Sub-regions: South America; Central America; Northern America
Countries: Peru [1991]; Ecuador [1991]; Colombia [1991]; Chile [1991]; Brazil [1991]; Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [1991]; Argentina [1992]; Paraguay [1992]; Mexico [1991]; Guatemala [1991]; Honduras [1991]; El Salvador [1991]; Nicaragua [1991]; Costa Rica [1991]; Panama [1991]; United States of America (Gulf Coast) [1992]
Host: Humans (general population in coastal and inland communities, including urban poor)
Event summary: The event began in January 1991 with explosive cholera outbreaks due to Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor Inaba in coastal Peru, rapidly affecting major urban centres and riverine communities across the country. Within months, the same seventh‑pandemic strain spread via travel, trade, and contaminated water along Pacific and inland corridors across most Andean and many Central American countries, later reaching Mexico and causing limited autochthonous transmission along the United States Gulf Coast, ultimately resulting in over one million reported cases and nearly 10,000 deaths by 1994. Intensified water and sanitation interventions, food safety measures, and public health campaigns gradually reduced transmission, and by the late 1990s cholera had receded to sporadic or focal incidence in most of Latin America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Re‑introduction of seventh‑pandemic El Tor V. cholerae O1 into a hemisphere that had been free of epidemic cholera for roughly a century; heavy reliance on untreated surface and municipal water; rapid urbanization and growth of peri‑urban slums; regional food trade, coastal shipping, and river transport; climatic variability (including El Niño events) affecting coastal ecology. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence in the regional context (introduction and dominance of seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineage over any residual classical strains); Enhanced Transmission linked to the strain’s environmental persistence and high proportion of asymptomatic infections, facilitating sustained water‑ and food‑borne spread over a vast geographic area.
Review: retain – Major, well‑documented event with >1 million cases in the Americas. Corrected geography: continent now includes both South America and North America, sub‑regions restricted to South America, Central America and Northern America, and Uruguay and the Caribbean islands removed because they reported no cholera cases during this wave.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020245299800025?utm_source=openai)) Event type adjusted from “inter‑continental emergence + re‑emergence” to “re‑emergence only”, in line with the rule that inter‑continental emergence should not be used when the organism is historically established on the continent and the apparent novelty is at strain level. Sources updated to emphasize PAHO/WHO and CDC MMWR over secondary summaries.

Countries: India [1992]; Bangladesh [1992]; Nepal [1993]; Pakistan [1993]; Thailand [1993]; Malaysia [1993]
Host: Humans (populations in cholera‑endemic coastal and riverine regions of the Bay of Bengal and neighbouring areas)
Event summary: In late 1992, severe outbreaks of cholera‑like illness began in Madras (Chennai) and other coastal areas of southern India, soon traced to a previously unrecognized serogroup, Vibrio cholerae O139 Bengal, arising on a seventh‑pandemic El Tor genetic background. During 1992–1993 the new serogroup rapidly displaced V. cholerae O1 across much of India and Bangladesh, causing very large epidemics with more than 100,000 reported cases and over 1,400 deaths in Bangladesh alone in the first few months, and spread to neighbouring countries around the Bay of Bengal and parts of South‑East Asia. By the mid‑1990s, O139 epidemics subsided as O1 El Tor re‑established dominance in many areas, but O139 persisted at low levels and occasionally resurged, and its abrupt emergence raised global concern about a potential eighth cholera pandemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high baseline vulnerability in the Bay of Bengal region due to dense populations relying on unsafe surface and groundwater, poor sanitation, and recurrent flooding; intense regional trade and population movement along coastal and riverine corridors. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – appearance of V. cholerae O139 Bengal via horizontal gene transfer and O‑antigen replacement in a seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineage, generating a serogroup against which existing population immunity to O1 offered little protection; Antimicrobial Resistance and altered virulence traits that facilitated large explosive outbreaks in settings already hyper‑endemic for cholera.
Review: retain – Newly added event that was missing from the original file but clearly qualifies among the most impactful post‑1990 cholera emergence events: a new epidemic serogroup (O139 Bengal) causing large epidemics in India, Bangladesh and neighbouring countries, with >100,000 cases and initial displacement of V. cholerae O1.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0140673693928117?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑emergence (strain‑level change) rather than first/global emergence, consistent with long‑standing cholera endemicity in this region.

Countries: Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo) – Goma and surrounding refugee camps [1994]; Burundi – refugee camps [1994]
Host: Humans (Rwandan refugees in emergency camps, local host populations)
Event summary: Following the 1994 Rwandan genocide, around a million predominantly Hutu refugees crossed into Zaire and Burundi, rapidly forming overcrowded camps around Goma and in northern Burundi with virtually no safe water or sanitation. Within days, explosive outbreaks of acute watery diarrhoea due largely to Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor and Shigella dysenteriae type 1 caused extremely high mortality, with crude death rates in some camps reaching tens of deaths per 10,000 persons per day and an estimated 12,000 or more cholera deaths in a few weeks. Massive international deployment of emergency water and sanitation interventions, rehydration therapy, and re‑organization of camp layouts gradually reduced cholera transmission over subsequent weeks, though the crisis left a large burden of mortality and became a paradigmatic example of cholera risk in mass displacement settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Sudden mass displacement of hundreds of thousands of people into densely packed camps; collapse of water, sanitation and health services; use of highly contaminated surface waters from Lake Kivu and nearby streams; severe malnutrition and co‑infections; insecurity and logistical constraints hampering aid delivery. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel strain or altered pathogen biology; the event represents re‑occurrence of existing seventh‑pandemic El Tor in an extreme humanitarian emergency.
Review: retain – Event is real and remains one of the most consequential cholera emergencies of the 1990s in terms of mortality among a concentrated population. Countries list has been narrowed to Zaire/DRC and Burundi, removing Rwanda which did not experience a comparably large in‑country epidemic during this episode; the main outbreaks were in refugee camps located in Zaire and Burundi.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673695903380?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑occurrence (no strain change, in a historically affected region) is appropriate.

Countries: Angola [2006]; Namibia [2006-2007] (first documented cholera outbreak with transmission in northern regions, linked to spread from Angola)
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban communities, including informal settlements, and populations along river and road corridors)
Event summary: The outbreak started in February 2006 in the Boa Vista neighbourhood of Luanda, Angola, and was rapidly recognized as a major cholera epidemic fuelled by grossly contaminated drinking‑water and inadequate sanitation in rapidly growing informal settlements. Over subsequent months, cholera spread along transport corridors and river systems to most Angolan provinces, ultimately causing more than 70,000–80,000 reported cases and around 3,000 deaths, while linked cross‑border spread caused Namibia’s first recorded cholera outbreak in northern border regions during 2006–2007. Expanded cholera treatment centres, emergency WASH interventions, health education, and seasonal decline in transmission eventually brought the epidemic under control, but Angola has since remained a recurrent hotspot for large cholera outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid post‑war urbanization and expansion of informal settlements lacking piped water and sewerage; heavy seasonal rains and flooding that overwhelmed drainage; weak surveillance, delayed outbreak recognition and response; intense population movement along roads and rivers including to/from Namibia; pervasive poverty and limited access to timely health care. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by atypical El Tor seventh‑pandemic lineages that reappeared after a decade‑long lull in cholera reports, with genomic studies documenting a new epidemic variant and wide geographic range expansion within Angola and into Namibia (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence plus Geographic Range Expansion).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3842873/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Angola 2006 remains one of the largest national cholera outbreaks of the early 21st century and also seeded Namibia’s first recorded cholera outbreak. Event type has been revised from “intra‑continental emergence + re‑occurrence” to “re‑emergence only”, to reflect (a) long‑standing cholera endemicity in Angola and the wider region, and (b) documented emergence of a new atypical El Tor lineage rather than first appearance on the continent or in a previously cholera‑free sub‑region in humans.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3842873/?utm_source=openai)) Geographic description clarified and a more specific genomic source added; flagged for review mainly to note this reclassification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Zimbabwe [2008]; South Africa [2008-2009]; Botswana [2008-2009]; Mozambique [2008-2009]; Zambia [2008-2009]
Host: Humans (urban and rural populations; particularly high impact in densely populated high‑density suburbs and informal settlements)
Event summary: Cholera re‑emerged in August 2008 in Chitungwiza and high‑density suburbs of Harare, Zimbabwe, against a backdrop of economic collapse, water system failure, and health‑system breakdown. The epidemic rapidly expanded nationwide, affecting all 10 provinces and leading to approximately 98,600 reported cases and over 4,300 deaths in Zimbabwe, while cross‑border spread caused additional cases in neighbouring South Africa, Mozambique, Botswana and Zambia, making it one of Africa’s largest cholera epidemics in recent decades. Intensified international response, repair of key water and sewage infrastructure, cholera treatment centres, and seasonal decline in transmission led to control of the epidemic by mid‑2009, although Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries have since experienced recurrent smaller outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe deterioration of municipal water treatment and sewage systems; collapse of solid‑waste management; health‑worker shortages and lack of basic medicines; high HIV prevalence and malnutrition; extensive cross‑border population movements and trade. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of circulating seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineages in a region with past cholera outbreaks; while some antimicrobial resistance was documented, the magnitude of the epidemic is best explained by infrastructural and socio‑economic collapse rather than major genetic changes.
Review: retain – Robustly documented as one of the largest modern African cholera epidemics with nearly 100,000 cases and >4,000 deaths.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Zimbabwean_cholera_outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence was incorrect because Zimbabwe, South Africa, Mozambique, Botswana and Zambia had all reported cholera in previous decades; this has been corrected to re‑occurrence only.([wrc.org.za](https://www.wrc.org.za/wp-content/uploads/mdocs/1398-1-051.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Countries and sub‑regions remain appropriate and are retained.

Host: Humans (rural riverine communities and urban/slum populations in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, with smaller outbreaks in Cuba and Mexico)
Event summary: In October 2010, months after Haiti’s devastating earthquake, cholera was introduced into the Artibonite River region—molecular and epidemiologic evidence later tracing the outbreak strain to South Asia—and rapidly spread through river systems and informal urban settlements with poor WASH infrastructure. Over subsequent years, Haiti experienced persistent transmission and multiple epidemic waves, accounting for more than half of the world’s reported cholera cases in 2010–2011 and ultimately causing over 812,000 reported cases and at least 9,600 deaths, with sustained transmission and spillover to the Dominican Republic and smaller linked outbreaks in Cuba and Mexico. Intensified investments in water and sanitation, large‑scale oral cholera vaccination campaigns, and strengthened surveillance progressively reduced incidence, and by early 2019 Haiti reported its last confirmed case in this epidemic, allowing the country to be considered cholera‑free for more than a year by 2020, although a new outbreak began in 2022 outside this event window.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑earthquake collapse and chronic weakness of water and sanitation infrastructure; contamination of the Artibonite River and irrigation canals; population displacement into camps and informal settlements; limited access to timely rehydration and health care; delayed recognition of cholera in a country that had not reported it for over a century. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence in the Hispaniola context through introduction of a South Asian seventh‑pandemic El Tor O1 Ogawa lineage with hybrid classical/El Tor traits, to an immunologically naïve population; Enhanced Transmission via prolonged environmental persistence in rivers and estuaries, facilitating spread to neighbouring Caribbean settings and Mexico.
Review: retain – This epidemic is unequivocally one of the largest cholera outbreaks ever recorded in a single country and had substantial regional spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7774537/?utm_source=openai)) Event type has been corrected from ‘intra‑continental emergence + re‑occurrence + re‑emergence’ to ‘re‑emergence only’, since cholera was historically present in the Americas and the novelty was the introduction of a new seventh‑pandemic lineage into a long‑cholera‑free region.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5948a4.htm?utm_source=openai)) Countries list and sub‑regions have been made explicit by adding Cuba and Mexico, for which small but genuine local outbreaks caused by the Haitian‑related strain were documented, while limiting the geography to settings with in‑country transmission (imported‑only cases elsewhere are referenced in the summary but not coded as part of the event).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3933092/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (displaced populations, urban poor, and rural communities across most Yemeni governorates)
Event summary: Cholera re‑emerged in Yemen in late 2016 amid escalating civil war, collapsing public services, and widespread displacement, initially causing tens of thousands of suspected cases in several governorates. After a brief lull, a second, much larger wave beginning in April 2017 spread nationwide, and by 2020 over 2.4–2.5 million suspected cases and more than 4,000 deaths had been reported, making it the largest documented cholera epidemic in modern history, with continued lower‑level transmission through at least 2020 and persisting vulnerability thereafter. Massive international deployment of rehydration services, large‑scale oral cholera vaccination in high‑risk districts, partial restoration of water and sanitation infrastructure, and evolving conflict frontlines gradually reduced case numbers, although Yemen remains at high risk for resurgence and has experienced renewed acute diarrhoea and cholera activity in recent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Protracted armed conflict destroying water and sewage infrastructure; salary interruptions and emigration of health workers; blockades and economic collapse limiting fuel, chlorine and medical supplies; large‑scale internal displacement into overcrowded, unsanitary conditions; widespread food insecurity and malnutrition that increased vulnerability to severe disease. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of circulating seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineages likely imported from the Horn of Africa/Red Sea region; Enhanced Transmission through dense, war‑affected settlements, but without clear evidence that major new genetic changes drove the scale of the epidemic.
Review: retain – Correctly identifies the largest recorded cholera epidemic to date with >2.4–2.5 million suspected cases and ~4,000 deaths in Yemen from 2016–2020, with ongoing vulnerability thereafter.([choleraalliance.org](https://www.choleraalliance.org/en/cholera-epidemic-yemen-overview-and-update?utm_source=openai)) Geographic scope has been narrowed in the countries field to Yemen only, since neighbouring Arabian Peninsula countries mainly reported imported cases without sustained transmission. Event type as re‑occurrence (no new continent or sub‑region; driven by conflict‑related system collapse) is appropriate.

Host: Humans (internally displaced persons, drought‑affected rural and peri‑urban populations in Somalia)
Event summary: After years of fragile health services and chronic WASH deficits, Somalia experienced a very large cholera outbreak in 2017, with over 78,000 suspected cases and about 1,150 deaths reported across 16 regions during a severe drought and food‑insecurity crisis. Although case numbers declined with intensified response, Somalia continued to report thousands of cases annually in 2018 and 2019, reflecting persistent foci of transmission among internally displaced persons and along riverine and urban corridors. Expanded early‑warning surveillance, cholera treatment centres, targeted oral cholera vaccination, and multi‑sectoral WASH interventions gradually reduced incidence, though cholera remains endemic and prone to resurgence in Somalia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Multi‑year drought leading to water scarcity and reliance on unsafe surface sources; armed conflict and insecurity limiting access to services; massive internal displacement into overcrowded camps; chronic underinvestment in water, sanitation and health systems. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of endemic seventh‑pandemic lineages; Enhanced Transmission facilitated by dense camps and high mobility rather than by major genetic change in the pathogen.
Review: retain – Somalia’s 2017 outbreak (>78,000 cases and >1,100 deaths) is among the largest recent national epidemics in the Horn of Africa and an important example of drought‑ and conflict‑associated cholera.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/29-march-2018-cholera-somalia-en?utm_source=openai)) Countries field has been simplified to Somalia only to avoid over‑stating direct epidemic linkage to contemporaneous outbreaks in Kenya and Ethiopia, which experienced their own large but not clearly subordinate epidemics during the regional drought; cross‑border context is retained in the narrative. Classification as re‑occurrence within an already endemic sub‑region is appropriate.

Host: Humans (rural lakeshore and river communities, urban populations in Kinshasa and other cities, internally displaced persons)
Event summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo, already a long‑standing cholera hotspot, saw a dramatic exacerbation of its recurrent outbreaks in 2017, culminating in more than 53,000 reported cases and over 1,100 deaths across multiple provinces. Transmission intensified along major river systems and in conflict‑affected eastern regions, with subsequent spread to the capital Kinshasa, which reported over 1,000 suspected cases between late 2017 and early 2018. Large‑scale case‑management efforts, improved surveillance, and targeted WASH and vaccination interventions reduced incidence after 2018, though DRC has continued to contribute a substantial share of global cholera burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronic poverty and lack of safe water in riverine and lakeshore communities; intense internal displacement and humanitarian crises; weak infrastructure for water treatment and waste management; heavy reliance on river transport facilitating long‑distance spread of infection. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of entrenched seventh‑pandemic El Tor strains; Geographic Range Expansion within national river networks as environmental reservoirs and human mobility enabled spread between distant basins.
Review: review – Event is valid and describes a very large outbreak (>53,000 cases, ~1,100 deaths) in one of the world’s most cholera‑affected countries.([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/sites/default/files/Cholera-Americas-D-PAHO.pdf?utm_source=openai)) However, when ranking global events strictly by impact and distinctiveness, this episode is borderline for inclusion among the ten most impactful post‑1990 cholera events once the 1992–1994 O139 emergence is added. Kept here with a ‘review’ recommendation so users can decide whether to retain it or drop it if they need exactly ten events per EPP.

Host: Humans (rural and peri‑urban populations, especially in northern and north‑eastern states, including conflict‑affected areas)
Event summary: After years of intermittent outbreaks, Nigeria experienced exceptionally large cholera waves during October 2020–October 2021, with about 93,600 suspected cases and roughly 3,300 deaths reported nationwide across 33 of 37 states, making it the largest documented cholera epidemic in the country’s history. The outbreaks disproportionately affected northern states with poor WASH infrastructure, insecurity and population displacement, and were further complicated by the concurrent COVID‑19 pandemic, which strained surveillance and response capacity. Intensified case management, risk communication, and WASH interventions, together with seasonal declines in transmission, brought case numbers down after late 2021, although Nigeria continues to report recurrent cholera activity and remains one of the countries with the highest estimated cholera burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Inadequate access to safe water and sanitation, particularly in rural northern states; conflict and displacement in the north‑east; heavy rainfall and flooding in some regions; overlapping health emergencies (COVID‑19 and others) diverting resources from cholera control. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of endemic seventh‑pandemic strains; possible contribution of antimicrobial resistance in some isolates, but epidemiologic patterns are primarily explained by environmental and systemic drivers.
Review: retain – Nigeria’s 2020–2021 epidemic (~93,600 cases and ~3,300 deaths) is the country’s largest documented cholera outbreak and one of the largest recent national epidemics globally, particularly notable for its interaction with the COVID‑19 response and for the breadth of states affected.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11770646/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑occurrence in a long‑affected sub‑region is appropriate. No geographical corrections were required.

Countries: Malawi [2022-2023]; Mozambique [2022-2023]; Zambia [2022-2023] (linked, smaller outbreaks within the same regional wave)
Host: Humans (communities across all 29 districts of Malawi, with high impact in peri‑urban slums and flood‑affected rural areas, and affected border regions in Mozambique and Zambia)
Event summary: In March 2022, Malawi declared a cholera outbreak that initially affected a limited number of southern districts but rapidly expanded following tropical storms and cyclones that damaged water and sanitation infrastructure and displaced communities. By mid‑2023 the country had reported roughly 59,000 cases and around 1,770 deaths, making this the largest and deadliest cholera outbreak in Malawi’s recorded history, with transmission documented in all 29 districts and linked spread to neighbouring Mozambique and Zambia as part of a wider southern Africa wave. Intensified national and international response—including large oral cholera vaccination campaigns, expanded treatment capacity, and WASH interventions—eventually brought cases down, and by mid‑2024 Malawi declared the outbreak contained, though the broader regional upsurge and underlying vulnerabilities persist.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe tropical cyclones and flooding damaging water systems and contaminating wells; chronic underinvestment in WASH; population displacement and crowding in temporary shelters; overstretched health services due to concurrent emergencies (including COVID‑19 and polio responses). Internal mechanisms: Genomic studies indicate introduction of a newly imported late‑wave seventh‑pandemic O1 Ogawa 7PET lineage distinct from historical local strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence) combined with Geographic Range Expansion and Enhanced Transmission via widespread environmental contamination, enabling unusually sustained nationwide and regional spread.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50484-w?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Malawi’s 2022–2023 outbreak (~59,000 cases, ~1,770 deaths) is the largest and deadliest in the country’s history and forms a key component of the 2021‑present multi‑country cholera upsurge in southern Africa, with documented genomic evidence of a newly imported 7PET lineage.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50484-w?utm_source=openai)) Event type has been simplified to re‑emergence (driven by introduction of a new lineage and exceptional expansion) rather than re‑occurrence + re‑emergence, to keep types mutually exclusive in line with the general guidance. The countries field has been expanded to explicitly include Mozambique and Zambia for which linked outbreaks within the same regional wave have been documented, while keeping Malawi as the primary burden centre.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%932024_Southern_Africa_cholera_outbreak?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans
Event summary: The outbreak began in late August 2000 in Gulu District in northern Uganda, where clusters of severe viral haemorrhagic fever were identified and laboratory testing confirmed Sudan virus as the cause. The epidemic expanded to Masindi and Mbarara districts, ultimately causing about 425 cases and 224 deaths before intensive case isolation, contact tracing, and safe burial practices brought transmission under control by January–February 2001. Uganda was declared free of Ebola after no new cases were detected for 42 days, ending what remains the largest known Sudan virus disease outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: nosocomial transmission in healthcare settings without adequate personal protective equipment, close family caregiving, and traditional funeral practices with contact with infectious corpses facilitated spread; delayed recognition of Ebola haemorrhagic fever also allowed early amplification in the community. Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis showed the outbreak strain was Sudan virus closely related, but not identical, to earlier Sudan virus isolates, and there is no strong evidence that major viral changes, increased virulence, or resistance were primary drivers; the event is best understood as a large re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion within Eastern Africa driven mainly by health‑system and behavioural factors rather than novel viral traits.
Review: review – Retain this as a major Sudan virus disease event but recode it from an intra‑continental emergence to a re‑occurrence. Sudan virus had already emerged in 1976 and 1979 in present‑day South Sudan (Eastern Africa), so the 2000–2001 Uganda outbreak represents spread into a new country within the same UNSD Eastern Africa subregion, which the project rules specify should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence. No changes were made to geography, timing or case counts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In 2004, cases of suspected viral haemorrhagic fever were reported from Yambio County in what was then southern Sudan (now South Sudan), and laboratory testing confirmed Sudan virus infection. The outbreak remained relatively limited, with 17 reported cases and 7 deaths, and transmission was largely confined to Yambio and nearby communities before strengthened surveillance, isolation of cases and safe, supervised burials interrupted spread. WHO declared the end of the outbreak on 7 August 2004, 42 days after the last laboratory‑confirmed patient died on 26 June 2004.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely spillover from a local animal reservoir in forested areas around Yambio followed by limited person‑to‑person spread in a remote area with constrained healthcare infrastructure; close contact during caregiving and funerals contributed to transmission. Internal mechanisms: no evidence was reported of major genetic change, novel strain properties, or resistance compared with earlier Sudan virus outbreaks; the event represents a re‑occurrence of Sudan virus disease in the same broader ecological focus as the 1976 and 1979 outbreaks rather than a clear virological re‑emergence.
Review: review – Retain the event but correct geography and magnitude. Yambio is in present‑day South Sudan, which the project classifies in Eastern Africa, so sub_regions has been changed from “Northern Africa” to “Eastern Africa” and the country from “Sudan [2004]” to “South Sudan [2004]”. The event summary has been updated to use WHO’s final figures of 17 cases and 7 deaths instead of an imprecise “dozen‑plus” description. Event type (re‑occurrence) and timing are unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2011, a 12‑year‑old girl from Nakisamata village in Luwero District, central Uganda, developed acute febrile illness with haemorrhagic signs and died shortly after admission to Bombo Military Hospital; testing at the Uganda Virus Research Institute confirmed Sudan virus infection, prompting declaration of an outbreak. Extensive contact tracing, active surveillance, and laboratory testing identified no additional confirmed secondary cases, and follow‑up of contacts for 21 days suggested the event was limited to a single recognized human infection. After the surveillance period elapsed without new cases, authorities declared the outbreak over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: probable zoonotic spillover in a rural community with close human–environment contact, combined with rapid recognition of viral haemorrhagic fever, early isolation of the patient, and strong infection‑prevention practices in the receiving hospital, which limited onward transmission. Internal mechanisms: full‑genome sequencing confirmed Sudan virus and showed the Nakisamata isolate to be very closely related (around 99% nucleotide identity) to the 2000 Gulu strain, with no evidence that viral evolution increased transmissibility or virulence; under the project definitions this episode is therefore more appropriately classified as a re‑occurrence arising from a new spillover rather than a mechanistic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event is real and should be kept, but the emergence type has been recoded from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence. Genomic analyses show the 2011 Nakisamata isolate is very closely related to the 2000 Gulu Sudan virus strain, and the primary publication describes this as “reemerging” disease in the sense of renewed occurrence rather than a novel, phenotypically distinct lineage; there is no evidence that viral change, rather than context, drove this single‑case outbreak. Mechanism text was updated accordingly; geography and dates were left unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In late July 2012, Uganda’s Ministry of Health reported clusters of severe illness and deaths in Kibaale District in western/mid‑western Uganda, and laboratory testing at the Uganda Virus Research Institute confirmed Sudan virus as the cause of the outbreak. The epidemic caused roughly two dozen cases with a high case‑fatality ratio, with transmission occurring mainly among household contacts and in healthcare settings before heightened control measures were implemented. Aggressive case isolation, contact tracing, public communication, and partner support brought the outbreak under control within weeks, and Uganda was declared Ebola‑free later in 2012 after the required 42‑day period without new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close contact in households and during funerals, limited early infection‑prevention and control in peripheral health facilities, and delayed recognition of Ebola contributed to spread within the district; mobility between neighbouring villages facilitated local dissemination. Internal mechanisms: virus characterization identified Sudan virus consistent with previously known lineages, with no clear evidence of novel virulence or resistance traits; the event is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a country with prior Sudan virus outbreaks rather than a fundamentally new variant‑driven emergence.
Review: retain – Event accurately represents the 2012 Kibaale Sudan virus outbreak as documented by WHO, CDC and ECDC, with correct geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa) and appropriate classification as a re‑occurrence in a country with prior Sudan virus activity. Case numbers are presented approximately (“roughly two dozen cases”), which is consistent with small differences between WHO and CDC summaries; no corrections to timing, location or emergence type were required.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In November 2012, Uganda detected new cases of Ebola haemorrhagic fever in Luweero District, and laboratory analysis confirmed Sudan virus as the aetiologic agent; additional linked patients were later identified in Luweero and Kampala Districts. This outbreak involved 7 cases (6 laboratory‑confirmed and 1 probable) and 4 deaths, with infections mainly linked through household exposure and health‑facility contacts before stringent infection‑prevention measures were implemented. After rapid deployment of response teams, reinforcement of infection‑prevention and control, and systematic contact follow‑up in affected districts, no additional transmission chains were identified and the event was declared over following the standard 42‑day observation period without new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely new zoonotic spillover or a short, initially undetected transmission chain in Luweero, with subsequent limited spread in family and healthcare settings and potential amplification risk due to proximity to Kampala; strengthened national surveillance capacity allowed relatively quick detection and response compared with earlier outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: virus typing indicated Sudan virus consistent with previous Ugandan strains, with no clear signal of novel genetic traits or resistance; thus the episode is treated as a re‑occurrence of Sudan virus disease in an already affected subregion rather than a mechanistically distinct re‑emergence.
Review: review – Retain this event but refine the description and sources. Case numbers in the summary have been aligned with WHO Disease Outbreak News (7 cases: 6 confirmed, 1 probable; 4 deaths) instead of the earlier vague “about seven cases with four fatalities”, and WHO DONs from 17, 23 and 30 November 2012 have been added to the source list to better document the episode. Geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa) and classification as a re‑occurrence remain appropriate.

Countries: Uganda [2022 – Mubende, Kassanda, Kyegegwa, Kagadi, Bunyangabu, Kampala, Wakiso, Jinja, Masaka and others]
Host: Humans
Event summary: On 20 September 2022, Uganda declared an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Sudan virus after a 24‑year‑old man from Madudu sub‑county in Mubende District tested positive at the Uganda Virus Research Institute following several unexplained community deaths. The outbreak spread across central and western Uganda with major transmission foci in Mubende and Kassanda and additional cases reported from districts including Kyegegwa, Kagadi, Bunyangabu, Wakiso, Kampala, Jinja and Masaka, resulting in 142 laboratory‑confirmed and 22 probable cases and 55 confirmed deaths before control measures took full effect. After 42 days with no new cases following the last patient’s outcome in late November 2022, national authorities and WHO declared the outbreak over on 11 January 2023.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suspected new spillover from a wildlife reservoir into a rural community, followed by human‑to‑human spread amplified in households, traditional burial practices, and health facilities where infection‑prevention and control measures were initially imperfect; population mobility from rural epicentres to trading hubs and to Kampala facilitated wider geographic dissemination. Internal mechanisms: genomic sequencing indicated the outbreak strain was closely related to the Nakisamata Sudan virus detected in Luwero in 2011, supporting a new spillover of a related lineage rather than continuation of earlier human transmission chains; no clear evidence of markedly increased transmissibility, virulence, or treatment resistance was identified, so under the project definitions this episode is treated as a large re‑occurrence rather than a mechanistic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event is correctly included as one of the most impactful Sudan virus outbreaks, but several corrections were required. The emergence type has been recoded from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because WHO, CDC and genomic analyses describe the virus as closely related to the 2011 Nakisamata lineage without evidence that viral evolution (e.g. substantially increased transmissibility or resistance) drove the outbreak; repeated zoonotic spillover and contextual factors better explain transmission. Case and death counts in the summary have been updated to the final official figures (142 confirmed and 22 probable cases with 55 confirmed deaths), and wording in the mechanism section was adjusted to reflect these interpretations. Geography and timing were left unchanged.

Countries: Uganda [2025 – Kampala, Wakiso, Mbale, Luwero, Jinja and other affected districts]
Host: Humans
Event summary: On 30 January 2025, Uganda’s Ministry of Health declared an outbreak of Sudan virus disease after post‑mortem samples from a 32‑year‑old nurse who died at Mulago National Referral Hospital in Kampala tested positive for Sudan virus in three national reference laboratories. Subsequent investigation and enhanced surveillance identified additional epidemiologically linked infections among healthcare workers and community contacts in Kampala and in districts connected to the index case’s movements, including Wakiso, Mbale, Luwero and Jinja, culminating in 12 confirmed and 2 probable cases and 4 deaths by late April 2025. Rapid activation of mortality surveillance, contact tracing, isolation and infection‑prevention measures, together with launch of a ring‑vaccination trial of a Sudan virus candidate vaccine, contained the outbreak, and the Ministry of Health declared it over on 26 April 2025 after 42 days with no new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: the index case was a mobile healthcare worker who sought care at multiple facilities in Kampala, Wakiso and Mbale and also visited a traditional healer while symptomatic, creating opportunities for nosocomial and community exposure before Sudan virus disease was suspected; urban density and inter‑district travel along major transport corridors increased the potential for spread, although strong preparedness and rapid response meant that high‑risk contacts were quickly traced, monitored and isolated. Internal mechanisms: genomic analysis of virus from the index case confirmed Sudan virus and showed close clustering with sequences from the 2012 Luweero outbreak rather than with the 2022 Mubende lineage, indicating an independent spillover from a wildlife reservoir or shared ecological focus rather than continuation of the 2022 transmission chain; no specific mutations associated with increased virulence or resistance have been implicated, so the event is best classified as another re‑occurrence of Sudan virus disease in Eastern Africa.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak centred on Kampala, which was missing from the original profile despite being one of only a small number of documented SVD outbreaks and therefore within the “top 10” events by default. Classification as a re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or mechanistic re‑emergence) follows WHO and CDC descriptions and genomic analyses indicating an independent spillover closely related to the 2012 Luweero lineage rather than continuation of the 2022 outbreak. Geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa), host system (humans), case counts (12 confirmed, 2 probable, 4 deaths) and end date are based on WHO Disease Outbreak News, CDC outbreak summaries and recent peer‑reviewed/technical reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (artisanal gold miners and close contacts in Durba and Watsa, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo)
Event summary: From October 1998, cases of severe haemorrhagic fever began appearing among gold miners working in the Goroumbwa mine near Durba and in the nearby town of Watsa in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak continued with sporadic primary cases and short transmission chains until late 2000, resulting in about 154 cases and 128 deaths, and constituting the first large community outbreak of Marburg virus disease recorded in Africa. Transmission declined after closure of the mine, intensified surveillance, isolation of cases, and community-based control measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense, poorly regulated underground gold mining in Goroumbwa mine with dense, prolonged human exposure in bat‑inhabited galleries; civil conflict and severely weakened health services that delayed recognition; limited infection prevention and control (IPC) in local facilities and traditional burial practices that facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: repeated zoonotic spillover from Egyptian rousette bats in the mine and concurrent circulation of multiple Marburg and Ravn virus lineages, illustrating substantial genetic diversity but no clear evidence of a fundamentally more transmissible or virulent variant compared with other African strains.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Retain this event as one of the two largest Marburg outbreaks, but reclassify it from re_emergence to intra_continental_emergence because it represents the first documented outbreak in the Middle Africa subregion (DRC) after earlier events in Europe, Kenya and South Africa, not a resurgence in a previously affected subregion.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa051465?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (primarily young children and caregivers; healthcare workers and community contacts in Uíge Province and a few other areas)
Event summary: Beginning in late 2004, clusters of unexplained haemorrhagic illness and deaths were reported in Uíge Province in northern Angola, with WHO confirming Marburg virus as the cause in March 2005. The outbreak spread mainly through families and health facilities, affecting several hundred people—disproportionately young children—and became the largest and deadliest Marburg virus disease outbreak on record. Sustained international support, strengthened IPC, community engagement, and safe burial practices eventually brought transmission under control, and Angola declared the outbreak over in November 2005.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: severely weakened health system in the post‑conflict period, including reuse of injection equipment, crowded paediatric wards, and inadequate barrier nursing; delayed laboratory confirmation; and high‑risk caregiving and funeral practices with intense contact with infectious body fluids. Internal mechanisms: circulation of an Angolan MARV lineage with extremely high observed CFR (~88–90%), together with extensive nosocomial amplification, consistent with re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion via a lineage associated with very severe disease rather than with an expanded host range.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Correct continent, subregion, timing (2004–2005) and country coding; event is clearly among the most impactful Marburg outbreaks globally. Classification as re_emergence within Middle Africa, driven by a highly virulent lineage and major nosocomial amplification, is reasonable under the given definitions.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2005_11_07a-en?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (gold miners and close contacts in Kamwenge and Ibanda Districts; some patients managed in Kampala)
Event summary: In mid‑2007, a miner from Kamwenge District was hospitalized and died in Kampala with haemorrhagic fever, and subsequent investigation identified Marburg virus infection in him and several other miners and contacts linked to the bat‑inhabited Kitaka gold mine in Kamwenge and health facilities in Ibanda District. The small outbreak, with four recognized cases and two deaths, marked Uganda’s first documented Marburg virus disease outbreak and focused attention on cave‑ and mine‑associated risk in the country. Closure of the mine and targeted IPC measures stopped further transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: renewed underground mining in Kitaka cave, where large colonies of Egyptian rousette bats roost; prolonged, unprotected exposure of miners to bats and contaminated cave environments; limited early recognition of viral haemorrhagic fever in rural facilities; and gaps in IPC. Internal mechanisms: zoonotic spillover of MARV/RAVV from Rousettus aegyptiacus followed by short human‑to‑human chains, with genetic data showing close relatedness to bat viruses from the same cave, consistent with re‑emergence from an established reservoir rather than a fundamentally altered virus.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event exists as described and is correctly placed in Eastern Africa/ Uganda with appropriate timing and scale (~4 cases). Treated as re_emergence within a previously affected subregion (Eastern Africa) and a critical event for understanding bat‑associated mining risk; impact is moderate but still within the plausible top‑10 set once geographic importance is considered.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3203392/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (community members in Kabale, Ibanda, Mbarara and Kabarole districts and Kampala; healthcare workers and family caregivers)
Event summary: In October 2012, Uganda detected a cluster of haemorrhagic fever cases in Kabale District that tested positive for Marburg virus at the Uganda Virus Research Institute, prompting declaration of an outbreak and rapid field investigation. The multidistrict outbreak ultimately involved 15 confirmed cases and four deaths across several western districts and Kampala, with transmission occurring in households and health facilities. Aggressive contact tracing, isolation, and IPC interventions ended transmission within weeks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ongoing human activity in areas with bat roosts in southwestern Uganda (including proximity to Kitaka mine), mobility between rural districts and Kampala, limited IPC in peripheral facilities, and traditional caregiving and funeral practices. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of MARV lineages closely related to earlier Ugandan bat and human strains, indicating repeated spillover from an established bat reservoir and efficient, but still limited, human‑to‑human transmission rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Correct country, subregion and year; 2012 is one of the larger post‑2000 MVD outbreaks (15 cases) and clearly within the ten most impactful. Event-type classification as re_emergence in Eastern Africa is consistent with prior Kenyan and Ugandan activity and phylogenetic evidence of related strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5649344/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (family cluster and contacts in Kween and Kapchorwa Districts; some cross-border contacts with Kenya)
Event summary: In October 2017, Uganda reported a confirmed case of Marburg virus disease in Kween District, traced to a male game hunter with probable exposure to bats or caves on the slopes of Mount Elgon, and subsequent investigation uncovered a small family cluster and additional suspected cases in neighboring Kapchorwa. The outbreak resulted in three confirmed cases and three deaths, all in close contacts. Rapid multi-sectoral response, isolation and contact follow‑up contained the event without wider spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑risk behaviors such as cave visitation and hunting of bushmeat in bat‑rich habitats along the Mount Elgon ecosystem; close caregiving and funeral contact within an extended family; and limited local diagnostic capacity, although national response capacity was strong. Internal mechanisms: repeated spillover of MARV from a long‑standing bat reservoir with viral genomes clustering with earlier Ugandan strains, consistent with re‑emergence in a known subregion rather than a novel evolutionary change.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event details (3 cases, 3 deaths in Kween/Kapchorwa, Eastern Uganda) and classification as re_emergence in an already affected subregion are correct. However, when Ethiopia 2025–2026 and Rwanda 2024 are added, this small cluster falls just outside a pure case‑count top‑10 ranking, so its inclusion versus other small but more geographically novel events (e.g. Guinea 2021) warrants user judgment depending on how strongly geographic expansion is weighted.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6438581/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (single adult male farmer in Guéckédou Prefecture; extensive traced contacts)
Event summary: In late July 2021, a 46‑year‑old farmer from Temessadou M’Boké village in Guéckédou Prefecture, southern Guinea, developed acute febrile illness with haemorrhagic signs and died in the community in early August; post‑mortem testing confirmed Marburg virus disease. Intensive investigation and contact tracing identified no additional cases, and the outbreak was declared over after one incubation period plus 21 days had elapsed without new infections. The case represented the first recorded Marburg virus disease in Guinea and in West Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close human interaction with forest ecosystems in Nzérékoré Region where fruit bats, including Egyptian rousettes, are present; rural health services initially focused on other endemic conditions; but strengthened VHF surveillance after recent Ebola outbreaks enabled rapid laboratory confirmation and targeted response. Internal mechanisms: first documented human spillover of MARV in West Africa, with viral genomes related to Angola‑like bat lineages from Sierra Leone, representing geographic range expansion of existing African lineages rather than emergence of a new species or dramatic shift in virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Correctly identified as the first documented Marburg virus disease event in West Africa (Guinea, Western Africa subregion), justifying inclusion despite only a single human case; classified appropriately as intra_continental_emergence for a new subregion, with no intra‑ or inter‑continental spread beyond West Africa.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2021-DON331?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (adult men and a 1‑year‑old child in Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions; healthcare and community contacts)
Event summary: In June–July 2022, Ghana’s health authorities reported two fatal cases of haemorrhagic fever in Ashanti Region that tested positive for Marburg virus, leading to declaration of the country’s first Marburg virus disease outbreak on 7 July 2022. Further investigation identified a third confirmed case linked to the initial cluster, with infections spanning Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions. Robust surveillance, contact tracing and isolation of suspected cases limited the outbreak to three confirmed infections and two deaths, and Ghana declared the event over in September 2022.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: livelihoods and travel in forest and savannah landscapes where fruit bats occur; population movement between affected regions; concurrent public‑health pressures (COVID‑19, yellow fever, mpox) that complicated response but also left strengthened surveillance infrastructure in place. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in the Western Africa subregion following the 2021 Guinea case, with genomic analyses showing Ghanaian sequences clustering with the Guinea 2021 virus and other Angola‑like MARV lineages, consistent with repeated spillover from a regional bat reservoir and limited human‑to‑human spread, without clear evidence of major changes in virulence or host range.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event is accurately described (three confirmed cases, two deaths across Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions) and correctly classified as re_occurrence within the Western Africa subregion following Guinea 2021. The previously cited 2021 ECDC CDTR PDF was not Ghana‑specific and has been replaced by WHO and national sources that more directly describe this outbreak.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/countries/ghana/news/ghana-declares-end-marburg-virus-disease-outbreak?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (community members in Kie‑Ntem, Litoral, Centro Sur and Wele‑Nzas provinces; healthcare workers and family caregivers)
Event summary: From late 2022 into early 2023, Equatorial Guinea experienced clusters of unexplained deaths from a haemorrhagic illness in villages of Nsok Nsomo and Ebibeyín Districts, Kié‑Ntem Province, and later in Bata and other districts. On 13 February 2023 the Ministry of Health declared a Marburg virus disease outbreak after a laboratory‑confirmed case, and subsequent investigations documented 16 laboratory‑confirmed and 23 probable cases across multiple mainland provinces with a very high case fatality. After several months of intensive response, including establishment of treatment centres, improved laboratory capacity and extensive contact tracing, the outbreak was declared over in June 2023.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely zoonotic spillover in forested areas of Kié‑Ntem followed by delayed detection in a health system with limited prior filovirus experience; expansion to several widely separated districts, including Bata—an economic hub with major transport links—under conditions of constrained surveillance, incomplete IPC, and funeral‑related exposures. Internal mechanisms: a single MARV lineage causing multiple, partly unlinked chains of transmission with CFR around 90%, representing re‑occurrence of MARV in Middle Africa; despite severity, genomic data support a virus related to known Angola‑like lineages rather than a fundamentally novel variant.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event exists and is correctly located in Middle Africa/Equatorial Guinea with multiple affected provinces; however, the start year has been updated from 2023 to 2022–2023 and the country start year to [2022] to reflect evidence of a probable index case with symptom onset in late December 2022. Classification as re_occurrence within Middle Africa remains appropriate, as the subregion was already affected (DRC, Angola). Wikipedia links have been replaced by WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/31/5/24-1749_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (community members and healthcare workers in Bukoba Rural District, Kagera Region)
Event summary: In March 2023, the United Republic of Tanzania reported a cluster of severe febrile illness and deaths in villages of Bukoba Rural District, Kagera Region; laboratory testing confirmed Marburg virus disease. The outbreak involved nine cases (eight confirmed, one probable) and six deaths, including infections among healthcare workers, all confined to Bukoba District. Rapid deployment of national and international teams, establishment of a Marburg treatment unit, and strengthened surveillance and border screening enabled containment within weeks, and the outbreak was declared over in June 2023.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: probable exposure to bat reservoirs or contaminated environments in rural Kagera, a region with caves and mining sites; close caregiving and health‑facility contact before MVD was suspected; limited prior national experience managing Marburg outbreaks despite experience with other VHFs. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in Eastern Africa, with genomes clustering with Ugandan bat and human strains and later with Rwanda 2024 and Tanzania 2025 viruses, indicating repeated localized spillover followed by short human‑to‑human chains rather than a qualitatively new viral phenotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event description (nine cases, six deaths, all in Bukoba district) and Eastern Africa/Tanzania coding align with WHO and CDC data, and classification as re_occurrence in an already affected subregion (Kenya, Uganda) with no inter‑continental spread is appropriate. This outbreak remains one of the more substantial post‑2000 events by case numbers and geographic significance.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2023-DON467))

Host: Humans (predominantly healthcare workers and hospitalized patients in Kigali, plus community contacts in affected districts)
Event summary: In September 2024, Rwanda declared its first-ever Marburg virus disease outbreak after a cluster of severe viral haemorrhagic fever cases was detected among intensive-care patients and staff in Kigali. Investigation traced the index case to a young adult man with bat‑cave exposure, followed by extensive nosocomial transmission across two major hospitals and limited community spread. By December 2024 the outbreak had caused 66 confirmed cases and 15 deaths, with an unusually high proportion of infections among healthcare workers, and was declared over after 42 days without new cases following the last patient’s recovery.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: zoonotic spillover linked to exposure in a cave inhabited by Egyptian rousette bats, followed by substantial nosocomial amplification in urban ICU settings where VHF-specific triage and full barrier precautions were initially absent; high patient turnover and close staff–patient contact in Kigali hospitals; heavy reliance on invasive procedures; and intense population movement in and out of the capital. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of a MARV lineage in Eastern Africa that was phylogenetically close to viruses from the 2014 Kampala case and later Tanzanian outbreaks, with limited genetic diversity within the outbreak; the scale of transmission was driven primarily by healthcare-associated exposure rather than demonstrably increased viral transmissibility.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added event capturing Rwanda’s first and globally the third‑largest documented MVD outbreak (66 cases, 15 deaths), correctly coded to Eastern Africa/Rwanda with 2024 start and end. Classified as re_occurrence because Eastern Africa was already affected (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania), and available genomic analyses show close relatedness to earlier regional strains rather than a novel species; clearly among the top‑impact events and should be included.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2024-DON541))

Host: Humans (rural residents in Katerela and Ruziba villages, Biharamulo District, including women and children; healthcare contacts)
Event summary: Between December 2024 and January 2025, a cluster of severe haemorrhagic illness and deaths occurred in villages of Biharamulo District, Kagera Region, northwestern Tanzania. On 20 January 2025 the government declared a Marburg virus disease outbreak after laboratory confirmation of a case, and retrospective investigation linked eight additional probable deaths to the same event. In total, ten cases (two confirmed and eight probable), all fatal, were identified, confined to Biharamulo District, and the outbreak was declared over on 13 March 2025 after 42 days without new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: limited early recognition of Marburg virus disease in a rural district with recent experience of other VHFs, late health‑seeking behavior with many deaths occurring before diagnostic sampling, and close household caregiving and funeral contact; proximity to wildlife reserves and bat habitats within the Kagera River basin ecosystem; but relatively rapid mobilization of national and international support once the outbreak was declared. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in Eastern Africa and in Tanzania specifically, with genomic data showing the 2025 viruses to be highly similar to those from the 2023 Tanzanian and 2024 Rwandan outbreaks, indicating repeated localized spillover and limited human‑to‑human transmission; the 100% observed CFR likely reflects under‑ascertainment of milder infections rather than a step‑change in virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added event; timing (symptom onset from December 2024 with outbreak declared January 2025), location (Biharamulo District, Kagera Region) and final size (10 cases, all fatal) match WHO and peer‑reviewed genomic analyses. Correctly classified as re_occurrence in Eastern Africa and in a country that already experienced MVD in 2023; not an intra‑continental emergence. Impact (10 cases, 100% CFR) places it clearly among the major post‑1990 events.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON559))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (community members and healthcare workers in Jinka, Malle and Dasench woredas, South Ethiopia Region, and Hawassa in Sidama Region)
Event summary: In November 2025, Ethiopia declared its first-ever Marburg virus disease outbreak after laboratory confirmation of suspected viral haemorrhagic fever cases in Jinka town, South Ethiopia Region. The outbreak, which began with symptom onset in late October 2025 in an adult patient, eventually involved 19 cases (14 confirmed and five probable) and 14 deaths across South Ethiopia Region and Hawassa in Sidama Region. Following intensive response efforts – including activation of national and regional emergency operations, deployment of a mobile laboratory, contact tracing of hundreds of exposed individuals, and establishment of treatment centres – the outbreak was declared over on 26 January 2026 after 42 days without new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: emergence in a remote area with limited prior VHF experience, likely linked to bat reservoirs in caves or other roost sites; delayed early recognition and health‑seeking, with several deaths before laboratory confirmation; movement of patients between woredas and to Hawassa; and constrained IPC capacity in some facilities prior to surge support. Internal mechanisms: first documented human MVD outbreak in Ethiopia but occurring in an already affected Eastern Africa subregion; MARV sequences cluster within known African lineages, and transmission patterns indicate one or a few zoonotic introductions followed by human‑to‑human spread in households and health facilities, without evidence of a qualitatively new viral phenotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added high‑impact event accurately summarized as Ethiopia’s first MVD outbreak (19 cases, 14 deaths) starting in late 2025, correctly coded to Eastern Africa/Ethiopia and classified as re_occurrence within an already affected subregion. Given its size, geographic novelty and documented multi‑district spread, it clearly belongs among the major emergence events and should be retained, while not being misclassified as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON592))

Host: Humans, primarily under-immunized children under 5 years (with some older children/adolescents)
Event summary: After the Americas were certified polio-free in 1994, pockets of very low oral polio vaccine (OPV) coverage in poor communities on Hispaniola allowed a Sabin type 1 vaccine strain introduced around 1998–1999 to circulate silently and diverge genetically. Between July 2000 and September 2001, 21 confirmed paralytic poliomyelitis cases (and additional compatible cases) occurred in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, caused by a vaccine-derived poliovirus type 1 that had regained neurovirulence and spread efficiently via the fecal–oral route in under-immunized neighborhoods. Intensified investigation, high‑coverage mop‑up OPV campaigns, and strengthened AFP surveillance stopped circulation by mid‑2001, and no further cVDPV1 transmission was detected in the Americas, though the event highlighted the risk of vaccine-derived outbreaks where coverage is low.([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/articlepdf/194465/jwr1212-1-1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Localized very low routine OPV coverage, absence of recent national immunization days, poverty, crowding, and poor sanitation in affected communities on Hispaniola permitted long-term person‑to‑person circulation of vaccine virus. Internal mechanisms: A Sabin 1 OPV strain acquired ~3% VP1 nucleotide divergence and recombined with other Enterovirus C genomes, regaining wild‑like neurovirulence and transmissibility; this constitutes the first recognized emergence of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 1 (cVDPV1) and a clear example of novel strain/genotype emergence from a vaccine strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570794/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Major cVDPV1 outbreak (21 confirmed paralytic cases, first recognized circulating vaccine-derived outbreak globally) that was missing from the original dataset; added as a dedicated event row with correct years, continent (South America), subregion (Caribbean), countries (Dominican Republic and Haiti), and classification as re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence from OPV; sources updated to primary CDC and peer‑reviewed descriptions.([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/articlepdf/194465/jwr1212-1-1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Northern Africa; Western Asia; Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: Nigeria [2003]; Niger [2003]; Chad [2004]; Cameroon [2004]; Burkina Faso [2004]; Benin [2004]; Côte d’Ivoire [2004]; Ghana [2004]; Togo [2004]; Sudan [2004]; Ethiopia [2004]; Somalia [2004]; Yemen [2005]; Indonesia [2005]; Nepal [2005]; other affected countries in West and Central Africa
Host: Humans, predominantly children under 5 years
Event summary: In 2003, several northern Nigerian states suspended oral polio vaccine campaigns after rumors and political/religious opposition, rapidly creating large cohorts of unvaccinated children and fueling explosive resurgence of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) in Nigeria. Over 2003–2006, genetically related WPV1 spread from northern Nigeria through much of West and Central Africa and onwards to the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and parts of South and South‑East Asia, re‑infecting at least 20 previously polio‑free countries—including large outbreaks in Sudan, Yemen (~478 cases) and Indonesia (~305 cases)—and accounting for more than half of global polio cases in 2005.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Intensified synchronized SIAs with monovalent OPV1, engagement of traditional and religious leaders, and improved surveillance progressively interrupted these importation‑related outbreaks by about 2006, although further waves of spread from Nigeria continued later in the decade.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Suspension of vaccination in parts of northern Nigeria due to mistrust of government and international agencies and rumors of vaccine contamination, combined with weak routine immunization, high population mobility, and conflict-affected or remote communities across West and Central Africa, created extensive immunity gaps and enabled long-distance spread of imported virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1831725/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved typical WPV1 genotypes exported from endemic northern Nigeria without evidence of major antigenic novelty; resurgence reflects amplification and geographic spread of existing wild virus driven by social, political and programmatic failures, fitting the re-occurrence category rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – This is correctly one of the most impactful post‑1990 polio events (over 1,000 importation-related cases across ≥20 countries). Countries list has been amended to include Nepal [2005] to justify inclusion of the Southern Asia subregion and better reflect WHO reports of importations into Nepal, and vague 'other affected countries in West and Central Africa' is retained to cover the full set of re‑infected states.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Event type remains re-occurrence (wild virus re‑introduced into previously polio-free areas due to immunity gaps) and not inter-continental emergence, since poliovirus was historically present on all affected continents. Wikipedia links used previously have been replaced at event level by WHO and CDC primary sources focused on this outbreak; recommend retaining Wikipedia only as a contextual background source at most.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, predominantly children in under-immunized northern Nigerian and neighboring communities
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2005, soon after widespread use of monovalent OPV1 and OPV3 replaced trivalent OPV in many supplementary immunization activities, northern Nigeria experienced the world’s largest documented outbreak of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2), with at least 315–400 paralytic cases detected through 2010 across 11 northern and three central states.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068031/?utm_source=openai)) Low type‑2 immunity allowed Sabin 2 vaccine virus to circulate, recombine with other Enterovirus C strains, and evolve into multiple independent cVDPV2 lineages that spread widely within Nigeria and caused sporadic importation-related cases in neighboring Niger (from 2006) and Chad (2010).([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/Mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5638a3.htm?utm_source=openai)) Intensified use of trivalent OPV in high‑risk areas, improved SIA quality, and stronger engagement of community and religious leaders gradually reduced incidence, with Nigeria’s last cVDPV2 case from these emergences reported in 2011 and no further related detections after 2014, although new cVDPV2 emergences later arose elsewhere in Africa.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6031a3.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronically low routine OPV coverage in northern Nigeria, heterogenous SIA performance, and extensive use of OPV formulations that omitted type 2 (mOPV1, bOPV) created large cohorts of children with little or no type‑2 immunity, enabling prolonged circulation of Sabin 2 in dense, often poor and remote communities.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068031/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Multiple independent cVDPV2 lineages emerged from Sabin 2, each acquiring >1% VP1 divergence, losing the temperature‑sensitive phenotype, regaining neurovirulence and exhibiting wild‑like transmissibility; this is a textbook example of novel strain/genotype emergence and sustained re-emergence of paralytic disease from vaccine virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068031/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Large Nigeria-centered cVDPV2 outbreak (≥315 paralytic cases and extensive geographic spread, plus importation-related cases in Niger and Chad) was missing from the original dataset; added as a distinct re-emergence event because it is among the ten most impactful post‑1990 poliovirus episodes by case count and its role in demonstrating cVDPV2 as a major eradication threat. Years, affected countries, and mechanisms are based on detailed CDC analyses of cVDPV2 epidemiology in Nigeria and neighboring states.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068031/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans, predominantly children but also adolescents and young adults
Event summary: In early 2010, after more than a decade without indigenous polio and eight years after the WHO European Region was certified polio‑free, Tajikistan detected a large outbreak of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) traced phylogenetically to importation from northern India in late 2009, ultimately confirming about 460 laboratory‑proven paralytic cases and additional compatible cases.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24576474/?utm_source=openai)) During 2010 the same outbreak strain spread into neighboring Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan and into the Russian Federation’s North Caucasus region, affecting mainly un- or under‑vaccinated children and young adults and revealing substantial immunity gaps despite prior polio‑free certification.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5943a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Aggressive outbreak response with multiple rounds of monovalent OPV1 and intensified AFP surveillance interrupted transmission in Tajikistan by mid‑2010 and in the wider region by early 2011, allowing the European Region to maintain its polio‑free status.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5943a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Declining or heterogeneous population immunity after years without cases, gaps in adult vaccination, high rates of labor migration and travel between India and Central Asia, and initial delays in outbreak recognition permitted a single importation to generate a large multi-country outbreak.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24576474/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The virus was a typical WPV1 lineage imported from India, without evidence of unusual virulence or novel antigenic properties; resurgence reflects re-occurrence of wild virus in previously polio‑free areas driven by immunity gaps rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – Correctly captured as one of the largest post‑1990 WPV1 outbreaks outside the traditional endemic zone (≈463 confirmed cases). Countries list has been corrected to remove Uzbekistan, which did not confirm indigenous cases (only possible undetected transmission inferred from one exported case to Russia); subregions and continents remain accurate.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2010_11_13-en?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (wild virus return to a previously polio‑free region due to immunity gaps) without inter‑continental emergence is consistent with project definitions. Sources are appropriate WHO and CDC outbreak reports and epidemiologic analyses; recommend no further changes beyond this geographic correction.

Countries: Republic of the Congo [2010]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2006]; Angola [2007]
Host: Humans, predominantly inadequately immunized adolescents and young adults
Event summary: Following re-establishment of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) transmission in Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from 2006 onward, virus spread north into the Republic of the Congo and, in late 2010, triggered an explosive outbreak centered in the coastal city of Pointe‑Noire after a decade without detected polio there.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Between September 2010 and February 2011, at least 445 confirmed paralytic cases and 179 related deaths were reported—mostly in young adults with low lifetime exposure to OPV—giving an unusually high case‑fatality ratio of about 40–47% and overwhelming intensive care capacity.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Intensive multi‑round immunization campaigns with monovalent OPV1 targeting the entire population, combined with strengthened surveillance and cross‑border coordination with Angola and DRC, brought the outbreak under control by early 2011, with no further cases linked to this lineage after January 2011.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/8/11-0195_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A decade without local wild poliovirus circulation, low adult vaccination coverage, and weak health systems in parts of central Africa created a large susceptible adult cohort; crowded urban living conditions and delayed recognition of early cases in Pointe‑Noire facilitated rapid spread and high mortality.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/8/11-0195_article?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses were WPV1 genetically related to strains circulating in Angola and DRC, with some studies suggesting relative resistance to neutralization by vaccine‑induced sera but no clear evidence of a fundamentally novel serotype or vaccine‑escape phenotype; overall this is best categorized as a severe re-occurrence of wild virus in a previously polio‑free country, not as re-emergence via new genotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai))
