Review: retain – Added as a missing high-impact event: the 2010–2011 Republic of the Congo WPV1 outbreak is one of the largest and deadliest post‑1990 polio outbreaks (≈445 cases, ~179 deaths, unusually high adult case‑fatality), and was not represented in the original dataset.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence because it reflects re‑introduction of wild virus into a previously polio‑free setting with large immunity gaps, without clear evidence of stable, fundamentally novel viral properties that would warrant re‑emergence classification.

Host: Humans, mainly under-immunized children in conflict-affected and displaced populations
Event summary: In October 2013, amid civil war and health system collapse, Syria confirmed wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) in Deir ez‑Zor and other governorates after more than a decade of polio‑free status, with sequencing linking the virus to strains circulating in Pakistan and indicating months of silent transmission.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2013_11_26polio-en?utm_source=openai)) Virus spread among displaced and under‑vaccinated children and crossed into Iraq in early 2014, resulting in a total of about 38 cases across the two countries and threatening neighboring polio‑free states in the Middle East.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6608a6.htm?utm_source=openai)) A large multi‑country emergency response, including synchronized OPV campaigns across eight countries, rapid social mobilization, and strengthened AFP surveillance, interrupted transmission in Syria by early 2014 and in Iraq by mid‑2014, with no further WPV1 detected in the region thereafter.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6608a6.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Armed conflict, mass population displacement, destruction of health infrastructure, and sharply reduced routine immunization coverage in parts of Syria created large immunity gaps, while refugee flows and cross‑border movement facilitated introduction into Iraq and threatened spread to surrounding countries.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6608a6.htm?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak virus was a typical WPV1 lineage imported from endemic areas (Pakistan/Afghanistan), with resurgence driven by social and health‑system disruption rather than viral evolution; thus it is appropriately coded as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Major conflict-associated WPV1 outbreak in the Middle East (≈38 cases across Syria and Iraq) with high geopolitical impact is accurately characterized and fits within the top tier of post‑1990 emergence events when considering both epidemiologic and political significance.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6608a6.htm?utm_source=openai)) Geographic classification (Western Asia, Syria and Iraq) and event-type coding as re-occurrence are correct; sources are appropriate WHO and CDC outbreak analyses.

Host: Humans, mainly children under 5 years in insecure and under-served areas
Event summary: In April 2013, Somalia confirmed its first wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) case since 2007 in a child from Mogadishu, marking the start of a major Horn of Africa outbreak that rapidly spread through inaccessible and chronically under‑served districts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10548859/?utm_source=openai)) Over 2013–2014, Somalia, Kenya and Ethiopia together reported about 223 WPV1 cases, many in older children and adults, reflecting long‑standing immunity gaps and multiple importations of Nigerian‑origin virus along the so‑called ‘importation belt’ of Africa.([panafrican-med-journal.com](https://www.panafrican-med-journal.com/content/series/27/3/22/full/?utm_source=openai)) Intensive regional coordination through a Horn of Africa outbreak coordination office, repeated synchronized SIAs, and strengthened surveillance progressively curtailed transmission, with the last related case in Somalia in August 2014 and the region subsequently regaining polio‑free status.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7613054/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Protracted conflict and insecurity in south‑central Somalia, large nomadic and displaced populations, weak routine immunization systems, and porous borders facilitated explosive cross‑border spread once WPV1 was imported, while uneven surveillance delayed recognition of early cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10548859/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Circulating viruses were WPV1 lineages genetically related to strains from Nigeria and other parts of West Africa without evidence of novel viral traits; the episode represents geographic re-occurrence of wild virus enabled by structural vulnerabilities rather than re‑emergence via new genotype.
Review: retain – Correctly represents a large Horn of Africa WPV1 outbreak (~223 cases across three countries), clearly among the most consequential post‑1990 importation-related events in Africa.([panafrican-med-journal.com](https://www.panafrican-med-journal.com/content/series/27/3/22/full/?utm_source=openai)) Geographic scope (Eastern Africa; Somalia, Kenya, Ethiopia) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; sources are high‑quality WHO and peer‑reviewed outbreak reports. No structural corrections beyond minor wording are required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, predominantly children in conflict-affected and hard‑to‑reach areas of Borno State
Event summary: In 2016, after more than two years without detected wild poliovirus, Nigeria’s Borno State reported four WPV1 cases in children from areas long inaccessible due to Boko Haram–related insecurity, revealing that low-level transmission had persisted undetected since at least 2011 and that circulating type 2 vaccine‑derived poliovirus (cVDPV2) was also present in the same region.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/06-october-2016-polio-nigeria-en?utm_source=openai)) These detections prompted declaration of a national and Lake Chad subregional public health emergency and triggered large-scale synchronized outbreak responses using bOPV and mOPV2, with intense efforts to reach children in partially liberated settlements and among displaced populations.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/news/polio-outbreak-response-assessment-and-lake-chad-coordination-review-meeting-underway-abuja?utm_source=openai)) Through innovative surveillance (including environmental sampling and mobile-phone–supported AFP reporting) and multiple SIAs, WPV1 transmission in Borno was again interrupted after 2016 and cVDPV2 incidence fell markedly, allowing Nigeria to be certified free of wild poliovirus in 2020, although other cVDPV2 lineages later emerged elsewhere in the region.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Armed insurgency, population displacement around Lake Chad, and areas inaccessible to health workers left large pockets of children unreached by both routine immunization and SIAs, permitting long-term undetected circulation of WPV1 and OPV2‑derived lineages.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of residual WPV1 and genetically divergent cVDPV2 strains (with multiple nucleotide changes from Sabin 2 and restored neurovirulence) represents viral evolution under selection in severely under‑immunized populations, fitting the re-emergence category through novel strain/genotype emergence coupled with geographic persistence in a security‑compromised reservoir.
Review: review – Event correctly highlights the discovery of hidden WPV1 transmission and cVDPV2 in Borno in 2016 and the intensive Lake Chad response, but the original version incorrectly implied confirmed cases in Niger, Chad, Cameroon and the Central African Republic starting in 2016; those countries mainly participated in synchronized response activities, and their later cVDPV2 outbreaks are better captured under the broader 2017–2023 African cVDPV2 event.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) Countries and subregion have therefore been restricted to Nigeria / Western Africa, and the row is flagged for review because, while epidemiologically important, its small paralytic case count (four WPV1 cases plus limited cVDPV2) means it may fall below the top ten post‑1990 polio emergence events when ranked purely by impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, mainly children in conflict-affected governorates with very low type‑2 immunity
Event summary: In June 2017, Syria detected an outbreak of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) causing paralytic disease in Deir ez‑Zor governorate, years after the country had eliminated wild polio and following the global withdrawal of type‑2–containing OPV in 2016.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Genomic analysis showed the outbreak strain differed by about 22 VP1 nucleotides from Sabin 2, indicating roughly a year of undetected circulation in an extremely under‑immunized population before the first recognized case, ultimately paralyzing 74 children in Deir ez‑Zor, Raqqa and Homs.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) A focused emergency response—with multiple rounds of mOPV2 in affected and neighboring areas and IPV campaigns among young children—interrupted transmission by late 2017, with no new cases in 2018 and the outbreak declared stopped after extensive follow‑up and external review.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged civil conflict, mass displacement, difficult access for vaccinators, and pre‑existing gaps in routine immunization led to very low type‑2 immunity, especially after the global tOPV–bOPV switch removed OPV2 from routine use; these conditions allowed a vaccine‑derived lineage to circulate unchecked.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak virus was a cVDPV2 lineage with substantial genetic divergence and restored neurovirulence relative to Sabin 2, representing classic novel strain/genotype emergence from vaccine virus and therefore qualifying as re-emergence driven by internal viral evolution.
Review: retain – Large cVDPV2 outbreak (74 paralytic cases) in a conflict setting that directly illustrates the risks created by the tOPV-to-bOPV switch and severe immunity gaps; appropriately classified as re-emergence with high-quality WHO and CDC documentation.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Minor source refinement has been made by replacing general background articles with EMRO outbreak situation reports; no further structural changes needed.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo [2017]; Somalia [2018]; Nigeria [2018]; Niger [2018]; Ethiopia [2019]; Angola [2019]; Central African Republic [2019]; Cameroon [2019]; Chad [2019]; Zambia [2019]; multiple additional African countries affected by distinct cVDPV2 emergences
Host: Humans, predominantly children in under-immunized communities across multiple African countries
Event summary: From about 2017 onward, numerous genetically independent outbreaks of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) emerged or expanded across West, Central, East and parts of Southern Africa, collectively accounting for the majority of global cVDPV2 emergences, outbreaks and virus detections after the global withdrawal of OPV2.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) These lineages, many arising in countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nigeria, Somalia, Ethiopia, Angola and the Central African Republic, spread widely across borders to affect >20 African countries and produced hundreds of paralytic cases during 2018–2023, particularly in chronically underserved, conflict‑affected or nomadic populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) The Global Polio Eradication Initiative mounted a continent‑wide response involving repeated outbreak assessments, large-scale use of monovalent OPV2 and, from 2021, novel OPV2 (nOPV2), along with intensified AFP and environmental surveillance; many outbreak lineages were closed by 2020–2023, but new emergences continued to appear, keeping cVDPV2 a major threat.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/circulating-vaccine-derived-poliovirus-type-2-global-update?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing weaknesses in routine immunization, fragile and conflict‑affected health systems, high population mobility (including in the Lake Chad basin and Horn of Africa), and logistical challenges in rapidly responding to multiple simultaneous outbreaks created conditions in which residual Sabin 2 and outbreak response use of mOPV2 could repeatedly seed new cVDPV2 lineages.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10354706/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Dozens of independent cVDPV2 emergences, each showing substantial VP1 divergence from Sabin 2 and restored neurovirulence, represent repeated novel strain/genotype emergence events; some lineages show evidence of enhanced fitness in low‑immunity populations, driving extensive geographic range expansion across multiple African subregions.
Review: retain – This aggregated event appropriately captures the highly impactful, multi‑country wave of post‑switch African cVDPV2 outbreaks that together account for the majority of global cVDPV2 burden since 2017, and is clearly among the top post‑1990 poliovirus emergence episodes by both case count and geographic spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) Event year has been adjusted from 2018–2023 to 2017–2023 to reflect early post‑switch cVDPV2 emergence and spread in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighboring countries; countries list remains illustrative rather than exhaustive, consistent with WHO summaries. Classification as re-emergence driven by multiple novel vaccine‑derived lineages is appropriate.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Northern America; Western Asia
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022]; United States of America [2022]; Israel [2022]
Host: Humans in high-income, previously polio-free countries; mostly asymptomatic or mild infections with few detected paralytic cases
Event summary: In 2022, enhanced environmental surveillance in London repeatedly detected vaccine-derived type 2 poliovirus in sewage samples from February onwards, and genetic analysis showed that these viruses were part of a cVDPV2 lineage that had acquired sufficient mutations to be classified as vaccine-derived and was spreading within under‑immunized communities.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673622018049?utm_source=openai)) Within months, closely related viruses were identified in wastewater in Jerusalem District, Israel, and in several counties in New York State, USA, where one unvaccinated adult developed paralytic polio, indicating transcontinental circulation of a single lineage likely originating from OPV use outside these high‑income countries.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON408?utm_source=openai)) Public‑health authorities mounted intensive responses including expanded AFP and wastewater surveillance, targeted IPV booster campaigns, and risk communication to affected communities; environmental detections declined during 2023, although low‑level circulation or sporadic importations remain possible and similar cVDPV2 detections have since been reported in other countries’ wastewater.([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/polio-global-eradication-nac-and-environmental-surveillance/environmental-surveillance-for-polio?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International travel and migration from regions still using type‑2–containing OPV introduced cVDPV2 into socio‑culturally cohesive subpopulations with lower vaccination coverage within otherwise highly vaccinated countries; reliance on IPV‑only schedules limited intestinal immunity, allowing mainly asymptomatic fecal‑oral transmission detectable via wastewater.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON408?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: A highly divergent cVDPV2 lineage, genetically adapted through prolonged circulation and displaying restored neurovirulence, spread across multiple continents and caused at least one paralytic case; this constitutes re-emergence of transmissible poliovirus in regions that had been free of any indigenous polio for decades, driven by novel strain/genotype emergence from OPV rather than wild virus.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673622018049?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This lineage represents the first documented instance of sustained cVDPV2 transmission detected in high‑income, long‑polio‑free settings in Europe and North America and therefore has high strategic importance despite relatively few paralytic cases.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON408?utm_source=openai)) Event-type coding has been corrected: inter_continental_emergence is now set to “false” because the poliovirus EPP has long been present on all affected continents; instead the event is treated as re-emergence of poliovirus transmission from a vaccine-derived lineage in previously polio‑free regions. Sources are focused on WHO DONs and detailed UK/US wastewater and case investigations.

Host: Humans (primarily rural agricultural workers and household contacts)
Event summary: From 1995 onwards, Kosovo experienced recurrent CCHF outbreaks centered in endemic rural foci, with major epidemic years in 1995 and 2001 and additional cases through at least 2013; across this period 228 human cases and a case‑fatality ratio of about 25–27% were documented. Most infections occurred in agricultural workers and household contacts exposed to Hyalomma ticks or infected livestock, with occasional nosocomial spread. Strengthened surveillance, infection‑prevention measures and community education gradually reduced the size of later outbreaks, but severe sporadic cases and small clusters continued to occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense human–tick–livestock contact in endemic foci, post‑conflict disruption of public health and veterinary services, and limited early infection‑control capacity in regional hospitals sustained recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: established Europe‑1 lineage CCHFV strains maintained stable enzootic cycles in ticks and livestock; available data support long‑standing endemicity with episodic amplification in humans rather than introduction of a novel viral variant.
Review: retain: Event represents a well‑documented long‑running re‑occurrence focus in Kosovo (with linked activity in neighboring Albania) and is among the most consequential European CCHF episodes by cumulative cases and deaths. Sub‑regions were corrected to "Southern Europe" only (removing the vague reference to Eastern Europe, since no specific Eastern European countries are listed in this row), and the event‑type coding was adjusted so that re_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, in line with evidence of long‑established Europe‑1 lineage circulation without clear viral change.

Host: Humans (ostrich farm and abattoir workers in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape Province)
Event summary: In October–November 1996, South Africa reported a large occupational CCHF outbreak among workers at an ostrich farm and slaughterhouse in the Oudtshoorn area of Western Cape, with around 17 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, more than 30 hospitalizations and at least one death. Infection was linked to handling of viremic ostriches and crushing of Hyalomma ticks during slaughter, and secondary transmission in healthcare settings was limited by the rapid institution of barrier nursing once the etiology was recognized. The outbreak led to temporary restrictions on South African ostrich meat exports and prompted extensive changes to tick‑control and biosafety practices in the ostrich industry, preventing further abattoir‑based clusters of similar magnitude.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of Hyalomma ticks on ostriches, intensive handling of tick‑infested birds and their blood in an abattoir with initially limited awareness of CCHF risk, and strong market demand for ostrich products combined to amplify occupational exposure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by long‑established Africa‑2 lineage CCHFV circulating in South African livestock and wildlife; there is no evidence for a novel strain or marked change in viral virulence, so this is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence driven by work practices and trade patterns rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain: Newly added event capturing the largest documented human CCHF outbreak in South Africa and its associated trade impact on the ostrich industry. Classified as re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic country, consistent with historical data showing human CCHF in South Africa since the early 1980s and absence of evidence for a novel viral variant.

Host: Humans (rural residents, agricultural workers and healthcare staff in southern Russia, especially Stavropol and Rostov regions)
Event summary: After a period of relatively low reported incidence, CCHF re‑emerged in southern Russia in 1999 with a localized outbreak in Rostov Province and additional cases in Stavropol, marking renewed activity in long‑known foci. Through the early 2000s, sustained transmission in the Southern and North Caucasus federal districts produced hundreds of cases and dozens of deaths; for example, in 2006 the Southern Federal District alone reported about 190–200 human cases, and cumulative 1999–2006 counts in Stavropol and Rostov each reached several hundred cases. Increased awareness, improved laboratory diagnosis and targeted vector control later reduced reported incidence somewhat, but sporadic cases and smaller clusters continued beyond 2006 and up to at least 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and increased activity of Hyalomma tick populations in southern steppe zones, climatic warming, changes in land use and livestock management, and greater human presence in tick habitats drove higher exposure, while socioeconomic changes after the Soviet period weakened some public‑health and veterinary controls. Internal mechanisms: sequencing shows circulation of Europe‑1 CCHFV lineages that have been present in the region for decades; the surge in human disease reflects re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel viral strain.
Review: retain: Newly added high‑impact event summarizing re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of CCHF in southern Russia, with large cumulative case numbers and substantial mortality. Classified as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic subregion (Eastern Europe), consistent with molecular data showing long‑standing Europe‑1 lineages and with WHO/EID descriptions of increasing incidence rather than a new introduction.

Host: Humans (livestock workers, butchers, household contacts and healthcare workers)
Event summary: Although CCHFV infection in livestock and ticks had been recognized in Iran since the 1970s, the first diagnosed human CCHF case was reported in 1999, quickly followed by additional cases and recognition of endemic transmission in several provinces. Between 1999 and 2011, around 870 human cases were reported nationally, with intense activity in Sistan‑va‑Baluchestan and notable nosocomial clusters in Fars, Isfahan, Mashhad and Birjand during the 2000s. Strengthened national surveillance, laboratory capacity and infection‑prevention measures in referral hospitals reduced the size of hospital outbreaks over time, but Iran continues to report sporadic and cluster‑based human CCHF cases annually.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of livestock trade and slaughter (often without adequate tick control), traditional animal‑handling practices, and initial gaps in barrier precautions in hospitals facilitated both zoonotic spillover and nosocomial transmission once human cases began to be recognized. Internal mechanisms: Asia‑1 lineage CCHFV strains had been enzootic in Iranian livestock and ticks for decades, and there is no clear evidence for a new viral genotype underlying the 1999 re‑appearance; the pattern is best explained as re‑occurrence in a previously known subregion driven by external and healthcare‑system factors.
Review: retain: Event accurately describes the major re‑occurrence of CCHF in Iran in 1999 and subsequent endemic transmission, which accounts for hundreds of cases and frequent nosocomial clusters. Emergence type has been corrected from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence to align with project definitions and the documented long‑standing presence of CCHFV in Iranian livestock and ticks; geographic coding (Southern Asia, Iran) and sources are appropriate.

Host: Humans (abattoir workers, butchers, livestock handlers, rural residents and healthcare workers)
Event summary: Following the first recognized human CCHF cases in 1976, Pakistan saw a marked rise in reported cases and outbreaks from around 2000 onwards, including notable nosocomial clusters such as a 2002 Rawalpindi outbreak linked to a surgical patient. Throughout the 2000s and early 2010s, dozens of cases were reported most years, with heightened activity around Eid‑ul‑Azha when large numbers of animals are slaughtered and moved through informal channels. By 2013, Pakistan was considered one of the highest‑burden CCHF countries globally, with persistent seasonal outbreaks and frequent infections among healthcare workers despite progressive improvements in surveillance and infection‑prevention practices.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high volumes of animal movement and slaughter during religious festivals, weak tick control in smallholder and cross‑border livestock trade, and gaps in hospital infection‑control programs facilitated repeated zoonotic and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: Pakistan’s CCHFV strains belong mainly to the Asia‑1 lineage and appear long‑established; resurgence after 2000 reflects re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing genotypes, not emergence of a novel viral variant.
Review: retain: This row captures Pakistan’s substantial CCHF burden since 2000, which ranks among the highest globally by case counts. The previous dual coding as both re_occurrence and re_emergence has been simplified to re_occurrence only, consistent with evidence that endemic Asia‑1 lineages, not new genotypes, underlie these outbreaks; all geographic fields and the main WHO/EMRO and EID sources remain appropriate.

Host: Humans (mainly rural residents and agricultural workers in the Kelkit Valley and surrounding north‑central provinces)
Event summary: CCHF was first recognized clinically in Türkiye in 2002, when an outbreak of severe febrile illness in the Kelkit Valley was confirmed virologically, and thereafter the country experienced the largest recorded national CCHF epidemic worldwide. Between 2002 and late 2015, nearly 9,800 human cases with around a 5% case‑fatality ratio were reported, peaking in the mid‑2000s and concentrated in north‑central Anatolia where Hyalomma ticks and livestock exposures are common. Intensive public‑health response including tick‑bite prevention campaigns, clinician training, strengthened laboratory diagnosis and better supportive care gradually reduced annual incidence and mortality, although seasonal cases have continued.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: agro‑ecological conditions in the Kelkit Valley favorable to Hyalomma ticks, extensive smallholder livestock farming, and increased human–tick contact in rural areas allowed rapid amplification once CCHF was recognized, while heightened surveillance initially inflated reported incidence. Internal mechanisms: Europe‑1 lineage CCHFV strains circulating in Turkish ticks and livestock appear closely related to those in neighboring Balkan countries; current evidence indicates re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Türkiye’s prolonged epidemic is the single largest CCHF event globally by number of reported cases and is essential for a top‑10 list. Event type has been reclassified from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence to reflect that CCHFV was already established in the wider Western Asia–Balkans region and that available data do not support a distinct new viral lineage in Türkiye. A generic German‑language Wikipedia URL was removed from the source list, leaving primary outbreak and review articles as the main references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (butchers, livestock handlers, family caregivers and urban residents in Nouakchott and nearby areas)
Event summary: Between February and August 2003, Mauritania experienced a major CCHF outbreak with 38 human cases (confirmed and probable) and an overall case‑fatality ratio near 30%, the majority of cases residing in the capital, Nouakchott. The epidemic began with a hospital‑based cluster linked to a butcher, followed by further nosocomial and community cases among butchers, livestock workers and family members, revealing previously unrecognized urban transmission. Rapid implementation of barrier nursing, case isolation, slaughterhouse hygiene measures and public risk communication helped to halt the outbreak, and only sporadic CCHF cases have since been reported from the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑risk slaughtering practices and direct exposure to blood and tissues of infected small ruminants in and around Nouakchott’s abattoirs, combined with limited early recognition of CCHF and inadequate infection‑control measures in hospitals, facilitated both animal‑to‑human and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: sequence data place Mauritanian viruses within Africa‑3 lineages that also circulate in other West and southern African countries; the 2003 epidemic is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence and amplification of established regional genotypes rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Newly added event representing the first large, predominantly urban CCHF outbreak recognized in West Africa, with substantial mortality and clear public‑health impact. Classified as re_occurrence within Western Africa, consistent with earlier evidence of CCHFV in the region; geographic fields align with the UNSD Western Africa subregion and sources are high‑quality outbreak descriptions.

Host: Humans (rural resident in northeastern Greece exposed to ticks and possibly livestock)
Event summary: In June 2008, Greece reported its first recognized fatal CCHF case in a woman from the Rhodopi area of northeastern Greece, despite previous isolation of a seemingly low‑pathogenic CCHFV strain (AP92) from ticks and high human seroprevalence in parts of the country. The patient likely acquired infection from a tick bite or contact with infected animal tissues in a rural setting, and virologic analysis showed that the responsible strain (Rhodopi‑2008) clustered with pathogenic Balkan CCHFV lineages and differed substantially from AP92. After this event, enhanced surveillance documented continued virus circulation in ticks and livestock but no further severe confirmed human cases for many years, suggesting persistent but low clinical incidence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movements of infected livestock and ticks across Balkan borders and expansion of Hyalomma‑infested habitats created opportunities for introduction of pathogenic CCHFV lineages into northeastern Greece, where people engage in outdoor agricultural activities. Internal mechanisms: the emergence of a pathogenic CCHFV strain distinct from the historically detected AP92 genotype in Greece is consistent with re‑emergence driven by strain differences within the Europe‑lineage viruses rather than de novo evolution after arrival in Greece.
Review: review: This single‑case but virologically important event marks the first severe, laboratory‑confirmed CCHF in Greece and the appearance of a pathogenic strain distinct from the earlier AP92 genotype. It has been re‑classified as re_emergence (reflecting strain change in a previously known Southern Europe subregion) and intra_continental_emergence has been set to No to comply with the rule that spread to a new country within an already affected subregion should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. Given its small case count compared with Turkey, Iran, Russia, Afghanistan and Iraq, it is flagged for review if a strict top‑10 cut is enforced, but is epidemiologically informative for Europe.

Host: Humans (rural residents, relatives caring for patients, and healthcare workers in Kordofan region)
Event summary: In late 2008, a nosocomial outbreak of hemorrhagic fever in a rural hospital in Al‑Fulah, West Kordofan, was confirmed as CCHF, with multiple healthcare workers and family caregivers infected while caring for a butcher who likely acquired infection from slaughtering infected livestock; additional sporadic cases and small clusters were recognized in nearby areas through 2009. Molecular characterization revealed CCHFV strains belonging to Africa‑3 lineages related to viruses from other parts of Africa, indicating previously unrecognized enzootic circulation in Sudan. Subsequent Sudanese epidemics in 2010–2011 involved larger numbers of cases in Kordofan, but the 2008–2009 events represent the first documented human CCHF emergence in Northern Africa and led to heightened clinical awareness and infection‑control measures in affected hospitals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense contact between pastoralist communities and viremic livestock, traditional bedside caregiving practices in rural hospitals, and severe limitations in infection‑prevention infrastructure allowed efficient nosocomial and household transmission once CCHF reached healthcare settings. Internal mechanisms: multiple Africa‑3 lineage variants were detected, suggesting long‑standing enzootic maintenance and movement of viruses with livestock rather than recent evolution of a novel strain; emergence in humans in Sudan is therefore best interpreted as intra‑continental emergence into a previously unaffected African subregion.
Review: review: Event correctly captures the first recognized human CCHF outbreaks in Sudan and, by UNSD definition, the first emergence of CCHF in the Northern Africa subregion; thus intra_continental_emergence has been set to Yes and re_emergence to No (earlier coding as re_emergence was inconsistent with lineage data showing established Africa‑3 viruses). However, case numbers (tens rather than hundreds) are modest compared with the largest national epidemics, so this row is flagged for review if the dataset must be pruned to 10 globally most impactful events; users may alternatively wish to expand the time span to 2008–2011 to encompass the larger 2010–2011 Sudan epidemics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (index livestock handler, family members and hospital staff in and around Ahmedabad, Gujarat)
Event summary: In December 2010–January 2011, India detected its first confirmed human CCHF outbreak near Ahmedabad in Gujarat, beginning with a probable livestock‑exposed index patient and followed by secondary nosocomial infections in a nurse, a physician and other hospital contacts; about five confirmed and several additional suspected cases were reported, with high case‑fatality. Molecular investigations identified CCHFV of the Asia‑1 lineage closely related to strains from Pakistan and Afghanistan in patient samples, local ticks and domestic animals, demonstrating establishment of a new endemic focus in western India. Aggressive infection‑control measures, contact tracing and tick‑control interventions limited onward transmission, although sporadic cases and small rural outbreaks have since been reported from Gujarat and neighboring states.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction or amplification of CCHFV‑infected livestock and ticks around Ahmedabad, close human contact with animals, and initial lack of CCHF‑specific infection‑control protocols in hospitals enabled both zoonotic spillover and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show that Indian viruses fall within the Asia‑1 lineage without clear evidence of novel genetic traits; the episode is best viewed as re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion of existing regional genotypes into India, with healthcare‑associated transmission acting as an amplifying context.
Review: review: This event is epidemiologically important as the first confirmed human CCHF outbreak in India and demonstrates spread of Asia‑1 viruses from neighboring countries into Gujarat, but involves relatively few cases compared with major national epidemics. Event type has been adjusted from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence within Southern Asia to align with project rules (no intra‑continental emergence for spread to a new country inside an already affected subregion). Retain if geographic expansion into India is a priority; otherwise, it is a candidate for exclusion under a strict top‑10 impact cut.

Countries: Spain [2013]; Spain (Ávila, Castilla y León; Cáceres, Extremadura; Salamanca, Castilla y León) [2016]
Host: Humans (rural residents and visitors exposed to Hyalomma ticks, and hospital staff exposed to index patients)
Event summary: Spain retrospectively identified an autochthonous human CCHF case from 2013 and, in 2016, reported two linked cases (a tick‑borne index patient from Ávila Province and a secondary nosocomial infection in a nurse), representing the first confirmed autochthonous human CCHF cases in the Iberian Peninsula. Extensive surveillance of ticks and wildlife from 2011 onward demonstrated established circulation of Africa‑3 lineage CCHFV in Hyalomma ticks feeding on wild ungulates and livestock across several regions, and additional sporadic human cases have been reported since 2016. National and EU‑level responses included strengthened tick and wildlife surveillance, public advisories on tick‑bite prevention, and enhanced preparedness for viral hemorrhagic fevers in hospitals, which have so far limited human involvement mostly to isolated cases and very small clusters.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: north‑westward spread of infected Hyalomma ticks into the Iberian Peninsula, likely via migratory birds and livestock movement, combined with suitable climatic conditions and increased human recreational and occupational exposure in tick‑infested habitats enabled CCHFV establishment. Internal mechanisms: introduction and local maintenance of Africa‑3 lineage viruses in Iberian ticks and wildlife constitute geographic range expansion of a known genotype; however, there is no strong evidence of novel functional viral traits, so this episode is treated as a re‑occurrence of existing African lineages in a new European focus rather than re‑emergence via viral evolution.
Review: retain: Despite low absolute case numbers, this event represents the first confirmed autochthonous human CCHF in the Iberian Peninsula and established Africa‑3 lineage circulation in Western EU tick and wildlife populations, making it a key emergence episode for Europe. Sub‑regions have been corrected to UNSD "Southern Europe" only (Spain is not in the Western Europe subregion as previously stated), intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags have been set to No, and the event is now coded as re_occurrence to reflect spread of a known African lineage into an already CCHF‑affected European subregion.

Host: Humans (livestock owners, butchers, household contacts and healthcare workers, mainly in Herat, Kabul and other high‑risk provinces)
Event summary: Although Afghanistan reported sporadic CCHF cases from the late 1990s onward, national surveillance documented a marked surge between 2016 and 2018, with 163 reported cases in 2016, 245 in 2017 and 483 in 2018, many of them severe and with high case‑fatality. Cases clustered in provinces such as Herat and Kabul and were strongly associated with animal slaughter, particularly around Eid‑ul‑Adha, as well as with contact with infected livestock, ticks and blood products; healthcare workers were also affected. Reactive control efforts—including public risk communication, improved infection‑prevention practices and limited tick‑control campaigns—helped reduce incidence somewhat after 2018, but recurrent seasonal spikes continue, and Afghanistan remains one of the highest‑burden CCHF countries globally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of small‑scale livestock keeping in peri‑urban areas, unregulated slaughter during religious festivals, conflict‑related disruption of veterinary and public‑health services, and limited laboratory capacity for early diagnosis contributed to large seasonal outbreaks once surveillance intensified. Internal mechanisms: Afghan viruses belong mainly to Asia‑1 lineages closely related to strains circulating in Iran and Pakistan; the 2016–2018 surge is best characterized as re‑occurrence and amplification of endemic lineages under changing social and ecological conditions, not emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Newly added event capturing one of the largest recent national CCHF burdens, with nearly 900 reported cases over three years and very high mortality. Classified as re_occurrence in a long‑endemic Southern Asia country and strongly recommended for inclusion among the global top 10 in terms of impact; dates, subregion coding and sources were checked against Afghanistan’s National Disease Surveillance and Response data and recent analytical studies.

Host: Humans (rural residents and health‑facility patients in Mopti Region)
Event summary: In January–February 2020, Mali notified WHO of an outbreak of suspected CCHF in Mopti Region, with 14 suspected cases and seven deaths, three of which were laboratory‑confirmed as CCHFV infection, yielding an apparent case‑fatality of about 50%. The index cases were linked to rural villages with livestock exposure, and investigation suggested both tick‑borne infection and person‑to‑person transmission through blood contact, raising concern about previously undocumented CCHFV circulation in central Mali. Rapid implementation of case isolation, contact tracing, community risk communication and reinforcement of infection‑prevention practices in local healthcare facilities appears to have prevented a larger secondary wave, although the true extent of enzootic virus circulation remains uncertain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unregulated livestock movements, minimal tick‑control practices and weak diagnostic capacity likely allowed silent circulation of CCHFV in animals prior to the recognition of severe human disease; concurrent attention to the emerging COVID‑19 pandemic may also have delayed thorough investigation. Internal mechanisms: available sequence data link Malian viruses to Africa‑3 lineages already found in West Africa, suggesting re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing regional genotypes into a new national focus rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: review: This small but high‑fatality outbreak documents the first confirmed human CCHF cases in Mali and extension of Africa‑3 lineage viruses into a new West African country, but involves few confirmed cases relative to larger regional epidemics (e.g. Mauritania 2003, Afghanistan 2016–2018, Iraq 2022–2023). Emergence type has been re‑coded from intra_continental_emergence/re_emergence to re_occurrence in Western Africa, reflecting previous CCHFV activity in neighboring countries. The row is flagged for review if only the very largest global events are to be retained.

Host: Humans (butchers, livestock handlers, rural residents and healthcare workers across multiple governorates)
Event summary: CCHF has been recognized in Iraq since at least 1979, but in 2022–2023 the country experienced its largest recorded outbreak, with WHO reporting over 200 cases and around 27 deaths by May 2022 and later national and regional summaries indicating roughly 1,300–1,400 suspected cases and more than 100 deaths for 2022 alone. Cases occurred across many governorates, especially in the south, and were strongly associated with slaughtering and handling of cattle, sheep and goats, with multiple nosocomial infections among healthcare workers during the peak. A multi‑sectoral One Health response involving intensified tick‑control on animals, safer slaughterhouse practices, improved laboratory capacity and broad public risk communication reduced incidence somewhat in 2023, but Iraq remains a major CCHF focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suspension or reduction of routine veterinary tick‑control and livestock spraying during the COVID‑19 pandemic, high demand for animal slaughter around religious festivals, and weak occupational protections for butchers and farmers markedly increased human exposure to infected ticks and animal blood. Internal mechanisms: Iraq’s CCHFV strains fall within Asia‑1 lineages already known from the region; the 2022–2023 surge is interpreted as a re‑occurrence and geographic/intensity expansion of endemic viruses rather than emergence of a new genotype, although higher exposure intensity likely contributed to severe disease and high case‑fatality.
Review: retain: This is Iraq’s largest documented CCHF epidemic and one of the highest recent global case burdens, with over a thousand suspected cases and more than 100 deaths, making it clearly among the top 10 events by impact. Event type has been simplified to re_occurrence only (earlier co‑coding as re_emergence lacked evidence for major viral change), and geographic fields and WHO/EMRO sources remain appropriate and specific to this episode.

Host: Humans
Event summary: From February 1996, a large outbreak of human mpox occurred in villages of the Katako-Kombe and Lodja health zones in Kasai-Oriental, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with hundreds of suspected cases and several deaths in a region where the virus was already known to be endemic. The outbreak developed with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission across multiple villages over 1996–1997, alongside sporadic zoonotic spillover, ultimately becoming the largest documented mpox outbreak to that time. Transmission declined after intensified surveillance and control measures, and case numbers fell by late 1997–1998, though mpox continued to be reported sporadically in the DRC thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cessation of smallpox vaccination leading to a growing cohort with no cross‑protective orthopoxvirus immunity, fragile health systems, and high dependence on bushmeat and wildlife contact in forest villages. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence of a novel strain; the event is best explained by increased susceptibility and opportunities for transmission (extended human-to-human spread) rather than major viral change.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the large 1996–1997 Kasai-Oriental outbreak in DRC, with appropriate geography (Middle Africa, Democratic Republic of the Congo) and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic subregion; no substantive changes were required.

Host: Humans (with infected pet prairie dogs and imported African rodents)
Event summary: In April–June 2003, mpox was introduced into the United States when a shipment of small mammals from Ghana, including African rodents, infected prairie dogs at a Midwest animal distributor, leading to 47 confirmed and probable human cases across six states—the first recognized human mpox outbreak in the Western Hemisphere. The outbreak expanded through contact with infected pet prairie dogs, causing febrile rash illness but no deaths, and investigations traced the virus to West African–origin clade II MPXV in the imported rodents. Aggressive animal quarantine, a federal ban on importation and movement of implicated rodents, euthanasia of exposed animals, and human contact tracing contained the outbreak by late 2003 with no sustained human-to-human transmission documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: global wildlife trade and movement of exotic pets from Ghana to the U.S.; mixing of imported African rodents with susceptible prairie dogs in commercial facilities; lack of prior awareness of mpox risk in the exotic pet trade. Internal mechanisms: clade II (West African) MPXV with relatively lower virulence compared with Central African clade I; no strong evidence that viral change, rather than ecological and trade pathways, drove this inter-continental emergence.
Review: retain – Event accurately describes the 2003 U.S. mpox outbreak (first documented human outbreak outside Africa), with correct North American geography and an appropriate classification as inter-continental emergence driven by imported rodents and local animal-to-human transmission; no corrections were needed.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In 2005, a cluster of human mpox cases was detected in Unity State of what is now South Sudan (then southern Sudan), representing the first reported human mpox outbreak in this dry savannah region outside the traditional Central/West African rainforest ecology. The outbreak involved around 10 confirmed, 9 probable and dozens of suspected cases across several villages, with up to five generations of human-to-human transmission and infection by a virus belonging to the Congo Basin (clade I) lineage but showing a novel genomic structural variation. Transmission waned by early 2006 after local and international response, and no further large mpox outbreaks were reported from this area for many years, although later mpox activity reappeared in the wider region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely zoonotic spillover from wildlife in a new, non‑rainforest ecological setting (savannah), coupled with limited clinical recognition and delayed laboratory confirmation, facilitated unnoticed spread. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel genomic variant within clade I (Congo Basin) MPXV and evidence of efficient person‑to‑person transmission over several generations justify classification as re‑emergence with novel strain/genotype characteristics in addition to intra-continental spread into a new African subregion.
Review: review – Corrected the countries field from 'Sudan (now largely South Sudan)' to 'South Sudan' to align with the UNSD country list and the fact that all known cases occurred in present-day South Sudan (Unity State); subregion 'Eastern Africa' remains appropriate. Classification as intra-continental emergence into a new African subregion plus re-emergence (novel clade I variant with efficient human-to-human spread) is retained but should be double-checked by the project team.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: Beginning in September 2017, Nigeria detected its first confirmed human mpox cases since the 1970s in Bayelsa State, with rapid recognition of a large, multi-state outbreak after decades of epidemiologic silence. The outbreak expanded during 2017–2018 to involve at least 118 confirmed cases (and many more suspected) across numerous states and the Federal Capital Territory, with several deaths and clear evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission, including in healthcare settings. By late 2018 incidence declined but mpox became newly established in Nigeria, with ongoing sporadic cases in subsequent years and this lineage later linked to exported cases and the 2022 global clade IIb outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: urbanization and changing land use in southern Nigeria, increased human–wildlife contact, weak routine surveillance, and waning population immunity after cessation of smallpox vaccination contributed to unnoticed re‑emergence and spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses indicate that the clade II (West African) viruses circulating in Nigeria from around 2014 evolved into the lineage (clade IIb) that later drove the 2022 global outbreak, implying adaptive changes associated with enhanced human‑to‑human transmissibility and geographic spread.
Review: review – Changed re_occurrence from true to false so that this event is classified primarily as re-emergence (involving an evolved clade II lineage with altered epidemiology) in a subregion where human mpox was known historically but absent for decades; years, geography, and sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2018]; Israel [2018]; Singapore [2019]
Host: Humans
Event summary: In 2018, travel-associated mpox cases were identified in the United Kingdom and Israel in travelers returning from Nigeria, representing the first documented exportation of West African clade mpox from Nigeria to non-African countries, with limited subsequent local transmission. The episode continued in May 2019 when Singapore detected its first laboratory-confirmed mpox case in a traveler from Nigeria, with extensive contact tracing and containment; in the UK, limited nosocomial and household transmission occurred from one imported case. These outbreaks ended without establishing endemic transmission in Europe or Asia, but they highlighted persistent under-recognized circulation of mpox in Nigeria and demonstrated the potential for repeated spread via air travel.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased international air travel from Nigeria, where mpox had re-emerged, combined with low clinician awareness in non-endemic countries but strong infection prevention capacity that limited onward spread. Internal mechanisms: viruses belonged to the Nigerian clade II lineage already circulating during the 2017–2018 outbreak; there is no strong evidence that additional viral change, beyond that, further altered transmissibility in these limited export events.
Review: review – Removed 'Western Europe' from the sub_regions list because no Western European country is listed in the countries field, and set inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence to false to reflect that these were small travel-associated clusters epidemiologically linked to the Nigeria outbreak, with only limited nosocomial/household spread and no sustained in situ transmission; the event is real and informative but may not meet the project’s threshold for a major emergence episode and could be merged with or referenced under the Nigeria 2017–2018 row.

Continent: Africa; Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Oceania
Sub-regions: Middle Africa; Western Africa; Eastern Africa; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern America; Caribbean; Central America; South America; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022]; Spain [2022]; Portugal [2022]; Germany [2022]; France [2022]; Italy [2022]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2022]; United States of America [2022]; Canada [2022]; Brazil [2022]; Peru [2022]; Mexico [2022]; Argentina [2022]; Chile [2022]; Nigeria [2022]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2022]; and many other affected countries across all inhabited continents
Host: Humans (predominantly adults, especially gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men; occasional infections in women and children)
Event summary: In May 2022, the United Kingdom reported a cluster of mpox cases without clear links to endemic regions, soon followed by multiple cases across Europe and North America, marking the start of the first large, multi-country mpox outbreak in non-endemic countries driven by sustained human-to-human transmission. Over 2022–2023 the clade IIb lineage linked to Nigeria spread through interconnected sexual networks, predominantly among men who have sex with men, causing tens of thousands of confirmed cases and hundreds of deaths worldwide, with the Americas and Europe initially most affected and later notable transmission also in other WHO regions. Intensive public health measures—including case isolation, contact tracing, risk communication targeting high‑risk sexual networks, and large-scale use of third‑generation smallpox/mpox vaccines and antivirals—led to a sharp decline in incidence by late 2022–2023, though low-level transmission persisted in several regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense international travel and social/sexual networks, particularly among MSM communities; overlapping HIV and STI epidemics; reduced orthopoxvirus immunity in the global population; and surveillance systems pre-focused on COVID-19 leading to some delays in early recognition. Internal mechanisms: emergence and dissemination of clade IIb mpox virus with genetic changes associated with accelerated mutation (e.g. APOBEC editing) and apparent adaptation for efficient human-to-human (especially sexual) transmission, representing a clear re‑emergence with a novel genotype and enhanced transmission compared with historically sporadic zoonotic outbreaks; this outbreak also entailed both inter-continental spread into previously unaffected continents (e.g. South America, parts of Oceania) and intra-continental spread into new subregions.
Review: review – Retained classification of this unprecedented multi-country outbreak as both inter-continental and intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence driven by clade IIb adaptation, but set re_occurrence from true to false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence; geography, scale, timing and mechanisms are consistent with WHO and CDC summaries, though case and country counts are necessarily summarized rather than exhaustive.

Host: Humans (including many children and women; evidence of sexual and close household transmission)
Event summary: From early 2023, the Democratic Republic of the Congo experienced a marked surge of clade I mpox, with suspected cases reported in the majority of provinces and a rapid rise in incidence compared with previous endemic levels. Over 2023–April 2024, DRC reported on the order of 15,000–20,000 suspected cases and hundreds of deaths, with increasing reports of sexual transmission, spread into large urban centers including Kinshasa, and cases among children and women, indicating changing epidemiology and transmission contexts. The outbreak continued into 2024 but with intensified national and international response planning, including enhanced surveillance, risk communication, and preparations for vaccination and clinical management to reduce incidence and mortality.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: persistent zoonotic reservoir in forested regions, high poverty and mobility, weak health systems, and limited access to vaccines and antivirals, combined with under-detection during the COVID-19 era, facilitated widespread re‑emergence and geographic expansion within DRC. Internal mechanisms: clade I viruses associated with higher case-fatality rates; recent analyses describe distinct clade I sublineages (e.g. Ia and Ib) and document sustained human-to-human transmission including sexual transmission in mining areas and urban centers, supporting classification as re‑emergence with altered transmission dynamics rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: review – Simplified the countries field to 'Democratic Republic of the Congo' (province-level spread, including Kinshasa, is now described only in the summary) and changed re_occurrence from true to false so that this large nationwide surge associated with new clade I lineages and sexual transmission is classified as re-emergence rather than both re-occurrence and re-emergence; magnitude, timing and mechanisms align with WHO and CDC sources, but ongoing evolution of the outbreak warrants continued monitoring.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: After several decades of mainly sporadic activity, chikungunya virus caused two large urban outbreaks in 1999–2000 in the Matete and Kingabwa townships of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, following periods of heavy rain. Contemporary investigations estimated around 50,000 human cases of febrile arthralgia, and virologic work confirmed chikungunya virus of a Central African lineage as the etiologic agent. Transmission declined after 2000 as vector densities fell and population immunity increased, but the episode signaled renewed epidemic potential in Central African cities and preceded later large outbreaks around the Indian Ocean and in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384432/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid urban growth in Kinshasa, poor drainage, and heavy rainfall created extensive Aedes breeding sites in densely populated neighborhoods, facilitating intense human–mosquito–human transmission. Limited arboviral surveillance and diagnostic capacity meant the chikungunya etiology was only recognized after substantial spread. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolates from this outbreak formed a distinct Central African chikungunya lineage, indicating evolutionary divergence from earlier East African strains and supporting classification as re‑emergence rather than simple recurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384432/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added because the 1999–2000 Kinshasa outbreaks (≈50,000 cases) are widely cited as a major modern re‑emergence in Africa and are among the most impactful post‑1990 chikungunya events. Classified as re‑emergence in Middle Africa with no inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence flags, since chikungunya was already established on the continent. Recommend retaining this event after manual verification of case estimates and locality.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Kenya [2004]; Comoros [2004-2005]; Mayotte [2005-2006]; Réunion [2005-2006]; Mauritius [2005-2006]; Seychelles [2005]; Madagascar [2005-2006]; Maldives [2006]
Host: Humans
Event summary: In 2004, chikungunya virus re‑emerged on the Kenyan coast (Lamu Island and Mombasa) after years of limited activity, then spread across the Comoros and other southwest Indian Ocean islands during 2004–2005. In 2005–2006 the same East/Central/South African lineage drove massive epidemics on Réunion (infecting roughly one third of the population, ≈200,000–260,000 persons) and large outbreaks in Mayotte, Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar and, slightly later, the Maldives, together totaling on the order of half a million cases. Transmission subsided by mid‑2006 as vector control intensified and susceptible populations were depleted, although low‑level circulation and sporadic cases persisted.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_03_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Drought conditions, water storage practices and rapid urbanization in coastal East Africa and the Indian Ocean islands increased household Aedes breeding sites, while intense human movement between Kenya and the islands enabled rapid seeding of new foci. Internal mechanisms: The East/Central/South African genotype acquired key envelope mutations (notably E1‑A226V) that enhanced replication in and transmission by Aedes albopictus, increasing epidemic potential in settings where this vector predominated and helping to explain the unprecedented scale of the Indian Ocean epidemics.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/214/suppl_5/S436/2632642?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Geographic scope and timing retained, but subregions corrected (removed incorrect “Western Africa” and nonstandard “Eastern Africa (island territories)” and restricted to Eastern Africa and Southern Asia). Emergence type recoded as re‑emergence only (no intra‑continental emergence) because affected territories all lie within already known African and Asian subregions. Source list pruned to keep Indian Ocean–focused WHO and JID articles; a Western Hemisphere–focused EID paper was dropped as less directly relevant.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: Seeded by viruses from the 2004–2006 Indian Ocean outbreaks, chikungunya re‑appeared in India in 2005–2006 after roughly three decades of apparent absence, spreading to at least 16 states and causing about 1.3–1.4 million suspected cases in 2006 alone. From 2006 onward, related East/Central/South African lineage viruses caused major epidemics in Sri Lanka and the Maldives and then moved through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and southern Thailand, where large outbreaks occurred in 2008–2009 after more than a decade without transmission. By around 2010, incidence had declined or become sporadic in many of these areas, but the virus established new endemic foci and left large cohorts with post‑epidemic rheumatologic sequelae.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_10_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Aedes aegypti in tropical urban and peri‑urban environments, inadequate vector control infrastructure, and intense human travel within South and South‑East Asia facilitated rapid dissemination once reintroduced. Large, immunologically naive populations supported explosive transmission, especially in densely populated Indian states and major cities in Indonesia and Thailand. Internal mechanisms: Continued spread of the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, including viruses bearing E1‑A226V and related mutations, increased fitness in Aedes albopictus and may have enhanced transmissibility, supporting re‑emergence across a wide climatic range in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4754000/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event narrowed to Asia only and extended through 2010 to capture the full South and South‑East Asian re‑emergence wave. Pacific island introductions (New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Yap) were removed from the country list and are treated separately in Oceania‑focused events. Emergence‑type flags were simplified to re‑emergence only: chikungunya was already known in Southern and South‑eastern Asia, and spread to new countries within the same subregions does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence under the project rules. Wikipedia and a Western Hemisphere EID paper were replaced with region‑specific WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In summer 2007, a traveler returning from India introduced chikungunya virus into the Emilia‑Romagna region of northeastern Italy, where Aedes albopictus was already established. Local transmission in the villages of Castiglione di Cervia and Castiglione di Ravenna produced about 200 symptomatic confirmed or probable cases, representing the first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in Europe. Intensive vector control, blood safety measures and the onset of cooler weather helped interrupt transmission by late September 2007.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/82980/cdc_82980_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑established Aedes albopictus populations in temperate Italy, combined with importation of a viremic traveler from an epidemic area in India, created conditions for local transmission. Warm summer temperatures, suburban housing with gardens and water containers, and high human mobility within Emilia‑Romagna facilitated mosquito–human contact. Internal mechanisms: The imported virus belonged to the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, adapted for efficient transmission by Aedes albopictus, demonstrating that this lineage could sustain transmission in a temperate European setting and highlighting the role of vector adaptation in enabling inter‑continental emergence.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/82980/cdc_82980_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Confirmed as the first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in Europe and therefore classified as an inter‑continental emergence event for this continent. The previous “re‑emergence” flag was removed because Europe was not a previously affected subregion. A nonessential Italian‑language Wikipedia link was dropped in favor of peer‑reviewed and official national/European sources.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2014, the first chikungunya infection in French Polynesia was detected in a traveler returning from Guadeloupe, and local transmission was documented from October 2014 onward. The virus then spread rapidly across Tahiti and most archipelagos, ultimately infecting an estimated 60,000–70,000 people (about one quarter of the population) and causing notable numbers of severe and atypical cases, including ICU admissions and deaths, as well as an increase in Guillain–Barré syndrome. Transmission declined by early 2015 as vector control was reinforced and a high proportion of residents became immune, but chronic rheumatologic sequelae persisted in many patients.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1341321X16301428?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of an Asian‑lineage virus from the Caribbean via air travel, together with high densities of Aedes aegypti and climatic conditions favoring year‑round vector abundance, enabled rapid amplification in densely populated island communities. Concurrent dengue and later Zika circulation complicated clinical recognition and further strained health services. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed an Asian genotype closely related to Caribbean strains, indicating long‑distance human‑mediated movement of an existing lineage rather than the emergence of a novel mutant; this outbreak is best characterized as intra‑continental emergence into the Polynesian subregion of Oceania.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6407142/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as the major high‑impact Pacific outbreak, with case numbers and severity (including ICU admissions and neurological complications) well documented. Emergence type recoded as intra‑continental emergence (Polynesia within Oceania) rather than first detection or inter‑continental emergence, because chikungunya had already established local transmission in Melanesia and Micronesia by 2011–2013. No changes to geography or timing; sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Saint Martin (French Part) [2013]; Sint Maarten (Dutch part) [2013-2014]; Martinique [2013-2014]; Guadeloupe [2013-2014]; Saint Barthélemy [2013-2014]; other Caribbean islands including Dominica, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, British Virgin Islands, US Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and others [2014]
Host: Humans
Event summary: In December 2013, autochthonous chikungunya transmission was first reported in the Western Hemisphere on the island of Saint Martin/Sint Maarten, where an Asian‑lineage virus caused locally acquired cases in residents without travel history. Over 2013–2014 the virus spread explosively throughout the Caribbean, with PAHO and CARPHA reporting several hundred thousand suspected and confirmed cases and some territories (e.g. Dominican Republic) recording hundreds of thousands of infections. By late 2014 transmission had declined in many islands, but the epidemic established chikungunya as an endemic arbovirus in the Caribbean basin and marked the first inter‑continental emergence of the virus into the Americas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of chikungunya into a wholly naive Caribbean population via air travel from endemic regions, combined with widespread Aedes aegypti (and, in some islands, Aedes albopictus), high human density and limited early vector control, allowed rapid expansion. Seasonal conditions favorable for dengue transmission similarly promoted Aedes proliferation and chikungunya spread. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic was driven by an Asian‑lineage virus already well adapted to transmission by Aedes aegypti, without evidence of a major new mutation; the key mechanism was geographic range expansion with efficient transmission in permissive vector and host populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4624217/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Confirmed as the first autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in the Americas and therefore appropriately classified as inter‑continental emergence. The previous use of “first_detection” for this regional introduction was removed to avoid confusion with global first detection in humans (1950s East Africa). Geography (Caribbean subregion under the South America continent code) and timing are consistent with PAHO/ECDC documentation.

Sub-regions: Caribbean; Central America; South America; Northern America
Countries: French Guiana [2014-2015]; Brazil [2014-2016]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2014-2016]; Colombia [2014-2016]; Suriname [2014-2015]; Guyana [2014-2015]; Costa Rica [2014-2016]; Nicaragua [2014-2016]; El Salvador [2014-2015]; Honduras [2014-2015]; Guatemala [2014-2015]; Mexico [2014-2016]; United States of America (Florida) [2014]
Host: Humans
Event summary: Following the 2013–2014 Caribbean introduction, chikungunya reached mainland South America in early 2014, with French Guiana reporting imported and then locally acquired cases and an estimated >16,000 clinical cases in Cayenne and surroundings. Over 2014–2016, autochthonous transmission was documented across most Central and South American countries and parts of Mexico, as well as small clusters of local transmission in Florida, USA; by late July 2016, the Region of the Americas had recorded roughly 2.9 million suspected and confirmed cases and nearly 300 deaths since the virus’s arrival. Co‑circulation with dengue and later Zika complicated diagnosis and strained health systems but also prompted major investments in Aedes control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high Aedes aegypti densities in urban centers across Latin America, coupled with water storage practices, inadequate housing and vector control gaps, allowed chikungunya to follow pathways previously established by dengue. Rapid regional air and land travel facilitated dissemination from Caribbean foci into mainland countries, where climatic conditions and existing vector populations supported sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: The same Asian lineage that seeded the Caribbean was the main driver of epidemics across mainland Americas; its traits supported efficient replication in Aedes aegypti but no single novel mutation was uniquely implicated. This event is best classified as intra‑continental emergence within the Americas following the initial inter‑continental introduction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as one of the highest‑impact events globally (>2.9 million reported cases across the Americas by mid‑2016). The continent field was cleaned (removal of duplicate “South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)” label), and the emergence type was recoded as intra‑continental emergence only, because the inter‑continental jump into the Americas is already captured in the 2013–2014 Caribbean event. Country list focuses on heavily affected mainland countries and the small but epidemiologically important Florida clusters.
