Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2016, Kenyan authorities reported a chikungunya outbreak in Mandera East sub‑county near the Somalia border, in a population that had not experienced major transmission since the mid‑2000s Indian Ocean wave. By late June, about 1,800 cases had been line‑listed, and WHO and national sources estimated that up to 80% of Mandera’s residents and roughly half of health‑care workers may have been affected, with linked cases reported across the border in Bula Hawa, Somalia. Transmission subsided later in 2016 after cross‑border coordination, vector control and community interventions were implemented, but the outbreak underscored the potential for large epidemics in East African border towns.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/news/chikungunya-kenya?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Aedes mosquitoes, widespread household water storage and fragile health infrastructure in a semi‑arid, insecure border area created ideal conditions for rapid spread once the virus was introduced. Cross‑border population movement between Somalia and Kenya facilitated virus circulation and complicated response operations. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed circulation of an ECSA lineage virus carrying additional mutations (e.g. E1:K211E, E2:V264A) associated with enhanced fitness in Aedes vectors, supporting classification of this episode as viral re‑emergence driven partly by genetic adaptation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493958/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event kept as an illustrative example of high‑attack‑rate re‑emergence in East Africa and of an adapted ECSA lineage but categorized solely as re‑emergence; an earlier “re‑occurrence” flag was removed to avoid overlapping categories. Country list clarified to name Somalia explicitly rather than “Somalia (border communities)”. Case estimates and attack rates rely on WHO AFRO and genomic/epidemiologic studies.

Host: Humans
Event summary: Pakistan reported its first recognized chikungunya outbreak in December 2016 in Karachi, Sindh Province, after weeks of unexplained febrile illness with severe arthralgia in densely populated neighborhoods. Over subsequent months, thousands of suspected cases were reported in Karachi and additional foci in Balochistan and other provinces, with WHO documenting roughly 1,000 suspected cases by March 2017 while local health authorities and clinical studies estimated more than 30,000 people affected. Transmission decreased later in 2017 as surveillance improved, vector control measures were intensified and seasonal declines in Aedes populations occurred, but chikungunya became established as a recurrent arboviral threat in major Pakistani cities.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6986857/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid, often unplanned urbanization in Karachi and other cities, poor solid‑waste management and abundant water‑holding containers favored proliferation of Aedes aegypti; weak baseline arboviral surveillance delayed recognition and response. High human mobility within and between provinces facilitated spread from initial foci. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked Pakistani strains to ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage viruses carrying additional mutations (including E1:K211E and E2:V264A) associated with enhanced transmission efficiency in urban Aedes populations, consistent with re‑emergence of an adapted lineage in a previously unaffected national setting.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8638460/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as a major first national outbreak in a large, densely populated South Asian country, but “first_detection” and “intra‑continental emergence” flags were removed because chikungunya had long been recognized in humans and in the Southern Asia subregion (India, Sri Lanka, etc.). The episode is more accurately classified as re‑emergence of an adapted ECSA lineage into a new national setting within an already affected subregion. Case‑number statements were harmonized with WHO EMRO and peer‑reviewed estimates.

Host: Humans
Event summary: After its first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in 2015–2016, Paraguay experienced a much larger resurgence beginning in October 2022, with national surveillance recording roughly 71,000–80,000 suspected, probable or confirmed cases by March 2023 and about 118,000 suspected and confirmed infections by early April. The epidemic, concentrated initially in Asunción and the surrounding Central Department, caused high hospitalization rates and at least 46 deaths, with severe disease observed particularly in infants and older adults, and coincided with co‑circulating dengue. Transmission declined later in 2023 as vector control was intensified and seasonal conditions became less favorable, but the wave highlighted the potential for high‑impact resurgence of chikungunya in subtropical South America.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7223a5.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High Aedes aegypti densities in urban Paraguay, warm and wet seasonal conditions and gaps in sustained vector control campaigns favored rapid amplification, while socioeconomic factors such as limited access to secure water and air‑conditioning increased human–mosquito contact. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed that the 2022–2023 wave was driven by an ECSA lineage that had circulated in Paraguay since mid‑2010s; the surge appears to reflect climatic and demographic drivers acting on a persisting lineage rather than a markedly altered viral phenotype, and is therefore classified as re‑occurrence rather than a distinct re‑emergence event.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8084490/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as a major recent resurgence with very high incidence and notable severity in Paraguay. Emergence type recoded as re‑occurrence only: available genomic data indicate epidemic expansion of an established ECSA lineage rather than emergence of a substantially new variant. Event summary updated to reflect more precise case and death counts from CDC MMWR and EID reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1991]; United Republic of Tanzania [1992]; United Republic of Tanzania [1993]; United Republic of Tanzania [1994]; United Republic of Tanzania [1995]; United Republic of Tanzania [1996]; United Republic of Tanzania [1997]
Host: Humans (predominantly bubonic plague, with occasional septicemic and pneumonic cases) in rural highland villages of Lushoto district and other foci in northern and central United Republic of Tanzania; reservoirs mainly commensal and wild rodents with flea vectors.
Event summary: After sporadic plague activity in the early 20th century, human plague re‑intensified in Tanzania from 1980, with Lushoto district becoming a highly active focus; between 1980 and 1996 more than 6,500 human cases and ≈530 deaths were recorded, with major peaks after 1990. From 1990–1997, national surveillance reported repeated large waves, including 364 cases in 1990, 1,293 in 1991, and 444–947 cases annually between 1994 and 1996, largely concentrated in Lushoto and neighbouring highland districts. Through the late 1990s, strengthened surveillance, improved rodent and flea control, and better access to antibiotics gradually reduced annual case numbers, though plague has persisted at lower incidence in a small number of endemic villages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: subsistence agriculture and food storage practices that attract rodents into mud‑and‑thatch housing; high household and peridomestic rodent densities in cool, humid highland environments; poverty, limited health infrastructure and delayed care‑seeking that allowed localised outbreaks to grow before control measures were deployed; land‑use and climate variability influencing rodent and flea population dynamics. Internal mechanisms: re‑activation and sustained transmission in long‑established natural foci of Y. pestis in Tanzanian highlands with classic flea‑borne transmission; available data do not indicate emergence of a novel genotype, host jump or antimicrobial resistance during this period, so the pattern is best classified as large‑scale re‑occurrence rather than evolutionary re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Added as a major omission: WHO regional summaries and Tanzanian field studies indicate >6,000 human cases and several hundred deaths in Lushoto and other foci between 1980 and 1996, with peaks of 1,293 cases in 1991 and >800 cases in several mid‑1990s years, making this one of the largest modern plague episodes globally.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0001706X9700096X?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because there is no evidence for a new strain, host jump, or resistance; changes are driven by social, ecological and climatic factors. Spatial resolution is national/highland rather than village‑level, so confidence set to 0.8.

Host: Humans (bubonic plague) in densely populated rural settlements of north‑central Namibia (especially Ohangwena and neighbouring regions) with commensal rodents and their fleas as the main zoonotic reservoirs.
Event summary: In 1991, Namibia experienced its worst recorded plague epidemic when approximately 1,092 persons in the north‑central regions developed suspected bubonic plague and about 45 died, following smaller outbreaks in the mid‑1980s. Surveillance data show continued high transmission in 1992 with a further 458 cases and 13 deaths, before activity fell sharply in subsequent years. Intensive outbreak response with antibiotic treatment, rodent and flea control, and public health education brought the epidemic under control, and later outbreaks, such as a 1999 cluster of roughly 39 cases, were much smaller in scale.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing natural plague foci in rodent populations of semi‑arid north‑central Namibia; overcrowded traditional homesteads and grain‑storage practices that favour rodent colonisation; drought and food insecurity promoting closer contact with rodents; delayed recognition of plague due to long inter‑epidemic intervals and limited diagnostic capacity. Internal mechanisms: re‑activation and amplification of established Y. pestis lineages in endemic rodent–flea cycles, with classical flea‑borne transmission to humans; no data indicate novel genetic variants or resistance, so this episode is best categorised as severe re-occurrence in known foci.
Review: retain – Added as a missing high‑impact event: WHO compilations and Namibian reports document ≈1,092 cases and 45 deaths in 1991 plus 458 cases in 1992, making this epidemic among the largest post‑1990 plague outbreaks worldwide.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5585619/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence (old foci with renewed intense transmission) rather than re-emergence, because the evidence points to amplification of existing enzootic cycles without demonstrated pathogen change.

Countries: Madagascar [1991]; Madagascar [1995]; Madagascar [1996]; Madagascar [1997]; Madagascar [1998]; Madagascar [1999]
Host: Humans (predominantly bubonic plague) in the coastal city of Mahajanga and surrounding urban/peri‑urban neighbourhoods, with Rattus rattus and the Asian house shrew (Suncus murinus) as key reservoirs and Xenopsylla cheopis and other fleas as vectors.
Event summary: In July 1991, after more than 60 years without reported human plague on Madagascar’s northwest coast, bubonic plague suddenly reappeared in the port city of Mahajanga, causing about 170 suspected cases and 41 confirmed or presumptive infections in shantytowns near the main market. Following a three‑year lull, four large annual urban epidemics from 1995–1998 produced roughly 1,800 suspected cases and over 200 bacteriologically or serologically confirmed human infections, spreading progressively into new quarters, with sporadic cases continuing into 1999. Intensive rodent and flea control, antibiotic treatment, and improved urban sanitation suppressed transmission, and after 1999 human plague again retreated mainly to the highland foci, although coastal rodent and shrew reservoirs persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of infected rodents and fleas from the highland plague foci to Mahajanga via trade and transport; rapid growth of informal settlements with poor housing, waste management, and high rodent densities; climatic conditions on the northwest coast that favoured flea survival and transmission during the July–November plague season. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion from highland to coastal urban environments and establishment of a novel coastal reservoir community in which the Asian house shrew S. murinus became a major maintenance host, alongside R. rattus, while efficient flea vectors sustained intense human exposure; emergence of new Y. pestis ribotypes in Madagascar and the first naturally occurring multidrug‑resistant strain were documented during the 1990s, although not restricted to Mahajanga.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/4/1/98-0114_article))
Review: retain – Event description, timing and magnitude agree with CDC and Malagasy data on the 1991 re‑introduction and four large Mahajanga epidemics totalling ≈1,800 suspected cases and over 200 confirmed infections.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/4/1/98-0114_article)) Classification as re-emergence is justified because Y. pestis re‑occupied a coastal urban niche that had been plague‑free for decades and adopted a new key reservoir host (Suncus murinus), representing ecological and host‑range changes rather than a simple recurrence in an unchanged focus.

Host: Humans (mainly bubonic plague, with sporadic septicemic and secondary pneumonic cases) in rural Andean and adjacent coastal districts of the northern departments of Cajamarca, La Libertad, Lambayeque and Piura.
Event summary: In October 1992, after many years with only scattered cases, bubonic plague re‑emerged in northern Peru, first in highland districts and then across parts of Cajamarca, La Libertad, Lambayeque and Piura, causing 120 reported human cases that year. National data compiled by WHO show a major escalation in 1993 with 611 cases and 31 deaths, followed by a further 420 cases and 19 deaths in 1994, making this the largest modern plague epidemic in the Americas. Intense control efforts—mass chemoprophylaxis for contacts, community flea control, rodent reduction campaigns and environmental sanitation—gradually reduced incidence after 1994, and by the late 1990s only smaller clusters persisted in the same rural foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing natural plague foci in rural Andean rodent populations; poverty and precarious adobe housing that allowed commensal rodents and their fleas to thrive; food storage practices and grain handling that increased human–rodent contact; climate variability, including El Niño–related rainfall anomalies, which likely boosted rodent and flea populations in the early 1990s; limited early plague surveillance and clinical suspicion after a long quiet period. Internal mechanisms: re‑amplification of entrenched Y. pestis foci with classic flea‑borne transmission to humans; available evidence from Peruvian and WHO reports does not indicate a novel genotype, host jump or resistance phenotype, so this multi‑year epidemic is best classified as a large-scale re-occurrence in previously affected subregions.
Review: retain – Added as a major missing event: WHO case tables and regional reviews document 120 cases in 1992, 611 in 1993 and 420 in 1994 (≈1,150 total, with ~46 deaths), making the 1992–94 northern Peru epidemic substantially larger than the 2009–2010 La Libertad outbreak originally highlighted by the LLM.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5585619/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence since it reflects resurgence in known highland and coastal foci without clear evidence of a novel strain or host expansion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (bubonic plague in rural Maharashtra and primarily pneumonic plague in the city of Surat and clusters in other states and Delhi).
Event summary: In late August 1994, after decades without recognised human plague in India, bubonic cases appeared in Mamla village, Beed District (Maharashtra), followed by a large urban pneumonic outbreak in Surat (Gujarat) and smaller clusters in several other states and the National Capital Territory of Delhi. Over the following two months, India reported thousands of suspected cases nationally; WHO and CDC analyses estimate 693 laboratory‑supported cases and 56 deaths from Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi, although the epidemic’s social impact was magnified by mass migration and international alarm. By late October 1994, intensified antibiotic treatment, vector control, disinfection, and environmental sanitation campaigns halted transmission and WHO declared the outbreak over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: urban flooding, refuse accumulation and poor drainage in Surat and other towns, which caused rodent die‑offs and flea dispersal; very high population density and overcrowded housing; inadequate early surveillance, clinical suspicion and laboratory capacity for plague; rapid mass internal migration that spread fear and may have disseminated infection; and intense media coverage that amplified socio‑economic disruption. Internal mechanisms: epidemiologic patterns are compatible with reactivation or importation of existing Y. pestis lineages into ecologically favourable urban environments, with flea‑borne transmission and person‑to‑person spread in pneumonic foci, but there is no strong evidence of a new genotype, increased intrinsic virulence or drug resistance.
Review: retain – This is correctly identified as one of the most impactful modern human plague outbreaks by case numbers and global socio‑economic disruption, with ≈693 lab‑supported cases and 56 deaths and substantial internal migration.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5585619/?utm_source=openai)) I recommend removing the non‑authoritative aggregator site (everything.explained.today) from the source list and relying on WHO and CDC primary reports and peer‑reviewed analyses instead.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (almost entirely bubonic plague) in rural districts of Tete Province—especially Mutarara—and later neighbouring areas, with sylvatic and commensal rodents and their fleas as reservoirs and vectors.
Event summary: After more than 15 years without reported human plague, Mozambique detected a bubonic plague outbreak in late 1994 in Mutarara District, Tete Province, resulting in about 216 cases and 3 deaths. Over the following years the same focus produced a much larger epidemic wave: WHO and national data indicate 825 cases and 18 deaths in 1997, followed by 430 cases (4 deaths) in 1998 and 316 cases (3 deaths) in 1999, making Mozambique one of the world’s largest plague hotspots in the late 1990s. Intensive case management, rodent and flea control, and community‑based environmental sanitation gradually reduced incidence, and by the early 2000s only small clusters of tens of cases were reported sporadically from the same endemic zone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: reactivation of a long‑silent natural plague focus in rodent populations of the Zambezi valley; food insecurity and grain‑storage practices that attracted rodents into dwellings; traditional housing with mud walls and thatched roofs providing abundant rodent harborage; limited health‑care access and under‑resourced vector control in remote districts; and possible climatic anomalies in the early–mid 1990s favouring rodent and flea population growth. Internal mechanisms: amplification of enzootic Y. pestis transmission in existing high‑risk landscapes with classical flea‑borne spread to humans; no evidence in available reports of a new genotype, resistance trait or host expansion, so these linked waves are best categorised as severe re-occurrence in known foci.
Review: retain – Added as a major missing episode: WHO surveillance and regional reviews show 216 cases in 1994, followed by 825, 430 and 316 cases in 1997–1999 (total ≈1,800 cases and >25 deaths), placing Mozambique among the top global contributors to plague burden in the late 1990s and clearly ahead of several small outbreaks originally included.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/1997_11_21a-en?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence because these outbreaks represent resurgence in a known endemic zone rather than spread to a new continent or evidence of pathogen change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo [2004]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2005]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2006]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2007]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2008]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2009]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2010]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2011]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2012]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2013]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2014]
Host: Humans (mainly bubonic plague, with repeated pneumonic and septicemic clusters) in rural highland and forest‑edge communities of Ituri and neighbouring districts in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Event summary: From 2004–2014, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo—especially the Ituri highlands and adjacent forest zones—experienced persistent plague transmission with numerous rural outbreaks, making DRC the single largest global contributor to reported human plague. WHO regional analyses estimate that DRC alone accounted for 8,379 of the 15,396 human cases reported worldwide over this period, with major peaks around 2005–2007 and recurrent pneumonic outbreaks in mining camps and remote villages. Despite targeted interventions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners, continuing insecurity, displacement and fragile health systems meant that human plague remained entrenched, although incidence showed a decreasing trend after the mid‑2000s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: chronic poverty and food insecurity; protracted armed conflict and population displacement into plague‑enzootic highlands and forest margins; overcrowded, poorly constructed housing with high rodent burden; weak surveillance and diagnostic capacity causing delayed detection and under‑reporting; and environmental conditions in tropical mountain ecosystems that support persistent rodent and flea populations. Internal mechanisms: long‑term maintenance of Y. pestis in multiple natural foci with recurrent amplification into human populations; major pneumonic outbreaks in 2005 and 2006 in a diamond mining camp and nearby villages underline how occupational crowding and poor conditions can trigger explosive respiratory transmission, but available genotyping does not indicate emergence of a novel dominant strain or resistance profile.
Review: retain – This multi‑year episode is well supported by WHO and CDC analyses, which show that DRC contributed ≈8,400 of ≈15,400 global plague cases during 2004–2014, far exceeding any other single country and clearly qualifying as one of the highest‑impact modern plague events.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/2/16-0122_article?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) is appropriate because repeated outbreaks reflect social, ecological and health‑system drivers in long‑established foci, without evidence for a novel strain or new host system.

Host: Humans (predominantly pneumonic plague with substantial numbers of bubonic and septicemic cases) in urban and peri‑urban settings across multiple districts, including Antananarivo and Toamasina, as well as traditional highland foci.
Event summary: In August 2017, an index patient with plague illness travelled by public transport from the endemic highlands to the coastal city of Toamasina via the capital Antananarivo, seeding pneumonic cases along the route and triggering an unprecedented urban epidemic. Between August and November 2017, Madagascar reported roughly 2,400–2,700 suspected, probable and confirmed plague cases and about 200 deaths nationwide, with around three‑quarters classified as pneumonic and many occurring in densely populated urban districts that had little prior experience with plague. Massive multi‑sectoral control measures—including rapid case detection and free antibiotic treatment, chemoprophylaxis of tens of thousands of contacts, cancellation of mass gatherings, large‑scale vector and rodent control, and international logistical support—brought the urban pneumonic wave under control by late 2017, although seasonal bubonic cases continue to recur annually in highland foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense human mobility between endemic rural highlands and major cities in overcrowded public transport; high population density and poor sanitation in urban neighbourhoods of Antananarivo and Toamasina; delayed recognition and laboratory confirmation of early pneumonic cases, allowing substantial exposure before control measures were activated; limited baseline preparedness for plague in large cities that had previously seen mainly sporadic imported cases. Internal mechanisms: repeated introductions of Y. pestis from highland foci into urban centres, with a clinical distribution skewed strongly toward highly transmissible pneumonic disease, but genetic investigations indicate multiple existing genotypes rather than a single novel strain, and susceptibility to frontline antibiotics remained generally preserved.
Review: review – This event is unquestionably one of the largest and most consequential modern plague outbreaks, with ≈2,400–2,700 reported cases and ≈200 deaths and a unique pattern of widespread urban pneumonic transmission.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/02-october-2017-plague-madagascar-en)) I have reclassified it from re_emergence to re_occurrence because available genomic and epidemiologic analyses indicate expansion of existing highland lineages into new urban settings under favourable social and environmental conditions, without clear evidence of a novel strain, resistance phenotype, or new host system. Duplicate WHO URLs were removed from the event’s source list, and reliance is placed on WHO DONs and peer‑reviewed outbreak reports; the Wikipedia entry is acceptable as a secondary source but not essential for core epidemiologic data.

Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo [2020]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2021]
Host: Humans (bubonic and pneumonic plague) in Rethy, Fataki and several neighbouring health zones of Ituri Province, including areas previously considered non‑endemic for human plague.
Event summary: Beginning in early 2020, the Rethy health zone in Ituri Province reported an unusual surge of suspected and confirmed plague cases, followed over 2020–2021 by further clusters, including pneumonic cases, in Fataki and nearby health zones. By mid‑2021, WHO regional bulletins described hundreds of suspected cases and several dozen deaths in Ituri, with some cases reported from localities that had not previously documented human plague, raising concern about geographic spread or under‑recognised foci. Despite insecurity, concurrent humanitarian crises and competing outbreaks, intensified surveillance, antibiotic supply, community education and vector‑control interventions were deployed, and reported case numbers declined by late 2021, although enzootic foci and human risk clearly persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: escalating armed conflict, population displacement and humanitarian crisis in Ituri, forcing people into or near plague‑enzootic forests and savannahs and into overcrowded camps with poor housing; weakened health services and attention diverted by other epidemics (e.g. Ebola, COVID‑19), delaying early detection and response; chronic poverty and food insecurity increasing contact with rodents and wild game. Internal mechanisms: renewed amplification of Y. pestis in longstanding Ituri foci with apparent extension of recognised risk into additional health zones and an increased share of pneumonic cases, but available reports do not suggest emergence of a novel genotype or resistance; instead, changing human settlement and security patterns appear to have expanded the pathogen’s effective reach.
Review: retain – This recent upsurge in Ituri is well documented by WHO and UNICEF, with several hundred suspected cases and dozens of deaths over 2020–2021 and spread into health zones that had not recently reported human plague, making it one of the more substantial 21st‑century events.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/2/16-0122_article)) Reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence because evidence points to renewed amplification and modest geographic extension of known foci under deteriorating security and socio‑economic conditions, rather than a demonstrably new strain or host transition.

Countries: United States of America (California – southern San Joaquin Valley counties, especially Kern and Tulare)
Host: Humans (residents of southern San Joaquin Valley counties, particularly Kern and Tulare)
Event summary: After several years of relatively low reported incidence, central California experienced a marked coccidioidomycosis upsurge beginning in 1991 following a prolonged drought and unusually wet winters in the southern San Joaquin Valley. During 1991–1994, annual reported coccidioidomycosis cases in California rose roughly tenfold above the historical baseline to more than 4,500 cases per year, with the great majority occurring around Bakersfield and neighboring Kern and Tulare counties, leading to thousands of illnesses and substantial healthcare costs. By 1995, case numbers declined toward pre‑epidemic levels, although they remained higher than in the 1980s, and subsequent analyses concluded that the epidemic reflected environmentally driven amplification of endemic strains rather than emergence of a single new clone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Interaction of a multi‑year drought in the late 1980s followed by periods of heavy rainfall in 1991–1992, which favored fungal growth and later dust generation, combined with population growth and housing expansion in high‑risk valley locations, increased occupational and outdoor recreational soil exposure, and many residents lacking prior immunity. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing of clinical isolates during the epidemic showed high genetic diversity and little linkage disequilibrium, indicating that no novel hypervirulent clone was responsible and supporting an interpretation of environmentally driven population increase of existing Coccidioides immitis lineages rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – New row added to capture the large 1991–1994 coccidioidomycosis epidemic in central California, during which annual reported cases rose from a long-term baseline of a few hundred to >4,500 per year, mainly in Kern/Tulare counties; this episode is clearly among the most impactful modern events and is well documented in CDC and J Clin Microbiol analyses. Classified as re-occurrence driven by climatic and demographic factors with no evidence for a novel epidemic clone.

Countries: Brazil (Northeast semi‑arid states Bahia, Piauí, Ceará, Maranhão, Pernambuco)
Host: Humans (rural residents and armadillo hunters in semi‑arid Northeast Brazil)
Event summary: From the late 1970s and particularly after 1991, clusters of acute coccidioidomycosis were recognized among armadillo hunters and rural workers in the semi‑arid Northeast of Brazil, initially in Bahia and Piauí and then in Ceará, Maranhão, and later Pernambuco. During 1991–2007, multiple outbreaks and case series documented dozens of autochthonous human and animal cases, supported by environmental detection of Coccidioides posadasii in local soils, establishing this semi‑arid belt as a new endemic area within South America. By the late 2000s, routine recognition and reporting of cases from referral centers demonstrated ongoing endemic transmission, with disease now considered a regional mycosis of Brazil’s Northeast rather than sporadic imported infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of agriculture and hunting into semi‑arid caatinga ecosystems; disturbance of armadillo burrows and dry soils during hunting and farming; limited clinical awareness leading to delayed but eventually concentrated recognition at reference centers. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of Coccidioides posadasii within Brazil’s semi‑arid interior, supported by molecular identification of the fungus in soil and clinical samples; no specific resistant or more virulent strain has been implicated, but establishment of new environmental foci in the Northeast represents spread into a previously unrecognized subregion.
Review: review – The episode correctly summarizes emergence of a new endemic focus of coccidioidomycosis in Brazil’s Northeast, supported by clinical, outbreak, and environmental data, and clearly merits inclusion as a major intra-continental emergence event. However, the original countries field mixed Brazilian states with pre-1990 date ranges that conflicted with the 1991–2007 event window; this has been simplified to list the affected Northeast states without internal dates, and re_emergence has been reset to false because this represents spread into a new South American subregion rather than reappearance in a previously affected one driven by documented pathogen change.

Countries: United States of America (Ventura County, California)
Host: Humans (general community in Ventura County)
Event summary: In January 1994, the Northridge (Mw 6.7) earthquake in southern California triggered landslides and large dust clouds in Ventura County, dispersing Coccidioides‑contaminated soil. In the weeks following the earthquake, approximately 200 acute coccidioidomycosis cases, including several deaths, were identified in Ventura County, far exceeding baseline incidence. Case numbers declined over subsequent months as dust settled and exposure conditions normalized, with no evidence of persistent new endemicity in this coastal area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major geophysical disturbance (earthquake) causing landslides and massive dust generation; intense short‑term community exposure to airborne soil; lack of awareness and respiratory protection among residents. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a new strain; the event was driven by environmental disturbance rather than pathogen change.
Review: retain – This row accurately represents the well-documented post‑Northridge earthquake outbreak in Ventura County (≈203 cases, 3 deaths), with correct geography, timing, and framing as a short-term re-occurrence driven by an environmental disaster rather than new endemicity; sources are appropriate CDC and USGS reports, so no structural changes are needed.

Countries: United States of America (Arizona, California, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah)
Host: Humans (general population in endemic U.S. states)
Event summary: Beginning in 1998, surveillance data from the United States showed a sustained and marked rise in reported coccidioidomycosis incidence in five traditionally endemic states. Incidence in these areas increased about sevenfold, from 5.3 per 100,000 in 1998 to 42.6 per 100,000 in 2011, corresponding to tens of thousands of cases annually and more than 100,000 reported cases overall. After 2011, incidence fluctuated but remained substantially above pre‑1998 levels, indicating a long-term elevation in burden rather than a brief spike.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic variability (periods of drought followed by rain affecting soil fungal growth and dust generation), rapid population growth and urban expansion into arid endemic zones, increased outdoor occupational and recreational exposures, and changes in surveillance such as mandatory laboratory reporting in California and national notifiability. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype has been linked to this rise; increased transmission and recognition are attributed mainly to environmental, demographic, and surveillance changes rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This event correctly synthesizes the large, well-characterized increase in reported coccidioidomycosis incidence across the core endemic U.S. states from 1998–2011, including the sevenfold rise from 5.3 to 42.6 cases per 100,000 in CDC analyses, and appropriately labels it as re-occurrence driven by climate, population growth, and surveillance changes without evidence for a new strain.

Countries: United States of America (California – Pleasant Valley State Prison [Coalinga], Avenal State Prison [Avenal])
Host: Humans (incarcerated adults and prison staff)
Event summary: Around 2005, extremely high rates of coccidioidomycosis were documented among inmates at Pleasant Valley State Prison and Avenal State Prison on the western side of California’s San Joaquin Valley, an area of intense endemicity. In 2005 these two institutions reported roughly 180 new cases, and in 2006 more than 600 additional cases were recorded, with incidence estimates at Pleasant Valley reaching several thousand per 100,000 inmates and multiple deaths. Following recognition of the outbreak, California authorities implemented measures such as restricting high‑risk inmates from hyperendemic prisons, dust control, and enhanced surveillance, which over subsequent years reduced but did not eliminate coccidioidomycosis risk in these facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incarceration of large numbers of medically vulnerable individuals in a hyperendemic, dusty environment; extensive soil disturbance from prison construction and surrounding agriculture; limited ability of inmates to avoid outdoor dust exposure; and lack of prior immunity among many transferees. Internal mechanisms: No specific resistant or hypervirulent strain identified; disease burden was driven by very high exposure intensity and a susceptible host population in an endemic setting.
Review: review – The outbreak among inmates at Pleasant Valley and Avenal prisons is correctly characterized as a major, localized re-occurrence in a hyperendemic area, with case counts and severity consistent with CDC and prison-focused investigations, and is clearly among the larger modern point-source outbreaks. The original source list relied heavily on Wikipedia; this has been strengthened by adding primary CDC/EID and PubMed reports documenting incidence, attack rates, and control measures, while retaining one Wikipedia link only as supplemental facility background.

Countries: United States of America (Washington State – Benton, Franklin, Yakima, and Spokane counties)
Host: Humans (local residents and outdoor workers)
Event summary: Around 2010, Washington State identified its first suspected locally acquired human cases of coccidioidomycosis in residents with no travel to known endemic areas. Subsequent investigations between 2010 and 2015 detected multiple autochthonous cases in eastern Washington and confirmed Coccidioides immitis in soil samples at exposure sites, with whole‑genome sequencing linking environmental and clinical isolates. After these detections, Washington instituted enhanced surveillance, and reported case counts slowly increased, indicating persistent but relatively low‑level endemic transmission in this newly recognized northern focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Possible climate warming and altered precipitation patterns enabling survival of Coccidioides further north; land disturbance from construction, agriculture, and recreational vehicle use in arid canyons; and increased clinical awareness once initial cases were recognized. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of Coccidioides immitis beyond its historic range in the southwestern United States; genomic analyses show Washington isolates nested within Californian lineages, consistent with relatively recent colonization rather than a long‑standing cryptic focus, but without evidence of a distinctive, more virulent clone.
Review: review – This row appropriately captures the first recognized autochthonous human infections and environmental isolations of Coccidioides in Washington State, a key northward range expansion, and justifies classification as intra-continental emergence. Re_emergence has been set to false, since this represents colonization of a new area within Northern America rather than reappearance in a previously affected subregion due to pathogen change; a Washington State Department of Health guideline has also been added as a primary source for timing and case counts.

Countries: United States of America (Arizona; California; Nevada; New Mexico; Utah; additional reporting states)
Host: Humans (general U.S. population, especially residents of western states)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2017, U.S. national surveillance recorded 95,371 reported coccidioidomycosis cases from 26 states and the District of Columbia, with Arizona and California accounting for the majority. During this interval, several states outside the traditional core endemic zones became reportable for coccidioidomycosis, and sporadic locally acquired cases were increasingly recognized in additional western areas. Although annual incidence fluctuated, the period represented a sustained high national burden of coccidioidomycosis compared with prior decades, rather than isolated outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued population growth and aging in endemic areas; widespread use of immunosuppressive therapies and increased numbers of transplant recipients; expansion of surveillance and mandatory laboratory reporting in selected states; and suspected effects of climate variability on dust exposure and fungal ecology. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain driving this nationwide burden has been identified; the pattern reflects re‑occurrence due to external, host-population, and surveillance factors rather than clear pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – The national 2011–2017 episode accurately reflects CDC surveillance data (95,371 reported cases across 26 states and DC) and highlights a prolonged period of elevated burden that is epidemiologically distinct from earlier decades; classification as re-occurrence driven by demographics, immunosuppression, climate, and surveillance expansion is appropriate and well sourced.

Countries: Brazil (national, with concentration in Northeast semi‑arid states – Piauí, Maranhão, Ceará, Bahia, Pernambuco)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with pulmonary and disseminated coccidioidomycosis)
Event summary: In 2016, Brazil’s national health data were analyzed to estimate the burden of coccidioidomycosis, identifying approximately 829 hospitalizations attributed to the disease, the highest number formally documented for any South American country to date. These hospitalizations reflected both recognized endemic transmission in the semi‑arid Northeast and cases from other regions, highlighting that coccidioidomycosis had become a significant but under‑appreciated cause of severe mycosis in Brazil. Following this analysis, Brazilian researchers and clinicians intensified efforts to characterize the epidemiology of coccidioidomycosis, leading to additional case series and ecological studies, but the true national burden likely remains underestimated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Improved recognition and coding of coccidioidomycosis in hospital information systems; concentration of susceptible rural workers in semi‑arid endemic zones; structural underdiagnosis in outpatient settings leading to hospitalization capture of more severe disease; and overall lack of mandatory notification. Internal mechanisms: No specific evidence of a new genotype; the apparent burden primarily reflects long‑standing endemic transmission that is being more completely documented rather than novel pathogen traits.
Review: review – The 829 coccidioidomycosis hospitalizations identified in Brazil in 2016 are well supported by national data syntheses and underscore a substantial, previously underappreciated South American disease burden, so the event is plausibly among the more impactful recent episodes for this pathogen. However, this row chiefly reflects retrospective quantification of severe cases across an already endemic country rather than a clearly bounded new outbreak or range expansion; it is therefore retained as a high-burden re-occurrence but flagged for potential future consolidation with the broader Northeast Brazil endemicity episode or reframing as a surveillance milestone.

Countries: United States of America (California – especially southern and Central Valley counties)
Host: Humans (California residents, with high incidence in southern Central Valley and southern coastal counties)
Event summary: In 2016 and 2017, California experienced a pronounced resurgence of reported coccidioidomycosis, with statewide case counts more than doubling compared with 2014–2015 and reaching historically high levels in several counties of the southern Central Valley and central coast. The increase manifested as a sharp rise in community‑acquired pneumonia due to Coccidioides, overwhelming some local public health resources and prompting statewide alerts to clinicians. After 2017, annual incidence in California declined somewhat but remained elevated compared with the early 2000s, indicating a re‑occurring pattern tied to environmental and demographic conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusual weather patterns in preceding years (severe drought followed by wet winters that may have promoted fungal growth and subsequent dusty seasons); expansion of residential and occupational activities in highly endemic areas; and improved laboratory reporting and clinician awareness. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a new, more virulent or resistant strain; the surge appears driven largely by environmental and surveillance factors superimposed on established endemicity.
Review: retain – This row accurately summarizes the documented resurgence of coccidioidomycosis in California in 2016–2017, including record or near-record incidence in southern Central Valley and coastal counties, and it is well aligned with CDC and CDPH analyses; treating it as a major re-occurrence driven by drought–rain cycles, exposure, and reporting changes is appropriate.

Countries: United States of America (Arizona – particularly Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties)
Host: Humans (Arizona residents, especially in major metropolitan and surrounding desert counties)
Event summary: Following several years of fluctuating incidence, Arizona experienced a substantial increase in reported coccidioidomycosis during 2017–2018, with case counts climbing notably above prior years in key counties such as Maricopa and Pima. The surge coincided with heightened clinician testing for Valley fever among patients with community‑acquired pneumonia and with meteorologic conditions favorable for dust generation. Subsequent years showed variable but generally high levels of disease, suggesting that the 2017–2018 period marked a significant re‑occurrence of coccidioidomycosis in Arizona’s already hyperendemic environment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions influencing soil moisture and dust storms in central and southern Arizona; urban sprawl and construction in desert fringes; and increased provider awareness and testing. Internal mechanisms: No definitive evidence of new virulence or resistance traits; the pattern is most consistent with environmentally driven re‑occurrence superimposed on a long‑standing endemic focus.
Review: retain – This event reflects the well-described 2017–2018 increase in Arizona coccidioidomycosis cases, including a >50% rise in reported cases during October 2017–March 2018 in Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties, and justifiably classifies it as a major re-occurrence driven by climate, land use, and testing practices rather than pathogen evolution.

Countries: Kenya [1990, western highlands including Kericho; major El Niño‑associated epidemics 1997–1998]; Uganda [early 1990s highland epidemics]; Ethiopia [mid‑1990s highland epidemics]; Rwanda [early 1990s highland epidemics]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990s highland epidemics]
Host: Humans (primarily Plasmodium falciparum in previously low‑transmission highland and semi‑arid populations)
Event summary: During the 1990s, highland and semi‑arid districts in Eastern Africa, especially the western Kenya highlands, experienced recurrent malaria epidemics after decades of low transmission, with hospital data from Kericho tea estates showing nearly annual outbreaks from 1990 to 1997, attack rates around 50% and substantial malaria‑attributable mortality. These epidemics intensified in the mid‑ to late‑1990s and peaked during the 1997–1998 El Niño event, when unusually heavy rains and flooding in previously marginal areas such as Wajir in north‑eastern Kenya triggered explosive outbreaks that affected tens of thousands of largely non‑immune people. National malaria programmes and partners responded with emergency indoor residual spraying, strengthened epidemic detection and early‑warning systems, and expanded access to effective treatment, and by the early 2000s malaria incidence and epidemic frequency in many highland settings had declined again.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climate variability (including El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole–related warm, wet anomalies), land‑use change (deforestation, swamp cultivation and agricultural expansion), rapid population growth and migration between lowland endemic zones and highland settlements, antimalarial drug resistance (notably to chloroquine and later sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine), and weakening of vector‑control and health‑care systems all increased epidemic risk. Internal mechanisms: No single novel parasite genotype was identified as causal; these epidemics largely reflect geographic range re‑occupation and amplification of existing Plasmodium falciparum lineages in populations with low immunity and failing first‑line drugs, so they are best coded as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: review – new high-impact resurgence episode added. Justification: 1990s highland and semi‑arid epidemics in Eastern Africa produced very large attack rates and substantial mortality in previously low‑transmission areas and are widely cited as a key example of climate‑ and drug‑resistance‑driven malaria re‑occurrence. Classified as re-occurrence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because Plasmodium falciparum was long established in Africa and no single novel genotype was identified; drivers are climate variability, land-use change, drug resistance and weakened control programmes. Country list and years are approximate and based on multi-country syntheses; should be checked by a human reviewer.

Host: Humans (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: After malaria had been reduced to only a few hundred cases a year in Tajikistan by 1990, civil war, economic collapse and the cessation of vector control led to a rapid resurgence of Plasmodium vivax and re‑establishment of local Plasmodium falciparum transmission from 1991 onward, especially in southern districts bordering Afghanistan. Official notifications rose from hundreds of cases in the early 1990s to 2,411 cases in 1994 and 29,794 cases in 1997, with contemporaneous estimates suggesting 200,000–500,000 infections that year as returning refugees and cross‑border movements seeded transmission into vulnerable communities. Beginning in 1998, intensive national and international control efforts—including renewed indoor residual spraying, mass radical treatment with primaquine, and establishment of specialized anti‑malaria centres—rapidly reduced incidence, halving reported cases by 1999 and setting the country on a trajectory that ultimately led to elimination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Armed conflict and population displacement, breakdown of health‑care and surveillance systems, suspension of mosquito‑control operations because of financial and logistical constraints, shortages of trained public‑health staff, and expansion of irrigated agriculture in arid southern valleys (creating Anopheles breeding sites) created ideal conditions for malaria resurgence once parasites were reintroduced from Afghanistan. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not implicate new parasite genotypes or antimalarial drug resistance as the primary cause; this episode is best characterized as a large‑scale re-occurrence of P. vivax and P. falciparum malaria in an area where transmission had previously been nearly eliminated.
Review: review – new large resurgence episode added. Justification: Malaria control collapse during Tajikistan’s civil war led to one of the largest documented post-elimination resurgences, with 29,794 officially reported cases and estimated 200,000–500,000 infections in 1997. Classified as re-occurrence in Central Asia (no evidence that parasite evolution or new drug resistance was the primary driver). Start and end years (1991–1999) chosen to bracket the period of sharp increase and subsequent decline; recommend expert review of exact temporal bounds and whether to split early vs peak years into separate rows.

Host: Humans (zoonotic Plasmodium knowlesi infections from macaque reservoirs via Anopheles mosquitoes)
Event summary: Between roughly 1998 and 2002, investigators in Kapit Division, Sarawak (Malaysian Borneo) documented a large cluster of human malaria cases initially diagnosed as Plasmodium malariae but subsequently confirmed by PCR, in 2004, to be Plasmodium knowlesi, revealing frequent naturally acquired zoonotic infections in humans in this forested region. This discovery showed that what had been considered rare simian malaria spillover was in fact a substantial and ongoing transmission cycle involving macaque reservoirs and Anopheles leucosphyrus‑group vectors, and subsequent surveillance identified many additional human P. knowlesi cases in other parts of Malaysian Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia. Control efforts have therefore focused on improving molecular species diagnosis, clinical management of knowlesi malaria and targeted vector control near forest–fringe communities, but because of the persistent macaque reservoir, human P. knowlesi infections have continued to occur rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deforestation, agricultural expansion, road building and human settlement in interior Sarawak increased human exposure to forest‑dwelling macaques and competent Anopheles vectors, while the introduction of species‑specific PCR assays allowed accurate differentiation of P. knowlesi from morphologically similar P. malariae that had previously masked its true incidence. Internal mechanisms: The event primarily reflects recognition and amplification of an existing zoonotic transmission cycle, rather than emergence of a clearly novel parasite genotype; it is therefore best treated as a re-occurrence driven by ecological change and improved detection, with host expansion (spillover into humans) occurring at clinically important incidence but likely predating the 1990s.
Review: review – retain event but reclassified and re-dated. Changes made: (1) Event years adjusted from 2000–2004 to 1998–2002 to align with the surveillance period underlying the 2004 Lancet description of the Kapit Division focus. (2) 'First detection' set to No because Plasmodium spp. were detected in humans long before 1990 and a naturally acquired human P. knowlesi infection was documented in 1965; this episode is the first recognition of a large zoonotic focus, not the first global detection. (3) Event type changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence, reflecting that current evidence points to ecological change and improved diagnostics rather than a clearly novel parasite genotype; host expansion is recognized but may have pre-dated the 1990s. Geography (Malaysia, South-eastern Asia) and sources are appropriate.

Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2007]; Brazil [spillover of imported and limited local transmission near border, mid-2010s]; Colombia [spillover, mid-2010s]; Guyana [2010s, increased imported cases linked to Venezuela]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2017, Venezuela experienced an explosive resurgence of malaria, with national cases rising nearly tenfold from around 41,700 to over 411,000 annually, largely concentrated in Bolívar state’s mining zones. The surge produced the largest malaria hotspot in Latin America, spilling over to neighbouring countries through mobile mine workers and displaced populations and contributing to more than half of all reported malaria cases in the Americas by 2017–2018, while imported cases from Venezuela became a dominant source of malaria in border areas of Brazil, Colombia and Guyana. Control efforts have since focused on emergency case management, vector control in mining and border regions, and regional containment plans, but high transmission has persisted and continues to strain regional elimination goals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe deterioration of Venezuela’s health system, shortages of antimalarials and diagnostics, reduced vector-control activities, rapid expansion of informal and illegal gold mining in forested areas that create vector-breeding habitats, and large-scale internal and cross-border human migration all contributed to the resurgence and cross-border spread. Internal mechanisms: No clearly dominant novel drug-resistant genotype has been identified as the primary driver; this episode is best described as a major re-occurrence due to socio-economic collapse and environmental change amplifying existing P. vivax and P. falciparum transmission.
Review: review – retain but adjust event type. Change made: 'Intra-continental emergence' set to No, leaving 're-occurrence' as Yes, because this is a massive resurgence of P. vivax and P. falciparum within an existing South America subregion rather than first establishment in a new subregion; this follows the rule that resurgence driven by health-system collapse and mining should be coded as re-occurrence, not intra-continental emergence. Summary and country list (Venezuela with spillover to Brazil, Colombia and Guyana) and impact metrics (≈10-fold increase from ~41,700 cases in 2007 to >400,000 in 2017 and majority of regional burden) are well supported by PAHO and PLOS sources.

Countries: Cambodia [2008]; Thailand [2008]; Viet Nam [2010]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2011]; Myanmar [2011]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: From about 2008 onward, delayed parasite clearance to artemisinin-based therapies and Pfkelch13 mutations were first documented in western Cambodia and along the Cambodia–Thailand border, indicating emergence of artemisinin-resistant Plasmodium falciparum. Over the following years, molecular surveillance showed spread and clonal expansion of resistant lineages into Thailand, southern Lao PDR, Viet Nam, and Myanmar across the Greater Mekong Subregion, undermining the efficacy of several artemisinin combination therapies in affected areas. In response, countries and partners implemented artemisinin-resistance containment projects, changes in first-line treatments, intensified vector control, and aggressive elimination strategies aimed at reducing the reservoir of resistant parasites.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use and sometimes misuse of artemisinin monotherapies and suboptimal combination regimens in Southeast Asia exerted intense drug selection pressure; high transmission pockets, cross-border population movement, and historically weak regulation of antimalarials in border regions facilitated spread of resistant parasites. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via multiple independent and then clonally expanding Pfkelch13 mutations (e.g., C580Y, Y493H) conferring partial artemisinin resistance, followed by acquisition of partner-drug resistance (e.g., plasmepsin2/3 amplification and pfcrt variants mediating piperaquine resistance), created multidrug-resistant lineages that significantly reduced ACT efficacy.
Review: review – retain as one of the most important evolutionary events but correct classification and subregion. Changes made: (1) Sub-regions narrowed from 'South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia' to 'South-eastern Asia' because all listed countries (Cambodia, Thailand, Viet Nam, Lao PDR, Myanmar) fall within that UNSD subregion. (2) 'Intra-continental emergence' set to No, leaving 're-emergence' as Yes, since this episode reflects emergence and clonal expansion of artemisinin- and partner-drug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum within an already endemic subregion, consistent with the instruction not to label new drug-resistant strains as intra-continental emergence. Event summary, host, and country list remain accurate for the 2008–2015 Greater Mekong resistance wave.
