Host: Humans (mainly Plasmodium vivax)
Event summary: After Greece was certified malaria-free in the mid-20th century, clusters of locally acquired Plasmodium vivax cases reappeared beginning in 2009 in agricultural and wetland areas such as Evrotas (Laconia, Peloponnese), followed by further foci and sporadic autochthonous infections through 2013. Transmission persisted over multiple seasons with more than 60 locally acquired cases documented and additional introduced cases among migrant workers, indicating re-establishment of limited P. vivax transmission in receptive areas. Intensified vector control, active case detection, and targeted chemoprophylaxis campaigns eventually interrupted these local chains of transmission, and no large sustained foci have been reported afterwards, although occasional introduced or sporadic local cases continue to be detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of P. vivax by migrant agricultural workers from endemic countries, combined with receptive ecological conditions (wetlands, irrigated agriculture, presence of competent Anopheles vectors) and reduced vigilance in a country considered malaria-free; economic austerity may have further constrained public-health capacity. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for markedly novel parasite genotypes or drug resistance driving this event; it is best characterized as geographic range re-occupation driven by human movement and ecology rather than parasite evolutionary change.
Review: retain – event appropriately describes the re-occurrence of locally acquired P. vivax malaria in Greece after mid-20th-century elimination and is among the most salient post-1990 European malaria events. Geography (Southern Europe; Greece), timing (2009–2013), and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) are consistent with WHO/ECDC reports. No data corrections required; minor case-count uncertainties (exact total of locally acquired vs introduced cases) are within the acceptable range for this level of aggregation.

Countries: Myanmar [2013, western and northern border regions with India and Bangladesh]; India [2014, West Bengal and northeastern states with emerging Pfkelch13 polymorphisms such as G625R, A675V and others associated with delayed parasite clearance]; Bangladesh [2018, K13-independent artemisinin resistance documented in Chittagong Hill Tracts bordering Myanmar]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum with emerging artemisinin-partial resistance signatures along the Greater Mekong–South Asia interface)
Event summary: During the 2010s, artemisinin-resistant Plasmodium falciparum that had first become established in the eastern Greater Mekong Subregion spread across Myanmar into its western and northern border regions abutting India, Bangladesh and China, with multiple Pfkelch13 mutant lineages documented there by 2013–2014. Subsequent therapeutic-efficacy and genetic studies identified candidate or confirmed resistance-associated kelch13 polymorphisms (such as G625R, A675V and others) and slowed parasite clearance in parts of eastern India and the northeastern states bordering Myanmar, as well as K13-independent artemisinin resistance in Bangladesh’s Chittagong Hill Tracts, raising concern that the historical east‑to‑west spread of antimalarial resistance could repeat. National malaria programmes and WHO responded with intensified molecular surveillance, cross-border coordination, and efforts to accelerate P. falciparum elimination in the eastern Greater Mekong to prevent fully resistant lineages from becoming entrenched in the high‑burden Indian subcontinent.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human mobility across porous international borders, continued use of artemisinin-based therapies with variable quality and adherence, and the long-recognized pattern of antimalarial resistance originating in the Greater Mekong and spreading westward toward the Indian subcontinent. Internal mechanisms: Westward geographic expansion and diversification of Pfkelch13 mutant parasite lineages originally arising in the Greater Mekong (including C580Y, F446I and regional variants such as G625R and A675V), along with K13-independent mechanisms that reduce artemisinin susceptibility in Bangladesh, represent a re-emergence of multidrug-resistance dynamics at the GMS–South Asia frontier rather than first presence of Plasmodium falciparum in these areas.
Review: review – retain as a distinct phase of the artemisinin-resistance crisis but correct geography and emphasis. Changes made: (1) Sub-regions expanded to 'South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia' and countries redefined to focus on Myanmar (western/northern border areas), India (West Bengal and northeastern states) and Bangladesh (Chittagong Hill Tracts), where kelch13 polymorphisms or K13-independent artemisinin resistance have been documented, rather than implying well-established resistance across all of South Asia by 2012–2014. (2) 'Intra-continental emergence' set to No to comply with guidance that new drug-resistant strains should be coded as re-emergence, not intra-continental emergence; 're-emergence' remains Yes. (3) Time window adjusted to 2013–2019 to better match available molecular and therapeutic-efficacy data. Because evidence for clinically significant resistance outside the Greater Mekong during this period is heterogeneous and evolving, this row should be reviewed by a malaria drug-resistance specialist.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Rwanda [2012, molecular detection of Pfkelch13 R561H and P574L]; Rwanda [2018–2019, therapeutic efficacy studies and in vitro confirmation of artemisinin partial resistance]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: From 2012 to 2015, molecular surveillance in Rwanda detected Pfkelch13 R561H and P574L mutations in Plasmodium falciparum, suggesting local emergence of genotypes analogous to Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistance markers; by 2018–2019, therapeutic efficacy studies linked R561H to delayed parasite clearance and ring-stage survival assays confirmed reduced susceptibility to dihydroartemisinin in isolates from southern Rwanda. The prevalence and geographic distribution of R561H increased over time, indicating clonal expansion and establishment of partial artemisinin resistance within Rwanda’s parasite population, although artemether-lumefantrine remained clinically efficacious in most sites. National control programs responded by intensifying therapeutic-efficacy monitoring, updating treatment guidelines as needed, and strengthening vector control and surveillance to track further spread of resistance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High ACT drug pressure in a setting of intense transmission, possible reductions in population immunity following earlier control successes, and limited capacity to rapidly change first-line regimens or fully enforce rational drug use created conditions favouring selection of resistant parasites. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of Pfkelch13 R561H and related alleles in African parasite populations, conferring partial artemisinin resistance as shown by delayed clearance and in vitro survival assays; genetic analyses support independent evolution in Rwanda rather than simple importation from Southeast Asia.
Review: retain – event accurately summarizes the independent emergence and spread of Pfkelch13 R561H (and related mutations) in Rwanda and is a key African evolutionary milestone. Dates (first detection in 2012–2015, clinical association and in vitro confirmation by 2018–2019), geography (Eastern Africa; Rwanda), and classification as re-emergence only (new genotype in an endemic pathogen) match the cited clinical, genetic, and in vitro evidence. No structural corrections were necessary, though precise end year (2020) is somewhat arbitrary and reflects the period over which data are available.

Countries: Uganda [2016, first detection of kelch13 mutations such as C469Y and A675V in northern Uganda]; Uganda [2020–2022, expansion of artemisinin-partial resistance and reduced lumefantrine susceptibility across northern and south‑western districts]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: Beginning around 2016, surveillance in Uganda detected multiple Pfkelch13 mutations (including C469Y, A675V, R561H and others) associated with delayed parasite clearance, with some—particularly C469Y and A675V—increasing in frequency through 2020–2022 in northern and south‑western districts. Laboratory studies confirmed reduced in vitro susceptibility of C469Y and related mutants to artemisinin derivatives, and ex vivo data showed decreased susceptibility to lumefantrine in parasites from northern Uganda by 2021, indicating that partner-drug tolerance was also emerging. These findings demonstrate indigenous emergence and clonal expansion of partially artemisinin-resistant and partner-drug-tolerant P. falciparum lineages in East Africa, prompting calls for intensified resistance monitoring and potential future treatment policy adjustments, even though current first-line ACTs still retain good efficacy in most settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Wide-scale ACT deployment with limited therapeutic-efficacy monitoring, high malaria transmission intensity, heterogeneous access to treatment and occasional sub-therapeutic drug exposures together created strong selection pressure for resistance. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and rapid selection of multiple Pfkelch13 mutant alleles (C469Y, A675V and others) conferring partial artemisinin resistance, coupled in some foci with reduced partner-drug susceptibility (e.g., lumefantrine), representing a major re-emergence of multidrug resistance dynamics within African parasite populations.
Review: retain – event is well supported by genomic and phenotypic studies documenting independent emergence and rapid expansion of multiple kelch13 mutations (especially C469Y and A675V) and reduced lumefantrine susceptibility in Uganda. Classification as re-emergence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate since the episode reflects new resistant genotypes in an endemic parasite. Timeline (from first detection around 2016 through documented spread by 2020–2022) and geography (Eastern Africa; Uganda) are consistent with current evidence. No corrections required beyond confirming that ACTs have remained largely efficacious to date.

Host: Humans (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum)
Event summary: Following unprecedented monsoon rains and flooding starting in June 2022, Pakistan experienced a dramatic surge in malaria, with WHO reporting more than 3.4 million suspected cases by August and subsequent estimates indicating roughly a five-fold increase in incidence and about 2–2.6 million additional malaria cases in 2022 compared with 2021. The outbreak was concentrated in heavily flooded provinces such as Sindh and Balochistan, where large displaced populations were exposed to extensive mosquito breeding sites in stagnant water and had limited access to health services. Emergency responses included mass distribution of rapid diagnostic tests and antimalarials, deployment of mobile clinics, and intensified vector control in camps and flood-affected communities, which gradually reduced, but did not fully eliminate, the elevated transmission risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme rainfall and large-scale flooding linked to climate variability and climate change, destruction of housing and health infrastructure, population displacement into temporary shelters with poor vector protection, and expansion of Anopheles breeding habitats in flooded areas all contributed to the surge. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel parasite genotype or drug-resistance trait has been identified as driving this increase; it represents a classic environmentally and socially driven re-occurrence of malaria in endemic areas.
Review: retain – event correctly highlights one of the largest recent environmentally driven malaria surges worldwide and a clear example of climate- and disaster-driven re-occurrence. WHO and World Malaria Report data confirm an approximately four- to five-fold increase in malaria incidence and roughly 2–2.6 million additional cases in 2022 compared with 2021 in Pakistan following catastrophic monsoon flooding. Classification as re-occurrence (with no intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) is appropriate; no corrections to timing, geography, or drivers were needed.

Host: Humans, predominantly adults with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and hematologic malignancies, including transplant and cancer patients in tertiary centers
Event summary: From the early 1990s through around 2010, India experienced a steady and marked rise in reported invasive mucormycosis cases, particularly among patients with poorly controlled diabetes and immunocompromising conditions. Multi-center case series and autopsy studies documented increasing incidence in tertiary care hospitals over this period, with mucormycosis transitioning from a rare curiosity to one of the most frequent invasive mold infections in some Indian centers. By the late 2000s and early 2010s, India’s estimated mucormycosis incidence had risen to many times higher than that of most developed countries, setting the stage for later explosive outbreaks during the COVID-19 era.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization, high and growing prevalence of poorly controlled diabetes, expanded use of corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapies, and improved mycological diagnostic capacity contributed both to true increases in incidence and to better recognition; environmental exposure to thermotolerant Mucorales in tropical/subtropical climates may further elevate baseline risk. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was identified as the primary cause of this long-term increase; rather, existing Mucorales species (notably Rhizopus arrhizus and Apophysomyces spp.) expanded their clinical impact in susceptible human hosts as underlying risk factors became more common.
Review: Retain – This row appropriately summarizes the well-documented long-term increase in mucormycosis incidence in India from the 1990s through about 2010 using large tertiary-centre series and burden estimates; geography and timeframe are reasonable, classification as re-occurrence (driven by rising diabetes, steroid and immunosuppressive use, and improved diagnostics) is consistent with definitions, and the sources are suitable. No substantive corrections are required.

Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2004]
Host: Adults and pediatric patients with hematological malignancies and bone marrow transplantation in a hematology–oncology unit
Event summary: In the mid-2000s, a hematology–oncology and bone marrow transplant unit at Queen Mary Hospital in Hong Kong identified a 6‑month outbreak of intestinal infection and colonization by Rhizopus microsporus in 12 patients receiving chemotherapy or transplant care. Intensified surveillance and a case–control study linked disease to ingestion of heavily contaminated oral allopurinol tablets and, to a lesser extent, certain prepackaged ready-to-eat foods, with isolates from patients, tablets, food and cornstarch excipient sharing closely related ITS genotypes. After switching to an alternative allopurinol manufacturer, enforcing boiled-food diets for high-risk patients, and confirming clearance of contamination, no further R. microsporus intestinal cases were detected during several months of follow-up.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of an oral allopurinol formulation and some ready-to-eat foods with high burdens of thermotolerant R. microsporus spores, combined with intense mucosal damage, neutropenia and immunosuppression in hematologic malignancy and transplant patients, enabled intestinal colonization and invasion. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain biology beyond the thermotolerance and digestive-tract survival typical of R. microsporus was identified; this episode represents point-source amplification and exposure rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added because this 12‑patient intestinal Rhizopus microsporus outbreak in a Hong Kong hematology/BMT unit is one of the largest single-hospital mucormycosis clusters described and illustrates high-impact, medication/food-borne transmission in immunocompromised hosts. Event is correctly classified as a healthcare-associated re-occurrence; the calendar years are approximated as 2004–2005 based on surveillance periods in the original report and should be checked against primary data in any downstream curation.

Host: Immunocompromised pediatric inpatients, mainly oncology and transplant patients, in a tertiary children’s hospital
Event summary: Between August 2008 and July 2009, a U.S. tertiary pediatric hospital observed five cases of fatal cutaneous or wound mucormycosis in oncology and other immunocompromised children, far exceeding background incidence. A CDC-led investigation showed that all five infections were hospital-associated and epidemiologically linked to exposure to ostensibly clean linens contaminated with Rhizopus species, with roughly 40% of environmental samples from freshly laundered linens, delivery carts and storage areas yielding Mucorales. After changing the external laundry vendor, modifying linen handling and storage practices, and implementing targeted use of sterile linens for highest-risk patients, no further outbreak-related mucormycosis cases were identified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavily contaminated reusable linens from an off-site laundry, inadequate protection of clean linen during transport and storage, and a high-risk pediatric oncology and transplant population created repeated high-dose environmental exposure. Internal mechanisms: Infections were due to typical Rhizopus species without evidence of novel virulence traits or host expansion; the outbreak reflects high inoculum and host susceptibility rather than evolutionary change in the fungus.
Review: Retain – New row capturing the 2008–2009 U.S. pediatric hospital linen-associated outbreak (five hospital-associated cases, all fatal), which is among the most consequential healthcare-associated mucormycosis clusters documented before the Arkansas event. Geography, timeframe, case numbers and linen-related mechanisms are well supported by the primary Clin Infect Dis report and follow-on remediation study; classification as re-occurrence is appropriate.

Host: Severely injured U.S. and coalition military personnel with blast-related traumatic wounds, often with lower-extremity amputations and extensive soft-tissue damage
Event summary: From June 2009 through August 2011, during combat operations in southern Afghanistan, 77 U.S. military casualties met a case definition for invasive fungal wound infection, with fungi from the order Mucorales isolated from roughly 40% of culture-positive wounds. Cases clustered among soldiers with dismounted blast injuries, large contaminated wounds and delayed wound closure, and were associated with higher amputation revision rates, longer times to wound closure and substantial mortality compared with similar trauma patients without mold infection. Development of a trauma-specific invasive fungal infection classification scheme, aggressive serial debridement protocols and early dual antifungal therapy, together with changes in battlefield evacuation and resuscitation practices, were followed by a decline in new IFI cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-energy improvised explosive device blasts causing massive soft-tissue injury, soil and organic debris heavily contaminating wounds, large transfusion requirements, and delayed definitive wound closure created ideal conditions for invasive mold infection; intensive care settings and prolonged broad-spectrum antibacterial exposure further increased risk. Internal mechanisms: Diverse Mucorales (notably Saksenaea spp. and other genera) were recovered without a single dominant outbreak clone; the event represents amplification of environmental molds in a unique trauma setting rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: Retain – Added to represent the large series of combat-related invasive fungal wound infections in Afghanistan (77 IFI patients between 2009 and 2011, with Mucorales recovered from about 40% of culture-positive wounds), which is a major modern trauma-associated mucormycosis episode. The event is correctly treated as a trauma-driven re-occurrence in Southern Asia rather than first emergence or inter-continental spread; users should note that reported case counts refer to all IFIs, with only a subset proven to be due to Mucorales.

Host: Civilians with severe traumatic injuries sustained during the 22 May 2011 EF5 tornado in Joplin, Missouri
Event summary: Following the 22 May 2011 EF5 tornado in Joplin, Missouri, clinicians identified a cluster of necrotizing soft-tissue infections among severely injured survivors, and 13 patients ultimately met a definition for tornado-associated cutaneous mucormycosis. Most patients had multiple deep lacerations and penetrating injuries contaminated with soil and debris; ten required intensive-care admission, and five died despite aggressive surgical debridement and amphotericin B–based therapy. After heightened clinical awareness, prompt debridement of contaminated wounds and targeted antifungal treatment were implemented, no further tornado-associated mucormycosis cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: An extremely violent tornado that lofted and injected soil and vegetative debris into traumatic wounds, creating massive, highly contaminated soft-tissue injuries, prolonged field exposure and delayed definitive surgical care, together with broad-spectrum antibiotic use, enabled mucormycete establishment. Internal mechanisms: Cases were caused predominantly by Apophysomyces trapeziformis, an environmental Mucorales fungus; no new genotype was implicated, and disease severity was driven by inoculum and host/wound factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – This 13‑case, 5‑death cluster of tornado-associated cutaneous mucormycosis in Joplin, Missouri, is a landmark natural-disaster–related mucormycosis event with strong primary documentation and clearly defined environmental drivers. It is appropriately represented as a major re-occurrence in Northern America rather than an inter-continental emergence episode.

Host: Adults with major burns in the University Hospital of Lille burn center
Event summary: Between approximately 2013 and 2016, the burn unit at the University Hospital of Lille, France, documented multiple cases of cutaneous mucormycosis, mainly due to Lichtheimia species, in severely burned patients. Two temporally distinct mini-outbreaks and individual cases prompted an investigation, which identified frequent contamination of unused, non-sterile crepe and elasticized bandages with Lichtheimia DNA and viable spores. After changes in bandage procurement, stricter wound-dressing protocols, and enhanced environmental monitoring, these clusters of burn-associated mucormycosis decreased and no further temporally linked outbreaks were reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Repeated use of non-sterile, fungi-contaminated bandages on large burn wounds and underlying severe tissue damage, often with concurrent broad-spectrum antibiotics and intensive care, provided favorable conditions for mucormycosis outbreaks; hospital supply-chain and sterilization gaps were central external drivers. Internal mechanisms: The isolates were typical Lichtheimia spp. adapted to high temperatures and necrotic tissue; no specific new genotype was required to explain the outbreak, which stemmed from point-source contamination and extreme host susceptibility.
Review: Retain – The seven-case Lichtheimia mucormycosis outbreak in the Lille burn unit (2013–2016) is clearly documented, correctly geolocated in France (Western Europe), and appropriately attributed to contaminated non-sterile bandages; classification as re-occurrence without inter-/intra-continental spread fits the definitions. It represents one of the major burn-unit mucormycosis episodes and should be retained.

Host: Severely burned adults cared for in the burn intensive care unit at Hôpital Saint-Louis in Paris and a related military burn unit in Clamart
Event summary: From late 2013 through early 2016, the burn intensive care unit at Hôpital Saint-Louis in Paris, with related cases in the nearby military burn unit at Hôpital d’Instruction des Armées Percy (Clamart), experienced an invasive wound mucormycosis outbreak due mainly to Mucor circinelloides f. circinelloides. Multiple patients developed deep wound infections within weeks of admission, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates showed numerous, largely patient-specific strains, consistent with repeated acquisition from a local environmental reservoir rather than single-strain transmission. After intensified infection-prevention measures, repeated environmental investigations, improved early molecular diagnosis, and changes in dressings and equipment handling, no additional linked cases were reported and incidence returned to baseline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive burn injuries requiring repeated debridement, high fungal exposure in the burn-unit environment, and likely contamination of dressings or equipment created conditions for repeated Mucorales inoculation; hospital infrastructure and infection-control gaps were central external drivers. Internal mechanisms: Isolates represented diverse environmental M. circinelloides strains with no clearly hypervirulent clone; the outbreak reflected environmental amplification and heavy exposure of highly susceptible burn patients rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – The original row mis-timed this outbreak (early 2010s) and vaguely described a single “military-affiliated” burn unit; the corrected version now reflects data from genomic and clinical studies showing an invasive wound mucormycosis outbreak spanning roughly 2013–2016 in the Saint-Louis Hospital burn ICU in Paris with related cases at the Percy military burn unit in Clamart. Classification as re-occurrence remains valid, but the updated dates and multi-centre nature of the event should be verified against national surveillance and burn-registry data; the row is recommended for retention with this clarification.

Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2015]
Host: Immunosuppressed adult inpatients (including oncology and transplant patients) at a tertiary hospital
Event summary: From 2 June to 18 July 2015, a tertiary hospital in Hong Kong SAR reported six immunosuppressed patients with pulmonary and/or cutaneous zygomycosis caused by Rhizopus microsporus, an unusually high number for such a short period. Epidemiologic investigation linked all cases to exposure to hospital linens supplied by a single substandard external laundry; cultures showed that roughly 28% of freshly laundered clothing and a smaller proportion of laundered linens were contaminated with R. microsporus. After the hospital suspended use of the implicated laundry, replaced linens, and tightened linen-processing and infection-control standards, no additional Rhizopus-related mucormycosis cases associated with that laundry source occurred and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of heavily contaminated hospital clothing and linen from a substandard commercial laundry, coupled with intensive care and immunosuppression, served as the main driver; excessive microbial loads on laundered fabrics far exceeded hygienic standards and enabled both inhalational and cutaneous exposure. Internal mechanisms: No new Mucorales genotype was identified; the outbreak was driven by high environmental inoculum and vulnerable hosts rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – The 2015 Hong Kong linen-associated Rhizopus microsporus outbreak (six cases in six weeks, all linked to linen from a single substandard laundry) is well described in primary and secondary sources; geography, timing and case numbers match published data, and classification as a healthcare-associated re-occurrence is appropriate. This row should be retained as a key example of contaminated-linen–driven mucormycosis.

Host: Hospitalized adults with hematologic malignancies, severe trauma, and other immunocompromising conditions at a large acute-care hospital in Arkansas
Event summary: Between June 2019 and May 2021, a large acute-care hospital in Arkansas, USA, experienced the largest reported single-center healthcare-associated mucormycosis outbreak in the country, with 16 confirmed cases of invasive disease among high-risk inpatients. Most affected patients had hematologic malignancies or recent major trauma, and several died, resulting in approximately 38% in-hospital mortality. A comprehensive investigation found Rhizopus spores on about 9% of newly arrived and in-hospital linens and identified multiple lapses in linen handling and storage; after the hospital changed laundry suppliers, reinforced linen-cart protection and cleaning, and addressed environmental mold sources, the cluster abated and no further outbreak-related cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contaminated healthcare linens from an external laundry, torn protective covers on linen carts, and suboptimal linen-handling practices created repeated exposure opportunities for highly immunocompromised patients; concurrent severe illness, intensive care, and frequent invasive procedures further increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved typical Mucorales species (mainly Rhizopus) without evidence of a novel hypervirulent genotype; high environmental burden and health-system factors, not pathogen evolution, underpinned this re-occurrence.
Review: Retain – The Arkansas acute-care hospital outbreak (16 healthcare-associated cases between June 2019 and May 2021) is currently the largest single-center mucormycosis outbreak reported in the United States; case numbers, timeframe, linen-related drivers and outcomes are well supported by the Open Forum Infectious Diseases report and associated CDC materials. Classification as a healthcare-associated re-occurrence is appropriate, and the row should be retained.

Host: Humans with recent or current COVID-19 infection, predominantly adults with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and recent corticosteroid therapy
Event summary: During the second wave of COVID-19 in 2020–2021, India experienced an unprecedented epidemic of COVID-19–associated mucormycosis (CAM), characterized by tens of thousands of cases of mainly rhino-orbital and rhino-cerebral disease in recently infected SARS-CoV-2 patients, most with uncontrolled diabetes and prior systemic steroid use. By June 28, 2021, official data from the Government of India reported about 40,845 mucormycosis cases and over 3,100 deaths nationwide, and mucormycosis was made a notifiable disease as case numbers surged in parallel with the Delta-variant COVID-19 wave. Following targeted clinical guidelines, improved control of steroid use, better diabetes management, and waning of the intense COVID-19 wave, the incidence of CAM declined from its peak, although India continues to bear a disproportionately high global burden of mucormycosis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptionally high community transmission of COVID-19, widespread and sometimes inappropriate use of systemic corticosteroids, high baseline prevalence of poorly controlled diabetes, possible hypoxic and iron-overload states in severe COVID-19, and healthcare system strain (including oxygen and ICU shortages) created a perfect storm for Mucorales infection; humid environments and high environmental spore loads further increased exposure. Internal mechanisms: No definitive novel Mucorales strain was proven to drive the epidemic—CAM appears to reflect a shift in host susceptibility and care practices rather than pathogen evolution—though some reports suggest changing species distributions (e.g., prominence of Rhizopus arrhizus and Apophysomyces spp.) under these conditions.
Review: Retain – India’s 2020–2021 COVID-19–associated mucormycosis epidemic (≈40,800 cases and >3,000 deaths reported nationally) is by far the largest mucormycosis event on record; dates, burden estimates and key drivers (COVID-19 surge, steroid overuse, uncontrolled diabetes, health-system strain) are well documented in WHO, NCDC and peer-reviewed sources. It is correctly classified as a massive re-occurrence rather than a first emergence event and is essential to retain in the dataset.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: United States of America [1990]; Canada [1990]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; France [1990]; Germany [1990]; other Western and Northern European countries with similar trends
Host: Humans (general adult population, people living with HIV, people experiencing homelessness, incarcerated persons)
Event summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, tuberculosis incidence, which had been declining for decades in North America and Western Europe, began to rise again, prompting renewed concern about TB control. Between about 1990 and 1993, increases in TB notifications were documented in the United States and several Western and Northern European countries, closely linked to the emerging HIV epidemic and weakening TB control programmes. In 1993, in response to this resurgence and rising global burden, WHO declared tuberculosis a global emergency and countries began to strengthen TB surveillance and control, which later helped reverse these early-1990s increases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: HIV epidemic expanding among marginalized populations, cuts and complacency in TB control programmes, overcrowding in shelters and prisons, and urban poverty led to increased transmission and reactivation of latent infection in North America and Western Europe. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new M. tuberculosis genotype dominated this episode; instead, existing strains resurged in populations with weakened immunity and disrupted public health infrastructure.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the early-1990s TB resurgence in North America and Western/Northern Europe linked to HIV and weakened control programmes, and correctly codes this as re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence. Geography, years and event type are consistent with WHO and historical descriptions; no changes made.

Countries: United States of America [1991]; Spain [1991]; Italy [1992]; other Western European countries reporting hospital and prison outbreaks
Host: Humans, especially people living with HIV, hospitalized patients, and prisoners
Event summary: In the early 1990s, clusters of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), resistant at least to isoniazid and rifampicin, were reported in New York City and other urban centers, particularly among HIV-infected patients. From about 1991 to 1995, nosocomial and prison outbreaks with high case‑fatality rates revealed that MDR-TB had become a major public health threat in the United States and several Western European countries. Intensified infection control in hospitals and prisons, improved TB/HIV management, and implementation of directly observed therapy (DOTS) subsequently contained these MDR outbreaks in many high-income settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Overcrowded hospitals and correctional facilities, inadequate TB treatment regimens, poor adherence, and co‑location of patients with HIV created conditions for selection and transmission of drug-resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: accumulation of resistance mutations to first‑line drugs, giving rise to MDR-TB with increased fitness under widespread antibiotic pressure and enabling sustained person‑to‑person transmission in congregate settings.
Review: retain – Event accurately describes early-1990s MDR-TB outbreaks in hospitals and prisons in the United States and parts of Western Europe, with correct re-emergence coding driven by antimicrobial resistance and no intra-/inter-continental emergence. Time window and locations match published outbreak reports; no structural changes required.

Countries: Russian Federation [1991]; Ukraine [1992]; Kazakhstan [1992]; Uzbekistan [1992]; Republic of Moldova [1993]; other newly independent states of the former Soviet Union through the 1990s
Host: Humans, including general population, prisoners, and people living with HIV
Event summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, tuberculosis incidence and mortality rose sharply in many Eastern European and Central Asian countries, reversing previous declines. Between roughly 1991 and 2005, severe epidemics of TB and MDR-TB emerged in the Russian Federation, Ukraine, Moldova, and Central Asian republics, fuelled by deteriorating health systems and explosive transmission in prisons. By the early 2000s, this region accounted for a large share of the world’s MDR and XDR-TB burden, and international programmes focused on scaling up DOTS-Plus and prison TB control to gradually stabilize the situation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Socioeconomic crisis, underfunded and fragmented TB services, irregular drug supply, and overcrowded prisons allowed incomplete or inappropriate treatment and extensive transmission; rising HIV prevalence in some areas further increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: independent evolution and spread of MDR and later XDR M. tuberculosis lineages (e.g., Ural and Beijing families) through stepwise accumulation of resistance mutations under intense selection pressure, with some strains later shown to expand clonally across Eastern Europe.
Review: review – Corrected misclassification of this episode as an intra-continental emergence event. TB was long established in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; the period 1991–2005 reflects resurgence and spread of MDR/XDR strains in an existing endemic area, which fits the project definition of re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than first presence in a new sub-region. Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false and retained re_emergence = true; years, regions and countries remain appropriate but should be checked by a human reviewer for final confirmation.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: South Africa [1990]; Botswana [1990]; Zimbabwe [1990]; Zambia [1990]; Malawi [1990]; Mozambique [1990]; Kenya [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Uganda [1990]; Ethiopia [1990]; Nigeria [1990]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [1990]; other sub‑Saharan African countries with rapidly rising TB/HIV co‑infection
Host: Humans, particularly adults living with HIV in sub‑Saharan Africa
Event summary: From 1990 to about 2005, tuberculosis incidence in sub‑Saharan Africa more than doubled, in stark contrast to stable or declining trends elsewhere. As generalized HIV epidemics expanded through the 1990s, countries such as South Africa and its neighbours experienced explosive growth in HIV‑associated TB, with millions of co‑infected individuals and overwhelmed TB programmes. By the mid‑2000s, regional and global initiatives to scale up antiretroviral therapy, improve TB/HIV collaborative activities, and strengthen DOTS began to slow and then partially reverse the rise in incidence, though TB burden remained extremely high.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Generalized HIV epidemics dramatically increased the risk of progression from latent infection to active TB, while weak health systems, poverty, and crowding promoted transmission and limited access to diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: mainly increased reactivation and transmission of existing strains in highly immunocompromised populations, with drug‑resistant TB emerging later as a compounding problem but not the initial primary driver of this regional resurgence.
Review: review – Two corrections made. (1) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because this episode is a dramatic HIV-driven resurgence of TB in an already endemic continent (re-occurrence) rather than first establishment of M. tuberculosis in new African sub-regions. (2) Expanded the country list to include illustrative high-burden countries from all four listed subregions (Eastern, Middle, Southern and Western Africa) so that the countries field better matches the stated sub-regional coverage; retained the phrase "other sub‑Saharan African countries" to reflect the region-wide nature of the crisis. Event remains coded as re_occurrence = true and should be retained after human review of the country examples.

Countries: South Africa [2005], especially KwaZulu-Natal Province (Tugela Ferry)
Host: Humans, especially people living with HIV attending rural hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal
Event summary: In 2005–2006, an outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant tuberculosis (XDR‑TB) was identified around the Church of Scotland Hospital in Tugela Ferry, KwaZulu‑Natal, with extremely high mortality among HIV‑infected patients. During 2005–2007, South African surveillance revealed that thousands of TB cases in KwaZulu‑Natal were multidrug resistant, and a significant fraction met criteria for XDR-TB, signaling that highly resistant strains were already transmitting widely. Over the following years, this Tugela Ferry XDR‑TB cluster became emblematic of drug‑resistant TB in southern Africa, and international reports documented spread of epidemiologically linked MDR/XDR cases to other countries, prompting intensive infection‑control efforts, treatment program expansion, and research into shorter MDR/XDR regimens.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High HIV prevalence, overcrowded hospital wards, delayed diagnosis, and limited drug‑susceptibility testing allowed undetected MDR cases to evolve further resistance and spread in health‑care settings; weaknesses in second‑line drug management also contributed. Internal mechanisms: stepwise accumulation of resistance mutations to first‑ and second‑line TB drugs produced XDR-TB strains with high-level resistance; despite some fitness costs, these strains transmitted efficiently among severely immunocompromised patients, representing a clear example of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance and enhanced transmission in a specific context.
Review: review – Narrowed the countries field to "South Africa [2005], especially KwaZulu-Natal Province (Tugela Ferry)" and removed the vague phrase about "later detection of linked cases outside South Africa" to avoid implying a separate inter-continental emergence episode; imported cases elsewhere are better treated as part of the same linked outbreak, consistent with the project rules. Implementation and scale‑up of DOTS and later MDR-TB programmes across China gradually improved detection and treatment, contributing to subsequent declines in TB incidence and better control of drug‑resistant disease, although absolute numbers remained high.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical use of non‑standard TB regimens, treatment interruptions, and health‑system gaps, especially among previously treated patients, selected for MDR strains; rapid urbanization and migration facilitated transmission. Event summary: By the mid‑2000s, India began reporting growing numbers of MDR-TB cases, initially concentrated in large cities and among previously treated patients, signaling a shift from sporadic resistance to a large‑scale MDR epidemic. Internal mechanisms: emergence and clonal spread of MDR M. tuberculosis strains through accumulation of resistance mutations under widespread, sometimes unsupervised, antibiotic exposure, with some lineages maintaining sufficient fitness for sustained community transmission.

Event summary: In 2020, the COVID‑19 pandemic severely disrupted TB services worldwide, leading to sharp reductions in TB case notifications and delays in diagnosis and treatment. Countries: Rwanda [1993]; Burundi [1993]; United Republic of Tanzania [1994]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [1994] (representative refugee-camp epidemics in the Great Lakes/Central Africa region)
Host: Humans (refugees and internally displaced persons, especially children)
Event summary: Beginning in late 1993, large epidemics of bloody diarrhoea due to Shigella dysenteriae type 1 struck refugee and displaced-person camps in Central Africa, first in Nzangwa camp in Rwanda and then in camps in Tanzania and eastern Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Over 1993–1995, at least 11 major Sd1 epidemics occurred in camps in Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Zaire, with attack rates often exceeding 10–30% and camp-level case-fatality ratios up to around 9%, contributing substantially to excess mortality during the Great Lakes refugee crisis. The epidemics gradually declined as safe water supplies, sanitation, effective antimicrobials and better camp management were put in place, but they highlighted the devastating potential of multidrug-resistant Sd1 in crowded humanitarian settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Armed conflict and genocide in Rwanda and neighbouring countries causing massive population displacement into overcrowded, poorly serviced refugee camps; extremely limited clean water (initially often <1–3 L per person per day), inadequate sanitation, and shortfalls in clinical care; large-scale cross-border movements facilitating regional spread. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (multiply drug-resistant Sd1 strains with resistance to first-line agents such as ampicillin and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, often with reduced susceptibility to nalidixic acid); Enhanced Transmission (very low infectious dose of Sd1 combined with high faecal–oral exposure in camp conditions, enabling explosive camp-wide outbreaks).

Classified as re-emergence of multidrug-resistant Sd1 in already affected African subregions, not as inter-/intra-continental emergence. Countries and dates are synthesised from Médecins Sans Frontières/WHO analyses and MMWR refugee surveillance; please verify the exact camp and country list for inclusion in a top‑10 event set.

Early outbreaks in Berlin and later in London during 2004–2005 were followed by recurrent clusters in other cities in the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, France and Germany, involving both Shigella flexneri and S. sonnei. Over this period, sexually transmitted shigellosis in MSM shifted from sporadic reports to a recurring and expanding problem, with fluctuating but persistent domestic transmission and growing recognition in European surveillance data.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing high-risk sexual practices and dense, interconnected MSM sexual networks across major European cities; international travel and mixing at sex venues and events; limited awareness of enteric pathogens as sexually transmitted infections. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (adaptation of existing Shigella lineages to efficient faecal–oral transmission within MSM networks, including prolonged shedding and asymptomatic carriage); in some lineages, Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (emergence of multidrug-resistance plasmids shared between MSM-associated S. flexneri and S. sonnei strains).

Countries: India [2007]; Pakistan [2007]; Bangladesh [2007]; Nepal [2008]; Viet Nam [2008]; Thailand [2008]; Cambodia [2009]; Indonesia [2010] (representative South and South‑East Asian countries where fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei became established)
Host: Humans (children and adults; mostly community-acquired diarrhoea)
Event summary: Around 2007, a fluoroquinolone-resistant Shigella sonnei clone emerged in South Asia following sequential accumulation of QRDR mutations, and rapidly increased in prevalence in local shigellosis cases. Over subsequent years, this resistant lineage clonally expanded and spread into neighbouring South‑East Asian countries, contributing to rising rates of treatment failure and antimicrobial-resistant diarrhoea in both children and adults. By about 2015, fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei was widely established across much of South and South‑East Asia, particularly affecting children in low‑resource, high-transmission settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy and often unregulated use of fluoroquinolones for diarrhoeal disease; high force of infection in densely populated areas with poor water, sanitation and hygiene; intense regional travel within Asia. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (single clonal fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei lineage within lineage III); Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (stepwise gyrA and parC mutations conferring high-level fluoroquinolone resistance); Enhanced Transmission (fitness of the resistant clone enabling clonal expansion in high-transmission environments).

Fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei arose around 2007 in South Asia and spread within Asia into regions where Shigella was already endemic; per the protocol, this represents re-emergence via a novel resistant clone rather than intra-continental emergence of the organism. Years, countries and narrative are consistent with genomic reconstructions by The et al. 2019 and related reviews.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015]

Event summary: In late 2015, Public Health England identified a cluster of Shigella sonnei infections in adult men with no travel history that carried an extended‑spectrum β‑lactamase plasmid and macrolide-resistance genes previously associated with MSM-linked Shigella flexneri 3a. The cluster signalled the emergence of an ESBL-producing, macrolide-resistant S. sonnei strain within domestic MSM networks in England. Classification as re-emergence (without intra-/inter-continental flags) is consistent with the protocol, and no corrections to geography, timing or sources were required, though the episode is nested within the broader 2001–2015 European MSM epidemic row.

Event summary: In 1997, a highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus of purely avian origin caused the first recognized human infections in Hong Kong, with 18 laboratory‑confirmed cases and 6 deaths linked to poultry exposures. Host: Humans (mainly poultry workers and household contacts presenting with conjunctivitis or mild influenza‑like illness, plus one fatal case of acute respiratory distress syndrome) in the context of a large poultry epizootic
Event summary: From February to April 2003, a highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H7N7) virus caused extensive outbreaks on poultry farms in the Netherlands, leading to culling of more than 30 million birds and major production losses. Zoonotic transmission to poultry workers and some household contacts produced at least 89 laboratory‑confirmed human infections, predominantly conjunctivitis or mild influenza‑like illness, and one fatal pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome. Implementation of large‑scale poultry depopulation, strict movement controls, antiviral prophylaxis for exposed workers and enhanced surveillance halted virus circulation in poultry and ended detection of new human cases by mid‑2003.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density commercial poultry production, frequent movements of birds and personnel between farms, and limited early use of personal protective equipment for workers enabled rapid amplification of H7N7 in poultry and intense human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a highly pathogenic H7N7 strain adapted to chickens; host expansion (spillover) from poultry to humans with marked conjunctival tropism; limited, non‑sustained human‑to‑human transmission documented among close contacts; genetic changes associated with partial adaptation to mammalian hosts.
Review: retain (added) – new event inserted because the 2003 Netherlands H7N7 outbreak, with at least 89 confirmed human infections and one death, is widely regarded as one of the largest documented outbreaks of a purely avian influenza virus in humans and was missing from the original list. Classified as 're-emergence' of influenza A via a novel highly pathogenic H7N7 subtype in Western Europe, not as first emergence, in line with WHO and peer‑reviewed analyses.

Host: Humans (severe pneumonia, mostly in children and young adults) with concurrent massive outbreaks in domestic poultry
Event summary: In late 2003, highly pathogenic H5N1 viruses genetically distinct from the 1997 Hong Kong strain re‑emerged in poultry in Viet Nam and Thailand, with the first new human cases detected in both countries and very high case‑fatality ratios. Through early 2004, H5N1 spread rapidly through poultry populations across several East and South‑East Asian countries, while Viet Nam and Thailand together reported dozens of human infections and more than 20 deaths associated with close contact with sick birds. Aggressive culling campaigns, temporary market closures, and improved surveillance reduced poultry outbreaks and human cases by mid‑2004, although the virus remained entrenched in parts of the regional poultry population, setting the stage for further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and integration of commercial and backyard poultry production, dense live‑bird marketing networks, and limited biosecurity in South‑East Asia promoted virus amplification and human exposure; regional poultry trade and wild‑bird migration aided geographic dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (e.g. Z‑genotype and related lineages) with high pathogenicity in poultry; enhanced transmission/vector adaptation in domestic poultry; host expansion as repeated zoonotic spillover to humans with severe disease.
Review: review – restricted the countries to Viet Nam [2003] and Thailand [2004], because WHO reports for this wave document human H5N1 infections only in these two countries while China, Japan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR and the Republic of Korea had poultry outbreaks but no confirmed human cases in 2003–2004. Sub_regions were therefore narrowed to 'South-eastern Asia', and the event is now classified solely as 're-emergence' (novel H5N1 clade in a region where influenza A was long endemic) rather than 'intra-continental emergence', in line with the rule that new serotypes in already affected subregions should be treated as re-emergence.

Intensified animal and human surveillance, mass poultry culling, and public‑health messaging eventually reduced human spillover, but H5N1 became endemic in poultry in several affected countries, particularly parts of Egypt and Indonesia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance migratory bird flyways, regional and international poultry trade, and inadequate farm biosecurity enabled trans‑continental spread from East and South‑East Asia into Western Asia and Africa; rural poverty and reliance on backyard poultry increased close human–bird contact. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (e.g. clade 2.2 and related lineages) with improved environmental stability and fitness in wild and domestic birds; geographic range expansion (inherent) into new ecological zones; continued host expansion to humans with very high observed case fatality.

Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic infection of backyard and commercial poultry in Indonesia, Viet Nam and neighbouring countries; dense live‑bird markets; cultural practices of home slaughter; limited early vaccine coverage and variable biosecurity. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing antigenic and genetic diversification of H5N1 lineages in poultry, with maintenance of high pathogenicity; geographic range expansion within the sub‑region; repeated host expansion/spillover to humans with very high observed CFR (~50–60%) but no sustained human adaptation.

Event summary: Beginning in 2006, Egypt experienced repeated waves of human H5N1 infections following the virus’s establishment in domestic poultry, rapidly becoming the country with the largest cumulative human case count worldwide. Over the decade 2006–2015, Egypt reported 359 laboratory‑confirmed human cases and 120 deaths, with major peaks in 2006–2008 and again in 2014–2015, often associated with winter poultry epizootics and household slaughter practices. Progressive strengthening of surveillance, vaccination and control measures in poultry, together with public‑health campaigns, eventually reduced human case numbers after 2015, although sporadic infections persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic H5N1 circulation in backyard and commercial poultry in the Nile Delta and other regions; widespread household poultry rearing and home slaughter; limited early vaccine coverage and inconsistent farm biosecurity; socio‑economic reliance on poultry as a protein source. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and local adaptation (Egypt‑specific clades, e.g. 2.2.1) with high fitness in domestic poultry; possible antigenic drift contributing to vaccine mismatch; sustained host expansion to humans with severe disease but little sustained human‑to‑human transmission.
Review: retain – event accurately summarizes Egypt’s prolonged high-burden H5N1 episode (359 cases, 120 deaths, with peaks in 2006–2008 and 2014–2015) and correctly treats it as both 're_occurrence' (strong external drivers such as endemic poultry infection and husbandry practices) and 're_emergence' (local clade evolution and antigenic drift) within Northern Africa; no structural changes needed.

Countries: Mexico [2009]; United States of America [2009]; Canada [2009]; Brazil [2009]; Argentina [2009]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009]; Spain [2009]; Russian Federation [2009]; China [2009]; India [2009]; Japan [2009]; South Africa [2009]; Australia [2009]; New Zealand [2009] (representative of >214 affected countries and territories)
Host: Humans (all age groups; disproportionately high burden in children and working‑age adults)
Event summary: In April 2009, a novel swine‑origin influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus was first detected in human patients in Mexico and the United States, prompting the World Health Organization to declare a pandemic by June 2009 as sustained human‑to‑human transmission spread across multiple regions. Over its first year (April 2009–April 2010), the virus caused an estimated 60.8 million illnesses, 274,304 hospitalizations and 12,469 deaths in the United States alone, and globally an estimated 151,700–575,400 deaths, with transmission documented in more than 214 countries and territories. By late 2010 the initial pandemic wave had subsided and WHO declared the post‑pandemic phase; the H1N1pdm09 virus then became established as a regular seasonal influenza A strain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive industrial swine production and global movement of pigs and people likely facilitated the generation and dissemination of the reassortant virus; rapid international air travel allowed swift inter‑continental seeding; limited pre‑existing immunity in younger age groups enabled large-scale epidemics. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment between swine, avian and human influenza lineages producing H1N1pdm09; enhanced transmission with efficient human‑to‑human spread; host expansion from pigs to sustained human circulation; partial immune escape relative to prior seasonal H1N1 viruses, particularly in children and young adults.
Review: review – replaced the nonstandard 'Global' label in 'sub_regions' with the full set of UNSD subregions across all inhabited continents and provided a representative list of high-burden countries while noting that transmission occurred in more than 214 countries and territories, since listing all would be impractical. 'First_global_emergence', 'first_detection', 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were changed from Yes to No and the event classified solely as 're_emergence', because influenza A virus was already globally established and the 2009 H1N1 pandemic reflects emergence and rapid spread of a novel reassortant strain within an existing EPP rather than first occurrence of influenza A on new continents.

Countries: China [2013] (provinces and municipalities including Shanghai, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Anhui, Henan, Guangdong, Hebei, Hunan and others); China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2013] (imported and limited local cases)
Host: Humans (mostly older adults with underlying conditions exposed to live poultry or live‑bird markets)
Event summary: In February–March 2013, China reported the first human infections with a novel avian‑origin influenza A(H7N9) virus, initially causing severe pneumonia in adults from eastern provinces with documented exposure to live poultry. Over five major epidemic waves through 2016–2017, H7N9 caused repeated surges of human zoonotic infections centred in eastern and south‑central China, ultimately leading to about 1,560–1,570 laboratory‑confirmed human cases and roughly 615–616 deaths, with the fifth wave alone accounting for approximately 766 cases. Large‑scale closure of live‑bird markets and roll‑out of poultry vaccination with H7‑containing vaccines in China from 2017 onward led to a rapid collapse in poultry infections and human spillover, with only a handful of human cases reported after 2018.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense networks of live‑bird markets in eastern China, movement of poultry from rural farms into urban markets, and high human visitation to markets facilitated zoonotic exposure; limited early awareness of H7N9 risk and pre‑existing poultry infections that were largely asymptomatic made control challenging. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of an H7N9 virus generated by reassortment among avian H7, N9 and H9N2‑like internal gene segments; host expansion (spillover) to humans with high case fatality (~39%); enhanced transmission in poultry with subsequent evolution of highly pathogenic H7N9 variants in later waves; partial geographic range expansion within China across multiple provinces.
Review: review – retained the time span, geography and burden estimates, which align with WHO and CDC summaries (~1,568 confirmed cases and ~616 deaths concentrated in eastern and south‑central China), but changed 'first_global_emergence' and 'first_detection' from Yes to No because influenza A virus was already endemic in humans globally; this episode is best characterized as 're_emergence' of the EPP via a novel reassortant H7N9 subtype causing severe zoonotic infection in Eastern Asia.

Event summary: In 2014, China reported the first recognized human infections with a novel reassortant avian influenza A(H5N6) virus, with early cases presenting as severe pneumonia in individuals exposed to poultry in Sichuan, Guangdong and Yunnan provinces. Over the subsequent decade, sporadic but often severe zoonotic H5N6 infections continued to be reported predominantly from mainland China, with at least 90–93 laboratory‑confirmed human cases (including a single confirmed case in Lao People’s Democratic Republic) and more than half fatal by the mid‑2020s. Continued veterinary control efforts and public‑health messaging have so far kept H5N6 from causing large human clusters, but the virus remains a significant zoonotic threat due to its high virulence and ongoing circulation in poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic circulation of multiple H5Nx and H9N2 viruses in Chinese poultry, high poultry densities and live‑bird market activity, and close human–poultry contact in affected provinces. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through reassortment, with H5N6 acquiring genes from H5N1‑like, H10N6‑like and H9N2/H7N9‑like viruses; increased virulence/pathogenicity in humans with high CFR (~60% among confirmed cases); host expansion (spillover) from birds to humans; ongoing genetic diversification within poultry populations sustaining the zoonotic risk.
Review: review – expanded the countries and sub_regions to include Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2021] and South-eastern Asia, reflecting the confirmed H5N6 human infection reported there, while keeping China [2014] as the primary locus of cases. 'First_global_emergence' and 'first_detection' were changed from Yes to No and the event classified as 're_emergence' of influenza A via a new H5N6 reassortant lineage, consistent with WHO/CDC summaries that describe >90 human infections (mostly in China, one in Laos) since 2014.

Host: Humans (hospital staff and patients)
Event summary: In March–April 2012, a cluster of 13 cases of severe pneumonia among healthcare workers and patients at a hospital in Zarqa, Jordan, including two fatalities, was investigated and later retrospectively confirmed by serology and RT‑PCR as infection with a previously unrecognized coronavirus, now known as MERS‑CoV. In June 2012, a 60‑year‑old man from Saudi Arabia who developed acute pneumonia and renal failure and was treated in Jeddah had a novel betacoronavirus isolated from respiratory samples, providing the first virological characterization of MERS‑CoV. Following these detections, additional sporadic and small cluster cases were identified in Saudi Arabia and Jordan as awareness and diagnostic capacity increased, marking the global first emergence and first detection of MERS‑CoV infection in humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: zoonotic spillover from infected dromedary camels in the Arabian Peninsula, with close human–camel contact in farm and market settings, and limited early infection prevention and control (IPC) measures in hospitals that allowed intra‑facility transmission. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of a bat‑related merbecovirus lineage into dromedary camels and then humans; viral traits enabling infection of the lower respiratory tract and efficient person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact healthcare settings, while maintaining a basic reproduction number near or below 1 in the community.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first recognized human MERS‑CoV cluster in Zarqa, Jordan, and the index virologically characterized Saudi case in 2012; timing, countries (Jordan, Saudi Arabia), subregion (Asia – Western Asia) and classification as first_global_emergence and first_detection are consistent with primary WHO, CDC and NEJM sources, so no structural changes were required.

Host: Humans (hospital patients, healthcare workers, visitors)
Event summary: Between April and May 2013, a major hospital‑associated outbreak of MERS‑CoV occurred in the Al‑Hasa region of eastern Saudi Arabia, involving 23 laboratory‑confirmed and 11 probable cases across four interlinked healthcare facilities and causing a high case‑fatality proportion. Transmission began from a presumed primary case admitted with severe respiratory illness and was amplified via shared dialysis units, inpatient wards and close contact among patients, visitors and healthcare workers. The outbreak was brought under control after strengthened infection‑control measures, patient cohorting and closure of affected units were implemented, although sporadic primary cases and small clusters continued to be detected in Saudi Arabia thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suboptimal early IPC practices, including delayed recognition of MERS, inadequate isolation, crowded dialysis units and frequent patient transfers between facilities, facilitated nosocomial spread among highly comorbid patients. Internal mechanisms: efficient human‑to‑human transmission of already circulating MERS‑CoV lineages in healthcare settings once introduced, without clear evidence of a distinct genotype responsible for the outbreak.
Review: review – Reclassified this cluster as re-occurrence (re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false) because it represents a substantial resurgence of an already circulating virus within the same Western Asia subregion driven by healthcare‑system factors, with no convincing evidence of a novel strain; other geography and narrative details were retained.

Countries: United Arab Emirates [2013]; Saudi Arabia [2013]; Oman [2013]; Qatar [2012]
Host: Humans (camel workers, household contacts, healthcare workers and patients); reservoir dromedary camels
Event summary: From early 2013 through mid‑2014, Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates documented 65 laboratory‑confirmed human MERS‑CoV infections, many occurring in defined clusters linked to healthcare facilities, households and dromedary camel holdings, while additional primary and secondary cases were detected in neighboring Gulf states including Qatar, Oman and Saudi Arabia. The episode was characterized by repeated introductions from infected camels into humans, followed by limited human‑to‑human transmission in hospitals and family settings across multiple countries within Western Asia, contributing substantially to the regional rise in MERS cases in 2013–2014. Intensified surveillance, improved IPC in healthcare settings and targeted control measures in camel farms and markets gradually reduced the frequency and size of clusters by mid‑2014.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close occupational and cultural contact with infected dromedary camels (farms, racing, markets), high utilization of tertiary care facilities, and expanded case finding through enhanced surveillance all contributed to increased detection and healthcare‑associated amplification across the Arabian Peninsula. Internal mechanisms: widespread camel reservoir infection with MERS‑CoV strains capable of zoonotic spillover and efficient transmission in healthcare and household settings, though transmission chains in the wider community typically remained short.
Review: review – Removed intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags and set re_occurrence=true to better reflect that this multi‑country Gulf episode was a major resurgence and geographic broadening of MERS within the already affected Western Asia subregion, driven by zoonotic exposure and healthcare‑associated spread rather than the virus entering a new UNSD subregion or acquiring clearly enhanced virulence.

Host: Humans (hospital patients, healthcare workers, visitors); reservoir dromedary camels
Event summary: In March–May 2014, Saudi Arabia experienced a sharp surge of MERS‑CoV cases centered on Jeddah, where a very large healthcare‑associated outbreak involving approximately 255 laboratory‑confirmed cases across multiple hospitals, including King Fahd General Hospital, was documented. Many infections were linked to overcrowded emergency departments, dialysis units and inpatient wards, with extensive involvement of healthcare workers and hospitalized patients, while primary camel‑linked cases continued to occur elsewhere in the country. Following international concern and a WHO mission in May 2014, aggressive IPC interventions, triage reforms and temporary closure of affected units were implemented, leading to a marked decline in new cases and deaths later in 2014, although lower‑level sporadic and cluster transmission persisted in Saudi Arabia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: crowded emergency rooms and inpatient wards, delayed case recognition, inadequate early application of standard, contact and airborne precautions, and frequent patient movement within and between hospitals created conditions for superspreading and rapid amplification. Internal mechanisms: existing MERS‑CoV lineages, with high intrinsic pathogenicity and a case‑fatality ratio around one‑third, proved capable of generating large healthcare outbreaks in the absence of robust IPC, without clear evidence that a fundamentally new genotype was necessary.
Review: review – Reinterpreted this Jeddah surge as a re-occurrence event (re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false) in Western Asia because the explosive outbreak reflects healthcare‑driven amplification of known MERS‑CoV lineages rather than emergence of a demonstrably more virulent or transmissible strain; country and temporal framing remain consistent with EID and NEJM descriptions.

Sub-regions: Europe – Western Europe; Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Southern Europe; Africa – Northern Africa; Asia – Western Asia
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]; Germany [2012]; France [2013]; Italy [2013]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2014]; Austria [2014]; Greece [2014]; Türkiye [2014]; Tunisia [2013]; Algeria [2014]; Egypt [2014]

Event summary: Beginning with imported cases to the United Kingdom and Germany in 2012 and accelerating over 2013–2014, several European and North African countries detected their first MERS‑CoV infections in travellers recently returned from the Arabian Peninsula, including the UK, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria, Greece, Türkiye, Tunisia, Algeria and Egypt. In a subset of these introductions, such as the UK family cluster, a French nosocomial transmission to a hospital roommate and a Tunisian family cluster, limited secondary spread occurred in households or healthcare settings, but transmission chains remained short and were rapidly contained. By 2015, Europe and North Africa together had reported only a few dozen cases and single‑digit deaths, and strengthened surveillance and IPC in receiving countries prevented any large‑scale outbreaks despite ongoing importation risk linked to travel and medical evacuation from the Middle East.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing international travel, labour migration and medical evacuation between the Arabian Peninsula and Europe/North Africa, combined with heightened clinical awareness and improved diagnostic capacity, led to detection of imported MERS cases and small secondary clusters. Internal mechanisms: the same Arabian Peninsula–derived MERS‑CoV lineages retained the capacity for human infection and limited person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings, but there was no evidence of adaptation for sustained community transmission in Europe or North Africa during this period.
Review: review – Updated the event year to 2012-2015 to match the first imported cases to the UK and Germany in 2012, corrected the geography to include Europe, Africa and Asia (for Türkiye) while removing the unsupported 'Europe – Eastern Europe' subregion, and reset first_detection to false while retaining inter_continental_emergence=true to reflect that this episode represents the first documented in situ transmission of MERS‑CoV in new continents (Europe and Africa) through small household and healthcare clusters.

Event summary: On 20 May 2015, the Republic of Korea reported its first laboratory‑confirmed MERS‑CoV case in a traveller recently returned from Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, who became the index patient for a large nosocomial outbreak. Over the following weeks, healthcare‑associated transmission in multiple hospitals generated 186 confirmed cases and 38 deaths in Korea, with one infected contact travelling to China and becoming that country’s first MERS case, making this the largest MERS outbreak outside the Middle East. Aggressive public health measures, including rapid case isolation, closure or restriction of affected hospitals, extensive contact tracing and quarantine of more than 16,000 contacts, eventually interrupted transmission, with the last case confirmed in early July 2015 and no further major outbreaks reported in Eastern Asia thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: delayed recognition of MERS in the index traveller, repeated healthcare‑seeking at multiple facilities, crowded emergency rooms and multi‑bed rooms, and gaps in early IPC allowed extensive hospital‑to‑hospital spread; high domestic mobility and international air travel facilitated introduction and limited exportation of cases. Internal mechanisms: MERS‑CoV strains imported from the Arabian Peninsula retained strong potential for nosocomial superspreading but did not show evidence of adaptation for sustained community transmission once robust control measures were in place.

Event summary: In mid‑2015, a substantial hospital‑associated MERS‑CoV outbreak occurred at King Abdulaziz Medical City, a large tertiary care facility in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, against a background of ongoing sporadic and cluster cases nationwide. The Riyadh hospital outbreak involved approximately 130 suspected MERS patients, of whom 81 were laboratory confirmed and 49 classified as probable, and contributed to a national cumulative total exceeding 1,100 cases and nearly 500 deaths by August 2015. Following this event, Saudi health authorities further strengthened national IPC programmes, outbreak preparedness and surveillance, and global MERS incidence declined markedly from 2016 onward, with only smaller camel‑linked primary cases and limited healthcare clusters reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: a high burden of vulnerable patients with comorbidities in tertiary hospitals, lapses in triage and isolation practices, crowded emergency departments, and persistent zoonotic pressure from infected camels maintained a high risk of repeated introductions into healthcare facilities. Internal mechanisms: circulating MERS‑CoV lineages continued to cause severe disease with high case‑fatality ratios and to spread efficiently in hospitals under suboptimal IPC, so this outbreak is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence driven largely by health‑system factors rather than by major viral genetic change, although recombinant viruses were documented during this period.

Host: Humans (hospital patients, healthcare workers, family caregivers); reservoir dromedary camels
Event summary: Between September 2014 and January 2015, a multifacility MERS‑CoV outbreak in Taif Governorate, Saudi Arabia, resulted in 38 laboratory‑confirmed cases across four healthcare facilities, with 21 reported deaths and frequent involvement of healthcare personnel. Transmission occurred in at least one dialysis unit and multiple hospital wards, with additional spread to family members and probable links between facilities suggesting unrecognized chains of transmission. Enhanced investigation, reinforcement of IPC measures, targeted screening of contacts and public health communication in Taif eventually interrupted the outbreak, although sporadic primary cases and small clusters continued to occur elsewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive use of dialysis and inpatient services by patients with chronic renal and other comorbid conditions, crowding within healthcare facilities, and incomplete early application of IPC precautions enabled sustained nosocomial spread across multiple hospitals. Internal mechanisms: MERS‑CoV strains circulating in Taif shared closely related spike gene sequences forming a discrete cluster, but there was no evidence of a fundamentally new phenotype; the high case‑fatality ratio instead reflected the vulnerability of affected patient groups and the healthcare‑associated nature of the outbreak.
