Host: Humans (hospital patients, visitors, healthcare workers, family contacts)
Event summary: During August–October 2015, Jordan experienced a multihospital outbreak of MERS‑CoV centered in Amman and Zarqa, in which 16 laboratory‑confirmed cases were identified across several hospitals and outpatient settings, with 7 deaths. Epidemiologic investigation showed that most cases were healthcare associated or close relatives of known cases, and genomic sequencing revealed distinctive in‑frame deletions in accessory open reading frames (ORF4a and ORF3) and, in some viruses, larger deletions spanning ORF4b and ORF5, indicating spread of a deletion variant lineage. Implementation of strengthened IPC, contact tracing and follow‑up of hundreds of healthcare and household contacts eventually halted further transmission, and no additional large clusters of the deletion variant were detected after the outbreak ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: exposure of susceptible patients, visitors and healthcare workers in busy hospitals, together with incomplete early recognition and isolation of MERS cases, facilitated nosocomial transmission within and between facilities. Internal mechanisms: emergence and onward transmission of MERS‑CoV deletion variants affecting several accessory genes (including ORF4a, ORF3, ORF4b and ORF5) mark this as a true re-emergence episode involving a genetically altered virus lineage that nevertheless retained the ability to cause severe clinical disease and human‑to‑human spread.

Event summary: From late May to June 2017, Saudi Arabia reported two contemporaneous healthcare‑associated MERS‑CoV outbreaks in Riyadh involving a large tertiary‑care hospital, a specialty pulmonary hospital, an outpatient clinic and a dialysis unit, together accounting for approximately 48 confirmed cases among patients, healthcare personnel and family members. Each hospital‑based cluster was seeded by a distinct index case, followed by multiple generations of transmission within emergency departments, inpatient wards and dialysis settings, with several asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic healthcare worker infections detected through screening. Event summary: In 2009, a previously unrecognized yeast was isolated from the ear canal of a hospitalized patient in Tokyo, Japan, and described as the new species Candida auris, marking its first confirmed occurrence in humans. Over the following years, additional isolates from Japan and retrospective identification of earlier Korean isolates clarified its clinical significance and distinctness from other Candida species. By around 2011, recognition of C. auris in microbiology laboratories ended this initial emergence period as targeted surveillance and species-level identification improved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Improved mycology diagnostics (e.g., sequencing, MALDI-TOF) and increased clinical attention to azole-resistant candidiasis enabled recognition of a previously misidentified yeast. Host: Humans with chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) and aspergillomas, predominantly as a sequel to pulmonary tuberculosis or other chronic lung diseases
Event summary: From 1990 onwards, India’s high incidence of pulmonary tuberculosis and improving TB survival created millions of patients with residual cavities and structurally damaged lungs, yet chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) remained rarely diagnosed and was often misclassified as smear‑negative or recurrent TB. In 2011, global burden modeling using TB incidence and limited CPA data suggested that hundreds of thousands of CPA cases worldwide were secondary to TB, with India contributing a large share, and subsequent India‑specific analyses incorporating local imaging and serology data further increased national CPA prevalence estimates to around 1.5 million people with CPA after TB and hundreds of thousands of new cases annually. By the late 2010s, it was evident that CPA had re‑emerged as a major, long‑term fungal consequence of TB control in India, with ongoing high morbidity and mortality driven largely by underdiagnosis and limited access to prolonged antifungal treatment rather than by discrete outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistently high TB incidence and improved survival in India generated large populations with cavitary and fibrotic lung disease that are predisposed to chronic A. fumigatus colonization and invasion; gaps in access to CT imaging, Aspergillus IgG testing, and mycology services led to frequent misdiagnosis of CPA as chronic or recurrent TB, delaying or preventing antifungal therapy; socioeconomic factors including poverty, malnutrition, and indoor air pollution further increased vulnerability. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel A. fumigatus genotype is consistently implicated; typical strains form chronic, often cavitary infections in pre-damaged lungs, sometimes with biofilm-like growth. Azole resistance (including TR34/L98H) can develop or be acquired in some Indian CPA patients and may worsen outcomes, but the key drivers of this event are external (TB epidemiology and health-system limitations).
Review: review – Retain this high-burden event describing CPA after TB in India, which is supported by global and India-specific modeling studies, but flag several approximations. Classification as re-occurrence (driven by external factors: TB burden, survival, and diagnostic gaps) is consistent with the definitions, as there is no evidence of a fundamentally altered fungus. The 1990–2020 window reflects the period in which TB control and survival generated very large pools of at-risk patients and CPA burden estimates were developed; a narrower period centered on the modeling era (approximately 2000s–2010s) could be considered in future revisions. Replaced general Wikipedia links with the original WHO Bulletin global burden paper, India-focused burden estimates, and a contemporary CPA review, which better document this emergence pattern.

Host: Humans with invasive or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis; environmental A. fumigatus in agricultural soils, compost, and urban environments in Iran and China
Event summary: During 2003–2009, clinical surveillance in Iran identified azole-resistant A. fumigatus in approximately 3% of patient isolates, with the earliest TR34/L98H-positive isolate recovered in 2005 and additional resistant strains found in both clinical and environmental samples, indicating an environmental origin. In parallel, global surveillance in 2008–2009 and subsequent multicenter studies in China documented clinical and environmental A. fumigatus isolates harboring TR34/L98H and TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I mutations across multiple provinces, with clinical resistance prevalences around 2–3% and environmental hot spots in intensively fungicide-treated areas. By around 2015, these findings established the Middle East (notably Iran) and East Asia (notably China) as important additional regional reservoirs of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus, contributing to the global dissemination of TR34/L98H-lineage resistance beyond Europe and India.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy and often repeated use of DMI azole fungicides in cereal, greenhouse vegetable, and ornamental crop production in Iran and China created strong selection pressure for azole-resistant A. fumigatus in soils, compost, and plant waste; rapid urbanization and construction, together with increased use of azoles in material preservation, may have further expanded environmental niches; limited routine susceptibility testing in many hospitals delayed recognition of resistance. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via TR34/L98H and composite TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I cyp51A promoter-repeat and coding mutations conferring high-level resistance to multiple medical azoles and many agricultural azoles; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with both globally distributed TR34/L98H clones and regionally distinctive TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I variants; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as these resistant lineages became established in human disease and diverse environments across western and eastern Asia.
Review: review – This row has been added as a missing major emergence event to capture the documented rise of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus in Iran and China, which together represent significant regional reservoirs beyond Europe and India. Classified as re-emergence because it reflects the spread of resistant genotypes (TR34/L98H and TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I) in regions where the species has long been present, rather than first detection of the EPP. The 2005–2015 window is anchored in the first Iranian TR34/L98H isolate (2005) and the 2008–2009 global surveillance and subsequent multicenter Chinese studies; precise country-specific start and end years may warrant fine-tuning as more longitudinal data emerge.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: South Africa [1990]; Uganda [1990]; Kenya [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Zambia [1990]; Zimbabwe [1990]; Malawi [1990]; Ethiopia [1990]; Nigeria [1990]; Botswana [1990]
Host: Humans (people living with HIV/AIDS with advanced immunosuppression)
Event summary: From about 1990 through the mid‑2000s, as the HIV pandemic expanded and many patients progressed to advanced immunosuppression, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis due to Candida albicans became one of the most frequent opportunistic infections, affecting an estimated 80–90% of HIV‑infected individuals at some point in their disease course in many high‑burden African settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3218701/?utm_source=openai)) Throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, clinics and hospitals in Eastern, Southern, and Western Africa reported very high caseloads of recurrent thrush and dysphagia requiring repeated azole therapy, creating a substantial clinical and healthcare burden.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2843789/?utm_source=openai)) With the scale‑up of effective antiretroviral therapy around 2000–2005, rates of mucosal candidiasis declined sharply in patients achieving viral suppression but remained high in areas with limited ART access or poor adherence, so the problem became more localized rather than fully resolved.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9684632/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global spread of HIV with large numbers of severely immunocompromised adults and children; delayed rollout and uneven coverage of effective antiretroviral therapy; malnutrition and co‑morbid infections; widespread but often intermittent use of fluconazole and other azoles for treatment and prophylaxis of recurrent mucosal candidiasis. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/host adaptation of C. albicans as an opportunistic pathogen in severely immunosuppressed hosts; later in the period, selection for azole‑resistant C. albicans and increased prominence of intrinsically less susceptible non‑albicans Candida species in some cohorts, setting the stage for subsequent resistance‑focused emergence events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3218701/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – New high‑impact event added to capture the extremely common HIV‑associated oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis epidemic (tens of millions of cases) that was previously omitted. Time window (1990–2005) and representative African countries are approximate and focus on high‑burden regions rather than an exhaustive global list, so this row should be retained but checked by a human curator for geographic scope and country listing.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (primarily people with advanced HIV infection receiving chronic fluconazole for recurrent oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis)
Event summary: In the early 1990s in the United States, clinicians began to report failure of fluconazole therapy for recurrent oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis in people with advanced HIV infection, linked to fluconazole‑resistant Candida albicans isolates with markedly elevated MICs.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7814530/?utm_source=openai)) Prolonged, repeated azole use in large HIV‑positive cohorts selected for resistant C. albicans strains, which then became an important cause of refractory mucosal and occasionally invasive disease in major urban HIV treatment centers. As combination antiretroviral therapy and more judicious azole use were adopted in the mid‑to‑late 1990s, the incidence of highly resistant C. albicans in HIV clinics stabilized or declined but remained a clinically significant problem in heavily pre‑treated patients.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread, long‑term fluconazole use for therapy and prophylaxis of recurrent mucosal candidiasis in people with AIDS; very high burden of immunosuppression and frequent healthcare exposure before effective ART. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance via stepwise azole resistance mechanisms (ERG11 target‑site mutations, efflux pump overexpression, loss of heterozygosity at ERG11), with clonal expansion of resistant lineages in some patients or centers; possible selection for strains with enhanced persistence at mucosal surfaces under drug pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7814530/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – Appropriately captures an early 1990s emergence of fluconazole‑resistant C. albicans in U.S. HIV populations, a major drug‑resistance milestone with substantial clinical impact. Classification as re‑emergence (pathogen change via azole resistance) and geography (United States, Northern America) are consistent with source literature; no structural changes beyond added citations are required.

Host: Humans (hospitalized adults and children with candidemia and other invasive Candida infections)
Event summary: From 1998 to 2000, a population‑based active laboratory surveillance program in Baltimore, Maryland and the state of Connecticut documented high incidence rates of Candida bloodstream infections, with C. albicans as the most common species and measurable fluconazole resistance among isolates.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387610/?utm_source=openai)) The study highlighted invasive C. albicans candidemia as a leading hospital‑acquired bloodstream infection in intensive care units and oncology wards, reflecting increased use of central venous catheters, complex surgery, chemotherapy, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics in high‑risk inpatients. After this surveillance period, C. albicans remained the dominant cause of candidemia in many U.S. centers, but with continued concern about antifungal resistance and a gradual shift towards more non‑albicans species in some settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive care medicine, use of central venous catheters, complex abdominal and cardiothoracic surgery, chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia, and prolonged broad‑spectrum antibiotic exposure among hospitalized patients; adoption of azole prophylaxis in selected high‑risk groups. Internal mechanisms: Increased biofilm formation and healthcare‑associated transmission on intravascular devices and hospital surfaces; limited but notable azole resistance in a subset of C. albicans strains, although the main impact of this event is high incidence of invasive infection rather than novel resistance mechanisms.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387610/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Event captures a major recognition of C. albicans candidemia as a leading nosocomial bloodstream infection in the U.S., but the main driver is healthcare practice (ICU care, devices, antibiotics) rather than pathogen change. Emergence type has been corrected from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence to better match the definition (incidence increase due to external drivers). Retain as one of the largest burden‑focused events, but a human curator should confirm that its impact justifies inclusion relative to other possible surveillance episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with invasive candidiasis treated with the echinocandin caspofungin)
Event summary: After caspofungin was approved in 2001, echinocandins were rapidly adopted in the United States as first‑line or salvage therapy for invasive candidiasis, including infections due to C. albicans.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.01653-05?utm_source=openai)) Between roughly 2001 and 2006, scattered clinical and laboratory reports documented the first C. albicans isolates with markedly reduced susceptibility to caspofungin, carrying FKS1 hot‑spot mutations and sometimes associated with treatment failure in animal models or patients. Following these early cases, echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans remained rare but became an established resistance phenotype, prompting routine susceptibility testing and development of molecular assays targeting FKS hot‑spot mutations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and increasing use of echinocandins (particularly caspofungin) for empiric and targeted therapy of invasive candidiasis in high‑risk inpatients. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance through novel FKS1 hot‑spot mutations in the 1,3‑β‑D‑glucan synthase complex, leading to elevated echinocandin MICs and reduced drug activity; early clonal expansion of mutant lineages within some hospital environments.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.01653-05?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – Represents the initial emergence of FKS1‑mediated echinocandin resistance in C. albicans following caspofungin introduction in the U.S., a key mechanistic and clinical turning point. Classification as re‑emergence (new resistance phenotype in an existing pathogen) with no intra‑ or inter‑continental component is appropriate; existing sources are relevant and sufficient.

Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with proven invasive candidiasis due to Candida albicans and other Candida spp. with acquired echinocandin resistance)
Event summary: From 2004 to 2010, the French National Reference Center for Mycoses and Antifungals collected and characterized clinical Candida isolates with elevated caspofungin MICs and FKS mutations, identifying 20 proven infections with acquired echinocandin resistance, including multiple C. albicans cases.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/11-0556_article)) These infections occurred in severely ill patients who had received prolonged echinocandin therapy and were often associated with prior wild‑type isolates from the same patient, documenting in vivo selection of resistant mutants. After 2010, echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans infections in France remained infrequent but continued to be detected, reinforcing the need for stewardship and molecular surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing echinocandin use in French tertiary hospitals for empiric and salvage treatment of invasive candidiasis, especially in ICU and hematology‑oncology patients with prolonged therapy and extensive device and antibiotic exposure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance via diverse FKS1 (and FKS2 in other species) hot‑spot mutations conferring elevated MICs; evidence of stepwise in‑patient evolution from susceptible to resistant isolates and occasional clonal spread within healthcare facilities.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/11-0556_article))
Review: Retain – This is a well‑defined national cluster of echinocandin‑resistant Candida infections in France (including multiple C. albicans cases) and clearly one of the most important resistance‑driven emergence events in Europe. Geography, time span and emergence‑type coding (re‑emergence only) are correct; this row should be kept as the primary European cluster, with the EUCAST methods study treated as supporting rather than a separate event.

Host: Humans (patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis in Austria in whom C. albicans acquired a double FKS1 hot‑spot mutation during prolonged echinocandin therapy)
Event summary: A detailed case report from Austria described a woman with long‑standing chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis who received repeated and then continuous echinocandin therapy (mainly caspofungin) from 2005 onwards, during which her initially echinocandin‑susceptible C. albicans isolates evolved a novel double FKS1 hot‑spot 1 mutation (R647R/G and P649P/L) by 2012.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4068606/?utm_source=openai)) Experimental work with clinical and engineered strains demonstrated that this double mutation substantially increased echinocandin MICs in vitro and reduced in vivo responsiveness in a murine disseminated candidiasis model, despite dose escalation. The case highlighted that stepwise accumulation of FKS1 mutations under prolonged drug pressure can produce high‑level resistance even in C. albicans, although such cases remain rare.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very long‑duration echinocandin therapy in a single immunocompromised patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, providing strong and sustained selection pressure for resistance evolution. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance via sequential acquisition of FKS1 hot‑spot mutations culminating in a heterozygous double mutation (R647R/G and P649P/L) in one allele, and demonstration that both heterozygous and homozygous double mutants markedly reduce in vitro and in vivo echinocandin susceptibility; exploration of fitness and virulence showed complex effects rather than simple attenuation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4068606/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Geography and timing were corrected: the double FKS1 mutation case is from Austria (Innsbruck/Vienna centers), not France, and the clinical course with progressive resistance spanned approximately 2005–2012 rather than 2011–2014. The event is appropriately coded as re‑emergence (novel resistance mechanism in an existing pathogen) with no inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence category. Although based on a single patient, it marks the first in vivo‑selected FKS1 double mutation in C. albicans and is mechanistically important enough to retain, but its inclusion as a top‑10 event should be reviewed by a human curator given the small case count.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (immunocompromised patient with invasive candidiasis due to echinocandin‑resistant Candida albicans)
Event summary: In 2017, clinicians in the Republic of Korea reported the country’s first documented case of echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans infection, involving an immunocompromised patient previously exposed to echinocandins.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5587835/?utm_source=openai)) The isolate carried an FKS1 hot‑spot mutation conferring resistance to multiple echinocandins and was associated with clinical failure of standard echinocandin therapy, prompting a switch to alternative treatment. Following this report, Korean mycology laboratories and clinicians enhanced surveillance for echinocandin resistance in Candida species, though subsequent C. albicans cases have remained very uncommon.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing use of echinocandins in Korean tertiary hospitals for prophylaxis and treatment of invasive candidiasis in high‑risk patients (e.g., hematologic malignancies, transplants). Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance via an FKS1 hot‑spot mutation in a locally circulating C. albicans strain, representing regional emergence of a resistance mechanism previously described in North America and Europe; this illustrates convergent evolution of FKS1‑mediated resistance under similar drug‑selection pressures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5587835/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Year corrected to 2017 to match the publication date of the Korean case report; the original 2016 date in the ChatGPT output was not supported by sources. Emergence‑type coding has been revised: this event is a national first report of echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans but not first detection of the species or an inter‑continental emergence of the EPP, so first_detection and inter_continental_emergence are now set to No and the event is classified solely as re‑emergence (drug‑resistant strain). Retain as an important marker of FKS1‑mediated resistance reaching Eastern Asia, but flagged for expert review on its relative impact compared with other surveillance data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (critically ill hospitalized patient with bloodstream infection due to pan‑echinocandin‑resistant Candida albicans acquired during prolonged echinocandin therapy)
Event summary: In May 2020, a 71‑year‑old man admitted to a tertiary hospital ICU in Catania, Italy developed C. albicans bloodstream infection and was treated with caspofungin, after which a subsequent blood culture yielded a pan‑echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans isolate associated with clinical deterioration and death from multiple organ dysfunction syndrome.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8224343/?utm_source=openai)) Sequencing revealed an S645P FKS1 hot‑spot mutation and elevated MICs to caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin, indicating high‑level class resistance. This case, one of the first detailed reports of pan‑echinocandin‑resistant C. albicans bloodstream infection in Europe, underscored that even C. albicans (for which echinocandin resistance remains <1% in surveillance) can occasionally evolve pan‑class resistance under intense drug pressure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8224343/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged echinocandin exposure in a critically ill ICU patient with multiple risk factors for invasive candidiasis (broad‑spectrum antibiotics, invasive devices, colonization at multiple sites). Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance resulting in pan‑echinocandin resistance due to an S645P substitution in Fks1p, coupled with adaptive changes in cell‑wall composition; this mutation pattern is known to markedly reduce echinocandin efficacy and is associated with breakthrough fungemia and treatment failure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8224343/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Year updated to 2020 (the documented admission and infection period in the Italian case report), replacing the original 2017–2019 range that did not match the published clinical timeline. The event is reclassified as re‑emergence only (novel pan‑echinocandin‑resistant strain), with first_detection set to No because C. albicans was long established in Italy. Given the single‑patient nature but high clinical significance (fatal breakthrough fungemia with pan‑class resistance), this event is retained but flagged for expert judgment on whether it ranks among the ten most impactful episodes for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Very low birthweight and preterm neonates in a tertiary hospital neonatal intensive care unit
Event summary:
From 1987 to 1991, a prolonged outbreak of Candida parapsilosis colonization and infection affected the neonatal intensive care unit at the Children’s Hospital, University of Helsinki, with a total of 58 colonized or infected infants; the 1990–1991 period falls within the tail of this episode, during which very low birthweight infants frequently developed C. parapsilosis sepsis and had markedly increased mortality compared with uninfected controls.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) Epidemiologic investigation found C. parapsilosis on the hands of several nurses but not in environmental reservoirs, supporting sustained patient-to-patient transmission in the unit.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak subsided after reinforcement of infection-control measures and the introduction of prolonged parenteral fluconazole prophylaxis for extremely preterm infants, which coincided with cessation of new cases.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Expansion of intensive care for extremely preterm, very low birthweight infants, extensive use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition, and high exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics created a setting highly permissive for exogenous C. parapsilosis transmission in the Helsinki NICU; hand contamination of nurses provided a key transmission route.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific antifungal resistance mechanism was documented during this episode; instead, the outbreak reflected the intrinsic ability of C. parapsilosis to colonize skin and catheter surfaces, form biofilms, and persist as one or a few successful clones in the unit.
Review: review – Added as a new high‑impact event capturing the 1990–1991 portion of a 55‑month NICU outbreak in Helsinki with 58 colonized/infected neonates and high mortality, which is repeatedly cited as a landmark C. parapsilosis outbreak. Classified as re-occurrence (no documented antifungal resistance), with continent/subregion/country fields aligned to the UN scheme. Although the outbreak began in 1987, only the 1990–1991 period is represented here to respect the ≥1990 time window; recommend curator confirmation that including this truncated yet epidemiologically coherent episode is acceptable.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Hospitalized adult patients, predominantly intensive care unit patients receiving central venous catheters and total parenteral nutrition
Event summary:
In 2001, a large outbreak of Candida parapsilosis bloodstream infections occurred in a community hospital in Mississippi, with 22 adult patients (15 confirmed, 7 possible cases) developing candidemia between April and October 2001, mostly among intensive care unit patients receiving total parenteral nutrition and central venous catheters.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing showed that nearly all case isolates belonged to a single clonal strain that also colonized the hands of a health-care worker and exhibited reduced (though not high-level) susceptibility to fluconazole and voriconazole, confirming sustained nosocomial transmission.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Following intensified infection-control measures and reinforcement of hand hygiene, incident cases declined and the outbreak resolved, although related strains continued to be sporadically recovered from blood and catheter tips.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition in ICU patients, suboptimal hand hygiene, and possible contamination of devices created conditions that favored nosocomial transmission of C. parapsilosis in the Mississippi community hospital.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: A single hospital-adapted clone with modestly decreased azole susceptibility and strong adhesion/biofilm capacity on catheters and skin dominated the outbreak, but high-level resistance was not the primary driver; hence the event is interpreted mainly as a control failure (re-occurrence) rather than resistance-driven re-emergence.
Review: retain – Event accurately represents the well-documented 2001 adult community-hospital outbreak in Mississippi (22 bloodstream infections linked to a single clone with moderately elevated fluconazole MICs); geocoding, host description and classification as a re-occurrence driven by ICU care, TPN, and hand transmission are consistent with primary sources, so only a narrative cross-check was needed.

Host: Neonates in a tertiary hospital neonatal intensive care unit
Event summary:
From 2002 through 2008, a tertiary-care university hospital NICU in São Paulo, Brazil, recorded 36 cases of Candida parapsilosis fungemia in neonates, with a marked outbreak peak between 2002 and 2004 when incidence rose to nearly 20 episodes per 1,000 admissions in some years.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) Almost all affected infants were premature, had central venous catheters, and received total parenteral nutrition, and 30-day mortality reached 45%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) An infection-control program was implemented during the outbreak, including reinforcement of catheter care and hand hygiene, after which incidence fell but C. parapsilosis remained an important neonatal pathogen in the unit.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Increased survival of very low birthweight neonates, extensive use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition, prolonged antibiotic exposure, and crowding in the NICU created a highly favorable environment for C. parapsilosis transmission and infection.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific resistance mutation was highlighted; the episode is best interpreted as amplification and persistence of one or more hospital-adapted clones with strong skin and device colonization and biofilm-forming capacity, consistent with a re-occurrence rather than resistance-driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the event window from “2003–2005” to “2002–2008” to match the full 7‑year NICU case series, in which the statistically significant outbreak peak occurred between 2002 and 2004, and simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2002]'. Classification as re-occurrence (no documented antifungal resistance) remains appropriate; event size and mortality justify retaining this outbreak among the largest C. parapsilosis emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Neonates and other hospitalized patients with candidemia, particularly in intensive care and neonatal units
Event summary: From around 2009 onward, South African sentinel surveillance and outbreak investigations documented a striking emergence of fluconazole-resistant Candida parapsilosis causing bloodstream infections, especially in public-sector neonatal units, with fluconazole resistance rates in some centers exceeding 50–60%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11973574/?utm_source=openai)) Many resistant isolates carried the ERG11 Y132F substitution and belonged to clonal lineages that persisted and spread within and between hospitals, making C. parapsilosis the leading cause of neonatal candidemia in some settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11973574/?utm_source=openai)) Despite targeted infection-control and antifungal-stewardship efforts, Y132F-bearing clones remained entrenched into the late 2010s, indicating durable re-emergence of resistant lineages rather than transient outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Heavy reliance on fluconazole for treatment and prophylaxis, combined with high burdens of ICU and neonatal patients with central lines, prolonged hospital stays, and challenges in infection prevention and control, created strong selective pressure and ample opportunity for clonal spread of resistant strains.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11911919/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal expansion of ERG11 Y132F substitutions, often together with additional resistance determinants, conferred high-level fluconazole resistance and sometimes cross-resistance to other azoles, allowing resistant clones to outcompete susceptible strains and persist in hospital environments and on patient skin; this pattern fits a re-emergence driven by novel resistant genotypes.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'South Africa [2009]' while keeping 2009–2020 as the event window for the multi-hospital wave of fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis, which surveillance data show to be among the highest-prevalence FRCP settings worldwide. Classification as re-emergence only (rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence) is consistent with definitions, because the species was long established in Southern Africa and the key novelties are resistant clones and their clonal spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Hospitalized adults with candidemia and other invasive Candida parapsilosis infections, including hematopoietic cell transplant recipients and ICU patients
Event summary:
Analysis of 2,318 Candida parapsilosis isolates collected between roughly 2010 and 2019 from 83 hospitals across China showed that, although overall fluconazole resistance remained low (~2–5%), resistant isolates were clustered in multiple hospitals and belonged to at least 10 clonal genotypes that persisted and transmitted for up to 29 months, many carrying ERG11 Y132F and additional resistance-associated mutations.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10761258/?utm_source=openai)) In parallel, echinocandin susceptibility testing of more than 2,500 C. parapsilosis isolates (2014–2019) identified decreased echinocandin susceptibility in a subset and documented the first pan-echinocandin- and multi-azole-resistant C. parapsilosis bloodstream isolate in China, carrying an FKS1 S656P mutation that conferred high-level echinocandin resistance in functional assays.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9793909/?utm_source=openai)) Together, these findings indicate a re-emergence of C. parapsilosis in Chinese hospitals in a more drug-resistant, clonally expanding form over the 2010s and into the early 2020s.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Increasing use of fluconazole and echinocandins for empiric and prophylactic treatment of invasive candidiasis, rapid growth in the number of high-risk ICU and hematology/oncology patients, and the ability of C. parapsilosis to persist on skin and hospital surfaces favored selection and spread of resistant lineages in Chinese hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10761258/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence of multiple fluconazole-resistant clones harbouring ERG11 Y132F and other azole-resistance mutations with clear evidence of clonal transmission, along with FKS1 hotspot mutations (e.g., S656P) mediating pan-echinocandin resistance in at least one invasive case, exemplify re-emergence driven by new multidrug-resistance mechanisms and enhanced tolerance rather than simple recurrence of susceptible strains.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'China [2010]' but otherwise retained this event, which accurately reflects multi-hospital surveillance demonstrating emergence and clonal transmission of ERG11 Y132F–bearing fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis clones and a rare pan-echinocandin-resistant FKS1 S656P isolate. Classification as re-emergence driven by new resistance mechanisms is consistent with the underlying studies and with the event-definition framework.

Host: Adult intensive care unit patients with candidemia
Event summary:
Between July 2011 and February 2012, a tertiary hospital intensive care unit in Brasília, Brazil, experienced a dramatic increase in candidemia, with 40 cases identified, 28 (70%) caused by fluconazole-resistant Candida parapsilosis that represented a sharp shift from the preceding five-year period.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Molecular analysis showed that most resistant isolates were closely related, consistent with dissemination of a single or few clonal FRCP strains among ICU patients who commonly had diabetes, central lines and prior antifungal exposure. After the outbreak was recognized, reinforcement of infection-control practices, catheter management and antifungal policies led to control of the cluster and a reduction in new fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis candidemia episodes.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High empiric and prophylactic fluconazole use, extensive central venous catheter utilization, and intense patient–health care worker contact in the ICU, particularly among patients with multiple comorbidities, provided strong selective and transmission pressures for a resistant clone.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Internal mechanisms: A hospital-adapted clone of C. parapsilosis with elevated fluconazole MICs, mediated by ERG11 target alterations and/or efflux-related changes, spread within the ICU and re-established the species as a difficult-to-treat pathogen in this setting, fitting the definition of re-emergence via a more drug-resistant lineage.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2011]' and left the 2011–2012 window unchanged; the description matches the published ICU outbreak in Brasília with 28 fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis candidemia cases. Classification as re-emergence (resistant clone) remains appropriate, and the event is of sufficient scale and impact to retain among the top episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Hospitalized adults, especially intensive care unit and surgical patients with invasive candidiasis
Event summary:
From 2012 to 2016, a Brazilian public university hospital medical center documented a prolonged outbreak and clonal persistence of azole-resistant Candida parapsilosis sensu stricto causing invasive candidiasis, particularly in ICU patients, with retrospective analysis revealing that a single dominant resistant clone had silently circulated for several years.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) During this period, C. parapsilosis complex became a leading cause of candidemia in the institution, and a substantial subset of isolates exhibited high MICs to fluconazole and other azoles; genotyping confirmed long-term clonal persistence across ICU and other wards. After recognition of the outbreak and characterization of resistance mechanisms, intensified infection-prevention measures and antifungal stewardship were implemented, which reduced but did not completely eliminate the resistant lineage.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Prolonged hospitalization, widespread use of intravascular catheters, high fluconazole exposure in a resource-limited setting, and unrecognized environmental reservoirs in high-dependency units allowed a resistant clone to persist and spread.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and long-term maintenance of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis sensu stricto clones with ERG11 mutations and likely efflux pump upregulation produced high azole MICs and enabled these clones to outcompete susceptible strains under local drug pressure, representing a clear re-emergence of the species in a more drug-resistant form.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2012]' and retained the 2012–2016 time span, which matches the clonal ICU outbreak and long-term persistence of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis at a Brazilian teaching hospital. Classification as re-emergence, driven by resistant clones documented with ERG11 mutations, is consistent with the primary study; the event remains one of the larger and better-characterized FRCP outbreaks and should be kept.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia
Countries: Italy [2014], Spain (Balearic Islands and other Spanish hospitals) [2015], France [2012], Türkiye [2007]
Host: Hospitalized adults (including ICU, cardiac surgery, oncology, and mixed medical-surgical wards) with candidemia and other invasive candidiasis
Event summary:
From the late 2000s through at least 2022, multiple hospitals in Italy, Spain, France and Türkiye experienced clonal outbreaks and subsequent endemicity of fluconazole-resistant Candida parapsilosis, often in intensive care and high-dependency units, with resistant isolates carrying ERG11 Y132F, K143R or G458S and becoming dominant among C. parapsilosis bloodstream isolates in some centres.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8092880/?utm_source=openai)) In Türkiye, a long-running outbreak at Ege University Hospital (approximately 2007–2019) involved pediatric and adult wards and was driven by Y132F- and Y132F+K143R-harbouring clones that became endemic.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7508617/?utm_source=openai)) In Europe, Italian and French tertiary hospitals reported clonal clusters of Y132F-bearing FRCP from about 2012 onward, and Spanish data from the Balearic Islands and the Madrid CANDIMAD surveillance programme showed a sharp rise in FRCP candidemia after 2015, with hospital-specific resistance rates reaching ≥70% of C. parapsilosis blood isolates in some centres and multiple genotypes spreading within and between hospitals during the COVID-19 era.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8092880/?utm_source=openai)) Collectively, these overlapping outbreaks constitute a prolonged regional re-emergence of fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis in Southern/Western Europe and Western Asia.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Heavy and often prolonged fluconazole use for empiric and targeted therapy in ICUs, surgical and oncology wards; high central-line and device use; overburdened infection-prevention systems (further strained during the COVID-19 pandemic); and frequent patient transfers within regional hospital networks all facilitated amplification and spread of resistant C. parapsilosis clones in Italy, Spain, France and Türkiye.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10634418/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Convergent acquisition and expansion of ERG11 Y132F-, K143R- and G458S-containing lineages, sometimes accompanied by additional resistance determinants (e.g. TAC1 or MRR1 mutations and efflux overexpression), produced high-level fluconazole resistance and, in some hospitals, broader pan-azole non-wild-type phenotypes; genotyping documented clonal transmission within and between hospitals in each of the affected countries, consistent with re-emergence driven by resistant genotypes rather than simple recurrence of susceptible strains.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8092880/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Reframed this row as a regional summary of several large, partially overlapping hospital outbreaks of fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis across Italy, Spain, France and Türkiye rather than a single unified outbreak, and expanded the event window to 2007–2022 to cover the long-running Y132F/K143R/G458S clonal episodes documented in these countries. Updated 'continent' to 'Europe; Asia' and aligned 'sub_regions'/'countries' with the UN classification (placing Türkiye in Western Asia), and changed the event type from 'intra-continental emergence + re-emergence' to 're-emergence only' because the species was already established in all affected subregions and the novelty is resistant genotypes. As this row aggregates distinct but parallel outbreaks, it is retained for now but explicitly flagged for possible future splitting into country-specific events if finer granularity is needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Hospitalized adults and some pediatric patients with invasive candidiasis, many in ICU and emergency services
Event summary:
Between 2014 and 2016, a general hospital in Mexico City (Hospital General Dr. Manuel Gea González) experienced a major increase in invasive candidiasis, with at least 74 cases identified; 38% were due to Candida parapsilosis and more than half of these C. parapsilosis infections were caused by fluconazole-resistant isolates.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8257413/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular analysis showed that many resistant isolates carried the ERG11 Y132F substitution and that microsatellite typing revealed a clonal cluster consistent with a hospital outbreak of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis. Following recognition of the outbreak, strengthened surveillance, infection-control measures and antifungal-stewardship interventions were implemented, which contributed to containment of the resistant cluster and a reduction in new fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis cases.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High case loads in ICU and emergency departments, substantial empirical use of fluconazole, widespread central venous catheter use, complex surgeries and delayed recognition of the outbreak all promoted selection and dissemination of resistant strains within the hospital.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8257413/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and expansion of ERG11 Y132F-mutant C. parapsilosis conferred fluconazole resistance, and some isolates also showed reduced susceptibility to other azoles, consistent with additional ERG11 overexpression or efflux-pump upregulation; these features support classifying the event as re-emergence via a resistant clone rather than simple recurrence.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Mexico [2014]' but otherwise kept this well-supported event, which mirrors the published Mexico City general-hospital outbreak with dozens of invasive candidiasis cases and a dominant ERG11 Y132F fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis clone. Classification as re-emergence is appropriate, and the event clearly ranks among the major FRCP episodes.

Host: Hospitalized patients with candidemia and other invasive or mucosal Candida parapsilosis infections
Event summary:
During a three-year multicentre laboratory-based surveillance study (2015–2017) in nine Indian tertiary hospitals, Candida parapsilosis emerged as a prominent cause of candidemia and other infections, with 32% of 199 isolates found to be non-susceptible to fluconazole and concentrated in clonal clusters in seven hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10512360/?utm_source=openai)) Many fluconazole-non-susceptible isolates carried a novel ERG11 K143R substitution or the previously known Y132F mutation, and genotyping showed two major resistant clusters circulating across multiple centres, indicating ongoing clonal transmission of resistant strains. Publication of these findings led to calls to enhance routine susceptibility testing, infection control, and antifungal stewardship across Indian hospitals.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Extensive use of fluconazole for empiric and prophylactic therapy, high burdens of ICU and post-operative patients with central lines, and limited routine antifungal susceptibility testing and molecular surveillance allowed resistant clones to spread between wards and hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10512360/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of ERG11 K143R in 92% of fluconazole-non-susceptible isolates and of ERG11 Y132F in others directly conferred high azole MICs; genotyping showing multi-hospital clusters is consistent with re-emergence via clonally expanding resistant genotypes.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'India [2015]' and kept the 2015–2017 window, which exactly matches the multicentre surveillance describing high (≈32%) fluconazole non-susceptibility and clonal spread of ERG11 K143R and Y132F mutants. The event is clearly a major resistance-driven re-emergence episode and merits inclusion among the top global events.

Countries: Brazil [2003]; Argentina [2008]; Chile [2008]; Colombia [2008]; Ecuador [2008]; Honduras [2008]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2008]
Host: Hospitalized adults and children with Candida bloodstream infection in tertiary‑care hospitals (Brazilian sentinel network and Latin America Invasive Mycosis Network)
Event summary: From March 2003 through December 2004, a nationwide sentinel surveillance study in 11 tertiary hospitals in nine Brazilian cities identified 712 candidemia cases with an incidence of 2.49 episodes per 1,000 admissions—2–15 times higher than many Northern Hemisphere series—with C. tropicalis the second most common species (20.9%) and a 30‑day mortality of 54%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/1594610/?utm_source=openai)) Building on these findings, the Latin America Invasive Mycosis Network conducted a 24‑month prospective laboratory‑based survey between November 2008 and October 2010 in 21 hospitals across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras and Venezuela, documenting 672 candidemia episodes (overall incidence 1.18/1,000 admissions) in which C. tropicalis accounted for 17.6% of bloodstream infections, particularly among adults, with 30‑day survival around 59%.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0059373&type=printable)) Together, these linked surveys revealed a persistently high regional burden of candidemia in Latin American tertiary hospitals where C. tropicalis is a leading non‑albicans pathogen, prompting region‑specific treatment and prevention recommendations despite generally low azole resistance during this period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high utilization of intensive care, central venous catheters, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, abdominal surgery and oncologic care in resource‑constrained Latin American public hospitals, combined with delays in blood culture diagnosis and limited early access to echinocandins, contributed to high candidemia incidence and mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/1594610/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: during 2003–2010 most C. tropicalis isolates remained susceptible to fluconazole and other triazoles, with only sporadic decreased susceptibility, so this episode reflects a re‑occurrence and consolidation of C. tropicalis as a major bloodstream pathogen driven primarily by host and healthcare‑system factors rather than by a distinct resistant clonal lineage.
Review: Review – New multi‑country Latin American high‑incidence candidemia episode added because previous output omitted Latin America despite very large burdens of candidemia with C. tropicalis comprising ~18–21% of hundreds of bloodstream infections and incidence up to 2.49/1,000 admissions; event is classified as re‑occurrence (species long established in the region, azole resistance still low) and aggregates the Brazil sentinel (2003–2004) and Latin America network (2008–2010) studies as a single linked emergence episode across neighboring countries.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Hospitalized adults and children with bloodstream infection in a tertiary‑care center (New Delhi)
Event summary: Between roughly 2004 and 2008, a large tertiary‑care hospital in New Delhi, India, observed a marked rise in candidaemia due to non‑albicans Candida, with C. tropicalis becoming the single most common species in later years and accounting for around 29% of bloodstream isolates, overtaking C. albicans.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3612330/?utm_source=openai)) This shift occurred alongside increasing ICU admissions, widespread use of central venous catheters and total parenteral nutrition, and heavy empirical fluconazole and broad‑spectrum antibacterial use, and was accompanied by notable fluconazole non‑susceptibility across Candida isolates. Even after the pattern was recognized and antifungal stewardship and catheter care were emphasized, C. tropicalis remained a dominant bloodstream pathogen in this center, signaling a broader regional shift toward non‑albicans Candida candidemia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive care capacity, frequent central venous catheterization, parenteral nutrition, prolonged hospitalization, and broad‑spectrum antibacterial use created ecological niches favoring non‑albicans Candida, particularly C. tropicalis, over C. albicans. Internal mechanisms: sustained exposure to fluconazole and other triazoles selected for more tolerant or less susceptible non‑albicans species, including C. tropicalis, although well‑defined azole‑resistant genotypes had not yet been systematically characterized in this period and resistance appeared polyclonal.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3612330/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This single‑center New Delhi episode captures an early, well‑documented shift from C. albicans to non‑albicans candidemia with C. tropicalis emerging as the leading species and substantial case numbers, appropriately classified as a regional re‑occurrence driven by intensive care expansion and antifungal/antibacterial selective pressure; geography (Southern Asia, India) and timeframe are consistent with the cited surveillance study.

Host: Adult hospitalized patients with C. tropicalis bloodstream infection (National Taiwan University Hospital and other Taiwanese centers)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2017, National Taiwan University Hospital and collaborating centers documented a rising proportion of fluconazole‑nonsusceptible C. tropicalis bloodstream isolates, with many azole‑resistant isolates belonging to a limited set of multilocus sequence types (e.g. DST225, DST506) within a clonal lineage (clade 4).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6711239/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing showed that these fluconazole‑nonsusceptible strains were highly related to each other and to resistant isolates previously reported from mainland China, suggesting regional dissemination of a drug‑resistant clonal population in Eastern Asia. Despite targeted antifungal therapy and infection‑control interventions, resistant C. tropicalis candidemia remained entrenched, highlighting a shift from sporadic resistance to clonal expansion of a high‑risk lineage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense clinical use of triazoles over preceding decades, high burdens of hematologic malignancy and ICU care, and frequent central‑line‑associated bloodstream infections fostered selection and nosocomial spread of azole‑resistant C. tropicalis in Taiwanese hospitals. Internal mechanisms: ERG11 mutations (including Y132F) and overexpression, together with upregulation of efflux pumps, conferred fluconazole and broad azole resistance; multilocus sequence typing and whole‑genome data demonstrated a clonal clade 4 lineage with reduced susceptibility and possible enhanced virulence, representing a clear novel strain/genotype emergence and re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6711239/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a major event but correct geography and event type: the underlying EID study is restricted to Taiwan, so the country list has been narrowed from “China, Taiwan Province of China” to “Taiwan Province of China” only, and the event is now classified solely as re‑emergence driven by a novel azole‑resistant clonal lineage in an already affected Eastern Asia subregion, not as intra‑continental emergence of the species.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans with candidemia and colonization linked to environmental reservoirs in fruit orchards and hospital environments in Taiwan
Event summary: From 2012 to 2018, surveys of mango and other fruit orchards in Taiwan identified widespread contamination by a predominant fluconazole‑resistant C. tropicalis clade 4 genotype that matched the main azole‑resistant lineage causing human candidemia, with detection frequencies increasing over time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11521182/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent hospital environmental surveillance around 2020 found the same genotype persisting in ICU environments, indicating that orchard and healthcare settings formed a linked reservoir for human infection. This multi‑year episode thus represents the establishment of a stable, environmentally and nosocomially maintained azole‑resistant C. tropicalis population that continues to seed invasive human disease despite enhanced surveillance and more cautious azole use.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑term agricultural use of triazole fungicides in Taiwanese orchards, environmental contamination of fruits and soils, and sustained clinical azole prescribing created a One‑Health selection gradient favoring the clade 4 genotype; persistence on hospital surfaces and in ICUs further promoted human exposure and transmission. Internal mechanisms: tandem duplications of ERG11 carrying the Y132F mutation and other ergosterol pathway alterations underlie high‑level azole resistance in clade 4 isolates, and genomic analyses demonstrate that these mutations are stably inherited within an expanding lineage that circulates between environmental niches and human hosts, illustrating novel genotype emergence, enhanced survival, and ecological range expansion within Eastern Asia.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43380-2?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a key One‑Health re‑emergence episode showing environmental and hospital reservoirs of a resistant clade 4 genotype, but intra‑continental emergence has been set to ‘No’ because C. tropicalis was already long established in Eastern Asia; this event reflects expansion and ecological diversification of a resistant lineage, not first occurrence of the species in a new Asian subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Southern Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: India [2014]; China [~2010]; Taiwan Province of China [2011]; Singapore [2009]; Thailand [2010]; Australia [2010]
Host: Hospitalized adults and ICU patients with invasive candidiasis in multicenter Asia‑Pacific hospitals
Event summary: From roughly 2010 onward, and particularly over 2014–2022, multilocus sequence typing and population‑genomic studies showed that an azole‑resistant C. tropicalis clade 4 lineage had become the dominant resistant population across much of the Asia‑Pacific region, being repeatedly recovered from invasive infections in mainland China, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand, India and Australia.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43380-2?utm_source=openai)) In several of these countries, azole resistance among C. tropicalis blood isolates reached 16–30%, with clade 4 accounting for the majority of resistant strains, and clinical series began to report treatment failures and the need to escalate empiric therapy to echinocandins. Despite greater awareness, shifts toward echinocandin‑based regimens and infection‑control efforts, the clade 4 population continued to expand geographically from East and South‑east Asia into South Asia and Oceania, establishing itself as the principal azole‑resistant C. tropicalis lineage in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive medical and agricultural triazole use across Asia‑Pacific, high ICU and oncology case loads, dense healthcare referral and patient‑transfer networks, and limited early molecular surveillance created a permissive environment for selection and spread of resistant clade 4 strains; regional travel and hospital‑to‑hospital transfers likely facilitated dissemination between countries and into Australia.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43380-2?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: ERG11 mutations (notably Y132F) frequently embedded in tandemly duplicated genomic segments, together with efflux pump overexpression and additional adaptive changes, conferred high‑level azole resistance and possibly enhanced virulence; MLST and whole‑genome phylogenies demonstrated that clade 4 is the predominant azole‑resistant population across sampled countries, indicating strong selection and a successful re‑emergent clonal expansion of the species in this region.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43380-2?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a major Asia‑Pacific re‑emergence episode driven by an azole‑resistant clade 4 lineage, but both intra‑continental and inter‑continental emergence flags have been set to ‘No’ because C. tropicalis was already established in all included continents and subregions; under the project definitions, the spread of a new resistant genotype across Asia and into Australia should be classified as re‑emergence of the species rather than first inter‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Hospitalized patients (ICU and non‑ICU) with invasive C. tropicalis infection across 27 hospitals in Delhi National Capital Region and neighboring states
Event summary: Between 2014 and 2022, a multicenter Indian surveillance program across 27 hospitals in Delhi and the surrounding National Capital Region collected 1,016 clinical C. tropicalis isolates and showed that C. tropicalis remained a leading cause of invasive yeast infection, with a substantial fraction demonstrating azole resistance. Whole‑genome sequencing and MLST revealed that a single azole‑resistant clade 4 lineage predominated among resistant isolates and was closely related across hospitals, indicating a smoldering regional outbreak with clonal spread facilitated by patient movement and suboptimal infection‑control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai)) The episode underscored high morbidity and mortality, treatment challenges and the need for routine species‑level identification and susceptibility testing, leading to recommendations for more restrictive azole use and enhanced fungal stewardship in Indian hospitals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high candidemia incidence in Indian ICUs and wards, widespread empiric fluconazole use, delays in accurate species identification, frequent patient transfers among Delhi‑NCR hospitals and limited early fungal stewardship promoted the rise and persistence of the clade 4 lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: clade 4 isolates harbored ERG11 mutations, copy‑number variation and transcriptional changes that increased azole resistance and upregulated virulence‑associated genes (e.g. adhesins, secreted proteases), consistent with emergence and regional dissemination of a specific high‑risk genotype with enhanced pathogenicity and transmission fitness.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a key Indian re‑emergence event dominated by clade 4, but re‑occurrence has been set to ‘No’ so that this episode is classified purely as re‑emergence driven by a novel resistant and virulent lineage; this aligns with project rules that re‑emergence (pathogen change) should not be conflated with re‑occurrence (purely external drivers) and reflects the genomic focus of the underlying mBio study.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Critically ill adult and pediatric ICU patients with ICU‑acquired candidemia across a multicenter Indian ICU network
Event summary: From approximately 2018 through the early 2020s, multicenter ICU surveillance in India, including a large network of ICUs monitored before and during the COVID‑19 pandemic, reported that C. tropicalis accounted for roughly 25–45% of ICU‑acquired candidemia episodes and was often the single most common Candida species, with 30–60% mortality in high‑risk groups.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39278818/?utm_source=openai)) These studies documented increasing proportions of non‑albicans Candida, high azole resistance and frequent need for echinocandin therapy; many C. tropicalis infections developed within 1–2 weeks of ICU admission and were linked to invasive procedures, broad‑spectrum antibiotic and corticosteroid use, and strained infection‑prevention resources during COVID‑19 surges. The episode represents a sustained, high‑burden re‑occurrence of C. tropicalis candidemia in Indian ICUs within an already clade‑4‑dominated resistance landscape.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensification and expansion of ICU care (including for COVID‑19), very high use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids, heavy reliance on central venous catheters and mechanical ventilation, and pandemic‑related pressures on staffing and infection‑prevention programs all promoted Candida colonization, transmission and progression to candidemia, with national surveillance indicating cross‑facility dissemination of high‑risk clones.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39278818/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: continued selection and spread of azole‑resistant clade 4 and other resistant lineages underlie rising non‑susceptibility, but by this period those genotypes were already established; this ICU‑focused event is therefore classified as re‑occurrence, driven largely by external clinical and health‑system stressors rather than by the first appearance of a new C. tropicalis genotype.
Review: Review – Retain as a distinct ICU‑focused high‑burden episode but reclassify it as re‑occurrence only: the excess burden of C. tropicalis candidemia during 2018–2023, especially around the COVID‑19 period, is best explained by external factors (ICU expansion, broad antibiotic and steroid use, infection‑control strain) acting on an already established resistant clonal background, rather than by emergence of a new genotype. This avoids double‑counting clade 4 emergence, which is captured in the 2014–2022 Delhi‑NCR and Asia‑Pacific events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America; Canada; Argentina; Brazil; Chile; Colombia; Uruguay
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with bloodstream infections in SENTRY-participating centers in the United States, Canada and several South American countries)
Event summary: During 1997–1998, the SENTRY Antimicrobial Surveillance Program documented Candida glabrata as the second most common cause of candidemia overall in North America, with its proportion of bloodstream infections increasing between 1997 and 1998 in the United States, Canada, and South American centers. This period marked an early shift away from Candida albicans toward non‑albicans species in many hospitals; in South America C. glabrata remained relatively infrequent but was present. By the end of this initial SENTRY period, C. glabrata was recognized as an important cause of candidemia in North America and an emerging contributor in South America, setting the stage for later resistance‑driven re‑emergence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rising use of fluconazole and other triazoles for prophylaxis and treatment in high‑risk hospitalized patients, broader deployment of central venous catheters, expansion of intensive care, and growing populations of elderly and immunocompromised patients favoured species that tolerate azole exposure. Internal mechanisms: C. glabrata has intrinsically higher azole minimum inhibitory concentrations and robust stress-response systems, allowing it to persist and increase in relative frequency under azole and antibiotic selection without requiring widespread new resistance mutations; this pattern is best interpreted as re‑occurrence (species shift) rather than emergence of a novel resistant lineage.
Review: review – Retain this as a major late‑1990s Americas episode but reclassify it as re-occurrence (species-level shift under azole and ICU selection pressure, without clear evidence for a new C. glabrata strain), correct the sub-region coding to “Northern America; South America” and the country list to the South American nations explicitly reported for SENTRY 1997 (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay; Mexico and Venezuela removed), and replace generic/Wikipedia links with primary SENTRY and CDC/clinical review sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (adults with candidemia identified through population-based surveillance in metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia, and Baltimore, Maryland, and in other North American hospital registries)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the early 2000s, U.S. population-based surveillance in metropolitan areas such as Atlanta and Baltimore showed a 10–40% increase in candidemia incidence together with a species shift toward non‑albicans Candida, particularly Candida glabrata. Around 2000–2005, C. glabrata accounted for roughly one quarter to one third of adult candidemia cases in many North American centers, and azole-resistant isolates became more common, establishing a high baseline burden of C. glabrata disease before echinocandins came into widespread first-line use.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased survival of patients with cancer, transplants, complex abdominal surgery, and other immunosuppressive conditions; extensive use of broad-spectrum antibacterials; central venous catheterization; and prolonged fluconazole prophylaxis all favoured non‑albicans species over C. albicans. Internal mechanisms: C. glabrata’s intrinsically reduced fluconazole susceptibility, together with the capacity to acquire azole-resistance mechanisms (e.g. PDR1 gain-of-function and efflux pump upregulation), enabled the species to expand under azole pressure; this episode is classified as re‑emergence because it reflects both external drivers and the increasing contribution of azole‑resistant C. glabrata to the candidemia burden.
Review: review – Retain this episode as an early‑2000s North American emergence of C. glabrata as a leading cause of candidemia and rising azole resistance; keep the re-emergence classification but clarify in the text that it reflects both external drivers and increasing azole resistance. Updated the Source URLs to emphasize the 1998–2000 U.S. population-based candidemia study, the MD Anderson hematogenous candidiasis paper, the MMWR surveillance summary, and a focused C. glabrata resistance review, and removed a generic Wikipedia link.

Continent: North America; South America; Europe; Asia; Oceania

Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with Candida bloodstream infections enrolled in the global SENTRY Antimicrobial Surveillance Program)
Event summary: In 2008–2009, the global SENTRY Antimicrobial Surveillance Program collected Candida bloodstream isolates from medical centers across North America, Latin America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Oceania and found that Candida glabrata isolates had the highest rates of resistance to both echinocandins and azoles among Candida species, with echinocandin resistance around 2–3% and azole resistance roughly 3.5–5.6% and the highest rates in North America. This period provided the first clear global documentation of C. glabrata strains with clinically meaningful resistance to first‑line echinocandins in addition to azoles, establishing C. glabrata as the main Candida species of concern for emerging dual azole–echinocandin resistance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid global uptake of echinocandins as first‑line therapy for invasive candidiasis in settings where C. glabrata had already become common, high antifungal exposure in intensive care and oncology units, and widespread use of indwelling devices and broad‑spectrum antibacterials in tertiary hospitals created strong selection for resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of hot‑spot mutations in FKS genes encoding the β‑1,3‑D-glucan synthase target of echinocandins, often in isolates already harbouring azole‑resistance mechanisms, produced multidrug‑resistant C. glabrata and marked a clear re‑emergence of the pathogen in a more treatment‑refractory form.

Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with Candida glabrata bloodstream infections at a large U.S. tertiary-care center)
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2010, a longitudinal study of 313 Candida glabrata bloodstream isolates at Duke University Hospital documented an increase in echinocandin resistance from 4.9% to 12.3% and an increase in fluconazole resistance from 18% to 30%. Many echinocandin‑resistant isolates harboured FKS1 or FKS2 mutations, and episodes involving these mutants were frequently associated with clinical failure when echinocandins were continued, highlighting the emergence of multidrug-resistant C. glabrata at a single U.S. tertiary-care center.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Stepwise antifungal therapy (long-term or repeated fluconazole use followed by echinocandin treatment), high antifungal consumption in oncology and transplant units, and concentrations of patients with central venous catheters and severe comorbidities created intense selection pressure for resistance. Internal mechanisms: Sequential acquisition of azole-resistance mechanisms (such as PDR1 gain-of-function mutations leading to efflux pump overexpression) followed by FKS1/FKS2 hot‑spot mutations conferring echinocandin resistance enabled C. glabrata to become multidrug‑resistant within individual patients and to persist or recur despite therapy, a prototypical re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major re-emergence episode documenting increasing echinocandin and multidrug resistance in C. glabrata at a large U.S. tertiary center. The timing, geography and re-emergence classification are appropriate. The Source URLs were tightened to emphasize the Duke 2001–2010 cohort and echinocandin-resistance reviews, dropping a generic ScienceDirect topic page.
