Countries: Brazil [2006] (Maranhão State; residential community in São Luís)
Host: Humans (residents, domestic workers, and employees in a gated community)
Event summary: In 2006, an infectious-disease specialist in São Luís, Maranhão, reported several acute toxoplasmosis cases among residents of a gated residential community, prompting a municipal and zoonoses-surveillance investigation. Of 110 residents, domestic workers, and employees interviewed, 90 agreed to serologic testing; 33 persons met a case definition for acute/recent toxoplasmosis, and all cases reported consuming water filtered by faucet‑mount or ceramic household filters, whereas bottled water use was less frequent. Environmental testing did not recover T. gondii from water or local cats, but epidemiologic analysis implicated a waterborne source related to well water used in the community and filtered at the point of use. Following public-health advice on water treatment and filter hygiene, and as exposed persons recovered, no further clusters were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of intermittently supplied well and public water with simple point-of-use filters, inadequate protection of water storage and distribution against fecal contamination, and limited awareness of oocyst resistance to routine chlorination and filtration, leading to waterborne transmission within a single residential complex. Internal mechanisms: Standard oocyst-borne infection via drinking water, with no evidence of a new parasite genotype or host shift; thus classified as re-occurrence linked primarily to infrastructural and behavioral factors.
Review: Retain. This 33‑case gated-community outbreak is one of the better-documented medium-sized waterborne events and is discussed in depth in a 2019 reanalysis. The main corrections are (i) to emphasize that the outbreak was concluded to be waterborne with a strong association to faucet-mount filtered water, and (ii) to provide the specific number of acute cases (33). Classification as re-occurrence is maintained. Flagged for review because the original summary underplayed the evidence for a waterborne source and overstated uncertainty.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2006] (São Paulo State; São Paulo city and Guarujá)
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming a raw beef dish, steak tartare)
Event summary: In November 2006, public health officials in São Paulo State investigated an outbreak of acute toxoplasmosis among people who had eaten at restaurants in São Paulo city and Guarujá. A field investigation and case–control study identified consumption of a raw-beef dish (steak tartare) at specific establishments as the main risk factor, and a small number of exposed diners developed clinically compatible illness with serologic evidence of recent infection. Withdrawal of the implicated meat batches and advisories discouraging consumption of uncooked beef were followed by an absence of further cases linked to this episode.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Serving and consumption of raw or undercooked beef prepared from carcasses of infected cattle, without freezing or other inactivation steps, in a context of changing culinary practices and varying background seroprevalence. Internal mechanisms: Meat-borne transmission via tissue cysts in beef, a well-established route for T. gondii; there is no evidence for a novel strain or host adaptation, so this small cluster is categorized as re-occurrence driven by food-handling and preparation practices rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. The outbreak is real and correctly geographically and temporally placed, and the principal source (Boletim Epidemiológico Paulista) is appropriate. However, it involved only a handful of cases (EID’s outbreak table lists a 6‑case beef-associated event for 2006 in Brazil), well below the scale of other events now included (e.g., Santa Isabel, Coimbatore, Izmir, açaí-related outbreaks). The key correction is reclassifying it from re-emergence to re-occurrence, because there is no evidence of parasite change—only meat-borne transmission via an already known route. Recommended: keep only if smaller foodborne clusters are desired for transmission-pattern illustration; otherwise mark for exclusion in a strictly “largest-impact outbreaks” list.
Review Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

Countries: Brazil [2009] (São Paulo State; large industrial plant)
Host: Humans (industrial-plant employees consuming cafeteria meals)
Event summary: In 2009, an industrial plant in São Paulo State with roughly 2,300 employees reported a cluster of workers with acute febrile illness compatible with toxoplasmosis. Investigation identified nine symptomatic and three asymptomatic employees with recent T. gondii infection (11 acute infections total) and used a case–control design to compare food and water exposures among 11 cases and 20 seronegative controls. Only consumption of green leafy vegetables from the factory cafeteria was significantly associated with illness, suggesting contamination of fresh produce by oocysts during production or handling. After reinforcing produce washing practices and reviewing supplier hygiene, no further clusters attributable to the cafeteria were observed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mass catering using raw green vegetables that had likely been contaminated with oocysts via irrigation water, soil, or handling, in the absence of adequate washing and sanitation procedures, allowed a small but clear foodborne outbreak in a large workforce. Internal mechanisms: Oocyst-borne transmission on fresh produce, highlighting an under-recognized food vehicle for toxoplasmosis; there is no evidence of a new genotype or altered virulence, so this is classified as re-occurrence driven by food-safety lapses.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. Corrections made: (i) clarified the year as 2009 (not “~2010”), in line with the primary case–control report and the CDC outbreak review; (ii) corrected the scale to 11 acute infections (rather than implying that “many” of the 2,300 workers became ill); and (iii) reclassified the event from re-emergence to re-occurrence, as the outbreak reflects a known route (oocyst-contaminated vegetables) without demonstrated parasite change. The outbreak is epidemiologically important for highlighting vegetable-borne transmission but is small in absolute impact relative to the major events now included.
Review Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

Host: Humans (family and close contacts sharing a lamb meal)
Event summary: In November 2010, public health authorities in Aveyron, southern France, investigated a cluster of acute toxoplasmosis among persons who had shared a family meal. Several attendees developed febrile lymphadenitis and serologic evidence of recent infection, and the common exposure identified was a single meal featuring undercooked lamb. No further spread beyond the exposed group occurred, and control actions focused on clinical follow-up—particularly of women of childbearing age—and reinforcing advice on thoroughly cooking lamb and other meats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cultural preference for rare or undercooked lamb and entry of infected small-ruminant meat into the food chain, combined with a population in which baseline immunity to T. gondii may be declining. Internal mechanisms: Conventional meat-borne transmission via tissue cysts in lamb, with no evidence of a novel genotype or shift in virulence; appropriately classified as a localized re-occurrence driven by food-preparation practices.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. This small family/meal-associated outbreak is correctly located and classified and uses high-quality national surveillance and peer‑reviewed sources. However, the number of affected persons is low compared with large Brazilian and Asian outbreaks and even some medium-sized waterborne events; it is not among the ten largest post‑1990 events by case count or geographic scope. Recommended: retain only if the dataset aims to illustrate diverse meat-borne scenarios; otherwise mark for exclusion in a strictly impact-focused list.
Review Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

Countries: Brazil [2011] (Rondônia State; Ji-Paraná, Ouro Preto do Oeste, Jaru)
Host: Humans (municipal residents consuming açaí juice)
Event summary: In 2011, Brazil’s Ministry of Health investigated a large outbreak of acute toxoplasmosis in three municipalities of Rondônia State—Ji‑Paraná, Ouro Preto do Oeste, and Jaru—after numerous residents presented with febrile lymphadenopathy. The investigation documented at least 141 persons with clinical and serologic profiles compatible with recent T. gondii infection, making it one of the largest non‑waterborne outbreaks recorded. Epidemiologic analysis implicated consumption of açaí juice prepared from pulp acquired outside the local production season as the common exposure, suggesting contamination with oocysts during harvesting or processing in endemic forest areas. Public health responses included enhanced surveillance, guidance to açaí vendors on hygienic processing, and community education, after which new cases declined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High consumption of raw açaí juice, sourcing of fruit from external producers during a period when local production was minimal, and insufficient sanitary controls in harvesting and pulping created conditions for contamination of açaí with T. gondii oocysts. Internal mechanisms: Typical oocyst-borne transmission via fruit beverages in a highly endemic Amazonian setting; no specific novel genotype was characterized in this investigation, so this event is considered a large-scale re-occurrence rather than confirmed re-emergence.
Review: Retain (added). This ≈141‑case multi-municipality outbreak linked to açaí consumption is described in detail in Brazilian public-health literature and highlighted in the CDC review as an example of large oocyst-borne outbreaks outside water systems. It was missing from the original dataset despite clearly ranking among the largest recent outbreaks by case count. Geography (South America | South America | Brazil, with Rondônia municipalities) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. Flagged for review primarily because detailed Ministry of Health bulletins were not directly accessed; if those are later obtained, case numbers and municipal breakdowns can be refined.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Brazil [2013] (Pará State; Ponta de Pedras, Marajó archipelago)
Host: Humans (municipality residents consuming açaí juice)
Event summary: In May 2013, clinicians and the municipal health service in Ponta de Pedras, in Pará State’s Marajó archipelago, noted several patients with febrile lymphadenopathy whose serology indicated acute toxoplasmosis, raising suspicion of an outbreak. A field investigation evaluated 270 residents and identified 73 individuals with clinical and laboratory profiles consistent with recent T. gondii infection; geospatial analysis showed strong clustering around three main points of sale for açaí juice. Consumption of açaí was the only exposure strongly associated with illness, and contamination of the juice with oocysts during fruit handling and pulping was considered the most plausible source. After intensified hygiene measures at açaí production sites and public education, incident cases subsided.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional consumption of raw açaí juice, use of processing practices that allow contamination of fruit with oocysts from cats or wild felids, and high demand during a period when fruit may have been sourced from areas with intense environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: Oocyst-borne transmission via açaí beverages, in line with an emerging pattern of Amazonian foodborne outbreaks; no confirmed novel genotype was reported in this specific outbreak, so it is treated as re-occurrence.
Review: Retain (added). This well-documented 73‑case outbreak, confirmed serologically and analyzed with geo-statistical methods, is explicitly featured in the CDC outbreak review as a representative example of açaí-associated toxoplasmosis. It clearly falls within the top tier of events by case count and public-health attention. Geography (Brazil, Pará, Marajó archipelago) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. Sources from the Pan-Amazonian Journal of Health and the CDC review are relevant and should be kept.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [2017] (Midwestern hunting retreat area); Canada [2018] (Quebec hunters returning from USA)
Host: Humans (deer hunters and family members consuming undercooked white-tailed deer meat)
Event summary: In November–December 2017, a group of hunters attending a deer-hunting retreat in the Midwestern United States consumed freshly prepared venison that was served rare; eight of ten attendees developed febrile illness with headache and myalgia, and all eight had serologic evidence of recently acquired T. gondii infection. In 2018, public health authorities in Quebec investigated several returning hunters with similar syndromes, ultimately linking their illnesses to consumption of undercooked venison from white‑tailed deer hunted in the same region and season. The outbreak underscored the risk posed by North American wildlife strains and the importance of thoroughly cooking wild game meat; communication campaigns and hunter-targeted guidance followed, and no further cases associated with this particular retreat were reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cultural practices of consuming freshly hunted deer meat rare or undercooked at hunting retreats, limited awareness of toxoplasmosis risk from venison, and circulation of T. gondii in white‑tailed deer populations. Internal mechanisms: Meat-borne infection with wildlife-associated T. gondii haplotypes common in North American cervids, causing sometimes severe but self-limited disease in immunocompetent adults; available data do not establish recent parasite evolution, so the event is best characterized as a notable re-occurrence highlighting a wildlife transmission cycle rather than confirmed re-emergence.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. This venison-associated outbreak is well documented and important for demonstrating the role of North American wildlife strains and hunting practices, but it involved only eight confirmed acute cases and is therefore small relative to the largest outbreaks. The main correction is to reclassify it from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since haplogroup 12 and other wildlife genotypes pre‑dated this event and there is no clear evidence of a new host jump or novel strain emerging at this time. Retain only if the dataset aims to capture illustrative wildlife/meat-borne clusters; otherwise consider exclusion.
Review Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

Countries: Brazil [2018] (Rio Grande do Sul State; Santa Maria)
Host: Humans (citywide population, including many pregnant women and newborns)
Event summary: In early 2018, Santa Maria, a city in Rio Grande do Sul, experienced a rapidly growing number of residents with febrile illness, lymphadenopathy, and serologic evidence of acute toxoplasmosis. By mid‑2018, state and municipal bulletins reported over 800 laboratory-confirmed recent infections and more than a thousand notifications overall, with hundreds of suspected or confirmed gestational cases and numerous congenitally infected newborns; the event has been described as the largest recorded outbreak of human toxoplasmosis. Intensive investigation suggested contamination of widely consumed food or water, and multiple studies isolated and genotyped T. gondii from human placentas, amniotic fluid, and animal sources, identifying highly virulent strains associated with severe fetal outcomes. Public health actions included mandatory notification of gestational and congenital toxoplasmosis, expanded prenatal screening and treatment, targeted environmental and food investigations, and extensive risk-communication campaigns.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High background environmental contamination with oocysts, dense domestic cat populations, complex food supply chains, and previously incomplete prenatal screening programs, in combination with one or more contaminated citywide food or water vehicles, enabled extensive exposure of reproductive-age women and the general population. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of highly virulent, atypical T. gondii genotypes in southern Brazil, demonstrated by isolation and genetic characterization from placental tissue and other specimens, with strong association to severe congenital disease and fetal demise—an archetypal re-emergence episode driven by genotype and virulence in a large urban population.
Review: Retain. The Santa Maria outbreak is widely recognized as the largest documented human toxoplasmosis outbreak, with several hundred to >800 confirmed acute cases and major gestational and congenital impact, and is therefore unquestionably among the top events by impact. Classification as re-emergence is appropriate given repeated isolation of atypical, highly virulent genotypes from human placentas and strong associations with severe fetal disease. Geography and timelines are correct; additional Brazilian state and municipal bulletins have been implicitly incorporated to refine case numbers but not individually listed as URLs to avoid redundancy. No structural corrections beyond clarifying approximate confirmed case counts and emphasizing its scale were necessary.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (rural residents and farmers in multiple Chinese provinces; principal reservoir Apodemus agrarius)
Event summary: From 1994 to 1998, China experienced a large national cluster of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), with statistically significant high-incidence spatial clusters in many rural counties across northeastern, central and eastern provinces where Hantaan virus is enzootic in Apodemus agrarius. The epidemic period was characterized by thousands of reported human cases annually and clear geographic clustering of high-risk counties, reflecting intense human–rodent contact in agricultural landscapes. Incidence declined somewhat after the late 1990s as vaccination, improved housing, and rodent control programs were expanded, although HFRS remained endemic in many of the same foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: agricultural expansion and intensification, high rodent (Apodemus agrarius) densities in rural fields and peri-domestic settings, and climatic variability influencing rodent population dynamics and human exposure patterns; improvements in surveillance also increased case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence for a novel HTNV genotype dominating this period—disease resurgence is best explained by ecological and socio-environmental factors rather than a major viral shift, so this is classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain: Correctly represents the mid‑1990s national HFRS cluster in mainland China based on spatial analysis of 1994–1998 surveillance data, with China as the only affected country in the event and HTNV long-established there; classification as a large re-occurrence (rather than intra-continental emergence) is appropriate and sources are well chosen.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans in multiple Chinese provinces (notably Shaanxi, Heilongjiang, Inner Mongolia and other northeastern and central provinces)
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2019, China reported 199,799 HFRS cases nationwide, with the burden concentrated in traditional HTNV-endemic areas of northeastern and north-central China and in emerging high-incidence clusters such as Shaanxi and parts of Inner Mongolia. The epidemic exhibited pronounced spatial–temporal clustering, with recurrent seasonal peaks and intensification of disease in several high-risk regions despite long-standing endemicity and vaccination programs. Toward the end of this period, some regions showed declining incidence attributed to expanded vaccination and rodent control, but others continued to experience substantial case numbers, maintaining HTNV-associated HFRS as a major public health problem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: changing agricultural practices, rapid urbanization at rural fringes, climatic fluctuations that favored rodent population booms, and demographic shifts (e.g., migrant workers) increasing exposure in high-risk landscapes, along with incomplete vaccine coverage and variable implementation of environmental management. Internal mechanisms: HFRS in China during this period was caused mainly by Hantaan and Seoul viruses; while phylogenetic analyses show regional HTNV lineages, there is no strong evidence that a single novel high-virulence genotype drove the nationwide burden, so this period is best characterized as a large-scale re-occurrence linked to ecological and socio-economic drivers.
Review: retain: Correctly summarizes the 2004–2019 national HFRS burden in China (≈200,000 cases) and identifies high-incidence HTNV-dominated provinces; treating this long, spatially structured epidemic as a single major re-occurrence episode is consistent with the project rules for linked multi-year episodes, though users could further subdivide it if more granular ranking of peaks is needed.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (college students and surrounding community in Xi’an, Shaanxi Province)
Event summary: From 2005 onwards, Xi’an City in Shaanxi Province experienced an increasing risk of HFRS associated with Hantaan virus, culminating in a documented outbreak among college students in 2012 in the northern urban area of the city. The outbreak involved multiple confirmed HFRS cases in students and residents; molecular typing of viruses from patients and local rodents showed they were all Hantaan virus closely related to strains circulating in the region since at least the 1980s. Following the outbreak, targeted HFRS vaccination of incoming freshmen and enhanced rodent control and education campaigns were implemented, which contributed to a reduction in cases in subsequent years in that campus population, although the wider region remained endemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of rodent reservoirs (Apodemus agrarius and commensal rodents) in and around student dormitories and campus green areas, suboptimal rodent-proofing and hygiene, and low initial vaccine coverage among students (0.29% in one college versus 72% in another). Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis showed the HTNV strains were closely related to earlier regional strains rather than representing a novel genotype with markedly increased virulence, so the event reflects re-occurrence driven by ecological conditions and gaps in vaccination rather than viral re-emergence.
Review: retain: Accurately reflects the 2012 Xi’an college outbreak (6 student cases, 2 deaths) and the broader 2005–2012 increase in HFRS risk around Xi’an, with virologic confirmation of HTNV and clear ecological and vaccination drivers; scale is modest but justified as a well-characterized urban re-occurrence hotspot rather than a new emergence, so the classification is appropriate.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (civilians and military personnel in multiple regions of the Republic of Korea, including newly affected southwestern areas)
Event summary: Between 1999 and 2003, reported HFRS cases in the Republic of Korea increased compared with the early 1990s, with 392 cases reported in 2003 and a notable shift in the geographic pattern of disease to include a substantial number of cases in the southwestern part of the country, in addition to traditional endemic areas near the Demilitarized Zone. The rise affected both civilians and military personnel and reflected wider spatial distribution of HTNV-infected rodents and human exposure. Ongoing use of inactivated Hantaan/Seoul vaccines, improved clinical management and public health education helped to stabilize incidence after the early 2000s, although year‑to‑year fluctuations persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: changes in land use and agricultural practices, urban expansion into rural rodent habitats, and favorable climate and food availability for Apodemus agrarius may have allowed HTNV-infected rodent populations to expand into new parts of South Korea, while broader recognition and surveillance also increased reported case numbers. Internal mechanisms: available data implicate endemic HTNV and Seoul virus without clear evidence of a novel genotype, so the event is considered a re-occurrence and geographic range expansion within the same UNSD subregion (Eastern Asia), rather than a distinct intra-continental emergence to a new subregion.
Review: retain: Supported by Korean surveillance data showing an increase to 392 reported HFRS cases in 2003 with a shift toward southwestern regions, and consistent with HTNV/SEOV co-circulation; treating this as a re-occurrence with intra-national range expansion (but not intra-continental emergence, since all locations remain in the same UNSD subregion of Eastern Asia) is appropriate.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (rural residents in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, especially northeastern districts)
Event summary: From 2000 to 2006, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in northern China was part of a second major regional HFRS epidemic: reported cases in the region peaked at 661 in 2000, the highest annual total on record there, and substantial numbers of cases continued in the early 2000s with marked spatial clustering. Phylogenetic analyses indicated that Hantaan virus was the principal cause of HFRS in northeastern Inner Mongolia, while Seoul virus predominated in central and western districts that first reported HFRS in the mid-1990s. During 2003–2006, targeted rodent and virologic surveys confirmed widespread circulation of HTNV in Apodemus agrarius in the northeast and SEOV in Norway rats elsewhere. Subsequently, rodent surveillance and public health interventions were strengthened, helping to delineate endemic foci and inform control efforts, although HFRS remained an important zoonosis in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: agricultural expansion and human settlement in grassland and forest–steppe habitats harboring Apodemus agrarius, along with climate-driven rodent population fluctuations, created favorable conditions for HTNV transmission to humans; enhanced surveillance in 2003–2006 also increased detection of cases and virus diversity, especially in newly affected central and western districts. Internal mechanisms: multiple hantaviruses were found co-circulating in rodents, including distinct HTNV lineages, but available data point to ongoing circulation and spread of existing HTNV variants rather than emergence of a radically novel strain, so the event is categorized as a large regional re-occurrence with geographic intensification in established and newly recognized HTNV-endemic zones.
Review: review: Original row dated the event as 2001–2006, but the Inner Mongolia analysis shows that the second major regional HFRS epidemic peaked at 661 cases in 2000 and that 2003–2006 rodent surveys documented HTNV and SEOV circulation; the time window has been adjusted to 2000–2006 and the summary updated to emphasize the 2000 peak and subsequent outbreaks, while retaining the classification as re-occurrence within an already endemic Chinese subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (sporadic HFRS patients and seropositive residents in northern and southern Vietnam) and rodents (Rattus norvegicus carrying Seoul virus; Niviventer confucianus carrying Hantaan-orthologous Da Bie Shan strains)
Event summary: Beginning with the first clinically recognized autochthonous HFRS case in Vietnam in 2008, in a nurse from Ho Chi Minh City infected by a Seoul virus–like hantavirus, subsequent serologic surveys in northern Vietnam identified low but measurable antibody prevalence against Hantaan 76–118 and Puumala antigens among residents and port workers. In the 2010s, molecular studies of rodents captured in northern Vietnam demonstrated Seoul virus circulation in Rattus norvegicus and, later, detection of Hantaan orthohantavirus Da Bie Shan–lineage sequences in Chinese white-bellied rats (Niviventer confucianus), showing that HTNV-lineage viruses had established in local rodent reservoirs in mainland Southeast Asia. Human HFRS cases attributable specifically to HTNV remain rare and often serologically cross-reactive, but together these findings mark the first confirmed ecological and likely low-level human presence of Old World hantaviruses, including HTNV-lineage viruses, in the UNSD South-eastern Asia subregion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased human encroachment into agricultural and peri-urban habitats in northern and southern Vietnam, trade and movement of commensal rodents across borders with China and through ports, and historically limited awareness and diagnostic capacity for HFRS likely facilitated the silent establishment and under-recognition of hantaviruses before their formal detection. Internal mechanisms: detection of Hantaan orthhantavirus Da Bie Shan strain in Niviventer confucianus represents geographic range expansion and host-range flexibility within the HTNV lineage, while human disease in Vietnam has thus far been dominated by Seoul virus; available data do not show a major change in virulence or transmissibility in humans compared with classic East Asian HTNV, so this event is classified primarily as intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion (South-eastern Asia) rather than as re-emergence driven by viral evolution.
Review: review: Kept as an intra-continental emergence event because it captures the first recognized human HFRS case in Vietnam (2008, due to Seoul virus) together with later confirmation of Hantaan-lineage Da Bie Shan virus in local rodents, marking extension of HTNV-lineage ecology into South-eastern Asia; however, HTNV-specific human disease burden remains very small and the event’s impact is modest compared with Chinese and Korean outbreaks. The sub_regions field has been restricted to South-eastern Asia and the countries field to Viet Nam [2008], dropping China because HTNV was already long established there; Wikipedia has been removed from the event-specific source list in favor of primary articles. Because attribution of human cases to HTNV versus SEOV is uncertain and the event is driven largely by rodent data, this row is flagged for expert review rather than unconditional retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Australia and New Zealand; Northern America; Western Europe
Countries: Japan [early 1990s]; Philippines [early 1990s]; Thailand [early-mid 1990s]; China [1990s]; Australia [mid-1990s]; United States of America (Hawaii [early 1990s–2000], California [1997–2002], other states [2000s]); United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [mid-late 1990s]; other Western European countries [late 1990s–2000s]
Host: Humans (sexually transmitted infection in heterosexual and MSM populations)
Event summary: From the early 1990s, fluoroquinolone-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae emerged in East and South‑East Asia and the Western Pacific and was soon detected in Hawaii and other parts of the United States, largely among infections linked to travel in Asia. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s and early 2000s these resistant lineages became established across Asia and Oceania and then in Northern America and Western Europe, with rapidly rising resistance proportions in sites such as Honolulu, California and the United Kingdom. By about 2007, fluoroquinolone resistance exceeded stewardship thresholds in many settings, leading countries (including a 2007 national change in US CDC guidelines) to stop recommending fluoroquinolones for gonorrhoea and leaving extended‑spectrum cephalosporins as the only routinely recommended class.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy and often indiscriminate use of fluoroquinolones to treat gonorrhoea and many other community infections in East/South‑East Asia and later globally; high partner change rates and dense sexual networks facilitating rapid dissemination; international travel and sex tourism linking Asian epicentres with Hawaii, North America and Europe. Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation of mutations in gyrA and parC conferring high‑level fluoroquinolone resistance; selection and clonal expansion of successful resistant lineages with adequate fitness that could compete with susceptible strains.
Review: Review – Major global emergence of fluoroquinolone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae correctly identified and supported by primary sources. Corrected the continent label to use 'Northern America', extended the end year to 2007 to reflect the US CDC decision to stop recommending fluoroquinolones, and reclassified the episode purely as re-emergence (removed intra- and inter-continental emergence) because resistance arose within an already global pathogen.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [early 1990s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990s]; Sweden [late 1990s]; other Western/Northern European countries [1990s–2000s]
Host: Humans (primarily men who have sex with men in urban centres)
Event summary: Across the 1990s, several Western and Northern European countries reported declining gonorrhoea incidence in the general population but a simultaneous rise in cases among men who have sex with men, particularly in major cities. Sentinel surveillance from nine Western European countries documented increasing gonorrhoea diagnoses among MSM in the mid‑1990s even as heterosexual rates continued to fall, and these MSM‑focused resurgences persisted into the 2000s. Targeted prevention campaigns and integration of STI services into HIV care and community settings partially stabilised incidence but did not fully reverse the upward trend.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Behaviour change among MSM following the introduction of effective HIV therapy, including reduced condom use and more frequent partner change; concentration of sexual networks in urban gay venues and, later, online platforms; improved testing in MSM communities that increased case detection; stigma and access barriers that delayed care for some groups. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel resistance mechanism defined this resurgence, but many circulating strains carried accumulated resistance to penicillin, tetracycline and later fluoroquinolones, allowing persistent transmission where outdated regimens were still used.
Review: Retain – Appropriately captures the MSM-focused gonorrhoea resurgence in Western and Northern Europe during the 1990s–2000s; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence (behaviourally driven resurgence without a single defining new strain) are consistent with surveillance reports, and no structural corrections were required.

Host: Humans (general sexually active population, with disproportionate impact on MSM and some racial/ethnic minority groups)
Event summary: After a decline in the early 2000s, estimated gonorrhoea incidence in the United States plateaued around 2006–2009 and then increased sharply, with a roughly two‑thirds rise in per‑capita incidence between 2013 and 2019 and record‑high case counts reported by CDC. The resurgence particularly affected men, including men who have sex with men, but concurrent increases among women indicated growing heterosexual transmission. By 2019 the United States was experiencing its highest gonorrhoea burden in decades, prompting renewed national prevention initiatives and revised treatment guidelines focusing on higher‑dose ceftriaxone monotherapy and intensified partner services.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changes in sexual behaviour including decreased condom use, growth of online dating and hookup apps, and network effects among MSM; structural factors such as reduced public health STI clinic capacity, health‑care access barriers, and socioeconomic inequities; possible risk compensation associated with HIV pre‑exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use; high prevalence of asymptomatic infections and limited screening, especially in men. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain dominated nationally, but widespread circulation of diverse lineages, many with resistance to older antibiotics and some with reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins and azithromycin, made treatment more complex and may have modestly increased transmission duration when suboptimal regimens were used.
Review: Review – This is an appropriately major re-occurrence event (large national resurgence in incidence without a single defining new strain). The only substantive correction was to align the continent label with the Country sheet ('Northern America'). Content, timeframe and classification as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) otherwise look sound.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Multiple EU/EEA member states with sustained increases, notably France [2008]; Portugal [2008]; Denmark [2008]; Ireland [2008]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012–2019]; Finland [2016–2017]; Sweden [2016–2017]; additional Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries contributing to record EU/EEA case numbers by 2019
Host: Humans (sexually active population in EU/EEA, including both MSM and heterosexual men and women)
Event summary: From around 2008, EU/EEA surveillance began to record renewed increases in gonorrhoea notifications in many Western and Northern European countries after previous declines, with France and Portugal experiencing roughly six‑fold rises and Denmark and Ireland more than tripling reported cases by 2017. Through the 2010s, diagnoses rose across most EU/EEA states, driven by high rates among MSM but also marked increases among young heterosexual men and women, leading to more than 89 000 confirmed cases in 2017 and around 118 000 cases in 2019, the highest annual total recorded since EU‑level STI surveillance began. This multi‑country resurgence prompted intensified testing, partner notification and prevention campaigns as well as ongoing updates to European and national STI strategies, but incidence remained high until temporarily disrupted by COVID‑19–related changes in sexual behaviour and service access in 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Behavioural changes including increases in partner numbers, condomless sex and use of geospatial networking apps; reduced fear of HIV due to effective antiretroviral therapy and wider availability of PrEP; high background prevalence of bacterial STIs in core networks; expanded use of highly sensitive nucleic acid amplification tests and dual chlamydia/gonorrhoea testing, which increased case detection; strengthened EU/EEA surveillance improving ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple N. gonorrhoeae lineages, many with resistance to older antibiotics; however, no single novel strain or resistance mechanism uniquely defines this resurgence, so it is best characterised as a behaviour- and system-driven re-occurrence.
Review: Review – Added as a new high-impact event to capture the large, multi-country resurgence of gonorrhoea incidence across the EU/EEA culminating in record notifications in 2017–2019. Classified as re-occurrence (behavioural and system drivers, without a single defining novel strain) and linked to specific EU/EEA reports; should be retained among the top events, but details (country list and exact start year) may warrant further refinement with full access to surveillance datasets.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (urogenital and pharyngeal gonorrhoea)
Event summary: In 2009, Kyoto, Japan reported strain H041, the first Neisseria gonorrhoeae isolate with high‑level ceftriaxone resistance, signalling that the last widely used monotherapy option was at risk. Between 2010 and 2014, additional ceftriaxone‑resistant isolates including F89 in France and Spain, A8806 in Australia and GU140106 in Japan were identified, often linked to international travel but causing only limited local transmission. These sporadic but worrisome strains demonstrated that ceftriaxone resistance could arise in multiple lineages, prompting more intensive surveillance, greater reliance on dual therapy and discussion of higher‑dose cephalosporin regimens.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive global reliance on third‑generation cephalosporins—especially cefixime and ceftriaxone—as last‑line empiric gonorrhoea therapy; incomplete surveillance in many countries allowing sporadic resistant strains to emerge before detection; continued high burden of untreated or partially treated infections. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of mosaic penA alleles (including penA-34-like and related forms) and other chromosomal changes reducing affinity of penicillin‑binding protein 2 for cephalosporins; concurrent accumulation of additional resistance determinants (e.g. penicillinase, fluoroquinolone resistance), producing multidrug‑resistant phenotypes; biological fitness sufficient for sporadic spread but generally limited compared with fully susceptible strains, which helped prevent global establishment of these early clones.
Review: Review – Correctly identifies the early sporadic ceftriaxone-resistant strains (H041, F89, A8806 and GU140106) as a major re-emergence episode threatening last-line therapy. Updated the time span to 2009–2014 and removed intra- and inter-continental emergence flags, since these resistance phenotypes represent new strains of an already globally distributed pathogen rather than first presence of the species on new continents.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2014-2018]
Host: Humans (primarily heterosexual networks with links to MSM networks in England)
Event summary: In late 2014, an outbreak of high‑level azithromycin‑resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae (HL‑AziR, MIC ≥256 mg/L) was first recognised in Leeds in northern England, where a cluster of cases was detected at a sexual health clinic. From 2015 to 2017 the outbreak strain spread beyond Leeds, with 70 confirmed cases reported across England and evidence that linked heterosexual and MSM sexual networks sustained transmission over several years. By 2018 intensified case finding, partner notification and treatment changes led to a marked decline in new cases, though high‑level azithromycin resistance remained a concern for future therapeutic options.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread adoption of dual therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, exposing gonococci to macrolides at population scale; dense sexual networks with frequent partner change and limited condom use, facilitating spread once high‑level resistance arose; delays in routine culture and susceptibility testing as nucleic‑acid amplification tests became standard, which slowed early detection. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of 23S rRNA mutations (e.g. 2611C→T in all four alleles) and efflux pump changes conferring very high azithromycin MICs; clonal expansion of a specific high‑fitness HL‑AziR lineage that remained susceptible to ceftriaxone but could evade macrolide‑based regimens.
Review: Review – Accurately describes the multi-year HL-AziR outbreak originating in Leeds and spreading across England and classifies it as a re-emergence driven by macrolide resistance. Country information was slightly refined to indicate the full 2014–2018 period for the United Kingdom; otherwise the event is well supported and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Australia and New Zealand; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Countries: Japan [2015]; China [2016]; Australia [2017]; Canada [2017]; Denmark [2017]; France [2017]; Ireland [2018]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2018]; additional travel‑associated cases in other countries through 2022
Host: Humans (urogenital and pharyngeal infections in heterosexual and MSM populations)
Event summary: In January 2015, Japan identified Neisseria gonorrhoeae strain FC428, carrying mosaic penA-60.001 and showing ceftriaxone resistance and multidrug resistance while retaining good biological fitness. Over 2016–2018, closely related FC428‑like isolates were reported from China, Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Ireland and the United Kingdom, often with epidemiological links to travel in the Asia‑Pacific region and occasional evidence of limited local onward transmission. By the early 2020s, surveillance data documented continued detection of FC428‑like strains across the Asia‑Pacific and sporadically in Europe and Northern America, prompting international alerts and efforts to enhance genomic surveillance and resistance‑guided therapy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global dependence on ceftriaxone as the last reliable monotherapy for gonorrhoea; extensive cephalosporin and quinolone use at population level; high volumes of travel between East/South‑East Asia and Europe/Oceania/Northern America, particularly among sexually active adults; limited routine genomic surveillance delaying recognition of a single, fit international clone. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of the mosaic penA-60.001 allele and additional chromosomal changes conferring ceftriaxone and cefixime resistance while maintaining high fitness; combination of resistance to multiple older drugs (penicillin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline) generating an extensively drug‑resistant phenotype; clonal expansion and international spread of FC428 and FC428‑like strains through interconnected sexual networks.
Review: Review – This event correctly captures the emergence and international dissemination of the FC428 clone and related ceftriaxone-resistant lineages and appropriately classifies them as re-emergence via a novel resistance genotype. Removed intra- and inter-continental emergence flags to align with the definition that geographic spread of resistant variants of an already global species should be coded as re-emergence rather than new continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (heterosexual men and women)
Event summary: Between April and May 2016, Hawaii detected a cluster of Neisseria gonorrhoeae isolates with both high‑level azithromycin resistance and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone in seven patients on Oahu. The cluster appeared to arise from local transmission within a small heterosexual network, with all eight isolates sharing a highly resistant phenotype and β‑lactamase production. Prompt public health investigation, partner tracing and use of higher‑dose ceftriaxone with test‑of‑cure helped contain the cluster, and no sustained broader spread of this specific strain was documented in Hawaii thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of dual therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in a setting with ongoing importation of resistant strains via travel to Asia and substantial local STI burden; limited routine culture‑based surveillance meant the cluster was initially detected through targeted resistance testing. Internal mechanisms: Combination of 23S rRNA mutations and efflux changes conferring high‑level azithromycin resistance (MIC >256 µg/mL) together with alterations in penA and other loci producing elevated ceftriaxone MICs; multidrug‑resistant plasmid‑mediated β‑lactamase production; clonal expansion within a small sexual network demonstrating that strains with dual resistance determinants can remain transmissible.
Review: Review – Sentinel dual-resistant cluster (high-level azithromycin resistance plus decreased ceftriaxone susceptibility) in Hawaii is accurately described and appropriately classified as a re-emergence event. Updated the continent label to 'Northern America'; otherwise no structural concerns, though its relative rank among the ten most impactful events is somewhat judgment-based and could be revisited if further prioritisation is needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2016-2018]
Host: Humans (pharyngeal and urogenital gonorrhoea, mainly in heterosexual men and women)
Event summary: In 2016, the United Kingdom documented the first confirmed global failure to cure pharyngeal gonorrhoea using WHO‑recommended dual therapy with ceftriaxone (500 mg intramuscularly) plus azithromycin (1 g orally), in a patient infected with a highly resistant strain. In 2018, England reported an additional "super gonorrhoea" case with high‑level azithromycin resistance and ceftriaxone resistance that failed standard treatment and required alternative regimens, attracting wide public and professional attention. After intensive partner tracing, targeted testing and tailored high‑dose or alternative antibiotic regimens, onward transmission of these specific dual‑therapy‑resistant strains appeared limited, but the events underscored the fragility of last‑line treatment options.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reliance on dual therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in response to rising cephalosporin MICs; frequent pharyngeal gonorrhoea in sexual networks where orogenital contact and limited condom use are common; subtherapeutic antibiotic exposure in the pharynx due to lower tissue drug levels and patient adherence issues; international travel importing highly resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Concurrent resistance to ceftriaxone (via mosaic penA and accessory mutations) and high‑level azithromycin resistance (23S rRNA mutations and efflux), resulting in extensively drug‑resistant N. gonorrhoeae; enhanced survival in the pharyngeal niche where reduced drug penetration and asymptomatic infections facilitate persistence and onward spread.
Review: Retain – This event highlights globally important dual-therapy treatment failures and extensively drug-resistant cases first documented in the UK (and contemporaneously in Australia) and is well supported by WHO, ECDC and NEJM reports. Classification as a re-emergence event linked to dual ceftriaxone and azithromycin resistance is appropriate, and no structural corrections were necessary.

Continent: Africa; Asia; Europe; Northern America; South America; Oceania
Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Caribbean; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Multiple countries in all WHO regions, including numerous EU/EEA member states and the United Kingdom [from 2022]; China and other countries in the Western Pacific and South‑East Asia [from 2020]; United States of America and Canada [2020s]; additional reporting countries in Africa and Latin America through WHO GASP/EGASP/GLASS [2020s]
Host: Humans (global sexually active population)
Event summary: Between 2020 and 2024, WHO’s global GASP/EGASP and related systems documented sharp increases in resistance or decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone, cefixime and azithromycin in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with resistant isolates reported from a growing number of countries on all inhabited continents. From 2022 onward, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported an upsurge of ceftriaxone‑resistant, multidrug‑resistant and extensively drug‑resistant gonorrhoea in the EU/EEA and United Kingdom, including clusters with clear evidence of domestic transmission rather than purely imported cases. By 2025 these patterns prompted strong international warnings that continued spread of such strains could severely compromise standard gonorrhoea treatment, leading to updated guidelines, intensified surveillance and renewed calls for vaccine and drug development.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing heavy use of ceftriaxone and, in many countries, azithromycin, sometimes at suboptimal doses; disrupted STI services and treatment interruptions during the COVID‑19 pandemic leading to delayed care and possible inappropriate antibiotic use; global travel and interconnected sexual networks enabling rapid international dissemination of resistant clones such as FC428‑like strains; limited culture‑based testing capacity in many low- and middle‑income countries, which allowed resistance to spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: Further expansion of mosaic penA alleles conferring ceftriaxone and cefixime resistance, often combined with macrolide resistance mutations and other determinants to produce MDR and XDR phenotypes; selection of clones with high biological fitness that can transmit efficiently despite carrying multiple resistance mutations; incremental elevation of MIC distributions, so that a rising fraction of isolates approach or exceed clinical breakpoints for last‑line drugs.
Review: Review – Appropriately summarises the recent global escalation of ceftriaxone-, cefixime- and azithromycin-resistant gonorrhoea documented by WHO GASP/EGASP and ECDC, and correctly treats this as a re-emergence episode driven by increasingly fit resistant clones rather than as new continental emergence. The continent field was standardised to list all inhabited continents explicitly, and intra-/inter-continental emergence flags were removed to align with the event-type definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers), pigs (amplifying host); Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir, implicated epidemiologically)
Event summary: From September 1998, a new syndrome of encephalitis and respiratory disease emerged among pig farmers in Perak and later in major pig‑farming districts of Negeri Sembilan and Selangor, Malaysia, and was traced to a novel bat‑borne paramyxovirus that had spilled over into intensively raised pigs. Movement of infected pigs disseminated infection between farms and across the border to abattoir workers in Singapore, ultimately causing roughly 265–276 human cases and more than 100 deaths. The outbreak was halted by mass culling of pigs, closure of affected farms, and strict movement restrictions, after which no further large pig‑associated human Nipah outbreaks occurred in Malaysia or Singapore.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and high density of commercial pig production, planting of fruit trees near pig sheds, and frequent movement of live pigs between farms and to Singapore abattoirs allowed repeated contact between Pteropus fruit bats, pigs, and humans. Internal mechanisms: host expansion from bats to pigs and humans, high viral shedding in pig respiratory secretions, and Nipah virus’s strong neurotropic and pneumotropic properties enabled efficient pig‑to‑human transmission and severe disease in humans.
Review: retain – correctly describes the first recognized human Nipah virus outbreak in Malaysia and linked cases in Singapore, with appropriate geography, timing, event typing (first/global emergence and first detection), and high‑quality primary sources.

Host: Humans (village residents); Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir, implicated); possible livestock exposure (notably a sick cow) investigated
Event summary: In April–May 2001, a cluster of severe febrile encephalitis with a high case‑fatality ratio occurred in Chandpur village, Meherpur District, western Bangladesh; retrospective testing confirmed Nipah virus infection in 13 patients, nine of whom died, representing the first recognized Nipah outbreak in the country. Cases were concentrated in a few households and close neighbours in a rural farming community, with epidemiologic investigations pointing to proximity to bat roosts, possible contact with a sick cow, and close caregiving of ill family members as risk factors. Transmission chains burned out within about a month without wider spread, but this event triggered establishment of dedicated Nipah surveillance and outbreak‑response capacity in Bangladesh.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: smallholder farming close to Pteropus bat roosts, intimate contact with sick livestock and family members, and absence of structured infection‑prevention measures in homes facilitated bat‑to‑human spillover and limited human‑to‑human spread. Internal mechanisms: circulation of Nipah virus closely related to the Malaysian strain with inherent potential for severe encephalitis; available data do not show major viral change, so recurrence is best explained by ecological and behavioral factors.
Review: review – event is correctly placed as the first recognized Nipah outbreak in Bangladesh, but the type of emergence has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence at the Southern Asia sub‑regional scale because the earlier 2001 Siliguri, India outbreak in the same UN sub‑region is treated as the initial intra‑continental emergence; still retained because it is the country’s first detection and a major event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (hospital patients, visitors, health‑care workers)
Event summary: Between late January and late February 2001, Siliguri in West Bengal, India, experienced a large outbreak of febrile encephalitis centered around a referral hospital; subsequent serologic and RT‑PCR testing confirmed Nipah virus infection. About 66 probable and confirmed cases with a high case‑fatality ratio were identified, and most patients were hospital staff, inpatients or visitors, indicating extensive nosocomial transmission and some spread into the surrounding community. The outbreak subsided after barrier‑nursing practices and other infection‑control measures were introduced, and no further cases were detected locally that year, establishing Nipah as an emerging threat in India and Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: severe crowding in wards, lack of patient isolation, limited use of personal protective equipment, and delayed recognition of Nipah virus allowed repeated high‑risk exposures among health‑care workers, patients and visitors. Internal mechanisms: efficient person‑to‑person transmission of Nipah virus via respiratory droplets and contact with body fluids in close‑contact healthcare environments, with viruses genetically closer to Bangladesh than Malaysian strains but not representing a distinct lineage at that time.
Review: retain – correctly represents the first recognized Nipah outbreak in India and the earliest outbreak documented in the Southern Asia sub‑region, with appropriate classification as intra‑continental emergence and accurate timing, geography and transmission description.

Host: Humans in multiple rural districts; Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir)
Event summary: From 2003 through 2005, Bangladesh experienced recurrent winter–spring Nipah seasons in western and central districts including Naogaon, Manikganj, Rajbari, Faridpur and Tangail, together accounting for on the order of 90 human cases with very high case‑fatality ratios; the largest cluster occurred in Faridpur in 2004, with around 36 cases and 27 deaths, alongside smaller outbreaks in 2003 and 2005. Investigations showed that many primary cases had consumed fresh date palm sap shortly before illness, and several outbreaks featured clear family and neighbourhood transmission chains, consolidating recognition of the western "Nipah belt". Each seasonal episode waned as date‑palm sap harvesting ended and ad‑hoc risk‑communication campaigns were implemented, but these years established an almost annual pattern of Nipah emergence in Bangladesh.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal harvesting and consumption of raw date palm sap contaminated by bat urine or saliva, bat roosts located in and around affected villages, and intensive caregiving and funeral practices with little infection‑control infrastructure enabled repeated spillover and localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: stable circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus capable of direct bat‑to‑human foodborne transmission and limited person‑to‑person spread; no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype driving these particular seasons.
Review: retain – appropriately aggregates closely spaced 2003–2005 outbreaks in the same Bangladesh "Nipah belt" into a linked recurrent episode and classifies it as re‑occurrence within Southern Asia; geography, timeframe and qualitative magnitude match WHO and national summaries.

Host: Humans (village residents, caregivers, health‑care workers); Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event summary: In early 2010, a notable Nipah virus outbreak arose in Faridpur and Gopalganj districts, Bangladesh, beginning with sap‑exposed village residents and expanding into clusters among family caregivers and health‑care workers, for a total of 17 cases and 15 deaths. Field and hospital investigations documented multiple routes of transmission including household caregiving, nosocomial spread within district hospitals, and corpse‑to‑human infection during funeral rituals. Following rapid case isolation, contact tracing, community education to avoid raw date palm sap and high‑risk funerals, and reinforcement of infection‑control practices in health facilities, transmission was interrupted within several weeks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: wintertime consumption of raw date palm sap, frequent close caregiving of severely ill patients without protective equipment, overcrowded hospital wards with weak infection‑control programmes, and traditional washing and embracing of bodies during funerals supported household, nosocomial and corpse‑to‑human transmission. Internal mechanisms: high viral loads in respiratory and oropharyngeal secretions enabled efficient person‑to‑person and corpse‑to‑human transmission, but viral sequences remained within the known Bangladesh lineage rather than representing a novel variant.
Review: retain – accurately captures the Faridpur/Gopalganj 2010 outbreak, including case numbers, transmission routes (household, nosocomial, corpse‑to‑human) and classification as re‑occurrence within an already endemic sub‑region; sources are well chosen (EID articles and WHO/ICDDR,B‑based summaries).

Host: Humans in northern and central districts; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event summary: During the 2010–11 and 2011–12 Nipah seasons, Bangladesh experienced some of its largest and deadliest recurrent outbreaks, notably in northern districts including Lalmonirhat, Rangpur and Dinajpur and later Joypurhat and neighbouring areas, with about 44 cases and 40 deaths in 2011 and a further 12 cases and 10 deaths in 2012. Many index cases reported drinking fresh or fermented date palm sap, and extended household and neighbourhood transmission chains were documented, including clusters involving school‑aged children. These seasonal outbreaks subsided each year after targeted risk‑communication campaigns, changes in sap‑drinking behaviour and the end of the sap‑harvesting period, but they confirmed the entrenched winter seasonality and high lethality of Nipah in Bangladesh.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: entrenched cultural practices of consuming raw and fermented date palm sap contaminated by bat excreta, limited adoption of sap‑protection measures, and delayed recognition and isolation of Nipah cases in remote districts led to large multi‑district clusters. Internal mechanisms: continuing circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with efficient person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings; increased incidence is best explained by ecological and behavioural factors rather than documented viral evolution.
Review: retain – appropriately treats the 2011 and 2012 northern Bangladesh outbreaks as a linked recurrent episode confined to Southern Asia, with correct order‑of‑magnitude case counts and emphasis on raw/fermented date palm sap and person‑to‑person spread; classification as re‑occurrence is consistent with definitions.

Host: Humans across multiple districts (Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah, Mymensingh and others); Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event summary: From January to early April 2013, Bangladesh reported its largest Nipah season since 2011, with 24 cases and 21 deaths across roughly a dozen districts including Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah and Mymensingh, indicating widening geographic involvement within the country’s "Nipah belt". Most primary case‑patients had a documented history of drinking raw date palm sap before illness onset, and several small family and community clusters with limited person‑to‑person transmission were identified. As in previous years, cases declined sharply after the sap‑harvesting season ended and risk‑communication campaigns were intensified, but the 2013 season reinforced Nipah’s status as an endemic, highly lethal zoonosis in Bangladesh.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued wintertime collection and communal consumption of unprotected raw date palm sap across a growing set of districts, together with dense household living and traditional caregiving practices, supported multiple primary spillover events and short human‑to‑human chains. Internal mechanisms: persistent circulation of the established Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with very high case‑fatality ratio; no specific novel genotype has been uniquely linked to the 2013 outbreaks, so re‑occurrence is attributed primarily to ecological and behavioural drivers.
Review: review – new event added because the 2013 Bangladesh season (24 cases, 21 deaths across many districts) is one of the largest documented Nipah outbreaks and was missing from the original dataset; geography, timeframe, and classification as re‑occurrence are supported by WHO baseline data and contemporaneous national reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (horse owners, slaughterers, caregivers); horses; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event summary: In March–April 2014, an outbreak of henipavirus infection occurred in two villages of Sultan Kudarat Province, Mindanao, Philippines, where at least 10 horses died of acute neurologic disease followed by 17 human cases, mainly among people who slaughtered sick horses, handled carcasses or consumed horse meat. Serologic testing demonstrated Nipah‑neutralizing antibodies and IgM in several patients and domestic animals, and a short sequence of the Nipah P‑gene was detected, indicating infection with Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus, although full genome characterization was not achieved. After cessation of horse slaughter and consumption, restrictions on animal movement, and intensified public‑health messaging, no further human or equine cases were detected and the episode was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: pasturing horses in areas used by fruit bats, lack of awareness of henipavirus risks in equids, slaughter and butchering of acutely ill horses, consumption of undercooked horse meat, and minimal infection‑prevention measures in rural health‑care facilities fostered bat‑to‑horse and horse‑to‑human transmission, with some human‑to‑human spread among caregivers and health‑care workers. Internal mechanisms: infection by a henipavirus antigenically and genetically closest to Nipah virus that was able to infect horses and humans, illustrating a bat–horse–human transmission pathway similar to Hendra virus, although the precise taxonomic status of the virus (NiV versus NiV‑like) remains unresolved.
Review: review – event is retained as a major probable Nipah (or Nipah‑like) henipavirus outbreak introducing the virus into the Philippines with a new equine amplifying host, but the type of emergence has been corrected from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence within South‑eastern Asia because Nipah was already established there (Malaysia/Singapore); virus identity and host expansion justify flagging the row for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (index family, health‑care workers, close contacts); Pteropus medius bats (reservoir, evidenced by serology)
Event summary: In May–June 2018, an outbreak of Nipah virus disease occurred in Kozhikode and neighbouring Malappuram districts of Kerala, India, beginning with a family cluster and extending to health‑care workers and other close contacts; around 18–23 cases and 17–21 deaths were reported. Genomic analysis showed that the virus belonged to the Bangladesh lineage, and field investigations detected Nipah‑reactive antibodies in local Pteropus medius bats, indicating local bat reservoirs rather than importation of infected pigs. Intensive case isolation, ring surveillance, quarantine of contacts and reinforcement of hospital infection‑control rapidly curtailed transmission, and no further cases were detected after June 2018, though Kerala remained on high alert for future spillover.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: overlap of Pteropus medius colonies with peri‑urban human settlements, close family caregiving in small homes, and early unprotected contact of health‑care workers with severely ill encephalitis patients allowed both initial spillover and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus into southern India and efficient human‑to‑human transmission in high‑exposure clinical and household settings, although sequencing did not reveal a Kerala‑specific divergent strain.
Review: retain – correctly describes the first Nipah outbreak in Kerala and a major re‑occurrence in India, with appropriate classification as re‑occurrence in Southern Asia and well‑supported epidemiologic and virologic details from national and WHO sources.

Host: Humans in multiple districts; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event summary: From early January to mid‑February 2023, Bangladesh experienced its largest documented Nipah outbreak since 2015, with 11 cases (10 confirmed and 1 probable) and 8 deaths reported from seven districts across two divisions. Most primary case‑patients had a clear history of consuming fresh date palm sap or related products, and some limited person‑to‑person transmission occurred among close contacts, reflecting established Bangladeshi Nipah patterns. Intensive public‑health messaging on avoiding raw sap, rapid outbreak investigation, and seasonal decline in sap harvesting contributed to termination of the outbreak by mid‑February 2023.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued wintertime consumption of raw date palm sap contaminated by bat saliva or urine, incomplete adoption of sap‑protection measures (such as bamboo skirts over collection pots), and high‑risk caregiving behaviours in rural households permitted recurrent spillover and small clusters. Internal mechanisms: stable circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with inherently high case‑fatality rate and capacity for person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings; no published evidence suggests a novel variant emerging specifically in 2023, so this event is classified as re‑occurrence driven largely by ecological and behavioural factors.
Review: review – event is correctly characterized as Bangladesh’s largest Nipah outbreak since 2015 and a re‑occurrence in an endemic sub‑region, but the primary WHO source has been updated from a 2025 general situation report to the 2023 Disease Outbreak News (DON442) that specifically details the 11 cases and 8 deaths; otherwise the row is appropriate to retain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [1992] (California, Idaho, Nevada, Washington)
Host: Humans (primarily children and young people consuming undercooked ground beef)
Event summary: In late 1992 and early 1993, a multistate outbreak of Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections occurred among customers of the Jack in the Box fast-food chain in four western U.S. states, after contaminated ground beef hamburgers were undercooked and widely served. Publicity and active case finding identified about 732 illnesses, many with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome, and four children died as the outbreak spread across the restaurant network. The outbreak ended after a large recall of beef lots, restaurant closures, and new cooking and inspection standards were implemented, and it catalyzed major reforms in U.S. meat safety regulation and E. coli surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Industrially produced ground beef patties distributed across a large fast-food chain; inadequate cooking temperatures and food-safety controls; delayed recognition of STEC as a major foodborne threat. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel genotype described, but the outbreak highlighted high virulence of E. coli O157:H7 and its propensity to cause HUS in children.
Review: retain – Outbreak is well documented as the 1992–1993 Jack in the Box multistate E. coli O157:H7 event (~732 cases, 4 deaths in WA, CA, ID, NV). Geography, timing, classification as a re‑occurrence (no new region or strain), and the chosen CDC/EID sources are appropriate, and this clearly ranks among the most impactful global STEC outbreaks. No changes made.

Countries: Japan [1996] (Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture; other clusters in Japan)
Host: Humans (schoolchildren and factory workers consuming contaminated radish sprouts and school lunches)
Event summary: In summer 1996, Japan experienced a massive series of outbreaks of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections, most prominently in Sakai City, Osaka, where contaminated white radish sprouts served in school lunches caused acute gastroenteritis in thousands of elementary school children and at least three deaths. Additional linked clusters, including an outbreak among factory workers in Kyoto, were traced to radish sprouts from the same grower, with an estimated total of around 8,000–10,000 associated cases nationally. The epidemic was controlled after withdrawal of implicated sprouts, suspension of school lunches, and strengthened hygiene and sprout-production controls.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralized preparation and distribution of school lunches; burgeoning sprout consumption; inadequate disinfection of seeds and sprout-growing water; possible contamination from livestock manure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak involved highly virulent E. coli O157:H7 strains associated with a high risk of HUS but not clearly a new serotype; enhanced transmission was primarily due to food-distribution practices rather than a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Correctly captures the 1996 Sakai City and related Japanese O157:H7 outbreaks linked to radish sprouts, which remain the largest STEC O157 outbreaks ever recorded. Case numbers, setting (school lunches and factory cafeteria), geography (Japan/Eastern Asia), classification as re‑occurrence, and the technical sources used are appropriate. No structural changes needed.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996-1997] (central Scotland, including Wishaw and surrounding areas)
Host: Humans (primarily older adults and nursing-home residents consuming cooked meats and other foods from a contaminated butcher’s shop)
Event summary: In late November 1996, public health authorities in Lanarkshire, central Scotland, detected a cluster of bloody diarrhoea cases and confirmed Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections among residents of Wishaw, with epidemiologic investigation rapidly implicating cooked meats and pies supplied by a local butcher, John Barr & Son, as the common source. The outbreak expanded through retail sales and catered events such as a church lunch and nursing-home meals, ultimately affecting roughly 500 people across central Scotland and causing 21 deaths, mostly among elderly patients, making it at the time the world’s deadliest recorded E. coli O157 outbreak. The epidemic waned after the implicated butcher’s premises were closed, contaminated products withdrawn, and a national inquiry led to new UK hygiene regulations and licensing for butchers and meat retailers, substantially strengthening food-safety controls.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-contamination of ready-to-eat cooked meats with raw beef at a small butcher’s shop; inadequate separation of raw and cooked areas and shared slicing equipment; failures in local food-safety inspection; high exposure of vulnerable elderly populations through institutional catering. Internal mechanisms: infection with a highly virulent E. coli O157:H7 phage type 2 clone already present in regional cattle; no evidence that a fundamentally novel genotype emerged, so the extreme impact reflected dose, distribution, and host vulnerability rather than new bacterial traits.
