Countries: Multiple EU/EEA countries including United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015]; Germany [2015]; France [2015]; Spain [2015]; Poland [2015]; others reporting outbreaks linked to eggs and egg products during 2015–2019
Host: Humans (consumers of eggs and egg products)
Event summary: From 2015 through 2019, EU/EEA surveillance documented numerous strong‑evidence food‑borne disease outbreaks of Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis, particularly sequence type 11 (ST11), linked to eggs and egg products, representing a substantial cumulative burden of illness and hospitalizations across several countries. Aggregated outbreak data indicate that, over this period, eggs and egg products accounted for thousands of S. Enteritidis outbreak cases and a large share of salmonellosis‑related hospitalizations in the EU, with multiple national and local outbreaks occurring each year. Strengthened monitoring, on‑farm controls, and targeted interventions in implicated egg production and processing facilities gradually reduced the frequency and size of these outbreaks by the end of the decade, although sporadic clusters continued to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale industrial egg production and distribution, occasional lapses in biosecurity and Salmonella monitoring in laying‑hen flocks, and high consumer exposure to eggs and egg‑containing foods allowed repeated contamination events to generate sizeable outbreaks across several EU countries. Internal mechanisms: Dominance of S. Enteritidis ST11 and related poultry‑adapted lineages, capable of contaminating eggs internally and externally (Enhanced Transmission through poultry‑egg adaptation); antimicrobial resistance was present in some isolates but not the primary driver of emergence in this aggregated episode.
Review: Review: EXCLUDE or MERGE (flagged). This row aggregates multiple, largely independent S. Enteritidis egg‑associated outbreaks (many not genetically linked) across 2015–2019 using summary statistics from EFSA/ECDC reports, rather than describing a single epidemiologically linked episode, and therefore does not strictly meet the project definition of an 'emergence event'.([efsa.europa.eu](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2022-02/ROA_Salmonella%20Enteritidis%20ST11_2022.pdf)) Much of its content overlaps with the specific multi‑country egg‑linked epidemic already captured in the 2012–2018 event, risking double‑counting. Recommended action: either drop this row entirely, or explicitly redefine and merge it with the 2012–2018 Polish‑egg‑linked epidemic if a more synthetic EU‑wide eggs event is desired; if retained, it should clearly be labeled as an aggregated burden summary rather than a discrete outbreak.

Countries: Pakistan [2016]; travel‑associated cases in other countries (e.g. United States of America [2016]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2017]) without sustained local transmission
Host: Humans (typhoid fever patients, mainly children and young adults)
Event summary: In November 2016, health authorities in Sindh Province, Pakistan, detected an outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant (XDR) Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi causing typhoid fever, initially centered in Hyderabad and later spreading to Karachi and other districts. Between 2016 and late 2018, over 5,000 XDR typhoid cases were laboratory‑confirmed among more than 8,000 typhoid cases in Sindh, with the outbreak strain resistant to first‑line drugs, fluoroquinolones and third‑generation cephalosporins and susceptible only to azithromycin and carbapenems; travel‑associated cases were subsequently reported in several high‑income countries but did not lead to sustained local transmission. While incidence has fluctuated and typhoid conjugate vaccine campaigns have been rolled out in Pakistan, XDR S. Typhi continues to circulate, posing ongoing treatment challenges and risk of wider regional or global spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy prior use and misuse of antibiotics in Pakistan, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, densely populated urban areas, and under‑resourced surveillance created an environment in which a highly resistant typhoid clone could emerge and disseminate; internal and international travel then exported cases abroad. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – evolution of an H58 S. Typhi clone harboring a promiscuous plasmid conferring resistance to fluoroquinolones and third‑generation cephalosporins; Antimicrobial Resistance – progression to an extensively drug‑resistant phenotype with very limited remaining oral treatment options; Enhanced Transmission – clonal expansion of this XDR lineage within endemic typhoid networks.
Review: Review: RETAIN. This event correctly captures the emergence of the XDR H58 S. Typhi lineage in Pakistan as a major re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance and clonal expansion, with imported cases elsewhere treated as part of the same epidemic but not counted as inter‑continental emergence because there was no sustained onward transmission in recipient countries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12090039/?utm_source=openai)) Emergence‑type coding (re_emergence only) and geographic scope (Southern Asia with travel‑associated cases noted) align well with the project rules; sources are authoritative (WHO DON, CDC MMWR, peer‑reviewed genomic and clinical analyses).

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022]; France [2022]; Germany [2022]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2022]; Belgium [2022]; Spain [2022]; Sweden [2022]; Norway [2022]; Italy [2022]; Ireland [2022]; Luxembourg [2022]; United States of America [2022]; Canada [2022]; other EU/EEA countries and North American states reporting linked cases
Host: Humans (primarily children consuming chocolate confectionery)
Event summary: In early 2022, public‑health authorities in the United Kingdom detected a cluster of multidrug‑resistant monophasic Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium sequence type 34 infections in young children, which was rapidly linked to Kinder‑brand chocolate eggs and related confectionery produced at a factory in Arlon, Belgium. By May 2022, WHO and ECDC/EFSA reported more than 150 genetically related cases initially, and later over 350–370 cases, across at least 14–16 countries in Europe and North America, with epidemiologic, microbiological and trace‑back evidence implicating specific chocolate products distributed to over 100 countries worldwide. Wide‑ranging recalls of Kinder products from the affected plant, temporary suspension of production, and extensive risk communication led to a gradual decline in new cases over the following months.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination within a high‑volume chocolate manufacturing facility, followed by international distribution of long‑shelf‑life confectionery popular with children, allowed a point‑source contamination event to generate cases across multiple countries; detection relied on coordinated genomic surveillance and international information exchange. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a monophasic S. Typhimurium ST34 variant with multidrug resistance and good survival in low‑moisture, high‑fat food matrices, illustrating Enhanced Transmission via adaptation to processed‑food environments rather than a change in human host range.
Review: Review: RETAIN with corrected geography, emergence type and sources. Expanded the country list and sub‑regions to reflect the multi‑country nature of the outbreak, including key EU/EEA states, the United Kingdom, and North American countries where linked cases were reported, rather than only the UK and Ireland.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON369?utm_source=openai)) Set 'intra_continental_emergence' to false and left 're_occurrence' as true because the event represents a large, but classical, food‑borne outbreak in regions where Salmonella is already endemic. Replaced Wikipedia‑only sourcing with WHO Disease Outbreak News, ECDC/EFSA rapid outbreak assessments and Eurosurveillance analyses, which more accurately document case counts, geographic spread, resistance profile and control measures.

Host: Humans (adults and children, including high-prevalence HIV-infected populations)
Event summary: From 1993 onward, surveillance at Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital and later nationally in South Africa documented large increases in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) and high proportions of penicillin-nonsusceptible and multidrug‑resistant S. pneumoniae, particularly among adults and children living with HIV infection. As the HIV epidemic expanded during the 1990s and early 2000s, HIV‑associated IPD incidence and resistant childhood serotypes (e.g., 6A/B, 9V, 14, 19A/F, 23F) rose sharply, with additional emergence of ceftriaxone‑nonsusceptible meningitis isolates by the mid‑2000s. After scale‑up of antiretroviral therapy and introduction of PCV7 in 2009 followed by PCV13 in 2011, national data to about 2012 show major declines in vaccine‑type and drug‑resistant IPD, although resistant strains and excess risk among people with HIV persisted. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9402377/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of the HIV epidemic generated a large immunocompromised population highly susceptible to pneumococcal disease, while heavy use of beta‑lactams, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, and other antibiotics in both community and hospital settings created intense selection pressure for resistant lineages and facilitated spread in overcrowded facilities. Internal mechanisms: Progressive accumulation and clonal expansion of antimicrobial resistance (penicillin, cotrimoxazole, and, for a subset, third‑generation cephalosporins) within established serotypes and lineages increased fitness under treatment pressure, resulting in re‑emergent, difficult‑to‑treat IPD until countered by ART scale‑up and PCV introduction.
Review: review – updated event years from 1993–2008 to 1993–2012 so that the episode now spans the period of rising multidrug-resistant IPD in South Africa, its amplification by the HIV epidemic, and the early post‑PCV7/PCV13 decline documented up to 2012; geography (Southern Africa/South Africa), focus on HIV‑associated disease, and classification as re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance remain appropriate.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [1996]; Belgium [1996]; France [1996]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996]; Norway [2004]
Host: Humans (primarily children <5 years, but also older children and adults)
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s through the 2000s, several Western and Southern European countries recorded increasing incidence of IPD due to non‑PCV7 serotypes, notably serotype 19A, even before widespread PCV7 use. After PCV7 introduction (2001 onward, with national implementation between roughly 2002 and 2006), surveillance in Spain, Belgium, France, England and Wales, and later Norway showed accelerated rises in 19A IPD, particularly in children, with doubling or more of incidence in some age groups by the mid‑2000s. As higher‑valent vaccines (PCV10/PCV13) were rolled out from 2009–2011, 19A disease burden declined, though country‑specific patterns varied and some additional non‑PCV13 serotypes began to increase. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/16/9/10-0102?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Progressive uptake of PCV7 and heterogeneous vaccine schedules across Europe altered serotype ecology, while ongoing macrolide and beta‑lactam consumption exerted selection pressure favoring resistant replacement serotypes. Internal mechanisms: Capsular switching, novel strain/genotype emergence, and clonal expansion of serotype 19A and other non‑vaccine serotypes—often with significant antimicrobial resistance—under vaccine and antibiotic selection drove re‑emergent IPD through serotype and lineage shifts rather than introduction into naïve regions.
Review: review – standardized the country name to the UN form 'United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland' (the underlying data come from England and Wales) but otherwise retained the 1996–2010 multi‑country European serotype 19A replacement episode; evidence base, geographic scope, and classification as re-emergence driven by serotype/genotype shifts under vaccine and antibiotic pressure are appropriate.

Host: Humans (children and adults with epidemic pneumococcal meningitis)
Event summary: Between 2000 and 2003, northern Ghana’s Kassena‑Nankana District in the African meningitis belt experienced a large outbreak of pneumococcal meningitis with epidemic characteristics, driven predominantly by serotype 1 S. pneumoniae belonging to the hypervirulent ST217 clonal complex and associated with case‑fatality rates around 40%. In neighboring Burkina Faso, surveillance from 2002 to 2005 documented similarly high, highly seasonal incidence of pneumococcal meningitis—again with serotype 1 accounting for a large share of cases—showing an epidemic pattern analogous to classic meningococcal outbreaks. These linked West African serotype 1 epidemics, occurring in the absence of a serotype 1–containing PCV, highlighted the exceptional invasiveness of ST217‑related clones and helped motivate the inclusion of serotype 1 in higher‑valent conjugate vaccines and targeted control strategies for the meningitis belt. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15962213/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Sahelian dry‑season conditions (low humidity, dust‑laden harmattan winds), crowded living conditions, and limited access to prompt care in the West African meningitis belt favored explosive meningitis transmission, while lack of conjugate vaccines targeting serotype 1 left populations highly susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and geographic expansion of the hypervirulent serotype 1 ST217 clonal complex—with high propensity to cause meningitis but generally low baseline antimicrobial resistance—constituted a biological change in the pathogen that enabled epidemic‑scale disease in previously affected subregions.
Review: review – new event added to capture the large serotype 1 pneumococcal meningitis epidemics in Ghana and Burkina Faso (2000–2005), which caused high incidence and case-fatality and are documented as hypervirulent ST217-driven outbreaks; classified as re-emergence due to the rise and spread of a particularly epidemic-prone serotype 1 clone in a previously affected subregion.

Host: Humans (primarily children <5 years, but also adults via herd effects)
Event summary: After the introduction of the 7‑valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV7) in the United States in 2000, rates of IPD from vaccine serotypes fell sharply by the early 2000s. Between about 2001 and 2008, however, IPD caused by non‑PCV7 serotypes—especially multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A, including ST320/CC320 and related clones—rose substantially in children and adults, partially offsetting vaccine gains. This replacement disease later declined after introduction of PCV13 in 2010, which directly targeted 19A and additional serotypes, leading to major reductions in 19A IPD and associated resistance. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5641a2.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread PCV7 use removed common, often resistant vaccine serotypes from carriage and disease, opening ecological space for non‑vaccine serotypes, while continued antibiotic pressure (e.g., macrolides, beta‑lactams) favored resistant lineages. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and expansion of multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A clones (e.g., ST320/CC320) with enhanced fitness under vaccine and antibiotic selection, along with beta‑lactam and macrolide resistance, drove increased incidence and severity of 19A IPD.
Review: retain – the post‑PCV7 emergence of multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A IPD in the United States is very well documented and clearly among the most impactful modern pneumococcal emergence events; years, geography, and classification as re-emergence via vaccine-driven serotype and genotype shifts are appropriate, and sources are highly relevant.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia
Countries: Denmark [2010]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]; France [2010]; Germany [2010]; Norway [2010]; Israel [2010]
Host: Humans (children and adults with invasive pneumococcal disease)
Event summary: Following introduction of PCV13 (and PCV10) into infant programs across most European countries and in Israel between 2009 and 2011, overall IPD incidence dropped further from PCV7‑era levels. Over the ensuing 4–5 years, surveillance networks such as SpIDnet documented persistent IPD caused by serotype 3 despite high PCV13 coverage, along with notable increases in non‑PCV13 serotypes (e.g., 8, 12F, 22F, 24F, 15A, 33F, 23A) in Denmark, England and Wales, France, Germany, Norway, and Israel. By around 2018, these shifts had reshaped the serotype landscape in older children and adults and helped motivate the development and deployment of higher‑valent vaccines (PCV15, PCV20) targeting additional serotypes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8714201/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High uptake of PCV13/PCV10 in infancy strongly suppressed vaccine serotypes but also created ecological space for non‑PCV13 serotypes, with demographic aging and comorbidity in adults maintaining a large susceptible population. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and clonal spread of non‑PCV13 serotypes and persistence of serotype 3 (potentially related to its capsule structure and suboptimal vaccine-induced immunity) led to re‑emergence of IPD via serotype replacement; these changes underpin the rationale for incorporating additional serotypes in PCV15/PCV20.
Review: review – corrected the sub-region list to match the included countries (removed Southern Europe, which was not represented) and standardized the UK country name; otherwise the PCV13-era persistence of serotype 3 and rise of non‑PCV13 serotypes in Europe and Israel is accurately described and appropriately coded as re-emergence, but it conceptually overlaps with the broader 2010–2019 North America/Europe replacement event and could potentially be merged with that episode in future harmonization.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United States of America [2010]; Denmark [2010]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]; France [2010]; Germany [2010]; Italy [2010]; Spain [2010]
Host: Humans (mainly older adults and high-risk groups with invasive pneumococcal disease)
Event summary: Following widespread adoption of PCV13 in infant schedules in the United States (2010) and many European countries (2010–2011), overall IPD incidence declined, especially for PCV13 serotypes such as 19A and 7F. Over the subsequent decade, however, multiple surveillance systems documented a growing share of IPD caused by non‑PCV13 serotypes—particularly serotypes 8, 10A, 12F, 15A, 22F, 24F, 33F, and others—most prominently in older adults and medically vulnerable groups. These accumulating data on replacement serotypes with substantial disease burden directly informed the design and licensing of higher‑valent conjugate vaccines (PCV15, PCV20, and later PCV21) that include several of these emerging serotypes in order to restore broader coverage in adult and high‑risk populations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8714201/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High coverage of PCV13 in children and resulting herd effects in adults suppressed vaccine serotypes but provided ecological opportunity for non‑PCV13 serotypes to expand; aging populations with substantial comorbidities in high‑income countries sustained a high underlying risk of invasive disease. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and clonal spread of non‑PCV13 serotypes with adequate invasive potential, some carrying notable antimicrobial resistance, led to a re‑emergent IPD burden that shifted toward serotypes now incorporated into PCV15, PCV20, and PCV21.
Review: review – standardized the UK country name and retained this episode as the broad North America/Europe post‑PCV13 emergence of non‑PCV13 serotypes in adults and high‑risk groups; evidence shows substantial burden and direct relevance to the development of PCV15/PCV20/PCV21, but note partial overlap with the more Europe‑focused 2010–2018 event, which future curators may choose to merge.

Host: Humans (primarily pediatric and adult respiratory and invasive infections)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2016, multicenter surveillance from 17 Chinese cities showed very high rates of macrolide and multidrug resistance among S. pneumoniae isolates from children and adults, with many strains also non‑susceptible to other commonly used agents. During this period, macrolides were widely employed as first‑line empiric therapy for community‑acquired pneumonia, and conjugate pneumococcal vaccines were not yet broadly incorporated into the national infant program, allowing circulation and expansion of resistant lineages. By the mid‑2010s, Chinese expert guidance increasingly recommended against macrolides as first‑line monotherapy for pneumococcal infection, and growing attention was given to PCV13 introduction and broader stewardship as complementary control strategies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5747162/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive and often inappropriate outpatient macrolide use, incomplete pneumococcal vaccination coverage, and dense urban healthcare utilization created strong selection pressure and opportunities for clonal spread of resistant pneumococci. Internal mechanisms: Very high macrolide resistance mediated largely by erm(B) and mef genes, together with multidrug resistance across several antibiotic classes and expansion of successful resistant serotypes and sequence types, resulted in re‑emergent, difficult‑to‑treat pneumococcal disease across China.
Review: retain – China’s nationwide multicenter data clearly demonstrate extremely high macrolide and multidrug resistance rates in pneumococci and major implications for empiric therapy; years, geography, and classification as re-emergence via antimicrobial resistance are appropriate, and the selected sources are specific and relevant.

Host: Humans (mainly older children and adults with pneumococcal meningitis)
Event summary: During the 2015–2016 meningitis season, Ghana experienced a large outbreak of pneumococcal meningitis in the Brong‑Ahafo region—outside the traditional meningitis belt—followed by increased pneumococcal meningitis incidence in the Northern and Upper West regions during 2015–2017, five years after infant PCV13 introduction. Across two seasons, most confirmed pneumococcal meningitis cases occurred in persons ≥5 years of age, and approximately 60%–70% of serotyped isolates were serotype 1, despite high infant PCV13 coverage using a 3+0 schedule without booster or catch‑up. These outbreaks and elevated incidence demonstrated that, in this high‑transmission setting, infant PCV13 had not yet generated sufficient herd protection against serotype 1 in older children and adults, raising concerns about schedule design and the need for complementary strategies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6128537/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent meningitis‑belt climatic conditions (dry season, dust, crowding), high baseline carriage and transmission, and use of a 3+0 infant PCV13 schedule without booster or catch‑up limited indirect protection for older age groups; health‑system constraints delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of highly invasive serotype 1 lineages (including ST217‑related clones) rather than a clearly novel variant suggests that external and programmatic factors predominated, so the episode is best characterized as re‑occurrence of epidemic serotype 1 disease in a known high‑risk subregion.
Review: review – new event added to represent the high-incidence serotype 1 pneumococcal meningitis outbreaks in Ghana (Brong-Ahafo and meningitis-belt regions) during 2015–2017 in the PCV13 era; classified as re-occurrence because the main drivers are climatic and programmatic (schedule and age targeting) rather than emergence of a completely new serotype 1 lineage, and its inclusion ensures that major African epidemic episodes are represented among the top events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (children and older adults with invasive pneumococcal disease and carriage)
Event summary: After Belgium switched its pediatric program from PCV13 to PCV10 in 2015–2016, surveillance recorded a rapid re‑emergence of serotype 19A invasive pneumococcal disease and carriage by 2017–2018. Whole‑genome sequencing of 19A isolates from children and adults showed diverse sequence types distinct from the earlier 19A clones that had expanded after PCV7 introduction, indicating a new wave of 19A lineages. As evidence accumulated of increased 19A disease following PCV10 use, Belgium and other countries reassessed vaccine policy, and some reverted to or favored higher‑valent formulations including 19A. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7014673/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The national policy change from PCV13 to PCV10 removed direct vaccine pressure on serotype 19A, allowing 19A lineages to expand again in a population where other vaccine serotypes remained suppressed; ongoing antibiotic use further supported selection of fit clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and diversification within 19A, including multiple new sequence types and frequent antimicrobial resistance, underpinned re‑emergence of 19A IPD and carriage despite prior control in the PCV13 era.
Review: retain – this Belgium-specific episode is clearly documented as a policy-driven re-emergence of serotype 19A after a switch from PCV13 to PCV10, with measurable increases in IPD and carriage and distinct new 19A clones; although more localized than some other events, it is informative for vaccine policy and currently fits within the top‑10 limit, but curators may reconsider its inclusion if future global ranking across many pathogens demands stricter impact thresholds.

Countries: Kenya [1997], Somalia [1997], United Republic of Tanzania [1998]
Host: Humans (pastoralists, farmers, slaughterhouse workers) and livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels) with human infections via mosquito bites and contact with infected animal blood/tissues.
Event summary: During the strong El Niño rains of late 1997, Rift Valley fever virus re‑emerged explosively in northeastern Kenya and spread into southern Somalia and northern Tanzania, infecting livestock and humans in multiple provinces and districts. The epidemic developed over several months with extensive livestock abortion storms and hemorrhagic disease, and hundreds of human RVF infections detected in Kenya alone, including severe hemorrhagic and neurologic cases; Somalia reported its first recognized human RVF cases during this episode, and Tanzania confirmed human disease as the outbreak spread southward. The outbreak waned by mid‑1998 as flooding subsided, vector populations declined, and control measures such as animal movement restrictions and public health messaging were implemented, although under‑ascertainment of both human and animal cases was substantial.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptionally heavy rainfall and flooding linked to the 1997–1998 El Niño event created widespread flooding of dambos and other mosquito breeding sites, driving explosive amplification of RVFV in livestock and spillover to humans; close contact between pastoralist communities and sick or aborting animals (slaughtering, butchering, handling fetuses) increased zoonotic transmission risk. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain was implicated, but the virus was already well adapted to multiple Aedes and Culex vectors and ruminant hosts; this event primarily reflects climate‑driven amplification and spread within endemic East Africa rather than emergence of a distinct new genotype.
Review: Retain – Well-documented major El Niño–associated outbreak in Eastern Africa; countries, timing (1997–1998), and classification as re-occurrence within an already endemic subregion are correct; sources are appropriate.

Host: Humans (rural residents and pastoralists) and livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels, donkeys) in and around Aioun El Atrouss, Hodh El Gharbi Region.
Event summary: In September 1998, Mauritanian health authorities detected clusters of febrile illness with hemorrhagic and icteric signs in the Aioun area of Hodh El Gharbi, and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection, following an earlier 1987 national epidemic. Between mid‑ and late September, approximately 300–400 human cases and six deaths were reported, concurrent with very high rates of abortion and mortality in sheep, goats and other livestock, with virologic investigations isolating multiple RVFV strains from humans, animals and vectors. Human and animal case numbers declined by late October as the unusually heavy rains that had triggered extensive flooding abated, mosquito populations decreased, and control measures such as animal movement restrictions, vector control and risk communication were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptionally heavy rainfall in September 1998—roughly three times the 10‑year average—created extensive temporary ponds in the arid Hodh El Gharbi region, supporting large populations of RVFV‑competent mosquitoes; dense pastoral livestock populations and close human–animal contact facilitated amplification and spillover. Internal mechanisms: Virologic work documented active circulation of RVFV with multiple virus isolates from humans, livestock and vectors, but these belonged to known West African lineages, indicating re‑occurrence of endemic virus strongly amplified by environmental conditions rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Review – Added major 1998 Mauritania outbreak (≈300–400 human cases, six deaths), which is explicitly listed among the nine largest RVF outbreaks 1997–2010; classified as re-occurrence in Western Africa. Should be retained when constructing a top-10 global events set.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (rural residents, herders, abattoir workers) with concurrent large‑scale infection in livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels).
Event summary: In September 2000, unexplained hemorrhagic fever associated with massive livestock abortions was reported along the southwestern border of Saudi Arabia and neighboring northern Yemen, and RVFV infection was quickly confirmed. The outbreak expanded over subsequent months, causing hundreds of laboratory‑confirmed human cases and more than 100 deaths in Saudi Arabia and Yemen combined, while also producing extensive losses in small ruminants; genetic analyses linked the viruses to East African lineages, indicating introduction via movement of infected animals or vectors. Human and animal cases declined by early 2001 following intensified vector control, animal movement restrictions, and the natural regression of favorable environmental conditions for mosquito breeding, but the event marked the first documented establishment and transmission of RVFV outside Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually high rainfall and flooding in the southwestern Arabian Peninsula created mosquito breeding habitats, likely interacting with importation of infected livestock or mosquitoes from East Africa; extensive cross‑border animal trade and limited awareness of RVF risk facilitated establishment. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed the Saudi Arabia and Yemen viruses were closely related to East African RVFV strains from the 1997–1998 Kenya and 1991 Madagascar outbreaks, indicating recent introduction of known virulent lineages rather than emergence of a novel genotype, but successful adaptation to local vectors and hosts enabled inter‑continental establishment.
Review: Retain – Correctly captures the first documented RVFV outbreak with autochthonous human transmission outside Africa (Saudi Arabia and Yemen); geography, timing and classification as inter-continental emergence are appropriate and supported by detailed virologic and outbreak reports.

Countries: Kenya [2006], Somalia [2007], United Republic of Tanzania [2007]
Host: Humans (particularly herders, farmers, butchers, veterinary and abattoir workers) and livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels).
Event summary: In late 2006, after periods of heavy rain and flooding, outbreaks of abortion and hemorrhagic disease in livestock were reported in northeastern Kenya and soon thereafter human cases of severe febrile illness and hemorrhagic fever were confirmed as RVF. The epidemic spread across multiple Kenyan districts and into neighboring Somalia and Tanzania, resulting in at least 684 reported human cases and hundreds of deaths across the region, while also causing extensive livestock losses; virus isolates from humans, animals, and mosquitoes revealed several co‑circulating lineages. Transmission declined by mid‑2007 as environmental conditions became less favorable for vectors, coupled with animal movement controls and heightened public health response, though subsequent outbreaks in Sudan and elsewhere showed the wider regional extent of this epidemic cycle.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and flooding associated with climate anomalies produced ideal mosquito breeding conditions in arid and semi‑arid zones, amplifying RVFV in livestock herds that serve as the main amplification hosts; close human contact with infected animals during herding and slaughter promoted spillover, while limited vaccination coverage and animal movement contributed to spread. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses of outbreak isolates documented multiple RVFV lineages co‑circulating across outbreak foci, but these were closely related to earlier East African strains; the event was driven primarily by environmental amplification and livestock‑vector‑human transmission dynamics rather than emergence of a fundamentally new variant.
Review: Retain – One of the largest modern RVF epidemics in humans and livestock; Eastern Africa countries, years and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic subregion match WHO/EID syntheses and need no correction.

Host: Humans (rural residents, farmers, herders) and livestock; large numbers of small ruminants and cattle were affected.
Event summary: In October 2007, Sudan’s Federal Ministry of Health requested international assistance to investigate a suspected hemorrhagic fever outbreak in several states, and RVFV was identified as the causative agent. The outbreak expanded across at least three states along the Nile and its tributaries, with official hospital records capturing hundreds of cases and over 200 deaths, while subsequent analyses estimated up to 75,000 human infections during this epidemic, concurrent with substantial livestock disease and abortions. Human and animal cases diminished by early 2008 as floodwaters receded and emergency control measures—including vector control, bans on animal movement from affected areas, and public education—were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and flooding along river systems, including areas influenced by irrigation and dam infrastructure, generated extensive mosquito breeding sites and sustained transmission among livestock, with socio‑economic dependence on livestock, close animal handling, and limited health infrastructure contributing to high human exposure and mortality. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a distinct new RVFV genotype in Sudan; instead, the large epidemic appears to reflect re‑introduction or persistence of endemic virus amplified under favorable environmental and ecological conditions.
Review: Retain – Large, well-documented outbreak in Sudan within the already affected Northern Africa subregion (following Egypt 1977–78 and later recurrences); classification as re-occurrence is appropriate and no geographic or timing corrections are needed.

Host: Humans (rural residents and people with contact to livestock) and livestock (mainly ruminants) with evidence of infection in animals and humans.
Event summary: During the rainy seasons of January–May 2008 and November 2008–March 2009, Madagascar experienced successive RVF outbreaks with laboratory‑confirmed human cases and concurrent livestock infections following unusually heavy rains. The outbreaks developed across several districts, including Fianarantsoa and areas near Lake Alaotra, with hundreds of laboratory‑confirmed and probable human infections reported across the two seasons, alongside serologic evidence of widespread animal infection. Transmission subsided after the rainy seasons ended and entomologic conditions became less favorable, though gaps in surveillance and reporting limited precise estimation of total human disease burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑normal rainfall and flooding during consecutive rainy seasons in Madagascar’s highland and lowland areas expanded mosquito breeding habitats, facilitating RVFV amplification in local livestock and spillover to humans; limited veterinary and public health surveillance reduced early detection and control. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization indicated that viruses from the 2008–2009 outbreaks clustered with Kenya‑1/1a East African lineages rather than earlier Madagascar strains, consistent with renewed introduction and replacement of prior lineages, so this episode is best viewed as re‑emergence driven by importation of distinct viral genotypes plus favorable climatic conditions.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-occurrence to re-emergence because sequence data show that 2008–2009 strains in Madagascar belong to Kenya-1/1a East African lineages distinct from earlier Madagascar viruses, indicating genotype replacement rather than simple climate-driven resurgence; geography and years are correct and sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers and rural residents) and livestock (especially sheep, goats, and cattle) across multiple South African provinces.
Event summary: Beginning in 2008, South Africa reported renewed RVF activity with a cluster of human cases linked to a dairy farm outbreak, foreshadowing larger epidemics in subsequent years. The situation escalated into widespread epizootics and epidemics during 2010–2011, when more than 14,000 animal cases were recorded across 8 of 9 provinces and at least 302 laboratory‑confirmed human infections, including around 25 deaths, were documented among people with close contact to infected livestock. Outbreak activity decreased after 2011 as rainfall normalized, vector populations declined, and control measures—such as targeted livestock vaccination, movement controls, and occupational protections—were strengthened, though sporadic smaller outbreaks (e.g., on a farm in 2018 with several human cases) have continued to occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Periods of above‑average rainfall and localized flooding in traditionally endemic regions triggered epizootics among sheep and other ruminants; high densities of susceptible livestock due to lapses in vaccination, animal movement between farms, and occupational exposure among farmers, veterinarians, and abattoir workers facilitated widespread zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular data suggest circulation of endemic RVFV lineages without clear emergence of a novel variant; the scale and geographic spread reflect environmental suitability and gaps in animal immunity rather than major viral change, with possible minor adaptations in local vector–virus–host interactions enhancing transmission efficiency.
Review: Retain – Multi-year South African cycle correctly summarized around the large 2010–2011 human epidemic; Southern Africa classification and re-occurrence status are consistent with a long history of RVF in the region and supported by national and CDC investigations.

Host: Humans (rural residents, livestock handlers) and livestock (small ruminants, cattle, camels) across southern Mauritania.
Event summary: In 2010, Mauritania experienced a major RVF outbreak affecting both animals and humans following heavy rainfall in southern regions, with cases reported from multiple wilayas. Epidemiologic investigations identified dozens of confirmed and probable human cases, including 13 deaths, along with widespread livestock abortions and deaths, representing one of several large RVF episodes the country has faced since the late 1980s. Human case reports declined towards the end of the year as rains diminished, vector densities decreased, and joint animal–human health responses were implemented, though RVFV has since continued to re‑emerge periodically in the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall events in the Sahelian and Saharan fringe zones of southern Mauritania created temporary ponds and flooded depressions that favored amplification of RVFV in domestic ruminants, with pastoral livelihoods and close animal contact exposing humans to infected blood and tissues; limited routine vaccination and vector control contributed to recurrent large‑scale outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolates from Mauritania during different outbreaks cluster with other West African RVFV lineages, consistent with persistence and local evolution of endemic strains rather than emergence of a radically new variant; the primary driver is climate‑mediated amplification and spread in livestock populations with accumulating susceptible animals.
Review: Retain – 2010 Mauritania outbreak is explicitly listed among major RVF epidemics (≈63 reported human cases, 13 deaths) and remains a relevant Western Africa re-occurrence; geography, timing and classification are correct.

Host: Humans (rural residents, herders, people with animal contact) and livestock in multiple southern regions of Mauritania.
Event summary: Following heavy rains and flooding in southern Mauritania in 2012, human cases of febrile and hemorrhagic illness were detected in several regions and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection. The outbreak unfolded between September and November 2012, with at least 34–41 confirmed human cases and 13–17 deaths reported across regions such as Tagant, Brakna, Trarza, Assaba, and Hodh El Gharbi, alongside evidence of livestock infection and ongoing animal abortions. Transmission diminished by late November as environmental conditions changed and a multisectoral response—strengthening surveillance, improving case management, and implementing measures in slaughterhouses and among farmers—was put in place.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and flooding created extensive breeding sites for RVFV mosquito vectors in southern Mauritania, leading to rapid amplification in local livestock; socio‑economic reliance on pastoralism and informal slaughter practices increased human contact with infected animals, and limited preventive vaccination enabled recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicated that the 2012 outbreak viruses were related to previous Mauritanian RVFV strains, suggesting re‑emergence of locally circulating lineages rather than a novel genotype, with geographic range expansion driven primarily by environmental and husbandry factors.
Review: Review – Moderate-scale Western Africa outbreak (≈34–41 cases, 13–17 deaths) with correct geography and classification as re-occurrence; however, once larger events such as Mauritania 1998, Mayotte 2018–2019 and the 2025 Mauritania/Senegal epidemic are included, this episode is unlikely to rank among the global top-10 by impact and could be excluded if strict prioritization is required.
Review Comment: Not top 10

Host: Humans (rural residents, pastoralists) with concurrent livestock infections (small ruminants and camels) in Tahoua Region, Niger.
Event summary: In August–September 2016, health authorities in Niger’s Tahoua Region detected clusters of severe febrile illness with hemorrhagic signs in pastoral communities, and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection, marking the country’s first documented RVF outbreak. The outbreak centered on Tchintabaraden and neighboring departments, with reports of approximately 78 human cases and 26 deaths during August–September and additional suspected cases identified through expanded surveillance, alongside evidence of widespread livestock disease. Case numbers declined after September 2016 as vector control, movement restrictions, and public health messaging were implemented and as seasonal ecological conditions became less favorable, but the event demonstrated RVFV’s expansion eastward within Western Africa into previously unaffected areas of the Sahel.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy seasonal rains in the Sahel produced temporary ponds and flooded grazing areas in Tahoua Region, promoting mosquito proliferation among transhumant herds; extensive livestock movements and trade from neighboring endemic areas likely facilitated virus introduction, followed by local transmission to humans through handling of sick animals and exposure to vectors. Internal mechanisms: Genetic sequencing of outbreak viruses showed close relatedness to known West African RVFV lineages from earlier Mauritanian outbreaks, suggesting geographic range expansion of existing strains rather than major evolutionary change, with successful establishment in a largely naïve human and livestock population.
Review: Review – Corrected emergence-type classification: removed previous ‘first_detection’ and ‘intra_continental_emergence’ flags (RVFV was already established in the Western Africa subregion via Mauritania and Senegal) and set ‘re_occurrence’ to true to reflect range expansion within an existing subregion into a new country (Niger). Event remains epidemiologically important but is smaller than several other global outbreaks; may be de-prioritized if only the very largest events are retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (residents of pastoral and agro‑pastoral communities in Wajir, Marsabit, and Siaya counties) and livestock (goats, sheep, cattle, camels).
Event summary: In May–June 2018, after reports of livestock abortions and deaths in northern Kenya, an RVF outbreak was confirmed in Wajir and Marsabit counties and later in Siaya, with human cases presenting with acute febrile and sometimes hemorrhagic illness. Over the course of the outbreak, investigations identified around 106 human RVF cases (probable and confirmed) across the three counties, with several fatalities, while thousands of small stock were reportedly lost and serologic studies revealed substantial infection in goats and other livestock. Human case numbers declined by late June as joint animal–human health teams implemented vector control, livestock movement restrictions, and risk communication, and as rains decreased and temporary breeding sites for mosquitoes dried up.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and localized flooding in arid and semi‑arid counties of northern Kenya increased mosquito breeding, while high densities of susceptible small ruminants and camels enabled rapid amplification of RVFV; pastoral practices involving slaughtering, butchering, and consumption of sick animals, combined with limited vaccination, facilitated spillover to humans. Internal mechanisms: Epidemiologic and serologic investigations indicate involvement of RVFV strains consistent with earlier Kenyan lineages rather than a novel variant, with environmental suitability and livestock management practices—rather than new viral traits—driving the observed resurgence and spread into multiple counties.
Review: Review – Outbreak is well described and classification as re-occurrence within an already endemic Eastern Africa subregion is appropriate. With 106 human cases and single-country spread, its impact is intermediate compared with the largest global RVF epidemics; depending on how strictly a top-10 threshold is applied, this event is a reasonable candidate for retention or exclusion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (residents of Mayotte with frequent livestock contact or exposure to animal fluids) and livestock (cattle and small ruminants) on the island.
Event summary: From November 2018 through July 2019, Mayotte, a French overseas department in the Comoros archipelago, experienced a prolonged RVF outbreak with autochthonous human transmission following increased virus circulation in local cattle. A total of about 142–145 laboratory‑confirmed human cases were reported, most in central and north‑western communes, with the majority of patients reporting direct or indirect contact with livestock, consumption of raw milk or involvement in slaughtering; more than 120 animal infection foci were also detected. Human case numbers and new animal outbreaks declined after mid‑2019 as vector control, animal health measures and risk communication were strengthened and the rainy season ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A tropical climate with abundant competent vectors, close proximity to RVF‑endemic areas in East Africa and the Comoros, importation and local movement of cattle and small ruminants, and intense human–animal contact around small backyard herds created favorable conditions for virus amplification and spillover; preceding increases in bovine seroprevalence signaled rising transmission. Internal mechanisms: Virologic and modeling studies indicate that the outbreak was driven by circulation of RVFV strains typical of Eastern Africa, with no evidence of a radically novel lineage, so the event represents a substantial re-occurrence in an area with prior evidence of endemic virus rather than a first detection in the human host system.
Review: Review – Newly added major island outbreak with ≈142–145 confirmed human cases and extensive animal involvement in Mayotte, classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Africa (Mayotte is listed under Eastern Africa in the provided country table). This episode is one of the larger RVF outbreaks since 2010 and should be considered among the top-10 global events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (pastoralists, livestock breeders, rural residents) and livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels, dromedaries) in multiple regions of Mauritania and Senegal.
Event summary: Between late September and late October 2025, Mauritania and Senegal reported an unusually large multicountry RVF outbreak in the Senegal River basin and adjacent Sahelian areas. By 30 October 2025, a total of 404 confirmed human cases and 42 deaths had been reported—46 cases (14 deaths) across 11 wilayas in Mauritania and 358 cases (28 deaths) across 22 health districts in eight regions of Senegal, most in Saint‑Louis, alongside numerous animal outbreaks with high abortion and mortality rates in small ruminants and camels. Human case incidence began to decline toward the end of October as national and international partners mounted a coordinated One Health response including vector control, animal movement restrictions, enhanced surveillance, and risk communication, although the event remains notable for its scale, severe cases and cross‑border spread within Western Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Periods of heavy rainfall and flooding along the Senegal River and in eastern Mauritania in 2025 created abundant breeding sites for Aedes and Culex mosquitoes, while dense livestock populations, extensive cross‑border transhumance, and trade between Mauritania and Senegal facilitated viral amplification and geographic spread; limited vaccination coverage and gaps in veterinary and human health surveillance contributed to delayed detection. Internal mechanisms: Current reports and risk assessments attribute the outbreak to re‑emergence of endemic West African RVFV lineages under favorable ecological conditions rather than to a newly evolved lineage; however, ongoing molecular analyses may refine understanding of viral diversity during this episode.
Review: Review – Added very large 2025 multicountry outbreak (404 confirmed human cases, 42 deaths) spanning Mauritania and Senegal, clearly among the most impactful RVF events since 1990. Classified as re-occurrence within the Western Africa subregion; details may need updating as final analyses are published but the event should be retained in any top-10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (primarily unvaccinated and undervaccinated children)
Event summary: Beginning in early 2018, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) experienced a protracted nationwide measles epidemic driven by low routine immunization coverage and gaps after supplementary campaigns. The outbreak intensified through 2019, ultimately affecting all 26 provinces and causing more than 450,000 suspected cases and over 8,000 reported deaths before large-scale vaccination and response activities gradually brought transmission under control by late 2020, when incidence declined and the epidemic was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: chronically low measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) coverage (around or below 60% in recent years), gaps in supplemental immunization activities, weak health systems, poverty, and concurrent crises that diverted resources, allowing accumulation of large susceptible cohorts. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of a fundamentally novel genotype driving this outbreak; the main mechanism is re-occurrence due to immunity gaps, with the inherently high transmissibility of circulating B3/H1-lineage strains facilitating rapid geographic expansion.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Large DRC epidemic (≈460,000 suspected cases and >8,000 deaths) is clearly among the most impactful modern measles events and is well documented by UNICEF and WHO/CDC sources. ([unicef.org](https://www.unicef.org/drcongo/en/press-releases/measles-deaths-democratic-republic-congo-top-4000)) Geographic, temporal and host information are correct; classification as re-occurrence (no first/inter-continental or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because measles has long been endemic in Middle Africa. No structural changes made beyond confirming that emergence-type flags remain all "No" except re_occurrence=Yes.

Host: Humans (mainly children, many unvaccinated)
Event summary: In September 2018, Madagascar detected an unusually large measles outbreak starting in Antananarivo that rapidly spread nationwide due to very low vaccination coverage. By late 2019, estimates suggested roughly 220,000–250,000 cases and over 1,000 deaths, making it the largest measles outbreak in the country’s history. The epidemic waned after multiple mass vaccination campaigns and strengthened surveillance, and incidence gradually returned toward pre‑outbreak levels once large susceptible cohorts had been partially depleted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing low MCV1 coverage (around 58% in 2017), high prevalence of childhood malnutrition, urban crowding, poverty, and overlapping health emergencies that strained the health system, allowing accumulation of susceptible children. Internal mechanisms: B3 genotype viruses already circulating in Africa were responsible; there is no evidence of a substantially novel measles strain, so the event is appropriately characterized as re-occurrence driven by immunity gaps and adverse socio-environmental conditions.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Madagascar’s 2018–2019 epidemic (≈225,000+ cases, >1,000 deaths) is one of the largest national measles outbreaks this century and fits the selection criterion based on burden. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/17-january-2019-measles-madagascar-en)) Country, sub-region (Eastern Africa), timing and drivers are consistent with WHO/UNICEF reporting. Classification as re-occurrence only is correct; measles has long circulated in Madagascar and no novel strain was implicated. No field changes required.

Host: Humans (primarily children, both unvaccinated and undervaccinated)
Event summary: From around 2013, the Philippines entered a large measles epidemic cycle as immunity gaps from declining vaccination coverage accumulated in successive birth cohorts. In 2014, WHO recorded more than 57,000 suspected cases and over 21,000 confirmed measles infections with about 110 deaths nationwide, with major outbreaks centered in Metro Manila and other urban areas. Intensified vaccination efforts and outbreak response activities in 2014–2015 reduced incidence, but persistent immunity gaps contributed to renewed resurgence in 2018–2019.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: declining routine measles vaccination coverage, high population density in urban centers, and health‑system constraints that hindered follow‑up campaigns and outbreak response. Internal mechanisms: circulating measles genotypes (notably D8) were not fundamentally new for the region; the outbreak reflects re-occurrence due to large susceptible cohorts rather than viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2013–2014 Philippines epidemic (tens of thousands of cases and >100 deaths) is a major Western Pacific/SE Asia event and seeded numerous international outbreaks, including in the U.S. and other high‑income countries. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/15-05-2019-new-measles-surveillance-data-for-2019?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate; measles was long-established nationally. No corrections to geography, timing or emergence-type flags were required, but users should note that case/death figures vary slightly by source and are approximate.

Host: Humans (mainly infants and young children)
Event summary: In early 2019, the Philippines experienced another major measles epidemic, with outbreaks declared in multiple regions including Metro Manila, Central Luzon, CALABARZON, Western Visayas and Central Visayas. By late February 2019, more than 12,000 suspected cases and over 200 deaths had already been reported, and national totals by year’s end reached many tens of thousands of mainly young, unvaccinated children. Aggressive emergency vaccination campaigns and risk‑communication efforts gradually curtailed transmission over 2019, but the episode underscored severe immunity gaps and eroded public trust in immunization following recent vaccine controversies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: substantial drops in measles vaccination coverage due to long‑term program weaknesses and, more recently, loss of public trust in vaccines, high birth rates, and intense urban crowding. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new measles variant was implicated; the epidemic reflects re-occurrence driven by large susceptible cohorts and frequent seeding between regions, with highly transmissible D8 genotypes already circulating in the Western Pacific Region.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2019 Philippines resurgence again produced very large national case and death burdens and contributed materially to global measles resurgence, so it is reasonable to include as a separate high-impact event following the 2013–2014 epidemic. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/15-05-2019-new-measles-surveillance-data-for-2019?utm_source=openai)) Emergence-type flags (re_occurrence only) and geographic classification are consistent with definitions and WHO reporting; no structural field changes made.

Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2017]; Brazil [2018]; Colombia [2018]; Ecuador [2018]; Peru [2018]
Host: Humans (children and adults, including indigenous populations)
Event summary: In mid‑2017, Venezuela reported a measles outbreak that marked the re-establishment of sustained transmission in a country and region previously verified as measles‑free, with 7,000+ confirmed cases and at least 80 deaths by 2019. From 2017–2019, the outbreak spread across borders, with genotype D8 virus exported to Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, where it caused outbreaks and led to loss of elimination status in Brazil and Venezuela. Intensive regional vaccination campaigns, including immunization of nearly 9 million children in Venezuela, eventually interrupted sustained transmission and brought the multinational episode under control by late 2019.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: severe collapse of Venezuela’s health system, economic crisis, and mass migration reduced vaccination coverage and facilitated regional spread, especially among vulnerable indigenous groups along the Venezuela–Brazil and Venezuela–Colombia borders. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was associated with circulation and regional establishment of measles genotype D8 (Hulu Langat lineage), already known globally; viral change did not fundamentally alter pathogenicity, so the event is classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence or true intra-/inter‑continental emergence.
Review: Decision: retain, with corrected emergence classification (flag for review). Change made: intra_continental_emergence was set from Yes to No because measles was historically endemic throughout the South American sub-region and had been eliminated but not absent historically; the 2017–2019 episode represents re-establishment of transmission and cross-border spread within a previously affected sub-region, fitting the definition of re-occurrence, not intra-continental emergence. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6945a6.htm?utm_source=openai)) Geography (South America, listed countries) and timing are appropriate; sources from PAHO, CDC and peer-reviewed literature are relevant. Event is important because it led to loss of elimination status in parts of the Americas Region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Ukraine [2017]; Romania [2017]; Italy [2017]; Greece [2017]; France [2017]; Germany [2017]; Bulgaria [2017]; Czechia [2017]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2018]; multiple other EU/EEA countries [2017]
Host: Humans (children, adolescents, and adults, including unvaccinated and under‑vaccinated groups)
Event summary: From 2017 onwards, the WHO European Region saw a major resurgence of measles, with large outbreaks in Ukraine, Romania, Italy, Greece, France, Bulgaria and several other countries after years of progress toward elimination. In 2017, reported EU/EEA measles cases more than tripled compared with 2016, and by 2018–2019 the region recorded over 80,000 and then more than 100,000 cases respectively, with Ukraine alone accounting for over half of cases in some periods. WHO and ECDC activated enhanced response measures, and expanded vaccination activities and targeted campaigns for at‑risk communities reduced incidence after 2019, although sporadic outbreaks continued where immunity gaps persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: declining or stagnating 2‑dose measles vaccine coverage in several countries, pockets of vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, health‑system gaps among marginalized communities (e.g. Roma, migrants), and high population mobility across European borders. Internal mechanisms: genotypes D8 and B3 predominated, but available evidence does not indicate markedly higher virulence; the resurgence is best characterized as re-occurrence in previously endemic sub-regions that had interrupted transmission but retained pockets of susceptibility.
Review: Decision: retain, with corrected emergence classification and minor consistency note (flag for review). Change made: intra_continental_emergence was set from Yes to No. The 2017–2019 resurgence occurred in European sub-regions with long-standing measles presence and previous elimination verification; per the definitions, this is a re-occurrence driven by immunity gaps, not first occurrence in a new sub-region. ([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/measles-cases-eu-treble-2017-outbreaks-still-ongoing)) The listed countries and sub-regions match ECDC/WHO reports, but the placeholder phrase "multiple other EU/EEA countries" is non-standard relative to the instruction to list all affected countries; if higher geographic resolution is needed, key additional countries (e.g. Albania, Serbia, Georgia) should be explicitly added in a future revision.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa
Countries: South Africa [2009]; Angola [2009]; Namibia [2009]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2009]; other WHO African Region countries with large outbreaks [2009]
Host: Humans (mainly children, but also adolescents and adults)
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2010, the WHO African Region experienced major measles outbreaks in multiple countries after several years of lower incidence following mortality‑reduction initiatives. Large epidemics were reported in South Africa, Angola, Namibia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and many other countries, with about 83,000 reported cases in 2009 and roughly 170,000 in 2010 region‑wide. Intensified supplemental immunization activities and renewed political commitment subsequently reduced incidence, but the episode demonstrated the fragility of gains and the potential for rapid measles resurgence when coverage goals are not sustained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suboptimal routine MCV1 coverage and incomplete or delayed follow‑up campaigns across many African countries created large susceptible cohorts, compounded by health‑system challenges and funding gaps. Internal mechanisms: several genotypes (B3, B2, D4, D8) circulated, but changes in virus genetics were secondary to immunity gaps; the event is best defined as a multi‑country re-occurrence within Africa rather than geographic emergence.
Review: Decision: retain, with corrected emergence classification (flag for review). Change made: intra_continental_emergence was set from Yes to No. The 2009–2010 African Region resurgence involved widespread outbreaks across already-affected African sub-regions and is described by WHO/CDC as a regional resurgence attributable to lapses in vaccination coverage, not first occurrence in new sub-regions. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6012a3.htm?utm_source=openai)) The "other WHO African Region countries" placeholder in the countries field departs from the ideal of listing all affected countries; however, given that ≥28 countries experienced outbreaks, summarizing the largest exemplars is a practical compromise. Event remains one of the largest modern regional measles resurgences and fits the "largest impact" criterion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Western Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Somalia [2020]; Ethiopia [2017]; Nigeria [2018]; Chad [2018]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2018]; multiple other African countries with major outbreaks [2019-2022]
Host: Humans (especially unvaccinated children in fragile and humanitarian settings)
Event summary: From roughly 2017 through 2022, the WHO African Region again saw widespread measles resurgence, with large outbreaks in countries such as Ethiopia, Nigeria, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and, later, Somalia. During 2019–2022, tens of thousands of measles cases were reported annually, and early 2022 data showed about a fourfold increase in regional measles cases compared with the same period in 2021, with at least 20 African countries reporting outbreaks in the first quarter of 2022. Emergency vaccination campaigns and strengthened outbreak preparedness reduced incidence in some countries, but persistent conflict, displacement and COVID‑19–related service disruptions left many areas at continued high risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: chronic under‑vaccination (regional MCV1 coverage stagnating near 69%), large displaced and hard‑to‑reach populations, health‑system disruptions from conflict and the COVID‑19 pandemic (which delayed vaccination drives and increased the number of children missing doses), and poverty‑related barriers to care. Internal mechanisms: re-occurrence driven primarily by widening immunity gaps and health‑system shocks; viral genotypes such as B3 were familiar, with no strong evidence that intrinsic viral evolution, rather than external drivers, was the main cause of resurgence.
Review: Decision: retain, with corrected emergence classification (flag for review). Change made: intra_continental_emergence was set from Yes to No. The 2017–2022 African resurgence reflects renewed, multi-country outbreaks in long-affected sub-regions, amplified by COVID‑19–related disruptions, rather than introduction into new African sub-regions. ([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/news/vaccine-preventable-disease-outbreaks-rise-africa)) Countries and timing are broadly consistent with WHO AFRO situation reports, though the "multiple other African countries" catch‑all again trades completeness for brevity. This row usefully captures the post‑2017 and early‑COVID measles surge and is appropriate to retain as a high-impact regional event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2014]; Canada [2015]; Mexico [2014]
Host: Humans (children and adults, especially unvaccinated travelers and their contacts)
Event summary: In December 2014, a measles outbreak linked to Disneyland Resort in California began after an infected traveler exposed visitors at the parks, leading to chains of transmission in several U.S. states and onward spread to Mexico and Canada. By February–April 2015, about 125 U.S. cases across multiple states were epidemiologically linked to the Disneyland exposure, and additional clusters occurred in Quebec, Canada, while concurrent importations from the large Philippines outbreak seeded other North American outbreaks. The episode ended by mid‑2015 after aggressive case finding, isolation and vaccination activities, but it highlighted vulnerabilities in measles‑eliminated settings where pockets of undervaccination persist and theme-park or travel hubs can amplify imported cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international travel from regions with large measles outbreaks (notably the Philippines), clusters of unvaccinated or under‑vaccinated individuals (including vaccine‑hesitant communities), and crowded theme‑park settings that facilitated exposure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by measles genotype B3, already widely circulating globally; re-occurrence in elimination settings was driven by human mobility and vaccination gaps, not novel viral traits.
Review: Decision: review (borderline for "top 10"; emergence classification corrected). Changes made: (1) Continent/sub-region and country fields were narrowed to North America and South America (via Mexico classified under Central America) with listed countries United States, Canada and Mexico; Brazil and a generic "other affected countries" phrase were removed because available CDC/WHO reports link the Disneyland-associated chains specifically to the U.S., Canada and Mexico, not to large outbreaks in Brazil, which were epidemiologically distinct. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm64e0213a1.htm)) (2) Intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence were both set from Yes to No. Per the project definitions, this episode is a re-occurrence in historically affected continents and sub-regions and involves imported cases with limited onward spread; it does not represent first occurrence of measles in a new continent or sub-region. The event is epidemiologically important because it exposed vulnerabilities in elimination settings, but with ~125 U.S. cases plus modest numbers in Canada and Mexico it is much smaller than other outbreaks listed. Dataset owners should decide whether to retain it within a strict "ten largest by burden" list or treat it as an illustrative policy case outside the core top 10.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (primarily unvaccinated children and members of tight‑knit religious communities, plus travelers)
Event summary: From late 2018 through 2019, the United States experienced its largest measles resurgence since 1992, with 1,249 confirmed cases and 22 outbreaks nationwide despite having eliminated endemic measles in 2000. The majority of cases were concentrated in long‑duration outbreaks in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York City and Rockland County, seeded by imported cases and amplified by low vaccination coverage, with smaller clusters across multiple states and some spillover into Canada. These outbreaks temporarily threatened the country’s elimination status but were brought under control just before a full year of continuous transmission elapsed, following intensive vaccination campaigns, emergency public‑health orders and community engagement efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: under‑vaccination and vaccine refusal in specific close‑knit communities, high population density and close social networks, frequent international travel importing virus from endemic regions (notably Israel, Ukraine and the Philippines), and sometimes delayed vaccination of infants. Internal mechanisms: circulating measles genotypes (mainly D8, with some B3) were not new to the U.S.; the episode is best classified as re-occurrence in an elimination setting due to local immunity gaps rather than viral evolution, though high intrinsic transmissibility meant relatively small drops in coverage yielded large outbreaks.
Review: Decision: review (high policy importance but modest burden relative to other events). No structural field changes were made: geography, timing, host, and emergence classification (re_occurrence only) align with CDC’s national update on the 2019 outbreaks and the definition of re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6840e2.htm)) However, with 1,249 U.S. cases and no reported deaths, the quantitative burden is far smaller than for African, European, or Philippine outbreaks listed here. Its inclusion is justified by its near‑loss of U.S. elimination status and the global attention it received, but if the dataset must strictly contain the ten largest events by cases/deaths, this row should be reconsidered for exclusion or treated as a secondary elimination-setting case study rather than a core top‑10 burden event.

Host: Humans
Event summary: From the early 1990s onward, Lyme disease in the United States intensified in the Northeast, Mid‑Atlantic, and Upper Midwest, building on foci first recognized in the 1970s and 1980s. Over roughly 1990–2010, incidence rose steadily and geographic foci expanded into suburban and peri‑urban areas as infected Ixodes scapularis ticks spread, leading to several hundred thousand treated human infections per year by the 2010s. The event has persisted through at least the mid‑2020s with high and fluctuating annual case numbers and no clear return to pre‑epidemic baselines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suburbanization and forest fragmentation that increased edge habitat and human exposure to ticks; recovery and high densities of white‑tailed deer and competent rodent reservoirs; increased outdoor recreation; and regional climate warming that lengthened tick activity seasons and favored Ixodes scapularis survival. Internal mechanisms: highly efficient enzootic transmission cycles of B. burgdorferi sensu stricto in Peromyscus and other small mammals and continued geographic range expansion of competent tick vectors (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation and inherent geographic range expansion), without strong evidence for a single novel hypervirulent strain dominating this period.
Review: retain – This row appropriately captures the long‑running increase and spread of Lyme disease incidence in the northeastern, mid‑Atlantic and upper midwestern United States from the early 1990s through at least the mid‑2020s, with correct continent/subregion/country coding and classification as a re‑occurrence event driven primarily by ecological and behavioral factors rather than pathogen change.

Event summary: Beginning around 2009, Canada experienced a marked emergence of Lyme disease as locally established Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus populations expanded northward from the United States and from coastal refugia. By around 2020, Lyme borreliosis was still non‑endemic but established as an emerging tick‑borne zoonosis in selected coastal zones of North and East Africa, raising concern that climate change, migratory birds and changing tick vectors could facilitate further spread in coming decades.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑distance movement of Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato into Africa via migratory birds carrying Ixodes and Hyalomma ticks from Europe; suitable humid Mediterranean and coastal climates in North and East Africa that allow survival of these vectors; movements of livestock, dogs and horses that help disseminate infected ticks; and limited awareness and diagnostic capacity that likely result in under‑recognition of human cases. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of Lyme group borreliae into new vertebrate reservoirs (including lizards) and probable adaptation to Hyalomma ticks as vectors in some settings, enabling sporadic autochthonous human transmission and constituting an inter‑continental emergence of the Lyme borreliosis system into African ecosystems.

Because case numbers are still low, some reports rely mainly on serology and molecular characterization is incomplete, this event is classified as an inter‑continental emergence episode of modest current burden and should be reviewed carefully by regional experts for confirmation of country start years and the strength of evidence for human infection.
