Host: Humans (adult and elderly urban residents, mainly in Bucharest and southeastern Romania)
Event summary: In summer–autumn 1996, Romania experienced a large outbreak of West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease centered on Bucharest and southeastern districts, marking a dramatic return of WNV encephalitis to Europe after decades of mainly silent circulation. The epidemic developed rapidly between July 15 and October 12, with 393 serologically confirmed or probable human cases, 352 presenting with central nervous system infection and 17 deaths predominantly among persons over 50 years of age. Transmission subsided with the end of the mosquito season and intensified vector control, after which only sporadic cases were reported until later European re-emergence episodes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: hot summer conditions, high densities of Culex mosquitoes in urban settings, and peri‑domestic bird populations facilitated intense local amplification; limited prior population immunity after a long inter-epidemic period likely increased the pool of susceptible adults. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel lineage was identified compared with earlier European/Mediterranean WNV lineage 1 strains, so the event is best characterized as a geographic and intensity resurgence without major documented viral genetic change (re-occurrence rather than re-emergence).
Review: retain: Major early European West Nile neuroinvasive outbreak (~393 confirmed cases, 17 deaths) in Eastern Europe; geography and classification as re-occurrence (no new continent or clearly novel strain) are consistent with published accounts, so no structural changes were made.

Event summary: During the summer of 1999, a large outbreak of West Nile fever and neuroinvasive disease occurred in southern European Russia, centered on the Volgograd Region with extension into neighboring Astrakhan and Rostov oblasts. From late July to early October, several hundred clinically compatible human cases were hospitalized (estimates around 800), including 84 meningoencephalitis cases with about 40 deaths, making this one of the largest recognized West Nile outbreaks in Europe and the Mediterranean to that time. Human transmission declined with the onset of cooler weather and intensified mosquito control, but subsequent surveillance documented continued endemic WNV circulation and recurrent seasonal cases in these regions.

Internal mechanisms: outbreak viruses belonged to WNV lineage 1 and were closely related to strains circulating in Romania and the eastern Mediterranean, without strong evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype; the event is therefore best interpreted as a major re-occurrence in an already endemic region driven mainly by climatic and ecological factors rather than by documented viral innovation.

Host: Humans (primarily older adults in New York City and surrounding counties)
Event summary: In late August 1999, unexplained clusters of encephalitis with muscle weakness were detected in Queens, New York City, and investigation identified the first domestic human cases of West Nile virus in the United States and the Americas. The outbreak evolved over August–September with around 60 hospitalized human cases and 7 deaths, accompanied by extensive bird mortality and WNV‑positive mosquito pools across New York City and neighboring counties, demonstrating rapid local establishment of a new zoonotic arbovirus. Human transmission waned with cooler weather and mosquito control measures, but the virus overwintered and seeded its subsequent continent‑wide spread across North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introduction of an infected human, bird or mosquito via international air travel or trade into New York, followed by amplification in abundant urban Culex pipiens mosquitoes and local bird populations; warm late‑summer conditions and dense human populations enhanced exposure. Internal mechanisms: the introduced lineage 1 strain was highly neuroinvasive in humans and birds, but genetic analyses suggest it belonged to the existing lineage 1 clade circulating in the Mediterranean rather than representing a fundamentally new genotype; the key mechanism was geographic range expansion and establishment in a naïve ecological and human context.

Event summary: Between August 1 and October 31, 2000, Israel experienced a nationwide epidemic of West Nile fever, following earlier animal outbreaks and detection of WNV activity in birds in 1998–1999. The epidemic involved 417 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, 326 hospitalizations and about 33 deaths, representing one of the largest and most severe WNV outbreaks recorded globally at that time. Human transmission declined with the end of the mosquito season and intensified vector control, but the event signaled renewed high‑impact WNV activity in an area with documented historical circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high late‑summer temperatures, irrigated agriculture and peri‑urban wetlands supported large Culex mosquito populations feeding on birds and humans; demographic aging and urbanization increased the proportion of susceptible older adults; prior detection of WNV in geese and migratory birds points to avian migration and local ecological change as key drivers. Internal mechanisms: sequence data indicate co-circulation of closely related lineage 1 clusters, including variants similar to those detected in Israel in 1998 and in New York and Russia in 1999, but without definitive evidence that a single new genotype alone explains the outbreak’s severity; the event is therefore treated here as a major re-occurrence in a region with prior human WNV activity.
Review: retain: Large 2000 nationwide outbreak in Israel (~417 confirmed cases, ~33 deaths) is well documented and clearly among the historically largest WNV outbreaks; geography and classification as re-occurrence (no new continent or sub-region, and only modest genotype differences within lineage 1) are acceptable for this dataset, so no structural changes were made.

Internal mechanisms: the epidemic was driven largely by the same lineage 1 strain introduced in 1999, with evidence of local adaptation of virus–vector–host systems but no single defining novel genotype; the key mechanisms were geographic range expansion and a high force of infection in a largely naïve continent, consistent with intra-continental emergence into new subregions.

Review: retain: The 2012 U.S. season (5,674 cases, 286 deaths) is one of the largest WNV epidemics recorded and is appropriately coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic continent driven largely by climatic and ecological factors; no structural changes were required.

Event summary: In 2021, the United States experienced a substantial West Nile virus season with an unprecedented focal outbreak in Maricopa County, Arizona, more than two decades after the virus became endemic. Nationally, about 2,445 human WNV cases and 165 deaths were reported, with Arizona accounting for roughly 1,487 cases, over 1,000 hospitalizations and 101 deaths concentrated in the Phoenix metropolitan area, the largest single‑county WNV outbreak ever recorded in the U.S. As the unusually wet 2021 Southwest monsoon ended and intensive vector control and public‑health messaging were implemented, human case numbers declined into late autumn, but the event highlighted the potential for extreme, climate‑linked WNV surges in established endemic regions.

Review: retain: The 2021 Maricopa County-focused outbreak (≈1,487 local cases, 101 deaths, within a U.S. total of ~2,445 cases) is well documented and represents one of the largest and most intense focal WNV outbreaks in an already endemic setting; geography and coding as re-occurrence without intra-/inter-continental emergence are appropriate, and no structural corrections were needed.

Countries: United States of America [1992-1993]; Canada [1992-1993]; France [1992-1993]; Japan [1992-1993]
Host: Humans (all ages; high illness burden especially among children and older adults)
Event summary: In the 1992–1993 Northern Hemisphere influenza season, influenza B viruses antigenically similar to B/Panama/45/90 (B/Yamagata-lineage) predominated in the United States and were responsible for epidemic influenza in many parts of the world, with B accounting for roughly 70–90% of early-season isolates in the US and being the first virus detected in countries such as France and Japan.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/00046025.htm?utm_source=openai)) As the season progressed, influenza A(H3N2) Beijing/32/92-like viruses increased and caused late-season outbreaks, but influenza B continued to contribute substantially to hospitalizations and excess pneumonia-and-influenza mortality, particularly among high-risk older adults.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/00046025.htm?utm_source=openai)) Activity declined by late winter and spring 1993, yet this season remains a reference example of large-scale influenza B predominance before the modern two-lineage era.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Typical wintertime environmental conditions, high mixing in schools and long-term care facilities, and limited prior immunity to B/Panama/45/90-like B/Yamagata viruses in younger age groups supported widespread transmission across North America, Europe and parts of Asia in the absence of a concurrent influenza A pandemic.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/00046025.htm?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenic drift within the B/Yamagata lineage produced B/Panama/45/90-like viruses that were sufficiently distinct from earlier Yamagata strains to cause substantial epidemics despite previous exposure and vaccination, but no new lineage or host shift occurred, so this episode is appropriately classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Decision: review – new high-impact event added for the 1992–1993 B/Yamagata-dominated season based on CDC surveillance and virological reports; geography is simplified to major well-documented countries (United States, Canada, France, Japan), but additional European and Asian countries almost certainly experienced similar patterns and may be added or refined in a subsequent expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Continent: Asia; Europe; North America; South America; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; South America; Southern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: China [2000-2002]; Japan [2000-2002]; Republic of Korea [2000-2002]; Singapore [2001-2002]; Malaysia [2001-2002]; United States of America [2001-2002]; Canada [2001-2002]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2001-2002]; Germany [2001-2002]; France [2001-2002]; Italy [2001-2002]; Spain [2001-2002]; Brazil [2002]; Argentina [2002]; Australia [2002]; New Zealand [2002]; South Africa [2002]
Host: Humans (all ages; notable burden in children and adolescents)
Event summary: After being largely restricted to eastern Asia throughout the 1990s, B/Victoria/2/87-lineage influenza B viruses re-emerged around 2000 in East Asia and then spread globally.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5038a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) During the 2000–2001 and especially 2001–2002 seasons, B/Victoria variants seeded seasonal epidemics in North America, Europe, South America, Oceania and parts of Africa, displacing B/Yamagata viruses in many countries and causing sizeable outbreaks in populations—particularly children—that had little prior exposure to this lineage.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5123a3.htm)) The episode concluded with inclusion of a B/Victoria-lineage virus (B/Hong Kong/330/01-like) in the 2002–2003 vaccine and long-term establishment of global co-circulation of the Victoria and Yamagata lineages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The concentration of B/Victoria viruses in East Asia during the 1990s created large susceptible cohorts elsewhere; increasing international air travel, especially between Asia and other continents, enabled rapid seeding of the lineage into North America, Europe, South America, Oceania and parts of Africa just as vaccine formulations still targeted B/Yamagata-lineage viruses, generating substantial lineage-level mismatch.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5123a3.htm)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenic drift within the B/Victoria lineage and reassortment with B/Yamagata-derived gene segments produced variants with reduced cross-reactivity to B/Yamagata-based vaccines and good fitness across climates, facilitating geographic range expansion and long-term re-establishment of this lineage in global circulation.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0042682202917198?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – corrected continents to include Africa, added Southern Africa and representative South-East Asian and African countries (Singapore, Malaysia, South Africa) based on surveillance reports, and reclassified the event as a lineage-level re-emergence rather than an inter‑continental emergence of influenza B (which was already globally established). Country-year annotations remain approximate and should be cross-checked against detailed national data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern America; Eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2005-2006]; France [2005-2006]; Germany [2005-2006]; Italy [2005-2006]; Spain [2005-2006]; Sweden [2005-2006]; Poland [2005-2006]; United States of America [2005-2006]; Canada [2005-2006]; Japan [2005-2006]; China [2005-2006]; India [2005-2006]
Host: Humans (especially children and adolescents, but with appreciable disease in adults)
Event summary: During the 2005–2006 influenza season, many European countries and parts of North America and Asia experienced epidemics in which influenza B viruses predominated early in the season, particularly in Europe where B viruses accounted for about 58% of all laboratory detections and consultation rates for influenza-like illness were similar to or higher than in 2004–2005.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17991413/?utm_source=openai)) Antigenic characterization showed that roughly 80% of circulating B viruses in the United States and Europe belonged to the B/Victoria lineage, whereas the trivalent vaccine contained a B/Yamagata-lineage component, leading to a substantial lineage-level mismatch and reduced vaccine effectiveness against influenza B.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5523a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) Influenza A activity increased later in the winter, and overall influenza circulation returned to low levels by late spring 2006, but this season became a key example used to motivate adoption of quadrivalent vaccines that include both B lineages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Wintertime climate, high contact rates in schools, and suboptimal vaccine protection due to inclusion of a B/Yamagata rather than B/Victoria antigen in the 2005–2006 trivalent vaccine allowed B/Victoria viruses to spread widely, with B accounting for one third to more than half of influenza detections in many settings.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17991413/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenic drift and lineage-specific population immunity favored B/Victoria-lineage viruses after several years of B/Yamagata-targeted vaccination, but no fundamentally new lineage or host shift occurred; this event represents a large recurrence of influenza B driven largely by vaccine mismatch and immunity patterns rather than intrinsic changes in host range or virulence.
Review: Decision: retain – new event added to capture the large 2005–2006 season in which B/Victoria-lineage viruses predominated in Europe and parts of North America and Asia and were mismatched to the B/Yamagata-lineage vaccine component; classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) reflects that the lineage was already globally established and genetic changes were modest, while the main driver was vaccine mismatch and population immunity.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012-2013]; Ireland [2012-2013]; Spain [2012-2013]; Italy [2012-2013]; Bulgaria [2012-2013]; Canada [2012-2013]; United States of America [2012-2013]; Germany [2012-2013]; France [2012-2013]
Host: Humans, with marked impact in children and older adults
Event summary: During the 2012–2013 Northern Hemisphere winter, all three seasonal influenza viruses circulated, but many European countries and parts of North America experienced a season in which influenza A(H3N2) viruses predominated early, followed by a later wave of influenza B that became predominant in a number of countries and contributed substantially to outpatient visits, pediatric hospitalizations and moderate to high severity indicators.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4102099/?utm_source=openai)) The episode waned by late spring 2013 as population immunity increased and seasonal transmission subsided, underscoring the recurrent contribution of influenza B to severe disease, particularly when lineage mismatch or suboptimal vaccine uptake occurs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Typical winter environmental conditions, intense mixing in schools and long-term care facilities, and the use of trivalent vaccines containing only one B lineage meant that in some settings circulating B viruses were of the opposite lineage or a drifted clade relative to the vaccine, contributing to breakthrough infections and a sizable late-season B wave.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/risk-assessment-seasonal-influenza-201213-europe-eueea-countries?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenic drift within both B/Victoria and B/Yamagata lineages generated partial immune escape, but no new lineage or host shift was identified; this event is therefore best interpreted as a re-occurring epidemic of established influenza B lineages.
Review: Decision: review – retained as a moderate-intensity but geographically widespread season with a substantial late influenza B wave; the sub-region list was corrected to include Eastern Europe (for Bulgaria), and the event is classified as re-occurrence of established lineages without inter- or intra-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Eastern Asia; Northern America
Countries: Japan [2017-2018]; Bulgaria [2017-2018]; Italy [2017-2018]; Spain [2017-2018]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2017-2018]; Germany [2017-2018]; France [2017-2018]; United States of America [2017-2018]; Canada [2017-2018]
Host: Humans, with prominent impact in school-age children and older adults
Event summary: In the 2017–2018 influenza season, many Northern Hemisphere countries experienced an unusually intense winter characterized initially by widespread A(H3N2) circulation, followed by a large wave of influenza B, predominantly of the B/Yamagata lineage, in Europe and parts of Asia and North America.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/seasonal-influenza-annual-epidemiological-report-2017-18-season?utm_source=openai)) The co-circulation of A viruses and a dominant B/Yamagata wave led to very high rates of influenza-like illness, hospitalizations and excess mortality across Europe and the United States, with many severe influenza B cases in middle-aged and older adults and significant pediatric involvement.([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/flu/about/burden/2017-2018/archive.htm?utm_source=openai)) As spring 2018 progressed, influenza B activity declined with rising population immunity, and the season strengthened the case for quadrivalent vaccines including both B lineages, because most trivalent vaccines in use contained only B/Victoria.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal winter conditions, substantial susceptible populations to B/Yamagata after several years of varying lineage dominance, and widespread use of trivalent vaccines targeting only the B/Victoria lineage in some countries contributed to high transmission and lineage-level vaccine mismatch.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5883452/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Circulating B/Yamagata viruses were antigenically similar to the B/Phuket/3073/2013-like component of quadrivalent vaccines but antigenically distinct from B/Victoria-lineage strains, so vaccinated persons who received trivalent vaccines lacking a B/Yamagata component had limited direct protection, while no major host shift or new genotype was documented; this episode is therefore classified as a strong re-occurring epidemic of an established lineage.
Review: Decision: review – geography was adjusted by removing the unsupported 'Southern Asia' sub-region so that sub-regions now align with the countries listed (Japan, European countries, United States, Canada), and the event is retained and classified as a re-occurrence of an established B/Yamagata lineage with major impact and documented B-lineage vaccine mismatch.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Central Asia; Eastern Asia
Countries: United States of America [2019-2020]; Canada [2019-2020]; Germany [2019-2020]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019-2020]; France [2019-2020]; Italy [2019-2020]; Spain [2019-2020]; Russian Federation [2019-2020]; Kazakhstan [2019-2020]; China [2019-2020]
Host: Humans, with especially high burden in children and adolescents
Event summary: The 2019–2020 Northern Hemisphere influenza season began unusually early with predominance of influenza B/Victoria-lineage viruses, particularly in the United States and parts of Europe and Central Asia, before later co-circulation with A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2) viruses.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/seasonal-influenza-annual-epidemiological-report-2019-2020?utm_source=openai)) In the United States this early B/Victoria wave led to very high pediatric hospitalization rates and a record 188 reported pediatric influenza deaths, nearly two‑thirds of which were attributed to influenza B, while in Europe lineage-typed B detections were overwhelmingly B/Victoria during late 2019 and early 2020.([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/flu/spotlights/2019-2020/2019-20-pediatric-flu-deaths.htm?utm_source=openai)) The episode concluded abruptly in March 2020 as widespread non-pharmaceutical interventions for COVID‑19 curtailed influenza transmission, sharply reducing further spread of both A and B viruses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8511754/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal conditions, intense transmission among school-age children, and gaps in vaccination coverage—especially among children and adolescents—amplified spread of B/Victoria viruses, while public health measures introduced for COVID‑19 (school closures, distancing, travel reductions) suddenly suppressed influenza circulation late in the season.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/73/4/e947/6121316?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenically drifted B/Victoria 1A(Δ3)B subgroup viruses (e.g. B/Washington/02/2019-like) became predominant in Europe and North America, representing a novel genetic and antigenic subgroup within B/Victoria that sustained early transmission and coincided with the first season since 1992–1993 in which B viruses predominated in the United States.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/influenza-virus-characterisation-october-2019?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – reclassified this episode as re-emergence (driven by the rise of B/Victoria 1A(Δ3)B viruses and a shift back to B predominance) rather than a combination of re-occurrence and re-emergence, to keep event types mutually exclusive as specified; geography and burden description are consistent with CDC and ECDC reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: China [2020-2022]; Japan [2020-2022]; Italy [2020-2021]; Germany [2020-2021]; France [2020-2021]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2020-2021]; United States of America [2020-2022]; Australia [2022]
Host: Humans, with continued susceptibility in children but markedly reduced overall influenza activity in 2020–2021
Event summary: Following the onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in early 2020, global influenza activity collapsed, but among the few influenza B detections almost all were B/Victoria-lineage and virological surveillance recorded no confirmed naturally occurring B/Yamagata-lineage viruses after March 2020.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) During the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 seasons, countries in East Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania that did observe influenza circulation reported overwhelming dominance of B/Victoria, while B/Yamagata remained undetected despite continued typing and sequencing.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/influenza-update-n-381?utm_source=openai)) By 2023–2024, WHO and national advisory bodies concluded that inclusion of a B/Yamagata antigen in seasonal vaccines was no longer warranted and recommended a transition back to trivalent vaccines containing only a B/Victoria component, marking a major reconfiguration of global influenza B ecology.([cdn.who.int](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/who-influenza-recommendations/vcm-southern-hemisphere-recommendation-2024/202309_recommendation.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=2c2cbebd_7&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Non-pharmaceutical interventions against COVID‑19 (travel restrictions, masking, school closures and distancing) dramatically reduced influenza transmission worldwide and disrupted the usual reseeding of influenza lineages between hemispheres; differences in local timing and stringency of these measures, along with prior immunity and vaccine use, appear to have favored persistence and reintroduction of B/Victoria viruses while pushing B/Yamagata to extremely low, and possibly zero, effective circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Pre‑existing antigenic properties and fitness of contemporary B/Victoria clades, together with B/Yamagata’s tendency to infect older age groups and its relatively antigenically stable vaccine strain, may have interacted with pandemic-era behavior changes to produce the first documented disappearance of an influenza B lineage in the genomic surveillance era, effectively re‑establishing a single-lineage influenza B population dominated by B/Victoria.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12325168/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – updated sub-regions to remove unsupported 'South-eastern Asia' (no specific countries listed) and reclassified the episode as re-emergence, reflecting the lineage-level restructuring of influenza B (apparent disappearance of B/Yamagata and dominance of B/Victoria) rather than a simple re-occurrence of typical seasonal activity; descriptions now align more closely with WHO and national vaccine‑composition recommendations.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [2005] (regions of Tuscany and Apulia; general adult population, archived sera)
Host: Humans (general adult population – residual serum samples from Tuscany and Apulia)
Event summary: From 2005 through 2017, random adult serum samples from Tuscany and Apulia contained IDV‑specific antibodies every year, with low baseline seroprevalence (~5–10%) in 2005–2007 rising sharply to 30–45% in 2008–2010 and again in 2013–2014 and 2016, indicating substantial and recurrent human exposure well before and after the formal discovery of IDV in swine. Seroprevalence peaks closely followed documented IDV outbreaks in cattle and pigs in Italy and neighboring countries, suggesting repeated spillover waves rather than sustained human‑to‑human transmission. By 2017, seroprevalence had fallen from peak levels but remained above the 2005 baseline, implying ongoing low‑level zoonotic exposure without any recognized, IDV‑attributable human epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic expansion of cattle and swine production in northern and southern Italy, frequent animal movements, and bovine respiratory disease outbreaks created sustained opportunities for zoonotic exposure at the human–livestock interface; human antibody peaks lagged behind livestock epidemics by roughly one year, consistent with spillover driven by animal infection dynamics. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – co‑circulation of multiple antigenic lineages (e.g. D/OK‑like and D/660‑like viruses) in European cattle; Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated infections of nearby humans; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – efficient replication of IDV in human airway epithelial cells and in ferret respiratory tracts suggests high compatibility with mammalian airways even though sustained human transmission has not yet been demonstrated.
Review: Review – Reclassified this Italian multi‑year episode as the earliest robust human evidence of IDV (first_detection = Yes) and extended the time span from 2005–2014 to 2005–2017 to match the underlying serosurvey. Removed previous labels of inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence, which were inconsistent with it being the global first detection and with limited evidence for virus‑intrinsic change in this period. This event now anchors the top‑level first_emergence_time/place fields and should be re‑checked by a subject‑matter expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (general adult population – residual sera from blood donors and other clinical collections)
Event summary: In 2011, a serologic survey of 316 human serum samples from the general population in the United States and Canada detected IDV hemagglutination‑inhibition antibodies in 1.3% of individuals, providing the first widely publicized indication that humans in North America had been exposed to influenza D virus. This low but measurable seroprevalence, identified after IDV had been isolated from swine and cattle, showed that zoonotic exposure was not confined to Italy and suggested that IDV or closely related viruses were already circulating silently in North American livestock and occasionally infecting humans. No discrete human outbreak or characteristic clinical syndrome could be linked to these serologic findings, and the episode is best interpreted as a baseline documentation of low‑level, previously unrecognized exposure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heightened interest in IDV following its 2011 isolation from pigs in Oklahoma and subsequent recognition of cattle as the primary reservoir prompted retrospective testing of available human sera from North America; extensive livestock movements and high cattle densities in U.S. and Canadian feedlot systems likely created undetected opportunities for past spillover. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – recognition of IDV as a distinct influenza species with antigenic properties separable from influenza C enabled specific serologic assays; Host Expansion (Spillover) – rare zoonotic infections from cattle or swine into humans inferred from low‑titer antibodies in a small fraction of the sampled general population.
Review: Review – Changed this event from first_global_emergence/first_detection to an inter‑continental emergence in North America, because archived Italian sera show earlier human IDV exposure from 2005 onward. Clarified that only 4 of 316 samples (1.3%) were positive and that these data reflect low‑level background exposure rather than a large clinical outbreak. Country and sub‑region assignments (United States, Canada; Northern America) are correct; event retained but downgraded in hierarchical importance relative to the Italian event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2016] (north‑central Florida; cattle‑exposed adults and non‑exposed controls)
Host: Humans (adult dairy and beef cattle workers; small comparison group of non‑cattle‑exposed adults)
Event summary: In a cross‑sectional serologic study published in 2016, serum from 35 cattle‑exposed adults and 11 non‑exposed adults in north‑central Florida was tested for IDV antibodies, revealing extremely high seroprevalence among cattle workers (91% by HI and 97% by microneutralization) and much lower seropositivity (18%) among controls, consistent with intense occupational exposure. The study was motivated by growing evidence of widespread IDV circulation in U.S. cattle and the earlier 1.3% seroprevalence estimate in the general population, and it demonstrated that frequent, mostly subclinical infections were occurring in a well‑defined worker population. The episode ended without identification of any IDV‑specific clinical outbreak, but it established cattle workers as a key risk group and prompted calls for more systematic occupational surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale dairy and beef operations in Florida with high animal densities, prolonged close human–cattle contact, and minimal respiratory protection created repeated opportunities for IDV exposure; the absence of targeted occupational surveillance before IDV’s discovery meant such infections went unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated zoonotic infections of cattle workers, as indicated by near‑universal neutralizing antibodies; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – established IDV lineages circulating in U.S. cattle herds by the mid‑2010s, maintaining a high environmental viral load in workplace settings.
Review: Review – Corrected the event type from re_emergence to re_occurrence because this represents resurgence of infection in the same sub‑region (Northern America) linked to occupational exposure and livestock management, without clear evidence of major viral genetic change. Adjusted the year from 2011–2012 to a single year (2016) aligned with the publication and contemporaneous cattle data, noting that the exact sampling year is not reported and should be verified in the full article. Countries/sub‑regions remain accurate (Florida, United States; Northern America).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Malaysia [2017] (Sarawak – Sibu and Kapit divisions; swine farms, abattoirs and live‑animal markets)
Host: Humans (swine farm, abattoir and live‑animal market workers; at least one worker with IDV‑positive nasal wash)
Event summary: During June–July 2017, a One Health surveillance study at the human–pig interface in Sarawak, Malaysia, collected nasal washes from 78 workers at pig farms, abattoirs and live‑animal markets, alongside animal and environmental samples. Among these workers, influenza D virus RNA was detected by rRT‑PCR in one nasal wash (1.3%), alongside detections of other respiratory and enteric swine viruses, providing the first molecular evidence of IDV infection in a human in Asia. No symptomatic outbreak was associated with this isolated detection, and follow‑up sampling was not performed, so the episode is interpreted as a sporadic zoonotic spillover event documenting that IDV can infect swine‑exposed workers in South‑eastern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense pig production in Sarawak, frequent close contact between humans and pigs in farms, abattoirs and wet markets, and limited consistent use of respiratory personal protective equipment facilitated occasional aerosol or contact exposure to multiple swine viruses, including IDV. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – zoonotic transmission from infected pigs or contaminated aerosols to at least one human worker; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – IDV’s ability to persist in bioaerosols and infect diverse mammalian hosts, together with experimental evidence of efficient replication in human airway cells and ferrets, underpins concern that such sporadic infections might presage broader adaptation.
Review: Review – Added this previously omitted event to capture the first molecular (PCR) detection of IDV in a human in Asia, as reported from Sarawak, Malaysia, in 2017; classified it as an inter‑continental emergence because it represents the earliest documented occurrence of human IDV infection on the Asian continent. Countries and sub‑region (Malaysia; South‑eastern Asia) were derived from the study sites (Sibu and Kapit). This event should be retained but flagged for expert review regarding its relative importance versus larger Asian seroprevalence studies.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America [2019] (Western and Southwestern United States; five large‑herd dairy operations)
Host: Humans (dairy cattle workers in large‑herd operations; nearby community members involved in related surveillance)
Event summary: Between May 2019 and January 2020, a NIOSH‑funded prospective study followed 31 workers at five large‑herd dairy operations in two U.S. states, collecting paired pre‑ and post‑shift nasal washes and personal bioaerosol samples over one to five consecutive workdays. IDV RNA was detected in nasal washes from 21 workers (67.7%) at least once and in 29.3% of all nasal‑wash specimens, with transient carriage patterns and no clear association with respiratory symptoms, demonstrating frequent, mostly asymptomatic nasal carriage of IDV among dairy workers across multiple facilities. The episode concluded without evidence of sustained human‑to‑human transmission, but it confirmed chronic occupational exposure and helped frame IDV as an under‑recognized hazard in industrial dairy environments.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Industrialization of U.S. dairy production with very large herds, high animal stocking densities, and open facilities that facilitate aerosolized virus exposure; lack of IDV‑specific surveillance before this study meant that such exposures were previously invisible; targeted occupational health research and molecular diagnostics enabled detection of transient infections. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated infection of cattle workers as incidental hosts; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – IDV’s ability to persist in aerosols and efficiently infect mammalian airways, including humans and ferrets, supports frequent acquisition and short‑term carriage; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – widespread circulation of multiple IDV lineages in U.S. cattle herds maintained a high force of infection at the human–animal interface.
Review: Review – Corrected the event years from 2018–2021 to 2019–2020 based on the study’s recruitment period (May 2019–January 2020) and removed an unrelated NIOSH annual report (cdc/101894) from the event‑level sources. Reclassified the event from re_emergence to re_occurrence because it represents repeated exposure and transient infection in the same sub‑region, driven by dairy production practices, without clear evidence of novel viral genotypes emerging in this setting. Countries and sub‑region (United States; Northern America) remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [2020] (Northeast China – urban and rural general population; outpatients with acute respiratory symptoms)
Host: Humans (general population in Northeast China; individuals with acute respiratory symptoms; subset with agricultural or animal‑contact backgrounds)
Event summary: Serologic surveillance in Northeast China using sera collected between 2020 and 2024 found very high IDV seropositivity in the general population (73.37%, 449/612) and even higher rates among patients with respiratory symptoms (96.67%, 58/60), while experimental infection studies showed that a contemporary cattle‑derived strain (D/HY11) replicated efficiently and transmitted via airborne routes between ferrets. These findings, combined with nationwide surveys showing IDV RNA in cattle across at least 13 of 16 sampled provinces and >90% IDV seroprevalence in cattle, indicate that IDV lineages, particularly those related to the D/Yama2019 lineage, are now widely established in Chinese livestock and have spilled over extensively into humans in Northeast China. By 2024, IDV exposure in this region appeared widespread and largely silent, without a clearly defined large clinical outbreak but with serologic and experimental evidence suggesting that some strains may have acquired the capacity for efficient mammal‑to‑mammal, and potentially human‑to‑human, transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High national IDV prevalence in cattle and documented circulation of multiple lineages (including D/Yama2019‑like and D/660‑like viruses) across at least 16 provinces, long‑distance movement and trade of cattle, and dense human–animal interfaces in Northeast China created persistent opportunities for zoonotic exposure; increased research interest after isolation of live IDV from Chinese cattle prompted focused human serosurveys. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – characterization of the D/HY11 strain with enhanced polymerase activity and association with the D/Yama2019 lineage; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – experimental demonstration of efficient airborne transmission of D/HY11 between ferrets, together with very high human antibody titers, suggests improved adaptation for mammalian respiratory spread; Host Expansion (Spillover) – extensive serologic evidence of infection in both rural and urban residents with and without direct cattle contact; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment and diversification of IDV lineages throughout East Asia underpins the broad geographic extent of human exposure documented in this episode.
Review: Review – Reclassified this event from inter_continental_emergence to intra_continental_emergence plus re_emergence because IDV had already been detected in a human in Asia (Malaysia, 2017) and because the Northeast China findings reflect spread into a new Asian sub‑region (Eastern Asia) combined with evidence of a newly dominant lineage (D/Yama2019‑like, including D/HY11) with enhanced airborne transmissibility in ferrets. Confirmed the 2020–2024 serologic surveillance window from the article abstract and related news coverage. Countries and sub‑region (China; Eastern Asia) are correct, but the contribution of human‑to‑human versus repeated animal‑to‑human transmission remains uncertain and should be interpreted cautiously.

Host: Humans (primarily children with acute respiratory illness)
Event summary: In early 1996, surveillance of children with acute respiratory illness in Yamagata City, Japan, identified a cluster of laboratory-confirmed influenza C infections marking a localized community outbreak after years of sporadic detections. The outbreak spread among children over the winter season, with multiple isolates belonging to a single antigenic group (C/Yamagata/26/81-like) recovered from pediatric outpatients and inpatients. Transmission declined by late spring 1996 as susceptible hosts were depleted and respiratory virus circulation shifted to other agents, and routine surveillance detected few or no influenza C cases in subsequent immediate seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Periodic accumulation of susceptible children in the community and winter respiratory seasonality favored localized transmission once influenza C was introduced or reintroduced into Yamagata; limited routine testing in prior years likely allowed low-level circulation to go unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak viruses were antigenically and genetically similar to previously circulating C/Yamagata/26/81-like strains, suggesting no major novel genotype, and periodic epidemic peaks are thought to reflect population immunity dynamics rather than marked changes in virulence or transmissibility.
Review: Decision: retain. This Yamagata City outbreak is a well-documented pediatric community epidemic with multiple C/Yamagata-lineage isolates and clear winter seasonality; timing, location, host, and classification as re-occurrence (not first or inter-/intra-continental emergence) are consistent with primary sources, so no corrections are needed.

Host: Humans (primarily children with acute respiratory illness)
Event summary: In 1998, Yamagata City, Japan, experienced a second documented outbreak of influenza C virus among children, following a relatively quiescent period after the 1996 epidemic. The 1998 outbreak again involved clusters of pediatric respiratory illness, with virologic surveillance detecting multiple closely related influenza C isolates in the same community setting. As with the earlier episode, circulation waned after the winter–spring peak, and the outbreak resolved without evidence of sustained high-level transmission into the following seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Similar to 1996, a build‑up of susceptible young children and seasonal winter conditions favored renewed community transmission once influenza C re-circulated. Internal mechanisms: Antigenic and genetic analyses showed 1998 strains highly homologous to the 1996 Yamagata outbreak viruses, indicating persistence of the same lineage rather than emergence of a distinct novel variant; the pattern is consistent with recurrent epidemic waves driven largely by host immunity cycles.
Review: Decision: retain. Represents the second Yamagata pediatric outbreak in the same community and lineage, with good virologic characterization; event timing, geography, and classification as a re-occurring wave of an established lineage are appropriate and require no changes.

Host: Humans (children and adults with acute respiratory illness)
Event summary: During the 1999/2000 winter season in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan, clinicians and public health laboratories documented an increased number of influenza C virus isolations from patients with respiratory illness, indicating a regional epidemic wave. Cases were identified across age groups, with most infections detected in the winter months through targeted virologic surveillance. As winter ended and overall influenza activity declined, influenza C detections fell, and the epidemic wave subsided without documented major spread beyond the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Routine winter respiratory virus seasonality, indoor crowding, and the presence of a susceptible pediatric population likely contributed to the regional 1999/2000 wave once influenza C began circulating. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization showed these Hiroshima strains were antigenically related to C/Yamagata-lineage viruses circulating in Japan through the 1990s, supporting a pattern of periodic re-occurrence of existing lineages rather than emergence of a new genotype with distinct virulence properties.
Review: Decision: retain. The Hiroshima 1999/2000 winter cluster is a clearly described regional epidemic with multiple confirmations; start year, location, and interpretation as a re-occurring wave of established Japanese lineages are appropriate, with no apparent misclassification or geographic errors.

Host: Humans (infants <24 months hospitalized with respiratory infections)
Event summary: From September 1999 through July 2003, a prospective study at Severo Ochoa Hospital in Madrid, Spain, followed infants under 24 months admitted with respiratory tract infections and identified influenza C virus as a non‑negligible cause of serious disease, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Among 706 hospitalized infants, 30 had influenza virus infections, of whom six were confirmed with influenza C, sometimes as co-infections with RSV or adenovirus. Seasonal circulation and hospital-based respiratory diagnostics showed that influenza C activity fluctuated over the four-year period, with occasional detections requiring hospitalization but no evidence of a large community-wide epidemic driven uniquely by influenza C.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban winter seasonality, high transmission in daycare and household settings, and limited preexisting immunity in very young children created conditions where influenza C could contribute to severe lower respiratory disease requiring hospitalization, especially in infants. Internal mechanisms: The Spanish cases fit within globally circulating influenza C lineages and did not show evidence of novel genotypes or altered virulence; the event mainly illustrates how a generally mild virus can nonetheless cause significant disease burden in vulnerable pediatric populations when conditions favor transmission.
Review: Decision: review. The original event year (2003-2004) has been corrected to 1999-2003 and the country tag updated to Spain [1999], matching the actual study period of hospitalized infants in Madrid. This series documents only six influenza C cases, so it is borderline in terms of "largest" events by case count but is valuable because it demonstrates that influenza C can cause hospitalization in young children; recommend keeping for now but flagging for possible exclusion if a strict top‑10-by-size filter is later applied.

Host: Humans (primarily children with acute respiratory symptoms)
Event summary: From January to July 2004, Japan experienced a nationwide epidemic of influenza C virus infections, with 131 laboratory-confirmed cases detected in children with acute respiratory illness across 10 prefectures. The epidemic began in early 2004 with increased detections in pediatric clinics and public health laboratories and expanded geographically as similar viruses were found in multiple prefectures through mid‑year. As the respiratory virus season waned and herd immunity in affected cohorts increased, case numbers declined, and nationwide surveillance showed a return to sporadic or no detections in subsequent seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The epidemic likely reflected a combination of winter–spring seasonality, high contact rates among school-age children, and a build-up of immunologically naïve cohorts after several years of low influenza C circulation, as well as expanded RT‑PCR–based surveillance that improved detection. Internal mechanisms: Antigenic and genetic characterization revealed relatively homogeneous viruses belonging to a C/Yamagata-lineage group, consistent with expansion of an established lineage rather than emergence of a fundamentally novel genotype or shift in host range; periodic large waves are thought to be driven more by population immunity than by major changes in viral pathogenicity.
Review: Decision: retain. This 2004 nationwide Japanese epidemic is one of the clearest large-scale influenza C outbreaks (131 confirmed pediatric cases across multiple prefectures) and appropriately classified as a re-occurring expansion of an existing lineage without evidence of new continent/subregion spread; no corrections required.

Host: Humans (children and adults with acute respiratory tract illness)
Event summary: Between November 2004 and April 2007, surveillance of 2,281 patients with acute respiratory tract infections in Normandy, France, documented influenza C virus circulation, with a marked peak in disease during the winter–spring season of 2005. The 2005 peak was characterized by higher influenza C detection rates relative to the following two seasons, during which only sporadic or few cases were identified. After this peak season, influenza C incidence decreased substantially, and surveillance over subsequent years indicated low-level or absent circulation, suggesting an episodic wave superimposed on otherwise low endemicity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal indoor crowding and winter humidity patterns, together with the accumulation of susceptible individuals, likely drove the 2005 peak, while improved multiplex RT‑PCR testing enhanced recognition of influenza C as a cause of respiratory illness. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses from French and other European isolates suggest that the viruses belonged to existing antigenic groups without clear evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype; the event represents a re-occurring seasonal wave within already established lineages rather than a distinct re-emergent strain.
Review: Decision: review. The event year has been adjusted from 2004-2005 to 2004-2007 to align with the actual surveillance period in Normandy, while still noting that the largest peak occurred in the 2005 season. Otherwise, geography, host, and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. The event is moderately sized (18 influenza C cases) and remains one of the better-characterized European series, but its inclusion among the top 10 most impactful events should be revisited once all candidates are compared.
