Countries: United States of America [1999] (citywide outbreak across 15 hospitals in Brooklyn, New York)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, predominantly ICU, with nosocomial A. baumannii infection or colonization)
Event summary: In 1999, a citywide clonal outbreak of multidrug- and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii was detected across 15 hospitals in Brooklyn, New York, with 419 unique patient isolates collected over a three‑month period. Molecular typing showed that a small number of epidemic clones, including carbapenem-resistant lineages, had spread between multiple hospitals, causing ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream, urinary, and wound infections. The outbreak was gradually controlled through intensified infection-prevention measures and antimicrobial stewardship, but carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii remained endemic in some facilities, marking an early large-scale urban emergence of this resistance phenotype in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High and heterogeneous use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (including carbapenems and cephalosporins) in a dense network of metropolitan tertiary hospitals, extensive use of invasive devices (ventilators, central lines, urinary catheters), and frequent patient transfers between facilities facilitated inter-hospital spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (dominance of epidemic A. baumannii clones with carbapenem resistance determinants), Antimicrobial Resistance (acquisition and spread of carbapenemase genes and other resistance elements leading to MDR and, in some isolates, panresistance), Enhanced Transmission (successful clones adapted to survive on hospital surfaces and equipment, supporting multi-hospital transmission).
Review: retain – Well-documented 1999 multicenter outbreak in Brooklyn with 419 A. baumannii isolates over July–September 1999; geography (United States, Northern America), timeframe, and classification as re-emergence of carbapenem-resistant clones are consistent with Landman et al. 2002 and related analyses, and the chosen URLs are appropriate primary sources.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Asia; Western Europe; Southern Asia
Countries: United States of America [2002]; Germany [2003]; Afghanistan [2002]; Iraq [2003]; Kuwait [2003]
Host: Humans (military personnel and other severely injured patients with war-related trauma, treated in forward facilities, Germany, and the USA)
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2004, multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter calcoaceticus–baumannii complex emerged as a major cause of bloodstream and wound infections among U.S. and coalition military personnel injured in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Kuwait, with 102 A. baumannii bloodstream infections identified in military treatment facilities and numerous additional extremity and wound infections reported. Molecular investigations suggested environmental and nosocomial acquisition of highly resistant clones in field hospitals and during aeromedical evacuation, followed by transmission in tertiary care hospitals in Germany and the United States. The outbreak was eventually mitigated through strengthened infection control, environmental decontamination, and changes in antibiotic use, but it highlighted the capacity of MDR A. baumannii to exploit war-related medical care networks for rapid multinational dissemination and led to the colloquial label “Iraqibacter.”
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: War-related trauma care in Afghanistan and the Iraq/Kuwait region, with heavy use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, substantial environmental contamination (dust, equipment, and surfaces), prolonged ICU stays, and rapid inter-facility transfers (from combat support hospitals to Landstuhl, Germany, and onward to U.S. military and Veterans Affairs hospitals). Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance (MDR and, in some cases, XDR phenotypes including carbapenem resistance, often leaving colistin as one of few treatment options), Enhanced Transmission (environmentally hardy clonal lineages able to persist on skin, equipment, and in austere hospital conditions), Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (distinct war-associated clones within the A. baumannii complex).
Review: review – The war-related MDR A. baumannii outbreak in injured service members (Afghanistan, Iraq, Kuwait with subsequent care in Germany and the USA) is accurately summarized and clearly a major global emergence episode. Sub-region coding has been corrected to include Southern Asia because Afghanistan is classified in Southern Asia in the country list; the sub_regions field is now “Northern America; Western Asia; Western Europe; Southern Asia” instead of only “Northern America; Western Asia; Western Europe.” In addition, both re_occurrence and re_emergence were previously marked true; under the provided framework these categories should be mutually exclusive, and this episode is best captured as re-emergence driven by the expansion of highly resistant clones, so re_occurrence has been set to false while re_emergence remains true.

Countries: Brazil [2003] (initial large outbreak in Curitiba; subsequent persistent endemicity and spread in southern Brazilian hospitals)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, especially ICU patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream, urinary tract, and wound infections)
Event summary: In 2003, a major outbreak of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii producing the OXA-23 carbapenemase occurred in a university hospital in Curitiba, Brazil, representing the first documented CRAB outbreak in the country and one of the earliest in South America. The outbreak involved numerous ICU patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia and bloodstream infections, and was followed over subsequent years by the persistence and regional spread of OXA-23-producing clones in southern Brazil, including hospitals in Porto Alegre and other cities, with high endemic rates of CRAB detected five or more years after the initial events. By the late 2000s, OXA-23-positive A. baumannii had become entrenched in local hospital networks, contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality and exemplifying the rapid regional establishment of a new carbapenemase-mediated resistance mechanism.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive carbapenem and broad-spectrum antibiotic use in ICUs, limited infection-control resources, overcrowding, and high patient turnover facilitated selection and intra- and inter-hospital spread of resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (introduction and expansion of OXA-23-producing A. baumannii lineages and later additional high-risk clones), Antimicrobial Resistance (broad MDR/XDR phenotypes including carbapenems, often leaving polymyxins and tigecycline as last-resort agents, partly mediated by AbaR-type resistance islands), Enhanced Transmission (epidemic clones able to persist in hospital environments for years, causing repeated outbreaks and sustained endemicity).
Review: retain – Accurately reflects the first documented Brazilian OXA-23 CRAB outbreak in Curitiba and subsequent long-term endemicity and clonal persistence in southern Brazil. The country and sub-region coding (Brazil, South America/South America) are correct, the 2003–2010 window reasonably captures the initial outbreak plus years of documented endemic transmission, and classification as re-emergence due to introduction and spread of OXA-23–producing clones is appropriate; sources are focused and highly relevant.

Countries: China [2013] (tertiary care hospital ICU with six-year longitudinal CRAB surveillance)
Host: Humans (ICU patients with pulmonary infections, bacteremia, and other healthcare-associated infections; extensive environmental contamination documented)
Event summary: From 2013 to 2018, a tertiary care hospital in eastern China conducted intensive surveillance of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in ICU rooms, documenting a sustained high burden of CRAB among critically ill patients and widespread contamination of environmental surfaces. Whole‑genome sequencing revealed persistent dissemination and replacement of closely related ST2 (international clone 2) CRAB lineages across rooms, patients, and surfaces over the six-year period, with limited success in eradicating these clones despite infection-prevention efforts. This prolonged episode illustrates the establishment of highly adapted CRAB clones within a Chinese ICU and reflects a broader national pattern of rising carbapenem resistance and dominance of ST2 among A. baumannii isolates in Chinese ICUs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged ICU stays, heavy carbapenem and broad-spectrum antibiotic use, high device utilization, inadequate environmental decontamination, and dense patient-to-patient contact favored persistence of CRAB in ICU environments. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (dominance and microevolution of global clone 2/ST2 lineages), Antimicrobial Resistance (carbapenemases such as OXA-23 and OXA-66 plus multiple additional resistance determinants leading to MDR/XDR phenotypes), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (ability to survive on high‑touch surfaces and form environmental reservoirs that sustained continuous transmission).
Review: retain – Captures a well-described six-year period of entrenched CRAB transmission and environmental contamination in a Chinese ICU, supported by WGS-based epidemiology and national ICU surveillance data. Country and sub-region (China, Eastern Asia) are correct, and classification as re-emergence of highly adapted ST2 CRAB lineages is in line with the definitions; no major geographic or event-type corrections are required.

Countries: Greece [2010] (tertiary care hospital in central Greece)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, predominantly ICU, with CRAB infections from clinical specimens including respiratory, blood, and wound samples)
Event summary: In 2010–2011, a tertiary care hospital in central Greece reported 174 carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates from clinical specimens, reflecting a rapid transition from largely susceptible strains in the 1990s to predominately carbapenem-resistant, OXA-23–producing lineages by the late 2000s. Molecular typing indicated dominance of international clone II and widespread carriage of OXA-23 and related carbapenemase genes, corresponding to endemic CRAB transmission in the hospital and mirroring high resistance rates in ICUs nationally. Subsequent infection-control interventions and antimicrobial stewardship programs were implemented to limit further spread, but CRAB remained an important cause of severe nosocomial infections in Greece and contributed to the country’s status as a European hotspot for carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High carbapenem and broad-spectrum antibiotic use in Greek hospitals, overcrowded ICUs, economic constraints, and challenges in maintaining robust infection-control practices enabled rapid selection and dissemination of resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance (acquisition and fixation of OXA-23 and other carbapenemase determinants in A. baumannii), Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (replacement of earlier local lineages by international clone II with high-level resistance), Enhanced Transmission (efficient clonal spread within ICUs and hospital networks).
Review: retain – Appropriately summarizes the rapid rise and hospital-level endemicity of OXA-23–producing IC2 A. baumannii in Greece around 2010–2011, supported by Eurosurveillance and molecular epidemiology studies. Geographic coding (Greece, Southern Europe/Europe) is correct, and classification as re-emergence driven by new carbapenemase-producing clones is consistent with the provided definitions.

Countries: Italy [2011] (nationwide cross-sectional survey of hospitals in multiple regions)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients across Italian acute-care hospitals, with CRAB isolated from respiratory tract, skin and soft tissue, urine, and blood)
Event summary: In mid-2011, a countrywide cross-sectional survey in Italy collected 232 carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates from 25 clinical microbiology laboratories, revealing epidemic diffusion of OXA-23–producing CRAB belonging mainly to international clone II. The study demonstrated that CRAB had achieved a level of distribution in Italian hospitals comparable to carbapenem-nonsusceptible Klebsiella pneumoniae, with isolates recovered predominantly from ICU patients and other severely ill inpatients. The survey documented that OXA-23–positive international clone II had largely replaced earlier lineages (including OXA-58 producers), and subsequent years saw continued endemic CRAB circulation in Italian hospitals, prompting intensified national infection-control and surveillance efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive carbapenem and broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing in Italian hospitals, high ICU bed utilization, and frequent inter-hospital patient transfers facilitated nationwide dissemination of resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (countrywide dominance of international clone II harboring blaOXA-23-like genes, displacing previous OXA-58 producers), Antimicrobial Resistance (multidrug and carbapenem resistance limiting therapeutic options), Enhanced Transmission (successful epidemic clone adapted to survive and spread in diverse hospital settings).
Review: review – The event is correctly based on the first cross-sectional countrywide survey of CRAB in Italy and appropriately characterizes nationwide diffusion of OXA-23–positive IC2 lineages. However, the underlying survey was conducted in mid-2011 rather than 2012, so the event year has been corrected from “2012” to “2011,” and the country annotation updated from “Italy [2012]” to “Italy [2011].” Classification as re-emergence (reflecting replacement of earlier clones by OXA-23–producing IC2) and the geographic coding (Italy, Southern Europe/Europe) remain appropriate; the event is flagged for review to confirm acceptance of the revised dating.

Countries: United States of America [2012] (eight metropolitan surveillance areas across multiple states)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with healthcare-associated CRAB infections and colonization across acute- and long-term care facilities)
Event summary: Between 2012 and 2015, the U.S. Emerging Infections Program conducted population-based surveillance for carbapenem-nonsusceptible Acinetobacter baumannii in eight metropolitan areas across several states, documenting over one thousand cases with high levels of multidrug resistance and substantial mortality. Most cases were associated with recent hospitalization, long-term acute care, mechanical ventilation, or invasive devices, underscoring CRAB’s role as a severe healthcare-associated pathogen in interconnected acute- and long-term care networks. While incidence decreased in some facilities following targeted interventions, CRAB remained endemic in several healthcare systems, highlighting recurrent and persistent emergence of carbapenem resistance in U.S. healthcare settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (including carbapenems), growth of long-term acute-care hospitals and skilled nursing facilities caring for highly complex patients, and frequent inter-facility patient movement promoted sustained CRAB circulation across acute and post-acute care. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance (high-level resistance to carbapenems and most other agents, often necessitating polymyxin-based or novel therapies), Enhanced Transmission (clonal spread via patient transfers, shared staff, and contaminated environments), Geographic Range Expansion (inherent traits enabling survival across diverse U.S. healthcare environments and facility types).
Review: review – This event correctly represents a large, multi-year U.S. surveillance episode documenting the burden and outcomes of carbapenem-nonsusceptible A. baumannii across eight metropolitan areas, and the geographic coding (United States, Northern America) matches the surveillance catchment. Previously, both re_occurrence and re_emergence were set to true; in line with the scheme’s intent that these be mutually exclusive, this episode is better described as re-emergence of carbapenem-resistant lineages across U.S. healthcare networks, so re_occurrence has been set to false and re_emergence retained as true.

Countries: United States of America [2020] (acute-care hospital in New Jersey during first COVID-19 wave)
Host: Humans (critically ill COVID-19 patients and other hospitalized adults with hospital-acquired CRAB infection or colonization)
Event summary: From February to July 2020, an acute-care hospital in New Jersey experienced a marked increase in hospital-acquired carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii during a surge of COVID-19 admissions, with 34 patients identified and 20 developing clinical infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia and bacteremia. Countries: Israel [2020] (Hasharon Hospital, converted into a dedicated COVID-19 facility)

Event summary: In 1996, the Netherlands reported 2,771 pertussis cases (18 per 100,000 population), more than eight times the 1995 incidence despite long‑standing whole‑cell vaccination and high coverage, signalling a national epidemic that was unprecedented in the vaccine era. Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Sweden [1998]; France [2004]; Netherlands [2004]; Norway [2007]; Italy [2012]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]
Host: Humans across age groups in countries using acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines
Event summary: Beginning in the late 1990s, serial collections of Bordetella pertussis isolates from multiple European countries started to reveal rare strains that no longer expressed the vaccine antigen pertactin, first detected in Sweden and later in France and the Netherlands. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, the proportion of pertactin‑deficient isolates rose steadily in France, Norway, Sweden, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, reaching around one quarter of all tested isolates overall and more than half in some countries by 2012–2015, while pertussis incidence remained cyclically elevated. By the mid‑2010s, pertactin‑negative, often ptxP3‑lineage strains had become established components of national B. pertussis populations across Western, Northern and Southern Europe, with no sharp end point but clear stabilisation of these vaccine‑escape variants at high frequency.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and high uptake of pertactin‑containing acellular pertussis vaccines created strong selection pressure favouring strains that could evade pertactin‑targeted antibodies, and sustained transmission in partially immune populations allowed such variants to spread between countries on normal travel and contact networks. Internal mechanisms: Multiple independent disruptive mutations in the prn gene (insertions, deletions and nonsense mutations) arose on successful ptxP3 genetic backgrounds and were repeatedly selected, leading to convergent loss of pertactin expression in diverse lineages; this pattern of antigen‑specific vaccine‑driven evolution and regional range expansion of pertactin‑deficient clones is characteristic of re_emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence rather than geographic introduction of the pathogen itself.
Review: review – Retain this as a major, Europe‑wide re_emergence episode capturing vaccine‑driven spread of pertactin‑deficient B. pertussis. Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting intra_continental_emergence to “false” (the pathogen was long established in all affected subregions; this is strain evolution, not first occurrence in new subregions) and kept re_emergence as “true”. Country labels and bracketed years were adjusted to match the earliest documented detection of pertactin‑negative isolates in each country according to EUpert I–IV and related studies; this row should be checked by a human reviewer for any finer adjustments to country‑specific onset years.

Host: Humans, with highest burden in infants and young children but many cases in older children and adults
Event summary: From 2008, Australia entered its largest recorded pertussis epidemic since national surveillance began, with notifications climbing sharply and peaking at nearly 40,000 cases in 2011, contributing to more than 140,000 reports between 2008 and 2012 and substantial infant hospitalisations. In nearby New Zealand, a linked regional resurgence began in August 2011 and lasted until December 2013, generating over 10,000 notifications, around 560 hospitalisations and three deaths in unimmunised young children, with incidence highest in deprived communities. Following intensified control efforts, including cocooning strategies, promotion of adolescent and adult boosters, and, in New Zealand, introduction and later optimisation of maternal vaccination, notifications gradually decreased by 2013–2014, though pertussis has remained cyclic and endemic in both countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: In both Australia and New Zealand, widespread use of acellular pertussis vaccines with relatively rapid waning of protection, together with several years since the previous large wave, allowed build‑up of susceptible older children and adults who then transmitted infection to very young infants; improved PCR diagnostics and clinician awareness further amplified detected incidence. Internal mechanisms: Genotyping of Australian isolates during the epidemic documented rapid expansion of ptxP3, prn2 and pertactin‑deficient lineages, mirroring global vaccine‑driven evolution, and similar ptxP3/pertactin‑variant profiles were seen in New Zealand; the rise of these fitter genotypes in highly vaccinated populations supports classification as re_emergence driven by antigenic evolution, superimposed on expected multi‑year epidemic cycling.
Review: review – Retain as a major Oceania epidemic episode, but the event year has been extended from 2008–2012 to 2008–2013 to capture the full New Zealand outbreak period (August 2011–December 2013). Emergence‑type coding has been adjusted so that only re_emergence is “true” (re_occurrence set to “false”), reflecting strong evidence for vaccine‑driven expansion of ptxP3 and pertactin‑deficient lineages alongside external drivers such as waning aP immunity and improved diagnostics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans across age groups, with severe disease concentrated in young infants
Event summary: In 2010, California reported over 9,000 pertussis cases, 809 hospitalisations and 10 infant deaths, its highest burden for more than 60 years and a warning sign of wider national resurgence. Over the next two years, large state‑level outbreaks culminated in 48,277 reported pertussis cases nationally in 2012, the largest US total since 1955, with states such as Washington declaring epidemics and recording historic highs in incidence. Subsequent expansion of Tdap booster recommendations, including routine maternal vaccination during each pregnancy, contributed to reductions in reported incidence after 2013, although national pertussis activity has remained well above the low levels of the 1980s and early 1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cyclic epidemic dynamics, waning immunity after childhood acellular vaccine series, suboptimal uptake of adolescent and adult Tdap boosters, and greater use of sensitive PCR assays all contributed to the high detected incidence during 2010–2012, particularly among school‑aged children, adolescents and their household contacts, who then infected undervaccinated or too‑young infants. Internal mechanisms: Molecular surveillance in the United States during this period showed increasing dominance of ptxP3 and pertactin‑deficient B. pertussis strains, indicating antigenic divergence from historical vaccine strains and improved fitness in vaccinated hosts; this pattern of vaccine‑driven evolution alongside external drivers justifies classification as re_emergence rather than pure re_occurrence.
Review: review – Retain this as one of the most impactful national resurgence episodes (largest US case count since the 1950s). Emergence‑type coding has been simplified to re_emergence = “true”, re_occurrence = “false”, in line with evidence that expansion of ptxP3 and pertactin‑deficient lineages under acellular‑vaccine pressure was an important part of the resurgence, alongside external factors like waning immunity and better diagnostics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans, with severe disease and deaths concentrated in young infants, especially those <6 months of age
Event summary: Around 2011, several South American countries experienced their largest pertussis burdens in decades, with Argentina reporting 10,395 suspected cases and at least 76 infant deaths in 2011 alone, and Brazil confirming 22,772 cases between 2011 and 2014, most in infants under one year. In 2012, Peru documented a national outbreak driven by B. pertussis genotypes carrying the globally emerging ptxP3–ptxA1–prn2 allelic profile, while neighbouring countries such as Chile also saw increased notifications and hospitalisations in young children during this period. Following rapid adoption of maternal Tdap immunisation in Argentina (2012) and later Brazil, together with strengthened surveillance and improved laboratory diagnostics, regional case counts and deaths declined after 2014, although further smaller cyclic peaks have recurred.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Despite long‑standing whole‑cell vaccination programmes, gaps in booster coverage, delayed or incomplete infant schedules, and social inequities led to large susceptible cohorts, while greater use of PCR and more systematic national reporting made the true scale of disease more visible; these factors together produced marked increases in detected incidence and infant mortality in 2011–2014. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies from Argentina, Brazil and Peru show that many circulating strains during these outbreaks belonged to the ptxP3–ptxA1–prn2–fim3 lineages that have spread globally and are antigenically divergent from older vaccine strains, indicating that pathogen evolution under vaccine pressure, not just external drivers, contributed to the severity and spread of the South American resurgence, consistent with classification as re_emergence.
Review: review – New row added to correct a major omission: the 2011–2014 resurgence across Argentina, Brazil, Peru and neighbouring countries clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 pertussis episodes in terms of cases and infant deaths. Classified as re_emergence because regional studies document both strong external drivers (coverage gaps, delayed vaccination, improved diagnostics) and expansion of globally emerging ptxP3/prn2 lineages. A human reviewer should confirm the exact list of countries included in this linked regional episode and adjust if additional South American countries are to be explicitly named.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]
Host: Humans, with a focus on severe disease and deaths in young infants <3 months
Event summary: In 2012, England and Wales experienced their largest pertussis outbreak for more than a decade, with almost 10,000 laboratory‑confirmed cases and 14 infant deaths, all in babies too young to be fully vaccinated. In response, the United Kingdom launched an emergency maternal pertussis vaccination programme in October 2012, offering Tdap during pregnancy to protect newborns via transplacental antibodies, and uptake rapidly reached high levels. Over 2013–2014, laboratory‑confirmed infant disease and deaths fell markedly while overall pertussis incidence declined from the 2012 peak but remained cyclic, and subsequent analyses showed sustained maternal vaccine effectiveness above 90% against infant disease and death.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Accumulation of adolescents and adults with waning aP‑induced immunity, incomplete and delayed infant schedules in some subpopulations, and natural multi‑year epidemic cycles combined to generate the large 2012 peak; improved laboratory testing also increased ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: As in neighbouring European countries, ptxP3 and often pertactin‑deficient B. pertussis strains were predominant in the UK by 2012, indicating that antigenic divergence under aP selection contributed to the outbreak’s intensity and age distribution; this supports classification as re_emergence rather than a purely control‑failure re_occurrence.
Review: review – Retain this row as it describes a well‑documented, high‑mortality outbreak that directly triggered the UK maternal vaccination programme. Emergence‑type flags have been simplified to re_emergence = “true”, re_occurrence = “false”, aligning with guidance that categories are generally mutually exclusive and recognising the documented role of evolving ptxP3/pertactin‑variant strains in addition to external drivers like waning immunity and coverage gaps.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (primarily children; macrolide‑treated pertussis cases across northern and eastern China)
Event summary: Around 2013, China reported its first documented macrolide‑resistant Bordetella pertussis isolates, initially from schoolchildren in Shandong and then from paediatric cases in Xi’an, prompting wider susceptibility testing. By 2013–2014, hospital‑based and multicentre studies in mainland China found that most clinical isolates in several northern and eastern provinces carried high‑level erythromycin resistance, and by 2014–2016 resistance prevalence exceeded 80% in some series while pertussis notifications were rising after years of apparent under‑reporting. These resistant lineages became established across multiple regions of China and persisted beyond 2016, transforming macrolide resistance from a rare curiosity into a dominant therapeutic challenge.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very frequent empirical use of macrolides for paediatric respiratory infections in China created strong antibiotic selection pressure, while gradual expansion of culture and PCR capacity uncovered pertussis cases that had previously been missed; high but imperfect coverage with whole‑cell and then acellular vaccines constrained severe disease but not transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genomic epidemiology revealed several highly clonal ptxP1–ptxA1–fhaB3 lineages carrying the 23S rRNA A2047G mutation that conferred high‑level macrolide resistance and expanded rapidly across China, representing a classic antimicrobial‑resistance–driven re_emergence with geographic spread of resistant clones rather than introduction of the pathogen into new areas.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first widespread emergence of macrolide‑resistant pertussis in China, which is both epidemiologically and clinically important. The time window (2013–2016), geographic scope (multiple regions of mainland China) and classification as re_emergence driven by antibiotic resistance are consistent with key surveillance and genomic studies, and no corrections to countries, dates or emergence‑type flags were required.

Host: Humans across age groups in Shanghai and other Chinese regions, with a post‑2020 shift toward older children and adolescents
Event summary: Between 2016 and 2022, detailed genomic surveillance of Bordetella pertussis in Shanghai showed macrolide resistance rising from roughly one third of isolates to more than 95%, coinciding with a local increase in pertussis cases and a shift in the age distribution from mainly young infants to a greater share of older children and adolescents after 2020. During this period, macrolide‑resistant ptxP1 lineages (notably MT195) that had become common in China were progressively displaced in Shanghai by a newly emerging macrolide‑resistant ptxP3 clone (MT28), which appeared after 2020 and rapidly became dominant. By the early 2020s, Shanghai had effectively fixed macrolide resistance in its B. pertussis population and become a focal point for the export of the MT28 ptxP3 macrolide‑resistant clone documented in international genomic datasets.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Sustained, often empirical prescribing of macrolides for respiratory illnesses, combined with high though imperfect vaccine coverage and waning immunity in older cohorts and dense urban contact networks, favoured both continued transmission and strong selection for resistant, immune‑evading lineages; COVID‑19–related perturbations may have further altered contact patterns and susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: Longitudinal genomic analyses in Shanghai demonstrate a stepwise evolutionary transition from predominantly ptxP1/prn1/fhaB3 macrolide‑resistant strains to near‑fixation of the MT28 ptxP3/prn2/fhaB1 sublineage after 2020, all carrying the 23S rRNA A2047G mutation; this combination of antimicrobial resistance, antigenic evolution and rapid clonal replacement within an already resistant population exemplifies a second‑stage re_emergence event with both genotype and age‑profile shifts.
Review: review – Retain this as a distinct follow‑on re_emergence episode highlighting the rise of the MT28 ptxP3 macrolide‑resistant clone in Shanghai, but it required substantial corrections. The event years were aligned with the main surveillance period (2016–2022 rather than 2018–2024), the country field was corrected to list only the sovereign state (China) rather than the non‑ISO entry “China, Shanghai”, and the summary/mechanism were revised to reflect the documented transition from ptxP1 MRBP to MT28 ptxP3 MRBP. Event‑level sources were updated to focus on the Shanghai‑specific genomic studies; a human reviewer should confirm that the chosen time window and framing remain appropriate as new data accumulate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In the early 1990s, Sweden documented a rapid rise in quinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni among human clinical isolates, shifting from previously rare resistance to high‑level resistance within a few years. Surveillance showed more than a 20‑fold increase in quinolone resistance, accompanied by the appearance of strains with characteristic gyrA and parC mutations. After awareness increased and antibiotic use policies were tightened, resistance levels stabilized, but quinolone‑resistant strains remained established in the human population and food‑animal reservoirs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics in humans and in food‑animal production, particularly poultry, created strong selection pressure for resistant C. jejuni; international travel also contributed to importation of resistant strains into Sweden. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of chromosomal mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC) conferred high‑level quinolone resistance in C. jejuni clinical isolates.
Review: Review – Event is real and well documented as an early sentinel of high‑level quinolone resistance in C. jejuni in Europe. Classification as re‑emergence (AMR‑driven) and the geographic assignment (Europe, Northern Europe, Sweden) are correct. Direct short‑term case counts are modest compared with very large waterborne outbreaks, so whether this remains in the final top 10 depends on how strongly AMR emergence is weighted relative to outbreak size; no field changes made.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans
Event summary: Between 1992 and 1998 in Minnesota, USA, surveillance detected the first locally acquired quinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni infections among patients who had not received quinolone therapy, after years in which no such resistance had been observed. Over this period, the proportion of human C. jejuni isolates resistant to fluoroquinolones rose markedly, in parallel with increasing detection of resistant strains in retail poultry products. Resistance levels remained elevated thereafter, indicating establishment of a resistant zoonotic reservoir and a sustained shift in the epidemiology of human campylobacteriosis in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Licensing and widespread use of fluoroquinolones in poultry production in the United States created strong selection pressure; contaminated poultry meat became a major vehicle for resistant C. jejuni into humans. Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation of mutations mediating fluoroquinolone resistance in C. jejuni, with resistant strains increasingly recovered from both human stool samples and chicken meat.
Review: Review – Event accurately reflects the early emergence of fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni in the U.S., including its link to poultry. Classification as re‑emergence (AMR‑driven) is appropriate, and geography is correct. Impact is substantial for antimicrobial resistance but modest in terms of documented outbreak case counts. Consider consolidating this with the Finland traveler‑associated resistance event as a single global fluoroquinolone‑resistance emergence episode in the final top‑10 list.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Africa; Western Asia; Northern America; South America
Countries: Finland (returning travelers); Spain; Thailand; multiple additional travel destinations in >40 countries on four continents
Host: Humans (travelers)
Event summary: From 1995 to 2000, surveillance of Finnish travelers returning with campylobacteriosis showed a rapid global rise in ciprofloxacin‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni infections acquired in numerous destination countries, after prior periods with little or no resistance. Across two collection periods, the proportion of traveler isolates resistant to ciprofloxacin increased sharply, with particularly high resistance levels linked to destinations such as Spain and Thailand and elevated resistance documented in at least 40 countries across four continents. By the end of the 1990s, fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni had become widespread in many travel destinations, making resistant strains a common cause of travelers’ diarrhea and imported infections into northern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of fluoroquinolone use in veterinary medicine and human healthcare across many countries, combined with intensive poultry production and growing international travel, facilitated dissemination of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance driven by chromosomal mutations conferring ciprofloxacin resistance, with diverse resistant genotypes emerging and spreading in poultry and other animal reservoirs and being transmitted zoonotically to humans.
Review: Review – Period and geographic scope have been corrected to 1995–2000 and to include the Americas, based on the original surveillance study showing traveler‑acquired resistant infections from 40 countries on four continents. This is an important global AMR re‑emergence signal but overlaps conceptually with the Sweden and Minnesota resistance events; treat as the primary global fluoroquinolone‑resistance emergence episode, and consider downgrading one of the more local AMR events if a strict top‑10 cap is enforced.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In August 1998, the municipality of Haukipudas in northern Finland experienced a large waterborne outbreak of campylobacteriosis when non‑chlorinated municipal groundwater became contaminated during water‑main repair work. A population survey indicated that roughly 18–19% of residents met the case definition for acute gastroenteritis, corresponding to an estimated 2,700 ill persons among about 15,000 inhabitants, and Campylobacter jejuni was isolated from stool samples of affected patients. The outbreak ended after chlorination of the distribution system and corrective actions to the mains were implemented, and it prompted wider recognition of the vulnerability of non‑chlorinated municipal groundwater systems to large Campylobacter outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of non‑chlorinated groundwater for municipal supply, mains repair that likely allowed fecal contamination to enter the distribution network, and absence of a disinfection barrier enabled widespread contamination of tap water. Internal mechanisms: No novel C. jejuni genotype was implicated; the event represents re‑occurrence driven by infrastructure failure and environmental contamination rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a new event because the Haukipudas 1998 outbreak is one of the largest documented C. jejuni waterborne outbreaks globally (≈2,700 estimated cases) and clearly meets the ‘major impact’ criterion. Classification as re‑occurrence (water‑system failure) and the geographic details are supported by the original outbreak investigation.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2000, the municipal water supply of Walkerton, Ontario became contaminated with manure‑derived pathogens, including Campylobacter jejuni and Escherichia coli O157:H7, after heavy rainfall washed farm runoff into a vulnerable well. Over subsequent weeks, more than 2,000 residents developed acute gastroenteritis, and several deaths were primarily attributed to E. coli O157:H7, with C. jejuni also playing an important role as a co‑pathogen. The outbreak ended after the contaminated wells were identified and taken offline, boil‑water advisories and alternative water sources were implemented, and extensive reforms to water testing, treatment, and regulation were instituted across Ontario and Canada.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Inadequate chlorination and monitoring of municipal groundwater supplies, regulatory and operational failures at the local water utility, and heavy rainfall events that facilitated runoff of livestock manure into a susceptible well. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel C. jejuni genotype was identified; this event is best characterized as a large re‑occurrence driven by environmental contamination and systemic water‑safety failures.
Review: Retain – Event exists and is among the most notable modern Campylobacter‑containing waterborne outbreaks in terms of illness burden and systemic impact on drinking‑water regulation. Classification as re‑occurrence and the Canadian geographic assignment are correct. Sources have been strengthened by explicitly including the EID outbreak characterization; no other field changes were required.

Host: Humans
Event summary: From the early 2000s, New Zealand experienced a prolonged national epidemic of campylobacteriosis, with notification rates peaking around 2003–2006 at roughly 380–400 cases per 100,000 population, the highest national incidence reported in the literature. Most cases were attributable to poultry, and the epidemic caused tens of thousands of illnesses annually, hundreds of hospitalizations, and measurable mortality and economic costs. In 2006–2007, a national Campylobacter risk‑management strategy targeting poultry production and processing was implemented, and by 2007–2008 notifications and hospitalizations declined by more than 50% compared with 2002–2006, ending the epidemic phase although campylobacteriosis remained the country’s most common foodborne illness.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High per‑capita poultry consumption, high contamination levels of fresh chicken meat, industrial consolidation of poultry processing, and initially limited regulatory controls sustained a prolonged high‑incidence epidemic; coordinated regulatory and industry interventions (process‑hygiene criteria, carcass‑contamination monitoring, and risk‑management targets) subsequently reduced human exposure. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic was driven mainly by established poultry‑associated C. jejuni genotypes; molecular epidemiology showed that reductions in poultry contamination translated into reductions in poultry‑attributed human infections rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Retain – National epidemic and subsequent sharp decline following poultry‑focused interventions are very well documented and represent a major high‑burden re‑occurrence event with clear control impact. Temporal span and classification as re‑occurrence (driven by food‑system changes, not pathogen evolution) are appropriate; minor wording in the summary was aligned more closely with reported incidence figures, but no structural changes were required.

Countries: United States of America (South Bass Island, Ohio)
Host: Humans
Event summary: In August 2004, South Bass Island, Ohio, a resort community receiving over half a million visitors annually, experienced a large waterborne outbreak of gastroenteritis when the island’s drinking‑water distribution system became contaminated. Approximately 1,450 persons reported illness, and laboratory investigation identified multiple pathogens, including Campylobacter jejuni, norovirus, Giardia intestinalis, and Salmonella enterica serotype Typhimurium, in stool samples from affected individuals. The outbreak was controlled after the contaminated groundwater wells and distribution system deficiencies were addressed, including infrastructural repairs and improved disinfection, and the event highlighted vulnerabilities of small island drinking‑water systems serving large transient populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of inadequately protected and intermittently contaminated groundwater sources for a high‑demand resort island, deficiencies in water treatment and distribution infrastructure, and heavy seasonal use of the system facilitated intrusion of fecal contamination. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel Campylobacter strain was reported; the event reflects re‑occurrence caused by infrastructure and environmental failures within a multi‑pathogen context.
Review: Review – Added as a new event because the South Bass Island outbreak is one of the largest U.S. Campylobacter‑associated drinking‑water outbreaks (~1,450 illnesses) and is cited internationally as a key example. However, Campylobacter was one of several pathogens implicated and the episode is multi‑etiologic; whether it remains in the final top 10 depends on how strictly mono‑etiologic C. jejuni events are prioritized.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2007, the town of Røros in Norway experienced a large waterborne outbreak of campylobacteriosis when untreated tap water from a groundwater source became contaminated, likely via defects and leakage in an aging distribution network. Retrospective cohort studies estimated that about 4 in 10 customers of the Røros waterworks, roughly 1,500 persons, developed acute gastroenteritis, and Campylobacter jejuni with identical PFGE profiles was isolated from many patients’ stools. The outbreak subsided after chlorination of the water supply was initiated and remedial actions were taken on the distribution system, and it has since been cited as one of Norway’s largest waterborne bacterial outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of untreated groundwater, an old and leaky distribution system with significant water losses, and likely intrusion of fecally contaminated surface water into the network created conditions for extensive contamination of tap water. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved a single C. jejuni clone without evidence of novel virulence; it is best characterized as a large re‑occurrence due to distribution‑system failures rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a new event because the 2007 Røros outbreak (≈1,500 cases) is one of the largest Campylobacter waterborne outbreaks reported in Europe and is repeatedly highlighted in national and international drinking‑water risk assessments. Classification as re‑occurrence and the Norwegian geographic details are well supported.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In late November 2007, the town of Nokia in southern Finland suffered a massive waterborne gastroenteritis outbreak when treated wastewater effluent was accidentally allowed to enter the municipal drinking‑water distribution network through a cross‑connection opened during maintenance work. More than half of the residents in the contaminated distribution area developed gastroenteritis, corresponding to over 8,000 illnesses, and multiple pathogens including Campylobacter jejuni, noroviruses, Giardia and Salmonella were identified in patient samples. The outbreak ended after the contaminated part of the network was isolated, extensive flushing and chlorination were performed, and longer‑term infrastructural and regulatory measures were implemented; the event remains Finland’s most significant recorded waterborne epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A misconnected valve between wastewater and drinking‑water lines, inadequate safeguards against backflow, and delayed detection of the incident allowed large volumes of sewage effluent to enter the municipal distribution system, exposing thousands of residents. Internal mechanisms: Campylobacter isolates were typical strains without evidence of novel evolutionary change; the event represents an extreme re‑occurrence driven by system design and operational failures and is notable for its long‑term sequelae, including reactive arthritis and prolonged gastrointestinal symptoms among affected residents.
Review: Retain – Added as a new event because the 2007 Nokia contamination is one of the largest documented waterborne outbreaks involving Campylobacter worldwide (>8,000 illnesses) and has extensive documentation of long‑term health and economic impacts. Classification as re‑occurrence and assignment to Finland, Northern Europe are correct; multi‑etiologic nature is noted but Campylobacter was a major pathogen.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In May 2010, the Danish town of Køge experienced a waterborne outbreak caused by a single clone of Campylobacter jejuni that contaminated the central municipal water supply. Forty‑five laboratory‑confirmed cases of campylobacteriosis were identified among residents served by the affected supply, and epidemiologic investigation implicated drinking tap water as the common exposure. After the contaminated part of the water system was identified and remediated and temporary control measures were instituted, new cases ceased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of a central community water supply, likely from environmental or fecal sources, combined with inadequate protection or integrity of the distribution system at the time of the incident. Internal mechanisms: A single clonal C. jejuni strain was responsible for the outbreak; there was no indication of novel virulence traits, so the event is best characterized as a re‑occurrence due to point‑source contamination of drinking water.
Review: Review – Event is real and correctly summarized, and has been cited internationally as a notable Danish Campylobacter waterborne outbreak (≈400 symptomatic cases estimated, 45 laboratory‑confirmed). However, its scale is smaller than several other newly added outbreaks (Haukipudas 1998, Røros 2007, Nokia 2007, Havelock North 2016, Askøy 2019). Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate and geography is correct. Recommend keeping this row for completeness but giving lower priority if a strict top‑10 selection is required.

Host: Humans
Event summary: In August 2016, the town of Havelock North in New Zealand experienced a massive outbreak of campylobacteriosis when Campylobacter jejuni contaminated the municipal groundwater supply feeding the town’s reticulated drinking water. Telephone surveys and routine surveillance indicated that roughly 5,500 of the town’s 13,000–14,000 residents developed gastroenteritis, and later modeling suggested up to about 8,000 cases in the wider area, making it New Zealand’s largest recorded waterborne disease outbreak and the largest documented Campylobacter waterborne outbreak to date. The outbreak was linked to heavy rainfall causing runoff from grazed paddocks into a poorly protected bore; it ended after the contaminated source was taken offline, chlorination and alternative supplies were implemented, and national drinking‑water regulations and oversight were strengthened.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy rain events leading to surface runoff from livestock paddocks, inadequate protection and sealing of a municipal bore head, lack of effective disinfection of groundwater designated as ‘secure’, and systemic regulatory and operational weaknesses in drinking‑water management. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical C. jejuni genotype; the event reflects environmental contamination and system failure rather than novel pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Event is well documented and widely recognized as the world’s largest recorded campylobacteriosis outbreak and New Zealand’s largest drinking‑water outbreak. Classification as re‑occurrence and the New Zealand geographic assignment are correct; case‑count estimates have been aligned with the latest survey and modeling data. Strong candidate for inclusion among the top global emergence events for this pathogen.

Host: Humans
Event summary: Between August 2016 and mid‑2017, Sweden reported a large nationwide increase in domestic Campylobacter jejuni infections, with surveillance estimating approximately 5,000 excess notified cases above expected baseline levels. The surge was temporally associated with changes in poultry production and processing that allowed higher Campylobacter contamination levels on broiler carcasses, and whole‑genome sequencing showed that many human and poultry isolates belonged to closely related lineages from a major producer. Case numbers gradually declined after enhanced control measures and stricter process‑hygiene criteria were introduced in the poultry sector, although incidence remained elevated compared with pre‑outbreak levels for some time.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changes in poultry production and slaughter practices, including problems with cleaning and disinfection of transport crates and processing equipment at a major producer, and high national poultry consumption, contributed to increased contamination of retail poultry meat and widespread foodborne transmission. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak largely involved existing poultry‑associated C. jejuni lineages; no single fundamentally novel strain was identified, so the event is best characterized as a large re‑occurrence driven by food‑chain and industry changes rather than new pathogen traits.
Review: Retain – Event is real, clearly described by the Swedish Public Health Agency, and represents a large, nationally important re‑occurrence driven by poultry‑sector changes, with thousands of excess human cases. Classification as re‑occurrence and assignment to Sweden, Northern Europe are correct; Wikipedia has been supplemented with the primary national outbreak report to strengthen sourcing.

Countries: United States of America (multistate: at least 18 states)
Host: Humans; companion dogs (puppies)
Event summary: From 2016 to 2018, and again in 2019–2020, the United States experienced multistate outbreaks of extensively drug‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni infections linked to contact with puppies sold through commercial pet stores, with at least about 113–120 confirmed human illnesses, around 17–24 hospitalizations, and no deaths documented during investigated periods. Whole‑genome sequencing identified a persistent clone (REPDBR01) circulating in puppies within the commercial breeding and pet‑store distribution chain, with isolates resistant to multiple first‑line antibiotic classes including macrolides and fluoroquinolones. The outbreaks subsided after enhanced infection‑control and antimicrobial‑stewardship measures in the pet industry and public‑health advisories, but the resistant clone has continued to cause sporadic illnesses, indicating ongoing zoonotic risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density commercial dog‑breeding and distribution networks, frequent movement of puppies between breeders, distributors, and pet stores, and widespread prophylactic and therapeutic antibiotic use in puppies created conditions for amplification and dissemination of resistant C. jejuni. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance and enhanced transmission—whole‑genome sequencing identified a persistent, extensively drug‑resistant C. jejuni clone (REPDBR01) with resistance to multiple antibiotic classes that caused repeated multistate outbreaks; efficient colonization of puppies facilitated zoonotic spillover to humans.
Review: Retain – Event is well documented by CDC and peer‑reviewed studies as an ongoing multistate outbreak series caused by an extensively drug‑resistant C. jejuni clone associated with puppies. Classification as re‑emergence (AMR and host‑associated clone) is appropriate; inclusion adds an important AMR‑and‑zoonosis dimension beyond large waterborne outbreaks.
