Host: Humans
Event summary: In June 2019, Askøy municipality in western Norway experienced a large waterborne outbreak of campylobacteriosis when Campylobacter jejuni contaminated a mountainside drinking‑water reservoir supplying about 15,000 inhabitants. Epidemiologic investigations estimated that more than 1,500, and possibly over 2,000, residents developed gastroenteritis, with at least around 70–80 hospitalizations and two deaths suspected to be associated with the outbreak. The contamination was traced to seepage of fecally contaminated surface water into an aging, partially cracked rock‑cavern reservoir following heavy rainfall. The outbreak ended after the affected reservoir was taken out of service, emergency chlorination and alternative supplies were provided, and extensive remedial works and national reviews of drinking‑water safety were initiated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Structural defects and aging infrastructure in a rock‑cavern drinking‑water reservoir, intrusion of fecally contaminated surface water following heavy rainfall, and lack of adequate disinfection allowed C. jejuni to contaminate the public water supply and infect a large proportion of consumers. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical C. jejuni genotype; the event represents a major re‑occurrence driven by infrastructure vulnerabilities and extreme‑weather‑related contamination, rather than novel pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a new event because the 2019 Askøy outbreak (≥1,500–2,000 cases) is one of the largest Campylobacter waterborne outbreaks in Europe and is extensively described in the scientific and public‑health literature. Classification as re‑occurrence and Norwegian geographic assignment are well supported and align with national summaries that highlight Askøy 2019 alongside Røros 2007 as major recent waterborne Campylobacter outbreaks.

Sub-regions: Europe | Western Europe; Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Southern Europe; Europe | Eastern Europe; Northern America | Northern America; Oceania | Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2003]; Belgium [2003-2004]; France [2003-2004]; Germany [2003-2004]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2004]; Sweden [2004]; Spain [2004-2005]; Italy [2004-2005]; Switzerland [2004-2005]; Poland [mid-2000s]; United States of America [2003-2004]; Canada [mid-2000s]; Australia [mid-2000s]
Host: Humans – primarily men who have sex with men (MSM), with occasional bisexual men; infection type mainly anorectal and inguinal lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) due to C. trachomatis serovar L2b.
Event summary: Around 2003, public health authorities in the Netherlands detected an unusual cluster of severe proctitis among men who have sex with men, which was confirmed as lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by a C. trachomatis serovar L2b strain that previously had been rarely recognized in industrialized countries. Subsequent enhanced surveillance and molecular typing showed rapid expansion of this L2b epidemic among MSM across multiple Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries and then to North America and Australia over the mid‑2000s, with hundreds to thousands of anorectal LGV cases reported in large urban sexual health clinics. The outbreak was gradually brought under better control after targeted awareness campaigns, improved diagnostic testing for rectal chlamydia in MSM, and guideline‑based doxycycline treatment of LGV cases and contacts, though L2b‑LGV remains an established STI among MSM in many affected countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The resurgence was linked to dense international sexual networks among MSM, high‑risk sexual practices (e.g. unprotected receptive anal intercourse, group sex, use of sex venues), overlapping HIV and STI epidemics, and increased travel between major cities in Europe, North America, and Australia, which facilitated long‑distance spread of an LGV strain that had previously been rare in these populations. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses identified a distinct L2b variant of C. trachomatis responsible for nearly all investigated LGV cases in MSM during this epidemic, indicating Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence combined with Enhanced Transmission within specific sexual networks rather than introduction of an entirely new species to these regions.
Review: Decision: review. The LGV L2b epidemic among MSM in Europe, North America and Australia is correctly identified as a major, epidemiologically linked re‑emergence episode of C. trachomatis. However, the event was misclassified as an inter‑continental emergence, which conflicts with the instructions that new serotypes/manifestations of an already‑endemic EPP in a continent should be treated as re‑emergence rather than inter‑continental emergence. I changed inter_continental_emergence from true to false and retained re_emergence = true to reflect a novel epidemic strain expanding within existing C. trachomatis–endemic regions. I also corrected the country name to “Netherlands (Kingdom of the)” to match the Country sheet. The listed countries and sub‑regions (including Poland as Eastern Europe) and approximate timing are supported by multi‑country LGV reviews and outbreak summaries and are appropriate to retain; no additional LGV‑related emergence events of greater impact were identified that would displace this episode from a top‑10 list for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Western Europe
Host: Humans – sexually active adolescents and adults with genital chlamydia infections detected in routine screening and diagnostic programmes.
Event summary: In the early 2000s, Sweden observed unexpected declines in reported Chlamydia trachomatis cases in some counties despite stable or rising test volumes, prompting investigation into potential diagnostic problems. In 2006, investigators discovered a new C. trachomatis variant (nvCT) with a 377‑bp deletion in the cryptic plasmid that removed the single NAAT target sequence used by Abbott m2000 and Roche Amplicor/TaqMan assays, allowing the strain to spread largely undetected for several years and to reach high prevalence in counties using these tests, while remaining detectable in counties and countries using alternative assays. After recognition of nvCT, Sweden and a few other European countries where sporadic nvCT cases were identified rapidly updated NAATs to include additional targets, undertook recall testing and partner notification, and by the late 2000s the proportion of nvCT among all chlamydia diagnoses in Sweden declined substantially as the diagnostic escape advantage was removed, with only limited transmission documented in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The emergence was facilitated by widespread use of single‑target nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) in routine chlamydia screening, creating strong diagnostic selection pressure in regions relying on Abbott and Roche assays that failed to detect the new variant; high screening coverage and sexual network connectivity in Sweden further supported rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The nvCT strain carried a 377‑bp deletion in the plasmid region targeted by these NAATs, representing Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with Diagnostic Escape, leading to apparent drops in case notifications and substantial under‑diagnosis until multi‑target assays and specific nvCT tests were introduced, after which its fitness advantage waned and its prevalence began to fall.
Review: Decision: review. The Swedish nvCT diagnostic‑escape episode is correctly included as a major re‑emergence event driven by a novel plasmid deletion variant and by NAAT testing practices, and classification as re_emergence (with all other emergence‑type flags set to false) is appropriate. However, the original row overstated the geographic extent and timing of nvCT spread outside Sweden by listing the United Kingdom and unspecified “other European countries” and by implying broader circulation. Based on national investigations and a Europe‑wide survey, there is strong evidence that nvCT transmission remained largely confined to Sweden, with only small numbers of confirmed cases in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France, and no confirmed circulation in the UK. I therefore (i) removed the United Kingdom and the vague “other European countries with sporadic detections” from the country list; (ii) restricted countries to Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France with starting years aligned to documented detections (Sweden 2002–2006 period of undetected spread; other countries 2007); and (iii) removed “Europe | Southern Europe” from sub_regions, as no Southern European country with nvCT circulation is well‑documented. Event years (2002–2009), host description and mechanism/driver text remain valid. Given these corrections, the event should be retained but flagged for expert review of the exact end year and any very small additional national clusters that do not substantially change its impact ranking.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [1996] (Alaska Native communities)
Host: Humans (primarily Alaska Native infants and young children)
Event summary: In 1996, after Alaska switched its Hib immunization schedule to a DTP-HbOC combination conjugate vaccine, invasive Hib disease reappeared in a previously well-controlled, highly vaccinated Alaska Native child population, with about 10 cases reported from May 1996 to April 1997 and additional cases in the late 1990s. The outbreak developed as ongoing Hib transmission persisted in remote communities despite high nominal coverage, revealing a reservoir of carriage in vaccinated children and breakthrough disease. Intensified surveillance, review and modification of vaccine policy, and targeted public‑health measures subsequently reduced invasive Hib incidence again in the affected populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Change in vaccine product and schedule (switch to a DTP-HbOC combination with lower functional immunogenicity), crowded living conditions and other socio-environmental risk factors in remote Alaska Native communities facilitated continued Hib transmission despite vaccination. Internal mechanisms: No major new strain or resistance mechanism was identified; re-occurrence was mainly driven by suboptimal vaccine-induced population immunity and persistent colonization rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – This event accurately reflects the well-documented re-emergence of invasive Hib disease in remote Alaska Native communities following a change in vaccine product and schedule, with timing, geography, and mechanism consistent with primary sources. No corrections to geography, timing, or event-type classification (re-occurrence driven by vaccine-program factors) are required, and the cited articles appropriately describe the episode.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999] (England and Wales)
Host: Humans (children and adults, with focus on children <5 years)
Event summary: Between 1999 and 2003, England and Wales experienced a nationwide resurgence of invasive Hib disease following several years of very low incidence after introduction of routine Hib conjugate vaccination in 1992. The increase developed gradually across age groups and was linked to reduced effectiveness of certain DTaP-Hib combination vaccines and waning immunity, particularly in cohorts primed with acellular combination products, with annual pediatric incidence peaking around 2002. A national Hib booster catch‑up campaign in 2003 for children aged 6 months to 4 years, alongside schedule and product adjustments, was followed by a marked fall in Hib disease back to very low levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of lower-immunogenicity DTaP-Hib combination vaccines, waning anti‑PRP antibody levels in cohorts without a robust booster dose, and continued circulation of Hib in school‑aged children acting as a reservoir; high but not uniformly optimal coverage. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a new, more virulent Hib clone; epidemiology points mainly to vaccine immunogenicity and immunity-gap issues rather than major pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – The description of the England and Wales Hib resurgence and the classification as re-occurrence (vaccine-program and waning-immunity driven) are appropriate and match national surveillance and serologic data. However, one non-existent placeholder URL (a BMJ Open link with “197/9/XXX”) was removed and replaced with the actual BMJ article describing the 2003 Hib booster campaign, and the UK Green Book chapter was confirmed as a suitable high-level source for time trends and policy response. Content is sound but the event is flagged for review because of these source refinements.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Canada [2000] (Northern Canada, including Arctic and sub‑Arctic regions); United States of America [2000] (Alaska and other North American Arctic regions)
Host: Humans (disproportionately Indigenous children in Arctic and sub‑Arctic communities)
Event summary: From 2000 through at least 2010, invasive Haemophilus influenzae serotype a (Hia) emerged as a major cause of invasive disease in the North American Arctic, where Hib had previously predominated before vaccination. Surveillance in Alaska and northern Canada documented that non‑b serotypes, especially Hia, rapidly increased to comprise most invasive H. influenzae cases and reached very high incidence levels in Indigenous children, in some northern regions approaching or exceeding historical Hib rates. The episode persisted over the decade, with ongoing high incidence but gradual strengthening of surveillance, clinical management and discussion of dedicated Hia vaccines rather than a clearly demarcated epidemic end.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High underlying burden of social and environmental risk factors in Indigenous Arctic communities (crowded housing, smoking exposure, limited healthcare access), combined with elimination of Hib by vaccination, likely created an ecological niche for non‑b serotypes. Internal mechanisms: Serotype replacement and expansion of particularly fit Hia lineages with high invasiveness; this represents a serotype shift and increased virulence or transmissibility of Hia in this setting, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by pathogen characteristics rather than spread into a truly new sub‑region.
Review: Review – The North American Arctic Hia episode is well supported by population-based incidence data and clearly qualifies as a major re-emergence event with serotype replacement and high disease burden in Indigenous children. However, the original classification as an intra-continental emergence has been corrected to re-emergence only, because H. influenzae (and probably Hia at low levels) was already present in Northern America and the episode reflects a serotype shift with increased incidence, not first presence in a new UN sub-region. No changes were needed to timing or geography, but the event is flagged for review due to this reclassification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Canada [2002] (northwestern Ontario and other northern regions); United States of America [2002] (Navajo and White Mountain Apache communities in the southwestern US, plus other regions with high Hia incidence); Australia [mid‑2000s] (Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory and other remote areas)
Host: Humans (primarily Indigenous children; some adults in high‑risk communities)
Event summary: Starting in the early 2000s, persistently high and sometimes increasing rates of invasive Hia disease were documented in multiple Indigenous populations beyond the core Arctic surveillance sites, including northwestern Ontario First Nations, Navajo and White Mountain Apache children in the southwestern United States, and Aboriginal communities in Australia. In several North American Indigenous groups, Hia incidence in young children reached levels comparable to pre‑vaccine Hib disease, whereas in Aboriginal Australian children Hia incidence was elevated but did not reach historic Hib levels. Over the mid‑2000s to late 2010s, these communities reported severe Hia manifestations such as meningitis, sepsis, and pneumonia, and these findings spurred intensified advocacy for Hia‑specific conjugate vaccines, strengthened local surveillance, and clinical management, without a discrete endpoint of the episode.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared structural determinants of health across Indigenous communities (overcrowding, poverty, limited access to timely care), and widespread effective Hib vaccination which may have opened ecological space for other capsulated serotypes. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of virulent Hia lineages in multiple geographic settings, constituting serotype shift and geographic range expansion of these lineages within continents that already harboured H. influenzae; this is best classified as re‑emergence via a different serotype rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence of the species itself.
Review: Review – This event correctly captures the extension of high-burden Hia disease from the Arctic into other North American Indigenous populations and into Aboriginal communities in Australia, drawing on multiple regional case series and reviews. The original labelling as both intra- and inter-continental emergence has been revised to re-emergence only, in line with project rules that new serotypes in regions where H. influenzae was already established should not be coded as intra-/inter-continental emergence. The event summary has been slightly tempered to clarify that Hib-comparable incidence applies to some North American populations, whereas Australian Hia incidence is elevated but clearly lower than historic Hib rates.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (children and adults with respiratory tract infections; some invasive cases)
Event summary: During the mid‑1990s in Japan, surveillance of Haemophilus influenzae from respiratory tract infections and some invasive cases revealed a marked and rapid increase in β‑lactamase‑negative ampicillin‑resistant (BLNAR) strains, with prevalence rising from rare in 1987–1989 to roughly 20% of isolates in 1995–1997 and remaining substantial thereafter. This episode developed as BLNAR clones with specific ftsI (PBP3) mutations disseminated widely in the community, complicating empirical use of ampicillin and some cephalosporins. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, BLNAR H. influenzae had become a major antimicrobial-resistance problem in Japan, leading to changes in recommended therapies and ongoing national surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High community use of β‑lactam antibiotics exerted selection pressure favouring BLNAR strains; outpatient treatment of respiratory infections with aminopenicillins and some cephalosporins was common. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and clonal expansion of BLNAR strains carrying multiple amino‑acid substitutions in PBP3 (ftsI) associated with reduced affinity for β‑lactams, representing a clear antimicrobial resistance mechanism and re‑emergence of H. influenzae disease in more drug-resistant form rather than appearance in a new geographic area.
Review: Review – The Japanese BLNAR episode is well supported by longitudinal susceptibility data and molecular studies and clearly qualifies as a major resistance-driven re-emergence of H. influenzae disease burden. The event is already correctly classified as re-emergence and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence, but is flagged for review because it is part of a broader global AMR trend and some readers may wish to confirm that its magnitude merits inclusion among the top resistance events for this species.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [1998] (multiple hospitals in a national respiratory isolate surveillance network)
Host: Humans (patients with community‑acquired respiratory tract infections)
Event summary: Between 1998 and 2001, U.S. antimicrobial surveillance programs identified the emergence and clonal dissemination of BLNAR H. influenzae strains in community respiratory infections, after such strains had been considered rare in North America. National surveillance in 2000–2001 detected BLNAR isolates at multiple hospitals and showed that a subset belonged to a closely related clone with unusually high ampicillin MICs, indicating recent spread. Over subsequent years, BLNAR and related β‑lactam resistant phenotypes became established at low but significant prevalence in North America, signalling an important shift in H. influenzae resistance epidemiology.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread community use of aminopenicillins and oral cephalosporins for respiratory infections; under-recognition of BLNAR due to standard susceptibility testing limitations, which may have facilitated silent spread. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of PBP3 (ftsI) mutations conferring high-level ampicillin resistance and clonal spread of these BLNAR lineages across geographically separated institutions, representing a clear re‑emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance evolution and enhanced success of certain clones.
Review: Retain – This event accurately summarizes the first clear identification and clonal spread of BLNAR H. influenzae in the United States, drawing directly on national surveillance and molecular characterization data. The timing, geography, and classification as an AMR-driven re-emergence (with no intra-/inter-continental component) are appropriate, and the sources are well chosen; no corrections were required beyond minor wording harmonization.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000]; other participating EU/EEA countries in invasive disease surveillance (e.g. Nordic, Western and Southern European states) [early 2000s]
Host: Humans (mainly older adults and persons with comorbidities; some children)
Event summary: From approximately 2000 to 2010, European surveillance documented a sustained increase in invasive disease due to non‑b encapsulated serotypes, especially H. influenzae serotypes e (Hie) and f (Hif), in countries such as England and Wales and several other European states. Over this period, Hib remained rare in vaccinated children, while Hie/Hif annual incidence rose with year‑on‑year increases and a high case‑fatality ratio in older adults and immunocompromised patients. By the end of the decade, Hie/Hif collectively constituted a significant proportion of invasive H. influenzae in several European countries, leading to recognition of non‑b disease as an important clinical and public‑health problem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Successful Hib vaccination created ecological space for other capsulated serotypes; aging populations with more malignancy and immunosuppressive conditions provided susceptible hosts. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of particular invasive Hie and Hif lineages, representing serotype shift and increased prominence of non‑b invasive clones; this fits re‑emergence mediated by serotype- and host‑adapted lineages rather than spread of H. influenzae into previously unaffected sub-regions.
Review: Review – The episode describing rising invasive Hie/Hif disease in Europe is well grounded in high-quality surveillance analyses from England and Wales and from the EU-IBIS network, and it appropriately focuses on increased incidence and severity in adults. The initial coding as an intra-continental emergence has been corrected to re-emergence only, because non-b serotypes were already present in Europe and the change reflects serotype replacement and demographic shifts rather than first occurrence of H. influenzae in new UN sub-regions. The event is flagged for review chiefly due to this classification correction and its partial overlap with the broader Europe-wide shift captured in the next event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Multiple European Union / EEA countries participating in invasive H. influenzae surveillance [1996] (e.g. Nordic, Western, Southern and some Eastern European states)
Host: Humans (all ages; children and adults with invasive or severe respiratory disease)
Event summary: Between 1996 and 2006, data from a multi‑country European invasive H. influenzae surveillance network showed a major epidemiologic transition: Hib cases plummeted following widespread Hib conjugate vaccination, while disease caused by non‑b serotypes and especially nontypeable H. influenzae (NTHi) increased and came to predominate invasive case counts. This shift developed gradually, with rising proportions of NTHi-associated bacteremia and pneumonia in older adults and high‑risk groups. By the end of the surveillance period, invasive NTHi and non‑b disease had clearly replaced Hib as the main form of invasive H. influenzae in many European settings, a pattern that has continued into the 21st century.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High Hib vaccine coverage eliminated most Hib carriage and invasive disease, allowing other serotypes and NTHi to occupy the same nasopharyngeal niches; demographic aging and more chronic disease increased susceptibility to NTHi. Internal mechanisms: Serotype replacement and expansion of NTHi lineages well adapted for colonization and opportunistic invasion, representing re‑emergence of invasive H. influenzae in new serotype and genotype configurations rather than first emergence of the organism on the continent or in new sub-regions.
Review: Review – This event appropriately captures a major Europe-wide epidemiologic shift from Hib-dominated invasive disease to predominantly NTHi and other non-b serotypes, supported by the EU-IBIS analysis and later clinical reviews. The original label as intra-continental emergence has been revised to re-emergence only, because the phenomenon is serotype and genotype replacement within countries where H. influenzae was long endemic, not first appearance in new UN sub-regions. The episode partially overlaps with the preceding, more Hie/Hif-focused event but is retained because it represents a broader and clearly high-impact change in invasive H. influenzae epidemiology; nonetheless, it is flagged for review due to this reclassification and overlap.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern America
Countries: Selected countries in Eastern Asia [2011] (e.g. Taiwan, based on northern Taiwan tertiary-care surveillance); multiple countries in Europe [2010s] (e.g. France, Italy, Norway and others reporting MDR NTHi or advanced BLNAR/BLPACR clones); United States of America [2010s]; Canada [2010s]
Host: Humans (patients with invasive disease and community‑acquired respiratory infections; adults and children)
Event summary: Over roughly the last decade, surveillance and genomic studies from East Asia, Europe and North America have documented the emergence and spread of multidrug‑resistant (MDR) nontypeable H. influenzae (NTHi) responsible for invasive disease and difficult‑to‑treat respiratory infections. A detailed study from northern Taiwan of invasive NTHi collected between 2011 and 2020 showed that most isolates were ampicillin resistant and over half were MDR, with novel resistance transposons carrying up to seven antibiotic-resistance genes, while European and North American series reported increasing proportions of BLNAR, BLPACR and fluoroquinolone- or macrolide-resistant NTHi among invasive and otitis media isolates. By the early 2020s, MDR NTHi had been reported from multiple continents, raising concerns about limited oral treatment options and driving calls for enhanced surveillance, stewardship, and new therapeutic approaches.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive outpatient use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics for respiratory tract infections, incomplete treatment courses, and transmission in community and healthcare settings; structural factors such as aging populations and frequent antibiotic exposure in high‑risk patients. Internal mechanisms: Transposon‑mediated acquisition of multidrug‑resistance gene clusters by NTHi lineages and accumulation of PBP3 and other target mutations, leading to expansion of specific MDR sequence types and resistant clonal groups; this represents a clear re‑emergence event characterized by antimicrobial resistance and enhanced survival under therapeutic pressure, rather than appearance of H. influenzae in new regions.
Review: Review – The original event appropriately recognized the global emergence of MDR NTHi but its geography and sourcing were overly centered on Europe and North America despite key primary data coming from a 2011–2020 invasive NTHi series in northern Taiwan. The event has been revised to explicitly include Eastern Asia (Taiwan) and to draw on additional European and U.S. susceptibility studies documenting MDR and BLNAR/BLPACR clones, while removing the intra-continental emergence label in line with guidance that new resistance phenotypes in regions with long-standing H. influenzae circulation should be coded as re-emergence only. Because of this broadened geographic framing and corrected classification, the event is flagged for review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (primarily children under 5 years of age; some older age groups)
Event summary: From 2017 through at least 2024, France has experienced a resurgence of invasive Hib disease in children despite high vaccination coverage with a 2+1 conjugate schedule and, more recently, mandatory vaccination. National surveillance and a detailed reference-centre analysis documented that the annual number and proportion of invasive Hib cases among children under 5 years increased over 2018–2024, with many cases occurring in appropriately vaccinated children classified as vaccine failures. The episode has persisted over several years, prompting epidemiologic, genomic, and immunologic investigations and policy discussions about schedule optimization and booster strategies; as of 2025–2026, Hib incidence remains higher than during the nadir in the 2000s but under continued monitoring.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of a 2+1 Hib-containing schedule with potential waning of antibody levels in some children before or shortly after the booster dose; possible disruptions or delays in routine immunization and healthcare-seeking associated with the COVID‑19 pandemic and broader respiratory epidemiologic shifts; and persistent Hib circulation in older age groups. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome sequencing to date indicates that circulating Hib isolates largely belong to established ST-6 clonal complex lineages without clear association between specific genotypes and vaccine failure, suggesting that programmatic and immunity-gap factors, rather than a fundamentally altered escape variant, are the dominant drivers of this resurgence.
Review: Review – The French Hib resurgence is strongly supported by a recent national reference-centre analysis (2017–2024) and by Santé publique France’s 2025 national bulletin, which document increasing Hib case numbers in young children despite high coverage and a 2+1 schedule. The event has been re-coded from combined re-occurrence and re-emergence to re-occurrence only, because available genomic data do not yet demonstrate a distinct vaccine-escape lineage and the pattern is better explained by waning immunity and programmatic factors, in accordance with project definitions. The geography, timing, and impact are otherwise appropriate, and the event is flagged for review because of this change in event-type classification and the rapidly evolving evidence base.

Countries: United States of America [1990] (multi‑hospital outbreaks in New York, Arizona, Florida, Massachusetts)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults, mainly patients exposed to clindamycin and other antibiotics)
Event summary: Between 1990 and 1992, four geographically separated U.S. hospitals experienced large outbreaks of severe Clostridioides difficile–associated diarrhea caused by a single clindamycin‑resistant epidemic strain (“J strain”), leading to sharp increases in CDI incidence and morbidity among inpatients. Molecular typing showed a predominantly clonal lineage carrying ermB‑mediated macrolide‑lincosamide‑streptogramin resistance, and restriction of clindamycin prescribing plus infection‑control interventions subsequently brought CDI incidence and the proportion of resistant isolates back down. The episode marked one of the first clear demonstrations that antibiotic‑resistant C. difficile lineages could rapidly emerge and dominate hospital outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive use of clindamycin and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics in acute‑care hospitals, coupled with high patient turnover and suboptimal infection‑prevention practices, created strong selection and ample transmission opportunities for a resistant clone. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – epidemic strains carried the ermB gene and were highly clindamycin‑resistant; Enhanced Transmission – clonal spread in multiple hospitals indicates traits favoring nosocomial transmission and persistence (spore formation, environmental hardiness).
Review: retain – Correctly describes the early 1990–1992 multi‑hospital outbreaks in New York, Arizona, Florida and Massachusetts caused by a clindamycin‑resistant J‑strain, including geography, timing and mechanism (antibiotic‑resistance‑driven clonal expansion). Emergence type as re‑emergence (new resistant lineage in a previously affected sub‑region) and country/sub‑region coding are appropriate and consistent with published outbreak reports.

Countries: United States of America [2000] (multiple hospitals in at least eight states)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults; predominantly healthcare‑associated CDI)
Event summary: From roughly 2000 to 2003, U.S. hospitals saw a marked rise in CDI, with national short‑stay hospital discharges listing CDI increasing from about 85,700 in 1993 to nearly 149,000 in 2001 and then continuing upward, while molecular investigations of large outbreaks in eight hospitals between 2000 and 2003 identified a new fluoroquinolone‑resistant epidemic lineage later defined as BI/NAP1/027. This hypervirulent strain was associated with more severe colitis, higher relapse and mortality rates, and rapidly became the dominant cause in many affected institutions. The expansion of BI/NAP1/027 and heightened awareness of CDI prompted enhanced surveillance and infection‑control efforts, which in some regions later helped stabilize or reduce hospital‑onset CDI rates.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of fluoroquinolones and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics, aging inpatient populations with more comorbidities, and high device and procedure use in acute‑care settings. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – emergence of BI/NAP1/027 with tcdC deletion, binary toxin and high toxin A/B production; Antimicrobial Resistance – high‑level fluoroquinolone resistance gave this clone a strong selective advantage; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – associated with more severe disease and efficient spread in healthcare facilities.
Review: retain – Accurately captures the early‑2000s rise of NAP1/BI/027 in multiple U.S. hospitals and the concurrent national increase in CDI discharges, with appropriate emphasis on fluoroquinolone resistance and hypervirulence. Geography (United States, Northern America) and classification as re‑emergence due to a novel, more virulent and resistant lineage are consistent with surveillance and outbreak data.

Countries: Canada [2002] (province of Quebec most heavily affected, spread to other provinces by 2004)
Host: Humans (primarily older hospitalized adults; healthcare‑associated CDI)
Event summary: Beginning around 2002 and peaking in 2003, hospitals in Quebec, Canada experienced a massive CDI epidemic with approximately a four‑fold increase in cases and a rise in 30‑day mortality from about 4.7% in 1991–1992 to 13.8% by 2003, driven largely by the hypervirulent NAP1/027 lineage. Molecular studies showed NAP1/027 becoming predominant in Quebec and then being detected across other Canadian provinces, coinciding with increased rates of toxic megacolon, colectomy, and CDI‑attributable deaths. Intensified infection‑control measures and improved antibiotic stewardship in subsequent years eventually reduced incidence and limited further explosive spread, although NAP1/027 remains an important lineage in Canada.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High use of fluoroquinolones and other broad‑spectrum agents, crowded tertiary‑care hospitals with frequent patient transfers, and initially unrecognized outbreak potential of NAP1/027. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – expansion of hypervirulent NAP1/027 with tcdC deletion and binary toxin; Antimicrobial Resistance – fluoroquinolone resistance; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – higher toxin production associated with greater severity and mortality; Enhanced Transmission – efficient nosocomial spread resulting in a province‑wide epidemic.
Review: retain – Well supported description of the 2002–2004 Quebec epidemic, including the four‑fold rise in incidence and tripling of 30‑day mortality associated with ribotype/NAP1/027, and spread to other Canadian provinces. Coded correctly as re‑emergence in Canada (Northern America) driven by a more virulent, fluoroquinolone‑resistant clone and external drivers such as high antibiotic use.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2003] (notably Stoke Mandeville Hospital, Buckinghamshire; Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust, Kent, and other English hospitals)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults; healthcare‑associated CDI)
Event summary: Between 2003 and 2006, several large CDI outbreaks occurred in England, beginning with a major 2003–2004 episode at Stoke Mandeville Hospital where 174 cases and at least 19 CDI‑related deaths were recorded, and followed by prolonged outbreaks at Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust and other hospitals, many linked to ribotype 027. The outbreaks were characterized by crowded wards, high antibiotic exposure, and lapses in isolation and environmental decontamination, leading to sustained hospital‑wide transmission and substantial excess mortality. Subsequent public inquiries, national surveillance, and strengthened infection‑prevention and stewardship programs contributed to a marked fall in CDI incidence and a decline in the proportion of cases due to ribotype 027 after 2007.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of high‑risk antibiotics (e.g., cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), inadequate isolation capacity, environmental contamination, and delayed recognition of CDI severity; organizational failures highlighted by national inquiries. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – spread of hypervirulent ribotype 027 into UK institutions; Antimicrobial Resistance – fluoroquinolone resistance in 027; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – higher toxin output associated with severe colitis and deaths; Enhanced Transmission – high environmental spore burden and ward‑level transmission sustained prolonged outbreaks.
Review: retain – Appropriately summarises major 2003–2006 CDI outbreaks in England (Stoke Mandeville, Maidstone & Tunbridge Wells and others) linked to ribotype 027, with correct geography (UK in Northern Europe) and emergence type (re‑emergence due to a hypervirulent, resistant lineage plus external drivers such as high‑risk antibiotic use and infection‑control failures).

Countries: Netherlands [2005]; Belgium [2005]; Ireland [2005] (multi‑hospital outbreaks of ribotype 027)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults; healthcare‑associated CDI)
Event summary: In 2005–2006, a Europe‑wide survey of 38 hospitals in 14 countries first detected the hypervirulent BI/NAP1/027 ribotype in hospitals in the Netherlands, Belgium and Ireland, where concurrent CDI outbreaks with unusually severe disease, high relapse, and elevated mortality were observed. In the Netherlands, a series of hospital epidemics between April 2005 and February 2006 involved ribotype 027 and prompted national CDI surveillance, with similar clusters reported in Belgian and Irish centers. Over time, better recognition, isolation, environmental cleaning, and antibiotic restriction led to a substantial decrease in 027 prevalence in these countries, although other ribotypes, including 078, later became more prominent.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High inpatient antibiotic pressure, including fluoroquinolones, and extensive regional patient transfers facilitated the rapid establishment of BI/NAP1/027 once it was introduced from North America/UK; limited initial awareness of strain‑specific virulence delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – continental introduction and expansion of BI/NAP1/027; Antimicrobial Resistance – fluoroquinolone resistance giving a competitive advantage; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – greater toxin production and environmental persistence drove large hospital outbreaks.
Review: retain – Correctly reflects emergence and spread of PCR ribotype 027 in Dutch, Belgian and Irish hospitals in 2005–2006, drawing on European surveillance and outbreak reports. Sub‑region coding (Western Europe for the Netherlands and Belgium; Northern Europe for Ireland) and classification as re‑emergence due to an epidemic strain in regions with pre‑existing CDI are appropriate.

Host: Humans (hospitalized and community‑onset adult CDI cases; linkage to pigs and food animals)
Event summary: From 2005 onward, Dutch surveillance documented a rapid rise of CDI due to PCR ribotype 078, initially noticed as an increasing share of cases among hospitalized patients and then recognized as a frequent cause of community‑onset CDI. Molecular studies showed ribotype 078 to be common in pigs and calves and present in retail meats, with some human isolates closely related to food‑animal strains, and its prevalence in Dutch CDI cases rose to around 9–10% as ribotype 027 declined. By the late 2000s this hypervirulent, multidrug‑resistant lineage had become an important cause of both hospital‑ and community‑associated CDI in the Netherlands, prompting continued veterinary and food‑chain investigations and human surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive livestock production with heavy antimicrobial use, potential foodborne exposure through contaminated meat, and community antibiotic prescribing likely facilitated zoonotic and community transmission of ribotype 078. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – emergence of hypervirulent ribotype 078 with increased toxin production; Antimicrobial Resistance – multidrug resistance, including to commonly used agents; Host Expansion (Spillover) – evidence of circulation in pigs and calves with probable spillover to humans; Enhanced Transmission – ability to cause community‑onset disease beyond traditional hospital settings.
Review: retain – Accurately describes emergence of ribotype 078 in the Netherlands from 2005 onward, including its rise to a substantial share of CDI cases and its close genetic relationship between human and pig isolates. Geographic coding (Netherlands, Western Europe) and classification as re‑emergence (new zoonosis‑linked, multidrug‑resistant lineage in a region with long‑standing CDI) are appropriate.

Countries: United States of America [2004] (e.g., Veterans Affairs hospital in North Carolina and other centers reporting community‑onset CDI)
Host: Humans (community‑associated CDI in adults, including otherwise healthy and peripartum individuals)
Event summary: Between about 2004 and 2007, U.S. surveillance and analytic studies identified a striking increase in community‑associated CDI, with a North Carolina Veterans Affairs hospital reporting that 35% of CDI cases from October 2004 to December 2005 had symptom onset in the community and national data showing rising CDI hospitalizations among younger adults and peripartum women without traditional healthcare exposures. These community‑onset cases were frequently linked to recent outpatient antibiotic use and, in some reports, proton‑pump inhibitor therapy, and often presented to hospitals with severe diarrhea requiring admission. Over subsequent years, awareness of community‑associated CDI led to guideline changes, improved outpatient prescribing stewardship, and more cautious use of acid‑suppressive therapy, which helped stabilize or reduce community CDI incidence in some regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased outpatient prescribing of broad‑spectrum antibiotics, widespread use of proton‑pump inhibitors and other gastric‑acid suppressants, and changing healthcare utilization patterns (more outpatient procedures and short‑stay admissions) shifted CDI risk into the community. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – circulation of epidemic healthcare‑associated lineages such as NAP1/027 and 078 into community reservoirs; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – adaptation of epidemic strains to survive and transmit outside traditional hospital environments, including in the community and household setting.
Review: retain – Provides a well‑supported summary of the mid‑2000s rise in community‑associated CDI in the United States, including the 35% community‑onset proportion reported from a North Carolina VA hospital and broader national trends. Correctly coded as re‑occurrence driven primarily by external factors (outpatient antibiotic and PPI use, changing healthcare patterns) rather than by a new species or lineage, and geography is accurate.

Countries: Republic of Korea [2006]; China [mid‑late 2000s]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2008]; Japan [mid‑late 2000s]; Singapore [mid‑late 2000s] (sporadic cases)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with CDI; sporadic cases, no sustained large 027/078 epidemics)
Event summary: In the mid‑ to late‑2000s, Asian hospitals began detecting the hypervirulent PCR ribotype 027 lineage: retrospective typing in Korea showed 027 present as early as 2006 with the first clinical case reported in 2009, single 027 cases without travel history were documented in Hong Kong, Japan and Singapore, and ribotype 078 was reported mainly from Korea and China. These detections occurred against a background of endemic CDI dominated by other ribotypes such as 017 and 018 and did not immediately produce continent‑wide 027/078 epidemics as seen in North America and Europe. Nevertheless, the appearance of 027 and 078 in Asian strain collections prompted heightened surveillance and infection‑control efforts to prevent local establishment of these hypervirulent lineages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing use of high‑risk antibiotics, aging hospital populations, and improved diagnostic capacity in Asian hospitals created conditions in which imported hypervirulent strains could be detected and potentially spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – regional introduction of ribotypes 027 and 078 into strain pools historically dominated by 017/018; Antimicrobial Resistance – similar fluoroquinolone resistance patterns to Western 027 strains; Enhanced Transmission – potential for rapid nosocomial spread, prompting early containment efforts.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the sporadic detection of hypervirulent ribotypes 027 and 078 in East and South‑east Asian hospitals during the mid‑ to late‑2000s, against a background of endemic 017/018 CDI and without large‑scale 027 epidemics. Sub‑regions were corrected to "Eastern Asia; South‑eastern Asia" to reflect inclusion of Singapore, and China was added to the country list to reflect reports of ribotype 078 there. The event summary wording was adjusted so that 078 is described as mainly reported from Korea and China, with 027 cases documented sporadically in Hong Kong, Japan, Korea and Singapore. Emergence is still best classified as re‑emergence (new hypervirulent genotypes in regions with established CDI rather than first continental emergence of the species).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia [2009] (first imported 027 case, Western Australia); Australia [2010] (first locally acquired 027 case, Victoria); Australia [2011–2012] (nationwide CDI incidence increase)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with healthcare‑associated CDI; some community‑onset cases)
Event summary: In 2009, Australia confirmed its first isolation of epidemic C. difficile PCR ribotype 027 in a patient in Western Australia who had apparently acquired the infection overseas, followed by the first locally acquired 027 infection in a Melbourne hospital in 2010, signalling the local establishment of the hypervirulent lineage. Over 2011–2012, national surveillance reported a significant increase in CDI incidence across Australian hospitals, although ribotype 027 remained less common than other ribotypes unique to the region. Subsequent antimicrobial stewardship and infection‑prevention initiatives were strengthened to prevent large‑scale 027‑driven epidemics like those seen in North America and Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rising use of high‑risk antibiotics and increasing complexity of hospitalized patients in Australia, combined with international travel and medical tourism, facilitated introduction of epidemic 027; delayed availability of routine strain typing initially limited early recognition. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – introduction and local spread of hypervirulent 027 into an immunologically naive hospital population; Antimicrobial Resistance – fluoroquinolone resistance similar to overseas 027 strains; Enhanced Transmission – potential for hospital outbreaks, prompting pre‑emptive surveillance and control measures.
Review: retain – Accurately describes Australia’s first imported (2009) and locally acquired (2010) ribotype 027 detections and the subsequent national increase in CDI incidence in 2011–2012, while noting that 027 remained less common than local ribotypes. Geographic coding (Australia within the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region) and classification as re‑emergence due to a novel strain in a region with pre‑existing CDI are appropriate, and imported‑only cases are not misclassified as inter‑continental emergence.

Countries: Poland [2008]; Poland [2011–2013] (multiple hospitals across the country)
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with healthcare‑associated CDI, including dialysis patients; multiple hospital outbreaks)
Event summary: From 2008 onward, Polish hospitals recorded a rapid rise in CDI driven by hypervirulent PCR ribotype 027 and its closely related ribotype 176, with some centers reporting 027 accounting for 48–65% of toxigenic isolates and numerous hospital outbreaks, including a documented 2012 nephrology‑ward outbreak among dialysis patients. National surveillance between 2011 and 2013 showed very high CDI incidence rates and a predominance of 027/176 across multiple regions, while broader nosocomial‑infection reports for 2011–2015 identified C. difficile as the leading cause of reported hospital outbreaks. Implementation of targeted infection‑control bundles and antibiotic stewardship is ongoing to curb 027/176 transmission and reduce the heavy CDI burden in Polish healthcare facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High hospital antibiotic use with frequent fluoroquinolone and cephalosporin exposure, aging inpatient populations, and limited early CDI diagnostics contributed to the rapid establishment of 027/176 and under‑recognition of cases. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – expansion of 027 and related 176 lineages; Antimicrobial Resistance – high rates of resistance in 027/176 compared with other ribotypes; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – association with severe disease and outbreaks; Enhanced Transmission – efficient hospital spread, as indicated by numerous nosocomial outbreaks and high ward‑level prevalence.
Review: retain – Correctly summarises the expansion of ribotypes 027 and 176 and the high CDI burden in Polish hospitals from 2008 onwards, including dialysis‑ward outbreaks and national data showing C. difficile as the most common cause of reported nosocomial outbreaks in 2011–2015. Coding as re‑emergence in Poland (Eastern Europe) is appropriate given the emergence of new epidemic genotypes in a country with pre‑existing CDI.

Continent: South America; Northern America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: South America – South America; Northern America – Northern America; Europe – Western, Northern, Southern, Eastern Europe; Asia – Eastern, South-eastern, Southern, Western Asia; Africa – Eastern, Western, Southern Africa; Oceania – Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Spain [1998]; Argentina [1999]; Japan [2002-2003]; Kenya [2003-2004]; China [2004]; multiple additional countries across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas and Oceania documenting BA genotype circulation by 2005-2006
Host: Humans (primarily infants and young children; also older adults)
Event summary: During the late 1990s, a new RSV group B genotype (BA), defined by a 60‑nucleotide duplication in the G glycoprotein gene, was first detected in Madrid, Spain (1998) and then in Buenos Aires, Argentina (1999), where it rapidly rose in frequency among hospitalized infants. Over the next 3–4 years, BA viruses were identified in Japan, China, Kenya and many other countries on all inhabited continents, progressively displacing previously circulating RSV‑B genotypes. By about the 2004–2006 seasons, BA and its descendant lineages (including BA9) accounted for almost all RSV‑B detections in multiple national and regional datasets, representing a global genotype replacement that reset the molecular baseline for subsequent RSV epidemics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2897623/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High global connectivity through human travel and year‑round RSV transmission in young children allowed rapid inter‑regional spread once BA viruses arose, and expanding molecular surveillance made it possible to document their rise. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain / genotype emergence (BA genotype with a 60‑nt duplication in the G gene that likely enhanced immune evasion and/or fitness), with inherent geographic range expansion as BA rapidly replaced earlier RSV‑B lineages across South America, Northern America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3963446/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Retain this event as a major re‑emergence episode (global replacement of RSV‑B by the BA genotype), but correct the start year to 1998 (first BA-like viruses with the 60‑nt duplication detected in Madrid, Spain) and adjust the countries list to Spain [1998], Argentina [1999], Japan [2002–2003], Kenya [2003–2004], and China [2004] based on molecular epidemiology studies. Also standardised the continent label from “North America” to “Northern America” to align with the Country sheet. Event type ‘re-emergence’ (novel genotype with global spread in regions where RSV was already endemic) remains appropriate; it is not classified as inter‑continental emergence because the EPP species was long established on all listed continents before BA appeared. Source URLs were refocused on detailed BA genotype descriptions and global spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Continent: Northern America; South America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Northern America – Northern America; South America – South America and Caribbean; Europe – Western, Northern, Southern, Eastern Europe; Asia – Eastern, South-eastern, Southern, Western Asia; Africa – Eastern, Western Africa; Oceania – Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Canada [Ontario, 2010]; Germany [2011-2012]; Kenya [2012]; China [2011-2012]; India [2011]; Japan [2012]; Panama [2012]; Paraguay [2012]; multiple additional countries across all continents reporting ON1 by the mid‑2010s
Host: Humans (primarily infants and young children; also adults)
Event summary: In winter 2010–2011, RSV group A viruses carrying a 72‑nucleotide duplication in the G gene (genotype ON1) were first identified in Ontario, Canada, initially as a minority of RSV‑A detections. Over the next 2–4 years, ON1 was reported from multiple countries in Europe (e.g. Germany), Asia (e.g. India, China, Japan, Republic of Korea), Africa (e.g. Kenya) and the Americas (including Panama and Paraguay), often rising quickly from sporadic detections to a substantial share of RSV‑A cases. By the mid‑2010s, ON1 had become the predominant RSV‑A genotype worldwide and diversified into numerous lineages, largely replacing earlier NA1/GA2‑like strains without clear, consistent changes in clinical severity but with important implications for antigenic drift and future vaccine design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3314658/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global air travel and intense mixing in childcare, schools and households enabled rapid dissemination of ON1 between and within continents, while expansion of genotyping networks improved detection. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain / genotype emergence (ON1 with a 72‑nt G‑gene duplication introducing additional O‑glycosylation sites and altered antigenic structure), followed by rapid lineage diversification and apparent fitness and/or immune‑escape advantages that allowed ON1 to out‑compete predecessor RSV‑A genotypes in most regions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3314658/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This event appropriately captures the emergence and rapid global spread of the RSV‑A ON1 genotype, which displaced earlier RSV‑A lineages across multiple continents. I harmonised the continent label to “Northern America”, clarified country‑specific years to better match published first-detection reports, and kept the classification as ‘re-emergence’ (novel genotype in regions with pre‑existing RSV circulation) rather than as first detection or inter‑continental emergence. The selected sources now emphasise detailed molecular epidemiology of ON1 (Ontario origin, early spread in Germany, China and Kenya) and its global predominance.

Continent: Global – Northern America; South America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Multiple: Northern America; South America and Caribbean; Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe; Eastern, South-eastern, Southern and Western Asia; Australia and New Zealand; selected African subregions with RSV surveillance
Countries: United States of America [2020-2021]; Brazil [2020-2021]; Chile [2020-2021]; France [2020-2021]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2020-2021]; South Africa [2020-2021]; Japan [2020-2021]; Republic of Korea [2020-2021]; multiple other surveillance countries with near-absence and then delayed RSV activity
Host: Humans (especially infants and young children; also adults)
Event summary: With the introduction of stringent COVID‑19 non‑pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) in early 2020, RSV circulation collapsed in many countries: the usual 2020–2021 winter RSV season was largely absent in Northern America, Europe, parts of South America and Asia, and several African and Oceanian settings. As NPIs were eased and schools and childcare reopened, a delayed and often off‑season reappearance of RSV activity was observed from late 2020 into 2021, typically at lower or moderate intensity compared with pre‑pandemic winters. This globally linked episode of suppression followed by atypical, shifted‑timing epidemics set up unusually large susceptible cohorts of infants and toddlers for subsequent RSV seasons. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/pdfs/mm7029a1-H.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Broad implementation of COVID‑19 NPIs (lockdowns, stay‑at‑home orders, school and daycare closures, mask use, reduced travel and gatherings) sharply reduced contact rates and RSV transmission, while later relaxation of these measures and reopening of schools altered the timing and strength of resurgent epidemics. Internal mechanisms: No major new RSV genotype has been implicated; changes are best explained by altered human behaviour and contact patterns, together with accumulation of RSV‑naïve children who missed exposure during 2020, rather than by viral evolution. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/pdfs/mm7029-H.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This event captures a clearly bounded, globally important re‑occurrence episode in which RSV activity was almost absent during the 2020–2021 winter and then reappeared in delayed, off‑season epidemics as COVID‑19 NPIs were relaxed. I standardised the continent label to “Northern America” to match the Country sheet and updated the source list to include key multi‑country and US surveillance analyses. Classification as ‘re-occurrence’ driven by external factors (NPIs and changed contact patterns) without evidence of a new genotype is appropriate; it should not be labelled inter‑continental emergence, because RSV was long endemic on all involved continents and imported cases were part of a single, globally disrupted episode.

Continent: Northern America; South America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Northern America; South America and Caribbean; Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe; Eastern, South-eastern and Western Asia; Southern and Eastern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [spring-summer 2021]; Brazil [2021]; Chile [2021]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2021]; France [2021]; Israel [2021]; Japan [2021]; Republic of Korea [2021]; South Africa [2021]; Australia [2021-2022]; multiple other surveillance countries with large, off-season RSV resurgences
Host: Humans (infants and young children; older adults also affected)
Event summary: Following the near‑absence of RSV in 2020–2021, many countries experienced unusually timed and often sizeable RSV resurgences beginning in spring or summer 2021, including large outbreaks in the United States, Brazil, Chile, multiple European states, Israel, South Africa, Japan, the Republic of Korea and Australia. These epidemics frequently peaked months earlier than traditional autumn–winter seasons, produced high paediatric hospitalization rates (sometimes exceeding prior off‑season baselines), and involved a broader age range of susceptible children, including older infants and toddlers who had not been infected during 2020. Through late 2021 and early 2022, RSV activity in many regions gradually shifted back toward more typical calendar timing, but incidence remained elevated compared with immediate pre‑pandemic seasons. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7214a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Relaxation of COVID‑19 NPIs, reopening of schools and childcare, and resumption of domestic and international travel markedly increased contact rates among children and families, while one to two unexposed birth cohorts (“immunity debt”) accumulated during the suppression period, amplifying epidemic size. Health systems in several countries were still coping with COVID‑19 waves, compounding the impact of RSV resurgences. Internal mechanisms: Genetic data indicate continued dominance of ON1 and BA9 lineages, with no single novel variant clearly linked to these resurgences, so the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by host and behavioural factors rather than viral change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9897071/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This row describes the first large, globally observed off‑season RSV resurgences in 2021–2022, which generated substantial hospitalization burden and are well documented in surveillance and clinical reports. I harmonised the continent label to “Northern America”, clarified that the epidemics begin in spring–summer 2021 and extend into early 2022, and updated sources to include key regional analyses (Europe, Japan, South Africa, United States). Classification as ‘re-occurrence’ (external drivers and immunity debt) without ‘re-emergence’ is consistent with the event-type definitions.

Continent: Northern America; Europe; selected parts of South America and Asia
Sub-regions: Northern America; Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe; parts of South America; selected Asian countries with enhanced RSV surveillance
Countries: United States of America [2022-2023]; Canada [2022-2023]; multiple EU/EEA countries including France, Spain, Germany, Italy, Netherlands (Kingdom of the), Sweden [2022-2023]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022-2023]; selected South American and Asian countries reporting concurrent RSV, influenza and COVID‑19 activity
Host: Humans (infants and young children, with substantial impact on pediatric services; older adults also affected)
Event summary: During the 2022–2023 Northern Hemisphere respiratory virus season, the United States, Canada and many European countries experienced very early and intense RSV epidemics, with activity beginning in late summer or early autumn and peaking weeks to months before typical pre‑pandemic winters. These surges drove sharp increases in paediatric emergency visits and hospital admissions, contributing to an overloading of children’s hospitals and intensive care units and to the widely publicised “tripledemic” of RSV, influenza and COVID‑19. By early 2023, RSV activity declined toward baseline, but hospitalization rates in young children in several settings remained higher than in 2018–2020 seasons, marking this as one of the most disruptive RSV epidemics in recent decades. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7214a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Residual immunity gaps from the suppressed 2020–2021 season, high contact rates after lifting most COVID‑19 restrictions, reopening of schools and childcare, and concurrent circulation of influenza and SARS‑CoV‑2 all contributed to early and large RSV epidemics and to health‑system strain. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses show continued circulation of ON1 (RSV‑A) and BA9 or related RSV‑B lineages, without evidence that a novel genotype was responsible for increased severity; the episode is therefore best interpreted as a large re‑occurrence driven primarily by demographic and behavioural factors. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7214a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This event corresponds to the well‑documented 2022–2023 “tripledemic” with very early, high‑intensity RSV activity and major paediatric care strain in North America and Europe. I standardised continent and country naming (e.g. “Northern America”, “Netherlands (Kingdom of the)”) and expanded the source list to include detailed burden estimates and ECDC risk assessments. Classification as ‘re-occurrence’ rather than inter‑continental emergence is appropriate, because the outbreaks occurred in regions where RSV was already long‑established and no new genotype or continent was involved.

Countries: France [2023-2025] (nationwide infant nirsevimab programme with reduced RSV bronchiolitis hospitalizations and surveillance-detected RSV-B variants carrying nirsevimab resistance-associated substitutions)
Host: Humans (infants in their first RSV season; focus on medically vulnerable and general infant population)
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑September 2023, France implemented one of the first nationwide programmes offering the long‑acting monoclonal antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) to almost all infants entering their first RSV season, which led to a substantial reduction in RSV bronchiolitis hospitalizations during the 2023–2024 season compared with pre‑programme years. Intensive virologic surveillance of infants with breakthrough RSV infections during 2023–2024 identified rare RSV‑B viruses carrying substitutions at the nirsevimab binding site (notably F:N208D and an I64M+K65R combination) that conferred marked reductions in in‑vitro susceptibility to nirsevimab. Subsequent national multicentre analyses across the first two programme seasons (2023–2025) documented additional resistant RSV‑B variants but still found resistance‑associated substitutions in only a small minority of sequenced breakthrough cases, highlighting the early emergence—but as yet limited spread—of monoclonal antibody–resistant RSV under large‑scale prophylactic pressure. ([santepubliquefrance.fr](https://www.santepubliquefrance.fr/en/node/35309?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Policy decisions to introduce universal or near‑universal nirsevimab prophylaxis for infants in France from 2023–2024 onwards, together with intense RSV circulation in the early post‑COVID period and strong laboratory surveillance networks, created both strong selective pressure at the F‑protein antigenic site Ø and the capacity to detect emerging escape variants. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial / monoclonal antibody resistance, via RSV‑B variants with amino‑acid substitutions in the nirsevimab binding site (e.g. N208D and related patterns) that substantially reduce neutralization in vitro; emergence and onward transmission of these escape variants represents a form of re‑emergence, although current data suggest that fitness costs are sufficient to keep their prevalence low so far. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39419046/?dopt=Abstract&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. I recommend retaining this event as an important early example of monoclonal‑antibody resistance emerging in RSV under national‑scale prophylaxis, but with caveats: resistant RSV‑B variants remain rare (a small fraction of sequenced breakthrough infections) and the clinical impact on overall RSV burden is limited so far. I kept the timeframe as 2023–2025 to capture the first two programme seasons and the 2026 multicentre resistance analysis, standardised country/region naming, and refocused the event summary on documented resistance frequencies rather than suggesting that resistant viruses account for a “meaningful minority” of all breakthrough cases. Classification as ‘re-emergence’ driven by antimicrobial resistance is appropriate, but continued surveillance will be needed to determine whether this ultimately qualifies among the ten highest‑impact emergence events for RSV.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (all ages with invasive group A streptococcal disease)
Event summary: From approximately 2009 onward, Canada’s national surveillance data showed a sustained increase in invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) disease incidence, rising from about 4.0 cases per 100,000 population in 2009 to roughly 8.1 cases per 100,000 by 2019, after earlier population‑based surveys in the 1990s and early 2000s had documented lower baseline rates. Over this decade, iGAS affected a broad age range with common clinical manifestations including necrotizing fasciitis, bacteremia without focus and pneumonia, and risk factors such as chronic disease, varicella in children, substance use, and social vulnerability were repeatedly identified, while multiple emm types circulated without a single nationwide clone completely dominating. The prolonged increase was not associated with a discrete outbreak endpoint but rather with establishment of a higher endemic level of iGAS, prompting continuing national notifiable‑disease surveillance and guidance on clinical management and chemoprophylaxis rather than specific time‑limited emergency measures. ([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2022-48/issue-9-september-2022/invasive-group-a-streptococcal-disease-surveillance-canada-2020.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Demographic changes including an ageing population, high prevalence of comorbidities (diabetes, heart and lung disease), varicella infections in children, crowding and socio‑economic disadvantage in some communities, and improved awareness and reporting likely contributed to the sustained rise in iGAS incidence. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing circulation and geographic range expansion of multiple virulent emm lineages with capacity for invasive disease, with some regional clonal expansions noted, but no single novel nationwide strain fully explains the trend; instead, the observed resurgence appears to result from the cumulative effect of diverse virulent S. pyogenes genotypes interacting with vulnerable populations. ([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2022-48/issue-9-september-2022/invasive-group-a-streptococcal-disease-surveillance-canada-2020.html?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event corresponds to the documented doubling of Canada’s national iGAS incidence between 2009 and 2019 and is one of the largest sustained country‑level increases. Reclassified from re-emergence to re-occurrence because Canadian surveillance reports attribute the trend mainly to demographic and social risk factors with multiple circulating emm types and no single novel epidemic clone; wording of the mechanism was adjusted accordingly, but continent, sub‑region, country and time span remain consistent with national data.
