Countries: China [2011]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2011]; China, Macao Special Administrative Region [2011]
Host: Humans (primarily children with scarlet fever and some invasive GAS cases)
Event summary: The event began in early 2011 with a sharp and unusual increase in notified scarlet fever cases in Hong Kong, coincident with rising reports from neighboring mainland China and Macao and associated with Streptococcus pyogenes emm12 and emm1 strains, some carrying novel genetic insertions and macrolide resistance. Throughout mid‑2011, large numbers of pediatric scarlet fever cases and several deaths were reported, and molecular studies documented multiclonal circulation of toxigenic emm12 lineages harboring integrative and conjugative elements encoding tetracycline and macrolide resistance as well as prophages encoding superantigens, while public health authorities implemented enhanced surveillance, school‑based control measures and cross‑border information sharing. Case numbers declined later in 2011 after control actions and the natural end of the transmission season, but the episode marked the onset of a broader, prolonged regional resurgence of scarlet fever in East Asia driven by these evolved S. pyogenes lineages. ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/201106/29/P201106290210.htm))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High population density and intense transmission in schools, seasonal respiratory virus circulation, and regional connectivity between Hong Kong, Macao and mainland China facilitated rapid spread; antibiotic selection pressure likely favored macrolide‑ and tetracycline‑resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (epidemic emm12 lineages carrying large integrative and conjugative elements with macrolide/tetracycline resistance genes and prophages encoding superantigens such as SSA and SpeC and DNase Spd1), antimicrobial resistance (high macrolide resistance among circulating scarlet fever strains), and increased virulence/pathogenicity through enhanced superantigen toxin gene content that likely contributed to disease severity and transmissibility. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507889/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Well-supported description of the 2011 Hong Kong/Mainland China/Macao scarlet fever upsurge linked to macrolide‑resistant emm12 lineages; continent, sub‑region and country list match UN geographies, and classification as re-emergence (strain change with enhanced virulence and resistance) is appropriate. Only minor formatting clean‑up and addition of citations were needed.

Countries: China [2011]; Republic of Korea [2011]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2011]
Host: Humans (children with scarlet fever, some adults and invasive cases)
Event summary: Beginning in 2011, China experienced a marked nationwide increase in scarlet fever incidence, with joinpoint analyses showing a break from previously low, stable rates and coinciding with contemporaneous surges in Hong Kong and South Korea. Over 2011–2016, surveillance documented persistently elevated annual scarlet fever rates across multiple provinces, with predominant GAS emm types varying by country (emm12 and emm1 in China, emm3 and emm28 in South Korea), indicating broad regional re‑emergence driven by multiple successful lineages. Although incidence fluctuated by year and region, disease burden remained substantially higher than pre‑2011 levels through at least 2016, and governments maintained strengthened surveillance and clinical guidance rather than declaring a discrete single‑year outbreak end. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29858148/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban crowding, high contact rates among school‑aged children, and regional travel likely enabled wide dissemination of epidemic clones; antimicrobial use patterns may have selected for resistant and highly fit emm12 and other lineages, while concurrent respiratory virus circulation may have amplified transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and geographic range expansion of epidemic emm types (notably emm12 and emm1 in China and emm3/emm28 in South Korea), with many strains carrying mobile genetic elements encoding superantigen toxins and macrolide resistance, leading to enhanced transmissibility and pathogenicity as well as antimicrobial resistance. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1473309918302317?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Correctly summarises the broader 2011–2016 East Asian scarlet fever resurgence in mainland China, Hong Kong and South Korea documented by national surveillance and Lancet Infectious Diseases analyses; the episode is epidemiologically linked to, but temporally broader than, the 2011 Hong Kong spike and appropriately classified as re-emergence driven by evolving emm12 and related lineages.

Host: Humans (all ages with invasive group A streptococcal disease)
Event summary: In 2012, Sweden reported a sharp rise in invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) infections, reaching an incidence of about 6.1 per 100,000 population, the highest since national notification began in 2004, and continuing at elevated levels into early 2013. During this period, surveillance identified a predominance and further increase of emm1/T1 isolates, a genotype previously associated with severe invasive disease, along with notable proportions of other emm types such as emm89, emm28 and emm3, indicating clonal shifts within the circulating S. pyogenes population. Although incidence remained elevated into 2013, the surge was gradually contained with continued clinical vigilance and public health monitoring rather than through specific outbreak‑control interventions, and the episode is recognized as a genotype‑linked re‑emergence of iGAS in Sweden rather than a new geographic introduction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23594518/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal respiratory transmission, population‑level susceptibility to particular emm1 clones, and improved case detection and reporting may all have contributed to the observed increase. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of a virulent emm1/T1 lineage that rose to around one‑third of typed invasive isolates, together with other virulent emm types, suggesting increased virulence/pathogenicity and transmission fitness of these clones compared with previously circulating strains. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23594518/))
Review: retain – Accurately reflects the documented 2012–2013 peak in Swedish iGAS incidence and the dominance of emm1/T1 and other virulent emm types; spatial classification (Northern Europe, Sweden) and treatment as a re-emergence driven by clonal shifts are well supported by Euro Surveill and national surveillance data.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2014]
Host: Humans (primarily children with scarlet fever; associated invasive GAS cases across age groups)
Event summary: Around 2013–2014, England began experiencing an abrupt increase in reported scarlet fever cases, with notification rates tripling between 2013 and 2014 and continuing to rise through the 2015 and 2016 seasons to the highest national levels in about 50 years. During this period, national surveillance and molecular studies showed changing S. pyogenes emm‑type distributions in respiratory and invasive isolates, with early association of the upsurge with emm3 and emm4 in northwest London and subsequent emergence and spread of a novel toxigenic emm1 lineage (M1UK) that became the dominant cause of upper respiratory and invasive disease in England. The large wave of scarlet fever activity persisted through 2016 before declining, but the M1UK lineage remained established in the population, and UK public health agencies instituted ongoing heightened surveillance and infection‑control guidance for schools and clinicians. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/increase-in-scarlet-fever-across-england))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cyclical population immunity to scarlet fever, dense school‑based mixing of young children, and possibly increased awareness and reporting contributed to the scale of the resurgence, while routine antibiotic use may have influenced strain selection. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and expansion, including increased circulation of emm3 and emm4 during the initial 2014 upsurge and subsequent emergence of the M1UK emm1 lineage distinguished from the global emm1 lineage by multiple SNPs and associated with higher expression of the SpeA superantigen, leading to increased virulence/pathogenicity and enhanced transmission that drove large increases in both scarlet fever and iGAS notifications. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6904876/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Row correctly characterises the 2014–2016 scarlet fever resurgence in England and the emergence and dominance of the M1UK lineage, drawing on UKHSA reports and detailed molecular epidemiology; geography, timing and classification as re-emergence (strain change with increased virulence) are appropriate.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: France [2022]; Ireland [2022]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2022]; Spain [2022]; Sweden [2022]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022]; Norway [2022]
Host: Humans (predominantly children <10 years with iGAS and scarlet fever; some adults)
Event summary: In late 2022, several European countries—including France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Sweden and the United Kingdom—began reporting an unexpected increase in invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) infections among children, often accompanied by rises in scarlet fever and non‑invasive GAS infections following a period of unusually low GAS circulation during the COVID‑19 pandemic; subsequent studies also documented marked paediatric and adult increases in Spain and Norway. Over the 2022–2023 winter season, WHO/Europe and ECDC compiled reports showing that paediatric iGAS case numbers and fatalities in some countries were several‑fold higher than pre‑pandemic levels, while typing data indicated circulation of familiar emm types (including M1UK in the UK and other lineages) without evidence for a novel emm gene sequence type or major shift in antimicrobial resistance. As the 2022–2023 season waned, incidence gradually declined toward more typical seasonal levels, with European health agencies issuing risk communications and reinforcing clinical guidance but assessing the overall population risk as low given established treatment options and the absence of a new highly resistant or hypervirulent S. pyogenes lineage. ([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/increase-invasive-group-streptococcal-infections-among-children-europe-including))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Relaxation of COVID‑19 non‑pharmaceutical interventions led to a rebound in transmission of common respiratory pathogens, including GAS, at a time when population‑level immunity—especially among young children who had experienced fewer infections during the pandemic—was relatively low; co‑circulation of respiratory viruses (e.g. influenza, RSV) appears to have increased susceptibility to invasive GAS disease, and heightened clinical awareness and testing may also have contributed to higher detection. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of endemic GAS lineages with enhanced transmission opportunities rather than emergence of a new genotype—surveillance in affected countries did not identify a novel emm sequence type or consistent new resistance pattern, so increased case numbers largely reflect external drivers acting on existing S. pyogenes populations. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON429))
Review: review – Multi-country 2022–2023 European iGAS/scarlet fever upsurge is correctly treated as a large re-occurrence driven mainly by post‑COVID changes in population mixing and concurrent viral epidemics; re-emergence was set to false to reflect the absence of a new emm type or resistance pattern in WHO/ECDC assessments. The country list was refined to name specific states with documented increases (France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, the UK and Norway) and to remove the non‑specific placeholder “other EU/EEA countries”; an additional European review article was added to the source list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (predominantly children and adolescents with invasive group A streptococcal disease; also adults)
Event summary: During the 2022–2023 respiratory virus season in the United States, CDC’s Active Bacterial Core surveillance and other systems detected an early and pronounced resurgence of invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) infections, with particularly notable increases among children and adolescents beginning in autumn 2022 in states such as Colorado and Minnesota. A December 2022 CDC Health Alert Network advisory highlighted pediatric iGAS increases above recent years, often occurring alongside high levels of respiratory syncytial virus and influenza activity, and by 2023 CDC estimated that the national number of serious group A strep infections had reached a roughly 20‑year high compared with pre‑pandemic seasons. Although incidence rose in all age groups, the surge in children was of special concern and prompted intensified surveillance, clinical alerts and public communications, after which activity gradually returned toward typical seasonal levels as the 2023–2024 winter progressed. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/han/2022/han00484.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The rapid relaxation of pandemic mitigation measures and the resulting “tripledemic” of SARS‑CoV‑2, influenza and RSV created high respiratory pathogen circulation and probable immunity gaps, especially among young children who had experienced fewer GAS and viral infections during 2020–2021; co‑infection with respiratory viruses is a recognised risk factor for iGAS, and increased clinical vigilance and testing may also have raised detection. Internal mechanisms: Genomic and surveillance data indicate circulation of common emm types, including emm1 and others, without identification of a single novel genotype or major shift in antimicrobial resistance driving the national increase, so this episode is best interpreted as a post‑pandemic re‑occurrence of endemic GAS lineages under altered host and environmental conditions. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/groupastrep/igas-infections-investigation.html?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New row added to capture the large 2022–2023 U.S. iGAS surge, which CDC reports as reaching approximately 20‑year highs in serious infections and which parallels the European post‑pandemic wave. Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because available CDC reports and MMWR analyses describe increases in common emm types without a new genotype or resistance pattern; continent, sub‑region and country fields follow the provided UN/CDC geography.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (mainly adults and older adults with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and other invasive GAS infections; some pediatric cases)
Event summary: In 2023, Japan recorded a record number of reported streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS) cases—around 941 in total—substantially exceeding the previous national high from 2019, with a large proportion attributable to group A streptococci and a high case‑fatality risk. National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID) bulletins and subsequent analyses noted that STSS and invasive group A streptococcal infections increased most sharply from mid‑2023 onward, with many cases occurring in adults over 50 years of age, and that reports continued at elevated levels into early 2024. Hospital‑based and regional studies from multiple Japanese centres documented parallel post‑pandemic increases in invasive GAS and severe paediatric GAS infections, again in the context of heavy circulation of respiratory viruses and relaxation of COVID‑19 control measures, leading domestic authorities and international commentators to characterise the situation as an unprecedented national surge in severe GAS disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11261432/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ageing demographics, high prevalence of comorbidities, and post‑COVID changes in social mixing and respiratory virus circulation likely contributed to the large pool of susceptible adults and older adults at risk for STSS and other iGAS manifestations; reductions in GAS transmission during 2020–2021 may have created immunity gaps that became evident when non‑pharmaceutical interventions were lifted. Internal mechanisms: Surveillance and early genomic investigations highlight increased contributions of emm1 and other established emm types, and Japanese risk assessments have raised the possibility that M1UK‑like sublineages may be present, but no single nationwide clone has yet been conclusively identified as the primary driver of the surge; at present the event is best interpreted as a pronounced re‑occurrence of severe disease caused by circulating GAS lineages under altered host‑population and ecological conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11261432/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New row added because Japan’s 2023–2024 STSS/iGAS surge, with record national case counts and high mortality, represents one of the largest recent country‑level increases in severe GAS disease. Classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence since current NIID and hospital‑based reports emphasise post‑pandemic epidemiologic drivers and increased incidence of known emm types; genomic work to clarify the role of M1UK‑like lineages is ongoing, so this classification should be revisited as more data emerge.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (children and adults with invasive group A streptococcal disease)
Event summary: In 2023, Argentina reported to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) a marked increase in invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) disease compared with previous years, with 926 nationally notified cases and 134 deaths (≈14% case‑fatality) according to subsequent regional updates. This increase, which affected both children and adults, prompted PAHO to issue an epidemiological alert for the Americas highlighting intensified surveillance in Argentina and the earlier signal from neighbouring Uruguay, and laboratory investigations in Argentina identified circulation of the hypervirulent M1UK lineage as well as a distinct emm1 sublineage carrying the SpeC superantigen, both of which were temporally associated with the rise in severe cases. By late 2023 and into 2024, PAHO continued to recommend strengthened clinical and genomic surveillance and early treatment rather than declaring a formal public health emergency, but the episode stands out as a major recent re‑emergence of virulent iGAS in South America. ([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/en/documents/epidemiological-alert-invasive-disease-caused-group-streptococci-28-november-2023?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑pandemic changes in social mixing and respiratory virus circulation, potential immunity gaps in paediatric populations, structural health‑system barriers and underlying chronic conditions likely contributed to the increased burden of invasive disease reported in Argentina. Internal mechanisms: PAHO reports and national data from Argentina document the detection and expansion of hypervirulent emm1 lineages, including M1UK clones and an emm1 sublineage harbouring the SpeC superantigen, consistent with a re‑emergence event in which pathogen evolution—rather than geography—plays a key role in driving incidence and severity. ([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/en/documents/epidemiological-alert-invasive-disease-caused-group-streptococci-28-november-2023?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is retained but substantially revised: the original row understated the role of new genotypes, whereas PAHO’s alert and subsequent update explicitly link Argentina’s excess 2023 iGAS burden to the emergence of M1UK and a SpeC‑positive emm1 sublineage. Classification was changed to re-emergence (not primarily re-occurrence), the placeholder “other South American countries” was removed from the country field to avoid conflating Uruguay’s earlier, smaller 2022 signal, and PAHO’s 2024 epidemiological update was added as a key quantitative source.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (initially mainly immunocompromised or otherwise medically complex adults, with later recognition of infections in immunocompetent individuals).
Event summary: From 1990 onward, clinicians and pathologists in the United States recognized fatal granulomatous amebic encephalitis cases in which brain tissue contained a free‑living amoeba distinct from Acanthamoeba, leading to the description of a new leptomyxid ameba later named Balamuthia mandrillaris. Early case reports in the early 1990s established B. mandrillaris as a cause of opportunistic meningoencephalitis in humans and other mammals, largely diagnosed at autopsy. By the mid‑1990s, Balamuthia was accepted as a distinct human pathogen with a very high case‑fatality rate, setting the stage for subsequent recognition of cases worldwide.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Improvements in neuropathology, immunohistochemistry, and reference‑laboratory support (e.g. at CDC) made it possible to distinguish Balamuthia from other free‑living amoebae in brain tissue, and publication of index cases raised global awareness. Internal mechanisms: Available data suggest this event primarily reflects recognition and characterization of a pre‑existing environmental amoeba rather than emergence of a new, more virulent strain; no specific genetic or phenotypic changes were linked to the initial human cases.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures first recognized human Balamuthia infections in the United States around 1990, consistent with J Clin Microbiol/J Eukaryot Microbiol descriptions and CDC summaries; geography, timing, and event‑type classification (first global emergence and first detection) are appropriate and no substantive corrections were needed.

Countries: Mexico [1997]; Peru [1999]; Argentina; Brazil; Venezuela (sporadic cases during the late 1990s and early 2000s).
Host: Humans, including children and young adults; many Latin American patients presented with chronic cutaneous lesions that later progressed to encephalitis.
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s, Balamuthia mandrillaris was increasingly recognized as a cause of fatal meningoencephalitis in Latin America, with a 4‑case Mexican series published in 1997 and additional cases described from Peru, Argentina, Brazil and Venezuela. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, clinicians in Peru and neighboring countries identified both encephalitic and cutaneous balamuthiasis, revealing endemic foci particularly in coastal and Andean Peru and documenting multiple fatalities. By the mid‑2000s, Central and South America together accounted for a substantial fraction of globally reported Balamuthia infections, firmly establishing the pathogen in a second continent beyond its original recognition in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High levels of soil and dust exposure in rural and peri‑urban settings (e.g. farming, outdoor labor) and limited access to advanced imaging and neuropathology contributed to both true risk and longstanding under‑recognition, with retrospective review of “unexplained brain abscess” deaths uncovering additional cases. Internal mechanisms: There is no single Latin American genotype clearly linked to this emergence; rather, environmental survival traits favoring warm, often arid or semi‑arid soils support broad establishment across diverse ecoclimates in the Americas (inherent geographic range extension documented through improved detection).
Review: review – Retain as the main inter‑continental emergence episode into Latin America, but the original row overstated Caribbean involvement and used speculative exact start‑years by country. Sub‑regions have been restricted to South America and Central America (no confirmed human cases from Caribbean islands, only environmental isolation in Jamaica), and country timing now reflects the 1997 Mexican 4‑case series and late‑1990s Peruvian reports, with other countries kept as undated late‑1990s/early‑2000s sporadic cases, consistent with MMWR and later reviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (cases detected in multiple states including California, Arizona, Texas, Mississippi, Hawaii, Georgia, Florida, New Mexico, Illinois, Virginia and Washington) [mostly 1999–2008].
Host: Humans across a wide age range, including immunocompetent children and adults as well as immunocompromised patients; some had preceding cutaneous lesions.
Event summary: Between 1999 and 2008, California and several other U.S. states recorded a noticeable cluster of Balamuthia mandrillaris encephalitis and cutaneous balamuthiasis cases, with 10 laboratory‑confirmed encephalitis cases identified through the California Encephalitis Project and additional cases reported elsewhere in the United States. During this period, Balamuthia disease was increasingly recognized among both immunocompromised and immunocompetent persons, often after prolonged diagnostic delays, and nearly all patients died despite aggressive therapy. By 2016, 109 U.S. cases overall (most occurring after 1990) had been documented, highlighting recurrent, geographically widespread risk within Northern America rather than isolated index cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enhanced encephalitis surveillance (especially the California Encephalitis Project) and wider use of MRI, brain biopsy, and reference‑laboratory testing greatly increased detection of rare CNS infections; soil exposure through gardening, agriculture, construction and outdoor recreation in warm, arid or semi‑arid regions was frequently documented as a risk factor. Internal mechanisms: No distinct emergent strain was implicated; the pattern is compatible with improved recognition of a previously underdiagnosed, environmentally widespread amoeba rather than new genetic adaptation, i.e. an apparent re‑occurrence driven by diagnostics and surveillance rather than true biological resurgence.
Review: review – Event correctly reflects a period of increased U.S. case detection centered on California and other southern states, supported by CDC’s 1974–2016 case series and the California Encephalitis Project data. However, the original row attached specific start‑years to individual states without direct evidence; the countries field has been simplified to list the United States with representative states and an approximate 1999–2008 window, which better matches CDC summaries while keeping the re‑occurrence classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Czechia [1998]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [early 2000s]; Portugal [2001]; additional isolated European cases recognized later in the 2000s.
Host: Humans, including children and adults, generally previously healthy or with limited immunosuppression, presenting with encephalitis sometimes initially suspected to be brain tumors.
Event summary: In 1998, a fatal case of amebic encephalitis in a 3‑year‑old child in Czechia was identified as Balamuthia mandrillaris, representing the first documented human infection in Europe. In the early 2000s, the first UK case was confirmed by post‑mortem culture, and in 2001 Portugal reported its first fatal Balamuthia encephalitis case initially misdiagnosed as a brain tumor, bringing the total to only a handful of European patients. Over subsequent years, a few additional isolated European cases were reported as specialist centers adopted immunofluorescence and PCR for diagnosis, demonstrating that Balamuthia could cause severe disease in Europe but that incidence remained extremely low and outcomes were usually fatal.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased neuropathology and molecular diagnostic capacity in European referral centers allowed recognition of Balamuthia among patients with idiopathic brain lesions, but there is no evidence of local outbreaks; cases remained sporadic. Internal mechanisms: No distinct European lineage has been described; emergence in Europe is best explained by global environmental distribution of the amoeba with rare spillover from soil exposure to humans, rather than human‑to‑human spread or strain‑specific changes.
Review: review – Retain as the inter‑continental emergence into Europe, but correct the original misstatement that the first European case occurred in the UK. Primary sources show the first confirmed human case was a Czech child in 1998, followed by UK and Portuguese cases in the early 2000s. Sub‑regions have been narrowed to Eastern, Northern and Southern Europe to match documented human cases during this period, and Turkey has been removed from the narrative because it is classified as Western Asia in the UNSD scheme, not Europe.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia
Countries: Japan (sporadic cases from the mid‑1990s); India (case reports emerging in the 2000s); Thailand [2004 – first recognized Southeast Asian case]; China (People’s Republic of China) [2002].
Host: Humans, including children and adults, often with chronic facial or limb skin lesions or sinus involvement preceding CNS disease.
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s onward, Balamuthia mandrillaris infections were reported from several parts of Asia, including Japan and India, indicating that the pathogen was present in both temperate and tropical Asian environments. In 2002, China documented its earliest known Balamuthia infection, and in 2004 Thailand reported the first recognized Southeast Asian case, followed by additional sporadic cases over the remainder of the decade. By around 2010, Balamuthia had been recognized across multiple Asian subregions, though reports remained sporadic and case‑fatality rates exceeded 90%.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of advanced neuroimaging, neurosurgery, histopathology and molecular diagnostics in large Asian referral hospitals enabled recognition of Balamuthia among patients with previously unexplained brain lesions or chronic granulomatous skin disease; widespread environmental contact with soil and dust in agricultural and peri‑urban settings likely provided exposure opportunities. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence supports a distinct Asian lineage or novel virulence trait; the pattern is compatible with long‑standing environmental presence and rare opportunistic human infection that became visible as diagnostic capacity improved, i.e. documentation of geographic range rather than de novo evolutionary expansion.
Review: review – This remains the appropriate inter‑continental emergence episode for Asia, but the original row placed the first Thai case around 2001–2002 and implied Asian cases started only in the early 2000s. Published reports show that Japan and India had cases by the mid‑to‑late 1990s and that the first clearly documented Southeast Asian case from Thailand was in 2004. The event window has been widened to 1993–2010 (matching CDC’s statement that Asian cases have been reported since 1993), country annotations have been adjusted accordingly, and the inter‑continental emergence classification remains justified.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China (People’s Republic of China) [2002], with later cases reported from multiple provinces across eastern, central and southern China.
Host: Humans of all ages, including children and older adults; both cutaneous balamuthiasis and CNS disease (encephalitis and encephalomyelitis) have been described.
Event summary: China’s earliest reported Balamuthia mandrillaris case had onset in 2002, but cases remained poorly recognized until systematic reviews revealed a growing series of infections over the following two decades. Between 2002 and September 2025, at least 66 confirmed Balamuthia infections were reported in China, with patients drawn from multiple provinces and many diagnosed using metagenomic next‑generation sequencing or species‑specific PCR. Despite occasional therapeutic successes, most Chinese patients died, and by the 2020s Balamuthia was increasingly recognized domestically as a rare but serious cause of granulomatous encephalitis and cutaneous disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of tertiary‑care capacity and of advanced diagnostic tools (particularly metagenomic next‑generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid and tissue, and wider availability of species‑specific PCR) enabled recognition of Balamuthia in patients who previously would have been labeled as having idiopathic encephalitis or brain tumors; increasing publication of case reports in Chinese and English amplified awareness. Internal mechanisms: Current data do not implicate a distinct, more virulent Chinese lineage; this episode is best interpreted as intra‑continental emergence of recognized disease into Eastern Asia, driven by diagnostics and reporting rather than newly evolved transmissibility or virulence.
Review: review – China clearly represents one of the largest national clusters (66 confirmed cases with onset from 2002 through 2025), supported by the recent Emerging Infectious Diseases review. However, the original row incorrectly marked this as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑occurrence; by definition re‑occurrence cannot co‑occur with intra‑/inter‑continental emergence and implies resurgence within a previously known subregion. The curated row treats China as an intra‑continental emergence episode within Asia, without tagging it as re‑occurrence; dates and case counts have been cross‑checked against the 2026 EID synthesis.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia [1997], with further cases including a successfully treated brain abscess reported around 2010 and additional cases originating from Western Australia and other regions in the early 2010s.
Host: Humans, including children and adults, some of whom survived after aggressive combination antimicrobial therapy and, in selected cases, neurosurgical excision.
Event summary: In 1997, clinicians in South Australia reported a fatal case of granulomatous amoebic encephalitis caused by Balamuthia mandrillaris, establishing the first documented human infection in Oceania. Over the following decade, additional Australian cases were identified, including a brain abscess successfully treated by complete surgical excision and prolonged multidrug therapy reported around 2010 and further encephalitis cases from Western Australia described in detailed neuropathological case reports. By the mid‑2010s, Australia had contributed several human cases, including rare survivors, demonstrating that Balamuthia is present in Australian soil and capable of causing severe CNS disease, even though reported incidence remained extremely low.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑level neurosurgical, radiologic and neuropathologic capacity in Australian tertiary hospitals enabled recognition of Balamuthia brain lesions and, in selected cases, allowed surgical management that contributed to survival; improved awareness and access to PCR and immunohistochemistry through collaboration with international reference laboratories facilitated species‑level diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not suggest a unique Australian strain; rather, cases illustrate that early diagnosis, surgical debulking and multidrug regimens can occasionally overcome the organism’s intrinsic high virulence, while the underlying environmental distribution appears similar to that in other warm regions.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified Australia as the site of Oceania’s emergence but treated a 2010 successfully treated brain abscess case as if it were the first local human infection. Earlier literature documents a fatal Balamuthia GAE case in South Australia in 1997, which is the continent’s first recognized human case. The event window has been extended back to 1997, the summary updated to include the earlier fatal case alongside later survivors, and the inter‑continental emergence classification retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – specifically a 3‑year‑old child with cutaneous lesions progressing to granulomatous amebic encephalitis, with no travel outside South Africa.
Event summary: In 2020, clinicians in South Africa reported what is considered the first definitively autochthonous African case of Balamuthia mandrillaris infection, in a young child from a rural area who developed a chronic facial skin lesion that later progressed to fatal granulomatous amoebic encephalitis; the child had never traveled outside South Africa. Detailed investigation confirmed Balamuthia infection by PCR and sequencing of biopsy material, and the case was published in 2022 as Africa’s first locally acquired Balamuthia GAE. To date, only this and possibly a handful of additional African cases have been documented, but the event demonstrates that Balamuthia is present in African environments and capable of causing severe disease there.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural environmental exposure to soil and dust, combined with diagnostic delays due to the rarity and unfamiliarity of the disease, likely contributed to disease progression; national and international laboratory collaboration was required to confirm the diagnosis and to attempt access to recommended antimicrobials. Internal mechanisms: Serologic studies suggest prior Balamuthia exposure in parts of Africa, but this child’s infection appears to represent the first molecularly proven autochthonous human case on the continent rather than emergence of a novel African lineage; the principal mechanism is thus documentation of continental range expansion and spillover from an environmental reservoir into a human host.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the first definitively autochthonous African human case in South Africa with onset in 2020, consistent with the detailed JPIDS case report and earlier EID correspondence noting that no African cases had been reported before. Geography, timing, and inter‑continental emergence classification are correct; no structural changes were required.

Countries: United States of America [1996–2000]; Canada [1996–1998]; Guatemala [1996–2000, as source of imported raspberries and other berries]
Host: Humans (adults and children consuming fresh imported berries at social events, restaurants and via retail)
Event summary: From spring through summer 1996, a very large multinational outbreak of cyclosporiasis occurred in North America, with approximately 1,465 outbreak-associated cases reported from 20 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Québec; epidemiologic investigations in both countries consistently implicated fresh raspberries imported from Guatemala as the vehicle of infection. Similar but somewhat smaller raspberry‑linked outbreaks recurred in 1997 and again in 1998, including a 192‑case, 13‑cluster event in Ontario, Canada, and further clusters in the United States, and in 2000 a 54‑case outbreak in Philadelphia and other clusters were again traced to Guatemalan raspberries or blackberries. This multi‑year episode ended only after Guatemalan growers, the Guatemalan Berry Commission, and U.S. and Canadian regulators suspended spring raspberry exports, implemented a stringent Model Plan of Excellence with improved water quality, hygiene and field sanitation, and restricted exports to vetted farms, after which raspberry‑associated Cyclospora outbreaks in North America ceased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of international trade in high‑value fresh berries from Cyclospora‑endemic Guatemala to North American markets; use of inadequately treated irrigation and wash water and poor sanitary infrastructure on some exporting farms; fragile raspberries with complex surface morphology that are difficult to wash effectively; and initially low awareness of Cyclospora among clinicians and laboratories in the United States and Canada, which delayed case recognition. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains or increased virulence during this episode; emergence was driven by repeated contamination of produce in endemic areas and its distribution into a naïve, high‑consumption market. Mechanism categories: Enhanced transmission via contaminated fresh berries entering new consumer markets and geographic range expansion of exposure (but not necessarily of long‑term parasite establishment) into Northern America.
Review: retain: This row correctly captures the large 1996–2000 North American epidemic linked mainly to Guatemalan raspberries, but the emergence type was misclassified. North American outbreaks were already recognized in 1990 and 1995, so this episode is not the first inter-continental occurrence on the continent. I reclassified it as re_occurrence, removed Peru from the country list (no strong evidence it was a major produce source in this specific episode), narrowed sub_regions to Northern America and Central America, and clarified that multiple years and clusters are grouped because they share a common Guatemala–North America raspberry supply chain. Event should be retained as one of the highest-impact global episodes for this parasite.

Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming mixed salads)
Event summary: In 2000, public health authorities in Germany investigated a foodborne outbreak of cyclosporiasis among patrons of a restaurant who had eaten mixed salads and had no recent travel to Cyclospora-endemic regions, resulting in several dozen laboratory-confirmed and probable cases. Epidemiologic studies implicated consumption of a particular mixed salad dish, although a single ingredient and its country of origin could not be conclusively identified, making this the first documented outbreak of locally acquired cyclosporiasis in central Europe. Once the implicated salad components were no longer served and awareness among clinicians and laboratories increased, no further linked clusters were detected and the episode ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of fresh salad vegetables into European food service from Cyclospora-endemic regions, combined with growing year-round consumer demand for raw mixed salads; limited familiarity with Cyclospora among European clinicians and diagnostic laboratories, which delayed recognition of locally acquired disease; and the intrinsic difficulty of detecting low-level contamination on mixed salad ingredients. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the outbreak is best explained by contamination of one or more salad ingredients during production or packing outside Germany. Mechanism categories: Inter-continental emergence of foodborne cyclosporiasis into Europe via globalized fresh-produce trade, with in situ transmission to consumers in a previously unaffected continent.
Review: retain: Corrected the year to 2000 (the German outbreak was confined to that year), restricted geography to Western Europe (Germany only), and removed an unsupported attribution of salad ingredients to Peru. Retained classification as inter_continental_emergence because this represents the first documented locally acquired foodborne outbreak in Europe. Given some remaining uncertainty about the exact produce origin and total case count, this row should be kept but could be revisited against the full EID article if further precision is needed.

Countries: United States of America [2005]; Peru [2005, as origin of imported fresh basil used in multiple Florida restaurants]
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons and catered-event attendees consuming dishes containing fresh basil or basil pesto)
Event summary: From March through May 2005, Florida experienced a very large statewide outbreak of cyclosporiasis, ultimately involving approximately 600 laboratory-confirmed and clinically compatible cases among residents and visitors who had eaten at numerous restaurants and catered events. Epidemiologic investigations identified fresh basil, used in pesto, salad dressings and garnishes, as the common exposure across multiple clusters, and traceback linked the basil to a single farm in Peru that supplied a wide network of Florida restaurant distributors. The outbreak was controlled after implicated basil shipments were no longer in distribution and U.S. and Peruvian authorities implemented enhanced field sanitation and export controls, with cyclosporiasis incidence in Florida returning to its usual seasonal baseline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-volume importation of fresh basil from Cyclospora-endemic Peru for use as a raw ingredient in salads, sauces and garnishes; use of contaminated irrigation and wash water on source farms; difficulty removing oocysts from delicate leafy herbs by routine washing; and widespread distribution of a single contaminated commodity through restaurant supply chains. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the outbreak reflects extensive environmental contamination of basil rather than intrinsic biological change. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a previously affected North American subregion driven by food-safety and agricultural practices in a South American source region, with enhanced effective transmission through a widely used raw herb.
Review: retain: Added this previously omitted 2005 Florida basil outbreak, which involved roughly 600 cases and is clearly among the ten most impactful post-1990 events for Cyclospora. Countries and subregions were set to reflect Florida as the main exposure location and a single Peruvian farm as the basil source. Classified as re_occurrence because Cyclospora had been recognized in North America for a decade and no parasite change was documented; the impact is due to a new high-volume herb vehicle rather than first emergence.

Countries: Sweden [2009]; Guatemala [2009, as probable source of imported sugar snap peas]
Host: Humans (Stockholm County residents consuming ready-to-eat salads containing imported sugar snap peas)
Event summary: During May–June 2009, Stockholm County, Sweden, detected an outbreak of cyclosporiasis with 12 laboratory-confirmed and six probable cases among persons without recent travel to endemic countries, representing the first reported outbreak in Sweden and only the second documented foodborne outbreak of cyclosporiasis in Europe. A case–control investigation implicated consumption of a ready-to-eat salad containing imported sugar snap peas, and traceback identified Guatemalan-grown peas as the likely common source. The outbreak waned once the implicated product was no longer on the market, and no sustained onward transmission in Sweden was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing European imports of fresh sugar snap peas from Cyclospora-endemic Guatemala; minimal processing and frequent consumption of peas in raw or lightly cooked form; routine produce surveillance that did not include Cyclospora; and very low baseline awareness of this parasite among Scandinavian clinicians and laboratories. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel lineages or enhanced virulence; the event is best explained by contamination of peas in Guatemalan production or packing environments. Mechanism categories: Intra-continental emergence within Europe, as cyclosporiasis extended from previously affected Western European areas into Northern Europe, driven by globalized fresh-produce trade and environmental contamination in the source region.
Review: retain: Corrected this row to specify sugar snap peas imported from Guatemala as the most likely vehicle, added Guatemala as a source country, and clarified that this was the first outbreak reported in Sweden and the second in Europe. Classification as intra_continental_emergence (spread to a new European subregion following earlier emergence in Germany) is appropriate. Event size is modest but it is important for documenting European spread, so it should be retained.

Countries: United States of America [2013]; Mexico [2013, as origin of implicated salad mix and cilantro]
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons and consumers of bagged salad mix and cilantro across many U.S. states)
Event summary: Between June and August 2013, the United States experienced an unusually large cyclosporiasis season, with 631 laboratory-confirmed cases reported from at least 25 states, greatly exceeding recent annual totals. Epidemiologic investigations identified at least two major, independent foodborne outbreaks within this season: a multistate cluster in Iowa, Nebraska and neighboring states linked to a prepackaged salad mix containing romaine lettuce and other vegetables imported from Mexico, and a series of clusters in Texas and nearby states linked to fresh cilantro from Mexico served at multiple Mexican-style restaurants. After implicated lots of salad mix and cilantro were withdrawn from commerce and the growing season ended, case counts declined toward baseline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-volume importation and centralized processing of fresh salad mixes and herbs from Cyclospora-endemic regions of Mexico; distribution of these ingredients through national restaurant and institutional food-service chains; and improved national surveillance and analytic capacity that allowed linkage of sporadic cases across jurisdictions into coherent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No convincing evidence of new strains or increased virulence; the high case numbers reflect repeated contamination events in produce supply chains rather than parasite evolution. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a previously affected North American subregion, with enhanced effective transmission via ready-to-eat salads and cilantro distributed widely through industrial food networks.
Review: retain: Minor corrections were made to explicitly list Mexico as the produce source country and to align sub-region coding with the Country sheet (Northern America and Central America). Classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate because large, imported-produce–linked outbreaks had already occurred in North America in the 1990s and early 2000s. This event is one of the highest-burden seasons and anchors the modern era of large U.S. Cyclospora outbreaks, so it should be retained.

Countries: United States of America [2014]; Mexico (Puebla state) [2014, as source of implicated cilantro]
Host: Humans (primarily restaurant patrons consuming dishes containing fresh cilantro)
Event summary: In the summer of 2014, U.S. surveillance identified another large cyclosporiasis season, with approximately 304 reported cases from at least 19 states, most of them in Texas. Multiple restaurant-associated clusters were investigated in which fresh cilantro served in salsa and other dishes was the only exposure strongly associated with illness, and traceback by state and federal investigators pointed to cilantro grown in the Mexican state of Puebla as the common source for a multistate outbreak involving about 60 cases. For many additional 2014 cases, a specific vehicle was not confirmed, but illness onsets clustered in late spring and summer and case counts returned toward baseline as the implicated cilantro and other seasonal produce left the market.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued heavy importation of fresh cilantro from Puebla, Mexico, where repeated environmental and hygiene deficiencies at farms and packing facilities were documented; the use of surface and irrigation water vulnerable to human fecal contamination; difficulty washing Cyclospora oocysts from delicate herb surfaces; and increasing year-round use of cilantro in restaurant cuisine. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for new parasite lineages or enhanced virulence; the increased incidence reflects recurrent contamination of cilantro and potentially other produce items. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a known North American subregion driven by persistent weaknesses in herb production and regulatory oversight in the exporting region.
Review: retain: This new row fills a clear gap by capturing the sizeable 2014 U.S. cyclosporiasis season (≈300 cases) and the documented multistate outbreak tied to cilantro from Puebla, Mexico. It is classified as re_occurrence, in line with similar cilantro-associated events in 2013 and 2015. Numbers and vehicles are based on CDC surveillance summaries, state investigations and regulatory reports; precise counts by state may warrant further fine-tuning, but the event is clearly among the top ten in impact and should be retained.

Countries: United States of America [2015]; Mexico (Puebla state) [2015, as origin of implicated cilantro]
Host: Humans (consumers of restaurant meals and other foods containing fresh cilantro across multiple U.S. states)
Event summary: In 2015, U.S. health departments reported 644 cyclosporiasis cases from 32 states and New York City, of which about 394 were domestically acquired and most had onset between May and August. Among these, a 61-case multistate outbreak involving patrons of unrelated Mexican-style restaurants in Texas, Georgia and Wisconsin was epidemiologically linked to fresh cilantro imported from the Mexican state of Puebla, and additional clusters in Texas were also associated with cilantro from the same production region. Although many domestically acquired cases had no single confirmed vehicle, overall case numbers again substantially exceeded pre-2013 baselines and declined only after targeted import alerts, field-level interventions in Puebla, and the end of the cilantro growing season.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing importation of fresh cilantro from Puebla, Mexico, where inspections repeatedly uncovered poor sanitation, human fecal contamination risks, and inadequate worker hygiene; widespread use of cilantro as a raw garnish and salsa ingredient; and improvements in surveillance and clinician awareness that increased recognition of cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a new Cyclospora strain or increased virulence; the pattern is consistent with recurrent environmental contamination of cilantro fields and rinsing water. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in the same North American subregion, driven by persistent supply-chain and agricultural issues in a specific exporting region and enhanced exposure through high-frequency cilantro use in restaurant dishes.
Review: retain: This row already captured the key features of the 2015 U.S. season, but I adjusted the narrative to align with CDC-reported totals (~644 cases, 394 domestically acquired) and emphasized the 61-case multistate outbreak associated with cilantro from Puebla, Mexico. Classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate, and the event is one of the largest cilantro-linked seasons. Wikipedia is kept only as a secondary synthesis source alongside primary CDC MMWR reports; the event should be retained.

Host: Humans (consumers of pre-packaged vegetable trays, fast-food chain salads and other fresh produce)
Event summary: During May–August 2018, U.S. public health authorities recorded 2,299 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases without recent international travel, the largest annual number since cyclosporiasis became nationally notifiable. Within this season, two major multistate foodborne outbreaks were identified: one linked to Del Monte pre-packaged vegetable trays containing raw broccoli, cauliflower, carrots and dip sold at convenience stores in the Upper Midwest, and another associated with salads (containing romaine lettuce, carrots and other leafy greens) sold at a large fast-food chain across multiple Midwestern states. These two outbreaks together accounted for several hundred illnesses, while many additional cases represented smaller clusters or sporadic infections linked to other fresh produce. Recalls of Del Monte vegetable trays and the fast-food chain’s salad products, combined with seasonal changes in produce sourcing, were followed by a decline in case reports to baseline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralized processing and wide distribution of ready-to-eat vegetable trays and pre-assembled salads from a small number of large facilities; challenges in maintaining hygienic conditions and effective produce washing that can remove or inactivate hardy Cyclospora oocysts in high-throughput environments; and heightened surveillance and diagnostic testing that improved outbreak recognition. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for novel parasite genotypes or enhanced virulence; the surge in cases is best explained by repeated contamination events affecting multiple types of produce. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence driven by industrial food-processing and distribution practices, with enhanced effective transmission through complex, widely distributed salad and snack products that obscure the specific contaminated ingredient.
Review: retain: This row accurately characterizes the very large 2018 U.S. season and the two main multistate outbreaks linked to Del Monte vegetable trays and Fresh Express salad mix supplied to a fast-food chain. I only clarified that many of the 2,299 cases were not directly tied to these two vehicles. The emergence-type classification as re_occurrence is appropriate, and the event clearly ranks among the most impactful and should be retained.

Countries: United States of America [2019]; Mexico [2019, as origin of basil implicated in a multistate outbreak]
Host: Humans (people in multiple U.S. states consuming fresh basil and other salads or herbs)
Event summary: In 2019, the United States again experienced a high-burden cyclosporiasis season, with 1,696 laboratory-confirmed non-travel-associated cases reported by late August from 33 states, the District of Columbia and New York City. Within this broader seasonal increase, a 132-case multistate outbreak affecting 11 states was traced to fresh basil imported from Mexico and served at several restaurants, while numerous additional clusters were associated with salads and other fresh produce but lacked a single confirmed vehicle. Although total case numbers did not surpass the 2018 peak, the 2019 season reinforced the pattern of recurrent large summertime waves driven by contamination of imported leafy greens and herbs. Illness incidence declined as the implicated basil and other suspect produce left the market and targeted advisories and inspections were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued reliance on imported herbs and leafy greens from Cyclospora-endemic regions, particularly basil from Mexico; complex distribution chains that disseminated contaminated basil to restaurants and retailers in many states; and improvements in diagnostic testing and surveillance that increased detection and linkage of cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for substantial genetic or phenotypic change in the parasite; increased incidence is attributable to environmental contamination of basil and other produce items. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a known North American subregion driven by globalized fresh-produce trade and seasonal environmental suitability in source regions, with enhanced effective transmission via widely distributed basil and mixed salads.
Review: retain: Added this new row to capture the large 2019 U.S. cyclosporiasis season (~1,700 domestically acquired cases) and the 132-case multistate outbreak linked to basil imported from Mexico. Treated as re_occurrence within the established pattern of large summertime waves; vehicles and case counts are drawn from CDC surveillance updates and recent reviews. Although many 2019 cases had no single confirmed vehicle, the scale and documented basil-linked outbreak justify inclusion among the top ten events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (consumers of Fresh Express bagged salad mixes and other fresh produce in the United States and Canada)
Event summary: From May through September 2020, a major North American cyclosporiasis episode occurred in the context of substantial seasonal case numbers. In the United States, at least 641 laboratory-confirmed illnesses and 37 hospitalizations in multiple Midwestern and neighboring states were linked to bagged garden salad mixes containing iceberg lettuce, red cabbage and carrots produced by Fresh Express at a facility in Illinois and sold under several brand names at large retail chains. Environmental sampling detected Cyclospora in an irrigation canal near a farm suspected of supplying red cabbage for the mixes. Canada concurrently reported 370 confirmed cyclosporiasis cases across six provinces and territories; some of these illnesses were associated with recalled Fresh Express salads, while others were linked to fresh herbs such as cilantro and parsley or had no identified vehicle. Extensive recalls of Fresh Express salad products, adjustments in sourcing and processing, and the close of the growing season were followed by a decline in new case reports.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralized production and interstate/international distribution of bagged salad mixes from a single processing facility serving both U.S. and Canadian markets; contamination of surface or irrigation water used on leafy greens; the resilience of Cyclospora oocysts to standard produce washing and processing steps; and seasonal climatic conditions favorable to parasite survival and sporulation in source fields. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence for novel parasite strains or increased virulence; outbreak dynamics primarily reflect contamination of salad ingredients and agricultural water. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence driven by environmental contamination and industrial-scale processing and distribution, with enhanced effective transmission through widely distributed bagged salads that combined ingredients from multiple fields and farms.
Review: retain: This row correctly represents the 2020 North American episode linked to Fresh Express bagged salads and contemporaneous Canadian cases. I clarified that Canadian illnesses comprised both salad-associated and herb-associated cases and limited the geography to Northern America (United States and Canada). Classification as re_occurrence is appropriate because similar large produce-associated outbreaks had occurred repeatedly in the preceding decade. Given its substantial binational case burden and strong documentation, this event should be retained.

Host: Humans (primarily adults with amoebic liver abscess and intestinal amebiasis in Tbilisi)
Event summary: Between late May and early September 1998, Tbilisi, Republic of Georgia, experienced a large outbreak of amebiasis, with 177 suspected cases (71 intestinal amebiasis, 106 probable liver abscess) identified and a case–control study confirming a strong association with municipal tap‑water consumption, implicating inadequate treatment or post‑treatment contamination of the city supply. Follow‑up investigations by international and national public health agencies documented numerous breakdowns in the water and sewer systems, and water‑treatment deficiencies, and control efforts focused on improving water treatment, repairing distribution infrastructure, and strengthening surveillance; reported incidence declined after 1999 but highlighted systemic vulnerabilities in urban water systems during the post‑Soviet transition period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ageing and poorly maintained municipal water infrastructure, frequent breaks and cross‑connections between drinking‑water and sewage lines, and inadequate filtration/chlorination allowed fecal contamination of the Tbilisi municipal supply, leading to high‑dose exposure to E. histolytica cysts in a large urban population. Socioeconomic disruption during the post‑Soviet transition likely reduced investment in maintenance and monitoring. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance phenotype was demonstrated; invasive disease (including liver abscess) matched known E. histolytica pathogenesis, so the event is best explained by increased exposure due to infrastructure failure rather than parasite evolution.
Review: retain – Event confirmed as the well‑documented 1998 Tbilisi waterborne amebiasis outbreak with 177 suspected cases; geography (Asia/Western Asia; Georgia) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. Summary was slightly tightened to use the documented case count rather than speculative ranges, but no structural corrections were needed.

Host: Humans (schoolchildren and some staff at a private school in Taichung City)
Event summary: In August–September 1993, a major outbreak of acute gastroenteritis struck a private school in Taichung City, Taiwan, sickening about 730 students; stool testing identified both Shigella sonnei and Entamoeba histolytica among cases, and environmental investigations traced the source to underground well water heavily contaminated by sewage from a nearby toilet due to defects in the 20‑year‑old water system. Teachers, who drank only city water, were spared, and the outbreak ended after closure of the contaminated well, repair of the water system, and a switch to safe municipal water, illustrating the potential for large mixed‑etiology protozoal and bacterial outbreaks from point‑source contamination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of an inadequately protected underground well as the school’s drinking‑water source, with cross‑contamination from a nearby toilet and structural failures in the well lining and overflow piping, allowed fecal contamination of the well and high‑dose exposure to enteric pathogens including E. histolytica. Limited treatment and lack of routine inspection of on‑site wells in institutional settings contributed. Internal mechanisms: No change in parasite genotype or virulence was reported; this is a classic fecal–oral, waterborne exposure scenario involving a known pathogen.
Review: review – The outbreak is real and well documented, but the original AI entry incorrectly used 2001 (publication year) instead of 1993 (outbreak year). Year and country annotation have been corrected to 1993, Taichung City, Taiwan (Eastern Asia). Classification as a large waterborne re-occurrence event is appropriate; a reviewer should confirm that including this mixed Shigella/E. histolytica outbreak among the top events is acceptable given its size (≈730 illnesses) and clear documentation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), many co-infected with HIV; some heterosexual adults and persons without travel to endemic areas
Event summary: From around 2000 through 2013, national surveillance and hospital series in Japan documented a marked rise in domestically acquired invasive amebiasis, shifting from a predominantly travel‑associated disease to a re‑emerging infection concentrated in large cities. Most new cases occurred in young to middle‑aged men, especially MSM and people living with HIV, with amebic colitis and liver abscess as common severe manifestations and no history of recent travel to highly endemic countries. Intensified awareness among clinicians, improved diagnostics (including serology and antigen tests), and targeted screening in HIV and STI clinics improved case ascertainment, but incidence in urban MSM networks remained elevated throughout the period, indicating sustained local sexual transmission rather than isolated importations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density urban MSM sexual networks with frequent oral–anal practices, a growing population of HIV‑infected men under care, and enhanced diagnostic testing (antigen assays, PCR, serology) led to both increased transmission and better detection of E. histolytica in Japan. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies show strain diversity but have not identified a single novel genotype or clear virulence shift responsible for the trend; the pattern is best characterized as behavioral and healthcare‑driven re-occurrence of a known pathogen in a low‑endemic country rather than re-emergence via parasite evolution.
Review: review – Event (multi‑year increase in domestically acquired invasive amebiasis in Japan, mainly in MSM with and without HIV) is well supported by surveillance and case‑series data. However, the original classification as “re-emergence” has been changed to “re-occurrence” because available evidence indicates a behavioral/diagnostic driver without clear demonstration of a new strain or host species, consistent with the project’s definitions. Sources were trimmed to peer‑reviewed articles and a global MSM review; a domain expert should confirm this reclassification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, exclusively men who have sex with men (MSM) with invasive intestinal amebiasis
Event summary: In October 2016 and again in January 2017, clinicians at an STI/HIV referral clinic in Barcelona, Spain, identified two short clusters (four cases each) of MSM presenting with proctocolitis due to invasive E. histolytica, none with recent travel to classic endemic areas. Epidemiologic interviews revealed high rates of oral–anal sex, multiple partners, sex‑party attendance, and sexual contacts linked to Latin America and the United Kingdom, suggesting introduction of pathogenic strains via international sexual networks followed by local transmission within Barcelona’s MSM community. All patients recovered after appropriate anti‑amoebic therapy; public health alerts to STI and HIV services increased awareness, and no large sustained outbreak followed, although sporadic MSM cases continued to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense MSM sexual networks in a major European city, frequent oral–anal practices, and globalized sexual contacts (including partners from endemic Latin American settings and other European hubs) enabled introduction and short‑range sexual transmission of E. histolytica in a population where waterborne exposure is rare. Limited prior clinical suspicion of amebiasis as an STI in Europe delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: No new genotype was defined; the clusters likely involved pathogenic zymodemes similar to those circulating in Asia‑Pacific MSM networks, and the episode is best viewed as re-occurrence of a known pathogen in a new behavioral niche rather than re-emergence through parasite change.
Review: review – Barcelona’s 2016–2017 MSM clusters are accurately summarized and documented by Eurosurveillance. Event type has been adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence, as there is no evidence of a novel parasite strain; this is a behavioral/sexual‑network driven outbreak in a non‑endemic, but previously exposed, subregion. Given the small case count (8), a reviewer should confirm that including this as one of the top events is justified on the basis of being Europe’s first clearly described MSM outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans, predominantly HIV-1–infected men who have sex with men (MSM), but also other adults living with HIV or with high‑risk sexual behavior
Event summary: In Taiwan, invasive amebiasis emerged as a significant opportunistic infection in people living with HIV from the mid‑1990s onward. A 9‑year retrospective review at a major referral hospital (1994–2003) identified 51 episodes of invasive amebiasis among 49 HIV‑infected patients, with markedly higher seroprevalence and intestinal colonization by E. histolytica among HIV‑positive MSM compared with HIV‑negative controls. Subsequent national analyses for 2006–2013 showed that a growing proportion of male amebiasis cases were diagnosed around the time of HIV infection and that sexual transmission (particularly male–male sex with oral–anal contact) had become a dominant route of acquisition. This multi‑year trend represents a re‑occurring, sexually transmitted niche for E. histolytica in a relatively low‑endemic, high‑income setting, with continued incident cases reported into the 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of HIV epidemics in MSM, high‑risk sexual behaviors including oral–anal sex, dense urban sexual networks, and improved access to HIV care and diagnostics together facilitated recognition and onward sexual transmission of E. histolytica. Increased use of serology and antigen/PCR tests in HIV clinics raised detection of both invasive disease and asymptomatic carriage. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence for a novel strain or drug resistance; risk appeared driven by host factors (HIV‑related immunity, sexual network structure) and exposure rather than intrinsic parasite evolution, supporting classification as re-occurrence.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well‑documented emergence of invasive and sexually transmitted amebiasis among HIV-infected MSM in Taiwan, which is consistently highlighted in the literature as a major focus of post‑1990 E. histolytica re-occurrence. Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because drivers are behavioral and host‑related, with no clear parasite genotype shift. A reviewer should confirm time bounds (1994–2013) are appropriate for representing this multi‑year episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans, exclusively men who have sex with men (MSM), most living with HIV, with invasive colitis and liver abscess
Event summary: Between December 2006 and October 2007, clinicians at a tertiary hospital in Sydney, Australia, reported five cases of invasive amebiasis (three amebic colitis, two liver abscesses) in MSM, four of whom were HIV‑infected, with minimal or no recent travel to highly endemic regions. These cases, together with earlier locally acquired infections and high background carriage of Entamoeba spp. in MSM, provided evidence that E. histolytica had established sexual transmission networks in Australian MSM, representing a shift from imported to autochthonous invasive disease in an otherwise low‑endemic country. All patients recovered with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent, but delays in diagnosis and severe complications in some cases highlighted limited awareness among clinicians.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑risk sexual behaviors in MSM (including oral–anal sex and sex‑on‑premises venues), intersecting HIV and STI epidemics, and under‑recognition of amebiasis as a sexually transmissible infection created conditions for local establishment and spread of E. histolytica in Sydney MSM. Internal mechanisms: No unique genotype or resistance pattern was identified; infections corresponded to typical invasive E. histolytica, again supporting classification as re-occurrence due to social/behavioral drivers.
Review: review – New event added to reflect the first clearly documented locally acquired invasive amebiasis in MSM in Australia (Sydney, 2006–2007), which is repeatedly cited as evidence that sexually transmitted E. histolytica has become established in MSM networks in several Asia–Pacific countries. Classified as re-occurrence; magnitude (small case series) is modest but important in the context of limited post‑1990 discrete outbreaks for this pathogen. A reviewer should confirm its inclusion among the top events.
