Host: Humans (secondary school students at Upper Hill School, Nairobi)
Event summary: In early March 2023, a large cluster of acute gastrointestinal illness occurred among students at Upper Hill School, a boys’ secondary school in Nairobi, Kenya, with around 90–100 students developing stomach pain, diarrhea and vomiting after eating rice, beans and beef in the school. Initial concern focused on cholera, but county health officials reported that rapid cholera tests were negative and that affected students instead tested positive for amoebiasis, with about 16–20 hospitalised at several facilities and the remainder treated and discharged. Public health teams collected water and food samples to investigate contamination of the school’s water supply or kitchen, and the outbreak subsided after supportive treatment and control measures; the episode occurred against a backdrop of water scarcity and broader cholera activity in Nairobi.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Acute water shortage and reliance on potentially unsafe sources, combined with inadequate food and water hygiene in a crowded boarding‑school environment, likely enabled fecal contamination of drinking water or food with E. histolytica cysts. Broader infrastructure challenges in Nairobi (drying boreholes, intermittent municipal supply) and concurrent enteric disease activity increased vulnerability to such outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No data indicate a new strain or resistance; this is a typical water/food‑borne re-occurrence of invasive amebiasis in a high‑burden region.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 2023 amoebiasis outbreak at Upper Hill School in Nairobi, where close to 100 students were reportedly affected and cholera was ruled out in favour of amoebiasis. While laboratory methods and species‑level confirmation are not fully detailed in media reports, the scale and clear attribution justify inclusion as a major recent re-occurrence event in Eastern Africa; a reviewer should confirm species assignment and any subsequent official investigation reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (adult women and men; predominantly women attending STI/vaginitis clinics)
Event summary: During the 1990s, clinicians in the United States and Canada increasingly reported sporadic cases of vaginal trichomoniasis that failed standard single- or short-course oral metronidazole therapy, and laboratory testing of isolates from many U.S. states and Canadian sites confirmed reduced susceptibility or resistance to metronidazole.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/153/5/948/927091?utm_source=openai)) Building on earlier case series from the mid‑1980s, research through the decade—including a 1999 New England Journal of Medicine report—characterized metronidazole‑resistant vaginal trichomoniasis as an emerging therapeutic problem rather than an isolated curiosity.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199907223410417?utm_source=openai)) By the end of the 1990s, high‑dose or prolonged nitroimidazole regimens, tinidazole, and topical agents were being used for a small but clinically important subset of women with persistent infection, and expert reviews began to frame nitroimidazole‑resistant T. vaginalis as a re‑emerging treatment challenge in Northern America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of single-dose or short-course metronidazole for trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis created strong selection pressure; incomplete partner treatment and reinfection also contributed to persistent infections that were heavily exposed to nitroimidazoles. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – clinical and in vitro metronidazole resistance associated with altered parasite redox metabolism and reduced drug activation (nitroimidazole resistance); molecular studies show diverse resistant genotypes, suggesting multiple evolutionary events rather than a single clone.
Review: review – Event concept (emergence and recognition of nitroimidazole-resistant T. vaginalis in Northern America) is well supported by case series and expert reviews and should be retained as one of the key high‑impact episodes. The event summary was revised to (a) describe resistance cases as rare but increasingly recognized, rather than implying large clustered outbreaks, and (b) attribute framing of resistance as an emerging problem mainly to clinical experts and literature (e.g. JID 1986 series and the 1999 NEJM report) rather than formal public-health authorities. No changes were made to geography, timing, or emergence-type classification (re‑emergence due to antimicrobial resistance).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: Uganda [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Kenya [1990]; Zimbabwe [1990]; South Africa [1990]; Malawi [1990]; Zambia [1990]; Nigeria [1990]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [1990]
Host: Humans (sexually active women and men in the general population and high‑risk groups)
Event summary: From 1990 through roughly 2010, trichomoniasis remained highly prevalent across many parts of sub-Saharan Africa, with community- and clinic-based studies in Rakai District (Uganda), Zimbabwe, South Africa, Malawi, Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of the Congo typically finding T. vaginalis infection in roughly one quarter to one third of sexually active women, and even higher levels in some high‑risk groups.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10195051/?utm_source=openai)) As large generalized heterosexual HIV epidemics expanded during the 1990s and early 2000s, longitudinal and case–control studies in Uganda, Zimbabwe, South Africa and other settings showed that T. vaginalis infection approximately doubled the risk of HIV acquisition in women, magnifying the public health impact of this otherwise often-neglected STI.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18275275/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2000s, intensified HIV prevention and STI control programs in several African countries were incorporating syndromic management and, in some programs, specific screening for trichomoniasis, yet the parasite remained endemic at high levels in many subregions and continued to act as an important cofactor in HIV transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Explosive heterosexual HIV epidemics with overlapping sexual networks; limited access to quality STI diagnosis and treatment; high background prevalence of other STIs; gender and socioeconomic factors constraining women’s ability to negotiate condom use; and health‑system weaknesses in laboratory capacity, surveillance, and routine screening. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance mechanism is clearly linked to this pattern; the episode represents sustained high transmission in widely infected sexual networks rather than biologically distinct re‑emergent variants. The main mechanistic role is that existing T. vaginalis infections increase genital inflammation and susceptibility to HIV, thereby amplifying HIV transmission.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the very high burden of trichomoniasis and its role as an HIV cofactor across sub-Saharan Africa and should be retained as one of the main high‑impact episodes. However, several corrections were made: (a) the statement that prevalence reached “up to half of women” in Rakai, Uganda, was inaccurate (Rakai surveys report ~24–31% T. vaginalis in women, with ~50% referring to bacterial vaginosis) and has been revised to describe more realistic ranges based on population-based and clinic-based studies; (b) the country list was expanded to include explicit examples from Eastern, Southern, Western, and Middle Africa (Malawi, Zambia, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of the Congo) consistent with published prevalence data; and (c) the emergence-type flag re_occurrence was changed from Yes to No, because available evidence indicates long-standing high prevalence rather than a clearly documented post‑1990 resurgence in incidence. The episode is now treated as a chronic high-burden pattern without a specific emergence-type label and is flagged for expert review of the chosen representation.

Host: Humans (women attending STD clinics in multiple U.S. cities)
Event summary: In 2009–2010, the U.S. CDC Sexually Transmitted Disease Surveillance Network conducted the first multisite evaluation of nitroimidazole susceptibility in T. vaginalis isolates from women in six U.S. cities, documenting clinically relevant metronidazole resistance and low-level tinidazole resistance across geographically diverse locations.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/22726?utm_source=openai)) Thousands of women with trichomoniasis were enrolled and a subset of isolates were tested, revealing metronidazole resistance in a measurable minority of samples and confirming that resistant parasites were no longer just sporadic case reports but a distributed problem in the national STD clinic population. In the years that followed, CDC developed reference susceptibility testing services and incorporated guidance on managing nitroimidazole-resistant T. vaginalis into national STI treatment guidelines,([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/hcp/laboratories/trichomonas-vaginalis-susceptibility-testing.html?utm_source=openai)) marking a shift from isolated case management to systematic recognition of resistance as a re‑emerging therapeutic threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive, long-term use of a single class of nitroimidazole therapy (metronidazole and tinidazole) for trichomoniasis and related infections; suboptimal partner treatment and reinfection, leading to repeated exposure of the same parasite populations to drug pressure; and limited routine resistance surveillance prior to 2009 that allowed resistant strains to circulate largely undetected. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – stable low- and high-level resistance to metronidazole, and rarer resistance to tinidazole, linked to alterations in hydrogenosomal and redox pathways that reduce activation of 5‑nitroimidazoles; these mechanisms represent biological re‑emergence through treatment failure and geographic dissemination of resistant genotypes.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the first systematic U.S. multisite surveillance of nitroimidazole resistance in T. vaginalis, with correct timing (2009–2010), geography (STD clinics in multiple U.S. cities), emergence-type classification (re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance), and highly relevant CDC/EID and guideline sources. No changes were made to the original event fields; it is appropriate to keep this as a major resistance-related emergence episode.

Sub-regions: Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Northern Africa
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo [1990]; Angola [1990]; Central African Republic [1990]; Sudan [1990]; South Sudan [1990]; Uganda [1990]
Host: Humans (primarily rural populations exposed to tsetse flies in Central Africa and Upper Nile regions)
Event summary: During the 1990s, gambiense human African trypanosomiasis resurged dramatically in conflict‑affected parts of Central Africa, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) at the epicentre and substantial transmission in Angola, Central African Republic and (South) Sudan, plus foci in northern Uganda.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3310607/?utm_source=openai))  Reported global HAT cases peaked at around 40,000 in 1998, two‑thirds of them in DRC (26,318 detected cases that year), before intensified screening and treatment campaigns from 2000 onwards began to reverse the trend.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3310607/?utm_source=openai))  Between about 2000 and 2003, large‑scale mobile screening and renewed investment in national control programmes reduced DRC’s detected HAT cases from ~26,000 to ~11,000 per year and initiated a sustained continental decline in gambiense HAT incidence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged civil wars and political instability in DRC, Angola and southern Sudan in the 1980s–1990s disrupted health systems, halted vector control and active screening, and displaced populations into highly tsetse‑infested areas, allowing intense transmission and late presentation with advanced disease.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3375795/?utm_source=openai))  Funding shortages and the collapse or decentralization of dedicated HAT programmes further reduced case detection until new public–private and WHO partnerships restored drug supply and control operations in the early 2000s.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-TRS-881?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points to resurgence driven mainly by increased human–vector contact and programmatic failure rather than emergence of novel, more virulent T. brucei gambiense strains (no consistent genotype shift has been linked to the 1990s epidemic).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4130665/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the major 1990s resurgence of gambiense HAT centred on DRC, Angola, CAR and (South) Sudan, with appropriate timing (1990–2003), countries and sub‑regions under the UNSD scheme, and correct classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence in long‑endemic foci without spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region). The magnitude and drivers (conflict‑related collapse of control and renewed screening reducing cases after 1998) align with WHO and EID data, so no structural changes to geography, timing or emergence type are recommended; only minor source consolidation has been done at the profile level.

Host: Humans (acute T. brucei rhodesiense sleeping sickness in rural communities); cattle (major reservoir influencing human risk)
Event summary: In late 1998, a new focus of acute human African trypanosomiasis due to Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense was detected in Soroti District in eastern/central Uganda, north of the traditional Busoga focus, in an area previously considered essentially free of this form of sleeping sickness.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673601057786?utm_source=openai))  Over the following years, cases spread into neighbouring Kaberamaido and the southern edge of Lira District, with more than 400–428 human cases reported between 1998 and 2004 and additional unreported cases inferred, making this one of the largest recent rHAT outbreaks in East Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3828156/?utm_source=openai))  Intensive interventions in the early–mid 2000s, including mass treatment of cattle reservoirs and localized tsetse control under the Stamp Out Sleeping Sickness (SOS) campaign, substantially reduced rHAT incidence in these newly affected districts by around 2005, although low‑level risk persisted and surveillance remains necessary.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑conflict restocking schemes and unregulated cattle trade moved T. b. rhodesiense–infected cattle from endemic southeastern Uganda into Soroti, Kaberamaido and Lira, all lying within the tsetse belt but previously free of human rHAT; high infection prevalence in market cattle seeded the new focus and drove its northward expansion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3851531/?utm_source=openai))  Weak veterinary services and limited clinical awareness in the newly affected districts led to delayed recognition of cases, with most patients presenting in late stage, and initial vector‑control measures were insufficient to prevent spread beyond Soroti.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1289320/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence indicates a novel parasite strain; molecular analyses suggest a genetically homogeneous population consistent with a founder effect from the existing Tororo/Busoga focus, so this episode reflects geographic range expansion within Eastern Africa driven by livestock movements rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3828156/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The Soroti–Kaberamaido–Lira rHAT focus is a well‑documented, high‑impact emergence within Uganda, and the time span (1998–2005) and country assignment are appropriate. However, under the project definitions, this should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence because it occurs within an already endemic UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Africa); instead it represents a major resurgence and geographic spread inside that sub‑region. The emergence type has therefore been corrected from intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence to re‑occurrence only, reflecting strong external drivers (post‑conflict cattle restocking and weak surveillance) and lack of evidence for parasite change. Users should review and confirm this reclassification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999]; Spain [2005]; France [2009]; Sweden [2009]; Switzerland [2012]; Belgium [2013]; Italy [2000s]; Portugal [2000s]; Germany [2000s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2000s]
Host: Humans (Latin American migrants with chronic T. cruzi infection; European recipients of blood, organs or vertically transmitted infection)
Event summary: From the late 1990s onward, Europe experienced a marked emergence of Chagas disease as millions of migrants from endemic Latin American countries settled primarily in Spain, Italy, France, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Portugal, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands, bringing an estimated 68,000–122,000 chronic T. cruzi infections by 2009.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21944556/?utm_source=openai))  Initially, Chagas was almost entirely unrecognized and under‑diagnosed, but during 1999–2013, accumulating reports of transfusion‑, transplant‑ and congenitally acquired cases led several countries to implement systematic or targeted screening of at‑risk blood donors and, in some settings, pregnant women (UK 1999; Spain 2005; France and Sweden 2009; Switzerland 2012; Belgium 2013), while others introduced donor deferral policies.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0953620517301772?utm_source=openai))  By 2013, Chagas disease had become a recognized public‑health concern in parts of Southern and Western Europe, with thousands of diagnosed cases but a large, mostly undetected reservoir of chronic infection in migrant communities and ongoing non‑vector local transmission via blood, organ transplantation and vertical routes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensified economic migration from endemic Latin America to Southern and Western Europe since the 1990s created sizeable populations of chronically infected yet often asymptomatic migrants, many of reproductive age, in health systems unfamiliar with Chagas disease.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0953620517301772?utm_source=openai))  Modern transfusion and transplant networks, combined with the absence of routine T. cruzi screening in blood banks until 1999–2013, enabled in situ transmission to European recipients, and unrecognized infection in pregnant women led to congenital cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4214631/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a new parasite genotype adapted to Europe; instead, multiple Latin American strains were imported, and emergence is driven by host‑population movements and health‑system gaps rather than evolutionary change in T. cruzi.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10747626/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The described emergence of Chagas disease in Europe is real and highly impactful, with strong support for substantial chronic infection burdens and documented transfusion and congenital transmission in multiple countries. The time span 1999–2013 aligns with the roll‑out of blood‑donor screening and initial policy responses in the UK, Spain, France, Sweden, Switzerland and Belgium, and the sub‑region and country lists are appropriate. However, the original row incorrectly set both inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence to “Yes”. Under the project definitions, Europe represents a new continent for human T. cruzi transmission, so inter‑continental emergence should be “Yes”, but re‑emergence should be “No” because there was no prior established Chagas presence in this region. This classification has been corrected accordingly; users should review and confirm.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (acute orally acquired T. cruzi infection in family and school clusters); triatomine bugs and wild/peridomestic mammalian reservoirs contaminating food (e.g. opossums, other sylvatic mammals)
Event summary: Beginning around 2000, Brazil’s Amazon region and later parts of Venezuela and Colombia saw a sharp increase in outbreaks of acute Chagas disease transmitted orally through contaminated foods and beverages, especially unpasteurized açaí and other fruit juices. In Brazil, surveillance data indicate that from 2000 to 2010 more than 1,000 acute cases occurred in 138 outbreaks, about 71% attributed to orally transmitted epidemics, predominantly in northern states such as Pará and Amapá.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  In Venezuela, the first large recognized urban food‑borne outbreak occurred at a school in Caracas in 2007, infecting 103 of roughly 1,000 exposed children and adults, followed by additional school and family clusters (e.g. Chichiriviche de la Costa in 2009), with at least 249 oral‑transmission cases reported nationally by 2015.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=6b81f946d6362f3da7750b2bf9b0f78c4159d5b5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))  Colombia documented dozens of family‑type oral outbreaks over this period—64 outbreaks and 302 affected individuals by 2023, with a case‑fatality rate around 11% and notable events such as the 2014 Paz de Ariporo outbreak with 41 cases—making oral transmission a major cause of acute Chagas disease in the Orinoco and Andean regions as well.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11262278/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of regional and extra‑regional demand for açaí and other fresh juices led to expanded harvesting and artisanal processing in sylvatic or peri‑urban settings where infected triatomines and marsupials (e.g. Didelphis spp.) are common, often without adequate washing, pasteurization or vector exclusion, facilitating contamination of juice and pulp with infected insects or their feces.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  Seasonal peaks in fruit harvest (e.g. November–January for açaí) coincide with warmer, wetter conditions that enhance triatomine activity and allow T. cruzi to remain viable for hours to days in moist foods, promoting micro‑epidemics with high attack rates among households, schoolchildren and workers sharing contaminated drinks.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing shows that specific T. cruzi discrete typing units (notably TcI and TcIV) are repeatedly associated with oral outbreaks, but there is no single novel lineage; the key change is the epidemiologic route—large inocula delivered to the oral mucosa or gastrointestinal tract—which is linked to more severe myocarditis and higher acute mortality than typical vector‑borne infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9113729/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This new row has been added because large food‑borne outbreaks of acute Chagas disease in Brazil, Venezuela and Colombia since about 2000 clearly qualify among the most impactful post‑1990 events for human trypanosomiasis, with >1,000 Brazilian cases in 138 outbreaks between 2000–2010, at least 249 oral cases reported in Venezuela by 2015, and 64 documented outbreaks affecting 302 people in Colombia by 2023, many with high case‑fatality. These episodes occur within long‑endemic South American sub‑regions and reflect a dramatic resurgence and shift in transmission route rather than spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region, so they are classified as re‑occurrence only. The temporal window (2000–2015) and country list focus on the period and locations where outbreak incidence and impact were highest; users may wish to refine the end date or extend the episode forward if acute oral outbreaks continue at similar scale after 2015.

Host: Humans (locally infected individuals via vectors, congenital transmission or transfusion); triatomine bugs; wildlife and domestic animal reservoirs (e.g. woodrats, raccoons, armadillos, dogs)
Event summary: Although Trypanosoma cruzi has circulated in wildlife and vectors in the southern United States for centuries, the early 2000s marked a period of heightened recognition of locally acquired human Chagas disease, with clusters of autochthonous acute and chronic infections documented in states such as Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee, California, Arizona and Missouri.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614205/?utm_source=openai))  Systematic reviews and public‑health reports identified roughly 29–31 confirmed and 47–47+ suspected locally acquired human cases during 2000–2018 (i.e. ≈76–78 persons), alongside high infection prevalence in triatomine bugs and peridomestic animal reservoirs, suggesting ongoing but hypoendemic vector‑borne transmission.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001706X19313166?utm_source=openai))  Introduction of routine blood‑donor screening for T. cruzi antibodies in 2007 (with nationwide coverage by 2012), together with state‑level notifiable‑disease systems and targeted investigations of suspected autochthonous cases, reduced transfusion‑related risk and improved detection, but many infections in exposed US residents—both imported and locally acquired—likely remain undiagnosed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ecological interfaces where humans live, work or recreate in close proximity to infected wildlife and triatomine habitats—such as substandard rural housing, peridomestic dog kennels, outdoor sleeping, hunting and military training—create opportunities for sylvatic cycles of T. cruzi to spill over into humans in the southern USA.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7470559/?utm_source=openai))  Urban and peri‑urban expansion into wildlife habitat, along with climate and land‑use changes that may alter vector distributions and seasonal activity, further modulate risk, while greater clinical and public‑health awareness and the advent of blood‑donor screening have increased case ascertainment relative to the past.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614205/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing enzootic transmission in wildlife and domestic animals provides a reservoir for host expansion to humans, and some triatomine species (e.g. Triatoma sanguisuga, T. gerstaeckeri) show adaptation to peridomestic environments; however, no specific novel parasite lineage or clear shift in virulence has been linked to these human cases, so the pattern is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by ecological and surveillance changes rather than parasite evolution.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7470559/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The pattern of increased recognition of autochthonous Chagas disease in the southern United States from 2000–2018 is well supported by multiple systematic reviews and CDC reports, and the event appropriately highlights a new appreciation of endemic (though low‑level) T. cruzi transmission in North America. However, the original row set both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence to “Yes”. Given longstanding evidence of enzootic T. cruzi circulation in US wildlife and vectors and the absence of clear parasite change, this episode fits the definition of re‑occurrence driven by ecological and surveillance factors rather than re‑emergence due to genetic or phenotypic shifts in the parasite. The classification has therefore been corrected to re‑occurrence=Yes and re‑emergence=No; inter‑ and intra‑continental emergence remain “No” because neither a new continent nor a new UNSD sub‑region is involved.

Countries: Mexico [1990] (Mexicali Valley, Baja California; irrigation canal exposure)
Host: Humans (children and young adults swimming or working in irrigation canals)
Event summary: In 1990, Mexico documented its first recognized outbreak of primary amebic meningoencephalitis when five residents of the Mexicali Valley, Baja California, developed fulminant meningoencephalitis after recreational or occupational exposure to local irrigation canals, and Naegleria fowleri was isolated from both patients and canal water. The cluster followed earlier isolated Mexican PAM cases in the late 1970s and 1980s but was the first multi‑case event clearly linked to recreational use of irrigation infrastructure in this hot desert environment. After the outbreak, health authorities issued warnings against swimming in canals and initiated environmental surveillance in the Mexicali region, and subsequent Mexican PAM reports have been sporadic rather than outbreak‑like.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high summer air temperatures in the Mexicali desert region; widespread informal recreational use of warm, slow‑moving irrigation canals that lack disinfection; limited public awareness of free‑living amoeba risks; and scarce early diagnostic capacity leading to delayed recognition of PAM. Internal mechanisms: Inherent thermotolerance and ecological flexibility of N. fowleri enabling persistence and proliferation in warm irrigation canals and other man‑made surface waters (Geographic range expansion – inherent into engineered canal networks), but no compelling evidence of a distinct, more virulent strain in this outbreak.
Review: retain (newly added major event; flag for review) – Added the 1990 Mexicali Valley, Mexico, irrigation‑canal outbreak (five PAM cases with N. fowleri isolated from patients and canal water) as one of the few documented multi‑case human episodes since 1990. Classified as re‑occurrence in the Central America subregion because N. fowleri and sporadic PAM cases were already reported in Latin America before 1990, and available sources do not demonstrate a novel strain or host jump. Evidence is drawn mainly from the Mexican Ministry of Health technical manual and Latin American reviews rather than a dedicated outbreak paper, so detailed epidemiologic parameters (exact case count, age distribution) should be re‑checked against primary Spanish‑language sources.

Countries: Guadeloupe [2008] (Dolé geothermal baths, French West Indies)
Host: Humans (9‑year‑old child bathing and diving in geothermal pool)
Event summary: In 2008, a previously healthy 9‑year‑old boy in Guadeloupe, French West Indies, developed rapidly fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis after swimming and diving in a popular geothermal bath at Dolé; laboratory testing confirmed Naegleria fowleri infection. The case represented both the first documented PAM case in Guadeloupe and the first recognized N. fowleri–associated death in the Caribbean subregion of the Americas, prompting concern about geothermal recreational waters as a new regional risk setting. Subsequent surveys of geothermal baths in Guadeloupe repeatedly detected N. fowleri and led to implementation of regular monitoring, risk communication, and engineering controls, after which no further large clusters were reported, though sporadic risk persists.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of untreated or minimally treated geothermal bath water for public recreation; naturally high water temperatures and organic load favoring Naegleria proliferation; limited historical awareness of PAM risk in Caribbean geothermal spas; and frequent head immersion and diving by children. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic thermophilic and environmental survival traits of N. fowleri enabling colonization of geothermal recreational waters (Geographic range expansion – inherent into a new climatic and hydrothermal niche in the Caribbean), without evidence that the Guadeloupe strain differed substantially in virulence from other global lineages.
Review: retain (newly added intra‑continental emergence; flag for review) – Added the 2008 fatal Guadeloupe case linked to the Dolé geothermal baths as the first documented PAM case in the Caribbean subregion and a clear intra‑continental emergence of N. fowleri from mainland Latin America into Caribbean island recreational waters. Event description and linkage to geothermal bathing are well supported by a detailed case report and subsequent environmental surveys. No correction to geography was needed, but classification was set to intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within South America), with the understanding that additional retrospective Caribbean cases, if uncovered, could alter this coding.

Host: Humans (all ages, predominantly young to middle‑aged adults)
Event summary: Beginning in 2008, Karachi, Pakistan, started to report recurrent summer clusters of primary amebic meningoencephalitis, with the first recognized case in a young adult man and subsequent series documenting dozens of confirmed and probable Naegleria fowleri infections over the following decade. Most patients had no history of freshwater recreation, and investigations increasingly implicated under‑chlorinated municipal and domestic water systems, with exposures occurring during bathing, showering, and ritual ablution rather than lake or river swimming. Despite intermittent chlorination campaigns, infrastructure upgrades, and public advisories, fatal cases continued to recur through the early 2020s, establishing Karachi as a persistent urban hotspot for PAM in Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High ambient summer temperatures and frequent heat waves warming municipal surface water sources and distribution systems; chronic under‑chlorination and aging, leaky pipe networks in Karachi’s water supply; heavy reliance on municipal water for domestic use and ritual nasal ablution; rapid urbanization and informal water storage practices that increase contact with warm, stagnant water. Internal mechanisms: Ecological plasticity and thermotolerance of N. fowleri enabling persistence in warm, low‑residual chlorinated distribution systems and household plumbing (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation; Geographic range expansion – inherent into engineered water infrastructure). Genetic analyses suggest circulation of thermotolerant Naegleria strains, but a distinct, more virulent Pakistan‑specific lineage has not been conclusively demonstrated.
Review: retain (reclassified event type; flag for review) – Karachi’s prolonged 2008–2023 series of summer PAM cases linked to municipal and domestic water is well documented and clearly belongs among the most impactful N. fowleri events worldwide in terms of cumulative case numbers and sustained transmission. I reclassified the event from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because available data implicate external drivers (rapid urbanization, inadequate chlorination, extreme heat) rather than a demonstrated new Naegleria strain as the primary cause of resurgence in the Southern Asia subregion. Geography, timing, and linkage to Karachi’s water system were retained and supported with additional Pakistani reviews and surveillance advisories; the multi‑year aggregation of cases into a single emergence episode remains appropriate but should be revisited as more granular case series become available.
