Event summary: In December 2011 and early 2012, several neonatal units in Northern Ireland reported clusters of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bloodstream infections, with four neonatal deaths attributed to P. aeruginosa bacteraemia. Environmental investigations demonstrated heavy colonization of tap outlets and flow straighteners in affected units, and variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) typing showed that many tap and patient isolates were closely related, implicating water outlets as an important source. In response, contaminated taps and components were replaced, water systems were remediated, and enhanced infection‑control measures were introduced across neonatal units. These incidents prompted UK‑wide development of a Water Action Plan, technical guidance on P. aeruginosa risks in augmented care units, and specific national recommendations for managing Gram‑negative outbreaks in neonatal units, after which outbreak‑related cases declined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Complex tap and mixer designs, inadequate monitoring of water quality, and use of hand‑wash outlets in close proximity to highly vulnerable preterm infants allowed biofilm‑associated P. aeruginosa to contaminate clinical environments and equipment; high device use and invasive procedures in NICU patients amplified the consequences of contamination. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain features were uniquely implicated; rather, the event illustrates P. aeruginosa’s inherent ability to form dense biofilms and persist in tap and mixer components, acting as a reservoir for recurrent introduction into susceptible hosts. The episode is therefore best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven by environmental and infection‑control factors rather than by emergence of new genotypes.
Review: review – The original event described a very broad 2005–2015 episode of sink‑associated P. aeruginosa outbreaks across “Western Europe,” with vague country attribution and sources drawn from several unrelated ICU outbreaks. This conflicted with the project rule that multi‑site events should be merged only when epidemiologically linked or representing continuous occurrence in the same area.([researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk](https://researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk/en/publications/investigation-of-healthcare-acquired-infections-associated-with-p/?utm_source=openai)) I have re‑scoped the event to focus on the well‑documented 2011–2012 neonatal outbreaks in Northern Ireland, where four neonates died and tap biofilms were clearly implicated, and to highlight the subsequent UK‑wide technical guidance and Gram‑negative outbreak management recommendations. Continent, sub‑region and country fields have been corrected to Europe / Northern Europe / United Kingdom, and the host description, time span, event summary, mechanism and source URLs have been updated accordingly. The event is now coded purely as re_occurrence, reflecting environmental contamination and infection‑control failures without evidence of novel genotypes. This episode remains an important high‑impact event for P. aeruginosa, but the narrowed geographic scope and dates should be reviewed against any additional UK neonatal outbreak documentation.

Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with serious infections in tertiary-care hospitals)
Event summary: From 2020 to 2022, hospitals in eastern China reported clonal spread of a high‑risk Pseudomonas aeruginosa sequence type 463 (ST463) co‑producing KPC‑2 and AFM‑1 carbapenemases, causing difficult‑to‑treat healthcare‑associated infections. During this period, ST463 became predominant among carbapenemase‑producing P. aeruginosa in the affected institutions, with isolates resistant to nearly all standard anti‑pseudomonal agents and only limited remaining therapeutic options. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and clonal expansion of ST463 co‑producing two potent carbapenemases, KPC‑2 and AFM‑1, representing convergence of class A and metallo‑β‑lactamase mechanisms in a single lineage and leading to extensively drug‑resistant phenotypes; associated mobile genetic elements and fitness traits enhanced survival and transmission in hospital environments.
Review: retain – The emergence of ST463 co‑producing KPC‑2 and AFM‑1 in eastern China during 2020–2022 is described in detail in an Emerging Infectious Diseases report and supported by broader reviews of carbapenemase genes and high‑risk clones in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10068724/?utm_source=openai)) The geographic and temporal fields match the primary report, and classification as re_emergence (new highly resistant clone of an established pathogen) is consistent with project rules, with no intra/inter‑continental emergence flags. Host: Humans (users of over-the-counter artificial tears; hospitalized patients with ocular and systemic infections)
Event summary: Between January 2022 and mid‑May 2023, U.S. public‑health authorities investigated a multistate outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections caused by a Verona integron‑mediated metallo‑β‑lactamase and GES β‑lactamase–producing strain (VIM‑GES‑CRPA) linked to contaminated over‑the‑counter artificial tears. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of a widely distributed preservative‑free artificial‑tears product during manufacturing or packaging, combined with global distribution and over‑the‑counter access, created an efficient vehicle for community and healthcare‑associated exposure to an extensively drug‑resistant P. aeruginosa strain; lapses in quality assurance and sterility control at the manufacturing facility were central non‑biological drivers. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of VIM‑80 and GES‑9 β‑lactamase genes in a high‑risk ST1203 background, yielding extensively drug‑resistant phenotypes nonsusceptible to nearly all standard anti‑pseudomonal agents; ability of the clone to survive in ophthalmic solution and cause severe ocular and systemic disease after topical use enhanced its transmission and clinical impact.
Review: review – This event clearly represents one of the most impactful recent P. aeruginosa outbreaks, involving 81 case‑patients across 18 U.S. states, four deaths, and multiple cases of vision loss and enucleation, all linked to a contaminated artificial‑tears product.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/79/1/6/7601234)) The original description underestimated case numbers and deaths based on early CDC HAN data; I have updated the event summary to reflect final counts and the formal case definition period (1 January 2022–15 May 2023) reported in the subsequent Clinical Infectious Diseases analysis. Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [early 1990s]; Ireland [mid-1990s]; Spain [late 1990s]; Portugal [late 1990s]; Italy [late 1990s]; Germany [late 1990s]; additional European countries [1990s-2000s]
Host: Humans (hospital-associated bloodstream infections, pneumonia, surgical-site and other invasive infections in inpatients)
Event summary: From the early 1990s, new epidemic methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus clones EMRSA-15 (ST22-MRSA-IV) and EMRSA-16 (ST36-MRSA-II) emerged in hospitals in the United Kingdom and rapidly displaced older MRSA lineages, driving steep increases in hospital-associated S. aureus bacteremia and other invasive infections. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s these highly transmissible clones spread into hospitals across Western and parts of Southern and Northern Europe, with several countries reporting that 30%–50% of S. aureus bloodstream isolates were methicillin-resistant and that EMRSA-15/16 accounted for the great majority of MRSA bacteremias. By around 2005, intensified infection-prevention programs and antibiotic stewardship started to reduce MRSA bloodstream infection rates in some countries, but EMRSA-15 in particular remained entrenched as the dominant hospital MRSA lineage in much of Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins) in European hospitals, high bed occupancy and frequent patient transfers, and initially limited or fragmented implementation of MRSA screening and isolation policies, all of which facilitated rapid within- and between-hospital spread. Internal mechanisms: emergence and clonal expansion of highly epidemic hospital-adapted MRSA lineages EMRSA-15 (ST22-MRSA-IV) and EMRSA-16 (ST36-MRSA-II) with multidrug resistance and traits favoring colonization and transmission in healthcare environments, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced transmission leading to large-scale re-emergence of S. aureus disease in hospitals.
Review: retain – Newly added event to capture the large hospital-associated MRSA epidemic in Europe driven by EMRSA-15 and EMRSA-16, which is a major global Staphylococcus aureus emergence episode after 1990 and was missing from the original list. Time window (1990–2005), geographic scope (mainly Western, Northern and Southern Europe) and classification as re_emergence (due to novel epidemic clones, not first detection) follow surveillance and molecular epidemiology studies; no intra- or inter-continental emergence flags are set because MRSA was already established in Europe and spread was largely within the continent.

Host: Humans (primarily community-associated skin and soft tissue infections, some invasive disease)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, non–multiresistant community-associated MRSA (CA‑MRSA) strains were first recognized causing infections among indigenous communities in remote Western Australia, marking a shift of MRSA from hospitals into the community. Through the mid‑ to late‑1990s and early 2000s, multiple CA‑MRSA clones (e.g., WA‑MRSA, ST93‑MRSA-IV ‘QLD clone’) spread across Western Australia, the Northern Territory, and into eastern Australian states, becoming a major cause of community-onset skin and soft tissue infections and some severe invasive disease. By the 2000s, CA‑MRSA was established across much of Australia (and subsequently New Zealand), with ongoing high incidence prompting national surveillance and infection-control responses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: overcrowding and poor housing in some remote communities, limited access to healthcare, high antibiotic use and selection pressure, and person-to-person transmission in households and congregate settings. Internal mechanisms: novel CA‑MRSA clones with SCCmec IV, often carrying PVL and other virulence factors, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to earlier hospital MRSA lineages.
Review: retain – Major early emergence of community-associated MRSA in Western Australia and then New Zealand; timing, geographic scope and characterization as re_emergence driven by novel CA-MRSA clones (WA-MRSA, ST93) are well supported by surveillance and molecular studies. No corrections to continent, subregion or event-type classification are recommended.

Host: Humans (primarily community-associated skin and soft tissue infections, with invasive disease including necrotizing pneumonia and sepsis)
Event summary: Around 1999–2000, the USA300 clone of CA‑MRSA was first identified in outbreaks of skin and soft tissue infections among a prison population in Mississippi and a sports team in Pennsylvania, marking the beginning of a new epidemic wave distinct from hospital MRSA strains. Between 2000 and the mid‑2000s, USA300 rapidly expanded across the United States, becoming the predominant cause of community‑associated MRSA infections nationwide and increasingly causing severe invasive disease and healthcare‑associated infections; Canada also reported growing CA‑MRSA burdens in community and hospital settings. By roughly 2010, incidence of invasive MRSA bloodstream infections in the US began to plateau or decline with improved infection control and awareness, although USA300 remained a dominant strain in many regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high levels of community antibiotic exposure, crowding and close-contact environments (e.g., correctional facilities, sports teams, military settings), and transmission into and within healthcare facilities. Internal mechanisms: emergence and clonal expansion of USA300 (ST8‑MRSA‑IV) with PVL and additional virulence determinants, representing novel strain/genotype emergence, increased virulence/pathogenicity, and enhanced transmission in community settings.
Review: retain – Correctly describes the large USA300-driven CA-MRSA epidemic in the United States and its subsequent spread and impact in Canada, with appropriate classification as re_emergence (new epidemic clone in a region where S. aureus and MRSA were already established). Continent/subregion coding (North America/Northern America) and approximate timing (1999–2010) are consistent with surveillance data; no structural changes required.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; Western Asia; Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: Japan [1997]; Republic of Korea [late 1990s]; China [2000s]; multiple other Asian countries [2000s]
Host: Humans (hospital-associated invasive infections, including bloodstream and postoperative infections; some community-onset infections)
Event summary: By the late 1980s and 1990s, MRSA had become highly prevalent in large tertiary hospitals in Japan and several other East Asian countries, and in 1996–1997 Japan reported the first clinical isolates of S. aureus with reduced susceptibility to vancomycin (hVISA/VISA), signalling a major escalation in resistance. During the late 1990s and 2000s, MRSA became endemic in many Asian hospitals and spread into community hospitals, while community-associated MRSA clones—especially ST59 (Taiwan/Asia-Pacific clone) and ST30—emerged as important causes of skin, soft tissue and invasive infections in Taiwan, parts of China and other Asian settings and increasingly spilled back into healthcare facilities. Into the 2000s, VISA and heterogeneous VISA phenotypes were documented at low but concerning prevalence in several Asian countries, prompting revisions of vancomycin breakpoints and the gradual introduction of stricter infection-control and antibiotic stewardship programmes, which stabilized but did not eliminate the regional MRSA burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: heavy and sometimes unregulated antibiotic use in hospitals and communities across much of Asia, high patient density and overcrowded healthcare facilities, widespread use of invasive devices, and variable infection-prevention infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: accumulation of multidrug resistance in long-established hospital MRSA lineages (e.g., ST239, ST5), stepwise mutations and cell-wall changes leading to VISA/hVISA phenotypes, and emergence of virulent CA-MRSA clones such as ST59 and ST30 that expanded in the community and increasingly contributed to hospital infections—collectively representing novel strain/genotype emergence, antimicrobial resistance escalation and enhanced transmission.
Review: review – Retain as a major event describing the explosive rise of MRSA and the first VISA/hVISA phenotypes in Asia, but the summary has been updated to reflect that community-associated MRSA clones such as ST59 and ST30 became major, not merely “occasional,” causes of disease in East Asia. Source URLs have been replaced with primary literature on MRSA and VISA/hVISA in Asian hospitals in place of more generic or VRSA-focused references. Event-type classification as re_emergence (rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence or first detection) remains appropriate.

Event summary: In 2002, Uruguay reported severe outbreaks of community-associated MRSA infections, and shortly thereafter Brazil documented the first confirmed CA‑MRSA infections in South America, signalling the arrival of CA‑MRSA clones in the region. During 2002–2010, CA‑MRSA lineages such as ST30‑SCCmec IV (related to the Southwest Pacific clone) and a Latin American variant of USA300 (ST8‑SCCmec IVc with COMER element) spread through Uruguay, Brazil, Argentina, Ecuador, Colombia, and other countries, becoming prominent causes of community-onset skin and soft tissue infections and serious invasive disease, with some clones moving into hospitals. Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [early 2000s]; France [early 2000s]; Spain [early 2000s]; Italy [2000s]; Germany [2000s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2000s]; multiple additional European countries [2000s]

Event summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Europe, which already faced entrenched hospital MRSA epidemics, began to detect increasing numbers of CA‑MRSA infections, often associated with PVL‑positive clones imported or related to lineages circulating in other continents. Through the 2000s, CA‑MRSA outbreaks and sporadic cases were reported in multiple European countries—including the UK, France, Spain, Italy, Germany and the Netherlands—with some spread of USA300 and other virulent CA lineages into both the community and healthcare facilities. By the mid‑2010s, CA‑MRSA remained less dominant in Europe than in North America or parts of Oceania, but had become a recognized and sometimes severe cause of skin, soft tissue, and invasive infections across several European subregions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international travel and migration introducing epidemic CA‑MRSA clones, antibiotic selection pressure in both community and hospital settings, and opportunities for transmission in households, sports teams, military settings, and hospitals. Internal mechanisms: introduction and secondary spread of PVL‑positive CA‑MRSA lineages (including USA300 and related strains) into a region already dominated by hospital MRSA clones, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to traditional hospital lineages.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2003]; Germany [mid‑2000s]; Belgium [mid‑2000s]; France [late 2000s]; Spain [late 2000s]; Denmark [late 2000s]; multiple other European countries [2000s]
Host: Humans (zoonotic and occupational infections, mainly carriers and skin/soft tissue infections, occasionally invasive disease)
Event summary: In 2003, a novel MRSA clone associated with pigs and cattle (sequence type ST398) was first identified in a human in the Netherlands, representing the emergence of livestock-associated MRSA (LA‑MRSA) as a new ecological form of S. aureus. Between 2003 and around 2010, LA‑MRSA ST398 spread widely in pig‑ and veal‑producing regions of the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and neighboring countries, leading to high carriage rates among farmers, veterinarians and slaughterhouse workers, with occasional infections in exposed persons and limited community spread. By the early to mid‑2010s, ST398 and related LA‑MRSA lineages were detected across much of Western and parts of Northern and Southern Europe, prompting changes in MRSA surveillance and infection-control policies focused on livestock contact as a specific risk factor.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive pig and veal calf production with high-density animal husbandry, frequent use of antimicrobials in livestock, close occupational contact between humans and colonized animals, and movement of animals within European trade networks. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a livestock-adapted MRSA lineage (ST398) with ability to colonize multiple animal hosts and spill back into humans, representing novel strain/genotype emergence, antimicrobial resistance selection in livestock, host expansion (spillover from animals to humans), and geographic range expansion within Europe.
Review: retain – Livestock-associated MRSA ST398 emergence in Dutch pig and veal production and subsequent spread to humans across several European countries is well documented and represents a distinct ecological expansion of S. aureus. Event years (2003–2015), subregions and countries are in line with surveillance and outbreak reports, and classification as re_emergence (novel livestock-adapted lineage spilling back into humans) without inter-continental flags is appropriate.

Countries: United States of America [2002, Michigan; 2002, Pennsylvania]
Host: Humans (severe invasive infections including chronic wound infection and bacteremia)
Event summary: In the summer of 2002, Michigan reported the first documented human infection worldwide with vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA), followed shortly by a second case in Pennsylvania, both in patients with chronic wounds and prior vancomycin exposure. Over the subsequent few years, additional VRSA cases were detected sporadically in the United States, all associated with severely ill patients and prior exposure to vancomycin and vancomycin-resistant enterococci. By the mid‑2000s, intensive infection-control measures and careful stewardship limited VRSA to rare, isolated cases, preventing broader dissemination despite the grave implications of vancomycin resistance in S. aureus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: prolonged vancomycin therapy for chronic MRSA infections, co-colonization or co-infection with vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), and healthcare settings where multidrug-resistant organisms coexisted. Internal mechanisms: acquisition of the vanA gene cluster from enterococci via horizontal gene transfer, leading to high-level vancomycin resistance, representing antimicrobial resistance escalation and novel genotype emergence within S. aureus, with potential for increased treatment failure.
Review: retain – VRSA remains exceedingly rare but the first two clinical infections in Michigan and Pennsylvania (2002) were globally significant as proof that high-level vancomycin resistance could transfer into S. aureus. Countries were reformatted to keep “United States of America” as the country name with state-level detail in brackets, and Wikipedia was replaced with primary clinical descriptions from NEJM and CDC/JAMA; classification as re_emergence (new resistance mechanism in an endemic pathogen) without inter-continental flags is appropriate.

Countries: Japan [1996–1997]; United States of America [late 1990s]; additional countries in Asia and North America [early 2000s]
Host: Humans (hospital-associated invasive infections in patients treated with vancomycin)
Event summary: In 1996–1997, Japan reported the first clinical isolates of S. aureus with reduced susceptibility to vancomycin (heterogeneous VISA precursor Mu3 and VISA strain Mu50) in patients receiving prolonged vancomycin therapy for MRSA infection, marking the first clinical warning that glycopeptide efficacy was eroding. Over the subsequent years, additional VISA and heterogeneous VISA (hVISA) isolates were reported in Japan and then in hospitals in the United States and other countries in Asia and North America, often in individuals with persistent MRSA bacteremia or deep-seated infections unresponsive to standard vancomycin dosing. By around 2005, VISA/hVISA had been detected in multiple hospitals, leading to changes in vancomycin breakpoints and treatment guidelines, though the overall prevalence of fully intermediate isolates remained low.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: prolonged and sometimes suboptimal dosing of vancomycin for chronic and deep MRSA infections, high MRSA prevalence in hospitals creating intense selection pressure, and limited early alternatives to glycopeptides. Internal mechanisms: stepwise mutations and cell-wall thickening mechanisms conferring reduced vancomycin susceptibility (VISA/hVISA), representing antimicrobial resistance evolution within existing MRSA lineages and, in some cases, increased persistence and treatment failure rather than classic increased virulence.
Review: review – This event appropriately highlights the emergence of VISA and hVISA as a major resistance step in MRSA, but the start year has been adjusted from 1997 to 1996 to include the first hVISA precursor strain (Mu3) reported in Japan. Wikipedia has been replaced by primary clinical and review articles on VISA/hVISA. The row still aggregates independent hospital-origin VISA/hVISA episodes in Asia and North America into a single global event; this is acceptable at the current granularity but should be revisited if a strictly outbreak-based, region-specific partitioning of events is required.

Countries: United States of America [2005]; selected Canadian provinces [late 2000s]
Host: Humans (healthcare-associated bloodstream infections and community-onset invasive disease)
Event summary: By 2005, MRSA had become a leading cause of healthcare-associated bloodstream infections in the United States, with data from CDC’s Emerging Infections Program showing high incidence of invasive MRSA across multiple surveillance sites amid ongoing circulation of both traditional hospital clones and newer strains like USA300. During 2005–2011, invasive MRSA incidence remained high but began to decline in many hospitals as infection-control interventions (central line bundles, decolonization, hand hygiene) expanded, even as USA300 and other CA‑MRSA lineages moved into healthcare settings and contributed to hospital-onset disease. By around 2016, the United States recorded substantial reductions in hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia but persistent burdens of community-onset invasive infections, indicating a shift in the epidemiology of serious S. aureus disease rather than full resolution.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: prior decades of endemic MRSA in hospitals, high device use and complex care, and subsequent implementation of multifaceted infection-prevention programs and antibiotic stewardship, which altered but did not eliminate MRSA transmission dynamics. Internal mechanisms: coexistence and partial replacement of older multidrug-resistant hospital MRSA clones by USA300 and other strains able to thrive in both community and hospital environments, reflecting novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission, and in some cases increased virulence/pathogenicity, which together produced a resurgence and then partial decline (re-emergence) of invasive MRSA.
Review: review – This episode captures the period when invasive MRSA bloodstream infections were at high incidence in the United States and then declined substantially with intensified infection-prevention programs, while community-onset invasive disease remained a major problem. The re_occurrence flag has been set to “No” because the pattern is dominated by the expansion and hospital penetration of new clones such as USA300 (an internal evolutionary change) rather than by purely external drivers in a previously quiescent subregion; re_emergence remains “Yes”. A Canadian CNISP report on MRSA bloodstream infections was added to support inclusion of Canadian provinces in the country list. The event is retained but flagged for review because it partly overlaps conceptually with the USA300 CA-MRSA event and mixes an epidemic plateau with a subsequent decline phase.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [1995]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1995]; Canada [1995]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1995]; Australia [1995]; New Zealand [1996]
Host: humans (all ages; high proportions of outbreaks in institutional settings such as hospitals, nursing homes and cruise ships)
Event summary: In 1995–1996 a new GII.4 strain, US95/96, became the predominant cause of norovirus outbreaks in the United States and the Netherlands, responsible for roughly half to four‑fifths of all typed outbreaks and marking the first clearly recognized global pandemic wave of GII.4 norovirus. In subsequent months and years, closely related US95/96‑like viruses seeded widespread epidemics across North America, Europe and parts of Australasia, with repeated institutional and community outbreaks. As population immunity accumulated and newer GII.4 variants arose, US95/96 activity waned by the early 2000s and was displaced by later pandemic variants such as Farmington Hills 2002 and Hunter 2004.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanding molecular surveillance in the mid‑1990s improved recognition of norovirus and linked geographically separated outbreaks, while increasing international travel and institutional crowding (e.g. long‑term care, cruise ships) facilitated rapid dissemination of a highly contagious virus with a very low infectious dose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (US95/96 GII.4 variant with antigenic properties that allowed escape from existing herd immunity); Enhanced Transmission (GII.4 lineage shows higher transmissibility and broader binding to host histo‑blood‑group antigens than many other genotypes).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event correctly captures the first recognized GII.4 pandemic wave (US95/96) and its major early-affected countries; classification as re-emergence (strain-driven resurgence in an already endemic virus) and not first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence is appropriate. Literature also documents US95/96 outbreaks in additional countries and continents (e.g. Brazil, China, Germany), but given the impracticality of listing every affected country and the stated approach of using illustrative high‑impact locations, the current geographic scope is acceptable; no field changes made, but future expansion of country lists could be considered if finer regional detail is needed.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [2002]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2002]; Germany [2002]; Australia [2002]
Host: humans (primarily adults and elderly in healthcare facilities, cruise ships and community settings, but also children in schools)
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2002, surveillance in the United States and Europe detected a sharp rise in acute gastroenteritis outbreaks linked to a newly identified GII.4 norovirus variant, Farmington Hills 2002, which rapidly became the dominant outbreak strain and was implicated in a large fraction of foodborne and person‑to‑person epidemics. Over 2002–2003 this variant, closely related to European and Australian outbreak strains, spread inter‑continentally and drove concurrent epidemic seasons across North America, multiple European countries and Australia. By 2004 the Farmington Hills wave was tapering as it was replaced by subsequent GII.4 variants such as Hunter 2004, although norovirus activity overall remained elevated compared with the pre‑US95/96 era.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global travel, cruise tourism, institutional crowding, and centralized food production (e.g. catered events) facilitated rapid seeding of the Farmington Hills variant between regions and continents, while improved RT‑PCR diagnostics and sequence‑based strain typing increased detection and linkage of outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (Farmington Hills GII.4 variant displacing earlier GII.4 US95/96 viruses); Enhanced Transmission and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity (mutations in the capsid P2 domain and HBGA‑binding interface likely increased binding breadth and transmissibility, enabling pandemic spread).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Correctly represents the Farmington Hills 2002 GII.4 pandemic wave, with appropriate timing, exemplar countries and emphasis on its role in global outbreak increases. Classification as re-emergence (novel variant supplanting previous GII.4 strain) is consistent with definitions; no geography or event-type corrections needed. Source set is appropriate and includes primary outbreak and molecular epidemiology descriptions.

Sub-regions: Australia and New Zealand; Western Europe; Eastern Asia; Northern America
Countries: Australia [2004]; New Zealand [2004]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2004]; Japan [2004]; China, Taiwan Province of China [2004]; United States of America [2004]
Host: humans (especially residents of nursing homes and hospitals, but also community and foodborne outbreak cases)
Event summary: In early 2004 surveillance in New South Wales, Australia, detected a marked rise in norovirus GII.4 activity dominated by a novel variant, later termed Hunter 2004, which rapidly became the main cause of institutional outbreaks in nursing homes and hospitals. During late 2004–2005 the Hunter virus was identified as the etiologic agent in hundreds of outbreaks and large epidemics in the Netherlands, Japan, Taiwan and other parts of Europe and Asia, indicating a new globally disseminated GII.4 pandemic wave. As with earlier GII.4 variants, Hunter circulation declined over the following seasons as it was displaced by still newer GII.4 strains, notably the 2006 Minerva/Den Haag variants that underpinned the 2006–2007 pandemic wave.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High contact intensity in long‑term care facilities, hospitals and other congregate settings, combined with ongoing international travel and trade, facilitated the rapid amplification and export of the Hunter 2004 variant from Australia to Europe, Asia and North America. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (GII.4 Hunter 2004 variant with >5% amino‑acid divergence in the capsid from previous strains and evidence of antigenic novelty); Escape from Herd Immunity and Enhanced Transmission (capsid changes in key blockade epitopes are associated with immune escape and increased outbreak activity, similar to prior and subsequent GII.4 pandemics).
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: New event added to capture the Hunter 2004 GII.4 variant, which is consistently identified in primary literature and reviews as one of the six major pandemic norovirus GII.4 variants and is clearly among the largest post-1990 emergence events. Countries and timing reflect documented large epidemic activity in Australia, the Netherlands, Japan, Taiwan and long-term care outbreaks in the United States; however, exact first-detection years by country are approximate and should be verified against national surveillance datasets. Event type (re-emergence driven by a novel variant in an already endemic virus) and overall geographic scope are consistent with current evidence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [2006]; Australia [2006]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2006]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2006]; France [2006]
Host: humans (especially residents of long‑term care facilities, hospital patients, cruise ship passengers and institutionalized populations)
Event summary: In 2006 the United States and several European and Australian jurisdictions reported unusually intense norovirus activity with hundreds of outbreaks, coinciding with the emergence of new GII.4 variants commonly termed Den Haag 2006b (Minerva) and 2006a (Laurens), which rapidly displaced earlier Farmington Hills and Hunter variants. Outbreaks occurred across diverse settings including cruise ships, long‑term care facilities, hospitals, schools and restaurants, with high attack rates and substantial morbidity among elderly residents and healthcare populations. By 2007 these 2006 GII.4 variants had become globally predominant and then gradually waned, as later GII.4 strains, notably New Orleans 2009, began to appear and take over in several regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High levels of person‑to‑person contact in healthcare and residential facilities, cruise travel, and widespread susceptibility to a novel GII.4 antigenic variant supported rapid amplification, while enhanced laboratory capacity (RT‑PCR, CaliciNet and similar networks) improved recognition of the surge. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (Den Haag 2006b/Minerva and related 2006 GII.4 variants with distinct capsid mutations); Escape from Herd Immunity and Enhanced Transmission (antigenic drift in GII.4 blockade epitopes enabling evasion of immunity to prior variants and sustaining large epidemic waves).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event accurately captures the Den Haag 2006b/Minerva GII.4 pandemic wave, with appropriate timing, exemplar countries and focus on institutional and cruise-ship outbreaks. Classification as re-emergence is correct; continents and subregions listed are consistent with the countries given, and sources are well chosen (CDC MMWR, EID, major reviews). No corrections needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [2009]; Canada [2009]; Italy [2009]; Australia [2009]; New Zealand [2010]
Host: humans (all ages; strong impact documented among children and elderly in institutional outbreaks and community settings)
Event summary: In late 2009, a new GII.4 variant termed New Orleans 2009 was first detected in U.S. CaliciNet data and quickly rose to account for the majority of typed norovirus outbreaks during the 2009–2010 winter season, displacing the 2006b/Minerva strain. Over 2010–2011 the New Orleans 2009 variant spread internationally and became predominant in several countries, including Italy and parts of Australia, where it drove consecutive epidemic seasons of acute gastroenteritis. By 2012, however, the New Orleans variant was itself overtaken in many regions by the emergent GII.4 Sydney 2012 strain, and New Orleans circulation dropped to lower, sporadic levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing global travel and high baseline susceptibility to new GII.4 variants enabled the New Orleans strain to spread between continents, while institutional crowding and food‑service exposures continued to amplify outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (GII.4 New Orleans 2009 with distinct capsid antigenic profile relative to Minerva 2006); Escape from Herd Immunity (serologic and blockade epitope analyses show antigenic differences between New Orleans 2009 and earlier GII.4 variants), leading to a new epidemic wave though with more modest increases in outbreak counts than some prior pandemics.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event appropriately represents the New Orleans 2009 GII.4 pandemic wave with correct timing and exemplar countries; classification as re-emergence is aligned with the appearance of a new variant within an established pathogen. Some sources note only modest increases in overall outbreak numbers compared with previous GII.4 waves, but New Orleans 2009 is consistently listed among the major pandemic variants, so inclusion as a top-impact event is justified; no field changes required.

Continent: North America; South America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Northern America; South America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Southern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Australia [2012]; New Zealand [2012]; United States of America [2012]; Canada [2012]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2012]; Italy [2012]; Japan [2012]; China [2012]; Bangladesh [2012]; Thailand [2012]; Brazil [2013]; South Africa [2013]
Host: humans (children and adults in community, school, healthcare and cruise‑ship outbreaks)
Event summary: In 2012 global norovirus surveillance detected a novel GII.4 variant, Sydney 2012, first identified in Australia in March 2012 and associated with rapidly increasing outbreaks; by late 2012 it had been confirmed on multiple continents and was replacing New Orleans 2009. During the 2012–2013 winter season, Sydney 2012 became the predominant outbreak strain in many countries including Australia, New Zealand, the United States, several European nations and parts of Asia and Latin America, and was linked to increased norovirus activity in some settings. By about 2014 its dominance began to decline as non‑GII.4 genotypes (e.g. GII.17, GII.P16‑GII.2) started to emerge regionally, although Sydney 2012 continued to circulate at lower levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High baseline global burden of norovirus, winter seasonality in temperate regions, and extensive international travel allowed the Sydney 2012 variant to spread almost simultaneously across continents, while institutional and food‑service outbreaks amplified local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (GII.4 Sydney 2012, phylogenetically distinct from Apeldoorn 2007 and New Orleans 2009); Escape from Herd Immunity and Enhanced Transmission (mutations in surface‑exposed P2 epitopes and HBGA‑binding interfaces correlate with antigenic changes and epidemiologic evidence of immune escape, enabling this variant to cause a new pandemic wave).
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event correctly identifies GII.4 Sydney 2012 as a major pandemic variant and captures its rapid global replacement of New Orleans 2009. However, the original version omitted Africa and underrepresented South and South‑East Asia despite clear evidence of Sydney 2012 predominance in South Africa, Bangladesh and Thailand; continents, subregions and countries have been expanded accordingly, and Bangladesh, Thailand and South Africa were added with approximate start years based on outbreak and surveillance reports. Because some country start years are inferred at annual resolution and additional affected countries are not listed exhaustively, this row should be reviewed against detailed national data before finalization.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Continent: Asia; Europe; Africa; North America; Oceania
Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Africa; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: China [2014]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2014]; Japan [2014]; Republic of Korea [2014]; Thailand [2014]; Germany [2015]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2015]; Italy [2015]; Romania [2015]; Russian Federation [2015]; South Africa [2015]; Australia [2015]; New Zealand [2015]; Canada [2015]; United States of America [2015]
Host: humans (primarily children and adults with acute gastroenteritis; many events documented among hospitalized patients and school or childcare outbreaks)
Event summary: In late 2014, a previously rare non‑GII.4 genotype, GII.17 (Kawasaki 2014/Kawasaki 308), emerged in East Asia, initially detected in large outbreaks of acute gastroenteritis in Guangdong and Hong Kong, China, and in Japan, where it rapidly became a predominant cause of hospital‑associated and community norovirus disease. Over 2015–2016, phylogenetic and surveillance data documented spread of GII.17 Kawasaki 2014 from its likely origin in East Asia to multiple countries across Asia, Europe, Africa, Oceania and North America, although outside East Asia it usually caused sporadic cases or limited outbreaks rather than fully replacing GII.4. By 2016 the GII.17 wave in China and Japan had subsided, with GII.4 Sydney and the emergent recombinant GII.P16‑GII.2 genotype taking over as predominant outbreak strains, and GII.17 persisted at lower background levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High population density and winter‑season congregation in East Asian megacities, plus extensive regional and international travel, favored rapid amplification and export of the emergent GII.17 lineage, while existing GII.4‑focused immunity may have left substantial susceptible populations to this antigenically distinct genotype. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (GII.17 Kawasaki 2014 lineage, inferred to have evolved from older African-origin GII.17 viruses around 2001 and acquiring mutations associated with epidemic capability); Enhanced Transmission and Geographic Range Expansion (rapid evolution in capsid and polymerase genes appears to have improved fitness and briefly challenged GII.4 dominance).
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event appropriately describes the GII.17 Kawasaki 2014 global wave and includes the main continents and exemplar countries supported by sequence-based analyses. Corrections made: (i) country name updated from “Hong Kong, China (Hong Kong Special Administrative Region)” to the UN/Country-sheet form “China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region”; (ii) the original subregion list omitted Northern America even though Canada and the United States were included in the country list—Northern America has been added; and (iii) an originally listed subregion (Northern Europe) with no corresponding country was removed to avoid inconsistency. Because inclusion of South Africa is supported by wastewater detection of GII.17 Kawasaki 2014 rather than large documented clinical outbreaks, and because several additional affected countries are not listed, this event is flagged for expert review of geographic detail.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Countries: China [2016]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2016]; Japan [2016]; China, Taiwan Province of China [2016]; Thailand [2016]; Malaysia [2016]; Germany [2016]; France [2016]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2016]; Denmark [2016]; Norway [2016]; United States of America [2016]; Canada [2016]
Host: humans (children and adults; many outbreaks in schools, kindergartens, universities and other congregate settings, plus hospitalized cases)
Event summary: From late 2016 a recombinant norovirus genotype, GII.P16‑GII.2, emerged almost simultaneously in multiple regions of China and Hong Kong, causing a sharp increase in norovirus outbreaks and rapidly becoming the predominant genotype in provinces such as Guangdong and in cities like Beijing, where outbreak numbers in 2016–2017 were roughly nine times higher than the previous year. During the 2016–2017 winter season the same GII.P16‑GII.2 lineage was reported in Japan, Taiwan, several European countries including Germany, and multiple other Asian locations such as Thailand and Malaysia, and it also spread to North America where GII.P16‑associated strains became prominent in CaliciNet data. By mid‑2017 the epidemic wave had peaked; GII.P16‑GII.2 circulation declined over 2017–2018 in China, Europe and North America as genotype distributions diversified again, although the recombinant lineage continued to circulate at lower levels and GII.P16 recombinants with other capsids remained important.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: School and childcare crowding, winter seasonality, and high mobility within and between East Asian, South‑East Asian, European and North American countries facilitated rapid amplification and geographic spread of GII.P16‑GII.2; enhanced molecular surveillance networks (e.g. CaliciNet China, CaliciNet US, national reference labs in Europe and Asia) enabled detailed characterization of the epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (recombinant GII.P16‑GII.2 viruses with a GII.P16 polymerase and GII.2 capsid, distinct from earlier GII.2 viruses); Escape from Herd Immunity and Enhanced Transmission (mutations in RdRp and the P2 domain of VP1 appear to have improved replication efficiency and immune evasion, allowing this non‑GII.4 genotype to temporarily outnumber GII.4 Sydney 2012 in several regions).
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event captures the major 2016–2017 global wave of recombinant GII.P16–GII.2 norovirus and correctly classifies it as re-emergence driven by a recombinant strain. Corrections made: (i) country names standardized to the Country-sheet/UN style (“China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region” and “China, Taiwan Province of China”); (ii) added Thailand and Malaysia to the country list to match the included South‑eastern Asia subregion and reflect documented large outbreaks there; and (iii) expanded continents and subregions to include Northern America, with the United States and Canada added, consistent with CaliciNet analyses showing GII.P16 recombinants (including GII.P16–GII.2 and GII.P16–GII.4 Sydney) becoming prominent in 2016–2018. Because some country start years are approximate (annual resolution) and the exact balance between GII.P16–GII.2 and GII.P16–GII.4 differs by country, this row is flagged for detailed surveillance cross-check.
