Host: humans (predominantly school‑age children and adolescents consuming catered meals, but also staff and some household contacts)
Event summary: In September–October 2012, eastern Germany experienced an exceptionally large foodborne norovirus outbreak linked to school and kindergarten catering, with nearly 11,000 cases of vomiting and diarrhoea among children and adolescents reported to health authorities, constituting the largest recorded foodborne outbreak in the country. Epidemiologic and virologic investigations traced the outbreak to imported frozen strawberries from China supplied in a specific batch to multiple large‑scale kitchens serving educational institutions, and identical or closely related GII norovirus sequences were recovered from both clinical samples and berries. After the contaminated batch was identified and withdrawn, affected facilities implemented control measures including exclusion of ill food handlers and intensified hygiene and the outbreak subsided over subsequent weeks, although the event spurred European audits and strengthened controls on frozen soft‑fruit imports.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Globalized food supply chains and import of frozen soft fruit from China, combined with centralized catering for many schools and kindergartens, enabled a single contaminated strawberry batch to seed thousands of cases across multiple federal states; the high environmental stability of norovirus and inadequate heat treatment of frozen berries contributed to persistence and transmission. Internal mechanisms: No major novel variant was implicated; instead, this was a classic re-occurrence event driven by foodborne exposure to an existing GII norovirus genotype without evidence of substantially altered virulence or transmissibility compared with contemporaneous strains.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This was Germany’s largest recorded foodborne outbreak with nearly 11,000 cases linked to a single contaminated frozen strawberry batch, making it a justifiable inclusion among the highest-impact norovirus emergence events despite its confinement to one country. Classification as re-occurrence (no evidence of a novel strain, with external drivers—globalized food trade and centralized catering—underpinning the event) is appropriate, and geographic labeling (Europe, Western Europe, Germany) is correct. Source set is focused and highly relevant (BfR and RKI primary reports); no field changes were required.

Host: Humans (residents of Panagyurishte and surrounding communities; exposure linked to infected goats and sheep)
Event summary: Beginning after a regional influenza wave in late 1992 and peaking in spring 1993, the town of Panagyurishte in central Bulgaria experienced a large epidemic of febrile respiratory illness. More than 2,000 residents were affected, hundreds had radiologically confirmed atypical pneumonia, and serologic testing of a convalescent cohort showed Coxiella burnetii antibodies in about 60% of patients, indicating that Q fever accounted for a major share of the epidemic. Control measures focused on investigating and managing heavily infected goat and sheep flocks around the town and improving public‑health awareness; after the spring peak, case numbers declined, although Panagyurishte has remained an endemic focus of Q fever.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense populations of goats and sheep around Panagyurishte, spring kidding and abortion coinciding with dry, windy conditions, and heavy contamination of pastures and village margins with birth products and manure that facilitated long‑range aerosol spread into town. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through the high environmental persistence and aerosolization potential of C. burnetii in contaminated dust, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) within Bulgaria as infection amplified from rural herds into predominantly non‑occupational urban and peri‑urban residents.
Review: Retain – major 1992–1993 Panagyurishte epidemic with >2,000 acute respiratory cases and a high proportion attributable to Q fever, clearly among the largest human Q fever outbreaks; newly added because it was missing from the original file. Classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) since Q fever was already established in Bulgaria; countries/region and timing were aligned with UNSD geography and published outbreak descriptions.

Host: Humans (general population and patients with community‑acquired pneumonia in Cayenne and nearby municipalities)
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s clinicians in French Guiana noted an unexpected rise in acute febrile respiratory illness and community‑acquired pneumonia around Cayenne, prompting systematic testing for atypical pathogens including Coxiella burnetii. Surveillance between 1996 and 2000 documented a very high annual Q fever incidence (around 37 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and showed that C. burnetii accounted for roughly a quarter of community‑acquired pneumonias, revealing French Guiana as a hyperendemic hotspot with the highest reported Q fever incidence worldwide and a locally unique C. burnetii genotype. Although incidence has remained elevated, empiric doxycycline treatment for pneumonia, continued clinical awareness and ongoing ecological investigations into the wild reservoir have helped stabilise severe disease burden even as the exact environmental source continues to be defined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of suburban settlements into rainforest fringes around Cayenne, creating interfaces between humans and a still‑uncertain wild reservoir (likely involving forest mammals), environmental conditions favouring survival and aerosolisation of C. burnetii, and historical under‑recognition of Q fever before targeted testing began. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (identification of a distinctive local genotype linked to unusually severe pneumonia), Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) in the sense of a newly recognised large, sustained human transmission focus in the Guiana Shield, and Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through efficient airborne spread from environmental reservoirs rather than classical domestic ruminant sources.
Review: Retain (with corrections) – strong evidence from surveillance and clinical studies that French Guiana became a hyperendemic Q fever focus with very high incidence and a distinct local genotype in the late 1990s, so this episode belongs among the major events. However, Q fever had been reported in humans and livestock in French Guiana and other South American countries since the 1950s, so the original first_detection and inter_continental_emergence flags have been set to No and the event reclassified as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion; summary wording was adjusted accordingly.

Host: Humans (visitors and vendors at a farmers’ market; exposure linked to a single heavily infected ewe)
Event summary: In May 2003 a large outbreak of atypical pneumonia was reported among persons who had visited an outdoor farmers’ market near Soest, Germany, leading to a focused epidemiologic investigation. A total of 299 notified Q fever cases were linked to the market, and analytic studies estimated roughly 500 symptomatic infections overall, with dramatically higher attack rates among vendors and visitors within a few metres of a small petting area containing a pregnant ewe that lambed during the event. After removal of the animals, cessation of similar displays, clinical follow‑up of affected persons and targeted public‑health messaging, no further cases associated with the market were detected and the episode was recognised as a classic, extremely large point‑source superspreading event.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: temporary co‑location of a heavily infected pregnant ewe with dense crowds in a confined market area, lack of physical barriers or respiratory protection for vendors and visitors, and unrecognised Q fever risk in an agritourism‑like setting. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via intense aerosolisation of C. burnetii during lambing and handling of contaminated bedding, producing highly efficient short‑range exposure, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) from typical farm environments into a mass‑gathering setting; no novel strain has been demonstrated.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the Soest farmers’ market outbreak produced 299 notified and an estimated ≈500 clinically ill Q fever cases, making it one of the largest point‑source Q fever events worldwide and clearly within the global top‑10 by case burden. The emergence type is adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence because investigations implicate a single infected ewe and environmental/behavioural conditions, with no evidence for a novel strain or host shift.

Host: Humans (prison inmates, prison staff, nearby residents and veterinary personnel in the Como urban area)
Event summary: From January to February 2003, clinicians in Como, northern Italy, observed a cluster of severe pneumonia cases among inmates at the local prison and some neighbouring residents, triggering investigation for atypical pathogens. Serologic testing subsequently identified 133 cases of acute Q fever linked to this outbreak, involving prisoners, guards, local residents and veterinary staff, with epidemiologic tracing implicating a flock of infected sheep and goats that had grazed in meadows adjacent to the prison in the weeks before the epidemic as the most likely airborne source. After management and treatment of the infected flock, environmental measures and heightened clinical awareness, no new outbreak‑related cases were reported, and the event was recognised as a large urban Q fever outbreak in a population with little direct animal contact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal pasturing of a large small‑ruminant flock on fields bordering an urban prison and residential area, lambing and abortions near the town, dry conditions that favoured aerosolisation of contaminated dust, and lack of prior awareness of Q fever risk in this urban setting. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via massive shedding of C. burnetii in birth products and manure with windborne spread, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of infection from traditional rural reservoirs into an urban, largely non‑occupational human population; no change in strain or host range has been reported.
Review: Retain – the 2003 Como prison/urban outbreak with 133 serologically confirmed human Q fever cases is one of the larger post‑1990 epidemics and merits inclusion among the major events. Classified as re-occurrence because Q fever was already endemic in Italy; the outbreak reflects amplification from infected sheep and goats grazing adjacent to the city rather than spread into a new continent or UNSD subregion.

Host: Humans (U.S. military personnel and other deployed forces; exposure to local livestock and dust in endemic rural environments)
Event summary: During the early phase of Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003, investigation of severe pneumonia among deployed U.S. soldiers first highlighted Coxiella burnetii infection as an under‑recognised cause of febrile respiratory illness in coalition forces, in a region where Q fever was already endemic in livestock and local populations. Subsequent surveillance and case‑finding documented more than 200 acute Q fever cases among U.S. military personnel over the 2003–2004 period and beyond, associated with exposures to sheep, goats and cattle, animal birthing sites, and dust‑laden environments during field operations, convoy movements and base construction. Increased awareness, preventive guidance for deployed personnel and improved clinical recognition and treatment of compatible febrile illnesses led to better case management and likely reduced incidence over time, although sporadic infections continued to occur in deployed forces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive military activity in rural and peri‑urban Iraqi environments where C. burnetii is endemic in livestock, frequent close contact with sheep, goats and cattle or their contaminated environments, high dust and aerosol exposure during patrols and base work in arid conditions, and limited initial awareness of Q fever as a threat among deployed medical staff. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) in the sense of high‑intensity zoonotic spillover from endemic animal reservoirs to large numbers of immunologically naïve foreign military personnel, and Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via persistence of C. burnetii in dust and aerosols that facilitated long‑range exposure in windy, semi‑desert environments.
Review: Retain – >200 acute Q fever cases reported in U.S. military personnel deployed to Iraq since 2003 constitute a substantial, well‑documented outbreak in a highly exposed, previously unexposed risk group and plausibly belong in the ten most impactful recent events when considering impact on a single host population. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because Q fever was already endemic in Iraq and there is no evidence that this episode represented first detection or spread into a new continent or subregion; geographic and temporal details were cross‑checked against CDC advisories and military surveillance reports.

Host: Humans (residents of Botevgrad and neighbouring towns; exposure linked to sheep and goat flocks grazing in or moving through urban areas)
Event summary: Between May and early June 2004, public health authorities in western Bulgaria investigated an outbreak of acute febrile illness and pneumonia in the town of Botevgrad. Case finding and serologic testing identified 220 human Q fever cases (168 from Botevgrad and the remainder from nearby villages), and epidemiologic investigation implicated flocks of sheep and goats that grazed in, or were herded along, town streets and gardens as the most likely source of airborne exposure. Control efforts, including restricting animal movements through residential areas, improving management and monitoring of small‑ruminant herds and increasing clinician and community awareness, were followed by a decline in incident cases and eventual cessation of the urban outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unusually close intermixing of small‑ruminant flocks with an urban population (sheep and goats grazing in streets and gardens), inadequate separation of livestock areas from residential zones, and slow initial recognition of Q fever leading to delayed implementation of control measures. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via heavy environmental contamination and aerosolisation of C. burnetii from infected flocks, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) from rural enzootic foci into a densely populated town; no evidence supports a novel strain or change in host range.
Review: Retain – the May–June 2004 Botevgrad outbreak with 220 human cases is one of the largest documented Q fever epidemics in Europe after Panagyurishte and the Dutch epidemic and was missing from the original dataset. It is correctly classified here as re-occurrence in an already endemic country and not as a first or inter‑continental emergence event.

Host: Humans (residents of Jena‑Winzerla suburb; exposure linked to nearby grazing sheep flock)
Event summary: In June 2005, general practitioners in Winzerla, a suburb of Jena in Thuringia, Germany, reported clusters of adults with acute febrile respiratory illness who lived near a hillside where a flock of sheep grazed and lambed, prompting an outbreak investigation. Investigators identified a large community outbreak with 331 reported Q fever cases, high attack rates among residents closest to the sheep pastures and strong epidemiologic evidence that lambing on pastures bordering housing had generated contaminated aerosols drifting over the residential area. Control measures included moving the flock away from homes, restricting access to contaminated pastures and providing clinical management and education for affected residents; after these interventions, incident cases declined, although follow‑up studies documented chronic Q fever and chronic fatigue syndrome in a subset of patients.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close proximity of a sizeable sheep flock to a densely populated residential area, lambing on open pastures immediately adjacent to housing, and favourable topography and wind conditions promoting down‑slope transport of contaminated aerosols; initial lack of awareness of Q fever risk in this suburban context delayed specific interventions. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through intense shedding of C. burnetii in birth products and environmental contamination from lambing sheep, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) into a suburban community in which large Q fever outbreaks had not previously been recognised; no novel genotype has been shown to drive this event.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the 2005 Jena‑Winzerla community outbreak with 331 reported Q fever cases is one of the largest European events and should remain in the major‑event set. The emergence type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence because available analyses attribute the epidemic to high local sheep density, lambing beside residential areas and meteorologic factors rather than to documented changes in the bacterium.

Host: Humans (students and staff at a religious boarding high school in an urban area of central Israel)
Event summary: In June 2005 health authorities in central Israel were notified of numerous febrile illnesses among students and staff at a religious boarding high school located in a densely populated urban area. A case–control investigation and serologic testing showed that 187 of 303 individuals reported compatible recent illness and 144 of 164 tested had evidence of acute C. burnetii infection, confirming a large Q fever outbreak likely linked to contamination of the school’s air‑conditioning system by infected stray cats or other animal reservoirs. After cleaning and modification of the ventilation system, restricting animal access to the premises and providing targeted clinical management and advice, no further school‑associated cases were detected, and the outbreak highlighted that Q fever can cause sizeable urban epidemics with little or no direct livestock contact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑density boarding‑school environment with shared dining and residential facilities, proximity of stray cats and other potential animal reservoirs in an urban setting, and contamination of a central air‑conditioning system that efficiently disseminated infectious aerosols throughout the school. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via the ability of C. burnetii to persist in dust and be aerosolised within ventilation systems, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of infection into an institutional urban population with limited traditional livestock exposure; there is no evidence of a novel strain.
Review: Retain – the 2005 Q fever outbreak in an urban boarding school in central Israel, with 187 ill individuals and 144 serologically confirmed infections, is one of the larger post‑1990 Q fever epidemics and was absent from the original file. It is correctly classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country, representing amplification in a specific institutional setting rather than spread to a new continent or UNSD subregion.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2006]
Host: Humans (workers at a meat processing plant in Scotland; exposure linked to a sheep lairage)
Event summary: In July 2006 a large outbreak of Q fever was detected among workers at a co‑located slaughterhouse and meat‑cutting plant near Stirling in Scotland, after a high proportion of staff developed febrile respiratory illness. National surveillance and outbreak reports identified approximately 138–142 human cases, making this the largest recorded UK Q fever outbreak since 2000, and epidemiologic investigation pointed to airborne transmission from a sheep lairage area processing post‑parturient ewes as the most likely source. Following modification of lairage and plant operations, enhanced environmental and engineering controls, and appropriate medical management of affected and at‑risk staff, no further plant‑associated Q fever cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: heavy throughput of small ruminants, including recently lambed ewes, in a large industrial slaughter facility, inadequate containment of aerosols generated in the sheep lairage and cutting areas, and limited prior recognition of Q fever risk in this workforce. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via massive aerosolisation of C. burnetii from heavily contaminated lairage environments and carcass handling, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) into a concentrated meat‑processing workforce; no evidence indicates a novel strain or altered host range.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the 2006 Scottish meat‑processing plant outbreak, involving roughly 140 cases, is the largest documented UK Q fever incident in the 2000s and belongs among the major post‑1990 events. The emergence type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the outbreak is explained by heavy occupational exposure to infected sheep in an endemic country, without evidence of pathogen change or expansion into a new continent/subregion.

Host: Humans (community residents and risk‑occupations; infection source linked to dairy goats and dairy sheep)
Event summary: The epidemic began in spring 2007 when clinicians in the southern Netherlands (notably Noord‑Brabant) reported clusters of atypical pneumonia among adults living near areas of intensive dairy‑goat farming, marking the onset of an unprecedented community Q fever epidemic. Over the following years, notified acute Q fever cases rose sharply to 168 in 2007, 1,000 in 2008 and 2,354 in 2009 (with >4,000 reported cases cumulatively and an estimated tens of thousands of infections), with strong spatial association to infected dairy‑goat and dairy‑sheep farms and environmental spread via aerosols from birthing products and manure; major veterinary measures, including mandatory vaccination of small ruminants and culling of more than 50,000 goats, were implemented. After large‑scale animal vaccination, movement controls, targeted culling and a suite of public‑health interventions, human case numbers declined steeply by 2010 and the epidemic was considered controlled, although chronic Q fever cases and associated mortality continued to be detected in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and expansion of dairy‑goat farming in the southern Netherlands, very high goat herd densities close to residential areas, delayed recognition of Q fever as a major zoonotic risk, and environmental dissemination of C. burnetii through contaminated aerosols and possibly manure management and particulate matter. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (dominance of a hyperabortigenic C. burnetii genotype in dairy goats and sheep), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (very high bacterial loads in birth products and manure facilitating efficient aerosol transmission to humans), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) within the Netherlands as the intensive goat sector expanded into new localities.
Review: Retain – the 2007–2010 Netherlands epidemic (>4,000 notified acute Q fever cases and at least dozens of acute and chronic Q fever–related deaths) is unequivocally the largest human Q fever outbreak ever reported and is correctly classified as re-emergence associated with a hyperabortigenic goat‑associated genotype and rapid intensification of dairy‑goat farming. Geographic scope, time span, case counts and control measures were cross‑checked against national (RIVM) and peer‑reviewed sources and are consistent.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (mainly unvaccinated rural and peri-urban residents, forestry and agricultural workers, and people engaging in outdoor activities)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia experienced one of the most dramatic upsurges of tick-borne encephalitis in Europe, with incidence in Latvia averaging nearly 28 cases per 100,000 during 1990–1999 and sharp increases also seen in Estonia and Lithuania compared with the 1970s–1980s. This resurgence developed as these newly independent Baltic states underwent rapid socio‑economic and land‑use changes that increased human exposure to infected Ixodes ticks, with particularly high incidence in forested rural counties. Toward the late 1990s local control measures, changing economic conditions, and in some areas improved vaccination coverage contributed to a decline from the mid-1990s peak, although incidence remained above pre‑1990 levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑communist socio‑economic transition (increased unemployment, subsistence activities, forest use and recreation), changes in agricultural practices and land abandonment leading to more suitable tick habitat, and incomplete or disrupted vaccination programs increased human contact with infected ticks and susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel viral lineage was identified as the primary cause; the upsurge is best explained as a re-occurrence driven by external socio‑economic factors acting on existing endemic foci rather than intrinsic viral change.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1876807/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This is a well-documented major 1990s upsurge in TBE incidence in the Baltic States, with some of the highest rates in Europe and clear socio‑economic drivers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1876807/?utm_source=openai)) Sub-region label corrected from "Northern Europe; Eastern Europe" to "Northern Europe" only, because Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are all classified as Northern Europe in the UNSD scheme used by the Country sheet. Event type (re-occurrence) and timing 1990–1999 are appropriate; sources are relevant and specific to this episode.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans living, working or recreating in forested regions of the Russian Federation, especially in Siberian and Ural natural-foci areas where Ixodes persulcatus is abundant
Event summary: From 1990 through the late 1990s, Russia experienced persistently high national tick-borne encephalitis incidence, representing the culmination of a roughly sevenfold increase in notified cases since the mid-1970s. Annual TBE case counts during this decade ranged from about 5,600 to over 10,000, with 89–166 deaths per year, and the burden was heaviest in Siberian and Ural regions where incidence far exceeded national averages.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Although incidence fluctuated seasonally and geographically, by the end of the 1990s TBE was recognized as one of Russia’s most important natural-focal infections before beginning to decline somewhat in the early 2000s in response to vaccination and other control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A combination of ecological and societal factors, including extensive forested landscapes supporting dense Ixodes persulcatus populations, expansion of human activity into tick-infested habitats, changing forestry and agricultural practices, and incomplete vaccination coverage, contributed to high transmission intensity in Siberia and the Urals.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Internal mechanisms: Available genetic data suggest co-circulation of established Siberian and Far Eastern TBEV subtypes rather than the emergence of a single novel lineage; the national-scale increase is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven predominantly by external ecological and socio-economic drivers acting on long-established foci.
Review: retain – Added because Russia’s 1990s TBE experience (5,593–10,298 cases and 89–166 deaths annually, with a sevenfold increase since the 1970s) clearly ranks among the most impactful global TBE emergence episodes in terms of absolute burden.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Classified as re-occurrence within an already endemic Eastern Europe subregion, driven by ecological and socio-economic factors; no evidence that this decade represented first/global emergence or intra-/inter-continental spread.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans living in or visiting coastal, archipelago and woodland areas of Sweden, especially Stockholm County and eastern coastal regions
Event summary: From the mid‑1980s into the 1990s and early 2000s, Sweden saw a substantial rise in TBE incidence, particularly in Stockholm County, with a tripling of human cases compared to earlier decades and record high years in the early–mid 1990s. The epidemic developed as milder springs and longer warm seasons favored higher densities and wider distribution of Ixodes ricinus ticks, while growing outdoor recreation in archipelago and forest areas increased human exposure. Expansion of risk areas and improved vaccination efforts in some high‑incidence regions, combined with public health messaging, helped stabilize or reduce incidence after peaks in the 1990s, though TBE remained an important endemic disease and has continued to increase again in the 21st century.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Documented regional warming with earlier springs and longer periods of tick activity, changes in wildlife host populations, and increased outdoor leisure and residence in peri‑urban forested areas all contributed to increased human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of established TBEV foci toward higher latitudes and altitudes, facilitated by climate suitability for Ixodes ricinus; no specific new viral genotype is implicated, so this represents climate‑ and behavior‑driven re-occurrence rather than a strain-driven re-emergence.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Sweden’s marked increase in TBE incidence from the mid‑1980s through the 1990s, especially around Stockholm, is well documented and commonly cited as a key climate‑associated resurgence in Northern Europe.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (no evidence for a novel strain) and focus on Northern Europe/Sweden are appropriate; no corrections to geography or timing are required. Sources from The Lancet and JAMA are suitable primary references; the French Wikipedia link is background only but not essential.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (primarily coastal residents and visitors in southern Norway exposed to Ixodes ricinus ticks)
Event summary: In 1997, Norway reported its first recognized human case of tick‑borne encephalitis, marking the appearance of clinically apparent TBE in a country previously considered non‑endemic despite proximity to Swedish foci. Over the following years, additional autochthonous cases were documented along the southern coastal areas, indicating establishment of local transmission in new natural foci at the north‑western fringe of the known TBEV range. The number of cases remained relatively low (0–2 per year through 2003) but persistent, and surveillance and vaccination recommendations were gradually adapted as TBE became an acknowledged emerging tick‑borne infection in parts of Norway.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely interplay of milder coastal climate, changing tick and wildlife host distributions, and increased human use of coastal recreational areas, enabling exposure where infected ticks were newly established. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of TBEV into coastal habitats in southern Norway that were previously unsuitable or unrecognized; available data do not demonstrate a distinct new viral genotype, so this is best considered re-occurrence of a known pathogen in a newly affected country within an already endemic Northern European subregion.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article))
Review: retain – Norway’s first documented autochthonous human TBE cases from 1997 onwards are important for tracking northwestward spread of the disease, but incidence remained low.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article)) Reclassified this episode from re-emergence to re-occurrence because published reports attribute it mainly to climate- and ecology-driven range expansion and improved testing, without evidence of a novel, more virulent TBEV strain. No changes to continent/subregion or timing are needed; sources (especially the CDC EID paper) are appropriate.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans in Novosibirsk Region, western Siberia, developing severe encephalitis with prominent hemorrhagic manifestations after tick bites
Event summary: During the summer of 1999, an unusual cluster of eight fatal tick-borne encephalitis cases with marked hemorrhagic syndrome was identified in Novosibirsk Region, Russia, among 447 serologically confirmed TBE patients. Affected individuals developed typical TBE symptoms followed by massive gastrointestinal and mucosal bleeding and multi-organ hemorrhages, and sequencing of viral E-gene fragments from archived brain samples showed that the responsible variants were closely related to the Far Eastern subtype but carried unique mutations.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) In the following two years, hundreds of TBE cases continued to occur in the region but no further hemorrhagic forms were documented, indicating that this severe phenotype represented a short-lived re-emergence of a more virulent TBEV variant within an already highly endemic area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 1999 cluster occurred against a background of intense TBEV transmission in western Siberia, where forest ecosystems, abundant ticks and rodent hosts, and frequent human exposure already sustained high incidence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis of E-gene sequences demonstrated that the hemorrhagic cases were caused by TBEV strains within the Far Eastern subtype that possessed distinct mutations compared with typical regional strains, and the abrupt appearance and disappearance of hemorrhagic TBE strongly suggest re-emergence linked to increased viral virulence or altered pathogenicity rather than to changes in surveillance alone.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article))
Review: retain – Added as a separate high-impact event because it represents the first well-documented cluster of hemorrhagic TBE, with eight fatal cases and molecular evidence of a distinct Far Eastern TBEV variant, thus fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by a change in pathogen virulence.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Geography and timing are clear; no intra-/inter-continental spread is involved.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans, predominantly farmers, domestic workers and forest workers in northeastern mountain forest regions (Inner Mongolia, Heilongjiang, Jilin), with additional sporadic cases in other provinces
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2013, mainland China reported 2,117 human TBE cases with 19 deaths, corresponding to an average annual incidence of about 4 cases per million and cases recorded in 189 counties across 17 provinces. The vast majority of infections (≈99%) occurred in northeastern endemic areas—northeastern Inner Mongolia, Heilongjiang and Jilin—where incidence rose sharply during 2009–2011 and the disease’s spatial distribution expanded southwestwards within these mountain forest zones, while smaller numbers of sporadic cases appeared in northwestern (Xinjiang) and southwestern (Yunnan) endemic areas.([eprints.soton.ac.uk](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/408106/1/1_s2.0_S1877959X1730167X_main.pdf)) By 2012–2013 incidence had declined from the 2011 peak but remained elevated in high‑risk counties, and TBE continued to pose an important occupational and environmental health risk in rural forested regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Spatial and temporal analyses linked human TBE risk to environmental factors such as cooler temperatures, higher altitude, extensive broadleaf and mixed broadleaf–conifer forest cover, and the distribution of the primary vector Ixodes persulcatus, with most cases occurring in early summer during peak tick activity; changes in forestry, agriculture and outdoor work patterns in northeastern China also increased exposure.([eprints.soton.ac.uk](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/408106/1/1_s2.0_S1877959X1730167X_main.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Circulating TBEV strains in China during this period belonged mainly to Far Eastern lineages already present in the region; no single novel genotype has been shown to drive the observed increase, so this is best interpreted as a large re-occurrence and spatial expansion within an already endemic Eastern Asia subregion rather than a new inter- or intra-continental emergence.
Review: retain – Added to capture a major Asian TBE episode: more than 2,000 reported cases and 19 deaths across 189 counties in 17 Chinese provinces (2006–2013), with a pronounced 2009–2011 peak and clear southwestward spatial expansion in the northeastern endemic focus.([eprints.soton.ac.uk](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/408106/1/1_s2.0_S1877959X1730167X_main.pdf)) This ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 TBE events outside Europe and Russia. Classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Asia (no evidence for a fundamentally new TBEV subtype), with environmental and occupational drivers.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Austria; Czechia; Estonia; Finland; France; Germany; Greece; Hungary; Latvia; Lithuania; Netherlands; Norway; Poland; Romania; Slovakia; Slovenia; Sweden
Host: Humans across EU/EEA countries with autochthonous TBE, including both traditionally endemic rural populations and residents of newly affected districts in central, northern and western Europe
Event summary: Between 2012 and 2020, EU/EEA surveillance recorded 24,974 TBE cases, of which about 24,600 were autochthonous, with nearly 79% hospitalized, 93 deaths and about 5% reported to have long‑term neurologic sequelae, representing a major regional burden compared with earlier decades. Over this period the epidemic showed an overall increasing trend, with notification rates peaking in 2020 and particularly high incidence in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Czechia, Slovenia and Finland, while spatial analyses documented a north‑westward spread into additional NUTS‑level regions of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden that were previously non-endemic or low-risk.([edoc.rki.de](https://edoc.rki.de/bitstream/handle/176904/12838/eurosurv-28-11-5.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1)) By the late 2010s, multiple new subnational regions across Central, Northern and Western Europe were reporting their first locally acquired TBE cases, and TBE had become a pan‑European public health concern, prompting revisions of vaccination recommendations and intensified surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A combination of environmental change (warmer temperatures, altered seasonality and mast years affecting rodent hosts), land‑cover and wildlife host changes, increased outdoor recreation, and heterogeneous or suboptimal vaccination coverage contributed to higher human exposure and susceptibility in many EU/EEA countries.([edoc.rki.de](https://edoc.rki.de/bitstream/handle/176904/12838/eurosurv-28-11-5.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Broad geographic range expansion of existing European TBEV lineages into new districts and towards the north and higher altitudes is evident, but without a single novel strain identified as the dominant driver; this episode is therefore coded as a large-scale re-occurrence within Europe rather than intra-continental emergence, consistent with the fact that all four European UNSD subregions were TBE‑endemic before 1990.
Review: retain – This multi-country EU/EEA episode (≈25,000 cases, 93 deaths, and 1,347 cases with sequelae 2012–2020) is one of the most impactful TBE events globally and clearly merits inclusion.([edoc.rki.de](https://edoc.rki.de/bitstream/handle/176904/12838/eurosurv-28-11-5.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1)) Corrected the countries list to include only those with autochthonous cases in the ECDC analysis (removed Ireland and Spain, which reported no local cases), and revised the host description accordingly. Reclassified event type from intra-continental emergence + re-occurrence to re-occurrence only, because all four European UNSD subregions were already TBE‑endemic before 1990 and because re-occurrence should not co‑occur with intra‑continental emergence under the provided rules.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (local residents and visitors in forested areas of the Netherlands, particularly Sallandse Heuvelrug and Twente regions)
Event summary: In spring 2016, TBEV was detected for the first time in questing ticks in the Sallandse Heuvelrug National Park in the Netherlands, triggering targeted clinical awareness and testing. Shortly afterward, in June–July 2016, the first confirmed autochthonous human TBE cases were diagnosed in patients without travel history outside the country, demonstrating local transmission in a nation where TBE had previously been considered purely imported. Over 2016–2020 additional locally acquired cases were reported, mostly linked to forested areas in the Twente and Sallandse Heuvelrug regions, establishing the Netherlands as a new endemic country with low but persistent TBE incidence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5356422/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction and establishment of infected ticks or wildlife hosts from neighboring endemic regions (e.g., Germany) combined with suitable forest habitat and recreational exposure; increased clinician awareness and testing after 2016 facilitated detection.([rivm.nl](https://www.rivm.nl/weblog/tekenencefalitis-nieuwe-ziekte-in-nederland-ib-04-2017?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host and geographic range expansion of existing European subtype TBEV into Dutch forest ecosystems is inferred, but no uniquely adapted strain has been demonstrated; this episode is therefore coded as re-occurrence of a known virus in a newly endemic Western European country within an already endemic subregion, rather than as intra‑continental emergence or strain‑driven re-emergence.
Review: retain – The Dutch emergence, with first TBEV-positive ticks and first confirmed autochthonous human cases in 2016 followed by continued local transmission, marks a genuine addition of a new endemic country in Western Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5356422/?utm_source=openai)) Reclassified the event from re-emergence to re-occurrence, because published analyses attribute it mainly to westward spread of existing European subtype strains and ecological suitability, without evidence of major viral change. Geography, timing and sources are appropriate.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (adults and children with forest exposure in Belgium, including hikers and residents in Ardennes and eastern forested regions)
Event summary: Beginning in 2018, Belgium detected its first possible and probable autochthonous TBE cases in patients without travel to known endemic countries, suggesting in‑country transmission for the first time. In 2020, three confirmed locally acquired human TBE cases were reported from different forested areas, formally establishing TBEV transmission in Belgium and prompting heightened clinical vigilance and serologic testing; from 2013 onwards, national data indicate a growing number of TBE diagnoses, including additional autochthonous and possibly autochthonous infections through at least 2024.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314842/?utm_source=openai)) In 2025, a household cluster of confirmed autochthonous TBE cases was described, reinforcing that TBEV has become a sporadic but established zoonosis in Belgian forest regions and raising concerns about further spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13211526/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely westward spread of infected ticks and wildlife reservoirs from neighboring endemic regions (Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, eastern France) into suitable Belgian forest habitats, coupled with increases in outdoor recreation and growing clinician awareness, which led to more frequent testing and case recognition.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314842/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of existing European subtype TBEV into Belgian tick populations; there is no evidence so far for a fundamentally new viral lineage, so this episode is interpreted as re-occurrence of a known pathogen in a newly affected Western European country.
Review: retain – Belgium’s emergence, starting with two possible/probable autochthonous infections in 2018, three confirmed autochthonous cases in 2020, accumulating additional local cases by 2024, and a household cluster in 2025, represents the establishment and early growth of TBEV transmission in a previously unaffected Western European country.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314842/?utm_source=openai)) Updated the event period to 2018–2025 and slightly revised the summary to reflect newer data. Reclassified the episode from re-emergence to re-occurrence, as available evidence points to spread of existing European TBEV lineages rather than emergence of a novel strain.

EPP common name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019]
Host: Humans (travellers and local residents exposed to woodland and rural areas in southern and eastern England and parts of Scotland)
Event summary: In 2019, TBEV was detected for the first time in questing ticks in parts of England, and the UK’s first probable locally acquired human TBE case was reported in a German child following a tick bite in southern England, overturning the previous assumption that all UK TBE cases were imported. Subsequent tick and wildlife surveillance confirmed TBEV-positive foci in several English locations, and in 2022–2023 enhanced surveillance and laboratory testing identified the first PCR‑confirmed autochthonous human TBEV infections without compatible travel history, providing definitive evidence of established local transmission foci in England and likely in parts of Scotland.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tick-borne_encephalitis?utm_source=openai)) By the early 2020s UK public health authorities had incorporated TBE into national risk assessments, issued travel and tick‑bite prevention advice, and recognized TBEV as an emerging zoonosis with patchy but expanding foci, though overall incidence remained very low compared to mainland Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely recent introduction and establishment of infected ticks or animal hosts from endemic regions in continental Europe, facilitated by ecological suitability of UK woodlands, increasing deer and tick populations, and improved tick and human surveillance that enabled detection.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tick-borne_encephalitis?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of the European subtype TBEV into British tick populations; no major novel strain has been implicated, so this represents re-occurrence of a known pathogen into a newly affected country within Northern Europe, with enhanced transmission sustained by suitable vectors and wildlife hosts.
Review: retain – The UK’s progression from detection of TBEV in ticks and a first probable local human case in 2019 to confirmed autochthonous PCR‑positive cases by 2022–2023 is a key recent expansion of the virus’s recognized range into a new country.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tick-borne_encephalitis?utm_source=openai)) Reclassified the event as re-occurrence (range expansion within an already endemic Northern European subregion) rather than re-emergence, as there is no evidence of a novel UK-specific lineage. Geographic and temporal details and sources are appropriate.

Host: Humans (primarily young adults; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event summary: In early 1993, clinicians in the Four Corners region of the southwestern United States (New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Utah) noted a cluster of previously healthy young adults presenting with rapidly progressive respiratory failure and high mortality, prompting an intensive epidemiologic investigation. The outbreak led to identification of a novel hantavirus, later named Sin Nombre virus, in association with deer mice and recognition of a new disease entity, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, with at least two dozen laboratory-confirmed cases and roughly half resulting in death in that initial episode. Intensive rodent control and public health education, along with the natural waning of the epizootic in deer mice after an El Niño–driven population boom, were followed by a marked decline in new human cases in the region, although sporadic cases have continued to occur in subsequent years across western North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually high precipitation and subsequent increases in vegetation and rodent (deer mouse) populations in the early 1990s in the Four Corners region increased human–rodent contact opportunities; many affected persons had substantial peridomestic or occupational exposures to rodent-infested dwellings or outbuildings, and limited prior awareness of hantavirus risk likely contributed to intense exposures. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate that a newly evolved, more virulent Sin Nombre strain triggered the event; instead, the outbreak represents first clinical recognition and laboratory detection of a long-circulating zoonotic virus with inherent capacity for severe pulmonary disease when aerosolized rodent excreta are inhaled by humans, i.e., geographic range and host association were pre-existing but previously undetected rather than newly evolved.
Review: retain – This row correctly represents the 1993 Four Corners outbreak of severe respiratory illness in the southwestern United States that led to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus and the definition of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, with appropriate geography and case-fatality characterization. Treating it as a first_detection (rather than first/global emergence) is justified because retrospective investigations have identified earlier HPS cases attributable to New World hantaviruses in the United States dating back to at least 1978 and even 1959, indicating that the virus was present in humans before 1993 but unrecognized. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/11/pdfs/18-0381.pdf))

Host: Humans (HPS/HCPS cases in western Canada; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event summary: Following media coverage of the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, clinicians in Canada retrospectively reviewed unexplained acute respiratory failure cases and prospectively investigated new severe respiratory illnesses, leading to laboratory confirmation of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in Canadian patients in 1994, including cases in British Columbia and Alberta. These early Canadian cases were linked ecologically and virologically to Sin Nombre virus maintained in local deer mouse populations, establishing SNV-associated HPS as a cause of severe disease across western Canada rather than being confined to the southwestern United States. After this first recognized Canadian emergence, active surveillance for HPS began in 1994 and the disease became nationally notifiable in 2000, with a low but persistent annual incidence of mostly sporadic Sin Nombre virus infections reported in western provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared ecological conditions across western North America—semi-arid to montane environments favoring deer mouse populations and human activities that disturb rodent-infested structures—enabled detection of Sin Nombre spillover into humans in Canada once awareness increased after the U.S. outbreak; enhanced clinical suspicion and laboratory capacity after 1993 were key drivers of detection. Internal mechanisms: Evidence supports that the Canadian HPS cases were caused by Sin Nombre virus strains closely related to those in the U.S. Four Corners area, implying geographic recognition and improved detection of an existing virus–host system rather than emergence of a novel variant; no clear changes in virulence, transmissibility, or host range were identified for this event.
Review: retain – This row accurately summarizes the first recognized Sin Nombre virus–associated hantavirus pulmonary syndrome cases in Canada in 1994 (initially in British Columbia and Alberta) and correctly places the event in Northern America with Canada as the affected country. The note that active surveillance began in 1994 and that HPS became nationally notifiable in Canada in 2000 is supported by national surveillance documents. Because this episode represents spread to a new country within the same UNSD subregion (Northern America) rather than to a new subregion or continent, and it is not a resurgence within a previously affected subregion, it does not map cleanly onto any of the six emergence-type categories; leaving all type flags as “no” is therefore acceptable, and no changes to the coded event types, geography, or sources are recommended. ([bccdc.ca](https://www.bccdc.ca/health-info/diseases-conditions/hantavirus-pulmonary-syndrome-hps))

Host: Humans (visitors to Yosemite National Park; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event summary: In summer 2012, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome occurred among overnight visitors to Yosemite National Park in California, United States, with confirmed Sin Nombre virus infection in at least ten persons who had stayed in certain tent cabins in Curry Village during June–August. Epidemiologic and environmental investigations linked the cases to heavy deer mouse infestation and structural design features of the insulated tent cabins that facilitated rodent nesting and human exposure to contaminated excreta; the outbreak was notable as the largest recognized Sin Nombre virus cluster in the United States since the 1993 Four Corners emergence. The affected tent cabins were permanently closed and removed, enhanced rodent control and public communication measures were implemented in the park, and no further large clusters associated with Yosemite lodging were reported in subsequent years, although sporadic Sin Nombre virus cases continue to occur in the western United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Structural features of the Yosemite Curry Village signature tent cabins, including double walls and insulation that permitted extensive deer mouse nesting, combined with high visitor density during peak tourist season, created an environment with intense human exposure to aerosolized rodent excreta; limited awareness of hantavirus risk among visitors and the park lodging sector likely contributed to inadequate rodent exclusion and control before the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by established Sin Nombre virus strains carried by deer mice rather than a new variant; the key mechanism was enhanced transmission opportunity through environmental and infrastructural factors (rodent infestation in human sleeping quarters) rather than evolutionary change in the virus, so it is best classified as a re-occurrence driven by ecological and structural conditions rather than re-emergence via viral change.
Review: retain – This row correctly describes the 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak among overnight visitors staying in Curry Village tent cabins, including the approximate number of confirmed Sin Nombre virus infections (10, with eight HPS cases and three deaths), the structural cabin design and rodent infestation as key drivers, and the implementation of cabin closure and enhanced rodent control as control measures. Classifying this as a re-occurrence (resurgence of disease within an already affected subregion of Northern America driven by ecological and infrastructural factors, without evidence of viral change or spread to a new continent) is appropriate, and primary sources from CDC MMWR, CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases, and Public Health Agency of Canada documents consistently identify this episode as the second major Sin Nombre virus outbreak after 1993. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6146a5.htm))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural and peri‑urban adults and children in western departments such as León, Chinandega, Estelí and Matagalpa)
Event summary: In October–November 1995, heavy rains and flooding in rural western Nicaragua triggered an epidemic of acute febrile illness with pulmonary hemorrhage centred on León and neighbouring municipalities. Investigations by the Ministry of Health, PAHO and CDC linked more than 2,000 suspected cases and several dozen deaths to leptospirosis, revealing that severe pulmonary forms of the disease were an under‑recognized cause of hemorrhagic fever in Central America. Transmission declined during 1996 after emergency surveillance, clinical training and environmental control measures were implemented, although endemic and recurrent outbreaks have continued in the same high‑risk areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense seasonal rainfall and flooding that contaminated soil and surface water with urine from infected livestock and free‑roaming dogs, poor rural housing and sanitation, and close occupational and household contact with muddy fields and streams. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel Leptospira strain was identified; the epidemic primarily reflected amplification of existing pathogenic Leptospira in animal reservoirs and recognition of a pulmonary hemorrhagic presentation that had often been misdiagnosed previously.
Review: review – Continent and subregion were corrected from 'North America/Central America' to 'South America/Central America' to match the UNSD-based country list. The outbreak is well documented as a severe pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis epidemic with >2,000 suspected cases and several dozen deaths and should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 events, but the revised geography should be checked in the master file.

Countries: Brazil (Rio de Janeiro State, including Rio de Janeiro city and western zones)
Host: Humans (urban residents in flood‑affected neighbourhoods)
Event summary: In early 1996, exceptionally heavy summer rains and flash floods in Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, led to widespread contamination of streets and homes with sewage‑laden floodwaters. State surveillance recorded roughly 1,425 human leptospirosis cases and 22 deaths, concentrated in low‑lying informal settlements in Rio’s western zone where drainage and sanitation were poor. After floodwaters receded and emergency drainage works, rodent control and public education campaigns were implemented, case numbers fell, though Rio and other Brazilian coastal cities have continued to experience seasonal urban leptospirosis after major rains.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense rainfall and flooding, deficient drainage and sewerage in informal settlements, high densities of commensal rats and extensive human contact with floodwater during and after the event. Internal mechanisms: disease was caused by endemic pathogenic Leptospira (e.g. L. interrogans) maintained in urban rodent reservoirs, without evidence of a novel genotype; the event represents environmentally driven re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic setting.
Review: retain – PAHO and Brazilian sources consistently describe this flood‑associated urban outbreak (≈1,425 cases, 22 deaths) as a major leptospirosis epidemic; continent/subregion coding already matches the UNSD scheme and classification as a re‑occurrence is appropriate. Recommended to keep as one of the largest post‑1990 events.

Countries: Thailand (nationwide, with focus on northeastern provinces)
Host: Humans (mainly male agricultural workers, especially rice farmers)
Event summary: From the late 1990s through the early 2000s, Thailand experienced a nationwide leptospirosis epidemic. Reported human cases rose from roughly 2,230 in 1998 to 6,080 in 1999 and about 14,286 in 2000, with most cases in northeastern rice‑growing regions, before gradually declining after 2003 as control efforts took effect. The epidemic was linked to intense monsoon seasons, increased exposure of farmers to flooded rice fields, and improved recognition and reporting of leptospirosis through national surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: heavy monsoon rains and flooding, high rodent reservoir density in rice ecosystems, barefoot and unprotected work in paddy fields, and heightened clinician awareness plus strengthened surveillance which increased detection. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing during the epidemic identified a widely distributed clone of L. interrogans associated with many cases, but available evidence still points primarily to environmental and occupational drivers in a country where leptospirosis was already endemic; classification as large-scale re‑occurrence is therefore reasonable.
Review: retain – National surveillance data confirm this multi‑year epidemic with peaks of >14,000 cases as one of the largest leptospirosis outbreaks ever recorded. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are consistent with definitions; although a dominant clone was reported, evidence for a clearly novel strain is limited. Recommended to retain as a core high‑impact event.

Countries: India (Maharashtra State, including Mumbai metropolitan region)
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban residents exposed to floodwaters)
Event summary: In July 2005, record‑breaking monsoon rains caused catastrophic flooding in Mumbai and surrounding areas of Maharashtra, leading to large numbers of water‑borne infections including a major leptospirosis outbreak. Hospital and municipal data reported hundreds of laboratory‑confirmed leptospirosis cases, with several wards recording tens of deaths and some city‑wide estimates suggesting more than 100 leptospirosis fatalities, and one tertiary hospital alone managed 432 suspected cases during the peak. As floodwaters receded and mass chemoprophylaxis, public education and extensive environmental cleanup were implemented, case numbers declined, although monsoon‑related leptospirosis has remained a recurrent seasonal threat in Mumbai.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme rainfall and urban flooding that overwhelmed drainage and sewage systems, dense informal settlements with poor sanitation, heavy contact with contaminated floodwater during commuting and cleanup, and high rodent infestation. Internal mechanisms: infections were caused by endemic Leptospira maintained in rodent and livestock reservoirs; no specific novel genotype or resistance pattern was implicated, so this is best categorized as environmental re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – Multiple clinical and epidemiologic reports support that the 2005 Mumbai floods were followed by one of India’s largest recorded leptospirosis outbreaks, with hundreds of confirmed cases and >100 deaths. Geography and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate and no structural corrections were needed; this event should remain in the high‑impact set.

Host: Humans (residents in heavily flooded urban and peri‑urban areas)
Event summary: From January to February 2005, historic flooding around Georgetown, Guyana, displaced more than 200,000 people and created extensive stagnant, contaminated water bodies. In the weeks following the flood, health authorities detected a leptospirosis outbreak among flood‑exposed residents, with 236 patients admitted to the main referral hospital as suspected cases and multiple deaths attributed to severe disease. The Ministry of Health, advised by PAHO/WHO, mounted a large‑scale response including mass doxycycline chemoprophylaxis, enhanced surveillance and public messaging; as floodwaters receded and interventions took effect, admissions for suspected leptospirosis declined markedly.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme coastal flooding with prolonged standing water, disruption of safe water and sanitation services, high rodent infestation in densely populated low‑lying settlements, and limited prior awareness of leptospirosis among clinicians and the public. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by endemic Leptospira circulating in animal reservoirs; no evidence suggests emergence of a new strain, so it represents environmentally driven re‑occurrence.
Review: review – This is a well‑documented flood‑associated outbreak (236 hospitalized suspected cases and several deaths) notable for the scale of the rapid doxycycline prophylaxis campaign and for representing a major event in the Caribbean region. However, its absolute magnitude is modest relative to the very largest global outbreaks; it should be carefully weighed against other candidates if the final list is constrained to ~10 highest‑impact events.

Countries: Sri Lanka (nationwide, with high incidence in major rice‑growing districts)
Host: Humans (primarily male paddy farmers and other agricultural workers, with additional rural residents)
Event summary: In 2008, Sri Lanka reported its largest recorded leptospirosis outbreak, with over 7,400 suspected cases and around 200 deaths notified nationally, particularly in major rice‑growing districts; elevated incidence persisted in 2009–2010 with thousands of additional cases each year. The epidemic coincided with heavy rainfall and flooding, intensive paddy cultivation and widespread occupational exposure, and led to Sri Lanka being recognized as one of the countries with the highest global leptospirosis incidence. Control efforts included national clinical management guidelines, farmer health education, and rodent and environmental control; although incidence decreased from the 2008 peak, leptospirosis has remained a major endemic zoonosis in the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: monsoon‑related flooding, expansion and intensification of rice agriculture, frequent barefoot field work, rodent infestations in paddy fields, and improved surveillance plus clinician awareness that increased recognition and reporting. Internal mechanisms: shifts in the predominant infecting serovars have been reported, but current evidence suggests that changing exposure patterns and climatic conditions, rather than a clearly defined novel strain, drove the large epidemic; thus the event is best classified as large‑scale re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – National surveillance and multiple analyses consistently identify the 2008–2010 Sri Lankan epidemic (over 7,000 cases and ≈200 deaths in 2008 alone, with sustained high incidence thereafter) as one of the largest leptospirosis outbreaks worldwide. Geography and classification as a re‑occurrence driven by rainfall, agriculture and exposure are appropriate; the row should be retained as a core high‑impact event.

Countries: Philippines (Metro Manila and surrounding flood‑affected areas)
Host: Humans (urban residents exposed to floodwaters after typhoons)
Event summary: Following Typhoon Ketsana (Ondoy) and severe flooding in September 2009, Metro Manila in the Philippines experienced a large leptospirosis outbreak. National authorities reported 2,299 leptospirosis patients and 178 deaths from 15 hospitals in Metro Manila, and a detailed investigation at San Lazaro Hospital documented 471 hospitalized patients with laboratory-supported leptospirosis, of whom 51 died (case-fatality ≈10.8%). After emergency doxycycline campaigns, risk communication and drainage of floodwaters, reported cases declined to baseline, but Manila and other Philippine cities have since faced recurrent monsoon‑associated leptospirosis clusters.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: torrential rainfall and catastrophic urban flooding from Typhoon Ketsana and subsequent storms, very high population density in informal settlements with poor drainage and sanitation, massive exposure to contaminated floodwaters and delayed presentation for care. Internal mechanisms: infections were caused by circulating pathogenic Leptospira maintained in rodent and animal reservoirs; the outbreak is best characterized as environmental re‑occurrence rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – Event summary has been updated to incorporate national surveillance totals (≈2,299 cases and 178 deaths) in addition to the 471 hospitalized cases and 51 deaths described at San Lazaro Hospital, while retaining classification as a large flood‑associated re‑occurrence. Geography is correct and the outbreak clearly ranks among the most severe post‑1990 events; the revised numbers should be cross‑checked against the cited reports in the master dataset.

Following emergency case management, health education, rodent control, and the strengthening of ELISA- and PCR-based diagnostics and surveillance, incidence declined, although Fiji has continued to experience smaller flood‑associated leptospirosis surges.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme tropical rainfall and flooding that inundated villages and towns, extensive exposure to contaminated river and flood water, close contact with livestock and peri‑domestic animals, and previously limited diagnostic capacity that had underestimated disease burden. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel serogroup was singled out; the event reflects environmental amplification and better detection of endemic pathogenic Leptospira rather than evolutionary change, so it is best regarded as large‑scale re‑occurrence.

Countries: India (Kerala State, especially flood‑affected districts such as Kozhikode, Ernakulam and Alappuzha)

Event summary: After catastrophic monsoon flooding in Kerala, India, in August 2018, the state experienced a major surge of leptospirosis ('rat fever'). Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme data up to September 11 documented approximately 2,598 suspected leptospirosis cases and 95 suspected deaths, including 1,318 laboratory‑confirmed cases with 53 confirmed deaths, far exceeding typical annual totals. Intensive chemoprophylaxis, public risk communication and clinical preparedness eventually curtailed transmission, but leptospirosis has remained a recurrent post‑monsoon threat in Kerala.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unprecedented flooding that contaminated wells and surface water with urine from infected rodents and livestock, accumulation of carcasses and debris, extensive wading and clean‑up work without adequate protective equipment, and gaps in uptake of recommended doxycycline prophylaxis despite health advisories. Internal mechanisms: no specific new Leptospira genotype has been implicated; the outbreak primarily reflects environmental exposure changes and high background endemicity, consistent with classification as re‑occurrence.

Countries: Sri Lanka (nationwide, with spread from historically high‑incidence southern districts into northern and central districts)
Host: Humans (agricultural workers and rural residents, as well as peri‑urban populations exposed to contaminated water)
Event summary: After a decade of elevated but relatively stable leptospirosis incidence, Sri Lanka entered a new phase of intensified transmission beginning in 2020, when 8,323 cases were reported nationally. Case counts remained high in 2021–2022 and then surged to 9,630 cases in 2023 and a record 13,328 cases in 2024, with high‑incidence clusters spreading from traditional rice‑growing southern districts into previously low‑incidence northern and central areas. Although stronger surveillance contributed to higher detection, spatiotemporal analyses suggest that increased rainfall and evolving agricultural and land‑use patterns helped drive this multi‑year resurgence, which was ongoing as of 2024.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑term climatic trends with heavier seasonal rainfall, expansion and intensification of paddy cultivation, changes in rodent and livestock ecology, and improved surveillance and diagnostic capacity that enhanced case ascertainment and revealed spread into new districts. Internal mechanisms: rodent reservoir studies document circulation of pathogenic L. interrogans and L. borgpetersenii in multiple small-mammal hosts, but available evidence points mainly to geographic expansion and environmental drivers rather than emergence of a distinctly new strain; the episode is therefore best classified as large‑scale re‑occurrence in a hyperendemic country.
Review: review – Added to represent Sri Lanka’s recent multi‑year resurgence, with national surveillance documenting 8,323 cases in 2020 and peaks of 9,630 cases in 2023 and 13,328 cases in 2024, the highest annual totals yet reported. Classified as re‑occurrence driven by climatic and agricultural factors in an already hyperendemic setting. This episode clearly ranks among the most impactful global leptospirosis events since 1990 and should be considered for inclusion in any top‑10 list, but the new data and interpretation should be reviewed in context with earlier Sri Lankan outbreaks.

Host: Humans (pregnant women, neonates, immunocompromised and elderly adults) infected after consuming contaminated ready‑to‑eat pork tongue in jelly and delicatessen meats
Event summary: In 1992, French surveillance detected a sharp rise in invasive listeriosis, and investigation between March and December identified 279 human cases caused by a single L. monocytogenes serotype 4b clone. A case‑control study and microbiologic testing traced infections primarily to contaminated ready‑to‑eat pork tongue in jelly from a national producer, with secondary contamination of delicatessen products via slicers and counters in retail shops. Large‑scale product recalls, withdrawal of implicated lots, and strengthened hygiene controls in meat processing and retail slicing ended the epidemic and returned incidence to baseline levels by early 1993.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Industrial‑scale production and wide distribution of a single ready‑to‑eat meat product, cross‑contamination of other meats at delicatessen counters, and extended refrigerated storage that allowed L. monocytogenes to multiply. Internal mechanisms: epidemic serotype 4b clone exploiting the species’ inherent psychrotrophic ability to grow at refrigeration temperatures and persist in meat‑processing environments; no clear evidence of a novel genotype or resistance trait (re‑occurrence driven by processing and hygiene failures).
Review: review – Event is correctly characterized as the large 1992 France outbreak (279 invasive cases, about 63 deaths) linked to pork tongue in jelly; continent/sub‑region and timing are correct. Countries field was simplified to “France [1992]” because primary sources document export of contaminated product but do not clearly quantify confirmed cases in other European countries. Classified as re‑occurrence in a long‑affected sub‑region with no evidence of a novel strain, which fits the provided definitions.

Host: Humans (schoolchildren and adult staff) with febrile gastroenteritis after consuming corn‑and‑tuna salad heavily contaminated with L. monocytogenes
Event summary: In May 1997, health authorities in two towns in northern Italy noted an unusual surge of febrile gastrointestinal illness among primary‑school pupils and staff eating at cafeterias served by a common caterer. A retrospective cohort investigation showed that 1,566 of 2,189 interviewed persons reported compatible symptoms and that illness was strongly associated with consumption of a cold corn‑and‑tuna salad; L. monocytogenes serotype 4b was recovered from leftover salad, stool samples and food‑handling environments. Withdrawal of the implicated salad from all cafeterias, cessation of its production, and enhanced hygiene controls in the catering operation rapidly ended the outbreak, and no linked cluster of invasive listeriosis was detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mass catering of a ready‑to‑eat cold salad prepared from contaminated canned or frozen corn, inadequate temperature control and holding times that allowed L. monocytogenes to reach very high concentrations, and serving to densely exposed school populations. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel strain or resistance; the event demonstrates that when ingested at extremely high doses, L. monocytogenes can cause self‑limited febrile gastroenteritis in immunocompetent hosts, reflecting dose‑dependent pathogenicity rather than evolutionary change (re‑occurrence driven by food handling).
Review: review – Added as the 1997 Italian school/corn‑and‑tuna salad outbreak, with 1,566 symptomatic cases and 292 hospitalizations but no reported deaths, widely cited as one of the largest documented L. monocytogenes foodborne outbreaks and as key evidence for non‑invasive listerial gastroenteritis. Classified as re‑occurrence in a region where the pathogen was already established, with impact driven by extremely high food contamination levels rather than emergence of a novel strain. Recommended for inclusion, but its prioritization versus smaller but more fatal outbreaks should be reviewed if a strict top‑10 list is enforced.
