Host: Humans (predominantly pregnant women, neonates, and immunocompromised adults) infected after consuming contaminated hot dogs and deli meats
Event summary: Between August 1998 and early 1999, US public health authorities detected a multistate cluster of invasive listeriosis caused by a rare L. monocytogenes serotype 4b strain. Epidemiologic and laboratory investigations linked approximately 100 illnesses and 21 deaths (including fetal losses) in at least 22 states to contaminated ready‑to‑eat hot dogs and deli meats produced at a Bil Mar Foods plant in Michigan. A massive recall of hot dogs and other meats from the facility, sanitation interventions, and public advisories to discard implicated products led to a rapid decline in new cases and termination of the outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralized industrial production and interstate distribution of ready‑to‑eat meat products, contamination and persistent colonization of processing equipment, and long refrigerated shelf‑life allowing L. monocytogenes growth. Internal mechanisms: epidemic‑prone serotype 4b clone but no clearly novel virulence or resistance trait reported; this outbreak mainly reflects environmental persistence and amplification of an established pathogenic lineage in a processing environment (re‑occurrence).
Review: retain – Event accurately describes the well‑documented 1998–1999 US Bil Mar hot‑dog/deli‑meat outbreak (~100 illnesses, 21 deaths across ≥22 states). Geography, timing, food vehicle and classification as a large re‑occurrence in an already affected region are appropriate, and sources include CDC MMWR and detailed molecular epidemiology studies; clearly among the major global listeriosis outbreaks.

Host: Humans (mainly older adults and pregnant women) with invasive listeriosis after consuming sliced ready‑to‑eat turkey deli meat
Event summary: From July to October 2002, surveillance in the northeastern United States identified a multistate cluster of invasive listeriosis caused by an uncommon L. monocytogenes strain. A case–control study and traceback investigation linked 54 cases, eight deaths and three fetal deaths in nine states to consumption of precooked, sliced turkey deli meat purchased at delicatessens, and the outbreak strain was recovered from the environment of one processing plant and from turkey products from a second plant. Recalls totaling more than 30 million pounds of ready‑to‑eat turkey and chicken meats, intensive sanitation at implicated facilities, and subsequent tightening of USDA–FSIS Listeria control regulations for ready‑to‑eat meat and poultry plants ended the outbreak and led to lasting changes in US regulatory policy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination and inadequate control of L. monocytogenes in large ready‑to‑eat turkey processing facilities, post‑cook contamination during slicing and packaging, widespread distribution of long‑shelf‑life deli meats, and frequent consumption of cold sliced turkey by high‑risk populations. Internal mechanisms: epidemic clone within an established serotype 4b lineage without evidence of novel resistance or markedly increased virulence; the event illustrates re‑occurrence driven by environmental persistence and industrial food‑processing practices rather than evolutionary change.
Review: review – New row added for the 2002 multistate US turkey deli‑meat outbreak (54 cases, 8 deaths, 3 fetal deaths across 9 states), which is consistently cited as one of the major post‑1990 listeriosis outbreaks and a key driver of strengthened US Listeria regulation. Classified as re‑occurrence in an already affected region; geography and timing based on CDC and peer‑reviewed summaries. Strongly recommended for inclusion among the top global events.

Host: Humans (mainly elderly or institutionalized adults, and other high‑risk groups) exposed to contaminated ready‑to‑eat deli meats
Event summary: In summer 2008, Canadian authorities observed an increase in invasive listeriosis cases in several provinces, especially Ontario, among elderly and institutionalized patients. Epidemiologic investigation and product testing linked 57 confirmed cases and approximately 22 deaths (where listeriosis was an underlying or contributing cause) to L. monocytogenes contamination of sliced ready‑to‑eat deli meats produced at a Maple Leaf Foods plant in Toronto. A nationwide recall of 191 meat products, closure and deep sanitation of the plant, and strengthened federal oversight and environmental monitoring of ready‑to‑eat meat controls brought the outbreak under control by late 2008.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent environmental contamination within a large ready‑to‑eat meat processing facility, use of large institutional meat packages sliced in hospitals and long‑term care homes, and high exposure of vulnerable institutionalized populations. Internal mechanisms: epidemic strain characteristics typical of invasive disease but no clear evidence of a novel genotype; the outbreak reflects long‑term persistence and growth of L. monocytogenes in processing environments rather than a new strain (re‑occurrence).

Event remains one of the deadliest listeriosis outbreaks in a high‑income country and appropriate to treat as re‑occurrence in an endemic region. Host: Humans infected after consuming a variety of contaminated foods of animal origin including cold meats (cecina, sausages), cheeses and other dairy products
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2008, Chile reported a sharp rise in listeriosis cases, particularly in Santiago, leading authorities to declare an epidemic in 2008–2009. Investigations attributed about 164 cases and at least 16 deaths to L. monocytogenes contamination across several ready‑to‑eat foods of animal origin, including cold meats, sausages, and cheeses from industrial producers. Progressive recalls of implicated products, closure and sanitation of affected plants, and strengthened national food‑safety controls on high‑risk ready‑to‑eat foods led to a decline in notified cases and the formal end of the outbreak in 2009.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of industrial production and distribution of multiple ready‑to‑eat meat and dairy products, insufficient control of L. monocytogenes in processing environments, and increased consumption of refrigerated ready‑to‑eat foods in urban populations. Internal mechanisms: no clearly documented novel genotype; the epidemic reflects environmental persistence and spread of virulent clones through several high‑risk food categories (re‑occurrence).
Review: retain – Event captures the major 2008–2009 Chile epidemic (≈164 cases, 16 deaths) linked to multiple ready‑to‑eat meats and dairy products. Geography (South America/Chile), timing and overall impact are consistent with Chilean and secondary sources. Appropriately classified as a severe re‑occurrence in a region with pre‑existing L. monocytogenes presence.

Host: Humans (hospitalized and community patients, mostly with serious underlying conditions) infected after consuming contaminated ice cream products
Event summary: Retrospective PulseNet analysis and a 2015 investigation uncovered a prolonged outbreak of listeriosis in the United States, with illnesses occurring from 2010 through 2015 that were linked to ice cream made by Blue Bell Creameries. At least 10 illnesses and 3 deaths were identified, including a hospital‑based cluster in Kansas where contaminated single‑serve ice cream products were served to high‑risk patients. In spring 2015, Blue Bell initiated a series of escalating recalls culminating in removal of all products from the market, temporary closure of production facilities for deep sanitation and re‑engineering, and implementation of more stringent environmental monitoring before distribution resumed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination of ice‑cream production lines in two facilities, inadequate environmental monitoring and corrective actions, and the practice of serving contaminated ready‑to‑eat frozen desserts to hospitalized high‑risk patients. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence of a novel genotype; instead, the event illustrates L. monocytogenes’ ability to persist long‑term in cold, wet processing niches and survive freezing, facilitating ongoing contamination of products over years (re‑occurrence via persistent factory colonization).
Review: review – Description of the 2010–2015 Blue Bell ice‑cream outbreak (10 illnesses, 3 deaths, large recalls and criminal penalties) aligns with CDC, FDA and legal documentation. Geography and timing are correct and classification as re‑occurrence in an endemic region is appropriate. Impact is substantial in terms of corporate and regulatory consequences but smaller in case and death counts than several other global outbreaks; flagged for expert review when finalizing a strict top‑10 list.

Host: Humans (pregnant women, elderly adults, and immunocompromised persons) infected after consuming contaminated fresh whole cantaloupes (cantaloupe melons)
Event summary: In late summer 2011, Colorado notified CDC of an unusual cluster of invasive listeriosis, and national surveillance quickly identified a large multistate outbreak. Investigation traced 147 infections, 33 deaths, and one miscarriage in 28 US states to L. monocytogenes contamination of whole cantaloupes grown and packed by Jensen Farms in Colorado, representing one of the deadliest US foodborne outbreaks in decades. A nationwide recall of the farm’s cantaloupes, changes in melon packing and sanitizing practices, and public warnings to discard implicated fruit halted new cases by October 2011.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of cantaloupes during post‑harvest handling at a packing facility with inadequate sanitation, use of equipment previously used for other commodities, lack of effective antimicrobial washing, and warm, wet pre‑cooling conditions that permitted L. monocytogenes growth on melon rinds. Internal mechanisms: multiple outbreak PFGE/WGS subtypes but no evidence of a novel hypervirulent lineage; risk was primarily related to pathogen survival and multiplication on moist melon surfaces during storage and distribution (re‑occurrence via new food vehicle and handling practices).
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2011 Jensen Farms cantaloupe outbreak (147 cases, 33 deaths, 1 fetal loss across 28 US states) and its control measures, in agreement with CDC and NEJM reports. Geography and classification as a severe re‑occurrence in an already affected region, involving a new produce vehicle but no clearly novel strain, are appropriate; clearly one of the top global listeriosis outbreaks.

Host: Humans (mostly elderly or severely ill adults) with invasive listeriosis after consuming contaminated ready‑to‑eat spiced meat rolls (rullepølse) and other cold cuts
Event summary: From late 2013 through 2014, Denmark detected an increase in invasive listeriosis cases that whole‑genome sequencing showed to belong to a single outbreak clone. Ultimately 41 cases and 17 deaths were identified nationwide, with interviews and trace‑back linking illness to contaminated ready‑to‑eat spiced meat rolls (rullepølse) and related cold cuts from a single producer, prompting recalls and plant closure. After removal of implicated products, deep sanitation at the facility and strengthened routine WGS‑based surveillance for human and food isolates, the outbreak subsided and incidence returned to background levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term environmental contamination of a ready‑to‑eat cold‑cut meat facility, distribution of contaminated rullepølse through retail and catering channels frequented by elderly and chronically ill consumers, and initially limited resolution of traditional subtyping. Internal mechanisms: outbreak caused by a single L. monocytogenes clone without reported novel resistance traits; impact arose from persistence and high exposure in vulnerable populations (re‑occurrence). The event illustrates the value of whole‑genome sequencing for outbreak detection and source attribution.

Geography (Northern Europe/Denmark) and classification as a severe re‑occurrence are appropriate. Given its high case‑fatality ratio and influence on adoption of routine WGS, this outbreak is a strong candidate for inclusion among the top global events and should be considered alongside other large outbreaks when finalizing the list.

Host: Humans in the United States and Canada infected after consuming contaminated frozen vegetables (including frozen peas and corn and mixed vegetables) processed by CRF Frozen Foods
Event summary: From 2013 onward, surveillance in the United States detected sporadic invasive listeriosis cases whose isolates later proved by whole‑genome sequencing to be linked to a common source. By 2016, nine cases in four US states (with three deaths, one attributed directly to listeriosis) were attributed to L. monocytogenes contamination of frozen vegetables processed at a CRF Frozen Foods plant in Pasco, Washington, with related products also distributed to Canada. Host: Humans (including children, pregnant women, older adults, and immunocompromised persons) with invasive listeriosis linked to commercially produced, prepackaged caramel apples made from contaminated whole apples
Event summary: In late 2014, US state health departments and CDC detected clusters of invasive listeriosis that whole‑genome sequencing showed to be closely related, and open‑ended interviews revealed an unusual common exposure to commercially produced, prepackaged caramel apples. Ultimately 35 outbreak‑associated cases were identified in 12 US states, with seven deaths and one fetal loss, and one genetically linked case was reported in Canada; traceback investigations implicated Granny Smith and Gala apples from a single California packing facility used by multiple caramel‑apple manufacturers. Voluntary recalls of implicated apples and caramel‑apple products, plant sanitation and equipment changes, and public advisories to avoid certain caramel apples brought the outbreak to an end by early 2015.

Internal mechanisms: no unique hypervirulent strain identified; risk was driven by the interaction between apple physiology, caramel coating, and storage conditions enabling growth of an established pathogenic lineage (re‑occurrence via a novel produce‑plus‑processing scenario).
Review: review – New row added for the 2014–2015 caramel‑apple outbreak in North America (35 US cases, seven deaths, one fetal loss plus a linked Canadian case), which is widely highlighted as a major listeriosis event and a key example of Listeria growth in an unexpected produce vehicle. Geography, timing and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate. Recommended for inclusion but, like Blue Bell and CRF, should be weighed against other large outbreaks when enforcing a strict top‑10 limit.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Austria [2015], Denmark [2015], Finland [2015], Sweden [2015], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015], Hungary [2016] (processing plant source)
Host: Humans in multiple European countries infected after consuming contaminated blanched frozen vegetables (especially frozen corn and mixed vegetables) produced at a frozen‑vegetable plant in Hungary
Event summary: From 2015 onwards, several EU Member States reported invasive listeriosis cases that whole‑genome sequencing later showed to share an L. monocytogenes serogroup IVb, sequence type 6 profile. By 2018, EFSA and ECDC had recognized a multi‑country outbreak with about 47–53 cases and 9–10 deaths in Austria, Denmark, Finland, Sweden and the United Kingdom, traced to blanched frozen vegetables—particularly frozen sweetcorn and mixed vegetables—processed at a single plant in Baja, Hungary. Coordinated EU‑wide recalls and withdrawals of frozen vegetable products from the implicated plant, closure and sanitation of the facility, and strengthened consumer advice to cook non‑ready‑to‑eat frozen vegetables thoroughly led to a decline in new cases and the eventual end of the outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term environmental contamination of a large frozen‑vegetable plant, wide distribution of private‑label frozen vegetables across many European retail chains, and consumer practices of under‑cooking or adding frozen vegetables directly to salads or minimally heated dishes. Internal mechanisms: expansion and persistence of a specific ST6 clone capable of surviving blanching and long‑term frozen storage and of colonizing processing equipment; this represents re‑emergence driven by clonal adaptation and persistence in frozen‑food processing environments rather than first introduction to new sub‑regions.
Review: review – Intra‑continental emergence and re‑occurrence flags were set to ‘false’ and re‑emergence retained as ‘true’ because L. monocytogenes was already endemic across the affected European sub‑regions; this event reflects clonal expansion and persistence of ST6 in a frozen‑vegetable plant, not first introduction to new sub‑regions. Countries and sub‑regions (Western, Northern, Eastern Europe) and time span are consistent with EFSA/ECDC rapid outbreak assessments. This multi‑country outbreak, with ~47–53 cases and 9–10 deaths and major EU‑wide recalls, is appropriately treated as a high‑impact re‑emergence event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: South Africa [2017] (implicated ready‑to‑eat processed meats also exported widely within Southern and Eastern Africa, but confirmed human outbreak largely confined to South Africa)
Host: Humans nationwide, including many neonates and pregnant women, infected after consuming contaminated ready‑to‑eat processed meat products (‘polony’ and related sausages)
Event summary: From early 2017, South Africa observed rising invasive listeriosis incidence, especially among neonates, and in December 2017 the Minister of Health formally declared a national outbreak. Epidemiologic investigations, supported by whole‑genome sequencing, linked 1,060 laboratory‑confirmed cases and about 216 deaths between January 2017 and July 2018 to a single L. monocytogenes sequence type 6 (ST6) clone contaminating ready‑to‑eat processed meat (polony) produced at an Enterprise Foods factory in Polokwane; related products were widely distributed domestically and exported to multiple African countries. A nationwide recall of all implicated processed meats, closure and decontamination of the plant, and strengthened food‑safety regulations led to a steep fall in new cases, and the outbreak was officially declared over in September 2018.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination of a large industrial processed‑meat facility, high consumption of affordable ready‑to‑eat polony among low‑income populations, limited routine environmental testing in factories before the outbreak, and extensive regional trade in processed meats. Internal mechanisms: dominance of a single hyperinvasive ST6 clone associated with high attack rates and severe disease, indicating clonal expansion of a particularly fit genotype; this fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by changes in the EPP (novel strain/genotype and enhanced transmission in processed‑meat environments).
Review: review – Re‑occurrence flag was changed to ‘false’ and re‑emergence left ‘true’ to align with definitions: this unprecedented outbreak was driven by expansion of a hypervirulent ST6 lineage in an already affected sub‑region, representing re‑emergence due to pathogen change rather than simple resurgence under unchanged conditions. Geography, timeline and magnitudes (1,060 cases, ~216 deaths; polony plant in Polokwane with exports to other African countries) match NICD, WHO and comparative analyses. Clearly one of the highest‑impact listeriosis events globally and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (especially elderly and immunocompromised adults, and pregnant women) infected after consuming contaminated rockmelons (cantaloupes) from a single New South Wales grower
Event summary: In early 2018, Australian authorities investigated a spike in listeriosis among elderly patients, which epidemiologic interviews linked to consumption of rockmelons (cantaloupes) from a farm in the Riverina region of New South Wales. The outbreak caused 22 laboratory‑confirmed cases across multiple states and at least 7 deaths plus a miscarriage, and led to temporary trade restrictions on Australian melons. A national recall and trade suspension of rockmelons from the implicated farm, combined with extensive risk communication advising vulnerable groups to avoid rockmelon, led to cessation of new outbreak‑related cases by April 2018, although the event severely impacted consumer confidence and melon sales.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental contamination of melon fields and packing operations—likely exacerbated by dust storms and challenging weather conditions—combined with inadequate hygiene controls in pre‑cooling and packing, national distribution of whole melons, and consumption of sliced melon by high‑risk individuals. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype reported; the outbreak reflects established invasive strains exploiting a produce vehicle in Australia, illustrating geographic and commodity expansion driven by environmental exposure and processing practices rather than evolutionary change (re‑occurrence).
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2018 Australian rockmelon outbreak (22 cases, at least 7 deaths and 1 miscarriage) and its consequences for melon trade and consumer confidence. Geography (Oceania/Australia) and classification as a severe re‑occurrence via a produce vehicle are appropriate, with WHO, CSIRO and national reports as sources. While smaller than some outbreaks in case count, it is highly impactful regionally and plausibly within a global top‑tier set.

Host: Humans (adults, pregnant women and neonates) infected after consuming ‘carne mechada’ (stuffed/roast pork) and other meat products from a single Andalusian producer
Event summary: Between July and late October 2019, the Andalusia region of Spain experienced a large outbreak of listeriosis linked to processed pork from one producer in Seville. Surveillance identified 207 confirmed cases, including three deaths and five pregnancy losses, with most cases occurring in Andalusia but some detected in other Spanish regions; whole‑genome sequencing confirmed a single outbreak clone in patient and food isolates from ‘carne mechada’ and related products. Withdrawal of implicated products, closure of the facility, extensive trace‑forward investigations, and national and international alerts issued via Spanish authorities and INFOSAN led to rapid decline in new cases and official closure of the alert in late September 2019.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Poor hygiene and environmental contamination in a small‑to‑medium‑scale meat‑processing facility producing popular ready‑to‑eat stuffed pork, wide local distribution including catering establishments, and delayed detection and recall despite early signals of clustered illness. Internal mechanisms: outbreak associated with a single L. monocytogenes clone without specific evidence of novel virulence traits; the event represents a major re‑occurrence with high case burden driven by processing and oversight failures rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New row added for the 2019 Andalusia (Spain) stuffed‑pork outbreak with 207 confirmed cases, 3 deaths and 5 pregnancy losses, documented in Eurosurveillance and Spanish government reports. Geography (Europe/Southern Europe, Spain) and classification as a large re‑occurrence are appropriate. Given its very high case burden and national and international alert, this event is a strong candidate for inclusion among the most impactful recent listeriosis outbreaks and should be weighed against other events in a strict top‑10 ranking.

Host: Humans (primarily adult men; HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma)
Event summary: From around 1990, population-based cancer registries in the United States and Canada began to show a steady increase in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma driven by HPV16 infection, particularly among middle‑aged men. Over the 1990s and 2000s, both the incidence of oropharyngeal cancer and the proportion of tumours that were HPV-positive rose several-fold, with HPV-positive OPSCC increasing by more than 200% between the late 1980s and early 2000s and becoming concentrated in younger, predominantly male, often non‑smoking patients. By the mid‑2010s, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had become the most common HPV-associated cancer in the United States and remained at high incidence with early signs of plateauing in some cohorts but no clear decline, so this re-occurrence episode is ongoing rather than fully resolved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Major cohort shifts in sexual behaviour (earlier sexual debut, more lifetime partners, and increased practice of oral sex), especially among men, leading to higher exposure to oral HPV infection; initially low HPV vaccination coverage in adults; and declining tobacco use, which reduced HPV-negative head and neck cancers and made HPV-driven disease a larger share of total oropharyngeal cancers. Internal mechanisms: No evidence to date for novel HPV16 genotypes, vaccine-escape mutants, or marked changes in intrinsic virulence or transmissibility; the epidemic appears to reflect existing oncogenic HPV16 lineages exploiting changing behavioural and demographic conditions. On this basis, the event is classified as re-occurrence rather than first detection, intra-/inter-continental emergence, or pathogen-change-driven re-emergence.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well-documented epidemic rise of HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma in the United States and Canada from ~1990 onward. Classified as re-occurrence (HPV already endemic; increase driven mainly by behavioural and cohort effects rather than new viral genotypes or geographic spread). Recommended for expert review to refine start/end years and confirm the choice of included countries, but the existence and general characterization of this epidemic are strongly supported by cancer registry and molecular evidence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; Sweden [1990]; Norway [1990]; Denmark [1990]; Finland [1990]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990]; Germany [1990]; France [1990]; Belgium [1990]; Switzerland [1990]; Austria [1990]
Host: Humans (primarily adult men; HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, clinical series and registry data from Northern and Western Europe (for example Sweden, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Germany) began to show that an increasing share of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas were HPV16-positive, alongside rising oropharyngeal cancer incidence. Through the 1990s and 2000s, the prevalence of HPV in oropharyngeal cancers and the incidence of HPV-positive OPSCC rose sharply across these countries, with some centres reporting that most tonsillar and base-of-tongue cancers were HPV-driven and describing this shift as an epidemic of viral-induced carcinoma. By about 2015, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had become a dominant subtype of head and neck cancer in many Northern and Western European countries, with incidence still rising or beginning to plateau, so the re-occurrence episode is ongoing rather than fully resolved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Birth-cohort-related increases in oral sexual practices and numbers of sexual partners, combined with delayed implementation of HPV vaccination in older cohorts and changes in tobacco and alcohol use that reduced HPV-negative head and neck cancers while leaving HPV-driven tumours relatively more common. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular studies show that these cancers are largely caused by established oncogenic HPV16 lineages rather than newly evolved variants, with no current evidence that vaccine-escape or substantially more virulent genotypes are responsible for the observed increase. Accordingly, this pattern is treated as re-occurrence prompted by external behavioural and demographic drivers, not as first detection, geographic emergence, or clear pathogen-change re-emergence.
Review: review – New event added to represent the marked increase in HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma across Northern and Western Europe since the 1990s, widely described as an emerging viral epidemic of cancer. Classified as re-occurrence because HPV was already present in these subregions and the rise is attributed mainly to behavioural and cohort effects rather than introduction into new areas or documented viral genotype shifts. Recommended for expert review to adjust the country list and time window, but underlying trend and classification are well supported by multi-country epidemiologic and molecular studies.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (primarily adult men; HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma)
Event summary: From the early 1990s, cancer registry analyses in Australia and New Zealand documented rising incidence of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, with an increasing proportion of tumours testing positive for HPV16 and related high-risk types. Between roughly 1990 and 2015, the proportion of HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers in both countries at least tripled, and age-standardized incidence rates of oropharyngeal cancer increased by several percent per year, mirroring the HPV-positive OPSCC epidemics seen in North America and Europe. By the mid‑2010s, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had become one of the most common HPV-associated malignancies in Australia and New Zealand and incidence was still rising or beginning to plateau, indicating an ongoing re-occurrence episode rather than a completed outbreak with clear resolution.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Shifts in sexual behaviour (including more frequent oral sex and higher partner numbers) in birth cohorts reaching middle age after 1990, limited HPV vaccination coverage in adults during the early years of vaccine rollout, and declining smoking prevalence that reduced HPV-negative oropharyngeal cancers while HPV-driven tumours increased. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work indicates that the great majority of these cancers are associated with established HPV16 lineages, with no demonstrated emergence of novel vaccine-escape or uniquely aggressive variants during this period. Consistent with the project definitions, this pattern is therefore interpreted as a major re-occurrence episode driven by external behavioural and demographic changes, not by first detection, geographic spread, or confirmed pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review: review – New event added to summarize the sustained increase in HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma in Australia and New Zealand since about 1990. Classified as re-occurrence reflecting rising incidence in an already affected subregion due chiefly to external behavioural drivers, with no evidence of new geographic spread or vaccine-escape variants. Recommended for expert review to refine the timing and ensure that Australia and New Zealand are the most appropriate focal countries, but the qualitative pattern and type-of-emergence classification are well supported by national cancer registry analyses and HPV-typing studies.

Host: Humans – nonpregnant adults (especially older adults and adults with diabetes, obesity, chronic heart disease and other comorbidities)
Event summary: From 1990 onward, population-based surveillance in selected U.S. states showed a steady rise in invasive group B streptococcal disease among nonpregnant adults, with incidence doubling from 3.6 to 7.3 cases per 100,000 population by 2007. The burden concentrated in older adults and those with chronic diseases, with skin/soft-tissue infection, bacteremia without focus, and urosepsis as common syndromes. By the late 2000s, invasive GBS in nonpregnant adults had become a major and growing component of the overall GBS disease burden in North America, prompting concern about adult-targeted vaccination and prevention strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: demographic aging, rising prevalence of diabetes, obesity, chronic heart and kidney disease, and improved survival of chronically ill adults increased the pool of susceptible hosts; widespread intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis reduced neonatal disease and shifted attention to adult disease. Internal mechanisms: no single new lineage identified as causal; rather, expansion of multiple existing invasive lineages under changing host and healthcare conditions (enhanced opportunities for invasive infection).
Review: retain – Event captures a major, well-documented rise in invasive GBS disease in nonpregnant adults in the United States, with incidence doubling between 1990 and 2007 and high case counts and mortality. Geography (Northern America), years, and classification as re-occurrence (driven by demographic and comorbidity changes without a clearly novel clone) are consistent with surveillance data and reviews; no corrections to countries, event type, or timing are required, and sources are appropriate for this large-scale trend.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: United States of America [1993]; Canada [1996]; Ireland [2000]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996]; France [1996]; Germany [1996]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1996]
Host: Humans – pregnant women, neonates, and adults with invasive and colonizing GBS
Event summary: Beginning in the mid‑1990s, surveillance in the United States and Canada detected increasing resistance of invasive and colonizing group B streptococci to macrolides (erythromycin) and lincosamides (clindamycin), coincident with large-scale use of intrapartum prophylaxis and macrolides in the community. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, European centers likewise reported high and rising frequencies of erythromycin and clindamycin resistance among both invasive and carriage isolates, often exceeding 10–30% for erythromycin and several percent to over 20% for clindamycin. By the mid‑2000s, macrolide- and clindamycin-resistant GBS had become widespread in North America and Western/Northern Europe, complicating prophylaxis for penicillin-allergic pregnant women and limiting alternative treatment options.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive use of macrolides and lincosamides in outpatient care and obstetric prophylaxis created strong selection pressure for resistant strains; guideline-driven intrapartum prophylaxis expanded antibiotic exposure among pregnant women. Internal mechanisms: emergence and expansion of macrolide- and lincosamide-resistant clones mediated mainly by erm family methylase genes and, to a lesser extent, mef efflux genes, frequently carried on mobile genetic elements; near-universal tetracycline resistance contributed to multidrug-resistant backgrounds (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission through antibiotic selection).
Review: retain – This event reflects a major, well-documented shift toward macrolide and clindamycin resistance in GBS across North America and parts of Europe in the 1990s–early 2000s, with clear clinical impact on intrapartum prophylaxis choices. Countries and subregions match the cited surveillance (Canada/USA, UK/Ireland, France, Germany, Netherlands), the time window (mid‑1990s to mid‑2000s) is appropriate, and classification as re-emergence due to acquired antimicrobial resistance is consistent with the definitions. No corrections to geography, timing, or event type are needed; sources are relevant and high quality.

Host: Humans – primarily pregnant women and neonates with invasive and colonizing GBS
Event summary: In Beijing and other parts of mainland China, susceptibility testing of clinical Streptococcus agalactiae isolates in the late 1990s documented substantial and increasing resistance to erythromycin and lincomycin, with erythromycin resistance rising from roughly 8% to 16% between 1998 and 1999 and notable proportions of isolates carrying ermB and mefA resistance genes. Over the early 2000s, additional studies across China showed persistently high macrolide resistance rates in GBS, mirroring trends in other streptococci in the country. By the mid‑2000s, macrolide- and lincosamide-resistant GBS had become entrenched in Chinese obstetric and pediatric populations, constraining alternative prophylaxis options for penicillin-allergic patients.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive macrolide use in China for respiratory and other community infections created strong selection pressure for resistance among streptococci, including GBS. Internal mechanisms: acquisition and spread of ermB and mefA genes mediating ribosomal modification and active efflux, often on mobile elements, leading to high-level macrolide resistance and reduced susceptibility to related agents (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission via selection of resistant clones).
Review: retain – The event describes the emergence and consolidation of macrolide/lincosamide-resistant GBS in mainland China in the late 1990s–early 2000s, supported by susceptibility and genotypic data and representing a large population with substantial implications for prophylaxis. Geography (Eastern Asia, China), timing (1998–2005), and classification as re-emergence driven by acquired resistance (not spread to a previously naïve region) are appropriate; no corrections to countries, subregions or event type are required, and sources are suitable.

Countries: Singapore [1995]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [1993]; Malaysia [2007]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2000]; Thailand [2007]; Viet Nam [2015]
Host: Humans – adults and neonates; aquaculture fish (tilapia and other freshwater fish) serving as reservoirs for human infection
Event summary: Retrospective genomic and surveillance work shows that from the early–mid 1990s onward, a hypervirulent serotype III sequence type 283 (ST283) clone of Streptococcus agalactiae caused invasive disease in adults in Hong Kong and Singapore and was later found in invasive collections from Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Thailand and Viet Nam, as well as in diseased tilapia and other freshwater fish across the region. During the 2000s and 2010s, ST283 became the dominant cause of invasive GBS in some hospital series from Laos and Thailand and was widely detected in human invasive disease and farmed tilapia in Singapore, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Thailand, Viet Nam and Malaysia. By around 2017, ST283 had established itself as a widespread regional lineage with bidirectional transmission between humans and aquaculture fish, recognized as a distinct, hypervirulent clone with major public health and aquaculture impacts in South-eastern and Eastern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of freshwater fish aquaculture and high per‑capita fish consumption in Southeast Asia; preparation and consumption of raw or undercooked freshwater fish dishes; warm tropical temperatures favoring bacterial survival in aquatic environments; regional trade in live and chilled fish facilitating dissemination. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a genetically distinct hypervirulent clone (ST283, clonal complex 283) with traits supporting invasion and survival in both humans and fish; acquisition of resistance determinants such as tet(M) on mobile genetic elements aiding persistence under antibiotic exposure in both human medicine and aquaculture; host expansion between humans and fish and possible enhanced transmission via adaptation to aquatic and human gastrointestinal niches (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion – inherent adaptation to regional aquatic–human interfaces).
Review: review – Event correctly highlights the emergence and regional spread of the hypervirulent ST283 clone in humans and fish across South-eastern and Eastern Asia and is clearly among the most impactful GBS emergence events. However, several corrections were needed: (1) start year adjusted from 1995 to 1993 to reflect earliest documented invasive ST283 disease in Hong Kong, while still capturing mid‑1990s first human cases in Singapore and Hong Kong; (2) Hong Kong entry standardized to “China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region” and first-detection year corrected from 2010 to 1993–1995 based on the 1993–2012 invasive series; (3) country list refined to Singapore, Hong Kong SAR, Malaysia, Lao PDR, Thailand and Viet Nam with approximate first-detection years drawn from invasive collections and fish outbreaks, and Myanmar was removed because only sparse, later reports exist and its contribution to this 1993–2017 regional emergence episode is uncertain; (4) “Western Asia” removed from sub_regions, as available data show ST283/CC283 is essentially confined to Asia with only very rare detections in Europe and no clear large-scale Western Asian emergence during this period; and (5) event type updated by switching intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No, keeping re_emergence as Yes, because the EPP (S. agalactiae in humans) was already established in these Asian subregions and this episode reflects re-emergence via a novel hypervirulent clone rather than first establishment of the species. An additional key source (Hong Kong 1993–2012 ST283 series) was added to the URL list to support the corrected Hong Kong dates and burden.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – predominantly previously healthy adults; freshwater fish used in ready-to-eat raw dishes (e.g. Asian bighead carp, snakehead) as the vehicle and reservoir
Event summary: In mid‑2015, hospitals in Singapore detected an abrupt epidemic of invasive group B streptococcal infections in adults, many presenting with sepsis, meningitis, and septic arthritis, which was rapidly linked epidemiologically and microbiologically to a serotype III ST283 clone and recent consumption of raw freshwater fish dishes. The outbreak peaked at around 26 reported invasive GBS cases per week and affected at least 140–150 persons, before public health authorities issued advisories in July 2015 and implemented bans on the sale of raw freshwater fish in ready‑to‑eat dishes in December 2015. Following removal of raw freshwater fish from the retail food chain, the incidence of invasive ST283 infections in Singapore fell sharply back toward baseline, although sporadic cases and low-level circulation of the clone in humans and fish have persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread consumption of ready-to-eat raw freshwater fish dishes, inadequate sourcing and hygienic handling of freshwater fish, and co-mingling of contaminated fish in markets created an efficient foodborne transmission route; delayed recognition of GBS as a foodborne pathogen allowed amplification before control. Internal mechanisms: the hypervirulent ST283 clone is capable of causing invasive disease in immunocompetent adults after gastrointestinal exposure; genomic analyses show close relatedness between human and fish ST283 isolates, supporting efficient cross-species transmission and adaptation to survival in aquatic hosts and human gastrointestinal tracts (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via carried determinants).
Review: retain – The 2015 Singapore ST283 outbreak is a clearly defined, high-impact foodborne epidemic (≈140–150 invasive cases, sharp temporal spike, and major policy response) and must be retained as a distinct re-emergence event of a hypervirulent clone with foodborne transmission. Countries, timing, and host description are accurate, classification as re-emergence (novel clone/route in a region where GBS was already present) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate, and the cited outbreak investigations and genomic analyses are the most relevant sources.

Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2021]
Host: Humans – adults with invasive GBS disease; freshwater fish and wet market environments as implicated reservoirs
Event summary: Between September and November 2021, public hospitals in Hong Kong detected an unusual cluster of invasive group B streptococcal infections in adults, more than half of which were caused by the hypervirulent sequence type 283 lineage previously associated mainly with Southeast Asia. During this period, ST283 was also isolated from freshwater fish and environmental samples from wet markets, indicating a shared or linked source similar to that seen in Singapore. After public health investigations, heightened food safety messaging and control of contaminated fish sources, the short‑term spike in invasive ST283 cases subsided, though Hong Kong authorities continue to monitor this lineage as an emerging foodborne and invasive pathogen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation and sale of freshwater fish from regions where ST283 is established, combined with traditional culinary practices and handling of raw or undercooked fish in wet markets, facilitated local introduction and amplification; high ambient temperatures during late summer and early autumn may have favored bacterial growth in fish and market environments. Internal mechanisms: dissemination of the same hypervirulent ST283 clone with demonstrated capacity for efficient foodborne transmission and invasive disease in adults, with genomic evidence of close relatedness between human and fish isolates, suggesting ongoing host switching and adaptation (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion within Asia).
Review: review – Event appropriately describes the 2021 Hong Kong surge of invasive ST283 infections (95 iGBS cases, 57 due to ST283) with linked detection of the same clone in freshwater fish and wet market environments, and it is clearly a major regional episode. However, the event type required correction: intra_continental_emergence has been set from Yes to No because ST283 had already been present in Hong Kong since the 1990s and this cluster represents a re-emergence/large flare-up of an existing hypervirulent lineage in a previously affected subregion, not first establishment of the species or lineage in a new Asian subregion. Classification as re_emergence (driven by a known hypervirulent clone and foodborne/handling exposures) and the geographic coding (Eastern Asia, Hong Kong SAR) and year (2021) are otherwise consistent with the outbreak description and added genomic/epidemiologic sources, including the detailed EID 2025 cluster report.

Countries: Russian Federation [1990]; Ukraine [1990]; Belarus [1990]; Republic of Moldova [1990]; Estonia [1991]; Latvia [1991]; Lithuania [1991]
Host: Humans (general sexually active population, with high incidence in sex workers, clients, and people who inject drugs)
Event summary: After relatively low syphilis rates in the 1980s, the early 1990s saw a dramatic resurgence of infectious syphilis across the Newly Independent States of the former Soviet Union, with reported incidence in Russia increasing roughly 50-fold by 1997 compared with 1990. The epidemic expanded rapidly through the mid‑1990s, fueled by rising sex work, injecting drug use, and social disruption, and spread widely across Eastern European successor states including Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the Republic of Moldova and the Baltic countries. Toward the late 1990s incidence began to plateau and then decline in several countries, though levels remained well above those of Western Europe and left a legacy of elevated STI and HIV risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Profound socio-economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union (unemployment, migration, weakening public health systems), rapid expansion of commercial sex, and increasing injecting drug use created dense sexual and injecting networks with limited access to condoms and STI care; reductions in organized STI control programs and stock-outs of diagnostics and treatment further weakened control. Internal mechanisms: No specific new Treponema pallidum genotype was identified as causal; the event is best understood as a resurgence of existing strains under changed social and health-system conditions (re-occurrence).
Review: review – Retain as one of the largest modern syphilis emergence events, but sub-region and country coding have been corrected: Baltic countries are now listed individually (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) and assigned to Northern Europe, while the event scope is restricted to Eastern European and Baltic successor states rather than all of Central Asia. Text of the event summary was adjusted to match this geographic scope. Classification as a large re-occurrence driven by socio-economic collapse (with no new strain) remains appropriate, but the row should be checked by a human reviewer to ensure the selected country list matches the intended modelling scope.

Host: Humans (general sexually active population, including sex workers, clients, MSM, and pregnant women)
Event summary: Following near-elimination of syphilis in China by the 1960s through mass screening and treatment, reported cases began to rise again in the 1980s and accelerated in the 1990s, reaching a national incidence of around 5 per 100,000 by the early 2000s. The epidemic expanded through coastal urban centers and along migration corridors, with high prevalence documented in sex workers, MSM and other key populations during the 1990s and 2000s. By the late 2000s and around 2010, syphilis had re-established as a major nationwide STI with sustained high incidence, prompting renewed government attention and control programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid economic liberalization, large-scale internal migration, growth of the sex industry, rising disposable income and new sexual networks, and initially weak STI surveillance and control systems all contributed to syphilis resurgence; concurrent HIV expansion, particularly among MSM, increased co-infection burdens. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain was identified as initiating the epidemic; the event reflects geographic and behavioral spread of existing T. pallidum lineages. Later in the period, increasing macrolide resistance was documented but played a secondary role in driving incidence.
Review: retain – Well-documented large-scale resurgence after near-elimination in China, with correct continent/sub-region, country, timing and classification as re-occurrence. No corrections needed; sources (national surveillance analyses and narrative reviews) are appropriate for one of the major global syphilis events.
