Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1997]; Ireland [1999]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1999]; France [1999]; Norway [1992, outbreak intensifying after 2000]; Germany [2001]; Spain [early 2000s]; Italy [early 2000s]; other EU/EEA countries with later MSM-focused outbreaks [2000s]
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), including many living with HIV; smaller contributions from heterosexual transmission and congenital cases
Event summary: After historically low syphilis incidence in Western and Northern Europe in the mid‑1990s, outbreaks of infectious syphilis were reported from 1997 onward, initially in UK cities and soon in Ireland, the Netherlands, France, Norway and other EU/EEA countries, largely concentrated among MSM. Through the 2000s and 2010s, case notifications rose steadily in many Western and Central European states, with particularly sharp increases among MSM and in urban centers, reversing previous declines. By around 2020, several European countries were reporting their highest syphilis rates in decades, with continued concentration in MSM and emerging concerns about congenital and heterosexual transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Behavioral changes in MSM populations after the advent of effective antiretroviral therapy for HIV (reduced fear of HIV, more condomless sex, higher partner numbers), internet and app-facilitated partner finding, chemsex practices, and sexual mixing within dense urban networks; reduced intensity of classic STI control programs and stigma or barriers limiting access to testing and treatment for MSM and migrants. Internal mechanisms: No dominant new T. pallidum strain has been shown to drive this resurgence; available data suggest circulation of multiple lineages, so this event is best classified as re-occurrence driven by social and behavioral factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Retain as a major event describing the MSM-focused resurgence in Western/Northern/Southern Europe, but the type-of-emergence coding has been corrected: intra_continental_emergence has been set to false so that this episode is treated purely as re-occurrence (syphilis was not new to these sub-regions). Countries are broadly correct but include a non-specific "other EU/EEA countries" category; a human reviewer may wish to expand this list for more granular country coverage.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2000]; Canada [early 2000s, smaller share of cases]
Host: Humans, predominantly MSM but with increasing involvement of heterosexual men and women over time
Event summary: After syphilis rates in the United States fell to historic lows around 2000 and near-elimination was considered achievable, cases began increasing again in the early 2000s, initially largely among MSM in major cities. Through the 2010s, reported primary and secondary syphilis rates rose steadily, with MSM continuing to bear the highest burden but incidence also rising in heterosexual men and women, including those who inject drugs. By the early 2020s, the United States and, to a lesser extent, Canada were experiencing a broad syphilis epidemic across many demographic groups, setting the stage for explosive growth in congenital syphilis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changing sexual behaviors related to HIV treatment optimism and decreased perceived HIV risk, increased partner concurrency and network connectivity among MSM, use of digital platforms for partner seeking, ongoing substance use and structural vulnerabilities (homelessness, incarceration), and erosion or underfunding of STI control programs. Internal mechanisms: No established penicillin resistance has been documented; most of the epidemic growth is attributable to behavioral and structural drivers. Macrolide-resistant strains became more common during this period but played a relatively modest role in overall incidence trends.
Review: retain – Accurately captures the large, long-running resurgence in the United States (and to a lesser degree Canada) from historic lows around 2000 to broad epidemics by the early 2020s. Geography, timing, and classification as re-occurrence (without intra- or inter-continental emergence) are appropriate; sources are strong (CDC surveillance and peer-reviewed analyses).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans – pregnant women and newborns (congenital syphilis)
Event summary: After very low congenital syphilis incidence in the late 1990s and early 2000s, reported U.S. congenital syphilis cases began to rise sharply from around 335 cases in 2012 to 3,761 in 2022, representing more than a tenfold increase. The epidemic expanded across many states, with disproportionate impacts in the U.S. South and West and among marginalized populations including people with substance use disorders and those with limited prenatal care access. By 2023 the United States recorded its highest number of congenital syphilis cases since the early 1990s, prompting urgent federal and state responses focused on prenatal screening and treatment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large increases in maternal syphilis linked to the broader adult epidemic, gaps in prenatal care coverage and quality (late or no prenatal care, missed or delayed testing, inadequate treatment), social determinants such as poverty, unstable housing, and methamphetamine or opioid use, and constraints in public health infrastructure and penicillin supply in some areas. Internal mechanisms: No specific new T. pallidum variant has been implicated; this is a classic re-occurrence driven by failures in prevention and care delivery rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This is a major, well-documented emergence event in terms of impact (tenfold increase and hundreds of preventable fetal and neonatal deaths). Geography, time window (2012–2023), and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate and supported by CDC data; no structural corrections required.

Host: Humans – general sexually active population, pregnant women, and newborns (congenital syphilis)
Event summary: From the early 2000s, Brazil documented rising rates of acquired syphilis, syphilis in pregnancy, and congenital syphilis, with over 300,000 congenital syphilis cases reported nationally between 2001 and 2022 and more than half occurring from 2017–2022. Throughout the 2010s, incidence of congenital syphilis increased in all macro-regions, particularly in the Northeast, and was associated with substantial fetal and infant mortality and adverse pregnancy outcomes. National action plans launched around 2010 and 2016 slowed growth in some regions but did not fully reverse trends, and high burdens persisted into the early 2020s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent social and regional inequalities, challenges in access to and quality of prenatal care, gaps in timely maternal testing and treatment, and delayed implementation of robust syphilis surveillance (acquired syphilis became notifiable nationwide only after 2010); contributing factors include urbanization, internal migration, and coexisting HIV and other STIs. Internal mechanisms: No specific resistant or more virulent T. pallidum lineage has been demonstrated as the main driver; the epidemic is mainly a re-occurrence fueled by health-system and social determinants.
Review: retain – Brazil’s large and sustained increase in acquired, gestational, and congenital syphilis is one of the most impactful national-level events, with very high case numbers and mortality. Geography, time span and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; event is strongly supported by multiple national and regional analyses.

Host: Humans – heterosexual men and women and MSM; small numbers of congenital cases
Event summary: After a long decline with only a few hundred annual cases by the early 2000s, Japan experienced a rapid increase in reported syphilis beginning around 2013, with annual cases rising from about 1,200 in 2013 to over 5,000 by 2017 and surpassing 10,000 by 2022. The surge was initially concentrated in major urban centers such as Tokyo and Osaka and, unusually compared with Western countries, involved large numbers of heterosexual men and women as well as MSM. By the early 2020s, syphilis had re-established as a major STI in Japan with sustained high incidence despite intensified public health messaging and surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changes in sexual behavior including increased casual and commercial sex, widespread use of smartphone dating apps, reduced condom use, and underestimation of syphilis risk due to historically low incidence; limitations in targeted prevention and early diagnosis for high‑risk groups also contributed. Internal mechanisms: High prevalence of macrolide-resistant T. pallidum (A2058G mutation in 23S rRNA) was documented in Japanese strains by the late 2010s, but penicillin remained effective; resistance may have complicated use of macrolides but is not thought to be the primary driver of incidence.
Review: retain – A well-supported major resurgence in Japan, with very large relative and absolute increases in national case counts and distinctive heterosexual involvement. Geography, years and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; sources include national surveillance summaries and peer-reviewed analyses.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Asia
Countries: United States of America (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Seattle, Baltimore) [1998–2002]; Canada (Vancouver) [2000–2002]; Ireland (Dublin) [early 2000s]; selected other European countries with documented macrolide-resistant strains [2000s]; China (Shanghai and other urban sites) [2000s]; Japan [late 2000s]
Host: Humans with syphilis receiving macrolide therapy (primarily MSM and other sexually active adults)
Event summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, clinically significant macrolide-resistant Treponema pallidum was identified, with azithromycin treatment failures linked to A2058G mutations in the 23S rRNA gene first reported in patients in San Francisco and then elsewhere in North America and Europe. During the 2000s, surveillance documented rapidly increasing proportions of macrolide-resistant strains in U.S. and Canadian cities and in several European and Chinese settings, making macrolide monotherapy unreliable for syphilis treatment. By around 2010, macrolide-resistant T. pallidum had become prevalent on multiple continents, and international guidelines moved away from macrolides toward penicillin-based regimens except in narrowly defined circumstances.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread, often empiric use of azithromycin and other macrolides for STI and respiratory infections, including off-guideline use of single‑dose azithromycin as a convenient alternative to injectable benzathine penicillin for syphilis in some settings; overlapping high‑transmission sexual networks in MSM facilitated dissemination of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal spread of point mutations (A2058G and later A2059G) in the 23S rRNA gene of T. pallidum conferred high-level macrolide resistance, a clear example of antimicrobial resistance–driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Retain as a key global re-emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance, but the type-of-emergence coding has been aligned with the project rules: intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence have been set to false, because the species was long present on all affected continents and this episode reflects the emergence and spread of resistant lineages (re-emergence) rather than first occurrence in new regions. Country list has been slightly expanded to name major documented sites (e.g. Seattle, Baltimore) while still summarising other affected European locations in aggregate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Caribbean; South America
Countries: High-burden countries in sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique, Nigeria) [2010]; South and South-eastern Asia (e.g., India, Bangladesh, Indonesia) [2010]; Latin American and Caribbean countries with high congenital syphilis rates, notably Brazil and others in the Americas [2010]
Host: Humans – pregnant women and fetuses/newborns (congenital syphilis)
Event summary: During the first half of the 2010s, WHO and partners estimated that congenital syphilis caused around 661,000 cases and 355,000 adverse birth outcomes in 2016 alone, including approximately 204,000 fetal and neonatal deaths, with the highest burdens in sub-Saharan Africa, South and South‑eastern Asia, and parts of Latin America and the Caribbean. Despite regional elimination initiatives launched in the Americas and global strategies aimed at reducing congenital syphilis, many countries reported stagnant or rising rates of maternal and congenital syphilis through the mid‑2010s. By the later 2010s these persistently high burdens highlighted major gaps in antenatal screening and treatment and positioned congenital syphilis as a leading cause of preventable stillbirths and neonatal deaths in several regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High background prevalence of syphilis among adults, limited access to or quality of antenatal care, insufficient or late syphilis testing in pregnancy, shortages of benzathine penicillin and other commodities, and structural barriers such as poverty, rural residence, and weak health systems; stigma and lack of awareness further reduced care-seeking. Internal mechanisms: No specific pathogen evolutionary change has been implicated at the global level; this is a re-occurrence driven almost entirely by health-system and social factors, although local strain heterogeneity is present.
Review: review – Retain as a single, global-scale event highlighting the very large burden of congenital syphilis (hundreds of thousands of adverse birth outcomes annually), but type-of-emergence coding has been corrected so that this episode is treated solely as re-occurrence (intra_continental_emergence set to false). More authoritative sources (WHO 2019 news release and the Korenromp et al. PLOS ONE global burden analysis) have been added alongside existing PAHO and background references. The aggregation of multiple high-burden countries into one multi-continent row is reasonable for a global-burden event, but a human reviewer may wish to refine the country list if more granularity is needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – initially Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in remote northern and central Australia, later also urban MSM and heterosexual populations including pregnant women and newborns
Event summary: After years of relatively low incidence, an outbreak of infectious syphilis was declared in 2011 among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in north‑west Queensland, followed by outbreak declarations in the Northern Territory (2013), northern Western Australia (2014) and parts of South Australia (2016), with spread across much of northern and central Australia over the following decade. National notification rates rose roughly fourfold from about 6 per 100,000 population in 2011 to around 24 per 100,000 by 2019, and congenital syphilis, previously rare, re-emerged with at least dozens of affected infants and multiple deaths reported since the mid‑2010s. By 2025 syphilis was affecting every state and territory, with particularly high rates among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and rising incidence in women of reproductive age, leading Australia’s Chief Medical Officer to declare syphilis a Communicable Disease Incident of National Significance and prompting a coordinated national response for 2023–2030.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing social and structural inequities affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities (including overcrowded housing, limited access to culturally safe sexual health services, and poverty), under-resourced regional public health systems, increased mobility between remote communities and towns, and later, broader behavioral and network changes in urban MSM and heterosexual populations contributed to the resurgence. Gaps in antenatal screening and timely treatment in affected regions facilitated a parallel rise in congenital syphilis. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that a novel, more virulent T. pallidum strain caused the Australian outbreaks; they are best understood as re-occurrence driven by social and health-system factors, with macrolide resistance present but not the primary driver of incidence.
Review: review – New event added. The multi-jurisdictional infectious syphilis outbreak beginning in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in 2011, and evolving into a nationwide resurgence with re-emergent congenital syphilis and a formal declaration as a Communicable Disease Incident of National Significance in 2025, represents a major Oceania-region event in terms of public health impact. Classified as re-occurrence (no new strain, but marked failures of prevention and care) with correct continent/sub-region and country coding. A human reviewer should confirm the chosen 2011–2025 window and whether any additional Pacific countries should be included or whether this row should remain Australia-specific.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Japan [1994] (Aomori Prefecture – elementary school and nearby park using untreated spring water)
Host: Humans (primary-school children and local residents)
Event summary: In July 1994, public health authorities in Aomori Prefecture, northern Japan, investigated an outbreak of febrile gastroenteritis among primary-school pupils and park visitors who had drunk from a local spring used as a school and public water source. Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:3 was identified in patients and in the implicated spring water, and 52 persons were reported as outbreak cases. Closure and disinfection of the spring, provision of alternative drinking water and communication about avoiding untreated surface water were followed by cessation of new Yersinia-associated illnesses from the area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of untreated spring water as a drinking source for a school and public park, lack of routine chlorination or microbiological monitoring, and high summer consumption of the spring water by children. Internal mechanisms: environmental persistence and cold-tolerance of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica O:3 in fresh water; no evidence for a novel strain, resistance pattern or host shift compared with other O:3 lineages, so this is best classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Added as a major post-1990 outbreak (≈52 cases) documented in Japanese national food-hygiene summaries. Classified as re-occurrence within an already endemic country (Japan); geography and case numbers are well supported by government tabulations, but clinical details and exact case definition remain sparse and could be cross-checked against any dedicated outbreak report.

Countries: India [1996] (North Arcot District, Tamil Nadu – village feast)
Host: Humans (adults and children attending a village feast)
Event summary: On 29 September 1996, 48 villagers in North Arcot District, Tamil Nadu shared a vegetarian feast that included rice dishes and buttermilk; within about 16 hours on average, 25 participants (52%) developed acute diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, vomiting and fever, and seven required hospital care. Investigators cultured toxigenic Yersinia enterocolitica serotype O:3 biotype 4 from one patient’s stool and from the borewell water used to dilute the buttermilk, and illness was strongly associated with buttermilk consumption. After the contaminated borewell was withdrawn from use and safe water and food-hygiene practices were reinforced, no additional outbreak-related cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of inadequately protected borewell water to dilute buttermilk for a mass community meal, probable faecal contamination of the well (likely from nearby livestock), and lack of routine outbreak investigation and water-quality monitoring. Internal mechanisms: a heat-stable enterotoxin–producing Y. enterocolitica O:3/biotype 4 strain able to proliferate in buttermilk at refrigeration and ambient temperatures; however, this bioserotype was already recognised in India and elsewhere, with no evidence for new virulence traits or resistance, so the event represents re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Newly added as the first well-documented foodborne Y. enterocolitica outbreak in India (25 cases, seven hospitalisations). Classified as re-occurrence in a country where the pathogen was already known from sporadic cases; geography, case counts and vehicle match the Indian Journal of Medical Research report.

Host: Humans (children and adults)
Event summary: In mid-December 2003, an outbreak of Yersinia enterocolitica 4/O:3 infection was detected in the coastal city of Kotka, Finland, when several patients presented with severe abdominal pain and fever, with some undergoing appendectomy before yersiniosis was recognised. Approximately 30 persons were affected, and 12 culture-confirmed isolates of Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3 showed a characteristic multidrug-resistant phenotype and clustered by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis and multilocus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis, distinguishing them from sporadic background strains. After investigation and control measures targeting the suspected local food vehicle and improvements in hygiene, reported cases declined and the outbreak ended in early 2004.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Local contamination of a shared food or water source in Kotka (likely a pork or fresh-produce item, though the precise vehicle was not definitively identified) and winter consumption patterns that favoured exposure among families. Internal mechanisms: circulation of a multidrug-resistant Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3 strain with a distinct PFGE/MLVA profile compared to sporadic isolates, consistent with re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance and clonal expansion rather than geographical spread to a new region.
Review: Retain: One of the few well-described European Y. enterocolitica outbreaks post-1990 (≈30 cases, 12 confirmed) and notable for a distinct multidrug-resistant 4/O:3 clone. Classification as re-emergence is justified by the resistance profile and clonal signature; inter-/intra-continental flags correctly remain negative. Sources (Finnish national surveillance report and BMC Microbiology paper) are appropriate and specific to the event.

Host: Humans (nursery school children, mainly 3–6 years old)
Event summary: In late July 2004, a nursery school in Nara Prefecture reported multiple children with abrupt high fever, intense right lower abdominal pain and, in some cases, diarrhoea, prompting an investigation by local health authorities. Among 182 enrolled children, roughly 40 met the clinical case definition (≈36–42 symptomatic), and Yersinia enterocolitica serotype O8 biotype 1B—a highly pathogenic bioserotype rarely seen in Japan—was isolated from 16 symptomatic children, from a mixed apple salad served at lunch on 23 July, and from a composite sample of its raw ingredients. School meals were temporarily halted, the kitchen and equipment were disinfected, remaining ingredients were discarded and food-handling practices were reinforced; no additional cases occurred after these measures and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Preparation and serving of a mixed apple salad (apple, cucumber, potato, carrot, ham and mayonnaise) in a nursery-school kitchen with insufficient controls against contamination, exposing a highly susceptible population of young children, and limited early awareness of Y. enterocolitica as a cause of paediatric pseudoappendicitis. Internal mechanisms: involvement of Y. enterocolitica serotype O8 biotype 1B carrying yst, ail and virF virulence genes—more virulent and less common than the usual O:3 strains in Japan—which supports classification as re-emergence of a particularly pathogenic lineage rather than simple re-occurrence of endemic strains.
Review: Retain: Newly added and clearly among the most impactful post-1990 Y. enterocolitica outbreaks (≈40 paediatric cases, 13 hospitalisations) and the first documented O8 biotype 1B food-poisoning outbreak in Japan. Classified as re-emergence owing to the unusually virulent O8/1B bioserotype; inter-/intra-continental flags correctly remain negative. Sources are strong and event-specific (Jpn J Infect Dis case report plus national hazard database entry).

Countries: Norway [2005] (two neighbouring counties in southern Norway)
Host: Humans (primarily older adults, one child)
Event summary: Between December 21, 2005 and February 6, 2006, Norway’s National Reference Laboratory identified 11 cases of Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:9 biotype 2 infection in residents of two neighbouring counties, far exceeding the expected incidence for this serogroup. A case–control study linked illness to consumption of a ready-to-eat Christmas pork product (spiced headcheese, “julesylte”) manufactured at a single facility; most cases were elderly, four required hospitalisation and two died, and several reported prolonged symptoms or reactive arthritis. Following withdrawal of the implicated product lot, improvements in production hygiene and public risk communication, no further outbreak-related O:9 cases were reported from the affected counties.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal production and high winter consumption of a vacuum-packed ready-to-eat pork product distributed regionally, combined with the ability of Y. enterocolitica to grow at refrigeration temperatures and gaps in hygienic control late in the processing chain. Internal mechanisms: emergence of an outbreak-associated O:9 clone in a setting where O:9 infections had been rare, with severe disease and mortality in vulnerable older adults; this shift in dominant serogroup and clinical impact is consistent with functional re-emergence of a distinct pathogenic lineage rather than mere fluctuation in incidence.
Review: Retain: Moderate-sized but high-severity outbreak (11 cases, two deaths) that played an important role in highlighting ready-to-eat processed pork as a vehicle for Y. enterocolitica O:9 in Scandinavia. Classification as re-emergence is reasonable given the rare serogroup and severe outcomes; treating this as inter- or intra-continental emergence would be incorrect because human Y. enterocolitica was already established in Norway.

Host: Humans (adolescents and adults)
Event summary: In early 2011, Norway’s reference laboratory detected a cluster of Yersinia enterocolitica O:9 isolates sharing an identical, previously unseen multilocus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis (MLVA) profile, prompting a nationwide investigation. Ultimately 21 laboratory-confirmed cases were identified across 10 municipalities; a matched case–control study implicated a particular brand of ready-to-eat mixed salad, and traceback pointed to imported radicchio rosso as the most likely contaminated ingredient. After voluntary withdrawal of all salad mixes containing radicchio rosso from the Norwegian market, no additional outbreak-strain infections were reported and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Globalised supply chains for fresh leafy vegetables, centralised industrial washing and packing of mixed salads, and extended cold storage that allowed psychrotrophic Y. enterocolitica to persist and reach consumers. Internal mechanisms: emergence or introduction of a Y. enterocolitica O:9 strain with a unique MLVA profile not previously recorded in Norway, demonstrating clonal expansion via a novel fresh-produce vehicle; this fits the definition of re-emergence rather than first or inter-continental emergence.
Review: Retain: Well-characterised 21-case outbreak that was the first clearly documented Y. enterocolitica outbreak associated with bagged salad mix and a distinct O:9 MLVA profile. Classification as re-emergence (new clone and vehicle within an endemic country) is appropriate; no changes to geography or timing are needed.

Countries: United States of America [2011] (southwestern Pennsylvania – Allegheny and surrounding counties)
Host: Humans (children and adults)
Event summary: Between March 24 and August 5, 2011, surveillance in four counties of southwestern Pennsylvania detected an unusual increase in Yersinia enterocolitica infections: 22 residents met the definition for culture-confirmed yersiniosis, compared with only three to five cases over comparable periods in previous years. Sixteen patients reported consuming pasteurised milk or ice cream from a single small dairy (Dairy A), and Y. enterocolitica with an indistinguishable pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern was isolated from unopened ice cream and homemade yogurt prepared from Dairy A milk. After Dairy A voluntarily halted production, recalled products and corrected deficiencies in post-pasteurisation handling, no further outbreak-associated Yersinia cases were identified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Inadequate pasteurisation and post-pasteurisation hygiene at a farm-based dairy using reusable glass bottles, combined with wide household distribution of its milk and ice cream and the pathogen’s ability to grow at refrigeration temperatures. Internal mechanisms: survival and growth of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in dairy matrices; no evidence that the outbreak strain was unusually virulent or resistant compared with other O:9 lineages, so the event is best classified as re-occurrence driven by process failures rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Substantial dairy-associated outbreak (22 confirmed cases, seven hospitalisations, three ICU admissions) with clear implications for pasteurised-milk safety. Event summary has been updated to reflect the full 22-case outbreak described in the detailed epidemiologic study rather than only the initial 16 cases in the MMWR "Notes from the Field". Reclassified to re-occurrence, as drivers were pasteurisation and hygiene failures, not documented organismal change.

Countries: Japan [2012] (Nagano Prefecture – mountain hotel used for high-school trip)
Host: Humans (high-school students and two accompanying staff)
Event summary: In August 2012, a Tokyo high school group staying at a mountain hotel in central Japan experienced an outbreak of gastroenteritis: 39 of the 41 guests (37 students and 2 staff) developed abdominal pain, diarrhoea and fever. Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was isolated from 18 of 28 stool specimens, but despite extensive testing the pathogen was not recovered from specific menu items or the hotel environment, so the precise contaminated food vehicle remained undetermined. After the hotel suspended food service, implemented hygiene improvements and cooperated with the investigation, the outbreak ended and no further associated cases were reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mass catering of multiple meals to a large group at a mountain hotel with limited kitchen infrastructure, potential cross-contamination among foods prepared for consecutive meals and inadequate temperature control of perishable ingredients. Internal mechanisms: infection with pathogenic O:8 strains of a lineage already established in Japan; no evidence of novel virulence markers or resistance compared with prior O:8 outbreaks, so the event is best viewed as a high-impact re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Newly added large O:8 outbreak (39 cases) investigated by the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Public Health and listed in national food-poisoning statistics. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because it reflects spread of an already established O:8 lineage via mass catering; geography, serogroup and case numbers are internally consistent across Japanese sources.

Countries: Japan [2012] (Morioka City, Iwate Prefecture – ryokan hosting seven primary schools)
Host: Humans (primary-school children and accompanying adults)
Event summary: On 6 September 2012, an outbreak of acute febrile gastroenteritis occurred among seven primary-school groups from Miyagi, Aomori and Iwate Prefectures that had stayed at the same ryokan (traditional inn) in Morioka City, Iwate. Of 261 pupils and staff who ate the inn’s meals, 92 developed fever, abdominal pain, malaise and diarrhoea, making this the first recorded Yersinia enterocolitica food-poisoning incident in the prefecture. Because stool samples were collected late in convalescence, Y. enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was eventually isolated only from three symptomatic pupils using prolonged low-temperature enrichment, but the epidemiologic link to the inn’s catering was clear. The ryokan suspended meal service, thoroughly cleaned and disinfected its kitchen and revised its food-safety procedures; no additional related yersiniosis cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale preparation and serving of multiple meals to school groups in a single kitchen, likely contamination of one or more menu items with Y. enterocolitica O:8, and the organism’s ability to survive and possibly multiply during refrigeration, allowing exposure across several days and school cohorts. Internal mechanisms: involvement of pathogenic O:8 strains with typical virulence determinants; there is no evidence that a new serovar or resistance phenotype emerged, so the event is best classified as re-occurrence within an endemic setting.
Review: Retain: Added as one of the largest post-1990 Y. enterocolitica outbreaks globally (92 symptomatic cases among 261 exposed), and the first recognised O:8 food-poisoning event in Iwate Prefecture. Treated as a single temporally and epidemiologically linked episode; classified as re-occurrence. Geographic fields (Asia/Eastern Asia/Japan) and the multi-prefecture school involvement via a single ryokan are now explicitly captured.

Host: Humans (students living in a dormitory and kitchen staff)
Event summary: In April 2013, a student dormitory in Tokyo reported a cluster of acute diarrhoea and fever among residents; investigation identified 52 affected students. Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was isolated from 21 students and three kitchen workers, and intensive microbiological testing of stored foods, including prolonged cold enrichment with immunomagnetic bead concentration, eventually yielded O:8 with the same characteristics from a fresh vegetable salad served in the dormitory cafeteria. Following withdrawal of the implicated salad, reinforcement of kitchen hygiene and monitoring of food handling, the outbreak subsided and no further Yersinia infections linked to the dormitory kitchen were reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralised preparation of large batches of minimally processed vegetable salad for dormitory meals, contamination of raw produce or salad during preparation, and refrigeration practices that allowed psychrotrophic Y. enterocolitica to persist in ready-to-eat salads. Internal mechanisms: pathogenic O:8 strains of an established lineage capable of colonising raw vegetables; no indication of novel virulence or resistance beyond what had been observed in earlier O:8 outbreaks, so this event is classified as re-occurrence.
Review: Retain: Newly added large fresh-vegetable–associated outbreak (52 dormitory residents and staff) that, together with the Norwegian salad outbreaks, illustrates the growing importance of produce vehicles for Y. enterocolitica. Classified as re-occurrence; geography, case counts and vehicle are well supported by the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Public Health publication and national summaries.

Countries: Norway [2014] (four military bases in northern Norway; civilian cases from several counties)
Host: Humans (military recruits and staff, plus civilian population)
Event summary: In May 2014, a gastrointestinal illness cluster due to Yersinia enterocolitica O:9 was reported from a military base in northern Norway, coinciding with an increase in Yersinia notifications among civilians in the national surveillance system. A national investigation ultimately identified 133 laboratory-confirmed cases with a shared, previously unrecorded MLVA profile (5-6-9-8-9-9), including 117 cases linked to four military bases supplied by common catering contractors and 16 civilian cases from geographically dispersed counties; mixed salad (containing iceberg lettuce and radicchio rosso from a common supplier) was identified as the most likely vehicle. After contaminated salad components were withdrawn from military catering and restaurant menus and the upstream supply of radicchio rosso was addressed, case counts declined and the prolonged outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralised catering systems in the Norwegian Armed Forces and civilian cafeterias that widely distributed a contaminated mixed-salad component sourced from a common supplier, coupled with long shelf-life and refrigerated storage of chicory products (radicchio rosso) that favour survival of Y. enterocolitica. Internal mechanisms: clonal expansion of a specific O:9 strain defined by a distinctive MLVA profile not previously seen in Norway, demonstrating re-emergence of a particular genotype within an existing endemic range via a fresh-produce vehicle rather than spread to a new continent.
Review: Retain: The largest documented Y. enterocolitica outbreak in the post-1990 period (133 confirmed cases, predominantly among military recruits) and a key example of national dissemination through centrally sourced mixed salads. Classification as re-emergence of a distinct O:9 clone via food-system changes is appropriate; this event should definitely be retained among the top-impact outbreaks.

Host: Humans (including many with and some without HIV or other immunosuppression)
Event summary: From 1990 onward, clinicians in mainland China increasingly reported cases of histoplasmosis in patients who had never left the country, revealing that the fungus was locally acquired rather than only imported from the classic endemic Americas. Through case series and national reviews, more than 300 human cases were collated by 2011, with around three‑quarters from provinces along the Yangtze River basin and most considered autochthonous based on lack of travel to known endemic regions. By the end of this period, China was being described as a new or newly recognized endemic area for histoplasmosis, with accumulating evidence of widespread exposure and ongoing sporadic disease in Eastern Asia.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23216676/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased HIV prevalence and other causes of immunosuppression in China, combined with greater clinical awareness and wider use of culture, histopathology and antigen testing, led to better detection of a previously under-recognized endemic mycosis. Environmental drivers include suitable ecological niches for Histoplasma along the Yangtze River basin, such as bat- or bird-guano enriched soils that favor fungal growth. Internal mechanisms: This event mainly reflects geographic range recognition rather than clear evidence of novel genotypes; phylogenetic work suggests multiple lineages in East Asia, likely introduced or dispersed over time by human activity or animal migration rather than a single new strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23216676/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the post‑1990 recognition of autochthonous histoplasmosis in China as a newly appreciated endemic focus in Eastern Asia. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) is appropriate because histoplasmosis was already known elsewhere in Asia (e.g. India, Southeast Asia) but not previously documented as locally acquired in China. Timeframe (1990–2011), geography (China, Eastern Asia) and sources are consistent with major reviews and mapping papers; no higher‑impact Asian emergence event was identified that would displace this one.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: French Guiana [1992]; Brazil [1990s]; Mexico [1990s]; other Latin American and Caribbean countries with advanced HIV (e.g. Colombia, Guatemala, Argentina, various Caribbean territories) [1990s‑2010s]
Host: Humans living with HIV, especially with advanced HIV disease (AIDS)
Event summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, disseminated histoplasmosis emerged as a leading AIDS-defining opportunistic infection and cause of death among people with advanced HIV in several Latin American settings, notably French Guiana and likely other South and Central American countries. Longitudinal cohorts from French Guiana documented hundreds of microbiologically proven disseminated cases from the early 1990s through the 2010s, with incidence rates up to 15 cases per 1,000 person‑years in HIV cohorts and case‑fatality comparable to or exceeding tuberculosis when diagnosis was delayed. Modelling and multicountry data later showed that, by around 2012, HIV-associated histoplasmosis incidence and deaths in Latin America rivalled or exceeded those due to tuberculosis in people living with HIV, cementing its role as a major, previously neglected killer in this region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6958354/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The HIV epidemic created large populations of profoundly immunosuppressed individuals in endemic Histoplasma regions of Latin America, dramatically increasing the probability of progression from latent or subclinical infection to disseminated disease. Health-system factors—limited awareness, misdiagnosis as tuberculosis, and poor access to rapid antigen testing and effective antifungals—contributed heavily to high mortality, making histoplasmosis a neglected opportunistic infection. External social drivers included poverty, delayed HIV testing, and late presentation to care. Internal mechanisms: No single new fungal genotype is implicated; rather, established Histoplasma lineages caused severe disease in immunocompromised hosts, demonstrating host-population expansion (high-risk HIV group) and clinical re-expression of an old pathogen under new immunologic conditions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10687118/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event summarizes the very large burden of HIV-associated disseminated histoplasmosis in Latin America and the Caribbean, which modelling shows to cause incidence and mortality comparable to or greater than tuberculosis among people with HIV in the region. The classification as re-occurrence (resurgence in already endemic subregions driven mainly by external factors: HIV epidemic, weak diagnostics, late ART) is appropriate; intra-/inter‑continental emergence are rightly not used. Countries and subregions match the UNSD structure for Latin America, though the country list is necessarily selective rather than exhaustive; this could be further detailed in future iterations but does not warrant exclusion.

Host: Humans (mostly immunocompetent or mildly immunosuppressed; some with underlying conditions)
Event summary: Between roughly 1990 and the early 2000s, European mycology centers began systematically reporting histoplasmosis cases, revealing that while most were imported from the Americas or Africa, a subset represented true autochthonous infections acquired within Europe. A multicountry survey by the European Confederation of Medical Mycology collected 118 human cases from 1995–1999, including several patients from Italy and Germany with no travel to known endemic zones, while separate studies isolated Histoplasma from soil in Italy’s Po River valley and documented positive histoplasmin skin tests in local residents. By the early 2000s, these findings had redefined Europe—from a region previously thought to see histoplasmosis only as an imported disease—to one with small but real endemic foci of Histoplasma in Southern and Western Europe.([air.unimi.it](https://air.unimi.it/handle/2434/49487?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental conditions along river valleys and caves or bat roosts in parts of Southern and Central Europe appear suitable for Histoplasma establishment, and increased surveillance plus case reporting in reference centers allowed recognition of locally acquired disease. Human travel and animal migration between endemic regions and Europe likely introduced diverse Histoplasma genotypes over time. Internal mechanisms: Genetic work indicates that European strains belong to an ‘Eurasian’ clade whose diversity suggests relatively long-standing presence rather than a single recent introduction; the emergence signal here is primarily geographic range recognition and renewed clinical attention (re-occurrence) rather than evolution of a new, more virulent variant.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9410202/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The original row incorrectly classified this episode as an inter‑continental emergence, but autochthonous histoplasmosis in Europe (especially Italy) was documented before 1990, and environmental isolation from Italian soil dates back to the 1960s. This period (1990–2004) is better interpreted as re-occurrence in previously known European subregions (Southern, Western Europe), driven by improved surveillance and recognition. Changes made: set inter_continental_emergence to false; set re_occurrence to true; removed Turkey from the country list because Turkey is in Western Asia under the UNSD scheme and its autochthonous cases are handled within Asian context, not this European event. Content and sources otherwise remain appropriate but should be rechecked by a domain expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [2005]; France [2005]; Italy [2005]; Ireland [2010s]; Switzerland [2010s]; Portugal [2010s]
Host: Humans, especially migrants and travelers from endemic areas, people living with HIV, and other immunosuppressed patients
Event summary: From 2005 onward, an increasing number of histoplasmosis cases were diagnosed in Europe, largely among migrants, travelers and immunosuppressed individuals cared for in tertiary centers. A systematic review of European cases from 2005–2020 found that most diagnoses occurred in Spain, France and Italy and were imported from Latin America or French overseas territories, but it also documented several autochthonous infections (four in Italy, two in Spain and one in Ireland) and growing environmental detections of Histoplasma in bats and soil in countries such as Portugal, indicating true local acquisition in scattered foci. By the late 2010s this pattern had established histoplasmosis as a persistent imported infection with small endemic foci in Western, Southern and Northern Europe, representing intra‑continental emergence into a new European subregion (Northern Europe) in addition to re-recognized foci in previously affected subregions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8231918/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased international migration and travel from highly endemic Latin American and African regions to Western Europe, together with better diagnostic capacity for fungal infections in European reference hospitals, led to higher recognition of both imported and rare indigenous cases. The growing populations of persons with advanced HIV, solid-organ transplants, or receiving biologic immunosuppressants created susceptible hosts in areas where Histoplasma had historically been absent or rare. Internal mechanisms: The event is driven more by movement and detection of pre‑existing Histoplasma lineages than by new variants; identification of an ‘Eurasian’ clade and molecular detection of Histoplasma in European bat guano (including in Portugal) suggest successful ecological establishment and geographic range expansion of certain lineages within Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9410202/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The original row combined European trends with the first autochthonous case from Israel and broadly labelled the whole episode as intra‑continental emergence. Here it has been restricted to Europe only, with subregions updated to include Northern Europe because the 2005–2020 review documents an autochthonous case from Ireland. Classification as intra‑continental emergence is retained to reflect extension of recognised endemicity into a new UNSD European subregion, while imported cases and small endemic foci in Western/Southern Europe are part of the same clinically and temporally linked pattern. Changes made: continent limited to Europe; sub_regions expanded to add Northern Europe; countries list extended to include Ireland, Switzerland and Portugal; references to Israel and the Middle East were removed from the summary and mechanism text. This row should be retained but reviewed for exact country‑year anchors as more detailed European data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (single documented autochthonous case: immunocompetent adult with laryngeal and probable disseminated histoplasmosis)
Event summary: Although Histoplasma had been isolated decades earlier from bat guano in a cave in northern Israel, no human infections were believed to be locally acquired in the Middle East. In 2018, clinicians reported an adult man from northern Israel with chronic hoarseness, weight loss and laryngeal lesions, with no travel history outside the country, whose biopsy, culture and molecular testing confirmed Histoplasma capsulatum infection, representing the first documented autochthonous histoplasmosis case from Israel and the wider Middle East. This report, together with older environmental isolates, triggered re‑evaluation of regional endemicity and raised the likelihood that additional pulmonary or disseminated cases in Western Asia had previously gone unrecognized or been misdiagnosed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: This emergence signal is driven mainly by improved clinical suspicion and access to histopathology and molecular mycology in Israeli tertiary hospitals, which allowed recognition of a case that might previously have been mistaken for malignancy or tuberculosis. Environmental drivers include bat‑inhabited caves and guano‑contaminated soils in northern Israel that can support Histoplasma growth, indicating that the fungus has likely been present locally for decades. Internal mechanisms: No novel lineage has been implicated; genetic data are limited, and the case is best interpreted as geographic range recognition and intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian subregion (Western Asia), rather than evolution of a new, more virulent strain.
Review: review – This is a newly added row to capture the first documented autochthonous human histoplasmosis case in Israel and the broader Middle East, which was previously folded into a combined Europe–Israel event. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) is appropriate: histoplasmosis was already known from other Asian subregions (Indian subcontinent, Southeast and East Asia), and the case demonstrates in situ infection in Western Asia rather than an imported episode. Because only a single autochthonous case is documented so far, this event is small in case count but justified as a key geographic range extension; it should be retained but flagged for expert review of the time window and whether additional Middle Eastern cases merit inclusion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans receiving tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α) blockers or other biologic immunosuppressive therapies; also people with HIV and other immunosuppression
Event summary: In the early 2000s, the widespread introduction of TNF‑α blockers and other biologic agents for autoimmune diseases in the United States led to recognition of a new high‑risk group for severe histoplasmosis within endemic areas. Analyses of U.S. hospitalizations for histoplasmosis from 2001–2012 showed substantial morbidity and mortality, while a multicenter review of nearly 100 patients on TNF‑α blockers who developed histoplasmosis between 2000 and 2011 found that over three‑quarters had disseminated disease, prompting the U.S. FDA in 2008 to issue a boxed warning about endemic mycoses with TNF‑α inhibitors. By the end of this period, histoplasmosis had re‑emerged as a significant iatrogenic opportunistic infection in biologic‑treated patients, altering risk profiles in endemic parts of Northern America.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/38201/cdc_38201_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid uptake of TNF‑α inhibitors and related biologic therapies for rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and other conditions created a growing population with impaired cell‑mediated immunity living in long‑established Histoplasma‑endemic zones. Clinical practice patterns (e.g. intensified immunosuppression prior to adequate screening or counseling about fungal risks) and limited early awareness of this association contributed to severe disease. Internal mechanisms: Histoplasma did not acquire known resistance or virulence changes in this setting; rather, host-population expansion to a new iatrogenically immunosuppressed group led to increased incidence and severity, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced opportunity for dissemination.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/38201/cdc_38201_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event appropriately highlights emergence of a large, clearly defined new risk group (patients receiving TNF‑α blockers and related biologic therapies) in a long‑endemic region. The classification as re-emergence (driven by host expansion rather than geographic spread or pathogen change) matches the definitions; intra-/inter‑continental emergence are correctly left as false because the fungus and disease were long established in North America. Timeframe (2001–2012) and sources align with hospitalization data and the TNF‑blocker case series and FDA warnings; no higher‑impact North American event of similar type was identified that would supersede this one.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Nigeria [2014]; multiple other African countries including Uganda, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Cameroon, Senegal and South Africa with documented histoplasmosis cases and increasing recognition in the literature [1990s–2010s, resurgence and underdiagnosis highlighted post‑2010]
Host: Humans, predominantly people with advanced HIV disease and patients misdiagnosed with tuberculosis
Event summary: Although histoplasmosis has long been present in Africa, from about the mid‑2010s onward new studies and reviews highlighted it as an emerging or neglected disease, particularly among people with advanced HIV. A continent‑wide review up to 2017 identified 470 documented cases from across Africa and emphasized likely large underdiagnosis, while work in Nigeria using histoplasmin skin tests and, later, Histoplasma antigen assays showed substantial prior exposure and that around 7–8% of advanced HIV patients with compatible syndromes had probable disseminated histoplasmosis. By the early 2020s, these data had reframed histoplasmosis as a significant, previously hidden contributor to morbidity and mortality among HIV‑infected Africans, especially in West Africa and Southern Africa, prompting calls to integrate antigen testing and antifungal treatment into HIV care packages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The generalized HIV epidemic in sub‑Saharan Africa created many individuals with profound cell‑mediated immunodeficiency, greatly increasing susceptibility to disseminated histoplasmosis. Concurrently, limited mycology capacity and high tuberculosis burden led to frequent misclassification of histoplasmosis as TB; expanded use of antigen detection, targeted prevalence studies and systematic reviews in the 2010s acted as drivers of apparent emergence by revealing previously overlooked disease. Socioeconomic factors like poverty, occupational exposure (e.g. farming, cave or mine work) and limited access to specialist care enhanced risk and delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a novel African Histoplasma genotype suddenly arising during this period; rather, long‑established H. capsulatum and H. duboisii lineages caused more recognized disease in the new context of widespread HIV, aligning with a re‑occurrence pattern dominated by external drivers.
Review: review – This row correctly treats the African signal as re-occurrence in long‑endemic subregions, driven by HIV, diagnostic limitations and health‑system factors rather than by new strains or spread to new continents. However, the original wording of sub_regions (“Western Africa; other African subregions”) was not aligned with the UNSD list; this has been corrected to explicitly name Western, Eastern, Middle and Southern Africa. The countries field has been clarified to list exemplar countries with documented HIV‑linked histoplasmosis or high exposure (Nigeria, Uganda, DRC, Cameroon, Senegal, South Africa), though many others also contribute. Because the exact start year of renewed recognition is somewhat arbitrary and cases span 1950s–2010s, this episode should be retained but kept flagged for expert review of the temporal bounds and country coverage.
