Countries: Brazil [1990s] – agricultural frontier states on the eastern Amazon border (Maranhão, Pará, Tocantins)
Host: Humans (primarily adult male rural workers engaged in agriculture, cattle ranching, and deforestation‑related activities)
Event summary: From the 1990s into the early 2000s, paracoccidioidomycosis was increasingly reported along the eastern border of the Brazilian Amazon, especially in the states of Maranhão, Pará, and Tocantins, where disease had previously been rare. As federal colonization programs, road construction, and expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching drove migration into newly deforested frontier zones, clinical series and sero‑epidemiologic data documented the establishment of new endemic and hyperendemic foci of paracoccidioidomycosis. By the early 2000s this eastern Amazon belt was recognized as part of an expanded endemic area, with sustained transmission among rural populations exposed to disturbed soils.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Government‑promoted colonization of frontier lands, highway building, deforestation, and rapid expansion of coffee, crops, and cattle ranching along the eastern Amazon border increased human encroachment into forest soils harboring Paracoccidioides and generated intense soil disturbance. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of established Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex lineages into newly deforested and cultivated zones; there is no evidence that a single novel genotype alone drove this spread, but pre‑existing strains colonized new ecological niches created by land‑use change.
Review: retain – Event corresponds to the well‑described expansion of paracoccidioidomycosis into the eastern Amazon border (Maranhão, Pará, Tocantins) linked to agricultural frontiers and migration. Geography (Brazil, South America | South America), time window (1990s–early 2000s), and classification as intra‑continental emergence into new Brazilian sub‑regions are consistent with major reviews. No changes made beyond minor wording; sources are appropriate and high‑quality.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Brazil [1997] – Rondônia state (especially southeastern Rondônia, Western Amazon)
Host: Humans (rural workers, migrants, and indigenous populations including Suruí people)
Event summary: Beginning around 1997, a pronounced increase in paracoccidioidomycosis cases was documented in Rondônia in Brazil’s Western Amazon, particularly in the southeastern part of the state. Case series, mortality data, and skin‑test surveys showed that this region had rapidly become a new hyperendemic focus, with incidence estimates in some localities reaching several tens of cases per 100,000 inhabitants per year. Through the 2000s the area remained a sustained hotspot, although later data suggest some gradual decline in incidence after the peak period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid deforestation of primary forest, settlement schemes, road building, cattle ranching, and expansion of coffee and other crops brought large numbers of non‑immune migrants and indigenous residents into recently disturbed forest soils. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of P. brasiliensis complex into the Western Amazon and establishment of stable transmission cycles in agro‑forestry mosaics; no specific single genotype has been identified as the sole driver, so the event is interpreted primarily as spatial expansion rather than strain‑level emergence.
Review: retain – Rondônia’s emergence as a hyperendemic area from 1997 onward is clearly documented and commonly cited as a major epidemiologic shift. Time frame and geography are appropriate, and classification as intra‑continental emergence into a new Amazonian sub‑region matches the definitions. No corrections to event coding were necessary; sources are relevant primary and review articles.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [early 2000s] – Midwestern and Northern regions including Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás, Rondônia, Pará
Host: Humans (patients with clinical paracoccidioidomycosis in Midwestern and Western Amazon regions)
Event summary: From the early 2000s into the 2010s, molecular and serologic studies of paracoccidioidomycosis cases from Brazil’s Midwest and parts of the Amazon revealed that many infections were caused by a phylogenetically distinct lineage, later named Paracoccidioides lutzii. Because standard P. brasiliensis–based serologic tests have reduced sensitivity for this species, its burden had been underestimated. Subsequent clinical series from Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás, Rondônia, and adjacent areas documented numerous P. lutzii‑associated cases and led to revision of Paracoccidioides taxonomy and diagnostic algorithms. Transmission of this lineage continues in these regions, contributing substantially to disease burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of agriculture and settlement into central Brazil and western Amazonia created and sustained foci where P. lutzii predominates, while improved access to mycology laboratories and molecular tools allowed species‑level identification. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype/species emergence within the Paracoccidioides complex (formal recognition of P. lutzii) with antigenic divergence that reduced the performance of traditional gp43‑based serologic assays. This represents re‑emergence through recognition and spread of a distinct species rather than simple geographic extension of previously known P. brasiliensis.
Review: review – Reclassified this event as re‑emergence only (intra‑continental emergence set to false) because, under the unified EPP "Paracoccidioides spp." for humans, the affected Brazilian sub‑regions were already endemic for paracoccidioidomycosis; the key novelty is species‑level differentiation and antigenic divergence (P. lutzii) rather than first presence of the genus. Removed the Wikipedia species URL in favor of peer‑reviewed sources documenting P. lutzii distribution and clinical relevance. Event remains one of the major post‑2000 emergence phenomena but should be interpreted as strain/genotype‑driven re‑emergence, not geographic first occurrence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Argentina [2010] – Northeast Argentina (Chaco and Corrientes provinces along the Paraná River/Yacyretá reservoir)
Host: Humans (children and adolescents 10–16 years with acute/subacute infant‑juvenile paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2012, clinicians in Northeast Argentina, historically an area with high incidence of chronic adult paracoccidioidomycosis but very few juvenile cases, detected several children and adolescents with acute/subacute disseminated disease. This represented an unusual cluster of the infant‑juvenile form in a region where only one such case had been reported in the previous decade. The cluster was temporally linked to the preceding 2009 El Niño–Southern Oscillation event and to major environmental changes in the Paraná River valley associated with the Yacyretá hydroelectric dam, and was characterized by severe systemic presentations requiring intensive management. After this period, juvenile cases have continued to be monitored, but no comparable explosive cluster has been described.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional climatic anomalies (strong El Niño‑related rainfall and flooding around 2009), extensive deforestation, agricultural expansion, and long‑term hydrological and ecological changes due to the Yacyretá dam altered soil moisture and vegetation in Northeast Argentina, likely increasing airborne dispersal of Paracoccidioides propagules and exposure of children and adolescents. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was identified; available data suggest the same Paracoccidioides lineages circulating in the area, so the event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence (a sharp increase in a previously rare clinical form) driven by environmental and social factors rather than intrinsic fungal change.
Review: retain – This event was missing from the original dataset and has been added because the 2010–2012 infant‑juvenile cluster in Northeast Argentina is repeatedly highlighted in the literature as a notable emergence of acute/subacute PCM linked to climatic and anthropogenic change. Classified as re‑occurrence (increase of a rare clinical form in a long‑endemic sub‑region) rather than intra‑continental emergence, since the area was already endemic for adult PCM. Time window, geography, and drivers follow the Medical Mycology case series and related Argentine epidemiologic reviews; sources are appropriate primary and review articles. Recommended to retain as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Brazil [2015] – Rio de Janeiro state (metropolitan area, Raphael de Almeida Magalhães ring‑road/highway corridor in Baixada Fluminense)
Host: Humans (mainly young adults and adolescents with acute/subacute paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event summary: During December 2015–December 2016, a reference center in Rio de Janeiro state diagnosed eight acute/subacute cases of paracoccidioidomycosis among residents of municipalities bordering the newly built Raphael de Almeida Magalhães Highway (Arco Metropolitano). This represented a more than five‑fold increase over the expected annual number of acute cases from the area, in a state where PCM was already endemic. The temporal and spatial clustering of cases near segments of highway constructed between 2008 and 2014, together with environmental sampling that detected Paracoccidioides DNA in soils along the road, supported interpretation as an outbreak linked to massive earthworks and deforestation. After completion of the most intense construction phases and with time for the exposed cohort to pass through the incubation window, incidence rates of new acute cases declined toward background levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale civil engineering for the Arco Metropolitano (2008–2014), including deforestation and removal of large volumes of soil in Atlantic forest remnants, generated dust plumes and altered local microclimates; a strong El Niño event in 2015–2016 further increased rainfall and soil humidity, conditions known to favor sporulation and aerial dispersion of Paracoccidioides conidia. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype has been uniquely associated with this cluster; it is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by intense environmental disturbance and increased inhalational exposure, rather than intrinsic fungal evolution.
Review: review – Corrected the event years to 2015–2016 (matching the documented diagnostic period for the Baixada Fluminense outbreak) and adjusted the country field to Brazil [2015]; original entry used 2014–2016, which blurred construction and clinical periods. Added two key sources: a study detecting Paracoccidioides DNA in soils along the highway and a Rio de Janeiro cohort describing temporal changes in acute PCM incidence, both reinforcing the environmental‑disturbance interpretation. Classification as re‑occurrence (in an already endemic state) without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2014] – Tocantins state (Northern region, Tocantins‑Araguaia basin) with adjacent areas of Goiás, Pará, Maranhão
Host: Humans (rural populations including farmers, fishers, and other workers in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin)
Event summary: In the mid‑2010s, a detailed clinical and eco‑epidemiological investigation in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin in northern Brazil identified 106 new paracoccidioidomycosis cases over 27 months, corresponding to more than 47 cases per year. This incidence ranked northern Tocantins and surrounding areas of Goiás, Pará, and Maranhão as a novel hyperendemic zone for the disease, in contrast to previous perceptions of only sporadic cases. The study led to calls for making PCM a notifiable disease in the region and for intensified surveillance and diagnostic capacity. Transmission remains active, and the basin is now recognized as part of Brazil’s northern endemic belt.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid land‑use change in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin, including deforestation of riparian forests, expansion of cattle and soybean production, road construction, hydro‑agricultural projects, and population inflows to new rural settlements, increased soil disturbance and human contact with Paracoccidioides reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) and consolidation of Paracoccidioides spp. in newly disturbed agro‑ecosystems; molecular assays could not fully discriminate species in this area, but there is no evidence that a single novel lineage alone explains the hyperendemicity.
Review: retain – The Tocantins‑Araguaia basin has been clearly defined as a new hyperendemic area with very high incidence (≈47 cases/year at a single reference hospital), and is widely cited as a major recent geographic expansion of PCM. The time window and geography in the original entry are consistent with the available data and with the linked eco‑epidemiologic study. Classification as intra‑continental emergence into a previously under‑recognized northern sub‑region is appropriate. No changes beyond minor wording; sources remain suitable.

Countries: Brazil [2016] – Ceará state (mountainous semi‑arid area in Northeastern Brazil, previously considered non‑endemic)
Host: Humans (adult male rural resident with chronic mucocutaneous paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event summary: In 2016, a man from a mountainous rural area of Ceará state, in Brazil’s semi‑arid Northeast, was diagnosed with autochthonous chronic paracoccidioidomycosis despite no travel to known endemic regions. Earlier reviews had characterized this part of Ceará as having very low endemicity with no confirmed local cases, so the report was interpreted as expansion of the recognized geographic range of Paracoccidioides within Brazil. Since publication in 2019, clinicians in the region have been alerted to consider PCM in differential diagnoses, although no large cluster from this microregion has yet been documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely related to localized environmental and land‑use changes (e.g., small‑scale agriculture, soil disturbance, and possibly microclimatic shifts in mountainous semi‑arid zones) combined with increased clinician awareness and access to mycological diagnosis in Northeastern Brazil. Internal mechanisms: Possible geographic range expansion or detection of a previously cryptic focus of Paracoccidioides in a new Brazilian sub‑region; there is no evidence for a novel strain, so the event is treated as intra‑continental emergence rather than classic re‑emergence.
Review: retain – The Ceará case is clearly framed in the primary report as the first autochthonous PCM from a mountainous area previously considered non‑endemic, justifying intra‑continental emergence into a new Brazilian sub‑region. Time, place, and interpretation are consistent with the literature. Because this is a single case rather than a cluster, its inclusion is justified mainly by its geographic significance; however, it still falls within the top tier of distinct emergence events for this pathogen. No coding changes were required.

Host: Humans (mainly immunocompetent or mildly immunocompromised adults); also domestic animals and wildlife (part of the same environmental focus but not the primary focus of this human event sheet)
Event summary: In 1999, Cryptococcus gattii emerged as a cause of cryptococcosis on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada, in a previously non‑endemic, temperate coastal forest environment, with the earliest recognized human and animal cases traced to that year and environmental isolation from trees and soil confirming local reservoirs. Over 1999–2007 more than 200 human cases were reported in British Columbia, with spread from Vancouver Island to mainland British Columbia and additional cases in residents and travelers exposed in the outbreak area, establishing a new temperate, coastal focus of disease distinct from earlier tropical and subtropical endemic zones.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) By the early 2010s, incidence in British Columbia had declined from its peak but C. gattii VGII lineages remained established in the environment, with continued sporadic human and animal cases in the broader Pacific Northwest region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely long‑distance dispersal of C. gattii VGII lineages (probably originating from South America or Australia) via movement of contaminated plant material, timber, soil, animals or shipping routes into coastal British Columbia, where mild, wet winters and dry summers, together with specific tree species and forestry/land‑use practices, favored establishment and aerosolization of infectious propagules.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23940707/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion into a novel temperate ecological niche; emergence and clonal expansion of hypervirulent VGIIa (and related VGII) genotypes capable of infecting predominantly immunocompetent hosts; and evidence of enhanced virulence/pathogenicity and efficient environmental persistence compared with many historical tropical strains.
Review: retain – The Vancouver Island/British Columbia episode is correctly captured as a major high‑incidence emergence in a new temperate niche and is among the largest global C. gattii events. However, inter_continental_emergence has been changed from Yes to No because C. gattii had already been documented clinically and environmentally in North America (southern California and the southeastern United States) well before 1999, so this episode represents a large regional re‑emergence and climatic range expansion within an already affected continent rather than first introduction.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/11/18-0975)) Countries, years and summary text remain consistent with major epidemiologic descriptions of the Vancouver Island and mainland British Columbia outbreak, so no further structural changes are recommended.

Host: Humans (both immunocompetent and immunocompromised adults), with linked infections in domestic animals and wildlife in the same region
Event summary: Beginning in 2004, clusters of autochthonous human C. gattii infections were recognized in Oregon and Washington, USA, in patients without travel to Vancouver Island, indicating that the pathogen had established environmental reservoirs in the U.S. Pacific Northwest in addition to those in British Columbia. Over 2004–2010, public health investigations documented dozens of locally acquired human cases, including infections caused by a novel VGIIc subtype apparently confined to Oregon alongside VGIIa and VGIIb strains closely related to the Vancouver Island outbreak lineage, and showed that clinical disease ranged from severe pneumonia to central nervous system cryptococcomas with substantial mortality.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) By around 2010, C. gattii was recognized as an endemic pathogen in parts of the U.S. Pacific Northwest, with ongoing sporadic cases and heightened clinical and laboratory awareness rather than unchecked epidemic growth.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued environmental establishment of C. gattii in forested and peri‑urban habitats of the U.S. Pacific Northwest, combined with human recreational and occupational exposure to contaminated trees and soils, sustained transmission within the region; increased clinical and laboratory awareness and targeted surveillance also enhanced case detection. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence, notably the VGIIc subtype in Oregon, representing a genetically distinct lineage associated with severe pulmonary and CNS disease; geographic range expansion within the Northern America subregion; and possible increased virulence/pathogenicity and environmental fitness of specific VGII lineages that enabled successful colonization of new microclimates and hosts.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13))
Review: retain – This row appropriately highlights the substantial number of autochthonous C. gattii cases and the emergence of the distinct VGIIc subtype in the U.S. Pacific Northwest, which together constitute a major re‑emergence episode within the broader Vancouver Island–Pacific Northwest outbreak.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) To better align with the event definition and country‑format rules, the countries field has been restricted to “United States of America [2004]” (removing Canada, which is already covered in the 1999–2013 event), and the summary has been lightly edited to emphasize that this episode reflects establishment and diversification of C. gattii in the U.S. rather than a separate inter‑continental emergence. The classification as re_emergence = Yes and intra_/inter‑continental emergence = No is appropriate, so the event is retained but flagged for review due to its partial overlap with the Vancouver Island episode; depending on how much granularity is desired, the two North American rows could alternatively be merged into a single linked episode in a later harmonization step.

Host: Humans (sporadic autochthonous cases, including immunocompetent adults) with linked environmental reservoirs identified in eucalyptus and carob trees and in forest habitats; additional cases in animals and travelers are epidemiologically linked but not the primary focus here.
Event summary: From the late 1990s onward, autochthonous C. gattii infections were documented in Mediterranean Europe, including clinical cases in Italy and Spain and associated environmental isolates from Eucalyptus camaldulensis and carob trees near patients’ residences, confirming that parts of Southern Europe harbored endemic foci rather than only imported infections.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) Around 2010–2012, environmental sampling in the Netherlands identified C. gattii in a forested area and linked it to a local human case, extending the known ecological range of the species into temperate Northern Europe and demonstrating that suitable niches exist beyond the Mediterranean climate zone.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/11-1190_article?utm_source=openai)) By the early 2010s, Europe was recognized as having both endemic Mediterranean clusters (largely AFLP4/VGI) and emergent temperate foci of C. gattii, with overall human case numbers still low but increasingly understood as a mix of locally acquired and travel‑related infections and reactivation of dormant infections acquired outside Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mediterranean and some temperate European climates, together with widespread planting of susceptible tree species (e.g. Eucalyptus, carob), appear to support environmental persistence of C. gattii, and international movement of trees, plant material and travelers from endemic tropical regions likely introduced and redistributed genotypes within Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion into new European subregions (Northern Europe) and climatic zones; local adaptation of predominant European AFLP4/VGI genotypes to Mediterranean and temperate tree hosts and environments; and a combination of reactivation of long‑dormant infections and in situ environmental transmission, consistent with re‑emergence driven by both host factors and pathogen ecology.
Review: review – The European episode is correctly identified as an important mix of autochthonous and travel‑related C. gattii infections with clear evidence of endemic Mediterranean foci and a newly recognized temperate niche in the Netherlands, and thus merits inclusion as one of the major global emergence/re‑emergence events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) To comply better with the country‑format guidance, the countries field has been updated from vague labels ("mid‑2000s", "2000s", "2010–2012") to approximate start years based on the first documented autochthonous clinical or environmental reports in each country (Italy [1997], Spain [2003], Netherlands [2010]); these dates should be treated as indicative rather than exact and therefore warrant a review flag. The dual classification as intra_continental_emergence = Yes (expansion into Northern Europe) and re_emergence = Yes (increased recognition and local adaptation of existing genotypes within Europe) is appropriate and has been retained.

Host: Humans (predominantly adults with advanced HIV infection, but including some HIV‑negative patients) in a high‑HIV‑prevalence province; no specific livestock production impacts documented in this series.
Event summary: Between March 2002 and February 2004, population‑based laboratory surveillance for cryptococcosis in Gauteng Province, South Africa, identified 46 patients infected with C. gattii, representing one of the largest documented series of C. gattii disease globally and occurring in the context of a generalized HIV epidemic.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Most patients presented with subacute meningitis or meningoencephalitis, often with severe immunosuppression due to AIDS, and cases were identified across multiple hospitals, indicating province‑wide risk rather than a single point‑source outbreak. After 2004, C. gattii has continued to account for a small but important fraction of cryptococcal disease in South Africa, but the 2002–2004 enhanced surveillance period remains the key episode defining the burden and clinical profile of C. gattii infection in this high‑HIV, Southern African setting.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high prevalence of advanced, untreated HIV infection in Gauteng during the early 2000s greatly increased the susceptible human population for cryptococcal disease, while the implementation of active, laboratory‑based surveillance and species‑level identification exposed the contribution of C. gattii within the broader cryptococcosis burden; environmental reservoirs of serotype C (VGIV) C. gattii in southern Africa, documented in earlier mycologic and environmental studies, likely provided longstanding exposure that became clinically manifest as HIV prevalence rose.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence that a novel genotype or major change in virulence drove this episode; instead, infections predominantly involved existing serotype C lineages, so the episode is best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven by external host and surveillance factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This newly added event captures a major, temporally bounded episode in Gauteng Province, South Africa, where population‑based surveillance during 2002–2004 identified 46 C. gattii infections, making it one of the largest documented series outside Australia and the Pacific Northwest and clearly within the top tier of global emergence episodes by case count.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Classification as re_occurrence = Yes (driven largely by the HIV epidemic and enhanced surveillance) with intra_/inter‑continental emergence = No and re_emergence = No appropriately reflects current evidence that C. gattii (especially serotype C/VGIV) was already present in southern Africa before 2002 and that no single new genotype has been implicated in this increase. Country, subregion and timeframe follow the original surveillance definitions; additional local series from Botswana and other provinces exist but have much smaller case numbers, so they are not added as separate top‑10 events.

Countries: South Africa [1990-2006]; Botswana [1990-2006]; Uganda [1990-2006]; Zambia [1990-2006]; Zimbabwe [1990-2006]; Malawi [1990-2006]; Kenya [1990-2006]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990-2006]; Ethiopia [1990-2006]; Nigeria [1990-2006]; Cameroon [1990-2006]; Burkina Faso [1990-2006]; Senegal [1990-2006]; Ghana [1990-2006]; India [1990-2006]; Thailand [1990-2006]; Viet Nam [1990-2006]; Indonesia [1990-2006]; Brazil [1990-2006]; other high HIV-burden countries across sub-Saharan Africa, South and South-eastern Asia, and Latin America [1990-2006]
Host: Humans (predominantly adults with advanced HIV infection and CD4 <100 cells/µL)
Event summary: During the 1990s and early-to-mid 2000s, the rapid global expansion of the HIV pandemic led to a dramatic rise in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South and South-eastern Asia, and Latin America. A 2009 analysis using 2006 data estimated about 957,900 annual cases of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis and 624,700 deaths worldwide, with the great majority of cases and deaths occurring in sub-Saharan Africa and much of the remainder in South/South-eastern Asia and Latin America. As ART access slowly improved in some regions toward the mid-2000s, incidence began to plateau or decline in better-resourced settings, but exceptionally high incidence and mortality persisted across many low- and middle-income countries where late HIV diagnosis and poor access to optimal antifungal therapy limited control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global spread and intensification of the HIV/AIDS pandemic created very large populations of adults with advanced immunosuppression, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia and Latin America, while ART availability, HIV testing, and linkage to care lagged badly in many settings. Weak health systems, limited access to amphotericin B and flucytosine, and reliance on suboptimal fluconazole monotherapy further amplified mortality. Internal mechanisms: No major pathogen change is implicated; the emergence reflects opportunistic infection by widespread environmental C. neoformans in a vastly expanded pool of severely immunocompromised hosts (host susceptibility expansion and health-system failure rather than fungal evolution).
Review: review: Event correctly captures the early HIV-driven global epidemic and uses appropriate burden estimates (≈957,900 cases and 624,700 deaths annually around 2006).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19182676/?utm_source=openai)) Main corrections were (i) replacing region labels such as “Sub-Saharan Africa” and “Latin America” in the Countries field with a list of high-burden countries using UN country names, while keeping the 1990–2006 range as an approximate active period per country, and (ii) removing Wikipedia as a primary source and adding the original global burden analysis by Park et al. 2009 (AIDS) as a key source.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19182676/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence) remains appropriate because the pattern is driven by HIV-related immunosuppression and health-system gaps rather than introduction into new continents or major pathogen evolution. Flagged for review to verify the list of exemplar countries and approximate date ranges per country against any country-level data available in the main project.

Host: Humans (adults with HIV infection; smaller number of HIV-uninfected patients)
Event summary: From 2000 to 2015, Botswana experienced a prolonged national epidemic of adult meningitis in which cryptococcal meningitis was the predominant identified etiology in the context of very high HIV prevalence. National meningitis survey data and linked registry analyses show that cryptococcal meningitis accounted for the majority of adult meningitis cases with an identified cause and that national incidence of cryptococcal meningitis remained extremely high into 2013–2014, despite substantial ART roll-out. Even in the mid-2010s, incidence among people living with HIV in Botswana was comparable to pre-ART era rates reported in South Africa, and in-hospital mortality remained substantial.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High adult HIV prevalence, persistent late presentation with advanced HIV disease, and gaps in early HIV testing and linkage to care created a large population at risk. Limited implementation of cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) screening and constrained access to preferred induction regimens (amphotericin B plus flucytosine) contributed to the sustained incidence and high in-hospital mortality. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel C. neoformans strain; this is best interpreted as re-occurrence driven by HIV-related immunosuppression and health-system constraints rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain: Botswana’s 2000–2015 national cryptococcal meningitis epidemic is well documented by the Botswana National Meningitis Survey and related analyses, which show (i) very high incidence nationally in 2013–2014 and (ii) cryptococcal meningitis as the predominant identified etiology of adult meningitis despite ART scale-up.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6679721/?utm_source=openai)) Geography (Southern Africa/Botswana), time span (2000–2015), and classification as re-occurrence driven by advanced HIV disease and incomplete ART/CrAg screening are appropriate. No structural corrections were needed; recommended to retain as a major national-level emergence episode.

Host: Humans (primarily HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis)
Event summary: Between roughly 2004 and 2014, studies from Botswana, South Africa, Zambia, and Uganda demonstrated that cryptococcal meningitis had become the leading identified cause of adult meningitis in much of southern and eastern Africa. National and referral-hospital data from Botswana indicated that cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 90% of microbiologically confirmed adult meningitis cases, mirroring earlier and contemporaneous data from high-HIV-prevalence provinces in South Africa and from Zambia. In a Ugandan cohort of HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis (2010–2012), cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 60% of all meningitis diagnoses, with bacterial and tuberculous meningitis much less common. Over this period, bacterial meningitis incidence declined with introduction of conjugate vaccines, but cryptococcal meningitis persisted as the dominant cause of adult meningitis in these settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high prevalence of advanced HIV disease, incomplete ART coverage and adherence, late care-seeking, and limited diagnostic capacity for alternative meningitis etiologies concentrated adult meningitis burden in cryptococcal disease. Introduction of bacterial conjugate vaccines reduced bacterial meningitis, increasing the relative share of cryptococcal meningitis among adult meningitis cases. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence for major pathogen evolution; the patterns reflect changing host susceptibility and competing etiologies rather than new cryptococcal strains.
Review: review: The overall event concept (cryptococcal meningitis becoming the leading cause of adult meningitis in parts of southern and eastern Africa) is well supported by Botswana national data and adult meningitis cohort studies from South Africa and Uganda.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6679721/?utm_source=openai)) Corrections made: (i) the Ugandan country period was changed from “Uganda [2004–2012]” to “Uganda [2010–2012]” to match the prospective cohort that found 60% of meningitis cases due to cryptococcal meningitis,([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4347329/?utm_source=openai)) and (ii) the Countries field was clarified to give explicit date ranges for South Africa and Uganda rather than vague descriptors such as “pre-ART era comparator.” Source URLs were updated to replace the Uganda 2015–2017 paper with the more relevant 2010–2012 cohort description (PMC4347329). The episode remains classified as re-occurrence; flagged for review to confirm the exact date ranges for Zambia and for consistency with any additional national datasets.

Continent: Africa; Asia; South America; Oceania; Europe; North America
Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa; Northern Africa (limited data); Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Caribbean; South America; Australia and New Zealand; selected high-burden subregions in Europe and North America
Countries: South Africa [2014]; Nigeria [2014]; Uganda [2014]; Kenya [2014]; Mozambique [2014]; United Republic of Tanzania [2014]; Zambia [2014]; Zimbabwe [2014]; Ethiopia [2014]; Cameroon [2014]; India [2014]; Indonesia [2014]; Thailand [2014]; Viet Nam [2014]; Brazil [2014]; other high-burden countries across sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Latin America, and smaller-burden countries in Oceania, Europe, and North America [2014]
Host: Humans (overwhelmingly people living with HIV with CD4 <100 cells/µL; smaller share in other immunosuppressed groups)
Event summary: A 2017 global burden analysis estimated that in 2014 about 278,000 people with advanced HIV infection were cryptococcal-antigen positive and there were approximately 223,100 incident cases of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, leading to an estimated 181,100 deaths worldwide that year; roughly 135,900 deaths (75%) occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite substantial ART expansion and some decline in incidence compared with estimates based on 2006 data, cryptococcal meningitis remained a major cause of AIDS-related mortality globally in 2014, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia and Latin America. Subsequent years have seen gradual reductions in incidence where ART coverage, CrAg screening, and improved induction regimens expanded, but high mortality and substantial burden persisted in many low-resource settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent gaps in early HIV diagnosis and ART initiation, continued high prevalence of advanced HIV disease, lack of routine CrAg screening in many countries, shortages of amphotericin B and especially flucytosine, and limited capacity for intensive supportive care sustained a very high global burden in 2014. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel fungal strain is required to explain the burden; the pattern is driven by opportunistic infection of severely immunocompromised hosts by globally endemic C. neoformans. The classification as re-occurrence reflects sustained high incidence and mortality relative to pre-HIV eras, driven primarily by external host and health-system factors.
Review: review: This event correctly represents the 2014 global burden episode described by Rajasingham et al., which estimated 223,100 incident cases of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis and 181,100 deaths worldwide, with ~75% of deaths in sub-Saharan Africa.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28483415/?utm_source=openai)) Corrections focused on the Countries field: generic phrases such as “Sub-Saharan African countries (e.g. …)” were replaced with an explicit list of exemplar high-burden countries (South Africa, Nigeria, Uganda, etc.) plus an “other high-burden countries” clause, and each listed country was assigned the event year 2014. Geography (all inhabited continents) and classification as a large re-occurrence episode remain appropriate. Flagged for review mainly to confirm whether any additional high-burden countries should be named explicitly, given space constraints.

Host: Humans (HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected adults; organ transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients)
Event summary: US hospital discharge data from 18 states for 1997–2009 showed that cryptococcal meningitis remained an important cause of hospitalization and death in the ART era. Over this period, hospitalizations for cryptococcal meningitis among people with HIV declined by more than half, reflecting expanded ART access and earlier HIV care, whereas the relative burden among HIV-uninfected patients—including solid-organ transplant recipients and people receiving intensive immunosuppressive therapy—became more prominent. In-hospital mortality remained substantial (around 11–12%), and by the end of the study period, cryptococcal meningitis persisted as a serious opportunistic infection with a shifting host profile toward non-HIV-related immunosuppression, without clear evidence of geographic spread into new areas of the United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread introduction of combination ART reduced HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, while increasing use of solid-organ and hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, chemotherapy, and biologic immunosuppressive agents expanded the population of non-HIV immunosuppressed patients at risk for cryptococcal disease. Improved diagnostics and awareness likely increased recognition of cryptococcal meningitis in non-HIV patients. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence for more virulent or drug-resistant C. neoformans strains driving the pattern; instead, changing patterns of host immunosuppression and medical practice underlie this re-occurrence.
Review: review: The US 1997–2009 episode is well supported by national hospitalization data, which document (i) a marked decline in HIV-related cryptococcal meningitis hospitalizations after ART scale-up and (ii) a rising relative share of cases in HIV-uninfected but otherwise immunosuppressed patients, with substantial in-hospital mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3574138/?utm_source=openai)) The main correction was to restrict the Countries field to the United States only, since the cited analysis covers US hospitalizations and does not provide parallel, linked data for Canada; including Canada would therefore overstate the documented geographic scope. Classification as re-occurrence due to changes in ART coverage and iatrogenic immunosuppression remains appropriate. Flagged for review only to confirm whether a separate event should later be created for C. neoformans disease trends in Canada using Canadian datasets, if those are considered in scope and distinct from C. gattii outbreaks.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Northern Africa (selected countries); Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: Burkina Faso [2000s-2010s]; Cameroon [2000s-2010s]; Ethiopia [2000s-2010s]; Kenya [2000s-2010s]; Senegal [2000s-2010s]; South Africa [2000s-2010s]; India [2000s-2010s]; additional African and Asian countries with documented high in-hospital case fatality for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis [2000s-2010s]
Host: Humans (primarily adults with advanced HIV infection hospitalized with cryptococcal meningitis)
Event summary: Between about 2000 and 2013, hospital-based studies from numerous African and Asian countries reported extremely high in-hospital mortality among adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. Case-fatality rates around 28–62% were documented in Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Ethiopia, India, Kenya, Senegal, and South Africa despite antifungal treatment, illustrating the severity of the epidemic under routine-care conditions in resource-limited settings. As ART programs expanded during the 2000s, incidence gradually declined in some hospitals, but many facilities continued to report high numbers of cases and persistently high early mortality, leading to recognition of cryptococcal meningitis as one of the leading causes of AIDS-related death in many high-burden countries, second only to tuberculosis in some analyses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Late HIV diagnosis, delayed or absent ART initiation, poor retention in care, and limited access to potent antifungal regimens (especially flucytosine) produced late presentation with high fungal burden and advanced disease. Amphotericin B toxicity, lack of capacity for serial lumbar punctures and intracranial pressure management, stockouts of antifungals, and scarce intensive-care resources further increased mortality. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence that a new C. neoformans genotype was responsible for these high case-fatality rates; they are better explained by severe host immunosuppression, high organism load, and treatment limitations. The episode is therefore classified as a large-scale re-occurrence in vulnerable populations rather than re-emergence driven by pathogen evolution.
Review: retain: This event accurately synthesizes multi-country evidence showing very high in-hospital mortality (often 30–60% or higher) among adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis across several African countries and India during the 2000s–early 2010s, as summarized in major reviews and burden-of-disease discussions.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40475-015-0045-z)) The geography (Africa and Asia), countries listed (Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Senegal, South Africa, India), and characterization as re-occurrence driven by late HIV diagnosis, limited ART, and inadequate access to optimal antifungal therapy are appropriate. No structural changes were needed; recommended to retain as one of the major high-mortality emergence episodes for this pathogen.

Host: Humans—mainly adults with hematologic malignancies (acute leukemias and other hematologic cancers) and one patient with prosthetic valve endocarditis
Event summary: Between 1989 and 1994, six Spanish tertiary centers documented 16 deep infections due to Scedosporium prolificans (now Lomentospora prolificans), largely in neutropenic patients with hematologic malignancies and including one prosthetic valve endocarditis case, providing the first substantial European case series and making this mold visible as a serious pathogen in oncology and hematology services. Most patients progressed quickly from localized infection or transient colonization to disseminated disease involving blood, lungs, central nervous system and skin, with all tested isolates showing high MICs to all available antifungals and an 87.5% mortality, which highlighted L. prolificans as an intrinsically multiresistant, highly lethal invader. After this multicenter experience, awareness, diagnostics and reporting improved, and while the initial surge abated, Spain and other European countries continued to report sporadic severe and disseminated lomentosporiosis in similar high‑risk populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of intensive chemotherapy and complex hematologic care in Spain, creating large numbers of profoundly neutropenic patients; use of invasive devices and prolonged hospitalization in environments where the fungus was already present in soil and dust. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B, azoles and flucytosine left clinicians with almost no effective fungicidal options; strong angioinvasiveness and ability to disseminate hematogenously favored multiorgan involvement and very high mortality.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Adjusted event_year from “1990–1994” to “1989–1994” to match the primary case-series, which reports 16 deep infections between 1989 and 1994 in six Spanish centers; this slightly predates the nominal 1990 cut-off but the majority of cases fall within the target window and the episode is the key early European emergence signal.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Removed the previous ‘re_emergence = true’ flag, as this episode represents the first substantial recognized emergence in Europe and is best classified as inter-continental emergence into a new continent rather than re‑emergence driven by documented pathogen change. (iii) Left geography (Europe, Southern Europe, Spain) and host description unchanged, as they are consistent with the source article. Flagged for manual review specifically regarding acceptance of the 1989 start year under the “1990 onwards” rule, but the event itself is valid and should be retained.

Host: Humans—neutropenic leukemia patients in a temporary hematology ward during hospital renovations
Event summary: In 1995, Hospital Central de Asturias in Oviedo, Spain, experienced a nosocomial outbreak in which four neutropenic leukemia patients housed in a temporary hematology unit during major renovations developed fatal disseminated Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans infection over about one month, representing one of the first clearly documented hospital outbreaks of this mold. All four patients had fungemia with widespread angioinvasive hyphae and conidia at autopsy, and in vitro testing showed uniformly high MICs to amphotericin B, azoles and flucytosine, with no survivors despite aggressive therapy. After the cluster was recognized, the two affected rooms were closed and infection‑control interventions implemented, and no further linked cases occurred in that ward, indicating a renovation‑associated re‑occurrence of L. prolificans in a previously affected European subregion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major construction and renovation activities around the hematology service likely increased airborne dust and fungal spores; relocation of profoundly neutropenic patients to a temporary unit without optimal protective air‑handling facilitated opportunistic acquisition. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic multidrug resistance (high MICs to amphotericin B and azoles) and strong angioinvasiveness produced rapidly fatal disseminated disease once spores were inhaled by neutropenic hosts.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Reclassified the event type from “re_emergence” to “re_occurrence” because the cluster occurred in a subregion (Southern Europe/Spain) where L. prolificans was already established from earlier deep infection cases, and the main drivers were external (renovation and suboptimal protective environment) rather than documented changes in the pathogen.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8586719/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Explicitly added location details (“Oviedo, Hospital Central de Asturias”) and clarified that this is a nosocomial construction‑associated outbreak rather than a new continental spread. Geography, timing and host description remain consistent with the primary J Clin Microbiol report. Flagged for review only to confirm alignment with the project’s operational definitions for re‑occurrence vs re‑emergence; the outbreak itself is well‑documented and should be kept.

Countries: Australia [1999] (single university hospital, New South Wales)
Host: Humans—immunocompromised adults including hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, patients with hematologic malignancies, solid organ transplants, HIV infection, and chronic lung disease; a minority of trauma-associated soft tissue infections
Event summary: From late 1999 through 2003, a large Australian university hospital documented the first local detections and invasive case series of Lomentospora (Scedosporium) prolificans, reporting eight patients with invasive L. prolificans infection within a broader 6.5‑year study of scedosporiosis. The fungus was first recognized in this center in December 1999, after which multiple invasive cases occurred—including pneumonia, disseminated fungemia and deep tissue disease—mainly in severely immunocompromised patients such as HSCT recipients, cancer patients and those with advanced HIV, with high mortality despite therapy. Isolation data showed that L. prolificans rapidly became the more invasive of the two main Scedosporium species at the hospital, with two temporal clusters of isolates coinciding with major construction work, thereby marking the inter‑continental emergence and establishment of this mold as a clinically important pathogen in Australasia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of transplant, oncology and HIV care in Australian tertiary hospitals created sizable populations of severely immunocompromised patients; hospital construction works with deep excavation were temporally associated with peaks in L. prolificans isolation, suggesting increased airborne exposure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2828065/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Compared with S. apiospermum, L. prolificans showed a higher propensity for invasive rather than colonizing infection and broad antifungal resistance, allowing it to exploit these high‑risk hosts and outcompete more susceptible molds in this setting.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Adjusted event_year from “1997–2003” to “1999–2003” and the country‑year tag from “Australia [1997]” to “Australia [1999]”, because the primary epidemiological study shows that S. prolificans was first detected at this hospital in December 1999, with subsequent invasive cases occurring thereafter; 1997–1998 belonged to the baseline Scedosporium apiospermum period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2828065/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Clarified that this episode is best classified as an inter‑continental emergence into Oceania (first documented regional series) rather than a re‑emergence, so ‘first_detection’ was set to false (global first occurred in 1984) and ‘re_occurrence’/‘re_emergence’ were set to false. The summary and mechanisms were reworded to align closely with the Australian data (including construction-associated clusters) without overstating case numbers. Flagged for review to confirm that the time window used for the “event” matches how the project wants to aggregate the early Australian emergence signal, but the underlying episode is robust and should be retained.
