Host: Humans—primarily adults with hematologic malignancies who developed bloodstream infection (fungemia), plus occasional other immunocompromised hosts
Event summary: Between 2000 and 2019, state-wide surveillance in Queensland, Australia, identified 22 incident episodes of bloodstream infection due to Scedosporium species and Lomentospora prolificans among 21 residents, 18 of which were caused by L. prolificans, documenting a rare but highly lethal pattern of fungemia in patients with hematologic malignancy. Nearly all patients had profound neutropenia during intensive chemotherapy or HSCT and deteriorated quickly after first positive blood cultures, with all patients with hematologic malignancy dying within a year and a median time to death of around 9 days despite antifungal therapy. This prolonged surveillance period demonstrates the recurrent re‑occurrence of L. prolificans fungemia as a uniformly or near‑uniformly fatal complication in Queensland leukemia care, reinforcing the species’ status as a critical threat in high‑risk hematology populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralization of hematology and HSCT services in Queensland created a repeated, well‑defined cohort of profoundly neutropenic patients exposed to environmental molds; statewide laboratory surveillance improved recognition of rare mold fungemias. Internal mechanisms: L. prolificans’ intrinsic multidrug resistance and strong angioinvasiveness confer a uniquely poor prognosis for bloodstream infection, with virtually no survivors among patients with hematologic malignancy in this series, suggesting that even modern combination antifungal regimens rarely alter the course without rapid immune recovery.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37599232/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Clarified that this event is a long-term population‑based surveillance signal from Queensland, not a discrete short outbreak, and that 22 bloodstream infection episodes (18 L. prolificans) were identified over 20 years.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37599232/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reclassified the event from ‘re_emergence’ to ‘re_occurrence’, as there is no evidence that pathogen evolution (new strain or host jump) drove this pattern; instead, it reflects the recurrent appearance of L. prolificans fungemia in an already endemic Australian setting driven by external factors (hematology service organization, patient mix, and surveillance). No geographic corrections were required. Flagged for review mainly to confirm that treating this entire 20‑year surveillance period as one aggregated “event” fits the project’s approach to temporally extended episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Spain [2001] (La Coruña, Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo)
Host: Humans—adult inpatients with acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia in a hematology isolation unit
Event summary: In the period leading up to a 2001 report, a hematology unit at Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo in La Coruña, Spain, experienced an airborne nosocomial outbreak in which six inpatients with acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia developed invasive Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans infection, all of whom died despite antifungal therapy. Phenotypic and genotypic analysis showed that isolates from patients and from the air of the isolation rooms were indistinguishable, indicating that a single clonal strain disseminated via the ward air, and implementation of intensified airborne infection‑control measures led to cessation of new cases. This outbreak represents a major re‑occurrence of L. prolificans disease in Southern Europe, demonstrating that the fungus can cause lethal, air‑transmitted epidemics in specialized hematology units.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Care of severely immunosuppressed leukemia patients in an isolation unit with inadequate control of airborne fungal contamination; likely environmental amplification of a single L. prolificans strain in or near the ward air‑handling or building fabric.([pascal-francis.inist.fr](https://pascal-francis.inist.fr/vibad/index.php?action=getRecordDetail&idt=972649&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic multidrug resistance and high virulence allowed the clonal strain to cause invasive infection and death in all six affected patients once inhaled, underscoring the pathogen’s capacity for point‑source airborne outbreaks in vulnerable hospital populations.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Substantially revised this row, which previously described an imprecise “around 1997” Spanish outbreak with multiple genotypes; it is now aligned with the well‑documented airborne outbreak described by Guerrero et al. in La Coruña, Spain, involving six acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia patients with invasive infection and 100% mortality.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11418156/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Updated event_year to 2001 (matching the outbreak report) and countries field to specify La Coruña and the Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo, and corrected the molecular description: genotyping showed a single clonal strain shared between clinical and air isolates, not multiple unrelated genotypes. (iii) Reclassified the event as ‘re_occurrence’ only (Southern Europe was already affected by earlier Spanish cases), removing erroneous ‘re_emergence’ and any implication that this was a new continental introduction. Flagged for review because this row has been materially reinterpreted; however, the updated version clearly corresponds to a major, well‑sourced outbreak that should be kept as one of the highest‑impact events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Republic of Korea [2004] (trauma‑associated knee and bone infection); Republic of Korea [2005] (fatal fungemia in relapsed AML)
Host: Humans—one immunocompetent child with post‑traumatic osteoarticular infection and one adult with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia and profound chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia
Event summary: In 2004–2005, clinicians in South Korea reported the earliest confirmed human infections with Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans from Asia: first, a 10‑year‑old immunocompetent boy who developed neglected bone and joint infection of the knee after laceration by a broken flowerpot, and then a 45‑year‑old woman with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia who developed fulminant S. prolificans fungemia during salvage chemotherapy and died within a day of starting amphotericin B. The orthopedic case established that this soil‑associated mold could cause musculoskeletal infection following traumatic inoculation in an Asian setting, while the subsequent Korean fungemia report explicitly noted that no bloodstream isolates of S. prolificans had previously been described in Korea or elsewhere in Asia. Together, these cases mark the inter‑continental emergence of L. prolificans in Eastern Asia and showed that both immunocompetent trauma patients and profoundly neutropenic leukemia patients in the region were at risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental exposure to contaminated soil or potted‑plant material in the community (flowerpot injury in the child) and increasing use of intensive chemotherapy for acute leukemia in Korean tertiary centers producing profound neutropenia (adult fungemia case).([jkoa.org](https://jkoa.org/pdf/10.4055/jkoa.2004.39.4.426?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The fungus’ ability to establish chronic osteoarticular infection in an otherwise healthy host, its intrinsic resistance to standard antifungals, and its high virulence in neutropenic hosts (with rapid progression to fatal sepsis) allowed these early Asian cases to occur despite empiric antibacterial and antifungal treatment, signaling that once introduced, L. prolificans could behave similarly to patterns seen in Spain and Australia.
Review: Decision: retain. New event added. Rationale and changes: (i) This row is newly introduced to capture Asia’s true early emergence signal, drawing on a 2004 Korean case of post‑traumatic knee bone/joint infection and a 2005 Korean case of fatal fungemia in a relapsed AML patient. The 2005 report explicitly states that S. prolificans fungemia had not previously been reported in Korea or Asia, indicating that these closely spaced cases represent the first recognized human infections by this species in the region.([jkoa.org](https://jkoa.org/pdf/10.4055/jkoa.2004.39.4.426?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Classified as ‘inter_continental_emergence’ for Asia, with ‘first_detection’ kept false at the global level (global first was in Minnesota in 1984). (iii) Countries and subregion were set according to the UNSD list (Republic of Korea, Eastern Asia). (iv) The event is temporally modest (two cases) but high‑impact for this rare EPP due to being the first confirmed Asian infections and illustrating both trauma‑associated disease and rapidly fatal disseminated infection. Flagged for review to confirm acceptance as one of the top global emergence events; if a strict cap of 10 events is enforced, this would still warrant inclusion given its continental significance.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans—diverse immunocompromised patients, predominantly with acute leukemias and other hematologic malignancies, and recipients of solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplants
Event summary: From 2005 to 2021, an Australian multicenter retrospective cohort of non‑Aspergillus mold infections documented 61 proven or probable invasive episodes due to Scedosporium/Lomentospora species, of which 37 (about 61%) were attributable to Lomentospora prolificans, confirming it as a leading non‑Aspergillus mold pathogen nationally. Patients frequently had acute leukemia or had undergone hematopoietic stem cell or solid‑organ transplantation, and nearly half of L. prolificans infections were disseminated, with high early and late all‑cause mortality despite combination antifungal therapy and aggressive supportive care. This prolonged observational period reflects a sustained re‑occurrence and consolidation of L. prolificans as a major opportunistic fungus in Australian tertiary centers, contributing to its inclusion on global fungal priority‑pathogen lists and stimulating interest in novel antifungal agents and combination regimens for lomentosporiosis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing growth and specialization of transplant and cancer services in Australia, with increasingly intensive immunosuppressive regimens and high‑risk hematology and HSCT populations; widespread use of mold‑active prophylaxis that may selectively suppress susceptible molds and leave niches for intrinsically resistant species such as L. prolificans. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic or high‑level resistance to nearly all licensed antifungals and a marked propensity for angioinvasion and dissemination underpin the very poor outcomes, and the apparent persistence of high case‑fatality over the 16‑year period suggests that any adaptive changes are outweighed by the fungus’s baseline virulence and resistance profile.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36861090/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Clarified that the 61 invasive episodes and 37 L. prolificans cases come from a formal multicenter retrospective cohort running 2005–2021, not a single‑center outbreak, and checked that timing, case numbers and underlying conditions match the Open Forum Infectious Diseases report.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36861090/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reclassified the event as ‘re_occurrence’ rather than ‘re_emergence’, because it represents continuing and expanding incidence in a continent where L. prolificans was already established by the early 2000s; there is no specific evidence for a new strain or host jump driving the increase. (iii) Updated the WHO fungal priority‑pathogen list URL to the current version for supporting context on the species’ recognized importance. Flagged for review to ensure the long time span and aggregation of diverse centers are acceptable as a single high‑impact event, but the data are strong and this episode clearly merits retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Japan [2011] (multiple centers; including Kobe and other tertiary hospitals)
Host: Humans—immunocompromised adults, mainly with acute myeloid leukemia and other hematologic malignancies; cases included infective endocarditis, disseminated infection, and severe ocular or CNS disease
Event summary: Starting in 2011, Japanese centers began reporting invasive Scedosporium/Lomentospora prolificans infections, including fungemia, infective endocarditis, ocular involvement and disseminated disease in patients with acute myeloid leukemia and other hematologic malignancies, marking the establishment of this pathogen in Japanese hematology and transplant practice. A 2015 endocarditis case report noted that the geographic distribution of S. prolificans infections had historically been limited to Australia, the United States and southern Europe, and that the first Japanese case had only been reported in 2011, with four cases recognized up to that time and a perceived increase in disseminated infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25630434/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent reports described additional invasive and disseminated lomentosporiosis in Japanese patients, indicating a growing, though still uncommon, presence of this intrinsically resistant mold in Eastern Asian hospitals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of high‑risk hematology and transplant programs in Japan and heightened awareness of non‑Aspergillus molds, together with improved fungal culture and species‑level identification, allowed recognition of a pathogen previously thought to be confined mainly to Spain, Australia and the southern United States. Internal mechanisms: The same intrinsic antifungal resistance and virulence profile seen elsewhere enabled L. prolificans to cause lethal disseminated disease in Japanese leukemia and transplant patients once introduced, but there is no evidence that Asian strains are biologically distinct; the emergence signal appears driven by host and healthcare‑system factors rather than major pathogen evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Removed incorrect flags for ‘first_detection’ and ‘inter_continental_emergence’, because earlier Korean cases (2004–2005) already document L. prolificans infection in Asia; this Japanese cluster is better interpreted as re‑occurrence within an already affected subregion.([acm.or.kr](https://www.acm.or.kr/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ACM-0802-15.pdf)) (ii) Removed the ‘intra_continental_emergence’ flag, as both Korea and Japan fall within the same UNSD Eastern Asia subregion, and the guidance specifies that spread to a new country within a subregion should generally be treated as re‑emergence or re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence. (iii) Tightened the event description to emphasize that published Japanese cases up to 2015 were still few (around four at the time of the key endocarditis report) but signaled a new, ongoing presence in Japanese hematology/transplant centers. Flagged for review to confirm the choice to represent Japan’s emergence as a separate high‑impact event in addition to the Korean continental‑first episode; from an epidemiological perspective, this is justified by the different healthcare systems and the clustering of severe invasive cases.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia [2015] (Western Australia, Perth—Fiona Stanley Hospital haematology unit)
Host: Humans—inpatients in a high‑risk haematology unit with hematologic disease and severe immunosuppression, including stem cell transplant recipients
Event summary: Over an approximately eight‑month period spanning 2015–2016, a haematology unit at Fiona Stanley Hospital in Perth, Western Australia, recorded a concerning cluster of four invasive Lomentospora prolificans infections in intensively treated patients, prompting a detailed outbreak investigation with whole‑genome sequencing. All four patients had severe underlying haematologic disease and profound immunosuppression, and developed invasive lomentosporiosis—including disseminated infection—with high morbidity and mortality owing to intrinsic antifungal resistance. Whole‑genome sequencing of clinical isolates from the cluster, together with two contemporaneous isolates from another hospital, demonstrated that the strains were genetically diverse (differing by >10,000 SNPs), arguing against a single point‑source clone and instead suggesting repeated environmental acquisition of L. prolificans by extremely vulnerable patients; after enhanced environmental assessment and strengthened infection‑control measures, no further temporal cluster was observed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Concentration of profoundly immunocompromised haematology and HSCT patients in a single ward in a region where L. prolificans is environmentally prevalent (Australian urban and semi‑arid settings), combined with possible micro‑environmental contamination in hospital spaces and air during a period of intense building activity in the broader healthcare system.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248584/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: A polyclonal set of intrinsically antifungal‑resistant strains capable of angioinvasion and dissemination repeatedly infected this ultra‑high‑risk population; genomic diversity implies that infection prevention must address broad environmental exposure rather than a single outbreak clone.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Confirmed that the cluster comprised four invasive L. prolificans infections over eight months in a haematology unit and that whole‑genome sequencing demonstrated polyclonality, not a single outbreak strain, which is now explicitly stated in the summary.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248584/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reaffirmed classification as a re‑occurrence event in an already endemic Australian setting rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence. (iii) Left geography and timeframe unchanged, as they are consistent with the published Medical Mycology Case Reports study. Flagged for review only in the sense that, if a strict 10‑event cap is later enforced, project leads may wish to weigh this four‑case hospital cluster against single‑case but continent‑first events; scientifically, it is one of the better‑documented outbreaks and merits retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans—adult patient after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo‑HSCT) for acute myeloid leukemia
Event summary: In 2016, a hematology team in Osaka, Japan, reported a fatal case of fungal meningitis caused by Lomentospora prolificans shortly after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia, described as the first documented instance of L. prolificans meningitis after allo‑HSCT. The patient developed central nervous system symptoms and imaging findings consistent with meningitis in the setting of profound post‑transplant immunosuppression, and despite systemic antifungal therapy, clinical status deteriorated and the patient died, underscoring the extremely poor prognosis of CNS lomentosporiosis. This case expanded the recognized clinical spectrum of L. prolificans in Eastern Asia to include HSCT‑associated CNS disease and highlighted diagnostic challenges when a very rare mold is responsible for post‑transplant meningitis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Highly immunosuppressive allo‑HSCT conditioning and post‑transplant regimens in a healthcare environment where L. prolificans had recently emerged, coupled with diagnostic delay due to the rarity of this pathogen in CNS infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27258644/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ ability to invade CNS tissues under conditions of profound immunosuppression and its intrinsic resistance to most antifungals permitted rapid progression despite treatment, illustrating how even sporadic cases can be almost uniformly fatal without early recognition and immune recovery.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: (i) This is a well‑documented and clinically important case—the first reported L. prolificans meningitis after allo‑HSCT—but it involves a single patient in a subregion (Eastern Asia/Japan) where the pathogen was already established, so its impact is more in expanding clinical phenotype than in geographic spread or case numbers.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27258644/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Event‑type flags were simplified to ‘re_occurrence’ only, removing earlier ‘re_emergence’ and inter‑/intra‑continental flags since there is no clear evidence of pathogen evolution and the case does not represent a new region. (iii) If a strict limit of 10 highest‑impact events is applied, this single‑case HSCT meningitis episode may be a candidate for exclusion in favor of continent‑first or larger multicase episodes (e.g., South American emergence or additional European clusters). For now it is retained as it illustrates the extreme severity of CNS lomentosporiosis, but it is flagged for strategic review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China [2019] (tertiary center caring for HSCT recipients)
Host: Humans—young adult with acute myeloid leukemia after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with chronic graft‑versus‑host disease
Event summary: In 2019–2020, a tertiary hospital in China reported a case of pulmonary Lomentospora prolificans infection in a 27‑year‑old man with acute myeloid leukemia following allo‑HSCT and severe chronic graft‑versus‑host disease, described as the first successfully treated post‑HSCT L. prolificans infection in the country. The patient developed pulmonary lomentosporiosis while receiving intense immunosuppression; combination therapy with voriconazole and terbinafine, alongside careful adjustment of immunosuppressive drugs, led to sustained clinical and radiologic remission—an exceptional outcome for this pathogen given its usual high mortality. Accompanying literature review suggested that L. prolificans infections were increasingly recognized in HSCT recipients worldwide but outcomes remained poor, making this Chinese case notable both as a first national report and as a rare therapeutic success.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of HSCT programs and intensive leukemia care in China, leading to more patients at risk for rare molds, and improved mycological diagnostics enabling species‑level identification of L. prolificans.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12297014/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: While intrinsic multidrug resistance constrained treatment options, partial susceptibility to voriconazole and terbinafine allowed for a synergistic combination regimen in this case, and some immune recovery likely contributed to successful control, illustrating that early aggressive multi‑agent therapy can occasionally overcome the fungus’s high virulence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: (i) This event is accurately described as the first successfully treated post‑HSCT L. prolificans infection reported from China and reflects growing recognition of the pathogen in Eastern Asia; however, it is a single case in a subregion where L. prolificans was already present (Korea and Japan), so its impact is more clinical (treatment breakthrough) than epidemiological.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12297014/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Event‑type flags were simplified to ‘re_occurrence’ only; earlier ‘first_detection’ and continental emergence flags were removed to align with definitions that reserve inter‑continental emergence for first presence in a continent (which is already captured by the earlier Korean episode). (iii) Because the project prioritizes the ten most impactful emergence events by case numbers and spread, this case may be considered for exclusion in a stricter pruning step, but it is currently retained as a high‑value example of successful therapy in a setting of growing regional incidence. Flagged for review with that caveat.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (mainly adults with hematologic malignancies, hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients and other severely immunocompromised patients)
Event summary: Between 1989 and 1999, multiple Spanish centres reported an accumulation of deep and disseminated infections due to Scedosporium prolificans (now Lomentospora prolificans), including at least 16 deep infections documented in six hospitals between 1989–1994 and a series of disseminated or colonising cases through 1999 with ≈88% mortality.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/)) Within this period, nosocomial clusters occurred in hematology units, notably airborne outbreaks during hospital renovation in which four to six neutropenic leukemia patients developed rapidly fatal amphotericin‑resistant fungemia over weeks to a month.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8586719/?utm_source=openai)) These clusters declined only after heightened environmental controls, better management of construction-related dust, and increased recognition of S. prolificans as a multiresistant pathogen in Spanish hematology and transplant services.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of high‑risk hematology and transplant populations in tertiary centres; prolonged profound neutropenia; extensive use of amphotericin B–based antifungal regimens that exerted little activity against S. prolificans; and hospital construction/renovation, which increased airborne mold spore loads in hematology units.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/)) Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance (intrinsic high‑level resistance of S. prolificans/Lomentospora to amphotericin B and azoles limiting treatment options and enabling ecological selection when susceptible molds are suppressed); increased virulence/pathogenicity (marked angioinvasiveness with rapid, disseminated infection and very high case‑fatality in neutropenic hosts).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/))
Review: Decision: retain. This row correctly captures one of the largest and best‑documented emergence episodes for Scedosporium spp. globally, namely the 1990s Spanish accumulation of deep and disseminated Lomentospora/S. prolificans infections and associated construction‑related nosocomial outbreaks. Geography (Europe, Southern Europe, Spain), host description and time span agree with multicentre Spanish series and outbreak reports, and classifying this as re-emergence is appropriate because it reflects the emergence of a multiresistant, highly virulent opportunist in an already colonised subregion rather than first detection.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/)) No corrections to countries, emergence-type coding or sources are needed, but the event is flagged as a key reference episode for subsequent Lomentospora outbreaks in other regions.

Host: Humans (solid-organ and hematopoietic cell transplant recipients at 23 tertiary-care centres)
Event summary: From 2001 to 2006, the US Transplant-Associated Infection Surveillance Network (TRANSNET) conducted prospective surveillance in 23 transplant centres and identified 27 invasive Scedosporium infections (≈16% of 169 non-Aspergillus invasive mold infections) in hematopoietic cell and solid-organ transplant recipients, predominantly due to S. apiospermum and S. prolificans.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/10828/cdc_10828_DS1.pdf)) These infections occurred alongside rising overall rates of non-Aspergillus mold disease in transplant patients and were associated with disseminated disease, frequent CNS involvement and high short‑term mortality despite intensive antifungal therapy.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/10828/cdc_10828_DS1.pdf)) By the mid‑2000s, Scedosporium spp. were recognised in North America as major contributors to non-Aspergillus mold infection burden in transplant recipients, prompting increased attention to pre‑transplant colonisation, antifungal prophylaxis choices and diagnostic strategies.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/10828/cdc_10828_DS1.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and increasing complexity of hematopoietic cell and solid-organ transplantation programs; prolonged and intensive immunosuppression for graft‑versus‑host disease and rejection; and widespread use of voriconazole and echinocandins, which suppress Candida and Aspergillus but have limited activity against Scedosporium, thereby selecting for intrinsically resistant non-Aspergillus molds.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/10828/cdc_10828_DS1.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance (intrinsic and often high‑level resistance of S. apiospermum and especially S. prolificans to amphotericin B and many azoles and echinocandins); enhanced ability to colonise damaged respiratory epithelium and vascular structures in heavily immunosuppressed patients.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/cmr.00039-07?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). This major emergence episode—27 invasive Scedosporium infections among US transplant recipients captured in the TRANSNET cohort—was missing from the original dataset but clearly ranks among the most impactful events for this pathogen in terms of cases, geographic spread and mortality.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/10828/cdc_10828_DS1.pdf)) Geography (Northern America, United States) and host description have been added and are consistent with the surveillance network’s scope. The event is classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or inter-continental emergence), since Scedosporium was already known in this region and the surge is driven by expanding transplant populations and antifungal selection rather than new pathogen traits; this aligns with the definitions provided. This row is flagged for review mainly to confirm that TRANSNET-based numbers remain the best single summary of early‑2000s North American transplant‑related scedosporiosis.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (adults and adolescents with chronic lung disease including cystic fibrosis and COPD/bronchiectasis, hematologic malignancies, and solid-organ or stem-cell transplants)
Event summary: Between January 2003 and December 2005, the Australian Scedosporium (AUSCEDO) Study conducted a nationwide, laboratory-based surveillance across 49 laboratories and documented 180 episodes of scedosporiosis, including 62 episodes meeting criteria for invasive disease, establishing Scedosporium spp. as a leading non-Aspergillus mold pathogen in Australian high‑risk patients.([researchers.westernsydney.edu.au](https://researchers.westernsydney.edu.au/en/publications/population-based-surveillance-for-scedosporiosis-in-australia-epi?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing of 146 clinical isolates from this period and earlier case collections showed that most infections were due to S. prolificans or S. apiospermum, but also revealed a third cluster corresponding to the newly described species Scedosporium aurantiacum, which accounted for about one‑third of clinical isolates in some centres and was prominent among cystic fibrosis lung isolates.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2600218/?utm_source=openai)) After 2005, awareness of scedosporiosis, improved culture conditions and new PCR assays led to better recognition and targeted management, but Scedosporium remained associated with substantial morbidity and mortality among Australian transplant, hematology and chronic lung disease populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122855/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing numbers of adults with advanced chronic lung disease and cystic fibrosis, expanding solid-organ and lung-transplant programs, and widespread use of amphotericin B and triazoles active against Aspergillus but less effective against Scedosporium spp., creating ecological niches for these intrinsically less susceptible molds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122855/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (formal description and clinical recognition of S. aurantiacum as a distinct species within the P. boydii/S. apiospermum complex in 2005, with high environmental abundance in Australia and frequent recovery from CF lungs); antimicrobial resistance (reduced susceptibility of S. prolificans and S. aurantiacum to most systemic antifungals); enhanced colonisation of structurally damaged airways and transplanted lungs facilitating persistent infection and occasional dissemination.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jcm.43.10.4930-4942.2005?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This row accurately summarises the large AUSCEDO population-based surveillance study (2003–2005) and the contemporaneous recognition of S. aurantiacum as a distinct, clinically important species in Australia, which together constitute one of the most substantial scedosporiosis emergence events worldwide.([researchers.westernsydney.edu.au](https://researchers.westernsydney.edu.au/en/publications/population-based-surveillance-for-scedosporiosis-in-australia-epi?utm_source=openai)) The continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and classifying the event as re-emergence is appropriate because it captures both the rise of a new species (S. aurantiacum) and the marked increase in burden and clinical recognition, rather than first detection in humans. To keep the event sheet focused on the single, country‑scale surveillance episode, I did not create separate rows for earlier non-clonal case clusters at Alfred and Westmead hospitals, but note them in the underlying literature; this choice is consistent with the definition of linked, country‑level episodes and should be reviewed if finer within-country resolution is later required.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/2/pdfs/07-0920.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (previously healthy or mildly comorbid adults and children who survived near-drowning during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and aspirated heavily contaminated seawater and sludge)
Event summary: Following the December 26, 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, several near-drowning survivors in southern Thailand developed severe Scedosporium apiospermum/Pseudallescheria boydii complex infections weeks after aspirating polluted tsunami waters, including cases of vertebral osteomyelitis and brain abscess with antecedent pneumonia (“tsunami lung”).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) A review of near-drowning-associated scedosporiosis identified at least two such tsunami survivors among 20+ global cases, highlighting extremely high mortality (≈70%) and a strong tendency for CNS dissemination, even in immunocompetent hosts.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17714363/?utm_source=openai)) As environmental contamination receded and acute disaster conditions resolved, no ongoing local transmission chains were documented, but these sentinel cases established Scedosporium spp. as key causes of invasive fungal disease in tsunami and near-drowning victims in tropical coastal settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme environmental disturbance from the Indian Ocean tsunami, which mixed soil, sewage, hydrocarbons and marine waters into stagnant pools and debris fields, producing high inocula of Scedosporium conidia in water aspirated by victims; prolonged entrapment in contaminated water, traumatic injuries and delays in definitive care that favoured tissue necrosis and secondary infection; and intensive antibacterial therapy that may suppress bacterial competitors while sparing Scedosporium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/host adaptation (ecological adaptation of S. apiospermum/P. boydii to sewage and polluted brackish water, enabling massive exposure during near-drowning); increased virulence/pathogenicity (marked angioinvasiveness with a strong propensity for hematogenous CNS and bone dissemination and delayed, insidious clinical presentation).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17714363/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). This row extracts the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami–related scedosporiosis cases in Thailand as a distinct, temporally and geographically bounded emergence episode, in line with the guideline that events should only be merged when epidemiologically linked or continuous within the same outbreak area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) It is correctly coded as re-occurrence rather than inter-continental or first-emergence, because Scedosporium was already present in South-eastern Asia and the spike in cases is driven by an external environmental catastrophe rather than novel pathogen traits. Countries and subregion follow the UNSD scheme, and the main sources now focus tightly on tsunami/near-drowning–associated disease rather than general Scedosporium epidemiology.

Host: Humans (previously healthy adults who nearly drowned in the March 11, 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami and developed delayed invasive scedosporiosis)
Event summary: After the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami of March 11, 2011, several near-drowning survivors developed severe Scedosporium infections, including a 59‑year‑old woman with lung and multiple brain abscesses due to S. apiospermum and later patients with tsunami-associated S. aurantiacum brain abscess and S. apiospermum vertebral osteomyelitis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) These cases occurred weeks to months after aspiration of heavily contaminated seawater mixed with soil and oil, and they were initially misdiagnosed as bacterial or Aspergillus infections before culture and molecular testing revealed Scedosporium spp.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) Following heightened awareness and targeted antifungal therapy (often voriconazole-based combinations), additional tsunami-related Scedosporium cases were not reported from the same coastal communities once acute disaster conditions and environmental contamination subsided.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale coastal flooding and infrastructure destruction from the 2011 tsunami, which created stagnant, oil- and sewage-contaminated seawater and debris fields where Scedosporium spp. thrive; near-drowning with aspiration of this water; prolonged intensive care and broad-spectrum antibiotics; and delays in recognising mold infection because of its subacute course and initial similarity to bacterial pneumonia or common molds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Enhanced adaptation of S. apiospermum and S. aurantiacum to polluted aquatic environments and damaged lung tissue; intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B with variable susceptibility to triazoles; and strong neurotropism and osteotropism leading to CNS abscesses and vertebral osteomyelitis after hematogenous spread.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24238227/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). This row isolates the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami–associated near-drowning scedosporiosis cases as a discrete emergence event in Eastern Asia, rather than aggregating them with the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which occurred in a different subregion and time period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) The coding as re-occurrence is appropriate because Scedosporium was already established in Japan, and the event reflects disaster-driven resurgence rather than new geographic or host-system introduction. Event years (2011–2013) are inferred from case-report timelines and the disaster date and should be double-checked against the full texts during final curation.

Host: Humans (predominantly immunocompetent adults who had undergone cardiac surgery with median sternotomy, later developing invasive Scedosporium boydii infection)
Event summary: Over a 14‑month period in the early 2010s, six immunocompetent patients treated at a single hospital in Germany developed invasive Scedosporium boydii infections; five had undergone cardiac surgery 1–14 months earlier, and at least two died despite antifungal therapy and surgical management.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26330287/?utm_source=openai)) Multilocus sequence typing of clinical isolates showed an identical genotype in five of the six patients, strongly suggesting a health‑care–associated cluster linked to the cardiac surgery unit, although no definitive environmental source was identified.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26330287/?utm_source=openai)) During a two-year observation window before and after this cluster, no further S. boydii infections were reported from the centre, indicating a temporally bounded emergence episode that resolved after investigation and infection-prevention measures.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26330287/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Complex cardiac surgery with prolonged sternotomy and use of prosthetic materials, creating susceptible mediastinal and sternal sites; possible contamination within the operating theatre or perioperative environment shared by most affected patients; and broad-spectrum antibiotic use that may have facilitated fungal overgrowth.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26330287/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: S. boydii’s ability to colonise surgical sites and prosthetic material and to cause deep-seated osteomyelitis and mediastinitis; intrinsic reduced susceptibility to many antifungal agents, making eradication difficult once infection is established.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/cmr.00039-07?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event, flagged for date verification). This German cluster of six S. boydii infections after cardiac surgery is one of the very few clearly documented health‑care–associated scedosporiosis outbreaks worldwide and therefore belongs among the major emergence events for this pathogen, despite modest absolute case numbers.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26330287/?utm_source=openai)) The continent, subregion and country coding are correct; the event is best classified as re-occurrence driven by procedural and infection-control factors rather than as intra- or inter-continental emergence. Because the original paper does not explicitly state the calendar years of the 14‑month cluster, I have approximated the period as “~2013–2014” based on the 2015 publication date and flagged this for review so that exact years can be updated when available.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Caribbean; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: United States of America [2005]; Puerto Rico [2005]; Singapore [2005]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2005]
Host: Humans (primarily soft contact lens wearers)
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2005, clinicians in the United States, Puerto Rico, Singapore and Hong Kong noted an unusual increase in severe Fusarium keratitis among soft contact lens users, typically without antecedent ocular trauma. Multicentre investigations coordinated by CDC and ophthalmology groups identified more than 130 culture‑confirmed cases in the United States plus sizeable national clusters in Singapore and Hong Kong, with a strong epidemiologic association between disease and use of Bausch & Lomb ReNu with MoistureLoc multipurpose solution; many affected patients required corneal transplantation and prolonged topical and systemic antifungal therapy. After the association with MoistureLoc was confirmed, affected lots were withdrawn and the product was permanently removed from the global market in 2006, after which the excess incidence of Fusarium keratitis subsided toward background levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and rapid global uptake of a specific multipurpose contact lens solution (ReNu with MoistureLoc) whose real‑world fungicidal performance proved inadequate under some storage and use conditions, combined with suboptimal lens‑care practices and large populations of soft lens wearers, created conditions for a multi‑country outbreak of Fusarium keratitis. International distribution of the product resulted in parallel clusters in multiple countries without requiring pathogen adaptation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing implicated multiple genotypes within the Fusarium solani species complex and related species, indicating opportunistic infection by diverse environmental strains under conditions of reduced disinfection efficacy rather than emergence of a single, highly virulent new lineage; no clear evidence of novel antifungal resistance or altered tissue tropism specific to this outbreak has been demonstrated.
Review: review – Retain this event as it corresponds to the well‑documented 2005–2006 multi‑country Fusarium keratitis outbreak linked to Bausch & Lomb ReNu with MoistureLoc. Countries, sub‑regions and timing (mid‑2005 to mid‑2006) are consistent with CDC MMWR, JAMA US and Singapore studies and the Hong Kong multi‑country analysis. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, because Fusarium keratitis pre‑dated this episode in all affected sub‑regions and no novel Fusarium lineage or new continent was involved; cases in different continents form a single healthcare‑product–associated episode and are not treated as inter‑continental emergence. Source URLs have been curated to emphasise primary outbreak investigations and comprehensive reviews, dropping a less informative secondary NEJM clinician summary and adding the multi‑country Hong Kong experience; no additional countries with substantial case numbers were identified that would alter the ranking of this event among major outbreaks.

Host: Humans (hematology/oncology and transplant patients in a tertiary‑care hospital)
Event summary: During the 1990s, a US university hospital caring for patients with hematologic malignancies, severe neutropenia and stem‑cell or solid‑organ transplants experienced recurrent invasive fusariosis cases without an obvious source. A detailed environmental investigation cultured the hospital water distribution system, documenting extensive Fusarium solani and Fusarium oxysporum colonization of storage tanks, plumbing, sink drains, faucets and showers, and molecular typing showed that multiple patient isolates were closely related to waterborne strains, establishing a prolonged, water‑associated cluster of fusariosis. After recognition of the potable water system as a reservoir and implementation of water‑management measures (including restrictions on tap‑water exposure for high‑risk patients and engineering controls), the facility reduced fusariosis risk and this work helped prompt broader guidance on waterborne mold prevention in high‑risk hospital units.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Complex hospital plumbing and storage systems permitted persistent Fusarium biofilm formation and inadequate disinfection for filamentous molds, while frequent exposure of profoundly neutropenic or transplant patients to unfiltered tap water via showers, sink use and other contacts created an unrecognized transmission pathway; intensification of chemotherapy and transplantation programmes expanded the susceptible host population. Internal mechanisms: A diversity of Fusarium solani complex and related genotypes was found in both water samples and clinical isolates, indicating environmental opportunism rather than a single emergent strain, but the ability of these molds to adapt to and persist in biofilms within chlorinated hospital water networks, with aerosolization from showers and faucets, supported efficient environmental persistence and exposure in this niche.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major hospital‑associated fusariosis cluster in a US tertiary‑care center where colonization of the potable water system was linked to invasive infections in highly immunocompromised patients. Event year 2001 reflects the principal Clinical Infectious Diseases investigation and publication rather than the full 1990s exposure window described in the paper; the precise start and end years of the cluster should be checked against the original article if finer temporal resolution is required. Geographic coding (North America, Northern America; United States of America) and host description are appropriate, and classification as re‑occurrence is justified because Fusarium infections in US hematology patients were already known and the increase was driven by environmental reservoir recognition and expanding high‑risk populations, not spread to a new region or a demonstrably novel genotype. Source URLs have been streamlined to focus on the original CID outbreak report and a major human fusariosis review, dropping a redundant ResearchGate link and a broad mycology review that added little event‑specific detail; flagged for review mainly to refine the exact temporal bounds if needed.

Host: Humans (patients undergoing cataract surgery with ophthalmic viscoelastic devices)
Event summary: In late 2020, ophthalmologists and public health authorities in the Republic of Korea detected an unusually large number of fungal endophthalmitis cases following cataract surgery across multiple hospitals nationwide. A national investigation identified around 150–160 affected eyes, most with Fusarium oxysporum isolated from intraocular specimens, and epidemiologic and microbiologic evidence linked cases to specific lots of a sodium hyaluronate ophthalmic viscoelastic device produced by a single manufacturer and distributed widely for cataract operations. Once the implicated viscoelastic batches were recalled and use was halted, along with intensified surveillance and treatment, the incidence of new Fusarium endophthalmitis cases associated with those products declined sharply and the outbreak gradually resolved, although many patients suffered substantial visual morbidity despite aggressive therapy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of widely distributed ophthalmic viscoelastic device lots used routinely in cataract surgery provided a direct route for intraocular inoculation of Fusarium spp., converting a rare opportunistic pathogen into the cause of a nationwide, iatrogenic outbreak; centralised procurement and rapid diffusion of the contaminated product across many facilities amplified the number of exposed patients. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was identified as Fusarium oxysporum, with genotypic identity between isolates from patients and from contaminated product, but the available data support clonal contamination and direct inoculation rather than the emergence of a distinctly more virulent or transmissible Fusarium lineage; disease severity mainly reflected the highly vulnerable intraocular site and delayed recognition rather than fundamental changes in pathogen biology.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the nationwide 2020 fungal endophthalmitis outbreak in the Republic of Korea linked to contaminated ophthalmic viscoelastic devices. Event years (2020–2021), geographic coding (Asia, Eastern Asia; Republic of Korea) and the host description align with national investigations and case series, and the approximate case numbers and linkage to specific viscoelastic lots are consistent with published data. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, because Fusarium ocular infections pre‑dated this episode in East Asia and the outbreak reflects contamination of a medical product rather than spread to a new region or a novel Fusarium lineage. Source URLs already point to the primary EID outbreak investigation and a large JAMA Ophthalmology clinical series and are suitable for documenting this event; no additional higher‑impact outbreaks of Fusarium endophthalmitis were identified that would supersede this episode in scale.

Host: Humans (predominantly obstetric and surgical patients receiving epidural or spinal anesthesia in Durango)
Event summary: From mid‑2022 into early 2023, clinicians in the state of Durango, Mexico, recognized an unusual cluster of subacute meningitis and meningoencephalitis, largely among women who had undergone cesarean sections or other procedures under neuraxial (epidural or spinal) anesthesia in several private hospitals. A retrospective cohort investigation identified roughly 1,800 patients exposed to neuraxial blockade between May 2022 and February 2023, of whom 80 developed Fusarium solani complex meningitis and 41 died, representing a case‑fatality rate of just over 50 percent; molecular testing of cerebrospinal fluid and anesthetic materials implicated contamination of specific bupivacaine batches used by one anesthesiologist as the source. After the contaminated anesthetic lots were withdrawn, exposed patients were traced and evaluated, and prolonged combination antifungal therapy was instituted for confirmed and probable cases, the incidence of new Fusarium meningitis cases declined and the outbreak was gradually controlled, although many survivors had severe neurologic sequelae.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Manufacturing or handling failures that led to contamination of bupivacaine batches used for neuraxial anesthesia, combined with high volumes of obstetric and surgical procedures and delayed recognition of a fungal etiology, created an efficient, high‑dose route of direct central nervous system inoculation; gaps in regulation and quality control for local anesthetic supplies and infection‑prevention practices in private clinics contributed to the scale and severity of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The Fusarium solani species complex strains involved showed the expected high minimum inhibitory concentrations to many systemic antifungals and marked neurotropism once introduced into the subarachnoid space, but available data suggest intrinsic resistance characteristics and route of exposure, rather than emergence of a demonstrably novel genotype, were the dominant drivers; the event is therefore best classified as a severe healthcare‑associated re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – Retain this event as it represents the largest documented outbreak of Fusarium solani meningitis, associated with neuraxial anesthesia in Durango, Mexico. The description has been updated to reflect more recent data from the Clinical Infectious Diseases cohort (approximately 1,801 exposed patients, 80 meningitis cases, 41 deaths), which supersede earlier provisional counts of 79 cases and around 35 deaths; the time window (mid‑2022 to early 2023), location (Mexico, Central America sub‑region under the South America continent grouping) and host profile are consistent with primary reports. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate: Fusarium was already known as a human pathogen in Mexico, and this event reflects contaminated anesthetic and procedural practices rather than first detection in a new region or emergence of a new strain. Source URLs have been refined to centre on the open‑access CID outbreak report, and less authoritative secondary summaries (for example general Wikipedia pages) have been removed; flagged for review mainly so that any future updates to case counts or follow‑up outcomes can be incorporated if the primary cohort is re‑analysed.

Host: Humans (medical tourists and local patients receiving cosmetic surgery under epidural anesthesia in Matamoros and subsequent care in Mexico or the United States)
Event summary: In early 2023, health authorities in Texas were notified of severe meningitis cases among US residents who had recently traveled to Matamoros, Tamaulipas, Mexico, for cosmetic procedures performed under epidural anesthesia, prompting a binational investigation. Public health agencies in Mexico and the United States ultimately identified hundreds of potentially exposed patients linked to two clinics (Clinica K‑3 and River Side Surgical Center) and documented at least two dozen confirmed and probable fungal meningitis cases among US residents plus additional affected patients in Mexico, with Fusarium solani species complex DNA detected in cerebrospinal fluid and a highly resistant F. solani strain isolated from at least one patient; about half of the confirmed and probable US cases died. Closure of the implicated clinics, international notification and screening of exposed individuals, and aggressive combination antifungal therapy and long‑term follow‑up led to progressive containment of the outbreak, though many patients experienced prolonged illness, neurovascular complications and significant morbidity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unsafe injection practices or contaminated anesthetic or related materials used for epidural anesthesia in high‑volume cosmetic surgery clinics that catered to international medical tourists created a direct route for Fusarium inoculation into the central nervous system, while cross‑border travel and delayed recognition of fungal meningitis facilitated a multinational outbreak spanning patients in Mexico and multiple US states. Internal mechanisms: The Fusarium solani complex isolates involved demonstrated high antifungal minimum inhibitory concentrations, consistent with substantial intrinsic resistance that complicated treatment, but current evidence points to contaminated procedures and direct CNS exposure rather than a fundamentally new, more transmissible or virulent Fusarium genotype; cases detected in the United States and any other countries are epidemiologically part of the same Matamoros‑centred healthcare‑associated episode and do not constitute separate inter‑continental emergence events.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major cross‑border outbreak of Fusarium solani meningitis among patients exposed to epidural anesthesia at two clinics in Matamoros, Mexico, with cases identified in multiple US states. Event year (2023), geographic coding (Central America for Mexico and Northern America for the United States) and the linked‑episode structure are appropriate; US and other non‑Mexican cases are correctly treated as part of the same healthcare‑associated episode rather than as separate inter‑continental emergence events, because exposure and presumed contamination occurred in Matamoros with no evidence of onward in‑country transmission. Case counts and fatality estimates in the summary are expressed qualitatively (dozens of confirmed and probable cases and roughly 50 percent mortality among the well‑characterised US cohort), which remain consistent with evolving surveillance data from CDC and Clinical Infectious Diseases reports; if finer numerical detail is needed, users should consult the cited cohort analyses. Source URLs have been curated to prioritise CDC Health Alert Network communications, the CDC HAI outbreak page and the detailed CID cohort description, and general Wikipedia pages have been removed; flagged for review mainly to ensure alignment with any future updates to case definitions or totals in official reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – predominantly adults with hematologic malignancies and other cancers receiving intensive chemotherapy and fluconazole prophylaxis
Event summary: At the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, USA, clinicians noted that Candida krusei, previously an uncommon cause of fungemia, began to account for an increasing proportion of bloodstream infections in cancer patients between 1989 and 1996. Over this 7‑year period, 60 cases of C. krusei fungemia were identified, with the proportion of fungemias due to C. krusei rising from about 5% in 1989–1992 to 10% in 1993–1996, and infections were strongly associated with leukemia, bone‑marrow transplantation, profound neutropenia, central venous catheters and widespread prophylactic use of fluconazole. The escalation was recognized as a serious therapeutic problem because of high mortality (~49% infection‑related) and intrinsic fluconazole resistance, leading to greater use of amphotericin B–based regimens and heightened awareness of drug‑resistant candidemia in high‑risk oncology settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of intensive chemotherapy and hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation programs created a large population of profoundly immunocompromised patients with central venous catheters and prolonged hospitalizations; widespread use of fluconazole prophylaxis and therapy exerted strong selective pressure favoring intrinsically fluconazole‑resistant Candida species; intensive antibiotic exposure and invasive procedures further disrupted host microbiota and barriers, increasing susceptibility to fungemia. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei and selection of this species under azole prophylaxis and therapy; enhanced transmission – likely healthcare‑associated spread within a high‑risk oncology population (temporal clustering and shared risk factors), although clonality was not formally assessed in this series.
Review: review – retain this event but correct the emergence‑type classification. This episode represents a marked re‑occurrence of C. krusei fungemia within an already affected subregion, driven mainly by external factors (introduction of fluconazole prophylaxis, expansion of intensive chemotherapy and transplant programs) rather than by a new strain or resistance mechanism. Accordingly, re_occurrence has been set to true and re_emergence to false; year range, geography, host description and case numbers match the MD Anderson series, and the cited sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – adults with hematologic malignancies and profound neutropenia in a hematology service receiving intensive chemotherapy and fluconazole‑containing antifungal prophylaxis
Event summary: At Erasmus MC University Medical Center in Rotterdam, Netherlands, a sudden rise in Candida krusei colonization and infection was observed among neutropenic hematology patients in the early 2000s, triggering a longitudinal outbreak investigation. During the study period, 39 patients were diagnosed with C. krusei carriage and/or candidemia, 13 developed bloodstream infection and three died, and genotyping showed that 25 patients shared a predominant outbreak genotype, indicating substantial nosocomial transmission under conditions of intensive fluconazole use. After antifungal prophylaxis was modified and stricter infection‑prevention measures were introduced, the incidence of new C. krusei colonization and candidemia dropped rapidly and the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Concentration of highly immunocompromised hematology patients with central venous catheters, mucosal damage from intensive chemotherapy and prolonged hospitalization; routine fluconazole‑based prophylaxis that suppressed susceptible yeasts and permitted intrinsically fluconazole‑resistant C. krusei to thrive; opportunities for cross‑transmission within shared inpatient wards. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei enabled it to escape azole prophylaxis and predominate once selected; enhanced transmission – clonal spread of a dominant genotype (genotype 1) among 25 of 39 patients demonstrated efficient healthcare‑associated transmission, although no novel resistance mechanism beyond baseline azole nonsusceptibility was identified.
Review: review – added as a new row to capture one of the largest documented C. krusei hospital outbreaks in Europe (39 colonized or infected hematology patients, 13 candidemias, three deaths). The time window is represented here as 2002–2003 to reflect the early‑2000s outbreak described by Vos et al. 2006, but exact start and end dates should be verified from the full text; therefore this row is flagged for review. Classified as re‑occurrence (a sharp increase within a previously affected Western European subregion driven by fluconazole prophylaxis and nosocomial spread) rather than re‑emergence, because no clearly novel strain or resistance mechanism is shown to underlie the outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans – adults with acute leukemia, other hematologic malignancies and selected solid tumors admitted to a hematology unit, many with severe mucosal injury, neutropenia and intensive cytotoxic therapy
Event summary: In February 2005, clinicians at the hematology unit of Oulu University Hospital in Finland recognized an unusual cluster of Candida krusei infections, with six patients developing bloodstream infection and a further six showing significant C. krusei growth from deep sites, in addition to several more patients with heavy mucosal colonization. Weekly surveillance cultures of all hematology patients between April and November 2005 identified widespread gastrointestinal colonization by C. krusei (up to 25% of patients in some months), but molecular typing showed mostly patient‑specific genotypes rather than a single dominant clone, suggesting repeated endogenous infections rather than a point‑source outbreak. After intensified hand hygiene, patient cohorting and discontinuation of routine fluconazole prophylaxis, invasive C. krusei infections ceased and no new colonization clusters were detected in subsequent surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑intensity chemotherapy and resulting mucosal injury in acute leukemia and other hematologic patients created portals of entry for gut colonizers; substantial prior antibacterial and some fluconazole exposure altered the mycobiota and likely favored intrinsically azole‑nonsusceptible C. krusei; close contact within a busy hematology ward provided opportunities for intermittent cross‑transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic resistance of C. krusei to fluconazole enabled it to persist under azole use, although this study did not demonstrate a new resistance mechanism; enhanced colonization of damaged gut mucosa and a tendency for endogenous invasion from the gastrointestinal tract rather than a single highly transmissible clone were emphasized.
Review: review – newly added event representing a well‑described 2005 cluster in a Finnish hematology unit (22 patients with C. krusei colonization or invasive infection, including 6 bloodstream infections), which is among the larger published C. krusei clusters in Northern Europe. Year and geographic classification follow Hautala et al. 2007; the event is classified as re‑occurrence because it reflects a surge within an already affected subregion driven mainly by host factors, chemotherapy‑associated mucosal damage and care practices, with no evidence for a fundamentally new strain or resistance phenotype. Sources focus on the original outbreak description; detailed case counts and relative contribution of colonization versus invasive disease should be checked in any downstream quantitative use, hence flagged for review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans – predominantly neonates and children (paediatric emergency and paediatric wards) with serious underlying illnesses
Event summary: At the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) in Chandigarh, North India, clinicians detected a sudden and sustained surge of Candida krusei candidemia beginning in early 2014, during which 316 candidemia cases were recorded over one year and C. krusei emerged as the single most common species (96 of 316 cases, 30%), especially among paediatric patients. Within this one‑year period, 82 paediatric C. krusei bloodstream infections occurred, with most isolations from the neonatal unit of the paediatric emergency department, and environmental and hand‑wash cultures identified C. krusei on a healthcare worker’s hands and in a washbasin; molecular typing (FAFLP) demonstrated clonality between blood and environmental isolates, confirming extensive cross‑transmission. After recognition of the outbreak, infection‑control measures (enhanced hand hygiene, environmental decontamination, and process changes for device care and antibiotic use) were intensified, which reduced C. krusei candidemia in subsequent years, although sporadic new strains continued to appear, indicating ongoing risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Marked overcrowding in the paediatric facility with high admissions and baby‑to‑bed ratios, frequent use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics – particularly carbapenems – and invasive devices created strong selection pressure and opportunities for bloodstream infection; lapses in hand hygiene and environmental cleaning allowed contamination of sinks and healthcare‑workers’ hands, enabling sustained nosocomial spread; heavy reliance on intensive care for critically ill neonates and children further increased exposure to central lines and parenteral nutrition. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei, combined with extensive antecedent antibiotic use, favored this species over more susceptible Candida spp.; enhanced transmission – clonal expansion of a single strain across patients and environmental reservoirs, demonstrated by FAFLP, reflects adaptation to the hospital environment and efficient healthcare‑associated transmission rather than a fundamentally new genotype with altered virulence.
Review: retain – this row accurately captures the very large 2014 paediatric C. krusei candidemia outbreak at PGIMER Chandigarh (96 C. krusei episodes, 82 in children) and is clearly among the highest‑impact events for this species worldwide. Geographic assignment (Asia/Southern Asia, India) and the 2014 time frame match the primary report; classifying the episode as re‑occurrence (a dramatic increase in incidence in a known subregion driven by overcrowding, antibiotic exposure and infection‑control failures) is consistent with the definitions, since no novel strain or resistance mechanism beyond intrinsic fluconazole resistance is implicated. No structural changes were needed; the event is recommended for retention as is.

Host: Humans – neonates and young infants in a tertiary‑care neonatal unit (Gauteng Province) with very low birthweight, prematurity, necrotizing enterocolitis and other serious comorbidities
Event summary: In 2014, a large tertiary neonatal unit in Gauteng Province, South Africa, experienced an explosive outbreak of Candida krusei candidemia, with 48 bloodstream infections occurring over just 4 months among highly vulnerable neonates, representing complete replacement of other Candida species during the peak months. Despite outbreak recognition and infection‑prevention interventions, the unit then experienced a second large C. krusei candidemia outbreak during April–July 2015 with 41 additional cases, in the context of recurrent fungal and bacterial bloodstream‑infection outbreaks linked to overcrowding and infrastructural constraints. The C. krusei outbreaks were eventually curtailed only after strengthened infection‑prevention and control, environmental remediation, and system‑level changes were implemented, although subsequent smaller fungal and bacterial clusters continued to occur through 2016.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe overcrowding (patient census above unit capacity), intermittent water supply, and structural limitations that prevented proper isolation of infected infants created conditions for sustained transmission; high baby‑to‑staff ratios and lapses in infection‑prevention and control practices (hand hygiene, handling of central lines, blood transfusions and total parenteral nutrition) promoted spread; the unit cared for extremely preterm and very low‑birthweight infants with fragile skin and mucosal barriers and frequent need for TPN and invasive devices, all recognized risk factors for candidemia. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission – epidemiologic patterns and repeated isolation of C. krusei from multiple infants over short intervals are consistent with nosocomial spread via healthcare workers’ hands and contaminated fomites, even though a specific environmental source was not identified; antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei likely conferred a survival advantage in a setting where fluconazole had been commonly used for empiric or prophylactic therapy, favoring persistence once the species was established.
Review: retain – the description, geography and timing of this event match the Emerging Infectious Diseases report of two linked C. krusei candidemia outbreaks in a Gauteng neonatal unit (48 cases in July–October 2014 and 41 cases in April–July 2015). Aggregating these closely spaced waves into a single 2014–2015 linked episode is consistent with the project’s definition of temporally and epidemiologically connected events, and classifying it as re‑occurrence within Southern Africa (rather than inter‑continental emergence) aligns with the fact that C. krusei was already known from the region. No corrections were required beyond adding this review note; the event should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – preterm and low‑birthweight neonates in a 24‑bed neonatal intensive care unit requiring intensive care, central venous access and broad‑spectrum antibiotics
Event summary: In a neonatal intensive care unit in Delhi, India, investigators using whole‑genome sequencing documented a protracted series of Pichia kudriavzevii (Candida krusei) bloodstream infections in hospital‑born neonates between 2015 and 2020, comprising at least two outbreak clusters separated in time. Across this five‑year period, 24 neonates were affected in two main clusters (one in 2015–2016 and another in 2020), and genomic analyses showed that infections were caused by multiple but closely related strain clusters that persisted and reappeared within the unit, with some isolates exhibiting higher fluconazole and itraconazole MICs and characteristic loss‑of‑heterozygosity events. Following recognition of these outbreaks and the implementation of strengthened infection‑prevention practices and antifungal stewardship in the NICU, transmission was reduced, though the study highlighted the potential for continued adaptation and persistence of P. kudriavzevii in this high‑risk setting.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High occupancy and prolonged hospitalization of critically ill neonates in a resource‑constrained NICU, extensive use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics and central venous catheters, and intermittent use of azole antifungals created strong ecological niches for intrinsically azole‑nonsusceptible P. kudriavzevii; repeated admissions and overlapping stays facilitated within‑unit transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection and genomic adaptation – whole‑genome and transcriptomic analyses identified distinct strain clusters with differing fluconazole and itraconazole MICs and frequent loss‑of‑heterozygosity events, indicating rapid evolution and selection of better‑adapted hospital lineages; enhanced transmission – recurrence of closely related genotypes across separate outbreak years suggests persistent colonization of the unit and repeated healthcare‑associated spread rather than de novo introduction each time.
Review: review – added as a new row to represent genomically documented P. kudriavzevii outbreaks in a Delhi NICU, involving roughly 24 neonates across two main clusters during 2015–2020, which places this episode among the more impactful neonatal C. krusei events worldwide. The time span and approximate case burden are drawn from Jain et al. 2025 and a recent neonatal invasive candidiasis review; finer subdivision into separate 2015–2016 and 2020 rows could be considered in future iterations. Classified as re‑occurrence within Southern Asia because the species was already established in India and the surge is driven by NICU ecology and adaptation of existing strains rather than first introduction to the region; users should verify exact case counts and any local mortality data before quantitative use, so this row is flagged for review.
