Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: United States of America; France; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Switzerland
Host: Humans with HIV/AIDS and other immunosuppressed adults
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the early 2000s, multiple centres in North America and Europe detected novel mutations at codons 55 and 57 in the dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) domain of Pneumocystis jirovecii, strongly associated with prior sulfonamide exposure, marking the global emergence of sulfa-associated P. jirovecii genotypes. Over this period the frequency of DHPS-mutant strains increased among HIV-infected patients receiving trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or dapsone prophylaxis or treatment, and such mutants were linked to prophylaxis failures and worse outcomes in several cohorts. By the early 2000s, mutant DHPS genotypes had been reported in clinical isolates from the United States, France, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and other countries, after which prevalence appeared to plateau or vary by locale as antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis practices evolved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3323267/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy use of sulfonamide-containing regimens (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, dapsone + trimethoprim) for PCP prophylaxis and treatment in HIV-infected and other immunosuppressed patients, creating strong drug-selection pressure; large HIV/AIDS-related PCP caseloads in urban referral centres. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (recurrent point mutations in the DHPS active site); Antimicrobial Resistance (functional studies in model systems demonstrate that analogous DHPS substitutions reduce susceptibility to sulfa drugs); possible Enhanced Transmission as mutant strains disseminated within high-burden patient networks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3323267/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain: Global emergence of DHPS mutations linked to sulfonamide exposure and worse outcomes in PCP is well documented from the early 1990s in Europe and North America; framing this as a high-impact re-emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance is appropriate, and the listed years and countries capture the main early study sites, although additional European centres (e.g. Denmark, Italy) were also involved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3323267/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Renal transplant recipients (HIV-negative adults)
Event summary: Around 1990–1991, a Swiss renal transplantation programme reported five cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia among HIV-negative kidney transplant recipients over a 22‑month period, after years with no PCP in this cohort, while AIDS patients with active PCP were being seen in the same outpatient facility. A case–control analysis showed that affected transplant recipients had more encounters in shared waiting and treatment rooms with AIDS patients who had, or later developed, PCP, suggesting transmission from HIV-infected patients to other immunosuppressed hosts. Following recognition of this unusual cluster, greater emphasis was placed on chemoprophylaxis and separation of high-risk transplant patients from AIDS wards, and no similar cluster was reported from this centre in subsequent years. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Co-location of renal transplant recipients and AIDS patients with PCP in the same outpatient clinic areas; lack of routine PCP prophylaxis for kidney transplant recipients beyond the early post-transplant period; episodes of acute graft rejection requiring intensified immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (epidemiologic evidence suggesting patient-to-patient spread from AIDS patients with PCP to renal transplant recipients); no specific novel genotype documented at that time. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The Lausanne cluster of five renal transplant recipients with PCP temporally associated with outpatient contact with AIDS patients is real and historically important for suggesting cross-group transmission, but small in absolute size; the year has been approximated to 1990–1991 to better align with the 22‑month period described in the 1991 AIDS report, the host field has been restricted to HIV-negative renal transplant recipients, the event type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence (no evidence of a novel strain), and the PubMed URL has been corrected. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Adult renal transplant recipients and HIV-infected adults sharing a renal/immunology/HIV building
Event summary: Between 1994 and 1996, a Lyon hospital building that housed both renal transplant services and HIV care units experienced a cluster of ten PCP episodes in renal transplant recipients alongside 36 cases in HIV-infected patients, after only one transplant PCP case in the preceding seven years. Molecular typing of Pneumocystis isolates showed that a single genotype (type 1) was disproportionately common among transplant recipients and was shared between several transplant and HIV-infected patients who had overlapping hospital stays, pointing to nosocomial person-to-person transmission within the building. After the outbreak was recognized, the centre implemented systematic trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for susceptible patients and HAART for HIV-infected individuals, and no further PCP cases occurred in renal transplant recipients through at least 2003. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High density of HIV-infected patients with PCP and renal transplant recipients in the same building; lack of, or suboptimal, anti-PCP prophylaxis in both groups during much of the period; intense immunosuppression in transplant recipients because of rejection episodes. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence that a predominant P. jirovecii type circulated between HIV and transplant patients); possible selection of type 1 in this local setting, but without clear evidence of novel virulence traits. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Review: review: This event has been corrected to reflect the Lyon Edouard-Herriot Hospital outbreak in 1994–1996 rather than 1998–2001, matching the period when ten renal transplant and numerous HIV-infected patients developed PCP in a shared building; it is reclassified as re-occurrence since it reflects nosocomial spread of an existing genotype (type 1) under inadequate prophylaxis rather than emergence of a new strain, and remains highly informative for transmission dynamics despite modest absolute size. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Adult renal transplant recipients
Event summary: In 1995, a Paris renal transplant centre (Hôpital Necker-Enfants Malades) reported an outbreak of Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) pneumonia in seven kidney transplant recipients who developed severe PCP a mean of about five months after transplantation, most following episodes of acute rejection and cytomegalovirus infection. The clustering of severe atypical pneumonia with high mortality in recently transplanted patients, in the absence of routine long-term prophylaxis, raised concern about cross-infection or a shared environmental source within the renal unit. After introduction of systematic cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for kidney transplant recipients and strengthened infection-control measures, the unit no longer observed similar clusters of PCP. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7758477/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive immunosuppression associated with acute rejection treatment, frequent cytomegalovirus co-infection, and lack of standardised long-term PCP prophylaxis in renal transplant protocols at that time; shared inpatient spaces facilitating airborne spread between transplant recipients. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (epidemiologic pattern consistent with nosocomial spread within a single transplant ward); no specific novel genotype or resistance mechanism was identified. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7758477/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The seven-case 1995 outbreak in a Paris renal transplant unit is accurately described and remains a key early example of nosocomial PCP in solid-organ transplantation; the event is retained but reclassified as re-occurrence because only external drivers (high immunosuppression burden, CMV co-infection, absence of prophylaxis) were demonstrated, not pathogen change, and its relatively small size means it is borderline among the ten most impactful events when compared to later national-level incidence shifts. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7758477/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
Host: Adults with hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants, chronic lung disease and other non-HIV immunosuppressive conditions, plus persons with HIV infection
Event summary: From 2000 to 2010, England recorded a steady rise in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia diagnoses, with hospital admissions increasing from 157 to 352 per year and national surveillance showing a marked shift from HIV-associated PCP towards non-HIV immunocompromised patients, especially those with haematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants and chronic lung disease. In the subsequent decade, population-level analyses indicate that PCP incidence in England more than doubled again between 2012 and 2020, with a growing burden among older adults and patients receiving modern immunosuppressive and biologic therapies, while HIV-related PCP continued to decline. Across this 20‑year period PCP re-emerged as a major, largely preventable opportunistic infection in non-HIV risk groups, prompting calls to broaden prophylaxis criteria and improve recognition of chronic lung disease and other conditions as important risk factors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3647665/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and ageing of non-HIV immunocompromised populations (haematologic malignancies, solid-organ and stem-cell transplantation, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases), increasing use of high-dose corticosteroids and biologic agents, and inconsistent application of PCP prophylaxis in these groups; improved diagnostics and coding may also contribute. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain has been implicated at the national level; changes are best explained by host- and healthcare-related drivers, though underlying genetic diversity of P. jirovecii may modulate clinical patterns in specific clusters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3647665/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This national-scale event is retained but the time window has been extended from 2000–2010 to 2000–2020 to incorporate newer data showing that PCP incidence in England continued to rise and more than doubled again between 2012 and 2020; the country field has been simplified to ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland’ (with England specified in the summary), and the event is now coded solely as re-occurrence because the increase is driven by expanding non-HIV immunosuppressed populations and changing prophylaxis rather than a demonstrably new strain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3647665/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Adults with HIV infection and non-HIV immunosuppressive conditions (hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, chronic lung disease, other immunosuppression)
Event summary: During 2001–2010, nationwide hospital discharge data from France documented substantial changes in invasive fungal infections, with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia incidence decreasing sharply among AIDS patients but increasing by more than 10% per year in non–HIV-infected patients, so that by the end of the decade non-HIV PCP incidence approximated that in persons with HIV. A multicentre cohort of 544 PCP cases from 2007–2010 further showed that 59% of patients had non-HIV immunosuppressive disorders, that non-AIDS patients had much higher in-hospital mortality than AIDS patients, and that many were receiving high-dose or prolonged corticosteroids or other potent immunosuppressants without PCP prophylaxis. Together these findings indicate a major re-occurrence of PCP in France’s non-HIV immunocompromised population, with increasing absolute case numbers and deaths despite declining HIV-related disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4073874/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rising numbers of patients with haematologic malignancies, solid-organ and haematopoietic stem-cell transplants, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases and chronic lung disease treated with intensive or prolonged immunosuppression; incomplete application of PCP prophylaxis in these groups; improved recognition and coding of PCP. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain has been implicated; changes are best ascribed to host and treatment factors, so this episode is treated as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4073874/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This is a newly added, high-impact national event capturing the well-documented shift in France between 2001 and 2010, where PCP incidence fell in AIDS patients but rose markedly among non-HIV immunosuppressed populations and non-AIDS PCP mortality exceeded that of AIDS-related PCP; it is coded as re-occurrence, driven by expansion of high-risk patient populations and immunosuppressive therapies rather than pathogen evolution, and warrants inclusion among the largest post‑1990 emergence events for this EPP. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4073874/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Pediatric renal transplant recipients and an infant with severe underlying disease
Event summary: In the early 2000s, a pediatric renal transplant unit in Heidelberg, Germany, which had reported virtually no PCP for two decades, experienced three consecutive cases of PCP among kidney transplant recipients over about five months, along with an infant on the same ward who developed PCP in the context of a mitochondriopathy. Single-strand conformation polymorphism typing showed that the three transplant recipients shared two identical P. jirovecii strains, and that the infant harboured multiple strains including these, strongly supporting nosocomial transmission from the infant index case or between the transplant patients themselves. Following recognition of the cluster, the unit introduced routine trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for pediatric renal transplant recipients and reinforced infection-control measures, after which no further linked PCP cases were reported in this population. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Absence of routine PCP prophylaxis in pediatric kidney transplant protocols owing to concerns about drug toxicity; close spatial clustering of highly immunosuppressed children and an index PCP case on the same ward; prolonged hospitalisations enabling repeated exposures. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence of interhuman spread of specific P. jirovecii strains among paediatric patients); no novel resistance or genotype with clearly altered virulence was identified. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Review: review: The Heidelberg pediatric renal transplant outbreak, with three paediatric graft recipients and one infant index case, is correctly described and supported by detailed molecular work; it is retained because it provides pivotal evidence for nosocomial transmission in a pediatric setting, but is reclassified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence and flagged as a relatively small event compared with later national-level incidence shifts, so could be deprioritized if a strict top‑10-by-case-count rule is enforced. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Adult kidney transplant recipients
Event summary: In the mid‑2000s, an Australian renal transplant service documented a cluster of 14 Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia cases among kidney transplant recipients, far exceeding the centre’s prior experience and occurring predominantly late after transplantation. Many affected patients required intensive care, two died and several lost their grafts, and contact mapping showed that cases were temporally and spatially linked through a busy outpatient transplant clinic and shared ward areas. Once the cluster was recognised, the service instituted blanket trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for all potentially exposed kidney transplant recipients and extended routine prophylaxis duration, together with strengthened infection-control measures, which was followed by rapid cessation of new outbreak-associated PCP cases. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing cohort of chronically immunosuppressed kidney transplant recipients, many years out from transplantation; limited baseline use or early discontinuation of PCP prophylaxis owing to toxicity concerns; dense patient contact networks in outpatient clinics and inpatient wards. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (epidemiologic clustering and multilocus sequence data consistent with person-to-person spread of closely related strains); no evidence of a unique, more virulent genotype driving the outbreak. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The Australian kidney-transplant cluster, involving 14 cases with high morbidity and strong epidemiologic evidence for clinic-based nosocomial transmission, is real and among the larger transplant-unit outbreaks; the event is retained but its type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since no novel strain or resistance mechanism was shown, and the summary has been aligned more closely with the details reported by Phipps et al. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Adult renal and liver transplant recipients
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2010, Denmark’s largest transplantation centre (Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen) experienced a major outbreak of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, with 29 cases among renal and liver transplant recipients in a setting where routine PCP prophylaxis was not used. Multilocus genotyping of respiratory specimens from cases and controls showed several distinct P. jirovecii genotypes circulating, with three predominant genotypes shared across clusters of renal and liver recipients, consistent with repeated nosocomial transmission along shared inpatient and outpatient pathways. After the outbreak investigation, the centre introduced systematic cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and enhanced infection-control measures for solid-organ transplant recipients, resulting in a marked decline in new PCP cases in this population. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High volume of solid-organ transplantation and follow-up without standard long-term PCP prophylaxis; shared outpatient facilities and inpatient wards linking renal and liver recipients; intensive immunosuppressive regimens including treatment for rejection and cytomegalovirus infection. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence for clustering of specific P. jirovecii genotypes within and between organ groups); multiple pre-existing strains were involved rather than a single novel outbreak lineage. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain: The 29-case Rigshospitalet outbreak in renal and liver transplant recipients (2007–2010) is accurately timed and located, and is clearly one of the largest documented nosocomial PCP outbreaks in solid-organ transplantation; it is retained as a key high-impact event, with classification adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence because several existing genotypes circulated under conditions of absent prophylaxis and intense patient contact. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Adults with and without HIV infection, including patients with hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants, autoimmune diseases, chronic lung disease and other immunosuppressive conditions
Event summary: From 2008 to 2012, national hospital discharge data from Spain identified 4,554 admissions with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and a nationwide analysis showed that while overall incidence remained relatively stable, the proportion and incidence of PCP among HIV-negative patients increased, whereas incidence among persons with HIV infection declined. Among HIV-negative cases, most had identifiable risk factors such as haematologic malignancies, chronic lung diseases and non-haematologic cancers, and mean in-hospital mortality and costs were high, highlighting PCP as an emerging public health problem in non-HIV immunocompromised Spaniards. This multi-year pattern represents a substantial re-occurrence of PCP in new patient groups at the national level, analogous to trends documented in the United Kingdom and France during overlapping periods. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changing epidemiology of immunosuppression in Spain, with more patients receiving chemotherapy, steroids and other immunosuppressants for cancers, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, and chronic lung conditions; declining HIV-related PCP due to effective antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis; underuse or late initiation of prophylaxis in non-HIV risk groups. Internal mechanisms: No specific new P. jirovecii strain was implicated; the emergence is best explained by host- and health-system-level changes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This newly added event summarises the first nationwide Spanish analysis of 4,554 PCP admissions during 2008–2012, which demonstrated rising incidence and high mortality among HIV-negative immunocompromised patients despite stable overall rates; it is classified as re-occurrence, driven by expanding and changing non-HIV risk groups, and merits inclusion among the major post‑1990 emergence events for P. jirovecii because of its national scale and clinical burden. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Adult renal transplant recipients
Event summary: In the early 2010s, a tertiary-care renal transplant centre in South India reported what was described as the first recognised outbreak of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia among its kidney transplant recipients, with a cluster of hospitalised patients developing PCP over a relatively short period after years in which the infection had been rare. Many affected patients were admitted for reasons other than suspected respiratory infection and only later developed respiratory failure with radiologic changes, underscoring low baseline awareness of PCP risk in this setting. After the cluster was recognised, the centre implemented more systematic cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and strengthened infection-control procedures, which were followed by a marked reduction in new PCP cases among their transplant recipients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of renal transplantation activity in India with limited routine use of prolonged PCP prophylaxis; high patient density and shared inpatient facilities in a large multispecialty hospital; delayed recognition of PCP as an important opportunistic infection in non-HIV immunocompromised patients in the region. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission is suspected based on temporal and spatial clustering in the transplant ward, but no detailed genotyping was reported; thus the episode is better framed as re-occurrence in a previously low-recognition setting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The South Indian renal-transplant outbreak is genuine and important as the first reported cluster in this population, but the exact outbreak window is not clearly stated in the abstract and may be shorter (around 2012–2013) than the 2010–2013 span used here; the event is therefore retained but coded as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence, and its start and end years should be verified against the full text if precise dating is required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Adult kidney transplant recipients
Event summary: Over an 11‑month period from July 2019 to May 2020, a US kidney-transplant centre (Yale) identified an outbreak of 19 Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia cases among kidney transplant recipients, many years after transplantation, in a setting where baseline PCP incidence had been low. Deep multilocus sequence typing with next-generation sequencing of respiratory samples from nine patients revealed coinfection with up to seven distinct P. jirovecii strains per patient and overlapping strain sets across cases, indicating multiple overlapping nosocomial transmission clusters rather than a single clone. A case–control analysis highlighted frequent transplant-clinic visits, belatacept-based immunosuppression, lower lymphocyte counts and non-White race as important risk factors, and implementation of extended trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and enhanced infection-control measures was followed by interruption of further outbreak-associated PCP cases. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-volume kidney transplant clinic with chronically immunosuppressed patients, including many receiving monthly belatacept infusions requiring frequent in-person visits; incomplete or time-limited PCP prophylaxis; dense patient–patient and patient–staff contact networks in outpatient and inpatient settings. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (NGS-based molecular epidemiology demonstrated repeated interhuman spread and complex coinfections with multiple genotypically related strains); no evidence that a single novel, more virulent strain was responsible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This US kidney-transplant outbreak has been substantially corrected: the event is now dated 2019–2020 rather than 2010–2015, the summary emphasises the 19 cases occurring over an 11‑month period with next-generation sequencing evidence for multiple overlapping transmission clusters, and the event type has been changed to re-occurrence since the outbreak was driven by clinic exposure and immunosuppression patterns rather than emergence of a single new strain; it should be retained as a major recent example of nosocomial PCP in North America. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – mainly adults with advanced HIV/AIDS; later smaller numbers of non-HIV immunocompromised patients
Event summary: From 1990 onwards, northern Thailand (especially Chiang Mai) experienced a sharp rise in disseminated Talaromyces marneffei infections as the HIV epidemic expanded, with talaromycosis becoming one of the leading AIDS-defining opportunistic infections in the country. Over 6,700 cases were diagnosed nationally between 1984 and 2004, with at least 1,843 cases seen at Chiang Mai University Hospital alone, and incidence peaked before widespread access to antiretroviral therapy. As antiretroviral therapy coverage improved in the early 2000s, incidence and mortality from talaromycosis began to decline, although the infection remained a major cause of morbidity and death among people with late-presenting HIV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Thailand created a large population of severely immunosuppressed adults, particularly in northern provinces, with high exposure to environmental niches harboring T. marneffei; limited early access to antiretroviral therapy and delayed HIV diagnosis amplified risk. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel fungal strain; emergence reflects opportunistic infection in an existing human host species (people with advanced HIV) rather than genetic change of the fungus itself.
Review: review – Retain this as a major high-impact event (nationally >6,000 Thai cases 1984–2004) but reclassify it from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the post-1990 surge is best explained by external drivers (the HIV epidemic and delayed ART access) without evidence for fungal genetic change; continent, sub-region, country, years, host, and sources are consistent with major epidemiologic reviews and national surveillance.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Thailand [1990]; Myanmar [early 1990s]; Cambodia [1990s]; Laos [1990s]; Malaysia [1990s]; Viet Nam [1996]; Philippines [late 1990s]
Host: Humans – primarily adults with advanced HIV/AIDS
Event summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, talaromycosis expanded from northern Thailand into a belt of neighboring Southeast Asian countries, with autochthonous AIDS-associated cases documented in Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Vietnam and later the Philippines. In Vietnam, the first AIDS-related talaromycosis cases were reported in 1996–1997, followed by a large cohort of patients managed at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City between 1996 and 2009, where talaromycosis became a common AIDS-defining illness. By the late 2000s, talaromycosis was recognized as an established endemic opportunistic mycosis across much of mainland South-eastern Asia, with incidence gradually modified by improving HIV testing and antiretroviral therapy programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional spread and maturation of the HIV epidemic throughout mainland South-eastern Asia, combined with ecological suitability (presence of bamboo rat reservoirs and favorable climate) and improvements in mycology diagnostic capacity in referral centers. Internal mechanisms: No specific new fungal genotype identified; the emergence is best explained by geographic expansion of recognized human infection due to increased exposure and susceptible hosts and by improved recognition rather than biological change of the pathogen.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the multi-country spread of HIV-associated talaromycosis within South-eastern Asia and should be retained as one of the largest regional episodes; however, the emergence type has been corrected from re_emergence to re_occurrence because expansion into additional countries within the same UNSD sub-region is driven by HIV epidemiology and improved detection rather than documented pathogen change, and it does not qualify as intra-continental emergence under the given rules.

Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [late 1980s–early 1990s]; China (Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Yunnan, Hunan) [early 1990s]; China, Taiwan [1994]
Host: Humans – mainly adults with advanced HIV/AIDS; later some HIV-negative immunocompromised patients
Event summary: From the early 1990s, talaromycosis emerged as a leading AIDS-defining illness in Hong Kong and southern mainland China, where it ranked just behind Pneumocystis pneumonia as a cause of AIDS-defining disease and was reported in up to around 8% of AIDS patients in Hong Kong. During the same decade, increasing numbers of cases were described in southern Chinese provinces such as Guangxi, Guangdong, Fujian, Yunnan and Hunan, indicating establishment of endemicity in southern China, and in 1994 the first locally acquired case was reported in Taiwan, followed by growing numbers of HIV-associated and later non-HIV cases. By the 2000s, talaromycosis was firmly recognized as an endemic opportunistic infection across southern China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, with incidence in HIV patients later declining as antiretroviral therapy coverage improved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of the HIV epidemic into southern China and Hong Kong, increased clinical awareness, and improved mycological diagnostics in tertiary centers; urbanization and internal migration likely increased contact between susceptible people and environmental reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype documented; this event represents intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD Asian subregion (Eastern Asia) and opportunistic infection in immunocompromised human hosts rather than change in the pathogen itself.
Review: review – Retain this event and keep its classification as intra_continental_emergence because it marks the first substantial establishment of talaromycosis in the Eastern Asia sub-region (southern China, Hong Kong, Taiwan); remove the re_emergence flag (now set to false) since there is no evidence of pathogen change, and ensure re_occurrence remains false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: India (Manipur state, northeastern India) [1994]; India (additional northeastern states) [late 1990s]
Host: Humans – adults with advanced HIV/AIDS
Event summary: In 1994, clinicians in Manipur state, northeastern India, reported the first four indigenous cases of disseminated T. marneffei infection in HIV-positive patients residing in India, all without travel outside the region, establishing that talaromycosis was endemic there rather than imported. Over the subsequent 19 months (1998–1999), an additional 46 HIV-infected patients with disseminated talaromycosis were diagnosed from the same area, confirming a substantial local disease burden and clinical similarity to cases from Thailand and southern China. By the late 1990s, talaromycosis was recognized as an important AIDS-defining opportunistic infection in northeastern India, extending the known endemic range westward in Asia, with cases continuing into the 2000s as HIV care programs expanded.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Local HIV epidemic in northeastern India bordering Myanmar, where talaromycosis was already endemic, coupled with improved diagnostic capacity and awareness; cross-border movement likely contributed to initial introduction or detection of the fungus. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain identified; this represents intra-continental emergence of recognized human infection into a new UNSD subregion (Southern Asia) rather than a change in fungal biology.
Review: review – Keep this as a distinct intra-continental emergence event because it documents the first confirmed endemic focus in the Southern Asia sub-region (Manipur and neighboring states) with dozens of autochthonous HIV-associated cases; remove the inappropriate first_detection and re_emergence flags (both now false), since global first detection occurred in 1973 and there is no evidence of pathogen change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Viet Nam (Ho Chi Minh City and southern provinces) [1996]
Host: Humans – adults with advanced HIV/AIDS
Event summary: Between 1996 and 1997, the first four AIDS patients with disseminated talaromycosis were reported from Ho Chi Minh City, marking the first recognition of the disease in Vietnam. In the following years, as HIV incidence rose and diagnostic capacity improved, hundreds of additional talaromycosis cases were managed at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City between 1996 and 2009, and the infection became a common cause of hospitalization and death among people with advanced HIV. With the rollout of Vietnam’s National Strategy on HIV/AIDS prevention and expanded antiretroviral therapy from the mid-2000s, talaromycosis incidence began to stabilize but remained a major opportunistic mycosis in southern Vietnam.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing HIV epidemic in southern Vietnam, delayed HIV diagnosis, and limited early access to antiretroviral therapy, combined with ecological suitability similar to neighboring endemic countries; strengthening of referral hospital laboratories enabled recognition and reporting. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of major genetic change in the fungus; emergence is due to opportunistic infection in a susceptible host population within an already endemic subregion and improved detection.
Review: review – Retain this as a separate high-impact event because large cohorts from Ho Chi Minh City document hundreds of AIDS-associated talaromycosis admissions and high mortality, but correct the emergence typing: this is a re-occurrence within the already endemic South-eastern Asia sub-region, not a first_detection or intra-continental emergence, and there is no evidence for pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans – predominantly HIV-negative adults with hematologic malignancies, autoimmune disease, or other immunosuppressive conditions; some HIV-positive patients
Event summary: From 2003 to 2014, hospitals in Guangxi, a highly endemic southern Chinese province, documented a growing number of disseminated T. marneffei infections in HIV-negative patients with underlying hematologic malignancies, autoimmune diseases, organ transplantation or other immunosuppressive states, alongside the ongoing burden in people with HIV. Retrospective analyses from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University showed that these HIV-negative infections could be severe and frequently fatal, challenging the previous view of talaromycosis as almost exclusively HIV-associated. By the mid-2010s, talaromycosis in HIV-negative immunocompromised hosts was recognized as a distinct and expanding clinical problem in southern China, prompting calls for broader diagnostic vigilance and prophylactic strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased use of immunosuppressive therapies for cancer, autoimmune disease and transplantation in Guangxi, coupled with better mycological diagnostics and awareness among clinicians. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of recognized disease into HIV-negative but immunocompromised human hosts; available data do not demonstrate a new fungal genotype or resistance phenotype, so this is treated as re-occurrence driven by changes in host populations and medical practices rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – This event usefully highlights the emergence of severe talaromycosis in HIV-negative but immunocompromised adults in Guangxi; classification has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence because the shift is best attributed to increased iatrogenic immunosuppression and improved diagnostics rather than documented fungal adaptation, while geographic fields and timing remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China (Guangzhou, Guangdong Province) [2004]; China (Hubei Province) [2006]; China (Shanghai Municipality, eastern China) [2014]
Host: Humans – mainly adults with advanced HIV/AIDS; some HIV-negative immunocompromised adults
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2011, serologic surveillance and clinical cohorts in Guangzhou (Guangdong Province) documented a high prevalence of talaromycosis among HIV-infected patients, indicating a substantial but previously under-recognized burden in this major southern Chinese metropolis. Building on this, a large retrospective cohort at Guangzhou Eighth People’s Hospital found 1,214 culture- or histopathology-confirmed talaromycosis cases among 7,575 hospitalized adults with HIV during 2011–2017, with talaromycosis accounting for roughly 16% of HIV-related admissions and showing an upward trend despite ART scale-up. From 2006 to 2013, 47 HIV-positive inpatients with culture-confirmed T. marneffei infection were identified in Hubei Province, a historically non-endemic central region, and between about 2005 and 2015 additional HIV-infected patients with talaromycosis were reported from Shanghai in eastern China, marking a spread of clinically significant disease into new urban centers within Eastern Asia. By the mid-2010s, talaromycosis was increasingly recognized as an important opportunistic infection among people with HIV both within and beyond the traditional southern endemic foci of China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Internal migration from southern endemic provinces to central and eastern Chinese cities, expansion of HIV epidemics into new regions, improved fungal diagnostics, and heightened clinician awareness led to increased detection in Guangzhou, Hubei and Shanghai; expansion of antiretroviral therapy programs may have subsequently tempered incidence. Internal mechanisms: This represents re-occurrence and geographic broadening of recognized disease within the Eastern Asia subregion, driven by changing human populations and healthcare access rather than documented genetic changes in the fungus.
Review: review – Retain this event but update it to cover 2004–2017 and explicitly include the large Guangdong cohort (≈1,200 HIV-associated cases and ~16% prevalence among HIV admissions), while keeping Hubei and Shanghai as examples of spread into central and eastern China; emergence type is corrected to re_occurrence only (no intra_continental_emergence or re_emergence), because these foci lie within the already affected Eastern Asia sub-region and the surge reflects HIV dynamics, migration, and diagnostics rather than first subregional occurrence or pathogen evolution.

Countries: China (Guangxi, Guangdong, Hong Kong SAR, Taiwan) [mid-2000s]; Thailand [mid-2000s]; Viet Nam [2010s]; other Southeast Asian endemic countries [2010s]
Host: Humans – primarily HIV-negative adults with adult-onset immunodeficiency due to anti–interferon-γ autoantibodies; other inborn errors of immunity and iatrogenic immunosuppression
Event summary: From around 2004 onwards, clinicians in Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong and southern China began reporting clusters of disseminated talaromycosis in HIV-negative adults with unexplained susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, which were later linked to high-titer neutralizing anti–interferon-γ autoantibodies and related adult-onset immunodeficiency syndromes. Over the 2000s and 2010s, multiple case series confirmed T. marneffei as a leading fungal pathogen in this new host group, often presenting with recurrent or relapsing talaromycosis and co-infections such as nontuberculous mycobacteria and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. By around 2020, talaromycosis associated with anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated adult-onset immunodeficiency and other inborn errors of immunity was widely recognized across endemic regions in East and Southeast Asia, representing a major re-occurrence of the pathogen in a non-HIV immunodeficient population and contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality despite antifungal therapy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Emergence and recognition of adult-onset immunodeficiency syndromes due to anti–IFN-γ autoantibodies and increased use of advanced immunosuppressive therapies for cancer and autoimmune diseases; improved immunologic and genetic diagnostics revealed underlying immune defects in previously unexplained non-HIV talaromycosis cases. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of recognized disease into new immunologic niches within the human host population (adult-onset neutralizing anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated immunodeficiency and other inborn errors of immunity); no specific fungal genetic change has been definitively linked, so the episode is treated as re-occurrence driven by changes in host immunity and medical practice.
Review: review – This event is retained as it captures a major shift of talaromycosis into HIV-negative adults with anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated and other immunodeficiencies across East and South-eastern Asia; the emergence type is standardized to re_occurrence (first_detection and re_emergence set to false), reflecting that the fungus exploits newly recognized human immune defects within already endemic subregions rather than representing a new global detection or documented pathogen-level re-emergence.

Host: Primarily HIV-seronegative infants and young children (≈3–26 months old) with and without diarrhea attending primary care clinics in Niamey; surveys also included a small series of immunocompromised adults with chronic diarrhea.
Event summary: From 1992 to 1993, investigators in Niamey, Niger conducted stool surveys for microsporidia among nearly 1,000 young, HIV-seronegative children at two primary care centers and in a smaller series of hospital patients. Using chromotrope-based staining and electron microscopy they detected Enterocytozoon bieneusi spores in about 0.8% of children and in roughly 7% of 60 mainly diarrheic, immunocompromised adults, showing that intestinal microsporidiosis was already established in both pediatric and adult populations in West Africa. The work ended as cross-sectional investigations rather than a defined outbreak, but provided some of the first well-documented evidence of endemic human microsporidiosis in West Africa and stimulated further surveys in African HIV and pediatric cohorts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Poor sanitation, limited access to safe drinking water, and high fecal–oral exposure in peri‑urban Niamey likely facilitated transmission of environmentally resistant microsporidian spores; limited diagnostic capacity meant infections in children and adults had previously gone unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was identified; the episode mainly reflects improved detection of existing Enterocytozoon bieneusi infections in a new African subregion and in largely immunocompetent young children, rather than documented pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Original row mis-characterized this event as involving HIV-positive adults only, mis-located it as an inter-continental emergence, and labeled it as a global “first detection.” Updated the timing to 1992–1993 with country tag Niger [1992], corrected the host to primarily HIV-seronegative young children (with a smaller adult series), rewrote the event summary and drivers to match the published Niamey surveys, changed the emergence classification to intra-continental emergence within Africa (first well-documented detection in West Africa) with first_detection and inter_continental_emergence set to false, and replaced hard-to-access or generic sources with focused reviews that explicitly summarize the Niamey data. Because these reconstructions rely on secondary summaries of the original AIDS 1993 abstract and related work, they should be cross-checked against the primary articles by Bretagne et al. and colleagues.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Adults with HIV infection and chronic unexplained diarrhea attending HIV clinics in Rio de Janeiro.
Event summary: Beginning in 1992, clinicians in Rio de Janeiro identified intestinal microsporidiosis in HIV-positive adults with chronic unexplained diarrhea and then undertook cohort and cross-sectional studies through the mid‑1990s. These investigations showed that microsporidia, predominantly Enterocytozoon bieneusi, were present in a substantial fraction of Brazilian AIDS patients with diarrhea and helped establish microsporidiosis as an endemic opportunistic infection in South American HIV care settings. The episode reflects a shift from isolated case reports to routine recognition of microsporidia as a significant cause of morbidity in Brazilian AIDS clinics rather than a contained outbreak with a clear end point.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of the HIV epidemic in Brazil increased the population of severely immunosuppressed persons, while urban crowding and deficiencies in water and sanitation likely supported fecal–oral transmission of microsporidian spores. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or virulence change was implicated; the emergence reflects geographic range expansion and clinical recognition of existing microsporidia in a new continent and high‑risk host population.
Review: review – Event is well-supported by Brazilian cohort and prevalence studies and appropriately captures the first well-documented human microsporidiosis series from South America. However, the original row incorrectly flagged this as “first_detection” in humans; global first detection occurred decades earlier in Japan and Europe/North America. Kept the classification as inter-continental emergence for South America but set first_detection to false and removed inline citation markup from the summary; geography (continent, subregion, country) remains correct.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans with advanced HIV infection and chronic diarrheal disease (outpatients and inpatients at major US HIV centers).
Event summary: Between 1993 and 1997, multiple US HIV treatment centers reported increasing numbers of patients with enteric microsporidiosis, including a multicenter chart review that identified 73 HIV-infected patients with gastrointestinal disease and confirmed intestinal microsporidia. During this period, intestinal microsporidiosis became established as a relatively common AIDS-associated opportunistic infection in North America, typically causing severe chronic diarrhea and wasting in patients with very low CD4 cell counts. Incidence declined sharply in the late 1990s and early 2000s as combination antiretroviral therapy became widely available, restoring immune function and reducing susceptibility to chronic microsporidial infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The HIV/AIDS epidemic created a large immunocompromised population highly susceptible to opportunistic infections, and improved diagnostic tools (light microscopy, special stains, small-bowel biopsies) in the early 1990s increased detection of microsporidia that previously went unnoticed. Internal mechanisms: No specific new strain was implicated; the episode primarily reflects host population-level immunosuppression and better recognition of an existing pathogen rather than documented microbial evolution.
Review: retain – This row accurately summarizes the large pre-HAART burden of intestinal microsporidiosis among US HIV patients, uses appropriate US-focused clinical sources, and correctly classifies the event as a re-occurrence (marked increase in incidence in a previously affected subregion driven by the HIV epidemic and improved diagnostics) without mislabeling it as first detection or inter-/intra-continental spread. No geographic or major classification corrections required.

Host: Humans with and without HIV infection, including pregnant women, exposed to contaminated segments of the municipal drinking-water distribution system in Lyon.
Event summary: In the summer of 1995, a large outbreak of intestinal microsporidiosis occurred in Lyon, France, with roughly 200 symptomatic cases among residents served by specific branches of the municipal water distribution network, including both HIV-infected and immunocompetent individuals such as pregnant women. Epidemiologic investigation linked illness to consumption of tap water from one of three water distribution subsystems, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi was identified as the etiologic agent in affected patients, making this the largest documented water-associated human microsporidiosis outbreak. The outbreak subsided after changes to water treatment and distribution and after the implicated water source was bypassed, and no sustained transmission outside the affected distribution area was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of a municipal drinking-water distribution system, likely from human or animal fecal sources, combined with the environmental resistance of microsporidian spores and limitations in standard water treatment and disinfection, permitted widespread exposure; use of inadequately treated surface or groundwater was implicated. Internal mechanisms: Efficient fecal–oral transmission of E. bieneusi via environmentally resilient spores facilitated waterborne spread, but no specific novel genotype or change in intrinsic virulence was demonstrated in association with this outbreak.
Review: review – The Lyon outbreak is correctly identified as the largest documented human microsporidiosis outbreak and the geographic information is accurate, but the original row misclassified it as “re-emergence.” Given that no new strain, host jump, or clear pathogen-level change was implicated, the episode fits the definition of re-occurrence (major increase in incidence in a previously affected subregion driven by environmental and infrastructure factors) rather than re-emergence. Updated the emergence-type flags accordingly and removed inline citation markup from the summary; underlying sources remain appropriate.

Host: Renal (kidney) transplant recipients, with additional cases among other solid organ transplant recipients, predominantly infected with Enterocytozoon bieneusi.
Event summary: From 2005 to 2019, the French TRANS-SPORE registry and associated surveillance networks documented a growing number of microsporidiosis cases among kidney transplant recipients, ultimately reporting 68 renal transplant patients with intestinal E. bieneusi infection across multiple centers. Over this 15‑year period, microsporidiosis emerged as an important cause of chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and acute kidney injury in this population, prompting routine inclusion of microsporidia in the differential diagnosis of post-transplant diarrhea. As awareness, diagnostic capacity, and treatment with fumagillin plus adjustment of immunosuppression improved, clinicians were better able to recognize and manage infections, and incidence appeared to stabilize despite the expanding transplant population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of solid organ transplantation and chronic immunosuppressive therapy created a growing population at risk for opportunistic intestinal infections; increased clinical awareness and access to molecular diagnostics improved case detection; ongoing exposure to contaminated water, food, or animal reservoirs likely provided sources of infection. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel strain was linked specifically to transplant recipients; the episode primarily reflects recognition of an existing human-adapted E. bieneusi pool in a new high-risk host group rather than a demonstrated pathogen-level change, although certain genotypes (e.g., genotype C and related group 1 genotypes) are particularly successful in immunosuppressed hosts.
Review: review – The French transplant episode is a major emergence event in a new high-risk human group and is well supported by the TRANS-SPORE registry paper and related reviews. However, the original row labeled it as re-emergence, even though available data point to expansion of a pre-existing human pathogen into a medically created at-risk group without clear evidence of new strain properties. Reclassified it as re-occurrence in a previously affected European subregion driven by changes in host population and clinical practice (transplantation and immunosuppression) and cleaned up the summary text; geography and sources are otherwise appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Primarily immunocompetent adults who ate at a hotel restaurant; some individuals had underlying conditions; infections were due to Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C.
Event summary: In October 2009, Swedish authorities investigated an outbreak of gastroenteritis among guests who had eaten at a hotel restaurant, with over 100 persons meeting the clinical case definition and at least 7 of 11 laboratory-investigated patients testing positive for Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C. Epidemiologic analysis linked illness to consumption of food served at the hotel, and the cluster was reported as the first documented foodborne outbreak associated with microsporidia in humans. Illness was generally self-limited over days to weeks, and once the implicated meal service ceased and hygiene measures were reinforced, no further transmission was detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A point-source contamination event, most likely involving fresh, ready-to-eat food items or ingredients handled or irrigated with contaminated water, combined with buffet‑style service that exposed many diners at once; the absence of specific food safety standards or monitoring for microsporidia in food allowed the contamination to go undetected. Internal mechanisms: Efficient fecal–oral transmission of E. bieneusi genotype C and its ability to infect immunocompetent hosts under conditions of high-dose exposure contributed to the outbreak, but there was no clear evidence that this genotype had acquired new virulence traits relative to other human-adapted strains.
Review: review – The Swedish hotel outbreak is a well-documented and widely cited first recognized foodborne microsporidiosis outbreak; continent, subregion, and country are correctly coded, and the host description is appropriate. The original row, however, marked this as re-emergence without evidence of pathogen change; given that the event reflects a foodborne point-source outbreak of an already circulating genotype in a previously affected region, it fits the definition of re-occurrence. Updated the emergence-type flags accordingly and removed an apparently invalid PMCID URL from the source list while retaining core outbreak references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Solid organ transplant recipients (kidney and lung transplant recipients) who acquired disseminated Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection from infected donors; several developed severe neurologic disease and at least one death occurred.
Event summary: In 2012, US public health authorities investigated a cluster of three solid organ transplant recipients who developed febrile illness and organ dysfunction several weeks after receiving organs from a common donor and were eventually found to have disseminated Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection, confirming donor-derived microsporidiosis. A subsequent investigation in 2014 described another cluster of three transplant recipients from a single donor who developed a severe neurologic syndrome due to donor-derived microsporidiosis, with one recipient dying despite intensive care. These linked clusters highlighted transplantation as a previously under-recognized transmission route for microsporidia, led to updated guidance to consider microsporidiosis in unexplained post‑transplant febrile or neurologic syndromes, and spurred increased awareness among transplant programs, effectively limiting further spread through enhanced vigilance and targeted treatment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth in solid organ transplantation and the use of potent immunosuppressive regimens created highly susceptible hosts, while the absence of routine donor screening for microsporidia and initially low clinical suspicion allowed donor-derived infections to occur and be misattributed to other pathogens. Internal mechanisms: The events demonstrate how existing microsporidia can exploit new iatrogenic transmission pathways (via viable spores in donor organs) rather than documenting emergence of a novel strain; host susceptibility and medical practices, rather than clear pathogen evolution, are the primary drivers.
Review: review – Donor-derived microsporidiosis clusters in US transplant recipients are real, well-documented events and qualify as major emergence episodes because they revealed a new iatrogenic transmission route with severe outcomes. The original row’s geography and narrative are sound, but classifying the episode as re-emergence overstates pathogen-level change; available evidence points instead to re-occurrence in a previously affected region mediated by changes in medical practice and host susceptibility. Adjusted the emergence-type flags accordingly and retained focused transplant and outbreak-investigation sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Predominantly immunocompetent adult employees at a single company who consumed catered food; infections were due to Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C.
Event summary: In November 2020, Danish public health authorities investigated a gastrointestinal illness outbreak among employees of a company and ultimately attributed the event to foodborne infection with Enterocytozoon bieneusi after at least 11 individuals tested PCR‑positive. Epidemiologic investigation linked cases to consumption of shared company meals, and detailed follow‑up characterized a median incubation period of around 9 days, prolonged fecal spore shedding in some individuals, and predominantly self‑limited diarrhea and abdominal discomfort in otherwise healthy adults. Once the contaminated food source was removed and workplace hygiene measures were strengthened, no additional transmission was detected, and the outbreak was reported as Denmark’s first recognized foodborne outbreak due to microsporidia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A point-source contamination of catered food, likely through ingredients or food handlers exposed to contaminated water or environments, combined with indoor shared meal settings, enabled clustered exposure among employees; the absence of regulatory controls or routine testing for microsporidia in food meant the contamination was not detected until illness occurred. Internal mechanisms: The human‑adapted E. bieneusi genotype C showed efficient fecal–oral transmission and prolonged shedding in immunocompetent adults, reflecting robust environmental survival and transmission potential rather than clearly novel virulence traits; together with the earlier Swedish outbreak, this event underscored the foodborne potential of existing genotypes.
Review: review – The Danish company outbreak is accurately described, with correct geographic coding and host characterization, and represents an important confirmation of foodborne microsporidiosis in Northern Europe. As with the Swedish outbreak, however, the original row incorrectly treated it as re-emergence; available data indicate a foodborne point-source outbreak of an already common human genotype rather than emergence of a new strain. Reclassified it as re-occurrence in a previously affected region, retained relevant national and peer‑reviewed sources, and removed inline citation markup from the summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (mainly pedal black-grain eumycetoma of the foot with subcutaneous and frequent osseous involvement)
Event summary: Between roughly 1991 and 2004, Brazil reported several eumycetoma cases in which the etiologic agent was identified morphologically as Madurella grisea, including a case series summarised by Severo et al. (1999) that reviewed nine Brazilian black‑grain eumycetomata attributed to M. grisea across multiple macro‑regions, and a later report from northern Brazil describing the first documented case from that region.([lume.ufrgs.br](https://lume.ufrgs.br/bitstream/handle/10183/23136/000295383.pdf)) These patients typically presented with long‑standing pedal masses and draining sinuses, often with bone involvement, and were managed with itraconazole and, in some instances, wide surgical excision. However, none of these Brazilian cases formed a temporally bounded outbreak; rather, they represent scattered, low‑incidence disease embedded in a national history of similar cases since the 1950s, and none of the Brazilian isolates have been confirmed as T. grisea by multilocus sequencing.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Most Brazilian cases occurred among rural residents in semi‑arid or agricultural settings, consistent with traumatic inoculation of environmental fungi into the foot and chronic disease progression under conditions of delayed diagnosis and limited access to mycology laboratories.([lume.ufrgs.br](https://lume.ufrgs.br/bitstream/handle/10183/23136/000295383.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Later taxonomic work shows that numerous Latin American clinical isolates historically labeled "M. grisea" in culture collections are actually Nigrograna mackinnonii, Emarellia spp. or other Pleosporalean fungi, and only a minority of human isolates worldwide are true Trematosphaeria grisea.([repository.naturalis.nl](https://repository.naturalis.nl/pub/531844/PERS2014033001007.pdf)) There is no clear evidence that the Brazilian cases represent a new T. grisea genotype, resistance phenotype or host shift; more likely they reflect ongoing, under‑diagnosed endemicity of several black‑grain agents misgrouped under the historical "M. grisea" label.
Review: Review – This row aggregates multiple Brazilian eumycetoma reports (including Severo et al. 1999 and Vilela et al. 2004) in which the agent was identified as Madurella grisea on phenotypic grounds and which, historically, represented some of the numerically larger clusters of "M. grisea" cases in any single country.([lume.ufrgs.br](https://lume.ufrgs.br/bitstream/handle/10183/23136/000295383.pdf)) However, subsequent multilocus sequencing work has demonstrated that many Latin American isolates historically labeled T. grisea instead belong to Nigrograna mackinnonii, Emarellia spp. and related taxa, and the Pleosporales revision explicitly highlights Vilela et al. 2004 as an unconfirmed T. grisea report.([repository.naturalis.nl](https://repository.naturalis.nl/pub/531844/PERS2014033001007.pdf)) The period 1991–2004 also does not represent a discrete emergence episode compared with earlier decades, but rather continued low‑incidence occurrence in a country with long‑standing "M. grisea" reports. For strict adherence to the emergence‑event definition (major, bounded episodes with clear spread or first occurrence), this Brazilian row could justifiably be excluded; if retained for historical context, its type classification has been simplified (no re‑occurrence flag) and the text now stresses the uncertainty around species‑level identification and the absence of outbreak dynamics.
Review Comment: Very long timeline, aggregated from multiple reports

EPP common name: Eumycetoma (black-grain eumycetoma due to Falciformispora senegalensis)
Countries: India [1991] (Tamil Nadu, Madras region; first culture-confirmed isolation in India)
Host: Humans (subcutaneous black-grain eumycetoma)
Event summary: In 1991, a histopathology and mycology review of 210 mycetoma biopsies from Tamil Nadu, India, reported isolation of Leptosphaeria species, including Leptosphaeria senegalensis (now Falciformispora senegalensis), in pure culture from several autochthonous black-grain eumycetoma cases, representing the first culture-confirmed documentation of this typically West African agent in India. The isolates occurred as a very small fraction of a much larger mycetoma burden dominated by Madurella mycetomatis, Actinomadura madurae and other agents, indicating that F. senegalensis was present at low endemic frequency rather than driving a noticeable increase in overall case numbers. Following this report, subsequent reviews and regional syntheses have continued to list F. senegalensis as an occasional eumycetoma cause in India, but without identifying any subsequent spikes in incidence or discrete outbreak clusters attributable specifically to this species.
Mechanism or driver: External drivers: most likely long-standing but previously unrecognized environmental presence of F. senegalensis in dry tropical soils and thorny vegetation in parts of Southern India, with traumatic inoculation during agricultural work analogous to West African settings, combined with improved culture and histopathology that enabled species-level identification in the 1991 review. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel genotype, increased virulence, host jump or enhanced transmissibility; the event appears to reflect diagnostic detection of a rare, pre-existing agent rather than true biological emergence or range expansion during the study period.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first culture-confirmed detection of Leptosphaeria senegalensis (now Falciformispora senegalensis) in India, based on Venugopal 1991 and later textbook summaries that list West Africa and India as the main regions where this species causes mycetoma.([ijdvl.com](https://ijdvl.com/prevalence-of-mycetomas-in-madras/)) The event is interpreted as an inter-continental emergence with in situ transmission in Southern Asia, but the underlying biopsies span an undefined period prior to 1991 and species-level identification historically suffered from misclassification, so the exact timing and magnitude of any true geographic spread remain uncertain. Retain this event for geographic-range context but flag for expert review of whether it should be considered a discrete emergence episode under the project’s strict criteria or treated purely as improved detection of long-standing background infections.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans – seven pale‑grain eumycetoma cases identified histologically in Madras, India; four cultured, with three Acremonium isolates (two A. kiliense, one A. falciforme) among 211 mycetoma biopsies.
Event summary: In 1995, investigators at Madras Medical College in southern India reviewed 211 biopsied mycetoma cases and found seven pale‑grain eumycetomas, four of which yielded etiologic fungi in culture, including two Acremonium kiliense and one Acremonium falciforme. These Acremonium cases occurred in adults from the traditional Indian mycetoma belt, typically with long‑standing pedal or lower‑limb lesions characterised by tumefaction, draining sinuses and pale grains. Patients were managed with combined surgical debridement and prolonged antifungal therapy, illustrating that Acremonium spp. function as rare but recurrent white‑grain eumycetoma agents within an established endemic setting.

Event summary: In 2006, dermatologists in New York, USA, reported a eumycetoma caused by Acremonium spp. in a cardiac transplant recipient, one of very few eumycetoma cases ever described in solid‑organ transplant patients. The infection likely originated from traumatic inoculation of soil saprophytes into subcutaneous tissue in an immunosuppressed host and progressed with chronic tumefaction and draining sinuses despite standard care. Targeted antifungal therapy and careful adjustment of immunosuppression eventually controlled the infection, and the case was highlighted as an example of emerging opportunistic Acremonium infection in transplant populations.

Internal mechanisms: Opportunistic behaviour of Acremonium spp. in profoundly immunosuppressed hosts, consistent with broader patterns of hyalohyphomycosis, but without a clearly defined novel strain; the key mechanism is the ability of hyaline septate hyphae to invade subcutaneous tissue and persist when neutrophil and cellular immune responses are impaired.

Host: Humans – 64‑year‑old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus in Florida, USA, with hand eumycetoma due to Acremonium spp. acquired during gardening.
Event summary: Around 2011, clinicians in Florida, USA, described a eumycetoma of the hand caused by Acremonium spp. in a 64‑year‑old diabetic man with a history of gardening exotic plants. Despite initial antifungal therapy with itraconazole and topical terbinafine, response was limited, underscoring therapeutic challenges and reinforcing Acremonium as an uncommon but emerging cause of eumycetoma in North American residents.

It is now coded as re_occurrence (true) and not re_emergence, because there is no evidence of strain change or new host species, only external risk factors (diabetes, gardening exposure) and diagnostic delay. Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

Event summary: By 2015–2016, clinicians in Birmingham, United Kingdom, reported a cutaneous mycetoma caused by Acremonium spp. in a patient with chronic granulomatous disease who was already receiving antifungal prophylaxis. Increased use of culture, reference mycology and species‑specific sequencing at the Delhi centre functioned as a detection driver, revealing Acremonium and Sarocladium agents that would previously have remained unidentified. Host: Humans, mainly immunocompetent rural adults with Madura foot–type lesions referred to a tertiary center in Rio de Janeiro; a minority had comorbidities or advanced bone involvement
Event summary: From 1991 to 2014, the Evandro Chagas National Institute of Infectious Diseases (FIOCRUZ) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, recorded 21 mycetoma patients, including 13 eumycetoma; Scedosporium apiospermum species complex was isolated in three of these, making it the most common identified fungal agent in the series. Cases originated mainly from semi‑arid rural areas of the Southeast and Northeast regions, presenting after years of evolution with tumefaction, draining sinuses and frequent bone involvement, and often requiring prolonged azole therapy plus surgery or even amputation. By the end of the period, increased clinical awareness and access to itraconazole and terbinafine allowed more limb‑sparing management, but morbidity, long treatment duration, and occasional treatment failure remained substantial.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Occupational exposure of agricultural workers walking barefoot in thorny, semi‑arid environments, low awareness of mycetoma among front‑line providers, and long travel distances to referral centers led to late presentations with extensive disease. Poverty and limited access to imaging and microbiology delayed diagnosis and contributed to chronicity. Internal mechanisms: The event does not reflect a new S. apiospermum strain; rather, it highlights the species’ longstanding ability to establish chronic, deep tissue infection with white grains and its intrinsic reduced susceptibility to many antifungals, which together make eumycetoma difficult to cure once established.
Review: Review – retain event, but updated source URLs to use the primary Rio de Janeiro mycetoma series on PMC and clarified that the UN sub-region is simply South America (cases largely originating from Brazil’s Southeast and Northeast macroregions). Classification as re-occurrence (and not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because S. apiospermum mycetoma had been documented in Brazil before 1990 and these 1991–2014 cases represent ongoing low-incidence disease in an already affected country. No larger Brazilian S. apiospermum eumycetoma cluster was identified that would displace this event among the top-impact episodes post‑1990.

Host: Humans, including immunocompetent patients with white‑grain eumycetoma and immunocompromised or chronically ill patients with lung fungus balls, sinusitis, peritonitis, brain abscess and other forms of scedosporiosis
Event summary: Between approximately 1990 and 2012, Brazilian clinicians reported an accumulated national experience of scedosporiosis due to Scedosporium apiospermum / Pseudallescheria boydii complex, synthesised in a 2013 case report and literature review that identified 24 Brazilian patients overall. Earlier reports had almost exclusively described subcutaneous eumycetoma in immunocompetent hosts, whereas post‑1982 and especially after 1990, additional cases appeared as pulmonary fungus balls in healed tuberculosis cavities, localized invasive infections in cancer and transplant patients, and a fatal central nervous system infection after near-drowning, alongside a new eumycetoma case successfully treated with oral voriconazole. By the end of this period, Brazilian authors recognized scedosporiosis as a diverse clinical entity with high morbidity and mortality in severely immunocompromised patients but potentially curable localized disease when diagnosed promptly and managed with surgery plus modern triazoles.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of transplant programs, chemotherapy, and intensive care in Brazil increased the pool of profoundly immunosuppressed patients at risk for invasive mould infections; chronic lung disease, especially post‑tuberculosis cavities, created niches for intracavitary colonization (fungus balls). Strengthening of mycology laboratories and case-reporting improved recognition of S. apiospermum in specimens previously labeled generically as hyalohyphomycosis or Aspergillus. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects the broad tissue tropism and intrinsic antifungal tolerance of S. apiospermum rather than a new genotype; its long-recognized capacity to cause both eumycetoma in immunocompetent hosts and invasive disease in compromised hosts underpins this re-occurring spectrum of disease. Voriconazole’s superior activity over older agents improved outcomes but does not represent a pathogen-level change.
Review: Review – retain event but corrected the event_year field to "1990-2012" (the original mixed the 1982–2012 literature window with a note about restricting to ≥1990) and set only re_occurrence = true, re_emergence = false, because the Brazilian series documents recurrent and increasingly recognized scedosporiosis by a historically known pathogen in an already affected country, without clear evidence for a novel strain or host jump. Event-level sources were updated to the primary Brazilian scedosporiosis review on SciELO plus the global Clinical Microbiology Reviews article on Scedosporium infections; the earlier semanticscholar PDF links are no longer needed.
