Countries: Bulgaria; Germany; Netherlands (Kingdom of the); Portugal; Slovenia; Spain; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Hungary

Event summary: From about 1990 to 2014, Europe accumulated a series of autochthonous mycetoma and other subcutaneous infections due to Scedosporium apiospermum / Pseudallescheria boydii in temperate, non‑endemic settings. A systematic review of mycetoma in Europeans identified 11 autochthonous S. apiospermum mycetoma cases across Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and the United Kingdom, mostly in immunosuppressed patients, and a later Hungarian report described a recurrent lower‑leg mycetoma cured with surgical excision and terbinafine after multiple relapses. The episode began as isolated “Madura foot”–like or post‑traumatic subcutaneous lesions in Southern and Eastern Europe and progressively expanded to other subregions as case reports accumulated. By the mid‑2010s, European clinicians recognized S. apiospermum as an important but rare cause of therapy‑refractory mycetoma and deep soft‑tissue infection in temperate climates and reported successful combined medical-surgical management, although relapses and functional impairment remained frequent.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased use of intensive immunosuppression (solid-organ and stem-cell transplantation, chemotherapy, long-term corticosteroids) in Europe amplified susceptibility to localized and invasive S. apiospermum infections; continued outdoor work with bare or minimally protected feet in Mediterranean and Balkan rural settings maintained environmental exposure. Improved diagnostic capacity, including fungal culture, histopathology, and, in later years, molecular identification, allowed recognition of S. apiospermum in lesions that might previously have been attributed to other eumycetoma agents. Internal mechanisms: Reported cases are consistent with the longstanding biology of S. apiospermum (environmental saprophyte with trauma-associated inoculation and intrinsic resistance or reduced susceptibility to many antifungals) rather than emergence of a demonstrably new, more virulent genotype.

Set intra_continental_emergence = true and turned off re_occurrence and re_emergence to avoid forbidden combinations and to reflect that the key signal is appearance of S. apiospermum mycetoma across multiple new European subregions outside the traditional mycetoma belt, rather than a pathogen-level shift. Increased diagnostic scrutiny, with species-level identification in specialized laboratories, likely contributed to recognizing S. apiospermum among numerous other white‑grain agents. Internal mechanisms: The Indian cases illustrate the existing capacity of S. apiospermum to produce white-grain eumycetoma rather than a new strain; there is no evidence of increased virulence, antifungal resistance shift, or host-species jump during this period.

Host: Humans, mainly adults with chronic lung disease (including cystic fibrosis and post-tuberculosis cavities), hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants and other forms of severe immunosuppression; a minority were immunocompetent with localized cutaneous or subcutaneous infection
Event summary: During 2003–2005, a nationwide, prospective, population-based surveillance study across 49 laboratories in Australia identified 180 episodes of scedosporiosis, of which 108 phenotypically and molecularly corresponded to the Scedosporium apiospermum / Pseudallescheria boydii complex and 72 to Lomentospora (Scedosporium) prolificans. About one-third (62 episodes) met criteria for invasive disease, including lung, disseminated, bone and joint, and CNS infections, with substantial mortality especially among patients with hematologic malignancy and profound neutropenia. This surveillance quantified an overall incidence of scedosporiosis of roughly one case per million population and highlighted S. apiospermum/P. boydii as an important opportunistic mould in Australian patients with chronic lung disease and post-transplant immunosuppression. By the study’s end, Australia was recognized as one of the countries with the highest documented burden of scedosporiosis worldwide.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of organ and stem‑cell transplantation, intensive chemotherapy, and survival of patients with cystic fibrosis and advanced chronic lung disease in Australia markedly increased the number of susceptible hosts, while national mycological surveillance and reference-laboratory support improved detection and species-level identification of Scedosporium isolates. Environmental exposure to nutrient‑rich, polluted soils and waters in urban and peri‑urban settings provided reservoirs for colonization and infection. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects the known propensity of S. apiospermum/P. boydii to colonize abnormal airways and cause invasive disease in immunocompromised hosts, together with intrinsic reduced susceptibility to many antifungals; no specific new genotype or resistance pattern was identified that would justify classifying this as re-emergence driven by pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – added this new event to correct an omission: the 2003–2005 Australian nationwide population-based surveillance for scedosporiosis, which documented 180 episodes (with the majority of isolates belonging to the S. apiospermum/Pseudallescheria boydii complex) and an incidence of about one case per million population. It is coded as re_occurrence (and not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because S. apiospermum infections had already been recognized in Australia before 2003 and the increased burden is largely attributable to growth of immunocompromised populations and enhanced surveillance rather than a new strain; detailed parameterization (e.g. exact S. apiospermum-only case counts) should be double-checked against the full article.

Host: Humans (adult rural farmer with foot eumycetoma)
Event summary: In 1999, Indian clinicians reported a 27‑year‑old male farmer from Tamil Nadu with a chronic black‑grain eumycetoma of the right foot, in which fungal culture and histopathology identified Curvularia lunata as the etiologic agent—regarded as the first well‑documented Curvularia eumycetoma in Asia. Host: Humans (older male farmer with foot eumycetoma)
Event summary: In 2007, a 65‑year‑old Indian male farmer presented to a North Indian tertiary center with long‑standing swelling of the right foot, multiple nodules, and draining sinuses exuding black granules; culture of grains yielded Curvularia lunata, confirming black‑grain eumycetoma due to this dematiaceous fungus. Host: Humans (adult woman with shoulder/chest wall eumycetoma; additional deep soft‑tissue eumycetoma cases)
Event summary: Around 2010–2012, Indian authors described a very rare eumycetoma involving the shoulder region and chest wall in a 27‑year‑old woman with a 12‑year history of nodular swellings and draining sinuses, where repeated biopsies and culture eventually identified Curvularia species as the causative agent. The case, managed with itraconazole and supportive surgery, differed from classic foot mycetoma by its upper‑trunk location but showed similar chronic, destructive evolution. In the same period, imaging‑based reports from India highlighted deep musculoskeletal eumycetoma with characteristic MRI “dot‑in‑circle” signs, and some of these series included Curvularia among the confirmed aetiologic fungi. Collectively, these scattered but culture‑confirmed detections marked continued re‑occurrence of Curvularia eumycetoma in India, including involvement of less typical anatomical sites, yet without any evidence for a temporally bounded outbreak or sharply rising incidence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing exposure of rural populations to contaminated soil and plant material, occasional penetrating trauma to exposed extremities or trunk, and increased use of imaging plus mycological work‑up in tertiary centers promoted recognition of deep Curvularia eumycetoma outside the classical pedal location. Internal mechanisms: Recognition of a distinct granulocyte‑tropic lineage within the broader Ehrlichia/Anaplasma complex represented novel strain/genotype emergence causing human disease in a region where monocytotropic ehrlichiosis was already present, with ecological conditions favoring establishment in Ixodes–rodent–deer cycles.

The event (1994–1997 recognition of human granulocytic ehrlichiosis in the upper Midwest and New York) is real and highly impactful, but the etiologic agent is now classified as Anaplasma phagocytophilum rather than an Ehrlichia species. I therefore turned off the first_global_emergence and first_detection flags and reclassified this as a re_emergence event (novel granulocyte‑tropic lineage within the ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis complex in a subregion where E. chaffeensis had already emerged). Curators should decide whether this episode should instead be moved to a dedicated Anaplasma phagocytophilum event sheet to avoid double counting.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (one symptomatic child and multiple adults with close contact to dogs)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, a 17‑month‑old girl in Venezuela with severe febrile illness and pancytopenia was retrospectively recognized as having ehrlichiosis based on platelet inclusions resembling those of canine Ehrlichia platys and compatible clinical findings, indicating previously unrecognized local transmission. In 1996, investigators isolated and molecularly characterized an Ehrlichia canis–like agent from an asymptomatic Venezuelan adult, and serologic and PCR-based studies of symptomatic children and dog‑exposed adults demonstrated infection with E. canis–reactive organisms, providing the first isolation and robust characterization of a human Ehrlichia species in South America. Although no large outbreak followed, these human infections in a setting where canine ehrlichiosis is endemic showed that zoonotic Ehrlichia spp. had silently established transmission cycles in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High prevalence of canine monocytic ehrlichiosis and dense dog–tick–human contact networks in tropical urban and peri‑urban Venezuela facilitated occasional zoonotic spillover from canine reservoirs; limited awareness and diagnostic capacity delayed recognition of human illness. Internal mechanisms: Spillover of a primarily canine pathogen (E. canis or a very closely related genotype) into humans represents host expansion of Ehrlichia lineages already established in dogs, with molecular data supporting infection of human mononuclear cells by strains nearly identical to local canine isolates.
Review: Decision: review. This event correctly reflects the earliest well-documented human infections with an E. canis–like agent in South America and is important as the first inter-continental emergence of human ehrlichiosis on that continent. I adjusted the event year from a single year (1996) to 1992–1996 to cover both the retrospectively described pediatric case and the 1996 adult isolate, and I turned off the first_detection flag so that this row now represents inter-continental emergence rather than global first detection. The timing and interpretation of the 1992 child case and its relationship to E. platys versus E. canis should be double-checked by a subject-matter expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Slovenia [1996]; Italy [1997]; other Western European countries [late 1990s]
Host: Humans (adult and pediatric patients with tick-associated febrile illness in Lyme borreliosis–endemic areas)
Event summary: In 1996–1997, clinicians in Slovenia reported the first molecularly confirmed human cases of granulocytic ehrlichiosis in Europe, with several adult and pediatric patients presenting with acute febrile illness, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after Ixodes tick bites in Lyme borreliosis–endemic areas. Shortly thereafter, additional cases were described from western Europe, including the Netherlands, showing that a granulocytic Ehrlichia‑like agent (subsequently recognized as Anaplasma phagocytophilum) was causing human disease on the continent. Over the following years, further autochthonous cases were confirmed in multiple European countries, establishing granulocytic ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis as an emerging tick‑borne infection in central and western Europe rather than a problem confined to North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared Ixodes ricinus tick vectors and reservoir hosts with Lyme borreliosis in central and western Europe provided ecological conditions favoring maintenance and spillover of granulocytic Ehrlichia/Anaplasma lineages; increased awareness in Lyme‑endemic regions led to targeted testing of atypical febrile illnesses after tick bites. Internal mechanisms: The same or closely related granulocytic lineages identified in North America appear to have been present in European Ixodes populations for some time, so this episode reflects inter‑continental recognition of an already widespread agent rather than de novo evolution in Europe.
Review: Decision: review. This episode accurately captures the first confirmed human granulocytic ehrlichiosis cases in Europe and the initial recognition that this disease (now classified as human granulocytic anaplasmosis) occurs on a second continent. I turned off the first_detection flag so that the row now represents inter-continental emergence rather than a second global “first detection” event. Because the etiologic agent is Anaplasma phagocytophilum and not a current Ehrlichia species, curators should consider whether to retain this event under the Ehrlichia sp. EPP or migrate it to an Anaplasma phagocytophilum sheet; the sub-region list (Southern, Western, and possibly Eastern Europe) may also be broader than what is documented for 1996–1997 and merits expert checking.

Countries: United States of America – Missouri [1996-1998 index patients], wider south‑central and southeastern states [late 1990s-2000s]
Host: Humans (adult patients with granulocytic ehrlichiosis, some immunocompromised)
Event summary: Between 1996 and 1998, four adult patients from Missouri with febrile illness, headache and thrombocytopenia were found by PCR and sequence analysis to be infected not with E. chaffeensis or the HGE agent but with a distinct Ehrlichia species previously recognized as a canine pathogen, leading in 1999 to the description of Ehrlichia ewingii as a newly recognized human pathogen. This initial cluster demonstrated that E. ewingii could cause granulocytic ehrlichiosis in humans, with clinical features overlapping those of E. chaffeensis infection and human granulocytic anaplasmosis, and most patients recovered with doxycycline. Over the 2000s, additional E. ewingii infections were documented in multiple south‑central and southeastern states, although they remained less common than E. chaffeensis, indicating sustained but geographically focal transmission in areas where Amblyomma americanum is abundant.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Amblyomma americanum ticks feeding on both dogs and humans in the south‑central United States facilitated cross‑species transmission of E. ewingii from canine reservoirs to people; improved molecular diagnostics allowed differentiation of E. ewingii from E. chaffeensis and A. phagocytophilum infections. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated capacity of E. ewingii, long recognized in dogs, to infect human granulocytes represents host expansion and novel genotype emergence as a human pathogen within an already endemic ehrlichiosis system.
Review: Decision: review. The NEJM and PubMed data clearly support this as the first recognized human infections with Ehrlichia ewingii, a new human-pathogenic Ehrlichia species in an area where E. chaffeensis was already endemic. I reclassified the event as re_emergence (novel species and host expansion within an established ehrlichiosis focus) rather than a second global first_emergence/first_detection for the genus-level EPP. I also removed general-purpose Wikipedia links in favor of primary clinical and taxonomic sources; these changes should be checked but the event itself should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural residents in forested/grassland areas with tick exposure)
Event summary: In 1999, clinicians in a forested area of Inner Mongolia, China, diagnosed the first confirmed case of human monocytic ehrlichiosis in Asia, identifying E. chaffeensis as the causative agent in a febrile patient with tick exposure. Before this report, HME had only been recognized clinically in North America, although serologic evidence and detection of E. chaffeensis DNA in ticks suggested exposure in parts of southern China and Thailand. Following the index case, sporadic additional human infections and serologic evidence of exposure were reported from several Chinese provinces, indicating low but real circulation of E. chaffeensis among rural populations with intense contact with local tick vectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanding tick populations, agricultural and forestry activities, and frequent human–tick contact in rural northern China created opportunities for spillover of E. chaffeensis maintained in wildlife and domestic animal reservoirs; increasing laboratory capacity and awareness of emerging tick‑borne rickettsioses prompted targeted testing of atypical febrile illnesses. Internal mechanisms: No clearly unique strain has been linked to Asian cases; available data are consistent with introduction or long‑standing presence of E. chaffeensis‑like lineages that have achieved geographic range expansion into East Asia where ecological conditions are suitable for enzootic maintenance.
Review: Decision: review. The evidence for a first clinically confirmed HME case in Inner Mongolia in 1999 is strong and this episode is appropriately treated as the first inter-continental emergence of human E. chaffeensis infection in Asia. I turned off the first_detection and intra_continental_emergence flags so that this row now specifically represents inter-continental emergence to Asia, consistent with the project definitions that reserve first_detection for the global host-system level and intra-continental emergence for spread between UN subregions. The timing and weight of earlier serologic data from Thailand and southern China are adequately handled in the narrative but could be revisited by curators if more detailed Asian data are added.

Countries: United States of America – Georgia [2005]; other southeastern United States where Panola Mountain Ehrlichia–infected Amblyomma americanum were detected [1998-2006]
Host: Humans (an adult patient with tick-associated febrile illness), domestic goats (index animal host)
Event summary: In the mid‑2000s, a previously undescribed Ehrlichia species closely related to E. ruminantium was identified in a goat experimentally exposed to Amblyomma americanum ticks from Panola Mountain State Park, Georgia, and later termed the Panola Mountain Ehrlichia. In 2005, clinicians reported the first human illness associated with this agent in a patient who developed fever and systemic symptoms after a lone star tick bite acquired at the same park, with Ehrlichia DNA detected in acute blood and rapid clinical response to doxycycline. Subsequent tick surveys between 1998 and 2006 detected Panola Mountain Ehrlichia DNA at low prevalence in A. americanum populations from multiple southeastern and some more northerly US states, indicating that this novel tick‑borne agent has been present at low levels over a broad area and can occasionally infect humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High human recreational and occupational exposure to lone star ticks in southeastern US parks and natural areas promoted detection of rare zoonotic transmission events; molecular surveillance of ticks across many states enabled recognition of genetically distinct Ehrlichia lineages that would previously have gone unnoticed. Internal mechanisms: The Panola Mountain Ehrlichia is genetically distinct from known Ehrlichia species and is closely related to E. ruminantium, representing novel strain/species emergence within the genus; its ability to infect both goats and humans and to be maintained by A. americanum indicates host expansion and adaptation to this tick vector, with evidence of a geographically widespread but low-prevalence enzootic cycle.
Review: Decision: review. This episode appropriately summarizes the discovery of the Panola Mountain Ehrlichia in goats and its subsequent association with human illness, and is one of the main re-emergence events driven by a newly recognized Ehrlichia lineage. I corrected the timing by setting the event window to 2005–2008, anchored on the first documented human illness in 2005 and the multi‑state tick surveys through 2006–2008, and simplified the country field to emphasize Georgia plus other US states with infected ticks, rather than an unsupported 2000–2002 timing. I also removed general Wikipedia links and added the broader tick-surveillance paper as a more informative source; the exact years to use for the event window could still be fine-tuned by curators.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (patients with undifferentiated febrile illness, some HIV-infected), domestic dogs and ticks as implicated reservoirs/vectors
Event summary: In the 1990s and early 2000s, isolated case reports from Mali and serologic surveys from several African countries suggested that human ehrlichial infections might be occurring but lacked definitive molecular confirmation. Between approximately 2004 and 2008, investigators in Cameroon conducted a systematic study of patients with undifferentiated febrile illness and detected Ehrlichia chaffeensis–specific DNA in a subset of blood samples, providing the first clear molecular and clinical evidence of human monocytic ehrlichiosis in sub‑Saharan Africa. These findings, together with prior serologic evidence and detection of E. chaffeensis and E. canis in local dogs and Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks, showed that human‑pathogenic Ehrlichia spp. are present and occasionally cause disease in African settings with high tick and HIV burdens, although diagnosed case numbers remain low and likely under-represent the true burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close human contact with dogs and livestock, abundant tick vectors (including Rhipicephalus sanguineus), and high prevalence of HIV infection in some sub‑Saharan settings increase both exposure to Ehrlichia spp. and susceptibility to severe disease; historically limited diagnostic capacity meant that ehrlichial infections were often misclassified among undifferentiated fevers. Internal mechanisms: The E. chaffeensis/E. canis lineages detected in African patients, dogs and ticks appear similar to those found elsewhere, suggesting long‑standing but previously unrecognized endemicity or historical inter‑continental spread rather than recent de novo evolution; this event is best interpreted as inter‑continental emergence in terms of human recognition and first confirmed autochthonous cases.
Review: Decision: review. This event appropriately represents the first molecularly confirmed human E. chaffeensis infections in Africa (Cameroon) against a background of earlier serologic hints from Mali and other countries, and qualifies as the inter-continental emergence of clinically recognized HME in Africa. I turned off the first_detection flag so that the row now cleanly encodes inter_continental_emergence, and I removed a duplicate PDF URL for the Frontiers review while retaining the main HTML article plus the earlier serosurveys as supporting context. The balance between treating the imported Mali case and the Cameroonian series as part of the same emergence episode versus separate events could be reconsidered, but the current aggregation is defensible.

Countries: United States of America – Wisconsin [2007, 2009], Minnesota [2009], other upper Midwest states [through 2013]
Host: Humans (at least 69 symptomatic patients), small mammals and Ixodes scapularis ticks as enzootic hosts and vectors
Event summary: In 2009, clinicians in Wisconsin and Minnesota identified a novel Ehrlichia species closely related to Ehrlichia muris in three symptomatic patients from Wisconsin and one from Minnesota, marking the discovery of the Ehrlichia muris–like agent (later named Ehrlichia muris subsp. eauclairensis) as a cause of human ehrlichiosis in the upper Midwest. Retrospective analyses of ticks collected in Wisconsin in the mid‑1990s showed that this agent had been present at low prevalence for at least a decade, and surveillance during 2007–2013 identified 69 symptomatic human infections, mostly in Wisconsin and Minnesota, with fever, cytopenias and occasionally severe disease. This emergence episode represented both recognition of a new human‑pathogenic Ehrlichia taxon and a change in the geographic pattern of ehrlichiosis, which previously had been considered rare or absent in the upper Midwest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive human exposure to Ixodes scapularis ticks in wooded and peri‑urban landscapes of the upper Midwest, together with ecological conditions favoring enzootic cycles in white‑footed mice and other small mammals, enabled recurrent spillover of the new Ehrlichia lineage; targeted molecular testing of ehrlichiosis suspects in a region previously thought to be non-endemic was critical to recognition. Internal mechanisms: Genetic divergence sufficient to warrant designation as Ehrlichia muris subsp. eauclairensis represents novel subspecies emergence within the genus; its adaptation to I. scapularis and small mammal hosts underpins geographic range expansion into cooler Upper Midwest environments and re-emergence of ehrlichiosis in a previously low-incidence area.
Review: Decision: review. The description of the Ehrlichia muris–like agent (E. muris subsp. eauclairensis) and its 69 recognized human cases in Wisconsin and Minnesota is accurate and clearly represents an important re-emergence event involving a newly defined Ehrlichia taxon. I reclassified the event as re_emergence only (novel subspecies in a region where ehrlichiosis as a syndrome was already known elsewhere in North America), turning off first_global_emergence, first_detection, and intra_continental_emergence to keep the type codes mutually exclusive and aligned with the genus-level EPP definition. I also removed the Wikipedia link in favor of primary NEJM and EID articles; the event should be retained but the genus-versus-species granularity should be checked against other EPP entries.

Countries: United States of America – southeastern, south‑central, and mid‑Atlantic states [2008]; expansion into some Midwestern states [by 2012-2013]
Host: Humans (nationally reported cases of E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii ehrlichiosis)
Event summary: From 2008 to 2012, US national surveillance documented a marked increase in reported cases and incidence of ehrlichiosis due to E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii, with over 1,500 E. chaffeensis infections reported in 2013 and incidence highest in the southeastern, south‑central and mid‑Atlantic regions but with an increasing number of cases identified in parts of the Midwest. During this period, the recognized geographic distribution of E. ewingii infections expanded and hospitalization numbers rose, although case‑fatality remained relatively low with prompt doxycycline treatment. This episode reflects both genuine increases in tick‑borne transmission linked to expanding Amblyomma americanum range and improvements in surveillance and diagnostics, cementing ehrlichiosis as a major nationally notifiable tick‑borne disease in the United States by the early 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Northward and westward expansion and increasing abundance of Amblyomma americanum, driven by land‑use changes, deer population growth, and climate‑related shifts in habitat suitability, increased human exposure to infected ticks; improved surveillance, revised case definitions, mandatory reporting and wider use of species‑specific PCR and serology substantially heightened ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that a single novel genotype drove the national increase; instead, sustained geographic range expansion and rising force of infection of existing E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii lineages, together with better detection, underpin this large re-occurrence of disease in previously affected US regions.
Review: Decision: review. This event appropriately summarizes the sharp rise in nationally reported E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii infections in the United States between 2008 and 2013 and is one of the largest episodes in terms of case numbers. I reclassified it as a re_occurrence event (strong increase in incidence driven by ecological and surveillance changes in an already endemic subregion) and turned off the intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags, because there is no clear evidence that spread to a new UN subregion or major intrinsic pathogen change was the primary driver. I also removed general Wikipedia URLs and retained the EID surveillance analysis together with the CDC statistics page as the most relevant sources for this national trend.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural residents near Chapare River, Cochabamba Department)
Event summary: In December 2003, a small cluster of acute hemorrhagic fever cases occurred in rural areas near the Chapare River in Chapare Province, Cochabamba Department, Bolivia, including a fatal index case from whom a previously undescribed arenavirus—Chapare virus—was isolated and identified as the cause of Chapare hemorrhagic fever. Investigations documented limited local transmission among residents during late 2003–early 2004 but no wider spread beyond the immediate outbreak area. The episode ended after supportive care and local control measures, with no further confirmed human cases reported in Cochabamba in the subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic exposure to infected wild rodents in rural agricultural settings, including poor-quality housing with rodent intrusion and close contact with rodent-infested crop storage, likely facilitated the initial spillover. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of a previously unrecognized mammarenavirus from its rodent reservoir into humans; possible inherent capacity for severe hemorrhagic disease but no evidence yet of enhanced transmissibility or distinct genotypic variants at this initial emergence stage.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2003–2004 Cochabamba/Chapare cluster with a single fatal, laboratory-confirmed case is well documented as the first identification and detection of Chapare virus in humans, and the location, timing, and case description match PLOS Pathogens, MedGen, CDC and WHO DON 2025 summaries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2277458/?utm_source=openai)) Continent, sub‑region, country coding and event-type flags (first_global_emergence and first_detection only) are consistent with definitions, and there is no evidence of any larger Chapare events in this period that should displace this row.

Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2019] (Caranavi and other municipalities in La Paz Department)
Host: Humans (rural residents and healthcare workers in La Paz Department)
Event summary: In 2019, Chapare virus re-emerged in rural areas of La Paz Department, Bolivia, with an outbreak centered in Caranavi that resulted in nine confirmed cases and four deaths, including infections in healthcare workers providing care to index patients. The outbreak demonstrated person-to-person transmission in healthcare settings and was associated with a Chapare virus strain genetically distinct from the 2003 Cochabamba strain, marking the first recognized spread of the virus into La Paz Department. Intensive epidemiologic investigation, infection-prevention measures, and rodent-focused environmental interventions halted further transmission, and no additional outbreak-related cases were reported after 2019.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural agricultural livelihoods with heavy rodent exposure, suboptimal housing and storage conditions promoting rodent infestation, and limited early recognition of Chapare hemorrhagic fever in health facilities contributed to zoonotic introduction and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence, with sequencing confirming a Chapare virus strain different from the 2003 strain; Enhanced Transmission in the sense of demonstrated efficient human-to-human transmission via contact with blood and body fluids in healthcare settings; possible Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Bolivia, enabling persistence in rodent populations of La Paz Department.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2019 Caranavi/La Paz outbreak with nine cases (four deaths) and documented nosocomial person‑to‑person transmission is consistently reported by NEJM, PAHO, Canada’s pathogen datasheet, CDC and WHO as the major modern Chapare event, and the description here (size, locations, involvement of healthcare workers, and genetic distinctness from 2003) matches those sources.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10245337/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re_emergence (new genotype and changed transmission pattern in a previously affected country and sub-region) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and consistent with the event definitions.

Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2021] (rural municipalities in northern La Paz Department)
Host: Humans (rural residents in northern La Paz Department)
Event summary: In 2021, a third documented Chapare hemorrhagic fever outbreak occurred in La Paz Department, Bolivia, involving three laboratory-confirmed human cases and two deaths in rural communities within the known at-risk zone of northern La Paz. This episode took place in the same broad ecological setting previously affected in 2019, indicating ongoing local zoonotic transmission from infected rodents rather than expansion to new regions or continents. The outbreak was contained through enhanced surveillance, clinical management, and community-level rodent control and public health messaging, with no evidence of sustained chains of human-to-human transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent ecological suitability for the rodent reservoir in rural northern La Paz, including jungle corridors with agricultural settlements, poor-quality housing, and ongoing rodent infestation in and around homes, underpinned repeated zoonotic spillover events. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven primarily by continued zoonotic transmission from the established reservoir rather than clear evidence of new viral genotypes or major changes in virulence; any human-to-human spread appears limited, without indications of substantially enhanced transmissibility compared with earlier events.
Review: Decision: retain. WHO’s 2025 Disease Outbreak News and subsequent reviews describe a third Chapare outbreak in 2021 in La Paz Department with three confirmed cases and two deaths, matching the case numbers and geography used here.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON553)) Detailed locality and driver information are necessarily more generic and largely inferred from descriptions of the established risk corridor (Caranavi–Teoponte–Palos Blancos), but remain consistent with the known ecology of the reservoir and with PAHO/WHO risk communication for rodent‑borne diseases in northern La Paz.([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/es/noticias/17-10-2022-pobladores-municipios-norte-paz-son-sensibilizados-capacitados-para-prevenir?utm_source=openai)) Event-type coding as re_occurrence (no new continent or UN sub‑region, and no documented novel genotype) is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2024] (northern La Paz Department – Teoponte/Muñecas–Alcoche area)
Host: Humans (25-year-old man from northern La Paz Department)
Event summary: In June 2024, Bolivia’s Ministry of Health confirmed a single laboratory-positive arenavirus infection attributed to Chapare virus in a 25-year-old man from the tropical north of La Paz Department, after field teams documented rodent exposure in rural communities such as Muñecas and Alcoche in Teoponte municipality. The patient was transferred to a referral hospital in El Alto and initially showed clinical improvement under intensive supportive care, but later developed severe pulmonary and neurologic complications and died in early August 2024; epidemiologic follow-up reported that 59 close contacts all tested negative for Chapare hemorrhagic fever. Health authorities delimited the affected area, implemented rodent-control and environmental sanitation measures, and provided additional training on Chapare hemorrhagic fever management in Caranavi and Teoponte, and no further confirmed human cases were reported in 2024, so this was treated as a localized zoonotic spillover event.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural agricultural settlements in northern La Paz with substantial infestation by the wild rodent Oligoryzomys microtis, substandard housing, and human encroachment into forest habitat likely enabled this spillover; the case was detected in the context of strengthened surveillance and rodent-borne disease control efforts in the Caranavi–Teoponte corridor. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by continued zoonotic transmission of an established Chapare virus lineage within Bolivia, with no current evidence of major genetic change or markedly increased human-to-human transmissibility in this event.
Review: Decision: review (corrected). The original row misattributed the December 19, 2024 adult male case described by WHO as part of the 2025 outbreak, and instead used that description for the 2024 event. I replaced the event_summary, host description and drivers with details from Bolivian Ministry of Health and SEDES La Paz communications, which document a distinct mid‑2024 Chapare hemorrhagic fever case in a 25‑year‑old man from Teoponte (northern La Paz), with 59 contacts tested and no secondary cases, and subsequent death from pulmonary complications.([minsalud.gob.bo](https://www.minsalud.gob.bo/8179-ministerio-de-salud-realizara-estudios-para-control-de-arenavirus-en-el-norte-paceno-y-descarta-caso-sospechoso-del-hospital-de-clinicas)) Event-type coding as re_occurrence in an already affected sub-region remains appropriate, and continent/sub-region/country fields are unchanged; I also updated source_urls to include the Bolivian primary reports and the June 2024 UK emerging infections summary as the most direct documentation for this outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2024] (rural municipalities in northern La Paz Department, including Bajo Inicua, Palos Blancos)
Host: Humans (adult male farmer and 7-year-old girl from rural northern La Paz Department)
Event summary: In late 2024 and early 2025, the fifth documented Chapare hemorrhagic fever outbreak in Bolivia occurred in the established risk corridor of northern La Paz Department and consisted of two confirmed human cases. The first patient, an adult male farmer aged about 50–60 years from a rural municipality in La Paz Department, developed fever, myalgia, arthralgia and gingival bleeding on 19 December 2024, was hospitalized on 24 December, and died on 30 December; Chapare virus infection was confirmed by real-time RT-PCR on a blood sample collected before death, and field investigation found intense rodent infestation in and around his wooden, dirt-floored home. A second laboratory-confirmed case was reported on 22 January 2025 in a 7-year-old girl from the indigenous Chimán community of Bajo Inicua in Palos Blancos municipality, whose symptoms began around 14 January; she required intensive care at Hospital del Norte but recovered, and comprehensive contact tracing, testing and rodent-control campaigns around both households found no further human cases, so authorities considered this a self-limited episode of repeated zoonotic spillover without sustained human-to-human transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Marked peri-domestic rodent infestation around smallholder farms in northern La Paz, wooden and metal housing with dirt floors, agricultural work that disturbs rodent burrows, and limited early recognition of Chapare hemorrhagic fever in remote facilities contributed to repeated zoonotic introductions; strengthened community surveillance and awareness allowed relatively rapid isolation and management once cases were suspected. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by ongoing circulation of Chapare virus in local rodent reservoirs, with no current evidence of new viral genotypes or markedly increased virulence compared with the 2019 strain; human-to-human transmission was not documented in either 2025 case, in contrast to the nosocomial spread seen in 2019.
Review: Decision: review (corrected). The original 2025 row conflated the December 19, 2024 adult male case with later sporadic cases and described that index case under the 2024 event as well, effectively double-counting it; it also did not clearly distinguish the mid‑2024 outbreak from the fifth outbreak spanning December 2024–January 2025. I have redefined this row to represent the fifth outbreak as described by WHO—beginning with the adult male farmer whose illness started on 19 December 2024 and was notified to WHO in early January 2025—and added the second confirmed 2025 case in a 7‑year‑old girl from Bajo Inicua, Palos Blancos, as documented by SEDES La Paz and a 2025 national case-series.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON553)) The year field is updated to 2024–2025 to reflect the cross-year onset and resolution, countries/host fields were corrected to emphasize northern La Paz municipalities, event_summary and drivers were rewritten to avoid overlap with the distinct 2024 Teoponte case, and confidence was increased to 0.9 given multiple convergent official and peer-reviewed sources; event-type classification as re_occurrence (no new continent or UN sub-region and no clear evidence of a novel genotype) remains appropriate.
