Host: Humans (rural agricultural workers and residents in Guanarito municipality and adjacent areas of Portuguesa State); wild rodent reservoirs including the short‑tailed cane mouse Zygodontomys brevicauda and Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni in surrounding agricultural fields and peridomestic habitats
Event summary: The event began when an epidemic of severe hemorrhagic fever was recognized in September 1989 among farmers near Guanarito, Portuguesa State, Venezuela; between May 1990 and March 1991, about 104 suspected cases with 26 deaths were recorded, almost all in small agricultural communities of the west‑central llanos.([wwwn.cdc.gov](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Arbocat/InformationExchange/54%20-%201991%20December%20searchable.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Virologic work in Venezuelan and international reference laboratories identified a novel arenavirus, later named Guanarito virus (Mammarenavirus guanaritoense), as the etiologic agent and linked infections to local rodent reservoirs, establishing Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever as a new zoonotic disease entity restricted to this rural focus.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article?utm_source=openai)) After this initial high‑incidence wave subsided in the early 1990s, transmission declined to a lower but persistent endemic level within the same geographic area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Agricultural expansion and intensification in the llanos of Portuguesa (grain, bean and cane cultivation) increased populations of the rodent reservoir Zygodontomys brevicauda and facilitated their incursion into fields and dwellings, elevating human exposure to infectious excreta; limited rural housing quality and poor rodent control further amplified risk.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: The emergence reflects zoonotic spillover from chronically infected wild rodents into humans in an area where Guanarito‑like mammarenaviruses appear to have been enzootic; there is no evidence that a dramatically more virulent or transmissible viral genotype appeared at this time, so environmental and social drivers, rather than viral evolution, are considered primary.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first and largest initial outbreak, but correct several details. Time span adjusted from 1990–1992 to 1990–1991 to match the best‑documented high‑incidence period (104 reported cases between May 1990 and March 1991).([wwwn.cdc.gov](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Arbocat/InformationExchange/54%20-%201991%20December%20searchable.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Country start year in brackets changed from [1989] to [1990] to align with the dataset’s 1990 start rule while still describing the 1989 onset in the text. The cotton rat reservoir species was corrected from Sigmodon hispidus (a North American species) to Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni, which is the species documented in Venezuela.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article)) The emergence‑type coding was revised to mark this episode as first/global emergence only (first_global_emergence = true, first_detection = false) because there is no long prior history of recognized human disease that would justify classifying it primarily as “first detection” of an ancient pathogen. Overall interpretation and geography (rural Portuguesa State, no spread beyond Venezuela) are well supported, but the event is flagged for expert review of exact year bounds and case counts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans in rural farming communities of Portuguesa State and nearby areas of Barinas State; wild rodent reservoirs (primarily Zygodontomys brevicauda, with co‑circulating arenaviruses in Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni) in cultivated fields and peridomestic habitats
Event summary: After the initial 1989–1991 epidemic, incident Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever cases decreased but did not disappear, and surveillance in the mid‑1990s documented a renewed period of higher transmission within the established focus of the west‑central Venezuelan llanos. Clinical and epidemiologic series covering 1989–1997 report a cumulative total of about 220 cases with a cyclic pattern of epidemic peaks every 4–5 years, indicating that a second wave of increased incidence occurred in the mid‑1990s among agricultural workers in Guanarito municipality and adjacent areas of Barinas State, but still without spread outside this rural region.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Toward the late 1990s, case numbers again fell back to the low‑level endemic background typical of inter‑epidemic periods in this area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The resurgence appears consistent with the cyclical ecology of rodent hosts and agricultural practices in the llanos—periods of favorable climate and cropping patterns lead to increased densities of Z. brevicauda and S. alstoni near human settlements, raising the frequency of exposure during planting and harvest seasons; chronic gaps in rodent control and rural health infrastructure likely allow such cycles to translate into episodic human outbreaks.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies of Guanarito virus isolates from the mid‑1990s show multiple co‑circulating lineages within western Venezuela but do not identify a clearly distinct, more virulent strain emerging during this period, so the episode is best treated as a re‑occurrence driven predominantly by external ecological and social‑economic factors rather than by major viral change.
Review: review – Retain this event as a mid‑1990s re‑occurrence within the same endemic focus, but flag for review because the exact start/end years and relative size of the mid‑1990s epidemic peak are only indirectly inferred from cumulative series (1989–1997) rather than from a clearly demarcated single‑outbreak report.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) The narrative, geography (Portuguesa/Barinas), and classification as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or continent affected, no strong evidence of a novel strain) are consistent with available data. The host description has been slightly adjusted to remove any implication that Sigmodon hispidus is a local reservoir and to emphasize Z. brevicauda and S. alstoni, which are the documented rodents in western Venezuela.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (predominantly male agricultural workers) in endemic rural areas of Portuguesa State; local wild rodent reservoirs including Zygodontomys brevicauda and Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni in surrounding fields and peridomestic environments
Event summary: Following several years of relatively low but persistent background transmission in the established endemic focus, a further upturn in Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever activity was reported around 2001–2002 within Portuguesa State, again affecting mainly young male farmers and rural residents. Spanish‑language epidemiologic summaries citing Ministry of Health data indicate roughly 30 clinically recognized cases during 2001–2002, representing a modest but notable increase over baseline, with cases remaining confined to the known endemic municipalities of Portuguesa (and sporadically Barinas) rather than appearing in new regions or countries.([es.wikipedia.org](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiebre_hemorr%C3%A1gica_venezolana?utm_source=openai)) After this episode, incidence again declined and, although sporadic infections continued to occur, no major geographic expansion was described in the published literature up to the mid‑2000s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: As with earlier waves, this re‑occurrence is plausibly linked to fluctuations in rodent reservoir abundance driven by agricultural cycles, climate variability in the llanos, and deteriorating rural socioeconomic conditions that increased exposure to rodents (e.g. food storage, housing quality), compounded by limited access to diagnostics that delayed recognition until clusters became apparent.([botica.xyz](https://www.botica.xyz/102/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: There is no published evidence of a distinct Guanarito virus lineage with altered virulence or transmissibility emerging in this period, so the episode is classified as a re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence; viral genetic diversity in western Venezuela appears longstanding and not clearly tied to specific human outbreak peaks.
Review: review – Retain this event as a smaller early‑2000s re‑occurrence, but keep it flagged for review. The existence of an early‑2000s uptick with approximately 30 cases is supported by Venezuelan sources cited in the Spanish‑language literature,([es.wikipedia.org](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiebre_hemorr%C3%A1gica_venezolana?utm_source=openai)) but Canada’s biosafety sheet summarizes a Guanarito virus outbreak in 2002–2003 without detailing whether it overlaps entirely with or extends beyond the 2001–2002 episode summarized here.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) The temporal bounds (2001–2002) should therefore be regarded as approximate. Host information has been corrected to refer to Sigmodon alstoni (Alston’s cotton rat) rather than S. hispidus, and the classification as a re‑occurrence (no new country or sub‑region affected, no clear viral change) is consistent with available data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans in rural communities of Portuguesa and Barinas States (principally agricultural workers and their household contacts); local rodent reservoirs (Zygodontomys brevicauda and Sigmodon alstoni) in fields and peridomestic settings
Event summary: Around the third quarter of 2011 and extending into early 2012, Venezuelan health and academic authorities reported a renewed epidemic of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever in the west‑central llanos, described in university council minutes as a “brote” with 86 cases occurring in the endemic zone of Portuguesa and Barinas.([medicinaucv.com](https://medicinaucv.com/documentos/ACTAS/2012/CF07-12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) This outbreak, occurring more than two decades after the initial emergence, followed the previously described pattern of affecting predominantly agricultural populations in the same municipalities, without spread beyond western Venezuela. After 2012, reported incidence again declined, although routine surveillance for febrile ictero‑hemorrhagic syndromes continued to include Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever as a target condition.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 2011–2012 outbreak fits the cyclic pattern of increased incidence every 4–5 years described for Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever and likely reflects favorable ecological conditions for rodent population growth (rainfall and agricultural cycles), ongoing poverty in rural communities, and limited rodent‑control and housing infrastructure that increase contact with infected excreta; incomplete public health surveillance and reporting may also have allowed local transmission to continue before the outbreak was widely recognized.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: Available summaries do not indicate emergence of a novel Guanarito virus strain or major changes in host range, so this episode is most consistent with re‑occurrence due to external ecological and social drivers rather than re‑emergence from viral evolution.
Review: review – New event added. Canada’s biosafety data sheet explicitly lists an outbreak of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever in 2011–2012 with 86 cases,([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) and minutes from the Faculty of Medicine at Universidad Central de Venezuela describe a recent FHV outbreak with 86 cases in the llanos of Portuguesa and Barinas, confirming this as a major epidemic wave within the endemic region.([medicinaucv.com](https://medicinaucv.com/documentos/ACTAS/2012/CF07-12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) This episode clearly meets the criterion of being among the largest post‑1990 events by case count and should be included. It is classified as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or continent, no evidence of viral change), with countries restricted to Venezuela; imported or potential cases elsewhere are not documented. Exact monthly start and end dates remain uncertain, so the 2011–2012 interval is approximate and merits expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans in rural agricultural communities of Portuguesa, Barinas, Apure and possibly parts of Guárico States; local rodent reservoirs (Zygodontomys brevicauda and Sigmodon alstoni) associated with croplands and peridomestic habitats
Event summary: In late 2015 and early 2016, Venezuelan public‑health experts and professional networks reported a new epidemic of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever, described in media interviews as the fifth recorded outbreak since the disease’s discovery in 1989.([elestimulo.com](https://elestimulo.com/salud-el-estimulo/2016-02-05/quinto-brote-de-fiebre-hemorragica-venezolana-se-extiende-en-tres-estados-del-pais/)) The outbreak was said to be affecting agricultural communities in Portuguesa, Barinas, Apure and parts of Guárico, with unofficial estimates of around 60 human cases and multiple deaths (including several members of the same family) and with under‑reporting suspected due to the absence of timely Ministry of Health bulletins.([elestimulo.com](https://elestimulo.com/salud-el-estimulo/2016-02-05/quinto-brote-de-fiebre-hemorragica-venezolana-se-extiende-en-tres-estados-del-pais/)) A biosafety data sheet from the Public Health Agency of Canada cites approximately 142 suspected cases associated with a 2016 outbreak, underscoring that this wave was one of the largest documented for Guanarito virus even though precise case counts and geographic spread remain uncertain.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) As the epidemic waned later in 2016, reports again dropped to sporadic cases, with continuing endemic transmission in the west‑central llanos.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Commentaries from Venezuelan epidemiologists attribute the 2015–2016 outbreak in part to severe drought and high temperatures linked to the El Niño climate pattern, which altered rodent ecology and intensified agricultural exposure, combined with worsening economic crisis, shortages of rodent‑control measures, and fragile rural health services that delayed diagnosis and isolation.([elestimulo.com](https://elestimulo.com/salud-el-estimulo/2016-02-05/quinto-brote-de-fiebre-hemorragica-venezolana-se-extiende-en-tres-estados-del-pais/)) Internal mechanisms: No specific Guanarito virus mutations or new host species were reported in association with this outbreak; available data instead point to a classic zoonotic spillover scenario recurring under stressed socio‑ecological conditions, so the event is best classified as a re‑occurrence within the same national endemic region rather than a re‑emergence driven by viral evolution. Spread involved additional Venezuelan states but did not cross national borders, so intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence categories are not triggered under the project definitions.
Review: review – New event added. Multiple sources, including Canada’s biosafety data sheet and Venezuelan press reports citing national epidemiology networks, agree that a substantial epidemic wave of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever occurred around 2015–2016 and describe it as the fifth recorded outbreak since 1989, with tens to more than one hundred suspected cases and several deaths.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) Because official Ministry of Health bulletins from this period are incomplete, the precise case count (e.g. 142 suspected cases in 2016) and spatial extent (reported involvement of Portuguesa, Barinas, Apure, and Guárico) remain somewhat uncertain; nevertheless, the episode clearly ranks among the largest post‑1990 events for this EPP and should be included. It is coded as a re‑occurrence localized within Venezuela, not as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, because all human transmission occurred in Venezuelan states within the same UN sub‑region and there is no evidence of sustained transmission outside the country. The 2015–2016 date range is approximate and flagged for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (index case in Zambia and healthcare workers in South Africa)
Event summary: Origin: In early September 2008, a female office worker living near Lusaka, Zambia developed an acute febrile illness that rapidly progressed to severe viral hemorrhagic fever; she was airlifted to Johannesburg, South Africa for treatment, where she later died. Development: Over subsequent weeks, four secondary nosocomial cases occurred—a Zambian paramedic involved in her evacuation and three South African healthcare or hospital workers—after unprotected exposure to the index patient’s blood and body fluids, creating a cluster of five epidemiologically linked cases with an approximately 80% case‑fatality rate and triggering intensive outbreak investigation and infection‑control measures. End: Following recognition of a probable viral hemorrhagic fever, barrier nursing, strict infection‑prevention and control practices, contact tracing, and isolation were implemented in Johannesburg, and no further cases occurred beyond the initial five; no additional human infections have been confirmed since this outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover from an as‑yet‑unidentified rodent reservoir in or near Lusaka, Zambia, followed by international medical evacuation of an undiagnosed severe febrile illness and initially inadequate infection‑prevention and control in the receiving hospital, which enabled limited nosocomial human‑to‑human transmission in Johannesburg. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from a rodent‑borne Old World arenavirus into humans, with documented person‑to‑person transmission via direct contact with blood and other body fluids in healthcare settings; there is no evidence to date of broader viral adaptation, sustained community transmission, or inherent geographic range expansion beyond this single, highly contained outbreak.
Review: review – Retain this event as the sole major emergence episode for Lujo virus (the 2008 Zambia/South Africa outbreak), which is well supported by primary literature and public‑health agency reports. Corrections applied: (1) event‑type coding adjusted to keep categories mutually exclusive for this single linked outbreak, setting first_global_emergence = Yes while changing first_detection from Yes to No and intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No, because all cases form one cross‑border nosocomial episode initiated by medical evacuation rather than independent emergence in a new sub‑region; (2) mechanism/driver text revised to remove unsupported reference to “Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)” and to emphasize zoonotic spillover plus limited nosocomial spread; (3) added the PLOS Pathogens genetic‑detection paper as a primary description of the same 2008 outbreak to both event‑level and profile‑level source lists. A human reviewer should confirm agreement with this coding choice (first/global emergence only) but no additional events appear to be missing or spurious for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Human laboratory workers; nude mice (Mus musculus) maintained in a cancer research institute
Event summary: In 1989, after an employee at a US cancer research institute developed lymphocytic choriomeningitis, an investigation identified a cluster of infections among staff linked to contact with LCMV‑infected nude mice used in tumor experiments. A retrospective cohort study found about 10% seroprevalence among employees, with infection strongly associated with cleaning cages, changing bedding, and handling water for nude mice. Control measures focused on improved rodent colony management, reduction of infected mouse populations, and stricter biosafety practices; the outbreak subsided once infected colonies were addressed and occupational exposure was reduced.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: occupational exposure to infected laboratory nude mice in a single institutional setting; high-density mouse colonies and recent expansion of experiments increased viral burden; limited prior awareness of LCMV risk in immunodeficient mouse strains. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel strain or change in virulence; the event reflects re-occurrence of an established zoonosis under high-exposure laboratory conditions rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – Year corrected from 1992 (publication date) to 1989 based on primary descriptions of the cancer‑research–institute outbreak. Geography, host description, and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic North American setting are appropriate. Because the corrected year falls just before the 1990 cut-off specified for event sheets, this outbreak should be treated primarily as historical context and considered for exclusion from the final 1990+ event list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Human solid-organ transplant recipients; reservoir rodents (likely house mice) not directly identified
Event summary: In December 2003, four solid-organ transplant recipients in the United States who shared a common donor developed severe febrile illness with meningoencephalitis, hepatitis, and multiorgan failure within weeks of surgery. Laboratory workup identified infection with an identical strain of LCMV in all recipients and in archived donor material, confirming donor-derived transmission in this cluster with high case fatality. The episode concluded without onward community spread but led to heightened awareness of LCMV as a cause of unexplained post‑transplant encephalitis and multisystem disease and informed subsequent donor‑evaluation guidance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: modern solid-organ transplantation providing an efficient iatrogenic route for LCMV transmission from a single infected donor to multiple highly immunosuppressed recipients; absence of routine LCMV screening in organ donors and unrecognized rodent exposure in the donor’s environment. Internal mechanisms: sequence data showed a single LCMV strain transmitted to all recipients, without clear evidence of increased intrinsic virulence; severe outcomes primarily reflected high inoculum via transplanted organs and profound host immunosuppression, consistent with re-occurrence of a known zoonosis in a novel clinical context.
Review: Review – Real and highly impactful donor-derived cluster with correct continent, subregion, country, and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic area. Event timing (2003–2004) and host description are appropriate. Source list was refined to retain the primary transplant-focused NEJM article and the CDC EID review of transplant-associated encephalitis, and to remove a rodent trace-forward article that primarily concerns the later 2012 feeder-rodent outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Human solid-organ transplant recipients; organ donor; pet hamster and pet-rodent distribution chain (Syrian hamsters and feeder/pet mice)
Event summary: In April 2005, a woman in Rhode Island died after a stroke and became an organ donor; all four recipients of her organs in Rhode Island and Massachusetts soon developed severe illness with hepatitis, coagulopathy, graft dysfunction, and multiorgan failure, and three died. Investigation identified LCMV in the donor, all recipients, and a recently purchased pet hamster in the donor’s household, and traced infection further back to a large commercial rodent-breeding and distribution operation that had shipped potentially infected hamsters and mice to multiple US states. The cluster ended without sustained human-to-human spread after implicated rodent stocks were quarantined or culled and public health authorities issued interim guidance for the pet-rodent trade and transplant community.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: commercial pet-rodent trade and large-scale interstate distribution of hamsters and mice, enabling wide dissemination of LCMV-infected animals; close human–pet contact in households; donor-derived transmission in heavily immunosuppressed transplant recipients; lack of routine LCMV screening for donors or rodent suppliers. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses showed unique donor-specific LCMV strains but no clear evidence of enhanced virulence; severe disease primarily reflected high viral load delivered through transplanted organs and host immunosuppression. This is best characterized as re-occurrence of known LCMV in a high-risk clinical and trade context.
Review: Retain – Well-documented high-fatality donor-derived outbreak linked to the pet-rodent trade, clearly among the most impactful modern LCMV events. Geographic assignment to the United States (North America, Northern America subregion) and classification as re-occurrence in an endemic region are appropriate, and the cited NEJM, MMWR, and EID articles are directly relevant. No corrections needed beyond acknowledging this event as a key driver of subsequent guidance on pet-rodent–associated LCMV risk.

Host: Human kidney transplant donor and two kidney recipients; presumed peridomestic rodents in donor environment
Event summary: In March 2008, a 49-year-old man in Massachusetts was hospitalized with fever and lymphocytic meningitis, progressed to anoxic brain injury, and subsequently became a kidney-only organ donor; both kidney recipients developed fever, hepatitis, coagulopathy, and multisystem organ failure within several weeks of transplantation. Testing at CDC showed acute LCMV infection in archived donor serum and in both recipients, with matching viral sequences, confirming donor-derived transmission in this cluster. Despite reduction of immunosuppression and ribavirin treatment in one recipient, both patients died, and the episode concluded without recognized secondary transmission but prompted a public health investigation of the donor’s rodent exposure history and reinforced guidance to consider LCMV when donors have unexplained encephalitis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: solid-organ transplantation providing an efficient route for LCMV transmission from an acutely infected donor to highly immunosuppressed recipients; lack of routine donor screening for LCMV; likely pre-hospital exposure of the donor to infected peridomestic rodents. Internal mechanisms: no indication of a uniquely virulent LCMV variant; severe outcomes are consistent with high viral load in transplanted organs and the immunosuppressed state of recipients, fitting a pattern of re-occurrence of an established zoonosis in a high-risk clinical niche.
Review: Review – Previously omitted but clearly documented donor-derived LCMV cluster in Massachusetts (2008) added, based on CDC MMWR and subsequent CDC EID summaries. Geography and host description are correct, and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic North American subregion is appropriate. Recommended to retain this event among the top LCMV emergence episodes given the 100% fatality among recipients and its role in shaping transplant safety guidance.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Human solid-organ transplant donor and four recipients; underlying rodent reservoir (house mice and/or peridomestic rodents)
Event summary: In late December 2010, a US adolescent with diabetic ketoacidosis and cerebral edema died and donated kidneys, liver, and lung to four recipients; within weeks to months, all recipients developed severe post‑transplant illness with hepatitis, encephalopathy, respiratory failure, and multiorgan involvement. CDC investigation in early 2011 identified LCMV infection in the donor and all four recipients by immunohistochemistry and RT‑PCR, with identical viral sequences confirming donor-derived transmission. Two recipients died and two survived after recognition of the etiology and adjustment of management; the cluster did not lead to further transmission but caused renewed alerts to transplant programs to consider LCMV when recipients develop unexplained fever, hepatitis, or encephalitis after receiving organs from donors with possible viral CNS infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: donor exposure to endemic LCMV (likely via household or community rodents), absence of donor screening, and intensive immunosuppressive regimens in recipients allowing high-level viral replication; increasing diagnostic capacity and awareness for arenavirus causes of post‑transplant encephalitis facilitated recognition. Internal mechanisms: molecular testing demonstrated a single LCMV strain transmitted to all recipients without evidence of a novel phenotype; this event is best interpreted as another severe re-occurrence of LCMV in transplant recipients within an endemic region.
Review: Retain – Donor-derived transplant cluster with substantial mortality and clear documentation, correctly placed in the United States (North America, Northern America subregion) and classified as re-occurrence in an endemic area. Source URLs (CDC EID article and associated CDC report) are directly relevant. No issues detected with timing, geography, or event-type classification.

Host: Employees of a large feeder-rodent breeding operation; feeder mice (Mus musculus) at multiple premises; downstream pet/feeder-mouse purchasers in multiple US states
Event summary: In April–May 2012, an Indiana rodent-breeding facility employee was hospitalized with aseptic meningitis and diagnosed with LCMV infection, prompting investigation of a large feeder-rodent operation with several premises. Serologic and molecular testing documented high LCMV prevalence in feeder mice and multiple infected employees, including several with meningitis, and trace-forward investigations showed that live potentially infected feeder mice had been shipped to numerous customers in other US states. The outbreak was contained through quarantine and stop‑movement orders on rodents from affected premises, culling and cleaning of facilities, and public health advisories to workers and customers, although LCMV persisted in wild and captive mouse populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive commercial production and interstate distribution of feeder mice without LCMV screening; crowded rodent housing conditions that favored viral maintenance and amplification; occupational exposure of employees to aerosolized excreta, bites, and contaminated dust; a growing feeder‑rodent market for reptile and exotic-pet owners that broadened the geographic reach of infected stock. Internal mechanisms: available data indicate endemic LCMV infection in mouse colonies without evidence of a novel genotype or altered virulence; this event represents re-occurrence driven primarily by industry practices and exposure intensity rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Large occupational and trade-related outbreak at a US feeder‑rodent operation, with multiple human infections and wide geographic distribution of infected mice. Geography and host description (employees and feeder mice within the United States, North America) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. The cited EID article, MMWR field note, and state-level guidance documents are all directly informative for this event; no corrections required.

Host: Two solid-organ transplant recipients (heart and kidney); peridomestic rodents in recipients’ home environments
Event summary: Around 2023–2024, two US solid-organ transplant recipients from different donors developed severe disseminated LCMV infection or meningoencephalitis, with one fatal outcome, despite no laboratory evidence of donor infection. Detailed investigation used metagenomic next‑generation sequencing and confirmatory molecular and serologic testing to attribute both infections to non–donor-derived LCMV acquired from substantial pre‑transplant rodent exposure in each recipient’s home environment. These cases did not generate secondary transmission but broadened recognition that environmental LCMV exposure can cause life‑threatening disease in transplant patients even when donors are uninfected, reinforcing guidance for clinicians to consider LCMV in severely immunocompromised hosts with compatible syndromes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: persistent endemic circulation of LCMV in peridomestic rodent populations; heavy household rodent infestation or contact in transplant recipients; profound immunosuppression related to transplant therapy; and improved diagnostic capacity through metagenomic next‑generation sequencing at reference laboratories. Internal mechanisms: viral sequences were consistent with known LCMV and did not demonstrate distinctive resistance or virulence markers; the key change is clinical and diagnostic recognition of severe non–donor-derived infection in this risk group rather than pathogen evolution. This episode is therefore categorized as re-occurrence in an endemic region.
Review: Retain – Small but clinically important series of severe non–donor-derived LCMV infections in US transplant recipients, highlighting environmental acquisition in an endemic region. Classification as re-occurrence, and restriction to North America/Northern America (United States), are appropriate. Year range (2023–2024) reflects the approximate clinical timeline reported in the primary case series; if finer temporal resolution is needed, the exact transplant and illness years can be cross-checked against the cited OFID article, but no major corrections are indicated.

Host: Humans in and around the town of Magdalena, Iténez Province, Beni Department (rural agricultural families and contacts)
Event summary: In July 1994, after almost two decades without confirmed cases, a Bolivian hemorrhagic fever outbreak began in an extended family in the town of Magdalena in Iténez Province, Beni Department, with seven relatives developing severe febrile hemorrhagic illness and six deaths; additional sporadic cases were identified in other residents of the endemic area, bringing the total to roughly one to two dozen probable infections. Bolivian authorities, assisted by international partners, carried out active case finding, rodent trapping, and environmental sanitation campaigns, and no further confirmed human cases were reported after late 1994, although the Machupo virus reservoir persisted in surrounding rural habitats. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: agricultural settlement and expansion around Magdalena into savanna and forest‑edge habitats, substandard housing, and grain‑storage practices that encouraged Calomys callosus infestation of dwellings facilitated intense human–rodent contact; gaps in local health infrastructure delayed recognition of the initial family cluster. Internal mechanisms: available virologic investigations show Machupo virus consistent with earlier strains, with no clear evidence of a novel genotype or change in virulence; the episode is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic focus driven by ecological and social factors rather than intrinsic viral evolution. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Review: Retain: This is a well‑documented major re‑occurrence in the historic endemic zone of Beni; timing, geography, case severity, and control measures match the CDC MMWR investigation and later reviews. No changes to event classification or geography are needed, and the source set appropriately prioritizes primary outbreak reports. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans in endemic rural communities of Beni Department
Event summary: In 1999, surveillance data summarized in clinical overviews indicate a small resurgence of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever in the traditional Machupo‑endemic zone of Beni Department, with approximately eight human cases reported over the year. Cases occurred in rural agricultural communities already known to harbor the Calomys callosus reservoir, without clear evidence of spread into new municipalities, and incidence declined again after targeted rodent‑control and health‑education activities. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: persistent ecological suitability for C. callosus in smallholder farming settlements, seasonal and interannual fluctuations in rodent densities, and limited rodent‑proofing of homes and grain stores likely enabled renewed spillover in a few foci; local socioeconomic conditions kept residents working and storing food in rodent‑infested environments. Internal mechanisms: no published data indicate emergence of a distinct Machupo lineage, increased virulence, or drug resistance, so this episode is best interpreted as endemic re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence driven by viral change. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain: Multiple standard references mention a cluster of ≈8 BHF cases in 1999 in Beni, with no indication of spread beyond the known endemic area; classification as a small re‑occurrence and the geographic coding are appropriate. Because information comes from secondary summaries rather than a formal outbreak report, case counts should be treated as approximate, but the event remains among the more substantial post‑1990 resurgences. Host: Humans in Beni Department (Magdalena, Huacaraje, San Ramón and nearby rural communities), including residents and health‑care workers
Event summary: From early 2007 into 2008, Beni Department experienced the largest recognized resurgence of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever since the 1960s. Surveillance first detected around 20 suspected BHF cases with three deaths near Magdalena and neighboring areas of Iténez Province, followed in February 2008 by reports of roughly 200 additional suspected cases and 12 deaths from municipalities including Huacaraje and San Ramón; a joint investigation by Bolivian authorities and CDC ultimately confirmed Machupo virus infection in five patients (three fatal), demonstrating active viral circulation across multiple rural communities. Intensive rodent‑control campaigns, reinforcement of infection‑prevention measures in local health facilities, and community education were deployed, and by late 2008 reported incidence had fallen back to low endemic levels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and improved road connectivity of rural communities in Beni, climatic variability and land‑use changes that likely boosted C. callosus populations, and persistent gaps in rodent‑proofing of homes and food‑storage structures created conditions for widespread human–rodent contact; limited infection‑prevention capacity in small health centers contributed to local amplification and infection of health‑care workers. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses of 2007–2008 Machupo isolates show close continuity with earlier strains rather than a distinct new genotype, and no evidence of altered virulence or host range, so this multi‑year episode is best understood as a pronounced re‑occurrence driven by ecological and social factors rather than intrinsic viral evolution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))

I have revised the narrative to distinguish suspected from laboratory‑confirmed cases and to align more closely with the CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases investigation and Bolivian surveillance reports, and I have pruned less authoritative sources (e.g., language‑specific Wikipedia and tertiary summaries) in favor of primary CDC and Ministry of Health documents. Because of discrepancies between suspected and confirmed counts, the event should remain flagged for expert review but clearly belongs among the top post‑1990 Machupo events. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (patients with Lyme-like illness); Ixodes scapularis ticks; small mammal reservoirs (e.g., Peromyscus spp.) in endemic Minnesota and Wisconsin foci
Event summary: This event began in 2013 when a Minnesota resident with Lyme-like illness was found to be infected with an atypical Borrelia that was subsequently detected in additional patients from Minnesota and Wisconsin and in Ixodes scapularis ticks collected in both states. Over 2013–2014, retrospective molecular analyses of more than 100,000 Lyme diagnostic specimens and targeted tick testing identified six human infections and a measurable, though low, prevalence of this novel Borrelia in blacklegged ticks in the Upper Midwest, leading to its formal description as Borrelia mayonii and recognition in 2016 as a new cause of Lyme disease. The episode concluded as the pathogen was incorporated into routine diagnostic algorithms and surveillance definitions, with only sporadic human cases reported thereafter and no evidence of large outbreaks, but with establishment of an endemic zoonotic cycle in parts of Minnesota and Wisconsin.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensified molecular surveillance and PCR-based genotyping of Lyme disease specimens at reference laboratories (Mayo Clinic and CDC) allowed discrimination of atypical oppA1 gene sequences from Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto; concurrent expansion and densification of Ixodes scapularis populations in Minnesota and Wisconsin, linked to land-use change (reforestation, suburbanization) and a warming climate, increased human–tick contact in the Upper Midwest. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel Lyme borreliosis genospecies within the B. burgdorferi sensu lato complex (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), characterized by higher spirochetemia and more diffuse rash and systemic symptoms than typical B. burgdorferi infection, which may facilitate detection via blood PCR and potentially alter transmission dynamics (Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: retain: Event appropriately captures the discovery and early characterization of Borrelia mayonii as a human Lyme disease agent in Minnesota and Wisconsin during 2013–2016, with correct timing, geography (Upper Midwest, United States), and event-type classification as both first global emergence and first detection in the human host system; no corrections were required.

Host: Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes angustus ticks; small mammal reservoirs (rodents); no confirmed human clinical cases as of 2019
Event summary: Following its recognition in the Upper Midwest of the United States, Borrelia mayonii or B. mayonii-like organisms were detected in the mid‑2010s in Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes angustus ticks and wild animal hosts in Ontario and British Columbia, marking spread of the enzootic cycle into Canadian foci without confirmed human illness. Through 2014–2019, national tick-borne disease assessments in Canada documented B. mayonii/B. mayonii-like detections in ticks and wildlife from these provinces while human Lyme disease remained dominated by Borrelia burgdorferi, suggesting silent geographic expansion of the novel genospecies. The episode is characterized as an ecological range expansion rather than a discrete outbreak, ending with B. mayonii recognized as present but rare in Canadian tick populations and as a potential future threat for human Lyme disease in Canada.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: northward and westward expansion of Ixodes scapularis and related tick species into higher-latitude and coastal regions of Canada due to climate warming, changing host distributions (e.g., deer and small mammals), and landscape changes that favor forested edge habitats; enhanced national tick and wildlife surveillance programs increased sensitivity for detecting rare pathogens. Internal mechanisms: no specific genetic or phenotypic changes in B. mayonii have been demonstrated for these Canadian detections; they are best interpreted as low-prevalence geographic range expansion of existing B. mayonii/B. mayonii-like lineages into new tick populations and ecozones, facilitated primarily by climate- and host-driven processes rather than documented novel adaptation.
Review: review: Event is retained as it reflects documented detection of Borrelia mayonii/B. mayonii-like organisms in ticks and wildlife in Ontario and British Columbia beginning around 2014, but the type-of-emergence classification has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence because this represents geographic spread within the same UN subregion (Northern America) driven mainly by climate- and host-mediated tick range expansion rather than demonstrated pathogen-level change; an obsolete CDC PRCATS URL (404) was removed from the source list, and the mechanism/driver text was edited to avoid speculative claims about specific adaptive changes in the bacterium.

Countries: United States of America [2025] (New York – Herkimer County)
Host: Humans (autochthonous Lyme disease case); Ixodes scapularis ticks as presumed local vector
Event summary: In July 2025, an adult resident of Herkimer County, New York, who had not traveled outside the state, was found by a commercial laboratory to be PCR‑positive for Borrelia mayonii, prompting investigation by the New York State Department of Health and CDC, and representing the first reported autochthonous human B. mayonii infection outside Minnesota and Wisconsin. Public health follow‑up confirmed absence of travel, transplant, or transfusion exposures and identified likely local tick exposure in upstate New York, indicating that B. mayonii had expanded beyond its previously recognized Upper Midwestern human range. The episode concluded as a single, severe but self‑limited Lyme disease case, with no identified secondary human transmission, but it led to heightened clinician awareness, inclusion of B. mayonii in regional Lyme diagnostics, and consideration of the pathogen in future tick and wildlife surveillance in the northeastern United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ongoing expansion and high density of Ixodes scapularis populations and Lyme disease risk in the northeastern United States, driven by reforestation, abundant deer and small mammal hosts, and climatic conditions favoring tick survival; increased clinician and laboratory awareness of B. mayonii and use of PCR assays capable of discriminating it from B. burgdorferi facilitated detection, together with targeted tick surveillance around the patient’s residence. Internal mechanisms: no specific genetic or phenotypic changes have yet been demonstrated for New York B. mayonii isolates; this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of previously recognized Upper Midwestern B. mayonii lineages into northeastern tick populations rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: review: Event is retained and reflects the first documented locally acquired human Borrelia mayonii infection and associated tick detections in New York State in 2025, but the type-of-emergence classification has been revised from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the episode represents spread within the same UN subregion (Northern America) without evidence for new host range or virulence traits; the host description was corrected for a typographical error ('autochthonous'), and the mechanism/driver narrative was adjusted to remove unsupported suggestions of increased virulence and to emphasize vector ecology, land-use/climate drivers, and enhanced surveillance as the primary explanatory factors.

Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with history of Ixodes persulcatus/Ixodes ricinus tick bites in the Yekaterinburg region)
Event summary: During the 2009 tick season, clinicians at Municipal Clinical Hospital No. 33 in Yekaterinburg, Russia, evaluated 302 patients admitted with suspected Ixodes-borne infections and identified 46 with PCR-confirmed Borrelia miyamotoi disease, representing the first recognized human cases worldwide. Patients had influenza-like illness with high fever, headache, myalgia and, in some, relapsing fever episodes or erythema migrans, in a region already endemic for Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne encephalitis. After patients received antimicrobial therapy and the tick season ended, case numbers declined, and publication of the findings in 2011 established B. miyamotoi as a human tick-borne relapsing-fever pathogen and spurred similar investigations elsewhere in the Northern Hemisphere.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/10/10-1474_article?source=govdelivery&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intense human exposure to Ixodes persulcatus (and locally I. ricinus) in mixed forest landscapes of the Ural region where multiple tick-borne agents co-circulate, together with deployment of specific PCR and improved serologic assays that allowed clinicians to distinguish B. miyamotoi from Lyme borreliosis and other febrile illnesses. Internal mechanisms: Spillover from rodent and bird reservoirs to humans via ixodid ticks and the relapsing-fever biology of B. miyamotoi, which supports persistent spirochetemia and recurrent fever episodes in the absence of treatment.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/10/10-1474_article?source=govdelivery&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Review. Adjusted the event to use 2009 as the year and Russian Federation [2009] as the country-specific start year, reflecting that all 46 patients in Platonov et al. were enrolled during the 2009 tick season even though the paper appeared in 2011. The summary was rewritten to clarify timing and avoid implying that illnesses occurred in 2011, while retaining classification as both first_global_emergence and first_detection in humans. Sources now emphasize the original case series and follow-up Russian work; a domain expert should confirm that using the case year (2009) rather than publication year (2011) is appropriate for this dataset.

Host: Humans (patients with history of Ixodes scapularis tick exposure in the northeastern United States, including an immunocompromised index patient with meningoencephalitis)
Event summary: In 2013, US clinicians reported Borrelia miyamotoi meningoencephalitis in an elderly immunocompromised man from New Jersey with presumed local Ixodes scapularis exposure and described additional febrile patients with serologic or PCR evidence of infection, providing the first recognized human cases in North America. These reports showed that B. miyamotoi had been silently circulating in blacklegged tick populations in the Northeast and Midwest and that a subset of patients with viral-like summer fevers after deer tick bites actually had hard-tick relapsing fever. Recognition of these cases prompted heightened clinical awareness and targeted testing, although early human infections remained sporadic and geographically focal.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMoa1209039?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Established and expanding populations of Ixodes scapularis associated with high white-tailed deer and rodent densities, reforestation and suburbanization that increase human–tick contact, and more intensive diagnostic work-ups of unexplained summer fevers in Lyme-endemic regions. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of B. miyamotoi within Ixodes complexes in North America and efficient transovarial transmission in ticks that maintain the spirochete in vector populations; in severely immunosuppressed hosts the organism can invade the central nervous system and cause meningoencephalitis.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/20/7/pdfs/v20-n7.pdf))

Retained 'inter_continental_emergence = true' because these were the first recognized human infections in North America with in situ transmission by I. scapularis. The summary was streamlined to focus on documented case series rather than speculative burden. A domain expert may wish to confirm whether illness-onset year (around 2011) should be used instead of publication year for this index US event.

Host: Humans (patients evaluated for suspected Lyme borreliosis or other tick-borne febrile illness in Hokkaido and other endemic regions)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, Japanese investigators re-examined stored sera from Lyme disease–suspect patients in Hokkaido and, in 2014, reported two indigenous Borrelia miyamotoi infections with illness onset in 2011 and 2013, providing the first confirmed human cases in Japan. Subsequent tick and patient-based surveillance from roughly 2013 to 2017 identified additional autochthonous infections among persons with febrile illness after Ixodes persulcatus bites, revealing that B. miyamotoi had been circulating unrecognized alongside Lyme borreliosis agents. Case numbers remained low and scattered, but this work established B. miyamotoi disease as an emerging hard-tick relapsing fever in Japan and, under the UNSD regional scheme, represents the first recognized human infections in the Asian continent outside Russia.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25061761/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing human exposure to Ixodes persulcatus in forested northern Japan and historically Lyme-focused diagnostics that did not initially target relapsing-fever group borreliae; expanded use of PCR and GlpQ-based serology in Lyme-suspect patients enabled both retrospective and prospective detection of B. miyamotoi. Internal mechanisms: Spillover from rodent reservoirs to humans via I. persulcatus and a clinical spectrum ranging from self-limited febrile illness to more severe disease, although most Japanese cases described to date have been mild to moderate.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25061761/))
Review: Decision: Review. Broadened the event period from 2013–2017 to 2011–2017 to reflect that the first two documented Japanese BMD cases had illness onset in 2011 and 2013 but were recognized through retrospective surveillance and reported in 2014. Simplified the country field to Japan [2011–2017] and clarified in the summary that this episode constitutes the first confirmed human infections in Asia outside Russia when the UNSD classification is applied, supporting 'inter_continental_emergence = true'. No additional type flags were changed.

Host: Humans (farmers and rural residents with tick exposure in northeastern China; Ixodes persulcatus and Haemaphysalis concinna ticks)
Event summary: From May 2013 through June 2015, clinicians at a forestry hospital in northeastern China enrolled 984 patients reporting recent tick bites and febrile illness and identified 14 (1.4%) with PCR-confirmed Borrelia miyamotoi infection, concurrently detecting the spirochete in about 3% of Ixodes persulcatus and some Haemaphysalis concinna ticks. These patients, drawn from forested and agricultural landscapes in Heilongjiang Province and neighboring areas, represented the first recognized human BMD cases in China and demonstrated that B. miyamotoi co-circulates with Lyme borreliosis agents and other tick-borne pathogens in the region. After this episode, B. miyamotoi was incorporated into the differential diagnosis for undifferentiated tick-associated fevers in northeastern China, but reported human case numbers remained modest.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5782893/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High occupational and recreational exposure to ticks among rural populations in northeastern China, ecological suitability for I. persulcatus and other competent vectors, and targeted field and clinical investigations that broadened molecular testing beyond Lyme disease alone. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of B. miyamotoi within Palearctic Ixodes populations and its ability to cause non-specific febrile illness that is easily overlooked without organism-specific PCR or sequencing.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5782893/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain. Clarified that 14 human cases were identified among 984 tick-exposed patients during 2013–2015 and specified the main affected provinces, but did not change any event type flags because this episode reflects recognition of human disease in an area where infected ticks were already present and does not correspond to a new UNSD subregion. Event sources were trimmed to prioritize the original EID article and its PMC version as the most relevant descriptions of the episode.

Host: Humans (severely immunocompromised patient with probable local Ixodes ricinus exposure in the Netherlands)
Event summary: In 2013, clinicians in Amsterdam reported a rituximab-treated patient with severe meningoencephalitis in whom Borrelia miyamotoi DNA was detected in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, constituting the first recognized symptomatic human case in the European Union after the Russian series. The illness was linked to presumed local Ixodes ricinus exposure rather than travel to Russia or Asia and was characterized by persistent fever, neurologic deficits, and inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid findings. The patient gradually improved with intravenous antibiotics, and this case prompted wider investigation of B. miyamotoi in ticks and humans throughout Western Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3987849/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Presence of B. miyamotoi in I. ricinus ticks in the Netherlands, as demonstrated by tick-testing studies, and growing use of molecular diagnostics in immunocompromised patients with unexplained central nervous system infections. Internal mechanisms: Neurotropism and persistence of B. miyamotoi in B-cell–depleted hosts, illustrating its capacity to cause severe CNS disease and highlighting the need to consider BMD in the differential diagnosis of meningoencephalitis in endemic Ixodes regions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3987849/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain. Classification as an intra-continental emergence event is appropriate because this was the first recognized human BMD case in Western Europe following the earlier Eastern European (Russian) series under the UNSD regional scheme. No changes were made to timing or type flags; the summary was modestly edited to emphasize local acquisition and its catalytic role for European surveillance. The selected sources continue to center on the original Lancet case report and related Dutch work that quantifies exposure in human-biting ticks.

Countries: Germany [2015]; France [2015-2018]; Sweden [2018]; Austria [2018, imported infection after tick bite in the United States]; other Western/Northern European countries with sporadic cases (e.g., Belgium, England, Norway, Poland)
Host: Humans (immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients with tick exposure in Western and Northern Europe)
Event summary: Following the Dutch index case, multiple countries in Western and Northern Europe reported autochthonous Borrelia miyamotoi disease between about 2015 and 2018, including neuroborreliosis-like CNS infections in Germany and Sweden and increasing numbers of systemic cases in France. A large French study of 824 patients with persistent polymorphic symptoms after tick bites identified 43 with B. miyamotoi DNA in blood, while additional single cases were documented in countries such as Norway and Poland and in Austria (where a European-type strain was detected in a patient reporting a tick bite in the United States). Together, these reports demonstrated that B. miyamotoi was widely established in Ixodes ricinus across Europe and capable of causing both acute febrile illness and meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised and immunocompetent persons, leading several centers to add B. miyamotoi testing to diagnostic algorithms for tick-associated fever and neuroborreliosis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059645/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Broad distribution and increasing densities of I. ricinus in Western and Northern Europe; high recreational and occupational exposure to ticks; and rising interest in non-Lyme tick-borne infections that prompted targeted PCR and GlpQ-based serology in patients with compatible syndromes. Internal mechanisms: Stable transovarial maintenance of B. miyamotoi in Ixodes populations and its ability to cause invasive CNS disease as well as persistent polymorphic symptom complexes; the emergence pattern here reflects geographic and diagnostic expansion of existing genotypes rather than appearance of a clearly novel strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7827671/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Review. Clarified that this multi-country episode represents extension of B. miyamotoi disease from the earlier Eastern and Western European foci into additional Western and Northern European settings, which supports 'intra_continental_emergence = true' at the UNSD subregional level. Expanded the country field to indicate that the Austrian case was probably imported after a tick bite in the United States (despite a European genotype) and to acknowledge other Western/Northern European countries with sporadic cases (e.g., Norway, Poland) that are not assigned separate rows. No further type flags were added. Because the included French cohort focuses on patients with chronic polymorphic symptoms and the clinical significance of B. miyamotoi DNA in that context is debated, this grouping and its interpretation as a major emergence event should be reviewed by a subject-matter expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America [2013-2019; 9 states with human surveillance cases, ≥19 states with B. miyamotoi–positive human-biting ticks]
Host: Humans (patients with tick exposure in northeastern, midwestern and some western US states, and human-biting Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus ticks)
Event summary: After the 2013 index reports, state health departments in the Northeast and upper Midwest implemented surveillance for hard tick relapsing fever caused by Borrelia miyamotoi, and during 2013–2019 they identified 300 human cases across nine US states, with about 55% classified as confirmed and 13% requiring hospitalization. In parallel, analyses of human-biting ticks submitted for testing during this period found B. miyamotoi in Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus from 19 states, indicating that exposure risk extended beyond the initial focal regions. Case detection increased over time as more laboratories adopted B. miyamotoi-specific PCR and GlpQ-based serology, and educational materials in some states began listing B. miyamotoi among monitored tick-borne pathogens, although incidence remained far lower than that of Lyme disease.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/29/9/22-1912_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and densification of I. scapularis populations driven by deer and rodent host dynamics, reforestation and suburbanization, climate-related lengthening of tick activity seasons, and enhanced clinician and public health awareness of emerging tick-borne pathogens, which together increased testing and reporting of B. miyamotoi. Internal mechanisms: Persistent, transovarial transmission of B. miyamotoi in Ixodes ticks enabling wide geographic spread at relatively low prevalence (~2% of ticks) and the capacity to cause a range of clinical syndromes from nonspecific febrile illness to neuroinvasive disease; there is no clear evidence in this period for major shifts in virulence or host range.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/29/9/22-1912_article))
Review: Decision: Review. Reframed this episode to emphasize the 300 human cases identified by public health surveillance in nine US states from 2013–2019, while still noting concurrent detection of B. miyamotoi in human-biting ticks from 19 states. Reset 're_occurrence' from true to false because there is no documented prior disappearance in Northern America; the pattern is better interpreted as gradual geographic expansion and improved recognition within the same UNSD subregion than as a resurgence. No intra- or inter-continental flags were added, since the event reflects within-country spread. Sources were updated to prioritize the 2023 EID surveillance paper alongside the tick-prevalence study and North American clinical review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (immunocompetent adults with undifferentiated febrile illness and recent tick bites in Slovenia)
Event summary: In a prospective study of adults with acute undifferentiated fever evaluated at the University Medical Centre Ljubljana during 2021–2025, investigators used metagenomic next-generation sequencing followed by specific PCR to identify Borrelia miyamotoi in two patients—one who sought care in July 2022 and another in May 2025—marking the first confirmed human cases in Slovenia. Both patients had recent Ixodes tick bites, moderate febrile illness with headache and mild cytopenias or liver enzyme elevations, and recovered without antimicrobial therapy. These locally acquired cases extended the documented range of human B. miyamotoi disease into Southern Europe and led authors to recommend that clinicians in Slovenia consider B. miyamotoi in the differential diagnosis of tick-associated febrile illnesses.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/8/26-0326_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Established Ixodes ricinus populations in forested and rural regions of Slovenia and the increasing use of unbiased metagenomic sequencing and targeted PCR to investigate unexplained fevers after tick bites. Internal mechanisms: Continued geographic spread of European-type B. miyamotoi within Ixodes populations and the organism’s ability to cause generally self-limited febrile illness in immunocompetent adults; no novel genotype or resistance phenotype was implicated in these cases.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/8/26-0326_article))
Review: Decision: Review. Changed the event year from 2025 to 2022–2025 and updated the country field to Slovenia [2022, 2025] to reflect that the first of the two confirmed locally acquired cases presented in July 2022, with a second in May 2025, as detailed in the 2026 EID report. Retained 'intra_continental_emergence = true' because this episode documents the first recognized human BMD infections in Southern Europe under the UNSD classification. Sources now focus on the Slovenian case series and a European overview; a subject-matter expert may wish to revisit whether any additional Southern European cases emerging after 2025 warrant a separate event row in future updates.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (four adolescent sisters and additional sporadic adult cases)
Event summary: In February 2003, a rural family in Tejuçuoca, Ceará State, northeastern Brazil, experienced a cluster of severe pneumonic sepsis in four adolescent sisters, from whom Burkholderia pseudomallei was first cultured, marking the first confirmed human melioidosis outbreak in Brazil. The event developed into a small but high‑mortality cluster and prompted investigation of additional sporadic human cases and environmental sources in Ceará over 2003–2004. Subsequent environmental sampling recovered B. pseudomallei from local soil and water, confirming previously unrecognized endemicity in this South American focus rather than continued large‑scale outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: agricultural and rural exposures to contaminated soil and surface water in a semiarid region with seasonal rains, combined with delayed clinical recognition and limited laboratory capacity in a non‑traditional melioidosis setting. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion and long‑standing cryptic environmental establishment of B. pseudomallei in northeastern Brazil revealed by improved surveillance and environmental sampling, rather than a demonstrably novel strain or major virulence shift.
Review: Review – Retain event but correct emergence type and sources. Autochthonous melioidosis had been reported elsewhere in South America (e.g. Ecuador 1962 and other countries) before 2003, so this Ceará cluster represents a major re-occurrence within an already affected sub-region rather than intra-continental emergence. Updated intra_continental_emergence to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed a non‑event‑specific Australian reference from source_urls.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (immunosuppressed adult woman)
Event summary: In January 2004, Mauritius reported its first autochthonous human melioidosis case when a 40‑year‑old woman on immunosuppressive therapy developed septic illness and B. pseudomallei was isolated, in a country where the organism had never previously been identified. The case evolved with severe systemic disease requiring prolonged hospitalization, and retrospective investigation linked her infection to chronic exposure to wet mud during a period of higher‑than‑average rainfall. After targeted public health and clinical awareness efforts, no large outbreak followed, but the case marked recognition of melioidosis as present in the western Indian Ocean region rather than remaining confined to classical Asian and Australian foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: higher‑than‑average seasonal rainfall increasing exposure to contaminated mud and surface water, and widespread diabetes and immunosuppressive conditions in the local population. Internal mechanisms: likely long‑standing low‑level environmental presence of B. pseudomallei in the western Indian Ocean islands uncovered through improved diagnostic awareness, without evidence for a distinct hypervirulent genotype.
Review: Review – Retain as a key sentinel case in the western Indian Ocean but adjust emergence classification and clean sources. Earlier human melioidosis exposures and cases linked to East Africa existed before 2004, so Eastern Africa was not a new sub-region for human infection; this event is better coded as a re-occurrence in a previously known African sub-region. Set intra_continental_emergence to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed a duplicate PMCID URL, keeping the primary EID case report and the regional review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (adult and elderly patients, many with comorbidities)
Event summary: From July through September 2005, shortly after a major typhoon brought flooding to southern Taiwan, clinicians identified an outbreak of 40 culture‑confirmed human melioidosis cases, far exceeding baseline incidence. The outbreak progressed with many patients presenting with severe pneumonia, sepsis and high rates of bacteremia and septic shock, and molecular typing showed multiple B. pseudomallei genotypes consistent with intense environmental exposure rather than a single clonal source. As floodwaters receded and targeted public health messaging and clinical management improved, case numbers declined back toward endemic levels in subsequent seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme rainfall and flooding associated with a typhoon, which likely mobilized B. pseudomallei from soil into surface waters and aerosols, increasing percutaneous and inhalational exposure; high prevalence of diabetes and chronic diseases in the affected population; and increased environmental disturbance in urban and peri‑urban areas. Internal mechanisms: no single novel strain was implicated; instead, enhanced transmission from multiple environmental sources during an extreme‑weather period explains the outbreak.
Review: Review – Event description and classification as a major re-occurrence in an already endemic area are appropriate, but the country field was standardized to the UN-style name used in the country list. Updated countries to “China, Taiwan Province of China [2005]”; otherwise retain the event and source set, which correctly emphasize the typhoon-associated cluster.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (adults and children, many with diabetes, alcohol use, chronic lung and renal disease)
Event summary: During the 2009–2010 monsoonal wet season, the Top End region of the Northern Territory, Australia, experienced record rainfall and simultaneously recorded its highest annual incidence of human melioidosis since prospective surveillance began in 1989. Case counts and severity rose sharply, with Royal Darwin Hospital reporting markedly increased admissions for pneumonic and septicemic melioidosis compared with the preceding 20 years, but intensive care and optimized therapy limited mortality to under 10%. As rainfall returned closer to normal in subsequent seasons, the incidence of melioidosis declined toward its long‑term endemic baseline, though strong rainfall‑incidence associations persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: record or near‑record wet season rainfall and associated flooding, which strongly increased environmental exposure to B. pseudomallei in soil and surface water, especially among people with diabetes, hazardous alcohol consumption, chronic lung disease or renal disease. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of a new genotype driving this surge; instead, enhanced transmission due to climatic anomalies in a highly endemic setting explains the re‑occurrence peak.
Review: Review – Retain this as one of the most impactful melioidosis seasons globally; coding as a re-occurrence in an already endemic sub-region is appropriate. Only a minor formatting change was made to the countries field (country plus years, without subnational detail) to align with the Excel specification; sources remain appropriate and event-level data are consistent with the primary MJA report.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (mainly Indigenous Aboriginal adults with comorbidities)
Event summary: In early 2011, after atypically intense rainfall and flooding in normally arid Central Australia linked to a strong La Niña event, six locally acquired human melioidosis cases were identified over four months in residents of the Alice Springs and Tennant Creek region, an area previously considered only marginally affected. The episode unfolded with severe sepsis and pneumonia in several patients, drawing attention because Central Australia had recorded only a handful of cases in the preceding two decades despite long‑running surveillance. As flood conditions resolved and public health alerts were issued, no sustained cluster persisted, but these cases demonstrated that B. pseudomallei is established in interior desert environments of Australia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: La Niña–associated record wet season in 2010–2011 causing unusual flooding in desert landscapes, increasing exposure to contaminated soil and water for local communities, particularly Indigenous populations with high burdens of diabetes and chronic disease. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion or previously under‑recognized endemicity of B. pseudomallei in arid central Australian soils revealed by extreme rainfall events; no clear evidence of a distinct, more virulent strain in this cluster.
Review: Review – Retain but correct event type and standardize the country field. Because melioidosis had long been endemic in the same UN sub-region (Australia and New Zealand) through Top End transmission, this central Australian desert cluster is best treated as a notable re-occurrence driven by extreme rainfall rather than intra-continental emergence. Updated intra_continental_emergence to false, re_occurrence to true, and simplified countries to “Australia [2011]”.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (adults with diabetes and other risk factors)
Event summary: Around 2010, a fatal and a subsequent nonfatal case of melioidosis in Puerto Rico, including one linked to exposure to floodwaters, triggered detailed investigations into possible local acquisition of B. pseudomallei. Over 2010–2012, case investigations, serosurveys and environmental sampling identified multiple autochthonous human infections and isolated B. pseudomallei from soil, confirming that melioidosis is regionally endemic in parts of Puerto Rico rather than limited to imported infections. After these studies, sporadic locally acquired cases continued to occur, but heightened clinician awareness and environmental data allowed more rapid diagnosis and management instead of large undiscovered outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: heavy rainfall and flooding episodes increasing contact with contaminated surface water and soil, plus high prevalence of diabetes and chronic conditions; in addition, improved diagnostic capacity and targeted field investigations after sentinel cases. Internal mechanisms: recognition of established environmental foci of B. pseudomallei in Puerto Rico and probable long‑standing low‑diversity local strain circulation, rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Review – Retain as a major re-occurrence event revealing endemicity in the Caribbean. Earlier sporadic human cases and environmental detections in the wider Caribbean meant the sub-region was not new; this 2010–2012 cluster, investigations, and soil isolation fit the definition of re-occurrence driven by external factors (rainfall and improved surveillance). The only change made was to standardize the countries field to “Puerto Rico [2010-2012]” to match the country list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (adults in Madagascar; contextual links to other western Indian Ocean island cases)
