Event summary: In 2012 and 2013, two adult patients from the coastal city of Mahajanga, Madagascar, were diagnosed with fatal autochthonous melioidosis, with B. pseudomallei of novel sequence types confirming local environmental circulation on the island. These cases, together with earlier recognition of a first autochthonous human case in nearby Mauritius in 2004 and several imported cases to Réunion Island epidemiologically linked back to Madagascar, collectively indicated previously unrecognized endemicity of melioidosis in the western Indian Ocean islands of Eastern Africa. After these sentinel events, awareness campaigns and limited environmental studies suggested ongoing but sporadic transmission rather than large, sustained outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: tropical climate with heavy rains, intensive exposure to wet soil and surface water in peri‑urban and rural settings, and high prevalence of diabetes and other comorbidities, combined with historically weak diagnostic capacity for melioidosis in African laboratories. Internal mechanisms: emergence and recognition of diverse, previously undescribed African B. pseudomallei sequence types with phylogenomic evidence of an Asian origin, consistent with re-emergence driven in part by pathogen diversity in a previously known African sub-region.
Review: Review – Retain this as a key western Indian Ocean emergence episode but adjust its scope and type. The original row inappropriately bundled the separate 2004 Mauritius case (already captured in its own event) and coded the episode as intra-continental emergence. Restricted the countries field to Madagascar [2012-2013] and reclassified the event as re-emergence (novel sequence types in an African sub-region where melioidosis had already been recognized historically), with intra_continental_emergence set to false.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (three adults with risk factors) and livestock (two animal cases)
Event summary: Between 2018 and 2021, Southern Africa documented an emergence cluster of three human and two animal melioidosis cases in South Africa and Namibia, with whole‑genome sequencing showing substantial diversity among B. pseudomallei isolates and supporting long‑term regional persistence. The episode unfolded as sporadic but clinically severe infections in persons with diabetes and other risk factors and in livestock, all initially unexpected because melioidosis had not previously been recognized in Southern Africa. Following these detections, the event stabilized into sporadic recognized cases with calls for enhanced environmental sampling and improved diagnostic capacity rather than a continuous high‑incidence outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: improved clinical awareness and reference laboratory support leading to identification of a pathogen that likely had been underdiagnosed; regional climatic and land‑use conditions conducive to B. pseudomallei survival; and common risk factors such as diabetes and hazardous alcohol use. Internal mechanisms: phylogenomic analyses indicate diverse B. pseudomallei lineages of Asian origin have become established in Southern Africa, reflecting geographic range expansion and long‑term environmental adaptation rather than a single recently introduced epidemic clone.
Review: Review – Retain and keep coded as intra-continental emergence. Prior African human cases and environmental detections were in other sub-regions (principally Eastern and Western Africa), whereas these are the first confirmed human and ovine cases from Southern Africa (South Africa and Namibia), representing spread into a new UN African sub-region. Countries were slightly standardized to “South Africa [2018-2021]; Namibia [2019]”; sources are appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (three adults with comorbidities)
Event summary: From July 2020 through 2023, three adults living near the Mississippi Gulf Coast developed severe melioidosis without travel to endemic countries, and B. pseudomallei with near‑identical genomes was isolated from both patients and nearby household soil and water, confirming local environmental establishment. The cluster unfolded over several years with each patient presenting with acute sepsis or pneumonia, prompting extensive epidemiologic and environmental investigations by CDC and state partners. After confirmation that B. pseudomallei is now endemic in the Mississippi Gulf Coast, public health authorities issued guidance on risk reduction and laboratory biosafety; additional locally acquired cases remain possible, but no large outbreak has yet been detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: suitable subtropical climate and soil conditions in the U.S. Gulf Coast that favor B. pseudomallei survival, combined with likely historical introduction via trade or movement from the Caribbean or Central/South America and underlying host risk factors such as diabetes and chronic disease. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion and documented environmental establishment of a distinct local strain (GCS2020) of B. pseudomallei in continental North America, representing a re-emergence of the pathogen within a continent where sporadic autochthonous cases had already been suspected.
Review: Review – Retain event but refine emergence coding and countries. Because earlier likely autochthonous cases in the continental United States (for example in Texas) had been described before 2020, the Mississippi cluster does not represent first or intra-continental emergence; instead it is best viewed as re-emergence in a previously affected sub-region, now with confirmed environmental establishment of a distinct local strain. Updated intra_continental_emergence to false, re_emergence to true, and standardized the countries field to “United States of America [2020-2023].”
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (four adults/children, at least two deaths)
Event summary: Between March and July 2021, four U.S. residents in Kansas, Texas, Minnesota and Georgia developed severe melioidosis with no travel to endemic regions, and genomic analyses showed their B. pseudomallei isolates were nearly identical, indicating a common source. The investigation progressed over several months until CDC detected the outbreak strain in a bottle of Better Homes & Gardens aromatherapy room spray imported from India found in the Georgia patient’s home, leading to a nationwide product recall and recognition of a novel consumer‑product exposure route. Once the contaminated aromatherapy line was withdrawn and households were advised on safe disposal and decontamination, no further linked cases were identified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: globalization of consumer products, with contamination of an imported aromatherapy spray manufactured in a melioidosis‑endemic country; use of the product in homes leading to inhalational or contact exposure in persons without travel history; and limited initial clinical suspicion in non‑endemic U.S. states. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by a single B. pseudomallei strain introduced via a manufactured product (novel exposure pathway), but there is no evidence of enhanced virulence or sustained environmental establishment from this source in the affected U.S. states.
Review: Review – Retain this as a major, widely documented outbreak illustrating a novel exposure route. Because transmission resulted from a contaminated imported consumer product with no evidence of onward environmental establishment in the United States, classification as a re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region (rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate. The countries field was simplified to “United States of America [2021]” to match the country list; otherwise the event description and sources are suitable.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Poultry slaughterhouse workers (abattoir employees, truck driver and maintenance mechanic) exposed to infected chickens or turkeys
Event summary: In 1990, occupational health authorities in western France investigated clusters of influenza‑like illness and atypical pneumonia among employees of a poultry abattoir and identified slaughterhouse exposure to aerosols from chlamydia‑infected chickens and turkeys as the likely source. Serologic testing of the workforce found 18 of 56 employees with evidence of recent Chlamydia psittaci infection, including six workers with pneumonia and four who required hospitalisation, prompting targeted antibiotic treatment and control measures in the plant. The outbreak subsided after medical management, improvements in hygiene and ventilation, and modifications to evisceration practices, with no evidence that sustained transmission occurred beyond the abattoir.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑throughput indoor poultry slaughter and evisceration with inadequate engineering controls, aerosol generation during gutting and defeathering, and limited early recognition of psittacosis risk in abattoir workers, resulting in prolonged unprotected exposure. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or altered virulence was reported; available data are consistent with exposure‑driven re‑occurrence of endemic C. psittaci in a high‑risk occupational setting rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New high‑impact occupational outbreak added. In 1990 a poultry abattoir in western France experienced psittacosis among 18 of 56 tested workers (six pneumonias, four hospitalisations) based on summaries in a systematic review of human psittacosis outbreaks; this size places it among the more substantial post‑1990 events. Classified as re‑occurrence in an already affected Western European subregion, with France correctly mapped to Western Europe. Because most numerical details are derived from secondary summaries rather than the original Goupil et al. report, a subject‑matter expert should verify final case counts and plant location against the primary paper before finalising the Excel sheet.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [1995] (Georgia; Florida bird distributor)
Host: Humans in households that purchased infected pet birds (parakeets, cockatiels, finches and other small birds) from Atlanta‑area pet stores supplied by a single Florida distributor
Event summary: In August 1995, a veterinarian in Georgia reported a dead pet bird with avian chlamydiosis, and tracing showed that more than 700 birds from a Florida distributor had been shipped to nine Atlanta‑area pet stores, after which several recent purchasers developed febrile respiratory illness. Follow‑up of 114 exposed households identified 46 persons among 428 exposed who met a clinical definition for psittacosis, and epidemiologic investigation plus serology confirmed a large outbreak linked to recently purchased psittacine and passerine birds from the infected shipment. Removal or treatment of infected birds, quarantine and record‑keeping measures under the Georgia Bird Dealer Licensing Act, and public health advisories to clinicians and bird owners were implemented, after which no additional outbreak‑related human cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large‑scale interstate trade in mixed‑species pet birds with minimal quarantine, limited infection control and record‑keeping in retail pet shops, and intense household contact with stressed, shedding birds shortly after transport. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci genotype or resistance phenotype was reported; the outbreak reflects amplification of endemic strains in commercial bird supply chains rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: review – Added as a major 1995 U.S. household outbreak, with 46 clinically defined psittacosis cases among 428 exposed persons linked to a shipment of >700 infected pet birds sold through nine Atlanta‑area pet shops. This event clearly ranks among the most impactful modern psittacosis outbreaks by case count and is well documented in primary sources; it is appropriately classified as re‑occurrence in Northern America. Final subdivision of cases into confirmed versus probable, and any small discrepancies in the exact number of affected households, should be checked against Moroney et al. (1998) and the Georgia Epidemiology Report when constructing the Excel table.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (visitors, staff and student interns) exposed to psittacine and other birds in an indoor commercial bird park
Event summary: In late 2001, public health authorities in Matsue City, Shimane Prefecture, Japan, detected several cases of severe atypical pneumonia among staff, student interns and visitors associated with an indoor bird park, and epidemiologic investigation implicated exposure to ill birds housed under closed‑air‑circulation conditions. Seventeen human psittacosis cases (12 visitors, three staff, two students) were confirmed serologically, most with radiographic pneumonia and many requiring hospitalisation, and environmental testing demonstrated C. psittaci DNA in fecal samples from multiple aviary cages. The bird park was temporarily closed, ill birds were isolated or culled and housing conditions were modified, after which no further human cases linked to the park were detected and operations later resumed under strengthened biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very high densities of exotic birds kept in enclosed hothouses with recirculating air, use of dehumidifiers and high‑pressure water sprays that aerosolised contaminated fecal material, absence of quarantine or veterinary oversight for imported birds, and lack of respiratory protection for staff and visitors. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain was described; outbreak behaviour was compatible with re‑occurrence of endemic C. psittaci genotypes under unusually conducive environmental and husbandry conditions.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the largest documented psittacosis outbreak in Japan, with 17 confirmed human cases linked to an indoor bird park in Matsue in winter 2001–2002. Country (Japan), continent (Asia), subregion (Eastern Asia), timing and exposure setting all match the primary outbreak report, and classification as a re‑occurrence (not first detection or inter‑continental spread) is appropriate given the long‑standing recognition of psittacosis in Japan. No corrections beyond verification of details were needed.

Host: Humans exposed to free‑ranging wild parrots and other birds in peri‑urban residential settings
Event summary: From March to June 2002, clinicians in the Blue Mountains district of New South Wales, Australia, noted an unusual surge of community‑acquired pneumonia among residents that was eventually linked to exposure to dead and free‑ranging wild birds, particularly parrots, around homes. Among 95 suspected cases, 59 patients had serologic evidence of acute C. psittaci infection and many required hospitalisation, with residence in the upper Blue Mountains, direct contact with wild birds, and lawn mowing without a grass catcher identified as strong risk factors in a case‑control study. The outbreak waned with the onset of colder winter weather, community advisories about avoiding contact with dead birds and using respiratory protection during high‑exposure outdoor activities, and no further large clusters were detected in the area once the event resolved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high local abundance and mortality of free‑ranging parrots and other wild birds in a forested peri‑urban area, frequent human contact with bird carcasses and droppings, and aerosolisation of contaminated material during lawn mowing and other yard work; limited baseline awareness of psittacosis risk in an endemic region also delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: there was no evidence of a novel genotype; epidemiologic patterns are consistent with geographic and intensity‑based range expansion of an endemic strain rather than genetic change, supporting classification as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This row accurately describes the large 2002 Blue Mountains outbreak (59 serologically supported cases) documented in Emerging Infectious Diseases and subsequent Australian work on endemic psittacosis. Continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence in an area with known psittacosis fits the definitions. No substantive corrections were required.

Host: Humans exposed to wild and domestic birds (particularly at garden bird feeders) in community settings, with some evidence of secondary transmission
Event summary: From 12 January to 9 April 2013, southern Sweden experienced an unusual increase in psittacosis notifications, with 25 cases detected—about three times the mean winter incidence in the previous decade—drawing renewed attention to psittacosis as a cause of atypical pneumonia. A matched case–control study found that cases were much more likely than controls to have cleaned wild‑bird feeders or otherwise been heavily exposed to wild‑bird droppings, and a separate investigation described a severe index case who appears to have transmitted infection to multiple close contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, indicating both strong environmental and limited human‑to‑human components. The spike in cases declined as the winter–spring season ended and targeted public‑health messaging on safe bird feeding and clinical awareness was implemented, with national incidence returning toward lower endemic levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal congregation of wild birds at garden feeders, frequent cleaning of heavily contaminated feeders by householders, and close contact with domestic birds in a temperate Northern European setting; increased clinician awareness and diagnostic testing during and after the outbreak likely amplified case detection. Internal mechanisms: while person‑to‑person transmission was documented from at least one severe index case, molecular data did not clearly implicate a novel, more transmissible strain; the event is best interpreted as an exposure‑driven re‑occurrence with rare secondary spread, rather than a re‑emergence of a new lineage.
Review: review – Retained as one of the larger modern psittacosis outbreaks (25 cases in southern Sweden with strong links to wild‑bird feeders and evidence of limited human‑to‑human spread). The original LLM row correctly captured size, timing, exposures, and classification as re‑occurrence, but relied mainly on a later case‑control paper; a dedicated 2013 Eurosurveillance outbreak report has now been added to the event‑level sources to better document case counts and risk factors. No changes to geography or emergence type were needed, yet the row is flagged for review so that final case numbers and the balance between environmental and secondary transmission can be cross‑checked directly against the Swedish outbreak reports when populating the Excel sheet.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (poultry slaughter‑plant workers) exposed to infected chickens and contaminated aerosols on processing lines
Event summary: During August–September 2018, clusters of severe respiratory illness and pneumonia among workers at two large chicken slaughter plants in Virginia and Georgia led to investigation by state health departments and CDC, ultimately identifying 82 employees who met a probable or confirmed psittacosis case definition, including 13 with C. psittaci infection confirmed by real‑time PCR. Most confirmed cases had radiologically verified pneumonia, high hospitalisation rates, and a small number required intensive care, and the outbreak was linked to intense exposure to infected chickens and aerosols generated during evisceration and further processing on fast, crowded production lines supplied by shared source farms. After plant‑level interventions—including temporary line slow‑downs, improved ventilation and sanitation, enhanced respiratory protection and clinical evaluation for workers, and sustained public‑health follow‑up—no further outbreak‑related cases were detected and national psittacosis surveillance in the United States returned to baseline levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive industrial poultry production with high bird throughput, close worker proximity to infected carcasses and contaminated aerosols, suboptimal respiratory protection and diagnostic suspicion before the outbreak was recognised, and structural factors that favoured rapid within‑plant amplification once C. psittaci entered the production system. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or resistance pattern was reported; molecular and epidemiologic data support classification as a large occupational re‑occurrence in a long‑recognised risk setting rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – The event row has been updated to reflect that this was the largest U.S. psittacosis outbreak in three decades, with 82 workers meeting probable/confirmed case definitions and 13 PCR‑confirmed infections across two poultry plants in Virginia and Georgia, as documented in both the Emerging Infectious Diseases article and a subsequent MMWR analysis. Country and subregion coding (United States, Northern America) and classification as a re‑occurrence are correct. Because the original summary understated the outbreak size, the revised text and numbers should be carefully aligned with CDC reports when finalising the Excel dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans with psittacosis (many with pneumonia) exposed mainly to wild birds and their droppings around garden bird feeders, with some cases linked to domestic psittacine birds
Event summary: Between November 2018 and March 2019, Sweden recorded an unusually high number of psittacosis cases, with around 60 notifications—several times higher than typical winter seasons over the preceding 20 years—predominantly from the southern and western regions of the country. Most affected patients reported direct or indirect exposure to droppings of small wild birds, especially through cleaning or handling garden bird tables and feeders, while a minority of cases were linked to domestic parrots and other captive birds, and many required hospital care for atypical pneumonia. Following public‑health communications advising the public to avoid contact with bird faeces and to take precautions when cleaning feeders, combined with the natural end of the winter wild‑bird feeding season, case numbers declined and the outbreak was declared over by the Public Health Agency of Sweden on 13 March 2019.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread winter feeding of small wild birds in gardens, frequent cleaning and handling of heavily contaminated bird tables and feeders, and heightened diagnostic attention once the signal was recognised, all occurring in a setting where C. psittaci circulates in wild birds; subtle ecological changes in wild‑bird populations may also have increased background infection pressure. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci genotype was reported; the pattern is consistent with an exposure‑ and surveillance‑driven re‑occurrence rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – New Swedish national winter 2018–2019 outbreak (approximately 60 reported cases, largely linked to wild‑bird feeders) added because it clearly exceeds normal seasonal incidence and is documented by both Folkhälsomyndigheten and ECDC. The country and subregion coding (Sweden, Northern Europe) and classification as a re‑occurrence in a country with longstanding psittacosis activity are appropriate. Exact numbers of laboratory‑confirmed versus suspected cases and the regional breakdown should be verified against Swedish surveillance tables before final Excel entry.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (duck slaughter‑ and processing‑plant workers and several close contacts) with severe community‑acquired pneumonia, including multiple human‑to‑human transmission chains
Event summary: In December 2020, a hospital in Shandong Province, China, notified authorities of a cluster of severe community‑acquired pneumonia among workers from a duck slaughter and processing plant and some of their close contacts, and metagenomic next‑generation sequencing together with PCR identified Chlamydia psittaci as the causative agent. Detailed field investigation documented 22 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, eight of whom developed severe pneumonia and one of whom died, with evidence of multiple person‑to‑person transmission chains in addition to intense primary exposure to infected ducks and contaminated aerosols in crowded indoor processing areas. After closure of the implicated plant, antibiotic treatment and quarantine of exposed workers and close contacts, and strengthened surveillance in the region, no further transmission was detected and the outbreak was considered contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large‑scale intensive duck production with high bacterial loads on carcasses, inadequate early respiratory protection, crowded indoor workstations enabling both zoonotic exposure and spread between workers, and delayed recognition of psittacosis as an etiology of severe pneumonia. Internal mechanisms: outbreak investigations showed the same C. psittaci genotype infecting multiple patients but did not conclusively demonstrate novel virulence determinants; the efficient human‑to‑human spread observed under very high‑exposure conditions suggests enhanced transmission potential yet, at present, is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence within an existing zoonotic system rather than a distinct re‑emergent lineage.
Review: review – New large 2020 outbreak in Shandong Province, China (22 confirmed cases, eight severe, one death, with well‑documented person‑to‑person transmission among duck‑plant workers and their contacts) added as one of the most impactful recent psittacosis episodes. Coding as Eastern Asia (China) and classification as re‑occurrence in a region with pre‑existing C. psittaci circulation are appropriate. Because numerical and some clinical details are synthesised from several English‑language summaries of the original Chinese investigations, national experts should confirm final case counts, case definitions and inferred transmission chains before the event is locked into the Excel dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Austria [2023]; Denmark [2023]; Germany [2023]; Sweden [2023]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2023]
Host: Humans with psittacosis, most with pneumonia, exposed mainly to wild birds and pet birds in community settings across multiple European countries
Event summary: From early 2023 through at least February 2024, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands reported through the EU Early Warning and Response System an unusual and unexpected increase in human psittacosis cases, with numbers rising sharply from November–December 2023 and five deaths recorded, prompting a WHO Disease Outbreak News notification. National investigations found that most affected patients had recent exposure to wild or domestic birds (often via garden bird feeders or hobby poultry) rather than to each other, and no common cross‑border point source or evidence of sustained human‑to‑human transmission or spread beyond Europe was identified, although many cases required hospitalisation for pneumonia. By late winter 2024, reported case numbers began to decline, and WHO and EU agencies assessed the overall public‑health risk as low while recommending continued surveillance, veterinary investigations in wild and domestic birds, and targeted risk communication on zoonotic transmission routes and timely antibiotic treatment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased seasonal exposure to infected wild and domestic birds across several Northern and Western European countries, including heavy use of garden bird feeders, possible underlying changes in avian population dynamics and infection prevalence, and enhanced clinical awareness and molecular testing once the multi‑country signal was detected; improvements in surveillance sensitivity may have amplified the apparent increase. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci variant has been implicated, and available evidence favours interpretation of this event as a regional re‑occurrence of psittacosis amplified by environmental and surveillance factors rather than emergence of a fundamentally new strain.
Review: retain – This multi‑country 2023–2024 European event is correctly represented as a substantial regional re‑occurrence involving at least five EU/EEA countries, with over a hundred reported cases and five deaths, and no evidence of sustained inter‑continental spread or primarily human‑to‑human transmission. Country list, subregions (Northern and Western Europe) and timing are consistent with WHO’s Disease Outbreak News and EU threat assessments, and the emergence‑type classification (re‑occurrence only) matches the definitions. Existing sources adequately document the event, so no further structural corrections are required.

Countries: Argentina [2024] (Buenos Aires Province; Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area)
Host: Humans with severe community‑acquired atypical pneumonia, many ultimately diagnosed with psittacosis and some with known or suspected contact with psittacine birds in urban and peri‑urban settings
Event summary: In March–April 2024, Argentina’s Ministry of Health, through severe acute pneumonia surveillance and intensive‑care networks, detected an increase in severe atypical pneumonia cases in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area and other parts of Buenos Aires Province, and enhanced etiologic investigation revealed an excess of psittacosis diagnoses within this group. National and provincial reports indicated roughly 60 suspected psittacosis cases, around 20 of which were laboratory‑confirmed C. psittaci infections, many in patients with no immediately obvious pet‑bird exposure although background information highlighted ongoing illegal trade and ownership of parrots and other captive birds and prior localised psittacosis clusters in the country. The episode led to epidemiologic alerts, clinical guidance to consider psittacosis in severe community‑acquired pneumonia, and public messaging on avoiding illegal bird trade and practising safe bird handling; as targeted control measures were implemented and winter progressed, case numbers declined and the event was assessed as a limited urban re‑occurrence rather than sustained widespread transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased recognition and systematic investigation of severe community‑acquired pneumonia within sentinel hospitals, in the context of urban and peri‑urban exposure to parrots and other birds (including through illegal wildlife trade and informal keeping), together with social and economic conditions that favour crowded bird‑keeping and limited veterinary oversight. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not implicate a novel genotype or clear change in virulence; the pattern is most consistent with a surveillance‑ and exposure‑driven resurgence of an endemic zoonosis rather than genetic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Retained as a recent, nationally recognised increase in psittacosis cases associated with investigations of severe atypical pneumonia in Buenos Aires Province, with around 60 suspected and approximately 20 laboratory‑confirmed infections according to official Argentine bulletins and contemporaneous reviews. Continent, subregion and country coding (Argentina, South America) and classification as a re‑occurrence fit the historical presence of psittacosis in the region. Because data are still evolving and detailed outbreak analyses are being published, final case counts, geographic spread within Argentina and degree of bird‑exposure documentation should be re‑checked against the most recent national epidemiologic reports before finalising the Excel event row.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (urban residents consuming traditional uneviscerated salted, fermented mullet fish “feseekh/faseikh” purchased in Cairo)
Event summary: In April 1991, Cairo hospitals reported 91 patients with severe paralytic illness and high mortality after eating traditional salted, uneviscerated mullet fish (feseekh), and investigation identified type E botulism with at least 18 deaths, making this the largest recorded type E outbreak and the first documented botulism outbreak in Egypt. The outbreak was traced to commercially prepared feseekh from a single shop, and national authorities rapidly banned sales from the implicated producer, inspected similar establishments, and warned the public against consuming uneviscerated salted fish around the Sham El‑Nessim holiday. Withdrawals of implicated product, strengthened regulation of salted‑fish production, and recurring seasonal risk‑communication campaigns ended the episode but did not fully eliminate recurrent, smaller fesikh‑associated outbreaks in later years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: mass seasonal consumption of feseekh during a spring holiday; use of uneviscerated fish stored for prolonged periods under warm, anaerobic, and often putrefactive conditions before salting; inadequate process control and oversight of small commercial producers; and limited public awareness of botulism risk. Internal mechanisms: high‑level production of botulinum neurotoxin type E by nonproteolytic C. botulinum in anaerobic, salted fish tissue; no evidence of a novel strain or host jump, so the event represents an extreme contamination and processing failure of an established pathogen.
Review: Decision: retain. This is a well‑documented, massive type E foodborne botulism outbreak in Cairo with 91 hospitalized patients and 18 deaths, described in a J Infect Dis investigation as the first documented outbreak in Egypt and the largest type E outbreak reported globally; it clearly belongs among the top‑impact human botulism events since 1990. Geography (Africa → Northern Africa → Egypt) and classification as re‑occurrence (long‑established pathogen; failures in traditional fish processing) are appropriate.

Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming potato‑ and eggplant‑based dips at a Greek restaurant in El Paso, Texas)
Event summary: In April 1994, a large restaurant‑associated outbreak of foodborne botulism in El Paso, Texas, affected 30 people after they ate potato‑ and eggplant‑based dips prepared from foil‑wrapped baked potatoes that had been held at room temperature for many hours to days. Epidemiologic investigation and laboratory testing identified botulinum neurotoxin type A in both dips and linked illness strongly to consumption of the potato dip, with four patients requiring mechanical ventilation, making this the largest U.S. botulism outbreak since 1978. Removal of the implicated foods, clinical deployment of antitoxin, and strengthened food‑safety guidance on time–temperature control of foil‑wrapped baked potatoes in commercial kitchens ended the outbreak and informed later U.S. and international prevention messaging.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: improper restaurant food‑handling, specifically leaving foil‑wrapped baked potatoes at ambient temperature for extended periods before incorporating them into cold dips, creating a warm, anaerobic, low‑acid environment ideal for C. botulinum growth and toxin production; gaps in staff training and regulatory enforcement regarding this specific risk. Internal mechanisms: classic proteolytic C. botulinum type A toxin production in a high‑risk food matrix without evidence of new strain characteristics or increased intrinsic virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. The El Paso ‘hazardous baked potato’ outbreak is a well‑characterized event with 30 cases and four ventilated patients, described as the largest U.S. botulism outbreak since 1978; it reasonably qualifies as one of the highest‑impact human botulism episodes globally in the 1990–present period. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are correct; only minor textual refinements (explicit case count and state) were added.

Host: Humans (schoolchildren in a rural residential school in Gujarat consuming a gram‑flour snack, sevu, stored at ambient temperature)
Event summary: In September 1996, 34 of roughly 310 pupils in a residential school in rural Gujarat, India, developed acute neuroparalytic symptoms compatible with botulism after eating several common foods, with epidemiologic and microbiological investigation implicating an improperly stored fried gram‑flour snack, sevu, as the likely vehicle. Toxigenic Clostridium butyricum capable of producing type E botulinum neurotoxin was isolated from leftover sevu and patient specimens, making this the first recognized large outbreak of type E botulism in India and a rare example of human foodborne botulism caused by a species other than C. botulinum. Intensified clinical care, withdrawal of suspect snack batches, and national alerts on safe storage of fried snacks brought the episode under control, and the event spurred debate and further research on neurotoxigenic C. butyricum as an emerging cause of botulism.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: mass catering of sevu in a boarding school, with bulk preparation and prolonged storage of a moist, fried gram‑flour product in inadequately ventilated containers at ambient temperatures; limited awareness among school staff of botulism risks from non‑canned foods. Internal mechanisms: emergence of neurotoxigenic C. butyricum producing type E toxin in human foodborne disease in India, representing a strain‑level change within the broader botulism complex rather than altered host or geography for C. botulinum sensu stricto.
Review: Decision: review. This is a large and influential outbreak (34 affected students, several deaths reported in some sources) linked to sevu contaminated with neurotoxigenic Clostridium butyricum type E and is widely cited as the first recognized foodborne botulism outbreak in India. However, the causative organism is C. butyricum rather than C. botulinum sensu stricto, and some official reviews note incomplete clinical confirmation; therefore inclusion under the species‑specific EPP “Clostridium botulinum” should be decided by project leads. Classification has been set to re‑emergence (novel toxigenic species/strain causing human botulism in this region) rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (consumers of rotten poultry and a processed meat product, ‘kashir’ sausage, in Algeria)
Event summary: In July 1998, reports from Algeria described a very large outbreak of suspected foodborne botulism affecting approximately 1,400 people, including at least 17 deaths, after consumption of rotten poultry and a processed meat sausage known as kashir. Contemporary summaries attributed illness to botulinum toxin produced in severely decomposed poultry and kashir that had been stored and sold without effective refrigeration or process controls, although detailed microbiologic characterization and toxin typing were not widely published. Emergency removal of implicated products from markets, public health warnings about consuming suspect poultry and sausages, and tightened oversight of small meat processors brought the explosive episode to an end.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread distribution and consumption of decomposed poultry and kashir from inadequately regulated producers, with profound temperature abuse and possible post‑processing contamination in the retail chain; limited enforcement of basic hygiene and cold‑chain standards in parts of the meat sector. Internal mechanisms: presumed classic botulinum neurotoxin production in anaerobic pockets of spoiled meat, but toxin type and precise clostridial species are not clearly documented in publicly available reports.
Review: Decision: review. Multiple risk‑assessment compilations cite a July 1998 Algerian outbreak involving approximately 1,400 illnesses and 17 deaths linked to rotten poultry and kashir sausage, based primarily on a ProMED report summarized in technical tables; however, peer‑reviewed clinical and laboratory details are sparse and toxin type is not reported. Because of its extreme reported size, this event is a plausible candidate for inclusion among the most impactful botulism outbreaks, but data quality is lower than for other events; it should be retained provisionally and validated against national or WHO reports if possible.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (villagers in northern Thailand consuming home‑canned bamboo shoots from a 20‑L can)
Event summary: In April 1998, 13 adults from two neighboring villages in northern Thailand developed severe neurologic illness consistent with botulism, including two deaths, after eating home‑canned bamboo shoots from a single 20‑liter galvanized container sold locally. Epidemiologic investigation and toxin testing of food confirmed foodborne type A botulism from inadequately processed low‑acid bamboo shoots, representing the first laboratory‑confirmed botulism outbreak reported in Thailand and prompting a provincial ban on remaining cans and public education about safe canning and reheating. Although modest in size compared with later Thai events, the outbreak served as an early warning about the risks of home‑canned bamboo shoots and led to strengthened control of home canning before a much larger 2006 outbreak in the same province.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: informal commercial production of low‑acid bamboo shoots in large, home‑made containers, with only boiling at atmospheric pressure before sealing and long‑term storage at ambient temperature; lack of acidification and pressure canning, limited producer awareness of botulism risks, and minimal regulatory oversight of small‑scale canning. Internal mechanisms: typical proteolytic C. botulinum type A spores surviving inadequate heat treatment, then germinating and producing toxin in an anaerobic, low‑acid environment.
Review: Decision: review. The 1998 Nan Province bamboo‑shoot outbreak (13 cases, 2 deaths) is accurately described here and was historically important as Thailand’s first lab‑confirmed botulism outbreak, but it is much smaller than the massive 2006 Nan outbreak (209 cases) and multiple other global events. With the addition of the 2006 Thai event, this 1998 episode is unlikely to remain among the ten most impactful post‑1990 outbreaks and could be excluded if a strict top‑10 size criterion is enforced; it may be retained if the project values country‑level firsts.
Review Comment: Not top 10

Host: Humans (residents of Casablanca and other areas consuming commercially produced mortadella sausage)
Event summary: In August 1999, Morocco experienced a major epidemic of foodborne botulism centred in Casablanca, where consumption of a contaminated commercial mortadella‑type sausage led to dozens of cases of flaccid paralysis and multiple deaths. Clinical series describe around 15 confirmed cases among 45 highly suspect patients with toxin type B detected, while food‑safety compilations cite up to 78 cases and approximately 20 deaths linked to mortadella from a single factory, making this one of the most lethal post‑1990 botulism outbreaks. National authorities seized large quantities of suspect sausage, closed the implicated facility, and intensified meat‑processing inspection and consumer warnings, which gradually ended the outbreak and reshaped botulism risk management for cured meat products in Morocco.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: industrial production of low‑acid cured sausage with inadequate heat treatment, salt/nitrite control, or hygiene, allowing survival and outgrowth of C. botulinum spores; wide distribution of a single contaminated product lot; limited early clinical recognition in a setting with little prior botulism experience. Internal mechanisms: classic proteolytic C. botulinum type B toxin production in a moist meat matrix, without evidence of a novel strain, so the event reflects a severe but conventional processing failure.
Review: Decision: retain. The 1999 Moroccan mortadella‑associated outbreak is a large, high‑fatality episode (on the order of several dozen cases and around 20 deaths) documented in clinical series and international food‑safety reviews, and ranks among the most severe modern botulism outbreaks linked to a commercial meat product. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate; case numbers in the literature vary, so they are described qualitatively and should be revisited if national surveillance data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural villagers attending a religious event and eating home‑canned bamboo shoots in Nan Province)
Event summary: From 15–26 March 2006, a massive outbreak of foodborne botulism struck Nan Province in northern Thailand, when home‑canned bamboo shoots served at a religious ceremony caused illness in 209 villagers, 134 of whom were hospitalized and 42 required mechanical ventilation. Investigations confirmed botulinum neurotoxin type A from contaminated bamboo shoots produced in unregulated home canneries, and shortages of antitoxin required urgent international mobilization of heptavalent antitoxin stocks. Emergency prohibition of the implicated bamboo‑shoot product, intensified regulation of home‑canned foods, and nationwide education on boiling and safely sourcing bamboo shoots ended the outbreak and led to creation of regional mechanisms for antitoxin sharing and botulism surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large‑scale informal production and sale of low‑acid bamboo shoots canned without pressure‑cooker sterilization, stored for long periods at ambient temperatures, and served in bulk at community gatherings; lack of enforcement of canning standards and limited awareness of botulism risks in rural areas. Internal mechanisms: high‑level proliferation of proteolytic C. botulinum type A in inadequately processed bamboo shoots; no new strain properties were reported, so the event reflects extreme exposure to a known hazard in a vulnerable food system.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2006 Nan Province bamboo‑shoot outbreak (209 cases, 42 ventilated) is one of the largest laboratory‑confirmed foodborne botulism outbreaks ever documented and had major implications for international antitoxin logistics and food‑safety policy in Thailand; it clearly belongs in any top‑10 list of impactful human botulism events after 1990. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate.

Host: Humans (adult consumers in the United States and Canada drinking commercially produced refrigerated carrot juice)
Event summary: In September–October 2006, an international outbreak of severe foodborne botulism was identified in the United States (Georgia, Florida) and Canada among adults who drank a commercially produced, pasteurized carrot juice that was inadequately refrigerated after purchase. Investigations confirmed botulinum neurotoxin type A in leftover juice and linked at least six severe cases—four in the United States and two in Canada, several requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation—to consumption of juice from specific lots, prompting recalls and consumer warnings in both countries. Regulatory actions, product reformulation and labeling changes, and public advisories on continuous refrigeration of low‑acid juices ended the outbreak and shaped subsequent risk‑assessment and guidance for minimally processed refrigerated beverages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: commercialization and wide distribution of a low‑acid vegetable juice that must remain refrigerated, combined with temperature abuse along the cold chain in retail and home storage and limited early regulatory guidance for such products. Internal mechanisms: growth and toxin production by proteolytic C. botulinum type A(B) in an anaerobic, low‑acid juice kept at permissive temperatures; strain characterization showed no unusual virulence traits, confirming that processing and handling failures rather than pathogen evolution drove the event.
Review: Decision: review. The carrot‑juice outbreak had only six cases but was highly influential for regulation of refrigerated low‑acid beverages and is one of the few modern botulism events prompting activation of a CDC emergency operations response. It is therefore impactful in a policy sense but remains small compared with large outbreaks in Thailand, Egypt, Morocco, Russia, and major U.S. outbreaks in Ohio 2015 and Mississippi 2016. Retain if the project incorporates regulatory impact alongside case counts; otherwise it could be deprioritized in a strict top‑10 by size.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (dinner guests consuming a commercially produced ground green‑olive tapenade in southeastern France)
Event summary: In 2008, a cluster of botulism cases occurred in southeastern France among guests at a private dinner who had eaten a commercial green‑olive tapenade, with five laboratory‑confirmed and several probable cases caused by botulinum neurotoxin type B. Traceback investigations linked illness to a single batch of olive–garlic–capers paste from a small producer, and the event received high media and regulatory attention as an EU example of botulism from a ready‑to‑eat, oil‑rich spread. Rapid recognition, product withdrawal, and EU‑wide risk communication ended the outbreak, and it contributed to European discussions on controlling C. botulinum in minimally processed, low‑acid, oil‑based foods.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: production of a low‑acid, oil‑rich olive spread with inadequate controls for C. botulinum (insufficient heating, acidification, or preservatives), potential post‑processing contamination, and extended shelf‑life with room‑temperature storage; growing consumer demand for artisanal, minimally processed delicatessen products. Internal mechanisms: standard proteolytic C. botulinum type B toxin production in a suitable anaerobic food matrix, without any identified novel strain properties.
Review: Decision: review. This French tapenade outbreak is well‑documented and important for EU risk management of ready‑to‑eat spreads but involved only about five confirmed cases, far fewer than the large African, Asian, and U.S. outbreaks now included. It should be retained only if the dataset aims to cover representative commercial‑product failures across regions regardless of size; otherwise it is a candidate for exclusion from a top‑10 impact‑based list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (adult attendees at a church potluck; many women and older adults)
Event summary: In April 2015, a large outbreak of foodborne botulism occurred among attendees of a church potluck in Lancaster, Ohio, after they ate potato salad prepared with improperly home‑canned potatoes processed in a boiling‑water bath. Among 77 persons who ate potluck food, 29 developed clinically compatible type A botulism, making this one of the largest U.S. outbreaks in decades; many required ICU care and mechanical ventilation, and one person died. Identification and recall of the implicated home‑canned potatoes, rapid antitoxin deployment, and extensive media coverage ended the outbreak and triggered renewed national outreach on safe home‑canning practices.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unsafe home‑canning of low‑acid potatoes using a boiling‑water bath rather than a pressure canner, possible failure to follow tested recipes, storage of jars at room temperature, and use of the contents in a large communal dish; low awareness of botulism risk in church and home‑preserving communities. Internal mechanisms: typical type A botulinum toxin production by proteolytic C. botulinum in an anaerobic, low‑acid, home‑canned vegetable; no evidence of novel strain traits.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2015 Ohio church‑potluck outbreak (29 cases, 1 death) is documented by CDC as one of the largest U.S. foodborne botulism outbreaks since 1978 and is prominent in modern epidemiologic summaries. It clearly belongs among the top‑impact events by case count and severity; geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate.

Countries: United States of America (Mississippi federal prison) [2016]
Host: Humans (incarcerated men consuming prison‑made illicit alcohol, “pruno” or “hooch” containing potatoes)
Event summary: In June 2016, a large outbreak of foodborne botulism occurred in a medium‑security federal correctional institution in Mississippi after inmates drank illicitly brewed alcohol (“pruno”) made with potatoes and other ingredients fermented in sealed plastic bags. Public‑health investigation identified 31 suspected, probable, or confirmed botulism patients linked to a single batch, several of whom required intensive care and antitoxin, representing the largest U.S. foodborne botulism outbreak of the 2001–2017 period. Removal of remaining pruno, restrictions on ingredients such as potatoes, and inmate and staff education halted the outbreak and led to tighter prison policies that have since reduced, though not eliminated, recurrence of pruno‑associated botulism.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: preparation of illicit alcohol in sealed plastic bags with starchy, low‑acid ingredients (including potatoes) and prolonged warm fermentation under strictly anaerobic conditions; social and structural factors in prisons that encourage shared consumption and hinder timely medical care; limited pre‑existing awareness of botulism risk from pruno despite earlier, smaller outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: conventional C. botulinum toxin production in an anaerobic, nutrient‑rich slurry; no evidence of new toxin variants or increased virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. With 31 affected inmates, this Mississippi prison pruno outbreak is one of the largest documented foodborne botulism outbreaks in recent U.S. history and a key example of behavior‑ and environment‑driven resurgence; it is appropriate to include among the top‑impact global events. The geographic coding and classification as re‑occurrence are correct.

Host: Humans (community adults purchasing ready‑to‑eat nacho cheese from a gas‑station market dispenser)
Event summary: From mid‑April to early May 2017, a serious outbreak of foodborne botulism occurred in Sacramento County, California, among customers who ate nacho cheese sauce dispensed from a warm‑holding dispenser at a gas‑station market. Ten patients with laboratory‑confirmed type A botulism were identified, nine of whom required mechanical ventilation and one of whom died, making it the largest known foodborne botulism outbreak in California. Environmental and laboratory investigations found botulinum toxin and C. botulinum in cheese sauce bags, and improper holding times and temperatures and extended use of an opened bag were implicated; public‑health orders to stop sales, recall implicated lots, and issue statewide alerts terminated the outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: prolonged use and inadequate temperature control of a bagged, commercially produced cheese sauce in a retail setting, including leaving an opened bag in a dispenser for extended periods and failure to follow manufacturer instructions on discard times and hot‑holding temperatures; insufficient staff training and oversight. Internal mechanisms: typical proteolytic C. botulinum type A growth and toxin production in anaerobic, nutrient‑rich cheese sauce under suboptimal hot‑holding conditions.
Review: Decision: review. Although the California nacho‑cheese outbreak involved only 10 confirmed cases, it had very high severity (90% ventilated, 1 death) and is widely cited as a major commercial‑product failure. It is smaller than several other events now included (e.g., Thailand 2006, Egypt 1991 and 2019, Morocco 1999, Russia 2024, U.S. Ohio 2015, Mississippi 2016), so its inclusion in a strict top‑10 by case count is debatable; it should be retained if severity and product type diversity are valued alongside size.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (San Diego County, California) [2017-2018]
Host: Humans (people who inject drugs, primarily black‑tar heroin users via subcutaneous or intramuscular injection)
Event summary: Between September 2017 and May 2018, San Diego County, California, experienced a prolonged outbreak of wound botulism among people who injected black‑tar heroin, many via ‘skin‑popping’ or intramuscular injection. Public‑health surveillance identified at least 13 confirmed wound botulism cases with typical neurologic signs and laboratory evidence of botulinum neurotoxin, all reporting recent black‑tar heroin injection and no shared food exposures. Intensive clinical alerts, harm‑reduction outreach, and education for people who use drugs and clinicians, along with prompt access to antitoxin, facilitated early recognition and treatment of additional cases and contributed to a decline in incidence after mid‑2018, although sporadic wound botulism continues to occur in association with black‑tar heroin in western North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread use of black‑tar heroin and injection practices (particularly skin‑popping and intramuscular injection) that introduce spores from the environment or contaminated drug supply into devitalized tissue under anaerobic conditions; limited access to sterile injection equipment and wound care; and ongoing circulation of contaminated heroin lots. Internal mechanisms: colonization of wounds by C. botulinum with in situ production of neurotoxin; no evidence of new toxin types or increased intrinsic virulence, so the outbreak reflects behavioral and drug‑market changes rather than microbial evolution.
Review: Decision: review. This San Diego black‑tar heroin–associated wound botulism cluster (≥13 cases) is one of the larger wound botulism outbreaks reported and is epidemiologically important for the growing injection‑drug–linked botulism burden. However, in terms of total case numbers it is still smaller than several massive foodborne outbreaks now included. It should be retained if the dataset aims to represent all major transmission routes (foodborne and wound); otherwise it could be deprioritized in a strictly size‑focused top‑10.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (residents of five Lower Egypt governorates consuming traditional fermented salted fish ‘feseekh’ during a celebratory period)
Event summary: On 24 September 2019, Egyptian authorities investigated a large‑scale botulism outbreak in five Lower Egypt governorates after 92 people developed neurologic or gastrointestinal illness following consumption of feseekh, a traditional fermented salted fish dish associated with the Sham El‑Nessim holiday. Case‑series review and field investigation linked illness to feseekh from informal producers and street vendors that had been prepared under warm, anaerobic conditions, echoing the earlier catastrophic Cairo 1991 outbreak but with lower mortality thanks to quicker recognition and supportive care. Product seizures, intensified seasonal warnings against unsafe feseekh, and targeted public‑health campaigns in affected governorates brought the outbreak under control and informed ongoing risk‑mapping and prevention planning for fesikh‑associated botulism in Egypt.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued popular consumption of uneviscerated, salt‑fermented fish prepared outside regulated factories; warm ambient temperatures and anaerobic storage conditions that favor toxin production; economic and cultural incentives to purchase cheaper, informally produced feseekh; and incomplete adherence to long‑standing Ministry of Health warnings. Internal mechanisms: type E botulinum neurotoxin production by C. botulinum in traditional salted fish; no new strain or host changes were documented, so this represents recurrent exposure to a known high‑risk practice.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2019 Lower Egypt feseekh‑associated outbreak (92 cases across five governorates) is a large, multi‑governorate botulism event directly linked to a well‑known high‑risk traditional food and explicitly framed in the literature as a ‘large‑scale outbreak’. It ranks among the major global botulism episodes by case count and geographic spread and complements the earlier Cairo 1991 outbreak in illustrating persistent fesikh‑related risk; geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate.

Host: Humans (general population consuming home‑preserved and small‑scale commercially prepared foods, including canned mushrooms, fish, and ready‑to‑eat salads)
Event summary: In 2024, the Russian Federation reported a dramatic surge in botulism cases across multiple regions, with national officials indicating that approximately 415 people had been affected and several had died, many linked to home‑preserved mushrooms and vegetables, fish products, and a widely distributed ready‑to‑eat salad brand. Media and official statements highlighted large clusters associated with bottled salads produced by a meal‑delivery company and marinated mushrooms sold through retail and online channels, raising serious concerns about food‑safety compliance among small producers and delivery platforms. Intensified inspections, seizure of over 170–200 tonnes of high‑risk products, temporary bans and recalls of implicated foods, and broad public warnings on safe home preservation and avoidance of unregulated canned goods were implemented, and incident reports declined later in the year as these measures took effect.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread domestic and small‑scale commercial canning of low‑acid foods (especially mushrooms and vegetables) with inconsistent application of modern processing standards; growth of online and app‑based food‑delivery businesses that may lack robust food‑safety management; economic pressures pushing consumers toward cheaper, informally produced preserves; and uneven regulatory enforcement across regions. Internal mechanisms: standard C. botulinum toxin production in improperly processed and stored low‑acid canned foods and ready‑to‑eat dishes; no clear evidence of new strain emergence, so the surge appears driven by socio‑economic and regulatory factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2024 Russia‑wide surge, with roughly 400–415 reported cases and multiple multi‑region clusters, is by far the largest recent national botulism event and had substantial public‑health and regulatory impact; it clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful modern botulism emergence/re‑occurrence episodes. Geography (Europe → Eastern Europe → Russian Federation) matches the UNSD classification used in the project, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate because the pathogen was long established and the drivers are food‑system and regulatory failures rather than geographic spread into a new continent.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2003]
Host: Humans (injecting drug users, mainly heroin users injecting subcutaneously or intramuscularly)
Event summary: From mid‑2003 through 2004 the United Kingdom detected an unusual national cluster of non‑neonatal tetanus almost entirely among people injecting heroin, with around 25 confirmed cases distributed across several regions. Many patients presented with severe generalized tetanus requiring intensive care and at least two deaths were reported, and investigations highlighted that most affected injecting drug users had never completed a primary tetanus vaccination course. After alerts to clinicians, targeted vaccination offers to people who inject drugs and harm‑reduction messaging about avoiding "skin‑popping" and seeking post‑injury care, the number of new tetanus cases in this group declined and the outbreak was considered over by 2004–2005.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑risk injecting practices among people who inject drugs (particularly subcutaneous or intramuscular "skin‑popping" of heroin), likely contamination of one or more heroin batches with soil‑borne C. tetani spores along the distribution chain, and very low coverage with basic tetanus immunization in this marginalized population. Internal mechanisms: No evidence that novel C. tetani genotypes, antimicrobial resistance, or increased virulence were involved; the outbreak reflects increased exposure via contaminated drugs and host immunity gaps rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review: Newly added to capture the ≈25‑case outbreak of tetanus among injecting drug users in the United Kingdom during 2003–2004, which is documented in BMJ, Eurosurveillance and later reviews; geography (Europe, Northern Europe; UK) and coding as a re-occurrence in an already endemic region are appropriate, but exact case counts and deaths should be cross‑checked against national surveillance summaries if greater precision is needed.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC546055/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (mainly adult tsunami survivors with traumatic, contaminated wounds)
Event summary: Following the 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, Aceh Province in Indonesia experienced a massive surge of traumatic injuries in a population with low baseline tetanus vaccination coverage. Over the first month after the tsunami, surveillance from fixed and mobile clinics and hospitals in the affected areas documented 106 clinically diagnosed tetanus cases, mostly among adults, with an overall case‑fatality ratio of about 19% as intensive‑care and antitoxin supplies were initially limited. As wound management, active and passive immunization, and broader emergency health operations scaled up in early 2005, the cluster was controlled and no further major tetanus outbreaks were reported from the tsunami‑affected districts in the acute phase.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major environmental disaster (earthquake and tsunami) causing extensive soft‑tissue trauma and contamination with soil and debris; overwhelmed and damaged health‑care infrastructure; historically low tetanus immunization coverage among adults in Aceh; and delays in wound debridement and post‑exposure prophylaxis for many injured survivors. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of novel C. tetani strains or increased intrinsic virulence; the event reflects amplification of endemic risk through mass injury and poor prior immunity rather than biological change in the pathogen.
Review: Retain: Event correctly captures the large Aceh 2004–2005 tsunami‑associated tetanus cluster (106 cases, CFR ≈19%) as a re-occurrence in South‑eastern Asia, with accurate timing, country assignment (Indonesia) and description of drivers; the cited Sante Publique France summary, J‑STAGE review and WHO emergency guidance together provide adequate documentation for this outbreak.([santepubliquefrance.fr](https://www.santepubliquefrance.fr/en/node/8505?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (adult and adolescent earthquake victims with traumatic wounds)
Event summary: On 8 October 2005 a catastrophic earthquake struck northern Pakistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, causing tens of thousands of deaths and severe trauma in millions of survivors. In the weeks after the earthquake, a tetanus outbreak was recognized among injured victims from the affected areas, with hospital‑based series documenting at least 32 hospitalized tetanus cases with high mortality and broader summaries noting a total of roughly 139 tetanus cases and 41 deaths associated with the disaster, largely in previously unimmunized adults. As emergency supplies of tetanus toxoid and tetanus immune globulin increased, wound‑care services expanded and public health responses intensified over late 2005, the surge in tetanus cases subsided and no further large clusters were reported from the earthquake zone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large shallow earthquake generating massive numbers of crush and penetrating injuries contaminated with soil and debris; severely disrupted health services and limited intensive‑care capacity; very low prior coverage with primary tetanus immunization among adults; initially inadequate stocks of tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin relative to the size of the affected population; and delays in wound debridement and prophylaxis. Internal mechanisms: No documented emergence of new C. tetani genotypes or resistance; disease severity and high case‑fatality were driven by host factors (lack of immunity), injury patterns and constrained critical‑care capacity rather than intrinsic pathogen change.
Review: Review: Retain as one of the largest documented post‑1990 tetanus outbreaks (≈139 cases, 41 deaths) following the 2005 Pakistan/Kashmir earthquake; year, country (Pakistan), sub‑region (Southern Asia) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. The original use of a general tsunami document and a Wikipedia page was replaced with Pakistan‑specific clinical data (Khurram & Mahmood 2007) and synthesis reviews that explicitly report the ≈139‑case, 29–30% CFR estimate, so sources now better support the event description.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5942249_Tetanus_in_post_2005_Pakistan_earthquake_scenario))

Host: Humans (earthquake-injured adults, predominantly older patients, with contaminated wounds)
Event summary: On 27 May 2006 a magnitude ~6.3–6.4 earthquake struck Yogyakarta Province and Central Java, Indonesia, injuring tens of thousands and disrupting local health services in an area with incomplete adult tetanus vaccination coverage. Post‑disaster surveillance by the Ministry of Health, WHO and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies identified 71 non‑neonatal tetanus cases among injured survivors by late June 2006, with 26 deaths (case‑fatality about 37%), most in older adults with contaminated limb wounds and delayed access to definitive care across eight hospitals. As wound debridement, tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin supplies and public‑health messaging were scaled up over subsequent weeks, the incidence of new tetanus cases fell back towards baseline and no further large tetanus outbreaks were reported from the affected districts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Destructive shallow earthquake causing large numbers of crush, laceration and puncture injuries; damage to transport and health‑care infrastructure; historically incomplete DTP/tetanus immunization in adults; and limited intensive‑care capacity, leading to late presentation and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of biologically novel C. tetani strains, antimicrobial resistance or altered virulence; the outbreak reflects amplification of endemic risk through mass trauma and existing immunity gaps rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review: Newly added because WHO, IFRC and peer‑reviewed analyses document 71 tetanus cases with 26 deaths (CFR 36.6%) after the 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake, making this one of the largest post‑1990 non‑neonatal tetanus clusters; year, country (Indonesia), sub‑region (South‑eastern Asia) and classification as re-occurrence are supported by J‑STAGE and BMC case‑series data and WHO/IFRC situation reports.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tjem/238/3/238_219/_html/-char/en))

Host: Humans (earthquake-affected population with traumatic wounds and pre-existing low tetanus immunity, including both adults and some neonates)
Event summary: On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake devastated Port‑au‑Prince and surrounding areas in Haiti, causing hundreds of thousands of injuries and overwhelming health facilities in a country where tetanus was already endemic and adult vaccination coverage had been low. During the first months of the response, the national Internally Displaced Persons Surveillance System recorded 18 tetanus cases among more than 23,000 consultations for priority syndromes in IDP camp clinics, and narrative reviews and PAHO/WHO reports describe additional post‑injury and neonatal tetanus cases that were likely under‑reported but did not reach explosive epidemic levels. As emergency vaccination campaigns with tetanus‑containing vaccines, improved wound care and routine disease surveillance were implemented through 2010, tetanus incidence declined and no large sustained outbreak was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Catastrophic earthquake producing large numbers of crush injuries and open wounds; extreme overcrowding and poor sanitation in temporary camps; long‑standing low coverage with tetanus toxoid in adults and women of childbearing age; disruption of routine health services and cold‑chain systems; and delays in wound debridement and prophylactic vaccination for many injured survivors. Internal mechanisms: No evidence that new C. tetani genotypes or increased virulence emerged; the observed cases reflect trauma exposure and immunity gaps in an already endemic setting rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review: Newly added to represent the moderate‑sized post‑earthquake tetanus cluster in Haiti; IDP camp surveillance documented 18 tetanus cases early in 2010 and reviews emphasize additional under‑reported post‑injury and neonatal cases in a population with low pre‑disaster vaccination coverage. Year (2010), geography (Caribbean, Haiti) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate, but true national case totals remain uncertain and should be revisited if more comprehensive Haitian data become available.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5930a2.htm))

Host: Humans (mainly older adults injured in the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami)
Event summary: On 11 March 2011 the Great East Japan (Tohoku) earthquake and subsequent tsunami caused extensive injuries and displacement in north‑eastern Japan, including many wounds contaminated by debris and muddy seawater. National infectious‑disease surveillance and case reports identified around 9–10 tetanus cases among injured survivors in the months following the disaster, predominantly in older adults who had not received full primary vaccination or booster doses, but with no deaths reported in this small cluster. With high baseline immunization in younger cohorts, rapid wound care and ready access to intensive care, tetanus incidence remained low and the disaster did not develop into a large‑scale tetanus epidemic, and routine background annual tetanus case numbers in Japan remained on the order of about 100 per year thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Combined earthquake–tsunami disaster causing contaminated traumatic wounds; concentration of cases among older adults born before routine tetanus vaccination was introduced, resulting in age‑cohort immunity gaps; and logistical challenges in early post‑disaster wound care and vaccination despite relatively strong health infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain, resistance, or host‑switching reported; this small re-occurrence mainly reflects pre‑existing susceptibility in specific age cohorts exposed to traumatic injuries during the disaster rather than evolutionary change in C. tetani.
Review: Retain: Event accurately summarizes the small but well‑documented post‑disaster tetanus cluster (~9–10 cases, no deaths) after the Great East Japan Earthquake, with correct geography (Asia, Eastern Asia; Japan) and classification as re-occurrence; NIID surveillance, BMC case‑series reports and J‑STAGE/WHO reviews all support the timing and limited scale described.([idsc.niid.go.jp](https://idsc.niid.go.jp/iasr/32/32s/me32s1.html?utm_source=openai))
