Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia
Countries: Russian Federation [1990]; Ukraine [1991]; Belarus [1991]; Republic of Moldova [1991]; Estonia [1991]; Latvia [1991]; Lithuania [1991]; Armenia [1991]; Azerbaijan [1991]; Georgia [1991]; Kazakhstan [1991]; Kyrgyzstan [1991]; Tajikistan [1991]; Turkmenistan [1991]; Uzbekistan [1991]
Host: Humans (mainly school‑age children and adults)
Event summary: Beginning around 1990 in the Russian Federation, diphtheria re‑emerged explosively after decades of control, then spread rapidly across all Newly Independent States and Baltic countries by the mid‑1990s, ultimately causing >150,000–200,000 cases and ~5,000 deaths between 1991 and 1998. As the epidemic expanded, large urban centers and militaries experienced intense transmission, with adults accounting for a substantial share of severe cases and deaths, and importations produced smaller clusters in parts of Europe and Mongolia. Aggressive mass vaccination campaigns targeting both children and adults and restoration of routine immunization gradually reduced incidence in the late 1990s, bringing the epidemic under control by the end of the decade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major geopolitical and socio‑economic disruption following the breakup of the Soviet Union led to breakdowns in vaccine production and supply chains, declining routine immunization coverage, large population movements, crowded living conditions (urban centers, military barracks), and weakened public health systems. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and dominance of a closely related epidemic clone of C. diphtheriae biotype gravis associated with many cases suggests strain‑specific advantages (novel strain/genotype emergence and possibly enhanced transmission).
Review: review – Correctly captures the major 1990s epidemic in the Newly Independent States as a top‑impact re‑emergent event. Sub_regions were narrowed to Eastern Europe, Northern Europe, Central Asia and Western Asia to align with where sustained epidemic transmission occurred, and intra_continental_emergence was set to 'false' because diphtheria was already present in these subregions long before 1990; importations into Western Europe and Mongolia are treated as part of the same episode but not as new‑subregion emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Indonesia [2011]; East Java Province as primary focus, with spread and repeated outbreaks within the province
Host: Humans (mainly children and adolescents)
Event summary: From 2011 onward, East Java Province, Indonesia, experienced repeated diphtheria outbreaks, leading to its declaration as an outbreak area as case numbers and mortality climbed sharply in 2011–2012. Over 2011–2016, hundreds of cases per year were reported in the province, contributing the majority of Indonesia’s national diphtheria burden and affecting multiple districts and age groups despite the presence of a national childhood immunization program. Successive rounds of outbreak response immunization (ORI) and intensified vaccination plus improved surveillance gradually reduced incidence, but East Java remained a hotspot feeding into the larger 2017 national surge.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Suboptimal and heterogeneous DTP coverage with immunity gaps in older children and adolescents, very high population density, and health‑system limitations in rapidly detecting and responding to cases enabled sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not emphasize a specific novel strain; the pattern appears driven primarily by accumulated susceptible cohorts rather than clear genetic shifts, so this is classified as re‑occurrence rather than strong re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Multi‑year East Java outbreaks generated several hundred cases annually and clearly contributed substantially to Indonesia’s and the global burden; classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) and geographic labeling are appropriate. No corrections needed.

Countries: Haiti [2014]; (smaller related transmission also reported in the Dominican Republic, not detailed here)
Host: Humans (mostly children and adolescents)
Event summary: Beginning in late 2014, Haiti reported renewed diphtheria transmission after years of very low incidence, with continuous suspected and confirmed cases recorded each year through at least 2020–2021. Over 2014–2021, Haiti documented roughly one thousand or more suspected cases and well over one hundred deaths, with multiple peaks and spread across several departments, signaling a prolonged nationwide re‑occurrence. Large‑scale catch‑up vaccination campaigns launched in 2018 and again in subsequent years, targeting millions of children, were deployed to close immunity gaps and curb persistent transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronic fragility of Haiti’s health system, political and economic instability, declining vaccination coverage with large numbers of under‑ or unvaccinated children, and difficulties maintaining cold chain and outreach all contributed to sustained circulation and high case‑fatality in some cohorts. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain, resistance, or virulence increase has been highlighted; the event reflects re‑occurrence in a setting where diphtheria was once largely controlled but resurged due to external drivers.
Review: retain – Haiti’s prolonged national outbreak (≈1,000+ suspected cases and high mortality) is among the larger modern diphtheria resurgences in the Americas; continents/sub‑regions and event‑type classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate. Minor numerical differences across PAHO reports are within expected uncertainty and do not require restructuring.

Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2016]; limited cross‑border spread with linked cases reported in neighboring countries including Brazil [2017] and Colombia [2018]
Host: Humans (children and adults)
Event summary: After more than two decades without reported diphtheria, Venezuela detected a new outbreak starting in July 2016, marking the country’s first cases since 1992. The epidemic evolved into a nationwide crisis through 2017–2019, with PAHO and national reports indicating around 2,500 confirmed or probable cases and multiple waves of transmission, affecting numerous states and age groups and contributing to regional spread through population movements, including clusters in Brazil and Colombia. Intensified vaccination campaigns, international support, and gradual strengthening of surveillance helped decrease reported incidence after 2019, though vulnerability remains amid broader health‑system collapse.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe economic and political crisis, health‑sector collapse, shortages of vaccines and antitoxin, deteriorating routine immunization coverage, and large‑scale migration created ideal conditions for re‑establishment and spread of diphtheria and exportation of cases to neighboring countries. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing showed circulation of toxigenic strains, but available data do not identify a clearly novel genotype or resistance mechanism as the primary driver; the episode is best characterized as re‑occurrence in a previously controlled setting.
Review: review – Outbreak scale (~2,500 cases) and geographic footprint justify inclusion as a major event. Intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence have been set to 'false' because diphtheria was long established throughout South America and available data implicate health‑system collapse and vaccination gaps rather than a clearly novel strain as the main driver; cross‑border spread to Brazil and Colombia is treated as part of the same re‑occurrence episode rather than new continental or subregional emergence.

Countries: Bangladesh [2017] (Cox’s Bazar district, especially Rohingya refugee camps and nearby host communities)
Host: Humans (predominantly Rohingya refugees, mainly children and adolescents; some cases among Bangladeshi hosts)
Event summary: Following the mass influx of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar into Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, in August 2017, a large diphtheria outbreak was first detected in November 2017 in overcrowded refugee camps. The epidemic spread rapidly through 2017–2018, ultimately generating approximately 8,400 suspected cases among the Rohingya population and lasting for over two years, with children and adolescents most affected and substantial morbidity but relatively low overall case‑fatality due to intensified clinical care and antitoxin use. Multiple rounds of mass vaccination, expansion of treatment centers, and strengthening of surveillance gradually brought the outbreak under control by 2019, though sporadic cases and ongoing vulnerability persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme overcrowding, poor sanitation, limited initial access to health care, low or uncertain prior vaccination coverage among Rohingya refugees, and the stress of forced displacement created ideal conditions for explosive transmission. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance pattern was highlighted; the outbreak mainly reflects intense spread in a highly susceptible displaced population, i.e., re‑occurrence facilitated by social and environmental drivers rather than genetic change.
Review: retain – Correctly identifies one of the three largest modern outbreaks (≈8,400 cases) and appropriately classifies it as re‑occurrence driven by extreme crowding and low prior coverage in a refugee setting. Geography, years, and sources are appropriate.

Host: Humans (children and adolescents, with some adults)
Event summary: In October 2017, amid protracted armed conflict and health‑system collapse, Yemen’s Ministry of Health and WHO announced a diphtheria outbreak after clusters were reported from Ibb governorate. Over 2017–2019, the outbreak spread to most districts in 23 of Yemen’s governorates, with several thousand suspected cases and hundreds of deaths recorded, making it one of the largest modern diphtheria emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Large‑scale emergency vaccination campaigns, deployment of antitoxin and antibiotics, and international support reduced incidence in later years, but continuing conflict and service disruptions mean that diphtheria transmission remains an ongoing risk rather than a clearly ended episode.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Devastating armed conflict, blockade‑related shortages, collapse of health infrastructure, overwhelmed services due to concurrent massive cholera outbreaks, population displacement, and low or interrupted vaccination coverage were key drivers of re‑occurrence and geographic expansion. Internal mechanisms: Available genomic work indicates circulation of toxigenic strains but does not clearly implicate a new lineage as the main cause; the event is best characterized as re‑occurrence driven by extreme external stressors rather than intrinsic pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Yemen’s protracted conflict‑associated epidemic (≈3,000+ cases) is among the most severe post‑1990 diphtheria events; classification as re‑occurrence without intra/inter‑continental emergence is consistent with long‑standing regional presence of C. diphtheriae. No structural corrections required.

Countries: Indonesia [2017] (multiple provinces across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Papua, with highest burden in East Java, West Java, Banten, Aceh, West Sumatra)
Host: Humans (children and adolescents, with adult cases)
Event summary: In 2017, Indonesia experienced a marked nationwide surge of diphtheria cases on top of ongoing endemic activity, prompting declaration of a national outbreak. Cases were reported from most major islands, with particularly high numbers in East Java (over 270 cases in January–November 2017) and additional clusters in West Java, Banten, Aceh, and West Sumatra, leading to hundreds of laboratory‑confirmed cases and significant mortality. Intensive outbreak response immunization campaigns targeting children and adolescents (and later some adults) in late 2017 and 2018, combined with improved clinical management, helped curb the national surge by 2018, though Indonesia has continued to report notable background incidence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent immunity gaps due to suboptimal and uneven DTP coverage, rapidly growing and densely populated urban centers, and mobility between provinces allowed accumulation of susceptibles and inter‑provincial spread, while limited adult booster policies left older groups partly unprotected. Internal mechanisms: Although studies document circulation of toxigenic strains and some reduced susceptibility to first‑line antibiotics in a subset of isolates, there is no clear evidence that a single novel genotype or resistance mechanism primarily drove the national outbreak; the episode is better viewed as re‑occurrence in a high‑burden, incompletely immunized population.
Review: review – National Indonesian outbreak (hundreds of confirmed cases and dozens of deaths) justifies its inclusion as a major event. Intra_continental_emergence has been set to 'false' because C. diphtheriae was long endemic throughout South‑eastern Asia; this surge represents re‑occurrence driven by immunity gaps and population density, not first arrival in a new Asian subregion. Other fields and sources are appropriate.

Countries: India [2000]; Nepal [2000]; (other countries in WHO South‑East Asia Region with sustained high incidence, especially India)
Host: Humans (primarily children and adolescents, with increasing share of older age groups)
Event summary: Throughout 2000–2017, India and some neighboring South‑East Asian countries maintained the highest global diphtheria case counts, with India alone accounting for the majority of reported cases worldwide each year and periods of increased incidence after 2010. Within India, surveillance analyses documented persistent endemic transmission with recurrent local outbreaks and a gradual shift toward older children and adults among reported cases. Intensification of routine immunization, supplemental activities, and discussions about life‑course booster strategies have been ongoing to address this chronic high‑burden situation, though diphtheria remains entrenched in several Indian states.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large population size, heterogeneous and often suboptimal DTP coverage in some states, socio‑economic disparities, and insufficient adolescent/adult booster policies sustain a large pool of susceptible individuals and recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence emphasizes immunity gaps and age‑shifts rather than a single novel strain or resistance pattern; this period is best considered a long‑running re‑occurrence and concentration of endemic disease rather than re‑emergence driven by a discrete pathogen change.
Review: review – Appropriately highlights India’s dominant contribution to global diphtheria incidence since 2000, but re_emergence has been set to 'false' because the sustained high burden and age‑shift are better explained by persistent immunity gaps and booster‑dose weaknesses than by clearly documented strain‑level changes. The time window (2000–2017) is broad but defensible as a linked period of chronic high incidence; a future refinement could focus on specific peak years or large state‑level outbreaks if finer granularity is desired.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Northern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Nigeria [2022]; Niger [2023]; Guinea [2023]; Mauritania [2023]; Gabon [2023]; Mali [2024]; Algeria [2024]; Chad [2025]; South Africa [2015, 2023–2025 clusters]
Host: Humans (predominantly under‑immunized children and adolescents, with cases in young adults)
Event summary: Beginning in May 2022, Nigeria detected unusually large numbers of diphtheria cases, with more than 1,400 suspected cases and 557 confirmed cases (73 deaths) reported from 21 states by April 2023, and tens of thousands of suspected and many thousands of confirmed cases reported thereafter across most states. From 2023 onward, linked or contemporaneous outbreaks were reported in Niger, Guinea, Mauritania, Gabon, Mali, Algeria, Chad and South Africa, so that by late 2024 the WHO African Region had recorded roughly 57,000 suspected cases and about 2,000 deaths in nine affected countries, followed by a further >17,000 suspected cases and nearly 900 deaths across eight countries during 2025. This multi‑country African resurgence, centered on northern Nigeria and neighboring Sahelian and West African countries, represents the largest documented diphtheria emergency since the 1990s New Independent States epidemic, with prolonged transmission and repeated waves despite large‑scale vaccination campaigns.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very low or heterogeneous DTP3 coverage with large zero‑dose child cohorts, protracted insecurity and humanitarian crises in parts of Nigeria, Niger, Mali and Chad, widespread poverty and overcrowding (including in camps and informal settlements), disruptions to routine immunization during the COVID‑19 pandemic, and constrained access to care and to diphtheria antitoxin created ideal conditions for re‑establishment and rapid spread of diphtheria across much of West and Central Africa. Extensive cross‑border movement across porous Sahelian frontiers facilitated spread between Nigeria, Niger, Guinea, Mauritania and Mali, while localized clusters in Algeria, Gabon, Chad and South Africa reflect the same regional immunity gaps. Internal mechanisms: Available typing data indicate circulation of multiple toxigenic C. diphtheriae lineages, with some penicillin non‑susceptibility, but no single clearly novel genotype has been identified as the primary driver; the pattern is best interpreted as large‑scale re‑occurrence in under‑immunized populations.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the very large 2022–2025 multi‑country African resurgence (≈57,000 suspected cases and ~2,000 deaths in 2023–2024, plus >17,000 suspected cases and ~900 deaths in 2025 across eight countries). Classified as re‑occurrence without intra/inter‑continental emergence because diphtheria was long established in all affected African subregions; localized clusters in Algeria, Gabon, Chad and South Africa are treated as part of the same regional resurgence rather than distinct emergence events. Human review is recommended to confirm final country list and time bounds, but inclusion as a top‑impact post‑1990 event is strongly supported by WHO regional situation reports and risk assessments.

Host: Humans (acute-care inpatients; multiple adult wards in a Bologna-area hospital)
Event summary: From 1–15 June 2012, active screening for carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in an Italian hospital identified eight patients colonized in the gut with a clonal Citrobacter freundii strain carrying the blaVIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase, representing a localized nosocomial outbreak of carbapenemase-producing C. freundii. All isolates showed multidrug resistance, shared the same multilocus sequence type, and were detected via rectal swabs following the discovery of a KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae case on the ward.
