Countries: India – Maharashtra [2016] (Sindhudurg district, Dodamarg and Sawantwadi talukas, later expansion to additional villages)
Host: Humans (village residents, forest and plantation workers); associated infected monkeys and ticks
Event summary: In early 2016, a major KFD outbreak was confirmed in Dodamarg taluka of Sindhudurg district, Maharashtra, marking the first recognized human cases in the state and affecting over 100 people with laboratory‑confirmed infection, alongside monkey deaths and positive tick pools.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26997635/)) Over subsequent seasons (2016–2019), KFD activity expanded to additional talukas and villages in Sindhudurg, with Maharashtra reporting roughly 129 cases in 2016, 202 in 2017, 109 in 2018 and 82 in 2019, forming part of a broader multi‑state Western Ghats episode that contributed to approximately 809 human cases nationwide in 2016–2017.([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf)) Intensified case detection, mass vaccination in high‑risk villages, restriction of forest access during peak season and tick‑control measures gradually curtailed outbreak intensity, although low‑level transmission persists in the region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6362715/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: spread of infection along the continuous Western Ghats ecosystem from Karnataka and Goa into Maharashtra, facilitated by movement of infected ticks on livestock and people, monkey migration, and expansion of cashew and other plantations into formerly forested areas; lack of prior vaccination or clinical suspicion in Maharashtra delayed early recognition.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/kyasanur-forest-disease)) Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of existing KFDV lineages into new districts and states; phylogeographic work indicates diversification within the Western Ghats but not a wholly distinct Maharashtra‑specific genotype, supporting classification as First detection and Re‑emergence in Maharashtra.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7005018/))
Review: review – This row accurately summarizes the first recognised human KFD outbreak in Maharashtra (Dodamarg taluka, Sindhudurg district) and its subsequent spread to additional talukas, with official reports documenting 129, 202, 109 and 82 cases in 2016–2019 respectively and >500 cases over the multi‑year episode.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26997635/?utm_source=openai))  I corrected the event‑type classification by changing first_detection from true to false, because within this dataset ‘first_detection’ refers to initial detection of KFDV in humans globally (1957 in Karnataka). The Maharashtra episode fits better as re_emergence driven by geographic spread of existing lineages along the Western Ghats, so re_emergence remains true; other fields and sources are retained.

Countries: India – Tamil Nadu [2016] (Nilgiris district, forest‑fringe communities along the Western Ghats border with Karnataka and Kerala)
Host: Humans in forest‑fringe communities and forest workers along the Western Ghats border with Karnataka/Kerala
Event summary: Following recognition of KFD in neighboring Kerala and Karnataka, isolated human KFD cases began to be reported from border areas of Tamil Nadu from 2016 onward, indicating the virus had crossed into new administrative territories along the Western Ghats.([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf)) Case numbers remained low (with official tallies reporting only a handful of confirmed infections per year between 2016 and 2019), but the detection of locally exposed forest workers and villagers suggested establishment of KFDV transmission in previously unaffected forest patches.([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf)) Targeted surveillance, focal vaccination and health education in these newly recognized foci helped limit spread, and no large explosive outbreak comparable to Goa, Kerala or Maharashtra was documented through 2019.([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: progressive west‑to‑east and north‑to‑south spread of KFDV along the Western Ghats forest belt, with human activity (grazing, fuelwood collection, forest work) and wildlife‑associated tick dispersal facilitating introduction into border districts of Tamil Nadu; initial absence of routine surveillance there likely delayed recognition of early cases.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32159030/)) Internal mechanisms: continued geographic range expansion of established KFDV lineages with no clear evidence of a Tamil Nadu–specific novel strain; therefore classified as Re‑emergence in a new state with relatively small but epidemiologically important impact.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7005018/))
Review: review – Evidence from the Karnataka operational manual, central government briefings and later reviews indicates that KFDV was detected in monkeys and ticks in Nilgiris district in 2012–2013, with the first human KFD case in Tamil Nadu reported in 2016 and low but persistent human case counts through 2019 (1, 1, 10 and 4 cases).([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf))  I therefore corrected the event year from 2015–2019 to 2016–2019 and specified Nilgiris district in the countries field. As with other state‑level expansions, I removed the mis‑used first_detection flag (global first detection was in 1957) and retained re_emergence to reflect geographic spread along the Western Ghats. Given the small absolute numbers but high epidemiological significance (establishment in a fifth Indian state), this event should be retained but kept flagged for expert review.

Host: Humans (rural residents, muskrat trappers and other residents of lake/steppe districts in Novosibirsk Oblast); wild small mammals (especially muskrats and voles) and ixodid ticks as reservoir/amplifying hosts and vectors within the natural focus
Event summary: After a prolonged inter‑epidemic period with very low or no recorded Omsk hemorrhagic fever (OHF) incidence following the 1945–1958 epidemic wave, surveillance in western Siberia detected renewed human OHF activity beginning in 1989, with sustained low‑to‑moderate incidence from 1990 through 1998 mainly in Novosibirsk Oblast of the Russian Federation. During this period, national data indicate 2–41 reported OHF cases per year in Novosibirsk, with the highest annual counts in 1990 and 1991, representing a clear resurgence compared with the preceding quiescent decades; most patients were muskrat trappers or rural residents exposed to tick‑infested wetlands and infected muskrats in long‑standing natural foci, while epizootic activity in muskrats and ticks was also documented in neighboring Tyumen, Omsk and Kurgan regions.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus)) By the late 1990s, public‑health messaging, changes in muskrat exploitation and ecological fluctuations appear to have reduced human exposure, and reported incidence declined again even though enzootic circulation of OHFV in wildlife persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reactivation of OHF natural foci in western Siberia driven by favorable ecological conditions for muskrats and voles around lakes and marshes, intensive muskrat trapping and skinning, and occupational/recreational exposure to tick‑infested habitats, combined with socio‑economic changes in the late Soviet and early post‑Soviet periods that likely reduced resources for systematic vector and wildlife management.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic and antigenic studies indicate that OHFV strains circulating in the 1990s belong to previously recognized western Siberian genotypes, with no clear evidence of major viral evolution or increased intrinsic virulence relative to earlier strains; the episode is therefore best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven primarily by ecological and behavioral factors rather than a genetic re‑emergence (no strong support for Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence or markedly Enhanced Transmission beyond the long‑established ecology).([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row appropriately captures the documented resurgence of OHF in the 1990s, with cases concentrated in Novosibirsk Oblast after a long quiescent period, and correctly classifies the episode as re‑occurrence in a long‑known natural focus rather than first emergence or inter‑/intra‑continental spread. I have revised the event summary to rely on primary reviews (Růžek et al. 2013; Control of Communicable Diseases Manual) rather than Wikipedia, removed a poorly sourced numeric estimate of "~240" cases in favor of qualitative wording linked to reported annual ranges, and clarified that most human cases were in Novosibirsk while neighboring oblasts mainly showed epizootic activity. These changes strengthen sourcing and reduce over‑precision but do not alter the basic structure of the event; further refinement of exact case counts would require access to detailed Russian surveillance tables.

Host: Humans (sporadic OHF cases, largely in Novosibirsk Oblast and possibly other western Siberian oblasts); wild small mammals (rodents including voles and muskrats) and ixodid ticks in western Siberia as reservoir hosts and vectors within established natural foci
Event summary: Russian‑language syntheses of OHF ecology describe a further period of elevated Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus natural‑focus activity beginning around 1999 and continuing through approximately 2007, particularly in Omsk Oblast, against a background of continued low‑level human OHF incidence in Novosibirsk Oblast. In this interval, OHFV circulation persisted in rodent–tick cycles around lakes and marshes in Omsk and adjacent western Siberian regions, and small numbers of human infections were reported among rural residents and people with occupational exposure to wetlands and muskrats, but no large explosive outbreaks comparable to the 1940s–1950s epidemic were documented and human disease remained rare.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/omsk-hemorrhagic-fever-virus?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2000s, available reports suggest that clinically apparent OHF cases had become sporadic while enzootic transmission in wildlife likely continued at a low level within long‑standing foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued maintenance of OHFV in established western Siberian landscapes characterized by wetlands, dense rodent populations and Dermacentor/Ixodes tick communities, together with ongoing but reduced human exposure through hunting, trapping and rural activities, underpinned recurrent sporadic human disease during 1999–2007, with Russian authors highlighting renewed epizootic activity in Omsk Oblast during this period.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/omsk-hemorrhagic-fever-virus?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Available genetic and ecological data do not indicate the emergence of a distinct new OHFV genotype or major change in virulence associated specifically with this interval; as with the 1990s episode, the period is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence driven by ecological cycles and human contact patterns, not a clear viral re‑emergence event.
Review: Decision: retain (with caution about precision). Rationale: This row reflects a later, relatively low‑intensity resurgence period (1999–2007) that is specifically noted in Russian reviews as a phase of renewed OHFV natural‑focus activity in Omsk and continuing sporadic human OHF in western Siberia, and its classification as a re‑occurrence episode in a long‑recognized endemic area is appropriate. However, quantitative human case data for this interval are sparse and largely inferred from secondary summaries of Russian sources. I have updated the narrative and sources to rely on these primary syntheses rather than Wikipedia and to emphasize the qualitative, low‑incidence nature of the episode. The event should be retained as one of the few identifiable post‑1990 resurgence phases for OHF, but future access to detailed Russian surveillance data could allow refinement of the time window and impact estimates.

Host: Humans (patients with meningitis or meningoencephalitis in Almaty city); wild rodents (multiple small‑mammal species) and ixodid ticks (Dermacentor marginatus, Dermacentor reticulatus, Ixodes persulcatus) in Akmola, West Kazakhstan, Almaty region and Almaty city as reservoir hosts and vectors within newly recognized natural foci
Event summary: Between 2016 and 2019, a cross‑sectional investigation in Kazakhstan provided the first direct evidence that Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus had spread beyond the historically recognized western Siberian focus in the Russian Federation: OHFV RNA was detected in Dermacentor marginatus ticks collected in 2016 from the Sandyktau area of Akmola Region, in additional tick pools from Akmola in 2018, in lung tissue of several rodent species trapped in West Kazakhstan Region in 2018–2019, and in cerebrospinal fluid from two patients with meningitis/meningoencephalitis treated in Almaty city hospitals in 2018–2019.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3aeb/b4a67588f1da5ba4ab630818570485207679.pdf)) These data demonstrated natural foci of OHFV in multiple regions of Kazakhstan and confirmed human infection up to ~1,600 km from the classic western Siberian endemic area, yet no large recognized outbreak of clinically classical Omsk hemorrhagic fever was described; instead, the virus appears to cause sporadic, previously unrecognized neurologic disease in Central Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Kazakhstan findings likely reflect a combination of long‑standing ecological continuity across the Russia–Kazakhstan border (shared steppe and forest‑steppe habitats, widespread muskrats and small rodents, and Dermacentor/Ixodes tick populations) and improved molecular surveillance for viral causes of undiagnosed febrile and neurologic illness, as suggested by the authors, with climate‑ and land‑use‑driven shifts in host and vector distributions potentially facilitating south‑ and west‑ward spread or detection of OHFV.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3aeb/b4a67588f1da5ba4ab630818570485207679.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Sequence analyses to date place Kazakh OHFV sequences within the known diversity of the virus rather than identifying a clearly distinct high‑virulence genotype, so the episode is best interpreted as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent and country for the human host system under the UNSD classification: Europe–Russian Federation to Asia–Kazakhstan) driven by geographic range expansion and improved detection, rather than as genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This new row has been added to capture an important emergence event omitted from the original dataset: the first confirmed detection of OHFV in humans, ticks and rodents in Kazakhstan between 2016 and 2019, which represents inter‑continental emergence from Europe (Russian Federation, per the UNSD classification used in the Country sheet) into Asia (Central Asia, Kazakhstan). The episode is supported by a detailed peer‑reviewed study (Wagner et al. 2022, Viruses) and clearly meets the criteria for an emergence event despite involving only a small number of recognized human cases, because it documents establishment of natural foci and autochthonous human infection in a new country and continent. Classification as inter‑continental emergence (with no first‑global‑emergence or re‑occurrence/re‑emergence labels) and the 2016–2019 time window are based on the sampling years reported in that study.

Countries: United States of America [1994] (Massachusetts [1994]; Maine, Vermont [1999–2001])
Host: Humans; ticks (primarily Ixodes cookei, with emerging involvement of Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (woodchucks, squirrels, other rodents as reservoirs)
Event summary: After several decades with only sporadic reports, Powassan virus reappeared in the northeastern United States when a neuroinvasive case was reported in Massachusetts in 1994, followed by a four‑case outbreak of Powassan encephalitis in Maine and Vermont during 1999–2001 that represented the first recognized cases in those states and the first U.S. cases since 1994. These cases marked renewed recognition of endemic foci in New England, with enhanced surveillance and serologic testing revealing that the virus had been circulating more widely than previously appreciated. The episode ended as incident cases again became rare after 2001, but it set the stage for subsequent expansion and increasing detection of lineage II (deer tick virus) in the same broader region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased clinical awareness and use of flavivirus serology in patients with encephalitis; expanding populations of ticks and wildlife hosts in New England due to land‑use change, reforestation, and growing deer populations; overlap with emerging Lyme disease ecology. Internal mechanisms: emergence and recognition of Powassan lineage II (deer tick virus) in Ixodes scapularis ticks in the northeastern U.S., representing a novel genotype associated with more efficient human exposure via a common human‑biting tick (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion (Spillover); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: review – Event is real and represents the key New England re‑emergence episode (Massachusetts 1994 case and the 1999–2001 Maine/Vermont outbreak). Updated the countries field to give state‑specific start years (Massachusetts [1994]; Maine, Vermont [1999–2001]) and left the event year span at 1994–2001 to cover this linked regional episode. Event type was restricted to re_emergence (re_occurrence kept at No) to comply with the project rule that categories are mutually exclusive except where re_emergence co‑occurs with inter/intra‑continental emergence. Added the CDC MMWR outbreak report as a primary source; recommend expert review of the chosen temporal grouping (single event versus splitting 1994 and 1999–2001) but keep the event as one of the major Powassan episodes.

Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: Beginning in 2002, Powassan virus was confirmed as the cause of severe neuroinvasive disease in a Michigan resident, and in 2003 Wisconsin reported its first recognized human case, after the virus had previously been confined to eastern Canada and the northeastern United States. Over 2002–2005, Wisconsin and neighboring Midwestern states documented several encephalitis cases and serologic evidence of wider exposure, indicating westward expansion of Powassan/deer tick virus into new endemic foci in the upper Midwest. Following this initial emergence period, Powassan virus became an established but rare zoonosis in the region, with recurring human cases and detections in Ixodes scapularis ticks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) range and density into the upper Midwest due to reforestation, abundant deer hosts, and changing climate; intensifying human use of forested recreation areas. Internal mechanisms: successful adaptation of Powassan lineage II (deer tick virus) to I. scapularis and associated rodent hosts in Midwestern ecotones (Host Expansion (Spillover); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence episode marking establishment of Powassan/deer tick virus in the upper Midwest, but correct details. Adjusted the event years from 2000–2005 to 2002–2005 and the country field to specify Michigan [2002] and Wisconsin [2003], based on case compilations showing the first Michigan case in 2002 and the first Wisconsin resident case in 2003. Kept the event type as re_emergence (linked to lineage II and I. scapularis adaptation) and not re_occurrence, since this period primarily reflects geographic and ecological emergence into new foci. Sources were focused on Michigan/Wisconsin case series and state surveillance; recommend expert review of whether to extend the end year slightly (e.g., through 2006–2007) to capture the full early cluster.

Countries: United States of America [2004] (New York – Lower Hudson Valley and surrounding counties)
Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: In the mid‑2000s, New York State identified a growing cluster of Powassan/deer tick virus encephalitis cases, including a fatal lineage II infection in a New York resident and additional confirmed neuroinvasive infections from 2004 onward. Between 2004 and 2012, a retrospective review documented 14 Powassan/deer tick virus encephalitis cases in New York, 72% from the Lyme‑endemic Lower Hudson Valley where Ixodes scapularis is abundant, indicating establishment of a new enzootic cycle involving deer ticks and rodents in this suburban region. After 2012, Powassan virus disease remained rare but continued to be reported almost annually from New York and neighboring states, with ongoing sporadic severe cases along the same ecological corridor.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of blacklegged ticks and white‑tailed deer in suburban forest fragments of the Lower Hudson Valley; intense human exposure to deer tick habitats due to outdoor recreation and expanding exurban development; improved arboviral surveillance and routine testing for neuroinvasive disease. Internal mechanisms: emergence and spread of deer tick virus (Powassan lineage II) within Ixodes scapularis–rodent cycles in New York, increasing human risk compared with the historical Ixodes cookei–groundhog cycle (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Host Expansion (Spillover)).
Review: review – Retain this event as the key Lower Hudson Valley lineage II emergence cluster. Corrected the event year span to 2004–2012 and aligned the country field to use 2004 as the New York start year, matching the retrospective series of 14 cases diagnosed during 2004–2012. Kept the event type as re_emergence, reflecting the establishment of a new deer tick virus transmission cycle rather than simple resurgence of an unchanged virus. No changes to geography or host listing were needed; main additions are clarification of dates and reliance on the EID case series and related NYS data as primary documentation.

Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: Minnesota reported its first confirmed human Powassan virus case in 2008, identified as a deer tick virus infection, marking the beginning of recognized endemic transmission in the state. Over the next several years, additional neuroinvasive cases accumulated, culminating in Minnesota’s first documented Powassan virus encephalitis death by 2011, which state and federal reports highlighted as evidence of a newly emerging tick‑borne disease risk in the upper Midwest. After this early emergence phase, Minnesota continued to report cases nearly every year, with Powassan virus added to state notifiable disease lists and integrated into routine arboviral surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: northward and westward expansion and increasing abundance of Ixodes scapularis in Minnesota forests and along river corridors, driven by land‑use changes, deer overabundance, and warming temperatures; enhanced clinician awareness and arboviral testing prompted by severe encephalitis cases. Internal mechanisms: establishment of Powassan lineage II in I. scapularis populations in Minnesota and efficient transmission to humans via relatively short tick attachment times (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Host Expansion (Spillover)).
Review: retain – Event corresponds well to the documented emergence of Powassan/deer tick virus in Minnesota, with 2008 as the first recognized case and a fatal encephalitis case reported in 2011. The event window, geographic scope, host listing and classification as re_emergence (linked to lineage II establishing in local Ixodes scapularis populations) are consistent with state and CDC sources. No corrections beyond routine wording refinement are required.

Countries: Canada [1994] (human cases reported from Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Manitoba; Powassan virus detected in Ixodes scapularis ticks in additional provinces including Prince Edward Island)
Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes cookei, Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (woodchucks, squirrels, rodents)
Event summary: Although Canada’s index Powassan virus case occurred in Ontario in 1958, additional human neuroinvasive cases began to be reported again from the late 1980s and 1990s onward, first in New Brunswick and Quebec and then in southern Ontario, marking renewed recognition of the virus in eastern Canada. Through the 2000s and 2010s, sporadic but often severe encephalitis cases continued to be documented in Ontario and Quebec, with isolated case reports from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador, while national surveillance and tick studies showed expanding populations of Ixodes scapularis carrying Powassan virus in multiple eastern provinces. In 2023, a severe encephalitis case acquired in Manitoba after a documented blacklegged tick bite demonstrated clinical spillover onto the central Canadian Prairies, and by the early 2020s at least 20–25 Canadian human cases had been reported overall, indicating slow but geographically broadening emergence overlapping Lyme disease risk areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: climate warming and changing land use facilitating northward and east–west expansion of Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes cookei; growth of deer and small mammal populations; rising outdoor recreation and awareness of tick‑borne risks leading to more diagnostic testing; national and provincial case definitions and surveillance guidance implemented by the Public Health Agency of Canada and provincial health authorities. Internal mechanisms: establishment and spread of deer tick virus within blacklegged tick populations in Lyme‑endemic areas, increasing opportunities for human spillover, and possible adaptation to a broader climatic envelope (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion (Spillover); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: review – Retain this as the main Canadian emergence episode but clarify geography and statistics. Rewrote the countries and event summary fields to distinguish provinces with documented human disease (Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, Manitoba) from provinces with only tick detections (e.g., Prince Edward Island), and to avoid overstating the scope of the often‑quoted figure of 21 Canadian cases, which applies specifically to Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. Kept the event type as re_emergence, reflecting the role of deer tick virus and expanding Ixodes scapularis range, and left the start year at 1994 while treating late‑1980s Atlantic Canada cases as historical context. Recommend expert review of precise provincial timelines, which remain partially approximate due to limited and dispersed case reports.

Countries: United States of America [2011] (Northeast and Great Lakes states including New York, Massachusetts, Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, and others)
Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis, Ixodes cookei); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: From 2011 through 2020, the United States experienced a marked increase in reported Powassan virus disease, with 194 human cases reported nationally over the decade, of which about 92% were neuroinvasive and 10%–15% resulted in death. Most cases occurred in the Northeast and Great Lakes regions, particularly Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York and neighboring states, reflecting multiple established foci linked to deer tick virus and blacklegged tick expansion. The episode persisted through 2020 with year‑to‑year variability but generally much higher case counts than in previous decades, indicating that Powassan virus had transitioned from an obscure curiosity to a recognized, though still rare, emerging arboviral threat in these regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued geographic and numerical expansion of Ixodes scapularis populations driven by climate change (warmer winters, longer tick seasons), reforestation, and abundant deer hosts; higher human outdoor exposure; improved clinician awareness and routine testing for arboviral causes of encephalitis; national notifiable disease reporting through ArboNET. Internal mechanisms: established enzootic cycles of Powassan lineage II in deer ticks and rodent hosts enabling sustained geographic range expansion while maintaining high neuroinvasiveness and virulence in humans (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – This decade‑long episode captures the major sustained increase in U.S. Powassan virus disease (194 cases, predominantly neuroinvasive). Corrected the event‑type coding so that it is classified as re_occurrence only, rather than both re_occurrence and re_emergence, in line with project rules that categories should be mutually exclusive except when re_emergence co‑occurs with inter/intra‑continental emergence. The period is characterized mainly by expansion and intensification of an already‑established deer tick virus cycle and greater detection, not by the appearance of a new lineage. Case counts and severity metrics are consistent with CDC and EID summaries; no geographic corrections were required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2023] (11 states in Northeast and upper Midwest – including Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York, Massachusetts, Maine and others)
Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis, Ixodes cookei); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: In 2023, U.S. national surveillance reported 49 Powassan virus disease cases from 11 states, at that time the highest annual number since Powassan became a separately reportable condition in 2004 and representing a sharp increase compared with most previous years. Cases were concentrated in northeastern and Great Lakes states where blacklegged ticks are abundant and overlapping Lyme disease risk is high, and most were neuroinvasive, contributing to substantial morbidity and several fatalities. Although numbers rose further in 2024, 2023 marked the first clear nationwide peak in the ongoing emergence of Powassan virus disease and prompted renewed public health messaging and clinical alerts about this rare but severe tick‑borne flavivirus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: record‑high densities and broad geographic distribution of Ixodes scapularis in the northeastern and upper Midwestern U.S., likely amplified by continued climate warming, changing wildlife communities, and increased human–tick contact; strengthened surveillance and diagnostic capacity capturing more neuroinvasive and some non‑neuroinvasive cases; concurrent public and clinician concern about tick‑borne diseases leading to more testing. Internal mechanisms: well‑established deer tick virus lineages maintaining efficient transmission in I. scapularis and causing severe neuroinvasive disease, with no evidence of attenuation (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Retain 2023 as a distinct emergence event because it is the first year with a pronounced national peak (49 cases across 11 states) documented in MMWR, but update its interpretation and classification. Changed the event type to re_occurrence only (removing re_emergence) and clarified that 2023 represented the highest annual count at that time, recognizing that 2024 subsequently surpassed it. No changes to geographic scope were required; sources now emphasize the 2023 arboviral surveillance summary and CDC historic data. This row should be evaluated together with the new 2024 event to confirm that both are among the top ten highest‑impact episodes for this pathogen.

Countries: United States of America [2024] (10 states in Northeast and upper Midwest – Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Wisconsin)
Host: Humans; ticks (Ixodes scapularis, Ixodes cookei); small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: In 2024, national ArboNET surveillance recorded 60 Powassan virus disease cases across 10 U.S. states, surpassing 2023 and representing the highest annual total reported since standardized surveillance began in 2004; at least nine deaths were documented, underscoring the virus’s high neuroinvasive case‑fatality rate. Cases again clustered in the northeastern and upper Midwestern states—particularly Minnesota (14 cases), Wisconsin (12), Massachusetts (11) and Maine (6)—where established deer tick virus foci overlap intensively with Lyme disease risk. This record‑high year confirmed that Powassan virus had become a persistent, regionally entrenched zoonosis with periodically high incidence, rather than a sporadic curiosity, and reinforced the need for expanded tick control, clinician awareness and diagnostic capacity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued expansion and very high densities of Ixodes scapularis populations in the Northeast and upper Midwest driven by climate warming, suburban reforestation and abundant deer and rodent hosts; sustained public and clinician awareness of tick‑borne diseases leading to more frequent arboviral testing; and systematic national reporting through ArboNET, which highlighted Powassan virus alongside West Nile virus and other arboviruses. Internal mechanisms: stable, well‑adapted deer tick virus (Powassan lineage II) lineages maintained in blacklegged tick–rodent cycles across multiple states, enabling efficient spillover to humans without evidence of attenuation (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – New event added to capture the 2024 record year, when 60 Powassan virus disease cases and nine deaths were reported from 10 U.S. states, exceeding the 2023 peak. Classified as re_occurrence, reflecting intensification of incidence in existing endemic foci rather than spread to a new continent or sub‑region or the emergence of a new lineage. Geographic coverage and state‑level counts are drawn from the national ArboNET table reproduced in the 2024 West Nile/arboviral update; the event clearly ranks among the most impactful Powassan episodes by case burden and severity and should be retained as one of the top events for this EPP.

Host: Humans (neuroinvasive encephalitis cases), with underlying transmission in passerine birds and Culex mosquitoes
Event summary: During 25 weeks in 1990–1991, central and south Florida experienced a major epidemic of St. Louis encephalitis, with approximately 222 laboratory‑diagnosed human cases and at least 14 deaths, representing the last large, classic SLEV outbreak in the United States. The epidemic developed over the late summer and autumn as intense bird–mosquito transmission in rural citrus groves and nearby communities led to widespread human neuroinvasive disease, particularly among older adults. Aggressive mosquito control, public health education to reduce evening outdoor exposure, and the seasonal decline in vector populations helped end transmission by early 1991, after which SLEV activity returned to low, sporadic levels in Florida.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A combination of climatic conditions (wet–dry rainfall cycles followed by heavy summer rains), expansion of flood‑irrigated citrus agriculture, and high densities of Culex nigripalpus and susceptible avian hosts created ideal conditions for explosive amplification and human spillover during 1990–1991. External factors such as land‑use change and mosquito habitat creation in irrigation furrows were key drivers, consistent with a re‑occurrence of an endemic lineage. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel SLEV genotype or major phenotypic shift was found; the epidemic is best interpreted as amplification of established lineage II strains, driven by environmental and demographic factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – updated Event Year to 1990–1991 to match the documented 25‑week Florida epidemic spanning late 1990 into early 1991 and clarified that approximately 222 laboratory‑diagnosed cases occurred across 28 counties. Replaced a generic ScienceDirect overview with the Florida‑specific epidemic analysis (Meehan et al. 2000) while retaining US‑wide and re‑emergence reviews; classification as re‑occurrence in an already endemic sub‑region without evidence of a new genotype remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (neuroinvasive encephalitis), with supporting evidence of transmission in local birds and Culex mosquitoes
Event summary: In August 2001, an outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis centered on Monroe and West Monroe, Louisiana, led to about 63 reported human cases and prompted a state emergency alert. The epidemic evolved rapidly over several weeks during peak mosquito season, with many cases recognized only after substantial transmission had already occurred. Intensified vector control, public health messaging to reduce evening mosquito exposure, and seasonal declines in mosquito abundance brought the outbreak under control by late summer, after which SLEV activity in Louisiana again became sporadic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warm, humid late‑summer conditions and abundant Culex quinquefasciatus breeding habitats in urban and peri‑urban areas, combined with delayed recognition of the outbreak and limited prior immunity in older adults, facilitated sustained transmission before control measures were escalated. Internal mechanisms: Available reports and molecular data do not indicate emergence of a distinct new genotype or strain; the event reflects ecological amplification of endemic virus rather than virologically driven re‑emergence, consistent with classification as a re‑occurrence.
Review: review – event timing and location (Monroe area, Ouachita Parish, Louisiana, 2001) and a scale of roughly 63 human cases agree with Louisiana Department of Health descriptions; classification as a re‑occurrence in an already endemic sub‑region without evidence of a novel strain is appropriate. Replaced Wikipedia with the state Saint Louis encephalitis manual while retaining Louisiana morbidity and annual reports as primary documentation, which strengthens source quality.

Host: Humans (encephalitis and meningoencephalitis), Culex pipiens/quinquefasciatus complex mosquitoes, local wild and domestic birds
Event summary: From January to May 2005, Córdoba Province, Argentina, experienced the first large documented outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis in the country, with 47 laboratory‑confirmed and probable human cases and nine deaths after decades of only sporadic detections. The outbreak began with clusters of neurologic disease in Córdoba City and spread through urban neighborhoods as infected Culex mosquitoes amplified genotype III SLEV in naïve bird populations. Intensive vector control, public advisories to reduce mosquito exposure, and the seasonal decline in mosquito abundance ended the outbreak by late autumn, although virologic and serologic studies showed that SLEV continued to circulate silently in birds and mosquitoes in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban expansion, local environmental conditions conducive to Culex breeding, and high densities of susceptible eared doves and other urban‑adapted birds facilitated explosive amplification once genotype III SLEV was introduced; limited prior human awareness and surveillance delayed recognition of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses identified re‑emergence of genotype III SLEV in Córdoba after at least 26 years of absence, and experimental work showed higher virulence and higher viremias in birds and mice compared with non‑epidemic strains, consistent with re‑emergence driven by a more pathogenic genotype.
Review: retain – event timing, location (Córdoba Province, Argentina), case and death counts, and characterization as re‑emergence driven by introduction of a more virulent genotype III strain are consistent across CDC and peer‑reviewed sources; no corrections to geography or event‑type coding are needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (encephalitis cases), Culex mosquitoes and local birds as transmission reservoirs
Event summary: In 2006, following the 2005 Córdoba epidemic, a new outbreak of Saint Louis encephalitis was reported in Paraná Province, Argentina, indicating spread of the emergent Argentine genotype III SLEV lineage into additional central regions. Neurologic cases occurred in residents after the summer mosquito season began, with epidemiologic evidence supporting local bird–mosquito amplification rather than isolated importations from Córdoba. Strengthened vector control, heightened clinical awareness, and the seasonal decline in mosquito populations brought the outbreak under control within the same season, confirming that the genotype III lineage had become established more broadly in central Argentina.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional bird movements and possible movement of infected vectors or hosts from Córdoba, along with warm, humid conditions and standing water that supported Culex populations, facilitated geographic spread to Paraná Province; human disease reflected spillover after enzootic cycles were established. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak is attributed to the same re‑emergent, more virulent genotype III lineage first identified in Córdoba, representing geographic expansion of an epidemic genotype with enhanced fitness in local ecological settings rather than de novo evolution in Paraná.
Review: retain – recognition of a 2006 outbreak in Paraná Province linked to the post‑2005 genotype III lineage, location within Argentina’s central region, and classification as re‑emergence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) are consistent with CDC and PAHO syntheses; case numbers remain incompletely documented but the event clearly qualifies as one of the major Argentine SLEV outbreaks after 2005.

Countries: Argentina (Buenos Aires Province [2010]; Córdoba Province [2010]; San Juan Province [2011])
Host: Humans (encephalitis and febrile neurologic disease), Culex mosquitoes, urban and peri‑urban birds (e.g., pigeons, sparrows, domestic fowl)
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2011, Argentina experienced a series of Saint Louis encephalitis outbreaks beyond Córdoba and Paraná, including confirmed clusters in Buenos Aires Province and the Andean province of San Juan, demonstrating multi‑provincial re‑emergence of SLEV as a human neurologic pathogen. In 2010, SLEV cases were detected in Buenos Aires and other central provinces during the warm season, and in early 2011 at least seven human cases were confirmed in San Juan, prompting provincial alerts and intensified vector‑control recommendations. Coordinated national and provincial mosquito‑control campaigns, public communication on personal protection, and seasonal declines in mosquito populations curtailed these outbreaks, but subsequent serologic and entomologic work indicated continued low‑level viral circulation in central Argentina.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued regional circulation of genotype III SLEV in birds and mosquitoes from earlier central‑Argentina outbreaks, urbanization, and climatic conditions favorable to Culex vectors promoted spread into densely populated Buenos Aires and more arid San Juan; human travel and movement of birds likely facilitated seeding of new foci. Internal mechanisms: The same re‑emergent genotype III lineage, associated with higher virulence, underpinned these outbreaks, representing ongoing geographic range expansion and repeated re‑emergence of a more pathogenic strain across multiple Argentine provinces rather than independent emergence of novel genotypes in each locality.
Review: retain – the 2010–2011 multi‑provincial Argentine outbreaks (Buenos Aires and San Juan) are correctly represented as linked re‑emergence of genotype III within Argentina, with appropriate timing, geography, and event‑type coding; sources from PAHO, national press, and CDC syntheses adequately support inclusion as one of the major SLEV emergence episodes since 1990.

Countries: Brazil (São José do Rio Preto, São Paulo State [2006])
Host: Humans (dengue‑like febrile illness, meningoencephalitis, and hemorrhagic manifestations), Culex mosquitoes, local birds in an urban setting with intense concurrent dengue transmission
Event summary: In the first half of 2006, during a large dengue virus serotype 3 outbreak in São José do Rio Preto (northwest São Paulo State, Brazil), investigators identified the first recognized community outbreak of Saint Louis encephalitis in the country, detecting SLEV RNA in six patients whose serum or cerebrospinal fluid had initially tested negative for dengue and yellow fever viruses. These SLEV‑infected patients presented with dengue‑like febrile illness, including three cases of viral meningoencephalitis and three with hemorrhagic signs, revealing that SLEV was co‑circulating with dengue in a densely populated urban center. As the dengue epidemic waned, vector control efforts intensified and arboviral transmission declined, but the outbreak highlighted that SLEV infections in Brazil were being missed and that SLEV could cause both neurologic and hemorrhagic disease during large arboviral seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high levels of dengue virus transmission (>15,000 suspected dengue cases) and associated vector control efforts focused primarily on Aedes aegypti created a context in which other arboviruses, including SLEV transmitted by Culex species, circulated largely unrecognized; urban crowding and year‑round mosquito breeding in water‑holding containers facilitated human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization indicated that the Brazilian outbreak strains were closely related to SLEV genotype V, which had been present in South America for decades; no clear evidence of a novel variant was identified. The episode is therefore best interpreted as re‑occurrence of pathogenic genotype V in humans, with clinical recognition improved by molecular diagnostics, rather than emergence of a new SLEV genotype.
Review: review – newly added event capturing the 2006 São José do Rio Preto community outbreak in Brazil, which primary sources describe as the first documented SLEV outbreak in the country with six RT‑PCR–confirmed human cases (three meningoencephalitis, three with hemorrhagic signs) during a large dengue‑3 epidemic. Classified as re‑occurrence (rather than first detection or inter‑continental emergence) because SLEV and human infections were already known from Brazil; the key impact is the shift from isolated infections to a recognizable outbreak and demonstration of hemorrhagic manifestations.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America (Arizona – Maricopa County [2015])
Host: Humans (23 confirmed infections, predominantly neuroinvasive disease), Culex mosquitoes, wild and peridomestic birds
Event summary: In summer 2015, Maricopa County, Arizona, experienced a notable outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis with 23 confirmed human cases, most neuroinvasive, and at least one to two deaths, occurring concurrently with a large West Nile virus outbreak. The outbreak began in July with detection of SLEV‑positive mosquito pools and rapidly progressed to clusters of human encephalitis cases in metropolitan Phoenix as a newly introduced genotype III lineage, closely related to Argentine strains, amplified in local bird–mosquito cycles. Intensive vector‑control interventions, public health messaging, and the seasonal decline of mosquito populations by October curtailed transmission, but subsequent phylogeographic work showed that the introduced genotype III lineage persisted and seeded onward spread across the western United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban heat islands, irrigated landscapes, and abundant Culex vectors and avian hosts in metropolitan Phoenix, together with low recent human exposure to SLEV, created favorable conditions for amplification once the virus was introduced; co‑circulation with West Nile virus underscored shared ecological drivers and strained surveillance systems. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing demonstrated that the Arizona outbreak strain belonged to genotype III, previously restricted to Argentina, representing cross‑continental introduction of a more virulent lineage with evidence of enhanced neuroinvasiveness and efficient transmission in local vectors and hosts, consistent with re‑emergence via novel genotype introduction rather than resurgence of historical US strains.
Review: retain – the 2015 Maricopa County outbreak is correctly dated, geographically located, and described in terms of human impact (~23 confirmed cases, including transplant‑associated infections) and linkage to an introduced genotype III lineage of South American origin; classification as re‑emergence via novel genotype introduction, without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence at the species level, is appropriate and well supported by phylogeographic analyses.

Countries: United States of America (California [2015]; Nevada [2015]; extended detections in California through 2020)
Host: Humans (sporadic neuroinvasive cases including a fatal Kern County case), Culex tarsalis and Culex quinquefasciatus mosquitoes, wild and sentinel birds (e.g., house finches, house sparrows, chickens)
Event summary: After an 11‑year apparent absence of detectable activity, St. Louis encephalitis virus reappeared in California in 2015, with SLEV‑positive mosquito pools and sentinel chicken seroconversions first detected in Riverside County’s Coachella Valley, concurrent with the Arizona outbreak and accompanied by detections in neighboring Nevada. Over 2015–2020, SLEV spread northward within California, with repeated detections in mosquitoes and sentinel chickens and sporadic human cases, including a fatal neuroinvasive infection in Kern County in 2016. Sustained vector surveillance, targeted larval and adult mosquito control, and public communication about personal protection limited human disease to relatively small numbers each year, although enzootic transmission of the introduced genotype III lineage became established across much of southern and central California.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive irrigated agriculture and urban water management in California’s Central Valley and southern deserts provided ideal habitats for Culex tarsalis and Cx. quinquefasciatus, while high densities of susceptible passerine birds supported enzootic amplification; long‑term surveillance focused on West Nile virus may initially have reduced sensitivity to SLEV reintroduction. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that all post‑2015 California SLEV isolates belonged to genotype III, closely related to 2005 Córdoba and 2014 Argentine mosquito isolates and to Arizona 2015 outbreak viruses, indicating re‑emergence via introduction of a South American genotype with traits supporting efficient transmission and long‑distance dispersal in western US ecosystems.
Review: retain – the 2015–2020 California (and associated Nevada) re‑emergence episode is correctly described as re‑introduction and sustained circulation of genotype III SLEV after extirpation from the state, with accurate timing, geography, and emphasis on the 2016 fatal Kern County case; classification solely as re‑emergence, without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, is appropriate.

Countries: United States of America (Arizona [2015]; California [2015]; Nevada [2015]; Texas [2015]; Idaho [2017]; Oregon [2017])
Host: Primarily birds (wild passerines and sentinel chickens) and Culex mosquitoes, with scattered human neuroinvasive cases documented in some western states
Event summary: Following its identification as the cause of a 2015 outbreak in Maricopa County, Arizona, a South American‑derived genotype III St. Louis encephalitis virus lineage spread across the western United States between 2015 and 2018, with first detections in mosquito pools in southeastern California and southern Nevada in 2015 and subsequent spread into central California, Texas, Idaho, and Oregon. This expansion unfolded over several transmission seasons as infected migratory birds and locally dispersing Culex mosquitoes seeded new enzootic foci, which were detected mainly through mosquito and sentinel bird surveillance rather than large human outbreaks. By 2018, molecular and surveillance data indicated that the introduced genotype III lineage had established persistent transmission across much of the arid and semi‑arid western US, after which its geographic range appeared to stabilize under ongoing vector‑control and arbovirus‑surveillance programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of infected migratory birds along western flyways, local dispersal of Culex vectors, and suitable climates and irrigated landscapes across western states enabled progressive colonization of new areas; sustained arboviral surveillance in mosquitoes and sentinel chickens was crucial to detecting spread before major human epidemics occurred. Internal mechanisms: Phylogeographic analyses demonstrated that all western US post‑2015 SLEV genomes clustered within the Argentine‑derived genotype III lineage introduced into Arizona, with rapid radiation into multiple clades and three main dispersal routes (Arizona to southern California, to central California, and to regions east of the Sierra Nevada), consistent with a successful, more fit genotype undergoing geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission in new ecological settings.
Review: review – corrected intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No because the expansion occurred entirely within the existing UN sub‑region Northern America, where SLEV had long been established, so this episode represents re‑emergence and geographic range expansion of genotype III rather than first occurrence in a new sub‑region. Updated the country‑level timing string to reflect genomic surveillance data (Texas first genotype III detection in 2015; Idaho and Oregon detections in 2017) and note that introduction into Arizona likely occurred by late 2014 even though the main outbreak and subsequent multi‑state spread were recognized from 2015 onward.

Host: Humans (febrile illness with rash and jaundice)
Event summary: In 2004, Usutu virus infection was confirmed in a 10‑year‑old patient in Burkina Faso who presented with fever, rash and jaundice, representing the first recognized human infection in Western Africa and the second documented human case globally after the 1981 Central African Republic case. The episode appears to have been a single sporadic zoonotic spillover detected through virological testing in the context of broader arbovirus studies, with no evidence of onward human transmission or additional recognized cases in the country. No sustained human outbreak followed, although virological and serological studies show that Usutu virus continues to circulate widely in birds and mosquitoes across several African countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing enzootic circulation of Usutu virus in African bird–mosquito cycles with occasional human exposure in rural settings where Culex mosquitoes are abundant and vector control is limited. Internal mechanisms: The case was caused by an African lineage strain typical of those circulating in birds and mosquitoes; there is no evidence that this infection involved a novel, more virulent genotype relative to other African strains.
Review: review – event retained; timing (2004), geography (Burkina Faso, Western Africa) and classification as intra‑continental emergence within Africa are supported by multiple reviews that document only two African human cases (Central African Republic in the early 1980s and Burkina Faso in 2004). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6669749/?utm_source=openai)) The only change made was to replace a generic ScienceDirect topic overview with a more specific peer‑reviewed review article on Usutu virus, which better documents the African human cases; no structural changes to dates, locations or emergence‑type flags were required.

Host: Humans (neuroinvasive disease – meningitis/meningoencephalitis, mainly in patients with comorbidities or immunosuppression)
Event summary: In 2008–2009, northern Italy (Emilia‑Romagna region) experienced the first recognized cluster of human Usutu virus infections outside Africa, with multiple neuroinvasive infections retrospectively detected in cerebrospinal fluid and serum samples from patients with encephalitis or meningoencephalitis in 2008–2009 and two immunocompromised patients with severe neuroinvasive disease diagnosed in real time in Modena in 2009. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1198743X16304256?utm_source=openai)) These cases occurred in an area where Usutu virus had already caused bird mortality and co‑circulated with West Nile virus, and were identified through pan‑flavivirus PCR and sequencing applied to patients with unexplained central nervous system disease. Following this episode, Italy continued to report sporadic neuroinvasive cases and numerous asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic blood‑donor infections in subsequent seasons, indicating that the virus had established persistent enzootic transmission with recurrent low‑level human spillover.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and establishment of African Usutu virus lineages into Italian bird–mosquito populations, favoured by suitable climate, wetlands, and abundant Culex pipiens mosquitoes, with enhanced diagnostic suspicion because of concurrent West Nile virus surveillance. Internal mechanisms: European Usutu virus lineages (notably Europe 2 and Europe 4) show genetic changes in structural and non‑structural proteins associated with neurotropism and efficient replication in birds and mosquitoes, which likely facilitated neuroinvasive disease in susceptible human hosts but do not yet appear to have generated sustained human‑to‑human transmission.
Review: review – event retained as the first documented human emergence of Usutu virus in Europe, but the event year has been corrected from 2009 to 2008–2009 to include neuroinvasive infections detected retrospectively in Modena in 2008 as part of the same episode. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1198743X16304256?utm_source=openai)) The ‘first_detection’ flag was set to No because the first human detection occurred in the Central African Republic in 1981; the appropriate classification for this event is inter‑continental emergence in humans (Africa to Europe). Source URLs were expanded to include the Modena retrospective study alongside the original 2009 case reports and European overviews.

Host: Humans (neuroinvasive disease – meningoencephalitis)
Event summary: In 2013, three patients in and around Zagreb, Croatia, were diagnosed with Usutu virus neuroinvasive infection (meningoencephalitis) during a concurrent West Nile virus outbreak, representing one of the earliest small clusters of severe human Usutu disease in southern Europe after the initial Italian cases. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25361698/?utm_source=openai)) The cases occurred in areas where Usutu virus had already been detected in birds and mosquitoes and followed earlier serologic evidence of viral circulation in horses and a human resident, indicating that the virus had become established before this clinical cluster. In subsequent seasons, Croatia identified additional neuroinvasive Usutu infections, including three more cases during the large 2018 West Nile virus outbreak, but no large‑scale human epidemic was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of enzootic Usutu virus transmission in continental Croatia, facilitated by favourable summer temperatures, wetlands that support dense bird and mosquito populations, and heightened surveillance during West Nile virus outbreaks that prompted testing for other flaviviruses. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of European Usutu lineages (notably Europe 2) capable of neuroinvasion, with human cases interpreted as spillover events during periods of particularly intense epizootic transmission rather than the emergence of a wholly novel strain, so this episode is treated as re‑emergence driven by viral persistence and ecological amplification in a subregion where the virus was already present in animals.

([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25361698/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑emergence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate because prior serologic evidence in horses and a human resident shows that the virus was already present in this sub‑region, and the definitions explicitly exclude spread to a new country within the same sub‑region from the intra‑continental category. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/13/9/1856?utm_source=openai)) The main changes were to enrich the source list with the primary Croatian case reports; no structural fields (year, geography, emergence type) required correction.

Host: Humans (neurologic disease – peripheral facial palsy, atypical presentation)
Event summary: In November 2016, a 39‑year‑old man from Montpellier in southern France was hospitalized with acute peripheral facial palsy and was retrospectively diagnosed with Usutu virus infection, representing the first documented autochthonous human infection in France and an atypical neurologic presentation of this flavivirus. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/5/17-1122?utm_source=openai)) The infection was identified through retrospective molecular testing of cerebrospinal fluid samples from patients with unexplained neurologic disease in an area where Usutu virus had been detected previously in birds and mosquitoes. Following this detection, French authorities strengthened arbovirus surveillance and subsequently documented continued enzootic circulation of Usutu virus and at least one additional febrile human infection in 2022, but only sporadic human cases have been reported and no sustained human outbreak has occurred.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Westward spread and intensification of enzootic Usutu virus transmission from central and southern Europe into southern France, promoted by warm summers, expansion of Culex mosquito populations, dense peri‑urban bird populations and enhanced diagnostic awareness in neurology and infectious‑disease services. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of European Usutu virus lineages with demonstrated neurotropism, with this case illustrating that the virus can cause atypical neurologic presentations (such as isolated facial palsy) in addition to classical meningoencephalitis; lineage‑specific genetic changes associated with neuroinvasion documented in European strains may have contributed to this clinical picture.
Review: review – event retained as the first documented autochthonous human Usutu virus infection in France with an atypical neurologic presentation, but the emergence‑type classification has been updated. Because an asymptomatic human Usutu infection had already been documented in a German blood donor in 2012, Western Europe as a sub‑region was no longer naive at the time of the French case; this event therefore does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence and is now classified solely as re‑emergence in an already affected sub‑region. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233929728_Detection_of_Usutu_virus_infection_in_a_healthy_blood_donor_from_south-west_Germany_2012?utm_source=openai)) No changes were required to year, geography or host description; sources remain focused on the Montpellier case report and European syntheses.

Host: Humans (mostly asymptomatic or mild infections detected in blood donors; occasional rash or nonspecific symptoms)
Event summary: From 2016 to 2017, Austria detected multiple Usutu virus infections in blood donors through nucleic acid amplification testing aimed at West Nile virus, revealing widespread but largely silent human exposure in central Europe. In 2016, one of four flavivirus NAT‑reactive blood donations and in 2017 six of seven such donations from eastern Austria were confirmed as Usutu virus infections, all from donors residing in areas with intense enzootic circulation in birds and mosquitoes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5710119/?utm_source=openai)) These findings prompted Austrian blood services to integrate Usutu virus into their risk assessments within West Nile virus screening algorithms, and subsequent seasons showed variable but generally low frequencies of Usutu‑positive donations, largely tracking variations in mosquito abundance and avian epizootics rather than indicating a sustained increase in clinically apparent human disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑intensity enzootic Usutu virus transmission in eastern Austria during warm summers, combined with extensive blood‑donor NAT screening for West Nile virus that cross‑detected or specifically tested for Usutu virus, thereby uncovering asymptomatic human infections; land‑use patterns (wetlands and river plains) and climate variability likely amplified Culex mosquito populations. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several European Usutu virus lineages (notably Europe 2 and Africa 3) capable of efficient replication in birds and mosquitoes, leading to frequent low‑level human spillover; most infected donors remained asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic, suggesting that genetic changes were associated more with transmission efficiency and overwintering than with a marked increase in virulence in humans.
Review: review – event retained to represent the substantial cluster of asymptomatic Usutu‑positive blood donations in Austria, but its scope and classification were corrected. The episode is now restricted to Austria, with Hungary moved to the 2018 multi‑country event, and the sub‑region set to Western Europe only. Year annotations for the country have been kept as Austria [2016] to reflect the start of donor infections, but the emphasis in the summary is on 2016–2017 when most cases were detected. Because Western Europe already had a documented human infection in Germany in 2012, this Austrian episode has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence to re‑emergence linked to intensifying enzootic circulation and systematic donor screening. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233929728_Detection_of_Usutu_virus_infection_in_a_healthy_blood_donor_from_south-west_Germany_2012?utm_source=openai)) Source URLs were replaced with primary reports on Austrian donor screening and ECDC synthesis documents.

Event summary: In 2018, Europe experienced a marked amplification of Usutu virus activity, with human infections documented in several countries including Italy, the Netherlands, Croatia, Hungary and Czechia, making this the largest recognized multi‑country episode of human Usutu infection to date. In northern Italy, eight cases (one neuroinvasive, six febrile and one viremic blood donor) were identified through targeted diagnostics and blood‑donor screening; Croatia detected three additional neuroinvasive cases during a large West Nile virus outbreak; Hungary confirmed its first human Usutu infection in a patient with aseptic meningitis; and the Netherlands identified seven RNA‑positive blood donors during West Nile virus screening. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31771697/?utm_source=openai)) This episode coincided with exceptional epizootic transmission and large‑scale bird mortality across central and western Europe, and after 2018 human detections continued at lower but persistent levels, reflecting established enzootic circulation and ongoing, though still relatively rare, human spillover events.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptionally warm summer conditions in 2018 that enhanced Culex mosquito abundance and competence, synchronized epizootics in wild and captive birds across much of Europe, and widespread blood‑donor NAT screening for arboviruses that increased detection sensitivity; land‑use factors (urban green spaces, river valleys, irrigated agriculture) and overlapping West Nile virus surveillance also contributed to increased ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple European Usutu virus lineages (notably Europe 2 and Europe 1) with demonstrated capacity for geographic expansion and overwintering in local mosquito populations supported broad range expansion within Europe, while lineage‑specific differences in neurovirulence (for example, Europe 2 strains over‑represented among severe infections in Italy, Croatia, Hungary and Czechia) likely contributed to the observed spectrum of neuroinvasive disease.
Review: review – event retained as the principal 2018 multi‑country amplification episode but edited to align with the documented pattern of human infections. Countries now listed (Italy, Netherlands, Croatia, Hungary, Czechia) all have confirmed 2018 human cases, while Belgium, Germany and France were removed because, to date, Belgium has only animal infections and German (2012, 2016) and French (2016) human cases occurred in earlier years. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10436690/?utm_source=openai)) Sub‑regions were corrected to Southern, Western and Eastern Europe, and the episode is now classified as both intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed human infections in Eastern Europe – Hungary and Czechia) and re‑emergence within already affected southern and western sub‑regions. Source URLs were replaced with primary reports on 2018 human cases (Italy, Croatia, Hungary, Czechia, Netherlands) and the ECDC EU/EEA synthesis.

Host: Humans (hantavirus pulmonary syndrome / hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome)
Event summary: In early 1995, physicians in El Bolsón, Río Negro Province, southern Argentina, recognized a cluster of severe respiratory illness consistent with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, and laboratory testing of autopsy tissue from one patient identified a novel hantavirus—later named Andes virus—as the etiologic agent. The event consisted of a small but severe outbreak centered in rural Andean Patagonia, prompting heightened surveillance, rodent investigations, and genetic characterization of the virus in humans and long‑tailed pygmy rice rats (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus). After this initial cluster subsided, Andes virus remained established in local rodent reservoirs and continued to cause sporadic and clustered human infections in Patagonia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased clinical awareness and expanded laboratory capacity for hantavirus pulmonary syndrome after the 1993 Four Corners outbreak in the United States facilitated recognition of similar severe disease in Patagonia; human encroachment into rodent habitats and agricultural/rural activities in the Andean forest ecotone increased opportunities for zoonotic exposure. Internal mechanisms: This event represents the first recognized spillover of an already circulating Andes virus lineage into humans rather than the emergence of a new genotype; no specific genetic changes were uniquely associated with the initial 1995 cluster.
Review: retain – Event correctly represents the first recognized Andes virus–associated HPS cases in El Bolsón in 1995, with appropriate designation as both first_global_emergence and first_detection and accurate placement in South America/South America; sources confirm timing, location, and etiologic characterization, and no earlier confirmed Andes virus event in humans with greater impact was identified.

Host: Humans (HPS)
Event summary: From September 22 to December 5, 1996, a large outbreak of Andes virus–associated HPS occurred among residents and visitors in El Bolsón, San Carlos de Bariloche, Esquel, and, via patient transfer, Buenos Aires, Argentina, following the 1995 recognition of the virus in the region. At least 18–20 epidemiologically linked cases were identified, including household contacts and health‑care workers, and molecular and epidemiologic evidence showed that many cases were connected by chains of person‑to‑person transmission rather than independent rodent exposures. The outbreak ended after isolation of cases, reinforcement of infection‑control practices, and public health interventions, after which only sporadic and smaller clusters continued to occur in southern Argentina.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close household contact, provision of care without adequate respiratory protection, and movement of infectious patients between towns and to Buenos Aires enabled human‑to‑human spread; ongoing rural exposures to infected Oligoryzomys longicaudatus rodents maintained background risk. Internal mechanisms: Sequence analysis identified a specific Epilink/96 strain of Andes virus associated with efficient person‑to‑person transmission during the prodromal phase, consistent with enhanced transmission capability (and possibly increased virulence) relative to more typical purely zoonotic hantavirus infections, and justifying classification as re‑emergence driven by viral lineage characteristics.
Review: retain – This is a well‑documented, high‑impact outbreak (≈18–20 cases) with the first confirmed person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus in Argentina; timing, geography and case numbers match primary reports, and classifying it as re_emergence (linked to the Epilink/96 strain with enhanced human‑to‑human transmission) is consistent with the project’s definition of re‑emergence driven by internal viral changes.

Host: Humans (HPS)
Event summary: In October 1995, Chile detected its first confirmed case of Andes virus infection in a patient from southern Chile (Cochamó, Los Lagos Region), shortly after virus identification in neighboring Argentina, marking the recognition of HPS in the country. Between July 1997 and January 1998, a substantial outbreak of 25 Andes virus–associated HPS cases, plus several mild and asymptomatic infections, occurred mainly in Regions X (Llanquihue) and XI (Aysén), including three family clusters with suspected limited person‑to‑person spread. The outbreak declined by early 1998 as rodent populations decreased and public health measures were implemented, establishing Andes virus as the principal cause of HPS in Chile with continuing sporadic and seasonal cases thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural and peridomestic exposures in Nothofagus forest and agricultural landscapes with high densities of Oligoryzomys longicaudatus and other sigmodontine rodents, combined with improved case recognition and enhanced national surveillance, led to detection of both the first Chilean case and the 1997–1998 outbreak; regional rodent "irruptions" related to bamboo flowering and favorable climatic conditions likely amplified human contact rates. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate that Chilean cases were caused by Andes virus lineages already circulating across southern Argentina and Chile rather than a distinct new genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as geographic recognition and amplification of an existing virus rather than emergence of a fundamentally altered strain.
Review: review – Corrected this row to (i) change the event year from 1997–1998 to 1995–1998 to cover both the first recognized Chilean HPS case in 1995 and the subsequent 1997–1998 southern Chile outbreak, and (ii) simplify the countries field from "Chile [1995], Argentina [1995]" to "Chile [1995]" because the linked Argentine cases are already captured in separate Argentina‑focused events; also set first_detection from true to false so that first_detection is reserved for the 1995 global emergence in Argentina, and left all emergence‑type flags as false since spread from Argentina to Chile occurs within the same South America–South America subregion and does not meet the project criteria for intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. These corrections align the row with UN subregion rules and outbreak descriptions from Chilean and CDC sources.
