Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rising burden of chronic diseases and immunosuppression in Saudi Arabia; expansion of tertiary‑care ICUs and oncology services with extensive device use and antibiotic exposure; initially limited awareness of Morganella as a significant pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance – frequent multidrug resistance in isolates complicating therapy; Enhanced Transmission – adaptation to ICU and hospital environments and to indwelling devices; Host Expansion – increasing prominence in critically ill and severely immunocompromised adults.
Review: retain: Event correctly summarizes the multicenter Saudi Arabian series of 75 Morganella morganii bloodstream infections (2015–2022). Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate, as the signal is a substantial burden of severe opportunistic infection in existing healthcare settings rather than expansion to new regions or a clearly new resistance mechanism. No geographic or temporal corrections were needed; the main refinement opportunity would be to specify more precisely the distribution of sources (urinary vs intra-abdominal vs skin/soft tissue) if desired.

Host: Humans (hospitalized patient with clinical infection due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: In 1992, a clinical Proteus mirabilis isolate from a human patient in the United States was found to produce TEM‑10, an extended‑spectrum β‑lactamase (ESBL), marking the first report of TEM‑10 production by this species and the first documented ESBL-producing P. mirabilis isolate recovered in the USA. The resistant strain was recovered during routine clinical microbiology and showed resistance to extended‑spectrum cephalosporins. Its characterization demonstrated that P. mirabilis could acquire ESBL determinants previously known from other Enterobacterales, foreshadowing broader ESBL dissemination in this species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing use of extended‑spectrum cephalosporins and other broad‑spectrum β‑lactams in US hospitals in the late 1980s and early 1990s created selection pressure for ESBL‑producing Enterobacterales, including Proteus mirabilis. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition and expression of a TEM‑10 ESBL gene on a mobile element by P. mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – ESBL production conferred resistance to extended‑spectrum cephalosporins and reduced susceptibility to other β‑lactams, narrowing treatment options.
Review: Review – Event is real and scientifically important as the first documented ESBL-producing Proteus mirabilis in the USA. However, it is a single‑isolate report and may be borderline in terms of inclusion among the ten most impactful events. Classification has been corrected from First detection=Yes to First detection=No and Re‑emergence=Yes to align with the definition that first_detection should refer to first description of the EPP in the human host system (which pre‑dates 1990), while acquisition of an ESBL determinant reflects re‑emergence via a novel resistant genotype.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (hospitalized, long‑term‑care, and some community patients with urinary tract and other infections caused by CMY‑type AmpC-producing Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: Between 1999 and 2008, a multidrug‑resistant Proteus mirabilis clone carrying chromosomal CMY‑type AmpC β‑lactamases of Citrobacter freundii origin (notably CMY‑16 and related variants) emerged and spread across multiple European countries, with earliest detections in Poland in 1999 and subsequent expansion to northern Italy and Greece from 2003 onwards. A focused investigation at an Italian hospital in Varese from 2004–2006 found that 43 of 2,070 P. mirabilis clinical isolates (prevalence rising from 0.3% to 4.6%) produced acquired AmpC‑type cephalosporinases, all harboring CMY‑16 and showing clonal relatedness, and similar CMY‑type chromosomal cephalosporinases were documented in Poland and Greece. This European‑wide clone caused difficult‑to‑treat urinary and other infections in elderly and fragile patients, and its persistent circulation over nearly a decade represented one of the largest documented emergence events of AmpC‑mediated cephalosporin resistance in P. mirabilis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Sustained use of third‑generation cephalosporins and other broad‑spectrum β‑lactams in European hospitals and long‑term‑care facilities favored selection and maintenance of AmpC‑producing Proteus mirabilis; high antibiotic pressure in elderly and chronically ill patient populations provided a niche for establishment of multidrug‑resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition of blaCMY‑type AmpC genes (especially CMY‑16) from Citrobacter freundii via ISEcp1-associated transposition modules (Tn6093), followed by stable chromosomal integration and clonal expansion; Antimicrobial Resistance – AmpC production conferred high‑level resistance to most penicillins and expanded‑spectrum cephalosporins and reduced susceptibility to β‑lactam/β‑lactamase inhibitor combinations; Enhanced Transmission – a successful CMY‑16‑producing P. mirabilis clone disseminated across multiple hospitals and countries in Europe.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the Europe‑wide clonal spread of CMY‑type AmpC-producing P. mirabilis (especially CMY‑16) documented between 1999 and 2008 in Poland, Italy and Greece, and associated with a substantial, measurable increase in cephalosporin resistance prevalence and dozens of clinical infections. This is clearly among the most impactful emergence episodes for Proteus spp. in humans and was missing from the original dataset. Classified as Re‑emergence=Yes (acquisition of a new cephalosporinase lineage and clonal expansion) without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence, because the species was already established in Europe and the event reflects evolution and spread of a resistant clone rather than first geographic presence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (hospital inpatients with urinary tract, wound, respiratory, bloodstream and other infections due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: Around 2001–2002, a one‑year survey at San Matteo Hospital in Pavia, northern Italy, found that 52% (147/282) of consecutive non‑duplicate Proteus mirabilis clinical isolates produced β‑lactamases, and 70 isolates (approximately 25% of all isolates) produced extended‑spectrum β‑lactamases (ESBLs). The ESBLs were identified as PER‑1 and TEM‑52, with PER‑1 reported for the first time in P. mirabilis, and clonal and plasmid analyses showed hospital‑wide dissemination of these ESBL‑producing strains. This represented a major local shift in epidemiology, with sustained circulation of multidrug‑resistant P. mirabilis causing frequent urinary and other nosocomial infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy use of expanded‑spectrum cephalosporins and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics in a large Italian tertiary‑care hospital promoted selection and persistence of ESBL‑producing lineages; nosocomial transmission, facilitated by urinary catheters, invasive procedures and cross‑ward patient movement, supported spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – first detection of PER‑1 ESBL in P. mirabilis and widespread TEM‑52 producers; Antimicrobial Resistance – plasmid‑borne ESBL genes and associated determinants generated multidrug‑resistant phenotypes; Enhanced Transmission – successful ESBL‑producing clones and conjugative plasmids disseminated across multiple wards and infection sites.
Review: Review – Event is well supported and clearly represents one of the largest documented ESBL outbreaks in P. mirabilis (70 ESBL-producing isolates in a single year with hospital‑wide spread). Classification has been adjusted from First detection=Yes to First detection=No and interpreted as Re‑emergence=Yes, reflecting emergence of new ESBL genotypes within an already established human pathogen rather than first detection of Proteus spp. in humans.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (community‑onset and hospital‑associated infections due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: In the early‑to‑mid 2000s, Proteus mirabilis strains carrying the blaVIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase (MBL) gene were identified in Greece, including an early cerebrospinal fluid isolate from 2003 and multiple clinical isolates from 2005–2006, representing the first descriptions of VIM‑1 carbapenemase production in this species. Subsequent prospective surveillance documented clonal VIM‑1‑positive P. mirabilis isolates causing community‑onset infections in outpatients as well as hospital‑associated cases, demonstrating transmission outside intensive‑care units and beyond hospital confines. This episode marked a transition from sporadic carbapenemase producers to wider dissemination of MBL‑mediated carbapenem resistance in P. mirabilis within southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive carbapenem use to treat ESBL‑producing Enterobacterales and endemic VIM‑1‑producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Greek hospitals created strong selection pressure for MBL‑producing strains; gaps in infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship allowed spread into non‑ICU wards and the community. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – first acquisition of blaVIM‑1 by Proteus mirabilis via a transferable plasmid; Antimicrobial Resistance – VIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase conferred high‑level carbapenem resistance, often combined with ESBLs and other resistance genes; Enhanced Transmission – a successful VIM‑1‑producing clone spread among hospitalized patients and community outpatients, expanding the resistant population beyond its initial niche.
Review: Review – Data support this as the first well‑documented VIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase emergence in P. mirabilis with confirmed community transmission in Greece, making it a high‑impact resistance event. Classification has been revised from First detection=Yes to First detection=No, with Re‑emergence=Yes to reflect appearance of a new carbapenemase genotype in an established pathogen rather than first detection of Proteus infection in humans.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (hospitalized adult with bloodstream infection due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: In 2008, a 53‑year‑old diabetic patient in the United States developed a bloodstream infection caused by Proteus mirabilis that was resistant to imipenem, meropenem, and ertapenem; molecular testing demonstrated carriage of the plasmid‑mediated blaKPC‑2 carbapenemase gene. The isolate displayed markedly elevated carbapenem MICs, and transfer of its plasmid to Escherichia coli conferred carbapenem resistance, confirming functional KPC‑2 activity. This case is regarded as the first reported instance of KPC‑mediated carbapenem resistance in P. mirabilis and highlighted the potential for epidemic KPC plasmids, already causing major outbreaks in Klebsiella pneumoniae, to disseminate into Proteus spp. and further complicate treatment of Proteus infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of carbapenems and other β‑lactams in US tertiary‑care settings selected for KPC‑producing Enterobacterales and facilitated interspecies plasmid transfer; a high‑risk patient with poorly controlled diabetes, recent major surgery, and prior antibiotic exposure provided a favorable niche for establishment of a highly resistant strain. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition of a transmissible plasmid carrying blaKPC‑2 by P. mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – KPC‑2 confers resistance to carbapenems and most other β‑lactams and is often associated with coresistance to multiple additional classes; Enhanced Transmission – broad‑host‑range plasmids capable of moving among diverse Enterobacterales, including Proteus spp., increase the risk of future nosocomial spread even when only a single index case is initially recognized.
Review: Review – Event accurately reflects the first documented KPC‑2 carbapenemase in Proteus mirabilis and is clinically important despite being a single‑patient report. Classification has been adjusted from First detection=Yes to First detection=No and interpreted as Re‑emergence=Yes, because the event represents acquisition of a new carbapenemase gene by an established human pathogen rather than first detection of Proteus spp. in humans.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (hospitalized adult with prolonged Proteus mirabilis bacteraemia)
Event summary: By 2009, Italy reported its first clinical case of prolonged bacteraemia due to a VIM‑1‑producing Proteus mirabilis, demonstrating that metallo‑β‑lactamase‑mediated carbapenem resistance in this species had extended beyond its initial focus in Greece. The patient experienced persistent bloodstream infection caused by a blaVIM‑1‑positive P. mirabilis strain that was highly resistant to carbapenems and multiple other agents. This case showed that VIM‑1‑producing P. mirabilis had reached Italian hospitals and reinforced concerns about limited therapeutic options for severe Proteus infections in southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional dissemination of carbapenemase‑producing Enterobacterales within southern Europe, together with ongoing carbapenem use in Italian hospitals, created opportunities for acquisition of blaVIM‑1 by local P. mirabilis strains; delays in detecting MBL producers and implementing control measures may have allowed silent spread. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence via Novel Genotype – introduction of the blaVIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase into Italian P. mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – broad resistance severely restricted treatment options; Enhanced Transmission – clonal spread and/or plasmid transfer from existing VIM‑1 reservoirs in other species facilitated appearance of resistant P. mirabilis in a new national setting.
Review: Review – Event corresponds to Italy’s first VIM‑1‑producing Proteus mirabilis and documents geographic extension of MBL-mediated carbapenem resistance within southern Europe, but it is based on a single patient and is therefore of limited size. It is nevertheless potentially among the top ten events for this EPP because VIM‑1 carbapenemase in P. mirabilis remains rare. Classification has been corrected by setting Intra‑continental emergence=No (the species was long present in Europe; this is a new resistant genotype) and ensuring the event is treated purely as Re‑emergence=Yes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (clinical Proteus mirabilis isolates from two geographically distinct US locations)
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2015, a novel metallo‑β‑lactamase gene, blaIMP‑27, was identified in unrelated Proteus mirabilis isolates from two geographically distinct sites in the United States, with one isolate recovered in 2009 and another in 2015. Both isolates carried blaIMP‑27 within a class 2 integron, and the later isolate harbored the gene on both chromosome and plasmids, indicating successful integration and potential for horizontal transfer. This marked the emergence of a new carbapenemase lineage in P. mirabilis within North America and expanded the diversity of carbapenem resistance mechanisms documented in this species, even though IMP‑27‑producing isolates remained rare.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued reliance on carbapenems and broad‑spectrum β‑lactams for severe infections in US hospitals created selection pressure for novel carbapenemase producers; integron‑ and plasmid‑mediated gene flow among Enterobacterales facilitated independent emergence of IMP‑27‑positive P. mirabilis in distinct regions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – first identification of the IMP‑27 metallo‑β‑lactamase in Proteus mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – IMP‑27 conferred resistance to carbapenems and other β‑lactams; Enhanced Transmission – localization of blaIMP‑27 in a class 2 integron and on plasmids increased mobility and the potential for broader dissemination across strains and institutions.
Review: Review – Event accurately summarizes the first reports of IMP‑27, the first IMP‑type metallo‑β‑lactamase identified in Proteus mirabilis, in two US locations over a six‑year span. It is mechanistically important but based on only two known isolates, so its ranking among the ten most impactful events is borderline and should be revisited as more epidemiological data accumulate. Classification has been corrected by changing First detection=No (reflecting that Proteus infections were long recognized) and Intra‑continental emergence=No, with the episode treated as Re‑emergence=Yes (novel carbapenemase genotype) rather than geographic emergence of the species.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (community and non‑tertiary‑care urinary tract infections due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, a study of uropathogens causing urinary tract infections in the Andaman Islands, India, reported the first detection of New Delhi metallo‑β‑lactamase‑1 (NDM‑1) in Proteus mirabilis, with two clinical isolates carrying the blaNDM‑1 gene among multidrug‑resistant uropathogens. These infections occurred largely in community or non‑tertiary‑care settings, indicating spread of NDM‑1 into P. mirabilis outside major referral hospitals. The episode signaled that NDM‑1, initially described in other Enterobacterales, had expanded its host range to Proteus spp., adding another highly problematic carbapenemase to the Proteus resistance repertoire in South Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Broad community and hospital use of carbapenems and other antibiotics in India, combined with high regional prevalence of blaNDM‑1 in Enterobacterales and environmental dissemination of NDM‑1 via sewage and water, created conditions for spillover of NDM‑1 into Proteus mirabilis; travel and referral networks likely facilitated wider regional spread of NDM‑positive strains. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – transfer of blaNDM‑1 from other Enterobacterales into Proteus mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – NDM‑1 confers resistance to nearly all β‑lactams (except aztreonam) and is often linked to additional resistance determinants, greatly limiting therapeutic options; Re‑emergence – introduction of a new carbapenemase genotype into an already resistant Proteus population, further increasing the risk of treatment failure and severe outcomes.
Review: Review – Event is supported by a peer‑reviewed study documenting the first NDM‑1‑producing Proteus mirabilis in the Andaman Islands and is highly significant because NDM‑1 is a globally important carbapenemase. Original sources pointing to secondary or less authoritative reports have been replaced with the primary article and major reviews. Classification has been corrected from First detection=Yes to First detection=No and interpreted as Re‑emergence=Yes, consistent with the definition that new resistance mechanisms in an existing pathogen constitute re‑emergence rather than first detection of the EPP in the human host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Host: Humans (sexually active adolescents and adults, predominantly 15–49 years)
Event summary: From roughly 1990 to 2010, genital herpes due to HSV-2 remained a major hidden epidemic in the United States and Canada. National estimates suggest that about 45 million Americans were already HSV-2-seropositive in the early 1990s, and modelling indicates roughly 1.6 million new HSV-2 infections in 2000 alone, with about 640,000 of these in 15–24-year-olds. Although U.S. HSV-2 seroprevalence among adults aged 14–49 years declined modestly from around 21% in 1988–1994 to about 15–16% by 2007–2010, the absolute number of infected adults and annual incident infections remained very high, concentrated in adolescents and young adults. By the late 2000s HSV-2 genital herpes was still one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in Northern America, with the vast majority of infected people unaware of their status and driving ongoing transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High levels of sexual risk behaviour (multiple partners, inconsistent condom use), urbanization, and overlapping HIV/STI epidemics during the 1970s–1990s created and then sustained a large pool of HSV-2-infected adults; persistent underdiagnosis and lack of routine screening meant that most infections were asymptomatic or unrecognized, facilitating silent spread. Internal mechanisms: No major new HSV-2 genotypes were implicated; this episode reflects persistence of high transmission in established sexual networks driven by external social and behavioural factors rather than virologic change, so it is best characterised as re-occurrence in an already endemic setting.
Review: review - Retain as a major regional burden episode for genital HSV-2 in Northern America. The event summary was revised to clarify that HSV-2 seroprevalence in the U.S. plateaued or modestly declined between 1990 and 2010 rather than continuously increasing, while still involving tens of millions of prevalent infections and roughly 1.6 million new infections in 2000 based on modelling. No changes were needed to geography or event-type classification (re-occurrence driven by external behavioural factors). Source set is appropriate and was left unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Australia and New Zealand; Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; Sweden [1990]; Norway [1990]; Denmark [1990]; New Zealand [1990]; Australia [1990]; United States of America [1990]; Canada [1990]
Host: Humans (sexually active adolescents and young adults with genital herpes)
Event summary: Between the early 1990s and about 2010, industrialized countries in Northern and Western Europe, Northern America, and Australasia documented a marked epidemiological shift, with HSV-1 causing an increasing proportion of first-episode genital herpes in young adults. Clinic and surveillance data from settings such as the United Kingdom, the United States, the Nordic countries, and Australia/New Zealand showed the share of genital herpes due to HSV-1 rising from a minority of cases in the 1970s–1980s to 20–50% or more of first-episode genital herpes by the mid-1990s and 2000s, and exceeding 50% in some younger cohorts by the 2000s. By the end of the period, genital HSV-1 had become a leading cause of new genital herpes episodes in younger age groups in several high-income countries, while HSV-2 remained dominant among older adults.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Improved hygiene and living conditions in childhood reduced oral HSV-1 transmission, leading to more HSV-1-seronegative adolescents and young adults who were susceptible to acquiring HSV-1 genitally via oral–genital sex; changes in sexual practices (especially more frequent oral sex among youth) further promoted genital acquisition of HSV-1. Internal mechanisms: No major novel HSV-1 strains were implicated; instead, the same virus shifted anatomic niche from predominantly oral to increasingly genital infection (a change in clinical and epidemiologic manifestation rather than host species). In line with the project guidance that new manifestations in an already affected host system should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence, this episode is classified as re-emergence within existing subregions.
Review: review - Retain as a key re-emergence event capturing the shift toward genital HSV-1 in high-income regions. Geography (Northern and Western Europe, Northern America, Australia/New Zealand) and time frame (1990–2010) are appropriate, and classification as re-emergence is consistent with the guideline that new clinical manifestations in a previously affected host system should be coded as re-emergence, not intra-/inter-continental emergence. Only minor editorial changes were made (removal of inline markdown links in the mechanism field); the existing source set remains relevant and high-quality.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: United States of America [1990]; Canada [1990]; France [1990]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; Germany [1990]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990]; Switzerland [1990]
Host: Humans (predominantly immunocompromised: people with AIDS, hematopoietic stem cell or solid-organ transplants, and other severe immunodeficiencies)
Event summary: From the late 1980s through the 1990s and 2000s, clinicians in North America and Western/Northern Europe increasingly reported severe, chronic mucocutaneous HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections that were clinically refractory to standard-dose acyclovir among patients with advanced HIV/AIDS and other profound immunosuppression. Early series from the United States and Europe described acyclovir-resistant HSV isolates in AIDS patients and transplant recipients, and by the mid-1990s surveillance and cohort data estimated resistance prevalences of roughly 3–7% among heavily treated immunocompromised populations, compared with well under 1% in immunocompetent individuals. Through the 2000s, acyclovir-resistant HSV became a recognised complication of long-term prophylaxis or therapy in immunocompromised hosts, necessitating alternative agents such as foscarnet and spawning ongoing surveillance and drug development efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread introduction and chronic use of nucleoside analogue antivirals (notably acyclovir and related drugs) for prophylaxis and treatment of HSV in the context of expanding HIV/AIDS and transplant programmes created strong selective pressure for drug-resistant variants; prolonged viral replication in immunocompromised hosts further favoured resistance emergence. Internal mechanisms: Antiviral resistance due to mutations in the viral thymidine kinase and, less commonly, DNA polymerase genes led to acyclovir and penciclovir resistance; resistant strains often retained pathogenicity and could cause extensive, persistent lesions. This episode is therefore classified as re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance within previously affected subregions.
Review: review - Retain as a major re-emergence event characterised by the development and spread of acyclovir-resistant HSV among severely immunocompromised patients in North America and Europe. The time frame and affected host groups are consistent with published case series and surveillance studies. No changes were needed to geography or event-type classification (re-emergence via antiviral resistance). Minor edits removed inline markdown links from the mechanism text; source URLs remain appropriate and focused on resistance mechanisms, prevalence, and clinical impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: South Africa [1990]; Botswana [1990]; Eswatini [1990]; Lesotho [1990]; Namibia [1990]; Zimbabwe [1990]; Zambia [1990]; Malawi [1990]; Mozambique [1990]; Kenya [1990]; Uganda [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Ethiopia [1990]; Nigeria [1990]; Ghana [1990]; Côte d’Ivoire [1990]
Host: Humans (sexually active adolescents and adults, especially women aged 15–49 years)
Event summary: From 1990 through at least 2016, countries across Eastern, Southern, Western and parts of Middle Africa experienced extremely high HSV-2 prevalence and genital ulcer disease burden, particularly among women of reproductive age. Regional modelling suggests that around one-third of adults aged 15–49 years in the WHO African Region—rising to about half of women aged 25–34 years—were living with HSV-2 infection by 2012–2016, with HSV-2 accounting for the majority of genital ulcer disease in many populations. In 2016 an estimated 420,000 of 1.4 million sexually acquired HIV infections worldwide were attributable to HSV-2 infection, with the largest share and highest population-attributable fraction in Africa, highlighting HSV-2 as a key cofactor sustaining the region’s generalised HIV epidemics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of heterosexual HIV epidemics, high rates of partner change in some sexual networks, limited access to condoms and STI care, gender inequality, and structural factors such as poverty and urbanisation created conditions in which HSV-2 spread widely and remained largely untreated. The biological synergy between HSV-2 and HIV—HSV-2 ulcers increasing HIV acquisition and transmission risk and HIV-related immunosuppression enhancing HSV reactivation—further amplified both epidemics. Internal mechanisms: No specific new HSV-2 lineage has been implicated; rather, long-established HSV-2 strains caused frequent genital ulcer disease in the context of overlapping HIV infection, so this is classified as a large regional re-occurrence of an endemic pathogen driven by external social and epidemiological factors.
Review: review - Added as a new high-impact event that was missing from the original dataset. Strong evidence shows that HSV-2 prevalence and HSV-related genital ulcer disease have been highest in the WHO African Region since at least the early 1990s, with roughly one-third of adults and up to half of women aged 25–34 years infected, and that about 420,000 new HIV infections in 2016 (≈30% of sexually acquired HIV globally, >35% in Africa) were attributable to HSV-2. This makes the sustained HSV-2/HIV syndemic in sub-Saharan Africa one of the most consequential HSV-related emergence patterns worldwide. Geography was focused on high-burden sub-Saharan countries, and the event is classified as re-occurrence (no clear viral change, but major externally driven amplification).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Continent: Africa; Asia; South America; North America; Europe; Oceania
Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa; Northern Africa; Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia; Central Asia; Caribbean; Central America; South America; Northern America; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand; Melanesia; Micronesia; Polynesia
Countries: Multiple countries across all listed subregions including, for example, South Africa [1990]; Nigeria [1990]; Kenya [1990]; India [1990]; China [1990]; Brazil [1990]; Mexico [1990]; United States of America [1990]; Russian Federation [1990]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; Australia [1990]; New Zealand [1990] (representative of global trends rather than an exhaustive list).
Host: Humans aged 15–49 years (sexually active population)
Event summary: From 1990 through 2021, global burden assessments documented a large and growing absolute number of genital herpes cases worldwide. Global Burden of Disease estimates indicate that incident genital herpes cases among people aged 15–49 years increased by about 52% over this period, from roughly 23.6 million new cases in 1990 to about 35.8 million in 2021, while the global incidence rate remained relatively stable (around 0.9% per year). By 2012–2016, approximately two-thirds of the world’s population under age 50 had HSV-1 infection and about 11–13% of individuals aged 15–49 years had HSV-2 infection, corresponding to more than half a billion people with genital HSV infection and tens of millions of new genital herpes episodes annually. By 2021, genital herpes remained one of the most prevalent STIs worldwide, with especially high HSV-2 prevalence and genital ulcer disease burden in sub-Saharan Africa and persistently high or increasing incidence in regions such as South Asia, Southern sub-Saharan Africa, and Central Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent high-risk sexual transmission dynamics (including inconsistent condom use, multiple partners, and overlapping HIV/STI epidemics), demographic growth in low- and middle-income countries, limited access to STI prevention and clinical services, and lack of vaccines or population-level HSV control programmes have maintained or increased the global burden; in some high-income regions, delayed HSV-1 acquisition in childhood and changes in sexual practices also contribute to genital HSV-1. Internal mechanisms: No single novel HSV lineage has been shown to drive global expansion; instead, the episode reflects sustained transmission of long-established HSV-1 and HSV-2 strains across diverse settings. It is therefore categorised as a large-scale re-occurrence (persistence and expansion of absolute case numbers and stable or rising incidence in several regions) of an endemic infection rather than new emergence.
Review: review - Retain as a global-scale re-occurrence event summarising the very large and growing absolute burden of genital herpes from 1990 to 2021. The narrative was updated to align with recent Global Burden of Disease analyses showing a ~52% increase in global incident cases between 1990 and 2021, stable overall incidence rates, and marked increases in incidence in regions such as South Asia, Southern sub-Saharan Africa, and Central Europe. Event type (re-occurrence), continents and subregions, and the choice to list representative rather than exhaustive countries for this global pattern are appropriate, though users should note that the country list is illustrative. Wikipedia URLs were removed from the event-specific source list in favour of primary WHO, GBD and modelling papers, and the WHO prevalence paper link was updated to an accessible PMC version.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Thailand (ethnic Lao Hmong refugee camp, Phetchabun Province)
Host: Refugees of all ages (children and adults), including pregnant women
Event summary: From late January to early May 2008, an explosive varicella outbreak swept through an ethnic Lao Hmong refugee camp in Phetchabun Province, northern Thailand, infecting 309 of 7,815 residents (attack rate about 4%). Transmission accelerated in the crowded barracks, with an unusually high proportion of adult cases and three adult hospitalizations, including one severe varicella pneumonia with respiratory failure. The outbreak waned as susceptible individuals were exhausted and basic clinical management was provided; no large-scale vaccination or antiviral campaign was implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high population density and close contact within the camp; many adult refugees from rural tropical areas with low childhood varicella exposure, resulting in a substantial pool of susceptible adults; absence of routine varicella vaccination. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel VZV strains; the event reflects demographic susceptibility and crowded refugee conditions rather than viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: with 309 cases and documented severe adult disease in a large tropical refugee camp, this outbreak is one of the better-characterized, higher-impact varicella events in low-vaccination humanitarian settings post-1990. Geography (Thailand, South-eastern Asia) and case counts align with the cited Conflict and Health report; emergence type as re-occurrence is appropriate because VZV was long-established in the region and no viral change is implicated.

Countries: Israel (detention facility for African immigrants in southern Israel)
Host: Adult male African immigrants (mostly from Eritrea and Sudan) detained in an Israeli facility
Event summary: Between June and December 2012, a prolonged primary varicella outbreak occurred in an immigration detention facility in southern Israel housing young adult men from Eritrea and Sudan, resulting in 109 clinically diagnosed cases over seven months. Initial control relied mainly on quarantine of ill detainees, but sustained transmission continued until national authorities recommended and implemented varicella vaccination for all susceptible detainees and staff in December. Following the first vaccine dose campaign, only one additional case was reported, and the outbreak effectively ended, demonstrating the impact of targeted vaccination in a highly susceptible, closed adult migrant population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: crowded, closed detention environment; high baseline susceptibility to varicella among young adult migrants from tropical regions where childhood VZV infection is less common; delayed introduction of vaccination as an outbreak-control tool. Internal mechanisms: no novel viral genotype or resistance detected; outbreak magnitude reflects host susceptibility and setting, not intrinsic viral change.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). Reason: this 109-case outbreak in a detention facility for African immigrants is well documented and among the larger adult varicella episodes in custodial migrant settings since 1990. It fills an important geographic gap (Western Asia) and is more impactful than several small U.S. clusters originally included. Emergence type as re-occurrence (driven by crowding and susceptible migrants) is appropriate.

Countries: Greece (refugee camps of Elliniko, Malakasa, and Raidestos on mainland Greece)
Host: Refugees (primarily Afghan and Syrian children and families) living in mainland camps
Event summary: From mid-2016 through mid-2017, four chickenpox outbreaks were documented across three large refugee camps (Elliniko, Malakasa, and Raidestos) on mainland Greece, together accounting for 203 varicella cases, mostly in young children but with some adolescent and adult infections. The largest outbreak at Elliniko between July 2016 and June 2017 affected nearly 7% of camp residents, while smaller but still substantial clusters occurred in Malakasa and Raidestos. Transmission gradually declined following routine clinical management and improvements in camp organization; no mass varicella vaccination was undertaken, but the episodes highlighted high susceptibility among refugee children from regions without universal varicella vaccination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: overcrowded camp conditions; frequent mixing of families from Afghanistan, Syria and other countries where childhood exposure to VZV and varicella vaccination coverage are lower; limited capacity for rapid isolation within camps. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of viral change; outbreaks reflect standard varicella transmission in a susceptible displaced population.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). Reason: the combined 203 cases across three Greek mainland refugee camps constitute a sizable and well-characterized varicella burden in European displacement settings, larger and more epidemiologically important than previously included small-cluster events. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because VZV was long established in Southern Europe, and the outbreaks were driven by crowding and susceptible refugee children.

Countries: United States of America (multiple Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers, including South Texas Family Residential Center and Port Isabel Service Processing Center)
Host: Detained migrants (children and adults) in U.S. ICE facilities
Event summary: Between January 1, 2017 and March 22, 2020, varicella circulated persistently across U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers, with 1,052 chickenpox cases identified among detained migrants and 26 distinct outbreaks documented in nine facilities. One family detention center in South Texas experienced a chickenpox outbreak that lasted 33 months, and nearly half of all varicella cases occurred in just two Texas centers. Transmission declined only after heightened awareness, limited vaccination efforts, and population turnover reduced the susceptible pool within affected facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme crowding, high population turnover, and frequent transfer of detainees between facilities; poor access to routine immunizations; many migrants originating from countries without universal varicella vaccination or with disrupted health services. Internal mechanisms: no novel VZV variants identified; outbreaks are driven by setting-related transmission dynamics and baseline susceptibility.
Review: Decision: retain, but note aggregation. Reason: this event aggregates 1,052 varicella cases and 26 outbreaks across interconnected ICE facilities over a 3-year period and is one of the largest documented VZV burdens in a detention system. Although individual outbreaks are spatially distinct, the prolonged, transfer-fueled transmission within the ICE network reasonably fits the "linked, recurrent episode in the same outbreak system" concept. Emergence type as re-occurrence is appropriate; no inter-continental or intra-continental emergence is involved because VZV was already endemic in North America.

Countries: Bangladesh (Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar District: Ukhia and Teknaf upazilas)
Host: Rohingya refugees (children and adults) living in displacement camps
Event summary: Beginning in late 2018, a massive varicella outbreak emerged in the densely populated Rohingya refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, and spread rapidly across camps from week 45 of 2018 through week 22 of 2019. Surveillance data recorded approximately 82,297 varicella cases during this period, with a weekly peak of over 10,000 cases, affecting children and adults in highly crowded shelters with limited prior varicella exposure or vaccination. The outbreak was eventually brought under control through the development and implementation of clinical management and reporting guidelines, enhanced surveillance and case recognition, and intensified health promotion, but no large-scale varicella vaccination campaign was mounted during the acute phase.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extreme overcrowding and poor living conditions in the world’s largest refugee settlement; very high numbers of susceptible children and young adults from Myanmar without routine varicella vaccination; constrained health infrastructure and difficulty isolating infectious cases; close contact in learning centers and communal spaces. Internal mechanisms: no newly described VZV strain; the extraordinary scale reflects a high force of infection in a large, immunologically naïve displaced population.
Review: Decision: retain with major correction. Changes: (1) Corrected the magnitude of the Rohingya varicella outbreak from hundreds of cases (~800) to approximately 82,297 cases between late 2018 and mid-2019, based on WHO-led EWARS data summarized in the PLOS ONE coordination paper, which documents 82,297 cases and a weekly peak of ~10,133. (2) Clarified the event period (week 45 of 2018 to week 22 of 2019) and emphasized that this was a camp-wide, multi-facility outbreak rather than a small, early cluster. (3) Updated source URLs to prioritize the detailed PLOS ONE analysis while retaining the WHO feature story as contextual support. Emergence type as re-occurrence remains appropriate: VZV was long established in Southern Asia, and the eruption was driven by external factors (crowding, susceptibility, disrupted services) rather than viral change.

Countries: United States of America (New York City; multiple migrant shelters and residential facilities)
Host: Recently arrived migrants (children, adolescents, and adults) living in New York City shelters and residential facilities
Event summary: After three linked varicella cases were identified in October 2022 among recent migrants in a New York City residential facility, health authorities detected an expanding multi-facility outbreak involving asylum-seekers arriving largely from Central and South America and other regions without routine varicella vaccination. Between September 12, 2022 and March 6, 2024, surveillance documented 873 outbreak-associated chickenpox cases, predominantly in children and adolescents, with 28 hospitalizations for complications such as encephalitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, and severe skin infection; one large family shelter alone reported nearly 200 cases. Transmission within major shelters subsided following intensive on-site varicella vaccination campaigns, which raised documented immunity among resident children from roughly one-quarter to over four-fifths, alongside improved isolation and linkage to primary care, although sporadic imported cases continued with new migrant arrivals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: sustained migration from countries where varicella vaccine is not routinely provided or where immunization programs have been disrupted; extreme crowding and mixing in NYC shelters and other temporary accommodations; initially limited systematic screening and vaccination of new arrivals. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel VZV strains; the outbreak reflects rapid spread of endemic VZV in a highly susceptible migrant population and demonstrates the effectiveness of large-scale catch-up vaccination in curtailing transmission.
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: with 873 reported cases and substantial morbidity in a large, multi-facility shelter system, this NYC migrant outbreak is among the largest documented varicella episodes in a high-income urban setting in the varicella vaccine era. Timeline, case counts, and hospitalization figures align with CDC MMWR reports. Emergence type as re-occurrence (re-surgence in a previously endemic subregion driven by under-immunized migrants and overcrowding) is appropriate; imported cases without onward spread outside shelters are correctly not coded as inter-continental emergence.

Countries: State of Palestine (Gaza Strip displacement camps in Khan Younis, Al Mawasi, Nuseirat, and other sites)
Host: Displaced Palestinian children and families living in overcrowded Gaza displacement camps
Event summary: In early summer 2026, a rapidly escalating chickenpox outbreak was reported across overcrowded displacement sites in the Gaza Strip, where more than 1.7 million people were living in tents and makeshift shelters after prolonged conflict. Within roughly two weeks, UN and health partners recorded over 9,300 suspected varicella cases—primarily among children—with local clinicians warning that true case numbers were likely higher due to under-reporting and limited access to care. As of mid-2026 the outbreak remained ongoing, with control efforts hampered by severe shortages of clean water, hygiene supplies, medicines, and functional health facilities, making effective isolation and routine vaccination extremely difficult.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: massive population displacement and intense overcrowding in tented camps; extensive damage to health, water and sanitation infrastructure from prolonged conflict; severe shortages of water, soap, and basic medical supplies; disruption of routine childhood immunization, leaving many children either unvaccinated or unable to complete vaccine series. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of new VZV variants; the scale and speed of spread are attributable to environmental and social collapse rather than intrinsic viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). Reason: this emerging 2026 outbreak, with more than 9,300 suspected cases reported in just two weeks across Gaza displacement sites and indications of a growing cumulative burden, is a major ongoing VZV event in a war-torn, severely resource-constrained setting. It fits the emergence-event definition as a large, temporally bounded episode in a specific outbreak area (displacement camps in Gaza). Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate: VZV has long circulated in Western Asia, and the outbreak is driven by conflict-related collapse of services and extreme overcrowding rather than viral change.

Host: Humans (horse trainer, stable worker, horse owner/trainer) infected after close contact with clinically ill or recently dead horses infected with Hendra virus
Event summary: In September 1994, a novel severe respiratory disease outbreak in thoroughbred racehorses in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, led to infection of a 49‑year‑old horse trainer (fatal pneumonic illness) and a 40‑year‑old stable worker (self‑limited influenza‑like illness), marking the first recognised human cases of Hendra virus. Subsequent retrospective investigations linked a second focus in Mackay, north Queensland, where two horses had died in August 1994 and a 36‑year‑old horse trainer who assisted with necropsy later developed aseptic meningitis and then fatal encephalitis 13 months after exposure, with Hendra virus confirmed as the cause. The episode ended after infected horses were euthanised, extensive tracing and surveillance of exposed humans showed no further infections, and the novel virus was isolated and characterised as a new henipavirus with flying foxes identified as the wildlife reservoir in later studies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Initial emergence reflected ecological interfaces between pteropid flying fox reservoirs and high‑density racehorse stabling in peri‑urban southeast Queensland, with likely exposure of horses to bat urine, faeces or birthing products and intense unprotected human contact with severely ill or dead horses during training and necropsy. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from bats to horses and then to humans, and enhanced transmission linked to high viral loads in acutely ill horses, but no evidence of a distinct new strain or adaptive genetic change within this initial emergence window.
Review: Retain – Verified against NSW Health’s human-case summary and other official and review sources: the 1994 Hendra (Brisbane) and 1995 Mackay human infections together represent the first recognised human emergence of Hendra virus, all within Queensland, Australia; timing, locations, host description and classification as both first_global_emergence and first_detection are consistent with the literature, and there is no evidence of additional, larger pre‑2000 human events or inter-/intra-continental spread that would alter this record.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (veterinarian) infected after extensive exposure to blood and respiratory secretions during necropsy of a horse presumed to have died of Hendra virus infection
Event summary: In late 2004, a veterinarian in her 20s in Cairns, north Queensland, performed a post‑mortem examination on a horse that was subsequently presumed, on clinical and epidemiologic grounds, to have had Hendra virus infection, resulting in extensive unprotected exposure to blood and respiratory secretions. About a week after exposure, she developed a mild influenza‑like illness and seroconverted to Hendra virus without progression to severe disease, while three other exposed individuals remained well and seronegative. The event concluded after public health follow‑up showed no secondary human transmission, and intensified infection‑control guidance for veterinarians and surveillance for equine cases in Queensland and northern New South Wales was implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued bat‑to‑horse spillover risk in tropical and subtropical Queensland combined with high‑risk veterinary procedures (post‑mortem examination of an undiagnosed horse without full respiratory protection) enabled a rare horse‑to‑human transmission event; recognition of this case prompted tighter infection‑control protocols for equine necropsy and suspect Hendra cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a new strain or altered virulence; disease pattern suggests typical zoonotic infection in a single highly exposed host without onward human transmission.
Review: Retain – NSW Health’s case summary documents a single serologically confirmed human infection in a Cairns veterinarian in late 2004 after necropsy of a presumptive Hendra-infected horse; year, location, host description and exposure circumstances in this record match those details. Classification as re_occurrence (in the same sub-region, with no evidence of a new strain or new geographic area within Oceania) and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate, and the listed sources are relevant and sufficiently specific for this event.

Countries: Australia [2008 Redlands (Thornlands area), suburban Brisbane, Queensland]
Host: Humans (two veterinary staff: veterinarian and veterinary nurse/technician) infected while caring for and performing invasive procedures and necropsies on multiple horses with acute neurological and respiratory disease due to Hendra virus in a veterinary hospital setting
Event summary: In July 2008, a veterinary hospital at Redlands, a suburb of Brisbane, Queensland, experienced an outbreak in which four horses with acute neurological signs tested positive for Hendra virus and a fifth became ill under quarantine, representing an intense focal equine outbreak in an enclosed clinical setting. Two veterinary staff members who had conducted high‑risk procedures—including nasal cavity lavage and necropsy—on the infected horses developed acute influenza‑like illness followed by encephalitis and seroconversion to Hendra virus, with one surviving and the other dying from severe neurologic disease. The incident ended after the clinic was quarantined, infected horses were euthanised, exposed staff and contacts were monitored and some given ribavirin, and no further human infections or secondary human‑to‑human spread were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak was driven by introduction of Hendra‑infected horses—likely infected via bat‑to‑horse spillover outside the clinic—into a high‑density veterinary hospital where intensive handling, aerosol‑generating procedures (nasal lavage, endoscopy, necropsy) and initially limited respiratory protection created multiple high‑dose exposure opportunities for staff, leading to the largest documented cluster of human cases. Internal mechanisms: Clinical description highlighted some ‘novel’ clinical features in horses and humans, but virologic characterisation did not demonstrate a distinct new genotype; the event is best interpreted as severe disease from the existing virus in an amplifying setting rather than strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: Retain – NSW Health’s case summary and the 2008 Redlands outbreak paper describe a veterinary hospital cluster in Redlands (Thornlands area) with two human infections (one fatal), matching the event year, location, host description and exposure setting recorded here. Classification as re_occurrence in the same sub-region (rather than re_emergence, because no distinct new genotype or host jump was demonstrated) is consistent with current evidence; all listed sources are relevant, though the ABC explainer and Wikipedia entry provide general background rather than primary epidemiologic detail.

Countries: Australia [2009 Cawarral near Rockhampton, central Queensland]
Host: Humans (veterinarian) infected while performing nasal endoscopy and other close‑contact procedures on a horse with undiagnosed Hendra virus infection at an equine nursery
Event summary: In August 2009, at an equine nursery in Cawarral near Rockhampton in central Queensland, a horse with fever and respiratory distress was examined by a 55‑year‑old veterinarian who performed nasal endoscopy without gloves or respiratory protection; the horse was later presumptively diagnosed with Hendra virus, and another horse on the property was laboratory‑confirmed infected. The veterinarian received post‑exposure ribavirin but developed influenza‑like illness 21 days after exposure, progressed to encephalitis and died, while three other highly exposed people from the same incident remained well and did not seroconvert. The human outbreak ended with this single fatal case; subsequent equine vaccination rollout from 2012 and strengthened biosecurity and PPE practices in horse medicine have been associated with the absence of further human Hendra virus infections after 2009 despite ongoing sporadic horse cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of recognised Hendra virus spillover risk into central Queensland, combined with invasive respiratory procedures on acutely ill horses without adequate PPE, created a high‑dose exposure setting that overcame existing informal precautions; the event underscored the occupational risk to equine veterinarians and drove subsequent policy and vaccine implementation. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel genetic variant; severe outcome is consistent with known high case‑fatality of Hendra virus encephalitis in heavily exposed humans.
Review: Retain – NSW Health’s case summary and Queensland/CSIRO documentation confirm a single fatal human infection in a veterinarian at Cawarral near Rockhampton in August 2009 following high-risk endoscopic procedures on an infected horse; the year, location, exposure circumstances and outcome in this record match those sources. Classification as re_occurrence (reappearance in the same sub-region driven by ongoing bat–horse spillover and occupational exposure) without intra- or inter-continental emergence or evidence of a new strain is appropriate, and the listed sources are relevant, though several focus primarily on equine outbreaks and control rather than human clinical details.

Host: Humans (febrile rural patients, mainly farmers; zoonotic spillover from shrews suspected)
Event summary: Origin: During sentinel surveillance of febrile patients with recent animal exposure at hospitals in Qingdao (Shandong) and Xinyang (Henan), China, in April 2018, metagenomic sequencing of a throat swab from one patient revealed a phylogenetically distinct henipavirus, later named Langya henipavirus (LayV), representing the first recognized human infections with this virus. Development: Expanded testing of similar febrile patients over 2018–2021 identified 35 sporadic human cases in rural parts of Shandong and Henan Provinces, most in farmers with animal contact, presenting with fever and sometimes pneumonia, with LayV as the only detectable pathogen in most acute cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. Ending/status: By August 2021, the surveillance period underlying the initial report concluded with no deaths and no large clusters, and subsequent monitoring and risk assessments up to at least 2024 describe LayV as an ongoing but rare zoonotic spillover threat confined to eastern China without documented spread to other countries or continents.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic exposure of rural farmers to infected small mammals, particularly shrews, likely through occupational or environmental contact in agricultural and peri‑forested settings; increased use of metagenomic next‑generation sequencing and targeted surveillance for febrile patients with animal exposure enabled detection of a pathogen that likely circulated previously at low levels. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – a shrew‑borne henipavirus (with high RNA prevalence in Ussuri white‑toothed shrews, Crocidura lasiura) spilled over into humans, causing sporadic febrile illness; no evidence has yet been found for substantial viral adaptations leading to efficient human‑to‑human transmission, increased virulence, or major antigenic change during this emergence episode.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Retain this event as the single major human emergence episode for Langya virus: 35 sporadic febrile cases detected through sentinel surveillance in Shandong and Henan, China, between April 2018 and August 2021, with no deaths and no sustained human-to-human transmission, consistent with NEJM, ECDC and subsequent reviews. The time window (2018–2021), geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China [2018]) and host description are correct, and no additional large or distinct human emergence events were identified up to at least 2025. The only substantive correction is to the type-of-emergence coding: to respect the guideline that event-type categories are generally mutually exclusive, this episode is best treated as a first/global emergence in humans (first_global_emergence = true) rather than being simultaneously coded as both first_global_emergence and first_detection, so first_detection has been set to false. Detections of Langya virus RNA in shrews in the Republic of Korea (Gyeonggi and Gangwon provinces) expand knowledge of the wildlife reservoir and geographic range but do not constitute a separate human emergence event and are therefore not encoded as an additional row for the human host system. No other columns or source URLs were changed, but this row is flagged for expert review to confirm the event-type coding choice.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America (North Carolina – onset November 1995, death June 1996)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – previously healthy 28-year-old male deer hunter
Event summary: In early November 1995, a 28‑year‑old man from North Carolina developed fever, myalgias, gastrointestinal symptoms and confusion after numerous mosquito bites while deer hunting in the southeastern United States. Virus isolation from blood and cerebrospinal fluid confirmed acute CVV infection causing severe meningoencephalitis with multiorgan failure, representing the first recognized human CVV disease case. He required prolonged intensive care, including dialysis and limb amputations, and ultimately died from pulmonary complications in June 1996, demonstrating that CVV can produce fulminant, often fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intense mosquito exposure during outdoor hunting in rural North Carolina, together with the absence of prior clinical recognition of CVV infection in humans, facilitated zoonotic spillover and delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Although no unique genotype was identified, this case showed that established North American CVV lineages possess marked neurotropism and the capacity to cause multiorgan failure in susceptible human hosts (increased virulence/pathogenicity expressed in a rare spillover event).
Review: Decision: retain. Event correctly captures the first recognized human CVV case in North Carolina in 1995–1996, with appropriate classification as first_detection (rather than first_global_emergence) and accurate geography; only narrative wording was clarified without changing interpretation.

Countries: United States of America (Wisconsin – suburban community on the Lake Michigan shore)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – generally healthy 41-year-old man
Event summary: In late October 2003, a 41‑year‑old man living near a landfill in a small city on the Lake Michigan shore in Wisconsin developed acute headache, fever, nausea, vomiting and fatigue. Cerebrospinal fluid findings were consistent with aseptic meningitis, and CVV was isolated from CSF and serum, confirming the second documented human CVV disease case presenting as non‑fatal aseptic meningitis. He gradually recovered with supportive care, illustrating sporadic re‑occurrence of human CVV neuroinvasive disease in the U.S. Upper Midwest without recognized onward transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Local enzootic circulation of CVV among mosquitoes and mammals in peri‑urban landfill and lakeshore environments, coupled with limited inclusion of CVV in routine arboviral diagnostic panels, allowed rare human spillover that was detected only through specialized virologic testing. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance phenotype was reported; the event reflects background zoonotic transmission of existing CVV lineages rather than adaptive viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Wisconsin 2003 aseptic meningitis case aligns with the original EID report in timing, location, clinical course, and laboratory confirmation; classification as re_occurrence in the already affected Northern America subregion is appropriate and no structural corrections were required.

Countries: Argentina (Córdoba City [2004], Jesús María and Colonia Caroya [2004-2005])
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – general urban and peri-urban residents sampled in serosurveys
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2005, investigators conducted reduction neutralization tests on human sera from Córdoba City and the nearby suburban towns of Jesús María and Colonia Caroya in central Argentina and found roughly 6–8% of samples with neutralizing antibodies to CVV. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18930511/?utm_source=openai)) These results provided the first documented evidence that people in South America had been infected with CVV or a closely related orthobunyavirus, expanding the recognized continental range of human infection beyond North America. No discrete clinical outbreak was linked to these infections, so this episode represents sero‑epidemiologic detection of past transmission rather than an identified epidemic of symptomatic disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing or expanding circulation of CVV‑like orthobunyaviruses and competent mosquito vectors in temperate regions of central Argentina, combined with focused serologic surveys, enabled recognition of prior human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Serologic cross‑reactivity within the Bunyamwera/Orthobunyavirus group complicates precise attribution to CVV, but there is no clear evidence for a novel genotype or host shift; the event reflects geographic range recognition of existing virus circulation rather than intrinsic viral adaptation.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly summarizes Tauro et al. 2009 and appropriately treats the finding as evidence of human CVV infection in Argentina, but the event-type coding has been corrected: first_detection is now set to false and inter_continental_emergence to true so that this episode is interpreted as first recognized occurrence in a new continent rather than a second global first_detection, in line with the largely mutually exclusive event-type definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America (New York State – upstate New York)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – 63-year-old immunocompetent woman
Event summary: In mid‑September 2011, a 63‑year‑old woman presented to a hospital in upstate New York with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a petechial rash after recent camping trips in rural New York, Vermont and New Hampshire. Cerebrospinal fluid was consistent with aseptic meningitis, and CVV was cultured from the CSF and identified by real‑time RT‑PCR and sequencing, yielding the complete viral coding sequences and documenting acute neuroinvasive CVV infection in an immunocompetent adult. ([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jcm.00252-13)) She recovered with supportive care, marking the third reported immunocompetent North American patient with acute CVV neuroinvasive disease and extending the known geographic range of clinically recognized cases to New York State.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recreational camping and outdoor exposure in wooded areas of the northeastern United States during late summer created opportunities for mosquito‑borne transmission, while the availability of molecular diagnostics and virus culture at reference laboratories enabled recognition of this rare infection. Internal mechanisms: No unique lineage was reported, and the case is best interpreted as sporadic re‑occurrence of neuroinvasive disease caused by circulating CVV strains in a new U.S. state within the already affected Northern America subregion.
Review: Decision: review (newly added event). This row has been added to capture the well-documented 2011 aseptic meningitis case from upstate New York described by Nguyen et al. 2013, which is one of the small number of published symptomatic human CVV infections and should be included among the major events for this EPP.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America (North and South Carolina; Michigan – probable exposure during travel in 2013); Australia (New South Wales – diagnosis and follow-up 2014-2016)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – 34-year-old man with X-linked agammaglobulinemia (primary immunodeficiency)
Event summary: Around 2013, a 34‑year‑old Australian man with X‑linked agammaglobulinemia traveled to North and South Carolina and Michigan and subsequently developed slowly progressive neuropsychiatric symptoms that evolved over several years into chronic meningoencephalitis with cognitive decline, speech slowing and mood disturbance. Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid and brain biopsy specimens performed in New South Wales identified CVV RNA, and immunohistochemistry confirmed CVV antigen in brain tissue, establishing CVV as the cause of a chronic central nervous system infection; CVV had not previously been detected on the Australian continent. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28628941/?utm_source=openai)) The patient’s condition stabilized somewhat with supportive and immunologic management but he remained severely neurologically impaired, and no secondary cases were detected, so this episode represents a single, protracted infection with a novel chronic disease phenotype likely acquired during travel to the United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International travel from Australia to endemic regions of the eastern United States, combined with profound B‑cell immunodeficiency due to X‑linked agammaglobulinemia, allowed persistent viral replication and chronic CNS infection that eluded standard diagnostic testing until unbiased metagenomic sequencing was applied. Internal mechanisms: The case documents CVV’s capacity for long‑term neurotropic infection and progressive meningoencephalitis in the setting of absent humoral immunity, representing re‑emergence of CVV disease with a new chronic manifestation in the already affected Northern America subregion rather than inter‑continental emergence in Oceania, because infection was probably acquired abroad and did not lead to onward transmission in Australia.
Review: Decision: retain. Travel history and clinical details match Wilson et al. 2017, and treating this as re_emergence (novel chronic disease phenotype in an immunodeficient host within the existing Northern America range) while explicitly not classifying it as inter-continental emergence is consistent with the project rule that imported cases without onward transmission should not be coded as inter-continental events.

Countries: United States of America (Missouri – northwest Missouri)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – man in his 60s with diabetes, coronary artery disease and prior thymectomy for malignant thymoma
Event summary: In September 2015, a man in his 60s from northwest Missouri presented with several days of high fever, chills, rigors, cough, abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and rapidly developed thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, respiratory failure and shock requiring intensive care. Whole blood sent to CDC for investigation of suspected emerging tick‑ or mosquito‑borne infection yielded a CVV isolate, and next‑generation sequencing showed an intraspecies reassortant virus, representing the first recognized case of severe non‑neuroinvasive CVV disease. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/73/9/1700/6149917)) The patient recovered after prolonged hospitalization, and the case was later reflected in national arboviral surveillance reports as a single CVV disease case from Missouri.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy exposure to mosquitoes during late summer in rural Missouri and underlying comorbidities (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, history of thymectomy) likely increased susceptibility to severe systemic illness, while targeted testing at CDC enabled detection of an unexpected pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing demonstrated a lineage I large‑segment intraspecies reassortant CVV strain associated with severe febrile, non‑neuroinvasive illness, supporting classification as re_emergence driven by emergence of a reassortant genotype and new clinical presentation within the existing Northern America range.
Review: Decision: review. This row has been substantially updated to align with the detailed Missouri case report by Baker et al. 2021: the case is now correctly described as severe non-neuroinvasive illness due to a reassortant CVV strain, and the event type has been changed from re_occurrence to re_emergence to reflect the documented genomic reassortment and novel clinical phenotype; a primary clinical article has been added to the source URLs.

Countries: United States of America (New York State – rural Cuba, NY)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – 58-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia on rituximab maintenance therapy
Event summary: In July 2016, a 58‑year‑old man from rural Cuba, New York, with chronic lymphocytic leukemia receiving rituximab maintenance therapy developed subacute confusion, memory loss, gait instability and fatigue. Extensive evaluation for autoimmune and infectious causes of meningoencephalitis was initially unrevealing, but repeat cerebrospinal fluid testing and molecular work‑up ultimately identified CVV infection, and the patient’s condition progressed to profound neurologic disability and death in August 2016. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6037180/?utm_source=openai)) This case documented fatal CVV meningoencephalitis in a B‑cell–depleted patient and provided evidence of CVV lineage 2 circulation in the northeastern United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The widespread use of B‑cell–depleting biologic therapies such as rituximab created a growing population of patients with severely impaired humoral immunity who are at high risk for severe arboviral infections after relatively modest mosquito exposure. Internal mechanisms: The report implicated CVV lineage 2 in the Northeast and showed dramatically increased neuroinvasive pathogenicity and prolonged viral persistence in a rituximab‑treated host, fitting the definition of re_emergence driven by both viral lineage characteristics and altered host immunity (increased virulence/pathogenicity in an immunocompromised population).
Review: Decision: retain. The New York 2016 rituximab-associated meningoencephalitis case is accurately summarized based on Yang et al. 2018 and subsequent reviews, with appropriate coding as re_emergence (new lineage and high severity in an expanding immunosuppressed host group) and correct geographic and temporal information.
