Countries: France [2022–2023]; Croatia [2022–2023]; Sweden [2022–2023]; Spain [2022–2023]; Italy [2023]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2023]
Host: Humans (primarily neonates in the first week of life; mothers with peripartum enterovirus infection)
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2022, France detected an unusual rise in severe neonatal infections due to a new echovirus 11 variant, with at least nine neonates hospitalized for sepsis‑like illness and hepatitis between July 2022 and April 2023, seven of whom died. By mid‑2023, additional severe neonatal E11 cases were reported from several EU/EEA countries including France, Croatia, Sweden, Spain, Italy, and the United Kingdom, prompting European and WHO alerts about a multi‑country event. The outbreak has persisted with fluctuating intensity, though increased clinical awareness, perinatal testing, and infection‑prevention measures in maternity and neonatal units aim to limit further severe neonatal cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: vertical and peripartum transmission from pregnant women with unrecognized enterovirus infection, high susceptibility and lack of immunity in neonates, and routine obstetric and neonatal care settings that may facilitate close contact and early transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of a new echovirus 11 variant associated with severe hepatitis and high case‑fatality in neonates; genomic studies indicate a distinct recombinant variant with apparent increased virulence/pathogenicity and possibly enhanced transmission in the perinatal setting. The multi‑country spread within Europe reflects both intra‑continental emergence of this variant and re‑emergence in subregions with prior E11 circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

Sub-regions: Asia: South-eastern Asia, Eastern Asia; Europe: Western Europe; North America: Northern America
Countries: Philippines [2008-2009]; Japan [2010]; Netherlands [2010]; United States of America – Georgia [2009-2010], Pennsylvania [2009], Arizona [2010]
Host: Humans (primarily children with severe acute respiratory infections and pneumonia)
Event summary:
From late 2008, clusters of severe lower respiratory tract infection and pneumonia in hospitalized children in the Eastern Visayas region of the Philippines were linked to EV-D68, marking the first clearly recognized multi-patient outbreaks of this serotype.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
During 2009–2010, additional clusters of acute respiratory illness caused by EV-D68 were reported in Japan, the Netherlands and several U.S. states (Georgia, Pennsylvania, Arizona), showing that the virus had shifted from sporadic detection to widespread regional outbreaks across three continents.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
By 2010, these temporally related outbreaks had subsided, but they revealed a re-emerging pathogen with the capacity for broader transmission and severe pediatric respiratory disease, setting the stage for larger epidemics later in the decade.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: increased use of molecular diagnostics and multi-pathogen respiratory panels enabled detection of EV-D68 that would previously have been misclassified as rhinovirus; sentinel and hospital-based surveillance in the Philippines, Japan, the Netherlands and U.S. sites highlighted an apparent rise in severe wheezing, pneumonia and asthma exacerbations linked to this virus.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses from Asia, Europe and North America show emergence and spread of novel EV-D68 lineages (early clades A and B) with changes in capsid and receptor-binding regions thought to favor respiratory tropism and more efficient transmission, consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence and early geographic range expansion of fitter variants.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7171721/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event corresponds to the six early multi-country clusters of EV-D68 respiratory illness described by CDC for 2008–2010 and is among the key pre‑2014 emergence episodes. The countries list has been corrected to remove New York (not part of the 2008–2010 clusters) and to drop the separate China [2006–2008] entry, which referred to sporadic circulation outside this episode and predates the 2008 start year; retained Philippines, Japan, the Netherlands and the U.S. states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Arizona with timing aligned to the MMWR description.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (predominantly children with asthma or reactive airway disease and otherwise healthy children; some adults)
Event summary:
In August 2014, pediatric hospitals in the United States (first in Kansas City, Missouri, and Chicago, Illinois) reported an unusual surge of children with severe respiratory illness requiring intensive care, and sequencing of respiratory specimens rapidly identified EV-D68 as the predominant pathogen, leading to recognition of a large, nationwide outbreak with at least 2,287 confirmed cases and multiple deaths.([repositorio.uchile.cl](https://repositorio.uchile.cl/handle/2250/153144?utm_source=openai))
Concurrently, Canada detected widespread EV-D68 circulation with hundreds of pediatric hospitalizations and at least one confirmed EV-D68–associated death, while in the U.S. clusters of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) with spinal gray matter lesions emerged in temporal and geographic association with the respiratory outbreak (about 120 AFM cases August–December 2014).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1473309915005435?utm_source=openai))
The respiratory epidemic waned by late autumn 2014 as the enterovirus season ended, but it marked a step-change in EV-D68 epidemiology with clear evidence of large-scale transmission, severe pediatric lung disease and probable neurotropism, after which EV-D68 became a recurrent biennial threat in North America.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: high susceptibility in the pediatric population after decades of limited circulation; dense mixing in schools and childcare settings during late summer and early autumn; widespread underlying asthma and reactive airway disease that increased risk of severe lower respiratory involvement; and initial use of diagnostic panels that did not distinguish EV-D68 from rhinoviruses, likely permitting early spread before targeted testing was introduced.([repositorio.uchile.cl](https://repositorio.uchile.cl/handle/2250/153144?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: molecular investigations showed co-circulation of multiple, closely related EV-D68 strains within clade B1/B2, with mutations in capsid and nonstructural proteins linked to enhanced replication at respiratory-tract temperatures and acquisition of poliovirus-like neurotropic features; this represents novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity, particularly in the lower respiratory tract and anterior horn cells, with enhanced transmission relative to historical strains.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28512577/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Large 2014 North American outbreak with severe pediatric respiratory disease and temporally associated AFM is well supported by U.S. and Canadian surveillance and descriptive studies; event timing, geography (United States and Canada), and classification as re‑emergence driven by clade B1 are appropriate, and no structural edits were required.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Norway [2014]; Denmark [2014]; Netherlands [2014-2015]; France [2014-2015]; United Kingdom (England, Wales, Scotland) [2014-2015]; Germany [2014]; Spain [2014-2015]; Sweden [2014-2015]; Italy [2014-2015]
Host: Humans (children and adolescents with severe respiratory illness and acute flaccid myelitis; some adults)
Event summary:
Following the 2014 North American epidemic, several European countries documented increased EV-D68 detections in children hospitalized with severe respiratory disease, including Norway where about 11% of pediatric respiratory samples in one hospital were EV-D68-positive and two children developed severe AFM.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/rapid-risk-assessment-enterovirus-68-detected-usa-canada-and-europe-second-update?utm_source=openai))
During late 2014 and through 2015, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy (along with Denmark and Germany reporting clusters of respiratory illness) all recorded EV-D68 circulation with smaller respiratory outbreaks and sporadic but severe neurologic cases, including the first recognized EV-D68–associated AFM clusters in Europe.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/microbiolspec.ei10-0018-2016?utm_source=openai))
By late 2015, European EV-D68 activity declined seasonally, but the region had transitioned from sporadic detections to a recognized pattern of EV-D68 outbreaks with associated AFM, preparing the ground for the larger pan-European AFM wave documented in 2016.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: increased clinician and laboratory awareness after the U.S. 2014 epidemic led to targeted EV-D68 PCR and sequencing in respiratory and AFM cases; school-term mixing and autumn seasonality favored transmission; and travel links with North America likely seeded introductions of the same or closely related clades.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/rapid-risk-assessment-enterovirus-68-detected-usa-canada-and-europe-second-update?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses showed European strains in 2014–2015 clustering with North American clade B1/B2 viruses and, in some locations, emerging B3-like lineages, consistent with rapid global dissemination of fitter variants that possessed enhanced respiratory tropism and, in a small subset of infections, neuroinvasive potential—supporting classification as re-emergence driven by novel strains with increased virulence/pathogenicity and enhanced transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5792700/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retain as the description of the initial European EV‑D68/AFM activity following the 2014 North American epidemic. The countries list has been expanded to include Denmark [2014] and Germany [2014], which reported EV‑D68 respiratory clusters during the same wave, while keeping Norway, the Netherlands, France, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy; sub‑regions and classification as re‑emergence remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (children with acute flaccid myelitis following respiratory illness)
Event summary:
In 2010, Osaka City, Japan experienced its first documented upsurge of EV-D68-associated acute respiratory infections in children, establishing the virus as a recognized respiratory pathogen in that setting.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0184335))
In August–December 2015, a nationwide survey of acute flaccid paralysis in Japanese children identified a cluster of AFM cases temporally associated with EV-D68 respiratory outbreaks, providing some of the earliest systematic documentation of EV-D68–associated AFM in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5850449/?utm_source=openai))
The AFM incidence declined after the 2015 enterovirus season, but this episode confirmed that the neuroinvasive phenotype observed in North America and Europe had also emerged in East Asia, with recurrent EV-D68 waves occurring in the same pediatric population.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: seasonal circulation of EV-D68 in late summer–autumn among school-age children; improved national AFP surveillance and virologic typing after the 2014 global experience; and high contact rates in schools and households.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5850449/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: sequencing from Osaka and nationwide surveillance demonstrated sequential replacement of EV-D68 clades between 2010, 2013 and 2015, with distinct B-lineage variants (including subclade B3) associated with the 2015 AFM cluster, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence and possible increased neurovirulence and transmissibility compared with older strains.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0184335))
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes Japan’s 2015 nationwide AFM cluster temporally associated with EV‑D68 outbreaks, drawing on longitudinal Osaka surveillance and national AFP data; geography, timing, and classification as re‑emergence due to distinct clades (including subclade B3) are appropriate, so no structural changes were made.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: France [2016]; United Kingdom (Scotland, Wales, England) [2016]; Sweden [2016]; Norway [2016]; Spain [2016]; Italy [2016]; Netherlands [2016]; other European countries participating in ENPEN network [2016]
Host: Humans (primarily children with acute flaccid myelitis and preceding respiratory illness)
Event summary:
In early 2016, European clinicians and laboratories reporting through ENPEN and ECDC noted increasing EV-D68 circulation in pediatric respiratory samples, particularly in northern and western Europe, following smaller waves in 2014–2015.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5718392/?utm_source=openai))
Between March and October 2016, a coordinated European case series identified 29 laboratory-confirmed EV-D68–associated AFM cases across 12 countries (including France, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Norway, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands) among more than 16,000 respiratory specimens screened, representing a >10-fold rise over 2014 and confirming a continent-wide AFM wave temporally linked to EV-D68 clade B3 circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6296836/?utm_source=openai))
As EV-D68 detections and AFM cases declined with the end of the 2016 enterovirus season, Europe established AFM working groups and highlighted the need for formal AFM surveillance, recognizing EV-D68 as a recurrent neurotropic outbreak pathogen.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: accumulation of a cohort of young children without prior exposure to newly circulating EV-D68 lineages after the 2014 wave; school- and daycare-based transmission during late summer and autumn; and enhanced case-finding via AFP/AFM surveillance and pan-European laboratory collaboration (ENPEN, ECDC), which increased ascertainment of both EV-D68 infection and AFM.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5718392/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses showed dominance of subclade B3 viruses across Europe in 2016, distinct from the B1/B2 strains prominent in 2014; these B3 strains display amino acid substitutions in capsid proteins and other regions associated with increased neurotropism and replication in neuronal tissue, constituting novel strain/genotype emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity and enhanced transmission in pediatric populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6296836/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the 2016 pan‑European AFM wave with 29 confirmed EV‑D68–associated cases in 12 countries and dominance of subclade B3; continent, sub‑regions, and re‑emergence classification are consistent with the case‑series data, and the generic reference to “other European countries participating in ENPEN” is acceptable given incomplete country-level reporting.

Host: Humans (primarily children with severe respiratory illness and acute flaccid myelitis)
Event summary:
In the late summer and autumn of 2016, two years after the initial U.S. epidemic, EV-D68 circulation again increased, with an outbreak in the Lower Hudson Valley region of New York alone yielding 160 laboratory-confirmed EV-D68 respiratory cases and genome sequencing showing a distinct subclade B3 that had replaced the 2014 B1 viruses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5430842/?utm_source=openai))
Nationally, AFM surveillance recorded a second large U.S. peak with 149 confirmed AFM cases in 2016, most in young children and clustered in late summer–fall, temporally aligned with EV-D68 activity and clinically similar to the 2014 AFM cases.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6827e1.htm?utm_source=openai))
By late 2016, both the B3-associated respiratory outbreak and AFM surge declined with the end of the enterovirus season, but this episode demonstrated that newly evolved EV-D68 lineages could repeatedly spark substantial outbreaks and AFM peaks in the same population.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: accumulation of susceptible children born after 2014 who lacked immunity to newly circulating EV-D68 variants; typical late-summer school and daycare mixing; and incomplete EV-D68-specific testing in many clinical laboratories, which likely led to under-ascertainment of respiratory cases outside sentinel sites.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5430842/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses from the Lower Hudson Valley outbreak showed that 2016 viruses formed a new subclade B3, with approximately 3–5% nucleotide divergence from the 2014 B1 strains and changes in capsid and non-structural regions consistent with antigenic drift and potential alterations in tissue tropism; together with the concurrent AFM peak, this supports classification as re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence with enhanced transmissibility and neurotropic potential.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5430842/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added to capture the documented 2016 U.S. EV‑D68 subclade B3 outbreak (e.g., 160 laboratory-confirmed respiratory cases in the Lower Hudson Valley and a national AFM peak of 149 confirmed cases), which was missing from the original list but represents one of the ten highest-impact EV‑D68 emergence episodes since 1990.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (children with acute flaccid myelitis following respiratory illness)
Event summary:
In 2016, following reports from North America and Europe, clinicians at a pediatric hospital in Buenos Aires, Argentina, prospectively investigated children admitted with acute flaccid paralysis under the national AFP surveillance program.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/25/3/pdfs/17-0897.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Over a four-month period they identified six children with AFM, four of whom had EV-D68 detected in respiratory samples by RT-PCR and sequencing, representing one of the first well-documented clusters of EV-D68–associated AFM in South America.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6390768/?utm_source=openai))
After this cluster, AFM incidence decreased, but the event highlighted that B3-lineage EV-D68 had spread to South America and could cause neuroinvasive disease similar to that seen in the Northern Hemisphere.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: regional circulation of EV-D68 introduced via international travel and seasonal spread; strengthened AFP surveillance and poliomyelitis eradication infrastructure enabled systematic identification and virologic investigation of non-polio AFM cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6390768/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analysis showed Argentine EV-D68 strains clustering with contemporary B3 lineage viruses implicated in AFM in Europe, suggesting that globally disseminated B3 variants—rather than locally unique strains—were responsible and that their inherent neurotropism and virulence underpinned this re-emergence of severe neurologic disease in a new region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6390768/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Cluster of EV‑D68–associated AFM in Buenos Aires (six AFM cases, four EV‑D68 positive) is well documented and represents the first clearly described neuroinvasive EV‑D68 event in South America; despite its modest size it is reasonable to include among the top events given the limited number of large global episodes, and no geographic or temporal corrections were required.

Host: Humans (children with acute flaccid paralysis)
Event summary:
In 2016, within the framework of poliomyelitis acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance in West Africa, investigators retrospectively tested stool specimens from children with AFP and identified EV-D68 RNA and subclade B3 sequences in several cases from countries including Guinea (Guinea-Conakry), Senegal and Niger.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7454047/?utm_source=openai))
These detections coincided temporally with the 2016 global wave of EV-D68-associated AFM and represented some of the first confirmed EV-D68 B3 infections linked to neurologic disease in Africa, though the clinical severity and numbers were smaller than in Europe and North America.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7454047/?utm_source=openai))
As the broader 2016 EV-D68 wave declined, West African AFP surveillance continued, but EV-D68-associated neurologic cases remained relatively rare, suggesting that while the virus had expanded its geographic and pathogenic range to West Africa, sustained large-scale outbreaks had not yet occurred or been documented.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: long-standing AFP surveillance for polio created a repository of samples that allowed retrospective identification of EV-D68; improved molecular typing in regional reference laboratories increased detection of non-polio enteroviruses; and cross-border movement and air travel likely introduced globally circulating B3-lineage EV-D68 into West Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7454047/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: sequencing confirmed that West African EV-D68 strains belonged to subclade B3, the same lineage associated with AFM in Europe and the Americas in 2016, implying that the emergence of a more neurotropic and transmissible genotype enabled both geographic range expansion and the capacity to cause sporadic neurologic disease in African children.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7454047/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retain as an important first description of EV‑D68 subclade B3 in West African AFP surveillance, but the countries list has been corrected to specify Guinea (Guinea‑Conakry), Niger and Senegal, removing the vague reference to “other neighboring West African countries,” because only these three of seven surveyed nations had EV‑D68–positive AFP cases in 2016; classification as re‑emergence remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [2018]; Canada [2018]; multiple European countries including France, Netherlands, United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Italy, Germany [2018]; Australia [2018]; New Zealand [2018]
Host: Humans (primarily children with severe respiratory illness and AFM)
Event summary:
After a relatively quiet EV-D68/AFM year in 2017, surveillance in the United States recorded a sharp rise in AFM cases in 2018 (about 238 confirmed AFM cases nationwide) temporally associated with renewed EV-D68 circulation in late summer and autumn, following the now-characteristic biennial pattern first observed after 2014.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6812a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Parallel increases in EV-D68 detections and AFM cases were documented across Europe in 2018, with ENPEN data showing that 2016, 2018 and later 2022 accounted for the majority of European AFM cases, and additional AFM cases with EV-D68 infection were recognized in Australia and New Zealand using AFP surveillance systems.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12124111/?utm_source=openai))
The 2018 wave subsided by winter, but it established EV-D68-associated AFM as a recurring global phenomenon with large peaks approximately every two years, aligning with shifts in population immunity and viral genetic evolution.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: accumulation of a birth cohort of young children lacking immunity to circulating EV-D68 clades following the 2016 wave; normal resumption of school and social mixing after the 2016 season; and increased awareness plus standardized case definitions for AFM leading to improved reporting.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6812a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: ongoing evolution within B3 and related clades, with evidence of antigenic drift and changing neutralization profiles, likely allowed escape from existing population antibodies and supported repeated large waves; combined with established neurotropic determinants, this produced re-emergence characterized by increased virulence/pathogenicity (AFM) and enhanced transmission on a biennial timescale.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/mra.00388-19?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event appropriately aggregates the substantial 2018 EV‑D68/AFM wave across the United States, Canada, multiple European countries and Australia/New Zealand, with case numbers and the biennial pattern consistent with NVSN and AFM surveillance data; no structural corrections to geography, timing or emergence type were needed.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United States of America [2022]; Canada [2022]; Finland [2022]; other European countries with increased EV-D68/AFM reports [2018-2022]
Host: Humans (children and adolescents with acute respiratory illness, asthma exacerbations, and occasional neurologic disease)
Event summary:
After non-pharmaceutical interventions for COVID-19 dramatically reduced circulation of many respiratory viruses, including EV-D68, in 2020–2021, U.S. surveillance detected a substantial increase in EV-D68-positive respiratory specimens and pediatric emergency visits for acute respiratory illness and asthma/reactive airway disease during July–September 2022, indicating a large nationwide EV-D68 respiratory outbreak.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7047a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
In the same year, Finland reported a notable EV-D68 outbreak with at least 56 hospitalized children with respiratory illness and one case of encephalitis, and ENPEN data showed that European AFM cases again clustered in EV-D68 circulation years (2016, 2018, 2022), though the 2022 AFM peak appeared lower than expected, possibly due to interference from other respiratory viruses or partial population immunity.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/29/6/22-1795_article?utm_source=openai))
By late 2022 the EV-D68 wave receded, but its timing after a skipped 2020 peak underscored how changes in contact patterns and competing respiratory viruses can modulate the biennial pattern of EV-D68 re-emergence, while the virus remains capable of causing sizeable respiratory outbreaks and sporadic neurologic disease.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: relaxation of COVID-19 mitigation measures restored typical contact patterns in schools and communities, allowing re-expansion of EV-D68; an immunity gap may have developed in children who missed exposure during 2020–2021; and concurrent circulation of SARS-CoV-2, RSV and other enteroviruses might have shaped both susceptibility and clinical expression, potentially blunting AFM incidence despite high respiratory circulation.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7047a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: 2022 viruses belonged to contemporary EV-D68 clades (including B3 and newer lineages) that have diversified antigenically since 2014, suggesting continued evolution under immune pressure with preserved or modestly enhanced transmissibility in the respiratory tract; however, AFM associations appeared weaker, raising the possibility that specific genetic determinants of neurovirulence, host immunity, or viral interference modulated clinical outcomes in this re-emergence wave.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ofid/article/doi/10.1093/ofid/ofad500.950/7448594?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the large 2022 EV‑D68 respiratory surge in the United States and Finland (and other European countries) after COVID‑19 mitigation was relaxed, including the notable decoupling between high respiratory circulation and relatively modest AFM counts; geography, timing, and classification as re‑emergence are consistent with available surveillance reports, so only editorial wording changes, not structural corrections, would be needed if further refinement were desired.

Host: Humans (older adults in a long-term care facility; human rhinovirus B14)
Event summary: In late autumn 2024, a long-term care facility in southeastern France experienced a cluster of severe respiratory illness and deaths among older adult residents of initially unknown cause; retrospective testing of stored nasopharyngeal swabs by metagenomic next-generation sequencing identified human rhinovirus B14 as the primary etiologic agent, with additional HRV-B14 detections in routine diagnostic samples from the surrounding region indicating concurrent community circulation. The facility outbreak resulted in 18 severe illnesses and 8 deaths among highly frail residents before subsiding, and there was no evidence of sustained transmission beyond the institution or of unusual regional spread of Rhinovirus B beyond its usual endemic background.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: congregate living conditions and close contact in a long-term care facility, high baseline frailty and comorbidity burden among very old residents, and seasonal community circulation of HRV-B14 created conditions for efficient transmission and unusually severe outcomes; delayed etiologic identification (only achieved via metagenomic sequencing) may have limited the timeliness of targeted infection control. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analysis suggested at least two closely related HRV-B14 strains were co-circulating during the outbreak, but there was no clear evidence of a novel genotype, antiviral resistance, or intrinsic increase in virulence relative to known B14 strains. Accordingly, this episode is best interpreted as a severe re-occurrence of an established Rhinovirus B type in a highly susceptible population rather than a strain-driven re-emergence or geographic expansion event.
Review: retain: Newly added event capturing the well-documented 2024 outbreak of HRV-B14 in a French long-term care facility (18 severe cases, 8 deaths). Classified as re-occurrence in Western Europe (France) because Rhinovirus B was long established in Europe and there is no evidence of first detection, new subregional or intercontinental spread, or virus-driven phenotypic shift; external drivers are the high-risk, congregate-care setting and host frailty. Event size is modest but likely among the most clearly characterized Rhinovirus B–specific severe outbreaks since 1990, so it is retained, with a recommendation to review its relative importance as more species-B-specific outbreak data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (children <5 years hospitalized with acute respiratory symptoms or fever, many with wheezing or asthma, in Davidson County, Tennessee, and Monroe County, New York)
Event summary: From October 2001 through September 2003, population-based surveillance in two US counties enrolled over one thousand children under five years of age hospitalized with acute respiratory illness or fever, and HRV was detected in around one sixth of cases. Subsequent sequencing of HRV-positive samples showed that approximately half belonged to the newly recognized HRV-C group, and these HRV-C infections were significantly more likely than HRV-A to occur in children with underlying high-risk conditions and to be associated with discharge diagnoses of asthma and wheezing, indicating a disproportionate role in asthma-related hospitalizations. The surveillance period ended in 2003, but this study established HRV-C as a major contributor to pediatric respiratory hospitalizations and asthma morbidity in high-income settings, reframing the clinical impact of this previously unrecognized rhinovirus species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prospective, population-based surveillance coupled with sensitive RT-PCR and sequencing for respiratory viruses enabled systematic identification and typing of HRVs in hospitalized children in the United States. Internal mechanisms: Molecular genotyping revealed a large burden of HRV-C infections with strong association with asthma and wheezing, implying that specific genetic features of HRV-C confer enhanced propensity to trigger lower airway inflammation and asthma exacerbations relative to other HRV species, consistent with subsequent mechanistic studies on HRV-C and asthma.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7112283/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: RETAIN as one of the top-10 events. Rationale: This event documents a large, well-characterized cohort of >1,000 hospitalized US children in which HRV-C accounted for nearly half of rhinovirus-associated hospitalizations and was strongly linked to asthma and wheezing, demonstrating substantial disease burden and redefining HRV-C as a major pediatric pathogen rather than a rare genotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7112283/?utm_source=openai)) It represents one of the most impactful early recognitions of HRV-C’s clinical importance. Classified as re-emergence because a newly delineated genetic group (HRV-C) within an already circulating virus complex was shown to drive a marked burden of severe disease (asthma hospitalizations) in a previously characterized subregion, reflecting a shift in recognized pathogen–host interaction rather than geographic spread. Geography (Northern America; United States of America) is correct and aligned with the Country sheet; source URL is an appropriate primary source.

Continent: North America; Africa; Asia; Europe; Oceania
Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Africa; Southern Africa; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United States of America [2004]; Australia [2003]; South Africa [2006]; Côte d’Ivoire [2006]; Nepal [2005]; India [2007]; Denmark [2007]; Spain [2003]; Germany [2007]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2004]
Host: Humans (infants, children, and adults with influenza-like illness, acute respiratory infections, and lower respiratory tract infections in hospital- and community-based surveillance)
Event summary: Between roughly 2003 and 2007, a genetically distinct rhinovirus clade later designated HRV-C was identified through MassTag multiplex PCR, pan-viral microarrays, and VP4/VP2 or VP1 sequencing in respiratory samples from patients with influenza-like illness in New York State, infants with bronchiolitis in Queensland, Australia, and then in children and adults with acute respiratory disease in South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, Nepal, India, Western Australia, Denmark, Spain, Hong Kong, Germany, and California. These investigations showed that viruses in this novel clade were associated with community outbreaks of acute respiratory illness and with severe lower respiratory tract infections and respiratory distress in infants and young children across Africa, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and North America. By 2007, phylogenetic and molecular-clock analyses indicated that this clade was as diverse and long-established as HRV-A and HRV-B and had likely circulated in humans for at least several hundred years, shifting the interpretation of HRV-C from a newly emerged pathogen to a long-endemic virus newly detected by advanced molecular diagnostics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deployment of broad-range molecular assays (MassTag PCR, multiplex PCR, microarrays) in respiratory virus surveillance and outbreak investigations enabled sensitive detection and typing of unculturable or previously untyped rhinoviruses, and coordinated sample sharing between laboratories in North America, Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania provided geographically diverse material. Internal mechanisms: Sequence and phylogenetic analysis revealed HRV-C as a deeply divergent, highly diverse clade within human rhinoviruses with long evolutionary history; its apparent association with pediatric lower respiratory tract disease and asthma exacerbations reflects inherent tropism and pathogenicity of this clade, but the key "emergence" driver for this episode was improved detection and taxonomic recognition rather than a recent viral change.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/6/08-0271_article))
Review: Decision: RETAIN with corrections. Changes made: (1) Continent and subregion fields have been standardized to match the UN/Excel classification and to include all relevant subregions actually represented in the cited surveillance (Northern America; Western and Southern Africa; Southern and Eastern Asia; Northern, Southern, and Western Europe; Australia and New Zealand).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/6/08-0271_article)) (2) The previous inclusion of "California, United States of America" as a separate country was removed as California is a state within the USA; the United States of America [2004] entry now covers both New York and California detections.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/6/08-0271_article)) (3) The event is reclassified as first detection only, with inter-continental emergence set to "No" because these studies showed that HRV-C was already globally distributed and long-established; there is no evidence for de novo spread between continents during this period, and the main novelty is species recognition and molecular detection rather than first occurrence in a genuinely naïve continent.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/6/08-0271_article)) (4) Duplicate JCM URLs were consolidated, and event-specific sources are now restricted to primary literature (global distribution paper and key molecular/clinical characterizations). Overall, this remains the central first-detection episode for HRV-C and clearly belongs among the top events for this EPP.

Host: Humans (children hospitalized at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Singapore with acute respiratory tract infections)
Event summary: From October 2005 through March 2007, a retrospective PCR-based study at Kandang Kerbau Women’s and Children’s Hospital in Singapore tested 500 nasopharyngeal swabs from hospitalized children with acute respiratory symptoms or fever for rhinoviruses, identifying HRV in about one eighth of cases. Molecular serotyping showed that most HRV detections were HRV-A or HRV-B, but two children carried HRV-C, one with asthma and one with bronchiolitis, with HRV-C detected either alone or as part of a co-infection with human bocavirus. The study period ended in early 2007, establishing the presence of HRV-C in hospitalized children in equatorial South-eastern Asia and suggesting, in conjunction with reports from nearby regions, that HRV-C may contribute to severe wheezing and bronchiolitis in this setting, although local sample sizes were small.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of PCR-based respiratory virus diagnostics in Singapore, including molecular serotyping methods originally developed in North America and East Asia, enabled identification of HRV-C in clinical samples that previously would have been reported only as unspecific rhinovirus. Internal mechanisms: Although the Singapore cohort contained only two HRV-C–positive children, both presented with significant lower respiratory involvement (asthma or bronchiolitis), in line with broader evidence that HRV-C is disproportionately associated with wheezing and more severe lower respiratory disease compared with other HRV species, but the small sample size limits firm conclusions about strain-specific virulence in this population.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/8/09-0321_article))
Review: Decision: REVIEW (borderline event). Changes made: (1) Reclassified from re-emergence to intra-continental emergence because the main significance is confirmation of HRV-C circulation in a new Asian UN subregion (South-eastern Asia) using molecular methods, rather than evidence of a novel, more virulent strain or a resurgence in a previously affected subregion. (2) Event summary and mechanisms have been rewritten to match the primary Singapore study, which detected HRV-C in only two of 64 HRV-positive children and did not claim that HRV-C was established as a major cause of severe pediatric respiratory disease in the country.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/8/09-0321_article)) (3) Overstatements about HRV-C being present in large numbers of Singaporean children with pneumonia and bronchiolitis and frequent co-infections with RSV have been removed; the revised text emphasizes the small sample size and the primarily confirmatory nature of this detection. Source URLs now clearly point to the primary letter and its open-access version plus a general HRV-C review for context. Given the very limited number of HRV-C cases, this event may not rank among the ten most impactful global HRV-C episodes and should be reconsidered for inclusion once other candidate events are compared.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (children with cystic fibrosis attending a reference center in São Paulo, Brazil, during routine follow-up visits and respiratory exacerbations)
Event summary: During 2006–2007, respiratory specimens were collected longitudinally from 103 children with cystic fibrosis at a reference center in São Paulo, Brazil, both at routine visits and during respiratory exacerbations, and tested by multiplex RT-PCR and sequencing. Rhinoviruses were the most frequently detected viruses overall, and HRV-C (together with HRV-A2) was significantly associated with respiratory exacerbations compared with routine visits, indicating that these genotypes were important triggers of clinical deterioration in this high-risk group. By the end of the study, HRV-C had been documented for the first time in South America and established as a major contributor to respiratory exacerbations among Brazilian children with cystic fibrosis, broadening both the known geographic range and the recognized clinical niche of HRV-C.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Implementation of comprehensive viral surveillance using RT-PCR and sequencing in a pediatric cystic fibrosis cohort in Brazil allowed for detailed typing of rhinoviruses that previously would have remained untyped; improvements in survival and specialist care for children with cystic fibrosis increased the size of the susceptible population with chronically damaged airways prone to viral-triggered exacerbations. Internal mechanisms: HRV-C and HRV-A2 subtypes were statistically associated with respiratory exacerbations, suggesting that specific genetic lineages have greater propensity to infect compromised lower airways and precipitate clinical worsening; this study also represents the first molecular confirmation of HRV-C circulation in South America, indicating long-standing but previously unrecognized endemic transmission on this continent.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/18215?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: RETAIN with minor reclassification. Rationale: This event likely represents the first published molecular confirmation of HRV-C in South America and documents a sizeable cohort of children with cystic fibrosis in whom HRV-C is significantly associated with respiratory exacerbations, making it both a major geographic range extension and a clinically important event in a high-risk host group.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/18215?utm_source=openai)) Classification has been adjusted by keeping inter-continental emergence = "Yes" (first documented occurrence on the South American continent) but setting re-emergence = "No" because the data do not demonstrate a new viral variant, resistance phenotype, or clear change in virulence relative to earlier HRV-C detections; the key novelty is formal detection and quantification of impact in a new continent and a specific chronic-lung-disease niche. Geography (South America; Brazil) and timing (2006–2007) correctly reflect the study, and the event-specific source set has been expanded to include both the main EID article and related open-access resources.

Host: Humans (hospitalized children with acute lower respiratory tract disease in Thailand)
Event summary: Between early 2006 and 2007, a retrospective study of Thai children hospitalized with acute lower respiratory tract disease tested respiratory specimens for human rhinoviruses and characterized positive samples by sequencing to determine species. HRV infections were common, and HRV-C was the predominant species among typed rhinoviruses, with many HRV-C–infected children presenting with wheezing, bronchiolitis, or asthma exacerbations, indicating that HRV-C accounted for a substantial share of severe pediatric lower respiratory illness in this tropical South-eastern Asian setting. With the end of the study period, HRV-C had been firmly documented as a leading rhinovirus species in Thai children with lower respiratory disease, providing one of the most substantial early demonstrations of its disease burden in South-eastern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of RT-PCR–based HRV detection and sequencing into Thai pediatric hospitals allowed species-level identification of HRV infections for the first time, in a context of high community circulation of respiratory viruses and frequent wheezing illnesses in young children. Internal mechanisms: The dominance of HRV-C among HRV-positive hospitalized children and its frequent association with wheezing and asthma exacerbations suggest that circulating HRV-C lineages in this setting have strong lower-airway tropism and pathogenicity, reinforcing global evidence that HRV-C is a key driver of severe pediatric respiratory disease rather than a benign “common cold” virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7172887/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: RETAIN as a major intra-continental emergence event. Rationale: This study shows that HRV-C was the most prevalent HRV species among hospitalized Thai children with acute lower respiratory tract disease and strongly associated with wheezing and asthma exacerbations, providing one of the earliest and clearest demonstrations of HRV-C’s substantial disease burden in tropical South-eastern Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7172887/?utm_source=openai)) It therefore represents an important intra-continental emergence into a new UN subregion (South-eastern Asia) in terms of documented presence and clinical impact. The continent/subregion/country fields have been populated to match the UN classification (Asia; South-eastern Asia; Thailand), and primary sources (PubMed and PMC versions of the Thai study) have been added. No misclassification of event type was present because this row is newly added; intra-continental emergence appropriately captures recognition of HRV-C in a new Asian subregion rather than first global detection.

Host: Humans (children hospitalized with acute lower respiratory tract infections at Beijing Children’s Hospital)
Event summary: From July through December 2007, nasopharyngeal aspirates from 258 children admitted to Beijing Children’s Hospital with acute lower respiratory tract infections were tested for common respiratory viruses and specifically for HRV-C using a dedicated RT-PCR targeting the 5′ untranslated region and VP4/VP2. HRV-C was detected in 14 children, often as the sole pathogen, with clinical diagnoses including pneumonia, bronchopneumonia, and peribronchiolitis, and three HRV-C–infected patients required intensive care; HRV-A and HRV-B were also present but did not dominate during a cluster of cases in October 2007, when HRV-C was the most frequently detected HRV species. The study concluded that HRV-C strains were circulating in Beijing, were genetically diverse yet closely related to HRV-C strains from Hong Kong, Germany, the United States, and Australia, and should be considered an important emerging cause of pediatric lower respiratory tract infections in China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incorporation of HRV-C–specific RT-PCR into routine testing of hospitalized children with lower respiratory tract infections in Beijing allowed identification of HRV-C in a setting where only HRV-A and HRV-B had previously been recognized, during months with high respiratory virus circulation. Internal mechanisms: The detection of HRV-C as the leading HRV type in a seasonal cluster, its association with clinical syndromes such as pneumonia and bronchiolitis, and phylogenetic evidence of multiple HRV-C lineages related to strains from Hong Kong, Germany, Australia, and the United States indicate both a diverse HRV-C population and a prominent role in severe pediatric lower respiratory disease; this is treated as re-emergence within Eastern Asia because HRV-C had already been described in Hong Kong, but now appeared as a significant cause of LRTI in mainland China.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/10/08-0545_article))
Review: Decision: RETAIN as a major clinical re-emergence event in Eastern Asia. Rationale: This episode documents a clear seasonal cluster of HRV-C infections among hospitalized children with lower acute respiratory tract infections in Beijing, including intensive care admissions and radiographically confirmed pneumonia/bronchiolitis, and provides strong evidence that HRV-C is an important pediatric LRTI pathogen in mainland China.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/10/08-0545_article)) It follows earlier identification of HRV-C in Hong Kong and other regions, so it is best classified as re-emergence in a previously affected UN subregion (Eastern Asia) with a more severe disease phenotype rather than as first detection. Geography (Asia; Eastern Asia; China) is aligned with the Country sheet. Event-specific sources now include the primary EID letter and its PubMed record, both of which are highly relevant to this event.

Host: Wild chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) in the Kanyawara community, Kibale National Park, with presumed human origin of the virus (reverse zoonosis from local people)
Event summary: In 2013, the Kanyawara community of approximately 56 wild chimpanzees in Kibale National Park, western Uganda, experienced a three-phase outbreak of severe respiratory disease over several months, during which most animals became ill and five (8.9%) died. Postmortem sampling of an infant chimpanzee that died in the early phase and subsequent noninvasive sampling of feces from other affected chimpanzees, combined with a commercial multiplex respiratory panel and deep sequencing, identified a recombinant HRV-C strain (designated RV-C45-cpz1-2013) throughout the respiratory tract, with viral loads comparable to those seen in HRV-C–infected children with acute wheezing; other respiratory pathogens were not detected. Epidemiologic modeling estimated the basic reproduction number around 1.8, similar to human common cold transmission, and genotyping of chimpanzees showed universal homozygosity for a CDHR3 allele that confers high susceptibility to HRV-C in humans, leading the authors to conclude that HRV-C of human origin had spilled over into chimpanzees and caused a lethal respiratory outbreak that threatens wild ape populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing spatial overlap and contact between humans and wild chimpanzees in Kibale National Park through research, tourism, and local resource use facilitated exposure of chimpanzees to human respiratory viruses. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak virus was a recombinant between HRV-C45 and HRV-C11 and used the cadherin-related family member 3 (CDHR3) receptor, for which chimpanzees (like susceptible human children) carry the high-risk Y529 allele, conferring species-wide genetic susceptibility; together, these viral and host genetic factors enabled efficient HRV-C infection and transmission in chimpanzees and severe lower respiratory tract disease with high mortality.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/2/17-0778_article?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: RETAIN as a key re-emergence/host-expansion event. Rationale: This well-documented outbreak shows HRV-C crossing from humans into wild chimpanzees and causing a lethal respiratory epidemic with nearly 9% mortality in an endangered ape community, supported by full-genome sequencing, qPCR viral load data, and epidemiologic modeling.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/2/17-0778_article?utm_source=openai)) It represents a major host expansion (spillover) and demonstrates that HRV-C, long considered a strictly human pathogen, can threaten wildlife conservation. Classified as re-emergence because the virus appears in a new host species within a continent (Africa) where human HRV-C circulation was already established, driven by internal mechanisms (recombinant HRV-C45/C11 strain and host genetic susceptibility) and external drivers (intense human–chimpanzee contact). Geography (Africa; Eastern Africa; Uganda) and timing (2013) are consistent with the primary EID report, and the event-specific sources are highly relevant.

Host: Humans (mainly prisoners, displaced persons, and highland rural populations; transmitted by human body lice)
Event summary: Beginning in late 1995, epidemic typhus caused by Rickettsia prowazekii was detected among inmates in Ngozi prison in northern Burundi, where laboratory testing of patients and lice confirmed louse‑borne typhus as the cause of a rapidly expanding febrile outbreak. The epidemic then spread from the prison into surrounding highland communities and refugee camps, and national surveillance recorded over 45,000 clinically diagnosed typhus cases by September 1997, with WHO contemporaneously describing nearly 24,000 cases reported in early 1997 and later analyses suggesting total case counts could have approached 100,000 across Burundi’s high‑altitude provinces. Intensive delousing campaigns, single‑dose doxycycline treatment of prisoners and high‑risk groups, and improvements in camp conditions gradually reduced transmission, and follow‑up surveys of body lice in refugee camps in 1998–2000 no longer detected R. prowazekii, indicating that this largest post–World War II louse‑borne typhus outbreak had been brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Civil war beginning in 1993 led to massive population displacement, overcrowded prisons and refugee camps, severe poverty, and limited access to hygiene facilities in Burundi’s highlands, creating ideal conditions for explosive proliferation of human body lice and louse‑borne transmission of epidemic typhus. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or altered host range was reported; the outbreak represents re‑occurrence of known R. prowazekii in a historically endemic central‑East African focus, with epidemic growth driven by socio‑political disruption and vector overabundance rather than documented genetic change in the pathogen.
Review: Decision: retain (with minor correction to event years). Changes made: Event year range adjusted from 1995–1998 to 1995–1997 to better match primary outbreak reports, which document intense transmission and >45,000 clinically diagnosed cases through September 1997, with subsequent 1998–2000 lice surveys demonstrating absence of R. prowazekii rather than continued epidemic activity. The continent, sub‑region, and country fields (Africa | Eastern Africa | Burundi) and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate because epidemic typhus had been documented repeatedly in Burundi and neighboring countries since the 1960s and 1970s. The event summary and drivers correctly capture the prison index cluster, national spread across high‑altitude provinces, and control via doxycycline and delousing, and the cited WHO WER, WHO Disease Outbreak News, Lancet, and EID articles are among the most relevant primary sources. Recommended status: RETAIN as the principal modern high‑impact emergence event for R. prowazekii.

Host: Humans (primarily institutionalized persons and/or homeless individuals infested with body lice)
Event summary: In the late 1990s, a cluster of epidemic typhus cases occurred in the Lipetsk region of the Russian Federation, including an institutional outbreak in a rural hospital where clinical features and serology were consistent with Rickettsia prowazekii infection amid heavy body‑louse infestation. Investigations linked the outbreak to one or more older patients with Brill–Zinsser disease (recrudescent epidemic typhus decades after primary infection) who served as index cases in an overcrowded facility, leading to secondary transmission among vulnerable, louse‑infested patients and staff; contemporary summaries describe 20–30 clinically compatible cases with most serologically confirmed and clothing heavily infested with lice positive for R. prowazekii. Implementation of delousing measures, antibiotic therapy, and improved heating, hygiene, and overcrowding within the institution curtailed further spread, and subsequent serologic and epidemiologic work treated the Lipetsk outbreak as a contained institutional re‑occurrence rather than a large regional epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Soviet socioeconomic instability, lapses in hospital infrastructure (including heating failures), and overcrowded institutional conditions facilitated body‑louse infestation and local transmission once Brill–Zinsser cases appeared; poor hygiene, shared bedding, and inadequate infection‑control practices were key external drivers. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was seeded by reactivation of latent R. prowazekii in elderly survivors of historical typhus (Brill–Zinsser disease), but available data do not indicate a novel strain, altered virulence, or expanded host range, so the event is best classified as re‑occurrence driven by latent human infection plus social and environmental conditions rather than genetic change in the pathogen.
Review: Decision: retain. Assessment: The existence of an institutional epidemic typhus outbreak in Lipetsk, Russia, in the late 1990s is well supported by Tarasevich et al.’s Lancet correspondence on an "outbreak of epidemic typhus in Russia" and by later summaries, which describe ≈23 patients and 6 staff with clinical typhus and 22 serologically confirmed R. prowazekii infections in a hospital with 100% clothing pediculosis. Secondary Russian‑language analyses identify this Lipetsk episode as a modern example of Brill–Zinsser–driven institutional epidemic typhus. The country (Russian Federation), region (Europe | Eastern Europe), and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate, as epidemic typhus was historically widespread in Russia and this event reflects recrudescence rather than geographic expansion. The 1997–1998 year range is plausible given discordant secondary sources (some cite 1997, others 1998); because original case‑year details are not fully accessible, I recommend leaving 1997–1998 but flagging for verification against Russian primary data. The event is smaller than the Burundian or Peruvian outbreaks but still among the few documented R. prowazekii outbreaks since 1990, and so deserves retention. Recommended status: RETAIN (no major structural changes; verify exact outbreak year if higher temporal precision is required).

Host: Humans in high-altitude rural Andean communities of Cusco department (impoverished villagers infested with body lice)
Event summary: From 1997 through 1999, the southern Andean highlands of Peru—particularly rural provinces of Cusco department such as Quispicanchis, Paucartambo, Calca and neighboring areas—experienced renewed activity of epidemic (exanthematous) typhus, historically attributed to Rickettsia prowazekii. Three outbreak foci investigated between May 1997 and April 1998 in Quispicanchis (including districts like Ccatcca and Chillihuani) involved clusters of febrile illness in heavily louse‑infested, high‑altitude communities. Official regional surveillance subsequently reported 136 probable exanthematous‑typhus cases in 1998 (≈70 laboratory confirmed) and 547 probable cases in 1999 (122 confirmed) across multiple Cusco provinces, making this one of the largest recognized foci of modern louse‑borne typhus in the Americas. Implementation of case‑finding, antibiotic treatment (notably doxycycline), and intensive insecticidal dusting campaigns in homes, combined with seasonal declines in louse populations, led to a marked drop in confirmed cases by 2000, although serosurveys and surveillance data indicate that epidemic typhus remains endemic at low levels in poor, cold, high‑altitude communities of southern Peru.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronic poverty, overcrowded and poorly constructed dwellings, limited access to water and bathing facilities, and cold high‑altitude climate in Andean communities of Cusco facilitated persistent body‑louse infestation and sustained transmission once epidemic typhus re‑appeared. Delayed recognition of outbreaks, incomplete application of vector control, and difficulties in reaching remote rural populations further contributed to spread. Internal mechanisms: Available Peruvian serologic and outbreak data indicate circulation of classic typhus‑group rickettsiae (treated operationally as R. prowazekii) in long‑established endemic highland foci; no specific evidence of a new strain, altered virulence, or host expansion was presented. Thus the episode is best classified as re‑occurrence of a known pathogen in an endemic region under permissive socio‑environmental conditions, not as genetically driven re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event to capture major Peruvian outbreaks). Rationale: Multiple Peruvian sources, including Morón (1999) and the regional laboratory study from Cusco, document that Cusco department has contributed more than half of the world’s notified exanthematous‑typhus cases in recent decades and that there were clear epidemic increases in 1997–1999, with at least 683 probable cases and nearly 200 laboratory‑confirmed infections across several highland provinces. These represent large, geographically coherent outbreaks and are substantially more impactful than the previously listed event based only on a small serosurvey. The continent (South America), sub‑region (South America), and country (Peru) entries are correct, and the classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, given long‑standing endemicity in the southern Peruvian Andes and lack of evidence for a novel strain or host jump. This row is added to ensure that one of the few sizeable R. prowazekii resurgence episodes in the Americas after 1990 is captured among the top impact events. Recommended status: RETAIN as a major late‑1990s emergence episode in South America.

Host: Humans (male adolescents and young adults in an overcrowded youth rehabilitation center with heavy body-louse infestation)
Event summary: In 2012, an outbreak investigation in a male youth rehabilitation center in western Rwanda identified a mixed outbreak of epidemic typhus and trench fever among residents living in severely overcrowded, unhygienic conditions with widespread body‑lice infestation. Between April and late 2012, investigators documented 199 suspected cases of acute febrile illness among approximately 1,910 residents (attack rate ≈10%), with seven reported deaths, and laboratory testing of a subset of patients and lice confirmed infection with Rickettsia prowazekii alongside Bartonella quintana. The outbreak was controlled after targeted antibiotic treatment, delousing of residents, improved laundering and bed‑linen hygiene, and better overcrowding management within the facility, and no evidence emerged of spread into the surrounding community, illustrating a localized institutional re‑occurrence of epidemic typhus in a country with historical louse‑borne typhus activity but no recent large‑scale epidemics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe overcrowding, poor structural conditions, and infrequent washing of clothing and bedding in the rehabilitation center created ideal circumstances for intense body‑louse transmission, and case‑control analysis showed that seeing lice on clothing and delayed washing of clothes and bed linen were strong risk factors for illness. Many residents may also have come from impoverished backgrounds with prior louse exposure, and the presence of older individuals with past infection raises the possibility of Brill–Zinsser recrudescence seeding the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate emergence of a novel R. prowazekii strain or altered virulence; instead, the episode is consistent with re‑occurrence of classic epidemic typhus in a previously endemic central‑East African region under renewed conditions of extreme crowding and poor hygiene.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added post‑2000 event). Rationale: A 2016 American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene paper and subsequent rickettsiosis reviews describe this 2012 youth‑center outbreak in Rwanda as a confirmed mixed epidemic typhus/trench fever episode with 199 suspected cases and seven deaths, and it is cited as the most recent documented outbreak of R. prowazekii‑associated epidemic typhus worldwide. The continent, sub‑region, and country fields (Africa | Eastern Africa | Rwanda) reflect the UNSD regional classification, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, because Rwanda has long been part of the central‑East African typhus focus and there is no evidence of a new strain or geographic expansion. Although smaller in absolute case numbers than the 1990s Burundian and Peruvian outbreaks, this is one of the very few modern institutional outbreaks and clearly qualifies as a high‑impact emergence event relative to the near‑absence of epidemic typhus elsewhere after 2000. Inclusion corrects the earlier meta‑description, which stated that 2005–2025 saw only sporadic cases and no outbreaks, and ensures adequate representation of recent African events. Recommended status: RETAIN as the key post‑2000 emergence episode.

Host: Humans (local residents in communities along the Senegal River and around Richard-Toll)
Event summary: Following completion of the Diama dam on the lower Senegal River in 1986, large freshwater bodies formed in the delta and around Lake Guiers in northern Senegal and southern Mauritania, an area where Schistosoma mansoni had not previously been recorded, though S. haematobium occurred at low, seasonal levels. Within a few years, explosive outbreaks of intestinal schistosomiasis occurred, with S. mansoni prevalence in the town of Richard‑Toll rising from under 2% in 1988 to around 60–70% by 1990–1991, and over 70% in some neighborhoods, indicating intense new local transmission. Transmission remained very high into the early 1990s until regional schistosomiasis control programmes with praziquantel mass treatment and snail habitat management began to reduce morbidity, though the Senegal River basin persists as one of the world’s most hyperendemic schistosomiasis foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Construction of the Diama anti‑salt dam and associated irrigation schemes dramatically expanded and stabilized freshwater habitat in a previously brackish/saline estuarine zone, promoting proliferation of Biomphalaria pfeifferi and other snail intermediate hosts; expansion of irrigated agriculture, sugar estates and daily water contact among workers and residents increased human exposure to cercariae. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (rapid growth and colonization of canals and reservoirs by Biomphalaria snails) and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as S. mansoni established sustained transmission in a part of the Western Africa sub-region where it had not been recorded before, representing re-occurrence driven by environmental change rather than novel parasite strains.
Review: review: Event is real and represents one of the largest dam-associated schistosomiasis outbreaks globally. Corrected emergence-type classification from intra_continental_emergence=Yes to intra_continental_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, because the outbreak occurred within the Western Africa sub-region where schistosomiasis was already known; under the project’s definitions, intra-continental emergence should only be used for spread to a new UN sub-region, not to a new focus within Western Africa. Years 1990–1994 reasonably capture the early hyperendemic phase, although initial cases began in 1988; no change made to the year field.

Host: Humans (local lakeshore communities, schoolchildren, tourists and expatriates exposed while swimming or diving in Lake Malawi)
Event summary: Until the late 1980s, the open waters and shorelines of Lake Malawi were widely regarded in travel medicine as essentially free of schistosomiasis, despite endemic transmission elsewhere in Malawi. In December 1991–1992, acute urinary schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma haematobium began to be reported in travelers and Peace Corps volunteers who had swum at Cape Maclear, and a 1993 CDC investigation found high seroprevalence of S. haematobium among expatriates whose only freshwater exposure was Lake Malawi. Subsequent surveys in the 1990s and early 2000s documented very high S. haematobium prevalence (often >50–70%, and up to >80% in some villages) among lakeshore schoolchildren along the southern and south‑western shores, demonstrating establishment of intense local transmission; these high prevalences persisted into the 2000s and early 2010s despite national control efforts, firmly establishing Lake Malawi’s southern shoreline as a major schistosomiasis risk for both residents and visitors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of shoreline settlements and agriculture, increased human use of the lake for bathing, washing and recreation, and changing hydrology and environmental management (including reduced snail‑eating fish and local water-resource developments) around the lake increased human–water contact and created suitable habitats for Bulinus globosus and endemic B. nyassanus. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent), as lacustrine Bulinus populations—especially B. nyassanus—acted as competent intermediate hosts and allowed S. haematobium to establish sustained transmission in lake habitats previously believed to pose little or no risk, representing a major re-occurrence of urogenital schistosomiasis within Eastern Africa rather than intra-continental emergence.
Review: review: Event is well supported by BMJ, MMWR, and subsequent Malawian epidemiological studies, and clearly represents a large re-occurrence/resurgence of urogenital schistosomiasis along Lake Malawi’s shores. Changed emergence-type classification from intra_continental_emergence=Yes to intra_continental_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, because the event occurred within Eastern Africa where S. haematobium was long endemic; under the project rules, spread within the same UN sub-region is re-occurrence, not intra-continental emergence. Host: Humans (rural residents, including farmers and fishermen, in hilly/mountainous and lake–marshland Schistosoma japonicum foci)
Event summary: By the early 1990s, large-scale schistosomiasis control programmes in China, supported by a World Bank Loan Project, had reduced Schistosoma japonicum infections from an estimated 11–12 million cases in the 1950s to under one million, with transmission interrupted or greatly reduced in many counties. From the mid‑1990s into the early 2000s, however, schistosomiasis re‑occurred in previously controlled hilly and mountainous areas of Sichuan and in lake and marshland regions along the Yangtze, with acute infections signaling renewed transmission in villages that had met prior control targets. By about 2004, national surveys showed that the prevalence of infection in endemic areas had plateaued or rebounded compared with 1995, prompting China to re‑elevate schistosomiasis to a top national public‑health priority and to adopt a new integrated transmission-blocking strategy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Termination of major external funding and the World Bank Loan Project in 2001, ecological changes including repeated flooding of the Yangtze River in the late 1990s, expansion of wetlands and irrigation schemes that created new Oncomelania hupensis snail habitats, increased mobility of infected humans and bovine reservoirs, and limitations of diagnostic tools that under‑detected residual infection. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence of major parasite genetic change; the episode is best characterized as Re-occurrence driven by environmental and programmatic factors, with Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (snail proliferation in modified landscapes) and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Eastern Asia.
Review: retain: Large-scale resurgence of S. japonicum in China during the late 1990s–early 2000s is well documented and clearly among the highest-impact schistosomiasis events since 1990. Geography (Eastern Asia, China) and classification as re_occurrence (with no first detection or inter-/intra-continental spread) are consistent with the project’s definitions; no changes made beyond minor source consolidation.

Host: Humans (local residents, vacationers and tourists in Porto de Galinhas, a coastal resort area in Pernambuco State)
Event summary: Around the September 7 national holiday in 2000, heavy rainfall caused the Ipojuca River to flood low‑lying neighborhoods in Porto de Galinhas, a major beach resort in Pernambuco, Brazil, leading to intense exposure of residents and visitors to contaminated floodwaters. An ensuing epidemic of acute Schistosoma mansoni infection was documented, with an epidemiological survey reporting 412 acute cases among about 2,800 residents across several localities, revealing a new, highly active urban–coastal transmission focus in an area better known for tourism than for rural parasitic disease. Over the subsequent decade, parasitological and malacological surveys showed that schistosomiasis became endemically established in Porto de Galinhas, with persistent human infection and infected Biomphalaria snails in peri‑urban water bodies despite control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid, unplanned urbanization and tourism‑driven population growth in Porto de Galinhas without adequate sanitation led to fecal contamination of surface waters, while flooding events connected contaminated streams, yards and informal drainage, exposing large numbers of people during a holiday period; migration of infected individuals from rural endemic zones introduced S. mansoni eggs into new peri‑urban aquatic habitats. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (Biomphalaria snail colonization of peri‑urban drainage, ditches and flood‑prone yards) and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent), as S. mansoni established a new urban–coastal focus within Brazil’s long‑endemic Northeast, representing a high‑impact re-occurrence rather than intra-continental emergence.
Review: review: Porto de Galinhas is a well-described large urban–coastal outbreak (≈400 acute cases, long-term endemisation) and clearly among the most impactful modern S. mansoni events in South America. Corrected emergence-type classification from intra_continental_emergence=Yes to intra_continental_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, as Brazil and the South America sub-region have long been endemic and this episode represents an urban re-occurrence within that sub-region. No changes to years, location or narrative.
