Host: Humans (French and other European tourists and local residents exposed while bathing in the Cavu River, southern Corsica; infection due to Schistosoma haematobium × S. bovis hybrids)
Event summary: In summer 2013, an unexpected outbreak of urogenital schistosomiasis occurred among tourists and residents who had bathed in the Cavu River in southern Corsica, France, with more than 100 locally acquired Schistosoma haematobium infections eventually identified through national and international surveillance, representing the first recognized cluster of autochthonous human schistosomiasis in Europe in decades. Subsequent investigations and serosurveys identified additional autochthonous infections linked to the Cavu in 2015 and 2016, and infected Bulinus truncatus snails plus molecular analyses confirmed a S. haematobium–S. bovis hybrid strain adapted to local conditions, indicating established transmission in this Western European river focus. Following targeted risk communication, restricted bathing, surveillance of snails and human cases, and treatment of identified infections, no further large clusters have been reported, but the event demonstrated that hybrid schistosomes can re‑emerge and sustain transmission in southern European freshwater ecosystems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Repeated introduction of S. haematobium and S. bovis by infected migrants or travelers from endemic African regions, high summertime tourist use of the Cavu River for bathing, and the presence of suitable Bulinus truncatus snail hosts created conditions for establishment of transmission; climatic and ecological conditions in southern Corsica provided a permissive environment for snail survival. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence through S. haematobium × S. bovis hybridization, which may have broadened host and environmental tolerances; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (successful exploitation of local B. truncatus populations) and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) into a Western European river system with no recent history of human schistosomiasis, fitting the project’s definition of re-emergence in a previously endemic continent.
Review: review: Event is robustly documented and highly significant despite modest case numbers, as it marks re-establishment of autochthonous human schistosomiasis in Europe driven by a S. haematobium × S. bovis hybrid. Corrected sub_regions from “Southern Europe” to “Western Europe” to align with the UN/UNSD classification for France, and adjusted year and country tag from 2011–2016/France [2011] to 2013–2016/France [2013] to match the documented start of the recognized outbreak, while still noting earlier bathing exposures in 2011–2012 in the summary. Classification as re_emergence (with no inter-/intra-continental emergence flag) is appropriate and retained.

Host: Humans (local residents in rural irrigation areas around Almería, southeast Spain, exposed to irrigation pools and channels)
Event summary: In 2003, a small cluster of urogenital schistosomiasis cases occurred among farmers in an irrigated agricultural area near Almería, southeast Spain, who had no history of freshwater exposure in endemic countries, implying local transmission. Retrospective outbreak investigation, including detailed patient histories and later environmental and malacological studies, documented autochthonous S. haematobium transmission associated with a local freshwater irrigation pond and Bulinus truncatus snail populations, representing the first recognized modern European focus outside Corsica. After belated recognition of the event years later, public‑health authorities implemented heightened clinical vigilance, snail surveys, and warnings against swimming in irrigation pools, and no sustained large-scale transmission has been documented since, though the episode highlighted ongoing risk given the presence of competent snail hosts and imported human infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of S. haematobium infection by migrants or travelers from endemic African regions into an area with suitable but previously overlooked B. truncatus snail populations, combined with use of small irrigation ponds and channels for recreation and hygiene by local residents. Internal mechanisms: Primarily a Re-occurrence event driven by human movement and environmental suitability rather than demonstrable parasite genetic change; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as S. haematobium exploited local B. truncatus habitats in southeastern Spain, reintroducing urogenital schistosomiasis into a Southern European sub-region with historical but long-interrupted transmission.
Review: retain: Autochthonous S. haematobium transmission in Almería is a real but small cluster (four confirmed local cases) that is nonetheless important as an early signal of renewed European receptivity. Geography (Southern Europe, Spain) and classification as re_occurrence with no intra-/inter-continental flags match the project definitions; sources have been trimmed to the most directly relevant outbreak and regional-overview papers.

Host: Humans (riverine villagers, schoolchildren and young adults living along the Mekong River in Khong and Mounlapamok Districts, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, and in Kratié and Stung Treng Provinces, Cambodia)
Event summary: After years of conflict and minimal surveillance in the Mekong region, severe schistosomiasis cases with hepatosplenic disease were rediscovered in the early 1990s among residents of Khong and Mounlapamok Districts in southern Lao People’s Democratic Republic and in villages along the Mekong in Kratié Province, Cambodia. Surveys in the mid‑1990s documented very high Schistosoma mekongi prevalence, often exceeding 60–70% and reaching over 70–80% in some communities, with frequent portal hypertension and variceal bleeding in adolescents and young adults. Recognition of this long‑neglected but highly focal endemicity prompted the launch of mass praziquantel treatment and health-education campaigns from 1994–1995 onward, eventually covering around 80,000 at-risk persons in Kratié and Stung Treng and the endemic districts of Lao PDR, and rapidly reducing infection prevalence and severe morbidity by the late 1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged civil conflict and weakness of health systems in Lao PDR and Cambodia, lack of safe water and sanitation, intense daily water contact with the Mekong River for fishing, bathing and household chores, and limited access to diagnosis and treatment allowed long-standing S. mekongi transmission and severe morbidity to go largely unrecognized until systematic surveys in the early–mid 1990s. Internal mechanisms: Transmission depends on the highly focal distribution of the intermediate snail host Neotricula aperta and involvement of animal reservoirs (e.g., dogs and pigs), but there is no clear evidence of major parasite genetic change in this period; the episode is best characterized as high-impact re-occurrence in a previously known South-eastern Asia sub-region.
Review: review: This row has been added to capture a major omission: the rediscovery and control of highly prevalent S. mekongi foci in Lao PDR and Cambodia in the 1990s, which involved tens of thousands of heavily infected people and substantial mortality and morbidity. Classified as re_occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because Mekong schistosomiasis had been known since the 1950s–1960s but was neglected during periods of conflict; geography and timing reflect the early–mid 1990s surveys and the first phase of mass drug administration. Event should be retained but is flagged for review and possible refinement of exact start/end years.

Host: Humans (residents of Khong and Mounlapamok Districts along the Mekong River in southern Lao People’s Democratic Republic)
Event summary: After several rounds of praziquantel mass drug administration in the late 1980s and 1990s, Schistosoma mekongi prevalence in Lao People’s Democratic Republic had fallen to around 2% in sentinel villages by the end of the 1990s. However, when mass treatment and health-education activities were discontinued after 1999 because of waning financial support, infection prevalence rebounded rapidly. A 2003 survey across 64 endemic communities in Khong District found an overall S. mekongi prevalence of 11% (with some villages up to 47%), and a joint Lao–Swiss study in 2005–2006 reported prevalence as high as 68% in Khong and 4% in Mounlapamok, with renewed hepatosplenic morbidity, bringing infection levels back to those seen before initial control. These findings triggered renewed national and international efforts toward elimination of Mekong schistosomiasis in Lao PDR.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Discontinuation of mass drug administration and health-education efforts after 1999, continued intense daily contact with the Mekong River, persistent poverty and lack of sanitation, and the presence of animal reservoirs allowed S. mekongi transmission to resurge quickly once control pressure was relaxed. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for major parasite genetic change; this is best interpreted as re-occurrence driven by programmatic and ecological factors, with Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and continued Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of Neotricula aperta snail habitats along sections of the Mekong.
Review: review: New row added to capture the documented re-emergence of S. mekongi in Lao PDR after interruption of MDA, which returned prevalence to very high levels (up to 68%) in the mid-2000s and is widely cited as a key example of control lapses leading to resurgence. Classified as re_occurrence since the parasite and its distribution were already known and the drivers were chiefly external (ending MDA, persistent exposure), not clear genetic change. Geography restricted to Lao People’s Democratic Republic, as control activities in Cambodia continued without a comparable rebound. Flagged for expert review of precise year range and wording.

Host: Humans (primary-school children and shoreline communities in Mangochi District, southern Lake Malawi, exposed at lakeshore sites and aquaculture ponds)
Event summary: In November 2017, malacological surveys in Mangochi District at the southern tip of Lake Malawi unexpectedly discovered populations of Biomphalaria pfeifferi snails in submerged Vallisneria beds, a species not previously known from the lake. By May 2018, additional B. pfeifferi populations were found at multiple shoreline sites, and a survey of 175 nearby schoolchildren showed intestinal schistosomiasis prevalence of about 34% by circulating cathodic antigen testing, with Schistosoma mansoni eggs confirmed in stool from several children and frequent co-infection with S. haematobium. Follow‑up cross-sectional surveys in 2019 across multiple shoreline schools demonstrated that intestinal schistosomiasis had transitioned from emergence to a wider outbreak, with ongoing high urogenital schistosomiasis prevalence, leading authors to call for intensified control and revised travel and health advice for Lake Malawi.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ecological changes in Lake Malawi, including lake‑level fluctuations, overfishing of molluscivorous fish such as Trematocranus placodon, and expansion of aquaculture ponds using pumped lake water, created favorable habitats for B. pfeifferi and increased human water contact at high‑risk sites; these changes occurred despite ongoing school-based praziquantel distribution targeting urogenital schistosomiasis. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent), as B. pfeifferi colonized new lacustrine and pond habitats and supported local S. mansoni transmission in an area previously thought to lack intestinal schistosomiasis, constituting a notable re-occurrence within Eastern Africa rather than a new continental emergence.
Review: review: This row has been newly added to represent the emergence and subsequent outbreak of intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni) along the southern shoreline of Lake Malawi from 2017 onwards, documented by discovery of B. pfeifferi in the lake and high infection prevalence in nearby schools. Classified as re_occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because Malawi and Eastern Africa were already endemic for S. mansoni; the novelty concerns new lacustrine foci. Years 2017–2019 align with first snail detection, confirmation of emergence (2018) and outbreak characterization (2019).

Event summary: From the mid‑1990s to early 2000s, previously rare serotype G9 rotaviruses (most often G9P[8]) expanded rapidly from initial detections in Bangladesh and India to become a major cause of pediatric gastroenteritis across Asia, the Americas, Europe, Africa and Australia. Surveillance sites reported seasons in which G9P[8] composed 70–90% of rotavirus infections and caused large outbreaks, such as the 2001 G9P[8] epidemic across central and northern Australia. By the mid‑2000s, G9 was recognised as the fifth globally common human rotavirus genotype, after which its prevalence began to oscillate as other genotypes and vaccines altered strain ecology.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High background transmission in largely unvaccinated child populations, extensive international travel and migration, and limited prior population immunity to G9 facilitated rapid multi‑continental spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through frequent reassortment among human Wa‑like strains (and occasional animal contributions) generated successful G9P[8] lineages, enabling re‑emergence of a once‑rare serotype as a globally dominant genotype.

Event summary: After a prototype G12 strain was described in the Philippines in 1990, G12 rotaviruses were rarely detected until they reappeared in 2002 in Thailand and the United States and then spread widely through the 2000s. By the mid‑2000s, G12 (often G12P[8] or G12P[6]) caused sizable fractions of hospitalizations in countries such as India, Hungary, Malawi and several Latin American and African sites, sometimes becoming a leading genotype in single seasons. Around 2010, G12 was established as a globally distributed human genotype, after which its prevalence fluctuated but it remained part of the dominant global genotype set into the early vaccine era.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High birth cohorts and intense transmission in low‑ and middle‑income countries, together with international travel and trade, promoted dissemination from initial foci in Asia to Africa, the Americas and Europe. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment created G12 lineages with human‑adapted Wa‑like genomic constellations; phylogenetic analyses show a rapid expansion of specific G12 lineages that mirrors the earlier global emergence of G9.

Host: Humans (mostly children <5 years, with some adult cases)
Event summary: In February–March 2005, Nicaragua experienced one of its largest recorded national outbreaks of severe acute gastroenteritis, with ≥64,000 cases and at least 56 deaths, predominantly among children under five years of age. Investigation of stool specimens showed that a newly introduced, mutated G4P[8] lineage Ic rotavirus, not previously seen in Nicaragua, accounted for most rotavirus‑positive cases, alongside smaller contributions from G9P[8] and mixed infections. Following emergency clinical and public‑health measures and the end of the seasonal peak, cases subsided; the event helped catalyse early introduction of rotavirus vaccination in Nicaragua in 2006.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A large susceptible child population with limited prior exposure to the specific G4 lineage, crowded living conditions and limited access to advanced care in some regions contributed to high incidence and mortality. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence—phylogenetic and structural analyses showed a distinct G4P[8] lineage Ic virus with amino‑acid changes in VP7, including an insertion at position 76 and substitutions in antigenic regions, which likely facilitated escape from pre‑existing population immunity and fuelled a nationwide outbreak.

Host: Humans (all age groups, with highest morbidity in children 0–5 years)
Event summary: During autumn 2005, Malatya City in Türkiye experienced a large waterborne outbreak of acute diarrhoea caused by group A rotavirus, with 9,907 patients aged 0–91 years presenting for care and the highest incidence among young children. Epidemiologic investigation linked cases to contamination of a large drinking‑water reservoir supplied by a well; rotavirus RNA was detected at high frequency in source water samples. After chlorination was intensified and the contaminated connection was closed, the outbreak wave declined and rotavirus incidence returned toward background seasonal levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Failure of drinking‑water treatment and distribution infrastructure (contamination of a municipal reservoir by faecally polluted well water) and reliance on a single water source for large urban districts enabled explosive spread of rotavirus via the water supply. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel antigenic genotype was reported; this event represents re‑occurrence of common group A rotaviruses driven primarily by environmental and infrastructure failures rather than viral evolution.
Review: review: Newly added event. Included because it is one of the best-documented, very large (>9,000 cases) rotavirus outbreaks in the 1990–present period and thus plausibly among the top 10 highest-impact emergence episodes for this EPP. Classified as re_occurrence (same species and common genotypes, externally driven by water contamination) with continent/subregion aligned to the Country sheet (Türkiye in Western Asia).

Shortly thereafter, similar DS‑1‑like G1P[8] strains rose to predominance among hospitalised children in Malawi soon after Rotarix introduction and were detected in Brazil and in archived pre‑vaccine samples from South Africa, indicating broader circulation. Host: Humans (severe neuroinvasive disease/encephalitis)
Event summary: Between 1990 and 1992, Massachusetts experienced a renewed episode of human eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), with four confirmed cases and one death after several quieter years, indicating cyclical resurgence in long‑established foci. The episode developed alongside intense equine and mosquito activity in freshwater swamp habitats of southeastern Massachusetts, prompting strengthened arboviral surveillance and targeted mosquito control. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel lineage or major viral change; this episode reflects cyclical amplification within established enzootic foci leading to spillover into humans (re-occurrence rather than re-emergence).
Review: retain – Massachusetts surveillance tables document four human EEE cases and one death during 1990–1992, with activity confined to long‑known foci; classification as re-occurrence, and the geography, hosts, and timing, are consistent with available data, so no structural changes were made.

Event summary: From 2004 to 2006, the northeastern United States, especially Massachusetts and New Hampshire, experienced an amplified EEE cycle that peaked in 2005, when New Hampshire reported seven locally acquired human cases and national totals reached about 21 cases, the highest annual count since national surveillance began. The outbreak developed as widespread EEEV activity was detected in mosquitoes, birds and equines across New England and parts of the Gulf Coast, leading to multiple human encephalitis cases and deaths. Transmission waned after 2006, but this episode established the modern pattern of episodic, regionally extensive human EEE outbreaks in the United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and warm summer conditions that enhanced larval habitats; extensive hardwood swamp ecosystems sustaining large Culiseta melanura populations; residential development and outdoor activity near swamp margins; improved clinical recognition and laboratory testing. Internal mechanisms: Available phylogenetic work indicates circulation of established North American Group I EEEV strains without clear evidence of a new genotype; the pattern is best characterized as cyclical re-occurrence driven by environmental and ecological amplification rather than viral innovation.

No evidence for a novel viral lineage; treating this as a large re-occurrence in long‑affected areas is appropriate, and country/subregion fields are correct.

Host: Humans (primarily adults and children in affected communities in south-central and southwestern Uganda)
Event summary: After more than three decades without recognized ONNV activity, clusters of acute febrile illness with severe polyarthralgia were detected starting in mid-1996 in Rakai District and other areas of south-central and southwestern Uganda, and virological investigation confirmed O'nyong-nyong virus as the cause. The epidemic spread rapidly through affected Ugandan districts during 1996–1997, with serosurveys estimating infection rates of roughly half or more of the local population in some villages and substantial short-term work absenteeism, but there was no evidence of spread outside Uganda comparable to the 1959–1962 multi-country epidemic.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/3/1/97-0112_article?utm_source=openai)) As immunity accumulated and vector densities declined, transmission waned and the epidemic ended by late 1997.

Event type as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) is defensible because available genetic data do not link viral changes to altered virulence or host range. I did not alter the row, but note that some secondary summaries ambiguously suggest spread to Kenya/Tanzania by conflating this epidemic with the 1959–1962 event; the conservative choice to list only Uganda is therefore appropriate but could be revisited if stronger evidence of in situ transmission in neighbouring countries emerges.

Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Occupational and travel-related exposure of a non-immune individual to local Anopheles vectors in rural southern Chad, combined with limited arboviral diagnostic capacity in the region such that ONNV circulation may have gone undetected until this imported-to-Europe case prompted detailed testing.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3291225/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic analysis showed the virus to be closely related to known ONNV strains, with no evidence of a distinct, more virulent genotype; the event is therefore interpreted as re-occurrence or documentation of existing transmission foci in Central Africa rather than re-emergence driven by viral evolution.
Review: review – This single confirmed ONNV infection in Chad is well documented and correctly located in Middle Africa, and the event type as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because ONNV had long been established in the African human host system and in neighbouring Central African countries. However, its impact (one recognized case, no onward transmission) is small compared with other post-1990 ONNV events; I am leaving it in the dataset because there are relatively few documented ONNV episodes since 1990 and first laboratory confirmation in a new country may be of analytical interest, but a human reviewer should decide whether it falls below the impact threshold for inclusion among the “largest” emergence events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (adults and children living in rural coastal villages in Kwale County, eastern Kenya)
Event summary: In 2009–2010, a large community-based serosurvey in coastal Kenya (two village clusters in Kwale County) tested 1,848 residents for alphavirus antibodies using ELISA and plaque-reduction neutralization tests and found very high O'nyong-nyong virus seroprevalence (around half of participants or more had ONNV-neutralizing antibodies), substantially exceeding chikungunya virus seroprevalence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4319898/?utm_source=openai)) Although this study did not correspond to a clinically recognized ONNV epidemic and the timing of individual infections could not be pinpointed, the results indicate intense or recurrent ONNV transmission in coastal Kenya during the 2000s, making this one of the most impactful post-1990 re-occurrence episodes in terms of cumulative human infections. No discrete epidemic endpoint was documented; instead, the data suggest sustained endemic or periodically epidemic transmission in this coastal focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent exposure of coastal Kenyan communities to efficient anopheline vectors in environments with abundant breeding sites (e.g. irrigated agriculture, standing water around homes), limited vector control, and frequent misattribution of febrile arthralgia to malaria or other causes, allowing ONNV transmission to proceed largely unrecognized.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4319898/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific viral genetic changes were identified as drivers of this high seroprevalence; instead, the study supports the view that ONNV is endemic in parts of East Africa, with periodic or continuous transmission driven by ecological and human behavioural factors rather than recent viral evolution.
Review: review – This is a newly added event row representing the very high ONNV seroprevalence documented in coastal Kenya in 2009–2010, which indicates a substantial cumulative burden of infection and is highlighted as a key epidemiologic finding in multiple reviews. Although the serosurvey does not define a sharp epidemic onset or end and infections likely accumulated over several years, the magnitude of exposure makes this one of the most impactful post-1990 ONNV re-occurrence episodes. Because interpretation depends heavily on serology with potential cross-reactivity to chikungunya virus and on assumptions about when infections occurred, this row should be reviewed by experts to confirm that treating it as a single temporally bounded “event” is acceptable for the project’s purposes.

Host: Humans (Pogosta disease in Finland, Ockelbo disease in Sweden, Karelian fever in north‑west Russian Federation); associated wild birds and ornithophilic mosquitoes (enzootic cycle)
Event summary: In late summer and autumn 1995, Finland experienced its largest recorded epidemic of Pogosta disease, with more than 1,300 serodiagnosed Sindbis virus infections concentrated in eastern and central regions but with cases reported across much of the country; contemporaneous increases in clinically similar Ockelbo disease and Karelian fever were noted in neighbouring Sweden and Russian Karelia, indicating a broader Fennoscandian outbreak. The epidemic followed the characteristic roughly seven‑year cyclic pattern of SINV activity in the region, with incidence peaking in highly endemic lake‑forest districts before declining over subsequent seasons as population immunity rose and vector densities fell. Transmission ended with the winter collapse of mosquito populations, after which SINV persisted at low levels in local bird–mosquito cycles during inter‑epidemic years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cyclic build‑up of susceptible human populations between major outbreak years; favourable weather in preceding seasons (warm, wet summers) that supported high densities of ornithophilic mosquitoes; high abundance of grouse and other reservoir birds in forested lake districts; outdoor recreational and subsistence activities (e.g. berry and mushroom picking) that increased human exposure to mosquitoes. Internal mechanisms: circulation of endemic European SINV genotype I without clear evidence of major new variants or expanded host range; the 1995 resurgence is best explained by ecological and climatic forcing superimposed on partial human immunity rather than by viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 1995 is consistently documented as the largest Pogosta/Ockelbo/Karelian fever outbreak (>1,300 confirmed cases in Finland) with concurrent activity in Sweden and Russian Karelia; geography, timing and classification as a re-occurrence in an established endemic focus are well supported by national surveillance and outbreak investigations, and no major corrections were required.

Host: Humans; migratory and resident birds (especially grouse); ornithophilic mosquitoes (e.g. Culex, Ochlerotatus spp.)
Event summary: In 2002, a major Sindbis virus epidemic struck Finland, producing approximately 600 serologically confirmed Pogosta disease cases nationwide with particularly high incidence (around 81 per 100,000) in the highly endemic North Karelia region and additional clusters in other eastern and central districts, while contemporaneous outbreaks of related Ockelbo and Karelian fever syndromes occurred in adjacent parts of Sweden and Russian Karelia. The outbreak developed over summer and early autumn following a build‑up of vector and bird reservoir populations and was accompanied by serological evidence of intense SINV circulation in both resident and migratory birds. Transmission subsided with the onset of colder weather and mosquito die‑off, after which case numbers returned to baseline, although chronic arthralgia persisted in a substantial subset of patients and SINV continued to circulate at low levels in bird–mosquito cycles.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: warm, wet conditions in preceding seasons that boosted mosquito populations; high densities of tetraonid birds (black grouse, capercaillie) acting as amplifying hosts; human outdoor activities in forested lake areas, such as berry and mushroom picking and fishing, increasing exposure to mosquitoes. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of SINV genotype I without strong evidence for a more virulent novel strain; the epidemic pattern largely reflects ecological amplification and periodic depletion and replenishment of human immunity rather than fundamental change in viral biology, although this outbreak also yielded the first human SINV isolates from Europe and confirmed SINV as the aetiologic agent of Pogosta disease.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2002 Finnish-led Fennoscandian outbreak is the second-largest recorded SINV epidemic (~600 cases in Finland) and a key event in which SINV was first isolated from European patients; the geography and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. The event description was retained but the Wikipedia citation was replaced with primary outbreak reports and analytic studies, and the role of this outbreak in yielding the first European human isolates was clarified.

Host: Humans; wild birds; mosquitoes
Event summary: In 2009, Fennoscandia experienced another, more moderate Sindbis virus outbreak year, with elevated Pogosta disease notifications in Finland and increased Ockelbo and Karelian fever reports in parts of Sweden and Russian Karelia compared with surrounding years, although far below the peaks of 1995 and 2002. The outbreak developed over the summer transmission season, following the characteristic approximately seven‑year periodicity of SINV activity linked to ecological cycles in reservoir and vector populations. As autumn progressed, human case numbers declined and the region returned to a low‑incidence state with sporadic infections and persistent subclinical circulation in birds and mosquitoes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cyclical dynamics of SINV in grouse and other birds and climatic conditions conducive to mosquito proliferation in 2009, superimposed on a partially immune human population after previous epidemics; intensified surveillance for arboviral disease in some Nordic countries. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence for novel strain emergence; phylogeographic studies indicate continued circulation of established SINV genotype I lineages across Fennoscandia, suggesting that the 2009 resurgence was primarily environmentally and demographically driven re-occurrence rather than re-emergence due to viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 2009 is consistently identified in analytical work as a Nordic Sindbis outbreak year with clearly elevated incidence, even if smaller than the 1995 and 2002 peaks; the geography and treatment as a re-occurrence in known endemic areas are appropriate, and no major corrections were needed.

Host: Humans; mosquitoes (e.g. Culex univittatus); wild and domestic animals in shared ecologies
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2010, South Africa recorded continuous laboratory‑confirmed Sindbis fever cases in humans, with a marked increase in 2010 when 208 of 2,025 suspected arboviral cases tested IgM‑positive for SINV, representing a sharp rise compared with 2006–2009 and indicating a substantial though under‑recognised outbreak mainly on the central plateau. The episode unfolded largely in late summer and early autumn in provinces such as Free State and Northern Cape, where SINV is endemic and where above‑average rainfall simultaneously fuelled a large Rift Valley fever epidemic in livestock and humans, suggesting shared climatic drivers for both arboviruses. As vector populations declined and drier conditions returned, Sindbis case detections fell back to background sporadic levels, with no severe or fatal human cases reported in this series but highlighting ongoing endemic transmission and the potential for larger future outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unusually high rainfall and flooding in 2009–2010 that increased breeding sites for Culex mosquitoes, coinciding with an extensive Rift Valley fever epizootic; agricultural and outdoor occupational exposure of farmers and farm workers in the central plateau; limited awareness and routine diagnostic testing for Sindbis fever leading to substantial under‑ascertainment except during intensified arbovirus investigations. Internal mechanisms: established South African SINV lineages maintained in bird–mosquito cycles with no evidence for new, more virulent genotypes; the 2010 spike is best interpreted as a climate‑driven re-occurrence of endemic SINV activity rather than true re-emergence due to viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2010 peak in Sindbis fever detections in South Africa (208 IgM-positive cases) is the largest well-characterised post-1990 outbreak there and clearly linked to climatic conditions that also drove widespread Rift Valley fever; geography, timing and classification as climate-driven re-occurrence are appropriate and supported by national surveillance data.

Host: Wild birds (e.g. hooded crow and other passerines); ornithophilic mosquitoes; incidental equids and other mammals; potential but as yet rarely documented human exposure
Event summary: From 2009 onward, Sindbis virus was repeatedly detected in Germany, beginning with isolation of SINV from Culex and Anopheles mosquitoes in the Upper Rhine valley in 2009 and, in 2010, from a hooded crow in Berlin, followed by multiple detections in mosquitoes and resident birds through at least 2016 during nationwide arbovirus monitoring. These findings confirmed for the first time an established bird–mosquito SINV transmission cycle in Germany, a country previously regarded as lying outside the main human disease foci in Fennoscandia and South Africa, and showed that at least two closely related genotype I lineages were co‑circulating. Despite serological evidence of past infection in blood donors and widespread enzootic circulation along river floodplains and wetlands, only isolated or no confirmed autochthonous human Sindbis fever cases were recognised, and the episode transitioned into low‑level endemicity while public and veterinary health attention increasingly focused on emerging flaviviruses such as West Nile and Usutu viruses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: westward expansion of SINV‑infected migratory birds from long‑established foci in Fennoscandia and eastern Europe; suitable wetland and floodplain habitats along German river systems supporting high densities of ornithophilic mosquitoes; enhanced entomological and wildlife surveillance from 2011 onward as part of broader mosquito‑borne virus monitoring. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show German SINV strains to be closely related to other European genotype I viruses, indicating geographic range expansion and local establishment of existing lineages rather than emergence of a distinct, more virulent variant.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Germany represents the first well-documented establishment of enzootic SINV circulation in Western Europe; the original time span (2011–2014) has been corrected to 2009–2016 to reflect initial mosquito detections in 2009 and subsequent findings in wild birds and mosquitoes. Classification as intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion is appropriate, but the near-absence of recognised human disease and the exact end year of the linked episode should be checked against national surveillance before final use.

Host: Humans; wild birds; mosquitoes
Event summary: In 2012, Finland experienced another sizeable Pogosta disease epidemic with 189 Sindbis virus infections recorded in the National Infectious Diseases Register, making it the largest Finnish outbreak since 2002; smaller contemporaneous increases in Ockelbo disease were noted in parts of Sweden. The outbreak began in late summer, with cases concentrated in traditional endemic eastern districts but also affecting additional areas, while virological work demonstrated multiple divergent but genotype I SINV strains circulating in humans and mosquitoes. As usual, human incidence declined sharply with the end of the mosquito season, leaving a new cohort of individuals with long‑lasting arthralgia and contributing to accumulated population immunity that reduced incidence in subsequent years until the very large resurgence in 2021.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: favourable climatic conditions for mosquitoes in 2012 and high densities of avian reservoirs in endemic forest–lake landscapes; outdoor recreational exposure and limited use of personal protection in affected communities; sensitive surveillance via mandatory notification and serological testing in Finland. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses of isolates from the 2012 outbreak revealed co‑circulation of several divergent but typical SINV genotype I lineages, implying multiple introductions or long‑standing micro‑foci rather than a single novel variant; disease resurgence is therefore best classified as ecological re-occurrence rather than re-emergence through major viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2012 Finnish outbreak (189 reported cases) is well documented and clearly among the largest post-1990 SINV epidemics; including Sweden reflects modest concurrent activity there. Geography and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate, and the source set (outbreak report plus ecological analyses) is relevant.

Host: Humans; wild birds; mosquitoes
Event summary: In mid‑August 2013, an unexpected outbreak of Sindbis virus infection (Ockelbo disease) occurred around the village of Lövånger in Västerbotten County, northern Sweden, a region previously considered non‑endemic, where the regional university hospital received 172 blood samples from suspected cases and 50 patients were confirmed by Sindbis‑specific IgM and IgG serology. The outbreak unfolded over late summer with intense local mosquito exposure and detection of a new SINV strain, Lovanger, in Culiseta morsitans mosquitoes captured near human case locations; phylogenetic analysis showed this strain to be closely related to recent Finnish genotype I viruses. Transmission ceased with the end of the mosquito season, but follow‑up 6–8 months later found that about 40% of patients still had persistent musculoskeletal pain limiting daily activities, underscoring the potential for sudden geographic shifts in SINV activity and substantial long‑term morbidity even from relatively small outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unusually warm and wet early summer conditions in northern coastal Sweden in 2013 that likely boosted local mosquito populations; human exposure during outdoor activities such as berry picking and recreation in an area where low‑level SINV circulation had previously gone largely unrecognised; heightened clinical suspicion and laboratory testing once clusters of rash and arthralgia were observed. Internal mechanisms: the Lovanger virus isolate clustered with established European SINV genotype I lineages without major genetic divergence, indicating geographic spread and ecological amplification of existing strains rather than emergence of a fundamentally new variant; the prominent chronic arthralgia reflects host response and disease natural history rather than demonstrable increased intrinsic virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2013 Lövånger outbreak is a well-characterised cluster with 50 confirmed cases and high rates of chronic arthralgia, occurring in a previously non-endemic part of Sweden; it represents both a sizable human event and a clear geographic expansion of recognised transmission within Northern Europe. It was missing from the original dataset and has been added using detailed outbreak and entomological investigations.

Host: Humans; wild birds (notably grouse); mosquitoes (Culex, Aedes/Ochlerotatus spp.)
Event summary: In 2021, Sindbis virus caused a very large Pogosta disease outbreak in Finland, with 566 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, representing the largest recorded SINV epidemic in the country since systematic surveillance began and the largest mosquito‑borne viral disease outbreak reported in the European Union that year. The outbreak started in late summer in traditional endemic eastern districts but showed marked geographical expansion westward and southward into areas with little previous documented SINV transmission, reflecting broader environmental suitability and possible shifts in bird and mosquito distributions. As temperatures dropped and mosquitoes disappeared in autumn, human transmission ceased, but the wide spatial footprint of the 2021 epidemic and concomitant serological evidence in birds indicated that SINV had established a wider endemic range within Finland than previously recognised, setting the stage for future cycles of re-occurrence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: a combination of climatic conditions (warm summer temperatures and precipitation patterns) favouring large mosquito populations, high densities of susceptible forest grouse and other birds, and a growing human population engaging in outdoor activities in newly affected areas; increased clinical awareness and laboratory testing likely enhanced case ascertainment compared with earlier years. Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis of 2021 Finnish SINV isolates showed them to belong to the established European genotype I lineage and to be closely related to prior Finnish, Swedish and German strains, implying that the main internal mechanism was geographic range expansion and amplification of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a new, more virulent strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2021 Finnish outbreak, with 566 confirmed cases and documented geographic expansion within Finland, is clearly one of the most impactful SINV events globally in the study period; the description, geography and classification as a large re-occurrence in an endemic region are well supported by surveillance and genomic data.

Host: Wild birds (African thrush, Turdus pelios, in wetland and savanna-edge habitats); ornithophilic mosquitoes (implied); potential incidental human exposure (not yet documented in this focus)
Event summary: During field sampling campaigns in 2022–2023 in and around the Amurum Forest Reserve in central Nigeria, Sindbis virus RNA was detected for the first time in West Africa in wild birds, with three of 504 sampled African thrushes testing positive and one yielding a complete SINV genome. These findings documented an enzootic transmission focus in Nigeria that had not previously been recognised, despite earlier serological evidence of human exposure from the 1970s, and indicated active local virus circulation rather than isolated introductions. No associated human Sindbis fever cases were reported during the study period, and after the surveillance campaign ended the extent and persistence of SINV transmission in Nigeria remained uncertain, but the detection nevertheless marked a clear intra‑continental range expansion of SINV into the Western Africa subregion with ecologies suitable for future spillover to humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely long‑distance introduction via migratory birds connecting eastern and southern African SINV foci with West African wetlands; suitable wetland and forest‑edge habitats and mosquito fauna in central Nigeria enabling local SINV maintenance; expanded ornithological surveillance and molecular diagnostics that increased the probability of detecting low‑prevalence infections in wild birds. Internal mechanisms: the detected Nigerian SINV strain clustered phylogenetically with known SINV genotype I lineages from Algeria, Spain and Kenya, suggesting geographic range expansion of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel lineage; any future human disease risk will depend on local vector competence, bird reservoir dynamics and human–mosquito contact patterns.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This event represents the first confirmed detection of Sindbis virus in wild birds in Nigeria and, more broadly, in West Africa, marking a major expansion of the known enzootic range with clear relevance for future human risk. The original dataset mis-dated the event to 2024; the event year has been corrected to 2022–2023 to reflect the documented sampling period, and the classification as intra-continental emergence (new African subregion) is appropriate, though continued surveillance will be needed to quantify its long-term importance.

Host: Humans; likely local wild birds and Culex mosquitoes maintaining the enzootic cycle (not directly sampled in this report)
Event summary: In July–August 2025, four autochthonous patients living in south‑eastern Tuscany, Italy, were hospitalised with acute neurological symptoms, and next‑generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid samples detected Sindbis virus RNA, providing the first unequivocal evidence of human neuroinvasive SINV infection and the first recognised cluster of locally acquired SINV disease in Italy. The cases occurred against a background of established but largely subclinical SINV circulation in southern Europe, where antibodies and viral RNA had previously been detected in birds and mosquitoes but no confirmed human outbreaks had been described. Following hospital management and supportive care, no wider community outbreak was identified, and transmission appeared to be limited to a small focus during the summer mosquito season, but the event highlighted the potential for SINV to cause severe central nervous system disease outside its traditional Northern European and South African strongholds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal abundance of competent Culex mosquitoes in lowland Tuscany during the warm summer of 2025; local enzootic circulation of SINV in birds that had gone largely undetected in routine surveillance; improved use of unbiased next‑generation sequencing in encephalitis diagnostics that enabled identification of SINV RNA where routine testing for other neurotropic viruses was negative. Internal mechanisms: available data indicate that the Italian viruses belong to the established SINV genotype I lineage known from Europe and Africa, and there is currently no clear evidence of major genetic change specifically associated with neuroinvasiveness; the event is therefore interpreted as a clinically important but probably surveillance‑driven re-occurrence of SINV infection in a region where the virus was already present, rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Tuscany 2025 cluster is small in case numbers but highly significant as the first confirmed neuroinvasive Sindbis virus infections and the first recognised autochthonous human cases in Italy; it therefore merits inclusion among major events. Because detailed clinical and genomic data are still emerging, the classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) and the absence of an intra-continental emergence label should be revisited once more evidence is available on whether these viruses differ biologically from previously circulating European strains.

Host: Humans (single severe encephalitis case in Argentina) with evidence of low-level post-epizootic WEEV circulation in local equine and vector populations
Event summary: In 1996, Argentina detected an isolated but severe human case of western equine encephalitis in a rural resident, occurring more than a decade after the major equine–human epizootics of 1972–1973 and 1982–1983 but within a region where WEEV had been historically established. The case likely arose from sporadic spillover out of residual avian–mosquito–equine transmission foci that persisted after the earlier epizootics, without evidence of a wider human outbreak or substantial onward transmission during that season. Following clinical management of the case and reinforcement of equine vaccination and vector surveillance, no further confirmed human WEE cases were reported in Argentina until the large 2023–2024 re-emergence, and human disease again fell into apparent silence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post-epizootic persistence of WEEV in avian–mosquito–equine cycles in central Argentina, together with climatic and ecological conditions that intermittently favored local Culex and Aedes vector proliferation, probably enabled sporadic spillover to humans despite the absence of a recognized equine epizootic. Internal mechanisms: Available data link the 1996 infection to the long-established South American WEEV lineage, without evidence for a novel genotype or increased intrinsic virulence, so this episode is best interpreted as a low-intensity re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion driven by environmental and surveillance factors rather than viral genetic change.
Review: retain – Verified that a single clinically and serologically confirmed human WEEV case occurred in Argentina in 1996 after the 1970s–1980s epizootics and that no additional human cases were recorded nationally until 2023. Continent, UNSD subregion (South America), country coding (Argentina [1996]), and classification as a re-occurrence (with no intra-/inter-continental emergence) are consistent with the protocol definitions and with WHO/PAHO and Argentine sources. No larger post‑1990 human WEEV emergence events were identified that would displace this event from the top‑10 list for this EPP.

Host: Humans (fatal encephalitis in a 14-year-old boy) with evidence of enzootic WEEV circulation in equine and mosquito populations in the broader Southern Cone region
Event summary: In April 2009, Uruguay recorded a fatal case of viral encephalitis in a previously healthy 14-year-old boy in Montevideo, with molecular testing identifying western equine encephalitis virus as the likely cause and representing the first documented human WEE case in the country. The illness progressed rapidly from febrile symptoms to severe encephalomyelitis and death, and intensive investigation did not identify additional temporally or spatially linked human cases, although serologic and entomologic surveys confirmed WEEV circulation in equine and mosquito populations in Uruguay and the wider Southern Cone. After this episode, Uruguay strengthened arboviral surveillance and vector control, and no further confirmed human WEE cases were reported until the multi-country 2023–2024 regional re-emergence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 2009 case most likely resulted from spillover from an established enzootic equine–mosquito–avian transmission cycle in the Southern Cone, with local climatic and ecological conditions favoring vector abundance in peri-urban environments around Montevideo and increasing human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analysis showed that the virus from the 2009 patient clustered within known South American WEEV lineages without marked divergence or evidence of enhanced virulence, indicating that this episode reflects re-occurrence of an existing lineage in a previously affected South American subregion and the first recognized human infection in Uruguay, rather than intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion or a genetically driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the emergence-type coding. Under the protocol, intra-continental emergence requires spread to a new UNSD subregion within a continent; Uruguay and Argentina both lie in the South America subregion, which was already known to harbor WEEV in humans. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence from “true” to “false” and re_occurrence from “false” to “true,” and rewrote the mechanism/driver text to describe this episode as a re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion and the first documented human case in Uruguay. Geography (South America/South America; Uruguay [2009]) and timing remain appropriate, and the event is retained as one of the small number of well-documented human WEEV emergence episodes after 1990.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (multiple neuroinvasive encephalitis and febrile cases), horses (large-scale neurologic epizootic), and at least one sheep; virus maintained in avian–mosquito cycles
Event summary: Beginning in November 2023, Argentina detected clusters of neurologic disease in horses in several northeastern and central provinces, with subsequent laboratory testing confirming western equine encephalitis virus and, on 20 December 2023, the country’s first laboratory-confirmed human WEE case in more than two decades in a rural worker from Santa Fe Province. Over the following months, the epizootic expanded widely, affecting horses in at least 17 Argentine provinces, multiple departments in neighboring Uruguay, and border municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, while human infections accumulated to more than 100 laboratory-confirmed cases (with roughly a dozen deaths) predominantly in Argentina and a smaller number in Uruguay, alongside many additional suspected infections. As mosquito activity waned by April 2024 and emergency vector control, compulsory equine vaccination, and enhanced human and animal surveillance were implemented across the affected areas, reported equine and human cases declined sharply and the regional outbreak was considered over, although genetic and ecological studies indicate that the responsible South American WEEV lineage has likely persisted in enzootic foci and could re-emerge under favorable conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Multiple external drivers contributed to this re-emergence, including climatic anomalies (high rainfall and elevated temperatures) that boosted floodwater and Culex mosquito populations, extensive irrigated agriculture and wetland habitats that favor vector breeding, and accumulation of susceptible equine populations after nearly 35–40 years without major WEE epizootics in Argentina, which reduced perceived risk and likely lowered vaccination coverage. Increased human exposure in rural and peri-urban areas, combined with strengthened clinical and laboratory surveillance once equine outbreaks were detected, facilitated recognition of human cases. Internal mechanisms: Molecular epidemiology of South American WEEV isolates from the 2023–2024 outbreak shows circulation of a South American genotype forming a distinct lineage (often termed lineage C) closely related to historical regional strains but with evidence of ongoing evolution; phylogenetic analyses indicate a coherent lineage responsible for the current epizootic and human infections, suggesting viral adaptation that may enhance maintenance and transmission in local vector–host networks rather than introduction of a completely novel serotype. This event is therefore classified as a re-emergence driven by both ecological/climatic drivers and lineage-level viral evolution, with geographic range expansion within South America but no spread to new continents.
Review: review – Updated the multi-country coding and narrative to align with current evidence and the protocol for linked episodes. Countries now list Argentina [2023], Uruguay [2023], and Brazil [2023], reflecting that the outbreak began in equines in Argentina in November 2023, spread to equines in Uruguay in early December 2023, and was confirmed in horses in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, later in December 2023, while human cases were documented in Argentina from late 2023 and in Uruguay from early 2024. The event summary was revised to incorporate PAHO/EID estimates of >100 laboratory-confirmed human cases and thousands of equine outbreaks across three countries and to note the equine component in Brazil, while retaining classification as a re-emergence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) in a historically affected South American subregion driven by both ecological/climatic drivers and evolution within a regional WEEV lineage.

Host: Humans (recipients of blood and blood components, mainly platelet concentrates and red cell units)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the mid‑1990s, multiple U.S. centers reported clusters of severe septic transfusion reactions that were ultimately linked to Serratia liquefaciens contamination of platelet concentrates and other blood components. These episodes, collated in national analyses, showed that S. liquefaciens could proliferate to high titres during room‑temperature storage of platelets, causing fulminant sepsis and death in some recipients and revealing a previously under‑recognized transfusion hazard. In response, blood services introduced stricter donor arm disinfection, diversion pouches and, later, routine bacterial screening of platelet units, which markedly reduced the incidence of Serratia‑associated transfusion sepsis in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Standard transfusion practices at the time—particularly storage of platelet concentrates at room temperature, incomplete donor skin disinfection, and absence of routine bacterial screening—created conditions in which environmental Gram‑negative bacteria introduced at donation could survive and multiply to dangerous levels. Internal mechanisms: S. liquefaciens, an environmental Serratia species not normally part of human flora, proved able to persist and proliferate in platelet bags and other blood components, effectively exploiting this artificial niche; this represents a host/exposure expansion and enhanced transmission in the context of blood products rather than a new geographic range.
Review: Review: Event is real and important as a national recognition of Serratia liquefaciens as a transfusion‑transmitted pathogen and catalyst for major blood safety changes. To comply with the event‑type rules, the classification has been corrected to re_emergence = true and re_occurrence = false (the episode reflects host/exposure expansion and regulatory failure rather than a simple incidence resurgence). Geographic fields and sources are appropriate; recommended to retain as one of the top 10 most impactful emergence events for Serratia spp.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (neonates in a governmental hospital NICU, Gaza City)
Event summary: Between January and December 2005, the NICU of a governmental hospital in Gaza City experienced a massive outbreak of Serratia marcescens septicaemia, with 159 culture‑confirmed nosocomial bloodstream infections in neonates. The outbreak was associated with high mortality—70 deaths (44% of cases)—and strongly linked to very low birthweight, prematurity and mechanical ventilation, indicating widespread transmission in a highly vulnerable population. Following recognition of the epidemic and identification of key risk factors, strengthened infection‑control measures and antimicrobial stewardship were implemented, ultimately reducing S. marcescens incidence, although the report emphasized the ongoing need for prevention in resource‑constrained settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Overcrowded NICU with limited staffing and infection‑control resources, high use of invasive procedures and mechanical ventilation, and broad‑spectrum empirical antibiotic use favored rapid dissemination of S. marcescens. Internal mechanisms: Isolates remained susceptible to imipenem and some fluoroquinolones, and no specific novel resistance determinant was highlighted; this event is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence driven primarily by environmental and health‑system factors rather than by major pathogen genetic change.
Review: Retain: This is one of the largest and deadliest documented Serratia marcescens NICU outbreaks worldwide (159 neonates infected, 70 deaths), clearly among the top 10 by impact. Geographic and temporal fields are correct (Gaza City, State of Palestine, 2005) and event type as re_occurrence (without strong evidence for novel strain properties) is appropriate. Minor clean‑up of secondary URLs was made (nonessential table‑of‑contents and Japanese summary links removed) but no substantive data corrections were required.

Host: Humans (primarily adult oncology and infusion‑center patients with central venous catheters, as well as home‑care patients, exposed to contaminated prefilled heparin or saline syringes)
Event summary: From October 7, 2007 through February 17, 2008, a multistate outbreak of Serratia marcescens bloodstream infections occurred in the United States, initially detected as clusters at an outpatient chemotherapy infusion center in Texas and in Chicago and subsequently recognized in nine states. Investigation linked 162 probable or definite S. marcescens BSIs to exposure to intrinsically contaminated prefilled heparin and isotonic sodium chloride flush syringes manufactured by a single company, with 4 deaths in which infection may have contributed. After epidemiologic and laboratory evidence implicated the syringes, a national recall of all prefilled heparin and saline syringes from the manufacturer was issued in December 2007–January 2008, and reports of new S. marcescens BSIs declined sharply thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Lapses in sterile manufacturing and quality‑control processes at a compounding/medical‑product company led to intrinsic contamination of nationally distributed prefilled heparin and saline syringes, seeding bloodstream infections across multiple states; extensive outpatient and home‑care use of these products amplified the scale of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical nosocomial S. marcescens capable of surviving and proliferating in aqueous syringe contents; no unusual resistance profile was highlighted, and impact was driven by contaminated product distribution rather than novel pathogen traits.
Review: Review: Major multistate product‑associated outbreak (162 BSIs across 9 US states with 4 associated deaths) that was missing from the original dataset and clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful Serratia events post‑1990. Added as a new event with continent/subregion/country fields and event type (re_occurrence) set according to published descriptions. Recommended to retain in the final top‑10 list; details could be further checked against the companion investigation of the Texas subset (Su et al., Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol 2009) if finer granularity is needed.

Host: Humans (neonates in the NICU of Alexandra General Hospital, Athens)
Event summary: Between December 2007 and September 2010, the NICU of Alexandra General Hospital in Athens, Greece, experienced three consecutive outbreaks of Serratia marcescens caused by genetically distinct clones. Over the 35‑month period, 57 neonates had S. marcescens isolated (37 colonized and 20 infected), and 9 of the 20 infected infants (45%) died, reflecting severe late‑onset sepsis and other invasive infections. Investigation linked the outbreaks to repeated introductions of new S. marcescens clones, with contaminated sinks and total parenteral nutrition implicated as possible reservoirs during specific waves, and intensified screening, cohorting and environmental control eventually halted the recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑risk NICU setting with extensive use of central lines and total parenteral nutrition, combined with intermittent environmental contamination (e.g., milk kitchen sink drain) and gaps in infection prevention, facilitated repeated introduction and spread of new S. marcescens clones. Internal mechanisms: Although multiple genetically distinct clones were identified, the report did not emphasize novel resistance determinants or unusual virulence; the event is best interpreted as a series of severe re‑occurrence episodes driven by infection‑control and environmental factors rather than by a single emergent high‑resistance lineage.
Review: Review: Large, prolonged NICU episode (57 colonized/infected neonates, 20 invasive infections, 9 deaths over 3 linked outbreaks) that was not captured previously and clearly ranks among the most clinically impactful Serratia NICU outbreaks post‑1990. Added as a new event, classified as re_occurrence (repeated introduction and spread of different clones without clear evidence of novel resistance). Recommended for inclusion in the top‑10 list, with details drawn from Maltezou et al. 2012 (American Journal of Infection Control).

Host: Humans (adult inpatients, predominantly medical and surgical ward and ICU patients in a tertiary hospital, "hospital H1")
Event summary: Following the introduction of colistin as salvage therapy in several wards of an Argentine tertiary hospital (H1) in 2005, the frequency of Serratia marcescens and Proteus mirabilis—both intrinsically colistin‑resistant species—increased markedly from 2006 onward. Between November 2007 and April 2008, H1 experienced an outbreak of multidrug‑resistant S. marcescens infections caused by a single epidemic cluster (cluster I), involving 32 patients with serious infections such as bloodstream infection and pneumonia and an attributable mortality of approximately 40% among infected patients. Molecular analysis showed that the outbreak clone carried complex class 1 integrons (In132::ISCR1::blaCTX‑M‑2) and additional resistance determinants (e.g., blaPER‑2, qnrB10), and implementation of strict infection‑control measures along with optimization of colistin use terminated transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy colistin use in response to other multidrug‑resistant Gram‑negative pathogens created strong ecological selection favoring intrinsically colistin‑resistant species like S. marcescens, and routine infection‑control measures were initially insufficient to prevent spread of the emerging MDR clone across multiple wards. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic S. marcescens cluster acquired complex class 1 integrons and extended‑spectrum β‑lactamase and plasmid‑mediated quinolone resistance genes, conferring multidrug and likely near pan‑drug resistance; this represents clear novel genotype emergence and re‑emergence of S. marcescens under polymyxin pressure.
Review: Review: Original row mis‑assigned this colistin‑associated outbreak to Italy in 2011 and treated the event dates imprecisely; primary sources show it occurred in an Argentine hospital (H1) with an epidemic period from November 2007 to April 2008 and ~40% mortality among infected patients. Continent, subregion, country and year fields have been corrected, and the event reclassified as re_emergence only (due to acquisition of complex resistance integrons and severe MDR phenotype). This outbreak is a key example of polymyxin‑driven selection of an epidemic S. marcescens clone and should be retained among the top 10 events, but details should be double‑checked against Merkier et al. 2013 (Journal of Clinical Microbiology) by a human reviewer.

Host: Humans (children, mostly outpatients and some inpatients, attending a rural health center)
Event summary: At Basse Health Centre in eastern Gambia, a healthcare‑associated outbreak of Serratia liquefaciens infections was detected in mid‑2010, when laboratory staff noticed a sudden rise in S. liquefaciens isolation from clinical specimens. Between 30 June and 16 September 2010, 44 children had clinical samples (including blood and respiratory specimens) positive for S. liquefaciens, and three infected children died with no other identified cause. Investigation traced the outbreak to contamination of multiple hospital consumables and solutions used for nebulization and intravenous infusion, and after removal and sterilization of the implicated fluids and equipment, the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Poor aseptic technique in preparation and handling of medications for nebulization and intravenous infusion, reuse of multi‑dose vials for multiple patients, and limited infection‑control awareness in a low‑resource rural health center allowed S. liquefaciens to contaminate fluids and spread to many children. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was environmentally adapted and able to persist in moist medical products, but no unusual resistance profile was emphasized; this represents a severe re‑occurrence of an environmental Serratia species in human patients driven by procedural and hygiene failures rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review: Original event correctly identified this as a major outbreak of S. liquefaciens in The Gambia but mis‑stated the timing (it occurred over 10 weeks in 2010, not 2013–2014) and gave an imprecise country/year notation. Event year has been corrected to 2010 (June–September) with countries updated to "Gambia [2010]" and the summary aligned to the primary report (Ikumapayi et al. 2016). Given 44 infected children, three deaths, and a clear demonstration of product contamination in a low‑resource setting, this event merits inclusion among high‑impact Serratia episodes.

Host: Humans (primarily adult cardiac‑surgery and ICU patients in a 600‑bed acute‑care hospital)
Event summary: Over a roughly 12‑month period beginning in mid‑2012, the 600‑bed Lucerne Cantonal Hospital in Switzerland experienced a hospital‑wide outbreak of Serratia marcescens, with most cases identified from respiratory samples among cardiac surgical intensive‑care patients but additional cases across wards. Standard CDC outbreak investigation, supplemented by Ishikawa "fishbone" root‑cause analysis, identified plausible sources including contamination of a transesophageal echocardiography probe used during cardiac surgery and deficiencies in surface disinfection logistics and products. After comprehensive re‑engineering of disinfection processes, targeted replacement or decontamination of implicated devices and reinforcement of infection‑control practices, the outbreak ended and hospital S. marcescens incidence returned to baseline; Swiss national data indicate approximately 91 cases over the 12‑month period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Complex cardiac surgical care with repeated use of a shared TEE probe and suboptimal disinfection processes created a persistent environmental reservoir and transmission route for S. marcescens, while broader weaknesses in surface disinfection logistics allowed contamination to spread hospital‑wide. Internal mechanisms: Isolates behaved as typical nosocomial S. marcescens without unique resistance features highlighted; re‑occurrence was driven chiefly by environmental persistence, biofilm formation on inadequately disinfected equipment and workflow problems rather than novel pathogen traits.
Review: Review: Event is real and high‑impact, with about 91 cases over 12 months in a Swiss teaching hospital, but the original row inaccurately dated the outbreak to an approximate 2014–2015 period. Based on the primary article and Swissnoso outbreak summary, the event year has been corrected to 2012–2013, and the country/subregion fields (Switzerland, Western Europe) are retained. Classification as re_occurrence (environmental/device‑associated outbreak without novel resistance) is appropriate. Recommended to keep as one of the top 10 events, with chronology verified by a human reviewer if greater precision is required.

Host: Humans (neonates and infants in the Targu Mures neonatal/paediatric units, with additional related adult cases in another hospital)
Event summary: From late 2014 through 2015, a neonatology unit in Targu Mures, Romania, experienced an outbreak of carbapenem‑nonsusceptible Serratia marcescens, characterized by colonization and invasive infections in neonates and infants, with related NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacterales also detected in the hospital and in a second hospital in Cluj‑Napoca. Whole‑genome sequencing of 33 S. marcescens isolates (27 NDM‑1 positive) and other Enterobacterales showed that a pKOX_NDM1‑like IncFIIY plasmid had been imported into Romania and disseminated between K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae and S. marcescens, with a clonal NDM‑1 S. marcescens strain causing a defined outbreak in the Targu Mures neonatal unit. Intensified infection‑control and active screening were used to monitor and contain the outbreak and associated plasmid spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of broad‑spectrum β‑lactams and carbapenems in Romanian hospitals, coupled with gaps in infection‑control infrastructure, facilitated introduction and spread of NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacterales, including S. marcescens, in neonatal and adult units. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and subsequent clonal expansion of S. marcescens strains carrying a pKOX_NDM1‑like plasmid conferred high‑level carbapenem resistance and multi‑drug resistance, representing clear novel genotype emergence and a re‑emergence of a more drug‑resistant Serratia lineage in this setting.
Review: Review: Event is real and important as one of the first detailed descriptions of an NDM‑1 S. marcescens neonatal outbreak in Europe and part of a broader multi‑species plasmid transmission network in Romania. The original row slightly simplified the broader context (multi‑hospital, multi‑species) but correctly located the main outbreak in the Targu Mures neonatal unit and classified it as re_emergence. An invalid placeholder PMC URL has been removed, and the summary clarified to match the WGS study. Recommended to retain as a top‑10 event, with any remaining numeric details (exact numbers of infected vs colonized neonates) cross‑checked by a human reviewer from the full article and supplementary tables.

Host: Humans (neonates and infants in multiple NICUs, neonatal units and a pediatric ICU at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Taoyuan)
Event summary: Beginning on 14 February 2021, a network of three NICUs and two neonatal units at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taoyuan, Taiwan, experienced an outbreak of carbapenem‑resistant Serratia marcescens in neonates and young infants. Fourteen infants developed serious infections during the acute phase, including sepsis, meningitis and pneumonia, and whole‑genome sequencing as part of longitudinal surveillance (through June 2023) showed that the main outbreak clone carried multiple resistance determinants associated with carbapenem resistance. After a comprehensive infection‑control package—enhanced hand hygiene, cohorting, dedicated staff, active screening and environmental and genomic surveillance—was implemented, the acute outbreak was contained within about 2.5 months, and over two years of follow‑up only one subsequent infection was genetically linked to the original epidemic clone, although unrelated S. marcescens infections continued to occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Complex care across co‑located NICUs and neonatal units with high antibiotic exposure provided fertile conditions for the emergence and spread of carbapenem‑resistant clones, and pre‑intervention infection‑control practices were insufficient to prevent rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain possessed multiple resistance genes, including determinants associated with carbapenem resistance, exemplifying novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced antimicrobial tolerance that enabled persistence under broad‑spectrum antibiotic pressure, making this a clear re‑emergence of a more drug‑resistant S. marcescens lineage in the NICU ecosystem.
Review: Review: Event is real and recent, documenting a carbapenem‑resistant S. marcescens outbreak in Taiwanese NICUs followed by two years of genomic surveillance. The original row’s basic description (14 infected infants, 2021 outbreak with follow‑up to 2023, multiple resistance determinants including an efflux pump associated with carbapenem resistance) matches the primary report, but one invalid placeholder PMC URL has been removed and the summary updated to align more closely with the Biomedical Journal article. Recommended to retain as a key AMR‑driven re‑emergence event; exact gene lists and case counts across the full 2021–2023 period should be checked by a human reviewer if further granularity is needed.
