Host: Humans (primarily older adults with serious underlying conditions cared for in hospitals across Norway; opportunistic infections with S. marcescens complex ct755)
Event summary: Between June 2021 and February 2023, Norway experienced a national outbreak of Serratia marcescens complex clone type 755 (ct755), first detected as a cluster of bloodstream infections in several hospitals and later recognized through whole‑genome sequencing as a widespread clonal outbreak. A total of 74 ct755 cases were identified across 33 hospitals, mostly in patients aged 60 years and older with substantial comorbidities, presenting with opportunistic infections typical of S. marcescens. Extensive case‑record review and interviews failed to identify common in‑hospital exposures, and the geographic spread and lack of clear nosocomial links suggested a community source, possibly a widely distributed product such as food. Despite the absence of a definitive source, the outbreak was eventually controlled through heightened surveillance and infection‑control vigilance, and S. marcescens complex ct755 highlighted challenges posed by opportunistic pathogens detected via high‑resolution WGS.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased use of clinical whole‑genome sequencing enabled recognition of a widely distributed S. marcescens complex clone that otherwise might have been dismissed as unrelated sporadic cases; the underlying driver appears to be a community‑distributed source (suspected nationally distributed product) rather than classic nosocomial reservoirs, with hospital‑based infection‑control measures playing a supporting role in limiting secondary spread. Internal mechanisms: The ct755 clone was non‑pigmented and largely antibiotic‑susceptible, with no major novel resistance mechanisms highlighted; its impact stems from clonal dissemination in the community and healthcare system rather than pathogen evolution, so this event is best categorized as a large re‑occurrence outbreak of an opportunistic Serratia lineage uncovered by WGS.
Review: Review: Newly added event capturing the recent Norway 2021–2023 national Serratia marcescens complex ct755 outbreak (74 cases across 33 hospitals) that was absent from the original dataset but clearly among the most impactful modern episodes. Classified as re_occurrence (large‑scale clonal spread without notable novel resistance) and located in Northern Europe / Norway based on the Eurosurveillance report. Strongly recommended for inclusion in the top‑10 list, with final details (e.g., exact case counts and ward‑level distribution) to be confirmed from the full article.

Host: Humans (predominantly adults co-infected with HIV: visceral leishmaniasis caused mainly by Leishmania infantum)
Event summary: Beginning around 1990, southern European countries with long-standing zoonotic L. infantum transmission experienced a sharp rise in visceral leishmaniasis among people living with HIV, as HIV-related immunosuppression exposed latent infections and increased progression from subclinical to clinical disease. Over the 1990–2001 period, more than 1,600 Leishmania/HIV co-infections were notified from Spain, Italy, France and Portugal, concentrated among people who inject drugs and other high-risk groups, before widespread antiretroviral therapy and improved HIV control gradually reduced incidence. As antiretroviral therapy coverage expanded in the late 1990s and early 2000s and harm-reduction measures improved, the incidence of new co-infection cases declined, though sporadic co-infections continued to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The HIV pandemic in Western and Southern Europe created large populations of severely immunocompromised adults, especially among people who inject drugs, in areas where zoonotic L. infantum was already endemic in dogs and sandfly vectors; poverty, marginalization and urban crowding in some neighborhoods increased vector exposure. Internal mechanisms: Increased clinical expression of existing infections under immunosuppression rather than a novel parasite strain; no strong evidence of major parasite change, so this is best characterized as a resurgence triggered by host-population and health-system changes rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – Correctly captures the well-documented 1990s Leishmania/HIV co-infection epidemic in Spain, Italy, France and Portugal, including scale (~1,600+ co-infections) and decline after HAART. Countries and sub-regions are consistent with UNSD classification, and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because the increase reflects HIV-driven susceptibility in an already endemic focus rather than spread to new regions or parasite change. No structural changes made.

Host: Humans (primarily anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania tropica in Kabul and other cities; zoonotic L. major in some northern foci)
Event summary: From around 1990 onward, Kabul and several other Afghan cities experienced a prolonged epidemic of anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis, against a backdrop of war-damaged infrastructure, mass displacement and collapsing health services. Cross-sectional surveys and WHO assessments in the early 2000s estimated that roughly 2%–3% of Kabul’s 2.5 million residents had active lesions and 15%–20% had scars at any time, implying tens of thousands of new cases annually and making Kabul the world’s largest single focus of cutaneous leishmaniasis. Through the 2000s, expansion of leishmaniasis clinics, provision of antimonial drugs and insecticide-treated nets and targeted health education gradually improved access to care and began to curb incidence and severity, but large numbers of new infections continued to occur each year, particularly in crowded, impoverished neighborhoods and informal settlements.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Decades of armed conflict, rapid unplanned urbanization, destruction of housing and sanitation, and massive internal displacement produced dense peri-urban settlements with abundant sandfly breeding sites and little vector control; shortages of diagnostic capacity and drugs limited early treatment and prolonged infectiousness. Internal mechanisms: Amplification of long-established L. tropica anthroponotic transmission cycles with humans as the main reservoir, without clear evidence of novel parasite genotypes, so this episode is best viewed as a large-scale re-occurrence driven primarily by socio-political and environmental change rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Review – Added as a new event because the prolonged anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis epidemic in Kabul (≈200,000 prevalent infections and ≈67,500 incident cases annually in early 2000s) clearly ranks among the most impactful Leishmania emergence episodes since 1990. Classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because leishmaniasis was already endemic in Afghanistan and the surge reflects conflict, urban crowding and collapse of control programmes rather than spread to a new continent/sub-region or parasite change. Time window 1990–2010 is approximate, chosen to encompass the documented multi-decade epidemic described in WHO and EID sources; details should be checked against any country program data before finalization.

Host: Humans (anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis, “kala-azar”, caused by Leishmania donovani)
Event summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, the contiguous visceral leishmaniasis focus spanning northeastern India (especially Bihar), central and western Bangladesh and southeastern Nepal experienced recurrent large epidemics, with Bihar alone estimated to have ≈250,000 cases in 1991 and realistic annual incidences of roughly 250,000 cases in India, 40,000 in Bangladesh and 3,000 in Nepal—about 60% of the global VL burden. Widespread failure of pentavalent antimonials in North Bihar, interrupted and patchy indoor residual spraying, and entrenched poverty, malnutrition and crowded rural housing allowed sustained high transmission and repeated peaks up to the early 2000s. In 2005 the three governments, in partnership with WHO, launched a regional kala-azar elimination programme, and by 2014 reported cases in Bangladesh, India and Nepal had fallen by about 75% compared with 2005, although residual hotspots, post–kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection continued to threaten elimination goals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large impoverished rural populations living in densely packed, poorly constructed houses; reduced or poorly targeted vector control after the malaria eradication era; weak health systems and delayed diagnosis; and high human mobility across porous borders contributed to intense and sustained VL transmission. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of high-level resistance to pentavalent antimonials in L. donovani in Bihar and neighboring areas, together with chronic human reservoirs such as post–kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis cases, represent parasite-level changes that helped maintain or resurge transmission, justifying classification as re-emergence rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Review – New multi-country event added to represent the very high-burden visceral leishmaniasis epidemics and subsequent elimination programme in India, Bangladesh and Nepal, which together accounted for ≈60% of global VL and included epidemic peaks of ≈250,000 cases in Bihar alone. Classified as re-emergence because sustained high incidence was closely linked to widespread antimonial drug resistance and long-lived human reservoirs, not to spread into a new sub-region or host system. Time window 1990–2014 approximates the late-20th‐century epidemic wave and the period up to the first major regional declines under the kala-azar elimination programme; exact start and end years may be refined using national programme data.

Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, mainly L. infantum; zoonotic cycle involving domestic dogs)
Event summary: From the 1980s into the 1990s and 2000s, Brazil saw a major shift of visceral leishmaniasis from rural endemic foci in the Northeast into urban and peri-urban environments, with large outbreaks in cities such as Teresina, São Luís, Natal, Belo Horizonte, Campo Grande, Araçatuba and Bauru. Between 1980 and 2005, Brazil reported nearly 60,000 VL cases, with an increasing proportion occurring outside the traditional Northeast region as the disease spread along migration and transport corridors and became established in medium and large cities; by 2001–2012, ten major urban centers accounted for about 15% of all Brazilian VL cases. Through intensified surveillance, canine reservoir control and vector-control measures in many municipalities after the mid‑2000s, some urban foci stabilized or declined, but VL remained endemic and highly spatially heterogeneous, with periodic urban outbreaks continuing beyond 2012.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid and often unplanned urbanization, rural–urban migration, peri-urban poverty, accumulation of infected domestic dogs as reservoir hosts, and favorable peri-domestic environments for sandfly vectors fostered the establishment of VL in cities; shortcomings in solid waste management and housing also increased vector density. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and ecological adaptation of phlebotomine vectors (e.g. Lutzomyia longipalpis) and domestic dog reservoirs to urban/peri-urban habitats, representing enhanced transmission and ecological niche expansion of existing L. infantum strains rather than a wholly novel species, justifying classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – Appropriately describes the major urbanization and geographic spread of visceral leishmaniasis in Brazil, a key global emergence pattern with tens of thousands of cases and establishment of multiple large urban foci. Classifying this as re-emergence (driven by ecological adaptation and geographic expansion of an existing zoonotic cycle) rather than intra-continental emergence is consistent with the UNSD sub-region scheme (all areas involved lie within the South America sub-region) and with the event definition. No changes to core fields were required.

Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis due to an atypical Leishmania donovani variant; occasional visceralized cases)
Event summary: Around 2001, clinicians in Sri Lanka began to identify increasing numbers of autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis cases, which were confirmed between 2001 and 2005 as being caused by L. donovani MON‑37, a parasite classically associated with visceral disease in neighboring India and East Africa. Over the next decade, surveillance documented thousands of CL cases with gradually widening spatial distribution across the island, seasonal transmission peaks, and rare visceralized or atypical presentations, indicating that this atypical L. donovani lineage had successfully established stable human transmission foci in multiple districts. After leishmaniasis was made a notifiable disease in 2008, reporting and control activities intensified, and although incidence remained substantial through at least 2013, enhanced diagnosis, awareness and control efforts helped limit the expansion and provided a clearer picture of the new endemic pattern.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely a combination of environmental changes, land-use and human mobility facilitating introduction or expansion of L. donovani into new ecologic niches on the island; limited early surveillance allowed the focus to grow before full recognition. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of an atypical L. donovani variant that predominantly causes cutaneous rather than visceral disease represents a novel strain/genotype emergence and a shift in clinical tropism; ongoing evidence suggests some capacity for visceralization, indicating altered host–parasite interactions and possibly enhanced transmission in skin tissues.
Review: Review – The original row misclassified this episode as “first detection” for Sri Lanka, but historical work documents leishmaniasis in the country since at least 1904 and modern locally acquired CL cases from 1992 onwards. The event has been reinterpreted as a re-emergence driven by an atypical, dermotropic L. donovani MON‑37 lineage, so the first_detection flag has been set to false while keeping re_emergence as true. Years, geography (Sri Lanka, Southern Asia) and the epidemiologic description are consistent with multiple peer-reviewed sources, but the revised classification should be checked and accepted by domain experts.

Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis with rising HIV co-infection; mainly L. donovani)
Event summary: During the early 2000s, Ethiopia’s long-standing visceral leishmaniasis endemicity evolved into a more complex public health problem as case numbers remained high (estimated 2,500–4,000 new VL cases annually) and VL–HIV co-infection emerged as a major challenge, particularly in northwest foci such as Humera, Metema and surrounding areas. Between roughly 2004 and 2014, national data showed sustained VL transmission across multiple regions (Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, Afar, Somali and SNNPR) and an increasing proportion of VL cases co-infected with HIV, complicating treatment and fueling relapses. In response, Ethiopia established a national leishmaniasis task force and expanded VL and CL treatment sites in the late 2000s and early 2010s, which, together with improved HIV care, began to moderate the impact of co-infection, though both diseases remained entrenched in vulnerable, mobile populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of commercial agriculture and labor migration into endemic lowlands, chronic poverty, malnutrition, and the growing HIV epidemic created large populations at risk of VL and of severe disease; limited access to early diagnosis and effective treatment further increased transmission and mortality. Internal mechanisms: The main mechanism is increased expression of severe VL in immunocompromised hosts rather than a novel parasite genotype; HIV co-infection amplifies parasite burden and transmission potential but does not imply a fundamentally new Leishmania lineage, so this is categorized as re-occurrence driven by host and health-system changes rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – Accurately summarizes the evolving national VL situation in Ethiopia, including sustained high incidence, emergence of high VL–HIV co-infection burdens and the public-health response. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) is appropriate because there is no strong evidence of parasite-level change; the surge reflects external drivers (HIV epidemic, labor migration, agriculture projects). No corrections beyond verification were required.

Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis among military personnel, mainly L. (Viannia) braziliensis; broader civilian CL and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis transmission)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, Colombia experienced a marked intensification of cutaneous leishmaniasis transmission, particularly affecting army personnel deployed in jungle and forested conflict zones in Meta, Guaviare and surrounding departments, with about 3,400 soldiers incapacitated by leishmaniasis in 2004 alone and roughly 13,000 cases reported nationally that year. Between 2005 and 2009, approximately 45,000 leishmaniasis cases (mostly CL) were reported nationwide, with high incidence in conflict-affected departments, reflecting both civilian and military exposure. After the mid‑2000s peak, case numbers gradually declined in the 2010s, influenced by changes in conflict dynamics and military operations (including the peace process with FARC), as well as improved prevention and treatment within the armed forces, though CL remained an important occupational disease for military and other populations entering enzootic forest areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged internal armed conflict and intensified military operations in Amazonian and Andean foothill jungles drove large numbers of susceptible soldiers into highly endemic forest habitats, while poverty, deforestation and settlement expansion also altered vector–host contact patterns; healthcare access for front-line troops and rural civilians was limited, increasing the clinical and operational impact of infections. Internal mechanisms: The surge reflects increased human exposure to existing zoonotic Leishmania transmission cycles rather than a clearly documented novel strain; multiple Leishmania (Viannia) species circulate in these areas, but the dominant driver of this emergence episode is socio-political (armed conflict) rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – This episode is well supported by military and national surveillance data and describes a clearly defined period of very high CL incidence (including ≈3,400 Colombian soldiers affected in 2004 and ≈45,000 national cases 2005–2009). Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because transmission intensified in long-endemic forest foci due to conflict-related exposure and limited control, without evidence of a new parasite or expansion into a new WHO/UNSD sub-region. No structural corrections were needed, though reliance on a general Wikipedia article for some figures should ideally be secondary to primary epidemiologic sources.

Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, primarily L. donovani)
Event summary: In 2003–2004, visceral leishmaniasis was recognized for the first time in the highland districts of Libo Kemkem and Fogera in South Gondar Zone, Amhara Region, Ethiopia, where VL had not previously been reported, marking the emergence of a new highland focus. The outbreak expanded rapidly through 2004–2005, ultimately affecting thousands of people (over 2,500 treated cases) with high case fatality, before control efforts and natural epidemic dynamics led to a sharp decline in new cases by 2006–2007. Following this peak, surveillance and treatment capacity were strengthened in the region, and subsequent surveys found low prevalence, suggesting that intensive control and partial herd immunity limited continued explosive transmission, though low-level endemicity likely persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Population movements from known VL-endemic lowland areas, changes in housing and agricultural practices, and possible climatic shifts enabling sandfly vectors to survive at higher altitudes contributed to the establishment of transmission in previously non-endemic highlands; poverty and limited health infrastructure facilitated rapid spread and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of L. donovani transmission into higher-elevation ecological zones represents geographic range expansion of existing parasite–vector systems, potentially aided by vector adaptation to new climatic conditions; there is no strong evidence of a distinct novel parasite strain, so this event is best interpreted as ecological expansion of an existing lineage rather than a new genotype.
Review: Retain – Correctly characterizes the Libo Kemkem/Fogera highland VL outbreak as a major new ecological focus of L. donovani in Ethiopia, with ≈2,400–2,500 treated primary VL cases between 2005 and 2007. The 2004–2007 time window and classification as re-emergence (geographic range expansion of an existing parasite–vector system within Eastern Africa, rather than first detection in humans) are supported by detailed outbreak investigations; no corrections were necessary.

Host: Humans (autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis, mainly L. mexicana and related species; also associated canine leishmaniasis due to L. infantum)
Event summary: Although sporadic autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis had been recognized in southern Texas since the early 20th century, from about 2001–2007 onward new clusters of locally acquired CL were detected farther north in Texas and into southeastern Oklahoma, with multiple confirmed cases prompting health alerts and field studies documenting local enzootic cycles. Between 2007 and the early 2020s, state and literature data indicate a steady trickle of autochthonous CL cases each year in Texas (often 6–15 cases annually) and rare cases in Oklahoma, Arizona and even North Dakota, suggesting gradual northward and westward expansion of Leishmania transmission and its rodent or canine reservoirs within the United States. By the early 2020s, reviews of U.S.-autochthonous leishmaniasis documented on the order of 80–90 confirmed locally acquired human cases (mostly CL) and highlighted concerns that climate change and land-use shifts could further expand suitable habitat for sandfly vectors and reservoir hosts, potentially increasing the frequency and geographic extent of human disease if surveillance and awareness do not keep pace.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changing climate (warmer temperatures and altered precipitation), land-use changes, expansion of peri-urban habitats, and human encroachment into areas with reservoir rodents and dogs have likely allowed both sandfly vectors and Leishmania reservoirs to expand northward; increased clinical awareness and diagnostics have also contributed to recognizing cases. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of existing Leishmania species (e.g. L. mexicana, L. infantum in dogs) and their vectors into previously unsuitable or marginal zones, potentially reflecting ecological and genetic adaptation to new climates and hosts; this constitutes re-emergence with inherent geographic expansion and enhanced transmission in new foci, superimposed on a background of long-standing but previously under-recognized endemicity in southern Texas.
Review: Review – The event accurately describes the gradual northward and westward expansion of autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis within the USA and is correctly reclassified here as re-emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) because it represents geographic and ecological expansion of existing enzootic cycles rather than a simple resurgence in a known focus. However, the absolute number of human cases (<100 confirmed autochthonous cases over several decades) is small compared with major epidemics in Afghanistan, South Asia, Brazil and East Africa. Recommended as a candidate for exclusion if a strict “top 10 by impact” filter is later applied, while still being epidemiologically noteworthy for range-expansion and preparedness in temperate regions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, L. donovani)
Event summary: Starting in late 2009, South Sudan—already known for cyclical VL epidemics—experienced a major new outbreak of visceral leishmaniasis in Upper Nile, Jonglei and other northern states, with more than 6,000 cases and over 300 deaths reported by late 2010 and ultimately over 28,000–30,000 cases reported by 2012. The epidemic expanded rapidly in remote, conflict-affected areas marked by population displacement, severe food insecurity and collapsing health services, overwhelming limited treatment centers until a multisectoral response scaled up diagnosis, case management and vector control. With intensified responses from national authorities, WHO and NGOs, case numbers gradually declined after the 2011 peak, although VL remained endemic with continued smaller outbreaks and substantial under-reporting in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Civil conflict, population displacement into endemic woodlands, malnutrition, and weak health systems created ideal conditions for high-intensity L. donovani transmission and high case fatality; climatic variability may also have affected vector and reservoir populations. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak appears to reflect amplification of established transmission cycles rather than a clearly distinct parasite lineage, so it is best characterized as re-occurrence driven primarily by socio-political and environmental conditions rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – Well-documented epidemic in South Sudan with ≈28,000–30,000 VL cases and substantial mortality, clearly qualifying as a major re-occurrence in an historically endemic Eastern African focus. Classification as re-occurrence (not inter-/intra-continental emergence) is correct because there was no spread to a new continent or UNSD sub-region and no evidence for a novel parasite strain. No corrections were needed.

Countries: Syrian Arab Republic [2011]; Lebanon [2012]; Jordan [2012]; Türkiye [2012]
Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania tropica and L. major, with cases largely among Syrian civilians and refugees)
Event summary: With the onset of the Syrian civil war around 2011, long-endemic cutaneous leishmaniasis in Syrian cities such as Aleppo and Homs surged dramatically as vector control and health services collapsed, leading to very high local incidence. From 2012 onward, large numbers of Syrian refugees carrying CL lesions were identified in Lebanon, Jordan and Türkiye, with Lebanon alone reporting more than 1,200 CL cases in 2012, almost all among refugees, and smaller numbers of locally acquired infections documented in host communities. Over the mid‑2010s, as conflict dynamics shifted and some control measures were introduced in refugee camps and host countries, reported cases in Lebanon and Jordan gradually declined, though the disease remained entrenched in parts of Syria and continued to pose a risk in overcrowded, under-served refugee settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Armed conflict, mass displacement, overcrowded refugee camps, breakdown of vector control and primary healthcare, and poor housing and sanitation in both war-affected Syrian neighborhoods and refugee settlements greatly increased human exposure to sandfly vectors and impeded timely diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects amplification and geographic redistribution of existing L. tropica and L. major transmission cycles rather than a newly evolved parasite genotype; key mechanisms are enhanced transmission via socio-environmental change and movement of infected hosts across borders, not intrinsic changes in virulence or tropism.
Review: Review – Countries and timing have been slightly corrected by changing Jordan’s start year from 2010 to 2012, in line with data showing that the marked increase in CL associated with Syrian refugees in Jordan occurred after the war began and refugees arrived in substantial numbers; Lebanon and Türkiye remain at 2012 consistent with outbreak reports. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because almost all cases were acquired within Western Asia and many were imported from Syria into neighboring countries, with only limited local transmission. This row should be rechecked against national surveillance time series, but the overall framing of a war- and displacement-driven CL resurgence is sound.

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Countries: Kenya [1990] (north‑west Turkana and other pastoral districts); Ethiopia [2000] (Dassanech, Nyangatom, Hamar and other pastoral communities in the south‑west)
Host: Humans in transhumant pastoral communities (Turkana in Kenya; Dassanech, Nyangatom, Hamar and Boran groups in Ethiopia)
Event summary: In eastern Africa, transhumant pastoralist groups such as the Turkana in north‑west Kenya and the Dassanech, Nyangatom, Hamar and Boran in southern Ethiopia have long experienced some of the world’s highest reported prevalences of human cystic echinococcosis, with ultrasound surveys in the 1980s–1990s in Turkana detecting liver or lung cysts in about 5–6% of residents and surgical series estimating annual incidence up to roughly 80–85 cases per 100,000 person‑years in some districts. Between about 1990 and 2012, repeated hospital record analyses and ultrasound campaigns in Turkana and later in Ethiopian pastoral zones such as South Omo documented persistently high but somewhat declining prevalence (for example, around 1.9–3.8% by ultrasound in Turkana in 2010–2012 and about 2–3% in some Ethiopian groups), indicating that large numbers of people remained infected despite local control efforts. By the mid‑2010s, cystic echinococcosis continued to impose a significant clinical and economic burden on East African pastoral communities, with cases concentrated in adults who had acquired infection in childhood, and these hyperendemic foci are repeatedly highlighted as among the highest‑prevalence CE areas worldwide.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transhumant pastoralism with large free‑roaming dog populations, routine home slaughter of sheep, goats and camels, feeding of uncooked infected offal to dogs, lack of formal abattoirs, scarce clean water and sanitation, and limited access to veterinary and human health services all sustain intense dog–livestock–human transmission in these communities. Internal mechanisms: Multiple Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato genotypes circulate in the Greater Horn of Africa, but available data do not indicate that recent parasite evolution, rather than environmental and husbandry factors, explains the high human burden; the event reflects long‑standing hyperendemic transmission in socio‑economically marginal pastoral settings.
Review: review – Added as a new event because WHO and regional reviews consistently highlight East African pastoralist communities (especially Turkana in Kenya and pastoral groups in southern Ethiopia) as having some of the world’s highest CE prevalences and substantial surgical incidence, making this hyperendemic belt clearly one of the top global high‑impact foci since 1990. Classified with all emergence‑type flags set to No, as the available evidence describes persistent hyperendemicity rather than re‑emergence after prior control or spread into new regions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans (exposed via domestic dog–sheep/cattle transmission cycles)
Event summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, human cystic echinococcosis in Kyrgyzstan rose sharply, with surgical incidence increasing from about 5.4 cases per 100,000 in 1991 to around 18 per 100,000 by 2000 and annual surgical cases rising from roughly 230 to more than 800 over the same period. Subsequent national surveillance analyses showed that high incidence persisted through the 2000s and early 2010s, with age‑standardised surgical incidence around 16–20 per 100,000 and widespread transmission across rural oblasts. From 2015 to 2020, more than 5,500 primary human CE cases were reported nationwide, indicating that the epidemic stabilised at a high endemic level rather than resolving and that CE remains one of Kyrgyzstan’s most important zoonoses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid socio‑economic changes after the Soviet collapse, including dismantling of collective farms, breakdown of state veterinary and meat‑inspection services, increased home slaughter of sheep, growth of free‑roaming dog populations and reduced routine dog deworming, greatly increased dog access to infected offal and environmental contamination with E. granulosus eggs. Internal mechanisms: No evidence supports emergence of a novel parasite strain or intrinsic changes in virulence; the rise and persistence of disease are explained by intensified transmission within pre‑existing dog–livestock cycles and increased human exposure driven by external socio‑economic shifts.
Review: review – Retain this event as one of the most important modern CE epidemics in terms of incidence, but extend the time span from 1991–2014 to 1991–2020 so that the event years match the inclusion of 2015–2020 surveillance data (over 5,500 primary CE cases) in the summary and sources. Clarified the textual description and removed in‑line web citations without changing the underlying epidemiological interpretation or the classification as re‑occurrence driven by post‑Soviet breakdown of control.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Countries: Peru [1991] (especially Junín Department and other central Andean highlands)
Host: Humans in rural Andean communities (sheep‑ and camelid‑raising areas)
Event summary: Hospital‑based surveillance in the central Andean department of Junín, Peru, recorded about 1,100 surgically treated human cystic echinococcosis cases between 1991 and 2002, confirming a long‑standing but very high endemic burden in highland sheep‑ and camelid‑raising communities. Subsequent community ultrasound surveys and national analyses in the late 2000s and early 2010s found annual incidence around 10 cases per 100,000 population in highly endemic regions and point prevalences of roughly 5–10% in some pastoral communities. By the mid‑2010s, cystic echinococcosis remained an important public‑health and economic problem in several Peruvian Andean departments, with improved imaging and reporting contributing to higher detection of cases compared with earlier decades.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent infection of dogs through access to infected sheep and camelid offal, backyard and informal slaughter with poor offal disposal, limited routine dog deworming and socio‑economic conditions favouring close human–dog contact sustained high transmission; expansion of ultrasound and CT imaging and referral to central hospitals also increased case detection. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel E. granulosus genotype has been implicated; the high burden is consistent with intense transmission of established sheep strains in a favourable ecological and husbandry context rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – Event retained as representing one of the world’s highest‑burden CE foci, but re_occurrence was changed from Yes to No because the Peruvian central Andes have been highly endemic for many decades and available data describe persistent high prevalence with better diagnosis, not a resurgence after prior control or absence. The summary was rephrased to emphasise chronic endemicity, and in‑line web citations were removed; no changes were made to geography or host classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans (primarily rural pastoral communities in Central Asian republics)
Event summary: Following independence of the Central Asian republics, Global Burden of Disease estimates and national surveillance data show that cystic echinococcosis incidence rose across Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan from the early 1990s, with particularly steep increases around 2000–2004. Over 1990–2019 these countries recorded some of the highest age‑standardised CE incidence rates worldwide, with ASIRs exceeding 120 per 100,000 in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, making CE one of the most prominent zoonotic neglected tropical diseases in the region. Although mortality and disability‑adjusted life years began to fall modestly after the mid‑2000s and some countries have seen partial control, incidence has remained elevated into the 2010s, consistent with a long‑lasting regional epidemic rather than isolated national outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Region‑wide socio‑economic transition after the Soviet collapse led to reduced funding for public and veterinary health services, weakened meat inspection and dog control, privatisation and informal home slaughter of livestock, and increases in unregulated dog ownership, collectively increasing human exposure to E. granulosus eggs in Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate emergence of new parasite genotypes or increased virulence in this region; the pattern is best explained by geographic and intensity expansion of long‑established dog–livestock transmission cycles under changed husbandry and control conditions.
Review: review – Retain this as a major post‑Soviet regional epidemic, but extend the event period from 1992–2004 to 1992–2019 to reflect that Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan maintained the world’s highest age‑standardised CE incidence over the full 1990–2019 GBD period, and adjust the summary so it no longer cites Kyrgyzstan (covered in a separate event) while highlighting these specific republics. Mechanism/driver text was clarified to reflect region‑wide breakdown of veterinary and meat‑inspection systems, and in‑line web citations were removed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans in pastoral and agro‑pastoral communities (notably Uyghur and other ethnic groups in north‑west China)
Event summary: In north‑west China, large community ultrasound screening campaigns and hospital data in the mid‑1990s documented extremely high burdens of human cystic echinococcosis in counties of Xinjiang, Gansu and neighbouring provinces, with surgical incidence reported as high as 43–80 cases per 100,000 in some areas and more than 21,000 hydatid surgeries recorded in Xinjiang alone by 1995. Follow‑up community surveys in Hoboksar County, Xinjiang from 2005 to 2008 showed persistent high prevalence and frequent reinfection despite treatment, indicating sustained intense transmission over more than a decade. WHO and Chinese technical reports estimated that by the early 2000s China harboured several hundred thousand human CE cases, making western China one of the world’s largest single‑country foci of cystic echinococcosis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: In endemic areas of Xinjiang, Gansu, Qinghai and adjacent provinces, traditional pastoral and agro‑pastoral systems with large dog populations, home slaughter of sheep and other livestock, use of dogs to guard herds and poor offal disposal created highly efficient dog–livestock cycles, while remoteness and limited access to health care delayed diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: Transmission is dominated by the globally common E. granulosus sensu stricto (G1) sheep strain; available evidence does not implicate any novel genotype or intrinsic change in the parasite, and the enormous burden is attributed to ecological and husbandry factors rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – Event retained as a major high‑burden focus, but re_occurrence was set from Yes to No because western China has been hyperendemic for CE since well before 1990 and available data describe long‑standing high incidence documented by ultrasound surveys and surgical series, not a resurgence after previous control. The summary now relies on quantitative estimates from WHO/Chinese reports, and in‑line web citations were removed; geography and host system are unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Countries: Argentina [1997] (Rio Negro Province and neighbouring Patagonian provinces)
Host: Humans in rural and peri‑urban sheep‑raising communities of Patagonian Argentina
Event summary: In Rio Negro Province in Argentine Patagonia, community ultrasound surveys in the mid‑1980s found cystic echinococcosis prevalence of about 5–6% among schoolchildren aged 6–14 years, prompting the establishment of a provincial hydatidosis control programme based on dog deworming, health education and ultrasound screening. From 1997 onwards the programme implemented annual ultrasound examinations of at‑risk schoolchildren and shepherds, and over 1997–2014 tens of thousands of people were screened, yet repeated community studies in small towns such as Ingeniero Jacobacci, Ñorquinco and Ramos Mexia still documented adult abdominal CE prevalences of roughly 4–7% and a substantial proportion of active cysts. Economic analyses estimated that human and livestock CE together caused large annual losses to the provincial health and agricultural sectors even as paediatric incidence declined, making Rio Negro one of the best‑documented but still heavily affected CE hotspots worldwide and an influential One Health control model.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive sheep farming with transhumant flocks, home slaughter and informal meat inspection, widespread dog ownership and feeding of raw infected offal, and historically limited access to diagnostic imaging in remote Patagonian communities created efficient dog–sheep–human transmission cycles; sustained provincial control activities (public education, dog deworming, ultrasound screening and deployment of the EG95 sheep vaccine) have reduced but not eliminated these risks. Internal mechanisms: Parasite populations are dominated by common E. granulosus sensu stricto sheep strains; there is no evidence that parasite evolution, rather than transmission intensity and the difficulty of maintaining long‑term control, explains the persistent human burden.
Review: review – Added as a new event because Rio Negro and neighbouring Patagonian provinces combine very high historical CE prevalence with sustained, well‑documented human and livestock economic losses and a long‑running integrated control programme; WHO and multiple reviews consistently cite this region alongside Peru, Central Asia, China and East Africa as among the highest‑burden CE areas globally. Classified without a specific emergence type because the event reflects chronic hyperendemicity under partial control rather than re‑emergence or spread into new regions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans (with parallel infections in sheep and dogs in Magallanes)
Event summary: In the Magallanes Region of southern Chile, a long‑running hydatidosis control programme that began in 1979 and markedly reduced infection in humans, sheep and dogs was terminated in 2004 after apparent success. In the years after the final mass praziquantel dosing of rural dogs, surveillance data showed a re‑emergence of Echinococcus granulosus infections in sheep and dogs and a parallel rise in human cystic echinococcosis incidence through at least 2021, reversing much of the progress achieved by the programme. The Magallanes experience is widely cited as a cautionary example that stopping dog deworming and surveillance too early can allow hydatidosis to bounce back in previously controlled areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The proximate driver was termination of a successful regional control programme (regular dog deworming, meat inspection and public education) in 2004, which allowed dog infection to rise again as dogs regained access to infected livestock offal; persistent pastoral practices meant the ecological context for transmission remained intact, so human exposure quickly increased once control pressure was removed. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for new genotypes or increased parasite virulence; this event exemplifies re‑occurrence driven by withdrawal of control measures rather than biological change in E. granulosus.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures a well‑documented regional re‑occurrence of CE in the Magallanes Region following termination of a successful dog‑deworming and surveillance programme; classification as re_occurrence (without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with the definitions. Minor editorial changes (removal of in‑line citations, clearer wording) do not affect the epidemiological content, so the event is retained as one of the key global examples of control programme failure leading to resurgence.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Poland; Lithuania; Latvia; Estonia; Slovakia; Hungary; Romania; Slovenia; Croatia; Belarus; Belgium; Netherlands; Italy
Host: Humans (mainly rural adults exposed to infected foxes and dogs; occasional pediatric cases)
Event summary: From the early 1990s onward, human alveolar echinococcosis began to be increasingly diagnosed outside the historical Alpine focus of France, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with rising numbers of autochthonous human cases reported in Poland, the Baltic states and other parts of Central and Eastern Europe. Over the 1990–2010s period, endemic foci were confirmed in fox populations and parallel clusters of human cases appeared across Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Slovakia and Hungary, later extending to Romania, Slovenia, Croatia, Belarus and into non‑traditional areas such as Belgium, the Netherlands and northern Italy, indicating a broad eastward and north‑westward expansion of transmission. By the 2010s–early 2020s, incidence had stabilized at high levels in some hotspots (e.g. northern Slovakia, parts of Poland and Lithuania), while new sporadic autochthonous human cases continued to be identified in additional European countries, showing that this long multi‑decadal episode represented a sustained geographic range expansion of the parasite in humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) Recovery and marked increase of red fox populations following oral anti‑rabies vaccination campaigns and hunting practice changes, which increased the density of the main wildlife definitive host; (2) urbanization and peri‑urbanization of foxes and raccoon dogs, bringing the sylvatic cycle into closer contact with humans and domestic dogs; (3) landscape and agricultural changes that favored rodent intermediate hosts; (4) improved imaging and serological diagnostics, establishment of national and European registries, and heightened clinical awareness that increased case detection and reporting, particularly in newly affected countries. Internal mechanisms: primarily geographic range expansion through existing parasite lineages; no dominant evidence for a novel, more virulent strain driving this European spread—human emergence appears largely host‑ and environment‑driven rather than due to major evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event correctly captures the large intra‑continental expansion of human AE from the historic Alpine focus into Central/Eastern and Baltic Europe and parts of Western/Southern Europe, and is clearly among the largest post‑1990 emergence episodes. However, the original sub‑region list omitted Southern Europe despite including Slovenia, Croatia and Italy in the country list, and Estonia (a clearly affected Baltic country) was missing from the country enumeration. Sub‑regions have been updated to include Southern Europe and Estonia has been added to the country list so that geography is consistent with published distributions. Event type (intra‑continental emergence) and time span (1990–2023) remain appropriate, but these geographic edits warrant human review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural communities reliant on small‑scale livestock and dogs, with intense contact with fox–rodent cycles)
Event summary: Between 1995 and the mid‑2010s, Kyrgyzstan experienced a marked emergence of human alveolar echinococcosis, with national surveillance data showing annual cases rising from fewer than three per year in the mid‑1990s to over 60 per year by 2011 and around 180 per year by 2014–2016, making it one of the highest‑incidence countries globally. The epidemic initially intensified in high‑altitude rural oblasts such as Naryn, Osh and Issyk‑Kul, where incidence in some districts exceeded 7 cases per 100,000 population per year, before spreading more widely across the country as infected dogs and foxes seeded additional foci. By the mid‑2010s, the disease had become a major public‑health burden in Kyrgyzstan, with large numbers of advanced cases requiring complex surgery or long‑term benzimidazole therapy and with little evidence of sustained decline through at least 2016 despite growing recognition and some control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) Profound socio‑economic changes after the collapse of the Soviet Union, including breakdown of centralized veterinary and public‑health services, which reduced dog deworming and meat inspection; (2) growth and poor management of free‑roaming dog populations that fed on infected offal and bridged the wildlife and domestic cycles; (3) poverty‑linked practices such as home slaughter of livestock and disposal of viscera accessible to dogs; (4) high prevalence of E. multilocularis in foxes and dogs in mountain pastoral systems. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence for a novel strain; emergence appears driven predominantly by intensified transmission in existing wildlife–dog cycles rather than genetic change, so this event is best characterized as intra‑continental emergence into a previously low‑incidence Central Asian human population.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This Kyrgyzstan epidemic is correctly identified as one of the most dramatic post‑1990 AE emergences, with very large increases in annual case numbers and incidence. However, the original time span (1995–2015) truncated the period of sustained high incidence documented through at least the mid‑2010s, and the narrative slightly overstated peak annual case numbers (>200/year) relative to published estimates (~180/year around 2014–2016). The event year has been extended to 1995–2016 and the case‑number description adjusted accordingly; classification as intra‑continental emergence (rather than first detection or re‑occurrence) remains appropriate but these temporal refinements should be checked.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China (particularly Qinghai; Tibet Autonomous Region; Sichuan; Gansu; Xinjiang; Ningxia; Inner Mongolia)
Host: Humans (predominantly Tibetan and other pastoral/agro‑pastoral communities in western China)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s, large‑scale national surveys and surveillance in China revealed that western provinces on the Tibetan Plateau harbored the vast majority of the world’s human alveolar echinococcosis burden, with China accounting for over 90% of an estimated 18,000 new AE cases globally each year and about nine million people at risk in high‑endemic counties. During 2004–2018, intensive ultrasound surveys and routine reporting documented very high village‑level prevalences and numerous advanced human cases in Qinghai, the Tibet Autonomous Region, Sichuan, Gansu, Xinjiang, Ningxia and parts of Inner Mongolia, confirming long‑standing hyperendemic foci and delineating their expansion along pastoral landscapes. Beginning in 2005, China implemented a national echinococcosis control program—including dog deworming, health education, and human screening—that gradually began to reduce transmission in some areas, although high‑risk pockets and substantial human disease burden persisted through at least the late 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) Traditional transhumant and semi‑nomadic pastoralism with large numbers of dogs, high densities of susceptible small mammals and close contact between humans, dogs and wildlife; (2) environmental and climatic conditions on the Tibetan Plateau that favor survival of E. multilocularis eggs and dense populations of arvicolid rodents; (3) poverty, limited access to veterinary services, and use of dogs for herding and protection, leading to low deworming coverage; (4) improved national surveillance, ultrasound screening and mapping, which brought to light the true scale of long‑underrecognized AE endemicity and guided control efforts. Internal mechanisms: predominantly maintenance and local spread of pre‑existing parasite populations; no single novel genotype is identified as the main driver, so the event is characterized as re‑occurrence (intensified recognition and burden) in historically endemic western China rather than de novo emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This event accurately represents the overwhelmingly dominant contribution of western China’s Tibetan Plateau region to global AE burden since 2000, with correct emphasis on national ultrasound surveys, very high endemicity, and the post‑2005 national control program. The time window (2004–2018), geographic focus, and classification as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic area driven by pastoral practices and improved detection are consistent with the literature. No corrections were required beyond verification, so the row can be retained as is.

Countries: Canada (British Columbia; Alberta; Saskatchewan; Manitoba; Northwest Territories; Ontario)
Host: Humans (autochthonous cases in western Canada and Ontario) and wildlife/domestic reservoirs (coyotes, red foxes, wolves, dogs)
Event summary: In 2009, a dog from Quesnel, British Columbia was found to harbor an alveolar hydatid cyst caused by a strain of Echinococcus multilocularis genetically closely related to European lineages, signaling the establishment of a European‑type strain in a part of North America where the parasite had not previously been detected in wildlife. Over the following decade, surveys of coyotes, foxes and other canids across western Canada and molecular analyses showed that European‑type haplotypes had become widespread in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, parts of British Columbia and the Northwest Territories, overlapping with native North American strains in complex mosaics. From 2013 to 2020, clinicians in Alberta documented a cluster of at least 17 locally acquired human alveolar echinococcosis cases, most of which were caused by these European‑like haplotypes, and additional autochthonous human cases were subsequently reported from other provinces such as Ontario, marking the emergence of a new human endemism linked to an introduced, apparently more virulent strain in Canada.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) Introduction and subsequent spread of European‑type E. multilocularis strains into western Canada, likely via movement of domestic dogs, translocated wildlife or other anthropogenic pathways; (2) expansion and urbanization of coyote and red fox populations, enabling establishment of efficient wildlife cycles in and around cities; (3) increasing densities of companion dogs with access to wildlife or rodent prey in endemic zones, enhancing spillover risk to humans; (4) improved imaging, histopathology and PCR diagnostics in Canadian centers, increasing the detection of AE. Internal mechanisms: clear evidence of Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence at the continental scale—the European‑type strain (including a Canada‑specific haplotype) appears more prone to cause canine and human AE than long‑established North American strains, and its invasion and establishment underlie the re‑emergence of human AE in Canada; this event thus represents re‑emergence of the disease in a region where the species was historically present but rarely pathogenic to people.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The event correctly captures introduction and establishment of European‑type E. multilocularis strains in western Canada and the associated cluster of locally acquired human AE cases, which is a key recent global emergence episode despite relatively low case numbers. However, the original classification incorrectly marked this as a first detection event in humans, whereas human AE due to E. multilocularis had been recognized in North America long before 1990. Under the project definitions, this Canadian episode is best treated purely as a re‑emergence driven by an introduced genotype, not as first detection, and ‘first_detection’ has therefore been set to false. No other structural changes were made, but the revised classification should be checked.

Countries: Japan (Hokkaido Prefecture; expansion from original coastal foci such as the Nemuro Peninsula and Rebun Island into central and western districts)
Host: Humans (predominantly rural residents of Hokkaido with exposure to infected red foxes and dogs)
Event summary: In Japan, human alveolar echinococcosis has long been endemic in Hokkaido, with early 20th‑century foci on Rebun Island and in eastern coastal regions; by the late 1980s those island outbreaks had largely ceased, but from the 1990s onward the parasite’s enzootic range and human disease burden shifted and expanded across Hokkaido. Epizootiologic and seroepidemiologic surveys during the 1990s demonstrated rapidly rising prevalence of Echinococcus multilocularis in red foxes and dogs, and identified new enzootic foci in central and western Hokkaido that closely paralleled increasing numbers of human AE cases, with roughly 9–27 new patients diagnosed annually since the mid‑1990s and a cumulative total of about 500 human cases by the mid‑2000s. Despite intensive local surveillance, dog deworming campaigns and public‑health education, Hokkaido has remained a hyperendemic focus for human AE into the 2010s, and sporadic cases continue to raise concern about potential spread of the parasite to other prefectures of Japan.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) High and increasing densities of red foxes in Hokkaido, partly linked to wildlife management changes and urban/peri‑urban adaptation, which amplified the sylvatic life cycle of E. multilocularis; (2) movements of infected foxes within Hokkaido and, historically, translocation of foxes between islands, facilitating the spread of infection from original foci to new districts; (3) close contact between humans, dogs and wildlife in rural communities, combined with limited regular deworming of dogs; (4) establishment of systematic ultrasound, serologic and veterinary surveillance in Hokkaido, which improved recognition of human and animal infections. Internal mechanisms: expansion and persistence of existing parasite lineages in suitable ecological niches rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent strain; this episode is therefore characterized as re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion within a historically endemic region of Eastern Asia.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event was missing from the original dataset but needs to be included because Hokkaido is one of the best‑documented long‑term foci of human AE and contributes a substantial fraction of non‑Chinese cases. The time window (1990–2018) captures the modern period of high incidence and geographic expansion within Hokkaido. Classified as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic area driven by changes in fox ecology, dog management and surveillance. Because this is a newly added row built from several sources, the narrative, dates and approximate case numbers should be checked by a subject‑matter expert.

Host: Humans (predominantly rural and small‑town residents in Siberian and Far Eastern federal districts, with exposure to infected wild canids and dogs)
Event summary: The Russian Federation has long been recognized as a major endemic area for alveolar echinococcosis, with historical human cases documented from the 19th century in Siberia and other regions; since 1990, sustained high case numbers and geographic spread within Russia have constituted one of the largest global AE burdens outside China. Systematic reviews and national reports for 1996–2021 indicate thousands of confirmed human AE cases, with estimated annual incidences on the order of 0.2 cases per 100,000 population and several hundred new cases per year, concentrated in the Siberian and Far Eastern federal districts but with increasing numbers of affected administrative units in European Russia as well. During the 2000s and 2010s, official data show AE being reported from an expanding set of federal subjects (rising from roughly 15 to more than 30), while case series from regions such as Tomsk, Krasnoyarsk and Yakutia highlight severe, often advanced hepatic disease requiring complex surgery or prolonged benzimidazole therapy. Although incidence may have plateaued or declined modestly in recent years in some regions, the 1990–2021 period represents a prolonged re‑occurrence phase with very high cumulative human AE burden in Russia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: (1) Extensive natural foci involving wild canids (red foxes and other species) and arvicolid rodents across Siberian taiga, steppe and tundra ecosystems, combined with rural livelihoods that bring humans and domestic dogs into contact with these cycles; (2) socio‑economic changes after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, including weakened veterinary and public‑health infrastructure, increased free‑roaming dog populations and informal slaughter practices, which likely facilitated transmission; (3) gradual expansion and better documentation of AE in additional federal districts, as diagnostic imaging, serology and reporting improved; (4) ongoing poverty and limited access to specialized surgical care in remote regions, contributing to high morbidity. Internal mechanisms: multiple E. multilocularis genotypes (Asian, North American, Mongolian, European) circulate in Russian wildlife, but current evidence does not implicate a single novel, highly virulent strain as the primary driver of increased human burden; the episode is therefore best framed as re‑occurrence and intensified recognition within a long‑endemic country.

Rationale: The original dataset omitted Russia, even though the Russian Federation accounts for a very large share of global non‑Chinese AE cases and is clearly among the highest‑burden countries between 1990 and 2021. This new event row summarizes Russia’s sustained high incidence and geographic spread, classifying it as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic area driven by ecological and socio‑economic changes plus improved diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of the O3:K6 clonal complex with tdh+, trh−, toxRS/new and ORF8 markers and multiple genomic islands, associated with increased virulence and epidemic potential; enhanced transmission via high bacterial loads in shellfish and efficient fecal–oral spread among exposed populations.

Internal mechanisms: Introduction and transient dominance of the pandemic O3:K6 clone (sequence type ST-3) and other novel genetic variants of V. parahaemolyticus in Peru, replacing pre-existing O4:K8 ST-88 lineages and contributing to increased virulence and epidemic potential.
Review: review – This event correctly highlights the El Niño-associated emergence of pandemic V. parahaemolyticus lineages in Peru, but it was previously misclassified as an intra-continental emergence and attributed solely to environmental drivers; it is now coded as re-emergence because a novel pandemic clone (ST-3 O3:K6 and related variants) displaced existing O4:K8 lineages in a country where the species was already present, and the mechanism text has been updated accordingly. Host: Humans (patients with watery diarrhea in Beira)
Event summary: From January to May 2004, 42 episodes of Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection were identified among diarrhea patients in Beira, Mozambique, marking the first systematically documented introduction of pandemic serovars O3:K6 and O4:K68 into sub-Saharan Africa. Following this episode, awareness of V. parahaemolyticus as a cause of diarrheal disease in eastern Africa increased, and the clone became part of regional etiologic differentials, although large recurrent outbreaks have been less frequently documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via international shipping and ballast water discharge or seafood trade from regions already colonized by the pandemic lineage, combined with suitable warm, subtropical coastal waters along the Mozambican coast. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment in Mozambique of pandemic O3:K6 and O4:K68 serovars with tdh+, trh−, toxRS/new, and ORF8 markers, representing a clonal lineage with enhanced virulence and epidemic potential compared with earlier local strains.

Event summary: Between 2001 and 2009, Hong Kong recorded 983 confirmed Vibrio parahaemolyticus food poisoning outbreaks affecting 4,604 persons, making V. parahaemolyticus the single most common cause of reported food poisoning in the territory. Internal mechanisms: A substantial proportion of isolates carried pandemic O3:K6 serovars and tdh virulence genes, but the large burden of illness over 2001–2009 reflects amplification of existing pathogenic lineages rather than the appearance of a completely new genotype, and is therefore best characterized as re-occurrence driven by food handling and environmental factors.

Event summary: In 2009, intensive shrimp farms in coastal China (e.g. Hainan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian) began to experience a novel "early mortality" syndrome characterized by high mortalities in the first weeks after stocking and a pale, atrophied hepatopancreas; the condition was later renamed acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND). As countries rolled out better diagnostics, biosecurity, pond management and stocking strategies, epidemic‑scale losses were partly reduced, but AHPND remains an important endemic constraint with periodic regional flare‑ups.

Event summary: By 2016, AHPND had been detected in commercial shrimp ponds in at least one South American country, with the pathogenic V. parahaemolyticus strain Ba94C2, isolated from diseased L. vannamei and characterized by Ecuadorian investigators, shown genomically to carry the canonical AHPND virulence plasmid, indicating establishment of the disease in the South American subregion. Although large‑scale collapses like those in early Asian epidemics have generally not been reported, AHPND has become one of several chronic bacterial constraints on intensive and semi‑intensive shrimp farming in South America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: AHPND‑causing strains were most likely introduced into South American farms via infected postlarvae or broodstock and regional trade in live shrimp seed, aided by shared water sources and high‑density culture of L. vannamei under conditions that favor Vibrio proliferation; the absence of early region‑wide diagnostics probably allowed low‑level circulation before formal recognition. Internal mechanisms: South American isolates such as Ba94C2 and the nine additional pirABvp‑positive V. parahaemolyticus strains analyzed by comparative genomics carry pVA1‑like plasmids closely related to Asian and Mexican AHPND plasmids, highlighting long‑distance dissemination of a mobile virulence element, while also showing local diversification in plasmid structure and chromosomal backgrounds that may influence virulence and host interaction (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: Review – Flag for review. This row has been revised to treat South America as an intra‑continental emergence within the broader "South America" continent (first presence in Central America/Mexico in 2013, then spread to the South America subregion in 2016), so inter‑continental emergence has been set to No and intra‑continental emergence to Yes.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0145305X25001338))  The start year is adjusted from ~2015 to 2016 in line with Restrepo et al. reporting the Ba94C2 AHPND isolate from South America, and the countries field now explicitly notes Ecuador as the inferred origin while acknowledging that many reports only specify "South America" without naming countries; these geographic details and the overall impact level warrant expert review but the event clearly represents one of the major regional emergence episodes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4992007/))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei)
Event summary: From 2016 onward, outbreaks of AHPND were documented in Penaeus vannamei culture systems in the Republic of Korea, initially in coastal farms and later in additional production areas, marking a northward extension of the disease within Eastern Asia. Korean studies subsequently characterized both canonical pirABvp‑positive V. parahaemolyticus strains (e.g. isolate 19‑021‑D1 from 2019) and a natural mutant V. parahaemolyticus that can cause AHPND‑like lesions despite a modified pir toxin gene complement, as well as AHPND‑causing Vibrio campbellii in some farms. These outbreaks were associated with stagnation or decline in national shrimp production in the early 2020s and prompted increased investment in diagnostics, selective breeding for tolerance and improved farm biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid recent expansion and intensification of L. vannamei culture in Korea, combined with imports of broodstock/postlarvae from AHPND‑affected regions, likely introduced pirABvp‑positive Vibrio strains; environmental conditions in Korean coastal and recirculation systems, including temperature and salinity regimes, permit establishment of these strains, and co‑infections (e.g. EHP) may exacerbate disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Korean AHPND outbreaks involve both typical pirABvp‑positive V. parahaemolyticus and variants with natural mutations in pir genes, as well as V. campbellii strains carrying pirVP, indicating ongoing diversification of AHPND etiologic agents within an already affected subregion (Re‑emergence via Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Enhanced Transmission; possible Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: Review – New row added. This event isolates the Korean AHPND situation from the previously conflated USA–Korea row and treats it as a re‑emergence within Eastern Asia driven by novel V. parahaemolyticus mutants and V. campbellii strains, consistent with recent Korean genomic and pathological studies that reference first outbreaks in 2016 and ongoing problems into the early 2020s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11475263/))  Because national‑scale production loss estimates and the exact temporal boundaries of the main epidemic wave remain somewhat uncertain, the 2016–2023 window and impact ranking should be reviewed by subject‑matter experts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei)
Event summary: In June 2017, mass mortalities occurred in intensive Penaeus vannamei farms in Texas, USA; diagnostic investigations detected pirA and pirB toxin genes associated with AHPND and identified the causative agent as V. parahaemolyticus bearing an AHPND virulence plasmid, with genotypes more similar to Mexican than Asian strains. This represented the first confirmed occurrence of AHPND in the United States and the first recognized incursion of the disease into the Northern America continent. Following targeted containment measures, heightened screening of imported broodstock and postlarvae, and strengthened farm biosecurity, no large‑scale multi‑state epizootics have been reported, but AHPND is now considered a notifiable and ongoing risk for US shrimp aquaculture and broodstock facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of AHPND‑causing V. parahaemolyticus into US shrimp farms was most likely via infected broodstock or postlarvae imported from endemic Latin American or Asian sources, together with the use of high‑density culture systems and water management regimes that favored Vibrio proliferation; the presence of US companies producing broodstock for export amplified concern about further regional and international spread. Internal mechanisms: US outbreak strains carried pirABvp on plasmids closely related to those in Mexican isolates, indicating spread of an established AHPND lineage rather than independent evolution, and showed genomic features consistent with adaptation to intensive culture systems (Novel Strain/Genotype Dissemination; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Review – New row added. This event now separately captures the first confirmed AHPND outbreak in the United States (Texas farms, 2017) and classifies it as an inter‑continental emergence into Northern America, in line with the primary case report and later reviews.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31019129/))  The 2017–2019 window reflects the outbreak year and the period over which it was investigated and reported; experts may wish to refine the end year if additional significant US epizootics are documented after 2019, but the event clearly belongs among the major global emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei)
Event summary: In 2023, mass mortalities with clinical signs and histopathology typical of AHPND were reported from multiple Litopenaeus vannamei farms in Egypt (e.g. Wadi‑Mariote, Berket Ghalyoun, Qarun Lake), and a four‑month surveillance study confirmed V. parahaemolyticus isolates carrying pirA and pirB toxin genes as the cause of these outbreaks, providing the first genetic confirmation of AHPND in Africa. Subsequent Egyptian studies have documented detailed hepatopancreatic lesions and metabolic responses in affected shrimp, indicating that AHPND has become an important emerging threat to the country’s expanding marine shrimp sector. Control efforts, including improved diagnostics, experimental evaluation of probiotic and fungal bioactive treatments, and enhanced farm management, are underway, but the longer‑term regional spread and economic impact across Africa remain unclear.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of intensive L. vannamei culture in Egypt and importation of seedstock from regions where AHPND is endemic likely facilitated introduction of pirABvp‑positive V. parahaemolyticus; environmental and management factors (eutrophic ponds, fluctuating salinity and temperature, co‑occurring pathogens) may promote disease expression and farm‑to‑farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Egyptian outbreak isolates carry both pirA and pirB genes on plasmids and produce typical AHPND lesions in challenge tests, and early microbiome work suggests that shifts in pond and gut bacterial communities may modulate pathogen proliferation and host susceptibility (Novel Strain/Genotype Dissemination into a new continent; Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion).
Review: Review – New row added. Recent Egyptian studies reporting pirA/pirB‑positive V. parahaemolyticus associated with mass shrimp mortalities in 2023 provide strong evidence that AHPND has now emerged in Northern Africa, making this an inter‑continental emergence event that was missing from the original dataset.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40054677/))  Because available reports are recent and largely limited to Egypt, the geographic scope, duration and overall impact rank of this African emergence should be revisited as more surveillance data from other African countries become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens); domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and wild boar (Sus scrofa) as main source animals
Event summary: Between 1990 and 1999, Romania experienced an exceptional resurgence of human trichinellosis, with around 20,000–28,000 reported cases and incidence peaking at more than 3,600 cases in 1993, making it the single largest national focus worldwide in this period. The surge followed the political and economic transition after 1989, which disrupted industrial pig production and official meat inspection and favoured backyard slaughter and informal marketing of pork products, leading to numerous wintertime outbreaks linked to raw or undercooked pork. Progressive restoration of veterinary services, improved inspection and public‑health interventions from the early 2000s gradually reduced incidence, though Romania has remained one of the principal contributors to EU trichinellosis notifications.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: profound socio‑political and economic changes after the fall of the communist regime, breakdown or weakening of centralized veterinary control, growth of backyard pig production with unsafe feeding practices, informal slaughter and sale of pork, and traditional consumption of inadequately cooked home‑made pork products; all of these increased human exposure to long‑established domestic and synanthropic Trichinella cycles. Internal mechanisms: infections were due mainly to known species (T. spiralis and T. britovi) without evidence of new genotypes or resistance, so the episode represents a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven by external drivers (food‑safety system disruption and food habits) rather than biological change in the parasite.
Review: retain – Added a multi‑year Romanian episode because published syntheses show that Europe accounted for ~86% of global trichinellosis cases in 1986–2009 and that about 28,564 of these occurred in Romania, mainly during 1990–1999, with a peak of 3,649 cases in 1993, clearly placing this wave among the most impactful post‑1990 events.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0896_article)) Coded as re‑occurrence (no novel species or resistance documented); years, country and sub‑region have been aligned with WHO/UNSD geography and the cited Romanian epidemiologic studies.

Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and wild boar (Sus scrofa) as key sources of infection
