Event summary: From the early 1990s through 2003, Bulgaria experienced sustained epidemic‑level trichinellosis, with 145 outbreaks and 238 sporadic cases recorded between 1990 and 2006 and a total of 4,108 human cases, with annual peaks of up to 12 outbreaks, mainly in 1994, 1997, 1998, 2002 and 2003. This prolonged wave of outbreaks followed political and economic transition in the early 1990s and was driven by consumption of inadequately cooked pork and wild boar meat products produced outside effective veterinary control. After 2003, strengthened surveillance and control measures led to some reduction in outbreak frequency and case numbers, although trichinellosis has remained an important zoonosis in Bulgaria.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: post‑1990 political and economic changes that weakened meat‑inspection systems, expansion of small‑scale pig rearing and hunting with home processing of pork and wild boar meat, traditional consumption of raw or undercooked sausages, and variable enforcement of inspection of game meat, all of which increased exposure to infected carcasses. Internal mechanisms: cases were attributed mainly to known domestic and sylvatic Trichinella species (chiefly T. spiralis, sometimes T. britovi), without evidence for new lineages or resistance; the episode is therefore classified as a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven by external socio‑economic and food‑safety factors.
Review: retain – Added this national wave because Bulgarian surveillance data show 145 outbreaks with 4,108 human cases between 1990 and 2006, with sustained high incidence from 1992–2003, making it one of the major post‑1990 trichinellosis burdens globally.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401708005852)) Classified as re‑occurrence linked to political and food‑production changes; years, geography and drivers follow the Bulgarian national review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as the main source animals, with occasional contribution from game such as mountain lion (Puma concolor)
Event summary: During 1990–1999, Argentina reported 5,217 human trichinellosis cases from 18 of 23 provinces, with about 90% of cases concentrated in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Santa Fe, reflecting repeated large food‑borne outbreaks rather than sporadic infections. Most outbreaks were linked to home‑produced or locally marketed pork products such as sausages and salami made from pigs raised under low‑biosecurity conditions and slaughtered without systematic inspection, and at least one outbreak involved meat from a mountain lion. Recognition of this substantial burden led to strengthening of surveillance and to replacement of trichinoscopy by more sensitive artificial digestion methods in official meat inspection, improving detection of infected pigs and helping to reduce human incidence in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive backyard and small‑scale pig production with poor biosecurity, feeding practices that allowed pigs access to infected carcasses or waste, limited coverage and sensitivity of traditional trichinoscopy in slaughterhouses, informal production and sale of cured pork products, and strong culinary traditions for lightly processed or undercooked pork. Internal mechanisms: infections were attributed primarily to T. spiralis, the long‑established species in Argentina, with no evidence for newly emerged lineages or resistance; the decade‑long wave is therefore best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence driven by production and food‑safety factors rather than parasite evolution.
Review: retain – Added this multi‑year Argentine episode because national data document 5,217 notified human cases between 1990 and 1999, making Argentina the country with the highest reported trichinellosis burden in the Americas and one of the largest post‑1990 foci worldwide.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11859488_Human_Trichinellosis_in_Argentina_Review_of_the_casuistry_registered_from_1990_to_1999?utm_source=openai)) It is coded as re‑occurrence driven by pig husbandry and inspection gaps; the country, sub‑region and years have been aligned with the UNSD country list and the Argentine national reviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; horses (Equus caballus) as the source animals for contaminated meat
Event summary: In December 1993, France experienced a very large multifocal outbreak of human trichinellosis, with 538 confirmed cases across several regions, caused by consumption of raw or rare horse meat from a single carcass imported from North America. Case–control investigations showed a strong dose‑response relationship between the quantity of horse meat consumed and disease, and parasitologic and typing studies identified Trichinella spiralis. The outbreak ended after the implicated batch of horse meat was withdrawn, and the episode triggered tighter European regulations and more sensitive digestion‑based protocols for systematic Trichinella screening of horse carcasses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in horse meat, limited sensitivity of then‑standard trichinoscopy and pooled digestion screening of horse carcasses, and strong culinary preferences in parts of France for raw or lightly cooked horse meat, which allowed a heavily infected carcass to seed hundreds of infections across multiple districts. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak strain was identified as T. spiralis, with no evidence of novel genotypes or increased virulence; the episode therefore represents a high‑impact re‑occurrence mediated by food‑safety system failure and consumer behaviour rather than biological change in the parasite.
Review: retain – Restricted this event to the well‑documented 1993 horse‑meat–associated outbreak with 538 cases, rather than combining it with the much smaller 1991 Auvergne outbreak (23 cases), and updated the year to 1993 and the country field to ‘France [1993]’ only.([courses.washington.edu](https://courses.washington.edu/zepi526/Papers09/ancelle_trichinellosis.pdf)) Classification as re‑occurrence in Western Europe is appropriate; this was not a first detection or inter‑continental emergence event because Trichinella was already endemic in European humans well before 1990.

Host: Humans; wild boar and domestic pigs (Sus scrofa) as source animals
Event summary: During 1994–1995, an outbreak of trichinellosis in Chumphon Province, southern Thailand infected 59 people, one of whom died, after communal meals that included undercooked wild pig and pork; muscle biopsy and serology identified the agent as the non‑encapsulated species Trichinella pseudospiralis. This was the first recognised human outbreak caused by T. pseudospiralis and highlighted that non‑encapsulated Trichinella species circulating in wildlife and domestic reservoirs in Southeast Asia could spill over into humans via traditional dishes made with raw or lightly cooked meat. The outbreak was controlled by clinical management of cases, tracing and removing contaminated meat, and intensifying education on proper cooking of pork and wild game.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rural and peri‑rural dietary practices involving consumption of raw or undercooked wild pig and pork, small‑scale pig production with weak veterinary inspection, and close ecological contact between domestic pigs and wildlife reservoirs harbouring non‑encapsulated Trichinella. Internal mechanisms: emergence of T. pseudospiralis as a recognised human pathogen in the region (a non‑encapsulated species with a broader host range, including birds, and different muscle pathology from T. spiralis), representing a re‑emergence event defined by a biologically distinct species infiltrating existing domestic and sylvatic cycles rather than purely by increased exposure to classic T. spiralis.
Review: retain – Corrected the year from 1998 to 1994–1995 and specified the location in Chumphon Province, based on the original clinical description of an outbreak affecting 59 people, including one death, which is cited as the first human outbreak caused by Trichinella pseudospiralis.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9455518/?utm_source=openai)) The event is appropriately coded as re‑emergence (novel non‑encapsulated species in humans) rather than first detection of Trichinella overall; Peromyscus‑focused and unrelated background URLs have been removed and replaced with a Thailand‑specific epidemiologic review as a more relevant source.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as main source animals
Event summary: In 1995, a large village‑wide outbreak of trichinellosis occurred in southern Lebanon after residents consumed home‑prepared pork products contaminated with Trichinella spiralis, leading to dozens of clinically and serologically confirmed cases. The outbreak struck a predominantly Christian rural community where pig keeping and pork consumption occur, and investigations linked illness to meat from locally slaughtered pigs rather than imported products. Control actions included culling of infected pigs, advising against further consumption of the implicated pork, treatment of cases and health education, after which no additional cases were reported from this episode.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: small‑scale, home slaughtering of pigs without veterinary inspection, production and consumption of inadequately cooked pork sausages in a resource‑limited rural setting, and limited awareness of trichinellosis and diagnostic capacity, which together led to a high attack rate once contaminated pork entered the local food chain. Internal mechanisms: infections were attributed to classic T. spiralis with no evidence of new lineages or resistance; this is thus a re‑occurrence of a known zoonosis in a vulnerable community on the eastern Mediterranean fringe, driven by husbandry and culinary practices rather than biological evolution of the parasite.
Review: review – The Lebanese village outbreak is real and correctly located in Western Asia, and it is epidemiologically notable because trichinellosis in the Eastern Mediterranean has been documented mainly among Christian communities consuming pork or wild boar.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2809009/?utm_source=openai)) However, available data suggest a moderate outbreak size compared with the very large multi‑year waves in Romania, Bulgaria, Argentina and the 2005 Laos outbreak now included here. Consider retaining this event for regional representativeness or first‑in‑region context, but it likely falls below the global top‑10 in terms of total cases and should be revisited during final prioritisation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2005] (Udomxay Province, northern Laos)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as the principal source animals, with evidence of infection in local swine herds and likely involvement of village‑raised pigs
Event summary: In 2005, a major outbreak of trichinellosis occurred in Udomxay Province in northern Laos after funeral and wedding ceremonies at which villagers consumed raw or fermented pork, with an estimated ≥650 people affected and more than 600 probable cases identified over the following year; no deaths were reported but many patients required hospital care. Serologic testing of suspected cases showed a high proportion with anti‑Trichinella antibodies, and muscle larvae of Trichinella spiralis were detected in at least one local pig not directly linked to the ceremonies, indicating established transmission in the local pig population. The outbreak revealed that trichinellosis was likely highly endemic yet under‑recognised in northern Laos and prompted calls for improved veterinary control and consumer education.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: free‑roaming smallholder pig husbandry with pigs accessing potentially infected carcasses or waste, cultural practices of sharing raw or fermented pork at communal ceremonies, low access to veterinary inspection and diagnostic services, and limited awareness of trichinellosis among health workers and communities, all of which allowed a large common‑source outbreak once heavily infected pork entered village feasts. Internal mechanisms: the causative species was identified as T. spiralis, with no evidence of new strains or resistance; the event is therefore best seen as a dramatic re‑occurrence in a setting where the parasite had likely long circulated undetected, brought to light by heightened clinical and serologic investigation.
Review: retain – Added this Laos episode because outbreak investigations estimated at least ~650 human trichinellosis cases in Udomxay in 2005, making it the largest documented outbreak in Southeast Asia and one of the major post‑1990 events globally; the outbreak also revealed previously unrecognised endemicity in northern Laos.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7611085/?utm_source=openai)) Coded as re‑occurrence in South‑eastern Asia (long‑standing but under‑detected circulation) rather than first detection; country name and sub‑region follow the UNSD list.

Countries: China [2006] (Yunnan Province; imported pork from Laos)
Host: Humans; pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as principal source animals via imported pork
Event summary: In December 2006, Yunnan Province in southwestern China recorded an outbreak of 49 human trichinellosis cases linked to pork imported from neighbouring Laos, which was identified as the first documented imported trichinellosis outbreak in China. Clusters of patients developed febrile myalgia and eosinophilia after shared meals containing undercooked pork, and investigations confirmed Trichinella larvae in leftover meat, while tracing showed that the meat had been brought in informally from across the Lao border. The outbreak subsided after remaining suspect meat was withdrawn, affected patients were treated and cross‑border trade in uninspected pork was more closely scrutinised.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: informal cross‑border trade in inadequately inspected pork from Laos into Yunnan, absence of systematic Trichinella testing for such imported meat, and culinary practices in rural communities that favour raw or lightly cooked pork, all of which enabled introduction of heavily infected meat into a consumer population with limited risk awareness. Internal mechanisms: available data do not indicate a novel genotype or altered virulence; the episode is best interpreted as a geographic re‑occurrence of classic T. spiralis infection associated with regional pork trade rather than a biologically driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the geographic coding by treating this as an outbreak in China (Yunnan) linked to imported pork from Laos, and therefore listing only China in the country field and restricting the sub‑region to Eastern Asia; Laos is better handled as the source of meat and now has its own major 2005 outbreak event.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) The event remains coded as a notable re‑occurrence and the first recorded imported trichinellosis outbreak in China, but its case count (49) is modest compared with the new large multi‑year waves; retain or down‑select depending on how strictly the top‑10 criterion is enforced.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as source animals
Event summary: In 2009, Lanping County in Yunnan Province, China, experienced a trichinellosis outbreak in which many residents developed fever, myalgia and eosinophilia after communal meals involving raw or undercooked pork, with laboratory confirmation of Trichinella infection in human sera and pork samples. The event formed part of a series of outbreaks reported from southwestern China in the 2000s, underscoring the persistently high burden of trichinellosis in Yunnan and surrounding areas where consumption of traditional raw pork dishes and backyard pig production remain common. Intensive case finding, antiparasitic treatment, health education and local improvements in meat inspection and pig‑rearing practices eventually halted transmission in the affected communities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: subsistence‑level pig production with inadequate housing and feeding, slaughter and distribution of pork outside formal inspection systems, and cultural traditions in parts of Yunnan for eating raw or lightly cooked pork during festivals and communal events, all of which repeatedly introduce infected pork into the human food chain. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not demonstrate a novel lineage or resistance phenotype; this outbreak is representative of ongoing re‑occurrence in an endemic focus driven mainly by food‑production and cultural factors.
Review: review – This Yunnan outbreak is consistent with Chinese national summaries that document multiple outbreaks (15 outbreaks, 1,387 cases and 4 deaths in southwestern provinces during 2004–2009), but the available literature suggests that it was one of several medium‑sized outbreaks rather than uniquely large.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) Recommend keeping it as a representative example of the sustained high burden in Yunnan, but its relative impact should be reassessed against larger national or regional episodes when enforcing a strict top‑10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Argentina [2010] (Pueblo General Belgrano and Gualeguaychú, Entre Ríos Province)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and possibly other local domestic animals as sources
Event summary: In July–August 2010, an outbreak of human trichinellosis occurred in the village of Pueblo General Belgrano and the nearby city of Gualeguaychú in Entre Ríos Province, Argentina, affecting 64 individuals after consumption of locally produced pork products from pigs slaughtered outside official inspection. The area had previously been regarded as free of Trichinella for more than 20 years, but outbreak investigations showed both human infections and the presence of Trichinella spiralis larvae in pigs and game animals, indicating an established local transmission cycle. Control measures included recall of implicated pork, testing and culling of infected animals, strengthened surveillance and intensive public education, which curtailed further human cases and highlighted the need not to assume absence of risk in nominally ‘Trichinella‑free’ zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of small‑scale pig and game‑animal production with inadequate biosecurity and meat inspection in a region considered low‑risk, informal marketing and home processing of pork products, and consumption of undercooked or poorly cured sausages. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing confirmed T. spiralis, a long‑established species in Argentina, without evidence of novel traits; the event is therefore interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a previously quiescent local focus driven by surveillance gaps and food‑safety practices, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – The Entre Ríos outbreak (64 confirmed cases) is accurately described and important because it revealed established transmission in a province officially considered Trichinella‑free, but it is smaller than the newly added national‑scale Argentine caseload (5,217 cases in 1990–1999).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S030440171400003X)) Retain it as a key local re‑occurrence illustrating hidden foci, but consider whether it should remain in a strict top‑10 list now that major multi‑year episodes have been added.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and wild boar (Sus scrofa) as sources
Event summary: In 2013, Lancang County in Yunnan Province, China, experienced another substantial trichinellosis outbreak associated with consumption of undercooked pork and possibly wild boar meat at communal events, with dozens of symptomatic cases presenting with myalgia, fever and eosinophilia. Trichinella infection was confirmed in human sera and in leftover meat, reinforcing evidence of persistent intense transmission in this region of southwestern China where domestic and sylvatic cycles overlap. Local authorities intensified surveillance, enforced meat inspection standards and issued risk‑communication campaigns about safe preparation of pork and game, bringing the outbreak under control but not eliminating the underlying endemic risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued high‑risk food practices involving raw or undercooked pork and wild boar, extensive overlap between domestic pig herds and wildlife reservoirs, and incomplete coverage of veterinary inspection in rural and mountainous areas, permitting heavily infected meat to reach consumers during festivals and communal meals. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel genotype or resistance phenotype has been described for this outbreak; it is another example of repeated re‑occurrence in a persistent endemic focus shaped by social and husbandry factors.
Review: review – This event is consistent with Chinese summaries that describe multiple outbreaks in Yunnan during the 2000s and early 2010s, but available data do not indicate that the Lancang outbreak was uniquely large relative to other Chinese clusters or to the newly added Romanian, Bulgarian, Argentine and Laotian waves.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) It should be retained as an illustrative example of ongoing intense transmission in southwestern China, but its inclusion in a strict top‑10 list should be revisited.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; wild boar (Sus scrofa) and possibly other game or backyard pigs as source meats, with infection by Trichinella britovi
Event summary: In 2020, EU/EEA surveillance recorded 117 confirmed trichinellosis cases, with 79 cases notified by Italy and a marked January peak that ECDC attributed largely to a food‑borne outbreak in Italy caused by Trichinella britovi, most likely linked to inadequately cooked meat from wild boar or pigs raised under non‑controlled housing. The outbreak was detected through national notification systems when clusters of patients with febrile myalgia and eosinophilia were found to share consumption of game or pork products, and subsequent trace‑back investigations focused on infected wild boar and backyard pigs. Control actions included tracing and removal of contaminated meat lots, clinical management of cases, expanded testing of wild boar and pigs, and renewed public‑health messaging about the risks of eating raw or undercooked game, which curbed further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased recreational hunting and consumption of wild boar and other game meats, incomplete application of Trichinella testing to hunted animals and pigs kept outside controlled housing, and culinary preferences in parts of Italy for undercooked or cured meat products, all of which periodically allow infected carcasses to enter the human food chain despite otherwise low national incidence. Internal mechanisms: the causative agent T. britovi has long circulated in European wildlife; no evidence has been reported of new variants or resistance, so this episode is coded as a re‑occurrence driven by human behaviour and game‑meat handling rather than genetic change in the parasite.
Review: retain – The 2020 Italian outbreak is corroborated by ECDC’s 2020 Annual Epidemiological Report, which notes 79 confirmed cases notified by Italy and a January peak in EU cases linked to a T. britovi food‑borne outbreak there;([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/Trichinellosis-AER_2020_Final.pdf)) while smaller than the large 1990s Eastern European and Argentine waves, it is one of the more substantial recent EU outbreaks and illustrates ongoing re‑occurrence linked to wild‑boar meat in Southern Europe.

EPP common name: Aujeszky’s disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (pseudorabies virus, PRV)
Host: Humans (encephalitis patients and occupationally exposed adults with serologic evidence of PRV exposure)
Event summary: From 2011, coinciding with widespread outbreaks of genotype II variant PRV in Chinese pig herds, retrospective metagenomic analyses identified PRV reads in cerebrospinal fluid from a young pork dealer with fatal encephalitis whose illness began in 2011, and follow-up sero-epidemiologic surveys of 1,335 encephalitis patients from nine Chinese provinces (samples collected in 2012, 2013 and 2017) detected PRV-reactive antibodies in a minority of cases at higher prevalence than in healthy controls. Although the serologic findings are complicated by potential cross-reactivity with other human herpesviruses and lack of virus isolation, together with the retrospectively documented 2011 encephalitis case they suggest that low-frequency, previously unrecognised zoonotic infections with pig-derived variant PRV were already occurring in Chinese encephalitis patients several years before clinicians began to recognise PRV routinely. This interval represents the earliest, low-visibility phase of a re-emergent zoonotic threat that later manifested as overt, molecularly confirmed encephalitis and ocular disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid spread of genotype II variant PRV in intensively farmed pigs in China from 2011 onward, with high seroprevalence in domestic swine; incomplete and voluntary vaccination coverage and reports of Bartha-K61 vaccine escape; dense pig production and trade networks; and frequent, often unprotected occupational contact of farmers, slaughterhouse workers, butchers and veterinarians with infected pigs, carcasses and farm effluents. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain and genotype emergence (clade 2.2 genotype II PRV variants displacing earlier strains in China), antigenic changes in major glycoproteins that can diminish vaccine-induced protection and may broaden host range, and early, inefficient host expansion with rare spillover into highly exposed humans, still without evidence of onward human-to-human transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Event retained as an early, low-confidence phase of human infection linked to emergence of genotype II PRV variants in Chinese pigs, but reinterpreted to focus on the retrospectively documented 2011 encephalitis case plus serologic surveys of encephalitis patients in 2012–2013 and 2017. Kept geographic scope (China, Eastern Asia) and re-emergence coding, while emphasising in the summary that evidence relies largely on serology and one retrospective mNGS-positive case and is therefore tentative. Updated source URLs to include the 2020 encephalitis sero-survey and the 2026 J Virol review, and to drop less directly relevant pig-only field studies.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Aujeszky’s disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (pseudorabies virus, PRV)
Host: Human (46-year-old female swineherd with ocular exposure to PRV-contaminated hoggery sewage)
Event summary: In June 2017, a 46-year-old swineherd from Jiangxi Province, China, developed high fever, headache and rapidly progressive visual loss after her eyes were splashed with sewage from a pig farm experiencing pseudorabies outbreaks. Vitreous humor obtained during vitrectomy yielded thousands of PRV sequence reads by metagenomic next-generation sequencing with over 80 percent genome coverage, findings that were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing, and subsequent testing showed PRV-specific antibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid. The patient’s systemic symptoms resolved but she was left with severe, permanent visual impairment. This case provided the first prospectively investigated, unequivocally molecularly confirmed human PRV infection in China and highlighted direct eye exposure to heavily contaminated farm effluent as a high-risk route, while still showing no evidence of central nervous system involvement or human-to-human spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Direct occupational exposure of the patient’s unprotected eyes to high-titer PRV-contaminated hoggery sewage on a farm with poorly controlled pseudorabies; high PRV prevalence in regional pig herds; limited mandatory vaccination and lack of routine eye and face protection for workers cleaning pig sties; and the growing use of unbiased metagenomic sequencing for atypical ocular infections, which enabled recognition of PRV in this case. Internal mechanisms: Novel genotype II variant PRV strains circulating in Chinese pigs with genetic differences from classical vaccine strains; probable enhanced neuro- and oculotropism of these variants that allows invasion of ocular tissues after mucosal exposure; and host expansion as these pig-adapted variants occasionally cross into humans with intense exposure, yet still without any documented capacity for human-to-human transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Event retained as a discrete, well-documented single-patient emergence episode representing the first widely recognised, molecularly confirmed human PRV infection in China, but first_detection has been changed from true to false because earlier suspected human infections (1914 onward) and at least one retrospectively analysed 2011 encephalitis case predate this event. Host description has been aligned with the case report (adult female swineherd in Jiangxi Province). Event-type coding otherwise remains focused on re-emergence driven by variant strains, with no intra- or inter-continental spread flags. Source list was streamlined to emphasise the primary case report and key contextual reviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Aujeszky’s disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (pseudorabies virus, PRV)
Host: Humans (adult farmers, butchers, veterinarians and other workers with recent exposure to PRV-infected pigs or raw pork)
Event summary: From mid-2016 onward, multicentre Chinese programmes that used metagenomic sequencing to investigate encephalitis of unknown cause began to identify clusters of adults with rapidly progressive panencephalitis, often accompanied by acute retinal necrosis, after close occupational contact with sick pigs or freshly butchered pork. Between 2016 and roughly 2019, at least a dozen such patients from provinces including Henan, Hubei, Shandong and others had PRV sequences detected in cerebrospinal fluid or ocular fluid, with characteristic MRI findings, high mortality and frequent severe neurological or visual sequelae; in 2019, a human PRV strain (hSD-1/2019) was isolated from CSF, showing close phylogenetic affinity to contemporary genotype II variant swine strains and high experimental virulence in pigs. Additional sporadic encephalitis and endophthalmitis cases have continued to be reported through at least 2022–2024, so that on the order of 30–35 molecularly supported human cases are now recognised, consolidating PRV as a rare but severe occupational encephalitic and ocular pathogen in Eastern China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High prevalence of genotype II variant PRV infection in intensively reared pigs across many Chinese provinces; dense swine production and marketing networks that sustain widespread viral circulation; common occupational practices that expose farmers, butchers and veterinarians with skin breaks or mucosal contact to raw pig tissues, blood and secretions; and the routine introduction of unbiased next-generation sequencing into diagnostic work-ups for encephalitis and severe ocular infections, which markedly increased detection of PRV in human clinical samples. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and subsequent dominance of genotype II variant PRV (clade 2.2) with mutations in key glycoproteins that confer partial immune escape from Bartha-K61-derived vaccines and may enhance neuroinvasiveness; increased virulence and neurotropism in animal models and in affected humans, evidenced by fulminant panencephalitis, respiratory failure and retinal necrosis; and host expansion in the form of rare but severe spillover into heavily exposed adult humans, while remaining incapable of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Event retained as the principal multi-year cluster of severe human PRV encephalitis and ocular disease in China, but the Event Year has been broadened from 2018–2019 to 2016–2024 to reflect published multicentre cohorts, virus-isolation work and systematic reviews showing confirmed cases beginning in mid-2016 and continuing sporadically through at least 2022–2024. Geographic scope remains restricted to China (Eastern Asia), and the event is still coded as re-emergence driven by genotype II variant strains rather than as intra- or inter-continental spread. Source URLs were updated to emphasise the key J Neurovirology cohort study, the Clinical Infectious Diseases report that first isolated a human PRV strain, several detailed case reports and the 2022 systematic review aggregating approximately a dozen encephalitis patients.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses; mules; donkeys; zebras (index introduction via imported zebras)
Event summary: After African horse sickness virus serotype 4 was introduced into a safari park near Madrid in 1987, probably via subclinically infected zebras imported from Namibia, the virus caused a multi-year epizootic in Iberia and the western Mediterranean. Large outbreaks occurred in southern Spain in 1988–1990 and spread to southern Portugal and northern Morocco in 1989, resulting in several hundred equine deaths and mass vaccination of more than 200,000 equids; Morocco continued to report cases until 1991. Intensive stamping-out, vaccination, movement restrictions and vector control ultimately led to official declaration of freedom from AHS in Spain and Portugal in 1991, ending the last recorded European AHS epizootic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of wild equids (particularly asymptomatically infected zebras from southern Africa), high densities of susceptible horses in southern Spain and Portugal, favourable climatic conditions for Culicoides vectors, and incomplete early vaccination coverage permitted AHSV-4 to overwinter and spread between Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate that the AHSV-4 strain involved was novel or unusually virulent compared with southern African strains; the episode is best interpreted as geographic re-introduction and amplification of an endemic African serotype into previously affected European and North African regions rather than evolution of a new viral variant.
Review: review – Retained as one of the major post-1990 AHS emergence episodes, but corrected the time span to 1987–1991 (to reflect the full Iberian/North African epizootic), simplified country annotations to first involvement years only, removed Algeria because primary OIE, EU and Spanish sources consistently list Spain, Portugal and Morocco but not Algeria for the 1987–1991 serotype 4 outbreak, and reclassified the event from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence since AHS had already occurred in Europe and North Africa during the 1965–1966 serotype 9 epizootic.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses (working and transport horses in rural Eastern Cape)
Event summary: From November 2000 through May 2001, a major outbreak of African horse sickness caused by virus serotype 2 struck the Transkei region of South Africa’s Eastern Cape Province, where large numbers of working horses are used for transport and draught. Veterinary reviews estimate that more than 1,000 horses died during this epizootic, making it one of the most severe AHS events in South Africa in recent decades and severely disrupting local rural livelihoods. Emergency vaccination campaigns, restrictions on horse movements and vector control were implemented, and reported cases declined after the 2000–2001 summer–autumn transmission season.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of unvaccinated or poorly vaccinated working horses, together with warm, wet seasonal conditions that favoured Culicoides vector abundance, allowed AHSV-2 to spread rapidly through villages in the coastal Transkei. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was associated with AHSV serotype 2 known from other African regions, with no clear evidence of a novel or unusually virulent lineage; the event is therefore interpreted as a climate- and management-driven re-occurrence of AHS in an endemic country rather than emergence of a new viral variant.
Review: retain – New row added because the 2000–2001 Transkei (Eastern Cape, South Africa) serotype 2 outbreak, with more than 1,000 horse deaths reported in veterinary reviews, is clearly among the largest recent AHS epizootics in South Africa; classified as re-occurrence in an endemic area driven mainly by climatic and management factors, with no strong evidence for novel viral evolution.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses; donkeys; mules (equids)
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2010, Ethiopia experienced extensive African horse sickness activity, with retrospective analyses documenting 737 outbreaks across multiple administrative regions and frequent severe disease in horses. Molecular typing showed co-circulation of AHSV serotypes 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9, with serotypes 4, 6 and 8 confirmed in Ethiopia for the first time, indicating substantial diversification of circulating virus populations. Control relied mainly on vaccination of horses and supportive care, and while AHS remained endemic, the intense multi-serotype outbreak activity subsided after 2010 as vaccine coverage and naturally acquired immunity increased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of susceptible horses and donkeys, environmental conditions highly favourable for Culicoides vectors, and incomplete vaccination coverage—particularly in donkeys, which can sustain subclinical infections—facilitated widespread transmission. Internal mechanisms: The appearance and co-circulation of several additional AHSV serotypes (2, 4, 6, 8 alongside endemic 9) represent re-emergence driven by expanded serotype diversity and genome reassortment, rather than simple resurgence of a single long-established lineage.
Review: review – Event retained but the countries field was standardised to show only the country-specific start year (Ethiopia [2007]) and the source list was streamlined to prioritise primary peer-reviewed articles documenting 737 outbreaks and the first detections of serotypes 4, 6 and 8; classification as re-emergence is appropriate because expansion of serotype diversity clearly contributed to this multi-year epizootic.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses
Event summary: Starting in March 2007, African horse sickness virus serotype 2, and to a lesser extent serotype 7, caused a nationwide epizootic in Senegal, beginning around Dakar and then spreading across multiple departments over roughly four months. Retrospective analyses documented 232 outbreaks and about 1,100–1,200 horse deaths, with the overall economic impact of mortality, lost traction power and control measures estimated at around €1.4 million. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign with polyvalent live-attenuated vaccine, combined with movement restrictions and vector control, brought the epidemic under control by late 2007, after which reported incidence returned to a lower endemic level.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of AHSV-2 (and 7) into a horse population in which previous circulation had been dominated by serotype 9, likely via movements of infected equids from neighbouring West African countries, together with high horse densities in the Niayes and Senegal River valley, abundant Culicoides vectors in the rainy season, and lack of pre-existing immunity to these serotypes, drove rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic is best characterised as re-emergence due to the incursion and amplification of new serotypes (2 and 7) in an already AHS-endemic system rather than simple climatic resurgence of serotype 9.
Review: retain – New high-impact event added because the 2007 Senegal epizootic (232 outbreaks, ≈1,100 horse deaths and ~€1.4 million in losses) is one of the largest modern AHS epidemics in West Africa and is explicitly linked to introduction of AHSV-2 (and 7) into a population previously dominated by serotype 9; classified as re-emergence within an endemic region rather than intra-continental emergence.

Host: Horses; donkeys; mules
Event summary: In 2011, Ethiopia experienced one of its largest recorded African horse sickness seasons, with retrospective veterinary reports indicating 208 outbreaks, 3,036 cases and 1,167 equid deaths across central, northern and western regions. Clinical cases were dominated by the cardiac and horse-sickness fever forms, and virological investigations identified only serotype 9 circulating in the affected areas, differing from the multi-serotype situation documented in 2010. Control consisted of vaccination, movement restrictions and supportive care; incidence decreased after 2011, although AHS remains endemic in Ethiopian equids.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High rainfall and suitable temperatures for Culicoides vectors, large populations of susceptible horses and donkeys, and uneven vaccination coverage created favourable conditions for intense transmission of endemic AHSV-9. Internal mechanisms: No evidence was reported for the emergence of new serotypes or major genomic variants during 2011; the episode is therefore classified as a re-occurrence of endemic serotype 9 driven mainly by climatic and management factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – New row added because the 2011 Ethiopian season, with 208 outbreaks, 3,036 cases and 1,167 deaths, is comparable in scale to the 2007–2010 multi-serotype period and clearly among the country’s largest modern AHS events; classified as re-occurrence of endemic serotype 9, since only AHSV-9 was detected and no substantial genetic novelty was reported.

Host: Horses; other domestic equids
Event summary: In 2011, southern Africa experienced a particularly severe African horse sickness season: SADC regional data record 720 outbreaks, 1,302 cases and 525 deaths across South Africa (675 outbreaks, 1,183 cases, 477 deaths), Namibia (44 outbreaks, 112 cases, 45 deaths) and Eswatini (1 outbreak, 7 cases, 3 deaths), the highest burden reported since systematic electronic recording began. Within this broader epizootic, an outbreak of AHSV-1 occurred in the African horse sickness controlled area of Western Cape Province in South Africa, centred on Mamre in the surveillance and free zones, with 73 laboratory-confirmed cases and about 70 deaths, leading to strict movement bans and a temporary suspension of horse exports. Following intensive vector control, quarantine, movement restrictions and blanket vaccination, cases in the controlled area ceased by May 2011 and regional outbreak numbers declined later that year, although AHS remains endemic in much of southern Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above-average rainfall and temperatures in early 2011, together with endemic AHS and extensive horse movements within southern Africa, were associated with a marked regional increase in outbreaks; the Mamre cluster most likely arose from movement of infected horses into the Western Cape controlled area. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome analyses showed that the AHSV-1 strains responsible for the 2004 and 2011 Western Cape controlled-area outbreaks were reassortants derived from live-attenuated vaccine viruses that had reverted to virulence, so the controlled-area component of the 2011 epizootic is a clear example of re-emergence via vaccine-derived viral evolution, whereas the wider regional peak reflects re-occurrence of endemic strains under favourable climatic conditions.
Review: review – Event retained but outbreak statistics were corrected to use SADC regional figures (720 outbreaks, 1,302 cases, 525 deaths across South Africa, Namibia and Eswatini in 2011) rather than South Africa-only counts, and the description was clarified to distinguish the vaccine-derived AHSV-1 outbreak in the Western Cape controlled area from the broader climate-driven regional epizootic; classification as both re-occurrence (regional upsurge) and re-emergence (vaccine-derived strains in the controlled area) is supported by surveillance and genomic data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses
Event summary: In 2014, another outbreak of African horse sickness occurred within the African horse sickness controlled area of Western Cape Province, South Africa, with clinical cases confirmed in the Porterville and Robertson areas among horses that should have been protected by strict vaccination and movement controls. Genetic sequencing of AHSV-1 isolates from this outbreak demonstrated close relatedness to components of the polyvalent live-attenuated vaccine, indicating reassortment and reversion to virulence rather than introduction of a wild-type field strain from elsewhere. Rapid implementation of quarantine, expanded movement bans, intensified surveillance and ring vaccination within and around the affected zones led to containment of the outbreak, and horse exports resumed after the required waiting period once no further cases were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of live-attenuated multivalent AHS vaccines in an endemic country, combined with dense equine populations and suitable Culicoides vectors in the Western Cape controlled area, created conditions in which vaccine-derived viruses could circulate and occasionally escape detection; movements of vaccinated but viraemic horses likely contributed to dispersal before the outbreak was recognised. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome sequencing confirmed that the 2014 outbreak viruses were reassortants between live-attenuated vaccine strains that had acquired combinations of genome segments associated with increased virulence, representing clear re-emergence through vaccine-derived genome reassortment and reversion to higher pathogenicity.
Review: retain – No major issues identified; the 2014 Western Cape outbreak in the AHS controlled area is well documented as a vaccine-derived AHSV-1 re-emergence episode with relatively limited case numbers but substantial trade and regulatory impact, and its classification as both re-occurrence (within a known AHS risk region) and re-emergence (vaccine-derived strain) without intra- or inter-continental spread is consistent with project definitions.

Host: Horses (working and riding horses; donkeys may also have been exposed)
Event summary: In 2019, African horse sickness reappeared prominently in Central Africa, with severe outbreaks reported in both Cameroon and Chad after decades without officially recognised clinical epizootics in the region. In Chad, veterinary reviews based on WOAH notifications describe 376 reported equine cases with more than 85% case-fatality, implying over 300 horse deaths, while veterinary services in Cameroon notified an epidemic of AHS in horses for the first time and undertook reactive investigations and control. The outbreaks mainly affected horses in savannah and Sahelian areas where they are essential for transport and draught, prompting emergency vaccination, restrictions on horse movements and vector control; reported clinical activity declined after 2019, although serological surveys indicate that AHSV continues to circulate in parts of Cameroon.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance trade and informal movement of horses between West and Central African countries where AHS is endemic, together with favourable environmental conditions for Culicoides vectors in riverine, irrigated and peri-urban zones, probably introduced and amplified AHSV in largely unvaccinated horse populations in Cameroon and Chad; limited veterinary infrastructure and delayed recognition likely contributed to the high apparent mortality. Internal mechanisms: Historical serological evidence shows that AHSV serotype 9 circulated in Central Africa (including Cameroon and Chad) decades earlier, and recent reviews suggest that additional serotypes (2, 4, 6, 7, 8) are now present in the region, but detailed molecular data for the 2019 viruses are still sparse; the episode is therefore conservatively classified as a high-impact re-occurrence of AHS pending more comprehensive genotypic characterisation.
Review: retain – New row added to represent the 2019 Central African outbreaks in Cameroon and Chad, which together involved at least 376 reported cases in Chad with >85% mortality and an officially recognised epidemic in Cameroon; classified as re-occurrence rather than intra-continental emergence because AHSV (particularly serotype 9) had already been documented serologically and virologically in Central African countries, including Cameroon and Chad, since the 1960s, although the apparent recent involvement of additional serotypes suggests ongoing viral diversification that merits continued monitoring.

Host: Horses (including racehorses and pleasure horses); zebras in captivity (probable source)
Event summary: In early 2020, horses in Pak Chong district of Nakhon Ratchasima Province, northeastern Thailand, developed peracute respiratory signs, oedema and rapid death, and laboratory testing in March–April 2020 confirmed African horse sickness virus serotype 1, marking the first confirmed AHS outbreak in Thailand and in South-eastern Asia. WOAH reports and subsequent studies documented 607 cases with an estimated case-fatality rate of about 93% in naïve horses, and spread to multiple provinces before emergency measures took full effect. Large-scale ring vaccination with live-attenuated AHS vaccine, strict movement bans, zoning and vector control were implemented, which eventually curbed further spread within Thailand, although intensive surveillance and vaccination continued over subsequent seasons as authorities sought to re-establish AHS-free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely illegal or poorly regulated importation of infected equids—particularly zebras—from Africa into Thailand shortly before the first detected cases, combined with abundant Culicoides vectors, a fully susceptible horse population and extensive local equine movements, facilitated rapid establishment and explosive spread; delays in recognising AHS as the cause further increased impact. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed that the outbreak strain was AHSV-1 closely related to southern African lineages rather than a novel serotype, with its impact driven primarily by highly efficient vector-borne transmission into an immunologically naïve horse population, representing intra-continental geographic range expansion within Asia rather than antigenic innovation.
Review: review – Event retained and remains one of the most consequential recent AHS outbreaks (607 cases with ~93% case-fatality in a naïve horse population), but the “first_detection” flag has been set to false because AHS was described and detected in equids long before 2020; the event is more accurately classified as an intra-continental emergence within Asia, representing spread of an established African serotype to a previously unaffected subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses (backyard and sport horses)
Event summary: In August 2020, horses on a property in Manir, Terengganu State on the Malay Peninsula developed fever and respiratory signs, and by early September the Malaysian veterinary authorities notified WOAH that five backyard horses had tested positive for African horse sickness virus, representing the first confirmed occurrence of AHS in Malaysia. Epidemiologic investigations and sequence data indicated that the Malaysian outbreak was caused by AHSV-1 closely related to the 2020 Thai outbreak strain, suggesting spread from Thailand into Malaysia with a limited number of clinically affected horses. Rapid implementation of quarantine, movement controls, targeted vaccination around affected holdings and heightened surveillance led to containment of the outbreak, with no evidence of wider establishment in Malaysia and subsequent suspension and later restoration of the country’s officially recognised AHS-free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional spread of AHSV-1 from Thailand—via either cross-border movement of infected equids or wind-borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges—into an AHS-free Malaysia, coupled with suitable tropical conditions for vectors and local horse movements, enabled in situ transmission in Terengganu; concurrent COVID-19-related disruptions may have complicated surveillance and logistics. Internal mechanisms: The virus was not a novel serotype but represented geographic range expansion of AHSV-1 within Asia, with high virulence in naïve horses; this event is best viewed as a small, epidemiologically linked extension of the Thai outbreak rather than a separate evolutionary shift.
Review: review – Event retained as part of the 2020 South-eastern Asian emergence episode and the first confirmed occurrence of AHS in Malaysia, but the “first_detection” flag has been set to false because AHS was detected and described in horses long before 2020; the event is best classified as an intra-continental emergence tightly linked to the Thai outbreak, with only limited local transmission in Terengganu.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Côte d’Ivoire [1996]; Benin [1997]; Togo [1997]; Nigeria [1997]; Ghana [1999]; Burkina Faso [2003]
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: In April 1996, African swine fever was reported for the first time in Côte d’Ivoire, where outbreaks around Abidjan rapidly devastated a previously expanding commercial and smallholder pig sector and triggered large-scale culling. Over 1997–2002, the same West African lineage ASF virus spread along coastal trade routes to Benin, Togo, Nigeria, Ghana and later Burkina Faso, causing near‑total loss of pigs in many affected areas and severe socio‑economic impacts on smallholders reliant on free‑ranging pigs. Intensive stamping‑out and movement controls eliminated ASF from Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana within a few years, but the virus became endemic in parts of the wider Western Africa region and permanently altered pig production and marketing systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of pig production in West African coastal countries, dominated by low‑biosecurity free‑range and backyard systems; informal cross‑border trade in live pigs and pork; swill feeding of uncooked waste; limited veterinary capacity and compensation, leading to under‑reporting and illegal sale of sick animals. Internal mechanisms: introduction and regional dissemination of genotype I viruses belonging to the West African lineage, maintained entirely in domestic pig cycles without a sylvatic reservoir, allowing sustained circulation and large‑scale geographic expansion within Western Africa without the involvement of new genotypes or resistance traits.
Review: retain – Added because the 1996–2002 West Africa epidemic in Côte d’Ivoire, Benin, Togo, Nigeria, Ghana and Burkina Faso is widely recognised as one of the most consequential ASF epizootics since 1990, with very high pig mortality and major livelihood impacts, and was missing from the original dataset. Classified as re‑occurrence within the Western Africa subregion (not intra‑continental emergence), since ASF was already present in parts of Western Africa (e.g. Senegal, Cape Verde) before 1996; countries and timing follow FAO and Brown et al. (2018).

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa
Countries: Kenya; Uganda; United Republic of Tanzania; Malawi; Mozambique; Zambia; Zimbabwe; Angola; Democratic Republic of the Congo; Congo; Cameroon; Nigeria; Ghana; Benin; Togo; Burkina Faso; Côte d’Ivoire; Senegal
Host: Domestic pigs; wild suids (warthogs, bushpigs)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s, African countries reported a marked increase and geographic expansion of African swine fever, with new or renewed outbreaks in many countries across Eastern, Middle and Western Africa after periods of partial control or under‑reporting. The disease spread among smallholder pig populations via local trade, swill feeding and movements of infected pigs and pork, causing repeated high‑mortality episodes and disrupting pig production and livelihoods. ASF persisted endemically in many affected areas through the 2010s, with recurrent local flare‑ups rather than clear eradication in most countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: growth of pig production in resource‑poor settings, extensive smallholder and free‑range systems, swill feeding, weak veterinary services and biosecurity, informal cross‑border trade, and limited compensation for culled animals promoted under‑reporting and virus maintenance. Internal mechanisms: long‑standing sylvatic and domestic cycles in African wild suids and soft ticks allowed persistent viral maintenance and gradual geographic expansion within already affected African subregions, but no specific novel genotype or resistance trait was the primary driver in this period.
Review: review – Retained as a high‑impact, multi‑country resurgence episode summarising increased ASF incidence and spread in sub‑Saharan Africa, but treated as a broad re‑occurrence rather than a discrete single outbreak. Corrected sub_regions to remove “Southern Africa”, which did not match the listed countries under the UNSD scheme, and changed the event type from mixed intra‑continental emergence plus re‑occurrence to re‑occurrence only, because all affected areas were in subregions where ASF was already known. Removed the vague “other affected African countries” phrase and limited the country list to explicitly mentioned, well‑documented countries; further subdivision into more granular national events could be considered if more detail is required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar
Event summary: In spring 2007, African swine fever appeared for the first time in the Caucasus, with an explosive outbreak in domestic pigs across most districts of Georgia that was traced to contaminated pork waste from ships and rapidly confirmed virologically. Over late 2007–2008 the same genotype II virus spread into Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Russian Federation (Chechnya and other regions), establishing infection in both backyard pigs and wild boar and extending beyond the Caucasus into key Russian pig‑producing regions. The virus was not eradicated and became entrenched in parts of the domestic pig and wild boar populations, seeding subsequent spread north and west into Eastern Europe and eastwards deeper into Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated pork or ship waste at a Black Sea port, low farm biosecurity, widespread backyard pig keeping, swill feeding, and uncontrolled movements of pigs and pork; later spread was aided by movement of animals and pork along trade routes and by wild boar movements. Internal mechanisms: introduction and establishment of a highly virulent genotype II strain with efficient transmission in domestic pigs and wild boar facilitated geographic range expansion from Africa and Europe into Asia under the UNSD classification, and re‑establishment of ASF in Eastern Europe after prior eradication.
Review: retain – Confirmed as a key high‑impact emergence event: the introduction of genotype II ASFV into the Caucasus and, under the UNSD scheme, the first occurrence of ASF in Asia, as well as re‑establishment in Eastern Europe. Corrected the event type by setting 'first_detection' to No (because global first detection occurred many decades earlier) and retaining 'inter_continental_emergence' = Yes to reflect the first occurrence of ASF in the Asian continent in this classification. Countries, years and hosts are appropriate and supported by primary literature and WOAH/FAO reports.

Host: Wild boar; domestic pigs
Event summary: In early 2014, African swine fever was detected for the first time in the European Union in wild boar and backyard pigs in Lithuania and almost simultaneously in eastern Poland, following earlier spread through Belarus and western Russia in 2013. Infection rapidly became established in wild boar populations in the Baltic states and eastern Poland, with a slowly expanding front and repeated spillover to domestic pigs, causing numerous outbreaks in backyard and some commercial farms despite intensive control efforts. By 2018, much of Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and eastern Poland was affected, and ASF had become endemic in local wild boar populations with recurrent outbreaks in pigs, rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infected wild boar across borders, human‑mediated long‑distance jumps via transport of contaminated pork products and fomites, low biosecurity in backyard farms, and difficulties in controlling infection in free‑ranging wild boar. Internal mechanisms: efficient transmission of the same highly virulent genotype II strain in wild boar and pigs supported sustained wildlife reservoirs and geographic range expansion within Eastern and Northern Europe, including first establishment in the Northern Europe subregion.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first introduction and establishment of genotype II ASFV in EU member states (Baltic countries and eastern Poland) and its spread into the Northern Europe subregion. Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting 'first_detection' to No (not a global first detection) and removing 're_occurrence', leaving 'intra_continental_emergence' = Yes to reflect spread from already affected Eastern Europe into the previously ASF‑free Northern Europe subregion. Simplified the Belarus entry to 'Belarus [2013]' while still acknowledging its epidemiological linkage.

Countries: Romania [2017]; Czechia [2017]; Hungary [2018]; Bulgaria [2018]; Slovakia [2019]; Republic of Moldova [2016]; Serbia [2019]
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar
Event summary: In July 2017, Romania detected its first African swine fever outbreaks in backyard pigs near the Ukrainian and Hungarian borders, followed by rapid spread during 2018 that produced a nationwide epidemic with thousands of outbreaks and large‑scale culling in both backyard and commercial herds. Around the same time, focal introductions of ASFV genotype II occurred in Czechia (2017), Hungary (2018), Bulgaria (2018), Slovakia (2019), the Republic of Moldova (2016) and Serbia (2019), typically beginning in wild boar with occasional spillover to domestic pigs. By 2020, many Central and South‑Eastern European countries had experienced repeated outbreaks, with some (e.g. Czechia) achieving eradication from wild boar while others, notably Romania, continued to report intense circulation and heavy production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infected pigs and pork from earlier affected Eastern European areas, poor biosecurity and backyard production in Romania and parts of the Balkans, swill feeding, informal trade, and human‑mediated long‑distance movement of contaminated materials leading to focal introductions in naïve wild boar populations. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of genotype II with high virulence and environmental stability, facilitating persistence in carcasses and wild boar populations and enabling further geographic spread and resurgence within already affected Eastern and Southern Europe subregions.
Review: retain – Verified as a major high‑impact episode dominated by the very large Romanian epidemic and repeated outbreaks in several Central and South‑Eastern European countries. Corrected the emergence‑type coding from 'first_detection' + intra‑continental emergence + re‑occurrence to re‑occurrence only, because all affected countries lie within subregions (Eastern and Southern Europe) where ASF was already present after 2007; spread here represents expansion and resurgence within existing subregions rather than first occurrence in a new subregion.

Countries: Belgium [2018]; Germany [2020 wild boar; 2021 domestic pigs]
Host: Wild boar; domestic pigs
Event summary: In September 2018, Belgium reported its first African swine fever cases in wild boar in the province of Luxembourg near the French border, marking the re‑appearance of genotype II ASFV in Western Europe and triggering extensive hunting bans and fencing measures to protect the commercial pig sector; the outbreak remained confined to wild boar and was declared eradicated by 2020. In September 2020, Germany detected its first ASF‑positive wild boar near the Polish border in Brandenburg, and in July 2021 confirmed the first outbreaks in domestic pigs in two farms, prompting strict movement controls and threatening a major European pork exporter. Germany has since experienced continuing ASF in wild boar but has aimed to contain and eradicate the disease in domestic pigs through stamping‑out and intensive surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑distance human‑mediated introduction of contaminated pork or materials into Belgium and, later, spread of virus in wild boar from heavily affected western Poland into eastern Germany; movement of wild boar across borders; high wild boar densities; and challenges in fencing and carcass removal. Internal mechanisms: persistence and efficient transmission of genotype II ASFV in wild boar, plus environmental stability of the virus in carcasses and the environment, enabled local establishment in wildlife in Western Europe despite strong veterinary services.
Review: retain – Confirmed as a distinct and high‑stakes episode marking the re‑appearance of ASF in Western Europe (Belgium and Germany) with major trade implications. Corrected the geography by restricting sub_regions to 'Western Europe' and removing uninfected neighbours from the country list, and changed the emergence‑type coding to re‑occurrence only, because ASF had occurred previously in the Western Europe subregion (e.g. earlier 20th‑century outbreaks in France, Belgium, the Netherlands). 'First_detection' was set to No because this is not a global first description.

Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (limited detection compared to pigs)
Event summary: On 3 August 2018, China reported its first African swine fever outbreak in Liaoning Province in northeastern China, with confirmation of genotype II ASFV from affected pigs and rapid identification of further outbreaks along major transport corridors. Over late 2018 and 2019, the virus spread to all provinces, leading to massive culling and mortality that reduced China’s pig herd by an estimated 40–50%, disrupted domestic pork supply and reshaped global pork markets. ASF persisted with recurrent outbreaks through at least 2022, despite large‑scale depopulation, movement controls and biosecurity campaigns, with emergence of additional viral variants and concerns about substandard vaccines contributing to continued virus circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large, highly integrated but unevenly biosecure pig production sector; long‑distance trucking of pigs and pork; widespread swill feeding and informal slaughter; complex supply chains; and delayed or incomplete reporting in some areas. Internal mechanisms: introduction of highly virulent genotype II ASFV into the previously ASF‑free Eastern Asia subregion, followed by emergence of additional variants/strains within China, potential selection pressure from experimental or illicit vaccines, and inherent viral stability that enabled sustained endemicity and widespread geographic range expansion across all Chinese regions.
Review: retain – This is by far the single most impactful ASF event globally in terms of pigs lost and market disruption. Under the UNSD classification, ASF had already reached Western Asia in 2007, so the appropriate type is intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian subregion (Eastern Asia), not inter‑continental emergence. 'First_detection' was set to No, as global first detection predates 1990. Countries, timing and impact are well supported by WOAH, FAO, USDA and peer‑reviewed sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Countries: Mongolia [2019]; Viet Nam [2019]; Cambodia [2019]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2019]; Myanmar [2019]; Philippines [2019]; Indonesia [2019]; Timor-Leste [2019]; India [2020]
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (limited reports, mainly Viet Nam and some others)
Event summary: Beginning in January–February 2019, African swine fever spread rapidly from China into neighbouring Asian countries, with Mongolia reporting its first outbreaks in January 2019, Viet Nam confirming its first outbreak in February 2019 and then experiencing nationwide spread within months, and Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar reporting their first outbreaks later in 2019; Viet Nam alone culled a large share of its pig herd and suffered major production losses. Over 2019–2020, the virus reached the Philippines, where outbreaks started near Manila and extended to multiple regions, and Indonesia, where North Sumatra recorded tens of thousands of pig deaths and widespread provincial spread, as well as Timor‑Leste, which reported severe losses in village pigs. From 2020 onward, ASF outbreaks were also confirmed in the north‑eastern states of India (Assam and Arunachal Pradesh), extending the epidemic into the Southern Asia subregion and causing tens of thousands of pig deaths and substantial livelihood impacts; ASF remained present in many of these countries through at least 2022, with repeated waves of outbreaks despite control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense cross‑border trade and informal movements of pigs and pork between China and neighbouring countries; backyard and smallholder production with low biosecurity and swill feeding; porous borders; limited veterinary resources; and movement of contaminated pork products by travellers. Internal mechanisms: the same genotype II virus introduced from China maintained high virulence and environmental stability, facilitating rapid geographic range expansion across Eastern Asia, South‑eastern Asia and into Southern Asia (India); no clear evidence of resistance emerged, although some viral variation occurred over time.
Review: retain – This episode represents the wider Asian spread of genotype II ASFV outside China and is clearly among the most impactful emergence events in terms of numbers of countries and pigs affected. The event has been expanded to include India and the Southern Asia subregion, reflecting first outbreaks in Assam and Arunachal Pradesh in 2020, and the sub_regions and countries fields were updated accordingly. 'First_detection' was set to No, and 'intra_continental_emergence' = Yes is retained, as this wave reflects first occurrence in new Asian subregions (South‑eastern and Southern Asia) rather than a new continent.

Host: Domestic pigs (village and smallholder); feral/free‑ranging pigs
Event summary: In March 2020, Papua New Guinea officially confirmed its first African swine fever outbreaks in free‑ranging village pigs in the Southern Highlands province, marking the arrival of ASF in Melanesia and the Oceania region and raising major concerns for Pacific biosecurity. The disease caused high mortality among village pigs in affected provinces, with reports of hundreds to around a thousand deaths in some areas and significant livelihood impacts for subsistence farmers. Intensive awareness campaigns, movement controls and targeted response efforts helped to limit the geographic extent of the outbreak, and authorities later reported that ASF was under control, though ongoing vigilance remained necessary.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introduction via infected pigs or pork products from ASF‑affected parts of Asia, combined with free‑ranging pig husbandry, communal scavenging, low biosecurity and limited veterinary infrastructure in rural Highlands communities. Internal mechanisms: high virulence and environmental stability of genotype II ASFV enabled rapid local spread once introduced into naive pig populations, but no evidence suggests novel viral traits beyond those circulating in Asia and Europe; the main significance of this event lies in its role as the first occurrence of ASF in the Oceania continent.
Review: retain – Verified as the first confirmed occurrence of ASF in Oceania (Papua New Guinea) and therefore an inter‑continental emergence event despite the relatively modest absolute number of pigs affected. Corrected the start year from 2019 to 2020 and aligned the country‑specific dates accordingly using WOAH/FAO reports, and changed the emergence‑type coding to 'inter_continental_emergence' = Yes and 'intra_continental_emergence' = No, since there was no prior ASF in Oceania. Replaced a Reddit link with an official and trade‑press confirmation (The Pig Site) for stronger sourcing.

Host: Domestic pigs; free‑ranging village pigs
Event summary: In July 2021, Dominican authorities confirmed African swine fever in domestic pigs after laboratory testing, representing the re‑appearance of ASF in the Americas and in Hispaniola roughly four decades after the 1970s–1980s Caribbean epizootic; widespread culling and movement controls were implemented to limit spread. In September 2021, Haiti notified WOAH of ASF detection in Artibonite Department, with outbreaks affecting smallholders and free‑ranging village pigs reminiscent of the historic epidemic that had previously led to mass pig culling in Haiti. Through 2022–2025, ASF continued to pose a major threat to Caribbean pig production and to the biosecurity of continental North and South America, prompting intensive regional surveillance and preparedness measures and substantial losses in parts of the Dominican and Haitian swine sectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: re‑introduction via infected pork products or live pigs, possibly related to trade or traveller‑carried meat from ASF‑affected regions; widespread low‑biosecurity backyard pig systems; free‑ranging pigs scavenging waste; and limited veterinary capacity and compensation mechanisms. Internal mechanisms: circulation of highly virulent genotype II ASFV similar to contemporary Eurasian strains, enabling rapid local spread. From a continental perspective this episode is best characterized as a geographic re‑occurrence in the Caribbean subregion of the Americas, rather than a new inter‑continental emergence or viral re‑emergence driven by evolutionary change.
Review: retain – This episode marks the re‑introduction and spread of ASF in Hispaniola after an absence of nearly 40 years and has major regional biosecurity significance. Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting 'inter_continental_emergence' and 'intra_continental_emergence' to No and 're_occurrence' to Yes, because the Americas (and the Caribbean subregion) experienced ASF previously in the 1970s–1980s; this event is a re‑occurrence rather than the first continental occurrence. 'First_detection' was set to No, as ASF was already known in this host system and region. The existing sources (USGS, USDA, WOAH, and a review of Haiti’s outbreak) are appropriate and were kept.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Commercial American bison (Bison bison) finished in a large Midwestern feedlot
Event summary: From early 1998 through late 1999, a large feedlot in the American Midwest experienced a devastating enteric disease syndrome in American bison, ultimately attributed to sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever caused by OvHV‑2. Retrospective and prospective necropsy and PCR investigations showed that malignant catarrhal fever had been present in the yard since at least 1993, but an intense epizootic began in January 1998, with an estimated 150 bison dying of the syndrome over two years and MCF becoming the leading cause of death in the 1,101‑animal consignment under study. A concurrent cohort study found that, among 300 monitored bison, 7.3% died and 15 of 22 necropsied animals had classic MCF lesions, and across the full consignment 75 of 98 deaths (75.5%) were attributable to MCF, underscoring its major impact on the commercial bison industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high animal density and prolonged confinement in a commercial feedlot, shipment and handling stress, and prior exposure of some bison to OvHV‑2‑infected sheep at source ranches likely increased susceptibility and triggered clinical disease; once infected animals arrived at the yard, repeated handling and other stressors were temporally associated with peaks in mortality. Internal mechanisms: Extreme species susceptibility of American bison to OvHV‑2, with a high proportion of infected animals developing fulminant alimentary‑form MCF and near‑100% case fatality; there was no evidence that a novel viral genotype caused the outbreak, so this represents a severe re‑occurrence of established SA‑MCF rather than a true viral re‑emergence.
Review: Retain: Added as a new event because the 1998–1999 sheep‑associated MCF epizootic in a US bison feedlot killed an estimated ~150 animals and accounted for >75% of deaths in a monitored 1,101‑head consignment, making it one of the most impactful malignant catarrhal fever outbreaks worldwide in terms of mortality and economic loss. Classified as a re‑occurrence in Northern America because OvHV‑2 and MCF were already established in North American bison prior to this outbreak and there is no evidence of first emergence or inter‑/intra‑continental spread.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: American bison (Bison bison) from eight Saskatchewan farms sold through a public auction market and mixed with resident bison on destination farms
Event summary: Following a November 2000 public auction of 163 bison from eight Saskatchewan farms at a market where 211 lambs were briefly present, an outbreak of sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever occurred on seven destination farms over the subsequent 7–8 months. Forty‑five of 163 sale bison (27.6%) became acutely ill and died between 50 and 220 days after the sale, with 21 animals confirmed as MCF cases by pathology and OvHV‑2 PCR and the remaining 24 classified as suspect cases based on clinical history; no cases occurred in unsold bison on the farms of origin or in resident bison mixed with the sale animals.
