The episode illustrated that a single short aerosol exposure to carrier lambs in an enclosed auction facility can cause high‑mortality SA‑MCF outbreaks in highly susceptible bison with no onward transmission between bison.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Brief but intense airborne exposure of naïve or subclinically infected bison to a large group of lambs shedding OvHV‑2 at a public auction market, followed by transport stress, regrouping and mixing on multiple destination farms, created conditions for widespread clinical disease after a common exposure event. Internal mechanisms: As in other SA‑MCF outbreaks, OvHV‑2 replicated in highly susceptible bison, producing a high case fatality rate with peracute to acute clinical courses; there was no evidence of virus adaptation or sustained transmission among bison, consistent with bison remaining dead‑end hosts.
Review: Retain: Added as a new event because detailed investigation showed that 45 of 163 bison (27.6%) exposed to sheep for less than a day at a Saskatchewan auction died of SA‑MCF, making this one of the best‑documented and most severe OvHV‑2 outbreaks in North American bison. Classified as a re‑occurrence within Northern America, since OvHV‑2 was already endemic in regional sheep and MCF had been reported previously in Canadian and US bison; there is no evidence of novelty in geographic range or viral genotype.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Indigenous Tanzanian shorthorn zebu cattle grazing near wildebeest calving grounds
Event summary: In April–June 2004, pastoral Maasai herds in Enguserosambu village, Ngorongoro District, northern Tanzania, experienced an outbreak of acute malignant catarrhal fever in zebu cattle following the wildebeest calving season. Cattle grazing at the wildlife–livestock interface developed high fever, corneal opacity, mucopurulent nasal discharge and high case fatality, and Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1 was confirmed by molecular characterization from affected animals. Losses subsided after cattle were moved away from wildebeest areas and surviving animals either died or recovered, but the episode highlighted the recurrent seasonal risk of wildebeest‑associated MCF in this pastoral ecosystem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal overlap of Maasai cattle with dense migratory wildebeest populations at shared grazing and water sources in Ngorongoro, together with semi‑nomadic management that brings susceptible cattle into close contact with wildebeest calves during peak viral shedding. Internal mechanisms: Long‑established circulation of AlHV‑1 in blue wildebeest, with very high viral shedding from calves around calving driving aerosol transmission to cattle; there is no evidence that a novel strain or host shift was involved, so this episode represents a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic risk system.
Review: Retain: Well‑documented wildebeest‑associated MCF outbreak in Maasai cattle in Enguserosambu (Ngorongoro District) with clear epidemiological linkage to wildebeest calving and substantial local livestock losses; continent/subregion/country coding and event‑type classification as re‑occurrence in Eastern Africa are appropriate, and the sources used are directly relevant to the event.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Dairy cows, pregnant dairy youngstock and calves in two intensive dairy herds co‑housed with lambing sheep (OvHV‑2 reservoir)
Event summary: Beginning in May 2012 and extending into early 2013, two large Dutch dairy herds that co‑housed cattle with lambing sheep experienced severe outbreaks of sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever. In the first herd, 10 dairy cows, 10 of 21 pregnant youngstock, one non‑pregnant heifer and one calf died or were euthanized over approximately three months; in the second herd, 5 cows, 20 pregnant youngstock and 10 calves died or were euthanized between September 2012 and January 2013. Clinical signs, pathology and OvHV‑2 PCR confirmed SA‑MCF, and mortality declined only after sick cattle were removed and strict separation from sheep was implemented, demonstrating the capacity of SA‑MCF to cause large multi‑animal losses in Western European dairy systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close indoor co‑housing of susceptible dairy cattle and calves with high densities of lambing sheep, especially during and after lambing when OvHV‑2 shedding peaks, combined with limited ventilation and lack of management awareness of MCF risk in mixed sheep–cattle enterprises. Internal mechanisms: High OvHV‑2 burden and intense virus shedding from lambs in enclosed barns, leading to efficient aerosol transmission to cattle; histopathology and virology indicated typical SA‑MCF without evidence of a novel viral strain, so the scale of losses reflects management‑driven exposure in herds located in a region where the virus was already endemic in sheep.
Review: Review: Retain as a major SA‑MCF outbreak but with corrected geography and sources. The Juniper paper documents two large outbreaks in Dutch dairy herds only; it does not describe a linked Belgian event, so Belgium has been removed from the countries field and the row is now restricted to the Netherlands. The Juniper URL has been corrected from an incorrect manuscript ID to JDVS.MS.ID.555672, and a Reddit mirror of the article has been treated as non‑primary and omitted from the source list. Event year (2012–2013), Western Europe subregion and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate. A separate row would be needed if the large peracute MCF outbreak in Belgian Blue cattle were to be included explicitly.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Ranch‑managed beef cattle herds at Kapiti Plains Ranch in a wildebeest interface area (Machakos County, Kenya)
Event summary: From 2014 to 2016, Kapiti Plains Ranch in south‑eastern Kenya recorded recurrent seasonal peaks of wildebeest‑associated malignant catarrhal fever in ranch cattle, with 325 animals showing clinical signs over three years and a substantial proportion confirmed as AlHV‑1 infections by PCR and ELISA. Disease incidence rose each year following the wildebeest calving season as cattle grazed within mixed wildlife–livestock landscapes, generating annual herd‑level losses that in some years approached 10% in parts of the ranch. Incidence declined after implementation of wildebeest‑avoidance measures and participation in experimental vaccination trials, but WA‑MCF remained an important seasonal constraint on cattle production in this ecosystem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term integration of ranch cattle with migratory wildebeest in unfenced savannah, increasing overlap at grazing and water points during and after calving; economic pressure to exploit high‑quality wet‑season pastures near wildebeest herds, and limited infrastructure to physically separate species at high‑risk times. Internal mechanisms: Endemic circulation of AlHV‑1 in wildebeest with intense shedding by calves, combined with high susceptibility of naïve cattle, produced recurrent high‑incidence outbreaks; there is no indication that novel viral variants were responsible, so this represents a major re‑occurrence within an established East African WA‑MCF focus.
Review: Review: Retain as a high‑impact WA‑MCF episode but correct the geographic scope. The cited BMC Veterinary Research paper documents recurrent outbreaks in Kapiti Plains Ranch (Kenya) from 2014–2016 with 325 clinically affected cattle; it does not provide evidence for a single epidemiologically linked 2014–2016 outbreak in Tanzania. The countries field has therefore been restricted to 'Kenya [2014‑2016]' and summary text adjusted to focus on Kapiti ranch, while Eastern Africa as the subregion and classification as re‑occurrence remain appropriate. Recommended for curator review of exact case counts and fatality estimates.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Bali cattle in smallholder mixed farms; nearby sheep and goats as OvHV‑2 reservoirs
Event summary: In 2016, veterinary services investigated reports of sudden deaths among Bali cattle in Musi Rawas District, South Sumatra, Indonesia, where affected animals showed fever, ocular and nasal discharge and erosive oral lesions consistent with malignant catarrhal fever. Field epidemiology linked the outbreak to close proximity of susceptible Bali cattle to small ruminants, and laboratory testing implicated OvHV‑2 infection, with multiple cattle in affected villages dying over a short period. Control efforts focused on movement restrictions, advising farmers to separate Bali cattle from lambing sheep and goats, and local awareness campaigns, although technical reports note that sporadic MCF cases continue to be reported from other Indonesian provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of mixed smallholder systems in South Sumatra where Bali cattle are kept in close proximity to growing populations of sheep and goats, often with free‑range management and minimal biosecurity, together with low farmer awareness of MCF and the risk posed by lambing sheep. Internal mechanisms: High inherent susceptibility of Bali cattle to SA‑MCF caused by OvHV‑2 circulating in Indonesian sheep, with high viral load in lambs and intense close contact driving localized outbreaks with high case fatality; no evidence has been published for emergence of new OvHV‑2 genotypes in this setting.
Review: Review: Outbreak reports and provincial risk‑management documents support a 2016 SA‑MCF episode in Bali cattle in Musi Rawas (South Sumatra), but detailed numbers of affected and dead animals in English are limited. Geographic coding (Asia → South‑eastern Asia → Indonesia) and classification as a re‑occurrence in an already endemic country are appropriate. Recommend a native‑language reviewer confirm herd sizes and mortality to judge whether this episode ranks among Indonesia’s largest documented MCF outbreaks and should be retained in a strict top‑10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Bali cattle on smallholder farms; nearby lambing sheep as OvHV‑2 reservoir
Event summary: Between January and September 2016, an outbreak of malignant catarrhal fever was documented in 231 Bali cattle on Lombok Island, West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. Twenty cattle died during the episode, 16 of which showed classical clinical signs including high fever, corneal opacity, mucopurulent nasal discharge, hypersalivation, enlarged superficial lymph nodes and characteristic necrotizing vasculitis on histopathology; nested PCR detected OvHV‑2 in peripheral blood leukocytes of surviving clinically affected cattle and in nasal, ocular and vaginal swabs from nearby adult sheep. The outbreak waned after the deaths and emergency culling, and control recommendations emphasized separating Bali cattle from lambing sheep and improving farmer awareness, with subsequent reports recognizing MCF as an endemic threat to Bali cattle in multiple Indonesian provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of mixed sheep–Bali cattle systems on Lombok with minimal separation between species, particularly during lambing, combined with relatively high stocking densities and housing that facilitated aerosol spread of ovine nasal secretions to cattle. Internal mechanisms: Established OvHV‑2 infection in Indonesian sheep spilling over into highly susceptible Bali cattle, producing high case fatality without clear evidence of a novel genotype; the outbreak’s severity reflects the inherent susceptibility of Bali cattle and management factors rather than recent viral evolution.
Review: Review: Corrected a major dating error. The cited Jurnal Veteriner paper clearly documents a Bali cattle MCF outbreak on Lombok Island occurring from January to September 2016 with 20 deaths among 231 cattle, not an early‑2000s event; the Event Year has been updated to '2016' and the country annotation revised to 'Indonesia [2016] (Lombok Island, West Nusa Tenggara)'. Confidence has been raised to reflect the strong primary data. Classification as a re‑occurrence of SA‑MCF in an already endemic Indonesian context remains appropriate. Recommended for curator verification of mortality figures and confirmation that this outbreak is among the country’s largest documented MCF episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Mediterranean water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) herds; co‑housed or neighboring sheep and goats as OvHV‑2/CpHV‑2 reservoirs
Event summary: In the early 2010s, two large commercial water buffalo farms in Southern Italy—one in Calabria housing ~200 buffalo and ~80 sheep, and one in Campania with ~650 buffalo surrounded by small ruminant farms—experienced outbreaks of malignant catarrhal fever characterized by fever, corneal opacity, mucopurulent nasal and ocular discharge and high mortality. Across the two farms, 12 buffalo developed clinical MCF and nine died within days of onset; real‑time PCR confirmed OvHV‑2 infection in nasal swabs and tissues from sick and dead buffalo, and genetic characterization of ORF50, ORF75 and Ov9.5 sequences showed that the outbreaks were caused by two distinct OvHV‑2 variants. Following the mortality peaks, surviving buffalo either recovered or were culled, and disease incidence declined after improved separation of buffalo from sheep and goats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density Mediterranean water buffalo production in Campania and Calabria in close proximity to small ruminants, including co‑housing of buffalo and sheep in the same paddocks on one farm and neighboring flocks on the other, facilitating interspecies aerosol transmission of OvHV‑2. Internal mechanisms: Sheep‑associated OvHV‑2 infecting a highly susceptible but previously under‑recognized host (water buffalo) in Southern Europe, with molecular analyses identifying distinct viral variants associated with the outbreaks; this host expansion and identification of specific OvHV‑2 strains in buffalo justify treating the episode as a re‑emergence of MCF with expanded host range in the Southern Europe subregion rather than a simple re‑occurrence.
Review: Review: Retain as an important SA‑MCF outbreak in Mediterranean water buffaloes in Southern Italy, but note that the current '2017' timing in the original file reflects the publication year of the Veterinary Microbiology paper rather than the exact outbreak years; the article indicates that the two outbreaks occurred 'recently' before 2014. The Event Year field has therefore been generalized to '~2010s (publication 2017)' pending manual extraction of precise dates from the full text. Geographic coding (Europe → Southern Europe → Italy) and the emphasis on host expansion and genetically characterized OvHV‑2 variants support classification as re‑emergence (with re‑occurrence also ticked), but this should be confirmed by a subject‑matter curator.

Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In August 2002, a large dairy herd of 286 cows in the canton of Grisons, alpine Switzerland, experienced an outbreak of severe hemolytic disease marked by fever, anorexia, agalactia, anemia and high culling, in a region where bovine anaplasmosis had previously been reported only sporadically and without major economic impact. Microscopy, serology and PCR confirmed Anaplasma marginale infection in nearly half the cows, alongside frequent co-infections with Babesia/Theileria spp. and Mycoplasma wenyonii, making this the first severe bovine anaplasmosis outbreak linked to multiple vector-borne pathogens in alpine Switzerland. After diagnosis, the entire herd was culled and regional surveillance showed very low but non-zero seroprevalence, indicating a dramatic re-occurrence of disease rather than first introduction of the pathogen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of A. marginale into a largely immunologically naïve high-yield dairy herd north of the Alps, with abundant tick and biting-fly exposure, created conditions for high within-herd transmission and severe clinical disease; regional cattle trade likely contributed to pathogen introduction. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel A. marginale genotype was reported; disease severity appears to have been amplified by polymicrobial co-infections (Babesia, Theileria, haemotropic mycoplasmas) and age-dependent susceptibility in adult cows.
Review: Retain: Well-documented 2002 alpine Switzerland outbreak with substantial morbidity and culling, confirmed by OIE notification and detailed clinical/molecular description, and representing a dramatic resurgence of bovine anaplasmosis in a previously low-impact area of Western Europe. Classification as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because earlier sporadic Swiss cases and established infection in other Western European countries pre‑date this event. No corrections needed beyond trimming sources to those directly describing the Swiss outbreak.

Host: Beef cattle (mixed-age herd of 75 animals)
Event summary: In late summer–early autumn 2009, a 75-head beef herd in northern Hungary developed an outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis in which Anaplasma marginale was first recognized in blood smears of 51 cattle and 5 animals showed acute clinical disease with lethargy, ruminal atony, anemia and organ pathology; 2 cows died within three days, and PCR showed at least 92% of animals were bacteraemic. Molecular typing of the msp4 gene revealed three previously undescribed A. marginale genotypes circulating in the herd and in Dermacentor reticulatus and Ixodes ricinus ticks, alongside concurrent infection with haemotropic mycoplasmas (“Candidatus Mycoplasma haemobos” and Mycoplasma wenyonii). Control measures focused on oxytetracycline treatment and tick removal, and the outbreak highlighted destabilisation of an endemic but subclinical situation by introduction of naïve cattle and novel A. marginale variants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Frequent introduction of newly purchased, naïve cattle into an area with established but subclinical A. marginale circulation disrupted endemic stability, while heavy tick infestation (especially D. reticulatus) facilitated rapid spread within the herd. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of several new A. marginale msp4 genotypes in the herd, together with widespread co-infection by haemotropic mycoplasmas, likely increased pathogenicity and contributed to the fatal clinical presentation, meeting the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogen genetic change and co-infection.
Review: Review: New event added because the 2009 northern Hungary outbreak is a well-characterised, high-prevalence (≈92% of 75 cattle) and partially fatal episode associated with novel A. marginale genotypes and concurrent haemoplasmosis, and is repeatedly cited as a key European emergence event. Classified as re-emergence (novel strain/genotype emergence in an already affected sub-region) rather than intra-continental emergence, since A. marginale was already endemic in Eastern Europe. Recommend retaining as one of the top global emergence/re-emergence events, but final inclusion should be confirmed by comparing its impact against other large Latin American or African outbreaks not individually documented here.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dairy cattle (≈680 lactating Holstein cows)
Event summary: In 2010, a large confinement dairy herd in northern Iowa (≈680 lactating Holstein cows) experienced a clinically recognized outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis, with many adult cows developing fever, anemia, weight loss and decreased milk production, prompting culling or death in a notable proportion of affected animals. Serologic follow-up in 2011 showed about 38% of cows seropositive for A. marginale, while roughly two-thirds of the herd remained susceptible, indicating substantial within-herd spread during the outbreak. Epidemiologic investigation implicated both tick exposure and iatrogenic mechanical transmission through reuse of needles and multi-dose oxytocin vials, and subsequent management changes (eliminating needle sharing, improved biosecurity and vector control) reduced clinical cases, although previously infected cows had persistently reduced milk yields in subsequent lactations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density confinement management, reuse of blood-contaminated needles and injection equipment, and presence of competent tick vectors in a region where bovine anaplasmosis had historically been considered of lower concern led to efficient within-herd spread among adult cows. Internal mechanisms: No novel A. marginale genotypes were implicated; the outbreak’s impact derived mainly from high force of infection in immunologically naïve adult animals, resulting in severe clinical disease and long-term subclinical carrier states with measurable production losses.
Review: Retain: Large, well-documented within-herd outbreak in a >600-cow U.S. dairy with clear evidence of economic impact (sustained milk loss) and mixed tick/iatrogenic transmission, consistent with a major re-occurrence event in a partially naïve herd in an endemic country. Geographic (Northern America) and temporal information match the primary sources, and the event is reasonably among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for this pathogen in North America.

Host: Dairy cattle (adult mixed-age cows)
Event summary: In 2013, the long-established San Miguel dairy farm in the municipality of Nariño, highland southern Colombia, reported its first-ever acute outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis after more than 50 years of cattle production without known cases, with 37 clinical cases and 6 deaths among predominantly high-producing adult cows. During the critical phase, affected animals showed fever, marked drops in milk yield, anorexia, emaciation, abortions and sudden deaths, and blood smears confirmed A. marginale with severe hemolytic anemia. Intensive treatment and improved vector control eventually halted the outbreak, but high abortion rates and abrupt cessation of milk production in surviving cows produced major economic losses and were interpreted locally as evidence of tick-borne disease expansion into previously cooler Andean zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional climate change and variability in the tropical Andes likely facilitated altitudinal expansion of tick vectors and A. marginale into historically cool, highland areas, and decades without exposure left the herd immunologically naïve. Internal mechanisms: No new A. marginale genotype was described; the event is better explained as geographic range expansion and exposure of adult naïve cattle, fitting the definition of re-occurrence driven by external climatic and management factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain: Case report clearly documents a sizeable acute outbreak with deaths, abortions and major production loss in a historically anaplasmosis-free Andean dairy area, aligning with a re-occurrence/range-expansion event in South America. Country, sub-region and timing are correct, and the event is among the relatively few well-quantified, high-impact emergence episodes in Latin American highlands since 1990.

Host: Beef and dairy cattle on an intensive farm
Event summary: In the early–mid 2010s, a large intensive cattle farm in Henan Province, central China, experienced a serious tick-borne disease episode in which bovine theileriosis and anaplasmosis occurred together, causing fever, anemia, weight loss and production losses in multiple animals. Microscopy and PCR identified mixed infections with Theileria annulata-like organisms and A. marginale, and this was reported as the first confirmed outbreak of theileriosis/anaplasmosis on a cattle farm in Henan Province. Following diagnosis, the farm implemented acaricide-based tick control and therapeutic regimens, which reduced clinical cases, and the authors recommended improved surveillance and control of bovine tick-borne diseases in central China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and increased activity of tick vectors (notably Rhipicephalus microplus) in central China, combined with intensification of cattle production, likely heightened exposure to tick-borne pathogens in an area where such mixed disease had not previously been recognized in farms. Internal mechanisms: No novel A. marginale genotype was described; the event represents a regional re-occurrence and recognition of mixed Theileria–Anaplasma infection in a major livestock province within China.
Review: Review: The Henan event is correctly characterised as the first confirmed mixed theileriosis/anaplasmosis outbreak reported from a cattle farm in that province and fits the definition of a re-occurrence/range-intensification event within Eastern Asia. However, the precise outbreak year is unclear from the accessible abstract; the current 2013–2015 range is an approximation inferred from study timing, and may well represent a single-year outbreak around 2014–2015. Recommend verifying the exact start year and duration from the full article and then narrowing the Event Year and country bracket (e.g. “Henan [2014]”) accordingly.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Lactating dairy cattle (local dairy herd)
Event summary: In March and again in September 2015, a dairy herd in Kırklareli Province in the Thrace region of Türkiye experienced an outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis in which 30 lactating cows developed fever, anemia, reduced milk yield, anorexia and respiratory distress, and A. marginale infection was confirmed by PCR. Genotyping of the major surface protein genes revealed several novel msp1a genotypes of A. marginale in the herd, and examination of placental tissues provided evidence of transplacental transmission to calves. After targeted therapy and reinforced tick control and herd management, clinical cases resolved, but the presence of highly pathogenic variants and vertical transmission indicated a worrisome re-emergence pattern with significant production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional abundance of competent ticks and possible introduction of infected animals or ticks into the herd likely seeded new A. marginale variants into adult dairy cows with limited prior immunity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of novel A. marginale msp1a genotypes associated with severe clinical disease and probable placental (vertical) transmission demonstrates pathogen evolution toward enhanced pathogenicity and transmission, justifying classification as re-emergence with internal genetic change rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Retain: Strongly supported by peer-reviewed data as an outbreak with novel genotypes and evidence of vertical transmission in a dairy herd, exemplifying re-emergence via pathogen genetic diversification in Western Asia. Country, sub-region and timing are appropriate under the UN classification used in the Country sheet (Türkiye in Western Asia). No corrections required beyond pruning less directly relevant secondary citations.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Croatia [2018] (Glina area and a second continental herd)
Host: Beef cattle (Simmental cows and other local breeds)
Event summary: From June to July 2018, a beef herd of about 50 Simmental cows near Glina in continental Croatia had an outbreak in which five adult cows died acutely with fever, anemia and icterus; spleen imprints and PCR confirmed A. marginale infection, representing the first indigenous lethal bovine anaplasmosis reported in Croatian cattle. A contemporaneous outbreak in another Croatian herd involved three cows that died from co-infection with A. bovis and Theileria orientalis, further demonstrating establishment of multiple tick-borne haemoparasites in local cattle. Following recognition of these outbreaks, Croatian veterinarians updated differential diagnoses and implemented stricter tick control and management practices to prevent additional lethal episodes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing presence of competent ticks (e.g. Dermacentor reticulatus) in continental Croatia and extensive pasture grazing promoted exposure of older, naïve cattle to A. marginale and other tick-borne agents; limited prior clinical recognition delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: No unique Croatian A. marginale lineage was reported; severe outcomes likely reflected infection of older animals and synergistic effects of co-infections (particularly A. bovis and T. orientalis) rather than clear pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain: The Croatian outbreaks provided the first reports of indigenous lethal bovine anaplasmosis in that country and signalled establishment of A. marginale and other tick-borne haemoparasites in continental Southern Europe. Sub-region and country assignments are correct, and classifying this as re-occurrence (rather than intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because A. marginale had long been present in other Southern European countries. No structural corrections required.

Host: Cattle (Leiqiong and Wagyu breeds), water buffalo, and Rhipicephalus microplus ticks
Event summary: From May to September 2020, researchers in northern Hainan, China collected 151 bovine blood samples (Leiqiong cattle, Wagyu cattle and buffalo) and 63 Rhipicephalus microplus ticks and, using PCR, detected Anaplasma marginale in 10.75% of all samples together with Babesia bovis and B. bigemina, with high mixed-infection rates in Leiqiong cattle. The work was presented as the first molecular detection of A. marginale, B. bovis and B. bigemina in cattle and R. microplus from the sampled northern coastal area of Hainan, complementing earlier province-level evidence of A. marginale circulation. Although not a point-source outbreak, the findings documented a substantial endemic focus of bovine anaplasmosis and piroplasmosis in an important subtropical island cattle area and prompted calls for improved tick control and surveillance to avert clinical losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warm, humid coastal climate in Hainan favors proliferation of R. microplus, and local husbandry practices with high tick exposure in Leiqiong cattle and buffalo enable persistent circulation of A. marginale and Babesia spp.; increasing animal movement and under-appreciation of tick-borne disease risk likely contributed to under-detection before this survey. Internal mechanisms: No novel A. marginale genotypes were highlighted; the event mainly reflects improved detection and recognition of endemic transmission in a specific region of Hainan rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review: The study robustly demonstrates A. marginale and Babesia spp. circulation in cattle and R. microplus in northern Hainan and can reasonably be treated as a regional emergence/re-recognition event, but it is a cross-sectional molecular survey rather than a clearly bounded clinical outbreak with quantified production losses. The event is classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Asia, consistent with prior evidence of A. marginale in Hainan and other Chinese provinces; it does not qualify as first detection for China or for the island as a whole. A non-specific Babesia review article previously listed as a source has been removed in favor of the primary preprint and ResearchGate versions of the Hainan study. Consider retaining this event only if the dataset aims to include important detection-based emergence signals alongside major clinical outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Poland [2021] (Białowieża Primeval Forest and Knyszyńska Forest)
Host: European bison (Bison bonasus), with potential spillover relevance for cattle
Event summary: In 2021, blood samples from free-ranging European bison in north-eastern Poland (Białowieża Primeval Forest and Knyszyńska Forest) were found by PCR and sequencing of the msp4 gene to be infected with Anaplasma marginale, marking the first confirmed occurrence of this pathogen in Poland, the first report in European bison, and the northernmost confirmed A. marginale record in Europe. Prevalence of A. marginale in sampled bison was about 17.8%, and phylogenetic analysis showed that the genotypes clustered with A. marginale strains from cattle in Hungary, Africa and Russia rather than with North or South American strains. Although no mass mortality event was described, the discovery revealed an autochthonous A. marginale cycle in a strictly protected wild bovid population and raised concern that bison could act as reservoirs posing spillover risk to sympatric cattle as the pathogen expands its range northward.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Northward expansion of competent tick vectors (e.g. Dermacentor reticulatus) and increasing spatial overlap between recovering European bison populations and cattle grazing areas in north-eastern Poland likely facilitated spillover and maintenance of A. marginale. Climate warming and land-use changes in Eastern Europe may be contributing to northward extension of both tick and pathogen ranges. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion from cattle into European bison represents re-emergence in a new wild host species within an already affected sub-region; phylogenetic evidence suggests recent cross-species transmission of cattle-like A. marginale genotypes rather than a long-standing, bison-adapted lineage.
Review: Review: Event year corrected from 2025 (publication year) to 2021 (sample collection year) based on the Parasites & Vectors article, and the country bracket updated accordingly. The event is appropriately classified as re-emergence via host expansion in Eastern Europe rather than intra-continental emergence, because A. marginale was previously established in neighboring Hungary. Two less relevant citations (a general South African A. marginale/A. centrale review and a paper on A. phagocytophilum in bison) have been removed from the event-level Source URLs to focus on the primary bison report and its bibliographic index. Recommended for retention as an important host-expansion event, but not a mass-mortality outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (smallholder farms)
Event summary: In a study published in 2024, investigators conducted the first molecular survey of Anaplasma marginale in healthy dairy cattle from 40 smallholder farms in Khon Kaen Province, north-eastern Thailand, and detected infection in 49 of 385 animals (overall prevalence ≈12.7%), with positives spread across multiple districts. Phylogenetic analysis of msp4 sequences showed Thai isolates clustering with A. marginale strains from Australia, China, Spain and the USA, indicating widespread international strain sharing. The findings demonstrated that bovine anaplasmosis is already endemic in the emerging dairy sector of north-eastern Thailand, where clinical disease may previously have been under-recognized, and led to recommendations for enhanced tick control, farmer awareness and diagnostic capacity to reduce future clinical outbreaks and productivity losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Smallholder dairy systems in north-eastern Thailand with frequent tick exposure, limited acaricide use and increasing cattle movement across the Mekong subregion create favorable conditions for establishment and spread of A. marginale. Internal mechanisms: No distinct Thai-specific lineage was identified beyond global msp4 similarity; the emergence pattern is driven mainly by geographic range expansion and recognition of under-detected endemic transmission rather than documented genetic change, making this a re-occurrence/intensification event rather than re-emergence.
Review: Review: The Khon Kaen study provides solid molecular evidence of established endemic A. marginale infection in dairy cattle in a previously under-studied area of South-eastern Asia, but it describes a prevalence survey rather than a discrete clinical outbreak with quantified production losses. It is therefore a borderline inclusion if the event list is restricted strictly to the most impactful outbreak episodes by cases or economic loss. Classification as re-occurrence within an already affected continent and sub-region is appropriate, and the country, sub-region and year are consistent with the primary article. Recommend retaining if the project values key detection-based emergence signals; otherwise consider deprioritising this event relative to large clinical outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (New York – Finger Lakes region, especially Keuka Lake)
Host: Wild American black ducks (Anas rubripes), mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) and other migratory waterfowl using Finger Lakes roosts
Event summary: In spring 1994, a major duck viral enteritis epizootic struck migratory waterfowl in the Finger Lakes region of New York, USA, killing roughly 1,200 American black ducks and mallards and constituting one of only two major wild-bird duck plague die-offs recorded in the United States, with diagnosis based on typical lesions and virologic confirmation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of migratory ducks concentrated on a few lakes during spring migration, environmental contamination of shared water by virus shed in feces, and potential contact with infected captive or resident waterfowl favored a large-scale die-off. Internal mechanisms: Virus characteristics matched previously circulating virulent strains; the severity appears driven by host aggregation and environmental persistence rather than documented increases in intrinsic virulence.
Review: retain – Large wild waterfowl epizootic (~1,200 ducks) highlighted in U.S. federal and Cornell wildlife health sources as one of the only major migratory-waterfowl duck plague mortality events; geography and classification as re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion are correct and the event merits inclusion among the highest-impact post‑1990 episodes.

Countries: United States of America (Illinois – private multispecies game bird facility)
Host: Domestic Muscovy ducks (Cairina moschata domesticus) in a resident flock; other domestic ducks and geese present but not clinically affected
Event summary: On a privately owned multispecies game-bird farm in Illinois, USA, duck viral enteritis caused an explosive outbreak in a resident population of domestic Muscovy ducks, killing 625 birds with nearly 100% mortality in affected adults, while other duck breeds and geese on the premises remained largely unaffected; diagnosis was confirmed by virus isolation and characteristic herpetic lesions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High stocking density of Muscovy ducks, co-housing with other domestic waterfowl species, and absence of prior DVE vaccination likely facilitated rapid within-flock transmission once virus was introduced, probably via infected replacement birds or contaminated water. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain characteristics were reported; the outbreak reflects high host susceptibility of Muscovy ducks to circulating virulent field strains rather than emergence of a new genotype.
Review: review – Epidemiology, host description, and U.S. geography are correct and classification as re-occurrence is appropriate, but the outbreak involved a single farm with 625 Muscovy ducks; given the addition of much larger multi-farm and regional epizootics (Bangladesh Haor, Chinese ‘new duck plague’, Egypt 2016–2018, large Indian and Chinese farm outbreaks), this event is unlikely to fall within the 10 highest-impact post‑1990 episodes and is a candidate for exclusion under a strict top‑10 filter.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Egypt (Gharbia Governorate – six commercial duck farms [2002-2004])
Host: Commercial Muscovy and local balady ducks on multiple farms in Gharbia Governorate
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2004, six outbreaks of duck viral enteritis with high mortality were diagnosed in commercial Muscovy and balady duck flocks in Gharbia Governorate, Egypt, with affected birds showing classic gross and histologic lesions of duck plague and confirmation by virus isolation and histopathology.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density commercial duck production in the Nile Delta with limited biosecurity, probable contact with infected wild or backyard waterfowl, and suboptimal vaccination facilitated repeated re-occurrence of DVE on multiple farms. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; lesions and virologic findings were consistent with established virulent Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1 strains circulating in Egypt since the first national report in the 1980s.
Review: retain – Added as a major African epizootic: six high-mortality outbreaks in commercial Muscovy and balady ducks in Gharbia (2002–2004) represent one of the best-documented, larger-scale DVE episodes in Egypt post‑1990. Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa/Egypt, where DVE has been present since 1986; event magnitude (multiple farms with high mortality) justifies inclusion, but exact flock sizes should be extracted from the full Benha Vet. Med. J. article for precise impact ranking.

Countries: Germany (captive multi-species duck and goose collections [2005])
Host: Numerous captive duck and goose species in zoological and ornamental collections kept under enforced indoor housing
Event summary: In 2005, an outbreak of duck viral enteritis occurred in multiple species of captive ducks and geese in Germany after flocks were moved indoors under strict biosecurity because of the regional threat of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1; within weeks, birds developed severe disease and high mortality, and duck plague virus was confirmed as the cause.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enforced in-house keeping of normally free-ranging waterfowl due to H5N1 concerns greatly increased stocking density and contact rates, likely allowing latent carriers to seed explosive transmission in naïve birds, while shared indoor water and fomites amplified virus spread. Internal mechanisms: The causative strain (later characterized as DEV 2085) showed virulent field-virus genomic features but no evidence of being a new species or continent-level introduction; this fits re-occurrence of DVE under altered husbandry rather than emergence of a novel agent.
Review: retain – Added as a key European event: the 2005 Germany outbreak in numerous captive duck and goose species, temporally linked to H5N1-driven indoor confinement, is one of the more severe and well-characterized DVE epizootics in Europe. Correctly coded as re-occurrence in Europe/Western Europe, Germany, with impact likely involving many hundreds of birds; flock numbers should be verified from the Kaleta et al. 2007 full text for precise impact comparison.

Countries: China (major duck-producing provinces, including Shandong and other eastern regions)
Host: Commercial domestic ducks (layer and meat types of various breeds) in intensive farms; occasionally geese and other waterfowl
Event summary: From about 2006 onward, Chinese investigators reported what they termed a ‘new duck plague’ in commercial duck farms, initially in Shandong and later in other major duck-producing regions, where severe outbreaks with high mortality and production losses occurred despite routine vaccination and classical duck plague vaccines or hyperimmune sera failed to protect affected flocks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and regional clustering of China’s duck industry, frequent movements of birds and equipment between farms, widespread but imperfect vaccination, and high duck densities around shared water bodies created strong selection and transmission opportunities for more virulent field strains. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies describe virulent field strains with distinct genetic features (including differences in the UL2 gene and other loci) relative to widely used attenuated vaccine strains, associated with vaccine escape and increased pathogenicity, fitting a re-emergence pattern driven by novel or highly adapted genotypes.
Review: retain – Captures a prolonged period of widespread, vaccine-breaking ‘new duck plague’ outbreaks in commercial ducks across eastern China, with strong evidence for genetically distinct, highly virulent field strains; classification as re-emergence is appropriate. Years (2006–2013) and geography (Eastern Asia/China) are broadly supported by Chinese and review literature, though exact onset year and provincial spread could be refined using additional primary outbreak reports; source list has been oriented toward primary Chinese articles and the Dhama et al. 2017 update rather than secondary abstract aggregators.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Bangladesh (Haor/wetland districts in the north-eastern region)
Host: Semi-scavenging and free-ranging domestic ducks (mixed local and commercial breeds) in village and small commercial flocks
Event summary: Between December 2012 and November 2014, recurrent duck plague outbreaks were documented on 50 farms among 450 investigated in five Haor (wetland) districts of north-eastern Bangladesh, affecting an estimated 175,467 ducks; PCR confirmed duck plague virus in 36 outbreaks, with farm-level morbidity of about 52%, mortality near 30%, and case fatality around 57%, indicating very large aggregate losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of ducks in Haor wetlands, extensive mixing of village and nomadic flocks on communal water bodies, low and irregular vaccination coverage, and weak biosecurity favored sustained transmission and repeated large-scale outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization showed Bangladeshi field isolates clustering with virulent strains from Vietnam and China without clear evidence of a distinct new genotype, supporting classification as re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental and management factors.
Review: retain – One of the best-quantified, highest-impact modern DVE episodes, with >170,000 ducks at risk and tens of thousands estimated dead; geography, host system, and classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/Bangladesh are correct and clearly supported by epidemiologic and molecular studies.

Host: Domestic ducks (primarily local meat and egg-type breeds reared in paddy-field-based systems) on commercial and smallholder farms
Event summary: During 2015–2016, a natural duck plague outbreak occurred in the high-density duck-farming Kuttanad region of Kerala, India, leading to significant mortality in domestic duck flocks and prompting isolation of a virulent strain designated DEV/India/IVRI-2016 from liver tissues of affected birds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional free-grazing of large duck flocks on flooded paddy fields, frequent flock movements, and close contact with wild waterfowl in a region already stressed by repeated avian influenza outbreaks created conditions for DVE re-occurrence and spread among commercial and backyard holdings. Internal mechanisms: Genomic sequencing of DEV/India/IVRI-2016 showed a virulent field strain closely related to Chinese and other Asian lineages rather than a vaccine-derived or novel species, fitting re-occurrence of a highly pathogenic lineage in an intensively farmed area.
Review: retain – Added because the Kuttanad outbreak from which DEV/India/IVRI‑2016 was recovered represents an important epizootic in one of India’s densest duck-farming regions; classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/India is appropriate. The year range and scale are inferred mainly from virological reports rather than a dedicated outbreak description, so flock numbers and losses should be refined if more detailed epidemiological data become available.

Host: Commercial and backyard ducks (especially Muscovy and local breeds) of various ages in multiple provinces
Event summary: From 2016 to 2018, Egypt experienced widespread duck viral enteritis outbreaks across several provinces, with examined flocks showing approximately 75% mortality and a 40% drop in egg production; diagnosis was confirmed through characteristic lesions, virus isolation in embryonated duck eggs, and PCR targeting the DEV DNA polymerase gene.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense duck production in the Nile Delta, inadequate or improperly implemented vaccination programs, poor biosecurity in both commercial and backyard systems, and potential involvement of migratory waterfowl contributed to high DVE incidence and severe flock-level impacts. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced isolates showed typical virulent DEV genomic features without strong evidence of a radically novel genotype, indicating re-occurrence of pathogenic field strains in a vulnerable production system rather than emergence of a taxonomically new variant.
Review: retain – Added as a major recent African epizootic: multi-province outbreaks with ~75% mortality and substantial production losses make this one of the largest documented DVE events in Egypt. Correctly coded as re-occurrence in Africa/Northern Africa, Egypt; provinces are listed explicitly from the primary study. Exact flock counts per outbreak are not given in the abstract and should be consulted in the full paper for precise quantitative ranking.

Host: Commercial domestic ducks (meat and/or layer flocks) on three intensive farms
Event summary: From February to June 2018, natural outbreaks of duck plague were reported on three commercial duck farms in Netrokona, Mymensingh and Nilphamari districts of Bangladesh, causing substantial mortality in flocks that had received duck plague vaccination; duck viral enteritis virus was confirmed by virus isolation and PCR targeting the DNA polymerase gene.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density commercial production, incomplete or suboptimal vaccination schedules, and likely exposure to contaminated surface waters or contact with infected scavenging ducks or wild waterfowl favored virus introduction and amplification on individual farms. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 2018 isolates were almost identical to previously reported Bangladeshi, Vietnamese and Chinese duck plague viruses, indicating re-occurrence of an established virulent lineage rather than the emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Well-supported, multi-farm outbreak with virologic confirmation and phylogenetic data linking Bangladeshi field strains to broader Asian lineages; classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/Bangladesh is appropriate. While smaller in scope than the Haor episode, its clear documentation and demonstration of vaccine-breakthrough infections justify keeping it among the higher-impact modern events.

Countries: India (Tamil Nadu – Kadavakathi village, Tirunelveli district [2019])
Host: Chara-Chemballi breed domestic ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus local indigenous type) in a commercial flock of 4,500 adults
Event summary: An outbreak of duck plague in a commercial flock of 4,500 Chara-Chemballi ducks in Kadavakathi village near Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, resulted in the death of about 2,000 birds (44.4% mortality), with affected ducks showing typical clinical signs and necropsy lesions; PCR amplification of the DEV polymerase gene confirmed duck viral enteritis virus infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recent long-distance movement of a large flock purchased from Kerala, transport stress during hot weather, and exposure to contaminated local water sources likely contributed to virus introduction and explosive within-flock spread. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and molecular testing indicated infection with virulent Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1 similar to other field strains in India; no novel genetic traits were reported, so this is best interpreted as a high-impact re-occurrence in a susceptible indigenous breed rather than emergence of a new variant.
Review: retain – Added because this single-farm outbreak caused 2,000 deaths among 4,500 Chara-Chemballi ducks (44.4% mortality), making it one of the more severe, well-documented duck plague events in India after 1990. Correctly classified as re-occurrence in Asia/Southern Asia, India. Event year is set to 2019, matching the case-report publication year; the paper does not explicitly state the outbreak year, so this timing should be confirmed against the full text if precise temporal ordering is critical.

Host: Commercial hemp ducks (approximately 5,000 birds around 310 days of age) on an intensive farm
Event summary: In December 2021, a severe duck plague outbreak occurred on a farm with about 5,000 hemp ducks in Qingyuan, Guangdong Province, China, causing high mortality among adult birds; pathological investigation and genomic analysis identified field strain DP-GD-305-21 as the causative duck enteritis virus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large, single-age cohort of adult ducks kept under intensive conditions, with potential gaps in vaccination and contact with contaminated water or fomites, enabled rapid farm-wide spread once virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome sequencing showed DP-GD-305-21 to be a virulent Chinese field strain closely related to other CHv/CV-like viruses, with several point mutations across genes such as UL12, UL41, UL47 and LORF11; these changes may influence virulence or antigenicity, but current evidence mainly supports continued circulation of an established virulent lineage rather than emergence of a wholly new subtype.
Review: retain – Added as a recent high-impact Chinese farm outbreak involving roughly 5,000 adult ducks with detailed pathological and genomic characterization; correctly located in Asia/Eastern Asia, China. Classified here as re-occurrence of virulent Chinese field lineages, but given documented gene-level differences from earlier strains, future work could justify re-emergence status if these mutations are shown to alter virulence or vaccine responsiveness.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei)
Event summary: In 1992 shrimp farmers in Guayas Province, Ecuador, near the Taura River, observed a new, acute disease in L. vannamei characterised by red tails, soft shells and high mortality, soon termed Taura syndrome. During 1992–1993 the syndrome spread rapidly among coastal farms, becoming the most important disease of farmed L. vannamei in the Western Hemisphere and causing major production losses. Subsequent investigations demonstrated a viral aetiology, and the causative agent was characterised and named Taura syndrome virus (now Aparavirus tauraense), marking its first known emergence in the shrimp host system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and expansion of L. vannamei aquaculture in coastal Ecuador, high farm and pond connectivity, and frequent movement of postlarvae and juveniles among farms facilitated the amplification and farm‑to‑farm spread of the newly emerged pathogen. Internal mechanisms: TSV, a positive‑sense RNA virus, likely arose as a novel agent in intensive shrimp culture with high mutation rates and efficient horizontal transmission, enabling rapid establishment in naïve farmed shrimp populations.
Review: Retain (minor corrections). Adjusted Event Year from 1991–1993 to 1992–1993 and standardised the country entry to Ecuador [1992], because multiple authoritative reviews place the first recognised Taura syndrome outbreaks in June 1992 near the Taura River even though phylogenetic work suggests a most‑recent common ancestor around 1991. Sources were focused on primary reviews and the WOAH manual rather than Wikipedia. No change in event type: this remains the first/global emergence in the shrimp host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: South America; Central America; Caribbean; Northern America
Countries: Peru [1993]; Colombia [1994]; Honduras [1994]; Guatemala [1994]; El Salvador [1994]; Nicaragua [1994]; Brazil [1994]; Belize [1995/1996]; Mexico [1995]; United States of America [1994-1995]; plus subsequent spread to most other shrimp-farming countries of the Americas by 1997
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, predominantly L. vannamei (with involvement of other cultured penaeid species in affected farms)
Event summary: Beginning in 1993, soon after its emergence in Ecuador, TSV‑associated Taura syndrome spread south to Peru and, from 1994, to Colombia, Brazil and the Pacific and Caribbean coasts of Central America, causing severe mortality in juvenile L. vannamei. By 1994–1995 the virus had reached Hawaii and coastal farms in Florida and Texas in the United States, and by 1995–1996 it had extended to Mexico and Belize, with further spread to virtually all major shrimp‑growing regions of the Americas by 1997. Cumulative industry losses during this American panzootic are estimated in the order of US$1–2 billion, and by the late 1990s TSV was widely endemic throughout the American shrimp‑farming belt.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: regional and international trade and movement of live postlarvae and broodstock L. vannamei of unknown health status, limited farm and hatchery biosecurity, and high pond and farm densities allowed rapid dissemination across national borders; expansion of intensive shrimp farming into new coastal sites greatly increased the susceptible host population. Internal mechanisms: TSV’s efficient oral and horizontal transmission, high viral loads in clinically and subclinically infected shrimp, and environmental stability in pond systems facilitated explosive epizootics as the virus entered immunologically naïve farm populations across multiple countries.
Review: Review (classification and geography corrected). Simplified the Continent field to South America; Northern America and standardised the Countries list to recognised country names, removing state‑level labels (e.g. “USA – Hawaii”) that are not in the Country sheet. Corrected Colombia’s first‑report year from 1993 to 1994 and aligned the overall spread sequence with FAO/OIE timelines. Set inter_continental_emergence = Yes and intra_continental_emergence = No, because this linked panzootic includes first establishment in a new continent (Northern America); under the project rules, intra‑continental and inter‑continental categories should not co‑occur for the same linked episode. Event remains one of the major global TSV emergence events and should be retained with these corrections.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (L. vannamei) in imported and locally cultured stocks
Event summary: Around 1999 TSV was first detected in Taiwan Province of China in L. vannamei broodstock imported from Central/South America, with multiple outbreaks reported to the OIE during 1999–2001 and hundreds of thousands of affected shrimp and substantial mortalities. In 1999–2000 the virus was also confirmed in Mainland China as L. vannamei and its pathogens were introduced with imported broodstock and postlarvae, leading to disease outbreaks in coastal farms and rapid recognition of TSV as a new, serious threat to East Asian shrimp aquaculture. By the early 2000s TSV had become established in affected Taiwanese and Chinese farming regions, with recurrent local epizootics and incorporation into regional surveillance and control programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: inter‑continental transfer of L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae from the Americas into Taiwanese and Chinese hatcheries and grow‑out farms without adequate TSV screening or quarantine was the primary driver of spread; rapid scaling‑up of L. vannamei culture in Taiwan and coastal China created dense, susceptible farm populations. Internal mechanisms: high viral loads in subclinically infected broodstock, vertical and early‑life transmission to progeny, and efficient horizontal spread in ponds allowed TSV to establish quickly in newly stocked farms once introduced.
Review: Retain (minor standardisation). Updated country names to match the Country sheet (Taiwan Province of China; China) and kept the 1999–2001 timeframe, which is well supported by OIE case reports and FAO documentation. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence from the Americas to Asia is appropriate, and there is strong evidence for major production losses, so this remains one of the top impact events.

Countries: Indonesia [2002]; Thailand [2003]; China (additional coastal provinces) [2002-2004]; Republic of Korea [2004]; Myanmar [2004]; Viet Nam [2004]
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, especially L. vannamei (with involvement of other cultured species where co‑cultured)
Event summary: Following its establishment in Taiwan and coastal China, TSV was detected in Indonesia in 2002 soon after the official introduction and rapid expansion of L. vannamei culture, and in Thailand around 2003 as farmers shifted from P. monodon to L. vannamei. By about 2004, TSV had been reported from additional coastal provinces in China and from farms in the Republic of Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam, where it contributed to high disease losses as the virus entered naïve shrimp‑farming areas. Over subsequent years, TSV became endemic in many East and South‑East Asian shrimp‑farming zones, co‑circulating with other major viral pathogens such as white spot syndrome virus (WSSV).
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intra‑Asian movement and trade of live L. vannamei postlarvae and broodstock, often sourced from previously infected regions within Asia, combined with rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp farming, drove TSV spread to new Asian subregions; limited biosecurity, water exchange among farms, and co‑culture or sequential culture of different penaeid species facilitated virus maintenance and spread. Internal mechanisms: TSV’s ability to infect multiple penaeid hosts and its efficient horizontal transmission allowed rapid establishment and persistence in new Asian production systems once introduced.
Review: Review (approximate timing). This event appropriately captures intra‑continental expansion of TSV within Asia from its initial foci in Taiwan/China to Indonesia, Thailand, Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam and is clearly among the major impact events. Countries and sub‑regions have been standardised to the UNSD list. However, the specific year assignments for Myanmar and Viet Nam are approximate (sources document that TSV was endemic in these countries by 2004 rather than giving exact first‑detection years), so the event is flagged for expert review of country‑specific start years while being retained as a major Asian spread episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed L. vannamei and L. stylirostris (including TSV- and IHHNV-selected resistant lines)
Event summary: In western Mexico, where TSV had already become endemic, a new strain of TSV emerged around 1998–1999 and caused massive epizootics in Penaeus stylirostris that had been selectively bred for resistance to earlier TSV variants. These outbreaks led to severe crop failures and effectively ended commercial interest in farming P. stylirostris in much of western Mexico, while also increasing disease pressure on co‑cultured L. vannamei. Through the early 2000s this more virulent strain contributed to renewed high mortalities and economic losses until producers shifted species and management strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑density shrimp culture in western Mexico with heavy reliance on a limited number of selectively bred TSV‑resistant P. stylirostris lines, combined with persistent endemic TSV circulation and concurrent introduction of WSSV in 1999, created strong selection pressures favouring TSV variants capable of overcoming host resistance. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel TSV strain/genotype (Type B) with altered antigenicity and increased virulence/pathogenicity in P. stylirostris is well documented, representing viral adaptation that negated prior genetic resistance and constitutes a clear re‑emergence driven by evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review (geographic scope narrowed). This event is strongly supported as a major re‑emergence driven by a new, more virulent TSV strain in western Mexico that overcame resistance in P. stylirostris, but the original JSON over‑generalised its spread to unspecified “multiple Latin American countries” and “USA–Mexico border regions” without clear primary evidence. The Countries field has been restricted to Mexico [1998–1999], and the timeframe adjusted to match WOAH and review‑article descriptions (1998–1999 with impacts continuing into the early 2000s). Classification as re_emergence = Yes remains appropriate. Further regional genetic/epidemiologic data could refine whether this strain caused major, distinct emergence episodes outside Mexico.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed giant tiger prawn (Penaeus monodon), Pacific white shrimp (L. vannamei) and other penaeids in mixed or sequential culture (e.g. Metapenaeus ensis in Taiwan)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, molecular surveys in Taiwan identified distinct TSV isolates in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis as well as in L. vannamei, showing that the virus had expanded beyond its original principal host into additional penaeid species with different susceptibility profiles. In Thailand, the first confirmed TSV outbreak in farmed L. vannamei was detected by RT‑PCR in early 2003, and subsequent work documented TSV infections in both L. vannamei and P. monodon, often as co‑infections with WSSV in mixed or sequential culture systems. Between about 2000 and 2006, increasing reports of TSV in P. monodon and other regional species contributed to complex disease presentations and additional losses in farms that had previously considered TSV primarily a risk for L. vannamei.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: diversification of shrimp farming in East and South‑East Asia, with overlapping culture of P. monodon, L. vannamei and other penaeids in shared water bodies and farm systems, created ecological opportunities for cross‑species transmission; limited species‑specific biosecurity measures meant viruses introduced with L. vannamei could spill over to resident species. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of TSV from its principal host L. vannamei into P. monodon and other penaeids, accompanied by genetic variation in capsid genes that affected host range and replication efficiency, represents a re‑emergence mediated by viral adaptation to new hosts rather than a purely geographic spread event.
Review: Review (host-range expansion; impact somewhat uncertain). Evidence from Taiwan (field and experimental infections in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis) and Thailand (molecular detection of TSV in P. monodon and L. vannamei, often with WSSV co‑infection) supports genuine host expansion and additional disease burden, justifying classification as re_emergence driven by host expansion and viral genetic variation. However, quantitative estimates of incremental production loss attributable specifically to TSV in non‑vannamei hosts are limited, and geographic coverage beyond Taiwan and Thailand is less clear. The event is retained as one of the main re‑emergence episodes but flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the top 10 TSV events and for potential refinement of the country list if stronger data on impacts in other South‑East Asian countries become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in grow-out ponds in the Lake Maracaibo and Paraguaná regions
Event summary: Until the early 2000s, Venezuela remained free of documented TSV despite extensive spread elsewhere in the Americas. In late 2004, farms in western Venezuela (notably in Lake Maracaibo and the Paraguaná Peninsula) experienced a severe epizootic in L. vannamei with classic Taura syndrome signs, high mortalities and pond survivals in some areas reportedly as low as 5–30%. Histopathology and RT‑PCR confirmed TSV infection, and the epizootic spread rapidly across the western shrimp‑farming region through 2004–2005, prompting OIE notifications and calls for urgent biosecurity and stock‑replacement measures. Subsequent genetic work on a Venezuelan isolate (TSV‑VE05) from this outbreak showed it to be a distinct variant within the global TSV phylogeny.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infected postlarvae and broodstock from neighbouring TSV‑endemic countries, inadequate on‑farm biosecurity, reuse of pond water, and mechanical transmission by birds and aquatic insects were all implicated in the rapid spread of TSV across western Venezuelan farms. Environmental stressors, particularly episodes of heavy rainfall and associated salinity drops in Lake Maracaibo, were associated with peaks in mortality. Internal mechanisms: the Venezuelan outbreak isolate TSV‑VE05 differed genetically from earlier American isolates (about 7% divergence from the HI94 reference strain in the genome sequence) and has been recognised as a new TSV variant; its virulence in experimental infections was comparable to highly pathogenic reference strains, supporting classification of this episode as a strain‑driven re‑emergence within the South American subregion.
Review: Retain (newly added major event). This large 2004–2005 epizootic in western Venezuela was missing from the original JSON despite clear evidence of severe regional impact (very low pond survivals and rapid spread) and its association with a genetically distinct Venezuelan TSV variant. It has been added as a re_emergence event (not intra‑ or inter‑continental, because TSV was already established elsewhere in South America) driven by novel strain emergence and poor biosecurity. Dates and impact are based on detailed clinical, histopathological and RT‑PCR descriptions from Venezuelan field studies plus genetic characterisation of TSV‑VE05. Further expert review could refine the exact start–end years, but the event clearly belongs among the top TSV emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cultured Indian white shrimp (Penaeus indicus) in intensive farms on the Red Sea coast
Event summary: During 2010–2011, intensive P. indicus farms on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia experienced severe disease outbreaks in which both WSSV and TSV were detected, with TSV first confirmed by RT‑PCR in mid‑2010. At affected farms, shrimp began dying about 30 days after stocking and survivals at harvest dropped to roughly 30–50%, with Taura syndrome disease persisting through 2010 and into 2011 and losses increasing further when WSSV appeared. Molecular analyses showed that Saudi TSV isolates formed a distinct lineage separate from previously described Americas, Belize, South‑East Asia and Venezuelan groups.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive P. indicus culture in Saudi Arabia, coupled with importation of P. vannamei and other shrimp stocks from TSV‑endemic regions, and limited initial biosecurity measures, created conditions for introduction and establishment of TSV in a previously unaffected Western Asian shrimp‑farming zone. High farm density and water exchange among ponds facilitated on‑farm and farm‑to‑farm spread, while co‑infection with WSSV exacerbated mortality and economic losses. Internal mechanisms: Saudi TSV isolates represent a distinct genotype within the global TSV phylogeny, suggesting evolutionary diversification as TSV spread into new environments and host species; this, together with confirmed disease in P. indicus, indicates re‑emergence with host expansion and genotype divergence within a new Asian subregion.
Review: Retain (new intra-continental re-emergence event). This 2010–2011 episode represents the first well‑documented establishment of TSV in Western Asia and in intensive P. indicus culture, with clearly described high mortalities and production losses, and a distinct Saudi TSV genotype. It has therefore been added as an intra_continental_emergence (new UNSD sub‑region within Asia) and re_emergence (new genotype and host expansion). This corrects the original assertion that there were no major 2005–2025 emergence events. The event should be retained as a key later‑phase emergence episode; additional regional surveillance data could clarify whether TSV has since spread widely in the Middle East or remained largely confined to Saudi farms.

Host: Wild and commercially harvested narrow‑clawed crayfish Pontastacus (Astacus) leptodactylus in major Turkish lakes and reservoirs
Event summary: In the mid‑1980s, intensive crayfish fisheries in western Anatolia began experiencing unexplained mass mortalities, first reported from Lake Çivril and other western Turkish lakes around 1985. Subsequent diagnostic work and field studies confirmed Aphanomyces astaci as the etiological agent of the disease, and the pathogen spread rapidly through the main lake and reservoir fisheries, driving national landings of Pontastacus leptodactylus down from roughly 5,000–7,000 tonnes in 1984 to a few hundred tonnes by 1991.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848603004290?utm_source=openai)) By the early 1990s most commercial crayfish stocks in Türkiye had collapsed, and the acute nationwide epizootic transitioned into a state of chronically depleted, fragmented populations with only localized harvesting.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: strong export demand from European markets led to heavy exploitation and large‑scale live crayfish trade, while translocations of crayfish among Turkish lakes and minimal biosecurity facilitated both the initial introduction of A. astaci from Europe and its rapid spread through inland waters.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848603004290?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the high susceptibility of P. leptodactylus to A. astaci, combined with efficient waterborne zoospore transmission in dense lake fisheries, produced explosive epidemics and near‑total mortality, representing a major geographic range expansion of the pathogen from Europe into Western Asia.
Review: Review – Retain this event as one of the most impactful emergence episodes (collapse of a major crayfish fishery and first well‑documented inter‑continental spread of A. astaci into Asia), but the original row mis‑used the 'first_detection' flag (now set to No, because global first detection occurred in 19th‑century Europe) and lacked clarity on the start year. The event period has been adjusted from 1984–1991 to 1985–1991 based on Turkish harvest and outbreak data, while acknowledging that some sources reference 1984 as the last pre‑plague baseline year; a human reviewer should confirm whether including this pre‑1990‑onset episode is acceptable under the "post‑1990" rule.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in three central Italian river systems
Event summary: In the summer of 2009, dense populations of the native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in three watercourses of central Italy suffered sudden mass mortalities over a few weeks. Laboratory examination of moribund and dead crayfish, including culture and PCR, identified Aphanomyces astaci as the cause of disease, representing the first crayfish plague outbreak in Italian A. pallipes populations to be confirmed by isolation of the pathogen in culture.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20481093/?utm_source=openai)) Following the die‑offs, affected reaches were left virtually devoid of native crayfish, and post‑outbreak management focused on local movement restrictions, surveillance and habitat protection rather than attempted eradication of the pathogen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑term spread of invasive North American crayfish (especially Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus) in Italian waters and human‑mediated transfers of live crayfish or contaminated fishing gear between catchments likely introduced A. astaci into these central Italian streams.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233799926_Crayfish_in_Italy_Distribution_threats_and_management?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the extreme susceptibility of A. pallipes to A. astaci and the rapid zoospore‑mediated transmission of the pathogen in small headwater streams led to near‑complete local extirpation once the fungus became established, exemplifying classic crayfish plague re‑occurrence in an already endemic European region.
Review: Review – Added as a new event because a large 2009 outbreak in wild Austropotamobius pallipes is widely documented and represents one of the most important post‑1990 European re‑occurrence episodes. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) because A. astaci has been established in Italy since the 19th century and no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype or host shift was identified in this outbreak; a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether concurrent 2009 epizootics in farmed Cherax destructor should be represented in a separate row or referenced only in the narrative.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii (feral pond and reservoir populations) and native burrowing crayfish Parastacus defossus and Parastacus pilimanus (low‑level infections)
Event summary: Around 2012–2013, molecular surveys of feral Procambarus clarkii populations in reservoirs and irrigation ponds in south‑eastern and southern Brazil provided the first confirmed record of Aphanomyces astaci in South America. Quantitative and conventional PCR assays detected the pathogen in multiple invasive P. clarkii populations and revealed low‑level ('agent level A2') infections in two native burrowing crayfish species, Parastacus defossus and P. pilimanus, occurring in sympatry.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306248212_First_detection_of_the_crayfish_plague_pathogen_Aphanomyces_astaci_in_South_America_a_high_potential_risk_to_native_crayfish?utm_source=openai)) Although large‑scale crayfish die‑offs had not yet been documented at the study sites, the findings showed that crayfish plague had been introduced to a continent with high endemic crayfish diversity, raising alarm about potential future epizootics and losses of native Parastacus species.
