Mechanism or driver: Drivers: decades of introductions and spread of P. clarkii for aquaculture, live food and the aquarium trade in Brazil created self‑sustaining invasive populations, and unregulated movements of live crayfish between waterbodies facilitated the silent spread of A. astaci.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306248212_First_detection_of_the_crayfish_plague_pathogen_Aphanomyces_astaci_in_South_America_a_high_potential_risk_to_native_crayfish?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: chronic, often subclinical carriage of A. astaci by P. clarkii and environmental overlap with susceptible native Parastacus species enabled pathogen spillover and establishment in a new continent (inter‑continental emergence), despite the absence of immediately obvious mass mortality events at the time of detection.
Review: Review – New row added because the Brazilian detection of A. astaci in feral Procambarus clarkii and sympatric native Parastacus species is the first confirmed record of crayfish plague in South America and therefore a key inter‑continental emergence event, even though documented mortality was limited at the time of study. Classified as inter‑continental emergence (South America) with 'first_detection' kept as No because this is not the first global description of the pathogen; a human reviewer should confirm the chosen event window (2012–2013), which follows the timing reported in global syntheses but is approximate in the primary Hydrobiologia paper.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Farmed redclaw crayfish Cherax quadricarinatus (Australian species introduced into freshwater aquaculture)
Event summary: Between November/December 2013 and January 2014, five freshwater crayfish farms in northern and southern Taiwan experienced outbreaks of an initially unknown disease in redclaw crayfish (Cherax quadricarinatus), with moderate to very high cumulative mortality and up to 100% losses at most affected farms. Histopathology and PCR with species‑specific ITS primers identified Aphanomyces astaci as the causative agent, confirming the first crayfish plague outbreaks in Asia involving an Australian Cherax species and the first report of C. quadricarinatus naturally infected by A. astaci.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201116300313?utm_source=openai)) Control measures, including fallowing and disinfection of ponds and adjustment of stocking practices, ended the acute mortality episodes, but the outbreaks raised serious concern about further spread of the pathogen in Asian aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in live redclaw crayfish and/or co‑stocked North American crayfish, together with movements of contaminated water and equipment among farms, likely introduced A. astaci into Taiwanese aquaculture, where high stocking density and water reuse favoured rapid farm‑level spread.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201116300313?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: host expansion into a highly susceptible non‑native Cherax species in a warm‑water Asian setting, combined with efficient zoospore production and transmission within dense pond populations, produced fulminant disease with very high mortality, marking the first documented intra‑continental emergence of crayfish plague from Western Asia into Eastern Asia.
Review: Review – Original event correctly highlighted this as a major outbreak but mis‑classified it as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence. Under the provided definitions, the Taiwan episode is best treated purely as intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed crayfish plague outbreaks in Eastern Asia), with 're_emergence' set to No because the sub‑region had not previously been known to harbour the pathogen. Event dates, host description and sources remain appropriate, but a human reviewer should confirm that the country label ('Taiwan (Province of China)') aligns with the project’s Country sheet conventions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Endemic Japanese crayfish Cambaroides japonicus in streams near Sapporo (Hokkaido), with invasive Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus acting as reservoir hosts
Event summary: In October 2014, mass mortality of the endemic Japanese crayfish Cambaroides japonicus was first reported from a stream in Sapporo, Hokkaido, prompting concern about a novel disease threatening this already declining species. Molecular analyses (ITS and mitochondrial rnnS/rnnL regions) and histology confirmed Aphanomyces astaci infection in C. japonicus and in sympatric invasive Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus, with evidence for both a known d1 haplotype and a novel d3 haplotype associated with P. clarkii.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884544/?utm_source=openai)) During 2014–2015 multiple C. japonicus populations around Sapporo suffered severe die‑offs, dramatically reducing local abundance and leading Japanese authorities and researchers to warn that crayfish plague now posed a serious extinction risk to Japan’s only native crayfish species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing introductions of North American crayfish (P. clarkii, P. leniusculus) in Japan created persistent reservoirs of A. astaci, and human‑mediated translocations of invasive crayfish, combined with habitat overlap with remnant C. japonicus populations, facilitated cross‑species transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884544/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel mitochondrial haplotype (d3) in P. clarkii and spillover of A. astaci into highly susceptible native C. japonicus represent pathogen genetic diversification and host expansion within an already infected sub‑region, justifying classification as re‑emergence rather than first introduction to Eastern Asia; the outbreaks caused the first confirmed crayfish plague epizootics in a non‑European native crayfish.
Review: Review – Event retained as a major episode but re‑classified: because A. astaci was already present in East Asia (in invasive crayfish) before the 2014–2015 die‑offs, this outbreak in Cambaroides japonicus is best coded as re‑emergence only, not as a new intra‑continental emergence. The narrative correctly emphasises the appearance of a novel haplotype and host shift, which fit the definition of re‑emergence; a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether earlier (2012–2013) Japanese detections in invasive crayfish should be represented as a separate, smaller emergence event or left as background to this high‑impact native‑host outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in multiple Irish river catchments (Erne and subsequent rivers)
Event summary: In August 2015, more than 600 dead white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes were reported from the Bruskey River in the Erne catchment in County Cavan, Republic of Ireland; laboratory testing confirmed Aphanomyces astaci as the cause, marking the first confirmed crayfish plague outbreak in Ireland since an unconfirmed event in 1987.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303035030_Outbreak_of_crayfish_plague_in_Ireland?utm_source=openai)) Over the following years, additional outbreaks and environmental‑DNA detections of A. astaci occurred in multiple river systems (including the Suir, Deel, Barrow, Nore, Shannon, Moy, Sligo and others), leading to severe declines or local extirpations of A. pallipes populations in affected catchments.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10819094/?utm_source=openai)) By about 2019, Ireland had established a National Crayfish Plague Surveillance Programme and strengthened biosecurity messaging, but once A. astaci became established it remained entrenched, threatening Ireland’s status as a stronghold for the species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental introduction of non‑native crayfish carrying A. astaci (likely through illegal stocking or releases) and the spread of spores on contaminated angling, boating and other water‑contact equipment between catchments are considered the most plausible drivers of these outbreaks.([fisheriesireland.ie](https://www.fisheriesireland.ie/news/media-releases/investigation-underway-into-cause-of-crayfish-plague-on-river-bruskey-near?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the extreme susceptibility of A. pallipes to A. astaci and rapid dispersal of zoospores in connected river networks produced rapid, near‑complete mortality once outbreaks began, characteristic of classic crayfish plague re‑occurrence in a region where the pathogen had probably been absent for decades.
Review: Review – New row added because the 2015–2019 Irish outbreaks eliminated or severely reduced many of the last large, relatively intact white‑clawed crayfish populations in Europe, clearly qualifying as one of the most impactful post‑1990 crayfish plague events. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental) because Ireland experienced at least one earlier outbreak in 1987 and there is no strong evidence that a fundamentally new strain or host shift drove the 2015+ epizootics; a human reviewer may refine the end year or split later outbreaks into a separate episode if more detailed genotyping data suggest multiple independent introductions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii (feral pond population) and coexisting freshwater crabs and shrimps in West Java
Event summary: Around 2018, field surveys in West Java documented an established outdoor population of the invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii and its widespread availability in Indonesian ornamental pet shops. Molecular diagnostics using species‑specific mitochondrial markers confirmed Aphanomyces astaci infection in the feral P. clarkii population and in P. clarkii held in at least one pet shop, and also detected A. astaci DNA in coexisting freshwater crab and shrimp species from the same locality, demonstrating that crayfish plague had entered Indonesian inland waters.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai)) No major mass mortality events were reported at the study sites during the survey period, but the combination of invasive host establishment and pathogen detection indicated successful introduction and early establishment of A. astaci in maritime South‑east Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation and domestic trade of live P. clarkii for food and as ornamental animals, together with releases into ponds and natural water bodies, facilitated both host and pathogen introduction in Indonesia, where regulations prohibited import of hazardous fish species but allowed aquaculture and internal transport of P. clarkii.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: chronic carrier status of P. clarkii and the ability of A. astaci to infect non‑crayfish decapods allowed the pathogen to persist and circulate in local decapod communities, representing an intra‑continental range expansion within Asia into a previously uninfected sub‑region with high endemic crustacean diversity and substantial aquaculture.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – New row added because the Indonesian detections represent the first confirmed establishment of A. astaci in South‑eastern Asia and thus a key intra‑continental emergence event, even though large die‑offs have not yet been documented. The event is coded as intra‑continental emergence (Asia) with no re‑occurrence/re‑emergence flags, reflecting that this is the first known presence in this sub‑region; a human reviewer should verify the precise onset year based on sampling dates in Putra et al. (2018) and any subsequent OIE reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Host: Mixed wild and cultured freshwater and low‑salinity/brackish fishes, notably Indian major carps (Labeo rohita, Catla catla, Cirrhinus mrigala), snakeheads (Channa spp.), walking catfish (Clarias batrachus) and other cyprinids and catfishes in ponds, rice fields, reservoirs and brackish lagoons (e.g. Chilika Lake; coastal backwaters of Kerala).
Event summary: Following first explosive outbreaks of epizootic ulcerative syndrome in Bangladesh and northeast India in 1988–1989, large seasonal EUS epizootics continued through the early 1990s across much of India and Bangladesh, with major events in low‑salinity lagoons such as Chilika (Odisha) in 1990 and in Kerala reservoirs and backwaters in 1991.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/veterinary-science-and-veterinary-medicine/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome?utm_source=openai)) During 1990–1994, recurrent cool‑season outbreaks caused heavy mortalities among carps, snakeheads and catfishes in inland aquaculture and wild fisheries, and similar lagoon epizootics were documented in eastern Sri Lanka in 1993–1994, severely affecting local fishing communities.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/3/y3610e/y3610e13.htm?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑1990s, incidence declined in some systems as husbandry improved, but EUS remained endemic in many South Asian floodplain and lagoon habitats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Monsoonal flooding, hydrological connectivity between ponds, rice fields and rivers, and cool‑season temperatures around 18–22 °C created ideal conditions for A. invadans sporulation and fish exposure; low alkalinity and hardness, organic pollution and residual organochlorine pesticides were repeatedly associated with high EUS incidence, while intensification and high stocking densities of carps and snakeheads amplified transmission.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No new genotype was identified in this period; disease expression reflects the inherent high virulence and broad host range of a single clonal A. invadans lineage interacting with environmental stressors, rather than documented evolution of resistance or increased intrinsic pathogenicity.
Review: Retain – This row correctly captures a major early‑1990s wave of EUS in South Asia as a re-occurrence following first late‑1980s outbreaks in Bangladesh and India; countries and sub-region (Southern Asia) align with UNSD definitions and key FAO/OIE reviews. Minor edits made: Sri Lanka timing clarified to 1993–1994, and Markdown-style inline links removed; classification as re-occurrence (without first_detection or intra/inter‑continental emergence) is consistent with the global first detection in Japan (1971) and with EUS already established in Southern Asia by 1988–1989.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Countries: Thailand [1990], Cambodia [1990], Lao People’s Democratic Republic [1990], Myanmar [1990], Viet Nam [1990], Indonesia [1990], Philippines [1990]
Host: Primarily intensively cultured snakeheads (Channa striata and related species), walking catfish (Clarias batrachus), gouramies and cyprinids in rice‑field ponds and canals, together with numerous wild freshwater and estuarine species in the lower Mekong and Central Thai floodplains.
Event summary: In South‑East Asia, epizootic ulcerative syndrome had first emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, with major epizootics in intensively cultured snakeheads and wild fishes; however, severe seasonal outbreaks continued into the early 1990s across Thailand and neighbouring Mekong‑basin countries.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/veterinary-science-and-veterinary-medicine/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome?utm_source=openai)) Between about 1990 and 1993, repeated cool‑season waves of EUS caused heavy mortalities in snakehead rice‑field culture and wild fish in Thailand, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Viet Nam and the Philippines, contributing to cumulative Thai losses estimated at over US$100 million for 1983–1993 and substantial livelihood impacts in small‑scale inland fisheries.([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/859739097/Epizootic-Ulcerative-Syndrome-EUS-Technical-Handbo?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑1990s, disease incidence declined in many intensively affected systems as awareness, diagnosis and management improved, though EUS remained an entrenched seasonal problem throughout much of South‑East Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of small‑scale aquaculture and rice‑field fish culture, extensive networks of canals and floodplains, and pronounced cool‑season temperature drops combined to favour EUS transmission; dense stocking of snakeheads and walking catfish, coupled with poor water quality and pesticide use in rice agriculture, increased stress and susceptibility.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/4/a0192e/A0192E07.htm)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks are attributed to the same clonal A. invadans lineage already established in the region; the high impact reflects ecological opportunity (susceptible hosts in modified floodplain systems) rather than emergence of a distinct strain or documented shifts in intrinsic virulence.
Review: Retain – Added as a missing major event: early‑1990s EUS epizootics in South‑East Asia caused very large fish mortalities and economic losses (particularly in Thai snakehead culture) and are repeatedly highlighted in regional reviews as among the most significant EUS episodes, with cumulative Thai losses alone >US$100 million over 1983–1993.([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/859739097/Epizootic-Ulcerative-Syndrome-EUS-Technical-Handbo?utm_source=openai)) Countries and sub-region now explicitly follow UNSD classifications; years in brackets are aligned with the 1990–1993 window of this linked episode, recognising that initial national emergence in several of these countries pre-dated 1990. Classified as re-occurrence (not first_detection or intra-/inter‑continental emergence) because EUS was already endemic in South‑East Asia by the late 1980s.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Host: Farmed snakeheads (Channa punctata and other Channa spp.), Indian major carps (Labeo rohita, Cirrhinus mrigala, Cirrhinus reba) and small cyprinids (Puntius spp.) in earthen ponds and connected Indus River floodplain systems in Punjab and Sindh provinces.
Event summary: In April 1996, Pakistan reported severe ulcerative disease outbreaks in farmed snakeheads in Punjab that were confirmed histologically as epizootic ulcerative syndrome caused by Aphanomyces invadans, representing the first recognised occurrence of EUS in the country but within an already affected South Asian region.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfp1966/33/4/33_4_321/_article?utm_source=openai)) During 1996–1998, EUS spread rapidly through pond systems and into the Indus River floodplain, with subsequent confirmation in Indian major carps and other cyprinids in Sindh and estimates that around 20% of farms were affected in some divisions following major floods.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfp1966/33/4/33_4_321/_article?utm_source=openai)) By the late 1990s, the disease was considered endemic in parts of the Indus basin, with ongoing but more localised outbreaks and continuing concerns about long‑term impacts on inland fisheries and rural livelihoods.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy monsoon flooding in 1996 facilitated movement of infected fish and water between ponds and river channels; extensive use of surface water, poor pond biosecurity and expanding semi‑intensive carp and snakehead aquaculture increased host density and connectivity, enabling rapid spread.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates Pakistan’s outbreaks were caused by the same Asian clonal genotype of A. invadans described elsewhere, without evidence of a novel strain; disease emergence here chiefly reflects geographic and host‑population expansion within Southern Asia, mediated by environmental and management factors, rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review – This event is rightly included as a high-impact national outbreak that extended EUS across much of Pakistan’s Indus basin, but the emergence type has been corrected. Because EUS was already established in Southern Asia (Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka) before 1990, Pakistan’s 1996 outbreak is not an intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD sub-region and should not be tagged as first_detection; it is best classified as a regional re-occurrence driven by flooding and aquaculture expansion.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Countries: United States of America [Atlantic coast estuaries from Delaware to South Carolina; inland ponds in Georgia and Louisiana]
Host: Primarily Atlantic menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus) with ulcerative mycosis in Atlantic coastal estuaries, plus bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) and channel catfish (Ictalurus punctatus) in inland warmwater ponds.
Event summary: Since at least the early 1980s, estuarine Atlantic menhaden along the U.S. East Coast experienced seasonal epidemics of deep skin ulcers termed ulcerative mycosis, but the aetiology remained uncertain.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/aphanomyces-invadans-atlantic-menhaden-along-east-coast-united-states?utm_source=openai)) In the 1990s, application of diagnostic tools developed for Asian EUS allowed successful isolation and molecular identification of Aphanomyces invadans from menhaden ulcers collected between Delaware and South Carolina, and from ulcerated bluegill in Georgia and channel catfish in Louisiana, demonstrating that the same pathogen causing EUS in Asia and Australia was present and transmitting in North American wild and farmed fish.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/aphanomyces-invadans-atlantic-menhaden-along-east-coast-united-states?utm_source=openai)) Publication of these findings in 2002 established EUS‑type disease due to A. invadans as an endemic problem in parts of U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coastal and inland waters and marked the first confirmed inter‑continental emergence of this pathogen into North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Atlantic menhaden in estuarine nursery areas, degraded water quality and other stressors (including temperature fluctuations and possibly algal toxins or co-infections) likely predisposed fish to skin damage and invasion by A. invadans; farmed bluegill and channel catfish were exposed through water transfers and movement of live fish among ponds.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/aphanomyces-invadans-atlantic-menhaden-along-east-coast-united-states?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: North American isolates show morphology, DNA sequence characteristics and temperature–salinity growth profiles identical to the globally distributed clonal A. invadans lineage; no distinct North American strain has been demonstrated, so the key internal feature is the pathogen’s broad host and habitat range rather than evolution of new genotypes.
Review: Review – This event appropriately represents the first confirmed establishment of A. invadans in North America and a large, long-running series of ulcerative mycosis epizootics in Atlantic menhaden and other fishes. It is correctly tagged as an inter-continental emergence, but the ‘first_detection’ flag has been set to false because global first detection in the host system occurred in Japan in 1971, not in the USA; other emergence-type flags remain false, in line with the episode’s role as a continental incursion rather than a re-occurrence or re-emergence.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Sub-regions: Southern Africa; Eastern Africa; Middle Africa
Countries: Namibia [2006], Botswana [2006], Zambia (Zambezi floodplain) [2007], Angola [by 2008], Malawi [by 2008], Mozambique [by 2008], Zimbabwe [2008-2010], South Africa (Western Cape and Okavango-linked systems) [2010-2011]
Host: Diverse wild freshwater fishes from floodplain rivers and wetlands of the Chobe–Zambezi–Okavango and connected systems, including multiple cichlids, tigerfish (Hydrocynus vittatus), various barbs (Barbus spp.) and catfishes (Clarias gariepinus, C. ngamensis) exploited by subsistence fisheries.
Event summary: In late 2006, unusually high numbers of ulcerated wild fish were first reported from the Chobe and upper Zambezi Rivers in Namibia and Botswana; subsequent investigations and histopathology confirmed these lesions as epizootic ulcerative syndrome caused by Aphanomyces invadans, representing the first recognised occurrence of EUS in Africa.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fishery/docs/DOCUMENT/aquaculture/aq2008_09/root/i0778e.pdf)) From 2007 to about 2010, active surveillance and FAO/WOAH missions documented spread throughout the upper Zambezi floodplain and associated river systems into Zambia, Angola, Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe, with heavy mortalities among key subsistence fish species and serious concerns for food security and aquatic biodiversity; by 2010–2011, infection was also confirmed in Western Cape Province of South Africa and in Okavango‑linked waters.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fishery/docs/DOCUMENT/aquaculture/aq2008_09/root/i0778e.pdf)) By around 2011, mortality in some Zambian reaches had declined towards enzootic levels, but EUS remained established across multiple southern African basins, with ongoing sporadic outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Hydrological connectivity of the Chobe–Zambezi–Okavango river–floodplain complex, extreme flooding in 2006–2008, and intense cross‑border movement of fish, fishing gear and possibly live bait fishes facilitated rapid transboundary spread; limited aquatic animal health infrastructure, absence of prior exposure in African fish populations and high reliance on wild fisheries increased both susceptibility and impact.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fishery/docs/DOCUMENT/aquaculture/aq2008_09/root/i0778e.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic and phenotypic analyses indicate that African isolates belong to the same clonal A. invadans genotype found in Asia and Australia, so this event reflects a major inter‑continental range expansion into a naïve continent rather than evolution of a new strain; its high impact is due to broad host susceptibility and favourable environmental conditions across African floodplain systems.
Review: Review – This is correctly one of the largest global EUS episodes, but the original classification conflicted with the scheme (simultaneously flagged as first_detection, inter- and intra-continental emergence, and re-occurrence) and inappropriately bundled the later Congo-basin outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Booleans are now set so that this event is purely an inter-continental emergence into Africa (first confirmed African occurrence in 2007 in Botswana, Namibia and Zambia); re-occurrence and intra-continental emergence are set to false, in keeping with the guideline that these categories are generally mutually exclusive and that re-occurrence should not co-occur with inter-continental emergence. The DRC 2015 outbreak has been removed from the country list and is treated as a separate Upper Congo event below.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Countries: Australia [2008-2010, Murray–Darling River System – Barwon-Darling reach between Bourke and Brewarrina, New South Wales]
Host: Wild native freshwater fishes including bony herring (Nematalosa erebi), golden perch (Macquaria ambigua), Murray cod (Maccullochella peelii) and spangled perch (Leiopotherapon unicolor); common carp (Cyprinus carpio) sampled during the same epizootic were not infected by A. invadans.
Event summary: In May 2008, Aphanomyces invadans was first isolated from ulcerated bony herring immediately upstream of Bourke Weir on the Barwon‑Darling River, marking the first confirmed diagnosis of EUS in the inland Murray–Darling River System (MDRS) of Australia rather than in coastal drainages where the disease had long been recognised as red spot disease.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0035568&utm_source=openai)) During routine sampling in June 2010, severe ulcers characteristic of EUS were observed in multiple native species (bony herring, golden perch, Murray cod, spangled perch) along a 200 km reach between Bourke and Brewarrina; histopathology and PCR confirmed A. invadans as the causative agent, indicating a recent invasion or expansion of the pathogen into the MDRS and several new host species.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0035568&utm_source=openai)) Following this large epizootic, Australia reported the event to WOAH/NACA, increased surveillance and highlighted biosecurity concerns about further spread within Australia’s largest river basin.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged low flows followed by flooding, altered flow regimes, and changes in water quality in the semi‑arid Barwon‑Darling River likely stressed native fishes and facilitated pathogen introduction and spread; hypotheses include movement of infected bait fishes or other carriers from coastal catchments and natural dispersal along connected waterways.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0035568&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The MDRS outbreaks were caused by the same clonal A. invadans lineage already established in Australian coastal waters, but involved marked host expansion to important inland species (Murray cod, golden perch, spangled perch), making this a re-emergence event driven by host expansion and geographic range extension into a new river system rather than by a demonstrably novel genotype.
Review: Retain – Added as a missing major emergence event. The 2008 first isolation and large 2010 epizootic in the Murray–Darling River System substantially extended A. invadans into Australia’s major inland basin and several new native host species, and are repeatedly cited as a key EUS emergence episode. Classified as re-emergence (host and basin expansion within an already affected country and sub-region), not as first or inter-continental emergence.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0035568&utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Countries: Canada [2010, Ontario – Lake Ontario, Hamilton Harbour]
Host: Brown bullhead (Ameiurus nebulosus) – wild adult catfish from Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario.
Event summary: In September and November 2010, moribund adult brown bullheads with deep ulcers on the head, fin bases and ventral body were collected in Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario, and submitted for laboratory investigation; histopathology revealed severe mycotic ulcerative dermatitis and necrotizing granulomatous myositis with non‑septate hyphae consistent with Aphanomyces invadans, and Canadian authorities recognised this as epizootic ulcerative syndrome in wild fish.([thefishsite.com](https://thefishsite.com/articles/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome-confirmed-in-canada?utm_source=openai)) The event was not accompanied by an obvious large‑scale fish kill, but represented both a new geographic record (Great Lakes basin, Canada) and a new susceptible species (brown bullhead) in North America, leading Canada to list EUS as an immediately notifiable disease while later relaxing some import controls once the limited nature of the outbreak was clear.([thefishsite.com](https://thefishsite.com/articles/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome-confirmed-in-canada?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent surveillance has not reported major additional EUS epizootics in Canadian waters.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Hamilton Harbour is an industrialised embayment with chronic contamination and ecological stress, conditions likely to predispose brown bullhead to skin damage and immunosuppression, creating portals of entry for A. invadans; Great Lakes fish movements and water transfers pose potential pathways for further spread, although no major secondary epizootics have been documented.([thefishsite.com](https://thefishsite.com/articles/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome-confirmed-in-canada?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: This episode reflects geographical and host expansion of the same clonal A. invadans genotype already present in U.S. estuaries and ponds, with host expansion to brown bullhead; there is no evidence of a new strain or altered intrinsic virulence.
Review: Review – This is a geographically and regulatory significant but biologically small outbreak: a limited number of wild brown bullheads in Hamilton Harbour, with no visible mass die-off, but representing the first confirmed presence of A. invadans in Canada and in the Great Lakes basin. It is therefore reasonable to retain it as a lower-impact emergence event (re-emergence via host and range expansion within an already affected continent), but misclassified emergence-type flags have been corrected: first_detection, intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence are now set to false, with only re_emergence marked true.([thefishsite.com](https://thefishsite.com/articles/epizootic-ulcerative-syndrome-confirmed-in-canada?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: A. invadans (syn. A. piscicida), A. piscicida (syn.)
Countries: Zambia (Bangweulu swamps – Upper Congo catchment) [2014], Democratic Republic of the Congo (Equateur and Ubangi basin rivers) [2014-2015]
Host: Wild freshwater fishes in the Upper Congo catchment, including Parachanna obscura (snakehead), Protopterus annectens (African lungfish), Clarias theodorae (snake catfish) and various mormyrids and cichlids important to local artisanal fisheries.
Event summary: Around 2014, the first outbreak of epizootic ulcerative syndrome in the Upper Congo catchment was reported from the Bangweulu swamps in northern Zambia, an inland delta supporting a large artisanal fishery; typical ulcerative lesions and subsequent diagnostics confirmed infection with Aphanomyces invadans in several native species.([uwcscholar.uwc.ac.za](https://uwcscholar.uwc.ac.za/bitstreams/14463e4c-ad21-49e7-9bce-0e2a6cbdf462/download?utm_source=openai)) In 2014–2015, serious fish disease outbreaks with similar lesions were reported from multiple rivers and markets in Equateur Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, prompting an FAO International Emergency Fish Disease Investigation Mission, which confirmed EUS by histopathology and PCR in snakeheads, lungfish and snake catfish and highlighted the risk of spread throughout the Congo River basin.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336826046_Report_of_the_International_Emergency_Fish_Disease_Investigation_Mission_on_a_Suspected_Outbreak_of_Epizootic_Ulcerative_Syndrome_EUS_in_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo)) These Upper Congo outbreaks signalled a major extension of A. invadans from southern African Zambezi/Okavango systems into Central Africa’s largest drainage, with significant implications for wild inland fisheries and food security.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive floodplain wetlands, seasonal flooding, and heavy reliance on wild-caught fish in Bangweulu and Equateur Province created conditions for rapid spread once A. invadans was introduced, while limited aquatic animal health capacity hindered early detection and control; possible pathways from the Zambezi–Chobe focus include informal fish movements or natural dispersal through interconnected wetlands.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336826046_Report_of_the_International_Emergency_Fish_Disease_Investigation_Mission_on_a_Suspected_Outbreak_of_Epizootic_Ulcerative_Syndrome_EUS_in_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo)) Internal mechanisms: Available evidence does not indicate a novel African genotype; as in prior southern African outbreaks, disease appears to be caused by the globally distributed A. invadans clone, with impact driven by expansion into a new river basin and naïve fish communities rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a missing, high-impact African event. FAO and peer-reviewed reports describe substantial EUS outbreaks in the Bangweulu swamps and multiple rivers and markets in Equateur Province around 2014–2015, marking the first confirmed incursion into the Congo River basin and the first occurrence in Middle Africa (DRC).([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336826046_Report_of_the_International_Emergency_Fish_Disease_Investigation_Mission_on_a_Suspected_Outbreak_of_Epizootic_Ulcerative_Syndrome_EUS_in_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo)) Classified as intra-continental emergence (new African UNSD sub-region and drainage) rather than as an extension of the 2006–2011 Zambezi–Okavango episode, due to the temporal gap and distinct catchment, though both likely share an epidemiological origin in earlier southern African infections.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cultured small abalone Haliotis diversicolor and subspecies (H. diversicolor supertexta, H. diversicolor aquatilis, H. diversicolor Reeve)
Event summary: In spring 1999, farms culturing small abalone in Fujian and neighbouring South China provinces reported explosive “low‑temperature viral disease” outbreaks in Haliotis diversicolor and subspecies, with most animals dying within days; histology and electron microscopy revealed severe lesions and virus‑like particles in multiple tissues, and later metagenomic and PCR work detected abalone herpesvirus (HaHV‑1) in archived samples alongside abalone shriveling syndrome virus. Over the next several years, similar high‑mortality events recurred at sites along the South China Sea coast and, by about 2003, mariculture facilities in Taiwan experienced acute ganglioneuritis and near‑100% mortality in H. diversicolor supertexta, from which the herpes‑like pathogen was formally described and linked by DNA‑polymerase sequencing to Australian HaHV‑1 isolates. As farms shifted species and culture practices and diagnostics improved, overt mass‑mortality outbreaks became less frequent, but HaHV‑1 DNA remained widely detectable in cultured abalone in South China and Taiwan, indicating establishment of the virus in regional aquaculture systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very rapid expansion and high density of abalone mariculture in South China and Taiwan, frequent movement of seed and stock among coastal farms, and seasonal periods of low water temperature that favoured expression of “low‑temperature viral disease” created conditions for explosive mortality events once HaHV‑1 was introduced or amplified. Internal mechanisms: a previously unrecognised neurotropic herpesvirus (later classified as Haliotid herpesvirus 1) with high pathogenicity for H. diversicolor and certain subspecies emerged or was introduced into intensive culture systems; its ability to cause acute necrotising ganglioneuritis with 70–100% mortality, to persist in subclinically infected animals, and to withstand short‑term exposure in cool seawater underpinned rapid establishment and geographic range expansion within Eastern Asia.
Review: Review – Retain this event as the earliest large Asian epizootic and treat it as the first/global emergence of HaHV‑1 in abalone, but not as a separate first_detection event. I have set first_global_emergence = "true" and first_detection = "false" to avoid double classification: the first officially reported herpesvirus infection of abalone occurred in Taiwan in 2003, whereas the 1999–2002 Chinese “low‑temperature viral disease” outbreaks are now considered probable HaHV‑1 events based on retrospective molecular work but involved incompletely characterised mixed infections. Continent, sub‑region and country assignments (Asia, Eastern Asia; China and Taiwan, Province of China) and the qualitative impact description are consistent with Corbeil 2020 and DFO/WOAH summaries, but because the exact contribution of HaHV‑1 versus AbSV to early South China mortality remains uncertain, the confidence score of 0.7 is appropriate and the row is flagged for expert review rather than uncritical retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed and wild abalone Haliotis rubra, Haliotis laevigata and their hybrids
Event summary: In late 2005, sudden mass mortalities occurred almost simultaneously on several land‑based abalone farms in south‑west Victoria, where histopathology revealed severe ganglioneuritis associated with a herpesvirus later confirmed as Haliotid herpesvirus 1. Through 2006 and subsequent years, abalone viral ganglioneuritis spread from farms into adjacent wild abalone beds along the Victorian coast between Portland and Cape Otway, with up to roughly 90% mortality in Haliotis rubra, H. laevigata and their hybrids and major cuts to total allowable catch; wild infection continued to be detected at least until January 2010, when the last cases were recorded near Cape Otway. Extensive movement controls, stock culling, decontamination of farms and long‑term closures of affected reef areas were implemented, and although acute outbreaks subsided after 2010, wild biomass remained depressed and Victoria maintained ongoing surveillance and strict biosecurity rules for abalone movements.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: the introduction of HaHV‑1 into Victorian land‑based farms is thought to have been mediated by movements of infected live abalone or product from endemic regions in Asia, after which high‑density holding in farms and processing facilities, discharge of untreated effluent into coastal waters, and along‑shore coastal currents enabled spillover into wild populations and rapid along‑coast spread. Internal mechanisms: the highly virulent HaHV‑1 strain complex responsible for Taiwanese disease showed strong neurotropism and rapid progression to death in multiple abalone species and proved capable of persisting and transmitting in cooler temperate waters, supporting a marked inter‑continental geographic range expansion into southern Australian ecosystems.
Review: Review – Retain this as the major Victorian farm and wild outbreak but adjust its temporal span and event typing. Based on Victorian government and FRDC sources, the epizootic in farms began in late 2005 with spread into wild reefs through 2006 and detections in the wild continuing until January 2010, so the event year has been widened from "2005-2007" to "2005-2010". Because first herpesvirus infection in abalone was documented in Taiwan in 2003, this Australian episode should not be coded as a first_detection event; first_detection has been set to "false" while inter_continental_emergence remains "true" (first establishment of HaHV‑1 in Oceania). Geography (Oceania; Australia and New Zealand; Australia [Victoria]) and the impact narrative match official reports and support retaining this as one of the highest‑impact events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed and wild-caught abalone held in facilities in Tasmania (Haliotis rubra and related commercial species)
Event summary: In January 2011, abalone farms and a processing facility at Bicheno on Tasmania’s east coast reported disease with signs consistent with abalone viral ganglioneuritis, and diagnostic tests confirmed infection with abalone herpesvirus closely related to Victorian HaHV‑1 strains; low‑level viral DNA was also detected in some nearby wild abalone. Over the following months, further detections occurred in farmed and processed abalone, including at a processing plant at Stanley in north‑west Tasmania in late 2011, prompting facility closures, stock destruction and strict movement controls to prevent wider spread. By 2012, intensified biosecurity procedures in farms and processors, together with zoning and harvest restrictions, helped to contain the outbreaks; clinical disease in wild Tasmanian abalone has remained intermittent and spatially restricted, but HaHV‑1 is now considered present at low levels and a continuing biosecurity concern for the state’s high‑value wild fishery.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: this emergence in Tasmania is attributed to secondary regional spread of HaHV‑1 from Victoria via movements of live abalone or contaminated product and water, with infection amplified in high‑throughput processing facilities and farms and then spilled into nearby coastal habitats; the economic importance of Tasmania’s abalone fishery motivated rapid implementation of biosecurity measures, but the state’s interconnected coastal trade and holding systems facilitated initial establishment in captive stocks. Internal mechanisms: no major new genotype was identified relative to Victorian isolates, so the event represents re‑occurrence of the same highly pathogenic HaHV‑1 lineage in a previously unaffected part of the same sub‑region, with its high virulence and efficient transmission enabling establishment in captive populations despite aggressive control efforts.
Review: Review – Retain this Tasmanian episode as a major regional outbreak in farms and processing facilities but clarify its classification. Evidence from Tasmanian incident reviews, ABC reporting and national summaries indicates that abalone viral ganglioneuritis was detected in farmed and processed abalone at Bicheno and Stanley in 2011, with limited detections of virus in nearby wild abalone and management measures continuing into 2012; large‑scale wild epizootics were not documented. The event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence within the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region driven by secondary spread from Victoria, not as a global first detection, so first_detection has been set to "false" while re_occurrence = "true" and inter-/intra‑continental emergence remain "false". No changes were made to continent, sub‑region or host fields, but because the extent of clinical disease in truly wild populations remains somewhat uncertain, this row is flagged for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wild abalone (Haliotis rubra, Haliotis laevigata and hybrids) in the western zone of the Victorian abalone fishery
Event summary: In early May 2021, divers operating off Cape Nelson in western Victoria reported a cluster of dead and weak abalone, and diagnostic testing confirmed abalone viral ganglioneuritis caused by HaHV‑1 in wild stocks in an area that had been free of detected disease since 2010. The Victorian government declared a control area from Bridgewater Bay to east of Narrawong, imposed broad fishing closures and gear‑movement restrictions, and launched intensified surveillance to delimit the extent of infection within the western zone abalone fishery. By late 2021 the acute outbreak had been contained and the specific control area revoked, but the episode demonstrated that latent or residual HaHV‑1 could re‑activate in western Victorian reefs after a decade‑long apparent hiatus, prompting renewed biosecurity planning and targeted research on virus persistence and transmission pathways.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: FRDC and Victorian investigations suggest this re‑occurrence most likely reflected reactivation and local amplification of HaHV‑1 persisting at low levels in western Victorian abalone populations, potentially triggered by environmental stressors (for example, unusual weather events) and/or human‑mediated movement of infected animals or contaminated equipment, with high local abalone densities and intensive fishing activity increasing the visible impact once disease flared. Internal mechanisms: no distinct new genotype has been reported relative to earlier Victorian isolates, and the outbreak is consistent with episodic expression of the same highly pathogenic HaHV‑1 lineage established during the 2005–2010 epizootic; the key internal mechanisms are herpesvirus latency and efficient water‑borne transmission in temperate reef systems rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Review – New event added. The original dataset omitted the 2021 re‑emergence of abalone viral ganglioneuritis in wild abalone in western Victoria (Cape Nelson/Portland area), which Victorian government and FRDC documents identify as a significant re‑occurrence after more than a decade without wild detections and as a key driver of renewed surveillance and research investment. Host: Wild abalone (commercial Haliotis species) in the Southern Zone Abalone Fishery on the south‑east coast of South Australia
Event summary: In February 2024, dead and dying abalone were reported at Breaksea Reef off Port MacDonnell in South Australia’s south‑east, and laboratory testing confirmed abalone viral ganglioneuritis caused by HaHV‑1 in wild stocks – the first detection of this disease in South Australian waters. Over the remainder of 2024, surveillance found additional infected reefs west of the initial site and the control zone for gear and fishing activities was progressively expanded along the Southern Zone Abalone Fishery to reduce the risk of human‑mediated spread. By early 2025, surveys indicated severe depletion of abalone (with losses approaching 96% at some sites), and on 6 March 2025 the South Australian government closed all commercial and recreational abalone fishing in the Southern Zone for at least 12 months to support stock recovery and prevent further spread while long‑term management and monitoring plans are implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: this outbreak appears to reflect continued regional spread of HaHV‑1 from endemic Victorian and Tasmanian waters into South Australia, facilitated by natural movement of infected abalone and possibly by fishing vessels, diving equipment and other gear that connect reef systems across the border; once introduced, dense wild abalone aggregations, strong coastal currents and ongoing fishing activity allowed the virus to establish and spread before its full extent was recognised. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses to date indicate that the South Australian virus is closely related to previously characterised southern Australian HaHV‑1 variants, with no clear evidence yet of a distinct new pathotype, so the main internal mechanism is the established lineage’s capacity for efficient transmission and high virulence in temperate Haliotis populations rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Review – Retain this as the major South Australian Southern Zone epizootic but update classification, timing and sources. The outbreak was first confirmed near Port MacDonnell in February 2024 and, according to PIRSA and FRDC risk assessments, the virus spread throughout the Southern Zone, with surveys in 2024–2025 indicating very high mortality at some reefs and prompting complete closure of the Southern Zone abalone fishery from 6 March 2025 for at least 12 months; the event year has therefore been standardised to "2024-2025" without the "ongoing" qualifier. As this represents spread of an existing southern Australian HaHV‑1 lineage within the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region, it is coded as re_occurrence only (first_detection reset to "false"). Event‑level source URLs have been revised to prioritise PIRSA and ABC reports and the FRDC 2023–25 risk assessment over generic Western Australian fact sheets, with the DPIRD WA page retained only as supporting context. Because the outbreak and its management are still evolving, this row is flagged for expert review.

Host: Commercial chickens (broilers and layers), later turkeys on Brazilian farms
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, avian metapneumovirus (primarily subtype A) was first detected in Latin America, with the earliest confirmed reports from Brazilian poultry flocks in 1995 based on field samples from chickens showing respiratory disease and swollen head syndrome. Over the following few years, serologic and virologic surveys showed the virus becoming established in Brazilian chicken and turkey operations across multiple regions, associated with respiratory signs and egg‑production losses. By the late 1990s the virus was considered endemic in much of the Brazilian poultry sector, prompting the development and introduction of vaccination and improved biosecurity measures to control recurring outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of Brazilian poultry production, high densities of broiler and layer farms, and limited prior immunity or vaccination against aMPV in Latin America facilitated initial establishment and spread; regional poultry movements likely dispersed infection between states. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of aMPV subtype A into a previously naïve continental poultry population (novel strain for the region) with efficient respiratory transmission in chickens and turkeys allowed rapid geographic range expansion and high within‑flock attack rates.
Review: Decision: retain. Evidence from Brazilian virological and serological studies confirms first isolation of aMPV from broiler‑breeder flocks in Brazil in 1995, with rapid spread and establishment in broilers and turkeys over subsequent years; Chilean detections in 1997 appear secondary and smaller in scale. Classification as first detection plus inter‑continental emergence for South America is appropriate, and no larger Latin American aMPV event in 1990–2025 was identified. No structural changes made.

Host: Commercial meat turkeys (Colorado, then Minnesota and other upper‑Midwest states); later other turkey flocks in the region
Event summary: In May 1996, a severe upper respiratory disease outbreak with sinusitis and conjunctivitis affected commercial meat turkeys in Colorado, and laboratory investigation at the US National Veterinary Services Laboratories identified avian metapneumovirus, later classified as the novel subgroup C, marking the first detection of aMPV in North American poultry. Over the late 1990s the virus spread from Colorado to major turkey‑producing states in the upper Midwest, including Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Iowa and Wisconsin, with a large proportion of turkey premises testing seropositive and industry losses estimated at roughly US$15 million per year from 1997–2000. As live‑attenuated vaccines and strengthened biosecurity and surveillance were implemented, incidence in US commercial turkeys declined, and by the early 2000s the multi‑state subtype C epizootic had largely subsided, leaving the virus under much better control in US flocks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of commercial turkey production in Colorado and the upper Midwest, movement of birds, equipment and personnel between farms, and concurrent circulation of other respiratory pathogens (e.g., avian influenza, mycoplasmas) promoted rapid farm‑to‑farm spread and exacerbated disease severity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a genetically and antigenically distinct subgroup C lineage compared with European A/B strains reduced detection by existing serologic assays and suggested prior evolution in wild birds, representing both a novel genotype and an inter‑continental range expansion into a naïve turkey population.
Review: Decision: review. The event window was expanded from 1996–1998 to 1996–2000 to reflect evidence that subtype C aMPV spread from Colorado to Minnesota and neighboring upper‑Midwest states and caused substantial economic losses through about 2000, rather than being confined to Colorado and Minnesota in the first two years. The previous flagging of this episode as 're_emergence' was removed, because the outbreak represents first continental introduction of aMPV into North American poultry rather than reappearance in a previously infected North American subregion. Additional US‑focused overview papers were added to better document the multi‑state extent and economic impact of the epizootic.

Host: Muscovy ducks and other farmed ducks in France; subsequent detections in wild ducks and other wild birds in Europe
Event summary: Around 1999, subtype C avian metapneumovirus was first isolated in farmed Muscovy ducks in France, representing the first detection of this subgroup outside North America and the emergence of a distinct Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage in waterfowl. Over the ensuing several years, aMPV‑C infections were documented in domestic ducks and in multiple wild bird species in Europe, indicating establishment of a duck‑ and wild‑bird–associated lineage that was genetically distinct from US turkey aMPV‑C strains and from European A/B viruses. As knowledge of this lineage grew, management responses focused on enhanced surveillance of ducks and wild birds and on considering duck and wild‑bird reservoirs in control strategies for poultry aMPV in Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close contact between domestic ducks and wild waterfowl, outdoor and free‑range duck production, and shared wetlands facilitated spillover and maintenance of the virus in duck populations and wild‑bird reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage with adaptation to ducks and wild waterfowl represents host expansion and genomic diversification within aMPV‑C, enabling efficient transmission and persistence in new host species while remaining antigenically distinct from A/B strains and from North American turkey aMPV‑C.
Review: Decision: review. Timing (starting in 1999) and classification as re‑emergence in a region where aMPV A/B were already endemic remain appropriate, but the event’s source list was revised to prioritize papers that directly describe the French Muscovy duck aMPV‑C isolates and their phylogenetic placement, rather than relying mainly on Chinese or generic systematic‑review articles. No evidence was found for a larger or earlier European duck aMPV‑C episode that would displace this event among the top‑impact post‑1990 episodes.

Host: Commercial chickens (broilers, layers, breeders) and turkeys on multiple Brazilian farms
Event summary: Beginning in the early 2000s, Brazil experienced increasingly frequent outbreaks of respiratory disease and production drops in chickens and turkeys, with aMPV detected by RT‑PCR and virus isolation in multiple geographic regions and production types, including the first confirmed isolation from turkeys. By 2003–2008, surveillance showed circulation of aMPV subtypes A and B in vaccinated and non‑vaccinated chicken and turkey farms across six Brazilian regions, associated with swollen head syndrome, reduced egg production, carcass condemnation from aerosacculitis, and notable economic losses. Subsequent years saw the incorporation of aMPV vaccination into broader respiratory disease control programs and ongoing molecular surveillance to track subtypes and vaccine performance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and geographic expansion of Brazil’s poultry sector, high farm densities, complex vertical integration networks, and incomplete or uneven vaccination coverage allowed aMPV to spread widely and persist; coinfections with Escherichia coli and other respiratory pathogens worsened clinical outcomes and carcass condemnation rates. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation and evolution of subtypes A and B in Brazilian flocks, with adaptation to local production systems, likely increased transmissibility and disease expression in intensively reared broilers and turkeys, representing geographic range expansion within Brazil and re‑emergence driven by subtype diversity and partial vaccine escape.
Review: Decision: review. This episode reflects amplification and geographic spread of aMPV A and B within Brazil, not first occurrence of the virus in a new South American subregion; therefore, 'intra_continental_emergence' has been changed from Yes to No. Retaining 're_emergence' as Yes captures the substantial resurgence and subtype diversification in an already affected subregion with clear production impacts. No other fields were altered, and the event still qualifies as a major post‑1990 aMPV episode in South America.

Host: Meat‑type commercial chickens (yellow‑feathered broilers) in southeastern China
Event summary: During February–April 2012, severe respiratory disease with conjunctivitis, sinus swelling, and up to 80% morbidity was observed in meat‑type commercial chickens on farms in southeastern China, and laboratory investigation identified aMPV subgroup C as the major pathogen. Molecular characterization of the JC strain showed it belonged to the aMPV‑C cluster but formed a distinct subcluster more similar to some wild‑bird and human metapneumovirus strains than to other aMPV‑C isolates, and experimental infection of specific‑pathogen‑free chickens produced marked respiratory lesions, demonstrating higher pathogenicity than previously recognized in chickens. Control of the affected flocks relied on culling and local biosecurity measures, and the episode spurred wider epidemiological studies documenting that aMPV‑C infection was likely widespread in Chinese chicken flocks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of broiler production, limited prior detection of aMPV in Chinese chickens, and possible introduction from wild birds or live‑bird markets facilitated rapid spread once the virus entered commercial flocks; lack of subtype C‑targeted vaccination in chickens likely contributed to high morbidity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct, highly pathogenic aMPV‑C variant (JC strain) in chickens, with closer genetic relatedness to some wild‑bird and human metapneumoviruses, represents novel genotype emergence, enhanced virulence in chickens, and re‑emergence of aMPV‑C within an already affected Eastern Asian subregion.
Review: Decision: review. The event window was narrowed to 2012 to match the documented period of the JC‑strain outbreaks in southeastern Chinese chickens, rather than the broader 2010–2013 range originally used. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was changed from Yes to No because aMPV (including subtype C) was already present in Eastern Asia (e.g. in Japan and South Korea); this episode reflects spread to a new country within the same subregion plus the emergence of a more pathogenic aMPV‑C variant, which is better captured as re‑emergence with novel strain characteristics. 'First_detection' is retained here to indicate first confirmed isolation of aMPV‑C from chickens in China.

Host: Muscovy ducks and other domestic ducks in China
Event summary: From around mid‑2010, outbreaks characterized by respiratory disease and egg‑production problems were reported in Muscovy ducks on farms in southern China, and virological investigation led to the isolation and characterization of subtype C aMPV strain S‑01 from affected ducks. The isolated virus caused respiratory and reproductive disease in experimental infections and showed close genetic relationships to North American aMPV‑C but clear distinction from subtypes A and B, indicating introduction and adaptation of aMPV‑C in Chinese duck populations. Over the subsequent years of this episode, serologic and molecular surveys suggested that aMPV‑C infection in domestic ducks and possibly wild ducks had become more widespread, raising concern about ducks as a reservoir for continued circulation and spillover to other poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species duck farming, contact between domestic ducks and wild waterfowl in rice‑paddy and wetland systems, and limited prior surveillance of aMPV in ducks enabled undetected introduction and amplification of aMPV‑C. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of the aMPV‑C lineage from turkeys and chickens into domestic ducks, with evidence of efficient replication and disease expression in Muscovy ducks, represents re‑emergence driven by host adaptation and geographic spread of the Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage within Eastern Asia.
Review: Decision: review. The time span was adjusted from 2010–2014 to 2010–2012 to better reflect the period emphasized in the primary S‑01 Muscovy‑duck paper, which describes severe disease beginning in 2010 without clearly documenting continuation of the same outbreak through 2014. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was changed from Yes to No because aMPV was already present in Eastern Asia; the key feature of this episode is emergence of a duck‑adapted aMPV‑C lineage and its spread among domestic ducks, which fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and viral adaptation within an already affected subregion. 'First_detection' is retained to denote first documented aMPV‑C isolation from Muscovy ducks in China.

Host: Sheldrake ducks (Fujian Province), other domestic ducks in affected area
Event summary: From about 2021, a novel aMPV subtype C variant, designated aMPV‑FJ21, was isolated from Sheldrake ducks in Fujian Province, China, during outbreaks of a severe hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome with reproductive tract lesions and reduced egg production. Phylogenetic analyses showed that FJ21 formed a distinct lineage within the aMPV‑C group, genetically distant from previously described North American and Eurasian aMPV‑C lineages, suggesting emergence of a new genetic lineage in Chinese ducks. Following characterization, affected flocks were managed through culling or enhanced flock‑level biosecurity, and the discovery prompted recommendations for increased surveillance and reconsideration of vaccine strategies in duck production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive duck production in southeastern China, regional movement of live ducks, and ongoing exposure to wild waterfowl likely created conditions for continued aMPV‑C evolution and the emergence of more pathogenic variants; limited or absent vaccination in ducks left populations immunologically susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence within subtype C (FJ21 lineage) with distinct genomic features and association with hydrosalpinx and severe reproductive pathology indicates increased pathogenicity and possible altered tissue tropism, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by viral evolution in ducks.
Review: Decision: retain. The FJ21 outbreaks in Sheldrake ducks are clearly documented as a newly emerged, genetically distinct aMPV‑C lineage causing significant reproductive disease and egg‑production losses in Chinese duck flocks from 2021 onward. This event is appropriately classified as re‑emergence (new variant in an already affected subregion) and appears to be one of the more impactful aMPV episodes in ducks during 2005–2025. No structural changes were made; sources already include the primary Virulence article and a recent systematic review.

Host: Broiler breeder chickens in Jiangsu Province, China
Event summary: In 2022, severe respiratory disease outbreaks occurred in broiler breeder chickens in Jiangsu Province, China, and investigation led to the isolation of an aMPV subgroup C strain designated GX22‑01 from affected flocks. The virus was confirmed by immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and sequencing of the nucleoprotein gene, and was associated with significant respiratory signs and production impacts in breeder flocks. After confirmation, affected farms implemented flock‑level management responses including targeted culling and heightened biosecurity, and the event added to evidence that aMPV‑C has become an important and evolving pathogen in Chinese chicken production systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density breeder operations, regional poultry movement networks, and ongoing circulation of aMPV‑C in Eastern China facilitated the appearance of outbreaks in previously unaffected breeder farms. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution of aMPV‑C in Chinese poultry populations and adaptation to broiler breeder chickens, represented by the GX22‑01 strain, underlie this re‑emergence, likely involving genotype diversification and potentially enhanced transmissibility or fitness in breeder flocks.
Review: Decision: review. The event year was narrowed from 2022–2023 to 2022 to match the period explicitly documented in the Jiangsu broiler‑breeder outbreaks from which GX22‑01 was isolated; current evidence does not yet support treating 2023 as part of the same epidemiologically linked episode. Classification as re‑emergence is retained because GX22‑01 represents another distinct aMPV‑C strain emerging in Chinese chickens in a region with prior aMPV circulation. The source list already includes the primary Jiangsu paper plus contextual Chinese aMPV‑C literature, so only the time span was corrected.

Host: Commercial turkeys and chickens in the United States (laboratory‑confirmed affected flocks)
Event summary: In January 2024, the US National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed avian metapneumovirus subtype B in poultry samples submitted through the National Animal Health Laboratory Network, marking the first confirmed detection of subtype B aMPV in US commercial poultry, where previous circulation had been dominated by subtype C and had been largely controlled by the late 2000s. Subsequent molecular and field investigations documented that both subtypes A and B had entered US poultry, with subtype B driving major outbreaks of respiratory and reproductive disease in turkeys and chickens in eastern states (including the Delmarva region) and subtype A detected more frequently in some western production areas. Throughout 2024 and into 2025, control efforts focused on intensive surveillance, flock‑level management and depopulation of affected premises, and rapid deployment of inactivated subtype B vaccines under special approvals, while national trade was maintained through targeted rather than nationwide movement restrictions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale integrated turkey and chicken production, dense networks for interstate movement of poults, hatching eggs, and live birds, and movement of equipment and personnel between complexes created conditions for rapid dissemination once aMPV‑A and aMPV‑B entered US systems; introduction pathways likely involved a combination of imported breeding stock, biologics, and/or wild‑bird reservoirs interacting with biosecurity gaps. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and early spread of genetically distinct aMPV‑A and aMPV‑B lineages into a poultry population where subtype C had been absent for more than a decade created a largely immunologically naive host population; sequence data indicate these lineages differ antigenically from historic US subtype C strains, implying genotype diversification with important consequences for diagnostic test performance and vaccine matching, and justifying classification as re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.
Review: Decision: review. The event is retained but its description was broadened from 'first detection of subtype B' to cover the concurrent introduction and spread of both subtypes A and B in US poultry, consistent with USDA and recent peer‑reviewed reports. Classification as 'first_detection' (for these subtypes in US poultry) plus 're_emergence' (reappearance of aMPV in a previously affected North American subregion with novel lineages) is appropriate, while 'inter_continental_emergence' remains No because aMPV as a species had already been present on this continent. The source list was updated to include the APHIS program update, detailed molecular epidemiology papers on subtype A and B introductions, and an extension fact sheet summarizing 2024 US subtype distribution and vaccine options.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Belgium [1990]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990]; France [early 1990s]; Germany [early 199s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [early 1990s]; Denmark [1998]; Spain [1990s]; Italy [1990s]
Host: Chickens (broilers and pullets; commercial layer and broiler operations)
Event summary: During the 1990s, very virulent infectious bursal disease virus (vvIBDV), first recognized in Europe in the late 1980s, caused a continent-wide wave of severe Gumboro disease outbreaks, beginning in Benelux countries and rapidly involving major poultry producers across Western and Northern Europe. The epizootic led to high flock mortality and heavy production losses, exemplified by a 1998 Danish episode affecting 36 broiler farms and causing the loss of over 200,000 broilers, while similar patterns of mortality and immunosuppression were reported in multiple European states. Improved vaccination strategies, biosecurity, and adaptation of control programs to vvIBDV pathotypes gradually reduced overt mortality by the late 1990s, though vvIBDV became enzootic in many European poultry sectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic concentration of broiler and layer production, dense poultry populations with high farm connectivity, and movement of live birds and hatching eggs facilitated rapid dissemination of vvIBDV between European countries; gaps in existing vaccination programs, designed for classical strains, left flocks vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of very virulent serotype 1 strains with increased virulence (increased virulence/pathogenicity) and enhanced capacity to cause high mortality and severe bursal damage; antigenic differences from classical and U.S. variant strains reduced protection from existing vaccines and favored geographic range expansion within Europe (geographic range expansion, inherent).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major vvIBDV epizootic in Europe, but change 'intra_continental_emergence' from Yes to No because vvIBDV arose within an already endemic IBDV population and, per the project rules, new pathotypes should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence. Geography, timing and impact are well supported by European reviews and outbreak reports, but the revised classification should be quality-checked.

Host: Chickens (intensive and semi-intensive commercial flocks)
Event summary: Around 1990, very virulent IBDV strains closely related to European vvIBDV were detected in Egypt, marking the appearance of this high-mortality pathotype in North African commercial poultry and causing severe outbreaks of Gumboro disease in young chickens. Through the early to mid-1990s, these vvIBDV strains spread within Egyptian poultry systems and likely into neighboring North African countries, leading to high mortality and immunosuppression in broiler and layer flocks despite vaccination. Over time, adaptation of vaccination schedules and introduction of more appropriate vaccines reduced overt losses, but vvIBDV became entrenched in regional poultry populations as an endemic, economically important pathogen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Poultry trade and movement of breeding stock and hatching eggs from Europe to North African production systems likely introduced vvIBDV; expanding commercial poultry sectors with limited early diagnostic capacity facilitated silent spread until large outbreaks occurred. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of very virulent genotypes belonging to the global vvIBDV lineage (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to African classical strains) with enhanced virulence and immunosuppressive capacity (increased virulence/pathogenicity) enabled successful establishment and regional range expansion within Africa (geographic range expansion, inherent).
Review: review: Keep this as the main early vvIBDV wave in North Africa (Egypt), but set 'inter_continental_emergence' to No and treat the episode purely as re-emergence because IBDV had been present in Egypt and elsewhere in Africa since the 1970s. The countries field was simplified to Egypt [~1990] to avoid speculative listing of 'likely affected' neighbors; timing and impact are consistent with reports that vvIBDV was first documented in Egypt around 1989–1990, so only the classification and country formatting required correction.

Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, very virulent IBDV strains emerged in East Asia, with Japan reporting vvIBDV-associated outbreaks in the early 1990s followed by rapid dissemination to China and other parts of the region, causing acute Gumboro disease with unusually high mortality in young chickens. Throughout the first half of the 1990s, East Asian poultry producers experienced repeated large outbreaks that overwhelmed existing control programs, resulting in substantial economic losses and widespread immunosuppression in affected flocks. As vaccination strategies were updated, vvIBDV became endemic but overt mortality in many large-scale operations was reduced, although recurrent episodes of disease and immunosuppression continued.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and industrialization of the East Asian poultry sector, extensive trade in live birds and hatching eggs, and limited early access to vvIBDV-adapted vaccines promoted rapid establishment of the introduced pathotype. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and subsequent regional expansion of a very virulent serotype 1 lineage derived from European vvIBDV (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to local classical strains) with heightened tissue tropism for the bursa and increased mortality (increased virulence/pathogenicity), enabling successful spread within East Asia (enhanced transmission/geographic range expansion).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major vvIBDV emergence in East Asia (Japan and China), but change 'inter_continental_emergence' to No because IBDV was already established in Asia before vvIBDV appeared; under the project rules this qualifies as re-emergence driven by a new pathotype. The time window and geography remain appropriate, matching reports that vvIBDV was introduced into Japan and then China in the early 1990s.
