Host: Chickens (backyard and commercial flocks)
Event summary: The first recognized infectious bursal disease outbreaks in Bangladesh were reported at the end of 1992, coinciding with reports of severe Gumboro disease in neighboring South Asian countries and marking the southward spread of vvIBDV within Asia into high-density poultry systems of the subcontinent. Through the 1990s, repeated, large-scale outbreaks with high mortality and marked bursal pathology occurred in broiler and layer flocks across Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, causing heavy production losses and predisposing birds to secondary infections. By around 2000, IBDV—often in very virulent form—was firmly established in South Asian poultry; improved vaccines and control programs subsequently mitigated but did not eliminate recurrent disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of commercial poultry production in South Asia, movement of day-old chicks and hatching eggs, and limited early diagnostic and surveillance capacity supported the introduction and spread of vvIBDV into Bangladesh and neighboring countries; concurrent endemic diseases amplified the impact of IBDV-induced immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and regional expansion of vvIBDV strains closely related to European/Asian very virulent lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to previously circulating or undetected IBDV) with high virulence and strong B-cell tropism (increased virulence/pathogenicity), combined with selection for variants able to escape partial vaccine immunity (antigenic diversification facilitating re-emergence).
Review: review: This South Asian wave of severe IBD (vvIBDV) should be kept as one of the major emergence events, but 'intra_continental_emergence' was set to No because the virus species was already endemic in the region and the new pathotype represents re-emergence rather than spread of a previously absent EPP. Otherwise, the timing (Bangladesh first recognized in 1992 with spread across India and Pakistan in the 1990s) and the listed countries align with primary reports and reviews.

Host: Chickens (industrial broiler and layer systems)
Event summary: By the late 1990s and early 2000s, very virulent IBDV spread into Latin America, with severe Gumboro disease outbreaks documented in Brazil and vvIBDV-like strains characterized from Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and other countries in the region, marking establishment of vvIBDV in South America and parts of the Caribbean. During this period, major Brazilian broiler-producing areas and Caribbean producers experienced acute disease with high mortality and significant economic losses, and similar patterns were reported from additional South American countries as vvIBDV became widespread. Over subsequent years, implementation of tailored vaccination programs and improved biosecurity reduced the frequency of catastrophic losses, although vvIBDV persisted as an endemic immunosuppressive threat to Latin American poultry production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensifying export-oriented broiler production, large-scale movement of breeding stock and hatching eggs from affected regions, and limited early awareness of vvIBDV in Latin America allowed rapid establishment of the introduced pathotype; dense vertically integrated systems facilitated farm-to-farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of vvIBDV genotypes belonging to the global very virulent lineage (novel strain/genotype emergence for South America) with greatly increased pathogenicity and mortality compared with classical IBDV (increased virulence/pathogenicity) and capacity to persist in the environment, supporting sustained regional range expansion (geographic range expansion, inherent).
Review: review: Keep this as the principal vvIBDV epizootic in Latin America/Caribbean, but reclassify it as re-emergence only by setting 'inter_continental_emergence' to No because IBDV had been present in the Americas since the 1970s. The event year range was broadened to 1999–2005 to reflect sequences showing vv-like viruses in Brazil and the Dominican Republic at the end of the 1990s, and the country list was revised to name Dominican Republic explicitly and to place Cuba around 2000; Wikipedia was replaced by primary Avian Diseases and regional genetic studies in the Source URLs.
