Host: Chickens (commercial broilers, layers, and smallholder flocks)
Event summary: From the mid-2000s through the early 2010s, West African countries such as Nigeria and Ghana reported recurrent, severe outbreaks of infectious bursal disease attributed to very virulent IBDV strains in both commercial and smallholder poultry, often in flocks that had been vaccinated. These outbreaks were characterized by high mortality, marked bursal lesions, and strong immunosuppression that exacerbated other endemic diseases, causing substantial economic losses and undermining farmer confidence in vaccines. Although updated vaccination regimes and improved husbandry gradually reduced disease severity in some large operations, vvIBDV remained enzootic in West Africa, and outbreaks continued to reappear in new locations and production systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of commercial poultry production in West Africa, frequent movement of chicks and live birds with limited biosecurity, and incomplete vaccine coverage or mismatches between field and vaccine strains facilitated resurgence; socioeconomic constraints limited consistent implementation of control measures. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of vvIBDV lineages confirmed by molecular characterization in Nigerian and Ghanaian flocks, including in vaccinated birds (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to earlier classical strains and evidence of vaccine escape); high virulence and immunosuppressive capacity (increased virulence/pathogenicity) supported repeated re-emergence and persistence despite control efforts.
Review: retain: This West African event is well supported by molecular studies and outbreak descriptions documenting vvIBDV in vaccinated flocks in Nigeria and Ghana; coding as both re-occurrence and re-emergence is appropriate because failures of control measures and virulent genotypes both contributed. Geography (Western Africa) and timing (mid‑2000s to early 2010s) are consistent with the literature, so no substantive corrections are required.

Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event summary: Between the early 2000s and early 2010s, China and other East Asian countries experienced repeated infectious bursal disease outbreaks associated with evolving vvIBDV lineages, including strains with distinctive VP2 and VP1 genomic features and reassortant genomes, in intensively reared chickens. These outbreaks caused significant mortality and bursal destruction in young birds and led to chronic immunosuppression problems in broiler and layer operations, despite extensive vaccination efforts. Over time, adaptation of vaccine strains and schedules to circulating vvIBDV and increased biosecurity helped reduce overt mortality, but genetically diverse vvIBDV strains persisted and continued to cause episodic disease and economic losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extremely dense and rapidly expanding poultry industries in China and neighboring countries, high farm connectivity, and intense vaccine usage created selective pressure and opportunities for viral evolution and spread; large integrated systems facilitated the rapid dissemination of successful viral variants. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution and diversification of vvIBDV strains, including novel VP2 hypervariable-region mutations and evidence of reassortment between classical and very virulent segment lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence and reassortment), sometimes associated with altered antigenicity and pathogenicity (increased virulence/pathogenicity and partial vaccine escape), underpinning repeated re-emergence events.
Review: retain: This event accurately captures the continued evolution and episodic impact of vvIBDV in East Asia during the 2000s, with appropriate classification as re-emergence and no intra- or inter-continental spread. The cited Chinese sequence and pathogenicity studies support both the timing and the description of reassortant vvIBDV lineages, so no major changes were needed.

Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event summary: From roughly the mid-2000s through the early 2010s, Indian poultry farms reported significant infectious bursal disease outbreaks linked to genetically drifting vvIBDV strains and reassortant viruses, despite widespread use of vaccination. These outbreaks were characterized by high morbidity, variable mortality, and severe bursal lesions in young chickens, leading to immunosuppression and production losses in both broiler and layer sectors across several Indian states. As monitoring improved, molecular characterization guided updates in vaccine strain selection and control strategies, which helped reduce disease severity in many large operations, although novel variants continued to arise and cause re-emergent disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanding commercial poultry production with high bird densities, complex live-bird marketing chains, and variable vaccine handling and coverage allowed ongoing circulation and selection of IBDV variants; economic pressures sometimes limited optimal vaccination schedules. Internal mechanisms: Accumulation of genetic drift and reassortment events in Indian IBDV populations, including unique VP1 and VP2 constellations that likely evolved from combinations of classical and vvIBDV segments (novel strain/genotype emergence, reassortment), altered antigenicity compared with vaccine strains, and maintained high immunosuppressive capacity (increased virulence/pathogenicity), driving re-emergence in vaccinated flocks.
Review: retain: The Indian re-emergence event (mid‑2000s to early 2010s) is well supported by molecular work documenting genetic drift and reassortment in vvIBDV strains, and the coding as re-emergence without geographic novelty is consistent with the project definitions. No corrections to geography, timing, or classification were required.

Countries: China [2015-2017]; Japan [2017]; Republic of Korea [late 2010s]; Malaysia [2017-2019]
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers, often subclinically affected)
Event summary: From the mid‑2010s, a novel variant IBDV genotype (nvIBDV, classified as A2dB1b) emerged in China and subsequently spread through East and parts of Southeast Asia, generating a large-scale epidemic characterized largely by subclinical infections with severe bursal atrophy and immunosuppression rather than classic high-mortality Gumboro disease. Over this period, nvIBDV became widespread in Chinese broiler and layer flocks and was detected in other countries such as Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Malaysia, undermining vaccine programs targeting classical and vvIBDV strains and contributing to increased susceptibility to other poultry pathogens. Adjustments to vaccination strategies, including development and deployment of variant-adapted vaccines and improved monitoring, have begun to address this challenge, but nvIBDV remains an important, immunosuppressive re-emergent form of the virus in Asian poultry systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High vaccine pressure against classical and vvIBDV phenotypes, dense poultry production, and extensive movement of birds and products across East and Southeast Asia promoted emergence and spread of variants better adapted to partially immune flocks; intensive production favored viruses that cause subclinical yet immunosuppressive infection. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the novel variant genotype A2dB1b with distinct VP2 antigenic properties and altered pathogenic profile (novel strain/genotype emergence), associated with strong bursal atrophy but often reduced overt mortality; partial escape from existing vaccine-induced immunity (antigenic variation/functional vaccine escape) allowed successful regional expansion (enhanced transmission/geographic range expansion).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major emergence of the Chinese novel variant nvIBDV (A2dB1b) and its subsequent spread in East and South‑eastern Asia, but update the period to 2015–2022 to match analyses showing reappearance of variants as novel strains in the mid‑2010s and their rapid expansion thereafter. The country list was refined to include only locations with documented nvIBDV (China, Japan, Republic of Korea, Malaysia), and 'intra_continental_emergence' was switched to No so the episode is coded purely as re-emergence of a new genotype within an already endemic virus species; Source URLs now point to primary Chinese and global analyses of A2dB1b rather than Middle East–focused papers.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Jordan [2023]; Lebanon [2023]; Iraq [2023-2024]; United Arab Emirates [2024]; Egypt [2021-2023]
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event summary: From the early 2020s, molecular surveillance revealed rapid spread of the novel variant IBDV genotype A2dB1b from its origin in East Asia into the Near East and North Africa, with first detections in Jordan and Lebanon in late 2023, followed by rapid establishment in the United Arab Emirates and evidence of related nvIBDV strains in Iraq. In parallel, Egypt reported nvIBDV A2dB1b in poultry flocks alongside existing vvIBDV strains, indicating further geographic expansion and leading to outbreaks characterized mainly by subclinical infection, bursal atrophy, and immunosuppression rather than high mortality. Ongoing circulation of these variants in the Middle East and North Africa has complicated control strategies based on classical and vvIBDV vaccines and raised concern about their long-term impact on vaccine performance and poultry health.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Trade in live birds and hatching eggs and regional integration of poultry supply chains between Asia, the Near East, and North Africa facilitated long-distance movement of nvIBDV; limited early awareness and diagnostic targeting of this genotype allowed silent spread before it was molecularly characterized. Internal mechanisms: The A2dB1b genotype possesses distinct VP2 antigenic signatures and is adapted to infect partially immune flocks previously vaccinated against classical and vvIBDV (novel strain/genotype emergence and vaccine escape), with a tendency toward subclinical yet strongly immunosuppressive disease (increased pathogenicity in terms of immune dysfunction rather than overt mortality), enabling re-emergence in regions where IBDV was already endemic and geographic expansion across Western Asia and into North Africa.
Review: review: This event is retained as the spread of nvIBDV A2dB1b into the Near East and North Africa, but the dates and geography were corrected using recent molecular surveillance: the wave now spans roughly 2021–2025, with nvIBDV first detected in Egypt around 2021–2023 and then in Jordan, Lebanon and the UAE from late 2023 onward, and Iraq added based on A2dB1b-classified sequences; Oman and Qatar were removed because current data primarily show other genotypes there. 'First_detection', 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were all set to No so the episode is treated strictly as re-emergence of a new genotype in continents where IBDV was long established; the sources now cleanly support these corrections and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final confirmation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990-1994]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In the early 1990s the United Kingdom’s existing BSE epidemic in cattle intensified, peaking in 1992 with over 37,000 confirmed clinical cases in that year alone and nearly 180,000 cases cumulatively by 2001. Despite an initial 1988 ban on feeding ruminant protein to ruminants and compulsory slaughter of affected cattle, large infected birth cohorts continued to age into clinical disease through the early 1990s. Only after reinforced feed bans, removal of specified risk materials, and large-scale culling did incidence begin a sustained decline, marking the turn of the main UK epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recycling of infected bovine offal and central nervous system tissues into MBM fed back to cattle; rendering practices that failed to inactivate prions; centralized feed manufacture and distribution amplifying and dispersing infectivity; late recognition of the new disease and of the feedborne transmission route. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and efficient feedborne transmission of a cattle-adapted classical BSE strain with high oral infectivity and long incubation periods, permitting extensive silent amplification in cohorts before clinical detection.
Review: retain – Core description (UK epidemic peak, order of magnitude of case counts, and control measures) is well supported by FAO, UK parliamentary statistics, and major reviews. The original classification of this episode as re-emergence has been corrected to re_emergence = No, because this period represents the growth and peak of the initial UK classical BSE epidemic rather than a reappearance driven by changes in the agent. No changes to geography or sources were required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: From 1989 through the early 1990s, BSE was detected for the first time in native-born cattle in several European countries outside the UK, beginning with Ireland in 1989 and followed by Switzerland and Portugal in 1990, France in 1991, and Italy in 1994. These detections, often in animals born and reared locally, were epidemiologically linked to earlier imports of contaminated MBM or live cattle from the UK, showing that the UK feed-borne epidemic had seeded infection into multiple European herds. Subsequent adoption of ruminant-to-ruminant feed bans and intensified surveillance across these countries gradually curbed incidence, though additional cases continued to arise for years from already-exposed birth cohorts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of MBM and live cattle from the UK during the 1980s before BSE risk was fully recognised; lack of early risk communication and harmonised feed controls in importing states; delays and inconsistencies in implementing effective ruminant protein bans at the European level. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of the classical BSE strain into new European subregions via contaminated feed chains; prolonged incubation periods that allowed infected cohorts to move through trade networks before clinical disease appeared.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the first indigenous BSE detections in key European countries outside the UK and is now aligned with FAO/EFSA tables: Ireland 1989, Switzerland 1990, Portugal 1990, France 1991, and Italy 1994. Countries whose first cases occurred later (Denmark, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands) have been removed from this row to avoid incorrect early-1990s dating and are instead represented in the later EU-wide 2000–2001 crisis event. The event year range has been adjusted from 1990–1994 to 1989–1994 to match the first Irish cases that were already cited in the original row. Type classification as intra-continental emergence and first detection (for these countries) is appropriate; no inter-continental or re-emergence flags are warranted.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: France [2000 – sharp rise in detected cases]; Germany [2000 – first domestic cases]; Spain [2000 – first domestic cases]; Denmark [2000 – first domestic cases]; Italy [2001 – widely publicised first domestic case]; other affected EU Member States with first domestic cases or sharp increases (e.g., Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Finland, Greece) [2000-2001]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: Around 2000–2001, several EU Member States experienced a marked rise in detected BSE cases, with France seeing rapidly increasing numbers and Germany, Spain, Denmark and Italy reporting their first clear domestic cases, triggering continent-wide public alarm. Active surveillance and mandatory testing of older slaughter cattle revealed that earlier controls had not fully prevented exposure in cohorts born during the 1990s, leading to what was widely perceived as a renewed ‘mad cow crisis’ in continental Europe. In response, the EU introduced stricter measures, including a comprehensive ban on MBM in feed for all farmed animals, systematic removal of specified risk materials and large-scale testing, after which incidence in affected birth cohorts progressively declined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Partial or delayed implementation and enforcement of feed controls in some Member States; continued cross-border trade in MBM and rendered by-products; intensified active surveillance and testing that uncovered previously undetected infections; strong consumer reaction and political pressure across the EU, which accelerated harmonised risk‑management actions. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of classical BSE in existing European subregions due to residual contaminated feed stocks and exposure of susceptible birth cohorts; no evidence for a fundamentally new strain, but continued low-level feedborne transmission until controls were fully effective.
Review: retain – This row appropriately represents the 2000–2001 EU-wide BSE ‘mad cow’ crisis. The event has been reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the surge reflects renewed or newly detected transmission of the existing classical BSE strain in already-affected European subregions, driven by incomplete feed controls and enhanced surveillance, rather than by a change in the agent. The country list and narrative have been updated to highlight Germany, Spain, Denmark and Italy’s widely reported first domestic cases in 2000–2001 and the sharp contemporaneous increase in France, while grouping other affected EU states in a general clause to avoid mis-dating smaller outbreaks.

Countries: Canada [1993 – single BSE case in a cow imported from the United Kingdom]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In 1993, Canada reported its first BSE-infected cow, an animal imported from the United Kingdom in 1987 that developed clinical disease several years after arrival, representing the first diagnosed BSE case in North America. Epidemiologic investigation concluded that the cow had probably been infected via contaminated feed in the UK prior to export, and no additional infected animals or domestic feed-borne transmission were identified in Canadian herds at that time. The incident nonetheless prompted precautionary surveillance, destruction of remaining high-risk UK imports, and tightening of import and feed policies in Canada and in trading partners concerned about potential BSE introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Pre-1990 trade in live cattle from the UK to Canada before the scale of the BSE epidemic was fully recognised; absence at that time of comprehensive controls on imports of potentially infected animals; limited early BSE surveillance capacity in North America. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the classical BSE strain via an already-infected imported cow, with no evidence for onward amplification in Canadian feed chains during this episode.
Review: review – The event is real and correctly described as a single BSE case in a UK-imported cow, with no documented indigenous spread in Canada. However, by the project’s criteria this imported-only, low-impact episode is unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful BSE emergence events globally, and imported cases without onward transmission should not be treated as inter-continental emergence. The row is therefore flagged for expert review, with a suggestion that it may be excluded in favour of higher-impact episodes (e.g., Canada’s 2003 indigenous outbreak) if a strict ‘top ten by impact’ filter is applied.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In May 2003, Canada confirmed BSE in a native-born beef cow in Alberta, the first recognised indigenous North American case and evidence of domestic feed-borne transmission. Intensive tracing, culling of cohorts, and expanded surveillance over 2003–2005 uncovered additional infected cattle from the same high-risk birth cohorts, while more than 30 countries imposed partial or total bans on Canadian beef and live cattle exports, causing severe economic disruption. Canada responded with stricter feed controls, specified-risk-material removal, and a large national surveillance programme, after which BSE incidence declined to very low levels and the country progressed toward, and ultimately achieved, negligible BSE risk status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical use of ruminant MBM in Canadian cattle feed prior to the 1997 ruminant-to-ruminant feed ban; possible importation of contaminated MBM from Europe; high-intensity commercial beef and dairy production; strong trade incentives that encouraged rapid surveillance and policy tightening once indigenous BSE was detected. Internal mechanisms: Inter-continental emergence of classical BSE in North American cattle herds with sustained amplification via contaminated feed; long incubation periods allowing infected birth cohorts to persist after initial control measures, until enhanced bans and removal of specified risk materials broke the cycle.
Review: retain – This is a major global BSE emergence episode: the first recognised indigenous classical BSE outbreak in North America, with substantial trade and production impacts. The inter_continental_emergence flag is appropriate because this is the first evidence of sustained feed-borne BSE transmission in a new continent (earlier Canadian and Omani cases were imported-only). The original re_emergence = Yes has been corrected to re_emergence = No, as there is no evidence of a new strain or prior elimination and reappearance in the same subregion; this is the initial establishment of classical BSE in North America.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In December 2003, the United States confirmed its first BSE case in a Holstein cow slaughtered in Washington State, which tracing showed had been imported from Canada and exposed there before the 1997 North American feed ban. The announcement triggered immediate domestic and international concern, leading many trading partners, including Japan and South Korea, to suspend imports of U.S. beef and provoking intensive media coverage and consumer anxiety. Through 2004, U.S. authorities implemented an expanded BSE surveillance programme, stricter feed and specified-risk-material rules, and trace-back investigations that found no additional classical BSE cases linked to the imported cow, helping to stabilise markets and lay the groundwork for gradual reopening of key export markets.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Pre-ban trade in live cattle between Canada and the United States; historical use of ruminant MBM in feed prior to the 1997 feed ban; limited pre-2003 active BSE surveillance in the U.S.; strong trade dependence on foreign beef markets that magnified the economic impact of a single confirmed case. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of classical BSE into the U.S. via an already-infected imported cow, with no evidence of sustained domestic amplification through U.S. feed chains during this episode; subsequent U.S.-born BSE cases were atypical and are treated as a separate, low-prevalence emergence pattern.
Review: retain – This row has been narrowed to focus on the 2003–2004 U.S. experience with its first detected BSE case (a Canadian-born classical BSE cow in Washington State) and the associated trade and policy response. The original version mixed this episode with later U.S.-born atypical cases (Texas 2005, Alabama 2006), which are now handled in a separate atypical-BSE event to avoid duplication. Event types have been simplified: first_detection = Yes (first BSE detected in the U.S.), with inter_continental_emergence = No (because continental emergence is attributed to Canada’s indigenous 2003 outbreak) and re_emergence = No (no prior U.S. BSE episode in this subregion).

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In September 2001, Japan confirmed its first domestic BSE case in a dairy cow, the first BSE case in a native-born animal reported outside Europe and the first recognised indigenous case in Asia, causing a collapse in domestic beef demand. In response, Japan rapidly implemented universal BSE testing of all slaughtered cattle and intensive farm-level inspections, which identified additional infected animals but showed that infection was largely confined to specific mid-1990s dairy cohorts at low overall prevalence. With a comprehensive feed ban on ruminant MBM, strict removal of specified risk materials, and sustained high-intensity surveillance, Japan’s BSE incidence declined sharply over the early 2000s, allowing gradual recovery of consumer confidence and cautious easing of some control measures while maintaining a very conservative safety regime.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical imports of MBM and possibly live cattle from BSE-affected regions before comprehensive bans; intensive dairy production systems; acute consumer and political sensitivity that led to adoption of universal cattle testing and conservative risk-management policies. Internal mechanisms: Inter-continental emergence of classical BSE in East Asia via contaminated feed, with a limited domestic epidemic focused on particular birth cohorts; long incubation periods delaying recognition until 2001, followed by rapid decline once strong controls took effect.
Review: retain – Japan’s 2001 BSE episode is well documented as the first indigenous BSE in a cow born outside Europe and marks inter-continental emergence into East Asia. The classification as inter_continental_emergence = Yes and first_detection = Yes (for Asia/Japan) is appropriate, and the time window 2001–2004 reflects the main period of intensive universal testing and case detection. No geographic or source corrections were needed.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In 2002, Israel reported its first and so far only BSE case, a 10‑year‑old dairy cow born and raised on a kibbutz farm in the Golan Heights, representing spread of BSE into Western Asia. Epidemiologic investigation suggested infection had probably occurred years earlier via imported feed ingredients that may have been contaminated with European MBM, but no further cases were identified despite extensive testing of slaughtered cattle and fallen stock. Israel quickly implemented precautionary measures including age-based slaughter policies, specified-risk-material controls, and long-term targeted surveillance, and no recurrence of BSE has been detected in its national herd.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dependence on imported protein meals (e.g., poultry or fish meals potentially contaminated with ruminant MBM); limited early awareness of BSE risk in the region; trade patterns linking Israel to European feed suppliers. Internal mechanisms: Intra-continental emergence of classical BSE within Asia, with a single recognised indigenous case and no evidence of sustained in-country amplification, implying a low-level point introduction rather than an established epidemic.
Review: review – The event is real (a single indigenous BSE case in Israel) and correctly described and classified as intra_continental_emergence within Asia. However, its impact in terms of case numbers and trade effects was modest compared with other BSE episodes (e.g., UK, EU 2000–2001, Japan, Canada, U.S., Brazil). It is therefore flagged for expert review as to whether a one‑case, non-epidemic event should remain among the top ten impact-focused emergence events for this EPP, or be deprioritised in favour of higher-burden episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In 2012, Brazil reported its first BSE case, an aged beef cow that had died in the state of Paraná in 2010 and was later confirmed to have atypical BSE after retrospective testing of archived brain tissue by national and international reference laboratories, constituting the first recognised BSE infection in South American cattle. The delayed disclosure led several importing countries to briefly suspend some Brazilian beef imports, despite risk assessments concluding that the case was a spontaneous atypical form with no evidence of feed-borne spread and that the carcass had not entered the food chain. Brazil retained its official negligible classical BSE risk status, but responded by reinforcing surveillance, validation of diagnostic procedures, and international communication to reassure trading partners.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large, export-oriented beef sector under intense international scrutiny; retrospective review of neurological cases and improved laboratory capacity that enabled detection of a single atypical case after the animal’s death; precautionary trade responses by importing countries sensitive to any BSE report. Internal mechanisms: Inter-continental emergence of atypical BSE in South America, most likely representing a sporadic prion strain arising in an older cow rather than feed-amplified classical BSE; no evidence for onward transmission, but confirmation that atypical BSE can occur at very low background levels in South American herds.
Review: retain – Brazil’s 2012 atypical BSE case is correctly identified as the first reported BSE infection in South American cattle and produced notable, if short-lived, trade impacts given Brazil’s role as a major beef exporter. Inter_continental_emergence = Yes is appropriate for the South American continent. The original re_emergence flag (used to denote a novel strain) has been set to No to avoid conflating first detection on a new continent with global re-emergence; atypicality is captured instead in the mechanism_or_driver narrative.

Countries: United States of America [2005-2023 – atypical BSE detections in older cattle at very low prevalence]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: Beginning in 2005, the United States identified its first native-born BSE case, an atypical form in a 12-year-old beef cow in Texas, followed by further atypical BSE detections in older cattle in Alabama (2006, 2017), California (2012), Florida (2018), South Carolina (2023) and possibly other isolated instances, all at extremely low prevalence under targeted surveillance of high-risk animals. These cases, classified as H-type or L-type atypical BSE, are considered sporadic events that arise in individual older cattle rather than from feed-borne exposure, and have not been associated with broader outbreaks or changes in classical BSE risk status. With reinforced feed bans and specified-risk-material removal already in place after 2003, no evidence of sustained transmission emerged, and the U.S. maintained or achieved negligible classical BSE risk designation while continuing long-term targeted surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post-2003 policy of intensive testing of high-risk cattle (fallen stock, emergency slaughter, neurologically abnormal animals) driven by international market scrutiny and WOAH risk-status criteria; improved diagnostic assays capable of distinguishing atypical from classical BSE. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence in the form of novel BSE phenotypes (H- and L-type atypical BSE) in older, predominantly beef cattle, likely arising sporadically without feed amplification; demonstration that such atypical forms occur at very low background levels in North American herds and can be detected under sustained, risk-targeted surveillance.
Review: retain – This row correctly summarises the long-term pattern of very rare, sporadic atypical BSE detections in U.S.-born cattle since 2005 and distinguishes these events from the earlier single classical BSE case imported from Canada. The classification as re_emergence = Yes is justified by the appearance of novel BSE strain types (H- and L-type) rather than by changes in incidence of classical BSE, while inter- and intra-continental emergence flags are kept at No because BSE was already present in North America. The time span through 2023 is in line with recent USDA and EFSA/WOAH summaries of atypical BSE reports.

Countries: Benin [2004]; Côte d’Ivoire [2005] (representing wider spread across West African cattle systems)
Host: Cattle in pastoral, agropastoral and mixed smallholder/commercial systems; Rhipicephalus microplus and other Rhipicephalus spp. ticks as vectors
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, the invasive Asian cattle tick Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus spread into West Africa, establishing in Benin and Côte d’Ivoire and progressively displacing local Boophilus ticks in many areas.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24258904/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent molecular and serological surveys documented appreciable prevalences and high incidence densities of Babesia bovis infection in cattle herds, for example around 10–15% prevalence and more than 15 new B. bovis infections per 100 cattle‑years in parts of Côte d’Ivoire, often with frequent co‑infection by Babesia bigemina and Anaplasma marginale.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1877959X17302637?utm_source=openai)) Through the 2010s and early 2020s, this vector–parasite complex turned bovine babesiosis from a sporadically recognized problem into a widespread health and productivity threat in multiple West African production systems, leading to increased emphasis on surveillance, diagnostics and integrated tick control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10064580/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance trade and movement of live cattle, including imports from Brazil and other endemic regions, introduced R. microplus into West Africa and allowed it to spread rapidly in the absence of stringent movement control; limited resources for acaricide treatment, emerging acaricide resistance and climate conditions favourable for one‑host ticks further supported establishment.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24258904/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel B. bovis genotype has been consistently implicated, but pairing of an efficient invasive vector with existing B. bovis lineages has increased transmission efficiency and geographic range (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation), leading to substantially higher infection pressure and more frequent clinical babesiosis in naïve or poorly immunised cattle.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1877959X17302637?utm_source=openai))
Review: Added as a major re‑occurrence event capturing the rise of Babesia bovis infections across parts of West Africa following invasion of the tick Rhipicephalus microplus from the mid‑2000s onward, supported by high prevalence and incidence density estimates in Benin and Côte d’Ivoire and modelling of the tick’s rapid regional spread.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24258904/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑occurrence (parasite long present in Africa and previously detected in West African cattle) rather than intra‑continental emergence, and flagged for review to refine exact country‑specific start years and the full list of affected countries as more detailed time‑series data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Commercial dairy and beef cattle plus a large feral cattle herd; Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks as vector
Event summary: In December 2007, Babesia bovis was accidentally introduced into previously babesiosis‑free New Caledonia when cattle vaccinated with a live tick‑fever (babesiosis/anaplasmosis) vaccine from Australia were imported into a territory already infested with the cattle tick Rhipicephalus microplus.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) During early 2008, clinical bovine babesiosis was confirmed on 22 commercial farms involving roughly 2300 high‑risk and 1600 suspect cattle, and infection also spread into a large feral cattle herd that served as a persistent reservoir.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) An intensive eradication campaign based on quarantine, repeated imidocarb treatment and aggressive tick control eliminated infection from commercial herds within about a year, followed by several years of targeted surveillance and feral‑cattle destocking to contain the last nidus of infection, after which New Caledonia again reported absence of bovine babesiosis.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of live vaccinated cattle into a naïve island territory, gaps in vaccine quality assurance allowing a B. bovis‑containing live vaccine to be used where the parasite was absent, and the presence of abundant competent R. microplus ticks and unmanaged feral cattle created ideal conditions for establishment and local spread of the vaccine strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence suggests the involvement of a novel B. bovis genotype or resistance trait; instead, the emergence reflects human‑mediated geographic range expansion of an existing live vaccine strain into a previously unexposed island population with pre‑existing tick vectors (geographic range expansion via host and vector movement).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events. Corrected classification from inter‑continental to intra‑continental emergence because Babesia bovis has long been endemic in northern Australia and other parts of Oceania, so New Caledonia represents spread to a new sub‑region, not a new continent.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babesiosis?utm_source=openai)) Set the 'first_detection' field to No, as global detection in cattle dates back to 1888 in Romania and B. bovis had been recognised in multiple continents well before 1990; this episode is the first detection in New Caledonia only.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4557164/?utm_source=openai)) Event‑level sources were pruned to focus on primary reports of the New Caledonia outbreak and eradication campaign (Barré et al., Hüe et al., WOAH/WOAH‑NC documents), removing generic references such as Wikipedia and broad factsheets that did not add event‑specific detail.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) Flagged for review only to confirm the chosen end year (2011) against the final eradication status of the feral herd in the most recent local reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2007] (Rio Grande do Sul state, Picada Café municipality)
Host: Beef heifers (Bos taurus / crossbred) recently introduced to endemic tick areas; Rhipicephalus microplus as vector
Event summary: In April 2007, a severe cerebral babesiosis outbreak caused by Babesia bovis occurred in a herd of 55 heifers recently brought onto a farm in Picada Café, Rio Grande do Sul, an area where bovine babesiosis is endemic.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Within five days, 28 animals (50.9%) died after acute fever, neurological signs, anemia and red‑coloured urine, and necropsy showed characteristic cherry‑pink discoloration of the gray matter of the brain with capillaries heavily congested by B. bovis‑infected erythrocytes.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Treatment of remaining cattle with imidocarb dipropionate, together with tick control and management changes, prevented further deaths during at least two months of follow‑up, after which surviving animals were sent to slaughter.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of immunologically naïve heifers into an area with heavy R. microplus infestation, along with management and environmental conditions favouring intense tick challenge, likely precipitated this high‑mortality cluster of cerebral babesiosis in an otherwise endemic region.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Internal mechanisms: The pathology and clinical pattern are consistent with typical highly virulent B. bovis strains that sequester in cerebral capillaries; no evidence was presented for a novel genotype or drug‑resistant phenotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic area rather than a genetically driven re‑emergence.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29))
Review: This row describes a well‑documented but highly localised outbreak confined to a single herd (28 deaths among 55 heifers over five days) in an area where Babesia bovis is already endemic.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) While clinically severe, its geographic scale and duration are small relative to continent‑wide spread or multi‑country emergence events; accordingly, it is unlikely to be among the ten most impactful global emergence episodes for B. bovis. Recommended decision: exclude from the final prioritised top‑ten event list, but retain the row in the working dataset as an example of severe re‑occurrence in an endemic South American setting and as a reference for cerebral babesiosis case descriptions.
Review Comment: we still keep althought it might not be the top 10 most impactful event

Host: Indigenous and improved cattle breeds in smallholder and pastoral systems along the Kenyan coast; R. microplus and other ticks as vectors
Event summary: Between roughly 2013 and 2020, cross‑sectional molecular surveys of 506 cattle in Kwale County on the Kenyan coast detected Babesia bovis DNA in 17.2% of animals, providing the first detailed evidence that this highly pathogenic species is present at substantial levels in Kenyan herds where bovine babesiosis had previously been attributed mainly to B. bigemina.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) The study showed marked spatial variation in infection prevalence across sub‑counties and coincided with recent records of the invasive tick Rhipicephalus microplus in the same region, raising concerns that babesiosis risk could increase along this busy livestock trade corridor linking Kenya and Tanzania.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Although most sampled cattle were clinically normal when bled, the authors warned that high underlying infection pressure could precipitate severe B. bovis outbreaks in susceptible herds and called for stronger surveillance and tick‑control programmes.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and spread of R. microplus into coastal Kenya via cross‑border movements of infested cattle, combined with expanding smallholder and commercial cattle production in humid coastal environments favourable for ticks, have increased opportunities for B. bovis transmission where earlier tick communities limited its impact.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Current evidence suggests geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission mediated by an invasive vector rather than a novel parasite strain; nevertheless, continuing evolution and local adaptation of B. bovis populations in East Africa remain possible and justify continued molecular surveillance.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain as a significant detection/re‑occurrence event but correct the event typing. The Parasites & Vectors study reports that Babesia bovis DNA had already been detected in Kenyan cattle before this survey and describes it as the first detailed report of a substantial level of occurrence, not the first detection in the host system; the 'first_detection' field has therefore been set to No.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Because B. bovis was documented in other parts of Eastern Africa, including Tanzania and the islands of Pemba and Unguja, well before 1990, this episode does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence at the UNSD sub‑region scale; that flag has been set to No and the event reclassified as a re‑occurrence linked to the recent invasion of R. microplus and changing tick ecology in coastal Kenya.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1702568/?utm_source=openai)) Event‑level source URLs have been focused on the Kenyan molecular survey and African tick‑range/epidemiology reviews; non‑specific references such as generic Wikipedia tick pages have been removed from this row.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle on smallholder and commercial farms on Santa Cruz Island; likely local tick vectors (exact species composition under investigation)
Event summary: In 2024, a molecular survey of 170 cattle from 19 farms on Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos detected Babesia bovis DNA in 11.2% of animals, alongside Babesia bigemina (14.7%), Trypanosoma vivax (14.7%) and a high prevalence of Anaplasma marginale (67.1%), documenting B. bovis on the islands for the first time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Earlier work had reported only B. bigemina from pooled tick samples on Santa Cruz, so the new findings indicate that B. bovis has recently been introduced and is now circulating within local cattle populations on at least a quarter of surveyed farms.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/13/10/910?utm_source=openai)) The authors highlighted that multiple haemoparasites and frequent co‑infections could impair productivity and potentially threaten endemic fauna if parasite–vector cycles expand further, and recommended Galápagos‑specific surveillance and integrated control strategies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of infected cattle or ticks from mainland Ecuador or other endemic areas, limited biosecurity for introduction of livestock to the islands, and environmental conditions suitable for tick vectors likely facilitated the introduction and establishment of B. bovis and other haemoparasites on Santa Cruz Island.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a novel B. bovis genotype; this event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion and re‑occurrence of a mainland parasite in a previously babesiosis‑free island ecosystem, with enhanced transmission risk due to multiple co‑circulating haemoparasites and naïve cattle hosts rather than documented genetic change in the parasite.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Added as a new emergence/re‑occurrence event because molecular surveys on Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos detected Babesia bovis DNA in 11.2% of sampled cattle and documented this parasite there for the first time, in a setting where only B. bigemina had previously been reported.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Although the absolute number of cattle is modest, the introduction affects a previously babesiosis‑free archipelago with conservation value and demonstrates establishment of B. bovis in about a quarter of sampled farms, justifying inclusion among major recent emergence episodes. Classified as re‑occurrence within South America (long‑endemic on the mainland) with no evidence yet of novel strain evolution. Flagged for review to confirm the sampling year underlying the 2024 publication and to monitor whether subsequent clinical outbreaks or spread to additional islands occur.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: France [pre-1990 endemic]; Spain [pre-1990 endemic]; Italy [pre-1990 endemic]; Germany [1990s]; Czechia [1990s]; Slovakia [1990s]; Poland [2000s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2000s]; Belgium [2000s]; Lithuania [2000s]; Latvia [2010s]
Host: Dogs
Event summary: From the early 1990s onwards, canine babesiosis caused mainly by Babesia canis expanded from long-standing endemic foci in southern Europe into central, western and northern European countries where cases had previously been rare and largely associated with travelled dogs. Over subsequent decades, autochthonous infections and new endemic foci were documented in Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland and later Baltic countries such as Lithuania and Latvia, in parallel with marked north- and westward expansion of the ornate dog tick Dermacentor reticulatus. By the 2010s, canine babesiosis was recognized as an emerging and in some regions rapidly spreading tick-borne disease across much of central and northeastern Europe, prompting increased surveillance and tick-control recommendations but no prospect of continent-wide elimination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climate warming with milder winters and longer vegetation seasons, land-use changes that created suitable meadow and riparian habitats, and changing wildlife host densities all favoured expansion of Dermacentor reticulatus into central and northern Europe; increased movement of pet dogs and greater veterinary awareness also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transovarial and transstadial transmission of B. canis in D. reticulatus and inherent geographic range expansion capacity of this tick species underpinned establishment of new endemic foci, with emerging reports of imidocarb treatment failures in some areas suggesting that drug resistance may be developing locally.
Review: retain – Large, multi-decade expansion of canine babesiosis due to Babesia canis and Dermacentor reticulatus into central, western and northern Europe is well supported by surveys and tick-distribution studies; the listed countries, broad time ranges and event types (intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence) are consistent with UNSD sub-regions and project rules, so no structural changes were made.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [2003]; Germany [2000s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000s]
Host: Dogs (including fighting breeds and imported dogs)
Event summary: In 2003, a dog in Spain with clinical babesiosis was confirmed by molecular testing to be infected with Babesia gibsoni, providing the first PCR-verified record of this predominantly Asian small Babesia species in a European dog. Over the 2000s and early 2010s, additional B. gibsoni infections were identified in dogs in Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries, often in American Pit Bull Terriers, American Staffordshire Terriers or other fighting breeds, some of which had links to imported dogs or organized dog fighting. Most cases were sporadic and concentrated in specific high-risk populations, but their recognition demonstrated that B. gibsoni had been introduced to Europe and could persist through dog-to-dog transmission, prompting broader diagnostic screening and guidance on preventing spread via bites and contaminated blood.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International movement and trade of dogs, particularly importation of fighting breeds from B. gibsoni-endemic regions in Asia and North America, and contact during dog fighting or other close-contact activities facilitated introduction and localized spread; increasing use of molecular diagnostics allowed differentiation of B. gibsoni from other small piroplasms. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of B. gibsoni in chronically infected carrier dogs and efficient non-tick transmission via blood exposure (bites, transfusions) enabled establishment in new canine populations despite the apparent absence of its primary tick vector in much of Europe; no clearly novel parasite lineage was implicated, so the event is best interpreted as inter-continental geographic spread of an existing lineage rather than true re-emergence.
Review: review – This event captures the emergence of Babesia gibsoni in European dogs, beginning with the first PCR-confirmed case in Spain in 2003 and subsequent cases in Germany and the UK; I reclassified it as an inter-continental emergence (inter_continental_emergence="true") and set first_detection, intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence to "false" because B. gibsoni had already been recognized in dogs in Asia and North America, and this episode reflects its spread into a new continent and several European sub-regions with mainly dog-to-dog transmission.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Equids (horses)
Event summary: In August 2008, equine piroplasmosis caused by Theileria equi (formerly Babesia equi) was detected in a Quarter Horse in Manatee County, Florida, in a country that had been considered free of the disease since 1988. Epidemiological investigation and extensive testing subsequently identified about 20 T. equi-infected horses on several linked premises, all associated with unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing, and tick surveillance did not find competent tick vectors infected with the parasite, pointing instead to iatrogenic transmission. Through 2008 and into 2009, aggressive quarantine, testing, euthanasia or removal of infected horses, and tightened biosecurity allowed authorities to contain and ultimately eradicate this focus, but the outbreak underscored vulnerabilities around blood-borne practices and illegal horse movements in maintaining EP-free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses, probably from Mexico, into an EP-free state; high-risk management practices in non-sanctioned racing (reuse of needles and syringes, possible blood transfusions, and multi-dose vials contaminated with blood) that amplified blood-borne spread; and initial lack of awareness of EP risk among participants. Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite genotype or change in vector competence was reported; the episode mainly reflects re-introduction and amplification of an established T. equi lineage in a previously cleared system, so it is best categorized as re-occurrence driven by failures in biosecurity and movement control rather than intrinsic parasite change.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the 2008 Florida equine piroplasmosis outbreak in Manatee County and is clearly among the largest recent equine Babesia episodes; I replaced less relevant or unstable URLs with peer-reviewed and official sources (JAVMA outbreak report, APHIS, an Australian EAD bulletin and a veterinary news article) but made no changes to the core timing, geography, host or event-type coding (re-occurrence).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Equids (horses)
Event summary: In 2009, a large Quarter Horse ranch in southern Texas that had not imported horses recently nor reported international travel detected equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi in multiple animals. Serologic screening showed that the majority of horses on the index ranch were infected, and field investigations documented heavy infestations with Amblyomma cajennense (now A. cajennense sensu lato/A. mixtum) and other ticks, with experimental work confirming A. cajennense as a competent vector under local conditions. The outbreak demonstrated sustained autochthonous tick-borne transmission of T. equi in a country long regarded as free of endemic EP, and eradication required years of quarantine, intensive tick control and either culling or prolonged imidocarb treatment of infected horses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density management and frequent movement of horses within and from the ranch, combined with abundant populations of Amblyomma cajennense and other ticks in south Texas, allowed efficient spread once T. equi was introduced; historical reliance on serologic surveillance alone may have missed chronically infected carriers. Internal mechanisms: Demonstration that A. cajennense could maintain and transmit T. equi in this ecosystem represents an important vector–parasite adaptation facilitating transmission in a setting where previous control programs had targeted other tick species; the event is therefore best treated as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion driven in part by changes in the effective vector assemblage.
Review: review – Retain this as a major equine piroplasmosis outbreak with well-documented local tick-borne transmission in south Texas; I set re_occurrence to "false" and re_emergence to "true" so that the event type matches the definition (reappearance in a previously affected subregion with clear new vector involvement) and respects the rule that re-occurrence and re-emergence are generally treated as mutually exclusive.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015]
Host: Dogs
Event summary: In the winter of 2015–2016, several severe cases of canine babesiosis due to Babesia canis were diagnosed in dogs with no travel history in Harlow, Essex, in the United Kingdom, which had previously been regarded as free from endemic canine babesiosis. Follow-up investigations through 2016–2017 identified additional locally acquired cases in Essex and Romford, and infected Dermacentor reticulatus ticks were found on affected dogs and in popular dog-walking fields, confirming an autochthonous transmission focus. Although local tick control, heightened veterinary awareness and owner education appeared to limit spread from the initial hotspot, the episode demonstrated that B. canis could establish enzootic transmission in parts of the UK given expanding D. reticulatus populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected dogs or ticks from continental Europe into areas of the UK where D. reticulatus populations were already present but under-recognized, combined with high dog traffic at affected recreational sites, created conditions for local transmission; warmer winters may have improved tick survival and activity. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and local establishment of D. reticulatus within the UK provided a competent vector able to sustain B. canis transmission in a country that had previously seen only imported cases, making this a re-emergent focus within a Northern Europe subregion already affected by B. canis in the Baltic states.
Review: review – The Essex/Romford outbreak represents the first clearly documented autochthonous focus of Babesia canis in the UK and should be retained as a distinct high-impact event; however, I changed intra_continental_emergence from "true" to "false" and left only re_emergence="true" because B. canis was already established elsewhere in the Northern Europe sub-region (e.g. Baltic countries), and spread to a new country within the same sub-region should not be classified as intra-continental emergence under the project rules.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (beef steers and local herd)
Event summary: In 2015, veterinarians investigated a severe outbreak of bovine babesiosis in the Dolores district of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, an area officially recognized as free from cattle fever ticks. The outbreak occurred after steers from Corrientes, a Babesia-endemic province, were moved into the district, bringing Rhipicephalus microplus ticks that successfully established on local pastures. Mixed infection with Babesia bovis and B. bigemina was confirmed by microscopy, serology and PCR, and around 140 cattle died with high fever, anemia and hemoglobinuria, making this one of the largest recent babesiosis losses reported from a South American tick-free zone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of parasitized steers from an endemic northern province into a nominally tick-free district breached the ecological and regulatory barrier that had previously protected Buenos Aires from cattle fever ticks; inadequate enforcement of tick-control measures at the interface between endemic and free zones, combined with local temperature and humidity conditions that allowed R. microplus to complete its life cycle, enabled rapid amplification of both ticks and Babesia parasites. Internal mechanisms: No new parasite genotypes were reported; the event reflects re-introduction and amplification of existing B. bovis and B. bigemina lineages via expansion of a well-known tick vector into a previously protected area, fitting the definition of re-occurrence rather than true re-emergence driven by intrinsic pathogen change.
Review: review – Added this new row to capture a 2015 bovine babesiosis outbreak in the Dolores district of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, where introduction of Rhipicephalus microplus–infested steers from Corrientes into a tick-free zone led to about 140 cattle deaths; coded as a high-impact re-occurrence within South America driven by animal movement and tick establishment rather than parasite evolution, and recommended for retention as one of the major livestock Babesia events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (beef herd)
Event summary: In 2018, an organic beef production farm in northern Germany with no previous history of redwater fever experienced an outbreak of bovine babesiosis caused by Babesia divergens, transmitted by Ixodes ricinus ticks. The initially naïve herd suffered substantial morbidity and mortality, with more than 20 adult cattle dying over a short period, and clinical cases clustered in one group of animals grazing pastures bordering a nature reserve with high tick exposure. After treatment of affected animals, changes in grazing management and intensified tick control, acute clinical cases declined, but follow-up studies showed that B. divergens had become endemic in the herd, highlighting the continued re-emergence potential of bovine babesiosis in northwestern Europe when herd immunity wanes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term decline in incidence of bovine babesiosis in parts of northern Europe led to reduced natural exposure and waning herd immunity, while suitable Ixodes ricinus habitats and wildlife reservoirs persisted in adjacent natural areas; the farm’s extensive grazing system increased cattle–tick contact on specific pastures. Internal mechanisms: No new parasite variants were identified; this outbreak is best understood as re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion driven by ecological and management changes that increased exposure of an immunologically naïve herd to an established B. divergens–tick cycle.
Review: retain – The 2018 Babesia divergens outbreak on a northern German beef farm, with more than 20 deaths in an otherwise naïve herd, is clearly documented and correctly coded as a re-occurrence (no evidence for new parasite variants or inter-/intra-continental spread); geography (Germany, Western Europe) and timing are accurate, and the cited sources are appropriate.

Host: Cattle, goats, sheep, and humans exposed through handling and consuming meat from sick or dead livestock
Event summary: From August 2009, multiple anthrax outbreaks began in cattle and small ruminants in northwestern Bangladesh (especially Pabna, Sirajganj and Tangail districts), leading to numerous animal deaths and slaughter of sick animals. Through 2009–2010, at least 14 linked village-level outbreaks were documented in these districts with 39 confirmed and 234 probable human cutaneous anthrax cases, and nationally about 607 suspected human cases were reported during August–October 2010 across 12 districts, all strongly associated with butchering and eating meat from diseased livestock. Emergency public health messaging, guidance on carcass disposal, and expansion of livestock vaccination gradually reduced human and animal case numbers after late 2010, although anthrax remains endemic in Bangladeshi livestock with recurrent smaller outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing endemic spore foci in floodplain and riverine soils; high densities of cattle and small ruminants linked to intensive dairy and draft use; historically low routine livestock vaccination coverage; economic pressure on poor households leading to slaughter and consumption of moribund animals; informal meat markets and unsafe carcass disposal. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing indicates circulation of several closely related B. anthracis genotypes but no evidence of a novel, more virulent lineage; the 2009–2010 spike reflects environmental and social drivers and heightened recognition rather than genetic re-emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row correctly captures the nationally important 2009–2010 wave of zoonotic anthrax outbreaks in Bangladesh, with timing, geography, host range and event-type (re-occurrence driven by endemic spores, low vaccination and risky slaughter/consumption practices) consistent with primary epidemiologic reports. I simplified the countries field to “Bangladesh [2009-2010]” to match the guidance for linked single-country episodes; no other structural changes were needed and the cited sources remain appropriate primary descriptions of the event.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009-2010]; Germany [2009-2010]
Host: Humans who inject heroin (persons who inject drugs), exposed via contaminated heroin; the source animal reservoir is presumed to be livestock in heroin-producing regions outside Europe
Event summary: In late 2009, clinicians in Scotland detected severe soft-tissue infections and sepsis among people who inject heroin, which were confirmed as anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis associated with contaminated heroin batches, marking the first recognized large cluster of injectional anthrax. Over 2009–2010, 119 affected heroin users were identified across Scotland, England and Germany (about half laboratory-confirmed), with a high case-fatality ratio, and molecular typing showed all isolates belonged to a single clonal strain contaminating the heroin supply. The outbreak waned by late 2010 after public health alerts, harm reduction messaging and depletion or removal of contaminated heroin batches, although sporadic cases and a later smaller multi-country wave in 2012–2013 demonstrated that this novel transmission route into a high-risk human subpopulation had not been completely eliminated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contamination of heroin during production or transit in regions where anthrax is endemic in livestock; globalized illicit drug trafficking that distributed contaminated product to multiple European countries; high-risk injection practices (“skin popping,” intramuscular injection into deep soft tissues) that create anaerobic conditions favorable for toxin production. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by a single clonal strain (e.g., Ba4599, Trans-Eurasian clade) without clear evidence of enhanced virulence compared with classical zoonotic strains; the public health importance lies in host expansion into people who inject drugs and the emergence of a new clinical presentation, not in a new genotype or geographic range.
Review: Decision: retain (but mark for thematic review). Rationale: This entry represents the defining, largest-ever outbreak of injectional anthrax globally (≈120 affected heroin users in Scotland, England and Germany) and is widely cited as a novel anthropogenic manifestation of B. anthracis infection in a new human risk group. I corrected the countries field to list “United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009-2010]; Germany [2009-2010]” and removed the subnational “England” label, while keeping the sub-region coding (Northern Europe; Western Europe) consistent with the UNSD country list. Event-type as re-emergence (host expansion/new clinical form) without intra- or inter-continental emergence remains appropriate. Because this episode is dominated by human cases but ultimately originates in animal-derived contamination, it should be cross-checked against the separate human-host anthrax sheet for consistency.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Hippopotamuses (Hippopotamus amphibius) in a game management area; humans in nearby villages exposed via handling and eating meat from carcasses
Event summary: During August–September 2011, an anthrax epizootic occurred among hippopotamuses along the South Luangwa River in Chama District, northeastern Zambia, with approximately 81–85 hippos found dead over several weeks. In the surrounding communities, about 511–521 suspected human anthrax cases and 5 deaths were reported, mostly cutaneous disease linked to butchering, carrying and eating meat from hippos found dead in the river. Following outbreak investigations, intensive community education on not handling or consuming carcass meat, and the eventual onset of the rainy season that reduced contact with contaminated riverbed sediments, human case numbers declined and the joint wildlife–human outbreak subsided, although similar wildlife-associated anthrax events have recurred in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe dry-season conditions and delayed rains in 2011 leading to water scarcity and concentration of hippos in shrinking pools and deepened riverbeds where spores had accumulated; long-term environmental contamination from previous wildlife epizootics; chronic food insecurity in nearby human communities that encouraged use of carcass meat despite health risks; close overlap of carcass sites and riverside settlements in a protected game management area. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel B. anthracis strain; disease reflects ingestion of long-persistent spores from river sediments and classic trophic transmission from wildlife carcasses to humans, i.e. environmentally driven re-occurrence rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is a very large, well-documented wildlife–human anthrax outbreak (≈85 hippos, >500 suspected human cases, 5 deaths) in Eastern Africa, with details on timing, location and risk factors tightly supported by primary reports. Geography, host description and classification as re-occurrence driven by dry-season ecology, food insecurity and carcass consumption are appropriate, and no structural corrections were required.

Host: Free-ranging wood bison (Bison bison athabascae) in the Mackenzie Bison Range
Event summary: In summer 2012, routine surveillance flights over the Mackenzie Bison Range in the Northwest Territories of Canada detected numerous dead wood bison, and laboratory investigation confirmed anthrax as the cause of mortality. The 2012 episode became the largest documented anthrax outbreak in this herd, with at least 440 bison deaths—over one-third of the population—leading to a drop below 1,000 animals and reversing previous recovery gains. Intensive carcass burning and chemical disinfection, herd monitoring and complete closure of hunting were implemented, and as seasonal conditions changed and carcasses were removed or decomposed, the outbreak ceased; however, anthrax remains a recurrent threat to northern Canadian bison populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic variability and sequences of flooding followed by drying that concentrate spores in low-lying meadows and wetland grazing sites; high local bison density and herd movements through historic anthrax foci; limited feasibility of preventive vaccination and handling for widely dispersed, free-ranging herds. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks in the Mackenzie herd are driven by exposure to persistent soil spore banks established during prior epizootics; serologic data from non-outbreak years show fluctuating but ongoing exposure, consistent with environmental re-occurrence rather than emergence of a novel strain or altered virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row correctly summarizes the largest known anthrax epizootic in the Mackenzie wood bison herd, with numbers (minimum 440 bison fatalities) and management actions aligned with territorial government and peer-reviewed accounts. Geography (North America / Northern America, Canada – Northwest Territories) and classification as environmentally driven re-occurrence in a long-recognized anthrax focus are appropriate, and no coding changes were required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) herds; humans in nomadic Nenets communities exposed mainly through handling or consuming infected animals
Event summary: In July–August 2016, after roughly 70 years without reported anthrax in the region, a severe outbreak occurred among semi-domesticated reindeer on the Yamal Peninsula in northwest Siberia, killing around 2,300–2,650 animals (about 6–7% of the local reindeer population) within a few weeks and prompting large emergency vaccination campaigns. Thirty-six human anthrax cases, mainly cutaneous and gastrointestinal, were reported among local Nenets herders and their families and workers, with at least one death, leading to extensive quarantines, evacuations of camps and restrictions on reindeer movements. With onset of colder conditions, intensive carcass disposal, large-scale vaccination of reindeer and movement controls, the outbreak subsided, but it highlighted the renewed risk of reactivating long-dormant anthrax foci under Arctic warming and permafrost thaw.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged regional warming and rapid thawing of permafrost over preceding years, including an exceptional summer heatwave in 2016, likely exposed buried carcasses from historic anthrax epizootics and released spores onto pastures grazed by reindeer; discontinuation or reduction of routine reindeer vaccination in the years before the outbreak; extensive long-distance movements of large semi-domesticated herds along traditional migration routes that traversed contaminated areas. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that the causative B. anthracis belonged to local lineages consistent with older outbreaks; the key mechanism was environmental reactivation and geographic re-expression of a dormant focus, not emergence of a new genotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is a globally significant, well-characterized outbreak linking climate-driven permafrost thaw to reactivation of an old anthrax focus, with reindeer and human case numbers, timing and geographic details consistent across multiple primary and review sources. Continent/sub-region classification (Europe / Eastern Europe, Russian Federation) follows the project’s treatment of Russia, and event-type as re-occurrence driven by environmental change (rather than emergence of a new strain) is appropriate; no structural edits were required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Hippopotamuses and Cape buffalo in Bwabwata National Park; potential spillover risk to nearby livestock and humans (no confirmed human or livestock cases)
Event summary: In late September 2017, wildlife authorities in northeastern Namibia detected a sudden die-off of hippopotamuses and Cape buffalo along the Kavango River in Bwabwata National Park, and field and laboratory testing confirmed anthrax as the cause. By early December, 155 hippopotamus and 86 Cape buffalo carcasses had been located and disposed of in the Mahango and Buffalo core areas, representing roughly 26% and 3.8% of the pre-epizootic local populations, respectively, making this one of the largest recorded wildlife anthrax events in Namibia. Intensive carcass burial and decontamination, vaccination campaigns in adjacent livestock, post-exposure prophylaxis and education for more than a thousand potentially exposed community members, and the onset of the rainy season together curtailed the outbreak, and no associated human or domestic animal cases were documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal drying of river levels and wetlands, which concentrated wildlife at shrinking water bodies and grazing sites where spores accumulated; high densities of hippos and buffalo on historically contaminated floodplains; limited feasibility of vaccinating free-ranging wildlife and promptly removing large carcasses; growing human presence and tourism along the river raising concern for spillover. Internal mechanisms: Anthrax in this area reflects persistent environmental spore banks and periodic wildlife epizootics driven by hydrological and ecological conditions; there is no evidence of a novel strain, so this event is best classified as ecological re-occurrence in a known endemic region.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The event itself is clearly among the major recent wildlife anthrax epizootics, but the original summary mis-stated carcass numbers by treating pre-outbreak population estimates (588 hippos, 2,216 buffalo) as deaths. I have corrected the narrative to report 155 hippopotamus and 86 Cape buffalo carcasses, and to explain that these correspond to ≈26% and 3.8% of local populations, following Cossaboom et al. (2019). Geography, host list and classification as re-occurrence in a well-known Namibian wildlife focus remain appropriate, and sources have been pruned to emphasize the primary EID article and contemporaneous national reports.
