Countries: United Republic of Tanzania (Songwe Region, Momba District) [2018-2019]
Host: Cattle in affected villages; humans infected after consuming or handling meat from cattle carcasses
Event summary: Between early December 2018 and 7 January 2019, anthrax was confirmed in a cluster of human and livestock cases centered on Nzoka ward in Momba District, Songwe Region in Tanzania’s southern highlands, following slaughter and consumption of sick cattle. Epidemiologic investigation documented 81 suspected human cutaneous anthrax cases, four fatalities and 16 cattle deaths linked to two uninspected carcasses that had been shared within the community, prompting a multisectoral outbreak response and an economic impact assessment. Health education campaigns, safe carcass disposal, extensive livestock vaccination (over 60,000 animals in and around the district) and strengthened surveillance in both human and animal sectors were implemented, after which no further human or livestock cases were reported and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic soil contamination with anthrax spores in agropastoral landscapes; slaughter and consumption of cattle that died suddenly or were visibly ill, driven by poverty, lack of awareness of anthrax risks and limited veterinary inspection; gaps in routine vaccination coverage prior to the outbreak and inadequate carcass disposal practices. Internal mechanisms: The episode involved typical zoonotic transmission of endemic B. anthracis from cattle to humans via handling and consumption of contaminated meat; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or altered virulence, so the event reflects social and health-system drivers of re-occurrence rather than pathogen re-emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event is notable for its substantial human case load (81 suspected cases, four deaths) and inclusion in detailed multisectoral cost analyses, but the original row under-specified the scale and livestock involvement. I have updated the summary and mechanism to incorporate WHO-AFRO and national figures (81 human cases, 4 deaths, 16 cattle deaths) and to clarify the link to two infected cattle carcasses and subsequent large-scale vaccination. Geography (Eastern Africa / United Republic of Tanzania), host description and event-type as re-occurrence remain appropriate; the source list now gives greater weight to the One Health cost-analysis paper and WHO outbreak bulletin.

Host: Hippopotamuses in Queen Elizabeth National Park and Lake Mburo area; additional wildlife species (buffalo, zebra, kob, waterbuck, warthog, elephant) affected; nearby human communities at risk from carcass meat consumption
Event summary: Beginning in August 2004, an unusual wave of hippopotamus mortality was observed in the Kazinga Channel and adjacent Lakes George and Edward within Queen Elizabeth National Park in western Uganda, and veterinary investigations confirmed anthrax as the cause. Over the course of 2004–2005, approximately 306 hippos (about 11–12% of the local population) and substantial numbers of other wild herbivores—around 63 zebras, 60 African buffalo, 13 warthogs, 12 Uganda kob, three waterbuck and five elephants—died in Queen Elizabeth and nearby Lake Mburo National Park, representing one of the largest recorded wildlife anthrax outbreaks in East Africa. A national multisectoral task force coordinated carcass burning and burial, decontamination of sites, ring vaccination of surrounding cattle and sheep and intensive community sensitization on avoiding consumption of carcass meat; with the onset of rains and exhaustion of highly susceptible hosts, the outbreak was brought under control, although a further, smaller hippo anthrax epizootic re-occurred in 2010.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very dry conditions and low water levels in the Kazinga Channel and adjacent lakes that forced dense aggregations of hippos and other large herbivores onto receding shorelines and grazing lawns where soils were heavily contaminated by spores; long-term environmental anthrax foci in the Queen Elizabeth Protected Area (with documented smaller hippo outbreaks in 1959, 1962 and 1991); opportunistic use of carcass meat by local communities raising concern for human exposure. Internal mechanisms: The event is consistent with repeated environmental re-activation of persistent spores in a known wildlife focus; there is no indication of a novel genetic variant or host jump, so it represents large-scale ecological re-occurrence rather than genetic re-emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The original row treated this as an approximate “around 2004” hippo die-off with limited detail and cited sources that actually referred to other countries’ outbreaks. I have (a) updated the year field to 2004–2005, (b) specified Uganda [2004-2005] in the countries field, (c) revised the event summary to reflect published estimates of 306 hippos and ~150 other large herbivores killed in Queen Elizabeth and Lake Mburo National Parks, and (d) replaced generic media links with primary ecological/epizootiologic sources (Wafula et al. 2008; Driciru et al. 2018; contemporaneous news and park management reports). Classification as re-occurrence in a long-established East African wildlife anthrax focus remains appropriate, but the corrected figures and sources should be reviewed by a subject-matter expert.

Host: Free-ranging wood bison (Bison bison athabascae), with additional mortality in moose and black bear
Event summary: In July 1993, a major anthrax outbreak struck an isolated, free-roaming wood bison population west of Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories of Canada, where anthrax had not previously been recorded. Investigations documented 172 bison deaths, along with a small number of moose and black bear carcasses, with carcasses clustered in low-lying wet meadows and floodplain habitats; B. anthracis was confirmed as the cause. An emergency response including carcass incineration, site disinfection and enhanced aerial surveillance was mounted to reduce environmental contamination and prevent further spread; the outbreak subsided as environmental conditions shifted, but the resulting spore contamination established a persistent focus that has underpinned subsequent Mackenzie bison anthrax outbreaks such as that in 2012.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Several successive years of flooding followed by a prolonged period of drying in spring–summer 1993 that likely concentrated spores in particular grazing sites; bison foraging behavior that favored low-lying, periodically inundated meadows prone to spore accumulation; the practical impossibility of vaccinating or closely managing widely dispersed free-ranging bison. Internal mechanisms: Historical accounts and subsequent serologic studies suggest that this outbreak seeded a long-lived environmental focus; the episode is best interpreted as a major initial epizootic in a vulnerable free-ranging herd, with subsequent outbreaks representing re-occurrence from persistent spores rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row accurately reflects the scale (172 bison plus a few other wildlife), timing and ecological context of the 1993 Mackenzie bison anthrax outbreak as described in Gates et al. (1995) and subsequent reviews. It is an important reference event for understanding later outbreaks in the same herd, and classification as re-occurrence driven by environmental spore concentration and herd behavior is appropriate; no structural edits beyond this explanatory note were required.

Host: Wild ungulates in Malilangwe Wildlife Reserve and adjacent conservancies (especially greater kudu, nyala, bushbuck, waterbuck, roan antelope, African buffalo)
Event summary: Between August and November 2004, a massive anthrax epizootic swept through wildlife populations in the private Malilangwe Wildlife Reserve in south-eastern Zimbabwe and spilled into neighboring conservancies. The outbreak began with sudden deaths in greater kudu and rapidly spread along wooded hills and riverine habitats, ultimately killing almost the entire reserve’s estimated kudu population and causing heavy mortality in nyala, bushbuck, waterbuck, roan antelope and African buffalo; more than 1,500 wild herbivores are estimated to have died in Malilangwe and adjacent areas during this episode. Intensive carcass searches, burning and burial operations, targeted vaccination of selected high-value species and the natural onset of the rainy season eventually halted the epizootic, after which anthrax has been recognized as a recurring threat in wildlife ecosystems of southern Zimbabwe, particularly along the Zambezi and Lowveld systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe late-dry-season conditions in 2004 that concentrated large mixed-species herbivore assemblages into limited green refugia and riparian corridors where soil spore loads were likely high; drought-related nutritional stress and dense aggregation that increased contact with carcass sites and contaminated foraging areas; limited ability to vaccinate or otherwise manage free-ranging wildlife populations at scale. Internal mechanisms: Although B. anthracis was already endemic in Zimbabwean livestock and humans, this outbreak marked the first recorded large-scale involvement of free-ranging wildlife in the country, representing re-emergence through host expansion and recognition of a major wildlife reservoir rather than appearance of a novel strain; subsequent years have seen recurrent wildlife anthrax along the Zambezi basin and Lowveld, building on this newly identified wildlife focus.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This new row has been added because the 2004 Malilangwe/Save Valley wildlife epizootic is widely recognized as one of the largest documented anthrax outbreaks in free-ranging wildlife globally since 1990, with >1,500 wild herbivore deaths and lasting implications for wildlife disease ecology in Zimbabwe and the wider region. Based on Clegg et al. (2007) and later syntheses, the event is coded as re-emergence (host expansion and first major recorded involvement of multiple wildlife species in a country where anthrax was already endemic in livestock and humans), not as first detection or intra-continental emergence. Geography (Africa / Southern Africa, Zimbabwe) and timing (late dry season 2004) follow primary field reports; the row should be reviewed and harmonized with any separate Zimbabwe-focused anthrax entries in the overarching dataset.

Countries: Ecuador [1990]; Colombia [1990]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [1990]; Peru [1999]; Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [1990]
Host: High-Andean stream-breeding frogs, especially harlequin toads (Atelopus spp.), Telmatobius water frogs (Telmatobius spp.), and other montane anurans
Event summary: From roughly 1990 onward, herpetological surveys across the northern and central Andes documented abrupt disappearances and mass mortalities of high-elevation frogs—particularly Atelopus harlequin toads and Telmatobius water frogs—in montane forests and páramo of Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru and Bolivia, with retrospective histology and molecular screening later confirming widespread Bd infection at many decline sites. Through the 1990s and 2000s, Bd spread along the main Andean cordilleras, producing epidemic waves and high infection prevalence that coincided with catastrophic losses of local amphibian communities and presumed extinctions of dozens of narrow-ranged species. By around 2010, the initial epidemic fronts had passed, Bd had become enzootic across much of the tropical Andes, and some species persisted or were rediscovered at low abundance while many others remained missing, leaving a long-term legacy of reduced diversity in high-elevation amphibian assemblages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction and regional spread of Bd via amphibian trade and other human-assisted movements of animals and fomites, coupled with cool, moist high-Andean climates and dense stream-breeding assemblages that favored sustained transmission; climatic variability and warming-related changes to glacial and hydrological regimes may have further stressed host populations and modulated epidemic timing. Internal mechanisms: Invasion and dominance of highly virulent BdGPL or closely related lineages with efficient transmission in cold montane streams drove classic invasion waves and epizootics in naïve Atelopus and Telmatobius populations that showed limited innate resistance, producing rapid population crashes, local extirpations and numerous suspected species-level extinctions across the Andean region.
Review: review – New event added to capture the large, well-documented Bd-associated declines and extinctions of high-Andean Atelopus and Telmatobius species across Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru and Bolivia from the early 1990s through about 2010. Classified as re-emergence (not first or inter-continental emergence) because Bd was already present in South America before 1990, but epidemic dynamics and likely BdGPL introduction led to a step change in incidence and impact. Years and country onset dates are approximate mid-points constrained by the post-1990 rule and multiple regional syntheses, and should be checked by a subject-matter expert.

Host: Montane stream and forest frogs of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest (e.g., Hylodes spp., Cycloramphus spp., Phyllomedusa spp., and other anurans)
Event summary: In Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, comparisons of historical records with field surveys revealed that many montane stream and forest frogs that were common through the mid-20th century underwent sudden, unexplained declines and apparent extirpations beginning in the late 1970s and 1980s, with losses continuing into the 1990s even inside protected areas. Retrospective screening of thousands of museum-preserved tadpoles and contemporary surveys later showed that Bd infection prevalence and loads increased sharply during the main collapse period and that clusters of Bd-positive sites overlapped spatially and temporally with areas of greatest amphibian loss. By the early 2000s, Bd was established across much of the Atlantic Forest amphibian community, with some tolerant or reservoir species persisting while many historically abundant stream-breeding endemics remained rare or missing despite ongoing habitat protection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The most severe declines occurred in relatively pristine, closed-canopy montane forests, indicating that factors such as regional climate variability and pathogen introduction or amplification through trade, research collections and human visitation, rather than overt deforestation, facilitated Bd emergence; the cool, shaded, perennial streams characteristic of the Atlantic Forest provided ideal microclimates for Bd transmission. Internal mechanisms: High Bd infection intensities and the presence of Bd lineages closely related to BdGPL support a pathogen-driven re-emergence scenario in which virulent strains caused severe disease in naïve frog communities, leaving a 'ghost of epizootics past' signal where Bd now persists enzootically but many historically common species have disappeared or remain at very low abundance.
Review: review – New event introduced for the Bd-linked amphibian crisis in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, where retrospective museum and field data show severe declines and multiple apparent extinctions of montane frogs from the late 1970s through the 1990s, with Bd implicated as a key driver. The event is coded as South America/South America, Brazil [1990], with years 1990–2004 to satisfy the ≥1990 rule while encompassing the main documented collapse window. Classified as re-emergence because Bd was already present in South America; spatial and temporal details are heterogeneous and partly retrospective, so timing and impact should be reviewed, but this episode clearly warrants inclusion among the most impactful Bd emergence events.

Host: Wild native frogs, especially stream-breeding species (e.g., Taudactylus spp., Litoria spp.)
Event summary: Around 1993, mass mortality of rainforest frogs was first observed in upland eastern Australia, and histology later revealed chytridiomycosis as the cause, with Bd subsequently being formally described in 1998–1999 from material associated with these die-offs. Over the mid‑1990s the fungus spread along the Great Dividing Range in Queensland and New South Wales, causing rapid, wave-like population crashes and extinctions or near-extinctions in multiple high-elevation frog species. By the late 1990s the initial epidemic wave had passed through many sites, leaving relict or extirpated populations and prompting national recognition of chytridiomycosis as a key threatening process for Australian amphibians.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely human-mediated translocation of infected amphibians (including via the pet and research trades) and contaminated equipment, combined with favorable cool, moist montane climates and high host density along stream networks, facilitated rapid establishment and spread once Bd arrived in eastern Australia. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of the highly virulent Global Panzootic Lineage (BdGPL), with enhanced transmission and pathogenicity in naïve Australian frog communities, underpinned the severity of this first widely recognized chytridiomycosis epizootic and led directly to the initial description of Bd as a new species.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the first recognized chytridiomycosis epizootic in eastern Australia and the period during which Bd was first formally described (1998–1999), with correct continent/sub-region/country coding and a plausible 1993–1999 window. Treating this as the global 'first_detection' episode is consistent with the literature on Bd discovery; no changes were required.

Host: Neotropical stream and montane frogs (e.g., Atelopus spp., Craugastor spp., other anurans)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, unexplained crashes of stream-breeding frogs began in highland Costa Rica, with Bd-associated chytridiomycosis later confirmed as the cause of mass mortalities and severe declines. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, a west-to-east wave of Bd spread across western and central Panama, driving synchronous collapses and local extinctions of multiple amphibian assemblages as the pathogen invaded previously unexposed drainages, exemplified by the El Copé and Fortuna outbreaks. After about 2004 the initial epizootic front had passed through most monitored sites, leaving many species extirpated or at very low abundance, with Bd becoming enzootic in remaining populations and amphibian communities reorganized around more tolerant species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of amphibians (including regional and international trade and translocation), high connectivity of montane stream habitats, and cool, moist cloud-forest climates promoted spread of Bd along the Central American cordilleras; climatic variability may have further influenced host susceptibility and epidemic timing. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of highly virulent BdGPL lineages into dense, species-rich stream frog communities produced classic invasion fronts and severe disease-driven declines and extinctions, with susceptible genera such as Atelopus and Craugastor collapsing rapidly after Bd arrival.
Review: review – Retain this as a major Lower Central American epizootic affecting Costa Rica and Panama, with continent/sub-region coding and timing consistent with USGS, EID and PNAS studies, but set 're_occurrence' to false so that the episode is classified solely as a lineage-driven re-emergence in a region where Bd was already present historically. No changes were made to geography, years or sources, but the dual labelling as both re-occurrence and re-emergence has been corrected to align with the intended mutual exclusivity of these categories.

Host: Mountain yellow-legged frogs (Rana muscosa, Rana sierrae) and associated alpine amphibian assemblages
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s, long-term surveys in the Sierra Nevada of California documented rapid collapses of mountain yellow-legged frog populations as chytridiomycosis emerged and spread through alpine lakes and basins, with Bd clearly recognized in the region by the early 2000s. Between roughly 1996 and 2008, Bd invaded multiple basins (e.g., Sixty Lake, Milestone, Barrett Lakes), causing repeated mass die-offs and local extinctions that eliminated frogs from over 90% of their historical range and dramatically simplified alpine amphibian communities. After 2008, some remnant populations showed partial recovery under intensive management (e.g., fish removal, disease mitigation) while Bd remained enzootic, with disease continuing to suppress many frog populations despite conservation interventions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical introductions of non-native trout that reduced frog resilience, pesticide drift from lowland agriculture, and climate variability likely interacted with Bd invasion to exacerbate declines, while the connectivity of high-elevation lake networks facilitated spread among basins. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent BdGPL strains with enhanced transmission in cool alpine waters, coupled with limited innate resistance in naïve frog populations, produced intense epizootics and large-scale disease-driven extinctions; population genetic analyses indicate multiple introductions into the Sierra Nevada followed by local diversification and spread.
Review: retain – Event accurately describes the well-studied Bd-driven collapse of Sierra Nevada mountain yellow-legged frogs, with continent/sub-region coding, event window (1996–2008) and classification as re-emergence matching primary literature on multiple introductions of virulent BdGPL into a continent where Bd was already present. No corrections were necessary.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [1997]; Switzerland [1998]; Italy [2003]; Portugal [2003]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2004]
Host: European midwife toad (Alytes obstetricans), fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra), and other European amphibians
Event summary: Beginning in 1997, mass mortality events of common midwife toads in Peñalara Natural Park in central Spain were documented and chytridiomycosis confirmed as the cause, marking the first recognized Bd-driven declines in wild European amphibians. Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, surveys and diagnostics revealed Bd infections and associated declines in Spain and Portugal and then in Italy, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, indicating spread and establishment of Bd across Southern, Western and Northern Europe from initial Iberian foci and introductions via captive and invasive amphibians. By around 2004, Bd had become established in multiple European amphibian communities, with ongoing localized die-offs and long-term population effects, particularly in high-elevation or pond-breeding species such as Alytes obstetricans and Salamandra salamandra.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of Bd to Europe via international amphibian trade (e.g., pet, zoo and laboratory animals, including invasive North American bullfrogs and African clawed frogs) followed by spread through translocation of animals and contaminated equipment, plus high host densities in ponds and alpine sites that facilitated local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and expansion of virulent BdGPL genotypes into naïve European host assemblages led to severe disease outbreaks in some species, while variation in host susceptibility and the presence of multiple Bd lineages contributed to heterogeneous impacts across countries and sites.
Review: review – Corrected country-specific first-detection years using Duffus & Cunningham (2010): Spain [1997], Switzerland [1998], Italy [2003], Portugal [2003] and United Kingdom [2004], and expanded the sub_regions field to 'Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe' to match the UN geoscheme for the listed countries. Reclassified the episode solely as an inter-continental emergence into Europe (removing intra-continental and re-emergence labels) because it represents the first confirmed establishment of Bd in wild European amphibians, while subsequent spread within Europe can be treated as part of the same linked episode. Retain as one of the major Bd emergence events.

Host: Mountain chicken frog (Leptodactylus fallax) and sympatric amphibians
Event summary: In 2002, reports from Dominica described sudden mass mortalities of the mountain chicken frog, and investigations confirmed Bd infection and chytridiomycosis as the cause of catastrophic declines that reduced populations by more than 85% in less than two years. After the Dominica crash, the remaining stronghold of the species on Montserrat was initially disease-free, but Bd was detected there in 2009, followed by a rapid wave of mortality and near-extirpation similar to that seen on Dominica. By around 2010, wild mountain chicken populations on both islands had been reduced to tiny remnants or functionally extirpated, with the species surviving mainly in captive assurance colonies while Bd remained established in local amphibian communities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of Bd to the Lesser Antilles via regional or international movement of infected amphibians (including invasive tree frogs) or contaminated fomites, with small, insular ranges and limited refugia greatly increasing the vulnerability of island populations. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent BdGPL strains caused intense epizootics with extremely high case fatality in Leptodactylus fallax, a highly susceptible host, driving rapid range collapses; high transmission in moist island habitats and limited genetic resilience in small, fragmented populations amplified the impact.
Review: review – Retain this as a major, well-documented Bd-driven collapse of an endemic Caribbean species, with continent/sub-region coding and timing (Dominica 2002; Montserrat 2009) supported by primary literature and conservation reports. 'Re_emergence' has been set to false because there is no evidence of earlier Bd presence in the Lesser Antilles; the episode is best characterized as an intra-continental emergence into a new sub-region (Caribbean) within the South America continent definition used by the project.

Host: Wild Malagasy frogs (multiple endemic species sampled across lowland and montane sites)
Event summary: Between 2005 and 2010, intensive surveys across Madagascar failed to detect Bd despite global concern about its potential arrival on the island. In 2010, Bd was first detected at low prevalence in wild amphibians from the Makay region and subsequent surveys up to 2014 documented patchy but increasing presence at additional sites, indicating recent introduction and early spread without clear, documented mass die-offs. By the mid‑2010s, Bd was considered present but not yet widely established or clearly epizootic in Madagascar, prompting ongoing surveillance and contingency planning to prevent or respond to large-scale chytridiomycosis outbreaks in the island’s highly endemic amphibian fauna.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable recent introduction via international or regional amphibian trade and/or movement of contaminated equipment, with biosecurity gaps allowing Bd to reach an island previously considered Bd-free; environmental heterogeneity and climate may have limited explosive spread during the initial years. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of Bd (likely BdGPL or a related lineage) into a naïve, highly endemic amphibian fauna represents geographic range expansion of the pathogen, but to date there is limited evidence for strong virulence expression or epidemic dynamics at the island scale, suggesting either an early invasion stage, lineage-specific differences, or host and environmental factors moderating disease expression.
Review: review – Retain this as the first confirmed detection and early spread of Bd in Madagascar, with Africa/Eastern Africa coding, a 2010–2014 window, and narrative all consistent with Bletz et al. (2015) and Kolby et al. (2015). 'First_detection' has been set to false because global first detection of Bd occurred in the late 1990s; classification as an intra-continental emergence within Africa (from other African or external sources into Madagascar) more accurately reflects its status and limited documented impact to date.

Host: Wild fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) populations in Het Bunderbos and Putberg forests (Limburg, Netherlands)
Event summary: Around 2010, mass mortalities and a >96–99% decline of fire salamanders were observed in Het Bunderbos in Limburg, Netherlands, with carcasses showing severe skin lesions and no known pathogens detected initially. Subsequent investigations isolated and described a novel chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, from affected salamanders in 2013 and experimentally confirmed it as the cause of lethal chytridiomycosis, marking the first recognized emergence and detection of Bsal in wild salamanders and its establishment at the outbreak site. By the mid‑2010s, field surveys found the local fire salamander population functionally extirpated and Bsal rarely or no longer detectable in the few remaining animals, indicating a crash‑and‑fadeout epidemic likely following introduction from Asian reservoir hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from East Asia via international trade in live salamanders and other amphibians, with infected but asymptomatic captive or traded animals bringing Bsal into Europe; lack of prior exposure in European fire salamanders, dense local populations, and suitable cool, moist forest habitats favored explosive spread and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and epidermis‑destroying pathology in naive fire salamanders, efficient transmission through aquatic zoospores and direct contact in communal habitats, and the capacity for rapid amplification in dense local populations enabled rapid host die‑off and local population collapse.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This is clearly one of the major Bsal events and should be retained. However, the original row incorrectly combined the global first-detection role of this outbreak with an inter-continental emergence label. Under the project rules, the Netherlands event is treated as the single global first detection of Bsal in this host system, so `first_detection` remains TRUE but `inter_continental_emergence` has been set to FALSE (categories are generally mutually exclusive, except for re-emergence). No changes were made to the country, subregion, or time span, which are consistent with the literature, though retrospective positives before 2010 are acknowledged in the quality notes rather than shifting the event start year.

Host: Wild fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and other urodele species in the Ardennes (Eupen, Robertville, Liège region, Belgium)
Event summary: In 2013, following reports of mass mortality of fire salamanders in eastern Belgium near Eupen, Bsal infection was confirmed and linked to severe chytridiomycosis and population declines in multiple monitored sites in the Ardennes. Over the next several years, longitudinal monitoring at Eupen, Robertville, and nearby localities documented extensive infection and high mortality in wild salamander populations, representing geographic spread of the Dutch index epidemic into adjacent parts of the same Western European subregion. By about 2017, many local populations in the affected area had undergone dramatic reductions in abundance, and Bsal became established as a persistent pathogen in parts of eastern Belgium.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural and possibly human‑mediated spread from the Netherlands outbreak area into adjacent forested regions of eastern Belgium, facilitated by connected salamander metapopulations, hydrological connectivity, and movement of infected animals or contaminated materials. Internal mechanisms: High host susceptibility and virulence similar to that observed in the Netherlands, with efficient skin colonization and lethal chytridiomycosis in fire salamanders, allowed Bsal to invade and decimate naive Belgian populations once introduced.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections: (1) The original row classified this as an intra-continental emergence event, but under the project definitions intra-continental emergence is reserved for spread to a *new UNSD subregion* within a continent. Belgium (like the Netherlands and Germany) lies in Western Europe, so this event reflects spread within the same subregion. The type has therefore been changed from `intra_continental_emergence = TRUE` to `re_occurrence = TRUE`, indicating resurgence and spread of the same pathogen within an already affected subregion. Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Germany [2013]; Netherlands [2013]; Belgium [2014]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015]; Spain [2015]; Sweden [2015]
Host: Captive collections of salamanders and newts (multiple urodele species, including European and Asian taxa) in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom
Event summary: Beginning in the early 2010s, Bsal was detected in captive salamander collections in Germany, initially associated with mass mortality of fire salamanders, and shortly thereafter in additional collections in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Epidemiological tracing showed that many affected private and zoological collections had imported salamanders from continental Europe and Asia, with Bsal infection often present in multiple species and sometimes causing clinical disease and die‑offs, while other taxa carried infections subclinically. These findings revealed that captive populations across several European subregions served as reservoirs and amplification hosts for Bsal and highlighted ongoing risk of repeated spillover into wild populations and long‑distance dissemination via the pet and zoo trade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International pet, zoo, and hobbyist trade moving live salamanders among Asia and multiple European countries, inadequate quarantine and pathogen screening of imported animals, and dense mixed‑species housing in private and institutional collections all facilitated establishment and spread of Bsal in captivity. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range among urodeles, the capacity for subclinical persistent infections in some Asian and European species, and efficient transmission in high‑density captive environments led to recurrent outbreaks and made captive collections important reservoirs and bridge populations for Bsal, enabling repeated introductions into new regions and host communities.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections and additions: (1) The original row only listed Germany and the UK and labeled the event as intra-continental emergence + re-emergence. EFSA and subsequent summaries show that major Bsal-positive captive collections with associated mortality were documented in Germany, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK by 2017, with additional asymptomatic infection documented in Swedish collections and evidence of infection in at least one Belgian collection. Countries and subregions have therefore been expanded to include Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom, and the sub_regions field updated to "Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe." Country start years are approximate mid‑2010s values reflecting earliest published detections and should be refined in any future update. (2) Under the project’s rules, intra-continental emergence is reserved for first occurrence in a new UNSD subregion in the wild; here, the same pathogen is appearing in captive populations across subregions that are already affected (or at risk) via trade. This event is therefore better treated as `re_emergence = TRUE` (expansion into new host communities and captive reservoirs) and `intra_continental_emergence = FALSE`. (3) Because multiple new countries and a type reclassification were introduced based on synthesis of several sources, this row is flagged for further expert review, but it should be retained as one of the major Bsal events given its role in amplifying and moving the pathogen across Europe.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and other urodeles in the Ruhr District and southern Eifel Mountains, Germany
Event summary: From about the mid‑2010s onward, Bsal was detected in wild fire salamander populations in western Germany, notably in the Ruhr District and southern Eifel Mountains, coinciding with emerging local declines. Long‑term field studies documented progressive spread of infection through regional metapopulations, severe disease signs, and substantial reductions or disappearance of larval and adult fire salamanders in multiple streams and forest sites over the following years. By around 2020, Bsal was established across several parts of western Germany, with evidence of widespread decline and local extirpations similar in character, though regionally patchy, to those seen earlier in the Netherlands and Belgium.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued natural spread from already affected Western European regions, facilitated by connected forest habitats, stream networks, and movements of infected salamanders, as well as possible human‑assisted translocation of animals or contaminated equipment. Internal mechanisms: High susceptibility and mortality of German fire salamander populations to the same highly virulent Bsal lineage allowed the pathogen to re‑appear and expand within the same UNSD subregion (Western Europe), leading to repeated, spatially separated but epidemiologically related outbreaks and severe population declines.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row accurately captures one of the four major wild Bsal epizootics in Europe, with substantial evidence for severe declines and local extirpations of Salamandra salamandra in the Ruhr and Eifel regions of Germany. Classifying it as `re_occurrence = TRUE` (and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence) is consistent with the definitions: Germany lies in the same UNSD subregion (Western Europe) as the Netherlands and Belgium, and this event represents continued spread within that subregion rather than emergence in a new subregion or continent. Dates, geography and host information match the key German field studies; no corrections were required beyond a slight rephrasing of the summary to emphasize that this is a continuation of the Western European outbreak rather than a distinct continental emergence.

Host: Wild urodeles in north‑eastern Spain, including fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and threatened endemic species in the Catalan and Montseny region
Event summary: In 2018, a disjunct Bsal outbreak was detected in north‑eastern Spain, marking the first confirmed presence of the pathogen in the Iberian Peninsula and raising particular concern for highly endangered local endemics such as the Montseny brook newt (Calotriton arnoldi). Subsequent surveillance between 2015 and 2021 showed Bsal infection in several urodele populations in Catalonia, with associated disease and mortality in some sites but a patchier impact than in north‑western Europe. Management responses focused on intensive monitoring, strict biosecurity, and consideration of ex situ assurance colonies in an effort to contain the outbreak and preserve Iberian salamander diversity in the face of this new chytrid threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via the amphibian trade or movements of infected animals or materials from already affected European regions or Asia into north‑eastern Spain, followed by establishment in suitable cool, moist mountain habitats in Catalonia. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of Bsal’s realized geographic and host range within Europe, including infection and high virulence in Iberian urodeles such as Triturus marmoratus and potential severe impacts on narrow‑range endemics like Calotriton arnoldi, is interpreted here as a re-emergence driven by host community composition and pathogen ecology in a new UNSD subregion (Southern Europe).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is the first and, to date, only confirmed wild Bsal outbreak in Southern Europe and the Iberian Peninsula and is clearly among the most impactful Bsal events due to the involvement of multiple native species and the proximity to highly threatened endemics. Classifying it as `intra_continental_emergence = TRUE` is appropriate, because it represents first occurrence in a new UNSD subregion (Southern Europe) within the already affected European continent. Given that it also involves spillover into new host assemblages (including species not previously recorded with natural Bsal infection), retaining `re_emergence = TRUE` is justifiable under the definition that allows re-emergence to co-occur with intra-continental emergence when expansion into new host niches is central to the event. No corrections to countries, subregion, or time span were necessary, but an explicit note about the management focus and restricted geographic footprint has been retained to distinguish this contained Iberian outbreak from the more extensive north‑western European epizootic.

Countries: Thailand [2013]; Viet Nam [2013]; Japan [2013]; China [2015]; Taiwan, Province of China [2015]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2020]
Host: Wild Asian salamanders and toads (multiple urodele species in Thailand, Viet Nam, Japan, China, Taiwan; a small‑webbed fire‑bellied toad, Bombina microdeladigitora, in Viet Nam and traded individuals; and occasionally imported amphibians in or via Hong Kong)
Event summary: Through retrospective and prospective surveys published from 2013 onward, Bsal DNA was detected in wild salamanders in Thailand, Viet Nam, and Japan without obvious associated mass mortality, leading to the hypothesis that East and South‑eastern Asia represent the pathogen’s endemic range. Subsequent broader screening demonstrated Bsal infection in additional wild urodele species in Viet Nam and China, in a small‑webbed fire‑bellied toad (Bombina microdeladigitora) in Viet Nam and the trade, and in some amphibians in Taiwan and Hong Kong, again largely without severe disease, indicating long‑term coexistence between local hosts and the fungus. By about 2020, these findings had firmly established East/South‑eastern Asia as a major reservoir region for Bsal, with numerous wild host species carrying the pathogen at low apparent impact but constituting a continuing source for global spread via trade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing natural presence of Bsal in East/South‑eastern Asian amphibian communities combined with rapidly expanding regional and international trade in wild‑caught and farmed salamanders and other amphibians, particularly from China and Viet Nam, has created conditions for intercontinental dissemination of the pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Co‑evolution of Bsal with Asian host lineages has produced many tolerant or reservoir hosts capable of harboring infection with minimal clinical disease, supporting persistent environmental circulation and wide geographic spread while maintaining overall low‑level prevalence in source populations. This reservoir dynamics underpins Bsal introductions to Europe and other regions via the amphibian trade.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections: (1) The original row labeled this Asian reservoir event as `first_detection = TRUE`, which conflicts with the Netherlands outbreak being the global first description and detection of Bsal. To avoid multiple first-detection events, `first_detection` has been set to FALSE here. (2) Instead, this episode is classified as `inter_continental_emergence = TRUE`, representing the first *documented* occurrence of Bsal in Asia as a continent following its initial description from Europe, and the subsequent recognition of East/South‑eastern Asia as the main natural reservoir. Although phylogenetic evidence indicates a long evolutionary history of Bsal in Asia, the project’s operational definitions are based on detection and documentation rather than inferred ancient presence. (3) Countries, subregions, and the broad 2013–2020 time range remain appropriate for an aggregated, linked episode of detections across multiple Asian countries in wild populations and traded animals, but the confidence score is kept at 0.85 to reflect residual uncertainty in exact first‑detection years per country. The event is retained because recognizing the Asian reservoir is essential for understanding the global emergence and trade‑driven risk profile of Bsal, but it is flagged for expert review due to the change in emergence-type classification and the conceptual nuance around endemicity vs. emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Raccoon (Procyon lotor) in captivity (zoos, traders, pets)
Event summary: In 1993, a survey of 291 captive and pet raccoons in Japan found Baylisascaris procyonis eggs in roughly 8–40% of animals depending on setting, providing the first detailed confirmation of this raccoon roundworm in Asia linked to imported pets. Infections were concentrated in zoo‑kept and trader‑held raccoons, whereas no eggs were found in the small number of wild animals examined, indicating establishment primarily within captive populations at that time. Limited, animal‑level deworming meant the parasite persisted in collections, setting the stage for environmental contamination of enclosures and eventual spillover into wildlife and other captive hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large‑scale importation of raccoons as pets to Japan from North America beginning in the late 1970s, escape and release of pets into the wild, and lack of systematic parasite screening or treatment programs in zoos and the pet trade. Internal mechanisms: high egg output by adult worms and the environmental resilience of eggs promoted establishment and long‑term persistence in captive raccoon populations despite sporadic deworming.
Review: Retain – Correctly represents the first well‑documented detection of B. procyonis in raccoons in Japan/Asia in 1993, based on Miyashita 1993. Continent, subregion, country and classification as first detection plus inter‑continental emergence into Asia are appropriate; sources are relevant and specific.

Host: Domestic rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) and raccoon (Procyon lotor) in a wildlife park
Event summary: Around 2000–2001, a small wildlife park in Japan experienced an outbreak of neurologic disease in housed rabbits that was subsequently confirmed as Baylisascaris procyonis larva migrans, reported in 2003 as the first proven outbreak in rabbits in the country. The event originated when a donated pet raccoon heavily infected with B. procyonis contaminated soil and enclosure areas adjacent to rabbit pens; rabbits ingested embryonated eggs likely dispersed during a flooding or overflow event, leading to widespread CNS larva migrans and deaths. Intensive anthelmintic treatment of raccoons, removal of contaminated soil, and flaming of substrates reduced transmission, but recurrent infections in young raccoons and sporadic rabbit cases persisted for months, illustrating how difficult it is to clear heavily contaminated environments.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of an infected pet raccoon into a mixed‑species park, close proximity of raccoon and rabbit enclosures, and flooding that spread contaminated feces into rabbit pens; incomplete deworming and environmental decontamination allowed eggs to persist. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into dense, susceptible paratenic hosts (rabbits) and extreme environmental persistence of eggs supported prolonged transmission despite control efforts.
Review: Retain – Accurately summarizes the first documented B. procyonis larva migrans outbreak in rabbits in Japan and its epidemiology, consistent with the 2003 J Vet Med Sci/ScienceDirect reports. Classifying this as re‑emergence (host expansion and new severe disease manifestation in an already colonized area) without intra/inter‑continental flags is appropriate.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Germany [long‑established core area], Netherlands [2010s], France [2010s], Poland [2010s], Czechia [2010s], Denmark [2010s], Norway [2010s], Austria [≈2020], Italy [≈2021], Luxembourg [2024]
Host: Wild invasive raccoon (Procyon lotor), various paratenic hosts (birds, rodents, captive mammals)
Event summary: Between roughly 2005 and the mid‑2020s, compiled occurrence data and new field surveys showed Baylisascaris procyonis spreading with invasive raccoon populations from core areas in central Germany into multiple other European countries. Free‑ranging raccoons infected with B. procyonis were successively reported from the Netherlands, France, Poland, Czechia and, later, from Denmark, Norway, Austria, northern Italy, Switzerland and, most recently, Luxembourg, indicating that the roundworm has become established across much of Central Europe and parts of Northern and Southern Europe. By the mid‑2020s, infection prevalences remained high in German core areas and the parasite’s European range was still expanding, with only a few diagnosed human cases but increasing recognition of zoonotic risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued spread and population growth of invasive raccoons across central and western Europe, facilitated by habitat generalism, synanthropic behaviour, lack of early large‑scale control and ongoing legal/illegal trade of raccoons as pets. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion driven by raccoon dispersal and the parasite’s life‑history traits (high prevalence, massive egg shedding, environmental persistence), rather than emergence of a novel genotype, underpins colonization of new European regions.
Review: Review – Kept this as the main intra‑continental emergence episode for Europe but corrected details to match recent syntheses. Sub_regions are expanded to include Western, Northern, Eastern and Southern Europe, and the countries list now explicitly names additional affected countries (Austria, Italy, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Denmark, Norway, Poland, Luxembourg) with approximate start years derived from the Parasitology Research review and subsequent country‑level reports. Because available data indicate geographic range expansion of an existing parasite with no clear evidence of a novel strain or host shift, the re_emergence flag was set to No; intra_continental_emergence remains Yes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild invasive raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event summary: From 2008 to 2018, necropsy surveys of 8,184 hunted or road‑killed raccoons across Germany (plus a smaller sample from Luxembourg) mapped the distribution of Baylisascaris procyonis and showed that the parasite was widespread and highly prevalent in central Germany. Many administrative districts within the long‑established Hesse and Harz raccoon populations had more than 40% of raccoons infected, whereas no B. procyonis were detected in raccoons from Luxembourg or from northeastern and some western German regions. By the end of this period B. procyonis was recognized as firmly entrenched in central German raccoon populations, prompting concern about human and wildlife health and the risk of future spread into parasite‑free raccoon populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: historic introductions of raccoons for fur farming and hunting, subsequent rapid population growth and urban colonization, and decades without targeted surveillance of raccoon parasites allowed B. procyonis to become common in central Germany before it was widely appreciated as a public‑health issue. Internal mechanisms: very high prevalence and egg shedding in raccoons, combined with their tendency to create communal latrines, maintain intense environmental contamination and favour further spread into neighbouring, initially parasite‑free raccoon populations.
Review: Review – The underlying event (large‑scale 2008–2018 survey) is valid, but the original row incorrectly implied widespread infection in Luxembourg and coded this as inter‑continental emergence. The EID 2020 analysis shows high prevalence restricted to central Germany and no detections in Luxembourg during the study period, so Luxembourg was removed from the countries field and the summary rewritten. Inter_continental_emergence was set to No because Europe had been colonized decades earlier, and the episode is better interpreted as a major re‑occurrence/intensification within an already affected Western European subregion (re_occurrence = Yes).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Captive raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2013, surveys of captive raccoons at multiple zoological and breeding facilities in China identified Baylisascaris procyonis eggs and adult worms, confirmed morphologically and by molecular sequencing, representing the first confirmed detection of this zoonotic parasite in the country. Infections were detected in several facilities, indicating that imported raccoons had introduced and maintained the parasite in captivity. No human cases were recognized during this period, but the study highlighted substantial environmental contamination potential and the risk of future spillover to humans and wildlife as raccoons spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation and breeding of raccoons for zoo display and the pet trade in China without systematic parasite screening or quarantine, and growing numbers of captive raccoons increasing environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: efficient fecal–oral transmission and high egg production enabling establishment in captive populations; genetic analyses showed close relatedness to North American and European B. procyonis, consistent with recent introductions rather than long‑standing endemic strains.
Review: Review – Retained as the first confirmed detection of B. procyonis in China, but removed the intra_continental_emergence flag. Japan and China are both classified in the same UN Eastern Asia subregion, and by definition intra‑continental emergence in this project refers to spread into a new subregion, not merely into an additional country within the same subregion. First_detection is kept to indicate first documented occurrence in China.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (children and adults) with neural and ocular larva migrans; raccoon (Procyon lotor) as definitive host
Event summary: From May 2013 through December 2015, CDC identified seven confirmed or probable human Baylisascaris procyonis infections with central nervous system or ocular disease in patients from six U.S. states, compared with 22 cases reported in the preceding four decades. Cases occurred in young children and adults living in raccoon‑prevalent areas of Oklahoma/Arkansas, Ohio, Massachusetts, California, Virginia and Minnesota, most with documented or likely exposure to raccoon latrines or contaminated soil. The cluster of severe, highly publicized cases prompted new clinical alerts and public‑health messaging but did not signal control of the parasite in raccoons, which remains widespread across North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing raccoon densities and human–raccoon contact in suburban and peri‑urban settings, limited public awareness of latrine‑associated risks, and improved diagnostic tools and surveillance (including use of a recombinant antigen immunoblot at CDC) that enhanced recognition of human cases. Internal mechanisms: pronounced neurotropism of B. procyonis larvae in paratenic hosts leading to severe neural larva migrans even with low‑level exposure; no novel strain was reported, but existing virulence combined with changing exposure patterns produced a perceptible re‑occurrence of severe disease.
Review: Review – Retained as a major human baylisascariasis episode but corrected geography and type. The original row listed several U.S. states that did not appear in the 2013–2015 case series; the countries field is now limited to “United States of America,” with specific states described in the narrative, consistent with MMWR 2016. Because the cluster occurred in an already endemic North American subregion and there is no evidence for a novel strain, intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence were set to No and the event is coded purely as a re_occurrence driven by exposure and surveillance changes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild raccoon (Procyon lotor) in urban and peri‑urban Greater Metropolitan Area
Event summary: During a 10‑month period in 2014, nuisance‑trapped raccoons from eight locations in the Greater Metropolitan Area of San José, Costa Rica were examined, and Baylisascaris procyonis was found in 10 of 20 animals, with 137 adult worms recovered and infections detected at all sites. Morphologic and molecular analyses showed the worms to be identical to North American B. procyonis, representing the southernmost and first confirmed detection of this parasite in free‑ranging raccoons in Central America. The study noted raccoon latrines in playgrounds and school yards and suggested that some previously diagnosed larva migrans cases in Costa Rican children might have been caused by B. procyonis rather than Toxocara spp., raising concern about under‑recognized zoonotic risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of raccoon populations into the densely populated Greater Metropolitan Area and increasing human–raccoon contact around houses, gardens, playgrounds and school yards, together with limited prior surveillance for B. procyonis in Central America. Internal mechanisms: high worm burdens and prolific egg shedding in raccoons and the long environmental persistence of eggs, combined with genetic identity to North American isolates, are consistent with recent introduction followed by rapid geographic range expansion into a new continent for this parasite.
Review: Review – Added as a missing but clearly major event. The 2016 EID letter documents high‑prevalence B. procyonis infection in raccoons from Costa Rica in 2014, representing the first confirmed occurrence south of the United States and the southernmost record at the time. Under this project’s geography (South America including Central America and the Caribbean), this is the first detection on a new continent, so inter_continental_emergence and first_detection are appropriately set to Yes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Wild raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event summary: In 2023–2024, a study of 46 raccoons from central and southern Mississippi documented Baylisascaris procyonis infection, with an overall prevalence of about 13% by necropsy and higher apparent prevalence by droplet digital PCR on feces, revealing a previously undocumented focus in the southeastern United States. Infected animals were found across several counties, and sequence data showed the worms to be indistinguishable from B. procyonis from other parts of North America and from introduced populations abroad. The authors concluded that B. procyonis is likely under‑recognized in the U.S. Southeast and recommended expanded surveillance and public‑health messaging as raccoons continue to thrive in peri‑urban and rural landscapes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued natural expansion and high densities of raccoons in parts of the southeastern United States, combined with limited previous parasite‑specific surveillance, meant that B. procyonis had gone undetected in Mississippi until targeted sampling was conducted. Internal mechanisms: straightforward geographic spread of an existing North American lineage via movement of infected raccoons, with no evidence of phenotypic or genetic change, demonstrating the parasite’s ability to colonize new ecological zones within its native continent.
Review: Review – Retained as an informative recent detection in the southeastern United States but corrected the emergence classification. Mississippi lies within the existing Northern America subregion where B. procyonis has long been endemic, and the EID 2025 study describes first state‑level detection and under‑recognized endemicity rather than spread into a new UN subregion or continent. The intra_continental_emergence flag was therefore set to No; no other emergence‑type flag clearly applies, so the row is left as a significant surveillance/first‑state‑detection event without a specific emergence category.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (two children) and raccoons as local reservoir
Event summary: In 2024, Los Angeles County reported two unrelated pediatric cases of severe baylisascariasis—one primarily neurologic and one ocular—in children with likely exposure to raccoon feces in urban settings, as detailed in an MMWR 2025 report. Both infections were linked epidemiologically to local raccoon activity and confirmed by serologic testing and characteristic neuro‑imaging or ocular findings, and one child experienced substantial, permanent neurologic and visual sequelae after a delay in diagnosis. The cases triggered extensive environmental assessments and a public‑health investigation and led to targeted educational outreach, but no raccoon population‑reduction program was undertaken, reflecting recognition that the parasite is already widely distributed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high raccoon densities and established raccoon latrines in densely populated urban neighbourhoods, unrecognized contamination of residential yards and play areas, and limited awareness among clinicians and the public of raccoon roundworm as a cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis. Internal mechanisms: the parasite’s strong neuroinvasive potential in paratenic hosts, combined with a lack of pre‑existing human immunity, results in severe disease even after low‑dose exposure; however, there is no evidence of a new strain or altered virulence in this episode.
Review: Review – Kept as a major, well‑described human event but adjusted the emergence typing. The Los Angeles cases occurred in a long‑endemic region of North America and the MMWR report attributes them to exposure circumstances and diagnostic delay, not to parasite changes or spread into a new subregion, so intra‑/inter‑continental emergence were left as No. Re_occurrence is set to Yes to reflect renewed occurrence of severe human disease in an already affected subregion; re_emergence was set to No because there is no evidence for a novel genotype, new host system or increased intrinsic virulence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wild raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event summary: In January 2024, investigators captured a juvenile raccoon in montane cloud forest in Veracruz, Mexico, that was severely ill and, on necropsy, harboured several adult roundworms morphologically and molecularly confirmed as Baylisascaris procyonis, the first documented finding of this parasite in Mexican wildlife. The infected animal likely reflects southward expansion of raccoons carrying B. procyonis from the United States into Mexico, and 28S rRNA gene sequences showed 100% identity with strains from the United States, China and Norway, indicating a widely disseminated lineage. The 2025 report emphasised that as raccoons continue to expand into human‑dominated regions of Mexico, environmental contamination with B. procyonis eggs will increase and there is an urgent need for surveillance and clinician awareness to prevent severe human baylisascariasis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: natural southward expansion and synanthropization of raccoons into suitable habitats in Mexico, possibly aided by human‑mediated movements, together with a lack of prior targeted surveillance so that the parasite’s arrival went unnoticed until necropsy of a clinically ill animal. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of an existing North American B. procyonis lineage via infected raccoons, with eggs that are environmentally resilient and capable of establishing new foci in forest and peri‑urban ecosystems once introduced.
Review: Review – Retained as a key expansion event but corrected details. The EID 2025 paper documents a single infected raccoon sampled in January 2024, so the event year was simplified to 2024 rather than 2024–2025. Because B. procyonis had already been confirmed on the South America (including Central America) continent in Costa Rica in 2014, this Mexican finding is not an inter‑continental emergence; the inter_continental_emergence flag was set to No. First_detection remains Yes to reflect the first documented occurrence in Mexico, and no intra‑continental flag is used because the parasite was already present within the same Central America subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe | Western Europe; Europe | Eastern Europe; Northern America | Northern America
Countries: Netherlands [1991]; Germany [1991]; United States of America [1992]; other Western European countries with early outbreaks (e.g. Belgium, France) are likely involved but primary first detections were in Germany and the Netherlands
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) in commercial herds
Event summary: In the late 1980s a new syndrome of reproductive failure and respiratory disease appeared in U.S. swine herds, and similar outbreaks were recognized in central Europe by 1990–1991, prompting investigation of a previously unknown pathogen. In 1991 the causative arterivirus was first isolated in the Netherlands (Lelystad virus, PRRSV-1) and in 1992 in the USA (VR‑2332, PRRSV-2), confirming a novel viral disease of pigs that had already spread widely across herds in both continents. By the mid‑1990s the virus was established and endemic in much of North America and Europe, leading to large, continuing production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high-density, intensifying pig production systems in Europe and North America, extensive animal movements and trade of breeding stock and semen, and inadequate early biosecurity allowed rapid amplification and spread once the virus entered domestic swine. Internal mechanisms: molecular phylogenetic analyses indicate Betaarterivirus suid 1 (PRRSV) evolved as two divergent genotypes (PRRSV‑1 and PRRSV‑2) that had already been circulating in swine or related hosts before clinical recognition, with independent emergence on the American and European continents; this pre-existing divergence underpinned antigenic and genetic differences that complicated diagnosis and control after emergence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7172856/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic pigs in commercial and smallholder systems
Event summary: In 1995 China reported its first recognized outbreaks of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, marking the introduction and establishment of Betaarterivirus suid 1 into East Asian pig populations. During the late 1990s PRRSV spread widely within Chinese pig herds, becoming one of the most important endemic viral diseases in the country and setting the stage for later highly pathogenic variants. By the early 2000s PRRSV was entrenched in Chinese swine production, contributing to chronic reproductive and respiratory losses across multiple provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and industrialization of the Chinese pig industry in the 1990s, large-scale pig and semen movements within and into China, and limited initial surveillance facilitated introduction and silent spread of PRRSV. Internal mechanisms: the viruses introduced to China were PRRSV‑2 (American‑like) strains that subsequently diversified locally; molecular studies suggest these ancestors were imported from North America during the 1990s and adapted to Chinese production systems. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4915/17/1/85?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic pigs of all ages in intensive and backyard herds
Event summary: In early 2006 a new, highly pathogenic variant of PRRSV-2 emerged in southern China, causing an epidemic characterized by high fever, severe respiratory disease and unusually high mortality in pigs of all ages, including vaccinated animals. The virus, later termed highly pathogenic PRRSV (HP‑PRRSV) and associated with characteristic deletions in the Nsp2 region, rapidly spread across many Chinese provinces in 2006–2007 and was estimated to have affected more than 2 million pigs with very high morbidity and mortality. By 2007 the initial epidemic wave had peaked, but HP‑PRRSV became endemic in China and continued to cause recurrent outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high pig population density, large commercial operations with frequent live‑pig movements between farms and provinces, and widespread but imperfect vaccination created conditions for rapid spread and potential selection of escape variants; limited early recognition and control facilitated broad dissemination. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel highly pathogenic PRRSV‑2 variant (HP‑PRRSV) characterized by ‘1 + 29’ amino acid deletions in Nsp2 and additional genomic changes associated with increased virulence, enhanced systemic replication and high mortality, representing a clear example of increased virulence/pathogenicity and possibly enhanced transmission within the existing PRRSV‑2 lineage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3165578/?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Asia | Eastern Asia; Asia | South-eastern Asia
Countries: China [2007]; Viet Nam [2007, 2010]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2008]; Cambodia [2008]; Thailand [2010-2011]; Malaysia [late 2000s]; Myanmar [late 2000s]; Philippines [late 2000s]; Singapore [late 2000s]
Host: Domestic pigs (breeding and grower-finisher herds) in commercial and smallholder systems
Event summary: Following its emergence in China in 2006, highly pathogenic PRRSV-2 spread into neighbouring East and South‑East Asian countries beginning around 2007, with early severe outbreaks reported in Viet Nam and subsequently in other Indochina countries. Between 2007 and 2011 multiple countries in the Greater Mekong and broader South‑East Asian region—including Viet Nam, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Thailand—experienced large HP‑PRRSV epidemics with high pig mortality, substantial numbers of outbreaks (e.g. over 500 outbreaks in Viet Nam in 2010) and major economic losses. After these epidemic waves, HP‑PRRSV became entrenched in regional pig populations, with continued circulation and localized outbreaks reported in several South‑East Asian countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense regional trade and movement of pigs and pig products among China and South‑East Asian countries, informal cross‑border movements, rapid growth of pig production in the Mekong region, and gaps in veterinary services and biosecurity facilitated geographic spread. Internal mechanisms: dissemination of the Chinese HP‑PRRSV-2 lineage into new sub‑regions represented geographic range expansion of this highly virulent variant, with phylogenetic studies indicating multiple introductions and subsequent diversification into distinct HP‑PRRSV clades in Thailand, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Viet Nam; these changes reflect both enhanced transmission and ongoing viral evolution within an already highly pathogenic background. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0021997515003370?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Northern America | Northern America; Asia | Eastern Asia
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial herds
Event summary: Around 2008 a new ‘highly virulent’ PRRSV-2 strain, later termed NADC30, was identified on a farm in Iowa, United States, associated with severe respiratory disease and production losses in pigs. Over subsequent years NADC30-like viruses spread within parts of the U.S. pig industry and were later detected in China from about 2013 onward, where they contributed to new waves of PRRS outbreaks and complex recombination patterns with endemic HP‑PRRSV strains. By the mid‑2010s these NADC30-like and recombinant viruses had become part of the diverse PRRSV-2 landscape in both North America and China, complicating control and vaccination strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive, highly connected swine production systems in the United States and China, extensive movement of pigs and possibly genetic material (semen, breeding stock) between systems, and widespread but imperfect vaccine use created ecological space for emergence and spread of new variants; global trade links likely facilitated inter-regional movement of lineages. Internal mechanisms: emergence of the NADC30 PRRSV‑2 strain with increased virulence and its subsequent recombination with other PRRSV‑2 lineages in China, generating novel genotypes with altered pathogenicity and antigenicity; these represent novel strain/genotype emergence, increased virulence, and enhanced genetic diversity within PRRSV‑2 that underlie this re‑emergence pattern. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378113521001917?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; Northern America; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2020]; United States of America [2020]; Belgium [2020]; France [2020]; Spain [2020]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2020] (representative early countries only)
Host: Companion animals (dogs, cats) living in households of human COVID-19 cases
Event summary: In early 2020, SARS-CoV-2 was first detected in a pet dog belonging to a COVID-19 patient in Hong Kong, with viral RNA repeatedly detected from nasal and oral swabs, followed shortly by detection in a second dog in Hong Kong and then companion cats and dogs in other countries. Over the course of 2020, sporadic infections were confirmed in pets in North America and Europe, nearly all linked epidemiologically to close contact with infected owners and generally causing mild or no clinical signs. These pet infections remained incidental spillover events with no evidence of sustained pet-to-human transmission, and control consisted primarily of guidance on hygiene and quarantine of animals from infected households rather than mass depopulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense human–animal contact in households during a period of explosive human community transmission, combined with heightened veterinary surveillance and targeted testing of pets belonging to COVID-19 patients in Hong Kong, the United States and Europe. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of a human-adapted virus into susceptible carnivores (dogs, cats) via shared ACE2 receptor compatibility; no clear evidence that these early pet infections involved distinct variants with increased virulence or transmission in animals. The main mechanism was repeated human-to-animal spillover without onward spread between animal populations.
Review: review – retain this event as the first documented natural infection of SARS-CoV-2 in the animal host system (pets) and hence the global first_detection/first_global_emergence entry. Inter_continental_emergence has been changed from 'Yes' to 'No' because pet infections in Europe and North America in 2020 were incidental, epidemiologically linked reverse-zoonotic spillovers during a single human pandemic episode, without sustained animal-to-animal transmission establishing new continental animal reservoirs; under the project rules such linked cases should not be coded as separate inter-continental emergences.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Netherlands [2020]; Denmark [2020]; Spain [2020]; Italy [2020]; Sweden [2020]; France [2020]; Greece [2020]; Lithuania [2020]; Poland [2021]; Latvia [2021]
Host: Farmed American mink (Neovison vison) raised for fur, with occasional infections in farm cats and other farm-associated animals
Event summary: Beginning in April 2020, SARS-CoV-2 was first detected on mink farms in the Netherlands, where mink showed respiratory signs and increased mortality and viral genomes closely matched local human viruses, before similar outbreaks were confirmed in Denmark and multiple other European fur-producing countries later that year. During 2020–2021 hundreds of European mink farms in at least ten countries experienced infection, with efficient mink-to-mink transmission, rapid within-farm spread, and repeated spillback events to farm workers, including emergence of mink-associated variants such as Denmark’s ‘Cluster 5’ that prompted intense public-health concern and large-scale culling. By late 2021, many affected countries had depopulated farms or brought forward bans on mink farming, and infection chains on remaining farms were progressively controlled through surveillance, biosecurity, and in some cases long-term cessation of production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very high animal densities, close confinement and poor ventilation on fur farms, frequent close contact between workers and animals, and high farm-to-farm connectivity through shared staff, equipment and animal movements; these factors created ideal conditions for virus amplification once introduced from infected humans. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into mustelids highly susceptible due to ACE2 receptor compatibility; rapid within-farm adaptation and geographic range expansion in farmed mink; emergence of novel mink-adapted variants with spike mutations (e.g. ‘Cluster 5’) that altered antigenic properties and raised concerns about reduced vaccine efficacy and increased transmissibility back to humans.
Review: review – retain as the major 2020–2021 European mink-farm epidemic. Corrected the country list by changing Poland’s first-detection year from 2020 to 2021 and adding Latvia [2021], in line with WOAH/EFSA reporting and later comprehensive reviews of mink outbreaks. No change was made to emergence-type coding: re_emergence='Yes' appropriately captures a large-scale re-emergence driven by host expansion, intensive-farming conditions and mink-adapted viral variants within a continent where animal infections (in pets) were already present.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed American mink (Neovison vison) and escaped/wild mink in the vicinity of mink farms
Event summary: In mid-2020, SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks with elevated mortality were reported on mink farms in the United States, initially in Utah and later in additional states, with viral sequencing linking mink and farm-worker infections and confirming human-to-mink and mink-to-human transmission similar to that seen in Europe.
