By late 2020 and into 2021, farm-associated outbreaks occurred in Canadian mink farms as well, including documented human–mink–human transmission chains and investigations showing infection in mink and farm workers. Active wildlife surveillance around affected US farms detected infection and antibodies in escaped and nearby free-ranging mink, raising concern that the virus could spill into wild mustelid populations, although sustained wildlife transmission outside farm settings remained poorly characterized and control focused on enhanced biosecurity, movement restrictions, and in some cases depopulation of infected farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of SARS-CoV-2 from infected farm workers during widespread human transmission in North America, combined with the same high-density, high-contact fur farming environment that facilitated rapid spread in European mink. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into mink with efficient mink-to-mink transmission and high mortality; potential geographic range expansion into free-ranging mink through escapees and environmental contamination; evolution of mink-associated lineages that, in at least one Michigan outbreak, were later linked to spillback into white-tailed deer in Ontario, suggesting a complex multi-host transmission network.
Review: review – retain as the principal North American mink-farm epidemic. Inter_continental_emergence has been changed from 'Yes' to 'No' because SARS-CoV-2 infections in animals (companion cats and dogs) had already been documented in North America earlier in 2020; these mink outbreaks therefore represent re_emergence and host expansion within an already affected continent, not the first inter-continental emergence of the virus in the animal host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Eastern Asia
Countries: United States of America [2020]; Canada [2020]; Netherlands [2020]; Sweden [2020]; Czechia [2021]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2020] (representative countries with major zoo outbreaks)
Host: Zoo and aquarium animals including large felids (tigers, lions, pumas, snow leopards), other carnivores, and great apes (gorillas) in captivity
Event summary: In April 2020, lions and tigers at the Bronx Zoo in New York became the first zoo animals reported with natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, showing respiratory signs after exposure to an infected keeper and testing positive for the virus, and similar cases in zoo felids were soon reported in other US facilities and in Europe. Over 2020–2022, additional outbreaks occurred in captive lions, tigers, pumas, snow leopards and other carnivores, as well as in gorillas in several zoos, with most animals experiencing mild to moderate respiratory illness but some felids suffering severe or fatal disease, and keepers often identified as the likely source. These outbreaks were managed through enhanced infection control for staff, temporary closure or distancing measures for visitors, and vaccination of susceptible zoo species where veterinary vaccines became available, and no long-term zoo-based reservoirs have been documented though repeated re-introductions from humans continued through successive waves of human infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close, prolonged contact between infected zookeepers and susceptible zoo species, high visitor traffic before implementation of strict biosecurity, and the global spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants that increased the chance of introduction into zoos. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into diverse carnivores and great apes with high ACE2 receptor compatibility; in some zoos evidence of animal-to-animal transmission within enclosures; but overall infections reflected repeated re-introduction of human-circulating variants rather than long-term independent viral evolution in zoo populations.
Review: review – retain as a single multi-continent episode of repeated zoo-animal infections with clear animal health and One Health relevance. Emergence-type coding has been revised: inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are now set to 'No', with only re_emergence='Yes'. These episodes reflect repeated reverse-zoonotic introductions and limited within-zoo spread in highly susceptible species on continents where animal infections were already established; re_occurrence cannot span multiple subregions or co-occur with inter-/intra-continental emergence under the project definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Free-ranging white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and, to a lesser extent, other cervids in the wild
Event summary: In 2020, experimental infections showed that white-tailed deer were highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 and capable of deer-to-deer transmission, prompting wildlife surveillance in the United States that soon detected widespread natural infection and antibodies in free-ranging deer across multiple states, with some populations showing very high seroprevalence. By late 2021 and 2022, US nationwide surveys found evidence of prior infection in large proportions of sampled deer across most of their range, while Canada reported its first detections in free-ranging deer in Quebec and Ontario in late 2021, confirming establishment of a wildlife reservoir in Northern America. Viral sequencing revealed that deer populations harbored multiple human-like variants and, in some locations, distinct deer-associated lineages persisting over time, raising concern that deer could serve as a long-term reservoir from which divergent viruses might spill back into humans or other wildlife even as human infections decline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive spatial overlap between dense deer populations and humans in suburban and rural landscapes, including deer habituation to human-dominated environments, anthropogenic feeding, and hunting practices, all facilitating repeated human-to-deer spillover; limited initial awareness and surveillance delayed recognition of the scale of infection. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into a highly susceptible cervid species with efficient deer-to-deer transmission and capacity for sustained transmission cycles; geographic range expansion across much of the North American deer range; and, in some locales, emergence of deer-associated viral lineages and documented deer-to-human transmission events, suggesting within-deer adaptation and potential increased fitness in this host.
Review: review – retain as a major emergence event marking establishment of SARS-CoV-2 in a free-ranging wildlife reservoir (white-tailed deer) in North America. Emergence coding has been simplified by setting re_occurrence to 'No' and keeping re_emergence='Yes', reflecting that the key feature is host expansion, sustained transmission and viral evolution in a new wildlife host within an already affected subregion, driven by internal viral adaptation rather than purely external drivers of resurgence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2021]
Host: Pet hamsters (Syrian and dwarf hamsters) in the commercial pet trade and households
Event summary: In December 2021–January 2022, Hong Kong authorities investigated a COVID-19 cluster linked to a pet shop, where multiple imported hamsters and environmental samples tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant AY.127 and genomic analysis suggested that infected hamsters were the source of infection for several human cases. Subsequent investigations identified co-circulation of Delta AY.127 and a B.1.258-like lineage in hamsters at a wholesale warehouse and pet shops, indicating infection before or during international transport, and further human cases were epidemiologically linked to exposure to hamsters or contaminated environments. To terminate the outbreak and prevent wider spread, authorities ordered the culling of more than 2,000 hamsters and other small mammals in pet shops and warehouses, suspended imports of small mammals, and advised owners to surrender recently purchased hamsters for euthanasia, after which the hamster-associated outbreak was brought under control with no evidence of sustained hamster-to-human transmission beyond the initial cluster.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international pet trade with hamsters likely infected in Europe or along transport routes before arrival in Hong Kong; dense housing, mixing of batches and high animal turnover in wholesale facilities and pet shops; and close contact between hamsters, shop workers, and customers in a city with otherwise strict COVID-19 controls. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into hamsters, a species experimentally known to support efficient SARS-CoV-2 replication and transmission; co-circulation of two distinct variant lineages within the hamster trade that evolved abroad; and enhanced transmission within hamster populations with at least one documented hamster-to-human spillback event, illustrating the potential of small-mammal trade networks to generate novel transmission chains.
Review: review – retain as a high-impact, well-documented outbreak linked to the international hamster trade in Hong Kong with clear public-health and animal-welfare consequences. Emergence coding has been adjusted by setting re_occurrence to 'No' and keeping re_emergence='Yes', because this episode represents re-emergence in a new, highly susceptible pet-trade host with distinct variant lineages in a subregion where SARS-CoV-2 infections in animals were already known, rather than a simple resurgence of prior animal infections driven solely by external factors.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Primarily domestic sheep in southern India; goats and cattle infected but with much lower apparent clinical impact
Event summary: In 1997, severe bluetongue outbreaks due to multiple serotypes (notably BTV‑1, ‑2 and ‑23) erupted among sheep flocks across Tamil Nadu, a state where the virus had been endemic since the 1980s, leading to rapid spread through densely stocked, largely unvaccinated rural flocks. Through 1997–1998 the epizootic caused extensive morbidity and exceptionally high mortality in small ruminants, with more than 300,000 sheep deaths reported by state authorities, before natural immunity, ad‑hoc movement controls and early vaccination efforts gradually reduced transmission. After 1998, bluetongue became an entrenched seasonal problem in southern India with recurrent but generally less catastrophic outbreaks, and efforts shifted toward development and deployment of multivalent inactivated vaccines tailored to the serotypes circulating in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic presence of BTV in southern India combined with high densities of susceptible indigenous and crossbred sheep, communal grazing, and abundant Culicoides vector populations during monsoon and post‑monsoon periods; limited early vaccination and reliance on clinical recognition favoured rapid amplification once climatic conditions triggered vector population booms. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several virulent serotypes (including BTV‑1, ‑2 and ‑23) in largely naïve flocks, but no clear evidence that a fundamentally new genotype or host shift was responsible; this episode is best interpreted as a dramatic climatic and management‑driven re‑occurrence of an established pathogen rather than a true genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Added as a new event because the 1997–1998 Tamil Nadu epidemic caused >300,000 sheep deaths and is clearly among the most impactful bluetongue episodes globally since 1990, yet was missing from the original dataset. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re‑emergence) because BTV had been endemic in India since the 1960s and there is no strong evidence that a novel strain or host shift, rather than climatic and husbandry factors, drove this severe wave. Country and timing are constrained to Tamil Nadu, India [1997], based on state‑level reports; broader Indian endemicity is not treated as separate events. This row should be reviewed by an expert familiar with Indian field data to validate impact estimates and confirm that no even larger Indian outbreak after 1990 has been overlooked.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Europe: Southern Europe, Eastern Europe; Africa: Northern Africa; Asia: Western Asia
Countries: Greece [1998], Turkey [1998], Bulgaria [1999], Tunisia [1999], Italy [2000], France [2000], Spain [2000], Algeria [2000], Croatia [2001], North Macedonia [2001], Serbia [2001], Montenegro [2001], Bosnia and Herzegovina [2002], Albania [2002], Cyprus [2003], Morocco [2004], Portugal [2004]
Host: Primarily domestic sheep, with goats and cattle infected and occasionally clinically affected in Mediterranean and Balkan regions
Event summary: Beginning in 1998, bluetongue virus serotype 9 was detected on Greek islands and quickly spread into mainland Greece, European Turkey and southern Bulgaria, marking renewed large‑scale circulation of BTV in the eastern Mediterranean after decades of sporadic activity. From late 1999 onwards, additional incursions of BTV‑2, ‑4, ‑9 and ‑16 moved west and north: BTV‑2 emerged in Tunisia in 1999 and Algeria in 2000 and spread into Sardinia, Sicily and southern mainland Italy, while related BTV‑2/4 strains later reached Corsica, mainland Spain and eventually Portugal, and BTV‑9 and ‑16 seeded extensive outbreaks across the Balkans. By 2005, repeated seasonal transmission of multiple serotypes across new parts of southern and eastern Europe and the Maghreb had generated thousands of outbreaks in naïve small‑ruminant populations, prompting large‑scale vaccination and vector‑control programmes that gradually curtailed spread, although BTV remained established around much of the Mediterranean Basin.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Windborne dispersal of Culicoides imicola and related vectors from endemic zones in sub‑Saharan and North Africa into the Mediterranean, coupled with long‑distance legal and illegal movements of live ruminants between North Africa, the Near East and southern Europe; progressive northward expansion of suitable climate niches for Culicoides vectors and warm, dry summers favourable for vector survival and viral replication. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and co‑circulation of several distinct BTV serotypes and topotypes (notably BTV‑1, ‑2, ‑4, ‑9 and ‑16) into previously unexposed Mediterranean and Balkan ruminant populations, with genetic evidence of reassortment among African and eastern Mediterranean lineages generating regionally adapted strains, particularly for BTV‑9 and BTV‑16.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Event appropriately represents the large 1998–2005 Mediterranean–Balkan–North African epizootic, which is one of the most important bluetongue emergence episodes on record. However, the original row omitted several affected countries and mis‑dated first outbreaks for others. Countries have been expanded and first‑year annotations corrected using EU and Mediterranean summaries: Turkey moved from 1999 to 1998; Spain set to 2000 (first BTV‑2 incursions) rather than 2003; Algeria adjusted to 2000; Morocco to 2004; and Cyprus, France (Corsica), Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina have been added. These changes better match OIE/EU tables and regional reviews while keeping the event as a single linked multi‑serotype episode. No change was made to event‑type coding (intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence), which remains justified because this wave reflects BTV expansion into new European sub‑regions (especially Eastern Europe) via novel serotype introductions. This row should be reviewed to verify that no additional Mediterranean islands or minor affected countries need to be appended.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe: Western Europe, Northern Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe
Countries: Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2006], Belgium [2006], Germany [2006], France [2006], Luxembourg [2006], Switzerland [2007], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2007], Denmark [2007], Czechia [2007], Italy [2008], Spain [2008], Sweden [2008], Austria [2008], Hungary [2008], Norway [2009]
Host: Domestic cattle and sheep (with clinical disease particularly severe in sheep); goats and some wild ruminants occasionally affected
Event summary: In August 2006, bluetongue virus serotype 8 was detected almost simultaneously in cattle and sheep in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, northern France and Luxembourg, causing the first bluetongue outbreaks ever recorded in much of western and northern Europe and resulting in over 2,000 infected holdings by the end of that vector season. After overwintering, BTV‑8 re‑emerged in 2007–2008 and, together with a contemporaneous but independent wave of BTV‑1 in south‑western Europe, spread across most of western, central and parts of southern and northern Europe, eventually affecting ruminant holdings in at least 15 countries, including the United Kingdom, Denmark, Switzerland, Czechia, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Austria, Hungary and Norway, and causing tens of thousands of outbreaks with substantial mortality and production losses. Emergency and then mass vaccination campaigns, coupled with movement restrictions and several colder winters, progressively reduced transmission, and by around 2010 BTV‑8 (and associated BTV‑1) circulation had largely ceased across the previously affected northern and western European regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually warm summers and mild winters in northern and western Europe that allowed high densities and extended seasons of Palearctic Culicoides complexes (notably the C. obsoletus and C. pulicaris groups); intense intra‑EU trade and movement of cattle and small ruminants; and frequent episodes of windborne spread between neighbouring states. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a novel BTV‑8 strain closely related to sub‑Saharan African isolates, showing efficient replication in new vector species and an ability to overwinter in temperate climates (probably via prolonged viraemia and vertical transmission in cattle), enabling dramatic geographic range expansion of BTV into regions previously considered climatically unsuitable.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: This row correctly captures the unprecedented 2006–2010 BTV‑8 (plus overlapping BTV‑1) epizootic in northern, western and parts of southern and eastern Europe, which is unquestionably one of the top global BTV emergence events by number of holdings affected and economic impact. The original country list was incomplete, omitting states such as Sweden, Austria, Hungary and Norway that experienced documented BTV‑8 circulation, and mis‑dating Italy and Spain (which were first affected in 2008, not 2006–2007). Country coverage and first‑year annotations have therefore been expanded and corrected using EU and OIE summaries, while still treating the pan‑European BTV‑8 wave and its BTV‑1 overlap as a single linked multi‑year episode. Event‑type coding as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence remains appropriate because this was the first sustained BTV circulation in the Northern and much of the Western and Central Europe UNSD sub‑regions. Users should review this row if a more exhaustive list of minor affected countries (e.g. with very few outbreaks) is required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe: Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, Western Europe; Asia: Western Asia
Countries: Greece [2014], Turkey [2014], Bulgaria [2014], North Macedonia [2014], Albania [2014], Serbia [2014], Montenegro [2014], Croatia [2014], Bosnia and Herzegovina [2014], Romania [2014], Hungary [2014], Cyprus [2014], Slovenia [2014], Italy [2014], Spain [2014], Portugal [2014], France [2016], Austria [2017], Switzerland [2017]
Host: Primarily domestic sheep; also goats, cattle, bison and wild ruminants such as mouflon and roe deer in affected Balkan and Mediterranean countries
Event summary: In May 2014, bluetongue due to serotype 4 was first recognised in sheep in southern Greece and rapidly expanded across the country, before spreading within months into European Turkey and neighbouring Balkan states including Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia, Montenegro, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Romania and Hungary, generating thousands of outbreaks in domestic ruminants. During late 2014 and 2015 the same multireassortant BTV‑4 strain moved westward and northward, seeding additional foci in Cyprus, Slovenia, Spain and Portugal and then, over 2015–2017, establishing sustained transmission in parts of Italy (notably Sardinia) and finally reaching Corsica, mainland France, Austria and Switzerland, with Italy alone reporting over 2,000 BTV‑4 outbreaks in 2017. Intensified vaccination campaigns, vector control and movement restrictions from 2015 onwards, together with seasonal declines in Culicoides activity, progressively reduced incidence, although BTV‑4 has remained enzootic in parts of the western Balkans and Italy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warm, humid summers and autumns that favoured abundant Culicoides vectors across the Balkans and western Mediterranean; extensive cross‑border movement of small ruminants and cattle among Balkan states and between Italy, Spain, Portugal and France; and topography and prevailing winds that supported midge dispersal from initial foci in southern Greece and the eastern Mediterranean towards central and western Europe. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of a multireassortant BTV‑4 strain whose genome segments derive from earlier African and Mediterranean BTV‑1, ‑2 and ‑4 lineages, with evidence of enhanced fitness and adaptation to local Culicoides species; rapid geographic expansion across multiple already BTV‑experienced UNSD sub‑regions, making this a major re‑emergence of the virus at continental scale rather than a first incursion into new sub‑regions.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: The original 2014–2015 BTV‑4 row correctly identified the major Balkan outbreak but truncated the wider 2014–2017 Mediterranean episode and mis‑classified it as intra‑continental emergence. The time span has been extended to 2014–2017 to encompass the epidemiologically linked spread of the same BTV‑4 strain from Greece and the Balkans into Cyprus, Iberia, Italy, Corsica, mainland France, Austria and Switzerland, consistent with EU epizootic summaries. Countries and first‑year annotations have been updated accordingly, and event‑type coding has been changed to "re‑emergence only" because BTV had circulated previously in the Southern, Eastern and Western Europe sub‑regions; this episode reflects the resurgence and geographic expansion of a new multireassortant BTV‑4 strain rather than the first appearance of BTV in a new UNSD sub‑region. This row should be re‑checked for completeness of the country list if very small national outbreaks (e.g. single‑holding detections) are to be exhaustively catalogued.

Host: Domestic cattle and sheep in affected western European countries
Event summary: In August 2015, bluetongue virus serotype 8 was unexpectedly detected in a ram in Allier, central France, despite BTV‑8 apparently having been eliminated from Europe since 2010, revealing silent re‑emergence of the serotype in French cattle and sheep. Over 2015–2017 the virus caused hundreds to thousands of mainly subclinical but epidemiologically significant infections across central and eastern France, and surveillance and serological studies showed low but widespread residual herd immunity and ongoing low‑level circulation, with subsequent limited spread to neighbouring Switzerland in 2017 and later to border regions of Germany and Belgium in 2018–2019. Renewed vaccination campaigns, targeted movement restrictions and the gradual build‑up of herd immunity, together with climatic variability, led to declining incidence after 2017, and by around 2019 the re‑emergent BTV‑8 wave in western and central Europe had largely subsided, though the virus has since persisted at low endemic levels in parts of France.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cessation or substantial relaxation of BTV‑8 vaccination after the apparent end of the 2006–2010 epizootic, leading to waning population immunity; continued movement of domestic ruminants within and between affected western and central European countries; and climatic conditions that periodically favoured Culicoides activity and virus transmission. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of a BTV‑8 strain genomically almost identical to the 2006–2010 northern European strain, strongly suggesting prolonged low‑level persistence or accidental reintroduction from a frozen or otherwise cryptic source rather than a wholly novel introduction; evidence of overwintering via prolonged or vertical infection in cattle; and re‑emergence in a partially immune but still substantially susceptible cattle and sheep population, resulting in focal outbreaks without the extensive, highly clinical pan‑European spread seen in 2006–2010.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: This row remains appropriate as a major BTV‑8 re‑emergence episode, but several corrections were required. First, event‑type coding has been changed from "intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence" to "re‑emergence only" because BTV had already circulated widely in the Western Europe sub‑region during 2006–2010; the 2015–2019 wave represents resurgence of the same serotype, not its first appearance in a new UNSD sub‑region. Second, the time span has been extended to 2015–2019 to reflect documented low‑level spread into Germany and Belgium by late 2018–2019. Third, the country list has been narrowed and re‑dated to focus on locations with clear evidence of autochthonous circulation (France 2015, Switzerland 2017, Germany 2018, Belgium 2019); Spain was removed because reports largely concerned proximity to the French restriction zone rather than clearly established in‑country transmission. The event summary was updated accordingly. Because there is some uncertainty about the extent of local transmission versus imported cases in Germany and Belgium, this row should be reviewed against the latest OIE/EU datasets before finalisation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle, sheep and goats on mixed and specialised ruminant farms across multiple Tunisian governorates
Event summary: In the summer of 2020, after years of enzootic bluetongue with intermittent use of live‑attenuated vaccines, bluetongue virus serotype 4 re‑emerged explosively in Tunisia, with climatic conditions and waning immunity allowing widespread infection of cattle, sheep and goats in numerous governorates. Between August and November 2020 the outbreak produced high morbidity and notable mortality in affected herds and flocks, with farmers reporting substantial losses in milk yield, growth and reproduction as well as treatment and replacement costs, and a detailed survey estimated heavy direct economic losses at the farm level. As vector activity declined with the end of the transmission season and emergency control measures, including vector control and improved clinical management, were implemented, clinical incidence dropped, but bluetongue remained a major ongoing threat in Tunisia within a broader pattern of multi‑serotype BTV circulation in North Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Favourable weather patterns in 2020 in Tunisia, including increased rainfall and temperatures that supported expansion of Culicoides vector populations; cessation of mass vaccination against BTV serotypes 1, 2 and 4 from 2017 onwards, which left large cohorts of susceptible small ruminants and cattle; and widespread smallholder and mixed farming systems with limited biosecurity that facilitated local spread. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of BTV‑4 in a region with a long history of BTV‑2 and BTV‑4 circulation, with no clear evidence so far that a fundamentally new genotype or host shift was involved; the heavy impact of this event appears to be driven primarily by external drivers and gaps in immunity rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Added as a new event because the 2020 BTV‑4 outbreak in Tunisia generated very substantial direct losses (estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros equivalent) and therefore ranks among the most economically impactful bluetongue episodes in the 2005–2025 period, yet was absent from the original profile. It is coded as re‑occurrence (not intra‑continental emergence or re‑emergence) because BTV‑4 and other serotypes have circulated in Tunisia since at least 1999; the 2020 episode reflects resurgence under favourable climatic and immunological conditions rather than appearance of a new strain in a previously unaffected UNSD sub‑region. This row relies heavily on one detailed economic‑epidemiological study, so it should be reviewed to confirm that no contemporaneous, even larger multi‑country North African BTV‑4 event warrants separate representation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Europe: Western Europe, Northern Europe, Southern Europe
Countries: Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2023], Germany [2023], Belgium [2023], France [2023], Spain [2023], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2023], Norway [2024], Sweden [2024]
Host: Domestic sheep and cattle (with especially severe clinical disease and mortality in sheep), and goats in some affected herds
Event summary: In early September 2023, a highly virulent bluetongue virus serotype 3 variant (BTV‑3/NET2023) was first confirmed in sheep on several farms in the central Netherlands, where it caused acute fever, oedema, oral lesions and high mortality in naïve flocks, marking a sharp contrast to the largely subclinical BTV‑3 infections previously observed in Italy and Tunisia. Over the autumn of 2023 and into 2024, this strain spread rapidly across much of the Netherlands, with thousands of premises testing PCR‑positive and more than a thousand holdings reporting clinical disease, and was soon detected with local transmission in neighbouring Germany and Belgium, followed by documentation of BTV‑3/NET2023 in additional western and northern European countries including France, Spain, the United Kingdom, Norway and Sweden. Emergency movement controls, heightened surveillance, vector studies and, from 2024 onwards, deployment of inactivated BTV‑3 vaccines in some countries began to reduce clinical impact in vaccinated flocks, but by 2025 the variant remained widely distributed in north‑western Europe and continued to pose a major threat to sheep and cattle production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of competent Palearctic Culicoides species in temperate north‑western Europe during warm, prolonged vector seasons; dense networks of small ruminant and cattle farms with frequent animal movements; and strong prevailing winds capable of carrying infected midges over tens to hundreds of kilometres, facilitating the rapid jump of the virus from the Netherlands to adjacent countries. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a novel BTV‑3 lineage (BTV‑3/NET2023) that is genetically distinct from earlier BTV‑3 strains circulating in Italy and Tunisia, associated with marked clinical virulence in both sheep and cattle and efficient replication in local Culicoides species; this qualifies as a clear re‑emergence of BTV via a new genotype in regions that had previously experienced BTV‑8 but not this serotype–strain combination. The episode also illustrates the capacity of BTV to re‑enter previously affected UNSD sub‑regions with substantially different clinical expression due to viral genetic change.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Added as a new event to capture the large, ongoing BTV‑3/NET2023 epizootic beginning in 2023 in the Netherlands and spreading across north‑western Europe, which has involved thousands of infected premises and unusually severe clinical disease in sheep and cattle and is therefore clearly among the most impactful bluetongue episodes of the 2005–2025 period. It is coded as re‑emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence because BTV had previously circulated widely in the same European sub‑regions (notably via BTV‑8), but the strain is genetically and clinically distinct from earlier BTV‑3 lineages in Italy and Tunisia. Country coverage beyond the core Netherlands–Germany–Belgium focus (France, Spain, United Kingdom, Norway, Sweden) is based mainly on compiled OIE/EU and review summaries indicating documented circulation; users should review and refine this list as more detailed national data become available and decide whether later years (post‑2025) merit splitting into a separate follow‑on event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Argentinean flat oyster Ostrea puelchana (cultured and wild beds)
Event summary: Between 1995 and 1996, Bonamia exitiosa caused a severe epizootic starting in a commercial culture of the native flat oyster Ostrea puelchana in San Antonio Bay (San Matías Gulf) and spreading into nearby natural beds along the northeastern coast of the gulf, producing about 95% mortality in cultured stock and high prevalence in wild beds; subsequent surveys showed marked and long‑lasting reductions in oyster density and mean size, with fisheries activity greatly curtailed as beds remained chronically depleted. Over the following decade and more, infection persisted at lower prevalence with altered size structure and reduced densities in surviving beds, indicating a long‑term restructuring of the population under ongoing disease pressure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely anthropogenic movement of infected oysters or shipping‑mediated transfer of the parasite into San Matías Gulf (culture site located near an international shipping wharf), coupled with intensive culture practices that amplified local transmission and facilitated spread from farms to adjacent wild beds. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was reported; molecular work places the Argentine Bonamia within the B. exitiosa clade, and the event is best characterized as geographic range expansion of an existing Southern Hemisphere B. exitiosa lineage into a new region and host population rather than a change in parasite phenotype.
Review: retain – Event corresponds to the well‑documented 1995–1996 San Matías Gulf epizootic in Ostrea puelchana with ~95% mortality and long‑term fishery impacts; continent/subregion/country coding (South America/South America/Argentina) and classification as an inter‑continental emergence from the original New Zealand focus are appropriate, and cited sources directly describe this outbreak and its aftermath.([ri.conicet.gov.ar](https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/bitstream/handle/11336/27736/CONICET_Digital_Nro.ddf883b0-3b3b-41d9-b8b1-82d59d456ebd_A.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=2&utm_source=openai))

Host: Chilean (dredge/Bluff) oyster Ostrea chilensis in the Foveaux Strait wild fishery
Event summary: After the initial Foveaux Strait bonamiosis epizootic of the late 1980s, a renewed and particularly intense wave of Bonamia exitiosa‑associated mortality occurred around 2000–2003 in the same oyster grounds, killing on the order of one billion wild dredge oysters and severely reducing stock size, which again depressed fishery yields and prompted intensive monitoring and adaptive management. Subsequent surveys through the 2000s and 2010s showed that bonamiosis‑driven mortality remained the principal driver of oyster abundance and spatial distribution, with disease pressure fluctuating with oyster density and environmental conditions as managers adjusted catch limits and other measures to allow partial population recovery.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High background prevalence of endemic B. exitiosa combined with high oyster densities and fishing‑related disturbance of benthic habitat likely promoted density‑dependent transmission and episodic outbreaks; environmental factors such as temperature and local hydrodynamics also influenced disease dynamics. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence for a novel strain or major genetic change in the parasite; the episode reflects recurrent epidemic expression of an established lineage in an endemic system, with geographic range largely unchanged but disease expression intensified when host population structure and environmental stressors favored transmission.
Review: retain – This row captures the major early‑2000s recrudescence of bonamiosis in Foveaux Strait, including the widely cited estimate of ~1 billion oysters lost and the recognition of B. exitiosa as the dominant mortality driver; classification as a re‑occurrence in an endemic area, without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags, is consistent with long‑term New Zealand data and fishery assessments.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/icesjms/article/62/1/3/667406?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America – North Carolina [2003]; United States of America – Florida [2007]
Host: Asian Suminoe oyster Crassostrea ariakensis (triploid experimental and candidate aquaculture stocks) with the native crested oyster Ostrea equestris/Ostrea stentina acting as a local reservoir host in parts of the southeastern USA
Event summary: Beginning in 2003, a Bonamia parasite later confirmed as Bonamia exitiosa was detected in non‑native Suminoe oysters Crassostrea ariakensis deployed to Bogue Sound, North Carolina, where infections reached high prevalence and caused mortality exceeding 80–100% in small oysters, effectively halting prospects for commercial introduction of the species. Follow‑up field deployments in 2005 in Bogue and Masonboro Sounds showed strong seasonality, with heavy Bonamia infection and high mortality in warm, euhaline summer conditions and little or no infection in cooler seasons, while concurrent surveys documented infection of the native crested oyster Ostrea equestris in the same area. By 2007, a genetically matching B. exitiosa strain was also detected in C. ariakensis and C. virginica exposed to ambient Atlantic waters of the Indian River Lagoon, Florida, confirming establishment of this Southern Hemisphere parasite on the Atlantic coast of Northern America and highlighting its capacity to infect multiple oyster hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction is strongly suspected to have been shipping‑mediated, with C. ariakensis and/or associated biota in port areas near Morehead City, North Carolina, providing an entry point from Southern Hemisphere B. exitiosa lineages, after which warm, high‑salinity estuarine conditions favored parasite transmission. Intensive experimental deployments of dense C. ariakensis cohorts in Bonamia‑enzootic waters amplified transmission and revealed the parasite’s impact, while the presence of infected native Ostrea equestris indicates a local reservoir that could sustain B. exitiosa independent of the introduced host. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses of SSU and ITS rDNA group the North Carolina and Florida Bonamia isolates with B. exitiosa from New Zealand, Argentina and Australia, indicating geographic range expansion of this species into a new continent and host genus (Crassostrea) rather than emergence of a distinct taxon; the severe mortality observed in small C. ariakensis cohorts reflects high susceptibility of this host under suitable environmental conditions.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well‑documented epizootic of B. exitiosa in experimentally deployed Crassostrea ariakensis and associated reservoir hosts in North Carolina and Florida, which produced very high mortalities and represents the first established occurrence of B. exitiosa on the North American continent; coded as inter‑continental emergence (not first global emergence) with no re‑emergence flag, and limited to the USA (North Carolina, Florida). Classification as B. exitiosa rather than an unnamed Bonamia sp. follows later molecular work and international fact sheets that place these isolates within the B. exitiosa clade.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5397965_Strong_seasonality_of_Bonamia_sp_infection_and_induced_Crassostrea_ariakensis_mortality_in_Bogue_and_Masonboro_Sounds_North_Carolina_USA))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [2006]; Italy [2007]; France [c. 2010]; Portugal [2016]; Croatia [2016]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2011; 2015]
Host: European flat oyster Ostrea edulis (mainly wild beds and culture sites), with Bonamia exitiosa also associated with dwarf oyster Ostrea stentina as a reservoir in parts of the Mediterranean
Event summary: In 2006, Bonamia exitiosa was first confirmed by histology and rDNA sequencing in European flat oysters Ostrea edulis from culture in the Ría de Arousa, Galicia (Spain), representing the first report of this Southern Hemisphere parasite in European waters and often co‑infecting oysters already affected by Bonamia ostreae. Over the following decade, B. exitiosa was detected at generally low to moderate prevalence in O. edulis from multiple European regions, including natural beds in the Manfredonia Gulf (Adriatic Italy), cultured stocks on the Spanish Mediterranean coast (Ebro Delta and other sites), flat‑oyster populations along the French Mediterranean, and later in southern Portugal and in Mali Ston Bay, Croatia, with occasional co‑occurrence in reservoir oysters such as O. stentina. In the United Kingdom, B. exitiosa was first reported in River Fal (Cornwall) in 2010–2011 and later detected ephemerally in adult and larval O. edulis from restoration and fishery sites in the Solent between 2015 and 2019, with subsequent surveys becoming negative; throughout Europe, infections have so far involved small proportions of sampled oysters and no large‑scale mortality events have been attributed solely to B. exitiosa, though concern persists about additive impacts alongside B. ostreae.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance human‑mediated movements of oysters and associated fouling/ballast, including transfers of O. edulis for aquaculture and restoration and potential reservoir hosts such as O. stentina and Pacific oysters Crassostrea gigas, are strongly implicated in introducing B. exitiosa from the Southern Hemisphere into multiple European coastal systems and in subsequent secondary spread within the Mediterranean and NE Atlantic. Internal mechanisms: European detections largely involve B. exitiosa lineages closely related (≈99% SSU rDNA similarity) to Southern Hemisphere strains, indicating geographic range expansion of existing genotypes rather than a novel species; co‑infection with B. ostreae, possible larval infection, and the presence of reservoir hosts may enhance transmission opportunities but have not yet been linked to altered virulence or dramatic, B. exitiosa‑driven mass mortalities.
Review: review – Years updated from 2007–2019 to 2006–2020 to reflect evidence that the first European detection occurred in Galicia in 2006 and that confirmed infections continued at least to 2020 in Croatia; country list expanded to include Portugal (Algarve) and clarified that UK detections encompass both the initial River Fal (Cornwall) outbreak and later ephemeral Solent detections. Inter‑continental emergence coding is appropriate because this is the first established occurrence of B. exitiosa in Europe, while re‑emergence is left ‘No’ given the absence of clear evidence for major parasite change driving these low‑prevalence detections; additional event‑level sources have been added for Spanish Mediterranean, Portuguese and UK outbreaks and an official UK factsheet.([ices.dk](https://www.ices.dk/sites/pub/CM%20Doccuments/CM-2010/ACOM/ACOM2910.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America – North Carolina [2012]; United States of America – Massachusetts [2013]
Host: Eastern oyster Crassostrea virginica (hatchery seed and cultured seed); with additional low‑level infection documented in C. virginica experimentally exposed in Florida waters
Event summary: In July 2012, Bonamia exitiosa was reported infecting hatchery‑produced seed of the eastern oyster Crassostrea virginica from Core Sound, North Carolina, followed in June 2013 by infection in cultured seed from Stage Harbor, Chatham, Massachusetts, during routine regulatory screening; these reports built on earlier experimental work showing B. exitiosa infections in C. virginica exposed in the Indian River Lagoon, Florida, and together established this dominant North American oyster as a susceptible host. The detections involved high infection prevalences in seed oysters but, at the time of reporting, no associated large‑scale field mortalities in wild or farmed C. virginica populations had been confirmed, though concern was raised about potential impacts on restoration and aquaculture and about trade restrictions triggered by the pathogen’s notifiable status. Subsequent advisories and surveillance recommended stringent movement controls and further research, and international assessments now treat C. virginica as a susceptible host while still noting the absence of major B. exitiosa‑driven outbreaks comparable to those seen in flat‑oyster hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely anthropogenic transfer of infected broodstock or seed oysters and/or associated fouling organisms between regions and continents, facilitated by intensive hatchery and grow‑out operations along the US East Coast, introduced B. exitiosa into hatchery and nursery lines of C. virginica in multiple states. Internal mechanisms: This episode represents host expansion of an already‑established North American B. exitiosa lineage (originally detected in Crassostrea ariakensis and reservoir Ostrea equestris) into C. virginica, greatly increasing the parasite’s potential epidemiological niche on the continent; available data do not indicate increased virulence in this host, and infections in C. virginica have so far been predominantly subclinical.
Review: review – The original row correctly captured the first widely reported infections of Bonamia exitiosa in hatchery and nursery seed of Crassostrea virginica in North Carolina and Massachusetts, but incorrectly coded this as an inter‑continental emergence; molecular and surveillance data show B. exitiosa was already present on the US Atlantic coast in Crassostrea ariakensis and Ostrea equestris by the mid‑2000s, so this event is now re‑classified as re‑emergence via host expansion within Northern America rather than first arrival on the continent. Summary text has been updated to acknowledge earlier experimental detections in Florida, and the ‘continent’ field has been standardised to ‘Northern America’ in line with the country list.([vims.edu](https://www.vims.edu/people/carnegie_rb/pubs/BexitiosaAdvisory_VIMS.HSRL_11Sept2013_FINAL1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Australian flat (native) oyster Ostrea angasi in farmed and adjacent wild populations in southern Australia (Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia)
Event summary: After Bonamia‑like disease had devastated experimental native oyster culture and nearby wild Ostrea angasi beds in parts of Australia in the early 1990s, renewed outbreaks occurred between about 2013 and 2017 on intertidal O. angasi farms in southern Australia, where molecular work confirmed the causative agent as Bonamia exitiosa. These more recent epizootics caused substantial mortality on farms and prompted detailed studies of infection dynamics, revealing seasonal patterns and high infection intensities in some cohorts, with concerns that disease in culture could spill over to remnant wild O. angasi populations. Management responses included enhanced biosecurity, movement restrictions, and research into farm design and husbandry practices to limit disease spread, and bonamiosis continues to constrain expansion of native‑oyster aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of O. angasi aquaculture (including use of intertidal farm systems), movements of oysters among hatcheries and grow‑out sites, and environmental conditions favoring transmission likely contributed to recurrent outbreaks; historical overfishing and habitat loss left wild populations fragmented and vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that the parasite affecting O. angasi in these outbreaks is B. exitiosa rather than B. roughleyi, and the event is best interpreted as repeated epidemic expression of an established B. exitiosa lineage in a highly susceptible host rather than emergence of a novel genotype; efficient oyster‑to‑oyster transmission under farm conditions underpins the severe farm‑level impacts observed.
Review: retain – This row appropriately describes the post‑2013 farm‑level epizootics of B. exitiosa in Ostrea angasi in southern Australia as a re‑occurrence of disease first recognised in the early 1990s, with correct continent/subregion coding and emphasis on aquaculture‑linked drivers; sources include both Australian project reports and peer‑reviewed work on infection dynamics and species identity, which are the key references for this emergence episode.([frdc.com.au](https://www.frdc.com.au/bonamiosis-farmed-native-oysters-ostrea-angasi?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in wild and cultured stocks
Event summary: In 1991–1992, Bonamia ostreae was detected at high prevalence in European flat oysters in the Damariscotta River estuary in Maine and in Tomales Bay, California, confirming that the parasite was established on both coasts of the United States and had extended its range within North America beyond earlier west-coast foci. Histological surveillance documented infection prevalences of about 34–45% in Maine and up to 31% in California, associated with increased mortality and concern for both wild and cultured O. edulis stocks. The episode led to strengthened movement controls and ongoing monitoring programmes that have since limited the further expansion of flat-oyster culture in these estuaries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical trans-Atlantic and coastal transfers of live flat oysters for aquaculture and restoration are implicated in the long-distance and regional spread of B. ostreae, with movements among hatcheries and grow-out sites likely seeding new foci in Maine and California. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission in dense cultured populations and the high host susceptibility of O. edulis facilitated rapid amplification once the parasite was introduced.
Review: retain – corrected the event type from intra-continental emergence to re-occurrence because Bonamia ostreae was already present elsewhere in the Northern America sub-region before 1991, and updated the country annotation to show infections in both Maine and California in 1991–1992; event still represents a well-documented, high-prevalence range extension within North America and should be kept, but a human reviewer may wish to confirm its ranking among North American episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ireland [Cork Harbour 1993; Clew Bay 1993; multiple bays 1990s–2000s]
Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in wild beds and cultivated stocks
Event summary: Following first detection of Bonamia ostreae in Cork Harbour in 1987, Ireland experienced continuing severe bonamiosis in multiple flat-oyster bays through the 1990s and early 2000s, with particularly heavy impacts on the Rossmore (Cork Harbour) and Clew Bay stocks. Repeated monitoring showed high infection prevalence and age-related increases in mortality, leading to substantial declines in native flat-oyster beds and a shift toward selective breeding for resistance. By the early 2000s, disease management, selective-breeding programmes and zoning regulations had reduced early-life mortalities, allowing some recovery in selectively bred stocks despite ongoing low-level infection pressure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing presence of B. ostreae combined with intensive flat-oyster cultivation and limited effective movement controls enabled re-occurring epizootics; environmental conditions in Irish bays (suitable temperature/salinity regimes) supported parasite persistence. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was clearly identified; instead, chronic infection in a highly susceptible host species (O. edulis) resulted in re-occurring outbreaks when environmental or farming stressors increased, with some host genetic adaptation (selective breeding) gradually reducing mortality.
Review: retain – this long multi-bay episode captures the major chronic impacts of bonamiosis on Irish flat-oyster populations, with high mortalities and the initiation of selective-breeding and management programmes; geography, timing and classification as re-occurrence are consistent with the literature, so no structural corrections were needed and the event should be retained as one of the highest-impact episodes.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in cultured stocks on oyster farms
Event summary: In 2004, Bonamia ostreae was detected for the first time in Canada when histopathology and PCR screening of European flat oysters from a British Columbia oyster farm revealed infections that were absent from archived samples collected prior to 2003. Follow-up surveys in 2005 found low but consistent prevalences (roughly 0.5–11%) of B. ostreae in O. edulis on three farms that had all been stocked with seed from Washington State, USA, where the parasite is endemic. Although Canada’s flat-oyster industry is small, this detection extended the known range of B. ostreae within North America and led to a change in Canada’s health status for the disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The introduction into British Columbia is inferred to have occurred via human-mediated transfer of infected O. edulis seed from enzootic areas in Washington State, illustrating the role of aquaculture-related transboundary movements in spreading B. ostreae. Internal mechanisms: The parasite’s ability to persist at low prevalence in cultured O. edulis and to be detected only with sensitive histological and molecular methods underpins its cryptic establishment in western Canada and the need for ongoing surveillance.
Review: retain – new event added to capture the first confirmed detection of Bonamia ostreae in Canada (British Columbia) in 2004–2005, which extended the parasite’s regulated range within Northern America and prompted restrictions on importing Ostrea edulis seed from endemic U.S. areas; classified as re-occurrence within the same UN sub-region rather than inter-continental emergence, and recommended for retention, with expert review to confirm its relative impact compared with other North American events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in farmed/wild stocks (exact production setting not always specified)
Event summary: Around 2005, Bonamia ostreae was confirmed for the first time in Morocco, representing the first documented occurrence of the parasite in North Africa and extending its known range from Europe and North America into a new continent. Diagnostic investigations linked the Moroccan detections to the global B. ostreae clade already present in Europe, raising concern for local flat-oyster stocks. Subsequent surveillance confirmed the parasite’s establishment in Morocco, prompting its inclusion in international reporting and regional biosecurity planning.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The introduction into Morocco is inferred to be via human-mediated movements of infected European flat oysters or associated stock from endemic regions, consistent with known patterns of B. ostreae spread linked to shellfish transfers and possibly shipping-associated fouling. Internal mechanisms: The parasite’s ability to infect O. edulis across a wide environmental envelope (temperature and salinity tolerance) supports its geographic range expansion into suitable North African coastal habitats.
Review: retain – event correctly captures the first confirmed occurrence of Bonamia ostreae in Africa (Northern Africa, Morocco) and its status as an inter-continental emergence; corrected the Source URLs by removing an unrelated Korean case report and keeping references that explicitly document the 2005 Laayoune detection and its context; geographic fields already matched the UN sub-region scheme, so only source curation was required.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) – primarily wild Limfjord stock, with some aquaculture involvement
Event summary: In 2014–2015, Bonamia ostreae was detected again in native flat oysters in the Limfjord, Denmark, which had long been managed as a bonamiosis-free zone after earlier transient introductions into relayed French oysters in the 1980s. The new detections indicated that B. ostreae had re-established and was now infecting the local wild O. edulis population, and monitoring over subsequent years documented increasing prevalence and associated stock declines. By the 2022–2023 season, the Limfjord flat-oyster fishery was suspended indefinitely due to low stock levels and ongoing disease pressure, marking a major socio-economic impact from the renewed bonamiosis in this key northern European fishery.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely re-introduction via movements of oysters or shellfish from infected European areas, combined with changing environmental conditions (including milder winters relative to earlier decades) that reduced the likelihood of climatic ‘culling’ of infected stock; high exploitation pressure on Limfjord oysters further increased their vulnerability. Internal mechanisms: Established capacity of B. ostreae to persist and transmit in dense O. edulis beds under suitable environmental conditions, with no evidence of a fundamentally new strain but clear evidence of successful re-establishment and sustained transmission leading to renewed population decline.
Review: retain – Limfjord represents a major re-occurrence of bonamiosis in a previously disease-controlled area, causing marked stock declines and eventual fishery closure; the event was re-typed from combined re-occurrence plus re-emergence to re-occurrence only, because the host species and parasite lineage are unchanged and there is no clear evidence for a novel strain or other intrinsic change in the parasite.

Host: Ostrea chilensis (New Zealand flat / dredge oyster) in farmed populations, with concern for wild fisheries
Event summary: In 2014–2015, high mortalities in farmed New Zealand flat oysters (Ostrea chilensis) in the Marlborough Sounds led to histology, PCR and sequencing that confirmed the first detection of the exotic parasite Bonamia ostreae in New Zealand, where the related parasite B. exitiosa was already endemic. A delimiting survey by Biosecurity New Zealand in 2015–2016 showed that B. ostreae was confined to the Marlborough Sounds and nearby Nelson area, and a Controlled Area Notice was implemented to restrict shellfish movements and protect major wild fisheries such as Foveaux Strait. Intensive surveillance and movement controls have continued since, and to date B. ostreae remains restricted to defined containment zones, although its presence has necessitated ongoing management costs and risk-mitigation measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction via international trade or transfer of infected Ostrea or possibly other oyster species from the Northern Hemisphere is strongly suspected, with aquaculture-related stock movements providing the most plausible pathway; subsequent spread risk is driven by aquaculture practices and vessel movements among bays. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion to O. chilensis (a species already heavily impacted by B. exitiosa) demonstrates the parasite’s ability to infect a new flat-oyster host, and its direct life cycle and high pathogenicity in Ostrea spp. promote efficient transmission once introduced.
Review: retain – this event correctly describes the first detection of Bonamia ostreae in New Zealand flat oysters and its arrival in the Southern Hemisphere, with strong evidence of an imported incursion and substantial management responses; classification as first_detection and inter-continental emergence is appropriate, and the re-emergence flag has been set to No because host expansion to O. chilensis occurs in a new UN sub-region rather than representing a biologically altered parasite reappearing in a previously known sub-region.

Countries: New Zealand [Stewart Island – Big Glory Bay 2017; ongoing containment surveys nationally 2016–2025]
Host: Ostrea chilensis (New Zealand flat / dredge oyster) in farmed and local wild oysters
Event summary: As part of national surveillance following the 2015 incursion, Bonamia ostreae was first detected in 2017 in farmed flat oysters in Big Glory Bay, Stewart Island, extending the parasite’s known range within New Zealand beyond the original Marlborough–Nelson focus. Subsequent delimiting and routine surveys through at least 2024 have not detected B. ostreae in key wild fisheries such as Foveaux Strait, but have repeatedly confirmed its presence within defined contained zones at Stewart Island and Marlborough. Strict movement controls for live oysters and enhanced biosecurity compliance (including enforcement actions against illegal transfers) have so far prevented the parasite from establishing in the main Bluff oyster beds, although the ongoing risk continues to constrain industry operations and planning.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Secondary spread within New Zealand has been linked to domestic movements of farmed oysters and potentially contaminated vessels or equipment, with intensive aquaculture around Stewart Island providing opportunities for local amplification; strong regulatory responses (Controlled Area Notices, surveillance) have acted as counter-drivers limiting wider establishment. Internal mechanisms: Once introduced into Big Glory Bay, the parasite’s efficient direct transmission in dense cultured O. chilensis stocks and its ability to persist in the environment under local temperature and salinity regimes underpin the sustained need for control measures.
Review: retain – Big Glory Bay detections from 2017 onwards represent secondary spread of an established incursion within the same UN sub-region (Australia and New Zealand) and have major implications for the Bluff oyster fishery and long-term biosecurity; event has been retyped from intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence to re-occurrence only, reflecting its status as spread within a previously infected sub-region without evidence of a novel strain or host shift, and should be retained as a distinct, high-impact episode linked to the 2015 incursion.

Countries: Republic of Korea [Gaeya Island, west coast – wild oysters collected November 2023; first report published 2026]
Host: Ostrea denselamellosa (wild flat oyster) in natural coastal populations
Event summary: In a study based on wild flat oysters (Ostrea denselamellosa) collected in November 2023 from the west coast of the Republic of Korea near Gaeya Island, Bonamia ostreae was molecularly and histopathologically confirmed, representing the first report of Bonamia infection in this host species and the first confirmed occurrence of B. ostreae in East Asian coastal waters. PCR, sequencing of SSU and ITS regions, and in situ hybridisation showed that the Korean parasite clustered tightly with European and North American B. ostreae isolates, suggesting a recent anthropogenic introduction, although infection intensity and associated pathology in sampled oysters were relatively low. The findings, published in 2026, have prompted calls for enhanced surveillance and biosecurity measures in Korean oyster aquaculture and conservation programmes to prevent wider spread and assess potential impacts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The phylogenetic similarity between the Korean B. ostreae isolates and Northern Hemisphere strains indicates likely introduction via human-mediated movement of live oysters or their pathogens (e.g. transfers of Crassostrea or Ostrea stock, aquaculture equipment, or ballast water) from endemic regions; expanding global trade in shellfish and seed stock is a key underlying driver. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion to O. denselamellosa, combined with the parasite’s broad tolerance of environmental conditions and efficient within-host replication, underpins its capacity for further geographic range expansion in East Asia; low observed infection intensity suggests that local host–parasite dynamics are still developing, but the establishment of infection in a novel wild host is an important warning sign for the region.
Review: retain – updated the Event Year from 2026 to 2023 to reflect the actual sampling date of wild Ostrea denselamellosa near Gaeya Island, and clarified the country annotation accordingly; kept classification as first_detection and inter-continental emergence (first confirmed occurrence of Bonamia ostreae in wild East Asian oysters) but set re-emergence to No, as there is no evidence of a biologically altered parasite reappearing in a previously infected Asian sub-region. Earlier reports from China involved B. ostreae detected in imported European oysters for consumption rather than established wild Asian populations, so this Korean record appropriately marks the first regional emergence event.

Host: Sheep (lambs in meat flocks)
Event summary: In 1997, an epidemic of severe post‑natal disease with unusually high mortality in lambs and concurrent abortions in ewes occurred in at least one Spanish sheep flock, prompting investigation of a suspected pestivirus outbreak. Virus was isolated from multiple lamb spleen samples and characterized as border disease virus, with five closely related isolates (ESP97‑1 to ESP97‑5) that reacted with BDV‑specific monoclonal antibodies and clustered phylogenetically with the highly pathogenic Aveyron (Av) strain from France, defining them as BDV‑5. As the outbreak progressed through the affected lamb cohort and susceptible animals were exhausted, mortality declined, but the episode demonstrated that introduction of virulent BDV‑5–like strains can cause marked production losses in otherwise typical Spanish sheep systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of lambs originating from France’s Aveyron region into the affected Spanish flock likely introduced the ESP97 virus, and close housing of susceptible lambs together with pregnant ewes facilitated efficient horizontal and vertical transmission; absence of BDV vaccination or targeted surveillance in the area allowed the outbreak to develop before it was recognized. Internal mechanisms: emergence and local amplification of a BDV‑5 genotype closely related to the Aveyron strain, apparently more pathogenic than endemic BDV‑4 strains circulating in Spain and capable of causing high mortality in post‑natally infected lambs as well as abortions in ewes, consistent with a strain‑driven re‑emergence of more virulent BDV in an already affected subregion.([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2015/pmc_26392884/pmc_26392884.pdf))
Review: Retain: Newly added event to capture the 1997 ESP97/BDV‑5 outbreak in Spain, which produced unusually high lamb mortality and is highlighted in later reviews as one of the few severe horizontal BDV epidemics in domestic sheep. Classified as re‑emergence (virulent new genogroup in an already affected subregion); other emergence‑type flags are left as No.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Pyrenean/southern chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica pyrenaica)
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2002, a previously unreported fatal disease emerged in Pyrenean chamois in the Alt Pallars–Aran National Hunting Reserve in the central Pyrenees of northeastern Spain, with many animals showing emaciation, alopecia, neurologic signs and pneumonia. A novel pestivirus within the BDV group was isolated from affected chamois and phylogenetically designated BDV‑4, and population monitoring indicated an approximate 42% decline in the local chamois population over the outbreak period. After two years the explosive epizootic waned as susceptible animals were depleted, leaving a much smaller, partially immune population and establishing BDV‑4 as a major new pathogen in this wild caprine host.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113506003919?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities and aggregation of chamois in alpine habitats, hunting management that encouraged concentration of animals in reserves, and lack of prior exposure to BDV in this wild population enabled rapid transmission and high mortality; harsh winter–spring conditions likely exacerbated case fatality. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of BDV from domestic small ruminants into Pyrenean chamois, with emergence of a distinct BDV‑4 genotype adapted to this host and associated with severe systemic and neurologic disease, representing a re‑emergence of BDV in Southern Europe driven by a new host species and genotype.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113506003919?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain: Major wildlife emergence event with large demographic impact (≈40% local population decline) and clear evidence of a new BDV‑4 genotype in a novel host. Corrected misclassification by setting first_detection to No, as BDV was long known in the animal host system before this host jump.

Host: Pyrenean chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica pyrenaica)
Event summary: Beginning in mid‑2005, a second major wave of BDV‑associated disease in Pyrenean chamois was detected in the Cadí and Cerdanya–Alt Urgell hunting reserves and neighboring areas of northeastern Spain, spreading over more than 120,000–130,000 hectares of alpine habitat. Over roughly 31 months, an estimated 3,000 chamois died and in the worst‑affected reserve numbers fell from about 3,458 animals in 2004 to 1,281 by mid‑2006 (≈63% decline), after which the outbreak gradually subsided as surviving chamois developed immunity and BDV‑4 transitioned to endemic circulation at lower prevalence. This multi‑year epizootic confirmed BDV‑4 as a key population driver for Pyrenean chamois and demonstrated the capacity for repeated, spatially expanding die‑offs in connected subpopulations.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/17726/cdc_17726_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement and spatial connectivity of chamois subpopulations across contiguous mountain reserves, high densities in preferred ranges, and limited feasibility of controlling infection in free‑ranging wildlife facilitated re‑introduction and spread of BDV‑4 beyond the initial outbreak area. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of the previously emerged BDV‑4 genotype in a largely immunologically naïve metapopulation, with no evidence for a fundamentally new strain but with demographic feedbacks (recruitment of susceptible juveniles) enabling a large re‑occurring epizootic. This fits the project definition of re‑occurrence in the same subregion driven primarily by ecological and management factors rather than additional viral change.
Review: Retain: Major follow‑on epizootic with very large wildlife mortality and range expansion within the Pyrenees. Re‑classified as re_occurrence (Yes) and re_emergence (No) because it reflects re‑appearance and geographic spread of the same BDV‑4 lineage rather than emergence of a new genotype.

Host: Sheep (single flock under investigation)
Event summary: During routine genetic typing of pestiviruses in India in 2009–2010, eight sheep from a flock with clinical signs compatible with border disease tested positive for pestivirus by real‑time RT‑PCR, and virus isolation followed by sequencing showed the agent to be a BDV‑3 strain rather than the BVDV‑1 or BVDV‑2 previously reported from Indian small ruminants. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the Indian isolate with BDV‑3 reference strains from Europe, and antigenic profiling showed clear differences from known BDV‑1, BDV‑5 and BDV‑7 strains. The affected flock was managed within broader pestivirus control efforts, and while the immediate outbreak was limited, this investigation provided the first virological confirmation of BDV infection in Indian sheep and demonstrated that BDV had extended its range into Southern Asia.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26851587/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: most likely introduction of BDV‑3 into India via movement of infected live sheep, germplasm or contaminated biologicals from BDV‑endemic regions, together with limited prior surveillance for BDV, allowed the virus to circulate undetected until this investigation. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of BDV‑3 into a new UNSD subregion (Southern Asia) and successful establishment in local sheep, with typical BDV genome structure and no strong evidence yet for altered virulence compared with European BDV‑3 strains.
Review: Retain: Important intra‑continental emergence event representing the first confirmed detection of BDV in Indian sheep and in the Southern Asia subregion. Corrected misuse of the first_detection flag (now No, because global first detection occurred in 1959), while keeping intra_continental_emergence as Yes.

Host: Goats (intensively managed fattening herds)
Event summary: From January to April 2012, four commercial goat fattening farms in Anhui and Jiangsu provinces in eastern China reported severe, unremitting diarrhea outbreaks in 150–200 goats per farm, with morbidity of roughly 28–37% and mortality of 10–15% despite antimicrobial therapy. Initial laboratory work‑ups considered BVDV, but virological testing, including RT‑PCR and virus isolation, identified three closely related pestivirus strains clustering within BDV‑3, providing the first virologically confirmed evidence of BDV infection in Chinese goat herds and, more broadly, the first documentation of BDV in China. Following these outbreaks, awareness of BDV increased and subsequent studies detected BDV in additional small ruminant populations in several Chinese provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive fattening operations that aggregated weaned goats purchased from multiple smallholder farms created high contact rates and introduced infected animals into naïve cohorts; lack of prior recognition of BDV in China delayed specific diagnosis and control. Internal mechanisms: intra‑continental geographic expansion of BDV‑3 into Eastern Asia with establishment in Chinese goat populations, with multiple closely related strains indicating either repeated introductions or short‑range spread; disease expression in these outbreaks was dominated by enteric signs rather than the classic congenital 'hairy shaker' syndrome, reflecting host age and infection route rather than a clearly new viral phenotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3602100/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain: Major intra‑continental emergence event marking the first confirmed BDV infections in China and Eastern Asia. Corrected emergence‑type classification by setting first_detection and re_emergence to No, and keeping intra_continental_emergence as Yes to reflect expansion of BDV into a new Asian subregion.

Host: Sheep (1,708 three‑month‑old feeder lambs)
Event summary: In 2019, a group of 1,708 mixed‑breed feeder lambs was transported from an open‑range operation in Colorado to an enclosed barn in New York State; approximately six weeks after arrival, an explosive outbreak of acute respiratory and systemic disease began. Daily mortality abruptly rose to 20–30 lambs, and over about three weeks more than 300 lambs died, for an overall mortality of roughly 18%, with necropsies revealing emaciation, bronchopneumonia, polyserositis and ruminal acidosis. Border disease virus was isolated from several lambs, whole‑genome sequencing confirmed BDV, and sequential serology showed rapid increases in BDV‑neutralizing antibodies among surviving lambs; after the most susceptible animals had either died or seroconverted, the outbreak subsided, but the episode highlighted BDV as an under‑recognized cause of high mortality in North American feedlot lambs moved over long distances.([vet.cornell.edu](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/about-us/news/20200123/border-disease-virus))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑distance shipment of a large group of young lambs from range conditions in Colorado to intensive indoor housing in New York, combined with the stress of transport, shearing and dietary change, likely suppressed immunity and facilitated rapid BDV transmission; the absence of routine BDV diagnostics in feeder lamb supply chains delayed recognition of the etiologic agent. Internal mechanisms: efficient horizontal spread of BDV from acutely or possibly persistently infected lambs in a dense, immunologically naïve group, leading to an acute, self‑limiting re‑occurrence of BDV disease without evidence of a novel genotype, but with substantial short‑term mortality.
Review: Retain: High‑mortality outbreak in a very large lamb cohort with clear virological confirmation and detailed epidemiologic description. No change to emergence‑type classification other than tightening numbers and timelines based on the USAHA abstract and Cornell report.

Host: Sheep (Composite ewe flocks; many persistently infected lambs)
Event summary: In 2019, two large commercial Composite ewe flocks in the South‑Western Slopes region of New South Wales experienced unexpectedly poor reproductive performance, with one property scanning only 69.9% of 3,500 maiden ewes pregnant and then marking just 1,922 lambs, implying loss of more than 500 lambs between scanning and marking. Diagnostic work identified resorbing fetuses, stillbirths and many weak or 'hairy' lambs, and BDV RNA was detected by BDV‑specific qRT‑PCR in most of 10 examined aborted or stillborn lambs, while a high proportion of surviving hairy lambs were BDV‑positive by pestivirus antigen ELISA. Cross‑sectional serosurveys across age groups revealed high BDV antibody prevalence in some cohorts and many still‑susceptible breeding ewes in others, and in a monitored group of 120 persistently infected lambs, only 21 were alive at 5 months and 14 at 12 months, illustrating the substantial cumulative reproductive and post‑weaning losses associated with this outbreak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12961243/?utm_source=openai))
