Mechanism or driver: Drivers: joining maiden ewes at a young age under drought conditions, together with intensive confinement feeding in drought lots, placed large numbers of immunologically naïve breeding sheep together during the critical early gestation window for fetal BDV infection; limited historic recognition of BDV in Australian sheep and the focus on BVDV in cattle meant BDV was not an early diagnostic priority. Internal mechanisms: establishment of BDV infection with transplacental spread leading to widespread fetal death, stillbirths and the birth of many persistently infected hairy lambs that shed virus efficiently, driving large‑scale flock‑level reproductive loss and poor lamb survival, even though the virus itself appears to belong to existing BDV lineages rather than a novel genotype.
Review: Retain: Newly added, high‑impact re‑occurrence event showing large‑scale BDV‑associated reproductive loss in Australian sheep, with thousands of ewes at risk and well‑documented fetal and lamb outcomes. Classified as re_occurrence driven by management and demographic factors rather than a new genotype or region.

Countries: United States of America [1991–2012] (Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Upper Midwest high-incidence states); Canada [mid-1990s onward, especially southern provinces]
Host: Primarily humans; domestic dogs widely used as sentinels, with high and increasing Borrelia burgdorferi seroprevalence in dogs in endemic states and provinces; incidental infections in horses and other companion animals.
Event summary: From 1991 onward, Lyme borreliosis caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato showed a marked rise in incidence in the northeastern, mid-Atlantic and upper Midwestern United States, with hundreds of thousands of human cases and parallel increases in Borrelia seropositivity in domestic dogs used as sentinels, indicating intense enzootic transmission in wildlife and companion animals. Over the 1990s and 2000s, reported human cases more than doubled, and large-scale canine serosurveillance (~16 million dog tests over 60 months) confirmed widespread and increasing exposure of dogs across many U.S. counties, reflecting expanding risk areas for both animals and people. By 2012, high-incidence foci were firmly established and still expanding, with Lyme borreliosis recognized as one of the most important emerging zoonoses in North America, and transmission became entrenched rather than ending in a discrete outbreak termination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reforestation and landscape changes after historical agricultural abandonment increased wooded habitat and ecotones favorable to Ixodes scapularis and wildlife hosts; recovery and high densities of deer and small mammals amplified tick populations; suburbanization increased human and pet contact with peri-urban tick habitats; and climate change lengthened tick activity seasons and enabled northward range expansion. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission and geographic range expansion inherent to Borrelia–Ixodes–wildlife systems, facilitated by high reservoir competence in rodents and birds, but without a single new strain being clearly responsible for this re-occurrence pattern in endemic regions.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures a major, long-duration resurgence and geographic expansion of Lyme borreliosis risk in the northeastern, mid-Atlantic and upper Midwestern United States and emerging foci in southern Canada, with substantial impacts on humans and companion animals. Countries, sub-region, and time span are consistent with U.S. and Canadian surveillance and large canine seroprevalence datasets; classification as re_occurrence (without intra- or inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because the event represents intensification and spread within an already affected continent rather than first detection in new continents or sub-regions. No corrections to geography, timing or event-type coding were required, and the listed sources are relevant for both human and animal aspects, so this event is recommended for retention as one of the top-impact episodes.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Sweden [early 1990s]; Norway [1990s]; Finland [1990s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990s–2000s]; Ireland [1990s–2000s]; Germany [1990s–2000s]; Austria [1990s–2000s]; Czechia [1990s–2000s]; Poland [1990s–2000s]; Baltic region countries such as Latvia and Estonia [late 1990s–2000s]; additional affected countries across central and southern Europe where Ixodes ricinus and Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato expanded into higher latitudes and altitudes.
Host: Primarily humans and wildlife (rodents, birds, cervids) with domestic dogs and, in some areas, horses serving as exposed hosts/sentinels; transmission maintained by Ixodes ricinus and related ticks feeding on wild vertebrates and domestic animals.
Event summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, Europe experienced a substantial increase and northward/altitudinal expansion of Ixodes ricinus populations and associated Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato transmission, leading to higher Lyme borreliosis incidence and emergence of new risk areas in northern and central Europe, including parts of Scandinavia and high-altitude sites. Field studies in Sweden in the early 1990s documented efficient transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi s.l. from reservoir mammals to I. ricinus, while multi-country analyses later in the 2000s showed rising Lyme incidence in at least nine European countries, coinciding with tick range expansion and increased reports of disease in humans and animals in newly suitable habitats. By around 2010, these processes had produced a continent-wide pattern of geographic expansion, with Lyme borreliosis now established further north and at higher elevations than previously recorded, and endemic transmission persisting in expanded foci rather than ending as a simple outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climate warming (milder winters and longer vegetation seasons) allowed I. ricinus survival and activity at higher altitudes in central Europe and higher latitudes in Scandinavia; changes in land use and habitat connectivity (reforestation, fragmentation creating ecotones) favored ticks and hosts; increases and redistribution of deer and other cervids provided abundant tick reproductive hosts; and human behavior (recreation in forested landscapes, outdoor work, pet ownership) increased exposure of people and domestic animals. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent adaptation of ticks and Borrelia to new climatic envelopes) and enhanced transmission efficiency in local enzootic cycles; no single novel Borrelia strain has been definitively linked to the overall expansion, though local differences in Borrelia genospecies composition influence host range and pathogenicity.
Review: review – This event appropriately summarizes a large, multi-country expansion of Ixodes ricinus and Lyme borreliosis risk across northern, central and parts of southern Europe, which is among the most impactful global emergence episodes for this pathogen complex in both humans and domestic animals. To comply with the event-type definitions (which treat re_occurrence as mutually exclusive with intra- and inter-continental emergence), I changed the classification by setting re_occurrence from true to false so that the event is coded purely as intra_continental_emergence, reflecting that the defining feature is spread into previously unaffected northern and high-altitude sub-regions rather than resurgence in historically endemic areas. I also replaced the non-specific tick-borne encephalitis Wikipedia link with a review focused on zoonotic tick-borne pathogens in domestic animals in temperate and cold regions of Europe, while retaining the key Ixodes ricinus range-change and Swedish Borrelia transmission studies and a modeling paper on Borrelia dynamics; countries, sub-regions, dates and narrative remain consistent with the literature. Because of these classification and source adjustments, this row is flagged for review but should be retained in the final top-10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [1992] (initially São Paulo state, then additional autochthonous foci in Rio de Janeiro and other southeastern, central-western, southern and Amazonian regions)
Host: Humans, with evidence of infection or exposure in horses, dogs and cattle; transmitted mainly by Amblyomma and Rhipicephalus ticks rather than Ixodes, with Borrelia burgdorferi-like organisms associated with Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome (Brazilian Lyme-like borreliosis).
Event summary: In 1992, Brazil reported the first locally acquired Lyme-like borreliosis cases in siblings from Cotia (São Paulo state) who developed erythema migrans, flu-like illness and arthritis after tick bites, with positive serology for Borrelia burgdorferi, marking the first recognized autochthonous Borrelia-associated borreliosis in South America. Through the 1990s and 2000s, additional human cases with similar clinical pictures were identified in multiple Brazilian regions and the syndrome was formally described and renamed Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome, while surveys detected Borrelia DNA or serologic evidence of exposure in horses, dogs and cattle in endemic areas, indicating a broader zoonotic cycle. By around 2015, Brazilian borreliosis/Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome was recognized as a controversial but persistent emerging tick-borne zoonosis distinct from classical Northern Hemisphere Lyme borreliosis, with endemic foci in several states and ongoing debate over the etiologic agent and case definitions rather than a clearly resolved outbreak end.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of human activity into tick-infested rural and peri-urban environments in southeastern and other regions of Brazil; high contact between humans, dogs, horses and cattle and Amblyomma and Rhipicephalus ticks in pasture and forest-edge settings; and limited early clinical awareness and diagnostic tools resulting in under-recognition and delayed control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and possible novel strain/genotype emergence, with evidence that Brazilian cases involve Borrelia burgdorferi-like spirochetes adapted to non-Ixodes hard ticks and possibly altered morphologic or antigenic features; enhanced transmission via abundant non-Ixodes vectors; and potential geographic range expansion within Brazil as ticks and reservoir hosts occupy varied ecosystems. The syndrome is often considered distinct from classic Lyme borreliosis, but is treated here as an inter-continental emergence of Borrelia-associated Lyme-like borreliosis in a new ecological and vector context in South America.
Review: review – This row is retained as the first clearly described autochthonous Lyme-like borreliosis/Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome event in South America, with documented human disease and evidence of exposure in horses, dogs and cattle, and it is appropriately coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence because it marks the first recognized occurrence of a Borrelia-associated Lyme-like zoonosis on this continent. The time span, country attribution (Brazil), and host description are consistent with clinical series and reviews, and there is no indication that this is a spurious or minor event relative to other first-detection episodes. However, there is substantial ongoing debate over whether the Brazilian agent(s) should be regarded as classical Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato or a distinct Borrelia entity, and case numbers remain much lower than in North America and Europe; for these reasons, I recommend keeping the event but flagging it for review when harmonizing taxonomy and inclusion criteria across EPPs.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Tunisia [1992–1996 clinical series; 1990s high Borrelia lusitaniae prevalence in Ixodes ricinus]; Morocco [1990s] (sporadic human Lyme borreliosis cases and B. lusitaniae-infected ticks); Algeria [2000s] (detections of Borrelia lusitaniae in ticks); Egypt [2000s] (Lyme-group Borrelia reports); Kenya [2000s] (Lyme-group Borrelia including B. garinii in ticks along the Indian Ocean coast); United Republic of Tanzania [2000s]; Mozambique [2000s].
Host: Humans (small case series with erythema migrans, neurologic and articular manifestations), domestic dogs and horses as potential exposed hosts, and wildlife including small mammals and lizards (e.g. Psammodromus algirus) serving as reservoirs; infection maintained mainly in Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes inopinatus in North Africa and, in some eastern African sites, in Hyalomma rufipes associated with migratory birds and livestock.
Event summary: In the early 1990s, clinical and serological studies in Tunisia identified patients with erythema migrans and compatible neurological and articular symptoms, together with high seroprevalence for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, providing the first recognized Lyme borreliosis cases in North Africa and coinciding with detection of Borrelia lusitaniae and related genospecies in Ixodes ticks. Subsequent work in the 1990s and 2000s documented very high prevalence of B. lusitaniae in I. ricinus and I. inopinatus ticks in Tunisia and Morocco and additional detections of Lyme-group Borrelia in ticks from Algeria and Egypt, while small human case series and serosurveys confirmed that Lyme borreliosis was present but non-endemic and likely underdiagnosed. During the 2000s, Lyme-group Borrelia, including B. garinii, were also reported from ticks along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique, associated with migratory birds and Hyalomma rufipes, indicating limited but genuine autochthonous establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia cycles in selected North and East African coastal ecosystems rather than mere importation of cases from Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Suitable Mediterranean and coastal climates in North African Maghreb countries and along parts of the western Indian Ocean coast provide humidity and vegetation structure favorable to Ixodes spp. and other ticks, while migratory birds moving between Europe and Africa likely introduced and help maintain Lyme-group Borrelia across the Mediterranean and into East Africa; local land use and presence of lizards, small mammals and livestock create additional reservoir and vector habitats. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of Lyme-group Borrelia and their tick vectors into African coastal environments, including adaptation of Borrelia lusitaniae to reptile reservoirs and Ixodes species prevalent in Mediterranean habitats, and possible spillover via Hyalomma ticks that feed on migratory birds and savanna animals. Overall incidence remains low and focal, but this represents the first documented establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia transmission cycles in African wildlife and domestic-animal systems.
Review: review – This is a new row added during peer review to capture first detections and limited emergence of Lyme-group Borrelia and Lyme borreliosis in Africa, based on clinical series from Tunisia in the 1990s and high Borrelia lusitaniae infection rates in Ixodes ticks in Tunisia and Morocco, together with later reports of Lyme-group Borrelia along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique. It is coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence because it represents the first autochthonous establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia cycles on the African continent in humans, wildlife and domestic animals, while remaining low-incidence and geographically restricted. Dates and country list are approximate and derived from regional reviews rather than harmonized surveillance data, so confidence is set lower (0.7) and this row is flagged for review in future iterations, but including it aligns the dataset with the rule that first continent-level detection events may be retained even when case numbers are modest.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein Friesian)
Event summary: In 1988–1989, a closed Holstein Friesian dairy herd of 220 pregnant heifers and bulls was imported from Minnesota, USA, to a governmental farm at Arab El‑Aoumar near Assiut in Upper Egypt, at a time when Egypt was considered free of enzootic bovine leukosis.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) In November 1996, cows in this herd developed weight loss, reduced milk yield, lymphadenopathy and other signs, and subsequent serological screening and PCR testing demonstrated high within‑herd BLV seroprevalence (≈38% in cattle <2 years and ≈73% in older animals) and confirmed BLV proviral DNA, establishing the first recorded outbreak of enzootic bovine leukosis in Egypt.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) Following diagnosis, strict quarantine and test‑and‑cull measures were implemented; OIE reported 46 clinical cases among 418 susceptible imported dairy cows in Assiut with 45 animals destroyed, and Egypt was later able to re‑establish official BLV‑free status by 1997 after stamping‑out.([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/downld/infos_san_archives/eng/1997/en_970613v10n24.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of BLV‑infected pregnant dairy cattle from the USA into a previously BLV‑free national herd, limited pre‑import and post‑arrival testing in the late 1980s, and close contact, shared needles and equipment within an intensively managed dairy herd facilitated rapid within‑herd transmission.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was implicated; the outbreak reflects geographic range expansion of an existing BLV lineage into a new country, aided by the virus’s inherent ability to establish lifelong infection and efficient blood‑mediated transmission in high‑density dairy systems rather than documented genetic change.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13151565/))
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The event correctly describes the first recorded BLV/enzootic bovine leukosis outbreak in Egypt and is likely among the most important post‑1990 country‑level emergence events, but the original classification of this row as a 'first detection' event has been changed to 'No' because BLV was identified as the cause of enzootic bovine leukosis globally in the late 1960s, long before this episode. The outbreak represents introduction into a new country within a continent and sub‑region where BLV was already established, which does not fit the definitions of first/global, intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence; all type‑of‑emergence flags are therefore left as 'No' and the event is retained but flagged for expert review of this categorisation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) in mixed buffalo–cattle systems
Event summary: Around 2000, investigators in northern Brazil sampled water buffaloes and co‑managed cattle from herds in Pará state to clarify whether bovine leukemia virus, long recognised in cattle, also circulated naturally in buffalo populations. Serologic testing for anti‑BLV antibodies and virological investigation of peripheral blood leukocytes demonstrated BLV infection and virus isolation from buffaloes kept alongside infected cattle, providing the first widely cited evidence of naturally occurring BLV infection in water buffalo rather than solely experimental susceptibility. Although no discrete clinical leukosis outbreak or national control response was reported, this finding established buffalo as a natural BLV host in South America and highlighted mixed buffalo–cattle systems as a previously unrecognised reservoir for virus maintenance and spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of buffalo husbandry in wetland and Amazonian areas of Brazil, frequent co‑grazing of buffalo with BLV‑infected cattle, and lack of BLV surveillance in buffalo herds created ecological and management conditions favouring spillover from cattle into buffalo and subsequent in‑herd transmission. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects host expansion and geographic range consolidation of existing BLV lineages into water buffalo rather than emergence of a demonstrably novel or more virulent genotype; buffalo infections appear to involve the same viral types circulating in sympatric cattle, with BLV’s inherent capacity for life‑long, cell‑associated infection enabling persistence in this additional domestic ruminant host.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row has been added because the 2000 Vet Record report of naturally occurring BLV infection in Brazilian water buffalo is widely regarded as the first clear demonstration of natural BLV infection in this major livestock species, with important implications for host range and epidemiology. The country, sub‑region, timing and host are consistent with the primary source, and classifying the episode as re‑emergence (via host expansion) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection labels aligns with the event‑type definitions.

Host: Yaks (Bos mutus/Bos grunniens)
Event summary: Until the 2010s, enzootic bovine leukosis was considered primarily a disease of cattle, and little was known about BLV status in domestic yaks grazing the high‑altitude rangelands of north‑western China. Between April 2013 and March 2014, a large serological survey of 1,584 black and white yaks from Gansu province found BLV antibody prevalence of about 21%, with similar infection levels in both colour types and no strong associations with age, sex or management factors, representing the first report of BLV infection in yaks in China. Subsequent molecular studies on nearly 800 yaks from Gansu, Qinghai and Sichuan confirmed BLV proviral DNA and identified multiple env genotypes (notably genotypes 6 and 10), indicating established, genetically diverse BLV circulation within yak populations on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau rather than sporadic spillover alone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional yak husbandry in Gansu, Qinghai and Sichuan involves communal grazing, shared watering points and frequent contact with BLV‑infected cattle and other ruminants, while routine BLV testing is rare in yak herds; these practices facilitate cross‑species transmission and silent establishment of infection. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects host expansion and maintenance of existing BLV genotypes in yak rather than emergence of a novel viral lineage, although env‑gene diversity suggests repeated introductions from cattle and subsequent adaptation to high‑altitude yak populations; this justifies classification as re‑emergence driven by host expansion rather than as a first‑detection or geographic emergence event.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This new row captures a major host‑range emergence event—documented BLV infection with moderate prevalence and multiple genotypes in large yak populations on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau—based on robust serologic and molecular surveys. The timing, geography and host classification are consistent with the primary studies, and labelling the episode as re‑emergence (via host expansion into yak) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection tags is aligned with the provided definitions.

Host: Dairy cattle in intensive production systems
Event summary: In China, enzootic bovine leukosis had been a major cause of neoplastic disease in cattle before 1985, but national control measures introduced in the late 1980s substantially reduced BLV prevalence through the 1990s. From around 2000 onward, however, surveys began to show renewed spread of BLV in rapidly expanding intensive dairy herds, culminating in large cross‑sectional studies in 2013–2014 that reported high infection levels in Chinese dairy cattle and widespread herd‑level positivity across multiple provinces. Subsequent molecular work on BLV env genes from dairy cattle in Henan and Ningxia provinces identified several genotypes (including genotype 4 newly recognised in China) and substantial sequence diversity, confirming that BLV had re‑established itself as an important endemic pathogen in China’s modern dairy sector after a period of relative decline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of China’s dairy industry since the 1990s, increased long‑distance movement and importation of breeding stock, high animal densities, reuse of needles and obstetric equipment, and limited BLV‑specific control policies created conditions that favoured resurgence of BLV transmission after earlier reductions. Internal mechanisms: Multiple BLV genotypes (at least 1, 4, 6, 7 and 10) have been detected in Chinese dairy cattle, indicating repeated introductions and genetic diversification, but there is no clear evidence that a single novel, more virulent strain triggered the re‑emergence; the episode is therefore best classified as re‑occurrence driven primarily by management and trade factors, with novel genotype detection noted as an internal mechanism but not treated as a separate emergence type.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This added row summarises the large‑scale post‑2000 re‑emergence of BLV in China’s dairy herds, documented by national and regional prevalence surveys and molecular data, which likely represents one of the highest‑impact BLV events in terms of numbers of infected cattle and economic consequences. It is appropriately classified as a re‑occurrence event (resurgence in a previously affected sub‑region driven by management and industry changes) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection labels; nonetheless, the exact start year of the resurgence is approximate and could be further refined by future country‑specific historical work.

Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) and co‑managed cattle
Event summary: By the mid‑2010s, bovine leukemia virus was already endemic in Colombian cattle herds, but its status in the rapidly expanding water‑buffalo industry of the central‑western coffee‑growing region remained unclear.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2020.00608/full)) During 2016–2017, a field study sampled 140 buffaloes from eight herds plus nearby cattle, sheep and humans, and nested PCR targeting the BLV env gene detected proviral DNA in 33.6% of buffalo blood samples and 3.4% of cattle, representing the first molecular confirmation of natural BLV infection in water buffaloes in Colombia and, according to the authors, the first PCR‑based report of BLV in buffaloes in the Americas.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en)) The outbreak did not manifest as a recognized clinical leukosis epidemic in buffaloes, and no immediate large‑scale control program was implemented, but the finding highlighted silent BLV circulation in mixed buffalo–cattle systems and prompted recommendations for enhanced surveillance and management changes to limit further cross‑species spread.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of water‑buffalo production in Colombia’s coffee‑growing region, frequent co‑grazing and co‑housing of buffaloes with infected cattle, shared handling equipment, and limited BLV testing in buffalo herds created ecological and management conditions favoring cross‑species transmission and establishment of infection in buffalo populations.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en)) Internal mechanisms: This event reflects host expansion and geographic range consolidation of existing BLV lineages into water buffalo within South America rather than emergence of a clearly novel genotype; BLV’s inherent capacity for lifelong infection and efficient blood‑borne spread underlies its successful spillover and maintenance in this new livestock host.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/enzootic-bovine-leukosis/))
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Colombian buffalo event represents an important regional host‑expansion episode with substantial within‑herd infection documented by PCR, and it is reasonable to include it among major post‑1990 BLV events. However, the narrative should be interpreted carefully: earlier reports provide serologic and virologic evidence of natural BLV infection in water buffaloes in Brazil and elsewhere, so phrases implying a global 'first' in buffalo should be read as referring specifically to PCR confirmation in Colombia or the Americas rather than worldwide novelty. The event type (re‑emergence via host expansion) remains appropriate, but the row is flagged for human review to ensure wording is adjusted if the dataset text is edited.

Countries: Uruguay [early 1990s, Tacuarembó Department – large survey and economic impact assessment]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams in commercial and stud flocks in a major sheep‑producing department)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, a comprehensive epidemiologic and economic study in Tacuarembó Department, Uruguay, where sheep production is highly concentrated, examined 1,529 rams from 40 flocks clinically and serologically using agar gel immunodiffusion and ELISA, finding 179 ELISA‑positive and 168 AGID‑positive rams and showing that 20% of small flocks and 74% of medium‑sized flocks were affected by Brucella ovis infection. The study demonstrated that B. ovis infection was widely established in the department, with meaningful reductions in lambing and weaning rates and associated economic losses, prompting recommendations for systematic testing and culling of positive rams and improved flock biosecurity. Despite these findings, no nationwide eradication was implemented; control has remained flock‑based and B. ovis continues to be recognized as an endemic cause of ram infertility and production loss in Uruguayan sheep systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High regional density of sheep, extensive grazing systems with frequent mixing of rams between flocks, and lack of systematic control programmes allowed B. ovis to become highly prevalent and persist in Tacuarembó, while increased diagnostic capacity (AGID, ELISA) enabled quantification of the infection and its economic impact. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or host jump was reported; the event reflects recognition and documentation of widespread infection by typical B. ovis strains in an already affected South American subregion.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to capture a major 1990s episode showing high B. ovis prevalence and substantial economic impact in a key South American sheep region. Classified as re_occurrence (not first_detection) because B. ovis was already recognized in South America and Uruguay before the study; the event’s importance lies in the scale of documented infection and economic analysis rather than global novelty. The time span (1993–1995) is inferred from the M.Sc. thesis and 1995 INIA technical bulletin and may require confirmation by a subject‑matter expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Italy [1994, first isolation in domestic rams; subsequent spread documented in multiple regions]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams; experimental work also conducted in mouflon, but natural mouflon infection not confirmed)
Event summary: In 1994, Brucella ovis was isolated for the first time in Italy from the genital organs of two domestic rams with epididymitis, providing the first documented confirmation of ovine epididymitis due to B. ovis in the country, although the pathogen was already known elsewhere in Europe and globally. Follow‑up bacteriological and serological studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s showed that infection was present in multiple Italian regions, particularly in northern areas such as Lombardia and the Triveneto, with measurable ram‑ and flock‑level prevalence. Control responses focused mainly on improved diagnosis and flock‑level management rather than a dedicated national eradication programme, and B. ovis became recognized as an endemic reproductive problem in Italian sheep populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of breeding rams and limited prior awareness of ovine epididymitis due to B. ovis allowed introduction and unnoticed spread into Italian flocks before the first isolation in 1994; targeted surveillance for B. ovis was limited compared with programmes for zoonotic Brucella species, delaying recognition. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain, host jump, or resistance was reported; the event reflects geographic range expansion and detection of an already globally distributed pathogen within Southern Europe.
Review: Decision: review. Corrected emergence‑type classification by setting first_detection=No and re_occurrence=Yes, because B. ovis was first detected in sheep in New Zealand and Australia in the 1950s and was already reported in several European countries before 1994; the Italian event is a first *country‑level* confirmation and range expansion within an affected subregion, not the first detection in the host system. The host field was also simplified to remove embedded citation formatting. Event timing and geography are otherwise sound and supported by Italian national information and experimental infection work that documents the 1994 isolation and subsequent spread.

Countries: Croatia [2002–2003, large‑scale survey documenting first confirmed presence]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in multiple counties)
Event summary: During 2002–2003, a national survey in Croatia tested 14,404 sheep from six counties and identified 1,014 seropositive and 2,060 suspect animals for Brucella ovis by serology, providing the first rigorous proof that B. ovis infection was widespread in Croatian sheep flocks. Clinical and pathological examinations of seropositive rams and some ewes found typical epididymal lesions, confirming ovine brucellosis due to B. ovis as an important reproductive disease. Control measures focused on flock‑level management, castration or culling of positive rams, and ongoing surveillance rather than rapid eradication, and B. ovis has persisted as an endemic infection requiring continued monitoring in Croatia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Implementation of organized serosurveys and improved diagnostics revealed substantial infection that had likely circulated undetected, while animal movements and transboundary trade within the Balkans probably facilitated spread before formal recognition. Internal mechanisms: Reports do not indicate emergence of a novel genotype, increased virulence, or host shift; the episode is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence and recognition of B. ovis within an already affected European subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Updated the year field from 2002 to 2002–2003 to match the survey period and changed the emergence‑type classification from first_detection to re_occurrence, because B. ovis was already globally and regionally established and FAO/OIE yearbooks list B. ovis in Croatia before this detailed survey. The event remains appropriate to retain as a large‑impact episode, given the very large sample size, high numbers of seropositive animals, and national implications for control programmes.

Countries: Romania [2005 outbreak; 2006 re‑occurrence with multiple foci in Salaj and Ialomita counties]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in affected flocks; clinical signs often mild or absent, detection mainly by serology)
Event summary: Romania reported ovine epididymitis (Brucella ovis) to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) in 2005 and, after declaring the initial outbreak ended, confirmed new infections again in November 2006, triggering an immediate notification as re‑occurrence of the disease. The 2006 episode involved several outbreaks in Salaj and Ialomita counties, including a large flock with nearly 1,000 sheep, where complement fixation testing identified infected rams and ewes despite limited overt clinical disease. Control measures included movement restrictions, screening, zoning and culling or slaughter of some infected animals, but B. ovis remained present at low prevalence, and Romania has subsequently maintained surveillance for ovine epididymitis within broader small‑ruminant brucellosis control programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incomplete elimination of infection after the earlier outbreak, continuing trade and possibly illegal movements of rams between flocks, and limited awareness of B. ovis contributed to re‑introduction or persistence in affected areas. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of antigenic shift, resistance, or host expansion was reported; the re‑occurrence reflects residual infection and renewed transmission following relaxation of control measures rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Decision: retain. The event is clearly documented in the WOAH immediate notification as a re‑occurrence following a 2005 outbreak, and the current classification (re_occurrence with no first_detection or inter/intra‑continental emergence) aligns well with the project’s definitions. No corrections to timing, geography or emergence type were required, although experts may wish to cross‑check whether the 2005 and 2006 episodes should be split into two rows or kept as a single linked re‑occurrence episode as done here.

Countries: Serbia [2008–2009, first identification in northern districts; 2014, confirmed outbreak in Pirot municipality]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in traditional flocks)
Event summary: Brucella ovis infection was first identified in Serbia in 2008–2009 during serological investigations in the northern region (South Bačka and Srem districts), where ELISA surveys detected substantial seroprevalence in rams and sheep, revealing B. ovis as an under‑recognized cause of reproductive disease in the country. Subsequent work characterized the epizootiological, clinical and pathological features of infected Serbian flocks, and in 2014 a detailed investigation in Pirot municipality in southern Serbia confirmed additional infected rams and flocks, indicating wider geographic spread at the national level. Control strategies have focused on improved diagnosis, culling of seropositive rams, and surveillance, but no national eradication has been achieved and B. ovis is now regarded as an endemic reproductive pathogen of Serbian sheep.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased awareness and availability of serological tests, together with targeted surveys, enabled detection of previously unrecognized infection, while movements of breeding stock between regions (north–south) likely contributed to dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The reports describe typical B. ovis strains without evidence of new genotypes, resistance, or altered virulence; the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence and geographic spread within an already affected Southern European subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Changed emergence‑type classification from first_detection to re_occurrence, since B. ovis had long been present in Europe and the event reflects country‑level detection and spread within an already affected subregion, not global first detection in the host system. The timing (2008–2014) and geography are supported by Serbian surveillance and case‑report papers; the event remains appropriate to retain given the relatively high reported seroprevalence and national implications.

Countries: Brazil [2010, first isolation in Paraíba State (Northeast); early 2010s, wider semiarid Paraíba surveys]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in semiarid, largely extensive flocks)
Event summary: In 2010, Brucella ovis was isolated and its DNA confirmed by PCR for the first time from sheep in Paraíba State in Brazil’s Northeast region, where the pathogen had not been previously reported despite earlier descriptions of B. ovis infection in southern Brazilian states such as Rio Grande do Sul. Follow‑up epidemiological studies in the semiarid Sertão mesoregion of Paraíba in the early 2010s documented flock‑level seroprevalence and identified management risk factors, confirming that B. ovis infection had become established and was spreading among extensive, non‑mechanized sheep flocks in the Northeast. Recommended control measures included testing and culling of positive rams and improved biosecurity, yet implementation in smallholder systems has been uneven, and B. ovis remains an endemic contributor to reduced fertility and lamb output in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of sheep production into Brazil’s Northeast, frequent animal movements from already infected southern states, and limited veterinary infrastructure and routine testing in smallholder systems facilitated introduction and establishment of B. ovis in a new regional production hub. Internal mechanisms: No evidence was reported for novel genotypes, increased virulence, or host shifts; the episode represents re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion of existing B. ovis lineages within South America.
Review: Decision: retain. The event is well supported by primary studies showing first isolation and high seroprevalence of B. ovis in the Brazilian Northeast, in the context of earlier endemicity in southern Brazil. Classification as re_occurrence (regional expansion within an affected continent) rather than first_detection or inter‑continental emergence is appropriate, and no corrections to timing, geography, or sources were required.

Countries: Spain [Aragón region – re‑emergence after withdrawal of Rev1 vaccination]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in regional flocks formerly included in B. melitensis eradication and Rev1 vaccination programmes)
Event summary: After Aragón (Spain) achieved official freedom from Brucella melitensis in small ruminants and stopped compulsory Rev1 vaccination in 2011, a regional surveillance programme monitored B. ovis infection in rams from 2010–2019 using a gel immunodiffusion test. Data presented in 2019 showed that, compared with the last year of Rev1 vaccination, the prevalence of B. ovis infection in rams and the proportion of positive flocks increased substantially during 2011–2019, with statistically significant disease clusters and bacteriological confirmation of B. ovis in multiple seropositive flocks. This re‑emergence demonstrated that withdrawing Rev1, which confers cross‑protection against B. ovis, without implementing a dedicated B. ovis control programme can lead to a major resurgence of ovine epididymitis, and similar patterns have been reported in other EU countries with comparable histories of Rev1 use.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The key driver was the policy decision to withdraw Rev1 vaccination after eradication of B. melitensis, removing cross‑protective immunity against B. ovis in a region where this pathogen persisted at low levels, combined with dense regional sheep populations and ongoing movements of breeding rams between flocks. Internal mechanisms: No novel B. ovis strain or resistance phenotype was reported; the episode is best interpreted as a vaccine‑driven re‑occurrence of an established pathogen rather than evolutionary re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to capture a well‑documented and high‑impact re‑emergence of B. ovis in Aragón after Rev1 withdrawal. Classified as re_occurrence because resurgence is clearly linked to external drivers (cessation of cross‑protective vaccination and regional husbandry patterns) rather than pathogen change. Exact quantitative prevalence values over 2011–2019 are summarized only in abstracts and conference materials, so an expert should confirm the chosen time span and wording of the impact description.

Host: Domestic sheep (ewes and rams in mixed small‑ruminant systems)
Event summary: Between roughly 2015 and 2018, a structured survey of 300 sheep from nine districts in Karnataka state, India, using serology and PCR, demonstrated antibodies and DNA of both Brucella melitensis and Brucella ovis in sheep, with 5.34% seropositive for B. ovis and species‑specific PCR confirming B. ovis DNA in a subset of samples. The study, conducted in a country already recognized as a brucellosis hotspot, showed that multiple districts (e.g. Yadgir, Tumkur, Raichur, Bagalkot) had non‑trivial levels of exposure to B. ovis and noted that only one prior B. ovis seroprevalence report in Indian sheep existed at the time. The findings highlighted B. ovis as a neglected component of ovine brucellosis in India and led to calls for national surveillance and tailored control strategies alongside existing B. melitensis programmes, although large‑scale B. ovis‑specific control has not yet been widely implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historically, Indian brucellosis control and surveillance have focused on zoonotic B. melitensis, with little routine testing for B. ovis in sheep; growing small‑ruminant populations and animal movements allowed B. ovis to become established with minimal detection until more advanced serologic and PCR methods were applied in this survey. Internal mechanisms: No novel B. ovis strain, increased virulence, or host expansion was described; the episode reflects re‑occurrence and recognition of existing infection in Southern Asia rather than a new evolutionary event.
Review: Decision: review. Changed emergence‑type classification from first_detection to re_occurrence, since B. ovis has been known globally since the 1950s and there was at least one earlier seroprevalence report from India; this episode is better framed as first robust documentation and regional recognition of an under‑diagnosed infection. The event is retained because it concerns a very large national sheep population and provides the first solid evidence that B. ovis is present and epidemiologically relevant in India.

Host: Domestic sheep (Valle del Belìce breed ewes and rams in a traditional farm; context of a wider Sicilian sheep population)
Event summary: Around 2019–2020, a confirmed outbreak of Brucella ovis infection was investigated in a traditional sheep farm in Trapani province, Sicily, within a district encompassing roughly 480 sheep farms and about 89,000 sheep, where B. ovis infection had been underestimated. The investigation found high within‑flock infection levels, with more than half of tested rams positive by complement fixation and an even higher proportion by ELISA, along with reproductive problems, indicating intense local transmission in a previously under‑surveilled area of Italy. The outbreak occurred against the backdrop of an earlier Sicilian serosurvey showing approximately 10% ram‑level B. ovis seroprevalence across 163 farms, highlighting substantial endemicity. Control actions centred on diagnostic testing, segregation and removal of positive rams, and farm‑level biosecurity improvements, but given the size of the surrounding sheep population and limited historical surveillance, B. ovis remains a concern for continued re‑occurrence in Mediterranean sheep systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional extensive management with close contact between rams and ewes, limited routine screening for B. ovis compared with zoonotic Brucella species, and dense local networks of small farms facilitated persistence and re‑occurrence of infection within the Sicilian sheep sector. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of new genotypes, altered virulence, or host shifts was reported; the episode represents a notable localized resurgence and better characterization of infection in a region where B. ovis has been present since at least the mid‑1990s.
Review: Decision: retain. The event is well documented and clearly represents a significant localized outbreak and improved detection of B. ovis in a major Italian sheep region, consistent with re_occurrence in an endemic area. Emergence‑type classification, timing, and geography are appropriate, and the selected sources (Sicilian outbreak report, prior Sicilian seroprevalence data and EFSA’s B. ovis assessment) are relevant; no substantive corrections were required.

Host: Cattle, sheep, goats, other small ruminants, and humans exposed through livestock contact or dairy products
Event summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union around 1991, brucellosis control programs in Central Asia collapsed, leading to a marked resurgence of infection in cattle and small ruminants and rising human incidence throughout the 1990s and 2000s. Throughout this period, Kazakhstan and neighboring republics reported brucellosis as one of their most challenging livestock diseases, with thousands of human cases annually and persistent infection in smallholder herds. By the late 2000s–early 2010s, partial reorganization of veterinary services and renewed vaccination campaigns began to stabilize or slowly reduce incidence in some areas, though the disease remains endemic and economically important.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Soviet economic and social transition causing fragmentation/privatization of collective farms, loss of centralized vaccination and test‑and‑slaughter programs, reduced veterinary funding, and increased uncontrolled livestock trade and movement. Internal mechanisms: No single novel genotype is implicated; re-occurrence reflects persistence and spread of existing Brucella abortus and B. melitensis lineages in newly vulnerable production systems, with geographic range expansion into newly established smallholder herds.
Review: review – Event is real and highly impactful, describing the well-documented post‑Soviet resurgence of brucellosis across Central Asia. Corrected emergence-type coding to re_occurrence=Yes and re_emergence=No to align with the given definitions (resurgence driven by system collapse and livestock movement, without evidence for a novel strain or host jump). Continent, sub-region, countries, timing, and narrative are consistent with cited sources; recommend retaining this as a major event but subject to expert review of the chosen 1990–2010 time window.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, and exposed humans (farmers, abattoir workers, rural households)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through 2009, Azerbaijan experienced a marked re-emergence of human brucellosis linked to infection in sheep, goats, and cattle, with human incidence increasing steeply in the 1990s and more than 11,000 reported cases over 1983–2009. The epidemic persisted into the 2000s, with hotspots in southeastern Azerbaijan where extensive small ruminant production and weak veterinary coverage coincided. Toward the end of the 2000s, Azerbaijan began developing a more explicit One Health strategy focused on strengthening animal vaccination and surveillance to curb ongoing transmission to humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Soviet deterioration of veterinary infrastructure, expansion of smallholder mixed farming, informal livestock trade, and limited access to pasteurized dairy, all facilitating sustained livestock infection and zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of endemic Brucella melitensis lineages rather than a single novel strain; the large increase in incidence is primarily due to system-level failures and geographic spread within the country, i.e. re-occurrence rather than pathogen change.
Review: review – Event accurately summarizes the substantial re-occurrence of brucellosis in Azerbaijan and is well supported by the main epidemiologic sources. Updated emergence-type coding so that only re_occurrence=Yes (re_emergence reset to No) because the resurgence is attributed to breakdown of control systems and husbandry changes, not to a documented new strain, host, or resistance phenotype. Geography and years are appropriate; recommend keeping as a distinct Central Asia/Caucasus episode but subject to expert confirmation of the 1990 start date.

Host: Primarily sheep and goats, with cattle involved in some areas; large numbers of human cases among herders and livestock workers
Event summary: After a period of relatively low incidence in the 1980s and early 1990s, human and livestock brucellosis re-emerged sharply in Inner Mongolia from around 1999, with tens of thousands of human cases reported between 1999 and 2008 and a major peak around 2010–2011. Brucellosis became the most serious zoonosis in the region, particularly in central and eastern pastoral counties where rapid expansion of sheep and goat production and long-distance live‑animal trade occurred. After 2011, intensive control efforts including expanded animal vaccination, movement controls, and improved case reporting gradually reduced or stabilized incidence, although Inner Mongolia remained one of China’s highest‑incidence regions by the mid‑2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of small ruminant herds to supply meat and wool, increased long‑distance live‑animal trade, inadequate animal vaccination, and improved but still incomplete human case detection; socio‑economic development and mobility spread infection to new counties. Internal mechanisms: Predominantly re‑expansion of endemic Brucella melitensis strains; available genetic data do not point to a single novel genotype. This episode is best coded as re-occurrence (resurgence and spatial spread within an existing endemic focus) rather than a new intra-continental emergence event.
Review: review – Inner Mongolia’s large, well-documented brucellosis resurgence is correctly captured and clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 events. Corrected type-of-emergence coding: set intra_continental_emergence=No and re_emergence=No, leaving re_occurrence=Yes, because the episode represents resurgence and expansion within an already endemic Eastern Asia sub-region without documented pathogen change. Countries field was simplified to China [1999] in line with the template (provincial detail retained in the summary). Recommended for retention, but expert review of exact end year (2010 vs 2011) is advised.

Host: Mainly sheep and goats, with cattle involved in some expanding agricultural areas; human cases among rural populations and slaughterhouse workers
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s but especially during 2004–2014, human brucellosis in China surged to historically high national levels, with incidence rising from very low levels in the early 1990s to several cases per 100,000 population by the mid‑2000s and peaking nationally in 2014; this reflected extensive underlying infection in livestock. During this period, the disease’s distribution expanded from traditional northern pastureland provinces (e.g., Inner Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet, Qinghai, Ningxia) into adjacent grassland and agricultural provinces (such as Shanxi, Heilongjiang, Jilin, Hebei, Shandong) and later into some southern provinces, representing major geographic spread within China. By the late 2010s, enhanced surveillance and vaccination, along with changes in livestock management, began to slow or partially reverse the expansion, though brucellosis remained a prominent zoonosis in northern China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: National-scale expansion and intensification of small ruminant husbandry, increased movement of sheep/goats and their products from northern pastoral to central and southern agricultural areas, gaps in animal vaccination and test‑and‑slaughter, and improved human case reporting. Internal mechanisms: Continued adaptation and spread of Brucella melitensis strains already present in China; no single novel lineage has been implicated. This is best classified as a large-scale re-occurrence episode (resurgence and range expansion within Eastern Asia) rather than intra-continental emergence or pathogen-driven re-emergence.
Review: review – This row captures the broader national re-occurrence and geographic expansion of brucellosis across China, which is clearly one of the largest global episodes post‑1990. Emergence-type coding has been adjusted to intra_continental_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, re_emergence=No, because spread occurred within the same UN sub-region (Eastern Asia) and there is no strong evidence for major pathogen change. Countries entry was simplified to China [2004]; specific provinces are described in the narrative. Because this event overlaps in time and space with the Inner Mongolia episode (previous row), a future consolidation into a single China-wide linked episode could be considered; recommend expert review for that decision.

Host: Sheep, goats, camels, cattle, and exposed humans, particularly in rural regions with traditional husbandry
Event summary: In Saudi Arabia, human brucellosis incidence rose through the 1980s to a documented peak of about 72 cases per 100,000 population in 1990, with very high regional rates exceeding 100 per 100,000 in some governorates, reflecting intense transmission from infected sheep, goats, camels, and cattle. During the early–mid 1990s the disease remained hyperendemic despite existing control policies, driven by high animal infection prevalence and strong cultural preferences for raw milk and fresh dairy. From the late 1990s onward, strengthened animal import controls, vaccination of livestock, and health‑education campaigns gradually reduced incidence, though brucellosis has persisted as an important zoonosis with substantial incidence in some regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional consumption of raw warm milk, importation of livestock for religious festivals and herd expansion, uncontrolled cross‑border movements of animals, and incomplete animal vaccination and surveillance. Internal mechanisms: Re‑amplification of existing Brucella melitensis and B. abortus infections in expanding animal populations; no specific novel strain or host shift is implicated, so this episode is coded as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.

Host: Small ruminants (sheep and goats), cattle, and exposed humans in affected municipalities
Event summary: Between 2005 and 2007, Bulgaria detected new foci of Brucella melitensis and B. abortus infection in livestock and humans after having been considered free of these forms of brucellosis since 1958, marking a notable resurgence in Eastern Europe. Initial cases were detected in goats and sheep along the country’s southern borders with Turkey, Greece, and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, followed by human infections in these high‑risk areas. Adjusted classification to intra_continental_emergence=No and re_occurrence=Yes, re_emergence=No, because Bulgaria lies within a historically endemic European sub-region and the episode reflects re-introduction and spread driven by animal movements rather than pathogen change. Host: Goats (source flock) and humans infected via locally produced raw goat cheese
Event summary: In 2008, an outbreak of human brucellosis occurred on the island of Thassos in northern Greece, linked to locally produced raw goat cheese contaminated with Brucella melitensis biovar 3 from an infected donor flock. The outbreak involved at least 55 confirmed human cases by mid-June 2008, against a background of endemic brucellosis in rural Greece, highlighting how unsafe artisanal cheese production can trigger concentrated epidemics even in areas considered livestock-brucellosis-free. Following investigation, authorities intensified surveillance of goat herds and enforced stricter controls on milk‑donor flocks and cheese‑processing practices on the island, which helped bring the localized outbreak under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Consumption of fresh, unpasteurized goat cheese; inadequate veterinary control of donor goat flocks and cheese hygiene; persistence of brucellosis in small ruminants in rural Greece despite formal eradication programs in many areas. Internal mechanisms: Local amplification of an endemic Brucella melitensis biovar 3 strain in a poorly controlled goat flock and contamination of cheese, leading to a point‑source foodborne outbreak in humans; no clear evidence of pathogen evolution, so this is coded as re-occurrence.
Review: review – The Thassos island cheese-associated outbreak is real and well described, but the original summary overstated its size. Updated the narrative to report ≥55 confirmed human cases (as documented in the EuroSurveillance preliminary report) instead of “more than 100,” and simplified the countries field to Greece [2008] with island details kept in the text. Re-coded emergence type to re_occurrence=Yes, re_emergence=No, reflecting a foodborne outbreak driven by unsafe processing of milk from an infected flock in an otherwise controlled setting. This is a moderate-size but clearly bounded event; recommend keeping it while noting that future prioritization could drop it if larger episodes are identified.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (dairy herds), sheep, goats, dogs, and associated human cases
Event summary: From about 2006 onward, Israel documented spillover of Brucella melitensis—traditionally endemic in sheep and goats—into previously brucellosis‑free dairy cattle herds, leading to several farm‑level outbreaks and secondary human infections through milk and direct contact. During the late 2000s and early 2010s, these bovine outbreaks occurred mainly near Bedouin and Arab pastoral areas where small‑ruminant brucellosis remained poorly controlled, and ritual slaughter practices and raw milk consumption facilitated human disease. Israeli veterinary and public‑health authorities responded by intensifying vaccination of small ruminants, culling infected cattle herds, and enhancing cross‑sectoral surveillance to limit further spillover and protect the status of commercial dairy farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large, uncontrolled Brucella melitensis reservoir in small ruminants (especially in Bedouin herds), close grazing and contact between sheep/goats and dairy cattle, cultural practices such as ritual slaughter and raw camel/goat milk consumption, and lapses in enforcement of small‑ruminant control programs. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced transmission of Brucella melitensis from sheep/goats into dairy cattle, with genomic analyses indicating clustering of bovine and human isolates within small‑ruminant‑associated lineages rather than a distinct bovine lineage; this justifies coding the episode as re-emergence (pathogen host expansion) rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: review – Spillover of B. melitensis into Israel’s dairy cattle from about 2006 is well documented and epidemiologically important because it represents a host expansion into previously brucellosis-free commercial herds. Adjusted emergence coding to re_emergence=Yes and re_occurrence=No, as the key feature is pathogen spread into a new livestock host niche within a region where small-ruminant brucellosis was already endemic. Countries field simplified to Israel [2006]; sub-regional details (Galilee, Golan Heights, Bedouin communities) remain in the text. Recommend retaining as a distinct re-emergence event focused on host expansion, with expert review of the chosen time window.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dairy cattle (two large herds), dogs, wildlife (e.g., jackals, wild boar), and one confirmed human case
Event summary: In 2021, Brucella abortus re-emerged in Israel after an apparent absence of several decades, causing an outbreak in two dairy farms where 82 of 137 cows were found infected and associated infections were detected in dogs and one human. The event was detected through clinical signs and laboratory confirmation, prompting extensive tracing and testing of neighboring herds and wildlife in the Golan Heights and Galilee to determine possible sources and extent of spread. Intensive control measures, including culling infected animals, investigating potential wildlife reservoirs, and reassessing cattle vaccination policy, were implemented to stop transmission and prevent re‑establishment of B. abortus in Israel’s dairy sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Discontinuation of routine cattle vaccination with B. abortus B19 in 2018, potential introduction via animal movements or wildlife reservoirs in ecologically complex border regions, and gaps in surveillance that allowed undetected persistence or reintroduction. Internal mechanisms: Re-establishment of B. abortus in cattle populations previously considered free, without clear evidence of a novel genotype or host jump; therefore classified as re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region rather than pathogen-driven re-emergence.
Review: review – The 2021 B. abortus outbreak in Israeli dairy herds is real, well characterized genomically and epidemiologically, and notable because it follows decades of apparent elimination. Re-coded this event as re_occurrence=Yes and re_emergence=No to align with the strict definitions (reintroduction after control lapse, but no clear evidence for a new strain or host range shift). All other fields (country, years, scale, and hosts) are consistent with the cited Emerging Infectious Diseases report; retain this event as a high-importance but geographically limited resurgence needing expert confirmation of its ranking among the top 10 by impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Primarily humans infected via dairy products; underlying reservoirs in dairy cattle, goats, and other livestock producing contaminated milk used for homemade or illegally sold cheese
Event summary: Between 1998 and 2011, the United States recorded multiple brucellosis outbreaks associated with consumption of unpasteurized dairy products—especially homemade or illegally sold Mexican‑style fresh cheeses (queso fresco) made from raw milk from infected livestock. These outbreaks affected primarily Hispanic communities in several states and were notable because they occurred in a country where bovine brucellosis had been largely controlled, demonstrating the continued risk posed by raw‑milk products and imported or home‑produced cheeses. Public‑health responses included outbreak investigations, targeted risk communication campaigns in affected communities, and enforcement actions against illegal cheese production and sale, which helped control each outbreak but did not entirely eliminate sporadic re‑occurrence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Consumption of raw milk and fresh cheeses made from unpasteurized cow or goat milk, informal or illegal cheese production and distribution (often in immigrant communities), importation of unpasteurized cheeses from endemic countries such as Mexico, and limited awareness of brucellosis risk among consumers. Internal mechanisms: Re-introduction of Brucella (mainly B. melitensis) via infected livestock or contaminated milk used in cheese production, leading to localized foodborne outbreaks in humans in an otherwise low‑incidence, highly controlled livestock setting; no novel strain or host range shift is invoked, so this is classified as re-occurrence.
Review: review – Clusters of brucellosis linked to unpasteurized Mexican-style cheeses in the US are well documented and demonstrate re-occurrence in a largely controlled setting. Adjusted emergence coding so that only re_occurrence=Yes (re_emergence=No), reflecting the absence of pathogen change and the foodborne nature of the outbreaks. Countries field was simplified to United States of America [1998] with state-level information kept in the text. While smaller in absolute case counts than some Asian and Middle Eastern episodes, this row captures an important pattern of re-introduction into a low-incidence system; recommend retaining but note that it could be deprioritized if a strictly case-number-based global top-10 is enforced.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (vaccine-factory workers, veterinary institute staff, and nearby residents) exposed to aerosolized Brucella abortus A19 vaccine strain; underlying production was for cattle vaccination, but a large parallel livestock outbreak was not reported.
Event summary: In 2019–2020, a massive outbreak of human brucellosis occurred in Lanzhou, Gansu Province, China, linked to emissions from the Zhongmu Lanzhou Biopharmaceutical Plant, which produced Brucella vaccines for livestock. During July–August 2019, the plant used expired disinfectants during fermentation of B. abortus vaccine strains, allowing live bacteria in waste gas to escape and form aerosols that drifted downwind to the nearby Lanzhou Veterinary Research Institute and surrounding residential areas. The first cluster of seropositive institute staff was detected in November 2019, and subsequent large-scale screening of residents identified more than 3,000 confirmed human cases by September 2020, making this the largest recorded laboratory- or vaccine‑factory–origin brucellosis outbreak. Once the source was identified, authorities halted vaccine production, revoked the plant’s license, and implemented mass testing, compensation, and long-term medical follow-up for exposed populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Serious biosafety failures at a veterinary vaccine plant, including the use of expired disinfectants and inadequate exhaust decontamination, combined with the facility’s proximity and downwind position relative to a veterinary research institute and residential areas. Internal mechanisms: Human infection caused by aerosolized Brucella abortus A19 vaccine strain, with no evidence of major genetic change; enhanced transmission resulted from high-concentration aerosol exposure rather than pathogen evolution. This episode is best coded as a large re-occurrence event triggered by a laboratory/vaccine manufacturing accident rather than as a new emergence in animals.
Review: review – New event added to correct a major omission: the 2019–2020 Lanzhou vaccine-factory–associated brucellosis outbreak, which multiple analyses identify as the largest recorded laboratory‑origin brucellosis cluster worldwide. Coded as re_occurrence (due to a biosafety failure and aerosol exposure of humans in an already endemic country) with no intra- or inter-continental emergence flags. Country, sub-region, timing, and scale (≈3,200–3,300 confirmed human cases; many more seropositive) follow the main peer-reviewed and official reports. Because this event is primarily human and laboratory-origin, but of exceptional magnitude, it should be retained in the top-10 list for Brucella spp. and closely reviewed by subject-matter experts.
