Host: Equids (horses, mules, donkeys)
Event summary: From 1999 to 2007, multiple outbreaks of glanders occurred in equids in Punjab Province, Pakistan, including a large cluster among Faisalabad Mounted Police horses and cases along major trade routes. Molecular epidemiology of 15 isolates demonstrated several closely related Burkholderia mallei genotypes circulating across different stables, consistent with persistent endemic lineages rather than a single point introduction. Despite local culling and movement controls, the disease remained entrenched in pockets of Punjab and continued to pose a risk of spread to other Pakistani provinces and neighbouring countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density working and mounted equid populations, communal watering points, and frequent animal movement for work and trade, combined with limited compensation for culled animals and weak enforcement of historical glanders legislation, favoured maintenance and repeated re-introduction of infection between districts. Internal mechanisms: VNTR and sequencing data showed distinct but related B. mallei genotypes persisting over several years, indicating long-term endemic lineages without clear evidence of substantially increased virulence, host range change or antimicrobial resistance; the event is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence in an already endemic sub-region rather than true intra-continental emergence.
Review: review – Retain this event, but correct its classification and geography. Intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because Pakistan lies within an already affected UN sub-region (Southern Asia) and the episode reflects resurgence/endemicity rather than first occurrence in a new sub-region. Countries have been restricted to Pakistan (1999–2007), removing the Afghanistan outbreak from this row to avoid double counting and to treat that small imported episode separately. The event remains one of the largest modern glanders episodes, supported by detailed molecular and outbreak data from Punjab.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [1999-2021]; key affected states include Pernambuco & Alagoas [1999], Maranhão [2007-2017], Rio de Janeiro [2012, 2015-2016], Pará, Piauí and others over time
Host: Equids (horses, mules, donkeys)
Event summary: After Brazil had been considered free of glanders since the 1960s, the disease reappeared in 1999 with confirmed equine cases in the northeastern states of Pernambuco and Alagoas, marking the start of a prolonged national re-emergence. From 1999 to 2021, official data recorded more than 3,000 equids and over 1,400 outbreaks across numerous states, with persistent foci in the Nordeste and later spread to other regions including Maranhão, Rio de Janeiro and parts of the Amazon and Centre-West. Implementation of a national surveillance and control programme (PNSE), mandatory testing before movements, and test-and-slaughter strategies have reduced but not eliminated transmission, and glanders remains endemic with recurrent clusters and trade restrictions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and movement of equids for agriculture, transport and sport, combined with decades without targeted surveillance, limited compensation for culled animals and incomplete implementation of PNSE in some states, enabled silent circulation and geographic spread from initial foci in Pernambuco and Alagoas to much of Brazil. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing has identified multiple B. mallei lineages in Brazil, including introduction of the so‑called "Turkey 10" lineage into the Northeast and evidence of regional clustering of genotypes, implying intercontinental movement of strains and regional adaptation. Although control failures are central, the establishment of previously absent lineages in Brazil justifies classifying this prolonged episode as a re-emergence event with a genotypic component rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: review – Retain but substantially revised. Start year moved from 2008 to 1999 to reflect the documented re-emergence of glanders in Pernambuco and Alagoas and continuous reporting thereafter, with >3,000 equids and >1,400 outbreaks recorded nationally between 1999 and 2021. Intra_continental_emergence was set to No because South America was already historically affected; re_emergence remains Yes to reflect the establishment of new B. mallei lineages (e.g. the Turkey 10 genotype) in Brazil. Sources were updated to include WOAH reports and recent Brazilian spatial/molecular analyses that better quantify the scale and duration of this event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Working equids (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, a cross-sectional serosurvey of nearly 1,000 working equids in central Ethiopia found approximately 3–4% seropositive for glanders using complement fixation and Western blot, demonstrating previously unrecognized but widespread infection in an area thought to be largely free of the disease. Subsequent WOAH reports from Eastern Africa recorded official presence of glanders in Eritrea in 2010 and suspected infection in Ethiopia in 2011, confirming that Burkholderia mallei was established in local horse and donkey populations. These findings revealed endemic foci of glanders in Eastern Africa and prompted increased attention to equine health surveillance, although resource constraints have limited comprehensive eradication efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High reliance on working equids for transport and draught power, congregation of animals at markets and watering points, low biosecurity, and limited access to veterinary services favoured silent persistence of B. mallei infection in Eastern Africa. Cross-border movements of animals and trade in equids from endemic parts of Asia or the Middle East may have contributed to historical introduction, but the modern event largely reflects recognition of long-standing infection rather than a discrete introduction. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of new strains, resistance, or altered virulence was reported; hence the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence of a long-established pathogen in a previously affected continent, newly documented through improved serological surveys.
Review: review – Added new event to capture a major, previously omitted modern focus of glanders. This row summarises serological evidence for endemic infection in working equids in central Ethiopia (≈3–4% seropositive) and official WOAH notifications from Eritrea and Ethiopia around 2010–2011, which collectively represent the main documented re-occurrence of B. mallei in Eastern Africa. Classified as re-occurrence (no internal pathogen changes demonstrated) and intra/inter-continental emergence set to No because Africa had historical glanders foci. Sources emphasise the original Ethiopian serosurvey, WOAH regional reports, and authoritative disease overviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses (outbreak in racing/performance and quarantine horses; equids generally)
Event summary: In 2004, glanders was detected for the first time in the United Arab Emirates in an official equine quarantine facility in Dubai, when imported horses from Syria tested positive and an outbreak spread among quarantined and high-value performance horses. At least 10 horses were confirmed infected and approximately 75 animals were ultimately euthanized as part of eradication efforts, with rapid notification to the OIE and extensive tracing of horse movements. Following strict test-and-slaughter, disinfection, and reinforced quarantine procedures, the outbreak was contained and the UAE subsequently regained and maintained official freedom from glanders, although the Dubai 7 strain later served as a molecular reference for related outbreaks in the Gulf region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International movement and trade of high-value horses, particularly from endemic countries such as Syria, combined with gaps in pre-export and post-import testing before 2004, enabled B. mallei to enter a previously disease-free national herd; high-density housing in quarantine and performance facilities facilitated transmission once introduced. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing of isolates defined the Dubai 7 strain but did not indicate exceptional virulence or novel host range; the event reflects re-occurrence of a known pathogen in Western Asia due to horse trade rather than emergence of a biologically changed strain.
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified. Intra_continental_emergence was set to No because Western Asia had long been affected by glanders; this episode is a re-introduction into a previously free country within an already affected sub-region. Re_emergence was changed to No and re_occurrence to Yes, in line with project definitions, because the outbreak was driven by horse movements from endemic Syria and not by documented changes in B. mallei biology. Source list was strengthened by adding the original WOAH notifications and a focused article on the Dubai outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: India [2006-2011]; affected states included Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttarakhand, Haryana, Punjab, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh and others
Host: Equids (horses, mules, donkeys)
Event summary: After India had remained free of reported glanders for about eight years, the disease reappeared in 2006 with outbreaks among equids in northern states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Punjab, followed by spread to additional states over the next several years. Between 2006 and 2010–2011, surveillance and outbreak investigations confirmed 164 infected equids in at least eight states, with major foci including a large outbreak in Maharashtra and repeated episodes in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, leading to extensive euthanasia of working and cart horses. Under strengthened national legislation, infected animals were culled and biosecurity and movement controls were tightened, reducing incidence but not preventing subsequent sporadic cases and later resurgence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Relaxation or uneven enforcement of historical glanders control laws, uncontrolled movement of working and pack equids between endemic and previously free districts, and increased movements for brick-kiln work and religious pilgrimages facilitated re-introduction and spread. Economic disincentives to report disease and cull infected animals, together with limited early diagnostic capacity, delayed containment in some states. Internal mechanisms: Available studies emphasize circulation of existing B. mallei strains without evidence of a novel genotype or marked change in virulence; the episode is therefore best viewed as a major re-occurrence driven by management and movement factors rather than re-emergence due to pathogen change.
Review: review – Retained as one of the largest modern glanders episodes, but emergence types adjusted. Intra_continental_emergence was set to No because India lies within the already affected Southern Asia sub-region; the outbreak represents resurgence within that sub-region, not first occurrence in a new one. Re_occurrence remains Yes and re_emergence is set to No, because the literature attributes the 2006–2011 resurgence to horse movements and control gaps, with no clear evidence for new strains or host shifts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Equids (horses); dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) in Bahrain
Event summary: Around 2010–2011, glanders was detected in equids in Kuwait and Bahrain, countries that had been regarded as free of the disease for decades despite its presence elsewhere in the Middle East. In Kuwait, surveillance initiated in 2010 identified infected horses and led to culling of positives, with the last confirmed case reported in December 2010. In Bahrain, an outbreak that began in April 2010 in horses imported via Kuwait resulted in multiple equine cases and, during a 2011 recrudescence in the same region, a total of about 50 horses and at least one dromedary camel testing positive for B. mallei. Intensive test-and-slaughter programmes, quarantine of affected premises and strict restrictions on equine imports were implemented, enabling both countries later to regain official freedom from glanders.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of horses from endemic areas (notably Syria and Pakistan) through regional trade and movement for racing and leisure, coupled with inadequate pre-import testing and quarantine prior to 2010, appears to have seeded the Kuwait and Bahrain outbreaks; high-value horses kept in dense stable environments amplified transmission once infection was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that strains from Bahrain’s horses and the infected camel were closely related to the UAE 2004 Dubai 7 strain but clustered into at least two distinct lineages, suggesting multiple introductions. The documented natural infection of a dromedary camel, with lesions indistinguishable from those in horses, highlights host expansion/spillover during this outbreak and justifies classification as re-emergence involving host-range expression of an established equine lineage.
Review: review – Event retained but re-dated and merged. Year span changed from 2008–2010 to 2010–2011 to match WOAH and regional reports indicating that Kuwait’s investigation programme and positive cases occurred in 2010 and Bahrain’s large outbreaks with camel involvement occurred in 2010–2011. Countries are now listed as Kuwait [2010] and Bahrain [2010–2011], and the camel spillover is included in this single multi-host, multi-country episode as per the project’s guidance on linked events. Intra_continental_emergence is set to No (glanders was already present in Western Asia), while re_emergence is kept Yes to reflect the host expansion to camels and the presence of at least two distinct B. mallei strain clusters in Bahrain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses (racetrack and associated premises)
Event summary: In 2011, Lebanon reported its first occurrence of glanders when horses at the Beirut Hippodrome racetrack and associated premises tested positive for B. mallei, after two recently imported horses from Syria developed clinical signs. Extensive tracing and testing of the country’s small equine population—approximately 1,700 horses—identified additional seropositive animals, leading to the euthanasia of at least 20–25 horses at the racetrack and further culling of positives elsewhere. Intensive surveillance, movement restrictions and disinfection were implemented, and after the outbreak was controlled and no further cases were detected, Lebanon pursued recognition of freedom from glanders.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses from endemic Syria, where glanders was still present, into a previously free national herd with limited prior experience of the disease, coupled with racetrack housing that favoured close-contact transmission, seeded the outbreak. Rapid recognition and large-scale testing of almost the entire Lebanese horse population were required to delimit infection and restore export confidence. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel B. mallei lineage or host shift was presented; the event is a re-occurrence in the already affected Western Asia sub-region, driven by equine trade rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New event added to capture a major, previously omitted outbreak. The 2011 Lebanon episode involved euthanasia of more than 20 horses at the Beirut Hippodrome and testing of almost the entire national horse population, with substantial trade and surveillance impacts, making it one of the largest modern glanders events by scale relative to national herd size. Classified as re-occurrence (re-introduction into Western Asia via horses imported from Syria) with no intra- or inter-continental emergence and no evidence of internal pathogen change. Sources prioritise WOAH bulletins and detailed racetrack outbreak descriptions.

Countries: India [2015-2018]; affected states included Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh and others with seropositive equids during national surveys
Host: Equids (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event summary: Between 2015 and 2018, India conducted extensive risk-based serological surveillance for glanders and clinical investigations in working and indigenous equids, testing more than 7,700 animals across multiple states and detecting an overall seroprevalence of about 1%. Surveillance revealed ongoing transmission in previously affected states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab and Maharashtra, as well as new foci in additional districts, with seasonal peaks in cases from March to June. Progressive culling of seropositive equids, movement restrictions and awareness campaigns were implemented, reducing apparent prevalence in some areas but not achieving national elimination, and underscoring the chronic endemic status of glanders in parts of India.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued movement of low-value working equids between endemic foci and new districts, reluctance of owners to present animals for testing or accept euthanasia due to economic constraints, and incomplete enforcement of the Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act contributed to persistent low-level transmission and repeated re-introduction into nominally cleared areas. Climatic seasonality and peaks in work demand may also have influenced temporal clustering of cases. Internal mechanisms: Studies did not identify clearly novel B. mallei lineages or increased virulence during this period; the pattern reflects recurrent flare-ups of existing strains under imperfect control and surveillance, fitting the definition of re-occurrence.
Review: review – Retained as a distinct later episode of national-scale surveillance and resurgence in India, but intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the disease was already established in Southern Asia; this is not first occurrence in a new sub-region. Re_occurrence remains Yes, with re_emergence No, reflecting recurrent outbreaks driven by equid movements and incomplete control rather than documented pathogen change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses
Event summary: In 2018–2019, serological surveys of horses in central and eastern Mongolia found glanders seroprevalence of about 7–8% using rose Bengal test and complement fixation, indicating substantial ongoing transmission in a country that had historically reported eradication of the disease. Positive animals were detected across multiple districts, demonstrating that B. mallei infection was more widespread than previously recognized. Following identification of seropositive horses, Mongolian authorities introduced targeted restrictions on horse movements from affected areas and considered renewed eradication campaigns, although full national elimination has not yet been documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased regional horse trade and movement for tourism, racing and traditional events, along with free-ranging husbandry practices and limited routine surveillance after earlier eradication campaigns, likely facilitated re-introduction or unnoticed persistence of B. mallei in Mongolian equids. The logistical difficulty of testing and culling free-ranging horses over vast areas hampers rapid control. Internal mechanisms: Available reports have not yet provided detailed genotyping of Mongolian isolates, and there is no evidence of novel virulence or host shifts; the episode is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence in Eastern Asia, with renewed recognition of infection in a country previously considered free rather than emergence of a fundamentally new strain.
Review: review – Retained as a major modern event documenting relatively high seroprevalence in Mongolian horses, but classification adjusted: intra_continental_emergence set to No because B. mallei was already present in Eastern Asia (e.g. China) and this represents renewed detection in a previously free country, not first entry into a new sub-region. Re_emergence was changed to No and re_occurrence to Yes, as no internal pathogen changes have yet been demonstrated; the emphasis in the literature is on re-introduction or persistence under limited surveillance.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: Between 1992 and 1994, Eastern Sudan experienced 35 reported outbreaks of camelpox in dromedary herds, with epizootics lasting 2–5 months and showing about 9% morbidity and 1.2% mortality overall, with deaths concentrated in young camels under three years of age. The disease spread mainly by direct contact at communal watering points, producing fever, facial and limb oedema, lymph node enlargement and generalized or localized pox lesions on the head, neck, legs and abdomen. Outbreaks were most frequent in the cooler winter months and eventually subsided as susceptible cohorts recovered and seasonal conditions changed, without evidence of a novel strain or spread to new sub‑regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic circulation of camelpox in camel‑rearing areas of Sudan, seasonal congregation of camels at shared watering points, and higher susceptibility of young stock supported efficient transmission and recurrent epizootics. Internal mechanisms: Clinical and epidemiological patterns were consistent with known CMLV strains, with no evidence for a distinct new genotype; this episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of endemic virus in a previously affected sub‑region.
Review: Decision: retain. Added as a new event to capture the large 1992–1994 epizootic in Eastern Sudan (35 outbreaks with 9% morbidity and 1.2% mortality), which is one of the better‑documented, higher‑impact African camelpox episodes within the 1990+ period and was missing from the original dataset; classified as re‑occurrence in Northern Africa with no evidence of a novel strain or new sub‑region, consistent with Khalafalla & Mohamed 1996 and WOAH/WOAH regional distribution data.

Countries: United Arab Emirates [1993], United Arab Emirates [1995]
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: Between the 1993–1994 and 1995–1996 winter/rainy seasons, multiple camelpox outbreaks occurred on camel farms in the United Arab Emirates, with at least 15 laboratory‑confirmed outbreaks in 1993–1994 and over 20 in 1995–1996, affecting numerous dromedaries with localized and, in some herds, generalized systemic lesions and a few deaths. The disease spread among intensively managed herds during the cooler, wetter months, prompting detailed virological investigations and the development and deployment of the live attenuated Ducapox camelpox vaccine. Subsequent seasons saw a marked reduction in severe disease as vaccination, improved husbandry and quarantine of affected herds were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of camel farming in the UAE, seasonal rainy‑season conditions favoring congregation and possibly arthropod vectors, and frequent movement of animals between farms facilitated rapid herd‑to‑herd spread. Internal mechanisms: Available virological studies showed typical CMLV strains without evidence for a novel genotype, so this episode reflects large‑scale re‑occurrence of endemic camelpox in a susceptible camel population.
Review: Decision: retain. Well‑supported multi‑season UAE outbreak series (1993–1996) with numerous farm outbreaks and vaccine development; continent/sub‑region coding (Asia/Western Asia) and classification as re‑occurrence are consistent with WOAH/UNSD frameworks and with primary UAE outbreak reports, and the cited sources are appropriate primary and review references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 1999 an eruptive moderate form of camelpox was reported in a dromedary herd in the Al‑Ahsa region of Saudi Arabia, with 100% morbidity but no recorded deaths and extensive skin lesions on the head, neck and limbs. The outbreak developed rapidly within the affected three‑ to four‑year‑old camels following an initial febrile phase and typical pox lesions, but remained confined to the herd without evidence of spread to new areas. Control relied mainly on isolation of sick animals and supportive care, complementing existing broader regional vaccination and surveillance activities, and the episode resolved without wider propagation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High stocking density and close contact among animals in the affected herd promoted efficient camel‑to‑camel transmission; regional endemicity and partial immunity in surrounding herds likely limited wider spread. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolation and characterization did not indicate a novel strain, and the clinical picture matched typical camelpox, so this event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of endemic CMLV within a previously affected country.
Review: Decision: review. The 1999 Al‑Ahsa herd outbreak is real and correctly located (Asia/Western Asia) and classified as a re‑occurrence, but it involves a single herd with moderate severity and no deaths, so its overall impact is smaller than multi‑herd epizootics in Sudan, the UAE and Kazakhstan; if a strict ‘top ten’ impact filter is applied, this event is a candidate for downgrading or exclusion in favor of larger or zoonotically significant episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In spring and summer 2005 the first documented outbreak of camelpox in Syria occurred in the provinces of Duma (near Damascus) and Hama, with estimated 30–90% morbidity, 1–15% mortality and very high abortion rates in affected herds. The outbreak began after introduction of infected camels that had been grazing east of Damascus, then spread between herds via communal grazing and contacts, producing generalized skin and mucosal lesions, respiratory signs and deaths mainly in young and pregnant animals. Movement restrictions, improved biosecurity and supportive treatment, together with confirmation of the etiological agent as camelpox virus by electron microscopy, virus isolation and PCR sequencing of the hemagglutinin gene, helped bring the episode under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of infected camels from desert grazing areas into naive herds, use of shared pastures and watering points, and limited prior immunity in Syrian camel populations enabled rapid spread and high abortion rates; potential involvement of ticks and other arthropods may have amplified transmission. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis showed the Syrian CMLV to be closely related to strains from Somalia and Saudi Arabia, indicating geographic range expansion of existing lineages within Western Asia rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: Decision: retain. The first documented Syrian outbreak is well supported by primary data (morbidity, mortality, abortions and laboratory confirmation), and mapping to Asia/Western Asia with classification as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) correctly follows the project rule that spread to a new country within an already affected sub‑region is not coded as intra‑continental emergence; the source set is adequate, though the generic ScienceDirect ‘topics’ page is non‑essential.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) and camel handlers (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: From December 2008 through 2010, a prolonged camelpox episode affected multiple districts in Rajasthan, India (including Bikaner, Jaisalmer and Barmer), the country’s main camel‑rearing region, causing widespread skin disease and some systemic cases in camels with associated production losses. During the 2009 phase of this outbreak, three camel attendants developed localized pox lesions on their hands and fingers, providing the first laboratory‑confirmed, genomically linked evidence of human camelpox infection associated with camel outbreaks. Control involved segregation of sick animals, improved hygiene, and later targeted vaccination and surveillance efforts, and the outbreak waned as herd immunity increased and management measures were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High camel density in western Rajasthan, seasonal and nomadic movements, poor nutritional status and absence of routine camelpox vaccination favored sustained transmission; movement of camels to Border Security Force (BSF) camps and regional markets likely spread infection among districts. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed Indian CMLV isolates to be closely related to other Orthopoxviruses while genomic comparisons of camel and human isolates demonstrated direct camel‑to‑human spillover; this episode therefore represents re‑emergence involving host expansion (spillover to humans) in a region with long‑standing camel infection rather than the appearance of a wholly novel strain.
Review: Decision: retain. This multi‑district Rajasthan outbreak with the first laboratory‑confirmed human camelpox cases is clearly among the most epidemiologically important and higher‑impact events (large camel involvement plus host expansion to humans); geography (Asia/Southern Asia) and dual re‑occurrence/re‑emergence coding are consistent with the definitions, and the key outbreak and virological sources are correctly cited.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) and camel herders (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In 2014, typical camelpox outbreaks were observed in two migratory dromedary herds near Showak in Gedarif State, Eastern Sudan, followed between September and December by pox‑like skin disease in three camel herders who worked closely with the affected animals. The human cases presented with erythematous, vesicular and pustular lesions on the hands, arms, legs, back and abdomen that resolved within about two months and showed no evidence of human‑to‑human transmission. Molecular testing, virus isolation and partial genome sequencing confirmed camelpox virus in samples from both camels and herders, demonstrating zoonotic transmission of CMLV in Eastern Sudan against a background of endemic camel infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Migratory camel husbandry with close daily contact between herders and sick animals, handling of camels with active skin lesions, and lack of personal protective equipment facilitated camel‑to‑human exposure; endemic camelpox in Eastern Sudan provided a persistent animal reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Comparative sequencing showed high similarity between camel and human CMLV isolates, supporting direct spillover; the event represents re‑occurrence of camelpox in a known sub‑region combined with re‑emergence via host expansion to humans, rather than emergence of a distinct novel lineage.
Review: Decision: retain. Added as a new event to represent the 2014 Showak (Gedarif State) outbreak involving dromedary herds and three camel herders, which provides key evidence for zoonotic CMLV transmission and was missing from the original list; coded as re‑occurrence in Northern Africa and re‑emergence due to host expansion to humans, in line with the primary case‑report and camel zoonosis reviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 2016 an outbreak of pox‑like skin disease occurred in camel herds in the Negev and southeastern Israel, where camelpox had not previously been diagnosed, leading to identification of CMLV as the causative agent. Affected camels showed fever, weakness, abortions and multifocal skin lesions, mainly in females, and infection was confirmed by electron microscopy, cell culture, immunological assays and sequencing of the full viral genome. Following diagnosis, on‑farm control measures including isolation of sick animals, improved hygiene and close monitoring were implemented, and the outbreak remained localized without documented wider spread across Western Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable introduction of infected animals or contaminated fomites from neighboring endemic countries, together with naive camel populations and lack of prior vaccination in Israel, allowed localized transmission in affected herds. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization showed the Israeli strain to be closely related to other known CMLV genomes within established diversity; this event represents geographic spread of existing lineages within Western Asia rather than emergence of a significantly different genotype.
Review: Decision: retain. The first diagnosed camelpox outbreak in Israel is well documented and appropriately mapped to Asia/Western Asia and classified as re‑occurrence within an already affected sub‑region; genomic data confirm that the virus clusters within known CMLV diversity, with no evidence of a novel lineage or inter‑continental emergence.

Host: Bactrian and dromedary camels (Camelus bactrianus, Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: From 2018 to 2020, a linked camelpox epizootic affected camel herds in the Balkan velayat of Turkmenistan and the adjacent Mangistau (Mangystau) region of western Kazakhstan in Central Asia. In 2018–2019, outbreaks in Balkan velayat caused disease and deaths in both young and adult dromedaries, after which, in June 2019, a major camelpox epidemic began in Kazakhstan’s Qaraqiya district and spread across multiple districts of Mangistau, ultimately affecting 2,336 camels, causing 27 confirmed fatalities and around 390 stillbirths or abortions before being brought under control through vaccination and movement management. Virological work during and after the epidemic, including genome comparisons with the historic M‑96 strain from Kazakhstan, showed that circulating viruses were closely related to earlier Central Asian CMLV lineages, and field trials of live and inactivated vaccines were conducted in 2019–2020 to help halt the outbreak and create a buffer zone along the Turkmenistan–Kazakhstan border.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of camels between Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, shared grazing areas in semi‑arid rangelands, limited historical vaccination coverage and environmental stressors contributed to re‑introduction and sustained spread across herds; regional trade and herd mixing facilitated dissemination within Mangistau. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicated close relatedness of contemporary outbreak isolates to the earlier Kazakh M‑96 strain, with no clear evidence of a novel genotype; the episode is therefore best interpreted as a large‑scale re‑occurrence of established CMLV lineages in a previously affected Central Asian sub‑region.
Review: Decision: retain. This new merged row replaces separate Turkmenistan 2018–2019 and Kazakhstan 2019–2020 rows and more accurately treats them as a single cross‑border 2018–2020 Central Asian epizootic, as suggested by temporal proximity and shared border; mapping to Asia/Central Asia and classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) align with the literature, and key impact metrics (2,336 camels affected, 27 deaths, ~390 abortions) are drawn directly from the Kazakh field‑trial reports.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In summer 2020 a severe systemic camelpox outbreak was reported in a large dromedary dairy herd in the United Arab Emirates, where camelpox had previously appeared only sporadically, causing generalized external and internal lesions, respiratory disease and measurable mortality, with about 56 clinically affected camels among 5,085 animals and five deaths (overall mortality 0.1%, case fatality rate ~8.9% among diseased animals). The outbreak developed rapidly after introduction of susceptible animals and coincided with reduced ectoparasite control at the start of the COVID‑19 pandemic and high burdens of Hyalomma dromedarii ticks. Following laboratory confirmation of CMLV, aggressive treatment of secondary infections, restoration of tick control and improved biosecurity measures, the outbreak was brought under control and used as a case study on virulence and pathogenesis of systemic camelpox.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High animal density and constant close contact in a commercial dairy herd, temporary lapses in tick and ectoparasite control associated with COVID‑19‑related disruptions, introduction of likely naive animals and abundant Hyalomma ticks and other vectors enhanced transmission and disease severity; management factors such as animal movement between units further facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Pathological and genomic analyses suggested particularly virulent circulating strains capable of causing generalized systemic disease, but still within known CMLV diversity; the event is therefore coded as re‑occurrence in an endemic country and re‑emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity in an intensively managed herd.
Review: Decision: retain. This well‑documented 2020 UAE outbreak in a large commercial herd had modest herd‑level mortality but unusually high case fatality among clinically affected animals and extensive systemic lesions; classification as re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence (increased virulence and severity in an endemic country) is consistent with the primary report and with project definitions.

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) – presumed source, and one human case (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: Around 2023, a 30‑year‑old male migrant worker in Qatar presented with painful pustular lesions on his arms and was diagnosed with camelpox, constituting the first documented human camelpox case in the country and likely linked to occupational exposure to infected or subclinically infected camels. The case occurred against a background of endemic camelpox in regional camel herds but without a reported large concurrent camel outbreak in Qatar, and there was no evidence of onward human‑to‑human transmission. The patient recovered with supportive management and infection‑control measures, and the episode prompted calls for stronger One Health surveillance integrating veterinary and human sectors for early detection of similar zoonotic spillover events.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close occupational contact between camel workers and infected or subclinically infected camels, together with limited use of personal protective measures, enabled zoonotic exposure in an endemic region; regional camel trade and husbandry maintain a persistent animal reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and clinical data indicate spillover of existing CMLV strains into a human host without evidence of sustained human‑to‑human spread or a novel viral lineage; this event is therefore coded as re‑emergence involving host expansion to humans in Qatar rather than a new continental or sub‑regional presence in camels.
Review: Decision: retain. The first confirmed human camelpox case in Qatar is well documented and epidemiologically linked to camel exposure in a region with established camelpox in camels; mapping to Asia/Western Asia is correct and classification as re‑emergence (host expansion to humans) without re‑occurrence reflects the absence of a major concurrent camel epizootic; the DeepDyve URL from the original draft is redundant given the open‑access PMC article and has not been retained here.

Host: Beef and mixed beef–dairy cattle herds (breeding bulls and cows) under extensive natural‑service systems
Event summary: From roughly 1999 through 2014, multiple large‑scale epidemiological surveys in the Southern Cone of South America showed that Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis infection was highly endemic in natural‑service beef systems in Uruguay, southern Brazil and La Pampa province in Argentina. A national survey in Uruguay (1999–2000) found Campylobacter fetus–positive bulls in about 37% of 230 beef herds and roughly 28% of 1,754 bulls tested, while a cluster‑based survey in the Pantanal region of Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, detected infection in about 52% of 327 bulls from 17 of 19 herds, and provincial surveillance in La Pampa, Argentina, reported bovine genital campylobacteriosis–positive bulls in roughly 2.3–10% of 3,700–6,000 bulls, prompting implementation of a Provincial Control and Eradication Program for venereal diseases. Together, these studies confirmed that bovine genital campylobacteriosis was a leading cause of infertility and early embryonic loss across major beef‑producing areas of the Southern Cone and motivated sustained control efforts based on bull testing, culling of positives and improvements in reproductive management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive beef‑cattle production with reliance on natural mating, large herd sizes, limited routine andrological and venereal‑disease testing of bulls, movement of untested breeding stock between ranches, and relatively low uptake of artificial insemination all favoured the long‑term maintenance and regional spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis. The lack of standardized, highly specific diagnostics in many laboratories (heavy reliance on direct immunofluorescence) also delayed accurate quantification and control. Internal mechanisms: the pathogen’s ability to establish chronic, asymptomatic colonization of the bull prepuce, to persist in cow reproductive tracts and to cause repeated early embryonic loss underpinned its endemic persistence; there is no clear evidence that novel strains or increased virulence were responsible for the high prevalences observed in these surveys.
Review: Decision: Review. The event is supported by multiple large post‑1990 prevalence surveys in the Southern Cone (for example, a Pantanal survey in 2002 that found ≈52% of 327 bulls DFAT‑positive in 17 of 19 herds, and a Uruguay national beef‑bull survey around 1999–2000 with ≈28% of 1,754 bulls positive and 37% of 230 herds affected, plus La Pampa surveillance showing 2.3–10% of 3,700–6,000 bulls infected and subsequent reductions under the provincial control programme). However, the original ChatGPT record mis‑specified the timing and countries. I updated the Event Year from 2003–2011 to 1999–2014 to better encompass the main survey and control‑programme period, removed Paraguay (no comparable post‑1990 BGC prevalence study could be located), and restricted the countries to Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay with country‑specific start years (Uruguay [1999], Brazil [2002], Argentina [2007]). The summary was revised to include quantitative prevalence figures and to note the La Pampa Provincial Control and Eradication Program. Coding as re‑occurrence remains appropriate because these data document high endemicity in regions where BGC was already established, without evidence of first introduction or novel strain emergence. Source URLs were adjusted to emphasise primary regional epidemiological sources (Pantanal and Uruguay) plus the South America review, rather than more generic diagnostic papers.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Breeding bulls and beef cows in Spanish beef herds managed under dehesa and mountain grazing systems
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2019, analysis of 5,182 breeding bulls from 1,950 Spanish beef herds submitted to the SALUVET veterinary diagnostic laboratory demonstrated sustained endemic infection with Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis, with about 7.7% of bulls and 12.2% of herds PCR‑positive and infection widely distributed across dehesa and mountain systems. Over this nine‑year period, bovine genital campylobacteriosis was repeatedly confirmed as a major contributor to early reproductive failure in natural‑service beef herds and was frequently detected together with bovine trichomoniasis, reinforcing its economic significance. Control recommendations focused on improved bull testing, biosecurity, strategic culling and increased reliance on artificial insemination, but the persistent detection of positive bulls throughout the study period illustrated the difficulty of eradicating the pathogen in extensive grazing systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive beef production with natural mating, especially under dehesa and communal mountain pastures, older breeding bulls, and co‑infection with bovine trichomoniasis were major risk factors for Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis infection; limited mandatory surveillance and the movement of breeding bulls between herds facilitated ongoing transmission. Internal mechanisms: long‑term, asymptomatic colonization of the bull prepuce and efficient venereal transmission allowed the pathogen to persist endemically without requiring major genetic change, so this episode reflects resurgence and continued detection of an established infection rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event closely reflects the national‑scale diagnostic‑laboratory dataset reported for Spain from 2011 to 2019, including the numbers of bulls and herds tested and the estimated prevalences (≈7.7% of bulls and 12.2% of herds PCR‑positive for C. fetus subsp. venerealis), and correctly emphasizes dehesa and mountain grazing systems as high‑risk settings. Spain is correctly placed in Europe | Southern Europe and the event is appropriately coded as re‑occurrence, as BGC has been endemic in Spain and other European countries for decades. The cited sources include the primary Spanish study, an official national factsheet and a recent global review, which are suitable references. No larger or more impactful post‑1990 BGC event in Europe was identified that would clearly supersede this episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Beef cows and breeding bulls in a commercial cow‑calf herd in Saskatchewan, Canada
Event summary: In 2011, a large commercial beef herd in Saskatchewan, Canada, experienced marked reproductive failure with reduced pregnancy rates and prolonged calving intervals, prompting a detailed outbreak investigation. A new real‑time quantitative PCR assay applied to preputial and reproductive samples identified Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis as the primary cause of bovine genital campylobacteriosis in the herd, confirming venereal transmission from infected breeding bulls to cows. Control measures including segregation and culling of infected groups, changes in bull management and enhanced record‑keeping led to improved reproductive performance in subsequent breeding seasons, illustrating both the substantial potential impact of BGC in North American beef systems and the value of molecular diagnostics in outbreak settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: reliance on natural service with limited pre‑breeding surveillance for venereal pathogens, introduction or persistence of carrier bulls, and large extensively managed breeding groups facilitated unnoticed spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis before diagnosis; the absence of routine vaccination or testing for BGC meant that infertility was initially attributed to other causes. Internal mechanisms: chronic, often asymptomatic colonization of the bull prepuce and efficient venereal transmission underpinned rapid within‑herd dissemination, but there was no evidence of a novel strain, antimicrobial resistance or host shift, so the outbreak represents re‑occurrence of a known pathogen rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: Retain. The description matches the documented Saskatchewan cow‑calf herd outbreak investigated with a novel real‑time PCR test, including the timing, clinical picture (marked reproductive losses) and subsequent improvement following targeted control. Canada is correctly assigned to Northern America | Northern America, and the event is suitably coded as re‑occurrence because BGC had long been present in North America and there is no evidence of first introduction, inter‑continental spread or a novel strain. Although the event involves a single herd, it is one of the better‑characterised high‑impact BGC outbreaks in a region where the disease is relatively uncommon due to widespread artificial insemination, and is reasonable to retain among the limited number of major post‑1990 episodes.

Host: Bulls in mixed pastoral and other management systems in northern Nigeria (with implications for cows in the same herds)
Event summary: In 2013, a large cross‑sectional survey in three northern Nigerian states collected preputial samples from 602 bulls in 250 herds and used culture and identification methods to estimate a true animal‑level Campylobacter fetus prevalence of about 16%, with roughly 81% of isolates identified as C. fetus subsp. venerealis and most of these as biovar intermedius, and a herd‑level prevalence of around 25%. Infection was particularly common in older bulls and in herds managed under pastoral systems, and there was a strong positive association with brucellosis, helping explain substantial, previously unquantified infertility and abortion losses. Subsequent work highlighted bovine genital campylobacteriosis as a key differential in reproductive failure investigations in the region and called for improved control programmes, although structural constraints in extensive systems have limited rapid reduction of disease burden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dominance of extensive pastoral and agro‑pastoral cattle systems with natural mating, frequent communal grazing and bull sharing, limited access to veterinary infrastructure and diagnostics, and high mobility of herds across porous borders provided ideal conditions for the maintenance and spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis; concurrent brucellosis further exacerbated reproductive losses. Internal mechanisms: predominance of C. fetus subsp. venerealis biovar intermedius strains adapted to the bovine genital tract enabled efficient venereal transmission and chronic carriage in bulls, but surveys did not implicate recent genetic changes as drivers of increased incidence, so the episode is best interpreted as documentation of endemic re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event accurately summarises the 2013 Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica survey in northern Nigeria, which sampled 602 bulls in 250 herds and reported a true animal‑level Campylobacter fetus prevalence of 16.4% and herd‑level prevalence of 25.5%, with most isolates classified as C. fetus subsp. venerealis biovar intermedius and a strong association with brucellosis. Nigeria is correctly assigned to Africa | Western Africa, and categorisation as re‑occurrence (long‑standing endemic infection documented with modern epidemiological methods) is appropriate. The cited sources include the primary paper plus a companion risk‑factor analysis, providing good coverage of both prevalence and drivers. No larger, clearly more impactful BGC event from sub‑Saharan Africa post‑1990 was identified that would unambiguously displace this episode.

Host: Dairy cows in herds using natural service in the state of Pernambuco, Brazil
Event summary: In 2013, a PCR‑based prevalence study of bovine genital campylobacteriosis and bovine trichomonosis in the state of Pernambuco, northeastern Brazil, analysed cervico‑vaginal mucus from 383 dairy cows in 21 herds. Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis DNA was detected in 1.8% of cows, and at least one positive cow was found in 28.6% of herds, while Tritrichomonas foetus DNA was identified in about one‑third of cows and over 90% of herds, confirming venereal pathogens as important contributors to reproductive inefficiency in the region. Herds larger than 100 animals and reliance on natural breeding were identified as significant risk factors for BGC, leading to recommendations for improved biosecurity, greater use of artificial insemination and, where feasible, testing and culling of bulls to mitigate venereal disease‑related production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive and semi‑intensive dairy systems in Pernambuco that rely on natural mating, large herd size, limited veterinary infrastructure and diagnostic capacity, and frequent mixing of animals all favoured the maintenance and spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis and Tritrichomonas foetus; the absence of systematic venereal disease control programmes meant infections remained largely unrecognised until targeted surveys were undertaken. Internal mechanisms: this episode reflects endemic persistence of established C. fetus subsp. venerealis lineages, with improved molecular diagnostics (PCR) revealing infections that may have been under‑detected by earlier methods, rather than emergence of novel genetic variants.
Review: Decision: Review. The underlying event corresponds to the 2013 PCR‑based study of bovine genital campylobacteriosis and trichomonosis in dairy cows from 21 herds in Pernambuco, Brazil, but the original row mis‑stated several details. I changed the Event Year from 2015 to 2013 to reflect the sampling period rather than the publication date and corrected the host description from 'breeding bulls and cattle herds' to 'dairy cows in herds using natural service', because only cervico‑vaginal mucus from cows was sampled. The event summary was re‑written to report the published prevalences (≈1.8% of cows PCR‑positive for C. fetus subsp. venerealis and 28.6% of herds with at least one positive cow) and to clarify that herd size >100 and natural breeding were risk factors. Coding as re‑occurrence remains appropriate given Brazil’s long history of BGC; there is no evidence of new introduction or novel strain emergence. The source list was streamlined to focus on the primary Pernambuco paper plus the regional South America review that contextualises these findings.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Breeding bulls in beef and dual‑purpose herds in central Tamaulipas, Mexico
Event summary: In 2022 (published 2023), a study of breeding bulls in the central zone of Tamaulipas, Mexico, examined semen and preputial samples and detected Campylobacter fetus, including Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis associated with bovine genital campylobacteriosis, by PCR and sequencing, documenting affected herds with reproductive problems. The authors emphasised that this represented the first report of C. fetus subsp. venerealis in Mexico confirmed by molecular methods and argued that venereal campylobacteriosis had likely been an unrecognised contributor to infertility and early embryonic loss in local cattle for some time. The work spurred calls for broader surveillance, routine testing of breeding bulls and strengthened control measures to prevent further spread and to improve reproductive outcomes in Mexican cattle systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: reliance on natural mating in many Mexican beef and dual‑purpose herds, limited routine pre‑breeding testing of bulls for venereal pathogens, low awareness of bovine genital campylobacteriosis among producers and veterinarians, and historically scarce access to molecular diagnostics allowed long‑standing but largely undetected circulation of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis. Increasing availability of PCR‑based tests triggered recognition of infections in regions such as Tamaulipas. Internal mechanisms: this episode primarily reflects improved molecular detection of an established pathogen in Mexican herds, rather than emergence of a novel strain, with venereal transmission and chronic colonisation of the bull genital tract underpinning reproductive losses before laboratory confirmation.
Review: Decision: Review. The 2023 SciELO study from central Tamaulipas does provide the first molecular confirmation of Campylobacter fetus (including C. fetus subsp. venerealis) in Mexican breeding bulls and supports the view that BGC has been under‑diagnosed in this region. However, bovine genital campylobacteriosis was already documented in Mexico long before this work, for example a 1975 bacteriological investigation of bovine genital vibriosis in Sonora beef herds and later sero‑epidemiological studies in tropical Mexican cattle, so this episode cannot be considered the first detection of the pathogen in the country. I therefore set first_detection to No and interpret the event as a re‑occurrence / re‑documentation of an endemic infection revealed by improved molecular diagnostics. The summary was adjusted to emphasise that the study reports the first PCR‑based confirmation in Mexico rather than true first occurrence. The source URLs were updated to include both the recent Tamaulipas molecular study and an earlier Mexican bacteriological report to substantiate this reinterpretation.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Spain [1990]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990]; Finland [early 1990s]; France [early 1990s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1993]
Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; cattle; pigs
Event summary: After approval of fluoroquinolone (e.g. enrofloxacin) use in food animals in several European countries around 1990, fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni rapidly emerged in poultry and other livestock, with high proportions of resistant isolates in Spain, the Netherlands and other countries documented within a few years. Surveillance in the early 1990s showed sharp increases in quinolone resistance among Campylobacter from both humans and food animals in mainland Europe, closely following veterinary licensing of enrofloxacin in Spain, the Netherlands and Finland. By the mid‑1990s, high levels of resistance were established in broiler and other livestock reservoirs across multiple European subregions, providing a sustained source of resistant zoonotic infection via meat and other animal products.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and rapid uptake of veterinary fluoroquinolones in poultry and other livestock, intensification of broiler production, and high consumption of poultry meat. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via point mutations in the gyrA gene and related mechanisms conferring fluoroquinolone resistance; Enhanced Transmission within poultry flocks and along slaughter/processing chains; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of resistant lineages across European livestock and food‑trade networks.
Review: retain – Well‑supported by multiple reviews and regulatory analyses linking licensing of enrofloxacin in European poultry to a rapid rise of fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni in chickens and human cases in Spain, the Netherlands, Finland, France and the UK.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2691575/?utm_source=openai)) Country names have been normalised to the Country sheet but no substantive content or classification changes were needed; this remains a key global AMR re‑emergence event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Thailand [1993]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [early 1990s]
Host: Broiler chickens; swine; cattle
Event summary: In the early 1990s, surveillance in Thailand and Hong Kong documented a sharp rise in fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni isolated from broilers and from humans, following the introduction of fluoroquinolones in food‑animal production. By the mid‑1990s, resistance frequencies in Campylobacter from poultry meat and from human infections in some Asian settings exceeded 50–80%, indicating a large‑scale resistance emergence in regional livestock reservoirs and associated human populations. These high resistance levels persisted, providing a long‑term source of resistant zoonotic infections linked to poultry and other animal products.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing fluoroquinolone use in intensive poultry and pig production, rapid growth of commercial animal agriculture, and limited early regulatory controls on antimicrobial usage. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via gyrA mutations and other resistance determinants; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through efficient colonization and spread within dense broiler and swine production systems and contamination of poultry meat.
Review: review – Event is well supported by syntheses showing that fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter was essentially absent in Asia before 1991 but reached >80% in Thailand and Hong Kong within a few years of veterinary fluoroquinolone introduction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2691575/?utm_source=openai)) Countries have been adjusted to align with the Country sheet (Taiwan, Province of China removed from the Countries field, while its role remains implied in the narrative). Classification as a resistance‑driven re‑emergence (rather than first/inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate.

Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; cattle (secondary)
Event summary: After fluoroquinolones were approved for use in U.S. poultry in 1995, previously rare ciprofloxacin‑resistant C. jejuni began appearing in human and animal isolates, with state and national surveillance from 1992–2001 documenting a clear upward trend in quinolone resistance linked partly to domestic poultry exposure. Retail chicken surveys in the late 1990s and early 2000s found Campylobacter contamination with notable levels of fluoroquinolone resistance in chicken and turkey products, indicating establishment of resistant strains in poultry production. In response to accumulating evidence that poultry use was driving resistant infections, the U.S. FDA withdrew fluoroquinolone approvals for poultry by 2005, after which monitoring focused on resistance trends in poultry‑associated C. jejuni.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Therapeutic and metaphylactic fluoroquinolone use in broiler and turkey production, high‑throughput poultry processing, and large‑scale distribution of contaminated meat. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via gyrA mutations and related mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission along the poultry production chain sustaining high colonization and contamination rates.
Review: retain – Strongly corroborated by U.S. surveillance data showing no fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni in 1990, rapid emergence after poultry approvals in 1995, rising resistance in human and poultry isolates in 1997–2001, and withdrawal of enrofloxacin for poultry in 2005.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3367372/?utm_source=openai)) Event framing as a resistance‑driven re‑emergence in U.S. food animals is appropriate and among the globally most consequential episodes.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Portugal [early 2000s]; Italy [early 2000s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2001]; other EU member states [2000s]
Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; pigs
Event summary: From the early 2000s, multiple European studies and surveillance programs reported that Campylobacter from broiler flocks and chicken meat frequently showed multidrug resistance, with very high rates of fluoroquinolone and tetracycline resistance and increasing macrolide resistance in some regions. In countries such as Portugal and Italy, surveys of broiler carcasses and retail poultry showed that the vast majority of C. jejuni and C. coli isolates were resistant to at least one and often several unrelated antibiotic classes, indicating establishment of MDR lineages in production systems. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, these MDR profiles persisted across many EU countries despite some regulatory tightening, sustaining a major reservoir for difficult‑to‑treat zoonotic infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical and ongoing use of multiple antimicrobial classes in European poultry and pig production, high‑density intensive farming, and slaughter/processing practices that facilitate flock‑to‑flock and carcass contamination. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance involving combined fluoroquinolone, macrolide, tetracycline, and other resistance determinants; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of MDR clonal complexes across European poultry and pig trade networks.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the consolidation of multidrug‑resistant Campylobacter in European poultry and pigs, supported by high MDR prevalence in broiler meat and flocks in Portugal, Italy and other EU states and by EU‑wide AMR summaries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9265442/?utm_source=openai)) No corrections to geography or classification are required; this episode is distinct from the earlier 1990s fluoroquinolone‑only emergence.

Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; beef cattle (retail beef); pigs (retail pork)
Event summary: Beginning in 2002, the U.S. National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System retail meat program systematically sampled chicken, turkey, beef and pork, finding Campylobacter contamination particularly common in poultry and documenting substantial resistance to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and other drugs. Over 2002–2007, a large fraction of C. jejuni and C. coli isolates from chicken breast and other meats were resistant to multiple antimicrobial classes, with many widely dispersed clones, defining a major emergence of MDR Campylobacter in U.S. animal‑source foods. This surveillance demonstrated that MDR Campylobacter had become entrenched in retail meat supply chains, informing subsequent control efforts in livestock production and processing.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Previous widespread antimicrobial use in poultry and other livestock, large industrial slaughter and distribution systems that amplify and disseminate colonized flocks and herds, and limited early‑2000s regulatory constraints on non‑therapeutic antimicrobial use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with combined resistance to macrolides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and other drug classes; Enhanced Transmission in slaughter and carcass processing environments and along retail distribution networks.
Review: retain – Supported by NARMS retail‑meat data showing high Campylobacter contamination of poultry and frequent multi‑class resistance in >2,000 isolates collected 2002–2007 across the United States.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3008252/?utm_source=openai)) This represents a distinct, highly impactful phase in which MDR Campylobacter became firmly established in the U.S. meat supply beyond the initial fluoroquinolone‑only emergence.

Host: Sheep (pregnant ewes and fetuses); cattle (reservoir)
Event summary: From about 2003 onward, investigators in the United States identified a highly virulent, tetracycline‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni clone (clone SA, for sheep abortion) that rapidly became the predominant cause of Campylobacter‑associated ovine abortions, responsible for the vast majority (>90% in some series) of diagnosed cases. Molecular epidemiology showed that clone SA was widely distributed in sheep flocks and also present in beef and dairy cattle and retail meats, indicating broad ruminant reservoirs and potential food‑borne transmission to humans. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, recurrent abortion storms associated with clone SA caused substantial reproductive losses in sheep operations and prompted development of targeted pathogenesis studies and vaccine candidates, marking a major re‑emergence event in ruminant health.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of tetracyclines as the main class of antibiotics approved for prevention and treatment of Campylobacter abortion in U.S. sheep, flock management practices that facilitate within‑flock spread, and intensive ruminant production systems. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (uniform tetracycline resistance in clone SA); Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity associated with a distinct capsular polysaccharide and other virulence determinants enabling systemic infection and placental invasion; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of clone SA within U.S. ruminant populations.
Review: review – New high‑impact event added. Multiple studies document that a single hypervirulent, tetracycline‑resistant C. jejuni clone (clone SA) emerged around 2003 as the predominant cause of ovine abortion in the United States, accounting for >90% of cases and being widely distributed in sheep and cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295108/?utm_source=openai)) This constitutes a major re‑emergence in the animal host system that was missing from the original list and clearly merits inclusion among the top 10 events; timeframe and geography are well constrained but should be checked against any national production‑loss data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Broiler chickens; chicken carcasses and retail meat; cattle (secondary)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, studies in Brazil and neighboring South American countries showed widespread C. jejuni and C. coli contamination of broiler carcasses and retail chicken meat, with a high proportion of isolates exhibiting multidrug resistance to three or more antibiotic classes. Surveys in Brazilian states such as Paraná and in the Federal District documented that roughly half to three‑quarters or more of Campylobacter isolates from chilled chicken carcasses and retail meats were MDR, and later national‑scale work confirmed frequent MDR profiles in meats from Brazil’s large poultry export sector. Through the 2010s these MDR Campylobacter populations became established in regional poultry production, with little evidence of substantial decline, representing a major resistance emergence in South American animal‑source foods with global trade implications.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of poultry production and export in Brazil and other South American countries, extensive therapeutic and metaphylactic antimicrobial use in broilers, and limited early routine surveillance of Campylobacter in animal products. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with multiple co‑existing resistance genes and phenotypes; Enhanced Transmission within broiler flocks and processing facilities that favors dominant MDR genotypes and widespread carcass contamination.
Review: retain – Brazilian and regional data consistently show very high Campylobacter contamination rates and a majority of isolates displaying MDR phenotypes in broiler carcasses and retail meats from the mid‑2000s onward, in a country that is the world’s largest chicken‑meat exporter.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25567139/?utm_source=openai)) This is plausibly one of the most impactful AMR emergence events for C. jejuni in food animals globally; no structural corrections are needed.

Host: Broiler chickens (domestic); imported broiler chicken meat; humans (secondary)
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2008, investigations in the Republic of Korea found that Campylobacter spp. from domestic chicken meat and from imported poultry products, including shipments from Brazil, commonly showed multidrug resistance, with approximately 95% of isolates from domestic chicken resistant to ciprofloxacin and many resistant to multiple other drugs. Molecular typing demonstrated that MDR Campylobacter genotypes were shared between domestic poultry, imported Brazilian chicken meat and human clinical isolates in Korea, indicating that resistant lineages were circulating in Korean poultry production and being exchanged through international poultry trade. This period therefore marked both the consolidation of a highly drug‑resistant Campylobacter reservoir in Korean broiler systems and inter‑regional dissemination of MDR strains via South American poultry exports.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global poultry trade linking South American exporters with East Asian markets, antimicrobial use in both Brazilian and Korean broiler sectors, and strong consumer demand for chicken meat. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with complex MDR profiles; Enhanced Transmission and colonization in intensive broiler production and processing; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of successful MDR lineages via international trade, with subsequent local circulation in domestic poultry systems.
Review: review – Years have been corrected to 2004–2008 to match the sampling period of the Korean domestic and imported chicken‑meat study rather than the publication year; Brazil has been explicitly listed as a second country because imported Brazilian chicken was an important source of MDR strains.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1089/fpd.2010.0553?download=true&utm_source=openai)) The event is reclassified purely as re‑emergence: although resistant South American lineages were introduced into Asia, C. jejuni was long established in both continents, and the guidelines specify that such strain‑level movements should not be coded as inter‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Broiler chickens; chicken meat at slaughter
Event summary: In 2016, a structured national survey of Campylobacter from chicken flocks and carcasses at slaughter across all major Australian meat‑chicken producers unexpectedly identified fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni and C. coli despite the absence of licensed fluoroquinolone use in Australian poultry. Genomic analyses showed that these resistant isolates carried the canonical gyrA Thr86→Ile mutation and were interspersed among international lineages, suggesting introduction from outside Australia rather than local selection by on‑farm fluoroquinolone use. The survey indicated that these resistant strains had achieved widespread colonization of commercial flocks across companies, marking a notable emergence of fluoroquinolone resistance in a previously largely susceptible national poultry reservoir.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of resistant strains via imported breeding stock, hatching eggs, or other indirect trade/traffic, combined with intensive vertically integrated poultry systems that can disseminate introduced clones widely even without local fluoroquinolone use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via gyrA mutations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of resistant international lineages into Australian broiler populations; Enhanced Transmission in large integrated production chains.
Review: review – Event year has been narrowed to 2016, aligning with the national slaughter‑survey that first detected fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter in Australian chickens, in a setting where such resistance had previously been absent due to lack of licensed fluoroquinolone use.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/AEM.02765-19?utm_source=openai)) The summary has been adjusted to remove implications of multi‑year monitoring before follow‑up studies and to emphasize the survey‑documented widespread colonisation; classification as a resistance‑driven re‑emergence remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dogs (pet store puppies); humans (secondary, zoonotic spillover)
Event summary: Between 2016 and 2020, U.S. public health investigations identified a multistate outbreak of multidrug‑ and extensively drug‑resistant C. jejuni infections linked to pet store puppies, with 168 epidemiologically or molecularly associated human cases across at least 30 states and strong evidence implicating dogs sourced through commercial breeding and retail chains. The outbreak strains were resistant to all recommended first‑line treatments and many other antibiotic classes and were traced back through puppy supply chains involving multiple breeders, transporters and pet store chains, indicating that high‑level resistant Campylobacter had become established in this companion‑animal network. Control efforts including revised antibiotic use practices, infection‑prevention guidance for pet stores and veterinarians, and public awareness campaigns helped reduce new outbreak‑associated cases after 2018, but XDR outbreak‑related strains continued to be detected through 2020, showing persistence of this new host‑system reservoir.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive commercial breeding and retail distribution of puppies, frequent prophylactic and empirical antibiotic use in puppies before and after sale, high‑density housing and transport stress, and close human–dog contact facilitating zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with extensive MDR and XDR profiles across multiple antibiotic classes; Host Expansion (Spillover) and establishment of highly resistant C. jejuni lineages in companion dogs as a distinct reservoir; Enhanced Transmission through shared kenneling, transport, and retail environments and across the pet trade network.
Review: retain – CDC outbreak reports and subsequent analyses confirm a large, multistate outbreak of MDR/XDR C. jejuni linked to pet store puppies from 2016–2020, with 100+ confirmed human cases and strains resistant to all recommended first‑line therapies.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/mm6737a3.htm?utm_source=openai)) This is a clearly defined, high‑impact re‑emergence involving a new companion‑animal reservoir and justifies inclusion as one of the top events.

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, mainly Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), with cases also in western blue shrimp (P. stylirostris) and other local penaeids.
Event summary: After its initial recognition in 1985, necrotising hepatopancreatitis continued to cause recurrent seasonal epizootics in shrimp farms along the Texas coast during the early 1990s, with microscopic and ultrastructural studies on samples collected in 1986–1991 confirming heavy infections of hepatopancreatic epithelial cells by a pleomorphic intracellular Gram‑negative bacterium.([int-res.com](https://www.int-res.com/articles/dao/13/d013p235.pdf)) These outbreaks developed during warm seasons with high salinity and were associated with 20–95% mortality and serious production losses in Pacific white shrimp grow‑out ponds.([units.fisheries.org](https://units.fisheries.org/fhs/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2017/08/6.2.1-Hepatopancreatitis-2014.pdf)) As better diagnostic tools and management practices were introduced in the mid‑1990s, farms reduced but did not eliminate NHP‑associated losses, and the disease became an endemic constraint in the region rather than an acute epizootic.
