Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive pond-based mariculture in Texas with high pond organic loads, elevated summer temperatures and high salinity (20–40 ppt) created favourable conditions for proliferation and transmission of the NHP bacterium; poor biosecurity and reuse of pond water facilitated within‑farm persistence.([units.fisheries.org](https://units.fisheries.org/fhs/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2017/08/6.2.1-Hepatopancreatitis-2014.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of novel strain emergence; the main factor was high baseline pathogenicity of Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei combined with host stress, leading to severe granulomatous hepatopancreatitis and high mortality in L. vannamei.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC168141/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. Evidence from Lightner et al. 1992 and subsequent reviews shows that NHP was first recognised in Texas shrimp farms in 1985 and caused severe seasonal losses (20–90% crop mortality) through the early 1990s, with multiple farms affected nearly every year.([int-res.com](https://www.int-res.com/articles/dao/13/d013p235.pdf)) Treating the 1990–1994 cluster as a linked re‑occurrence episode in an already affected subregion (Northern America) is consistent with the event definitions, and no larger unrecorded NHP events are evident for this period; geography, host list and sources are appropriate and need no correction.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in commercial grow‑out ponds.
Event summary: In January–February 1993, a severe epizootic of necrotising hepatopancreatitis appeared in penaeid shrimp farms in the Tumbes region of north‑western Peru and adjacent farms in Ecuador, marking the first major spread of the Texas NHP agent beyond North America and its arrival in South America.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak rapidly affected numerous commercial ponds stocked with L. vannamei, with histology and TEM revealing massive intracellular infections of hepatopancreatic epithelium by a pleomorphic Gram‑negative bacterium closely resembling the Texas NHP agent and causing up to 90–95% mortality and severe production collapse.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) By June 1993 nearly half of Peru’s 44 active shrimp farms in the affected area were forced to close or suspend operations, and control relied on pond fallowing, improved water management and biosecurity to limit further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of L. vannamei farming in Peru and Ecuador using stock movements and shared water sources likely introduced the NHP bacterium from Texas into new farms; high ambient temperatures and high salinity in the Tumbes region favoured rapid amplification and farm‑to‑farm spread.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The etiologic agent showed close genetic and morphological similarity to the Texas NHP bacterium, later classified as Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing highly virulent strain rather than a novel variant.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. The 1993 Peru/Ecuador outbreak is well documented as a severe epizootic with very high mortalities and closure of roughly half of Peru’s active shrimp farms, and is widely recognised as the first confirmed spread of NHP from Texas to the South American continent.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) Classifying this event as an inter‑continental emergence (North America to South America) is appropriate; Peru and Ecuador with 1993 onset years correctly capture the main affected countries, and the chosen Aquaculture and molecular papers are the most relevant sources for this episode.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and western blue shrimp (P. stylirostris) in coastal ponds in Sonora and Sinaloa, Mexico.
Event summary: Necrotising hepatopancreatitis was first reported in Mexican shrimp aquaculture in 1999, when farms in Sonora and Sinaloa on the Pacific coast recorded outbreaks of hepatopancreatic disease and confirmed NHP infections in L. vannamei and P. stylirostris.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) During the subsequent 2–3 years, affected ponds experienced summer mortalities ranging from about 20% to 80%, particularly when water temperatures reached or exceeded 34 °C and salinity rose to around 45 g/kg, leading to notable production losses and increased diagnostic and control efforts.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) As farmers improved biosecurity, adjusted stocking densities and modified water management, the intensity of NHP outbreaks declined, and the disease transitioned toward an endemic but better‑managed problem in the main shrimp‑farming regions of north‑western Mexico.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional expansion of intensive shrimp farming in north‑western Mexico, coupled with movements of post‑larvae and possible use of infected broodstock from regions already affected by NHP, likely introduced the pathogen; extreme summer water temperatures and high salinity strongly predisposed ponds to outbreaks and high mortalities.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks were attributed to the same NHP bacterium later named Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei, with no strong evidence for a distinct Mexican strain; pathogenicity expressed as severe hepatopancreatic necrosis in stressed shrimp populations rather than through documented novel genotypes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. A recent peer‑reviewed history of shrimp diseases in Mexico clearly states that NHP was first reported there in 1999 in farmed P. vannamei and P. stylirostris in Sonora and Sinaloa, with 20–80% summer mortalities under very warm, hypersaline conditions.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) This supports the 1999 onset year and the description of impact. Because Peru/Ecuador (South America subregion) were already affected in 1993, the first detection in Mexico (Central America subregion) is correctly classified as intra‑continental emergence within the broader South America continent defined in the Country sheet, rather than as a new inter‑continental event. WOAH and national sources corroborate Mexico as part of the endemic Western Hemisphere range, so no geography or type changes are needed.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/app/uploads/2021/03/microsoft-20word-20--20nhp-20disease-20card-20-draft-.pdf))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp including Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and black tiger shrimp (Penaeus monodon) in coastal ponds in northern Viet Nam (Quảng Ninh) and later other farming areas.
Event summary: Around 2002, Vietnamese authorities first detected necrotising hepatopancreatitis, caused by a Rickettsia‑like Gram‑negative bacterium referred to locally as NHPB, in farmed penaeid shrimp in Quảng Ninh province, representing the first confirmed occurrence of the disease in Asia.([vbpl.vn](https://vbpl.vn/quangtri/Pages/vbpq-toanvan.aspx?ItemID=26839&Keyword=&utm_source=openai)) In the following years, NHP was recognised as present in parts of the Asia–Pacific region and officially reported from Viet Nam, where affected ponds showed slow growth, lethargy, soft shells and hepatopancreatic degeneration with reported mortalities up to 50–100% over several weeks.([library.enaca.org](https://library.enaca.org/Health/FieldGuide/pdf/Necrotising%20hepatopancreatitis.pdf)) As diagnostic standards and shrimp health management improved and attention shifted to other emerging hepatopancreatic diseases such as AHPND, NHP remained a recognised but comparatively less prominent bacterial threat, managed through biosecurity, pond hygiene and avoidance of extreme temperature–salinity combinations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of penaeid shrimp aquaculture in Viet Nam, combined with imports or movements of seed from regions where NHP was endemic, likely introduced Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei into Asian farms; local pond conditions with high temperature and salinity episodes facilitated disease expression.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7172736/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The agent was described as a Gram‑negative, Rickettsia‑like bacterium consistent with NHPB, implying geographic range expansion of an already virulent lineage into a new continent and additional host species (including P. monodon) rather than evolution of a new strain; host expansion within penaeids is recognised but not clearly linked to novel genotypes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: REVIEW. NACA’s regional field guide and multiple reviews affirm that NHP has been officially reported from Viet Nam and is the only confirmed focus in the Asia–Pacific region, with Vietnamese regulations indicating first detection on farmed shrimp in Quảng Ninh around 2002.([library.enaca.org](https://library.enaca.org/Health/FieldGuide/pdf/Necrotising%20hepatopancreatitis.pdf)) This justifies classifying the 2002–2005 Viet Nam episode as an inter‑continental emergence event (first establishment in Asia). However, the original OIE disease‑card URL used in this row is now obsolete; I have replaced it with the current WOAH disease page, which links to the Aquatic Code and Manual chapters on infection with Hepatobacter penaei.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/necrotising-hepatopancreatitis-hepatobacter-penaeiv/)) Event timing, geography, and host range look consistent with available sources, but given limited quantitative impact data, human review of the exact year range and severity is recommended.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in commercial ponds in Brazil experiencing high mortality attributed to NHP bacterium.
Event summary: Around 2010, Brazilian shrimp farms reported significant mortalities in L. vannamei stocks, and diagnostic investigations on shrimp from a commercial farm with high losses confirmed necrotising hepatopancreatitis bacterium infection through wet mounts, histopathology and PCR.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak developed as a severe on‑farm epizootic, with high prevalence of advanced NHP lesions in broodstock and grow‑out shrimp that contributed to production declines in parts of the national industry already challenged by other diseases.([globalseafood.org](https://www.globalseafood.org/advocate/disease-risk-factors-shrimp-production-brazil/?utm_source=openai)) Following implementation of improved broodstock screening, pond management and biosecurity, Brazilian producers reduced the impact of NHP, although the pathogen remains present in the region as part of a complex of shrimp bacterial diseases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of infected broodstock and post‑larvae, high stocking densities, and suboptimal pond management likely allowed re‑establishment and amplification of NHP bacterium in Brazilian ponds that had previously reported the disease; environmental stressors and co‑infections may have exacerbated clinical expression.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel Brazilian strain; rather, the episode reflects re‑occurrence of Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei in an already affected subregion, with disease severity associated with high infection loads and host stress rather than documented genetic change in the bacterium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. The 2010 Brazilian episode is supported by a peer‑reviewed diagnostic study documenting high NHP‑attributed mortalities on a commercial farm, and by broader regional analyses that list Brazil among the Latin American countries where NHP is established.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) Because South America (Peru/Ecuador) was already affected in 1993, this event fits best as a major re‑occurrence within the same subregion rather than as a new intra‑continental emergence; the current classification reflects that and no geography or host corrections are needed, though the exact national-scale production impact remains less quantified than for the Peru/Ecuador epizootic.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in ponds in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica.
Event summary: During 2014, an outbreak (brote) of necrotising hepatopancreatitis occurred in L. vannamei cultured in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica, exacerbated by El Niño–related conditions of unusually high water temperatures and salinities; histopathology confirmed characteristic NHP lesions in affected shrimp.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) The episode caused significant on‑farm morbidity and mortality and was recognised nationally as an important climatic‑driven disease event in Costa Rican shrimp aquaculture. As environmental conditions normalised and management measures were implemented, mortalities decreased, and NHP remained one of several bacterial diseases monitored in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 2014 El Niño event produced elevated sea surface temperatures and salinity in the Golfo de Nicoya, stressing shrimp and creating favourable conditions for expression and transmission of NHP in existing farm systems; management practices and stocking densities likely modulated outbreak severity.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates involvement of the typical NHP bacterium (Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei) with no demonstration of novel strains or resistance traits, so this episode reflects environmentally driven re‑occurrence rather than pathogen evolution or host‑range shift.
Review: REVIEW. This new row has been added to capture the well‑documented 2014 outbreak of NHP in farmed L. vannamei in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica, which the primary case report explicitly describes as a brote associated with El Niño–type high temperature and salinity conditions.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) Because Central America was already affected via earlier spread to Mexico and other countries, this is best classified as a re‑occurrence event within an endemic subregion driven by climatic factors, not as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. Quantitative national production‑loss data are limited, so a human reviewer should confirm that this episode merits inclusion among the top‑impact events for this pathogen, but current evidence suggests it is one of the more significant recent NHP outbreaks in Central America.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America; Mexico (Baja California)
Host: Primarily wild black abalone (Haliotis cracherodii), with impacts also on other wild abalones such as H. rufescens, H. fulgens and H. corrugata
Event summary: In the mid‑1980s, withering abalone syndrome that began at the Channel Islands spread through dense black abalone populations across the southern California islands and adjacent mainland, and during the 1990s extended southward into northern Baja California, causing catastrophic declines. Surveys and fishery data documented >95–99% reductions in black abalone at many southern California sites by the late 1990s, with local extirpations on several islands and substantial losses reported around Bahía Tortugas in Baja California during warm‑water years. By the end of the decade, populations across much of the species’ warmer‑water range in the USA and Mexico had effectively collapsed and fisheries were closed or severely curtailed, marking the culmination of this initial large epizootic wave.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High abalone densities and historical overfishing left populations dominated by larger, more susceptible adults; strong El Niño events in the late 1980s and 1990s elevated seawater temperatures, which promoted disease expression and transmission; currents facilitated spread along the coast of California and Baja California. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and coastal range expansion of the rickettsiales-like bacterium Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis in black and other abalones led to chronic wasting, high mortality and effective geographic range expansion of the pathogen from initial foci at the Channel Islands into the broader Southern California Bight and northern Baja California.
Review: Review – Retained as a major linked epizootic in southern California and northern Baja California; the event start was extended back to 1985 to reflect first observations of withering syndrome at the Channel Islands, while the end year (1999) was left unchanged. The inter_continental_emergence flag is kept as Yes because spread into Baja California (Mexico, classified in the project as South America–Central America) represents first establishment in a new continent, but re_emergence was set to No because this episode represents the initial emergence and coastal spread of the pathogen rather than a resurgence driven by pathogen change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America; Mexico (Baja California)
Host: Wild black abalone (Haliotis cracherodii) and other sympatric abalone species
Event summary: During the strong 1997–1998 El Niño, anomalously warm sea temperatures in southern California and Baja California triggered a renewed and intensified wave of withering syndrome in already depleted black abalone populations. Disease expression and mortality rates surged at numerous Channel Islands and mainland sites, with monitoring programs reporting that by 1998 less than 1% of the historic southern California black abalone population remained and many monitoring plots fell to zero individuals. As cooler post‑El Niño conditions returned in 1999, acute mortality rates declined, leaving scattered remnant populations and a long‑term legacy of extreme depletion that has slowed subsequent recovery efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 1997–1998 El Niño produced persistently elevated sea surface temperatures and altered upwelling in the Southern California Bight and northern Baja California, conditions known to exacerbate withering syndrome and increase abalone metabolic stress; continued high local densities in some refugia and limited management tools further facilitated transmission. Internal mechanisms: Temperature‑dependent expression of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis infections led to enhanced pathogenicity and rapid progression of chronic infections to clinical disease and death, causing an acute re‑occurrence peak within an already established endemic system.
Review: Retain – The 1997–1998 El Niño–associated mortality peak in already affected southern California and Baja California populations is well documented and fits the definition of a re_occurrence (temperature‑driven resurgence in an existing outbreak area) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. Geographic coding and event‑type assignment are consistent with the project scheme, so no structural changes are recommended.

Countries: United States of America; Mexico (Baja California)
Host: Multiple abalone species in wild and culture (Haliotis cracherodii, H. rufescens, H. fulgens, H. corrugata and others)
Event summary: In 2000, researchers formally described the rickettsiales-like organism associated with withering abalone syndrome along the west coast of North America and proposed the provisional name Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis based on isolates from multiple abalone species in California and Baja California. This taxonomic description followed a decade of unexplained mass mortalities in wild and cultured abalones and clarified the etiological link between the intracellular bacterium and the chronic wasting disease. Once the pathogen was characterized and diagnostic tools were developed, surveillance and management programs in California and Mexico began to incorporate targeted detection of C. Xenohaliotis californiensis to monitor disease prevalence and support conservation and aquaculture biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Advances in marine pathology, microscopy and molecular techniques (e.g. 16S rDNA sequencing) enabled the identification of the previously uncharacterized rickettsiales-like organism responsible for withering syndrome; longstanding concern over fishery collapse in California and Baja California focused research efforts on determining the causal agent. Internal mechanisms: Recognition that a specific intracellular bacterium, Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis, was consistently associated with disease lesions and experimental infections established a clear etiological pathway and allowed definition of this monomorphic pathogen as the primary agent of withering abalone syndrome.
Review: Review – Geographic coding was updated so that this formal 2000 description of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis, which used material from both California (USA) and Baja California (Mexico), now lists both North America and South America in the continent field, matching the project convention that places Mexico in South America (Central America subregion). The first_detection classification for the pathogen in the abalone host system remains appropriate and no other structural changes were needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America (California – Channel Islands, mainland southern and central California)
Host: Cultured red abalone (Haliotis rufescens) and other farmed abalones in California, with spillover risk to nearby wild populations
Event summary: From the early 1990s through about 2010, withering syndrome became established in most California abalone farms, with many facilities experiencing recurrent outbreaks and heavy losses of cultured red abalone and other species. Chronic infection with Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis led to stunted growth, foot atrophy and high mortality in tanks and raceways, and in at least one documented case, pathogen‑laden effluent from an infested farm was shown to discharge into adjacent coastal habitat used by wild abalones. Over time, improvements in biosecurity, culling, and antibiotic bath protocols, combined with better siting and temperature management, reduced the frequency and severity of clinical disease on farms, although the pathogen persists in some captive stocks and continues to pose a spillover threat to wild populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of land‑based and nearshore abalone aquaculture in California led to high host densities, animal movements among facilities, and sometimes warm or nutrient‑rich effluent discharges into coastal waters; early operations often lacked effective biosecurity and effluent treatment, enabling persistence and amplification of the pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis infections were shown to be temperature sensitive, with warmer culture conditions promoting disease expression; chronic colonization of the digestive gland and shedding of bacteria in feces created sustained infection pressure within farms and into receiving waters, thereby enhancing transmission and effectively expanding the pathogen’s realized ecological niche in association with aquaculture systems.
Review: Retain – Recurrent withering syndrome outbreaks and heavy losses in California abalone farms over this period are well documented, including evidence that infected farm effluent can discharge the pathogen into nearby wild habitats. Coding this as a re_emergence (same subregion and country, but expanding into cultured hosts and high‑density farm environments) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is consistent with the event‑type definitions, and no corrections to timing or geography were required.

Sub-regions: South America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia
Countries: Chile; Iceland [2004]; Spain [2004]; Ireland [2006]; France; China; Chinese Taipei (Taiwan, Province of China); Japan; Thailand; Israel
Host: Primarily farmed red abalone (Haliotis rufescens), with subsequent detections in other cultured abalones including European abalone (Haliotis tuberculata) and Asian species such as Haliotis discus discus
Event summary: Beginning around the early 2000s, withering syndrome associated with Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis was introduced, largely via trade in infected Californian red abalone seed and broodstock, into overseas abalone aquaculture operations in Chile, several European countries (Iceland, Ireland, Spain, France) and parts of Asia (China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand, Israel). As the international abalone industry expanded, the pathogen was detected in cultured Haliotis rufescens in Chile and subsequently in European and Asian abalone species, with official notifications including a 2004 report from Iceland, a 2004 report of infection in Haliotis tuberculata in Spain, and a 2006 OIE report from Irish farms, followed by additional detections in France and multiple Asian hatcheries. Over the following decade and a half, affected countries implemented surveillance, movement controls, and husbandry changes to limit spread, and many farms adopted selective breeding, antibiotic treatments and improved biosecurity to manage the disease and maintain production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid globalization of abalone aquaculture and trade in live seed and broodstock from California facilitated long‑distance translocation of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis to South America (notably Chile), Europe (including Iceland, Ireland, Spain and France) and Asia (China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand and Israel); limited early awareness and diagnostic capacity in importing regions delayed detection; intensive culture conditions in new environments promoted establishment. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s ability to infect multiple Haliotis species, survive transport with infected hosts, and persist in culture systems under a range of temperatures enabled successful colonization of new geographic regions and host species; in some European stocks of Haliotis tuberculata and cultured red abalones, infection dynamics and susceptibility patterns indicate host expansion and strain adaptation consistent with re‑emergence in novel host–environment combinations.
Review: Review – Retained as a single linked international aquaculture emergence episode capturing long‑distance spread of the pathogen via trade in Californian red abalone seed and broodstock. Sub_regions and country coding were expanded so that Chile (South America), Iceland and Ireland (Northern Europe), Spain and France (Southern and Western Europe), and China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand and Israel (Eastern, South‑eastern and Western Asia) are explicitly represented, and bracketed first‑detection years were added where supported by OIE notifications or primary reports (notably Iceland 2004, Spain 2004, Ireland 2006). Event types (inter_continental_emergence plus re_emergence through host expansion into European and Asian abalone species) and the 2000–2015 time window remain appropriate but the row is flagged for review to ensure consistency with any future updates on Asian detections.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (central and northern California coastline, including Diablo Canyon and northward)
Host: Wild black abalone (Haliotis cracherodii) and red abalone (Haliotis rufescens), with involvement of other local abalone species
Event summary: From roughly 2005 to 2015, withering syndrome continued to move north from its original southern California foci into parts of central California, with detections of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis and episodic disease impacts in black and red abalone at sites such as Diablo Canyon and other central coast locations. Management and survey reports documented that the pathogen and/or disease had spread north of Point Conception into central California by the early 2000s, although cooler temperatures and lower host densities limited mortality compared with the catastrophic losses farther south, and populations north of about the Monterey/San Luis Obispo County line largely remained free of obvious withering syndrome signs. This period nonetheless marked an expansion of the pathogen’s realized range along the California coast and prompted increased recovery, translocation and disease‑risk assessments for endangered abalone species in central California refugia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Progressive along‑shore spread of the pathogen via coastal currents, anthropogenic movements of infected animals (including conservation outplanting), and episodic warm‑water events enabled withering syndrome to move into historically cooler central California habitats; continued low but non‑zero fishing pressure and other stressors may have reduced resilience of northern populations. Internal mechanisms: The inherent capacity of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis to survive at cooler temperatures, albeit with reduced disease expression, supported gradual geographic range expansion, and variation in host susceptibility among abalone species (e.g., higher susceptibility of black abalone than red abalone) shaped local outbreak severity and recovery potential in newly affected areas within the same subregion.
Review: Review – This episode was re‑interpreted primarily as a re_emergence and range expansion within the existing Northern America subregion rather than an intra‑continental emergence, because spread north of Point Conception into central California occurs within a single UNSD subregion and country. The intra_continental_emergence flag was therefore changed from Yes to No, while re_emergence was retained to reflect biological expansion into cooler habitats and new parts of the California coast. The event summary was also softened to acknowledge that, although the pathogen and disease extended into central California, documented impacts north of the Monterey/San Luis Obispo County line remained much lower than in southern California.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: African lion (Panthera leo); domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris) as source reservoir; other sympatric carnivores (e.g. hyenas, jackals) involved in transmission
Event summary: In early 1994, a morbillivirus closely related to canine distemper virus spilled over from infected domestic dogs into the lion population of Serengeti National Park and adjacent Maasai Mara, initiating an explosive epidemic. The outbreak rapidly spread through the high‑density lion population, killing roughly one‑third of Serengeti lions and causing marked neurological signs and pneumonia, with domestic dogs to the west of the park identified as the most likely infection source. The epidemic waned as susceptible lion numbers were depleted and herd immunity rose, leaving CDV established in the broader carnivore community with recurrent but less catastrophic circulation thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density, poorly vaccinated domestic dog populations surrounding the protected area created a large, persistent reservoir of CDV; close spatial overlap and occasional contact between dogs and wildlife at park edges facilitated repeated spillover; climatic extremes and associated tick‑borne co‑infections (e.g. Babesia) amplified case fatality in lions. Internal mechanisms: Highly transmissible CDV lineages already circulating in regional dogs and wild canids spilled over into immunologically naïve lions; co‑infection with hemoparasites increased apparent virulence and mortality, but viral genetics were consistent with a local dog‑origin lineage rather than a completely novel genotype, in line with classification as re‑emergence rather than first emergence.
Review: review - Retain as a top-impact wildlife CDV emergence event. Corrected the event year from '1993-1994' to '1994' and aligned country-specific years for Tanzania and Kenya to 1994 because primary descriptions date the lion epidemic to early 1994 with no clear evidence for 1993 case onset; Maasai Mara involvement is contemporaneous. Event type (re_emergence due to spillover into naïve lions) and geographic coding (Africa | Eastern Africa; Tanzania, Kenya) are otherwise consistent with the literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe
Countries: Kazakhstan [1997, 2000-2001]; Azerbaijan [2000-2001]; Turkmenistan [2000-2001]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [2000-2001]; Russian Federation [2000-2001]
Host: Caspian seal (Pusa caspica)
Event summary: Beginning with a mass mortality in 1997 and followed by larger epizootics in 2000 and 2001, CDV emerged as a major cause of death in Caspian seals, with thousands of animals found dead along the coasts of Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Iran and the Russian Federation. The 2000 event was characterized by acute respiratory and neurological disease, widespread CDV infection confirmed by serology and RT‑PCR, and mortality affecting a large proportion of hauled‑out seals across the basin. Outbreaks subsided after 2001 as immediate susceptible cohorts were removed, but CDV has since been recognized as an ongoing conservation threat to this endemic marine mammal, with sporadic deaths and concern about future die‑offs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High seal aggregation at breeding and molting haul‑outs promoted intense transmission once CDV was introduced; possible nutritional stress and contaminant burdens (e.g. organochlorines such as PCBs and DDTs) may have compromised immunity and increased mortality; proximity to coastal dog and carnivore populations likely provided the initial spillover route. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a terrestrial CDV lineage into a naïve marine mammal population, with a distinct Caspian strain detected from 1997 onward; high viral transmissibility in dense moulting aggregations and age structure effects led to repeated mass mortality events, consistent with re‑emergence in a new host rather than first emergence at the animal‑system level.
Review: review - Retain and correct. This multi-year, multi-country series of epizootics caused CDV-attributed mortality in the thousands (>10,000 seals estimated dead in 2000) and is clearly among the most impactful CDV emergence events since 1990. Updated 'continent' from 'Asia' to 'Asia; Europe' because the affected coasts span Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan (Central Asia), Azerbaijan and Iran (Western Asia), and the Russian Federation (Eastern Europe) under the UNSD scheme. To respect the event-type rule that only inter-/intra-continental emergence can co-occur with re_emergence, set 're_occurrence' to false and retained 're_emergence = true', reflecting sustained host expansion of CDV into Caspian seals across recurrent die-offs.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Santa Catalina Island fox (Urocyon littoralis catalinae); domestic dogs and/or raccoons as likely introduction vectors
Event summary: In the late 1990s, a virulent CDV epidemic swept through the endemic island fox population on Santa Catalina Island, California. Fox numbers on the island crashed from an estimated ~1,300 adults in 1990 to roughly 100 animals by 1999–2000, with foxes east of the Two Harbors isthmus suffering an ~85–90% decline following detection of CDV in carcasses. The epidemic burned through the immunologically naïve population until emergency measures—including captive breeding, translocation of foxes from the unaffected western subpopulation, and widespread CDV vaccination—stabilized numbers and initiated a slow recovery, though CDV remains a central long‑term threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of CDV to an isolated, previously unexposed island fox population via an infected domestic dog or raccoon arriving by boat from mainland California; high local fox densities and close proximity to human settlements facilitated rapid fox‑to‑fox transmission once CDV was introduced; small population size and restricted range greatly increased extirpation risk. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a dog-lineage CDV strain into an insular canid with no prior immunity, producing very high case fatality and a population crash; subsequent models and monitoring show that even infrequent CDV incursions can drive quasi‑extinction without continued vaccination and biosecurity.
Review: review - Newly added event. A CDV epidemic on Santa Catalina Island (USA) in 1998–2000 reduced the endemic island fox population by ~85–90% (from ~1,300 to ~100 animals) and is widely regarded as a near-extinction event that triggered ESA listing and intensive management, so it clearly qualifies among the top global CDV emergence events post-1990. Classified as 're_emergence' (host expansion and severe impact in a new wildlife host within the animal system) rather than first_detection or inter-continental emergence. Years, geography (North America | Northern America; United States) and host assignment follow King et al. 2014, Kohlmann et al. 2005 and related sources and should be retained but could be fine-tuned further if more precise onset dates are desired.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: African wild dog (Lycaon pictus) in a captive breeding program
Event summary: In December 2000, an acute infectious disease compatible with CDV swept through a captive breeding group of African wild dogs in Tanzania, beginning shortly after routine handling and vaccination procedures. Within two months, 49 of 52 animals died, and serology and virology confirmed CDV infection as the primary cause of the epizootic. The outbreak burnt out as almost the entire captive pack succumbed, resulting in a severe setback for African wild dog conservation efforts in the region and prompting changes in vaccination and management strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High animal density and close confinement in the captive facility allowed rapid CDV spread once introduced; intensive handling and recent vaccination may have caused stress and transient immune suppression; circulation of CDV in surrounding domestic dogs and wild carnivores provided a likely reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of CDV in an extremely susceptible, immunologically naïve endangered host; potential vaccine–wild-type interactions were investigated but evidence supported infection by a field virus closely related to regional dog and wildlife strains; high virulence in African wild dogs magnified conservation impact even though absolute case numbers were modest.
Review: retain - This outbreak (49 of 52 captive African wild dogs dying in Mkomazi Game Reserve, Tanzania) is well documented and remains one of the most consequential CDV events for this endangered species. Event-year range, geography (Africa | Eastern Africa; United Republic of Tanzania) and re_emergence classification are consistent with primary sources; no field corrections were required.

Host: Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica); Amur leopard (Panthera pardus orientalis); sympatric wild carnivores and domestic dogs as reservoirs
Event summary: From the early 2000s, CDV began to be recognized as a cause of neurological disease and death in wild Amur tigers in the Russian Far East, with confirmed tiger deaths in 2004 and a spatial cluster of cases around 2010 in the Sikhote‑Alin Biosphere Reserve. Surveillance and modeling showed that CDV exposure was widespread in tigers and other carnivores, and that the 2010 cluster coincided with a localized decline in the Sikhote‑Alin tiger population from roughly 25 to 9 individuals by 2012. The outbreak subsided as affected animals died and targeted interventions (dog vaccination, carcass removal and increased monitoring) were implemented, but CDV remains a recognized extinction‑threatening pathogen for Amur tigers and leopards in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High CDV prevalence in local domestic dogs and wild mesocarnivores (e.g. raccoon dogs, foxes, martens) created multiple opportunities for spillover into low‑density tiger and leopard populations; expanding human settlements and dog populations in Primorsky Krai increased cross‑species contacts; fragmented tiger ranges amplified the demographic impact of losing even a few breeding adults. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and re‑emergence of an Arctic‑like CDV lineage adapted to multiple wild carnivores; genetic analyses show tiger and leopard viruses cluster with broader regional Arctic‑like and Asia‑4 lineages, indicating ongoing viral evolution; pronounced neurotropism and high virulence in big cats translated into severe clinical disease and death, making even sporadic infections a major conservation threat.
Review: review - Retain as a major CDV emergence episode in endangered Amur tigers and leopards. Corrected event-type coding by setting 'first_detection' to false because CDV has been recognized in the animal host system for centuries; this cluster is best described as 're_emergence' with host expansion into big cats, not first detection at the host-system level. Year range and geographic coding (Europe | Eastern Europe; Russian Federation per UNSD, although biologically in the Far East) remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis); domestic dogs as source reservoir
Event summary: In late 2005, CDV spilled over from local domestic dogs into Ethiopian wolves in Bale Mountains National Park, initiating an outbreak that spread rapidly through multiple contiguous packs. During 2005–2006, mortality reached catastrophic levels in affected subpopulations, with some wolf packs losing most or all members and the event described as the most severe single disease episode recorded for the species. The epizootic declined as infected packs collapsed and limited reactive vaccination and dog control were implemented, but it left Bale’s wolf population greatly reduced and more vulnerable to subsequent disease waves.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High contact rates within tightly social wolf packs promoted very efficient within-pack CDV transmission after spillover from unvaccinated village dogs; continued encroachment of people and dogs into Afroalpine habitat increased cross‑species contact; recent severe rabies outbreaks had already reduced wolf numbers, limiting demographic resilience. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of CDV in an endangered canid with no prior widespread immunity; high virulence and possible interaction with prior rabies‑driven demographic thinning intensified population impact; CDV’s broad carnivore host range enabled establishment in sympatric dogs and carnivores, sustaining the threat.
Review: retain - This 2005–2006 epizootic in Ethiopian wolves caused 43–68% mortality in affected subpopulations of one of the world’s rarest canids and is clearly among the highest-impact CDV events in wildlife post-1990. Its coding as re_emergence (host expansion into an endangered canid within the animal system) and geographic placement (Africa | Eastern Africa; Ethiopia) are aligned with primary sources; no field-level corrections were needed.

Host: Rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) in breeding farms and research facilities; cynomolgus monkey (Macaca fascicularis) in a Japanese facility
Event summary: In 2006, a measles‑like respiratory disease emerged among rhesus macaques at a breeding farm in Guangxi, southern China, where subsequent investigations identified CDV as the etiologic agent, marking one of the first confirmed natural CDV outbreaks in nonhuman primates at scale. Related CDV outbreaks then occurred in rhesus monkeys at a Beijing animal center and in 2008 in cynomolgus monkeys at a facility in Japan, with genetic analyses showing closely related strains circulating across facilities. Control was achieved through culling, quarantine and enhanced biosecurity, but these events established CDV as an emerging pathogen of captive Old World monkeys in East Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density housing of macaques in breeding and research facilities, with frequent animal movements between farms and centers, created ideal conditions for CDV amplification; likely contact with infected dogs or contaminated materials introduced canine lineages of CDV into naïve primate colonies; limited prior recognition of CDV risk in primates delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover and subsequent adaptation) of CDV into nonhuman primates; molecular analyses showed that monkey strains clustered with contemporary dog CDV lineages (Asia‑1), with specific mutations in the H gene associated with altered receptor usage that may facilitate infection of primate SLAM receptors; ongoing chains of CDV transmission within primate colonies highlight efficient transmission in the new host once established.
Review: review - Retain as a top-impact event because outbreaks in Chinese breeding farms and a Japanese primate facility involved ~10,000 infected monkeys with substantial mortality, and represent a clear, well-characterized host expansion of CDV into nonhuman primates. Corrected event-type coding by setting 'first_detection' to false (CDV was long known in the animal host system); the event is best classified as 're_emergence' driven by host expansion and viral adaptation in primates. Geographical coding (Asia | Eastern Asia; China and Japan) is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis); domestic dogs as source reservoir
Event summary: Around 2010, only about four years after the 2005–2006 CDV epizootic and a major rabies outbreak, CDV re‑emerged in Ethiopian wolves across Bale Mountains National Park. The virus again spread rapidly among closely knit packs, causing high mortality and the eradication of several packs before waning as susceptible animals were exhausted and emergency vaccination and dog control were intensified. This second CDV wave further fragmented and depressed the already weakened wolf population, demonstrating the short inter‑epizootic interval and the chronic threat posed by CDV in this system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent CDV circulation or repeated reintroduction from surrounding domestic dogs where vaccination coverage was low; rapid demographic turnover and incomplete vaccination of wolves limited the build‑up of long‑term herd immunity; continued land use change and high dog density kept wolves in close proximity to reservoir populations. Internal mechanisms: Reappearance of the same or closely related CDV lineage in a partially recovered but still vulnerable host population, with virus life‑history traits (short infectious period, high transmissibility in social canids) favoring frequent epizootic waves rather than a distinct new genotype.
Review: review - Retain as a major follow-on event in Ethiopian wolves but adjust classification. This 2010 outbreak is a resurgence of CDV in the same Bale Mountains subregion shortly after the 2005–2006 outbreak, driven primarily by external factors (ongoing dog reservoir, incomplete vaccination, demographic recovery after rabies), with no evidence that a novel viral strain or host expansion occurred. Accordingly, recoded as 're_occurrence = true' and 're_emergence = false'; years, geography and host details were left unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed American mink (Neovison vison); red fox (Vulpes vulpes), raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and wild ferret (Mustela putorius furo) as key wildlife reservoirs
Event summary: Following several years with little or no detected disease, a major CDV outbreak began in Danish farmed mink in late summer 2012 and continued into early 2013, ultimately affecting 64 mink farms on the Jutland peninsula. The same CDV strain was also detected in local wildlife—especially red foxes, raccoon dogs and a wild ferret—indicating that a wildlife reservoir seeded infections on multiple farms. Although precise mink mortality numbers were not reported, high morbidity and mortality on large commercial farms resulted in substantial production losses before the outbreak waned under improved vaccination and tightened biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense housing of thousands of mink per farm, coupled with incomplete vaccination and lapses in farm biosecurity (e.g. wildlife access across fences), allowed rapid farm‑level amplification once CDV was introduced; a widespread, endemic reservoir of infected red foxes and other wild carnivores provided repeated opportunities for farm introduction; management practices that did not fully exclude wildlife or their feces facilitated between‑farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of a European‑lineage CDV strain that had likely persisted in regional fox populations since at least 2008, with high genetic identity across mink and wildlife isolates; although some mink viruses carried an Y549H substitution in the H gene, the outbreak is best viewed as a re-occurrence of CDV in a previously affected subregion and host group, rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: review - Newly added event. The 2012–2013 Danish outbreak, which involved 64 commercial mink farms and parallel infection in local foxes, raccoon dogs and ferrets, is one of the most significant CDV epizootics in production animals in the post-1990 period and thus warrants inclusion among the top-10 events. Classified as 're_occurrence' because Denmark had prior mink outbreaks and the 2012–2013 wave reflects resurgence of a European-lineage virus from wildlife reservoirs under suboptimal biosecurity, rather than a first or inter-continental emergence. Years, geography (Europe | Northern Europe; Denmark) and host description are based on Trebbien et al. 2014 and Gregers-Jensen et al. 2015.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) in captivity; domestic dogs and other carnivores as potential reservoirs
Event summary: Between December 2014 and March 2015, an outbreak of CDV occurred at the Shaanxi Rare Wildlife Rescue and Breeding Research Center in China, initially affecting one giant panda and then spreading to other pandas in the facility. Five infected giant pandas that developed clinical signs—characterized by respiratory, gastrointestinal and neurological disease—died within 7–34 days of onset, and genomic sequencing of virus from one panda (giant panda/SX/2014) showed it belonged to the Asia‑1 CDV cluster with mutations associated with cross‑species infection. After aggressive quarantine, relocation of uninfected pandas, and strict biosecurity, the outbreak was contained, but it highlighted that any future CDV incursion in panda range could endanger both captive and wild populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Housing of pandas in a rescue/breeding facility near human settlements and domestic dogs likely facilitated introduction of CDV; limited use of CDV vaccination in pandas before the outbreak meant high susceptibility; fragmented wild panda habitats and increasing numbers of captive animals magnify the consequences of disease introduction. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of an Asia‑1 canine CDV lineage into giant pandas, with H‑gene mutations such as Y549H implicated in overcoming host barriers; the strain showed high virulence in pandas, causing rapid progression and death despite intensive care; genomic work demonstrated that the panda virus was closely related to dog‑origin CDV, underlining the role of ongoing viral evolution and adaptation in enabling new host jumps.
Review: review - Retain as a key emergence event because the 2014–2015 Shaanxi outbreak is the best-documented example of CDV causing fatal disease in giant pandas and has significant conservation implications. Corrected event-type coding by setting 'first_detection' to false (CDV was long recognized in animals); categorized as 're_emergence' via host expansion into pandas (Asia-1 lineage with Y549H in the H gene). Years, geography and host description remain appropriate and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Japan [2002] (Nagano Prefecture index farm; national surveys [2002-2004])
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat breeds)
Event summary: In 2002, caprine arthritis/encephalitis was detected for the first time in Japan in a large dairy goat herd in Nagano Prefecture, where numerous goats showed carpal arthritis and occasional pneumonia and CAEV infection was confirmed by histopathology, serology and virus isolation. Subsequent national surveillance from 2002 to 2004 found about one-fifth of 3,102 tested goats seropositive, indicating that the virus had already spread beyond the index herd and was present at low-to-moderate prevalence in multiple Japanese herds. Control on the affected farm and nationally relied on testing and culling or segregation of positives, kid-rearing and colostrum management, and movement restrictions, which reduced prevalence substantially but did not completely eradicate CAEV from Japan.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected breeding stock into what had been assumed to be a CAE‑free national herd, probably via international trade in high-yield dairy goats, combined with intensification in a few large herds that facilitated close contact, shared milking equipment and kid-rearing practices favouring lactogenic transmission. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; persistence of infection and efficient milk‑borne and horizontal transmission typical of CAEV enabled several years of silent spread in Japan before the first clinical outbreak was recognised.
Review: retain – corrected the emergence-type classification: intra_continental_emergence was set from true to false because CAEV had already been present in the same UN subregion (Eastern Asia) in China since 1988, so Japan represents spread to a new country within an already affected subregion rather than a new subregion. Marked this instead as a major regional re_occurrence (true) reflecting renewed detection and substantial prevalence in Eastern Asia. Slightly broadened the year range to 2002–2004 to align with the documented outbreak and early national surveys, but left geography and impact description unchanged; event is clearly among the major post‑1990 CAEV episodes and should be retained.

Countries: Brazil – Paraíba state (Cariri region) [2004-2008]; Brazil – multiple Northeastern states (Piauí, Maranhão, Sergipe, Alagoas, Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Ceará) [2008-2010]
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat) in semi-arid smallholder and breeder herds
Event summary: Between the mid‑2000s and around 2010, several epidemiological and serological studies in Northeast Brazil documented CAEV as an important emerging infection in goat herds, starting with surveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba state that found notable seroprevalence across 60 herds, followed by broader studies of breeder goats in seven Northeastern states. These investigations showed that CAEV was present in multiple states with herd-level seroprevalence associated with more technified/intensive production, buck use, and inter‑herd animal movement, implying that the virus had spread widely through regional trade and breeding networks. Recognition of CAEV as endemic in major goat‑producing areas of Northeast Brazil led to calls for control programmes focused on testing, culling or segregating positives, and adjusting breeding practices, but full eradication has not been implemented and subsequent work continues to find CAEV in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of goat production in the semi‑arid Northeast, movement of breeding animals among states, shared use of bucks, and limited historical testing all facilitated regional dissemination; semi‑intensive and intensive management systems were associated with higher seroprevalence. Internal mechanisms: Circulating SRLV strains in Northeastern Brazil were phylogenetically related to CAEV‑type lentiviruses; no uniquely more virulent variant was reported, and the main internal factor was the virus’ capacity for persistent infection and efficient transmission in dense herds.
Review: retain – this episode aggregates the earliest large-scale serosurveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba and subsequent multi‑state breeder surveys in Northeast Brazil, which together represent one of the most substantial documented CAEV emergence/re-occurrence events in South America in terms of herd numbers and regional spread. Geographic scope, timing and host description are consistent with the cited Brazilian studies; no major corrections to dates, regions or emergence-type classification (re_occurrence in an already affected continent) are needed. Event is appropriately counted among the top global CAEV emergence episodes.

Countries: Oman [2007-2008] (Batinah, Dakhiliya, Sharqiya, Dhahra, Wusta regions)
Host: Domestic non-dairy indigenous goats (slaughtered and field herds)
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2008, a large serological survey of 1,638 indigenous goats from five regions of the Sultanate of Oman found that 5.1% of samples were positive for antibodies against CAEV, providing the first serological evidence that CAEV was circulating in Omani goat populations. Seropositive animals were detected in several regions, with older age classes more frequently positive, indicating that infection had been present for some time and was not confined to a single imported herd. The findings confirmed that CAEV had become established in the Gulf region and prompted recommendations for improved biosecurity, control of animal movements from endemic source countries and better management of colostrum and kid rearing, although no formal national eradication programme has yet been implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing importation of live goats from countries such as Somalia and other CAEV‑affected areas into Oman, combined with traditional extensive or pastoral management that allows mixing between indigenous and imported animals, likely introduced and disseminated the virus. Internal mechanisms: Standard SRLV biology (lifelong infection, delayed seroconversion and persistent shedding) facilitated silent establishment of CAEV in indigenous goats without overt clinical indicators, rather than emergence of a new strain or host jump.
Review: retain – added this event as a major regional re_occurrence in Western Asia, representing the first documented CAEV serological evidence in Oman based on a large, multi‑region survey with >1,600 goats and clear management-related risk factors. Classified as re_occurrence (not intra_continental_emergence) because CAEV had already been reported in the same UN subregion (Western Asia) in Jordan and Saudi Arabia before 2007. Countries, years and host system align with Tageldin et al. 2012; event should be considered among the globally important post‑1990 CAEV emergence episodes.

Countries: Somalia (Somaliland – Togdheer and Waqoyi Galbed districts) [2008]
Host: Domestic goats in pastoral and agropastoral herds
Event summary: In 2008, a cross-sectional survey of 1,198 goats from 34 randomly selected herds in northern Somalia (Somaliland) found an overall CAEV seroprevalence of 6.0% and herd-level infection in 24 of 34 herds, providing the first solid evidence that CAEV was circulating in a country with one of Africa’s largest goat populations. Multivariable analysis showed that older age, larger herd size and rearing goats together with sheep were significant risk factors for seropositivity, indicating ongoing within- and between-herd transmission in the main goat-producing districts. The study, set against the backdrop of an earlier global survey in the 1980s that had found no reactors in Somali goats, signalled a substantial regional emergence of CAEV in Eastern Africa and highlighted the need for surveillance and movement control in a livestock-dependent economy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and commercialization of goat production in Somaliland, close contact between goats and sheep, and regional trade and movements of animals (including imports for slaughter and breeding) likely introduced CAEV into previously negative populations and supported its spread. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported; the emergence pattern is consistent with introduction of typical CAEV/SRLV genotypes into high-density pastoral systems, with persistent infection and slow seroconversion leading to under-recognition until systematic serological surveys were undertaken.
Review: retain – added this as a key African re_occurrence event: it documents CAEV establishment in northern Somalia using a large sample (1,198 goats) and herd-level analysis in a country with ~12 million goats, and explicitly contrasts the new positives with earlier global data showing no reactors from Somalia. Classified as re_occurrence (not first_detection or intra_continental) because CAEV had already been reported in Eastern Africa (e.g. Kenya) by the mid‑1980s; the main novelty is the virus’ emergence in Somalia’s large pastoral goat sector. Event clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 CAEV emergence episodes and should be retained.

Host: Domestic goats (dairy Saanen and other breeds)
Event summary: Around 2010, a dairy goat farm in South Korea that had been considered free of CAEV began to experience lameness, carpal joint swelling and neurologic signs in goats; nested PCR and sequencing of the gag gene confirmed CAEV infection and the episode was reported as the first recognized outbreak of CAE on a Korean farm. Subsequent testing on the index farm found more than half of the adult Saanen goats and a substantial fraction of kids PCR-positive, while nearby farms keeping only native Korean black goats remained negative, indicating localized establishment of infection in imported dairy breeds. Follow-up serological and molecular work showed that Korean isolates clustered with known CAEV strains, and control on the affected farm focused on testing, culling of positives and improved kid-rearing practices rather than a national eradication programme.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of infected Saanen or other dairy breeding stock into a previously CAEV‑naïve commercial farm, limited historical testing, and increasing interest in intensive dairy goat production created conditions for silent spread before overt clinical disease emerged. Internal mechanisms: The Korean isolates showed close sequence homology to known CAEV strains, suggesting that endemic establishment was driven by efficient lactogenic and horizontal transmission in intensive herds rather than by a novel genotype or increased virulence.
Review: retain – adjusted the event year from an imprecise 2005–2010 range to 2010, corresponding to the first confirmed outbreak and molecular characterization reported by Park et al. (2010) and later detailed clinically in a 2021 case report, and clarified the country/time annotation accordingly. Kept emergence-type coding as a regional re_occurrence (CAEV was already present in Eastern Asia in China and Japan) and not as intra_continental_emergence, which is reserved for first appearance in a new UN subregion. Event remains one of the key post‑1990 CAEV emergence reports in Eastern Asia.

Countries: Malaysia [2010], Malaysia (Peninsular – Selangor and other states) [2010-2013]
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat goats) and sheep in mixed small-ruminant farms
Event summary: Around 2010, Malaysia reported its first confirmed CAEV outbreak when a large commercial herd of about 2,000 goats in Selangor recorded around 20 animals with nervous signs and progressive arthritis that were diagnosed as CAE. Subsequent years saw follow‑up investigations and the first dedicated serological surveys in Peninsular Malaysia, which documented CAEV seroprevalence in goats and sheep in multiple states (e.g. Selangor and neighbouring regions), demonstrating that infection was already established in several herds. These findings prompted recognition of CAEV as an emerging transboundary disease in Malaysian small ruminants, with recommendations for routine serological surveillance, improved biosecurity, and kid‑rearing practices; however, eradication has not yet been achieved and CAEV remains a low‑to‑moderate prevalence problem in intensive and semi‑intensive herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth and partial intensification of small‑ruminant production in tropical Southeast Asia, with increased importation of dairy breeds and breeding stock from CAEV‑endemic regions; limited historical testing allowed the virus to become established before detection. Internal mechanisms: No unique Malaysian genotype was highlighted; the key internal factor is the virus’ ability to persist and transmit via colostrum and close contact, enabling silent spread in mixed goat–sheep systems.
Review: retain – this is appropriately coded as an intra_continental_emergence event, as Malaysia represents the first well-documented occurrence of CAEV in the South‑eastern Asia UN subregion, with a clinically apparent outbreak followed by state‑level serosurveys. Countries, timing and impact (large index herd, multiple affected states) are consistent with Noordin et al. 2010 and Jesse et al. 2018. No changes to dates or geography were required; event is clearly among the top post‑1990 emergence episodes for CAEV and should be retained.

Host: Domestic goats (dairy, meat and breeding herds)
Event summary: Between March 2011 and October 2012, a large-scale serological survey of 3,437 goats from 65 goat farms across Taiwan found an overall CAEV seropositive rate of 61.7% and herd-level infection in 98.5% of farms, demonstrating that CAEV infection was widespread in both dairy and meat goat operations. Prevalence was highest in dairy herds (over 80% of animals positive in some regions), and positive farms were detected in northern, central, southern and eastern parts of Taiwan, with only one surveyed farm remaining negative. These results provided the first national-level picture of CAEV infection in Taiwan and led to recognition that the virus was endemic and a major constraint on goat productivity, highlighting the need for ongoing surveillance and targeted control measures, particularly in intensive dairy systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of dairy goat farming in Taiwan, including importation of high-yield breeds from CAEV-endemic countries and frequent animal movements between regions, likely underpinned the high prevalence detected in the survey. Internal mechanisms: The study did not identify a novel genotype driving spread; rather, the very high within-herd and herd-level prevalence is consistent with long-standing circulation of typical CAEV strains in dense dairy herds, aided by efficient transmission via colostrum/milk and close contact.
Review: retain – added this event because the 2011–2012 nationwide survey in Taiwan is one of the largest and highest-prevalence CAEV datasets worldwide (3,437 goats, 65 farms, 61.7% individual and 98.5% herd seropositivity), making it clearly among the top ten post‑1990 CAEV emergence/re-occurrence events by impact. Classified as a regional re_occurrence in Eastern Asia, since CAEV had already been present in China and Japan; not marked as intra_continental_emergence. Noted Taiwan as “China (Taiwan)” to align with UN-style nomenclature, but this may need harmonization with the project’s country list.

Countries: Thailand [2011] (Ratchaburi, Phetchaburi, Kanchanaburi provinces – western Thailand)
Host: Domestic goats (smallholder and commercial herds)
Event summary: In 2011, a cross‑sectional serological survey in the western part of Thailand (Ratchaburi, Phetchaburi and Kanchanaburi provinces) revealed that CAEV antibodies were present in goats, with an individual‑animal seroprevalence of about 5–6% and higher herd-level prevalence, providing one of the first clear demonstrations that CAEV was circulating in Thai goat populations. The study identified older age, larger herd size and introduction of new goats as significant risk factors for seropositivity, indicating ongoing transmission dynamics within and between herds in these western border provinces. Awareness of CAEV in Thailand increased following these findings, and recommendations were made for improved movement control, testing of new stock, and enhanced kid‑rearing management to curb further spread; however, subsequent national surveys still detect SRLV infection, showing that CAEV remains endemic at low to moderate levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of goat production and cross‑border trade of animals in western Thailand; herd expansion via purchase of replacement stock from multiple sources was statistically associated with infection. Internal mechanisms: Standard CAEV/SRLV biology – lifelong persistent infection, late seroconversion and efficient lactogenic and horizontal transmission – contributed to under‑recognition and ongoing endemic circulation rather than any novel genotype or virulence shift.
Review: review/exclude – this survey is an important early documentation of CAEV in Thai goats but is smaller in scale and shows lower prevalence than several other events now included (e.g. Taiwan and the Philippines). It has been reclassified as a regional re_occurrence within South‑eastern Asia (Malaysia already documents first introduction to the subregion), which is appropriate. If the dataset must be limited strictly to the ten most impactful post‑1990 CAEV emergence events, this Thai episode is a candidate for exclusion in favour of higher-prevalence or broader national studies; otherwise it can be retained as a secondary regional event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil – Paraná and other southern/midwestern states [2015-2022]
Host: Domestic goats in commercial and breeding herds
Event summary: From about 2015 onwards, CAEV was increasingly recognized in southern and midwestern Brazil, with seroepidemiological studies in goat herds in Paraná and other states documenting measurable CAEV seroprevalence and its association with higher levels of herd technification and intensive dairy production. These later surveys built on Northeastern findings and showed that CAEV had expanded well beyond earlier foci, becoming an issue across several Brazilian regions and in both dairy and meat goat systems. The expansion prompted calls for national-level CAEV control policies and integration of CAEV testing into broader small‑ruminant health programs, but most interventions have remained herd‑level (testing, biosecurity, and management changes) rather than coordinated national eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued intensification and geographic expansion of commercial goat farming in Brazil, with frequent animal movements between regions and importation of high‑yielding breeds; higher technification and larger herd size were statistically linked to seropositivity. Internal mechanisms: As in other regions, persistent infection and efficient transmission via milk and close contact sustained endemicity; phylogenetic studies reveal typical CAEV‑like SRLV genotypes without strong evidence of a novel lineage driving spread in southern Brazil.
Review: retain – this event captures the documented southward and westward spread of CAEV in Brazil into Paraná and other southern/midwestern states, supported by serological surveys linking infection to intensive and technified herds. Although less dramatic in prevalence than some Asian events, it represents important geographic range expansion in one of the world’s main goat-producing countries and appropriately remains coded as a regional re_occurrence in South America. No corrections to geography or timing beyond the broad 2015–2022 window are required given the underlying literature.

Host: Domestic goats (local breeds) in smallholder systems
Event summary: Between roughly 2019 and 2021, a serological survey of goats in several goat‑dense districts of Bangladesh detected CAEV antibodies and provided the first detailed documentation of CAEV infection in Bangladeshi goat populations, with district‑level seroprevalence varying but clearly demonstrating circulation. The study identified risk factors including management system, herd size, and introduction of new animals, showing that CAEV was spreading in typical smallholder settings in Southern Asia where it had previously received little attention. Following publication around 2023, CAEV was recognized as an emerging constraint on goat productivity in Bangladesh, and the authors recommended enhanced surveillance, improved biosecurity and kid‑rearing practices, though no formal eradication program has yet been initiated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and commercialization of goat production in Bangladesh, increased animal movement between districts, and lack of prior testing allowed introduction and silent establishment of CAEV before the first focused serosurvey. Internal mechanisms: Standard SRLV biology—lifelong infection, delayed seroconversion and persistent shedding—enabled under‑recognition; the study compiled international prevalence data (e.g. from Malaysia, Brazil, Jordan, Oman, Turkey, Mexico, Pakistan, Iraq, Somalia, Italy), suggesting that global strain diversity and multiple importation routes may have contributed to introduction into Bangladesh rather than emergence of a distinct local variant.
Review: retain – corrected the emergence-type classification by setting intra_continental_emergence from true to false and re_occurrence from false to true. CAEV had already been documented in the Southern Asia subregion (e.g. in India and parts of Iran/Pakistan) before the Bangladeshi survey, so this episode reflects a regional re-occurrence and country-level first detection rather than first emergence in a new UN subregion. Countries, timeframe and impact description are consistent with the 2019–2021 sampling and 2023 publication; event merits inclusion among major post‑1990 CAEV emergence events for Southern Asia.

Host: Domestic goats in commercial and smallholder farms
Event summary: From January 2021 to December 2022, a nested PCR survey of 1,334 goats from 24 farms across Luzon, Philippines, detected CAEV proviral DNA in 31.4% of animals and 91.7% of farms, revealing a high positivity rate and suggesting that CAEV is widespread in the main goat‑producing island. Farm-level infection ranged from about 1.5% to over 90% of sampled animals, and many farms reported histories of arthritis, pneumonia, mastitis and emaciation in goats, consistent with chronic CAE. These findings led Philippine authorities and researchers to classify CAE as an emerging/re‑emerging notifiable disease in the country and underscored the need for surveillance, movement control and improved kid‑rearing and biosecurity practices to limit further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth of goat production in Luzon, inter-farm trade in breeding animals, and a lack of prior systematic testing allowed CAEV to become established and disseminate widely before this molecular survey. Internal mechanisms: The very high within-farm positivity detected by nested PCR reflects the sensitivity of proviral detection in chronic lentiviral infections and long-standing circulation of CAEV in intensive and semi‑intensive herds rather than emergence of a novel strain; standard SRLV features (lifelong infection, efficient milk‑borne and horizontal transmission) underpin the observed high prevalence.
Review: retain – added this event because the Luzon nested-PCR study is one of the most striking recent CAEV re-occurrence episodes globally, with 31.4% of 1,334 goats and 22 of 24 farms testing positive, and CAE recognised as a notifiable emerging/re-emerging disease in the Philippines. Classified correctly as a regional re_occurrence in South‑eastern Asia, since CAEV had already been detected in the subregion (Malaysia and Thailand). Years, geography and host system are consistent with the VirusDisease 2024 report; event is clearly within the top ten CAEV emergence events by impact.

EPP common name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Sheep (primarily), goats (exposed and culled in mixed flocks)
Event summary: In November 1994, sheep pox re‑appeared in Evros Prefecture in north‑eastern Greece, near the land border with Türkiye, after the country had been free of clinical disease for several years. The outbreak evolved into a prolonged regional epidemic lasting until December 1998, involving 249 infected premises in Evros and neighbouring areas, with extensive culling, movement restrictions and other control measures implemented. By late 1998 the epidemic was stamped out through depopulation of affected and at‑risk flocks and strict biosecurity, although a single reappearance in 2000 triggered renewed control before the disease was again eliminated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated introduction of virus across the Evros land border from endemic areas in Türkiye, high densities of small‑ruminant farms, and practical challenges in enforcing movement controls in a transboundary grazing zone. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host shift was described; dynamics reflected high susceptibility of naïve or under‑vaccinated flocks and efficient direct and aerosol transmission within and between holdings.
Review: retain – Well-supported major epidemic in Evros, Greece, 1994–1998 with correct continent/sub‑region assignment and appropriate classification as re‑occurrence in a historically affected area; no structural changes made.

EPP common name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Goats (small ruminants, primarily local breeds)
