EPP common name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Goats (primary affected herds in Argentina and Chile); cattle (bovine abortions in La Pampa, Argentina)
Event summary: In 2012, during the spring kidding season, a commercial goat herd in Mendoza Province, Argentina (400 criollo does) experienced a six‑week episode in which about 70 does aborted late‑term fetuses or delivered weak kids, prompting detailed pathological and laboratory investigation. Histopathology, immunohistochemistry and PCR on placental tissue confirmed Chlamydia abortus as the etiologic agent, while contemporaneous diagnostic work in Argentina detected C. abortus DNA in bovine reproductive losses in La Pampa and Chilean SAG laboratories documented multiple caprine abortion foci in the Metropolitan, Biobío and Atacama regions with real‑time PCR confirmation of C. abortus, together constituting the first laboratory‑confirmed C. abortus abortion outbreaks in Chile and Argentina within a continent where serologic evidence and isolated reports from Brazil and Uruguay had already suggested prior circulation. The affected herds controlled the outbreaks through improved hygiene at kidding/lambing, culling or segregation of aborting animals and broader awareness and testing, leading to a return toward baseline abortion rates while establishing C. abortus as a recognised cause of small‑ruminant and bovine abortion in southern South America rather than a new continental incursion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and partial intensification of small‑ruminant and cattle production in southern South America; increased movements of animals between regions and countries; and, critically, the progressive introduction of modern laboratory diagnostics (ELISA, PCR, real‑time PCR) in Argentina and Chile that enabled recognition of C. abortus in abortion material where it had previously gone undetected. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or resistance phenotype was reported; phylogenetic analysis showed close homology with existing ovine and caprine strains from Europe and China, consistent with long‑standing but previously under‑diagnosed presence followed by geographic range expansion and local amplification within the already infected South America sub‑region; this episode is therefore best classified as a regional re‑occurrence and recognition event, not a true inter‑continental emergence or global first detection.
Review: Decision: review (retain with corrected classification and sources). Changes made: (1) Removed the earlier claim that this episode represents inter‑continental emergence or a global first detection of C. abortus in South America; serologic and molecular data from Brazil and other countries show the pathogen was present in the region before 2012, so this outbreak is re‑classified as a re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?lng=en&pid=S0100-736X2012001100002&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en&utm_source=openai)) (2) Set first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to "No" and re_occurrence to "Yes" to align with the definitions, because the episode reflects recognition and spread in new countries (Argentina and Chile) within an already infected sub‑region rather than the first presence on the continent. (3) Clarified in the event summary that Chilean multi‑herd caprine abortion outbreaks with PCR‑confirmed C. abortus in 2012 are documented by SAG’s BVO report and that bovine reproductive losses in La Pampa, Argentina, also involved C. abortus.([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/bitstream/handle/10915/107832/Documento_completo.pdf?sequence=1)) (4) Added the SAG BVO 2014 document as a key source for the Chilean component of the event and retained the Argentinian caprine outbreak and La Pampa bovine abortion articles; these are more specific than the generic background review previously used. Overall, the event remains important as the first well‑documented C. abortus abortion outbreaks in Chile and Argentina, but should not be interpreted as a continent‑wide first emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) in a large semi‑intensive dairy camel operation
Event summary: In the 2018–2019 calving seasons a large, semi‑intensive dairy camel farm in northern Saudi Arabia, which had previously recorded ≤2–3% annual abortions, experienced a sudden abortion storm in the last trimester of pregnancy, with 71 of 210 pregnant she‑camels (33.8%) aborting without prominent systemic illness. Field veterinarians implemented enhanced surveillance and submitted sera, placental tissue, amniotic fluid and a preputial wash from a breeding male for laboratory testing; ELISA indicated prior exposure to several abortifacient pathogens, while real‑time PCR performed at a regional reference laboratory detected C. abortus DNA in 6 of 8 sampled aborted females and in one breeding male, and ruled out Toxoplasma gondii, Coxiella burnetii, Brucella spp. and Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis as primary causes, thereby implicating C. abortus as a major contributor to the abortion storm. Following implementation of strict segregation of calving areas, repeated mass doxycycline treatments, removal of the infected male and improved hygiene and disinfection protocols, abortion rates fell back to around 4% in the 2019–2020 season and the episode was considered controlled, although subsequent serologic surveys in the region have confirmed that C. abortus remains an important abortifacient in camels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth and intensification of dairy camel production in Saudi Arabia, high stocking densities, shared calving and milking infrastructure, and seasonal movement between grazing and calving units created favourable conditions for efficient transmission, while limited prior abortion investigation meant chlamydial infections in camels were under‑recognised despite earlier serologic evidence in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries.([researchopenworld.com](https://researchopenworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/IJVB-5-531.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: there is no evidence in this outbreak of a novel genotype, new host jump or antimicrobial resistance; rather, existing C. abortus lineages exploited intensive management conditions to cause high‑level infection and shedding in dromedary camels, leading to a marked but reversible increase in abortion incidence. On this basis the episode is best characterised as a severe re‑occurrence of C. abortus‑associated abortion in an already exposed camel population in Western Asia, not as first detection or host‑expansion re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review (retain with reclassified emergence type). Changes made: (1) Re‑evaluated the event in light of serologic and uterine‑infection studies demonstrating C. abortus infection in camels in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries before 2018, which shows that camels were already a recognised host in this region.([researchopenworld.com](https://researchopenworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/IJVB-5-531.pdf)) (2) Set re_occurrence to "Yes" and re_emergence to "No", and left inter_continental_emergence and intra_continental_emergence as "No", because the episode represents an unusually large outbreak in an already infected host population in Western Asia rather than a new host expansion or geographical first. (3) Adjusted the mechanism/driver description to focus on intensive management, high stocking density and gaps in surveillance as key external drivers, and removed the stronger claim of host expansion as an internal mechanism; no novel strain or adaptation specific to camels was documented. The event remains a high‑impact abortion storm (33.8% abortions) and is appropriate to retain among major emergence episodes, but its type has been corrected to align with the project’s definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Sheep (approximately 200‑ewe flock; both previously vaccinated and unvaccinated ewes)
Event summary: In the mid‑2010s a French sheep farm with about 200 ewes, where 36 replacement ewes had been vaccinated two years earlier with a live C. abortus 1B vaccine, experienced a major abortion storm affecting both vaccinated and unvaccinated sheep. Vaginal swabs from aborting ewes and tissues from 12 of 13 dead fetuses tested strongly positive for C. abortus by real‑time PCR, and molecular typing showed that the infecting strain was indistinguishable or nearly indistinguishable from the commercial 1B vaccine strain, confirming a vaccine‑derived abortion outbreak. The episode subsided only after strict biosecurity, culling or segregation of affected animals and reassessment of live‑vaccine use, and it contributed to broader genomic work demonstrating that the 1B vaccine strain is not truly attenuated and can cause field abortion storms similar to those induced by wild‑type strains.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive use of the live, temperature‑sensitive 1B C. abortus vaccine for enzootic abortion control in European flocks, combined with management practices that allowed persistence and spread of vaccine‑derived organisms (e.g. incomplete separation of vaccinated ewes and replacements, re‑use of contaminated lambing areas). Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence mediated by a vaccine‑derived strain—whole‑genome comparisons have shown that the 1B vaccine strain is genetically very close to its virulent parent AB7 and to field isolates recovered from vaccinated and in‑contact ewes that aborted, supporting the conclusion that 1B can revert or behave as a fully virulent strain under field conditions rather than remaining attenuated.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6005232/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This event is appropriately classified as a re‑emergence episode driven by a vaccine‑derived strain, consistent with project definitions that include emergence of new strains or altered pathogenicity under the re‑emergence category. The French abortion storm is well documented by case and genomic studies, and fits into a broader pattern of 1B vaccine–associated abortion outbreaks first characterised in Scotland and later in other European countries.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20554095/?utm_source=openai)) No changes were made to the event type flags, geography or core narrative, but the mechanism text was reviewed to ensure it accurately reflects the genomic evidence that 1B is not a genuinely attenuated strain. This episode is judged to be among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for C. abortus because of its implications for global vaccination policy, even though the absolute number of affected ewes is moderate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Sheep (multiple flocks in Sulaimani province – Kalar, Said Sadiq, Chamchamal)
Event summary: During the 2017 lambing season, veterinarians in Sulaimani province, northern Iraq, reported widespread abortions in several sheep flocks in districts including Kalar, Said Sadiq and Chamchamal. Thirty aborted fetuses from five affected herds were examined; conventional PCR and embryonated‑egg culture identified C. abortus DNA in one fetus from Kalar, while the remaining 29 fetuses were positive for Brucella abortus, indicating a mixed‑etiology abortion problem dominated by brucellosis but with documented C. abortus involvement in at least one herd. Control recommendations focused on strengthening diagnosis and control of both brucellosis and chlamydial abortion (improved lambing hygiene, biosecurity and strategic antibiotic use), and the acute abortion episode subsided, although subsequent surveys have shown that enzootic abortion and other infectious causes remain important contributors to reproductive loss in Iraqi flocks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high small‑ruminant density with limited biosecurity and vaccination coverage, co‑circulation of multiple abortifacient agents (notably Brucella abortus) in the same flocks, and generally weak surveillance and diagnostic capacity at the flock level in northern Iraq, all of which predisposed to recurrent abortion episodes. Internal mechanisms: no novel C. abortus genotype or clear change in pathogen biology was reported; the single C. abortus‑positive fetus isolated in this study clustered phylogenetically with other regional isolates, and the event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of C. abortus within an endemic Western Asian sub‑region where the pathogen has long been present alongside other abortifacients.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7256821/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review (candidate for exclusion on impact grounds). Rationale: The Sulaimani study clearly documents C. abortus isolation and molecular characterisation from one aborted fetus and provides useful evidence of the pathogen’s presence in Iraqi sheep.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7256821/?utm_source=openai)) However, only 1 of 30 fetuses (3.3%) was C. abortus positive, whereas 29 (96.7%) were positive for Brucella abortus, indicating that the abortion storm in these flocks was overwhelmingly driven by brucellosis rather than by C. abortus. In comparison with numerous large C. abortus‑dominated abortion outbreaks documented in Europe and Asia (e.g. the many flocks in Iran in which C. abortus was the leading diagnosed cause of abortion),([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9684225/?utm_source=openai)) this episode is unlikely to rank among the top ten most impactful C. abortus emergence events globally. The event type (re_occurrence in a long‑endemic Western Asian sub‑region) and geography are appropriate, but given its relatively small direct C. abortus contribution it is recommended that this row be considered for exclusion if the dataset needs to be restricted strictly to the highest‑impact events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Year: ~2014-2017 (samples collected in the mid‑2010s; study published 2018)
Host: Farmed fur animals – foxes, raccoon dogs and mink in intensive fur farms
Event summary: In the mid‑2010s, several intensive fur farms in northeastern China reported frequent reproductive failures in foxes, raccoon dogs and minks, including abortions, stillbirths and weak offspring, for which routine diagnostic workups had not identified a clear cause. A targeted investigation collected reproductive tissues and swabs from affected animals and used PCR and sequencing to test for Chlamydia spp., demonstrating that many farmed foxes, raccoon dogs and minks harboured C. abortus DNA, with molecular evidence linking the bacterium to the ongoing reproductive problems and confirming the first infection of farmed fur animals with C. abortus worldwide. Following recognition of C. abortus as a cause of reproductive disease in these species, affected farms implemented stricter biosecurity at whelping, improved hygiene and, where necessary, culling of heavily affected breeding stock; abortion problems were reduced, but the findings highlighted a new domestic animal reservoir and potential cross‑species and zoonotic transmission risks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of the fur‑animal industry in northeastern China, with very high animal densities, close confinement, and possible exposure to contaminated feed or environmental sources (e.g. products from infected small ruminants or other livestock), together with a near absence of prior surveillance for chlamydial pathogens in fur animals so that abortions were initially unexplained. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of C. abortus from traditional ruminant hosts into canid and mustelid species under intensive farming conditions, with molecular evidence that infection can cause clinically significant reproductive disease in these novel hosts; no distinct new genotype was described, so the event is best interpreted as a re‑emergence via host expansion into a new production system rather than a new strain or global first detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6287152/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review (retain with corrected emergence typing). Changes made: (1) Confirmed that this study is explicitly described as the first report of C. abortus infection in farmed fur animals (foxes, raccoon dogs and mink), establishing a novel domestic animal reservoir and clinically relevant reproductive disease in these hosts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6287152/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Set first_detection to "No" and kept re_emergence as "Yes" to reflect that, under the project’s definitions, this is a host‑expansion re‑emergence event within the livestock/animal host system rather than a global first detection of C. abortus, which occurred decades earlier in small ruminants. (3) Left the geographic coding (Asia – Eastern Asia, China) unchanged, as this aligns with the UN sub‑region classification. The event is retained as a major emergence episode because it documents a clear, well‑characterised shift of C. abortus into new intensively farmed host species with associated production and potential public‑health implications.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Mexico [first reports of chlamydiosis in sheep and goats and role of Chlamydia in ewe abortions ~1996; first isolation of C. abortus from goats 1997; zoonotic outbreak linked to infected goat herd 2001]
Host: Sheep and goats (mixed rural and dairy herds)
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s to 2001, Mexican investigators documented chlamydial infection in sheep and goats, first linking Chlamydia spp. to ewe abortions, then isolating C. abortus (then classified as C. psittaci serotype 1) from goats, and finally describing a zoonotic outbreak in which a pregnant woman developed severe systemic infection and aborted after contact with an infected goat herd. These linked investigations provided the first clear evidence that C. abortus was established as an abortifacient in Mexican small ruminants, marking emergence of ovine/caprine chlamydiosis in the Central America sub‑region of the Americas. Following recognition, infection appears to have become endemic in affected flocks and herds, with later work focusing on improved diagnostics and risk‑factor characterization rather than discrete, explosive outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of goat and sheep production in central Mexico, animal movements without biosecurity, and limited awareness of chlamydial abortion created conditions for introduction and undetected spread of C. abortus into local small‑ruminant systems, with close human–animal contact enabling occasional zoonotic cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a unique genotype is presented; this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of established C. abortus lineages into a new Americas sub‑region and recognition of their role in abortion (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)), rather than de novo evolution of a novel strain.
Review: ADDED EVENT. Rationale: Mexico’s 1990s reports and first isolation of C. abortus in goats, plus the 2001 zoonotic outbreak linked to an infected goat herd, represent the first well‑documented establishment of C. abortus as an abortifacient in the Central America sub‑region and are more consequential than some later, purely serologic surveys. Classification changes: Marked as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD sub‑region within the South America ‘continent’ grouping) and not as first detection or inter‑continental emergence, which are reserved for global/continental milestones. Scope: Treated as a single linked episode (1996–2001) covering initial reports, isolation, and zoonotic transmission. Flag: RETAIN as a major emergence event; recommended for inclusion in any top‑10 list for this EPP because it defines the appearance of C. abortus‑associated abortion in Central America.

Countries: Brazil [Pernambuco 2009; Paraíba 2012; Alagoas 2013; additional northeastern semi‑arid states by early 2010s]
Host: Sheep and goats
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2013, a series of studies in northeastern Brazil documented moderate to high seroprevalence of antibodies to C. abortus in sheep and goats in Pernambuco, Paraíba, Alagoas and neighboring semi‑arid states, with some flocks showing substantial exposure levels and histories of reproductive problems. These surveys and risk‑factor analyses provided the first robust evidence that enzootic abortion associated with C. abortus was established in Brazilian small‑ruminant populations, complementing earlier reports from Andean countries and helping to reframe reproductive losses in the region as part of a broader South American chlamydial abortion problem. By 2020, Brazil was officially reporting infection with C. abortus (enzootic abortion of ewes, ovine chlamydiosis) as present in its sheep and goat populations to the World Organisation for Animal Health, confirming national‑level establishment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of hair‑sheep and goat production in Brazil’s semi‑arid northeast, frequent animal movements among smallholder flocks without quarantine, limited reproductive health surveillance, and low clinician awareness of chlamydial abortion favoured silent spread and under‑diagnosis until systematic serologic surveys were undertaken. Internal mechanisms: Available data are consistent with introduction and geographic range expansion of existing C. abortus lineages within a sub‑region of South America (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)), without clear evidence for a distinct hyper‑virulent strain or major host shift.
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, SUBSTANTIALLY REVISED. (1) Time span and geography: Expanded year range from 2010 to 2009–2013 and clarified that earlier serologic evidence in Pernambuco (2009) and subsequent work in Paraíba and Alagoas represent a multi‑year, multi‑state emergence pattern in northeastern Brazil. Countries field now lists Brazil with key states and years; host updated from ‘Sheep (ewes)’ to ‘Sheep and goats’ to reflect mixed‑species studies. (2) Event type: Set first_detection = false and inter_continental_emergence = false because C. abortus was present in South America (e.g. Colombia and Peru) well before 1990, so Brazilian reports are neither global first detection nor the first occurrence in the continent. Intra_continental_emergence is also set to false because Brazil lies in a sub‑region (South America) where C. abortus was already documented; per instructions, spread to additional countries within the same sub‑region should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. Marked as re_occurrence at the sub‑regional scale, reflecting broader recognition and probable increase in incidence across South American flocks. (3) Impact: While these are largely seroprevalence and risk‑factor studies rather than a single, dramatic outbreak, they do document establishment of C. abortus in a large new national small‑ruminant population. Flag: REVIEW – likely retain as one of the larger Latin‑American emergence events, but its inclusion in a strict global top‑10 list should be reconsidered against other regional events.
Review Comment: Not top 10

Host: Yaks (Bos grunniens)
Event summary: In 2012, a cross‑sectional study of 674 yak sera from six counties in Qinghai Province found a C. abortus seroprevalence of about 17.7%, indicating widespread infection in yak herds on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau; subsequent work isolated and genetically characterized C. abortus from aborted yak fetuses and tissues in the same region. Together, these studies showed that C. abortus infection was common in yaks and associated with abortion and reproductive losses, establishing yak as a significant livestock host for this pathogen in Eastern Asia. By the mid‑2010s, enzootic abortion due to C. abortus had been recognized as an important constraint on yak productivity in the high‑altitude pastoral systems of Qinghai and neighboring provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and commercialization of yak husbandry on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, co‑grazing of yaks with sheep and goats, and limited biosecurity and veterinary infrastructure likely facilitated spillover and maintenance of C. abortus in yak herds, with environmental and nutritional stressors at high altitude exacerbating abortion impacts. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects host expansion of existing C. abortus lineages into yaks (Host Expansion (Spillover)) and geographic range expansion within Eastern Asia (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)); available genomic work suggests relatively conserved lineages adapted to local ruminant populations rather than a radically novel genotype.
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, RETAINED WITH TYPE CORRECTION. (1) Classification: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence have been set to false because C. abortus was long established in Chinese and wider Asian sheep and goats before 2012; this episode documents its characterization in a new livestock host rather than first presence in Eastern Asia. Re_emergence remains true to reflect a host‑expansion event within a previously affected sub‑region, consistent with the definition that links re‑emergence to changes in the pathogen such as expanding to a new host. (2) Content: The summary is slightly reframed to emphasize host expansion and systematic investigation in yaks, noting prior evidence of chlamydial abortion in yak herds but limited characterization before these studies. (3) Impact: Because yaks represent millions of animals in the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau and reproductive rates are intrinsically low, this host‑expansion event is considered one of the most consequential emergence episodes for C. abortus. Flag: RETAIN as a major emergence event.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Host: Yaks (Bos grunniens)
Event summary: Between roughly 2018 and 2020, a survey of 938 yak sera from six areas of the Tibet Autonomous Region reported an overall C. abortus seroprevalence of about 11.1%, with infection detected across age groups and locations, providing the first systematic data on C. abortus in Tibetan yak populations. These findings extended earlier Qinghai and Gansu reports to show that C. abortus infection in yaks is widespread across the broader Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, with endemic transmission rather than isolated spillover. By the time of publication in 2021, C. abortus was recognized as an established reproductive pathogen of yaks in Tibet, reinforcing its importance in high‑altitude pastoral systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional free‑ranging yak production, communal alpine grazing, seasonal transhumance, and limited segregation of pregnant animals likely facilitated regional spread and maintenance of C. abortus following earlier introduction into yak populations, while sparse veterinary infrastructure and lack of routine abortion diagnostics delayed recognition in Tibet. Internal mechanisms: Available data suggest dissemination of previously established yak‑adapted C. abortus strains from neighboring provinces rather than a new genotype; the episode therefore represents regional geographic range expansion and re‑occurrence of C. abortus‑associated abortion within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, RETAINED WITH TYPE CORRECTION. (1) Classification: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence are set to false because C. abortus infection in yaks had already been documented in other Chinese provinces (Qinghai, Gansu) before this survey. The event is now coded as re_occurrence (ongoing endemic transmission and spread within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region) without re_emergence, as no clear host switch or novel genotype was reported. (2) Event year and countries: Years left as 2018–2020, matching the approximate sampling period underlying the 2021 publication; countries field simplified to Tibet Autonomous Region with bracketed year. (3) Impact: This event is important mainly as consolidation and geographic extension of the earlier yak emergence on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, rather than a distinct, higher‑impact wave. Flag: RETAIN but marked for REVIEW when prioritizing a strict top‑10 list, as it could be merged with the Qinghai yak event into a single plateau‑wide emergence episode depending on desired granularity.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Countries: Mexico (Guanajuato and surrounding central states) [2012; broader dairy and meat goat herds in multiple states by mid‑2010s]
Host: Goats (commercial dairy and mixed breeds)
Event summary: From about 2012 to 2015, intensive studies of commercial dairy goat farms in Guanajuato, Mexico, found C. abortus seroprevalence of roughly 5% at the animal level, with seropositive does present in two‑thirds of herds and PCR detection of C. abortus in aborting goats, followed by isolation and characterization of the bacterium from vaginal swabs and tissues. These investigations, building on earlier 1990s reports and 1997 isolation of C. abortus in Mexican goats, demonstrated that the pathogen was widely established in modern dairy and meat goat production systems in central Mexico and was a significant cause of abortion and reproductive loss. Subsequent multi‑state surveys, including work in Sinaloa and other regions, confirmed C. abortus infection in goats with abortion problems across a broad swath of the country, indicating a transition from sporadic recognition to acknowledged endemicity in Mexican goat herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth and intensification of dairy and meat goat production in hot central and north‑western Mexican regions, high between‑herd animal movement, limited biosecurity, and historical classification of enzootic abortion as an ‘exotic’ disease (which impeded access to reagents and diagnostics) all likely contributed to undetected spread and accumulation of infection before comprehensive surveys and isolation studies were conducted. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication of a novel genotype; this episode mainly reflects re‑occurrence and amplification of existing C. abortus lineages within goat populations and production systems, underpinned by management and trade drivers rather than intrinsic pathogen change.
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, RETAINED BUT REINTERPRETED. (1) Historical correction: Earlier work showed that chlamydiosis in Mexican sheep and goats and the role of Chlamydia in ewe abortions were first reported in the 1990s, with the first isolation of C. abortus in goats in 1997 and a documented zoonotic outbreak in 2001. Therefore, this 2012–2015 Guanajuato episode cannot be coded as first detection for the country or region. first_detection has been set to false accordingly. (2) Event type: intra_continental_emergence is set to false because C. abortus was already present in the Central America sub‑region (Mexico) by the late 1990s; under project rules, spread within the same sub‑region should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. The event is now classified as re_occurrence, reflecting a marked increase in recognized incidence and impact in intensively managed goat systems driven by external management factors. re_emergence is set to false because there is no strong evidence of host expansion or a novel strain during this period. (3) Scope: The summary has been expanded to acknowledge both the prior 1990s work and subsequent broader multi‑state surveys, while keeping the temporal focus on the early‑ to mid‑2010s when intensive diagnostic investigations in commercial dairy herds occurred. Flag: RETAIN as a major emergence/re‑occurrence event in Central American goat systems, but noted for REVIEW when ranking relative to other Latin‑American episodes.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Countries: Chile (Atacama Region 2010; Metropolitan Region and Biobío Region multiple outbreaks 2012); Argentina (Mendoza Province 2018)
Host: Goats (with some ovine involvement in Chile)
Event summary: From 2010 onward, Chilean surveillance identified serologic evidence of enzootic abortion in goats in several regions, and in 2012 multiple abortion outbreaks in goat herds in the Metropolitan and Biobío Regions were investigated using histopathology and molecular methods, leading to the first confirmed detection of C. abortus in Chile and laboratory implementation of PCR diagnostics for abortion cases. Subsequently, a 2018 report from Mendoza Province, Argentina, described a major abortion outbreak in a goat herd (70 of 400 does aborting) in which placental lesions, immunohistochemistry and PCR sequencing identified C. abortus as the etiologic agent, representing the first confirmed caprine abortions due to C. abortus in Argentina. Together, these findings show that during the 2010s C. abortus emerged as a recognized cause of caprine abortion across parts of the Southern Cone, expanding the known distribution of enzootic abortion in South American goats beyond earlier Andean foci and contributing to significant reproductive losses in affected herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of goat production in arid and semi‑arid areas of Chile and Argentina, frequent movement of replacement animals without specific biosecurity measures, and historically limited diagnostic capacity for chlamydial abortion likely facilitated introduction and spread of C. abortus before its formal recognition. Increased surveillance and adoption of molecular diagnostics during the 2010s then revealed its role in recurrent abortion outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No distinct Southern Cone C. abortus genotype has been highlighted; this episode is best viewed as re‑occurrence and geographic extension of existing C. abortus lineages into additional goat populations within a previously affected South American sub‑region (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)), rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: ADDED EVENT. Rationale: The first molecular confirmation of C. abortus–associated abortion outbreaks in Chilean goat herds (2010–2012) and the large 2018 caprine abortion outbreak in Argentina (70/400 does) together represent a substantial recognition and spread of C. abortus as an abortifacient in Southern Cone goat populations. These have wider regional impact than some single‑state serosurveys and thus merit inclusion among the major post‑1990 events. (1) Classification: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence are set to false because C. abortus had been present in the South America sub‑region for decades (e.g. Colombia, Peru, Brazil); per project rules, spread to new countries within the same sub‑region should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. The event is coded as re_occurrence, reflecting a pronounced increase in recognized incidence and geographic extent of C. abortus‑associated caprine abortion within the South America sub‑region, driven largely by external husbandry and diagnostic factors. (2) Aggregation: Chile and Argentina are treated as a single, regionally linked emergence episode (2010–2018) because they are neighboring countries in the same production zone and share similar diagnostic and epidemiologic narratives; if finer granularity is preferred, this could be split into separate national events. Flag: RETAIN as a major Latin‑American emergence/re‑occurrence event, recommended for inclusion in any top‑10 list for this EPP.

Countries: United States of America [1967 Colorado captive mule deer; early 1980s free-ranging deer and elk in Colorado and Wyoming]
Host: Captive mule deer; captive elk; wild mule deer; wild elk; wild white-tailed deer (early foci)
Event summary: From 1967 through the early 1980s, chronic wasting disease was first recognized as a progressive wasting syndrome in captive mule deer held at a Colorado wildlife research facility near Fort Collins, then shown in 1978 to be a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy of cervids. In the early 1980s, natural infections were documented in free‑ranging mule deer and elk in Colorado and Wyoming, revealing that the agent had escaped captive settings and established in wild populations in the central Rocky Mountain region. By the mid‑1980s, this Colorado–Wyoming focus was recognized as the original endemic area for CWD in North America, providing the source population for subsequent geographic spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term confinement of mule deer and elk at high densities in experimental pens where they were likely exposed to contaminated environments, and possible historical contact with scrapie‑infected sheep pastured at the same facilities; subsequent translocation of captive and wild cervids within the central Rockies. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a novel cervid prion strain capable of efficient horizontal transmission, with strong environmental persistence of prions in soil and enclosures, allowing infection to amplify in captive herds and then spill over into adjacent free‑ranging mule deer and elk populations.
Review: retain – New event added to capture the first global emergence of CWD in captive mule deer and subsequent early wild cases in Colorado and Wyoming (1967–1980s), in line with the instruction to include first global emergence even if pre‑1990. Classification set to first_global_emergence=true and other event‑type flags false; geography (United States of America, Northern America) and hosts follow standard UN sub‑region definitions and historical sources.

Countries: Canada [1996 first farmed elk case in Saskatchewan; 2000 first wild mule deer case in Saskatchewan; 2005 first wild cases in Alberta]
Host: Farmed elk and deer; wild mule deer; wild white-tailed deer
Event summary: Beginning in 1996, chronic wasting disease was first detected in Canada in farmed elk in Saskatchewan, followed by additional detections in farmed cervids on other prairie game farms and then in wild mule deer along the Saskatchewan–Alberta border in 2000. Over the early 2000s, surveillance revealed continued spread and establishment of localized endemic areas in wild mule deer and, in subsequent years, in white‑tailed deer in the same region, with Alberta confirming its first wild cases in 2005. By around 2005, CWD was recognized as established in wild cervid populations in parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta, prompting large-scale depopulation of infected game farms and intensive wildlife testing programs, and shifting management from attempted eradication toward long-term control and surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance translocation and trade of farmed elk and deer from CWD-affected areas of the United States into Canadian game farms; high animal densities and fence-line contact on farms; movement of infected animals between farms and into the wild via escapes or improper carcass disposal. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced environmental persistence and indirect transmission of prions in contaminated enclosures and pastures; geographic range expansion enabled by infected wild deer dispersing along river valleys and agricultural landscapes.
Review: review – Event retained as representing the first major Canadian emergence of CWD involving farmed elk and early wild deer, but reclassified from 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' to 're_occurrence' because the pathogen was already established in the Northern America sub‑region. Timeline and geography adjusted to note first farmed elk case in Saskatchewan in 1996, first wild mule deer case in Saskatchewan in 2000, and first wild cases in Alberta in 2005; species wording softened so that wild white‑tailed deer are described as being detected in the early 2000s rather than specifically in 2000. Source list updated to emphasize the Saskatchewan government overview, CFIA national CWD page, and a Canadian review article, dropping the less directly relevant British Columbia CWD plan.

Countries: Republic of Korea [2001 elk imports, 2001–2004 outbreaks]
Host: Farmed elk (Cervus elaphus nelsoni)
Event summary: In 2001, South Korea detected CWD for the first time in an imported Canadian elk showing progressive neurologic disease, marking the first report of CWD outside North America. Over the next several years, additional farmed elk herds tested positive, leading to a national control response involving depopulation and surveillance of cervid farms. By about 2004, these initial outbreak herds had been culled and intensive surveillance temporarily reduced detected CWD activity in Korean farmed cervids.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in live farmed elk from CWD-endemic Canadian herds; high-density confinement on deer farms facilitating transmission; limited early awareness of CWD risk in Asian cervid industries. Internal mechanisms: Efficient horizontal transmission of CWD prions among elk via contact and environmental contamination; prion environmental persistence on farms enabling infection of multiple animals after introduction by a small number of imported carriers.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the first detection of CWD outside North America in farmed elk in the Republic of Korea and associated culling of infected herds. To align with the event‑type definitions, 'first_detection' has been set to false (global first detection occurred in Colorado in 1967), while 'inter_continental_emergence' remains true to reflect first establishment in Asia with demonstrated farm‑to‑farm transmission. No changes to geography, hosts, timeline or sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus); captive white-tailed deer
Event summary: In 2002, Wisconsin confirmed its first CWD-positive wild white-tailed deer near the border with Iowa County, representing the first detection of CWD east of the Mississippi River and far from the original Rocky Mountain endemic area. Subsequent intensive surveillance through the 2000s revealed a core endemic focus in southern Wisconsin with rising prevalence, including detection in both free-ranging and captive white-tailed deer herds, prompting aggressive management actions such as special hunts and carcass movement restrictions. By around 2010, CWD was firmly established in parts of Wisconsin’s deer population, and management shifted from attempted local eradication to long-term control and monitoring of disease spread within the state.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historic translocation and trade of captive elk and deer from CWD-endemic regions of the western United States into the Midwest; high local deer densities, supplemental feeding, and baiting practices increasing deer-to-deer contact; human movement of carcasses and heads spreading contaminated tissues. Internal mechanisms: Long incubation period and environmental persistence of prions allowing undetected buildup before recognition; efficient horizontal transmission among white-tailed deer in dense Midwestern populations, enabling rapid local amplification once introduced.
Review: review – Wisconsin’s outbreak is correctly included as the first large CWD focus east of the Mississippi and an important management turning point. In line with the definitions, 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' have been set to false because CWD was already known in the Northern America sub‑region; the episode is now classified solely as 're_occurrence', reflecting geographic expansion and sharp local increases in prevalence driven by external factors such as cervid translocation and high deer densities. Event summary, hosts, and sources from Wisconsin DNR and Emerging Infectious Diseases remain appropriate.

Countries: Canada [2005 first Alberta wild cases; ongoing spread in Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec (captive red deer), British Columbia]
Host: Wild mule deer; wild white-tailed deer; wild elk; wild moose; farmed cervids
Event summary: Starting in 2005, Alberta confirmed its first wild CWD-positive deer along the Saskatchewan border, extending the known Canadian wild-endemic area beyond the initial Saskatchewan focus, and subsequent surveillance revealed ongoing spread along river valleys and prairie landscapes. Through the 2010s and early 2020s, CWD prevalence increased in wild mule deer and white‑tailed deer in parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta, with later detections in additional provinces including a large outbreak on a red deer farm in Quebec in 2018, wild mule and white‑tailed deer in Manitoba from 2021, and wild white‑tailed deer in British Columbia beginning in 2024, as well as occasional cases in wild elk and moose. By the mid‑2020s, CWD had become enzootic across large portions of the Canadian Prairies and present in multiple provinces, necessitating long-term hunter-based surveillance, carcass movement controls, and adjustments to deer harvest regulations to mitigate population impacts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural dispersal of infected wild deer along interconnected prairie and riverine habitats; extensive hunter harvest and carcass transport that can redistribute infected tissues; expanding road networks and agricultural development facilitating deer movements; historical movement of infected farmed cervids seeding multiple areas. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by environmental prion persistence in heavily used riparian and agricultural areas; infection of multiple cervid species, including moose, increasing the host community reservoir; potential selection for prion strains adapted to regional host genotypes, sustaining high prevalence foci.
Review: review – Event appropriately summarizes the long‑term spread and intensification of CWD in Canadian wild cervids beyond the original Saskatchewan focus, including first wild cases in Alberta and later detections in Manitoba, Quebec (captive red deer), and British Columbia (wild deer). Event‑type flags were adjusted: 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_emergence' are set to false and 're_occurrence' to true, since this represents continued expansion within an already affected UN sub‑region driven largely by host movements and management, rather than a new sub‑region or clearly novel strain. The summary was lightly edited to distinguish first wild cases in Saskatchewan (2000), Alberta (2005), wild deer in Manitoba (2021) and wild deer in British Columbia (2024), while keeping the single linked episode 2005–2024.

Countries: Republic of Korea [2010 re-emergence; 2016-2024 annual cases]
Host: Farmed elk; farmed red deer; farmed sika deer
Event summary: After several years with no detected CWD following early-2000s control efforts, CWD reappeared in South Korea in 2010 in farmed cervids, indicating that the pathogen had persisted or been reintroduced. During 2016–2024, national surveillance documented recurring cases almost every year in multiple farmed elk, red deer, and sika deer herds across the country, with repeated depopulations and economic losses in the farmed deer industry. By the early 2020s, CWD had become an entrenched management problem for Korean farmed cervids, requiring ongoing testing, movement controls, and herd culling to limit further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued commercial farming and movement of multiple cervid species within South Korea; incomplete elimination of prions from previously infected premises; economic incentives to expand or restock deer farms after earlier depopulations; possible reintroduction via imported animals or contaminated products. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence driven by persistent environmental prion contamination on farms and efficient multi-species transmission among elk, red deer, and sika deer, supporting sustained transmission cycles despite control measures.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re‑emergence episode of CWD in South Korean farmed cervids after several apparently disease‑free years, but the event type has been simplified: 're_occurrence' is kept as true to reflect renewed transmission in an already affected country, while 're_emergence' is set to false because current evidence points mainly to persistence and re‑introduction of existing strains rather than clear pathogen change. No adjustments to geography, hosts, or timeline were required.

Countries: United States of America [multiple states including original western focus and expansion into Midwest, South, and Atlantic states]; Canada [multiple provinces beyond initial prairie focus]
Host: Wild white-tailed deer; wild mule deer; wild elk; farmed deer and elk; wild moose (localized)
Event summary: From roughly 2010 onward, surveillance data documented rapid geographic expansion of CWD across North America, with detections in ever more U.S. states and Canadian provinces outside the original Rocky Mountain and prairie foci, ultimately exceeding 30 U.S. states and several Canadian provinces by the early 2020s. Many of these newly affected regions reported initially low but increasing prevalence in wild white-tailed and mule deer, occasional cases in wild or captive elk, and localized management responses including surveillance zones, carcass restrictions, and targeted culls. By the mid‑2020s, CWD had become a continent‑wide wildlife health concern with multiple high‑prevalence hotspots and mounting evidence of demographic impacts on some local deer populations, prompting long-term adaptive management rather than short-term eradication attempts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance translocation of live cervids and carcasses, both historically and in the early 21st century; high deer densities near urban, agricultural, and supplemental feeding sites; wildlife management practices (baiting, winter feeding, game farms) that concentrate cervids; incomplete biosecurity at captive facilities leading to spillover into free-ranging populations. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion driven by mobile infected deer dispersing into naïve areas; persistent environmental prions in soils and vegetation along movement corridors; possible emergence and spread of prion strains better adapted to white‑tailed deer and to varied climatic conditions across North America.
Review: review – North America–wide expansion from roughly 2010 onward is appropriately treated as a single, long, epidemiologically linked episode capturing spread into many additional U.S. states and Canadian provinces with rising prevalence. To match the definitions, 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_emergence' are set to false and the event is classified as 're_occurrence', reflecting major resurgence and geographic spread within the same sub‑region. Source URLs were updated to prefer CDC and APHIS over Wikipedia for the continental overview, while retaining Alberta management documents that discuss surveillance and control.

Host: Wild mountain reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus)
Event summary: In March 2016, Norway diagnosed CWD in a free-ranging wild reindeer from the Nordfjella herd in southern Norway, representing the first detection of the disease in Europe and the first confirmed natural CWD case in reindeer. Intensive follow-up surveillance during 2016–2018 identified additional classical CWD cases within Nordfjella Zone 1, leading authorities to implement a drastic management campaign that culled the entire wild reindeer population in that zone to prevent further spread to other reindeer areas. By 2018, culling in Nordfjella Zone 1 had been completed and ongoing national surveillance indicated no further classical CWD cases in reindeer outside the original outbreak zone, though vigilance remained high.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Possible introduction of CWD prions into the Nordfjella landscape via historical importation of infected cervids or contaminated animal products from North America, or via environmental contamination from other prion sources such as scrapie in small ruminants grazing in the region; high local reindeer densities and seasonal aggregation facilitating within-herd transmission. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of a classical CWD strain capable of efficient transmission in wild reindeer, with environmental persistence of prions on shared ranges; disease dynamics in a migratory, herd-living host leading to rapid amplification once the pathogen became established.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the 2016 detection of classical CWD in the Nordfjella wild reindeer herd, the first recognized occurrence in Europe and globally the first natural infection in reindeer, and the subsequent eradication cull of Nordfjella Zone 1. To conform with the schema, 'first_detection' was set to false (global first detection predates this event), while 'inter_continental_emergence' remains true to mark first establishment of CWD in the European continent. No changes were needed for geography, timeline, or sources.

Host: Wild moose (Alces alces); wild red deer (Cervus elaphus)
Event summary: Following the 2016 detection of classical CWD in Nordfjella reindeer, Norway’s expanded cervid surveillance identified several atypical CWD-like prion cases in older wild moose and a small number of red deer in other parts of the country, genetically and pathologically distinct from the classical CWD strain in reindeer and North American cervid strains. These moose and red deer cases were rare, typically single animals detected over multiple years, and did not show evidence of clustered transmission comparable to the Nordfjella outbreak, but they extended the known host range and prion strain diversity of CWD-like diseases in Europe. By the early 2020s, Norway recognized these atypical moose and red deer cases as a separate epidemiological phenomenon requiring continued surveillance but different management emphasis than the classical reindeer outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive, nationwide active surveillance of wild cervids following the Nordfjella outbreak, leading to detection of sporadic atypical prion cases that might previously have gone unnoticed; aging moose and red deer populations in some regions where older individuals are more likely to express atypical transmissible spongiform encephalopathies. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of atypical or Nor16CWD-like prion strains in individual moose and red deer, possibly arising spontaneously in older animals rather than through sustained horizontal transmission; host expansion of cervid prion disease manifestations to additional species in Norway, with limited onward transmission demonstrated to date.
Review: review – Norway’s atypical CWD‑like cases in moose and red deer are retained as a distinct event because they represent new prion phenotypes (Nor16CWD and related strains) and host expansion within Northern Europe. Event‑type flags were simplified: 're_emergence' is kept true to reflect emergence of novel, likely sporadic strains and new affected hosts in a previously infected sub‑region, while 're_occurrence' is set to false to avoid double classification. Otherwise, geography, hosts, and timing remain consistent with Norwegian surveillance reports and EFSA’s European CWD overviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wild moose (European elk, Alces alces)
Event summary: In March 2018, Finnish authorities reported the country’s first CWD-like transmissible spongiform encephalopathy case in a 15‑year‑old wild moose found dead near Kuhmo in eastern Finland, representing the first such detection in the country and extending the known European distribution of cervid prion disease. Subsequent investigations concluded that this case resembled the atypical CWD-like prion pattern previously described in Norwegian moose rather than the classical, highly transmissible North American form, and intensified surveillance of cervids was implemented in Finland and neighboring EU member states. No large clusters or clear transmission chains were identified in Finland after this index case, but it established Finland as part of the European region where atypical cervid TSEs occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: EU- and nationally coordinated cervid surveillance programs that increased sampling intensity after CWD was detected in Norway; detection in an older moose possibly linked to age structure and longevity in local populations. Internal mechanisms: Likely spontaneous or low-transmissibility atypical prion strain in moose, similar to Nor16CWD reported in Norway, representing a re-emergent form of cervid prion disease in a new national population and host context; host expansion within Northern Europe from Norwegian to Finnish moose populations.
Review: review – The 2018 Finnish moose case near Kuhmo is retained as a key milestone showing that atypical cervid prion disease occurs beyond Norway. Event‑type flags have been revised so that 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' are set to false (Europe was already affected and this is a new country within the same Northern Europe sub‑region), while 're_emergence' is set to true to reflect appearance of a Nor16CWD‑like, likely sporadic strain in a new national host population. Sources from the Finnish government, Yle, and veterinary reports remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild moose (Alces alces)
Event summary: In March 2019, Sweden reported its first CWD-positive wild moose, extending the known occurrence of cervid prion disease to another Nordic country and indicating that atypical moose CWD-like cases were not confined to Norway and Finland. Over 2019–2022, Sweden detected an additional small number of isolated CWD-like cases in older moose in northern counties, and surveillance also intensively sampled semi-domesticated reindeer in northern regions for potential infection, highlighting concern over possible spread into Sámi reindeer herding areas. These findings positioned Sweden within the broader Scandinavian pattern of atypical cervid TSEs, prompting continued targeted surveillance and risk assessments for moose populations, although no confirmed reindeer cases have been reported in Sweden.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Targeted surveillance of older moose following European Commission and Nordic responses to Norwegian CWD findings; increased diagnostic capacity and awareness leading to identification of rare, atypical cases. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of atypical CWD-like prion strains in individual moose, possibly sporadic and age-associated, representing a re-emergent prion disease phenotype in new national and host settings; potential, but still uncertain, capacity for spillover into reindeer, motivating precautionary monitoring.
Review: review – Swedish moose cases are correctly included as part of the Scandinavian pattern of atypical CWD‑like disease, but several corrections were made. The event period was extended to 2019–2022 to cover all four confirmed moose cases reported through 2022, the host list was restricted to wild moose since no CWD cases have been detected in reindeer in Sweden, and event‑type flags were adjusted so that 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' are false while 're_emergence' is true (new atypical strain and host occurrence in a country within an already affected sub‑region). Source URLs were updated to add the Swedish Veterinary Institute’s CWD pages and to drop the less essential French‑language Wikipedia article.

Host: Wild mountain reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus)
Event summary: After the culling of the Nordfjella reindeer herd, Norway continued intensive surveillance and in 2020 identified a classical CWD case in a wild reindeer on the Hardangervidda plateau, home to Europe’s largest wild reindeer population, indicating that classical CWD had either spread beyond Nordfjella or arisen independently. This detection triggered renewed concern and risk assessments, as Hardangervidda supports many thousands of reindeer and is ecologically and culturally important, leading authorities to consider further targeted removals and strengthened monitoring. In the early 2020s, ongoing testing of Hardangervidda and other reindeer areas continued to search for additional cases to guide long-term management of CWD risk in Norway’s remaining wild reindeer populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Residual or previously unrecognized circulation of CWD prions in Norway’s interconnected reindeer ranges, potentially influenced by animal movements between management areas, shared grazing grounds, and historic livestock use of the same mountain pastures. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of classical, transmissible CWD in a second major wild reindeer population, highlighting the capacity of this prion strain to persist and spread within reindeer metapopulations despite localized eradication efforts in Nordfjella; environmental persistence of prions in alpine ecosystems sustaining risk over multiple years.
Review: review – The detection of classical CWD in a Hardangervidda wild reindeer in 2020 is appropriately treated as a separate high‑impact event because it involves Europe’s largest wild reindeer population. Event‑type classification was simplified by setting 're_emergence' to false and keeping 're_occurrence' true, since available data indicate the same classical strain as in Nordfjella rather than a new variant; the episode is thus best interpreted as renewed occurrence in another population within the same Northern Europe sub‑region. Geography, timeline (2020 onward), and Norwegian Veterinary Institute sources remain valid.
