Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [1995]; Iraq [1996]; Bahrain [1996]; Kuwait [1997]; Qatar [1999]; Saudi Arabia [1999]; United Arab Emirates [1999]
Host: Sheep; goats; cattle; camels; humans (sporadic wound myiasis)
Event summary: The event began when Old World screwworm myiasis due to Chrysomya bezziana was reported as an outbreak in livestock in Khuzestan Province, southern Iran, in spring 1995, and then appeared suddenly in the Mesopotamia valley of Iraq in September 1996, likely introduced or amplified via movement of infested sheep and goats in a period of trade disruption and constrained veterinary services. Within 1996–1997 the infestation spread along the Tigris–Euphrates system and across at least 13 Iraqi governorates, generating an estimated 54,000–60,000 myiasis cases in livestock with multi‑million‑dollar losses, while contemporaneous infestations were documented in Bahrain (mid‑1990s), Kuwait, Iran, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia from the late 1990s, predominantly affecting small ruminants. From the late 1990s to early 2000s, a regional emergency program led by AOAD, FAO, IAEA and partners implemented intensive surveillance, wound treatment, and feasibility work on sterile insect technique, after which reported case numbers declined and the epidemic wave subsided, leaving C. bezziana established but under better control in Gulf livestock populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of sheep and goats with frequent tail‑docking and other husbandry practices that create wounds, coupled with limited access to veterinary care and insecticides under economic sanctions and regional instability, created abundant oviposition sites and delayed treatment; movement of infested livestock among Gulf states facilitated transboundary spread along trade routes and river valleys, while climate in the Mesopotamia valley and Gulf lowlands provided optimal warm, humid conditions for screwworm development. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain is clearly implicated, but genetic studies reveal structured haplotypes in Middle Eastern C. bezziana populations consistent with geographic range expansion from existing endemic foci; the outbreak reflects the species’ inherent high reproductive capacity, strong flight dispersal, and biological traits favoring geographic range expansion and efficient transmission in dense small‑ruminant systems rather than a major shift in virulence or host range.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the large mid‑1990s invasion of Iraq and regional Gulf outbreaks as a single epidemiologically linked wave across Western and Southern Asia. However, based on FAO and WOAH summaries, these infestations occurred in a subregion (Gulf / Western Asia) where C. bezziana was already present before 1990, and available studies do not demonstrate a novel strain or host shift; therefore the emergence type has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence, with intra‑ and inter‑continental emergence kept as “No”. Country lists and approximate country‑specific start years (Iran 1995; Iraq 1996; Gulf states late 1990s) are broadly consistent with regional syntheses but should be cross‑checked against primary national reports (e.g. for Oman, which may also have been substantially affected) if more granular dating is required.

Host: Sheep; goats; cattle; camels; dogs; donkeys; humans (sporadic)
Event summary: The event originated when Old World screwworm was first officially reported from Yemen in late 2007, after sudden incursions into Sa’dah Governorate near the Saudi border, most likely introduced via movement of infested livestock from neighboring endemic areas into susceptible small‑ruminant and camel herds in Yemen’s north‑western lowlands. During 2008, a severe outbreak of traumatic myiasis developed in sheep, goats, cattle, camels, dogs and other animals across several coastal and adjacent inland governorates, with thousands of cases reported and major concern about southward and highland spread and potential spillover into wildlife and humans; by 2009, further outbreaks were reported from central governorates such as Taiz, Ibb and Dhamar. Coordinated surveillance and control activities under regional AOAD/FAO/IAEA programs, including wound treatment campaigns, larvicide supply, awareness efforts and movement management, reduced reported case numbers after 2008–2009, although C. bezziana likely remained established and Yemen has since been considered at continued risk of screwworm re‑incursion and renewed outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of small ruminants and camels from endemic neighboring countries, limited veterinary and surveillance infrastructure, and high livestock densities in climatically suitable coastal and lowland areas fostered establishment once the fly arrived; extensive pastoral systems, frequent untreated wounds (including around docking, branding and other procedures), and delayed treatment amplified local transmission. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak represents geographic range expansion and resurgence of existing Middle Eastern C. bezziana lineages into a previously less‑affected country within the same Western Asia subregion, exploiting the species’ inherent capacity for dispersal and high reproductive output, rather than emerging from a newly evolved strain or a shift in host range; enhanced transmission in dense small‑ruminant populations and along trade pathways was the key biological driver.
Review: retain – Yemen’s 2007–2009 wave is one of the best‑documented large OWSW emergence episodes after 2000, with thousands of animal cases and strong regional concern. Consistent with project rules, it is not coded as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence because Western Asia already harboured C. bezziana in other Gulf countries; instead, the emergence type has been changed from re_emergence to re_occurrence, reflecting reappearance and dramatic increase within an already affected subregion driven largely by external factors (animal movements, service disruption, climate). Event years and host range are well supported by FAO/IAEA reports and later reviews, but detailed governorate‑level burden estimates remain uncertain and could be refined from national Yemeni data if available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle; sheep; goats; donkeys; dogs; cats; other domestic livestock; wild mammals (various wildlife species reported locally)
Event summary: The event began during the 2023 rainy season when veterinarians and livestock keepers in several regions of Senegal started reporting unusually aggressive traumatic myiasis in small ruminants, cattle, equids and companion animals, with larvae later confirmed by the national veterinary laboratory and an FAO/IAEA mission as Old World screwworm (Chrysomya bezziana). Between July 2023 and January 2024, the infestation spread across at least five departments, including coastal and inland areas such as Dakar–Thiès–Fatick and parts of Tambacounda and Ziguinchor regions, where field investigations documented about 1,900 confirmed screwworm myiasis cases and many additional farmer‑reported cases, leading to deaths, culling and marked loss of productivity in affected herds. Following emergency support from FAO, WOAH and national services—focused on larvicide treatment of wounds, farmer and veterinarian awareness campaigns, and enhanced surveillance—the wave of cases subsided with the end of the rainy season in early 2024, but authorities highlighted that pupae surviving in the soil, continued animal movements and climatic suitability mean that further outbreaks during future rainy seasons in Senegal and neighboring West African countries remain a significant risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A wet 2023 rainy season, high densities of small ruminants and other livestock, frequent untreated or poorly treated wounds (including around tail docking, castration and traditional husbandry practices), and limited prior awareness of screwworm facilitated rapid amplification once C. bezziana was introduced or re‑introduced into Senegal; animal movements within West Africa and across ecological zones likely aided spread among departments. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects the establishment and resurgence of an already widely distributed African C. bezziana lineage in a country that had not reported the parasite for decades, exploiting its inherent high fecundity, broad host range and capacity to complete multiple generations over a rainy season; there is currently no evidence of a novel strain, resistance, or major shift in host range, so the episode is interpreted as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: review – New event added because FAO and WOAH report that Senegal experienced its first confirmed large outbreak of Old World screwworm between July 2023 and January 2024, with roughly 1,900 recorded cases in five departments and thousands of animals affected during the 2023 rainy season, making this one of the most significant recent emergence events in Africa. Consistent with the project definitions and historical records of C. bezziana in other West African countries, this episode is classified as re_occurrence within the Western Africa subregion rather than intra‑continental emergence or first detection, and there is currently no evidence of a distinct strain or host‑range shift that would justify re_emergence coding. As the situation is relatively recent and surveillance is still being strengthened, case numbers, host range and any subsequent spread to neighboring countries should be revisited when more detailed WAHIS and national data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event summary: After CSF had been close to eradication in much of the EU, Germany experienced a prolonged resurgence beginning in the early 1990s, with 424 outbreaks in domestic pigs and widespread infection in wild boar recorded between 1990 and 1998. Intensive control measures, including culling and movement restrictions, were implemented as CSF became endemic in wild boar in several regions, repeatedly seeding infections into pig farms. By 1998, the last outbreak in domestic pigs was eliminated and Germany regained CSF‑free status for domestic herds, although infected wild boar remained a concern for some time.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High pig density and extensive trade/movements of pigs and pig products within Germany and neighboring EU states; hunting and feeding practices that facilitated contact between wild boar and domestic pigs; difficulties in biosecurity implementation at small farms. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission via establishment and maintenance of CSFV in wild boar populations, which acted as a wildlife reservoir repeatedly infecting domestic herds rather than a clearly novel viral genotype.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within wildlife reservoirs.
Review: retain – major 1990s German CSF epizootic with >400 domestic-pig outbreaks and a large wild boar reservoir; geography, timing and impact are consistent with primary sources. Event correctly coded as a re-occurrence in Western Europe without intra- or inter-continental spread; no structural changes made.

Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: Belgium, which had previously reduced CSF to low levels, experienced a substantial resurgence in 1993–1994 when virus introduced via regional pig movements spread in high-density pig areas, particularly in northern Belgium. Over roughly four months, around two dozen herds became infected and several hundred thousand pigs were slaughtered or destroyed under EU stamping-out policies, resulting in multi-million-euro losses and trade disruption. Following strict movement controls, tracing of animal movements and intensified surveillance, the outbreaks were eliminated and Belgium later regained CSF‑free status in domestic pigs, although it was affected again on a much smaller scale during the wider 1997–1998 Western European epizootic.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High pig density and strong trade and animal‑movement links with neighboring countries, particularly Germany and the Netherlands; rapid spread once the virus entered integrated production systems; delays in early detection on some farms. Internal mechanisms: Infection involved genotype 2 CSFV similar to strains circulating elsewhere in Western Europe; there is no evidence that unusually high virulence, rather than trade and husbandry factors, drove the epidemic.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via interconnected production and trade networks.
Review: retain (after correction) – original row mis-dated the main Belgian epidemic as 1995–1998 and over-emphasised the 1997–1998 wave. Timing has been corrected to 1993–1994, when ≈23 outbreaks and large-scale culling occurred, and the summary/mechanism text updated accordingly. Geography and classification as re-occurrence in Western Europe remain appropriate; recommend expert review of final outbreak and loss estimates.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (backyard and commercial herds)
Event summary: After roughly two decades without recognised cases, Cuba reported re‑emergence of classical swine fever in 1993, with virus introduction into commercial and backyard pigs leading to an epizootic that became endemic and generated several hundred recorded outbreaks nationwide between 1993 and 1997. From this focus, CSF spread to neighboring Haiti in 1996 and to the Dominican Republic in 1997, where more than two hundred outbreaks were reported in 1998, causing high mortality in smallholder herds and prompting regional trade restrictions and concern about spread toward the mainland Americas. Control relied on intensive vaccination, stamping‑out in affected foci, and movement controls, which progressively reduced outbreak numbers but did not fully eliminate CSF, leaving the virus endemic in parts of the Caribbean.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Regional trade in live pigs and pork between Cuba and Hispaniola; insufficient and inconsistently applied vaccination and biosecurity in backyard and smallholder systems; informal movement of animals and pork and feeding of uncooked swill; limited veterinary infrastructure in some affected areas. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of CSFV genotypes within Caribbean pig populations, followed by local diversification and adaptation to backyard production and marketing networks, facilitating long-term persistence and repeated seeding of new foci.
Internal mechanisms coded: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (regional establishment and diversification of new genotypes); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through adaptation to dense informal trade and backyard systems.
Review: retain – new event added to capture the 1993–1998 Caribbean epizootic centred on Cuba with subsequent spread to Haiti and the Dominican Republic, which together generated hundreds of outbreaks and substantial pig losses and clearly rank among the most impactful post‑1990 CSF episodes. Countries, timing and epidemiological linkage are based on OIE/USDA documentation and Cuban molecular‑epidemiology studies; classified as re-emergence in an already affected subregion rather than as intra-continental emergence.

Host: Domestic pigs; free‑ranging pigs; wild boar
Event summary: After earlier control successes, Italy continued to report CSF outbreaks in domestic pigs and wild boar through the mid‑ to late‑1990s, with notable activity from about 1995 in mainland regions and in Sardinia. Molecular typing of isolates from outbreaks between 1985 and 2000 showed at least two separate introductions affecting both domestic pigs and wild boar, indicating sustained circulation and repeated spillover. By late 1999, Italy declared itself free from CSF in domestic pigs except on Sardinia, where endemic infection persisted in free‑ranging pigs and wild boar, necessitating ongoing control programs into the 2000s.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Extensive smallholder and free‑ranging pig husbandry in mountainous and forested areas; close contact between domestic pigs and wild boar; challenges enforcing biosecurity and movement controls; mixed infections with other pig diseases complicating surveillance. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicated multiple CSFV lineages but not a single novel hypervirulent genotype; persistence was instead linked to maintenance in wildlife and traditional production systems.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (maintenance in wild boar and free‑ranging pigs); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within island and mountainous habitats.
Review: retain – Italy (including Sardinia) experienced recurrent CSF with substantial involvement of wild boar and free-ranging pigs in the 1990s, forming part of the core Western European problem recognised by WOAH. Countries field has been simplified to 'Italy [1995]' (Sardinia now specified in the narrative), but geography, timing and classification as re-occurrence in Southern Europe remain appropriate.

Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: In February 1997, classical swine fever was detected in a mixed sow and finishing herd in the pig‑dense regions of the Netherlands, triggering one of the largest modern CSF epizootics. The virus spread through intensive pig production areas, ultimately infecting 429 herds and leading to culling of several million pigs, including more than 1.1 million pre‑emptively slaughtered in 1,286 herds at risk. By 1998, strict stamping‑out, movement controls, and pre‑emptive slaughter brought the epidemic to an end and the country regained CSF‑free status, though at enormous economic and social cost to the pig industry.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Very high pig and herd density, frequent animal movements, and complex trade networks within and beyond the Netherlands; late detection in a densely connected production system; policy of non‑vaccination which required extensive culling once virus was established. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by CSFV subgenotype 2.1a, but there is no strong evidence that intrinsic increases in virulence drove spread; rather, management and network factors dominated.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (via dense production and movement networks).
Review: retain – Netherlands 1997–1998 epidemic is correctly characterised as one of the largest CSF outbreaks ever recorded, with ≈429 infected herds and millions of pigs culled; geography and timing match EU and WOAH reports. Coding as a major re-occurrence in Western Europe without inter-continental spread is appropriate and sources are highly relevant.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000]
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: In August 2000, the United Kingdom detected classical swine fever in a pig farm in Suffolk, East Anglia, the first confirmed outbreak since national eradication in 1966. The disease spread to a total of 16 farms in the high‑density pig region of East Anglia, leading to the culling of about 75,000 pigs and substantial trade disruption. Through rapid stamping‑out, movement controls, and zoning, the outbreak was contained and officially ended by early 2001, allowing the UK to maintain its overall CSF‑free status.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Reintroduction most likely via movement of infected pigs or contaminated pork products into a previously CSF‑free, high‑density pig production area; high farm connectivity and animal movements facilitated early spread; absence of vaccination meant all control relied on culling and movement bans. Internal mechanisms: No major new genotype or virulence change was identified; the event is best explained by reintroduction and production‑network drivers.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (through dense farm network, not virological change).
Review: retain – UK 2000 East Anglia outbreak is correctly described as a nationally important re-occurrence with 16 infected farms and ~75,000 pigs culled, causing major trade impacts. Geography (Northern Europe/UK) and event-type coding as re-occurrence only are appropriate; no structural corrections were needed.

Countries: Bulgaria [2006]; Slovakia [2006]; Lithuania [2009]; Latvia [2010-2012]; Hungary [2008-2009]; Germany [2008]
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar
Event summary: Following major control efforts in Western Europe, CSF reappeared intermittently in Eastern and Central European member states from about 2005 onward, with outbreaks in farmed pigs and extensive infection in wild boar in countries including Bulgaria, Slovakia, Lithuania, Latvia, Hungary, and parts of Germany. These outbreaks marked renewed spread of CSFV into areas that had been free or nearly free of the disease in domestic herds, often seeded by infected wild boar or movements of subclinically infected pigs. Through coordinated EU surveillance, wild‑boar vaccination, and strict stamping‑out in domestic herds, the number of outbreaks declined and by the early 2010s cases in commercial pig farms had become sporadic.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Expansion and increased density of wild boar populations in Eastern and Central Europe; movement of infected wild boar across borders; variable biosecurity and smallholder pig production systems that allowed spillover; increased hunting and trade in game meat. Internal mechanisms: No single novel genotype dominated, but long‑term maintenance in wild boar and occasional farm introductions illustrated the virus’s ability to persist in wildlife and exploit gaps in biosecurity.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (wild‑boar maintenance); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Eastern European sub‑regions.
Review: retain (with classification correction) – this row appropriately summarises a multi-country 2005–2012 wave of CSF in wild boar and domestic pigs in Eastern/Central Europe, supported by EFSA and EU data. To align with definitions, the original co-classification as both intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence has been simplified to intra-continental emergence only (spread into Eastern European subregions that had become CSF-free), and 'Germany – Eastern regions' has been standardised to 'Germany [2008]' in the countries field. Exact country-specific start years remain approximate and should be checked by a regional expert.

Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event summary: Japan, which had reported no CSF outbreaks since 1992, confirmed re‑emergence of the disease in September 2018 at a pig farm in Gifu Prefecture, central Honshu, after pigs began dying in August. Genetic analysis showed the virus belonged to subgenotype 2.1 and differed from strains causing earlier Japanese outbreaks, and the infection rapidly spread to numerous pig farms and wild boar populations in Gifu and neighboring prefectures, with nearly 900 notifications in domestic pigs and wild boar by August 2019. Through extensive culling, movement controls, vaccination of wild boar, and eventually vaccination of domestic pigs in affected prefectures, Japan progressively brought the epidemic under control, though control and eradication efforts continued beyond 2021.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Dense pig production in central Japan, frequent movements of pigs and vehicles among farms, and contact between farm environments and abundant wild boar populations; probable introduction of CSFV via contaminated live pigs or pig products from endemic regions; delay in recognition due to long absence of CSF. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of a novel CSFV subgenotype 2.1 lineage distinct from historic Japanese strains, with efficient transmission in both domestic pigs and wild boar and genetic evidence of ongoing evolution; maintenance in wild boar created a persistent wildlife reservoir.
Internal mechanisms coded: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion (Spillover and maintenance in wild boar reservoir); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of 2.1 lineage into previously free Japan.
Review: retain – the 2018–2021 Japanese CSF epidemic, with re-introduction of genotype 2.1 after 26 years of freedom and hundreds of notifications in pigs and wild boar, is clearly one of the major modern CSF emergence events. Geography, timing, host range and classification as re-emergence are appropriate, and the source set is strong and outbreak-specific.

Host: Domestic pigs (commercial and backyard); wild or free‑ranging pigs in some areas
Event summary: Although Brazil had achieved CSF‑free status in its main commercial swine‑producing regions, from August 2018 classical swine fever re‑emerged in the non‑free Northeast zone, with the first outbreak detected in Forquilha municipality (Ceará). Over 2018–2019, a total of about 68 CSF outbreaks with thousands of cases were reported across dozens of municipalities, predominantly in Ceará and Piauí, with additional outbreaks in Alagoas, largely affecting smallholder and backyard systems but posing a risk to the national industry. Intensified surveillance, zoning to protect the free area, and, more recently, targeted vaccination campaigns in the non‑free Northeast progressively reduced outbreak numbers by 2020 and initiated a long‑term eradication effort for this region.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Concentration of low‑biosecurity backyard and smallholder pig systems in the Northeast, with frequent animal movements and informal trade; feeding of swill and limited access to veterinary services; socio‑economic constraints that hampered rapid detection and response; strong trade connections between non‑free and CSF‑free zones necessitating strict zoning. Internal mechanisms: Phylodynamic analyses indicate a long‑standing CSFV subgenotype 1.5 lineage circulating and evolving in Northeast Brazil, so the 2018–2020 surge reflected amplification and spatial expansion of an endemic lineage under suboptimal control rather than appearance of a completely new strain.
Internal mechanisms coded: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Brazil’s Northeast; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through adaptation to backyard and smallholder systems.
Review: retain (with mechanism and country-field correction) – the 2018–2020 CSF outbreaks in Brazil’s non-free Northeast zone (mainly Ceará, Piauí and Alagoas) involved dozens of outbreaks and thousands of pigs and were highly significant because of the risk to Brazil’s large CSF-free export regions. Countries have been standardised to 'Brazil [2018]; Brazil [2019]' and internal mechanisms recoded to reflect amplification of an endemic 1.5 lineage (re-occurrence) rather than de novo strain emergence; otherwise the event is appropriately characterised and clearly merits inclusion among major CSF emergence events.

Host: Sheep and goats in feedlots and mixed small‑ruminant flocks
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, two severe outbreaks of type C and type D botulism in South Africa caused catastrophic losses in small ruminants: in one feedlot, 329 of 900 sheep died within 9 days, and in another mixed flock about 100 of 330 sheep and goats died over roughly three weeks. Both episodes began soon after animals were moved onto rations or feedlot conditions that exposed them to preformed C. botulinum toxins, resulting in acute flaccid paralysis and rapid death in many animals. Mortality halted once contaminated feed sources were identified and withdrawn and surviving animals were protected from further exposure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive feeding of sheep and goats in feedlots using inadequately controlled rations and possible inclusion of carcass‑contaminated material created high‑risk anaerobic conditions for toxin formation. Internal mechanisms: Laboratory work identified classical type C and type D toxins in feed and intestinal contents without evidence of novel variants, so these outbreaks are best interpreted as large re‑occurrence events in an endemic area driven by management and feeding practices rather than evolutionary change in the bacterium.
Review: review – Event is real and clearly high‑impact (hundreds of small ruminants dead in two outbreaks). I replaced the vague year label “1990s” with 1995, approximated from the publication date of the primary case report, and kept both outbreaks merged into one row because they are similar in scale, country and time period. However, the two South African outbreaks are not known to be epidemiologically linked, so a future refinement could split them into two rows if greater temporal precision becomes available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (California – Salton Sea)
Host: Wild fish‑eating waterbirds, especially American White Pelican, California Brown Pelican and other piscivorous birds
Event summary: In summer 1996, the Salton Sea in southern California experienced a massive outbreak of type C avian botulism in fish‑eating birds, with nearly 20,000 pelicans and other species reported sick or dead, including about 9,000 American White Pelicans, over 2,000 endangered California Brown Pelicans and roughly 4,500 birds from about 60 additional species. The episode escalated as pelicans and other birds fed on tilapia and other fishes that harbored C. botulinum type C toxin, leading to the largest pelican die‑off ever recorded from any cause. The outbreak was gradually controlled through intensive carcass collection, bird rehabilitation and seasonal changes in water temperature and fish mortality patterns, but avian botulism has recurred at the Salton Sea in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term salinization and eutrophication of the Salton Sea from agricultural runoff created warm, shallow, low‑oxygen conditions ideal for C. botulinum growth, while mass die‑offs of tilapia supplied carcasses that supported toxin production; dense aggregations of pelicans and other fish‑eating birds at this artificial lake amplified the carcass–maggot–bird transmission cycle. Internal mechanisms: The event involved typical type C toxin without any reported novel strain; severity was driven by environmental degradation and an introduced fish reservoir (tilapia) rather than pathogen evolution, so it is classified as a major re‑occurrence.
Review: review – This large wildlife event was missing from the original LLM output but is clearly among the most consequential C. botulinum outbreaks since 1990, with nearly 20,000 birds affected and major conservation and management implications. Added as a new row with geography, host range and magnitude taken from USGS summaries. Classified as re‑occurrence because avian botulism was already known at the Salton Sea and globally; the episode reflects extreme environmental and food‑web conditions rather than a new strain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus) on multiple intensive farms
Event summary: In June 2002, a large type D bovine botulism episode began in southern Israel, affecting vaccinated Holstein dairy herds on dozens of farms after total mixed rations containing fermented poultry manure became contaminated with C. botulinum neurotoxin D. The initial multi‑farm outbreak, together with additional outbreaks between July 2002 and May 2005, led to at least 14 documented herd‑level outbreaks and about 210 clinically affected cows and calves in detailed investigations, with catastrophic losses in some herds. Control relied on withdrawing contaminated rations, tightening poultry‑manure handling and revisiting national vaccination protocols; no comparable nationwide multi‑herd episode has been reported from Israel since, although sporadic cattle botulism cases continue to occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of inadequately processed fermented poultry manure in dairy total mixed rations and centralized feed mixing/distribution allowed contamination of many herds with high doses of BoNT/D; vaccine protection was incomplete when animals were heavily exposed. Internal mechanisms: Laboratory work and serology identified classical type D toxin with no evidence of a novel variant, so this cluster is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence driven by feed practices and possible vaccine‑performance issues rather than evolutionary change in C. botulinum.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified a major type D dairy outbreak in Israel and the role of poultry manure, but overstated mortality as “more than 600 cows” without a clear source. I rewrote the summary to align with the published immunoglobulin/vaccine‑efficacy study, which documents 14 herd‑level outbreaks and about 210 affected animals between mid‑2002 and 2005, and retained the 28‑dairy‑farm figure only where it is explicitly supported. Classification as re‑occurrence (not first detection or re‑emergence) is appropriate because bovine botulism and vaccination were already long‑established in Israel.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (Devon; eight premises)
Host: Beef and dairy cattle on multiple premises
Event summary: In 2006, a notable cluster of bovine botulism outbreaks in Devon, United Kingdom, affected eight cattle premises that had used or stored broiler litter, with one intensively documented herd losing 52 of 378 at‑risk cattle (around 14%) and additional deaths across other farms. The cluster unfolded over several weeks as cattle accessed stacked or spread poultry litter or litter‑contaminated silage, leading to progressive flaccid paralysis and high case fatality. The situation was brought under control after broiler litter sources were removed or fenced off, advisory measures were issued nationally, and greater emphasis was placed on vaccination and on prohibitions against using carcass‑containing litter as fertiliser or bedding for ruminants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of broiler litter as fertiliser or bedding on grazing or silage ground, sometimes containing decomposed poultry carcasses, provided a potent environmental reservoir of C. botulinum type C/D toxin; wind, scavengers and manure handling allowed contamination of pasture and feed across several premises. Internal mechanisms: No new toxin variant was reported; disease reflected high environmental toxin loads in an endemic setting and is best classified as re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – The Devon cluster is well documented in UK government and advisory reports as a multi‑premises bovine botulism episode linked to broiler litter, with around 52 deaths in one major herd and multiple affected farms. Geography and timing (Northern Europe, 2006, UK) and the classification as re‑occurrence driven by poultry‑litter management are appropriate. I did not alter the original event substantially and recommend keeping it as a representative large European cattle‑botulism cluster.

Countries: United States of America (Florida – EquiTransfer embryo transfer facility)
Host: Horses (primarily adult mares at a large embryo‑transfer facility)
Event summary: In October 2008, a catastrophic equine botulism event occurred at the EquiTransfer embryo‑transfer farm in Marion County, Florida, when hay or haylage suspected to be contaminated with C. botulinum toxin was fed to the resident herd of roughly 400 mares. Within hours to days of exposure, more than 100 horses developed rapidly progressive neuromuscular weakness and respiratory compromise, and approximately 100–114 horses were euthanized or died despite intensive veterinary care, making it one of the largest recorded equine botulism outbreaks. The event ended after the suspect forage was withdrawn, surviving horses received antitoxin and supportive care, and heightened awareness led to changes in forage sourcing and handling; smaller, independent equine botulism clusters (e.g. in Vermont) were reported elsewhere in the U.S. the same year but were not epidemiologically linked to the Florida incident.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Feeding a large, high‑value group of horses with a single contaminated batch of hay or haylage under intensive management conditions created a point‑source exposure with devastating consequences; the absence of routine botulism vaccination for many adult horses and delays in recognizing the toxin source contributed to high mortality. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved established C. botulinum toxin (likely type B or C) rather than a novel strain, so it is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by forage contamination and management factors.
Review: review – The original row correctly highlighted the Florida 2008 equine botulism outbreak and gave an appropriate order‑of‑magnitude death toll, but it conflated this with small, unrelated clusters in Vermont and other states and formatted U.S. states as pseudo‑countries in the “countries” field. I restricted the event to the well‑documented Florida EquiTransfer incident, kept the overall case and death range consistent with veterinary media reports (≈100–114 horses), and clarified that other 2008 clusters were independent and are not treated as part of the same outbreak. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein–Friesian cows and offspring)
Event summary: In spring–summer 2009, a severe outbreak of bovine botulism occurred in a Saxony‑Anhalt dairy herd in Germany, where 122 of 286 Holstein–Friesian cows and youngstock showed signs of flaccid paralysis and 115 animals (about 40% of the herd) died or were euthanized. The outbreak likely followed ingestion of C. botulinum type D/C toxin via contaminated feed or farm environmental sources, producing progressive weakness, recumbency and respiratory failure in affected animals. After contaminated material and possible toxin sources were identified and removed and farm management was adjusted, no further cases occurred and the outbreak subsided.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive indoor dairy management and contaminated grass or mixed rations, possibly linked to poorly preserved silage or environmental contamination, allowed high‑dose exposure to type D/C toxin in a single large herd; lack of mandatory botulism reporting in Germany may delay recognition in similar situations. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved known D/C mosaic toxin, with no evidence of a novel genotype or host range change, and so is treated as a major re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This event is well substantiated by German and international veterinary sources and clearly qualifies as a major dairy herd loss (≈115 cattle) in Western Europe. Geography, timing and event‑type classification as re‑occurrence are consistent with the literature, and the sources used are appropriate case‑report and national‑level documents. I recommend retaining this row without substantive changes.

Host: Feedlot beef cattle (steers)
Event summary: In August 2017, a catastrophic outbreak of type C botulism struck a feedlot in Midwestern Brazil after 1,700 steers began receiving a batch of corn silage contaminated with C. botulinum neurotoxin type C. About 1,100 steers were affected and 1,090 died within just four days once clinical signs—progressive flaccid paralysis and recumbency—appeared, giving a mortality rate of 64.7% and lethality of 99.1% in clinically affected animals. The event ended only after the contaminated silage source was identified and removed and the remaining steers were managed with antitoxin therapy and changes in feeding practices.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density feedlot management and feeding of improperly preserved, non‑acidified corn silage that allowed carcass contamination and anaerobic conditions for BoNT/C production created a point‑source exposure for the entire cohort. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved classical BoNT/C and illustrates vulnerability of unvaccinated or improperly vaccinated cattle to massive toxin doses; there is no evidence of a novel strain, so this is a very large re‑occurrence event driven by feed and storage conditions.
Review: retain – This is one of the clearest and best‑documented large bovine botulism events worldwide (≈1,090 steers dead on a single farm), with detailed peer‑reviewed description of epidemiology and clinical course. Location, numbers and classification as re‑occurrence are accurate, and the sources used (Anaerobe case report and a review summarizing it) are appropriate. No corrections needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle on a mixed dairy–broiler poultry farm
Event summary: In winter 2018, a massive outbreak of bovine botulism due to C. botulinum type D/C occurred on a mixed dairy and broiler farm in eastern France, with extensive illness and deaths in the dairy herd after contamination of feed and the environment. The episode began after broiler flocks carrying C. botulinum D/C asymptomatically shed the organism into litter; manure handling and use of the same tractor bucket to remove broiler litter and then mix cattle rations led to widespread contamination of ration ingredients and barns. The outbreak was gradually brought under control through withdrawal of contaminated feed, vaccination of the herd, depopulation and intensive cleaning of the poultry house, and environmental decontamination that eventually eliminated detectable C. botulinum from the system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close integration of broiler and dairy production on a single site, repeated use of broiler litter as a fertilizer and failure to segregate equipment between the poultry house and cattle feed preparation allowed cross‑contamination of cattle feed and housing, while structural features such as contaminated ventilation systems sustained environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: The investigation showed persistent carriage of a known type D/C strain in broilers and environmental reservoirs and its spread via equipment, but did not document a novel genotype; thus this is best classified as a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic region driven by production‑system design and hygiene gaps rather than re‑emergence due to pathogen evolution.
Review: review – The original row accurately captured the mixed dairy–broiler context and the importance of asymptomatic carriage in broilers, but it marked both “re_occurrence” and “re_emergence” as Yes. Based on the detailed Frontiers in Microbiology investigation, there is no evidence of a novel toxinotype or host jump—rather, an existing D/C strain exploited poor biosecurity between poultry and cattle. I therefore kept re_occurrence = Yes and set re_emergence = No to align with the project definitions (external drivers predominating). This event should be retained as a major European cattle‑botulism outbreak and a key example of cross‑sector contamination.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: India (Rajasthan – Sambhar Salt Lake and surrounding wetlands)
Host: Wild and migratory waterbirds (various waterfowl and shorebird species)
Event summary: In November 2019, a massive die‑off of wild and migratory birds occurred at Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan, India, with government and scientific reports estimating over 18,000–23,000 birds dead within roughly 10 days across the lake and nearby wetlands. Field investigations and laboratory testing by Indian veterinary and wildlife institutes confirmed avian botulism due to C. botulinum toxin as the principal cause, and carcass scavenging and a carcass–maggot–bird cycle amplified mortality among densely congregated migratory birds. Mortality declined after carcasses were systematically removed and as water levels, salinity and temperature shifted away from the extreme conditions that had favored toxin production, and the event has been described as the first documented large avian botulism outbreak in India.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusual hydrological and climatic conditions following monsoon rains—rapid water level fluctuations, increased salinity as water receded, high organic loading and probable eutrophication—created anaerobic microhabitats for C. botulinum growth in lake sediments, while mass congregation of migratory birds and delayed carcass removal sustained a carcass–maggot–bird transmission cycle. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was identified; C. botulinum and avian botulism were already known globally and C. botulinum had likely long been present in the region, so this outbreak is best treated as a re‑occurrence in an ecosystem newly recognized as vulnerable, rather than as global first detection of the pathogen in animals.
Review: review – The original row correctly emphasized the scale of the Sambhar Lake die‑off and its confirmation as avian botulism, but it set “first_detection” = Yes as if this were the first global detection of C. botulinum in animals, which contradicts the project definition (first description in the host system worldwide). I reset first_detection = No and reclassified the event as re_occurrence, driven by extreme environmental conditions in a region where C. botulinum almost certainly pre‑existed but had not previously caused a documented mass avian mortality. I also relied more heavily on government and peer‑reviewed reports rather than Wikipedia for the core description.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America (Oregon–California border – Lower Klamath and Tule Lake National Wildlife Refuges)
Host: Wild waterfowl and shorebirds (dabbling ducks, geese, coots, grebes and other waterbirds)
Event summary: In the summer and early autumn of 2020, the Klamath Basin National Wildlife Refuge Complex on the Oregon–California border suffered its worst recorded avian botulism outbreak, with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service staff and partner organizations estimating that roughly 60,000 waterfowl and other waterbirds died, mainly at Lower Klamath and Tule Lake National Wildlife Refuges. As prolonged drought and upstream water diversions left most wetlands dry or extremely shallow, birds were forced into a few warm, stagnant pools laden with decaying organic matter, where C. botulinum type C toxin production and carcass–maggot–bird transmission rapidly escalated mortality. Emergency carcass collection, establishment of a rehabilitation hospital and, where possible, delivery of additional water to key refuge pools eventually reduced the die‑off, but the event highlighted the extreme vulnerability of the refuges under ongoing water shortages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Multi‑year drought coupled with extensive irrigation withdrawals left historic marshes largely desiccated, concentrating millions of migratory birds into small, shallow, nutrient‑rich ponds that warmed rapidly and developed anoxic conditions ideal for C. botulinum growth; carcass accumulation and insect scavengers then propagated a classic carcass–maggot–bird botulism cycle. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved the usual type C toxin; its magnitude is attributable to hydrological stress and habitat loss rather than the emergence of a new strain, so it is classified as a major re‑occurrence event.
Review: review – A very large Klamath Basin botulism outbreak (≈60,000 birds) was not represented in the original dataset, even though it clearly ranks among the most consequential avian botulism events globally in the past few decades. I added this row based primarily on U.S. FWS–linked reporting and conservation‑group summaries that quantify the 2020 mortality and describe the hydrological context. Event type is classified as re_occurrence (environmentally driven) in an already endemic system. Given the importance of this site for the Pacific Flyway, this event should be considered for inclusion among the top 10.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America (cases in Colorado, Louisiana, New Mexico, Texas, and a later case in Kentucky)
Host: Horses (multiple breeds; mostly adult horses)
Event summary: From December 11, 2022 to March 24, 2023, a multi‑state equine botulism outbreak in the United States was traced to contaminated commercial alfalfa cubes (“Top of the Rockies”) distributed to horse owners in at least four states (Colorado, Louisiana, New Mexico, Texas), with an additional late case in Kentucky. Epidemiologic and regulatory investigations documented at least 98 affected horses and 57 deaths, most occurring within days of feeding from specific lots that contained carcass material contaminated with C. botulinum type C toxin. After the feed was recalled nationwide, regulatory warnings were issued and awareness of the risk from improperly screened alfalfa‑cube production increased, new cases ceased and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Industrial‑scale manufacture and wide interstate distribution of contaminated alfalfa cubes allowed a single feed product, adulterated with small carcass fragments containing C. botulinum type C, to poison horses across multiple U.S. states; gaps in feed‑safety controls and traceability delayed full recognition of the scope of the event. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved established type C toxin without evidence of a new strain; disease severity reflects high‑dose exposure via feed rather than pathogen evolution, so it is classified as a large re‑occurrence associated with modern feed manufacturing and distribution networks.
Review: review – The original description of this event and its classification as a large re‑occurrence were sound, but the “countries” field mixed the country name with U.S. states and year tags, which are intended only for multiple‑country episodes. I simplified “countries” to the United States with states noted in parentheses and clarified that an additional late case occurred in Kentucky, as described in the peer‑reviewed outbreak investigation. This event should be kept as one of the most significant modern equine botulism outbreaks linked to manufactured feed.

Host: Wild and migratory waterbirds
Event summary: In late 2024, Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan, India, again experienced elevated bird mortality attributed to avian botulism, with reports indicating at least about 600 migratory birds found dead over a relatively short period. The event followed the catastrophic 2019 outbreak and began as large numbers of migratory birds assembled at the wetland under conditions of variable water levels and high organic loading. Prompt carcass collection, increased surveillance and public awareness stemming from the 2019 event appear to have limited the 2024 mortality compared to the earlier episode, and deaths declined as environmental conditions improved and carcasses and suspected toxin sources were removed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recurrence of environmental conditions at Sambhar Lake favourable for C. botulinum—fluctuating water levels, extreme weather and changes in water quality and depth that produced localized, warm, organic‑rich, low‑oxygen zones—likely triggered a smaller‑scale repeat of the carcass–maggot–bird cycle seen in 2019; ongoing anthropogenic pressures on the wetland (e.g. illegal salt extraction) may contribute to chronic vulnerability. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported, and the event is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence in the same subregion driven by climatic, hydrological and carcass‑management factors.
Review: review – The original row correctly captured the order‑of‑magnitude mortality (~600 birds) and attribution to avian botulism as a recurrence in the same wetland, and its classification as re_occurrence is appropriate. However, given the existence of much larger avian botulism events worldwide (e.g. Klamath Basin 2020, Salton Sea 1996) and even at Sambhar itself in 2019, this 2024 episode is unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful global events for this EPP, though it is important as evidence of site‑level recurrence. I recommend keeping it marked as re_occurrence but flagging it for possible exclusion if a strict top‑10 filter is imposed across all available events.

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, primarily Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), Chinese white shrimp (Fenneropenaeus chinensis) and kuruma shrimp (Marsupenaeus japonicus).
Event summary: Beginning in 2002, shrimp farmers in coastal China observed a new chronic mortality syndrome in intensive ponds, with moribund shrimp remaining on pond bottoms and cumulative losses sometimes reaching about 80% early in the culture cycle; this condition became more prominent by 2009 and was recognized as covert mortality disease (CMD) or viral covert mortality disease (VCMD). Through the 2000s, CMD/VCMD caused substantial and recurrent production losses in Pacific white shrimp and other penaeid species in multiple coastal provinces, often overlapping with other major diseases such as AHPND. In 2014, Chinese researchers identified a novel alphanodavirus, covert mortality nodavirus (CMNV), from diseased shrimp and fulfilled viral causality criteria, establishing CMNV as the etiological agent of VCMD and enabling the development of specific molecular diagnostics and disease nomenclature.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and geographic expansion of penaeid shrimp aquaculture in coastal China, with high stocking densities, fluctuating temperatures and co‑occurring pathogens (e.g. AHPND), created strong amplification conditions for a previously unrecognized viral agent; extensive movement of post‑larvae and broodstock among hatcheries and ponds facilitated its silent spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence – CMNV represents a newly characterized alphanodavirus species associated with shrimp disease, distinct from previously known nodaviruses; enhanced transmission/vector adaptation – the virus efficiently infects multiple penaeid shrimp species and can be shed into pond water, supporting rapid within‑pond transmission once introduced.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Adjusted Year from 2002–2013 to 2002–2014 so that the event explicitly covers both the first observation of covert mortality disease in Chinese shrimp ponds (initially reported in 2002, with major impact from 2009) and the virological identification of CMNV as the causative agent in 2014, which is when the EPP itself was first confirmed and described in this host system. (2) Clarified the summary to distinguish early disease reports from later confirmation of CMNV, in line with reviews indicating initial CMD observations in 2002 and serious industry-wide losses since 2009, with CMNV identified in 2014. (3) Retained classification as first_global_emergence = Yes and first_detection = Yes for this event because there is no evidence of earlier confirmed CMNV infection in any host system before Chinese farmed shrimp, and the 2014 work by Zhang et al. represents the first detection and description of the virus itself. Rationale for review: the 2002 start year and continuous episode framing are supported mainly by secondary syntheses and may warrant expert confirmation against detailed Chinese surveillance data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (L. vannamei, F. chinensis, M. japonicus) and multiple wild and farm-associated crustaceans including ridgetail white prawn (Exopalaemon carinicauda), red swamp crayfish (Procambarus clarkii), swimming crabs and intertidal crabs.
Event summary: From about 2009 through the mid‑2010s, covert mortality disease intensified and became highly prevalent across China’s coastal shrimp-farming regions, with CMNV-positive shrimp and crustaceans detected in ponds from essentially all coastal provinces and recurrent crop failures. During this period, CMNV was also found at high prevalence in multiple crustacean species inhabiting ponds and adjacent waters, including ridgetail white prawn, crayfish and various crabs, revealing establishment of complex reservoir and vector networks around shrimp farms. By around 2017, studies had demonstrated vertical transmission of CMNV in Exopalaemon carinicauda and widespread infection in wild and farm-associated crustaceans, cementing CMNV as an entrenched endemic pathogen repeatedly causing severe production losses in Chinese shrimp aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued intensification and year‑round operation of shrimp farms, reuse of water, and reliance on infected seed stocks allowed persistent circulation and frequent reintroduction of CMNV into ponds; suboptimal biosecurity and lack of CMNV-specific surveillance in the early years hindered effective control; hydrological connectivity between ponds, drainage canals and coastal habitats facilitated exchange of infected reservoir species. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) – CMNV successfully infected numerous crustacean species in and around ponds, creating persistent vertebrate‑free reservoir communities; enhanced transmission/vector adaptation – high prevalence in resident species such as Exopalaemon carinicauda, combined with demonstrated vertical transmission in this host, increased environmental viral loads and ensured long‑term maintenance; geographic range expansion (inherent) – CMNV spread from initial outbreak zones to nearly all coastal shrimp-farming provinces in Eastern China, representing a major re‑emergence and intensification within the same subregion.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Set re_occurrence from Yes to No and retained re_emergence = Yes to comply with the rule that event types are generally mutually exclusive except for re_emergence co-occurring with intra/inter-continental emergence; this episode is best interpreted as re-emergence driven by expanded host range (new reservoir crustaceans, vertical transmission) and intensification within the same subregion, rather than as a separate purely external-driver re-occurrence. (2) Left the 2009–2017 year range unchanged, as it is consistent with reports that CMD/VCMD became a major problem from 2009 and that high-prevalence surveys and vertical transmission studies were conducted between 2013 and 2017. Rationale for review: although splitting the Chinese experience into a first-emergence event (2002–2014) and this subsequent re‑emergence/intensification event is defensible, experts may wish to consider whether a single, longer linked episode with a single event year (e.g. 2009–2017) would better match their outbreak-bounding conventions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Thailand [2014]; Indonesia [2014]; Malaysia [2014]; Viet Nam [2014]; India [2014]
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), other penaeid shrimp and, in some systems, farmed freshwater prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii).
Event summary: From around 2014, CMNV was detected by molecular assays in shrimp-farming systems in several Asian countries outside China, including Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam and India, often in ponds experiencing chronic mortalities or running mortality syndrome not fully explained by other agents. Subsequent surveys showed CMNV-positive shrimp and pond-associated crustaceans in multiple coastal farming regions within these countries, indicating that the virus had established local transmission cycles with ongoing low to moderate mortality and growth retardation in affected crops. By the late 2010s, VCMD/CMNV was recognized in regional disease cards, biosecurity manuals and risk assessments as an important emerging viral threat to shrimp and freshwater prawn aquaculture across South-eastern and Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transboundary movement of live shrimp and prawn broodstock and postlarvae from China and other sources, often with limited CMNV-specific screening, likely introduced the virus into hatcheries and farms in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam and India; regional trade in live crustaceans, shared coastal water bodies and limited farm-level biosecurity facilitated subsequent spread within and between national industries; co-occurrence with other major shrimp diseases (e.g. AHPND, WSSV) complicated attribution and delayed targeted management. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) – the ability of CMNV to persist in multiple crustacean hosts and environmental matrices allowed successful establishment in new tropical farming environments across South and South‑east Asia; host expansion – detection in farmed Macrobrachium rosenbergii and diverse crustaceans broadened the susceptible host community, reinforcing persistence; enhanced transmission – chronic, often subclinical infections in broodstock and postlarval supply chains enabled silent dissemination prior to overt disease expression.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Added Indonesia to the list of affected countries based on epidemiological summaries indicating CMD/VCMD problems and CMNV-positive ponds in Thailand, Indonesia, India and Ecuador, and on later genomic work noting CMNV detections in Thailand, India, Malaysia, Viet Nam and other countries since 2014. (2) Reformatted the Countries field to include approximate country-specific start years in square brackets (all set to 2014, reflecting that regional reports describe CMNV as present in these countries “since 2014” rather than providing exact first-detection years), in line with the requested convention for multi-country linked episodes. (3) Replaced an inaccessible training-manual link with more robust sources (Virus Research genomic characterization article, RT-LAMP diagnostic paper, NACA disease card, and Australian prawn import risk assessment) that collectively document spread to these Asian countries and recognition as an emerging regional disease. Rationale for review: first-detection years for individual countries are approximate and would benefit from confirmation against national reports; the assumption that these national outbreaks form a single intra-continental emergence episode driven by shared broodstock trade should also be validated.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in intensive hatchery and grow‑out systems.
Event summary: Starting around 2014, CMNV was detected in farmed whiteleg shrimp in Mexico and Ecuador, coinciding with unexplained chronic mortalities, soft-shell problems and growth retardation in intensive hatcheries and grow‑out ponds in parts of Latin America. Diagnostic investigations of disease complexes such as Las Bolitas syndrome in hatcheries, along with broader surveillance, identified CMNV RNA in affected shrimp, indicating that the virus had become established in some production clusters on both the Pacific coast of Mexico and Ecuador. By about 2020, regional scientific reviews and government risk analyses acknowledged CMNV as an emerging viral pathogen of shrimp aquaculture in the Americas and raised concern about further spread within the hemisphere.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance trade in live Litopenaeus vannamei broodstock and postlarvae from Asian and other sources into Latin American hatcheries, in the absence of CMNV-specific certification, provided plausible introduction routes; intensive monoculture of L. vannamei at high densities, frequent co-infections with other shrimp pathogens (e.g. IMNV, TSV, WSSV), and limited early awareness of CMNV in the region likely increased susceptibility and masked its contribution to disease; regional trade in seed and harvested product may have facilitated secondary dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) – CMNV’s ability to infect L. vannamei and persist in intensive production environments supported its establishment on a new continent; enhanced transmission – chronic infection, environmental stability and potential survival in chilled product streams may contribute to spread along hatchery and processing networks; possible host expansion to local wild crustaceans and other fauna, though still under investigation, could provide additional reservoirs supporting persistence in coastal ecosystems.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Reformatted the Countries field to include approximate first-detection years (Mexico [2014]; Ecuador [2014]) based on statements that CMNV-positive samples have been found in Mexico and Ecuador “since 2014” and that CMD/VCMD was documented in Latin American hatcheries in the mid‑2010s. (2) Clarified the event as a single inter-continental emergence episode capturing initial establishment of CMNV in intensive shrimp aquaculture in the Americas, rather than separate country-level events, because both introductions are plausibly linked to similar long-distance broodstock/postlarvae trade from Asia. (3) Retained classification as inter_continental_emergence = Yes, with no re_emergence or re_occurrence flags, since this is the first confirmed presence of CMNV in the South America macro‑continent rather than a resurgence in a previously affected subregion. Rationale for review: precise years and epidemiological linkage between Mexican and Ecuadorian occurrences (e.g. whether they represent independent introductions or a stepwise spread) remain uncertain and warrant expert confirmation.

Host: Wild and farm-associated fish and invertebrates including the goby Mugilogobius abei, Japanese flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), cyprinid fish such as goldfish/carp (Carassius auratus), sea cucumber (Apostichopus japonicus), large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea), crabs and other non-penaeid hosts, with later reports of infection in additional invertebrates such as bivalves.
Event summary: From 2018 onward, CMNV was detected for the first time in a widening range of non-penaeid hosts in and around shrimp-farming areas in China, beginning with natural infection of the intertidal goby Mugilogobius abei collected near affected ponds and soon followed by reports of CMNV infection in farmed Japanese flounder, cyprinid fishes, and coastal crabs. Subsequent studies documented CMNV nucleic acid and lesions in sea cucumber (Apostichopus japonicus), large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea) and other aquaculture or wild species from environments connected to shrimp production, demonstrating that the virus had spilled over across multiple animal phyla. By around 2022, experimental and field data showed that these new hosts could harbor CMNV with associated histopathological changes, implying that CMNV had undergone substantial host expansion and established additional reservoirs in coastal ecosystems adjacent to shrimp farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continuous discharge of CMNV-contaminated effluents and sediment from shrimp ponds into surrounding coastal and estuarine waters, plus physical connectivity between ponds, drainage canals and nearshore habitats, repeatedly exposed wild fish and invertebrates to high viral loads; mixed and proximate aquaculture of shrimp with fish, sea cucumbers and other species increased inter-species contact, while growing demand for polyculture systems intensified these interfaces. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) – CMNV successfully infected and replicated in new vertebrate and invertebrate hosts (e.g. gobies, Japanese flounder, cyprinids, sea cucumbers, bivalves), indicating a marked broadening of its host range beyond penaeid shrimp and pond crustaceans; enhanced transmission/vector adaptation – infection of wild fishes, echinoderms and other invertebrates created additional reservoirs and potential biological or mechanical vectors capable of reintroducing virus into shrimp ponds; increased virulence/pathogenicity in some new hosts is suggested by observed lesions in nervous, muscular and other tissues, though the full production impact in these species is still being elucidated.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Adjusted Year from 2015–2020 to 2018–2022 to align more closely with the timing of published host-jump reports: natural infection of the goby Mugilogobius abei (2018), farmed Japanese flounder (2019), sea cucumber (2021), and large yellow croaker (2022), as well as more recent evidence of CMNV in bivalves. (2) Expanded the Host description and event summary to explicitly mention key new vertebrate and invertebrate hosts documented in the literature, framing this as a major multi-phyla host expansion within Eastern Asia. (3) Updated sources to prioritize primary research articles on cross-species transmission and new host detections, while retaining one recent Aquaculture article on CMNV in bivalves as support for later host range broadening. Rationale for review: although there is strong evidence for host expansion in coastal China, the exact start year of spillover into each taxon and the magnitude of associated production losses in non-shrimp species remain uncertain and warrant further expert assessment.

Host: Humans (patients with persistent ocular hypertensive viral anterior uveitis, POH‑VAU) with frequent exposure to CMNV-infected seafood or aquatic animals, alongside the established aquatic animal hosts.
Event summary: From around 2019, ophthalmology clinics in China began to recognize a distinct form of chronic anterior uveitis with elevated intraocular pressure and progressive vision loss, later termed persistent ocular hypertensive viral anterior uveitis (POH‑VAU), in patients who often reported frequent occupational or dietary exposure to seafood and other aquatic animals but whose etiologic agent was unknown. A case–control and metagenomic investigation published in 2026 in Nature Microbiology demonstrated CMNV RNA and specific immune responses in ocular samples from 70 POH‑VAU patients and found strong statistical associations between CMNV exposure and disease, thereby linking this emerging eye condition to zoonotic infection with CMNV. Over the 2019–2023 period covered by the study, accumulating POH‑VAU cases and experimental infection data established that CMNV can infect mammalian ocular tissues and cause pathology, identifying a novel, localized human disease manifestation originating in an area where CMNV was already endemic in aquatic animals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High and sustained human exposure to CMNV through handling, processing and consumption of infected aquatic animals (especially shrimp and fish), combined with practices such as processing without eye protection and consumption of raw or undercooked seafood, likely created rare opportunities for cross-species transmission to ocular tissues; the rapid growth of intensive aquaculture producing large volumes of CMNV-infected biomass increased environmental and foodborne viral burdens in coastal communities. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) – CMNV demonstrated the capacity to infect human ocular tissues, representing a major host jump from invertebrates and fish to humans within the same geographic subregion; enhanced tissue tropism – the virus is able to establish persistent infection in the anterior chamber and associated structures, leading to chronic inflammation and ocular hypertension; this event reflects re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion (Eastern Asia) via expansion into a new host species and tissue niche, rather than a new geographic range expansion.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Reclassified this episode from first_global_emergence = Yes and first_detection = Yes to first_global_emergence = No, first_detection = No, re_emergence = Yes, to reflect that CMNV was first detected and globally emerged in farmed shrimp in China in 2014; the human POH‑VAU association represents a later host expansion and re‑emergence in a new host species within an already affected subregion, consistent with the definition of re-emergence (changes in the EPP such as host expansion). (2) Adjusted Year from 2019–2025 to 2019–2023 to align with the time window documented in the 2026 Nature Microbiology case–control study (which analyzes patients over several recent years but does not yet provide evidence for cases beyond the study period) and to avoid extrapolating incidence trends beyond published data. (3) Replaced the previous mix of Wikipedia and secondary commentary with the primary Nature Microbiology research article as the main source, supported by the associated News & Views piece and the WOAH disease card for broader context; Wikipedia is retained only as a concise secondary summary. Rationale for review: while the link between CMNV and POH‑VAU is strongly supported by the Nature Microbiology study, the broader public health impact, possible under-ascertainment of cases, and any subsequent geographic spread of human disease remain uncertain and should be monitored; classification as a re‑emergence via host expansion should be confirmed against the project’s conventions for cross-host events in EPPs listed under non-human host systems.

Host: Domestic goats (primary animal source), sheep (present but less implicated), humans (spillover cases)
Event summary: In late 1992 and early 1993, after an influenza epidemic, a very large community outbreak of Q fever occurred around the town of Panagyurishte in southern Bulgaria, with goats in their periparturient period identified as the main animal reservoir and period of intense environmental contamination. During spring 1993, human cases of atypical pneumonia and febrile respiratory illness peaked from April to June, coinciding with goat kidding and sporadic abortions, while sheep grazing further from town were considered less likely sources. The outbreak subsided after the kidding season and with implementation of control measures and changing exposure patterns, but subsequent waves in the mid‑1990s showed that Q fever remained endemic in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑communist economic and social changes in Bulgaria led to a tripling in goat numbers, closer contact between goat owners and animals, and increased consumption of raw goat milk and products, which shifted the main source of human C. burnetii infection from cattle and sheep to goats; seasonal concentration of kidding and abortions near populated areas amplified airborne exposure. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel strain was highlighted; the event is best characterized as re-occurrence driven by intensified goat husbandry and environmental aerosolization rather than a new genotype.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the major Panagyurishte outbreak described as the largest Bulgarian/European Q fever outbreak of the early 1990s, with goats as the main source and >2,000 acute respiratory cases where Q fever contributed substantially.([cureus.com](https://www.cureus.com/articles/150529-a-narrative-review-of-q-fever-in-europe?utm_source=openai))  Country (Bulgaria), subregion (Eastern Europe) and years (1992–1993) are consistent with published accounts, and classification as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because Q fever had been recognized in Bulgaria for decades.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2640784/?utm_source=openai)) No structural changes made; retained as one of the top global events.

Host: Domestic goats (including imported goats), humans (farm workers, pub patrons and community)
Event summary: In April 1993, an explosive Q fever epidemic occurred in the village of Jedľové Kostoľany in Nitra District, Slovakia, after an abortion storm in a large-capacity goat breeding center whose animals included stock imported from Bulgaria. A total of 113 persons developed Q fever, most infected indirectly when goat attendants repeatedly visited the local pub wearing contaminated work clothes, enabling aerosol spread of Coxiella burnetii to other patrons, while a smaller group acquired infection directly through occupational contact with the goats. After recognition of the outbreak, tracing of the coxiellosis epizootic in the goat herd and application of veterinary and public-health measures, no further waves of community transmission were reported from this locality.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement and trade of goats, including importation from an endemic Bulgarian herd, introduced heavily infected animals into a Slovak village; lack of hygiene barriers between farm and community (e.g. workers visiting pubs in soiled clothing) created an unusual indoor aerosol transmission setting. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not identify a novel genotype or altered virulence; the outbreak is interpreted as re-occurrence of endemic Q fever in Eastern Europe facilitated by livestock movements and social-behavioural factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Case numbers (113 human infections) and the unusual route of pub-based aerosol transmission from goat attendants’ contaminated clothing match the primary Slovak and Bulgarian reports.([cejph.szu.cz](https://cejph.szu.cz/artkey/cjp-199704-0007_An-explosive-outbreak-of-Q-fever-in-Jedlove-Kostolany-Slovakia.php?utm_source=openai))  Country, subregion and year are correct, and classification as re-occurrence (not intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because Q fever was already present in Slovakia and no new subregion or strain emergence is documented. No column changes required; event is clearly among the larger post‑1990 outbreaks.

Host: Sheep (slaughtered in open municipal abattoir, primary source), cattle (possible contributing source), humans (town residents and abattoir‑adjacent workers)
Event summary: From March to June 1996, the small Alpine town of Briançon in southeastern France experienced a large outbreak of acute Q fever with about 200 diagnosed human cases, many presenting with atypical pneumonia. Epidemiologic investigation linked illness to a municipal abattoir located in the town centre where infected sheep and cattle were slaughtered and waste was left uncovered, and helicopter traffic and local winds were thought to disperse contaminated aerosols over nearby residential areas. After the abattoir was closed or modified and infected animal waste was properly managed, incident Q fever cases declined and the urban epidemic came to an end.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Location of an open abattoir in the town centre, inadequate covering and disposal of infected sheep offal, and strong valley winds and helicopter downdrafts that favoured long-distance aerosol spread from slaughter activities to densely populated neighbourhoods. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel Coxiella genotype or host jump was reported; this event is best viewed as a re-occurrence of endemic French Q fever under high‑risk slaughter and land‑use conditions.
