Review: retain – Added as a new row because multiple reviews identify the 1996 Briançon urban/abattoir outbreak (~204 Q fever cases) as one of the largest European events in the 1990–2010 period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88923/?utm_source=openai))  France/Western Europe classification and timing (1996) follow standard UNSD groupings and outbreak reports. Treated as re-occurrence since Q fever was long endemic in France and the key drivers were abattoir siting and aerosolisation of slaughter waste, not first detection or spread to a new subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Sheep and goats grazing near town (probable main reservoirs), cattle (possible minor role), humans (residents of Etropole and nearby villages)
Event summary: In spring 2002, the mountain town of Etropole in Sofia district, central-western Bulgaria, experienced a sizeable Q fever outbreak with roughly 120 laboratory-confirmed human cases, many presenting with atypical pneumonia. Cases clustered among residents living in a valley area below pastures where flocks of sheep and goats grazed and lambed, and serological surveys in local livestock indicated substantial C. burnetii circulation in these herds. As lambing ended and flock movements and grazing near the town were restricted, new human infections declined and the outbreak resolved without evidence of spread to other Bulgarian regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Town topography in a narrow valley with prevailing winds from surrounding slopes, outdoor lambing and grazing of infected sheep and goats close to residences, and dry conditions that favoured aerosolisation of birth products and contaminated dust; these features match patterns seen in other mountainous Q fever hotspots.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235756073_Q_fever_in_humans_and_farm_animals_in_four_European_countries_1982_to_2010?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host expansion was highlighted; the event is a re-occurrence of endemic Bulgarian Q fever driven by livestock management and environmental factors.
Review: retain – Newly added because comparative analyses of Q fever in Bulgaria, France, Germany and the Netherlands list the Etropole 2002 outbreak (≈121 human cases) as one of the larger European events linked to livestock in the post‑1990 era.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235756073_Q_fever_in_humans_and_farm_animals_in_four_European_countries_1982_to_2010?utm_source=openai))  Year, location and livestock sources have been aligned with those summaries, and the event is correctly classified as re-occurrence rather than first detection or geographical emergence.

Host: Single lambing ewe and associated sheep flock at farmers’ market, humans (market visitors, stall holders and nearby residents)
Event summary: In May 2003, health authorities in Soest district, Germany, detected an unusual cluster of atypical pneumonia among visitors to a spa-town farmers’ market where a pregnant ewe had lambed in a public petting area. Subsequent investigation identified 299 notified human Q fever cases linked to this event, with risk strongly associated with time spent near the ewe’s pen and short-distance crowding around the animal. After the market ended, the flock was removed and no continued local source existed, so case numbers declined and no broader geographic spread beyond this point-source outbreak was observed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a heavily infected pregnant ewe into a crowded farmers’ market created a classic super‑spreading scenario, with lambing and heavily contaminated bedding generating high loads of C. burnetii aerosols in a confined public space; the lack of awareness of Q fever risk in this non‑occupational setting meant no respiratory protection or separation from visitors. Internal mechanisms: genotyping did not implicate a special high‑virulence strain; this is a re-occurrence event driven by extreme exposure conditions to a single infected ewe rather than by pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Added as a new row because the Soest 2003 farmers’ market outbreak with 299 notified Q fever cases is repeatedly cited as one of the largest community point‑source Q fever outbreaks in Europe and worldwide.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1618839/?utm_source=openai))  Germany/Western Europe classification and year are straightforward, and treatment as re-occurrence is appropriate since Q fever was endemic in Germany and the event reflects an intense single-source exposure, not spread to a new subregion.

Host: Sheep flock grazing and lambing on meadows near prison and urban neighbourhoods, humans (prisoners, prison staff, nearby residents and veterinary personnel)
Event summary: Between January and early March 2003, a large Q fever outbreak struck the city of Como in northern Italy, initially recognised when multiple prisoners from a local facility were hospitalised with acute pneumonia. Active case-finding identified 133 persons with acute Q fever, including inmates, guards, nearby residents and veterinary staff, and epidemiologic investigation implicated a flock of sheep that had grazed and lambed on meadows adjacent to the prison and urban area as the most likely source. After the infected flock was treated and movement and grazing near the town were curtailed, environmental contamination fell and no further waves of Q fever were detected in Como.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Grazing and lambing of infected sheep directly adjacent to densely populated urban and prison settings enabled windborne and local aerosol spread from contaminated meadows to persons with no agricultural occupation; diagnostic vigilance and serologic screening then revealed the full scale of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not indicate emergence of a new Coxiella genotype or host range; this is a re-occurrence of endemic Italian Q fever precipitated by high‑risk land use and flock management.
Review: retain – Newly added because the Como 2003 outbreak with 133 acute Q fever cases in prisoners, staff and local residents is recognised as a major post‑1990 European epidemic linked to sheep grazing and lambing near an urban area.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/1/03-0467_article?utm_source=openai))  Italy/Southern Europe assignment and classification as re-occurrence (not first detection) follow national Q fever histories; no evidence suggests inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence.

Host: Flocks of sheep and goats grazing in and around town, humans (urban residents and nearby villagers)
Event summary: From early May to early June 2004, the town of Botevgrad (Sofia district, western Bulgaria) experienced a large Q fever outbreak with 220 clinically and serologically confirmed human cases, producing attack rates of about 8 per 1,000 inhabitants in the town. Most patients had no direct contact with livestock, but flocks of sheep and goats routinely grazed along roads and in gardens within and around Botevgrad, and a major dust storm early in May likely dispersed contaminated particles over residential areas. Following public‑health advisories, restriction of small-ruminant grazing inside town limits, and the natural end of the lambing season, incidence fell and the urban epidemic was considered over by mid‑June.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of sheep and goats grazing and lambing in and around an urban municipality, combined with a documented dust storm, created conditions for long-range airborne spread of C. burnetii from infected small ruminants into the town; most cases occurred in people without occupational animal contact.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26331870_An_outbreak_of_Q_fever_in_Bulgaria?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host expansion was reported; the event represents a dramatic re-occurrence of Q fever in an already endemic Bulgarian focus driven by land use and meteorological conditions.
Review: retain – Added as a new major event because the Botevgrad 2004 outbreak (220 cases) is described as Bulgaria’s largest Q fever epidemic in the preceding decades and is widely cited in comparative European analyses.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26331870_An_outbreak_of_Q_fever_in_Bulgaria?utm_source=openai))  Bulgaria/Eastern Europe classification and 2004 timing are consistent with outbreak reports; re-occurrence is appropriate as the region had long-standing Q fever activity and this episode did not involve spread to a new continent or subregion.

Host: Domestic sheep (flock grazing and lambing near town), humans (nearby residents and exposed persons)
Event summary: In June 2005, a large Q fever outbreak was identified in the Jena suburb of Winzerla, Germany, when residents living adjacent to a meadow developed febrile respiratory illness later confirmed as C. burnetii infection. Investigation traced the source to an infected flock of sheep that had been grazing and lambing on pasture bordering residential areas, leading to massive environmental contamination with birth products, dust and aerosols carrying the bacterium, and a total of 331 human cases were reported. After removal or relocation of the flock, environmental decontamination and public health messaging, the outbreak declined and new cases subsided.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density sheep grazing and lambing very close to a suburban residential area, combined with dry and windy conditions, enabled windborne dispersal of contaminated aerosols over the town; lack of prior awareness of Q fever risk in suburban sheep farming allowed this practice to continue until after the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain, resistance, or host expansion was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence driven by environmental exposure and land‑use patterns rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This row is consistent with detailed German reports describing the 2005 Jena-Winzerla outbreak (331 reported cases) as one of the largest Q fever epidemics in Europe, with sheep grazing and lambing immediately adjacent to housing as the main driver.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870892/?utm_source=openai))  Continent/subregion mapping and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; no corrections needed.

Countries: Israel [2005, central Israel boarding high school]
Host: Humans (boarding high school students and staff); external animal reservoir not fully defined but likely regional livestock or other mammals, with contaminated aerosols recirculated indoors via air-conditioning
Event summary: In June 2005, numerous febrile respiratory illnesses were reported among 322 students and employees of a boarding high school in an urban area of central Israel, and subsequent investigation identified a large Q fever outbreak that had begun about two weeks earlier. Overall, 187 of 303 interviewed individuals reported compatible illness and C. burnetii infection was serologically confirmed in 144 of 164 persons tested, with risk highest among boarding students and those dining regularly in the school cafeteria. Environmental sampling demonstrated C. burnetii DNA in dust from the dining hall air-conditioning system, suggesting that contaminated aerosols from an external animal source were drawn into and recirculated within the building; after the summer break and cleaning/disinfection of the ventilation system, no further school-associated cases were documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density boarding-school setting with shared dining facilities, combined with contamination of the air-conditioning system that likely drew in and recirculated aerosols originating from infected animals in the surrounding region, allowed extensive indoor exposure of susceptible students and staff; awareness of Q fever risk in this fully urban context was initially low.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20415568/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: although later genotyping work in Israel has identified local Coxiella strains, this outbreak is not clearly driven by a novel genotype or host expansion, and is best classified as a re-occurrence of endemic Q fever presenting in an unusual urban/indoor transmission setting.
Review: retain – Added because the central Israel boarding-school outbreak (187 illnesses, 144 serologically confirmed Q fever infections) is a well-documented large epidemic and is repeatedly cited as a key example of urban/indoor Q fever transmission.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20415568/?utm_source=openai))  Continent and subregion (Asia/Western Asia) align with UNSD groupings; given long-standing endemicity of Q fever in Israel, classification as re-occurrence rather than first detection or inter-continental emergence is appropriate.

Countries: Netherlands [2005 – first dairy goat abortions; 2007-2010 – large epidemic]
Host: Dairy goats (primary source), dairy sheep (minor role), cattle (background reservoir), humans (large community outbreak)
Event summary: From 2005, C. burnetii was first diagnosed as a cause of abortion waves on Dutch dairy goat farms, and between 2005 and 2007 abortion storms were confirmed on multiple large dairy goat and a few dairy sheep farms in the southeastern Netherlands. In 2007 a community Q fever outbreak was recognized, which evolved into the world’s largest recorded Q fever epidemic between 2007 and 2010, with about 4,000 notified human cases, strongly clustered around intensive dairy goat farms with abortion problems and PCR‑positive bulk tank milk. After 2009–2010, a comprehensive control programme including mandatory vaccination of dairy goats and dairy sheep, movement restrictions, bulk tank milk PCR surveillance, and culling of pregnant animals on infected farms led to steep declines in both animal shedding and human cases, and the epidemic was brought under control by around 2011–2012, though endemic circulation in livestock persisted at lower levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of the Dutch dairy goat sector following changes in European cattle milk quotas and prior livestock disease crises led to very large herds kept in close confinement, often near densely populated villages; high stocking density and concentrated kidding seasons resulted in massive environmental contamination with C. burnetii in barns and surrounding areas; low baseline human seroprevalence created a highly susceptible human population, and meteorological conditions facilitated windborne dispersal of contaminated aerosols into nearby communities. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing showed that a single predominant C. burnetii genotype was responsible for most cases in dairy goats, sheep and humans in the epidemic area, consistent with a clonal expansion of an outbreak strain with efficient transmission in goats and to humans, representing a re-emergence driven by genotype amplification and enhanced transmission in an intensified production system rather than initial introduction of the species to the region.
Review: retain – This row accurately reflects the 2007–2010 Dutch epidemic, which all major reviews agree is the largest Q fever outbreak ever recorded with >4,000 notified human cases and extensive abortion storms in dairy goats.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0399077X14000535?utm_source=openai))  Western Europe subregion, time span and emphasis on intensive dairy‑goat farming as the driver are correct. Classifying this as re-emergence (clonal expansion of a predominant genotype in an already endemic country) is consistent with molecular epidemiology papers; no corrections to emergence type are required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (slaughterhouse and animal-market workers, animal skin processors), dromedary camels, imported cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In 1994, a cluster of severe hemorrhagic fever cases occurred among abattoir workers and livestock traders in the United Arab Emirates, leading to investigation of a suspected viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak. Over 1994–1995, more than a dozen human cases with high case-fatality were confirmed as Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and linked epidemiologically to slaughtering or handling imported livestock infected with CCHFV. Intensified infection-prevention measures in slaughterhouses and better control of animal imports and ticks curtailed the outbreak, after which only sporadic cases were reported in the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale importation of cattle, sheep and goats from CCHF-endemic countries in Asia and Africa for slaughter, combined with inadequate tick control and poor abattoir biosafety, created intense exposure of workers to infected animal blood and Hyalomma ticks; earlier nosocomial transmission in Dubai in 1979 shows the virus was already present but under-recognized in the country. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate circulation of existing CCHFV lineages rather than a novel strain, and the event is best explained by amplification of endemic virus in livestock under high-intensity trade and slaughter conditions, increasing spillover risk to humans.
Review: Decision: retain (with reclassification). CCHF was first reported in the UAE in a nosocomial outbreak in Dubai in 1979, so the 1994–1995 abattoir-associated episode cannot be coded as first_detection; first_detection has been set to false and re_occurrence to true while keeping other emergence-type flags as no. The year range, country (United Arab Emirates), subregion (Western Asia) and occupational focus are well supported by outbreak investigations, and the sources are appropriate, but this event should be flagged as borderline if a very strict top‑10-by-impact filter is later enforced because of its moderate case numbers.

Host: Humans (ostrich abattoir workers), ostriches, cattle, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In October 1996, an outbreak of acute hemorrhagic fever occurred among workers at an ostrich abattoir in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape Province, South Africa, where CCHFV was already known to circulate in livestock and ticks. Seventeen abattoir workers developed compatible illness, with at least one death, and investigations linked infection to handling viremic ostriches and possibly crushing infected Hyalomma ticks during slaughter and processing. Control measures including temporary closure of slaughter operations, improved personal protective equipment, and stricter tick control on ostriches and other livestock ended the outbreak, and subsequent years saw only sporadic occupational cases in South Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of commercial ostrich farming and export in the Klein Karoo increased human contact with ticks and blood from CCHFV-infected birds and other livestock; limited awareness and insufficient protective measures in abattoirs heightened risk. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects amplification of an established South African CCHFV lineage in ostriches and ticks rather than a novel strain, with occupational exposure and high tick burdens driving re-occurrence in a known endemic focus.
Review: Decision: review (borderline for top‑10). This row accurately represents the 1996 ostrich-abattoir outbreak in Oudtshoorn, including timing, location (South Africa, Southern Africa subregion), host range and classification as re_occurrence in an already endemic country, and the cited WHO and South African sources are appropriate. However, with 17 human cases it is smaller than several later multi‑province outbreaks (e.g. Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, Mauritania), so it may fall below the ten most impactful global events, although it remains epidemiologically important for the animal host system and ostrich industry.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (rural residents, healthcare workers, slaughterhouse workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In June 1999, clusters of severe hemorrhagic fever were recognized in Sistan and Baluchestan Province in southeastern Iran, triggering investigations that confirmed Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in an area where sporadic human and animal infections had been reported since the 1970s but no large outbreak had been documented. Between 1999 and the early 2000s, hundreds of suspected and confirmed cases, including nosocomial clusters and infections among butchers and animal handlers across several provinces, were reported, making this the first major nationally recognized CCHF epidemic in Iran. Expanded surveillance, public health education, hospital infection-control measures and veterinary tick control gradually reduced incidence after the early 2000s, though the virus remained endemic with recurring human and animal infections in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing but under-recognized circulation of CCHFV in livestock and ticks, increased animal movement across the Iran–Pakistan–Afghanistan borders, and poor infection control in rural hospitals led to spillover and nosocomial amplification; enhanced laboratory capacity and surveillance converted previously cryptic transmission into a documented epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies place Iranian strains mainly within the Asia-1 lineage and do not indicate a major novel variant driving the surge; the episode is best interpreted as a large re-occurrence in an endemic system fueled primarily by external drivers rather than substantial viral change.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections). National and provincial data show sporadic CCHF infections in humans and livestock in Iran from the 1970s onward, with 1999 marking the first large, multi-province outbreak rather than the first detection; accordingly, first_detection has been set to false and re_occurrence to true, and the narrative has been revised to remove the claim that only ticks and livestock were previously infected. The country, subregion (Southern Asia), time window (1999–2004), scale (hundreds of cases) and external drivers are consistent with primary Iranian and regional sources, justifying inclusion as one of the most impactful CCHF episodes.

Host: Humans (rural residents, agricultural workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In 1999, an outbreak of severe febrile illness with hemorrhagic manifestations occurred in Stavropol Territory in southern European Russia, resulting in about 65 CCHF cases and 6 deaths and representing the first large, laboratory-confirmed CCHF outbreak reported from this region after several decades without recognized disease. During 1999–2000 and subsequent years, additional cases were reported from adjacent regions including Rostov, Astrakhan, Volgograd and Kalmykia, indicating establishment of new endemic foci in southern Russia. Intensified tick-control campaigns in livestock, public education and better surveillance mitigated case numbers over time, though hundreds of cases continued to occur sporadically in 1999–2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Agricultural development, increased livestock grazing and human encroachment into steppe and semi-desert habitats favored Hyalomma tick expansion and human exposure; cross-border livestock movements from neighboring endemic areas likely introduced CCHFV into new Russian territories. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses show Russian strains grouped within the Europe 1 lineage, indicating geographic range expansion of known genotypes into new ecological zones rather than the emergence of a novel lineage.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections). Because CCHF was recognized in Crimea and other parts of the former Soviet Union long before 1999, the Stavropol outbreak cannot be considered first_detection; I set first_detection to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed re_emergence, while keeping the emphasis on renewed activity after a prolonged lull in this territory. The year span (1999–2000), location in southern European Russia (Eastern Europe subregion), and approximate magnitude are in line with WHO outbreak reports and Russian surveillance data, supporting its inclusion as a major re-activation and geographic expansion event.

Host: Humans (rural residents, family contacts, healthcare workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In spring and summer 2001, Kosovo (then part of Yugoslavia/Serbia) experienced a notable outbreak of CCHF, with 69 suspected cases, 18 confirmed or clinically compatible infections, and 6 deaths concentrated in rural areas. The outbreak originated in villages where residents had close contact with livestock and ticks, and spread included nosocomial and household transmission among caregivers and health staff. Enhanced surveillance, barrier nursing and public education on tick avoidance and safe handling of livestock and patients ended the outbreak by late summer, although sporadic cases and smaller clusters continued to occur in later years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High Hyalomma tick densities in pastoral areas, close contact with cattle and small ruminants, and limited infection-control practices in local hospitals allowed virus maintained in livestock and ticks to spill over repeatedly and spread within households and healthcare facilities. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analysis of Kosovo strains indicated continuity with long-established Balkan CCHFV lineages, and the event is best interpreted as a large resurgence in a known endemic focus rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Decision: retain (with minor source cleanup). This row correctly captures the size, timing and setting of the 2001 Kosovo outbreak and appropriately classifies it as re_occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence in a long-recognized Balkan focus. I recommend replacing the earlier Italian-language Wikipedia citation with primary descriptions from Emerging Infectious Diseases and related reviews, as done here, but otherwise the event is well supported and merits inclusion as one of the more substantial European CCHF episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (farmers, animal handlers, healthcare workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: Beginning in 2002, Türkiye detected its first recognized CCHF cases in the Kelkit Valley region of north-central Anatolia, initially as sporadic severe febrile illnesses among rural residents and animal handlers, with virologic confirmation in 2003. Over 2002–2008, a rapidly expanding epidemic produced more than 1,800 confirmed cases by 2007 and over 3,000 by 2008, with a case-fatality rate around 5%, and the virus became endemic across multiple provinces, with most cases occurring in spring and summer among persons exposed to ticks or livestock. Following the establishment of a national surveillance system, clinical guidelines and public health campaigns emphasizing tick avoidance and safe animal handling, incidence stabilized at lower but persistent levels, making Türkiye one of the world’s major CCHF foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of livestock grazing in tick-infested hilly regions, increased human interaction with Hyalomma-infested cattle and small ruminants, and limited early awareness of CCHF in the medical community facilitated rapid amplification of infection; occupational exposures among farmers and healthcare workers further propagated the epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Turkish CCHFV strains belong to the Europe-1 lineage, closely related to Balkan viruses, consistent with geographic range expansion and establishment of a large endemic focus; seroprevalence and molecular data suggest long-standing but previously under-recognized circulation that intensified under changing land-use and climate conditions, so this episode is best viewed as the first detected national epidemic driven mainly by eco-epidemiologic change rather than a novel viral genotype.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections). Türkiye’s 2002–2008 epidemic is clearly one of the largest CCHF events worldwide and should be kept, but I corrected the emergence coding: intra_continental_emergence is set to false because Türkiye lies in Western Asia where CCHF was already endemic, and re_emergence is set to false so the event is classified solely as first_detection at national level, consistent with the rule that types are generally mutually exclusive. I also replaced the earlier specific case/death figures with wording that reflects national surveillance totals (over 1,800 confirmed cases by 2007 and >3,000 by 2008) to avoid understating the magnitude.

Host: Humans (urban residents, healthcare workers, family caregivers), goats and other small ruminants, Hyalomma and other ticks
Event summary: In February 2003, a woman from Nouakchott who had recently butchered a goat was hospitalized with severe hemorrhagic fever in Mauritania and infected multiple relatives and healthcare workers, revealing a nosocomial outbreak of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the capital. Subsequent investigation identified additional community-acquired and hospital-linked cases for a total of about 38 patients with an overall case-fatality ratio near 30%, most of them urban residents but epidemiologically linked to contact with infected livestock or their tissues. Implementation of barrier nursing, heightened clinical awareness, and tick and animal surveillance around slaughterhouses halted the outbreak by late August, although CCHFV has since caused sporadic human cases in Mauritania.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Slaughter of viremic small ruminants in and around Nouakchott, limited veterinary oversight of urban livestock marketing and holding areas, and lack of basic infection-prevention and control in the referral hospital enabled efficient transmission from an animal-associated index case to healthcare workers, family members and other patients. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses grouped outbreak viruses within an established Africa-3 lineage previously detected in Mauritanian ticks and earlier human cases, indicating that this was a major re-occurrence of an endemic strain rather than emergence of a new genotype, with urbanization and animal-movement patterns acting as key external drivers.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). The 2003 Nouakchott outbreak, with roughly 38 cases and high case-fatality and extensive nosocomial transmission, is the most impactful documented CCHF episode in West Africa during the period and was missing from the original dataset. I classified it as re_occurrence rather than first_detection because the first confirmed human CCHF case in Mauritania occurred in 1983, and assigned it to Western Africa (Mauritania [2003]) with hosts spanning humans, small ruminants and ticks, in line with WHO and Emerging Infectious Diseases reports.

Host: Humans (rural residents, butchers, healthcare workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In 2008, Afghanistan reported its first well-documented multifocal CCHF outbreak, with human cases occurring in several areas of Herat and other provinces and involving rural residents, butchers and health workers exposed to livestock and ticks. The outbreak emerged against a background of previously sporadic or poorly documented CCHF activity, and was recognized through enhanced surveillance prompted by neighboring epidemics in Iran and Pakistan. Targeted public health interventions, including awareness campaigns before religious festivals involving mass animal slaughter and improved infection control in hospitals, reduced transmission after the initial peak, though the virus has since remained endemic with intermittent outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensified livestock movements and informal cross-border trade with Iran and Pakistan, combined with low veterinary and public health infrastructure in post-conflict Afghanistan, likely facilitated introduction and wider dissemination of CCHFV; religious festivals and backyard slaughtering increased direct exposure to viremic animals. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses place Afghan strains within the Asia-1 clade circulating regionally, indicating geographic expansion and amplification of existing lineages rather than novel genotype emergence.
Review: Decision: retain (with minor correction). The 2008 Herat-centred multifocal outbreak is correctly placed in Afghanistan (Southern Asia) with a realistic description of hosts and drivers and is appropriately coded as a high-impact resurgence. I have set intra_continental_emergence from true to false because Afghanistan belongs to the Southern Asia subregion, where CCHF was already established in Pakistan and Iran; this event is better characterized as re_occurrence within an endemic subregion rather than spread into a new subregion.

Host: Humans (rural index case, treating physician, nurse), cattle, buffalo, goats, sheep, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: In late 2010 and January 2011, a cluster of severe hemorrhagic fever cases in a tertiary hospital in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, including a rural index patient, the treating physician and a nurse, was investigated and confirmed as Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, representing the first recognized human CCHF outbreak in India. Subsequent field and laboratory studies detected CCHFV RNA and antibodies in Hyalomma ticks and domestic animals (cattle, buffalo, goats, sheep) around the patient’s village, indicating previously undetected enzootic circulation in western India. Aggressive infection-prevention measures, contact tracing and awareness campaigns around abattoirs and healthcare facilities limited the outbreak to a small nosocomial cluster, although sporadic cases and further outbreaks have since been reported in Gujarat and neighbouring states.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Undetected circulation of CCHFV in livestock and ticks in western India, combined with unprotected clinical care of a severely ill index patient and lack of awareness of CCHF among clinicians, facilitated nosocomial transmission to healthcare workers. Internal mechanisms: Viral sequences from Gujarat clustered within the Asia-1 lineage shared with Pakistan and Iran, suggesting cross-border introduction and local establishment of an existing genotype rather than emergence of a new strain; the key novelty is geographic range expansion and first detection in India.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). The 2010–2011 nosocomial outbreak in Ahmedabad was the first confirmed human CCHF event in India and documented established infection in local livestock and ticks; given India’s size and its role in regional livestock trade, omitting this event would leave a major gap in the depiction of south-Asian range expansion. I coded it as first_detection at national level without intra- or inter-continental flags and specified hosts across humans, cattle, buffalo, small ruminants and Hyalomma ticks, consistent with outbreak and molecular reports.

Host: Humans (butchers, animal handlers, healthcare workers, rural residents), cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, camels, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: CCHF has been recognized in Pakistan since 1976, but from 2012 to 2013 the country experienced one of its largest and most geographically widespread episodes, with around 140–200 human cases and more than 30 deaths reported nationally, and outbreaks affecting multiple provinces including Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Sindh, Islamabad Capital Territory and Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The episode coincided with intensive movements and slaughter of livestock associated with Eid-ul-Adha and increased trade through porous borders with Afghanistan and Iran, leading to clusters among butchers, animal traders and healthcare workers; WHO and national authorities described the 2012–2013 activity as among Pakistan’s worst CCHF outbreaks to date. Strengthened surveillance, issuance of national CCHF guidelines and targeted risk communication to high-risk occupational groups helped control the surge, but CCHF has remained entrenched with recurrent seasonal spikes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic CCHFV in livestock and ticks, combined with heightened animal movements and informal slaughter around religious festivals, poor biosafety in abattoirs and tanneries, and suboptimal infection prevention in health facilities, drove re-occurring outbreaks and broad geographic spread; cross-border livestock trade with Afghanistan and Iran further seeded high-risk areas. Internal mechanisms: Available genetic data suggest continued circulation of Asia-1 lineages with some diversity but no single novel genotype explaining the surge; the episode reflects amplification of existing strains under socio-economic and cultural drivers rather than a distinct new viral variant.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2012–2013 period in Pakistan produced one of the country’s largest documented CCHF surges, with multi-province spread and high case-fatality described by WHO EMRO and several national analyses, and clearly qualifies as a major re-occurrence episode. The geography (Southern Asia, Pakistan), host spectrum and classification as re_occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence are appropriate, and the cited WHO and peer-reviewed sources provide a solid evidentiary basis.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (hikers, rural residents, healthcare workers), wild ungulates (e.g. deer), livestock (cattle, sheep), Hyalomma ticks, migratory birds
Event summary: In August 2016, Spain reported its first two autochthonous human CCHF cases in the province of Ávila, Castile-León—a hiker likely infected by a tick bite and a secondary case in a nurse who cared for the index patient—marking the first recognized clinical CCHF infections in Spain and in south-western Europe. Subsequent surveillance detected CCHFV RNA and antibodies in Hyalomma ticks, wild ungulates and livestock in several Spanish regions, and sporadic additional human cases were reported between 2013 and 2021, confirming that the virus had established new foci on the Iberian Peninsula. Implementation of enhanced tick and wildlife surveillance, occupational guidance for farmers and hunters, and hospital preparedness limited human case numbers, but ecological establishment of CCHFV in local tick–host systems suggests a durable range expansion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Northward and westward expansion of Hyalomma ticks, possibly facilitated by climate warming and land-use changes, along with introduction of infected ticks via migratory birds and livestock trade from endemic African and eastern Mediterranean regions, enabled CCHFV to colonize Iberian wildlife and livestock. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic studies show Spanish viral genomes belong to lineages closely related to African and Balkan strains, with evidence of reassortment events, indicating that long-distance dispersal and genetic mixing have produced novel segment combinations suited to local tick and host communities, supporting classification as re-emergence through geographic range expansion and reassortment.
Review: Decision: retain (with minor correction). Spain’s 2016–2021 experience—first autochthonous human cases in Spain and south‑western Europe, followed by demonstration of established CCHFV foci in ticks, wildlife and livestock and several additional human cases—is highly impactful as a westward range expansion and warrants inclusion. To align with the rule that emergence types are generally mutually exclusive, I set re_occurrence from true to false while retaining first_detection and re_emergence as true, reflecting that this is both the first recognized national detection and a re-emergence driven by reassortant genotypes in a new part of Southern Europe; geography and sources from ECDC, Viruses and EID remain appropriate.

Host: Humans (housewives, butchers, livestock breeders, rural and peri-urban residents), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event summary: From early 2022, Iraq experienced an unprecedented surge of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, with 212 cases (97 confirmed, 27 deaths) reported by late May 2022 and more than 380 confirmed cases and over 100 deaths recorded nationally in 2022, far exceeding previous yearly totals. Cases occurred across at least 13 governorates, with nearly half of confirmed patients from Dhi Qar and many working as butchers, livestock breeders or housewives in close contact with cattle, sheep and goats and tick-infested animal barns. Intensified surveillance, vector control on livestock, public risk-communication campaigns around Eid-ul-Adha slaughtering and improved hospital infection-prevention measures reduced incidence after the 2022–2023 peak, but CCHF remains endemic and Iraq continues to report high numbers of suspected and confirmed cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense livestock populations around household compounds, widespread Hyalomma tick infestation, informal slaughtering practices and limited veterinary and public-health infrastructure—exacerbated by economic hardship and climatic conditions favouring ticks—created ideal conditions for explosive amplification of CCHFV and broad geographic spread; religious festivals with mass animal slaughter further increased exposure. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence data indicate circulation of multiple existing CCHFV lineages rather than a single novel strain, so this episode is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence in an endemic country driven primarily by ecological and socio-economic factors.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). The 2022–2023 epidemic in Iraq produced several hundred confirmed CCHF cases and more than 100 deaths across many governorates and is described by WHO and regional analyses as the largest recorded outbreak in Iraq and the Eastern Mediterranean Region, so it clearly belongs among the most impactful global events. I coded it as re_occurrence in Western Asia (Iraq [2022]) without intra- or inter-continental flags, because CCHF has been endemic in Iraq since 1979 and current evidence points to ecological and behavioural drivers rather than a new viral genotype as the main cause of the surge.

Host: Mixed livestock (piglets, calves, lambs, goats) on traditional farms
Event summary: In 1993, a cross‑sectional parasitological survey of livestock in Trinidad and Tobago documented Cryptosporidium oocysts in calves, lambs, goat kids and piglets on multiple smallholder farms, providing the first systematic evidence of cryptosporidial infection in farm animals in the country. The study showed that infection occurred across species and age groups, indicating established environmental contamination and ongoing transmission on traditional mixed farms rather than a single explosive outbreak. Although no specific control campaign followed, the findings highlighted Cryptosporidium as an unrecognized endemic problem in Caribbean livestock and a potential zoonotic reservoir for human infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional mixed‑species farming with close confinement of young stock, shared housing and limited hygiene likely facilitated faecal contamination of pens and water sources, supporting sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: High environmental robustness and low infectious dose of C. parvum oocysts allowed maintenance of infection cycles across multiple juvenile host species in the absence of targeted control.
Review: review: Keep this event as the earliest systematic documentation of Cryptosporidium infection in livestock in Trinidad and Tobago (and one of the first for Caribbean livestock), which fits the “first detection” category at national/subregional scale. The original second URL pointed to an Estonian calf‑cryptosporidiosis thesis and has been replaced by the AGRIS record for Kaminjolo et al. 1993; PubMed 8408755 is likely the corresponding Veterinary Parasitology article but could not be fully inspected because of reCAPTCHA. Year, geography and host description match secondary summaries, but the event should be rechecked against the full paper before final acceptance as a top‑tier emergence event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Neonatal dairy calves
Event summary: Around 2010, veterinary investigations in the Metropolitan Region (Santiago) of Chile documented Cryptosporidium spp., later confirmed as C. parvum, in diarrhoeic neonatal dairy calves, with a high proportion of infected animals among scouring calves on affected farms. The study concluded that C. parvum was a major parasitic agent in neonatal calf diarrhoea on Chilean dairy farms, building on an earlier initial report of Cryptosporidium infection in Chilean cattle rather than representing the first occurrence. Although no specific nationwide control programme followed, the findings increased awareness of cryptosporidiosis among Chilean veterinarians and producers and encouraged its inclusion in routine diagnostic panels for calf scours.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing intensification of dairies in central Chile, with close housing of neonates and accumulation of faecal contamination in calving and calf pens, favoured faecal–oral transmission. Internal mechanisms: Efficient C. parvum transmission in highly susceptible neonatal calves, often in the context of mixed infections with other enteropathogens, underpinned outbreak‑scale morbidity; no new subtype or resistance phenotype was highlighted.
Review: review: This row should be kept as an important South American example of neonatal calf disease due to C. parvum, but its event type and narrative required correction. The underlying paper explicitly notes that the first report of Cryptosporidium infection in Chilean cattle was by Gorman et al., so this 2010 study is not a first_detection event; the type has been reclassified to re_occurrence in an already affected country. The summary has been rephrased to remove claims of being the first national report while still capturing its role in defining C. parvum as a major neonatal diarrhoea agent in Chile. Geography and sources appear appropriate, but the event is probably of lower global impact than the largest Chinese and Indian outbreaks and should be reviewed for possible deprioritisation if a strict top‑10 list is enforced.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy and dairy‑beef calves with diarrhoea across multiple farms
Event summary: In the late 2000s and early 2010s, a cross‑sectional study of 597 diarrhoeic calves from 84 Australian dairy and dairy‑beef properties found that C. parvum was among the most common enteric pathogens detected, confirming that cryptosporidiosis was a major contributor to calf scours nationally. Many enrolled farms were experiencing multi‑pathogen diarrhoea episodes with substantial morbidity, dehydration and growth setbacks in pre‑weaned calves, implying significant cumulative production losses even if herd‑level mortality was usually modest. The study prompted broader recognition of Cryptosporidium as a key endemic pathogen in Australian calf health, with subsequent emphasis on hygiene, colostrum management and strategic prophylaxis (e.g. halofuginone) on high‑risk farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of dairy and dairy‑beef calf‑rearing systems, high stocking densities, group housing of neonates and imperfect hygiene in calving and calf pens created high environmental oocyst loads and exposure. Internal mechanisms: The high infectivity and environmental resilience of C. parvum, together with frequent coinfection with rotavirus, coronavirus and enterotoxigenic E. coli, drove recurrent scours outbreaks across farms; no specific novel subtype was singled out.
Review: retain: No structural or classification changes were made to this event. The multicentre Australian study documents widespread C. parvum‑associated diarrhoea across 84 farms and hundreds of calves and is widely cited as evidence that cryptosporidiosis is a major endemic production and welfare issue in Oceania’s dairy sector. Event coding as a re_occurrence (rather than first_detection or inter/intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate, and the geography and sources match the underlying Australian Veterinary Journal article.

Host: Pre‑weaned dairy calves on a large dairy farm in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region (north‑western China)
Event summary: In October 2013, a large dairy farm in the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region of north‑western China experienced a devastating outbreak of neonatal calf diarrhoea in which essentially all 396 pre‑weaned calves developed severe watery diarrhoea and 356 died despite treatment. Molecular investigation of faecal samples showed that nearly all infected young calves carried C. parvum, and all C. parvum isolates were identified as the gp60 subtype IIdA15G1, whereas older animals on the farm harboured other, largely non‑pathogenic Cryptosporidium species. The outbreak subsided only after replacement of affected cohorts and improvements in calf management and hygiene, and it is widely cited as the first major bovine cryptosporidiosis outbreak caused by subtype IIdA15G1 in China and one of the most lethal calf cryptosporidiosis episodes reported worldwide.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of large‑scale dairy operations in semi‑arid north‑west China with high densities of young calves, limited isolation of sick animals and heavy faecal contamination of calf housing created ideal conditions for explosive faecal–oral transmission. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and dominance of the highly pathogenic C. parvum subtype IIdA15G1 in very young calves led to exceptionally high oocyst shedding and severe villous atrophy, driving high case‑fatality; the subtype is now recognized as an important virulent lineage in Chinese cattle.
Review: review: This is a newly added event capturing the 2013 Ningxia outbreak, in which 356 of 396 pre‑weaned calves reportedly died, making it clearly one of the most impactful bovine cryptosporidiosis episodes globally. It is coded as re_emergence because it involves a highly pathogenic subtype (IIdA15G1) causing a severe outbreak in a region where Cryptosporidium was already present, not a first detection. Geography and timing are taken from Cui et al. 2014; details of management changes and exact case counts should be checked against the full Parasites & Vectors article before final inclusion, but the event almost certainly belongs among the top ~10 emergence events for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Calves 30–45 days old (approx. 400‑head cohort) on a large beef‑type herd in southern Rio Grande do Sul
Event summary: In 2014, a large beef‑type herd in southern Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, reported an outbreak of severe diarrhoea in a cohort of about 400 calves aged 30–45 days, of which 35 became clinically ill and 16 died. Affected calves were born weak and soon developed profuse yellow diarrhoea, progressive weight loss, dehydration and depression, with death typically 10–15 days after onset of signs; necropsy and histopathology revealed villous atrophy and Cryptosporidium stages adherent to enterocytes. The episode led the authors to warn of cryptosporidiosis as a primary cause of diarrhoea and economic loss in beef calves in southern Brazil and to recommend management and hygiene measures to reduce environmental contamination and protect animal and public health.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Calving and early rearing of large numbers of calves in contaminated pastures and corrals, with limited ability to separate sick from healthy animals, likely increased environmental oocyst load and exposure intensity. Internal mechanisms: Heavy intestinal infection with Cryptosporidium spp. in naïve calves produced severe villous damage and malabsorptive diarrhoea, and the lack of effective specific therapy for cryptosporidiosis in this setting contributed to the high fatality proportion; no novel genotype was singled out, so the event is treated as a severe re_occurrence in an already endemic region.
Review: review: Added to capture a well‑documented South American outbreak in which 35 of 400 calves fell ill and 16 died, a substantial loss for a single beef herd and one of the clearer high‑mortality calf cryptosporidiosis events outside China. Event type is coded as re_occurrence because Cryptosporidium was already known in Brazilian cattle; the outbreak appears driven by management and exposure rather than emergence of a new subtype. The sources (Pesquisa Veterinária Brasileira article and its PDF) directly describe the episode; details such as exact herd type and any concurrent pathogens should be checked on full‑text review, but the event likely merits retention among major emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Neonatal dairy calves in peri‑urban Punjab (Ludhiana)
Event summary: Between the early 2010s and mid‑2010s, veterinarians in peri‑urban Ludhiana, Punjab, investigated 17 outbreaks of severe neonatal calf diarrhoea on small and medium‑sized dairies, where C. parvum, often together with other enteropathogens, was identified as a key causal agent. The outbreaks involved high morbidity among unweaned calves, with profuse watery diarrhoea, dehydration and substantial mortality, contributing to heavy economic losses for affected dairy farmers. Control measures centred on improved colostrum management, hygiene, and calf housing, but recurrent outbreaks underscored the entrenchment of cryptosporidiosis in intensifying peri‑urban dairy systems in northern India.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of peri‑urban dairy farming around Ludhiana, characterized by overcrowded calf housing, poor sanitation, and inconsistent colostrum feeding, created high susceptibility and exposure. Internal mechanisms: Heavy C. parvum oocyst shedding and environmental persistence, often in combination with rotavirus, coronavirus, Salmonella and E. coli, amplified disease severity and outbreak size; no specific novel genotype was identified, so the event is treated as a severe re_occurrence in a known endemic area.
Review: retain: This multi‑farm series of 17 outbreaks in peri‑urban Punjab clearly documents heavy calf mortality and substantial economic loss attributable to C. parvum in combination with other enteropathogens, and it is one of the few detailed descriptions of repeated large‑scale outbreaks in South Asia. The event appropriately remains coded as re_occurrence in a long‑affected region, and the country, subregion and sources match the BMC Veterinary Research article. No structural changes were made, so the row can be retained as a major emergence event.

Host: Neonatal dairy calves on a large industrial dairy farm (Jiangsu Province)
Event summary: From January to April 2016, a large industrial dairy farm in Jiangsu Province, East China, experienced a catastrophic outbreak of severe diarrhoea in over 400 neonatal calves, of which approximately 360 died despite treatment. Investigation showed that 73 of 79 Cryptosporidium‑positive calves were infected with C. parvum, and all C. parvum isolates belonged to the gp60 subtype IIdA19G1, with other common enteric pathogens unable to explain the pattern of disease. Control was eventually achieved through improved hygiene, isolation of scouring calves and adjustments in colostrum and housing management, and the outbreak is considered the first major bovine cryptosporidiosis epizootic caused by subtype IIdA19G1 in China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density housing of very young calves, persistent contamination of calving and calf pens, and absence of effective specific prophylaxis allowed rapid spread between cohorts on this large farm. Internal mechanisms: The highly pathogenic C. parvum IIdA19G1 subtype, with very high oocyst shedding and strong association with watery diarrhoea, represents novel strain/genotype emergence in Chinese dairy calves and underpins the classification of this episode as re_emergence rather than simple re_occurrence.
Review: review: This event remains one of the largest reported calf cryptosporidiosis outbreaks globally (≈360 deaths among >400 neonatal calves) and clearly deserves inclusion as a top‑impact emergence episode. The event type re_emergence is appropriate because it involves a highly virulent subtype (IIdA19G1) in a region where Cryptosporidium was already present. The second source URL has been corrected: the previous DOI (10.1111/tbed.13976) actually refers to a different outbreak (IIdA20G1 in Hebei/Heilongjiang) and has been replaced with the correct International Journal for Parasitology article (doi:10.1016/j.ijpara.2019.02.006).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Pre‑weaned dairy calves on a large dairy farm in Heilongjiang Province (north‑east China)
Event summary: In November and December 2018, a diarrhoea outbreak occurred in more than 150 pre‑weaned calves on a dairy farm in Heilongjiang Province, north‑east China, with approximately 60 calves dying during the episode. Diagnostic investigations showed that C. parvum and group A rotavirus were the dominant pathogens in diarrhoeic calves, with C. parvum detected in about three‑quarters of sampled calves during the outbreak and all C. parvum isolates identified as subtype IIdA20G1. The outbreak tapered after the affected cohort passed the highest‑risk age window and management and hygiene were reinforced, and it has been interpreted as a case where coinfection of a highly pathogenic C. parvum subtype with rotavirus drove severe watery diarrhoea and high mortality.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive dairy management with large numbers of pre‑weaned calves housed in close proximity, combined with inadequate environmental hygiene and lack of effective specific prophylaxis, created conditions for rapid spread of both C. parvum and rotavirus. Internal mechanisms: The zoonotic C. parvum subtype IIdA20G1 showed strong association with watery diarrhoea and high oocyst shedding, and its concurrence with rotavirus in many calves likely intensified villous damage and fluid loss, making this episode a clear example of re_emergence driven by a virulent subtype and pathogen synergy.
Review: review: Newly added to capture the Heilongjiang 2018 outbreak, in which >150 pre‑weaned calves were affected and ≈60 died, making this one of the largest documented calf‑mortality events linked to Cryptosporidium (IIdA20G1) and rotavirus coinfection. The event is coded as re_emergence because it involves a virulent C. parvum subtype causing a severe outbreak in a setting where Cryptosporidium was already established. Geography (Heilongjiang, Eastern Asia) and sources (PubMed entry and Transboundary and Emerging Diseases article, doi:10.1111/tbed.14496) are consistent with the primary report, but the exact numbers and management changes should be reconfirmed from full text.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Neonatal dairy calves on a large Estonian dairy farm
Event summary: During the first quarter of 2015, a large dairy farm in central Estonia with more than 1,800 cows experienced an outbreak of cryptosporidiosis in neonatal heifer calves, with 144 calves born over a two‑month period followed prospectively. Despite the use of halofuginone, diarrhoea was common and 14.6% of the calves died during a three‑month observation window, and Cryptosporidium parvum infection was significantly associated with diarrhoea, inflammatory responses and impaired short‑term weight gain. Following adjustments to halofuginone use and calf management practices, clinical disease declined, although C. parvum remained endemic on the farm, illustrating the difficulty of eradicating the parasite in intensive European dairy systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High calf density, continuous calving and contaminated housing surfaces on a large intensive dairy farm created sustained exposure pressure, and incorrect or inconsistent halofuginone prophylaxis reduced, but did not eliminate, infection and disease. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transmission of existing C. parvum strains to highly susceptible neonatal calves, often in the context of mixed infections with other protozoa, drove morbidity and mortality; no novel subtype or specific resistance was reported, so this episode is best treated as re_occurrence with management‑linked drivers.
Review: review: This event represents one of the better quantified European cryptosporidiosis outbreaks in calves, with 21 deaths among 144 tracked calves and clear demonstration of production losses, so it should remain in the candidate list of major events. The event year and country annotation have been corrected from 2018/Estonia [2018] to 2015/Estonia [2015], aligning with the reported birth and follow‑up period (January–March 2015) in Niine et al. The event type has been changed from re_emergence to re_occurrence, as no novel genotype or resistance pattern is described; the outbreak is primarily driven by management and exposure. The source list has been updated to pair the Estonian thesis (which includes full outbreak context) with the primary Research in Veterinary Science article (doi:10.1016/j.rvsc.2017.12.015), while a generic long‑term impact paper previously cited at the row level is retained only in the profile‑level sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Neonatal calves on a large mixed‑breed cattle farm in Hebei Province (northern China)
Event summary: From December 2018 to April 2019, a large cattle farm in Hebei Province, northern China, reported watery diarrhoea in roughly 200 neonatal calves, with more than 40 deaths despite supportive care. Diagnostic work during and after the outbreak identified C. parvum as the main pathogen associated with diarrhoea, and all C. parvum isolates from sick calves belonged to the gp60 subtype IIdA20G1, while older animals carried other Cryptosporidium species. After the outbreak, C. parvum prevalence in calves declined but the subtype remained detectable, and the episode has been highlighted as one of several severe calf diarrhoea outbreaks in China driven by highly pathogenic IId subtypes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensively reared cohorts of neonatal calves on a large mixed‑breed cattle operation, with inadequate segregation of age groups and high faecal contamination of housing, favoured rapid spread of enteric pathogens. Internal mechanisms: Dominance of the virulent C. parvum IIdA20G1 subtype in very young calves, with strong association with watery diarrhoea and high oocyst shedding, underpins classification as a re_emergence event in a setting where Cryptosporidium was already present; older cattle on the same farm carried non‑pathogenic species, underscoring age‑linked pathogenicity.
Review: review: This row has been newly added to capture the Hebei IIdA20G1 outbreak explicitly, which involved diarrhoea in ≈200 neonatal calves and >40 deaths and is described in Zhang et al. (Transboundary and Emerging Diseases, doi:10.1111/tbed.13976). The event is coded as re_emergence because it represents another highly pathogenic IId subtype outbreak in an already endemic country; it is clearly among the most severe cryptosporidiosis episodes reported in calves. Some Chinese reviews group discussion of this and other IIdA20G1 outbreaks, so the exact farm location and denominators should be confirmed from the final published article when available, but the event almost certainly belongs in the top‑impact set.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: ≤14‑day‑old scouring Holstein‑Friesian calves on two commercial dairy farms (Al Ain region)
Event summary: Around 2020, two large dairy farms in the Al Ain region of the United Arab Emirates reported clusters of severe diarrhoea in neonatal calves, and a study of 36 scouring calves found C. parvum antigen in 29 animals and Cryptosporidium oocysts in 27, frequently alongside other enteric pathogens. At least one necropsied calf showed severe necrohaemorrhagic colitis, indicating substantial welfare impacts, and the authors described the episode as the first report of C. parvum, E. coli K99, Salmonella spp., rotavirus and coronavirus in ≤14‑day‑old scouring calves in the UAE. The investigation concluded with recommendations for improved neonatal management, hygiene and broader epidemiological surveillance of calf scours pathogens across the rapidly expanding Emirati dairy sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid development of large‑scale dairies in arid environments, with indoor housing of very young, high‑value calves and limited prior experience with cryptosporidiosis, likely facilitated introduction and amplification of C. parvum and other scours pathogens. Internal mechanisms: High environmental persistence and shedding of C. parvum, combined with frequent coinfections (E. coli K99, rotavirus, coronavirus), drove severe enteritis and high morbidity, though the study did not implicate a novel subtype or resistance trait.
Review: review: This episode is appropriately treated as a first_detection event for C. parvum‑associated neonatal calf diarrhoea in the UAE, but the original coding also set intra_continental_emergence to “yes,” which is not justified given prior widespread reports of bovine cryptosporidiosis elsewhere in Western Asia; intra_continental_emergence has been reset to “no.” The geographical information and sources match the Veterinary Parasitology: Regional Studies and Reports paper. Impact is moderate (tens of cases, no quantified large‑scale mortality), so its relative priority versus other large‑mortality outbreaks should be considered when selecting the final top‑10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dairy and beef cattle (calves and older animals) in St. Elizabeth Parish
Event summary: In a study posted in 2022, a molecular survey of 119 faecal samples from dairy and beef cattle on 10 farms in St. Elizabeth Parish, Jamaica, provided the first confirmation of Cryptosporidium infection in Jamaican cattle, detecting C. parvum in several calves and, notably, C. hominis in a diarrhoeic calf. The work reported an overall Cryptosporidium PCR‑positivity of 8%, with most PCR‑positive samples coming from diarrhoeic animals, especially younger cattle, and gp60 subtyping identified C. hominis IbA9G2 in a calf, a subtype more commonly associated with humans. Although not linked to a single explosive on‑farm outbreak, the study established that Jamaican cattle can harbour zoonotic Cryptosporidium species and subtypes and raised concerns about livestock acting as reservoirs for human infection in mixed‑species grazing systems along the Black River and tributaries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed grazing of cattle with other livestock species along riparian pastures, close proximity between animals and human communities, and limited water and sanitation infrastructure may foster cross‑species transmission and environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: Detection of both zoonotic C. parvum and human‑adapted C. hominis IbA9G2 in calves suggests host expansion and complex transmission cycles involving livestock and humans; this underpins the classification as first_detection plus re_emergence (new host involvement for C. hominis), though no evidence of a new subtype per se is presented.
Review: review: The year has been corrected from 2023 to 2022, corresponding to the posting date of the “First Report of Cryptosporidium spp. in Cattle from Jamaica” preprint; sampling likely occurred earlier but is not precisely dated. The original second URL pointed to a Chinese calf outbreak (PMC7089608) and has been replaced by the study DOI; together with the Research Square PDF these now accurately reference the Jamaican work. Event coding as first_detection is appropriate for cattle in Jamaica, and re_emergence is retained solely to reflect detection of a largely human‑adapted C. hominis subtype in a calf. Because this represents a low‑prevalence survey rather than a large outbreak, its priority relative to the very high‑mortality Chinese and Brazilian events should be reviewed before final selection of the main emergence set.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Western Europe; Asia – Western Asia; Northern America – Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996 – archival confirmation of CyHV‑3 in wild and farmed carp from unexplained mortality events]; Germany [1997 – first formally described KHV outbreaks in koi carp]; Israel [1998 – mass mortalities of farmed common carp and koi]; United States of America [1998 – mass mortalities of ornamental koi in New York State and other sites]
Host: Ornamental koi carp (Cyprinus carpio koi) and farmed/common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in ponds and intensive culture systems in Europe, Israel and the United States
Event summary: Cyprinid herpesvirus 3 was present by 1996 in the United Kingdom, where retrospective testing of archived tissues from unexplained mass mortalities of wild and cultured carp revealed CyHV‑3 DNA, but the disease was not recognized as a distinct syndrome at the time. In 1997–1998, severe outbreaks with 80–100% mortality in koi and common carp were reported independently from Germany, Israel and the United States, and virological investigations showed that a single, previously undescribed herpesvirus was responsible for these contemporaneous events. Following depopulation, disinfection and ad‑hoc movement controls at affected facilities, acute mortalities subsided locally, but the virus established latent and subclinical infections in surviving carp and, aided by international trade in live koi, seeded further spread to other regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of the ornamental koi trade and international movement of live koi and common carp with minimal health screening, high stocking densities and frequent mixing at shows and in holding facilities, and water temperatures in the 18–28 °C range that favor CyHV‑3 replication and acute disease expression. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel carp herpesvirus (CyHV‑3) with high virulence and efficient direct-contact and waterborne transmission, the ability to establish latent infections in survivors, and a broad capacity to infect both cultured and feral carp, enabling silent dissemination followed by explosive outbreaks when conditions are permissive.
Review: review – Retain this event as the global first emergence of CyHV‑3 but extend it to 1996–1998 and add the United Kingdom as the earliest confirmed location, based on archival detections of CyHV‑3 in UK carp from 1996 and subsequent mass‑mortality outbreaks in Germany, Israel and the USA in 1997–1998. Updated subregions and country list to reflect UK (Northern Europe) and clarified that this episode is classified as first/global emergence only (not also as first detection or inter‑continental emergence), in line with definitions that reserve the first‑emergence category for genuinely new pathogens in the host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Europe – Western Europe; Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Southern Europe; Europe – Eastern Europe
Countries: Belgium [1999]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2001]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000 – first confirmed KHV isolation in England and Wales with numerous outbreaks by 2002–2003]; Denmark [2002]; France [2003]; Austria [2003]; Switzerland [2003]; Italy [2003]; Luxembourg [2003]; Poland [2003-2004]
Host: Primarily ornamental koi carp and farmed common carp in ponds and aquaculture facilities; occasional infections in feral or wild carp noted later in the period
Event summary: After the initial recognition of koi herpesvirus disease in the late 1990s, from 1999 onward CyHV‑3 was detected in rapid succession in many Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries, causing high mortalities in koi collections and substantial losses in carp farms. National and international surveillance summarized by an early European workshop documented first detections and repeated outbreaks in Belgium, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Denmark, France, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Luxembourg and Poland between 1999 and 2004, often linked to imports of infected koi. Emergency measures such as movement restrictions, culling of affected stocks and improved diagnostics reduced epidemic peaks in some areas, but the virus became established and now recurs sporadically in carp populations across Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intra‑European trade in ornamental koi and carp (including koi shows and private pond stocking), expanding and intensifying carp aquaculture, and initially limited diagnostics and non‑notifiable status that allowed the virus to spread undetected. Internal mechanisms: efficient CyHV‑3 transmission in dense culture systems and latent infection in asymptomatic carrier carp, enabling spread through apparently healthy fish into new countries and subregions; no distinct novel strain is implicated beyond the original emergent CyHV‑3 lineages circulating in Europe.
Review: review – Retain as a major intra‑European emergence episode but correct geography and country details: removed Germany (initial 1997 outbreaks are captured in the global first‑emergence event) and Czechia (no confirmed KHV outbreaks reported in this period), added Eastern Europe to subregions to reflect Poland, standardized country names (United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Luxembourg) and checked first‑outbreak years against the Haenen et al. 2004/Pokorová 2005 country table.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ornamental koi carp and farmed common carp in ponds and freshwater aquaculture systems in South Africa
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2003, South Africa reported outbreaks of koi herpesvirus disease with high mortality in koi and common carp, marking the first confirmed presence of CyHV‑3 in Africa. Affected ornamental and food‑fish facilities experienced rapid onset of gill necrosis and heavy losses in recently imported or contact‑exposed carp, and diagnostic work confirmed CyHV‑3 infection. Control responses focused on culling infected stocks, imposing movement controls and tightening biosecurity, which helped curtail acute outbreaks, although the virus likely persisted in carrier carp populations in some systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of infected koi or carp from Europe or Asia into South African ponds and farms via international trade with limited health screening, combined with subtropical water temperatures favorable for disease expression. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of CyHV‑3 into African freshwater systems through infected hosts, facilitated by the virus’s environmental stability in water and its capacity for subclinical infection and latency that allow long‑distance movement and later recrudescence.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the first documented emergence of CyHV‑3 in Africa (South Africa 2001–2003), with correct continent/subregion coding and classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode. Timing and interpretation match regional summaries (Haenen et al. 2004; Pokorová et al. 2005; Biodiversity Explorer), and no major omissions or misclassifications were identified.

Sub-regions: Asia – South-eastern Asia; Asia – Eastern Asia
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2001-2002]; Indonesia [2002 – widespread carp and koi mortalities beginning in Blitar, East Java]; Taiwan (reported as Taiwan Province of China) [2002-2004]; Thailand [2004 – koi exports to Europe found KHV-positive]
Host: Farmed common carp for food and ornamental koi carp in ponds, tanks and lake/river cage culture systems; infections later detected in some feral or wild carp populations in affected areas
Event summary: From 2001 to 2004, koi herpesvirus disease spread within Asia from its earlier focus in Western Asia to new subregions in Eastern and South‑eastern Asia. Confirmed outbreaks occurred in Hong Kong in 2001 and in both Indonesia and Taiwan in 2002, where mass mortalities of koi and common carp in ponds and cage‑culture systems reached 80–100% in many farms and caused substantial economic losses and disruption of carp aquaculture. By 2004, additional detections, including KHV‑positive koi exports from Thailand and further outbreaks in Taiwan and neighboring areas, indicated that CyHV‑3 had become established across multiple Asian countries. Emergency responses led by national veterinary and fisheries services, often with FAO–NACA support, introduced movement controls, culling and improved diagnostics, which reduced acute epidemic peaks but could not prevent long‑term endemicity in the region’s carp sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive regional trade and redistribution of koi and common carp (including export‑oriented ornamental sectors), high‑density cage and pond culture in lakes and reservoirs, initially limited diagnostic capacity and awareness, and widespread water temperatures in the permissive range for CyHV‑3 replication. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of existing high‑virulence CyHV‑3 genotypes from Western Asia into Eastern and South‑eastern Asia, with efficient waterborne and direct‑contact transmission and the ability to establish latent infections that facilitate spread via apparently healthy carrier fish.
Review: review – Retain this episode as the main intra‑Asian emergence wave but adjust the start year to 2001 to capture the confirmed Hong Kong outbreak and restrict the countries and subregions to Eastern and South‑eastern Asia (removing Israel and Japan, which are described in other events). These changes align the event with the definition of intra‑continental emergence as spread into new Asian subregions and avoid double counting Japanese outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed common carp in net pens and ponds (e.g. Lake Kasumigaura and other culture sites) and wild/feral common carp in Lake Biwa and connected water bodies
Event summary: Beginning in October 2003, large market‑size common carp reared in net pens in Lake Kasumigaura, Japan, experienced mass mortalities with koi herpesvirus disease confirmed by PCR and experimental infections, prompting major depopulation and disinfection campaigns. In spring 2004, CyHV‑3 spread into wild and feral common carp in Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest lake, where approximately 70–80% of the wild carp population (on the order of 100,000 fish) died, and viral DNA and histopathologic lesions consistent with CyHV‑3 infection were documented.
