Countries: Chile – Magallanes Region (including Tierra del Fuego) [2004]
Host: Sheep (especially older animals) and rural dogs, with associated human cystic echinococcosis cases
Event summary: In Chile’s Magallanes Region, including the island province of Tierra del Fuego, a hydatid control programme begun in 1979 and based largely on regular praziquantel treatment of rural dogs led by the early 2000s to a dramatic reduction of Echinococcus granulosus infection in dogs (from around 60% to well below 1%) and in sheep (from about 80% to under 1%), alongside marked declines in human cystic echinococcosis. After the last official mass deworming of dogs in 2004 and termination of the programme, abattoir condemnation data from 1999–2023 showed a steady rebound in ovine hydatidosis, with prevalence in sheep over two years of age reaching about 32.5% in 2023, comparable to levels at the start of the programme, and dog faecal PCR surveys across rural Magallanes and Tierra del Fuego detected substantial clusters of E. granulosus DNA, with around 6–7% of sampled dog faeces positive on Tierra del Fuego. Human incidence also increased again within the region, and by the early 2020s the re-established dog–sheep cycle was recognised as a major One Health concern requiring renewed long-term dog deworming, enhanced surveillance and consideration of sheep vaccination to prevent further expansion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Termination of the long-standing regional dog deworming and surveillance programme removed the principal control pressure on the dog–sheep cycle, while large and in some areas growing rural and peri-urban dog populations, extensive sheep production (Magallanes holds more than half of Chile’s sheep), continued access of dogs to carcasses and infected offal, and difficult logistics in remote communities all favoured rapid re-establishment and amplification of transmission. Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been presented for a novel parasite genotype or anthelmintic resistance; the resurgence is consistent with classic post-programme rebound in a high-sheep-density region, with older sheep acting as long-term infection accumulators rather than reflecting an intrinsically more virulent or transmissible strain.
Review: Review – Retain as a single merged regional event. The original draft split Magallanes and Tierra del Fuego into two separate rows even though both describe re-occurrence following the termination of the same long-running control programme in one administrative region and share tightly linked dog–sheep transmission dynamics; these have been combined into a single linked episode covering Magallanes Region including Tierra del Fuego, in line with the guidance to merge epidemiologically connected, geographically contiguous episodes. Classification as re-occurrence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate, and the source list has been refined to focus on the key regional sheep and dog studies; the superseded Tierra-del-Fuego-only row is flagged for exclusion below.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Austria; France; Germany; Switzerland; Belgium [1990s]; Poland [1990s]; Czechia [1990s]; Slovak Republic/Slovakia [1990s]; Italy [2002]; Denmark [2000]; Luxembourg [1990s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1998]; Liechtenstein [1990s]
Host: Red foxes (Vulpes vulpes); voles and other small rodents; humans (sporadic and emerging cases in newly affected countries)
Event summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, Echinococcus multilocularis expanded its known range in European fox populations from four core endemic countries (Austria, France, Germany, Switzerland) to at least eight additional central, western, northern and southern European countries, with first records in foxes in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy and several central‑eastern states. As surveillance of red foxes and small mammals intensified, more newly infected areas were documented and occasional human cases began to be recognized in some of these countries. By the early 2000s, ecological and surveillance data confirmed that the parasite’s geographic range in Europe was far wider than previously thought, establishing new endemic foci across western and central Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large increases in red fox populations across Europe driven by oral rabies vaccination, hunting changes and urbanization, combined with high rodent densities in agricultural and peri‑urban landscapes, allowed the parasite to spread along expanding fox ranges and colonize new territories. Intensified wildlife surveillance and improved diagnostic tools (necropsy, copro‑PCR) increased detection probability and helped map the expanding range. Internal mechanisms: This episode reflects geographic range expansion of existing sylvatic cycles rather than a clearly distinct strain, although local adaptation of the parasite to new ecological settings likely supported establishment.
Review: Decision: review – Event is real and high‑impact, but several geographic details needed correction. (1) Sub‑regions expanded to include Northern and Southern Europe because Denmark and Italy are affected as documented in Oksanen et al. 2016 and subsequent Italian fox studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Event window extended to 1990–2002 so that Italy’s first fox detections in the early 2000s fall within the episode, consistent with Manfredi et al. and later confirmations from Alto Adige.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7789758/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Country list edited to remove non‑standard tags like “[historic]” and to reduce spurious precision (e.g. “Belgium [1991]”→“Belgium [1990s]”; “Netherlands [1996]”→“Netherlands [1998]” to match first published Dutch fox detections).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401798002635?utm_source=openai)) Event type kept as intra‑continental emergence only, which matches spread to multiple new European sub‑regions; no re‑occurrence flag is used because these are genuinely new endemic areas rather than resurgence in previously endemic ones. Because of these adjustments and remaining approximate dating for some central‑eastern countries, this row should be checked against national fox surveillance summaries before final use.

Countries: Japan [1990] (Hokkaido – Rebun Island and eastern Hokkaido; occasional spillover to pigs and dogs on Honshu)
Host: Humans; red foxes (Ezo red fox, Vulpes vulpes schrencki); domestic dogs and cats; gray‑backed voles and other small rodents; pigs (as intermediate hosts)
Event summary: By the late 20th century, a long‑standing focus of alveolar echinococcosis in Hokkaido, Japan, centred on Rebun Island and eastern Hokkaido, had evolved into a major endemic area, with several hundred cumulative human cases and widespread infection in foxes and voles. From 1999 to 2018, Japan’s national surveillance system recorded 425 human echinococcosis notifications, about 400 of them alveolar echinococcosis and over 95% from Hokkaido, corresponding to roughly a dozen or more new AE patients each year. Despite intensive control measures, including baiting programmes to deworm wild foxes, routine praziquantel treatment of dogs and public health campaigns, Hokkaido remained a persistent high‑burden focus by 2018, with continuing human and canine cases and concern about spread to Honshu and other islands.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical anthropogenic translocations of infected foxes to Hokkaido followed by decades of ecological change, including dense fox and vole populations, have sustained intense transmission; modern land use, urban expansion and tourism increased human exposure to contaminated environments. National legislation making echinococcosis notifiable in 1999 and improved imaging and serology greatly increased case detection, revealing the true scale of the problem. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular data indicate that the parasite population in Hokkaido derives from introductions of existing northern haplotypes rather than a newly evolved strain; the key processes are ecological and anthropogenic spread rather than major changes in virulence.
Review: Decision: review – This new event was added because Hokkaido is one of the largest long‑term AE foci outside China. National surveillance (1999–2018) reports 425 human echinococcosis cases, of which 400 are AE and >95% from Hokkaido, with mean annual notifications on the order of 20 cases.([id-info.jihs.go.jp](https://id-info.jihs.go.jp/niid/en/iasr/8695-469te.html)) Fox infection prevalences around 50% and a long history of human cases since 1937 are documented in Japanese mammalogy and NIID reviews.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/mammalstudy/30/Supplement/30_Supplement_S101/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai)) This magnitude makes Hokkaido comparable in impact to the better‑documented European and Central Asian foci and clearly among the top 10 global AE events. The event is coded as re‑occurrence rather than first detection because both human disease and wildlife cycles long predate 1990; recent decades represent continued high incidence under modern surveillance and control. Further refinement of the start and end years (e.g. distinguishing Rebun vs. mainland Hokkaido phases) could be done if more granular Japanese data are used.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: China [1991] (Gansu, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Qinghai, Sichuan, Tibet Autonomous Region, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region)
Host: Humans; domestic dogs; foxes; small rodents (e.g. Microtus, Cricetulus, Eospalax spp.)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, mass ultrasound and serological surveys in rural south Gansu revealed a very large, previously under‑recognized focus of human alveolar echinococcosis in central China, with about 5% of residents in some communes affected, after scattered clinical case reports from the 1960s–1980s. Subsequent field surveys through the 1990s and early 2000s documented extremely high prevalences across multiple western provinces on and around the Tibetan Plateau, with dogs, foxes and small rodents sustaining intense transmission in poor upland farming and herding communities. By the mid‑2000s, these Chinese plateau regions were recognized as accounting for more than 90% of an estimated ~18,000 new AE cases per year globally, making them the dominant global hotspot of the disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional pastoral/agropastoral livelihoods on the Tibetan Plateau with large dog populations, free‑roaming owned dogs, close human–dog contact, high densities of arvicoline rodents in upland grasslands, and limited access to veterinary care and anthelminthics created ideal conditions for intense parasite cycling and human exposure. Deforestation, land‑use change and poverty exacerbated exposure risks, while the introduction of mass ultrasound screening revealed many previously undiagnosed chronic infections. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain has been clearly implicated; instead, the parasite’s ecological adaptation to plateau ecosystems, combined with demographic and behavioural factors, underpinned sustained high transmission, representing amplification and geographic consolidation in human populations rather than a distinct genotype‑driven shift.
Review: Decision: review – The event (large plateau focus in China) is clearly one of the largest global AE episodes and should be retained, but the event‑type coding was incorrect. China had published AE case series since at least the 1960s, and the Gansu focus itself was first documented in 1991–1992 mass ultrasound surveys and follow‑up work rather than being the first detection of AE in the country or in Eastern Asia.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/014067369292693A?utm_source=openai)) Therefore the ‘first_detection’ flag was set to No and the event re‑classified as re‑occurrence, reflecting a dramatic increase in recognized incidence and visibility in a previously known subregion driven by environmental and social changes plus improved case finding. ‘Intra‑continental emergence’ was set to No to avoid conflating this intensification within Eastern Asia with true spread to new Asian sub‑regions (which is better captured in the Kyrgyzstan event). Sources were also refined to focus on the original Lancet description of the Gansu focus, subsequent ecological work, China‑wide prevalence meta‑analysis and the global burden estimates that underpin the statement that China accounts for >90% of new AE cases.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0000722))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Poland [1990s]; Czechia [1990s]; Slovak Republic/Slovakia [1990s]; Hungary [2000s]; Lithuania [2000s]; Latvia [2000s]; Slovenia [2000s]; Romania [2000s]; Denmark [2000s – wildlife only]; Italy [late 1990s–2000s]; Belgium (northern) [1990s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [late 1990s]; Luxembourg [1990s]; Sweden [2011 – wildlife only]
Host: Humans (in most listed countries); red foxes; domestic dogs; small rodents
Event summary: From the 1990s through the 2000s, human alveolar echinococcosis emerged in central‑eastern and Baltic Europe and in several western and southern European countries that had previously reported no or very few locally acquired cases, including Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia, Romania, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and parts of northern Italy. These new human reports coincided with confirmation of Echinococcus multilocularis in foxes and small mammals in many of the same countries, often first detected in the mid‑1990s or early 2000s, while in Denmark and Sweden the parasite was found only in wildlife with no confirmed autochthonous human cases during this period. By around 2015, several hundred human AE cases had been collated from these newer endemic areas, indicating that the parasite’s public health impact had expanded well beyond the historic Alpine foci into much of central, northern and eastern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued spread and densification of infected fox populations across Europe, facilitated by rabies vaccination, landscape change, agricultural intensification and high rodent prey densities, enabled colonization of new subregions and countries. Greater diagnostic awareness, improved imaging and serology, and the creation of national and multinational registries led to better identification and reporting of AE cases in countries where the disease had previously gone unrecognized or had been misdiagnosed. Internal mechanisms: The emergence mainly reflects colonization of new geographic areas by existing parasite lineages adapted to fox–rodent cycles; no single novel hyper‑virulent strain is required to explain establishment, though local genotypic differences and ecological contexts likely modulate human risk.
Review: Decision: review – This event appropriately captures the multi‑country emergence of human AE in central‑eastern, Baltic and parts of western Europe and should be kept, but several clarifications were needed. (1) Denmark and Sweden were annotated as ‘wildlife only’ because up to at least 2015 no confirmed autochthonous human AE cases had been reported there, even though infected foxes and rodents were found.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304401715003763?utm_source=openai)) (2) The summary text was edited so that human emergence is not implied for Denmark and Sweden, but rather linked explicitly to Poland, the Baltic states, Hungary, Slovenia, Romania, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and northern Italy, in line with European registry data and the 2019 global review.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2958541/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Event coding as ‘first_detection’ and ‘intra‑continental emergence’ was retained because, at the continental scale, these represent new European countries and sub‑regions acquiring documented human AE transmission. Given the complexity of overlapping time windows with the fox‑range expansion event and the core Alpine re‑occurrence, this row should be cross‑checked against country‑by‑country incidence tables before final use, but it clearly represents one of the major human AE emergence patterns.

Host: Humans; domestic dogs; foxes; small mammals
Event summary: The first recorded human alveolar echinococcosis case in Kyrgyzstan was reported in 1996, with only 0–3 cases per year recorded until the early 2000s. Over the subsequent decade, national surveillance documented a sharp rise to dozens of human AE cases per year by about 2010 and more than 200 cases annually by the mid‑2010s, giving Kyrgyzstan some of the highest reported surgical incidences of AE worldwide. By around 2018, incidence appeared to plateau or slightly decline, but AE remained a major public health problem with persistent rural hotspots, especially in southern mountain valleys.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Socioeconomic disruption following the dissolution of the Soviet Union led to breakdown of state veterinary services, increased numbers of free‑roaming dogs, more home slaughtering of livestock, and reduced access to routine dog deworming, all of which facilitated parasite amplification in dog–rodent cycles with spillover to humans. Rural poverty and reliance on backyard slaughter, pastoralism and dog ownership increased human exposure to dog and fox feces. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points mainly to intensified transmission via dogs and wildlife rather than the emergence of a novel, more virulent strain; thus this represents first detection and rapid amplification of a long‑established wildlife cycle under new social and economic conditions rather than a genotype‑driven shift.
Review: Decision: review – The Kyrgyzstan epidemic is unquestionably one of the most important AE emergence events and should be retained, but the event‑type coding conflicted with the scheme. The original row simultaneously set ‘first_detection’, ‘intra_continental_emergence’ and ‘re_occurrence’ to Yes, even though re‑occurrence is defined as mutually exclusive from intra‑/inter‑continental emergence. Surveillance data show that the first recognized human AE cases in Kyrgyzstan appeared in 1996, with a marked rise after 2000 linked to post‑Soviet breakdown of control systems, which fits the ‘first_detection’ definition for this country and an intra‑continental spread of documented human AE from China and other Asian foci into Central Asia.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/19/7/12-1405_article?utm_source=openai)) ‘Re_occurrence’ was therefore set to No; the dramatic increase in incidence is captured in the narrative and drivers rather than by a separate category. Because earlier Soviet‑era human AE may have gone unrecorded and wildlife cycles were already endemic across Central Asia, regional experts may wish to revisit whether a supplementary re‑occurrence event for Central Asia as a whole is warranted, but the current coding aligns better with the provided definitions.

Host: Humans; red foxes; domestic dogs
Event summary: In core endemic Alpine regions of Switzerland, Germany, France and Austria, human alveolar echinococcosis incidence rose in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with Switzerland documenting a statistically significant increase in annual incidence from about 0.10 to 0.26 per 100,000 population between 1993–2000 and 2001–2005. Parallel data showed increasing prevalence of Echinococcus multilocularis in foxes, including the establishment of dense, infected urban fox populations in German and Swiss cities. By the mid‑2000s, these countries reported growing numbers of human AE cases linked to peri‑urban or rural residence, leading to heightened concern and sustained clinical and veterinary surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rabies control and hunting changes allowed fox populations to grow and colonize peri‑urban and urban areas, increasing proximity between infected foxes, domestic dogs and humans. Urban green spaces and peri‑urban farmland supported high rodent and fox densities, while lifestyle patterns involving outdoor recreation and gardening increased exposure to contaminated environments. Improvements in imaging and serology increased case detection but do not fully explain the observed incidence rises. Internal mechanisms: The main mechanism appears to be enhanced transmission via expanding and urbanizing fox and dog populations rather than clearly documented increases in parasite virulence or new genotypes.
Review: Decision: retain – This event correctly describes the well‑documented increase in human AE incidence in the historic Alpine core (Switzerland, southern Germany, eastern France, western Austria) around 2001–2005, driven by fox population growth and urbanization.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/13/6/06-1074_article?utm_source=openai)) The geographic scope, timing and mechanism are well supported by Swiss registry analyses and European reviews, and the event‑type classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence in a long‑established endemic area driven by external ecological change) is appropriate and mutually exclusive of intra‑/inter‑continental categories. No structural changes were necessary beyond minor source consolidation.

Countries: China [2004] (Gansu, Ningxia, Qinghai, Sichuan, Tibet Autonomous Region, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Inner Mongolia)
Host: Humans; domestic dogs; foxes; small rodents; livestock (economic impact through dog–livestock interface rather than direct infection)
Event summary: Building on earlier recognition of large foci in the 1990s, nationwide echinococcosis surveillance and control programmes in China from 2004 onwards revealed sustained, very high burdens of alveolar echinococcosis across Tibetan Plateau provinces, with repeated county‑level surveys showing some of the highest prevalences and incidence rates in the world. Over 2004–2022, tens of thousands of echinococcosis cases were recorded nationally, with AE accounting for a substantial share of the disease burden and disability in plateau counties, and new foci documented in areas such as parts of Inner Mongolia and western Gansu. Despite gradual scale‑up of dog deworming, fox and dog management and health education, AE remained entrenched, though some local reductions in prevalence were observed toward the end of this period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing pastoral systems with large free‑roaming dog populations, high small‑mammal densities in high‑altitude grasslands, climate conditions favouring egg survival, and persistent poverty and limited access to healthcare allowed AE transmission to remain intense despite control efforts. Expansion of national programmes for ultrasound screening and control improved detection and treatment coverage, changing the apparent incidence and burden over time. Internal mechanisms: Continued high transmission is largely ecological and behavioural rather than driven by identifiable novel genotypes; survival analyses and burden estimates indicate chronic, entrenched endemicity rather than a short‑term outbreak, although local micro‑evolutionary changes in parasite populations cannot be excluded.
Review: Decision: review – This row usefully summarises the long period of very high AE burden under national surveillance and control in China after 2004 and should be kept, but it does not fit neatly into any single emergence‑type category. The original coding as ‘re_occurrence’ implied a resurgence after prior decline, whereas available data suggest persistent hyperendemicity punctuated by improved case finding and gradual, spatially heterogeneous effects of control measures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7362549/?utm_source=openai)) Accordingly, all six emergence‑type flags have been set to No and the episode is framed as a continuation and national scaling‑up of the plateau hotspot first highlighted in the early 1990s (now captured in the 1991–2005 event). Experts may wish ultimately to merge these two Chinese rows into a single long episode, or to split them into more precise phases (e.g. pre‑ and post‑national control programme) if detailed Chinese surveillance data are to hand; this is why the row is flagged for review rather than retain.

Countries: Canada [2009] (British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, southern Ontario)
Host: Coyotes; red foxes; domestic dogs; humans; small rodents
Event summary: Although Echinococcus multilocularis has been present in North American wildlife since the mid‑20th century, from 2009 a European‑type strain was identified in a dog in British Columbia with no travel history outside the province and subsequently in urban coyotes and dogs in western Canada, indicating recent introduction and establishment of a more pathogenic lineage. By the early 2010s, high prevalences were documented in urban coyotes around Calgary, Alberta, and autochthonous human alveolar echinococcosis cases began to be recognized in western Canada, a condition previously almost unheard of there. Over the following decade, further human cases and widespread wildlife infection suggested an emerging public health concern linked to this introduced strain in prairie and urban ecosystems in several western and central provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International movement of dogs (e.g. importation or rescue of infected dogs from endemic European regions) is thought to have introduced the European strain into western Canada, where expanding urban coyote and dog populations and close human–pet contact facilitated establishment and spillover to humans. Urban growth and green space expansion increased overlap between humans, coyotes, dogs and rodent intermediate hosts, while limited awareness of AE delayed diagnosis and reporting. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of European‑type genotypes with higher propensity to cause disease in dogs and humans, and apparent competitive displacement of some native North American strains, represents re‑emergence driven by parasite genetic change superimposed on a pre‑existing wildlife transmission system.
Review: Decision: review – The introduction and spread of European‑type E. multilocularis lineages in western Canada, with emerging human AE in Alberta and neighbouring provinces, is a key modern event and should be retained, but the original classification as ‘inter‑continental emergence’ was incorrect because E. multilocularis has been endemic in North American wildlife (e.g. Arctic foxes, coyotes) since at least the mid‑20th century.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0000722)) The event better fits the definition of re‑emergence, driven by internal change (introduction of more pathogenic genotypes) on top of an existing host–parasite system, so only ‘re_emergence’ is set to Yes. The countries list has been restricted to Canada, where the European‑type strain and most documented human cases are clearly established; evidence for similar genotypes in the USA is emerging but largely post‑2020 and beyond the temporal scope of this event.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2024-50/issue-9-september-2024/human-echinococcosis-incidence-2000-2020.html?utm_source=openai)) Because strain attribution and spatial spread in North America are evolving rapidly, this row should be revisited as new genomic and surveillance data accumulate.

Host: Red foxes; voles and other small rodents; domestic dogs (potential definitive hosts)
Event summary: National fox surveillance in Sweden, ongoing since 2000, detected Echinococcus multilocularis for the first time in a red fox shot in December 2010 in the south‑west of the country, with a second infected fox found nearby in March 2011. Follow‑up investigations confirmed low‑prevalence but established infection in local wildlife, and subsequent rodent studies during 2013–2015 identified competent intermediate hosts, indicating that the parasite had recently colonized Sweden from neighbouring endemic regions. Over the subsequent few years, further wildlife and rodent studies substantiated an emerging local transmission cycle, prompting long‑term monitoring, risk assessments and communication to veterinarians and the public, although no autochthonous human AE cases had been confirmed by 2015.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural dispersal of infected foxes from endemic areas in Denmark, Germany or Poland, combined with suitable Swedish habitats and rodent communities, likely introduced the parasite; increasing fox population densities and mobility, including across borders, underpinned establishment. Implementation of systematic surveillance enabled early detection at very low prevalence. Internal mechanisms: The event represents geographic range expansion of existing European strains into a new northern subregion rather than a novel genotype with altered virulence.
Review: Decision: review – This event correctly captures the first detection and establishment of E. multilocularis in Swedish wildlife and is relevant as a first‑detection episode in a previously parasite‑free country.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21492529/?utm_source=openai)) However, the original host list and wording implied possible human involvement, whereas up to at least 2015 no confirmed autochthonous human AE cases had occurred in Sweden.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304401715003763?utm_source=openai)) The host field has therefore been restricted to foxes, rodents and potential dog definitive hosts, and the summary now explicitly notes the absence of human cases in this period. Event coding as ‘first_detection’ and ‘intra‑continental emergence’ (spread to a new European sub‑region) remains appropriate. Because Sweden is also mentioned in the broader European emergence row, users should be aware this country appears in two linked but conceptually distinct episodes: a continental‑scale emergence in many countries and this more detailed national first‑detection event.

Countries: Kazakhstan [~1991]; Kyrgyzstan [~1991]; Uzbekistan [~1991]; Tajikistan [~1991]; Turkmenistan [~1991]; Mongolia [1990s]
Host: Dogs and other canids (definitive hosts); sheep, goats, cattle, camels and other livestock (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, indicator of intense dog–livestock transmission)
Event summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union around 1991, cystic echinococcosis (CE) due to Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato re‑emerged across the newly independent Central Asian republics, with sharp rises in human surgical cases and high infection prevalences in dogs and livestock documented during the 1990s and 2000s. In Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, official data showed rapid post‑1991 increases followed by sustained high incidence of human CE (often 5–25+ cases/100,000/year) and high infection levels in rural dogs by the 2000s, while similar resurgences were reported in neighbouring post‑socialist Mongolia. By the mid‑2010s, CE remained highly endemic across Central Asia and Mongolia despite some control efforts, indicating long‑term re‑establishment of dog–livestock transmission cycles driven by socio‑economic transition rather than parasite change.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Profound socio‑economic transition after the Soviet collapse led to fragmentation/privatization of collective farms, growth of smallholder flocks, uncontrolled home slaughter, unsafe offal disposal, reduced dog management, and collapse of state veterinary and public‑health services, greatly increasing dog exposure to infected livestock viscera and human contact with infected dogs.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3713972/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Amplification of pre‑existing E. granulosus s.l. lineages under altered transmission conditions, with increased force of infection driven by growth and changed management of dog and livestock populations rather than emergence of novel genotypes.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This event clearly represents one of the largest post‑1990 CE resurgences worldwide and should be retained as a major emergence episode. I removed western China from the country list and narrative to avoid double‑counting with dedicated China events, restricting this episode to the post‑Soviet Central Asian republics plus Mongolia, which share the same socio‑economic transition driver. Based on the definitions, I reclassified the event as re‑occurrence only (no re‑emergence), because the literature documents resurgence due to external socio‑economic and veterinary‑service collapse, with no evidence of novel parasite strains or resistance; intra‑ and inter‑continental emergence appropriately remain “No.” Sub‑regions (Central Asia; Eastern Asia) are still appropriate because Mongolia is assigned to Eastern Asia in the UNSD scheme. Source set is generally appropriate; the scispace link duplicates peer‑reviewed material and could be dropped in later curation.

Countries: Kyrgyzstan [AE first recorded 1996; rapid increase from 2000s]
Host: Dogs (definitive host); foxes and other wild canids (likely definitive hosts in some foci); small mammals (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, clinical AE cases)
Event summary: Alveolar echinococcosis (AE) caused by Echinococcus multilocularis was first officially recorded in humans in Kyrgyzstan in 1996, with only 0–3 cases per year until 2003, after which reported human AE cases increased steeply, reaching around 148 cases by 2013 and very high incidences in certain oblasts such as Naryn (≈7 cases per 100,000 per year). National analyses describe concurrent increases in cystic echinococcosis (CE), so that by the early 2010s AE and CE together were recognized as among the most important zoonoses in Kyrgyzstan, with sustained high case numbers despite limited control, indicating entrenched local transmission cycles involving dogs, foxes and rodent intermediate hosts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3713972/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Soviet economic decline, reduced veterinary services, increased numbers of owned and stray dogs, more home slaughter of livestock, and poor offal management created favourable conditions for both CE and AE; in southern Kyrgyzstan, dense dog populations, fox–rodent communities and rural poverty further amplified exposure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3713972/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Available data support geographic range expansion and amplification of existing E. multilocularis populations under changing ecological conditions (fox and rodent communities, dog ecology) rather than emergence of a distinct new genotype; the episode is therefore best treated as re‑occurrence driven by external/ecological change rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This is a well‑documented, high‑impact epidemic of AE (and CE) in Kyrgyzstan and should be retained. I corrected the emergence‑type classification to re‑occurrence only: the event occurs in a subregion (Central Asia) where E. multilocularis was already present pre‑1990, and the literature attributes the surge primarily to socio‑economic and ecological change (dog management, wildlife–livestock interfaces) rather than parasite evolution. Intra‑continental emergence remains “No” because the subregion (Central Asia) was already known to be endemic before 1990, and first_detection is correctly “No” at the global host‑system scale. No changes to geography were required.

Countries: Lithuania [1997]; Poland [first human AE cases early 1990s, strong increase after 2000]; Latvia [2000s]; Estonia [2000s]; Belarus [2000s]; Hungary [first autochthonous AE ~2000s]; Romania [first AE reports late 2000s]
Host: Red foxes and raccoon dogs (definitive hosts); small mammals (intermediate hosts); domestic dogs (occasional definitive host); humans (accidental intermediate host, clinical AE)
Event summary: From the late 1990s onward, Baltic and eastern‑central European countries recorded large new foci of Echinococcus multilocularis infection in foxes and raccoon dogs, accompanied by rising numbers of human AE cases, representing a major northward and eastward expansion from the classic endemic core in France, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Lithuania diagnosed 96 human AE cases between 1997 and 2008 alongside very high fox infection intensities, while Poland documented over 120 human AE cases from 1990–2011 with a marked rise during 2000–2009 and clustering in the north‑east bordering Lithuania; similar first or early autochthonous human AE cases were reported in Latvia, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Romania during the 2000s. By around 2010, AE was recognized as emerging across large parts of the Baltic and eastern‑central Europe, with sustained fox infection and continuing human case detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and urbanization of red fox populations following rabies vaccination campaigns, landscape changes increasing rodent intermediate hosts, expanding raccoon dog populations, and improved imaging/serology together created new and denser E. multilocularis transmission cycles and increased detection of human AE.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of E. multilocularis within Europe, with high worm burdens in foxes indicating enhanced transmission; at continental scale, spread is best explained by wildlife ecology and control of rabies rather than emergence of a single novel strain.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This episode represents a major intra‑European expansion of AE into the Baltic and eastern‑central European countries and is clearly among the largest post‑1990 emergence events. I corrected the emergence‑type classification: first_detection was set to “Yes” in the draft but should be “No” at the global host‑system scale, and there is no strong evidence that parasite evolution (as opposed to wildlife ecology and rabies control) is the primary driver, so re_emergence was changed to “No.” Intra‑continental emergence remains “Yes” because transmission was newly documented in UNSD subregions (Northern Europe – Baltics; Eastern Europe) beyond the pre‑1990 Alpine core. I also recommend removing the general Echinococcosis Wikipedia link in favour of more specific peer‑reviewed sources and have added a key EU‑wide systematic review of E. multilocularis distribution in wildlife as a more relevant source.

Countries: France [pre‑1990 endemic, marked fox infection and AE increase 1990s]; Germany [1990s-2000s]; Switzerland [1990s-2000s]; Austria [1990s-2000s]; neighbouring areas of Czechia and Slovakia [1990s-2000s]
Host: Red foxes (primary definitive host); domestic dogs and cats (occasional definitive hosts); small mammals (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, AE cases)
Event summary: In the 1990s and early 2000s, traditionally endemic areas of western‑central Europe (eastern France, southern Germany, Switzerland and western Austria, with spill‑over into Czechia and Slovakia) experienced sharp increases in E. multilocularis prevalence in foxes and corresponding rises in human AE case numbers. Fox population recoveries following successful oral rabies vaccination, along with urban expansion and landscape changes, led to higher fox densities and increased contamination of peri‑urban and rural environments with parasite eggs, while domestic dogs and occasionally cats provided additional links to humans. By around 2010, AE was considered an emerging or re‑emerging zoonosis in these countries, with mortality and chronic morbidity persisting despite improved treatment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recovery and expansion of red fox populations after rabies control, fox urbanization, agricultural and land‑use changes favouring rodent intermediate hosts, and greater human use of peri‑urban green spaces together increased human and dog contact with fox‑contaminated environments.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission within fox–rodent cycles and adaptation to peri‑urban habitats, but no clear evidence that a novel parasite strain is the primary driver; overall pattern reflects re‑occurrence of an existing parasite under new ecological conditions.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This is a core European AE resurgence with substantial human and wildlife impact and should be retained. I corrected the sub‑region label from the non‑standard “Central and Eastern Europe” to the UNSD‑conformant combination “Western Europe; Eastern Europe,” since the event covers France, Germany, Switzerland and Austria (Western Europe) plus neighbouring parts of Czechia/Slovakia (Eastern Europe). The episode is best classified as re‑occurrence, driven by fox population recovery and landscape change, rather than re‑emergence sensu stricto because there is no strong evidence for a new strain or resistance; therefore re_emergence was set to “No” while re_occurrence remains “Yes.” I also replaced general Wikipedia links with more specific systematic reviews and EU‑level analyses that better document fox infection and human AE trends.

Countries: China – high‑altitude western and north‑western provinces/autonomous regions including Sichuan (Ganzi, Shiqu), Qinghai, Tibet (Xizang), Xinjiang, Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia, Yunnan, Shaanxi [2000s]
Host: Dogs (owned and semi‑feral, definitive host); foxes and other wild canids (definitive hosts, especially in pastoral areas); sheep, yaks, goats and other livestock (intermediate hosts for CE); small mammals (intermediate hosts for AE); humans (accidental intermediate host; high village‑level prevalence)
Event summary: From roughly 2000 to the mid‑2010s, large‑scale ultrasound and serological surveys in western China documented extremely high co‑endemicity of cystic and alveolar echinococcosis, especially among Tibetan pastoral communities on the eastern Tibetan Plateau (western Sichuan and adjoining Qinghai) and in other western and north‑western provinces. In Shiqu County, Sichuan, village‑based surveys between 2000–2002 found overall human echinococcosis prevalences exceeding 10% with both CE and AE present, and subsequent national surveys during 2012–2016 estimated around 170,000 human cases and tens of millions at risk, with particularly high prevalence in Tibet and Qinghai. By 2016, China accounted for the majority of global AE cases and a major share of CE burden, with sustained high transmission in dogs, foxes, livestock and small mammals despite intensified control in some areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847145/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional transhumant and sedentary pastoralism with large dog populations, home slaughter of yaks and sheep, feeding of uncooked viscera to dogs, limited dog deworming and slaughterhouse controls, poverty, and ecological conditions favouring high densities of small mammal intermediate hosts all promoted intense transmission; remoteness limited access to diagnosis and care.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847145/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing E. granulosus s.l. and E. multilocularis lineages maintained in high‑altitude ecosystems, with geographic expansion into additional counties documented; the very high force of infection reflects ecological suitability and dense host networks more than emergence of novel genotypes, so the episode is best characterised as re‑occurrence in a pre‑existing endemic zone.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This episode captures the exceptional CE/AE burden in Tibetan and other western Chinese pastoral areas and is clearly among the most impactful global events. However, I reclassified it as pure re‑occurrence: western China was well known to be endemic for CE and AE before 1990, and the high prevalences observed from 2000 onward represent amplification and better documentation of long‑standing transmission, not first detection or spread to a new continent/sub‑region, nor emergence of a new strain. Thus intra‑continental and inter‑continental emergence and re_emergence were set to “No.” Geographic scope (western and north‑western Chinese provinces within Eastern Asia) and years remain appropriate.

Countries: China – nine western endemic provinces/autonomous regions (Xinjiang, Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Yunnan, Shaanxi) [2004]; additional non‑endemic provinces reporting sporadic cases [2004-2020]
Host: Dogs and other canids (definitive hosts); livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, yaks) and small mammals (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, notifiable cases)
Event summary: Following the introduction of nationwide notifiable disease reporting and echinococcosis surveillance in China in 2004, a sustained high burden of both CE and AE was documented through 2020, with more than 66,000 reported cases concentrated in nine western endemic provinces/autonomous regions and additional sporadic cases reported from non‑endemic provinces. Annual case numbers remained substantial throughout this period, with the Tibetan Plateau and adjacent highland areas consistently showing the highest notification rates and prevalence, while routine reporting newly delineated risk in many counties and identified occasional locally acquired infections in previously non‑endemic provincial‑level units. Despite stepped‑up control efforts (dog deworming, health education, improved slaughter hygiene), transmission persisted in core pastoral areas into the late 2010s.([jsczz.cn](https://www.jsczz.cn/EN/10.12140/j.issn.1000-7423.2022.04.009?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Systematic surveillance primarily revealed the scale and geography of a long‑standing problem, but also highlighted continuing drivers including extensive dog ownership, low deworming coverage, pastoral production systems, wildlife reservoirs, environmental contamination, and migration of people and livestock from endemic to non‑endemic provinces.([jsczz.cn](https://www.jsczz.cn/EN/10.12140/j.issn.1000-7423.2022.04.009?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Largely persistence and gradual geographic range expansion of existing parasite populations within suitable ecological zones; no convincing evidence that emergence of new genotypes at the country scale is the primary driver of the post‑2004 burden.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This nationwide Chinese episode is high‑impact and should be retained, but it is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of a known endemic problem under modern surveillance rather than intra‑continental emergence. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence to “No” and kept re_occurrence as “Yes.” The event appropriately captures recognition of the true scale of burden (66,000+ reported cases 2004–2020 and many more likely unreported) in the nine endemic western provinces plus sporadic cases elsewhere, consistent with national surveillance analyses. The geography (China, Eastern Asia) and years are appropriate, and the source set (endemic status paper plus national burden analyses) is suitable for this event type.

Countries: Argentina – Neuquén and other Patagonian sheep‑rearing provinces (Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego) [1990s-2000s]; Chile – southern regions (Los Lagos, Aysén, Magallanes) and Coquimbo/north‑central highlands [1990s-2000s]; Uruguay [1990s-2000s]; Brazil – Rio Grande do Sul [1990s-2000s]; Peru – Andean departments such as Junín, Pasco and Ica/Chincha [1990s-2000s]; Bolivia – Andean highlands [1990s-2000s]
Host: Dogs (definitive host); sheep and other small ruminants plus cattle (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, surgical CE cases)
Event summary: From about 1990 to 2010, the Southern Cone and Andean countries of South America (Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, southern Brazil, Peru and Bolivia) experienced a persistently high burden of cystic echinococcosis (CE) despite decades of control programmes. In Patagonia Argentina, intensive dog deworming and slaughter‑control programmes initiated in the 1970s greatly reduced CE but surveillance from 1995–2004 in Neuquén Province still showed heterogeneous surgical incidence (declining from ≈44 to ≈19 cases per 100,000 person‑years but remaining ≥15 per 100,000 in many localities), indicating residual high‑transmission pockets.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1383576907000104?utm_source=openai)) Similar high or very high surgical incidences were documented in southern Chile and north‑central highlands such as Coquimbo, and ultrasound and hospital‑based studies in Andean Peru and Bolivia reported prevalences up to several percent and surgical incidences exceeding 10–30 per 100,000 in some communities.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401709007304?utm_source=openai)) Regional reviews estimate roughly 5,000 new human CE cases annually across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Peru and Uruguay during this period, with substantial associated livestock production losses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6431127/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incomplete or heterogeneous application of dog deworming, stray dog control and safe offal disposal, particularly among smallholder and subsistence sheep producers in remote rural areas, allowed continuing infection of dogs and contamination of the environment; socio‑economic constraints, limited veterinary/public‑health resources, and program fatigue limited the sustainability and reach of Southern Cone and Andean control projects.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9236943/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence of fundamentally new parasite genotypes driving this episode at regional scale; persistence reflects survival of E. granulosus s.l. (especially sheep‑strain lineages) in residual high‑risk dog–sheep microfoci and slow decline even under prolonged but uneven control.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. The original Neuquén‑focused event captured only part of a much larger Southern Cone/Andean CE problem. I expanded the geography and timeframe to reflect the well‑documented, long‑lasting high burden across Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, southern Brazil, Peru and Bolivia from roughly 1990–2010, which collectively account for thousands of human cases and substantial livestock losses annually according to PAHO/WHO and regional reviews. The event remains classified as re‑occurrence (continuation of long‑standing endemicity with incomplete control) with no evidence for parasite‑driven re‑emergence. The broader country list and references now better match the definition of a major, multi‑country linked episode and ensure that Andean Peru—a globally important CE hotspot—is explicitly represented without creating a separate, overlapping event.

Countries: Canada – British Columbia (Quesnel region) [2009]; Alberta (Calgary and Edmonton metropolitan areas and surrounding regions) [2009-2010s]; Saskatchewan [2010s]; Manitoba [2010s]; Ontario [2010s]; United States of America – north‑central and midwestern states within the historic endemic zone (e.g. Minnesota and neighbouring states) and isolated new foci (e.g. Missouri) with locally acquired canine and occasional human AE cases [2010s]
Host: Wild canids (coyotes, foxes) as definitive hosts; domestic dogs (definitive host with severe clinical AE); small mammals (intermediate hosts); zoo primates and other captive mammals (aberrant intermediate hosts); humans (locally acquired AE cases)
Event summary: From 2009 onward, Echinococcus multilocularis exhibiting European‑type genotypes was detected in dogs and wild canids in western and central Canada, including British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and later Ontario, extending well beyond the historically recognized Arctic and north‑central endemic zones. Molecular studies of a 2009 dog case in British Columbia showed the parasite to be closely related to European strains rather than traditional North American lineages, and subsequent surveys found increasing E. multilocularis prevalence in urban coyotes around Calgary and other cities, along with a growing number of severe canine AE cases and at least several locally acquired human AE cases in Alberta and sporadic locally acquired infections in the United States.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3358155/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s, Canadian experts characterized E. multilocularis, particularly introduced European‑type strains, as an emerging and costly zoonotic problem in North America with expanding geographic range and host spectrum.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International and interprovincial dog movements (including imported dogs from Europe and endemic regions without mandatory Echinococcus testing or treatment), urban expansion into wildlife habitats, increasing and urbanizing coyote and fox populations, and low awareness and deworming coverage in dogs facilitated introduction and establishment of European‑type E. multilocularis in new regions.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1471492212000517?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of more pathogenic or highly zoonotic European‑type haplotypes into North America, followed by geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission in urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; this represents strain‑level re‑emergence of AE risk in regions where the species was previously absent or rare, rather than first continental introduction of E. multilocularis itself.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (borderline for inclusion). This event describes the strain‑level invasion of European‑type E. multilocularis into western and central Canada (and, to a lesser extent so far, parts of the USA). I corrected the emergence‑type classification: North America has long been endemic for E. multilocularis, so this is not an inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence at the species level, nor a first_detection event globally. Instead, it is best treated as re‑emergence driven by introduction of more zoonotic European haplotypes and their establishment in new urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; accordingly, only re_emergence is set to “Yes.” I also refined the country list to focus on provinces and states where European‑type strains and locally acquired AE have been documented. Although the absolute number of human cases remains small compared with China, Central Asia or South America, the combination of novel genotype introduction, wide geographic spread in wildlife and dogs, and high per‑case costs gives this event strategic importance; whether it should remain among the top 10 highest‑impact events depends on how strictly impact is defined (current DALYs vs future risk), so it is flagged for further expert review rather than automatic exclusion.

Host: Goats (domestic small ruminants)
Event summary: In the 1990s, heartwater was already endemic in southern Mozambique, but post-civil-war livestock restocking moved naïve goats from the relatively low-risk northern province of Tete into heavily infested southern provinces. A serological survey found markedly different exposure levels between northern (8.1%) and southern (65.6%) goat populations, and a small translocation experiment showed that about half of the transplanted goats either died of clinically confirmed heartwater or seroconverted within five weeks, indicating substantial restocking-associated mortality. This high-loss episode, reported in 2001, subsided as the most susceptible restocked animals died or acquired immunity and as awareness of the heartwater risk in restocking programs improved, although the disease remains endemic throughout Mozambique.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement and restocking of naïve goats from the lower-risk north into highly endemic southern Mozambique created a large pool of susceptible hosts exposed to infected Amblyomma ticks, compounded by limited tick control and insufficient risk awareness in restocking schemes. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance phenotype was implicated; this event reflects amplification of an existing endemic pathogen in a newly assembled, highly susceptible host population rather than genetic change in Ehrlichia ruminantium.
Review: Decision: retain (flagged for review). This is a well-documented, high-impact heartwater episode linked to post-war goat restocking in Mozambique, based on Bekker et al. 2001. I simplified the 'countries' entry to 'Mozambique' to follow the country list and removed the embedded '1990s–2000' date range, and I rephrased the summary so the serological work is described as a north–south comparison rather than a nationwide survey. Classification as re-occurrence (endemic pathogen causing a surge in mortality in an already affected subregion, without evidence of a new strain or new subregion) remains appropriate, but a subject-matter expert should confirm whether using the 2001 publication year as the event year is acceptable for this largely 1990s restocking period.

Host: Cattle and goats (domestic ruminants)
Event summary: Heartwater became endemic in Guadeloupe in the 1980s following introduction of Amblyomma variegatum and Ehrlichia ruminantium from West Africa, with clinical cases confirmed there by 1980 and serological surveys in the early 1990s documenting infection in cattle and goats in Guadeloupe and nearby islands. From the 1990s through the early 2020s, heartwater remained stably endemic on the main Guadeloupe islands, but a 2024 archipelago-wide survey found seropositive goats on all major islands, including Les Saintes, which had previously been considered heartwater-free. This first serological evidence of E. ruminantium circulation in Les Saintes represents a geographically limited expansion of the endemic Caribbean focus, increasing the area at risk and underlining the potential for further spread to additional Caribbean islands and eventually the American mainland.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term establishment of Amblyomma variegatum in the Lesser Antilles, routine movement of livestock between islands within the Guadeloupe archipelago, suitable tropical climate and vegetation for tick survival, and the difficulty of sustaining intensive tick-control programs likely facilitated gradual spread of both vector and pathogen from the main islands to the smaller Les Saintes group. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance phenotype was identified in recent surveys; the event is best interpreted as local geographic range expansion of an established Ehrlichia ruminantium–Amblyomma variegatum system rather than emergence of a genetically distinct variant.
Review: Decision: retain (flagged for review). The event correctly captures ongoing endemic heartwater in Guadeloupe and the newly documented serological presence of Ehrlichia ruminantium in Les Saintes based on Dufleit et al. 2025 and earlier Caribbean work. I changed the emergence-type classification: spread to Les Saintes occurs within the same UN subregion (South America - Caribbean) and the same 'country' (Guadeloupe), so it does not meet the definition of intra-continental emergence and is now coded with all six emergence-type flags as 'No'. I also simplified the 'countries' field to 'Guadeloupe [2024]' and removed speculative mention of sheep from the host list, restricting it to cattle and goats documented in the 2024 survey. This remains a geographically important but relatively small-scale expansion; a domain expert should confirm that it merits inclusion among the top heartwater emergence events and whether the event year should later be broadened to 2024–2025 if Les Saintes outbreaks in winter 2025 are to be explicitly included.

Host: Ticks (Hyalomma dromedarii, Rhipicephalus annulatus, Rhipicephalus rutilus) parasitizing camels, cattle and sheep
Event summary: Until recently, heartwater and its agent Ehrlichia ruminantium were regarded as confined in Africa to sub-Saharan regions and nearby Indian Ocean islands, with no confirmed presence in the countries of Northern Africa including Egypt. A four-year PCR-based survey of 3,940 ticks collected from camels, cattle and sheep in north and north-western Egypt detected E. ruminantium DNA in 16.5% of Hyalomma dromedarii, 2.5% of Rhipicephalus annulatus and 0.3% of R. rutilus ticks, and phylogenetic analysis of the pCS20 locus showed Egyptian sequences clustering with other African E. ruminantium isolates, leading the authors to describe this as the first report of the agent in Egypt. The study inferred that repeated importation of livestock infested with Amblyomma ticks from endemic sub-Saharan countries likely introduced the pathogen, and although no large clinical heartwater outbreaks have yet been reported in Egyptian livestock, the demonstrated establishment of E. ruminantium in local tick populations represents an important northward range expansion and has prompted calls for strengthened surveillance and movement controls.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intense legal and informal trade in camels, cattle and small ruminants into Egypt from sub-Saharan Africa, some of them carrying Amblyomma ticks, coupled with favourable ecological conditions for Hyalomma and Rhipicephalus ticks in the Middle East and North Africa, likely enabled introduction and silent spread of Ehrlichia ruminantium. Internal mechanisms: Sequence data did not indicate a novel genotype; the Egyptian pCS20 sequences clustered with previously described African strains, so this event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion mediated by tick and livestock movements rather than evolution of a new strain or host adaptation.
Review: Decision: retain (new event; flagged for review). This row has been added to capture the first molecular detection of Ehrlichia ruminantium in Egypt, based on a four-year PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases study that found pCS20-positive ticks on camels, cattle and sheep and explicitly states that this is the first report of E. ruminantium in the country. Egypt lies in the UN 'Northern Africa' subregion, where heartwater had not previously been reported, so the event is classified as intra-continental emergence (new African subregion) rather than first global emergence. Because evidence is currently limited to infection in ticks and a small number of clinically affected cattle, and no large-scale heartwater epidemics have yet been described in Egypt, a specialist should confirm that this range-expansion event warrants inclusion among the top post-1990 emergence events for this pathogen.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia
Host: Domestic pigs (breeding sows, suckling and weaned piglets, and fattening pigs) in intensive commercial herds; wild boar in adjacent hunting areas showed serologic evidence of circulation but limited clinical disease
Event summary: From 1990 to 2001, encephalomyocarditis virus caused hundreds of clinical outbreaks of myocarditis and reproductive failure in pig herds across Greece, Italy, Belgium, and Cyprus, with Belgium alone reporting about 320 affected farms and Italy 110, plus high seroprevalence in endemic areas and infection documented in wild boar. In Italy, after initial cases in the late 1980s, the disease reappeared with a severe outbreak in a 2,000‑sow farm in Friuli‑Venezia Giulia in 1996 (over 1,900 piglet deaths), then became endemic in parts of southern Lombardy with dozens of additional herd outbreaks; Belgium and Greece also experienced recurrent seasonal clusters, and Cyprus reported several outbreaks followed by widespread vaccination. Intensified rodent control, enhanced biosecurity, and improved diagnostic surveillance gradually reduced the frequency of clinical outbreaks by the early 2000s, although serologic data showed that subclinical circulation persisted in both domestic pigs and wild boar in affected regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density, intensive pig production with large farrow‑to‑finish systems, abundant commensal rodents on farms, and seasonal spikes in rodent populations created repeated opportunities for spillover via feed and water contaminated with rodent excreta; trade and movement of pigs and feed within endemic regions likely facilitated spread between holdings. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and serologic studies indicated co‑circulation of at least two EMCV genotypes in European pigs and wild boar, but there is no clear evidence that a single novel, more virulent lineage triggered these outbreaks; the epizootic is best interpreted as intra‑continental expansion and endemic maintenance of pre‑existing EMCV lineages under favorable ecological and husbandry conditions.
Review: Decision: retain. Added as a new high‑impact event omitted in the original file, representing 451 documented clinical EMCV outbreaks in pigs across Belgium, Italy, Greece, and Cyprus between 1990 and 2001, with thousands of animals affected; this clearly belongs among the top global EMCV emergence events. Host: Captive baboons (Papio spp.) in a 3,060‑animal research and production colony at the Southwest Foundation for Biomedical Research (San Antonio, Texas)
Event summary: Over a 9‑month period spanning 1990–1991, an epizootic of encephalomyocarditis virus infection in a large baboon colony in San Antonio, Texas caused approximately 80 deaths among animals aged from neonates to 22 years, with sudden death and signs of acute congestive heart failure the most common presentations. Necropsy and histology revealed severe nonsuppurative necrotizing myocarditis with pulmonary edema, and EMCV infection was confirmed by virus isolation, serology, and electron microscopy; concurrent investigation identified EMCV‑infected feral rats on the premises as the most likely source. Implementation of aggressive rodent control coincided with rapid cessation of new cases, and no associated human infections or disease in co‑housed chimpanzees were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Outdoor housing of a large primate colony in an area with substantial feral rat populations, combined with ready access of rodents to primate feed and housing, enabled sustained rodent‑to‑baboon transmission over many months until targeted rodent control broke the transmission chain. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was attributed to a cardiotropic EMCV strain causing severe myocardial infection but, based on available descriptions, did not clearly represent a novel genotype; this episode is therefore interpreted as a major re‑occurrence of endemic EMCV in a highly susceptible primate population driven by environmental and management factors rather than virus evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. New row added to capture a large, well‑documented EMCV epizootic with ~80 baboon deaths, which clearly ranks among the highest‑impact non‑domestic animal events post‑1990 and was missing from the original dataset. Classified as re‑occurrence (not first detection or intra/inter‑continental) because EMCV was already recognized in North American pigs and zoo mammals, and the main drivers are rodent exposure and husbandry rather than spread to a new continent or sub‑region or emergence of a demonstrably novel lineage. Geography (United States of America; Northern America sub‑region) follows the provided country sheet.

Host: Domestic pigs (mainly 3–5‑month‑old growers and adult pigs) on four smallholder farms in Bingerville, Azito, and Grand‑Bassam
Event summary: In 1992–1993, a series of four outbreaks of acute myocarditis compatible with EMCV occurred in pigs in Côte d’Ivoire: an initial episode on a nucleus farm near Bingerville in early 1992 that killed 13 adult pigs, followed by smaller outbreaks in Azito (four 5‑month‑old pigs), Grand‑Bassam (42 3‑month‑old pigs), and another herd near Bingerville (three 4‑month‑old pigs). Affected pigs died suddenly, with necropsies reporting severe myocardial lesions as the principal pathology, consistent with EMCV infection as later summarized in FAO and EMCV outbreak databases. These outbreaks marked the first recognized EMCV‑associated pig disease episodes in West Africa, after earlier swine disease reports in southern Africa, and prompted international attention to rodent‑borne viral threats in emerging pig sectors in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of pig production around Abidjan, together with limited rodent control and storage of feed in structures accessible to commensal rodents, likely facilitated viral introduction from infected rodents into naive herds; climatic variability and feed availability may have influenced rodent population peaks. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence from available summaries that these outbreaks involved a distinct EMCV lineage with altered virulence or host range; the episode is best interpreted as geographic expansion of existing African EMCV lineages into a new West African pig‑producing area, i.e. intra‑continental emergence without clear viral evolutionary change.

New row added to represent the first documented EMCV pig outbreaks in West Africa (Côte d’Ivoire, 1992–1993), which, while smaller than the major European epizootics, are important for capturing intra‑African geographic spread into a new sub‑region. Host: Free‑ranging African elephants (Loxodonta africana) in Kruger National Park; myomorph rodents (especially Mastomys spp.) served as reservoir hosts but were not the primary clinical host in this event
Event summary: Between December 1993 and November 1994, Kruger National Park in South Africa experienced a major outbreak of EMCV‑associated acute myocarditis in free‑ranging African elephants, beginning with a cluster of deaths in late 1993 and peaking in January 1994; in total, 64 elephants died, most of them adult bulls. Virus isolation from elephant myocardium and serologic analysis of archived sera showed that EMCV had been present in the population since at least 1987, and concurrent studies documented a marked increase in rodent abundance and EMCV antibody prevalence in myomorph rodents that coincided with the elephant mortality peak. As rodent populations and infection prevalence subsequently declined and targeted rodent control was implemented around key elephant use areas, new elephant deaths abated and no similar large‑scale EMCV die‑off in Kruger elephants has been reported since.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A rodent population boom, probably related to ecological and environmental conditions in Kruger National Park, substantially increased environmental contamination of elephant foraging and watering sites with EMCV‑infected rodent urine and feces, amplifying exposure of susceptible elephants; human management responses focused on rodent control rather than changes in elephant management. Internal mechanisms: Available virologic and serologic data do not indicate emergence of a novel EMCV strain in this outbreak; instead, the episode reflects a dramatic re‑occurrence of disease caused by an already circulating cardiotropic EMCV lineage in elephants, driven by reservoir population dynamics and exposure intensity rather than viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. This is correctly captured as one of the most consequential EMCV events in wildlife (64 free‑ranging elephants dead in Kruger National Park). Geography (South Africa in Southern Africa) and timing (December 1993–November 1994, summarized as 1993–1994) match the primary outbreak description. Classification as re‑occurrence (not first detection, intra‑, or inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate because serology shows prior circulation in the same sub‑region and the main driver is a rodent population surge, not spread to a new region or viral change. Source selection is appropriate, with the primary Onderstepoort paper and a recent non‑domesticated‑species review providing detailed outbreak data; Wikipedia is used here only as background and could be removed without loss of core information if a stricter primary‑literature‑only policy is desired.

Host: Captive orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus and P. abelii) and sporadically other zoo mammals at the Singapore Zoological Gardens
Event summary: Between July 2001 and January 2002, an outbreak of fatal acute myocarditis occurred in orangutans at the Singapore Zoological Gardens, during which four orangutans of different ages died over about eight months and EMCV was isolated from the hearts and lungs of the two juveniles. Epidemiologic investigation indicated that this represented the first documented EMCV infection in Singapore and South‑East Asia, and virus isolation from tissues of several species in the collection showed that the outbreak affected orangutans most severely but coincided with infection in other zoo mammals. Genetic and antigenic characterization revealed that the Singapore isolates formed a highly divergent lineage (proposed EMCV serotype 3) within Cardiovirus A, making this both a geographic expansion of EMCV into a new Asian sub‑region and an important example of a distinct viral variant causing severe disease in great apes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A tropical zoo setting with substantial rodent activity in and around primate enclosures, combined with shared feed and water sources and high densities of susceptible captive primates, likely enabled repeated spillover from infected rodents into orangutans and other species; routine zoo management practices may have facilitated within‑collection spread. Internal mechanisms: Sequence analyses demonstrated that the orangutan isolates (e.g. Sing‑M100‑02) are highly divergent from previously known EMCV‑1 and EMCV‑2 strains and tentatively represent a third EMCV serotype, consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence and host expansion into new primate species; this justifies classifying the episode as both intra‑continental emergence (first detection in South‑Eastern Asia) and re‑emergence (driven by a distinct lineage).
Review: Decision: review. The original row understated this event as a single fatal orangutan case “around 2002” and relied only on the US zoo outbreak paper; it has been corrected to reflect a multi‑animal outbreak between July 2001 and January 2002 affecting four orangutans (and sporadically other species) at the Singapore Zoological Gardens. The emergence type has been updated to intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence, because this is the first documented EMCV infection in South‑East Asia and involves a highly divergent lineage (proposed EMCV‑3). The primary source URL has been changed to the dedicated Virology Journal article on the Singapore outbreak, with the US “zoological transmission” paper retained only as supporting context for strain nomenclature; these changes and the reliance on a small number of key sources warrant human verification, but the event clearly merits inclusion among major EMCV emergences.
