Host: Captive African elephant (Loxodonta africana) and commensal rats at the Réserve Africaine de Sigean zoo in southern France
Event summary: In November 2013, a captive African elephant at the Réserve Africaine de Sigean zoo in southern France died suddenly with gross and histologic evidence of acute myocarditis, and EMCV RNA and infectious virus were detected in heart and other tissues. Follow‑up trapping of commensal rats in the zoo identified EMCV infection in rodents, and sequencing showed 98–100% identity between elephant and rat strains, confirming active rodent‑mediated circulation of EMCV within the collection. After intensified rodent control and biosecurity measures were implemented, no further EMCV‑associated elephant deaths were reported at this facility, and the event is regarded as a contained but high‑impact recurrence of EMCV disease in European zoo megafauna.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of commensal rats with access to feed stores and elephant housing, together with limited initial rodent control, created conditions for sustained EMCV circulation on the premises and spillover into a highly susceptible captive elephant; improved housing hygiene and rodent control sharply reduced risk after the case. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization showed that the elephant and rat viruses were typical EMCV Cardiovirus A1 strains closely related to other European swine and wildlife isolates, without evidence of a novel genotype, so the episode reflects re‑occurrence of an established lineage in a new individual host rather than virus evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. The original description of this event is accurate and appropriately sourced from the detailed French zoo case report. Geographic coding (Europe | Western Europe; France) and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate, because EMCV was long established in European pigs and wildlife and there is no indication of a new lineage; intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence are not justified. No major changes were required beyond minor wording edits for clarity, so this row can be kept as one of the principal zoo‑based EMCV emergence events.

Host: Multiple captive zoo mammals in the southeastern United States, including an African elephant, an East African hippopotamus, and a common brown lemur (Eulemur fulvus), plus associated rodents on zoo grounds
Event summary: Between approximately 2018 and 2020, a series of fatal EMCV infections occurred in US zoological collections in the southeastern states, including an East African hippopotamus at a Texas zoo in 2018 (isolate N‑19‑013), a common brown lemur at a south Florida facility in 2020 (N‑20‑413), and an index African elephant case (N‑037‑19) that prompted detailed investigation and vaccine development. Within at least one affected institution, multiple susceptible species died over a period of only a few weeks, with necropsies showing severe necrotizing myocarditis and pulmonary edema consistent with EMCV. Following diagnosis, zoos implemented intensive rodent control, improved enclosure and feed‑storage hygiene, and, in at least one case, an autogenous inactivated EMCV vaccine program for elephants and other high‑value species; after these measures, EMCV‑associated deaths in the involved collections declined sharply, though EMCV remains a recognized recurrent threat in North American zoos.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Co‑housing of diverse, often immunologically naive zoo mammals in outdoor or semi‑outdoor enclosures where synanthropic rodents can access feed and bedding created repeated opportunities for spillover; shared feed sources and occasional animal transfers may have contributed to within‑ and between‑facility spread. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses of N‑037‑19, N‑19‑013, and N‑20‑413 showed that these viruses belong to EMCV serotype 1 and share close capsid antigenic profiles with other recent EMCV‑1 strains rather than representing a novel species or serotype; the episode is therefore best viewed as a re‑occurrence of endemic EMCV in high‑value zoo hosts with enhanced transmission at the wildlife–rodent interface, rather than emergence of a fundamentally new lineage.
Review: Decision: retain. The timeframe (2018–2020), host range (elephant, hippopotamus, lemur), and characterization of this as a multi‑facility zoo outbreak cluster are consistent with the recent "zoological transmission" study; no substantive corrections were needed beyond phrasing. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, given long‑standing EMCV presence in North American pigs and zoo mammals and the lack of evidence that these isolates constitute a new serotype; intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is not supported. Because the event description aggregates several closely linked fatal cases across facilities but the exact start and end dates are approximate, a human reviewer may wish to refine the date range if more detailed facility‑level timelines are needed, but the event clearly qualifies as a major modern zoo emergence episode.

Host: Growing–finishing pigs on two commercial farms in the state of Mato Grosso, with infected commensal rats (Rattus rattus) trapped on the premises
Event summary: After a 38‑year gap since the last documented swine case in 1985, two growing–finishing pig farms in Mato Grosso, midwestern Brazil, experienced outbreaks of sudden death among 120–130‑day‑old pigs investigated in April 2023, with batch‑level mortalities around 9–10% compared with expected losses of <2%. Necropsy and histopathology of seven pigs showed severe myocardial necrosis, dystrophic mineralization, fibrosis, and lymphoplasmacytic myocarditis, and EMCV RNA was detected by RT‑PCR in multiple pig organs and in the brains and feces of trapped rats; VP1 sequencing indicated that pig and rat viruses were nearly identical and closely related to strains previously reported from humans in Peru. These findings represent the third recorded occurrence of EMCV in Brazil, the first with molecular characterization, and a clear re‑emergence of EMCV as a swine pathogen with significant mortality in South American commercial herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term absence of diagnosed EMCV in Brazilian swine created large, immunologically naive pig populations; growing pig production and trade in the midwestern region, combined with local rodent infestations and gaps in rodent control and biosecurity, likely allowed introduction and establishment of EMCV on the affected farms. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analysis showed that the Brazilian pig and rat strains belong to Cardiovirus A1 and are closely related to Peruvian human isolates, consistent with regional circulation of a specific lineage that recently entered Brazilian herds; the notably high mortality and detection in both pigs and rats support classification as a re‑emergence event driven by introduction of a distinct lineage into a naive host population rather than simple re‑occurrence of an endemic strain.
Review: Decision: review. The original row mis‑timed this event as “early 2020s” (2020–2023); it has been corrected to 2023 based on the study’s report of outbreaks investigated during farm visits in April 2023 and the stated 38‑year gap since the previous pig case in 1985. The event summary has been rewritten to align closely with the primary article (two farms in Mato Grosso, mortality levels, histopathology, RT‑PCR results, and phylogenetic link to Peruvian strains), and the classification as re‑emergence has been retained because this is explicitly framed as a re‑emergence of EMCV in Brazilian swine involving a characterized lineage. Reviewers should verify whether any additional Brazilian EMCV pig outbreaks occurred after the study period that would warrant extending the end year or adding linked rows, but as currently documented this 2023 episode clearly belongs among the top global EMCV emergence events in livestock.

Host: Primarily Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp); later also Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei in Thai farms
Event summary: In the early 2000s, Thai farms culturing Penaeus monodon experienced a “monodon slow growth syndrome” with severe size disparity and poor growth, causing national production losses estimated at around 13 000 million baht (~USD 300 million) by 2002.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15460852/?utm_source=openai)) In 2004, histopathology of slow‑growing shrimp from commercial ponds in Thailand revealed a previously undescribed cytoplasmic microsporidian infecting hepatopancreatic tubule epithelial cells, and this parasite was formally described in 2009 as Enterocytozoon hepatopenaei, marking the first confirmed detection of EHP in penaeid aquaculture.([scielo.cl](https://www.scielo.cl/pdf/lajar/v51n1/0718-560X-lajar-51-01-0001.pdf)) During 2004–2009 the pathogen became established in Thai shrimp production—initially in P. monodon and later also in P. vannamei—leading to chronic growth retardation and entrenched economic losses, after which improved diagnostics and on‑farm biosecurity helped stabilize but not eliminate endemic infection.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification of shrimp aquaculture in Thailand with high stocking densities, large‑scale movement of broodstock and postlarvae, and limited early adoption of biosecurity, together with reuse of pond water and sediments, facilitated pond‑to‑pond and farm‑to‑farm transmission of EHP. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion and amplification of a previously unrecognized microsporidian within intensive farm systems, with efficient horizontal transmission via ingestion of spores in feces and detritus and chronic hepatopancreatic infection that primarily impairs growth rather than causing acute mortality, as shown in experimental cohabitation and challenge studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5216530/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Reclassified this episode as a global 'first detection' rather than 'first/global emergence' because earlier, morphologically similar but undescribed microsporidians had been reported from shrimp in Malaysia and Australia, implying that EHP may have been present but unrecognized before 2004. Also clarified that the ≈USD 300 million loss estimate refers to the broader early‑2000s slow‑growth crisis in Thailand and not solely to EHP. Geographic fields and host list remain correct, but the event should be re‑checked by a subject‑matter expert before finalization.

Host: Primarily Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (whiteleg shrimp), also Penaeus monodon in parts of the region
Event summary: From 2010 onward, shrimp farms in Viet Nam and later in other South‑eastern Asian countries began reporting slow growth, size variation and white feces in P. monodon and especially P. vannamei, with histology, PCR and in situ hybridization confirming EHP as a key pathogen associated with these syndromes.([ouci.dntb.gov.ua](https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/4aBVkKz5/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s EHP was widely detected in shrimp farms across Viet Nam, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia—Indonesia and Malaysia reporting confirmed farm outbreaks by 2016—contributing to chronic production losses and complex disease situations involving co‑infections such as AHPND.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27530403/?utm_source=openai)) Control efforts across the subregion emphasized improved pond preparation, biosecurity, screening of broodstock and postlarvae, and better management of co‑infections, but EHP remained highly prevalent and entrenched in shrimp‑farming areas of South‑eastern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive regional trade and movement of live shrimp (broodstock and postlarvae) between farms and countries, high farm densities along shared coastlines, shared water sources and equipment, and inadequate pond disinfection between cycles facilitated transboundary spread and persistence of EHP throughout South‑eastern Asia. Internal mechanisms: high environmental resilience of spores, efficient horizontal transmission via ingestion of contaminated feces and detritus, and probable vertical transmission from broodstock to larvae demonstrated experimentally, together with widespread adoption of P. vannamei, allowed the parasite to maintain high prevalence in the region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5216530/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Extended this linked South‑eastern Asia episode to 2010–2016 and updated country onsets to Viet Nam [2010] and Indonesia and Malaysia [2016], reflecting the timing of first peer‑reviewed reports and regional summaries. Retained the 're_occurrence' label because this represents intensification and geographic widening of EHP within an already affected sub‑region, not spread to a new UNSD sub‑region, and kept 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_emergence' as 'No'. Event is broadly well supported but should be re‑checked for whether additional SE Asian countries (e.g. Philippines, Brunei) warrant explicit inclusion.

Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (whiteleg shrimp) cultured in China
Event summary: Starting in 2013, EHP was detected for the first time in Chinese shrimp farms, initially in coastal provinces such as Jiangsu and Shandong, where P. vannamei showed reduced growth, size disparities and hepatopancreatic lesions similar to those described previously in Thailand and Viet Nam.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352513420306773?utm_source=openai)) As surveillance expanded, EHP was recognized as an important cause of chronic production problems in whiteleg shrimp along much of China’s coastline, with epidemiological surveys in the 2010s and early 2020s documenting substantial farm‑level prevalence and serious associated economic losses.([yykxjz.ijournals.cn](https://yykxjz.ijournals.cn/yykxjz/article/abstract/20230215002?st=article_issue&utm_source=openai)) Chinese farms responded by integrating EHP diagnostics into routine health monitoring, adopting improved biosecurity and pond management, and adjusting stocking densities, although the pathogen is now considered endemic in major shrimp‑farming areas of Eastern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation and domestic movement of broodstock and postlarvae from EHP‑endemic South‑eastern Asian sources, rapid intensification of P. vannamei farming in coastal China, and frequent water exchange with surrounding environments likely facilitated introduction and dissemination of EHP; co‑occurrence with other hepatopancreatic diseases such as AHPND further stressed farms.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0044848616307141?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: efficient horizontal transmission in intensive pond systems and possible vertical transmission, together with chronic, growth‑retarding infection rather than acute mortality, allowed EHP to establish and spread before it was widely recognized, necessitating the development of new molecular diagnostics and on‑farm control guidelines.
Review: review – Corrected the start year and country‑specific onset from an imprecise '≈2010' to China [2013], based on Chinese reports that EHP has been detected in cultured shrimp there since 2013 and became widespread thereafter. Classification as an intra‑continental emergence (spread from South‑eastern to Eastern Asia) is consistent with UNSD sub‑regions and has been retained. No other structural changes were made, but a human reviewer should confirm the chosen end year for this early‑phase Chinese emergence window.

Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei and Penaeus monodon cultured in India
Event summary: Around 2014, Indian farms culturing specific‑pathogen‑free P. vannamei on the southeast coast began reporting severe growth retardation and marked size variation, and investigations using histopathology, electron microscopy, PCR and in situ hybridization confirmed EHP infection in affected shrimp, marking the first confirmed emergence of EHP in India.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0044848615303045?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent surveys of slow‑growth ponds across major shrimp‑farming states showed very high EHP prevalence in both P. vannamei and P. monodon, demonstrating rapid spread and making EHP a major contributor to chronic production losses.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27503918/?utm_source=openai)) Indian authorities and research institutes incorporated EHP into routine surveillance, developed improved diagnostics and training materials, and recommended strengthened hatchery screening, pond drying, disinfection and biosecurity to limit further spread.([ciba.res.in](https://www.ciba.res.in/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/EHP%20training%20manual%202021.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive whiteleg shrimp farming in India, large‑scale importation and domestic movement of broodstock and postlarvae, and suboptimal biosecurity and pond hygiene created opportunities for EHP introduction and dissemination; co‑farming of multiple shrimp species and frequent co‑infection with viral pathogens such as white spot syndrome virus and AHPND‑causing Vibrio exacerbated disease impact.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0044848615303045?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion from South‑eastern to Southern Asia, efficient transmission via contaminated pond water, sediment and feces, and probable vertical transmission contributed to high prevalence; the predominantly chronic, growth‑retarding infection phenotype allowed the parasite to become widespread before being recognized as a distinct problem.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first confirmed emergence of EHP in Indian shrimp aquaculture (2014) and its rapid spread and high prevalence, with appropriate classification as an intra‑continental emergence from South‑eastern to Southern Asia and well‑matched peer‑reviewed sources. No structural corrections were required, though a minor update could later refine the end year if more detailed epidemiological data become available.

Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (whiteleg shrimp) cultured in Venezuela
Event summary: In 2016, Venezuelan shrimp farms experiencing slow growth, size variation and white feces in cultured P. vannamei were found to be infected with EHP alongside Taura syndrome virus, providing the first confirmed report of EHP in Latin America and the first confirmation of the parasite outside Asia.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S004484861731030X?utm_source=openai)) Histopathology, in situ hybridization and PCR showed typical hepatopancreatic microsporidiosis lesions, and phylogenetic analyses indicated that Venezuelan EHP sequences clustered closely with, but were distinguishable from, Asian isolates, consistent with introduction from Asia followed by some local diversification.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S004484861731030X?utm_source=openai)) The combined impacts of EHP and re‑emerging Taura syndrome virus raised concern over compounded production losses in Venezuela and highlighted the risk of further spread of EHP within South America, prompting increased regional awareness and surveillance.

Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (Pacific whiteleg shrimp) and, later, giant freshwater prawn cultured in Korea
Event summary: In April 2020, indoor shrimp farms in the Republic of Korea culturing Pacific whiteleg shrimp with growth disorders were confirmed to harbor EHP, representing the first detection of the parasite in Korean aquaculture and extending its known range within the Eastern Asia subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8614486/?utm_source=openai)) Follow‑up investigations detected EHP in additional P. vannamei farms and, by 2022, in farmed giant freshwater prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii), indicating host expansion beyond marine penaeids.([kci.go.kr](https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/landing/article.kci?arti_id=ART003091386&utm_source=openai)) Phylogenetic analyses showed that Korean EHP isolates formed a distinct clade relative to previously reported strains from Thailand, Viet Nam, China and India, and although overall prevalence remained lower than in heavily affected South‑eastern Asian countries, Korean authorities classified EHP as an emerging disease requiring routine monitoring, biosecurity and quarantine measures to prevent wider establishment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8614486/?utm_source=openai))

'Re_emergence' is retained as 'Yes' to reflect host expansion to Macrobrachium rosenbergii and the distinct Korean clade reported by phylogenetic analyses. Country, year of first detection (2020), and Eastern Asia sub‑region coding remain consistent with the primary reports but should be double‑checked by an expert.

Countries: Italy [1992]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1992]; Belgium [1993]; Spain [1993]; Portugal [1995]
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: After a period of low SVD activity in Europe, a new antigenic–genetic SVDV variant (the fourth European lineage) became established in Italy and was first recognized in both Italy and the Netherlands in 1992. Over the next few years, movement of infected pigs and contaminated vehicles seeded linked outbreaks in other Western and Southern European countries, including Belgium and Spain in 1993 and Portugal in 1995, prompting EU‑wide control measures and trade restrictions. Through aggressive stamping‑out, movement controls and intensified serological surveillance, these Western European outbreaks were eliminated by the mid‑1990s, leaving Italy as the main remaining reservoir of the new lineage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of intra‑European trade in live pigs and pig products, movements of infected animals from Italy and possibly from Far‑Eastern source regions, and contaminated trucks and equipment facilitated spread into high‑density pig areas in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain and Portugal; detection was hampered by the clinical similarity of SVD to other vesicular diseases. Internal mechanisms: molecular and antigenic studies show that this wave was driven by a distinct fourth antigenic–genetic variant of SVDV derived from earlier strains, consistent with viral evolution and selection facilitating renewed spread in European pig populations (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Enhanced transmission in intensive pig systems; Geographic range expansion within Europe).
Review: review – Corrected the event window to 1992–1995 (reflecting that the fourth antigenic SVDV variant was first reported in Italy and the Netherlands in 1992), and added Portugal [1995] as an affected country in this wave based on EU, WOAH/OIE and review data. Also removed a duplicate ScienceDirect URL and added more specific outbreak documentation (EU decision on Dutch outbreaks; OIE reports for Spain and Belgium). Classification as a re-emergence driven by a novel European lineage remains appropriate and is retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: After the 1992–1995 European resurgence, SVDV remained endemic mainly in central and southern Italy, with sporadic but persistent outbreaks in commercial and backyard pig farms. During 1996–2005, repeated re‑introductions via pig movements and environmental persistence on farms produced a background of low‑level cases that triggered EU safeguard measures and led to the implementation and later strengthening of the Italian national surveillance and eradication programme. These outbreaks gradually declined in number toward the mid‑2000s but the virus was not eliminated, setting the stage for a large epidemic in northern Italy in 2006–2007.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense pig production in parts of Italy, frequent movement of pigs and pig transport vehicles, and inadequate cleansing/disinfection of vehicles and premises allowed virus persistence and re‑seeding between herds; non‑compliance in some smallholder and informal production systems hindered eradication. Internal mechanisms: persistence of established Italian lineages with strong environmental stability and long survival in pork products supported ongoing low‑level transmission, but there is no strong evidence that novel, more virulent genotypes drove this phase (primary mechanism: external drivers and environmental persistence rather than major viral change).
Review: retain – Evidence from WOAH/OIE documentation, Italian surveillance data and genomic studies shows that after the early‑1990s European wave, SVDV persisted endemically in central and southern Italy with recurrent low‑level outbreaks through the late 1990s and early 2000s. The chosen time window, country coverage (Italy only) and classification as re-occurrence driven mainly by movement, biosecurity and environmental persistence are consistent with published information, so no structural changes were made.

Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: In late 1997, SVDV re‑emerged in Taiwan (reported by WOAH/OIE as Taipei China) after several years without recognized cases, with a laboratory‑confirmed infection in a backyard sow from Pingtung/Kaohsiung that was initially suspected to be foot‑and‑mouth disease. Subsequent years saw additional outbreaks in 1998 and 2000 and serologic evidence of wider endemic circulation, which complicated diagnosis and control during Taiwan’s concurrent 1997 FMD epizootic and led to enhanced surveillance for vesicular diseases. Control measures linked to the FMD response, together with culling, movement controls and improvements in garbage‑feeding and market hygiene, were followed by disappearance of reported SVD, and WOAH/OIE records indicate that the last recognized SVD case in the Far East occurred in Taiwan in 2000.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high pig density, widespread use of untreated swill, movement of pigs through live markets and informal channels, and limited early laboratory capacity for differentiating SVD from FMD allowed continued circulation and intermittent detection of SVDV in Taiwan during 1997–2000; the simultaneous FMD crisis delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: recent phylodynamic work suggests that these Taiwanese outbreaks formed part of a broader pattern in which human Coxsackievirus B5–like lineages repeatedly recombined and spilled over into pigs to generate SVDV, so this episode is best characterized as re-emergence via novel strain/genotype emergence and host expansion from humans to pigs rather than simple re-occurrence of a long‑established endemic lineage.
Review: review – Added this new row to capture the re-emergence of SVDV in Taiwan (reported as Taipei China) in 1997, 1998 and 2000, which multiple sources identify as the last recognized SVD activity in the Far East and as part of the same anthropo‑zoonotic lineage complex that seeded European outbreaks. Because detailed outbreak counts are scarce and country naming conventions are politically sensitive, the event is represented as a single multi‑year episode under Eastern Asia with China [Taiwan, 1997] as the country label, and is flagged for further expert review of timing, magnitude and nomenclature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, SVDV reappeared in the Iberian Peninsula via Portugal, which reported outbreaks in 2003 and 2004 and a further incident in 2007 in pig‑dense regions with active trade links to Italy. Genetic analyses showed that the Portuguese viruses were closely related to contemporary Italian strains, indicating re‑introduction from the long‑standing Italian reservoir rather than the emergence of an independent endemic focus. Through intensified stamping‑out, movement restrictions and targeted serological surveillance, Portugal eliminated SVDV again by the late 2000s, and no further outbreaks have since been reported there.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cross‑border trade and movement of live pigs and possibly contaminated pork products from infected Italian regions into Portugal, combined with gaps in farm and transport biosecurity and delays in detecting mild vesicular signs, facilitated re‑introduction into Portuguese pig herds and created risks for neighboring Iberian production. Internal mechanisms: the Portuguese viruses belonged to the same European lineage circulating in Italy and do not represent a fundamentally new genotype; the episode is therefore best explained by animal movements and environmental stability of the virus rather than major viral innovation (Re-occurrence driven by trade and environmental persistence).
Review: review – Restricted this episode to Portugal only and removed Spain from the country list and narrative, because WOAH/OIE summaries and later reviews indicate that Spain’s last SVD outbreaks occurred in 1993 and that only Portugal (2003–2004 and 2007) and Italy reported SVD in the 2000s. Updated the event summary and drivers accordingly while retaining the classification as re-occurrence driven by re-introduction from the Italian reservoir via trade.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: In mid‑2006, a new recombinant SVDV lineage within the long‑circulating European fourth antigenic variant was introduced into northern Italy, probably entering high‑density pig‑producing areas in Lombardy (e.g. Brescia) and remaining undetected for some weeks before the first case was recognized at slaughter in Bergamo. Between 2006 and 2007 this epidemic led to roughly 140 notified outbreaks and the slaughter of more than 150,000 pigs, with spread largely driven by movements of infected animals and contaminated transport vehicles between commercial farms, dealers’ premises and slaughterhouses. Intensive epidemiological tracing, strengthened farm and transport biosecurity, regionalization and stamping‑out measures ultimately contained the epidemic by the end of 2007, although related viruses continued to circulate at lower levels in parts of southern Italy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of infected pigs or contaminated transport into intensive pig systems in northern Italy, combined with very high herd density, extensive within‑country pig movements and incomplete cleansing and disinfection of vehicles and premises, allowed rapid farm‑to‑farm spread before controls were tightened; traders’ premises and long‑distance movements played a key role. Internal mechanisms: whole‑genome sequencing shows that the 2006–2007 epidemic was driven by a distinct recombinant lineage within the established European variant, closely related to viruses detected earlier in Portugal and southern Italy, with evidence of recombination and adaptive evolution that may have facilitated its successful spread (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Geographic range expansion within Italy; Enhanced transmission in intensive pig production systems).
Review: review – Restricted the country list for this event to Italy, because WOAH/OIE and genomic analyses treat the 2006–2007 epidemic as an Italian outbreak genetically related to but not epidemiologically continuous with earlier Portuguese cases; Portugal is instead covered in a separate 2003–2007 re-occurrence event. Updated outbreak numbers to align with OIE reports (approximately 140 outbreaks and >150,000 pigs culled) and clarified that this wave represents re-emergence driven by a recombinant lineage within the European variant.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [2008]; Italy [2015, last recorded outbreak worldwide]
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event summary: Following the 2006–2007 epidemic in northern Italy, SVDV continued to circulate at low levels in a few regions of Italy, causing sporadic outbreaks detected through the strengthened national surveillance and eradication programme. Between 2008 and 2015, these residual foci were repeatedly re‑ignited by illegal or poorly controlled pig movements, insufficient farm biosecurity and environmental persistence of the virus, prompting EU measures specifically targeting SVD in Italy and progressive enlargement of control zones. Implementation of enhanced surveillance, trace‑back and strict movement controls ultimately led to the last recorded clinical outbreak in Calabria in 2015, after which only seropositive pigs were detected (until 2017), and SVDV was subsequently declared eradicated from Italy and, by extension, from domestic pigs globally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued movement of pigs from non‑compliant or illegal holdings, vehicles contaminated with manure or pork products, and the virus’s marked environmental stability allowed sporadic re‑introductions into Italian farms despite control programmes; policy tools such as EU Decision 2005/779/EC and intensified national measures were required to progressively close these gaps. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new genotypes were identified in this late phase; rather, persistence of existing Italian lineages and their ability to survive in the environment and in pork products underpinned recurrent flare‑ups (Re-occurrence driven by external factors and environmental persistence; geographic spread remained confined to already affected Italian subregions).
Review: retain – The 2008–2015 window, restriction to Italy, and characterization as low-level re-occurrence following the 2006–2007 epidemic are consistent with Italian eradication programme reports and WOAH/EU documentation, which show continued sporadic outbreaks through 2015 and only serological positives through 2017. No structural changes were needed, so this event is retained as-is apart from minor wording harmonization with updated Italy-wide eradication data.

Countries: Australia (Lake Burrinjuck [1990], Lake Burley Griffin [1991; 1994], Lake Ginninderra [1994], Googong Reservoir [1994], all in the upper Murrumbidgee River / Canberra region of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory)
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) as the confirmed host; co‑occurring native species such as Macquarie perch (Macquaria australasica) were shown experimentally to be highly susceptible and were almost certainly exposed in some affected impoundments, but clinical EHN has not been definitively documented in native fish during this episode.([ewater.org.au](https://ewater.org.au/archive/crcfe/freshwater/publications.nsf/3eb684c73f8449acca256f1200284afb/9ffa733471131b0aca25725f00244a04/%24FILE/Macq%20Perch%20reintrod%20Qbyn%20R%20-%20Web%202006.pdf))
Event summary: From 1990 to 1994, EHNV caused recurrent mass mortality events in wild redfin perch across several impoundments in the upper Murrumbidgee River catchment, including Burrinjuck Dam, Lake Burley Griffin, Lake Ginninderra and Googong Reservoir, representing a major wave of spread north from the original Victorian focus into the Canberra region.([ewater.org.au](https://ewater.org.au/archive/crcfe/freshwater/publications.nsf/3eb684c73f8449acca256f1200284afb/9ffa733471131b0aca25725f00244a04/%24FILE/Macq%20Perch%20reintrod%20Qbyn%20R%20-%20Web%202006.pdf)) These outbreaks produced sudden die‑offs dominated by juvenile redfin but also occasionally affecting adults, and coincided with areas holding threatened native species such as Macquarie perch, which were likely exposed to the virus. Following this wave, EHNV became established as an endemic pathogen in redfin populations of the upper Murrumbidgee system, with later surveillance detecting the virus at low prevalence even as overt epizootics became less frequent.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread illegal and legal translocation of redfin perch within south‑eastern Australia, hydrological connectivity among Murrumbidgee impoundments, recreational boating and fishing gear moving between lakes, and altered flow regimes associated with dams all facilitated the stepwise spread of EHNV into new reservoirs.([ewater.org.au](https://ewater.org.au/archive/crcfe/freshwater/publications.nsf/3eb684c73f8449acca256f1200284afb/9ffa733471131b0aca25725f00244a04/%24FILE/Macq%20Perch%20reintrod%20Qbyn%20R%20-%20Web%202006.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV shows high environmental stability and extreme virulence in redfin perch, enabling rapid amplification after introduction into naïve populations and supporting long‑term persistence in invaded catchments even when large epizootics become rare.
Review: REVIEW – retain event but with corrected classification and clarified host description. Re‑emergence has been set to false (re‑occurrence remains true) because there is no evidence that this wave was driven by viral genetic change or a novel host strain; it represents geographic spread and repeated outbreaks within an already affected UNSD sub‑region.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) The host field has been adjusted to avoid implying confirmed clinical disease in Macquarie perch, reflecting that their involvement in these specific outbreaks is inferred from susceptibility studies rather than direct diagnostic confirmation. Overall spatial and temporal framing, and listed waterbodies, are well supported by Lintermans (2006), Whittington et al. (1996) and later syntheses, so the event is recommended for retention with these clarifications.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia (multiple commercial rainbow trout farms in the Murrumbidgee River catchment, New South Wales, and at least one farm in the Shoalhaven River catchment, plus affected farms in Victoria)
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), mainly 0+ post‑hatchery fingerlings and small growers, with infection pressure maintained by co‑endemic EHNV reservoirs in nearby wild redfin perch populations.
Event summary: Between 1986 and 1992, EHNV was repeatedly detected on commercial rainbow trout farms in south‑eastern Australia, particularly in the Murrumbidgee and Shoalhaven River catchments of New South Wales, following establishment of the virus in redfin perch within the same drainage systems.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) Outbreaks typically involved low‑to‑moderate increases in mortality among 0+ fingerlings less than 125 mm long, with laboratory testing showing high proportions of clinically affected and dead fish positive for EHNV but very low prevalence in in‑contact survivors. As awareness and surveillance improved, farms adopted stricter biosecurity and stocking practices, and subsequent cohorts often cleared the virus, limiting long‑term persistence on farms but demonstrating that EHNV had expanded its effective host range from wild redfin to intensively reared salmonids in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of live trout fingerlings between hatcheries and grow‑out farms, use of potentially contaminated transport water, and proximity to EHNV‑infected wild redfin perch populations in shared catchments created repeated opportunities for spillover into aquaculture facilities. Poor water quality, high stocking density and low water‑exchange rates on some farms were correlated with clinical disease expression.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV is highly virulent but relatively poorly transmissible in rainbow trout, leading to outbreaks characterized by low infection prevalence but high case‑fatality among infected fingerlings; the virus’s ability to infect both redfin and trout represents a host‑expansion dynamic and justifies classification of this multi‑year farmed‑fish episode as re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: REVIEW – correct and retain, but adjust timing and classification. The main epidemiological work on EHNV in farmed rainbow trout documents five outbreaks on a New South Wales farm from 1986–1992 and similar episodes on other farms, with no strong evidence that outbreaks continued through the late 1990s; the event period has therefore been corrected from 1990–1999 to 1986–1992 to match the published data.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) To reflect that this event primarily represents host expansion from wild redfin to farmed trout rather than a simple resurgence in an already affected host, re_emergence is set to true and re_occurrence to false. Users who wish to strictly enforce the 1990‑onward time window could, if necessary, treat this as a 1990–1992 subset of the same multi‑year episode, but epidemiologically the 1986–1992 interval is more coherent.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – lower Murray River system including Lake Alexandrina and Lake Albert, Mount Bold Reservoir near Adelaide, and subsequent detections further upstream near Renmark and in metropolitan reservoirs)
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) experiencing mass mortalities; co‑occurring native species such as Murray cod, silver perch and other Murray–Darling natives were at risk of exposure, but confirmed EHN disease in native species was not reported in this wave.
Event summary: In 1991–1992, EHNV was first confirmed in South Australia when die‑offs of redfin perch in the lower Murray River system were diagnosed as epizootic haematopoietic necrosis, with affected sites including Lakes Alexandrina and Albert at the Murray mouth and Mount Bold Reservoir in the Mount Lofty Ranges.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287841352_Silver_Perch_A_Resource_Document)) Reports compiled in the early 1990s indicated that the virus was subsequently detected further upstream near Renmark and in metropolitan Adelaide reservoirs, revealing a rapid downstream and lateral spread through South Australian waters following its earlier establishment in upstream Victorian and New South Wales catchments. After this wave, official reporting indicates that EHN has not been recorded again in South Australia since the early 1990s, although redfin and other susceptible species remain present and surveillance continues.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance human‑mediated movement of redfin perch (both deliberate stocking and illegal translocations), combined with river regulation and impoundments along the Murray that facilitate the accumulation and downstream transport of infected fish and carcasses, likely introduced EHNV into South Australian waters.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287841352_Silver_Perch_A_Resource_Document)) Internal mechanisms: As in other regions, high virulence of EHNV in redfin perch and its capacity to persist in water and fish tissues for extended periods underpinned conspicuous mass‑mortality events once the virus reached naive redfin populations in large lower‑river lakes and reservoirs.
Review: REVIEW – new event added to capture a major 1991–1992 emergence episode omitted from the original dataset. Silver perch recovery documents and national field guides identify 1991 as the first confirmed detection of EHNV in South Australia, with mass redfin mortality in Lakes Alexandrina and Albert and Mount Bold Reservoir and subsequent spread to other reservoirs, and WOAH/DAWE summaries list EHN as historically present in SA with last reports in the early 1990s.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287841352_Silver_Perch_A_Resource_Document)) This episode is among the most geographically extensive and impactful wild‑fish events since 1990 and should be included; it is classified as re‑occurrence because it represents further spread within the already infected Australia & New Zealand sub‑region without evidence of viral genetic change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (Lake Ginninderra, Australian Capital Territory [outbreaks confirmed in December 2008 and December 2010])
Host: Wild juvenile European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis); endangered Macquarie perch and other native species in nearby catchments were considered at high risk but no confirmed EHN cases in natives were reported from this lake.
Event summary: In December 2008, EHNV was confirmed as the cause of a large mortality event in juvenile redfin perch in Lake Ginninderra in the Australian Capital Territory, marking a clear resurgence of EHN at a site with severe epizootics documented in the early 1990s.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) A further outbreak in December 2010 again produced conspicuous die‑offs of juvenile redfin, demonstrating that EHNV persisted within the upper Murrumbidgee endemic focus and could periodically re‑emerge when susceptible cohorts accumulated. Intensive surveillance conducted between 2007 and 2011 found EHNV to be absent from redfin outside the upper Murrumbidgee endemic area, underscoring the localised but persistent nature of this focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued dominance of invasive redfin perch in Canberra‑region lakes, frequent movement of anglers and recreational craft between impoundments, and stable cool‑water conditions that favour EHNV replication and transmission all contributed to periodic re‑appearance of disease at Lake Ginninderra.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Long‑term environmental persistence of EHNV in endemic catchments and its high virulence for juvenile redfin underpin episodic mass‑mortality events when large naive cohorts are present, even if overall prevalence in the redfin population remains low between outbreaks.
Review: REVIEW – retain event but adjust classification. Evidence from Becker et al. (2019) and associated surveillance shows that these 2008 and 2010 Lake Ginninderra outbreaks are classic re‑occurrence in an established endemic focus, with no indication of a novel strain, new host, or inter‑/intra‑continental spread; accordingly, re_emergence has been set to false while re_occurrence remains true.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) All other fields, including timing, location and host, align well with published data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Australia (Blowering Dam, upper Murrumbidgee River catchment, New South Wales [December 2009])
Host: Wild juvenile European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis); other susceptible native and introduced fishes in the upper Murrumbidgee system were at risk of exposure but disease was only confirmed in redfin during this event.
Event summary: In December 2009, EHNV was confirmed in juvenile redfin perch from a fish‑kill event in Blowering Dam, a major impoundment in the upper Murrumbidgee River catchment of New South Wales that had experienced earlier, largely anecdotal EHN outbreaks in the late 1980s and early 1990s.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) The 2009 detection involved conspicuous disease in redfin but did not result in documented clinical cases in native fishes, and subsequent basin‑wide surveys indicated that EHNV remained restricted to the known endemic focus rather than spreading into other catchments. This event nonetheless highlighted ongoing circulation of EHNV in one of the Murray–Darling Basin’s largest headwater reservoirs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent redfin populations in Blowering Dam, angler‑mediated movement of live bait and fishing gear, and the dam’s large volume and cool‑water regime, which favour dense redfin assemblages, set the stage for periodic EHN outbreaks when environmental conditions and host demography allowed.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: As in other reservoirs, EHNV’s capacity to remain at low prevalence between outbreaks, coupled with high case‑fatality in juvenile redfin, leads to episodic but sometimes dramatic mortality events without necessarily leaving strong serological signatures in surviving fish.
Review: REVIEW – retain event but adjust classification. The 2009 Blowering Dam episode is well supported by the 2007–2011 surveillance work and subsequent syntheses as a re‑occurrence within the upper Murrumbidgee endemic area; there is no evidence that it involved a novel strain or first detection in a new UNSD sub‑region, so re_emergence has been set to false while re_occurrence remains true.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Location, timing and host information are consistent with available sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Australia (Lake Hume, upper Murray River, on the Victoria–New South Wales border – especially around Lake Hume Resort [2021])
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis); low numbers of fish with lesions consistent with EHN were reported, and other species were under surveillance but not confirmed infected during this episode.
Event summary: In 2021, cases of suspected and confirmed EHNV infection were reported from redfin perch caught near Lake Hume Resort on Lake Hume, a large Murray River impoundment on the Victoria–New South Wales border where EHNV‑associated disease had previously been recorded in the 1980s.([finterest.au](https://www.finterest.au/stories/redfin-perch-and-the-ehn-virus?utm_source=openai)) Anglers and local authorities noted redfin with skin lesions and a history of prior EHN outbreaks, prompting renewed diagnostic testing and public advisories, although observed mortality levels appeared modest compared with the major epizootics of earlier decades. The event nevertheless demonstrated that EHNV persists or can re‑enter historically affected Murray headwater storages and remains a contemporary management concern.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued widespread distribution of redfin perch in the upper Murray, intensive recreational fishing around Lake Hume, and potential upstream or lateral movement of infected fish or contaminated equipment from other EHNV‑positive waters likely facilitated re‑introduction or re‑activation of the virus in this reservoir.([finterest.au](https://www.finterest.au/stories/redfin-perch-and-the-ehn-virus?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV’s environmental robustness and ability to persist at low levels in fish populations or in the environment enable sporadic clinical re‑occurrence even when surveillance has not detected the virus for many years.
Review: REVIEW – newly added event with moderate confidence. Multiple secondary sources, including a targeted outreach article and a recent systematic review, report EHNV cases at Lake Hume in 2021 and emphasise their significance as evidence of continuing circulation and potential range shifts, but detailed quantitative information on mortality and diagnostic methods is limited and partly derived from media interviews.([finterest.au](https://www.finterest.au/stories/redfin-perch-and-the-ehn-virus?utm_source=openai)) The episode is therefore included as a re‑occurrence in a historically affected headwater storage with a conservative confidence score and should be revisited if more formal primary data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (New South Wales – Central Tablelands and Central West: Lake Wallace at Wallerawang [late 2023; early 2024], Oberon Dam [2023; 2024], Waratah Dam near Orange [late 2023], and Lake Burrendong [early 2024])
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) with large, conspicuous mortality events; endangered Macquarie perch populations in nearby sub‑catchments were considered highly threatened by potential spillover but were the target of protective closures rather than confirmed cases.
Event summary: From late 2023 into early 2024, epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus was confirmed as the cause of substantial fish kills of redfin perch across several Central Tablelands and Central West New South Wales impoundments, including Lake Wallace at Wallerawang, Oberon Dam, Waratah Dam near Orange and Lake Burrendong.([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-11/endangered-macquarie-perch-in-grave-danger-of-virus/103304738?utm_source=openai)) NSW authorities documented hundreds of dead redfin at multiple sites and temporarily closed parts of the Winburndale catchment to recreational fishing to reduce the risk of human‑mediated spread and to protect a nearby reintroduction population of the endangered Macquarie perch. These outbreaks represented the first confirmed extension of EHNV from its long‑recognised upper Murrumbidgee and lower Murray foci into the Central Tablelands region and highlighted the capacity of the virus to colonise new river basins within south‑eastern Australia after a period of relative quiescence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human‑assisted dispersal of redfin perch between inland dams (for angling and illegal stocking), movement of contaminated boats and equipment, and hydrological connectivity among Central Tablelands impoundments likely underpinned the rapid appearance of EHNV at multiple sites.([nationaltribune.com.au](https://www.nationaltribune.com.au/temporary-fishing-closure-to-protect-endangered-fish-from-ehnv/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The same traits responsible for earlier epizootics—high virulence in juvenile redfin and environmental stability of the virus—enabled intense but spatially patchy mortality once EHNV entered these previously uninfected lakes.
Review: REVIEW – newly added linked episode covering multiple Central Tablelands / Central West impoundments. Official NSW DPI communications and independent news reports consistently attribute significant 2023–2024 redfin kills at Lake Wallace, Oberon Dam, Waratah Dam and Lake Burrendong to EHNV and note associated emergency management actions; together these constitute a major, epidemiologically linked expansion of EHNV into a new set of catchments within the same UNSD sub‑region.([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-11/endangered-macquarie-perch-in-grave-danger-of-virus/103304738?utm_source=openai)) The episode is therefore classified as re‑occurrence (spread within an already affected sub‑region rather than a new continent or UNSD sub‑region) and merits inclusion among the major post‑1990 events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (Talbingo Reservoir, Tumut River catchment, New South Wales [February–March 2025])
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) in Talbingo Reservoir, in which infection with EHNV was detected by qPCR in a small number of sampled fish; no overt clinical disease or large‑scale fish kill was reported at the time of detection.
Event summary: In early 2025, targeted disease surveillance carried out under the Snowy 2.0 Biosecurity Risk Management Plan detected epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus in redfin perch from Talbingo Reservoir using quantitative PCR, marking the first confirmed presence of EHNV in this major Snowy Mountains storage.([snowyhydro.com.au](https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Snowy-2.0-Biosecurity-Risk-Management-Plan_Annual-Report-for-the-Financial-Year-ended-30-June-2025.pdf)) All sampled fish appeared externally healthy and only two positive detections were obtained among more than 250 individuals, so the event is best interpreted as detection of subclinical infection rather than a visible epizootic. Nonetheless, the finding triggered a revision of the surveillance program to focus on preventing spread into upstream Tantangara Reservoir, which is currently considered redfin‑ and EHNV‑free but supports habitats of high conservation value including Macquarie perch and stocky galaxias.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The long‑standing presence of redfin perch in Talbingo Reservoir, combined with regional movements of anglers and potential water transfers associated with Snowy 2.0 infrastructure, created a realistic pathway for EHNV introduction from known endemic areas in the upper Murrumbidgee and other Murray–Darling catchments.([snowyhydro.com.au](https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Snowy-2.0-Biosecurity-Risk-Management-Plan_Annual-Report-for-the-Financial-Year-ended-30-June-2025.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV’s ability to persist at low prevalence without overt disease, together with its potential to spread via infected fish or contaminated water, motivates precautionary surveillance and control efforts even when only subclinical infections are detected.
Review: REVIEW – newly added surveillance‑based emergence event. The WOAH Quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease report for Q1 2025 and the Snowy 2.0 Biosecurity Risk Management Plan annual report both document qPCR‑confirmed EHNV infection in wild redfin from Talbingo Reservoir and describe associated changes to surveillance priorities, but they do not report a conspicuous fish kill or clinical disease.([rr-asia.woah.org](https://rr-asia.woah.org/app/uploads/2025/07/Australias-QAAD-Q1-2025.pdf)) The event is therefore classified as a re‑occurrence (detection of infection in a new reservoir within the same UNSD sub‑region) with high confidence in occurrence but uncertain short‑term impact; it is included because of its clear management importance and demonstration of northward range expansion within the Snowy–Murrumbidgee system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Beef and dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In late summer 1997, a large epidemic of Ibaraki disease occurred in western Japan when cattle developed fever, salivation, dysphagia and bluetongue‑like oral lesions, and EHDV belonging to a strain later reclassified as serotype 7 was isolated from sick animals and aborted fetuses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC85817/?utm_source=openai)) Over the 1997–1998 season the virus spread across southern and western Japan, causing widespread clinical disease and more than 1,000 reported abortions and stillbirths in infected pregnant cows, making it one of the most severe EHD‑associated cattle outbreaks recorded.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf)) The epidemic waned with the end of the vector season and implementation of vaccination against Ibaraki disease, but established EHDV‑associated Ibaraki‑like disease as a major recurring arboviral threat to Japanese cattle.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: warm, humid late‑summer conditions in western and southern Japan favoring Culicoides midges; dense dairy and beef cattle populations with limited prior immunity; movement of animals between affected prefectures. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence—an EHDV lineage now attributed to serotype 7 caused classical Ibaraki disease signs and extensive reproductive losses; host adaptation and increased virulence for cattle compared with earlier Ibaraki virus outbreaks; potential reassortment within the EHDV serogroup.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf))
Review: Decision: retain (added). Rationale: Major 1997–1998 Ibaraki disease epidemic in Japanese cattle is well documented, caused by an EHDV strain now attributed to serotype 7, and resulted in widespread clinical disease and >1,000 abortions/stillbirths, clearly placing it among the 10 most impactful EHDV emergence events since 1990.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf)) Classification set to re-emergence (new pathogenic EHDV lineage in a previously affected subregion) with other emergence-type flags left false to align with provided definitions.

Host: Wild white‑tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and other wild ruminants
Event summary: In mid‑August to late September 1999, a large epizootic of hemorrhagic disease due to EHDV‑1 occurred along the eastern United States from Georgia to New Jersey, affecting white‑tailed deer across over 100 counties in at least 10 states and causing thousands of deer deaths.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak developed rapidly over late summer with widespread deer mortality and characteristic hemorrhagic lesions, making it the largest documented EHD outbreak in U.S. deer since the 1970s.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai)) The epizootic waned as vector activity declined in autumn, but highlighted the potential for large‑scale, climate‑linked recurrence of EHD in North American cervids.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: warm late‑summer conditions and abundant Culicoides vectors in the eastern U.S.; high densities of susceptible white‑tailed deer across multiple states; landscape changes and agricultural water sources favoring midge breeding. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel genotype implicated; this represents a major cyclical re‑occurrence of endemic EHDV‑1 with high transmission intensity rather than a new strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 1999 eastern U.S. HD epizootic is well documented as one of the largest modern EHD outbreaks in wild deer, with broad geographic extent and high mortality. Geography (United States, Northern America) and classification as re-occurrence without intra/inter-continental or first-detection flags are consistent with definitions and literature.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef)
Event summary: From 2004 in Morocco and then in 2006 in Algeria and Tunisia, EHDV serotype 6 (strain 318) caused outbreaks of febrile illness with oral lesions, lameness and production losses in cattle, representing the first confirmed EHDV circulation in the Maghreb.([openveterinaryjournal.com](https://www.openveterinaryjournal.com/index.php?html=1&mno=62057&utm_source=openai)) The disease spread within Northern Africa over the 2004–2006 seasons, with morbidity in affected herds and evidence of regional movement of the EHDV‑6 strain among Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2941451/?utm_source=openai)) The epizootic subsided after winter vector breaks, but serological surveys in subsequent years showed continued low‑level EHDV‑6 circulation in cattle and dromedaries, establishing the virus in the region.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/324415695_Epizootic_haemorrhagic_disease_virus_circulation_in_Tunisia?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of an exotic EHDV‑6 strain into Northern Africa, likely via movement of infected ruminants or wind‑borne Culicoides from endemic sub‑Saharan or Middle Eastern areas; suitable Mediterranean climate and abundant midge vectors. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (regional introduction and establishment of EHDV‑6 strain 318 into a previously EHD‑free subregion); geographic range expansion into Maghreb climates; increased apparent pathogenicity in cattle compared with earlier African reports.([openveterinaryjournal.com](https://www.openveterinaryjournal.com/index.php?html=1&mno=62057&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false because EHDV had been detected in ruminants and vectors in Africa and Asia decades earlier; this Maghreb episode is not the first detection in the host system but the first in the Northern Africa subregion.([fr.wikipedia.org](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maladie_h%C3%A9morragique_%C3%A9pizootique?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Left intra_continental_emergence=true and re_emergence=true to reflect expansion of EHDV into a new African subregion (Northern Africa) and emergence of a more pathogenic EHDV‑6 lineage in cattle, which is consistent with the definitions.([openveterinaryjournal.com](https://www.openveterinaryjournal.com/index.php?html=1&mno=62057&utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein and other breeds)
Event summary: In late September 2006, Israel recorded a severe orbiviral outbreak in dairy cattle characterized by fever, oral ulcers, lameness, reduced milk yield and high morbidity; virological investigation identified EHDV‑7 as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed EHD outbreak in Israeli cattle.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) Over the summer and autumn, the outbreak spread through multiple dairy farms with substantial production losses, making it one of the first and most severe cattle‑dominated EHD events globally.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) The epidemic declined with the onset of cooler weather and reduced vector activity, but EHDV‑7 became established in the region and contributed to subsequent EHDV diversity in Israel.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10885110/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of EHDV‑7 into densely managed Israeli dairy cattle populations, probably via movement of infected animals or wind‑borne midges from neighboring endemic areas; climatic suitability for Culicoides vectors in summer–autumn; high herd densities favoring local spread. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/host adaptation—EHDV‑7 closely related to Australian strains but showing reassortment with African/Middle Eastern segments and associated with unusually severe clinical disease and milk loss in cattle; enhanced transmission via competent local Culicoides spp.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false, because EHDV had been described in the livestock/wildlife host system long before 2006; this event is the first detection in Israel but not in the host system globally.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false, as EHDV was already present in other Western Asia countries (e.g. Oman) before 2006, and spread to a new country within the same subregion does not meet the definition of intra‑continental emergence.([fr.wikipedia.org](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maladie_h%C3%A9morragique_%C3%A9pizootique?utm_source=openai)) (iii) Kept re_emergence=true to reflect emergence of a new, clinically important EHDV‑7 lineage in a subregion where EHDV was already known.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle
Event summary: In July 2007, a 7‑week outbreak of bluetongue‑like disease began in cattle in Muğla Province in western Türkiye, with affected animals showing fever, stomatitis, facial edema, lameness, udder erythema and reduced milk yield; laboratory testing confirmed infection with EHDV‑6 closely related to North African strain 318.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) Similar clinical cases were soon reported from neighboring provinces including İzmir, Çanakkale and İstanbul, confirming that the North African EHDV‑6 lineage had spread into Western Asia and could cause clinically apparent disease in Turkish cattle.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) The outbreak subsided toward the end of August 2007 as temperatures cooled and Culicoides activity decreased, but established EHDV‑6 as part of the regional orbivirus fauna.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: spread of EHDV‑6 strain 318 from North Africa across the eastern Mediterranean, likely via wind‑borne Culicoides and/or movement of infected ruminants; suitable summer climate and vector habitat in western Türkiye; limited pre‑existing immunity in local cattle. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of a fit EHDV‑6 epidemic lineage with demonstrated pathogenicity in cattle; potential enhanced fitness in local Culicoides populations enabling establishment in Western Asia.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Restricted this row to the 2007 cattle outbreak in Türkiye only and removed Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia from the countries field to avoid double‑counting the 2006 Maghreb epizootic already captured in the 2004–2006 event. (ii) Updated continent and subregion to Asia/Western Asia only, which matches the territorial classification for Türkiye. (iii) Set first_detection=false because EHDV was long known in the host system, and inter- and intra‑continental emergence are not appropriate (EHDV was already present in Asia); retained re_emergence=true to reflect expansion of the EHDV‑6 Maghreb lineage into an already affected subregion with a changed strain profile.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; captive cervids; cattle and other domestic ruminants (limited clinical disease)
Event summary: In 2007, the United States experienced one of its most extensive orbivirus years, with widespread hemorrhagic disease in white‑tailed deer across eastern and midwestern states and concurrent bluetongue activity, involving EHDV‑2 and detecting EHDV‑6 for the first time in U.S. deer.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) Deer mortality was reported from many counties in at least 11 states, with both wild and captive cervid herds affected and sporadic disease in domestic ruminants.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) The epizootic declined in late autumn as midge activity fell, but contributed to recognition of a trend toward more frequent and severe EHDV years in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: favorable warm, dry late‑summer conditions promoting Culicoides abundance; high deer densities and anthropogenic water sources creating vector habitat; cyclical build‑up of susceptible deer cohorts following lower‑impact years. Internal mechanisms: detection of exotic‑derived EHDV‑6 in North American deer alongside endemic serotypes, but 2007 is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence of multi‑serotype EHDV activity rather than a single novel genotype event.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 2007 is recognized in surveillance summaries and USAHA reports as a major HD year with extensive deer mortality and the first detection of EHDV‑6 in North American cervids, justifying inclusion among high‑impact events.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) Event geography and classification as re-occurrence (without intra/inter-continental or re-emergence flags) are consistent with definitions and current knowledge.

Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; captive cervids; cattle and bison
Event summary: During the summer and fall of 2012, an unusually large EHD outbreak occurred across the United States, affecting domestic cattle and bison herds as well as wild and captive white‑tailed deer, and involving multiple serotypes including EHDV‑2 and the emerging EHDV‑6.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak produced notable cattle morbidity and death in some herds, with average within‑herd morbidity of about 7% in cattle/bison and 46% in captive deer, and viral detections across roughly 15 states in the Midwest and Southeast.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai)) Transmission declined with the onset of cooler weather, but molecular epidemiology later showed reassortant viruses containing segments from exotic EHDV‑6 and endemic EHDV‑2, raising concerns about future emergence potential.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread drought and high late‑summer temperatures in 2012 that favored midge breeding and increased wildlife–livestock congregation at remaining water sources; expansion of captive deer farming and dense cattle herds in affected regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence—evidence of reassortant EHDV combining exotic (EHDV‑6) and endemic (EHDV‑2) genome segments in U.S. herds; increased virulence/pathogenicity in cattle compared with earlier North American experience; enhanced transmission efficiency of these reassortants through abundant Culicoides vectors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Change made: re_occurrence was set from true to false and re_emergence left true, because the 2012 outbreak is distinguished by emergence of reassortant EHDV-6/EHDV-2 strains with altered host impact rather than solely by external drivers; under the provided definitions, this better fits re-emergence (EPP change in a previously affected subregion) rather than simple re-occurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (mainly), with likely infection of wild ruminants
Event summary: In 2020, EHDV re‑emerged in the eastern Mediterranean with outbreaks in cattle in Türkiye and several North African countries attributed primarily to EHDV‑6, after a period of apparent low‑level circulation following the mid‑2000s Maghreb epizootics.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai)) Disease episodes presented with bluetongue‑like signs in cattle and were confirmed by molecular testing, indicating renewed regional spread of EHDV‑6 in the Mediterranean basin.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai)) Transmission declined after the 2020 vector season, but this resurgence set the stage for subsequent introduction and spread of EHDV‑8 in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ongoing climate warming in the Mediterranean ‘hotspot’ increasing vector seasons and high‑altitude suitability for Culicoides; animal movements between North African and Near‑Eastern countries; limited targeted surveillance for EHDV allowing silent spread. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of EHDV‑6 lineages with demonstrated cattle pathogenicity; geographic range re‑expansion within Western Asia and Northern Africa from previously established foci.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false, as these outbreaks represent resurgence of EHDV‑6 in subregions (Northern Africa, Western Asia) where the virus had already been established since 2006–2007, not spread into new UNSD subregions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10885110/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Retained re_emergence=true to capture the renewed activity of established EHDV‑6 lineages under changing climatic and ecological conditions. Country list (Türkiye, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia) follows recent regional syntheses but should be checked against official WOAH notifications, so the event is flagged for further review of exact 2020 country involvement.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (primary); wild cervids likely exposed
Event summary: Between September and November 2021, Tunisia experienced a severe outbreak of EHD in cattle caused by EHDV serotype 8, representing the first major circulation of this serotype in North Africa and globally.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai)) Affected herds showed fever, anorexia, lameness, oral lesions and production losses, with molecular and phylogenetic analyses confirming a distinct EHDV‑8 lineage circulating in Tunisian cattle and Barbary deer.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10383031/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak waned with the end of the 2021 vector season, but EHDV‑8 remained established and later served as the source for spread into Algeria, Morocco and ultimately southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction and local amplification of a previously undetected EHDV‑8 lineage under favorable climatic conditions and abundant vector populations in coastal and inland Tunisian cattle areas. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence (regional emergence of EHDV‑8 with distinct VP2/VP5 signatures); increased virulence/pathogenicity in cattle relative to earlier regional EHDV‑6 events; geographic range expansion of EHDV‑8 within North Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false because EHDV was already long known in ruminants; this episode is the first detection of serotype 8 in North Africa but not the first detection of the EPP in the host system.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false in line with the rule that new serotypes in a region where the organism is already present should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence.
