(iii) Retained re_emergence=true to capture the appearance of a new, epidemiologically important EHDV‑8 lineage in a previously affected subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Northern Africa; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Tunisia [2021]; Algeria [2022]; Morocco [2022]; Italy (Sicily, Sardinia) [2022]; Spain (Andalusia, other regions) [2022]; Portugal [2023]; France [2023]
Host: Cattle (primary); wild red and fallow deer; sheep (subclinical and occasional clinical infections)
Event summary: Building on the 2021 Tunisian outbreak, EHDV‑8 spread westward across North Africa in 2022 and then crossed the Mediterranean to Europe, with first European detections in cattle in Sicily and Sardinia (Italy) in October 2022 and in Andalusia (Spain) in November 2022.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37081599/?utm_source=openai)) The virus subsequently expanded during the 2022–2023 seasons to affect large areas of southern Spain, Portugal and southern France, as well as additional parts of Italy, causing thousands of cattle outbreaks and confirmed infections in wild cervids and, later, some sheep.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai)) By late 2023 the initial wave of transmission had slowed with winter vector decline, but EHDV‑8 had become established in both North Africa and southern Europe, fundamentally changing the regional orbivirus landscape.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12341390/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: climate warming and extended warm seasons in the Mediterranean ‘hotspot’ enhancing Culicoides survival and competence; strong north–south livestock trade and probable wind‑borne carriage of infected midges from North Africa to southern Europe; high densities of susceptible cattle and wild cervids in affected regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence and geographic range expansion—EHDV‑8 lineage originating in Tunisia with near‑identical genomes in North African and European isolates; efficient transmission via European Culicoides species; host expansion with significant clinical disease documented in cattle and wild red deer, and confirmed infections in sheep.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12341390/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false, because EHDV was already known globally in ruminants; this event represents the first detection in Europe, which is captured via the inter‑continental emergence flag. (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false to avoid co‑classification, in line with guidance that emergence types are generally mutually exclusive and that this episode’s defining feature is first occurrence of EHDV in a new continent (Europe). (iii) Set re_emergence from true to false, as Southern and Western Europe were previously free of EHDV; the event is better characterized as de novo inter‑continental emergence of an existing lineage rather than re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37081599/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Spain [2023]; Portugal [2023]; France [2023]; Italy (Sardinia, other regions) [2023–2024]
Host: Cattle; wild red and fallow deer; sheep (documented infections)
Event summary: In 2023, following initial detections in late 2022, EHDV‑8 caused explosive expansion within the Iberian Peninsula and parts of France and Italy, with Spain alone reporting over 3,000 EHD outbreaks within two months of intense transmission.([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/66cdc8160671fa213911b341/14_August_2024_Epizootic_Haemorrhagic_Disease_in_Europe.pdf?utm_source=openai)) The virus spread northward and westward within Spain and into Portugal and southwestern France, and further cases were recorded in domestic cattle and wild deer populations in Sardinia and mainland Italy, with occasional infections documented in sheep.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai)) As temperatures dropped and control measures were implemented, the number of new outbreaks decreased into 2024, though surveillance indicated overwintering of the virus in parts of southern Europe and the need for continued vector and movement controls.([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/epizootic-haemorrhagic-disease-in-europe/28-november-2023-epizootic-haemorrhagic-disease-in-europe?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: exceptionally warm summers and mild winters in southern and parts of western Europe, extending vector seasons; dense and mobile cattle populations; limited prior immunity to EHDV‑8; cross‑border animal movements within the EU. Internal mechanisms: ongoing geographic range expansion and establishment of EHDV‑8 as an endemic orbivirus in southern Europe; likely adaptation to local Culicoides species enhancing transmission efficiency; broader host involvement including wild cervids and sheep, indicating altered host range compared with earlier EHDV lineages.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false because this wave represents continued spread and intensification of EHDV‑8 within Southern and Western Europe where the virus had already emerged in 2022, not first occurrence in a new UNSD subregion. (ii) Set re_occurrence from false to true and re_emergence from true to false, treating 2023–2024 as a major re-occurrence ( resurgence and geographic amplification) of the same EHDV‑8 lineage in already affected European subregions rather than emergence of a new lineage.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (beef and dairy herds)
Event summary: Between January and April 2003, a bluetongue‑like disease outbreak occurred in cattle across much of Réunion Island, with 3,607 animals in affected herds and 235 showing clinical signs including fever, lameness and torpor, and occasional death after a protracted course. Virological investigations identified epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus, primarily serotypes 2 and 6, as the causal agent, representing the first recognized EHD epizootic in cattle on Réunion and the wider south‑west Indian Ocean region. As Culicoides activity declined later in 2003 the outbreak subsided, but subsequent surveys documented continued circulation of EHDV alongside bluetongue virus in the island’s cattle population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and establishment of EHDV‑2 and EHDV‑6 on Réunion via infected Culicoides midges, probably linked to animal and wind‑borne vector movements from nearby African mainlands, combined with climatic conditions favorable to high midge abundance and widespread exposure of largely naïve cattle. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of EHDV into the south‑west Indian Ocean and emergence of clinically apparent disease in cattle, with serotypes and strains showing sufficient virulence to cause overt illness and mortality in a previously unexposed cattle population.
Review: Retain – newly added major cattle epizootic on Réunion (2003) involving >3,600 cattle and confirmed EHDV infection; classified as intra‑continental emergence into Eastern Africa plus re‑emergence due to expansion of pathogenic serotypes into a new island ecosystem. Sources updated to include the original outbreak description and quantitative data on herd involvement.

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event summary: In 2006, severe bluetongue‑like disease with fever, facial edema, oral lesions and production losses was reported in cattle herds across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, where EHDV infection had not previously been recognized as a cause of clinical disease in domestic ruminants. Molecular characterization showed that these outbreaks were caused by epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6), closely related to the 318 strain, and that the North African viruses formed a distinct cluster associated with pathogenicity in cattle. Following the 2006 vector season the acute epizootics waned, but EHDV‑6 established in the Maghreb, with subsequent serologic and virologic detections indicating continued circulation in regional ruminant populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Wind‑borne movement of infected Culicoides midges from endemic areas, coupled with local animal movements and climatic conditions in 2006 favorable to vector proliferation and survival across the Maghreb. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and geographic range expansion of a pathogenic EHDV‑6 lineage into North African cattle populations, with strain‑specific traits associated with clinical disease in bovines and subsequent regional persistence.
Review: Retain – event is well documented as the first major EHDV‑6 incursion into the Maghreb with substantial cattle morbidity and economic losses; continent, sub‑region, countries and 2006 timing align with OIE and peer‑reviewed sources. No changes to classification were required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds); likely subclinical infection in local wild ruminants
Event summary: In late summer and autumn 2006, a large‑scale outbreak of bluetongue‑like illness occurred in Israeli dairy and beef cattle herds that had not previously experienced confirmed EHDV disease, with reports from dozens of localities along the Jordan Valley and adjacent regions. Laboratory investigations isolated epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 7 (EHDV‑7) from affected cattle, and epidemiologic analyses documented involvement of more than 80–100 herds with fever, oral lesions, lameness, milk drop and occasional deaths, causing major economic losses. Clinical cases declined after the end of the Culicoides transmission season, but EHDV became established in Israel and was followed in later years by additional outbreaks caused by other serotypes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of EHDV‑7 into Israel, probably via wind‑borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges or regional animal movements from North Africa or the Arabian Peninsula, in a setting of dense dairy cattle populations and favorable summer climate for vector activity. Internal mechanisms: Geographic expansion of an exotic EHDV‑7 lineage from the Asia–Pacific/African–Middle Eastern region into Western Asia, with high pathogenicity in cattle compared to historically mostly subclinical EHDV infections, representing both intra‑continental emergence into a new UNSD sub‑region and re‑emergence through a novel serotype causing severe disease in cattle.
Review: Review – corrected classification: set inter_continental_emergence to No because EHDV was already present in Asia (e.g. Japan) before 2006, and set intra_continental_emergence to Yes to reflect first incursion into the Western Asia sub‑region. First_detection was changed to No because global first detection of EHDV predates this event. Event remains a major outbreak and should be retained after expert review of the revised coding.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: White‑tailed deer and other wild cervids; some farmed/captive deer; sporadic cattle
Event summary: In 2007, an exceptionally widespread hemorrhagic disease epizootic affected wild white‑tailed deer across large areas of the eastern and Midwestern United States, with wildlife surveillance reporting thousands of cases across many counties and multiple states. Virological investigations documented co‑circulation of multiple EHDV serotypes, including endemic EHDV‑1 and EHDV‑2 and the recently introduced EHDV‑6, making this one of the most extensive orbivirus outbreaks in U.S. deer on record. Case reports declined rapidly after the first hard frosts reduced Culicoides vector populations, but local deer populations in some regions suffered substantial short‑term declines and heightened management concern.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Hot, dry summer conditions in 2007 that concentrated deer around shrinking water sources heavily infested with Culicoides midges, along with high deer densities in agricultural and suburban landscapes and limited prior immunity to EHDV‑6. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by the simultaneous circulation of multiple EHDV serotypes, including the newly established EHDV‑6, with possible serotype‑specific differences in virulence and transmission contributing to unusually broad geographic spread and high deer mortality.
Review: Retain – this event is well supported as one of the largest documented hemorrhagic disease outbreaks in U.S. deer, with multi‑state spread and high mortality. Geographic coding and classification as re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence (due to the recent introduction of EHDV‑6) are consistent with the project definitions and supporting reports.

Host: White‑tailed deer, other wild cervids, and domestic ruminants (especially cattle, but also bison, yak, elk and sheep)
Event summary: In the summer and autumn of 2012, the United States experienced an unusually large EHD outbreak that affected both domestic ruminants and wild white‑tailed deer across much of the country, with 129 cattle herds, 65 captive deer herds, and additional bison, yak, elk and sheep flocks confirmed PCR‑positive. Clinical disease in cattle and bison was concentrated in the central Great Plains and Midwest, while captive and free‑ranging deer were heavily affected in several Midwestern and eastern states. Virological testing showed that EHDV‑6 accounted for the majority of isolates from diseased deer, displacing historically dominant serotypes. Transmission decreased over the winter of 2012–2013, and while localized activity and residual population impacts persisted into early 2013, cases returned to baseline as Culicoides activity fell.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe drought and record high temperatures in 2012 across large parts of the central United States, which shortened the extrinsic incubation period of EHDV in Culicoides and concentrated deer and cattle at limited water sources, amplifying transmission. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence characterized by dominance of the relatively recently introduced EHDV‑6 serotype in both wildlife and domestic ruminants, reflecting a shift in the serotype landscape and possible fitness advantages of EHDV‑6 in North American hosts and vectors.
Review: Review – country list was corrected to remove Canada, as the 2012 domestic ruminant epizootic is documented from the United States, whereas Canadian detections in 2013 represent separate, small‑scale events. Classification was updated to remove intra_continental_emergence (this is not a spread into a new UNSD sub‑region) and emphasize re_occurrence plus re_emergence driven by the rise of EHDV‑6. Event is clearly among the highest‑impact global episodes and should be retained after checking that the revised description and coding match project conventions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America – especially Illinois and neighboring Midwestern states [2013]
Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; some cattle
Event summary: Following the large 2012 event, another major hemorrhagic disease year occurred in 2013, particularly in the Midwestern United States. In Illinois, wildlife surveillance recorded over 1,200 reported cases of hemorrhagic disease in wild white‑tailed deer across more than 60 counties, with substantial local mortality and hunter‑observed declines in some herds. Similar but patchier activity was reported in neighboring states. As in other temperate outbreaks, reported cases declined sharply after the first hard frosts reduced Culicoides midge populations and terminated transmission for the season.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued high deer densities, favorable summer conditions for Culicoides vectors in the Midwest, and residual susceptibility in cohorts not heavily exposed in 2012, leading to another year of intense localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: This episode is best characterized as a re‑occurrence of cyclical hemorrhagic disease activity in previously affected sub‑regions, with serotypes similar to earlier years; there is no strong evidence that a novel serotype or significantly altered viral phenotype dominated in 2013.
Review: Retain – this event represents one of the largest documented state‑level hemorrhagic disease epizootics in wild deer (e.g. >1,200 reported cases in Illinois alone) and captures the continued high impact of EHD in Midwestern cervid populations after 2012. Classification as re‑occurrence only (without intra/inter‑continental emergence or first detection) aligns with the project definitions; sources were refined to include quantitative Illinois data.

Host: Beef and dairy cattle
Event summary: From October 2015 over a three‑month period, a febrile illness affecting cattle was reported in Hyogo Prefecture in western Japan, with 46 animals (40 Japanese Black beef cattle and 6 Holstein dairy heifers) on 38 farms showing fever, anorexia, cessation of rumination, swollen eyelids, oral lesions, difficulty swallowing and, in some cases, abortions. Seven cattle died and two were euthanized because of poor prognosis, making this the most substantial EHD‑like disease event in Japanese cattle since classical Ibaraki disease episodes. Laboratory investigations confirmed infection with epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6), and phylogenetic analyses indicated that the strain belonged to an Asia‑Pacific lineage distinct from the North African/Mediterranean EHDV‑6 cluster.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic and ecological conditions in western Japan favorable to Culicoides vectors, with likely introduction or amplification of EHDV‑6 in local ruminant populations that had little recent exposure to this serotype. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of clinically significant EHD in Japanese cattle driven by an EHDV‑6 lineage with pathogenic features reminiscent of, but genetically distinct from, historic Ibaraki virus (EHDV‑2), representing intra‑continental emergence into parts of Eastern Asia where EHDV‑6 had not previously caused recognized cattle outbreaks.
Review: Review – newly added event to represent a major Eastern Asia emergence of EHDV‑6 in cattle (46 affected animals on 38 farms with multiple deaths), which is highlighted in the primary literature as a notable outbreak. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (first substantial EHDV‑6 cattle outbreak in this part of Eastern Asia) plus re‑emergence due to a new pathogenic lineage; this should be checked by domain experts but appears consistent with regional EHDV history.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dairy and beef cattle (including pregnant cows); aborted fetuses
Event summary: In September 2015, a country‑wide epizootic of febrile illness and production loss was recognized in Israeli dairy and beef cattle herds, with clinical signs including reduced milk yield, weakness, drooling, lameness, recumbency, fever, mild oral and nasal mucosal erythema, weight loss and abortions; deaths and cachexia occurred in a minority of animals. Virological testing (ELISA, real‑time RT‑PCR and VP2 sequencing) confirmed epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6) infection, and the outbreak involved multiple geographic foci including northern Israel and the Dead Sea region. After the Culicoides season ended, the epizootic declined, but serologic data and subsequent detections indicated continued EHDV circulation in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Favorable conditions for Culicoides vectors in Israeli dairy and beef production areas, combined with movement of infected animals or midges from neighboring EHDV‑6‑endemic countries, facilitated spread into densely stocked herds. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of EHD in Israel associated with a different serotype from the 2006 EHDV‑7 outbreak, with EHDV‑6 causing widespread clinical disease and abortions, reflecting both viral genetic diversification and changing host–virus dynamics in a region where multiple EHDV serotypes now co‑circulate.
Review: Review – newly added event to capture the large 2015 EHDV‑6 epizootic in Israeli cattle, which caused substantial production losses and abortions and is cited as a major cattle outbreak in recent global reviews. Classified as re‑occurrence and re‑emergence within Western Asia rather than new continental emergence; inclusion brings the dataset closer to representing the ten most impactful post‑1990 EHD episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds); Barbary red deer (Cervus elaphus barbarus); Culicoides vectors
Event summary: In late September 2021, Tunisian authorities detected outbreaks of bluetongue‑like disease in dairy and beef cattle herds in central‑western Tunisia, and laboratory investigations identified a novel epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 strain (EHDV‑8 TUN 2021) not previously detected in the field since the prototype strain was isolated in Australia in 1982. During 2021–2022, this EHDV‑8 lineage spread among Tunisian cattle, causing fever, facial edema, oral ulcers, respiratory distress, reduced milk production, reproductive problems and occasional deaths, and was also confirmed in Barbary deer and in Culicoides midges along the Tunisian–Algerian border. As vector activity decreased and targeted control and surveillance measures were implemented, clinical cases declined, but virological and serological evidence showed that the new EHDV‑8 lineage had become established in North Africa and posed a risk of onward spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic and ecological conditions in central‑western Tunisia favorable for Culicoides vectors, including irrigated agriculture and high cattle densities, together with limited pre‑existing immunity to EHDV‑8 in local ruminant populations and animal movements within border regions. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of EHD via the first field detection in decades of a genetically distinct EHDV‑8 lineage (EHDV‑8 TUN 2021) capable of infecting cattle, wild Barbary deer and Culicoides vectors, representing novel strain/genotype emergence within a region already known for EHDV‑6 activity.
Review: Review – corrected first_global_emergence and first_detection to No, because EHDV was recognized decades earlier and EHDV‑8 had been described as a prototype strain in Australia; this event instead represents the first documented field circulation of a new EHDV‑8 lineage since 1982 and a major re‑emergence in a region already affected by EHDV‑6. Classification as re_emergence only (without intra/inter‑continental emergence) now aligns with project rules; event remains one of the most consequential recent EHD episodes and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy (Sardinia, Sicily, mainland) [2022–2023]; Spain [2022–2024]; Portugal [2023–2024]; France [2023–2024]
Host: Cattle; domestic small ruminants to a lesser extent; wild red deer (Cervus elaphus), fallow deer (Dama dama) and mouflon (Ovis orientalis musimon)
Event summary: In autumn 2022, epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 closely related to the Tunisian 2021 EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 strain was detected for the first time in Europe in cattle in Sardinia and Sicily (Italy) and in southern Spain, marking the first incursion of EHD into European livestock and wildlife. During 2022–2023 the same EHDV‑8 lineage spread widely across mainland Spain, into neighboring regions of Portugal and southern France and into mainland Italy, causing numerous outbreaks in cattle herds with fever, oral lesions, edema, milk drop and occasional deaths, as well as significant mortality and clinical disease in European red deer, fallow deer and mouflon. By late 2023 the disease had affected all regions of mainland Spain and multiple regions in Portugal, France and Italy, with control responses including movement restrictions and accelerated development and deployment of inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines; activity continued into 2024 and beyond, raising concern that EHD may become endemic in parts of southern and western Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely wind‑borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges across the Mediterranean from North Africa into southern Europe, in the context of a warming climate and shifting vector distributions, followed by dense livestock networks and game‑estate management practices that facilitated virus amplification and within‑continent spread between Italy, Spain, Portugal and France. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental emergence and rapid geographic range expansion of the EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 lineage into naïve European cattle and cervid populations, with marked pathogenicity in both domestic and wild hosts, alongside rapid development and deployment of new inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines that may influence future viral evolution and disease dynamics.
Review: Review – classification was adjusted by setting first_detection to No (global first detection predates this event) while retaining inter_continental_emergence as Yes to reflect the first occurrence of EHDV in Europe and intra_continental_emergence as Yes to capture subsequent spread from initial foci in Southern Europe (Sardinia, Sicily, Andalusia) into Western Europe (France). The event is clearly one of the most impactful in the history of EHD, with multi‑country spread, severe cattle and wildlife disease, and major regulatory and vaccination responses, and should be retained as a cornerstone emergence episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses (pregnant mares in a riding-school herd)
Event summary: In early 1991, a riding school in the Netherlands experienced an EHV-1 abortion storm: seven of twelve pregnant mares aborted late-term and one live-born foal died at eight days of age, with virus isolation from aborted foals confirming EHV-1. Most abortions occurred within about two weeks after an initial February abortion, and clinical illness remained largely confined to the affected mares, with no clear evidence of spread beyond the facility. Isolation of aborting mares, strengthened hygiene, and the natural decline in virus shedding led to cessation of new abortions and the outbreak ended later that spring.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High stocking density and close contact in a riding-school setting, including recent transport of at least one pregnant mare, created conditions for rapid respiratory spread and heavy exposure of mares late in gestation. Internal mechanisms: Serologic data and timing support reactivation of latent EHV-1 in an index mare triggered by transport or management stress, followed by typical abortion-storm pathogenesis; there is no evidence for a novel genotype or geographic range expansion, so this is best interpreted as a local re-occurrence of endemic virus.
Review: Review – Event is real, well documented, and correctly coded as a re-occurrence of endemic EHV-1 rather than any form of first emergence. I corrected the country name to the standardized "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)" and updated the summary to reflect the published case numbers (7 of 12 mares aborting plus one foal death). However, this is a single-farm abortion storm with fewer than 10 foal losses and is likely not among the ten highest-impact global EHV-1 events since 1990; retain if a representative abortion-storm example is desired, otherwise consider exclusion under a strict top‑10 criterion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2003] (University of Findlay English Equestrian Center, Ohio)
Host: Horses in a university English riding / equestrian program (mixed breeds; school and show horses)
Event summary: In January 2003, an outbreak of EHV-1 at the University of Findlay’s English equestrian center in Ohio affected most of the 135 horses on the premises: 117 developed clinical signs of infection and 46 showed neurologic deficits consistent with equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM), with 12 horses ultimately dying or being euthanized. The disease began with fever and respiratory signs before progressing to ataxia, weakness, and recumbency in a subset of mainly older horses, leading the university to suspend riding classes and competitions for several months while strict isolation, movement controls, and intensive nursing care were implemented. Over subsequent weeks, no new neurologic cases occurred, surviving horses gradually recovered, and the facility was able to reopen under enhanced biosecurity and revised vaccination and entry policies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high-density housing of school and show horses, frequent movement between barns and arenas, and intensive training of older, highly used equids promoted rapid virus transmission once introduced, while continual horse turnover complicated early control. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic work on this outbreak linked severe neurologic disease to infection with neuropathogenic EHV-1 strains harboring the ORF30 D752 (G2254) variant, and risk-factor analysis identified older age and high peak fever as strong predictors for EHM, supporting classification as a re-emergence event driven by strain virulence interacting with host factors.
Review: Retain – The original row mis-identified this outbreak as occurring at a California racetrack; it actually took place at the University of Findlay English equestrian center in Ohio, where 117/135 horses became ill, 46 developed neurologic signs, and 12 died. I corrected the location, host description, and narrative using Henninger et al. (2007) and contemporaneous reports, and kept the classification as re-emergence because the event involved a neuropathogenic EHV-1 variant causing unusually high neurologic morbidity and mortality. This is clearly one of the largest and most influential EHV-1/EHM outbreaks in the post‑1990 period and should be retained as a top‑tier event.

Countries: United States of America [2006] (clusters at Florida showgrounds and racetracks, Kentucky racetracks, Maryland tracks including Pimlico and Bowie)
Host: Horses at Thoroughbred racetracks and high-level show / training facilities
Event summary: From late 2006 into early 2007, multiple EHV-1 outbreaks with neurologic cases occurred at major U.S. equine venues, including a highly publicized episode at Pimlico Race Course in Maryland and contemporaneous outbreaks at Florida showgrounds and Kentucky tracks. At Pimlico, several barns were quarantined for weeks, at least three horses were euthanized, and movement of racehorses into and out of Maryland was heavily restricted, while related concerns at Bowie and other training centers further disrupted the Mid-Atlantic racing circuit. Similar EHM events at Florida training and show facilities and at Kentucky racetracks triggered quarantines, race cancellations, and widespread interstate movement controls, and collectively these clustered outbreaks prompted USDA to classify neurologic EHV-1/EHM as an emerging equine disease and spurred development of national guidance on outbreak management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Concentration of large numbers of race and show horses at racetracks and winter show circuits, frequent interstate transport, and shared stabling / training environments allowed rapid dissemination of EHV-1 once infected horses were introduced. Internal mechanisms: Many neurologic cases were associated with neuropathogenic ORF30 D752 EHV-1 strains, and high viral loads in blood and nasal secretions in some horses, combined with host factors such as age and intense training stress, contributed to severe EHM expression and the perception of a newly emerging neurologic form of EHV-1.
Review: Retain – This row reasonably summarizes the 2006–2007 cluster of neurologic EHV-1 outbreaks at Florida show facilities and Mid‑Atlantic/Kentucky racetracks (notably Pimlico and associated tracks) and correctly treats them as a major re-emergence of neuropathogenic EHV‑1 rather than first emergence. Geographic attribution to the United States with specification of affected tracks is appropriate, and the time window 2006–2007 matches regulatory reports. I recommend retaining this as a single linked episode representing the mid‑2000s racetrack/showground EHM cluster; no structural changes are required, though additional primary sources (state veterinary and USDA reports) could be added if more detail is desired.

Countries: Germany [2009] (mixed riding and breeding facility in southern Germany)
Host: Horses at a mixed riding and breeding farm (pregnant mares, youngstock and sport horses)
Event summary: In early 2009, a riding and breeding facility in southern Germany experienced a severe EHV-1 outbreak that began with an index abortion and rapidly progressed to multiple additional abortions, febrile illness in many horses, and a cluster of equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) cases. Neurologic horses showed ataxia, weakness, and urinary dysfunction, but with intensive care all survived, while pregnant mares suffered repeated late-term losses over several weeks. Implementation of strict isolation of febrile and neurologic horses, separation of pregnant mares, enhanced temperature monitoring, and stable-level biosecurity measures eventually halted new cases and prevented wider spread beyond the farm, although the episode highlighted the potential for EHV-1 to cause concurrent abortion storms and neurologic disease on a single premises.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High intra-farm contact rates, shared housing of pregnant mares and performance horses, and delayed recognition of early febrile cases facilitated within-farm transmission after introduction or reactivation of EHV-1. Internal mechanisms: Virologic work identified a neuropathogenic EHV-1 strain and emphasized the role of ORF30 polymorphism and endothelial tropism in the pathogenesis of both abortion and neurologic disease, making this a clear example of re-emergence driven by strain characteristics within an already endemic region.
Review: Retain – This event corresponds closely to a well-described 2009 German farm outbreak with combined abortions and EHM, and the location, hosts, and clinical pattern in the row match the primary literature. Classifying it as re-emergence (neuropathogenic strain causing unusually severe disease on a premises where EHV‑1 was already present) rather than first emergence or intra-/inter-continental spread is appropriate. I recommend retaining this as one of the larger European EHV‑1 outbreaks in the period.

Countries: United States of America [2011], Canada [2011] (multistate / multiprovince spread originating at Ogden, Utah)
Host: Cutting and western performance horses at the National Cutting Horse Association Western National Championships and linked home facilities
Event summary: During late April and early May 2011, EHV-1 spread extensively among horses attending the National Cutting Horse Association Western National Championships in Ogden, Utah, with initial fever and respiratory signs followed by numerous horses developing equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM). After exposed horses returned home, secondary outbreaks occurred across western U.S. states and parts of Canada, ultimately exposing more than 2,000 horses at over 240 premises, with at least 84 confirmed EHV-1/EHM cases and around a dozen deaths. Coordinated federal–state response, extensive quarantines, event cancellations, and aggressive communication through the AAEP, EDCC precursors, and state animal health officials gradually contained the outbreak over about a month, and the episode became a landmark case in recognizing and managing large-scale EHM events.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A large interstate gathering of cutting horses under crowded conditions, followed by rapid dispersal of exposed animals back to many states and provinces, created an extensive contact network; limited initial biosecurity and delayed recognition of neurologic cases allowed widespread silent dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of neuropathogenic EHV‑1 strains capable of causing EHM, together with host factors such as older age and intense training/travel stress, underpinned the high neurologic case load and cemented EHM’s status as an emerging equine disease in North America.
Review: Retain – This row accurately reflects the scale and epidemiology of the 2011 Ogden cutting-horse outbreak, but I have added Canada to the country list to acknowledge documented Canadian secondary cases. The description and numbers (over 2,000 exposed horses, ~84 confirmed cases, ~12 deaths) match federal and peer‑reviewed summaries, and classification as a major re-emergence event without new continental spread is appropriate. This is unambiguously one of the highest-impact EHV‑1 events since 1990 and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America [2012] (Hawthorne Race Course, Illinois)
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses at Hawthorne Race Course
Event summary: Beginning in October 2012, Hawthorne Race Course near Chicago, Illinois, experienced an outbreak of neurologic EHV-1 in backstretch horses, with multiple animals developing fever that progressed to ataxia and recumbency and at least six to seven fatalities over the course of the event. The Illinois Department of Agriculture imposed a prolonged quarantine of the track, racing officials dropped at least seven race days, and other jurisdictions temporarily restricted entry of Illinois-based racehorses, generating substantial economic losses and logistical disruption. After several weeks of strict isolation of affected barns, enhanced monitoring, and no new neurologic cases, quarantine was lifted, but the event prompted long-term regulatory changes including specific EHV-1 vaccination and entry requirements for horses racing at Illinois tracks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density stabling and continual movement of racehorses into and out of Hawthorne, together with the financial pressure to maintain racing, initially hampered rapid control and facilitated EHV-1 transmission once an infected horse was present. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved the neurologic form of EHV‑1 (EHM) and likely neuropathogenic genotypes, illustrating how racetrack management conditions can amplify an otherwise endemic virus into a high-impact neurologic outbreak, justifying its classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – The Hawthorne 2012 outbreak is correctly located and characterized as a neurologic EHV‑1 event with multiple deaths and substantial economic impact. The sources cited specifically describe this outbreak, and classifying it as re-emergence (severe clinical expression of an endemic virus in a racetrack environment) is appropriate. I recommend keeping this as one of the larger racetrack EHM events in the dataset.

Countries: United States of America [2016] (Sunland Park Racetrack, New Mexico)
Host: Thoroughbred and Quarter Horse racehorses at Sunland Park Racetrack
Event summary: In early 2016, an EHV-1 outbreak at Sunland Park Racetrack in New Mexico resulted in dozens of confirmed infections, multiple neurologic EHM cases, and quarantine of roughly 3,000 horses at Sunland Park and connected facilities. Racing was suspended for 19 days, the Grade III Sunland Derby and Sunland Park Oaks were cancelled, and approximately 72 races with several million dollars in purses were lost while regulators and track management implemented stringent testing and movement controls. With sustained quarantine, isolation of affected barns, and progressive decline in new cases, the outbreak was brought under control and restrictions were gradually lifted, and the episode became a key case study in large-scale racetrack EHV‑1 risk and economic impact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large numbers of racehorses housed in close quarters, frequent movement between barns and training centers, and intense racing schedules created ideal conditions for rapid amplification of EHV‑1 once introduced, with substantial economic incentives initially favoring continued operations. Internal mechanisms: The occurrence of neurologic EHM cases in a partially immune population suggests involvement of neuropathogenic EHV‑1 variants and high within-barn viral loads; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-emergence of severe EHV‑1 disease in a racetrack setting rather than a new geographical introduction.
Review: Retain – This row accurately summarizes the 2016 Sunland Park EHV‑1 outbreak, including the scale of quarantine and cancellation of the Sunland Derby and Oaks, and correctly codes it as re-emergence in an endemic region. I adjusted the summary to emphasize the approximate number of horses under quarantine and the documented racing and economic impacts based on New Mexico Livestock Board and racing-industry reports. This remains one of the more impactful racetrack-associated EHV‑1 events and should be retained.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia; Northern America
Countries: Spain [2021], France [2021], Belgium [2021], Germany [2021], Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2021], Switzerland [2021], Italy [2021], other European countries with linked cases [2021], Qatar [2021], United States of America [2021] (imported cases linked to returning horses)
Host: International show-jumping and sport horses (primarily warmbloods and sport-horse breeds)
Event summary: In February 2021, an international show-jumping tour at the CES Valencia venue in Spain became the epicenter of one of the most serious EHV-1 outbreaks recorded in Europe, with several hundred horses exposed, a very high proportion developing fever and respiratory disease, and many progressing to equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM), resulting in at least 18 deaths. As exposed horses traveled home, epidemiologically linked cases were reported across at least ten European countries and beyond, including Qatar and a small number of North American cases in horses that had attended European events, prompting the FEI to suspend international competitions in mainland Europe and triggering extensive quarantines and heightened surveillance throughout the sport-horse sector. Over the following months, stringent movement restrictions, mandatory monitoring of temperatures and clinical signs, and strengthened biosecurity and vaccination protocols eventually curtailed new cases, and by late spring 2021 the international competition calendar gradually resumed under much tighter EHV‑1 risk-management rules.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A multi-week, high-density international equestrian event hosting 700–850 horses, limited initial isolation capacity, and substantial horse and human movement between barns enabled rapid amplification of EHV‑1 within the Valencia venue; subsequent long-distance transport of exposed horses without full quarantine disseminated infection widely across Europe and to Qatar and North America. Internal mechanisms: Genomic studies showed closely related EHV‑1 strains associated with high rates of EHM among affected horses, although some were of the so-called non-neuropathogenic ORF30 genotype, underscoring the role of viral load, host factors, and intense exposure in driving severe neurologic disease during this large re-emergence event.
Review: Review – The Valencia 2021 episode is correctly portrayed as one of the largest EHV‑1/EHM outbreaks in Europe, with at least 18 deaths and cases in ~10 countries, and the list of affected countries and inclusion of Qatar and the U.S. as destinations of returning horses are appropriate. I changed the emergence-type coding: previously it was marked as both intra- and inter-continental emergence, but because EHV‑1 was already endemic in Europe, Asia, and North America and all extra‑European cases were epidemiologically linked exports from Valencia rather than first continental introductions, this outbreak should be treated purely as a large re-emergence event, not a new inter-continental emergence. Recommended status: retain as a top‑tier event, with corrected classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2024] (aged working equids at a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains, California)
Host: Aged working horses and one mule (trail and ranch-type equids in a single closed operation)
Event summary: In the summer of 2024, an outbreak of EHV-1 myeloencephalopathy was documented in a population of 33 aged working equids at a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California, with 18 animals developing clinical disease. Fourteen horses developed neurologic signs consistent with EHM (ataxia, weakness, urinary incontinence, recumbency), and several others exhibited only fever and respiratory signs; six neurologic horses were euthanized due to severity of deficits. Strict on-farm quarantine, supportive treatment (including antivirals, anti-inflammatories, and anticoagulants), and monitoring of all exposed equids led to a gradual decline in new cases, and by about three weeks after onset, viral shedding had ceased and surviving horses stabilized, though some retained long-term neurologic deficits.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: An older equid population with waning immunity, chronic work-related stress, and close contact in a single operation created conditions for efficient spread once EHV‑1 was introduced or reactivated, while limited resources constrained options for referral or extensive isolation facilities. Internal mechanisms: Quantitative PCR documented high viral loads in blood and nasal secretions in many clinically affected animals, and all typed isolates were of the non-neuropathogenic N752 genotype, illustrating that EHM can arise in older horses even without the classic neuropathogenic marker and supporting classification as re-emergence driven by host and viral-load factors rather than expansion into new areas or hosts.
Review: Review – The original row incorrectly placed this outbreak in Nevada and implied an uncertain 2023–2024 time span; I corrected the location to a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California and the year to 2024, and updated the host description and case numbers to match the Viruses case report. Classification as re-emergence (unusually severe EHM in a closed, aged herd within an endemic region) remains appropriate. Scientifically this is a valuable illustration of EHM in older working equids, but in terms of absolute scale it is smaller than major multi-state or multi-country events; I therefore recommend flagging it as below the top tier of impact and potentially excluding it if a strict "10 largest events" filter is enforced, while retaining it for now as a well-documented local outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2022] (Desert International Horse Park, Thermal, California, with linked cases and quarantines across multiple California counties and western states)
Host: Show-jumping and hunter/jumper sport horses at a multi-week winter circuit
Event summary: In February 2022, Desert International Horse Park (DIHP) in Thermal, California, reported an outbreak of EHV-1 during its multi-week Desert Circuit, with an initial neurologic EHM case confirmed on-site and subsequent detection of additional febrile and neurologic horses. Over the following weeks, at least a dozen confirmed EHV-1 cases (including several EHM) were identified at the venue, one horse was euthanized, and show management ultimately cancelled the remaining Desert Circuit weeks and Desert Dressage IV to limit spread. Horses that had competed at DIHP seeded secondary cases at other California shows and training barns, leading to a multi-county outbreak, extensive quarantines, and heightened surveillance; by late March, after nearly six weeks of movement controls, temperature monitoring, and targeted testing, California authorities began lifting quarantines and the outbreak was considered contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large numbers of high-value show horses from many states stabled in close quarters for a prolonged winter circuit, together with early horse movement off-site before full recognition of the outbreak, facilitated regional dissemination of EHV-1. Internal mechanisms: Investigations showed that both neuropathogenic and non-neuropathogenic EHV‑1 genotypes could be associated with EHM, and risk-factor analyses identified older age and certain management practices (e.g., discipline, housing patterns) as contributors to infection and neurologic disease, supporting interpretation of this episode as a major re-emergence event in a dense sport-horse network.
Review: Review – The previous row conflated this outbreak with speculative, later "recurrent" events and labeled the period 2021–2025; I have restricted the event to the well-documented 2022 DIHP Desert Circuit outbreak and updated the narrative to align with peer-reviewed analyses and official reports. Location (Thermal, California) and the multi-county nature of the episode are now explicitly described, and sources have been changed to DIHP- and California-specific outbreak reports and epidemiologic studies rather than to the separate 2025 Pusterla et al. management case, which describes a smaller, distinct outbreak at a multi-week event. Classification as re-emergence (severe disease expression in an endemic region with high sport-horse mobility) remains appropriate. Recommended status: retain as a major sport-horse EHV‑1 event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2025] (multi-state outbreak originating at the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race, Waco, Texas; cases reported in Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Washington, South Dakota, Louisiana and other states)
Host: Barrel racing and rodeo horses attending the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race, plus secondary cases in exposed performance and ranch horses across multiple states
Event summary: In November 2025, an outbreak of EHV-1 and equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) began among horses competing at the Women’s Professional Rodeo Association (WPRA) World Finals and Elite Barrel Race in Waco, Texas, and rapidly expanded as exposed horses returned home. By late November, official and industry summaries reported at least 50 confirmed EHV-1–positive horses, including around 28 with neurologic EHM, and more than 150 exposed horses distributed across multiple U.S. states, with numerous deaths reported by treating clinics. State animal health agencies and the Equine Disease Communication Center issued urgent advisories, many barrel races and rodeo events were cancelled or postponed, and multiple states imposed new testing and entry requirements for horses returning from Texas and Oklahoma. Intensive quarantine, contact tracing, and public outreach over subsequent weeks gradually reduced new case reports, but the episode underscored the vulnerability of large rodeo and barrel-racing circuits to widespread dissemination of endemic EHV‑1.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A very large, multi-day barrel racing and rodeo event with extensive interstate participation, shared stabling, and frequent horse movement between events allowed rapid amplification and long-distance dissemination of EHV‑1 from a single venue. Subsequent long-haul transport of exposed horses into diverse boarding, training, and competition environments, sometimes before clinical signs were recognized, further widened the outbreak footprint, while the economic and competitive pressures of high‑stakes events initially impeded rapid containment. Internal mechanisms: Early reports describe the strain as clinically aggressive with a high proportion of neurologic cases, but definitive genomic characterization is still limited; in the absence of clear evidence for a novel genotype, the episode is best treated as a large re-occurrence of severe disease caused by endemic EHV-1 under high-risk management and movement conditions rather than a true viral re-emergence in a new host or region.
Review: Added – The original dataset omitted the large 2025 multi-state EHV‑1/EHM outbreak linked to the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race in Waco, Texas, despite its clear importance: at least 50 confirmed positive horses (roughly half with neurologic EHM) and more than 150 exposed animals across numerous U.S. states, with multiple deaths and widespread event cancellations. I created a new row to capture this episode, coded it as a re-occurrence (large-scale resurgence of endemic virus driven by event structure and horse movements) rather than first emergence, and drew on EDCC alerts, extension summaries and state/regional advisories for dates and approximate scale. This outbreak is comparable in impact to the 2011 Ogden and 2021 Valencia events and should be retained among the major post‑1990 EHV‑1 events.

Host: Polo horses (Thoroughbred–Criollo crosses and related sport-horse types) in a large Chilean polo operation
Event summary: In early 2025, Chile reported its first documented outbreak of equine herpes myeloencephalopathy in a large polo-horse operation housing more than 500 horses, where EHV-1 infection had previously been associated only with respiratory disease and abortion. During the outbreak, numerous horses developed fever and respiratory signs and a subset progressed to neurologic deficits such as hindlimb ataxia, weakness and urinary incontinence, prompting notification of the national animal-health authority and the implementation of strict on-farm quarantine, movement restrictions, and enhanced hygiene measures. Over several weeks, targeted isolation of clinical cases, temperature monitoring, and restricted horse movement gradually reduced transmission; by the end of the official quarantine period in April 2025 no new cases were detected, although a minority of affected horses retained residual neurologic deficits.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density stabling, intense training and competition of polo horses, and frequent within-operation mixing likely facilitated rapid EHV‑1 transmission once a neurologically virulent strain or reactivated infection entered the herd; increased clinical and laboratory surveillance following recognition of neurologic signs enabled the first formal identification and reporting of EHM in Chile. Internal mechanisms: This outbreak represents re-emergence of EHV‑1 with a new clinical phenotype (EHM) in a country where the virus was already endemic for respiratory and reproductive disease, reflecting the role of neuropathogenic or high‑viremia infections in shifting disease expression toward neurologic involvement among adult performance horses under stress.
Review: Retain – This row aligns closely with the published case report describing the first recognized EHM outbreak in Chile, including host type (polo horses), the large operation size, the onset and end of quarantine, and the classification of EHM as a new clinical manifestation of an already endemic EHV‑1. Coding this as re-emergence (new disease expression in an existing host population and region) rather than first detection of the virus itself is appropriate. Given its status as the first reported EHM outbreak in Chile and a significant regional event, this row should be retained among the major emergence events.

Host: Horses at a riding establishment near Barcelona (mixed riding horses, various breeds)
Event summary: In 1992, an outbreak of equine viral arteritis occurred at a riding establishment near Barcelona, Spain, affecting 31 of 186 horses with fever, depression, edema of the limbs and ventrum, and vesicular–erosive stomatitis but no recorded mortality. Serologic testing confirmed recent infection with equine arteritis virus, representing the first confirmed clinical EVA outbreak reported from Spain, although the virus was already recognized elsewhere in Southern and Western Europe. The outbreak remained confined to the riding establishment and resolved with management measures, after which Spain reported no further major clinical EVA outbreaks for many years despite later serologic evidence of low‑level EAV circulation in horse populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable introduction of an infected horse or semen from other European regions into a largely naïve Spanish riding population, together with close housing and intensive use of horses at a single establishment, facilitated efficient respiratory spread. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient horse‑to‑horse respiratory transmission of an established EAV lineage into an immunologically naïve group; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment of clinical EVA in a new national population within Southern Europe without evidence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Event is well documented as the first recognized clinical EVA outbreak in Spain and of moderate regional impact. Corrected emergence classification: set intra_continental_emergence to false because EAV was already established in Southern Europe (e.g. Italy) before 1992; treated instead as a re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion with first national recognition.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1993]
Host: Non‑Thoroughbred breeding horses (stallions and mares) on a stud in south Nottinghamshire and horses on five linked premises
Event summary: In 1993, equine viral arteritis was diagnosed for the first time in the United Kingdom when an outbreak began on a non‑Thoroughbred stud in south Nottinghamshire after use of a recently imported Anglo‑Arab stallion. Infection spread to five additional premises via chilled semen used for artificial insemination and via movement of acutely or subclinically infected mares, resulting in typical EVA signs including pyrexia, depression, conjunctivitis, and limb and genital edema in about 100 horses. Voluntary movement restrictions, tracing of exposed mares, and control measures on the six affected premises contained the outbreak, after which EVA was made notifiable in the UK and long‑term serologic surveillance programmes for stallions and mares were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in breeding stallions and chilled semen from continental Europe into a naïve UK horse population, combined with widespread artificial insemination and return movement of bred mares, enabled rapid dissemination; absence of prior EVA vaccination and limited awareness further amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient venereal and respiratory transmission from a persistently infected carrier stallion and acutely infected mares; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – first confirmed establishment of clinical EVA in the Northern Europe subregion with onward spread between multiple premises.
Review: retain – Widely recognised as the first recorded EVA outbreak in the UK, involving six premises and around 100 horses and prompting major regulatory changes. Corrected type classification by setting first_detection to false (global first detection was in 1953 in Ohio); retained intra_continental_emergence as true because this represents spread of clinical EVA into the Northern Europe subregion.

Countries: United States of America (Illinois [1993], Kentucky [1993], Iowa [1993], Nebraska [1993])
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses on the Arlington Park racetrack in Illinois and subsequently at other linked racetracks in Kentucky, Iowa and Nebraska
Event summary: In the summer of 1993, a large epizootic of equine viral arteritis occurred over roughly eight weeks among Thoroughbred racehorses at Arlington Park racetrack in Illinois, with more than 200 horses developing clinical illness characterized by fever, respiratory signs, edema and urticaria. Infected horses subsequently moved to other racetracks, and related EVA cases were reported at Churchill Downs (Kentucky), Prairie Meadows (Iowa) and Ak‑Sar‑Ben (Nebraska), disrupting race meetings and training schedules across several US states. Track‑level movement controls, enhanced biosecurity, and natural resolution of clinical cases brought the multi‑track outbreak under control, after which EVA remained sporadic in US racehorses until larger Quarter Horse breeding‑farm outbreaks later in the 2000s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of incubating or subclinically infected racehorses between racetracks in the Midwestern racing circuit, combined with dense stabling, shared airspace and equipment, and lack of routine EVA vaccination in Thoroughbreds, created ideal conditions for intense respiratory spread and rapid dissemination along the racing network. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient droplet and aerosol transmission of an existing EAV lineage in confined stabling; no clear evidence for a novel genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence driven mainly by horse movements and management factors rather than viral change.
Review: retain – This multi-track epizootic (>200 clinical cases across several US racetracks) is consistently cited as a major EVA event. Countries field updated to reflect spread from Illinois to additional US states, and the event summary expanded beyond a single racetrack; classification as a national re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate.

Host: Warmblood breeding horses (stallions, mares and foals) on a single Warmblood breeding farm in Pennsylvania
Event summary: In spring 1996, an imported Warmblood stallion that was a known carrier of equine arteritis virus seeded an extensive outbreak of equine viral arteritis on a Warmblood breeding farm in Pennsylvania, USA. Over several weeks, clinical EVA was recorded in 23 horses on the farm (four stallions, seven mares and 12 foals), with one late‑term abortion and three foal deaths, as virus spread from the carrier stallion to in‑contact stallions, mares and foals via both venereal and respiratory routes. Emergency vaccination of clinically unaffected horses with modified‑live vaccine, strict on‑farm biosecurity, and management of carrier stallions eventually curtailed the outbreak but highlighted the risk posed by imported Warmblood carriers to North American sport‑horse breeding operations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of a persistently infected Warmblood stallion from Europe into a susceptible Warmblood breeding herd, combined with intensive on‑farm breeding and close stabling of stallions, mares and foals, enabled rapid venereal and aerosol spread; prior absence of EVA vaccination and limited screening of imported stallions amplified the risk. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – selection of a single EAV variant from the carrier stallion’s semen that was efficiently transmitted both vertically and horizontally on the farm; Genetic Stability – molecular analyses showed the outbreak strain remained highly stable as it spread through mares and foals, indicating that re-occurrence was driven by introduction and management factors rather than emergence of a markedly divergent genotype.
Review: retain – This Warmblood breeding‑farm outbreak (23 clinical cases, foal deaths and abortion) is explicitly highlighted in major reviews as a notable international EVA event and is likely among the top 10 post‑1990 outbreaks by impact. New row added and classified as a re-occurrence within an already endemic US subregion, driven by introduction of a carrier stallion; no evidence supports inter- or intra-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Equids in South Africa, primarily donkeys and selected horse populations associated with carrier stallions (exact outbreak locations and case numbers not well documented)
Event summary: National disease‑status reporting in South Africa lists 1998 as the date of the last officially recorded outbreak of equine viral arteritis, in a country where earlier work had demonstrated widespread equine arteritis virus seropositivity in donkeys and lateral transmission among Lipizzaner stallions but few confirmed clinical cases in horses. Published studies from the 1990s document high EAV seroprevalence in South African donkeys and identification of a highly divergent asinine EAV genotype in donkey semen, as well as lateral spread between stallions at the Lipizzaner Centre, suggesting localized circulation of distinct EAV lineages. The 1998 entry most likely reflects limited recognized EVA cases or confirmation events rather than a large clinical epidemic, and no further officially reported outbreaks in South Africa were noted through at least the mid‑2010s, although EAV or its asinine variants persisted serologically in donkeys.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing endemic EAV circulation in South African donkeys and close contacts between donkeys and selected horse or stallion populations, coupled with limited historical surveillance of EVA in horses, likely allowed silent maintenance and occasional spillover events; regulatory focus on other equine diseases may have delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular work identified a highly divergent South African asinine EAV genotype with only 60–70% nucleotide identity to reference strains, implying prolonged independent evolution; Host Expansion (Spillover) – experimental and field data indicate potential for transmission from donkeys to horses; these virological features justify treating the African situation as a re-emergence involving new genotypic diversity rather than simple range expansion.
Review: review – South Africa’s official disease-status report lists 1998 as the last EVA outbreak, but no detailed, peer-reviewed description of a sizeable clinical outbreak in horses could be traced, and other sources state that no confirmed EVA cases in horses have occurred since the late 1980s while documenting high-prevalence donkey infection and divergent asinine genotypes. The current row therefore reinterprets this as a low‑detail re-emergence linked to divergent African strains rather than a major clinical epidemic; impact and even existence as a discrete 1998 outbreak should be checked by a human expert, and the event could be excluded if only clearly high-impact episodes are retained.
Review Comment: a low‑detail re-emergence

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2004] (index stallion infected during transport from the Netherlands, Kingdom of the [2004])
Host: Imported stallion and in‑contact horses in Great Britain (non‑Thoroughbred; Dutch stallion and associated consignment)
Event summary: In 2004, the United Kingdom reported a new occurrence of equine viral arteritis, classified by the World Organisation for Animal Health as a re‑occurrence of a previously listed infection in a country that had been free since the 1993 outbreak. During transport from the Netherlands to Great Britain, a Dutch stallion that was subsequently confirmed as an EAV carrier shared transport with other horses, and an outbreak involving 18 equines (one clinical case and 17 in‑contacts) was detected, with most infections subclinical and no deaths reported. National veterinary authorities imposed investigation, movement restrictions, and testing around the affected premises, and the incident was rapidly contained, reinforcing UK controls on imported stallions and semen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of a carrier stallion within the European single market, shared transport conditions, and absence of stringent pre‑movement EVA testing for stallions at that time allowed re-introduction of EAV into previously free UK premises. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – venereal exposure and close-contact respiratory transmission from a persistently infected carrier stallion led to infection of in‑contact horses; this represents a regulatory and surveillance‑driven re-occurrence of known EAV lineages rather than the emergence of a new viral genotype.
Review: retain – Well supported by OIE/WOAH notification as a limited but policy‑relevant re-occurrence in a country that had been EVA-free since 1993. No changes to type classification were needed; row retained as a smaller but still notable re-introduction event within Europe.

Countries: United States of America (New Mexico [2005], Kansas [2006], Montana [2006], Oklahoma [2006], Utah [2006], Alabama [2006] and additional affected states)
Host: Quarter Horse breeding stock (stallions, mares and foals) on multiple breeding farms in several US states
Event summary: From late 2005 through 2007, equine viral arteritis emerged as a major problem in the American Quarter Horse breeding industry when EVA was first recognized on a large breeding farm in New Mexico, where early pregnancy losses and abortions were traced to EAV infection. During 2006–2007, the outbreak expanded into a multi‑state occurrence, with EVA confirmed on premises in at least six US states (including Kansas, Montana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Utah and Alabama) and additional respiratory disease, abortions, neonatal pneumonia and foal deaths, largely linked to movements and semen of infected Quarter Horse stallions. Quarantine of affected premises, extensive testing of stallions and mares, restrictions on shipment of semen, and increased vaccination and biosecurity measures gradually controlled the outbreak by 2007, but it caused substantial economic disruption and cemented EAV’s status as an important emerging reproductive pathogen in the US Quarter Horse sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive interstate trade in breeding stallions and cooled-shipped semen within the Quarter Horse industry, concentration of large numbers of pregnant mares on a few breeding farms, and historically low EVA vaccination coverage in Quarter Horses enabled rapid venereal and respiratory spread across multiple states; export and competition restrictions for affected horses amplified the economic impact. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular epidemiology showed that the multi‑state outbreak was driven by a distinct EAV strain with characteristic insertions in nsp2 and ORF3 shared among isolates from several western and midwestern states; Enhanced Transmission – the carrier‑stallion state and efficient venereal transmission via semen were central to persistence and dissemination; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – rapid spread of this variant across a wide geographic area of the US within a single subregion.
Review: retain – This multi‑state Quarter Horse outbreak is universally described as one of the most significant EVA events since the 1984 Kentucky epidemic, with abortions, foal deaths, and widespread trade disruption. Minor edits were made to clarify that additional states beyond those listed were affected; type classification as a re-emergence driven by a distinct outbreak strain remains appropriate.

Countries: France [2007] (mainly Normandy and other western departments)
Host: Breeding and sport horses on multiple premises in Normandy and western France (various draught, warmblood and sport‑horse types)
Event summary: In summer 2007, France experienced its first major recorded occurrence of equine viral arteritis when a virulent EAV strain emerged in Normandy, causing clinical EVA with abortions, neonatal deaths and occasional adult mortality in affected foals and horses. The epidemic spread through the breeding season to at least 18–30 premises in five western departments, with index, primary and secondary premises linked through movements of stallions, mares and shipped semen, and more than 200 horses affected overall. Intensive surveillance, use of real‑time RT‑PCR for rapid diagnosis, movement restrictions, and targeted control measures in breeding stallions and mares brought the epidemic under control by late summer, although less pathogenic EAV strains and sporadic cases continued to be detected in France thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density breeding activity and frequent movements of stallions and mares within Normandy and neighbouring western regions, limited pre‑existing EVA vaccination in French breeding populations, and intensive use of shipped semen and competition horses created a highly connected network that facilitated rapid farm‑to‑farm spread; the outbreak also prompted heightened regulatory and industry responses. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – virological studies demonstrated that the epidemic was driven by an emergent EAV variant arising from a persistently infected carrier stallion, distinct from previously circulating low‑pathogenic French strains; Enhanced Transmission – this variant showed high clinical impact with abortions and foal deaths and efficient spread in both breeding and sport‑horse populations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – swift dissemination within western France from a single carrier‑stallion source.
Review: retain – The 2007 Normandy epidemic is clearly one of the largest and best documented EVA outbreaks in Europe, with >200 affected horses, multiple premises, foal deaths and abortions, and demonstration of a novel outbreak strain. Existing classification as a re-emergence linked to a new variant is consistent with the literature; only minor wording changes were made to align case numbers and affected departments with primary sources.

Countries: Argentina [2010] (San Antonio de Areco, Buenos Aires Province)
Host: Thoroughbred breeding mares and foals on a Thoroughbred stud farm in San Antonio de Areco, together with related sport-horse mares inseminated with imported frozen semen
Event summary: In March 2010, Argentina experienced its first reported clinical outbreak of equine viral arteritis when an abortion storm associated with EAV infection occurred on a Thoroughbred breeding farm in San Antonio de Areco, Buenos Aires Province. Abortions and reproductive losses were detected in Thoroughbred mares after they had been mixed with showjumping mares that had recently been inseminated with frozen semen imported from the Netherlands, and EAV was isolated from semen straws and fetal or placental material; epidemiologic investigation and genetic analysis later confirmed that the outbreak strain (GLD-LP-ARG) belonged to the European EU-1 group. In response, the national veterinary authority (SENASA) imposed temporary restrictions on horse movements in Buenos Aires Province, expanded testing of stallions and semen, and strengthened the national EVA surveillance and control programme, after which the outbreak was contained and no wider dissemination into other regions of Argentina was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A largely EAV-naïve national horse population with very low background seroprevalence, combined with the importation and use of infected frozen semen from a European carrier stallion, provided the conditions for an abortion outbreak in highly valuable Thoroughbred breeding stock; the lack of permitted EVA vaccination in Argentina at that time and extensive mixing of Thoroughbred and sport-horse mares on the affected premises further increased vulnerability. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Introduction – molecular characterisation showed that the outbreak was caused by a European-type EU‑1 strain closely related to certain Belgian and previously isolated Argentinean strains, representing re-emergence of EAV disease in Argentina through introduction and amplification of a virulent genotype; Enhanced Transmission – the ability of the imported strain to cause abortions and limited lateral spread among mares and foals underscores its pathogenicity in an otherwise naïve population.
Review: retain – This 2010 abortion outbreak, with provincial movement restrictions and the first documented clinical EVA in Argentina, is consistently highlighted in international reviews as a major recent EVA event and is likely one of the top 10 globally by impact since 1990. New row added and classified as a re-emergence driven by introduction of a European EU‑1 strain into a largely naïve South American horse population; not coded as inter-continental emergence because EAV had been present serologically and virologically in Argentina prior to 2010.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Breeding horses on stud farms in south‑eastern France (including foals and mares)
Event summary: In 2011, several years after the major 2007 Normandy epidemic, a localized outbreak of equine viral arteritis was detected in south‑eastern France, with clinical EVA reported on at least one stud farm, including abortion and the death of a foal. Case numbers and geographical spread were modest compared with 2007, but the episode confirmed that EAV continued to circulate at low levels in French breeding populations outside Normandy. Rapid diagnosis, tracing of exposed animals, and reinforcement of existing surveillance and biosecurity protocols in breeding stallions and mares limited the outbreak, and France has since reported sporadic EVA cases and small clusters but no epidemic on the scale of 2007.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Residual EAV circulation in regional breeding populations and movement of subclinically infected horses or semen into south‑eastern holdings enabled re-occurrence; uneven vaccination uptake and lower surveillance intensity outside core breeding regions may have contributed. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by persistence of existing French EAV lineages rather than emergence of a novel genotype; Enhanced Transmission – local horse‑to‑horse contact and breeding activity sustained a small outbreak that was rapidly halted once detected.
Review: retain – A modest but well-documented re-occurrence confirming ongoing low-level EAV circulation in France with abortion and a foal death. Kept because, once higher-impact events are included, there is still room within the approximate top 10 for a representative smaller re-occurrence; type classification as re-occurrence without emergence was confirmed, and no major corrections were required.

Host: Horses (sport and breeding horses treated with or epidemiologically linked to contaminated hyperimmune plasma)
