Event summary: In 2006, equine infectious anaemia was unexpectedly detected in Ireland in a cluster of sport and breeding horses, after several animals on premises in County Meath that had received imported equine hyperimmune plasma developed acute EIA, revealing the country’s first recorded outbreak in many decades. Subsequent investigations showed that the index infections were linked to a contaminated plasma batch, with additional clinically apparent and subclinical cases identified on multiple farms and in referral facilities in Ireland and one linked premises in Northern Ireland through iatrogenic transmission and horse movements. The episode was contained over the following months through extensive tracing, testing and culling of infected horses, strict movement controls, and enhanced surveillance, after which Ireland regained its EIA-free trade status with no evidence of endemic circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in inadequately screened equine hyperimmune plasma and its therapeutic use in multiple horses seeded infection, while subsequent spread was driven by iatrogenic transmission (shared veterinary equipment, surgical procedures) and movement of treated horses between farms and clinics. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that Irish viruses were closely related to those involved in a contemporaneous Italian plasma-associated outbreak, with no evidence of a new, more virulent EIAV strain; the episode reflects re-introduction and amplification of established EIAV lineages rather than evolutionary change.
Review: retain – Real 2006 Irish outbreak seeded by contaminated hyperimmune plasma, with multiple linked premises and cross-border spread to Northern Ireland. Classification as re-occurrence in Northern Europe is consistent with prior EIAV presence in the subregion, and host, geography and timing are correct; sources include national reports and detailed outbreak investigations. Minor nuance: the outbreak ultimately involved more than two premises, but the summary captures the main drivers and control measures, so no structural changes are required.

Host: Horses (mainly sport and working horses in central and other Italian regions)
Event summary: In 2006, Italy experienced a notable outbreak of equine infectious anaemia when horses that had received contaminated hyperimmune plasma developed EIA in central regions, leading to recognition that EIAV infection was more widespread in the national horse population than previously appreciated. As investigations and follow-up testing proceeded, additional infections were detected on neighbouring and more distant farms, including animals with no direct plasma exposure, implicating mechanical transmission by blood-feeding flies and possible iatrogenic spread, and prompting Italy to launch a comprehensive National Surveillance Plan that actively screened the entire equid population between 2007 and 2012. Over this 2006–2012 episode, testing of over a million equids identified EIAV-seropositive animals on more than a thousand holdings, but systematic serological screening, notification, culling or permanent isolation of positive equids and movement controls progressively reduced infection prevalence, after which surveillance shifted to a risk-based approach and reported occurrence declined to low levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of untested or inadequately screened equine plasma products, combined with horse movements between farms and extensive use of shared equipment, seeded the initial outbreak, while favourable vector conditions and dense equid populations in some rural areas facilitated ongoing mechanical transmission by horseflies and stable flies; the absence of prior nationwide testing meant many inapparent carriers had accumulated undetected. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses of Italian field isolates revealed typical EIAV gag sequences, including close relatedness between the Irish and Italian 2006 plasma-associated strains and other historical North American and Asian isolates, without evidence of a novel hypervirulent genotype; re-occurrence is best explained by persistence and amplification of existing EIAV lineages in high-risk ecologic niches rather than viral innovation.
Review: review – Year span adjusted from 2006–2007 to 2006–2012 to reflect that the initial 2006 plasma-associated outbreak directly triggered Italy’s National Surveillance Plan, during which over 1 million equids were tested and EIAV-positive animals were found on >1,000 holdings through 2012, making this a multi-year national re-occurrence episode rather than a short, two‑year event. Geography, host, and classification as re-occurrence remain appropriate; sources now clearly support the extended surveillance period and magnitude.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses (primarily saddle and sport horses, with some cases on rescue or mixed-use premises)
Event summary: From 2009 to 2012, France experienced a multi-year episode of sporadic but impactful equine infectious anaemia re-occurrence after a long period of very low prevalence, with around 15 cases in several outbreaks in 2009 (notably in the Var department and one case in Dordogne), 10 infected horses across seven foci in 2010 in multiple regions, and eight cases in two foci in 2012 in the Gard and Vaucluse departments. The episode consisted of geographically scattered clusters affecting mainly saddle and sport horses, including foci epidemiologically linked to imports of Romanian-origin horses via Belgium as well as apparently autochthonous infections, leading to intensive national surveillance and detailed outbreak investigations. Each focus was controlled through euthanasia of positive horses, movement restrictions, tracing and testing of in-contact and neighbouring equids, and expanded testing within affected departments, and by 2014 only two isolated cases were detected in the Gard department, indicating that this re-occurrence phase had been largely contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses from endemic areas (especially Romania) through intra-EU trade, together with frequent movements of sport and leisure horses for competition and sale, initiated several French outbreaks, while local transmission was favoured by vector exposure and, in some instances, potentially by management practices that allowed blood contamination between animals; heightened surveillance also increased detection of latent carriers. Internal mechanisms: No French-specific EIAV genotype with clearly increased virulence or altered host range has been reported; phylogenetic and serological data suggest that re-occurrence reflects repeated introductions and local persistence of existing EIAV strains rather than emergence of a distinct, more pathogenic lineage.
Review: review – Evidence from French surveillance reports and the RESPE network confirms the cluster sizes and distribution summarised here (≈15 cases in 2009, 10 in 2010, 8 in 2012) and supports classification as a national re-occurrence episode confined to Western Europe. To strengthen sourcing, official French outbreak and surveillance reports (RESPE alert on the 2012 Gard focus; Gaudaire et al. 2012 surveillance overview) have been added alongside the OIE regional report and the French Wikipedia synthesis; the NDCC equine disease alert is no longer relied upon as a primary source. Geography, timing and event type remain appropriate, but the row is flagged for review to allow a future curator to decide whether pre‑2009 French foci (2001, 2005, 2007) should be merged into a longer linked episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Equids (horses, mules and donkeys, primarily in extensively managed western herds)
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2012, Canada’s national equine infectious anaemia control program documented a substantial burden of endemic EIAV in western and northern regions when federal disease investigations identified 409 EIA-positive equids on 288 holdings, with 397 of these cases in the western provinces and territories (Yukon, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan) and only 12 in eastern Canada (Québec). The episode unfolded not as a single point-source outbreak but as a concentration of infections detected through case-triggered testing in remote, extensively managed equid populations where owner-requested surveillance coverage was low, prompting concern that EIAV remained entrenched in parts of western Canada despite very low national prevalence. Control measures during this period involved investigation of each positive case, tracing and testing of in-contact equids, mandatory movement restrictions and, where required, destruction or permanent quarantine of infected animals, and the findings contributed to federal discussions and consultations on revising Canada’s national EIA disease control program.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive outdoor management of equids in remote western regions, low levels of voluntary owner-requested testing, and abundant tabanid and stable fly populations facilitated ongoing mechanical transmission of EIAV and allowed infection to persist in sparsely monitored herds; movements of untested or infrequently tested equids between ranches further propagated infection. Internal mechanisms: Available Canadian studies emphasize long-term circulation and genetic heterogeneity of EIAV gag sequences in naturally infected horses rather than the emergence of a new high-virulence strain, so this multi-year pattern represents re-occurrence and persistent endemicity in specific ecological niches rather than viral re-emergence driven by genetic change.
Review: review – New event added to capture a clearly major post‑1990 EIAV episode: 409 positives detected during federal disease investigations from 2009–2012, overwhelmingly in western Canada, which is of greater numerical impact than several small European clusters. Classified as re-occurrence because EIAV has been present in Canada since the 19th century, with no evidence of a novel strain; continent, subregion and host assignments follow the project’s geography schema. Summary and drivers are based on peer‑reviewed analyses of Canada’s EIA control program and CFIA guidance, but the row is flagged for expert review to refine the narrative once full-text Canadian reports are consulted without access limitations.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Equids (horses, working equids and other equines)
Event summary: In 2010, Romania—where EIAV had been endemic for decades—reported a dramatic surge in detected equine infectious anaemia when intensified testing under an eradication program revealed 1,331 outbreaks involving 1,389 seropositive equids during the first half of the year, mainly in rural areas with high densities of working horses. As the episode unfolded, Romanian authorities implemented extensive control measures and the European Commission adopted protective legislation that required pre-movement testing, restricted exports of Romanian equidae and imposed additional safeguards in EU Member States receiving Romanian horses, during a period when infected Romanian-origin horses were linked to outbreaks in Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the United Kingdom. Through 2011–2012, continued surveillance, culling of positives and strengthened movement controls reduced the number of newly reported outbreaks, but low-level endemicity persisted in some regions, and Romania remained a primary European source of EIAV infection in traded equids.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing endemic EIAV in Romania combined with large populations of susceptible working equids, informal horse movements without systematic pre-movement serological testing, and abundant blood-feeding flies created conditions for high local transmission, while Romania’s integration into the EU internal market made it economically important to document infection status, leading to intensified testing that revealed the full extent of infection. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data do not indicate emergence of a novel, hypervirulent EIAV strain in Romania during this period; the apparent ‘explosion’ in case numbers is better explained by improved surveillance superimposed on existing endemicity, combined with continued mechanical transmission and movement of asymptomatically infected equids.
Review: retain – The row accurately reflects the scale of Romania’s 2010 EIAV epizootic (1,331 outbreaks; 1,389 positive equids in the first half of 2010), its role as the main endemic source for subsequent Western European incursions, and the EU protective measures enacted via Decision 2010/346/EU. Classification as a re-occurrence in Eastern Europe is appropriate because EIAV was long-established in the region, and there is no evidence of strain-driven re-emergence; no corrections to geography, timing or event type are needed.

Host: Horses (imported Romanian horses and resident horses on affected premises)
Event summary: In early 2010, Belgium detected equine infectious anaemia in a horse in West Flanders that had been imported from Romania, representing the country’s first recorded occurrence of EIA and triggering concern because many Romanian-origin horses had entered Belgium in preceding years. Epidemiological investigations and targeted serological surveys of horses imported from Romania between 2007 and 2009 revealed additional EIAV-positive animals on several premises, confirming that asymptomatically infected horses had been moved through Belgian dealer networks and sold on to other EU countries. Belgian authorities imposed emergency measures including on-farm quarantine, tracing and testing of contact and similarly imported horses, culling of infected equids and strict movement controls, and were able to demonstrate freedom from infection on affected premises three months after removal of the last positive animals, although re-occurrence with new foci was documented again in 2012.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of live horses from endemic Romania without sufficiently stringent or effectively enforced pre-export testing, coupled with commercial dealer movements of poorly documented animals, was the primary driver of EIAV introduction into Belgium; once in-country, infected but clinically normal horses posed a risk of further spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization of Belgian EIAV isolates showed close relatedness to Romanian field strains, consistent with direct introduction rather than in situ viral evolution, and no new genotype with increased virulence or altered tropism was identified; the event thus reflects re-occurrence mediated by trade rather than viral change.
Review: review – The Belgian 2010 episode is real, well documented and of regulatory importance, but the row has been updated to add the national AFSCA epidemiological summary as a primary source describing that seven outbreaks were detected, all involving Romanian-origin horses, and that Belgium considered this its first recorded EIA occurrence. Event classification remains re-occurrence at the Western Europe subregional scale, which already had EIAV via earlier French outbreaks; timing and geography are correct. Flagged for review mainly to ensure future harmonisation of how first-ever detections at country level are handled within the global classification scheme.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]
Host: Horses (imported and resident horses, mainly in dealer and livery premises)
Event summary: In 2010, the United Kingdom confirmed equine infectious anaemia in an imported horse in Northumberland that had been part of a consignment of Romanian-origin horses routed via Belgium and the Netherlands, during a wider period of EIAV incursions into Western Europe linked to trade from Romania. Over 2010–2012, Great Britain detected a small number of additional cases and very small clusters on dealer and livery premises receiving horses from continental Europe, including two linked cases in Devon and Cornwall in 2012, each of which prompted extensive tracing and testing of in-contact horses and horses from the same import consignments. All incursions were managed by immediate euthanasia of infected horses, imposition of movement restrictions and intensive surveillance of associated premises, and by the end of this period Great Britain remained officially free of endemic EIAV, with national guidance documents describing EIA as a rare, sporadic, mostly import-related infection and indicating that the last outbreaks occurred in 2012.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade and movement of horses from endemic Eastern European areas, often via intermediary countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, without fully effective pre-export or pre-movement screening, was the primary driver of EIAV incursions into the UK; concentration of imported horses in dealer premises increased the risk of onward spread to local horses. Internal mechanisms: Sequence data for UK isolates show close relatedness to Romanian and other European strains and do not indicate the emergence of a novel, more virulent lineage; re-occurrence is therefore best attributed to repeated introduction of existing EIAV genotypes combined with opportunities for mechanical and iatrogenic transmission.
Review: review – The UK 2010–2012 incursions are genuine and policy‑relevant, and the event is correctly framed as a series of small, import-related outbreaks rather than a new endemic focus. To better ground the narrative, official Defra guidance (confirming outbreaks in 2010 and 2012 and the UK’s otherwise EIA‑free status) and the detailed epidemiological report on the 2012 Devon/Cornwall cases have been added as sources. Classification as re-occurrence in Northern Europe remains appropriate; the row is flagged chiefly so future curators can consider whether all Romania-linked 2010 incursions in Western/Northern Europe should be consolidated into a single, multi-country episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Equids (horses and mules, mainly working animals in Pantanal wetlands and northeastern states)
Event summary: From 2010 to 2014, multiple large-scale serological surveys in Brazil highlighted an exceptionally heavy endemic burden of equine infectious anaemia, particularly in the Pantanal wetland region and in northeastern states, revealing that EIAV remained widely disseminated despite existing control regulations. In 2010, testing of 5,615 equids from 209 municipalities in the northeastern states of Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte and Ceará found 151 seropositive animals (2.7%), with infection present year-round and in all three states, while a survey in the Poconé municipality of the northern Pantanal found EIAV antibodies in approximately one-third of sampled equids and on more than half of surveyed farms, with prevalence exceeding 40% among animals kept on regularly flooded pastures. A 2014 statewide study in Mato Grosso, encompassing the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal biomes, subsequently reported 6.6% animal-level and 17.2% herd-level seroprevalence among 3,858 equids in 1,067 herds, with the highest infection levels in the Pantanal zone, underscoring that EIAV is entrenched across multiple biomes and prompting calls to re-evaluate Brazil’s EIA control programme and strengthen prophylactic measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive, low-biosecurity management of working equids in flooded wetlands and cattle-ranching systems, sharing of saddles, tack and veterinary equipment, incomplete segregation or culling of seropositive animals, and abundant populations of blood-feeding flies in the Pantanal and other humid regions all favoured efficient EIAV transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies of Brazilian EIAV from Pantanal horses show high genomic variability within endemic strains but do not implicate a single emergent hypervirulent variant; the high prevalence and farm-level clustering reflect long-term adaptation of EIAV to local equid populations and ecologic conditions rather than a recent evolutionary shift, making this a major endemic re-occurrence episode rather than a distinct re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: review – New event added to represent the very high-burden, post‑1990 endemic situation in Brazil, particularly in the Pantanal/Mato Grosso and northeastern states, where herd- and animal-level seroprevalence (up to ≈52% of farms and ≈30% of animals in parts of Pantanal; ≈6–7% of animals at state level in Mato Grosso) clearly make this one of the most impactful EIAV episodes by numbers infected. Classified as re-occurrence because EIAV has been recognized as endemic in Brazil for decades and the studies describe entrenched infection rather than first introduction or novel-strain emergence. Geography and timing align with survey periods, but the row is flagged for review so that a future curator can refine spatial granularity (e.g. separate Pantanal vs. northeast) if desired.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cattle (feedlot and dairy; healthy carriers)
Event summary: In 1990, a U.S. study systematically detected and characterized verotoxin-producing E. coli in feces of healthy cattle, showing that roughly 10% of animals carried VTEC/STEC strains and confirming that feedlot and dairy cattle could serve as major asymptomatic reservoirs for human-pathogenic serotypes. Follow‑up work through the early 1990s established similar carriage patterns in other North American herds and helped embed cattle reservoirs into quantitative risk assessments for beef and dairy products. This research phase concluded with STEC being recognized in North American policy and industry guidance as a critical pre‑harvest hazard in cattle production systems rather than a purely human clinical problem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of feedlot beef and large dairy operations in North America, high stocking densities, and fecal–oral transmission within herds favoured amplification and maintenance of STEC, while improved laboratory methods (Shiga/verotoxin assays, DNA probes) enabled detection in asymptomatic cattle. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects recognition, rather than de novo evolution, of STEC lineages in cattle; no specific novel strain or host expansion is implicated relative to earlier VTEC reports in calves and other domestic species.
Review: review – Study accurately documents early large-scale detection of VTEC/STEC in healthy U.S. cattle and the role of cattle as reservoirs, but it is primarily a surveillance milestone rather than a discrete, high-impact emergence episode (no single major outbreak, policy shift, or geographic jump is tied to 1990 alone). I removed the previous re_emergence flag so that all emergence-type indicators are now No, because there is no clear evidence of a qualitative pathogen change or new host adaptation compared with earlier 1980s VTEC detections in calves and other animals. Consider excluding this row if a strict “top 10” list of highest-impact events is enforced.
Review Comment: it is primarily a surveillance milestone rather than a discrete, high-impact emergence episode

Host: Humans (primarily children) infected via undercooked beef patties; beef cattle as upstream reservoir
Event summary: From late 1992 through early 1993, undercooked beef patties contaminated with E. coli O157:H7 served at a fast‑food chain caused a multistate outbreak in the United States, with more than 700 laboratory‑confirmed cases and at least four child deaths. Investigation traced the outbreak to ground beef produced from cattle carrying O157:H7, revealing widespread contamination risks in centralized grinding and distribution systems. In 1994, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) responded by declaring E. coli O157:H7 an adulterant in raw ground beef and implementing routine regulatory testing, marking a step‑change in how STEC hazards in cattle and beef were managed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Centralized, high‑volume grinding of beef from multiple feedlot sources, inadequate cooking procedures at retail outlets, and limited pre‑existing regulatory control of STEC in beef dramatically increased human exposure to O157:H7. Public alarm and intense media coverage prompted a strong regulatory response, including FSIS’s 1994 zero‑tolerance policy for O157:H7 in ground beef, which in turn drove major investment in pre‑ and post‑harvest control measures in cattle and the beef supply chain. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical O157:H7 with stx2 and eae; there is no evidence of unusual virulence evolution beyond known EHEC traits, so the episode is best viewed as a large re‑occurrence driven by exposure and processing failures rather than by qualitatively new pathogen biology.
Review: retain – Added as a major re_occurrence episode because the 1992–1993 Jack-in-the-Box O157:H7 outbreak (≈732 cases, 4 deaths) and the subsequent 1994 FSIS decision to classify O157:H7 as an adulterant in ground beef together had enormous impact on cattle/beef STEC control. Classified solely as re_occurrence (no intra- or inter-continental emergence) since O157:H7 was already established in North America; the event’s importance stems from the scale of human disease and the regulatory shift, not from first detection. Sources include the outbreak summary and Microbiology Spectrum review detailing the 1994 adulterant policy.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (residents and refugees) exposed via beef and contaminated surface water; cattle as asymptomatic reservoir shedding O157 into dung and water
Event summary: In late 1992, during a severe drought in Eswatini and neighbouring areas of South Africa, a massive outbreak of diarrhoeal disease occurred, initially characterised by bloody diarrhoea consistent with E. coli O157 infection and later complicated by cholera. Investigations identified E. coli O157 from human stools, surface and drinking water, sewage, cooked maize, and from cattle dung on affected sugar plantations and nearby communities, implicating stressed cattle herds and contaminated water as key sources. The episode, which likely involved tens of thousands of human infections, represented the first well-documented large outbreak of O157 in Africa and highlighted cattle as a central reservoir in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged drought forced cattle to graze around dwindling surface waters, increasing faecal contamination of rivers and waterholes that were then used for drinking and cooking; bans on cattle imports and economic pressures led to slaughter and consumption of distressed or dead animals, while abattoir hygiene was poor. These environmental and management conditions greatly amplified O157 contamination of beef and water supplies. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain (O157:NM with stx1 and stx2) showed no unique virulence features compared with other O157:H7 lineages; the event reflects geographic spread and intense exposure in a new continent rather than novel strain evolution.
Review: retain – Added as a key inter_continental_emergence event. The 1992 Eswatini/South Africa epidemic is widely regarded as the first major, well-characterised O157 outbreak in Africa and provides direct evidence of E. coli O157 in cattle dung and surface waters in the region. I classified it as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence (for Africa) and did not use intra-continental or re-emergence flags, because the main importance is appearance of STEC O157 in a new continent’s human and cattle populations on a large scale. Source is the detailed Emerging Infectious Diseases investigation.

Host: Cattle (beef and dairy; healthy carriers)
Event summary: Between 1992 and 1994, a large survey of 387 cattle in Japan tested more than 2,000 E. coli isolates and found that roughly one quarter of animals shed verotoxin‑producing E. coli, identifying both O157:H7 and numerous non‑O157 VTEC/STEC serotypes. These data provided the first comprehensive evidence that Japanese cattle were a major reservoir of STEC strains, including those implicated in human disease. Subsequent to these findings, STEC was incorporated into national zoonotic surveillance and food safety programs, laying groundwork for understanding and responding to large school‑based O157 outbreaks later in the decade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of Japanese cattle production and the introduction of sensitive diagnostic methods (PCR and verotoxin assays) permitted detection of previously under‑recognized STEC carriage. Internal mechanisms: Maintenance of STEC lineages with stx1, stx2 and other virulence genes in the bovine gastrointestinal tract, with efficient fecal shedding but little or no clinical disease in cattle, confirming their role as asymptomatic reservoirs of human‑pathogenic strains.
Review: retain – This event appropriately captures the first large-scale demonstration that Japanese cattle were important reservoirs of STEC, and its timing (1992–1994) precedes and informs Japan’s subsequent large O157 outbreaks. Coding as first_detection (for Japan) and intra_continental_emergence (expansion of known Asian STEC from South Asia to East Asia) is reasonable. No geography corrections were needed; the sources (Itoh et al. Vet Microbiol 1998 plus a later characterization paper) are suitable primary references.

Host: Cattle (beef and dairy; healthy carriers), beef and dairy products; pediatric human cases linked to bovine and food isolates
Event summary: In 1994, a survey of healthy cattle in Galicia, Spain, showed verotoxin-producing E. coli on most farms and confirmed that a diversity of VTEC serogroups, including O157:H7 and O26:H11, circulated widely in regional herds. A few years later, a one‑year prospective study in central France (1997–1998) concurrently examined cattle feces, beef, cheese and hospitalized children, finding high prevalence of stx-positive cattle and food samples and directly linking bovine and food isolates to pediatric STEC infections. Together, these studies marked the first comprehensive documentation that cattle and beef/dairy products in southern and western Europe formed an important reservoir–exposure pathway for STEC, reshaping regional risk assessments.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth and regional concentration of beef and dairy industries in Iberia and France, combined with intensified microbiological surveillance of slaughter cattle, carcasses and foods, revealed widespread contamination that had previously gone undetected. Internal mechanisms: Persistence and diversification of STEC serotypes in European cattle populations, including both O157 and multiple non‑O157 groups, with demonstrated spillover to children via contaminated beef and dairy products; no single novel strain dominates, so the significance lies in geographic range expansion and recognition of the reservoir.
Review: review – Corrected the timing and geography: Spain is now coded as Spain [1994] based on Blanco et al. (Epidemiol Infect, cattle sampled February–July 1994), and France as France [1997] reflecting the 1997–1998 prospective study in Clermont-Ferrand (J Clin Microbiol 38:1023–1031). Event year was updated to 1994–1998 accordingly. I retained first_detection and intra_continental_emergence, interpreting this as first comprehensive documentation of bovine and food STEC reservoirs in Spain and central France within an already affected European continent. The previous citation to the Japanese cattle study was replaced with the Spain cattle paper to better match the described event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (primarily children with HUS and hemorrhagic colitis); cattle as emerging reservoir of sorbitol-fermenting O157:H−
Event summary: In the mid–late 1990s, sorbitol-fermenting Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H− emerged in Germany as a distinct lineage causing severe hemolytic uremic syndrome in children, with a notable outbreak in Bavaria in 1995–1996. Follow‑up investigations identified cattle as a reservoir for these strains, and by 2000 sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− STEC had been isolated from bovine feces, supporting a zoonotic link. By the end of this episode, this unusual O157 lineage was recognized as an important, highly pathogenic variant established in regional cattle herds and repeatedly causing pediatric HUS.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density cattle production, slaughtering of regionally sourced animals, and close integration of cattle, the food chain and human populations in central Europe facilitated maintenance and transmission of the new lineage. Enhanced clinical and veterinary surveillance following severe pediatric HUS clusters prompted targeted studies that eventually detected the sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− strains in cattle. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of a sorbitol‑fermenting, usually nonmotile O157:H− STEC lineage with distinct phenotypic traits and virulence gene combinations, representing re-emergence of STEC in the same subregion through evolution of a highly pathogenic clade rather than simple spread of pre‑existing O157:H7.
Review: review – This episode correctly describes the emergence of sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− as a distinct, highly pathogenic lineage in Germany and its subsequent detection in cattle. To align with the rules that new strains in already affected regions should be coded as re-emergence rather than intra-continental spread, I set intra_continental_emergence to No and retained only re_emergence as Yes. First_detection is interpreted here as first recognition of this specific SF O157:H− lineage in cattle, not first STEC in Western Europe more generally.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (three pasture-based herds in southeast Queensland; healthy carriers) and farm environments
Event summary: Over a 12‑month period in the late 1990s, a longitudinal study of three Australian dairy herds in southeast Queensland collected nearly 600 cattle fecal samples and over 140 environmental samples, documenting Shiga toxin–producing E. coli in about 17% of cattle feces and 4% of environmental samples. The work identified serotypes including O26:H11 and O157:H7 and showed persistent contamination of water and pasture on these pasture-based farms. Publication of these findings around 2000 provided the first detailed, large-scale evidence that Australian dairy cattle and their farm environments were an established reservoir of multiple STEC serotypes of human health concern.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and modernization of the Australian dairy sector and increasing concern over export-market requirements for pathogen control motivated systematic surveillance for STEC on dairy farms. Internal mechanisms: Stable colonization of dairy cattle and environmental persistence of STEC serotypes, including O157:H7, in a new continental setting, indicating that globally distributed STEC lineages had become entrenched in Oceania’s ruminant reservoirs even though O157-associated human disease remained relatively rare in Australia.
Review: review – Adjusted the timing to reflect the actual sampling period (a 12‑month longitudinal study in the late 1990s) rather than the 2000 publication year and interpreted this as the first large-scale documentation of STEC (including O157:H7) in Australian dairy cattle. Given the lack of earlier published evidence of STEC reservoirs in Oceania’s cattle and the paper’s prominence in later reviews, I set first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to Yes for the animal host system, while leaving intra_continental_emergence at No. This event is retained as the main representation of STEC establishment in cattle in Oceania.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef; healthy carriers)
Event summary: In 1999, a survey of 197 fecal samples from healthy dairy and beef cattle and slaughter cattle in Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, used PCR screening for stx genes and culture on CT‑SMAC to detect STEC. Approximately 71% of samples were positive for stx, with higher prevalence in dairy cattle, and 15 STEC strains representing 11 serotypes were isolated; notably, three O157:H7 strains were recovered. The authors reported this as the first isolation of O157:H7 from cattle in Brazil and highlighted the high background prevalence of STEC in cattle as a potential source of contamination for beef and dairy products.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of dairy and beef production in southeastern Brazil, combined with improved laboratory methods (PCR for stx genes and selective media for O157), allowed detection of widespread STEC carriage that had previously gone undocumented. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects geographic documentation of STEC, including O157:H7, in Brazilian cattle rather than clear evidence of a novel strain; it establishes Brazil as part of the global network of STEC‑infected cattle reservoirs with multiple human‑pathogenic serotypes.
Review: retain – Added to cover South America, using Cerqueira et al. (Vet Microbiol 1999) which showed very high stx gene prevalence in cattle and reported the first isolation of O157:H7 from Brazilian cattle. Classified as first_detection for Brazil without intra- or inter-continental flags, because STEC was already established in South America (notably in Argentina) before 1999. No evidence of a specific new strain or resistance profile was highlighted, so re_emergence was left No.

Host: Cattle (feedlot and range; asymptomatic reservoirs of multiple non-O157 and O157 serogroups)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s through 2011, large surveys in U.S. feedlot and range cattle documented widespread shedding of multiple non‑O157 STEC serogroups—especially O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, and O145—alongside O157:H7, with these "top-7" serogroups increasingly implicated in severe human illness and outbreaks. Molecular work showed that many cattle isolates carried stx2 and other virulence factors associated with human disease, and by 2011 the U.S. FSIS responded by declaring six non‑O157 STEC serogroups adulterants in non-intact beef. This sequence of surveillance, attribution and regulatory action marked a qualitative shift in how diverse STEC lineages in cattle were viewed and controlled in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale feedlot finishing, mixing of cattle from diverse sources, and high-throughput slaughter facilitated dissemination and amplification of multiple STEC serogroups. Enhanced diagnostic methods (Shiga toxin immunoassays, multiplex PCR panels) greatly improved detection of non‑O157 STEC in both human and cattle samples. Policy and market pressures to reduce STEC risk further incentivized surveillance and control. Internal mechanisms: Expansion and diversification of non‑O157 STEC serogroups within cattle populations, including emergence of highly virulent O26, O103, O111 and other serotypes, and accumulation of virulence and, in some cases, resistance determinants, justifying classification as re-emergence driven by qualitative changes in the STEC population rather than a simple recurrence.
Review: review – Retained as a major global re-emergence episode in cattle, centered on diversification and regulatory recognition of non-O157 STEC in the U.S. beef chain. I simplified the event typing to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to No) to emphasize that the key feature is the rise and formal recognition of new virulent serogroups in cattle, culminating in the 2011 adulterant policy, rather than just a resurgence in incidence. The existing sources (USDA ARS cattle surveys, FSIS policy announcement, and methodological papers on non-O157 detection) remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Calves (young dairy/beef calves with diarrhea, enteritis, and occasional septicemia) and humans with HUS
Event summary: Beginning around 2009, attaching–effacing and Shiga toxin–producing E. coli of serotype O80:H2 (AE-STEC/EPEC) were increasingly detected in diarrheic calves in Belgium and in pediatric hemolytic uremic syndrome cases in Belgium and neighbouring countries. Retrospective work showed that related O80:H2 strains had been present in calves as early as the late 1980s, but the 2009–2015 period saw a marked rise in detection and evidence that this hybrid pathotype had become established in local bovine populations and was causing severe extraintestinal disease in both calves and humans. By the mid‑2010s, O80:H2 was recognized as an emerging hybrid STEC/EPEC/ExPEC pathotype in western Europe, prompting calls for targeted surveillance in cattle.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive calf-rearing systems, animal movements within and between farms, and slaughter of young calves created opportunities for amplification and spread of the O80:H2 lineage. Heightened clinical and veterinary attention following unusual pediatric HUS presentations led to more targeted diagnostic testing and retrospective identification of O80:H2 in historical calf isolates. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and expansion of a hybrid AE‑STEC/EPEC O80:H2 pathotype combining attaching–effacing capacity, Shiga toxin production (particularly stx2), and extraintestinal virulence traits, representing a clear re-emergence of STEC in an already affected region through evolution of a new, highly virulent lineage.
Review: review – Recast this episode explicitly as a re_emergence event. Retrospective data show that O80:H2 strains were present in calves before 1990, so coding 2009 as first_detection would be misleading; instead, the 2009–2015 period reflects increased detection and expansion of a hybrid pathotype causing severe disease in calves and humans. I therefore set first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to No and retained only re_emergence as Yes. The Clinical Microbiology Reviews article and the EID report are appropriate key sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (dairy cows and native beef cattle; healthy carriers of increasingly multidrug-resistant STEC)
Event summary: In 2010–2011, abattoir-based surveys in the Republic of Korea demonstrated that a substantial fraction of cattle carried STEC, and that among isolates there was a sharp rise in multidrug resistance between 2010 and 2011. Many isolates showed resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics commonly used in livestock, raising concern about the potential for transmission of difficult-to-treat STEC infections to humans. The surveys coincided with large-scale culling and restocking of cattle due to a national foot‑and‑mouth disease outbreak, suggesting that changes in herd structure and antimicrobial use may have altered STEC ecology and selected for resistant clones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive antibiotic use in Korean livestock, including metaphylaxis and growth promotion, and the major perturbation of cattle populations due to foot-and-mouth disease control measures (mass culling and restocking), likely created strong selection and dissemination pressures for multidrug-resistant STEC. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and expansion of multidrug-resistant STEC lineages in cattle, representing a re-emergence of STEC in the same subregion driven by internal resistance mechanisms rather than simple changes in exposure alone.
Review: review – This event accurately summarises the Korean data on rising multidrug resistance among STEC isolated from cattle around 2010–2011 and is coded as re_emergence (antimicrobial resistance development) without intra-/inter-continental flags. However, its impact is largely national and based on surveillance rather than a large outbreak or major policy change, so its inclusion among the very top global STEC emergence events is debatable. I therefore recommend retaining it provisionally but flagging it for further review if the list needs to be pruned to the 10–12 most consequential episodes.

Countries: Egypt [1994], Egypt (Nile Delta governorates) [1994], Egypt (Qena/Upper Egypt) [2009]
Host: Buffalo, cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys (multiple domestic ruminants, with buffalo and cattle most heavily infected)
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s onward, fasciolosis caused mainly by Fasciola spp. (with F. gigantica and F. hepatica/hybrid forms varying by zone) intensified along the Nile Valley in Egypt, with buffalo and cattle in the Middle and Eastern Nile Delta showing high infection rates and heavy economic losses from liver condemnation and productivity losses. National statistics and abattoir surveys through the 1990s and 2000s reported substantial prevalences in slaughtered ruminants, while farm-based studies and reviews began to describe fascioliasis as hyper-endemic in livestock and an important zoonosis in Nile Delta and Upper Egypt governorates. By the early 2010s, repeated abattoir and farm-based studies confirmed persistently high burdens and widespread infection across multiple animal species, indicating a sustained high-burden hyper-endemic situation rather than isolated outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of irrigated agriculture along the Nile (canals, rice paddies, irrigation schemes) created extensive habitats for lymnaeid snail intermediate hosts; year-round irrigation and favorable microclimates on smallholder mixed farms (buffalo, cattle, sheep, goats) maintained continuous transmission; limited strategic deworming and constraints in veterinary services contributed to persistently high burdens. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or resistance trait was documented for this period; the episode reflects intensification and geographic consolidation of an already long-endemic parasite focus rather than a new strain, although mixed F. hepatica/F. gigantica and hybrid populations are recognized in Egypt. Abattoir surveys and epidemiological reviews quantify high prevalence and economic losses and frame fascioliasis as a major, re-occurring parasitic problem in Egyptian livestock.
Review: retain (with corrections): This is a clearly documented, large-scale, long-term hyper-endemic situation with substantial economic impact in Nile Delta and Upper Egypt, and it merits inclusion among the major post‑1990 F. gigantica-related events. I changed the event type to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because available data indicate intensification driven by irrigation and management in a long-established focus, without evidence for a new strain or host-range shift. I also slightly edited the summary wording to avoid calling it a sustained “re-emergence” and to emphasize chronic high burden. Countries and sub-region are correctly assigned (Egypt, Northern Africa), and the 1994–2015 window is a reasonable representation of the modern high-burden period. Sources are appropriate and based on primary Egyptian epidemiological and economic studies and specialized reviews; no further URL changes needed here.

Host: Cattle (communal grazing systems in highveld and lowveld areas)
Event summary: Between late 1998 and 2000, longitudinal coprological surveys in communal grazing cattle in Zimbabwe’s highveld and lowveld regions revealed substantial burdens of F. gigantica, with marked seasonal peaks corresponding to wet periods. The work demonstrated that fasciolosis was a widespread and significant constraint in communal livestock production rather than a localized problem, with infection detected across multiple grazing areas and water sources. The disease persisted across consecutive years with seasonally recurring peaks, indicating endemic re-occurrence driven by environmental and management conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal rainfall patterns in highveld and lowveld communal areas created and renewed wet habitats suitable for lymnaeid snail intermediate hosts; communal grazing at shared water sources increased exposure; limited access to regular flukicide treatment in communal systems allowed build-up of infection. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or resistance was described; the episode reflects sustained endemic transmission and seasonal re-occurrence rather than genetic change. Epidemiological studies in Zimbabwe documented F. gigantica infection patterns in cattle and linked them to climatic seasonality and communal grazing practices.
Review: retain (with minor corrections): The Zimbabwe communal-grazing studies are real, well described and regionally important, but they are more moderate in scale than some national-level events. I corrected the event years to 1998–2000 to match the published longitudinal surveys rather than 1999–2000, and updated the country/year notation accordingly; sub-region (Eastern Africa) and country assignment (Zimbabwe) are correct per the UNSD country list. Classification as re_occurrence (with re_emergence set to No) matches the evidence that seasonal climate and grazing management, not parasite change, drove the observed patterns. Sources appropriately point to the primary OJVR field study and a global re-emergence review; no URL replacement is needed.

Countries: Kenya [1990-2004], Kenya (Taveta division, semi-arid coastal area) [1990-2004]
Host: Cattle, sheep, goats (slaughtered animals at coastal abattoirs; F. gigantica predominant)
Event summary: From 1990 through 2004, a retrospective analysis of slaughter records in Taveta division of semi-arid coastal Kenya showed persistently high rates of liver condemnation due to F. gigantica in cattle, sheep and goats. Across the 15‑year period, bovine fasciolosis accounted for about 26% of condemned bovine livers and roughly 79.5% of total financial losses from liver condemnation, with cumulative losses of approximately 3.5 million Kenyan shillings attributed to F. gigantica. The consistently elevated condemnation rates over many years demonstrated that fasciolosis was a long‑standing, economically important constraint in coastal production systems rather than a short-lived outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Irrigated and low-lying coastal areas with canals, streams and marshy fields provided favorable snail habitats despite the overall semi-arid climate; year-round grazing near water points and communal use of wet pastures promoted ongoing exposure to metacercariae; limited strategic fluke control meant that chronic infections accumulated in slaughter stock. Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite strain was reported; the pattern reflects chronic endemic re-occurrence in a known endemic focus. Abattoir-based studies in Taveta quantified F. gigantica-related condemnation rates and cumulative economic losses over 1989/1990–2004, highlighting fasciolosis as a major parasitic problem in coastal Kenya.
Review: retain (with corrections): The Taveta coastal Kenya series provides a strong, long-term economic-impact assessment and is reasonably among the major African F. gigantica episodes. I corrected the event window to 1990–2004 (covering the retrospective slaughter-data period) instead of 2004–2006, and adjusted the summary so that the 3.5 million KES loss is correctly described as a cumulative loss over the study period, not an annual figure. Sub-region (Eastern Africa) and country are correct. The event is best classified as re_occurrence only; therefore I set re_emergence to No. Sources now explicitly reference the Tropical Animal Health and Production paper providing the primary data, supplemented by a global review used only for broader context.

Countries: Ethiopia [2005], Ethiopia (multiple regions including Arba Minch, Boloso Bombe, Kombolcha, other municipal abattoir sites) [2005-2020]
Host: Cattle primarily; also sheep and goats in some surveys (bovine fasciolosis dominated by F. gigantica at lower altitudes and F. hepatica at higher altitudes)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s through at least 2020, numerous abattoir and farm studies across Ethiopia documented very high prevalences of bovine fasciolosis and substantial economic losses, with F. gigantica predominating in lowland and mid-altitude zones and F. hepatica more common at higher altitudes. Site‑specific investigations (e.g. Arba Minch, Boloso Bombe, Kombolcha) reported significant annual losses from liver condemnation and carcass weight reduction, while a recent national systematic review and meta-analysis estimated direct annual losses from liver condemnation alone at over 40 million Ethiopian birr. The disease remained highly prevalent and economically important across diverse production systems despite ongoing anthelmintic use, indicating persistent high endemic burden and control failure rather than isolated outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated agriculture and wetlands, communal grazing around water bodies, and large-scale movement of cattle from various agro-ecological zones to municipal abattoirs all facilitated transmission; limited access to, or improper timing of, flukicide treatments contributed to persistently high burdens; climate variability (rainfall patterns, flooding) influenced snail habitats and seasonal peaks. Internal mechanisms: Altitude-related partitioning of F. hepatica (highlands) versus F. gigantica (lowlands) reflects ecological adaptation of the two fasciolids and their snail hosts, but no new strain or resistance phenotype has been clearly documented in Ethiopia for the period considered. Systematic reviews and site-specific studies highlight very high prevalence, major economic losses, and the predominance of F. gigantica in lowland and mid-altitude cattle.
Review: retain (with corrections): Ethiopia’s large national cattle population, very high pooled fasciolosis prevalences and multi‑million‑birr annual losses clearly make this one of the most impactful F. gigantica–associated events and it should be retained. The original classification as both re_occurrence and re_emergence was inconsistent with the definitions; I changed the event to re_occurrence only, as the evidence points to expansion and persistence driven by environment and management rather than documented parasite change. I also removed a low-quality Reddit link from the event-level sources, keeping primary abattoir studies and the national meta-analysis instead. Years, country/sub-region assignment and overall storyline are appropriate, but the event should be interpreted as a long-lasting high-endemicity episode rather than a discrete outbreak.

Countries: Pakistan [2008-2010], Pakistan (Punjab – Toba Tek Singh district) [2008-2010]
Host: Dairy cattle and water buffalo (lactating bovines)
Event summary: Between about 2008 and 2010, a detailed field study in Toba Tek Singh district, Punjab, Pakistan, documented a high point-prevalence of fasciolosis in dairy cattle and buffalo, with F. gigantica the predominant species and significant reductions in milk yield associated with infection. In a sample of 2,400 lactating bovines, 27.3% were positive for Fasciola eggs, and F. gigantica infections were more frequent and heavier than F. hepatica. Chemotherapeutic intervention with oxyclozanide led to measurable increases in milk production, quantifying substantial subclinical production losses. Subsequent Pakistan-wide systematic reviews covering 2000–2020 confirmed that fascioliasis in ruminants was widespread and economically important across multiple provinces, framing it as a significant constraint on the livestock sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Flood irrigation, rice-based cropping and canal systems in Punjab created extensive snail habitats; year-round grazing and use of surface water increased exposure; limited routine fluke control in smallholder dairy systems allowed accumulation of chronic infection; intensification of dairy production amplified the economic consequences of productivity losses. Internal mechanisms: F. gigantica dominance in lowland Punjab reflects ecological adaptation to warm, irrigated environments, but no specific novel genotype or resistance trait was reported. The Toba Tek Singh study quantified F. gigantica prevalence and milk-yield impact at herd level, while national meta-analyses highlight high Fasciola prevalence across ruminant hosts and large aggregate economic burdens.
Review: retain (with corrections): This Pakistan dairy-herd episode is well supported by a primary J Helminthology study and contributes important quantitative evidence on production losses, so I recommend retaining it. The event is best categorized as re_occurrence (re_emergence set to No) because it documents a high-prevalence, high-impact situation in an already endemic area without evidence of parasite change. I removed the duplicate Semantic Scholar PDF in favor of the open-access Pathogens meta-analysis. The 2008–2010 timing is approximate (the paper does not clearly state calendar years), but fits the publication date; if more precise study dates are needed, they should be extracted directly from the full article in a later pass.

Host: Sheep and goats (small ruminants), with both F. hepatica and F. gigantica detected
Event summary: In 2012, an investigation in Sargodha district, Punjab, Pakistan, reported notable prevalences of fasciolosis in small ruminants, with both F. hepatica and F. gigantica present and economically significant losses from liver condemnation and carcass depreciation over a six‑month study period. Microscopical examination of faecal samples from sheep and goats showed over 40% of animals infected with Fasciola spp., and an economic analysis quantified the value of condemned livers and weight loss in slaughter stock. The study highlighted that fasciolosis, long recognized as a constraint in cattle and buffalo, was also a substantial and previously underappreciated burden for sheep and goat production in irrigated areas of Punjab.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared grazing of sheep and goats with cattle and buffalo on irrigated pastures and canal banks increased small‑ruminant exposure to metacercariae; expansion of mixed crop–livestock systems and limited species-specific parasite control allowed Fasciola spp. to establish in small-ruminant flocks; environmental conditions in irrigated Punjab (warm temperatures, standing water, rice-based systems) favored Fasciola transmission. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects host expansion (spillover) and consolidation of Fasciola spp. infection in small ruminants in a region where the parasite was already well established in large ruminants, consistent with re-emergence in an additional host group within the same sub-region. The Sargodha study provides direct prevalence and economic-loss estimates for sheep and goats.
Review: retain (with reclassification and source adjustment): The Sargodha small-ruminant study documents high Fasciola prevalence and clear economic losses in sheep and goats within a major irrigated livestock region, which justifies its inclusion as one of the more impactful host-expansion events. I reclassified the event as re_emergence (re_occurrence set to No) because its main significance is the consolidation of fasciolosis as a production-limiting disease in small ruminants, i.e. host expansion within the same sub-region. I removed the Mardan District prevalence paper from the event-level sources (it is geographically different and only provides general Pakistan context) and instead paired the primary Vet Ital Sargodha study with the Pakistan-wide meta-analysis. Sub-region, country and year (2012) are correct.

Host: Cattle, water buffalo (carabao), horses (large livestock in South Cotabato)
Event summary: In September 2007, veterinary authorities in South Cotabato province in the southern Philippines warned of a potential outbreak of liver fluke disease after laboratory testing of samples from cows, carabaos and horses in the province’s towns and lone city showed an infection level of about 89.5%. This abrupt surge in fasciolosis, attributed to erratic weather and heavy rains, was described as alarming and prompted calls for immediate treatment to avert complications and associated diseases. Later parasitological work in the Philippines, including intensive surveys in Northern Samar, confirmed that F. gigantica infections can reach very high prevalences in bovines in some areas, underscoring the country’s vulnerability to episodic spikes on top of a background of endemic fasciolosis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusual or erratic weather patterns, including heavy rains and flooding, expanded and prolonged wet habitats for snail intermediate hosts in South Cotabato; livestock grazing on flooded or waterlogged pastures ingested large numbers of metacercariae; limited routine fluke control allowed rapid build-up of infections to very high levels. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic changes were reported; the event reflects enhanced transmission efficiency under favorable environmental and husbandry conditions in an already endemic setting. Contemporary news reports and later parasitological surveys corroborate very high F. gigantica infection levels in Philippine bovines and link them to climatic and land-use factors.
Review: retain (with major source improvements and clearer framing): The 2007 South Cotabato episode is a well-documented example of extremely high fasciolosis prevalence (≈89.5%) in large livestock, widely cited in subsequent literature, and is a reasonable candidate among the top events for South‑eastern Asia. I retained the basic storyline but anchored it to primary or near-primary sources: a contemporaneous newspaper report reproduced in the New Light of Myanmar and compiled WHO documentation, and a PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases study from Northern Samar that independently demonstrates very high F. gigantica prevalences in Philippine bovines. I removed English and Spanish Wikipedia from the event-level sources, as they are secondary compilations rather than primary evidence. The event is correctly classified as re_occurrence (environmentally driven spike in an endemic area) and not as inter- or intra-continental emergence.

Countries: Nigeria [2005-2020], Nigeria (multiple states including Maiduguri, Oyo/Ibadan and others) [2005-2020]
Host: Cattle primarily; also other ruminants in some surveys
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, multiple abattoir and field studies in Nigeria documented moderate to high prevalences of bovine fasciolosis dominated by F. gigantica and substantial economic impacts due to liver condemnation, reduced carcass weight and productivity losses. A recent economic model estimated annual national losses from bovine fasciolosis at about US$26 million, based on an 18.3% prevalence and national herd and slaughter parameters. Reviews of bovine trematodiasis further highlighted fasciolosis as one of the most common causes of liver condemnation in abattoirs, with high prevalence in several ecological zones and major financial implications for the Nigerian livestock industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive and transhumant grazing systems with cattle moving through floodplains, riverine pastures and irrigated fields created repeated exposure to infected snail habitats; inadequate or poorly timed flukicide treatments and limited veterinary coverage enabled chronic infection; expansion of irrigated rice and vegetable cultivation in some regions likely increased snail habitats and transmission. Internal mechanisms: Some authors speculate that the parasite may be well adapted to a diversity of lymnaeid snail hosts in Nigeria, but clear evidence for recent genetic change is lacking; the episode is better viewed as re-occurrence and intensification of a long-established problem. Economic modelling and reviews quantify large national-level financial losses and describe tropical fasciolosis (F. gigantica) as a major parasitic constraint in Nigerian cattle.
Review: retain (with reclassification and source refinement): Nigeria’s combination of large cattle population, high Fasciola prevalence in multiple zones and an estimated US$26 million in annual losses places this event squarely among the most impactful F. gigantica-related episodes and it should be retained. I reinterpreted the event type as re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No), since drivers are predominantly grazing systems, irrigation and inadequate control rather than demonstrated parasite change. I also replaced a SciSpace-hosted PDF of the national review with the canonical Cambridge journal link, and kept the FAO/AGRIS economic-model record and the Ibadan abattoir study as key sources. Sub-region (Western Africa) and country coverage are correct.

Countries: Cameroon [2016], Cameroon (Western Highlands – Bamenda and Bafoussam abattoirs) [2016-2020]
Host: Cattle (slaughtered at Bamenda and Bafoussam municipal abattoirs)
Event summary: Between about 2016 and 2020, studies at Bamenda and Bafoussam abattoirs in the Western Highlands of Cameroon found notable prevalences of bovine fasciolosis and calculated significant annual financial losses due to liver condemnation. The work highlighted fasciolosis as an economically important but under-recognized disease in one of Cameroon’s key livestock-producing regions, with condemnation rates high enough to represent appreciable losses to local producers and traders. The disease persisted over several years of surveillance, indicating ongoing endemic transmission and economic impact rather than a one-off outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Highland and mid-elevation pastures with streams, irrigation channels and swampy areas favored lymnaeid snails; communal grazing and movement of cattle from surrounding rural areas to urban abattoirs facilitated parasite circulation; limited targeted fluke control in smallholder systems contributed to persistent infection. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects sustained endemic re-occurrence of Fasciola-driven fasciolosis in cattle; no specific genetic or resistance changes were reported. Prevalence and economic-loss estimates from Western Highlands abattoirs underscore the regional importance of the disease.
Review: retain (with sub-region correction and reclassification): This event documents clear economic impact of fasciolosis in a major livestock-producing region of Cameroon and is worth retaining as a representative Middle African focus, although its absolute impact is smaller than that of Ethiopia, Nigeria or Bangladesh. I corrected the sub-region from Western Africa to Middle Africa to match the UNSD classification where Cameroon is listed, and left the country as Cameroon. I also set the event type to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No), as the data reflect persistent endemic infection driven by environmental and husbandry factors. The main source is an open-access Veterinary Medicine and Science article; the global review is kept only as high-level context.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Bangladesh [2011-2013], Bangladesh (national passive-surveillance data across all districts) [2011-2013]
Host: Cattle, water buffalo, goats, sheep (domestic ruminants)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2013, analysis of national passive-surveillance data in Bangladesh identified 1,723,971 reported cases of fascioliasis in domestic ruminants (cattle, buffalo, goats and sheep) across all districts, with multiple statistically significant spatial and space–time clusters. The disease, caused solely by F. gigantica or closely related hybrid fasciolids in this low‑elevation tropical setting, showed particularly high case burdens in intensively cultivated floodplain areas with dense dairy and draft-animal populations. Subsequent systematic reviews confirmed pooled Fasciola prevalence around 20% in ruminants, and recent abattoir studies in floodplain areas estimated annual economic losses from liver condemnation alone at roughly US$ 278,000, indicating a very large, nationally distributed burden rather than isolated local outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive low-lying floodplains, monsoon-driven rainfall and rice-based agriculture create ideal habitats for Lymnaea auricularia and other snail intermediate hosts; high densities of cattle and buffalo used for milk, meat and draft power, often grazing on irrigated rice stubble and canal banks, maintain intense transmission; limited access to veterinary services in many districts and suboptimal timing of flukicide use allow chronic infections to accumulate. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work in Bangladesh has revealed complex hybrid Fasciola populations, but from an epidemiological perspective the 2011–2013 national pattern primarily reflects high endemic transmission of F. gigantica-type fasciolids in suitable landscapes, i.e. re-occurrence and intensification in a long-endemic country. National surveillance, meta-analyses and economic-loss studies jointly demonstrate that Bangladesh bears one of the heaviest post‑2000 fasciolosis burdens among tropical livestock systems.
Review: add (new major event): Bangladesh was missing from the original list despite very strong evidence of an exceptional national fascioliasis burden dominated by F. gigantica. National passive-surveillance data for 2011–2013 report over 1.7 million ruminant cases and identify persistent spatial and space–time clusters, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses plus recent economic studies document high pooled prevalence and substantial annual losses from liver condemnation. Given the scale of affected livestock populations and the magnitude of case numbers, this multi-year national episode clearly belongs among the top 10 most impactful F. gigantica-related emergence/re-emergence events. I classified it as re_occurrence (long-endemic parasite with environmentally driven intensification), assigned it to Southern Asia with country Bangladesh per the UNSD list, and linked it to primary national and meta-analytic sources.
