EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Wild cervids (primarily red deer Cervus elaphus and fallow deer Dama dama); occasional roe deer and mouflon
Event summary: From the late 1980s onward, fascioloidosis outbreaks were recognised in cervids of the Danube floodplain forests, first in red deer in south‑western Slovakia and shortly afterwards in north‑western Hungary, signalling the formation of a new central European natural focus. During the 1990s and early 2000s the parasite spread along the Danube into floodplain and adjacent forests of eastern Austria, Croatia’s Baranja region and, by around 2007, northern Serbia near the Danube–Sava confluence, with very high prevalences and heavy liver pathology in local red and fallow deer. By the mid‑2000s the Danube floodplain forests had become a persistent multinational natural focus of F. magna, raising concern about long‑term effects on cervid populations and the risk of spillover to livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transboundary movements and natural migration of red and fallow deer along the Danube corridor, historical translocations and intensive game management, and extensive wet floodplain forest habitats that favour Galba truncatula and other lymnaeid snails promoted establishment and spread of the parasite. Internal mechanisms: Strong geographic range expansion supported by the parasite’s ability to maintain high intensities in definitive cervid hosts and to complete its life cycle in European lymnaeid snails allowed consolidation of a large, contiguous Danube focus.
Review: retain – This is the key multi‑country Danube floodplain emergence episode and should be retained as one linked event. Corrected the Serbian start year from an imprecise “early 2000s” to 2007 based on published reports, and reclassified the event as re_occurrence (geographic expansion within already affected European subregions driven by host movements and habitat) rather than intra‑continental emergence or re_emergence. Also refined the source list to emphasise genetic and epidemiological work on the Danube focus. Flag for manual review to confirm acceptance of these typology changes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: Wild red deer and fallow deer; roe deer and mouflon as aberrant hosts; occasional cattle
Event summary: Building on earlier 20th‑century introductions, systematic mapping during the 2000s showed Fascioloides magna expanding from long‑affected southern and central Bohemia into western, northern and other parts of Czechia, with several newly recognised foci near the German and Polish borders. In some managed red and fallow deer populations, local prevalence exceeded 90%, and roe deer and mouflon were increasingly found with severe lesions, highlighting the parasite’s impact on wild ungulates. By around 2012, the Bohemian focus functioned as a major European reservoir with ongoing geographic expansion and documented spillover risk to livestock in overlapping pasture and meadow systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth and connectivity of managed cervid populations, increased deer densities in forest and game preserves, and overlapping use of wet pastures by wildlife and cattle facilitated local spread and cross‑species transmission. Internal mechanisms: Efficient maintenance of the life cycle in multiple deer species and in Galba and Radix snail populations supported sustained transmission and progressive range expansion within Czechia.
Review: retain – This event captures the major post‑2000 expansion and consolidation of the long‑standing Bohemian focus, which clearly qualifies as a large‑impact emergence episode. Reclassified it as re_occurrence (intensification and spread within an already affected Eastern European subregion) rather than intra‑continental emergence or re_emergence, since no novel strain or host shift is implicated at this scale. Recommended for retention, but flagged for manual review of the precise date range (start of systematic surveys vs. earlier presence) if finer temporal resolution is needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Countries: Poland [2012, Lower Silesian Wilderness; 2015, Bory Zielonogórskie; 2016, Podkarpackie Province (farmed fallow deer)]
Host: Wild red deer; farmed fallow deer
Event summary: After a single mid‑20th‑century record, Fascioloides magna was rediscovered in 2012–2013 in red deer faecal samples from the Lower Silesian Wilderness in south‑western Poland, confirming renewed local presence. In 2015 eggs were again detected in red deer in the nearby Bory Zielonogórskie forests, and by 2016 adult flukes were reported in farmed fallow deer in Podkarpackie Province in south‑eastern Poland, with mitochondrial genotyping linking these parasites to central European foci. Together, these findings documented both a re‑occurrence in historical Polish range and the establishment of an expanding second European natural focus involving multiple regions within Poland.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movements of red deer between Czech/Slovak and Polish forest complexes, trade and movement of farmed deer, and suitable wetland and forest habitats enabled recolonisation of former range and establishment of a new farmed‑deer focus. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion within cervid hosts, with parasites genetically traceable to existing central European populations, allowed F. magna to re‑establish and persist in Polish wild and farmed cervids.
Review: retain – This episode represents a substantial re‑establishment and spread of F. magna within Poland, including creation of a genetically characterised second European natural focus with both wild and farmed hosts, and should be retained. Corrected the emergence‑type classification to re_occurrence only, because it reflects recolonisation and intensification within an already affected Eastern European subregion rather than a new subregion or strain. Manual review is advised to confirm that no additional intra‑continental emergence label is desired at a finer spatial scale (e.g. at the level of ‘natural focus’ rather than UN subregion).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Countries: Germany [Upper Palatinate Forest, Bavaria; first lesions noted 2007–2009, focus documented in the 2010s]
Host: Wild red deer; fallow deer; roe deer; sika deer
Event summary: In north‑eastern Bavaria’s Upper Palatinate Forest, unusual dark hepatic lesions were first noted in harvested red and fallow deer around 2007–2009, and subsequent parasitological work in the early 2010s confirmed Fascioloides magna in wild cervids, representing a modern German focus distinct from the historic single 1930s record near Görlitz. Surveys showed infections in red and fallow deer and also in roe and sika deer, indicating an established multi‑host transmission cycle along the Czech border. This emergence signalled a westward extension of the central European fascioloidosis belt and raised concern about further spread into other German forest complexes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of cervids from heavily infected Bohemian and Danube‑adjacent areas, high local deer densities under hunting management, and suitable wet forest and wetland habitats permitted establishment of the parasite in Bavarian hunting grounds. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and successful use of several European cervid species as definitive hosts facilitated persistence after introduction into the Upper Palatinate Forest.
Review: retain – The Upper Palatinate focus represents a clear national‑scale emergence in Germany, with multiple wild host species involved and potential for onward spread, and should be retained as a major event. Updated the emergence classification to re_occurrence only, since Germany (Western Europe) had historical records of F. magna and this focus reflects renewed establishment driven by deer movements and habitat, not a novel strain or continent/subregion jump. Replaced generic Romanian/Austrian references with dedicated German studies documenting this focus. Manual verification of the approximate date span (first lesions vs. confirmed diagnostics) is recommended if higher temporal precision is required.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: Horse (Equus caballus; natural infection in an endemic area)
Event summary: In 2005 a 25‑year‑old mare in Minnesota was euthanised for unrelated reasons and found at necropsy to harbour multiple adult Fascioloides magna flukes in the liver, representing the first documented natural infection of this species in a horse. The case occurred in a region where the parasite is enzootic in white‑tailed deer, indicating spillover from local cervid reservoirs rather than establishment of a new geographic focus. Although the episode ended with the individual animal’s death, it expanded the recognised host range of F. magna and highlighted the need to consider the parasite in differential diagnoses for horses in endemic regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared pasture or habitat between horses and infected wild cervids in an endemic North American focus allowed accidental ingestion of metacercariae on contaminated forage. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion to a non‑typical dead‑end host (horse) and the ability of immature and adult flukes to survive in equine hepatic tissue underpin this re‑emergence in a new host species within the animal host system.
Review: review – This is an important first report of natural equine infection (host expansion and new clinical context), but it involves a single animal in an already long‑endemic North American focus and has limited population‑level impact. Reclassified as re_emergence only (host expansion) rather than first_detection of the parasite in the animal host system. Recommend keeping this row under review: it may be retained as one of the top 10 events if host‑range changes are prioritised, but could be excluded if strict ranking by numbers of affected animals or countries is applied.
Review Comment: retained as one of the top 10 events if host‑range changes are prioritised

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: Highland cattle; wild red deer; Radix labiata snails (intermediate host)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, investigations in the Czech Republic documented adult Fascioloides magna in two Highland cattle bulls grazing in areas shared with infected red deer, along with larval stages in naturally infected Radix labiata snails. Molecular identification confirmed both cattle and this Radix species as hosts, providing the first natural confirmation of R. labiata as an intermediate host and a rare example of patent infection in cattle in Europe. These findings showed that fascioloidosis had moved beyond a strictly wildlife issue in at least one locality, with a competent local snail reservoir and domestic livestock involved in the life cycle.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Overlap of grazing cattle with heavily infected deer populations on wet meadows and floodplain pastures, together with diverse local lymnaeid snail fauna, created opportunities for cross‑species transmission and involvement of domestic livestock. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion to domestic cattle and natural use of Radix labiata as an additional intermediate host increased the ecological breadth of F. magna and the potential for sustained transmission in mixed wildlife–livestock systems, justifying classification as re_emergence.
Review: retain – This episode marks a genuine re_emergence through documented expansion of both definitive and intermediate host range (Highland cattle and Radix labiata) and has clear implications for livestock and transmission ecology. Adjusted the year to the publication year (2014) as a conservative approximation of first confirmed findings and classified it solely as re_emergence (not intra‑continental). Recommended for retention as one of the top 10 events, but manual checking of the underlying sampling years may further refine the start date.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: Steer (beef cattle)
Event summary: In 2014 a clinical case report from North America described a steer with fatal pulmonary haemorrhage in which Fascioloides magna cysts and flukes were found in the liver and lung, representing the first reported death of an adult bovine directly attributed to this parasite. The animal originated from a region where F. magna is enzootic in wild cervids, and the case demonstrated that cattle, typically considered dead‑end hosts with subclinical liver involvement, can occasionally suffer severe, life‑threatening disease due to aberrant fluke migration. The episode ended with the steer’s death but increased awareness of fascioloidosis as a differential diagnosis in cattle with unexplained hepatic and pulmonary lesions in endemic areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shared ranges or pastures between cattle and infected deer in an endemic area allowed accidental ingestion of metacercariae on contaminated vegetation. Internal mechanisms: Aberrant migration of F. magna into the lungs and associated increased pathogenicity in a dead‑end host represent a notable change in disease manifestation, fitting a re_emergence in terms of new clinical presentation within the existing animal host system.
Review: review – This is a notable first report of fatal pulmonary disease due to F. magna in cattle, highlighting a new and severe disease manifestation in a common livestock species, but it is based on a single case in an already endemic region. Classified as re_emergence due to the novel clinical presentation rather than geographic spread. Recommend keeping this row under review: its inclusion among the top 10 events depends on how heavily unique clinical impact in livestock is weighted relative to broader wildlife‑level range‑expansion episodes.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: European fallow deer (Dama dama) in hunting estates; background wild red deer populations in neighbouring countries
Event summary: Between December 2021 and January 2023, livers and faecal samples from 72 fallow deer culled on 11 hunting grounds in Arad County, western Romania, were examined, and adult Fascioloides magna and eggs were confirmed by sequencing as the parasite, with four animals testing positive. This study provided the first documented report of F. magna in Romania and completed the chain of Danube and Pannonian foci spanning neighbouring Hungary and Serbia. By the time of publication in 2024, the Romanian focus was recognised as a new national occurrence of an invasive parasite in wild cervids, with concern about further spread into Carpathian deer populations and potential spillover to domestic ruminants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural movement and management of fallow and red deer across the Romania–Hungary–Serbia border region, together with suitable wetland and forest habitats along the lower Mureș and Danube systems, facilitated incursion of F. magna into Romanian hunting grounds. Internal mechanisms: Continued geographic range expansion from existing central European natural foci into a previously unaffected country within the same Eastern European subregion, without evidence of a novel strain or host shift, best fits re_occurrence driven by host dispersal and habitat connectivity.
Review: retain – This is the first national report for Romania and an important extension of the Danube/Pannonian fascioloidosis belt into a new country, directly affecting wild fallow deer populations. Reclassified it as re_occurrence within Eastern Europe (new country in an already affected subregion) rather than first_detection or intra‑continental emergence, and removed re_emergence since no host shift or novel strain is implicated. Recommended for retention as a major event, with manual review to confirm that the national ‘first report’ status is adequately captured in narrative rather than via the first_detection flag.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: Wild red deer (Cervus elaphus), fallow deer (Dama dama) and roe deer (Capreolus capreolus)
Event summary: During the summer and winter of 2024, professional gamekeepers in two special‑purpose state hunting grounds in the Prekmurje region of north‑eastern Slovenia submitted 22 deer livers with extensive lesions from red deer, fallow deer and roe deer for examination. Post‑mortem, parasitological and ITS2‑based molecular analyses confirmed Fascioloides magna in 11 red deer, 4 fallow deer and 3 roe deer, providing the first documented and molecularly confirmed report of the parasite in Slovenia. The cases occurred close to the borders with Hungary and Croatia, in landscapes similar to known Danube and Pannonian foci, and were recognised as establishing a new national focus of an invasive parasite with potential for further spread and for wildlife–livestock transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of cervids from heavily infected regions in Croatia and Hungary, together with connected forest and wetland habitats in the Prekmurje region, allowed colonisation of Slovenian cervid populations. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing geographic range expansion within Europe, with effective transmission in red, fallow and roe deer and local lymnaeid snail hosts, underpinned establishment in this new national focus; this is best classified as re_occurrence in a previously unaffected country within an already affected Southern European subregion.
Review: retain – Slovenia’s first confirmed occurrence of F. magna, involving three wild cervid species and clearly linked to spread from neighbouring foci, is a major recent emergence event and should be retained. Corrected the event year to 2024 (the documented sampling period) rather than 2024–2025 and reclassified the event as re_occurrence (new country within an already affected Southern European subregion), removing the first_detection and intra‑continental emergence flags. Also updated the host list to reflect all three infected deer species reported. Manual review is advised to ensure this interpretation of the emergence‑type scheme is acceptable to end‑users.

Host: Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi) in south Florida
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2004, FeLV was detected for the first time in free‑ranging Florida panthers in south Florida after almost two decades of negative surveillance, with infections clustered in and around Okaloacoochee Slough, the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge, and parts of Big Cypress. Five panthers were confirmed antigen‑positive and at least three to five deaths were attributed wholly or partly to FeLV‑associated disease in a small, endangered population. An intensive management response, including widespread FeLV vaccination of panthers and nearby domestic cats, capture and removal of clinically affected animals, and sustained monitoring, eliminated detectable FeLV infection from the population by 2004 and no further FeLV‑positive panthers were found again until 2010.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The epizootic was most likely initiated by cross‑species transmission from an FeLV‑infected domestic cat at the wildland–urban interface, facilitated by landscape fragmentation, increasing overlap between free‑ranging domestic cats and panther habitat, and the very small, genetically depauperate Florida panther population that heightened vulnerability to infectious disease. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization showed that the outbreak strain FeLV‑Pco was a FeLV‑A virus closely related to the highly virulent domestic cat strain FeLV‑945, indicating introduction of a particularly pathogenic genotype into a naive non‑Felis host lineage. This episode represents host expansion (spillover) from domestic cats into Florida panthers coupled with novel strain/genotype emergence in this host, resulting in severe disease and high case fatality.
Review: Review – Retain this as a major FeLV emergence episode in wildlife, but correct the event window to 2001–2004 (five antigen‑positive panthers with three to at least five FeLV‑associated deaths and no additional cases detected from 2004–2010) and reclassify it as re‑emergence rather than first_detection, because FeLV was already long established in domestic cats in North America and in Florida. Geography (North America / Northern America, United States) and host specification (Florida panther) are appropriate. The J Wildl Dis epizootiology paper has been added as a key source alongside the EID articles and FWC summary. A human reviewer should verify the preferred start/end years and reconcile minor discrepancies among sources in the exact number of FeLV‑attributed deaths.

Host: Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) in the Doñana area (Coto del Rey and nearby subpopulations), southern Spain
Event summary: From December 2006 through August 2007, a severe FeLV outbreak occurred in the northern Doñana population of Iberian lynx in southern Spain, following earlier sporadic detections of FeLV provirus in individual lynx during the 1990s and early 2000s. Over roughly six months, 13 lynx in Coto del Rey and adjacent subpopulations became FeLV‑infected, many developed acute anemia and bone‑marrow aplasia, and six died, a substantial demographic shock to a global population then estimated at under 200 animals. Through aggressive management measures—capture and testing, vaccination of uninfected lynx, removal or isolation of infected individuals, and control of contact with domestic/feral cats—the outbreak was confined to the initial subpopulations, and no further FeLV‑related clinical cases or new FeLV‑positive lynx were detected in Doñana after August 2007, although low‑level FeLV circulation persisted at very low prevalence in Iberian lynx populations during subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak was likely initiated by spillover from an FeLV‑infected domestic or feral cat at the edge of Doñana, with impact amplified by extremely small, fragmented lynx subpopulations, low genetic diversity, and human‑modified landscapes that increase overlap among lynx, domestic cats, and their prey. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that lynx viruses were FeLV‑A closely related to pathogenic domestic cat strains and exhibited unexpectedly high virulence in this host; the event therefore fits re‑emergence driven by a particularly pathogenic strain and host expansion from domestic cats into Iberian lynx, rather than a first detection, because FeLV infection had already been sporadically documented in lynx and was long present in domestic cats in Southern Europe.
Review: Review – Retain this event as the major FeLV outbreak in Iberian lynx but adjust the case numbers to 13 infected lynx with six deaths within about six months, as reported by PLoS ONE and Animal Conservation, and emphasise that earlier single FeLV‑positive lynx in the 1990s mean this is not a first_detection event. Classification as re_emergence is appropriate because a pathogenic FeLV‑A strain spilled over from domestic cats into an already exposed, highly endangered lynx metapopulation in a region where FeLV was long present in domestic cats. Continent, sub‑region and country (Europe / Southern Europe, Spain) are correct. The J Vet Diagn Invest paper on the initial FeLV detections in Iberian lynx has been added as a supporting source. A reviewer should confirm that no additional multi‑fatality FeLV episodes in lynx rival this one in impact and thus warrant separate rows.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi) in south Florida
Event summary: After an apparent absence of FeLV cases in Florida panthers between 2004 and late 2010, FeLV infections reappeared in the population from 2010 to 2016, with six of 214 necropsied panthers testing FeLV‑antigen positive and at least one death attributed primarily to FeLV‑associated disease. These contemporary cases occurred west of the historic outbreak zone and mostly involved animals killed by vehicle collisions in more human‑populated areas, indicating renewed spillover rather than simple persistence of the earlier virus. Continued vaccination of panthers and local domestic cats, combined with surveillance and case management, limited the scale of this re‑emergence and FeLV remained at low prevalence, although repeated introductions from domestic cats remain a recognised threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The re‑emergent FeLV infections arose in south and southwest Florida where panthers increasingly overlap with free‑ranging domestic cats around ranches, rural residences, and roads, consistent with repeated cross‑species transmission driven by human land‑use change, expanding residential development, and incomplete vaccination and management of local domestic cat populations. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses of FeLV from contemporary (2010–2016) panthers showed viruses clustering with domestic cat FeLV‑A strains and provided evidence of FeLV‑B recombinant virus, indicating multiple introductions from domestic cats and ongoing viral evolution. This episode is therefore classified as re‑emergence involving repeated host expansion (domestic‑cat–to‑panther spillover) and novel strain/genotype dynamics in a population that had already experienced a prior FeLV outbreak.
Review: Review – Retain this as the second, lower‑intensity FeLV episode in Florida panthers, characterised by six antigen‑positive necropsied animals during 2010–2016 after a six‑year period with no detected cases. Classification as re_emergence is consistent with the event‑type definitions and molecular evidence for repeated domestic‑cat spillover and the presence of FeLV‑B; no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is involved because FeLV was already present in North America and in Florida. Geography and timing (North America / Northern America, United States; 2010–2016) match the primary sources, but a human reviewer should confirm whether any post‑2016 FeLV‑positive panthers represent additional linked episodes or isolated cases that would warrant updating the end year or adding a new event row.

Host: Pigs (primary), with limited involvement of other cloven-hoofed livestock
Event summary: In March 1997, Taiwan, previously free of FMD for decades, detected a devastating outbreak of FMDV serotype O (O/Taiwan/97) that was highly adapted to pigs and initially recognized in Hsinchu; the virus spread explosively through Taiwan’s dense pig industry, infecting over 6,000 farms and more than 4 million pigs between March and July 1997 and leading to massive culling and collapse of the island’s pork export trade. The epidemic was eventually controlled through large‑scale stamping out, movement restrictions, and vaccination, and Taiwan subsequently implemented long-term eradication and surveillance programs that culminated in official recognition of FMD freedom without vaccination many years later.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high pig density and intensive production systems; extensive movement of live pigs and pork products; evidence of introduction via smuggled pigs or illegal slaughter by sea from neighboring regions; delayed detection and initial diagnostic challenges. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a pig‑adapted FMDV serotype O Cathay topotype (O/Taiwan/97) with strong host restriction to swine, high transmissibility within pigs, and rapid farm‑to‑farm spread, representing a notable novel strain/biotype and enhanced transmission phenotype in the local context.
Review: review – major, well-documented 1997 Taiwan FMDV serotype O/Cathay epidemic in pigs (≈6,000 farms; >3.8–4 million pigs culled)([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/4/y3649e/y3649e02.htm?utm_source=openai)). Geography, timing, hosts and sources are appropriate. Event type has been corrected to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) to reflect emergence of a pig-adapted lineage as the primary internal driver rather than a simple resurgence in an unchanged virus population.

Sub-regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: India [1990s]; Nepal [1993]; Saudi Arabia [1994]; multiple Middle Eastern countries [mid‑1990s]; Bangladesh [1996]; Bhutan [1998]; mainland China [1999]; China, Taiwan Province of China [1999 distinct from 1997 pig‑only strain]; Thailand [1999]; Malaysia [1999]; Russian Federation [2000]; Mongolia [2000]; Republic of Korea [2000]; Japan [2000]; South Africa [2000]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2001]; Ireland [2001]; France [2001]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2001]; Bulgaria [1996]; Greece [1996]; Türkiye (European Thrace) [1996]
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, and other cloven‑hoofed livestock
Event summary: From the early 1990s through 2001, a single genetic lineage of FMDV serotype O (topotype ME‑SA, PanAsia strain) that emerged in northern India expanded its range, first spreading across South Asia and the Middle East and then into East Asia, the Russian Federation, and parts of Africa. Between 1998 and 2001 this PanAsia strain caused widespread outbreaks across multiple Asian subregions, reached South Africa, and culminated in major incursions into previously FMD‑free or long‑free areas of Europe in 2001, including the large United Kingdom epidemic and additional outbreaks in Ireland, France, and the Netherlands, with millions of animals ultimately culled and severe trade disruption. Control relied on rapid slaughter policies, emergency vaccination in some settings, strict movement controls, and coordinated international surveillance, after which the pandemic wave subsided although related ME‑SA lineages remain endemic in parts of Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and globalization of livestock production and trade; long‑distance movement of live animals and animal products across Asia, the Middle East, and into Europe; porous borders and informal trade networks; limitations in regional vaccination coverage and strain matching at the time of spread. Internal mechanisms: emergence of the highly successful O/ME‑SA PanAsia lineage with genetic changes in VP1 and related regions conferring enhanced fitness, broad host range, and strong transmissibility, enabling rapid geographic range expansion and repeated re‑emergence in regions that were previously disease‑free or had long intervals since the last FMD outbreaks.
Review: review – retained as a single linked episode describing the global spread of the O/ME-SA PanAsia lineage from India across South and West Asia into East Asia, parts of Africa and Europe, consistent with molecular and historical reconstructions([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387408/?utm_source=openai)). Event_year was broadened from 1998–2001 to 1990–2001 to align with first detection of PanAsia in India. Subregions were expanded (adding South-eastern Asia and Southern Europe) to match the listed countries. Event-type flags were simplified to re_emergence only (intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence set to false) because FMDV itself was already established on all affected continents and subregions; the key feature is emergence and global dissemination of a highly fit new lineage rather than first presence of the virus in those areas.

Countries: Argentina [2000]; Uruguay [2000]; Brazil (notably Rio Grande do Sul State) [2000-2001]
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, and other domestic ruminants and swine
Event summary: In 2000, shortly after Argentina had been declared free of FMD without vaccination, FMDV was reintroduced into the Southern Cone of South America, causing extensive outbreaks in Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil, including the state of Rio Grande do Sul. The virus spread across border areas with dense cattle populations and intense trade, reversing years of regional progress and leading to large numbers of affected herds, major emergency vaccination and culling campaigns, and temporary loss of FMD‑free status with severe impacts on beef export markets. Through coordinated regional control—mass vaccination, movement controls, and surveillance—countries progressively contained the outbreaks, regained FMD‑free status over subsequent years, and incorporated lessons learned into updated regional eradication strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive cross‑border movement of cattle and other livestock in the Mercosur region; relaxation or changes in vaccination policies following achievement of FMD‑free status; gaps in biosecurity at production and marketing nodes; economic incentives for long‑distance live animal transport. Internal mechanisms: introduction of at least two distinct FMDV type O viruses into the Southern Cone, with efficient transmission in naïve or partially vaccinated cattle populations; these introductions represented re‑emergence of epidemic strains in previously controlled zones rather than new serotypes, but their high transmissibility in large, concentrated cattle systems amplified impact.
Review: review – retained as a major resurgence in the Southern Cone shortly after Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Brazil had achieved FMD‑free status, with thousands of infected premises and large regional trade losses documented([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1978293/?utm_source=openai)). Event narrative and geography are appropriate. Event-type coding has been adjusted to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to false), because available evidence indicates reintroduction and spread of existing serotype O epidemic strains into previously controlled zones, driven mainly by control-policy changes and livestock movements rather than clear emergence of a fundamentally new viral variant.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2001]; Ireland [2001]; France [2001]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2001]
Host: Cattle, sheep, pigs, and other domestic ruminants
Event summary: On 19 February 2001, the United Kingdom detected FMD in pigs at an abattoir in Essex, with tracing revealing infection in multiple farms and confirming that an O/ME‑SA PanAsia strain had already spread widely before diagnosis; the epidemic ultimately infected over 2,000 premises, led to the culling of more than six million animals, and caused devastating economic and social disruption in rural communities. Through February–March 2001, linked outbreaks were detected in Ireland, France, and the Netherlands following movement of infected animals, prompting intensive surveillance, culling, and in some locations emergency vaccination to prevent further spread. The crisis was brought under control by late September 2001 via slaughter policies, national standstills on animal movement, disinfection, and enhanced biosecurity, after which affected countries regained FMD‑free status but significantly revised contingency planning and EU‑wide policies for transboundary animal diseases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High levels of livestock movement within and between EU member states; initial undetected spread from an infected pig unit supplying an abattoir; deficiencies in early detection and tracing systems; rendering and waste‑feeding practices that amplified virus spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction of the highly transmissible O/ME‑SA PanAsia strain into largely non‑immune livestock populations in a densely stocked and highly connected production system, representing a re‑emergence of FMD with enhanced epidemic potential compared with previously circulating European strains.
Review: review – this is correctly one of the most consequential FMD events globally, with ≈2,000 infected premises and ~6 million animals culled in the UK alone, plus linked outbreaks in Ireland, France and the Netherlands and very large economic and social impacts([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387408/?utm_source=openai)). Geography, hosts and narrative are accurate and well sourced. Event-type coding has been simplified to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) because the episode reflects introduction and explosive spread of the PanAsia O lineage into largely FMD‑free European livestock populations, rather than a generic increase in incidence of pre‑existing European strains; FMDV itself was long established in Europe, so inter-/intra-continental emergence are correctly left as ‘no’.

Host: Cattle, pigs, goats, sheep (cloven‑hoofed livestock in Miyazaki Prefecture)
Event summary: On 20 April 2010, Japan reported its first FMD outbreak since 2000 when FMDV serotype O was confirmed in beef cattle in Miyazaki Prefecture, an important livestock‑producing area in southern Japan; subsequent investigations found rapidly increasing numbers of infected cattle and pigs across the prefecture. Over the following months, the epidemic expanded to hundreds of farms and led to the culling of approximately 290,000 animals, with major economic losses and disruption of Japan’s high‑value beef and pork sectors. Intensive stamping‑out, movement bans, creation of vaccination and culling zones, and strengthened biosecurity eventually stopped transmission by July 2010, after which Japan again moved towards FMD‑free status with heightened long‑term surveillance and stricter controls on animal and product imports.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of cattle and pig farms in Miyazaki Prefecture; frequent animal movements within production networks; possible introduction via imported animal products, fomites, or travelers, though the exact source remained uncertain; initial delays before full recognition of the extent of spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an FMDV serotype O strain of the Southeast Asia topotype, lineage Mya‑98, with efficient transmission in intensive livestock systems; re‑emergence of FMD in a fully susceptible population that had not been exposed for a decade, resulting in unusually large epidemic size for Japan.
Review: review – large and well-documented Miyazaki Prefecture epidemic (~292 outbreaks and about 290,000 animals culled, the worst FMD outbreak in Japan in a century)([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvms/74/4/74_11-0271/_article?utm_source=openai)). Hosts, geography and course of the outbreak are accurately summarised and supported by primary Japanese and international sources. Event-type coding has been refined to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) to emphasize that the key driver was the introduction and rapid spread of a new serotype O Mya‑98 lineage into a previously FMD‑free population, rather than a generic resurgence of pre-existing virus.

Host: Pigs (primary), cattle, and other cloven‑hoofed livestock
Event summary: On 28 November 2010, the Republic of Korea detected FMDV serotype O in a pig complex in Andong, Gyeongbuk Province, marking the beginning of a massive nationwide epidemic that followed smaller incursions earlier in 2010; over the next 145 days, FMD spread through much of the country, heavily affecting pig and cattle industries. The outbreak resulted in the culling of hundreds of thousands to millions of animals and substantial economic losses, leading authorities to shift from targeted slaughter to large‑scale emergency vaccination combined with movement restrictions to halt spread. By April 2011, active transmission was brought under control through this combination of vaccination, culling, and strict controls, and Korea subsequently worked to re‑establish its FMD‑free with vaccination status and to strengthen border biosecurity and routine vaccination policies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High livestock densities with large industrial pig and cattle operations; frequent animal and vehicle movements; introduction of virus likely linked to regional circulation of O/SEA/Mya‑98 lineages in East and Southeast Asia; initial underestimation of the scale of spread before nationwide measures were implemented. Internal mechanisms: circulation of a virulent serotype O Mya‑98 strain with strong transmissibility in intensive production settings, coupled with partial gaps in population immunity prior to emergency vaccination; the epidemic represented a major re‑emergence driven by both viral fitness and susceptible host structure.
Review: review – correctly captures the largest FMD epidemic in Korea’s history, with ≈3.48 million animals culled and thousands of farms affected, caused by the O/SEA/Mya‑98 lineage and controlled through a shift from stamping-out to nationwide vaccination([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3647416/?utm_source=openai)). Geography and trajectory are consistent with primary epidemiological reports. Host: Cattle (high mortality in calves), buffalo, small ruminants
Event summary: In early 2012, Egypt experienced a large FMD outbreak caused predominantly by FMDV serotype SAT2 topotype VII, a serotype not seen in the country since around 1950, with confirmation by the World Reference Laboratory following detection by the Egyptian Animal Health Research Institute; tens of thousands of cattle were infected and nearly 10,000 animals died, particularly young stock. Genetic studies showed that the Egyptian SAT2 viruses fell into at least two distinct lineages within topotype VII and were related to, but distinct from, SAT2 viruses detected in Libya and sub‑Saharan Africa, suggesting multiple introductions into North Africa; concurrent SAT2 outbreaks were reported in Libya, indicating regional spread and a broader emergence episode. Emergency measures—including movement controls, intensified surveillance, and development and deployment of vaccines including SAT2 antigens—gradually reduced case numbers later in 2012, but SAT2 has since become part of the complex of endemic FMDV serotypes circulating in Egypt and neighboring regions, requiring ongoing tailored vaccination and cross‑border control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement and smuggling of live animals between sub‑Saharan Africa, Libya, and Egypt; inadequate vaccination coverage and absence of SAT2 antigen in existing vaccines at the time of introduction; live‑animal markets and uncontrolled animal transport; limited early laboratory capacity to distinguish new serotypes. Internal mechanisms: geographic expansion and host shift of FMDV SAT2 topotype VII from sub‑Saharan wildlife–livestock interfaces into North African domestic livestock populations; emergence of multiple distinct SAT2 VII lineages, indicating repeated introductions and viral diversification; re‑emergence in Egypt after >60 years of absence, driven by novel strain introduction and subsequent adaptation to local cattle and buffalo populations.
Review: review – accurately describes the 2012 emergence of FMDV serotype SAT2 topotype VII in Egypt with linked outbreaks in Libya, including high mortality in calves and molecular evidence for multiple introductions into North Africa([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23025522/?utm_source=openai)). Geography, hosts and control measures are well supported. Event-type coding has been corrected: intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are set to false and re_emergence retained as true, because the EPP (FMDV) was already present in North Africa; what is new is the incursion and establishment of a previously absent serotype/lineage, which fits the project’s definition of re‑emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence.

Host: Cattle, sheep and goats (small ruminants) and other domestic cloven-hoofed livestock in affected herds
Event summary: Beginning in 2013, FMDV serotype O, topotype ME-SA, lineage Ind‑2001d was detected in Libya after emerging from the Indian subcontinent and Middle East; over the following two years closely related viruses spread westward across the Maghreb. In 2014–2015 this lineage caused substantial epidemics in Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco, with hundreds of outbreaks reported in cattle and small ruminants, disrupting regional livestock production and triggering large-scale vaccination campaigns and movement controls. By 2015 the main epidemic wave had been brought under control through intensified vaccination with matched O/Ind‑2001d antigens, surveillance and restrictions on animal movements, but the episode highlighted North Africa’s vulnerability to repeated introductions of novel FMDV lineages from neighboring endemic regions and the need for sustained vaccine-matching and cross-border coordination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High volumes of formal and informal trade in live ruminants and animal products between the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East and North Africa; political instability and limited veterinary capacity in Libya acting as a gateway for virus introduction; gaps in vaccination coverage and use of vaccine strains poorly matched to the incoming O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001d lineage; extensive live-animal markets and cross-border livestock movements within the Maghreb. Internal mechanisms: emergence and geographic range expansion of the O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001d lineage from its endemic focus in South Asia into North Africa, with phylogeographic analyses indicating at least two independent introductions into Algeria and onward spread to Morocco; successful establishment of this lineage in domestic cattle and small ruminants required rapid adaptation to local husbandry systems and generated antigenic novelty that necessitated updated vaccine formulations.
Review: review – new multi-country event added to capture the O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001d epidemic that spread from Libya to Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco between 2013 and 2015, with hundreds of outbreaks and major vaccination responses documented by WRLFMD, phylogeographic analyses and North Africa reviews([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6168464/?utm_source=openai)). Classified as re_emergence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because FMDV was already endemic in North Africa; the defining feature is incursion and establishment of a new serotype O lineage. Geography, timing and drivers are well supported, but users may wish to confirm its prioritisation against any other mid-sized Ind‑2001-related episodes when finalising the top-10 list.

Host: Cattle, buffalo, goats, sheep and pigs (cloven-hoofed livestock across multiple Indonesian provinces)
Event summary: After more than three decades without reported FMD and recognition as FMD-free without vaccination since 1990, Indonesia confirmed new FMD outbreaks in cattle in East Java and Aceh in May 2022; laboratory characterization showed serotype O viruses belonging to the O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001e lineage. The disease spread rapidly through 2022, eventually affecting livestock in more than 20 provinces and hundreds of thousands of animals, severely disrupting smallholder beef and dairy production and prompting national concern over potential regional spread and impacts on religious festival slaughter. In response, Indonesia declared an animal health emergency, rolled out mass FMD vaccination, imposed movement controls and biosecurity measures, and implemented compensation schemes; incidence declined through 2023, though sporadic cases and ongoing vaccination needs indicate that FMD has not yet been fully eradicated from the archipelago.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large, largely naïve cattle and buffalo population following decades without vaccination; intensive movements of live animals for trade and religious festivals, including movements around Eid al-Adha; porous borders and informal trade or animal movements with neighboring countries where Ind‑2001 lineages are endemic; initially limited awareness and diagnostic capacity for FMD after a long disease-free period. Internal mechanisms: introduction of FMDV serotype O, O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001e lineage into a fully susceptible national herd, with high transmissibility and broad host range leading to rapid geographic expansion; phylogenetic analyses support close relatedness to contemporary Ind‑2001e viruses in Southeast Asia, consistent with recent transboundary spread rather than persistence of old Indonesian strains.
Review: review – new row added for Indonesia’s first FMD outbreaks in more than 30 years, starting in 2022 with detection of serotype O/ME-SA/Ind‑2001e in East Java and Aceh and subsequent spread to livestock in over 20 provinces, with national economic losses estimated in the range of US$1.37–6.6 billion and severe disruption of smallholder production([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9933659/?utm_source=openai)). Classified as re_emergence (FMDV had circulated historically in Indonesia but was reintroduced as a new lineage into a largely naïve population) and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence. Given its scale, geographic extent and documented economic impact, this episode is judged to belong among the largest modern FMDV emergence events and warrants inclusion in the curated top-10 list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic pigs (intensive commercial pig sector; minimal involvement of cattle/sheep)
Event summary: In March 1997, Taiwan detected FMD serotype O in pigs near Hsinchu after decades of national FMD freedom, and within weeks the virus spread explosively through the very dense commercial pig population across the western coastal plain. Control relied on mass depopulation, movement controls and emergency vaccination, leading to culling of about 3.8–3.9 million pigs on over 6,000 farms and collapse of Taiwan’s lucrative pork export trade, before the epidemic was brought under control by mid‑1997 and the country gradually rebuilt its pig sector under routine vaccination.([bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1136/vr.145.25.731?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extremely high pig density, feeding of untreated swill, proximity of farms to slaughterhouses and ports, and probable introduction via illegally imported pigs or pork products near a major smuggling port created ideal conditions for rapid spread and widespread seeding. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – the outbreak was caused by an O/Taiwan/97 swine-adapted serotype O virus that infected pigs almost exclusively and had not previously circulated in Taiwan’s intensive pig industry, enabling explosive transmission in a highly susceptible, naïve population.([bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1136/vr.145.25.731?utm_source=openai))},{
