Event summary: From about 2015, GI‑23 (Var2‑like) infectious bronchitis viruses of Middle Eastern origin were first detected in European poultry, initially in Poland and Romania and soon after in Italy and other Southern and Eastern European countries, indicating successful establishment of this lineage outside its original range. Following introduction, GI‑23 strains spread in European broiler and layer flocks and were linked to respiratory and nephropathogenic disease, often in vaccinated birds, though their overall field pathogenicity was still being assessed. By the late 2010s, GI‑23 had become one of several co‑circulating IBV genotypes in parts of Europe, raising concern about further expansion of this vaccine‑escape lineage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of live poultry, hatching eggs or contaminated equipment between the Middle East and Europe, together with high connectivity of European poultry trade networks, likely facilitated long‑distance spread; existing vaccine programs based on Mass and 4/91 provided incomplete protection. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – GI‑23 showed the capacity to establish outside its original Middle Eastern/North African range; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Recombination – European GI‑23 viruses were closely related to Egyptian/Israeli Var2 strains, some showing recombinant genomes; Antigenic divergence from standard vaccines allowed re‑emergence in vaccinated European flocks, contributing to its establishment.
Review: Flagged for review. Published phylodynamic and surveillance data indicate that GI‑23 (Var2‑like) was first recognized in Europe around 2015–2016 in Poland and Romania, with subsequent spread to Italy, Greece and Germany; the event years and country list have been updated accordingly, and Western Europe has been added as a sub‑region. Because IBV was long established in Europe, this wave has been re‑coded from 'first_detection' and 'inter_continental_emergence' to 're‑emergence' associated with introduction of a new lineage; re‑occurrence has been set to 'No' to avoid double counting. Several additional European detections (e.g. in other Eastern European states) are not explicitly listed but fall within the same regional episode.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Host: Commercial layer and breeder chickens
Event summary: In 2015, IBV strains closely related to the U.S. Delmarva/1639 (DMV/1639) genotype were first detected in Canadian poultry, marking the introduction of this nephropathogenic GI‑17 lineage into Canada. From 2015 onward, DMV/1639‑like viruses spread through eastern Canadian layer and breeder flocks, where they were associated with cystic oviduct lesions, false‑layer syndrome and marked reductions in egg production, causing substantial economic impact. By around 2019, DMV/1639 had become a significant IBV genotype in eastern Canada, prompting evaluation of existing vaccines and experimental vaccine‑challenge studies to determine effective control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of poultry, hatching eggs or contaminated equipment between U.S. and Canadian production systems likely introduced DMV/1639 into eastern Canada; limited initial awareness of this genotype and use of vaccines developed for other IBV serotypes contributed to unchecked spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – DMV/1639 expanded its range from U.S. to Canadian poultry; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – Canadian DMV/1639 strains caused severe reproductive tract pathology and persistent infection in experimental studies; Antigenic mismatch with commonly used vaccines and evidence of recombination among DMV/1639 variants supported classification as a re‑emergent, vaccine‑escape lineage in the new host population.
Review: Flagged for review. The introduction of DMV/1639 into Canada is a significant regional emergence, but IBV had been present in Canadian poultry for decades, so the previous 'first_detection' flag has been cleared and the episode is now coded as re‑emergence driven by a new nephropathogenic lineage. The 2015–2019 time frame and focus on eastern Canada match genotyping and pathogenicity studies; no additional North American countries have been identified with comparable DMV/1639 impact to warrant inclusion in this row.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Host: Commercial broiler and layer chickens
Event summary: From late 2018, China experienced a large wave of infectious bronchitis outbreaks in commercial broiler and layer flocks despite extensive vaccination programmes, with molecular analyses showing that most field viruses belonged to the GI‑19 (QX‑like) genotype. During 2018–2020 these GI‑19 viruses, including a newly recognised subtype with substantial divergence from the QXL87 vaccine strain, became dominant in many regions and were repeatedly isolated from respiratory and nephropathogenic disease cases and egg production drops. The upsurge of GI‑19 outbreaks led to re‑evaluation of vaccine strategies and stimulated development and deployment of updated or genotype‑matched vaccines as authorities and producers sought to bring the situation back under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term, intensive use of a limited set of IBV vaccines (e.g. H120, 4/91, LDT3‑A, QXL87) in a very large and dense poultry population created strong immune selection pressure favouring escape variants; rapid turnover and transport of birds across Chinese provinces enabled widespread dissemination of successful GI‑19 variants. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – within GI‑19, a new subtype with less than 90% nucleotide identity to the QXL87 vaccine and multiple amino‑acid substitutions in S1 emerged; Antigenic drift under vaccine pressure led to reduced protection and vaccine breakthroughs; Enhanced Transmission – dominant GI‑19 variants outcompeted other genotypes, driving a marked re‑emergence of clinical IB despite vaccination.
Review: Retain. Recent Chinese studies document a pronounced surge of GI‑19 (QX‑like) outbreaks from 2018 onward, dominated by a newly diverged subtype with reduced cross‑protection from existing vaccines; this fits the definitions of both re‑emergence (strain change) and re‑occurrence (vaccine and management pressures) within an already endemic EPP. The focus on China, Eastern Asia, and the 2018–2020 period is appropriate to capture the initial explosive phase of this genotype shift, though GI‑19 activity has continued beyond 2020 and could be covered in future updates.

Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr in the River Batnfjordselva
Event summary: From 1991 to 1994, intensive field studies in the Norwegian river Batnfjordselva documented extremely high burdens of Gyrodactylus salaris on multiple year classes of Atlantic salmon parr, with prevalence close to 100% and seasonal median parasite loads often reaching several hundred to over a thousand worms per fish, contributing to severe juvenile mortality and collapse of the local wild salmon stock. The river had been infected since around 1980 following introduction of infected hatchery smolts, and by the early 1990s the epizootic represented a mature, high‑impact phase of the wider Norwegian G. salaris epidemic. Infection pressures only began to decline after subsequent eradication attempts, including rotenone and later aluminium‑based treatments, as part of Norway’s broader eradication programme for the Driva infection region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated introduction of G. salaris via stocking of infected salmon juveniles from Norwegian hatcheries seeded the Batnfjordselva infection in the early 1980s; continued use of the river for angling and salmon management, together with cold freshwater conditions supporting high host densities, facilitated sustained transmission and heavy parasite burdens. Internal mechanisms: The event mainly reflects the high intrinsic virulence and reproductive potential of the Atlantic Norwegian G. salaris lineages on naïve Atlantic salmon hosts—parasites reproduced explosively on parr skin and fins, with no evidence that a novel genotype arose during this period; host immunity and density‑dependent processes, rather than parasite evolution, eventually limited parasite numbers locally.
Review: retain – This row correctly describes a major early‑1990s high‑burden epizootic in Batnfjordselva: timing (1991–1994), location (Norway, Northern Europe), host, and the classification as re‑occurrence in a river infected since ~1980 are consistent with Appleby & Mo’s population‑dynamics work and Norwegian management reports. No changes to geography, timing, or event‑type flags were needed; only additional supporting references were added for context.

Countries: Norway [1996] (Lærdalselva and Rauma river systems, Sognefjord region, western Norway)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and sea trout (Salmo trutta) in Lærdalselva and Rauma river systems
Event summary: In autumn 1996, Gyrodactylus salaris was first detected on Atlantic salmon parr in Lærdalselva and in the Rauma system, marking spread of the parasite into a previously uninfected, highly valued wild‑salmon region on Norway’s west coast and triggering a major crisis for one of the country’s flagship salmon fisheries. Lærdalselva was treated with rotenone in 1997 in an attempt to eradicate G. salaris, but the parasite reappeared by 1999 and persisted at damaging levels through the early 2000s, causing severe declines in wild salmon and necessitating prolonged restrictions on angling. This pre‑2005 phase set the stage for more radical eradication strategies using aluminium‑based treatments later in the decade and cemented Lærdalselva and Rauma as focal points in Norway’s national action plan against G. salaris.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Anthropogenic translocation of infected salmon or rainbow trout from already infected facilities or rivers, combined with intensive fishery use and river regulation in the Sognefjord region, most likely introduced G. salaris into Lærdalselva and Rauma; stocking and movement of fish within and among rivers increased host contact rates and amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was driven by the high virulence of established G. salaris lineages on naïve Atlantic salmon in these western rivers rather than by a clearly novel genotype; failure of the initial rotenone eradication attempt is attributed to limitations of coverage and refugia for hosts and parasites, not demonstrable evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: review – The original row mixed the early detection/rotenone phase with later aluminium treatments and incorrectly flagged the episode as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑occurrence. I have (i) adjusted the event years to 1996–2004 so this row covers the initial detection in Lærdalselva/Rauma and the 1997 rotenone phase up to just before large‑scale aluminium treatments began in 2005, (ii) changed intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No because spread occurred within the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe), and (iii) retained re_occurrence as Yes, reflecting renewed high incidence of G. salaris within a sub‑region where the parasite was already known (Baltic area and other Norwegian rivers). A Store norske leksikon entry for Lærdalselvi was added as a more authoritative narrative source. Please review this split together with the 2005–2017 Lærdalselva eradication event to ensure it matches your preferred episode structure.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Finland [1984] (multiple salmon-smolt farms in northern Finland)
Host: Baltic Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in hatchery and smolt-production farms
Event summary: From 1984 through 1993, long‑term monitoring of several salmon smolt farms in northern Finland documented persistent but generally low to moderate prevalence of Gyrodactylus salaris on Baltic Atlantic salmon stocks, with infections recurring over 6–7 years at some facilities without causing catastrophic mortality. The parasite, already endemic in Baltic salmon elsewhere, became established in roughly 40% of surveyed Finnish salmonid farms and provided a key case study of how relatively resistant Baltic salmon can carry G. salaris with sublethal effects. By the early 1990s, Finnish authorities used these data to strengthen surveillance and movement controls to prevent spillover from farms into wild Atlantic salmon rivers shared with Sweden and Russia and to limit the risk of exporting infection to more susceptible Atlantic populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transfers of salmon broodstock and smolts among Finnish farms and from the wider Baltic basin, together with farm‑level management factors such as changes in water intakes, occasional holding of wild fish and movements of fish between units, allowed repeated introduction and persistence of G. salaris across multiple facilities. Internal mechanisms: The episode primarily reflects the partial resistance of Baltic salmon to G. salaris—parasite burdens increased on older year classes and before stocking but seldom reached levels associated with mass mortality, in contrast to the explosive growth and severe disease observed on East‑Atlantic salmon stocks in Norway and the White Sea.
Review: review – The event is real and provides one of the main long‑term data sets on G. salaris in Baltic salmon farms, but the original classification as both first_detection and intra‑continental emergence was not consistent with the definitions: the parasite was first described on Baltic salmon in Sweden in the early 1950s and was already present in the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe). I have therefore set first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to No and flagged re_occurrence as Yes to reflect renewed establishment and increased incidence within a sub‑region where G. salaris was already known. The time span (1984–1993) slightly predates 1990 but is retained because the episode extends into the 1990s and is likely still among the ~10 most important events for this EPP; if strict adherence to a 1990 start is required, this row should be truncated to 1990–1993 or excluded.
Review Comment: Accept after correction

Countries: Russian Federation [1992] (Keret River, Republic of Karelia, White Sea basin)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr and smolts in the Keret River (White Sea drainage)
Event summary: In 1992, Gyrodactylus salaris was first recorded on juvenile Atlantic salmon in the Keret River in the White Sea basin of Russian Karelia, a region that had previously lacked this parasite on anadromous salmon. Within about four years the infestation spread throughout the river system and some tributaries reached 100% prevalence and very high intensities, leading to an estimated 25–200‑fold reduction in salmon parr densities and a comparable collapse of the adult salmon stock. After this acute epizootic phase, parasite abundance and host densities fluctuated, with G. salaris sometimes undetectable in particular years but persisting as a chronic threat, and Russian authorities initiated long‑term monitoring and risk‑mitigation measures for White Sea and Barents Sea rivers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Keret outbreak was strongly linked to anthropogenic transfer of infected juvenile salmon from the Vyg hatchery and Lake Onega in the Baltic basin into the Keret catchment during the late 1980s, using shared transport equipment (e.g. canvas bags) and lacking adequate biosecurity, which introduced a virulent Baltic strain into a naïve White Sea salmon population. Internal mechanisms: The imported G. salaris lineage, well adapted to Baltic salmon, proved highly pathogenic to Keret’s East‑Atlantic salmon; rapid parasite reproduction on juvenile salmon skin and fins produced extreme burdens, overwhelming host immune responses and causing mass mortality, with no evidence that additional novel genotypes beyond this introduced strain were needed to drive the epidemic.
Review: retain – This high‑impact White Sea epidemic, omitted in the original file, clearly belongs among the most important global emergence events for G. salaris: it was the first pathogenic outbreak in a Russian Atlantic‑salmon river, with 25–200‑fold reductions in parr and adult stocks linked to anthropogenic introduction of a Baltic strain. The Keret River lies in Eastern Europe, a sub‑region where G. salaris was already present in Baltic drainages, so I classified the episode as re_occurrence (dramatic incidence increase within a known sub‑region) rather than first_detection or intra‑continental emergence. New, well‑documented Russian and NASCO sources were added; this row should be retained and used to represent the White Sea component of the G. salaris range expansion.

Countries: Sweden [1989] (Atlantic-draining west-coast rivers including Säveån, Ätran system, Fylleån, Nissan, Viskan, Rönne å and other salmon rivers south of Anråse å, plus Munkedalsälven [2025])
Host: Wild Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr and smolts in multiple Swedish west-coast rivers; occasionally farmed salmon and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) as carriers
Event summary: Beginning with first detection of Gyrodactylus salaris on wild Atlantic salmon in Säveån (Göta älv system) in 1989, the parasite spread during the 1990s and 2000s to most Swedish Atlantic‑draining west‑coast salmon rivers south of Anråse å, with detections in at least twenty rivers and tributaries including Ätran, Fylleån, Nissan, Viskan and Rönne å, and into some fish farms. A national monitoring programme established from 2001 onward has shown that while G. salaris can reach high burdens on individual fish and negative trends in juvenile salmon densities have occurred in several rivers, overall population‑level effects have generally been much less severe than in Norwegian rivers, likely reflecting differences in host susceptibility and environmental conditions. In 2025, the parasite was confirmed for the first time in Munkedalsälven, a tributary of Örekilsälven north of Göta älv, indicating northward extension of the west‑coast infection zone and reinforcing Swedish concerns about ongoing risk to remaining uninfected stocks and to neighbouring Norwegian rivers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Multiple introductions from infected Baltic salmon and rainbow trout farms, including stocking of smolts and escapes or transfers of farmed fish, together with movements of fishing gear and boats without proper disinfection, are considered the main sources of G. salaris into Swedish Atlantic‑draining rivers; the parasite cannot easily cross high‑salinity coastal stretches unaided. Internal mechanisms: Several mitochondrial haplotypes of G. salaris have been detected on the Swedish west coast, indicating multiple introduction events, but there is no clear evidence of novel, more virulent strains compared with other Baltic‑derived lineages; instead, host–parasite interactions and local environmental factors modulate disease impact, with west‑coast salmon appearing more susceptible than Baltic salmon yet less catastrophically affected than Norwegian Atlantic salmon.
Review: retain – This new row has been added to cover the long‑running emergence of G. salaris in Swedish Atlantic‑draining west‑coast rivers, which was entirely missing from the original dataset despite being a key range‑expansion event highlighted by NASCO and Swedish authorities. I have set the event years to 1990–2025 (noting first detection in 1989 in Säveån) to comply as far as possible with the 1990 cut‑off while capturing subsequent spread to many rivers and the important 2025 detection in Munkedalsälven. Because G. salaris was already endemic in the Baltic part of the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe), the episode is classified as re_occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence or first_detection. High‑quality Swedish and NASCO sources documenting detection years, monitoring results and impact were added; this row should be retained as one of the major emergence events for this EPP.

Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and sea trout (Salmo trutta) in Lærdalselva
Event summary: Following the failure of the 1997 rotenone treatment to eradicate Gyrodactylus salaris from Lærdalselva, Norwegian authorities launched full‑scale chemical eradication trials using acidified aluminium sulphate (AlS) in 2005–2006, dosing the main river stem and major tributaries and sacrificing large numbers of salmon and sea trout in the process. Initial monitoring after the 2005–2006 treatments showed a sharp decline in G. salaris, but low‑level survival and reinfestation led to further Al‑based and supplementary rotenone treatments in 2008 and again in 2011–2012, while angling closures and strict biosecurity remained in place. After extensive post‑treatment surveillance, Lærdalselva was finally declared free of G. salaris from 2017 onwards, making this prolonged eradication phase one of the most technically challenging and costly, but ultimately successful, control campaigns for the parasite in a major Norwegian salmon river.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Strong economic and cultural value of the Lærdalselva salmon fishery and the need to prevent spread of G. salaris within the Sognefjord region prompted development and large‑scale deployment of novel aluminium‑based eradication methods, supported by national funding and regulatory approvals; hydraulic regulation and complex side channels made complete coverage difficult and required repeated campaigns. Internal mechanisms: The eradication phase targeted the same highly virulent G. salaris strain introduced in the 1990s, but the parasite’s ability to persist at low densities in refugia and possibly on non‑salmonid hosts allowed re‑establishment after initial treatments; the episode illustrates resilience of the parasite’s direct life cycle under intense control pressure rather than evolution of new genotypes.
Review: review – The original 2005–2007 Lærdalselva eradication row accurately captured the early aluminium treatments but truncated the episode before the additional 2008 and 2011–2012 treatments and the eventual declaration of freedom in 2017, effectively under‑representing the duration and impact of this eradication phase. I have therefore extended the event years to 2005–2017 and updated the summary to include later treatments and the 2017 ‘friskmelding’, while keeping the classification as re_occurrence (continued presence of the same introduced strain in a known sub‑region) consistent with Norwegian sources. More detailed Norwegian technical reports and SNL’s Lærdalselvi entry were added or emphasised as primary references. Please check that this extended time span fits your event‑selection rules; if you prefer shorter, more discrete interventions, the episode could be split differently.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus) – anadromous and resident forms; sympatric Atlantic salmon and rainbow trout as comparators
Event summary: Around 2006–2007, molecular and morphometric analyses demonstrated that Gyrodactylus salaris infecting anadromous Arctic char in the River Signaldalselva in northern Norway and resident Arctic char in Lake Pålsbufjorden in southern Norway were true G. salaris, confirming the first viable wild populations of this parasite on a host species in the absence of Atlantic salmon. Parasites on Signaldalselva char shared mitochondrial haplotypes with those on sympatric Atlantic salmon, while the Pålsbufjorden parasites carried a haplotype previously associated with rainbow trout, indicating at least two independent host‑switch events within Norway. Recognition of Arctic char as a competent reservoir host raised concerns that G. salaris could persist and spread even where salmon are absent or eradicated, complicating eradication strategies and requiring expanded surveillance and risk assessments for non‑salmon hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated introductions of G. salaris via stocking of salmon and rainbow trout and movements of equipment likely seeded infections into Signaldalselva and the upstream Lake Pålsbufjorden system, where hydroelectric development and multi‑species fisheries brought char into repeated contact with infected salmonids. Internal mechanisms: Clear host expansion and lineage diversification were documented—G. salaris on Arctic char exhibited mitochondrial haplotypes and subtle morphometrics distinct from some salmon‑associated strains, yet maintained reproductive success and transmission; this expansion of the host range and creation of new wild reservoirs justifies classification as re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission potential.
Review: retain – This event accurately summarizes the 2006–2007 demonstration that Arctic char can serve as a competent wild host and reservoir for G. salaris in Signaldalselva and Lake Pålsbufjorden, based on robust molecular and morphometric evidence. The classification as re_emergence (driven by host expansion and new reservoir formation within an already affected sub‑region) is appropriate, and the geography, timing and host description match the primary Parasitology paper and related Norwegian reports; no corrections beyond minor wording clarifications were required.

Countries: Norway [2014] (remaining infection regions with multiple infected rivers in central, western and south-eastern Norway)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) populations in numerous Norwegian rivers; other salmonids (brown trout, Arctic char, rainbow trout) acting as carriers or secondary hosts
Event summary: Between roughly 2014 and 2020, Norway implemented an updated national eradication programme for Gyrodactylus salaris under a formal action plan and EEA‑approved national measures, targeting residual infection regions such as Rana, Vefsn, Skibotn, Steinkjer, Driva and Drammenselva while many previously treated rivers were being declared parasite‑free. During this period, G. salaris had historically been detected in over 50 Norwegian rivers, but coordinated chemical treatments (mainly rotenone and aluminium‑based methods), stricter movement controls and enhanced diagnostics progressively reduced the number of actively infected rivers to fewer than ten, concentrated in a few infection regions. The episode culminated in substantial progress towards the national goal of eradicating pathogenic G. salaris strains from all Norwegian rivers and farms, while also documenting continued re‑occurrence in a small subset of rivers where eradication had not yet succeeded, setting up final eradication campaigns in the 2020s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Strong policy and economic incentives to restore wild Atlantic salmon stocks and protect angling tourism, coupled with evolving European fish‑health regulations and EFTA Surveillance Authority approvals, underpinned Norway’s intensified national eradication plan, which used integrated piscicide and aluminium treatments, zoning and long‑term surveillance. External drivers included improved availability of piscicides, development of aluminium‑based methods, and advances in diagnostic tools (microscopy, molecular assays, eDNA), enabling more targeted interventions. Internal mechanisms: Persistent low‑level G. salaris infection in some rivers appears to reflect the parasite’s capacity to survive in refugia and exploit multiple salmonid hosts within complex catchments rather than emergence of new genotypes, so the episode is best treated as re_occurrence in a shrinking set of infection foci under sustained control pressure.
Review: retain – This row provides a reasonable synthesis of the 2014–2020 national eradication programme and its impact on the number of infected Norwegian rivers, consistent with Mo (2024), the Norwegian Fish Health Reports and the EFTA Surveillance Authority decision approving updated measures. Classification as re_occurrence (persistence and local resurgence within a long‑affected sub‑region) rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence is appropriate, and the geographic scope (Norway, Northern Europe) matches the country sheet. No structural changes were necessary; I only tightened the linkage to key official sources.

Countries: Norway [2022] (Driva infection region: Rivers Driva, Litldalselva, Usma, Batnfjordselva and Gylelva, Møre og Romsdal)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and other salmonids in the Driva infection-region river systems
Event summary: From 2022 to 2024, Norway carried out an intensive, multi‑river eradication campaign against Gyrodactylus salaris in the Driva infection region, treating the rivers Driva, Litldalselva, Usma, Batnfjordselva and, following a 2023 detection, Gylelva with a combination of rotenone and chlorine. The operations required complex logistics to ensure that all salmonid hosts and parasite refugia throughout these interconnected catchments were exposed to lethal concentrations, while parallel environmental monitoring and eDNA surveys documented treatment efficacy and the absence of surviving parasite populations. By 2024, Norwegian authorities reported completion of the chemical treatments with no subsequent detections of G. salaris in 2023–2024 sampling, and a formal post‑treatment surveillance (friskmeldings) programme starting in 2025, marking one of the final and most challenging steps toward eradicating G. salaris from all Norwegian wild salmon rivers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing recognition of the ecological and economic value of Driva‑region salmon stocks and Norway’s national and international commitments to eradicate G. salaris led to major investments in this final eradication phase, implemented through a multi‑agency partnership involving the Environment Agency, Food Safety Authority, regional governors, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, NINA and NIVA. Internal mechanisms: As in other Norwegian rivers, the campaign targeted established high‑virulence G. salaris lineages that had persisted since the 1980s; the key biological challenge was eliminating parasites surviving in refugia or on non‑target hosts within a cold, complex river network, rather than coping with newly evolved strains, justifying classification as re_occurrence under intense control rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This event is a well-documented, recent large‑scale eradication campaign in the Driva infection region and clearly among the most consequential late‑phase episodes for G. salaris in Norway. The timing (2022–2024), river list and description of combined rotenone and chlorine treatments align with Veterinary Institute reports and regional management documents, and classification as re_occurrence (removal of a long‑standing infection focus rather than new emergence) is appropriate. No corrections were required beyond minor wording changes and adding the newly published 2026 summary report as a key source.

Host: Horses; humans
Event summary: In August–September 1994, clusters of acute, high‑fatality respiratory and neurological disease in horses at a racing stable in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, and retrospectively linked deaths of two horses near Mackay revealed a previously unknown paramyxovirus infecting horses. Laboratory investigation isolated the virus, later named Hendra virus, and showed that in total 22 horses on the two properties and three people were infected, with two human deaths, establishing the pathogen as a bat‑origin zoonosis spilling over to horses and then to humans. Control was achieved through quarantine of affected properties, euthanasia of infected or high‑risk horses, movement restrictions and enhanced infection‑control measures, after which no further equine or human cases occurred from this episode.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense housing and close contact among racehorses in the Hendra stable, intensive husbandry and high‑risk procedures (nursing of severely ill horses without respiratory protection) amplified horse‑to‑horse and horse‑to‑human exposure once spillover occurred; limited prior awareness of bat‑borne henipaviruses delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from pteropid flying fox reservoirs into domestic horses and then into humans, with the novel henipavirus showing a strong tropism for vascular endothelium and the respiratory and central nervous systems, resulting in severe systemic disease in equids and people.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review: review – Retain this row as the primary description of the original 1994–1995 Hendra/Mackay emergence but correct the emergence classification: this episode represents the global first emergence of Hendra virus in horses (and humans), so first_global_emergence is set to true and first_detection to false, consistent with the definitions for newly recognised pathogens. The host field is expanded to include humans because three human infections (two fatal) occurred in this episode. Timing, location and horse/human counts match Queensland Health’s event table, CDC case descriptions and the Hendra virus historical summaries, so no changes to year or geography were required.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses; humans (veterinarian)
Event summary: In late 2004, a horse on a property near Gordonvale, about 25 km south of Cairns in northern Queensland, died with illness later presumed on clinical and epidemiologic grounds to be due to Hendra virus infection. A young veterinarian who had performed an autopsy and been heavily exposed to the horse’s blood and respiratory secretions developed a mild influenza‑like illness about a week later and was found to have seroconverted to Hendra virus, representing a non‑fatal human infection associated with a single‑horse spillover. No further animal or human cases occurred once the property was investigated, exposed contacts monitored and guidance on personal protective equipment for veterinary procedures reinforced.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued overlap between horse grazing areas and flying fox foraging and roosting habitat in tropical north Queensland enabled sporadic bat‑to‑horse spillover; limited early use of respiratory and barrier protection during necropsies on unexplained horse deaths increased occupational risk for veterinarians. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects geographic re‑occurrence of the known Hendra virus phenotype in a previously affected subregion rather than any documented change in viral genotype or virulence; transmission to the veterinarian again occurred via intense exposure to blood and respiratory secretions from an infected horse.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review: review – New event added: the 2004 Gordonvale/Cairns episode (one infected horse plus a seroconverting veterinarian) is one of only four known Hendra outbreaks with human infection and therefore clearly belongs among the top‑impact post‑1990 events. Classified as re_occurrence within the existing Australia and New Zealand subregion, since earlier spillovers had already occurred in Queensland and there is no evidence of a novel strain. Year, location and animal/human counts follow the Queensland Health event table and narrative description and the Hendra virus history on Wikipedia; no competing, larger 2000–2005 events were identified that would displace this episode from the top ten.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses
Event summary: In October 2006, Hendra virus infection was confirmed in a single horse near Murwillumbah in northern New South Wales, representing spread of recognised equine risk beyond previous foci in Queensland into another eastern Australian state. The case followed sporadic spillover events in coastal Queensland and triggered heightened awareness and surveillance for Hendra virus in horses in NSW, but no other horses or people on the property were found to be infected. Strict quarantine of the premises, movement controls and the introduction of more rigorous biosecurity guidance for veterinarians limited the event to a single‑horse outbreak.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing ecological overlap between flying fox colonies and horses along the subtropical east coast, including shared use of pastures and potential contamination of feed and water by bat excreta, enabled rare spillover into New South Wales; increased clinical suspicion of Hendra virus outside Queensland facilitated diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: This event reflects geographic re‑occurrence of the existing Hendra virus lineage in a new administrative jurisdiction but not in a new UNSD subregion, and there is no evidence of genetic change or altered host range compared with earlier Queensland outbreaks.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review: retain – This row correctly represents the first recognised Hendra virus infection in New South Wales and is a reasonable inclusion among the most impactful events because it extended recognised risk beyond Queensland. Classification as re_occurrence (with intra_continental_emergence set to false) is consistent with the UNSD framework, since Queensland and NSW are in the same 'Australia and New Zealand' subregion, and the horse and human case counts and timing match Queensland Health and Business Queensland incident tables; no corrections to year, geography or sources were required.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))

Host: Horses; humans
Event summary: In June–July 2008, a major outbreak of Hendra virus occurred at an equine veterinary clinic in the Redlands/Thornlands area near Brisbane, Queensland, where five horses were confirmed infected, several additional equine deaths were epidemiologically linked, and three staff members developed illness, two with confirmed Hendra virus infection and one fatality. The virus spread between closely housed horses under intensive veterinary care, providing strong evidence for efficient horse‑to‑horse transmission in confined clinical settings and exposing a large number of veterinary personnel. The outbreak ended after quarantine of the clinic, euthanasia of infected and in‑contact horses, environmental decontamination and the introduction of strengthened infection‑control protocols and personal protective equipment guidance for equine practices.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density stabling and intensive procedures at an equine veterinary clinic (including invasive diagnostics and close‑contact nursing) amplified transmission among horses and dramatically increased opportunities for staff exposure; at the time, PPE practices for managing suspect Hendra cases were still evolving. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence data show that the virus in Redlands was closely related to earlier HeV isolates, so the outbreak is best explained by amplification of an existing lineage in a high‑contact environment rather than emergence of a new strain; the episode nonetheless highlighted the inherent potential of HeV for efficient horse‑to‑horse transmission in stabled settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3294518/))
Review: review – This outbreak is appropriately included as one of the most consequential Hendra events because it involved the largest documented horse‑to‑horse transmission cluster after 1994 and caused two human infections with one death. The main correction is to the host field, which now explicitly lists humans as well as horses; classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate, as genomic analyses show no major viral divergence and the severity is attributable to high‑risk clinical settings. The narrative of case numbers, human outcomes and control measures is consistent across Queensland Health, Business Queensland and CDC EID reports.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses
Event summary: In July 2008, shortly after the Redlands clinic outbreak, multiple horses on a property near Proserpine in north Queensland died or became severely ill, and three horses were confirmed infected with Hendra virus, with at least one additional death considered a probable but untested case. This Proserpine outbreak occurred more than 900 km from Redlands yet within the same winter season, and together the two independent multi‑horse incidents signalled unusually broad HeV activity in bat reservoirs and spillover into horses across eastern Queensland. Quarantine of the affected property, destruction of infected and high‑risk horses and movement controls contained the Proserpine outbreak, and no human infections were documented despite substantial equine case numbers.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Similar environmental conditions to Redlands—winter season with increased shedding of virus by flying foxes and close proximity of horses to bat foraging areas—likely favoured bat‑to‑horse spillover at Proserpine, while on‑property husbandry practices and delay before recognition of Hendra virus contributed to multiple equine infections. Internal mechanisms: Sequence comparisons indicate that the Proserpine and Redlands viruses represent closely related variants within the known HeV diversity, so this episode is best understood as geographic re‑occurrence and local amplification of an established lineage rather than emergence of a new strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3182206/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the Proserpine 2008 outbreak involved three confirmed and at least one probable equine case and is highlighted in ecological and genomic analyses as one of two large, geographically separated outbreaks in winter 2008, placing it clearly among the top HeV emergence events. It is classified as re_occurrence within the same subregion because it represents another multi‑horse spillover without evidence of a distinct strain or new host. Horse numbers, timing and the concurrent nature of this outbreak with Redlands were cross‑checked against Queensland Health, Business Queensland and the Queensland Ombudsman review.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses; humans
Event summary: In August 2009, an equine nursery near Cawarral, close to Rockhampton in central Queensland, experienced a Hendra virus outbreak in which four horses were confirmed or strongly suspected to be infected, all of which died or were euthanised. A 55‑year‑old veterinarian who had performed a nasal endoscopy and other procedures on an infected horse without full respiratory protection developed encephalitis and died, becoming the fourth recorded human fatality from Hendra virus. The outbreak was controlled through destruction of affected horses, long‑term quarantine of the property, widespread tracing and risk assessment of human contacts, and a major review of infection‑control practices in equine veterinary medicine.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close confinement of horses in a multi‑paddock nursery, coupled with high‑risk veterinary procedures conducted before Hendra virus was suspected, increased within‑property transmission and intense human exposure to respiratory secretions and blood; the event occurred against a background of increasing horse movements within Queensland. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that the Cawarral virus was highly similar to other HeV isolates, so the severity of this outbreak is attributable to exposure conditions rather than novel viral traits; bat‑to‑horse spillover followed by limited horse‑to‑horse transmission in a confined setting best explains the pattern of cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3294518/))
Review: review – This Cawarral outbreak remains one of the highest‑impact events because it involved multiple equine cases and a fatal human infection in a veterinarian. The main correction is to the host field, which now includes humans; the event is still best classified as re_occurrence since viral genome comparisons show high conservation with earlier strains and there is no evidence of a novel genotype. Timing, horse and human case counts and control measures are consistent across Queensland Health, Business Queensland, parliamentary and media reports.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses; dog (domestic)
Event summary: Between June and October 2011, eastern Australia experienced an unprecedented spike in Hendra virus activity, with 17 documented property‑level spillover events in Queensland and New South Wales and 21 horse deaths across multiple locations. Within this cluster, a property near Mount Alford/Boonah in south‑east Queensland with three infected horses also yielded the first naturally infected domestic dog, which was seropositive for Hendra virus antibodies, indicating that the virus’s recognised domestic host range extended beyond horses. Intensive surveillance, property quarantines, destruction of infected horses and enhanced risk communication eventually saw the number of new incidents decline after winter, and no sustained transmission beyond affected properties or any human infections were documented during this surge.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe weather events in late 2010 and early 2011, including major flooding in south‑east Queensland and northern New South Wales and Cyclone Yasi, likely disrupted flying fox food resources and roosts, increasing nutritional stress and driving bats into closer contact with horses, while heightened awareness and testing probably improved detection of spillovers. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion from horses into a companion dog on the Mount Alford property demonstrated that HeV can infect domestic canids under field conditions, and the marked, climate‑associated increase in spillover incidence within an already affected subregion is treated here as re_emergence even though no specific new genotype was identified.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review: review – This row is retained as a synthetic description of the June–October 2011 spike, which comprised 17 separate property‑level spillovers causing 21 horse deaths and the first recorded natural HeV infection in a dog. It explicitly aggregates multiple independent bat‑to‑horse spillover events into a single episode because they were temporally clustered, geographically proximate and plausibly driven by shared climatic and ecological conditions; users should note that most incidents are not linked by horse‑to‑horse transmission. The event is kept as re_emergence due to the combination of a marked incidence increase and documented host expansion to a dog, and the overall magnitude and chronology match Queensland Health, Business Queensland and secondary syntheses.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses; dog (domestic)
Event summary: In June–July 2013, Hendra virus infection was confirmed in an unvaccinated horse on a property near Macksville on the mid‑north coast of New South Wales, and the farm was quarantined while remaining horses, cats and dogs were monitored. Subsequent testing detected Hendra virus RNA and neutralising antibodies in a quarantined dog that had close contact with the sick horse, confirming the second naturally infected dog recorded and extending recognition of canine involvement to NSW. No human infections occurred, and the outbreak was declared over after follow‑up testing of in‑contact animals remained negative and movement restrictions were lifted.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendra_virus))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued bat–horse interface in coastal NSW, together with low vaccine uptake in the region, created susceptible horse populations in close proximity to flying fox contamination; farm dogs had unrestricted access to paddocks and sick horses, facilitating cross‑species exposure. Internal mechanisms: This event represents geographic re‑occurrence of the previously documented ability of Hendra virus to infect dogs, now in a different state, rather than emergence of a new host species or genotype; available virologic data show no novel variant, and there was no evidence of dog‑to‑human or dog‑to‑horse onward transmission.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/12/15-1324_article?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the 2013 Macksville outbreak is included because it documents the second naturally infected dog and demonstrates that canine Hendra virus infection can occur outside Queensland, an important host‑range and geographic consideration. It is classified as re_occurrence within the same subregion since dog infection had already been documented in 2011 and no new genotype was identified. Horse and dog involvement, timing and the scope of the public‑health and veterinary response are drawn from CDC EID’s detailed case report, ABC coverage and the Business Queensland incident table.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/12/15-1324_article?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses
Event summary: In June 2019, Hendra virus infection was confirmed in an unvaccinated older mare on a small non‑Thoroughbred property near Scone in the Upper Hunter Valley, New South Wales, marking the first equine case in the Hunter region and, at that time, the furthest south that infection in a non‑bat host had been documented. An urgent One Health response involving NSW Health, the Department of Primary Industries and local veterinarians quarantined the property, traced and risk‑assessed ten human contacts and monitored in‑contact horses, with no additional equine or human infections detected. Extensive media and industry communication followed, and vaccination uptake in the Hunter Valley increased, while quarantine was lifted once follow‑up testing of animals remained negative.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of flying fox foraging and roosting into the horse‑dense Upper Hunter region, combined with variable adoption of the Equivac HeV vaccine, created conditions for spillover into an area previously believed to be low risk; climate variability and broader environmental changes affecting bat ecology may also have contributed. Internal mechanisms: Viral characterisation did not show a novel genotype, so this event is interpreted as geographic range expansion of spillover within the same subregion rather than emergence of a distinct strain, prompting revised risk mapping and biosecurity guidance for the thoroughbred and broader equine industries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the 2019 Scone case is widely recognised as the first equine Hendra virus infection in the Hunter Valley and, at the time, the southernmost non‑bat case, with substantial implications for risk mapping and vaccination behaviour. It is therefore justifiably among the top ten emergence events even though it involved only a single horse, and is classified as re_occurrence within the Australia and New Zealand subregion because no new genotype was identified. The description of the case, One Health response and impact on vaccine uptake is based on NSW Health surveillance reports, veterinary case descriptions, Business Queensland data and ABC news coverage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses; flying foxes (fruit bats)
Event summary: In October 2021, a horse near West Wallsend in the greater Newcastle region of New South Wales died with acute neurological signs and was confirmed infected with Hendra virus genotype 2 (HeV‑g2), the first equine case in which this divergent lineage was prospectively diagnosed and, at that time, one of the southernmost confirmed HeV infections in a horse. Genomic surveillance over the preceding decade had identified HeV‑g2 RNA in grey‑headed and other flying foxes across eastern, southern and western Australia, and application of the new PCR assay also led to retrospective recognition that at least one 2015 horse case in Gympie, Queensland, had been caused by HeV‑g2. The West Wallsend outbreak was confined to the index horse thanks to rapid diagnostic confirmation, property quarantine and risk communication, and surveillance and messaging were expanded southwards to reflect the broader distribution of the variant in bat reservoirs and horses.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensified genomic surveillance of flying foxes and horses and the development of an HeV‑g2‑specific molecular assay enabled detection of this genotype in bats across a wide geographic range and its identification in horses, including the Newcastle case; ongoing habitat change and urban encroachment continue to bring flying foxes and horses into contact over a broader latitudinal band. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence—HeV‑g2 is substantially divergent from the prototype Hendra virus yet retains the capacity to infect horses—and inherent geographic range expansion of this lineage in bat reservoirs underpin its classification as re_emergence, with spillover now documented in horses further south and, retrospectively, as early as 2015 in Gympie.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11905374/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This row is retained as the key description of Hendra virus genotype 2 emergence in horses but updated to reflect subsequent evidence that at least one 2015 Gympie horse case was retrospectively reclassified as HeV‑g2 and that the lineage has a broad distribution in flying foxes. The event remains appropriately classified as re_emergence because it documents recognition of a divergent viral genotype and southward expansion of confirmed spillover into horses, rather than a simple recurrence of the prototype strain. Hosts, geography and timing are consistent with the primary veterinary case report, CSIRO communications and Australian government sources, while the text now clarifies the relationship between the 2021 diagnostic breakthrough and earlier, retrospectively reinterpreted cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11905374/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ethiopia [1999] (Debre Zeit, Mojo, Nazareth, Bako, Ejaji and 28 additional cart‑horse and cart‑mule towns)
Host: Equids – primarily carthorses and cart‑mules used for urban and peri‑urban transport
Event summary: From December 1999 to January 2001, a cross‑sectional study of 2,907 carthorses in Debre Zeit, Mojo and Nazareth in central Ethiopia found Histoplasma farciminosum infection in 26.2% of animals, demonstrating rampant endemic epizootic lymphangitis in key cart‑horse towns.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Between November 2002 and April 2003, 21% of 309 cart‑mules in Bako and Ejaji in western Ethiopia were affected, and between January 2003 and June 2004 a survey of 19,082 carthorses in 28 towns recorded 18.8% prevalence, with highest burdens in warm, humid mid‑altitude towns and in larger horse populations.([colab.ws](https://colab.ws/articles/10.1016%2Fj.prevetmed.2004.09.008?utm_source=openai)) Taken together, these linked investigations (1999–2004) confirmed that epizootic lymphangitis had re‑occurred as one of the most important constraints on working equids across much of Ethiopia, without any coordinated national control effort.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of urban and peri‑urban cart‑horse and cart‑mule transport, concentration of equids at parking stations and markets, poor harness design causing chronic skin trauma at the chest, neck and limbs, limited owner awareness and access to antifungal treatment, and climatic suitability (warm, humid mid‑altitude towns) that favours survival of Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: field and phylogenetic studies to date have not identified a novel epizootic lineage during this period; disease resurgence is best explained by increased transmission opportunities and work‑related skin injury, so the event is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event retained but the time span has been adjusted from “2002–2005” to “1999–2004” to reflect the actual periods of the major Ethiopian prevalence studies (2,907 carthorses in three central towns in 1999–2001; 309 cart‑mules in Bako/Ejaji in 2002–2003; 19,082 carthorses in 28 towns in 2003–2004).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Countries and sub‑region are correctly coded as Ethiopia, Eastern Africa; event type is appropriately coded as re‑occurrence (no evidence for new continent or sub‑region invasion or for emergence of a new strain). Sources have been updated to include the 2002 Journal of Veterinary Science study and to remove inline URLs from the Countries field; a human reviewer should confirm that merging these linked surveys into a single 1999–2004 episode matches the project’s outbreak‑episode criteria.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ethiopia [2010] (Bahir Dar, Amhara Region – cart‑mule population)
Host: Equids – primarily cart‑mules, with related burden in local cart‑horses
Event summary: Baseline screening in 2010 of 430 cart‑mules in Bahir Dar, a major lake‑side city in Amhara Region, found epizootic lymphangitis prevalence of 23.9%, confirming a heavy local burden of chronic, debilitating disease similar to that seen in other Ethiopian towns.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) From 2010 to 2017, an integrated community‑based control programme led by The Donkey Sanctuary and partners introduced improved diagnosis and treatment, owner education, better harnesses and carts, and euthanasia of advanced cases, with annual cross‑sectional surveys documenting a decline in prevalence to around 5–6%, a transient rise to 10% in 2016, and 5.9% (58/981) in 2017.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) Despite substantial reductions in clinical case burden and improved welfare, epizootic lymphangitis remained endemic in Bahir Dar at the end of the programme.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: before intervention, high prevalence was linked to poorly fitting harnesses and carts that produced chronic harness wounds, overcrowded working and stabling conditions, and limited access to effective antifungal therapy, all of which prolonged infectiousness and favoured mechanical transmission by biting flies and contaminated equipment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) The control programme demonstrated that improving harness design, clinical management, owner awareness and municipal regulation can markedly reduce transmission in an endemic focus, but that underlying environmental suitability and reliance on working equids continue to sustain low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or change in virulence was identified during this period, so the episode is coded as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event retained with minor corrections: Countries field simplified to “Ethiopia [2010] (Bahir Dar, Amhara Region)” and inline URLs removed; classification as re‑occurrence (with all other emergence‑type flags set to No) is consistent with the description of a long‑standing endemic focus experiencing control‑driven changes in prevalence rather than spread to a new continent/sub‑region or emergence of a new strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) Source list appropriately emphasises the Frontiers 2021 community‑based intervention paper and supporting local prevalence studies; a human reviewer should confirm that treating the entire 2010–2017 control period as a single episode meets the project’s temporal‑linkage rules.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ethiopia [2018] (17 cart‑horse towns across multiple regions including Kombolcha, Gondar and Debre Birhan)
Host: Equids – carthorses
Event summary: Between October 2018 and June 2019, a cross‑sectional survey of 4,162 carthorses in 17 Ethiopian towns found an overall epizootic lymphangitis prevalence of 16.67% (95% CI 15.6–17.8) and detected disease in 16 of the 17 towns, with town‑level prevalences up to 33.3% at Kombolcha.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) This large, multi‑site study confirmed that, more than a decade after earlier nationwide surveys and despite local control efforts, epizootic lymphangitis remained widely endemic in the cart‑horse sector across diverse climatic zones in Ethiopia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: logistic‑regression analyses indicated higher epizootic lymphangitis prevalence in warmer, more humid mid‑altitude towns and in areas with larger carthorse populations, supporting the role of climate suitability, urban aggregation of working equids, and associated harness‑related skin trauma as key external risk factors.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) Limited access to affordable antifungal treatment and weak surveillance further allow chronic cases to persist and spread infection. Internal mechanisms: molecular studies of Ethiopian Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum isolates show a relatively conserved equine‑associated lineage without evidence of a newly emerged hypervirulent strain during this period, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added to capture the large 2018–2019 multi‑town survey of 4,162 carthorses in 17 Ethiopian towns, which is among the largest post‑1990 datasets on epizootic lymphangitis and demonstrates widespread endemic re‑occurrence across the country.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) Event is coded as re‑occurrence (all other emergence‑type flags No) because the pathogen and affected host system were long‑established in Ethiopia and no new continent or UN sub‑region was involved. Countries and sub‑region are coded as Ethiopia, Eastern Africa; a human reviewer should confirm that treating this survey as a distinct emergence episode, separate from earlier 1999–2004 studies and the 2010–2017 Bahir Dar control period, aligns with the project’s episode‑definition guidelines.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [2002-2003] (Mississippi broiler belt – 5 broiler-breeder and 29 broiler flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial broilers in an immunologically naïve broiler industry; breeder flocks also affected)
Event summary: From December 2002 to March 2003, a localized infectious laryngotracheitis outbreak occurred in Mississippi, United States, affecting five broiler‑breeder and 29 broiler flocks in a state that had been free of ILT for the preceding 15 years.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The virus spread among closely spaced farms in an otherwise immunologically naïve commercial broiler population, leading to marked respiratory disease, mortality, and production losses.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak was controlled by depopulating infected flocks, implementing ring vaccination with live CEO vaccines around affected sites, tightening movement controls on litter and personnel, and improving house cleaning and down‑time, after which no further ILT‑positive flocks were detected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of ILTV into a naïve broiler region, high farm density, movement of company service crews and suppliers between farms, and shared litter‑removal equipment were all statistically associated with ILT introduction on case farms.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The viruses were typical CEO‑like field/vaccine strains; there is no evidence of a novel genotype, and the episode is best interpreted as amplification of existing ILTV lineages under intensive production and suboptimal biosecurity.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event clearly represents one of the larger post‑1990 US ILT epizootics (34 commercial flocks) and should be retained, but event description was updated to include the documented number and types of flocks and to rely primarily on the Mississippi risk‑factor study.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) Non‑specific or tangential sources were removed from this row.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2002-2003] (Bastos region, São Paulo State – intensive commercial layer area of ~14 million hens)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial laying hens in large multi-age layer farms)
Event summary: At the end of 2002 and throughout 2003, a severe ILT epidemic struck the Bastos region of São Paulo State, Brazil, the country’s largest egg‑production hub with around 14 million commercial layers, causing typical respiratory disease, high flock morbidity and mortality reported up to 20%, and major egg‑production losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular characterization showed that most outbreak isolates grouped into distinct field virus clusters, clearly differentiated from some vaccine strains used in Brazil at that time.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21154050/?utm_source=openai)) Following extensive vaccination with live attenuated vaccines, strengthened biosecurity, and regulatory control on bird and litter movements, clinical disease declined, although ILTV has remained endemic in Brazilian commercial poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very dense layer populations in multi‑age complexes, frequent movement of personnel, equipment and litter between barns and farms, and pre‑existing respiratory co‑infections created ideal conditions for rapid farm‑to‑farm spread and large cumulative losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses belonged mainly to established field lineages rather than novel recombinants; subsequent Brazilian work documents long‑term persistence of both field and vaccine‑origin ILTV, with latency and vaccine virus maintenance contributing to continued re‑occurrence in the same production region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9679056/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: This São Paulo (Bastos) epidemic is widely cited as one of the largest modern ILT outbreaks, affecting an exceptionally dense layer region and causing substantial mortality and production loss; geography and emergence type (re-occurrence within an already affected country/continent) are correct. Minor wording changes were made to emphasise scale and to align with Brazilian primary sources.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America [2005-2008] (Central Valley, California – 57 broiler ranches from two integrators)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial broilers on large integrator ranches)
Event summary: Beginning in 2005, a large vaccinal ILT outbreak in California’s Central Valley affected 57 broiler ranches belonging to two integrators, with birds showing respiratory disease, increased mortality and condemnation losses, and viruses indistinguishable from chicken‑embryo‑origin (CEO) vaccine strains.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak persisted through multiple production cycles despite standard cleaning, disinfection, and vaccination, leading companies and state authorities to implement a coordinated regional depopulation, extended down‑time, and intensive biosecurity audit programme across affected ranches.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) After completion of extended down‑time and strengthened sanitation in early 2008, ILT diagnoses fell sharply; only two of the previously affected ranches recorded further cases, and both integrators subsequently regained LT‑free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high broiler densities in multi‑house ranches, reuse and movement of contaminated litter, incomplete down‑time between flocks, and frequent movements of personnel and equipment facilitated sustained circulation of vaccinal ILTV over a wide area.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was driven by CEO‑vaccine–like viruses that had spread and persisted in the field; there is no evidence for a novel recombinant genotype, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence of vaccine‑origin ILTV maintained under intense production pressure.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event is correctly identified as a major vaccinal ILT epizootic in California, but the event period has been adjusted from 2005–2007 to 2005–2008 to reflect the documented duration of coordinated control efforts in Chin et al. 2009.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) is retained because the causative viruses were CEO‑like and not novel recombinants.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia [2007-2015] (commercial poultry regions of New South Wales and Victoria)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers; some backyard flocks also affected)
Event summary: From late 2007 onward, eastern Australia experienced an unprecedented series of ILT outbreaks in commercial poultry in Victoria and New South Wales, with many flocks showing severe respiratory disease and high mortality.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai)) Molecular epidemiology demonstrated that most outbreaks between 2007 and 2009 were caused by two novel, highly virulent recombinant ILTV genotypes (classes 8 and 9) that arose through recombination between pre‑existing Australian live vaccine strains (SA2, A20) and the newly introduced European Serva vaccine strain; by 2009–2015, an additional recombinant (class 10) emerged and became predominant in parts of New South Wales.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai)) Despite intensive control measures and changes in vaccine policy, these vaccine‑derived recombinants displaced previously circulating class 2 field strains and continued to cause economically important outbreaks over several years before improved vaccination strategies and regulatory changes reduced their impact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of the Serva live ILT vaccine into an industry already using other live attenuated vaccines, combined with dense industrial poultry production and heavy vaccine use, fostered frequent co‑infection of birds with multiple ILTV strains and created strong selection for fitter recombinants.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Natural recombination between distinct live vaccine strains generated novel class 8, 9 and later class 10 ILTV genotypes with higher virulence and transmission, representing a clear example of vaccine‑driven novel strain/genotype emergence (re‑emergence) within an established endemic setting.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4365042/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: The Australian recombinant‑vaccine epizootic is one of the most impactful and scientifically important ILT events worldwide, illustrating vaccine‑driven re‑emergence of more virulent genotypes; geography, timing and classification as re‑emergence are consistent with primary molecular epidemiology studies.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai))

Countries: Brazil [2010-2011] (Mantiqueira Highlands egg-production region, Minas Gerais State – multi-age layer complexes)
Host: Domestic chickens (large multi-age commercial laying-hen flocks)
Event summary: In November 2010, an extensive ILT outbreak was reported in a high-density egg‑production area in the Mantiqueira Highlands of Minas Gerais, Brazil, where approximately eight million layers were housed in multi‑age complexes with individual farm sizes up to 2.9 million birds.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Over subsequent months, multiple farms experienced increased mortality (roughly 1–9% per month) and sudden drops in egg output, with necropsy revealing characteristic necrotic and fibrinous laryngotracheitis and molecular tests confirming ILTV infection.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) As movement restrictions, improved biosecurity, and (later) vectored‑vaccine programmes were implemented by producers and the official veterinary service, mortality gradually returned toward baseline, although ILTV persisted in the region and prompted long‑term surveillance and control efforts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12172900/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extremely dense layer populations in multi‑age systems, restrictions on removal of birds and litter once the disease was recognized, and co‑circulation of other respiratory pathogens created a setting in which ILTV could spread rapidly and cause large cumulative losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate involvement of virulent field strains related to earlier Brazilian ILTV genotypes rather than a fundamentally new recombinant; this episode therefore represents major re‑occurrence of established lineages in a new high‑density production pocket within the same country and subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This large Minas Gerais outbreak, affecting an egg‑production region with ~8 million hens, was missing from the original list despite being highlighted in Brazilian surveillance papers as a major ILT episode distinct from the Bastos epidemic.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) A new row has been added and classified as re-occurrence in South America; geography and timing follow Brazilian primary reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China [2010-2014] (multiple provinces – Guangdong, Guangxi, Jiangsu, Jiangxi, Hainan and others reporting outbreak isolates)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial broilers and layers in intensive systems)
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2014, numerous ILT outbreaks were reported in at least five Chinese provinces, with 19 ILTV strains isolated from dead or diseased chickens showing typical respiratory signs and variable mortality (roughly 0.5–10% in documented flocks).([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1040638715618230?utm_source=openai)) Molecular characterization of these isolates revealed a mix of virulent and low‑virulence field strains, many closely related to CEO or TCO vaccine strains, indicating widespread endemic circulation of vaccine‑like and field ILTV lineages in major poultry areas.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1040638715618230?utm_source=openai)) Expanded vaccination, improved diagnostics, and biosecurity measures reduced clinical incidence in some regions, but ILT persisted as part of a broader respiratory disease complex in Chinese commercial poultry.
