Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of the Chinese poultry industry, high flock densities, and frequent co‑infections with other respiratory pathogens (e.g. avian influenza, Newcastle disease virus, infectious bronchitis virus) created favourable conditions for repeated ILT outbreaks and wide geographic spread of existing viruses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7241549/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Most outbreak isolates were low‑virulence or vaccine‑related ILTV strains with limited genetic divergence; there is no indication of a single novel recombinant dominating nationwide, so this period is best interpreted as multi‑province re‑occurrence of previously established lineages rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event is retained as a representative multi‑province ILT episode in China, but the original classification as intra‑continental emergence has been corrected to re-occurrence, because ILT has been present in China and Eastern Asia for decades and the 2010–2014 isolates mainly reflect endemic circulation of field and vaccine‑related strains.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1040638715618230?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Namibia [2018] (commercial farms near Windhoek and one farm in northern Namibia – three linked outbreaks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers)
Event summary: Between July and August 2018, two ILT outbreaks near Windhoek, Namibia, caused the death of over 116,000 commercial layers and broilers on two farms; a third outbreak in September 2018 occurred roughly 800 km to the north in a smaller broiler flock.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Affected flocks exhibited severe respiratory distress, 23–70% reported mortality, and marked drops in egg production on the layer farm, with necropsy revealing classic fibrinous and haemorrhagic laryngotracheitis.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Molecular analysis showed that outbreak viruses were essentially identical to the Nobilis ILT live vaccine strain, indicating reversion to virulence and spread of a vaccine‑derived virus.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Despite movement bans, illegal transport of birds and likely airborne spread between nearby farms contributed to wider dissemination; by late 2018 over 200,000 chickens had been lost, before improved vaccination practices and enforcement of movement controls brought the epizootic under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incorrect administration of live Nobilis ILT vaccine (aerosol spray instead of eye‑drop), unavailability of registered vaccine locally leading to probable off‑label sourcing, illegal movement of birds despite movement bans, shared worker housing, and windy seasonal conditions all contributed to vaccine‑virus spread between farms separated by up to 800 km.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Internal mechanisms: Molecular epidemiology demonstrated that the outbreaks were caused by a reverted‑to‑virulence vaccine strain genetically indistinguishable from Nobilis ILT, exemplifying how live attenuated vaccines can re‑emerge as field pathogens when misused, but representing the first documented ILT outbreaks in southern Africa rather than a new genotype at global scale.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content))
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This high‑mortality Namibian episode (>116,000 birds dead and >200,000 birds lost overall; first documented ILT outbreaks in southern Africa) was missing from the original dataset and clearly qualifies among the most impactful modern ILT events.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) It has been added and classified as intra‑continental emergence (new subregion within Africa) driven by vaccine‑strain reversion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Egypt [2018], [2019], [2020], [2021] (multiple governorates including Behera, Giza, Qalyubia, Monofiya, Sharkia, Fayoum and others)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers – cross-bred and intensive flocks)
Event summary: From approximately 2018 through at least 2021, Egypt experienced intense ILT activity in commercial poultry, with outbreaks documented in multiple governorates among both layer and broiler flocks showing severe respiratory signs, high mortality and egg‑production losses.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Molecular characterization of outbreak isolates from layers and broilers in Behera, Qalyubia and other provinces revealed that many circulating viruses were closely related to chicken‑embryo‑origin (CEO) and tissue‑culture‑origin (TCO) vaccine strains, indicating that vaccine‑like ILTVs were driving field outbreaks rather than classical wild‑type strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8072874/?utm_source=openai)) As official and private control programmes strengthened diagnostics, refined vaccination schedules and improved on‑farm biosecurity, reported clinical incidence declined in some areas, but ILT remained part of a complex endemic respiratory disease landscape in Egyptian poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high poultry densities, frequent co‑infections with avian influenza, infectious bronchitis, Newcastle disease and other agents, extensive but variably applied live‑vaccine use, and heterogeneous biosecurity practices created conditions for vaccine‑derived ILTV to persist and flare into major outbreaks.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03079457.2014.886004?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Sequencing of Egyptian isolates consistently shows close relationship to CEO‑ and TCO‑type vaccine strains and evidence of vaccine‑derived viruses circulating and evolving in the field, supporting classification as re-emergence of modified vaccine lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence within an endemic region) rather than simple re‑occurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8072874/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Egyptian ILT outbreaks in 2018–2021 are major in scale and clearly linked to vaccine‑like CEO/TCO strains, but the original row marked both re-occurrence and re-emergence. In line with the schema (where re-emergence denotes pathogen change), classification has been adjusted to re-emergence only, while retaining the event as a key example of vaccine‑driven ILTV resurgence in North Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8072874/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Türkiye [2014-2018] (Konya and other commercial poultry regions; commercial layers, broilers and some backyard flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers; backyard flocks in some studies)
Event summary: In the mid‑ to late 2010s, Türkiye documented multiple ILT outbreaks and high seroprevalence in commercial layer flocks, particularly in the Konya region where ELISA surveys found ILTV antibodies in over 40% of sampled birds and 64% of sampled farms.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29424631/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent investigations detected ILTV DNA in broiler and layer flocks with respiratory disease in several Turkish provinces, and nationwide surveys reported PCR‑positive ILTV in about 14% of 119 flocks examined, indicating widespread endemic infection in the country’s commercial poultry.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40101513/?utm_source=openai)) Control responses have focused on improved surveillance, strain characterization and targeted vaccination, with ILT now recognised as an economically significant contributor to respiratory disease in Turkish poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of the Turkish poultry industry, high stocking densities, incomplete biosecurity, and possible spillover between commercial and backyard flocks facilitated the spread and entrenchment of ILTV in previously under‑recognised areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11960647/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Sequencing of Turkish ILTVs has revealed genetic diversity in gB, gG and ICP4 genes but does not yet point to a single dominant vaccine‑derived recombinant; available data are most consistent with geographic expansion and increased detection of existing and imported genotypes rather than major novel‑strain emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Türkiye has reported ILT since at least 2003, and 2014–2018 episodes represent expansion and intensification within an already affected Western Asian country rather than first introduction to a new subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17449712/?utm_source=openai)) The intra‑continental emergence flag has therefore been set to "No" and the event reclassified as re-occurrence, while retaining it as one of the larger recent ILT episodes in Western Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2021] (Northern Ireland – mainly Armagh and Tyrone counties near Dungannon; ~19 affected flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (mostly commercial poultry flocks of varying production types; some small flocks)
Event summary: From early May 2021, Northern Ireland experienced a notable ILT outbreak centred around the Dungannon area, with 17–19 poultry flocks (mostly commercial) reported infected and roughly 250,000 birds estimated to have been affected.([fbcc.ca](https://www.fbcc.ca/file.aspx?id=9be515c1-49ba-466c-bacb-504e0d19812f)) Clinical signs were mainly respiratory, with generally low mortality but significant temporary production losses in recovering birds; ILT was already considered endemic in the region but had not caused a major commercial‑sector outbreak for nearly a decade.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/infectious-laryngotracheitis-ilt?utm_source=openai)) DAERA treated ILT as a production disease rather than imposing compulsory culling, instead emphasising strict farm biosecurity, careful handling and storage of litter, and targeted vaccination; by mid‑June 2021, the rate of new case reports had slowed and the outbreak was regarded as stabilising.([farmersjournal.ie](https://www.farmersjournal.ie/news/news/poultry-industry-getting-on-top-of-ilt-629101))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ILTV is endemic in Northern Ireland, and officials believe initial spread in 2021 likely involved wind‑borne transmission between closely sited poultry houses, followed by further dissemination via contaminated litter and farm traffic in a dense poultry region.([farmersjournal.ie](https://www.farmersjournal.ie/news/news/poultry-industry-getting-on-top-of-ilt-629101)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been published of a novel genotype; available information suggests re-occurrence of existing ILTV lineages in commercial flocks that had previously been protected primarily through biosecurity and controlled vaccine use.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This Northern Ireland episode, affecting nearly 250,000 birds across ~19 flocks, is one of the larger recent European ILT events and was missing from the original dataset.([fbcc.ca](https://www.fbcc.ca/file.aspx?id=9be515c1-49ba-466c-bacb-504e0d19812f)) A new row has been added and classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic Northern European region; geography and scale are based on DAERA and independent surveillance summaries.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: In 1990–1991, Norway experienced the historical peak of its initial ISA epidemic, with around 80 new farm outbreaks in 1990 alone among marine-phase Atlantic salmon, causing heavy mortality and major economic losses. Following rapid spread along much of the Norwegian coast, authorities intensified control with movement restrictions, slaughter of infected cages, and improved hygiene and water-treatment regulations. These measures, together with better farm management, reduced the annual number of ISA outbreaks in Norway to generally fewer than 20 per year after 1993, although sporadic cases have continued.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and high density of Norwegian salmon aquaculture in the 1980s, common use of untreated seawater, and shared equipment and well boats facilitated farm-to-farm spread before strong biosecurity standards were implemented. Internal mechanisms: No single new genotype is implicated at this peak; the event primarily reflects efficient horizontal transmission of existing virulent ISAV strains rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: retain – Peak 1990–1991 Norwegian epidemic with ~80 farm outbreaks is correctly identified as a major high‑impact event. Geography and timing match Norwegian Veterinary Institute and other sources. Coded as re‑occurrence in a previously affected subregion without evidence for a new genotype, which fits the definitions. Updated the source list to remove a Chile‑specific paper and instead cite Norwegian and general ISA references; otherwise no structural changes.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Countries: Canada [1996 – New Brunswick]; United States of America [2001 – Maine]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: From 1996 to 2003, ISA was first detected and then became epidemic in salmon farms in southwest New Brunswick, Canada, and subsequently in 2001 spread to farms in Cobscook and Passamaquoddy Bays in neighboring Maine, USA, marking the first major establishment of ISAV outside Europe. The virus spread through densely stocked sites in the Bay of Fundy–Quoddy region, leading to slaughter of hundreds of thousands of salmon and tens of millions of dollars in compensation and control costs on both sides of the border. Aggressive depopulation, fallowing, movement controls and increasingly strict biosecurity regulations gradually reduced outbreak frequency in Atlantic Canada and Maine, although ISA has persisted at low levels in the wider region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High farm density in the Bay of Fundy–Quoddy region, shared service vessels and equipment between Canadian and Maine farms, and strong tidal exchange created an area‑wide contact network that promoted rapid local spread once ISAV was introduced. Limited early surveillance and gaps in bay‑management zoning delayed containment, and cross‑border movements of well boats and fish further linked Canadian and U.S. sites. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of virulent European‑lineage ISAV to North America (likely via movements of fish or eggs) followed by efficient horizontal transmission; available evidence does not point to a novel North American genotype during this first inter‑continental emergence wave.
Review: review – Expanded this row to cover the whole 1996–2003 Bay of Fundy–Quoddy epidemic, which encompassed both New Brunswick (from 1996) and epidemiologically linked outbreaks in Maine (from 2001). According to the event definitions, this cross‑border, hydrodynamically connected episode should be treated as a single linked event with multiple countries listed and country‑specific start years, rather than split across separate rows. Reclassified the event type so that it remains the first inter‑continental emergence of ISA into North America (inter_continental_emergence = true) but no longer uses first_detection, which should refer to the first global detection in 1984. Mechanism text was updated to integrate hydrodynamic and cross‑border risk factors previously described in the Maine‑only row. The original Maine‑specific row is therefore recommended for exclusion to avoid double counting (see that row’s Review).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1998 – Scotland]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: In May 1998, ISA was first detected in a salmon farm in Loch Nevis on the Scottish west coast, representing the first recognized occurrence of clinical ISA in the United Kingdom. Over 1998–1999 the disease spread to multiple Scottish farms, leading to substantial mortalities and mandatory slaughter of affected and contact sites under an ISA control program. Through enforced depopulation, fallowing, movement controls and an industry Code of Practice, the 1998–1999 Scottish epidemic was brought under control, with no new clinical outbreaks reported by 2000.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of well boats and other service vessels between infected and uninfected sites, combined with high farm density in sea lochs and limited early awareness of ISA, facilitated long‑distance seeding of infection; tidal circulation patterns in sea lochs further promoted spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a virulent ISAV strain into Scottish farms, likely via imported fish or eggs from already affected regions in Northern Europe, followed by efficient horizontal transmission; no clearly defined novel genotype beyond importation is highlighted for this episode.
Review: review – Retained as one of the major global ISA events, but reclassified. Because ISA had already been present in Northern Europe since the mid‑1980s, the Scottish 1998–1999 epidemic is a re‑occurrence within a previously affected subregion rather than a global first_detection event; first_detection has therefore been set to false and re_occurrence to true. The country name has been standardised to match the Country sheet (“United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland”) while retaining Scotland as location detail in brackets.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: In March 2000, ISA was first suspected and then confirmed in a salmon sea farm in the Faroe Islands, initiating an epidemic that raged from 2000 to 2005 and affected most of the archipelago’s salmon farms. The disease spread widely among marine sites, causing very high cumulative mortalities and leading to near collapse of the Faroese salmon aquaculture industry, with extensive depopulation and trade restrictions imposed by the EU and OIE. A complete restructuring of production with large fallowing zones and strict biosecurity, combined with eradication of infected stocks, eventually ended the epidemic by 2005; no further clinical ISA was seen until a re‑emergent outbreak in 2014.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High concentration of farms in fjords with limited water exchange, lack of pre‑existing ISA‑specific management plans, and extensive movements of fish, equipment and personnel promoted rapid island‑wide dissemination; limited early fallowing and zoning delayed control. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of virulent HPR‑deleted ISAV variants from a background of non‑virulent HPR0 viruses circulating in Faroese broodstock, smolt farms and marine sites, representing a transition from endemic low‑pathogenic infection to highly virulent epidemic strains.
Review: review – The Faroese 2000–2005 epidemic is correctly captured as one of the most severe ISA events globally, with near collapse of the local industry. It is not a global first_detection (Norway 1984) and occurs in a subregion where ISA was already known, so first_detection has been set to false. Given strong evidence that virulent HPR‑deleted variants emerged from endemic HPR0 in Faroese production, coding as re_emergence is appropriate. Country name has been aligned with the Country sheet (“Faroe Islands”) while retaining the first detection year.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: From 2003 to 2005, Norway experienced a renewed cluster of 32 ISA outbreaks distributed along much of its coast, despite earlier success in reducing cases after the 1990 peak. The disease reappeared at multiple marine sites, with variable clinical severity and substantial local mortalities, prompting renewed concern about farm‑to‑farm spread. Genotyping and epidemiological investigation showed that many outbreaks were linked by shared viral genogroups and risk factors such as proximity and operational contact, and strengthened biosecurity plus rapid depopulation again reduced annual outbreak numbers after 2005.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Horizontal transmission associated with geographic proximity of farms, shared workboats and service infrastructure, and movements of fish contributed to spread; increasing farm biomass and complex contact networks created recurrent opportunities for re‑introduction. Internal mechanisms: Multiple ISAV genogroups circulated, with evidence that virulent HPR‑deleted variants arose repeatedly from non‑virulent HPR0 backgrounds and then spread locally, representing recurrent re‑emergence driven by mutation and selection for virulence under farming conditions.
Review: review – Retained as a major post‑control resurgence in Norway, but recoded from a combined re_occurrence + re_emergence to re_emergence only. The 2003–2005 cluster occurred in a long‑affected subregion, and molecular work shows repeated emergence of pathogenic HPR‑deleted variants from HPR0; this fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by viral change. Using only re_emergence avoids overlapping event‑type labels, which are intended to be mutually exclusive except for co‑occurrence with intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch); farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: In the late 1990s, ISA virus was first isolated from farmed salmon in Chile, with clinical disease in coho salmon and later in Atlantic salmon recognized and characterized by 2001. Early Chilean cases were limited to a small number of farms and did not yet cause widespread industry disruption, though they confirmed establishment of ISAV in South American aquaculture. Surveillance and sporadic control actions were implemented, but the virus persisted at low levels in southern Chilean farming regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of Chile’s salmon industry in the 1990s, high farm density and importation of eggs from Northern Hemisphere sources likely facilitated introduction of ISAV into Chile; limited initial regulation and biosecurity meant early detections did not trigger comprehensive containment. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a North American‑genotype ISAV strain causing jaundice syndrome in coho salmon, with subsequent detection in Atlantic salmon, but with relatively restricted spread and impact during this early phase. The later large‑scale Chilean epidemic (2007–2009) was driven instead by introduction and expansion of a distinct European‑genotype HPR‑deleted lineage, treated as a separate re‑emergent event.
Review: review – This row correctly represents the first establishment of ISAV in South America, based on North American‑genotype virus detected in coho salmon in 1999 and later in Atlantic salmon. It is therefore appropriately coded as inter_continental_emergence for the continent, but not as a global first_detection. The original mechanism text incorrectly implied that a European‑like lineage introduced in the mid‑1990s underlay these early cases; this has been corrected to reflect that the initial Chilean detections involved NA‑genotype ISAV with limited farm‑level impact, while the later 2007–2009 crisis was caused by a separate European‑genotype HPR‑deleted lineage.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: Beginning in June 2007, Chile experienced a massive ISA epidemic centered in the Los Lagos and Aysén regions, which over 2007–2009 led to catastrophic losses and a two‑thirds decline in national Atlantic salmon production. The virus spread rapidly through a highly concentrated network of farms, forcing extensive culling, abandonment of sites and closure of many companies, with major unemployment in salmon‑dependent communities. Emergency regulations, new zone‑management schemes, mandatory fallowing and stricter controls on stocking density and egg imports were progressively introduced, and by around 2010–2011 the epidemic curve declined and production began a slow recovery towards pre‑outbreak levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high farm density and synchronized production cycles in southern Chile, weak initial biosecurity and scant zoning, heavy movement of fish and equipment between sites, and limited government regulation allowed sustained amplification and long‑distance spread; rapid industry expansion and inadequate control of imported eggs have been highlighted as key management and policy failures. Internal mechanisms: A virulent ISAV lineage of European genotype (notably HPR7b) that diverged from Norwegian strains in the mid‑1990s appears to have been introduced into Chile and widely disseminated by about 2005, with HPR‑deleted mutations and other changes associated with enhanced virulence and transmissibility driving a classic re‑emergent epidemic from a previously established, but low‑impact, lineage.
Review: review – This Chilean 2007–2009 epidemic is correctly captured as one of the most impactful ISA events worldwide, with major production losses and socio‑economic impacts. It is not an inter‑continental emergence, because ISAV had already been detected in Chile in 1999, but it does meet the definition of re_emergence: a dramatic resurgence in a previously affected subregion driven by introduction and spread of a virulent European‑genotype HPR‑deleted lineage. Accordingly, re_occurrence has been set to false and re_emergence retained as true. Event‑level sources have been refined to rely on primary Chile‑specific epidemiological studies and contemporary economic reporting rather than general topic pages or non‑authoritative summaries.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2008 – Scotland, Shetland Islands]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: A decade after the first Scottish epidemic, ISA re‑emerged in 2008 in farms in the Shetland Islands and adjacent areas, with several confirmed outbreaks in 2008–2009 despite existing control measures. The disease caused significant local mortalities and prompted rapid depopulation and extended fallowing of infected and neighboring sites under an updated ISA control program. Through aggressive culling, movement restrictions and enhanced surveillance, these re‑emergent Scottish ISA outbreaks were successfully eradicated by the end of 2009.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Residual infection reservoirs in the farming area, farm connectivity through shared service infrastructure, and possibly lapses in full compliance with biosecurity codes facilitated re‑introduction and local spread; Shetland’s clustered farm geography increased infection pressure among neighboring sites. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic investigation point to emergence of virulent HPR‑deleted ISAV from non‑virulent HPR0 sources rather than simple persistence of the original 1998–1999 strain, indicating true re‑emergence via within‑region viral evolution.
Review: review – Shetland’s 2008–2009 outbreak is appropriately included as a distinct major event, given multiple affected farms and notable local economic losses. Consistent with Scottish and EU reporting, it represents a re‑emergence in a subregion previously affected in 1998–1999, driven by evolution of virulent HPR‑deleted virus from HPR0 rather than simple persistence of the original strain; it has therefore been coded as re_emergence only, with re_occurrence set to false to avoid overlapping event‑type labels. The country field has been standardised to the UN country name with Shetland and Scotland retained as location detail.

EPP common name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Countries: Canada [2012 – Nova Scotia]; Canada [2012 – Newfoundland and Labrador]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event summary: In 2012, new ISA outbreaks occurred in eastern Canada, with confirmation at a commercial aquaculture facility in Nova Scotia and the first recorded ISA outbreak in Newfoundland and Labrador, each leading to the destruction of hundreds of thousands of farmed salmon. The virus was contained largely to individual sites or local areas, but depopulation orders, movement controls and surveillance were implemented across affected provinces. These 2012 events marked a significant re‑occurrence of ISA in Atlantic Canada, after earlier Bay of Fundy epidemics, and triggered further tightening of federal–provincial fish‑health regulations and ongoing localized outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued high farm densities in parts of Atlantic Canada, waterborne spread within embayments, and possible wildlife or equipment‑mediated transmission provided pathways for ISA re‑introduction into Nova Scotia and for first establishment in Newfoundland and Labrador; detection was aided by routine surveillance programs. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence is attributed to spread of existing virulent ISAV lineages circulating in the North Atlantic rather than to a clearly identified new genotype; localized outbreaks demonstrate the virus’s capacity to persist in the broader region and re‑invade farms when biosecurity is insufficient.
Review: retain – The 2012 Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador outbreaks are accurately represented as a re‑occurrence of ISA within a long‑affected North Atlantic subregion, with the Newfoundland event also being the first provincial establishment. Event impact (hundreds of thousands of salmon culled and national regulatory response) justifies inclusion among the most important post‑2005 episodes. Country entries have been reformatted so that “Canada” matches the Country sheet, with provincial detail and starting year moved inside brackets.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Cultured marine finfish, especially red sea bream (Pagrus major) and at least 30 other warm‑water marine species in net‑pen aquaculture
Event summary: In 1990, a novel iridoviral disease (later recognized within the ISKNV/RSIV megalocytivirus complex) caused mass mortalities in cultured red sea bream in Shikoku, southwestern Japan, marking the first recognized emergence of this pathogen complex in marine finfish aquaculture. Over the 1990s the virus spread through marine net‑pen farms across western and southern Japan, infecting at least 31 cultured marine fish species across 18 prefectures and causing recurrent seasonal outbreaks with high cumulative mortality and major economic losses. Improved biosecurity, vaccination, and husbandry changes gradually reduced outbreak frequency and severity by around 2000, although the virus became enzootic in Japanese marine aquaculture populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and expansion of marine net‑pen aquaculture in southwestern Japan, high host densities, and seawater temperatures favorable to viral replication promoted initial emergence and farm‑to‑farm spread; extensive movement of juvenile fish and limited early biosecurity facilitated wider dissemination. Internal mechanisms: a megalocytivirus (RSIV/ISKNV complex) with high environmental stability and broad host range caused systemic infection with megalocytic cells in spleen and kidney, enabling efficient amplification and shedding in crowded culture environments.
Review: review – Event is real and clearly one of the globally most impactful ISKNV/RSIV‑complex episodes. Corrected the type classification by setting re_occurrence from true to false so that this row reflects a single linked first‑emergence episode in Japan; re_occurrence should describe later resurging incidence after prior establishment, not the continuation of the initial 1990s epizootic. Geography, time span and sources are appropriate; recommend retaining this event as the global first emergence episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Freshwater mandarin fish (Siniperca chuatsi) and later largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) in pond and cage culture
Event summary: From 1994 onwards, a severe systemic disease with high mortality was recognized in cultured freshwater mandarin fish in southern China, and the causative agent was identified as infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV), representing the first characterization of this genotype in freshwater aquaculture and in this host. During 1994–1998 the virus spread among mandarin fish farms in southern China, and experimental studies showed high susceptibility of mandarin fish and largemouth bass, with typical megalocytic cells in spleen and kidney and substantial production losses. Although improved management and the development of vaccines subsequently reduced catastrophic losses, ISKNV became established in Chinese freshwater culture systems and provided a source for later spillover into additional freshwater species and regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive freshwater mandarin fish culture in southern China with high stocking densities, warm water temperatures, and limited early diagnostics or control allowed extensive undetected spread before the virus was fully characterized; live fish movements among farms enhanced dissemination. Internal mechanisms: host expansion and ecological shift of an ISKNV genotype into freshwater systems, with high virulence and efficient systemic replication in spleen and kidney tissues of mandarin fish and largemouth bass, leading to severe disease in naïve freshwater hosts and supporting subsequent adaptation to additional freshwater fishes.
Review: review – Event corresponds to the well‑documented 1994–1998 ISKNV epizootic in mandarin fish and is among the major global episodes. Adjusted the event years from “1994–1999” to “1994–1998” to match primary reports, changed the country string from “China [1990s]” to “China [1994]”, and reclassified the emergence type: intra_continental_emergence and first_detection were set to false, while re_emergence was set to true to reflect host expansion and genotype emergence within an already affected sub‑region rather than spread into a new UN sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Countries: China [~1998], China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [~1998], Republic of Korea [1998]
Host: Multiple cultured marine finfish species (e.g. red sea bream, groupers, sea bass, rock bream, turbot) in coastal net‑pen aquaculture
Event summary: Following the initial 1990 red sea bream outbreaks in Japan, similar severe iridoviral diseases were reported in the late 1990s and early 2000s in marine food fish in coastal farms in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and the Republic of Korea, where viruses closely related to the ISKNV/RSIV megalocytivirus complex (e.g. sea bass iridovirus, rock bream iridovirus, turbot reddish body iridovirus) were identified. These outbreaks represented major spread and diversification of the ISKNV/RSIV complex across new marine aquaculture industries and hosts within Eastern Asia, with high mortalities and recurring seasonal epizootics in groupers, rock bream, turbot and other species. Over about a decade, improved diagnostics, vaccination for RSIVD, movement controls and husbandry changes reduced the frequency of explosive outbreaks, but ISKNV‑like megalocytiviruses became enzootic across many Eastern Asian marine aquaculture sectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid regional expansion and intensification of marine cage‑culture in coastal waters of China, Hong Kong SAR and Korea, combined with trade in live juveniles and broodstock and limited early biosecurity, facilitated cross‑border dissemination of megalocytiviruses. Internal mechanisms: emergence and diversification of multiple closely related ISKNV‑like genotypes (e.g. RSIV, RBIV, TRBIV, SBIV) with broad host ranges and high virulence represented both novel genotype emergence and geographic range expansion within permissive warm‑water marine environments.
Review: review – This regional episode, aggregating RSIV/ISKNV‑complex outbreaks in China, Hong Kong SAR and Korea, is justified as a high‑impact intra‑regional spread event. Removed Japan from the country list to avoid double‑counting the original Japanese emergence, updated country‑specific years to approximate first detections, and reclassified the event as re_emergence only (intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence set to false) because spread occurred within the already affected UN sub‑region (Eastern Asia) and involved new genotypes and hosts rather than first presence in a new continent or sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Murray cod (Maccullochella peelii) in freshwater aquaculture; imported ornamental dwarf gourami (Trichogaster lalius) as source host
Event summary: In 2003, an outbreak of severe systemic disease with very high mortality occurred in farmed Murray cod in Victoria, Australia, and a megalocytivirus closely related to infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus and dwarf gourami iridovirus was identified as the cause, representing the first confirmed incursion of this virus complex into Australian aquaculture. Epidemiological and molecular evidence linked the Murray cod infections to imported ornamental dwarf gourami carrying the virus, indicating inter‑continental introduction from Asian ornamental fish production systems and onward transmission to a high‑value native food fish. Following recognition of the outbreak, affected Murray cod stocks were culled and Australia progressively tightened biosecurity, quarantine and health certification requirements for imported ornamental fish to prevent further establishment and spread of ISKNV‑like megalocytiviruses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in live ornamental gouramis from Southeast Asia, inadequate pre‑import screening and biosecurity, and the practice of co‑housing or feeding imported ornamental fish to Murray cod broodstock enabled cross‑species and cross‑system transmission; intensifying Murray cod aquaculture created dense, susceptible populations. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of an ISKNV‑like megalocytivirus (dwarf gourami iridovirus lineage) and host expansion from ornamental gouramis to a new high‑value native host (Murray cod), with high virulence demonstrated experimentally and in field outbreaks, facilitated by the virus’s environmental stability and capacity to infect multiple freshwater species.
Review: review – The Murray cod outbreak is well documented and important as the first establishment of an ISKNV‑like megalocytivirus in Oceania and as a major driver of stricter ornamental fish import policy. Narrowed the event period to 2003, when the main farm outbreak occurred, and simplified the emergence classification to inter_continental_emergence only (removing first_detection and re_emergence) to align with definitions that reserve first_detection for the first description in the host system globally and treat this episode primarily as an inter‑continental incursion with local transmission.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Freshwater ornamental fishes (e.g. pearl gourami Trichogaster leeri, silver gourami T. microlepis, dwarf gourami, livebearers, cichlids, tetras, angelfish) in farms and international trade
Event summary: Between about 2005 and 2008, Korea documented multiple outbreaks of disease and detections of infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus in at least 10 species of freshwater ornamental fish hatched locally or imported from other Asian countries, marking the first systematic recognition of ISKNV infection in the ornamental fish trade. Affected gouramis and other ornamentals in Korean facilities showed systemic disease and high cumulative mortality, and experimental infections confirmed high virulence of the ISKNV isolate (originally from pearl gourami) in several gourami species. Surveillance also revealed widespread low‑level infection in asymptomatic ornamental stocks, raising concern that the global ornamental trade was disseminating ISKNV silently across regions and continents.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: globalization and intensification of freshwater ornamental fish production and trade in East and Southeast Asia, high stocking densities in hatcheries and export facilities, mixed‑species holding systems and frequent international movements without routine ISKNV testing facilitated silent spread and periodic high‑mortality outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: broad host range and high virulence of ISKNV in labyrinth and other freshwater ornamental fishes, combined with the ability to produce subclinical infections, allowed the virus to persist in trade networks while intermittently causing explosive disease episodes.
Review: review – The Korean ornamental‑fish episode is well supported by primary literature and is a major emergence in terms of new host range and global dissemination risk. To align with the definitions, the geography was restricted to the location of documented disease (Republic of Korea), and the emergence type was simplified to re_emergence only (removing first_detection, intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence) to reflect host expansion and ecological shift of ISKNV within an already affected sub‑region rather than spread into a new UN sub‑region or continent.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Farmed barramundi/Asian sea bass (Lates calcarifer) in coastal sea‑cage systems in Vietnam and inland freshwater culture systems in Thailand
Event summary: From around 2012, disease outbreaks with high mortality and pathology consistent with megalocytivirus infection were reported in farmed barramundi in Vietnam, and infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus was confirmed as the primary agent in affected farms, where losses substantially impaired production. In subsequent years, closely related ISKNV strains were isolated from diseased barramundi in Thailand, including 2018 outbreaks in inland freshwater culture with cumulative mortalities of roughly 40–50% in some grow‑out populations. These episodes signalled the establishment of ISKNV as a major emerging viral pathogen of barramundi/Asian sea bass in Southeast Asia, prompting calls for improved surveillance and vaccine development for this high‑value species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid regional growth of barramundi aquaculture in Vietnam and Thailand, with intensive sea‑cage and pond systems, high stocking densities, and extensive movement of juveniles between hatcheries and grow‑out sites, created conditions favoring virus amplification and farm‑to‑farm spread; limited early diagnostics for megalocytiviruses delayed targeted response. Internal mechanisms: host expansion and genotype diversification of ISKNV within Southeast Asia, including emergence of both genotype I and genotype II lineages infecting barramundi, supported efficient replication in spleen and kidney and high mortality under commercial farming conditions.
Review: review – This high‑impact barramundi/Asian sea bass episode was missing from the original dataset and has been added as a distinct event because ISKNV outbreaks in Vietnam and Thailand caused substantial mortalities in a major marine finfish commodity and broadened the recognized host and ecological range of the virus. Classified as re_emergence (novel host and genotype emergence within an already affected continent) rather than intra‑/inter‑continental emergence, and aggregated Vietnam [2012] and Thailand [2018] into a single linked Southeast Asian episode as the outbreaks are epidemiologically and virologically related.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and tilapia hybrids in Lake Volta cage culture, with spillover to some native fishes
Event summary: In late 2018, massive mortalities of cage‑cultured tilapia on Lake Volta in Ghana were investigated and infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus was identified as the primary viral agent, representing the first confirmed detection of ISKNV in farmed tilapia in Africa. Over subsequent months and years, the virus spread rapidly among farms on Lake Volta, causing mortality rates of 60–90% in affected cages and daily losses reportedly exceeding 10 tonnes of fish at the height of outbreaks, with co‑infections by Streptococcus agalactiae and other bacteria further exacerbating losses. By 2023, genomic surveillance of water and fish showed that ISKNV had become established in Lake Volta, and while improved biosecurity and management reduced acute mortality on some farms, recurrent outbreaks and significant economic impacts persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of tilapia cage aquaculture on Lake Volta with very high stocking densities, extensive movement of fingerlings from a limited number of hatcheries, limited early biosecurity and disease diagnostics, and likely introduction of the virus via imported broodstock or fry promoted explosive spread once ISKNV entered the system. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a highly virulent ISKNV strain capable of efficient transmission in warm tropical freshwater and high replication in spleen and kidney of tilapia, combined with frequent co‑infections that may enhance disease severity, facilitated large‑scale geographic range expansion of the virus to a new continent and sustained, high‑impact epidemics.
Review: review – The Ghana Lake Volta epidemic is one of the most impactful ISKNV events globally and should be retained. Corrected the emergence classification by setting re_occurrence and re_emergence to false, leaving inter_continental_emergence as the primary type, because this episode represents the first confirmed establishment of ISKNV in Africa rather than a resurgence in a previously affected African sub‑region or evidence of viral change driving re‑emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Farmed giant gourami (Osphronemus goramy) in freshwater ponds
Event summary: Around 2019–2020, large‑scale mortality events were reported in farmed giant gourami in India, and infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus infection was confirmed by molecular diagnostics and histopathology, marking the first documented ISKNV‑associated disease outbreaks in this species and region. Affected farms experienced severe systemic disease and high cumulative mortality, and experimental challenge studies showed approximately 60% mortality in giant gourami injected with ISKNV‑positive homogenates, confirming high virulence in this host. Control efforts focused on improved on‑farm biosecurity, culling of affected stocks and awareness among farmers, which reduced further explosive outbreaks but did not eliminate ISKNV circulation in gourami culture areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of giant gourami pond culture in parts of India with high stocking densities and limited historic surveillance for megalocytiviruses created a receptive environment; regional movement of gourami seed and possible introduction from ornamental or food‑fish trade likely facilitated virus entry. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of ISKNV into a large‑bodied food‑fish gourami, with efficient systemic replication in spleen and kidney and high virulence demonstrated experimentally, allowed rapid amplification and severe disease once introduced into naïve farm populations.
Review: review – This event is supported by primary reports of ISKNV‑associated large‑scale mortality in farmed giant gourami in India and represents a notable host expansion in South Asia. To match the event‑type definitions, intra_continental_emergence and first_detection were set to false (the Southern Asia sub‑region was already affected by megalocytiviruses), and re_emergence was retained to capture emergence in a new major host within an existing endemic sub‑region.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in reservoir and pond aquaculture, with spillover to some native free‑living fishes
Event summary: In June 2020, outbreaks of severe disease and high mortality were reported in farmed Nile tilapia in Brazil, and virions were confirmed as infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus by PCR, sequencing and electron microscopy, representing the first report of ISKNV in farmed tilapia in South America. Subsequent investigations documented ISKNV infection in tilapia on multiple farms and demonstrated spillover to native free‑living fish species in affected water bodies, indicating environmental establishment of the virus beyond farmed stocks. Control measures, including heightened biosecurity, stock management changes and surveillance, have reduced but not eliminated outbreaks, and ISKNV is now recognized as an important emerging pathogen in Brazilian tilapia aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of tilapia aquaculture in Brazil, high fish densities in reservoirs and ponds, and movements of live fish and eggs (including possible introduction of infected broodstock or fry from other regions) likely facilitated introduction and spread of ISKNV; inadequate early surveillance delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a virulent ISKNV strain capable of efficient replication and shedding in tilapia, combined with ecological adaptability allowing survival and transmission in South American freshwater ecosystems, enabled both farm‑level epidemics and spillover into native fish communities (host and geographic range expansion).
Review: review – The Brazilian tilapia outbreaks are clearly a major inter‑continental emergence event and should be retained. Corrected the event period and country annotation to start in 2020 (the first documented outbreak) rather than 2018, and simplified the emergence classification to inter_continental_emergence only, setting re_occurrence and re_emergence to false to reflect that this was the first confirmed establishment of ISKNV in South America rather than a resurgence in a previously affected South American sub‑region.

EPP scientific name: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus
Host: Food‑fish gouramis, especially snakeskin gourami (Trichopodus pectoralis) and sympatric three‑spot gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus) in pond culture
Event summary: In 2022, severe disease outbreaks with skin haemorrhage, scale loss, visceral organ degeneration and high mortality were reported in farmed snakeskin gourami and co‑reared three‑spot gourami in Thailand, and natural infection with infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus was confirmed by molecular and histopathological analyses. These outbreaks caused cumulative mortalities exceeding 60% in affected ponds, demonstrating that ISKNV can cause high‑impact disease in gouramis farmed primarily as food fish in Southeast Asia. Following recognition of the etiologic agent, farmers and authorities implemented improved biosecurity and husbandry measures, which reduced outbreak frequency at some sites, but ISKNV remains a recognized threat in regional gourami aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing commercialization and intensification of gourami pond culture in Thailand, high fish densities, and water quality stress created conditions conducive to virus transmission; use of shared earthen ponds and fry sources likely contributed to spread between ponds and farms. Internal mechanisms: expansion of ISKNV host range into new Trichopodus food‑fish species, with high tissue tropism for spleen and kidney and high virulence at warm tropical pond temperatures, allowed the virus to establish and cause major production losses in a previously minor host group within an already endemic region.

Updated the event year to 2022, clarified that this is a recent host‑expansion event within Southeast Asia, and replaced secondary sources (Wikipedia, HandWiki, generic aggregators) with the primary Journal of Fish Diseases article. Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [1997]
Host: Domestic chickens and other domestic poultry (ducks, geese, quail)
Event summary: In 1997, a highly pathogenic H5N1 lineage of goose/Guangdong origin spread through poultry farms and live bird markets in Hong Kong, culminating in territory-wide infection of domestic chickens and other poultry. The epizootic intensified through late 1997, coinciding with the first recognized human H5N1 cases and leading authorities to order territory-wide depopulation of all live poultry. The outbreak was brought under control when approximately 1.3–1.5 million birds were slaughtered over several days, combined with market disinfection and tighter poultry import and farm biosecurity controls.([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/isd/news/dec97/kill-chi.htm?utm_source=openai))

Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence of H5N1 goose/Guangdong lineage with high virulence in chickens and capacity for zoonotic infection; enhanced transmission in crowded live bird market environments.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2004_01_24-en?utm_source=openai))

Host: Commercial turkeys, broilers, layers and other domestic poultry
Event summary: Around 1999, low-pathogenic H7N1 avian influenza circulating in Italian poultry evolved into a highly pathogenic form and caused large outbreaks in the country’s intensive poultry sector. Over 1999–2001 the epidemic spread widely across northern and central Italy, affecting numerous commercial farms and requiring massive depopulation campaigns. EPP common name: HPAI H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b, high pathogenicity avian influenza in cattle)
Countries: United States of America [late 2023–Texas/Kansas/New Mexico; 2024–multiple states across the central, western and southern U.S.]
Host: Primary: dairy cattle (Bos taurus); secondary spillover on affected farms to domestic cats and wild birds, with sporadic human infections in exposed farm workers
Event summary: In late 2023, a reassortant HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype (B3.13) circulating in wild birds in North America spilled over into U.S. dairy cattle, with retrospective analyses placing the cattle virus ancestor in this period and the first recognized clinical illness appearing in older lactating cows in Texas, Kansas and New Mexico in early 2024.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07849-4?utm_source=openai)) On March 25, 2024, HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b was first confirmed in a Texas dairy cow, and over 2024–2025 the virus spread efficiently within and between dairy herds via contaminated milking equipment, animal movements and shared infrastructure, ultimately infecting hundreds of herds in at least 17–18 states and causing marked drops in milk yield, severe mastitis and economic losses, alongside multiple infections in farm cats and at least two confirmed human cases linked to infected cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11210653/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak was gradually brought under partial control by federal orders restricting interstate movement of lactating cattle, enhanced bulk-tank milk surveillance, herd quarantines, and on‑farm biosecurity improvements, though sporadic new detections continued into 2025.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density, inter-connected commercial dairy systems with frequent live-animal movements facilitated rapid lateral spread once the virus entered cattle; contaminated milking parlors and equipment enabled repeated udder exposure to virus-laden milk; and co-circulation of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in wild birds and poultry in the same regions increased opportunities for initial spillover and occasional spillback.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07849-4?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from birds to cattle with adaptation to replicate to high titers in mammary tissue and be shed in raw milk; enhanced transmission via the intramammary route during machine milking; emergence of a distinct bovine-associated genotype (B3.13) within clade 2.3.4.4b; and molecular changes that broadened receptor binding breadth while maintaining avian-type receptor preference, potentially facilitating efficient infection of bovine mammary epithelium without widespread systemic disease.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08063-y?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: In 1998, severe respiratory disease outbreaks occurred in multiple US swine herds, and virological investigation identified novel H3N2 triple‑reassortant swine influenza A viruses containing gene segments from human, avian and classical swine lineages. Over 1998–2000 these triple‑reassortant H3N2 viruses rapidly spread across major US pig‑producing regions, displacing classical H1N1 as the dominant cause of swine influenza and generating associated H1N2 and reassortant H1N1 variants. By 2000, the novel H3N2 reassortants were widely established in US swine, fundamentally changing the genetic landscape of swine influenza there.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑density, year‑round intensive pig production in the US Midwest, frequent animal movements, and close contact with humans and birds in production systems facilitated co‑infection and reassortment. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (triple‑reassortant H3N2 with human, avian and swine genes), Enhanced Transmission/Adaptation in swine (efficient pig‑to‑pig spread), and rapid Geographic Range Expansion within US herds once established.
Review: retain – Correctly captures the well-documented 1998 emergence and rapid spread of triple‑reassortant H3N2 swine influenza in US pigs; geography, timing and classification as a re‑emergence event in a previously affected subregion are appropriate.

By about 2005, North American swine populations harboured a complex co‑circulating assemblage of H1N1, H1N2 and H3N2 reassortants derived from the 1998 triple‑reassortant backbone.

Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense human H1N1pdm09 activity with close contact between infected workers and pigs, large integrated pig industries in Canada, the United States and Mexico, and frequent long‑distance movement and commingling of pigs at markets and fairs. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from humans back into pigs, Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence through reassortment of H1N1pdm09 with classical and triple‑reassortant swine viruses, Enhanced Transmission associated with the pandemic M gene and other internal segments, and greatly increased antigenic and genetic diversity of swine influenza in the region.
Review: retain – Added as a missing major event: repeated reverse‑zoonotic introduction and establishment of H1N1pdm09 in North American pigs, with multiple reassortant genotypes, is clearly among the most consequential recent SIV emergence episodes; classified as re‑emergence (new strain in a long‑affected subregion) rather than inter‑continental emergence.

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: In 2009, the novel H1N1pdm09 virus that caused the human 2009 influenza pandemic was introduced into Chinese pig herds, with infections detected in multiple central and eastern provinces during August 2009–April 2010. From 2009–2012, intensive surveillance in Chinese pigs showed rapid establishment of H1N1pdm09‑derived viruses and extensive reassortment with endemic Eurasian avian‑like H1N1 and North American triple‑reassortant lineages, producing numerous distinct reassortant genotypes carrying pandemic‑origin internal genes. By around 2012, H1N1pdm09‑origin internal genes had become entrenched in many Chinese swine influenza viruses, increasing viral diversity and zoonotic potential.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: massive concurrent human pandemic with frequent human‑to‑swine transmission, high‑density pig farming and movement networks within China, and limited prior immunity to H1N1pdm09 in pigs. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (H1N1pdm09 and multiple reassortant genotypes with pandemic internal genes), Host Expansion (Spillover) from humans back into pigs, Enhanced Transmission in pigs through adaptation of pandemic‑origin internal genes, and Geographic Range Expansion of the new lineages across Chinese production regions.
Review: review – Retain as a major event, but intra‑continental emergence has been set to No because H1N1pdm09 represents a new strain of an already present pathogen in East Asia; classification as re‑emergence (strain‑level change with major epidemiologic impact) is appropriate, and the subregion label is simplified to the UNSD term Eastern Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Sub-regions: Southern Europe, Western Europe, Northern Europe, Eastern Europe
Countries: Italy [2009], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010], France [2010], Germany [2010], Spain [2010], Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2010], Denmark [2010], Poland [2011], Sweden [2011], other European Union Member States [2010-2013]
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: Soon after its emergence in humans in 2009, H1N1pdm09 virus infected European pigs, with the first documented outbreak on a swine breeder farm in Italy in November 2009 followed by detection in pig herds in the United Kingdom and other EU countries during 2010. From 2009–2013, surveillance across Europe revealed that H1N1pdm09 became established in swine populations and reassorted with endemic European avian‑like H1N1, human‑like H3N2 and H1N2 viruses, increasing the number of co‑circulating lineages and viral genotypes. By 2013, pandemic‑origin genes formed a stable component of the European swine influenza gene pool, and multiple reassortant viruses of concern for human health were identified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high incidence of pandemic H1N1 in humans with frequent human‑to‑swine spillover, dense commercial pig sectors in EU Member States, and intra‑EU pig trade enabling rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (H1N1pdm09 lineage in pigs plus many reassortants with European swine viruses), Host Expansion (Spillover) from humans to pigs, Enhanced Transmission in swine following adaptation, and expansion of antigenic diversity contributing to re‑emergence of swine influenza in previously affected subregions.
Review: review – Event is well supported and clearly among the largest recent SIV emergence episodes, but under the project definitions the arrival of H1N1pdm09 in European pigs is a strain‑level change of an established pathogen; intra‑continental emergence is therefore set to No and the event is classified as re‑emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: After the 2009 human pandemic, H1N1pdm09 virus was repeatedly introduced from humans into South American swine herds. In Brazil, the first documented farm outbreaks of acute respiratory disease in pigs were reported from 2010 onward in southern states, including Santa Catarina, and phylodynamic analyses of viruses collected from Brazilian pigs during 2009–2012 showed rapid human‑to‑swine transmission, widespread establishment of H1N1pdm09 in multiple states, and further reassortment with pre‑existing human‑origin H1N2/H3N2 lineages that had circulated undetected in Brazilian pigs for over a decade. In Argentina, H1N1pdm09 was detected in large commercial pig farms from mid‑2009, and reassortant viruses combining pandemic and endemic swine gene segments were soon described, indicating rapid regional integration of the pandemic lineage into South American swine influenza ecologies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intense human H1N1pdm09 transmission with close contact between farm staff and pigs, growth of industrial pig sectors in Brazil and neighbouring countries, and historically limited systematic surveillance that allowed long, unnoticed circulation of human‑origin strains in swine. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (H1N1pdm09 in South American pigs and multiple reassortants with older human‑origin H1N2/H3N2 and classical swine viruses), Host Expansion (Spillover) from humans to pigs, Enhanced Transmission in dense herds, and Geographic Range Expansion of pandemic‑origin genes within South American pig populations.
Review: review – Retain as a major event because H1N1pdm09 became widely established and reassorted in South American pigs, but intra‑continental emergence is set to No (new strain of an existing pathogen), and the country list is trimmed to Brazil and Argentina where swine outbreaks and reassortants are clearly documented; spread to other South American producers is left implicit in the summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Countries: Australia [2009] (New South Wales [2009], Queensland [2009-2010], Victoria [2010], Western Australia [2010-2011])
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: In July 2009, a 300‑sow farrow‑to‑finish herd in New South Wales experienced an outbreak of acute respiratory disease, and testing confirmed infection with the pandemic H1N1 2009 virus (H1N1pdm09), representing the first recorded detection of influenza A virus infection in Australian pigs. Over 2009–2011, further reverse‑zoonotic introductions of H1N1pdm09 from humans into pigs were detected on commercial farms in Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia, and the virus spread within affected herds. These events established influenza A as a new endemic respiratory pathogen of pigs in Australia and marked the first documented occurrence of swine influenza viruses in Oceania’s commercial pig sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of H1N1pdm09 into an immunologically naive national pig herd via infected farm staff during the human pandemic, absence of prior swine influenza experience in Australia, and close contact between workers and pigs on affected farms. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from humans to pigs, Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence in a new continental pig population, and subsequent limited reassortment of H1N1pdm09 with human‑origin influenza lineages already known in the region.
Review: retain – Added as a missing key event: the 2009–2011 introduction of H1N1pdm09 into Australian pigs constitutes both the first detection of influenza A in Australian swine and an inter‑continental emergence of swine influenza viruses into Oceania; classification is therefore first detection and inter‑continental emergence, without re‑emergence.

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Host: Domestic pigs; occasional human infections among swine workers
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2018, large‑scale surveillance of pigs at slaughterhouses and veterinary hospitals across ten Chinese provinces identified a recently emerged genotype 4 (G4) Eurasian avian‑like H1N1 swine influenza virus bearing internal genes from H1N1pdm09 and triple‑reassortant lineages. G4 Eurasian avian‑like H1N1 viruses increased in frequency and, by around 2016, became the predominant swine influenza genotype in many Chinese pig farms, where they caused severe respiratory disease and high morbidity and showed serological evidence of frequent infection in swine workers. The lineage persisted endemically through at least 2018, and subsequent reports of sporadic human infections indicated ongoing re‑emergence risk and zoonotic potential rather than clear termination.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of China’s pig industry, high levels of co‑circulation of multiple influenza subtypes in pigs, and limited availability of strain‑matched vaccines allowed the new genotype to out‑compete others. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (G4 Eurasian avian‑like H1N1 with pandemic and triple‑reassortant internal genes), Host Expansion (Spillover) with demonstrated human seropositivity and several confirmed human infections, Enhanced Transmission and adaptation in pigs (dominance of G4 in herds), and Geographic Range Expansion of this genotype across multiple Chinese provinces.
Review: review – This is correctly identified as one of the most important recent re‑emergence events for swine influenza (G4 Eurasian avian‑like H1N1 becoming predominant in Chinese pigs), with appropriate classification as re‑emergence; however, newer data show that G4 viruses continue to circulate beyond 2018, and users may wish to extend the end year or explicitly link this national‑scale episode with the Guangxi 2018–2023 surveillance described in a separate (recommended-for-exclusion) row.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Sub-regions: Northern Africa, Western Africa, Eastern Africa
Host: Domestic pigs
Event summary: From about 2010 onward, surveillance studies began to document influenza A virus infections in African pigs, including detection of pandemic H1N1pdm09 in pigs in Cameroon and on Réunion Island, virological and serological evidence of infection with avian H5/H9 and human/swine H1N1 viruses in pigs around Cairo, Egypt, and later detection of H1N1pdm09 and other influenza A viruses in Nigerian and Kenyan pigs. These findings indicated that pandemic H1N1/2009 and other swine influenza lineages had been introduced into African pig populations and were circulating with limited clinical recognition in both backyard and commercial systems. By the late 2010s, OFFLU and other networks reported established, though still poorly quantified, circulation of influenza A viruses in pigs in several African countries, highlighting Africa as an emerging region for swine influenza evolution and zoonotic risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: under‑resourced veterinary surveillance, rapid growth of smallholder and peri‑urban pig sectors, frequent close contact between pigs, poultry and humans, and informal live‑animal trade created opportunities for cross‑species transmission and silent spread. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of human pandemic H1N1pdm09 and avian H5/H9 viruses into pigs, Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence through reassortment in a new ecological context, and Geographic Range Expansion of swine influenza viruses into African pig populations where they had previously been little documented.
Review: review – Retain as a continental‑scale re‑emergence episode summarising the delayed but important establishment of influenza A viruses in African pigs after 2009; intra‑continental emergence is set to No because swine influenza was already reported in parts of Africa before 1990, and the countries list is expanded to include well-documented detections (Cameroon, Réunion) while recognising that additional countries have evidence only from sparse surveys.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: China [1992]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [1997]
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers), quail and other domestic poultry species in southern and eastern China live poultry markets; predominantly H9N2 LPAI viruses (BJ94-, G1- and G9-like genotypes).
Event summary: In 1992, low pathogenic H9N2 avian influenza viruses were first isolated from chickens in Guangdong Province, southern China, signalling the emergence of a new poultry-adapted lineage in East Asia. Through the mid-1990s, related BJ94-, G1- and G9-like H9N2 genotypes became established in chickens and quail in live poultry markets in southern China and Hong Kong, and by 1998–1999 H9N2 viruses accounted for the great majority of influenza isolates from Chinese chickens as the subtype spread to most provinces. As the virus became endemic, large-scale vaccination programmes and market interventions were introduced around 1999–2000, reducing explosive outbreaks but not eliminating circulation, and H9N2 has since remained the dominant low-pathogenic influenza subtype in Chinese poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of China’s poultry industry, dense networks of live poultry markets where birds from many farms and species were commingled, and long-distance movement of live birds allowed H9N2 viruses introduced in the early 1990s to spread quickly across eastern and southern China and persist at high prevalence in chickens and minor poultry. Internal mechanisms: evolution of poultry-adapted BJ94-, G1- and G9-like H9N2 genotypes with HA and NA changes that enhanced replication and transmission in chickens, broadened host range to multiple domestic species, and enabled the viruses to donate internal genes to other zoonotic lineages such as H5N1 and H7N9, exemplifying re-emergence driven by viral adaptation rather than simple geographic spread.
Review: Retain (added new event). This large-scale emergence of H9N2 LPAI in Chinese poultry in the 1990s is very well documented and clearly among the most impactful LPAI episodes globally, with H9N2 becoming the predominant influenza subtype in Chinese chickens and a major gene donor for later zoonotic strains.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/proteincell/article/6/1/18/6803253)) It was missing from the original dataset and has been added as a re-emergence event (new poultry-adapted genotypes in a region where LPAI already circulated).

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Primarily intensively reared turkeys and chickens in high-density poultry areas of northern Italy (Veneto, Lombardia); LPAI H7N1 also detected in other domestic birds (guinea fowl, quail, pheasants, ducks, ostriches).
Event summary: In late March 1999, low pathogenic H7N1 avian influenza virus was detected in turkeys and chickens in the densely populated poultry regions of northern Italy, marking the start of a large LPAI epidemic that spread through commercial flocks. Over 1999–2000 the virus caused hundreds of outbreaks and, after several months of circulation, mutated to a highly pathogenic H7N1 variant that led to mass mortality in turkeys and chickens and the culling or death of over 13–16 million birds. Intensive stamping‑out, movement controls and depopulation in affected areas progressively eliminated the epidemic lineage, and by 2001 surveillance showed only sporadic detections and eventual disappearance after major changes in industry biosecurity and vaccination policies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high poultry density and intensive turkey and chicken production in the Po Valley, together with extensive movements of live birds and shared equipment between farms and slaughterhouses and limited early surveillance, facilitated rapid spread of LPAI H7N1 before strict control measures were implemented. Internal mechanisms: emergence and evolution of a novel H7N1 lineage within Italian poultry, including stepwise genetic changes in the HA cleavage site that increased virulence and converted an initially low-pathogenic virus into a highly pathogenic form, making this a classic example of re-emergence driven by viral evolution in a densely populated poultry system.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12062787/))
Review: Retain. The Italian 1999–2001 H7N1 epidemic is correctly captured as a major LPAI episode that evolved into HPAI, with appropriate geography (Italy/Southern Europe) and host description. Classification as re-emergence (due to mutation of an LPAI virus to HPAI in a region where avian influenza was already known) is consistent with project definitions and supported by detailed outbreak analyses.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12062787/))

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: Saudi Arabia [1998]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [1998]; United Arab Emirates [1999]; Israel [2000]; Jordan [2003]
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens (broilers, layers, breeders), turkeys and quail; primarily G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses.
Event summary: Around 1998, H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza viruses were first detected in chickens in Saudi Arabia and Iran, marking the introduction and establishment of G1-lineage H9N2 into poultry flocks in the Middle East. Over the late 1990s and early 2000s, related H9N2 viruses became enzootic in commercial and backyard poultry in Gulf and Levant countries including the United Arab Emirates, Israel and Jordan, causing repeated respiratory disease outbreaks, drops in egg production and increased mortality in the presence of co-infections.
