By the mid-2000s, vaccination programmes were widely adopted but H9N2 remained endemic across much of Western Asia, with distinct regional genetic lineages established in different countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of poultry production in the Middle East, high volumes of regional and international trade in live birds and hatching eggs from Asia, and suboptimal farm and market biosecurity allowed G1-lineage H9N2 introduced from southern China to spread and become endemic across multiple Middle Eastern countries. Internal mechanisms: emergence and regional diversification of poultry-adapted G1-lineage H9N2 genotypes with molecular markers of mammalian adaptation and efficient replication in chickens, representing re-emergence of LPAI in the region through introduction and evolution of a new lineage rather than simple spread of existing local LPAI strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9148743/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Iran was previously listed under Western Asia only, which conflicts with the UNSD classification (Southern Asia); sub_regions has been updated to "Western Asia; Southern Asia" and the countries field now lists specific countries with documented first H9N2 detections and approximate start years (Saudi Arabia, Iran, UAE, Israel, Jordan) instead of a vague "other Gulf and Levant countries".([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9148743/)) The event is reclassified as re-emergence only: per project rules, spread of a new H9N2 lineage within Asia into regions where LPAI was already present should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. First_detection remains No because H9N2 and LPAI influenza A were detected in poultry well before 1998 in other continents.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Commercial broiler, layer and breeder chickens and backyard poultry throughout Pakistan; G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses (particularly genotype A5) becoming the dominant avian influenza subtype.
Event summary: In 1998, low pathogenic H9N2 avian influenza was first reported in commercial chickens in Pakistan, introducing a new LPAI subtype into a rapidly expanding poultry industry already affected by other avian influenza subtypes. Through the early 2000s, H9N2 spread widely in broiler and layer flocks, causing recurrent respiratory disease outbreaks and substantial mortality and egg-production losses, with major epidemics reported in densely populated poultry areas such as Karachi and Punjab. By the mid-2000s and into the 2010s, H9N2 had become hyper-endemic in Pakistani poultry, prompting widespread vaccination and control efforts, yet the virus continued to circulate and occasionally infected humans, illustrating a long-running re-emergence driven by an established poultry-adapted lineage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Densely concentrated commercial poultry production near major urban centres, frequent movements of birds and eggs between farms and live bird markets, inadequate farm-level biosecurity, and co-infections with other respiratory pathogens fostered rapid establishment and persistence of H9N2 across Pakistan. Internal mechanisms: introduction and subsequent evolution of G1-lineage H9N2 viruses, with genotype A5 and related variants becoming dominant, acquiring gene segments through reassortment and mutations associated with mammalian receptor binding and efficient replication in chickens, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogen change in a region where LPAI was already present.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/world-s-poultry-science-journal/article/abs/emerging-threat-of-h9n2-viruses-in-poultry-of-pakistan-and-vaccination-strategy/FC522C91F1147508165198500E4E2D6C))
Review: Retain (added new event). Pakistan’s long-running H9N2 LPAI epizootic, beginning in 1998 and now endemic with large documented economic losses and occasional human infections, is widely recognised as one of the most important H9N2 foci globally and was missing from the original dataset.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/world-s-poultry-science-journal/article/abs/emerging-threat-of-h9n2-viruses-in-poultry-of-pakistan-and-vaccination-strategy/FC522C91F1147508165198500E4E2D6C)) It is therefore added as a major re-emergence event in Southern Asia.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: United States of America [2002] (Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina)
Host: Commercial turkeys and chickens (broilers and layers) in the Shenandoah Valley and adjacent regions; LPAI H7N2 subtype.
Event summary: In March 2002, an outbreak of low pathogenic H7N2 avian influenza was detected among commercial turkey and chicken operations in Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley, signalling a major regional epizootic rather than sporadic LPAI detections. Over roughly four months, the virus spread to nearly 200 affected flocks in Virginia, West Virginia and North Carolina, prompting large-scale depopulation, movement controls and intensive surveillance. By mid-2002, stamping‑out of about 4.7 million birds, carcass disposal, disinfection, and surveillance activities brought the outbreak under control, and virus circulation was no longer detected in commercial operations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High poultry density in the Shenandoah Valley, frequent movement of live birds and shared equipment between premises, and delayed initial detection allowed extensive farm-to-farm spread before full control measures were implemented; logistical challenges with rapid depopulation and carcass disposal further complicated the response. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel genotype was implicated; the episode represents a major re-occurrence and amplification of an H7N2 lineage already circulating in the eastern United States, driven more by management and trade networks than by marked viral change.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063870701900401))
Review: Retain. The 2002 Shenandoah Valley H7N2 LPAI outbreak is correctly described as a large regional re-occurrence of an existing lineage with ~4.7 million birds depopulated and nearly 200 infected premises, and the geography (USA/Northern America) matches the UNSD scheme.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063870701900401)) Classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental spread) aligns with project definitions.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: Bangladesh [2006]; spread within subsequent years across multiple districts and production systems.
Host: Primarily chickens (commercial broilers, layers, breeders and backyard flocks), with detections also in live bird markets; LPAI H9N2 viruses related to G1-lineage strains.
Event summary: In 2006, H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza was first detected in domestic poultry in Bangladesh, marking the introduction of this subtype into a densely populated poultry system in Southern Asia. Over the following years, H9N2 spread widely through commercial and backyard flocks and became endemic, with repeated respiratory disease outbreaks and production losses, especially in broiler and layer chickens and in urban live bird markets. By the early 2010s, phylogenetic analyses showed a relatively homogeneous endemic H9N2 genotype of Pakistani and Middle Eastern origin circulating throughout Bangladesh, prompting intensified surveillance and control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of Bangladesh’s poultry sector, high bird densities, poor biosecurity in backyard flocks and live bird markets, and extensive live-bird movement within the country facilitated establishment and onward spread of the introduced H9N2 lineage. Internal mechanisms: introduction and subsequent local evolution of a G1-lineage H9N2 genotype carrying multiple gene segments from Pakistani H7N3 and other H9N2 viruses, with molecular markers associated with mammalian adaptation and efficient replication in chickens, underpinning re-emergence as a dominant endemic LPAI subtype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12123974/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Evidence confirms first detection of H9N2 in Bangladeshi poultry in 2006 and subsequent endemic circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12123974/)) However, per the event-type definitions, this episode should not be coded as "first_detection" (LPAI and H9N2 were already known globally) nor as intra-continental emergence (Bangladesh is in the same UNSD subregion as Pakistan, where H9N2 had circulated since 1998). The event is now coded solely as re-emergence driven by introduction and evolution of a new lineage in an already affected subregion.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens, turkeys and quail in Egypt; LPAI H9N2 co-circulating with endemic HPAI H5N1 in poultry.
Event summary: In early 2010, active surveillance in Egyptian poultry first identified H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza in broiler chickens in northern Egypt, and soon afterwards in turkeys and quail, indicating introduction of this subtype into North African poultry. During 2011–2013 the virus spread widely and became enzootic in commercial and backyard flocks, often detected alongside endemic H5N1, and was associated with respiratory disease, reduced egg production and substantial economic losses. Following this initial explosive spread, H9N2 became entrenched and diversified into several closely related clusters in Egypt, with routine detection in surveillance and concern about reassortment with H5 and other avian influenza viruses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely importation of infected birds or hatching eggs from neighbouring Middle Eastern countries where H9N2 is endemic, dense mixed-species poultry production with limited biosecurity, and co-circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens facilitated establishment and spread; live bird markets and backyard flocks provided additional maintenance reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: introduction of G1-like H9N2 viruses that subsequently diversified within Egypt, with genetic markers for mammalian adaptation and reassortment with wild-bird-origin gene segments, representing a clear re-emergence of LPAI driven by viral adaptation in a new ecological and geographic setting.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6383604/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Multiple sources agree that G1-lineage H9N2 was first detected in Egyptian poultry in 2010, with rapid diversification and endemic establishment thereafter.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6383604/)) In the original row this episode was incorrectly coded as both "first_detection" and "inter-continental emergence"; LPAI (and H9N2) were already well documented globally and in other African countries (e.g. Libya 2006, Tunisia 2010–2012), so under the project rules it should be treated as a re-emergence event within Africa rather than a first or inter-continental emergence.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: China [2013] (initially Shanghai and neighbouring eastern provinces, then multiple eastern and southern provinces over successive waves).
Host: Primarily chickens (especially in live poultry markets), also other domestic poultry species; H7N9 LPAI virus in birds, with later emergence of H7N9 HPAI in poultry.
Event summary: In March 2013, China reported the first human infections with a novel H7N9 avian influenza virus, and within days low pathogenic H7N9 was detected in chickens and environmental samples from live poultry markets in Shanghai and nearby provinces, revealing widespread silent circulation in poultry. Over multiple epidemic waves from 2013 to about 2017, H7N9 LPAI circulated in poultry across many eastern Chinese provinces, driving major live poultry market closures, mass culling and restructuring of the live poultry supply chain, and later gave rise to highly pathogenic H7N9 variants in poultry. After aggressive interventions including large-scale vaccination of poultry and permanent or prolonged closure of many live bird markets, reported H7N9 detections in poultry and humans declined sharply by the late 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive live poultry market networks in eastern China, mixing of birds from many sources, high human–poultry contact, and complex poultry value chains allowed a newly reassorted H7N9 LPAI virus to spread widely before detection; subsequent control relied on large-scale market closures, culling and changes in marketing practices. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel reassortant H7N9 virus derived from multiple avian influenza lineages, exhibiting efficient replication in chickens with minimal clinical signs, enhanced zoonotic potential, and later mutations that converted some lineages to HPAI, which together constitute a major re-emergence event driven by viral evolution and enhanced transmission in an existing LPAI ecosystem.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6652192/))
Review: Retain with corrections. The description of timing, geography, and control measures for the H7N9 LPAI/HPAI episode in China is accurate and well sourced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6652192/)) However, the event was originally coded as "first_detection" and "intra-continental emergence"; because H7N9 viruses existed before 2013 and LPAI influenza A was long established in East Asia, the 2013 episode is better classified as re-emergence of a novel reassortant lineage rather than as global first detection or intra-continental emergence.

EPP common name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: Burkina Faso [2017]; Ghana [2017]; Benin [2017]; Togo [2017]; Nigeria [2019]; Senegal [2019]
Host: Backyard and small-scale commercial chickens (layers and broilers) and other domestic poultry in West Africa; G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses, with reports of increased pathogenicity in some flocks.
Event summary: In 2017, G1-lineage H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza virus was first reported in poultry in Burkina Faso and soon afterwards in Ghana, signalling spread of this lineage from North Africa and the Middle East into West African poultry populations. Over the subsequent years, H9N2 detections became more frequent in backyard and commercial poultry in Ghana, Benin, Togo, Nigeria and Senegal, with outbreaks associated with respiratory disease, production drops and occasional higher mortality in some flocks. Control efforts including culling, movement restrictions and heightened surveillance were implemented during outbreaks, but H9N2 has continued to circulate at low to moderate levels in West African poultry, and more recently human H9N2 infections have been reported in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of H9N2 via regional poultry trade and informal movements of live birds and hatching eggs from North Africa and the Middle East, combined with widespread backyard farming and open live bird markets with low biosecurity, promoted establishment and spread of the virus in West Africa. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a G1-lineage H9N2 genotype closely related to viruses from Morocco and the United Arab Emirates, followed by local diversification and adaptation to chickens, with molecular markers favouring mammalian receptor binding; the appearance of a human H9N2 infection in Ghana and later in Senegal underscores re-emergence driven by viral adaptation and geographic range expansion within Africa.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/50213/cdc_50213_DS1.pdf))
Review: Retain with corrections. West African H9N2 emergence is a major geographic expansion of the G1 lineage and is well documented beginning with Burkina Faso in 2017 and subsequent detections in Ghana, Benin, Togo, Nigeria and Senegal.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/50213/cdc_50213_DS1.pdf)) The original row mentioned only Ghana and treated the event as "first_detection" and "intra-continental emergence"; the countries field has been expanded to include other affected West African states with approximate first-detection years, and, following the project rules for new serotypes in regions where LPAI is already established, the event is now coded purely as re-emergence rather than first or intra-continental emergence.

Countries: China [~1993]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2001]; Thailand [2001]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: From the early 1990s, surveillance in southern and eastern China identified avian-origin H1N1 influenza A viruses in pigs that clustered phylogenetically with the Eurasian avian-like swine H1N1 lineage, indicating independent introductions of avian H1N1 into Asian pig populations. Over the 1990s and early 2000s, these Eurasian avian-like H1N1 (EA H1N1) viruses spread within Chinese pig herds and were detected in pigs in Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and Thailand by around 2001, co-circulating with classical swine H1N1 and human-like H3N2 and gradually increasing in prevalence. By roughly 2005, EA H1N1 had largely replaced classical H1N1 as the dominant H1 lineage in many Chinese pig populations, establishing an endemic reservoir that subsequently reassorted with triple-reassortant and 2009 pandemic H1N1 viruses and contributed key gene segments to later globally important swine influenza genotypes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of pig production in China and neighbouring regions, frequent movement of pigs between farms and through live markets, and close proximity of pigs to domestic poultry and wild birds created sustained opportunities for avian H1N1 viruses to spill over and become established in swine herds. Limited structured influenza surveillance in pigs during the 1990s meant EA H1N1 viruses could circulate and spread widely before they were fully recognised and genetically characterised. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via host expansion of a Eurasian avian-like H1N1 lineage into pigs and subsequent adaptation in this mammalian host, followed by geographic range expansion of EA H1N1 across eastern and south-eastern Asia; these EA H1N1 viruses later donated NA and M segments to the 2009 H1N1 pandemic strain and internal genes to reassortant genotypes such as G4, illustrating their central role in SIV evolution.
Review: Review (newly added event). A major post‑1990 SIV emergence episode missing from the original dataset was the introduction and establishment of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 viruses in Asian pigs. Multiple virologic and phylogenetic studies document avian-origin European-lineage H1N1 viruses entering Chinese pigs in the early 1990s and forming an Asian EA sublineage, detection of EA H1N1 in pigs in Hong Kong SAR and Thailand by about 2001, and progressive replacement of classical H1N1 by EA H1N1 as the predominant H1 lineage in Chinese swine herds by around 2005.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC190877/?utm_source=openai)) This episode is widely regarded as a key shift in the global SIV gene pool and an important precursor to both the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus and later G4 EA H1N1 genotypes, so it qualifies as one of the top emergence events. I coded it as re-emergence (new strain and bird-to-pig host expansion within an already SIV-endemic region) with no first- or inter-continental emergence flags, and restricted the explicit country list to China (including Hong Kong SAR) and Thailand where early establishment is best documented. A subject-matter expert should review the chosen year range (1993–2005) and country timing, but this event should be retained among the largest SIV emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1994]; France [late 1990s]; Germany [~2000]; Italy [~2000]; Belgium [~2000]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [~2000]; Spain [~2000]; Denmark [~2000]; Sweden [~2000]; Czechia [2002–2003]; Poland [2002–2003]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: In 1994, a novel H1N2 swine influenza A virus emerged in pigs in the United Kingdom, generated by reassortment between human seasonal H1N1 and existing European swine H3N2 and avian-like H1N1 lineages and causing outbreaks of respiratory disease in pig herds. Over the late 1990s and early 2000s, this reassortant H1N2 lineage spread widely across western, northern and parts of southern and eastern Europe, becoming detectable in pigs in countries including France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Spain, Denmark, Sweden, Czechia and Poland and co-circulating with avian-like H1N1 and human-like H3N2. By the early 2000s, H1N2 was established as one of three main SIV subtypes in European pig populations, with infections transitioning from obvious outbreaks to an endemic pattern of recurrent respiratory disease with ongoing antigenic drift and further reassortment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and modernisation of European commercial pig production, dense pig populations, and intra-European trade in live pigs facilitated dissemination of the new H1N2 lineage between herds and across borders; limited virological surveillance in pigs during the 1990s delayed recognition of the virus’s broader spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment between human seasonal H1N1 and existing European swine H3N2 and avian-like H1N1 lineages produced a new H1N2 virus with human-origin HA and NA and internal genes from established swine lineages, representing a clear re-emergence event driven by genetic innovation rather than introduction of influenza A into a naïve host system.
Review: Review. This event correctly captures the emergence of European H1N2 SIV in UK pigs in 1994 and its spread across much of western and northern Europe, supported by ECDC and EID data on the UK origin and subsequent endemic establishment in continental Europe and by seroprevalence data from multi-country surveys in 2002–2003.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/swine-influenza/factsheet?utm_source=openai)) The classification as re-emergence (a novel reassortant genotype within an already SIV-endemic continent) and the decision not to label this as intra- or inter-continental emergence are consistent with the project rule that new serotypes or manifestations in regions where the organism is already present should be treated as re-emergence. I added Czechia and Poland to the country list, with approximate dates 2002–2003, to match the inclusion of Eastern Europe as a subregion and align with serologic evidence of H1N2 circulation there, and otherwise retained the year range and subregions. The event should be kept as one of the major post‑1990 SIV emergence episodes, but the amended country list and approximate timings warrant expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), with occasional spillover to turkeys and other poultry
Event summary: In 1998, outbreaks of influenza-like illness in U.S. pig herds revealed the sudden emergence of a novel H3N2 swine influenza virus containing the so‑called triple reassortant internal gene (TRIG) cassette, with genes derived from human H3N2, classical swine H1N1 and North American avian influenza viruses; these viruses rapidly caused widespread disease in multiple U.S. states. During the following years, the TRIG internal gene constellation became established across U.S. swine populations and reassorted further with classical swine H1N1 to generate additional H1N2 and H1N1 variants, while similar triple-reassortant H3N2 viruses were detected in Canadian pigs by 2005, indicating regional spread within northern North America. By the mid‑2000s, triple‑reassortant lineage viruses (trH3N2, trH1N2 and trH1N1) had become dominant in North American swine, replacing classical H1N1 as the sole major lineage and establishing a genetically diverse, enzootic swine influenza ecosystem that persists and continues to generate novel reassortants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density, multi-site pig production and frequent movement of weaned pigs between breeding and finishing units favoured rapid spread of the new TRIG lineage across North American herds; close contact between pigs and humans and between pig and poultry operations created repeated opportunities for multi-host infection and reassortment. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through complex reassortment among human H3N2, classical swine H1N1 and avian influenza viruses produced the triple‑reassortant internal gene (TRIG) cassette, which conferred high fitness in pigs and subsequently seeded reassortant H1 and H3 subtypes; this represents re-emergence through genetic innovation, geographic range expansion of the TRIG lineage within North America, and enhanced transmission potential in pig populations.
Review: Retain. The emergence of triple-reassortant H3N2 viruses with the TRIG internal gene cassette in U.S. pigs in 1998 and their rapid establishment and diversification across North American swine, including detection in Canadian pigs by 2005, is extensively documented and widely recognised as one of the most important modern SIV emergence events.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168170200001544?utm_source=openai)) The geographic scope (United States and Canada), approximate year range (1998–2005), host description and classification as re-emergence (novel reassortant genotype in an already SIV-endemic region) are all consistent with published evidence and with the project’s rule to treat genotype shifts, rather than the long-standing presence of influenza A in pigs, as re-emergence. The event’s sources are highly relevant primary virologic studies; no corrections were required, and this row should be retained as is.

Continent: North America; South America; Europe; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub-regions: Northern America; Central America; South America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Australia and New Zealand; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: Mexico [2009]; United States of America [2009]; Canada [2009]; Brazil [2009]; Argentina [2009]; Colombia [2010]; Chile [2010]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009]; Germany [2010]; Italy [2010]; Finland [2009]; Spain [2010]; China [2009]; Japan [2009]; Viet Nam [2010]; Thailand [2010]; India [2010]; Australia [2009]; Cameroon [2010]; Kenya [2011]; Nigeria [2010]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: In 2009, the novel pandemic H1N1 (H1N1pdm09) influenza A virus, a complex reassortant derived partly from North American triple‑reassortant swine viruses and Eurasian avian-like swine viruses, spilled over from swine into humans in Mexico and the United States and rapidly spread worldwide in humans; soon after, reverse zoonotic transmission from infected people led to introduction of H1N1pdm09 into domestic pig herds in multiple countries on six continents. From 2009 to roughly 2013, H1N1pdm09 viruses were repeatedly introduced into swine populations in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Oceania and Africa, where they established sustained pig-to-pig transmission and reassorted extensively with locally endemic SIV lineages, as documented in countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Australia, Finland and Cameroon, and later detected in African pigs in Cameroon, Kenya, Nigeria and other countries. By the mid‑2010s, H1N1pdm09-derived gene segments had become entrenched in the global swine influenza gene pool, with numerous reassortant genotypes co-circulating in pigs across six continents and contributing to sustained endemic respiratory disease and an expanded reservoir of zoonotic viruses with pandemic potential.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The large human H1N1pdm09 pandemic with widespread, intense transmission across the globe created repeated opportunities for human-to-swine virus introductions via infected farm workers and animal handlers; international trade and movement of live pigs and limited biosecurity in some intensive systems facilitated onward spread and establishment in pig populations, including in regions where swine influenza viruses had previously been poorly characterised. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through reassortment between North American triple-reassortant and Eurasian avian-like swine influenza lineages produced H1N1pdm09, which then reassorted further with endemic H1N1, H1N2 and H3N2 SIVs in each region; this represents a major global re-emergence event characterised by host expansion (sustained spillback from humans to pigs), extensive genetic diversification in pigs and geographic range expansion of H1N1pdm09-derived gene segments within continents.
Review: Review. This row appropriately describes the global reverse-zoonotic seeding and establishment of pandemic H1N1 2009 (H1N1pdm09) viruses in pigs on all major continents between 2009 and roughly 2013, consistent with phylogenetic work showing at least dozens of independent human-to-swine introductions and subsequent reassortment in swine in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Oceania and Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3541789/?utm_source=openai)) However, I changed inter_continental_emergence from Yes to No, leaving only re-emergence marked as Yes, because influenza A viruses had been documented in pigs on all affected continents (including Africa) before 2009; under the project rules, introduction of a new strain/serotype where the EPP organism (swine influenza A virus) is already present on the continent should be treated as re-emergence rather than inter-continental emergence.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113514005951?utm_source=openai)) I also standardised the Nigeria timing from the vague “2010s” to “Nigeria [2010]” based on evidence of H1N1pdm09 infection and serologic exposure in Nigerian pigs from 2010 onward.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5897404/?utm_source=openai)) The listed countries remain a representative, not exhaustive, subset of the many countries where H1N1pdm09 has been reported in swine; overall the event is clearly among the top SIV emergence episodes and should be retained, but the revised coding and dates should be reviewed by an expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), with zoonotic spillover to humans at agricultural fairs
Event summary: Around 2010–2011, U.S. surveillance detected variant H3N2 swine influenza viruses (trH3N2) in pigs that carried the internal TRIG cassette and acquired the matrix (M) gene from the 2009 H1N1pdm09 virus, with infections documented in exhibition and commercial herds and occasional human infections linked to agricultural fairs. Over the next several years, these reassortant H3N2 viruses spread within U.S. swine populations and were repeatedly associated with human variant H3N2 (H3N2v) cases, including a multi-state outbreak in 2012 with hundreds of fair-associated infections, highlighting intense bidirectional transmission at the human–swine interface without causing catastrophic pig mortality but contributing to widespread respiratory disease and production impacts in affected herds. By the mid‑2010s, H3N2 viruses carrying the pH1N1 M gene had become part of the diverse North American SIV landscape, continuing to reassort with H1 lineages in pigs and persisting as an important zoonotic risk during swine exhibitions while being managed in herds through vaccination, improved fair biosecurity, and enhanced surveillance rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense mixing of pigs from multiple sources at agricultural fairs and exhibitions, along with close human–pig contact, facilitated amplification and cross‑species transmission of the novel H3N2 variants; movement of pigs between production sites and variable vaccine match further supported their spread and persistence in commercial and exhibition herds. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment between endemic triple‑reassortant H3N2 SIVs and the H1N1pdm09 virus resulted in H3N2 viruses carrying the pH1N1 M gene, which may enhance transmissibility and adaptation; this constitutes a re-emergence driven by genetic change and recurrent host expansion (frequent spillover to humans) within an already SIV-endemic subregion.
Review: Review. The event correctly describes the emergence in U.S. pigs of H3N2 variant viruses that carry the H1N1pdm09 M gene and their strong epidemiologic link to H3N2v human infections associated with agricultural fairs from 2011 onward, as documented in CDC MMWR and EID reports.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6051a4.htm?utm_source=openai)) Classifying this as re-emergence only is appropriate, because these viruses represent a new reassortant genotype within an already SIV-endemic subregion and do not meet the criteria for first/global, intra- or inter-continental emergence of the EPP. To improve the relevance of sources, I replaced a tangential Nigerian H5N1/H1N1pdm09 serology paper with targeted CDC MMWR and EID articles on H3N2v transmission at fairs and on subclinical infection in exhibition swine, while retaining the broader CDC swine/variant flu background page. The geography (United States only), time frame (2011–2014) and emphasis on fairs are reasonable simplifications of a complex situation, but this row should be reviewed to confirm that no larger SIV events are being crowded out by this choice.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: From approximately 2016 onward, surveillance in Chinese pig farms identified a dominant genotype of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza, termed G4 EA H1N1, which had arisen through reassortment and began to replace earlier EA H1N1 lineages in pigs, causing endemic respiratory disease across major swine-producing regions of China. Over 2016–2020, G4 EA H1N1 viruses became the predominant H1N1 genotype detected in Chinese pigs and serologic studies found substantial exposure in swine workers, indicating widespread circulation in pigs and frequent human–pig contact with the lineage, though without recognised large human outbreaks to date. By 2020, G4 EA H1N1 was firmly entrenched in Chinese swine populations, continuing to evolve and co-circulate with other SIV lineages and prompting international concern and preparedness activities because of its genetic makeup and demonstrated ability to infect humans, even though pig herds were managed through routine influenza control measures rather than emergency depopulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and consolidation of China’s intensive pig industry, high pig densities, and complex live-pig marketing chains favoured replacement of older EA H1N1 lineages by fitter reassortant G4 viruses; relatively sparse systematic swine influenza surveillance before 2016 allowed the lineage to spread widely before its predominance was fully recognised. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through reassortment between Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine viruses and internal genes from H1N1pdm09 and triple-reassortant swine influenza lineages created the G4 genotype, characterised by a specific constellation of polymerase, nucleoprotein, matrix and non-structural genes that support efficient replication in pigs and infection of humans; this is a clear re-emergence event involving genetic innovation and geographic range expansion within Chinese pig populations.
Review: Review. This event accurately summarises the emergence and rapid predominance of the G4 genotype of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza viruses in Chinese pigs since about 2016, as described in the original PNAS report and subsequent risk assessments and EID analyses that show G4 viruses becoming the main EA H1N1 genotype and infecting a notable fraction of swine workers.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/swine-flu/comm-resources/cdc-prepare-swine-flu.html?utm_source=openai)) Coding it as re-emergence (a novel reassortant genotype within a long‑infected host population) and not as a first or inter-continental emergence event is consistent with the project definitions. To strengthen the evidence base, I replaced the general Swine influenza Wikipedia link with the primary PNAS article on G4 and an EID paper on its zoonotic threat, while retaining the CDC preparedness page that contextualises public-health concern. The year range (2016–2020) captures the documented rise to predominance but may need updating as more recent surveillance shows whether G4 remains dominant; therefore this row is flagged for expert review rather than unconditional retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: In the early 2010s, a severe episode of ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma was recognized in sheep flocks in Shandong Province, China, where OPA had been reported historically but rarely characterized with modern virology. Development: Clinical, pathological, and RT‑PCR investigations confirmed numerous cases caused by exogenous JSRV, with phylogenetic analysis linking the Shandong strain closely to a Kenyan JSRV isolate and indicating widespread infection within affected flocks. End: The outbreak subsided only after heavily affected animals were removed and diagnosis clarified, but the study emphasized that JSRV‑associated OPA remains endemic and economically important in Chinese sheep production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density sheep production, close housing, and movement of infected but subclinically affected animals facilitated flock‑level spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or clear virulence shift was reported; the outbreak reflected efficient transmission and long incubation of endemic exogenous JSRV rather than emergence of a distinct genotype.
Review: retain – Well‑documented severe OPA outbreak in Shandong, China, with molecular characterization and clear production impact. OPA was first reported in China in the 1950s, so classification as re_occurrence (not first_detection) is appropriate, and the Asia/Eastern Asia/China coding is consistent with the UNSD scheme. No changes made beyond confirming that this episode merits inclusion as one of the major post‑1990 outbreak‑scale events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3909617/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: In the mid‑2010s, ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma was identified histologically and by PCR as an incidental finding in sheep from two flocks in Southern Jutland, Denmark, representing the first documented, laboratory‑confirmed OPA cases in the country. Development: A subsequent national abattoir-based survey of 1,480 sheep and lamb lungs in 2016 found no confirmed OPA cases, suggesting that OPA prevalence remained very low or highly focal despite earlier detections. End: The incidental detections and the negative 2016 survey indicated that JSRV was present but probably at low prevalence in Denmark, prompting recommendations for continued surveillance using histology and immunohistochemistry rather than gross inspection alone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via live animal trade or shared breeding stock from neighboring European countries where OPA is endemic; diagnostic intensification (histology, IHC, PCR) enabled detection of otherwise overlooked cases. Internal mechanisms: No specific evidence of a novel JSRV strain or altered pathogenicity was presented; the event mainly reflects detection of low‑level endemic infection rather than biological change.
Review: retain – The Danish article explicitly notes that OPA had previously been detected only as incidental PCR‑confirmed cases in two Southern Jutland flocks, and that its national prevalence was unknown before this work, supporting use of first_detection for Denmark. Time and place (Europe, Northern Europe, Denmark) are correct. The 2014 date is inferred rather than directly stated in the source and may need refinement from the original Maedi–Visna prevalence study cited as reference 18, so this event should be kept but the exact year could be checked in a future pass.([dvt.ddd.dk](https://dvt.ddd.dk/bladarkiv/2018/nr-10/proportion-of-ovine-pulmonary-adenocarcinoma-in-danish-sheep-at-slaughter/))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: Although OPA had been clinically suspected and is a notifiable disease in Ireland, its causative virus had not previously been confirmed, and an abattoir survey of adult sheep lungs was undertaken in the mid‑2010s. Development: Using gross examination, histopathology, JSRV‑specific RT‑PCR, and immunohistochemistry, researchers documented multiple OPA cases and, for the first time in Ireland, molecularly confirmed JSRV infection in affected sheep, enabling preliminary estimates of national prevalence and distribution. End: The study concluded that JSRV‑associated OPA was present but underdiagnosed in Ireland and recommended improved surveillance and control measures, marking a key diagnostic emergence event within the Irish sheep industry rather than a new introduction of the virus globally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enhanced abattoir surveillance combined with modern molecular methods revealed existing infection rather than a sudden biological change; movement of breeding sheep within and into Ireland likely sustained low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain, resistance, or virulence change was identified; the primary mechanism was improved detection of endemic exogenous JSRV.
Review: retain – Lee et al. (2017) explicitly frame this as the first PCR confirmation of JSRV in Ireland and provide a national abattoir prevalence estimate, so classification as first_detection in this country is appropriate. The event is epidemiologically important despite modest case numbers and fits the brief to include major diagnostic emergence events. Geographic coding (Europe, Northern Europe, Ireland) is correct and source selection is appropriate.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5735933/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: In the late 2010s, the status of OPA in Romania was poorly defined despite endemic reports from other European countries, prompting abattoir-based investigations in Transylvania. Development: Lung samples from 2,693 slaughtered adult ewes (2017–2019) were examined, revealing 34 cases of OPA (1.26% prevalence) associated with exogenous JSRV type 2 (exJSRV2); histopathology, immunophenotyping, electron microscopy, and molecular assays confirmed infection and described both classical and atypical anatomical forms, the latter not previously documented in Eastern Europe. End: The study, published in 2020, provided the first detailed virological and pathological characterization of OPA (including atypical forms and exJSRV2) in Romanian flocks and highlighted that, although less prevalent than in high-incidence areas like South America, South Africa, and Scotland, JSRV is established in parts of Romania and requires targeted control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Systematic abattoir surveillance and growing concern about production losses led to detection of both classical and atypical OPA forms; historical sheep trade within Europe likely introduced exJSRV2 earlier. Internal mechanisms: Identification of exJSRV2 and atypical OPA lesions in Romania reflects the regional emergence/recognition of distinct viral lineages and pathological variants already known elsewhere, rather than a globally novel genotype, and fits the definition of re‑emergence via new manifestation in an already affected subregion.
Review: review – Evidence from Romanian pathology and review articles indicates that pulmonary adenomatosis had been recognized locally before 2017, with the 2020 BMC study providing the first comprehensive virological and pathological characterization and the first documentation of atypical OPA and exJSRV2 in Romania/Eastern Europe. Accordingly, first_detection has been set to No and re_emergence to Yes to reflect a new manifestation/strain in a subregion where OPA was already present, in line with the project’s definition of re‑emergence. Event dates (2017–2019, published 2020) and Eastern Europe/Romania coding are correct, and the primary source is appropriate.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32807166/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: Increasing numbers of sheep in some Mongolian regions were observed with chronic respiratory signs and lung tumors consistent with pulmonary adenomatosis, prompting efforts to confirm the etiologic agent. Development: A 2021 study performed histopathology and nested PCR on lung tissues from clinically affected slaughtered sheep, demonstrating typical OPA lesions and amplifying JSRV proviral 5′‑LTR sequences, which clustered phylogenetically with Chinese, American, Indian, and Scottish strains, suggesting introduction from abroad rather than a distinct local lineage. End: The work established the presence of exogenous JSRV causing OPA in Mongolian sheep and concluded that rapid molecular diagnostic capacity was needed to manage a disease whose incidence appeared to be rising in some areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via international or regional trade in breeding stock from countries where JSRV is endemic; extensive grazing and limited routine post‑mortem diagnostics may have allowed silent spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced proviral fragments did not form a distinct Mongolian clade but grouped with existing global strains, indicating geographic range expansion via animal movement rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – The Mongolian Journal of Agricultural Sciences paper describes the first molecular confirmation of OPA/JSRV in Mongolia and explicitly interprets the infection as likely imported from abroad, matching the intended use of first_detection at the country level. Eastern Asia/Mongolia coding is correct and the event is a reasonable inclusion among major modern emergence events given the size of the national sheep population and evidence for increasing case recognition.([mongoliajol.info](https://mongoliajol.info/index.php/MJAS/article/view/1910))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Origin: In the early 2020s, veterinarians at Mosul city abattoirs in northern Iraq increasingly observed lung lesions suggestive of OPA in slaughtered sheep, against a background of earlier reports of the disease elsewhere in the country. Development: A recent study collected lung samples from suspect carcasses at Mosul slaughterhouses and butcher shops; histopathology demonstrated characteristic OPA tumors and RT‑PCR detected JSRV, representing the first molecular identification of the virus in Mosul city and confirming JSRV-associated OPA as an important cause of chronic respiratory disease in local flocks. End: This work highlighted that JSRV‑associated OPA is present and likely under‑recognized in parts of Iraq, underscoring the need for broader surveillance and flock‑level control strategies in Western Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of diagnostic capacity and targeted abattoir surveillance in Mosul enabled recognition of OPA; regional sheep movements across Western Asia probably introduced or maintained JSRV circulation without earlier molecular confirmation. Internal mechanisms: The study focused on confirming infection rather than viral evolution, and no evidence of a unique strain, altered virulence, or resistance was reported; the event reflects re‑occurrence/recognition in a country where OPA had already been described.
Review: review – The Iraqi study clearly states that OPA has been documented previously in Iraq and that its RT‑PCR results represent the first molecular identification of JSRV in Mosul city specifically, not the whole country. Therefore, first_detection has been changed from Yes to No and re_occurrence set to Yes to reflect renewed recognition of an existing disease focus in Western Asia. The event year has been left as ~2024, based on the 2024 submission and 2025 publication dates, but ideally should be refined to the actual sampling period if available. The geographic coding (Asia, Western Asia, Iraq) and choice of primary source are appropriate.([vetmedmosul.com](https://www.vetmedmosul.com/article_186015.html))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Countries: Thailand [pre-1990s]; Cambodia [pre-1990s]; Viet Nam [1990s]; China [1990s]; Japan [1990s]; Republic of Korea [1990s]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [1990s]; Indonesia [1990s]; Malaysia [1990s]; India [2000s]; Nepal [2000s]; Sri Lanka [2000s]
Host: Domestic pigs; wild and domestic birds; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through about 2010, genotype I strains of Japanese encephalitis virus emerged and spread across much of East, Southeast and parts of South Asia, progressively displacing the historically dominant genotype III in pigs, mosquitoes and humans. Phylogeographic analyses indicate that genotype I lineages diverged in mainland Southeast Asia (Thailand/Cambodia) and then spread northward through Viet Nam and China to Japan and the Republic of Korea, while also circulating in other parts of tropical Asia, coinciding with extensive pig production and rice‑paddy mosquito habitats. By the late 2000s, genotype I had become the predominant lineage in many endemic countries, altering the genetic landscape of JEV circulating in animal reservoirs and vectors even though endemic transmission continued rather than ending abruptly.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of pig production, proliferation of irrigated rice agriculture supporting Culex tritaeniorhynchus breeding, and regional connectivity likely facilitated rapid movement and establishment of genotype I viruses across multiple countries. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and subsequent dominance of a novel genotype (genotype I) with evidence of favorable evolutionary and epidemiologic dynamics compared with genotype III, suggesting enhanced fitness and possibly increased transmissibility in mosquito–pig–bird cycles, representing classic re‑emergence driven by viral genetic change.
Review: retain – This long multi-country episode (1990–2010) describing genotype I replacing genotype III across East, Southeast and parts of South Asia is well supported by phylogeographic analyses and pig/mosquito data, and fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by viral genetic change without constituting a new continental or subregional presence. Subregions and country groupings are consistent with published spread patterns, and no higher‑impact genotype‑shift episode has been identified that would displace this event from the top set.

Host: Domestic pigs; feral pigs; waterbirds; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event summary: In 1995, Japanese encephalitis virus was detected for the first time in recognized natural transmission cycles in the Australasian region during an outbreak centered on Badu Island in the Torres Strait, where three human cases (two fatal) occurred and JEV infection was demonstrated in local pigs and mosquitoes, indicating establishment of a transmission cycle in domestic swine and wildlife. Subsequent investigations showed active JEV circulation in southern Papua New Guinea, with virus isolated from Culex mosquitoes and serologic evidence in humans and pigs during the late 1980s–1990s, likely serving as the source, and by 1997–1998 JEV was isolated from mosquitoes in Western Province PNG and from pig blood and mosquitoes in the Torres Strait, confirming an epizootic/enzootic focus spanning PNG and northern Australia. By 1998, virus activity had extended to mainland northern Australia (Cape York Peninsula), after which enhanced surveillance and vector control reduced detectable circulation, although low‑level activity persisted in the Torres Strait in later years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Strong cyclonic weather systems and prevailing winds in the Gulf of Carpentaria likely transported infected Culex mosquitoes from high‑transmission foci in southern Papua New Guinea into the Torres Strait and Cape York; the co‑location of piggeries, waterbird habitat, and rice or wetland environments provided ideal conditions for sustained transmission. Intensified regional travel and trade may also have facilitated movement of infected vectors or birds. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was implicated; instead, existing Asian JEV lineages expanded their geographic range into a previously non‑endemic continent (Oceania), representing geographic range expansion enabled by suitable vectors and amplifying hosts rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – This is the well-documented first establishment of JEV transmission in Oceania, covering the 1995 Torres Strait outbreak and subsequent spread to Cape York. Continent, subregions (Australia and New Zealand; Melanesia) and country assignments (Australia, Papua New Guinea) match the UNSD scheme and the literature. Coding as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent, with in situ pig–mosquito cycles) without first/global emergence or re‑emergence flags is appropriate; while 1995 and 1998 may represent separate incursions, treating 1995–1998 as a single linked early Australasian episode is defensible and does not misclassify the event type.

Host: Domestic pigs; waterbirds; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event summary: In 2005, a very large Japanese encephalitis outbreak occurred in northern India (notably Uttar Pradesh) and adjoining districts of Nepal, where several thousand suspected human cases and more than a thousand deaths were reported in areas with extensive pig farming and rice cultivation. The episode built on long‑standing endemic circulation but represented a major resurgence, with pigs and waterbirds serving as key amplifying hosts sustaining high mosquito infection rates in rural communities. After emergency vector control and rollout of human vaccination campaigns, along with seasonal decline in mosquito populations, the outbreak subsided, although JE remained endemic in pigs and humans in the affected Terai and Gangetic plain districts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of unvaccinated children, extensive irrigated rice cultivation favoring Culex breeding, close proximity of pigs to human dwellings, monsoon‑related increases in vector populations, and limited initial vaccination coverage contributed to explosive amplification from the usual pig–bird reservoirs into humans. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel genotype was uniquely implicated in this particular year; the event is best interpreted as a dramatic re‑occurrence driven mainly by environmental and socio‑economic factors that intensified transmission in an already endemic pig–mosquito–human system.
Review: retain – The 2005 epidemic in Uttar Pradesh and neighboring Nepal is widely recognized as one of the largest recent JE outbreaks by human cases and deaths, occurring in a long‑endemic Southern Asian focus with intensive pig and rice production. Geography (Southern Asia; India and Nepal) and classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence in a known subregion driven by external factors rather than a new genotype or new region) are consistent with the definitions, and no more impactful post‑1990 JE outbreak in this region has been omitted that would supersede it.

Host: Domestic pigs; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event summary: Until the late 2000s, Tibet on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau was considered non‑endemic for Japanese encephalitis because its high altitude was thought to preclude sustained mosquito–vertebrate transmission cycles. In 2009, however, investigations following human JE cases identified JEV‑specific IgM antibodies in one‑third of sampled piglets in Mainling and Medog counties and viral RNA in local Culex mosquitoes, demonstrating that pigs were newly participating in local transmission cycles in this previously unsuitable high‑altitude environment. Subsequent surveillance confirmed ongoing, though still relatively limited, JEV circulation in plateau areas, marking a durable range expansion of the virus in Chinese domestic pig populations rather than a one‑off incursion that disappeared.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warming temperatures, changes in land use and agriculture, and development of pig production and irrigation in parts of Tibet likely improved habitat suitability for Culex vectors and facilitated introduction and maintenance of JEV. Internal mechanisms: The event represents geographic range expansion into high‑altitude ecological zones where JEV transmission had not previously been sustained, consistent with re‑emergence driven by climatic and ecological shifts combined with the virus’s inherent capacity to exploit new environmental niches, rather than by a specifically identified new genotype unique to Tibet.
Review: retain – This event is well supported by primary data showing IgM‑positive piglets and infected Culex mosquitoes in high‑altitude counties of Tibet previously regarded as JE‑free. Coding as re‑emergence (range expansion into new ecological zones within an already affected country and subregion) without intra‑/inter‑continental tags is appropriate, and Eastern Asia/China placement matches the UNSD regional scheme.

Host: Humans; potential reservoir hosts such as domestic pigs and aquatic birds and local Culex mosquitoes are inferred but were not directly investigated in this event.
Event summary: In March 2016, during a large yellow fever outbreak in Angola, genomic analysis of blood from a 19‑year‑old man in Cunene Province who had not travelled outside Angola revealed co‑infection with yellow fever virus and Japanese encephalitis virus, with phylogenetic analysis showing the JEV genome to be genotype III closely related to Asian strains; this provided the first documented evidence of locally acquired JEV infection on the African continent. Only this single human case with detectable JEV RNA was identified, but the finding in a rural Angolan resident, in a setting where competent Culex vectors and potential amplifying hosts such as pigs and aquatic birds are present, indicated that JEV had been introduced into, or was newly recognized within, African transmission cycles. After the yellow fever epidemic waned, no further confirmed JEV cases were reported from Angola, but the event prompted international calls for targeted serologic and entomologic surveillance in humans and animals in Angola and neighboring countries to determine whether the virus had become established.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased human movement and trade between Asia and Africa during the 2010s likely provided opportunities for introduction of JEV into Angola, and extensive clinical sampling during the yellow fever outbreak enabled its unexpected detection; the presence of irrigated agriculture, domestic pigs and waterbirds, and competent Culex vectors in southern Angola provides ecological conditions in which JEV could circulate once introduced. Internal mechanisms: The Angolan virus belonged to known genotype III rather than a novel lineage, so this episode is best interpreted as an inter‑continental geographic range expansion of existing Asian JEV lineages into Africa, facilitated by human and possibly bird or mosquito movement, rather than by documented viral genetic innovation.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first documented autochthonous JEV infection in Africa (Angola, 2016), which is widely cited as the continent’s initial evidence of local transmission and is clearly among the most important post‑1990 emergence events despite direct data only from a human case. Classified as inter‑continental emergence into Middle Africa because the infection was locally acquired and not imported. Animal hosts (pigs/birds) are inferred but not directly documented, so this row should be retained but flagged for expert review of host listing and to confirm that including a primarily human case in the animal‑host sheet is acceptable for the project’s cross‑host framing.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Commercially reared domestic pigs
Event summary: Between about 2017 and 2021, serological surveys of commercially reared pigs in four states of southwestern Nigeria found JEV‑specific IgG antibodies in roughly one‑third of sampled animals, providing the first evidence that pigs in Africa had been naturally exposed to Japanese encephalitis virus. These findings, in unvaccinated pigs across multiple farms and age groups, indicate that local transmission cycles involving pigs and competent Culex vectors had become established or had been introduced into West Africa, even though no large, clinically recognized animal or human outbreaks were reported at the time. Following publication of these data, JEV exposure in Nigerian pigs has been recognized as a potential emerging zoonotic risk, prompting calls for integrated surveillance in pigs, vectors and humans to clarify the extent and dynamics of this new African focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Presence of JEV mosquito vectors such as Culex tritaeniorhynchus in southwestern Nigeria, growth and intensification of pig farming with limited biosecurity, and suitable climatic conditions likely enabled introduction and silent circulation of JEV in pig herds following its initial appearance in Africa. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not yet identify a distinct novel genotype or phenotype; this event is interpreted as intra‑continental emergence of JEV from its first recognized African focus into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and establishment of transmission in domestic pigs, rather than as a separate inter‑continental emergence or genotype‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – The underlying pig serosurvey is robust and documents substantial JEV antibody prevalence in unvaccinated pigs in southwestern Nigeria, supporting inclusion of this event as a major development for animal hosts in Africa. However, the event type has been corrected from inter‑continental emergence to intra‑continental emergence, because the first documented African JEV infection occurred in Angola (Middle Africa) in 2016; the Nigerian findings therefore represent spread into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and first confirmation in domestic pigs, not the initial continental incursion. Given remaining uncertainty about possible cross‑reactivity in serologic assays and limited virologic confirmation, this row should be retained but kept flagged for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs; feral pigs; Culex mosquitoes; sentinel chickens; an alpaca; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event summary: In late 2021 and early 2022, Japanese encephalitis virus was detected in piggeries across south‑eastern mainland Australia (Victoria, New South Wales, southern Queensland and South Australia), far south of its previous known range in northern Australia and the Torres Strait, signalling a major epizootic in domestic and feral pigs. By late 2022, JEV had been reported from more than 80 commercial piggeries and feral pig populations across multiple states, with concurrent detections in mosquitoes, sentinel chickens, an alpaca and humans; molecular analysis showed involvement of genotype IV, a lineage not previously reported in Australia. With the onset of cooler, drier conditions and implementation of vector‑control, animal movement controls and targeted vaccination of at‑risk humans, reported transmission declined, though JEV is now considered an emerging endemic risk in southern Australia’s pig‑farming and wetland regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged La Niña conditions and widespread flooding created extensive mosquito breeding habitats along river systems such as the Murray, while high densities of domestic and feral pigs and waterbirds in irrigated agricultural landscapes provided abundant amplifying hosts; movement of infected birds and mosquitoes likely facilitated rapid spread among piggeries. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of JEV genotype IV in Australia, coupled with southward geographic range expansion into temperate regions with largely naïve pig and human populations, constitutes a clear re‑emergence based on viral genetic change and range expansion within an already affected country, with potential implications for transmission efficiency and overwintering in local vectors and hosts.
Review: retain – The large 2021–2022 genotype IV–associated outbreak in eastern and southern Australian piggeries is a clearly major epizootic, with strong documentation of >80 affected piggeries, feral pig involvement and multiple human cases. Treating this as a re‑emergence event (new genotype and major southward range expansion within Oceania, rather than a new continent) is consistent with the definitions and with prior JEV presence in northern Australia; geography and sources are appropriate, so the row should be kept as is.

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Host: European brown hare (Lepus europaeus); mountain hare (Lepus timidus)
Event summary: Around 1990, EBHSV caused a major epizootic wave in free-living European brown hares and mountain hares in Finland, with at least 136 confirmed EBHS cases in mountain hares between 1990 and 2002 and evidence of widespread exposure in brown hares. The disease became established in northern and central Finland during the early 1990s and recurred seasonally over more than a decade, contributing to marked declines and fluctuations in local hare populations. By the early 2000s, reported EBHS cases and associated mortality began to decline, likely reflecting reduced host density and increasing herd immunity rather than eradication of the virus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high hare population densities and cyclic dynamics in boreal Finland, aggregation at feeding sites, and environmental conditions favouring indirect transmission facilitated sustained circulation; landscape connectivity across northern Fennoscandia enabled spread from earlier Scandinavian foci. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence of a novel EBHSV strain driving this episode; disease pattern is consistent with geographic range and incidence expansion of an established lineage rather than a newly emergent genotype.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the large 1990–2002 EBHS epizootic in Finnish hares documented in primary literature, with appropriate geography (Finland, Northern Europe) and classification as re-occurrence within an already affected Northern European subregion. No structural changes were required; this remains the only post‑1990 EBHSV event clearly among the most impactful for this EPP.

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: France [2010]; Spain [2011]; Portugal [2011]; Italy [2011]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2012]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2013]; Azores, Portugal [2013-2014]; Canary Islands, Spain [2013-2014]
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: In 2010, a new pathogenic lagovirus variant, later designated Lagovirus europaeus GI.2 (RHDV2), was first identified during rabbit haemorrhagic disease outbreaks in domestic rabbits in France, where it caused high mortality despite vaccination against classical RHDV. Over 2011–2013 the virus spread explosively through Iberia (Spain, Portugal), Italy, the Netherlands, the UK, and other European countries, and by 2013–2014 it had reached several Atlantic islands including the Azores and Canary Islands, causing large die-offs in both farmed and wild rabbits. By about 2014–2015, RHDV2 had become widely established across Europe and many island systems, partially or fully replacing classical RHDV (GI.1) as the dominant cause of rabbit haemorrhagic disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive rabbit production and trade, movement of live rabbits and rabbit products, high hunting and translocation pressure in wild rabbit populations, and dense, interconnected European rabbit metapopulations facilitated rapid geographic spread on the continent and to offshore islands. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel genotype (GI.2/RHDV2) with distinct antigenic properties and partial vaccine escape relative to GI.1, increased ability to infect younger rabbits, and evidence of recombination with non-pathogenic lagoviruses likely enhanced its fitness and allowed it to outcompete endemic GI.1 strains. Mechanisms include novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion inherent to the lineage.
Review: review – Corrected event-type coding so this early multi-country European wave of GI.2/RHDV2 is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by a new genotype, rather than as first/global emergence, first detection and intra-continental emergence. Geography (France, Iberia, Italy, the Netherlands, UK and Atlantic islands) and the 2010–2015 time window remain appropriate for one of the most impactful global events, but a human reviewer may wish to verify whether any additional highly affected European countries should be named explicitly.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub-regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Tunisia [2015-2018]; Morocco [2017-2021]; Algeria [2018-2021]; Egypt [2018-2020]; Benin [2015]; Côte d’Ivoire [≥2016]; Ghana [2019]; Nigeria [2020-2021]; Senegal [2020]; South Africa [2022]
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in commercial and backyard systems; occasional wild/feral rabbits
Event summary: In February 2015, RHDV2 was first reported in Africa during severe outbreaks in commercial rabbit farms in Kairouan, Tunisia, where it caused high mortality and major economic losses, and molecular data showed multiple introductions of GI.2-like strains from Europe. Over the next several years genetically related viruses were detected in North African countries including Morocco, Algeria and Egypt, and by 2015–2020 RHDV2 had appeared in multiple West African nations such as Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal, where large outbreaks—most notably the 2019 epidemic in Ghana and the 2020 wave in Nigeria—devastated rapidly growing rabbit industries. By 2022, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, with outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs, indicating that the new genotype had become established across several African subregions with recurrent, often high-mortality production losses rather than remaining a series of isolated incursions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation of live rabbits and rabbit genetic stock from Europe and Asia, movement of rabbit meat and byproducts into coastal West African port cities, rapid expansion of semi-intensive rabbit production as a protein source, and limited biosecurity in smallholder and peri-urban farms facilitated introduction and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward dissemination of the globally successful GI.2 genotype with high transmissibility, broader age susceptibility, and partial vaccine escape relative to earlier GI.1-based vaccines, together with largely naïve African rabbit populations, underpinned severe production losses. Mechanisms include novel genotype-driven geographic range expansion, enhanced transmission, and, in some countries, further diversification via recombination documented in African RHDV2 genomes.
Review: review – Updated the time span from 2015–2019 to 2015–2022 and corrected several country-specific first-detection windows (e.g. Nigeria from 2017–2019 to 2020–2021, Senegal to 2020, South Africa to 2022, Algeria to 2018–2021, Tunisia to 2015–2018) in line with WOAH and recent outbreak reports. Re-coded the episode as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype in an already RHD-affected continent, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags to comply with the event-type definitions; the event should be retained but remains flagged for expert review of exact country-year ranges.
