EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: In May 2015, RHDV2 was first detected in Australia, which previously hosted only deliberately released and naturally introduced GI.1 variants used for biocontrol and an emergent GI.1a strain along the east coast. Over the subsequent 18 months, RHDV2 spread rapidly across much of the Australian mainland and Tasmania, causing frequent mortality events in wild rabbits and disease episodes in domestic rabbits. By 2016–2017, field studies showed that RHDV2 had largely replaced endemic GI.1 lineages as the dominant circulating lagovirus in many Australian regions, substantially altering the virological landscape of rabbit biocontrol and complicating management strategies that relied on older strains.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive contiguous wild rabbit populations targeted for biocontrol, widespread use and movement of classical RHDV (GI.1) biocontrol strains, and high connectivity among rabbit populations across farming landscapes enabled rapid establishment and dissemination of the newly introduced GI.2 virus. Internal mechanisms: RHDV2’s broader age susceptibility, partial immunity escape in rabbits previously exposed to GI.1 biocontrol strains, and high transmissibility allowed it to outcompete existing viruses and persist across variable environmental conditions. Mechanisms include novel genotype emergence in a continent with long-standing Lagovirus presence, enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion with competitive replacement of endemic strains.
Review: review – Reclassified the arrival and spread of GI.2/RHDV2 in Australia and Tasmania as a re-emergence event within an already Lagovirus-endemic continent, removing the previous inter-continental and re-occurrence flags that conflicted with the definitions. Country information has been consolidated so Tasmania is treated as part of Australia rather than as a separate country label. The timing and impact (rapid continent-wide spread and replacement of control strains) remain well supported, but the row is flagged for expert confirmation of the chosen 2015–2017 window as the main emergence phase.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Continent: North America; South America (Central America and Caribbean)
Countries: Canada [2016, 2018-2019]; United States of America [2018-2022]; Mexico [2020-2022]; Cuba [2019]
Host: Domestic European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in pet, backyard and commercial settings; multiple native North American lagomorphs including black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus), cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus spp.), and endangered riparian brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani riparius)
Event summary: RHDV2 was first detected in the Americas in 2016 during an outbreak among feral rabbits in Mont-Joli, Québec, Canada, which was rapidly contained, followed by a genetically distinct 2018 outbreak centred on feral and domestic rabbits in British Columbia. In March 2020, after earlier detections in Cuba (2019) and isolated U.S. pet rabbit cases in 2018–2019, a large, sustained epizootic began in New Mexico and spread across domestic and wild rabbits and hares in the southwestern United States, northern Mexico and later additional U.S. states, causing hundreds of reported outbreaks and substantial mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered riparian brush rabbits. By 2022, RHDV2 was established across a broad swath of western North America and parts of the Americas, triggering emergency vaccination campaigns, movement restrictions and long-term surveillance before incidence began to decline somewhat with increased awareness and vaccine uptake.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infected domestic rabbits and possibly contaminated fomites between Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean; limited early access to RHDV2 vaccines in North America; and dense populations of susceptible wild lagomorphs in arid southwestern landscapes all facilitated widespread transmission once the virus arrived. Internal mechanisms: the broad host range of RHDV2 across lagomorph species, high environmental stability and contagiousness, and partial immune escape from prior GI.1-based immunity enabled rapid multi-species spillover and establishment in novel native hosts, leading to severe mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered brush rabbits. Mechanisms include host expansion (spillover), enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion, with re-emergence in continents that had previously experienced only sporadic or eradicated RHD incursions.
Review: review – Harmonised event-type coding so this North America–Central America–Caribbean episode is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype and host expansion, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags. Adjusted country-year annotations to distinguish early, self-limited Canadian incursions (Québec 2016, British Columbia 2018–2019) from the large 2019–2022 epizootic affecting the southwestern United States, Mexico (from 2020) and Cuba (2019). This row intentionally aggregates several genetically and spatially linked outbreaks for parsimony; a human reviewer may consider splitting early Canadian incursions into a separate, lower-impact event if finer temporal resolution is required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: New Zealand, long free of RHDV2 despite endemic classical RHDV since 1997, experienced its first confirmed detections of RHDV2 in wild rabbits and domestic rabbits during late 2017 and 2018, initially recognised in Bay of Plenty and Marlborough. Following introduction, likely via a single incursion into the North Island around 2016–2017, the virus spread through local wild rabbit populations and into domestic rabbits at multiple sites, sometimes co-circulating with or co-infecting alongside existing RHDV1 biocontrol strains. By 2018–2019, genomic analyses indicated that RHDV2 had become established in both islands, adding a new, more variable and potentially vaccine-escaping pathogen to New Zealand’s lagovirus complex and complicating rabbit biocontrol and pet health management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: unregulated or inadvertent introduction of RHDV2 (possibly via illegally imported biological material, live rabbits or contaminated fomites), combined with widespread susceptible wild rabbit populations and ongoing use of RHDV1 biocontrol strains, enabled silent establishment before official detection. Internal mechanisms: the introduced GI.2 lineage showed close genetic affinity to European/Australian strains, with high transmissibility and partial escape from existing RHDV1-based immunity and vaccines; mixed infections with RHDV1 suggested opportunities for recombination and further viral diversification. Mechanisms include novel genotype introduction into a previously RHDV2-free country, enhanced transmission, and potential for increased virulence or immune escape relative to earlier strains.
Review: review – Re-coded this episode as a pure re-emergence event (introduction of GI.2 into a country already endemic for pathogenic Lagovirus via RHDV1), removing the previous re-occurrence flag to comply with the event-type rules. Updated the country-year annotation to New Zealand [2017–2019] in line with retrospective detection and circulation studies. The event clearly remains one of the major emergence episodes for this EPP in Oceania and merits retention, but is flagged for expert confirmation of the end date as RHDV2 continues to circulate at lower levels.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Host: European brown hare (Lepus europaeus); Iberian hare (Lepus granatensis) alongside European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: Following the emergence of RHDV2 in European rabbits after 2010, sporadic but epidemiologically important spillover infections were documented from rabbits into European brown hares and Iberian hares in Italy and Spain from the early 2010s onward, where disease presentations resembled classical EBHS. Over the 2010s, longitudinal studies in northeastern Iberia and other Mediterranean agro-ecosystems showed overlapping circulation of EBHSV (GII.1) and RHDV2 (GI.2) in sympatric hare and rabbit populations, with occasional severe disease episodes in hares linked to RHDV2 infection and the appearance of recombinant lagoviruses combining hare and rabbit virus genomic segments. By around 2020, these mixed lagovirus dynamics had established a new, more complex disease ecology in hare populations, with co-circulation, cross-species transmission and recombinant viruses reshaping EBHS epidemiology rather than a simple replacement of EBHSV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close ecological overlap between dense wild rabbit populations infected with RHDV2 and sympatric European and Iberian hare populations in Mediterranean agro-ecosystems, shared hunting grounds, and limited biosecurity at the wildlife–domestic interface promoted cross-species exposure. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of RHDV2 into hares and documented recombination between EBHSV and RHDV2 genomic segments generated novel chimeric lagoviruses, raising concerns about altered virulence and antigenicity in hares; these represent classic re-emergence mechanisms driven by host expansion, recombination and potential antigenic change rather than simple reintroduction of an unchanged virus. Mechanisms include host expansion (spillover), novel strain/genotype emergence via recombination, and possible increased virulence/pathogenicity in hare hosts.
Review: review – Left the classification as re-emergence because this episode is driven by host expansion of RHDV2 into hares and the appearance of recombinant lagoviruses rather than spread of an unchanged virus, but tightened the event year from 2010–2020 to 2011–2020 to better reflect the timing of well-documented hare cases. Country coverage (Italy and Spain) and the focus on Southern Europe are appropriate, yet the exact onset and end years for hare involvement remain approximate; the row should be retained but is flagged for specialist review of the temporal window and the balance between EBHSV and RHDV2 impacts in hares.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: After first recognition of rabbit haemorrhagic disease in domestic rabbits in northern Italy in 1986, RHDV spread rapidly through the Mediterranean region, causing major epidemics in wild and domestic European rabbits in Spain from 1988 and Portugal from 1989, and by 1990 affecting large parts of France. Across the late 1980s and early 1990s, mortality in wild rabbit populations in the Iberian Peninsula and southern France often reached 55–75%, with severe losses in commercial rabbitries. By the mid‑1990s, as host immunity, vaccination and improved management developed, RHD became enzootic with lower but recurrent mortality.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid dissemination via trade in live rabbits and rabbit meat, movement of infected carcasses and fomites, and dense wild rabbit populations in Mediterranean agro‑ecosystems with little pre‑existing immunity to RHDV. Internal mechanisms: introduction and establishment of highly virulent classical RHDV1 (GI.1) lineages capable of efficient fecal–oral and fomite transmission; no clear evidence of a novel strain within this period, so the global significance of this episode lies in its role as the first establishment of RHDV in Europe and its massive demographic impact on wild rabbits rather than in viral evolution per se.
Review: review – Retain this event as one of the largest global RHD episodes, but reinterpret it as the Europe‑wide emergence/establishment of classical RHDV1. Corrected: (i) event years widened to 1986–1993 to cover the initial Italian outbreaks that are epidemiologically linked to the early 1990s Iberian epidemic; (ii) sub_regions expanded from only Southern Europe to "Southern Europe; Western Europe" because France is in Western Europe; (iii) countries list updated to add Italy and correct first reported years (Italy 1986, Spain 1988, Portugal 1989, France circa 1990) based on regional reviews; (iv) event type changed from a re‑occurrence to an inter‑continental emergence, because this episode represents the first establishment of RHDV in Europe following the 1984 Chinese emergence, not a resurgence in a previously affected European sub‑region. These changes should be checked against project‑wide conventions on whether multi‑year pre‑1990 start dates are allowed when outbreaks continue past 1990.

Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: Rabbit haemorrhagic disease was first reported in domestic rabbits in Sharkia Governorate, Egypt, in 1991, marking the recognized introduction of RHDV1 to Africa. Subsequent outbreaks in the early to mid‑1990s caused substantial mortality and economic losses in commercial rabbitries in Egypt, and by 1992–1993 RHD was also confirmed in Tunisia. By the late 1990s, classical RHDV was considered established in parts of North Africa and managed through biosecurity and vaccination rather than eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of infected breeding stock or rabbit products from Europe or Asia, high‑density commercial rabbit production with limited initial biosecurity, and lack of prior immunity in North African rabbit populations. Internal mechanisms: establishment of classical RHDV1 (GI.1) lineages in a previously naïve continent, with high virulence but no strong evidence that distinct African‑specific antigenic variants arose during this early period.
Review: review – Retain as the first well‑documented introduction of RHDV1 to Africa, representing an inter‑continental emergence. Corrected: (i) countries field now lists Egypt [1991] plus Tunisia [1992–1993] instead of a vague reference to "probable spread to neighbouring countries," using primary reports from Egypt and Tunisia; (ii) clarified in the narrative that this represents the recognized continental incursion of classical RHDV, not RHDV2. Event type (inter_continental_emergence = yes; others = no) is appropriate and should be kept.

Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: In late 1988, rabbit haemorrhagic disease was introduced into Mexico, likely via imported frozen rabbit meat from China, leading to a major epidemic of RHDV1 in domestic rabbitries from 1989 to 1991. Mexican authorities implemented extensive stamping‑out, movement controls, disinfection and serologic surveillance, ultimately destroying more than 120,000 rabbits as part of eradication efforts. The last outbreak was reported in 1992, and Mexico was declared free of RHD thereafter, with subsequent detections linked to later RHDV2 introductions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction through contaminated rabbit meat or live rabbits from endemic regions, rapid spread via movement of animals and contaminated equipment between farms, and lack of prior awareness or immunity. Internal mechanisms: establishment of virulent RHDV1 (RHDVa) in a naïve domestic rabbit population in the Americas; no new genotype is implicated, and disease control relied on depopulation and movement restrictions rather than evolutionary changes in the virus.
Review: review – Retain as the key event representing the first introduction and subsequent eradication of RHDV1 in the Americas. Corrected: (i) event years adjusted from 1990–1992 to 1988–1992 to reflect the documented start of the epidemic in late 1988 with control and eradication completed by 1992; (ii) this remains classified as an inter‑continental emergence because it is the first recognized occurrence of RHDV in the Western Hemisphere. Country and sub‑region coding (Mexico in South America | Central America) are consistent with the project’s country sheet.

Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: The Czech CAPM 351 RHDV1 strain was imported into Australian quarantine facilities in 1991 as a potential rabbit biocontrol agent and released to field‑trial sites on Wardang Island in 1995, from where it accidentally escaped to mainland South Australia and spread rapidly across much of the continent, causing large declines in wild rabbit populations. The virus was then deliberately released nationwide in 1996 and became established as a key biocontrol tool. In 1997, RHDV1 was illegally introduced into New Zealand, where it likewise caused major reductions in feral rabbit numbers before settling into enzootic circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: deliberate importation and field trials for biological control in Australia, accidental escape from quarantine, intentional releases by land managers, and extensive feral rabbit populations in arid and agricultural landscapes with minimal prior immunity. Internal mechanisms: high virulence and efficient transmission of the Czech CAPM 351 strain in wild European rabbits, with subsequent selection for host resistance and attenuation over time but no major antigenic shift at introduction.
Review: retain – This is an essential event representing the deliberate and accidental introduction of RHDV1 as a biocontrol agent in Oceania, with very large ecological and economic impacts. Country and sub‑region assignments (Australia and New Zealand; Oceania) and classification as an inter‑continental emergence are appropriate. Source set already relies mainly on primary and governmental documents; Wikipedia could be dropped at a later clean‑up stage but is not critical.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: France [2010], Spain [2011], Portugal [2012], Italy [2011], Netherlands [2011-2012], United Kingdom (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland) [2013-2014], Ireland [2014], additional European countries and islands by 2014
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus); some hare species (Lepus spp., including Sardinian Cape hare)
Event summary: In 2010, a novel pathogenic lagovirus with distinct antigenic and genetic characteristics, later designated RHDV2 or Lagovirus europaeus/GI.2, was identified in domestic and wild rabbits in north‑western France, including cases in previously vaccinated and younger animals. Over the next several years, RHDV2 spread rapidly across continental Europe and nearby islands—including Spain, Portugal, Italy, the Netherlands, the UK and Ireland—often replacing classical RHDV1 as the dominant circulating strain. By around 2014, RHDV2 had become enzootic in much of Western and Southern Europe, with recurrent outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs and initial documented spillover into hares.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive movement of domestic rabbits and rabbit products across Europe, high densities of wild European rabbits, and widespread vaccination programs targeting only RHDV1 which provided limited cross‑protection to RHDV2. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a recombinant GI.2 genotype with a distinct antigenic profile, broader age susceptibility (including young rabbits), partial escape from existing RHDV1 immunity and vaccines, and enhanced fitness relative to classical strains, resulting in rapid replacement of GI.1 and clear re‑emergence mediated by novel strain/genotype emergence and host expansion.
Review: review – Retain as the foundational global event for RHDV2 emergence but adjust classification. This episode represents (i) first detection of GI.2/RHDV2 globally and (ii) re‑emergence of the EPP in Europe driven by a novel genotype with altered antigenicity and host range. However, per project definitions, it should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence because RHDV (the EPP) was already widespread in all the affected European sub‑regions; spread of a new serotype within an already infected continent is to be treated as re‑emergence. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to "false" while first_detection and re_emergence remain "true".

Sub-regions: Australia and New Zealand (Australia focus for this event)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: Serologic data indicate that RHDV2 was circulating in Australian wild rabbits by spring 2014 and was first confirmed virologically in May 2015 in a wild rabbit in New South Wales. Within roughly 18 months, RHDV2 had spread across all Australian states and territories, rapidly displacing existing RHDV1 field strains and causing average declines of around 60% in monitored wild rabbit populations. By 2016–2017, RHDV2 had become the predominant lagovirus biocontrol agent in Australia, complicating planned releases of additional RHDV1 strains but significantly suppressing rabbit numbers in many regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive connectivity of wild rabbit populations across open landscapes, mechanical spread by insect vectors and fomites, and strong selection pressure from existing RHDV1 biocontrol leading to partial host immunity. Internal mechanisms: introduction and rapid geographic expansion of RHDV2/GI.2 with apparent fitness advantages over RHDV1, including infection of younger age classes, broader host range and partial vaccine/immunity escape, resulting in both inter‑continental emergence of GI.2 into Oceania and re‑emergence of RHD as a more effective biocontrol agent.
Review: retain – Keep as a major event, representing the rapid establishment and dominance of RHDV2 as a biocontrol agent in Australia. Classification as both inter‑continental emergence (for GI.2 into Oceania) and re‑emergence (novel genotype supplanting existing RHDV1 in an already affected sub‑region) is consistent with the project rules. Country, timing and impact are well supported by primary sources.

Sub-regions: Northern America; South America | Central America
Countries: Canada [2016], United States of America [2018-2019 domestic; 2020 wild], Mexico [2020]
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus); native North American rabbits and hares (Sylvilagus spp., Lepus spp., Brachylagus idahoensis)
Event summary: RHDV2 was first detected in North America in August 2016 in domestic rabbits in Quebec, Canada, followed by outbreaks in pet and feral rabbits in British Columbia and sporadic introductions into U.S. domestic rabbits in 2018–2019. In early 2020, a large multi‑state outbreak began in the southwestern United States, with RHDV2 detected in domestic, feral and then wild lagomorphs in New Mexico, Arizona, Texas and neighbouring states, and subsequently spreading to wild populations in at least 14 U.S. states and into northern Mexico. During 2020–2022, the virus became established across much of the western and parts of central U.S. and in regions of Mexico, affecting multiple native cottontails, jackrabbits and pygmy rabbits as well as domestic and feral European rabbits, while some Canadian incursions (e.g. British Columbia 2018, 2020) were successfully contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movements of infected domestic rabbits, fomites (equipment, feed, carcasses) and possibly contaminated products among Canada, the USA and Mexico; abundant susceptible wild lagomorph populations in arid and semi‑arid habitats; and initially limited vaccination coverage in domestic rabbits. Internal mechanisms: RHDV2’s broader host range (multiple Sylvilagus species, Lepus spp. and pygmy rabbits), ability to infect young animals, and partial vaccine escape facilitated successful establishment and rapid geographic range expansion, constituting both inter‑continental emergence into the Americas and re‑emergence of the EPP through host expansion and novel genotype dominance.
Review: retain – This event appropriately summarizes the inter‑continental emergence and subsequent establishment of RHDV2 across Canada, the United States and Mexico, including spillover to native North American lagomorphs. Continent and sub‑region coding (North America overall, with Northern America and South America | Central America to capture Mexico’s classification) is acceptable, and the event correctly distinguishes between early, contained domestic outbreaks and the large 2020–2022 southwestern U.S.–Mexico epizootic. Event‑type classification as inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence (novel genotype with host expansion) is appropriate.

Sub-regions: Australia and New Zealand (New Zealand focus for this event)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: New Zealand, which had experienced illegal introduction of RHDV1 in 1997, remained free of RHDV2 until its first confirmed detection in 2018 during surveillance following the legal release of RHDV1‑K5, with retrospective evidence of circulation in wild rabbits since at least late 2017. From 2018 to 2021, RHDV2 spread widely through feral rabbit populations and occasionally affected domestic rabbits across multiple regions, co‑circulating with several RHDV1 variants. By the early 2020s, RHDV2 was considered established across much of New Zealand, prompting updated vaccination strategies for pet and farmed rabbits.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: probable unauthorized or inadvertent introduction of an exotic RHDV2 strain, movement of infected carcasses and rabbits within New Zealand, and extensive feral rabbit populations already under selection pressure from RHDV1 biocontrol. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward spread of a distinct New Zealand RHDV2 recombinant lineage (GI.3P‑GI.2) capable of efficiently infecting wild rabbits and co‑circulating with RHDV1, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by novel strain emergence and competitive replacement dynamics within an already infected sub‑region.
Review: review – Retain as a major RHDV2 event in Oceania but adjust event‑type classification. Because the UN sub‑region "Australia and New Zealand" already contained RHDV2 from 2014 via Australia, spread to New Zealand represents expansion to a new country within the same sub‑region rather than to a new sub‑region. Under the project rules, such spread should not be labeled intra‑continental emergence. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to "false" and the episode is treated purely as re‑emergence driven by introduction and establishment of a new GI.3P‑GI.2 lineage in a country where RHDV (the EPP) was already present (via RHDV1).

Sub-regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Morocco [2017], Côte d’Ivoire [≥2016], Egypt [2018], Tunisia [2018], Ghana [2019], Nigeria [2020], Benin [2020], Senegal [2020], South Africa [2020]
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: Following its emergence in Europe, RHDV2 was reported in northern Africa by 2017, with a recombinant GI.1b/GI.2 strain detected in Morocco and subsequent detections in Egypt and Tunisia. Molecular evidence indicates that RHDV2 had reached Côte d’Ivoire by at least 2016, and from 2018–2020 the virus spread widely through West Africa, causing high‑mortality outbreaks in commercial rabbitries in countries such as Ghana, Nigeria, Benin and Senegal. In Ghana alone, a 2019 outbreak affected approximately 11,350 rabbits and killed about 6,000 animals across multiple farms. By around 2020, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, and the virus became a major cause of losses in domestic rabbits across several African sub‑regions, with repeated outbreaks and ongoing risk of further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased legal and illegal trade in breeding stock and rabbit meat between Europe, North Africa and West Africa; limited biosecurity and high animal densities in small‑scale and commercial rabbitries; and scarce access to vaccines matched to RHDV2. Internal mechanisms: introduction and establishment of RHDV2/GI.2 and recombinant variants (e.g. GI.1b/GI.2 in Morocco) into regions that were previously free of RHD, creating intra‑continental emergence into new African sub‑regions (West and Southern Africa) while also causing re‑emergence in North African areas where classical RHDV1 had circulated earlier.
Review: review – Retain as a continent‑scale RHDV2 emergence episode but correct geography and clarify mechanisms. Changes: (i) sub_regions expanded from "Northern Africa; Western Africa" to include "Southern Africa" because South Africa is involved; (ii) countries list updated to explicitly name Côte d’Ivoire, Tunisia and South Africa with approximate first‑detection years drawn from WOAH/WAHIS‑based reviews, while keeping Morocco 2017 and Ghana 2019; (iii) event classification kept as both intra‑continental emergence (first occurrence of the EPP in new African sub‑regions, notably West and Southern Africa) and re‑emergence (replacement of RHDV1 by RHDV2 in North Africa), which is consistent with the rule that re‑emergence can co‑occur with intra‑continental emergence. Because some country‑level start years remain approximate, this row should be double‑checked against the project’s preferred cutoff dates.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Italy [2011-2012], Spain [2011-2014], Sardinia (Italy) [2011], Sicily (Italy) [2012], France [2013], Sweden [2016-2017], Germany [2017], Netherlands [2017], Ireland [2018-2019], United Kingdom [2018-2019]
Host: Multiple hare species (Lepus capensis mediterraneus, Lepus europaeus, Lepus timidus, Lepus corsicanus, Lepus granatensis, Lepus townsendii in introduced populations) and European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: Beginning around 2011, RHDV2—which initially emerged as a rabbit pathogen—was confirmed as the cause of fatal hepatitis outbreaks in Sardinian Cape hares in Italy, and soon after in Italian hares in Sicily. Over the 2010s, additional spillover and sometimes sustained outbreaks were documented in European brown hares, mountain hares, Iberian hares and Irish hares in several European countries, including Italy, Spain, France, Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland and the UK, typically in areas where RHDV2 was enzootic in sympatric rabbit populations. By the late 2010s, these events had established RHDV2 as a multi‑host lagovirus within European lagomorph communities, with ongoing sporadic mortality in multiple hare species of conservation and hunting importance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high ecological overlap between dense European rabbit populations and sympatric hare species, landscape connectivity enabling frequent contact with contaminated carcasses and environmental virus, and absence of prior immunity to RHDV2 in hares. Internal mechanisms: host expansion and partial breakdown of species barriers by RHDV2/GI.2, likely facilitated by recombination and antigenic changes broadening cell tropism, resulting in re‑emergence of the EPP in existing European sub‑regions through infection of new host species without major additional geographic expansion.
Review: review – Retain this event because cross‑species establishment of RHDV2 in multiple European hare species is a globally important host‑expansion episode, but correct its classification and country coverage. Adjustments: (i) intra_continental_emergence set to "false" because the EPP (Lagovirus europaeus) was already present throughout the listed European sub‑regions; this event reflects host expansion within existing areas, not first occurrence in new sub‑regions; (ii) re_emergence remains "true" as this is a classic case of re‑emergence via host expansion; (iii) countries list expanded to include France and the Netherlands, and to clarify Sardinia and Sicily as separate island foci, based on detailed reports and reviews. The time window (2011–2019) and focus on major, well‑documented hare outbreaks remain appropriate.

Countries: Brazil [urban foci first widely recognized 1990s, expansion across 1990s–2010s]; Paraguay [1990s–2000s, spread from Brazil border]; Argentina [late 1990s–2000s, northern provinces]; Uruguay [2000s, emergence from Brazil/Argentina corridors]
Host: Domestic dogs (primary reservoir), with incidental infection in humans; occasional infection in other domestic animals and peri‑domestic wildlife
Event summary: Beginning in the late 1980s–early 1990s, Brazil experienced a marked urbanization and geographic spread of canine visceral leishmaniasis (CVL) caused by Leishmania infantum, with new urban foci in large northeastern cities like Natal and later expansion west and south into central and southern states. Throughout the 1990s–2010s, dispersal of the sandfly vector Lutzomyia longipalpis along highways, pipelines and peri‑urban settlements, together with movement of infected dogs, drove sustained transmission and establishment of CVL in dozens of municipalities, including border areas with Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay. By the mid‑2010s, autochthonous canine and human VL had been reported in roughly a quarter of Brazilian municipalities and in neighboring Southern Cone countries, reflecting a continent‑wide re‑emergence and range expansion rather than isolated outbreaks, with control efforts (dog culling, insecticide spraying, collars) proving only partially effective before incidence began to plateau locally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid and unplanned urbanization with expansion of peri‑urban slums, deforestation and ecosystem modification, major infrastructure projects (roads, dams, gas pipeline) facilitating vector and dog movement, internal migration from rural endemic zones to cities, poverty and poor sanitation, and inconsistent implementation of vector and reservoir control programs. Internal mechanisms: enhanced transmission/vector adaptation (Lutzomyia longipalpis adapting to peri‑domestic and urban habitats and to feeding on dogs and humans), and possible geographic range expansion traits in the vector–parasite system; no single novel parasite genotype dominates, but L. infantum’s adaptation to urban dog populations underpins sustained transmission. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001706X16301231))

Countries: United States of America [first recognized 1999–2000 in Virginia and other eastern states]; Canada [early 2000s, Ontario and neighboring provinces]
Host: Foxhounds (kenneled hunting dogs) as primary affected population; other dog breeds occasionally; humans rarely exposed
Event summary: In the summer of 1999–2000, severe systemic illness compatible with visceral leishmaniosis was recognized in foxhounds in a Virginia kennel, and Leishmania infantum was subsequently isolated and characterized, revealing an unsuspected endemic focus in North American dogs. Over the next 5–6 years, intensive surveillance showed spread of infection through foxhound networks, with seropositive dogs detected in at least 60 kennels across 22 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces, largely via movement of breeding and hunting dogs and non‑vector routes such as vertical and dog‑to‑dog transmission. Control measures including culling of severely affected dogs, kennel hygiene, and movement restrictions slowed the epidemic within foxhound populations, but low‑level infection persisted and seeded later autochthonous cases in other breeds and species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense kennel housing, frequent interstate and cross‑border movement of foxhounds for breeding and hunts, lack of prior awareness or screening for leishmaniosis, and absence or scarcity of competent sandfly vectors in much of the affected area leading to reliance on non‑vector routes. Internal mechanisms: host expansion and enhanced non‑vector transmission (vertical, venereal, bite‑associated) among dogs, allowing maintenance of L. infantum without classical sandfly transmission; no clear evidence of a novel genotype, but adaptation to vertical and direct transmission may have been selected in this closed dog population. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2824922/))

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Portugal [endemic focus with increasing prevalence 2000s]; Spain [northward expansion from Mediterranean to interior and northern regions 2000s–2010s]; Italy [expansion from traditional southern foci to north‑central regions 2000s–2010s]; Greece [endemic with fluctuating incidence]; France [Mediterranean coast endemic, emergence further inland]; Germany [sporadic autochthonous canine cases from 2000s, increasing risk up to 2020s]; Switzerland [sporadic autochthonous infections 2010s]; Austria [emergent foci in 2010s–2020s]; Hungary [first autochthonous canine cases reported 2000s–2010s]; Czechia [autocthonous Leishmania martiniquensis in horses 2019–2023 but canine exposure documented]; United Kingdom [imported canine cases throughout, occasional suspected local transmission]; Sweden [imported canine cases and potential vector establishment]
Host: Domestic dogs (primary reservoir host for L. infantum); increasing recognition of infection in cats and horses as secondary hosts in some countries
Event summary: From the early 2000s onward, canine leishmaniosis in Europe shifted from a largely Mediterranean‑bounded disease toward broader distribution, with rising prevalence in traditional endemic areas of Portugal, Spain, Italy and Greece and gradual northward expansion into central and northern countries such as France, Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Hungary, supported by occasional autochthonous canine infections. During the 2010s–early 2020s, surveillance and serological studies revealed increasing seropositivity in dogs in previously non‑endemic or marginal regions, coinciding with detection of competent Phlebotomus vectors in more northerly zones and large numbers of infected imported dogs from southern Europe. Control initiatives including vector repellents, vaccination of dogs, and awareness campaigns have mitigated incidence in some endemic foci, but climatic warming, dog movements and shifting sandfly distributions continue to drive re‑emergence and intra‑continental spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: climate warming and milder winters enabling northward expansion and higher seasonal activity of Phlebotomus sandflies; increased movement and trade of pet dogs (including rescue/import of infected dogs from Mediterranean shelters); urbanization, peri‑urban green spaces and peri‑domestic chicken/pigeon rearing creating suitable vector habitats; and socio‑economic changes affecting dog ownership and outdoor exposure. Internal mechanisms: enhanced transmission/vector adaptation (Phlebotomus spp. adapting to peri‑domestic and urban environments), geographic range expansion traits in vectors and possibly parasites, and host expansion to non‑canine species; no single new parasite genotype dominates, but microevolution and strain turnover are documented. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11206782/))

Countries: United States of America [multiple states in the Midwest, South and Southwest with autochthonous animal cases]; Canada [sporadic foxhound and other dogs infected with L. infantum]
Host: Dogs (foxhounds and other breeds), domestic cats, horses, wild canids and small mammals in some foci
Event summary: Following the initial foxhound outbreaks, autochthonous leishmaniosis in animals became increasingly recognized across the United States and Canada from the early 2000s onward, with surveys documenting L. infantum‑infected hunting dogs, sporadic infections in other breeds, and occasional infections in cats, horses and wildlife in regions where competent sandfly vectors such as Lutzomyia shannoni and Lutzomyia vexator occur. Between 2006 and 2019, a large retrospective dataset of canine samples from the U.S. and Canada showed that around 6% of dogs clinically suspected of leishmaniosis were infected, with many cases linked to travel or importation but a subset meeting criteria for local acquisition in areas such as Texas, Oklahoma and the Midwest. Despite continued absence of widespread human visceral disease, this period established a low‑level but persistent animal reservoir with both vector and non‑vector transmission routes, complicating eradication and introducing ongoing risk of zoonotic transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: sustained foxhound reservoir after 1999–2005 outbreak; increasing international and interstate movement of dogs (including rescues and military working dogs) from endemic regions; presence and gradual documentation of competent sandfly vectors in southern and central U.S.; changing land use, suburbanization and outdoor dog housing practices that increase vector–host contact. Internal mechanisms: host expansion to non‑foxhound dog breeds, cats, horses and wildlife; enhanced non‑vector transmission pathways (vertical, venereal, transfusion) enabling maintenance of L. infantum in areas with marginal vector presence; possible adaptation of parasites and/or host immune selection but no clearly defined novel genotype. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12654226/))

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Spain [equine and feline cases increasingly reported from 2010s]; Italy [equine and feline cases 2010s]; Portugal [feline cases 2010s–2020s]; France [equine/feline cases 2010s]; Germany [first reports of L. martiniquensis and L. infantum infections 2010s]; Switzerland [L. martiniquensis infections 2010s]; Austria [equine L. martiniquensis 2019–2023]; Czechia [equine L. martiniquensis 2019–2023]; Greece [feline cases]
Host: Horses and donkeys (equine cutaneous leishmaniosis, primarily L. infantum and L. martiniquensis); domestic cats (feline leishmaniosis) as emerging hosts; dogs as established reservoirs in same areas
Event summary: During the 2010s, veterinary case reports and small series from Spain, Italy, Portugal, France and other European countries documented increasing numbers of autochthonous equine cutaneous leishmaniosis cases, mostly caused by L. infantum but also by the Mundinia species L. martiniquensis, initially recognized in central Europe in Germany and Switzerland and then reported in horses in Austria and Czechia between 2019 and 2023. In parallel, feline leishmaniosis emerged as a recognized clinical entity in cats living in, or imported from, endemic canine leishmaniosis areas of southern Europe, with prevalence in cats ranging from near zero to more than 60% in some surveys and a growing body of evidence that cats may act as secondary reservoirs. By the early 2020s, these findings established horses and cats as important non‑canine hosts involved in the broader Leishmania transmission cycle in Europe, prompting updates to veterinary guidelines and heightened awareness among practitioners.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high environmental force of infection in endemic areas due to abundant infected dogs and competent sandflies; increased diagnostic awareness and use of molecular tests in veterinary practice; movement and trade of horses and cats across Europe; and climate‑driven changes in sandfly distributions. Internal mechanisms: host expansion/spillover (Leishmania spp., particularly L. infantum and L. martiniquensis, adapting or being recognized in equine and feline hosts); enhanced transmission via broader vertebrate host range; and, in the case of L. martiniquensis, likely geographic range expansion and possibly novel genotype introduction into central Europe. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/31/9/25-0254_article))

Countries: Spain [feline and canine cases with recognized reservoir role 2010s]; Italy [feline cases 2010s–2020s]; Portugal [feline cases 2010s–2020s]; Greece [feline cases 2010s]; France [feline cases in endemic areas and imported cats]
Host: Domestic cats (primary focus for this event) with concurrent canine reservoirs and human cases in the same environments
Event summary: From around 2010, reports from southern European countries began to highlight feline leishmaniosis as an emerging disease, with case series and serosurveys showing that cats in endemic canine leishmaniosis regions of Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece and France were frequently infected with L. infantum and occasionally developed clinical disease. Over the 2010s–early 2020s, accumulating evidence of high seroprevalence in some cat populations, natural infection of sandflies feeding on cats, and detection of parasite DNA in feline tissues shifted the perception of cats from rare incidental hosts to potential secondary reservoirs in certain foci. This recognition led to increasing inclusion of feline leishmaniosis in diagnostic differentials for feline dermatologic and systemic disease in endemic and even some non‑endemic European areas receiving imported cats, though the exact quantitative contribution of cats to human and canine transmission remains under study.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high background transmission intensity in Mediterranean canine foci; expanding domestic cat populations with outdoor lifestyles; importation and movement of cats between endemic and non‑endemic regions; and wider use of sensitive molecular and serologic diagnostics that detect subclinical infections. Internal mechanisms: host expansion/spillover (L. infantum increasingly infecting and adapting to cats); possible changes in feline immunity or co‑factors (e.g., retroviral infections) enhancing susceptibility; and enhanced transmission through increased diversity of mammalian hosts available to vectors. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feline_leishmaniosis))

Countries: French Guiana [2016 emergence of autochthonous canine L. infantum]; France [military working dogs seroconvert after deployment to French Guiana and return to mainland France]
Host: Domestic dogs (including military working dogs) as reservoirs; humans at risk for zoonotic infection
Event summary: In 2016, molecular surveys in Cayenne, French Guiana, identified autochthonous Leishmania infantum infection in local dogs with an estimated prevalence of about 3%, marking the first clear evidence of a local canine visceral leishmaniasis transmission cycle in this previously non‑endemic part of the Guiana Shield. Around the same time, military working dogs deployed from France to French Guiana and tested negative before deployment were found infected on return, further confirming local transmission in South America’s northeastern coastal region. Subsequent years saw continued detection of infected dogs and sandflies, although the focus remained geographically limited, and public health responses concentrated on vector control and monitoring of canine and human cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: environmental changes and urban/peri‑urban development in and around Cayenne creating suitable habitats for sandfly vectors; movement of domestic and working dogs between Europe and French Guiana; and limited prior surveillance masking earlier low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of L. infantum to a new part of the South American coast; host expansion and establishment of dogs as a local reservoir; and efficient transmission via competent local Lutzomyia vectors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11061994/))

Countries: Costa Rica [first autochthonous canine L. infantum infections in 2023–2025, following earlier imported case from Spain]
Host: Domestic dogs (clinically affected and subclinical carriers); humans potentially exposed but not the primary focus of this event
Event summary: Between 2023 and 2025, veterinarians in Costa Rica diagnosed a series of dogs with clinical signs compatible with visceral leishmaniosis and confirmed infection with Leishmania infantum using serology and PCR, establishing the first autochthonous canine visceral leishmaniasis cases in the country after a prior imported case from Spain. Phylogenetic analysis of kinetoplast DNA revealed that Costa Rican L. infantum sequences clustered with Old World strains rather than typical Brazilian isolates, suggesting recent introduction from Europe rather than spread from traditional South American foci. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of an Old World L. infantum lineage into Central America; host expansion/establishment in local dog populations; and enhanced transmission potential where appropriate Lutzomyia vectors are present. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12870656/))

Countries: Morocco [urban and peri‑urban expansion of CVL 1990s–2010s]; Tunisia [similar expansion 1990s–2010s]; Algeria [endemic CVL with fluctuating incidence 1990s–2010s]
Host: Domestic dogs as main reservoir for zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis; humans as spillover hosts; occasional infection in other domestic animals
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the mid‑2010s, canine visceral leishmaniasis in North African countries such as Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria transitioned from primarily rural, focal transmission to more widespread urban and peri‑urban circulation as dogs and vectors adapted to changing environments. Over this period, multiple studies documented increasing prevalence of L. infantum infection in dogs in expanding peri‑urban belts around major cities, with associated rises and periodic outbreaks of human zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis in children. Control efforts, including dog culling, insecticide use and environmental management, produced only partial and temporally limited reductions in incidence, and the disease is now considered entrenched in many urban and peri‑urban settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: urbanization and peri‑urbanization, expansion of irrigated agriculture and peri‑domestic animal husbandry, poverty and inadequate waste management, and climatic variability affecting Phlebotomus sandfly populations. Internal mechanisms: enhanced transmission/vector adaptation (Phlebotomus spp. adapting to peri‑domestic habitats and urban environments); geographic range expansion of both vectors and parasites within North Africa; and possible strain selection under control pressure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11206782/))

Countries: Türkiye [expansion of canine leishmaniosis from Aegean/Mediterranean coast to inland regions 2000s–2010s]; Israel [CVL in dogs in peri‑urban and rural settings 2000s–2010s]; Cyprus [endemic CVL with urban spread]; Greece [bridge between Asian and European foci, expansion in northern regions 2000s–2010s]
Host: Domestic dogs (primary reservoir host), with infection in cats and potentially wildlife in some areas
Event summary: Between roughly 2005 and 2020, canine leishmaniosis in the Eastern Mediterranean region encompassing Türkiye, Israel, Cyprus and Greece underwent notable geographic expansion and intensification, with previously marginal or non‑endemic inland and northern zones reporting increasing canine seroprevalence and clinical cases. This period was marked by greater recognition of L. infantum infection in owned and stray dogs in peri‑urban belts, ports and tourist centers, and by increasing documentation of infection in cats and wildlife near human settlements. Control initiatives varied among countries but generally lagged behind the pace of spread, and by around 2020 the region was recognized as a major trans‑continental corridor for Leishmania circulation between Asia and Europe through dog movement and vector dispersal.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: climate and environmental changes favoring Phlebotomus vectors; growth of peri‑urban settlements and stray dog populations; high volume of dog movement associated with tourism, trade and informal rescue networks; and limited, fragmented control programs. Internal mechanisms: enhanced transmission/vector adaptation and geographic range expansion of both vectors and parasites; host expansion to cats and wildlife contributing to re‑emergence and maintenance of transmission. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11206782/))

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; South America; Northern America
Countries: Italy [example of intensive use of canine leishmaniosis vaccines and collars]; Brazil [pilot and large‑scale use of dog culling and insecticide‑impregnated collars]; United States of America [use of repellents and monitoring in foxhounds and other dogs]
Host: Domestic dogs (primary reservoir and vaccination target); indirectly, humans and other animals benefiting from reduced transmission risk
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, large‑scale deployment of control tools targeting canine reservoirs—including leishmaniosis vaccines, insecticide‑impregnated collars and culling of seropositive dogs—was rolled out in highly endemic countries like Brazil and in parts of southern Europe such as Italy and Spain, affecting the epidemiology of CVL at regional scales. Over the following decade, these interventions led to transient declines in canine and human visceral leishmaniasis incidence in some areas, but the disease repeatedly re‑emerged due to operational challenges, incomplete coverage and ecological compensation by sandflies and other hosts. By approximately 2020, it had become clear that while these measures could reduce incidence, they did not eliminate canine leishmaniosis, and new waves of infection and geographic expansion continued to appear in Latin America, the Mediterranean and North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: public health policy and programmatic changes introducing new control strategies; socio‑economic constraints limiting sustained high‑coverage implementation; and community reactions to dog culling influencing program adherence. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence driven by partial selection for parasite or vector traits under insecticidal and immunological pressure; potential shifts in strain composition; and maintenance of L. infantum transmission through alternative hosts and non‑vector pathways when canine infection is partially suppressed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4211574/))

Host: Iberian hare (Lepus granatensis), European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus, including O. c. algirus), domestic rabbits
Event summary: In early summer 2018, a novel recombinant myxoma virus strain (often termed ha-MYXV/MYXV-Tol) spilled over from long-established rabbit reservoirs to Iberian hares in central and southern Spain, causing high mortality and the first documented large-scale myxomatosis outbreaks in this endemic hare species. The virus rapidly spread across multiple regions of Spain during 2018–2019 and was soon detected in Iberian hares and sympatric wild rabbits and domestic rabbits in neighbouring areas of Portugal. By 2020, myxomatosis had become enzootic in Iberian hares across much of the Iberian Peninsula, with marked declines in hare abundance and hunting bags but with incidence stabilizing as populations partially adapted and management and surveillance were strengthened.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term endemic circulation of myxoma virus in European wild and domestic rabbits in the Iberian Peninsula created a high-force-of-infection environment; high densities and artificial aggregation of lagomorphs in game-managed estates, together with overlapping habitats of rabbits and Iberian hares, facilitated cross-species transmission; environmental conditions in Mediterranean agroecosystems and vector presence (arthropods) supported efficient spread; intensive hunting and translocations of lagomorphs likely contributed to wider dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – a natural recombinant myxoma virus (ha-MYXV/MYXV-Tol) acquired genetic material that enabled efficient infection and severe disease in Iberian hares, a species previously considered largely resistant, representing a major host-range expansion; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – genomic analyses revealed that the outbreak was caused by a distinct recombinant lineage derived from classic European rabbit MYXV strains, with insertions and rearrangements in virulence-associated genes; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – the recombinant virus caused peracute to acute fatal disease in Iberian hares with high case fatality and substantial population impacts; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – while specific vector adaptations remain under study, high viral loads and clinical presentation favored mosquito/flea transmission, sustaining epidemics over multiple seasons; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – once established in hares, the recombinant virus spread across much of Spain and Portugal, occupying new ecological niches in hare populations beyond the long-standing rabbit reservoir.
Review: retain – Event accurately represents the 2018–2020 emergence of the hare‑adapted recombinant myxoma virus (ha-MYXV) in Iberian hares and sympatric rabbits in Spain and Portugal, including timing, affected hosts, geography (Southern Europe; Spain and Portugal), and major impacts on hare populations. Classification as re-emergence (new recombinant lineage and host expansion within a subregion where MYXV was already endemic in rabbits) and not as first detection or intra-/inter‑continental emergence is consistent with the definitions in the protocol, and the cited literature and official reports substantiate the storyline and mechanisms. No changes required.

Host: European brown hare (Lepus europaeus), European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event summary: From 2023, sporadic cases of severe myxomatosis were detected in European brown hares in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, in an area where myxoma virus had long circulated only in rabbits, and retrospective testing confirmed infection with the hare-adapted recombinant lineage ha-MYXV. In summer–autumn 2024, reports of sick and dead brown hares with classic myxomatosis-like lesions surged on both sides of the Germany–Netherlands border, and laboratory investigations in Germany and the Netherlands documented a large regional outbreak of ha-MYXV in brown hares, with some sympatric wild rabbits infected by either ha-MYXV or classical MYXV. During 2024–2025, surveillance showed radial and northward spread within this border region and continuing high hare mortality, prompting coordinated cross-border wildlife disease monitoring while the longer-term population impacts and potential for further spread across Western and Northern Europe remained under active assessment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued circulation of the hare-adapted MYXV lineage (ha-MYXV) in the Iberian Peninsula, combined with natural movements and possibly human-assisted translocations of hares and rabbits or contaminated fomites, likely facilitated long-distance introduction into the Germany–Netherlands border region; landscape connectivity and sympatry of rabbits and European brown hares in agricultural and peri-urban habitats favored cross-species transmission; climatic conditions and abundant arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, fleas) in this temperate region supported establishment and seasonal amplification of the virus. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – the same recombinant ha-MYXV lineage that had adapted to Iberian hares demonstrated the capacity to infect and cause lethal disease in European brown hares, representing further host-range expansion within Lepus spp.; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – genomic sequencing showed that German and Dutch ha-MYXV isolates clustered within the Iberian recombinant clade, confirming spread and ongoing evolution within this lineage rather than a de novo recombinant; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – infection in European brown hares produced classic myxomatosis lesions with high case-fatality, indicating high virulence in this new host; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – the virus maintained efficient transmission in cooler, more temperate Western European conditions compared with the Mediterranean origin area, implying robust transmission traits that support persistence across a broader climatic gradient; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – this event represents intra-continental spatial expansion of ha-MYXV from Southern to Western Europe, establishing new foci in hare populations outside the original Iberian range, even though MYXV as a species was already endemic in Western European rabbits.
Review: review – Event is retained as a major episode but I corrected the emergence-type classification and timing and expanded the supporting sources. Specifically: (1) intra_continental_emergence has been set from true to false because MYXV has been endemic in rabbits in Western Europe since the 1950s, so this outbreak represents spread of a recombinant lineage and host expansion within an already affected subregion and should be classified solely as re-emergence under the protocol definitions; (2) the event year has been extended from 2023–2024 to 2023–2025 to reflect evidence from Dutch surveillance that ha-MYXV continued to cause new municipal-level outbreaks and high hare mortality in the Netherlands during 2025 as part of the same regional epizootic; and (3) DWHC outbreak reports (2024 investigation of increased hare mortality and the 2026 focus-species note summarizing 2024–2025 spread) have been added to the source list to complement the primary Emerging Infectious Diseases article, while one background-only Australian evolution paper has been dropped from the event-specific sources.

Host: Humans; reservoir hosts including dogs, rats and other peridomestic mammals; cattle and pigs suspected as additional sources
Event summary: In October–November 1995, rural communities in western Nicaragua experienced an epidemic of acute febrile illness with severe pulmonary hemorrhage after periods of intense rainfall and flooding, and investigations identified leptospirosis caused mainly by L. interrogans serovars in the Canicola and Pyrogenes groups as the principal etiology, with more than 2,000 febrile illnesses evaluated and dozens of deaths. The outbreak developed rapidly among residents heavily exposed to creeks, irrigation channels and flooded fields contaminated with urine from infected dogs, rodents and livestock, and Leptospira were isolated from both human patients and local animals. Transmission declined after floodwaters receded, risk factors such as walking in creeks and dog ownership were publicized, and targeted environmental and rodent-control measures were implemented, but the episode signalled that severe pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis could emerge in Central America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall and flooding inundated rural settlements and farmlands, increasing human contact with water and soil contaminated by urine from infected dogs, rodents, pigs and cattle, while limited sanitation and protective equipment amplified exposure. Internal mechanisms: The event involved highly pathogenic L. interrogans serovars already circulating in local animal reservoirs rather than a demonstrably new genotype, so it represents environmentally driven re-occurrence of virulent lineages rather than de novo microbial evolution.
Review: Retain – Event corresponds to the well-documented 1995 western Nicaragua epidemic with pulmonary hemorrhage; geography and timing match, and classification as re-occurrence (environmentally driven resurgence in an already endemic Central American setting) is appropriate. Minor textual clean-up applied by removing inline citation tags from the host field; case and death magnitudes are within the documented range from CDC/MMWR and subsequent analyses.

Host: Humans; urban rats as primary reservoir; dogs and livestock present in affected communities
Event summary: In 1996, the city of Salvador in northeast Brazil and the state of Rio de Janeiro experienced major urban leptospirosis outbreaks after heavy seasonal rains and flooding, with Rio de Janeiro alone reporting about 1,425 cases and 22 deaths and other coastal cities also affected. The epidemics were concentrated in densely populated low-income neighborhoods with poor drainage, accumulated refuse and heavy rat infestation, where residents were extensively exposed to contaminated floodwater. As rainfall decreased and municipal authorities implemented emergency rodent control, drainage works and public health messaging, case numbers fell, although flood-associated urban leptospirosis has remained a recurring problem in Brazilian coastal cities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intense rainfall and flooding in rapidly urbanizing, informal settlements with inadequate storm-water and solid-waste management led to explosive growth of rat populations and widespread contamination of floodwaters with Leptospira, while poverty, crowding and limited access to protective gear heightened human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate efficient transmission of endemic L. interrogans serovar Copenhageni and related serovars maintained in rodents rather than emergence of a novel genotype, so the episode is best interpreted as a severe, environmentally driven re-occurrence.
Review: Retain – Large, well-characterized urban outbreaks in Rio de Janeiro and Salvador with >1,000 cases and documented deaths; regional coding (South America/South America, Brazil) and re-occurrence classification are consistent with PAHO and Lancet descriptions. Only cosmetic change was removal of inline citation markers from the host field.

Host: Humans; cattle and water buffalo as major livestock reservoirs; pigs and dogs; commensal rodents
Event summary: During the late 1990s, Thailand saw a steep rise in leptospirosis incidence, culminating in a nationwide peak in 2000 with around 14,285 reported human cases, particularly in the northeastern rice-growing provinces. The outbreak was concentrated among agricultural workers exposed to flooded paddy fields and irrigation water contaminated by urine from infected cattle, buffalo, pigs, dogs and rodents, with serosurveys in livestock showing very high infection prevalence in the same regions. After leptospirosis was recognized nationally as a major flood-associated zoonosis and targeted surveillance, health education and some animal-health interventions were implemented, reported incidence declined and stabilized at lower but still substantial levels in subsequent years.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/13/1/06-0718_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of rice agriculture, high-density cattle and buffalo grazing in paddy landscapes, and widespread seasonal flooding greatly increased human–animal–water contact, while earlier under-recognition of the disease meant many cases were previously missed but now captured through improved surveillance. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic primarily reflected intense transmission of existing pathogenic L. interrogans serovars maintained in livestock and rodents, rather than a demonstrably new genotype, fitting re-occurrence driven by environmental and agricultural change.
Review: Retain – Thailand’s 2000 peak (≈14,285 cases) is one of the largest modern leptospirosis outbreaks; geographic coding (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Thailand) and classification as re-occurrence (environmental and occupational drivers without clear evidence of novel strains) are appropriate. Host list and narrative correctly emphasize cattle/buffalo and rodents as key reservoirs; only inline citation text in the host field was removed.

Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event summary: In 2003, Sri Lanka recorded a marked increase in leptospirosis, with about 2,235 notified cases nationwide, representing the country’s first large modern outbreak since systematic surveillance began in the early 1990s. Cases clustered in wet agricultural districts where rice farmers and other rural workers were exposed to waterlogged fields and irrigation channels contaminated with urine from infected cattle, buffalo, pigs, rodents and dogs. Notifications fell after the main rainy season and acute control and awareness efforts, but the event marked the start of a period of recurrent large seasonal epidemics in the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High rainfall, paddy agriculture, close contact with infected cattle and buffalo, and rodent infestation in rural areas created ideal conditions for environmental contamination and human exposure, while improved case recognition and reporting increased apparent incidence. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not implicate a particular novel strain or host jump; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-occurrence of endemic L. interrogans lineages under favorable climatic and occupational conditions.
Review: Retain – Surveillance data confirm a substantial national increase (~2,235 cases) in 2003, making this a reasonable choice as the first large modern Sri Lankan epidemic. Subregion and country coding (Asia/Southern Asia, Sri Lanka) and re-occurrence classification (environmental and occupational drivers, no clear new strain) are appropriate; host list and sources are adequate, though the primary paper "Leptospirosis in Sri Lanka 2003–2012" should be used rather than generic Wikipedia pages.

Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event summary: In 2008, Sri Lanka experienced its largest recorded leptospirosis outbreak, with about 7,400–7,500 suspected cases and roughly 200 deaths reported nationally, particularly in districts such as Matale, Kegalle, Kandy and Kurunegala. The epidemic followed periods of heavy rainfall and widespread flooding coinciding with intensive paddy cultivation and close contact with cattle, buffalo, pigs and rodents, and many patients presented with severe pulmonary and multi-organ involvement. After the peak, notifications declined but remained much higher than in the pre-2003 era, indicating that leptospirosis had become a high-incidence, frequently epidemic zoonosis in Sri Lanka.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3163869/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme rainfall and flooding, extensive rice agriculture, lack of personal protective equipment for farmers, and gaps in livestock vaccination and rodent control were central in amplifying transmission, while heightened awareness improved reporting. Internal mechanisms: Multiple pathogenic L. interrogans serovars were circulating, but no single novel genotype was clearly linked to the epidemic; re-occurrence driven by climatic and agricultural factors remains the most appropriate classification.
Review: Retain – 2008 is clearly documented as Sri Lanka’s largest leptospirosis outbreak (~7,400 cases, ~200 deaths), and thus belongs among the top global events. Regional coding and classification as re-occurrence (strong climatic and occupational drivers, without clear evidence of a new strain) are correct; event summary has been slightly tightened and cross-checked against national surveillance and detailed outbreak analyses.

Host: Humans; primary reservoirs rats (Rattus spp.) in dense urban settlements; dogs and livestock (notably pigs and cattle) as additional sources contaminating floodwaters
Event summary: After Typhoon Ondoy (Ketsana) caused catastrophic flooding across Metro Manila in late September 2009, a large leptospirosis outbreak occurred, with Philippine Department of Health reports indicating about 2,299 suspected cases and 178 deaths across 15 hospitals, and detailed investigation at San Lazaro Hospital documenting 471 hospitalized patients and 51 deaths. The epidemic developed rapidly among mostly young male residents of low-lying urban districts who had waded through deep floodwaters contaminated by urine from infected rats, dogs and livestock, and many fatal cases showed pulmonary hemorrhage, acute renal failure and multi-organ dysfunction. Case numbers fell to baseline by early November as floodwaters receded, emergency response and clinical management improved, and public warnings were issued, but the event has since been regarded as a benchmark example of flood-associated urban leptospirosis risk in South-east Asia.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/10-1892_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: An intense tropical cyclone produced extreme rainfall and prolonged flooding that submerged densely populated, poorly drained urban areas with inadequate drainage, sanitation and solid-waste management, greatly increasing contact with Leptospira-contaminated water; delayed access to care and dialysis further increased mortality. Internal mechanisms: Available data implicate pathogenic L. interrogans serogroups already endemic in local rat populations rather than a new genotype, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by climatic extremes and urban vulnerability.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2009 Metro Manila outbreak (≈2,300 suspected cases, 178 deaths) is one of the most severe modern leptospirosis epidemics globally and clearly meets the “top-10 impact” criterion. Geography and timing (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Philippines [2009]) and classification as re-occurrence (large flood-associated surge in an already endemic country) are appropriate. Recommend retaining as a major event and, if a strict limit of 10 events is enforced later, considering replacement of smaller-scale episodes such as the Italy Hardjo herd outbreaks or the Puerto Rico 2017 cluster.

Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event summary: In early 2011, Sri Lanka experienced another major leptospirosis epidemic, with surveillance data indicating about 6,700 suspected cases and 100 deaths nationally, and a particularly intense flood-associated outbreak in the dry-zone district of Anuradhapura. The epidemic was driven by extensive flooding of agricultural land and irrigation schemes, exposing farmers to contaminated water, but molecular analyses showed that many cases in Anuradhapura were caused by Leptospira kirschneri, a species not previously recognized as a common cause of human leptospirosis in the country, and associated with severe cardiac and renal complications. Case numbers declined after the rainy season ended and control measures were strengthened, yet the shift in infecting species and severe clinical pattern highlighted a genuine re-emergence phenomenon within Sri Lanka’s long-standing leptospirosis problem.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3894175/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and flooding of irrigation schemes and paddy fields, intense human contact with contaminated surface water, high rodent and livestock infection prevalence, and limited personal protective equipment sustained high transmission risk. Internal mechanisms: Unlike earlier outbreaks dominated by classical L. interrogans serovars, the 2011 Anuradhapura cluster was largely due to L. kirschneri, indicating a shift in the infecting Leptospira species and supporting classification as re-emergence driven in part by changes in pathogen populations rather than purely by environmental factors.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-occurrence to re-emergence because PLOS NTD analyses show that the 2011 Anuradhapura outbreak was predominantly caused by Leptospira kirschneri, previously not a common human pathogen in Sri Lanka, representing a shift in infecting species. Regional coding and overall description remain valid, but the mechanism section was updated to emphasize this internal pathogen change; human expert review is recommended to confirm the balance between environmental drivers and pathogen evolution.
