Host: Dogs (companion animals); urban wildlife reservoirs including raccoons, skunks and rodents; incidentally humans
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the early 2000s, North America saw a marked resurgence of canine leptospirosis, with increasing case series and serosurveys documenting rising prevalence in dogs in the United States and Canada and a shift from traditional vaccine-covered serovars Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae to emerging serovars such as Autumnalis, Grippotyphosa, Pomona and Bratislava. The problem became particularly evident by the late 1990s and early 2000s in regions such as Ontario and across the US, where the proportion of positive canine microscopic agglutination tests increased and disease clustered in urban and peri-urban areas with abundant raccoon and rodent populations. Expanded vaccination that incorporated additional serovars and increased awareness among veterinarians helped to reduce severe disease in some areas, but canine leptospirosis has remained an important re-emerging zoonosis in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urbanization and expansion of suburbs into wildlife habitats increased contact between dogs and reservoir hosts such as raccoons and rodents; changes in pet management (e.g. more outdoor access) and lagging updates to vaccines left many dogs susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence was closely associated with a shift in dominant infecting serovars in dogs toward Pomona, Grippotyphosa, Bratislava and Autumnalis, reducing protection from older bivalent vaccines and representing both novel strain/genotype prominence and effective host expansion within dog populations, which justifies classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – The multi-country, multi-year resurgence of canine leptospirosis with a clear shift to non-classical serovars in the US and Canada is a major animal-health emergence event and fits the definition of re-emergence due to changes in circulating genotypes and host ecology. Geography, timeframe and sources are appropriate; no classification changes were needed beyond text clean-up.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Germany [1995]; France [1995]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1995]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1995]; Italy [1995]; Greece [1995]; other European countries with reported canine cases
Host: Dogs (companion animals); wildlife reservoirs such as rodents and hedgehogs; livestock (pigs, horses, cattle) as maintenance hosts for some serovars
Event summary: From the mid-1990s onward, multiple European countries reported a re-emergence of canine leptospirosis, with increasing clinical cases and a shift in predominant serovars away from the classical Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae toward Grippotyphosa, Bratislava, Pomona and others maintained in wildlife and livestock reservoirs. This trend was documented across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe as serosurveys in dogs and wildlife and case series highlighted rising exposure to these non-classical serovars and concerns that older bivalent vaccines no longer provided adequate coverage. Progressive roll-out of multivalent canine leptospirosis vaccines and adjustments in vaccination policies followed, reducing severe disease risk in some regions but leaving infection widely established in dogs and wildlife.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased contact between dogs and wildlife (especially rodents and hedgehogs) in urban and peri-urban environments, pet travel and trade within Europe, and incomplete vaccine coverage against the newly important serovars all contributed to the resurgence. Internal mechanisms: The growing importance of non-classical pathogenic serovars such as Grippotyphosa and Bratislava in canine infections represents a shift in serovar ecology and effective host expansion within dog populations, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by changes in the pathogen repertoire rather than simple environmental fluctuation.
Review: Review – Intra-continental emergence was set to “Yes” in the original file, but available evidence shows longstanding leptospirosis across European subregions; the 1995–2015 pattern is best characterized as re-emergence with changing dominant serovars rather than first introduction into new subregions. The intra_continental_emergence flag has therefore been changed to false, with re_emergence kept as true; otherwise, geography and description are appropriate. Recommended status: retain as a major animal-health re-emergence episode but flagged for expert confirmation of the selected timeframe.

Host: Dairy cattle; humans occupationally exposed to infected herds
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2011, two documented abortion outbreaks caused by Leptospira serovar Hardjo (Hardjo-bovis/Hardjo-prajitno complex) were detected in dairy cattle herds in northeastern Italy, a region where bovine leptospirosis was already known to occur. Affected herds experienced increased abortions, stillbirths, infertility and milk drop, and investigations confirmed herd-level leptospiral infection with evidence of chronic carrier cows shedding organisms. Implementation of an integrated outbreak management plan including enhanced biosecurity, whole-herd antibiotic treatment and vaccination against Hardjo controlled clinical disease and reduced shedding, but Hardjo-associated leptospirosis remains an endemic production and zoonotic risk in Italian dairy systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density dairy farming with frequent animal movements between farms, incomplete vaccination against Hardjo in some herds, and environmental exposure to contaminated water and possible wildlife reservoirs allowed within-herd transmission and re-introduction. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks involved a cattle-adapted Hardjo maintenance serovar already established in Italy rather than a novel genotype, so they are better viewed as re-occurrence of endemic infection facilitated by gaps in herd immunity and management rather than true re-emergence.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the Italian dairy outbreaks involved Hardjo, a long-established cattle maintenance serovar, with no clear evidence of a new strain or host jump; the main drivers were management practices and incomplete vaccination. The event is genuine but relatively localized (a few herds) compared with very large human outbreaks and continent-wide canine re-emergence; it should therefore be considered a candidate for exclusion if the dataset must be trimmed to the 10 highest-impact global events.

Host: Humans; livestock (cattle, pigs); dogs; rodents as major maintenance hosts contaminating surface water
Event summary: In early 2012, two successive tropical depressions caused severe flooding in western Fiji, leading to the largest recorded leptospirosis outbreak in the Pacific region, with approximately 576 reported cases and around 40–44 deaths and a case fatality near 7%. The epidemic was concentrated in flood-affected rural and peri-urban communities where people were exposed to turbid floodwaters and muddy soils contaminated by urine from infected cattle, pigs, dogs and abundant rodents, and many severe cases presented with pulmonary hemorrhage and acute renal failure. Following intensified clinical awareness, public messaging, and environmental and veterinary interventions, case numbers fell, but recurrent flood-associated leptospirosis outbreaks have continued to pose a major One Health challenge in Fiji.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4731082/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Successive extreme rainfall and flooding events in a tropical island setting with limited sanitation, dense livestock and dog populations, and high rodent abundance dramatically increased human contact with contaminated water and soil, while constraints in diagnostic capacity delayed recognition and treatment. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak appears to have been driven by intense transmission of existing pathogenic L. interrogans serovars endemic in local animal reservoirs rather than emergence of a new genotype, so it is best classified as a severe flood-driven re-occurrence.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2012 Western Fiji outbreak (≈576 cases, ~40–44 deaths) is documented as the largest leptospirosis epidemic in the Pacific and represents a major flood-associated zoonotic event. Coding as Oceania/Melanesia (Fiji [2012]) and as re-occurrence is appropriate given pre-existing endemicity; however, inclusion as a top-10 event should be confirmed by subject-matter experts when balancing global human and animal impact.

Host: Humans; reservoir hosts including rats, dogs and livestock (cattle, pigs) contaminating floodwaters
Event summary: After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, causing widespread flooding and severe damage to water and sanitation infrastructure, surveillance data and retrospective reviews documented several dozen to roughly one hundred suspected and confirmed human leptospirosis cases and at least four confirmed deaths, with some analyses suggesting additional undetected fatalities. The outbreak developed as displaced residents, emergency workers and others were forced to rely on unsafe surface and groundwater sources and were heavily exposed to debris and standing water contaminated by urine from infected rats, dogs and livestock. Reported cases gradually decreased as floodwaters drained, emergency response operations restored safer water supplies, and risk communication and clinical awareness improved, although endemic leptospirosis transmission linked to animal reservoirs has continued on the island.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A major hurricane caused prolonged flooding, disruption of piped water supplies, population displacement, and strain on clinical and laboratory systems, substantially increasing opportunities for exposure to Leptospira-contaminated water and delaying diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: No evidence indicates the emergence of a new Leptospira strain; the event reflects environmentally and infrastructurally driven re-occurrence of pathogenic L. interrogans maintained in rat and domestic animal populations.
Review: Review – Outbreak is real and clearly hurricane-associated, but reported case numbers (tens to low hundreds of suspected and confirmed cases and a handful of confirmed deaths) are modest compared with very large outbreaks in Thailand, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Fiji. Classification as re-occurrence and Caribbean/South America coding are appropriate; however, given the aim to capture roughly the 10 most impactful events globally, this Puerto Rico episode should be considered for exclusion or down-weighting in favor of larger outbreaks, while still being noted in narrative reviews because of its political and surveillance implications.

Host: Dogs (companion dogs)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through at least 2007, canine leptospirosis re-emerged in the United States and Canada, with rising seropositivity among dogs tested by microscopic agglutination test and a shift toward serovars such as Grippotyphosa, Pomona, Autumnalis, and Bratislava. The epizootic developed as an increasing number of clinical and subclinical infections were recognized across many US regions, with spatial and spatio-temporal clusters of seropositive dogs identified between 2000 and 2007. By the mid‑2000s canine leptospirosis was widely regarded as a re-emerging infection in North American dogs, leading to changes in vaccination recommendations and greater clinician awareness.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urbanization and peri-urban expansion bringing dogs into closer contact with wildlife reservoirs (notably rodents), changing climate and rainfall patterns favoring environmental survival of Leptospira, and evolving dog management practices (e.g., more outdoor recreation and boarding) contributed to increased exposure. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and serovar shift in the canine population (emerging importance of serovars Grippotyphosa, Pomona, Bratislava, and Autumnalis rather than the classical Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae) increased disease incidence and challenged older bivalent vaccines, representing re-emergence of disease driven by changing serovar ecology and partial immune mismatch.
Review: retain: This row appropriately summarizes the continent‑wide re‑emergence of canine leptospirosis in the United States and Canada from the mid‑1990s through the 2000s, characterized by rising seroprevalence and a major shift toward serovars Grippotyphosa, Pomona, Bratislava and Autumnalis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2705070/)) Event timing (1990–2007) and geography (Northern America: United States and Canada) are a reasonable approximation of the best‑documented period of increase, and classifying the event as 're_emergence' (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags) matches the literature. No corrections recommended.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Germany [1990], France [1990s], Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1990s], Belgium [1990s], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990s], Italy [1990s], other European countries with reported canine cases [1990s-2003]
Host: Dogs (companion dogs)
Event summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, leptospirosis re-emerged in dogs across several European countries, with surveillance data from Germany documenting 99 canine leptospirosis cases between 1990 and 2003 and reports from other European states describing similar trends. The epizootic involved a shift from traditional vaccine-targeted serovars (Canicola, Icterohaemorrhagiae) toward emerging serovars such as Grippotyphosa and Bratislava, which were increasingly identified among diagnosed dogs. By the early 2000s, leptospirosis was recognized as an emerging or re-emerging zoonotic disease of dogs in Europe, prompting revisions to canine vaccination protocols and renewed emphasis on environmental and rodent control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased recognition and diagnostic testing in companion animals, higher dog densities in urban and peri-urban environments, and persistent rodent and wildlife reservoirs facilitated exposure. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/serovar emergence and selection—particularly Grippotyphosa and Bratislava—in the European dog population, together with limited cross-protection from existing bivalent vaccines, drove re-emergence marked by increased virulence in incidental hosts and enhanced transmission within dog–environment–rodent cycles.
Review: retain: This row captures the widely recognized re‑emergence of canine leptospirosis across multiple European countries in the 1990s and early 2000s, driven by a shift from classical vaccine serovars Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae to serovars such as Grippotyphosa and Bratislava.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3371786/)) Event timing (1990–2003), geography (Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe) and classification as 're_emergence' are consistent with multi‑country serologic and clinical reports; the described serovar–vaccine mismatch is appropriate. No corrections are needed, though the list of affected countries could be expanded in a future iteration if finer national detail is required.

Host: Pigs (2600-sow commercial breeding herd)
Event summary: Around 2000, a large outbreak of leptospirosis occurred in a 2600-sow breeding herd in Thailand, where approximately 5% of sows aborted over a short period, causing a marked spike in reproductive losses. Subsequent investigation using expanded serological testing (including additional serovars sejroe, hardjo, and bratislava) identified Leptospira interrogans serovars Bratislava and Sejroe as the cause of the abortion storm. After herd-wide antimicrobial treatment and implementation of rodent control and feed-box protection to reduce contamination, clinical signs and abortions ceased and the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density intensive swine production with inadequate biosecurity and rodent access to feed likely allowed heavy environmental contamination with leptospires, while absence of targeted vaccination against the causative serovars facilitated rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: Infection of a largely naive breeding herd by already circulating Leptospira interrogans serovars Bratislava and Sejroe, which were only identified after an expanded serologic panel was applied, led to a severe abortion storm; this represents re-occurrence of endemic serovars in a susceptible herd rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review: Event corresponds closely to a documented abortion storm in a 2600-sow herd in Thailand, but it represents re-occurrence of endemic serovars rather than emergence of a novel strain. Reclassified the event from 're_emergence' to 're_occurrence' and rewrote the mechanism/driver text accordingly; timing (publication year 2000 used as an approximation of outbreak year) and geography (Thailand, South‑eastern Asia) are correct.([digital.car.chula.ac.th](https://digital.car.chula.ac.th/tjvm/vol30/iss3/2/)) Impact is substantial at herd level but smaller than continent‑wide canine and pinniped epizootics, so this row should be kept provisionally and revisited when ranking the global top 10 events for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [California, Oregon, Washington 2004], Canada [British Columbia 2004]
Host: California sea lions (Zalophus californianus), with involvement of other pinnipeds in some locations
Event summary: In 2004, a major leptospirosis epizootic caused by Leptospira interrogans serovar Pomona affected California sea lions along the Pacific coast, with high numbers of sick and dead animals recorded from central and southern California northward into Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia. The outbreak developed over the second half of the year, with widespread stranding of clinically affected sea lions and evidence of a high proportion of the population being exposed during this period. Following this large epidemic wave, leptospirosis incidence in sea lions declined but the pathogen persisted endemically, contributing to recurrent seasonal outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Demographic and environmental factors, including a large susceptible cohort of subadult and adult sea lions, seasonal aggregation at rookeries and haul-outs, and oceanographic conditions influencing prey distribution and animal condition, facilitated intense transmission. Internal mechanisms: Chronic shedding and maintenance of L. interrogans serovar Pomona in the California sea lion population allowed persistence and periodic large epidemic waves along the eastern Pacific coast; this outbreak is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence of endemic infection in a long-established reservoir host, not as intra-continental emergence or a novel strain event.
Review: review: Large 2004 leptospirosis epizootic in California sea lions from California north to British Columbia is well documented and clearly among the highest‑impact wildlife events for this EPP.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tbed.12201)) However, Leptospira interrogans serovar Pomona had been established in this host population and in the same Northern America subregion since at least the 1970s, with recurrent 3–5‑year outbreak cycles, so this episode does not meet the definition of intra‑continental emergence or re‑emergence driven by pathogen change. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence to 'false', re_occurrence to 'true', and re_emergence to 'false' and adjusted the mechanism/driver text to emphasise recurrent epizootics in an endemic marine reservoir.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dairy cattle (dairy herds in northeastern Italy, province of Padua)
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2009, two dairy herds in the province of Padua, northeastern Italy, experienced significant leptospirosis outbreaks characterized by high seroprevalence and reproductive problems, with the first outbreak detected in October 2007 showing nearly half the herd seropositive. The outbreaks developed with ongoing reproductive losses and evidence of active leptospiral shedding, prompting intensive investigation and implementation of an integrated outbreak management plan. After application of enhanced biosecurity, rodent and wildlife control, environmental sanitation, movement restrictions, and vaccination and treatment of affected cattle, reproductive performance improved and the outbreaks were brought under control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction or amplification of Leptospira within intensively managed dairy herds—likely via contaminated water sources, wildlife or other livestock contact, and suboptimal pest and manure management—allowed rapid spread once the pathogen entered naïve or insufficiently vaccinated herds. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks represented re-occurrence of bovine leptospirosis in an already endemic region, driven by failure of control measures and high within-herd transmission rather than the emergence of a novel strain; the main mechanisms involved chronic renal shedding and efficient transmission in moist environmental conditions typical of dairy operations.
Review: retain: Outbreak description (two dairy herds in the province of Padua, northeastern Italy, 2007 and 2009) matches published case reports and an integrated outbreak management study, including timing, location, host (dairy cattle) and association with Leptospira borgpetersenii serovar Hardjo.([research-portal.uu.nl](https://research-portal.uu.nl/en/publications/application-of-an-integrated-outbreak-management-plan-for-the-con/)) Classified as 're_occurrence' (not first detection or new strain), which is consistent with leptospirosis being endemic in Italian cattle herds; no changes required.

Host: Dairy cattle (mixed-age cows in a commercial dairy herd)
Event summary: In 2015, a dairy herd in northeastern Brazil experienced a major leptospirosis-associated reproductive outbreak in which, between January and July, 17% of 106 cows aborted, 5.7% delivered stillborn calves, and 11.3% showed repeated estrus, indicating substantial herd-level reproductive failure. Serological and epidemiological investigation implicated leptospirosis as the likely primary cause of the abortion and stillbirth cluster. Following implementation of control measures including vaccination, antibiotic treatment, and management interventions, the incidence of new reproductive problems declined and the outbreak was contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Tropical environmental conditions with high rainfall, pasture flooding, and contact with contaminated surface water, combined with possible wildlife and rodent reservoirs and incomplete prior vaccination, facilitated intense exposure and transmission in the dairy herd. Internal mechanisms: This event represented re-occurrence of endemic bovine leptospirosis leading to a pronounced abortion cluster, driven mainly by high within-herd transmission and persistent renal shedding rather than the documented emergence of a new serovar or genotype; the primary internal mechanism was efficient reproductive-tract and transplacental infection leading to abortion and stillbirths.
Review: retain: The 2015 abortion‑associated outbreak in a Brazilian dairy herd (Maranhão State, Northeastern Brazil), with approximately 17% abortions and additional stillbirths and repeat estrus, is accurately summarized and is well supported by the primary case report and recent reviews of bovine genital leptospirosis.([repositorio.unesp.br](https://repositorio.unesp.br/server/api/core/bitstreams/fce4777b-5e58-4a63-86d8-0248cf91021f/content)) Event type 're_occurrence' is appropriate because bovine leptospirosis is long‑endemic in Brazil and no novel serovar or host jump was documented; geography and timing are correct; no corrections made.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep and goats (small ruminants) with listerial encephalitis on two silage‑fed farms in New York state
Event summary: In the early 1990s, two epizootic outbreaks of listerial encephalitis occurred in one sheep flock and one goat herd in the northeastern United States, with multiple animals in each flock showing circling disease and brainstem lesions. Listeria monocytogenes was isolated from brain tissue and from associated silage, and random amplified polymorphic DNA typing linked clinical and silage isolates, providing strong evidence that poorly fermented, heavily contaminated silage was the infection source. The outbreaks resolved after removal of contaminated silage and improved feeding and hygiene, and the investigation became a widely cited model for molecularly linking ruminant listeriosis to on‑farm feed sources.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Feeding of heavily contaminated silage with high L. monocytogenes counts, together with winter housing and close confinement, facilitated high‑dose exposure and epizootic encephalitis in small ruminants. Internal mechanisms: multiple L. monocytogenes strains were present in silage, but encephalitis was associated with particular silage subtypes rather than a demonstrably novel genotype; disease expression reflected high environmental load and exposure rather than an emergent strain.
Review: review – Event is real and well documented (Wiedmann et al. 1994 J Clin Microbiol). Countries/continent/sub‑region are correct, but the use of 1994 as the outbreak year likely reflects the publication year rather than the exact outbreak dates; this should be verified from the full article. Classification as re‑occurrence (endemic disease linked to contaminated silage) is appropriate. Sources were corrected to use the primary J Clin Microbiol outbreak paper plus the Nightingale et al. 2004 farm‑ecology study; an unrelated Brazilian PVB link was removed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (multiple farm outbreaks of meningoencephalitis)
Event summary: Between 2000 and 2007, veterinarians in the southern Brazilian states of Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná documented seven outbreaks of neurological disease in sheep attributable to Listeria monocytogenes, with affected flocks showing around 3% morbidity and nearly 100% lethality among clinically ill animals. Cases occurred mainly in summer and early spring and were confirmed by the presence of unilateral brainstem microabscesses and immunohistochemical detection of L. monocytogenes in the brain. Control relied on removing affected animals, improving feed and water hygiene and, in some flocks, preventive antibiotic treatment of in‑contact sheep, after which new clinical cases ceased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental contamination of pastures, water and possibly roughage in intensive and semi‑intensive sheep systems in southern Brazil, combined with climatic conditions favouring survival and transmission, promoted recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: no particular novel genotype was reported; the events represent re‑occurrence of classical encephalitic listeriosis in a region where the pathogen is present but often under‑diagnosed.
Review: retain – Multi‑farm outbreak series in southern Brazil is well supported by the Pesquisa Veterinária Brasileira case series and clearly qualifies as a high‑impact regional event (multiple outbreaks, high case‑fatality). Geography, time span, and host species are correctly represented and classification as re‑occurrence (endemic pathogen, no described novel genotype) matches the primary report.

Host: Sheep (flock outbreak of septicaemic listeriosis with encephalitic involvement)
Event summary: In winter 2001, an outbreak of septicaemic listeriosis occurred in a sheep flock in eastern Saudi Arabia, principally affecting adult and pregnant ewes with clinical signs of fever, weakness, respiratory distress, keratoconjunctivitis, circling and occasional encephalitis. Listeria monocytogenes was isolated in pure culture from affected animals, and morbidity and mortality were estimated at 7.1% and 2.4%, respectively. Hygienic measures and antibiotic treatment of in‑contact animals halted further cases, and this episode was published as the first reported outbreak of ovine listeriosis in Saudi Arabian livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely exposure to contaminated feed or environmental sources under arid husbandry conditions, combined with naïve flock immunity and limited prior awareness of listeriosis in the region. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel genotype or virulence change was reported; the key emergent feature was recognition and laboratory confirmation of the disease in a new national setting, rather than true appearance of a new strain or expansion into a new continent.
Review: review – The outbreak is real and clearly described as the first reported ovine listeriosis in Saudi Arabia (Al‑Dughaym et al. 2001 Rev Sci Tech). However, the previous version incorrectly flagged this as “first detection” in the host system; listeriosis in ruminants has been recognised globally since the early 20th century and had been reported in other Asian countries and neighbouring Türkiye before 2001. The event has therefore been reclassified as re‑occurrence of an endemic pathogen in a new national context, with first_detection set to false. An unrelated small‑ruminant Johne’s disease PDF link was removed and replaced with the primary Rev Sci Tech article; manual review is recommended to confirm whether this event should remain among the top 10 given the much larger 2020 Qassim outbreak now added.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy sheep (flock producing raw‑milk ewe cheese)
Event summary: In 2005, a clinical listeriosis outbreak occurred in a 55‑ewe dairy sheep flock in Austria that also produced raw‑milk cheese, with several ewes showing neurological signs and abortions. Investigation by Wagner and colleagues isolated Listeria monocytogenes from affected animals, from heavily contaminated grass silage and along the on‑farm cheese production chain, demonstrating transmission from silage to sheep and onward contamination of bulk milk and raw‑milk cheese. After withdrawal of contaminated silage, changes in feeding and milking routines, and stricter dairy hygiene, clinical cases stopped and L. monocytogenes contamination in raw‑milk cheese dropped to below detectable levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of poorly fermented grass silage with very high L. monocytogenes loads (~10^5 CFU/g) and lack of physical separation between animal housing and cheese production areas enabled amplification and spread through animals, milk and cheese. Internal mechanisms: no distinct new genotype was highlighted; disease expression was driven by high environmental load and repeated exposure, making this a classic example of re‑occurrence in an endemic setting.
Review: retain – This Austrian dairy sheep outbreak is a key, well‑documented event linking ruminant listeriosis, silage contamination, and raw‑milk cheese contamination (Wagner et al. 2005 Vet Rec). Geography, host and year are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate. The event‑level sources were strengthened by adding the primary Vet Rec paper; the general MDPI review is kept as contextual secondary literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (mixed herd of milking cows, dry cows, and heifers)
Event summary: In early 2009, a U.S. dairy herd of about 315 cattle experienced an outbreak of encephalitic listeriosis affecting nine animals, of which seven died or were euthanised within days. Diagnostic work identified Listeria monocytogenes serotype 4b belonging to the otherwise rare lineage III, and multilocus sequence analysis showed that the outbreak strain represented a unique genotype not previously described among hundreds of isolates. The outbreak ended after treatment of clinical cases and management changes, including adjustments to feed handling, and the study concluded that this was the first report of a particularly severe clinical course of bovine listeriosis associated with a lineage III strain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely exposure to contaminated silage or farm environment, as is typical for bovine listeriosis, with management and feeding practices permitting high‑dose exposure. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a unique lineage III serotype 4b genotype associated with unusually severe neurological disease and high case‑fatality in cattle, consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence and possibly increased virulence compared with background bovine strains.
Review: retain – Outbreak details, host species, and geography match the J Vet Diagn Invest report (unique lineage III serotype 4b strain and severe clinical course). Classification as re‑emergence (novel genotype associated with enhanced pathogenicity in cattle) is consistent with the authors’ conclusions; no intra‑ or inter‑continental spread is implied. Sources are appropriate and specific to this outbreak.

Host: Sheep (flock with mixed clinical forms: rhombencephalitis, enteric disease, abortions)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, an outbreak on a Swiss sheep farm led to multiple animals developing different clinical manifestations of listeriosis, including rhombencephalitis, enteric disease and abortions, over a single episode. Detailed microbiological and molecular investigations showed that all clinical cases, along with Listeria monocytogenes isolates from soil and water on the premises, belonged to a single strain, indicating a hypervirulent clone that had colonised the farm environment. After fencing off heavily contaminated areas, discarding implicated feed and improving hygiene, new clinical cases stopped and environmental detection of the outbreak strain declined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination of soil and water on the farm and probable contamination of feed created multiple exposure routes for sheep over time, sustaining transmission. Internal mechanisms: dominance of a single hypervirulent L. monocytogenes strain associated with ruminant rhombencephalitis sequence types in both animals and the environment, representing clonal environmental adaptation and enhanced transmission/virulence rather than background strains.
Review: retain – The Swiss sheep outbreak with a single hypervirulent clone colonising animals and the farm environment is well supported by the Vet Microbiology paper (Dreyer et al. 2015) and later neuropathology work. Geography, host and timing are correctly captured, and classification as re‑emergence (clonal, hypervirulent strain with environmental adaptation) is justified. No changes beyond minor wording and confirmation of sources are required.

Host: Beef cattle (heifers in a large research beef herd)
Event summary: In late winter and early spring of 2014, a major abortion outbreak occurred in beef heifers at the United States Meat Animal Research Center (USMARC) in Nebraska, with 28 late‑term abortions over 36 days, 24 of them clustered within 12 days. Listeria monocytogenes was cultured from 19 of 23 fetal and post‑abortion clinical submissions, and isolates were also recovered from silage and water sources. Whole‑genome sequencing showed that most clinical, silage and water isolates belonged to a single lineage III strain, while additional clinical cases were caused by two distinct lineage I strains. Disposal of several hundred tons of contaminated silage, management changes and monitoring led to cessation of abortions attributable to L. monocytogenes in the following calving season.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy contamination of shared feed (maize silage) and water sources with L. monocytogenes in a large heifer group created intense exposure during late gestation, in combination with stressors associated with winter feeding and herd management. Internal mechanisms: multiple existing lineages (III and I) were involved, but there is no evidence of a novel genotype; the outbreak represents a severe re‑occurrence of endemic strains under high‑exposure conditions rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: review – New high‑impact event added. The 2014 USMARC beef‑heifer abortion outbreak (Whitman et al. 2020 BMC Vet Res) involved 28 abortions in 36 days and large‑scale silage disposal, clearly making it one of the more consequential post‑1990 livestock listeriosis events. Countries, sub‑region and host system are correctly assigned, and classification as re‑occurrence (severe outbreak of endemic strains driven by feed and water contamination) aligns with the genomic investigation. Recommended to retain as part of the top‑impact set; figures and dates should be double‑checked against the published article during manual curation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Fattening pigs (large commercial pig holding)
Event summary: In 2018, Austrian authorities recorded an outbreak of fatal listeriosis on a pig farm in Lower Austria, affecting a commercial holding of about 450 fattening pigs and resulting in 35 deaths attributed to Listeria monocytogenes. Epidemiological investigation by the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES) identified maize silage produced under inappropriate ensiling conditions as the most likely infection source, with high bacterial loads exposing many pigs in a species where clinical listeriosis is usually rare. Following replacement of the defective silage and improved management and hygiene, the outbreak subsided and no further clusters of deaths were reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of poorly fermented maize silage with inadequate acidification created a heavily contaminated feed source, and the intensive fattening system exposed a large population of pigs to high infectious doses; delayed recognition occurred because pigs are not typical sentinel species for listeriosis. Internal mechanisms: the public report does not provide evidence of a novel genotype or host‑adapted variant; the outbreak is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence of endemic L. monocytogenes in an atypical host population driven by feed and management factors.
Review: review – Event is clearly documented in the Austrian national zoonoses report as an outbreak of fatal listeriosis in 450 fattening pigs with 35 deaths and maize silage as the likely source. The previous version incorrectly flagged this as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence without evidence of a novel genotype or host‑range shift; classification has been corrected to re‑occurrence only, with re_emergence set to false and mechanism text revised to remove unsupported speculation about evolutionary change. Geography and host are correct; retain event but review if more detailed strain data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (large mixed‑age flock with predominantly neurological listeriosis)
Event summary: In January 2020, a major outbreak of listeriosis occurred in a 700‑head sheep flock in Qassim Region, central Saudi Arabia, with 400 animals (57.1%) showing neurological signs such as ataxia, head tilt and circling, and 350 deaths, yielding a 50% flock‑level mortality and 87.5% case‑fatality rate. Listeria monocytogenes was cultured from brain and liver tissues of affected animals, confirming neurolisteriosis as the cause. The outbreak occurred in winter, in animals grazing by day and housed and fed fodder rolls at night; there was no clear association with silage feeding. Early treatment of clinically affected sheep with penicillin and flunixin had some success, whereas late‑stage cases generally died, and prophylactic sulfonamide‑trimethoprim in in‑contact animals helped reduce new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high stocking density, winter environmental conditions and possible contamination of fodder or environment with L. monocytogenes, in a previously naïve flock with no prior vaccination or known exposure, contributed to exceptional morbidity and mortality. Misdiagnosis as coenurosis and initial use of antiparasitic rather than antimicrobial therapy likely exacerbated losses. Internal mechanisms: the study did not report a novel genotype; the event represents an unusually large re‑occurrence of classical neurolisteriosis in a highly susceptible flock, rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New event added and should almost certainly be included among the top 10 livestock listeriosis events post‑1990 because of its extreme impact (400 clinical cases and 350 deaths in a 700‑animal flock) documented by Osman et al. 2021 (Int J Vet Sci). Continent, sub‑region and country are correct. Classified as re‑occurrence: a very large outbreak of endemic pathogen in a naïve flock with strong environmental/management drivers and no evidence of a new strain. Recommended for retention; manual review should confirm that no even larger small‑ruminant outbreaks have been overlooked.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Sheep (coastal flocks in Sunnhordland and Sørlandet); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); likely involvement of local cervids and willow ptarmigan as reservoir hosts
Event summary: In the early 1990s, louping ill—previously regarded as a disease of the British Isles—was recognised causing encephalomyelitis in sheep flocks in coastal areas of Sunnhordland and Sørlandet in southern Norway, and virus isolates from affected sheep were shown by antigenic and sequencing studies to be classical louping ill virus closely related to British strains. These outbreaks produced neurological disease and deaths in local sheep and demonstrated that LIV had established at least transient natural foci on the Norwegian coast, with serologic evidence of exposure also detected in game birds and deer. Following these limited epizootics and increased awareness, no further clinical outbreaks in Norwegian livestock have been reported since 1991, although later wildlife and livestock serosurveys show that closely related tick‑borne flaviviruses may continue to circulate at low levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected Ixodes ricinus ticks into coastal pastures in southern Norway—most plausibly via movement of sheep or game animals from infected areas or by migratory birds—combined with humid, tick‑suitable hill grazing and local deer populations, enabled establishment of a new LIV focus outside the British Isles. Internal mechanisms: Molecular comparison of the Norwegian virus with British LIV strains showed >95% nucleotide and >98% amino‑acid identity in the envelope gene, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing lineage rather than emergence of a genetically distinct, more virulent strain.
Review: retain: Added this event to capture the early‑1990s Norwegian outbreaks that confirmed classical louping ill virus outside Great Britain and Ireland. Timing (1991), geography (Norway in Northern Europe) and the description of sheep as the main clinical host with I. ricinus as vector are consistent with Norwegian public‑health and veterinary sources and with Gao et al. (1993). Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate under the project rules (spread within an already affected UN subregion, no novel genotype), and despite relatively few reported flocks this episode is highly important for geographic range and should be retained as one of the core post‑1990 events.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1994]
Host: Sheep (upland hill flocks); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); red grouse as an important wildlife host in the same upland system
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, intensive serologic and ecological studies in hill sheep flocks in the Forest of Bowland, Lancashire, England, revealed very high prevalence of louping ill virus exposure and ongoing production losses in an upland grazing system where sheep and red grouse served as key hosts for both ticks and virus. From 1994 onwards a coordinated control programme combining vaccination of lambs and yearlings, acaricide use and grazing management was implemented across multiple farms, and follow‑up surveys through 1999–2000 and into the early 2000s showed marked reductions in LIV force of infection in flocks that sustained these measures, although spatial heterogeneity in risk persisted. As management practices were adjusted based on these findings, disease incidence and tick burdens declined, and this Bowland focus transitioned from a major emergence concern to a better‑controlled endemic system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Ixodes ricinus ticks on rough upland pasture, abundant competent hosts (unvaccinated sheep and red grouse) and management geared toward both sheep production and grouse shooting created conditions for intense local LIV circulation, with significant economic impact. Implementation of systematic vaccination, acaricide treatment and tick‑aware grazing regimes then altered host–vector contact rates and reduced virus transmission, illustrating how land use and husbandry practices drive re‑occurrence and control of this endemic flavivirus. Internal mechanisms: Available data show no evidence of a novel LIV strain in this focus; the event reflects amplification and subsequent suppression of an established lineage through ecological and management change rather than genetic evolution of the virus.
Review: retain: This event correctly summarises the Forest of Bowland (Lancashire) focus studied during 1994–2001, where high LIV seroprevalence in hill sheep and associated grouse led to implementation and evaluation of a structured vaccination and tick‑control programme. The year range, location (UK within Northern Europe), hosts and classification as re‑occurrence (intensification and subsequent control of endemic infection) are all consistent with the epidemiologic literature. No corrections to timing, geography, event type or sources are required; the event should be retained as one of the main high‑impact post‑1990 episodes for this EPP.

Host: Ticks (Ixodes ricinus) collected from goats and sheep in northern Greece; goats and sheep as presumed vertebrate hosts in this natural focus
Event summary: Greek goat encephalitis virus (GGEV), a louping ill–like member of the LI/TBE complex first isolated from a newborn goat with encephalitis in northern Greece in 1969, was revisited in the early 2000s when large‑scale tick surveys were undertaken in rural northern Greece. Between 2003 and 2006, over 3,000 ixodid ticks collected from goats and sheep were screened by RT‑PCR, and two pools of Ixodes ricinus were positive for GGEV, confirming continued, low‑level circulation of this LIV‑related subtype in livestock‑associated tick populations decades after the original goat case. Because no sizeable contemporary livestock outbreaks were reported during this period, the episode is best regarded as renewed detection of a persistent natural focus rather than a major new epizootic, and its prominence waned once surveillance data had documented the virus’s limited prevalence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional small‑ruminant grazing in wooded, tick‑infested mountainous pastures and limited vaccination or acaricide use maintain ecological conditions under which GGEV can persist at low prevalence in local Ixodes ricinus populations. The main proximate driver of this event was expanded molecular surveillance of ticks in 2003–2006, which revealed viral persistence that had gone undocumented rather than a true surge in incidence. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that contemporary GGEV sequences clustered closely with the historical Vergina strain and related southern European LIV‑like viruses, indicating evolutionary continuity rather than emergence of a distinct, more virulent genotype.
Review: review: The row accurately reflects the 2003–2006 tick‑survey work in northern Greece, where only two of 3,144 Ixodes ricinus tick pools tested positive for Greek goat encephalitis virus, confirming long‑term persistence of this LIV‑like subtype at very low prevalence but without documented large livestock outbreaks. I corrected the host field to remove explicit mention of the original 1969 goat case (pre‑1990) and instead describe goats and sheep as presumed vertebrate hosts in the surveyed flocks, in line with project rules against mixing hosts from other episodes. Because the impact in terms of clinical cases and production loss appears minimal, this episode is borderline for inclusion among the “top 10” emergence events and should be reconsidered for possible exclusion or down‑weighting in the final dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Goats (Bermeya breed); ticks (Ixodes ricinus and related species)
Event summary: In autumn 2011, a severe neurologic disease outbreak occurred in a herd of Bermeya goats in Asturias, north‑western Spain, with 17 goats dying over four months and clinical and pathologic signs closely resembling classic louping ill. Virologic investigation showed that the causative agent was a louping ill–like flavivirus genetically distinct from both British/Irish LIV and the previously recognised Spanish sheep encephalitis virus that had affected Basque sheep in the 1980s, and the new subtype was designated Spanish goat encephalitis virus (SGEV), representing an expansion of recognised LI‑lineage activity into goats in this region. After the affected herd was investigated and management adjustments were made, the outbreak subsided, but the event firmly placed SGEV and north‑western Spain within the wider LI/TBE complex distribution and stimulated targeted surveillance of ticks, wildlife and livestock on the northern Iberian Peninsula.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional grazing of goats on tick‑infested mountainous pastures, animal movements between farms within Asturias and the absence of specific vaccination or awareness of LI‑like flaviviruses in Spain created favourable conditions for intensive local exposure to infected Ixodes ticks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that the outbreak virus formed a distinct phylogenetic lineage, Spanish goat encephalitis virus, separate from classical British/Irish LIV and from Spanish sheep encephalitis virus, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence within the LI/TBE complex together with clear host expansion to goats as a prominent clinical host in this focus.
Review: retain: This event is well documented by the 2011 Bermeya‑goat outbreak in Asturias caused by Spanish goat encephalitis virus, a novel LIV‑lineage subtype that produced high mortality and expanded both the known host range and geographic range of LI‑like viruses in Iberia. I corrected the host field to restrict it to goats and tick vectors involved in the 2011 episode, removing sheep that relate only to the earlier 1987 Spanish sheep encephalitis virus epizootic (which lies outside the 1990–cut‑off period) in order to avoid mixing hosts from separate events. Classification as re‑emergence (new genotype and host expansion within a subregion where related LI‑like viruses already circulated) is appropriate, and the event clearly belongs among the major post‑1990 emergence episodes.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019]
Host: Sheep (yearling ewes moved to hill grazing); ticks (Ixodes ricinus)
Event summary: In April 2019, a group of about 200 yearling ewes was moved onto tick‑infested hill grazing on a farm near Oswestry on the English/Welsh border, and within 2–3 weeks 10 animals developed neurological signs including torticollis, fitting, head shaking and recumbency, with several later found dead. Post‑mortem examination of an affected ewe showed non‑suppurative encephalitis, and serology plus RT‑PCR on hindbrain tissue confirmed infection with louping‑ill virus, with sequencing demonstrating >99% identity to existing LIV sequences from Aberystwyth in west Wales and clear distinction from northern‑England isolates. After diagnosis, management changes and heightened awareness limited further losses, but the incident was reported as a North‑East Wales outbreak and underscored the ongoing risk that naïve sheep moved into upland tick habitats can experience significant losses from LIV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The key external drivers were movement of immunologically naïve, unvaccinated yearling ewes into an upland pasture with high densities of Ixodes ricinus ticks, lack of prior exposure in the flock and environmental conditions favouring tick survival and activity, which together enabled rapid infection and focal outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterisation showed the virus to be closely related to previously circulating Welsh LIV strains rather than a novel variant, so this event is best interpreted as ecological re‑occurrence of endemic LIV in a high‑risk grazing system rather than strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: retain: This added event reflects the 2019 North‑East Wales outbreak documented in Access Microbiology, where ~10 of 200 yearling ewes developed neurologic disease and some died after being moved onto hill grazing, with LIV confirmed by serology, PCR and sequencing. Geography (United Kingdom within Northern Europe), timing (2019) and classification as re‑occurrence in an already endemic region without evidence of a novel viral lineage are consistent with the primary report. Given its clear clinical impact and formal documentation as an outbreak, it should be retained as one of the principal post‑1990 emergence episodes for this EPP.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2025]
Host: Sheep (Cheviot hoggs and lambs); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); possible co‑infection with Anaplasma phagocytophilum causing tick‑borne fever
Event summary: In spring 2025, SRUC Veterinary Services reported two clusters of louping ill in sheep on neighbouring farms near St Boswells in the Scottish Borders, an area where the disease had not been diagnosed since 2003, marking a notable return after more than two decades. The first cluster involved homebred Cheviot hoggs grazing rough tick‑infested hill ground that developed classic neurological signs and were confirmed as LIV‑positive by serology, PCR and histopathology; the second involved multiple deaths among 4‑week‑old lambs in a bought‑in ewe flock, where non‑suppurative encephalomyelitis and LIV infection were similarly confirmed. Following diagnosis, advice on tick control, flock management and awareness of concurrent tick‑borne fever was implemented, and the outbreaks subsided, but they highlighted renewed LIV activity in the Scottish Borders and prompted calls for greater veterinary vigilance and development of replacement vaccines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Local land‑use changes that increased suitable tick habitat, rising deer populations, climate warming that may allow Ixodes ticks to complete more life‑cycle stages per year and movement of naïve, unvaccinated ewes into a high‑risk area all likely contributed to renewed LIV transmission in these flocks. Co‑infection with tick‑borne fever (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) in the hoggs probably exacerbated immunosuppression and clinical severity, while the absence of a currently available commercial LIV vaccine in the UK left farmers reliant on acaricides and grazing management. Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been presented for a genetically novel LIV strain in these cases; the pattern is best interpreted as ecological and management‑driven re‑occurrence of endemic LIV at the southern edge of its Scottish range.
Review: retain: This event is well supported by the SRUC Veterinary Services report describing two distinct but nearby farm outbreaks near St Boswells in 2025, after more than 20 years without diagnosed cases in the Scottish Borders. The year, location (Scottish Borders within the UK and Northern Europe), host description and classification as re‑occurrence (reappearance of endemic LIV driven by ecological and management factors, with no evidence of a new strain) are all consistent with that source and broader UK surveillance summaries. No corrections to the row were needed; it should be retained as a recent, clearly defined re‑occurrence episode.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa; Middle Africa
Countries: Ethiopia [2006]; Sudan [2006]; Kenya [2007]; Uganda [2007]; United Republic of Tanzania [2007]; Zambia [2008]; Zimbabwe [2008]; South Africa [2008]; Botswana [2009]; Namibia [2009]; Nigeria [2010]; Ghana [2010]; Mali [2011]; Niger [2011]; Cameroon [2011]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2012]; Mozambique [2012]; others in endemic belt with recurrent outbreaks
Host: Domestic cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus); occasional water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) and small ruminants as spillover
Event summary: From about 2006, lumpy skin disease re‑intensified across multiple endemic regions of sub‑Saharan Africa, with WOAH data showing marked fluctuations and overall high outbreak numbers through 2013. The disease repeatedly resurged in East, Southern and West African cattle populations, causing substantial production losses and prompting vaccination campaigns in several countries. By around 2013, incidence in many affected African countries began to stabilize or decline, although the virus remained widely endemic and served as a source for later transboundary spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities and seasonal abundance of blood‑feeding vectors (biting flies, mosquitoes), increased intra‑ and transboundary cattle movements, and limited vaccination coverage or vaccine access in pastoral and smallholder systems contributed to recurrent large outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No single new genotype was implicated; rather, the long‑established African LSDV lineages continued to circulate, with range and incidence patterns influenced by climate variability and livestock trade rather than demonstrably novel viral traits.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures a prolonged high-incidence phase in endemic African countries identified in WOAH-based time-series and reviews, with appropriate African subregions and classification as re-occurrence rather than new intra-/inter-continental emergence. No geography or emergence-type corrections were required, though the exact per‑country start years are approximate.

Countries: Egypt [2011]; Israel [2012 re-occurrence]; Lebanon [2013]; Jordan [2013]; Iraq [2014]; Syrian Arab Republic [2012]; Türkiye [2013]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [2014]; Saudi Arabia [2013]; Yemen [2013]; Oman [2013]; Kuwait [2014]; Qatar [2014]; United Arab Emirates [2014]; Bahrain [2014]; Sudan [2012]; others in the Middle East/North Africa corridor
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo in parts of Egypt and the Middle East
Event summary: Between roughly 2012 and 2015, LSDV caused a major multi‑country epizootic across the Middle East and adjoining North African states, following prior limited incursions into the region in the late 1980s and 2000s. Outbreaks spread progressively through Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula, Iran and Türkiye, with hundreds of reported outbreaks and substantial cattle losses. Intensive vaccination, movement controls and stamping‑out in some herds gradually reduced reported outbreaks by around 2015, although the region remained a bridgehead for further spread into Europe and deeper into Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of live‑cattle trade and informal animal movements among North Africa, the Levant and the Gulf region, together with abundant vector populations in irrigated and peri‑urban systems, facilitated rapid dissemination. Conflict‑related disruption of veterinary services in several Middle Eastern countries likely exacerbated spread. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed viruses closely related to African field strains; there is no strong evidence that intrinsic viral changes, rather than ecological opportunity and movement networks, were the main drivers in this wave.
Review: review – Event kept as a major multi-country Middle East/North Africa wave, but Libya was removed from the country list because WOAH and FAO/WOAH sources indicate first detections in Libya, Algeria and Tunisia only from 2023–2024, not 2012. The remaining countries and 2012–2015 timing are consistent with EMPRES-i/WAHIS-based analyses of 2012–2015 outbreaks; classification as re-occurrence (rather than first or intra-/inter-continental emergence) remains appropriate because most listed countries had earlier LSD presence.

Countries: Greece [2015]; Bulgaria [2016]; North Macedonia [2016]; Albania [2016]; Serbia [2016]; Kosovo [2016]; Montenegro [2016]; Bosnia and Herzegovina [2017, limited]; Türkiye (European Thrace) [2015]; Russian Federation (southern European parts) [2016]
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo locally
Event summary: In August 2015, LSDV was first detected in the European Union in cattle in northern Greece near the Turkish border, marking the first recognized establishment of the virus on the European continent. During 2015–2017, the virus spread extensively through Greece and into multiple Balkan countries, with thousands of outbreaks reported and severe trade and production impacts. A coordinated mass vaccination campaign and movement controls across the Balkans and EU member states led to a sharp decline in outbreaks after 2017, with most affected countries regaining disease‑free status in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction from the infected Middle East/Türkiye region, likely via wind‑borne or mechanically transported vectors and/or short‑distance animal movements, followed by regional spread under favorable climatic conditions for vector flies and ticks. Substantial movements of cattle among Balkan states and to EU markets amplified dissemination before control measures were harmonized. Internal mechanisms: Viruses belonged to the classical field strain lineage; no major genetic shifts were necessary for establishment, but the virus showed efficient transmission by local vector species, highlighting vector‑adaptation compatibility with European climates.
Review: review – Retained as the first confirmed inter-continental emergence of LSDV into Europe, but the continent and sub-region fields were corrected from “Europe; Asia / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Asia” to “Europe / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe” because the outbreaks listed here occurred only in European territories (Balkans, European Thrace, European Russia). Emergence-type coding as inter-continental emergence (first occurrence in Europe) is consistent with EFSA and WOAH timelines.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Western Asia; Central Asia
Countries: Russian Federation [2016]; Georgia [2016]; Azerbaijan [2016]; Armenia [2016]; Kazakhstan [2016-2017]; others in the Caucasus and adjacent regions
Host: Domestic cattle
Event summary: Following the 2015 incursion into south‑eastern Europe, LSDV extended its range north and east between 2016 and 2019 into the Caucasus, southern Russia and Kazakhstan, establishing endemic foci beyond the Balkans. Initial outbreaks appeared in the Caucasus republics and southern Russia, with further spread into Kazakhstan and neighboring areas in subsequent years. By around 2019, sustained vaccination and control campaigns had reduced reported outbreak numbers in many of these newly affected territories, although the virus became entrenched in some border regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Progressive spread along cattle movement routes and contiguous grazing areas from the Balkans and Türkiye into the Caucasus and Central Asia, aided by suitable climatic conditions for vector flies over extended summers. Limited early vaccination coverage and challenges in coordinating control across multiple jurisdictions facilitated continued expansion. Internal mechanisms: Viruses in this wave were closely related to earlier European/Middle Eastern field strains; geographic range expansion was driven mainly by host and vector ecology and movement patterns rather than clearly defined novel viral adaptations.
Review: retain – This row appropriately represents the onward spread from the Balkans into the Caucasus, southern Russia and Kazakhstan as intra-continental emergence within Europe and Asia, supported by EFSA/WOAH data and genomic studies showing close relatedness to earlier Balkan/Middle Eastern field strains. No corrections to geography or emergence type were required.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia
Countries: Russian Federation [2017]; Kazakhstan [2017]; China (Xinjiang) [2019, recombinant-like ancestry]; Mongolia [2019-2020]
Host: Domestic cattle
Event summary: From 2017 onwards, molecular surveillance in Russia and Kazakhstan identified multiple vaccine‑like recombinant LSDV strains emerging in cattle populations that had been vaccinated with live‑attenuated capripox vaccines. These recombinant viruses caused field outbreaks and then spread eastward, with related genotypes later detected in parts of Asia including western China and Mongolia during the first local LSD incursions. Control measures in affected countries were progressively adjusted, including review of vaccine strains and strategies, as outbreaks linked to these recombinants were brought under better control by around 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of live‑attenuated capripox vaccines in settings with concurrent circulation of field strains created ecological conditions favorable for recombination, while large cattle populations and imperfect vaccination coverage allowed onward spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via recombination between vaccine and field LSDV strains led to multiple distinct vaccine‑like recombinant lineages with field‑virus behavior; these represented genuine viral re‑emergence with altered genomes and in some cases possibly modified virulence or transmission potential.
Review: review – Event retained as a distinct re-emergence episode driven by vaccine–field strain recombinants, but the sub-region list was expanded to include Eastern Asia because recombinant-derived strains seeded initial outbreaks in western China and Mongolia. Emergence type remains correctly set to re-emergence (novel genotypes) without marking additional intra-/inter-continental spread, which is handled in separate geographic events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [2019]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2021]; Taiwan [2020, Kinmen Island]; Mongolia [2021]
Host: Domestic cattle
Event summary: In August 2019, China reported its first LSD outbreak in cattle in Xinjiang, representing the first recognized establishment of the disease in East Asia, followed soon by further outbreaks in Inner Mongolia and other provinces. During 2020–2021, related outbreaks were detected in additional eastern Asian territories, including Taiwan (Kinmen) and Hong Kong SAR, and Mongolia, with trade disruptions and targeted culling in some affected herds. Intensive surveillance, quarantine of infected farms and rapid vaccination responses gradually contained many of these foci, though LSDV has since become established in parts of western China and neighboring areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction likely occurred via movement of infected cattle or vectors from Central Asian or Russian foci into north‑western China, with subsequent dissemination through domestic cattle trade networks and communal grazing. Rapid intensification of cattle production and long‑distance transport in China further facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses indicated that early Chinese isolates were closely related to vaccine‑like recombinants circulating in Russia and Kazakhstan, suggesting introduction of a recombinant strain; however, no clear evidence of substantially increased virulence compared with other field strains was reported.
Review: review – Retained as the major East Asian geographic expansion, but the country list was corrected: (i) Mongolia’s first outbreak is now dated to 2021 rather than “2019–2020”, (ii) the Republic of Korea was removed because its first LSD outbreak occurred only in October 2023, and (iii) Taiwan (Kinmen Island, 2020) was added as part of this wave. The ‘first_detection’ flag was set to false because global first detection of LSD in cattle dates to 1929; this event is best classified purely as intra-continental emergence into a new Asian subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Bangladesh [2019]; India [2019 limited, wider 2020]; Sri Lanka [2020]; Nepal [2020]; Bhutan [2020]; Pakistan [2021]
Host: Domestic cattle; Asian water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) in some countries
Event summary: Starting in 2019, LSDV was first reported in Bangladesh and then in neighboring parts of India, marking the initial recognized spread of the virus into South Asia. During 2020–2021, outbreaks were notified in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan, with tens of thousands of affected cattle and buffalo and substantial milk yield losses across the region. Emergency vaccination campaigns, movement restrictions and farmer awareness programs gradually improved control by late 2021, though the virus became endemic in many South Asian cattle populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border cattle trade and informal livestock movements from already infected areas in the Middle East and Central Asia into South Asia, combined with abundant vector populations in monsoon climates and dense smallholder cattle systems, underpinned rapid spread. Limited prior exposure meant high susceptibility in regional herds. Internal mechanisms: Viruses were closely related to recombinant vaccine‑like strains and field strains from the Middle East and Central Asia; range expansion into a naïve host population, rather than a major intrinsic change in virulence, explains much of the high impact.
Review: review – Kept as the main introduction and early spread of LSD into South Asia (Bangladesh 2019, India 2019–2020, Nepal/Bhutan/Sri Lanka 2020, Pakistan 2021), with intra-continental emergence correctly marked. The ‘first_detection’ flag was changed from true to false because first detection refers to the host system globally (1929), not to the subregion; otherwise the row aligns with WOAH and regional review timelines.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Viet Nam [2020]; Myanmar [2020]; Cambodia [2021]; Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2021]; Thailand [2021]; Malaysia [2021]; Indonesia [2022, continuation of wave]; Singapore [2022, mainly import-related detections]
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo in parts of mainland Southeast Asia
Event summary: From late 2020, LSDV spread for the first time into mainland Southeast Asia, with initial large outbreaks reported in Viet Nam and Myanmar, followed in 2021 by major epizootics in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia. Morbidity in many affected herds exceeded 15–30%, with notable economic losses in smallholder and commercial beef and dairy systems throughout the Mekong region. Regional vaccination programs, movement controls and improved surveillance progressively reduced outbreak numbers by late 2021, although the virus continued its southward spread into Indonesia and other areas in 2022.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction from South Asia and China via formal and informal cattle trade, transboundary grazing and possibly wind‑borne or mechanically transported vectors, followed by rapid intra‑regional spread facilitated by dense cattle populations, limited prior immunity and warm, humid climates highly favorable to vector flies. Internal mechanisms: Viral genotypes in Southeast Asia were closely related to recombinant and field strains circulating in South and East Asia; enhanced transmission in this region was largely attributable to ecological suitability and host movement rather than documented new viral traits.
Review: review – This row is retained as the first major Southeast Asian wave but the event year was broadened from “2020–2021” to “2020–2022” to match the inclusion of Indonesia and Singapore (first affected in 2022). As with other regional spread events, the ‘first_detection’ flag was reset to false (global first detection is historical), while intra-continental emergence remains appropriate for the first occurrence in the South-eastern Asia subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: India [2022]; Pakistan [2022]; Nepal [2022]; Bhutan [2022]; Bangladesh [2022 resurgence]
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo in some affected districts
Event summary: In 2022, South Asia experienced an exceptionally severe LSD epidemic, with India reporting widespread outbreaks across many states and the death of tens of thousands of cattle within a few months, alongside major production losses. Neighboring Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh also recorded large numbers of cases, often in regions that had seen only limited disease in earlier years. Accelerated rollout of homologous and heterologous LSD vaccines, stricter movement controls and heightened farmer awareness gradually brought the large 2022 wave under better control by early 2023, though the virus is now entrenched in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High baseline prevalence following initial introduction in 2019–2021, intense livestock movement after easing of COVID‑19 disruptions, and warm, humid conditions that favored vector proliferation combined to trigger a large secondary epidemic wave. Gaps in early vaccination coverage and cold‑chain/logistics issues further allowed explosive spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses from India indicated that 2022 outbreak strains were distinct from earlier 2019 isolates and represented a separate genetic lineage circulating under vaccine and immune pressure, consistent with Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; reports of more severe disease in some areas support classification as viral re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: review – This severe South Asian wave is retained as a major re-emergence episode, but the emergence coding was adjusted so only ‘re_emergence’ is true (re_occurrence was set to false) to respect the guideline that event types are generally mutually exclusive, with re-emergence reserved for episodes involving clear viral genetic change. Genomic work from India demonstrates that 2022 strains form a distinct lineage from 2019 isolates under vaccine/immune pressure, justifying re-emergence classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic cattle
Event summary: After several years without EU cases following successful control of the Balkan outbreaks, LSDV reappeared in 2025 with a first case reported in Sardinia (Italy), followed shortly by outbreaks on mainland Italy, a major epizootic in France beginning in summer 2025, and detections in Spain later that year. The French outbreak caused significant trade disruptions and required large‑scale vaccination, movement restrictions and emergency response measures over roughly eight months. By early 2026, French authorities reported that the national crisis was largely under control and remaining regulated zones were being lifted, although surveillance and vaccination remained in place to prevent renewed spread in Western Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of LSDV into previously free parts of Western and Southern Europe likely occurred via importation of infected animals or vectors, possibly linked to trade or movement of cattle or vector‑carrying goods under climatic conditions that allowed vector activity well into autumn. High cattle densities, intense trade within the EU and initial gaps in immunity in Western European herds facilitated rapid spread before emergency vaccination scaled up. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests involvement of strains related to recombinant and field lineages circulating in Asia and eastern Europe; the event is best characterized as re‑emergence in a previously cleared region and intra‑continental emergence into new European subregions, with viral traits sufficient for efficient transmission via European vector species but without clear proof of substantially increased virulence.
Review: review – Retained as a major re-emergence and intra-continental emergence event in Western and Southern Europe (Italy, France, Spain) starting in mid‑2025, consistent with WOAH and EU/Swiss summaries. The source list was revised to prioritise WOAH, EFSA, EU and UK official outbreak assessments plus detailed French press reports, and to remove reliance on Wikipedia for this recent episode. Emergence typing as both intra-continental emergence (new European subregions) and re-emergence (return to a previously cleared continent) is justified.
