Countries: United States of America [mid-Atlantic and northeastern states 1990]; Canada [Ontario 1999]
Host: Wildlife, predominantly raccoons (Procyon lotor), with secondary involvement of skunks and other mesocarnivores; occasional spillover to domestic animals
Event summary: During the 1990s, an epizootic of raccoon-associated rabies virus that had been introduced into the US mid-Atlantic region in the late 1970s expanded rapidly north and south along the eastern seaboard, establishing sustained wildlife transmission in most eastern states and reaching southern Ontario, Canada, by 1999. The epizootic caused many thousands of raccoon, skunk and other wildlife cases and shifted the national rabies ecology so that raccoons became the most frequently reported rabid species, driving large increases in animal-testing, human post-exposure prophylaxis and local control costs. By the late 1990s, large-scale oral rabies vaccination (ORV) programs using vaccine baits were deployed along an “immune barrier” from the Gulf of Mexico to the Great Lakes to slow or halt further westward spread of the raccoon variant, where it remains enzootic but partially contained by continuing ORV belts and wildlife surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human-mediated translocation of raccoons from rabies-enzootic areas of the southeastern United States to the mid-Atlantic region for hunting in the 1970s, followed by natural dispersal of dense raccoon populations through forested and suburban landscapes; limited early capacity to detect and respond to wildlife rabies; and high availability of anthropogenic food and den sites in peri‑urban environments that sustained high raccoon densities. Internal mechanisms: The epizootic was driven by geographic range expansion of an established raccoon-variant RABV lineage rather than emergence of a novel strain, with no evidence of markedly increased virulence; disease impact stemmed from host ecology and spatial spread rather than major viral innovation. Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (adaptation to raccoon reservoir maintained over decades).
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the eastern North American raccoon rabies epizootic (1990–1999) as a major wildlife rabies emergence episode, based on CDC surveillance summaries and spatial analyses showing thousands of animal cases annually and progressive spread from the mid-Atlantic into the Northeast US and southern Ontario. Classified as re-occurrence (not inter- or intra-continental emergence) because RABV was long-established in the Northern America sub-region and the epizootic reflects range expansion of an existing raccoon variant rather than first presence on a new continent or UN sub-region. Please review whether this event should be retained among the top 10 by impact and whether the end-year should be truncated (e.g. 1990–1998) to emphasise the main expansion phase.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China [southern provinces incl. Guangxi, Hunan, Guizhou from 1996; progressive spread into central and some northern provinces by mid‑2000s]
Host: Primarily domestic dogs (Canis familiaris), with extensive spillover to livestock (especially cattle, pigs) and occasional wildlife
Event summary: After a nadir of reported human rabies cases in 1996, China entered a fifth major epidemic wave in which dog-mediated rabies resurged from historically affected southern provinces and spread into many new rural and peri-urban counties across eastern and central China. Between 1996 and a peak around 2007, annual human deaths increased more than twenty-fold, with over 3,000 deaths per year at the peak and expansion of reported rabies into most provinces except Tibet and Qinghai; many counties reported their first recognised rabies epidemics in dogs and humans during this period. From 2008 onward, intensified national attention to dog vaccination, post-exposure prophylaxis and dog population management gradually reduced incidence, but dog-maintained rabies remained widely distributed and continued to cause substantial animal and human disease into the 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid economic and social change increased dog ownership, especially in rural and peri-urban areas, without matching investment in mass dog vaccination or coordinated dog population management; large free-roaming dog populations, limited awareness of rabies risk, poor access to affordable high-quality post-exposure prophylaxis in rural areas, and gaps in coordination between human and veterinary sectors all contributed to resurgence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies show multiple established classic RABV lineages co-circulating in China, with lineage turnover in some regions but no single novel, more virulent genotype clearly responsible for the wave; the epidemic is best explained by demographic, programmatic and behavioural factors rather than major viral innovation. Re-occurrence driven by external factors; no intra-continental emergence flagged because Eastern Asia as a UN sub-region already harboured dog-mediated rabies long before 1996.
Review: Review – EXISTING EVENT MODIFIED. (i) Time span updated from 1999–2007 to 1996–2008 to match national surveillance analyses that define the post‑1996 increase and peak in 2007–2008 as a single epidemic wave with 19,806 human cases during 1996–2008. (ii) Removed the intra_continental_emergence flag and retained only re_occurrence, because rabies was already endemic in Eastern Asia and the wave represents a resurgence and geographic widening within an existing UN sub-region rather than first detection in a new sub-region. Narrative and mechanisms were adjusted to emphasise external drivers (dog demography, vaccination gaps, PEP access) rather than viral novelty. Recommend retaining this as one of the highest-impact global rabies emergence events, but ask for expert review of the chosen start/end years and classification (re-occurrence vs possible additional re-emergence flag if lineage displacement is to be emphasised).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Indonesia [Flores Island, East Nusa Tenggara – first canine rabies detection Larantuka, East Flores 1997; spread to multiple regencies 1998–2003]
Host: Primarily domestic dogs (Canis familiaris), with frequent spillover to cattle and other livestock and resultant human exposures
Event summary: In September 1997, three infected dogs brought by fishermen from the rabies-endemic island of Buton (Sulawesi) introduced rabies to the previously rabies-free island of Flores in eastern Indonesia, with the first local dog cases detected soon afterwards in Larantuka and the first human death recorded in March 1998. Over the next several years, rabies spread across much of Flores despite intensive but delayed dog-culling campaigns and limited dog vaccination, resulting in at least 113 documented human deaths by 2003 and large numbers of dog and livestock losses. Following expansion of mass dog vaccination, public education and more targeted dog population management in the early 2000s, incidence in animals and humans decreased, but rabies became entrenched and Flores shifted from explosive emergence to endemicity requiring ongoing control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human-mediated movement of infected dogs by boat from rabies-endemic Sulawesi into a naive island dog population; high densities of largely free-roaming owned dogs valued for cultural and practical reasons; limited initial access to vaccines, diagnostics and rabies awareness; and reliance on mass culling rather than early, sustained island-wide dog vaccination. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic work indicates the Flores outbreak strains cluster with existing Indonesian dog RABV lineages, with no evidence of a radically novel genotype; emergence reflects geographic range expansion and ecological suitability rather than major evolutionary change. Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent).
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the Flores Island canine rabies epidemic (1997–2003), a previously omitted but very high-impact emergence episode with at least 113 human deaths on a formerly rabies-free island and extensive dog and livestock losses. Classified as intra_continental_emergence (new, sustained enzootic focus within South‑eastern Asia) with no re-occurrence or re-emergence flags because this was the first known establishment of dog-maintained rabies on Flores. Please review whether this classification is acceptable given that UN sub-regions are coarser than the island level, and whether you prefer to shorten the event window to the core epidemic years (e.g. 1998–2003).

Countries: Bhutan [eastern districts including Trashigang, Trashiyangtse, Mongar and neighbouring areas 2005–2007]
Host: Domestic dogs and cattle, with smaller numbers of horses and cats
Event summary: Between May 2005 and late 2007, Bhutan experienced a major rabies outbreak in its eastern districts after several years with no reported cases in this part of the country, with dozens of villages affected along the Indian border. The epidemic resulted in more than 250 reported domestic animal cases, predominantly in cattle and dogs, and at least one human death, and spread along roads and settlements where free-roaming dogs were abundant. Control measures included emergency dog culling, dog vaccination and intensified public awareness, which eventually contained the outbreak, although Bhutan has continued to face sporadic reintroductions along its southern and eastern borders in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely repeated incursions of rabid dogs from adjacent rabies-endemic areas of India into previously low-incidence eastern districts; large populations of free-roaming dogs around towns and highways; limited prior dog vaccination coverage and surveillance in rural Bhutan; and resource constraints that favoured reactive dog culling over sustained vaccination. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolates belonged to regional canine RABV lineages already circulating in India; no clear evidence of a new, more virulent strain driving the outbreak. Re-occurrence driven mainly by cross-border dog movement and dog ecology in a country that had reduced but not eliminated rabies risk.
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the 2005–2007 eastern Bhutan outbreak as a distinct high-impact re-occurrence episode in Southern Asia, based on detailed epidemic investigations documenting >250 domestic animal cases and significant control costs in a resource-limited country that had enjoyed several years with few or no cases in the east. Classified as re_occurrence (no intra- or inter-continental emergence) because rabies was historically present in Bhutan and the wider Southern Asia sub-region, and there is no evidence for a novel strain or host jump. Please review whether this outbreak warrants inclusion among the top 10 global events given its animal-impact and strategic importance for Bhutan’s national programme.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic dogs and cattle, with a few horses
Event summary: From January to July 2008, rabies re-emerged in Chhukha District in south‑western Bhutan after years without reported cases there, with the outbreak believed to have started in dogs near the border with India and then spreading northwards along road corridors. The episode caused the deaths of nearly 100 animals, predominantly cattle and dogs, and generated substantial concern about further spread into Bhutan’s interior. Intensive outbreak response, including dog culling, emergency vaccination of dogs and cattle, and public education, eventually halted transmission in the district, though Bhutan has continued to experience sporadic border-area incursions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable cross-border introduction of rabid dogs from rabies-endemic Indian states into a region of Bhutan with many free-roaming dogs and close human–livestock–dog contact along trade routes; limited routine vaccination in dogs and cattle in the affected subdistricts; and delayed recognition of early cases in an area that had been considered low risk. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses place Bhutan’s viruses within established South Asian dog RABV lineages; no evidence of a novel strain or host shift driving the Chhukha outbreak. Re-occurrence due to external drivers in a previously affected sub-region.
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the 2008 Chhukha District outbreak as a separate Bhutanese re-occurrence episode, following the original literature which treats the eastern (2005–2007) and south‑western (2008) outbreaks as distinct incursions on different parts of the India–Bhutan border. Classified as re_occurrence only, consistent with prior endemicity in Southern Asia and lack of evidence for a novel viral variant. Please review whether you prefer to collapse the eastern and Chhukha events into a single 2005–2008 linked episode for simplicity, or retain them as two rows to reflect their differing geography and control responses.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Primarily domestic dogs (Canis familiaris); occasional spillover to livestock and wildlife
Event summary: In late 2008, rabies virus was introduced into the previously rabies-free island of Bali, Indonesia, most likely via movement of an infected dog from a neighbouring rabies-endemic island, leading to rapid establishment of sustained transmission in Bali’s large free-roaming dog population. Over 2008–2010 the epidemic spread to all districts, with thousands of confirmed rabid dogs, tens of thousands of human exposures, and more than 130 human deaths before effective mass dog vaccination campaigns were implemented island-wide. Successive island-wide dog vaccination rounds from 2010–2011 achieved coverage near or above 70%, sharply reducing animal and human rabies incidence, although dog-mediated rabies has persisted at low levels, requiring continued vaccination and surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of an infected dog by boat into a naive island dog population; high densities of owned but free-roaming dogs; lack of pre-existing dog vaccination and bite-surveillance systems; and initial reliance on dog culling and limited ring vaccination rather than rapid, high-coverage mass dog vaccination. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses show Bali outbreak viruses are closely related to existing Indonesian dog RABV lineages, consistent with a single or very limited number of introductions from other endemic islands; there is no evidence of a major new strain with altered virulence. Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent).
Review: Retain – EXISTING EVENT MOSTLY ACCEPTED. The Bali 2008–2011 dog-mediated rabies outbreak is correctly described as a major emergence on a previously rabies-free island, with appropriate emphasis on dog ecology and delayed shift from culling to mass vaccination. Classification as intra_continental_emergence (new enzootic focus within South‑eastern Asia) is defensible given the creation of a major new focus in a region that was otherwise endemic, although strictly speaking UN sub-regions are coarser than the island level. No changes were made to the event type flags, but more specific primary sources (social and virological studies) were added and the generic ‘Prevalence of rabies’ link was dropped at event level as non-essential. Marked as “retain” but flagged here for minor conceptual review of the intra-continental label across all Indonesian island incursions to ensure consistency.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [north‑eastern regions including Friuli Venezia Giulia, Veneto and Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol 2008]
Host: Wildlife, predominantly red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), with occasional spillover to other wild mammals and domestic animals
Event summary: After the last fox rabies case in 1995 and recognition as rabies-free in 1997, Italy experienced re-introduction of fox-mediated rabies into its north‑eastern regions at the end of 2008, linked phylogenetically to epidemic lineages spreading westward from the Balkans and Slovenia. From 2008 through early 2011, several hundred animal cases—mostly in red foxes but also in badgers, roe deer and domestic species—were detected in the Triveneto area as the epidemic front moved south and west despite early control efforts. Intensified and geographically extended oral rabies vaccination (ORV) campaigns, coordinated with neighbouring countries, progressively contained the outbreak, with the last Italian case reported in early 2011 and rabies-free status for terrestrial animals re-recognised in 2013.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance natural dispersal of infected foxes from endemic foci in the Balkans into previously rabies-free north‑eastern Italy; incomplete or insufficiently extended ORV belts before the incursion; high fox densities in recovering wildlife populations; and challenges coordinating cross-border vaccination fronts. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses indicate that the viruses belong to established Central/Eastern European fox RABV lineages, with no evidence of a novel Italian-specific variant; this episode reflects geographic spread of existing wildlife lineages rather than major viral innovation. Re-occurrence driven chiefly by wildlife movement and ORV programme gaps.
Review: Retain – EXISTING EVENT. The 2008–2011 Italian fox rabies episode is appropriately characterised as a re-occurrence in a previously rabies-free country within Southern Europe, with correct timing and host focus and no misclassification as inter-continental emergence. I have pruned and refocused the sources to emphasize detailed outbreak and ORV evaluations (and dropped generic rabies overview pages), but made no changes to the event types. Recommended to retain as a key European wildlife rabies re-introduction event, though its relative ranking among the global “top 10” could be revisited if the list becomes overfull.

Host: Primarily domestic dogs, with spillover to humans and some livestock
Event summary: Around early 2010, a large rabies outbreak was recognised on Nias, an island off North Sumatra that had previously been considered rabies-free, after the death of the local health chief and multiple other residents from dog‑mediated rabies. By mid‑ to late‑2010, provincial reports indicated at least 20–31 human deaths and hundreds of dog-bite cases on Nias alone, prompting declaration of an extraordinary event (KLB) and emergency bans on movement of dogs, cats and monkeys from the island. Intensified dog vaccination campaigns, culling of unowned dogs and public awareness efforts were rolled out from late 2010 into 2011, gradually reducing incidence, but Nias and surrounding North Sumatran districts continued to report rabies cases and dog bites for several years thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of infected dogs from rabies-endemic mainland or nearby islands into a naive island dog population; rapid spread among free-roaming, largely unvaccinated dogs; limited public awareness and PEP access in remote communities; and challenges implementing coordinated vaccination and dog population management in the aftermath of earlier earthquake and infrastructure disruption. Internal mechanisms: Available information suggests viruses belong to established Indonesian dog RABV lineages; there is no clear evidence for a novel strain. Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent).
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the Nias Island outbreak (2010–2011) as another major Indonesian island incursion that was missing from the original dataset, supported by Indonesian Ministry of Health reports and provincial data showing >20 human deaths and declaration of a rabies emergency (KLB) in a previously rabies-free island. Classified as intra_continental_emergence (new persistent focus within South‑eastern Asia) without re-occurrence or re-emergence flags, analogous to Flores and Bali. Please review whether grouping Flores–Bali–Nias into one multi-island “Indonesian islands” episode would better fit your event-linking rules, or if keeping them as separate high-impact island emergences is preferable.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Greece [northern regions including Kozani, Kastoria, Florina and surrounding areas 2012–2014]
Host: Wildlife (red foxes) with additional cases in dogs and livestock
Event summary: In October 2012, Greece detected its first rabies case in 25 years in a red fox found near Kozani in northern Greece, ending the country’s officially rabies‑free status that had been in place since 1987. Over 2012–2014, dozens of rabies cases were confirmed in wild foxes, a few dogs and some livestock in northern regions bordering other Balkan countries where wildlife rabies remained endemic, prompting extensive oral vaccination campaigns for foxes and strengthened domestic animal vaccination and surveillance. Following several rounds of ORV and intensified surveillance, no further animal rabies cases were detected after 2014, and Greece subsequently self-declared freedom from rabies virus infection while maintaining preventive ORV along high‑risk borders.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border spread of fox-mediated rabies from endemic foci in neighbouring Balkan countries into previously rabies-free northern Greece; high densities and movements of wild foxes; and the absence of pre-emptive ORV in Greece despite ongoing wildlife rabies in adjacent states. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses link Greek viruses to established Central/Eastern European fox RABV variants; there is no evidence of a novel strain unique to Greece. Re-occurrence in a previously free country due to regional wildlife movement and delayed ORV implementation.
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the 2012–2014 northern Greece outbreak as a separate Southern Europe wildlife rabies re-occurrence, given its importance as a loss and subsequent regaining of rabies-free status and the need for extensive ORV campaigns. Classified as re_occurrence only, consistent with prior rabies presence in Southern Europe and genetic evidence connecting Greek viruses to existing Balkan fox lineages. Please review inclusion of this event among the global top 10; if space becomes constrained, it could be deprioritised relative to higher-burden Asian dog-mediated outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Primarily domestic dogs, with spillover to cats and other mammals
Event summary: In 2017, Sarawak on the island of Borneo, historically regarded as free of dog-mediated rabies for decades, reported its first human rabies cases in children and an associated dog outbreak in Serian Division, with investigations pointing to introduction from neighbouring West Kalimantan, Indonesia. Following declaration of a state rabies outbreak on 1 July 2017, the virus spread to many divisions of Sarawak despite extensive dog culling, vaccination campaigns and movement controls, and by the mid‑2020s more than 80–90 human cases (with >90% fatality) and tens of thousands of animal bite incidents had been recorded, alongside vaccination of hundreds of thousands of dogs and cats. Large-scale, multi-year dog vaccination, improved bite-management and surveillance systems are ongoing, with the state aiming to eliminate human rabies cases by the mid‑2020s and dog rabies by around 2025, but transmission persists in some foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of infected dogs from rabies-endemic West Kalimantan into a previously rabies-free state; large numbers of free-roaming owned and stray dogs in rural and peri-urban Sarawak; limited historical experience and infrastructure for rabies control; and logistical challenges in delivering high vaccination coverage across dispersed communities and difficult terrain. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence data link Sarawak viruses to Indonesian dog RABV lineages from Kalimantan; there is no indication of a novel, unusually virulent strain. Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent).
Review: Review – NEW EVENT. Added the Sarawak (Malaysian Borneo) dog-mediated rabies outbreak (2017–present) as a major South‑East Asian emergence episode, with >80–90 human cases and high fatality in a state that had been rabies-free for decades. Classified as intra_continental_emergence because it represents establishment of a new enzootic focus within South‑eastern Asia following cross-border introduction from Indonesia, rather than re-occurrence in a historically endemic sub-region. The end year is set to 2025 to fit the requested time window while acknowledging that transmission is ongoing; please review this choice and whether to truncate at 2024 (last year with complete published data) in your final dataset.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae and early juveniles in intensive hatchery and nursery systems
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, hatcheries in Pointe‑Noire, Guadeloupe, began to report episodes of almost 100% mortality in M. rosenbergii post‑larvae characterized by rapid onset of whitish, opaque tail muscles, with a major outbreak in 1997 prompting detailed investigation and recognition of white tail disease (WTD). Similar losses were soon documented in Martinique, and electron microscopy and molecular work from these outbreaks demonstrated a novel nodavirus (MrNV) consistently associated with an extra‑small satellite virus (XSV), establishing the viral aetiology of WTD. After initial emergency responses focused on culling, hatchery disinfection and improved broodstock management, catastrophic epizootics became less frequent by the late 1990s, although MrNV is believed to have persisted at low levels in regional stocks and possibly other Caribbean sites.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of freshwater prawn hatcheries in the French West Indies, high larval stocking densities, limited early biosecurity and exchange of post‑larvae among Caribbean facilities created ideal conditions for amplification and recognition of a previously unnoticed viral pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Emergence or recognition of a highly virulent nodavirus (MrNV), with a strong tropism for striated muscle in larvae and post‑larvae and frequent co‑infection with the helper virus XSV, led to explosive tank‑wide mortalities and facilitated both horizontal and probable vertical transmission within hatchery populations.
Review: retain: Corrected event year to 1995–1999 (to reflect reports of mortality beginning in the mid‑1990s and the 1997 outbreak described by Arcier et al.) and clarified that the event covers both Guadeloupe and later Martinique. Classification as first/global emergence and first detection is appropriate, and continent/sub‑region assignment (South America | Caribbean) matches the provided country list. Sources are authoritative (Arcier 1999, WOAH manual, Sahul Hameed & Bonami 2012), so this row should be retained as the index global emergence event.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: China [Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shanghai, Guangxi, Guangdong; ~2000 onwards]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae and juveniles in coastal Chinese hatcheries and nursery ponds
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, Chinese hatcheries culturing M. rosenbergii in several eastern and southern coastal provinces began to experience a new epidemic of whitish muscle disease in post‑larvae and juveniles, with rapid whitening of tail muscles and near‑total tank mortalities. Virological studies, including the seminal work by Qian et al. (2003), demonstrated nodavirus and XSV particles in affected prawns and confirmed that these Chinese outbreaks were caused by MrNV, closely related to French West Indies strains, marking the first large‑scale establishment of WTD in Asia. Over the next few years, the industry adopted RT‑PCR screening of broodstock and post‑larvae and improved hatchery hygiene; these measures reduced catastrophic die‑offs but did not eliminate MrNV, which remains enzootic in some production areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very rapid expansion of freshwater prawn aquaculture in China, the development of large commercial hatcheries and likely importation or movement of infected broodstock or post‑larvae from already affected areas created conditions for inter‑continental introduction and amplification. Internal mechanisms: Chinese MrNV isolates showed high sequence similarity to French West Indies strains, indicating successful geographic range expansion of an already highly virulent lineage with efficient horizontal and vertical transmission in densely stocked larval systems.
Review: retain: Event correctly represents the first well‑documented establishment of MrNV in Asia, with China as the entry point, and is appropriately classified as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent relative to the Caribbean focus). Country, continent and sub‑region assignments are consistent with the country list, and the time window (2000–2003) matches the period covered by Qian et al. and related surveillance. No major structural changes were needed; row should be retained as one of the major impact events.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae and juveniles in hatcheries, nursery ponds and some grow-out ponds
Event summary: From about 2003, many scampi hatcheries and nursery ponds in Nellore, Vijayawada and Chennai on India’s east coast reported devastating episodes of white tail disease in M. rosenbergii post‑larvae and early juveniles, with tanks often suffering close to 100% mortality within a few days of tail muscle whitening. RT‑PCR surveys conducted during 2003–2004 confirmed the presence of MrNV and XSV in affected larvae and post‑larvae and showed that infection was widespread in hatchery and farm stocks across major producing districts. In response, Indian hatcheries progressively implemented broodstock screening, larval testing, water disinfection and stricter seed movement controls, reducing but not eliminating WTD‑related economic losses; later work from India has focused on improved diagnostics and immunoprophylaxis, indicating that MrNV remains an important endemic constraint.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Accelerated expansion and intensification of freshwater prawn culture in coastal Southern India, coupled with extensive movement of post‑larvae among hatcheries without biosecure quarantine, likely allowed rapid spread once MrNV was introduced, probably via infected seed or broodstock from other regions. Internal mechanisms: The Indian outbreaks were caused by MrNV/XSV co‑infection with very high virulence in larval stages and efficient waterborne and probable vertical transmission, leading to synchronized tank‑wide mortalities; no major genotype shift was reported relative to earlier strains, implying that introduction of an existing high‑virulence lineage into a naïve production system drove the impact.
Review: retain: Adjusted event years to 2003–2004 to align with FAO/NACA reports and the first Indian RT‑PCR detection paper, and removed penaeid shrimp from the host field because natural WTD outbreaks in P. monodon and P. indicus are documented later (Ravi et al., 2009) and are now treated as a separate re‑emergence event. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (first establishment in a new Asian sub‑region – Southern Asia) is appropriate, and India is clearly one of the highest‑impact countries; row should be retained.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Taiwan Province of China [Kaohsiung and Pingtung counties]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae and juveniles in hatcheries and nursery ponds
Event summary: In 2006, hatcheries and nursery ponds rearing M. rosenbergii in southern Taiwan reported outbreaks of white tail disease in post‑larvae and juveniles, with whitening of tail musculature and rapid tank‑wide mortalities resembling cases in China and India. Virological work by Wang and co‑workers demonstrated MrNV infection in affected prawns using RT‑PCR and in situ hybridization and showed that the Taiwanese isolates formed a distinct cluster within the global MrNV phylogeny, confirming that these outbreaks were part of the same trans‑regional WTD problem. Following these investigations and earlier reports of “whitish muscle disease” in Taiwanese prawn culture, the industry increased broodstock and seed screening and improved hatchery water treatment, which appears to have moderated but not completely removed the risk of large WTD episodes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing intensive freshwater prawn farming in southern Taiwan, trade in broodstock and seed within East and Southeast Asia and possible introduction of infected animals or contaminated water from already affected regions likely underpinned the appearance of MrNV‑associated WTD in Taiwan. Internal mechanisms: Taiwanese MrNV isolates are closely related to those from other parts of Asia and the Caribbean, indicating continued geographic dissemination of a successful high‑virulence lineage rather than an independent viral origin; strong tropism for striated muscle and efficient transmission in hatchery conditions again drove high mortality among early life stages.
Review: review: Corrected the time window from 2001–2003 to 2006–2007 to match the documented MrNV‑positive WTD outbreaks in Kaohsiung and Pingtung and to separate them from earlier, bacterially caused white muscle disease events in Taiwan. Removed the previous classification as “re-occurrence” because at the sub‑regional level this represents continued spread within Eastern Asia rather than a clearly defined resurgence, and left all emergence‑type flags as ‘No’. Added the primary Taiwan virology paper as a source; recommend keeping the event but treating its overall impact ranking as slightly lower than that of the China and India episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Thailand [major hatchery and farm areas in the central and eastern regions]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae, juveniles and broodstock in hatcheries, nursery ponds and farms
Event summary: By the early to mid‑2000s, Thai freshwater prawn hatcheries and farms began reporting severe white tail disease outbreaks in M. rosenbergii post‑larvae and juveniles, with classic tail muscle whitening and rapid mortality that caused substantial production losses in several key farming provinces. A 2006 study documented high MrNV prevalence in diseased Thai post‑larvae and frequent MrNV/XSV co‑infection in broodstock, confirming that these epizootics were part of the same WTD phenomenon seen in the Caribbean, China and India. In subsequent years, Thailand implemented broader use of molecular diagnostics, broodstock testing, culling of infected spawners and improved hatchery biosecurity, which reduced the frequency and scale of catastrophic WTD outbreaks while MrNV remained entrenched in some prawn culture systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of M. rosenbergii aquaculture in Thailand, widespread movement of broodstock and post‑larvae within the country, and limited early screening of freshwater prawn seed and broodstock enabled MrNV to invade and spread within South‑eastern Asia once introduced, probably via infected seed from other Asian countries. Internal mechanisms: High infection rates and co‑infection of broodstock with MrNV/XSV favored vertical transmission to larvae, seeding heavily infected batches; the virus’s strong muscle tropism and high virulence in juvenile life stages generated the dramatic mortality patterns observed in Thai hatcheries and farms.
Review: retain: This event correctly captures the first major establishment of MrNV in the South‑eastern Asia sub‑region, with Thailand as the main focus, and is appropriately classified as intra‑continental emergence (new Asian sub‑region). The time window and geographic focus align with Yoganandhan et al. and subsequent WOAH/NACA summaries. No structural changes beyond minor wording were needed; given the scale of Thai production and documented impact, this row should be retained as one of the key high‑impact events.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Australia [Flinders River catchment, Queensland; later detections in additional river systems including the Murray–Darling Basin]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii broodstock, juveniles and wild or stocked freshwater prawns; other native or introduced freshwater crustaceans as potential carriers
Event summary: In mid‑2007, Australian authorities recorded an index case of white tail disease in adult broodstock M. rosenbergii captured from the Flinders River in western Queensland, with juveniles from the same family showing white muscle lesions and chronic high mortality, and MrNV/XSV infection confirmed by RT‑PCR. Subsequent surveillance and genetic studies revealed that MrNV had become established in cultured prawns and some wild or stocked populations in additional catchments, including parts of the Murray–Darling Basin, raising concern about long‑term persistence in natural freshwater systems. Australia responded by listing infection with MrNV as a nationally notifiable exotic disease, strengthening import controls on prawn broodstock and product, and imposing movement restrictions, monitoring and biosecurity measures to reduce the risk of further spread within and beyond the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The most plausible route of introduction into Australia is movement of infected M. rosenbergii seed or broodstock from MrNV‑endemic Asian sources prior to strict import controls, followed by escape or release into river systems via aquaculture activities and stocking. Internal mechanisms: Australian MrNV strains show high genetic similarity to overseas isolates with evidence of reassortment between introduced and potentially endemic nodaviruses, implying that once introduced, the virus adapted to local crustacean hosts and freshwater environments; its ability to infect multiple decapod species and cause persistent infections in adults facilitates environmental maintenance and complicates eradication.
Review: retain: Updated the event window to 2007–2009 to reflect the documented index case in 2007 and the 2009 description of disease in Australia, and clarified that the sub‑region label “Australia and New Zealand” is geographic rather than implying occurrence in New Zealand. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence (first confirmed establishment of MrNV in Oceania) is correct, and the event is clearly of high regulatory and ecological importance; row should be retained.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Malaysia [Perak River (Sungai Perak), Sungai Timun and a hatchery in Negeri Sembilan]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii larvae, post-larvae and juveniles from rivers and hatcheries
Event summary: From about 2007 onwards, Malaysian hatcheries and river‑based prawn fisheries reported increasing problems with larvae and post‑larvae of M. rosenbergii showing white tail muscles and elevated mortalities reminiscent of WTD elsewhere in Asia. A detailed survey published in 2011 detected MrNV RNA in prawns collected from the Perak and Timun rivers and from a commercial hatchery in Negeri Sembilan, and phylogenetic analysis placed Malaysian isolates among other Asian MrNV lineages, confirming that WTD had become established in Malaysian freshwater prawn populations. In subsequent years, Malaysian researchers and authorities focused on characterizing local MrNV strains, developing diagnostics and strengthening broodstock and seed health management, helping to reduce catastrophic losses even though MrNV remains a recognized risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional trade in broodstock and post‑larvae, the use of wild‑caught berried females from rivers already harboring MrNV, and limited early screening of seed likely mediated introduction and spread of MrNV into Malaysian hatcheries. Internal mechanisms: Malaysian MrNV isolates cluster closely with other Asian strains, indicating ongoing spread of a successful lineage; high susceptibility of early life stages and probable vertical transmission from infected wild or broodstock prawns support recurrent mortality episodes once the virus gained a foothold in local river and hatchery systems.
Review: review: Corrected the emergence‑type classification by setting intra‑continental emergence to ‘No’, because MrNV was already established in the South‑eastern Asia sub‑region via Thailand before its detection in Malaysia; at the sub‑regional scale this represents additional national spread rather than a new sub‑region. The event itself is well supported by J Fish Dis and review articles and likely had substantial local impact, so it should be kept, but its ranking among the absolute top 10 events may warrant further review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Viet Nam [Mekong Delta hatcheries and nurseries (e.g. Cần Thơ area)]
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae and juveniles in hatcheries and nursery ponds
Event summary: During the mid‑ to late 2000s, regional FAO/NACA reports and Vietnamese research projects from the Mekong Delta documented outbreaks of white tail disease in M. rosenbergii seed production systems in southern Viet Nam, with affected post‑larvae showing white tail muscles and high mortality. A Cần Thơ‑based study (2006–2010) investigating “white muscle disease” in giant freshwater prawn seed concluded that MrNV and XSV were the principal viral agents responsible for these lesions, indicating that WTD had become established in Vietnamese freshwater prawn hatcheries. Over time, Viet Nam incorporated MrNV diagnostics and broodstock health management into broader aquatic animal health programs; while detailed quantitative impact data are scarce, WTD is recognized regionally as one of several important constraints on prawn seed production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of M. rosenbergii aquaculture in the Mekong Delta, frequent movement of broodstock and seed within and between hatcheries, and connectivity with other WTD‑affected South‑eastern Asian countries likely underlay the emergence of MrNV in Viet Nam. Internal mechanisms: As in neighboring countries, co‑infection of broodstock with MrNV/XSV and high susceptibility of early life stages probably drove episodic but severe hatchery losses once the virus was introduced.
Review: review: Tightened the event window to 2006–2010 to match the timeframe of Vietnamese work in the Mekong Delta and clarified that this event is inferred primarily from regional FAO/NACA reports and a national research project rather than a single detailed outbreak paper. Set intra‑continental emergence to ‘No’ because South‑eastern Asia was already affected via Thailand; this row represents further spread within the same sub‑region. Given the indirect nature of the evidence and uncertainty about scale, the event is flagged for review regarding both its timing and whether it belongs among the top 10 highest‑impact episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Host: Macrobrachium rosenbergii post-larvae in a commercial hatchery
Event summary: In December 2011, a large M. rosenbergii hatchery near Yogyakarta, Indonesia, experienced a severe outbreak of white tail disease in post‑larvae, with rapid tail muscle whitening followed by high mortalities that threatened its multi‑million‑PL annual production. Laboratory investigations using RT‑PCR and infection trials demonstrated that the disease was caused by MrNV, often with XSV, and that the virus could be transmitted via immersion and through Artemia used as live feed, firmly establishing MrNV as the etiologic agent of this Indonesian WTD event. Following confirmation, the hatchery and local authorities culled affected lots, tightened broodstock and water treatment protocols and strengthened health screening, which controlled the immediate outbreak, although MrNV remains a concern for Indonesian prawn seed production and trade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation or regional movement of infected broodstock or post‑larvae from other WTD‑endemic South‑eastern Asian countries, combined with highly intensive, centralized seed production for much of Java and other islands, likely facilitated MrNV introduction and amplification in the Yogyakarta hatchery. Internal mechanisms: The Indonesian outbreak involved MrNV strains closely related to other Asian isolates, indicating continued regional spread of a high‑virulence lineage; high susceptibility of post‑larvae, efficient waterborne transmission and the demonstrated role of live feeds as vectors contributed to the rapid escalation and economic significance of this single‑hatchery event.
Review: retain: This event is well documented as the first confirmed WTD outbreak in Indonesia with clear linkage to MrNV and substantial hatchery‑level economic impact. Corrected the emergence‑type classification by setting intra‑continental emergence to ‘No’, because South‑eastern Asia already harbored MrNV; at the sub‑regional level this is additional national spread. Despite being geographically localized, the hatchery’s production scale and the detailed virological evidence justify retaining this row as a major event, though users may wish to reassess its relative ranking against broader regional episodes.

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: India [marine shrimp hatcheries co-located with M. rosenbergii seed production; mainly on the east coast]
Host: Penaeus (Penaeus) monodon and Penaeus (Fenneropenaeus) indicus post-larvae in marine hatcheries; nearby Macrobrachium rosenbergii stocks as likely source hosts
Event summary: In the late 2000s, Indian marine shrimp hatcheries that produced P. monodon and P. indicus seed in close proximity to M. rosenbergii hatcheries began to experience outbreaks of white tail‑like disease in penaeid post‑larvae, with abdominal muscle whitening and high mortalities. Studies by Ravi and co‑workers showed that affected P. monodon and P. indicus post‑larvae were infected with MrNV and XSV, and that the clinical and histopathological picture matched WTD in M. rosenbergii, representing the first confirmed natural WTD outbreaks in marine penaeid shrimp. The outbreaks prompted warnings about mixed or adjacent culture of freshwater prawn and penaeid shrimp, and led to recommendations for stricter separation of systems, improved broodstock and larvae screening and stronger biosecurity barriers between prawn and shrimp sectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Co‑location of M. rosenbergii and penaeid shrimp hatcheries, use of common water sources and shared infrastructure, and the absence of strict barriers between freshwater and marine seed production created opportunities for MrNV from infected freshwater prawns to spill over into penaeid systems. Internal mechanisms: These events represent a clear host‑range expansion of MrNV, with documented natural infection and high mortality in P. monodon and P. indicus post‑larvae; this biological shift fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and underscores the capacity of MrNV/XSV to cause severe disease beyond their traditional freshwater prawn host.
Review: review: Added this new row to capture the first documented natural WTD outbreaks with high mortality in penaeid shrimp (P. monodon and P. indicus) in India, which were omitted from the original dataset but clearly represent a major host‑range expansion and thus a re‑emergence under the project’s definitions. Classified only the re‑emergence flag as ‘Yes’ to reflect host expansion within an already affected sub‑region; all geographic emergence flags are ‘No’. Because quantitative data on national‑scale production loss are limited, the event is flagged for review regarding whether it should displace any existing rows if a strict cap of 10 events is enforced, but it should be present in the curated list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV; white tail disease virus)
Countries: Multiple P. vannamei-farming countries in East and Southeast Asia (samples from farms in at least Thailand and Taiwan Province of China; additional locations not consistently specified)
Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (Pacific white shrimp) in marine/brackish farms with white muscle lesions; Macrobrachium rosenbergii in nearby or associated culture systems (continuing host)
Event summary: Between roughly 2006 and 2012, investigators re‑examining Pacific white shrimp (P. vannamei) from Asian farms that had experienced episodes of white muscle disease and high mortality but tested negative for known agents IMNV and PvNV found that some of these samples were positive for MrNV by RT‑PCR and genome sequencing. Bioassays in which P. vannamei were fed MrNV‑infected M. rosenbergii tissue demonstrated that MrNV could replicate and cause increased mortality in P. vannamei under low‑salinity, low‑temperature conditions, confirming that this important marine shrimp species is naturally susceptible to MrNV. These findings, together with field detections in farmed P. vannamei and earlier Indian cases in P. monodon and P. indicus, expanded concern about MrNV from a primarily freshwater prawn pathogen to a broader crustacean threat and prompted recommendations for stricter separation of freshwater prawn and marine shrimp production and targeted surveillance of white‑muscle cases for MrNV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The expansion of intensive P. vannamei culture across Asia, frequent co‑location or proximity of freshwater prawn and marine shrimp farms, shared water or intake canals and movement of potentially infected live crustaceans created repeated opportunities for MrNV originating in M. rosenbergii to encounter P. vannamei. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated natural infection of P. vannamei with MrNV and experimental confirmation of disease and mortality under certain environmental conditions indicate a further host‑range expansion of MrNV; although pathogenicity in P. vannamei appears more context‑dependent than in M. rosenbergii, this broadened host spectrum justifies classification as a re‑emergence event driven primarily by biological host expansion rather than purely by management changes.
Review: review: Reworked the original host‑expansion event to: (i) align the timing with the Aquaculture 2012 study (samples from 2006–2007, paper published 2012) rather than 2010–2018; (ii) focus specifically on P. vannamei while acknowledging associated M. rosenbergii sources; and (iii) replace a French Wikipedia citation with the primary Aquaculture paper and relevant WOAH/Pathogens reviews. Geographic detail on which countries contributed P. vannamei samples is incomplete, so the countries field remains partly generic; the event is therefore flagged for review, both because of this uncertainty and because its overall economic impact relative to large M. rosenbergii epizootics is less well quantified.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (imported Merino and Awassi; indigenous Menz and other central highland sheep)
Event summary: From the mid‑1980s, serology at Debre Berhan breeding centres detected Maedi–Visna virus infection for the first time in Ethiopia, initially in imported Merino sheep and then in local Menz and crossbred flocks in the central highlands.([repository.au-ibar.org](https://repository.au-ibar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/efd11302-ba60-4ad1-a656-985d54b21213/content)) During the 1990s and early 2000s, surveys of government ranches and nearby smallholder flocks found very high MVV seroprevalence (often >70%) and increasing chronic respiratory disease, leading to recognition of ovine progressive pneumonia as a major emerging cause of pneumonia in central Ethiopian sheep.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/)) By about 2003, microscopic examination of pneumonic lungs from highland sheep confirmed typical maedi‑visna lesions alongside pulmonary adenomatosis, indicating that MVV had become endemic in improved and crossbred highland flocks while remaining rare in lowland small ruminants.([ilri.org](https://www.ilri.org/knowledge/publications/pulmonary-adenomatosis-and-maedi-visna-ethiopian-central-highland-sheep))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale importation of exotic wool and dairy breeds (Merino, Awassi, Romney, Dorper) into Ethiopian government ranches from the 1960s onwards, and subsequent dissemination of crossbred rams to farmers around Debre Berhan and other highland areas, introduced MVV and facilitated its spread into previously naïve central Ethiopian sheep populations.([repository.au-ibar.org](https://repository.au-ibar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/efd11302-ba60-4ad1-a656-985d54b21213/content)) Intensive management and housing at breeding centres, with high stocking densities and close confinement at lambing, further amplified transmission before the disease was widely recognised.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/)) Internal mechanisms: No unique Ethiopian MVV lineage has yet been defined; the event reflects typical SRLV biology—lifelong infection, delayed seroconversion, and efficient dam–lamb and close‑contact transmission—which allowed extensive silent spread prior to formal detection.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/))
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (i) changed first_detection from Yes to No and flagged re_occurrence as Yes, because MVV was first serologically detected in imported Merino sheep in Ethiopia in 1986 (with subsequent infection in local sheep) and thus global first detection lies decades earlier; (ii) adjusted the time span to 1986–2003 to cover the documented introduction and early establishment phase, while keeping the focus on post‑1990 emergence; (iii) rewrote the event summary to rely on primary Ethiopian studies (Ayelet/Woldemeskel and later surveys) rather than implying that recognition only began “around 1990”; and (iv) updated sources to include the AU‑IBAR review and ILRI microscopic study instead of generic MVV reviews alone. This event remains one of the largest and most consequential modern emergence episodes for MVV and should be retained, but a subject‑matter expert should verify exact start/end years and whether to split additional sub‑events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (south‑western Finnish flocks)
Event summary: Finland, previously regarded as free of Maedi–Visna, detected MVV infection in eight sheep flocks in the south‑west during a 1994 serological survey; epidemiological investigation indicated that the virus had been introduced by imported sheep around 1981.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) Over the mid‑to‑late 1990s, infection remained geographically limited while a government‑approved voluntary control programme using repeated ELISA testing, culling of reactors and movement restrictions was implemented in affected and at‑risk flocks.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) By about 2000, Finland reported successful eradication of MVV from programme flocks and regained national MV‑free status, making this a well‑documented incursion and elimination episode.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected breeding sheep from other European countries into southwestern Finland, followed by local trade of live animals between a small number of flocks, seeded MVV into a country that had been free of the infection.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) The subsequent voluntary control programme—with systematic serological surveillance, removal of positive animals and tight movement controls—minimised further spread and allowed eradication. Internal mechanisms: No novel MVV strain or host shift was reported; the event reflects re‑occurrence of established SRLV genotypes in a previously free national population via trade.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7222820/))
Review: Decision: review. Changes: (i) set first_detection from Yes to No to align with the definition that first detection refers to the host system globally (MVV was already widespread in Europe long before 1994); (ii) set re_occurrence to Yes, as this episode represents a re‑occurrence/incursion into a previously free country within a sub‑region (Northern Europe) where MVV was already endemic; and (iii) clarified in the summary that the event is a national incursion and eradication episode, not a global or continental first. The event is well supported by the Finnish voluntary control programme paper and remains a useful example of successful eradication, so it should be retained among the major events, but the re‑classification should be checked against how other country‑level first‑detections are coded in the broader dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1998] (mainly Scotland)
Host: Sheep (pedigree lowland flocks, especially Texel and Suffolk flocks in Scotland)
Event summary: In the late 1990s, a major outbreak of Maedi–Visna was recognised in pedigree sheep flocks in Scotland, traced to a heavily infected source flock that had sold breeding stock widely to other high‑value flocks.([fwi.co.uk](https://www.fwi.co.uk/news/beware-of-risks-following-maedi-visna-outbreak)) Over the following few years, targeted serological testing and culling revealed further linked infections, prompting re‑evaluation of the UK MV accreditation scheme and biosecurity around pedigree sheep movements.([fas.scot](https://www.fas.scot/article/maedi-visna-mv-increase/)) By the early 2000s, most affected pedigree flocks had been culled or heavily depopulated, but the episode highlighted how MVV could re‑establish in accredited populations when pre‑purchase testing and quarantine were inadequate, with substantial economic losses in high‑value breeding stock.([qmscotland.co.uk](https://qmscotland.co.uk/news/sheep-farmers-urged-step-vigilance-maedi-visna))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Concentration of susceptible pedigree sheep in a limited number of flocks, frequent movement of breeding animals between accredited and non‑accredited flocks, and inadequate pre‑movement MVV testing allowed rapid dissemination from a single heavily infected flock into multiple high‑value flocks.([fwi.co.uk](https://www.fwi.co.uk/news/beware-of-risks-following-maedi-visna-outbreak)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel genotype or host expansion was reported; the outbreak largely reflects amplification of endemic MVV in intensively traded pedigree populations where the long incubation period and iceberg nature of infection facilitated undetected spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482963/))
Review: Decision: retain. This event fits the definition of a re‑occurrence (control breakdown with expansion of an endemic agent) within a long‑affected sub‑region, and the narrative and timing are supported by specialist UK industry sources and later epidemiological reviews. I did not identify major factual errors in the geography, dates or type‑of‑event coding (re_occurrence only), and the flock‑level impact (including at least one later 4,000‑ewe cull linked to MVV) argues for retaining a representative UK pedigree‑flock episode among the top events. Minor refinements (e.g. more precise dates or including explicit flock sizes) could be added at a later curation step but are not essential.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (various meat and wool breeds in multiple Brazilian states)
Event summary: Maedi–Visna virus was first identified in Brazil in the late 1980s, when AGID testing found seropositive sheep in Rio Grande do Sul on farms with a history of importing animals.([revistas.ufg.br](https://revistas.ufg.br/vet/article/download/4454/9257?inline=1)) During the 2000s, additional serological and molecular studies documented low but widespread MVV infection in sheep from several states, including São Paulo, Paraná, Pernambuco, Ceará and Sergipe, indicating that infection had become established across both southern and northeastern production systems.([bjvm.org.br](https://bjvm.org.br/BJVM/article/view/521)) By around 2012, Embrapa and national reviews described maedi–visna as a widely distributed but under‑recognised disease of Brazilian sheep with potential economic impact, especially in intensive and semi‑intensive flocks.([embrapa.br](https://www.embrapa.br/web/caprinos-e-ovinos/cim-inteligencia-e-mercado-de-caprinos-e-ovinos/zoossanitario-maedi-visna))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Initial introduction of MVV into Rio Grande do Sul via imported sheep was followed by internal trade in purebred and crossbred breeding stock, which disseminated infection to other states over subsequent decades; limited routine testing, long incubation periods and often subclinical infection allowed the virus to remain largely undetected until targeted surveys were undertaken.([revistas.ufg.br](https://revistas.ufg.br/vet/article/download/4454/9257?inline=1)) Internal mechanisms: No specific Brazilian MVV lineage or virulence shift has been linked to this period; the process is best interpreted as geographic range expansion and endemic establishment of pre‑existing SRLV genotypes across Brazilian flocks under varied management conditions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9924038/))
Review: Decision: retain. The event correctly captures the timing and nature of MVV emergence in Brazil: first serological detection in Rio Grande do Sul in 1987–1989, followed by documentation of infection in multiple additional states during the 2000s and recognition of maedi–visna as an emerging national problem. I left the classification as re_occurrence (expansion of an established global pathogen into new national regions) and did not mark first_detection, because global first detection and emergence occurred long before. Sources have been focused on primary Brazilian studies and Embrapa summaries; the event is one of the few describing MVV expansion in South America and should be kept as a major episode.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (Norwegian commercial flocks in Nord-Trøndelag and connected ram circles)
Event summary: After many years of low‑prevalence maedi under a national control programme, Norway detected new cases in November 2002 and January 2003 when post‑mortem examinations from two farms in Nord‑Trøndelag revealed histopathological lesions consistent with maedi.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Subsequent tracing and serological screening of more than 15,000 sheep from about 300 flocks identified around 50 infected flocks linked to this cluster, triggering strict movement restrictions, repeated whole‑flock testing and culling of seropositive animals.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) By 2005, the outbreak had been largely contained and surveillance estimated national prevalence below 0.2% positive flocks, but the episode demonstrated that MVV could re‑enter and spread within Norway despite long‑standing surveillance and control measures.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak was associated with infected animals entering organised ram circles that supply breeding stock to many commercial flocks, allowing extensive contact networks and movement of potentially infected rams between holdings before MVV was detected.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not suggest a novel or more virulent strain; rather, the re‑occurrence is consistent with the epidemiology of conventional SRLVs in high‑contact breeding networks, aided by long incubation, intermittent seroconversion and incomplete sensitivity of single‑time‑point ELISA screening.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921448823002456))
Review: Decision: review. Adjustments: (i) narrowed the original very broad 2000–2010 time span to 2002–2005, matching Norwegian surveillance reports that date this specific Nord‑Trøndelag outbreak; (ii) clarified that about 50 flocks were found seropositive after screening ~300 flocks and 15,000 sheep, which better conveys the scale; and (iii) confirmed that this episode is best categorised as a re_occurrence in a country with a long‑running control programme, not as first_detection or intra‑continental emergence. The event appears to be of substantial epidemiological and economic importance and should be retained, but I recommend expert review of the exact flock counts and whether to merge or separate it analytically from the later 2019–2020 Norwegian outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (Menz, Awassi and crossbred flocks at Debre Berhan and Amed Guya sheep multiplication centres)
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2007, a severe Maedi–Visna outbreak forced closure of the Debre Berhan and Amed Guya sheep breed multiplication centres in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, which had been central to national crossbreeding programmes. MVV serosurveys at Amed Guya during this period found very high flock‑level seroprevalence (around 87%) across Menz, Awassi and crossbred sheep, and concurrent respiratory disease caused major production losses.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) The crisis led to suspension of ram distribution, mass culling of seropositive animals—reports indicate that at Amed Guya roughly 2,300 of 3,000 sheep were slaughtered—and temporary closure of both ranches.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) By 2007, the centres had been partially restocked with MVV‑negative flocks, but later studies still documented high seroprevalence, underscoring how deeply MVV had become entrenched in these improvement herds.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Crossbreeding projects that imported Awassi and other exotic breeds into Debre Berhan and Amed Guya from the 1960s onwards, combined with their mandate to supply thousands of improved rams to surrounding smallholders, created large, densely stocked ranches that acted as both amplifiers and dispersal hubs once MVV was introduced.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) Limited early MVV surveillance and biosecurity at these centres allowed infection to reach very high within‑flock prevalence before it was detected and control measures—closure, testing and mass culling—were imposed. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence for emergence of a novel Ethiopian strain; the episode is best explained by typical SRLV dynamics in crowded breeding flocks with high dam–lamb contact and close housing during the cold season, leading to sustained high infection pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/))
Review: Decision: review. New event added. Rationale: multiple Ethiopian sources report that the Debre Berhan and Amed Guya multiplication ranches were closed between 2004 and 2007 because of a major MVV outbreak, with very high seroprevalence and large‑scale culling (about 2,300 of 3,000 sheep at Amed Guya). This represents a discrete, high‑impact episode distinct from the earlier introduction/establishment phase and clearly qualifies as one of the most consequential MVV emergence events globally in the post‑1990 period. I created a dedicated row to capture this outbreak, coded as re_occurrence (no evidence for a new strain), and sourced it directly from detailed seroprevalence and programme reports. A domain expert should verify the approximate numbers culled and ensure there is no double‑counting with the broader 1986–2003 Ethiopia event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: India [2016] (Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh; abattoirs in northern India)
Host: Sheep (slaughtered and farmed) and goats (serology in mixed small‑ruminant flocks)
Event summary: Around 2016, investigators in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, reported ELISA evidence of Maedi–Visna and caprine arthritis–encephalitis virus antibodies in sheep and goats, giving the first published indication of SRLV circulation in that region of India.([ndpublisher.in](https://ndpublisher.in/admin/issues/JARV6N13.pdf)) In 2017, a pathology study on 888 slaughtered sheep from Indian abattoirs identified lungs with lesions consistent with maedi and confirmed MVV proviral DNA by PCR in a subset, which the authors described as probably the first molecular confirmation of maedi‑visna infection in India.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29263606/)) Subsequent work from the same group has demonstrated MVV nucleic acid and antigen in various tissues of spontaneously affected sheep and goats, indicating that SRLV infection is established in parts of the Indian small‑ruminant population, although national prevalence and economic impact remain poorly quantified.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11327649/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of sheep and goat production in some Indian states, together with movement or importation of exotic and crossbred animals for genetic improvement, likely introduced MVV and related SRLVs into previously unrecognised foci; limited prior surveillance meant that infection could circulate silently for years before serological and molecular tools were applied.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29263606/)) Internal mechanisms: Early reports have not identified a unique Indian lineage associated with changed virulence; observed lesions and tropism match typical SRLV infections. Long incubation periods, multisystemic pathology and variable antibody responses complicate diagnosis and control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11327649/))
Review: Decision: review. Updates: (i) changed first_detection from Yes to No, since MVV was globally recognised long before and there is evidence of SRLV infection in other Southern Asian countries (e.g. Iran) before 2016; (ii) set re_occurrence to Yes, interpreting this as emergence of MVV/SRLVs in a new country within a continent and sub‑region where they were already present; and (iii) clarified that 2017 represents the first molecular confirmation in India rather than necessarily the first true presence. The event is important for documenting the entry of MVV into Indian small‑ruminant populations, but final weighting among the ‘top 10’ should be checked against any future evidence of larger, multi‑flock outbreaks in the region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: Brazil [2018] (Rio Grande do Sul, Salvador do Sul municipality)
Host: Sheep (Texel flock, southern Brazil)
Event summary: In January 2018, a closed flock of 96 Texel ewes in Salvador do Sul, Rio Grande do Sul, developed an outbreak of respiratory and neurological disease; 14 animals showed clinical signs such as weight loss, dyspnoea and hindlimb ataxia and 14.5% of the flock were seropositive for MVV.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) Histopathology and PCR confirmed concurrent maedi (lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia) and visna (encephalitis), and the authors reported this as the first well‑documented outbreak of clinical visna‑maedi disease in a Brazilian sheep flock.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) All seropositive sheep were eventually culled, representing a major loss for the pedigree meat flock and illustrating the potential for severe disease expression where MVV enters a naïve, intensively managed system.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The flock had acquired replacement ewes from multiple external sources without MVV testing and used artificial insemination with semen of uncertain lentiviral status; combined with semi‑intensive management (indoor housing at night, high stocking density), these practices facilitated efficient within‑flock spread once MVV was introduced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was identified; the episode shows how typical SRLV strains can cause overt maedi and visna when introduced into large, genetically susceptible and previously unexposed flocks, with chronic infection and high contact rates leading to cumulative pathology and production loss.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/))
Review: Decision: review. Correction: reclassified this episode from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the clinical outbreak involved typical MVV strains in an already infected country and there is no evidence for a new genotype, host switch or change in intrinsic viral properties; the severe expression is best explained by introduction into a naïve, intensively housed Texel flock. The event is flock‑scale (≈100 animals) but is notable as the first fully documented clinical visna–maedi outbreak in Brazil and helps to illustrate the production impact of MVV in South American systems; it should likely be retained but may be ranked slightly below the very largest multi‑flock events (e.g. Ethiopia and Norway) when enforcing a strict top‑10 cut‑off.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (commercial and breeding flocks in Trøndelag)
Event summary: In 2019, the Norwegian SRLV surveillance programme detected a new case of maedi in a sheep flock in Trøndelag county after more than a decade without detected cases.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Tracing of animal movements and intensive regional screening in northern Trøndelag led to the identification of an outbreak cluster; surveillance reports and subsequent analyses describe nine initially recognised infected flocks, with extended investigations revealing well over a hundred infected flocks overall and necessitating culling of thousands of sheep.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) By 2020, aggressive test‑and‑cull measures, movement controls and targeted surveillance had again reduced apparent prevalence to very low levels, but the outbreak underscored the diagnostic challenges of eliminating SRLVs and the risk of re‑introduction even in countries with long‑standing control programmes.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The 2019–2020 outbreak appears to have stemmed from undetected introduction of MVV‑infected animals into a regional breeding network with extensive movement of rams and ewes between flocks, coupled with earlier surveillance strategies that focused on specific flock types and may have allowed infection to persist unrecognised in other holdings.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate emergence of a novel, more virulent MVV strain; instead, the outbreak is consistent with the known epidemiology of SRLVs—long incubation, intermittent seropositivity and focal high within‑flock prevalence—interacting with imperfectly sensitive serological tests and incomplete coverage of prior surveillance.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11225221/))
Review: Decision: review. New event added.
