Rationale: more recent Norwegian reports and outbreak analyses show that the 2019–2020 Trøndelag episode involved a substantial number of infected flocks (on the order of 100–200) and culling of thousands of sheep, clearly marking it as one of the most impactful modern MVV re‑occurrence events. I therefore added a dedicated row rather than subsuming it under the earlier 2002–2005 outbreak. The event is coded as re_occurrence, with no evidence for a new strain or inter‑continental introduction. Precise numbers of infected flocks (e.g. the figure of 179 reported in at least one analysis) should be verified and harmonised across the dataset by a Nordic expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2021] (Scotland; Northern Ireland)
Host: Sheep (lowland and hill flocks, accredited and non‑accredited)
Event summary: In 2021, veterinary authorities in Northern Ireland confirmed Maedi–Visna infection in homebred sheep linked to movements from Scotland, prompting intensive tracing and control actions; industry reports also noted increasing concern about chronic viral infections such as MVV in UK flocks in the early 2020s.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/maedi-visna-mv)) Over 2021–2022, additional affected flocks were identified through targeted serological sampling of imports and contact holdings, and movement controls, flock restrictions and culling of reactors were implemented to limit further spread.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/maedi-visna-mv)) MVV remains endemic at relatively low prevalence in the British national flock, but this episode led to renewed emphasis on MV accreditation, quarantine and testing of purchased breeding sheep.([fas.scot](https://www.fas.scot/article/maedi-visna-mv-increase/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased movement of breeding sheep between Scotland, Northern Ireland and other parts of the British Isles, purchasing from non‑accredited or inadequately monitored flocks, and high stocking densities in some lowland systems contributed to renewed MVV incursions into flocks previously believed to be free, while greater surveillance focused on chronic viral diseases increased detection.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/maedi-visna-mv)) Internal mechanisms: No novel MVV genotype has been implicated; the event reflects re‑introduction and persistence of existing SRLV strains in partially susceptible populations, aided by long incubation periods and the limitations of single‑round serological screening.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482963/))
Review: Decision: retain. This event accurately captures a documented recent re‑occurrence of MVV in the UK and Northern Ireland, supported by DAERA communications and industry briefings, and is correctly coded as re_occurrence only. While the total number of affected flocks is modest compared to Ethiopia or Norway, its policy relevance (renewed control measures and industry messaging) argues for keeping it in the curated list. Further refinement (e.g. explicit flock counts, whether cases also occurred in the Republic of Ireland) could be added in a future update but are not essential for current purposes.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in natural beds and coastal fishing grounds of the Gulf of Thessaloniki / Thermaikos Gulf (northern Aegean Sea)
Event summary: Between about 1994 and 1998, native flat‑oyster beds in the Gulf of Thessaloniki (Thermaikos Gulf) in northern Greece suffered progressive, multi‑year mass mortalities and a dramatic decline in landings, leading to closure of the local O. edulis fishery and functional extinction of natural beds. Subsequent investigations demonstrated high prevalences of Marteilia sp. consistent with M. refringens in the remaining oysters and documented that infection was largely confined to this gulf (≈46% prevalence in sampled oysters, with other Greek sites testing negative), strongly implicating marteiliosis as a primary driver of the collapse. Follow‑up work through the 2000s confirmed persistence of Marteilia infections in both oysters and farmed mussels in Thermaikos Gulf, with temperature‑linked peaks in parasite activity but no recovery of the original flat‑oyster stocks.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: chronic environmental stress in Thermaikos Gulf (eutrophication, reduced water quality and elevated summer temperatures) combined with intensive shellfish exploitation, which likely reduced host condition and resilience and favoured sustained marteiliosis transmission. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of M. refringens in a new national setting within an already endemic Mediterranean sub‑region, with high infection intensities in O. edulis but no clear evidence of a novel strain or host jump; the impact is best characterised as a severe resurgence in a previously uninfected local population rather than a taxonomically novel re‑emergence.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))
Review: review: Added this event as a major, previously omitted emergence episode: the marteiliosis‑associated collapse of Greek flat‑oyster beds in the Gulf of Thessaloniki / Thermaikos Gulf during 1994–1998, explicitly cited in the DFO synopsis as a dramatic decrease in O. edulis production linked to M. refringens.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))  Classified it as re‑occurrence (not intra‑continental emergence) because the parasite was already endemic in the Southern Europe sub‑region (France, Spain, Italy) and there is no evidence of a distinct strain or host jump in this case, even though it was the first detection in Greece.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))  A national expert review is recommended to refine the exact starting year (the production decline begins in the mid‑1990s and some Greek sources frame the extinction of oyster beds as occurring over the preceding decade) and to ensure that the role of co‑occurring stressors (other diseases, pollution) is properly weighted relative to marteiliosis in the event summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in Mediterranean coastal lagoons and nearby farms
Event summary: In 2006, Marteilia refringens was officially reported for the first time in European flat oysters Ostrea edulis from Moroccan Mediterranean waters, based on OIE notifications and subsequent summaries, representing the first confirmed detection of the parasite in North Africa. This finding extended the known range of M. refringens southwards from endemic European areas into a new continent, although available reports did not document large‑scale mortality comparable to historic French outbreaks. Following the report, Moroccan and international authorities incorporated the affected lagoons into marteiliosis surveillance and trade‑control frameworks to limit further spread within North Africa and across the Mediterranean.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introduction via movements of infected oyster seed or adults from enzootic European sources into Moroccan lagoons, combined with suitable local temperature and salinity regimes that allowed establishment of the parasite life cycle; limited prior surveillance may have delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of established M. refringens lineages into a new continent (Africa) without evidence of marked changes in virulence or host range relative to European populations.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))
Review: review: Retained this event as the first confirmed detection of M. refringens in North Africa and thus a valid inter‑continental emergence, supported by OIE/WOAH and DFO distribution summaries.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))  However, reset the ‘first_detection’ flag from Yes to No because, under the project’s definitions, first detection/global emergence should refer to the earliest record in the host system overall (which occurred in France in the late 1960s), not to country‑level firsts; the appropriate type label here is inter‑continental emergence.  No strong evidence was found for major mortality or production loss in Morocco comparable to Greek or historical French events, but given its status as the first African record and its regulatory importance, it still belongs among the top emergence events and is flagged for expert review mainly to confirm that no better country‑level case series are available than the current summary sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Ostrea stentina (dwarf oyster) in coastal sites near Monastir and along nearby Tunisian shores
Event summary: Around 2009–2010, dense populations of the dwarf oyster Ostrea stentina along the central Tunisian coast (near Monastir and adjacent areas) experienced episodes of severe mortality. Histology, TEM and PCR subsequently demonstrated heavy infections by Marteilia refringens in O. stentina, with prevalences up to 90–100% and massive parasite burdens in digestive tissues, representing the first confirmed report of this host–parasite combination and of marteiliosis in Tunisian oysters. The outbreaks caused marked physiological impairment and collapse of local O. stentina aggregations, and later surveys showed that M. refringens remained established in this host and region as an endemic infection.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201112002728?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑density O. stentina aggregations in sheltered, warm coastal habitats, elevated summer temperatures and local environmental stressors (eutrophication, pollution) that likely increased host susceptibility; possible introduction or amplification via regional shellfish movements from other Mediterranean foci. Internal mechanisms: clear host expansion of M. refringens into O. stentina with very high infection intensities and severe pathology, consistent with a re‑emergence event in an already affected Northern Africa sub‑region driven by parasite–host adaptation and efficient transmission in a new oyster host.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201112002728?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: Corrected the event‑type flags: set ‘first_global_emergence’ and ‘first_detection’ to No because M. refringens was first detected and globally emerged in flat oysters in France decades earlier, and this Tunisian episode represents a new host and country within a continent where the parasite was already present (Morocco).([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.811284/full?utm_source=openai))  Retained ‘re_emergence’ = Yes to reflect the documented host expansion into O. stentina with very high prevalence and severe pathology in an already affected Northern Africa sub‑region, which fits the project’s re‑emergence definition.  The event remains one of the most impactful post‑1990 marteiliosis episodes (massive local dwarf‑oyster mortality), but is flagged for review so an expert can confirm whether it should be represented as a single Tunisian event or as part of a broader Mediterranean O. stentina emergence episode including later findings in Iberia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) and Ostrea stentina (dwarf oyster) in southern Portugal (Ria Formosa lagoon) and nearby southern Spain (Carreras River and other sites)
Event summary: Between about 2011 and 2012, targeted surveys of flat‑oyster and dwarf‑oyster populations in southern Portugal and adjacent southern Spain detected Marteilia refringens in Ostrea edulis for the first time in Portugal and in O. stentina at both Portuguese and Spanish sites. Histology and ITS‑1 sequencing showed O‑type M. refringens infecting O. edulis in the Ria Formosa lagoon, while both O‑type and M‑type genotypes were detected in O. stentina, marking the first confirmed occurrence of M. refringens in this host species in Europe. These findings extended the known range of marteiliosis westwards along the Iberian Atlantic coast and revealed that O. stentina could act as an additional susceptible host in European waters, prompting integration of the affected areas into EU/WOAH surveillance and movement‑control frameworks.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201115001287?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: regional transboundary movements of oysters and mussels for aquaculture and restocking among France, Spain and Portugal; natural dispersal of parasite stages by coastal currents along the Alboran–Gulf of Cádiz–Algarve corridor; and favourable lagoon environments (temperature, salinity, retention) for parasite development. Internal mechanisms: expansion of M. refringens into a new oyster host species (O. stentina) within Europe and continued spread within endemic Southern Europe, consistent with a re‑emergence event driven by host‑range broadening and geographic expansion of existing lineages rather than by purely external resurgence factors.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201115001287?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: Retained this episode as a major Iberian range‑expansion and host‑expansion event but reclassified it from pure ‘re‑occurrence’ to ‘re‑emergence’ to emphasise the demonstrated expansion of M. refringens into O. stentina in European waters, in line with the project definition that re‑emergence involves intrinsic pathogen changes such as host expansion.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201115001287?utm_source=openai))  Confirmed from the primary paper that the Portuguese detections indeed represent the first report of M. refringens in Portugal, with O‑type sequences in O. edulis and both O‑ and M‑type sequences in O. stentina; however, the ‘first_detection’ flag remains No because first detection for the host system occurred decades earlier in France.  Spain is kept in the ‘countries’ field as a historically affected neighbour where linked infections were documented, but the impact narrative focuses on the Portuguese emergence; this compounded nature should be flagged for expert review to ensure it matches how other multi‑country linked episodes are handled.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) in a closed colony of 53 animals at Everland Zoological Gardens, Yongin, Republic of Korea
Event summary: Between December 1992 and March 1993, an outbreak of natural measles virus infection occurred in a colony of 53 Japanese macaques at Everland Zoological Gardens in Yongin, Republic of Korea, probably originating from exposure to infected human visitors while the monkeys were on outdoor public exhibit. Over roughly four months, 12 macaques aged 7 months to 22 years developed dermatitis, diarrhea, neurologic signs and systemic disease and died, and necropsy with histopathology, immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization and electron microscopy confirmed widespread measles virus antigen and characteristic paramyxovirus nucleocapsids in multiple tissues together with frequent opportunistic co-infections. Clinical cases ceased after the most severely affected animals died and the colony was managed in new outdoor enclosures, and no further measles cases were reported from this group, highlighting the high susceptibility of unvaccinated macaques and the risk posed by human visitors. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of human measles virus into a closed, unvaccinated Japanese macaque colony at a public zoo, most likely via aerosol exposure to infected human visitors, with recent transfers between enclosures and associated handling stress likely contributing to immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: A standard wild-type human measles virus caused profound immunosuppression in affected macaques, predisposing them to high rates of secondary infections (including disseminated cytomegalovirus infection, bacterial pneumonia and Candida-associated lesions) and contributing to about 21% colony mortality, but there is no evidence of a novel NHP-adapted strain; pathogenesis closely mirrored severe human measles with opportunistic infections. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))
Review: review – Newly added high-impact event based on a detailed veterinary pathology case report describing a 1992–1993 measles epizootic in 53 Japanese macaques at Everland Zoological Gardens, Yongin, Republic of Korea (12 deaths; approximately 21% colony mortality). This outbreak clearly meets criteria for inclusion among the largest MeV emergence events in non-human primates since 1990 and fills an omission in the original dataset. Classified here as a re-occurrence in Asia rather than first detection or intra-continental emergence, because measles epizootics in captive NHPs were already well documented in Asia and elsewhere before 1990, but this choice should be confirmed by a human reviewer given incomplete historical reporting for Eastern Asia. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Old World non-human primates (Cercopithecidae), including cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis), rhesus macaques (M. mulatta), and pig-tailed macaques (M. nemestrina) housed in two primate research facilities
Event summary: In 1996, a large measles outbreak occurred in two U.S. facilities housing Old World non-human primates, following introduction of wild-type human measles virus during a period of ongoing community measles transmission. Over approximately two months, 94 monkeys developed evidence of acute measles infection, with clinical illness and serologic confirmation indicating rapid within-facility spread. The outbreak was brought under control through quarantine measures, restriction of human–primate contact, and emergency vaccination of both non-human primates and at-risk human staff, after which no further MeV transmission was detected in the colonies. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reverse zoonotic transmission from humans to NHPs during a concurrent human measles outbreak in the United States, facilitated by close contact between animal-care staff and primates and incomplete measles immunity among staff; high-density housing of susceptible macaques in indoor research facilities enabled rapid aerosol spread once the virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain specific to NHPs was identified; the outbreak virus was a circulating wild-type human measles virus, so the principal mechanisms were the inherent high transmissibility of MeV and the high susceptibility of Old World primates rather than viral adaptation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event is real and extensively documented (94 Old World non-human primates with acute measles infection over about two months in two U.S. research facilities) and is clearly among the most impactful MeV epizootics in NHPs since 1990. Geographical assignment (North America | Northern America; United States of America) and timing (1996) are correct, and classification as a re-occurrence driven by reverse zoonosis and gaps in vaccination or staff immunity is consistent with the literature; no corrections beyond minor wording and citation additions were needed. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in a non-human primate quarantine facility south of Manila, with concurrent Reston ebolavirus infection in some animals
Event summary: In August 2015, a non-human primate quarantine facility south of Manila, Philippines, detected unusual rash illness and sudden deaths in six cynomolgus macaques during routine monitoring, in the context of a large human measles outbreak nationally. Investigation and testing of 174 sera from the colony identified Reston ebolavirus infection in the dead animals and eight macaques with serologic evidence of recent measles virus infection, including two coinfected with RESTV, and the MeV strains corresponded to genotype B3 viruses circulating in humans in the Philippines at that time. The measles component of the outbreak was contained through quarantine, enhanced biosecurity, and close monitoring of the colony, and no onward spread of MeV from this facility to other NHP colonies was reported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reverse zoonotic spillover of measles virus from humans to captive macaques during a large national measles outbreak in the Philippines in 2015, facilitated by close human–NHP contact in a quarantine facility and concurrent biosecurity lapses that also permitted Reston ebolavirus transmission; high animal density and internal movements within the facility likely aided within-group spread. Internal mechanisms: The measles virus detected in macaques was a human genotype B3 strain rather than an NHP-adapted lineage, so cross-species transmission and limited onward spread reflected the inherently high transmissibility of MeV and host susceptibility rather than emergence of a novel variant specific to NHPs; there is no evidence in the report for increased virulence or other viral changes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is real and supported by a detailed Emerging Infectious Diseases case report on the 2015 Reston ebolavirus outbreak in cynomolgus macaques in the Philippines, which documents concurrent measles virus infection in eight animals; this outbreak is one of the few well-characterized post‑2005 MeV events in NHPs and should be retained as a major emergence episode. The original row misclassified this as first detection in the host system; measles infection in non-human primates was documented globally, including in Asia, many decades earlier, so the First_detection flag has been set to false and the event classified as a re-occurrence in an already affected sub-region of Asia driven by a large human measles epidemic and facility-level biosecurity gaps. The source list has been updated to prioritize the peer‑reviewed Emerging Infectious Diseases article (and its CDC stacks/PMC copies) as primary references, with the earlier conference abstract retained only as a supplementary citation; a human curator should verify that the balance between Reston ebolavirus and MeV content in the summary is appropriate for this EPP profile. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Net-pen–cultured marine red sea bream (Pagrus major) in coastal farms around Shikoku Island
Event summary: In 1990, a severe systemic disease with anemia, splenomegaly and very high mortality appeared in net‑pen–reared red sea bream on Shikoku Island, Japan. Virological investigation identified a large icosahedral DNA virus (red sea bream iridovirus, RSIV) as the cause and linked it to heavy losses in juvenile and grow‑out fish in southwestern Japan. Emergency culling and management changes reduced acute losses on affected farms, but RSIV became established in regional mariculture and prompted development of the first commercial marine‑fish vaccine in Japan.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of red sea bream mariculture in southwestern Japan, dense stocking in coastal net‑pens and warm summer seawater temperatures (~20–25 °C) facilitated initial emergence and farm‑to‑farm spread. Internal mechanisms: First recognized emergence and detection of a highly virulent RSIV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 adapted to sparid hosts, with efficient waterborne and horizontal transmission in young red sea bream.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the globally recognized first outbreak and first detection of red sea bream iridoviral disease in marine finfish aquaculture (Japan 1990); geography, timing and event‑type flags are consistent with the literature.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Multiple cultured marine finfish species (>30 species including red sea bream, yellowtail, groupers, flounders and others) in Japanese coastal mariculture
Event summary: During the 1990s, RSIVD spread from initial foci in Shikoku to many marine fish farms across southwestern and western Japan. By the late 1990s the virus had been confirmed in 17–18 prefectures and nearly 30 farmed marine species, causing recurring summer mass mortalities and major economic losses in red sea bream, yellowtail, groupers, flounders and other high‑value fish. Introduction of a formalin‑inactivated vaccine in 1999, together with movement controls and improved husbandry, reduced the scale of outbreaks, although RSIVD remained an endemic seasonal constraint on Japanese marine aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continuing expansion and diversification of Japanese marine finfish aquaculture, frequent transfer of juvenile fish between hatcheries and grow‑out sites, and high summer temperatures promoted rapid farm‑to‑farm spread and recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated broad host range and host expansion of the RSIV lineage within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to at least 30 cultured marine species, allowing persistence in multi‑species rearing systems and re‑emergence each warm season despite vaccination efforts.
Review: review – Event retained but (i) the time span was adjusted from 1991–1995 to 1991–2000 to match documentation of RSIVD expansion across Japanese mariculture through the late 1990s, and (ii) emergence‑type flags were simplified to re_emergence = true, re_occurrence = false to reflect major host‑range expansion and intensification within the same sub‑region rather than a generic 're‑occurrence'.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Net‑cage–cultured marine red sea bream (Pagrus major) around the Penghu (Pescadores) Islands off the southwestern Taiwan area
Event summary: From 1993 onward, outbreaks of a severe viral disease with abnormal swimming, lethargy and cumulative mortalities of 50–90% over roughly two months were reported in net‑cage–cultured red sea bream around the Penghu Islands off southwestern Taiwan. Virological and molecular analyses showed the causative agent to be closely related to Japanese RSIV, indicating introduction of red sea bream iridoviral disease into the Taiwan region. Farm‑level losses declined after affected cohorts were removed and stocking practices were modified, but RSIV/ISKNV‑like megalocytiviruses subsequently became established in Taiwanese marine aquaculture and were detected in additional host species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of infected but asymptomatic seed fish or broodstock from RSIVD‑endemic areas of Japan, combined with high‑density cage farming in sheltered island waters and warm seasonal temperatures, promoted rapid farm‑level spread and heavy mortality. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of an existing RSIV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 into a new country inside the Eastern Asia sub‑region, with high virulence in red sea bream but no clear evidence for major genomic change relative to Japanese isolates.
Review: review – Event retained but (i) the Country field was corrected to 'China [1993]' to comply with the project Country list while the text still specifies the Penghu/Taiwan location, and (ii) first_detection was set to false (global first detection is Japan 1990), leaving the episode classified as a major re_occurrence within Eastern Asia driven by transboundary seed‑fish movements.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Freshwater pond‑cultured mandarin fish (Siniperca chuatsi) in southern China
Event summary: From about 1994, large‑scale outbreaks of a systemic disease with splenic and renal necrosis caused catastrophic mortalities, often 90–100% in affected ponds, in pond‑reared mandarin fish in southern China. The causative agent, later named infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV), was identified as a megalocytivirus and linked to severe economic losses across multiple provinces during the late 1990s. As diagnostic tools and vaccines were developed and disseminated, farmers adopted control measures that reduced the frequency of explosive outbreaks, although ISKNV remained an important constraint on mandarin fish culture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of high‑value mandarin fish aquaculture with very high stocking densities, warm summer temperatures and frequent live‑fish movements between farms created conditions for efficient introduction and amplification of ISKNV. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct ISKNV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 able to cause peracute systemic disease in mandarin fish and later infect additional freshwater and marine species, representing a major genotype and host expansion of the species within Eastern Asia.
Review: review – New event added to capture the mid‑1990s emergence of infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV) in pond‑reared mandarin fish in China, which was omitted from the original file despite being one of the most impactful Megalocytivirus pagrus1 epizootics worldwide; classified as re_emergence (new genotype and host within the previously affected Eastern Asia sub‑region).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cultured rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus) and other marine finfish (e.g. red sea bream, sea perch, black porgy, rockfish) in coastal marine farms
Event summary: By the mid‑1990s, RSIV‑like systemic disease causing mass summer mortalities was recognized in cultured marine fish in the Republic of Korea, with rock bream particularly affected. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, recurrent epizootics produced annual die‑offs and major economic losses in rock bream and co‑reared species, and experimental infections demonstrated near‑100% mortality at typical rearing temperatures. Expanded surveillance, vaccination and changes in stocking and temperature‑management reduced, but did not eliminate, RSIVD as a major pathogen of Korean marine finfish aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of rock bream and other marine finfish farming, frequent movement of juveniles among farms, and seasonal seawater temperatures of roughly 25–30 °C that trigger disease expression in subclinically infected stocks all favoured repeated outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Adaptation and host expansion of RSIV genotype I within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to rock bream, which shows very high susceptibility and can act as an efficient amplifying host, underpinning re‑emergence of the virus within the Eastern Asia sub‑region.
Review: review – Event retained but emergence‑type flags were corrected: first_detection was set to false (global first detection in Japan), and re_emergence is now used (with re_occurrence = false) to emphasize the marked host expansion and repeated severe outbreaks of RSIVD in rock bream within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed turbot (Scophthalmus maximus) in intensive cold‑water marine culture in northern China (e.g. Shandong Peninsula)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, turbot farms in northern China began reporting a 'viral reddish body syndrome' in juveniles and adults, characterized by skin reddening, lethargy and high mortality. A new megalocytivirus, turbot reddish body iridovirus (TRBIV), was isolated from affected fish and linked to repeated outbreaks between about 2001 and 2006 that caused substantial production and economic losses in the rapidly expanding turbot industry. Subsequent development of diagnostics, vaccines and improved husbandry reduced the frequency of severe TRBIV epizootics, although the virus remains present in cultured flatfish populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of intensive turbot aquaculture in northern China, high stocking densities in recirculating or flow‑through systems and sub‑optimal husbandry facilitated spread once TRBIV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct TRBIV lineage within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 adapted to cold‑water flatfish hosts, with high virulence and efficient transmission in turbot, representing a major genotype and host shift within the species.
Review: review – New event added for turbot reddish body iridovirus (TRBIV) outbreaks in farmed turbot in northern China in the early 2000s, which represent a major genotype‑specific emergence of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 with high mortality and economic losses; classified as re_emergence in Eastern Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed Murray cod (Maccullochella peelii) in freshwater recirculating aquaculture in Victoria, exposed via feeding imported dwarf gouramis (Trichogaster lalius)
Event summary: In early 2003, a Murray cod farm in Victoria, Australia experienced a severe outbreak of systemic disease with roughly 90% mortality among fingerlings and broodstock after imported dwarf gouramis were fed to broodfish. Laboratory investigation showed the outbreak was caused by a megalocytivirus closely related to ISKNV/dwarf gourami iridovirus, representing the first confirmed incursion of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 into Australian aquaculture. Affected stocks were destroyed and heightened biosecurity and import‑risk assessments for ornamental fish were implemented; no further confirmed farmed‑fish outbreaks have occurred in Australia since.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International ornamental fish trade introduced an ISKNV‑like megalocytivirus into Australia, and the unsafe practice of feeding imported gouramis to broodstock, combined with elevated water temperatures and dense holding, enabled efficient virus transmission and severe disease in Murray cod. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of an ISKNV‑cluster megalocytivirus from ornamental dwarf gourami to a novel freshwater percichthyid host, with high virulence, demonstrating the capacity of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to infect non‑native species and establish on a new continent.
Review: review – Event retained as the first documented establishment of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 in Oceania, but first_detection was set to false (global first detection in Japan 1990) while inter_continental_emergence = true and re_emergence = true were kept to capture both the new continent and host expansion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in intensive freshwater aquaculture in the United States
Event summary: In 2012, a severe systemic disease outbreak occurred in a commercial Nile tilapia facility in the United States, causing approximately 50–75% cumulative mortality over about two months in affected cohorts. Histopathology, virus isolation and sequencing identified the causative agent as infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV), marking the first confirmed Megalocytivirus pagrus1 epizootic in tilapia and the first documented farm‑level outbreak in North America. Following culling, movement restrictions and strengthened biosecurity, the outbreak was brought under control and subsequent surveillance has focused on preventing re‑introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density tilapia production in recirculating or pond systems, combined with probable introduction of ISKNV via live‑fish imports (food or ornamental) and limited initial awareness of this pathogen, facilitated establishment and spread within the affected farm. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of the ISKNV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to a new major host (Nile tilapia), with high virulence in juvenile and grow‑out fish, representing both host expansion and inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – New event added for the 2012 ISKNV outbreak in farmed Nile tilapia in the United States, which represents both the first major Megalocytivirus pagrus1 epizootic in tilapia and the first confirmed farm‑level emergence in North America; classified as inter_continental_emergence with re_emergence (host expansion).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed giant sea perch / Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) fingerlings in coastal cage farms in southern Taiwan area (Kaohsiung and Pingtung)
Event summary: From April to October 2017, multiple coastal cage farms rearing giant sea perch (Asian seabass, Lates calcarifer) in southern Taiwan experienced epizootics of systemic disease with up to 90% mortality in fingerlings. Molecular characterization showed that the causative agents were megalocytiviruses within the RSIV/ISKNV complex, and one isolate clustered closely with viruses from fingerlings recently imported from Thailand, indicating transboundary introduction through regional seabass seed trade. Mortalities declined after affected cohorts were culled or harvested early and stricter health management and sourcing controls were implemented, although megalocytivirus infection remains an ongoing risk for L. calcarifer culture in the area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional trade in Asian seabass seed from Southeast Asian hatcheries, high stocking densities of fingerlings in coastal cages and warm seasonal temperatures facilitated introduction and rapid spread of megalocytiviruses into seabass farms in southern Taiwan. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated host expansion of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 (RSIV/ISKNV genotypes) to Asian seabass, a euryhaline marine–brackish species, with high virulence in fingerlings, representing re‑emergence of the species complex in a new cultured host within Eastern Asia.
Review: review – Event retained but (i) the Country field was adjusted to 'China [2017]' to comply with the project Country list while the narrative retains the southern Taiwan location, and (ii) emergence‑type flags were simplified to re_emergence = true (host expansion within Eastern Asia) with re_occurrence = false.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cage‑cultured Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) in estuarine and coastal farms along the west coast of India
Event summary: In 2018, severe mortality events (approximately 50–90% losses) were reported in cage‑cultured Asian seabass along the west coast of India, and diagnostic investigations identified red sea bream iridovirus (RSIV) genotype II as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed Megalocytivirus pagrus1 outbreak in Indian marine finfish aquaculture. A second major outbreak in 2020 affected additional seabass farms in the same region, confirming local establishment and spatial spread of RSIVD in Southern Asia. Following these episodes, Indian research institutes and authorities initiated targeted surveillance, diagnostic test development and vaccination trials, which have helped reduce but not eliminate the risk of further high‑mortality outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of RSIV genotype II via importation of infected Asian seabass seed or broodstock from endemic countries, rapid expansion of open estuarine and coastal cage culture with high stocking densities and limited biosecurity, and warm tropical waters promoted efficient transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of RSIV genotype II within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 into a new sub‑region (Southern Asia) and continued adaptation to Asian seabass as a major cultured host, leading to re‑emergence in a new ecological and production context.
Review: review – Event retained but emergence‑type flags were corrected so that the episode is classified as intra_continental_emergence (first major establishment in Southern Asia) with re_emergence (new sub‑region and genotype/host context), while first_detection and re_occurrence were set to false to avoid multiple overlapping categories.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cage‑cultured Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and hybrids in intensive floating cages on Lake Volta
Event summary: From late 2018, intensive tilapia cage farms on Lake Volta in Ghana experienced unprecedented mortalities, with some operations reporting 60–90% losses and daily deaths exceeding 10 tonnes of fish during the peak of the outbreak. Histopathology, virus isolation and PCR confirmed infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV) as the causative agent, and follow‑up surveys in 2019–2020 showed the virus had become endemic across multiple production zones on the lake. Although mortality rates declined after emergency culling, stocking reductions and adoption of management measures such as heat‑shock treatment and vaccination on some farms, ISKNV continues to cause recurrent losses, particularly in juvenile tilapia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of cage‑based tilapia aquaculture on Lake Volta, very high stocking densities, frequent live‑fish movements among hatcheries and grow‑out sites, and limited initial biosecurity enabled rapid spread once ISKNV was introduced, likely via movement of infected seed or broodstock. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to tilapia in Africa and efficient transmission in high‑density cage systems allowed the virus to establish and re‑emerge in successive cohorts, representing inter‑continental emergence with major production impacts.
Review: review – New event added to represent the large‑scale ISKNV epidemic in cage‑cultured tilapia on Lake Volta, Ghana, from 2018 onward, which accounts for some of the highest reported mortality and production losses for Megalocytivirus pagrus1 worldwide; classified as inter_continental_emergence with re_emergence (host expansion and establishment in Africa).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: Retrospective testing of archived sera from Saudi Arabian dromedary camels collected from 1992 through 2010 showed very high MERS-CoV antibody seroprevalence, revealing that the virus had been endemic in Arabian Peninsula camel populations long before the first recognized human cases in 2012.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) Subsequent analyses linked these long-standing camel infections to the clade B MERS-CoV strains associated with human outbreaks in Saudi Arabia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) The event is considered ongoing, with continued widespread circulation in Saudi camels and periodic zoonotic spillover into humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-established intensive camel husbandry and dense dromedary populations in the Arabian Peninsula, with frequent animal movements for trade and cultural practices (racing, dairy, meat), maintained high transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) Internal mechanisms: Long-term adaptation of MERS-CoV to dromedaries with efficient upper-respiratory replication and shedding, but relatively mild disease, favored silent maintenance and geographic expansion (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – Event is valid and should be retained as a major emergence episode, documenting long-term MERS-CoV circulation in Saudi dromedaries and first documented introduction of camel infection into Asia (inter-continental emergence from Africa). However, it was misclassified as a re-emergence; re_emergence has been set to No because there is no earlier recognized camel event in Western Asia and no clear evidence of a novel strain causing a resurgence in this subregion. A more specific primary source (the mBio Saudi camel infection paper) has been added and the generic Wikipedia link removed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: Archived sera from dromedary camels in Somalia, Sudan and Kenya collected in the early 1980s and 1990s showed about 81% MERS-CoV–neutralizing antibody seropositivity, indicating intense, long-term endemic circulation in Eastern Africa; similar high seroprevalence was later documented in camels from Ethiopia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4257824/)) During 2009–2013, additional surveys in Kenyan herds confirmed that high seroprevalence persisted in both nomadic and farmed camels, suggesting sustained transmission.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/8/14-0596_article)) The event remains ongoing, with Eastern Africa recognized as a major endemic reservoir for camel MERS-CoV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High camel densities, nomadic and transboundary trade systems in the Greater Horn of Africa facilitated frequent mixing of herds and sustained virus circulation across national borders.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4257824/)) Internal mechanisms: Stable adaptation of MERS-CoV to dromedaries with efficient respiratory shedding in juveniles maintained viral circulation without causing noticeable disease, allowing unrecognized persistence for decades (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – This event correctly highlights Eastern Africa as a long-term endemic reservoir and should be retained, but two corrections were needed. (1) Somalia and Sudan were removed from the country list because all published sera from these countries with MERS-CoV antibodies were collected in 1983–1984 (pre-1990) and thus are now represented only in the first_emergence_time/background, not as ≥1990 event entries. The remaining countries, Kenya [1992] and Ethiopia [2011], match the earliest post‑1990 camel serologic evidence. (2) intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence have been set to No: Eastern Africa is the original known subregion for camel MERS-CoV, and these data represent long-standing endemicity rather than spread to a new subregion or a resurgence driven by external factors.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: Serologic surveys of camel sera collected between 2009 and 2011 in Tunisia (North Africa), Nigeria (West Africa) and Ethiopia (East Africa) revealed widespread antibodies to MERS-CoV or a closely related virus, demonstrating that infection was not confined to the Horn of Africa but extended across multiple African subregions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4111168/)) These findings extended the recognized endemic range of camel MERS-CoV throughout North, West and East Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) The event reflects long-standing, rather than newly introduced, circulation but marks the first documentation of infection in these subregions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional camel trade networks connecting Eastern Africa with North and West Africa, and movements for slaughter and pastoralism, likely allowed long-term spread and homogenization of MERS-CoV across the continent.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for major viral change in this period; the event mainly represents improved serologic surveillance uncovering pre-existing endemic infection (no specific internal mechanism identified beyond existing host adaptation).
Review: review – This multi-country survey is an appropriate intra-continental emergence event, documenting first evidence from North and West Africa as well as additional data from East Africa, and should be retained. However, Nigeria’s start year has been corrected from 2009 to 2010 to align with the reported sampling period (2010–2011) in the African geographic-distribution serosurvey. No other changes to classification, geography, timing, or sources are required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Eastern Africa
Countries: Egypt [2013]; Tunisia [2013]; Senegal [2013]; Uganda [2013]; Burkina Faso [2013]; Morocco [2013]; Nigeria [2010]
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: From about 2010 onwards, large-scale serologic and virologic surveys across North, West and East Africa identified very high MERS-CoV seroprevalence and, in some countries, viral RNA and full genomes in dromedary camels in Egypt, Tunisia, Senegal, Uganda, Burkina Faso, Morocco and Nigeria, confirming continental-scale endemicity.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) Genetic analyses showed that many African camel viruses formed a distinct clade C, differentiating them from Arabian clade B strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) The event is ongoing, with African clade C viruses continuing to circulate in camel populations without recognized large human outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of virologic surveillance in camels, combined with long-standing cross-border trade and movement of live animals from East and West Africa to North Africa and the Middle East, revealed and may have facilitated dispersion of distinct viral lineages.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and maintenance of African clade C lineages (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence) and their adaptation to local camel populations, with genetic divergence from clade B viruses circulating in Arabia, represent viral evolution associated with this re-emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/))
Review: review – This event captures the large-scale, multi-country African surveys and the genetic definition of African clade C viruses and should be retained. Two adjustments were made. (1) intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because North, West and East Africa were already known to harbor infected camels from earlier (2009–2011) work; this episode reflects intensified sampling and genomic characterization rather than first spread to new African subregions. (2) Nigeria’s start year was aligned to 2010 to reflect earlier serologic evidence, though the main clade C sequencing work dates from 2013 onward. Re_emergence=Yes remains appropriate as this event is driven by the recognition of distinct viral lineages with sequence-level changes (novel strain/genotype emergence).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: A serologic study of 651 dromedary camel sera from the United Arab Emirates found that 151 samples collected in 2003 and 500 collected in 2013 had high titers of antibodies neutralizing MERS-CoV or a conspecific virus, demonstrating that camels in the UAE had been heavily infected at least a decade before human MERS was recognized.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) The 2013 samples confirmed that high camel seroprevalence persisted during the early human epidemic period.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) The event illustrates long-standing endemic infection in Gulf-region camel populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive camel farming and trading systems in the UAE, including movements to and from neighboring Gulf countries, likely facilitated stable viral maintenance, while serologic studies initiated after the human epidemic revealed pre-existing infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel viral properties were identified; rather, this event highlights the silent, well-adapted host reservoir state of MERS-CoV in dromedaries (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: review – The UAE serologic evidence for widespread camel infection in 2003 and 2013 is robust and the event should be kept. However, intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the virus was already established in Western Asia (Saudi Arabia) and the UAE lies within the same subregion; spread to a new country within a subregion does not meet the intra-continental emergence definition. No other changes to timing, geography or sources are needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 2013, a comparative serologic study detected high prevalence of MERS-CoV–neutralizing antibodies in dromedary camels in Oman and about 14% seropositivity in camels in the Canary Islands of Spain, demonstrating widespread infection in the Arabian Peninsula and providing the first documented evidence of MERS-CoV–like infection in European camels.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/middle-east-respiratory-syndrome-coronavirus-neutralising-serum-antibodies-dromedary)) Subsequent follow-up testing in the Canary Islands found no active viral shedding despite persistent antibodies, suggesting past exposure rather than ongoing circulation.([cidrap.umn.edu](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/mers-cov/report-finds-no-active-camel-mers-canary-islands)) The event expanded the recognized geographic range of camel infection to Europe, although no human cases were linked to European camels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International movement and trade of dromedaries between Northwest Africa, the Middle East and Spanish territories likely introduced MERS-CoV–infected camels into the Canary Islands, while local management practices limited onward circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel viral traits were reported; the event mainly represents geographic range expansion documented through serology (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) inferred rather than newly evolved).
Review: retain – This event accurately summarizes the comparative serologic study demonstrating widespread camel infection in Oman and first documented evidence of MERS-CoV–like infection in European camels (Canary Islands, Spain). The geography (Asia; Europe; Western Asia; Southern Europe), timing (2013), and classification as inter_continental_emergence=Yes are consistent with definitions, and the cited sources are appropriate. No corrections are recommended.

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 2013, investigations of two human MERS cases on a farm in Qatar identified MERS-CoV RNA and later virus isolates in nasal swabs from several dromedary camels in the same herd, with near-identical genome sequences between one camel and the human patient, providing direct evidence of active infection and zoonotic transmission on farm premises.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2013_11_29-en)) The farm study showed transient shedding and seroconversion in the camels, confirming ongoing in situ camel-to-camel and camel-to-human transmission.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMoa1401505)) Subsequent control measures focused on farm biosecurity and reducing close contact with sick camels, but camel infections and intermittent human cases have continued in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close occupational contact between farmers and camels, including handling of camels with respiratory symptoms and use of raw camel products, enabled zoonotic spillover.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2013_11_29-en)) Internal mechanisms: Efficient replication and shedding of MERS-CoV in the upper respiratory tract of camels facilitated high-titer exposure to humans in farm settings (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), though no distinct new viral genotype was implicated.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – The Qatar farm outbreak is a key event demonstrating direct camel-to-human transmission and should be retained, but it was previously misclassified as re_occurrence. Because Western Asia was already known to host endemic camel infection and there is no documented prior control followed by resurgence in Qatar, re_occurrence has been set to No, leaving this as an important but untyped emergence event in the classification scheme. In addition, the Lancet Infectious Diseases outbreak investigation has been added as a primary source and the generic Wikipedia link removed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 2013–2014, studies in Egypt detected very high seroprevalence of MERS-CoV antibodies in domestic and imported dromedary camels and identified near–full-genome MERS-CoV sequences from camel nasal swabs, confirming active infection and viral shedding in North African herds.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24079378/)) Phylogenetic analysis grouped Egyptian camel viruses with other African clade C MERS-CoV strains distinct from Arabian Peninsula clade B.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) The event firmly established that African camel viruses formed a separate lineage, with ongoing circulation but no large recognized human outbreaks in Egypt.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large national camel population in Egypt and substantial imports of camels from Sudan, Somalia and other African exporters created mixing of herds and opportunities for viral introduction and persistence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) Internal mechanisms: Evolution and maintenance of clade C viruses with distinct phylogenetic signatures compared with Middle Eastern clade B strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), but without evident increase in pathogenicity in camels.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/))
Review: retain – This event correctly describes high seroprevalence and active infection with genetically distinct clade C viruses in Egyptian camels and is appropriately coded as a re_emergence episode (novel strain/genotype emergence within a previously infected Northern Africa subregion). Years, geography, and sources are consistent with the literature, and no corrections are required.

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius; some Bactrian camels also sampled)
Event summary: Serologic surveys of camels in Punjab, Pakistan, using samples collected from 2012 to 2015, found high prevalence of MERS-CoV–specific antibodies, with evidence of infection in camels born in Pakistan, indicating established local transmission.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28221127/)) A subsequent countrywide survey reported about 76% seropositivity among Pakistani dromedaries, while no neutralizing antibodies were detected in sampled humans, suggesting silent but widespread animal infection without recognized human disease.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6235758/)) This event marks the first documented establishment of MERS-CoV in camels in Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of camels from the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, combined with growth of domestic camel populations and trade within Pakistan, likely introduced and then maintained MERS-CoV in South Asian herds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382745/)) Internal mechanisms: No distinct South Asian lineage was defined; viruses were similar to known camel strains, suggesting geographic expansion of established genotypes rather than novel evolution (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Pakistan represents the first documented establishment of camel MERS-CoV in Southern Asia and is correctly classified as intra_continental_emergence (spread from Western Asia to a new Asian subregion). The event should be retained, but the “countries” field has been simplified to a single entry, “Pakistan [2012]”, as required by the specification of one country with its starting year per linked episode. Details of the 2014 national survey remain in the event summary. No other changes to timing, geography or sources are needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 2015, serologic testing of dromedary camels at livestock markets and quarantine sites in Bangladesh found MERS-CoV antibodies in about 31% of animals, with higher seroprevalence in adults than juveniles, indicating exposure and likely circulation of the virus in Bangladeshi camel populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) Many seropositive camels had been imported, but detection in younger animals suggested local transmission as well.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) The event represents extension of documented camel MERS-CoV infection into another country of Southern Asia, though no human MERS cases have been confirmed in Bangladesh.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of camels from the Middle East and Africa into Bangladesh for slaughter and religious festivals, together with market crowding and limited biosecurity, provided opportunities for introduction and local spread of MERS-CoV.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) Internal mechanisms: The viruses are presumed similar to previously characterized camel strains, with no specific new genotype reported; the event mainly reflects geographic expansion following trade (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – The Bangladesh survey documenting MERS-CoV antibodies in market and quarantine camels is well supported and should be kept, as it shows further geographic expansion of camel infection within Southern Asia. However, intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the subregion “Southern Asia” was already established as infected by 2012–2015 data from Pakistan; spread to an additional country in the same subregion does not satisfy the intra-continental emergence definition. No adjustments to timing, geography or sources are otherwise required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: India [1994, first major spread beyond Tamil Nadu; nationwide endemic by the 2000s]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep (small ruminants); limited serological evidence also in other domestic ruminants
Event summary: From 1994 through roughly 2010, PPRV spread from initial foci in Tamil Nadu and neighboring southern states to become endemic across most of India, with repeated village‑ and district‑level outbreaks and high mortality in naïve goat and sheep populations. The expansion produced thousands of officially recorded outbreaks and tens of thousands of reported deaths, with the heaviest burden between about 2000 and 2007, causing substantial production losses and major constraints on small‑ruminant development. These impacts prompted progressive rollout of a national PPR control and then eradication programme based on mass vaccination, after which reported outbreaks and deaths began to decline, although PPRV remains endemic in some areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of small‑ruminant production, extensive movement and trade of sheep and goats (including live‑animal markets and long‑distance transport), and limited early diagnostic capacity allowed PPRV to spread widely before systematic control began; concurrent rinderpest eradication drew attention and resources, delaying targeted PPR control. Internal mechanisms: Circulating lineage IV strains established sustained transmission in large, immunologically naïve small‑ruminant populations, with high intrinsic transmissibility supporting endemic maintenance across diverse agro‑ecological zones rather than any single novel strain.
Review: Retain – this is clearly one of the globally most impactful PPR episodes, with thousands of outbreaks and ~95,000 reported deaths in India between 1995 and 2019, and a major shift from regional to nationwide endemicity.([nivedi.res.in](https://www.nivedi.res.in/Nadres_v2/pdf/Left_bar_articles/5.viruses.pdf)) The start year has been tightened from 1990 to 1994 and the end to 2010, to match evidence that PPR was largely confined to southern India until outbreaks spread northward after 1994 and that the pre‑control high‑burden period runs to about 2010.([nivedi.res.in](https://www.nivedi.res.in/Nadres_v2/pdf/Left_bar_articles/5.viruses.pdf)) One SciDirect citation that referred primarily to Ethiopia has been replaced with the India‑specific Viruses 2021 epidemiological analysis; other sources remain appropriate. Type‑of‑emergence is left as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or major new lineage), which is consistent with the definitions. Recommended decision: retain (with edits applied).

Countries: Türkiye [1999, first official reports in southeastern, eastern and Mediterranean regions; spread to central, Aegean, Marmara and Thrace regions by 2004]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep
Event summary: In 1999 Türkiye officially reported its first PPR outbreaks in southeastern, eastern and Mediterranean regions, documenting establishment of the virus in a previously unaffected national population within the already affected Western Asia sub‑region. Over the following years, the disease became widespread, with repeated outbreaks in central, Aegean and Marmara regions and eventual spread into Thrace near the Bulgarian and Greek borders, raising concerns about potential incursion into the European Union. By around 2004, extensive vaccination and control measures were in place and reduced outbreak frequency, although PPRV remained endemic in much of the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border livestock movements and informal trade from endemic neighbouring countries, together with dense flocks and mixed farming systems, facilitated introduction of PPRV into naïve Turkish small‑ruminant populations and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: Existing lineage IV PPRV strains established in new ecological and husbandry settings; there is no clear evidence that a fundamentally novel, more virulent strain drove this episode, which instead reflects regional re‑occurrence and geographic expansion within Western Asia.
Review: Retain – this episode marks the major establishment of PPR in Türkiye, including spread into the Thrace region bordering EU Member States, and is widely emphasised as a key step in the westward advance of the virus.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/4/y5932e/y5932e03.htm)) However, under the project definitions, intra‑continental emergence must involve spread to a new UN sub‑region, not simply a new country within Western Asia; PPR was already endemic in the Arabian Peninsula and other Western Asian countries by the 1980s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6751262/)) Accordingly, the intra_continental_emergence flag has been set to false and re_occurrence set to true to reflect a major resurgence and geographic expansion within an already affected sub‑region. Sources (FAO EMPRES bulletin and molecular studies from Türkiye) are appropriate and retained. Recommended decision: retain (classification corrected; flag for review of categorisation details if needed).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Kenya [2006], Uganda [2007], United Republic of Tanzania [2008]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep in pastoral and agropastoral systems; limited involvement of other domestic ruminants in some areas
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2008, PPRV spread for the first time into the arid and semi‑arid small‑ruminant populations of northern Kenya, the Karamoja region of Uganda and northern Tanzania, triggering a large, regionally linked epidemic in Eastern Africa. In Kenya the disease was first recognised in Turkana in 2006 and then advanced southwards, with some national estimates suggesting over one million and possibly up to 2.7 million sheep and goats lost during this wave. Uganda and Tanzania experienced subsequent outbreaks (Karamoja 2007–2008; northern Tanzania 2008–2009), with heavy losses and culling, including about 64,661 animals culled in Tanzania as part of control measures. Emergency vaccination campaigns, movement controls and strengthened veterinary services gradually brought the epidemic under control by the late 2000s, but PPR became established as an endemic disease in many affected areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive transboundary pastoralism, porous borders and high dependence on small ruminants for livelihoods in the arid and semi‑arid lands created dense, mobile networks of susceptible hosts; limited prior awareness of PPR and gaps in surveillance and vaccination allowed explosive spread once the virus entered Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies indicate that Asian lineage IV PPRV had recently been introduced into Africa and was responsible for many of these outbreaks, representing a re‑emergence driven by the incursion and regional amplification of a new genetic lineage rather than de novo evolution within East Africa.
Review: Added – this 2006–2008 Eastern Africa epidemic was missing from the original dataset but is one of the best‑documented high‑impact PPR events, with FAO estimating 1.2 million small‑ruminant deaths in Kenya and 64,661 animals culled in Tanzania, and some Kenyan sources citing losses of up to 2.7 million sheep and goats.([rr-africa.woah.org](https://rr-africa.woah.org/app/uploads/2019/10/a-i6316e.pdf)) It also marks the incursion and regional spread of Asian lineage IV into East Africa. The event is treated as a single, epidemiologically linked episode covering Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, with re_emergence set to true to reflect the role of a newly introduced lineage; intra/inter‑continental emergence are kept false because East Africa was already a known PPR sub‑region before 1990. Recommended decision: retain as a major added event (flagged for expert review of exact country‑specific start years if finer resolution is desired).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China [Tibet (Ngari) 2007, additional limited foci in Tibet 2008]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep in border areas of western Tibet; serological evidence of infection in local small ruminant populations
Event summary: In mid‑2007 China officially reported its first confirmed PPR outbreak in Ngari Prefecture in western Tibet, representing the first recognised incursion of PPRV into Chinese territory and into the Eastern Asia sub‑region. The outbreak involved small ruminants in remote high‑altitude border areas, with clinical signs typical of PPR and virological and serological confirmation of infection. Rapid culling of affected and in‑contact animals, movement controls and emergency vaccination led to elimination of detectable transmission by early 2008, and PPR was considered provisionally controlled in China until further incursions several years later.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of PPRV via cross‑border movements of small ruminants or informal trade along high‑altitude pastoral routes that connect Tibet with endemic regions of South Asia, combined with limited prior familiarity with PPR among local veterinarians, delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of established lineage IV strains into a previously unexposed small‑ruminant population allowed short‑term local amplification before control was achieved; there is no evidence that a distinct new genotype arose in Tibet during this event.
Review: Retain – this is the first confirmed PPR occurrence in China and in the Eastern Asia sub‑region, well documented by national and international sources.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/17364)) The original classification incorrectly marked this as a global first detection; that flag has been set to false because PPR was first detected in West Africa in 1942, long before this event. Intra‑continental emergence remains true, as this is the first occurrence in a new UN sub‑region (Eastern Asia) within Asia. The French‑language Wikipedia link has been replaced by primary outbreak reports (EID article and DAFF Exotic Animal Diseases Bulletin) and a recent synthesis of emerging small‑ruminant viruses in China. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected emergence‑type and improved sources).

Host: Domestic sheep and goats
Event summary: In mid‑2008 Morocco detected its first PPR outbreaks, with more than one hundred foci reported across many provinces and particularly heavy losses in sheep flocks, marking the first recognised incursion of Asian lineage IV PPRV into the Maghreb and a major re‑emergence of the disease in Northern Africa, where PPR had previously been reported in Egypt in the late 1980s. During 2008 the epidemic spread widely within Morocco, threatening millions of small ruminants and posing a risk of further spread across the Maghreb and to southern Europe. A national emergency programme combining mass vaccination campaigns from 2008 to 2010 with strict movement controls and outbreak containment dramatically reduced transmission; subsequent serological surveys indicated high vaccine‑derived immunity and an absence of active virus circulation in previously affected regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction is thought to have occurred via movement of infected small ruminants from endemic regions in sub‑Saharan Africa or the Middle East into Moroccan markets or grazing systems; internal livestock trade and congregation at markets and religious‑festival gatherings amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by PPRV lineage IV, a genetic lineage that had recently spread into Africa and represented a shift from the previously circulating African lineages, consistent with re‑emergence driven by introduction of a new genotype into a largely naïve small‑ruminant population.
Review: Retain – this is a key high‑impact event, signalling the jump of lineage IV PPRV into the Maghreb and creating substantial risk for the western Mediterranean.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/Outbreak-of-%27peste-des-petits-ruminants%27-in-Morocco/en)) However, the original record incorrectly treated it as both first detection and intra‑continental emergence for Northern Africa; PPR had already been documented in Egypt in 1987–1989, so Northern Africa was not a new sub‑region by 2008.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10093352/)) The intra_continental_emergence and first_detection flags have therefore been set to false and re_emergence to true, reflecting the introduction and amplification of a new genetic lineage in a previously affected sub‑region. The event summary has been updated to acknowledge prior Egyptian outbreaks while still emphasising the significance of the Moroccan incursion. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected classification and narrative).

Countries: China [Xinjiang 2013; wider northern, central and eastern provinces 2014–2016]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep; serological and virological evidence of infection in wild small ruminants in some regions
Event summary: Beginning in late 2013, PPR re‑emerged in China with outbreaks first detected in Xinjiang and then spreading rapidly eastward, leading to a large, multi‑provincial epidemic through 2014–2015. By early 2016, China had officially reported nearly 40,000 clinical PPR cases in sheep and goats from 22 provinces, autonomous regions and municipalities, including major livestock‑producing areas far from the initial focus. Intensive control measures, including mass vaccination, large‑scale culling and strict restrictions on inter‑provincial movement of small ruminants, progressively reduced transmission, and by 2016 the epidemic wave had subsided, although PPRV remained a continuing risk necessitating ongoing vaccination and surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of sheep and goats and extensive internal trade and transport, including long‑distance movement for fattening and slaughter, enabled rapid dissemination from western border regions to central and eastern China; gaps in vaccination coverage and low baseline immunity in many provinces facilitated explosive spread. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses indicate expansion of lineage IV PPRV closely related to strains circulating in neighbouring Central and South Asian countries, with evidence of multiple introduction clusters and a sharp increase in viral population size during the 2013–2014 epidemic; changes in host connectivity and immunity appear more important than major shifts in virulence.
