Review: Retain – this nationwide epidemic is one of the largest recent PPR events in terms of recorded cases and geographic extent (22 provinces and nearly 40,000 reported clinical cases).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921448817302316)) The original classification improperly combined intra‑continental emergence and re_occurrence; because PPR had already occurred in the Eastern Asia sub‑region (Tibet 2007–2008), this episode represents a large re‑occurrence within the same sub‑region rather than spread into a new sub‑region. The intra_continental_emergence flag has therefore been set to false while re_occurrence remains true. Event description and sources remain appropriate. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected emergence classification).

Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [multiple northern and central provinces 2014–2016]
Host: Wild goats (Capra aegagrus), wild sheep (Ovis orientalis and related taxa), with epidemiological linkage to domestic sheep and goats
Event summary: Between 2014 and 2016, Iran experienced a series of PPRV‑associated die‑offs in wild caprine and ovine populations in several protected areas in northern and central provinces, with more than 1,000 wild goats and wild sheep reported dead and evidence that outbreaks were linked to concurrent infection in nearby domestic small ruminants. These wildlife mortality events shifted perceptions of PPRV from primarily a disease of domestic sheep and goats to a serious threat to vulnerable wild ungulate populations in Iran. Control efforts focused on ring vaccination of domestic flocks around protected areas, restrictions on livestock access to wildlife rangelands and water sources, and enhanced wildlife disease surveillance, which together reduced but did not eliminate the risk of further spillover.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High overlap between domestic flocks and wild ungulates at shared pastures and water points, particularly under drought or resource scarcity, increased contact rates at the wildlife–livestock interface; incomplete PPR control in some domestic herds near protected areas maintained a source of infection. Internal mechanisms: Spillover of lineage IV PPRV from domestic animals into multiple wild Caprinae species represents host expansion, with viral strains in wildlife closely related to contemporary domestic strains; this constitutes re‑emergence driven by host‑range expansion rather than by a fundamentally new genotype.
Review: Retain – this episode is well documented and represents one of the most consequential wildlife PPR events, with >1,000 wild goats and sheep reported dead in Iran and clear demonstration of sustained spillover from domestic flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5367395/)) Classification as re_emergence (host‑range expansion in a previously affected sub‑region) is appropriate and has been retained; no intra/inter‑continental spread is involved, and no evidence suggests a novel viral lineage beyond the widespread lineage IV. Sources (EID articles and follow‑up analyses) are relevant and sufficient. Recommended decision: retain (no structural changes).

Countries: Mongolia [2016 domestic livestock in western provinces; 2016–2017 Mongolian saiga and other wild ungulates]
Host: Domestic sheep and goats; Mongolian saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica mongolica); Siberian ibex (Capra sibirica); goitered gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa); argali sheep (Ovis ammon)
Event summary: In 2016 PPR was officially reported for the first time in domestic sheep and goats in western Mongolia’s Khovd and Gobi‑Altai provinces, followed within months by a devastating outbreak among critically endangered Mongolian saiga antelope and other wild ungulates in the same region. From late 2016 through early 2017, an estimated 50–80 percent of the Mongolian saiga population died, alongside confirmed infections and deaths in ibex, argali and goitered gazelles, making this one of the most severe wildlife PPR events recorded. Mongolia implemented emergency livestock vaccination, strict movement controls, targeted carcass collection and destruction, and enhanced wildlife monitoring; by late 2017 active outbreak activity had declined, although population surveys in early 2018 still reflected the massive saiga losses and long‑term demographic impacts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of PPRV likely via cross‑border movement of infected small ruminants from endemic neighbouring regions, combined with close spatial overlap of livestock and wild ungulates on winter ranges and around limited water sources, facilitated rapid spillover and sustained wildlife transmission; harsh winter conditions and nutritional stress may have exacerbated mortality. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses show that the Mongolian outbreak viruses belonged to lineage IV closely related to strains circulating in China, with evidence that PPRV circulated undetected in livestock before wildlife cases; this episode exemplifies re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission in novel wild hosts rather than emergence of a distinct new viral lineage.
Review: Retain – this is a globally important event for both livestock and biodiversity, with ~50–80% of the Mongolian saiga population lost and substantial mortality in other wild ungulates following introduction of PPR into Mongolia in 2016.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6924898/)) The event year range has been tightened from 2016–2018 to 2016–2017, reflecting that major livestock and wildlife outbreaks occurred during this period, while 2018 mainly captured post‑epidemic population assessments. The first_detection and intra_continental_emergence flags have been set to false: the event is country‑level first detection within a sub‑region (Eastern Asia) where PPR was already present due to the Tibet outbreaks, and first/global detection occurred decades earlier. Re_emergence remains true, capturing the major host‑range expansion into several wild species. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected dates and classification).

Host: Domestic sheep (notably Tushuri breed) and goats in affected flocks
Event summary: In early 2016 Georgia reported its first PPR outbreaks in sheep flocks located near Tbilisi, representing the first officially recognised incursion of PPRV into the South Caucasus and, from a WOAH regional perspective, into continental Europe. Laboratory investigation confirmed infection with lineage IV PPRV closely related to strains circulating in neighbouring countries in the Middle East and Central Asia. Aggressive stamping‑out, movement controls and ring surveillance limited the outbreak to a small number of flocks, and Georgia has not reported further confirmed PPR outbreaks since 2016, although the wider Caucasus region remains under heightened surveillance given ongoing circulation in surrounding countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement and trade of small ruminants, including transhumant flocks moving between Georgia and neighbouring endemic areas, likely introduced PPRV into previously free Georgian sheep populations; gaps in awareness and surveillance delayed early detection but rapid response once detected limited spread. Internal mechanisms: The viruses involved belonged to lineage IV, already widespread in Western and Central Asia; the episode reflects geographic range expansion of an existing lineage into a new country within an already affected sub‑region rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: Added – this 2016 outbreak in Georgia was missing from the original dataset, yet it is epidemiologically and policy‑wise important as the first officially recognised PPR incursion into the South Caucasus and the first detection in Europe in WOAH’s regional reporting (even though Georgia is classified under Western Asia in the UNSD scheme used here).([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/peste-des-petits-ruminants/)) Because PPR was already endemic in Western Asia, the event is coded as re_occurrence rather than intra/inter‑continental emergence. The event summary emphasises its bridgehead role toward Europe while keeping continent/sub‑region labels consistent with the project’s country table. Recommended decision: retain as a major added event (flagged for review only if a strict cap of 10 events forces trade‑offs with other small but symbolically important incursions such as Bulgaria 2018).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Bulgaria [2018, Burgas and Yambol regions near the border with Türkiye]
Host: Domestic sheep and goats in smallholder flocks; heightened concern for nearby wild small ruminants (no large confirmed wildlife die‑offs during this initial incursion)
Event summary: In mid‑2018 Bulgaria confirmed several PPR outbreaks in small ruminant flocks in the Burgas region near the border with Türkiye, representing the first recognised incursion of PPRV into the European Union and into Eastern Europe as defined in this project. The outbreaks affected smallholder sheep and goat farms, with clinical disease and virological confirmation indicating local transmission rather than isolated imported cases. Bulgaria rapidly implemented EU‑supported control measures including culling of affected and at‑risk flocks, movement bans, intensive surveillance and zoning; by July 2018 no further cases were detected, and the incursion was declared successfully contained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from endemic areas in neighbouring Türkiye via informal cross‑border movements or trade of small ruminants, with local husbandry practices and close flock contact enabling limited spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiological evidence indicates that the viruses involved were closely related to lineage IV strains circulating in the region; the event reflects inter‑continental geographic range expansion into a new regulatory and ecological context rather than emergence of a novel variant, and rapid control prevented broader establishment.
Review: Retain – although relatively small in animal numbers, this event is highly significant as the first confirmed PPR incursion into the EU and into the European continent under the UNSD country classification used here (Georgia 2016 being treated as Western Asia).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3381390/)) The inter_continental_emergence flag is therefore appropriate and has been kept. The first_detection flag has been set to false, as global first detection occurred decades earlier. The event summary has been slightly edited to avoid ambiguous wording about ‘one of the first events on the European continent outside Türkiye’s European part’ and instead focuses on its role as the first EU/Eastern Europe incursion. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected emergence‑type flag and clarified wording).

Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines
Event summary: In 1990, rinderpest was diagnosed in cattle in Georgia, representing the first incursion of the disease into this Transcaucasian republic for many decades and the first penetration into the wider European region since 1949. The outbreak occurred amid severe political instability and weakening of veterinary services, raising concern about wider regional spread, but was rapidly identified and stamped out through emergency control and vaccination. Although small in absolute numbers, the episode was epidemiologically important as a warning of renewed transboundary risk in the post-Soviet space and was later linked by molecular studies to Asiatic lineage viruses also detected on the Mongolia–Tuva–Chita border.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Civil unrest and fragmentation of state institutions in the late Soviet period weakened surveillance, animal-movement control and border veterinary services, facilitating re-introduction of rinderpest into Georgian cattle. Informal cross-border livestock trade and transhumance from endemic areas likely provided the source of infection. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization showed the virus belonged to an existing Asiatic lineage rather than a novel strain, and there was no evidence of altered virulence; the event therefore reflects re-occurrence of a known lineage under conditions of reduced control, not viral evolution.
Review: retain – Structured fields (year, geography, emergence-type classification) closely match FAO descriptions of the 1990 Georgian incursion, which was small but epidemiologically significant as the first penetration into the European region since 1949. Georgia is correctly coded to Asia | Western Asia per the project’s UNSD-based country sheet, despite some sources describing this as an outbreak “into Europe.” No structural corrections were needed; wording of the summary was slightly tightened and supplemented with explicit reference to its linkage to Asiatic lineage viruses.

Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in southern Indian states (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala)
Event summary: During the early 1990s, rinderpest persisted mainly in the southern Indian states despite decades of vaccination, with recognized infection from at least 1990 and the last bovine outbreak reported in Karnataka in January 1995. Transmission occurred as sporadic outbreaks in pockets with low vaccination coverage, but overall incidence fell sharply after India launched the National Project on Rinderpest Eradication and Operation Rinderpest Zero. No clinical cases were detected after late 1995, allowing India to document freedom from clinical rinderpest and ultimately achieve official recognition as free from infection by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) in 2006.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incomplete and uneven vaccine coverage, very large cattle and buffalo populations, and logistical constraints in reaching smallholders and remote areas allowed continued low-level circulation into the early 1990s. Progressive improvements in funding, organization and coverage under national eradication programmes closed immunity gaps and strengthened surveillance, accelerating fade-out of infection. Internal mechanisms: Available virological evidence does not indicate emergence of a new strain or altered virulence; the pattern is best interpreted as declining re-occurrence of long-established endemic lineages under gradually intensifying control rather than re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: retain – This is a major endemic focus and “endgame” episode for South Asia, with timing and geography well supported by FAO and Government of India sources (last outbreaks in southern states with disappearance by late 1995). Classification as re-occurrence (control-system driven fade-out of existing lineages) rather than re‑emergence is appropriate. No structural corrections were required.

Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines in the Awash Valley and adjacent Afar pastoral areas; possible involvement of wildlife
Event summary: From the early 1990s until the mid‑1990s, rinderpest persisted in cattle in the northern Awash Valley and Afar Region of Ethiopia, forming one of the last significant classic rinderpest foci in Africa. Infection circulated in mobile pastoral herds, generating periodic outbreaks that maintained regional risk even as incidence declined elsewhere on the continent. Intensive campaigns combining community-based animal health workers, mass vaccination and strengthened surveillance progressively reduced case occurrence, and no outbreaks were confirmed in Afar or elsewhere in Ethiopia after late 1995, allowing the focus to be declared extinguished.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Semi‑arid pastoral systems with frequent long-distance herd movements, limited infrastructure and intermittent insecurity hampered consistent vaccine delivery and surveillance, permitting low-level persistence and re-introduction of rinderpest. Operational challenges in reaching mobile herds and maintaining cold chains created immunity gaps among young stock. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates that viruses circulating in the Awash–Afar focus belonged to pre-existing African lineages without clear evidence of altered virulence or host range; the persistence is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence maintained by ecological and programmatic factors, not re-emergence due to viral change.
Review: review – The time span has been extended from 1991–1993 to 1991–1995 and the country string adjusted to Ethiopia [1991–1995] to reflect FAO reports that rinderpest persisted in the Awash–Afar focus until no outbreaks were confirmed after late 1995. This brings the episode into line with descriptions of Afar as one of the last classic African foci. Emergence-type classification as re-occurrence remains appropriate. A human reviewer should verify that the chosen period and geographic scope match any additional national data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (and some domestic buffalo) in eastern Türkiye, northern Iraq and north‑western Iran
Event summary: In September 1991, Türkiye experienced a major rinderpest outbreak, its first since 1971, with rapid spread through eastern provinces: 516 herds in 44 localities were affected within two months, leading to about 2,700 cattle deaths, 12,000 animals slaughtered and emergency vaccination of roughly 12.5 million cattle. Intensive control measures eliminated clinical disease within four months. In March–April 1994, new outbreaks occurred in eastern Türkiye, northern Iraq and north‑western Iran, consistent with an endemic focus in Kurdish border areas fed by animal movements from more easterly endemic zones. Coordinated emergency vaccination and culling again contained the epizootic, and no further rinderpest has been reported from these countries since the mid‑1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Gulf War disruption of animal-health services, porous borders in Kurdish regions, and active trade and unofficial movements of cattle from endemic areas in South and Central Asia created conditions for re-introduction and spread of rinderpest into Türkiye, Iraq and Iran. The need for rapid, large‑scale vaccination campaigns illustrates how declines in routine immunity can permit explosive re-occurrence once the virus is re‑seeded. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked these viruses to known Asiatic lineages, and there is no clear evidence of a novel genotype, altered virulence or host expansion; the events represent major re-occurrence of existing strains under conditions of weakened control.
Review: review – This large West Asian epizootic (major 1991 outbreak in Türkiye and 1994 outbreaks spanning Türkiye, Iraq and Iran) was missing from the original ChatGPT output despite clear evidence of high impact (thousands of deaths, extensive culling and vaccination, and multi‑country spread). A new row has been added with years, countries and magnitude drawn from FAO technical reports and EMPRES bulletins. Emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because all affected subregions had historical rinderpest, and there is no evidence for a new strain. Given the importance of this cluster, a human reviewer should confirm the chosen year range and country list against detailed national records.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Oman [1992-1995]; Saudi Arabia [1992-1996]; Yemen [1995]; United Arab Emirates [1995]
Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines (with some involvement of small ruminants and camels in parts of the Arabian Peninsula)
Event summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, rinderpest caused a series of outbreaks on the Arabian Peninsula following introduction from endemic foci to the north. Oman reported a large epidemic in 1992 with well over 100 outbreaks, and rinderpest continued to be detected there until the mid‑1990s. Related incursions affected cattle in Saudi Arabia, and rinderpest remained present in hill cattle in Yemen until at least 1995 despite annual vaccination campaigns, with additional outbreaks reported in the United Arab Emirates in the mid‑1990s. Coordinated regional efforts under the West Asian Rinderpest Eradication Campaign (WAREC) and GREP, including intensified vaccination, movement control and improved surveillance, progressively eliminated these foci, so that by the late 1990s rinderpest was believed to persist only in Yemen.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing trade and movement of live cattle and other livestock from endemic areas in South and West Asia into Gulf states, combined with incomplete routine vaccination and weaknesses in border control, allowed repeated re-introduction of rinderpest. The early 1990s regional instability following the Gulf War likely exacerbated gaps in veterinary services. In Yemen, difficult terrain and dispersed hill cattle systems impeded high vaccine coverage, favouring endemic persistence until targeted campaigns closed remaining immunity gaps. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication that these outbreaks were driven by a novel strain or altered virulence; they are best interpreted as re-occurrence of known Asiatic lineages in a high‑risk trade hub.
Review: review – This multi‑country Arabian Peninsula focus, including a large epidemic in Oman and persistent endemic infection in Yemen with additional outbreaks in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, was absent from the original dataset but is clearly highlighted in FAO/OIE sources as one of the remaining rinderpest reservoirs in the mid‑1990s. A new row has been added with approximate year ranges and country‑specific last-report dates based primarily on regional summaries and OIE workshop data. Because detailed national outbreak timelines are heterogeneous and not always fully accessible, this event is flagged for human review to confirm the per‑country start years and relative weighting of Oman versus Yemen.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Pastoral cattle herds and wild bovids (notably African buffalo and antelopes) in the southern Sudan ecosystem and contiguous areas of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia
Event summary: From 1993 to the late 1990s, classic rinderpest persisted in the southern Sudan ecosystem and neighbouring pastoral areas of Uganda, Kenya and western Ethiopia, forming one of the last major African reservoirs of virulent lineage‑1 virus. Widespread outbreaks in cattle and associated wildlife occurred in southern Sudan and Karamoja (Uganda) in 1993–1995, with further activity in border districts of Kenya and Ethiopia, before intensive control efforts reduced incidence. The final laboratory‑confirmed outbreak in this ecosystem was recorded near Torit in what is now South Sudan in 1998, after which no further confirmed rinderpest occurred, paving the way for verification of eradication in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Protracted civil conflict in southern Sudan, insecurity in parts of Uganda and Kenya, and very limited state presence severely constrained veterinary services, vaccination coverage and disease reporting. Large, mobile pastoral herds moved across porous borders with little control, sustaining transmission in an ecological “southern Sudan axis” even as other African regions became free. Only with the introduction of community‑based animal health workers, targeted vaccination in high‑risk corridors and improved surveillance under PARC/PACE and GREP was this reservoir finally extinguished. Internal mechanisms: Virological data indicate circulation of established lineage‑1 rinderpest viruses rather than a novel strain; the episode is thus characterized as re-occurrence of classic rinderpest maintained by conflict and pastoral ecology rather than re-emergence driven by virus evolution.
Review: review – This major East African focus, often described as the “southern Sudan axis,” was missing from the original output despite being identified in GREP analyses as one of the last two African reservoirs of classic virulent rinderpest. A new row has been added summarizing widespread outbreaks in southern Sudan and contiguous parts of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia during 1993–1998, culminating in the final confirmed outbreak near Torit. Country list and time ranges are approximate and should be cross‑checked against national datasets; emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is supported by lineage‑1 virology and the strong influence of conflict and service breakdown.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in pastoral systems, and wild African buffalo and other susceptible wildlife in the Somali pastoral ecosystem
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s, a mild lineage‑2 rinderpest virus persisted in the Somali pastoral ecosystem spanning north‑eastern Kenya, south‑eastern Ethiopia and southern Somalia, representing the last enzootic focus of rinderpest worldwide. The virus caused only low‑grade or inapparent disease in cattle but was associated with severe mortality in wildlife, being detected in Tsavo East National Park (Kenya) in 1994–1995 and in Nairobi National Park in 1996, and later in African buffalo in Meru National Park in 2001, the final confirmed natural infection globally. Despite sporadic reports of “mild rinderpest” in cattle up to the early 2000s, intensive participatory surveillance and wildlife monitoring after 2001 failed to detect further virus circulation, supporting eventual global eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Highly mobile Somali pastoralist systems, cross‑border livestock movements, and chronic insecurity hindered conventional surveillance and mass vaccination, allowing a virus causing mostly mild disease in cattle to circulate cryptically at the livestock–wildlife interface. Gaps in vaccination left cohorts of young cattle and wildlife susceptible while older animals remained partially immune, favouring maintenance of low‑level transmission. Internal mechanisms: The virus in this focus belonged to African lineage 2 and showed an unusually mild clinical phenotype in cattle yet retained the capacity to cause severe disease in certain wild artiodactyls. Its distinct genotype and attenuated presentation, which enabled long‑term, largely inapparent persistence, justify classification of this episode as re-emergence driven by viral lineage characteristics, rather than simple re-occurrence of classic rinderpest.
Review: review – The time span has been adjusted from 1993–2001 to 1994–2001 to align with FAO EMPRES reports that first recognized mild lineage‑2 rinderpest in Tsavo East National Park in 1994, with subsequent detections in Nairobi and Meru National Parks, and no confirmed virus after 2001. Country‑specific start years have been updated (Kenya [1994–2001], Somalia [1994], Ethiopia [1996]) based on descriptions of spread from the Kenya–Somalia border and later suspicion in southern Ethiopia. Generalist sources (Wikipedia and a broad ScienceDirect topic page) were replaced with more focused FAO bulletins and peer‑reviewed articles. Because precise timing of first infection in each country is still approximate, this row is flagged for human review, but the classification as re-emergence linked to lineage‑2 virus is well supported.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo (with prior involvement of small ruminants in earlier outbreaks)
Event summary: Sri Lanka experienced its last recognized rinderpest outbreak in 1994, following a notable reintroduction in 1987 that had prompted detailed virological studies. The 1994 episode, which occurred against a backdrop of civil conflict and incomplete vaccine coverage, affected cattle and buffalo herds in areas where rinderpest had previously been endemic but was rapidly contained through intensified vaccination and control measures. No further clinical cases were reported after 1994, and Sri Lanka subsequently documented freedom from rinderpest as part of regional eradication efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: War-related disruption of veterinary services, difficulties in sustaining high vaccination coverage in conflict-affected and remote areas, and ongoing livestock movements contributed to the re-occurrence of rinderpest up to 1994. Targeted national and international support strengthened surveillance and immunization, enabling elimination. Internal mechanisms: The virus responsible for Sri Lanka’s outbreaks belonged to established Asian lineages; experimental work on the 1987 strain focused on host range and pathogenicity but did not demonstrate a novel genotype capable of explaining the 1994 recurrence. The 1994 event is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence due to gaps in control rather than re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures Sri Lanka’s last rinderpest activity in 1994 as a re-occurrence following the 1987 reintroduction, in line with FAO and national epidemiology bulletins. The emergence-type classification and geographic coding are appropriate, and the sources are specific to the event. No structural corrections were required.

Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in the Northern Areas (now Gilgit‑Baltistan) and adjoining regions
Event summary: Between April 1994 and November 1995, northern Pakistan experienced the most severe rinderpest epidemic reported globally for more than a decade, affecting cattle and buffalo in remote highland districts and killing an estimated tens of thousands of animals. Infection spread along roads and trade routes as livestock were moved for markets and social obligations, overwhelming local veterinary capacity and threatening spread into neighbouring countries. Emergency vaccination campaigns, movement controls and intensified surveillance under the GREP framework eventually curtailed transmission, and Pakistan later documented absence of circulation leading up to official recognition as free from rinderpest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major gaps in prior vaccination coverage, challenging mountainous terrain and remote communities, and extensive cattle and buffalo movements along trade and social networks allowed rapid spread once the virus was introduced. Delays in detection and laboratory confirmation, combined with limited resources for mass vaccination, greatly amplified the epidemic’s scale. Internal mechanisms: Virological evidence indicates circulation of a known Asian lineage of rinderpest without clear signs of increased virulence or a novel genotype; the epidemic is therefore categorized as dramatic re-occurrence driven by failures in vaccination coverage and surveillance rather than re-emergence arising from viral evolution.
Review: retain – This is clearly one of the largest and best-documented rinderpest outbreaks of the 1990s, with magnitude and chronology supported by detailed clinical and modelling studies. Geography, host range and emergence-type (re-occurrence) are appropriate. No structural corrections were needed; sources are highly relevant and event-specific.

Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo
Event summary: In 1995, Afghanistan reported a rinderpest outbreak that was epidemiologically linked to movement of infected cattle from Pakistan, extending the South Asian epidemic zone. The disease spread among local cattle and buffalo herds in areas already stressed by prolonged conflict and population displacement but was limited in overall size compared with the Pakistani epidemic. Emergency vaccination and ad‑hoc control measures, supported by regional GREP activities, eventually interrupted transmission, and Afghanistan subsequently reported no further rinderpest cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unregulated cross-border livestock movements from Pakistan into Afghanistan, combined with conflict-related displacement, poor veterinary infrastructure and limited vaccination, facilitated re-introduction and local spread of rinderpest. The broader context of civil unrest impeded systematic surveillance and coherent response. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved the same Asian lineage implicated in Pakistan’s epidemic; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or altered virulence, so the event is classified as re-occurrence driven by animal movement and governance factors rather than by viral change.
Review: retain – The Afghan outbreak is correctly portrayed as a spillover from the major Pakistani epidemic, with year, geography and emergence-type (re-occurrence) matching FAO descriptions. While detailed case counts are sparse, its inclusion is justified by its role in extending the South Asian epidemic zone. No structural corrections were required.

Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies
Event summary: Beginning in 1996, the small hive beetle (Aethina tumida), previously confined to sub‑Saharan Africa, was first detected in honey bee colonies near Charleston, South Carolina, with further detections in Florida in 1998 and rapid spread across much of the southeastern and mid‑Atlantic United States during the late 1990s and early 2000s. By 2002 the beetle had been reported from Manitoba, Canada, confirming its establishment in Northern America outside its native range. Infestations caused honey and pollen fermentation, brood damage and, in heavily infested operations, significant colony losses and economic disruption, marking the first inter‑continental establishment of this pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international movement of bees and bee products (especially package bees and beeswax) from southern Africa facilitated introduction of Aethina tumida into North American apiaries, while high densities of managed colonies and migratory beekeeping supported rapid regional spread. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion and adaptation of small hive beetle to European‑derived Apis mellifera strains, with strong reproductive success in large colonies and warm climates, resulted in severe damage where bees lacked co‑evolved behavioural defences.

Event summary: In October 2002, small hive beetle was first detected in commercial honey bee hives near Richmond, New South Wales, and in Queensland, representing its introduction into Australia and, for the first time, the Oceania region. Over the subsequent decade the beetle spread widely along the eastern seaboard and into additional states, becoming established in many beekeeping regions and causing comb destruction, brood damage and honey spoilage in susceptible colonies. By the late 2000s small hive beetle was recognised as a major, ongoing pest of Australian beekeeping, while neighbouring New Zealand remained free of the beetle but intensified biosecurity and surveillance because of the regional threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental importation of infested bee colonies or hive products from already infested regions, likely via international trade in live bees or bee products, is considered the most plausible route of entry into Australia, followed by domestic movement of hives for pollination and honey production that facilitated rapid spread across suitable climatic zones. Internal mechanisms: adults’ ability to fly long distances, high reproductive capacity in warm, humid conditions, and the absence of co‑evolved defensive behaviours in European‑derived A. mellifera stocks greatly increased invasive success and damage potential in Australian apiaries.
Review: retain – Corrected the Australian first-detection year for small hive beetle from 2001 to 2002 based on multiple official Australian sources and restricted the ‘countries’ field to Australia only, as New Zealand remains free of SHB (its status is mentioned only in the narrative). Classification as inter‑continental emergence (first established presence in Oceania) is appropriate. Replaced less specific literature with Australian government and industry sources that clearly document the first detection and subsequent spread. Internal mechanisms: the beetle’s broad climatic tolerance, ability to reproduce in dense A. mellifera apiaries with limited behavioural resistance and capacity for adult dispersal allowed establishment and persistence despite aggressive control measures, raising concern about potential onward spread across Europe.
Review: retain – Substantially revised this event to reflect that the only 2004 European record was an interception of larvae in imported queen cages in Portugal, with no evidence of establishment, and that the first confirmed establishment of small hive beetle in Europe occurred in Calabria (and later Sicily), Italy, in 2014. Event summary: From about 2000 onward, Switzerland experienced a prolonged epidemic of European foulbrood caused by Melissococcus plutonius, with annual numbers of infected apiaries rising sharply compared with earlier decades and reaching several hundred newly infected apiaries per year by the mid‑2000s.
