Review: retain – Swiss federal and peer‑reviewed sources confirm that European foulbrood reached epidemic proportions in Switzerland between roughly 2000 and 2010, with case numbers far exceeding historic baselines and then declining after strengthened control measures. The episode is appropriately coded as a re‑emergence driven by changes in pathogen strain composition and virulence, rather than as inter‑ or intra‑continental spread. Event remains one of the clearest, highly documented re‑emergence episodes for European foulbrood and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies (brood)
Event summary: Throughout the 1990s, American foulbrood (AFB) caused by Paenibacillus larvae was recognised as the most serious honey bee disease in New Zealand, with concern that incidence was increasing as government funding for control programmes was reduced. In response to rising case numbers and industry pressure, the Biosecurity (National American Foulbrood Pest Management Strategy) Order 1998 came into force in 1999, creating a national elimination strategy that mandated systematic inspection and destruction of infected colonies and contaminated equipment. Over the subsequent decade to around 2008, national surveillance and coordinated beekeeper action progressively reduced AFB prevalence, transforming a major resurgence threat into a managed elimination programme, although sporadic cases persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: earlier relaxation of government‑funded control efforts and variable beekeeper compliance had allowed AFB prevalence and spore reservoirs in equipment and honey to build up by the early 1990s, increasing disease pressure and threatening export markets for honey and live bees. Internal mechanisms: the extreme environmental persistence of P. larvae spores in hive materials, honey and the environment, coupled with management practices such as exchange of contaminated equipment and robbing behaviour, underpinned the disease’s resilience and necessitated strict destruction‑based control rather than reliance on antibiotics.
Review: retain – Event captures a nationally important resurgence and subsequent large‑scale management response to American foulbrood in New Zealand, supported by government and industry documents. Coding as a re‑occurrence (resurgence driven primarily by external management and compliance factors, not major pathogen change) is appropriate. Time span 1990–2008 reflects both the build‑up phase and the first decade of the national Pest Management Strategy; the event is retained as one of the most impactful AFB episodes in the period.

EPP common name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Countries: Australia [2022 – initial detection in sentinel hives at Port of Newcastle; 2022-2023 spread within eastern states]
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies and feral colonies
Event summary: In June 2022, Varroa destructor was detected for the first time in Australia in sentinel hives at the Port of Newcastle, New South Wales, ending the country’s long‑standing varroa‑free status. A large‑scale eradication programme was launched, including statewide movement bans on hives, destruction of tens of thousands of colonies in red zones and baiting of feral bees, but ongoing detections through 2022–2023 showed that the mite had spread widely within eastern New South Wales and into parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia. In September 2023 the National Management Group concluded that eradication was no longer technically feasible and agreed to transition to long‑term management, marking the beginning of a new era in which Varroa destructor is expected to become endemic across much of Australia with major implications for pollination‑dependent industries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction likely occurred via accidental importation of infested bees or equipment despite strong biosecurity controls, with high volumes of international shipping and trade providing opportunities for breach. Before detection, extensive movement of hives for pollination and honey production within eastern Australia allowed the mite to disperse beyond the initial port area, complicating eradication. Internal mechanisms: Varroa destructor’s high reproductive rate in sealed brood, efficient transmission of deformed wing virus and other viruses, and the absence of evolved mite resistance in Australian A. mellifera stocks underpin rapid colony decline and necessitate adoption of intensive miticide and integrated pest‑management strategies as the mite becomes established.
Review: retain – Added this new event to capture the 2022–2023 Varroa destructor incursion and subsequent abandonment of eradication in Australia, which ends the last major honey‑producing region previously free of Varroa and has large projected impacts on beekeeping and pollination‑reliant agriculture. All six emergence‑type fields are set to false because Oceania already harboured Varroa destructor (New Zealand) and this episode represents spread to a new country within the same sub‑region rather than emergence in a new continent or sub‑region; it is also not a re‑occurrence or re‑emergence in Australia, which had no prior established Varroa populations. Strongly supported by Australian government outbreak reports and national media; event should be retained and treated as one of the most impactful recent episodes for this complex.

Host: Humans (laboratory worker and research personnel) exposed to macaques and materials infected with simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) and other NHP retroviruses
Event summary: In the early 1990s, a laboratory worker in the United States who handled SIV-infected macaques and laboratory cultures was identified with a documented simian immunodeficiency virus infection acquired directly from non-human primate materials, representing the first confirmed direct SIV zoonotic infection in a human rather than via established HIV lineages. Subsequent serosurveys and linked surveillance of workers in SIV laboratories showed additional evidence of occupational exposure but no human-to-human transmission, framing this as a contained laboratory-acquired zoonosis. The episode concluded without secondary spread but triggered formal CDC and NIH guidance, strengthened biosafety protocols, and long-term monitoring of simian retrovirus spillover risks in primate research centers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive experimental use of SIV-infected macaques and high-titer viral cultures in biomedical laboratories, frequent handling of infectious blood and tissues, and initially underappreciated occupational zoonotic risk facilitated exposure. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of SIV from macaques to a human via percutaneous or mucosal exposure; available evidence indicated no substantial adaptation for sustained human-to-human transmission, with infection remaining an isolated event.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first well-documented direct SIV infection in a laboratory worker in the United States and its impact on biosafety guidance. Year, geography, host description, and the absence of onward human-to-human transmission are consistent with NEJM and CDC MMWR reports. The case count is small but the scientific and biosafety impact justifies inclusion among the top events for this multi-pathogen NHP zoonosis complex.

Countries: United States of America [1995]; Canada [1995]; Germany [1997]
Host: Humans occupationally exposed to captive non-human primates (laboratory workers, animal caretakers, zoo personnel) in primate research centers and zoos
Event summary: From 1995 through around 2000, serologic and molecular studies in cohorts of primate facility and zoo workers in North America and Europe provided the first clear, reproducible evidence that simian foamy viruses (SFV) had zoonotically infected humans, with multiple laboratory and animal‑house staff testing positive for persistent SFV infection. Initial reports of three infected laboratory or monkey-house personnel were followed by CDC-linked surveillance in U.S. and Canadian primate centers and a Lancet report of infected North American zoo keepers, documenting that roughly 1–5% of heavily exposed workers could become SFV infected. No disease clusters or human-to-human transmission were observed, but these findings firmly established SFV as a common occupational NHP zoonosis and led to long‑term follow‑up of infected workers and strengthened biosafety guidance in primate facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of large primate research colonies and zoos, with frequent bites, scratches, mucosal splashes and contact with saliva and blood, created sustained opportunities for SFV spillover into humans; limited early awareness and inconsistent use of personal protective equipment contributed to risk. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of highly prevalent, saliva-borne SFV from chimpanzees, baboons, macaques and other NHPs into humans, with viral properties favoring lifelong integration of proviral DNA but not efficient human-to-human transmission; no consistent evidence of increased virulence was found in infected workers.
Review: review – Updated the year to 1995–2000 to reflect the initial Schweizer et al. 1995 report and subsequent CDC cohort and zoo keeper studies; clarified that infections occurred in the United States, Canada, and at least one European facility (here represented by Germany). Removed vague phrasing about “likely additional industrialized countries” and specified countries with documented infections. Kept the classification as first_detection (first clear evidence of SFV infection in humans) and set other emergence-type flags to No. Human expert should confirm whether to further disaggregate North American and European sub-episodes or retain this as a single occupational SFV-recognition phase.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (research assistant) exposed to rhesus macaques infected with Macacine herpesvirus 1 (B virus) at a primate research center
Event summary: In 1997, a research assistant at the Yerkes (Emory) National Primate Research Center in Georgia, United States, was splashed in the eye with biological material from an infected rhesus macaque and subsequently developed fatal encephalomyelitis due to B virus infection, becoming one of the most widely publicized modern cases of this rare but deadly occupational zoonosis. Extensive contact tracing and testing of more than one hundred close contacts and healthcare workers detected no secondary cases, confirming that transmission in this episode was limited to direct macaque-to-human exposure. The incident spurred major overhauls in macaque-handling biosafety practices, including mandatory eye and mucous-membrane protection, structured bite and splash exposure protocols, and heightened institutional awareness of B virus risks in primate facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close, incompletely protected contact with macaque body fluids during routine primate research, rapid growth of macaque use in biomedical research, and gaps in consistent use of eye and mucosal protection created conditions for ocular inoculation. Internal mechanisms: Long-established host expansion (spillover) of B virus from macaques to humans via contact with saliva or tissues, with very high neurovirulence in humans; no new strain or resistance mechanism was implicated, and the severity reflected intrinsic properties of B virus rather than recent viral evolution.
Review: review – Reinterpreted this case as a severe but sporadic occupational B virus infection rather than a formal re-occurrence event under the project’s definitions; all emergence-type flags are now set to No. Replaced the general Wikipedia facility page with the NIOSH case report on the 1997 ocular exposure and retained CDC clinical and EID review articles as primary sources. Event remains high-impact given the fatal outcome and its role in driving major biosafety changes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (rural hunters and villagers) bitten or scratched by wild apes and monkeys; source hosts included gorillas and several monkey species
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2005, focused field studies in remote forest villages of southern Cameroon identified a cluster of at least 13 persons persistently infected with simian foamy viruses after severe bites or other traumatic contacts with wild apes and monkeys, providing the first strong evidence of natural SFV transmission to humans in Central Africa. Molecular analyses showed that each human SFV strain closely matched viruses circulating in local gorillas or monkeys, indicating repeated, independent cross‑species transmission events linked to hunting and bushmeat handling rather than a single outbreak. No human-to-human spread or SFV-associated disease clusters were detected, but this work established Central African hunting communities as a hotspot for primate retrovirus spillover and motivated sustained longitudinal monitoring and risk-reduction campaigns.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-intensity human–wildlife contact through subsistence hunting and butchering of apes and monkeys, increasing forest access via logging roads, land-use change and deforestation that intensify encounters with NHPs, and lack of protective equipment during carcass handling all promoted repeated SFV spillover. Internal mechanisms: Repeated host expansion (spillover) of diverse SFV lineages from wild apes and monkeys into humans, with phylogenetic analyses showing independent cross-species transmission events; viruses established lifelong infection in humans but showed no evidence of adaptation for efficient human-to-human transmission or increased virulence.
Review: review – Corrected the sub_regions field to Middle Africa only and restricted countries to Cameroon, removing unsupported references to neighboring countries without documented human SFV infections in this study. Reclassified the event as an inter-continental emergence (first recognized natural SFV infections in humans in Africa) rather than a mix of intra-continental emergence and re-emergence, since SFV had not previously been documented in humans in this continent. Event summary and mechanism remain appropriate for a major Central African SFV spillover episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (monkey temple workers, local residents, pet owners, urban residents, and some tourists) exposed to free-ranging macaques; source hosts were mainly Macaca fascicularis, Macaca mulatta, Macaca assamensis, and other macaque species
Event summary: From 2000 to 2007, multi-country surveys in South and South‑East Asia documented simian foamy virus infections in eight persons living and working alongside free-ranging macaques in Indonesia, Thailand, Nepal, and Bangladesh, representing the first clear description of endemic SFV spillover in Asian community and temple settings. Human SFV sequences from infected temple workers, pet owners, and village residents clustered closely with local macaque strains, and serosurveys suggested that a measurable fraction of frequently exposed people at monkey temples and in urban interfaces could become infected. No human-to-human transmission or SFV-associated clinical disease clusters were observed, but these findings shifted attention to commensal macaque–human interfaces as important foci for primate-associated zoonoses and informed risk communication for workers and tourists.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense commensal macaque populations in urban and temple environments, cultural practices of feeding and close contact, rapid urbanization, wildlife tourism, and limited awareness or use of protective measures against bites and scratches collectively increased opportunities for macaque-to-human SFV transmission. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of endemic macaque SFV strains to humans, with geographic range expansion of recognized zoonotic transmission into South and South‑East Asian urban, religious, and village sites; viral genetics indicated stable, host-associated lineages without major new genotypes linked to increased human virulence.
Review: review – Adjusted the year span to 2000–2007 to match the sampling period, corrected the country list and timing based on the Asia SFV survey (Indonesia 2000/2003, Thailand 2002 and 2004–2005, Nepal 2003, Bangladesh 2007), and removed unsupported mention of India. Reclassified the event as an inter-continental emergence of human SFV infections in Asia (new continent for recognized human SFV zoonoses) and set other emergence-type flags, including first_detection and re_emergence, to No. This episode remains one of the most important SFV spillover events given its multi-country scope and demonstration of risk in non-occupational settings.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Gabon [2010]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2012]
Host: Humans (bushmeat hunters, women involved in hunting and butchering, and other rural residents) exposed to wild non-human primates; source hosts included mandrills and several monkey species
Event summary: Between roughly 2010 and 2013, expanded field investigations in Gabon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo documented additional naturally acquired SFV infections in hunters and rural residents, including several women infected by viruses from different monkey species, thereby broadening the demographic and host-range context of African SFV zoonoses beyond the earlier Cameroon cohorts. Detailed molecular studies showed that each human infection was closely related to SFV strains circulating in local non-human primate populations and that multiple distinct genotypes from mandrills and monkeys had independently crossed into humans. No evidence of onward human-to-human transmission or consistent clinical disease was found, but these results consolidated the view of Central African forests as a persistent source of genetically diverse SFV spillover and supported ongoing programs to monitor NHP-borne retroviruses and counsel high-risk groups about safe hunting and handling practices.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued reliance on bushmeat, expansion and professionalization of bushmeat trade networks, and evolving gender roles in hunting and butchering in Central Africa maintained or increased high-risk human contact with NHP blood and saliva; weak clinical and virologic surveillance systems meant asymptomatic infections were rarely recognized outside targeted studies. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergent host expansion (spillover) of diverse SFV genotypes from multiple monkey and mandrill species to humans within a subregion where SFV zoonoses were already known, with evidence of multiple independent cross-species transmission events; viral evolution reflected high genetic diversity in reservoir hosts but did not indicate enhanced human pathogenicity or transmissibility.
Review: review – Left geography unchanged (Middle Africa: Gabon and DRC) but changed emergence typing from intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence to re_emergence only. Because SFV spillover to humans had already been documented in the same subregion (Cameroon), these new infections represent additional, genetically diverse spillover events rather than spread into a new subregion of Africa. Event remains important as it documents broader host and demographic range for African SFV zoonoses.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans occupationally exposed to New World and Old World non-human primates (animal handlers, general helpers, veterinarians, and other staff) at a Brazilian primate center and zoo; source hosts included multiple New World monkey species (e.g., capuchins, marmosets, howler and spider monkeys) and some Old World primates
Event summary: From 2011 to 2014, longitudinal screening of 56 workers at the Rio de Janeiro primate center and city zoo in Brazil identified simian foamy virus infections in 10 persons (about 18%), providing the first confirmed zoonotic infections with New World simian foamy viruses and the first well-documented human SFV infections in South America. Infected workers, most of whom had a history of bites and other high-risk accidents while handling primates, showed durable serologic responses and, in some cases, detectable proviral DNA in blood or buccal cells, although no associated disease or human-to-human transmission was observed. This episode demonstrated that New World SFV lineages can cross into humans in occupational settings and highlighted primate facilities in Latin America as important but previously overlooked interfaces for NHP retrovirus spillover.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth of primate research and conservation breeding programs in Brazil, intensive daily handling of a wide range of New World primate species, frequent bites and scratches in the absence of uniformly applied protective measures, and limited prior awareness of SFV risk in New World species facilitated spillover. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genetically divergent New World SFV lineages into humans, with clear evidence of multiple independent infections; this represents both geographic range expansion of recognized human SFV zoonoses into South America and evolutionary diversification of the infecting SFV lineages, although no adaptation for human-to-human transmission has been demonstrated.
Review: review – Added this event because the Brazilian cohort provides the first documented human infections with New World simian foamy viruses and the first sizable series of SFV-infected primate workers in South America (10 confirmed infections), making it one of the largest and most geographically important emergence events for this EPP. Classified it as an inter-continental emergence (new continent for recognized human SFV infections) and re_emergence (new viral lineages and host expansion), with geography and timing based on the study’s 2011–2014 sampling.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (two workers at a macaque facility in Japan) with chronic neurologic disease linked to Macacine alphaherpesvirus 1 (B virus) infection; source hosts were macaques (likely rhesus macaques) managed at a pharmaceutical research facility
Event summary: In 2019, Japanese investigators identified B virus infection in two workers from the same macaque facility who had long-standing neurologic disease, marking the first confirmed human Macacine alphaherpesvirus 1 infections in Asia after decades of cases being reported almost exclusively in North America. Molecular testing of cerebrospinal fluid and archived brain tissue demonstrated high copy numbers of B virus DNA and sequences matching rhesus-genotype strains, and both patients had a history of occupational exposure to macaques. No epidemiologic link between the two patients was found beyond working at the same facility, and no secondary human-to-human transmission was detected, but these cases showed that severe B virus disease can occur in Asian macaque workers and underscore the need for surveillance and strict biosafety in regional primate centers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term occupational exposure to macaques at a research facility in Japan, international trade in macaques, and previously limited consideration of B virus risk in Asian primate centers contributed to undetected infection and delayed diagnosis; improved molecular diagnostics eventually enabled retrospective confirmation. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of B virus from macaques to human workers with subsequent CNS involvement; the detected strains were typical rhesus-genotype viruses without evidence of unusual virulence or adaptation, indicating that recognized cases reflect pre-existing viral properties rather than recent viral change.
Review: review – Added this event because it documents the first confirmed human B virus infections in Asia (two occupational cases in Japan), representing an inter-continental emergence of recognized B virus zoonosis beyond North America. Year range reflects the period from the earlier patient’s clinical presentation (2014) through virologic confirmation of both cases in 2019. Emergence-type flags are limited to inter_continental_emergence to avoid conflating these sporadic, unrelated cases with re-occurrence or re-emergence dynamics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Human (veterinarian working with non-human primates at a research and breeding facility in Beijing) exposed to macaques carrying Macacine alphaherpesvirus 1 (B virus)
Event summary: In 2021, China reported its first confirmed human infection with monkey B virus in a 53-year-old male veterinarian involved in breeding and experimental work with macaques in Beijing, who developed severe neurologic disease and died despite intensive care. Real-time PCR testing of cerebrospinal fluid detected B virus DNA, while testing for other viral pathogens and all samples from close contacts were negative, indicating a single zoonotic infection without onward human-to-human spread. This case followed the earlier identification of B virus infections in Japan and demonstrated that severe B virus disease can occur among macaque workers in Chinese facilities, prompting heightened awareness and recommendations for strict adherence to macaque injury management and B virus diagnostic protocols in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of macaque breeding and experimental use in China, frequent close contact between workers and macaques, and limited prior experience with diagnosing B virus infection created conditions for delayed recognition of this fatal zoonosis. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of B virus from macaques to a human via occupational exposure, leading to encephalitis and death; virologic data are consistent with known B virus neurovirulence, without evidence of novel genetic features linked to increased transmissibility. The case represents re-occurrence of B virus disease within Eastern Asia after the earlier Japanese cases rather than spread to a new continent or subregion.
Review: review – Added this event as the first documented human B virus infection in China, an important follow-on to the Japanese cases that confirms B virus zoonotic risk in Chinese primate facilities. Classified as re_occurrence within Eastern Asia (same subregion as the Japanese cases) rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence, in line with the project rules that spread to additional countries within the same subregion should not be coded as intra-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Avian mycobacteriosis (Avian tuberculosis; typically Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium)
Host: Lesser flamingo (Phoeniconaias minor), free‑ranging wild waterbirds at Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru
Event summary: From August to mid‑November 1993, a major mortality event occurred among lesser flamingos (Phoeniconaias minor) congregating at Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru in Kenya’s Rift Valley, an area where avian tuberculosis had been reported previously. More than 18,500 flamingos died over about three months; necropsies found granulomatous lesions mainly in spleen and liver, frequent isolation of Mycobacterium avium serovar 1, and concurrent septicemia with Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, while lesions typical of algal toxicosis were absent. The epizootic waned as environmental conditions and bird densities at the lakes changed, with no evidence of sustained spread to other bird or mammal species frequenting the lakes, and was interpreted as a large flare‑up of endemic mycobacteriosis complicated by bacterial sepsis rather than a new geographic incursion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10231756/))
Mechanism or driver: External drivers likely included drought‑related crowding of flamingos at the soda lakes, associated changes in water quality and algal blooms, and nutritional stress, which together would have increased contact rates and reduced host resilience, predisposing birds to infection and septicemia. Internal mechanisms reflected amplification of an already endemic M. avium infection (serovar 1) in this wild population rather than emergence of a novel genotype or host shift; chronic mycobacterial lesions appear to have interacted with opportunistic bacterial sepsis to produce the observed high mortality. In line with these features and the absence of new subregions or continents affected, this episode is best classified as a high‑impact re‑occurrence of avian tuberculosis within Eastern Africa, rather than an intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – newly added major epizootic (>18,500 lesser flamingos dead in 1993 at Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru, Kenya) attributed in part to Mycobacterium avium; classified as a high‑impact re‑occurrence event in Eastern Africa with no evidence for new subregions or continents affected. Event details (timing, location, host and pathology) derived from Kock et al. 1999 and subsequent syntheses; recommended for inclusion among the largest Mycobacterium avium avian outbreaks but flagged for expert confirmation of classification and summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Avian mycobacteriosis (Avian tuberculosis; typically Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium)
Host: Commercial layer hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) in a large cage‑layer flock
Event summary: Around 2002, a severe outbreak of avian tuberculosis was reported in Spain in a commercial flock of approximately 38,500 48‑week‑old layer hens, after a gradual decline in egg production and feed intake and a rise in mortality. Necropsy findings showed granulomatous nodules in infraorbital sinuses, liver, intestine and other organs, with abundant acid‑fast bacilli, and PCR confirmed Mycobacterium avium as the etiologic agent, indicating extensive flock‑level infection in an otherwise standard intensive production unit. Control relied on flock depopulation and biosecurity measures at farm level; the outbreak remained confined to this operation but represented a rare, very large commercial poultry episode of avian tuberculosis with substantial production losses.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/10979729_Outbreak_of_Avian_Tuberculosis_in_48-Week-Old_Commercial_Layer_Hen_Flock?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: This outbreak likely reflected a combination of external drivers typical for long‑cycle layer systems, including high stocking densities, reuse of housing with accumulating contaminated litter and dust, and the advanced age of birds, which together allow endemic Mycobacterium avium to build up and spread within the flock. Internal mechanisms such as novel strain emergence or host expansion were not reported; the infecting organism was consistent with previously recognized M. avium subsp. avium. Accordingly, the event is interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence of endemic avian tuberculosis in a Southern European commercial flock rather than an intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – newly added large commercial poultry outbreak (~38,500 48‑week‑old layer hens) in Spain, documented by González et al. 2002 and widely cited in later reviews. Treated here as a severe farm‑level re‑occurrence of endemic Mycobacterium avium infection in Southern Europe without evidence of broader regional spread; recommended for inclusion among the most impactful events but flagged for expert verification of year, flock size and production‑loss estimates used in the summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Avian mycobacteriosis (Avian tuberculosis; typically Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium)
Host: Commercial Pekin breeder ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domestica) on a large farm in Sichuan Province
Event summary: In July 2015, a commercial farm in Sichuan Province, China, housing about 2,500 46‑week‑old Pekin breeder ducks experienced a marked increase in mortality, progressive emaciation and decreased egg production, prompting investigation. Necropsy of affected ducks revealed multifocal granulomatous nodules in multiple visceral organs, abundant acid‑fast bacilli, and culture plus PCR (IS901 and 16S rRNA) confirmed Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium infection, representing the first described outbreak of avian tuberculosis in commercial domestic duck flocks. Over roughly four weeks, cumulative flock mortality reached about 20%, after which culling of diseased birds and hygiene measures were implemented and the outbreak remained limited to this farm, with no reports of onward spread in regional duck production.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/307969101_Outbreak_of_Avian_Tuberculosis_in_Commercial_Domestic_Pekin_Ducks_Anas_platyrhynchos_domestica))
Mechanism or driver: The outbreak occurred in older breeder ducks kept at high density, conditions that favour environmental build‑up and transmission of M. avium, and underscores that waterfowl—although often relatively resistant—can develop clinical disease when chronically exposed. The source of infection was not definitively identified, but contamination from the wider environment, introduction via feed or undetected carrier birds were considered more plausible than emergence of a new genotype, and there was no evidence for spread beyond the index premises. This episode is therefore interpreted as a rare, localized re‑occurrence of endemic avian tuberculosis in intensive duck production in Eastern Asia rather than a new intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence event.
Review: review – newly added rare but high‑impact outbreak in a 2,500‑bird Pekin breeder duck flock in Sichuan, China (2015), documented by Zhu et al. 2016. Classified as a localized re‑occurrence of Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium in commercial ducks within an already endemic region; inclusion is recommended because of flock size and documented economic impact, but the event is flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among other, less well‑quantified outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Avian mycobacteriosis (Avian tuberculosis; typically Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium)
Host: Commercial Bourbon Red breeder turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) on two farms in Markazi and Qazvin Provinces
Event summary: During winter 2018, a chronic outbreak of avian mycobacteriosis began in a 45‑week‑old breeder flock of 250 Bourbon Red turkeys in Saveh, Markazi Province, Iran, with progressive wasting, lameness and falling egg production. After the flock was moved to a second farm in Takestan (Qazvin Province), mortality continued, and over six months (December 2018–May 2019) about 80% of birds died; necropsy showed granulomatous nodules in liver, spleen, ovary and ribs with acid‑fast bacilli, and PCR targeting 16S rRNA, IS1245 and IS901 confirmed Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium infection. Epidemiologic investigation linked the outbreak to reuse of an old poultry house with poor biosecurity and close proximity to a loft harbouring more than 1,000 feral pigeons, and after laboratory confirmation the remaining birds were slaughtered and the premises cleaned and disinfected under veterinary authority guidance, with no reports of spread to other commercial farms.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03079457.2020.1740167?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Key external drivers included inadequate biosecurity in a repurposed poultry facility and intense local exposure to feral pigeons, which likely served as an environmental reservoir and direct or indirect source of Mycobacterium avium for the turkeys, compounded by the advanced age of breeder birds and chronic housing of a small flock on contaminated premises. Internal pathogen changes such as novel genotype emergence, host shift or clearly increased virulence were not demonstrated; the isolate behaved as typical M. avium subsp. avium. Consequently, this episode is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence of endemic avian tuberculosis within Southern Asia, rather than a new intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence, albeit one with high within‑flock impact and clear links to wildlife reservoirs and management practices.
Review: review – newly added high‑mortality outbreak in a 250‑bird breeder turkey flock in Iran (December 2018–May 2019) with ~92% morbidity and 80% mortality, documented by Rahimi et al. 2020. Treated as a localized re‑occurrence driven by poor biosecurity and exposure to feral pigeons within a region where Mycobacterium avium is already endemic; recommended for inclusion among major events and flagged for expert confirmation of UN subregion coding (Iran assigned to Southern Asia) and completeness of the event description.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Around 1990–1993, surveillance reports in New Zealand documented a rapid increase in sheep flocks known to be infected with Johne’s disease, with official figures showing a marked rise in the number of infected flocks compared with the 1980s. The situation evolved as MAP spread within commercial sheep enterprises, reflected by year‑on‑year growth in the number and proportion of flocks with clinical losses. The episode stabilised into an endemic pattern with Johne’s disease recognised as a significant chronic wasting disease of New Zealand sheep, prompting ongoing on‑farm management changes and later integration into broader national paratuberculosis control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of New Zealand’s sheep industry with high stocking densities and pasture-based management favoured MAP transmission within and between flocks, while improved veterinary awareness and surveillance increased reporting of clinically affected flocks. Internal mechanisms: No specific new MAP strain was implicated; the episode represents amplification of endemic MAP infections under favourable management and environmental conditions rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event correctly captures an early‑1990s increase in recognised Johne’s‑infected sheep flocks in New Zealand and associated transition to endemic disease status, based on New Zealand surveillance data and later national reviews of MAP control in pastoral livestock. Geographic assignment (Oceania | Australia and New Zealand; country New Zealand) and classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence of an established pathogen driven by management and surveillance changes) are appropriate; no evidence supports first detection or inter/intra‑continental emergence in this period. Sources are relevant and specific to New Zealand sheep; no corrections required, but human reviewer may wish to confirm quantitative details from the original Surveillance 21(1) 1994 article.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep and goats (ovine Johne’s disease; some spillover to cattle)
Event summary: Following first recognition of ovine Johne’s disease (OJD) in Australian sheep in 1980, infection spread widely through flocks in New South Wales and neighbouring states, and by the 1990s had developed into a major epidemic causing substantial mortality, production losses and trade restrictions. During the 1990s the number of infected flocks and the extent of infected areas increased markedly, leading to quarantine of properties, interstate movement controls, and strong industry and community concern. From 1998 a A$40.1‑million National Ovine Johne’s Disease Control and Evaluation Program, and from 1999–2009 a large‑scale vaccination and abattoir‑surveillance campaign in New South Wales (over 12 million ovine vaccinations and 7.6 million carcass examinations), progressively reduced lesion prevalence and helped stabilise the epidemic, although OJD remains endemic in some regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement and sale of breeding and store sheep, communal grazing and agistment, and high stocking densities in key wool‑growing regions drove rapid geographic spread; regulatory changes and market incentives for flock expansion likely increased animal movement; strong economic dependence on the sheep industry heightened the impact and political pressure to act. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic primarily involved the ovine (S) strain of MAP already present in Australia; there is no clear evidence that a novel, more virulent strain emerged during this period, although cross‑species infections (sheep strain in some cattle) were detected and considered in control strategies.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This episode is widely documented as one of the most impactful MAP events globally, with large-scale mortality and production losses in Australian sheep, a national A$40.1‑million control programme, and millions of vaccinations and carcass inspections. Year range (1990–2009) appropriately covers the major epidemic and control phase; continent/sub‑region/country assignments are correct. Classification as re‑occurrence (intensification and geographic expansion of endemic MAP infection under changed trade and management, without evidence of a new strain) is appropriate. Sources (Australian Veterinary Journal articles, NSW government and Senate reports) are highly relevant; no changes needed but this event should be retained as a key high‑impact episode.

Host: Dairy and beef cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: Clinical Johne’s disease was first recorded in Ireland in 1920 in an imported cow, and available evidence suggests that prevalence remained very low for many decades, with sporadic cases only. After the creation of the EU Single Market in 1992 and removal of certain quarantine checks, Ireland experienced increased cattle imports from continental Europe, and analyses of trade and surveillance data indicate that MAP infection became more widely established in Irish cattle herds during the 1990s. By 2005, a national survey estimated a true herd‑level prevalence of approximately 20.6% of dairy herds (animal‑level prevalence ~2.9%), and later modelling of herds enrolled in a pilot control programme in 2013–2014 suggested around 28% herd prevalence, confirming Johne’s disease as a significant problem in Irish dairy production. In response, Ireland implemented the Irish Johne’s Control Programme (IJCP), beginning with pilot herds in late 2013 and scaling to a national voluntary control programme by 2017, which continues to aim at reducing MAP prevalence and safeguarding market access.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased intra‑European cattle trade following EU market integration, particularly importation of breeding stock from higher-prevalence countries, likely introduced additional MAP infection into previously low‑prevalence Irish herds; traditional management practices such as pooled colostrum and waste‑milk feeding to calves, use of calving pens for sick or lame cows, and limited awareness of Johne’s risk further promoted within‑herd and between‑herd spread. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates the presence of typical bovine MAP strains rather than a novel variant; the emergence reflects increased introduction pressure and conducive management systems rather than a change in pathogen genotype or virulence.
Review: Decision: retain, flag for review. Changes made: (1) Sub‑regions adjusted from "Northern Europe; Western Europe" to "Northern Europe" because the event, as defined, concerns infection dynamics and control in Ireland only; origin countries in Western Europe are part of the driver narrative, not part of the outbreak area. (2) Event-type classification changed: this episode is not first detection of MAP in Irish cattle (clinical JD was first recorded in 1920) and does not represent spread into a new continental sub‑region, so first_detection and intra_continental_emergence have been set to false. Instead, it is re‑occurrence, reflecting resurgence and wider establishment of an existing pathogen in a previously low‑prevalence country due to external drivers (EU Single Market trade and management practices), consistent with Irish surveillance and IJCP descriptions. (3) The event summary has been updated to explicitly mention the 1920 first record, emphasise historically low prevalence prior to 1992, and avoid implying that MAP was entirely absent from Ireland before the 1990s. Mechanism/drivers remain consistent with published analyses. Recommendation: retain this as a major European emergence/re‑occurrence episode, but human expert should confirm the chosen time span (1992–2017) and emphasis on trade‑driven introduction versus amplification of existing infection.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed deer (primarily red deer Cervus elaphus and red–elk hybrids)
Event summary: Johne’s disease was first confirmed in New Zealand farmed deer before 1990, but by the mid‑1990s to early 2000s it had shifted from a rare diagnosis to a significant health and production problem in the expanding deer industry, with increasing numbers of clinically affected animals and herd‑level losses reported. During this period, abattoir surveillance and field investigations documented a steady rise in the incidence of MAP‑associated enteritis in deer, with some outbreaks affecting up to 10–15% of young deer in affected groups and high case‑fatality rates, prompting industry concern and research into disease epidemiology and control. By the early 2000s the emergence of Johne’s disease in deer resulted in coordinated industry responses, including advisory material, proposed assurance schemes, and ultimately the establishment of Johne’s Management Limited (JML) in 2007 to support sustained control of Johne’s disease in New Zealand deer.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of farmed deer production in New Zealand, high stocking rates, and movement of stock among farms facilitated MAP transmission; increasing deer densities and stressors such as weaning and winter feeding heightened susceptibility, while improved diagnostic recognition in deer herds and systematic abattoir monitoring increased case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Both bovine and ovine MAP strains have been implicated in deer, but no specific novel genotype was singled out during this period; instead, high susceptibility of young deer and the high force of infection under intensive conditions led to severe clinical disease and high mortality compared with cattle and sheep, effectively amplifying the impact of existing MAP strains.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: New Zealand’s farmed deer epidemic of Johne’s disease, with hundreds of infected farms and outbreaks causing up to 10–15% mortality in groups of young deer, is one of the clearest examples of MAP emerging as a major production disease in a relatively new farmed host. The 1995–2005 window reasonably captures the transition from sporadic cases to widespread recognition of a serious industry problem, as reflected in national case–control studies and abattoir‑based surveillance. Continent/sub‑region/country fields are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence and spread of an existing pathogen into a rapidly growing host industry) is appropriate; there is no strong evidence for a novel strain or true host‑range jump that would justify re‑emergence. Sources (Vet Clin North Am review, NZSAP 2002 proceedings, deer epidemiology PhD thesis, industry fact sheets) are well-matched to the event; no structural changes required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In 1996, the NAHMS Dairy ’96 study in the United States provided the first robust national estimate of Johne’s disease status in dairy cattle, indicating that about 21.6% of dairy herds had evidence of MAP infection and that affected herds suffered substantial production losses per cow. Over the following years, recognition of the high herd-level prevalence and economic impact, combined with growing concern about possible public‑health implications, led to intense discussion among veterinarians, industry groups and regulators about how to control Johne’s disease. By 1998–2001 this culminated in development of the U.S. Voluntary Johne’s Disease Herd Status Program for Cattle and, subsequently, USDA’s Uniform Program Standards for the Voluntary Bovine Johne’s Disease Control Program, marking the start of coordinated national efforts aimed at reducing MAP prevalence through testing and management‑based control at the herd level.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large, increasingly concentrated U.S. dairy herds with intensive calf‑rearing, high animal movements, and manure management practices facilitated MAP transmission; national surveillance and economic analyses revealed previously under‑recognised production losses, creating strong incentives for industry and regulatory response. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects amplification and better detection of existing bovine MAP strains rather than emergence of new genotypes; no specific evidence of increased virulence or antimicrobial resistance driving this episode has been identified.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This event describes the point at which Johne’s disease emerged as a nationally quantified and economically significant problem for the U.S. dairy industry, triggering the NAHMS Dairy ’96 survey and development of national voluntary control standards. The time window (1996–2001) reasonably brackets the first national prevalence estimates and early implementation of the Voluntary Johne’s Disease Herd Status and USDA uniform control programmes. Geographic fields are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence (surge in recognised incidence and control response for an endemic pathogen) is appropriate. Sources (NAHMS technical reports and the National Academies monograph on control principles and programs) are central references for this episode; no corrections are needed, though users should note that large‑scale control efforts continued beyond 2001.

Host: Dairy and beef cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: Bovine paratuberculosis was first detected in Japan in an imported dairy cow that died in 1959, and the disease was made notifiable in 1971; case numbers increased gradually through the 1980s, reaching more than 200 diagnosed cases per year in the mid‑1990s. In 1998, Japan strengthened its national control programme by introducing compulsory active surveillance using a Mycobacterium phlei‑absorbed ELISA on all adult cattle at 5‑year intervals, with animals that were repeatedly ELISA‑positive or culture‑positive subjected to compensated slaughter. During 1998–2000 alone, 2,469 ELISA‑ or culture‑positive cattle (about 1,500 dairy and 969 beef) were culled under the programme, and a further 3,181 high‑risk animals (mainly progeny and cohorts of infected cattle) were slaughtered with subsidies, representing a major national test‑and‑cull effort. Through the 2000s and 2010s, this compulsory surveillance and eradication framework continued, with regular testing of infected herds every 3–6 months until all animals tested negative, maintaining pressure on MAP infection and supporting Japan’s broader goals for control of high‑impact bovine diseases and protection of trade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rising numbers of diagnosed paratuberculosis cases in the 1980s and 1990s, combined with Japan’s emphasis on controlling serious bovine diseases and safeguarding export markets and public confidence in dairy products, led to adoption of an intensive national surveillance and culling programme. Government funding for testing and compensation facilitated producer participation and allowed repeated whole‑herd testing at defined intervals. Internal mechanisms: The programme targeted existing bovine MAP infections; there is no clear evidence that a novel strain or resistance trait emerged in this period—the impact derives from policy‑driven removal of infected and high‑risk animals on a national scale rather than a change in pathogen biology.
Review: Decision: added event, flag for review. Rationale: A major national bovine paratuberculosis control programme in Japan, initiated before 1998 and substantially intensified that year with compulsory ELISA screening of all adult cattle and test‑and‑cull with compensation, resulted in the slaughter of at least 2,469 confirmed infected cattle and 3,181 high‑risk animals during 1998–2000 alone, and continued as an active control framework into the 2010s. Given the scale of culling, compulsory surveillance, and Japan’s sizeable dairy and beef sectors, this episode is among the most impactful MAP control/emergence events globally post‑1990 and was missing from the original dataset. Geographic fields (Asia, Eastern Asia, Japan) and classification as re‑occurrence (intensified control and reduction of an established pathogen driven by external regulatory decisions) are appropriate; no evidence supports first detection or intra/inter‑continental emergence during this period. The chosen year range (1998–2018) is meant to capture both the initial surge of test‑and‑cull and the continuation of the compulsory national programme, but exact end‑year should be confirmed from Japanese regulatory sources. Human expert review is recommended to refine the upper time bound and to check whether this event should be split into separate phases (initial eradication campaign vs. long‑term maintenance).

Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: In 1998, a national survey in the Netherlands estimated that 31–71% of dairy herds were infected with MAP (true animal‑level prevalence approximately 2.7–6.9%), highlighting Johne’s disease as a widespread endemic infection in one of Europe’s most intensive dairy industries. Around 2000, similar surveillance in Denmark reported an estimated 8.8% of dairy cows testing positive in a milk‑ELISA survey, confirming that MAP was an important, though variably distributed, production disease in Northern European dairy systems. These findings made clear that Johne’s disease was a large‑scale problem in high‑intensity European dairy sectors and spurred or reinforced national and regional control efforts in several countries, including herd‑assurance schemes, risk‑based testing, and integration of Johne’s control into broader bovine health programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing MAP infection in intensive dairy systems in the Netherlands and Denmark, combined with improved diagnostic tests (ELISA, culture) and structured national surveys, converted largely hidden endemic infection into a recognised large‑scale health and economic issue; intra‑EU cattle trade also contributed to cross‑border dissemination. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain is reported in these surveys; the episode represents enhanced detection and documentation of widespread endemic MAP leading to coordinated control efforts, rather than a discrete genetic or virulence shift.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row appropriately summarises the first robust national‑scale evidence of high MAP prevalence in intensive European dairy herds (Netherlands and Denmark) and the role of these surveys in catalysing or reinforcing control efforts. The time span (1998–2000) aligns with the key survey dates. Geographic coding (Europe; Western Europe for the Netherlands and Northern Europe for Denmark) and classification as re‑occurrence (recognition and response to high endemic prevalence) are consistent with definitions. Sources (Irish prevalence paper for comparative European data, USDA Johne’s 2002 report summarising Danish data, and the 48‑country control review) are relevant; no major corrections are needed, though human experts may wish to consider whether subsequent major expansions of European programmes (e.g. in Germany or the UK) warrant additional separate events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Mixed pastoral livestock (deer, cattle, sheep)
Event summary: By the mid‑2000s, Johne’s disease caused by MAP had become a recognised multi‑species problem in New Zealand’s pastoral systems, particularly affecting farmed deer and dairy cattle, leading industry and government stakeholders to seek coordinated solutions. In 2007, the deer industry established Johne’s Management Limited (JML) to support practical control in farmed deer, and from 2008–2016 the Johne’s Disease Research Consortium (JDRC) operated as an industry–science partnership to generate epidemiological, genetic and management tools for Johne’s control across cattle, sheep and deer. Over its lifespan this coordinated programme developed risk‑based management recommendations, improved diagnostic approaches and provided resources to farmers, helping to reduce clinical disease incidence and embed Johne’s control in New Zealand’s broader herd and flock health strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Accumulated economic losses and animal‑welfare concerns from Johne’s disease in high‑value deer and dairy sectors, together with evidence of widespread infection from abattoir and on‑farm data, drove creation of industry‑funded and government‑supported research and management programmes; the collaborative structure allowed coordinated interventions across multiple livestock species. Internal mechanisms: Research under JDRC explored host genetics and MAP–host interactions, but the episode is primarily characterised by improved understanding and control of existing MAP infections rather than clear emergence of novel strains or resistance traits.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Although this event is framed around control initiatives rather than a discrete outbreak, it reflects a major coordinated multi‑species response to a burdensome endemic disease across New Zealand’s pastoral industries, including a national abattoir‑based surveillance system for deer and cross‑sectoral research investment. The 2007–2016 window corresponds to the establishment of JML (2007) and the life of the JDRC (2008–2016). Geographic and host fields are appropriate, and classification as re‑occurrence (ongoing management of a recognised endemic problem) is consistent with definitions. Sources (JDRC website, DRL/JML resources, Gautam et al. 2018) provide good coverage. Because this row sits at the boundary between “emergence event” and “control era,” human reviewers may wish to confirm its inclusion relative to other possible control‑focused events, but its impact on national MAP management justifies retention.
