Host: African buffalo (Syncerus caffer); cattle (Bos taurus); other wildlife (e.g., lions, kudu) in and around Kruger National Park
Event summary: In 1990, bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis was first detected in a free-ranging African buffalo in Kruger National Park, South Africa, indicating recent cattle-to-buffalo spillover into this major wildlife population.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, infection prevalence increased and spread northwards through the park’s buffalo metapopulation, with subsequent spillover to other wildlife species and concern for transmission to adjacent communal cattle.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) By about 2006, the infection front had reached the northern boundary of Kruger, establishing a large, persistent sylvatic reservoir that complicated prospects for regional bovine TB control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059242/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from infected cattle at the wildlife–livestock interface, high buffalo density, drought stress in the early 1990s, and park management practices that facilitated within-park animal movements and contacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870607/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from cattle into African buffalo followed by establishment of a new wildlife maintenance host population; Enhanced Transmission via dense, socially structured buffalo herds; and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within the park as infected subpopulations seeded new areas over time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870607/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Well-supported major wildlife re-emergence event: M. bovis spilled over from cattle into Kruger African buffalo in 1990 and spread northwards to infect most herds by the mid‑2000s, creating a persistent multi-species wildlife reservoir.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new wildlife maintenance host within a long-endemic region) and the Africa/Southern Africa/South Africa geographic coding are appropriate; no changes made.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); farmed deer (Cervus spp.); brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula); other wildlife (e.g., ferrets, feral pigs, wild deer)
Event summary: During the 1980s and early 1990s, bovine tuberculosis control in New Zealand stalled as widespread infection became established in brushtail possum populations, leading to a rapid rise in infected cattle and farmed deer herds and expansion of wildlife vector risk areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Herd infection prevalence peaked in 1994–1995 with around 1,700 infected herds (≈3.8–3.9% of all cattle and deer herds) and TB‑infected wildlife occupying roughly a third of the country, threatening export markets and prompting creation of a national pest management strategy focused on wildlife vectors.([ospri.co.nz](https://www.ospri.co.nz/our-programmes/the-tbfree-programme/history?utm_source=openai)) From the late 1990s through about 2011, large‑scale possum control, intensified livestock testing, and movement controls progressively reduced infected herds to under 100 nationwide and shifted programme goals from control to staged eradication of M. bovis from both livestock and wildlife reservoirs.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00480169.2015.1013581?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reduced funding for possum control in the late 1970s and early 1980s, high possum densities in forest–pasture mosaics, and close spatial overlap between possums, cattle and farmed deer allowed wildlife infection to become widespread and to drive recurrent breakdowns in domestic herds across an expanding vector risk area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment and consolidation of brushtail possums—and locally ferrets, feral pigs and wild deer—as maintenance hosts of M. bovis; Enhanced Transmission via dense possum populations and shared feeding sites; and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of M. bovis lineages across large areas of New Zealand’s pastoral landscape, although no single novel genotype has been implicated.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Added because the 1990s wildlife‑driven bovine TB epidemic in New Zealand (peaking at ~1,700 infected cattle and deer herds and TB wildlife over ~39–40% of the country) is clearly among the most impactful global M. bovis emergence episodes in the post‑1990 period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (resurgence driven mainly by external control and policy factors rather than a new strain) and the Oceania/Australia and New Zealand/New Zealand geographic coding are appropriate.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990s]; Ireland [1990s]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); European badger (Meles meles); other wildlife (e.g., deer)
Event summary: From the early 1990s onward, Great Britain and Ireland experienced a marked resurgence of bovine tuberculosis in cattle herds after earlier control successes, with rising herd incidence particularly in southwest England, Wales, and parts of Ireland.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) During 2003–2015, analyses documented substantial and sustained increases in breakdown rates in high‑risk and edge areas of England and localized hotspots in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, while Scotland remained largely free.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, enhanced testing, badger culling/trial interventions, and tightened cattle movement controls had slowed but not eradicated the epidemic, leaving bovine TB as a major economic and policy challenge.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changing cattle demographics (larger herds, increased movements), historical gaps in testing during the 2001 foot‑and‑mouth disease outbreak, and the presence of a dense badger wildlife reservoir in many high‑incidence areas all contributed to re‑occurrence; social and political constraints on wildlife control also limited rapid intervention.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2018.00109/full?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No clear novel strain appears to have driven this resurgence; instead, the key internal factor is Enhanced Transmission via long‑standing badger reservoirs and complex cattle–badger–cattle transmission cycles, allowing sustained high incidence despite control measures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3377356/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Major long‑running re-occurrence episode with large economic impact: marked post‑1990 resurgence of bTB in cattle associated with badger reservoirs in Great Britain and Ireland is thoroughly documented and clearly among the highest‑impact events for M. bovis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-occurrence (external drivers dominating, no clear novel strain) and the Europe/Northern Europe/UK and Ireland geographic assignment are appropriate; no changes made.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); wild boar (Sus scrofa); red deer (Cervus elaphus); other wild ungulates
Event summary: From the 1990s onward, Spain reported increasing Mycobacterium bovis infection in wild boar and red deer, with some hunting estates reaching extremely high prevalences and frequent spillover to cattle, marking a shift to a multi‑host wildlife–livestock maintenance system in parts of the Iberian Peninsula.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3377356/?utm_source=openai)) In the 2000s, similar patterns were documented in Portugal, where wild boar and red deer became recognized maintenance hosts and new M. bovis clonal complexes (e.g., Eu2, Eu3) emerged and spread among wildlife and cattle across ecological corridors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10484045/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, high animal TB prevalence in these multi‑host communities persisted despite cattle control programs, forcing adoption of integrated wildlife and livestock surveillance and management strategies.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-77713-8?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and fencing of game estates, high densities of wild boar and red deer, artificial feeding and watering that concentrate animals, and overlapping ranges of wildlife and cattle at the interface increased contact rates and environmental contamination.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1755436522000731?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment of wild boar and red deer as true maintenance hosts; Enhanced Transmission via multi‑host transmission cycles; and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence plus Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of European clonal complexes (e.g., Eu2, Eu3) that adapted to circulate efficiently in wildlife and spill back to cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11218495/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Strongly supported large re-emergence event: the Iberian multi-host wildlife–livestock system (wild boar and red deer as maintenance hosts plus new Eu2/Eu3 clonal complexes) has major, long‑term impacts on cattle TB control and is widely cited as a key global M. bovis hotspot.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3377356/?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-emergence and the Europe/Southern Europe/Spain and Portugal geographic coding are appropriate; no changes made.

Countries: Canada [1992] (Manitoba – Riding Mountain National Park ecosystem)
Host: Elk (Cervus elaphus manitobensis); cattle (Bos taurus); white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus)
Event summary: In 1992, the first case of bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis was confirmed in a free-ranging bull elk shot near Rossburn, Manitoba, representing the first reported infection in wild elk in North America and linking wildlife to a nearby infected cattle herd.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, additional infected elk and at least 11 infected cattle herds were detected around Riding Mountain National Park, leading authorities to designate a Riding Mountain TB Eradication Area and implement intensive surveillance and control measures for both wildlife and livestock.([digitalcommons.unl.edu](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/michbovinetb/49/?utm_source=openai)) By about 2010, prevalence in elk and deer had declined and no new cattle outbreaks were detected for several years, but the area continued to be managed as one of Canada’s last wildlife-associated M. bovis foci because of persistent low‑level infection in elk.([gov.mb.ca](https://gov.mb.ca/agriculture/animal-health-and-welfare/animal-health/bovine-tuberculosis.fr.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High local elk densities, supplemental winter feeding practices that concentrated elk and cattle on shared hay bales, and overlap between elk wintering grounds and cattle pastures facilitated indirect transmission at feeding sites, while initial lack of targeted wildlife surveillance delayed recognition of elk as a reservoir.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment of free-ranging Manitoban elk as a wildlife maintenance host for M. bovis, sustained elk‑to‑elk transmission in a relatively sedentary subpopulation, and spillback to cattle and occasionally to white‑tailed deer, consistent with a re-emergence event driven by a new multi‑host reservoir rather than by a novel bacterial lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Added as a major wildlife host-expansion event: the Riding Mountain National Park elk–cattle system is one of the few documented free-ranging M. bovis wildlife reservoirs in Canada, with repeated cattle outbreaks and a long-running eradication programme, and is widely recognized in the global wildlife TB literature.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new elk maintenance host within an already endemic region) and North America/Northern America/Canada geographic coding are appropriate.

Host: White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus); cattle (Bos taurus); humans (spillover)
Event summary: In 1994, Mycobacterium bovis was identified in a hunter-harvested free-ranging white-tailed deer in northeastern Michigan, marking the beginning of a recognized wildlife epidemic in cervids in North America.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Over the subsequent decade, bovine TB became endemic in the local deer population, with repeated spillback infections in nearby cattle herds and documented zoonotic cases in humans with exposure to deer or unpasteurized products.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570927/?utm_source=openai)) By around 2007, intensive management (deer population reduction, feeding restrictions, cattle surveillance) reduced but did not eliminate transmission, leaving a persistent deer reservoir that continues to threaten cattle herds.([michigan.gov](https://www.michigan.gov/en/emergingdiseases/home/bovine-tuberculosis?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High deer densities, supplemental feeding and baiting practices that aggregated deer, close proximity of cattle farms to deer habitat, and historical under-recognition of TB in wildlife allowed M. bovis to establish in free-ranging deer.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment of white-tailed deer as a new wildlife maintenance host; Enhanced Transmission via dense winter feeding aggregations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of deer-associated strains within northeastern Michigan; and intrinsic pyrazinamide resistance of M. bovis complicating treatment in spillover human cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570927/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This is the archetypal North American wildlife host-expansion event: Michigan’s endemic white‑tailed deer reservoir with recurrent cattle and human cases is clearly one of the highest‑impact M. bovis episodes globally since 1990.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new maintenance host), with North America/Northern America/USA (Michigan) geographic coding, is appropriate; no changes made.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002] (England, Wales, Northern Ireland)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); humans (zoonotic TB due to M. bovis)
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2014, surveillance in England, Wales and Northern Ireland recorded a small but statistically significant increase in human tuberculosis cases caused by Mycobacterium bovis amid a background of rising bovine TB in cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) During this period, most human M. bovis patients had exposures such as contact with TB‑affected cattle or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products, highlighting ongoing zoonotic risk despite historical declines after pasteurization and cattle control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) By 2014, overall human M. bovis incidence remained low but stable, with public health guidance emphasizing continued control of bovine TB in cattle and risk‑based messaging to farmers, veterinarians, and consumers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Re-occurrence of bovine TB in cattle herds in high‑incidence regions, occupational and food‑borne exposures (raw milk, contact with infected livestock or wildlife), and travel or migration leading to exposure in high‑incidence rural areas were key external drivers of zoonotic cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No major novel genotype or increased virulence was identified in human M. bovis isolates; the increase reflects spillover from expanding or persistent animal reservoirs that themselves were sustained by wildlife–livestock transmission cycles, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence linked to broader bovine TB dynamics.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Geographic coding has been corrected to remove the Republic of Ireland, because the underlying surveillance study and notification data cover only England, Wales and Northern Ireland.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (low but increasing zoonotic cases reflecting spillover from resurgent animal reservoirs) is appropriate, but the overall human case numbers are modest relative to the major animal and wildlife events; recommend retaining the row to document the zoonotic dimension while flagging it for expert review of whether it should rank among the top 10 emergence events for this host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Free-ranging sika deer (Cervus nippon); cattle (Bos taurus); European badger (Meles meles)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, surveillance in Ireland increasingly detected Mycobacterium bovis infection in free‑ranging sika deer populations co‑occurring with cattle and badgers in endemic bovine TB areas, particularly in County Wicklow.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Through the 2010s, detailed epidemiologic and genetic studies showed that in some foci sika deer had infection prevalences and transmission patterns consistent with an independent maintenance host, rather than acting solely as spillover from cattle or badgers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) By around 2020, evidence had accumulated to classify sika deer as a new wildlife maintenance host of bovine TB in Ireland, adding complexity to eradication efforts that had previously focused mainly on cattle and badgers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanding and increasingly dense free‑ranging sika deer populations in parts of Ireland, habitat overlap with cattle and badgers, and shared pasture and feeding areas created conditions for sustained deer–deer and cross‑species transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) transitioning to a true wildlife maintenance reservoir role for sika deer; Enhanced Transmission via multi‑host networks; and possible Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of local M. bovis strains into new deer habitats, though without clear evidence of a fundamentally novel genotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This free‑ranging sika deer event documents the emergence of a new wildlife maintenance host within a high‑incidence area (County Wicklow) and has clear implications for Ireland’s eradication strategy, making it a plausible member of the top‑10 set despite its geographically localized nature.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-emergence (new maintenance host in a long‑infected region) and Europe/Northern Europe/Ireland geographic coding are appropriate; no field-level corrections needed.

Countries: Greece – national small-ruminant sector (acute contagious agalactia outbreaks 1994–1997)
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (dairy small ruminants)
Event summary: Between 1994 and 1997, Greece experienced a wave of acute contagious agalactia outbreaks in dairy sheep and goat flocks nationwide, caused predominantly by Mycoplasma agalactiae in a long‑endemic Mediterranean small‑ruminant system. Official analyses estimated annual financial losses of around €24.5 million from reduced milk production, abortions, neonatal deaths and culling, indicating widespread clinical disease in many flocks despite acknowledged under‑reporting. After this period, strengthened control measures, movement restrictions and vaccination reduced, but did not eliminate, CA incidence, and the disease has since persisted as an endemic and periodically resurging problem in Greek small‑ruminant production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense small‑ruminant dairy populations, transhumant grazing and communal pastures, frequent movement and trading of replacement stock, and incomplete or inconsistently applied vaccination programmes, together with farmer reluctance to notify because of strict regulatory consequences, all favoured rapid amplification and under‑reporting of outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: available data point to classical M. agalactiae strains rather than a single novel variant; this episode is best interpreted as a large‑scale re‑occurrence of an established pathogen driven primarily by husbandry, movement and surveillance constraints rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – new event added to capture the 1994–1997 epidemic wave of contagious agalactia in Greece, which incurred estimated losses of ~€24.5 million per year; classified as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic Southern European country rather than first detection or inter‑/intra‑continental emergence, based on OIE-linked economic analyses.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: North Macedonia – Debar and Gostivar regions
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (small ruminants)
Event summary: From 1997 to 1999, severe outbreaks of contagious agalactia occurred first in the Debar region and later in the adjoining Gostivar prefecture of what is now North Macedonia, affecting almost 80% of local small‑ruminant flocks. Laboratory investigation of the 1999 incidents, including bacterial isolation and serology, confirmed Mycoplasma agalactiae as the causative agent, documenting the pathogen’s presence in this Balkan country within a broader Southern European endemic zone. The episode prompted proposals for serological surveillance and control measures, and CA has since been recognised as present but not among the most commonly reported small‑ruminant diseases nationally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cross‑border animal movements and trade within the western Balkans, traditional transhumant grazing systems and limited prior diagnostic capacity likely allowed unnoticed introduction and amplification of CA in local flocks before confirmation. Internal mechanisms: the available data do not indicate novel strain characteristics; this episode is best interpreted as a marked regional re‑occurrence of classical M. agalactiae‑associated CA within an already affected Southern European subregion rather than a first detection or intra‑continental emergence under the UN sub‑region definitions.
Review: review – corrected the event years to 1997–1999 (matching the reported Debar and Gostivar outbreaks) instead of 2001, clarified that the affected areas were Debar and Gostivar within North Macedonia, and reclassified the episode as a re‑occurrence in the Southern Europe sub‑region rather than as a 'first detection' or 'intra‑continental emergence', which would conflict with the instruction not to treat spread to a new country within the same sub‑region as intra‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Spain – Andalusia (Sierra Nevada and other Andalusian ranges; free‑ranging Spanish/Iberian ibex populations)
Host: Wild Iberian (Spanish) ibex (Capra pyrenaica)
Event summary: In 1998, an outbreak of contagious agalactia due to Mycoplasma agalactiae was recognised for the first time in free‑ranging Spanish ibex in the Sierra Nevada, Andalusia, causing keratoconjunctivitis, mastitis, arthritis and high mortality, with 17 of 40 infected ibex dying during the episode. Subsequent surveillance and epidemiologic studies up to 2003 showed continued M. agalactiae infection across several Andalusian ibex metapopulations, with age, sex and location influencing infection risk and indicating sustained circulation rather than isolated spillover from domestic flocks. Although structured research campaigns ended, the work demonstrated that M. agalactiae had become established in Iberian ibex populations in southern Spain, raising concern about a two‑way reservoir at the wildlife–livestock interface.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of wild ibex in some Andalusian mountain ranges, spatial overlap and potential contacts with domestic sheep and goat flocks (shared pastures, salt licks and water sources), and long‑term endemicity of CA in regional small ruminants created conditions for cross‑species transmission and maintenance. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover and apparent establishment of M. agalactiae in a wild caprid species), and geographic range expansion at the wildlife–livestock interface as infected ibex move among metapopulations; strains in ibex were closely related, suggesting spread from a parental clone. This constellation fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and strain adaptation rather than primary emergence.
Review: review – retained this wildlife host‑expansion episode as a major re‑emergence event but adjusted the years to 1998–2003 (to cover the initial 1998 Sierra Nevada outbreak and subsequent Andalusian surveillance), clarified that it is confined to Andalusia, and added the primary epidemiological studies in free‑ranging Spanish ibex; classification as re‑emergence driven by host expansion is consistent with the evidence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Brazil – Paraíba state (two dairy goat and mixed small-ruminant herds, August 2001–January 2002)
Host: Domestic goats (predominantly) and sheep (does, bucks, kids and lambs)
Event summary: Between August 2001 and January 2002, two major outbreaks of contagious agalactia occurred in dairy goat and mixed goat–sheep herds in Paraíba state, north‑eastern Brazil, with mastitis, agalactia, polyarthritis, keratoconjunctivitis, fever and high morbidity affecting adults, kids and lambs and causing notable mortality and culling. Mycoplasma agalactiae was isolated from milk, joint fluid, nasal swabs and external ear‑canal washings, and its identity confirmed by immunoperoxidase and PCR, establishing it as the causative agent in both outbreaks. This study documented the first confirmed occurrence of M. agalactiae‑associated contagious agalactia in Brazil, signalling inter‑continental spread of the pathogen into South America’s small‑ruminant dairy sector and raising concern about its potential endemic establishment there.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of infected animals from commercial dairy goat herds in other Brazilian states into previously unaffected flocks in Paraíba, together with intensive dairy management, close confinement and shared milking equipment, favoured within‑herd transmission once the agent was introduced. Internal mechanisms: the outbreaks were caused by classical M. agalactiae strains without evidence of novel virulence factors; their significance lies in geographic range expansion and inter‑continental emergence into South America (first detection in this continental small‑ruminant host system) rather than in documented strain evolution.
Review: review – added as a missing high-impact event: the first confirmed M. agalactiae‑associated contagious agalactia outbreaks in Brazil (2001–2002), which also represent inter‑continental emergence into South America; classified as 'first detection' and 'inter‑continental emergence' rather than as a generic re‑occurrence, based on explicit wording in the Brazilian report that these were the first such cases detected in the country.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe (France – Savoy region, French Alps)
Countries: France – Savoy region (Vanoise National Park and surrounding Alpine massifs)
Host: Wild Alpine ibex (Capra ibex), with some involvement of sympatric chamois
Event summary: From 2003 onwards, an abnormal mortality episode associated with pneumonia was detected in Alpine ibex in the Savoy region of the French Alps, where necropsies of carcasses repeatedly yielded Mycoplasma agalactiae from lung lesions alongside other bacteria. Between 2003 and 2010, around 60 ibex carcasses and additional live‑captured animals were sampled, and genomic analyses showed that the ibex‑associated M. agalactiae strains formed a highly related, atypical lineage carrying a new prophage and displaying unusual tissue tropism and virulence compared with classical small‑ruminant strains. Although the exact contribution of M. agalactiae to individual deaths cannot be fully disentangled, demographic studies indicate that this epizootic had long‑lasting effects on ibex survival and population structure in the affected massifs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: relatively high ibex density in certain Alpine massifs, limited possibilities for intensive interventions in protected wildlife populations, and historical co‑occurrence of mycoplasmal infections in nearby domestic sheep and goats all created ecological conditions favouring emergence and maintenance of infection. Internal mechanisms: emergence of an atypical M. agalactiae strain lineage harbouring a novel prophage, with altered tissue tropism (frequent lung involvement) and apparent increased virulence in ibex and associated infection of sympatric chamois; combined with host expansion from domestic small ruminants to a protected wild mountain ungulate, this fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by strain evolution and host adaptation.
Review: review – narrowed the geography from a broad 'Alpine region in several countries' to the well-documented Savoy region of the French Alps, extended the years to 2003–2010 to match the sampling period, and retained classification as re‑emergence driven by atypical strains and host expansion into Alpine ibex; this episode is an important wildlife-focused emergence event and should be kept.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic dairy sheep (small ruminants)
Event summary: In 2008, Mycoplasma agalactiae re‑emerged as a major cause of contagious agalactia in dairy sheep flocks in the Western Pyrenees basin of France, particularly in the Pyrénées‑Atlantiques department, where official data recorded 98 new CA outbreaks in that year. Affected flocks experienced sharp drops in milk yield, mastitis, arthritis and keratoconjunctivitis consistent with classical CA in an area where the disease had long been present but had previously been better controlled. Subsequent implementation of vaccination and movement‑control programmes reduced the prevalence of M. agalactiae infection in sheep flocks in the region to below 5%, although the basin has remained a recognised focus of CA activity in France.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of dairy sheep, seasonal transhumance between valley farms and mountain pastures, intensive trading of replacement animals and incomplete adoption of preventive measures contributed to resurgence of CA in this endemic basin. Internal mechanisms: there is no clear evidence that a novel strain drove this wave; available information indicates a strong regional re‑occurrence of established M. agalactiae lineages in response to management and movement factors rather than strain evolution.
Review: review – redefined this event as the well-documented 2008 re‑emergence of M. agalactiae in the French Western Pyrenees with 98 new outbreaks, rather than an imprecise 'late 1990s–early 2000s' France–Spain episode; restricted the geography to France where data are available and kept the classification as a major re‑occurrence in an endemic basin.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) – national small-ruminant sector (cumulative 968 outbreaks reported to OIE over 2014–2018)
Host: Domestic dairy sheep and goats (small ruminants)
Event summary: Over the four-year period ending in 2018, Iran reported a cumulative 968 outbreaks of contagious agalactia to the OIE, the highest officially notified CA burden worldwide in that interval. These outbreaks, affecting dairy sheep and goat flocks across multiple provinces, reflected intense circulation of Mycoplasma agalactiae and related mycoplasmas in a major small‑ruminant‑producing country, with substantial but incompletely quantified losses from milk reduction, animal deaths and disease control expenditures. Despite ongoing vaccination and treatment, CA remained entrenched in Iranian small‑ruminant systems during this period, highlighting gaps in surveillance, vaccine performance and farm‑level biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very large national populations of sheep and goats managed in extensive and semi‑intensive systems, seasonal movements of flocks, frequent trading of animals, and variable access to high‑quality vaccines and diagnostics favoured persistent transmission and repeated outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: the epidemic wave is best interpreted as a high‑intensity re‑occurrence of established CA in Iran; there is no indication from available summaries that a single new strain with markedly altered virulence or host range dominated the 2014–2018 outbreaks.
Review: review – new aggregated national event added to represent the exceptionally high burden of CA in Iran (968 outbreaks reported over 2014–2018), which is clearly among the most impactful recent emergence waves; classified as a large-scale re‑occurrence in an already affected Southern Asia country rather than as first detection or inter‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Mongolia – national small-ruminant sector (cumulative 380 outbreaks reported to OIE over 2014–2018)
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (pastoral small ruminants)
Event summary: During the same four-year period to 2018, Mongolia officially reported 380 outbreaks of contagious agalactia in small ruminants, indicating substantial Mycoplasma agalactiae activity in pastoral sheep and goat systems of Eastern Asia. These outbreaks occurred in predominantly nomadic or transhumant livestock systems and added to the burden of other endemic diseases, contributing to milk losses, morbidity and the need for culling in affected flocks. Control remained challenging because of the vast grazing areas, flock mobility, limited laboratory infrastructure and economic constraints on sustained vaccination, allowing CA to persist as a recurrent problem.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive nomadic and semi‑nomadic management of sheep and goats, large flock movements over long distances, harsh climatic conditions and constrained veterinary resources impeded early detection and systematic control of CA outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: as in Iran, the wave is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of known M. agalactiae infection; existing evidence does not single out a novel genotype as the main driver, but aggregated OIE data indicate that CA reached a nationally significant level of impact during 2014–2018.
Review: review – new national-level event added for Mongolia, which reported 380 CA outbreaks over 2014–2018; this represents one of the largest recent epidemic waves outside the Mediterranean basin and merits inclusion as a major re‑occurrence episode in an Eastern Asian pastoral system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Italy – Sicily (Enna district; large mixed sheep–goat dairy farm)
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (large mixed dairy flock of >1,000 animals)
Event summary: In 2015–2016, a large mixed sheep–goat dairy farm of over 1,000 animals in the Enna district of Sicily experienced a severe contagious agalactia outbreak in which daily milk production dropped from about 650 litres to roughly 100 litres, and clinical CA spread to around 30% of susceptible ewes and many goats. The infection, introduced with a group of apparently healthy Etna goats purchased in March 2015, led to weak kids, unexpected milk drop and progressive spread through the flock, ultimately necessitating the slaughter of 200 sheep and 240 goats, culling of lambs and kids, and extensive vaccination and restocking. Total direct costs to the farmer were estimated at over €100,000, illustrating the high economic impact a single CA incursion can have in an intensively managed Mediterranean dairy small‑ruminant system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of unscreened replacement goats from a CA‑infected area, high animal density on the farm, close contact during milking and housing, and delayed recognition of disease signs allowed rapid amplification of infection once M. agalactiae was introduced. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by classical M. agalactiae strains; its importance lies in the magnitude of economic losses and the illustration of how breakdowns in biosecurity can trigger high‑impact re‑occurrence at farm level in an endemic region rather than in the emergence of a novel strain.
Review: review – new high-impact farm-level event added to reflect the well-documented 2015–2016 CA incursion on a large Sicilian mixed sheep–goat dairy farm, with direct losses exceeding €100,000; retained as a major re‑occurrence episode in Southern Europe driven by animal movements and on‑farm biosecurity failures.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Countries: Türkiye (Thrace region – European part of the country) [2002]
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event summary: From 2002, unusually severe respiratory disease with high morbidity and mortality was observed in goat herds in the Thrace region of Turkey, and laboratory investigations confirmed contagious caprine pleuropneumonia caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae, representing the first recognized CCPP outbreak in Turkish Thrace and the first confirmed occurrence on the European landmass since outbreaks reported in Greece in the 1920s–1930s. Over the following decade the disease spread within Thrace and became established, with serological surveys in 2014 showing an overall CCPP seroprevalence of just over 8% in goats and repeated PCR or culture detections from lung samples up to 2015. After intensified surveillance and control, Mccp was no longer detected from clinical lung samples after about 2015, suggesting local extinction or a marked reduction of clinical circulation in the region. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30964465/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of infected carrier goats through regional trade or informal transboundary movements from endemic areas in Anatolia or the broader Middle East into the relatively naïve goat population of Thrace, followed by local spread facilitated by flock mixing, animal markets and delayed recognition of CCPP. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing indicates close relatedness of Thrace strains to those circulating elsewhere in Turkey and the Middle East, with no evidence of a novel highly divergent lineage, supporting interpretation of this event as geographic re‑occurrence and establishment in a previously free area within an already affected sub‑region rather than de novo evolution of a new strain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8787594/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is genuine and important: it captures the first documented CCPP outbreak in Turkish Thrace with subsequent endemic circulation until 2015, consistent with Özdemir et al. 2018 and EFSA assessments. The emergence-type coding has been corrected from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence, because CCPP was already known from Europe (Greece in the 1920s–1930s) and, under the UNSD scheme used in this project, Türkiye is classified in Asia–Western Asia rather than in the Europe continent. Geography (Asia; Western Asia; Türkiye) and the temporal span 2002–2015 are retained but should be checked against the primary papers for exact start/stop years and prevalence figures.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2007, Iran officially reported to the OIE a large epizootic of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with about 478 outbreaks and approximately 16,000 goats affected nationwide, indicating that Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae had become widely established in domestic goat populations of the country. These outbreaks occurred across multiple provinces and reflected rapid spread in naïve or insufficiently immunized herds within a region where CCPP has historically been present in neighbouring Southern Asian countries such as India, leading to substantial production losses before systematic diagnosis and reporting were in place. After this two‑year wave, CCPP has continued to be recognised in Iran, with sporadic or localized outbreaks reported and later laboratory confirmation in several provinces, while national control policies and vaccination strategies have gradually been developed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of goats within and into Iran from enzootic neighbouring regions of Western and Southern Asia, combined with extensive pastoral and transhumant systems, limited early diagnostic capacity, and gaps in targeted vaccination against CCPP, favoured rapid establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: Available accounts emphasise typical virulent Mccp strains without evidence for a distinct new lineage; this episode is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence and geographic expansion of existing strain complexes into Iran within an already affected Southern Asia sub-region, rather than as emergence into a previously naïve sub-region or as re-emergence driven by marked genetic change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This row correctly captures a nationally important CCPP wave in Iran in 2006–2007 (≈478 outbreaks, ≈16,000 goats), as summarised in Abdollahi et al. 2023 and in recent reviews. However, the original classification as intra-continental emergence was inappropriate because CCPP has been reported in the Southern Asia sub-region (e.g. India) since at least the early 20th century; the event reflects a large re-occurrence and spread within an already affected sub-region. Emergence-type coding has therefore been changed to re-occurrence (yes) with intra-/inter-continental emergence set to no; geography (Asia – Southern Asia – Iran) is consistent with the UNSD country list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Captive wild ungulates (Nubian ibex Capra ibex nubiana; wild goat Capra aegagrus; Laristan mouflon Ovis orientalis laristanica; gerenuk Litocranius walleri) and domestic goats in a mixed collection
Event summary: In 2007, an outbreak of severe respiratory disease compatible with CCPP occurred in a large mixed collection of captive wild ungulates and goats at Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation in Qatar, with high morbidity and mortality among wild goats, Nubian ibex, Laristan mouflon and gerenuk as well as domestic goats; Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae was isolated and confirmed as the causative agent. The disease spread rapidly through enclosures housing these conservation‑relevant species, demonstrating that multiple wild Caprinae and related antelopes are highly susceptible once exposed to infected goats and that wildlife collections can act as intense transmission foci. Intensive veterinary intervention, strict biosecurity measures, and separation of species, alongside treatment and culling of affected animals, eventually contained the outbreak, but only after substantial losses in the captive wild populations. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17469281/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density mixed‑species housing in a wildlife collection, close contact between domestic goats and exotic ungulates, and likely introduction of infected goats or subclinically infected wildlife facilitated cross‑species aerosol transmission of Mccp. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated ability of circulating Mccp strains to infect multiple wild Caprinae and antelope species indicates host expansion and enhanced transmission across species barriers; this episode fits a re-emergence pattern driven by host expansion into new wild hosts rather than by a clearly novel genotype. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17469281/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event accurately summarises the well-documented 2007 outbreak in captive wild ungulates and goats at Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation (Qatar), including affected species and confirmation of Mccp as the agent. I updated the source list to prioritise the primary case report (J Zoo Wildl Med 2007, cited via PubMed) plus a recent arid-lands mycoplasma review and the comprehensive CCPP review, and removed reliance on ResearchGate as the main primary-source link. Classification as re-emergence (host expansion into multiple wild species in a region where CCPP is already enzootic) with no intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event summary: Between 2008 and 2009, Oman experienced a major national epizootic of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with nearly 600 reported outbreaks affecting about 30,000 goats, making it one of the largest documented CCPP waves in recent decades. Outbreaks were recorded across multiple governorates, with morbidity in affected herds often very high and mortality reported at roughly 10% of clinically affected animals, leading to severe production and livelihood losses in a goat-dense livestock sector. Following recognition of the scale of the problem, Omani authorities strengthened surveillance, introduced or expanded vaccination and treatment campaigns, and began more systematic epidemiological and serological studies, but CCPP has remained an important threat to the country’s goat industry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High national goat densities, frequent internal animal movements, and climatic stressors (high temperatures and seasonal rainfall peaks) likely contributed to increased transmission and the synchronised appearance of many outbreaks, while limited prior vaccination coverage and incomplete diagnostic capacity delayed effective control. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not indicate emergence of a new lineage; instead, the episode reflects large-scale re-occurrence and amplification of endemic Mccp strains in a previously affected Western Asia country, underscoring how environmental stress and management factors can precipitate very large epizootics without major genetic change. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374586864_Contagious_caprine_pleuropneumonia_A_review_of_the_global_situation_with_a_special_reference_to_Oman))
Review: review – New event added because multiple authoritative sources (Yatoo et al. 2019; EFSA 2017; Ali et al. 2023) report nearly 600 CCPP outbreaks in Oman during 2008–2009, affecting about 30,000 goats, which clearly qualifies this as one of the largest CCPP epizootics since 1990. It is coded as a re-occurrence in Western Asia rather than as intra-continental emergence, because CCPP and Mccp had been present in Oman and the wider region for decades. Quantitative figures are taken from secondary syntheses of OIE data and should be verified against original national/OIE reports, but the overall scale and timing are well supported.

Internal mechanisms: There is no strong evidence that the 2013 wave was driven by a new strain; instead, it reflects re-occurrence of endemic Mccp lineages under favourable transmission conditions, illustrating how external drivers (animal movement, climate, gaps in control) can generate large multi-country flare-ups without major evolutionary change. EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Arabian oryx (Oryx leucoryx) and Arabian sand gazelle (Gazella marica) in captivity; proximal domestic goats likely source at regional scale
Event summary: In 2014, a severely emaciated captive Arabian oryx in the United Arab Emirates died with respiratory signs and pleuropneumonia, and pleural fluid culture followed by genotyping identified Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae, with the sequence type matching that of Mccp strains from an ongoing CCPP outbreak in adjacent sand gazelles housed in a neighbouring enclosure. This episode provided the first documented evidence that members of the Hippotraginae subfamily, specifically Arabian oryx, are susceptible to CCPP, expanding the known wild host range beyond Caprinae and gazelles. After recognition of the link, management measures including separation of susceptible species, improved biosecurity, and control of CCPP in nearby goats and gazelles were implemented to prevent further cross‑species transmission. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113514003265?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species captive management with close proximity between Arabian oryx, sand gazelles and potentially goats, combined with movement of infected animals into the collection, created conditions for aerosol or close‑contact transmission of Mccp across species barriers. Internal mechanisms: Molecular genotyping confirmed that the oryx infection was caused by the same Mccp strain as in nearby sand gazelles, indicating host expansion of an existing lineage to a new wild host (Arabian oryx) without major genetic divergence; this represents re-emergence driven by host expansion and high virulence in a naïve Hippotraginae species. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113514003265?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly reflects the first reported fatal CCPP case in an Arabian oryx in the UAE with concurrent infection in sand gazelles, as described by Chaber et al. 2014 and cited in EFSA and WOAH documents. Geography (Asia; Western Asia; United Arab Emirates), host description and classification as re-emergence via host expansion are appropriate, and no structural corrections are required.

EPP common name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus) in a large commercial herd (~2,000 head)
Event summary: In August 2021, a large herd of approximately 2,000 goats near Tehran, Iran, experienced a severe outbreak of respiratory disease with pleuropneumonia; clinical investigation recorded substantial morbidity and a high case fatality rate among affected goats, and PCR on lung samples confirmed Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae as the cause. This outbreak provided the first detailed, peer‑reviewed description of a CCPP outbreak in Iran with laboratory confirmation of Mccp, complementing earlier OIE reports of CCPP without etiologic confirmation in 2006–2007. The disease spread rapidly through the herd before diagnosis, causing major losses, but was brought under control through whole‑herd antibiotic treatment followed by vaccination with an inactivated Pulmovac‑In Mccp vaccine, after which no further severe CCPP episodes were reported in this herd in the short term. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A history of malnutrition and heat stress in the preceding two months likely reduced herd immunity, while dense stocking and internal movement of animals facilitated rapid aerosol spread once CCPP was introduced; initial lack of specific vaccination against CCPP and delayed laboratory confirmation also contributed to the severity. Internal mechanisms: Pathology and clinical course were typical of virulent Mccp infection, with no evidence of a novel genotype; this represents re-occurrence of endemic disease in a susceptible large herd, with severity shaped largely by management and environmental stressors rather than by new pathogen traits. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event summarises the 2021 Tehran-region herd outbreak described by Abdollahi et al. 2023, correctly highlighting it as the first peer-reviewed, Mccp-confirmed CCPP outbreak report from Iran while acknowledging earlier OIE-notified epizootics. Classification as re-occurrence (in a country and sub-region known to be affected) without intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate; detailed morbidity and case-fatality figures should still be checked directly against the article before final publication.

Host: House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus), American goldfinch (Spinus tristis) and other wild passerine species
Event summary: In the winter of 1993–1994, house finches with severe conjunctivitis were first observed at bird feeders in the Washington, D.C.–mid‑Atlantic region of the eastern United States, and a novel strain of Mycoplasma gallisepticum was isolated from affected birds, representing the first recognized involvement of this poultry pathogen in wild songbirds. Over the next three years, mycoplasmal conjunctivitis spread rapidly through the introduced eastern range of house finches, with citizen‑science surveillance documenting a sharp rise in disease reports and high prevalences across much of the eastern United States and into eastern Canada by the mid‑ to late‑1990s, and by late 1995 the outbreak also involved American goldfinches and other passerines, accompanied by marked declines in local house finch abundance. The initial epidemic wave peaked within a few years, after which disease incidence declined from early epidemic highs as some host populations crashed and infection transitioned toward an endemic pattern with ongoing but fluctuating transmission in eastern North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities and frequent aggregation of house finches and other passerines at backyard bird feeders in suburban and urban landscapes facilitated efficient transmission and allowed continent‑scale surveillance of spread; the house finch is an introduced species in eastern North America with relatively low genetic diversity and no prior exposure to MG, likely increasing susceptibility; long‑distance movements and dispersal of finches helped propagate the epidemic front across the eastern range. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover of a poultry‑adapted pathogen into a novel wild passerine host community), emergence of a genetically distinct house‑finch‑associated MG clade (novel strain/genotype emergence) that produced severe conjunctivitis and high early mortality, and traits favoring efficient conjunctival and respiratory transmission that allowed rapid establishment and spread in dense feeder‑aggregated populations.
Review: review — MG was already a well‑known poultry pathogen in this host system long before 1990, so this event is not a first detection at the host‑system level. Reclassified the event type from first_detection=true to first_detection=false and re_emergence=true to reflect a major host shift and emergence of a novel finch‑adapted MG lineage within a subregion where MG was previously present in domestic poultry. Corrected the Canadian introduction year from 1996 to 1995 based on early outbreak reports indicating that mycoplasmal conjunctivitis was widespread in the eastern United States and Canada and had spread to American goldfinches by late 1995.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/3/1/97-0110_article?utm_source=openai)) This event clearly ranks among the most impactful MG emergence episodes (large geographic extent, severe population declines in house finches) and should be retained after quality control.

Host: House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus), American goldfinch (Spinus tristis) and multiple other wild passerine species
Event summary: Following the initial mid‑1990s epidemic in eastern house finches, Mycoplasma gallisepticum infection persisted in wild passerine populations in the eastern United States and Canada, with recurrent seasonal peaks of mycoplasmal conjunctivitis and evidence of ongoing transmission. During this period, the house‑finch‑associated MG strain expanded its host range to additional songbirds such as American goldfinches, purple finches, evening grosbeaks, chickadees and other passerines, and longitudinal studies documented changing patterns of virulence, prevalence and disease severity as both pathogen and host populations evolved. By the late 2000s, MG‑associated conjunctivitis had become an established endemic wildlife disease across much of eastern North America, with episodic outbreaks continuing in finches and other susceptible species but at generally lower overall population‑level impact than the initial crash in the 1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued widespread feeding of wild birds at backyard feeders maintained high contact rates among finches and other passerines; seasonal breeding pulses and winter aggregations created strong temporal variation in host density that supported recurrent epidemic waves; absence of targeted control in wild birds allowed long‑term circulation. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence was driven by adaptation of the MG strain to its new passerine hosts, including documented evolution in virulence and transmissibility over time; expansion of host range from house finches to multiple other wild songbird species (host expansion) increased the ecological niche and maintenance opportunities for the pathogen; genetic diversification within the house‑finch MG clade (novel strain/genotype emergence) likely contributed to variable clinical outcomes and persistence of infection in different host species.
Review: retain — This row captures the transition from an explosive epidemic to long‑term endemic circulation of the house‑finch‑associated MG lineage in eastern North America, including expansion to additional passerine hosts and documented evolutionary changes in virulence and transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4111589/?utm_source=openai)) The geographic scope (United States and Canada within the same UN subregion) and lack of a discrete new subregion mean it is best classified as re_emergence (driven by host expansion and pathogen evolution) rather than intra‑continental emergence; existing type coding (re_emergence=true) is therefore appropriate. No corrections to geography or dates are clearly warranted, but event boundaries (1998–2008) are approximate and could be refined with more detailed incidence data; recommend retaining the event but treating the time window as approximate in downstream analyses.

Host: House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus) and other wild passerines
Event summary: In the early 2000s, surveillance data and field observations indicated that the house‑finch‑associated Mycoplasma gallisepticum strain, initially confined to the introduced eastern range of the species, had crossed the central North American barrier posed by the Rocky Mountains and begun infecting house finches in the native western range, with first detections in the Rocky Mountain region (e.g. Montana) in 2002. Over the subsequent several years, mycoplasmal conjunctivitis became established in western house finch populations and was documented in multiple western U.S. states and western Canadian provinces, including British Columbia by the mid‑2000s, marking a major geographic extension of the wildlife reservoir within the same UN subregion. By around 2010, MG‑associated conjunctivitis was recognized as occurring annually in house finches across most of the continental United States and parts of southern Canada, with disease dynamics shifting toward a background endemic presence punctuated by local flare‑ups rather than a single synchronized epidemic front.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural dispersal and migration of house finches, including movements across and along the Rocky Mountains and across the northern Great Plains, facilitated westward spread; backyard feeding and urban/suburban aggregation in western North America created similar high‑contact environments that had supported epidemics in the east; lack of MG‑specific management in wild bird populations allowed unimpeded geographical expansion and establishment in new western populations. Internal mechanisms: The same poultry‑derived MG lineage that had adapted to house finches in the east retained sufficient fitness to survive in new climatic and ecological conditions in western North America (geographic range expansion) and showed evidence of evolutionary change in virulence during spread, with some western isolates exhibiting altered pathogenicity; its efficient conjunctival and respiratory transmission supported establishment in naïve western finch populations and occasional spillover to other passerines, representing a spatial re‑emergence and further geographic range expansion of an already emergent wildlife pathogen rather than appearance of a completely novel strain.
Review: review — The original row correctly identified the westward spread of house‑finch‑associated MG across North America as a major emergence episode but misclassified the event type and under‑reported Canadian involvement. Reclassified the event as re_emergence (re_occurrence=false, re_emergence=true), because MG had not disappeared from the Northern America subregion between 1994 and 2002; this episode reflects spatial expansion of the same emergent lineage rather than a simple resurgence after control. Updated the countries field to "United States of America [2002]; Canada [2004]" to reflect first detections in the Rocky Mountain region in 2002 and documentation of MG conjunctivitis in western Canadian house finches (e.g. British Columbia) by the mid‑2000s.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225627780_Dynamics_of_Mycoplasmal_Conjunctivitis_in_the_Native_and_Introduced_Range_of_the_Host?utm_source=openai)) Source list was adjusted to emphasize studies and summaries that explicitly describe continent‑scale spread and occurrences in Canada and the western United States; this event should be retained but flagged for expert review of the exact start/end years and provincial timing.

Host: Commercial broiler breeder chickens, turkey breeders, broiler chickens, growing turkeys and a large commercial egg-layer complex (Gallus gallus domesticus, Meleagris gallopavo)
Event summary: After Mycoplasma gallisepticum had been largely eradicated from U.S. commercial broiler chicken and turkey breeder flocks, extensive MG outbreaks were detected in the fall of 1999 in North Carolina, involving numerous broiler and turkey breeder flocks as well as associated broiler chicken and growing turkey operations. Over the following 1–2 years, MG infection affected at least 54 breeder and grow‑out flocks in North Carolina and contributed to the first MG outbreaks in over two decades in the Delmarva broiler production region, including infection of a one‑million‑bird commercial egg‑layer complex, prompting large‑scale depopulation, movement controls and intensive regional surveillance. Through aggressive biosecurity measures, culling of infected breeder and layer flocks, and tighter controls on movement and sourcing of MG‑free breeder stock and hatching eggs, these outbreaks were gradually contained by the early 2000s, although MG has continued to cause occasional outbreaks in U.S. commercial poultry thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Re‑introduction of MG into commercial systems via movement of infected broiler breeder stock and hatching eggs, breakdowns in biosecurity and multi‑age production systems allowed rapid farm‑to‑farm spread in a region that had been largely MG‑free for years; dense poultry production in North Carolina and the Delmarva region amplified transmission and economic impact. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak appears to have involved re‑introduction and dissemination of virulent field strains rather than a fundamentally new genotype; MG’s inherent ability for vertical (transovarian) and horizontal transmission in poultry flocks, combined with stressors and co‑infections, contributed to severe respiratory disease and production losses but there is no clear evidence that this episode was driven primarily by novel strain evolution rather than external drivers.
Review: review — The initial LLM output omitted a major late‑1990s re‑occurrence of MG in U.S. commercial poultry, despite its clear impact on flock numbers and industry concern. A new event row has been added to capture the 1999–2001 North Carolina and Delmarva outbreaks, during which MG reappeared in at least 54 broiler and turkey breeder, broiler chicken and growing turkey flocks in North Carolina and caused the first MG outbreak in over 22 years in the Delmarva broiler region, including a one‑million‑bird egg‑layer complex.([nimss.org](https://nimss.org/projects/view/mrp/outline/3840)) This episode fits the definition of re_occurrence (re‑appearance and expansion in a previously controlled subregion driven mainly by external factors such as movement of infected stock and lapses in biosecurity) rather than re_emergence driven by new strain properties; it is therefore coded as re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false. Because this event is geographically limited to the United States but involves very large numbers of commercial birds and substantial economic impact, it likely ranks among the top MG emergence events since 1990 and should be retained after expert review of flock counts and precise temporal bounds.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Kenya [early 1990s]; Uganda [early 1990s]; Rwanda [1994]; Burundi [1997]; Democratic Republic of the Congo – Ituri region [1990s]; Ethiopia [1990s]; Namibia [1990s]; Zambia [1997]; Botswana [1995]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbred beef and dairy cattle in pastoral and agropastoral systems)
Event summary: From about 1990, CBPP re‑emerged explosively in East and parts of Southern Africa, with infection moving from long‑standing foci in Angola, Sudan and the Horn via Uganda and Kenya into northern Tanzania (Ngorongoro, Arusha Region) and then into Kagera on the Uganda border. Over roughly 1990–2003, linked epidemics spread through much of Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, the Ituri region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Namibia, Zambia and Botswana, reinvading countries that had been free for decades and greatly expanding the geographic range of a largely homogeneous African epidemic lineage. By the early 2000s, coordinated regional vaccination, movement control and stamping‑out campaigns had reduced outbreak numbers, but CBPP remained entrenched and endemic in many of these subregions and continued to threaten neighboring free areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: FAO and WOAH analyses attribute the 1990s–early 2000s CBPP resurgence in Africa to weakened veterinary services and vaccination programs during economic crises and conflict, coupled with extensive formal and informal cattle movements along trade and transhumance routes that carried infection from long‑standing endemic foci in Angola and the Horn into previously free countries such as Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Zambia and Botswana. Dense pastoral networks, porous borders, and inadequate quarantine and surveillance allowed the disease to spread widely across Eastern, Middle and Southern Africa, with economic losses for Africa as a whole estimated in the billions of US dollars and hundreds of thousands of cattle deaths in Tanzania alone during 1990–2003. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing shows that most 1990s outbreaks in East and Southern Africa were caused by closely related MmmSC strains, including a distinct African/“southern African” lineage and, in Botswana, a novel biotype with phenotypic differences from classical strains, consistent with clonal expansion of established African lineages and, in some areas, emergence of new biotypes. This episode thus represents both intra‑continental emergence into new subregions and re‑emergence driven by pathogen lineage expansion and chronic carrier states rather than by a completely new species or host jump.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this row as the major 1990–2003 regional CBPP wave in East/Middle/Southern Africa, which is well documented as re‑invading many previously free countries and causing very large losses (e.g. Tanzanian losses alone estimated at ~350,000 cattle deaths and >US$40 million). Corrected the list of countries to remove Angola as a purely pre‑1990 endemic source and to add Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri) in line with FAO descriptions of newly infected/re‑invaded areas in the 1990s. Kept classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence, as the episode involved spread of established African lineages and at least one novel biotype into new subregions and countries, rather than a first detection on the continent.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Kenya [source region, late 1980s–early 1990s]; Uganda [source region, early 1990s]
Host: Cattle in pastoral and agropastoral systems in northern, western and central Tanzania
Event summary: After Tanzania had eradicated CBPP and been considered free since the 1960s, the disease was re‑introduced in June 1990 into Ngorongoro District (Arusha Region) via transboundary cattle movements from northern Kenya, followed by a separate outbreak in Kagera Region in 1991–1992 linked to southern Uganda. Through the 1990s CBPP spread widely within Tanzania, with official records indicating more than 160 outbreaks and several thousand cases and deaths by about 2001, heavily affecting pastoral and mixed crop–livestock communities. Intensive national control efforts combining vaccination, movement control and surveillance gradually reduced outbreak numbers in the early 2000s, although abattoir and serological surveys showed that CBPP remained widespread and endemic in many regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of infected and carrier cattle from endemic areas in Kenya and Uganda into northern Tanzania initiated the re‑introduction, and internal cattle trade and seasonal transhumance then disseminated infection into western and central regions. Structural adjustment and constrained veterinary budgets reduced surveillance, vaccination and movement‑control capacity just as CBPP was re‑introduced, while farmers’ need to move cattle for grazing and markets during droughts expanded contact networks. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular and field data indicate that Tanzanian outbreaks in the 1990s were caused by African MmmSC lineages closely related to those circulating in neighboring countries, without clear evidence of a fundamentally new strain in Tanzania itself; the episode is therefore best interpreted as re‑occurrence of CBPP in a previously free country driven primarily by re‑seeding and spread of existing lineages and the persistence of chronic carriers.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this event as a major national re‑occurrence in Tanzania, but correct several details: (i) extended the start year from 1992 to 1990 to include the first documented outbreak in Ngorongoro (Arusha Region) introduced from Kenya, in line with Tanzanian and FAO/OIE reports; (ii) clarified Kenya and Uganda as source regions rather than countries with in situ outbreaks in this specific event row; and (iii) changed the emergence‑type coding from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence, because the resurgence in Tanzania reflects re‑introduction and spread of existing African MmmSC lineages under weakened control systems rather than emergence of a clearly novel strain.

Host: Beef cattle in communal and commercial systems in Ngamiland and adjacent districts, Botswana
Event summary: In February 1995, after about 50–56 years of national freedom from CBPP, Botswana detected an outbreak in Ngamiland District, with infection traced to transboundary spread from long‑endemic foci in Angola and northern Namibia. The disease spread within northern Botswana during 1995, prompting declaration of an infected zone and the subsequent slaughter, under a stamping‑out campaign in 1996, of roughly 320,000 cattle in Ngamiland to regain international disease‑free status. By the end of 1997, after restocking and continued surveillance, Botswana again reported freedom from CBPP, with trade access progressively restored.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The key external driver was uncontrolled or poorly regulated movement of infected and carrier cattle across the borders from endemic areas in Angola and northern Namibia into Ngamiland, facilitated by porous borders, traditional transhumance routes and the high value of cross‑border livestock trade. Delays in recognizing CBPP, logistical challenges in enforcing movement controls and the need to protect export markets led policy‑makers to adopt an aggressive stamping‑out policy that magnified the economic impact through mass culling. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization of MmmSC isolates from the Botswana outbreak revealed that most strains were closely related to other African epidemic isolates, but at least one isolate showed phenotypic and genotypic properties consistent with a novel biotype distinct from classical strains, supporting classification of this event as re‑emergence driven in part by emergence of a new biotype within the existing species, in addition to re‑introduction from endemic reservoirs.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this event as one of the most impactful CBPP episodes globally because of the slaughter of ~320,000 cattle and severe trade disruption, but simplify the “countries” field to Botswana [1995] only; Angola and Namibia are better treated as endemic source areas described in the narrative rather than as participating outbreak countries in this row. Kept the emergence type as re‑emergence, as molecular work demonstrates a distinct Botswana biotype within MmmSC, consistent with pathogen change contributing to the episode.
