Host: Cattle in smallholder, pastoral and agropastoral systems in western and north‑western Zambia
Event summary: Zambia, which had previously controlled CBPP and reported freedom by the mid‑1990s, experienced re‑occurrence of the disease with new outbreaks detected from 1997 onwards in Sinjembela and other areas of Western Province bordering Angola and Namibia. During the late 1990s and early 2000s, serological surveillance and field investigations revealed that CBPP was more widespread than initially thought, with infection extending into North‑Western Province and prompting concern about onward spread into Namibia, Zimbabwe and Botswana. Control campaigns combining vaccination, quarantine, movement restrictions and targeted culling continued into the early 2000s, gradually reducing reported outbreak numbers but failing to completely eliminate CBPP foci within Zambia during this period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of cattle from endemic areas of Angola and, to a lesser extent, from neighboring infected zones in Namibia and Tanzania were the most likely sources of re‑introduction into Zambia’s Western Province, while internal cattle trade and seasonal movements along the Zambezi floodplain facilitated wider dissemination. Limited resources for sustained vaccination and surveillance, logistical difficulties in remote border areas, and broader regional relaxation of structured eradication campaigns in the 1990s contributed to delayed detection and incomplete containment. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not indicate emergence of a new MmmSC strain in Zambia; instead, the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of CBPP due to re‑seeding by existing African lineages and subsequent local spread, with chronic carrier animals and subclinical infections complicating eradication.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this national‑level event but extend the end year from 2000 to 2003 to align with FAO/OIE reports that CBPP spread beyond Western Province into North‑Western Province and was still being detected in 2002–2003. Kept the classification as re‑occurrence (rather than re‑emergence or intra‑continental emergence) because Zambia had a prior history of CBPP and the resurgence is attributed to re‑introduction from neighboring endemic areas and incomplete control, with no clear evidence of a novel strain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Ethiopia – western highlands (Boji district, West Wellega Zone) [2000-2002]; Ethiopia – north‑western region at periphery of proposed disease‑free zone [2003-2005]
Host: Cattle in mixed crop–livestock systems in the Ethiopian highlands and north‑western export‑oriented zones
Event summary: Around 2000, Ethiopian veterinary services reported a resurgence of CBPP in the western highlands (Boji district, West Wellega), where a 16‑month longitudinal study from June 2000 to January 2002 documented that about one‑third of cattle in monitored herds seroconverted and that clinical cases and mortality were substantial. In the early to mid‑2000s, additional outbreaks were documented on the southern edge of a planned north‑western disease‑free export zone, with official records noting one outbreak in 2003 and at least two more in 2004–2005 that threatened Ethiopia’s ambitions to establish a CBPP‑free export region. Strengthened surveillance, targeted vaccination along trekking routes from endemic pastoral areas, and movement management into the proposed free zone subsequently reduced reported outbreak numbers, although CBPP remained an important constraint on Ethiopia’s cattle sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of trekking routes and cattle trade from more heavily infected southern and western lowland areas into highland districts such as Boji and into the periphery of the north‑western export zone underpinned these resurgence events, with mixed crop–livestock systems and communal grazing favoring local spread. Farmer responses centered on informal antibiotic treatment and ad hoc isolation, which, combined with gaps in formal vaccination coverage and diagnostic capacity, were insufficient to interrupt transmission. Internal mechanisms: Epidemiological and modeling work from Boji shows typical CBPP dynamics dominated by chronic carriers and slow within‑herd spread, without evidence of a novel strain; the key internal factor is the ability of MmmSC to persist in chronically infected animals and to spread insidiously in smallholder herds, allowing geographic range expansion of existing African lineages within Ethiopia.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this as an important Ethiopian resurgence episode, but correct the timing and structure: (i) adjusted the start year to 2000 to match the Boji district longitudinal study (June 2000–January 2002) rather than 2003–2004; (ii) treated the Boji highlands (2000–2002) and the 2003–2005 outbreaks at the southern edge of the proposed north‑western disease‑free zone as a single linked national episode of re‑occurrence; and (iii) kept the classification as re‑occurrence, since the evidence indicates resurgence of existing African CBPP lineages driven by cattle movements and control gaps, not emergence of a new strain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ethiopia – Western Oromia (Bako Agricultural Research Center and surrounding districts) [2011]
Host: Research and nearby smallholder cattle herds in Western Oromia, Ethiopia
Event summary: In May 2011 a severe outbreak of respiratory disease consistent with CBPP occurred in the cattle herd of the Bako Agricultural Research Center in Western Oromia, Ethiopia, with many animals becoming sick and some dying before infection with MmmSC was confirmed. Subsequent serological surveys in surrounding districts showed appreciable CBPP seroprevalence, indicating that the research herd outbreak formed part of a wider local focus rather than an isolated incursion. Following this episode, control measures including vaccination, improved biosecurity and movement management were implemented at the research farm and in nearby communities, and later surveys reported lower but still notable CBPP seroprevalence, suggesting partial control but continued endemicity in the broader region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected or carrier cattle from surrounding endemic areas into the Bako research herd, likely through routine purchases or exchanges, combined with close confinement and high contact rates in the research setting, amplified transmission and triggered the severe farm‑level outbreak. Regional cattle movement patterns and trade from higher‑prevalence western zones into Western Oromia created ongoing risk, while delays in etiologic diagnosis slowed implementation of specific CBPP measures. Internal mechanisms: Serological and epidemiological data suggest involvement of endemic Ethiopian MmmSC lineages rather than a novel variant; the key internal feature was the capacity of chronic carrier animals to introduce infection silently into a largely naïve, high‑value herd and to sustain efficient within‑herd transmission under intensive management, making this a clear re‑occurrence rather than a novel emergence.
Review: RETAIN – This event is accurately described and supported by detailed local epidemiological studies documenting the 2011 Bako outbreak and surrounding seroprevalence. Although smaller in geographic scope than the major 1990s and early‑2000s epizootics, it represents one of the best‑characterized post‑2005 CBPP resurgence episodes and reasonably belongs among the top documented emergence/re‑occurrence events for this pathogen.

Host: Dairy and beef cattle herds in northern Italy (particularly Lombardy and neighboring regions)
Event summary: In October 1990, after roughly a century of national freedom from CBPP, Italy detected a new outbreak in cattle in northern regions, marking re‑introduction of the disease into Europe’s commercial cattle sector. Between 1990 and 1993 a total of 94 outbreaks were notified, mainly in northern Italy, leading to the slaughter of more than 17,000 cattle under a government‑funded stamping‑out program and strict movement controls. By late 1993 the last Italian outbreak had been eliminated, and following continued surveillance Italy regained official CBPP‑free status in the mid‑1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Italian epidemic is believed to have originated from importation of infected cattle from CBPP‑affected regions, followed by local spread facilitated by intensive cattle movements and farm‑to‑farm contacts in high‑density dairy and beef systems in northern Italy. Rapid implementation of active surveillance, movement restrictions and large‑scale culling was essential to eradicate the disease but also imposed substantial economic costs, including loss of animals and trade disruptions. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses have shown that European MmmSC strains isolated since 1990 form a distinct lineage characterized by an ~8.8‑kb chromosomal deletion affecting the glycerol transporter operon and a surface lipoprotein gene, representing a specific “European” biotype with somewhat different pathogenicity profiles compared with many African strains; thus this episode is best classified as re‑emergence involving a distinct biotype in a region with prior historical CBPP rather than simple re‑occurrence of unchanged strains.
Review: REVIEW – Added this new row because the 1990–1993 Italian CBPP epidemic, with 94 outbreaks and over 17,000 cattle slaughtered, is clearly one of the most impactful modern CBPP events outside Africa and had been omitted. Classified as re‑emergence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence), since CBPP had long been known in Europe and molecular data show a distinct European MmmSC biotype rather than a first detection on a new continent.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Beef and mixed cattle herds in northern Portugal (Iberian Peninsula)
Event summary: In 1999, Portugal reported new CBPP outbreaks in northern regions, representing a resurgence of the disease in the Iberian Peninsula after earlier control efforts and constituting the last recorded CBPP cases in Europe and the European Union. The outbreaks were controlled through stamping‑out, strict movement restrictions and intensified surveillance, with all affected herds depopulated and trade safeguards imposed until freedom could be demonstrated. Following these measures, CBPP was eliminated in Portugal and the country, along with the rest of the EU, has since been officially recognized as free of CBPP.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Portuguese outbreak is generally attributed to re‑introduction of infection into Iberia via movements of infected cattle, either from residual foci in southern Europe or from imports originating in endemic regions, with local spread facilitated by animal movements within affected northern zones. High‑value export markets and EU regulations mandated rapid containment and eradication through depopulation, surveillance and movement controls, which, while effective, caused significant though localized economic losses. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence does not indicate emergence of a novel MmmSC strain specific to Portugal; the episode is best categorized as re‑occurrence of CBPP in a previously affected region of Southern Europe driven by re‑introduction of existing European lineages and subsequent limited local transmission.
Review: REVIEW – Added this row because the 1999 Portuguese outbreak is widely documented as the last occurrence of CBPP in Europe and the EU and, although smaller than the Italian epidemic or the major African wave, is highly significant in terms of geographic range and trade impact. Classified as re‑occurrence in Southern Europe (CBPP had been present in Portugal and Spain previously) without strong evidence for a novel strain, and not as inter‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Europe – Western Europe, Northern Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe; Asia – Eastern Asia, Southern Asia; Oceania – Australia and New Zealand; South America – South America
Countries: Netherlands [2008]; Germany [2010]; Italy [2010]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]; France [2009]; Japan [2010]; Republic of Korea [2010]; Australia [2012]; Brazil [2012]; Poland [2014]; India [2017]
Host: Commercial layer chickens (multiple breeds); occasionally broiler breeders and backyard layers
Event summary: Beginning in 2008, layer flocks in the Netherlands started to show a novel eggshell pathology characterized by thinning, increased translucency and cracks localized at the apex of the egg, which field and experimental work linked to infection of the oviduct by particular Mycoplasma synoviae genotypes and termed eggshell apex abnormalities (EAA). Over the following decade, similar MS‑associated EAA outbreaks were reported across Europe (Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, France, Poland), Asia (Japan, the Republic of Korea and later India), Australia and Brazil, causing significant drops in egg production and increased downgrading and breakage of affected eggs. As farms improved MS monitoring, implemented live MS vaccines, strengthened biosecurity and, in some integrated systems, adopted eradication or depopulation policies, the incidence of severe clinical EAA was reduced in many regions, although EAA‑inducing MS strains have remained endemic in commercial layers and continue to cause localized economic losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of commercial layer production and multi‑age farm structures that facilitated persistent MS circulation; regional and international trade in hatching eggs and day‑old chicks disseminating specific EAA‑associated MS genotypes between countries; incomplete biosecurity and reliance on antibiotics rather than eradication in some systems. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence – distinct MS genotypes with tropism for the reproductive tract were associated with EAA and experimentally reproduced the syndrome; Increased virulence/pathogenicity – these strains caused more severe reproductive tract pathology and egg‑quality losses compared with typical respiratory MS strains; Geographic range expansion (inherent) – spread of EAA‑associated MS genotypes from an initial focus in the Netherlands to multiple regions in Europe, Asia, Oceania and South America via movements of poultry and hatching eggs.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the emergence of the eggshell apex abnormality (EAA) syndrome as a genotype‑driven re‑emergence of Mycoplasma synoviae, but the original time span (2000–2015) and several country start‑years were inconsistent with the literature. I have (i) reset the episode to 2008–2017, anchored on the first observation of EAA in the Netherlands in 2008 and subsequent spread during the 2010s; (ii) updated the country list and years using earliest published field reports (e.g. Germany and France 2009–2010, Italy and the UK around 2010, Korea 2010, Australia and Brazil from about 2012, India 2017, and mid‑2010s evidence from Poland); (iii) expanded the European sub‑regions to include Eastern Europe and added Southern Asia to reflect India; and (iv) added the Indian case report as a source. Classification as re‑emergence driven by novel MS genotypes remains appropriate but should be double‑checked by a subject‑matter expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Native Chinese chicken breeds and commercial chickens (layers and broilers)
Event summary: Beginning in 2010, large numbers of flocks of native‑type and commercial chickens in multiple Chinese provinces developed infectious synovitis with lameness and joint swelling, and epidemiological investigations identified Mycoplasma synoviae as the primary causative agent. Between 2010 and 2015, surveillance and serological surveys showed that MS infection became widespread across at least 16–21 provinces, affecting thousands of broiler and breeder flocks and causing substantial morbidity and production losses, representing a marked increase in incidence and geographic spread compared with earlier sporadic reports. Control efforts based mainly on mass antibiotic medication, improved hygiene and disinfection reduced clinical impact on some farms, but MS remained highly prevalent and continues to be an important production‑limiting disease in Chinese poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of the poultry industry in China with large populations of native and commercial breeds; multi‑age production systems and high flock densities facilitating horizontal MS transmission; extensive movement of birds between farms and regions; limited use of specific MS vaccines during the study period, leading to dependence on antimicrobials and hygiene alone. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission – high within‑flock prevalence and efficient respiratory and contact spread documented during the 2010–2015 outbreaks; possible, though not fully characterized, strain diversity (including a distinct K‑group genotype) contributing to variable clinical severity between flocks rather than a single novel genotype.
Review: review – This event represents a very large, well‑documented wave of MS‑associated infectious synovitis in China between 2010 and 2015 and should be retained as one of the major emergence episodes. I have not altered the geographic scope or event classification (re‑occurrence driven mainly by industry expansion), but I replaced one source that was focused on 2016–2019 antimicrobial resistance with more relevant serological and meta‑analytic studies documenting the scale and distribution of the 2010–2015 epidemic. Recommended for retention with these updated references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Commercial chickens (broilers and layers) in China
Event summary: From 2016 to 2019, systematic minimum‑inhibitory‑concentration testing of Mycoplasma synoviae isolates from Chinese chicken farms showed that all field strains had very high MIC values to enrofloxacin and variable but sometimes elevated MICs to macrolides and other commonly used drugs, indicating widespread fluoroquinolone resistance and emerging multidrug resistance in circulating MS populations. During the same period, MS infection was recognized as one of the most prevalent and economically important bacterial diseases of chickens in China, and treatment failures with standard antibiotic regimens were increasingly reported in flocks with synovitis and respiratory disease. These findings raised serious concerns about the sustainability of antibiotic‑based MS control and prompted calls for more judicious antimicrobial use, better susceptibility testing, and greater reliance on vaccination and biosecurity to reduce circulation of resistant MS strains.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy and often prophylactic use of enrofloxacin, macrolides, tetracyclines and other antibiotics in Chinese poultry production, frequently without susceptibility testing; large flock sizes and continuous production cycles providing strong selection pressure and transmission opportunities for resistant clones; limited regulatory oversight of on‑farm antimicrobial use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – field isolates showed uniformly high MICs to enrofloxacin and variably elevated MICs to macrolides and other classes, with point mutations identified in the quinolone‑resistance–determining regions of parC, gyrA and parE and in 23S rRNA; selection and persistence of multidrug‑resistant MS strains in commercial systems under continued antibiotic exposure.
Review: retain – The time window, geographic focus (China), and classification of this episode as an antimicrobial‑resistance–driven re‑emergence are well supported by MIC data from Chinese isolates collected between 2016 and 2019 and by global reviews of resistance in veterinary mycoplasmas. I have only refined the wording of the summary and mechanism to emphasize the predominance of enrofloxacin resistance and the specific mutations described; no structural changes to the event are needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Europe – Western Europe, Northern Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe; Asia – Eastern Asia, Southern Asia, South-eastern Asia; South America – South America; Oceania – Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Representative countries with documented resistant MS or significant concern include: Netherlands [2009]; Italy [2012]; Hungary [2010]; Poland [2010]; Israel [1996]; China [2016]; India [2010]; Thailand [2015]; Brazil [2018]; Australia [2010]
Host: Commercial chickens (layers and broilers), turkeys and other poultry in multiple regions
Event summary: From the late 2000s onward, and especially throughout the 2010s and early 2020s, multi‑country MIC surveys and reviews from Europe, Asia, South America and Oceania increasingly highlighted Mycoplasma synoviae as a key contributor to rising antimicrobial resistance in poultry mycoplasmas, with many field isolates showing elevated MICs or clear resistance to fluoroquinolones and, in some settings, to macrolides and lincosamides. Large datasets from Italy and central/eastern Europe revealed uniformly high enrofloxacin MIC90 values and variable resistance to macrolides and lincomycin, while similar resistance patterns and resistance‑associated mutations were documented in isolates from China, India, Thailand, Brazil and other producing countries, and treatment failures were reported in layer and breeder flocks experiencing synovitis, respiratory disease and EAA. In response, industry and regulatory bodies in several regions promoted reduced metaphylactic antibiotic use, greater emphasis on vaccination (e.g., live MS‑H and MS1 vaccines), and the development of rapid molecular tools to detect resistance mutations and to distinguish vaccine from wild‑type strains, yet resistant MS lineages have remained entrenched in many intensive poultry systems up to at least 2025.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Global reliance on a limited set of antibiotic classes (macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, lincosamides, pleuromutilins) for control of mycoplasmal infections in poultry; long‑term flock medication and mass treatments via feed or water; large, highly connected poultry industries (including international trade in hatching eggs and chicks) enabling dissemination of resistant lineages between regions; uneven implementation of antimicrobial‑stewardship policies despite increasing regulatory and consumer pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – emergence and spread of MS strains harboring point mutations in 23S rRNA and in the quinolone‑resistance–determining regions of gyrA, parC and related genes, often conferring high‑level resistance to enrofloxacin and reduced susceptibility to macrolides and lincosamides; Novel strain/genotype emergence – accumulation of distinct resistant genotypes within MS populations in multiple regions; Enhanced transmission – resistant strains persisting in multi‑age farms and vaccinated flocks, with co‑infections and immunosuppression further favoring their maintenance.
Review: review – This episode is conceptually valid as a global re‑emergence of Mycoplasma synoviae driven by antimicrobial resistance, but the original version compressed the chronology and under‑represented some regions. I have (i) extended the time span to 2009–2025 to reflect that high enrofloxacin and macrolide MICs in MS were already common in Europe and Israel by the late 2000s and that large MIC surveys and resistance‑focused reviews continued through the 2010s and early 2020s; (ii) broadened the sub‑regions to include Eastern Europe and South‑eastern Asia and updated the representative country list (Netherlands, Italy, Hungary, Poland, Israel, China, India, Thailand, Brazil, Australia) using documented MIC surveys and resistance reports; and (iii) expanded the source list to include key multi‑country MIC studies and region‑specific surveys as well as recent Chinese work on isolates collected between 2018 and 2025. Because AMR patterns are complex and continuous rather than a single discrete outbreak, an expert should review whether representing them as one global re‑emergence event is the most appropriate summarization.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: In 1993, Nairobi sheep disease virus (NSDV) was officially reported in Côte d’Ivoire, marking the first confirmed epizootic of Nairobi sheep disease in West Africa and indicating spread beyond the long‑recognized East African focus. Based on OIE/WOAH reporting summarized by USDA APHIS, affected flocks of sheep and goats experienced acute hemorrhagic gastroenteritis compatible with classical Nairobi sheep disease. No subsequent large NSDV epizootics have been documented from Côte d’Ivoire, and the event is generally cited as an isolated westward incursion rather than the establishment of a persistent West African focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely long‑distance movement of infected small ruminants and/or infested Rhipicephalus ticks from endemic East or Central African areas into West African production systems, facilitated by regional trade and transhumance, provided the opportunity for NSDV to reach susceptible flocks in Côte d’Ivoire, though direct movement chains were not documented.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Environmental suitability of savanna and mixed crop–livestock systems in West Africa probably allowed short‑term maintenance of the tick–ruminant cycle during the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of existing African NSDV lineages into a new African sub‑region; available sequence data do not indicate a distinct Côte d’Ivoire specific genotype or altered virulence compared with East African strains.
Review: retain – The 1993 Côte d’Ivoire outbreak is explicitly listed in the USDA APHIS Nairobi sheep disease technical fact sheet as an officially reported NSD epizootic (“Cote d’Ivoire (1993)”), based on WOAH/OIE data.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Coding of continent (Africa), sub‑region (Western Africa), and country is accurate given the UNSD classification, and classification as intra‑continental emergence into a previously unaffected African sub‑region is consistent with available historical distribution data, which place earlier foci in East and Central Africa.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/nairobi_sheep_disease.pdf)) The narrative about introduction via movements of infected animals or ticks is plausible but inferential; no concrete trade tracebacks are reported in the primary sources. No structural changes to this event row are recommended.

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: By 2003, Nairobi sheep disease virus remained endemic in East Africa, and official notifications compiled by WOAH/USDA APHIS list outbreaks in Kenya and the United Republic of Tanzania as the last reported NSD epizootics in these countries. In these outbreaks, naïve or poorly immune sheep and goats introduced into tick‑infested enzootic areas developed severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with high mortality, consistent with classical NSD. Following short‑lived control efforts and natural decline in vector abundance, disease reports subsided, and subsequent decades have not seen similarly documented large NSD outbreaks from Kenya or Tanzania despite continued enzootic circulation in ticks and livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of susceptible small ruminants from low‑tick or NSDV‑free areas into endemic East African grazing systems, combined with periods of favorable rainfall and vegetation that support high densities of Rhipicephalus appendiculatus and other competent ticks, likely precipitated renewed NSD outbreaks in Kenya and Tanzania around 2003.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/nairobi_sheep_disease.pdf)) Gaps in routine tick control, lack of vaccination, and marketing of animals through centralized abattoirs where they are exposed to infected ticks probably amplified transmission. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that these outbreaks were driven by emergence of a novel NSDV strain; they are best interpreted as re‑occurrence of endemic virus triggered by ecological and management factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – USDA APHIS, drawing on WOAH’s World Animal Health Information Database, identifies Kenya and Tanzania with outbreaks “last seen in 2003,” immediately preceding the 2007 Somalia episode.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Treating these as a late re‑occurrence in the long‑standing East African endemic focus and not as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is aligned with the given event‑type definitions and with regional distribution summaries that place NSDV as historically endemic in Uganda, Ethiopia, Somalia, Tanzania, Kenya and neighboring countries.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) The main uncertainties concern the magnitude of these epizootics (case and death counts are not published in detail), but there is no evidence they fall outside the intended ‘major outbreak in endemic area’ category. No coding changes are recommended.

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: In 2007, Somalia notified WOAH of an outbreak of Nairobi sheep disease affecting small ruminants in pastoral systems in the Horn of Africa, summarized in USDA APHIS documentation as the most recent officially reported NSD outbreak worldwide. Sheep and goats in affected Somali flocks developed acute febrile illness and hemorrhagic diarrhea typical of NSD, with high mortality in naïve animals. The event occurred in an area already known to be at ecological risk for NSDV, and disease activity subsided after the episode without evidence of wider regional spread or subsequent large-scale epizootics, although enzootic circulation in ticks and livestock is thought to persist.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Pastoral transhumance and cross‑border livestock movement across the Horn of Africa, coupled with heavy rains associated with regional climate anomalies that favor proliferation of Rhipicephalus appendiculatus and other tick vectors, likely underpinned the 2007 Somali re‑occurrence of NSD.([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/downld/infos_san_archives/eng/1998/en_980306v11n10.pdf)) Weak veterinary infrastructure and insecurity in Somalia may have delayed detection and response, allowing considerable flock‑level impact before recognition. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or phenotypic viral changes were reported for this episode; it is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of endemic NSDV disease driven by ecological and management factors rather than by major viral evolution.
Review: retain – The 2007 Somalia outbreak is directly cited in the USDA APHIS technical fact sheet as the “most recent outbreak” of Nairobi sheep disease reported to WOAH, with earlier outbreaks in Kenya and Tanzania in 2003.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Multiple reviews describe NSDV as historically endemic in the Horn of Africa, including Somalia,([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) so coding this event as a re‑occurrence (and not as intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) in Eastern Africa is appropriate. The lack of detailed quantitative outbreak data limits precise impact ranking but does not challenge the event’s inclusion; no field corrections are required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ticks (predominantly Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks collected from sheep and goats); vertebrate maintenance hosts presumed to include sheep and goats, although clinical disease had not yet been reported
Event summary: In 2013, Nairobi sheep disease virus RNA was first detected in ixodid ticks collected from small ruminants in northeastern China (Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces), revealing previously unrecognized circulation of NSDV in East Asia beyond its known African and South Asian range. Viral metagenomic analysis and segment sequencing showed that the Chinese NSDV ("NSDV China") formed a distinct phylogenetic clade separate from Kenyan and Indian/Sri Lankan strains, indicating a geographically structured lineage established in local tick populations. Although no concurrent clinical outbreaks in sheep or goats were recognized at the time, repeated detection of NSDV RNA in Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ticks in subsequent surveys suggested ongoing, cryptic maintenance cycles in the region, raising concern that ecological change or introduction of highly susceptible flocks could precipitate overt disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and high abundance of Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks in northeastern China, influenced by land‑use change and climate warming, together with growing small‑ruminant production, created suitable conditions for establishment of a NSDV transmission cycle in East Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9836300/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses of S, M and L segments showed that Chinese NSDV sequences clustered together yet were distinct from African and South Asian lineages, consistent with geographic range expansion accompanied by local genetic diversification into a Chinese clade; however, this diversification occurred in a new Asian sub‑region rather than representing reappearance in a previously affected area.
Review: review – The 2013 detection of NSDV RNA in ticks from sheep and goats in Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, China is securely documented by Gong et al. (2015, Emerging Infectious Diseases) and multiple subsequent tick‑virome studies, which together demonstrate a distinct Chinese NSDV lineage in Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4378503/?utm_source=openai)) Treating this as an intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian sub‑region (Eastern Asia) is appropriate, because NSDV/Ganjam virus was already recognized in India and Sri Lanka (Southern Asia) by the mid‑20th century.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004268220291514X?utm_source=openai)) However, the original row incorrectly also marked this event as “re‑emergence”, which by the project definition requires reappearance in a previously affected sub‑region with viral change; China represents a novel sub‑region rather than reappearance, so `re_emergence` has been set to `false`. No other structural fields were altered, but this change in event‑type coding should be reviewed by a domain expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: In the early 2020s, definitively reported in a 2025 Journal of Virology article, Nairobi sheep disease virus was for the first time identified causing infection and clinical disease in sheep and goats in China, converting prior tick‑only detections into recognized livestock disease foci in East Asia. Meta‑transcriptomic sequencing of diseased small ruminants revealed high NSDV abundance in spleen tissue, and follow‑up field investigations documented approximately 4.1% NSDV RNA positivity and around 30% seroprevalence in sampled herds, with some animals experiencing severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and mortality.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00006-25?af=R)) Subsequent control and heightened awareness helped limit the recognized outbreaks to a small number of farms, but the discovery highlighted that NSDV has become established in Chinese small‑ruminant production systems with the potential for broader epizootics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth and spatial expansion of small‑scale and medium‑scale sheep and goat farming in China, combined with the established presence of NSDV‑infected Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks since at least 2013 and evidence of wider tick‑borne NSDV circulation in multiple Chinese provinces, created conditions for spillover from ticks into naïve or partially naïve flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9836300/?utm_source=openai)) Limited prior awareness of NSDV in China and lack of specific preventive measures likely allowed the virus to circulate undetected until severe cases were investigated with high‑throughput sequencing. Internal mechanisms: Chinese NSDV isolates from ticks and sheep/goats form several distinct but related sub‑clades that are clearly separated from Kenyan and Indian strains, implying local genetic diversification and adaptation to Chinese tick and vertebrate hosts.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) This combination of established vector‑borne circulation followed by emergence of clinically apparent disease in livestock driven by locally evolved NSDV lineages supports classification of this episode as re‑emergence within an already infected sub‑region, rather than as a new intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – First confirmed NSDV infections and clinical Nairobi sheep disease in Chinese sheep and goats are clearly documented by Yao et al. (2025, Journal of Virology), which reports high viral loads in diseased animals, approximately 4.1% RNA prevalence and 29.9% seroprevalence in sampled herds, and experimental confirmation that the isolated Chinese strain is highly pathogenic for sheep.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00006-25?af=R)) Coding this as a re‑emergence event (appearance of livestock disease in an area where NSDV was already established in ticks and has diversified into a distinct Chinese clade) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is consistent with the project’s definitions and with recent reviews emphasizing eastward expansion and Chinese clade diversification.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) The main residual uncertainty is the exact calendar window of field cases and sampling; the article is published in mid‑2025 and does not, in the limited accessible text, clearly delimit outbreak onset and end dates, so the “2023–2024” range in this row should be treated as an informed estimate and validated against the full primary data. No other fields have been altered, but because of this timing uncertainty the event is flagged for expert review.
