Countries: Malaysia [1998–1999 – Perak, Negeri Sembilan, Selangor]; Singapore [1999 – Singapore]
Host: Domestic pigs; humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); companion animals (dogs, cats)
Event summary: From late 1998, intensive pig farms in peninsular Malaysia experienced a new respiratory–neurological disease in pigs accompanied by highly fatal encephalitis among pig handlers, initially misdiagnosed as Japanese encephalitis. Movement of infected pigs spread infection between major pig-producing states and into abattoirs in Singapore, leading to roughly 265 human encephalitis cases with over 100 deaths and the culling of more than a million pigs. The epidemic ended after aggressive pig depopulation, movement bans, farm closures and slaughterhouse controls removed the amplifying host populations and stopped human exposure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and high density of pig production, frequent live-pig movements between Malaysian states and to Singapore, and siting of pig farms under fruit trees created close interfaces between Pteropus fruit bats and pigs; early misattribution to Japanese encephalitis delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of a bat-borne henipavirus into pigs and then humans; enhanced transmission through high-titer virus shedding in pigs acting as amplifying hosts; inherent ability of the Malaysia genotype to spread efficiently within pig herds and from pigs to humans through close contact.
Review: retain – Correctly represents the first recognized NiV emergence in pigs and humans in peninsular Malaysia with linked cases in Singapore; continent, sub-region and countries match UNSD classifications; event-type coding as first global emergence/first detection (without intra- or inter-continental flags) is appropriate and the outbreak is clearly one of the two largest Nipah events globally.

Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus medius/giganteus reservoir); occasional livestock contact (e.g. sick cow near index case)
Event summary: In April–May 2001, a cluster of acute encephalitis cases occurred in Chandpur village, Meherpur District, north-western Bangladesh; retrospective investigations and serologic testing later confirmed Nipah virus infection, making this the first recognized NiV outbreak in Bangladesh. Most patients had close contact with the index case and some had contact with a sick cow, while subsequent animal investigations found serologic evidence of NiV infection in local Pteropus bats, supporting bat-to-human spillover with limited human-to-human transmission. The outbreak ended after the deaths of the small cluster and basic infection-prevention measures were introduced in the district hospital and community awareness increased, although NiV was not conclusively identified as the cause until 2003.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human settlements and small-scale livestock keeping in close proximity to Pteropus bat roosts, intimate caregiving of severely ill patients in households and limited infection-prevention capacity in the Meherpur district hospital facilitated initial spillover and short transmission chains. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the NiV-Bangladesh lineage into humans via bat contamination of food or the environment and efficient transmission among very close contacts; no intermediate amplifying livestock host (such as pigs) was identified.
Review: review – Original ChatGPT row incorrectly combined Meherpur (Bangladesh) and Siliguri (India) into a single cross-country event and labeled it as both intra-continental emergence and re-emergence; this row has been restricted to Meherpur only and coded as intra-continental emergence of NiV into Southern Asia without re-emergence. The event is historically important as Bangladesh’s first recognized NiV outbreak but is smaller than several later Bangladesh outbreaks; a human reviewer should decide whether to retain it in addition to the 10 largest events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (patients, family caregivers, health-care workers, visitors); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir, suspected)
Event summary: During January–February 2001, a large outbreak of febrile encephalitis with high mortality occurred in several hospitals in Siliguri, West Bengal, India. Later testing of stored clinical specimens demonstrated Nipah virus infection genetically closer to Bangladesh strains than to Malaysia strains, and most cases had clear hospital-associated exposure, indicating extensive human-to-human transmission among patients, visitors and health-care workers. Transmission chains were interrupted after enhanced infection-prevention measures, isolation of suspected cases and the natural exhaustion of susceptible close contacts, and this episode became the first recognized NiV outbreak in India and one of the largest Nipah events globally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Crowded referral hospitals, frequent patient transfers between facilities, lack of routine use of personal protective equipment and close contact between caregivers and severely ill patients created an environment conducive to nosocomial NiV spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage into India with demonstrated capacity for efficient person-to-person transmission via respiratory secretions in hospital settings; no domestic animal amplifying host was identified in this outbreak.
Review: retain – Added as a new row because the 2001 Siliguri outbreak (≈66 cases, ≈45 deaths) is one of the largest NiV outbreaks and the first recognized event in India; it was previously merged with the Meherpur event, which obscured its size and nosocomial nature. Coded as intra-continental emergence into Southern Asia with no re-emergence flag, consistent with its timing and genotype evidence.

Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); probable indirect involvement of domestic animals and contaminated environment
Event summary: In early 2004, Bangladesh experienced its largest recorded Nipah season when linked clusters of encephalitis occurred in Rajbari and neighbouring Faridpur Districts, with more than 60 cases and very high case fatality. Outbreak investigations implicated wintertime consumption of raw date-palm sap contaminated by fruit bats as the main route of bat-to-human transmission, followed by substantial household and caregiving-associated human-to-human spread. The epidemic waned after the end of the date-palm sap harvesting season, intensive public-health messaging to avoid raw sap and contact with sick individuals, and strengthened isolation and barrier precautions in local health facilities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal harvesting and widespread consumption of raw date-palm sap accessible to feeding Pteropus bats, dense household contact networks during illness and funerals, and limited early isolation capacity in rural hospitals. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of the NiV-Bangladesh lineage with efficient person-to-person transmission; no strong evidence for a major genetic shift compared with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks, so re-occurrence within the same subregion is considered the dominant pattern.
Review: retain – Row updated to include both Rajbari and Faridpur districts and to reflect that the combined 2004 Bangladesh season involved >60 cases and high mortality; event is clearly among the largest NiV outbreaks and appropriately coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia driven by date-palm sap exposure and close-contact transmission.

Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); limited involvement of domestic animals
Event summary: In early 2007, Bangladesh reported several Nipah clusters in Thakurgaon District in the northwest and in Kushtia/Pabna/Natore and Naogaon Districts, together accounting for about 18 cases and nine deaths. Detailed investigations in Thakurgaon and Kushtia documented both primary infections linked to bat-contaminated food or environment and secondary person-to-person transmission among family caregivers and health-care contacts. These geographically separated but temporally linked clusters reinforced the pattern of seasonal NiV re-occurrence in Bangladesh’s “Nipah belt” and highlighted the importance of both bat-to-human and human-to-human transmission routes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing winter consumption of fresh date-palm sap accessible to bats, household caregiving practices with intense contact with severely ill patients, and limited use of personal protective equipment in district hospitals enabled repeated spillover and short chains of transmission. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe encephalitis with high case fatality; available sequence data do not indicate a distinct new genotype compared with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks, so this is treated as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – Added as a new row to capture the aggregated 2007 Bangladesh season (≈18 cases, 9 deaths across multiple districts), which WHO-derived outbreak tables list among the larger NiV outbreaks; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia without intra-continental or re-emergence flags, consistent with repeated seasonal outbreaks driven by date-palm sap consumption and close-contact transmission.

Countries: Bangladesh [2010 – Faridpur, Rajbari, Gopalganj, Madaripur Districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event summary: Between February and March 2010, Bangladesh experienced a substantial Nipah outbreak season centered on Faridpur, Rajbari, Gopalganj and Madaripur Districts, with about 16 recognized cases and 14 deaths. Epidemiologic investigations found that many primary cases had recently consumed raw or fermented date-palm sap, while several secondary cases arose from close contact with severely ill Nipah patients in households or health facilities. The outbreak subsided after the sap-harvesting season ended and after intensified public messaging and infection-prevention measures reduced high-risk exposures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal production and consumption of raw date-palm sap contaminated by bats, combined with intimate caregiving of encephalitic patients and inadequate barrier precautions in district hospitals, sustained repeated spillover and limited person-to-person spread. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing transmission of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe encephalitis with high case fatality; genetic analyses from 2008–2010 outbreaks show moderate diversity within a single lineage rather than emergence of a clearly distinct new strain, supporting classification as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added because WHO- and CEPI-based outbreak tables list the 2010 multi-district Bangladesh outbreak (≈16 cases, 14 deaths) among the 10 largest Nipah events; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia with no intra-/inter-continental or re-emergence flags, in line with its epidemiology and sequence data.

Countries: Bangladesh [2011 – Lalmonirhat, Rangpur, Dinajpur, Rajbari and other affected districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event summary: In January–February 2011, Bangladesh experienced its largest documented Nipah season, with several clusters of encephalitis in northern districts such as Lalmonirhat, Rangpur and Dinajpur and additional cases in central districts including Rajbari, totaling about 44 cases and 40 deaths. Many primary case-patients reported drinking raw date-palm sap, and detailed field investigations identified extensive person-to-person transmission within households and some health-care–associated spread. The season ended after the sap-harvesting period and following intensified public-health messaging, contact tracing and isolation of suspected Nipah cases through the national sentinel surveillance system.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High seasonal availability and consumption of raw date-palm sap, geographic clustering of bat roosts in the so-called Nipah belt, and close household and hospital contacts with severely ill patients combined to produce Bangladesh’s largest recorded Nipah season. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage with efficient human-to-human transmission in close-contact settings; no distinct new genotype has been defined relative to earlier Bangladesh viruses, so the pattern is best described as re-occurrence in a known high-risk subregion.
Review: retain – Added to capture the 2011 Bangladesh season (≈44 cases, 40 deaths), which is clearly one of the largest NiV outbreaks worldwide and a key driver of enhanced national Nipah surveillance; appropriately coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia, not as intra-continental emergence or re-emergence.

Countries: Bangladesh [2013 – Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah, Mymensingh and other affected districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event summary: In January–February 2013, Bangladesh again reported multiple Nipah clusters across several northern and central districts, including Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah and Mymensingh, with around 24 cases and 21 deaths. As in previous years, most primary cases had consumed fresh date-palm sap shortly before illness onset, and subsequent infections occurred among family caregivers and other close contacts. Strengthened event-based and sentinel surveillance enabled earlier recognition and targeted control efforts, which, together with the end of the sap-harvesting season, brought the season to a close.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistently popular consumption of raw date-palm sap in high-risk districts, close household care of gravely ill patients, and limited but improving infection-prevention in smaller health facilities maintained the conditions for recurrent NiV-Bangladesh outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses with high case-fatality and capacity for limited chains of human-to-human transmission; no evidence of major viral change relative to earlier Bangladesh seasons, so this episode is treated as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added to represent the 2013 Bangladesh Nipah season (≈24 cases, 21 deaths), which ranks among the ten largest Nipah outbreaks by case numbers; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia with drivers and mechanisms consistent with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks.

Countries: Bangladesh [2014 – multiple districts including Manikganj, Magura, Faridpur, Rangpur, Shariatpur, Kushtia, Rajshahi, Dinajpur, Chapai Nawabganj, Naogaon]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event summary: During February 2014, Bangladesh experienced another dispersed Nipah season with smaller clusters and sporadic cases reported from about 13 districts, totaling roughly 18 cases and nine deaths. Most primary cases again reported drinking raw date-palm sap during the cool months, and several secondary infections occurred among caregivers and family members in affected communities. Compared with earlier seasons, improved surveillance and faster outbreak investigation facilitated earlier risk communication and patient isolation, helping to limit the overall size of the season.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued harvesting and consumption of unprotected date-palm sap and close contact with severely ill patients in homes and local facilities sustained recurrent Nipah transmission in known high-risk districts, even as awareness and surveillance improved. Internal mechanisms: Recurrent circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe disease; no clear evidence for emergence of a fundamentally new viral genotype or host range, so this event is classified as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added because the aggregated 2014 Bangladesh season (≈18 cases, 9 deaths across many districts) is listed among the largest Nipah outbreaks in WHO/CEPI compilations; appropriately coded as re-occurrence in a known endemic subregion and helps capture the sustained burden of NiV-Bangladesh in the 2010s.

Countries: Philippines [2014 – Sultan Kudarat and South Cotabato Provinces, Mindanao]
Host: Horses; humans (horse owners, slaughterers, meat consumers); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event summary: In 2014, a henipavirus outbreak occurred in villages in Sultan Kudarat and South Cotabato Provinces on Mindanao Island, Philippines, when horses developed acute, often fatal neurologic and respiratory disease followed by severe illness in people who slaughtered sick horses or ate their meat. Seventeen human cases with high case fatality were documented, with evidence for horse-to-human and limited human-to-human transmission, and molecular analyses indicated infection with Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus, most similar to the Malaysia lineage. The outbreak was controlled after cessation of slaughter and consumption of sick horses, quarantine and movement restrictions on equids, and community education to avoid contact with ill horses and bats, with transmission chains burning out once these measures were in place.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Backyard and free-grazing horse management under fruit trees frequented by Pteropodidae bats, slaughter and consumption of visibly ill horses, and lack of initial awareness of henipavirus risks in both animal and human health sectors. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and amplification in horses as intermediate hosts, with efficient horse-to-human transmission, and re-emergence of a NiV-Malaysia–like lineage in a new country within South-eastern Asia, justifying classification as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion.
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2014 Mindanao horse–human henipavirus outbreak, which WHO and EID describe as probable Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus and which involved 17 human cases; coded as re-emergence in South-eastern Asia due to reappearance of a Malaysia-like lineage with a new amplifying host (horses), and is among the ten largest Nipah outbreaks.

Countries: India [2018 – Kozhikode and Malappuram Districts, Kerala]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus medius reservoir, confirmed serologically); possible limited domestic animal exposure
Event summary: In May 2018, Kerala state in southern India detected its first Nipah virus outbreak when an index case with encephalitis in Kozhikode was linked to multiple generations of infection among family members, other patients, companions and health-care workers across Kozhikode and neighboring Malappuram District. Laboratory investigations confirmed NiV infection and sequencing showed a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage, while serologic surveys identified NiV-reactive Pteropus medius bats near the index case’s home. Aggressive contact tracing, strict isolation of cases, establishment of dedicated treatment and quarantine facilities, and extensive community risk communication contained the outbreak within about a month, with roughly 19–23 cases and a very high case-fatality ratio.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense and busy hospital environments where the first cases were not immediately recognized as Nipah, close caregiving contact in households, and bat roosts and orchards near human dwellings created opportunities for both bat-to-human spillover and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of NiV-Bangladesh–like virus in a new ecological setting in southern India with demonstrated capacity for sustained human-to-human transmission in clinical settings; genomic analyses show close relatedness to Bangladeshi strains, so despite the new geography this is best classified as re-occurrence within Southern Asia rather than emergence of a distinct new lineage.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the size, geography and nosocomial nature of the 2018 Kerala outbreak and uses appropriate sources; emergence coding has been adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence in a known subregion because sequencing indicates a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage without clear evidence of a novel strain, while the outbreak itself is among the ten largest Nipah events.

Countries: Germany [1991]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1994]; Ireland [1997]
Host: Farmed turbot (Scophthalmus maximus) in land‑based and tank‑based marine aquaculture facilities in Germany, on the Scottish island of Gigha, and at commercial farms in southwest Ireland; associated wild marine fish in adjacent North Sea and northeast Atlantic waters.
Event summary: In 1991, VHSV was identified as the cause of a severe disease episode in farmed turbot in Germany, representing one of the first natural VHS outbreaks in a high‑value marine flatfish. In 1994 a further outbreak occurred in a commercial turbot farm on Gigha in western Scotland, where mortality was modest but approximately 14 tonnes of fish were culled as part of eradication, and by 1997 similar VHSV genotype III–associated disease was reported from Irish turbot farms. These linked outbreaks led to strict stamping‑out policies and movement controls, and although genotype III VHSV remains part of the marine virus pool around the British Isles, major turbot farm epizootics have been rare since the late 1990s.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Rapid development and intensification of turbot aquaculture in northern Europe, using raw seawater supplies in regions where VHSV was already present in wild marine fishes, provided large populations of susceptible, high‑value hosts with limited initial biosecurity. Movements of fish, equipment and seawater between facilities and hatcheries likely facilitated regional spread once virus entered captivity. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of marine genotype III VHSV from wild fish into turbot, a species shown experimentally to be highly susceptible; enhanced transmission and amplification in dense tank systems; and the emergence and farm‑level dominance of a turbot‑adapted strain such as UK‑860/94 associated with higher virulence in turbot than historical freshwater trout isolates.
Sources emphasize the German 1991 and Scottish 1994 farm outbreaks, subsequent reports from Ireland, and the role of genotype III in turbot mariculture.
Review: review: New event added to represent the major 1991–1997 VHS outbreaks in farmed turbot in Germany, Scotland and Ireland, which are widely cited as high‑impact marine aquaculture episodes for VHSV (now Novirhabdovirus piscine). Classified as re‑emergence (host expansion of genotype III within an already affected European region) rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, consistent with the long‑standing presence of VHSV in European trout aquaculture and marine fish. Years, country list and scale of culling (e.g. ~14 t at Gigha) are based on secondary reviews rather than original farm reports, so a regional expert should verify detailed mortality and production‑loss estimates and confirm that no additional turbot outbreaks of similar magnitude after 1997 should be merged into this episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine sea‑cage aquaculture on the British Columbia coast; associated wild marine fish reservoirs (especially Pacific herring and other pelagic species) in the Northeast Pacific Ocean.
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, genotype IVa VHSV, already endemic in wild marine fishes of the northeastern Pacific, was repeatedly isolated from Atlantic salmon held in marine net‑pen farms in British Columbia, marking the first confirmed infections of farmed Atlantic salmon by this virus in the region. Most detections were associated with low to moderate mortality or subclinical infections rather than explosive die‑offs, but they demonstrated that farmed Atlantic salmon could become infected following spillover from wild herring and other marine fishes and prompted enhanced surveillance and risk assessments for the sector. Since about 2000, VHSV IVa has remained an enzootic marine pathogen in Pacific Northwest fish communities, with intermittent detections in farmed Atlantic salmon but few documented large‑scale mortality events.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and high stocking densities of Atlantic salmon sea‑cage aquaculture in coastal British Columbia placed large, naïve farmed salmon populations in close contact with an enzootic marine VHSV IVa reservoir in Pacific herring and other wild fishes; schooling behavior of herring and their tendency to enter net pens likely facilitated viral transfer into cages. Regulatory attention and surveillance increased because of concerns over pathogen exchange between wild and farmed fish and potential impacts on wild salmon. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype IVa VHSV from wild marine fishes to Atlantic salmon; viral persistence in infected Atlantic salmon tissues even when overt disease was limited; and continued low‑level circulation of genetically similar IVa strains in wild and farmed populations, maintaining an ongoing risk of viral adaptation toward greater virulence in this host.
Review: review: Event retained but re‑dated and reframed. Evidence from Canadian and U.S. risk assessments and surveillance documents indicates that genotype IVa VHSV has been periodically detected in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia since the mid‑1990s, with infections acquired from wild marine reservoirs and usually causing low‑level or subclinical disease rather than catastrophic farm losses. The original 1992–1995 timing appears to have conflated the well‑known 1992–1996 IHNV epizootics in Atlantic salmon with VHSV; the year range is adjusted here to 1995–2000 as an approximate window for the first confirmed VHSV detections and early investigations. Because outbreaks have generally been modest in scale compared with other VHSV events, a human reviewer should decide whether this host‑expansion episode merits inclusion among the top 10 emergence events or should instead be treated as contextual background for Pacific Northwest VHSV ecology.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Japanese flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus) in marine net‑pen aquaculture in the Seto Inland Sea; wild Japanese flounder and other marine fish in surrounding Japanese coastal waters.
Event summary: In 1996 a severe rhabdoviral disease outbreak occurred in market‑sized farmed Japanese flounder in the Seto Inland Sea, and the causative agent was identified as viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, representing the first confirmed VHSV outbreak in cultured fish in Japan and the first recognized VHS disease event in Asia. Over subsequent years, additional VHSV isolates were recovered from both farmed flounder and apparently healthy wild Japanese flounder in the Inland Sea and Sea of Japan, demonstrating establishment of a broader marine reservoir and continued local circulation. Control of the disease in Japanese flounder farms relied on improved biosecurity, husbandry changes and stock management, and VHSV has persisted as an endemic marine pathogen in Japanese coastal waters with ongoing but more localized outbreaks in farmed flounder.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of Japanese flounder mariculture in coastal Japan during the 1990s, combined with high stocking densities and use of local seawater, increased opportunities for contact between farmed flounder and VHSV‑infected wild marine fishes; movements of fish or eggs for aquaculture may also have contributed to viral introduction and spread. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype IVa‑like VHSV from wild marine fishes into intensively cultured Japanese flounder; probable emergence of local strain clusters adapted to this flatfish host as indicated by genetic analyses of Japanese isolates; and enhanced transmission under net‑pen conditions, where crowding and handling stress can amplify clinical disease expression.
Review: review: Event retained and re‑classified as an inter‑continental emergence because the 1996 Seto Inland Sea outbreak in farmed Japanese flounder is widely recognized as the first confirmed VHS disease outbreak in Asia, expanding the virus from its historical European and North American range into a new continent. Re‑emergence is kept as ‘yes’ to reflect the appearance of a new genotype/host combination and marked host‑range expansion within the global fish host system. Dates, geography and main impacts align with primary Japanese fish pathology reports; no corrections to timing or country are needed, but a regional expert could refine the end year of the linked episode if more detailed outbreak chronologies are desired.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Denmark [1998]; Sweden [1998]; Norway [1998]; Finland [1998]; Germany [1998]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1998]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1998]
Host: Wild marine fish (e.g. herring, cod, whiting, turbot and other demersal species) in the Baltic Sea, Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and adjacent North Atlantic coastal waters; incidental spillover into nearby marine aquaculture sites.
Event summary: By the late 1990s, coordinated surveys in the Baltic Sea, Kattegat, Skagerrak and North Sea documented widespread infection of wild marine fishes with VHSV, and from around 1998 several mass‑mortality or high‑prevalence events in multiple species were attributed to marine VHS‑like viruses. As surveillance expanded, multiple marine genotypes (notably I and II) were detected in diverse species and locations around the Baltic and North Sea, demonstrating that VHSV had established a substantial and genetically structured marine reservoir beyond its traditional association with freshwater rainbow trout farms. Although acute mass‑mortality episodes subsequently decreased in frequency, marine VHSV has remained enzootic in these European shelf seas and continues to pose a risk of spillover into susceptible marine aquaculture species such as turbot and sea‑farmed rainbow trout.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term anthropogenic changes in the Baltic and North Sea, including eutrophication, altered food webs and intensive fishing, likely reshaped host population structure and stress levels in ways that favored VHSV transmission and persistence; international movements of fish and eggs for aquaculture and stocking may also have helped redistribute viral genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Geographic and ecological niche expansion of genotypes I and II from freshwater rainbow trout aquaculture into a wide array of wild marine fish species; diversification of marine VHSV lineages and population structure as shown by nucleoprotein and glycoprotein gene analyses; and efficient transmission linked to dense schooling behavior and overlapping spawning aggregations of susceptible pelagic and demersal fishes.
Review: retain: This event appropriately summarizes the late‑1990s recognition of a broad marine VHSV reservoir in wild fish across the Baltic, Kattegat, Skagerrak and North Sea, which had important implications for European aquaculture and fisheries risk. Countries and subregions listed match those most intensively surveyed, and classification as re‑emergence (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) is consistent with VHSV’s long history in European trout farming and earlier sporadic marine detections. Start–end years (1998–2000) should be regarded as an approximate window centered on the main survey and mass‑mortality period and could be fine‑tuned with more detailed national survey timelines if needed.

Host: Sea‑reared rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in marine net‑pen farms on the west coast of Sweden; wild Baltic/North Sea herring (Clupea harengus) in adjacent coastal waters acting as a reservoir and putative source of infection.
Event summary: In 1998, VHSV genotype Ib was detected in diseased sea‑reared rainbow trout on the west coast of Sweden, marking the start of a marine net‑pen epizootic in an area previously considered free of VHS. Despite stamping‑out measures, infection re‑occurred in 2000, and identical or near‑identical VHSV Ib strains were isolated from herring caught close to affected trout farms, implicating spawning herring as a repeated source of virus introduction. Recurrent outbreaks, coupled with the difficulty of excluding infected herring from open cages, ultimately made rainbow‑trout farming in this coastal area untenable, and the affected region transitioned away from this form of aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Use of open marine net‑pen systems for rainbow trout in coastal areas frequented by large schools of spawning herring created sustained opportunities for virus transfer from wild to farmed fish, while repeated restocking of cages and movements of equipment and service vessels facilitated farm‑to‑farm dissemination once VHSV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype Ib from wild herring into rainbow trout; apparent local adaptation of marine Ib strains to cause clinical disease in trout; and efficient waterborne transmission and amplification within densely stocked sea‑cage populations in relatively confined coastal embayments.
Review: review: New event added to capture the repeated VHSV genotype Ib outbreaks in sea‑reared rainbow trout on Sweden’s west coast around 1998–2000, where infected herring were strongly implicated as a reservoir and where trout farming was ultimately abandoned in the affected area. Classified as re‑emergence in Northern Europe, not intra‑continental emergence, because VHSV was already established in the same UNSD subregion through Danish and other Nordic aquaculture and marine reservoirs. Dates and impact (initial detection in 1998, recurrence in 2000, and eventual cessation of rainbow trout farming) are drawn from later Finnish and Norwegian syntheses citing Nordblom & Norell (2000); a regional expert should confirm the exact number of farms, total production losses and whether any post‑2000 residual cases should be folded into this episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in brackish‑water net‑pen farms in the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Finland, primarily in the Åland Islands and selected mainland coastal sites.
Event summary: In spring 2000, VHSV was diagnosed for the first time in Finland from four rainbow trout farms in brackish water along the Baltic coast, signalling introduction of the virus into Finnish marine‑influenced aquaculture. Between 2000 and 2004 the infection spread despite control efforts, and by the end of 2004 VHSV had been isolated from 24 farms in three separate coastal areas, causing notable production losses and triggering extensive stamping‑out, movement restrictions and the designation of a large restriction zone in the Åland Islands. Following aggressive eradication and progressive strengthening of on‑farm biosecurity, the Finnish brackish‑water VHS epizootic was brought under control, although a nearby marine reservoir in wild fish continues to pose a risk of re‑introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of rainbow trout farming in brackish Baltic coastal waters increased contact between farmed fish and marine VHSV reservoirs, while frequent movements of live fish, shared service vessels and waterborne pathways enabled farm‑to‑farm spread once the virus was introduced; cross‑border trade and regional movements of fish or eggs may also have played a role. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of VHSV in a new production niche via spillover from marine lineages closely related to historical Danish freshwater isolates; partial adaptation of genotype Id to rainbow trout under brackish conditions; and enhanced transmission associated with semi‑open net‑pen systems and high stocking densities.
Review: retain: The 2000–2004 Finnish brackish‑water rainbow trout epizootic is well documented (24 farms in three Baltic coastal areas) and clearly ranks among the largest VHSV emergence events in European aquaculture after 1990. Country, subregion, timing and description of control measures match primary Finnish and international sources, and coding as re‑emergence (genotype Id spreading into a new production setting within an already affected Northern European region) is appropriate. No structural corrections are required, though the continuation of low‑level detections in Åland after 2004 is acknowledged in the cited thesis and could be treated as an extended tail of this episode in future, more granular datasets.

Host: Numerous wild freshwater fish species (>30) including freshwater drum (Aplodinotus grunniens), muskellunge (Esox masquinongy), smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu), yellow perch (Perca flavescens), gobies and many others in the Laurentian Great Lakes and connected inland waters; incidental detections in baitfish and aquaculture‑related movements.
Event summary: In spring 2005 a large mortality event in freshwater drum in the Bay of Quinte, Lake Ontario (Canada) led to the isolation of a previously unrecognized VHSV strain, later designated genotype IVb, and additional detections that year and in 2006 signalled that the virus had entered the Great Lakes basin. During 2006–2007 the new IVb genotype caused dramatic multi‑species fish kills across several of the Laurentian Great Lakes and connected inland lakes and rivers on both the Canadian and U.S. sides, and surveillance ultimately documented infection in more than 30 freshwater fish species with a rapidly expanding geographic range. After 2008, the magnitude of die‑offs declined as host populations and management adjusted, but genotype IVb has persisted as an enzootic freshwater pathogen in the Great Lakes with ongoing low‑level circulation and occasional localized outbreaks and continuing regulatory concern.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable introduction of a marine‑origin VHSV strain from the North American Atlantic coast into the freshwater Great Lakes via human‑mediated pathways such as ballast water discharge, movement of infected baitfish or other live‑fish transfers; extensive regional trade and recreational movements of baitfish and boats then accelerated spread among basins and into inland lakes. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a novel freshwater‑adapted genotype/subgenogroup IVb, closely related to but distinct from marine genotype IVa; large‑scale geographic range expansion from coastal marine to large freshwater lake systems; rapid host expansion to numerous new freshwater fish species, some experiencing high mortality; and high mutation rates and haplotype diversification of IVb following introduction, potentially facilitating adaptation to multiple hosts and environments.
Review: review: This event correctly characterizes the emergence of genotype IVb VHSV in the Laurentian Great Lakes as a major, multi‑species, multi‑jurisdiction outbreak and a paradigmatic aquatic emerging infectious disease. The original row, however, assigned 2005 as the start year for both Canada and the United States; available chronologies indicate that index mortality and isolation occurred in Canadian waters of Lake Ontario in 2005, with confirmed U.S. detections following in 2006. The country‑specific start year for the United States has therefore been corrected to 2006, while keeping 2005–2008 as the overall window of most intense emergence. Coding as re‑emergence (novel genotype, new freshwater range and broad host expansion within a continent already known to harbor VHSV) remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sea‑farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in marine net‑pen farms in Storfjorden, western Norway; associated wild marine fish in surrounding fjord and coastal waters.
Event summary: In autumn 2007, an outbreak of VHS occurred in sea‑farmed rainbow trout in Storfjorden on Norway’s west coast, and the causative virus was identified as a genotype III strain previously known only from wild marine fish in the North Sea and Skagerrak, representing the first confirmed VHS outbreak caused by this genotype in farmed salmonids. The episode involved several farms within one fjord system, with elevated but moderate mortality and clinical signs of both neurological disease and septicemia, and genomic analyses showed that the outbreak strain differed from low‑virulence marine genotype III isolates. The affected farms were depopulated and strict control measures implemented, and while genotype III VHSV remains present in Norwegian marine fish, major outbreaks in rainbow trout farms have been rare or absent since this event.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of rainbow trout mariculture along the Norwegian coast increased contact between farmed salmonids and wild marine fish harboring genotype III VHSV, while waterborne spread within the fjord and routine animal and equipment movements likely connected farms during the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of genotype III from non‑salmonid marine hosts to rainbow trout, with molecular studies identifying specific amino acid substitutions in the nucleoprotein and other genes associated with increased virulence in trout; enhanced transmission in dense sea‑cage populations within a semi‑closed fjord system; and demonstration that even genotypes previously considered low‑pathogenic for salmonids can, after limited genetic change, cause clinical VHS in rainbow trout.
Review: retain: The 2007 Storfjorden outbreak in sea‑farmed rainbow trout is accurately described and supported by detailed virological and epidemiological investigations, with correct timing, geography and identification of genotype III as the causative strain. Classification as re‑emergence (host expansion and increased virulence of a previously low‑pathogenic marine genotype in a subregion where VHSV was already present) is consistent with the event definition, and no changes to the coded emergence types or main narrative are required.

Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater raceways and flow‑through farms across multiple major trout‑producing provinces in Iran.
Event summary: From 2015 onward, Iran—then one of the world’s largest producers of freshwater rainbow trout—began reporting severe viral disease outbreaks in trout farms, and molecular investigations identified VHSV alongside IHNV as causes of multiple clinical epizootics in several provinces. Between 2015 and 2019 at least a dozen VHSV‑positive outbreaks were documented, with farm‑level cumulative mortalities often in the 20–70% range and substantial economic losses in heavily affected regions of this nationally important food‑fish sector. Phylogenetic analyses showed that Iranian VHSV isolates clustered within European genotype I lineages, suggesting introduction via infected eggs or fry, and authorities and industry responded by strengthening surveillance programs, biosecurity measures and controls on imported trout eggs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very rapid expansion and high stocking densities in Iran’s rainbow trout industry, combined with heavy reliance on imported eggs and frequent movements of fry and market fish among provinces, created strong opportunities for introduction and dissemination of novirhabdoviruses; limited early on‑farm biosecurity and warm‑season water temperatures further exacerbated outbreak severity. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of genotype I VHSV lineages in a previously naïve, highly intensive freshwater trout system; co‑circulation and possible interactions with IHNV; and ongoing viral evolution within farms under strong transmission and selection pressures, as suggested by molecular‑epidemiology data.
Review: review: New event added because 2015–2019 VHSV outbreaks in Iran occur in one of the world’s largest rainbow trout industries and involve repeated high‑mortality episodes and multi‑province spread, making them among the most consequential recent VHSV emergence events globally. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed establishment of VHS disease in Southern Asia as an UNSD subregion) and re‑emergence (introduction of genotype I lineages into a previously naïve but intensively farmed host population). The number of VHSV‑positive outbreaks, mortality ranges and relative contribution of VHSV versus IHNV are taken from molecular‑epidemiology studies rather than complete national surveillance summaries; a regional expert should cross‑check these figures against official veterinary statistics and consider whether post‑2019 events should be treated as a continuation of the same emergence episode.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine net-pen aquaculture; nearby wild Pacific salmonids as reservoir hosts (e.g. sockeye salmon, Oncorhynchus nerka)
Event summary: In July 1992, IHNV was detected for the first time causing disease in sea-cage–reared Atlantic salmon in British Columbia, Canada, triggering an epidemic that affected multiple marine farms between 1992 and 1996 and caused substantial cumulative mortalities and stock culls. The virus, originating from endemic wild Pacific salmon, spread between net-pen sites via waterborne transmission and farm-to-farm movements of infected fish, prompting area-wide surveillance and control programs. By the mid‑1990s, improved biosecurity, coordinated area management, and fallowing allowed the initial epidemic wave in Atlantic salmon to subside, although IHNV remained endemic in wild salmon and a risk for farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a naïve, highly susceptible host (Atlantic salmon) into IHNV-endemic coastal waters; rapid expansion and high stocking densities of marine net-pen aquaculture; limited early biosecurity, including movement of subclinically infected fish between farms; hydrodynamic connectivity facilitating waterborne spread among sites. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from native Pacific salmonids into farmed Atlantic salmon; possible selection for variants with enhanced fitness in Atlantic salmon within high-density net-pen conditions, although the epidemic is largely attributed to ecological and management drivers rather than a single clearly defined novel genotype.
Review: retain – Major 1992–1996 epizootic of IHNV in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia; timing, hosts, and drivers match primary outbreak descriptions. Only change was to standardize the sub-region field to 'North America | Northern America'; event-type classification as re-emergence (host expansion into Atlantic salmon within an already endemic sub-region) is consistent with the scheme.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine net-pens
Event summary: In August 2001, a new epidemic of IHNV began in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia, Canada, with the first reported case that year and successive outbreaks through June 2003 across multiple marine farms. The epidemic developed through farm-to-farm spread within coastal production areas, again linked to contacts among net-pen sites and exposure to endemic virus in wild salmon. The wave of outbreaks was eventually controlled by strengthened movement restrictions, culling of affected cages, area-based fallowing, and enhanced surveillance, after which large-scale IHNV epidemics in BC Atlantic salmon subsided.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued intensive Atlantic salmon farming in IHNV-endemic waters; high connectivity among farms through live-fish transfers and shared water masses; initial gaps in coordinated area management; environmental mixing with wild salmon migration corridors. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of IHNV in wild salmonid reservoirs and in farmed stocks; available genetic data indicate continuity with earlier BC strains, so the epidemic is primarily associated with management and ecological risk factors rather than the emergence of a clearly distinct new genogroup.
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence episode, but the event type has been corrected. The 2001–2003 wave represents a large re-occurrence of IHNV in the same sub-region and host species as the 1990s BC epidemic, driven mainly by farm management and connectivity; evidence for a distinct new viral lineage is limited, so 're_occurrence = true' and 're_emergence = false' better match definitions. Sub-region string was also standardized.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss); other farmed salmonids in freshwater
Event summary: In 1992, IHNV was detected for the first time in Germany and Belgium, following earlier introductions into France and Italy in the late 1980s, marking spread of the virus into new parts of Western Europe’s trout-farming sector. The event was associated with outbreaks in rainbow trout farms and detection in imported fish and eggs, indicating both local transmission and repeated introductions from other European countries. Subsequent control measures and EU‑supported eradication programs focused on culling infected stocks, disinfection, and movement controls, which reduced but did not entirely eliminate IHNV from European freshwater aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International and intra‑European trade in live salmonids and eggs, particularly rainbow trout movements from Italy and France into Germany and Belgium; high farm densities and shared watercourses facilitating downstream spread; limited early screening for IHNV in broodstock and eggs. Internal mechanisms: Establishment and dissemination of European IHNV lineages derived from North American M-genogroup viruses in additional Western European countries; current evidence points to spread of existing European strains rather than emergence of a novel genotype at this time.
Review: review – Event retained as a key step in the expansion of IHNV within Western Europe, but the emergence type was corrected. Because IHNV was already established in the same UNSD sub-region (Western Europe) following 1987 outbreaks in France and Italy, this 1992 spread to Germany and Belgium should not be tagged as intra-continental emergence. It fits better as a re-occurrence within a previously affected sub-region driven by trade and farm connectivity. A general Wikipedia link was removed in favour of more specific reference-laboratory and molecular-epidemiology sources.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and grayling (Thymallus thymallus) in freshwater farms
Event summary: In August 1999, Austria reported an IHNV outbreak in a trout farm with high acute mortality, and over the following decade multiple farms across the country tested positive for IHNV infections. The initial outbreak was linked to recent introduction of infected fish, and subsequent surveillance revealed additional farms infected with European M‑genogroup viruses of two distinct lineages. Through progressive implementation of testing, culling, and movement controls, IHNV-positive farms were reduced and later surveillance of import consignments after 2004 found no further IHNV-positive lots destined for Austria, indicating containment of the earlier wave of introductions and spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Purchase and introduction of infected rainbow trout from other European sources; waterborne spread along connected streams; limited historical health screening prior to stock movements. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of European M-genogroup lineages (including M‑Eur1 and M‑Eur2) in Austrian farms, but available data suggest these lineages reflect diversification of the original European introduction rather than a wholly new strain arising in Austria; the outbreak is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence due to trade and farm connectivity in a previously affected sub-region.
Review: review – Retain as a significant European episode, but adjust interpretation: IHNV was already present in Western Europe, and Austrian outbreaks are best classified as re-occurrence within that sub-region driven by movements of infected trout rather than as re-emergence due to a newly evolved strain. The re_emergence flag was therefore set to false, while re_occurrence remains true.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries and grow-out farms
Event summary: In 1991, the Republic of Korea recorded its first outbreak of IHNV in a rainbow trout hatchery in Gangwon‑do Province, following earlier establishment of the virus in Japan and China. The outbreak caused mass mortalities in hatchery fry and led to subsequent detection of IHNV in additional Korean trout farms, confirming local establishment of the pathogen. Control efforts comprised culling of affected lots, disinfection, and revised sourcing of eggs and fry, but IHNV has since persisted as a recurrent problem in Korean rainbow trout aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected rainbow trout eggs or fry from other IHNV‑endemic regions of East Asia (particularly Japan); intensification of coldwater aquaculture in Korea with high-density hatcheries and farms using shared water sources. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of Asian J‑genogroup IHNV variants in Korean farms with evidence for multiple introductions from Japan and subsequent local diversification, but no clear indication that a novel genotype (as opposed to imported Japanese lineages) drove the 1991 emergence.
Review: review – This event reflects the first detection of IHNV in Korea but not in the animal host system globally. The previous 'first_detection' flag has therefore been removed to keep that category reserved for global first description. Given IHNV was already established in the Eastern Asia sub-region (Japan and China), the Korean outbreaks are better classified as a re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region associated with egg trade and aquaculture expansion.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries and grow-out farms
Event summary: IHNV was first detected in Iranian rainbow trout farms in the early 2000s (around 2003–2004), marking the arrival of the virus in Southern Asia and initiating a period of recurrent outbreaks in trout hatcheries and broodfish facilities. Over the mid‑2000s, IHNV became widespread in Iranian trout-producing regions, with surveillance studies documenting infection in multiple reproduction and grow-out centers. By the late 2000s, the disease had contributed, together with other viral diseases, to a reduction in national rainbow trout production and forced the eradication or restructuring of some farms, after which improved health management, diagnostics, and biosecurity began to stabilize production despite ongoing endemic circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of infected rainbow trout eggs and broodstock from Europe or other IHNV‑endemic regions; rapid expansion and intensification of Iran’s rainbow trout industry with dense stocking and limited early biosecurity; shared water supplies among farms in mountainous regions facilitating downstream spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of IHNV of the European E genogroup into naïve trout populations in a new Asian sub-region, with subsequent local diversification documented in Iranian isolates; this fits both intra‑continental emergence (into Southern Asia) and re-emergence driven by spread of a distinct genogroup into new production systems.
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence episode representing the introduction of E-genogroup IHNV into Southern Asia. The earlier 'first_detection' flag has been removed because first detection in the animal host system occurred decades earlier in North America; however, classification as both intra-continental emergence (new Asian sub-region) and re-emergence (spread of a distinct genogroup into new host populations) is appropriate and allowed by the scheme.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout fry and fingerlings (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries
Event summary: In 2016, Iran experienced several severe IHNV outbreaks in rainbow trout hatcheries in provinces including Tehran, East Azerbaijan and Kermanshah, with reported cumulative mortalities of up to 90% in fry at some sites and 50–60% at others. These mass-mortality events occurred against a backdrop of broader IHN/VHS-like disease problems that over the preceding decade had reduced national trout production from roughly 140,000 tonnes to about 100,000 tonnes as many farms were depopulated or closed. Enhanced diagnostics, genetic analysis confirming E‑genogroup viruses closely related to Italian isolates, and strengthened control measures were rolled out after this crisis period, helping to reduce catastrophic fry mortalities in subsequent production cycles.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density fry production and continuous throughput in hatcheries; ongoing introduction of infected or subclinically infected broodfish or eggs; limited early vaccination or specific antiviral tools; economic pressures favouring rapid restocking that may have reintroduced virus into recovering farms. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of highly virulent E‑genogroup IHNV strains in Iranian farms, with molecular analyses indicating close relationships to European isolates; the severity of these outbreaks reflects amplification of virulent lineages under favourable environmental and management conditions rather than emergence of a wholly new genotype.
Review: review – The event is retained as a distinct, high-impact wave of IHNV outbreaks in Iran, but the timing has been corrected: the key detailed description of ~90% fry mortality and associated national production impacts refers to outbreaks investigated in 2016, not 2014–2015. Event year and country bracket have been updated accordingly, and the re_emergence flag has been cleared so the episode is treated as a severe re-occurrence within an already affected sub-region driven mainly by management, trade and high infection pressure.

EPP common name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Countries: China [2010]; multiple provinces including Heilongjiang, Gansu, Ningxia, Sichuan and other coldwater-farming regions [2010-2014]
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and other cultured salmonids in freshwater and flow-through systems
Event summary: Although IHNV was first reported in China in the mid-1980s, between roughly 2010 and 2014 it caused large-scale disease problems in the rapidly expanding rainbow trout industry across at least seven provinces. During this period, multiple outbreaks with high mortalities were documented, including a severe 2014 episode in Dujiangyan, Sichuan Province, where juvenile trout suffered about 40% mortality and fingerlings about 80% mortality. By the end of this interval, IHNV had become endemic in most Chinese rainbow trout farms, prompting intensified surveillance, molecular epidemiology studies, and development of vaccines and management guidelines to mitigate ongoing losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of coldwater aquaculture in several Chinese provinces; frequent movement of eggs and fry between regions; limited initial use of IHNV-specific vaccines or rigorous health certification; environmental conditions (cold, flowing water) favouring virus transmission. Internal mechanisms: Establishment and spread of Asian J‑genogroup IHNV lineages, with phylogeographic analyses indicating repeated introductions and subsequent regional diversification; the severe 2014 Sichuan outbreak illustrates a pronounced resurgence driven by high farm-level infection pressure and circulation of virulent lineages adapted to intensive rainbow trout production.
Review: review – Retain as the main Chinese emergence episode in the post-1990 period, but adjust event typing. The outbreaks represent a major resurgence and geographic spread within China (still entirely inside the Eastern Asia sub-region), not an intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD sub-region. Evidence points to repeated introductions and amplification of existing J-genogroup lineages under intensified farming rather than a clearly defined new global genotype, so this event is best coded as re-occurrence only.

EPP common name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Host: Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp) in intensive coastal pond culture
Event summary: The event began in 1990 when farmers in central/eastern Thailand observed sudden mass mortalities of grow-out Penaeus monodon with yellowing of the cephalothorax and gills, later termed yellow head disease and associated with a previously unrecognized virus that was formally described in 1991–1993. The disease spread rapidly along the eastern and western coasts of the Gulf of Thailand to southern farming regions, causing near-total crop losses within days of onset and becoming the first major viral disease problem in Asian shrimp farms. By 1993 the epidemic intensity in Thailand declined as management practices changed and white spot syndrome virus emerged as a dominant cause of mortality, and yellow head disease shifted from catastrophic, widespread outbreaks to more sporadic events.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification of P. monodon aquaculture in Thailand during the late 1980s with very high stocking densities, poor biosecurity, and extensive water and stock movements between farms facilitated explosive within-country spread; limited diagnostic capacity initially allowed cryptic circulation before recognition. Internal mechanisms: the virus (later classified as Okavirus flavicapitis genotype 1) is intrinsically highly virulent in P. monodon, with efficient waterborne and cannibalism-mediated transmission, enabling acute epizootics; available evidence suggests the event reflects geographic range expansion and exploitation of a highly susceptible intensively farmed host rather than a newly evolved genotype at that time.
Review: Retain – This row accurately represents the globally first recognized emergence and description of yellow head disease / YHV1 in Thailand around 1990, with timing, geography (central and coastal Thailand), host (P. monodon), and impact (near-total crop losses, first major viral disease of Asian shrimp aquaculture) all well supported by FAO guidance and multiple virology reviews. The classification as both first/global emergence and first detection in the host system is appropriate for this relatively recently evolved pathogen, and no corrections to countries, regions or emergence-type coding were needed. This event clearly belongs among the top-impact emergence episodes for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Countries: China [early 1990s, including Chinese Taipei/Taiwan Province of China]; Philippines [early 1990s]; Indonesia [mid-1990s]; Malaysia [mid-1990s]; Viet Nam [mid-1990s]; Sri Lanka [1998]; India [late 1990s–early 2000s]
Host: Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp) in intensive and semi‑intensive coastal farms; occasional reports in other penaeid shrimp in Asia
Event summary: Following its initial recognition in Thailand, disease consistent with acute yellow head virus infection and/or confirmed YHV genotype 1 was reported during the 1990s from major shrimp‑farming countries across East, South‑east and South Asia, including coastal farming regions of China (including Chinese Taipei), the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam, Sri Lanka and later India. As shrimp industries in these countries expanded, yellow head disease caused episodic mass mortalities in P. monodon grow‑out ponds, often in combination with other viral pathogens such as white spot syndrome virus, leading to major regional production and economic losses. By around 2000, YHV1 and related yellow‑head‑complex viruses had become widely endemic in P. monodon populations throughout much of the Indo‑Pacific range, and overt yellow head disease outbreaks became more sporadic as farm management practices evolved and other viral diseases (e.g. white spot) dominated the mortality profile.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp aquaculture across Asia, widespread movement of live broodstock and post‑larvae between hatcheries and grow‑out farms, and poor on‑farm biosecurity promoted transboundary spread of YHV1; coastal water exchange between farms and inadequate fallowing further amplified transmission. Internal mechanisms: high intrinsic virulence and efficient horizontal transmission of YHV1 in P. monodon supported explosive outbreaks when introduced into naïve farm populations; no single novel genotype is consistently implicated in this Asian spread, which appears predominantly driven by host- and systems-level changes rather than by a distinct genetic shift, although multiple related genotypes in the yellow head complex were detected in subclinical infections.
Review: Review – This row appropriately captures the major wave of intra‑continental spread of yellow head disease/YHV1 from Thailand into other Asian shrimp‑farming countries, which is clearly one of the largest emergence episodes for this EPP in terms of geographic extent and production impact. However, the original version used specific pre‑1990 onset years for some countries (e.g. 1986–1989 for Taiwan, 1989 for China and the Philippines) derived from secondary reviews that discuss possible earlier, retrospectively attributed epizootics; these dates conflict with the project rule to document events from 1990 onwards and are not robustly supported by primary outbreak reports. I have therefore (i) reset the event period to 1992–2000 to reflect the main documented expansion phase following first recognition in Thailand; (ii) replaced exact country years with qualitative time windows (early/mid/late 1990s) consistent with regional FAO/QAAD and review data; (iii) removed a separate entry for “Taiwan (China, Taiwan)” and instead note Chinese Taipei/Taiwan under China, because Taiwan is not listed as a separate country in the project’s Country sheet; and (iv) removed the comment about Madagascar from this Asian event, as African occurrence is handled in a dedicated row. The emergence-type coding as intra‑continental emergence within Asia remains appropriate. Because country‑specific onset years remain approximate and should ideally be cross‑checked against national surveillance or outbreak reports, this event is flagged for further review rather than treated as fully final.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Countries: Madagascar [first WOAH reports of infection with yellow head virus genotype 1 during 2019–2025; exact initial year, spatial extent and outbreak severity remain uncertain]
Host: Penaeus monodon (giant tiger prawn) in marine shrimp aquaculture and associated wild or farm-adjacent populations
Event summary: Between approximately 2019 and 2025, infection with yellow head virus genotype 1 (YHV1) was reported as present or suspected in Madagascar through WOAH’s World Animal Health Information System, representing the first official detection of YHV1 in Africa. Available information suggests detection in farmed or farm‑associated Penaeus monodon stocks, but there are as yet no widely cited descriptions of explosive, Thailand‑style yellow head disease epizootics or national‑scale production crashes linked to YHV1 in Madagascar. The event therefore appears to mark a transition from historical freedom from YHV1 in East African P. monodon broodstock to at least sporadic detection of the virus, with uncertain but potentially significant implications for regional aquaculture and wild shrimp populations. As of 2025, the situation seems to be one of localized or low‑level presence requiring enhanced surveillance and strengthened biosecurity rather than a fully documented, large continental epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (inferred): the most plausible pathway is introduction via international movements of live P. monodon broodstock or post‑larvae, or possibly contaminated crustacean products, from YHV1‑endemic Asian sources into Madagascan hatcheries or farms, facilitated by historical perceptions that East African P. monodon were free of major shrimp viruses and by limited specific screening for YHV1. Expansion of commercial shrimp aquaculture and use/export of East African broodstock may have masked early incursions until more sensitive genotype‑specific diagnostics and structured surveillance were in place. Internal mechanisms: this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of existing highly virulent YHV1 lineages from Asia into a previously free region; there is currently no evidence of a distinct African YHV1 genotype or of viral change driving the emergence, and the limited available data do not yet demonstrate major re‑emergent disease dynamics in local shrimp populations.
Review: Review – The original row described a late‑1990s to early‑2000s emergence of YHV1 in both Madagascar and Mozambique, implying that classical yellow head disease became established in African aquaculture during that period. Closer examination of primary sources shows this is problematic. WOAH’s YHV1 manual and subsequent genetic studies indicate that Mozambique has detections of non‑YHV1 yellow‑head‑complex genotypes (e.g. GAV and genotypes 3–6) predominantly in healthy P. monodon, with no clear evidence of major YHV1‑associated yellow head disease outbreaks there, so Mozambique should not be treated as a confirmed YHV1 emergence site. Conversely, recent WOAH crustacean situation reports list infection with yellow head virus genotype 1 as present or suspected in Madagascar—but not Mozambique—during the last five years, implying a relatively recent first detection confined, so far, to Madagascar. I have therefore (i) removed Mozambique from the countries field; (ii) re‑dated the event to 2019–2025 to align with the period covered by WOAH reports of YHV1 in Madagascar rather than speculative late‑1990s dates; (iii) rewritten the summary and drivers to describe this as a recent, surveillance‑driven inter‑continental range expansion into Africa with currently uncertain production impact, instead of a large early‑2000s epidemic; and (iv) updated the emergence‑type coding so only inter‑continental emergence is marked ‘Yes’ and first_detection is ‘No’, given that global first detection occurred in Thailand in 1990. Because the exact onset year, outbreak scale and economic consequences in Madagascar remain poorly documented, this event is flagged as provisional and should be revisited as more African data become available; depending on final impact, it may or may not merit inclusion among the top‑10 highest‑impact events for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Countries: Mexico [from at least 1999 on the north‑west Pacific coast (Sonora, Sinaloa, Nayarit), later also detected in inland low‑salinity P. vannamei farms in Colima]
Host: Litopenaeus vannamei (whiteleg shrimp) and Litopenaeus stylirostris (blue shrimp) in coastal grow‑out farms on the northwest Pacific coast and, later, inland low‑salinity L. vannamei farms
Event summary: From at least 1999, Mexican researchers using RT‑PCR and hybridization assays began to detect yellow head virus–like infections in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei and L. stylirostris on the northwest Pacific coast of Mexico, representing the first confirmed presence of YHV1‑consistent viruses in shrimp farms in the Americas. Over the subsequent decade, YHV‑like infections were repeatedly documented in cultured and wild penaeids from the Gulf of California region and from inland low‑salinity P. vannamei farms in Colima, but most reports described low-virulence or apparently avirulent genotypes and did not record the explosive mass‑mortality outbreaks characteristic of classical yellow head disease in Asian P. monodon ponds. By around 2010, YHV1 or closely related yellow‑head‑complex variants were considered established but of limited direct clinical impact in Mexican shrimp farming, though their presence raised substantial concern for potential evolution toward higher virulence or problematic co‑infection scenarios and led to strengthened surveillance and import controls across the Americas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: globalization of shrimp aquaculture and movement—both formal and informal—of live shrimp stocks and broodstock between Asia and the Americas likely introduced YHV1‑like viruses into north‑west Mexico; high farm connectivity along the Pacific coast, shared water sources, and contact between farmed and wild shrimp facilitated their subsequent spread among local farms and into wild populations. Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis of Mexican isolates shows close genetic relatedness to YHV1, but field observations indicate markedly reduced virulence in local penaeid hosts compared with the classical Thai YHV1, suggesting genotype- or host‑specific differences in pathogenicity; despite currently low apparent virulence, the presence of YHV1‑consistent viruses in American shrimp populations maintains an ongoing risk that recombination or mutation could generate more pathogenic variants.
Review: Review – This event correctly identifies Mexico as the first documented site of YHV1‑consistent infections in shrimp in the Americas and appropriately classifies it as an inter‑continental emergence, with limited clinical impact but high strategic importance. However, the original row dated the event to 2006–2010 and marked it as a “first detection” event. More recent syntheses show that viruses essentially indistinguishable from YHV1 at key genomic regions were present in farmed L. vannamei and P. stylirostris in north‑west Mexico from at least 1999, with repeated detections through the 2000s, and that earlier presumptive reports from US farms were later considered erroneous. I have therefore (i) extended the event period back to 1999 to encompass the earliest well‑supported detections while retaining coverage of repeated findings through roughly 2010; (ii) simplified the sub‑region to “Central America” to align exactly with the project’s Country sheet entry “South America | Central America” for Mexico; (iii) updated the countries field to note both the coastal Pacific states and later inland low‑salinity farms; and (iv) set first_detection to ‘No’, since global first detection in the host system occurred in Thailand in 1990 and this Mexican episode is better captured solely as an inter‑continental emergence. The overall narrative, host description and mechanistic interpretation remain valid. This row is retained as one of the major emergence events but flagged for review regarding the precise temporal bounds, which could be tightened further if detailed sampling years from the primary Mexican studies are extracted.
