EPP common name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Host: Litopenaeus vannamei (whiteleg shrimp) farmed in intensive inland freshwater ponds (Ratchaburi Province, central Thailand)
Event summary: In 2009, high mortalities with classical yellow head disease–like signs were observed in intensive freshwater inland ponds culturing Litopenaeus vannamei in Ratchaburi Province, central Thailand, with affected shrimp testing positive for yellow head virus by RT‑PCR. From June 2009 to January 2010, multiple farms in this inland production zone experienced acute YHV outbreaks, leading to large crop losses and demonstrating that YHV1 could cause severe disease in P. vannamei under Thai farming conditions after earlier decades in which dramatic outbreaks were mainly associated with P. monodon. The outbreaks subsided after emergency control measures, including fallowing, improved biosecurity, and stocking from YHV‑screened hatcheries, although YHV continues to be regarded as an important transboundary risk for inland and coastal P. vannamei culture in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid conversion of inland freshwater ponds in central Thailand to intensive L. vannamei culture, sometimes with suboptimal biosecurity and use of untested post‑larvae, created new ecological niches for YHV; movement of infected seed or exposure to contaminated water or equipment linking inland and coastal areas likely introduced the virus to these inland systems. Internal mechanisms: molecular characterization of outbreak samples showed they were caused predominantly by a distinct subtype, YHV type 1b, with a characteristic deletion in the ORF3 region encoding gp116, indicating a novel genotype within YHV1 that was associated with severe disease in L. vannamei at a range of salinities; this represents viral genetic diversification, host expansion from P. monodon to P. vannamei, and geographic range expansion into freshwater/inland production environments, collectively constituting a re‑emergence driven by novel strain dynamics and host/environmental shift.
Review: Retain – This row accurately describes the well-documented 2009–2010 outbreaks of yellow head disease due to YHV1b in inland freshwater L. vannamei farms in central Thailand, which are widely regarded as a major re‑emergent episode because they involve a new YHV1 subtype, a host shift from P. monodon to intensively farmed P. vannamei, and expansion into atypical low‑salinity inland systems. The timing, location (Ratchaburi Province), host species, and association with the YHV1b genotype are well supported by Thai field studies and subsequent impact assessments. The classification as re‑emergence (rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate because YHV1 was already endemic in Thai shrimp populations, and this event reflects a genotype/host/environment shift rather than initial introduction into a new region. No corrections to geography, host or emergence-type coding were required; the row is retained as one of the major emergence events for this EPP.

Host: Captive black rat snake (Pantherophis obsoletus, formerly Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta) with severe facial mycotic granuloma
Event summary: In 2009, veterinarians in the United States investigated a captive black rat snake with chronic facial masses and granulomatous dermatitis, from which a previously undescribed Chrysosporium-like fungus was isolated and characterized. The fungus was formally described as Chrysosporium ophiodiicola (later reclassified into the new genus Ophidiomyces), establishing the first definitive species-level description of O. ophiodiicola as a pathogen of snakes. This index description ended without documented onward transmission in the collection but provided the taxonomic and diagnostic framework that enabled subsequent recognition of snake fungal disease in wild populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased diagnostic capacity and mycological investigation in captive reptile medicine enabled recognition and description of a previously overlooked keratinophilic fungus. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype characterization (formal delineation of O. ophiodiicola from the Chrysosporium anamorph Nannizziopsis vriesii complex) rather than a newly evolved pathogen per se; no specific adaptation event is implicated in this captive case.

Host: Multiple free-ranging snake species including timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus), eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus), mud snake (Farancia abacura), various Nerodia, Pantherophis, Thamnophis and other colubrids and viperids
Event summary: From 2006 onwards, wildlife biologists in the eastern United States began observing severe facial and body skin lesions and high mortality in timber rattlesnakes in New Hampshire and other pitviper populations, with similar disease later confirmed in eastern massasauga rattlesnakes in Illinois in 2008 and other species across the eastern and Midwestern states. Over the subsequent decade, targeted field studies and diagnostic testing linked these outbreaks to Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and documented its presence in dozens of wild snake species, with USGS reporting the pathogen in at least 20 eastern states and widespread clinical snake fungal disease by the mid‑2010s. By the end of this episode, some localized populations such as Illinois eastern massasaugas and New England timber rattlesnakes showed marked declines and high disease-associated mortality, while surveillance and management responses (e.g., monitoring and treatment trials) were ramped up but the disease had become entrenched regionally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Habitat loss and fragmentation, small and isolated snake populations, environmental stressors, and possibly changing climate conditions are thought to have increased host susceptibility and facilitated emergence and recognition of disease; expanding wildlife health surveillance and molecular diagnostics also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain has been conclusively proven to underlie this emergence, but O. ophiodiicola shows traits consistent with environmental persistence and effective transmission in cool, humid microhabitats, supporting geographic range expansion (inherent) and enhanced transmission in stressed pitviper populations; the event is therefore categorized primarily as re-occurrence driven by external ecological change rather than clear pathogen innovation.

Host: Free-ranging eastern foxsnake (Pantherophis gloydi/vulpinus) and additional wild snakes in southern and central Ontario
Event summary: In March 2015, wildlife health authorities in Ontario, Canada, diagnosed an adult female eastern foxsnake near Lake Erie with severe dermatitis caused by Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola, representing the first confirmed case of snake fungal disease in Canada and the first documented wild snake infection outside the United States. Subsequent targeted testing in 2015–2017 detected the pathogen at several other sites in southern and central Ontario, sometimes without overt disease, indicating wider environmental presence and exposure in Canadian snake communities. The episode led to the inclusion of snake fungal disease considerations in provincial survey protocols for species-at-risk snakes and stimulated ongoing monitoring, but no broad-scale Canadian population collapses attributable solely to SFD have yet been documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely natural or human-assisted movement of infected snakes or contaminated substrates across the U.S.–Canada border within connected Great Lakes and agricultural landscapes; increased awareness and targeted diagnostics following U.S. reports facilitated recognition. Internal mechanisms: No distinct Canadian lineage has been implicated; the event likely reflects geographic range expansion of existing North American clades into adjacent habitats rather than novel strain evolution.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]; Czechia [2015]
Host: Free-ranging grass snakes (Natrix natrix), dice snake (Natrix tessellata), and other natricine and viperid snakes from Great Britain and Czechia
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2016, researchers screened hundreds of carcasses and shed skins from wild snakes in Great Britain and the Czech Republic and identified Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola by PCR and culture in multiple grass snakes and a dice snake with characteristic skin lesions, constituting the first confirmed detections of the pathogen and snake fungal disease in free-ranging European snakes. Analysis revealed that O. ophiodiicola was widely distributed in England and Wales and present at least at a point site in the Czech Republic, indicating continental circulation beyond North America. Subsequent retrospective work on museum specimens from Natrix and Vipera snakes showed that the fungus had actually been present in Europe since at least 1959, so the 2010–2016 episode reflects renewed recognition and re-occurrence of clinically apparent disease rather than a novel continent-wide introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enhanced wildlife disease surveillance and application of O. ophiodiicola-specific molecular diagnostics to both contemporary and historical material enabled recognition of an endemic but previously undiagnosed pathogen; environmental changes (e.g., altered land use, climate variability) may have increased disease expression in some populations. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses revealed at least one European clade distinct from North American lineages, suggesting long-term regional evolution, with occasional detection of North American-like clades in Switzerland indicating historical intercontinental exchanges; however, no single recent mutation has been clearly tied to this emergence pattern.

Countries: United States of America [2013]; Puerto Rico [2015]
Host: Multiple wild snake species across the continental United States (58 species tested) and native snakes in Puerto Rico on U.S. military lands
Event summary: From roughly 2013 onward, coordinated surveillance across 56 U.S. Department of Defense installations tested 657 snakes representing 58 species for Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and documented widespread infection and ophidiomycosis across much of the eastern, midwestern, and newly the western United States, as well as on military lands in Puerto Rico. This large-scale effort revealed the pathogen’s presence in regions where it had not previously been reported, including western states such as California and Idaho and Caribbean habitats in Puerto Rico, thereby extending its known geographic and host range. By the end of the 2010s, O. ophiodiicola was recognized as a broadly distributed pathogen across North America, with population-level effects still being evaluated but concerning signs of disease in multiple snake communities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of snakes and contaminated substrates via military logistics, trade, and other human activities, combined with natural dispersal, likely facilitated spread into western U.S. regions and Puerto Rico; intensified targeted surveillance on military lands substantially increased detection probability. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen shows ecological flexibility and environmental persistence that support geographic range expansion (inherent) into diverse climates and habitats, but there is no evidence of a single newly evolved, highly transmissible strain driving this expansion; thus the event is treated as inter- and intra-continental emergence largely mediated by host and human movement.

Host: Captive snakes in Japan (including imported rat snakes and other colubrids held in private collections)
Event summary: Around 2019–2021, veterinarians in Japan investigated dermatitis outbreaks in multiple captive snakes, some originating from overseas trade, and histopathology and culture identified Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola as the etiologic agent, marking the first confirmed report of ophidiomycosis in Asia. The disease manifested as severe crusting and necrotic skin lesions in several snakes housed in the same facility, suggesting in situ transmission within captivity. Affected animals were treated and biosecurity measures recommended, but the event raised concern that infected captive snakes could act as reservoirs for spillover into native wild snake populations if escapes or releases occurred.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International wildlife trade in live snakes introduced O. ophiodiicola into Japanese collections, with captive-husbandry conditions (high stocking density, shared enclosures, and environmental stress) favoring pathogen transmission and disease expression. Internal mechanisms: This episode illustrates host expansion and geographic range expansion mediated by human movement of hosts rather than documented new strain evolution; available genotyping suggests these Asian cases are closely related to previously characterized lineages.

Host: Free-ranging coastal carpet pythons (Morelia spilota mcdowelli), eastern bandy-bandy (Vermicella annulata), white-crowned snake (Cacophis harriettae) and other squamates in South East Queensland
Event summary: Between April 2023 and September 2024, clinicians at the Australia Zoo Wildlife Hospital in South East Queensland received multiple free-ranging snakes with severe, disfiguring dermatomycosis, including a coastal carpet python admitted in August 2024 with extensive crusted lesions and dysecdysis; skin testing identified Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and confirmed snake fungal disease as the cause, representing the first documented cases of this pathogen in free-ranging Australian snakes. Additional cases in coastal carpet pythons, an eastern bandy-bandy, and a white-crowned snake were subsequently confirmed, indicating that the fungus was already established in local wild reptile communities. By early 2026, these findings had been synthesized in an Australian Veterinary Journal paper and widely publicized, prompting concern over potential long-term impacts on Australia’s exceptionally diverse reptile fauna and calls for rapid surveillance and management responses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The introduction pathway is not definitively proven but is strongly suspected to involve international movement of captive reptiles or contaminated materials, combined with climatic changes in eastern Australia that favor survival of Onygenaceae fungi and high local densities of susceptible hosts; increasing clinical awareness and diagnostic capacity also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: The cases demonstrate geographic range expansion of O. ophiodiicola into a new continent and host expansion within Australian squamates, but current data do not yet implicate a uniquely virulent Australian strain; impacts appear linked to the pathogen’s general ability to cause severe, chronic skin disease in ectothermic hosts under suitable environmental conditions.

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Wild birds, especially double-crested cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) and associated colonial waterbirds
Event summary: Beginning in late summer 1990, virulent Newcastle disease virus caused heavy mortality in double‑crested cormorant colonies in western Canada, killing more than 10,000 birds and marking the first recognized large‑scale ND epizootic in North American cormorants.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/51388595_Newcastle_disease_in_wild_water_birds_in_western_Canada_1990?utm_source=openai)) In 1992, closely related viruses produced another major epizootic in juvenile cormorants across several northern U.S. states and a Canadian province, confirming that NDV had become established in this wild reservoir with recurrent die‑offs in shared breeding areas.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/1992-epizootic-newcastle-disease-double-crested-cormorants-north-america?utm_source=openai)) Mortality declined as colonies dispersed after each breeding season, but NDV has since recurred intermittently in cormorants and other wild waterbirds in the region.([pubs.usgs.gov](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/2001114?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense colonial nesting, accumulation of fecal contamination in roosts, and congregation of juveniles at breeding sites facilitated intense fecal–oral transmission and large die‑offs once virulent NDV was introduced.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/1992-epizootic-newcastle-disease-double-crested-cormorants-north-america?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a novel genotype specific to these outbreaks; they are best interpreted as re‑occurrence of virulent NDV already present in North America, amplified by ecological conditions in cormorant colonies rather than major viral evolutionary change.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8236515/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain this event as a major wildlife NDV episode but correct it to a linked 1990–1992 cormorant epizootic affecting both Canada and the United States. Updated the year range, added the United States of America to the country list, and clarified that the mechanism is re-occurrence (no clear novel genotype). Event-level sources were adjusted to include primary descriptions of the 1990–1992 cormorant outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Domestic poultry (primarily commercial and backyard chickens), with some involvement of other domestic birds
Event summary: In 1993–1994, South Africa experienced one of its most severe Newcastle disease epizootics when a newly introduced genotype VIIb virus, probably originating from Europe and ultimately the Far East, spread rapidly through commercial and backyard chicken flocks across multiple provinces.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14991446/)) Within months the virus had spread throughout Southern Africa, causing devastating losses in all classes of poultry, with contemporary reports estimating up to roughly one million poultry deaths per week at the epidemic peak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) Intensive vaccination campaigns, movement controls and biosecurity improvements eventually brought the 1993/1994 epidemic under control, although genotype VIIb viruses continued to be detected sporadically until the late 1990s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and geographic expansion of intensive poultry production, movement of live birds and hatching eggs between regions, and gaps in vaccination coverage and farm-level biosecurity favored rapid spread once genotype VIIb NDV was introduced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by the incursion of a novel, highly virulent genotype VIIb lineage that displaced earlier endemic genotype VIII viruses and formed part of the wider fourth ND panzootic caused by genotype VII.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Reinterpreted this row to represent the major 1993–1994 genotype VIIb epizootic in South Africa, rather than a generalized 1990–1994 genotype VIII resurgence. Adjusted the event years, emphasized the scale of mortality, and clarified that this is a re-emergence episode driven by introduction of an exotic genotype VIIb virus, not an intra- or inter-continental emergence. Existing South Africa–specific molecular epidemiology sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens (broilers, layers), with occasional infection of other domestic and wild birds
Event summary: From the mid-1990s, China began to detect class II genotype VII Newcastle disease viruses (notably subgenotypes VIIc and VIId) during severe outbreaks in chickens, and over the late 1990s and early 2000s these viruses spread from eastern into southern and southwestern regions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai)) By the early 2000s, genotype VII NDVs had become the predominant field genotype across most of China, associated with frequent vaccine‑break outbreaks and substantial economic losses despite intensive use of traditional LaSota‑like vaccines.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai)) After around 2005, genotype VII remained endemic but incidence fluctuated as vaccination strategies were updated and other genotypes co‑circulated, with ND persisting as a major endemic disease rather than a single explosive epidemic.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and geographic expansion of China’s poultry industry, high densities of commercial flocks, and imperfect matching between commonly used genotype II vaccine strains and emerging genotype VII field viruses favored recurrent large outbreaks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and selection—genotype VII viruses with enhanced fitness and partial antigenic divergence under widespread vaccination became dominant and seeded the fourth ND panzootic.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Corrected the start year from 1995 to 1996 to align with reports that genotype VII outbreaks in mainland China were first documented in the mid- to late 1990s, while retaining 2005 as an approximate end to the main emergence phase. Classification as re-emergence (novel predominant genotype in a region with longstanding NDV circulation) is appropriate; no intra-continental emergence flag was added because NDV as a species was already established in Eastern Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1997]; Ireland [1997]
Host: Commercial chickens, turkeys and other domestic poultry in large integrated operations and smaller flocks
Event summary: In early 1997, virulent Newcastle disease reappeared in previously disease‑free Northern Ireland and was soon detected in multiple large commercial poultry units in Great Britain, with a linked outbreak confirmed in the Republic of Ireland in a flock that had recently imported day‑old chicks from the North.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/newcastle-disease)) Antigenic and genetic analyses showed that viruses from 11 outbreaks in Great Britain, 12 in Northern Ireland and one in Ireland were essentially identical and belonged to a genotype VII lineage closely related to strains circulating elsewhere in Europe.([bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bvajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1136/vr.145.15.417?utm_source=openai)) Control was achieved through stamping‑out, stringent movement restrictions and, in some areas, emergency vaccination; around 1.4 million poultry were slaughtered in Northern Ireland alone and trade in live poultry and hatching eggs within and from the island of Ireland was temporarily suspended.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/newcastle-disease))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of NDV into a non‑vaccinating, high‑density poultry sector in Northern Ireland, followed by movements of live birds and hatching eggs within the British Isles, allowed rapid spread before detection; trade patterns with continental Europe were the most likely source of the initial incursion.([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1997-03-06/debates/23df5983-338e-4d41-8d05-5e4d70e1035b/NewcastleDisease?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence associated with the incursion of a highly virulent genotype VII virus that was antigenically distinct from traditional vaccine strains and part of the wider fourth ND panzootic, rather than evolution of an endemic UK lineage.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378113512002970?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Added this missing high-impact event representing the 1997 genotype VII Newcastle disease epizootic in Northern Ireland, Great Britain and the Republic of Ireland, during which roughly 1.4 million poultry were culled and significant trade disruptions occurred. Classified as re-emergence driven by introduction of a virulent genotype VII lineage into a region with prior ND history, rather than as intra- or inter-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Domestic poultry (commercial chickens), with possible involvement of backyard flocks
Event summary: From 1998 to 2000, Australia experienced its first recorded outbreaks of virulent Newcastle disease when previously endemic low‑virulence NDV strains circulating in chickens in New South Wales evolved into highly virulent forms, causing outbreaks on multiple farms in the Mangrove Mountain and western Sydney regions.([www1.health.gov.au](https://www1.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/cda-pubs-cdi-1998-cdi2210-cdi2210i.htm?utm_source=openai)) The initial 1998 outbreaks and subsequent flare‑ups in 1999 and 2000 led to the destruction of around two million chickens and major disruption of regional egg and meat production.([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/science/news/stories/1999/42994.htm?utm_source=openai)) Through depopulation of affected flocks, strict movement controls, surveillance and enhanced biosecurity, authorities eradicated the virulent viruses and Australia regained ND‑free status, with only low‑virulence NDV remaining in poultry.([outbreak.gov.au](https://www.outbreak.gov.au/prepare-respond/identify-pests-diseases/emergency-animal-diseases-field-guide?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density commercial poultry production, movements of birds and equipment among farms, and prior circulation of lentogenic NDV strains created conditions in which virulent variants could arise and spread rapidly once they emerged.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19184867/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Clear re‑emergence driven by increased virulence/pathogenicity, as molecular analyses showed stepwise acquisition of multiple basic amino acids at the fusion protein cleavage site in a previously low‑virulence genotype I lineage, converting it into a velogenic virus capable of causing severe disease and high mortality in chickens.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19184867/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain this event as a key example of in situ evolution of virulent NDV in a previously NDV-free country for velogenic strains, but improve documentation. Replaced generic North American references with Australian outbreak reports and molecular epidemiology papers, and confirmed classification as re-emergence driven by virulence increase in endemic lentogenic viruses rather than by new continental introduction.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Backyard gamefowl and exhibition poultry, village poultry, and commercial layer and broiler chickens
Event summary: Beginning in the late 1990s, virulent NDV outbreaks caused by subgenotype Vb viruses were reported widely in poultry in Mexico, including a major 2000 outbreak in the La Laguna region; related viruses became endemic in village and commercial flocks and spread into parts of Central America.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai)) In October 2002, a closely related virulent strain was confirmed in backyard gamefowl in southern California, USA, and over 2002–2003 the disease spread through backyard flocks in California, Nevada, Arizona and Texas, with spillover into commercial egg operations and the depopulation of about 3–4 million birds.([ars.usda.gov](https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=155202&utm_source=openai)) Aggressive stamping-out, quarantine and movement controls eventually eradicated the outbreak in the United States, but genetically similar virulent genotype Vb viruses have continued to circulate endemically in parts of Mexico and neighbouring countries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive informal trade and illegal movement of fighting cocks and backyard poultry between Mexico, Central America and the southwestern USA, dense networks of small flocks, and inadequate biosecurity facilitated spread across national and subregional boundaries; live‑bird markets and shows served as amplifiers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence associated with sustained circulation and diversification of a virulent class II genotype V lineage (subgenotype Vb) in Mexico and Central America that repeatedly seeded new foci, rather than the emergence of a new genotype in North America; the key change was geographic range expansion of an already virulent lineage within and between the South American (Central America) and North American subregions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain this as a major Mexico–USA NDV epizootic but correct geography and emergence classification. Updated the continent field to reflect that Mexico (Central America) falls under the South America continent category in the project schema, removed the intra-continental emergence flag because NDV was long established in both subregions, and emphasised that this is a re-emergence and range expansion of genotype Vb rather than first continental introduction.

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Village chickens and other rural poultry, plus small-scale and commercial chicken flocks across all agro-ecological zones
Event summary: In 2008, endemic Newcastle disease in Nigeria culminated in a nationwide epizootic in which an estimated 78,526 outbreaks were reported across the country, mostly in village chickens and smallholder or semi‑intensive commercial flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) The epidemic imposed an estimated financial burden of 8.9 billion Nigerian naira on the rural chicken sector alone, underscoring the heavy, often under‑reported toll of ND on poultry‑dependent livelihoods.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) Despite these losses, ND remained endemic after 2008, with recurrent outbreaks in backyard and commercial systems and growing recognition of the diverse virulent genotypes circulating in West Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive movement of live birds through live‑bird markets, weak biosecurity in village and peri‑urban flocks, limited access to quality vaccines, and incomplete cold‑chain and dosing practices created conditions for explosive spread and persistence of NDV nationwide.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The event reflects amplification of multiple virulent NDV lineages (including genotype V sublineages and genotype XVII) already present in Nigeria rather than emergence of a single new genotype, so it is best categorized as a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven mainly by management and marketing factors.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19052688/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Added this row to capture the 2008 nationwide Newcastle disease epizootic in Nigeria, documented to involve more than 78,000 reported outbreaks and very large economic losses, which clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful recent ND events. Classified as re-occurrence driven primarily by systemic control and biosecurity gaps rather than by the appearance of a single novel genotype.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Sub-regions: South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Western Asia
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens, occasionally other domestic birds (e.g. turkeys)
Event summary: Between 2011 and 2013, a new sub-genotype of genotype VII Newcastle disease virus (often designated VIIi or closely related lineages) emerged and caused severe disease on poultry farms in Indonesia and Pakistan before being detected in outbreaks in Israel and parts of the Middle East.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12455?utm_source=openai)) The outbreaks were characterised by high mortality in vaccinated flocks and rapid spread within each country, raising concern that this lineage could seed a new ND panzootic.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12455?utm_source=openai)) Through intensified surveillance, updated molecular characterisation and adjustments to vaccination and biosecurity, affected countries eventually reduced the largest waves of disease, although genotype VII lineages have remained endemic across much of Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high poultry densities and extensive live-bird marketing in Indonesia, Pakistan and Israel, combined with frequent movement of hatching eggs, chicks and live birds, promoted wide dissemination of the emerging VIIi sub-genotype within and between Asian subregions.([kci.go.kr](https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART001432236&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence (sub-genotype VIIi within genotype VII) with evidence of enhanced transmission and partial immune escape in vaccinated flocks, and geographic range expansion across distinct Asian subregions, all within a continent where NDV was long established.([kci.go.kr](https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART001432236&utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain this event as a key wave in the fifth ND panzootic driven by sub-genotype VIIi, but remove the intra-continental emergence label because NDV was already established in all affected Asian subregions; under the project definitions this should be treated purely as re-emergence associated with a novel lineage and vaccine-break outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Commercial chickens (broilers, layers), backyard poultry, and domestic pigeons; occasional wild birds
Event summary: Around 2013, South Africa experienced a new wave of Newcastle disease outbreaks caused by genotype VIIh viruses that replaced earlier circulating genotypes (VIII, VIIb, VIId), initially detected in KwaZulu-Natal and subsequently spreading to other provinces.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) By late 2013 the same genotype VIIh strain had been confirmed in neighbouring Zimbabwe, indicating rapid regional dissemination and causing substantial losses in commercial and smallholder poultry.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai)) Over the following two years, strengthened vaccination programmes and movement controls reduced outbreak frequency, but genotype VIIh became established as the dominant virulent NDV lineage in the subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of poultry and informal trade in live birds, together with gaps in vaccination coverage and biosecurity in both commercial and smallholder sectors, facilitated regional dissemination of the newly introduced genotype VIIh virus.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence linked to a novel genotype (VIIh) with high virulence that replaced prior endemic genotypes and expanded geographically within Southern Africa, illustrating genotype turnover and ongoing viral evolution in the region.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This event accurately captures the introduction and spread of genotype VIIh Newcastle disease virus in South Africa and Zimbabwe from 2013 onward, including its displacement of earlier genotypes and regional spread. The geographic scope, timing and classification as re-emergence driven by a novel genotype are consistent with detailed South African and broader African molecular epidemiology studies.

EPP common name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Backyard gamefowl and exhibition chickens, smallholder flocks, and commercial layer operations in California
Event summary: In May 2018, virulent Newcastle disease was detected in a backyard exhibition flock in Los Angeles County, California, and over the next two years the outbreak spread widely through backyard gamefowl in southern California, with occasional transmission to commercial layer farms.([outbreak.gov.au](https://www.outbreak.gov.au/prepare-respond/identify-pests-diseases/emergency-animal-diseases-field-guide?utm_source=openai)) By the time California and federal authorities declared the state free of virulent ND in 2020, more than 1.2 million birds had been euthanized and hundreds of premises in Los Angeles, Riverside and San Bernardino counties had been affected.([cdfa.ca.gov](https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/ahfss/Animal_Health/newcastle_disease_info.html?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak was eventually contained through extensive depopulation, quarantine zones, movement restrictions and intensive outreach to gamefowl communities, echoing earlier major California outbreaks in 1971–1974 and 2002–2003.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659000/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense networks of backyard and gamefowl flocks in urban and peri‑urban southern California, frequent informal movement and trade of birds (including illegal imports), and limited biosecurity in small flocks created ideal conditions for sustained transmission and spillover into commercial operations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659000/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Virus characterisation showed close similarity to virulent NDV lineages circulating in Mexico and to previous California outbreaks, with no evidence of a substantially novel genotype; the event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by anthropogenic movement and management factors rather than by a fundamentally new viral variant.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This row accurately describes the scale, timing and drivers of the 2018–2020 virulent Newcastle disease outbreak in southern California, including the approximate number of birds culled, affected counties and the predominance of backyard gamefowl, and correctly classifies it as a major re-occurrence rather than emergence of a new genotype.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Germany [2011]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2011]; Belgium [2011]; France [2012]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]; Luxembourg [2012]; Switzerland [2012]; Austria [2012]; Denmark [2012]; Sweden [2012]; Norway [2012]; Finland [2012]; Ireland [2012]; Italy [2012]; Spain [2012]; Czechia [2012]; Poland [2012]; Estonia [2012]; additional EU countries with serological evidence of exposure by 2013 [2012-2013]
Host: Domestic ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats); wild ruminants including cervids (e.g. red deer, roe deer) and European bison in affected regions
Event summary: Origin: Between August and October 2011, a previously unknown orthobunyavirus was detected in dairy cattle with fever, diarrhoea and acute milk drop in North Rhine‑Westphalia (Germany) and across the Netherlands, and was identified and named Schmallenberg virus after the town where the index samples originated. Development: Over the 2011 and 2012 Culicoides midge seasons, SBV spread explosively across western and northern Europe and then into southern and parts of eastern Europe, with more than 5,700 infected farms officially reported by August 1, 2012 and high national‑level seroprevalence by 2013, causing tens of thousands of congenital malformations, abortions and stillbirths in calves, lambs and goat kids as naïve pregnant animals were infected in mid‑gestation. Ending: By 2013–2014, very high within‑herd and regional seroprevalence, together with the seasonal nature of the midge vectors, led to a marked decline in new clinical cases and a transition from epidemic spread to low‑level endemic circulation and sporadic congenital disease in previously unexposed or replacement stock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive populations of competent Culicoides biting midges across northern and central Europe, favourable summer–autumn climatic conditions for vector survival and long‑distance windborne dispersal, high densities and connectivity of cattle and small‑ruminant herds, and a wholly naïve European ruminant population to Simbu‑group viruses collectively enabled rapid continental spread once SBV was introduced. Enhanced veterinary surveillance following the 2006–2008 bluetongue serotype 8 epidemic aided early detection and case documentation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate SBV is a novel or recently derived Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyavirus, likely arising via reassortment, representing a novel strain/genotype; its efficient replication in Culicoides vectors and ruminant hosts, and strong transplacental tropism leading to arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly syndrome in fetuses, underpinned its high apparent impact in immunologically naïve European herds, although virulence appeared relatively stable throughout this initial epidemic wave.
Review: Review – Retain as the foundational global emergence/European epidemic event, but country‑specific first‑detection years were corrected for France, the United Kingdom and Denmark (now starting in 2012 based on national reports), and the intra‑continental emergence flag was set to “false” to keep event‑type categories mutually exclusive, leaving this row classified primarily as first global emergence/first detection. Sources are appropriate EFSA/EID/ANSES syntheses plus national summaries; Wikipedia links are treated as supplementary only.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic ruminants (dairy cattle in central, southern and western Ethiopia; cattle, sheep and goats in Zambezia Province, Mozambique)
Event summary: Origin: In the wake of SBV’s 2011 emergence in Europe, cross‑sectional serosurveys of dairy cattle sampled between September 2011 and May 2012 in central, southern and western Ethiopia and of cattle, sheep and goats sampled in September 2013 in Zambezia Province, Mozambique, revealed very high apparent seroprevalence of SBV antibodies using commercial competitive ELISAs, with about 56–58% of Ethiopian animals and 83% of herds seropositive and near‑100% cattle seroprevalence on sampled Mozambican farms, coinciding with increased reports of reproductive disorders in dairy herds. Development: These findings, together with the absence of prior vaccination and the known spread of SBV across Europe, were interpreted as evidence that SBV, or a closely related Simbu‑serogroup virus indistinguishable in the ELISA, had reached eastern Africa by 2011–2013 and was circulating widely in domestic ruminants, although no viral RNA or isolates were obtained and cross‑reactivity with endemic Simbu viruses could not be ruled out. Ending: After these initial surveys, only limited follow‑up studies have been published and no large, clinically obvious, multi‑year epidemic comparable to the north‑western European episode has been documented; African evidence for SBV remains largely serologic, and the true burden of reproductive loss specifically attributable to SBV versus other Simbu viruses is still uncertain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers include long‑distance movement of infected Culicoides midges on prevailing winds from Europe or the Middle East, trade in live breeding cattle and possibly infected semen from Europe, and high densities of susceptible dairy cattle and mixed ruminant herds in tropical environments that support abundant Culicoides populations. Internal mechanisms: If the serologic signals indeed reflect SBV rather than another Simbu virus, the episode represents geographic range expansion of the European epidemic lineage into the African continent, exploiting existing vector species and host niches rather than documented viral innovation; genetic confirmation is lacking, so the exact relationship of these African infections to European SBV strains is unresolved.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the first strong serologic evidence for SBV (or a very closely related Simbu virus) in Africa; classified as an inter‑continental emergence based on timing and high prevalence, but confidence is limited because only ELISA data are available and authors explicitly note possible cross‑reactivity with other Simbu viruses. Recommended for expert review of pathogen attribution and whether this should be attributed specifically to Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense or treated more cautiously as “SBV‑like” circulation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Domestic ruminants: dairy cattle, yellow cattle, buffalo and goats on commercial farms in Guangdong Province
Event summary: Origin: To investigate possible spread of SBV beyond Europe, researchers collected 317 ruminant sera from multiple farms in subtropical Guangdong Province, southern China, between 2012 and 2015 and tested them with a commercial SBV competitive ELISA and a real‑time RT‑PCR; high seroprevalence was observed, particularly in dairy cattle (often 30–100% seropositive by farm), and temporal patterns suggested that SBV infection in Guangdong could be traced back at least to 2012. Development: No SBV RNA was detected in the sera and virus isolates were not obtained, but the authors argued that the combination of high seroprevalence across several years, stronger summer–autumn signals and known importation of European bull semen and breeding stock made recent introduction of SBV into East Asia plausible, potentially via contaminated semen or wind‑borne Culicoides, although they acknowledged possible ELISA cross‑reactivity with other Simbu serogroup viruses. Ending: After 2015, no confirmed large‑scale clinical SBV epidemics were reported in Chinese ruminant populations, and the initial study emphasized the need for molecular confirmation and broader surveillance; subsequent global reviews still treat this as preliminary serologic evidence for SBV presence in East Asia rather than definitive proof of endemic circulation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers include importation of semen and breeding cattle from heavily affected European countries, which could introduce SBV into naïve herds, and potential wind‑assisted spread of infected Culicoides from Europe or western Asia along expanding trade routes such as air travel and the China–Europe rail corridor. Guangdong’s warm, humid climate and abundant arbovirus vectors provide ecological conditions conducive to establishment once introduced. Internal mechanisms: Assuming the ELISA signal reflects true SBV infection, the episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of the European SBV lineage into East Asia, exploiting existing Culicoides fauna and ruminant hosts; no viral genomes were obtained, so viral evolution or reassortment cannot be evaluated.
Review: Review – New event capturing the first published serologic evidence for SBV infection in East Asia; classified as an inter‑continental emergence into Asia because infection appears to date back to 2012, likely predating or paralleling detections in Türkiye. However, like the African serosurveys, this relies solely on ELISA without VNT or PCR confirmation and may cross‑react with other Simbu viruses; pathogen attribution and the choice to treat this as definite SBV emergence warrant expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic ruminants (primarily beef and dairy cattle, with evidence of exposure in small ruminants) in central Anatolia and later other western and southern Turkish regions
Event summary: Origin: Following the large 2011–2013 SBV epidemic in Europe, serologic and molecular surveys of cattle herds in central Anatolia in 2013 detected SBV RNA in approximately 3% of blood samples and neutralizing antibodies in about 24% of sera, with S‑segment sequences showing 98–99% nucleotide identity to European SBV strains, indicating introduction of the virus into Turkish ruminant populations. Development: Additional surveys and case reports over the following years found further seropositivity and evidence of exposure in several Turkish regions, and later work in the Eastern Mediterranean region documented around 29% ELISA seropositivity and low‑level PCR positivity in ruminants between 2015 and 2017, but no explosive epidemic with congenital malformations on the scale seen in north‑western Europe was recorded. Ending: After 2017, SBV appears to have circulated at low to moderate levels in Türkiye, with sporadic detections rather than sustained large outbreaks, suggesting that local herd immunity and climatic/vector conditions may have limited clinical impact despite established circulation within the Western Asia sub‑region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers include windborne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges from affected parts of south‑eastern Europe across the Bosporus and Aegean, cross‑border movement of ruminants and possibly trade in infected semen, combined with limited initial awareness of SBV in Türkiye, which may have delayed its recognition. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced Turkish SBV strains were highly similar to European isolates, indicating introduction of the existing epidemic lineage rather than the emergence of a novel variant; this episode therefore mainly reflects geographic range expansion within Asia and establishment in Western Asia, supported by competent local Culicoides vectors and largely naïve ruminant hosts, rather than viral innovation.
Review: Review – Existing event retained but reclassified from inter‑continental to intra‑continental emergence because earlier serologic data from China indicate that Asia was already affected by SBV (or an SBV‑like virus) by 2012; this Turkish episode is therefore best interpreted as the first confirmed spread into the Western Asia sub‑region rather than the first appearance on the Asian continent. The narrative was updated to reference both early RT‑PCR and later serologic work in Türkiye, and the evidence base (Tonbak 2016 and subsequent regional studies) is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Ireland [2016-2017]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2016-2017]; France [2016-2017]; Belgium [2016-2017]; Germany [2016-2017]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2016-2017]; other previously affected western and northern European countries with evidence of renewed circulation [2016-2017]
Host: Domestic ruminants, especially dairy and beef cattle and sheep, in previously exposed regions of western and northern Europe
Event summary: Origin: After several years of very low clinical incidence following the initial 2011–2013 epidemic, Schmallenberg virus activity reappeared around 2016 in western and northern Europe, with renewed detection of SBV RNA and congenital malformations in calves and lambs in Ireland, Great Britain, France, Germany, the Netherlands and neighbouring countries. Development: Molecular sequencing of SBV from malformed lambs and calves in Great Britain in 2016–2017 revealed a second distinct genetic clade circulating alongside viruses closely related to the original epidemic strain, while bulk‑milk and serologic surveillance in Ireland and France documented substantial re‑circulation in cattle herds and the birth of congenitally affected offspring, indicating that waning population immunity and the accumulation of naïve youngstock had created conditions for a new wave of infection. Ending: By late 2017, reported clinical cases again declined and serologic data suggested increasing immunity in affected regions, with SBV returning to a pattern of low‑level endemic circulation and reinforcing the need for ongoing vector and serologic surveillance to detect future re‑emergence episodes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Key external drivers included the gradual replacement of highly immune adult animals from the 2011–2013 epidemic by susceptible youngstock, waning herd immunity over time, favourable climatic conditions for Culicoides midges in 2015–2016, and continued high densities of susceptible ruminants in intensive production systems. Internal mechanisms: Whole‑genome analyses comparing SBV sequences from the 2011–2013 outbreak with those from 2016–2017 in Great Britain and elsewhere identified a second distinct genetic clade, indicating viral diversification during the inter‑epidemic period; this genetic divergence, together with altered population immunity, supports classification of this episode as a re‑emergence driven partly by novel or diverged genotypes, even though clinical severity and manifestations remained broadly similar to the original epidemic.
Review: Retain – The 2016–2017 western/northern European wave is correctly captured as a major re‑emergence event with good support from genomic and surveillance data, and classification as “re‑emergence” (without co‑flagging re‑occurrence or inter/intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate given the identification of a distinct SBV clade during this period. No substantial corrections were needed beyond clarifying that affected countries are those with documented renewed circulation and congenital cases.

Host: Domestic ruminants (cattle and sheep) on dairy and mixed farms, and Culicoides biting midges, in multiple regions of Israel
Event summary: Origin: As part of national arbovirus surveillance, monthly sampling of Culicoides biting midges and diagnostic testing of malformed newborn ruminants between June 2018 and December 2019 in Israel revealed SBV RNA in multiple pools of C. imicola, C. oxystoma and other Culicoides species and in the brains of three malformed lambs and one malformed calf, demonstrating local viral circulation and congenital disease in Israeli ruminants. Development: Positive midge pools and affected farms were distributed across several climatic regions, and phylogenetic analysis showed the Israeli SBV sequences to be closely related to European strains, suggesting recent introduction followed by in situ transmission rather than long‑standing endemicity; although the total number of confirmed congenital cases was limited, the combined entomological and clinical findings indicated that SBV had become established in parts of Israel’s ruminant and vector populations. Ending: After 2019, published reports suggest continuing but low‑level SBV activity rather than large‑scale outbreaks, and Israel is now considered part of the broader Western Asian region in which SBV or closely related Simbu viruses episodically circulate, warranting ongoing surveillance in both vectors and livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers for this episode include windborne spread of infected Culicoides from neighbouring endemic regions (e.g. Türkiye or Mediterranean Europe), cross‑border movement of infected ruminants or semen, and favourable ecological conditions for C. imicola and allied species in Israel’s coastal and Jordan Valley regions. Internal mechanisms: Genomic data indicate that the viruses detected in Israeli midges and ruminants belong to known SBV lineages rather than a novel variant, so this event primarily represents re‑occurrence of SBV within the already affected Western Asia sub‑region, driven by repeated introductions and vector‑borne circulation in largely naïve local herds.
Review: Review – New event added to recognize the well‑documented 2018–2019 SBV circulation in Israel confirmed by genomic detection in both Culicoides vectors and malformed ruminant neonates. Classified as a re‑occurrence within Western Asia (the sub‑region was already affected via Türkiye), not as a new inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence. Evidence is strong, but the scale of clinical impact appears moderate; experts may wish to confirm that its inclusion among the top SBV events is appropriate based on impact criteria.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Small ruminants (sheep and goats) in semi‑intensive and intensive flocks in Peninsular Malaysia
Event summary: Origin: Motivated by concern over transboundary spread of SBV and reproductive problems in Malaysian small ruminants, investigators conducted a serologic survey of 362 sheep and goats from seven farms in Negeri Sembilan and Terengganu states between January and October 2019, using a commercial multi‑species SBV competitive ELISA. Development: Overall apparent seroprevalence was about 21.5% (true prevalence ~22%), with all seven flocks having at least some seropositive animals and intra‑flock prevalence ranging from 2.2% to over 55%; risk‑factor analysis showed higher odds of seropositivity in semi‑intensively managed flocks and in certain breeds (e.g. Malin and Barbados Black Belly sheep, Boer goats), consistent with vector exposure and possible introduction via imported breeding stock. Ending: The study, which did not include RT‑PCR or virus isolation, concluded that SBV infection (or infection with an antigenically similar Simbu‑group virus) was present in Peninsular Malaysia and posed a potential emerging threat to small‑ruminant productivity; subsequent reviews cite Malaysia as having serologic but not yet pathogen‑confirmed evidence for SBV, and further genomic work is still needed to clarify the virus involved and its impact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers include importation of live breeding sheep and goats from Europe or West Asia, movement of infected semen or embryos, and abundant Culicoides and mosquito vectors in Malaysia’s warm, humid, forested environments, with semi‑intensive management systems increasing animal–vector contact. Internal mechanisms: Without viral genomes, this episode cannot be firmly attributed to a specific SBV lineage, but assuming SBV is involved it represents intra‑continental emergence into the South‑eastern Asia sub‑region, driven by geographic range expansion and adaptation of existing SBV strains to local vector assemblages and small‑ruminant production systems.
Review: Review – New event added to cover the first published serologic evidence for SBV infection among small ruminants in Peninsular Malaysia and, by extension, South‑eastern Asia. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (new Asian sub‑region) and first detection for Malaysia. As with Ethiopia, Mozambique and China, attribution to SBV is based solely on ELISA, and cross‑reactivity with other Simbu viruses is possible; experts should review whether to treat this definitively as SBV emergence or as SBV‑like exposure pending molecular confirmation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Wild ruminants (red deer, roe deer, mouflon) in western Germany, with presumed concurrent infection in domestic ruminants given the enzootic status of SBV
Event summary: Origin: After earlier post‑epidemic re‑circulation events in 2014 and 2019, serologic surveillance of wild red deer, roe deer and mouflon in western Germany during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 hunting seasons found a low SBV antibody seroprevalence of about 4.9% in 2022 but a dramatic increase to roughly 40% overall in 2023, with around 32% of juveniles seropositive, indicating intense SBV transmission in summer–autumn 2023. Development: Parallel monitoring of Culicoides biting midges from 2019–2023 showed continuous low‑level detection of SBV RNA with a marked rise in minimum infection rates in 2023, supporting a substantial re‑circulation wave in vector populations; given Germany’s dense domestic ruminant herds and enzootic SBV status, these wildlife and vector data strongly imply widespread re‑infection of naïve cattle and small ruminants in affected regions, even though only a fraction of clinical cases would be detected. Ending: As in previous cycles, this 2022–2023 wave is expected to subside as younger cohorts acquire immunity, reinforcing the pattern of SBV as an enzootic virus in central Europe with cyclic re‑occurrence every 2–3 years and highlighting the need for continued surveillance and targeted vaccination of susceptible breeding animals to mitigate fetal losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The primary external driver is the progressive decline in herd‑level immunity in both domestic and wild ruminants as immune animals from earlier waves are replaced by naïve youngstock; favourable weather patterns for Culicoides activity and high densities of susceptible hosts in western Germany further facilitate explosive local transmission when virus is re‑introduced or persists at low levels. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses from earlier re‑circulation episodes (e.g. 2019) show that circulating SBV strains remain highly similar (≈99–100% nucleotide identity) to earlier European lineages, suggesting that cyclic re‑occurrence is driven more by immunity dynamics and vector ecology than by major viral change; accordingly, this event is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2022–2023 increase in SBV seroprevalence in German wild ruminants (from ~5% to ~40%) and associated high infection rates in Culicoides vectors indicate a large, recent re‑occurrence wave with substantial though incompletely quantified impact on ruminant populations. Classified as re‑occurrence (driven mainly by waning immunity and vector dynamics) rather than re‑emergence, since available data show little genomic change. Domestic livestock impacts are inferred rather than explicitly quantified, so experts should confirm whether this episode ranks among the top SBV emergence events by the chosen impact metrics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In early 1995, a large Ebola virus disease outbreak caused by Zaire ebolavirus began in Kikwit and surrounding areas of southwestern Democratic Republic of the Congo following suspected zoonotic spillover. The outbreak expanded through nosocomial transmission and unsafe caregiving and funeral practices, ultimately causing 315 reported cases and 250–254 deaths before intensive infection prevention, isolation, and community interventions reduced transmission. By mid‑1995, coordinated control measures and exhaustion of susceptible contacts brought the epidemic to an end, with no further local transmission documented.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebola?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Limited infection prevention and control in hospitals, reuse of needles, and close caregiving and burial practices facilitated amplification in Kikwit after a zoonotic introduction. Weak surveillance delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of major viral change; this event is best characterized as re-occurrence of an established Zaire ebolavirus lineage in its historical Central African focus.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In 2000, an outbreak of Ebola virus disease due to Sudan virus began around Gulu in northern Uganda, representing the first recognized Ebola outbreak in Uganda and in the Eastern Africa subregion. The epidemic spread within health facilities and communities in several districts, eventually reaching 425 reported cases and 224 deaths despite rapid national and international response. By early 2001, aggressive isolation, contact tracing, and community engagement interrupted transmission and the outbreak was declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover likely from bats into rural communities, compounded by limited early detection, high household caregiving exposure, and insufficient infection control in health facilities. Internal mechanisms: This event represented geographic range expansion of Sudan virus into a new country and UNSD subregion (Eastern Africa), indicating inherent capacity of this lineage to colonize new ecological and social settings (classified here as re-emergence alongside intra-continental emergence).

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: From late 2001 to 2003, several linked Ebola virus disease outbreaks due to Zaire ebolavirus occurred in forested border areas of northeastern Gabon and northwestern Republic of the Congo following presumed wildlife exposure. Transmission repeatedly spread from hunters and carcass handlers into villages on both sides of the border, resulting in roughly 300 reported cases and high case fatality, with outbreaks responding slowly to control because of remoteness and community mistrust. By the end of 2003, intensive surveillance, safe burials, and movement controls curtailed cross‑border chains of transmission and these outbreaks subsided.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-risk contact with infected great apes or other wildlife, cross-border movement in remote forest regions, limited access to healthcare, and delayed outbreak recognition fostered repeated spillover and community spread. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests circulation of Central African Zaire ebolavirus lineages without clearly documented novel genotypes driving the outbreak; thus this is treated primarily as re-occurrence in a known ecological focus.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In late 2007, an outbreak of Ebola virus disease was detected in Bundibugyo District in western Uganda, and viral characterization identified a previously unknown species, Bundibugyo virus. The epidemic caused about 149 cases and 37 deaths, with spread largely confined to rural communities and local health facilities before intensified surveillance and control measures took hold. By early 2008, after isolation of cases, safe burials, and community mobilization, transmission chains were interrupted and the Bundibugyo virus epidemic was declared over.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON602?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely zoonotic spillover from bats or other wildlife in a forested area, with amplification through household care and health‑facility exposure in settings with limited infection control. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a novel ebolavirus species (Bundibugyo virus) with distinct genetic characteristics represents clear Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and geographic range expansion within Africa, so this is classified as re-emergence in an already affected subregion.

Countries: Uganda [2012]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2012]
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In 2012, Uganda experienced multiple Ebola virus disease outbreaks, including Sudan virus disease in Kibaale District and a separate outbreak later in the year, while Democratic Republic of the Congo reported a contemporaneous Zaire ebolavirus outbreak in Orientale Province. These outbreaks involved dozens of cases each, with transmission driven by close contact and limited infection prevention, but were detected and responded to more quickly than earlier events. By late 2012, strengthened surveillance, case isolation, and safe burials in both countries halted transmission and the outbreaks were declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))

Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed circulation of previously known Sudan virus and Zaire ebolavirus lineages rather than a clearly novel variant; these events are thus treated as re-occurrence in previously affected subregions.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Countries: Guinea [2013]; Liberia [2014]; Sierra Leone [2014]; Nigeria [2014]; Senegal [2014]; Mali [2014]; Spain [2014]; United States of America [2014]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2014]; Italy [2014]
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In December 2013, Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus emerged in southeastern Guinea, marking the first known Ebola outbreak in West Africa and likely originating from a zoonotic spillover in a village near forested areas. Through the first half of 2014, undetected transmission and highly connected population movements allowed the virus to spread widely within Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone and then to additional African countries and, via travel, to Europe and North America, culminating in more than 28,000 reported cases and over 11,000 deaths, the largest Ebola epidemic on record. By early 2016, after massive international response, improved case management, safe burials, and community engagement, all known chains of transmission in West Africa and secondary affected countries were interrupted and the epidemic was declared over, though surveillance continued for flare‑ups.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/ebola-outbreak-2014-2016-West-Africa?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely bat‑to‑human spillover in a remote village, rapid urbanization, porous borders, traditional burial practices, weak health systems, delayed recognition, and intense regional and international mobility all contributed to explosive spread; later, international deployment of resources, novel vaccines, and community-based interventions helped suppress transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies documented adaptive mutations during prolonged human transmission, but the core driver was geographic range expansion of Zaire ebolavirus into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and new continents with in situ transmission (Europe, North America), so this event is classified as both intra-continental and inter-continental emergence and as re-emergence of an existing virus in new ecological and social settings.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In mid‑2014, separate from the West African epidemic, an Ebola virus disease outbreak due to Zaire ebolavirus was detected in Équateur Province in northwestern Democratic Republic of the Congo after cases linked to handling infected bushmeat. The outbreak resulted in several dozen confirmed and probable cases and a high case-fatality ratio, but rapid recognition and deployment of control teams limited geographical spread to a small area. By late 2014, aggressive isolation, contact tracing, and safe burials ended transmission and the outbreak was declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic exposure to infected wildlife in a rural setting, combined with traditional caregiving and funerary practices, triggered localized transmission; however, prior experience with Ebola response in DRC allowed faster containment than in 1995. Internal mechanisms: Virological analyses indicated a Central African Zaire ebolavirus lineage consistent with earlier DRC outbreaks, and there is no clear evidence of major new viral traits, so this event is best categorized as re-occurrence.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In mid‑2018, Ebola virus disease due to Zaire ebolavirus was detected in North Kivu Province of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, soon spreading to neighboring Ituri Province in a conflict‑affected region near the borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and South Sudan. Despite deployment of experimental vaccines, advanced treatment centers, and international support, persistent insecurity, community mistrust, and high mobility allowed the outbreak to continue for nearly two years, with over 3,400 cases and more than 2,200 deaths, making it the second‑largest Ebola outbreak recorded. In June 2020, following extensive vaccination campaigns, improved security in key areas, and sustained surveillance, the outbreak was finally declared over after no new cases were detected for multiple transmission cycles.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recurrent zoonotic spillover in an area with chronic armed conflict, population displacement, porous borders, and weak health infrastructure fostered prolonged transmission, while attacks on health workers and treatment centers impeded response operations. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed ongoing evolution within the Zaire ebolavirus lineage but no clearly defined new species; the event is thus treated as a major re-occurrence of Ebola in an already affected Central African subregion.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In May 2018, Democratic Republic of the Congo reported an Ebola virus disease outbreak in Équateur Province, including cases in the city of Mbandaka on the Congo River, raising concern about spread to other provinces and neighboring countries. Rapid activation of response mechanisms, including ring vaccination with an experimental Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, improved case management, and strengthened surveillance, limited the outbreak to several dozen cases. By July 2018, after two incubation periods without new cases, the Équateur outbreak was declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely wildlife-to-human transmission in a rural area followed by movement into a dense riverine city created potential for wider dissemination, but early detection, rapid international support, and rollout of vaccination curbed spread. Internal mechanisms: The virus belonged to the Zaire ebolavirus species already endemic to DRC, without evidence that novel viral properties primarily drove the event, so it is categorized as re-occurrence.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In mid‑2020, an Ebola virus disease outbreak was detected again in Équateur Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with cases scattered across remote forested health zones and riverine communities. The outbreak accumulated more than 100 reported cases and a high case‑fatality ratio, but benefited from rapid deployment of vaccination, mobile teams, and strengthened surveillance capacities established during earlier DRC outbreaks. By late 2020, after intensive field operations and expanded vaccination coverage, no new cases were detected and the outbreak was officially declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Either fresh spillover from a wildlife reservoir or reintroduction from a persistent human or animal source in an area with limited health access, combined with river transport and rural mobility, enabled multi-focal spread. Internal mechanisms: Genome data (where available) suggest continued circulation of Zaire ebolavirus lineages closely related to prior DRC outbreaks, with no clear step-change in viral traits, so this is classified as re-occurrence.

Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event summary: In early 2021, Guinea reported a new cluster of Ebola virus disease cases in N’Zérékoré Region, near areas heavily affected during the 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic. Genomic analyses indicated that the virus was closely related to strains from the previous epidemic and likely arose from viral persistence in a survivor rather than a fresh zoonotic spillover, leading to a localized outbreak of several dozen cases. Through rapid case isolation, ring vaccination, and robust contact tracing, transmission was contained within months and the flare‑up was declared over later in 2021.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Viral persistence in a human survivor, combined with gaps in follow‑up care, stigma, and ongoing close-contact social networks, enabled reintroduction into the community; improved surveillance and response capacities from the prior epidemic limited spread. Internal mechanisms: This event exemplifies re-emergence driven by long‑term viral persistence and delayed relapse in human hosts, illustrating enhanced capacity of Ebola virus to maintain low‑level infection reservoirs and trigger new outbreaks years after the main epidemic ended.
