Host: Humans; presumed wildlife reservoir (likely bats) with occasional spillover
Event summary: In early 1995, Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus reappeared in and around the city of Kikwit in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, decades after the first known outbreak in Yambuku in 1976. The Kikwit epidemic resulted in about 315–316 cases and roughly 250 deaths, with substantial nosocomial transmission and high infection rates among health-care workers. Rapid implementation of barrier nursing, safe burial practices, and community education allowed control, and the outbreak ended later in 1995.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely spillover from forested areas near Kikwit into a charcoal worker, followed by extensive hospital transmission in settings lacking personal protective equipment and with reuse of needles, compounded by traditional burial practices. Internal mechanisms: The virus was a Zaire ebolavirus lineage similar to earlier Central African strains, so the event is best characterized as a severe re-occurrence driven by health-system vulnerabilities rather than major viral genetic innovation.
Review: retain – Kikwit 1995 is a well-documented large Ebola outbreak in Middle Africa (≈315 cases, ≈250 deaths) and clearly ranks among the major pre‑West‑Africa events. Geographic fields (continent Africa, sub-region Middle Africa, Democratic Republic of the Congo) and event-type coding as a re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion without intra- or inter-continental emergence are consistent with the definitions. Existing CDC/WHO sources appropriately document this outbreak.

Host: Humans; strong epidemiological link to cave/ mine-dwelling bats (Rousettus spp.)
Event summary: From October 1998 through September 2000, a prolonged outbreak of Marburg virus disease occurred among gold miners and nearby residents in Durba and Watsa, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The epidemic involved about 154 cases and 128 deaths, with repeated introductions linked to miners working deep underground and subsequent limited spread into the community. Eventually, improved surveillance, closure or reduced activity of implicated mine galleries, and strengthened infection prevention and control halted new cases, ending the outbreak by late 2000.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive underground gold mining with high bat exposure, poor occupational safety, and crowded living conditions fostered repeated zoonotic spillovers and close-contact transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses revealed multiple distinct Marburg virus lineages co-circulating in the mine environment, indicating frequent independent emergence events from a bat reservoir and supporting classification as re-emergence driven by host–reservoir interface changes rather than a single expanding strain.
Review: review – This outbreak is correctly included as one of the largest Marburg virus disease events. However, its event-type coding has been adjusted: intra_continental_emergence is set to Yes and re_occurrence to No because this was the first documented Marburg outbreak in Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo), representing spread of the EPP into a new African subregion. Re_emergence remains Yes to reflect the multiple distinct viral lineages detected in the mine, consistent with novel genotypes within the genus.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; likely spillover from wildlife (reservoir not fully defined)
Event summary: In mid‑2000, a cluster of hemorrhagic fever cases in Gulu District, northern Uganda, was identified as Sudan ebolavirus, representing the first recognized Ebola virus disease outbreak in Uganda. From August 2000 to January 2001, 425 presumptive cases and 224 deaths were reported across Gulu, Masindi, and Mbarara districts, making it one of the largest pre‑West‑Africa Ebola outbreaks. Intensive international support, establishment of isolation wards, strict infection prevention in hospitals, and community engagement eventually interrupted transmission, and the outbreak was declared over in early 2001.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover in a rural community with close contact with wildlife and limited early diagnostic capacity, combined with nosocomial amplification in under-resourced hospitals and traditional caregiving and burial practices, facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by Sudan ebolavirus, a known species with high but somewhat lower case fatality than Zaire ebolavirus; no specific novel genotype or resistance phenotype was central to emergence, so changes in health-system and social context, rather than viral change, dominated.
Review: retain – The Gulu 2000–2001 Sudan ebolavirus outbreak (425 cases, 224 deaths) is correctly captured as a major event and as the first large Ebola outbreak in Uganda and in the Eastern Africa subregion. Coding as intra-continental emergence (new African subregion) without first/global emergence, and with no inter-continental spread, matches the project definitions and the geography in the Country sheet. Sources (MMWR, EID, CDC) are appropriate.

Host: Humans; frequent contact with infected great-ape and other wildlife carcasses (gorillas and chimpanzees) implicated in spillover
Event summary: From October 2001 through December 2003, a series of linked outbreaks of Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus occurred in forested border areas of northeastern Gabon (Ogooué-Ivindo Province) and northwestern Republic of the Congo (Cuvette-Ouest Region). Together these outbreaks caused roughly 300 human cases and more than 250 deaths, often following handling of carcasses of gorillas and chimpanzees and subsequent amplification through household caregiving and funerals. An intensive international response, including surveillance for wildlife die-offs, isolation of patients, safe burials, and community engagement, progressively interrupted transmission in both countries, and the last outbreak was declared over by late 2003.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Repeated zoonotic spillover associated with hunting and butchering of infected great apes and other wildlife in remote forests, coupled with limited access to health care, unsafe caregiving and funeral practices, and delayed recognition of Ebola, fuelled successive outbreaks on both sides of the Gabon–Congo border. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiologic analyses indicate multiple independent introductions of Zaire ebolavirus rather than a single expanding transmission chain, and there is no clear evidence for major new viral traits; this episode is therefore best classified as a severe re-occurrence within an already affected subregion.
Review: review – Newly added event. The 2001–2003 series of Zaire ebolavirus outbreaks spanning northeastern Gabon and northwestern Republic of the Congo (≈300 cases, >250 deaths in at least five linked episodes) was missing from the draft but is widely recognized as one of the largest Ebola outbreaks prior to 2013. It is coded here as a re-occurrence within Middle Africa (Ebola had already been documented in this subregion since the 1976 and 1995 DRC and 1994–1997 Gabon outbreaks) with no intra- or inter-continental emergence flags. This event should be retained among the top high-impact Orthoebolavirus episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; likely bat reservoir with human spillover
Event summary: In late 2004, cases of severe hemorrhagic fever emerged in Uíge Province in northern Angola and were confirmed in March 2005 as Marburg virus disease. By August 2005, Angola had reported around 250 cases and over 220 deaths, with most cases in children and an overall case-fatality rate near 88–90%, making it the largest and deadliest Marburg outbreak recorded. Intensive international response focusing on infection control, contact tracing, and community engagement gradually interrupted transmission, and the outbreak was brought under control later in 2005.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak likely arose from a zoonotic introduction in a setting with weak infection control, delayed recognition, and extensive transmission in hospitals and households, particularly among pediatric patients, with burial practices amplifying spread. Internal mechanisms: No uniquely novel genotype or resistance trait was identified; the extreme impact reflected the combination of a virulent Marburg lineage with fragile health infrastructure and late detection, representing a major re-occurrence within Middle Africa rather than spread into a new subregion.
Review: review – Angola 2004–2005 is correctly included as the largest Marburg virus disease outbreak (252 cases, 227 deaths), but the event-type coding needed adjustment. Because Marburg had already been documented in Middle Africa (Durba/Watsa, DRC 1998–2000), this event is not an intra-continental emergence into a new subregion; instead it is reclassified as a re-occurrence within the same subregion (intra_continental_emergence set to No; re_occurrence set to Yes; re_emergence left as No). Geography (Angola, Middle Africa) and sources are appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; likely wildlife reservoir (bats) with spillover; domestic animals not primary hosts
Event summary: In mid‑2007, a hemorrhagic fever outbreak began in Bundibugyo District in western Uganda and was confirmed in November 2007 as Ebola virus disease caused by a previously unknown species, later named Bundibugyo ebolavirus. Between August 2007 and February 2008, the outbreak caused over 100 suspected cases with a lower case-fatality ratio (~25%) than typical Zaire or Sudan ebolavirus outbreaks and remained largely confined to Bundibugyo and Kikyo areas. Implementation of isolation wards, training of health workers, and community-based control measures led to a decline in cases, and Uganda declared the epidemic over in February 2008.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover in a forested border region with close human–wildlife contact and delayed recognition of Ebola due to atypical clinical severity facilitated early spread; limited health resources also contributed. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis demonstrated that the causative agent was a distinct filovirus species, Bundibugyo ebolavirus, representing true viral re-emergence via novel strain/species emergence within the Orthoebolavirus group, with implications for vaccine and therapeutic effectiveness.
Review: review – This outbreak correctly highlights the first recognition of Bundibugyo ebolavirus as a new species, justifying the re_emergence flag. However, first_global_emergence has been set to No because Orthoebolavirus spp. (Ebola/Marburg viruses) were recognized in humans decades earlier (1960s–1970s). The event occurred in Uganda within the already-affected Eastern Africa subregion, so intra-/inter-continental emergence flags remain No. A Wikipedia link was removed in favor of primary WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs; humans with asymptomatic infection (farm and slaughterhouse workers); likely co-circulation in bats and non-human primates
Event summary: In 2007–2008, increased mortality in pigs on farms in Bulacan, Pangasinan, and other provinces in the Philippines led to investigations that identified Reston ebolavirus infection in swine, marking the first detection of any ebolavirus in domestic pigs. Subsequent serologic testing revealed antibodies in several pig workers and abattoir staff, indicating asymptomatic or mild human infections linked to pig exposure, and prompted a joint FAO–OIE–WHO mission and a national control strategy. Pig depopulation, movement controls, and enhanced surveillance and biosecurity in affected farms were implemented, and no evidence of widespread human disease emerged; viral activity in pigs appeared to subside after control measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and expansion of commercial pig production in the Philippines, with high animal densities and co-infection with porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) virus, likely facilitated amplification and detection of Reston ebolavirus in swine, while close human–pig contact created opportunities for spillover. Internal mechanisms: This event represented a significant host expansion of Reston ebolavirus from non-human primates to domestic pigs and then asymptomatic human infection, with potential adaptation for efficient replication and shedding in pigs, raising concern about future viral evolution toward greater human pathogenicity.
Review: review – The Philippines Reston ebolavirus event is appropriately included because it marks the first detection of an ebolavirus in domestic pigs and asymptomatic infections in pig-exposed humans, representing a major host expansion with economic and zoonotic implications. However, first_detection has been set to No because Orthoebolavirus spp. were detected in animals and humans prior to 1990 (e.g. Reston virus in macaques and humans in 1989–1990); this episode is better coded purely as re-emergence via host expansion in a new domestic species within the animal host system. Geography (Asia, South-eastern Asia, Philippines) and sources (WOAH/FAO/WHO and peer‑reviewed risk assessments) are appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Guinea [2013]; Liberia [2014]; Sierra Leone [2014]; Nigeria [2014]; Senegal [2014]; Mali [2014]
Host: Humans; likely spillover from bats (wildlife reservoir not fully confirmed)
Event summary: In late 2013, Zaire ebolavirus spilled over into humans in rural southeastern Guinea, initiating the first known Ebola outbreak in the Western Africa subregion and rapidly spreading to Liberia and Sierra Leone. Through 2014–2015 the epidemic expanded into dense urban settings and across borders, ultimately causing about 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, with limited secondary transmission in Nigeria, Mali, and single imported cases in Senegal and outside Africa. Aggressive international response, improved case isolation, safe burials, and deployment of experimental vaccines and therapeutics progressively reduced transmission, and WHO declared the end of the West Africa Ebola epidemic in 2016, with flare-ups linked to viral persistence in survivors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High baseline mobility across porous borders, care-seeking and funerary practices involving direct contact with bodies, weak health systems overwhelmed by the scale of transmission, delayed recognition of Ebola in a region without prior history, and dense urban transmission corridors all amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: Not primarily associated with a radically novel strain, but high viral load and efficient human-to-human transmission of Zaire ebolavirus, combined with documented long-term viral persistence in immune-privileged sites of survivors that caused late flare-ups, contributed to the epidemic’s scale.
Review: retain – The 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic is correctly represented as the largest Ebola outbreak in history and an intra-continental emergence into the Western Africa subregion, where sustained human transmission had not previously been documented. Imported and limited secondary cases in Europe and North America are appropriately treated as part of the same linked episode without triggering an inter-continental emergence flag. Countries and years match WHO/CDC timelines, and the chosen sources provide authoritative coverage.

Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo [2018]; Uganda [2019]
Host: Humans; likely spillover from bats or other wildlife reservoir
Event summary: In August 2018, Zaire ebolavirus was confirmed in North Kivu Province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, marking the country’s tenth recorded Ebola outbreak and the first in this conflict-affected region. The epidemic persisted for nearly two years, causing roughly 3,470 cases and 2,287 deaths across North Kivu, Ituri, and South Kivu provinces and spilling over briefly into neighboring Uganda, where a few family-cluster cases were detected. Massive ring-vaccination campaigns with rVSV‑ZEBOV‑GP, enhanced surveillance, and eventually improved security coordination enabled control, and the outbreak was declared over in June 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronic armed conflict, population displacement, attacks on health facilities, mistrust of authorities, and cross-border movement hindered contact tracing and infection prevention, sustaining intense transmission. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved Zaire ebolavirus strains similar to earlier Central African lineages without evidence of major new virulence traits; its scale was driven more by context than by viral novelty, although survivor persistence and rare reintroductions likely contributed to prolonged transmission.
Review: retain – The 2018–2020 North Kivu/Ituri Ebola outbreak is accurately depicted as the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, with correct geography (Middle Africa for DRC, Eastern Africa for spillover cases in Uganda) and classification as a re-occurrence in already affected subregions rather than a new intra-continental emergence. Sources from WHO and CDC are suitable and specific to this episode.

Host: Humans; likely wildlife reservoir spillover (Sudan ebolavirus)
Event summary: On 20 September 2022, Uganda declared an outbreak of Sudan virus disease after a fatal case from Mubende District tested positive for Sudan ebolavirus, marking the country’s first Sudan virus outbreak in over a decade. The epidemic spread across several central districts and ultimately resulted in 164 cases (142 confirmed and 22 probable), 55 confirmed deaths, and 87 survivors before being controlled. Aggressive public health measures—including isolation of cases, contact tracing, movement restrictions, and enhanced community engagement in the absence of a licensed Sudan virus vaccine—brought transmission to an end and the outbreak was declared over in early 2023.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover in a rural area with close interaction with wildlife, delayed detection of the index cluster, suboptimal infection prevention in some facilities, and population movement along trade routes facilitated early spread. Internal mechanisms: This was a re-occurrence of Sudan ebolavirus in Uganda rather than a new virus species; available evidence suggests a typical Sudan virus lineage without major novel genetic traits, but the event underscores gaps in cross-protective vaccination (no licensed Sudan-specific vaccine at the time) and the importance of strain-specific countermeasures.
Review: retain – The 2022 Sudan virus disease outbreak in Uganda (164 cases) is appropriately included as one of the larger recent filovirus outbreaks and as a re-occurrence of Sudan ebolavirus in an already affected Eastern Africa subregion. Event-type coding (re_occurrence only) accords with the definitions, and the WHO and peer‑reviewed sources provide robust epidemiological and molecular detail.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Peromyscus maniculatus (deer mouse reservoir); humans
Event summary: In spring 1993, a cluster of acute respiratory failure and high‑fatality illness was detected among residents of the Four Corners region in the southwestern United States. Epidemiologic and laboratory investigations identified a previously unrecognized New World hantavirus, later named Sin Nombre virus, carried by deer mice and causing a new clinical entity termed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). Intensive rodent control, public health messaging on rodent exposure, and improved clinical recognition led to a decline from the initial explosive cluster into sporadic, seasonally linked HPS cases in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually wet El Niño conditions in the early 1990s increased primary productivity, boosting deer mouse populations and human–rodent contact in rural housing and peridomestic settings. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and first recognition of a previously undescribed Sin Nombre orthohantavirus lineage capable of causing severe pulmonary disease in humans (novel strain/genotype emergence), with efficient aerosol transmission from infected rodent excreta to people.
Review: retain – Major global event: first recognition of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and Sin Nombre virus in humans in North America. Coding as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence is appropriate, geography (United States; Northern America) is correct, and sources are primary (CDC/EID plus supporting reviews), so no structural changes were needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Oligoryzomys spp. and other sigmodontine rodents; humans
Event summary: Following recognition of HPS in the United States, similar severe respiratory illnesses were retrospectively and prospectively identified in Brazil in 1993 and then in Argentina and Chile from 1995 onward, with laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection and description of distinct South American virus lineages such as Andes and Juquitiba viruses. By the mid‑1990s, confirmed HPS cases had been reported in multiple Southern Cone countries, establishing South America as an additional focus of New World hantavirus disease with increasing annual case counts. National surveillance systems and rodent studies were expanded, and HPS incidence stabilized at lower levels after initial emergence but has persisted as an endemic–epidemic zoonosis in several South American countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Improved clinical awareness post‑1993, expansion of diagnostic capacity, and land‑use change in rural/agro‑forestry areas increased recognition and true exposure to sigmodontine rodent hosts. Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing but previously undetected circulation of multiple South American orthohantaviruses (e.g., Andes, Laguna Negra, Juquitiba and related strains) with inherent capacity to cause HPS; the event represents first detection of these lineages in humans on a new continent rather than de novo viral evolution.
Review: review – Event correctly captures early emergence of HPS in the Southern Cone, but country-specific onset years have been corrected to Brazil [1993], Argentina [1995], Chile [1995], Paraguay [1995], and Uruguay [1997] based on PAHO and national reports. Classification as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence for South America remains appropriate, and the episode is clearly among the most impactful Orthohantavirus emergences; retain after these geographic corrections.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Oligoryzomys longicaudatus (long‑tailed pygmy rice rat); humans
Event summary: In September–December 1996, an outbreak of HPS occurred around El Bolsón, Bariloche and Esquel in southern Argentina, involving at least 18 confirmed cases linked by close social and family contact rather than shared rodent exposure. Molecular and epidemiologic investigations demonstrated person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, providing the first conclusive evidence that a hantavirus could spread directly between humans. Intensive contact tracing, isolation of symptomatic contacts and strengthened infection‑control measures eventually interrupted transmission and terminated the outbreak after several generations of human‑to‑human spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural housing with high rodent infestation, close‑knit family and social networks, and delayed recognition of secondary cases facilitated chains of transmission. Internal mechanisms: Andes virus lineage with traits permitting limited human‑to‑human transmission via respiratory secretions (enhanced transmission/host adaptation) and higher viral loads in some patients, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by viral properties rather than simple ecological resurgence.
Review: retain – The 1996 El Bolsón/Esquel Andes virus cluster is the first well-documented person-to-person transmission of a hantavirus and is rightly classified as re_emergence driven by enhanced human-to-human spread. Countries have been restricted to Argentina [1996] to avoid implying contemporaneous Chilean involvement in this specific outbreak. Event remains high-impact despite moderate case numbers and should be retained.

Host: Myodes glareolus (bank vole) and other small rodents; humans
Event summary: From April 1997 through March 1998, the Republic of Bashkortostan in the European part of the Russian Federation experienced an unprecedented epidemic of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, with 10,057 registered cases and extremely high regional incidence peaking in autumn and early winter 1997. The outbreak occurred in an area where hantaviruses had been endemic but typically at much lower incidence; serologic investigations implicated Puumala orthohantavirus and related rodent-borne lineages maintained in bank voles and other small mammals. Emergency rodent-control campaigns, intensified public guidance on avoiding rodent exposure, and subsequent declines in vole populations were followed by a sharp reduction in HFRS incidence, although Russia has continued to experience recurrent multi‑year epidemic peaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Favorable climatic conditions and mast years leading to explosive bank vole population growth, expansion of human housing and agricultural activity into forest-edge habitats, and limited pre-existing immunity in the local population created conditions for intense spillover. Internal mechanisms: Established Puumala and related orthohantaviruses in local rodents caused disease; available data do not support emergence of a fundamentally novel strain, so the event represents very large-scale re_occurrence driven primarily by host and environmental dynamics rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – Newly added event to represent the extremely large 1997–1998 HFRS epidemic in Bashkortostan (~10,000+ cases), which was missing despite being one of the highest-burden Orthohantavirus outbreaks worldwide since 1990. Coded as re_occurrence in an already endemic Eastern European subregion with no clear evidence for a novel strain; geography (Russian Federation; Eastern Europe) and hosts follow Russian and international epidemiologic reports. This event clearly belongs among the top-impact episodes.

Countries: China [2006] (nationwide spread across multiple provinces through 2012)
Host: Apodemus agrarius (striped field mouse); Rattus norvegicus (brown rat); humans
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2012, China experienced sustained high incidence of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, with more than 77,000 reported cases and hundreds of deaths, and marked geographic spread into new counties and provinces compared with earlier decades. Surveillance analyses showed large annual case burdens and shifting hotspots, particularly in northeastern, central and eastern provinces where rodent hosts and human agricultural activities overlapped. Expansion of vaccination, intensified rodent control and health‑education campaigns eventually reduced incidence and severity in many high‑risk areas after this peak period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid socio‑economic change, agricultural expansion, rodent habitat alteration, climate variability affecting rodent abundance, and increased rural–urban migration amplified contact between people and rodent hosts; improved surveillance increased detection. Internal mechanisms: Continued spillover of established Hantaan and Seoul orthohantaviruses from Apodemus and Rattus reservoirs (no major new strain), representing re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion within Eastern Asia driven primarily by environmental and demographic forces.
Review: review – This episode correctly summarizes a very large 2006–2012 HFRS resurgence in China (tens of thousands of cases), clearly among the most impactful Orthohantavirus events. However, intra_continental_emergence has been changed from 'true' to 'false' because hantaviruses and HFRS were long endemic throughout Eastern Asia; spread was within the same UNSD subregion rather than to a new subregion. The event is best classified as large-scale re_occurrence; geography and sources remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Myodes glareolus (bank vole); humans
Event summary: After statutory notification of hantavirus infection began in Germany in 2001, three large national outbreak years occurred in 2007, 2010 and 2012, dominated by nephropathia epidemica caused by Puumala virus. The 2010 outbreak alone involved roughly 2,000 notified cases distributed across several federal states, with similar or larger peaks in 2012 and smaller but notable peaks in other years. Following these years with exceptional case burdens driven by bank‑vole population booms, incidence declined again, although localized outbreaks continue to recur in mast years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cyclic masting of beech and other trees increased food resources, leading to bank‑vole population surges and higher virus prevalence, while recreational and forestry activities heightened human exposure; enhanced surveillance improved case capture. Internal mechanisms: Established Puumala orthohantavirus lineages circulating in bank voles caused disease; the emergence pattern reflects re‑occurrence in known endemic subregions linked to rodent–food web dynamics rather than major viral evolution.
Review: review – This event appropriately highlights Germany’s major Puumala virus outbreak years (2007, 2010, 2012), with some of the largest documented European hantavirus case counts. Host: Oligoryzomys longicaudatus and related sigmodontine rodents; humans
Event summary: From late October 2018 through early 2019, a large outbreak of Andes virus HPS centered in Epuyén, Chubut Province, Argentina, produced around 30–34 confirmed cases and 11 deaths, with one linked case detected in Chile. Detailed epidemiologic reconstruction and genomic sequencing showed multiple generations of person‑to‑person transmission within households and social gatherings, making it the largest documented human‑to‑human Andes virus outbreak to date. Geography (Argentina with one linked case in Chile), classification as re_emergence (enhanced transmission) without new continental spread, and sources (WHO DON, NEJM, CDC) are appropriate. Event summary: In early May 2022, the United Kingdom reported a cluster of mpox cases, some without travel links to endemic regions, soon followed by rapid detection of additional cases across multiple European countries and North America, revealing sustained human‑to‑human transmission of a clade IIb lineage in non‑endemic populations. By mid‑ to late‑2022, the outbreak had expanded into a global multi‑country epidemic with more than 80,000–90,000 confirmed cases across over 100 countries, predominantly associated with close and often sexual contact among men who have sex with men, leading WHO to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in July 2022. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species smallholder systems common in Northeast Brazil, with close contact between goats and cattle and shared milking or handling equipment, likely facilitated spillover of BPVs from cattle into goats; limited biosecurity and extensive management may have supported ongoing circulation. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of BPV‑2 and related viruses into goats, together with detection of putative new BPV types and co‑infections, reflects re‑emergence driven by both host‑range expansion and novel genotypes, suggesting that BPVs can adapt to new domestic ruminant hosts under suitable ecological and management conditions.
Review: Review – Event retained as an important host‑expansion episode but corrected in several ways. (1) Timing: the original row dated this to 2015–2018, but the only directly cited source is a UFRPE doctoral thesis (defended June 2024) that describes a cross‑sectional survey of 58 farms and 1885 goats; in the absence of explicit field sampling years, the thesis defence year 2024 is used as a proxy for the event year. (2) Countries field updated to Brazil [2024] and to specify the three northeastern states. (3) The original classification as first_detection has been removed; papillomaviruses were already long known in livestock, and caprine papillomatosis had been described elsewhere, so this episode is better treated as re‑emergence with host expansion and novel genotypes rather than global first detection of the EPP. Recommend future users consult the full thesis (and any derived peer‑reviewed articles) to refine the exact sampling period; nonetheless, this represents a meaningful, if numerically modest, emergence of papillomatosis in a new livestock host system within Brazil.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Dairy cattle (cutaneous papillomas on body skin)
Event summary: In the early 2020s, veterinarians in Taiwan recognized cutaneous papillomas in lactating dairy cows on several farms, leading to the first systematic investigation of bovine papillomaviruses in Taiwanese cattle. Eight papilloma samples collected from six dairy farms were analyzed and found to contain BPV‑1, BPV‑2 and a novel BPV genotype, demonstrating that BPVs were circulating and associated with skin papillomatosis in Taiwan where little prior disease information had been reported. The lesions were generally benign but raised concerns about animal welfare and potential progression to more serious neoplastic disease. The documented cases were managed at farm level through surgical removal and supportive care rather than large‑scale control programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and previously unrecognized circulation of BPVs in Taiwanese dairy herds likely occurred over time via cattle and semen movements, but only became evident when visible lesions were investigated with modern diagnostics. Internal mechanisms: Detection of BPV‑1, BPV‑2 and a novel genotype in Taiwanese cattle indicates both geographic range documentation in a previously unsurveyed area and ongoing genetic diversification of BPVs; this is best viewed as re‑emergence mediated by novel strain appearance and improved detection capabilities, not as first detection of the EPP in the region.
Review: Review – Event retained but corrected. (1) Timing: the original row dated this event to 2016, but the Transboundary and Emerging Diseases article describing these cases was published in 2025, with sample identifiers suggesting collection in 2023; the year has therefore been updated to 2023–2023, and the country field to China [2023] (Taiwan Province). (2) Event type: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence flags have been removed, because bovine papillomatosis was already known in Eastern Asia; instead, this episode represents re‑emergence via detection of BPV‑1/2 plus a novel genotype in a previously unsurveyed national context. (3) Sources: limited to the primary article and its PDF mirror; a general Papillomaviridae Wikipedia link used only for background has been removed from the per‑event sources. Overall this is a modest‑size but well‑documented re‑emergent event in a new national setting that should remain in the dataset, but users should treat the 2023 date as approximate pending more precise sampling information.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2016] (Rio Grande do Sul; Passo Fundo and Farroupilha; multiple source herds)
Host: Dairy cattle (teat papillomas; animals sent to slaughter from affected herds)
Event summary: In 2016, researchers in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil, collected teat papilloma samples at abattoirs from milking cows that had been culled from herds because of teat lesions and milking problems, representing the tail end of severe papillomatosis episodes in those herds. In total, 23 teat wart samples from cows originating from Passo Fundo and Farroupilha were analyzed, revealing at least 26 complete BPV genomes corresponding to numerous known types and 14 new BPV types (provisionally named BPV‑30 to BPV‑43), indicating remarkable viral diversity in teat papillomatosis. Parallel work on a larger set of slaughtered dairy cows from the same region documented 73 animals with teat papillomas and at least 24 different BPV types, including 10 putative new types, reinforcing the picture of extremely diverse co‑infections in cull cows with chronic teat disease. While these investigations sampled animals at slaughter rather than during active on‑farm outbreaks, they showed that extensive and genetically complex papillomatosis was contributing to culling and production losses in southern Brazil. The immediate herd‑level events ended with removal of affected cows, but the work suggested that similar undetected diversity underlies ongoing teat papillomatosis problems in regional dairies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Chronic teat papillomatosis in high‑producing dairy cows, combined with economic pressures favoring culling of animals with milking difficulties, led to concentration of severe cases in slaughter populations; intensive milking practices and environmental exposures likely facilitated persistent herd‑level transmission in the source herds. Internal mechanisms: Frequent co‑infection with many BPV genotypes, including 14 newly described types (BPV‑30 to BPV‑43) and numerous other known and putative types, points to rapid viral diversification and complex papillomavirome communities driving re‑emergent and persistent teat disease; this represents re‑emergence driven by extensive novel strain/genotype emergence and potentially altered immune interactions in affected cows.
Review: Retain – This event captures a major, well‑documented focus of papillomatosis in southern Brazil: multiple herds in Rio Grande do Sul supplying slaughtered dairy cows with chronic teat warts, from which investigators characterized both high case numbers (73 culled animals with teat papillomas) and extraordinary BPV genetic diversity (14 newly described types plus many known types). It clearly meets criteria for a large, impactful emergence episode in terms of production loss (culling and milking problems) and viral evolution. The year 2016 reflects the slaughter and sample collection period reported in the Animal Microbiome and Brazilian Journal of Microbiology papers. Classification as both re_occurrence (persistent disease pressure in an endemic subregion) and re_emergence (numerous novel genotypes) is appropriate; there is no evidence that this represents first detection or inter‑/intra‑continental emergence. The previous separate Brazilian “2010–2013 multi‑herd” row duplicated much of this content and has been recommended for exclusion; this 2016 row should be retained as the main Brazilian teat papillomavirome emergence event.

Countries: Portugal [2000] (Azores archipelago; especially São Miguel Island)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef; mainly adult cows)
Event summary: From roughly 2000 through 2006, bovine enzootic haematuria (BEH) associated with urinary bladder tumours in cattle grazing bracken fern–infested pastures remained hyper‑endemic in the Azores archipelago of Portugal, causing substantial economic losses. Investigations during this period demonstrated a strong association between bovine papillomavirus type 2 (BPV‑2) infection and proliferative and neoplastic bladder lesions in affected cattle, with viral DNA and E5 oncoprotein detected in urothelial tumours. BEH had been recognized in the Azores for decades, but work in the early 2000s clarified the viral co‑carcinogenic role of BPV‑2 alongside bracken fern toxins and documented that bladder cancer attributable to this complex caused an estimated €4 million in losses between 2000 and 2006. Control efforts have focused on reducing bracken exposure and managing affected animals, but the disease complex remains a major constraint in certain high‑risk grazing areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term grazing of cattle on pastures heavily infested with bracken fern (Pteridium aquilinum), whose carcinogenic compounds act as co‑factors, combined with traditional management systems that kept cattle on these pastures for years, created chronic exposure conditions favoring bladder tumour development. Limited pasture alternatives and economic constraints perpetuated this pattern. Internal mechanisms: Persistent BPV‑2 infection of the urinary bladder mucosa, with expression of the viral E5 oncoprotein, acts synergistically with bracken‑derived carcinogens to drive neoplastic transformation of urothelial cells; this represents re‑emergence of papillomavirus‑associated neoplasia in a well‑known endemic focus, with improved molecular understanding and quantification of impact rather than first occurrence of the disease. The dramatic economic burden and long‑standing high incidence justify inclusion of this chronic, geographically focused disease complex as a major emergence event.
Review: Retain (newly added event) – This row has been added because bovine enzootic haematuria (BEH) in the Azores represents one of the most impactful papillomavirus‑associated disease complexes in livestock during the 1990–2025 period, with documented heavy economic losses (on the order of €4 million between 2000 and 2006) and strong evidence implicating BPV‑2 in bladder tumour pathogenesis alongside bracken fern exposure. The event is framed as a chronic, geographically bounded re‑emergent disease complex rather than a single acute outbreak, consistent with the literature. Classification as both re_occurrence (long‑standing endemic disease with continued high incidence linked to external environmental drivers) and re_emergence (clarified and ongoing role of BPV‑2 in neoplasia) is appropriate; there is no basis for first‑detection or inter‑/intra‑continental emergence flags, as BEH was recognized in the Azores before 1990. The 2000–2006 time window is chosen because economic impact was explicitly quantified for this period in the cited sources; users may refine this range if more detailed temporal data are compiled.

Host: African lions (Panthera leo; primary affected wildlife host); domestic dogs (maintenance reservoir); spotted hyenas, bat-eared foxes and other wild carnivores (spillover hosts)
Event summary: In late 1993–early 1994, a morbillivirus closely related to canine distemper virus spilled over from large domestic dog populations surrounding Serengeti National Park in northern Tanzania into lions, causing sudden-onset neurologic disease and pneumonia. Over subsequent months, approximately 85% of Serengeti lions seroconverted and about one-third of the population died, while the epidemic spread northward into Maasai Mara lions in Kenya and affected other carnivores such as hyenas and bat‑eared foxes. As herd immunity built up in lions and dog vaccination began in surrounding communities, case numbers declined and the outbreak burned out by late 1994, although CDV has continued to circulate endemically at lower impact in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density, largely unvaccinated domestic dog populations around the Serengeti–Mara ecosystem provided a persistent CDV reservoir; close spatial overlap of dogs and wild carnivores at livestock/wildlife interfaces facilitated cross-species transmission; severe drought and heavy tick infestations increased Babesia co-infections in lions, greatly amplifying mortality. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced pathogenicity of canine distemper virus in non-canid carnivores, with unusually high mortality in lions and other species; efficient lion-to-lion transmission once established in prides, leading to rapid spread through an otherwise CDV-naïve lion metapopulation.
Review: retain – Added as a missing major paramyxovirus event. The 1993–1994 canine distemper epidemic in Serengeti–Mara lions caused ~30% lion mortality with >80% seroprevalence and affected multiple carnivore species, clearly ranking among the most impactful wildlife morbillivirus events. Classified as re-emergence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because CDV was long present in domestic dogs in East Africa; this outbreak reflects dramatic host expansion and increased virulence in wildlife within an already affected subregion.

Host: Horses (clinical spillover host); flying-fox bats (Pteropus spp., reservoir identified later)
Event summary: In September 1994, a previously unknown paramyxovirus (later named Hendra virus) emerged in a Thoroughbred training complex in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, Queensland, killing 13 horses and a horse trainer with severe respiratory disease. Subsequent investigation linked the outbreak to spillover from flying-fox bats into horses, and extensive testing of nearly 2,000 horses showed no prior circulation, confirming it as a new henipavirus infection of horses and humans. Quarantine, movement controls and culling of affected horses ended the cluster, and no wider spread in Australian livestock occurred at that time.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density racehorse stabling with intense close contact, horse paddocks located under or near trees used by flying-foxes, and encroachment of horse facilities into bat foraging ranges in peri-urban Brisbane. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a novel henipavirus from bats to horses, followed by efficient horse-to-horse transmission via respiratory secretions once spillover occurred; ecological adaptation of the virus to local bat populations allowed long-term maintenance in the wildlife reservoir.
Review: retain – Event correctly describes the first recognized emergence of Hendra virus with accurate location, hosts, and approximate horse and human fatalities. Classification as first_global_emergence and first_detection is appropriate at the virus-species level (Hendra virus), even though paramyxoviruses in general were long endemic in animals. Geographic coding (Oceania; Australia and New Zealand; Australia) and timing (1994) are correct; sources are authoritative (state health departments, WOAH, peer-reviewed reviews).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (primary amplifying host); humans (spillover); dogs (incidental spillover); fruit bats (Pteropus spp., reservoir)
Event summary: Between late 1998 and mid-1999, a novel paramyxovirus (Nipah virus) caused severe respiratory and neurologic disease in pigs on farms in peninsular Malaysia, with at least 265 associated human encephalitis cases and over 100 deaths among pig farmers and abattoir workers, and 11 additional human cases linked to imported pigs in Singapore. The outbreak spread from initial foci in Perak through movement of infected pigs to large commercial farms in Negeri Sembilan and to abattoirs in Singapore, prompting intensive investigations that identified a new henipavirus closely related to Hendra virus. Drastic control measures, including culling of around one million pigs and bans on pig movement, ultimately stopped transmission in pigs and ended human cases by mid-1999.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deforestation and agricultural expansion in peninsular Malaysia pushed fruit-bat reservoirs into closer contact with intensive pig production systems; large-scale, high-density pig farming with frequent animal movements facilitated rapid farm-to-farm and cross-border spread; initial misdiagnosis as Japanese encephalitis delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a bat-borne henipavirus to pigs and then to humans, with highly efficient pig‑to‑pig respiratory transmission and high viral loads in respiratory secretions; geographic range expansion from localized bat reservoirs into intensive pig belts through livestock movements.
Review: retain – This is correctly identified as the first global emergence and detection of Nipah virus, with accurate description of pig and human case numbers, geographic spread within Malaysia and into Singapore, and control measures (mass pig culling and movement bans). Event classification focuses on virus-level emergence (henipavirus) rather than the broader paramyxovirus family, which is reasonable for this EPP entry. Sources (CDC MMWR, WHO, peer‑reviewed articles) are appropriate and more informative than general summaries.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Denmark [2002]; Sweden [2002]; Norway [2002]; Germany [2002]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2002]; Belgium [2002]; France [2002]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]; Ireland [2002]
Host: Harbour seals (Phoca vitulina; primary affected host); grey seals (Halichoerus grypus; some cases)
Event summary: In May 2002, unusually high mortality among harbour seals was first detected around the Danish island of Anholt in the Kattegat, marking the start of a second major phocine distemper virus (PDV) epizootic in northwestern Europe following the 1988 outbreak. Over roughly nine months, the infection spread through seal colonies along the North Sea and Baltic coasts of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, the United Kingdom and Ireland, killing an estimated 21,700–30,000 seals, or about half of the North Sea harbour seal population. As population immunity increased and the seasonal pupping period ended, new cases declined and the epidemic subsided by late 2002, leaving long-lasting demographic impacts on many regional seal populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A large, immunologically naïve generation of harbour seals born since the 1988 epizootic, high seal densities at haul-out sites in the Wadden Sea and other coastal areas, and seasonal movements and mixing of colonies facilitated rapid virus spread; migrating Arctic or sub-Arctic seals have been hypothesized as carriers introducing PDV into North Sea populations. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of PDV in an already affected seal metapopulation, with efficient seal‑to‑seal transmission and high case-fatality leading to catastrophic mortality; no major genomic shift compared with the 1988 virus, but waning population immunity created conditions for a second large-scale outbreak.
Review: retain – Added as a missing event. The 2002 phocine distemper virus epizootic killed roughly 20,000–30,000 harbour seals (≈50% of the North Sea population) across multiple Northern and Western European countries, clearly placing it among the most impactful animal paramyxovirus events since 1990. Classified as re-occurrence (second major PDV epizootic in the same subregions, with no evidence of a fundamentally novel strain) and not as inter-continental emergence; subregions and affected countries have been expanded and corrected using CDC EID and other primary sources.

Host: Sheep; goats; wild bharal (Pseudois nayaur) in affected highland areas
Event summary: In July 2007, peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV), a morbillivirus of sheep and goats, was confirmed for the first time in China during multiple outbreaks in four counties of the remote Ngari region of southwestern Tibet, causing high morbidity and mortality in small-ruminant flocks and infections in free-ranging bharal. Over 2007–2008, diagnostic surveys and molecular testing documented several distinct outbreak foci in Tibetan villages, indicating sustained in situ transmission rather than isolated introductions, and showed the virus belonged to lineage IV circulating in neighboring South Asian countries. Emergency control measures, including movement restrictions and ring vaccination, were implemented and successfully halted reported outbreaks in Tibet by 2008, after which no further Chinese PPR outbreaks were reported until the large epidemic beginning in 2013.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of small ruminants along traditional transhumance and trade routes linking Tibet with infected regions of South Asia; limited veterinary infrastructure, challenging terrain and low prior awareness of PPR in Tibetan pastoral systems impeded early recognition and control. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of endemic lineage IV PPRV into a new Asian subregion (Eastern Asia) and a previously unaffected country (China), with highly efficient transmission and severe disease in naïve sheep and goat populations and demonstrated ability to infect wild caprines.
Review: review – Epidemiologic details (first confirmation of PPR in China in Ngari, Tibet in 2007; lineage IV; involvement of bharal) and spatial coding (Asia; Eastern Asia; China) are correct. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence is appropriate for PPRV at the country/subregional level. However, in a strict top‑10 ranking for all animal paramyxoviruses, this episode is of moderate scale compared with later China-wide and African PPR epidemics and the large PDV/CDV events; consider retaining for its importance as the first incursion into Eastern Asia, but it could be deprioritized if the list must be reduced to exactly ten events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: In mid-2008, PPR was confirmed for the first time in Morocco, where outbreaks in sheep and goats were reported in numerous provinces and posed a major threat to approximately 22 million small ruminants. FAO and national assessments indicated that this was the first incursion of PPR into North Africa, implying spread across the Sahara from endemic zones further south. Morocco rapidly launched nationwide vaccination campaigns from 2008 to 2010, combined with movement controls and outbreak containment measures, successfully controlling the epidemic, with the last reported case in November 2008.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of infected small ruminants along trans-Saharan pastoral and trade routes from endemic Sahelian countries; difficulty controlling animal movements in nomadic and transhumant systems in southern Morocco and neighboring regions. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV from sub-Saharan Africa into a new subregion (Northern Africa), with high morbidity and mortality in immunologically naïve sheep and goat populations amplifying the impact of the initial incursion.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first documented occurrence of PPR in Morocco and the broader North African subregion, with accurate timing (summer–autumn 2008), host species, and approximate population at risk. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence is appropriate for PPRV. Source set has been strengthened by ensuring inclusion of FAO, ONSSA (Moroccan veterinary authority) and a global PPR review, with Wikipedia kept only as supporting historical context.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Goats; sheep
Event summary: From 2008 onward, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), previously considered PPR-free, began experiencing outbreaks of severe disease in goats and sheep across several provinces, culminating in a large epidemic recognized by 2012 that killed more than 75,000 goats and affected tens of thousands more small ruminants. Retrospective molecular studies of tissues from dead goats collected in Tshela in 2012 showed circulation of lineage IV PPRV closely related to viruses from neighboring Gabon and Nigeria, and revealed that at least four of eleven provinces had been affected between 2008 and 2012. FAO and national authorities mounted emergency vaccination campaigns (e.g. in Bandundu Province) and strengthened surveillance and border controls, which reduced but did not immediately eliminate PPR, and subsequent outbreaks in 2016 and 2018 involved additional viral lineages, indicating complex re-emergence dynamics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Porous borders and largely uncontrolled movements of small ruminants between DRC and infected neighboring countries; limited veterinary services and public awareness; political instability and population displacement facilitating long-distance livestock movements; lack of systematic vaccination and quarantine infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: Intra-continental emergence of lineage IV PPRV into a new central African country followed by re-emergence and diversification of viral lineages (II, III and IV) over time, aided by viral genetic diversity and the ability of PPRV to persist and spread in mixed production systems and at the wildlife–livestock interface.
Review: retain – Well-supported as one of the largest PPR epidemics in central Africa, with >75,000 goat deaths and multi-province spread in a previously PPR-free country. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence (first incursion into Middle Africa) combined with re_emergence (multiple lineages detected over 2008–2012 and again later) is consistent with the project rules, which allow re-emergence to co-occur with intra-continental emergence. Country, subregion and timing match FAO and peer‑reviewed molecular epidemiology sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: Peste des petits ruminants was first confirmed in northern Tanzania in 2008, and by early 2010 a major wave of outbreaks was recognized in northern and central regions, with FAO warning that the epidemic could spread southward into countries of the Southern African Development Community. The 2010 outbreaks threatened more than 13 million Tanzanian small ruminants and an estimated 50 million sheep and goats in up to 15 southern African countries if not contained, prompting an emergency regional response. Emergency vaccination in northern Tanzania, restrictions on animal movements, and strengthened surveillance in neighboring states helped to limit further southward spread, but PPR has since become endemic in much of Tanzania and remains a source of risk for southern Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities and frequent movement of small ruminants for trade and pastoralism across East Africa; long, porous borders with Kenya and other endemic neighbors; limited prior PPR vaccination and delayed recognition of the disease after its initial introduction to Tanzania in 2008. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence and southward geographic spread of PPRV within the Eastern Africa subregion into new areas of Tanzania that were previously unaffected, driven by high transmissibility of lineage III PPRV in largely unvaccinated flocks rather than by clear viral genetic change.
Review: retain – Revised the event summary to clarify that PPR was first confirmed in Tanzania in 2008, while the 2010 wave represented a large re-occurrence and southward extension with major regional risk (threat to ~50 million small ruminants across up to 15 SADC countries). Classification as re_occurrence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because PPRV was already established in Eastern Africa and in Tanzania by 2008. Event is borderline in a strict global top‑10 ranking but is retained here given its scale, policy importance for the SADC region, and strong FAO documentation; flagged for possible down‑selection if further prioritization is needed.

Countries: China (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region [2013]; Heilongjiang Province [2014]; multiple other northern provinces during 2013–2014 wave)
Host: Sheep; goats; various wild small ruminants in affected regions
Event summary: In November–December 2013, China reported new PPR outbreaks in Huocheng County of Xinjiang after several quiet years following the 2007 Tibetan outbreaks, marking re-emergence of the virus and signaling a fresh introduction into northwestern border areas. Over 2013–2014, lineage IV PPRV spread widely across northern China, with confirmed outbreaks and virus detections in Xinjiang, Heilongjiang and more than 20 other provinces, ultimately affecting over 20–22 provinces and more than 260 counties and causing tens of thousands of sheep and goat cases and over 16,000 deaths. Large-scale vaccination campaigns, culling in outbreak foci, and strengthened movement controls gradually contained the epidemic by mid-2014, although PPRV has continued to pose a risk of further spread within China and to neighboring countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement and trade of small ruminants across China’s western and northern borders and between provinces; dense sheep and goat populations (over 300 million animals) with limited prior PPR immunity outside earlier Tibetan foci; gaps in routine vaccination and surveillance that allowed undetected spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Rapid geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV across Eastern Asia following a likely single introduction around mid‑2013, as inferred from full-genome phylogenetics; high transmissibility and adaptation to sheep and goats facilitated extensive spread, with viruses from multiple provinces forming a closely related genetic cluster indicative of a recent common ancestor.
Review: retain – Corrected the event-type classification by setting intra_continental_emergence to false and retaining re_emergence = true. PPRV had already been detected in Eastern Asia (Tibet, China) in 2007, so the 2013–2014 wave represents a major re-emergence and nationwide expansion within an existing subregion rather than first intra-continental emergence. Country, subregion and timeline (Xinjiang index in late 2013, spread to Heilongjiang and >20 provinces through mid‑2014) and impact metrics (tens of thousands of cases, >16,000 deaths, risk to ~300 million small ruminants) are consistent with CDC EID and Chinese epidemiologic analyses.

Host: Sheep; goats; Mongolian saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica mongolica); goitered gazelles and other wild ungulates
Event summary: In September 2016, Mongolia reported its first-ever PPR outbreaks in domestic sheep and goats in western provinces bordering China, representing a new country incursion of lineage IV PPRV into a naïve small-ruminant population. In early 2017, the virus spilled over into the critically endangered Mongolian saiga antelope and other wild ungulates in the Great Lakes Depression, causing mass mortality that reduced the saiga population from roughly 25,000 animals to fewer than 9,000 within a few months. Intensive vaccination of livestock, targeted carcass disposal and wildlife surveillance eventually interrupted active transmission by mid-2017, but the event left the saiga population severely depleted and highlighted PPR as a major biodiversity as well as livestock threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border livestock movements from infected areas of China into western Mongolia; close spatio-temporal overlap of domestic sheep and goats with saiga and other wild ungulates on shared rangelands; limited prior PPR vaccination and wildlife health surveillance in Mongolia. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV into a previously unaffected country; highly lethal host expansion into multiple wild ungulate species (especially Mongolian saiga), with intense transmission at the livestock–wildlife interface enabling rapid spread and catastrophic wildlife mortality.
Review: retain – Adjusted event-type flags by setting intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence to false and treating this as first_detection of PPRV in Mongolia. Under the project’s definitions, intra-continental emergence is reserved for first appearance in a new UNSD subregion (Eastern Asia was already affected via China), and re-emergence requires prior presence in the same subregion, which did not apply at the country level. The event’s very high impact on both livestock and critically endangered Mongolian saiga and its status as Mongolia’s first PPR incursion justify retaining it among the major emergence events.

Sub-regions: Europe: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe. Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia. North America: Northern America.
Countries: Italy [2000, CPV-2c first officially recognised and rapidly expanding]; Germany [retrospective detection of 426E CPV-2c-like viruses in samples from 1996]; Spain [2006, first CPV-2c detection associated with a fatal kennel outbreak]; Switzerland [early 2000s, CPV-2c detected]; Czechia [early 2000s, CPV-2c detected]; Sweden [2011, first CPV-2c detection]; Viet Nam [2004, first CPV-2c reported; CPV-2c ~97% of parvovirus isolates by 2016-2018]; China [from ~2009-2010 onwards, CPV-2c increasingly reported and rising in prevalence]; United States of America [2006-2007, CPV-2c detected in multiple states alongside CPV-2b].
Host: Domestic dogs (primarily puppies and young dogs with hemorrhagic gastroenteritis); occasional domestic cats infected by CPV-2c in parts of Europe.
Event summary: Around 2000, a new antigenic variant of canine parvovirus type 2 carrying a Glu-426 substitution in VP2 (later designated CPV-2c) was first recognised in dogs in Italy, with retrospective data showing closely related 426E strains already circulating in Germany in the mid-1990s. Over the following decade CPV-2c spread across much of Europe—being documented in Spain, Switzerland, the Czech Republic and later Sweden—and progressively replaced earlier CPV-2a/2b variants in many dog populations. By the mid-2000s to early 2010s, CPV-2c had also been reported from Asian countries such as Viet Nam and China and from North America, where it co-circulated with CPV-2a/2b, contributing to large numbers of severe enteritis cases in puppies despite vaccination and establishing multiple regional CPV-2c lineages.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of companion-dog populations; intensive breeding and shelter environments with high densities of susceptible puppies; global movement and trade of dogs; incomplete or improperly timed vaccination leading to windows of susceptibility; environmental persistence of parvoviruses in kennels and public spaces. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – CPV-2c (Glu-426 VP2 mutant) exhibits distinct antigenic properties relative to CPV-2a/2b and shows evidence of strong fitness, enabling replacement of earlier variants in many regions. Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – very high environmental stability, intense faecal shedding and efficient dog-to-dog transmission allowed CPV-2c lineages to disseminate and become endemic across diverse climates and husbandry systems.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). Corrections made: (i) restricted this event to Europe, Asia and North America and moved South American details to the dedicated South American CPV-2c event to avoid double counting; (ii) updated country timelines (CPV-2c first recognised in Italy in 2000 with retrospective detection in Germany in 1996; first report in Spain in 2006; first CPV-2c detections in China around 2009–2010; CPV-2c predominance in Viet Nam documented for 2016–2018 rather than the mid-2000s); (iii) reclassified the event from “inter-continental emergence + re-emergence” to “re-emergence only”, in line with the project rule that new antigenic variants of an already established EPP should not be coded as inter-continental emergence; and (iv) pruned and refocused the source list on primary molecular-epidemiology studies rather than Wikipedia or duplicate PDF links. The episode clearly represents a major CPV-2c-driven wave of disease and should remain among the key post-1990 emergence events for this EPP, but final coding should be checked by a human reviewer.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Argentina [2003, CPV-2c first detected and increasingly common; predominant by 2008]; Uruguay [2007, first report of CPV-2c, quickly becoming a major variant]; Brazil [2008-2010, CPV-2c predominant among typed canine parvovirus strains in several southern and southeastern states].
Host: Domestic dogs (mainly puppies and young dogs) with severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis.
Event summary: From 2003, CPV-2c was first identified in dogs in Argentina and rapidly increased in frequency, becoming the predominant variant affecting domestic dogs there by about 2008. Over subsequent years, CPV-2c was documented in neighbouring Uruguay and then Brazil, where molecular surveys between 2008 and 2010 showed CPV-2c as the main circulating subtype in diarrhoeic dogs, indicating swift replacement of earlier CPV-2a/2b variants. This regional shift was accompanied by widespread outbreaks of severe gastroenteritis in puppies and young dogs and marked a major South American amplification phase of the global CPV-2c pandemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High proportions of unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated dogs, especially in low-income urban and peri-urban settings; dense dog populations and informal breeding and kennelling systems; substantial cross-border movement of dogs between Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil; limited early genomic surveillance. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – introduction and subsequent dominance of CPV-2c, which exhibited greater fitness than co-circulating CPV-2a/2b variants in local dog populations. Possible Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity or partial immune escape relative to existing vaccine strains was suggested by severe disease in some vaccinated or maternally immune puppies, although vaccines based on CPV-2b generally remained protective at the population level.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). Evidence from Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil confirms a rapid rise and regional predominance of CPV-2c between 2003 and 2010 with substantial clinical impact, justifying inclusion as a major emergence episode. I reinterpreted the event type from an “intra-continental emergence + re-emergence” combination to a pure re-emergence event, because canine parvovirus had been endemic in South America since the early 1980s and the project rules state that spread of a new antigenic variant of an existing EPP within a continent should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. The time window and affected countries are otherwise well supported by the cited molecular-epidemiology studies, but a human reviewer should confirm that separating this South American episode from the broader 2000–2015 CPV-2c event is the preferred granularity for the final dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: North America: Northern America. Europe: Southern Europe; Western Europe.
Countries: United States of America [2010, 10-month series of confirmed and suspected FPV cases in a large open-admission shelter in the Midwestern USA]; Italy [2010-2013, multi-year FPV outbreak in a large feline shelter in north-western Italy with 177 hospitalised cats and high mortality]; Netherlands [2010s, recurrent feline panleukopenia outbreaks in Dutch animal shelters highlighted in a 2018 outbreak-management article].
Host: Domestic cats in animal shelters and rescue facilities (mainly kittens and juveniles).
Event summary: Around 2010–2013, multiple large feline panleukopenia (FPV) outbreaks were documented in shelter populations in North America and Europe. In the USA, an adoption-guarantee shelter experienced a 10-month series of confirmed and suspected FPV cases with high morbidity and mortality in kittens, while in north-western Italy a multi-year outbreak originating in a single large shelter generated 177 hospitalised FPV cases over three years and became effectively endemic. Similar recurrent outbreaks and associated guidance on outbreak management were published for Dutch animal shelters, together indicating that FPV remained a leading cause of severe disease and death in shelter kittens despite long-standing availability of effective vaccines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High turnover and crowding of cats in open-admission and large municipal or charity shelters; intake of many unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated kittens; delays in vaccination at intake; incomplete adherence to isolation, cohorting and sanitation protocols; high environmental stability of FPV with inadequate disinfection of rooms, cages and fomites. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel FPV genotype has been consistently implicated in these outbreaks; FPV and occasionally CPV-like strains were already endemic, so these episodes are best interpreted as re-occurrence events driven largely by management and population-risk factors rather than by major viral change.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). I refined the continent and subregion coding to “North America; Europe” with explicit reference to Northern America, Southern Europe (Italy) and Western Europe (Netherlands), and updated the country list to name the specific shelters and regions described in the main case-series and guideline papers. The event type has been changed from a generic multi-type coding to “re-occurrence only”, because FPV was long endemic in all these subregions and the outbreaks are best explained by shelter-level drivers (crowding, intake of unvaccinated kittens, breakdowns in vaccination and biosecurity) rather than by the emergence of a distinct new viral strain. The cited sources are appropriate for a composite shelter-outbreak episode, but human review is advised to confirm that aggregating multiple shelters and countries into a single 2010–2013 re-occurrence event meets the project’s expectations for event granularity.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia. Africa: Western Africa; Northern Africa. Europe: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe. North America: Northern America.
Countries: China [from 2009-2010 onwards, CPV-2c of Asian lineage increasingly detected and by the mid-2010s representing a substantial share of isolates]; Viet Nam [CPV-2c first reported 2004; by 2016-2018 CPV-2c accounted for ~97% of parvovirus-positive dogs across three regions]; Thailand [2010s, CPV-2c of Asian lineage reported in dogs and cats]; Myanmar [2020s, CPV-2c of Asian origin predominant among sampled dogs]; India [2010s, reports of Asian-like CPV-2c emergence in dogs]; Nigeria [from 2016 onwards, introduction and spread of Asian-like CPV-2c with partial replacement of older CPV-2a and CPV-2b variants]; Côte d’Ivoire [2025, detection of Asian CPV-2c clade viruses in multiple dogs]; Egypt [2010s, CPV-2c co-circulating with CPV-2a/2b in several governorates]; Italy [late 2010s, Asian-like CPV-2c introduced via imported dogs from Thailand and subsequently detected in local clinical cases including in Sicily]; Romania [late 2010s–early 2020s, widespread Asian-like CPV-2c in dogs across the country]; Canada [mid-2010s, sporadic detection of Asian CPV-2c in dogs].
Host: Primarily domestic dogs (puppies and juveniles with hemorrhagic gastroenteritis); occasional infections documented in wild canids and non-carnivoran wildlife such as pangolins, but these are not the main drivers of the event.
Event summary: Phylogeographic analyses indicate that an “Asian” CPV-2c lineage originated in Asia around 2008 and remained largely confined there until roughly 2012, when it underwent a marked expansion in population size and geographic range. Over the following decade, viruses from this lineage became widespread and often predominant in many parts of Asia (including China, Viet Nam, Thailand, Myanmar and India), and were introduced repeatedly into Africa, Europe and North America, with documented establishment in countries such as Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Egypt, Italy, Romania and Canada. This lineage displaced earlier CPV-2 variants in many settings, contributed to numerous outbreaks and endemic cases of severe canine parvoviral enteritis and further diversified into regional sublineages, representing a second major CPV-2c-driven re-emergence wave superimposed on existing CPV endemicity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing international and regional trade and movement of pet dogs (including import of dogs from Asian countries to Europe and Africa), rescue and rehoming chains, and informal dog movements; sustained pools of unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated dogs in many low- and middle-income regions; urbanisation and dense free-roaming dog populations; limited molecular surveillance delaying recognition of the lineage’s spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – the “Asian” CPV-2c lineage harbours a characteristic constellation of VP2 and non-structural gene mutations (e.g. at residues 5, 267, 324 and 370) associated with enhanced receptor binding and possibly increased fitness, enabling it to outcompete earlier CPV-2a/2b and prototype CPV-2c strains in multiple regions. Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion – strong evidence of multiple long-distance introductions from Asia followed by local establishment and onward spread in Africa, Europe and North America, sometimes accompanied by partial replacement of prior variants; limited but notable spillover into wildlife (e.g. raccoon dogs, pangolins) illustrates an expanded host range but remains epidemiologically secondary to dog-to-dog transmission.
Review: Decision: review (new event to retain). This row was added because multiple phylogenetic and molecular-epidemiology studies identify the emergence and transcontinental spread of the “Asian” CPV-2c lineage (originating around 2008 and expanding out of Asia after 2012) as a distinct and highly impactful evolutionary episode, associated with replacement of pre-existing CPV variants and large numbers of clinical cases in dogs across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. In accordance with project rules, it is coded as a re-emergence event (novel high-fitness strain) rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence, since canine parvovirus itself was already established globally. Country lists and years are approximate and reflect first detections and documented predominance rather than exhaustive coverage; a human reviewer should confirm that the selected countries and 2012–2022 window best capture this lineage’s emergence for the purposes of the dataset and that overlap with the earlier 2000–2015 CPV-2c event is acceptable.
