Sub-regions: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand. Asia: Western Asia.
Countries: Australia [2014-2018, multiple large FPV outbreaks in eastern states including Victoria and New South Wales after decades without major epizootics]; New Zealand [2016-2018, FPV outbreaks following a long period with few reported epidemics]; United Arab Emirates [2017, FPV outbreak in Dubai region associated with a distinct viral lineage].
Host: Domestic cats (mostly unvaccinated kittens and young cats, many in shelters, rescue facilities and urban stray colonies).
Event summary: Clinical feline panleukopenia (FPV infection) had become rare in Australia by the early 2010s, with no large reported outbreaks for roughly four decades, largely due to widespread vaccination. In 2014, severe FPV outbreaks re-emerged in eastern Australia and continued through 2015–2018 in multiple regions, causing hundreds of cases and high mortality, while contemporaneous outbreaks were reported in New Zealand (2016–2018) and the United Arab Emirates (2017). Sequence analysis showed that the Australian and New Zealand outbreaks were caused by closely related FPV lineages distinct from those in the UAE, and that intensified vaccination and outbreak control subsequently reduced reported case numbers, although FPV remains a recurrent threat in under-vaccinated cat populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Declining or inconsistent FPV vaccination coverage in pet, shelter and stray cats; accumulation of large populations of unvaccinated urban strays and feral colonies; high-density housing and population turnover in shelters and rescue facilities; movement of cats between shelters, rescue groups and regions; probable introduction of FPV into naïve subpopulations via inter-regional movement of cats (particularly relevant for the UAE outbreak). Internal mechanisms: While phylogenetic studies identified distinct FPV lineages associated with the Australian/New Zealand and UAE outbreaks, the major drivers appear to have been immunity gaps and management factors rather than a clearly more virulent virus, so this is best considered a re-occurrence event; nonetheless, ongoing evolution of FPV with regional clustering underscores the potential for future strain-related changes in epidemiology. Enhanced Transmission – high environmental stability and heavy faecal shedding of FPV facilitated rapid spread once vaccination gaps existed.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). The timing and geography (eastern Australia 2014–2018, New Zealand 2016–2018, United Arab Emirates 2017) match well-documented large FPV epizootics after decades of low clinical incidence in these regions, clearly qualifying this as a major re-emergent episode. I changed the event-type coding from a combination of intra-continental emergence, re-occurrence and re-emergence to “re-occurrence only”, because FPV was historically present in both Oceania and Western Asia and the literature identifies waning population immunity and vaccination lapses, rather than a fundamentally new viral phenotype, as the primary drivers of these outbreaks. The source list was also refocused on the key outbreak and seroprevalence papers and a general shelter-medicine FPV guidance resource. A human reviewer should confirm that the balance between external drivers and any putative strain effects is appropriately reflected in the re-occurrence classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cape cormorant (Phalacrocorax capensis), African penguin (Spheniscus demersus) – wild seabirds in breeding colonies
Event summary: In 1991, a severe avian cholera outbreak off western South Africa caused high mortality of Cape cormorants, marking the first major Pasteurella multocida epizootic recorded in the region’s seabird colonies. From 2002 to at least 2006, repeated outbreaks on Dyer Island and nearby colonies produced large die‑offs of Cape cormorants—over 7,000 birds in 2004 alone—and sporadic mortality of African penguins, with carcass‑removal and colony‑management interventions used to limit spread. Although outbreaks subsided intermittently, avian cholera became an entrenched recurrent threat contributing to ongoing regional cormorant declines and adding disease pressure to already threatened African penguin populations.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=0e425bef5c3efbc52c2d3788f00f42edbc5c555a&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density colonial nesting on small guano islands, food shortages linked to shifts and overexploitation of pelagic fish, and climate‑driven variability in prey availability increased stress and aggregation of Cape cormorants and African penguins, promoting rapid fecal–oral and carcass‑mediated transmission; restricted roosting habitat and limited freshwater also favoured environmental persistence of P. multocida. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates repeated outbreaks caused by virulent serotype‑1 lineages already circulating in regional seabirds and poultry, without clear demonstration of a novel genotype, so the episode is best interpreted as geographic and temporal re‑occurrence of an established pathogen in dense seabird colonies.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=0e425bef5c3efbc52c2d3788f00f42edbc5c555a&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retain this event as a major seabird epizootic; corrected the event year from 1991–2005 to 1991–2006 to reflect documentation that Dyer Island outbreaks with thousands of cormorant deaths continued through 2005–2006. Geographic assignment to Southern Africa/South Africa and classification as re‑occurrence (rather than first/global or intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) are supported by primary seabird and African penguin sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Lesser snow goose (Anser caerulescens caerulescens) – wild migratory light geese on Banks Island breeding grounds
Event summary: During the summers of 1995 and 1996 on Banks Island in the western Canadian Arctic, avian cholera caused catastrophic die‑offs of breeding lesser snow geese, killing at least 30,000 birds in 1995 and 20,000 in 1996 as infection swept through dense nesting aggregations. The outbreaks followed decades of population growth and habitat degradation by overabundant light geese and raised concerns that Banks Island colonies could act as major reservoirs contributing to disease spread along flyways. After 1996, mortality at Banks Island declined, but the events underscored the role of Arctic goose concentrations in amplifying P. multocida and seeding recurrent cholera outbreaks elsewhere.([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2001-10-12/pdf/01-25612.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid population increase of lesser snow geese, high nesting densities on limited wetlands, and associated habitat degradation created ideal conditions for intense bird‑to‑bird and environment‑mediated transmission; seasonal congregation of large numbers of geese on staging and moulting areas further promoted epidemic spread. Internal mechanisms: Isolates were typical serotype‑1 P. multocida strains already associated with light geese in North America, and there is no evidence of major genetic novelty; the episode reflects amplification of endemic lineages in a highly dense host population rather than emergence of a new strain.([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2001-10-12/pdf/01-25612.pdf))
Review: retain – Event is well documented (≥30,000 and 20,000 lesser snow geese killed in 1995 and 1996, respectively) and clearly among the largest post‑1990 avian cholera mass mortalities; no changes to geography or event‑type classification were needed.

Countries: Denmark [1996 wild birds; 2001-2004 free-range layer and duck farms]; Sweden [1998 wild birds]
Host: Free-range layer chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus), farmed ducks; wild birds (gulls and waterfowl) as reservoir hosts
Event summary: Beginning with the first recorded outbreak of fowl cholera in Danish wild birds in 1996, a highly virulent Pasteurella multocida subsp. multocida clone circulated for nearly a decade among wild waterbirds in Denmark and Sweden and subsequently spilled into outdoor poultry. By 2001–2004, the same outbreak clone had established in commercial free‑range layer farms in Denmark, causing recurrent episodes of elevated mortality in flocks of several thousand birds despite vaccination and biosecurity measures, and was also linked to earlier outbreaks in farmed ducks. Molecular typing showed that isolates from wild birds (Denmark 1996, 2001, 2003; Sweden 1998) and from multiple Danish poultry flocks were virtually indistinguishable, indicating long‑term clonal persistence across wild and domestic hosts. Cholera incidence in Danish poultry declined after 2004, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability of expanding free‑range systems to infection from local avifauna.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of free‑range and organic layer production in Denmark increased direct and indirect contact between domestic birds and infected wild waterfowl and gulls, while shared equipment, lack of strict hygiene barriers, presence of other domestic animals, and imperfect vaccination facilitated farm‑level transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: A specific P. multocida ssp. multocida clone, originally detected in Danish wild birds in 1996 and later in Swedish wild birds in 1998, showed high virulence for domestic poultry and gamebirds and remained genetically stable across years and hosts, consistent with re‑emergence driven by a successful, highly pathogenic genotype that expanded from wild birds into free‑range poultry.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence of a virulent clone linking wild birds and free‑range poultry, but broadened the event period from 2001–2004 to 1996–2004 and clarified the country field to reflect epidemiologically linked wild‑bird outbreaks in Denmark (1996, 2001, 2003) and Sweden (1998) that predated and seeded the poultry epizootics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: French Southern Territories [Amsterdam Island – Falaise d’Entrecasteaux seabird cliffs, ~1996-2015]
Host: Indian yellow-nosed albatross (Thalassarche carteri), sooty albatross (Phoebetria fusca), northern rockhopper penguin (Eudyptes moseleyi), Amsterdam albatross (Diomedea amsterdamensis) – breeding seabirds
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s through at least the mid‑2010s, recurrent outbreaks of avian cholera became a chronic problem in seabird colonies on Amsterdam Island in the southern Indian Ocean, where more than 20,000 pairs of Indian yellow‑nosed albatross, thousands of northern rockhopper penguins and other species breed on the Falaise d’Entrecasteaux cliffs. Annual bacterial epizootics, attributed mainly to Pasteurella multocida, caused large die‑offs of albatross and penguin chicks and occasional adult mortality, severely depressing breeding success and driving long‑term declines in Indian yellow‑nosed and Amsterdam albatross populations. Despite intensified monitoring and, more recently, experimental vaccination of albatross chicks, avian cholera has remained entrenched, and the episode is now considered one of the dominant disease threats to several globally threatened Southern Ocean seabirds on the island.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0197291&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and maintenance of P. multocida on a small, isolated island are suspected to involve domestic livestock or feral animals (e.g., cattle, rats) historically present on Amsterdam Island, with predator and scavenger species potentially contributing to spread among dense seabird colonies; high nesting densities on a restricted cliff system and environmental contamination by carcasses allow efficient transmission and environmental persistence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and serological work confirms circulation of P. multocida in multiple seabird species, and repeated high chick mortality with limited adult disease suggests strong age‑related susceptibility rather than a single explosive introduction; the episode is best classified as re‑emergence of a poultry‑associated pathogen that has expanded into a novel seabird community, becoming endemic with substantial demographic effects on endangered albatross and penguin populations.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0197291&utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added to capture the long‑running series of avian cholera epizootics on Amsterdam Island that have caused chronic chick mortality and population declines in Indian yellow‑nosed and Amsterdam albatrosses. Dates (mid‑1990s to mid‑2010s) are approximate and should be fine‑tuned against colony‑specific time series, but the episode clearly ranks among the most impactful for this pathogen.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Common eider (Somateria mollissima dresseri) – breeding sea ducks in St. Lawrence Estuary colonies
Event summary: In 2002, long‑monitored common eider colonies on islands in the St. Lawrence River estuary, Québec, experienced an exceptionally severe and synchronous avian cholera epizootic, in contrast to more localized outbreaks documented in earlier decades. Approximately 7,000 eiders were found dead and as many as 10,000 may have died—around one‑fifth of the regional breeding population—with heavy female bias in mortality, leading to major breeding failures and sharp local population declines. After 2002, avian cholera continued to recur intermittently in the estuary, but intensified monitoring, habitat management and natural demographic processes gradually stabilised some colonies, even as disease remained an important limiting factor.([cwhc-rcsf.ca](https://www.cwhc-rcsf.ca/docs/newsletters/newsletter11-1en.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense nesting of common eiders on a limited set of islands, combined with environmental conditions that favour P. multocida survival in poorly drained soils and dense vegetation, facilitated explosive local transmission; regional movements and shared down‑harvesting activities likely enhanced connectivity among colonies, contributing to the near‑simultaneous epizootic on multiple islands. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate re‑occurrence of established P. multocida lineages in an enzootic system rather than emergence of a new genotype; the magnitude of the 2002 event appears driven more by colonisation density, environmental conditions and the build‑up of susceptible adults than by documented genetic change in the bacterium.([cwhc-rcsf.ca](https://www.cwhc-rcsf.ca/docs/newsletters/newsletter11-1en.pdf))
Review: review – Retain as a major event; augmented the summary with quantitative estimates from Canadian Cooperative Wildlife Health Centre reports (7,000–10,000 eiders dead, ~20% of the estuary population) and added the CWHC newsletter as a key source. Classification as a large re‑occurrence in an already enzootic system remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Canada [Northern Québec – Nunavik colonies 2004, 2006-2007; Nunavut – Southampton Island (East Bay/Mitivik Island) 2005-2012]
Host: Northern common eider (Somateria mollissima borealis), with involvement of lesser snow geese and other waterfowl as carriers
Event summary: From 2004 onward, the first recorded Arctic outbreaks of avian cholera occurred in northern common eiders at nesting colonies in northern Québec (Nunavik) and at East Bay (Mitivik Island), Southampton Island, Nunavut, causing repeated mass mortalities of breeding females and chicks. The most severe epidemic at East Bay in 2006 killed more than 3,200 eiders—over 40% of nesting females that year—with further large outbreaks through 2007 and continued, lower‑level epidemics documented up to 2012. As surveillance and carcass‑removal improved and herd immunity built up, annual mortality declined and the epidemic eventually faded out, but stochastic population models showed that a continuation of high‑intensity cholera years would likely have driven the colony toward extinction.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-79888-6?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Northward shifts and increasing densities of migratory waterfowl (especially lesser snow geese) linked to broader flyway population growth, climate‑driven changes in Arctic sea‑ice and open‑water phenology affecting nesting schedules, and extremely dense nesting of eiders on small islands created conditions for introduction and explosive spread of P. multocida; carcass accumulation in colonies further amplified environmental contamination and exposure. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data show circulation at East Bay of multiple P. multocida serotypes, including serotype 1 strains typical of Central and Mississippi flyways and serotypes 3, 4, and 3×4 typical of Atlantic systems, implying long‑distance host‑mediated introduction of new genotypes into previously unaffected Arctic eider populations and supporting classification as re‑emergence via host expansion and enhanced transmission in a novel high‑density host system.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0029659&utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retain this as one of the most consequential events, but corrected the event period from 2000–2012 to 2004–2012 (first documented Arctic outbreaks in Nunavik colonies and at East Bay) and changed “intra‑continental emergence” from Yes to No, because within the UN classification North America has a single subregion (“Northern America”) and avian cholera was long established in that subregion. Re‑classification as a re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence due to host and geographic expansion within an existing continent is consistent with published epidemiology.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [Inner Mongolia – Hongjian Nur Lake (Ordos wetland) 2007]
Host: Wild migratory waterfowl (11 species of ducks and shorebirds, including ruddy shelduck and other Anseriformes and Charadriiformes)
Event summary: In late August 2007, routine surveillance at Hongjian Nur Lake in the Ordos wetland of Inner Mongolia detected dead waterfowl, and over an 11‑day period more than 3,300 wild ducks and shorebirds of 11 species were found dead. Laboratory investigation isolated Pasteurella multocida subsp. multocida serotype A1 from multiple tissues of dead and sick birds, confirming avian cholera as the cause of the die‑off and revealing infection in eight species not previously reported with P. multocida infection. The outbreak, the first documented fowl cholera epizootic in wild waterfowl in China, subsided after early September as birds dispersed from the lake and carcass‑removal and local management reduced environmental contamination.([bioone.org](https://bioone.org/journals/journal-of-wildlife-diseases/volume-45/issue-4/0090-3558-45.4.1194/An-Outbreak-of-Avian-Cholera-in-Wild-Waterfowl-in-Ordos/10.7589/0090-3558-45.4.1194.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Hongjian Nur Lake is an important breeding and staging site where large numbers of migratory ducks congregate in late summer; crowding on shrinking water surfaces during a warm season likely facilitated intense contact and contamination of shared foraging areas, while limited local surveillance before 2007 meant earlier small outbreaks, if any, may have gone unnoticed. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved P. multocida serotype A1, which was already known globally from poultry and waterfowl; the main novelty lies in expansion to multiple wild waterfowl species in this region and first recognised infection in eight species, so the event is best viewed as re‑emergence via host expansion and first confirmed establishment of wild‑waterfowl cholera in China rather than emergence of a new strain.([bioone.org](https://bioone.org/journals/journal-of-wildlife-diseases/volume-45/issue-4/0090-3558-45.4.1194/An-Outbreak-of-Avian-Cholera-in-Wild-Waterfowl-in-Ordos/10.7589/0090-3558-45.4.1194.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added because the 2007 Hongjian Nur Lake outbreak (3,300+ wild waterfowl deaths and first report of fowl cholera in wild waterfowl in China) is both sizeable and epidemiologically important, representing notable host and geographic expansion within Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [Utah – Great Salt Lake 2007]
Host: Eared grebe (Podiceps nigricollis) – wild migratory waterbirds staging on the Great Salt Lake
Event summary: In the autumn of 2007, an avian cholera outbreak at Utah’s Great Salt Lake killed approximately 15,000 Eared Grebes during migration, with carcasses washing up along shorelines as birds congregated in dense rafts on shrinking areas of open water. Previous cholera events had been documented at the lake in the 1990s and early 2000s, but the 2007 episode was unusually severe in both daily death rates and total mortality. As the outbreak progressed, die‑off intensity decreased once cold weather, dispersal of birds and management actions reduced grebe densities and removed carcasses from affected areas.([wildlife.utah.gov](https://wildlife.utah.gov/diseases/avian-cholera))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Great Salt Lake hosts millions of staging Eared Grebes each autumn; in 2007, high bird densities combined with local hydrological conditions to concentrate birds in limited open‑water habitat, while carcasses in the water and along shorelines served as focal points for infection and environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: No unusual strain characteristics were reported; the event reflects a severe re‑occurrence of endemic P. multocida in a system with repeated prior outbreaks, driven primarily by crowding and environmental factors rather than documented changes in bacterial genotype or virulence.([wildlife.utah.gov](https://wildlife.utah.gov/diseases/avian-cholera))
Review: review – New event added because the 2007 Great Salt Lake epizootic (≈15,000 Eared Grebes dead) is one of the better quantified and larger modern avian cholera die‑offs in North America; clearly more impactful than the smaller 2015 Idaho event retained below for exclusion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [California–Oregon – Klamath Basin National Wildlife Refuge Complex 2012]
Host: Mixed migratory waterfowl (dabbling ducks, snow and Ross’s geese, and American coots) using the Klamath Basin refuges during spring migration
Event summary: In early 2012, severe water shortages in the Klamath Basin National Wildlife Refuge Complex on the California–Oregon border forced an estimated two million migrating ducks and geese into a fraction of the normal wetland area, triggering the worst avian cholera outbreak there in more than a decade. Over 10,000 waterfowl—by some estimates up to 15,000–20,000, mainly Northern Pintails, snow geese, Ross’s geese and coots—died over several weeks as infection spread rapidly through overcrowded flocks on the Lower Klamath and Tule Lake refuges. Mortality declined once additional water was delivered, refuge wetlands re‑flooded, and carcass‑removal teams reduced environmental contamination, but the event highlighted how drought and water‑allocation decisions can precipitate large‑scale cholera epizootics.([kqed.org](https://www.kqed.org/news/60809/avian-cholera-kills-thousands-of-birds-in-northern-california))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptional water scarcity linked to drought and upstream water management left key refuge marshes largely dry during peak spring migration, concentrating millions of birds into a small number of shallow wetlands and dramatically increasing bird density and contact rates; carcasses accumulating in crowded wetlands further contaminated water and sediments with P. multocida. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved typical North American waterfowl strains of P. multocida in an area with a long history of cholera; there is no evidence of novel genotypes or resistance traits driving the epizootic, which is best classified as an extreme re‑occurrence of an endemic disease under unusually severe crowding and environmental conditions.([wildfowlmag.com](https://www.wildfowlmag.com/editorial/disease-decimating-california-waterfowl/280320?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added because the 2012 Klamath Basin epizootic (≥10,000–20,000 waterfowl dead) is one of the largest modern avian cholera die‑offs in the Pacific Flyway and clearly exceeds the impact of the smaller 2015 Idaho outbreak; classification as a severe re‑occurrence driven by drought‑induced crowding is well supported.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [California – commercial broiler ranch 2025]
Host: Commercial slow-growing broiler chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) on a large broiler ranch
Event summary: Around 2025, a severe outbreak of acute fowl cholera in a commercial slow‑growing broiler system in California resulted in the complete loss of a 25,000‑bird flock on a 262,500‑broiler ranch. Over the 14‑week production cycle, successive spikes in mortality prompted necropsy submissions at 5, 11 and 14 weeks of age, and diagnostic workups confirmed P. multocida infection; by the time of scheduled processing, cumulative mortality in the affected flock had reached 100%. The episode drew attention to the particular vulnerability of slow‑growing broiler systems to fowl cholera and prompted recommendations for strengthened biosecurity and consideration of targeted vaccination in such operations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40643942/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Slow‑growing broiler lines remain on farms for much longer than conventional broilers, increasing cumulative exposure time to environmental contamination, wild birds and rodents; barn‑level management factors and potential gaps in biosecurity and preventive vaccination likely contributed to introduction and rapid flock‑wide spread. Internal mechanisms: The causative P. multocida isolate was typed as serovar 1 with a common fingerprint (HhaI 0001), not reported as genetically novel, and the outbreak is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence of a known virulent lineage in a production system with heightened susceptibility due to longer grow‑out and management practices, rather than as a distinct strain‑emergence event.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40643942/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added because complete loss of a 25,000‑bird slow‑growing broiler flock from acute fowl cholera represents a major modern poultry outbreak with clear economic impact and management implications. Classified as a dramatic re‑occurrence of established P. multocida serovar‑1 lineages in a vulnerable production system rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/indicus), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event summary: From 2000 to 2005, participatory disease surveillance across Pakistan documented haemorrhagic septicaemia as one of the most prevalent and economically important livestock diseases, with high reported prevalence and perceived importance in many districts of Punjab, Sindh, North-West Frontier Province/Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and the Northern Areas, and annual economic losses in Punjab alone estimated at more than 2.17 billion Pakistani rupees. HS was identified as a leading cause of cattle and buffalo mortality in susceptible stock, with farmers consistently ranking it above or alongside other major transboundary diseases in terms of economic impact. The episode represents a period of intense endemic circulation and repeated local outbreaks, which spurred calls for improved vaccination coverage, surveillance and coordinated national control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of cattle and buffalo in smallholder systems, seasonal monsoon-associated humidity, fodder scarcity, heavy work stress in draught animals, and gaps in vaccination coverage and surveillance enabled widespread HS transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks were attributed to endemic Pasteurella multocida serotypes B:2/E:2; there is no evidence that novel genotypes or resistance profiles were central to this period, so the episode is best characterized as large-scale re-occurrence driven by environmental and management factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a new multi-year national episode because participatory disease surveillance (2000–2005) shows HS as one of Pakistan’s most prevalent and economically important bovine diseases, with very large estimated annual losses. Classified as re-occurrence (endemic disease with external drivers; no evidence that novel strains drove this period). Geography (Asia/Southern Asia, Pakistan) and timeframe follow the surveillance and economic-loss data; sources focus specifically on HS epidemiology and impact in Pakistan.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/indicus), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event summary: During the early 2000s, India experienced intense HS activity in bovines, with particularly high incidence in Karnataka state, where retrospective analysis of outbreak and farm-level data showed HS outbreaks increasing from 2002 and peaking in 2005. Numerous farm outbreaks caused high morbidity and mortality and substantial economic losses via reduced milk production, loss of draught power and replacement costs, with state-level projected economic losses from HS running into tens of millions of US dollars under high-incidence scenarios. Following this peak, targeted mass vaccination campaigns and improved management and awareness led to a marked decline in reported HS outbreaks and associated financial losses in Karnataka.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense bovine populations in small and medium farms, suboptimal housing and nutrition, and monsoon-associated humidity and temperature were linked to repeated HS outbreaks; limited vaccine coverage at the start of the period contributed to high susceptibility, while expanding vaccination programs later reduced incidence. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks were caused by endemic Pasteurella multocida serotype B:2; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or resistance trait driving emergence, so the episode reflects re-occurrence driven by environmental stress and inadequate herd immunity rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Large, well-documented regional episode with quantified outbreak trends and substantial projected economic losses for Karnataka, making it one of the most impactful HS episodes in India during 1990–2010. Updated the 'countries' field to explicitly indicate India [2002–2005] and Karnataka state as the focal area; classification as re-occurrence (environmental and vaccination-coverage driven) is consistent with the epidemiological analysis and no evidence for novel strains.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), cattle (Bos taurus/indicus)
Event summary: In late September to mid-October 2003, a severe HS outbreak occurred in Banir and Bidor areas of Batang Padang district, Perak State, Malaysia, affecting shared-grazing buffalo and cattle herds. In Banir, 11 buffalo herds (572 animals) and two cattle herds (56 animals) were involved, with 200 buffalo and four cattle deaths, while an additional small buffalo herd in Bidor also suffered high mortality; Pasteurella multocida serotype B:2 was isolated from heart blood and nasal swabs. The epidemic curve showed an explosive,-short duration event with most deaths occurring in the first week, and the outbreak was described as the largest HS episode in the country in the preceding decade. After emergency vaccination and management changes, mortality subsided and no further major HS cases were reported in the affected herds during the investigation period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of apparently healthy but carrier cattle from an HS-endemic region into an immunologically naïve, poorly vaccinated buffalo population, combined with heavy rainfall and use of shared ponds and swamps for wallowing and drinking, created ideal conditions for rapid transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by typical HS-associated P. multocida B:2; there was no indication of novel genotypes or resistance, so this episode represents a catastrophic re-occurrence in an endemic country triggered by animal movement and environmental conditions rather than pathogen change.
Review: Retain – Added as a new high-impact outbreak representing South-eastern Asia; mortality of over 200 buffaloes plus cattle and characterization as Malaysia’s largest HS outbreak in a decade justify inclusion among major events. Classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country (no evidence of new strain or new region); geography (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Malaysia; Perak State) and scale are taken directly from the outbreak investigation report.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Countries: Ethiopia [2007-2015] (Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ Regional State)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus)
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2015, retrospective surveillance in Ethiopia’s Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ Regional State documented 1,496 reportable cattle disease outbreaks, with haemorrhagic septicaemia accounting for 393 outbreaks (26.3%) and thousands of bovine cases and deaths across multiple zones. HS outbreaks occurred in diverse agro-ecological zones and were concentrated after the long rainy season, indicating persistent endemic circulation with periodic large flare-ups that together caused substantial productivity losses. Despite vaccination efforts, repeated HS outbreaks over this nine‑year period underscored gaps in coverage, under-reporting and challenges in timely response, prompting recommendations for strengthened surveillance and targeted immunization before high-risk seasons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic HS presence combined with seasonal climatic patterns (highest outbreak frequency in early dry season after heavy rains), variable access to veterinary services, and inconsistent vaccination campaigns drove recurrent outbreaks across zones; under-reporting and weak outbreak investigation capacity impeded effective control. Internal mechanisms: Available data attribute outbreaks to typical bovine HS due to P. multocida serogroup B/E; no specific novel variants or resistance patterns were implicated, so this episode reflects sustained re-occurrence linked primarily to environmental and programmatic factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Multi-year surveillance shows HS responsible for over a quarter of all reported cattle disease outbreaks in SNNPRS, with thousands of cases and hundreds of deaths, making this one of the better-quantified high-burden HS episodes in Africa. Geography (Africa/Eastern Africa, Ethiopia; SNNPRS) and timeframe are consistent with the retrospective study; classification as re-occurrence is appropriate since environmental seasonality and incomplete vaccination, not pathogen change, explain the pattern. Removed a redundant Mendeley catalog URL in favor of the primary journal PDF and WOAH manual.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica), with related bovine HS strains in cattle
Event summary: From 2010 to 2015, several mass mortality events affected saiga antelope populations in Kazakhstan, culminating in an unprecedented die‑off in May 2015 in the Betpak‑Dala population in which around 200,000 animals died within weeks, wiping out entire calving aggregations and reducing the global population by more than two-thirds. Necropsy, bacteriology and molecular work confirmed haemorrhagic septicaemia caused by Pasteurella multocida serogroup B as the proximate cause of death, with earlier, smaller die‑offs in 2010–2012 also linked to P. multocida. Following the 2015 catastrophe, surviving saiga populations began to recover under intensive conservation measures, but the events highlighted the potential for an opportunistic bovine pathogen to cause explosive, climate‑triggered mortality in a wild antelope host already under demographic pressure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually warm and humid conditions during calving in 2015 (and likely in earlier events), high animal density at calving sites, and limited dispersal are inferred to have triggered systemic activation of normally commensal P. multocida in saiga tonsils, leading to synchronized septicemia and mass mortality; historical over‑exploitation and habitat pressures left populations especially vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that saiga isolates were P. multocida serogroup B closely related to bovine HS strains (e.g. ST64) with multiple virulence genes; this represents host expansion and re-emergence of haemorrhagic septicaemia in a wild ungulate, where bacterial traits and host physiology under climatic stress enabled rapid progression from commensal carriage to fatal septicaemia across entire calving aggregations.
Review: Retain – This is an exceptionally high-impact event, with ≈200,000 saiga deaths in 2015 plus earlier die-offs, and clear attribution to P. multocida-associated haemorrhagic septicaemia under extreme climatic conditions; it also represents a major host expansion for a classical bovine pathogen. Corrected the emergence classification so that only re-emergence is marked "true" (reflecting host expansion and altered disease expression), removing the simultaneous re-occurrence flag to comply with the project rule that re-emergence should not co-occur with re-occurrence. Geography (Asia/Central Asia, Kazakhstan; Betpak-Dala and Ural saiga populations) and timeframe are consistent with the EID, Science Advances and BMC Microbiology analyses.

EPP common name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), cattle (Bos taurus)
Event summary: During the large 2011–2012 SAT2 foot-and-mouth disease epidemic in Egypt, an associated outbreak of haemorrhagic septicaemia was documented in 5,630 fattening buffalo and cattle calves from 25 farms along the Alexandria–Cairo desert road in Alexandria province. Approximately 4,616 animals (81.9%) showed clinical signs of FMD, and among these, 2,600 calves (56.3%) developed HS with 362 deaths (case fatality ~14%), with buffalo calves showing much higher HS morbidity and mortality than cattle; P. multocida serotype B:2 was isolated from lung, liver and heart blood. After antibiotic treatment, emergency vaccination and improved management, the combined FMD–HS mortality declined and the outbreak was brought under control, but the episode illustrated how immunosuppression from FMD can precipitate large HS die-offs in intensively reared young stock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A major SAT2 FMD outbreak caused immunosuppression and stress in densely stocked fattening calves, facilitating overgrowth and systemic spread of P. multocida; additional drivers included high animal density, shared management across multiple large farms, and initial gaps in HS vaccination. Internal mechanisms: The HS component was caused by typical P. multocida B:2 strains with usual virulence traits; there is no indication of novel strain emergence, so this episode is best seen as a severe re-occurrence of HS precipitated by viral co-infection and management conditions rather than by pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a major outbreak episode in Northern Africa with thousands of at-risk calves, 2,600 HS cases and over 360 deaths, clearly linked to SAT2 FMD co-infection and supported by detailed epidemiological data. Classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country, since HS was already present in Egypt and the main drivers were FMD-associated immunosuppression, stocking density and vaccination gaps, not new HS strains. Geography (Africa/Northern Africa, Egypt; Alexandria province) and year (2012) are derived from the Life Science Journal outbreak report and related FMD timeline.

Countries: India [1995] (multiple states including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Punjab and others)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus, Bos taurus and crossbreds), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event summary: Between 1995 and 2003, India experienced a prolonged period of very high hemorrhagic septicemia (HS) activity in cattle and buffalo, with P. multocida serogroup B:2 causing tens of thousands of reported outbreaks across most Indian states, particularly in the southern zone. Spatio‑temporal analyses of national surveillance data show that states such as Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka consistently accounted for a large share of annual HS outbreaks, indicating sustained, large‑scale transmission and heavy livestock losses. Toward the end of this period, increasing vaccination and control efforts coincided with a gradual decline in reported outbreaks in several regions, although HS has remained endemic thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large cattle and buffalo populations kept in smallholder and mixed-farming systems, seasonal stress associated with monsoon rains and heat, animal movements, and uneven vaccination coverage created conditions for extensive, recurrent HS outbreaks. Weak veterinary infrastructure and reliance on passive surveillance likely contributed to under-reporting but also to delayed control in many districts. Internal mechanisms: Circulating P. multocida serogroup B:2 lineages exhibit virulence-associated factors typical of HS (capsule, iron-acquisition systems, outer-membrane proteins) that support rapid septicemia and high case fatality, but there is limited evidence that major novel variants arose specifically to drive the 1995–2003 peak; this episode is therefore best categorized as severe re-occurrence rather than strain-driven re-emergence.
Review: Review – Event clearly represents one of the largest documented HS burdens globally and should be retained. Emergence type has been corrected from combined re_occurrence + re_emergence to re_occurrence only, because available outbreak and genomic data show long-established B:2 lineages and do not demonstrate a specific novel variant driving this period. Country, continent and sub-region assignments are correct. Text remains somewhat general on exact numbers but consistent with national analyses; human expert may refine quantitative impact estimates.

Host: Feedlot cattle (bovine respiratory disease complex)
Event summary: From 2011 to 2016, investigations of bovine respiratory disease (BRD) mortalities in North American feedlots identified a high and concerning prevalence of multidrug-resistant Pasteurellaceae, including P. multocida and Mannheimia haemolytica, in lung tissue from fatal cases across numerous feedlots in the United States and Canada. These isolates, collected from large commercial operations, demonstrated resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes commonly used in BRD metaphylaxis and therapy, indicating widespread dissemination of MDR strains within the feedlot sector. Although BRD and P. multocida had long been endemic in the region, the emergence and documentation of MDR profiles raised concern about compromised treatment efficacy and prompted increased emphasis on antimicrobial stewardship and alternative control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of antimicrobials in feedlot cattle for metaphylaxis and treatment of BRD, combined with large‑scale confinement, high stocking densities and commingling of calves from many sources, created strong selection pressures and transmission opportunities for resistant P. multocida and other Pasteurellaceae. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and spread of multiple antimicrobial resistance genes (including those conferring resistance to macrolides, tetracyclines and other drug classes) in P. multocida and M. haemolytica represent a clear case of antimicrobial resistance–driven re-emergence within an existing disease complex, without evidence that the pathogen was geographically new to the region.
Review: Retain – This multi-year, multi-country episode documents widespread MDR P. multocida in a major livestock sector, with clear implications for morbidity, mortality and treatment failure in BRD. It fits the definition of re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than geographic spread. Continent, sub-region and country coding are correct; event years align with the sampling frame of the cited study. No major corrections needed beyond clarifying that some resistance patterns may reflect pre-existing selection rather than a simple monotonic rise, which does not change its importance as a major AMR-related emergence event.

Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, rabbits, poultry and companion animals with respiratory or systemic pasteurellosis
Event summary: Between 2012 and 2017, data from the French national veterinary antimicrobial resistance network (RESAPATH) showed that P. multocida isolated from respiratory infections in food-producing animals and pets was widespread, and that in cattle isolates in particular, resistance to several veterinary antimicrobials (notably tetracyclines and some older agents) was present at non-trivial levels. Although overall resistance to critically important antimicrobials such as third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones remained low, the surveillance highlighted distinct resistance profiles in cattle compared with other host species and provided evidence that selection for resistance was occurring despite national efforts to reduce antimicrobial use. These findings informed national guidelines and stewardship initiatives aimed at preserving the efficacy of key BRD treatments in French livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing, widespread use of oral and injectable antimicrobials for respiratory disease in cattle and other species in France, including metaphylactic regimens, provided selection pressure for resistance. The structure of French livestock production, with integrated systems and animal movements between farms and regions, facilitated dissemination of successful resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Progressive accumulation and dissemination of resistance determinants in P. multocida, particularly in cattle isolates (e.g., genes mediating resistance to tetracyclines and older antimicrobials), represent antimicrobial resistance–mediated re-emergence of the pathogen as a more difficult-to-treat cause of respiratory disease. Most isolates remained susceptible to high-priority critically important drugs, but the documented resistance patterns signal evolutionary responses to past drug exposure.
Review: Review – This event reflects a large national surveillance dataset (thousands of isolates) and is important for understanding AMR-driven re-emergence. However, the original draft slightly overstated uniformly increasing resistance trends and underplayed that overall resistance to several key classes remained low. The summary has been rephrased for closer alignment with published RESAPATH and EFSA descriptions. Classification as re_emergence via AMR is appropriate. Geographic coding (Western Europe, France) and years (2012–2017) match the main study period, but a human expert should confirm quantitative thresholds and whether France should indeed be prioritized over other European countries with similar surveillance data in a strict top‑10 ranking.

Host: Free-range and intensive pigs and cattle (acute septicemia and respiratory disease due to P. multocida type B)
Event summary: From 2009 onward, Spain documented the emergence of P. multocida capsular type B, classically associated with hemorrhagic septicemia, as a cause of acute septicemic pasteurellosis in free-range pigs, wild boar and later cattle. An initial outbreak of acute septicemia in free-range pigs in 2009 was followed by additional type B outbreaks in swine and wild boar, and in February 2015 the first documented outbreak of bovine hemorrhagic septicemia caused by P. multocida type B occurred on a free-range beef farm in southern Spain, affecting calves and one cow with characteristic HS lesions. Over the period 2010–2018, at least 70–80 type B isolates from pigs and cattle with acute septicemia were characterized, revealing shared capsular type B biovar 3 profiles and, in many isolates, reduced susceptibility to commonly used antimicrobials. Autogenous vaccination and targeted antimicrobial therapy were implemented to control farm-level outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of free-range and mixed-species livestock systems in parts of Spain, with close contact between pigs, cattle and wildlife (e.g., wild boar, deer), likely facilitated the introduction and circulation of type B P. multocida lineages historically associated with HS in Asia and Africa. Animal movements and environmental conditions in extensive systems also favored persistence and spillover between host species. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization shows Spanish type B isolates clustering with global HS-associated lineages and sharing virulence-associated genes typical of hemorrhagic septicemia, while antimicrobial susceptibility testing of pig and cattle isolates revealed resistance to several commonly used drug classes (e.g., tetracyclines, some older agents). Together, these findings support classification as re-emergence via geographic expansion of HS-associated type B lineages into Iberian livestock and partial evolution of antimicrobial resistance, rather than a first detection of P. multocida in the region.
Review: Review – Spain’s type B episode is epidemiologically important because it marks the appearance and spread of HS-associated P. multocida lineages in Iberian pigs, wild boar and, for the first time, cattle, with documented acute septicemia and economic impact. The event year range has been updated to 2009–2018 to encompass the first reported pig outbreak and the 2015 bovine HS outbreak. Hosts and event summary have been broadened accordingly, and key primary sources (Acta Veterinaria Hungarica short communication on the 2015 bovine HS outbreak and the Vet Microbiol AMR paper on type B isolates) have been added. Classification as re_emergence (host expansion/geographic expansion plus AMR) remains appropriate. A human reviewer should confirm whether to treat pig and cattle outbreaks as a single linked episode (as done here) or as separate events in a more granular dataset.

Countries: Brazil [2010] (southern Brazil poultry and swine production)
Host: Commercial chickens and turkeys, grower-finisher pigs
Event summary: In the early 2010s, a study of 96 P. multocida strains from clinical cases in southern Brazil documented frequent isolation of the bacterium from repeated outbreaks of pasteurellosis in intensive poultry and swine operations, together with high frequencies of virulence-associated genes and multidrug resistance. Isolates from diseased birds (liver and heart) and pigs (lungs) showed resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes, including sulfonamides, tetracyclines and macrolides, and many carried combinations of adhesin, outer-membrane and iron-acquisition genes. These findings indicated that virulent, multidrug-resistant P. multocida lineages had become established in Brazilian pig and poultry production, increasing the difficulty of controlling respiratory and septicemic disease complexes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High antimicrobial use in Brazilian poultry and swine industries for treatment and metaphylaxis, dense industrial production with rapid turnover, and frequent movement of animals between farms favored selection and dissemination of resistant P. multocida. Internal mechanisms: Many isolates carried multiple virulence-associated genes (e.g., ompH, oma87, ptfA, iron-acquisition and sialidase genes) alongside resistance determinants to several antimicrobial classes, exemplifying re-emergence of P. multocida as a more difficult-to-control pathogen in these sectors through combined virulence and multidrug resistance.
Review: Retain – This episode represents a major AMR- and virulence-associated re-emergence of P. multocida in a key livestock region, with repeated clinical outbreaks across poultry and swine and clear documentation of multidrug resistance in many isolates. Continent, sub-region and country coding (South America, Brazil) and years (2010–2014) match the sampled period. No geographic or event-type corrections are needed; classification as re_emergence driven by AMR and virulence gene combinations is appropriate. A human reviewer might consider adding more explicit production-loss estimates if available, but the event meets the criteria for inclusion among the major global episodes.

Host: Commercial poultry (chickens, ducks, geese) with fowl cholera
Event summary: Between roughly 2012 and 2016, repeated fowl cholera outbreaks in poultry in southwest China led to the isolation and detailed characterization of 45 P. multocida strains from clinically affected flocks. These outbreaks affected multiple avian species and farms and were associated predominantly with capsular type A strains carrying numerous virulence genes, along with a range of antimicrobial resistance determinants. By the end of the study period, florfenicol- and streptomycin-resistant isolates harboring floR and strA genes, respectively, had been detected, underscoring a shift toward more resistant avian P. multocida populations in this region’s commercial poultry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of poultry production in southwest China, combined with routine antibiotic use and potential exposure to wild bird reservoirs, facilitated repeated introduction and spread of virulent, partially resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Isolates exhibited diverse capsular–LPS genotypes, high prevalence of virulence genes, and the presence of resistance genes such as floR and strA, indicating concurrent evolution of virulence and antimicrobial resistance. This pattern is consistent with re-occurrence of endemic fowl cholera combined with re-emergence of more resistant and genetically diverse P. multocida lineages.
Review: Retain – This event aggregates several years of recurrent fowl cholera outbreaks in a major poultry-producing region, with clear evidence of virulent and increasingly resistant P. multocida populations. Geographic coding (Eastern Asia, China) and years align with the study. Classification as both re_occurrence (repeated outbreaks in an endemic area) and re_emergence (novel genotype and AMR patterns) is justified by the molecular data. No major corrections identified; human review may refine the description of outbreak sizes and economic impact if additional national data are available.

Host: Pigs with respiratory disease/pasteurellosis
Event summary: From approximately 2013 to 2018, veterinary laboratories in Viet Nam collected and characterized 83 P. multocida isolates from pigs showing clinical signs of pasteurellosis and respiratory disease, reflecting recurrent outbreaks in commercial herds in central Vietnam. Molecular analysis revealed high prevalence of multiple virulence factors and capsular serotypes among these isolates, together with several antimicrobial resistance genes. The findings suggest that virulent and partially multidrug-resistant P. multocida lineages had become entrenched in Vietnamese pig production, complicating control of respiratory disease complexes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of Vietnam’s swine industry, high animal densities, and the use of antimicrobials for growth promotion and disease prevention created favorable conditions for emergence and spread of virulent, resistant P. multocida strains. Internal mechanisms: Many isolates carried clustered virulence genes and antibiotic resistance determinants (including genes conferring resistance to tetracyclines and sulfonamides), consistent with re-emergence driven by acquisition of resistance and maintenance of a robust virulence arsenal in pig-adapted lineages.
Review: Retain – This episode documents the establishment of virulent, AMR-associated P. multocida lineages in a rapidly intensifying swine sector, with repeated clinical disease and clear molecular evidence of resistance and virulence factors. Geographic coding (South-eastern Asia, Viet Nam) and years are in line with the study. Event-type assignment as re_emergence (rather than mere re-occurrence) is appropriate given the focus on virulence and resistance genes. No major inconsistencies were identified; human review could strengthen the link to specific production-loss estimates if available from national sources.

Host: Chickens (broilers and layers), other domestic birds, rabbits
Event summary: Between about 2015 and 2020, multiple Egyptian studies on diseased chickens and other domestic birds documented frequent isolation of P. multocida from fowl cholera outbreaks, together with increasing detection of antimicrobial resistance and diverse virulence profiles; parallel work in rabbits identified multidrug-resistant P. multocida strains causing pasteurellosis. These investigations, mainly in governorates such as Sharkia and Ismailia, indicate repeated outbreaks in commercial and smallholder flocks and rabbitries, often with high mortality and significant economic losses. Over time, detection of numerous resistance genes and, in some studies, new virulence-associated markers such as luxS highlighted a shift toward more resistant and potentially more adaptable P. multocida populations in Egyptian poultry and rabbits.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive poultry production with variable biosecurity, widespread antimicrobial use in flocks and rabbitries, and co-circulation of other respiratory pathogens created ecological niches for expansion of resistant P. multocida strains. Backyard and smallholder systems further facilitated persistence and transmission. Internal mechanisms: Isolates carried multiple resistance genes (e.g., for tetracyclines, sulfonamides, trimethoprim) and numerous virulence genes; some studies reported luxS and other traits associated with quorum sensing and biofilm formation. These features together represent re-occurrence of endemic fowl cholera and snuffles combined with re-emergence via antimicrobial resistance and potential enhancement of transmission or persistence traits.
Review: Retain – Egypt has experienced sustained, economically important P. multocida problems in poultry and rabbits during this period, with multiple independent studies documenting MDR and virulence traits. Geographic and sub-regional coding (Northern Africa, Egypt) are correct and event years reasonably summarize the overlapping study periods. Classification as both re_occurrence (repeated outbreaks in an endemic setting) and re_emergence (AMR and virulence evolution) is well supported. One source URL has been updated to a journal-hosted version of the Sharkia governorate study rather than an intermediate repository. Human review could refine which specific years and governorates contributed the largest economic losses.

Countries: Kazakhstan [2015] (Betpak-Dala region and other calving areas)
Host: Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica)
Event summary: In May 2015, a catastrophic mass die-off of saiga antelopes occurred in central Kazakhstan, with approximately 200,000 animals – more than half of the global population at the time and virtually all animals in affected herds – dying over about two weeks during the calving period. Necropsy, microbiology and molecular investigations identified hemorrhagic septicemia caused by P. multocida serotype B as the proximate cause of death, with consistent gross and histopathologic lesions and high isolation rates from carcasses. The episode followed an unusually warm and humid spell, and there was no evidence of other primary infectious agents; the die-off caused a dramatic, temporary collapse of saiga numbers and spurred intensive international conservation and disease-ecology research.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme short-term climatic anomalies (unusually high humidity and temperature) coinciding with dense calving aggregations likely triggered systemic invasion by P. multocida carried latently in the tonsils and upper respiratory tract of apparently healthy saigas. High local densities during calving, limited dispersal options and prior population stressors contributed to near-100% mortality in affected herds. Internal mechanisms: Characterization of P. multocida isolates from the die-off indicated capsular type B strains closely related to HS-associated lineages from domestic livestock in Asia and Europe, with no unique novel virulence determinants clearly distinguishing them from other B:2/B:3 HS strains. The event is therefore best interpreted as a climate- and host-context–driven re-occurrence of hemorrhagic septicemia in a susceptible wildlife host, rather than a re-emergence driven by pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – This event was missing from the original draft yet is arguably one of the most impactful P. multocida-associated episodes since 1990, with ~200,000 saigas (≈60–70% of the global population) dying over a short period. It has now been added as a major re-occurrence event in Central Asia wildlife. Continent, sub-region and country assignments (Asia, Central Asia, Kazakhstan) are correct. Classification as re_occurrence (climate-triggered activation of latent P. multocida) rather than re_emergence is supported by genomic analyses showing close relatedness to existing HS lineages. Because the host system of interest for this EPP entry is livestock/poultry, inclusion of this wildlife-focused event should be explicitly approved by domain experts, but it fits the instructions to include major events even in hosts outside the primary system.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei (Penaeus vannamei)
Event summary: From 2002, intensive L. vannamei farms in Piauí State, northeastern Brazil began reporting episodes of idiopathic myonecrosis with whitening of abdominal muscles and slow but high cumulative mortalities that in some ponds approached 70%. Over 2003–2005 the condition spread along Brazil’s northeast coast into additional states, causing repeated crop failures and national losses estimated in the hundreds of millions of US dollars as productivity in affected areas dropped sharply. Investigations during this period purified a 40 nm dsRNA virus from diseased shrimp, which was designated infectious myonecrosis virus (IMNV), and adoption of improved biosecurity, specific-pathogen-free (SPF) stocks and movement controls subsequently reduced the frequency of catastrophic IMN outbreaks, although the virus remained endemic in parts of Brazil.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of L. vannamei aquaculture in northeastern Brazil, with high stocking densities, long grow-out periods, and frequent environmental stressors (temperature and water-quality fluctuations), together with extensive movement of postlarvae and juveniles among farms, created ideal conditions for emergence and farm-to-farm spread of a previously unrecognised virus. Internal mechanisms: IMNV is a novel dsRNA virus tentatively assigned to the Totiviridae, with a chronic infection profile, high viral loads in skeletal muscle and ability to persist in surviving shrimp; these traits support efficient horizontal transmission within ponds (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) and facilitated geographic range expansion and establishment in Brazilian farmed L. vannamei populations (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Review – Retain this event as the first global emergence and detection of IMNV in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in Brazil, but expand the event period from "2002-2004" to "2002-2005" to reflect that IMN-related epizootics and large productivity losses in northeastern Brazil clearly continued through 2004–2005; geography and emergence-type coding remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: In 2006, farms in the Situbondo District of East Java, Indonesia, experienced outbreaks of a myonecrosis disease in L. vannamei characterised by whitening of abdominal musculature and chronic mortalities reminiscent of Brazilian infectious myonecrosis. RT-PCR and sequencing of the viral capsid gene from affected shrimp showed IMNV highly similar to the Brazilian reference strain, confirming introduction of the virus into Indonesia and its spread during 2006–2007 to additional shrimp-growing areas with substantial economic losses in intensive farms. Control measures including stricter screening and control of broodstock and postlarvae movements, farm biosecurity upgrades and adjusted stocking practices gradually reduced catastrophic mortality, although IMNV became endemic and later genotypes have continued to be detected in Indonesian production systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: transboundary movement of live L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae from IMNV-endemic Brazil, often without adequate health certification or screening, combined with rapid intensification of L. vannamei farming in Indonesia, enabled introduction and establishment of IMNV in Southeast Asia. Internal mechanisms: Indonesian isolates from the initial outbreaks were nearly identical to Brazilian strains, indicating direct geographic spread of an existing lineage; chronic infection dynamics and efficient horizontal transmission in high-density ponds (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent) underpinned rapid farm-to-farm dissemination once the virus entered the country.
Review: Review – Event appropriately represents the first confirmed IMNV outbreaks in Indonesia and the first inter-continental emergence of IMNV into Asia; I set re_emergence to false (previously true) because early Indonesian isolates were essentially identical to Brazilian strains and there is no evidence that a novel variant drove this initial incursion, so this episode is best classified purely as inter-continental geographic spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: In May 2015, a grow-out facility for juvenile L. vannamei on the Korean coast experienced sudden mortalities in two tanks, with about 40% of 500,000 stocked shrimp dying over three days; histology revealed typical IMN lesions (coagulative skeletal muscle necrosis and lymphoid organ spheroids), and nested RT-PCR followed by sequencing confirmed IMNV infection. A subsequent epidemiological investigation in 2015 tested broodstock, imported polychaete lugworms used as maturation feed, rearing water and surrounding organisms from five hatcheries, detecting IMNV in one of six broodstock and in 25–40% of the imported lugworms but not in culture water or local wild invertebrates, indicating introduction via infected biological inputs. Following diagnosis, Korean authorities implemented quarantine and movement restrictions on affected facilities, strengthened import controls and diagnostics for broodstock and feeds, and later national surveillance has not reported additional large-scale IMNV epizootics in Korean farms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Korea’s emerging whiteleg shrimp sector relied on imported SPF broodstock and frozen or chilled polychaete lugworms for broodstock maturation; the discovery of IMNV in both broodstock and lugworms from one hatchery indicates that infected live or fresh inputs, rather than the environment, were the most plausible introduction pathway. High-density juvenile culture and limited prior experience with IMNV in Korea facilitated rapid amplification once it entered the facility. Internal mechanisms: IMNV’s capacity to establish persistent infections in broodstock and survive in fresh or frozen biological materials (feeds) allows long-distance movement without obvious clinical signs, and its chronic but often substantial mortality profile in L. vannamei supports its establishment in intensive hatchery and nursery systems when biosecurity is breached (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Review – Added this event to capture the first confirmed IMNV outbreak in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in the Republic of Korea in 2015, which is largely omitted from global timelines; classified it as intra-continental emergence into the Eastern Asia subregion with country-level first detection, and based the description on the national epidemiological investigation that links introduction to infected broodstock and imported lugworm feed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: In 2016, shrimp farms in Purba Medinipur District, West Bengal, India reported disease outbreaks in L. vannamei characterised by muscle opaqueness, reddish discolouration of distal abdominal segments and gradually increasing mortalities of roughly 20–50%, with routine PCR tests negative for common DNA shrimp viruses. RT-PCR with IMNV-specific primers, histopathology and experimental infection of naïve shrimp identified IMNV as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed report of IMNV in Indian aquaculture and demonstrating local farm-to-farm spread in affected coastal areas. Subsequent surveillance showed that IMNV infections remained sporadic but persistent in Indian L. vannamei culture, prompting inclusion of IMNV in national health management plans and SPF breeding and screening programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of L. vannamei farming in India, heavy reliance on imported and domestically multiplied broodstock, and imperfect screening and biosecurity created pathways for IMNV introduction, while high stocking densities, environmental stress and co-infections likely amplified disease impact once the virus was present. Internal mechanisms: available sequence and epidemiological data suggest that Indian IMNV represents geographic range expansion of existing Asian/Brazilian lineages rather than a uniquely Indian variant; the chronic infection dynamics and high susceptibility of L. vannamei favour establishment in new farming regions once introduced (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: Review – Event correctly describes the first confirmed IMNV outbreaks in India in 2016 and treats them as intra-continental emergence into the Southern Asia subregion with country-level first detection; I removed a later generic surveillance paper that did not specifically document these West Bengal outbreaks and retained the primary 2017 J Fish Diseases article and key reviews as sources.

Countries: Brazil [2016] (notably farms in Pará, Maranhão, Piauí, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe and Bahia)
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: Beginning around 2016, many intensive L. vannamei farms in Brazil’s northeastern states again reported IMN-like disease, but with faster progression and in some cases cumulative mortalities reportedly reaching up to 80%, causing significant production losses through at least 2019. Molecular diagnostics on moribund shrimp from multiple states showed high IMNV loads and little or no WSSV, and whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate from Ceará in 2018 revealed a novel IMNV strain, designated Br-1, whose 8.2 kb genome shared about 98% identity with the historic Brazilian reference but clustered more closely with Indonesian strains in phylogenetic analyses. Awareness of this more virulent variant led Brazilian producers and breeding programmes to strengthen IMNV screening of broodstock and postlarvae, review the use of imported genetic lines, and further enhance biosecurity and health management to mitigate a renewed wave of IMNV-driven losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: renewed growth and intensification of shrimp farming in northeastern Brazil, coupled with informal or poorly controlled movements of L. vannamei genetic lines between Brazil and Indonesia, likely facilitated introduction and selection of a novel IMNV variant in areas where the original strains had been partially controlled. Internal mechanisms: genomic analysis shows Br-1 is a distinct IMNV lineage more closely related to Indonesian strains, consistent with either re-introduction or evolution under new selection pressures; the associated outbreaks featured more rapid and sometimes higher mortalities than earlier IMNV epidemics, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and increased pathogenicity (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: Review – Added this re-emergence event to represent the 2016–2019 wave of unusually severe IMNV outbreaks in northeastern Brazil associated with the Br-1 variant; classified it as re_emergence in a previously affected South American subregion driven by emergence of a novel, more virulent strain, without additional intra- or inter-continental spread, using the 2022 Aquaculture paper and related summaries as primary sources.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: In 2018, Malaysian authorities reported an outbreak of disease consistent with infectious myonecrosis in cultured L. vannamei in Melaka, Peninsular Malaysia, with affected shrimp showing muscle atrophy and reddish discolouration of the tail region; national reporting to the NACA/WOAH Quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease system listed infection with IMNV as the causative agent. During 2018–2019, IMNV was recognised as a new viral threat for Malaysian shrimp farming, with positive PCR findings in affected farms raising concern over possible introduction from IMNV-endemic neighbours and prompting review of broodstock and postlarvae import controls. In response, Malaysia implemented enhanced biosecurity, tighter regulation of live shrimp imports and inclusion of IMNV among screened and notifiable pathogens, which appears to have limited more widespread epizootics while leaving IMNV as an ongoing regional risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introduction of IMNV via regional trade in live L. vannamei broodstock or postlarvae from endemic parts of Asia, combined with high-intensity culture and previously limited routine screening for IMNV, facilitated this re-occurrence within the South-eastern Asia subregion. Internal mechanisms: available sequence information and the regional context suggest the Malaysian outbreaks were caused by IMNV lineages closely related to Indonesian/Indian strains rather than a novel variant; the event is therefore best interpreted as geographic range expansion within Southeast Asia, with impact driven by the inherent high susceptibility of L. vannamei and the chronic, production-sapping nature of IMNV infection (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Retain – QAAD 2018/2 and associated Malaysian reports support a genuine IMNV outbreak in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in Melaka in 2018 with measurable mortality; classification as first_detection for Malaysia and re-occurrence within an already affected South‑eastern Asia subregion (without new subregion or continent) is consistent with the event definitions, and no corrections to timing, geography or emergence type were required.

Host: Cultured penaeid shrimp, primarily Penaeus semisulcatus (also posing risk to L. vannamei)
Event summary: From around 2018, disease outbreaks with muscle necrosis, reduced growth and abnormal appearance were reported in cultured penaeid shrimp (notably P. semisulcatus) on private farms in Damietta and North Sinai provinces along Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Clinical examination, histopathology and PCR testing of affected shrimp confirmed IMNV infection with typical myonecrosis lesions, representing the first documented presence of IMNV in African aquaculture and indicating local establishment on the north coast. Repeated detections over subsequent production cycles raised concern about the virus’s impact on Egypt’s expanding shrimp industry and its potential spread to other Mediterranean and Red Sea aquaculture areas, prompting recommendations for stricter import controls, targeted surveillance and improved farm biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introduction of IMNV into Egypt via importation of infected broodstock or postlarvae from endemic Asian sources, combined with rapid local development of penaeid shrimp aquaculture and limited prior familiarity with this virus, facilitated the first inter-continental jump of IMNV to Africa. Internal mechanisms: IMNV’s ability to infect multiple penaeid species, including P. semisulcatus, and to persist in apparently healthy or mildly affected shrimp promotes establishment in new host populations and environments (Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), even though distinct Egyptian genotypes have not yet been clearly defined.
Review: Retain – Evidence from Aly et al. (2020) and subsequent diagnostic reviews supports genuine IMNV outbreaks with characteristic myonecrosis lesions in cultured penaeid shrimp on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast beginning around 2018; classification as first_detection for Egypt and inter-continental emergence of IMNV into Africa is appropriate, and no corrections to timing, geography or emergence type were needed.
