Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: In July 2020, the first confirmed case of IMNV infection in cultured L. vannamei in China was detected in Liaoning Province, after years in which official surveillance had reported other shrimp pathogens but no IMNV-positive cases. Subsequent targeted and routine surveillance through 2023 identified additional IMNV-positive farms in coastal China, and molecular analysis showed the Chinese CN-20-1 IMNV isolate to be closely related to Indonesian strains, suggesting relatively recent introduction associated with regional trade in broodstock or postlarvae. In response, Chinese authorities incorporated IMNV into national diagnostic proficiency testing and surveillance programmes, and farms increased screening and biosecurity measures to prevent wider dissemination into the country’s large shrimp farming sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high-volume importation and domestic movement of L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae across East and Southeast Asia, combined with the scale and intensity of shrimp aquaculture in China and prior focus on other pathogens, created conditions for delayed but eventual introduction of IMNV into Chinese farms; expanding molecular diagnostic capacity in the early 2020s then facilitated detection. Internal mechanisms: close phylogenetic affinity of Chinese isolates to Indonesian IMNV lineages indicates continued geographic range expansion of established Asian strains rather than emergence of a novel lineage, with IMNV’s chronic infection dynamics and host susceptibility favouring establishment in new intensive farming regions (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: Review – Event accurately represents the first confirmed IMNV case in China in 2020 and subsequent detections in 2020–2023, and its coding as intra-continental emergence into the Eastern Asia subregion with country-level first detection is appropriate; I removed the re_occurrence flag so that it no longer co-occurs with intra_continental_emergence, in line with the event-type definitions that restrict re_occurrence to events confined within an already known subregion.

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Countries: Mexico; Guatemala; Honduras; Nicaragua; Costa Rica; Panama; Colombia; Ecuador; Peru; Brazil; Venezuela
Host: Farmed and wild penaeid shrimp, primarily Penaeus (Litopenaeus) stylirostris, Litopenaeus vannamei and other American penaeid species
Event summary: From 1990 through the late 1990s, IHHNV/PstDV1 became widely established in farmed and wild shrimp along the Pacific coasts of Mexico, Central America and the west coast of South America, causing catastrophic losses in cultured P. stylirostris and contributing to collapse of the wild L. stylirostris fishery in the northern Gulf of California, Mexico. As infection became enzootic in wild and farmed populations from Mexico to Peru, large farms increasingly shifted from highly susceptible P. stylirostris to more tolerant L. vannamei, in which IHHNV caused chronic runt deformity syndrome (RDS) and growth retardation rather than acute mass mortality. During the strong 1997–1998 El Niño, Ecuador experienced well-documented IHHNV epizootics in both L. stylirostris and L. vannamei, with elevated prevalence and production losses linked to stressful low-salinity, high‑temperature conditions and heavy use of wild post-larvae, after which IHHNV was regarded as enzootic throughout much of the American shrimp-farming region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of IHHNV from Southeast Asia with live P. monodon broodstock in the 1970s; rapid expansion and intensification of penaeid shrimp aquaculture in the Americas in the 1980s–1990s; extensive regional trade in live broodstock and post‑larvae; high farm stocking densities; and environmental stressors such as the 1997–1998 El Niño that exacerbated disease expression in Ecuador. Internal mechanisms: high virulence of IHHNV for P. stylirostris but largely sublethal, deforming infections in L. vannamei that allowed widespread, persistent circulation; efficient vertical and horizontal transmission in farmed and wild shrimp; and limited genetic variation among American isolates tightly clustered with a Philippine isolate, consistent with a single, relatively recent introduction followed by rapid expansion.
Review: Retain – This is a major, well-documented multi‑country episode encompassing the 1990 collapse of wild L. stylirostris stocks in the Gulf of California and the high‑impact 1997–1998 IHHNV epizootics in Ecuador. I corrected the event window to 1990–1998 to explicitly include the El Niño‑related Ecuador outbreaks, removed 'Caribbean' from the sub_regions (no Caribbean countries are listed) and added Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Colombia to the country list to better reflect the documented Pacific and Central American distribution. The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence plus re‑occurrence was not consistent with definitions; I reclassified this as re‑emergence (dramatic increase and host shift to L. vannamei driven by viral properties) without intra‑ or inter‑continental tags. Sources were updated toward primary regional and phylogenetic studies and the USDA IHHNV pathways assessment for detailed country coverage.

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Countries: China; Taiwan, Province of China; Philippines; Thailand; Indonesia; Malaysia; Viet Nam
Host: Farmed Penaeus monodon and, later in the decade, introduced Litopenaeus vannamei
Event summary: During the 1990s, improved histological and PCR diagnostics revealed that IHHNV was widespread and essentially endemic in farmed P. monodon across much of Southeast and East Asia (e.g. the Philippines, Thailand, Taiwan, Indonesia, Malaysia), where infections were usually subclinical but associated with stunting and deformities. At the same time, early introductions of L. vannamei broodstock and seed from the Americas carried infectious type 1/2 IHHNV genotypes into Asian grow‑out systems, where the virus established persistent infections and contributed to chronic runt deformity problems, often overshadowed by more acute viral diseases such as WSSV and YHV. Molecular comparisons showed close relationships between American and Asian type 1/2 isolates and tighter clustering of American isolates with a Philippine P. monodon strain, supporting a historical origin of the American epidemic in Southeast Asian P. monodon and subsequent bidirectional exchange of virus lineages via live shrimp movements.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing endemicity of IHHNV in wild and farmed P. monodon across Southeast and East Asia; rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp aquaculture during the 1980s–1990s; and increasing importation of L. vannamei broodstock and post‑larvae from the Americas without systematic IHHNV screening. Internal mechanisms: IHHNV’s ability to cause mostly sublethal, chronic infections in P. monodon and L. vannamei, thereby persisting in broodstock and seed; circulation of genetically distinct but related Asian and American genotypes (type 1 and type 2), with Asian isolates showing greater sequence diversity; and efficient vertical and horizontal transmission that allowed the virus to remain ubiquitous despite control efforts focused mainly on other pathogens.
Review: Retain (with corrections) – Asia is the ancestral source region for IHHNV, not a new continent of introduction, so the original classification as 'first_detection = Yes' and 'inter_continental_emergence = Yes' was incorrect. I reclassified this 1990s episode as a re‑emergence event capturing intensified recognition and impact of an already endemic virus in Asian P. monodon, plus early host expansion into L. vannamei via imported broodstock. Inter‑ and intra‑continental emergence flags were set to 'No', and the narrative was revised to emphasize Asia’s source role and bidirectional movements between Asia and the Americas. Primary molecular‑epidemiology sources (Tang et al. 2003; Rai et al. 2012) and global reviews were prioritised over Wikipedia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Countries: Madagascar; Mauritius; United Republic of Tanzania
Host: Wild and farmed Penaeus monodon carrying integrated IHHNV-related (type A/B or type 3) genomic sequences
Event summary: In the early 2000s, routine PCR screening of P. monodon from Madagascar, Tanzania and nearby western Indian Ocean locations repeatedly produced IHHNV-positive results, yet experimental challenge of specific‑pathogen‑free P. monodon and L. vannamei with these shrimp did not result in infection or disease. Sequencing revealed highly divergent "type A" and "type B" IHHNV-related genomes integrated into the host genome rather than circulating infectious virus, with flanking sequences showing shrimp microsatellite and retrotransposon-like DNA. Follow‑up work demonstrated that these type A/B elements, now commonly grouped as "type 3" or EVE‑like lineages, are noninfectious endogenous viral elements in P. monodon from East Africa and Australia that can be amplified by standard IHHNV PCR assays.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: wider adoption of molecular diagnostics and genome‑walking techniques in shrimp virology during the early 2000s, which led to systematic screening of P. monodon populations from Africa and Australia and the discovery of unexpected PCR‑positive but noninfectious cases. Internal mechanisms: historical integration of partial IHHNV-like genomes into the P. monodon germ line, generating type A/B (type 3) endogenous viral elements that are ~8–14% divergent from epidemic IHHNV strains; these elements retain parvoviral replication initiator and helicase motifs but are embedded within host DNA and are not transmissible in infection bioassays, creating a major source of false positives for conventional IHHNV PCR tests and prompting the development of diagnostic methods that distinguish infectious virus from EVEs.
Review: Review – This row accurately captures the discovery of noninfectious, genome‑integrated IHHNV-related sequences (type A/B or type 3) in East African P. monodon and their importance for diagnostics and taxonomy. However, this episode is primarily a molecular/evolutionary finding with little direct documented production loss in Africa, so whether it belongs among the ten largest emergence events (defined by impact on cases/production/countries) is debatable. I corrected the timing to 2000–2006 to match the main Virus Research papers, removed the earlier 'first_detection' and 'inter_continental_emergence' flags (Africa was not newly infected by an emergent epidemic strain) and reclassified it as re‑emergence to reflect the recognition of a distinct, integrated genotype class. Event is flagged for further review on inclusion in a strict top‑10 impact list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Sub-regions: South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia
Countries: China; Viet Nam; Thailand; Indonesia; Malaysia; Philippines; India
Host: Introduced Litopenaeus vannamei and existing Penaeus monodon stocks in intensive commercial farms
Event summary: From the early 2000s, rapid, region‑wide adoption of L. vannamei in place of P. monodon across Asian shrimp industries led to pervasive establishment of infectious IHHNV in both species, with many ponds reporting chronic runt deformity syndrome, slow growth and reduced harvest weights rather than large die‑offs. Molecular surveys during this period showed high IHHNV prevalence in farmed stocks and broodstock lines in China, Viet Nam, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and, increasingly, India, with Asian type 1/2 genotypes closely related to American strains, consistent with repeated introductions via imported broodstock. By the late 2000s, IHHNV infection was considered enzootic in many Asian production systems; its direct impact on L. vannamei survival had declined due to use of tolerant or resistant lines, but chronic growth penalties and interactions with other pathogens (e.g. WSSV, IMNV, EHP) remained an important constraint.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very rapid expansion and intensification of L. vannamei farming in Asia, often at high stocking densities and with limited initial biosecurity; large‑scale importation of broodstock and post‑larvae from IHHNV‑endemic regions of the Americas; and co-circulation of multiple shrimp viruses that complicated disease management and encouraged hidden persistence of IHHNV. Internal mechanisms: host expansion and adaptation of IHHNV to L. vannamei with predominantly sublethal but economically important effects (RDS and growth retardation); circulation of infectious type 1/2 genotypes with relatively high substitution rates and region‑specific diversity; and coexistence of integrated IHHNV‑like elements in P. monodon that complicated diagnostics but may have contributed to long‑term viral "accommodation" in some host lineages.
Review: Retain – This episode captures the decade in which IHHNV became essentially ubiquitous in Asian L. vannamei and P. monodon aquaculture and caused chronic but large‑scale production losses, making it one of the key high‑impact events for this virus. The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence plus re‑occurrence and re‑emergence overstated geographic novelty: by 2000 IHHNV was already present in both Southeast and East Asia, and the event is best viewed as a resurgence and host/strain‑driven re‑emergence within existing subregions. I therefore set 'intra_continental_emergence' to 'No' and retained 're_occurrence' and 're_emergence' to reflect increased incidence driven by farming practices and host/genotype changes. Sources were tuned toward comprehensive reviews on Asian shrimp pathogens and IHHNV’s chronic impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Host: Farmed Litopenaeus vannamei co-infected with IHHNV and infectious myonecrosis virus (IMNV)
Event summary: In the late 2000s, shrimp farms in northeastern Brazil culturing L. vannamei experienced episodes of high mortality and muscle necrosis in which natural co-infections with IHHNV and IMNV were documented, demonstrating that IHHNV was widely circulating in Brazilian stocks and could exacerbate disease outcomes in combination with IMNV. These co-infections were associated with substantial production losses and highlighted IHHNV’s role as a contributor to complex disease syndromes and growth depression rather than as a solitary acute killer. As farms improved biosecurity, implemented targeted diagnostics and adjusted management, overt IHHNV–IMNV co-infection outbreaks declined, but IHHNV remained endemic in Brazilian shrimp populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive L. vannamei culture in Brazil; introduction and establishment of IMNV and other viral pathogens; high stocking densities and environmental stress (e.g. temperature and salinity fluctuations) promoting multi‑pathogen infections; and initially limited awareness of IHHNV’s contribution to disease complexes. Internal mechanisms: chronic IHHNV infection creating a background of compromised health and growth, which, when combined with IMNV, produced more severe pathology and mortality; high viral loads of both agents in affected ponds; and efficient horizontal transmission within farms that sustained recurrent co‑infection outbreaks until biosecurity and husbandry were improved.
Review: Retain – Co‑infection of IHHNV with IMNV in Brazilian L. vannamei caused clearly documented production losses and exemplifies IHHNV’s role as a component of high‑impact multi‑virus disease syndromes in a major shrimp‑producing country. The geographic and temporal framing (Brazil, late 2000s–early 2010s) and classification as a re‑occurrence event driven by external factors (intensive culture, introduction of IMNV, management practices) are appropriate. No changes to emergence-type flags were needed; I only clarified that this is not a first detection or spread into a new subregion, but a resurgence of impact in an already IHHNV‑positive country, and retained primary Aquaculture and review sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Host: Farmed Penaeus monodon (and later L. vannamei) in hatcheries and grow-out ponds along India’s east and west coasts
Event summary: Between roughly 2006 and 2011, Indian investigators used PCR and histopathology to show that slow‑growing P. monodon from farms in multiple coastal states often carried IHHNV, sometimes together with other growth‑retarding viruses such as HPV and LSNV. In 2011, the complete genome of an Indian PstDV1/IHHNV isolate from P. monodon was sequenced, and comparative analyses showed that this strain clustered with other Asian infectious genotypes from Taiwan and Thailand, while Indian P. monodon also harboured integrated type A IHHNV-like sequences. These findings confirmed that IHHNV was widely established in Indian hatcheries and farms and contributed to chronic growth problems in P. monodon, and they catalysed broader diagnostic screening and incorporation of IHHNV into Indian shrimp health management as L. vannamei farming expanded.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp farming along India’s coasts; use of P. monodon seed and broodstock with limited viral screening in the early 2000s; and initial focus on WSSV and other acute pathogens, which delayed recognition of IHHNV’s role in slow‑growth syndromes. Internal mechanisms: circulation of an infectious Indian PstDV1 genome closely related to Taiwanese and Thai isolates (infectious type 1/2 genotypes) alongside type A IHHNV-related endogenous sequences in P. monodon; association of infectious IHHNV with slow growth and deformities in Indian P. monodon; and the potential for EVEs to confound PCR diagnosis and mask the true prevalence and impact of infectious strains.
Review: Review – India is a major shrimp producer, and the 2006–2011 recognition and genomic characterization of infectious IHHNV in P. monodon (with concurrent discovery of integrated type A sequences) likely had substantial influence on diagnostics and management, so this event is a plausible candidate for inclusion among the largest IHHNV emergence episodes. However, the original row incorrectly labeled 2011 as the first detection and implied that India’s infections were newly emergent at that time; PCR‑based reports of IHHNV in slow‑growing Indian P. monodon predate the genome publication. I expanded the time window to 2006–2011 to capture both early PCR detections and the complete genome, set 'first_detection' to 'No', and reclassified the event as a re‑emergence reflecting characterization of a regional infectious genotype and recognition of its role in chronic production losses. Because this episode overlaps conceptually with the broader 2000–2010 Asia event, I flag it for expert review when finalising a strict top‑10 list.

EPP common name: PstDV1 (Infectious hypodermal and haematopoietic necrosis virus, IHHNV)
Countries: United States of America (New Mexico; California; Texas; Florida) [2019]; Canada [2019]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019]
Host: Farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in land-based recirculating aquaculture and biosecure facilities in North America, with linked detections in imported stocks in the United Kingdom
Event summary: After more than two decades without reports from U.S. shrimp farms, IHHNV was again detected in 2019 in specific‑pathogen‑free L. vannamei cultured in fully contained systems in New Mexico, California, Texas and Florida, with whole‑genome sequencing of Texas and Florida isolates showing they were infectious type 2 lineages nearly identical to an Ecuadorian strain. Immediate notifications to WOAH in 2019–2020 also documented first occurrences of IHHNV in four Canadian indoor L. vannamei facilities and at two sites in the United Kingdom (an experimental facility with high mortality in imported shrimp and a commercial facility receiving apparently healthy but infected post‑larvae), all epidemiologically linked to movements of live shrimp from the Americas. Although large‑scale mortalities were not reported in most affected North American farms, the episode demonstrated renewed transboundary spread of infectious IHHNV into high‑biosecurity systems, prompted quarantines and depopulation of affected units, and raised concern about chronic growth impacts and potential spillover to additional facilities or wild shrimp.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in live L. vannamei broodstock and post‑larvae between Ecuador, the United States and other countries; gaps in pre‑movement viral screening and certification that allowed IHHNV‑positive lines to be designated as specific‑pathogen‑free; and ongoing expansion of high‑density, land‑based shrimp culture in North America and Europe that creates new opportunities for pathogen introduction. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an infectious type 2 IHHNV lineage capable of persistent, often subclinical infection in L. vannamei; high genetic similarity between U.S. isolates and the Ecuador strain, implying a recent common source; and the virus’s ability to cause measurable reductions in growth and survival even in tolerant lines when viral loads in post‑larvae are high, as illustrated by experimental work estimating substantial per‑hectare economic losses at high infection intensities.
Review: Retain – This is a major recent re‑emergence episode in which an infectious type 2 IHHNV lineage linked to Ecuador was detected in multiple U.S. states and, via live‑shrimp movements, in Canada and the United Kingdom, triggering international notifications, quarantine and depopulation measures. I expanded the geographic and temporal scope to align with WOAH and USDA reporting (New Mexico and California as well as Texas and Florida; Canada and UK detections in 2019) and reworded the countries field accordingly. In line with the project’s rules and the Ebola example, I did not classify this as an inter‑continental emergence event for Europe, because the UK detections occurred in closed facilities with no documented onward establishment; instead, I treat them as part of a linked transboundary re‑emergence centered on North America. The original 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_occurrence' flags were removed and the event is now coded purely as re‑emergence, reflecting introduction of a new infectious lineage into a previously infected continent with clear implications for modern high‑biosecurity production systems.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Central America; South America
Countries: United States of America [1990]; Mexico [1990]; Guatemala [early 1990s]; El Salvador [early 1990s]; Honduras [early 1990s]; Nicaragua [early 1990s]; Panama [early 1990s]; Ecuador [early 1990s]; Peru [early 1990s]
Host: Farmed Penaeus (Litopenaeus) stylirostris; Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei; other farmed penaeid shrimp
Event summary: Around 1990–1995, IHHNV became widely established in intensive shrimp farms along the Pacific coasts of North, Central and parts of South America, where earlier 1980s outbreaks in Hawaii and Mexico had already caused catastrophic mortality in Penaeus stylirostris and prompted a shift towards the more IHHNV‑tolerant P. vannamei. During this period the virus spread throughout major farming areas from Mexico to Peru and into adjacent wild shrimp populations, leading to recurrent acute epizootics in P. stylirostris and chronic runt deformity syndrome with severe growth retardation in P. vannamei, with estimated production losses of 10–50% per crop in some operations. As resistant or tolerant lines were adopted and farm management and biosecurity improved, IHHNV’s impact transitioned from dramatic die‑offs to a more endemic, production‑limiting infection across much of the eastern Pacific shrimp industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp aquaculture on the eastern Pacific coasts; high‑density pond culture with limited early biosecurity; extensive transboundary movement of broodstock and post‑larvae; waterborne spread between neighboring farms; and likely historical introduction of IHHNV from the Philippines with imported P. monodon broodstock. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion within the Americas; host expansion and adaptation from highly susceptible P. stylirostris to chronic infection and runt deformity syndrome in P. vannamei; and possible selection for viral variants well adapted to intensive culture conditions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7169130/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected the emergence-type classification: set intra_continental_emergence=Yes (spread into the South America sub-region along the Pacific coast) and re_emergence=Yes (host expansion and changing disease expression), and set re_occurrence=No so that categories conform to the rules that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7169130/?utm_source=openai)) Bracket years for individual Central and South American countries remain approximate because most sources report regional spread during the late 1980s–early 1990s rather than precise first-detection years by country; these should be treated as indicative and may warrant refinement in a later expert pass.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf))

Countries: Belize [late 1990s]; Honduras [late 1990s]; Nicaragua [late 1990s]; Panama [late 1990s]; Cuba [late 1990s]; Dominican Republic [late 1990s]; Trinidad and Tobago [late 1990s]; Brazil [late 1990s]; Colombia [late 1990s]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [late 1990s]
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (primarily P. vannamei and P. stylirostris), some wild penaeid species
Event summary: Between roughly 1996 and 2000, IHHNV expanded from Pacific farming areas into shrimp farms and some wild stocks in the Caribbean basin and Atlantic coasts of Central and South America, becoming widely distributed in cultured white shrimp and associated penaeid species. The virus was introduced into multiple Caribbean and Atlantic farming countries through movement of infected post‑larvae and broodstock from Pacific sources, after which it became established in local farm systems and, in some areas, nearby wild shrimp populations, contributing mainly to chronic growth retardation and deformities in P. vannamei rather than dramatic acute die‑offs. As farms in these regions began managing multiple viral threats (including Taura syndrome and white spot disease), IHHNV persisted as an endemic agent causing economic losses via reduced growth performance and survival, but its impact was often masked by co‑occurring, more acutely lethal pathogens.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: regionalization of shrimp seed and broodstock trade from Pacific to Caribbean and Atlantic farms; limited early diagnostic capacity, allowing silent spread; mixing of farmed and wild stocks in coastal lagoons and estuaries. Internal mechanisms: continued geographic range expansion of established IHHNV genotypes into new sub-regions (Caribbean and Atlantic coasts of South America); establishment of chronic infection with runt deformity syndrome in P. vannamei causing reduced growth and higher feed conversion; co-infections with other shrimp viruses that may have modified apparent disease impact.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf))
Review: Decision: review. Corrected geography so that the continent is South America only, because all listed countries fall under the project’s South America continent (Central America and Caribbean sub-regions are defined under South America in the Country sheet). Set re_emergence=No, as this episode primarily reflects intra-continental spread of existing American genotypes into new sub-regions (Caribbean/Atlantic) rather than resurgence driven by demonstrable viral change in already affected sub-regions.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf)) Bracket years by country are retained only as approximate indicators of late-1990s spread and should be treated cautiously pending country-specific literature review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Penaeus monodon; Fenneropenaeus indicus; penaeid hatchery stocks
Event summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, IHHNV was detected for the first time in Indian shrimp hatcheries and farms, primarily affecting Penaeus monodon and Fenneropenaeus indicus in coastal aquaculture zones, at a time when the virus was already present elsewhere in Asia. Initial reports described co‑occurrence of IHHNV with other viral pathogens in commercial hatcheries, indicating that the virus had arrived via imported or domesticated broodstock and was circulating in seed production systems before field recognition. As Indian shrimp aquaculture intensified and later shifted toward P. vannamei, IHHNV became one component of a broader viral disease complex, contributing mainly to subclinical infections and growth loss rather than overt mass mortality. Improved PCR-based screening, biosecurity guidelines, and import regulation for broodstock gradually reduced the risk of high-impact IHHNV outbreaks, although enzootic infection has persisted in many farmed populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of shrimp hatchery and farm capacity along the Indian coast; limited early viral screening of broodstock and post‑larvae; importation or informal movement of broodstock and nauplii from other IHHNV‑affected regions of Asia or the Americas. Internal mechanisms: intra-continental emergence of IHHNV into the Southern Asia sub-region; adaptation of circulating genotypes to new host genetic backgrounds, including P. monodon and F. indicus; and subsequent diversification of Indian IHHNV lineages documented in genomic studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/))
Review: Decision: review. Reinterpreted this episode as an intra-continental emergence into a new Asian sub-region rather than an inter-continental emergence or first detection globally. Evidence shows IHHNV was already present in East Asia by 1986 (quarantined P. vannamei in Taiwan) and in other Asian countries before 1993, so India does not represent the first inter-continental jump from the Americas to Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/)) Accordingly, first_detection has been set to No (global first detection was in Hawaii in 1981) and inter_continental_emergence to No, with intra_continental_emergence set to Yes to reflect spread into Southern Asia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: China [2001]; China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [1999]; China, Macao Special Administrative Region [1999]; Thailand [2000]; Philippines [1996]; Indonesia [2000]; Viet Nam [2000]; Malaysia [2000]; Singapore [2001]; Taiwan (Province of China) [1998]
Host: Farmed P. monodon and P. vannamei; other cultured penaeid shrimp
Event summary: From the late 1990s into the early 2000s, IHHNV became highly prevalent in the rapidly growing shrimp aquaculture industries of East and South‑east Asia, including China, Taiwan, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Viet Nam, Malaysia and Singapore, where both P. monodon and, increasingly, introduced P. vannamei were farmed. Building on earlier introductions documented in the mid‑1990s (for example in the Philippines), the virus disseminated widely through regional and international trade in infected post‑larvae and broodstock and then between farms via water exchange, shared equipment and local stock movements, often alongside other major viral pathogens. Acute mass mortality due to IHHNV was less prominent than in the early American outbreaks, but chronic runt deformity syndrome, growth retardation and increased susceptibility to co‑infections resulted in substantial, though often under‑reported, production losses across Asian shrimp farming. Over time, enhanced diagnostic capacity, selective breeding for tolerance and improved biosecurity reduced the visible impact of IHHNV, although high prevalence in many hatcheries and farms has persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: explosive growth and intensification of Asian shrimp farming; large‑scale import and regional redistribution of specific‑pathogen‑free (SPF) or non‑certified P. vannamei broodstock; dense farm clusters with shared water sources and limited early biosecurity. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence and amplification of at least two infectious IHHNV genotypes within already affected East and South‑east Asian sub‑regions; host expansion and sustained chronic infection phenotypes in P. monodon and P. vannamei manifesting as runt deformity syndrome and increased vulnerability to other infections.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/))
Review: Decision: review. Updated the mechanism and classification to reflect that this episode represents re-emergence and amplification within already affected Asian sub-regions, not the initial intra-continental spread into new sub-regions. Evidence indicates IHHNV was present in Taiwan by 1986 and in the Philippines by 1996, before the 1998–2005 intensification captured here.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/)) Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence is now set to No and re_emergence to Yes. The start years for China (2001, based on national survey data) and the Philippines (1996, based on first detection reports) were adjusted to match published timelines; other country years remain approximate and should be refined with country-level literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Madagascar [2003]; Mauritius [2003]; Mozambique [2003]; United Republic of Tanzania [2003]
Host: Wild and broodstock Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, molecular studies of wild and broodstock Penaeus monodon from Madagascar, Mauritius, Mozambique and Tanzania identified IHHNV‑related DNA sequences integrated into the shrimp genome, representing genotypes 3 and 4 (Type A and Type B) that are distinct from the infectious IHHNV genotypes circulating in the Americas and much of Asia. These integrated endogenous viral elements (EVEs) did not produce clinical disease or transmissible infection in experimental bioassays, but their discovery demonstrated long‑standing historical exposure of African tiger shrimp lineages to IHHNV‑like viruses and revealed a major source of false positives for standard PCR assays designed to detect infectious IHHNV. The findings led to refinement of diagnostic methods and to guidance aimed at avoiding unwarranted trade restrictions on African P. monodon broodstock based solely on EVE-positive PCR results.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased genetic and virological surveillance of wild P. monodon stocks for aquaculture broodstock sourcing and international trade; global concern over shrimp viral diseases triggering more intensive pathogen screening. Internal mechanisms: presence of ancient, non‑infectious IHHNV‑related EVEs (genotypes 3 and 4) integrated into the genomes of African P. monodon populations, which complicate molecular diagnosis of infectious IHHNV and required the development of discriminating PCR assays that can distinguish EVEs from active viral infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/))
Review: Decision: review. This row correctly describes the discovery of non-infectious IHHNV-related endogenous viral elements in African P. monodon but the original classification as inter-continental emergence and first detection of infectious IHHNV was misleading; all emergence-type flags have been set to No to avoid implying introduction or resurgence of infectious virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/)) Because these EVEs have no demonstrated direct disease or production impact, but do have important diagnostic and trade implications, this episode sits at the margin of the project’s emergence-event definition and should be reviewed by domain experts to decide whether to retain it as one of the top events or treat it only as contextual information.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild and farmed Penaeus monodon; other penaeid prawns and hybrids
Event summary: Archived samples and subsequent surveillance revealed that IHHNV or closely related viruses had been present in Australian penaeid prawns since at least 1993, when an infectious IHHNV strain was retrospectively identified in cultured P. monodon from northern Australia using IHHNV‑specific PCR and sequencing, while later work also demonstrated the presence of integrated, non‑infectious IHHNV‑related sequences in Australian P. monodon. In 2008, an infectious form of IHHNV closely related to South‑east Asian isolates was reported from farmed P. monodon in northern Queensland, prompting official notification to the World Organisation for Animal Health and incorporation of IHHNV into national surveillance and risk assessments. Although no major farm‑level mortality events attributable solely to IHHNV were documented, endemic infection and/or EVE carriage in wild and farmed P. monodon raised concerns about potential growth impacts and about maintaining the health status of Australian shrimp for domestic production and international trade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expanding prawn aquaculture in northern Australia and associated health surveillance; international concern about shrimp viral diseases stimulating retrospective testing of archived material and targeted screening of wild broodstock. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental emergence and establishment of infectious IHHNV in Oceania, likely via historical movements of infected stock; coexistence of infectious IHHNV with integrated genotype 3 IHHNV-related sequences in Australian P. monodon, which complicates PCR diagnosis and necessitated development of assays that can distinguish EVEs from active infection.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15584422/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Substantially revised this row to align with the published timeline: (i) earliest infectious IHHNV in Australia is now dated to archived P. monodon from 1993, with official reporting of an infectious strain from farmed P. monodon in 2008, rather than a vaguely defined 2002–2006 window; (ii) the emergence type is set to inter_continental_emergence=Yes to reflect the first confirmed occurrence of infectious IHHNV in the Oceania continent, while first_detection, intra_continental_emergence, re_occurrence and re_emergence are set to No.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15584422/?utm_source=openai)) Because documented production losses in Australia attributable solely to IHHNV appear modest relative to other viruses, but endemic infection and EVEs are epidemiologically important, this event should be retained but flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the top emergence events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2019]; Canada [2019]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019]
Host: Farmed Penaeus vannamei (Pacific white shrimp) in indoor and outdoor aquaculture facilities
Event summary: In 2019, IHHNV reappeared in North American shrimp aquaculture after a long absence from US farms and was reported for the first time from Canada and from Europe (United Kingdom), in a set of epidemiologically linked events associated with international trade in post‑larval P. vannamei. The United States reported two disease events in indoor facilities: a recurrence of IHHNV infection in New Mexico with subsequent movement of infected shrimp to a facility in California, and the first reported occurrences in Texas and Florida aquaculture facilities, prompting quarantine and depopulation of affected tanks. In the same year, Canada reported its first occurrence of IHHNV in four of its five indoor P. vannamei culture premises, traced to importation of infected post‑larvae from a common overseas supplier, and the United Kingdom reported its first detections in an experimental facility and a commercial aquaculture site, both linked to imported shrimp from an IHHNV‑positive source. These detections highlighted ongoing risks of long‑distance spread of IHHNV through international trade in ostensibly SPF post‑larvae and led to strengthened import controls, surveillance and on‑farm biosecurity in the affected countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: globalization of shrimp broodstock and post‑larval trade; reliance on indoor or recirculating aquaculture systems sourcing stock from international hatcheries; incomplete or inconsistent pathogen screening in export chains; and high animal movements between facilities within and across countries. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental emergence of infectious IHHNV into Europe (first confirmed detection in the United Kingdom) and renewed establishment in previously affected North American production systems, with predominantly chronic infection phenotypes in P. vannamei causing reduced growth and economic losses rather than dramatic acute mortality.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf))
Review: Decision: retain. Cleaned the country list to include only the three countries for which immediate notifications of cultured-shrimp IHHNV events were reported to WOAH in 2019 (United States, Canada, United Kingdom) and removed Mexico and the subnational entry “Texas, Florida aquaculture facilities”, which are either endemic-background or subnational and therefore inappropriate in the Countries field.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf)) Reclassified the emergence types so that this episode is treated primarily as an inter-continental emergence into Europe (first detection in the UK) plus a recurrence in North American facilities described in the narrative, but without tagging re_occurrence or re_emergence at the row level to avoid violating the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with inter-continental emergence in a single event row.

Countries: United States of America [1990] (Delaware Bay, New Jersey; coastal New York; coastal Massachusetts to Cape Cod)
Host: Primarily Crassostrea virginica (eastern oyster) in wild and fished estuarine populations
Event summary: Between 1990 and 1992, Perkinsus marinus infections surged in intensity and prevalence in estuarine oyster populations from Delaware Bay north to Cape Cod, where the parasite had previously been rare or absent at epizootic levels. This episode developed into large-scale epizootics across a roughly 500‑km stretch of the northeastern U.S. coast, causing heavy mortality of C. virginica and sharply reducing fishery and aquaculture landings. The epizootic subsided to lower but persistent endemic levels after several years, with continued northward persistence of the parasite and concern about future outbreaks under warmer conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A period of unusually warm winters and positive North Atlantic Oscillation phases increased winter and spring sea-surface temperatures, while decades of oyster translocations from enzootic southern areas had repeatedly introduced the parasite into mid‑Atlantic and New England estuaries. Internal mechanisms: Increased fitness of P. marinus under warmer winter conditions and circulation of more virulent genotypes allowed high parasite burdens to build in previously marginal, colder habitats, effectively expanding the realized thermal niche of the parasite and increasing associated mortality.
Review: retain - This row accurately describes the well-documented 1990–1992 northward epizootic from Delaware Bay to Cape Cod, including timing, geography, host and impact. Classification as re-emergence (without intra- or inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because P. marinus was already long established within the Northern America subregion before this outbreak. No corrections were required.

Countries: Mexico [1992] (Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon system, Tabasco State, southern Gulf of Mexico)
Host: Crassostrea virginica (American/eastern oyster) in wild and fished beds in coastal lagoons
Event summary: In 1992, surveys of American oysters Crassostrea virginica in the Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon complex of Tabasco, southern Gulf of Mexico, revealed very high prevalences and heavy intensities of Perkinsus marinus infection, with weighted prevalence values consistent with severe disease. These findings provided the first confirmed report of P. marinus in Mexico and in the project’s 'South America' continent grouping, and suggested that the parasite was an important but previously unrecognized contributor to sporadic oyster mortalities blamed locally on pollution. Subsequent work documented persistent infections and seasonal variation in disease levels, indicating that P. marinus had become enzootic in these lagoons.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical movements of live oysters and spat from U.S. Gulf of Mexico and other infected areas into Mexican coastal lagoons likely introduced P. marinus to Tabasco, where warm, relatively high-salinity lagoon conditions favored establishment and proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of established Gulf of Mexico parasite lineages into new southern habitats, with heavy infections reflecting the high susceptibility of C. virginica and the absence of prior host adaptation in these lagoon populations.
Review: review - New row added to capture the 1992 detection of P. marinus in the Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon system (Tabasco, Mexico), which is the first confirmed occurrence in Mexico and, under the project’s continent scheme, the first inter-continental emergence into 'South America'. Impact is supported by high prevalences and heavy infections reported by Burreson et al. (1994), but quantitative production-loss estimates remain limited; recommended to retain as a major event but for a human reviewer to confirm its ranking and wording.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [1995] (Maine coastal embayments)
Host: Crassostrea virginica (eastern oyster) in wild and managed beds near the northern limit of the species
Event summary: In 1995, Perkinsus marinus was first reported in Maine oyster populations, marking a notable northward jump beyond earlier reports that had reached only as far as Cape Cod. Following its detection, local C. virginica stocks experienced elevated infection intensities and episodic mortality events that raised concern about the viability of oyster restoration and aquaculture at this poleward range edge. Over subsequent years, disease levels fluctuated with environmental conditions, but the parasite remained established in Maine waters as a chronic constraint on oyster production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional warming trends and milder winters in the Gulf of Maine increased the duration of periods with water temperatures exceeding about 20 °C, promoting parasite proliferation at higher latitudes than previously considered suitable. Internal mechanisms: The same P. marinus lineages responsible for the early‑1990s northeastern U.S. epizootics were able to persist and transmit in cooler Maine estuaries, representing a climate-mediated geographic range expansion within the Northern America subregion rather than a new continental emergence.
Review: retain - This row correctly captures the first documented record of P. marinus in Maine (1995) and its significance as a poleward range extension linked to warming, as reported in the range-expansion literature. Treating the event as re-emergence (further spread within an already affected Northern America subregion) rather than intra-continental or first-detection is consistent with the project definitions; no structural corrections were needed.

Countries: Mexico [2006] (Gulf of California, Sonora coast, northwest Mexico)
Host: Crassostrea gigas (Pacific oyster) in intensive aquaculture; likely infection source from Crassostrea virginica stocks moved within Mexico
Event summary: In July–August 2006, mass mortalities of farmed Pacific oysters Crassostrea gigas were reported in coastal farms along the Sonoran shore of the Gulf of California, northwest Mexico, and were attributed in part to Perkinsus marinus infections acting together with stressful environmental conditions. The outbreak developed rapidly during warm summer conditions, causing large production losses in affected farms and highlighting the vulnerability of C. gigas to P. marinus in Mexican Pacific systems. Mortalities declined after environmental conditions moderated and management responses reduced stocking densities, but the episode established P. marinus as a recognized threat to Pacific oyster aquaculture in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High summer water temperatures, elevated salinities, and culture conditions characterized by high stocking densities and limited water exchange created stressful conditions that exacerbated disease susceptibility and mortality in farmed oysters. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced transmission, as P. marinus—likely introduced via transfers of infected C. virginica or other bivalves from Gulf of Mexico sources—successfully infected and caused severe disease in C. gigas, demonstrating that this parasite can utilize non-native oyster species as epidemiologically important hosts in new ocean basins.
Review: retain - The 2006 mass mortality of C. gigas in the Gulf of California attributed to P. marinus is well documented and clearly among the most impactful emergence episodes for this pathogen outside its native Atlantic–Gulf range. Country, subregion and host assignments are correct, and treating this as re-emergence (host and basin expansion within an already affected continent) rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence matches the definitions. Only a more specific article on the event was added to the source list; otherwise the row is retained.

Countries: Mexico [2006] (Nayarit, Pacific coast lagoons including Boca de Camichín and Pozo Chino); Mexico [2010] (Sinaloa, additional Pacific coastal lagoons)
Host: Crassostrea corteziensis (native Cortez oyster, farmed and wild) and Saccostrea palmula (native rock oyster) on the Pacific coast of Mexico
Event summary: Beginning in late 2006, Perkinsus marinus was detected in cultured populations of the native oyster Crassostrea corteziensis in Nayarit State on Mexico’s Pacific coast, marking establishment of the parasite in this native host and ocean basin. Over the subsequent years, surveys showed low to moderate prevalence infections in C. corteziensis in Nayarit and, by around 2010, in native rock oysters Saccostrea palmula across multiple coastal lagoons in Sinaloa, generally without dramatic mass mortalities but with evidence of sublethal effects. By the mid‑2010s, P. marinus was recognized as widely but patchily distributed in native oyster assemblages along sections of the Mexican Pacific, prompting concern about its longer-term impact on native oyster resources and aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical and ongoing movements of live oysters and other bivalves from the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coast for aquaculture and restoration are strongly implicated as the source of P. marinus introductions to Pacific lagoons, with local environmental conditions (warm temperatures, moderate to high salinity) supporting parasite establishment. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and geographic range expansion, as P. marinus successfully colonized new native hosts (C. corteziensis and S. palmula) and ecosystems on the Pacific side, aided by parasite genotypes closely related to U.S. Atlantic and Gulf strains that tolerate regional temperature–salinity regimes.
Review: review - Start year and within-country timing were corrected to reflect evidence that P. marinus was first detected in C. corteziensis in Nayarit in 2006 and subsequently in S. palmula in Sinaloa around 2010, based on Cáceres-Martínez et al. (2008, 2012, 2016) and related work. The event is retained as a single, linked re-emergence episode representing sustained host and geographic expansion within the Mexican Pacific, still not qualifying as intra-continental emergence because it remains within the existing 'Central America' subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Brazil [2013] (Paraíba State, Paraíba River estuary, northeastern Brazil)
Host: Crassostrea rhizophorae (mangrove oyster) in wild and small-scale harvested intertidal beds
Event summary: In 2013, Perkinsus marinus was confirmed by histology and molecular methods in mangrove oysters Crassostrea rhizophorae from the Paraíba River estuary in Paraíba State, Brazil, representing the first species-level identification of P. marinus on the Atlantic coast of South America. The study documented very high infection prevalence (often exceeding 70–90%) and heavy parasite burdens in many oysters, indicating an established and intense epizootic in this estuarine system. Although the disease did not immediately cause a well-documented regional fishery collapse, the findings signaled a newly recognized, ongoing epizootic that threatened mangrove oyster stocks exploited by local communities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected bivalves—likely through historical or recent movements of oysters or other molluscs between the Gulf of Mexico/Pacific Mexico and northeastern Brazil—combined with warm, moderately saline estuarine conditions that favor parasite proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of P. marinus in C. rhizophorae populations in a new UNSD subregion ('South America') within the South America continent grouping, supported by parasite genotypes closely related to Mexican strains and capable of high virulence in mangrove oysters.
Review: review - The event correctly represents the first confirmed P. marinus record on the Atlantic coast of South America (Paraíba, Brazil) and is appropriately classified as intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion ('South America'). However, the original row misused the 'first_detection' flag for this regional first report; this has been reset to 'No' because first detection in the host system occurred decades earlier in the Gulf of Mexico. All other fields are retained.

Countries: Brazil [2014] (Rio São Francisco estuary, Sergipe State); Brazil [2015] (Mamanguape River estuary, Paraíba State)
Host: Crassostrea gasar (= C. brasiliana; native mangrove/estuarine oyster) and Crassostrea rhizophorae in northeastern Brazil
Event summary: Following the 2013 confirmation in Paraíba, subsequent studies in 2014–2015 documented Perkinsus marinus infecting native oysters Crassostrea gasar and C. rhizophorae in additional northeastern Brazilian estuaries, including the Rio São Francisco estuary in Sergipe State and the Mamanguape estuary in Paraíba. These surveys showed moderate to high infection prevalences, evidence of tissue damage, and concern about sublethal and lethal impacts on both wild and cultured oysters. Over the next several years, the parasite became recognized as widely distributed among northeastern Brazilian estuaries and capable of infecting multiple native oyster hosts, indicating an expanding and consolidating regional epizootic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued spread of P. marinus within interconnected coastal systems of northeastern Brazil, facilitated by natural dispersal of infective stages via currents, as well as local trade and movement of oysters for consumption and culture, in estuarine conditions favorable to parasite survival. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence through host expansion and increasing strain diversity, as P. marinus established in C. gasar—an important native cultured species—while maintaining high prevalence in C. rhizophorae, thereby enlarging the parasite’s host and ecological niche in the South Atlantic.
Review: review - This row appropriately summarizes the post-2013 spread of P. marinus to C. gasar and additional estuaries in northeastern Brazil and is best viewed as a re-emergence episode driven by host expansion and geographic consolidation within the same UNSD subregion ('South America'). Countries: Brazil [2013-2014] (Santa Catarina State, coastal farms around Balneário Barra do Sul and São Francisco do Sul); Brazil [2015-2017] (continued detections in native Crassostrea sp. and farmed Crassostrea gigas in Santa Catarina aquaculture areas)

Countries: Canada [2024] (New Brunswick: Spence Cove; Nova Scotia: Merigomish); Canada [2025] (Newfoundland and Labrador: Notre Dame Bay; further confirmed sites in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Prince Edward Island)

Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence associated with low-temperature–tolerant P. marinus strains and geographic range expansion within the existing Northern America subregion, allowing the parasite to maintain infections and transmission in cooler Canadian estuaries that were previously unsuitable, thereby extending the species’ realized climatic niche.

Using updated CFIA location lists and regional summaries, the countries field has been expanded to include 2025 detections in Quebec and Prince Edward Island, while 'first_detection' has been reset to 'No' (because global first detection in the host system occurred in the mid‑20th century) and 'intra_continental_emergence' to 'No' (spread occurs within an already affected Northern America subregion). Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum (wild and cultured)
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s, high prevalences of Perkinsus olseni were documented in Manila clam beds in Japan and on the west coast of Korea, coinciding with marked declines in clam production and recurrent summer mortality episodes. The parasite became established with infection prevalences often approaching 100% and high infection intensities in many intertidal flats, contributing to density‑dependent growth reduction and mortality in heavily exploited or farmed beds. Through the early 2000s, these infections remained endemic with recurrent mortality peaks but did not lead to complete stock collapse everywhere due to ongoing recruitment, translocations and local management interventions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of Manila clam aquaculture and maintenance of very high natural densities in intertidal mudflats, combined with warming summer temperatures, eutrophication and occasional hypoxia, increased host stress and facilitated parasite transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and establishment of P. olseni in East Asian Manila clam metapopulations, together with its high tolerance of warm, low‑oxygen conditions and ability to reach very high tissue burdens, drove a major re‑emergence of disease expression in this host, even though the parasite species was already known from other regions and hosts.
Review: review – Retain this as a major East Asian emergence episode, but I corrected the country‑specific start years to Japan [1998] and Republic of Korea [1997] based on Hamaguchi et al. 1998 and Choi & Park 1997, and recoded the event as re‑emergence only (host/geographic expansion and entrenched high‑intensity infection) instead of both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence, to keep emergence categories mutually exclusive as specified.

Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum; carpet shell clam Ruditapes decussatus
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, perkinsosis caused by Perkinsus olseni (then often termed P. atlanticus) was linked to severe mortality episodes in Manila and carpet shell clams in estuaries of Portugal and Spain, building on earlier outbreaks and causing substantial production losses. Through the late 1990s the parasite became widespread along Iberian Atlantic coasts and was also detected along the French Atlantic coast, sometimes with infection prevalences near 100% in affected beds. Mortalities abated somewhat after initial peaks but the parasite remained entrenched as an endemic, production‑limiting pathogen in European clam aquaculture and wild fisheries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Co‑introduction and large‑scale translocation of Manila clams for aquaculture in Europe from the 1970s onwards, together with eutrophication and warming coastal waters, facilitated establishment and spread of P. olseni between estuaries. Internal mechanisms: The parasite’s broad host range allowed spillover from introduced Manila clams to native Ruditapes decussatus and other venerids, and its capacity for very high proliferation in gill and digestive tissues impaired filtration, growth and condition, driving a re‑emergence of high‑impact disease in clam fisheries despite earlier recognition of the parasite in the region.
Review: review – Event is real and clearly among the highest‑impact global outbreaks (Portugal, Spain, France), but I recoded it as re‑emergence only. Earlier work (e.g. Azevedo 1989) shows that severe mortalities in R. decussatus began in the 1980s, so the 1994–2000 period represents continued and expanded epizootics rather than a simple re‑occurrence driven purely by external factors; host expansion from introduced Manila clams and sustained high parasite loads justify re‑emergence as the primary category.

Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum
Event summary: Perkinsus olseni was first detected in Manila clams in northern Adriatic lagoons of Italy in 1991 without clear attribution to major mortality, although low‑ to moderate‑level infections were present in farmed stocks. In autumn 2011, the southern part of the Lagoon of Venice experienced a severe, spatially extensive mortality of farmed Manila clams, and histopathology identified extensive lesions and heavy P. olseni infections as the primary cause. Following this episode, the disease became recognized as a major constraint on intensive clam culture in the lagoon, prompting enhanced monitoring and biosecurity efforts to limit further high‑mortality outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High stocking densities and altered sediment and water‑quality conditions in clam farming zones of the Venice Lagoon, together with warm, stratified summer waters, favored parasite proliferation and host stress, tipping an endemic infection into acute mass mortality in 2011. Internal mechanisms: No new Perkinsus species or host shifts were implicated; instead, chronic high infection intensities of P. olseni in clams, combined with environmental stressors, led to a dramatic re‑occurrence of disease expression in an already infected system.
Review: review – Retain this high‑impact Italian episode; it correctly captures first detection in 1991 and the 2011 mass mortality in the Venice Lagoon. I recoded it as re‑occurrence (dramatic resurgence under changed culture and environmental conditions) rather than both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence, because there is no clear evidence of a novel strain or host shift relative to earlier European P. olseni infections.

Host: Blacklip abalone Haliotis rubra; greenlip abalone Haliotis laevigata; Roe’s abalone Haliotis roei and other abalone spp.
Event summary: After its original description in South Australian abalone in 1981, Perkinsus olseni was associated with increasing abalone morbidity and localized depletions in South Australia and New South Wales by the late 1990s, prompting dedicated investigations into Perkinsus‑related mortality from about 1997 onward. Through the 2000s, surveys and FRDC projects documented chronic infections and recurring mortality in blacklip and greenlip abalone along much of southern Australia, with substantial impacts on wild fisheries and concern for farmed stocks. By around 2010, P. olseni was recognized as an endemic, economically important pathogen of multiple abalone species in Australia, with management focusing on surveillance, movement controls and improved diagnostics rather than eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High fishing pressure, warming coastal waters and other environmental stressors on nearshore reef habitats likely reduced abalone condition and resilience, while movement of infected abalone and other molluscs facilitated spread among reefs and jurisdictions. Internal mechanisms: P. olseni exhibits efficient transmission among abalone and other molluscs and can reach high tissue burdens; repeated temperature‑associated mortality episodes in the 1980s and 1990s show that environmental forcing of an established parasite, rather than a demonstrably new strain, underlies this long‑running re‑occurrence of disease.
Review: review – This is a key long‑term Australian abalone episode; the timing and impacts are broadly supported by national reports and FRDC studies. I simplified the emergence coding to re‑occurrence only, because recurrent mortality in long‑infected abalone populations is best explained by environmental drivers and host stress, whereas evidence for novel parasite variants in this period is limited; host range within abalone was already established before 1990.

Host: New Zealand cockle / little neck clam Austrovenus stutchburyi and other native bivalves
Event summary: Around 2000, Perkinsus olseni was first confirmed in New Zealand cockles Austrovenus stutchburyi and other native bivalves from estuaries near Auckland, representing the first recognized occurrence of this parasite in New Zealand molluscs. Over the subsequent decade, surveys showed that P. olseni was present in multiple harbours and estuaries and established in several bivalve species, although large‑scale mortality directly attributed to the parasite in New Zealand remained uncommon. Its presence raised concern for potential sublethal effects on growth and reproduction and for possible spillover into commercially important shellfish sectors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of molluscs and planktonic stages within the southwest Pacific, including historical trade in shellfish seed and ballast water, likely introduced or redistributed P. olseni within the Australia–New Zealand subregion. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range and capacity for chronic, often subclinical infections in several native bivalve hosts facilitated silent establishment and geographic range expansion; this represents re‑emergence of a known parasite species in a new national fauna and host assemblage rather than a novel pathogen.
Review: review – Retain this as an important Oceania range‑expansion/host‑expansion event, but I (i) adjusted the event start to 2000 and the country tag to New Zealand [2000], based on national surveillance reporting P. olseni in clams from Mangamangaroa Stream in May 2000, and (ii) recoded emergence types: first_detection and intra‑continental emergence were set to "No" because the species was already known from the animal host system (abalone in Australia) and Australia and New Zealand fall within the same UNSD subregion, so spread between them does not meet the project definition of intra‑continental emergence; the event is best coded as re‑emergence via host and geographic expansion.

Host: Black-footed abalone Haliotis iris
Event summary: In July 2013, Perkinsus olseni was first reported from New Zealand’s black-footed abalone (pāua) Haliotis iris in farmed stocks, marking a new host record and raising concerns for the high‑value pāua fishery. Initial detections occurred during targeted health surveillance of cultured abalone, with infected individuals showing histological evidence of systemic infection but no associated large‑scale mortality. Subsequent work confirmed that P. olseni was also present at low prevalence in wild pāua populations, prompting proactive management and ongoing monitoring despite the absence of major die‑offs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural or anthropogenic movement of infected molluscs and their larvae within the southwest Pacific, potentially from Australian waters where abalone perkinsosis is endemic, likely introduced or facilitated contact between P. olseni and New Zealand abalone. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of P. olseni to Haliotis iris, facilitated by its demonstrated ability to infect multiple abalone species elsewhere, constitutes a re‑emergence of the parasite in a new high‑value gastropod host within Oceania.
Review: review – Keep this event as it documents a clear host expansion into New Zealand pāua and triggered WOAH immediate notification, but I recoded it: first_detection and intra‑continental emergence are now "No" because those categories apply at host‑system/continent level, not for individual new host species within the same subregion; the event is best classified as re‑emergence through host expansion in an already infected country.

Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum (wild beds, west coast tidal flats)
Event summary: In the summer of 2015, intertidal Manila clam beds on the west coast of Korea experienced marked surfacing behavior and mortality during a period of unusually high air and sediment temperatures. Field investigations showed that clams with high P. olseni burdens were more likely to surface and die, and infection prevalences in major beds often approached 100% with very high infection intensities. As temperatures declined after the heatwave, mortality subsided, leaving depressed clam densities and reinforcing the role of P. olseni as a key contributor to episodic summer die‑offs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A short but intense summer heatwave raised air and sediment temperatures above about 33–34 °C for roughly ten days, exacerbating physiological stress in dense intertidal clam populations and creating conditions favorable for parasite proliferation and sediment hypoxia. Internal mechanisms: High chronic P. olseni infection loads compromised host immune function and condition; under extreme thermal stress these chronic infections translated into acute mortality, illustrating a re‑occurrence of outbreaks in an already heavily infected region without any demonstrated change in parasite strain or host range.
Review: retain – This is a well‑documented, high‑impact Korean heat‑wave–associated mortality episode in a region with long‑established perkinsosis. The geographic scope, host, timing and classification as a re‑occurrence (environmentally triggered mortality in an endemic area) are appropriate and consistent with the Parasites & Vectors study and related Korean literature.

Host: Mediterranean mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis (farmed and wild)
Event summary: During routine monitoring of Mediterranean mussel farms and natural banks in Campania (Italy) from 2019 onward, histology and molecular diagnostics first revealed Perkinsus olseni infections in Mytilus galloprovincialis, a host not previously reported for this parasite in Europe. In parallel, mussel mortality events in Catalonia (Spain) in 2020 were associated with similar Perkinsus infections, with prevalence up to about 20% at some sites and inflammatory lesions in digestive and gonadal tissues. By 2021, P. olseni had been confirmed as an emerging pathogen of Mediterranean mussels in both countries, raising concern for mussel aquaculture and prompting recommendations for broader surveillance of cross‑species transmission from clams to mussels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive bivalve aquaculture with co‑cultured clams and mussels, movements of seed and market shellfish, and regional hydrodynamics likely facilitated spillover of P. olseni from heavily infected clam populations into mussel stocks; ongoing warming and environmental stress may have enhanced disease expression and host susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a generalist parasite to M. galloprovincialis, with molecular analyses indicating distinct haplotypes in mussels compared to classic European clam isolates, represents a re‑emergence driven by cross‑species transmission and possible intraspecific genetic diversification toward a new host.
Review: review – This recent mussel event is well-supported by Carella et al. 2023 and clearly constitutes a host‑expansion episode with potential production impacts. I recoded emergence types by removing first_detection (which should apply at host‑system scale, not to individual new host species) and retaining re‑emergence to reflect cross‑species transmission of an established parasite within the same European subregion.

Host: Chilean mussel Mytilus chilensis (cultured); other regional bivalves (background)
Event summary: By the 2000s, Perkinsus olseni had been reported in South American bivalves, including the venerid clam Pitar rostrata in Uruguay, indicating that the parasite had successfully colonized parts of the southwest Atlantic. In 2022, a study from the Beagle Channel reported the first occurrence of P. olseni in cultured Chilean mussels Mytilus chilensis in Argentine waters, documenting histological lesions and confirming parasite identity by species‑specific PCR and sequencing. This finding signaled host expansion into an important aquaculture mussel species in southern South America and highlighted the potential for wider spread in regional mussel farming areas, though large‑scale mortality events directly attributed to P. olseni in M. chilensis remain limited so far.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of mussel aquaculture in the Beagle Channel, together with regional movements of seed and harvest stock, likely facilitated contact between mussels and infected bivalve reservoirs where P. olseni was already present (e.g. in clams from Uruguay). Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of P. olseni to Mytilus chilensis, supported by its broad host range and capacity to infect diverse bivalves, represents re‑emergence in a new cultivated host within South America and raises concern about future adaptation toward higher virulence under changing environmental conditions.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first confirmed occurrence of P. olseni in cultured M. chilensis in Argentine waters and its interpretation as a host‑expansion/re‑emergence episode building on prior presence in Uruguayan clams. No changes to timing, geography or emergence type were required, other than ensuring that inter‑continental emergence is not claimed here because South America was already infected via Uruguay.

Host: Venerid clam Pitar rostrata (natural beds)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, a health survey of natural populations of the venerid clam Pitar rostrata from the Uruguayan coast revealed infections with a Perkinsus sp. in about 22% of animals, with severe hemocytic infiltration and tissue damage in affected clams. Sequencing of the ITS‑5.8S rDNA region confirmed that the parasite was Perkinsus olseni, providing the first confirmed record of this species in South America and, at the time, the western hemisphere. Although mass mortality of P. rostrata was not explicitly documented, the finding marked a major geographic range expansion of P. olseni into a new continent and host species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance transfers of molluscs and planktonic stages within global shellfish trade and shipping, as well as regional oceanographic connectivity in the southwestern Atlantic, likely introduced P. olseni into Uruguayan clam populations from previously infected regions. Internal mechanisms: Successful establishment of P. olseni in Pitar rostrata reflects both host expansion (a new venerid clam host for this parasite in South America) and inter‑continental geographic range expansion, making this a key inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence event despite limited documented production losses at the time of first detection.

I classified it as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent with in situ infection) and as re‑emergence because it also represents host expansion to P. rostrata.
