Countries: United States of America [2000]; Canada [2005]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2005]
Host: New World camelids (alpacas, llamas) in close contact with cattle
Event summary: From approximately 2000, bovine viral diarrhea virus-1 (Pestivirus bovis) was increasingly recognized as an emerging cause of disease in New World camelids, beginning with reports of BVDV infection in alpacas and llamas in North America and culminating in a 2005 abortion outbreak with a persistently infected cria in an Ontario herd. Over the following years, additional cases and small clusters of infection and persistent infection were documented in alpaca herds in the United States, Canada and later the United Kingdom, often linked to contact with infected cattle or contaminated biological products, prompting concern and targeted surveillance in the camelid industry. As awareness increased and biosecurity and testing were implemented, these outbreaks were generally contained at herd level, though low‑level circulation and occasional PI animals persist in some camelid populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: growth and commercialization of New World camelid farming in North America and the UK, frequent close co-housing or fence-line contact of camelids with cattle, animal movements between farms and shows, and use of bovine-derived biological products (e.g. colostrum, semen) from BVDV‑infected cattle herds created opportunities for cross‑species transmission. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of established BVDV-1 lineages from cattle into New World camelids with the same capacity to generate persistently infected offspring as in cattle, but without clear evidence for a distinct camelid-adapted genotype during this period; this represents re-emergence of the virus in a new domestic host species within regions where BVDV-1 was already endemic in cattle.
Review: review – Event is well supported as a major host-expansion episode of Pestivirus bovis into New World camelids. Corrected the event period to 2000–2010 to capture earlier published infections in US camelids, cleaned the countries field to list only UN-standard country names with country-specific start years, and added primary case reports from Canada and the UK plus an early US camelid series and the ACVIM consensus review as source URLs. Classification as re_emergence (host expansion in regions where BVDV-1 was already endemic in cattle) and the decision not to mark this as inter- or intra-continental emergence remain appropriate, but the relative ranking among the top global BVDV-1 events should be confirmed by human review.

Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein heifers)
Event summary: In May 2004, a large Holstein dairy in California experienced an outbreak among first-calf heifers in late gestation in which 19 of 37 animals aborted or delivered premature calves with striking skeletal and neurologic deformities, and bovine viral diarrhea virus-1 subtype b (Pestivirus bovis) was isolated from affected fetuses and calves. Over a four-week period, multiple stillborn and live premature calves showed brachygnathism, hydranencephaly, hydrocephalus and other malformations, and experimental inoculation of calves with the outbreak strain demonstrated that it induced marked thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia and leukopenia, an unusual phenotype for BVDV-1. Following recognition of the outbreak, management changes and vaccination were implemented and the episode subsided, but the highly pathogenic BVDV-1b strain has since been used as a challenge virus in experimental work and is considered a notable example of increased virulence within BVDV-1.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of a virulent BVDV-1b strain into a large California Holstein herd, likely via movements of replacement heifers or contact with infected animals, combined with incomplete protection from existing vaccination protocols that did not fully match the infecting strain, resulted in widespread fetal infection in susceptible late-gestation heifers. Internal mechanisms: increased virulence/pathogenicity of a specific BVDV-1b field strain, which, unlike most BVDV-1 isolates, produced severe congenital malformations and experimentally induced thrombocytopenia, expanding the recognized pathogenic spectrum of Pestivirus bovis and fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by viral change rather than by geography alone.
Review: review – Added as a new major re-emergence event capturing a well-documented 2004 California outbreak in which a BVDV-1b strain caused numerous late-term abortions, premature births and congenital defects, and experimentally demonstrated thrombocytopenia. Classified as re_emergence (increased virulence and atypical pathology of BVDV-1b within an already endemic US region), with no intra- or inter-continental spread. Geography (Northern America, United States) and year are taken directly from the case report; a human expert should confirm that this episode is indeed among the top BVDV-1 events by impact compared with other severe but more localized outbreaks.

Host: Beef cattle (feedlot and pasture)
Event summary: In 2008, a severe outbreak of acute bovine viral diarrhea due to a BVDV-1b (Pestivirus bovis) strain was reported in Brazilian beef cattle, with high morbidity characterized by fever, diarrhea, erosive and hemorrhagic lesions of the gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory signs in affected herds. The outbreak spread within and between herds in the affected region of Brazil over a short period, causing substantial clinical and production losses in growing beef cattle in an area where BVDV was already endemic. Clinical disease waned following removal of severely affected animals, enhanced biosecurity, and, in some operations, implementation of vaccination and testing strategies, but BVDV-1b remained part of the bovine pestivirus pool in southern Brazil.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high-density beef production systems with movement of young cattle between farms and feedlots, limited prior vaccination against BVDV, and mixing of animals from multiple sources facilitated rapid within- and between-herd transmission in an endemic setting. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak strain belonged to subtype BVDV-1b and appeared particularly pathogenic in this context, but available data do not indicate a clearly novel genotype or altered host range, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re-occurrence driven primarily by management, animal movements and contact patterns rather than fundamental viral change.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects a well-documented severe BVDV-1b outbreak in Brazilian beef cattle and is appropriately classified as re_occurrence in an endemic region, without intra- or inter-continental emergence. Country and subregion match the UN list, and the primary outbreak description plus a general review on persistent infection are suitable sources. No structural corrections were required, but a human reviewer may still wish to compare its impact against other severe but localized BVDV-1 outbreaks in South America.

Host: Dairy cattle, beef cattle, yaks (Bos grunniens), and water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2013, a large cross-sectional investigation in China documented very high seroprevalence and widespread active infection with BVDV-1 (Pestivirus bovis) across four bovine species—dairy cattle, beef cattle, yaks, and water buffalo—across eight provinces, revealing extensive and often under-recognized circulation of the virus. Molecular typing showed that all characterized field viruses were BVDV-1 but belonged to multiple subtypes, including 1b and 1m and, importantly, a distinct new cluster designated subtype 1u, alongside other work in China around this time describing the first isolation and pathogenic characterization of a BVDV-1a strain in dairy cattle. Although BVDV-1 had been present in China for decades, the discovery of high infection pressure and newly recognized subtypes prompted calls for nationwide control and reconsideration of vaccine strain composition.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of dairy and beef production in multiple Chinese provinces, frequent long-distance movement of calves and replacement stock, and variable or absent vaccination programs allowed sustained transmission and intermixing of BVDV-1 lineages across species and regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence and increasing genetic diversity of Pestivirus bovis, with phylogenetic analyses identifying a new subtype (BVDV-1u) and documenting first isolation of subgenotype 1a from Chinese dairy cattle; this constellation of changes supports classification as re-emergence driven by viral diversification rather than simple persistence.
Review: review – Event correctly treats the nationwide 2010–2013 Chinese surveys as a re-emergence episode characterized by high prevalence and the recognition of new BVDV-1 subtypes rather than as first detection. The continent, subregion and country fields have been cleaned so that only China (with its start year) is listed, and the provinces are instead described in the summary. Primary sources documenting prevalence, subtype 1u, and first isolation of BVDV-1a in China are appropriate; a human reviewer should verify that this episode is among the most impactful BVDV-1 events when considering its broad geographic scope and implications for vaccination.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) in proximity to cattle operations
Event summary: On 5 June 2022, a farmed white-tailed deer in central Florida experienced a stillbirth involving two mummified fetuses that were submitted for diagnostic investigation and found to be infected with BVDV-1 (Pestivirus bovis), representing the first confirmed natural case of BVDV-1–associated fetal mummification in farmed white-tailed deer. Subsequent virological and molecular testing of maternal and fetal tissues confirmed vertical transmission of BVDV-1 in this deer herd, in a region with nearby cattle operations in which bovine BVDV is endemic, highlighting ongoing cross‑species circulation at the wildlife–livestock interface. The herd implemented enhanced biosecurity, diagnostic screening, and management changes to reduce contact with cattle and prevent further spillover, and the case has been used to recommend inclusion of BVDV in the differential diagnosis of abortions on deer farms, although broader surveillance data on follow-on cases remain limited.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close geographic proximity and potential fence-line contact between farmed white-tailed deer and BVDV-infected cattle or contaminated environments, combined with limited routine pestivirus surveillance in deer farms, facilitated spillover of an endemic cattle virus into a managed wildlife population. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of Pestivirus bovis from cattle into white-tailed deer with successful vertical transmission and fetal infection; although BVDV infection in wild deer had been recognized experimentally and serologically before, this case documents a natural, clinically significant reproductive outcome in farmed deer and is therefore treated as a re-emergence event at the wildlife–livestock interface rather than a first detection in the species.
Review: review – Event accurately reflects the first reported natural BVDV-1–associated fetal mummification in farmed white-tailed deer in Florida and appropriately classifies it as re_emergence via host expansion in a region where BVDV-1 is already endemic in cattle, not as first detection or inter-continental spread. The country field has been corrected to use only the UN-standard country name with the start year (state-level detail moved to the summary), and primary case and extension reports plus a general host-range consensus paper are retained as sources. Because this is a single-herd event focused on a novel host rather than large case numbers, a human reviewer should assess whether it merits inclusion among the top-impact BVDV-1 emergence events or should instead be reserved for a more host-centric dataset.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle, water buffalo, sheep, goats, camels
Event summary: In mid‑1993, after a 12‑year lull following Egypt’s massive 1977–1978 Rift Valley fever epizootic, clusters of acute visual loss after febrile illness were recognized in rural Aswan Governorate, and serologic surveys showed recent RVFV infection in roughly 8–12% of villagers together with concurrent abortions in cattle and buffalo. Surveillance subsequently detected additional human and animal infections in multiple Nile Valley and Delta governorates, indicating renewed widespread RVFV circulation in Egyptian ruminant populations along the irrigated Nile corridor. Intensified livestock vaccination, vector control and enhanced animal and human surveillance were implemented from late 1993 onward, and reported human and animal cases gradually declined, although serologic data suggest low‑level enzootic transmission persisted in livestock.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely re‑introduction of RVFV into southern Egypt via movement of infected ruminants from endemic areas in Sudan, combined with dense populations of cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats and camels along irrigated farms and abundant Culex mosquito breeding sites in Nile irrigation canals, facilitated amplification and spread. Limited immunity in younger livestock cohorts and incomplete vaccination coverage contributed to abortion storms and widespread seropositivity. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate recurrence of previously circulating Egyptian/Nile RVFV lineages rather than emergence of a markedly divergent strain, so this episode is best characterized as a trade‑ and irrigation‑driven re‑occurrence rather than viral evolutionary change.
Review: Retain – New row added for the 1993 Egypt recurrence, which is widely documented as a major RVF outbreak with substantial livestock abortions and widespread human and animal serologic evidence along the Nile Valley. Geography (Northern Africa, Egypt), timing (1993) and classification as re‑occurrence (virus already established since the 1977–1978 epizootic, with no strong evidence for a novel strain) are supported by CDC and Egyptian reviews; this episode merits inclusion among the most impactful post‑1990 animal outbreaks.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Kenya [1997], Somalia [1997], United Republic of Tanzania [1998]
Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels and other domestic ruminants
Event summary: Following exceptionally heavy El Niño‑associated rains from late 1997, a large Rift Valley fever epizootic began in northeastern Kenya and southern Somalia, with massive abortion storms and mortality in sheep, goats, cattle and camels and concurrent human hemorrhagic fever cases. The outbreak expanded across flooded lowland areas of Kenya, into Somalia and parts of Tanzania through early 1998, causing widespread livestock losses and disrupting pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods. As seasonal rains subsided and floodwaters receded in early 1998, mosquito populations crashed, livestock infections declined, and the epizootic gradually ended, leaving endemic foci and substantial economic damage in the affected districts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme El Niño‑driven rainfall and flooding in East Africa created extensive temporary wetlands and dambos, triggering mass hatching of infected Aedes mosquitoes and secondary amplification by Culex species, while dense concentrations of sheep, goats, cattle and camels in flood‑prone pastoral areas facilitated explosive transmission and abortion storms; limited vaccination and veterinary infrastructure, and movement of animals between flooded grazing areas, further propagated the epizootic. Internal mechanisms: Although multiple RVFV lineages were circulating in East Africa in the 1990s, there is no clear evidence that a novel, more virulent genotype drove this event; it is best viewed as a major amplification of endemic virus under extreme climatic and ecological conditions rather than evolutionary re‑emergence.
Review: Retain – Event accurately captures the 1997–1998 El Niño‑associated RVF epizootic in Kenya, Somalia and Tanzania. Countries, Eastern Africa sub‑region and timing (1997–1998) match FAO, WHO and CDC accounts, and classification as re‑occurrence (large amplification of endemic virus, without clear evidence for a novel strain) is appropriate. No corrections to geography or event type are required; this is clearly one of the largest RVF livestock outbreaks on record.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels
Event summary: In September 2000, Rift Valley fever was detected for the first time outside Africa when unexplained hemorrhagic disease in humans and massive abortions and deaths in sheep, goats and camels were reported in Jizan Province of Saudi Arabia and adjacent Wadi Mawr areas of Yemen. The outbreak spread across irrigated wadis and farming areas along the Saudi–Yemeni border through late 2000 and early 2001, with large numbers of affected small ruminants and camels and major disruption of regional livestock trade. Intensive vector control, animal movement restrictions, and depletion of mosquito populations as seasonal rains waned led to progressive decline of cases, and by early 2001 the epizootic was brought under control, though concerns about RVFV establishment in the Arabian Peninsula remained.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected livestock from the Horn of Africa via long‑standing Red Sea trade routes, combined with unusually heavy rains and irrigation that created abundant breeding habitat for Aedes and Culex mosquitoes in wadis and irrigated plains, enabled virus establishment and amplification in largely naïve Saudi and Yemeni herds; dense livestock populations and active trade and movement along the border facilitated spatial spread and severe economic impact, including trade embargoes. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses show the Arabian viruses were closely related to East African lineages from the 1997–1998 and earlier outbreaks without evidence of major reassortment, so the key mechanism was geographic range expansion enabled by livestock movement and suitable vector ecology rather than evolution of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: Retain – Correctly describes the first documented RVF epizootic outside Africa in Saudi Arabia and Yemen in 2000–2001. Continent and sub‑region (Asia, Western Asia), countries and timing match WHO, FAO and EID reports, and classification as inter‑continental emergence (with neither first_global_emergence nor first_detection ticked) aligns with the definitions. Event summary and mechanisms accurately reflect livestock trade and rainfall as key drivers; sources are appropriate.

Countries: Kenya [2006], Somalia [2007], United Republic of Tanzania [2007]
Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels and other domestic ruminants
Event summary: After satellite‑based early warning indicated high risk in late 2006, Rift Valley fever re‑emerged in northeastern Kenya with heavy rainfall, flooding and reports of mass abortions and deaths in sheep, goats, cattle and camels alongside severe human disease. Through early 2007, the epizootic spread across multiple foci in Kenya, into southern Somalia and northern Tanzania, affecting thousands of livestock and causing serious economic losses for pastoralists and mixed farmers in flood‑prone lowlands. As the rainy season ended and vector breeding sites dried, integrated response measures including livestock movement controls and vaccination in some areas helped suppress new infections and the epidemic waned by mid‑2007, though the virus persisted enzootically in parts of East Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and flooding in semi‑arid and low‑lying grazing areas, high densities and movements of small ruminants and cattle, and limited pre‑emptive vaccination enabled rapid amplification of RVFV following activation of infected Aedes eggs; regional livestock trade and transhumance facilitated spread between districts and across borders. Internal mechanisms: Genomic studies of viruses from livestock, mosquitoes and humans revealed multiple co‑circulating RVFV lineages and reassortment among genome segments between the 1997–1998 and 2006–2007 outbreaks, indicating ongoing viral evolutionary dynamics and supporting classification as re‑emergence with novel genotype combinations that may influence transmission patterns.
Review: Retain – Geography (Kenya, Somalia, United Republic of Tanzania in Eastern Africa), timing (late 2006–2007) and emphasis on multiple co‑circulating lineages and reassortment are consistent with outbreak investigations and genetic studies. Treating this as re‑emergence (novel genotype combinations on a background of established endemicity) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is aligned with the provided definitions. No changes to core fields are needed.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels
Event summary: In October 2007, Sudanese authorities requested international assistance after suspected viral hemorrhagic fever cases were detected in White Nile and Sinnar States, coinciding with reports of abortions and deaths among sheep, goats, cattle and camels. Subsequent investigations confirmed a large Rift Valley fever outbreak centered in irrigated and flood‑prone areas of White Nile, Gezira and Blue Nile States, with extensive livestock disease, trade disruption and a high number of associated human cases and deaths. As surveillance, mosquito control, animal movement restrictions and public health measures were implemented and seasonal flooding receded toward the end of 2007, animal and human case numbers gradually declined and the outbreak was brought under control, though RVFV remained a threat in Sudan’s irrigation schemes and pastoral zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy seasonal rains and expanding irrigation projects along the Nile created ideal breeding habitat for RVFV mosquito vectors, while dense mixed herds of sheep, goats, cattle and camels kept close to human dwellings increased human–animal contact; limited vaccination coverage, weak veterinary services and disruption of livestock markets amplified economic and health impacts. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate that the outbreak was driven primarily by ecological and management factors and by amplification of existing East African lineages rather than by emergence of a substantially different viral strain, so it is best categorized as re‑occurrence in an endemic country.
Review: Retain – The 2007 Sudan event is well documented as a large RVF outbreak affecting White Nile, Gezira, Blue Nile and nearby states, with significant livestock and human impact. Assigning Sudan to the Northern Africa sub‑region (per the project’s UN‑based country list) and classifying the event as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) are correct, as RVFV was already known from Sudan. No substantial corrections are needed.

Host: Cattle (zebu), goats, sheep
Event summary: During the 2008 and 2008–2009 rainy seasons, Madagascar experienced a major Rift Valley fever epizootic after abnormal mortality and abortions were reported in cattle in coastal and central highland districts, with RVFV infection confirmed in ruminants and humans across at least 19 districts. Nationwide serosurveys among high‑risk slaughterhouse workers and livestock demonstrated recent RVFV circulation in all regions and evidence of virus activity in 70–92 of Madagascar’s 111 districts, indicating widespread infection of zebu cattle and small ruminants. As rainfall decreased and targeted animal and human surveillance and movement controls were strengthened, reported animal cases declined by mid‑2009, although subsequent studies show that RVFV has persisted enzootically in Malagasy ruminant populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually wet rainy seasons created extensive mosquito breeding sites in coastal and highland rice‑growing areas, while large‑scale trade and movement of zebu cattle between southern, highland and northern regions disseminated infection; limited vaccination and veterinary capacity favored explosive amplification once RVFV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses indicate that the 2008–2009 Malagasy outbreak viruses clustered with Kenya‑1 lineages from the 2006–2007 East African epizootic, supporting classification as re‑emergence via introduction of established East African strains into Madagascar rather than long‑term local maintenance or a novel genotype.
Review: Retain – New row added for the 2008–2009 Madagascar epizootic. Multiple outbreak and phylogenetic studies identify this as a major RVF event with widespread livestock infection and national‑scale spread, and locate Madagascar within the Eastern Africa sub‑region in the project’s scheme. Classification as re‑emergence (introduction of Kenya‑related lineages into largely susceptible Malagasy herds) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is appropriate. This event should be counted among the most significant post‑1990 livestock outbreaks.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, wildlife (notably game species)
Event summary: Beginning in 2008, Rift Valley fever re‑appeared in South Africa after decades without major epizootics, with small outbreaks in several provinces that presaged a much larger wave. Between 2008 and 2011, repeated RVF epizootics culminated in an explosive and geographically extensive 2010 outbreak affecting hundreds of farms across Free State, Northern Cape, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Mpumalanga, North West and Gauteng provinces, with more than 19,000 reported animal cases and thousands of deaths, particularly in sheep and young stock, and linked outbreaks were also reported in neighboring Namibia and evidence of spread into southern Botswana as the virus moved westwards and into coastal regions. As rainfall patterns normalized, large‑scale vaccination campaigns were implemented and herd immunity increased, the incidence of new animal infections declined and the multi‑year regional epizootic wave subsided after 2011, though localized outbreaks have recurred since.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and flooding in interior plateau and later coastal areas created extensive mosquito breeding habitat, while high densities of sheep, goats and cattle in commercial and emerging farming systems, gaps in routine vaccination coverage, and movement of animals between farms, provinces and neighboring countries facilitated rapid spread; economic losses were amplified by trade impacts and mortality among high‑value breeding and game animals. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic analyses indicate that repeated outbreaks between 2008 and 2011 involved related but distinct RVFV lineages (with lineage C in earlier years and lineage H predominating in 2010–2011) and reassortant strains, consistent with viral re‑emergence in new ecological niches and some genetic diversification within the region rather than simple climatic re‑occurrence.
Review: Review – This row correctly captures a major multi‑year RVF epizootic wave in Southern Africa and should be retained as one of the top‑impact events. However, published outbreak summaries and SADC yearbooks document that genetically related RVFV strains caused outbreaks not only in South Africa but also in Namibia and likely Botswana in 2010–2011. To reflect this, the 'countries' field has been expanded to 'South Africa [2008], Namibia [2010], Botswana [2010]' and the animal case count in the summary adjusted to 'more than 19,000 reported animal cases' based on regional tallies, while keeping classification as re‑emergence (not intra‑continental emergence) because all affected states lie within the UN 'Southern Africa' sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Camels, sheep, goats, cattle
Event summary: In late 2010, after unusually heavy rains in northern Mauritania, suspected Rift Valley fever was reported in camels and small ruminants in Adrar and Inchiri Provinces along with human hemorrhagic fever cases, marking a notable re‑emergence of RVF in this largely arid region. Further south, a subsequent outbreak in 2012 followed markedly above‑average rainfall in southern Mauritania, with widespread abortions among cattle, sheep and goats and confirmed human infections in several regions, forming a linked multi‑year episode of virus activity in Mauritanian livestock. Vector control, animal movement restrictions, heightened surveillance and the end of the unusually wet conditions helped curtail active transmission after late 2012, although serologic evidence indicates continued low‑level circulation in local ruminant populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall events in both northern oasis and southern agro‑pastoral zones created temporary wetlands favoring vector breeding in otherwise dry landscapes, while high densities of camels and small ruminants around oases and in transhumant systems, together with limited vaccination and veterinary oversight, allowed rapid amplification; movement of camels and small ruminants for trade and grazing likely linked northern and southern foci. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses of the 2010 and 2012 viruses show close relationships to earlier West African lineages and to each other, highlighting re‑activation of RVFV with detectable genetic variation and particularly prominent involvement of camels in severe disease, consistent with re‑emergence featuring lineage diversification and host‑impact shifts rather than a purely climatic recurrence.
Review: Retain – The 2010 northern and 2012 southern Mauritania outbreaks are correctly treated as a linked episode in a single country, with Western Africa sub‑region and 2010–2012 time span supported by WHO and EID reports. Genetic work shows that 2012 viruses cluster with 2010 strains, supporting re‑emergence from an enzootic focus rather than independent introductions. Classification as re‑emergence (with camel‑dominated disease and lineage diversification) is appropriate; no changes to core fields are needed.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels
Event summary: In May–June 2018, Kenyan authorities confirmed a new Rift Valley fever outbreak after reports of numerous abortions and deaths in small ruminants and camels and suspected human cases in several pastoral counties. The epizootic was concentrated in eastern and northeastern counties such as Wajir and Marsabit, where high livestock mortality and abortions in sheep, goats and camels were documented and human cases were epidemiologically linked to handling or consuming products from sick animals. Implementation of livestock movement restrictions, targeted vaccination in affected herds, and health messaging to reduce high‑risk animal contact during slaughter and milking, together with the end of the rainy season and associated decline in mosquito vectors, helped to bring the outbreak under control later in 2018.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal heavy rains and flooding in arid and semi‑arid counties created ideal vector‑breeding habitats, and nomadic pastoral systems with dense mixed herds and extensive trade in live animals and animal products facilitated rapid spread and human exposure; prior vaccination coverage was incomplete, leaving many herds susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests circulation of known East African RVFV lineages rather than a novel genotype, so this event is best characterized as re‑occurrence driven by climatic conditions, livestock movement and immunity gaps (enhanced transmission via favorable ecology and management rather than intrinsic viral evolution).
Review: Review – The 2018 Kenya outbreak caused substantial abortion storms and notable livestock losses (e.g. government estimates of roughly 3,700 small stock lost across several counties) and is one of the larger recent RVF episodes, though still smaller than the 1997–1998, 2006–2007 or 2010 Southern Africa events. Countries, Eastern Africa sub‑region, timing and classification as re‑occurrence are consistent with WHO and national reports, and sources are appropriate. Because its scale is intermediate relative to other candidates (e.g. Egypt 1993, Madagascar 2008–2009, Sudan 2019–2020), its inclusion among the final top ten should be revisited by subject‑matter experts rather than assumed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels (primarily small ruminants)
Event summary: In 2019, after unusually heavy rains and flash flooding across much of Sudan, Rift Valley fever re‑emerged with human and animal cases first detected in River Nile State and then in Red Sea and several other northern and eastern states, accompanied by abortions and deaths in goats and sheep. Between late September 2019 and early 2020, national and WHO reports documented around 500–600 confirmed human cases with multiple deaths and laboratory confirmation of RVFV infection in small ruminants in River Nile and Red Sea states, prompting bans and controls on livestock movements from affected areas. Implementation of One Health response teams, enforcement of animal‑movement restrictions, and the end of peak vector season led to a gradual decline in new human and animal cases by early 2020, although Sudan remains at high risk for further RVF activity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive flooding created abundant breeding sites for mosquito vectors in wadis and irrigated zones, and intense movement of sheep, goats and other livestock through major markets such as Eldamar and Port Sudan facilitated dissemination of RVFV between herding areas and export points; limited veterinary surveillance and vaccination exacerbated spread. Internal mechanisms: Available genetic analyses indicate that 2019 Sudan viruses fall within known East African/Nile RVFV lineages, with no compelling evidence of a substantially novel strain, so this outbreak is best described as a large re‑occurrence in an endemic country driven by climatic conditions and livestock‑movement patterns rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Review – New row added for the 2019–2020 Sudan outbreak, which produced approximately 576 confirmed human cases across several northern and eastern states and documented animal infection in goats and sheep, along with major disruption of livestock movements and exports. Assignment to Northern Africa (Sudan) and classification as re‑occurrence (in a country with prior large outbreaks) are supported by WHO and EID reports. Because animal surveillance data are sparse and the precise livestock burden is uncertain, this episode appears to be a substantial recent RVF event but its exact ranking among the top ten should be cross‑checked against other candidates during expert review.

EPP common name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (newborn calves from pregnant cows infected during gestation; similar risk in sheep and goats in affected regions)
Event summary: In July 1998, Japan experienced a severe epizootic of congenital abnormalities in calves, with numerous herds across southern and other regions reporting newborn calves with arthrogryposis, ataxia and hydranencephaly, leading to widespread reproductive and welfare losses. Pathology and serology from more than a hundred affected calves examined at Miyazaki University showed lesions typical of Akabane disease and high neutralizing antibody titres against Akabane virus, implicating heavy virus circulation in pregnant cows during mid‑gestation. As the 1998–1999 calving season ended, the wave of malformed calves subsided with the decline in Culicoides vector activity and accumulation of immunity in breeding stock, although Akabane virus remained endemic in southern Japan, setting the stage for later episodic outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: After a period of low Akabane activity, several years of births from naïve heifers and cows created a susceptible breeding cohort, and favourable warm, humid conditions in 1997–1998 supported high densities of Culicoides vectors in key cattle‑rearing areas, allowing extensive infection of pregnant cows within a narrow gestational window. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not point to a single novel Akabane strain; the outbreak is best interpreted as a large re‑occurrence of endemic virus with geographic spread across much of Japan, following the classic teratogenic pattern in which transplacental fetal infection during specific gestational stages leads to arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly rather than a fundamentally altered pathotype.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to capture the severe 1998 Akabane congenital outbreak described as occurring in "most areas of Japan" with numerous malformed calves examined at Miyazaki University, supported by Uchida et al. 2000 and Akabane reviews.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/104063870001200605)) Classified as re‑occurrence (large epidemic of an endemic virus) rather than first/global emergence or intra‑/inter‑continental spread. National scale and quantitative impact (numbers of affected herds/calves) should be cross‑checked against Japanese surveillance data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (dairy herds; evidence of related infections in other domestic ruminants)
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2003, Israel experienced a major resurgence of Akabane virus infection in cattle, with outbreaks initially centered in northern regions and subsequently extending to the Arava Rift Valley and other areas, causing waves of abortions, stillbirths and calves with arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly and other congenital malformations. Serologic surveys and virus characterization demonstrated widespread AKAV circulation in affected herds and showed that the 2002–2003 epizootic involved a distinct viral lineage compared with the earlier 1969–1970 outbreak. After this epidemic phase, clinical incidence declined as herd immunity increased, although Simbu‑group viruses, including Akabane and Shuni viruses, continued to circulate in Israel and periodically cause reproductive losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions favoring Culicoides and mosquito vectors, including warm, humid seasons and windborne movement of infected midges, facilitated southward and longitudinal spread of Akabane virus within Israel; intensively managed dairy herds with many susceptible pregnant cows amplified the epizootic. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data indicated that a new Akabane virus lineage was responsible for the 2001–2003 outbreak, consistent with re‑emergence driven by viral genetic change and possibly altered antigenicity or tropism, rather than simple cyclical recurrence of the earlier lineage.
Review: Decision: retain (no structural corrections). The 2001–2003 Israel Akabane outbreak is well documented as a major epizootic involving a new virus lineage and large numbers of malformed calves, and classification as re‑emergence is consistent with Stram et al. 2004 and subsequent Israeli reviews.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419647/?utm_source=openai)) The exact start year (2001 vs. 2002) and geographic extent are reasonable but should be re‑checked against full national surveillance data; no changes were made to timing, geography, or emergence‑type flags.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (adult beef and dairy cattle with encephalomyelitis; background infections in cattle, sheep and goats)
Event summary: In summer and autumn 2006, southern Japan experienced the first large‑scale epidemic of Akabane virus–associated encephalomyelitis in adult cattle, distinct from the classical congenital malformation syndrome previously linked to the virus, with hundreds of cattle developing acute neurologic signs such as ataxia, recumbency and hypersensitivity. Virologic investigations identified Akabane virus genogroup I a strains in the central nervous system of affected cattle and showed that virus had recently invaded the region after an apparent year without detectable circulation. The epidemic waned as the vector season ended and herd immunity rose, and subsequent control efforts focused on vaccination of heifers and improved vector monitoring in high‑risk areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High seasonal abundance of competent Culicoides vectors in warm, humid regions of southern Japan, coupled with movement of infected animals or vectors from endemic areas, introduced and amplified the encephalitogenic Akabane strain in largely naïve adult cattle populations. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a genogroup I a strain with increased neurotropism and virulence for postnatal cattle, representing re‑emergence driven by viral genetic evolution that expanded the clinical spectrum beyond in utero teratogenesis to include severe encephalomyelitis in adult animals.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2006 southern Japan outbreak of Akabane encephalomyelitis in adult cattle is a clearly documented, high‑impact event with hundreds of clinical cases and strong evidence for invasion by a genogroup I a strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2443122/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑emergence (novel strain with changed clinical expression) and restriction to Eastern Asia/Japan are appropriate, and no corrections to geography, timing or emergence‑type flags were required.

EPP common name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Germany [2011]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2011]; Belgium [2011]; France [2012]; Luxembourg [2012]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]; Italy [2012]; Spain [2012]; Denmark [2012]; Switzerland [2012]; Ireland [2012]; Finland [2013]; Sweden [2013]; Austria [2013]; Norway [2013]; Poland [2013]; Estonia [2013]
Host: Domestic ruminants (primarily cattle, sheep and goats)
Event summary: In late summer and autumn 2011, dairy cattle in western Germany and the Netherlands developed a new febrile syndrome with milk drop and diarrhea, from which a novel Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyavirus—Schmallenberg virus (SBV)—was identified, marking the first known member of this virus group to cause disease in European ruminants. Over winter 2011–2012 and into 2013, SBV spread rapidly across western, northern and southern Europe via Culicoides midges, with malformed lambs, kids and calves reported in many countries as in utero infections during the 2011 vector season translated into congenital arthrogryposis, hydranencephaly, stillbirths and neonatal mortality, and tens of thousands of holdings ultimately reporting cases. After this epidemic phase, the virus transitioned to low‑level endemic circulation with occasional localized outbreaks, as high seroprevalence, changes in breeding management and, in some countries, voluntary vaccination limited the scale of subsequent waves.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a novel Simbu‑serogroup virus into a naïve European ruminant population—originating likely from endemic regions in Africa or Asia through movement of infected vectors or animals—followed by efficient onward transmission by abundant Culicoides biting midges whose activity was favored by temperate climatic conditions; dense, seasonally breeding sheep and goat populations, and autumn pregnancies that coincided with peak vector activity, amplified the impact through synchronized congenital disease. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (SBV as a previously undescribed orthobunyavirus, probably a reassortant between Sathuperi‑ and Shamonda‑like viruses) conferring effective replication in European Culicoides species and high fetal neurotropism, enabling rapid geographic range expansion and high levels of congenital disease in susceptible herds and flocks.
Review: Decision: review. This event correctly captures the major 2011–2013 SBV epidemic in European ruminants and its classification as an inter‑continental emergence of Simbu‑group viruses into Europe is appropriate.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587714000828?utm_source=openai)) However, the earlier version mis‑labelled it as first_global_emergence and first_detection, which properly refer to the 1970s Akabane emergence in Japan for this grouped EPP; these flags have been set to false. The list of affected countries was expanded to include Ireland, Norway and Estonia, based on national reports and EFSA/ECDC syntheses, though some country‑specific start years (2012–2013) are approximate and should be validated against EFSA datasets.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Sheep (pregnant ewes; malformed lambs), with potential risk to goats and other small ruminants
Event summary: During the 2011–2012 and 2012–2013 lambing seasons, several sheep flocks in Ontario and Québec, Canada, reported unusually high rates of late‑term abortions, stillbirths and lambs born with severe skeletal and central nervous system malformations, including arthrogryposis, scoliosis and hydranencephaly. Diagnostic investigations by the Animal Health Laboratory and federal laboratories identified Cache Valley virus in fetal tissues by RT‑PCR and virus isolation, and serology of ewes confirmed recent infection, representing the first laboratory‑confirmed outbreaks of CVV‑associated congenital disease in Canadian livestock and implicating a genetic variant distinct from previously described North American strains. Following these seasons, the acute wave of malformed lambs subsided, but serosurveys and later case reports indicated that CVV had become an established, intermittently manifest cause of reproductive loss in small‑ruminant flocks in eastern Canada.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warm, wet late summers and autumns in 2011 and 2012 favored mosquito proliferation in eastern Canada, overlapping with breeding schedules that placed many ewes in early gestation during peak vector activity, while most flocks had no prior immunity to CVV, resulting in high attack rates among pregnant ewes. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis of Ontario isolates demonstrated a CVV genetic variant distinct from existing reference sequences, suggesting re‑emergence via introduction or evolution of a new lineage with efficient vertical transmission in sheep; nevertheless, the teratogenic pattern closely matched previously described CVV‑induced arthrogryposis‑hydranencephaly syndromes in North American flocks.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to represent the first confirmed CVV congenital malformation outbreaks in Canadian sheep flocks (Ontario and Québec, 2011–2013), supported by AHL newsletters and Canadian arbovirus reviews.([uoguelph.ca](https://www.uoguelph.ca/ahl/sites/uoguelph.ca.ahl/files/June%202012.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑emergence of an endemic North American virus via a distinct genetic variant in a new national setting; impact is regional but substantial for affected flocks. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points to geographic range expansion and local amplification of established Akabane virus lineages in the Middle East, rather than emergence of a markedly new genotype; thus the event is best viewed as a major re‑occurrence within an already affected continental and subregional context driven mainly by environmental and management factors.

This event accurately reflects a large Akabane outbreak in a massive dairy herd on Iran’s Mughan plain, but earlier serologic surveys and case reports show that Akabane virus had circulated and caused disease in other parts of Iran before 2021; therefore, the previous classification as first_detection and intra‑continental emergence was inappropriate.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11260222/)) The event has been reclassified as a major re‑occurrence/range expansion within Southern Asia. Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus)
Event summary: In the winter of 1991–1992, increased mortality of harbour and grey seals was documented along the western North Atlantic from eastern Canada through the northeast United States (e.g. Gulf of St. Lawrence, Maine, Long Island), where morbillivirus infection with serologic and antigenic profiles consistent with phocine distemper virus was first recognized in North American pinnipeds. The event unfolded as a localized but distinct mortality peak with dozens of seals showing characteristic PDV lesions and PDV‑biased neutralizing antibody profiles, indicating that PDV had entered western North Atlantic seal populations. Strandings declined back toward baseline by spring 1992, leaving behind seropositive survivors and evidence of low‑level endemic circulation of PDV‑like virus in harbour and grey seals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: natural movements and seasonal dispersal of harp, grey, and harbour seals between Arctic/Canadian breeding areas and the Gulf of St. Lawrence/New England region likely facilitated trans‑Atlantic or Arctic introduction of PDV into previously naïve western North Atlantic harbour seal populations; concurrent circulation of avian influenza viruses may have contributed to overall strandings but PDV‑specific pathology and serology support a morbilliviral component. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental geographic range expansion of PDV from its original northeastern Atlantic focus into the western North Atlantic, with establishment of infection in an immunologically naïve pinniped metapopulation; efficient respiratory and contact transmission in dense haul‑out aggregations produced a recognizable but smaller‑scale mortality event than the 1988 European epidemic.
Review: review – Event is real and corresponds to the first confirmed PDV‑associated mortality episode in North American harbour and grey seals, supported by pathology and serology, but NOAA’s UME summaries note that the 1991–1992 Northeast pinniped UMEs were initially classified as ‘undetermined/suspect avian influenza’ and later work showed co‑circulating influenza and PDV. Classification has been corrected by setting first_detection to No (global first detection and emergence occurred in Europe in 1988) while retaining inter_continental_emergence = Yes to mark the first North American occurrence. Countries and sub‑region (United States and Canada, Northern America) are appropriate but the precise state‑level range remains somewhat uncertain, justifying the moderate confidence score and a recommendation for expert review of final inclusion and attribution strength.

Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus); Hooded seal (Cystophora cristata); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus)
Event summary: From 1998 through 1999, a marked increase in strandings of juvenile harp and hooded seals, and to a lesser extent harbour and grey seals, was recorded along the northwestern Atlantic coast of Canada and the northeastern United States. Diagnostic investigations and serology indicated circulating PDV infection in these populations, representing a recurrence of PDV activity following the 1991–1992 event rather than a new continental incursion. Mortality was geographically widespread but of lower intensity than the catastrophic European epizootics, and strandings gradually returned toward baseline by 1999–2000, while serologic data suggested continued enzootic PDV circulation in multiple sympatric seal species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal movements and mixing of large harp and hooded seal populations from Canadian breeding grounds with harbour and grey seals in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and New England likely maintained and redistributed PDV, with environmental factors such as prey shifts and ice conditions influencing aggregation and stranding patterns. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of PDV in an already exposed western North Atlantic multi‑host pinniped metapopulation, without clear evidence for a novel viral lineage or major host jump compared with the early 1990s; multi‑species maintenance in harp, hooded, harbour, and grey seals enabled recurrent peaks of mortality when cohorts of susceptible juveniles accumulated.
Review: review – This episode is supported mainly by longitudinal strandings and serologic/RT‑PCR data summarized in the 2014 PDV review, which links the 1998–1999 harp and hooded seal strandings in the northwest Atlantic to confirmed PDV circulation but does not correspond to a formally declared NOAA UME with a PDV aetiologic label. The event is therefore retained as one of the major North American PDV recurrence peaks, but its emergence type has been corrected from re_emergence to re_occurrence because there is no strong evidence of a new strain or novel host expansion relative to the 1991–1992 event; PDV was already present in the same sub‑region and host community. Countries and sub‑region are consistent with the available descriptions, but the moderate confidence score and reliance on secondary synthesis justify flagging this row for further expert review.

Countries: United States of America [2000] (Alaska – eastern Aleutian Islands, South Alaska Peninsula, Kodiak Archipelago)
Host: Northern sea otter (Enhydra lutris kenyoni)
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, a PDV‑like morbillivirus was introduced into northern sea otter populations in the North Pacific off south‑central and southwestern Alaska, with retrospective serology showing substantial exposure by 2004–2005 and RT‑PCR detection of viral RNA closely related to North Atlantic PDV strains. The event unfolded as part of a broader period of elevated sea otter mortality in the eastern Aleutians, South Alaska Peninsula, and Kodiak Archipelago, with PDV implicated as one of several contributing disease agents rather than a single explosive cause of die‑off. By the mid‑2000s, seroprevalence in live‑captured otters had stabilized at high levels and overt PDV‑associated morbidity waned, consistent with establishment of the virus (or a very closely related morbillivirus) in this new host and region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: progressive loss of Arctic sea ice, shifts in oceanographic conditions, and resulting changes in migration routes of ice‑associated seals likely facilitated east–west movement of infected pinnipeds through the Arctic, allowing PDV to cross from the North Atlantic into the North Pacific and reach Gulf of Alaska ecosystems; long‑distance movements of harp and other Arctic seals acted as a potential vector bridge. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of PDV from true seals (phocids) into northern sea otters, a mustelid marine mammal, and geographic range expansion into the North Pacific via an Arctic corridor; available partial P‑gene sequences show close relatedness to North Atlantic PDV, indicating that only modest viral adaptation was needed to infect otters, and that infection in this new host manifested as chronic health impacts and contribution to background mortality rather than a short, catastrophic epizootic.
Review: review – Strong field and laboratory evidence indicates that a PDV‑like morbillivirus infected northern sea otters in Alaska in the early 2000s, representing both a host expansion and a major geographic range expansion into the North Pacific. However, full‑genome sequence data remain limited and some publications describe the agent as “PDV‑like” rather than definitively PDV, so the event is retained but classified conservatively as re_emergence (host expansion and geographic range expansion) without any first_detection or (intra/inter‑)continental emergence flags. The country, region, and timing (Alaska, early 2000s with confirmation by 2004–2005) are consistent with CDC and NOAA reports, but uncertainty about the precise year of initial incursion justifies the approximate 2000–2005 date range and the high‑but‑not‑maximal confidence score.

Countries: Denmark [2002]; Sweden [2002]; Norway [2002]; Germany [2002]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2002]; Belgium [2002]; France [2002]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]; Ireland [2002]
Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus)
Event summary: Beginning in May 2002, an outbreak of respiratory and neurologic disease in harbour seals was first detected near Anholt Island in the Kattegat (Denmark), marking the onset of a second major PDV epizootic in European harbour seals. Over the following 8–9 months, the infection spread north and west through Danish and Swedish Kattegat–Skagerrak colonies and south and west across the Wadden Sea and North Sea into German, Dutch, Belgian, French, British, and Irish waters, ultimately killing an estimated ~21,700–30,000 harbour seals—about half or more of some regional populations. By late 2002 and early 2003, mortality had fallen back to near‑baseline levels as the susceptible pool was depleted and herd immunity increased, leaving heavily reduced but recovering harbour seal populations across the North Sea–Kattegat–Skagerrak system, with grey seals widely exposed but much less affected clinically.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of harbour seals at coastal haul‑out sites, seasonal aggregation during moulting and breeding, and strong connectivity among colonies in the Wadden Sea, Kattegat–Skagerrak, North Sea, and parts of the southern Baltic facilitated rapid regional spread; possible re‑introduction from Arctic harp or ringed seal reservoirs or via long‑range movements of grey seals, combined with environmental stressors such as contaminants and prey shifts, may have increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of PDV in European harbour and grey seals 14 years after the 1988 epidemic, involving a genetically distinct PDV lineage introduced into an immunologically renewed population with low post‑1988 antibody prevalence, leading to another severe, fast‑moving epidemic with high case fatality; spatial ‘jumps’ in epidemic spread suggest movement via more mobile carrier species (likely grey seals) rather than solely via local harbour seal transmission.
Review: review – This row correctly captures the scale, timing, and geography of the 2002 European PDV epizootic, which caused ~22,000–30,000 harbour seal deaths across the Wadden Sea, North Sea, and Kattegat–Skagerrak and is one of the largest marine mammal mass‑mortality events on record. However, the emergence type has been corrected: intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because PDV was already established in the same European subregions (Northern and Western Europe) during the 1988 outbreak, so this event represents a re‑introduction/re‑emergence in previously affected populations rather than first occurrence in a new sub‑region. The sub_regions field has been amended to remove ‘Southern Europe’, which is not supported by the documented country list, and the vague phrase about ‘additional adjacent Baltic and North Sea states’ has been dropped so that only countries with strong evidence of involvement (Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, the UK, Ireland) are listed explicitly. Sources now focus on detailed European outbreak analyses (Härkönen et al. 2006; Rijks et al. 2005; Müller et al. 2004 and related work), and the event is retained as a key global PDV re‑emergence.

Countries: United States of America [2006] (Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia)
Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus); Harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus); Hooded seal (Cystophora cristata)
Event summary: From spring 2006 through autumn 2007, an unusual mortality event involving pinnipeds was declared along the US northwest Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia after a sharp increase in strandings of harbour, grey, harp, and hooded seals. Virological investigations during this UME isolated a PDV strain (PDV USA 2006) from affected harbour seals, and molecular analyses showed it was most similar to the 1988 European PDV isolate rather than the 2002 European strain, indicating a distinct North American lineage. Approximately 800–1,500 seal deaths were attributed to this outbreak, which remained regionally contained and subsided by late 2007 as strandings declined toward baseline, after which PDV persisted at low levels within the regional multi‑species pinniped community.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: dense aggregations of multiple seal species at haul‑out sites in New England and the Mid‑Atlantic, expanding grey seal populations, and seasonal peaks in juvenile abundance created favourable conditions for cross‑species PDV transmission; regional prey and oceanographic patterns likely influenced the timing and concentration of susceptible animals alongshore. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of PDV in northwestern Atlantic seals with a distinct North American lineage (PDV USA 2006) genetically closer to the 1988 European virus than to the 2002 strain, suggesting independent re‑introduction and/or long‑term circulation of multiple PDV lineages in the North Atlantic; multi‑host transmission among harbour, harp, hooded, and grey seals increased viral maintenance potential and produced a substantial, though not Europe‑scale, mortality event.
Review: retain – This event corresponds directly to the 2006–2007 Northeast Pinniped UME (Maine–Virginia) that NOAA attributes to infectious disease with PDV confirmed as the primary agent, and to the PDV USA 2006 strain described in CDC’s Emerging Infectious Diseases paper. The event year range, geographic extent (United States Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia), host species involved, and magnitude (≈800–1,500 pinniped deaths) are consistent with primary sources. Classification as re_emergence (a distinct North American PDV lineage in an already infected sub‑region) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags matches the definitions and current phylogenetic understanding; no corrections beyond verification were necessary, and the row should be retained as one of the major PDV emergence events.

Countries: United States of America [2018] (Atlantic coast from Maine to New Jersey)
Host: Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus); Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus)
Event summary: Between January 2018 and May 2019, a large pinniped unusual mortality event was recorded along the US northeast Atlantic coast from Maine through the Mid‑Atlantic, with 2,107 stranded grey, harbour, and harp seals documented. NOAA investigations concluded that infection with phocine distemper virus was the primary cause of mortality in grey and harbour seals, whereas the cause for harp seals was classified as undetermined but likely related to demographic and ice‑related ecological factors. By mid‑2019, stranding rates of the affected species had declined to background levels and the UME was formally closed, although PDV remains an endemic disease threat in northwest Atlantic pinnipeds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapidly growing grey and harbour seal populations along the New England and Mid‑Atlantic coasts, with high densities at haul‑out sites from Maine through Rhode Island and southward, facilitated efficient PDV transmission; changing sea‑ice conditions and prey distributions likely altered harp seal movements and survival, contributing to elevated harp seal strandings even where PDV was not clearly established as the primary cause. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of PDV in a northwest Atlantic pinniped community with established endemic circulation, where periodic large outbreaks occur when cohorts of susceptible juveniles accumulate and herd immunity wanes; viral phylogenetic analyses indicate that PDV sequences from the northwest Atlantic in 2011–2018 form a single clade consistent with a long‑standing incursion rather than a novel strain, so the 2018–2019 UME represents a resurgence of existing lineages rather than a genetically distinct re‑emergence.
Review: review – The 2018–2019 Northeast Pinniped UME is well documented by NOAA as a major mortality event (2,107 seals) with PDV confirmed as the primary cause in grey and harbour seals, and ecological factors implicated for harp seals. The event is therefore correctly included as one of the largest PDV‑associated emergence episodes in the 2005–2025 window. However, the emergence classification has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence: phylogenetic work on northwest Atlantic PDV shows that viruses from 2011–2018 fall within a single clade consistent with a long‑standing incursion rather than a new strain, and there is no evidence of a novel host system or major shift in virulence driving the 2018–2019 UME. The country‑level location description has been refined from “Maine to New York” to “Maine to New Jersey” to match NOAA’s UME summaries for harbour and grey seals. Because this row combines UME‑level statistics with inferred PDV evolutionary context, it is flagged for expert review of the final wording and emergence‑type coding.

Host: Multiple endemic and native birds including New Zealand dotterel (Charadrius obscurus) chicks, mohua/yellowhead (Mohua ochrocephala), brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli) and little penguin (Eudyptula minor), as well as introduced passerines acting as reservoirs
Event summary: From 1996 onward, avian malaria parasites (mainly Plasmodium relictum and related lineages) caused successive mortality events in previously unexposed New Zealand endemic birds, first noted in New Zealand dotterel chicks in 1996 and then in other threatened species. Although Plasmodium spp. had been present in introduced passerines in New Zealand since the early 20th century, these late-1990s and 2000s outbreaks marked a major expansion of disease impact in native species, with additional outbreaks documented in mohua in 2004, brown kiwi in 2010–2011 and little penguins, each associated with significant local mortality and concern for small conservation populations. Control focused on managing mosquito exposure around captive and translocated populations, but the parasite became established in wild bird and mosquito communities, making eradication unrealistic and requiring ongoing vector and translocation-risk management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and establishment of exotic passerines and mosquitoes provided reservoir hosts and competent vectors, facilitating spillover from introduced birds into naïve endemic species; conservation translocations inadvertently moved susceptible hosts into higher-risk sites with infected vectors; landscape changes around captive facilities and restoration sites increased mosquito breeding habitat. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion/spillover of established Plasmodium relictum and P. elongatum lineages from tolerant introduced passerines (e.g. blackbirds) into highly susceptible endemic species; enhanced transmission via competent local Culex vectors; possible geographic range expansion of particularly virulent lineages such as GRW4 within New Zealand.
Review: retain: Event corresponds to a well-documented series of avian malaria outbreaks in multiple threatened New Zealand bird species (dotterel, mohua, kiwi, little penguin) from the mid‑1990s onward; geography and host information are correct and supported by national reviews. Emergence classification has been tightened to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false), because Plasmodium spp. were already established in the subregion and the key novelty is expansion into highly susceptible endemic hosts rather than simple resurgence in a previously known system.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [Marwell Zoo, Hampshire 1999]
Host: Captive African penguin (Spheniscus demersus) and macaroni penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus) colony at Marwell Zoo
Event summary: In 1999, Marwell Zoo in Hampshire, UK, lost its entire mixed colony of 27 penguins (22 African and 5 macaroni) to an outbreak of avian malaria attributed to Plasmodium spp., one of the earliest widely reported total penguin-colony losses in a European zoo. The outbreak occurred over a short period during the mosquito season, with birds dying rapidly despite veterinary care, and the colony was not restocked with the same species immediately afterwards. The event highlighted the extreme susceptibility of penguins housed outdoors in temperate regions where Plasmodium is endemic in wild passerines and helped catalyse more systematic malaria surveillance and mosquito-control programmes in European zoological collections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Outdoor penguin exhibits in a temperate region with abundant local Culex mosquitoes and infected wild birds; lack of prior exposure and immunity in African and macaroni penguins; limited mosquito-control infrastructure around the exhibit in the late 1990s. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and spillover of endemic European Plasmodium lineages (especially P. relictum) from tolerant local passerines into naïve penguin species, with high virulence and rapid clinical progression typical of avian malaria in penguins.
Review: retain: Added as a new event because the 1999 Marwell Zoo outbreak, which wiped out all 27 penguins in the colony, is widely cited as one of the most severe avian malaria episodes in European zoos and is more impactful than some later, smaller UK outbreaks. Classified as re_emergence (spillover of endemic European Plasmodium into highly susceptible captive penguins); geography and timing are based on Marwell Zoo’s own history and secondary reviews, and no corrections to the underlying narrative were needed.

Countries: South Africa [Table View, Western Cape – SANCCOB Rietvlei rehabilitation centre 2001-2013]
Host: African penguin (Spheniscus demersus) undergoing rehabilitation at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds (SANCCOB) following oiling, injury or disease
Event summary: From the early 2000s through roughly 2013, African penguins admitted to the SANCCOB seabird rehabilitation centre near Cape Town experienced sustained high exposure to avian malaria, with serological and blood-smear surveys showing frequent new Plasmodium infections during summer months and substantial malaria-related mortality among oiled and injured birds. The problem intensified after large oil spills, when thousands of penguins were brought inland for long-term care, and avian malaria became a leading cause of death among rehabilitated penguins until comprehensive mosquito-exclusion and vector-control measures were implemented around 2008. After vector control was improved, malaria prevalence and mortality dropped markedly, demonstrating that the episode was driven by changes in host and vector ecology rather than by any demonstrable change in parasite biology.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mass rehabilitation of oiled and injured penguins inland from coastal colonies, increasing exposure to mosquito vectors; high densities of stressed, immunocompromised birds kept in outdoor pools; warm summer conditions and adjacent wetland habitats favouring Culex mosquito breeding around the facility. Internal mechanisms: Repeated spillover of endemic Plasmodium lineages (including P. relictum and P. juxtanucleare) from local wild birds into naïve African penguins, with severe disease and high case fatality; no clear evidence that parasite traits changed during this period, so resurgence is attributed mainly to altered host density and vector exposure rather than parasite evolution.
Review: retain: Added as a new event to capture the prolonged period (early 2000s–2013) during which avian malaria caused substantial mortality in African penguins at SANCCOB, where prevalence and malaria-specific deaths were high until mosquito-proofing was introduced. Evidence from Botes et al. 2017 and related summaries shows that malaria became a major cause of death during rehabilitation and then declined sharply once vector exclusion was implemented, fitting the definition of re_occurrence driven by external ecological changes rather than parasite evolution; geography and timing have been set accordingly.

Host: Galápagos penguin (Spheniscus mendiculus)
Event summary: Between 2003 and 2005, blood sampling of Galápagos penguins on multiple islands revealed the first detection of a Plasmodium blood parasite in any bird in the Galápagos archipelago, indicating that avian malaria parasites had newly reached or recently established in this previously isolated island system. Molecular analyses showed the parasite to be closely related to virulent mainland Plasmodium lineages known to cause severe disease in captive penguins elsewhere, raising concern for an endangered, geographically restricted host. Subsequent monitoring has detected Plasmodium DNA intermittently but without documented mass mortality, suggesting low-prevalence circulation that nonetheless remains a conservation threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased human movement and trade in birds and mosquitoes between mainland South America and the Galápagos, together with climate conditions that began to allow survival of suitable mosquito vectors on the islands; possible inadvertent introduction of infected birds or vectors via ships. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a mainland Plasmodium lineage into a naïve island penguin population; geographic range expansion of avian malaria lineages into new oceanic island ecosystems where susceptible endemic hosts lack evolved resistance.
Review: review: Confirmed that this event correctly represents the first documented Plasmodium infection in any Galápagos bird but not the first detection of the parasite in the animal host system globally. Emergence classification has been recoded from first_detection + intra_continental_emergence to re_emergence only, as the parasite was already present on the South American mainland and the novelty lies in host and geographic expansion within the same UNSD subregion. The source list was pruned to retain the Galápagos-specific Biological Conservation article and remove a generic Hawaii-focused avian malaria source that was not directly relevant to this event.

Host: Native Hawaiian forest birds, especially honeycreepers (Drepanidinae) such as ʻiʻiwi (Drepanis coccinea), Hawaiʻi ʻamakihi (Chlorodrepanis virens) and related species
Event summary: Although Plasmodium relictum and the invasive mosquito Culex quinquefasciatus were introduced to Hawai‘i many decades earlier, the period from roughly 2005 to 2015 saw a marked upslope expansion of avian malaria transmission into mid- and higher-elevation forests as temperatures warmed, coinciding with sharp declines in several native honeycreepers. Field studies documented year-round or seasonal malaria transmission at elevations that had previously been disease refugia, with extremely high mortality in susceptible species following single infective bites. Management responses focused on mosquito control (including landscape-level suppression pilots) and habitat protection at the remaining cool, high-elevation refuges, but ongoing warming continues to erode these safe zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Anthropogenic climate change increased temperatures at mid and high elevations, removing thermal constraints on development of both Culex quinquefasciatus and P. relictum within mosquitoes and extending the transmission season; habitat alteration and the presence of feral ungulates created more mosquito breeding sites in native forests. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission due to a highly competent invasive vector; climate-facilitated geographic range expansion of P. relictum into previously unsuitable high-elevation zones; potential selection for parasite strains better adapted to local bird communities, although external climatic forcing is the primary documented driver.
Review: review: Event is well supported by multiple field and modelling studies as a major climate-driven upslope expansion of avian malaria in Hawaiian forest birds, with strong population impacts on honeycreepers. Emergence classification has been adjusted to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to false) because the resurgence and range shift are clearly linked to external climatic and habitat drivers rather than demonstrated parasite evolution; geography, years and primary references remain appropriate.
