Host: Magellanic penguin (Spheniscus magellanicus) undergoing rehabilitation
Event summary: In the austral summer of 2009, a rehabilitation centre in Florianópolis, southern Brazil, experienced a major outbreak of avian malaria in Magellanic penguins, with at least 28 birds infected and high mortality attributed to multiple Plasmodium species, including P. tejerai and other lineages. The outbreak emerged during the warm season, likely after mosquitoes fed on infected local wild birds and then on the penguins, with evidence that penguin-to-penguin transmission via mosquitoes may have occurred later in the episode. Control measures included intensified vector management and chemoprophylaxis, which reduced new cases once the main mosquito season passed and infected birds either died or recovered, but highlighted the high vulnerability of rehabilitated penguins housed outdoors in endemic regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal abundance of local mosquitoes around outdoor rehabilitation pools; proximity to wild reservoir birds harbouring Plasmodium spp.; prolonged captivity of weakened penguins through the high-transmission summer period. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and spillover of multiple Plasmodium lineages from native bird fauna into highly susceptible Magellanic penguins; potentially higher virulence of certain lineages (e.g. P. tejerai) in penguins; enhanced transmission within dense captive groups at the rehabilitation facility.
Review: retain: This is a large, well-characterised outbreak at a Brazilian rehabilitation centre, involving at least 28 Magellanic penguins and multiple Plasmodium lineages with substantial mortality, and is among the most impactful South American avian malaria events in non‑human hosts. The geography, timing and emergence classification as re_emergence (spillover from local avifauna into a novel, highly susceptible host under rehabilitation) are supported by detailed parasitological and epidemiological work; no corrections beyond minor wording adjustments were required.

Host: African penguin (Spheniscus demersus) in two Italian zoos
Event summary: Between 2015 and 2019, two zoos in the Lazio region of central Italy (Bioparco and Zoomarine) recorded the deaths of eight African penguins from avian malaria, accounting for 80% of penguin mortality at these facilities during the study period. Necropsy, histopathology and molecular analyses confirmed infection with Plasmodium matutinum in all eight penguins, and entomological surveillance identified P. matutinum and P. vaughani in local Culex pipiens mosquitoes around the enclosures. Implementation of intensified mosquito control and chemoprophylaxis followed, and no further clusters of sudden deaths attributable to malaria were reported after the main outbreak years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of Culex pipiens and other mosquitoes in and around outdoor penguin exhibits in a Mediterranean climate; presence of infected wild passerines in the zoo landscape acting as reservoirs; warmer summer conditions favouring vector proliferation and parasite development. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and spillover of P. matutinum (and P. vaughani in vectors) from local avifauna into African penguins; enhanced transmission via a competent local Culex population; possible strain-specific virulence of particular P. matutinum lineages (e.g. AFTRU5) in penguins.
Review: review: Confirmed as a significant multi-year cluster of avian malaria mortality (eight African penguins) in two Italian zoos caused by P. matutinum, with strong parasitological and entomological evidence. The UNSD subregion has been corrected from Western Europe to Southern Europe for Italy; emergence classification as re_emergence (spillover from endemic avian Plasmodium into a novel captive host) remains appropriate and sources centred on the Frontiers in Veterinary Science case series are suitable.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [Chester Zoo 2017-2018]
Host: Humboldt penguin (Spheniscus humboldti) colony at Chester Zoo, plus local wild birds and mosquitoes
Event summary: From late September 2017 to January 2018, Chester Zoo experienced a major mortality event in its Humboldt penguin colony: 22 of 44 penguins died, with histopathology and PCR confirming avian malaria as a cause or strong suspect in several cases. Concurrent entomological studies showed high Plasmodium infection prevalence in local mosquitoes (up to around 30% weekly positivity in mid-summer), and molecular analyses linked penguin infections with parasite lineages detected in mosquitoes and wild birds around the zoo. Following relocation of the penguins to an indoor facility and strengthened mosquito control, no further malaria-associated deaths were reported once the outbreak ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high seasonal abundance and infection prevalence of Culex mosquitoes in and around the outdoor penguin exhibit; landscape features of the zoo (water bodies, vegetation) supporting mosquito breeding; wild local passerines acting as Plasmodium reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Spillover and enhanced transmission of one or more avian Plasmodium lineages from wild birds to penguins via dense mosquito populations; high intrinsic susceptibility and acute disease course in Humboldt penguins; potential adaptation of certain lineages to penguin hosts as suggested by repeated detection in penguin tissues and in local vectors.
Review: retain: Chester Zoo’s 2017–2018 mortality event, in which 22 of 44 Humboldt penguins died and Plasmodium infection was confirmed in multiple birds with matching lineages in local mosquitoes and wild birds, is one of the best-documented and more severe avian malaria outbreaks in European zoos. The subregion has been corrected to Northern Europe for the UK, but the emergence classification as re_emergence (spillover from endemic avian Plasmodium into a managed penguin colony) and the main sources, especially the detailed International Journal for Parasitology: Parasites and Wildlife case study, remain appropriate.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [Dudley Zoo, West Midlands 2021-2022]
Host: Humboldt penguin (Spheniscus humboldti) colony at Dudley Zoo
Event summary: Around the winter of 2021–2022, Dudley Zoo in the West Midlands, UK, suffered one of the largest recorded avian malaria outbreaks in captive penguins, losing about 50 of 69 Humboldt penguins—roughly 70% of its colony—to confirmed Plasmodium infection. The outbreak developed rapidly over several weeks, with birds showing few signs before sudden death, and was widely recognised in media and zoo reports as the largest such outbreak in England in decades. Subsequent years saw intensive mosquito control, prophylactic treatment and importation of new penguins, and by 2024 the colony had begun to recover with successful breeding reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually favourable weather for mosquitoes in the preceding season, with mild, wet conditions that promoted vector breeding; outdoor exhibit design that allowed mosquito access; ongoing circulation of Plasmodium in local wild bird communities. Internal mechanisms: Highly efficient transmission of avian Plasmodium (likely P. relictum or similar) through dense, susceptible penguin populations; high virulence of the parasite in Humboldt penguins leading to rapid, often peracute mortality; possible involvement of particularly pathogenic lineages suggested by the high case fatality.
Review: retain: The Dudley Zoo outbreak, in which roughly 50 of 69 Humboldt penguins (around 70% of the colony) died, is one of the largest captive-penguin malaria events documented worldwide and clearly qualifies as a top‑impact emergence episode. Subregion has been corrected to Northern Europe for the UK; emergence classification as re_emergence (spillover and intense transmission of endemic Plasmodium into a large susceptible colony) is appropriate, and the main news and zoo sources agree on the scale and timing of the event.

Countries: Thailand [multiple zoological gardens, including a northeastern Thailand zoo, 2022-2025]
Host: Humboldt penguin (Spheniscus humboldti) and other avian hosts in Thai zoos
Event summary: In February 2022, a Humboldt penguin housed at a zoo in northeastern Thailand died and was confirmed as the first documented fatal case of avian malaria in a penguin in the country, prompting broader surveys of haemosporidian infections in birds across Thai zoological collections. Subsequent work from 2022 to 2025 identified Plasmodium and related haemosporidian parasites in additional Humboldt penguins, other captive birds and local mosquitoes at several zoos, indicating ongoing circulation of avian malaria lineages such as P. collidatum in these facilities. Thai zoos responded by heightening vector surveillance and control around bird exhibits and incorporating malaria into routine diagnostic investigations for penguin and other avian mortalities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of penguin husbandry into tropical South‑eastern Asia where competent mosquito vectors and local Plasmodium reservoirs are abundant; outdoor or semi‑outdoor enclosures allowing exposure to endemic vectors; regional climate favouring year‑round mosquito activity. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of local Plasmodium lineages, including P. collidatum, into a novel penguin host species with no prior exposure; enhanced transmission potential due to continuous vector presence in tropical climates; potential for emergence of lineages with increased virulence in penguins, as suggested by fatal cases.
Review: retain: This event captures the first confirmed fatal avian malaria case in a Humboldt penguin in Thailand and the subsequent detection of Plasmodium (including P. collidatum) in penguins, other birds and mosquitoes across multiple Thai zoos from 2022–2025, representing an important host-expansion episode in tropical Asia. The event years have been broadened to 2022–2025 to match the surveillance period, and the emergence type has been recoded as re_emergence only, because avian Plasmodium was already endemic in South‑eastern Asia and the novelty lies in infection of captive penguins rather than intra‑continental or global first detection; the source list has been expanded to include the full open‑access article.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) in high-health commercial herds
Event summary: In the early 1990s, a novel wasting disease later termed postweaning multisystemic wasting syndrome (PMWS) was first recognized in high‑health pig herds in western Canada, characterized by progressive wasting, respiratory signs, and enlarged lymph nodes in nursery and grow–finish pigs. Investigations during 1991–1996 linked the syndrome to a previously unrecognized porcine circovirus now designated PCV2, with acute outbreaks causing marked increases in post‑weaning mortality compared to historical baselines. The event subsided as affected herds implemented improved biosecurity and management, but PCV2 infection became recognized as endemic in Canadian swine populations and a potential driver of future disease outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of pig production in high‑health herds, high stocking density, and extensive movement of pigs likely facilitated efficient transmission; co‑infection with other respiratory and enteric pathogens and immunostimulation were later shown to be key external co‑factors for full expression of PCVAD. Internal mechanisms: Recognition of a distinct pathogenic circovirus lineage (PCV2) separate from the non‑pathogenic PCV1, with PCV2 causing lymphoid depletion and multisystemic lesions that define PMWS; however, this event represents first clinical detection rather than de novo viral emergence, as retrospective serology suggests prior silent circulation of PCV2 in pigs.
Review: Decision: retain. The event appropriately represents the first recognized PMWS/PCVAD outbreaks in western Canada in the early 1990s and their linkage to PCV2, with correct continent/sub‑region assignment, host specification, and classification as the first detection of this disease entity in domestic pigs. No clearly larger or earlier PCVAD emergence event in swine was identified that would displace this episode, and the listed sources are relevant to its documentation.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999]; France [1998]; Spain [1998]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [1998]; Denmark [1999]; Germany [1999]
Host: Domestic pigs in intensive commercial herds
Event summary: From about 1998, large outbreaks of PMWS/PCVAD were reported almost simultaneously in several European countries, including France, Spain, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, in herds that had previously not experienced this syndrome. Over 1999–2002, herd‑level breakdowns spread from initial foci in southern England to much of the UK and across Western and Northern Europe, with affected farms reporting sharp increases in post‑weaning mortality and wasting and widespread detection of PCV2 in diseased pigs. Disease incidence stabilized after several years as management adapted, but PCV2 became widely endemic throughout European pig populations, providing a reservoir for ongoing PCVAD problems and later genotype shifts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High pig density and extensive live‑pig and semen trade within Western and Northern Europe facilitated rapid transboundary spread of PCV2‑associated PMWS once introduced from North America; contemporaneous disruptions (e.g. 2001 foot‑and‑mouth disease movement changes) altered surveillance and reporting but did not initiate PCVAD. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of pathogenic PCV2 lineages into naïve or partially naïve European herds with co‑infections (PRRSV, Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, swine influenza virus) and immune stimulation acting as critical co‑factors; viral genetic variants present in Europe were closely related to North American PCV2 strains, consistent with recent inter‑continental introduction rather than long‑standing endemicity.
Review: Decision: retain. This row captures the major multi‑country PMWS/PCVAD epidemic in Europe and the first inter‑continental emergence of PCVAD outside North America. While France and Spain reported similar syndromes from about 1994 onward, the 1998–2002 window corresponds to the most impactful epidemic phase affecting multiple Western and Northern European countries, and the continent/sub‑region and country assignments follow the UNSD-based Country sheet. No structural corrections were required.

Countries: China [2000]; Republic of Korea [1999]; Japan [1999]; Viet Nam [2002]
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial herds, including large integrated systems in China and neighboring East Asian countries
Event summary: Around 2000, China reported its first PMWS cases linked to PCV2, followed by a major expansion of PCV2 infection and PCVAD outbreaks across coastal and central provinces by 2002–2003, with high seroprevalence in post‑weaning and grower pigs and heavy economic losses. During this period, PCV2‑associated disease was also documented in other East Asian countries such as Korea and Japan, indicating rapid regional establishment after initial incursions from North America/Europe. By the mid‑2000s, PMWS/PCVAD had become one of the most significant viral diseases of pigs in China and East Asia, prompting widespread diagnostic and control efforts and setting the stage for later genotype shifts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and expansion of pig production in China and neighboring countries, high farm densities, and extensive movements of pigs and pig products (including genetic stock importation from Europe and North America) facilitated PCV2 establishment; limited early awareness and absence of vaccines allowed large outbreaks before control measures were developed. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and local evolution of multiple PCV2 genotypes (initially PCV2a, then PCV2b) with high prevalence and frequent co‑infections (PRRSV, CSFV and others) that enhanced disease severity; genomic studies indicate widespread circulation and diversification of PCV2 in China from 2000 onward, which underpinned later shifts toward more fit genotypes such as PCV2d.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) Event Year adjusted from “2000-2003” to “1999-2003” so that the episode now includes the first published PMWS/PCV2 detections in Japan and the Republic of Korea in 1999, while still covering the early‑2000s expansion and major outbreaks in China and Viet Nam; (2) an additional primary source documenting the first PMWS‑associated PCV2 detection in Japan was added to the Source URLs. Continent and sub‑region labels and classification as an inter‑continental emergence event for Asia remain appropriate.

Countries: Brazil [2000, with spread from initial diagnosis in Santa Catarina to herds in the Southeast region and Rio Grande do Sul by 2002–2003]; Mexico [2001]
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial herds, including farrow‑to‑finish operations
Event summary: In the early 2000s, PMWS/PCVAD was first recognized in Latin America, with Brazil reporting cases from 2000 in Santa Catarina and subsequent outbreaks in the Southeast and Rio Grande do Sul by 2002–2003, and Mexico confirming its first PMWS cases in 2001 despite retrospective evidence of earlier silent PCV2 infection. During 2000–2004, affected Brazilian farms experienced increased mortality in four‑month‑old weaned pigs and typical histologic lesions and PCV2 antigen in lymphoid tissues, while Mexican herds showed longstanding PCV2 seropositivity but only newly emerging clinical PMWS with production impacts. After several years, disease became endemic across major pig‑producing states in Brazil and Mexico, adding PCVAD to the list of key constraints on swine production in South and Central America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and industrialization of swine production in Brazil and Mexico, with importation of breeding stock and semen from Europe and North America likely serving as introduction pathways; dense pig populations and limited early diagnostic capacity facilitated undetected spread until overt PMWS occurred. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of PCV2b‑dominated lineages and interaction with local co‑infections and management stressors triggered transition from subclinical PCV2 infection to clinically apparent PMWS; retrospective tissue analyses in Brazil and Mexico show PCV2 had been present for decades, indicating that shifts in management, co‑infections, or viral variants likely underpinned disease emergence rather than initial viral presence alone.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) standardized the Sub-regions field to “South America; Central America” to match the UNSD-based Country sheet, removing the explanatory parenthetical text; (2) consolidated duplicate Brazil entries in the Countries field into a single Brazil entry that notes sub‑national spread (Santa Catarina, Southeast region, Rio Grande do Sul) and the 2000–2003 window. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence into the South/Central American macro‑region is retained, and treating Mexico within the ‘Central America’ sub‑region under the South America macro‑continent is consistent with the input Country sheet.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs in commercial and breeding herds in New Zealand
Event summary: In 2003, New Zealand, previously considered free of many major pig diseases, confirmed its first PMWS/PCVAD outbreak in a farrow‑to‑finish herd in the Waikato region, with epidemic non‑responsive wasting and elevated post‑weaning mortality. Over the next several years, further cases were detected and investigations concluded that the outbreak represented a new disease incursion, as PCV2 infection was ubiquitous serologically but clinical PMWS had not previously been seen. Following intensive industry and governmental response, including tightened biosecurity and control measures, PMWS spread remained limited relative to Europe and North America, and New Zealand maintained a reputation for relatively favorable pig health status despite the presence of PCV2.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of pathogenic PCV2‑infected pigs or genetic material into a pig population with high health status and little prior exposure to virulent PCV2 lineages, combined with intensification and relatively naïve herd immunity, enabled clinical PMWS to emerge; concerns about trade and biosecurity prompted rapid governmental response. Internal mechanisms: PCV2 was already widespread serologically in New Zealand herds, but emergence of clinical PMWS likely reflected either introduction of a more virulent strain or changes in co‑infection patterns and management stress, allowing PCV2 to cause the full PCVAD syndrome rather than subclinical infection.
Review: Decision: retain. This event correctly represents the first recognized PMWS/PCVAD incursion into Oceania via New Zealand in 2003 and its limited spread through 2006. The continent/sub‑region assignment ('Oceania' / 'Australia and New Zealand'), the focus on New Zealand, and the classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode are appropriate, and the cited thesis and outbreak reports substantiate the storyline. No structural changes were required.

Host: Domestic pigs in nursery and grower/finisher units in Ontario and Quebec, Canada
Event summary: In late 2004, swine herds in Ontario experienced unusually severe PCVAD outbreaks characterized by higher mortality and more extensive lesions than previously typical PMWS cases, soon followed by similar problems in Quebec herds. Molecular investigations during 2005–2006 identified a new PCV2 variant (RFLP type 321, corresponding to genotype PCV2b) that rapidly became dominant in affected Canadian herds and was associated with more severe lymphoid and systemic lesions compared with the previously dominant RFLP 422 strains. After several years, widespread adoption of PCV2 vaccination and improved control measures markedly reduced clinical PCVAD incidence, although PCV2b and related variants remained endemic in Canadian pig populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High pig density in Ontario and Quebec, frequent movement of pigs between herds and regions, and limited prior vaccination created conditions for rapid expansion of a fitter viral variant; concurrent infections and production stressors further amplified disease severity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and rapid spread of a novel PCV2b strain (RFLP 321) with distinct ORF2 (capsid) gene sequence and evidence of higher virulence—histological comparisons showed more severe lesions in pigs infected with RFLP 321 than with older strains—constitute a clear example of novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence; this episode is classified as both re‑occurrence (marked resurgence of disease in a previously affected subregion) and re‑emergence (due to genetic change in the virus).
Review: Decision: review. Correction made: consolidated duplicate Canada entries in the Countries field into a single entry (“Canada [2004, mainly Ontario and Quebec 2004–2006]”) while retaining the emphasis on Ontario/Quebec as the focus of this severe PCV2b-associated episode. Event timing, geography, and the dual classification as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence (due to emergence and dominance of the PCV2b/RFLP 321 variant) remain consistent with the cited Canadian studies.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: United States of America [2004]; Canada [2004]; France [2003]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2003]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2003]
Host: Domestic pigs in intensive swine production systems in North America and Western/Northern Europe
Event summary: Between approximately 2003 and 2007, many pig‑producing regions in North America and Western/Northern Europe reported a wave of severe PCVAD outbreaks, with sharp increases in diagnostic submissions and field reports linking high nursery and grow‑finish mortality to PCV2, often of the emerging PCV2b genotype. In the United States and Canada, these outbreaks were characterized by high case fatality, extensive co‑infection with PRRSV and other respiratory pathogens, and substantial economic losses, while in Europe, similar increases in PMWS/PCVAD incidence were observed in France, the Netherlands, and the UK despite previous experience with PMWS. The wave of severe disease largely subsided after 2006–2007, coinciding with rapid rollout of effective PCV2 vaccines in major pig markets and widespread incorporation of vaccination into routine herd health programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High global pig densities, intensive production practices, extensive movement of animals within continents, and frequent co‑infection with PRRSV and other pathogens created conditions for widespread expression of severe PCVAD; economic pressures and management changes (e.g., all‑in/all‑out, larger batch sizes) increased immunological stress and pathogen mixing. Internal mechanisms: Increasing dominance of PCV2b over PCV2a in North America and Europe, along with high viral loads and strong immunostimulation, contributed to more frequent and severe PCVAD episodes; although the primary internal mechanism was genotype replacement rather than a single novel strain, the resulting disease surge represents a major re‑occurrence and re‑emergence of PCVAD in already affected subregions, mitigated only after vaccination dramatically reduced clinical cases.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) set Intra-continental emergence to “No”, because all listed sub-regions (Northern America; Western/Northern Europe) were already affected by PCVAD in earlier events and this represents a severe resurgence rather than first occurrence in a new sub-region; (2) set Re-emergence to “Yes” to reflect the global genotype shift from PCV2a to PCV2b associated with increased disease impact; (3) expanded the Event Year from “2005-2007” to “2003-2007” to encompass early PCV2b-associated surges in Europe as well as the 2004–2007 peak in North America; and (4) adjusted country-specific start years for the United States and Canada to 2004 so they fall within the revised event window. The event is thus interpreted as a large multi-continental re-occurrence and re-emergence episode driven by PCV2b genotype replacement.

Countries: China [2008]; China (Guangxi, Hebei, Henan, Shandong, Jiangsu, Heilongjiang and multiple other provinces) [2008-2019]
Host: Domestic pigs across diverse production systems in China (backyard to large-scale commercial)
Event summary: From around 2008 onward, Chinese swine herds experienced a prolonged phase of PCVAD activity associated with a genotype shift from previously dominant PCV2a/2b strains to PCV2d, with PCV2d becoming the predominant genotype in many provinces by the early to mid‑2010s. During 2008–2019, PCV2d was repeatedly detected at high prevalence in herds across central, eastern and southern China (e.g., Guangxi, Hebei, Henan, Shandong), often in pigs with respiratory disease or systemic signs, and field and experimental data suggested that some PCV2d strains replicated to higher titers than earlier genotypes and were less well matched by PCV2a‑based vaccines. Although PCV2 vaccination generally kept catastrophic PMWS‑like outbreaks in check, persistent subclinical infection, sporadic clinical PCVAD, and co‑infections combined with genotype shifts resulted in a sustained, economically important re‑emergence of PCV2‑related disease across Chinese pig production during this decade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high pig densities, rapid expansion and restructuring of the Chinese swine industry, and frequent mixing of pigs from different sources allowed rapid circulation and selection of fitter viral variants; widespread but imperfect vaccine coverage (mostly PCV2a‑based) and ongoing co‑infection pressures (PRRSV, CSFV, etc.) created an epidemiological environment favoring immune‑escape or better‑fit PCV2 variants. Internal mechanisms: Documented genotype transitions (PCV2a→PCV2b, then PCV2b→PCV2d) with PCV2d becoming dominant after about 2008–2010, and evidence of higher amino‑acid diversity in key capsid epitopes and higher viremia in some PCV2d strains compared with PCV2b, indicate novel strain/genotype emergence and possible enhanced fitness; this event is classified as both re‑occurrence (renewed disease impact in previously affected subregions) and re‑emergence (strain replacement with altered antigenicity and potential partial vaccine escape).
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) standardized the Sub-regions field to the UNSD-compatible label “Eastern Asia”, moving the description of central and southern Chinese provinces into the Countries field; (2) set Intra-continental emergence to “No”, because PCV2/PCVAD was already established in Eastern Asia and this event reflects genotype shifts and renewed disease impact within previously affected areas rather than first occurrence in a new sub-region; and (3) adjusted the Event Year from “2009-2019” to “2008-2019” to better align with molecular data indicating PCV2d began replacing PCV2b around 2008 while still covering the decade-long period of PCV2d predominance and associated re-emergence.

Countries: Japan [early 1990s]; Republic of Korea [early 1990s]; China [1990s]; Thailand [mid-1990s]; Philippines [1990s]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), mainly suckling piglets, weaners and growers
Event summary: In the early 1990s, PEDV became widely established in East and parts of South-east Asia, emerging as a major cause of neonatal diarrhea and mortality in piglets in Japan, South Korea and China and later in Thailand and the Philippines. The virus spread between intensive breeding and finishing farms, producing repeated waves of severe diarrhea in seronegative herds and becoming endemic in multiple countries. By the late 1990s, PEDV was enzootic across much of Eastern Asia and parts of South-eastern Asia, with recurrent local outbreaks but limited international reporting.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of commercial pig production in East and South-east Asia, high pig densities, frequent live-pig movements between farms and regions, and limited early biosecurity standards facilitated establishment and regional spread. Internal mechanisms: Progressive genetic diversification of PEDV relative to the European prototype strain (CV777), particularly in the spike gene, likely supported persistence and adaptation under field conditions, but no single discrete novel high-pathogenicity genotype dominates reports from this period.
Review: review - Retain this event as it captures the early 1990s establishment of PEDV across East and parts of South-eastern Asia, which is a major step in global spread. Reclassified it from re-occurrence to intra-continental emergence to reflect first confirmation in new Asian sub-regions (notably South-eastern Asia) and added the Philippines to the country list. Country-specific years remain approximate and should be refined against national reports.

Host: Domestic pigs in farrow-to-finish systems, including sows, suckling piglets and growers
Event summary: After PEDV activity in Europe had become sporadic by the late 1990s, Italy experienced renewed, severe PED outbreaks in 2005–2006 on seronegative breeding farms, with acute watery diarrhea and notable mortality in neonatal piglets. The epidemic spread between multiple farms and regions within Italy over two production years, causing substantial economic losses but remaining largely confined to the country. Disease incidence declined again after control measures and herd immunity increased, and Europe overall returned to a pattern of low-level or sporadic PEDV activity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High farm-level pig densities, limited prior PEDV immunity in Italian herds, and movements of replacement stock between breeding and finishing sites facilitated spread once PEDV was reintroduced. Internal mechanisms: The Italian outbreaks were associated mainly with classical (CV777-like) PEDV rather than a clearly distinct high-pathogenicity variant, suggesting that host susceptibility and management rather than viral innovation were the dominant drivers.
Review: retain - Well-documented epidemic in northern Italy during 2005–2006, correctly located in Southern Europe and classified as re-occurrence driven by reintroduction of classical CV777-like strains into largely naïve herds. Sources adequately describe epidemiology and impact; no structural changes recommended.

Host: Domestic pigs on commercial farms, predominantly suckling piglets and weaners
Event summary: Beginning in late 2007, Thailand reported large PEDV outbreaks starting in Nakhon Pathom province and rapidly spreading to multiple provinces and swine farms nationwide. The epidemic caused extensive diarrhea and high piglet mortality in affected herds, with virus detected on dozens of farms over several months. By early 2008 the initial national wave subsided, but PEDV remained endemic in Thailand with recurrent local outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a PEDV strain closely related to contemporary Chinese viruses, frequent movement of pigs and insufficient gilt acclimatization, and biosecurity gaps (e.g. contaminated transport vehicles and equipment) were implicated in rapid national dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Thai isolates showed high genetic similarity to Chinese field strains and divergence from the European vaccine strain CV777, with molecular evidence of more recent GII epidemic lineages; this supports classification as re-emergence driven by introduction of more virulent genotypes into a region where PEDV had circulated previously.
Review: review - Retain this event as one of the major PEDV epizootics in South-eastern Asia but reclassify it from intra-continental emergence to re-emergence, because Thailand already had documented PEDV circulation in the 1990s and the 2007–2008 wave was caused by newer, Chinese-like GII variants. Geography and timing are appropriate; no changes to countries, but the event type correction should be reviewed and accepted.

Host: Domestic pigs of all ages, with very high mortality in neonatal suckling piglets
Event summary: From October 2010, China experienced a large-scale PED epizootic in which severe diarrhea with 80–100% mortality in suckling piglets spread rapidly among previously vaccinated sow herds in multiple southern and eastern provinces. During 2010–2012, genetically related PEDV variants displaced classical strains and caused repeated farm-level outbreaks despite routine use of CV777-based vaccines, leading to major piglet losses and economic damage to the Chinese swine industry. Outbreak intensity gradually declined as updated control measures and partial population immunity developed, although the new variant lineage became endemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density industrial pig production, extensive inter-provincial pig and piglet movements, and inadequate farm biosecurity allowed rapid geographic expansion; reliance on vaccines based on classical CV777 strains created strong selection for immune-escape variants. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of highly virulent GII variant strains with substantial spike-gene divergence from CV777 (reducing neutralization), increased intestinal tropism and high viral loads in the small intestine produced increased virulence and vaccine breakthrough, representing classic novel strain emergence with increased pathogenicity.
Review: retain - This is one of the highest-impact PEDV events globally and is accurately described as a re-emergence episode in China driven by highly virulent GII variants that broke through CV777-based vaccination. Geography, timing and mechanisms are well-supported by multiple primary EID reports and later molecular-epidemiology reviews; no structural corrections needed.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Central America; Caribbean; South America
Countries: United States of America [2013]; Mexico [2013]; Peru [2013]; Dominican Republic [2013]; Canada [2014]; Colombia [2014]; Ecuador [2014]
Host: Domestic pigs in all commercial sectors, particularly neonatal piglets in sow farms
Event summary: In April–May 2013, highly virulent PEDV was first detected in the United States, where it rapidly spread to swine farms in dozens of states within months, causing very high morbidity and up to 95% mortality in suckling piglets and an estimated loss of more than seven million piglets during the first year. During late 2013 and 2014, the same Asian-like lineage was reported with in situ transmission in Mexico, Peru, the Dominican Republic, Canada, Colombia and Ecuador, establishing PEDV across much of North, Central and South America. Intensive control efforts, including enhanced biosecurity, transport and rendering/feed-chain sanitation, and sow exposure or vaccination, eventually reduced outbreak frequency, but PEDV became enzootic at lower levels throughout the Americas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of an Asian-derived, high-virulence PEDV GII lineage into a largely naïve Western Hemisphere pig population; extensive movements of pigs, piglets and contaminated transport vehicles; shared slaughter and rendering networks; and possible contamination of feed ingredients collectively drove rapid cross-border dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The invading strains belonged to genetically distinct, highly pathogenic GII lineages with spike-gene changes associated with enhanced virulence and efficient replication; in the absence of pre-existing population immunity, this produced explosive epidemics and very high piglet mortality across multiple American countries.
Review: review - Event retained as a major global episode but expanded from a North American focus (USA, Canada, Mexico) to cover the documented 2013–2014 inter-continental introduction of PEDV into the wider Americas (adding Peru, Dominican Republic, Colombia, Ecuador) and corrected continent/sub-region coding accordingly. The event type was adjusted so it is classified purely as inter-continental emergence (not first detection at the host-system level, which occurred decades earlier in Europe). Source list was strengthened by adding detailed Canadian and Mexican outbreak reports and the Lv et al. 2016 review while dropping reliance on Wikipedia; exact national start months and loss estimates remain approximate and warrant further checking.

Countries: Republic of Korea [2013]; Japan [2013]; Japan [2014]; Japan [2015]; Japan [2016]
Host: Domestic pigs, especially suckling piglets on commercial farms
Event summary: After earlier PEDV activity in the 1990s and 2000s, Eastern Asia experienced a major re-emergence of highly virulent GII PEDV from late 2013 onward. South Korea reported widespread PED outbreaks in late 2013–2014, while Japan, after several quiet years, saw a large-scale epidemic beginning in late 2013 that spread to most prefectures by 2014 and continued with substantial herd-level losses into 2016, with hundreds of thousands of pigs estimated to have died. Taiwan also experienced severe PEDV outbreaks in 2013–2014, with near-100% mortality in suckling piglets on many affected farms. Molecular analyses showed that East Asian outbreak strains were closely related to contemporary U.S. epidemic and recent Chinese variants, indicating re-introduction of high-virulence lineages rather than resurgence of older endemic viruses. Intensive control measures gradually reduced outbreak numbers, but these variant lineages became endemically established in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely repeated introductions of US-/China-like high-pathogenicity PEDV strains into East Asian pig industries via regional trade, biological products or other contaminated fomites, combined with high pig density, complex movements between breeding, nursery and finishing systems, and gaps in farm-level biosecurity, enabled rapid national and regional spread in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan. Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses clustered within highly virulent GIIa lineages and showed near-identity in the spike gene to North American epidemic strains but clear divergence from historical local PEDV, consistent with re-emergence driven by new, more virulent and transmissible genotypes that partially escaped existing vaccine-derived immunity.
Review: review - Original row describing only South Korea (2013–2014) was broadened to represent the full Eastern Asia re-emergence of highly virulent GII strains affecting South Korea, Japan and Taiwan and the time span was extended to 2013–2016 to capture the prolonged Japanese epidemic. Classification as re-emergence (rather than inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because all affected subregions had prior PEDV circulation. Country coverage and approximate years should be checked against national surveillance data, but this remains one of the largest PEDV episodes and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Viet Nam [2013]; Viet Nam [2014]; Viet Nam [2015]; Philippines [2014]; Philippines [2015]
Host: Domestic pigs on commercial and smallholder farms, with highest mortality in neonatal and suckling piglets
Event summary: From 2013, South-eastern Asia experienced new high-virulence PEDV outbreaks associated with GII variants closely related to recent Chinese strains. In Viet Nam, genotype IIb PEDV was detected in multiple herds in 2013 and recurred over subsequent years, while in 2014–2015 the swine industry in the Philippines suddenly suffered large PED outbreaks characterized by severe watery diarrhea and near-100% mortality in suckling piglets on many affected farms. These episodes caused marked piglet losses and production disruptions in both countries, and PEDV remained enzootic with intermittent severe flare-ups despite increasing awareness and control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of pig production in Viet Nam and the Philippines, high densities of pigs around urban and peri-urban areas, extensive movement of pigs and feed ingredients within and between countries, and limited early biosecurity and vaccine coverage favored introduction and onward spread of Chinese-origin PEDV. Internal mechanisms: The Vietnamese and Philippine outbreaks were caused by GIIb/GIIa variants with spike-gene changes linked to high virulence and close genetic relatedness to recent Chinese field strains, indicating re-emergence driven by novel, more pathogenic genotypes rather than persistence of older classical CV777-like viruses.
Review: review - New row added to capture major 2013–2015 re-emergence of high-virulence PEDV in South-eastern Asia, particularly genotype IIb/IIa outbreaks in Viet Nam and the large 2014–2015 epidemic in the Philippines with very high piglet mortality. These outbreaks are clearly among the more impactful regional episodes yet were missing from the original list; classification as re-emergence (not first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence) is consistent with earlier PEDV presence in the region. National data could further refine the duration and relative impact in each country.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Germany [2014]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2014]; Belgium [2015]; France [2014]; Austria [2014]; Czechia [2014]; Hungary [2015]; Italy [2014]; Portugal [2015]; Slovenia [2015]; Ukraine [2014]
Host: Domestic pigs on breeding, farrow-to-finish and fattening farms
Event summary: In 2014, Europe saw re-emergence of PEDV when epidemic diarrhea was reported on German pig farms, including a large 1,200-head fattening operation in southern Germany, followed by outbreaks in sow and farrow-to-finish herds. Over 2014–2016, closely related S-INDEL PEDV strains, genetically akin to the U.S. OH851 variant, were detected in the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Austria, Italy, Portugal, Slovenia and several Central and Eastern European countries including Czechia, Hungary and Ukraine, causing variable but sometimes high piglet mortality and widespread herd infection. By 2016, reported outbreaks had decreased, but PEDV persisted at low levels in parts of Europe, raising concern about ongoing viral evolution and sporadic severe episodes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long gaps without significant PEDV activity left many European herds immunologically naïve, while intense intra-European pig movements, shared transport networks, and initial lack of awareness created favorable conditions for dissemination of reintroduced strains. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies showed that most 2014–2016 European strains formed a relatively homogeneous S-INDEL cluster related to, but distinct from, U.S. high-virulence strains, suggesting one or a few recent introductions followed by regional evolution with generally reduced but still variable virulence; in Ukraine, more virulent GIIa US-like viruses were also detected, illustrating co-circulation of different re-emergent genotypes.
Review: review - Event retained as the principal 2014–2016 European re-emergence but the country list was expanded (adding Netherlands, Austria and Slovenia) and some start years were corrected (for example Ukraine to 2014 and Belgium to 2015) based on comprehensive European reviews. Classification as re-emergence (rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence) remains appropriate because PEDV was already present in Europe. Given reliance on regional syntheses for some dates, country-specific onset years should be double-checked against national outbreak reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs in industrial systems, particularly neonatal piglets despite prior vaccination
Event summary: Following the large 2010–2012 PED epizootic, China continued to experience recurrent PEDV outbreaks from 2017 onward, with episodes of severe diarrhea and high piglet mortality reported on vaccinated farms across multiple provinces. During this period, genomic surveillance documented ongoing diversification of variant GII strains, with emergence of subgroup lineages such as GII-a (e.g. strain HM2017) showing high virulence in experimental infections. These recurrent outbreaks gradually declined in some regions as biosecurity and updated vaccine strategies improved, but PEDV remained an important endemic and periodically epidemic pathogen in Chinese pig production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent high-density industrial pig production, incomplete vaccine coverage, and continued long-distance movement of pigs and piglets sustained viral circulation and periodic re-introduction into susceptible herds. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution of GII PEDV variants, including accumulation of mutations and recombination in the spike gene, produced sub-lineages with maintained or increased virulence and partial immune escape from existing CV777-based and early variant vaccines, exemplifying re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and possible enhanced transmission.
Review: retain - This row appropriately captures the post-2016 pattern of recurrent, variant-driven PEDV outbreaks in China as a re-emergence episode with ongoing diversification of GII sub-lineages. Geography, time span and mechanisms are consistent with recent molecular-epidemiology reviews; detailed quantification of impact varies between sources but the episode clearly ranks among the major recent events, so no structural changes are recommended.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Greece [1994-1998] (Evros prefecture near the border with Türkiye)
Host: Sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: Between 1994 and 1998 a protracted epidemic of sheep pox caused by capripoxvirus affected the Evros prefecture in northern Greece, with repeated seasonal waves in local sheep flocks near the Turkish border. The epidemic caused major economic losses from mortality, culling, movement bans and trade restrictions on small ruminants and their products. Intensive stamping-out, movement control, and biosecurity improvements gradually interrupted local transmission by the late 1990s, although sheep pox remained a regional threat in neighbouring countries and sporadically reappeared in Greece in later years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of susceptible sheep flocks with limited prior immunity; cross-border movements of animals and products from endemic areas in neighbouring countries; environmental conditions favouring mechanical vector transmission and farm-to-farm spread; limited early vaccination coverage. Internal mechanisms: This episode is best characterised as a re-occurrence of an established capripoxvirus in a known region, driven by external factors rather than clear viral change; no specific novel strain has been consistently implicated.
Review: Retain – Well-documented multi-year sheep pox epidemic in Evros, Greece with large numbers of affected flocks and substantial economic impact; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence within Southern Europe are consistent with primary sources. No structural changes made.

Countries: United States of America [2003]; Ghana [source rodents, 2003]
Host: Prairie dogs (Cynomys ludovicianus, primarily black‑tailed prairie dogs); various African rodents (Gambian pouched rats, dormice, rope squirrels and others) involved in the import consignment
Event summary: In spring 2003 monkeypox virus (clade II) was introduced into the United States via a shipment of wild-caught African rodents from Ghana that were co‑housed with prairie dogs in a pet distribution facility. Over subsequent weeks infected prairie dogs were distributed to pet stores and swap meets in multiple Midwestern states, leading to a multi‑state epizootic with numerous sick or infected prairie dogs and at least dozens of human zoonotic cases linked to direct animal contact, representing the first documented occurrence of monkeypox in the Western Hemisphere. Federal authorities responded by tracing and quarantining exposed animals, restricting importation of African rodents and trade in prairie dogs, and by late 2003 the epizootic and associated human cases had been contained without evidence of sustained wildlife establishment in North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Globalisation of the exotic pet trade and importation of wild African rodents; co‑housing of multiple rodent species and prairie dogs under crowded conditions; lack of prior awareness of monkeypox risk in the pet industry; absence of pre‑existing immunity or surveillance for orthopoxviruses in North American pet rodents. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of monkeypox virus from endemic African rodent reservoirs to prairie dogs; Enhanced Transmission through high-density housing and close contact, although no clear adaptive mutations were documented; Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) across continents via trade rather than natural dispersal.
Review: Retain – Accurately describes the 2003 U.S. monkeypox epizootic with appropriate classification as first detection and inter-continental emergence (established transmission among imported/exotic rodents in North America, not just single imported cases). No changes needed.

Countries: India [Tamil Nadu 2004; Maharashtra (Aurangabad, Kolhapur) and other states 2006–2008, 2009–2010]
Host: Domestic water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis); dairy cattle; humans (milkers, dairy workers, and a few laboratory staff)
Event summary: Between 2004 and roughly 2010 India experienced a series of large buffalopox outbreaks caused by vaccinia‑like buffalopox virus, starting with a notable 2004 episode in Tamil Nadu involving over 120 lactating buffaloes and 40 cows plus multiple infected milkers, and followed by severe epizootics in Maharashtra and other states during 2006–2008 and 2009–2010. These outbreaks caused high morbidity, significant mortality in young buffalo calves and substantial reductions in milk production in some affected herds, along with numerous occupational infections in dairy workers and occasional laboratory-associated cases. Control was achieved through improved hygiene in milking, segregation of sick animals, temporary disruption of trade, and better awareness among veterinarians and farmers, but buffalopox continues to re‑emerge sporadically in Indian dairy systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density dairy buffalo and cattle herds with close human–animal contact during hand milking; lack of specific vaccination against buffalopox; animal movements and shared milking equipment spreading virus between farms; sometimes poor farm-level biosecurity. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of vaccinia‑like buffalopox virus in new dairy regions, with evidence that the virus has evolved locally in Indian buffalo and cattle populations; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity is suggested by severe disease and high calf mortality in some outbreaks; zoonotic potential demonstrated by repeated human infections in dairy workers and, on at least one occasion, in a laboratory setting.
Review: Retain – Outbreaks and impacts are well supported by veterinary and zoonotic case reports from India, and classification as repeated re-occurrence and re-emergence (local evolution plus recurrent severe outbreaks) is justified. No structural edits required.

Sub-regions: Southern Asia; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Africa; Eastern Africa
Countries: India [recurrent 2005–2022]; Pakistan [2006–2012]; Bangladesh [2007–2019]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [multiple years]; Kazakhstan [1993; intermittent to 2008 and later]; Russian Federation (southern regions, intermittent to 2008 and later); Morocco [2010]; other endemic or newly affected countries in Africa and Asia
Host: Sheep; goats
Event summary: From about 2005 to 2022 sheep and goat pox viruses caused recurrent and sometimes expanding waves of outbreaks across Africa and Asia, with occasional incursions into previously disease-free areas of Central Asia and Eastern Europe, such as Kazakhstan and parts of the Russian Federation. Individual country epizootics were often intense, involving thousands of outbreaks and major production and trade losses, but collectively they formed a pattern of persistent endemicity with periodic geographic expansion into new administrative regions and some new countries. Continued use of capripox vaccines, improved surveillance and targeted control campaigns have helped limit spread in some regions, but sheep and goat pox remain among the most important transboundary small-ruminant diseases in Afro‑Eurasia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanding small-ruminant populations in low- and middle‑income countries; increased live animal trade and transboundary movement; low vaccination coverage and uneven veterinary infrastructure; socio-economic factors (e.g. conflict, poverty) reducing capacity for routine control; environmental conditions that facilitate congregation and long-distance movement of animals. Internal mechanisms: Predominantly geographic range expansion (inherent) of existing capripoxvirus lineages into new districts and some new countries; although genetic diversity exists, no single novel global lineage has been shown to drive this 18‑year pattern, so it is best described as repeated intra-continental emergence episodes rather than a discrete novel-genotype event.
Review: Review – Retained as a single high-level episode summarising major sheep and goat pox activity and geographic spread since 2005, but the event-type flags were adjusted: intra-continental emergence remains “Yes” to reflect spread into new subregions (e.g. Central Asia, Eastern Europe), while re-occurrence was set to “No” to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra- or inter-continental emergence. Country list still mixes historical first-detection years (e.g. Kazakhstan [1993]) with the 2005–2022 focus period and should be interpreted as indicative; consider refining these years in a future pass.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: India [2008–2009, especially Rajasthan (Barmer, Bikaner, Jaisalmer) and Delhi]
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius); humans (camel attendants and handlers)
Event summary: In 2008–2009 a major outbreak of camelpox occurred among dromedary camels in north‑western India (Rajasthan and Delhi), with widespread skin lesions and production losses in affected herds. During this episode, several camel attendants developed pox‑like lesions on their hands and fingers, and laboratory investigations confirmed camelpox virus infection, providing the first conclusive evidence of zoonotic transmission of camelpox to humans. Veterinary control measures, including isolation of sick camels, improved hygiene and, in some areas, vaccination, helped bring the outbreak under control, but camelpox remains endemic in camel-rearing regions of South Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of camels in arid pastoral systems with close daily contact between animals and handlers; seasonal stress and climatic fluctuations after the monsoon; limited prior vaccination and veterinary access in remote camel-rearing areas; animal movements for trade and cultural uses. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects re-emergence of endemic camelpox virus with documented Host Expansion (Spillover) to humans under close-contact conditions, rather than emergence of a clearly distinct viral strain; available molecular analyses show Indian isolates clustering with known CMLV lineages.
Review: Review – Retained as an important regional event and as the first confirmed zoonotic transmission of camelpox to humans, but event-type flags were modified: intra-continental emergence was set to “No” (the disease was already endemic in Southern/Western Asia), and re-emergence was set to “Yes” to reflect reappearance with new host range (humans).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Sheep; goats (Capra hircus, to a lesser extent)
Event summary: In 2010 Morocco experienced a notable epidemic of sheep pox (and associated sheep and goat pox) that represented a major resurgence of capripoxvirus disease in North Africa. The outbreak began in Moroccan sheep flocks with rapid spread in affected regions, causing high morbidity, notable mortality in lambs, and serious trade disruptions for small ruminants and their products. Aggressive control measures including movement bans, culling and vaccination gradually controlled the epidemic over the following years, although sheep and goat pox remained endemic or recurrent in many African and Asian countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large populations of susceptible sheep with limited recent exposure; increased movements related to trade and religious festivals; possible underinvestment in routine vaccination and veterinary services; environmental conditions favouring animal congregation and mechanical transmission. Internal mechanisms: This epidemic is primarily a re-occurrence of endemic sheep/goat pox viruses rather than emergence of a clearly novel genotype; molecular studies show close relatedness between field and vaccine strains despite the unusual nodular clinical form.
Review: Review – Event is real and regionally important, but intra-continental emergence was incorrectly flagged in the original version. Because sheep and goat pox were already long endemic in Northern Africa, the event is best classified as a re-occurrence; intra-continental emergence has been set to “No”.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Israel [2012]; Lebanon [2013]; Jordan [2013]; Türkiye [2013–2014]; Iraq [2014]; other Middle Eastern countries with reported outbreaks
Host: Cattle; occasional water buffalo
Event summary: After initial transcontinental introduction of lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) from Africa into Israel in the late 1980s, the disease re‑emerged strongly from 2012, with outbreaks in Israel and neighbouring Middle Eastern countries indicating sustained establishment in western Asia. From 2013 to 2015 the disease spread widely through Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq and adjacent states, causing substantial cattle production losses and prompting emergency vaccination and movement restrictions. By around 2015 improved vaccination coverage and surveillance began to reduce the frequency of large epidemics in some western Asian countries, although the virus persisted endemically and served as a source for onward spread into Europe and further into Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross‑border trade and informal movement of cattle from endemic African and Middle Eastern regions; favourable climate for vector-borne transmission in irrigated and coastal areas; gaps in vaccination programmes and veterinary infrastructure; regional conflicts and displacement complicating animal health services. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV within Western Asia from earlier foci in Israel and Egypt, followed by establishment in local vector–host systems; no specific novel genotype has been consistently linked to this regional wave, so changes are best characterised as range expansion and re-occurrence rather than major viral innovation.
Review: Review – Retained as a major re-emergence and expansion of LSDV within Western Asia, but intra-continental emergence has been set to “No” because the spread was within the existing Western Asia sub-region rather than into a new sub-region. Country name “Turkey” was standardised to “Türkiye” to match the Country sheet.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Greece [2015–2017]; Bulgaria [2016]; North Macedonia [2016–2017]; Serbia [2016]; Albania [2016–2017]; Montenegro [2016]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbreds); water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event summary: In August 2015 lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) was confirmed for the first time in the European Union in cattle herds in Evros, northern Greece, following progressive northward spread from endemic foci in Africa and the Middle East. During 2016 the disease spread rapidly across the Balkans, affecting Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia, Albania and Montenegro and causing thousands of outbreaks, production losses and extensive trade restrictions. Mass vaccination campaigns using live homologous capripox vaccines and movement controls from 2015–2017 progressively contained the disease, and by 2018 the Balkans were considered free of active LSDV transmission although the virus remained endemic in parts of Africa and Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of live cattle trade and informal animal movements between Türkiye and neighbouring Balkan countries; abundant blood-feeding arthropod vectors (biting flies, mosquitoes) favoured by warm, wet summers; limited prior immunity in Balkan cattle populations; initial gaps in vaccine supply and rollout; high-density dairy and beef systems facilitating spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV from Africa–Middle East into the European continent; available genomic data indicate that the viruses in south‑eastern Europe were closely related to Middle Eastern field strains without major adaptive change.
Review: Review – This event has been refocused to the 2015–2017 Balkan and EU epidemic only (first occurrence of LSD in Europe), with Israel and Türkiye now covered under the Western Asia event. The year span was corrected from “2012–2016” to “2015–2017”, continent simplified to “Europe”, and inter-continental emergence is retained as “Yes” because this represents the first establishment of LSDV on the European continent. Kosovo*, while epidemiologically affected, is not listed as a separate country because it is absent from the provided Country sheet.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia
Host: Cattle; domestic water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event summary: From 2015 lumpy skin disease virus spread north and east from the Middle East and Türkiye into the Caucasus and the Russian Federation, with the first Russian outbreaks reported in 2015 and a major epidemic in 2016 that caused nearly two thousand recorded outbreaks and substantial cattle losses in southern regions. In 2016 LSDV was also confirmed in western Kazakhstan, marking the first occurrence of the disease in Central Asia, and in subsequent years the Russian epidemic front advanced along the border with Kazakhstan, with recurrent seasonal clusters through about 2020. Intensive vaccination campaigns using homologous and later recombinant vaccines, combined with movement controls and surveillance, progressively reduced outbreak numbers, though LSDV and recombinant vaccine-like strains have persisted locally in parts of Russia and neighbouring countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of cattle and vectors between endemic areas of Türkiye, the Caucasus and southern Russia; summer conditions favourable to blood-feeding insects; limited prior immunity in Russian and Kazakh cattle; delayed deployment and suboptimal coverage of homologous vaccines during early years; possible contribution of illegal or heterologous vaccines. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV into new subregions (Eastern Europe and Central Asia) accompanied by the emergence and maintenance of recombinant vaccine-like strains detected in Russia and Kazakhstan, consistent with re-emergence driven partly by viral genetic change.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the large and well-documented LSD epizootic in the Russian Federation and Kazakhstan (plus neighbouring Caucasus states), which is comparable in scale and impact to the Balkan and Asian LSD waves and should be among the top events for this EPP. Classified as intra-continental emergence (new subregions in Europe and Asia) and re-emergence (appearance and spread of recombinant vaccine-like strains); recommended for expert review of country list and exact end year.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Iberian hare (Lepus granatensis); European wild rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus, endemic host)
Event summary: In mid‑2018, after roughly six decades of endemic myxomatosis in European wild rabbits, a recombinant myxoma virus variant spilled over for the first time into Iberian hares in Spain, causing severe myxomatosis with high mortality. During 2018–2019 the disease spread rapidly across multiple Spanish regions and into Portugal, producing large estimated declines in local hare populations and major ecological and hunting impacts. Surveillance and evolving host–pathogen dynamics over 2019–2020 suggested some stabilisation as hare populations partially adjusted, but the new myxoma virus lineage has become established as a significant emerging pathogen of Iberian hares.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities and overlapping ranges of infected rabbits and susceptible hares; human-mediated landscape changes (agriculture, water management) that concentrate lagomorphs and insect vectors; climatic conditions favouring vector activity. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of a recombinant myxoma virus strain from rabbits to hares; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence involving recombination events; likely changes associated with Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity in the new hare host, as evidenced by high mortality; geographic range expansion within the Iberian Peninsula as the variant spread into new areas.
Review: Review – Retained as a major host-jump and wildlife-impact event, but (i) the sub-region list was corrected to “Southern Europe” only, since both Spain and Portugal fall under this sub-region in the Country sheet, and (ii) the “first_detection” flag was set to “No” because poxviruses in lagomorphs were long known; this event instead represents re-emergence with host expansion within the animal host system.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Southern Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Countries: Bangladesh [2019]; India [2019, 2022]; China [2019]; Nepal [2020]; Sri Lanka [2020]; Viet Nam [2020]; Myanmar [2020]; Thailand [2021]; Pakistan [2022]; Indonesia [2022]; Afghanistan [2022]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus and Bos indicus and crossbreds); domestic water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, some countries)
Event summary: In mid‑2019 lumpy skin disease was reported for the first time in Bangladesh, soon followed by outbreaks in eastern India and western China, marking a rapid eastward jump from earlier foci in the Middle East and western Asia. Between 2019 and 2021 the virus spread widely across South Asia and parts of South‑East Asia, becoming established in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Viet Nam, Myanmar, Thailand and other countries with growing cattle sectors. In 2022 particularly severe waves in India and Pakistan caused very high morbidity and large numbers of cattle deaths, before intensified vaccination, movement controls and farmer awareness campaigns began to reduce incidence, although the disease remains endemic across much of Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensifying regional trade and informal movement of live cattle and buffalo; increased vector abundance linked to monsoon-related rainfall and climate variability; low vaccination coverage and limited access to homologous LSD vaccines prior to 2021; rapid growth and intensification of dairy sectors in South Asia. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV into new climatic zones of South and South‑East Asia; genomic studies indicate that viruses from the 2019 and especially 2022 waves in India and Pakistan form distinct lineages compared with earlier African and Middle Eastern strains, suggesting Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and potentially altered virulence or transmission efficiency.
Review: Review – Kept as a single large Asian LSD emergence episode, but (i) Kazakhstan was removed from the country list because its first outbreak in 2016 belongs more naturally to the Russia/Central Asia wave, and (ii) re-occurrence was set to “No” to respect the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-continental emergence. Re-emergence remains “Yes” in light of evidence for distinct 2019 and 2022 viral lineages.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius); humans (camel attendants and handlers)
Event summary: In 2008–2009 a major outbreak of camelpox occurred among dromedary camels in north‑western India and in Delhi, with widespread skin lesions and production losses in affected camel herds. During this episode, several camel attendants developed pox‑like lesions on their hands and fingers, and laboratory investigations confirmed camelpox virus infection in humans as well as camels, providing the first conclusive evidence of zoonotic camelpox. Veterinary measures such as isolation of sick camels, improved hygiene and vaccination in selected herds helped bring the outbreak under control, but camelpox remains endemic in camel-rearing regions of South Asia and the wider Middle East.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High camel densities in pastoral and paramilitary herds with close human–animal contact; seasonal stress after the monsoon; historically low vaccine coverage and limited veterinary services in remote camel-rearing areas; transhumant and trade-related animal movements. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of endemic camelpox virus with demonstrated Host Expansion to humans, rather than emergence of a genetically novel virus; molecular analyses show Indian human and camel isolates clustering with existing CMLV strains.
Review: Review – This camelpox event is regionally important and documents first confirmed zoonotic transmission, but the original classification (intra-continental emergence plus re-occurrence) conflicted with the scheme. It has been reclassified as re-emergence only (no intra-continental emergence or re-occurrence) because the disease was already endemic in Southern/Western Asia and the key novelty was expanded host range.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Kenya [1990]; South Africa [1990]; Namibia [1990]
Host: African lions (Panthera leo) – free-ranging populations in Serengeti ecosystem (Tanzania/Kenya) and in Kruger and Etosha National Parks (South Africa, Namibia)([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/))
Event summary: From the late 1980s into the 1990s, serosurveys of free-ranging African lions in East Africa (Serengeti ecosystem) and Southern Africa (Kruger and Etosha National Parks) revealed very high prevalences (often >70–90%) of antibodies and lentiviruses closely related to FIV, indicating that lion-specific FIV-like viruses (FIVple) were endemic across multiple lion populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, follow-up epidemiologic and molecular studies confirmed widespread infection and multiple divergent FIVple subtypes, documenting natural history and patterns of multiple infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC371036/)) The episode continued as an essentially stable, enzootic infection without clear mass die-offs, but raised conservation concerns regarding potential long‑term health impacts and risks of moving infected lions into naïve populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8877134/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-standing, high-density lion populations with frequent aggressive contact (fighting, biting) that facilitate efficient lentiviral transmission; translocation and management of lions between reserves with limited prior virological screening, raising concern over virus introduction into naïve populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8877134/)) Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and long-term adaptation of FIV-like lentiviruses to lions, yielding lion-specific FIVple strains; novel strain/genotype emergence (multiple distinct FIVple subtypes and co-infections in individual lions), and possible increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to domestic cat FIV, as suggested by immunopathologic changes in some lion populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/))
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected emergence classification: SIV/FIV were already known in African primates and domestic cats before FIVple was characterized in lions, so this episode is not the first detection of the EPP in the animal host system nor clearly an intra-continental emergence into a new African sub-region. Instead it represents recognition of a long-established, host-adapted FIV lineage and associated novel clades in lions. I therefore set first_detection=No and intra_continental_emergence=No, and kept re_emergence=Yes to capture host expansion/novel genotype emergence. Geography, timing and sources remain appropriate but the row should be reviewed as part of a linked long-term enzootic rather than a short outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Countries: Australia [1990]; New Zealand [1995] (FIV recognized in domestic cats in both countries, with detailed data from eastern Australia)([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/))
Host: Domestic cats (Felis catus) – pet, stray, and feral populations in eastern Australia and later New Zealand([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/))
Event summary: In the early 1990s, retrospective testing and prospective serosurveys in eastern Australia demonstrated that FIV had been present in domestic cats since at least the 1970s and had become widely established by the 1990s, with reported seroprevalence ranging from about 4% to over 30% in some populations of adult cats.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) Through the mid‑1990s, additional surveys in Australia and subsequently New Zealand documented FIV across pet, stray and feral cat populations, confirming that the virus was firmly endemic in Oceania and associated with outdoor access and fighting behavior.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) By the late 1990s, FIV was recognized as a major chronic infection of cats in the region and became an important consideration for vaccination, testing policies and cat population management.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth of outdoor and feral cat populations, high densities in urban and peri‑urban areas, and frequent bite-related contact promoted efficient horizontal transmission; limited early awareness and absence of control programs enabled silent spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) Internal mechanisms: FIV exhibits relatively low virulence and chronic infection with prolonged asymptomatic carriage, facilitating long-term survival and onward transmission; genetic subtypes (notably subtype A in Australia) demonstrate geographic structuring but no evidence of sudden virulence shifts during this emergence period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/))
Review: Decision: retain. FIV-Fca was first isolated in California in 1986, so this episode is not the global first detection of the EPP but rather its establishment in a new continent. I therefore set first_detection=No and retained inter_continental_emergence=Yes to reflect the spread and endemic establishment of FIV in domestic cats in Oceania. Timing (early–mid 1990s) and geography (Australia and New Zealand) are consistent with published seroprevalence and molecular data, though the exact start year is approximate and should be treated as such.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Domestic cats (Felis catus) – companion and clinic-presenting cats in Japan([cir.nii.ac.jp](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1361981468536525184))
