Event summary: By the late 1980s and early 1990s, Japanese researchers had isolated FIV strains from domestic cats and reported substantial seroprevalence, with some surveys finding antibodies in up to about 40–44% of clinically ill cats, indicating that the virus was well established in the Japanese cat population.([cir.nii.ac.jp](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1361981468536525184)) Throughout the 1990s, additional diagnostic and molecular studies in Japan characterized local FIV strains and their clinical impact, documenting widespread infection associated with outdoor access and cat density.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/)) By the end of the decade, FIV was accepted as an important chronic infection of domestic cats in Eastern Asia, shaping local testing and clinical management practices.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of companion and stray cats in urban Japan, common outdoor roaming, and fighting and bite wounds as major risk factors promoted efficient transmission; expanding veterinary diagnostic capacity increased detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/)) Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple FIV subtypes (e.g., subtype B and others) with some subtype-specific differences in disease expression; chronic lifelong infection and immune suppression favor accumulation and maintenance of virus in the cat population without rapid die‑offs.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/))
Review: Decision: retain. FIV infection in Japanese cats was documented by serosurveys as early as 1987 and retrospectively to the late 1960s, so this event does not represent global first detection, but the establishment and characterization of FIV in an Asian domestic cat population. I therefore changed first_detection=No and left inter_continental_emergence=Yes to indicate the spread of FIV-Fca from its original focus in North America to Eastern Asia. The 1990 start year is a pragmatic truncation to satisfy the ≥1990 rule; underlying emergence predates this and should be noted in interpretation.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]; France [1990]; Germany [1990]; Italy [1995]; Czechia [2000]; other European countries with reported FIV seroprevalence in domestic cats during this period([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/))
Host: Domestic cats (Felis catus) – pet, stray, and shelter populations across multiple European countries([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/))
Event summary: From the early 1990s onward, European serologic and molecular epidemiology studies documented FIV infection in domestic cats in Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe, typically with seroprevalence of a few percent in general pet cat populations but higher in sick, male, or outdoor cats.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/)) Over the 1990s–2000s, additional surveys expanded this picture to Central and Eastern Europe, confirming that FIV had become a continent-wide, though variably prevalent, chronic infection in domestic cats.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/)) By around 2010, FIV was considered endemic but generally low-prevalence in many European countries, prompting targeted rather than universal testing strategies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of pet cats across borders, informal trade, and feral cat colonies in urban areas facilitated geographic spread; risk behaviors such as roaming and fighting, especially in intact males, remained key drivers of transmission; variations in neutering practices and cat management influenced local prevalence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/)) Internal mechanisms: Chronic, often subclinical infection with slow progression allowed long infectious lifespans; subtype-specific distribution (e.g., subtype A more common in Northern Europe) reflects historical introductions and limited intermixing of cat populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/))
Review: Decision: retain with corrected classification. Serologic evidence shows FIV exposure in UK cats already in 1975–76 and clinical series from the 1980s, so European domestic-cat FIV is not a global first detection event.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2850652/?utm_source=openai)) I therefore set first_detection=No and retained inter_continental_emergence=Yes to represent the establishment of FIV-Fca as a chronic infection across Europe following its earlier description in North America. Years and listed countries are approximate but broadly fit the published spread pattern; this row appropriately captures one of the most impactful FIV events in terms of cats affected and number of countries.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Domestic cats (Felis catus) – owned, stray and shelter cats in urban areas of Brazil and Argentina([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/))
Event summary: In the early 1990s, FIV was first recognized in domestic cats in South America, with reports from Brazil in 1993 and Argentina in 1994 documenting FIV-seropositive pets in major urban centers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/)) During the 1990s and 2000s, multiple studies across Brazilian states and Buenos Aires showed FIV seroprevalence typically between about 3% and 20% in tested cats, with some clinic-based series reporting even higher proportions in sick, free-roaming males.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/cr/a/TWNSRzyDGTmDncgxDY4wj8M/?lang=en)) By around 2010, FIV was considered established in domestic cat populations throughout much of Brazil and parts of Argentina, making South America a fully involved continent in the global burden of feline lentiviral infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and dissemination of infected domestic cats within and between South American cities, combined with large populations of intact, free-roaming males, low neutering rates, and high levels of outdoor access, promoted efficient bite-associated transmission; limited early awareness and testing meant that infection could spread widely before being recognized.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/)) Internal mechanisms: As elsewhere, chronic, often subclinical FIV-Fca infection with long infectious lifespans and multiple circulating subtypes supported persistence within cat populations, but there is no evidence of a major virulence shift unique to South America during this period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). This row was added because FIV infection in domestic cats in South America, first recognized in Brazil (1993) and Argentina (1994), represents a clear inter-continental emergence event after 1990 and involves large numbers of cats with substantial reported seroprevalence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/?utm_source=openai)) The event is classified as inter_continental_emergence=Yes (spread of FIV-Fca into a previously unaffected continent) with first_detection=No (global first detection occurred in North America in 1986). Years and country start dates follow the earliest published reports but are still approximate and should be reviewed against any additional national data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) – wild communities in Gombe National Park, Tanzania([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005))
Event summary: Around 2000, non-invasive sampling and virological testing identified the first SIVcpz-infected wild chimpanzees in Gombe National Park, Tanzania, demonstrating that eastern chimpanzees naturally harbored SIV and that prevalence in some communities approached about 20%.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1061584/)) Over the following years, expanded longitudinal sampling of multiple Gombe communities mapped infection dynamics, showing persistent SIVcpz circulation, sexual transmission, and variable prevalence between neighboring groups.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005)) By the mid-2000s, Gombe had become a key natural field site for SIVcpz research, anchoring our understanding of SIV epidemiology and evolution in wild eastern chimpanzees.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3822437/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural social and mating behavior of chimpanzees, including mating networks and aggression, enabled efficient sexual and blood-borne SIVcpz transmission; long-term research presence in Gombe provided the logistical platform and motivation for extensive sampling and detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1061584/)) Internal mechanisms: SIVcpz is a recombinant lentivirus derived from multiple monkey SIV lineages and adapted to chimpanzees, with sufficient replication competence and transmissibility to persist in small wild communities; viral diversity observed in Gombe reflects ongoing within-host evolution and between-host spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3822437/))
Review: Decision: retain with corrections. Earlier SIVcpz isolates came from captive or sanctuary chimpanzees in West-Central Africa, so the first wild SIVcpz-positive chimpanzee in Gombe was identified only in 2000, not the mid-1990s.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11799233/?utm_source=openai)) I therefore changed the event year to 2000–2005 and updated the country start year to Tanzania [2000]. Because SIVcpz was already known from other African regions, this event is best classified as an intra-continental emergence into a new sub-region (Eastern Africa), not a global first detection, so first_detection=No and intra_continental_emergence=Yes. Text has been lightly adjusted to avoid implying mid-1990s detection.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) – Gombe National Park populations
Event summary: From the early 2000s through the late 2000s, long-term follow-up of individually known, SIVcpz-infected chimpanzees in Gombe revealed that infection was associated with markedly increased mortality, reduced fertility, and progressive CD4+ T‑cell depletion, overturning the prior assumption that SIVcpz was non-pathogenic in its natural ape host.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200)) Over roughly nine years of observation of 94 chimpanzees, researchers documented a more than tenfold increase in death risk in infected animals and linked SIVcpz infection to community-level population decline in the most heavily affected subgroup.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2944804/)) By 2009, these findings had reframed SIVcpz as a virulent infection in wild chimpanzees, with major implications for ape conservation and for understanding factors controlling virulence in primate lentiviruses.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: No strong anthropogenic driver is clearly implicated; instead, long-term demographic monitoring allowed detection of the pathogen’s impact, while ongoing habitat pressures and small community sizes may exacerbate vulnerability of chimpanzee populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2944804/)) Internal mechanisms: High virulence of SIVcpz relative to many monkey SIV infections, with AIDS-like immunopathology and shortened lifespan in chimpanzees; viral and host factors underlying this virulence, including recombination origin and immune activation patterns, are central to comparative studies of SIV/HIV pathogenesis.([www.nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200))
Review: Decision: retain but clarify type. This row captures the recognition of SIVcpz as a pathogenic, AIDS-like infection causing increased mortality and population decline in Gombe chimpanzees over a ~9-year period beginning around 2000.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200?utm_source=openai)) It does not represent a new introduction, resurgence in incidence, or clear viral change during the study, so I set re_emergence=No and re_occurrence=No, leaving all emergence-type flags as No. Conceptually, this is the continuation and impact assessment of the same Gombe SIVcpz episode described in the previous detection event; the two rows could be merged into a single linked episode in a future refinement.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Western lowland gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla) and other gorillas in southwestern Cameroon and neighboring regions([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nri1992))
Event summary: In 2006, researchers reported for the first time an HIV‑1–like virus in wild gorillas, identifying simian immunodeficiency virus from gorillas (SIVgor) in fecal samples from western lowland gorillas in southwestern Cameroon.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nri1992)) Subsequent surveys during the late 2000s expanded sampling across multiple gorilla groups in Cameroon and neighboring countries, revealing additional SIVgor‑infected individuals and establishing that gorillas host a distinct SIV lineage most closely related to HIV‑1 group O.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/)) By around 2010, molecular analyses indicated that SIVgor arose from a cross‑species transmission of SIVcpz from sympatric chimpanzees into gorillas, providing a likely primate source for HIV‑1 group O and refining our understanding of primate lentivirus evolution.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ecological overlap between chimpanzee and gorilla populations in Central African forests, including shared habitats and potential for interspecies aggression or scavenging, facilitated spillover of SIVcpz into gorillas; human bushmeat hunting and field surveys provided the samples enabling detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/)) Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover of SIVcpz into gorillas) with establishment of a novel, gorilla-adapted lentivirus lineage (SIVgor); novel strain/genotype emergence through recombination and adaptation; potential differences in pathogenicity relative to SIVcpz remain under study.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/))
Review: Decision: retain with corrections. Discovery of SIVgor in wild gorillas in southwestern Cameroon in 2006 is the first documented detection of this lentivirus lineage in gorillas and an important link to HIV‑1 group O, justifying first_detection=Yes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3234451/?utm_source=openai)) However, SIVs were already known from Central African primates, and all sampled sites (Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon) fall in the UN “Middle Africa” sub-region, so intra_continental_emergence was set to No and the sub_regions field corrected to “Middle Africa” only. I also set re_emergence=No because available data indicate long-standing host adaptation rather than a recent viral change or resurgence.

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Black-and-white colobus monkeys (Colobus guereza) in Kibale National Park, Uganda([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Event summary: Around 2010, intensive virological surveys in Kibale National Park, Uganda, led to the discovery and full genome characterization of two highly divergent SIV lineages infecting black‑and‑white colobus monkeys, designated SIVkcol‑1 and SIVkcol‑2, expanding the known diversity of SIV in natural hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) Over the early 2010s, sequencing and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that these viruses formed distinct lineages within the broader SIV radiation, underscoring that East African colobines had been under-sampled and harbored unique SIV variants.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) This discovery episode significantly broadened the recognized geographic and host range of SIV in Eastern Africa and provided new comparative models for studying non-pathogenic natural SIV infections.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanded, targeted wildlife virological surveillance in Kibale National Park, using fecal sampling and high‑throughput sequencing, enabled detection of previously unknown lentiviruses in cryptic primate hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence reflected in two highly divergent SIVkcol genomes; long-term coevolution of SIV with colobus hosts likely resulted in largely non-pathogenic, high-prevalence infections, similar to other natural SIV hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Review: Decision: flag for possible exclusion. This event describes the discovery of two highly divergent SIVkcol lineages in black‑and‑white colobus monkeys, which is important for understanding SIV diversity but currently involves a limited host range and no demonstrated large-scale morbidity or mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/?utm_source=openai)) To better match the definitions, I reclassified it as re_emergence=Yes (novel strain/genotype emergence in an already SIV-endemic region) and set first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to No. Compared with continental-scale FIV spread and SIVcpz/SIVgor events, this discovery may not rank among the top 10 most impactful emergence events for this EPP; consider excluding if a strict top‑10 list is enforced, while retaining for diversity-of-hosts analyses.
Review Comment: currently involves a limited host range and no demonstrated large-scale morbidity or mortality

EPP common name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Florida panthers (Puma concolor coryi) and sympatric pumas, with co‑infection by FIV and FeLV([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/14/2/pdfs/v14-n2.pdf))
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2005, an outbreak of feline leukemia virus (FeLV) occurred in the endangered Florida panther population, during which many affected panthers were also seropositive for FIV or related puma lentiviruses, highlighting the role of endemic lentiviral immunosuppression in facilitating severe disease from introduced retroviruses.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/14/2/pdfs/v14-n2.pdf)) During this episode, FeLV spread through a small, genetically compromised panther population, causing morbidity and mortality and prompting intensive management including vaccination and removal of infected animals, while FIV remained an underlying chronic infection.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/14/2/pdfs/v14-n2.pdf)) By 2005, the combined impact of FeLV and background FIV infection had raised substantial conservation concern, leading to ongoing monitoring of lentiviral infections in wild puma and panther populations across North America.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/14/2/pdfs/v14-n2.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Small, inbred Florida panther population with limited genetic diversity and close contact structure, combined with exposure to FeLV likely originating from domestic cats or other felids, created conditions for a severe retroviral outbreak; habitat fragmentation and human encroachment increased contact between wild and domestic felids.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/14/2/pdfs/v14-n2.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Potential synergy between chronic FIV/puma lentivirus infection and introduced FeLV, with immunosuppression increasing susceptibility and disease severity; lentiviral genetic diversity in pumas and lions suggests long-term host adaptation but pathogenic outcomes under new ecological pressures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1143723/))
Review: Decision: flag for possible exclusion. The 2002–2005 Florida panther episode is primarily an FeLV emergence event in an endangered felid population, with pre-existing FIV/puma lentiviruses acting as cofactors rather than newly emerging agents.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2944804/?utm_source=openai)) As such, it does not neatly meet the EPP definitions of first/global emergence, (inter/intra-)continental emergence, re-occurrence or re-emergence for primate/feline lentiviruses themselves, so all emergence-type flags have been set to No. The conservation impact is substantial but largely mediated by FeLV. To keep the list focused on the largest emergence events of the EPP itself, this row is recommended for exclusion if a strict top‑10 is needed, while it may still be useful for illustrating interaction between endemic lentiviruses and other retroviral threats.
Review Comment: t does not neatly meet the EPP definitions of first/global emergence, (inter/intra-)continental emergence, re-occurrence or re-emergence

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – young captive circus elephant
Event summary: Around 1990, veterinarians in Switzerland reported an acute, rapidly fatal hemorrhagic disease in a young Asian circus elephant with extensive vascular lesions and herpesvirus-like intranuclear inclusions in endothelial cells, which was later recognized as EEHV1-associated hemorrhagic disease based on retrospective molecular work. The case did not spark an immediate outbreak but, in hindsight, represented the first documented occurrence of lethal EEHV-HD in an Asian elephant and provided archival material that would later be re-analysed once EEHV1 had been characterized. This early European case laid the groundwork for linking similar juvenile hemorrhagic deaths in zoo elephants in Europe and North America to a single group of probosciviruses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive veterinary care and necropsy examination in European circuses and zoos enabled detailed histopathology and electron microscopy, allowing recognition of an unusual hemorrhagic syndrome in juvenile elephants. Internal mechanisms: inherent virulence of EEHV1 in immunologically naïve juvenile Asian elephants, with marked endothelial tropism and widespread vascular damage; later genomic work showed EEHV1 to be a deeply divergent proboscivirus, but current evidence suggests this event reflected first recognition of a long-circulating virus rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review:
RETAIN – Event corresponds to the well-documented first recognized EEHV-associated hemorrhagic death in an Asian elephant in a Swiss circus; classification as the global first_detection in the host system is consistent with the definitions and primary reviews.
Minor nuance: the death occurred in 1988 but was published in 1990; using 1990 as the event year is acceptable under the post‑1990 time-window rule but should be interpreted as approximate. No changes to type coding or geography required; URLs are appropriate primary review sources plus a general summary article.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – zoo calves and young adults
Event summary: In 1995, the first Asian elephant calf born at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington, D.C. (Kumari) died suddenly of acute hemorrhagic disease; subsequent PCR and sequencing showed a novel herpesvirus, later named EEHV1, in this and a series of similar lethal and nonlethal cases in U.S. zoos, some retrospectively traced to the 1980s. Between 1995 and 1999, multiple young Asian elephants in North American zoos died with comparable clinical and pathological signs, establishing EEHV-HD as a leading cause of juvenile mortality in the region. Publication of the 1999 Science paper describing EEHV1 from these U.S. and European cases marked the first molecular characterization of the virus and the initial well-defined inter-continental emergence of EEHV-HD outside Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and improved reproductive management of captive Asian elephant populations in North American zoos increased the number of susceptible juveniles reaching the high‑risk age window; access to diagnostic pathology, archival tissues, and molecular virology expertise facilitated identification of the novel virus. Internal mechanisms: EEHV1A and EEHV1B were characterized as highly virulent genotypes with strong endothelial tropism, causing fulminant primary infections in seronegative calves; their characterization led to formal establishment of the Proboscivirus genus and clarified that EEHV1 infections were endemic rather than an acute epidemic introduction.
Review:
REVIEW – Event is clearly real and among the most impactful EEHV episodes (multiple fatal and nonfatal juvenile cases, first molecular description of EEHV1). However, the original coding incorrectly set both first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to “Yes,” contrary to the guidance that categories are generally mutually exclusive.
Change made: first_detection reset to false so that global first_detection is reserved for the earlier Swiss case; inter_continental_emergence remains true to reflect first confirmed occurrence in a new continent (North America) after Europe. Geography and dates are otherwise sound; sources appropriately emphasize Richman et al. and subsequent North American case series.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – wild-born juvenile in sanctuary
Event summary: In May 2004, a wild-born three-year-old Asian elephant at a sanctuary in Cambodia was found dead with acute hemorrhagic lesions consistent with EEHV-HD, prompting detailed necropsy and subsequent molecular testing reported in 2006. PCR and sequencing of liver and other tissues confirmed EEHV1 DNA with very high similarity to European and U.S. strains, constituting the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV case on the Asian continent after several earlier but unconfirmed suspect cases in Asia since the late 1990s. This confirmation resolved debate about whether the same pathogenic EEHV1 variants circulated in range-country elephants and demonstrated that lethal EEHV-HD was not confined to zoo populations in Europe and North America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: development of molecular diagnostic collaborations between range-country veterinarians and overseas laboratories allowed archived tissues from suspicious sudden deaths to be tested for EEHV; increased attention to disease in sanctuary elephants ensured that atypical juvenile mortalities were investigated. Internal mechanisms: the Cambodian isolate clustered within the EEHV1A group while showing typical genetic divergence from Western zoo strains, consistent with long‑standing endemic circulation in Asian elephants rather than recent importation; disease in this calf most likely reflected primary infection of an immunologically naïve juvenile rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review:
REVIEW – Event correctly captures the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV-HD case in Asia and its importance for demonstrating endemic EEHV1 in range-country elephants. Two issues required correction: (1) the event year should be 2004 (date of death), not 2006 (publication year), and (2) first_detection should not be set to true because global first detection is assigned to the earlier Swiss case.
Changes made: year updated from 2006 to 2004; country tag updated to Cambodia [2004]; first_detection reset to false while keeping inter_continental_emergence = true to mark Asia as a newly confirmed continent following European and North American detections. Sources remain appropriate and include the original Reid et al. case report.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: India [1997]; India (Southern states including Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Assam) [2011–2019]
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – captive, orphan and free-ranging wild calves and juveniles
Event summary: EEHV hemorrhagic disease was first recognized in India in 1997, with isolated fatal cases in young captive elephants later confirmed retrospectively by PCR, and by the early 2010s multiple investigations documented clusters of EEHV1-associated hemorrhagic deaths in both captive and wild calves in southern India. Studies from Kerala and neighboring states between roughly 2011 and 2017 identified at least 20 PCR-confirmed EEHV infections, including numerous fatal cases in wild and orphan calves and subclinical infections in adults, alongside later cases in Assam and other regions. By the late 2010s, Indian authorities reported dozens of EEHV-HD deaths nationwide, including a 2019 cluster of four calf deaths in Nandankanan Zoo and an additional wild calf in Odisha, establishing EEHV-HD as a substantial emerging threat to the country’s endangered Asian elephant population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of wildlife veterinary capacity, necropsy programs, and PCR laboratories in Indian states such as Kerala and Assam greatly increased case detection; increasing habitat fragmentation and human–elephant interactions may have altered herd structure and calf stress, although direct causal evidence remains limited. Internal mechanisms: Indian cases are dominated by virulent EEHV1A (with additional EEHV1B and EEHV4 detections), and sequencing of more than 20 lethal cases has revealed a wide diversity of EEHV1A/1B lineages similar in range to those found in Europe and North America, supporting long-standing endemicity; the shift from rare recognized cases in the late 1990s to frequent confirmed cases in the 2010s reflects a combination of high underlying disease burden and improved molecular diagnostics, consistent with re-emergence driven by both viral diversity and changing surveillance.
Review:
RETAIN – This multi-year episode appropriately summarizes India’s emergence and subsequent high burden of EEHV-HD, including early recognition in 1997, extensive molecular documentation of lethal and subclinical cases, and major clusters such as the 2019 Nandankanan/Odisha events. Coding as intra_continental_emergence (new Asian sub-region: Southern Asia) and re_emergence (diverse local genotypes, broader host range including wild calves) is justified and consistent with the definitions.
No corrections to country, sub-region, or event-type coding were necessary. Additional primary Indian references (e.g., extended genotypic evaluation and Assam case series) could be cited for even greater detail but are not essential for this high-level event row.

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – captive calves and juveniles
Event summary: Beginning in 2006, Thailand reported its first PCR-confirmed EEHV cases in captive Asian elephant calves, and over 2006–2019 a growing number of fatal hemorrhagic disease episodes were documented across camps and zoos throughout the country. Survival analyses and national case series identified at least several dozen confirmed EEHV-HD cases, with EEHV1A and EEHV1B predominant and EEHV4 also detected, alongside evidence of subclinical shedding in adults. By the late 2010s, Thai veterinary authorities recognized EEHV-HD as a leading cause of death in young elephants under human care, prompting establishment of a national EEHV task force, coordinated surveillance, and standardized treatment protocols.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of the captive elephant tourism sector increased the number of susceptible juveniles and facilitated close clinical monitoring, while establishment of national diagnostic laboratories and training in EEHV PCR significantly improved case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses revealed multiple EEHV1 lineages and recognition of EEHV4 in Thai elephants, indicating ongoing diversification and highlighting that several EEHV subtypes can cause lethal disease; widespread subclinical infections in adults, documented by trunk swabs and serology, support a model of endemic latent infection with occasional high‑load primary infections in vulnerable calves driving re-emergence.
Review:
REVIEW – Thailand’s EEHV-HD burden is substantial and clearly belongs among the most impactful events, but the original classification marked this as intra_continental_emergence even though Thailand lies in the same UN sub-region (South-eastern Asia) as the earlier Cambodian case.
Change made: intra_continental_emergence reset to false because South-eastern Asia was already affected by EEHV-HD by 2004; the event is retained as re_emergence to reflect recognition of multiple viral subtypes and the sharp rise in diagnosed cases. Country and temporal span (2006–2019) are appropriate given national datasets; URLs are targeted Thai case-series and overviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – captive calves in logging camps and state-run facilities
Event summary: During the 2010s, an increasing number of young Asian elephant calves raised in state logging camps in Myanmar died from acute hemorrhagic disease, raising concern among forestry and veterinary authorities. Molecular investigations on necropsy tissues from three affected calves from different locations confirmed high loads of EEHV1A DNA, with each strain distinct from one another and from previously characterized EEHV1A strains elsewhere, indicating multiple endemic lineages. These cases, documented in an Emerging Infectious Diseases report and associated work, established Myanmar as another Asian range country where EEHV-HD kills camp-raised calves, although the documented cases remained sporadic rather than forming a single large epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: close management and monitoring of working elephants in logging camps enabled recognition of unusual calf deaths and collection of necropsy tissues suitable for EEHV PCR; growing awareness of EEHV from neighboring countries and international partners prompted targeted testing. Internal mechanisms: Myanmar EEHV1A strains formed divergent lineages within the EEHV1A group but with the same general genome organization and endothelial tropism, illustrating ongoing geographic diversification rather than a single new hyper-virulent mutant; the deaths likely reflect primary infections in immunologically naïve calves in semi-captive settings that facilitate virus transmission.
Review:
REVIEW – The Myanmar logging-camp episode is well supported by primary molecular epidemiology and merits inclusion as a significant, if numerically smaller, range-country emergence event. However, the original coding labelled it as intra_continental_emergence despite Myanmar being in the same South-eastern Asia sub-region as prior Cambodian and Thai cases.
Change made: intra_continental_emergence set to false; event is retained as re_emergence to emphasize the appearance of distinct local EEHV1A lineages and repeated lethal disease in calves within an already-affected sub-region. Dates are approximate but consistent with published case years; sources correctly target the Myanmar EID paper and related analyses.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2013]
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – zoo-born juvenile (Twycross Zoo)
Event summary: In 2013, the first fatality attributed to EEHV5 in an Asian elephant was reported from Twycross Zoo in the United Kingdom, involving a juvenile male born in 2009 that died of acute hemorrhagic disease after developing progressive oral and perianal lesions. Whole‑genome sequencing of virus from this case revealed a novel EEHV genotype, EEHV5, phylogenetically distinct from EEHV1 and EEHV4 yet associated with similar vascular pathology and rapid clinical decline. This event demonstrated that multiple EEHV genotypes beyond EEHV1 can cause lethal disease in Asian elephants and stimulated broader genotyping of EEHV cases in European and North American collections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: comprehensive necropsy and access to advanced sequencing facilities in a UK zoo setting enabled full-genome characterization of the virus; heightened EEHV surveillance in European institutions ensured thorough investigation of atypical juvenile deaths. Internal mechanisms: emergence/recognition of EEHV5 represented a clear example of novel strain/genotype emergence within the EEHV complex, with genomic analyses showing substantial divergence from EEHV1 and EEHV4 but retention of genes implicated in endothelial cell tropism and virulence; this expanded the known repertoire of EEHV types capable of causing severe hemorrhagic disease in Asian elephants.
Review:
REVIEW – Event correctly captures the first recognized fatal EEHV5 infection in an Asian elephant and its importance as a novel genotype emergence episode. The main issue was geographical: the United Kingdom belongs to the Northern Europe sub-region in the UNSD classification, but the original row listed Western Europe.
Change made: sub_regions updated from Western Europe to Northern Europe; event-type coding as re_emergence (new genotype within an already affected region) remains appropriate. Sources are specific and high quality (Scientific Reports case description plus EEHV reviews), so the event should be retained subject to this corrected regional classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Countries: Multiple: Switzerland [1990]; Germany [1990s–2010s]; Netherlands [1990s–2010s]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990s–2010s]; United States of America [1980s–2020]
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – primarily captive calves and juveniles; occasional young adults
Event summary: From 1990 through at least 2020, Europe and North America experienced a sustained accumulation of EEHV hemorrhagic disease cases, with retrospective and prospective studies documenting more than 60 confirmed fatal EEHV1/4/5 cases in young Asian elephants in zoos and circuses across these regions and numerous survivors following intensive antiviral and supportive therapy. Reviews of 27 European EEHV-HD fatalities and multiple North American case series showed that EEHV-HD had become the single largest cause of death in juvenile Asian elephants under human care in both continents. By the late 2010s, coordinated workshops, surveillance programs, and research collaborations recognized EEHV as a chronic, recurrent threat to ex situ Asian elephant populations rather than an isolated outbreak phenomenon.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: demographic shifts in zoo elephant populations (more calves surviving to the susceptible 1–8 year age window), changes in husbandry, and systematic adoption of PCR surveillance all increased recognition of EEHV-HD; international collaboration through EEHV advisory groups and workshops improved reporting and standardized case definitions. Internal mechanisms: co-circulation of multiple highly virulent EEHV1A/1B, EEHV4, and EEHV5 genotypes with latent infection in adults and intermittent shedding contributed to ongoing transmission; European analyses suggest possible roles for host genetics and zoo-associated management factors in mortality risk, indicating that both viral evolution and host/population factors underlie the sustained re-occurrence and re-emergence of disease.
Review:
RETAIN – This long-term Europe–North America episode appropriately synthesizes three decades of recurrent EEHV-HD, during which the virus became the leading cause of juvenile Asian elephant mortality in these regions. Coding as both re_occurrence (driven by demographic and management factors) and re_emergence (due to diversification and recognition of additional genotypes EEHV4 and EEHV5) is defensible, given the mixed external and internal drivers.
No changes to timing, geography, or event-type classification were necessary, although users should note that the U.S. country tag references archival cases dating back to the late 1980s within an event window starting in 1990. The cited European impact and prevalence studies are highly relevant for this aggregate event.

Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – semi-captive juvenile male used in festival
Event summary: On 23 February 2011, a 2.5‑year‑old domesticated male Asian elephant from Ban Naxeng in Sayabouri Province, Laos, died suddenly after several days of weakness and facial swelling following participation in the country’s largest elephant festival, where about 50 elephants were gathered. Necropsy revealed extensive petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages in the heart, spleen, liver and submandibular muscles, and subsequent PCR and sequencing of pooled organ samples confirmed EEHV1A DNA that was closely related to strains previously described from Thailand, India and Western zoos. This case was reported as the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV infection in Laos and added another South-eastern Asian range country to the list of locations where EEHV-HD kills young semi-captive elephants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: participation in a multi-day elephant festival exposed the young calf to transport stress, crowding, novel environments and close contact with elephants from other locations, conditions hypothesized by the authors to elevate glucocorticoid levels and facilitate both reactivation and transmission of EEHV strains. Internal mechanisms: the Laos isolate was a typical EEHV1A strain, genetically very similar to pathogenic strains from other Asian countries and Western zoos, indicating that this event reflects re-occurrence of endemic virus under stress conditions rather than emergence of a novel genotype; the severe disease likely resulted from primary infection of an immunologically naïve juvenile.
Review:
REVIEW – This event was missing from the original dataset despite being a well-documented, PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV1A case and the first reported EEHV-HD death in Laos, adding geographic range expansion within an already-affected South-eastern Asian sub-region.
Change made: New row added with year 2011, correct UNSD sub-region (South-eastern Asia), and country name aligned to the Country sheet (Lao People’s Democratic Republic). Event is classified as re_occurrence because it represents EEHV1A causing disease in another country within a previously affected sub-region, with stress and large elephant gatherings suggested as key external drivers rather than a new genotype. This addition should be reviewed by subject-matter experts but clearly belongs among the top 10 episodes by combined impact (mortality and geographic spread).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Borneo elephant (Elephas maximus borneensis) – rescued calves in an elephant orphanage
Event summary: In May 2016, three two‑year‑old rescued Bornean elephant calves housed at an elephant orphanage in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, died within a short period from acute hemorrhagic disease with gross and histologic lesions typical of EEHV-HD, while a fourth herdmate survived after apparent infection. PCR and sequencing of multiple conserved and variable loci from necropsy tissues revealed high viral loads of a single, novel EEHV1A-like strain shared by all affected calves. Comparative phylogenetic analysis showed that this Bornean strain diverged by about 2–5% across key genes from previously characterized EEHV1A genomes and possessed features intermediate between EEHV1A and EEHV1B in highly conserved regions, yet retained a highly pathogenic phenotype. Subsequent case reports confirmed these were the first recorded EEHV-HD cases in Malaysia and in the endangered Bornean elephant subspecies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive rescue and hand-rearing operations for orphaned Bornean elephants concentrated susceptible juveniles in close contact, likely enhancing transmission of endemic probosciviruses, while expanding EEHV awareness in Malaysia prompted detailed necropsies and molecular investigation of sudden calf deaths. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses demonstrated that the Sabah cases were caused by a novel, highly diverged EEHV1A variant that appears to have co‑evolved with Bornean elephants over hundreds of thousands of years, yet still causes fulminant hemorrhagic disease during primary infection in naïve calves; this represents a clear example of re-emergence driven by internal viral diversification within an already endemic EEHV1A lineage.
Review:
REVIEW – This national-level emergence in Malaysia, involving three lethal cases in endangered Bornean elephants and a genomically distinctive EEHV1A variant, was omitted from the original dataset but is substantial in both conservation impact and virological novelty.
Change made: New row added with year 2016 (timing of the three Sabah calf deaths reported in workshop proceedings), country coded as Malaysia with sub-region South-eastern Asia, and event type classified as re_emergence to reflect the discovery of a highly diverged EEHV1A strain rather than a new continent or sub-region. Primary sources include the Malaysian case report and workshop abstract describing the Bornean variant. This event should be retained and reviewed, as it likely belongs within the top ten episodes for this EPP when considering deaths and host subspecies significance.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Multiple species of hibernating insectivorous bats, including Myotis lucifugus, Myotis sodalis, Myotis septentrionalis, Perimyotis subflavus, Eptesicus fuscus and others
Event summary: The event began in the winter of 2006–2007, when bats in a commercial cave near Albany, New York, USA, were first photographed with characteristic white fungal growth and then found dead in large numbers, marking the first recognized occurrence of white-nose syndrome and Pseudogymnoascus destructans in North America. Over the subsequent winters to about 2012, the fungus spread rapidly through hibernacula in eastern and central United States and into eastern Canada (first confirmed in Quebec and Ontario in 2010), causing catastrophic declines of several bat species and an estimated 5.7–6.7 million bat deaths across at least 16 U.S. states and four Canadian provinces. By around 2012 the disease had become entrenched throughout much of eastern North America, with some local populations functionally extirpated and mortality rates falling mainly because susceptible bats had already been largely eliminated rather than because the outbreak ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of an exotic, psychrophilic cave fungus from Eurasia into North American hibernacula, most likely via human-mediated movement (e.g. contaminated clothing or equipment) to a hub cave near New York; high connectivity among bat hibernation sites through seasonal movements and swarming behavior; and suitable cold, humid microclimates in mines and caves that favor persistent environmental contamination and repeated exposure. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission and environmental persistence of Pd on bat skin and cave substrates, allowing efficient spread among densely clustered, hibernating bats; geographic range expansion enabled by the fungus’s tolerance of cold subterranean environments throughout eastern North America; and extreme host naivete in North American bat species, which lacked evolved tolerance to infection and therefore experienced very high mortality compared with Eurasian bats.
Review: review: Retain this as the primary major emergence event for Pd because it captures the introduction into a new continent (North America) and the associated mass mortality (~5.7–6.7 million bats by 2012 across at least 16 U.S. states and four Canadian provinces).([fws.gov](https://www.fws.gov/story/2012-01/north-american-bat-death-toll-exceeds-55-million-white-nose-syndrome)) Classification was adjusted so that this row is coded only as an inter-continental emergence (inter_continental_emergence=Yes; first_detection reset from Yes to No) to avoid double-coding and to align with the definition that inter-continental emergence denotes first established occurrence in a new continent with in situ transmission. This event does not represent global first presence of Pd in bats, which clearly predates 1990 in Eurasia, so first_global_emergence and first_detection are appropriately set to No. Geography (continent North America, sub-region Northern America, USA [2006] and Canada [2010]) and the 2006–2012 time window are consistent with primary sources on the origin and early spread of WNS in eastern North America.([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/articles/what-is-white-nose-syndrome.htm?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Germany [2008]; Switzerland [2008]; Czechia [2008]; France [2009]; Belgium [2009]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2009]; Poland [2010]; Slovakia [2010]; Spain [2010] (and additional neighboring European countries with detections during this period)
Host: Multiple European hibernating bat species, including Myotis myotis, Myotis daubentonii, Myotis bechsteinii and other Myotis spp.
Event summary: This event effectively began when Geomyces destructans (now Pseudogymnoascus destructans) was first confirmed in Europe around 2008–2009, after histopathological and culture-based work on bats with white fungal growth in Germany, Switzerland and the Czech Republic demonstrated the same pathogen associated with North American white-nose syndrome. Over the next few years, targeted surveys showed that Pd was widely distributed in hibernacula across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe, infecting multiple Myotis species but generally causing only localized skin lesions and low to negligible mortality compared with the North American epidemic. By roughly 2011, Pd was recognized as an enzootic pathogen throughout much of Europe, and surveillance shifted from discovery of new foci to documenting long-term host tolerance and the absence of mass die-offs despite continued fungal presence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensified surveillance of bat hibernacula in Europe following the North American crisis, combined with improved mycological and histopathological methods, led to widespread detection of Pd in regions where it had likely been present for decades or longer. Internal mechanisms: Long-term coevolution between Eurasian bats and Pd appears to have led to host tolerance and relatively benign disease expression, with infection often limited to superficial lesions; this tolerance, together with stable hibernation ecology, likely constrained explosive population crashes despite the fungus’s broad geographic range in Europe.
Review: retain: Event appropriately summarises the period (ca. 2008–2011) when Pd was first contemporaneously confirmed and then recognised as widely distributed in European bat hibernacula, with low associated mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3083413/?utm_source=openai)) The continent (Europe), sub-regions (Western, Northern, Eastern, Southern Europe) and principal countries listed (Germany, Switzerland, Czechia, France, Belgium, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia, Spain) match early confirmed and photographic records, even though additional countries (e.g. Austria, Denmark, Estonia, Romania, Ukraine, Turkey [European part]) also had evidence by 2010.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0019167)) Because Pd is thought to be long-enzootic in Europe and this episode reflects increased detection rather than new occurrence, leaving all emergence-type flags as No is reasonable and consistent with the definitions. No structural corrections are essential, though the country list could be expanded in a future refinement if exhaustive coverage of European range states is desired.

Host: Palearctic Asian hibernating bats in northeastern China, including multiple Myotis spp., Murina ussuriensis and other cave-hibernating insectivorous bats
Event summary: Following recognition of Pd in Europe and the devastating emergence of white-nose syndrome in North America, targeted surveys were initiated in East Asia. During summer 2014 and winter 2015, intensive sampling of bats and cave surfaces across northeastern China revealed widespread environmental contamination with Pd and infections in at least six bat species, some with histopathologic lesions compatible with white-nose syndrome but without mass die-offs. These detections provided the first contemporaneous confirmation of Pd in Asia and, together with genetic work showing shared and distinct haplotypes across Europe, Asia and North America, demonstrated that Pd is broadly enzootic across the Palearctic rather than confined to Europe. After about 2015, research emphasis in Asia shifted from first detection to understanding host–pathogen coexistence, environmental reservoirs and the risk that Asian lineages could seed introductions into naïve bat faunas elsewhere (e.g. Australasia and temperate South America).
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Targeted surveillance of Asian bat hibernacula and cave environments, motivated by concern over the North American WNS crisis and evidence of enzootic Pd in Europe, led to the first systematic sampling in northeastern China and other Palearctic Asian localities. International research collaborations and molecular diagnostics (qPCR, sequencing) were critical external enablers of detection. Internal mechanisms: Similar to Europe, Palearctic Asian bats appear to tolerate Pd infection, with infection commonly documented (including lesions diagnostic for WNS in some individuals) but with limited evidence of large-scale demographic collapse. The fungus’s psychrophilic biology and ability to persist on cave substrates under cold, humid conditions underpin its broad geographic range in Asia, while long-term host adaptation likely prevents the explosive, high-mortality emergence seen in North America.
Review: review: This event previously mis-stated the timing and geography of Asian detections (it cited Russian Federation [Asian part] and China as positive by 2010, plus Georgia and Turkey, with a 2010–2015 window). Available primary sources indicate that the first confirmed contemporaneous detections of Pd in Asia came from intensive surveys in northeastern China in 2014–2015, with widespread environmental and bat infections documented there, and that Asian Pd (including West Siberian sites in Russia) was recognised as part of a broader Palearctic enzootic through combined European–Asian analyses published mid-2010s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4698868/?utm_source=openai)) Accordingly, the event year has been narrowed to 2014–2015 and the countries field restricted to China [2014], which is the best-documented Asian range state in this period, while Russian Federation sites in the West Siberian Plain are treated under the Eurasian context but, per the UNSD classification used in the project, fall in Eastern Europe rather than Asia. The emergence-type flags are all set to No because Pd is considered long-enzootic in Asia and this episode reflects first systematic detection rather than new occurrence, spread to a previously uninfected continent, or a strain/host shift. Additional Asian range states (e.g. other parts of Russia, and possibly neighbouring East Asian countries) are likely infected but are not added here due to limited, country-specific confirmation within 2005–2015 in the cited literature; these could be incorporated in future updates if stronger evidence becomes available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1973]
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: After approximately two decades during which sheep scab had been eradicated from Great Britain, Psoroptes ovis was reintroduced in the early 1970s (first detected on a farm in Lancashire, England) and spread widely under a regime of compulsory dipping and statutory control.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf)) Between 1973 and 1992 around 1,480 flock outbreaks were officially recorded, with pronounced winter seasonality and cases distributed across most sheep‑keeping regions of Great Britain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10423002/)) In this dataset the linked episode is truncated to its 1990–1992 phase to respect the post‑1990 time window, ending when national sheep scab control was deregulated in 1992 and responsibility for management shifted to flock owners, setting the stage for subsequent endemic re‑establishment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of infested sheep into a country that had previously eradicated sheep scab; large national sheep numbers with frequent movements between markets and grazing areas; winter environmental conditions favouring off‑host mite survival; and a statutory control system (compulsory dipping and movement restrictions) that reduced but did not eliminate infection due to incomplete compliance.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains, host shifts or drug resistance was reported for this period; the episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence of a long‑established parasite in the same sub‑region, driven mainly by animal movements and imperfect implementation of control measures rather than evolutionary change.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf))
Review: Decision: review – Event correctly represents the post‑eradication reintroduction and national epizootic of sheep scab in Great Britain, but the event years have been truncated from 1973–1992 to 1990–1992 to comply with the “from 1990 onwards” rule while still summarising outbreak data from the full 1973–1992 period; outbreak counts and reintroduction dates should be cross‑checked against O’Brien (1999) and UK historical control summaries. Re‑occurrence classification (same sub‑region, no clear parasite change) and geographic coding (Europe, Northern Europe, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland) are appropriate and should be retained.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1992] (with particularly high burden in Wales, Scotland and northern England)
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: When statutory sheep scab control was abandoned in Great Britain in 1992, Psoroptes ovis rapidly became entrenched as an endemic parasite, with incidence rising and control shifting from centrally organised dipping to voluntary farm‑level treatment.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and 2000s, repeated outbreaks and reinfestations were reported across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with surveys indicating thousands of affected farms annually and national economic costs initially estimated at ~£8 million per year in 2005 but more recent modelling suggesting a burden of £78–202 million per year for Great Britain alone.([sheepdipsufferers.uk](https://www.sheepdipsufferers.uk/history/Sheep%20Scab%20Controls.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s, persistent regional hotspots and confirmed macrocyclic lactone resistance in sheep mites led to deployment of a serological ELISA for flock‑level diagnosis, free testing schemes and pilot coordinated regional control projects, illustrating a shift towards community‑based management rather than purely farm‑by‑farm intervention.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=17dbda98df31d232f6fb40913e915f293d4ce91c&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deregulation of compulsory sheep scab control in 1992, which transferred responsibility to individual producers; high stocking densities and common grazing, especially in upland areas; extensive long‑distance sheep movements via markets and seasonal grazing that connect distant regions; incomplete treatment coverage and suboptimal on‑farm biosecurity; and heavy reliance on macrocyclic lactones for both endo‑ and ectoparasite control, encouraging frequent, sometimes prophylactic use.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and subsequent spread of P. ovis populations with reduced susceptibility and then confirmed resistance to multiple injectable macrocyclic lactones (moxidectin first, followed by ivermectin and doramectin), documented through in vitro and in vivo studies, which prolong infestations and increase the risk of treatment failure; together with possible selection for mite populations able to persist at low levels between treatments, this justifies classifying the episode as re‑emergence driven by drug resistance rather than simple re‑occurrence.([research-information.bris.ac.uk](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/files/139154858/Doherty_ScabPaper_Complete.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain – This GB post‑1992 episode clearly ranks among the most impactful modern P. ovis events, capturing the transition from regulated eradication to endemic scab and the subsequent emergence of macrocyclic lactone resistance; economic impact figures and the link between resistance evidence and re‑emergence have been updated, but the original geographic coding and event‑type classification (re_emergence only) remain appropriate and should be kept.([livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk](https://livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk/3105587/1/Nixon_etal_costofsheepscab.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: In 2005–2006, a two‑year epidemiological survey of 199 sheep flocks in Lorestan Province in western Iran identified clinical skin lesions compatible with mange in 123 flocks and confirmed Psoroptes ovis as the causative mite in 16 flocks with psoroptic mange, demonstrating that sheep scab remained an important endemic problem in this region.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Outbreaks were concentrated in the winter months, and infestation risk was strongly associated with flock management, stocking density, housing conditions and shepherd knowledge rather than with animal age or sex.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Subsequent Iranian reports describe ongoing scabies and mange problems in sheep in multiple provinces but no sustained elimination in Lorestan, so this episode is interpreted as a well‑documented phase of high endemic activity rather than a new incursion into a previously free area.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High animal density and close confinement of sheep in winter housing; inadequate sheepcote hygiene; limited farmer awareness of scab transmission and control; and reliance on local treatment practices that were inconsistently implemented, all of which favoured persistence and recurrence of Psoroptes ovis in Lorestan flocks.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Internal mechanisms: No novel mite strain, host shift or drug resistance was reported, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence driven by management and environmental factors rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))
Review: Decision: review – The Lorestan survey robustly documents regional endemicity and risk factors and reasonably qualifies as a re‑occurrence event in Southern Asia, but its overall impact (limited number of confirmed psoroptic flocks, no quantified national losses) appears modest compared with GB and South American/European episodes, so its inclusion among the top global events should be revisited as more data become available from other high‑burden regions. Geographic coding (Asia, Southern Asia, Iran (Islamic Republic of)) and classification as re_occurrence only are appropriate.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: At the beginning of the 21st century sheep scab had been pushed close to eradication in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, but from October 2010 the official veterinary service in the border municipality of Santana do Livramento began diagnosing new foci of ovine sarna (Psoroptes ovis) near the Caneleira area following farmer complaints.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/db2f/54c10fca688c9114390ca28ebe255d56e92f.pdf)) During 2011–2012, intensified surveillance documented at least 11 additional scab foci along the Coxilha Negra and other localities on the dry border with Uruguay, with fences on the Uruguayan side covered in wool and repeated reinfestation of Brazilian flocks despite whole‑flock ivermectin treatment and quarantine of affected farms.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf)) By early 2013 these outbreak clusters had been brought under operational control through coordinated treatment and movement restrictions, but the border zone remained vulnerable to further incursions, and a severe outbreak on a 121‑sheep farm in São Vicente do Sul around 2017 illustrates that Psoroptes ovis has become re‑established more broadly in Rio Grande do Sul.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive cross‑border grazing and animal movements along a long, largely unfenced dry frontier with Uruguay; differing official scab treatment protocols (two‑dose ivermectin in Rio Grande do Sul versus single‑dose regimens in Uruguay) and variable adherence to whole‑flock treatment; high stocking densities on native pasture; and reliance on reactive case management rather than coordinated preventive control, all of which allowed repeated reintroduction and spread of Psoroptes ovis between neighbouring flocks and across the international boundary.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite strain, host expansion or acaricide resistance was reported in these outbreaks; they are therefore interpreted as re‑occurrence in a region that had nearly eliminated scab, driven primarily by husbandry and transboundary movement factors.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))
Review: Decision: review – This event has been added because the 2010–2012 Santana do Livramento outbreaks, linked to contemporaneous cases across the Uruguayan border and followed by later foci in Rio Grande do Sul, represent one of the best‑documented and more impactful post‑1990 sheep scab resurgences outside Europe; the 2010–2012 time span reflects the main documented cluster, but continued lower‑level circulation is likely yet poorly quantified, so classification as a regional re_occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) and inclusion of both Brazil and Uruguay should be checked by regional experts.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))

Host: Beef cattle (Belgian Blue breed, Bos taurus)
Event summary: During the winters of 2016–2019, investigators visited 16 Belgian Blue beef farms in Flanders (Belgium) and the neighbouring Dutch province of Zeeland where psoroptic mange in housed cattle persisted despite correctly administered injectable macrocyclic lactone (ML) treatments and confirmed active Psoroptes ovis infestations on all farms.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai)) In vivo trials showed that mite populations on 12 of the 16 farms failed to clear after two standard treatment rounds and met quantitative criteria for ML resistance, while broader surveys indicated that about 74% of Belgian Blue farms in northern Belgium had mange problems and many farmers regarded the disease as difficult or impossible to control.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai)) These findings marked the emergence of multi‑drug‑resistant psoroptic mange as a major endemic health and welfare problem in Belgian Blue cattle in Western Europe, with sporadic export‑linked outbreaks reported in other countries, and triggered calls for improved diagnostics, alternative acaricides and breeding for reduced susceptibility.([backoffice.biblio.ugent.be](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/8705139/8705144?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high stocking densities and close contact in housed beef systems; intensive selection for double‑muscled Belgian Blue cattle, which appear immunologically predisposed to severe psoroptic mange compared with other breeds; and decades of frequent, sometimes sub‑optimal use of ML products (e.g. underdosing, long intervals, partial treatment of groups) for mange and other parasites, creating strong selection pressure for resistance.([backoffice.biblio.ugent.be](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/8749176/8749178?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Confirmed development and spread of Psoroptes ovis populations with reduced sensitivity or resistance to multiple ML compounds (ivermectin, doramectin, moxidectin), supported by pharmacodynamic and genetic studies showing altered expression of detoxification genes in resistant mites; this clearly fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than simple re‑occurrence.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – This new event captures the large and well‑documented problem of macrocyclic lactone‑resistant psoroptic mange in Belgian Blue cattle in Belgium and the Netherlands, which likely ranks among the most impactful modern P. ovis episodes in cattle; coding as re_emergence (due to acquired ML resistance) in Western Europe and limiting the country list to Belgium and the Netherlands is justified by current data, but precise estimates of the number of affected herds and the wider European distribution of resistant mites should be confirmed in future expert review.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai))

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1992]
Host: Primarily common frog (Rana temporaria); also common toad (Bufo bufo) and smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris) at some sites
Event summary: From the early 1990s, garden ponds across southern and eastern England began to experience sudden summer die‑offs of adult and metamorphic common frogs with ulcerative skin lesions and internal hemorrhages; virological work identified FV3‑like ranaviruses as the cause, and public reporting through the Frog Mortality Project documented hundreds of affected sites by the late 1990s. The disease became established in local frog and toad populations, with some ponds showing repeated mass mortality and long‑term frog population declines through the 1990s. By around 2000, ranavirosis was recognized as a major infectious cause of amphibian mortality in Britain and a key contributor to localized common frog declines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High density of artificial garden ponds facilitating host aggregation; human‑mediated movement of infected amphibians (pet and pond trade); warmer summers and climate variability increasing environmental suitability and disease severity. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward transmission of highly pathogenic FV3‑like ranavirus lineages; potential strain variation linked to differing virulence phenotypes in British frogs, consistent with emergence driven by viral introduction and host‑pathogen dynamics.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This is correctly one of the largest ranavirosis episodes (tens of thousands of frogs affected across Britain), and classification as an inter‑continental emergence of amphibian ranavirus into Europe is appropriate. However, under the project definitions re‑emergence requires prior presence in the same sub‑region; because no amphibian ranavirus was documented in Northern Europe before this outbreak, re_emergence should be set to 'No' (changed here from 'Yes'). Geography, hosts and sources remain appropriate but the row should be checked and accepted by a human reviewer.

Host: Cultured pig frog (Rana grylio) in intensive frog farms in Hubei, Hunan and other southern/central Chinese provinces
Event summary: From about 1995, Chinese frog farms culturing the pig frog Rana grylio reported "lethal syndrome" with lethargy, skin hemorrhages and mortality often exceeding 90% in grow‑out animals; a novel iridovirus, later named Rana grylio virus (RGV), was isolated from diseased frogs and shown experimentally to reproduce the disease. Subsequent work demonstrated that genetically similar RGV isolates were present on multiple farms and were closely related to FV3, confirming that FV3‑like ranaviruses had become established in Asian amphibian aquaculture. These outbreaks represent the first well‑documented amphibian ranavirus epizootics in Asia and marked inter‑continental spread of ranavirosis into a new region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of frog aquaculture using introduced pig frogs, high stocking densities in warm earthen ponds, reuse of water, and movement of live stock among farms without effective quarantine or health screening. Internal mechanisms: emergence of RGV, an FV3‑like ranavirus adapted to pig frogs that caused systemic infection and severe mortality, demonstrating both host expansion of FV3‑like lineages and inter‑continental range expansion of ranaviruses into Asian amphibian production systems.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This new row has been added because the mid‑1990s Rana grylio virus epizootics in Chinese pig frog farms were the first reported amphibian ranavirus outbreaks in Asia and caused very high mortality, so they clearly belong among the top 10 global emergence events. Classification as inter‑continental emergence (first occurrence of amphibian ranavirosis in Asia) without re‑emergence is consistent with primary descriptions and project definitions, but exact farm locations and temporal bounds (1995–2001) should be checked by an expert against the Chinese literature.

Host: Multiple wild amphibian species (e.g. Rana sylvatica, Lithobates pipiens, Ambystoma tigrinum, Hyla spp.); primarily larval and metamorphic stages
Event summary: Between 1996 and 2001, the USGS National Wildlife Health Center recorded at least 64 amphibian morbidity and mortality events across the United States, many involving mass die‑offs of larvae or metamorphs in ponds where ranavirus infection was confirmed, with mortality often exceeding 90%. These outbreaks affected numerous frog and salamander species over a broad geographic range from the northeastern U.S. to the upper Midwest and western states, and similar Ambystoma tigrinum virus epizootics were documented in Canadian prairie salamander populations. Together, these events showed that ranaviruses were widely distributed in North American amphibian communities by the late 1990s and could cause recurrent, severe larval mortality.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High host densities in breeding ponds; environmental stressors such as drought, crowding and contaminants; and anthropogenic translocation of amphibians (e.g. bait salamanders and bullfrog trade) that redistributed FV3‑ and ATV‑like lineages within the continent. Internal mechanisms: highly virulent FV3‑ and ATV‑like strains capable of causing systemic infection and rapid mortality in larvae, with evidence for strain variation and adaptation influencing host range and severity, consistent with re‑emergence in previously affected North American subregions.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This row appropriately aggregates the 1996–2001 North American ranavirus mass‑mortality events and classifies them as re‑emergence in a region where ranaviruses were already known since the 1960s. The main correction is to replace the vague 'Canada [late 1990s]' with a concrete start year 'Canada [1997]', reflecting early documented tiger salamander die‑offs in Saskatchewan and other provinces; the rest of the description, geography and sources are suitable for retention.
