Review: retain – this row appropriately captures the major SAV3‑associated pancreas disease epidemic in Norway beginning in 2003, which is one of the largest SAV emergence episodes by number of affected farms and production loss. I have made only minor wording adjustments to emphasise the geographic spread from western to northern coastal counties and to align drivers with Norwegian surveillance and risk‑factor studies; the time window 2003–2010 and classification as a re‑occurrence driven by production and connectivity, rather than by a new SAV3 variant, remain justified. Wikipedia has been removed from the event‑level sources in favour of primary and official references.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (Scotland) [2006]; Norway [2010]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in seawater (marine SAV2 infections)
Event summary: Around 2006, marine infections of Atlantic salmon with Salmonid alphavirus genotype 2 (SAV2), previously mainly associated with sleeping disease in freshwater rainbow trout, were first identified in seawater farms in north‑west Scotland, particularly in Shetland and Orkney. In 2010, the first detections of marine SAV2 in Norway were reported from pancreas‑disease outbreaks in Atlantic salmon, and sequence analyses showed Norwegian marine SAV2 strains to be closely related to Scottish marine SAV2 viruses, consistent with recent translocation between the two areas. During the late 2000s and early 2010s, marine SAV2 caused notable PD outbreaks at affected Scottish and some Norwegian sites but remained more spatially restricted than SAV1 in Ireland and Scotland or SAV3 in Norway, and enhanced surveillance, movement controls and vaccination helped limit its broader establishment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infected fish or eggs and shared supply chains between Scottish and Norwegian salmon industries, together with high local farm densities and waterborne spread within fjords and island archipelagos, likely facilitated the jump of SAV2 from freshwater trout systems into marine salmon sites and its subsequent spread between regions. Internal mechanisms: the capacity of SAV2 to replicate efficiently and cause pancreas disease in marine‑reared Atlantic salmon represents both novel strain/genotype behaviour in this production niche and host/life‑stage expansion from rainbow trout in freshwater, fitting the definition of re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – the event correctly represents the emergence of marine SAV2 infections in Atlantic salmon in Scotland and their subsequent introduction into Norway, a pattern that is epidemiologically and genetically distinct from earlier SAV1 and SAV3 outbreaks. Years and countries are consistent with sequence‑based studies and WOAH/OIE subtype‑distribution tables. I have kept the classification as re‑emergence (new host and production niche for SAV2) and not marked this as intra‑continental emergence because the spread occurred between countries within the same UN Northern Europe sub‑region, which under the project’s rules does not qualify as a separate intra‑continental event. Event‑level sources have been focused on molecular epidemiology and official surveillance reports.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (Scotland) [2018]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in freshwater hatchery / pre‑smolt culture (SAV1‑associated pancreas disease)
Event summary: In May 2018, a freshwater hatchery on the west coast of Scotland reported increased mortality and reduced performance in Atlantic salmon parr and pre‑smolts, initially suspected to be infectious pancreatic necrosis. Diagnostic testing instead detected Salmonid alphavirus subtype 1 (SAV1), and histopathology showed pancreas, heart and skeletal muscle lesions consistent with pancreas disease, representing the first published description of a clinical SAV outbreak causing PD in freshwater‑reared Atlantic salmon. The episode led to removal of affected cohorts and implementation of enhanced hygiene and stocking measures, and although the outbreak was confined to this facility it raised concern that freshwater systems could act as additional reservoirs feeding infection into the marine production phase.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: concentration of large numbers of salmon in intensive freshwater hatchery units, reuse of water and equipment, and movements of fish between tanks likely favoured persistence and spread of SAV1 within the site; seeding from infected marine stocks or other facilities via water or fish movements is a plausible source. Internal mechanisms: expression of overt pancreas disease at the freshwater life stage indicates host/life‑stage expansion and altered epidemiology of an existing SAV1 lineage, fitting the definition of re‑emergence rather than first detection in the host system as a whole.
Review: review – the original row described extensive SAV1‑associated freshwater pancreas disease outbreaks in Ireland during 2011–2017, for which I could not find supporting evidence in the primary or official literature. I have replaced it with the first well‑documented clinical field outbreak of SAV1‑associated pancreas disease in freshwater Atlantic salmon, which occurred in a Scottish hatchery in 2018 and clearly fits the definition of re‑emergence in a new production niche (freshwater life stage). However, this episode involved only a single facility and its overall contribution to system‑wide losses is modest compared with the large marine PD and SD epidemics; I therefore recommend that this corrected event be kept for now but flagged for further review regarding whether it should remain among the top‑impact events for this EPP.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild caprine ungulates, primarily Iberian ibex (Capra pyrenaica hispanica)
Event summary: In 1992, sarcoptic mange was recognized as an epizootic in the Iberian ibex population of the Sierra Nevada Natural Park in southern Spain, with Sarcoptes scabiei confirmed from skin scrapings and mange prevalence averaging over 20% across 1992–1996 and reaching almost 45% in a core focus area. During this period the disease spread spatially within the park, with highest prevalence and mortality in a western focus but without complete collapse of the overall ibex population, which continued to increase in density. By the late 1990s the outbreak transitioned toward endemic circulation with fluctuating prevalence modulated by climate and host demography, and later work documented partial host resistance and generally lower mange prevalence into the 2000s and 2010s.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High ibex density within a protected mountain habitat, overlap and potential contact with domestic small ruminants in surrounding areas, and climatic conditions (cooler, wetter months) that favored mite survival and transmission have been implicated in sustaining the epizootic and shaping its seasonality. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiologic work in Iberian wild ruminants supports introduction of a host‑taxon–adapted Sarcoptes scabiei strain from domestic goats or sheep and its establishment in Iberian ibex, consistent with re‑emergence driven primarily by host expansion (spillover from domestic small ruminants) and geographic range expansion of an existing strain within southern Spain.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic goats/sheep to Iberian ibex); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: retain – Well‑documented mange epizootic in Sierra Nevada Iberian ibex from 1992–1996 with 20–45% prevalence and clear spatial spread, matching Pérez et al. 1997 and subsequent ibex disease syntheses. Timing, geography (Spain, Southern Europe), and classification as re‑emergence (spillover of a goat‑derived strain into a wild ibex population within an already affected subregion) are consistent with primary literature. Earlier, more catastrophic Iberian ibex outbreaks in Cazorla (1987–1991, >90% mortality) are correctly omitted here because their onset precedes the 1990 cutoff. No changes to event fields recommended; mechanism text already emphasizes domestic‑origin strain and host expansion, which aligns with current evidence, though detailed strain pathogenicity remains an active research topic.

Host: Non-native Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia) introduced to Spain
Event summary: Between 1991 and 1995, a severe sarcoptic mange epizootic affected the introduced Barbary sheep population in Sierra Espuña Regional Park, southeastern Spain, with Sarcoptes scabiei confirmed in affected animals. Over the course of the outbreak, population monitoring documented an approximately 86% decline in Barbary sheep numbers, transforming a previously overabundant exotic ungulate population into a small remnant. Following intensive management and natural fade‑out of the epizootic, the surviving population remained at much lower density, and mange became enzootic at low levels rather than continuing as a high‑mortality wave.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: The Barbary sheep population in Sierra Espuña had been introduced and allowed to increase to high densities in a relatively small protected area, facilitating rapid transmission once sarcoptic mange was introduced; contact with domestic small ruminants or other sympatric ungulates is considered a likely source of introduction, and rugged terrain made carcass removal and other interventions difficult. Internal mechanisms: The event represents establishment of Sarcoptes scabiei in a non‑native wild Caprinae host within the Iberian Peninsula, probably via spillover of a host‑taxon–adapted strain from domestic or other wild ruminants, consistent with re‑emergence driven by host expansion and geographic range expansion of an existing mite lineage.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover into non‑native Barbary sheep); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: review – Added as a missing major event: the 1991–1995 sarcoptic mange epizootic in non‑native Barbary sheep (arruí) in Sierra Espuña Regional Park, Spain, which caused an ≈86% population decrease and is repeatedly cited as a high‑impact example in later mange literature. Years, host, location and impact are based on the Journal of Wildlife Diseases paper and the associated University of Murcia thesis, with additional confirmation from Ferreyra et al. 2022 referencing this outbreak. Classified as re‑emergence (spillover and establishment of Sarcoptes in a new wild host population within an already affected subregion), not intra‑continental emergence, because Sarcoptes was already established in Iberian wildlife. Recommend expert review of the summarized drivers and internal mechanism tags, but inclusion of this event among the top‑impact epizootics is well supported.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cantabrian chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica parva) with spillover to other wild ungulates (e.g., red deer, roe deer, mouflon)
Event summary: In May 1993, an epizootic of sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first detected in Cantabrian chamois in the Cantabrian Mountains of northwestern Spain, where mange had not previously been reported in this wild caprine. Over the mid‑1990s and 2000s, the disease front spread progressively eastwards across the range at an estimated 2.6–4 km per year, causing marked local population declines and high mortality in affected chamois units and also infecting sympatric wild cervids and other ungulates. By around 2008, the main epidemic wave had traversed most of the chamois range and transitioned into lower‑level endemic circulation with sporadic mortality, leaving long‑term effects on population structure and demography in affected areas.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Close contact between wild caprines and domestic goats and sheep grazing on mountain pastures is strongly implicated as the original source of S. scabiei, while protected‑area management and increasing wild ungulate densities facilitated sustained transmission; the metapopulation structure of chamois along a linear mountain chain shaped the speed and pattern of spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work indicates host‑taxon–derived mite strains with high pathogenicity in naive chamois, representing a host‑adapted strain spilling over from domestic small ruminants and establishing persistent transmission in wild populations, consistent with re‑emergence via host expansion and geographic range expansion within Southern Europe.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic goats/sheep to wild chamois); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (host‑taxon–specific variant in Cantabrian chamois); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: retain – Major long‑duration mange epizootic in Cantabrian chamois beginning in 1993 with eastward spread over ~15 years and substantial local population impacts, as described by Fernández‑Morán et al. and summarized in later reviews and the Cantabrian chamois species account. Years, host, and geography (Spain, Southern Europe) are correct, and the epidemic wave classification as re‑emergence (domestic goat/sheep–derived strain establishing in a new wild caprine population) matches microsatellite evidence that links these outbreaks to small‑ruminant sources. No corrections to emergence‑type flags are needed; intra‑continental emergence is not triggered because the event remains within the Southern Europe subregion. The Wikipedia URL is secondary but accurate; primary scientific articles already provide the core documentation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [1995] (Belluno Province, Dolomites); Italy [1997] (Bolzano Province); Italy [2000] (Trento Province)
Host: Alpine chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra rupicapra), with Alpine ibex (Capra ibex) and other sympatric ungulates as secondary hosts
Event summary: In October 1995, sarcoptic mange was first recorded in Alpine chamois in the Province of Belluno (Dolomites, northeastern Italy), marking the start of a new epizootic wave in this mountain region. Over subsequent years, the outbreak spread westward, reaching Bolzano Province in 1997 and Trento Province by 2000, and caused high mortality and demographic collapse in several chamois populations while also affecting sympatric Alpine ibex. By the mid‑2000s, after roughly a decade of intense impact, mange had become established and largely endemic across much of the regional chamois metapopulation, with episodic flare‑ups but reduced overall mortality compared to the initial epizootic front.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High densities and connectivity of Alpine chamois across contiguous alpine massifs facilitated progressive spread once mange was introduced, and climatic conditions in high‑elevation habitats (cool, moist periods) favored mite survival off‑host. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic reflects geographic expansion of a host‑taxon–adapted Sarcoptes scabiei strain among largely naive chamois subpopulations, with possible spillover between chamois and Alpine ibex, consistent with re‑emergence driven by geographic range expansion of an existing strain and traits that permit efficient transmission in caprine hosts in alpine environments.
Internal mechanism tags: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within the Alps); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Host Expansion (among closely related wild Caprinae).
Review: retain – Large, well‑documented mange epizootic in Alpine chamois and ibex in the Dolomites beginning with the first Belluno case in 1995 and spreading into Bolzano (1997) and Trento (2000), as detailed by the SEI model paper and surveillance studies using detector dogs. The 1995–2005 window appropriately captures the main high‑mortality phase, although surveillance shows continued endemic presence beyond 2005; treating this as a single long episode is consistent with the linked‑episode definition. Classification as re‑emergence (expansion of an established host‑taxon–specific strain within Southern Europe) is appropriate, with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence involved. No geography or timing corrections required; event could be further refined by extending the end year if a longer endemic phase is of interest, but it is already one of the highest‑impact Caprinae outbreaks in the period.

Countries: United States of America [2013] (Bakersfield, California); United States of America [2019] (Taft, California)
Host: Endangered San Joaquin kit fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica), with likely involvement of domestic dogs and possibly other canids as reservoir or source hosts
Event summary: In spring 2013, sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first documented in an urban subpopulation of endangered San Joaquin kit foxes in Bakersfield, California, where this disease had not previously been reported in the subspecies. Between 2013 and about 2020, the epidemic expanded to encompass the entire Bakersfield urban population and, by early 2019, was detected in a satellite kit fox population in the town of Taft, leading to at least 90 clinically confirmed cases and substantial additional undetected mortality, with camera‑based indices indicating an approximate 50% decline in kit fox abundance in Bakersfield. Following intensive monitoring and some treatment and collar‑based interventions, reported case numbers dropped sharply around 2020, but mange remains an ongoing management concern with potential for re‑emergence or further spread to other fragmented kit fox populations.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Urbanization has concentrated San Joaquin kit foxes at high densities around anthropogenic food and water sources, while dense networks of artificial dens and frequent contact with domestic dogs and possibly red foxes created opportunities for cross‑species transmission and rapid intra‑population spread; small, fragmented populations and the endangered status of the subspecies amplify conservation impact. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiological data support a canine‑derived S. scabiei strain that adapted to San Joaquin kit foxes and spread between foxes, representing host expansion (spillover from domestic or other canids) and efficient fox‑to‑fox transmission, consistent with re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission in a new, highly susceptible canid host.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic/other canids to kit foxes); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within North America).
Review: retain – High‑impact mange epidemic in an endangered canid with clear onset (Bakersfield, March 2013), documented spread to Taft by early 2019, and strong evidence for a ~50% decline in the urban Bakersfield population based on camera detections, as reported by FWS, Cypher et al., Foley et al., and related studies. Location (USA, Northern America), host, and timing match these sources, including first Taft detection in 2019. Classification as re‑emergence (new host expansion of a canine‑derived Sarcoptes strain in an already mange‑affected continent) is appropriate; imported cases without onward transmission are not involved, so no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence applies. No corrections to event fields or URLs recommended.

Countries: Australia [2010] (Narawntapu National Park, central north Tasmania)
Host: Common wombat / bare-nosed wombat (Vombatus ursinus), primarily Tasmanian subspecies, with mange also affecting other common wombat populations in south‑eastern Australia
Event summary: Around 2010, a severe outbreak of sarcoptic mange emerged in the common wombat population of Narawntapu National Park in central north Tasmania, a site previously known for high wombat density but within a region where mange had already been present historically. From 2010 to 2016, systematic spotlight and monitoring surveys documented a catastrophic 94% decline in the resident wombat population attributable to mange, making this event one of the most extreme local impacts recorded for the species. By 2016 wombat numbers in Narawntapu had effectively collapsed, while wombat populations elsewhere in Tasmania were generally stable or increasing, and the outbreak prompted ongoing research and trials of novel single‑dose mange treatments and management strategies to prevent similar localized crashes.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Historical introduction of S. scabiei to Australia with European settlers and domestic animals in the 19th century, combined with high local wombat density in improved pasture landscapes around Narawntapu, limited effective treatment options, and landscape features that promoted local host aggregation, created conditions for intense, localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: The Narawntapu event reflects a severe resurgence of an established human/domestic‑origin Sarcoptes strain in wombats rather than emergence of a novel genotype or new host association; efficient transmission through shared burrows and high contact rates drove a travelling epidemic wave and extreme local mortality, without evidence to date of major new parasite adaptations.
Internal mechanism tags: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (burrow sharing, high host density); Geographic Range Expansion (fine‑scale within Tasmania).
Review: review – The Narawntapu outbreak is correctly identified as an exceptionally severe mange episode in common wombats, with a 94% local population decline between 2010 and 2016 documented by Tasmanian monitoring programs and Martin et al. (2018). However, Sarcoptes scabiei has been present in wombats and other Australian mammals for over a century, and wombat mange was already widespread in south‑eastern Australia; this event is therefore best interpreted as a dramatic re‑occurrence in an already affected host and subregion, not as re‑emergence driven by a new strain or host expansion. Re‑emergence has been set to "No" and re‑occurrence to "Yes", and the mechanism text has been adjusted to emphasize external drivers (host density, land use, limited treatment) and intense local transmission of an established strain rather than novel host adaptation. Recommend expert review of the precise end year (2016 captures the documented crash, though lower‑level persistence likely continues) and of any future evidence for parasite evolution in wombats.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Argentina [2014] (San Guillermo National Park and Biosphere Reserve, San Juan Province)
Host: Wild South American camelids: vicuña (Vicugna vicugna) and guanaco (Lama guanicoe); probable source in domestic llamas (Lama glama) introduced near the park
Event summary: In 2014, sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first diagnosed in vicuñas and guanacos in San Guillermo National Park, Argentina, a protected area that previously supported one of the country’s largest sympatric wild camelid populations and had no recorded mange outbreaks in native camelids for at least five decades. Between 2014 and intensive surveys in 2017–2019, the outbreak expanded rapidly, with transect data showing 68% and 77% short‑term declines in vicuña and guanaco densities between 2017 and 2018 and an overall 95–98% decline in abundance relative to pre‑outbreak levels; by April 2019, surveys recorded no living vicuñas or guanacos along park transects, indicating near‑extirpation. Genetic data on mites and the timing and location of infected domestic llamas point to recently introduced llamas as the most likely source, and by the end of the study period the park’s wild camelid populations remained functionally collapsed with uncertain prospects for natural recovery.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: A provincial livestock incentive program introduced domestic llamas into areas adjacent to San Guillermo Biosphere Reserve from 2009 onward, some reportedly affected by mange; spatial and temporal overlap between infected llamas and wild camelids, the absence of prior mange in local livestock and wild camelids for decades, and small, isolated wild populations created ideal conditions for a severe spillover event and rapid, density‑dependent transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multilocus genotyping of mites from vicuñas and guanacos supports a recent, exogenous introduction of Sarcoptes scabiei with limited time for co‑evolution, representing host expansion from domestic llamas into previously naive wild camelids and resulting in an aggressive, high‑mortality epizootic—i.e. re‑emergence driven by host expansion and novel strain/genotype introduction within South America.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic llamas to wild vicuñas and guanacos); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (recent introduction into the wild camelid community); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within South America).
Review: retain – One of the most extreme documented Sarcoptes outbreaks in wild mammals, with PLOS ONE and associated reports showing 68–77% short‑term density declines and 95–98% overall reductions in vicuña and guanaco abundance, culminating in near‑absence of live animals on 2019 transects in San Guillermo. The 2014–2019 window correctly brackets first detection and the last intensive surveys; host species, location (Argentina, South America) and linkage to recently introduced domestic llamas as the likely source are well supported by genetic and epidemiologic analyses. Classification as re‑emergence (host expansion and novel introduction of mites into previously mange‑free wild camelids in this area) is appropriate. No changes to event fields or URL set recommended.

Countries: United States of America [Pennsylvania 1991; later increasing reports from neighboring eastern states through the 2010s]
Host: American black bear (Ursus americanus) populations in the northeastern and mid‑Atlantic United States
Event summary: In 1991, the first American black bear with sarcoptic mange was documented in Pennsylvania, marking the beginning of an emerging disease issue in this species in the eastern United States. Through the 1990s and 2000s, case reports and surveillance data indicated an expanding distribution of mange in black bears across Pennsylvania and neighboring states, with increasing clinical severity and concern among wildlife managers. By the 2010s, sarcoptic mange was recognized as a re-emerging parasitic disease in regional black bear populations, with locally high case burdens but limited evidence for sustained, large-scale population collapse, and it remains a focus of surveillance and research into landscape, host and co-infection drivers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of black bear populations into peri‑urban and agricultural landscapes, increased contact with domestic dogs and sympatric canids, and possible nutritional or environmental stressors likely facilitated spillover and establishment of Sarcoptes scabiei in bears. Internal mechanisms: This represents host expansion and re‑emergence of S. scabiei in a historically rarely affected host, with a bear‑adapted mange presentation now observed more frequently; genetic studies to date suggest circulation of canid-derived mite lineages rather than a wholly novel bear-specific genotype.
Review: Decision: Review (borderline top‑10). Rationale: This is a well‑documented emerging issue in eastern U.S. black bears, but available syntheses emphasize that North American mange generally has not produced the extreme population crashes documented in other wildlife hosts (e.g. wombats, vicuñas, raccoon dogs).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599944/?utm_source=openai)) Classification changes: (i) First_detection reset from true→false because S. scabiei was long known in animals and in North American carnivores before 1991; the event is a first major emergence in this host species and region, not the first detection in the animal host system overall. (ii) Re_emergence kept as true to reflect host expansion from canids into black bears; re_occurrence remains false. Geography/timing: Years 1991–2020 and the listed states remain approximate but consistent with the cited review and thesis; no country/subregion change needed. Sources: retained the North American wildlife review and the Pennsylvania‑focused thesis as the most directly relevant references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Iberian ibex (Capra pyrenaica) in the Sierra Nevada Natural Space, southern Spain
Event summary: In 1992, a major sarcoptic mange epizootic caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was recognized in Iberian ibex in the Sierra Nevada Natural Space in southern Spain, following an earlier catastrophic outbreak in another Iberian ibex population at Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas in the mid‑1980s. The disease spread through the Sierra Nevada ibex population during the 1990s, causing high morbidity and mortality and driving marked declines before transitioning to an endemic situation with lower prevalence as host immunity and management interventions developed. Since the 2000s mange has persisted at low but recurrent levels, with ibex populations partially recovering yet remaining under long‑term surveillance and management focused on monitoring, selective culling and treatment to limit further large epizootics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High ibex densities in Mediterranean mountain habitats, interactions with infested domestic goats and other ungulates, and climatic conditions favoring mite survival and transmission facilitated the rapid spread and long-term persistence of sarcoptic mange. Internal mechanisms: This severe re‑occurrence in a region where ibex mange had already been documented (Cazorla complex) likely reflects establishment and spatial expansion of an ibex‑adapted S. scabiei lineage in susceptible subpopulations, with host–parasite coevolution and changing host immunity influencing the shift from acute epizootic to endemic dynamics rather than clear evidence of a novel mite strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4641373/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major global event). Evidence: Long-term work on Sierra Nevada ibex documents a large, sustained epizootic beginning in 1992 with severe mortality and long‑term endemicity.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4641373/?utm_source=openai)) Classification changes: (i) Re_occurrence set true and re_emergence set false (was the reverse), because mange was already established in the same UN subregion (Southern Europe) in Iberian ibex (Cazorla outbreak in 1985–1986); there is no clear evidence for a distinct novel strain driving this specific wave. (ii) First_detection remains false, as the parasite was long known in European ungulates. Geography/timing: Years and location consistent with major ibex disease syntheses; no changes to continent/subregion/country fields. Sources: existing ibex-focused papers are appropriate and were retained.

Countries: Spain [Cantabrian Mountains, Asturias and adjacent areas 1993; progressive spread eastwards through the 2000s]
Host: Cantabrian chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica parva) in the Cantabrian Mountains, north‑western Spain
Event summary: In May 1993, sarcoptic mange was first detected in Cantabrian chamois in the Cantabrian Mountains of north‑western Spain, representing a new and severe disease focus for this subspecies. The epizootic spread through central and eastern Asturias and adjacent areas during the late 1990s and 2000s, leading to substantial local population declines and progressive expansion of the affected range by roughly 40 km eastward over about 15 years. By around 2010, more than half of the total Cantabrian chamois population and distribution range had been affected, with mange persisting as an ongoing threat despite partial demographic recovery in some areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High local chamois densities in rugged mountain terrain, concentration at shared foraging cliffs and passes, and probable spillover from infected ungulates in neighboring regions (including ibex and red deer) facilitated disease establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: This event reflects re‑emergence driven by host expansion of S. scabiei from previously affected wild ungulates into a naïve chamois subspecies, with high susceptibility and lack of prior immunity producing severe outcomes and sustained, spatially advancing epidemic waves.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304401797000617?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major regional event). Evidence: Primary epizootiological studies and later syntheses show a large, long‑lasting mange outbreak in Cantabrian chamois, affecting >50% of the population and range by the late 2000s.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304401797000617?utm_source=openai)) Corrections: (i) End year extended from 2001→2010 to reflect continued spread and impact through at least 2008–2010. (ii) First_detection changed to false (was true), because S. scabiei was already long recognized in European wildlife and wild caprines; 1993 marks first detection in this host/subpopulation, not in the animal host system. (iii) Intra_continental_emergence set to false (was true); all involved areas lie within the same UN subregion (Southern Europe), and guidance specifies that spread within a subregion or country should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. (iv) Re_emergence kept true (host expansion from previously affected ungulate hosts into Cantabrian chamois). Overall structure and country/subregion assignments remain appropriate.

Countries: Italy [Dolomites, province of Belluno 1995; spread to Bolzano 1997 and Trento 2000]
Host: Alpine chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra) in the Dolomites (northeastern Italy)
Event summary: In October 1995, the first recorded case of sarcoptic mange in Alpine chamois in the Dolomites was detected in the province of Belluno, initiating a new epidemic wave in this mountain population. The epidemic front moved westward over subsequent years, reaching Bolzano in 1997 and Trento in 2000, with at least 417 recorded mange cases on the Dolomiti di Sesto massif between 1995 and 2002. Following extinction of the epizootic focus on that massif around 2002, mange continued to circulate at lower or cyclic levels in chamois in other Dolomite massifs, requiring ongoing surveillance and management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Contiguous alpine habitats and movements of chamois across massifs enabled progressive spread of mites, and high densities around shared foraging and resting areas increased contact rates; infection may have been introduced via contact with already infected chamois or domestic goats from neighboring Alpine regions. Internal mechanisms: This epidemic represents a pronounced re‑occurrence of sarcoptic mange in Alpine chamois within a region where the disease has recurred in cycles since at least the early 20th century, rather than a first emergence or clearly novel strain; repeated epidemic waves are characteristic of mange dynamics in this host.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17513750902883283?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major Alpine event). Evidence: Dolomites outbreaks are among the best quantified mange epizootics in European mountain ungulates, with hundreds of recorded chamois cases and clear epidemic wavefront dynamics.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17513750902883283?utm_source=openai)) Corrections: (i) First_detection changed from true→false; mange in Alpine chamois was described in multiple European regions decades to over a century earlier. (ii) Intra_continental_emergence changed from true→false, because the Dolomites are not a new UN subregion for S. scabiei in Europe; previous outbreaks occurred in both Austrian and Italian Alps. (iii) Re_occurrence set true and re_emergence set false, emphasizing this as a new epidemic wave of an established host–parasite system rather than a clearly strain‑driven re‑emergence. Geography and years remain consistent with the cited SEI‑model and surveillance papers.

Countries: Japan [Kanagawa Prefecture, including Yokohama and surrounding municipalities 1995–2002]
Host: Japanese raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides viverrinus) in Kanagawa Prefecture
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s, sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei triggered a severe epizootic in wild raccoon dogs in Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, with particularly well‑documented dynamics around Yokohama. Wildlife rescue and surveillance data indicate that mange prevalence increased sharply from the mid‑1990s, peaking between about 1995 and 2002, during which time the affected raccoon dog population declined by roughly 90% before slowly recovering. Mange has since remained present at lower levels in the regional raccoon dog population, but the 1995–2002 outbreak stands out as an intense wave with major demographic impacts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High raccoon dog densities in peri‑urban landscapes, reliance on anthropogenic food resources, and close proximity to domestic dogs facilitated frequent contacts and spillover of S. scabiei between domestic and wild canids; landscape fragmentation and road networks also shaped movement and rescue patterns. Internal mechanisms: Genetic work has shown co‑circulation of mite genotypes typical of companion dogs and raccoon dogs, supporting re‑emergence via host expansion and repeated introductions from domestic reservoirs, followed by efficient transmission within raccoon dogs and strong disease‑induced mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11554625/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (added as new major event). Evidence: State‑space modelling of rescue data for Kanagawa raccoon dogs estimated a ~91% reduction in population size during the mange outbreak, comparable in severity to classic Swedish red fox epizootics and more severe than many other canid events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11554625/?utm_source=openai)) This clearly belongs among the most impactful mange events since 1990. New row: This event was missing from the draft but added here with timing, geography and impact drawn from recent quantitative work and earlier epidemiological descriptions. Classification: Re_emergence set true (host expansion and repeated introductions from domestic dogs plus strong demographic impacts); first_detection left false; intra-/inter‑continental emergence left false because mange in domestic dogs and other wildlife was long present in Eastern Asia. Sources: Added the 2023 state‑space analysis and earlier Japanese raccoon dog mange studies as primary references.

Countries: Switzerland [mid‑1990s re-emergence and nationwide spread completed by ~2017]; Norway [southeastern Norway camera-trap epizootic clusters ~2009–2014]
Host: Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) populations in Switzerland and parts of Scandinavia experiencing large-scale mange epizootics and endemic circulation
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s through the 2010s, European red fox populations experienced renewed and widespread sarcoptic mange activity. In Switzerland, retrospective and prospective surveillance over more than 60 years showed that mange, known since the 19th century, re‑emerged in the mid‑1990s and progressively spread to cover the entire country by around 2017, with fluctuating local prevalence and recurrent epizootic peaks. In southeastern Norway, camera‑trap monitoring from 2009 to 2014 documented low to moderate apparent prevalence but persistent spatial clusters of mangy foxes near human settlements, illustrating long‑term endemicity and localized epizootics within a population already heavily impacted by earlier large mange outbreaks in the 1970s–1980s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High fox densities in peri‑urban and rural landscapes, anthropogenic food subsidies, and landscape features concentrating fox movements near settlements and refuse sites enhanced transmission and supported recurrent epidemics. Internal mechanisms: These events represent severe re‑occurrence of an established red‑fox–adapted S. scabiei lineage; long‑term studies in Norway suggest host/parasite adaptation over time, with declining proportions of clinically mangy but seropositive foxes after the initial outbreak decade, rather than emergence of a single new strain.([sonar.ch](https://sonar.ch/global/documents/177970))
Review: Decision: Retain (major long-term European event). Evidence: Switzerland’s 60+ year dataset documents re‑emergence and nationwide spread of mange from the mid‑1990s onward, and Scandinavian work shows entrenched enzootic mange with earlier epizootics causing fox population declines of 50–90% in parts of Sweden and Norway.([sonar.ch](https://sonar.ch/global/documents/177970)) Corrections: (i) Sub_regions expanded from Western Europe only→"Western Europe; Northern Europe" to reflect inclusion of both Switzerland and Norway. (ii) Year range adjusted from 1990–2015→1995–2017 to better match the documented Swiss re‑emergence mid‑1990s and spread to nationwide endemicity by 2017. (iii) Classification retained as re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false: mange has been endemic in European red foxes since at least the 19th century, and current patterns are best interpreted as re‑occurring epizootics and enzootic persistence rather than a distinct new strain or host expansion. (iv) Removed a North Carolina advisory fact-sheet URL in favor of the more directly relevant long-term Swiss and Norwegian research articles.

Host: Bare-nosed (common) wombat (Vombatus ursinus) in Narawntapu National Park, central‑northern Tasmania
Event summary: Around 2006, following a period of severe drought, a sarcoptic mange outbreak in bare‑nosed wombats intensified in Narawntapu National Park in central‑northern Tasmania, where mange had previously occurred at low levels. Between 2010 and 2016, repeated transect surveys documented a dramatic ~94% decline in wombat abundance, with some sectors of the park experiencing near‑complete local population collapse as a travelling wave of infection moved from east to west. After 2016 the epidemic subsided, leaving only a small remnant wombat population at very low density, and subsequent management and research have focused on monitoring recovery and testing population‑level treatment strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of S. scabiei to Australian fauna in the 19th century, high local wombat densities before the outbreak, severe drought and environmental stress, and the ecology of wombat burrows (which can act as environmental reservoirs) all contributed to intense transmission along a travelling wave front. Internal mechanisms: This event is best characterized as a severe re‑occurrence of an established wombat‑adapted mite lineage, causing catastrophic local host mortality without clear evidence for a novel strain; however, the epidemic likely imposed strong selection on both mites and wombats.([australiasnaturehub.gov.au](https://www.australiasnaturehub.gov.au/action-inventory/common-wombat-population-monitoring-and-mange-prevalence?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major global event). Evidence: Government monitoring and detailed ecological analyses show a 94% decline in wombat abundance in Narawntapu between 2010 and 2016, with effectively 100% mortality behind the wave front.([australiasnaturehub.gov.au](https://www.australiasnaturehub.gov.au/action-inventory/common-wombat-population-monitoring-and-mange-prevalence?utm_source=openai)) Classification: Original coding as re_occurrence=true and re_emergence=false is appropriate; the event is a dramatic resurgence of an introduced parasite in a previously affected host population rather than a first emergence or host/strain shift. Sources: Re-ordered and slightly streamlined the URLs, emphasizing quantitative and official Tasmanian reporting; content remains essentially as in the draft.

Countries: Australia [Tasmania, Bronte Park and nearby central plateau sites late 2000s–mid‑2010s]
Host: Bare-nosed wombat (Vombatus ursinus) populations in the Bronte Park region, central Tasmania
Event summary: In the late 2000s and early 2010s, sarcoptic mange intensified in bare‑nosed wombats around Bronte Park and adjacent central Tasmanian areas, where the parasite had previously been present at low prevalence. Monitoring and retrospective analyses indicate that the local wombat population declined by roughly 80% during this epizootic as mange spread and persisted through the region. Following the peak of the outbreak, wombat numbers appear to have stabilized at much lower densities, with continued low‑level mange and active research into improved single‑dose and remote treatments for free‑ranging wombats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Similar to Narawntapu, local environmental conditions, high pre‑epizootic wombat densities, and the ecology of burrow sharing likely amplified S. scabiei transmission and disease severity in this central Tasmanian focus. Internal mechanisms: This event represents a severe re‑occurrence of an existing wombat‑adapted S. scabiei lineage without confirmed evidence of a novel genotype, but with substantial demographic impacts due to high virulence and small, semi‑isolated host populations.([parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com](https://parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13071-024-06275-9.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major Tasmanian event). Evidence: Recent reviews of mange impacts in wombats state that Narawntapu and Bronte Park populations experienced approximately 94% and 80% declines, respectively, due to sarcoptic mange.([parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com](https://parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13071-024-06275-9.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Corrections: (i) Removed a generic ‘Sciencedirect topics’ URL that does not specifically describe the Bronte Park event and replaced it with the Tasmanian government monitoring report as a more appropriate contextual source. (ii) Classification as re_occurrence (not re_emergence) retained, because there is no clear evidence of a novel mite strain or host jump; this is a second major Tasmanian focus in the same host species. (iii) Years remain approximate (late 2000s–mid‑2010s); confidence kept at 0.72 to reflect some temporal uncertainty.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus) in the Borgafjäll subpopulation, Swedish mountains
Event summary: In April 2013, sarcoptic mange was again detected in Arctic foxes in the Borgafjäll subpopulation of the Scandinavian mountains, decades after a smaller outbreak in 1986–1987 had been controlled. Intensive field monitoring and wildlife camera data showed that in 2013–2014 about 30% of individuals in this already endangered subpopulation exhibited mange symptoms, with infected foxes present at most den sites and subsequent recurrent outbreaks documented in 2017, 2019, 2020 and 2021. Despite aggressive bait‑based treatment efforts, these mange waves reduced reproductive output and litter size, and threatened the fragile recovery of this small, fragmented Arctic fox population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climate warming and associated expansion of red foxes into sub‑Arctic tundra have increased interspecific competition and opportunities for transmission of red‑fox–adapted S. scabiei to Arctic foxes; anthropogenic food subsidies that support red foxes may further exacerbate this process. Internal mechanisms: This event is best interpreted as re‑emergence and host expansion of existing S. scabiei variants from red foxes into a naïve endangered Arctic fox population, with high virulence and demographic impacts but no evidence of a wholly new mite lineage.([rasmuserlandsson.net](https://www.rasmuserlandsson.net/publication/wallen-etal-2024/wallen-etal-2024.pdf))
Review: Decision: Retain (major event in an endangered host). Evidence: Long-term monitoring of the Borgafjäll Arctic fox subpopulation documents repeated mange outbreaks beginning in 2013, with ~30% of individuals affected in 2013–2014 and demonstrated negative effects on reproduction and population growth.([rasmuserlandsson.net](https://www.rasmuserlandsson.net/publication/wallen-etal-2024/wallen-etal-2024.pdf)) Corrections: (i) Year range updated from an imprecise 2000–2015→2013–2021 to match the documented modern epizootic and subsequent outbreaks; the earlier 1986–1987 event is pre‑1990 and treated as historical context rather than as part of this post‑1990 event. (ii) Countries narrowed from “Sweden; Norway” to Sweden only, as the best evidence for repeated mange outbreaks with quantified demographic effects is from the Swedish Borgafjäll subpopulation; Norwegian Arctic fox mange is acknowledged in reviews but less clearly documented as a single large epizootic. (iii) First_detection reset from true→false; mange in Arctic foxes in Scandinavia was recorded at least as early as 1986–1987. (iv) Re_emergence retained true (host expansion and recurrent epizootic in a previously affected but still highly vulnerable subpopulation).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [California, Bakersfield urban area 2013]
Host: San Joaquin kit fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica) – endangered urban population in Bakersfield, California
Event summary: On 13 March 2013, sarcoptic mange was first detected in endangered San Joaquin kit foxes in Bakersfield, California, when kit foxes with severe skin lesions were reported near Meadows Field airport. The epidemic subsequently spread through urban Bakersfield over the next several years, with annual case detections peaking around 2015–2016 at roughly 90–100 identified cases per year and an estimated suppression of the urban kit fox population to around half its pre‑mange size. By 2020, mange remained endemic at lower levels, with the kit fox population and disease co‑persisting under intensive management, including experimental acaricide collars and localized den treatments to mitigate further declines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High local kit fox densities in a patchy urban habitat, shared den use, and proximity to infected domestic dogs and other carnivores likely facilitated introduction and sustained transmission of S. scabiei in this small, isolated population. Internal mechanisms: This outbreak is a clear example of re‑emergence through host expansion of S. scabiei into a new endangered canid host with severe demographic effects; disease persistence has been influenced by kit fox social structure and the spatial arrangement of family groups, which maintain mange in semi‑discrete clusters over many years.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_kit_fox?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain (major endangered‑canid event). Evidence: Detailed PLOS ONE analyses show sustained high case counts and an estimated ~50% reduction in the urban San Joaquin kit fox population during the peak of the mange epidemic.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_kit_fox?utm_source=openai)) Corrections: (i) First_detection changed from true→false, as S. scabiei had been known in North American canids for decades; 2013 is first detection in this specific kit fox population. (ii) Re_emergence retained true (host expansion into a new endangered canid host and clear demographic impact). (iii) Source list trimmed slightly to emphasize peer‑reviewed and official conservation sources most directly describing the Bakersfield outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Argentina [San Guillermo National Park, San Juan Province 2014–2019]
Host: Vicuña (Vicugna vicugna) and guanaco (Lama guanicoe) in San Guillermo National Park
Event summary: In 2014, sarcoptic mange was first detected in wild vicuñas and guanacos in San Guillermo National Park in the Andean highlands of Argentina, a protected area established to conserve these camelids. Between 2013 and 2017–2018, population surveys documented catastrophic declines of about 95% in guanacos and 98% in vicuñas, with nearly all examined carcasses showing mange lesions; by 2019, no vicuñas or guanacos were observed on transects, indicating near‑extirpation of both species from the park. Genetic analysis of mites from several camelids indicated a single recent source, and epidemiological investigation pointed to introduction from mange‑infested domestic llamas brought near the park under a livestock incentive program.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of mange‑infested domestic llamas near park boundaries through a governmental livestock program provided a likely source of S. scabiei for spillover into naïve wild camelid populations; lack of early detection and control, combined with the open, shared grazing landscape and harsh high‑Andean environment, facilitated rapid spread and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: This is a striking example of re‑emergence and host expansion of S. scabiei from domestic camelids into wild vicuñas and guanacos, with a single mite genotype causing severe, multi‑year epizootics and local functional extinction of key herbivores.([vetmed.ucdavis.edu](https://www.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/news/mange-outbreak-decimated-wild-vicuna-population-argentina))
Review: Decision: Retain (added; one of the most severe known events). Evidence: Field surveys and PLOS ONE analyses show 95–98% declines in guanaco and vicuña densities between 2013 and 2018, with no animals detected on transects by 2019; this outbreak locally erased both wild camelid species from a national park that had been created to protect them.([vetmed.ucdavis.edu](https://www.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/news/mange-outbreak-decimated-wild-vicuna-population-argentina)) New row: This globally important event was missing from the draft and clearly belongs among the top 10 highest‑impact sarcoptic mange events since 1990. Classification: Re_emergence=true (host expansion from domestic llamas and novel introduction into this wild camelid community), re_occurrence=false; first_detection=false because mange in South American camelids is documented elsewhere prior to 2014. Geography and timing follow the primary field and news reports.

Host: Sheep (with later recognition in goats, but index description is ovine)
Event summary: In 1998, Norwegian veterinarians identified several scrapie cases in sheep with highly unusual neuropathology and prion protein profiles, later termed Nor98 or atypical scrapie. Detailed characterization showed distinctive cerebellar and cerebral cortical vacuolation and a unique low–molecular weight PrPSc band pattern, clearly separating these cases from classical scrapie. The finding led to recognition of atypical/Nor98 scrapie as a distinct prion strain and motivated adjustments to Norway’s TSE surveillance to ensure such cases would be detected going forward.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (first description of the atypical/Nor98 scrapie strain with distinctive PrPSc phenotype, lesion distribution and biochemical signature). Drivers – Availability and application of improved neuropathological and biochemical diagnostic methods within Norway’s scrapie surveillance allowed recognition of this divergent strain, which likely had been overlooked previously.
Review: retain – Event accurately captures the first recognition of atypical/Nor98 scrapie in Norwegian sheep in 1998, with correct geography (Northern Europe, Norway), host, timing and classification as re_emergence due to a novel strain; no corrections required.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]; France [2002]; Germany [2002]; Spain [2003]; Italy [2003]; Belgium [2003]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2003]; Ireland [2003]; Sweden [2003]; Portugal [2003]; Denmark [2003]; Estonia [2003]; Lithuania [2003]; Switzerland [2003]; Iceland [2003]
Host: Sheep (with later detection in goats in some countries)
Event summary: From 2002, implementation of EU‑mandated active TSE surveillance in small ruminants, including abattoir and fallen‑stock testing, led to the detection of atypical/Nor98‑like scrapie across Great Britain and many EU member states. Between roughly 2003 and 2007, atypical cases were reported from an expanding set of Northern, Western and Southern European countries, and in some areas they accounted for a substantial proportion of diagnosed scrapie relative to classical disease. Despite this wider recognition, atypical scrapie has generally remained a low‑prevalence, sporadic infection of older sheep, without large flock‑level epidemics but with a now well‑documented pan‑European distribution.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (continent‑wide recognition and circulation of the atypical/Nor98 prion strain within European sheep populations). Possible Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of this strain within already scrapie‑endemic regions. Drivers – Regulatory and technological drivers, particularly EU Regulation 999/2001 and associated active surveillance with rapid TSE tests, generated the sampling intensity and laboratory sensitivity needed to detect atypical cases widely across Europe.
Review: review – Corrected two issues: (1) removed Falkland Islands from the country list and restricted this episode to European countries, because the Falkland case represents a separate Southern Hemisphere event rather than part of the EU surveillance wave; and (2) set intra_continental_emergence to false, since atypical scrapie represents a new strain emerging in regions where scrapie was already endemic and, per the scheme rules, such strain changes should be coded as re_emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence. Per‑country start years remain approximate and should be cross‑checked in any future refinement.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (classical scrapie)
Event summary: After a long period with very few confirmed events, Norway’s national scrapie surveillance programme detected several small classical scrapie outbreaks in sheep flocks beginning in 2001. Through 2009, classical cases recurred intermittently in a limited number of flocks, while atypical Nor98 scrapie was detected more regularly in other holdings, prompting targeted tracing, culling and movement controls around affected premises. By 2009, classical scrapie remained rare and geographically limited, and Norway continued to document its low‑incidence status while maintaining intensive surveillance and control, after which only atypical cases have been reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers – Livestock management and animal movement patterns, as well as environmental persistence of prions, likely facilitated sporadic re‑introduction and within‑flock transmission of classical scrapie into a small number of Norwegian flocks; enhanced surveillance increased the probability of detection and thus the apparent incidence. Internal mechanisms – No strong evidence of a novel strain in these classical outbreaks; these episodes are best interpreted as re‑occurrence of classical scrapie in a country with long‑standing but low‑level presence under stringent control.
Review: retain – Event appropriately characterizes Norway’s small number of classical scrapie outbreaks detected between 2001–2009, uses correct geography and time span, and classifies them as re_occurrence (resurgence of a known disease without evidence of a new strain); despite relatively modest global impact, it is reasonable to retain as one of the main post‑1990 emergence episodes for this EPP.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]
Host: Sheep (classical and atypical scrapie)
Event summary: From 2002 onward, Great Britain conducted large‑scale abattoir and fallen‑stock surveys for scrapie alongside the National Scrapie Plan, leading to greatly increased detection of both classical and newly recognised atypical scrapie compared with prior passive reporting. Over the following decade, hundreds of flocks were identified with classical scrapie and more than a hundred holdings with atypical scrapie, revealing substantial underlying infection that had previously gone largely unrecognised. Genotype‑based breeding for resistance, compulsory culling in infected flocks and continued testing progressively reduced classical scrapie incidence even as atypical cases continued to appear sporadically, illustrating shifting strain dynamics under genetic selection and control pressure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers – Strong policy and surveillance drivers (EU TSE regulations, the UK National Scrapie Plan, and public concern in the wake of BSE) produced intensive testing and PRNP‑genotype‑based breeding for resistance, as well as culling of infected flocks. Internal mechanisms – Re‑emergence dynamics shaped by host genetic selection (favouring ARR and other resistant genotypes) altered the balance between classical and atypical scrapie, and the broader recognition of atypical scrapie highlighted the diversity of circulating prion strains.
Review: review – Reclassified this episode as re_emergence only (removed re_occurrence) because scrapie was already endemic in Great Britain and the apparent rise in case numbers after 2002 was largely due to intensified active surveillance and recognition of atypical scrapie, rather than a true resurgence driven by external failures of control. Geography, time span and overall description remain appropriate, but coding now aligns more closely with the event‑type definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (atypical/Nor98‑like scrapie)
Event summary: Between 2006 and the late 2000s, the U.S. National Scrapie Eradication Program’s slaughter surveillance detected several sheep with biochemical and histopathological profiles consistent with atypical/Nor98 scrapie, representing the first recognition of this strain in North America. A 2009 report described the first six U.S. cases in detail, while enhanced surveillance in Canada subsequently identified three atypical scrapie cases reported in 2010, all occurring in older sheep and showing Nor98‑like diagnostic signatures. Following these detections, both countries incorporated atypical scrapie into national TSE surveillance definitions and risk communication, while eradication efforts continued to focus primarily on classical scrapie in sheep and goats.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence recognised in the North American context (re_emergence of the scrapie prion as an atypical/Nor98 strain in populations already affected by classical scrapie). Drivers – Expansion and refinement of U.S. and Canadian scrapie surveillance, including the deployment of rapid tests and confirmatory methods capable of detecting atypical scrapie, together with international awareness of Nor98 following its description and spread in Europe, prompted retrospective and prospective case identification.
Review: review – Updated this event to encompass the first recognised atypical/Nor98 scrapie cases in both the United States (detected since 2006) and Canada (three cases reported in 2010), extending the year range to 2006–2010 and adding Canada to the country list. Re‑coded the event as re_emergence only (removed first_detection and inter_continental_emergence) because classical scrapie was already endemic in North America and, under the scheme rules, the appearance of a new strain in an already affected continent should be treated as re_emergence rather than inter‑continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (atypical scrapie); historical background of classical scrapie in sheep
Event summary: Japan, which had recorded classical ovine scrapie outbreaks beginning in the early 1980s, identified its first case of atypical scrapie in a sheep in 2016 during active TSE surveillance using modern immunohistochemical and biochemical assays. The atypical case occurred in a flock in which overall scrapie incidence was very low but surveillance intensity was high due to national concern over prion diseases such as BSE. Following confirmation, authorities refined elements of their prion surveillance strategy, and no large‑scale epidemic of atypical scrapie has been reported, with scrapie remaining a rare diagnosis in Japanese flocks.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (first detection of atypical/Nor98‑like scrapie in Asia) and re_emergence in a country with prior classical scrapie but a long interval without major outbreaks. Drivers – Enhanced prion surveillance capacity and diagnostic technology in Japan following BSE‑related investments, and sustained testing of fallen stock and risk animals, enabled recognition of a single atypical scrapie case decades after the country’s initial classical scrapie outbreaks.
Review: review – Removed coding as first_detection, intra_continental_emergence, inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence, because scrapie (classical form) had been present in Japan and Asia since the early 1980s and the 2016 case represents the emergence of the atypical/Nor98 strain in an already affected continent. Event is now coded solely as re_emergence in line with the definitions, while geography, host and timing remain supported by the primary Japanese reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Sheep and goats (classical scrapie; large mixed‑flock epidemic)
Event summary: From the mid‑1980s and throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Cyprus experienced a major epidemic of classical scrapie in sheep and, increasingly, in goats, with disease spreading widely through mixed small‑ruminant flocks across much of the island. By the 2000s, annual case numbers in goats and sheep numbered in the hundreds to thousands, and scrapie was reported from more than 1,000 holdings, meaning roughly one fifth of all Cypriot small‑ruminant farms were affected and around 90% of EU goat scrapie cases in 2007 came from Cyprus. Intensive surveillance, large‑scale culling, movement controls, and the introduction of breeding programmes for PRNP genotypes associated with resistance gradually reduced incidence toward 2010, although many infected flocks still required long‑term management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers – High densities of mixed sheep–goat flocks, extensive within‑island animal movements, and initial lack of effective control measures allowed classical scrapie to amplify and persist at high prevalence. Internal mechanisms – Host genetic susceptibility, particularly PRNP codon 146 polymorphisms in goats that strongly influenced risk, created highly vulnerable goat populations; later, genotype‑based breeding programmes exploited protective alleles as a control tool but only after the epidemic was well established.
Review: retain – New event added to capture the long‑running, high‑prevalence classical scrapie epidemic in Cyprus, which affected >1,000 small‑ruminant holdings and accounted for around 90% of reported EU goat scrapie cases in 2007; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for the scrapie prion. Coded as re_occurrence in Western Asia (Cyprus) because it represents a large resurgence of an already present disease driven mainly by host genetics and management, without strong evidence for a novel scrapie strain.

Host: Sheep (single detected case of atypical/Nor98 scrapie)
Event summary: In 2005, TSE surveillance on sheep in the Falkland Islands identified an animal whose brain tissue showed atypical, Nor98‑like scrapie on histopathology and western blot, despite the absence of any prior reports of classical scrapie in the territory. The case was confirmed based on a distinctive low–molecular weight PrPSc band and cerebellar‑predominant lesions, and was reported as the first atypical scrapie case in the Southern Hemisphere. No additional cases or evidence of flock‑level spread were documented in subsequent years, and the event is interpreted as a rare, sporadic occurrence that nevertheless expanded the recognised geographic distribution of atypical scrapie.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence expressed as atypical/Nor98 scrapie in an otherwise classical‑scrapie‑free sheep population, with epidemiology consistent with a sporadic, poorly transmissible prion disease. Drivers – Deployment of rapid TSE tests and confirmatory methods as part of international surveillance programmes allowed detection and characterization of this single atypical case in a remote sheep‑farming territory.
Review: retain – New event introduced to represent the first reported atypical/Nor98 scrapie case in the Falkland Islands (2005), which was also the earliest Southern Hemisphere report of this strain. Classified as re_emergence (novel strain in a continent where classical scrapie had already been present for decades, e.g. Brazil) rather than inter‑continental emergence, in accordance with the rule that new strains of an existing EPP in a continent should not be coded as inter‑continental emergence.

Host: Sheep (atypical/Nor98 scrapie; isolated cases)
Event summary: In 2009, brain tissue from a New Zealand sheep submitted as presumed negative control material for European scrapie rapid‑test evaluations yielded discordant test results and was ultimately confirmed, via detailed western blotting and immunohistochemistry, as atypical/Nor98 scrapie – the first recognised scrapie case of any form in New Zealand. Subsequent active and retrospective surveillance did not reveal further cases there, and similar diagnostic approaches later identified five atypical scrapie cases in Australia described in 2016, again in older Merino or Merino‑cross sheep with cerebellar‑predominant vacuolation and Nor98‑like PrPSc signatures. These detections, although rare and without evidence of onward flock‑level transmission, demonstrated that atypical scrapie can occur sporadically even in countries considered free from classical scrapie and prompted refinement of TSE surveillance and risk communication in both New Zealand and Australia.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence of atypical/Nor98 scrapie in small but important populations historically recognised as free of classical scrapie, with epidemiology consistent with a sporadic or very low‑transmissibility prion disease. Drivers – Use of highly sensitive rapid TSE screening tests and thorough confirmatory methods in the context of international surveillance and test‑validation programmes enabled recognition of isolated atypical cases that would previously have remained undetected.
Review: retain – New combined event added to capture the first recognised occurrence of scrapie prion disease (as atypical/Nor98 scrapie) in Oceania, namely a single New Zealand case detected in 2009 and a small series of Australian cases reported in 2016. Coded as inter_continental_emergence (first occurrence of the scrapie prion in Oceania) co‑occurring with re_emergence (novel strain), which is explicitly allowed under the scheme rules; geography, timing and low‑prevalence, sporadic character are supported by the primary NZ and Australian reports.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Multiple long‑affected carp‑producing countries including (but not limited to) Germany, France, Hungary, Czechia, Poland, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Italy and others where SVCV was already endemic in carp culture and wild carp populations.
Host: Primarily common carp (Cyprinus carpio) and cultured strains (including food carp); other cyprinids and related species occasionally affected.
Event summary: From approximately 1990 through 2010, spring viraemia of carp virus caused recurrent high‑mortality outbreaks in carp aquaculture and, less frequently, wild carp fisheries across many European countries where the pathogen had been established for decades. Epizootics were most severe in intensively managed pond and reservoir systems, especially among yearling carp during spring temperature windows favourable for SVCV transmission, leading to substantial annual production losses despite improved diagnostics and control measures. Over time, enhanced farm biosecurity, surveillance, and selective breeding for more resistant carp strains helped reduce the frequency of catastrophic losses, although SVCV remains an important endemic threat in parts of Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high‑density carp aquaculture, extensive pond and reservoir systems, movements of live carp and koi between farms and countries, and spring temperature conditions (roughly 10–17 °C) that maximise SVCV replication and disease expression. Internal mechanisms: no single novel genotype is clearly linked to this period; outbreaks largely reflect ongoing circulation of established European SVCV genogroups with efficient waterborne transmission, occasionally aided by mechanical vectors such as leeches and carp lice, rather than discrete viral evolutionary shifts.
Review: retain – This row appropriately aggregates major recurrent SVC outbreaks in long‑endemic European carp aquaculture between 1990 and about 2010 and classifies them as re_occurrence only, which fits the definitions because SVCV was already widespread in all listed European subregions before 1990. No changes to geography or event types were needed; only minor text tidying (removal of inline markdown citations) was performed, while OIE and review articles remain cited in Source URLs as the main references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Brazil [1998, outbreak of spring viraemia in goldfish (Carassius auratus) in a lake in São Paulo State].
Host: Goldfish (Carassius auratus) maintained in a lake in São Paulo State, Brazil (ornamental cyprinids).
Event summary: In 1998, an outbreak of haemorrhagic disease in goldfish kept in a lake in São Paulo State, Brazil, was investigated and SVCV was identified as the causative agent, confirming spring viraemia of carp in South America for the first time. The event, which involved clinically affected goldfish likely derived from international ornamental fish trade, represented the first confirmed occurrence of SVCV in the Americas and outside its long‑recognised European range. The outbreak was controlled by culling and sanitary measures at the affected site, and no further confirmed SVCV outbreaks in Brazilian finfish have been reported, but the episode triggered increased surveillance and highlighted the risk of inter‑continental spread via ornamental fish.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international movement of ornamental cyprinids, probably from SVCV‑endemic regions, with limited pre‑import testing and biosecurity at the receiving site allowed introduction of the virus into a Brazilian lake. Internal mechanisms: the virus involved appears to belong to the classic SVCV genogroup I, with no evidence of a novel genotype; the key biological factor was SVCV’s ability to cause acute haemorrhagic disease in susceptible cyprinids introduced into naïve environments rather than viral innovation.
Review: review – New row added to capture the 1998 SVCV outbreak in goldfish in a São Paulo lake, which OIE and CFSPH identify as the first confirmed occurrence of SVCV in the Americas and thus the inter‑continental emergence of SVCV into the South America continent. Classified as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence; magnitude of fish losses is not fully quantified in accessible summaries, so key outbreak details should be cross‑checked directly against Alexandrino et al. 1998 before final use.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [2002 North Carolina koi farm; 2002 Cedar Lake, Wisconsin wild carp; 2003–2004 additional detections including wild carp in an Illinois waterway linked to Lake Michigan; 2004 Washington pet koi; 2004 Missouri farmed koi; 2007 Upper Mississippi River, Minnesota and Wisconsin wild carp]; Canada [2006 Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario wild carp].
Host: Koi carp (Cyprinus carpio koi) in ornamental/farm settings; common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in wild lakes and river systems; other North American freshwater fishes experimentally or incidentally exposed.
Event summary: In 2002, SVCV was detected for the first time in North America during a severe outbreak at a koi farm in North Carolina, where about 15,000 koi died and roughly 135,000 additional fish were culled during eradication efforts. In the same year, a major kill of wild common carp occurred in Cedar Lake, Wisconsin, and subsequent detections between 2003 and 2007 included wild carp in an Illinois water channel linked to Lake Michigan, pet and farmed koi outbreaks in Washington State and Missouri in 2004, asymptomatic infected common carp in Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario, Canada in 2006, and wild carp in the Upper Mississippi River near Minnesota and Wisconsin in 2007, indicating establishment and limited spread in wild and cultured cyprinids. Intensive surveillance, movement controls, and destruction of affected cultured stocks curtailed further spread in commercial aquaculture, though SVCV persists in some wild carp populations in the Great Lakes–Upper Mississippi basin.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in live koi and carp from endemic regions, inadequate pre‑import virological screening, and subsequent movement of infected fish within North America facilitated introduction and secondary spread of SVCV into wild and farmed cyprinid populations. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show North American isolates cluster within genogroup Ia and are closely related to Asian strains associated with Chinese ornamental fish, suggesting recent introduction from Asia; SVCV’s capacity for subclinical infection and shedding in survivor carp and broad cyprinid host range enhanced its invasive potential in novel freshwater ecosystems.
Review: review – This episode is well supported by Goodwin (2002), Dikkeboom et al. (2004), Canadian surveillance and U.S. extension/USGS summaries and clearly represents the first detection and establishment of SVCV in North America with substantial mortality and culling. Event types have been corrected so that it is coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence only (removing re_occurrence, which should not co‑occur with inter‑continental emergence); geography (USA and Canada, 2002–2007) remains accurate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [latent infections detected in ornamental carp and goldfish exported from Beijing in the late 1990s; multiple isolates from ornamental carp and koi in northern China (including Beijing/Miyun) between 2002 and 2006; first confirmed outbreak in cultivated common carp reported in 2004].
