Host: Ornamental cyprinids (including koi and related carp strains) and, from 2004, cultivated common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in Chinese aquaculture.
Event summary: In the early 2000s, SVCV was confirmed for the first time in fish in Asia when isolates genetically matching SVCV were obtained from ornamental carp and goldfish associated with Beijing and, subsequently, from ornamental carp farms in northern China between 2002 and 2006. In 2004, an SVCV outbreak was confirmed in cultivated common carp in China, and surveillance of thousands of ornamental fish demonstrated low‑prevalence but established infection in some farms, indicating that SVCV had become enzootic in parts of the Chinese ornamental and food‑fish carp sectors. Control responses focused on culling infected stocks, strengthening quarantine and movement controls for ornamental carp exports, and developing diagnostic and molecular tools to support ongoing surveillance, thereby limiting but not eliminating SVCV circulation in Chinese aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of carp and koi farming in China, dense stocking densities, and active domestic and international trade in ornamental fish created conditions for the introduction, amplification and dissemination of SVCV in East Asia. Internal mechanisms: Chinese isolates fall within genogroup Ia and are closely related to isolates from koi and goldfish exported from China and from North American outbreaks, indicating long‑distance spread via live‑fish movements of an existing lineage rather than emergence of a highly divergent novel strain; viral traits such as efficient waterborne transmission and the ability to persist subclinically in ornamental stocks underpinned establishment.
Review: review – Retained as the first confirmed detection and establishment of SVCV in Asian aquaculture, supported by OIE, PLOS ONE and Virologica Sinica reports. The start year has been adjusted from 2003 to 2002 to reflect earlier Chinese isolates from cultured carp and koi (2002–2004), and the event remains coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence because no earlier confirmed Asian field outbreaks in fish were identified. Minor text edits removed inline markdown links, relying instead on the Source URLs column.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [Khuzestan Province (Ahvaz) 2006–2007; Gilan Province (Astaneh Ashrafieh) 2006–2007, outbreaks in Indian carp farms].
Host: Indian carp species farmed in Iran – rohu (Labeo rohita), mrigal (Cirrhinus mrigala) and catla (Catla catla) in pond aquaculture.
Event summary: Between May 2006 and September 2007, mortality events in Indian carp (rohu, mrigal and catla) on farms in Khuzestan and Gilan provinces in Iran were investigated and confirmed as spring viraemia of carp by nested PCR targeting the SVCV glycoprotein gene and supporting histopathology. All sampled Indian carp from affected farms were PCR‑positive, indicating active SVCV infection in multiple carp species within these freshwater systems and representing the first documented SVCV presence in these hosts and in Iranian carp aquaculture. Control focused on improved diagnostics, on‑farm hygiene, and quarantine/isolation of infected stocks, and the findings prompted concern about further spread of SVCV within the Middle East and highlighted the need for regional surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of warm‑water carp aquaculture in Iran using dense pond systems and movements of seed and broodstock, likely including fish or eggs sourced from regions where SVCV was already present, created pathways for virus introduction into Indian carp farms. Internal mechanisms: this episode reflects both geographic range expansion within Asia from earlier foci in Eastern Europe/China into Southern Asia and host expansion of SVCV into Indian major carps, qualifying as re_emergence driven by host range extension; available data do not indicate a distinct novel genotype, but the virus showed typical SVCV genetic features.
Review: review – New row added to represent 2006–2007 SVCV outbreaks in Indian carp species in Iran, documented by Haghighi‑Khiabanian Asl et al. (2008), which provide the first confirmed SVCV detections in Iranian carp aquaculture. Classified as intra_continental_emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) and re_emergence (host expansion into Indian carps); provincial timing and any subsequent control outcomes should be double‑checked against the original article and national reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Mexico [2015, wild common carp in the Tecocomulco natural lagoon in central Mexico].
Host: Wild common carp (Cyprinus carpio) inhabiting Tecocomulco Lagoon, a natural, apparently hydrologically isolated freshwater lagoon in central Mexico.
Event summary: In October 2015, ten wild common carp showing septicaemia, exophthalmia, moderate abdominal distension and external and internal haemorrhages were collected from Tecocomulco Lagoon, a closed freshwater system in central Mexico with no previous reports of SVCV. Laboratory investigation using cell culture, semi‑nested RT‑PCR, gene sequencing and electron microscopy confirmed infection with SVCV genogroup Ia, representing the first confirmed detection of SVCV in Mexico and documenting its presence in a natural water body in Central America. Although no large‑scale fish kill was reported, the finding extended the known southern range of SVCV in the Americas and led Mexican authorities to inform SENASICA and recommend enhanced surveillance and stricter controls on carp movements and ornamental fish imports.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: the precise route of introduction into Tecocomulco Lagoon is unknown, but likely involved previous human‑mediated translocation of infected carp for stocking, movements of contaminated equipment, or introduction via susceptible ornamental cyprinids or possibly waterfowl, reflecting regional trade and stocking practices. Internal mechanisms: the Mexican isolate showed typical SVCV molecular features and clustered within genogroup Ia alongside North American and Asian isolates, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing lineage into a new subregion of the Americas rather than evolution of a novel genotype; the confined lagoon setting highlighted how even hydrologically isolated systems can harbour exotic fish viruses once introduced.
Review: review – Kept as the first confirmed detection of SVCV in Mexico, supported by the 2019 Journal of Fish Diseases case report; however, event‑type coding has been corrected. Because SVCV had already been reported from Brazil (1998) within the same South America continent, this episode is now classified as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence (new Central America subregion) rather than inter_continental_emergence. The summary also clarifies that no mass mortality was documented, and the event is important primarily for range extension.

Internal mechanisms: this outbreak reflects host expansion (spillover) of an established SVCV Ia lineage from carp into P. pingi without major detectable genomic divergence, consistent with re_emergence driven by extension of host range rather than evolution of a new genotype.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures the 2016 SVCV‑associated mass mortality event in cultured Percocypris pingi in Sichuan, China, as described by Xiao et al. No issues with geography or time span were identified, and no changes were made beyond relying on the cited Aquaculture article as the primary source.

Host: Cattle (Bos indicus and cross-bred beef and dairy cattle)
Event summary: From 2005 to about 2016, abattoir-based surveys collated by Hiko & Seifu and later meta-analyses showed bovine cysticercosis to be widely endemic across Ethiopia, with meat-inspection prevalences ranging from roughly 1.9% in Addis Ababa to around 26% in Hawassa and consistent detection in many other slaughterhouses. Published economic assessments from five local studies together reported direct losses of about 4.05 million Ethiopian Birr (≈US$0.21 million) from carcass downgrading, condemnation and human taeniasis treatment, while the authors stressed that these figures substantially underestimate the true national burden. Event summary: Between 2007 and 2014, routine meat inspection of more than 23 million cattle in Goiás, a major beef-producing state in central Brazil, showed a mean bovine cysticercosis prevalence of about 0.53%, with marked spatial clustering and significantly elevated risk in the Central mesoregion and the Goiânia microregion. (2017, Parasitology Open) and the Brazil meta-analysis: the period (2007–2014), mean prevalence (~0.53%), spatial clustering in the Central mesoregion and estimated producer losses of roughly US$9.3–11.3M all match the published data. Event summary: From 2017 to 2019, analysis of more than 6.27 million bovine carcasses slaughtered in São Paulo State found an apparent bovine cysticercosis prevalence of about 1.41%, with widespread but spatially heterogeneous distribution across mesoregions and municipalities. During these three years, detection of viable and non‑viable cysticerci at meat inspection was estimated to cost cattle farmers on the order of US$5–6 million through carcass downgrading, freezing treatment and condemnation. The period did not mark a new introduction but highlighted ongoing re-occurrence and economic relevance of T. saginata in one of Brazil’s principal export‑beef regions.

Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel genotypes or resistance; transmission dynamics reflect a stable host–parasite system whose geographic range is maintained by cattle trade and human infection reservoirs.
Review: retain – The time window (2017–2019), prevalence (~1.41% in 6.28M slaughtered cattle) and magnitude of farmer losses (~R$33M, ≈US$5.8M at contemporary exchange rates) are consistent with Comin et al. (2021, Prev Vet Med) and related conference summaries. The event is clearly a high-impact, state-wide endemic peak rather than a new incursion, so classification as re-occurrence only is appropriate. No structural changes recommended.

Host: Beef cattle supplying an export abattoir in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
Event summary: In 2019–2020, surveillance of about 70,600 cattle slaughtered by an export abattoir in Rio Grande do Sul revealed a bovine cysticercosis prevalence of roughly 3.44%, with markedly higher risk in regions including Porto Alegre, Caxias do Sul, Santa Maria, Ijuí and Passo Fundo. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Export-focused cattle production with regional clusters of intensive finishing operations, incomplete rural sanitation and persistent human taeniasis in surrounding communities created localised hotspots of environmental contamination; complex trade networks moved asymptomatically infected animals into the export slaughter chain. Internal mechanisms: no parasite changes were documented; continued circulation represents re-occurrence driven by sanitation and management shortcomings, with spatial aggregation of risk linked to cattle density, water sources and proximity to human settlements.

The original row incorrectly cited a Goiás-specific article for this event; I replaced that with the dedicated Rio Grande do Sul paper (hdl:11449/202099) and retained the Brazil meta-analysis only as general background. Event classification as re-occurrence and the basic narrative are sound, but the source correction should be checked and mirrored in any linked bibliographies.

Host: Beef and dairy cattle in Catalonia (North‑Eastern Spain)
Event summary: From March 2005 through at least 2015, routine meat inspection in Catalonia detected bovine cysticercosis every year, with apparent prevalences typically between about 0.015% and 0.02% and clear spatial clustering of infected farms. In 2005–2007, 284 infected cattle from 67 farms were recorded, and later analyses estimated that by 2013–2015 the combined annual cost of bovine cysticercosis and associated human taeniasis in Catalonia was around €155,000, dominated by meat inspection, carcass treatment and follow‑up procedures. Infection persisted at low but stable levels throughout the decade, representing a chronic re-occurrence in a high‑standard European beef industry rather than emergence in new areas.

Internal mechanisms: no novel genotypes or resistance were reported; the low‑prevalence but persistent pattern suggests a stable host–parasite interaction, with clusters linked to human population density and specific farm management practices.

(2009) and Laranjo‑González et al. (2018). I removed an unrelated Brazil-focused meta-analysis URL from this event’s sources so that only Catalonia-specific papers remain. Host: Cattle in Belgium (national beef and dairy herds)

During these years, the largest share of total economic loss fell on cattle owners, who faced about €3.4 million per year in value losses and insurance costs linked to carcass freezing, downgrading and occasional destruction, while slaughterhouses and the public health sector bore additional inspection and treatment expenses. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Longstanding but low‑level human taeniasis, historical patterns of wastewater and manure use near cattle farms, dense cattle populations and continuous trade within Belgium and neighbouring countries maintained T. saginata transmission despite modern meat inspection; economic incentives and the availability of insurance often favoured post‑slaughter management (freezing, deboning) over costly upstream investments in sanitation or behavioural change. (2018) provide robust national estimates of annual costs (≈€4.25M total, ≈€3.41M borne by animal owners) and show that bovine cysticercosis remained endemic over many years; the broader European review supports the interpretation as a long-term economic hotspot rather than new emergence. Event summary: From the early 2000s to around 2018, a series of regional studies and a national systematic review documented bovine cysticercosis as one of the most frequently detected zoonoses in Brazilian slaughterhouses, with meat-inspection prevalences typically between about 0.4% and 3–4% depending on state, abattoir and inspection sensitivity. Over this period, major beef‑producing states including Paraná, Goiás, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul and Espírito Santo reported substantial carcass downgrading, freezing and condemnation, with individual state‑level losses reaching several to over twenty million US dollars and contributing to a large cumulative national economic burden. Despite gradual improvements in meat inspection and awareness, the parasite remained entrenched across Brazil’s expanding beef supply chain, constituting a protracted, multi‑state re-occurrence episode of high national impact rather than a single local outbreak.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of Brazil’s cattle industry, complex internal animal movement patterns from high‑risk to export-oriented regions, uneven adoption of good agricultural practices, persistent gaps in rural sanitation and widespread use of surface water sources maintained extensive environmental contamination with T. saginata eggs. Rainfall patterns, seasonal agricultural labour and local human taeniasis prevalence were repeatedly identified as risk factors in state‑level analyses. The prevalence ranges, list of key states (Paraná, Goiás, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul, Espírito Santo) and description of cumulative economic impact are consistent with those sources. Host: Feedlot and slaughter cattle in commercial South African beef feedlot systems
Event summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, bovine cysticercosis was reported as the leading health problem in South African feedlot cattle, with meat-inspection data indicating prevalences high enough to make cysticercosis the dominant cause of carcass downgrading and freezing in some intensive systems. Based on these data, Giesecke (1997, cited in later work) estimated that annual losses to the South African feedlot industry alone were on the order of US$3.3 million due to condemnation, refrigeration and reduced carcass value. Although the infection had been present for decades, recognition of its major economic impact in this period prompted investigations into feedlot-specific risk factors and contributed to subsequent risk‑based control efforts, even though endemic transmission persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Highly concentrated commercial feedlot operations drawing cattle from diverse sources, combined with contamination of feed and water by human faeces (including sewage overflows and informal settlements near grazing areas), created conditions for ‘cysticercosis storms’ when batches of animals were exposed to heavy T. saginata egg contamination. Inadequate wastewater treatment and occasional use of sewage-irrigated pastures were highlighted as important risk factors. Internal mechanisms: there is no indication of parasite genetic change; the outbreaks and sustained losses reflect intense, human‑driven exposure in feedlots within an already endemic national setting, making this a re-occurrence driven by management and sanitation rather than re-emergence.
Review: review – New event added. The estimate that cysticercosis was the “top health problem” in South African feedlots with annual losses of about US$3.3M for the feedlot industry comes from Giesecke (1997), as cited in Phiri et al. (2002) and later South African feedlot risk-factor work. The temporal window (1990–1997) is approximate and intended to capture the mid‑1990s situation leading up to that estimate; it should be refined if more detailed national time-series become available. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate, as T. saginata was long-established and the high losses clearly reflect external drivers (sewage-contaminated feed/water, intensive feedlot management), not parasite change.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999]

Event summary: Around 1999, a European review drawing on UK industry data estimated that bovine cysticercosis in the United Kingdom caused losses of roughly £100 per infected carcass and about £4.0 million per year in total when condemnation, downgrading, refrigeration, handling and transport were taken into account. Although meat-inspection prevalences were low, the size and value of the national cattle herd meant that even sporadic infections translated into substantial economic costs. Subsequent UK work focused on farm-level risk factors and cattle movement networks, and while prevalence has since remained low, bovine cysticercosis continues to recur sporadically, prompting interest in risk-based meat inspection rather than reflecting any true emergence into new regions or hosts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Identified UK risk factors include cattle grazing or accessing surface water contaminated with human effluent, use of sewage sludge on farmland, proximity to camping sites and other areas with uncontrolled defecation, and complex movement of cattle through markets and finishing units, which can spread infection from a small number of heavily contaminated source farms. Internal mechanisms: studies have not demonstrated new T. saginata variants; the 1999 cost estimate reflects long‑standing endemic infection recognised under stringent meat-inspection and food-safety requirements, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by environmental contamination and animal movements.
Review: review – New event added. Laranjo‑González et al. (2016) report that costs due to bovine cysticercosis in England were estimated at about £100 per carcass and £4.0M annually in 1999, which is comparable in magnitude to the Belgian national burden and clearly among the largest quantified economic impacts globally. I set the event year to 1999 to match that estimate and used later UK case–control work only to characterise risk factors. The country/subregion coding is correct and the event is appropriately treated as a re-occurrence episode in an already endemic system, but UK specialists should confirm whether additional years or regional breakdowns warrant separate entries.

Host: Cattle in Kenya (commercial and pastoral systems)

Although T. saginata had long been present, these analyses in the 1990s crystallised awareness of cysticercosis as a major recurring constraint on the beef sector, prompting calls for improved sanitation, meat inspection and risk-factor control, while endemic transmission continued into the 2000s.

Studies identified grazing area, distance of pastures from homesteads, and deworming patterns of household members as significant risk factors for bovine infection, consistent with a cycle driven by human taeniasis and environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: there is no evidence for parasite genetic change; the mid‑1990s losses represent re-occurrence and continuing endemicity rather than emergence or re-emergence due to altered parasite biology.

Host: Sheep and goats (coenurosis – Taenia multiceps)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through at least the mid‑2010s, Taenia multiceps coenurosis remained a major endemic disease of small ruminants across parts of the Middle East and adjoining North Africa, with multiple reports documenting high prevalences and significant economic losses in sheep and goats in Türkiye, Iraq, Jordan, Egypt and Oman. Studies during this period described both acute and chronic neurological disease (‘gid’) with prevalence estimates exceeding 20% in some flocks, indicating that coenurosis was persisting or resurging at high levels despite long-standing awareness of the parasite. Control efforts based on dog deworming and management, together with culling of clinically affected animals, were implemented intermittently, but no sustained, region-wide decline of the disease has been documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of small-ruminant production without parallel improvement in dog management and deworming; large populations of semi-owned and stray dogs with access to infected offal; limited access to veterinary services in rural areas; and low farmer awareness of the dog–sheep/goat transmission cycle. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular and epidemiological data do not show distinct new T. multiceps lineages during this period; the high burden is driven mainly by husbandry and dog management rather than clear parasite evolution, so the pattern is treated as prolonged re-occurrence of a historically endemic infection rather than true re‑emergence.

Egypt is classified as Northern Africa, so the continent field has been updated to 'Asia; Africa' and the sub_regions field to 'Western Asia; Northern Africa'. Country-specific start years for Jordan and Oman were adjusted to 1996 and 1999 respectively, based on first published coenurosis reports, while Türkiye, Iraq and Egypt are left at 1990 to indicate that the infection was already present by the start of the 1990s. Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event summary: In 1997, a large abattoir and field survey in the Eastern and Southern provinces of Zambia examined over a thousand pigs and found very high prevalences of porcine cysticercosis, with around a fifth of slaughtered pigs infected by routine meat inspection and substantial proportions positive on tongue examination. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the very high prevalences reflect amplification of long-standing T. solium transmission under changing husbandry and sanitation conditions, consistent with re-occurrence of an under-recognized endemic infection rather than first emergence.

The 1997 survey in Eastern and Southern provinces of Zambia documented some of the highest reported prevalences of porcine cysticercosis worldwide and large absolute numbers of infected pigs, clearly qualifying it as a major post‑1990 animal Taenia solium event. These findings increased awareness among veterinary authorities, highlighted the role of close human–cattle contact and casual labour on farms in sustaining transmission, and informed recommendations on improving meat inspection and sanitation, although endemic transmission in rural areas has likely persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional and feedlot cattle husbandry overlapping with areas of poor human sanitation, the presence of untreated human T. saginata carriers, and limited diagnostic capacity, which had led to under-recognition of infections by meat inspection alone. Host: Cattle (feedlot beef cattle; Taenia saginata – Cysticercus bovis)
Event summary: In late 1999, feedlot cattle in Alberta, Canada, were exposed to Taenia saginata eggs, likely via fecal contamination from a human tapeworm carrier, leading to heavy Cysticercus bovis infection in one cohort. In April 2000, 11 of 139 slaughtered animals from this feedlot cohort were condemned for C. bovis infection at a United States plant, triggering traceback and investigation on both sides of the border. Follow-up work and control measures focused on improving sanitation, strengthening meat inspection and raising awareness among producers and abattoir workers, reducing apparent prevalence in some municipalities but not eliminating the parasite.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive cattle production in areas with suboptimal human sanitation and occasional free defecation leading to pasture contamination with T. saginata eggs; movement of cattle from high-risk areas to slaughter without pre-slaughter control; and limited sensitivity of routine meat inspection, which underestimates light infections and allowed sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a new strain or altered pathogenicity; the event reflects persistence and geographic expansion of cattle production into areas with poor sanitation and thus re-occurrence of a long-established parasite.
Review: Review – retain. The 2000 SIF 1710 survey in Paraná is correctly geo-referenced (South America/South America, Brazil) and appropriately coded as re-occurrence of endemic bovine cysticercosis, not first detection. It documents widespread infection and associated condemnations in a major beef-producing state and serves as an early abattoir-based benchmark. Later statewide studies (e.g. 2004–2008 in Paraná, 2009–2012 in Espírito Santo) show even greater aggregate losses; one of these (Espírito Santo 2009–2012) has been added as a new event. Depending on how strictly the final dataset is limited to the single largest episodes, this 2000 episode can be kept as important context or deprioritized.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – mainly Taenia solium, with possible contribution from other Taenia spp.)
Event summary: By the early 2000s, fragmented data suggested that porcine cysticercosis persisted in parts of Eastern Europe despite prior control efforts. In 2003, official veterinary reports from Poland recorded 4,487 porcine cysticercosis cases detected at slaughter, representing an unusually high burden for the region. Subsequent years showed a decline in reported numbers, interpreted as the combined result of improved meat inspection and control measures, changes in pig production systems and possibly underreporting, while low-level transmission likely continued in backyard and smallholder herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistence of backyard and smallholder pig production with poor sanitation and lack of controlled housing, allowing pigs access to human feces; incomplete surveillance and inconsistencies in meat inspection and reporting in earlier years that had masked the scale of endemic infection. Internal mechanisms: No specific evidence of a novel T. solium genotype or altered virulence; the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence or renewed recognition of a large endemic focus rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: Review – retain. The 2003 Polish episode is supported by official veterinary notification data collated in a systematic review and represents an exceptionally large number of porcine cysticercosis cases for Europe. It is correctly coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic country (Europe/Eastern Europe, Poland), without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, and the chosen source (systematic review of taeniosis/cysticercosis in Eastern Europe) is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (bovine cysticercosis – Taenia saginata, Cysticercus bovis)
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2012, analysis of records from federal and state‑inspected slaughterhouses in Espírito Santo State, Brazil, showed that bovine cysticercosis remained a significant sanitary and economic problem. Out of roughly 1.34 million cattle slaughtered in the period, just under 1% were condemned or partially condemned for Cysticercus bovis, resulting in more than 1.5 million kilograms of beef being rejected and direct financial losses on the order of 9 million Brazilian reais. The burden was greater during the rainy season and concentrated in particular municipalities, prompting subsequent spatial risk-mapping work and reinforcing the need for improved sanitation and control of human taeniasis to safeguard the beef industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High cattle densities in municipalities with inadequate household sewage coverage, reliance on surface water and flood‑prone pastures contaminated by human feces from untreated T. saginata carriers, and incomplete control of human tapeworm infection and rural sanitation. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel T. saginata lineages or altered pathogenicity; the event reflects re-occurrence and spatial clustering of a long‑established parasite under favourable environmental and sanitation conditions, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review – added as a new event. The 2009–2012 slaughterhouse analysis from Espírito Santo documented very large absolute economic losses from bovine cysticercosis (over 1.5 million kg of beef condemned and about 9 million BRL in direct losses) and directly informed spatial risk-mapping and control planning for the state. It is correctly geo-coded (South America/South America, Brazil) and classified as re-occurrence in a country where bovine cysticercosis has long been endemic, with no evidence of new strains or inter‑continental spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event summary: Using epidemiological and economic data from across the United Republic of Tanzania, a national burden-of-disease assessment estimated the societal cost of Taenia solium taeniasis/cysticercosis for the year 2012. Modelling suggested that roughly 12% of the national pig population—on the order of 180,000 animals—were infected with porcine cysticercosis, leading to potential production losses of around US$2.8 million in that year, alongside a much larger human health burden from neurocysticercosis-associated epilepsy. The study’s findings highlighted T. solium as a major public health and agricultural problem and spurred calls for a national One Health control strategy integrating human, pig and environmental interventions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of smallholder pig production with predominantly free-ranging husbandry, low latrine coverage and open defecation allowing pigs access to human feces, backyard slaughter and informal pork markets with little veterinary inspection, and limited access to anthelmintic treatment for both humans and pigs. Internal mechanisms: No specific new parasite genotypes or heightened virulence were identified; the high burden is attributed to social, economic and husbandry factors, so the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence of a long‑established infection rather than true re‑emergence.
Review: Review – added as a new event. The 2012 national assessment for Tanzania estimated that porcine cysticercosis affected on the order of 180,000 pigs (about 11–12% of the herd) and caused pig production losses of approximately US$2.8 million in a single year, making it one of the largest well-quantified animal-sector Taenia solium events globally in the post‑1990 period. It is correctly coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic country (Africa/Eastern Africa, United Republic of Tanzania) with no evidence for new parasite strains or new continental spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event summary: A national economic evaluation for Mexico using 2015 data estimated the monetary burden of Taenia solium cysticercosis by combining epidemiologic information with cost data for both human disease and animal production. The study concluded that cysticercosis imposed overall societal costs exceeding US$200 million annually, of which roughly US$19.5 million were attributable to porcine cysticercosis through carcass condemnation and price reductions for infected pigs. These findings underscored that, despite long-standing awareness and partial control, porcine cysticercosis continues to generate major economic losses for the Mexican pig industry and provided quantitative justification for renewed investment in integrated control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistence of traditional pig-rearing systems in many rural regions with free-ranging or backyard pigs, inadequate sanitation and sewage infrastructure, incomplete coverage and enforcement of meat inspection (particularly in informal slaughter), and ongoing human taeniasis maintaining environmental contamination with T. solium eggs. Internal mechanisms: The study did not implicate any novel parasite variants; the large losses reflect the scale of endemic transmission and its economic impact rather than evolutionary change, so the event is classified as re-occurrence in a long‑affected country.
Review: Review – added as a new event because the 2015 national cost-of-illness study for Mexico quantified very large annual losses due to porcine cysticercosis (around US$19.5 million), in addition to substantial human health costs, making it one of the highest documented animal-sector burdens for Taenia solium worldwide. Coded as re-occurrence in an already highly endemic country (South America/Central America, Mexico) with no evidence of new parasite strains or spread to a new continent. Geography follows the UNSD-based Country sheet, where Mexico is grouped under the South America continent and Central America sub-region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses (mares on affected studs)
Event summary: In 2001, Türkiye reported its first confirmed occurrence of contagious equine metritis when Taylorella equigenitalis was isolated from infertile or endometritic mares during routine screening and outbreak investigation, representing the first recognised presence of CEM in the country within the Asian continent. The outbreak appeared to be confined to one or a few studs, with infection detected by culture from genital swabs and managed through treatment of positive mares and movement controls on breeding animals. Follow‑up testing did not reveal widespread dissemination, and available reports suggest the episode was limited in scale compared with large outbreaks elsewhere.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of a carrier breeding animal through international horse trade from CEM‑affected European countries into Turkish studs, combined with limited pre‑import or pre‑breeding screening at the time, facilitated the first recognised establishment of Taylorella equigenitalis in Türkiye. Internal mechanisms: Venereal transmission during natural service and the ability of T. equigenitalis to persist in the genital tract of infected mares and stallions without obvious clinical signs underpinned local spread, but no novel strain, host shift or resistance pattern was reported for this event.
Review: review – Event is real and should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 occurrences because it documents the first confirmed detection of CEM in Türkiye and Western Asia. However, according to the event‑type definitions, 'first_detection' refers to the first detection in the host system globally (which occurred in the UK in 1977), not the first detection in an individual country. I therefore changed first_detection from true to false and left intra_continental_emergence as true to reflect spread of an already known pathogen into a new Asian sub‑region. I also replaced generic review‑style URLs with the specific Vet Record case report (Ozgur et al. 2001) and a molecular epidemiology review that explicitly cites this first Turkish isolation as the main sources for this event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses (Lipizzaner stallions; limited exposed mares)
Event summary: In 2006, contagious equine metritis was re‑introduced into the United States when several imported Lipizzaner stallions housed at a breeding and research facility in Wisconsin were found culture‑positive for Taylorella equigenitalis during breeding soundness examinations and follow‑up testing. Trace‑back investigations showed that infection was confined to a small number of imported stallions and a limited group of mares, with no evidence of wider spread into the domestic Thoroughbred or Quarter Horse sectors. Federal and state authorities implemented quarantine, testing and treatment of all infected and exposed horses, and the outbreak was declared eradicated, allowing the United States to regain CEM‑free status prior to the larger 2008–2010 incident.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International movement of high‑value breeding horses from endemic European regions, combined with imperfect pre‑export and post‑import testing protocols, allowed carrier Lipizzaner stallions to enter the United States and introduce T. equigenitalis into a previously CEM‑free population. Internal mechanisms: Chronic, asymptomatic colonisation of stallions and efficient venereal transmission to mares enabled silent carriage and limited spread before detection, but there is no evidence that this event involved a novel, more virulent or resistant strain compared with other European isolates.
Review: retain – The 2006 Lipizzaner‑associated incident in Wisconsin is well documented in U.S. reviews and technical factsheets and represents an important re‑introduction of CEM prior to the major 2008–2010 outbreak. Event year, country (United States), and classification as a re‑occurrence following earlier eradication are consistent with WOAH notifications and U.S. summaries. No corrections were needed beyond tightening sources to focus on the JAS review, CFSPH disease card and a 2006 foreign‑animal‑disease bulletin that describe this specific episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [2008]; widespread exposure across 48 U.S. states by 2010
Host: Horses (stallions, mares, one gelding; multiple breeds)
Event summary: In December 2008, a Quarter Horse stallion in Kentucky tested culture‑positive for Taylorella equigenitalis during semen‑export testing, triggering investigation of what became the largest recorded contagious equine metritis outbreak in the United States. From late 2008 through 2010, federal and state authorities traced and tested roughly 1,000 exposed horses in 48 states, ultimately confirming 22 infected stallions, one gelding and five mares as T. equigenitalis‑positive carriers, all epidemiologically linked to a Fjord stallion imported from Europe in 2000. After extensive quarantine, standardized genital treatment and repeated negative testing of all infected and exposed animals, the outbreak was declared eradicated and the U.S. again considered CEM‑free, although the event highlighted the vulnerability of artificial insemination networks to silent dissemination from a single carrier horse.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread use of artificial insemination and shipped cooled semen, together with lapses in hygiene and incomplete screening of breeding stallions, enabled a single imported carrier stallion to disseminate Taylorella equigenitalis widely via semen distribution and shared handling equipment. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of T. equigenitalis in asymptomatic stallions and some mares, efficient venereal transmission and the organism's ability to survive in semen and on breeding equipment underpinned the large geographic footprint of the outbreak; molecular typing showed that U.S. isolates from this incident were closely related but did not identify a uniquely more virulent or resistant strain.
Review: retain – This multi‑state U.S. outbreak is clearly one of the most impactful modern CEM events, with detailed peer‑reviewed documentation of case numbers, geographic spread and control measures. The existing event narrative correctly reflects the scale (about 1,000 exposed horses across 48 states with 28 culture‑positive animals) and its classification as a major re‑occurrence rather than a new continental emergence. I retained the event as written, keeping the key Preventive Veterinary Medicine investigation, the Equine Veterinary Journal review and official U.S. extension materials as primary sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Portugal [2008]; Germany (source country of the imported stallion) [2008, source only]
Host: Horses (stallions and mares at a single Lusitano stud farm)
Event summary: In 2008, Portugal documented its first outbreak of contagious equine metritis when a Lusitano stallion recently imported from Germany and two mares at the same stud farm tested positive for Taylorella equigenitalis on routine pre‑breeding examination. Comprehensive testing of all 30 equids on the premises identified four additional infected horses (three mares and one stallion), but no evidence of spread beyond the affected stud or into the wider Portuguese horse population. All culture‑positive animals underwent standard topical treatment and repeated culture testing, and subsequent national surveillance of more than 2,000 genital swabs from other farms failed to detect further cases, indicating this was a self‑limited introduction event.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing international trade in Lusitano horses and importation of a breeding stallion from Germany with a false‑negative or incomplete CEM status provided the pathway for introduction of Taylorella equigenitalis into Portugal, while concentration of breeding at a single stud and initial lack of comprehensive screening allowed several additional horses to become infected before detection. Internal mechanisms: The ability of T. equigenitalis to persist in carrier stallions and mares with mainly subclinical or transient infertility favoured silent spread within the stud prior to testing, but no new genotype, host jump or antimicrobial resistance pattern was reported in relation to this episode.
Review: review – This event accurately captures Portugal’s first confirmed CEM outbreak and should be retained as a key intra‑continental emergence in Southern Europe. However, in line with the event‑type definitions, I changed first_detection from true to false because global first detection occurred in 1977 in the UK; the Portuguese episode instead represents spread of an established pathogen into a previously unaffected country within Europe, appropriately coded as intra_continental_emergence. I also simplified the sub_regions field to Southern Europe and left Germany only in the countries field as the epidemiological source, and focused the sources on the Open Veterinary Journal case report (including its PMC version), which provides the primary quantitative description of this outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses (stallions and mares in Lipizzaner and sport‑horse populations)
Event summary: In May 2011, South Africa, previously considered free of contagious equine metritis, reported its first confirmed cases of Taylorella equigenitalis infection to the World Organisation for Animal Health after detection of CEM in stallions at an artificial breeding centre in Gauteng, with epidemiological evidence pointing to introduction via Lipizzaner or Warmblood stallions imported from Europe in the late 1990s. National stallion‑screening and extensive tracing during 2011–2012 identified at least 43 PCR‑ or culture‑positive horses on the index premises and 12 additional properties across three provinces, revealing that T. equigenitalis had silently persisted for years within a closed Lipizzaner population before being disseminated more widely through assisted reproduction and fomites. All infected and exposed horses were quarantined, treated according to WOAH‑aligned protocols and repeatedly re‑tested, and, with industry cooperation, the outbreak was brought under control, although South Africa continues to treat CEM as a controlled disease with ongoing surveillance and import screening.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑standing importation of Lipizzaner and Warmblood stallions from endemic European regions, combined with limited early surveillance and later adoption of artificial insemination and other assisted reproductive techniques, allowed Taylorella equigenitalis to establish a hidden reservoir in a closed Lipizzaner population and then spread horizontally via contaminated breeding equipment and management practices. Internal mechanisms: Persistent, asymptomatic carriage in stallions and some mares, efficient venereal and fomite transmission, and the ability of particular clonal lineages to circulate for many years without obvious clinical signs underpinned the scale of the South African outbreak, but available molecular typing suggests introduction of existing European genotypes rather than in situ evolution of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: review – This multi‑premises South African outbreak was missing from the original dataset but clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful post‑1990 CEM events: it represents the first confirmed occurrence of Taylorella equigenitalis in Africa, involved dozens of infected horses across multiple provinces and is repeatedly highlighted in major reviews as a paradigm‑changing episode linked to artificial reproduction. I added this new event row, classified it as inter_continental_emergence (first establishment of CEM in Africa) rather than re‑occurrence, and based the summary and scale on South African veterinary reports, anipedia’s detailed chapter and international surveillance summaries. This row should be retained but reviewed by domain experts for any desired adjustment to case counts or the exact end year of the linked episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]
Host: Horses (non‑Thoroughbred mares and a stallion)
Event summary: On 28 March 2012, Defra confirmed Taylorella equigenitalis infection in a retired 15‑year‑old Thoroughbred mare in Gloucestershire after a voluntary pre‑breeding clitoral swab tested positive by PCR and culture, marking the first UK isolation of the contagious equine metritis organism in many years and occurring outside the regulated Thoroughbred sector. Epidemiological tracing led to identification of further contacts, and CEM was subsequently detected on a second premises in a non‑Thoroughbred mare and a non‑Thoroughbred stallion; overall, four horses on two premises were confirmed positive while several traced in‑contacts tested negative under restriction. All infected horses underwent treatment and repeated testing under the Horserace Betting Levy Board Code of Practice, affected premises remained under movement restrictions until all equidae tested negative, and the incident was considered resolved later that year without spill‑over into the UK Thoroughbred breeding population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of Taylorella equigenitalis into non‑Thoroughbred horses via artificial insemination with semen from imported European stallions, together with lower levels of routine CEM screening in some non‑Thoroughbred sectors compared with regulated Thoroughbred studs, allowed silent carriage to develop before detection. Internal mechanisms: Long‑term asymptomatic carriage in stallions and subclinical infection in mares enabled venereal and possibly fomite‑mediated transmission within and between a small number of premises, but available reports do not indicate emergence of a novel or more virulent genotype; rather, this episode exemplifies the risk posed by established T. equigenitalis lineages when biosecurity and screening are suboptimal.
Review: review – This 2012 UK outbreak, involving four confirmed CEMO‑positive horses on two premises and documented in the DEFRA/AHT/BEVA Equine Quarterly Disease Surveillance Report and later UK reviews, was not present in the original JSON but is repeatedly highlighted in the scientific literature as a key example of CEM associated with artificial reproduction in non‑Thoroughbreds. I added it as a distinct re‑occurrence event (not an intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) because CEM had been present in the UK since 1977 and in the same Northern Europe sub‑region. The new row should be retained, but details such as the exact number of traced in‑contacts could be refined if more granular UK surveillance data are integrated later.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses (primarily Icelandic and Fjord breeds)
Event summary: From 2019 through 2023, Denmark recorded multiple cases of Taylorella equigenitalis infection in horses, with contagious equine metritis recognised as the only WOAH‑listed equine disease present in the country during this period and 16 cases confirmed in 2023 alone, mainly in Icelandic and Fjord breeds. These detections, arising in breeding populations monitored through CEM surveillance linked to stud activity and international trade, represented a renewed and more sustained occurrence of CEM in Denmark following earlier sporadic isolations in 2001–2003. Danish authorities revised national procedures for handling CEM‑positive horses in 2023, imposing mandatory treatment, movement restrictions and a prohibition on breeding use until infected animals had completed prescribed treatment and three consecutive series of negative tests, contributing to declining annual case numbers after 2020 and apparent containment within monitored subpopulations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing intra‑European movement and breeding of horses, particularly in Nordic leisure and native breeds, together with increased surveillance that both detected and clustered cases, maintained a background risk of re‑introduction and local circulation of Taylorella equigenitalis. Internal mechanisms: Chronic or subclinical carriage in stallions and some mares, with efficient venereal transmission, allowed persistent low‑level circulation and occasional flare‑ups; there is no evidence from available data that these Danish cases were associated with a distinct, more virulent or resistant strain compared with other European T. equigenitalis populations.
Review: review – The Danish 2019–2023 series is well supported by national 'Animal Health in Denmark' reports and is large enough (including 16 cases in 2023) to warrant inclusion as a major modern episode in a previously affected country. I retained the event but clarified in the summary that Denmark had documented T. equigenitalis in 2001–2003, so this episode is correctly coded as a re‑occurrence rather than a first detection or intra‑continental emergence. I also noted the specific breeds affected and kept Denmark as a single‑country, multi‑year linked episode, which aligns with the guidance for recurrent, epidemiologically continuous events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2021]
Host: Horses (stallion and in‑contact mares)
Event summary: On 9 June 2021, a stallion at an equine premises in Devon, United Kingdom, tested positive for Taylorella equigenitalis, initiating a small cluster of contagious equine metritis cases in West Devon in a country where the disease had first been described in the 1970s. National notifiable‑disease surveillance and application of the Horserace Betting Levy Board CEM Code of Practice led to tracing and testing of in‑contact mares and linked breeding premises, with three CEM cases ultimately confirmed in West Devon during this episode. Affected horses were placed under movement restrictions, removed from breeding, treated and repeatedly re‑tested until negative, and the event was managed as a localised re‑occurrence with no evidence of widespread dissemination beyond the involved premises.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued live‑cover breeding and importation of non‑Thoroughbred breeding stock from mainland Europe, where CEM remains endemic in some populations, sustain a low‑level risk of CEMO incursion into the UK despite long‑standing control codes and surveillance. Internal mechanisms: As in previous outbreaks, asymptomatic stallion carriage and efficient venereal and procedure‑related transmission account for the risk of sporadic flare‑ups; available evidence does not indicate that this 2021 cluster involved a novel strain, host shift or resistance that would justify classification as re‑emergence.
Review: review – This 2021 Devon cluster is a documented, recent UK re‑occurrence and is small but still within the likely top 10 modern CEM events for this pathogen, given the overall rarity of sizeable outbreaks since 1990. I kept the event but slightly expanded the summary to align with GOV.UK updates indicating three confirmed cases in West Devon, and I maintained its classification purely as re_occurrence (not intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence), because CEM has long been established in the UK and Northern Europe. The VetTimes article was added as an additional contextual source since it summarises recent UK experience with CEM under the industry‑led protocol.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [2024]; positive horses on premises in Florida, Iowa, Maine, Maryland, North Carolina and South Carolina, with exposed horses traced and quarantined in additional states
Host: Horses (domestic ponies, riding horses and draft horses; predominantly geldings with some stallions and mares)
Event summary: In May 2024, the U.S. National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed Taylorella equigenitalis infection in an 11‑year‑old pony mare and subsequently in pony stallions on a farm in Orange County, Florida, revealing the first U.S. detection of CEM since the 2008–2010 outbreak and an infection that retrospective tracing showed had been present on the index farm since at least 2017. Intensive testing through late 2024 and early 2025 identified a total of 53 T. equigenitalis‑positive horses, including ponies, riding horses and draft horses, with 41 cases on the index farm and additional positive geldings on multiple trace‑out premises in Florida, Iowa, Maine, Maryland, North Carolina and South Carolina, while exposed horses in several other states were quarantined and tested. All infected and exposed horses were placed under regulatory quarantine, treated with standard genital cleansing and antimicrobial protocols and repeatedly re‑tested; by April 2025 most positive animals had cleared infection and further tracing was ongoing, but the outbreak appeared to be confined to a defined network linked to the original Florida premises.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term undetected carriage of T. equigenitalis in geldings and stallions on a Florida farm, combined with shared semen‑collection and sheath‑cleaning equipment, movement of horses off the property over several years and limited suspicion of CEM in non‑breeding geldings, allowed the organism to circulate silently from at least 2017 until detected in 2024. Internal mechanisms: The capacity of Taylorella equigenitalis to persist for years in asymptomatic male horses and to spread via contaminated equipment rather than overt breeding activity, together with genomic evidence that the incident isolates form a distinct clade not matching earlier U.S. outbreaks, underpinned this large re‑occurrence, although there is no current indication of increased virulence compared with other strains.
Review: review – This Florida‑centred, multi‑state outbreak detected in 2024 and still under investigation in 2025 was entirely absent from the original dataset but clearly ranks among the most consequential post‑1990 CEM events, with 53 confirmed positive horses and extensive interstate tracing. I added it as a re_occurrence event in a country previously affected by CEM, using the USDA APHIS incident summary as the primary quantitative source and a Florida state FAQ as supporting context. The event should be retained, but the end year and final case counts will need updating once the U.S. investigation is formally closed.

Countries: Belarus [1996], Ukraine [1996], Latvia [1997], Republic of Moldova [2002], Romania [2002], Russian Federation [2004]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) in commercial and backyard systems
Event summary: From 1996 to 2005, multiple outbreaks of teschovirus encephalomyelitis were reported to WOAH/OIE from Eastern European countries including Belarus, Ukraine, Latvia, Republic of Moldova, Romania and the Russian Federation, indicating renewed clinical circulation of neuroinvasive porcine teschoviruses in regions where the virus had historically circulated but had become rare. The outbreaks caused neurologic disease and paresis/paralysis in pigs on affected farms but remained limited to local or national scales rather than continent‑wide epizootics. Control relied mainly on culling affected groups, movement control and improved biosecurity, after which reports of new severe outbreaks declined.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑Soviet restructuring of the pig sector, variable veterinary services, increasing pig densities in some areas, and gaps in biosecurity likely contributed to renewed expression of endemic teschoviruses as clinical disease. Internal mechanisms: No single novel serotype was consistently implicated; available data suggest resurgence of existing neuroinvasive PTV‑1 or related strains rather than emergence of a new genotype.
Review: retain – Well supported by WOAH/OIE listings summarised in the Teschovirus review, including the same countries and approximate years; correctly classified as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic European region without evidence for a novel genotype driving the episode.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7123469/))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs in smallholder and backyard systems
Event summary: Between 1996 and 2005, outbreaks of teschovirus encephalomyelitis were reported from Madagascar and Uganda, reflecting renewed clinical expression of Teschen‑like disease in African pig populations where severe teschovirus encephalomyelitis had already been documented in the mid‑20th century. Affected village and smallholder pigs showed neurologic signs consistent with classical Teschen disease, but available reports provide limited quantitative data on herd‑level morbidity and mortality. After targeted local control measures and improvements in surveillance, no large, sustained continent‑wide wave of outbreaks was reported beyond the early 2000s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and gradual intensification of pig production in parts of Eastern Africa, low baseline immunity in younger pigs, and limited biosecurity and diagnostic capacity likely contributed to renewed detection and spread of virulent PTV strains. Internal mechanisms: Historical reports indicate Teschen disease was already established in Madagascar by the 1950s, and no clearly novel genotype was described in the 1996–2005 episodes, so these events are best interpreted as re‑occurrence of existing virulent PTV‑1–like strains rather than first emergence or new strain evolution.
Review: review – Classification corrected: historical sources document major Teschen disease outbreaks in Madagascar in the 1940s–1950s, so these 1996–2005 episodes are not first detections or inter‑continental emergence for Africa but re‑occurrence in previously affected countries. Updated event types to set first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to false and re_occurrence to true; event remains among the major modern African episodes but timing and case counts should be checked against full WOAH archives.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/bavf_0001-4192_1951_num_104_4_12333))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs in intensive and mixed production systems
Event summary: Around 2000–2004, clinically apparent teschovirus encephalomyelitis was reported from several East Asian locations: outbreaks in Taiwan in 2000 and 2004, an outbreak in Japan in 2002, and the first recognized PTV‑associated neurologic disease in pigs in mainland China in 2003. These events confirmed that neuroinvasive PTV strains were causing disease in East Asian pig herds where subclinical circulation had likely been present for years. After enhanced diagnostics and improved biosecurity, severe Teschen‑like disease became sporadic in East Asia, although later severe outbreaks due to specific serotypes reappeared in China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of pig production, increasing pig densities and movements within East Asia, and improved laboratory capacity for viral diagnostics together favored both spread and recognition of clinical teschovirus encephalomyelitis. Internal mechanisms: While early reports did not always assign serotype, subsequent work from the region documents multiple PTV serotypes and genetic diversity, but these early‑2000s outbreaks are best interpreted as clinical expression of existing PTV‑1 and PTV‑2 lineages rather than emergence of a new species‑level taxon.
Review: review – Updated the country list and timing to distinguish Taiwan [2000, 2004], Japan [2002] and the first recognised PTV‑associated neurologic disease in mainland China [2003], in line with WOAH listings and later Chinese virology studies. The event is still classified as re‑occurrence (PTV already widespread in Asia) rather than intra‑continental emergence; human curator should verify exact country names versus the project’s Country sheet (especially treatment of Taiwan).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7123469/))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs on commercial farms in western Canada
Event summary: From 2002 through approximately 2008, a small number of pig farms in western Canada reported 4–7‑week‑old pigs with bilateral hind‑end paresis or paralysis; necropsy revealed nonsuppurative polioencephalomyelitis centered in the brainstem and spinal cord. Virologic workup excluded other neurotropic swine pathogens and confirmed porcine teschovirus infection in central nervous tissues, representing the first confirmed teschovirus encephalomyelitis cases in Canada, with low within‑herd morbidity but high case fatality among clinically affected pigs. Control focused on culling affected groups, strengthening biosecurity and monitoring, and no large regional epizootic was documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Commercial intensification, movements of young pigs between sow, nursery and finisher sites, and lack of prior herd‑level immunity to virulent PTV‑1 strains likely allowed sporadic emergence of severe disease on a subset of farms. Internal mechanisms: The clinical pattern suggests introduction or amplification of neuroinvasive PTV‑1 variants into partially susceptible herds; although the precise genotype is incompletely described, this episode reflects re‑emergence of severe clinical teschovirus encephalomyelitis in a new national setting rather than a new species‑level agent.
Review: review – Corrected the event period from a single year (2011) to 2002–2008, matching the retrospective Canadian case series and the CFSPH summary that places most outbreaks between 2002 and 2008; updated the event summary to remove the implication that this was the first North American occurrence after Haiti. The event remains among the major modern teschovirus episodes but is a multi‑year, low‑morbidity cluster rather than a single 2011 outbreak.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21398466/))

Host: Backyard pigs of various ages in smallholder systems
Event summary: In February–March 2009, a large outbreak of severe teschovirus encephalomyelitis occurred in backyard pigs in the Lower Artibonite Valley and Lower Plateau regions of Haiti, with around 1,500 pigs affected and approximately 40% dying or being euthanized; morbidity approached 60% with prominent posterior ataxia progressing to paresis and paralysis, and laboratory testing confirmed PTV‑1 while ruling out classical and African swine fever. Subsequent investigations and serologic surveys showed that the same or closely related PTV‑1 strains were also present in pigs with neurologic signs in adjacent regions of the Dominican Republic, indicating spread of the outbreak within the island of Hispaniola. The epidemic was eventually curtailed through community awareness campaigns, movement restrictions and loss or sale of affected pigs, and is regarded as the first appearance of the severe Teschen‑like form of teschovirus encephalomyelitis in the Americas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a virulent PTV‑1 strain into largely naive backyard pig populations with low biosecurity, frequent uncontrolled animal movements between villages and across the Haiti–Dominican Republic border, and limited veterinary infrastructure facilitated explosive spread and delayed diagnosis and control. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that the Haitian and Dominican viruses were closely related neurovirulent PTV‑1 variants associated with unusually high morbidity and mortality, representing a re‑emergence of a classic Teschen‑like phenotype in a new geographic region; increased virulence/pathogenicity and efficient faeco‑oral transmission in naive pigs likely underpinned the high impact.
Review: review – Expanded the country list to include the Dominican Republic, which molecular and serologic studies show was affected by the same Hispaniola PTV‑1 epidemic, and clarified that the event represents the first appearance of the severe Teschen‑like form—not of PTV in general—in the Americas. Kept classification as re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence because a virulent PTV‑1 strain exploited low herd immunity and poor biosecurity, but did not label it as inter‑continental emergence since PTV was already present in the region and the Dominican cases are epidemiologically linked to the Haitian outbreak.([digitalcommons.unl.edu](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/zoonoticspub/186/))

Host: Weanling and growing pigs on commercial Dutch farms; likely domestic pigs with possible wild boar exposure
Event summary: In 2014–2015, two Dutch pig farms experienced outbreaks of neurologic disease in weanling pigs characterized by non‑suppurative encephalomyelitis without other major lesions, and virological investigations identified porcine teschoviruses as the sole consistent agents in affected central nervous tissues. Sequencing showed that the causative viruses were novel strains closely related to PTV serotypes 3 and 11 but forming distinct genotypes within Teschovirus A, and epidemiologic evidence strongly implicated them as the cause of the clinical outbreaks. Following heightened awareness, biosecurity measures and herd‑level management changes, similar severe outbreaks remained sporadic, although the study underscored ongoing emergence of new neuroinvasive PTV strains in Western Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density commercial pig production, pig and semen movement between herds, and increased diagnostic scrutiny of unexplained polioencephalomyelitis facilitated both emergence and recognition of these outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated that the Dutch strains were novel genotypes within PTV‑3 and PTV‑11 lineages, consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence and increased neurotropism/virulence compared with many endemic, subclinical PTV strains.
Review: review – Adjusted the event period from 2014–2017 to 2014–2015 to match the Dutch case series and CFSPH summary that place the outbreaks in 2014–2015; otherwise the description and classification as re‑emergence of novel neuroinvasive PTV genotypes in a previously affected continent are appropriate.([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7014746/))

Host: 6–7‑week‑old growing pigs in two commercial herds in Spain

Approximately 20% of pigs in affected batches developed clinical signs and case fatality among sick pigs approached 60%, making this one of the highest‑mortality PTV outbreaks reported since the mid‑20th‑century European epizootics; after diagnosis, enhanced biosecurity and management measures were implemented and the outbreaks subsided.

Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis showed that the virus represented a distinct serotype (PTV‑13), consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence; the unusually high mortality and severe neurologic signs indicate increased virulence and neurotropism relative to many endemic PTV strains.

Host: Suckling piglets and young pigs on a large‑scale commercial farm in Henan Province
Event summary: In June 2020, a severe disease outbreak struck a large‑scale pig farm in Henan Province, China, initially affecting suckling piglets, which showed severe diarrhea, lethargy, locomotor ataxia, nystagmus, hind‑limb paralysis and coma; mortality among suckling pigs reached about 38%, which is remarkably high for porcine teschovirus infections. After diagnosis, affected cohorts were culled or managed with supportive care and strict biosecurity, and the outbreak subsided, but the event highlighted the capacity of emergent PTV‑2 variants to cause high‑mortality encephalomyelitis in modern Chinese herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑throughput pig production with dense, highly susceptible piglet populations and frequent internal animal movements facilitated rapid dissemination of the novel PTV‑2 strain, while limited prior immunity to this genotype likely exacerbated losses. Internal mechanisms: Genome and capsid analyses showed that the HeNZ1 strain was genetically distinct from previously described PTV‑2 isolates and associated with unusually high mortality, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence combined with increased virulence/neurotropism and effective evasion of host innate immune responses.
Review: review – Corrected the event year from 2023 to 2020 and specified Henan Province as the location, in line with the outbreak description in the original BMC Veterinary Research article; classification as a high‑mortality re‑emergence event driven by a novel PTV‑2 strain is appropriate and supported by molecular and clinical data.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9810521/))

Host: Nursery and growing pigs on a commercial swine farm in southern Brazil
Event summary: On a piglet production farm unit in southern Brazil with about 1,200 weaned piglets, an outbreak of neurologic disease occurred in which approximately 40 piglets showed motor incoordination, paresis and paralysis of the hind limbs, evolving over about 4 days. Histologic examination revealed nonsuppurative encephalomyelitis and ganglioneuritis, and molecular analysis of central nervous system, cerebrospinal fluid and feces identified Teschovirus A in all CNS samples, with frequent co‑detection of porcine sapelovirus A and enterovirus G. This case series represents the first detailed report of severe swine polioencephalomyelitis associated with PTV infection in South America, and after diagnostic confirmation, adjustments to herd management and biosecurity reduced clinical cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased intensification of swine production in southern Brazil, high nursery pig density, and co‑circulation of multiple enteric neurotropic viruses likely contributed to the occurrence of clinical polioencephalomyelitis; movement of weaned pigs between units may have helped disseminate infection within the farm. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing showed the PTV detected in CNS tissues was closely related to PTV‑6, and its clear association with neurologic disease indicates re‑emergence of a neurotropic PTV strain in a region where infections are usually subclinical; coinfections with sapelovirus and enterovirus G may have enhanced pathogenicity via synergistic tissue damage or modulation of host immunity.
Review: review – Updated the event year from an imprecise 2014–2016 range to 2021 and clarified that this represents the first well‑documented severe PTV‑associated polioencephalomyelitis in South America, based on the Brazilian case report and SHIC/CFSPH summaries; the event remains appropriate to include among major global episodes given its novelty for the continent, but herd‑level scale is modest.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34024036/))

Host: Commercial pigs (including suckling piglets) in western Chinese production regions (Gansu)
Event summary: In 2022, a pig farm in Gansu Province, western China, experienced an outbreak characterized by diarrhea with high mortality, respiratory distress, paralysis and neurologic signs in piglets, prompting virome analysis of diarrheic samples. A porcine teschovirus strain belonging to genotype 5 was enriched and subsequently isolated; experimental infections demonstrated that this PTV‑5 variant caused severe interstitial pneumonia, watery diarrhea, paralysis and high mortality in challenged pigs, confirming a highly pathogenic phenotype. After recognition of the new strain and implementation of stricter biosecurity and movement controls, the on‑farm outbreak was brought under control, but the episode underscored that highly pathogenic PTV variants can still emerge in modern Chinese production systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive pig production into western regions such as Gansu, long‑distance movement of pigs and possibly contaminated fomites or feed ingredients, and high within‑farm stocking densities likely facilitated introduction and rapid amplification of the PTV‑5 strain. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed that the Gansu isolate shared only about 90% identity with the most closely related known PTV strain and contained multiple mutant clusters in VP1, consistent with a distinct, highly pathogenic PTV‑5 variant; animal challenge studies confirmed markedly increased virulence and broader tissue tropism compared with typical low‑pathogenicity PTVs.

Countries: United States of America [2008] (Florida – multiple premises linked to unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing)
Host: Horses (Equus caballus) on unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing premises and associated farms in Florida
Event summary: In August 2008 a 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding in Florida developed fever, anemia and dark urine and was diagnosed with equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, triggering a foreign animal disease investigation in a country declared EP‑free since 1988. Testing of roughly 200–210 horses on about 25 epidemiologically linked premises identified 20 T. equi–infected horses on seven unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing farms, most of which were clinically inapparent carriers but all of which posed a regulatory and trade concern. Affected premises were quarantined, infected horses were euthanised or removed from the state, and with intensive tracing, testing and tick surveillance, authorities reported eradication of this outbreak from Florida by early 2009.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of chronically infected horses (likely imported from endemic areas such as Mexico) into Florida’s unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing circuit, combined with extensive iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission through practices such as blood‑doping, reuse of needles and syringes, and sharing of multidose drug vials, allowed T. equi to spread despite the absence of demonstrated local tick vectors. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel strain or increased virulence; the event reflects efficient mechanical transmission from long‑term carrier horses in a high‑risk management system rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: review – Event correctly represents the 2008 Florida re‑emergence of T. equi in an officially EP‑free United States and is among the largest recent outbreaks, so it should be retained. I corrected the description of scale to match regulatory and case‑report data (≈20 infected horses, seven epidemiologically linked premises, ~200–210 horses tested) and clarified that this was a re-occurrence in a previously endemic subregion rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence. Source list was kept but augmented with a primary outbreak description and USDA reporting documents; classification as re-occurrence with no re-emergence (no clear pathogen change) remains appropriate.
