Countries: United States of America [2009] (Jackson County, Missouri)
Host: Horses, ponies and mules on a boarding stable in Jackson County, Missouri (index 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding plus six additional equids)
Event summary: In early June 2009 a 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding from a stable in Jackson County, Missouri was hospitalized in Kansas with acute fever, jaundice and anemia, and laboratory testing at the National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed Theileria equi infection, initiating a foreign animal disease investigation in another U.S. state previously regarded as EP‑free. Quarantine and testing of 63 equids (horses, ponies and mules) on the premises identified six additional T. equi–positive animals, for a total of seven infected equids, while intensive examination of the animals and premises found no competent tick vectors, pointing instead to blood‑borne spread via shared needles or other contaminated injection equipment. Positive horses were euthanised or otherwise removed under a stamping‑out policy, the premises remained under quarantine until repeat testing of remaining animals was negative, and the outbreak was declared resolved with no evidence of further local or interstate transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of a T. equi–infected horse of uncertain origin onto a Missouri boarding stable, together with unsafe parenteral medication practices (reuse of needles, syringes or multidose vials), created an opportunity for iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission in an area lacking established EP vector ticks. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel or more virulent T. equi strain; the event is best explained by amplification of a chronically infected carrier horse through mechanical transmission, similar in mechanism to the 2008 Florida outbreak, and therefore reflects re-occurrence rather than pathogen re-emergence.

I added it as a separate re-occurrence event for Northern America, using official surveillance summaries and veterinary reports for timing, case numbers and transmission route, and classified it as re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence. Countries: United States of America [2009] (large ranch in south Texas)
Host: Horses (primarily Quarter Horses and other equids) on a large ranch in south Texas
Event summary: In October 2009 a ranch horse in south Texas was diagnosed with equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, revealing widespread infection on a large ranch in a country officially declared EP‑free since 1988. Serologic screening of approximately 2,500 horses linked to the ranch identified about 292 of 360 horses on the index ranch, and more than 400 horses in total, as T. equi–infected, and field plus experimental work demonstrated efficient tick‑borne transmission, particularly by the cayenne tick Amblyomma cajennense (now A. mixtum) and the American dog tick Dermacentor variabilis, with horse movements between the Texas ranch and an EP‑endemic sister ranch in Brazil considered the most likely source. The outbreak was gradually controlled and T. equi eradicated from the ranch through long‑term quarantine, aggressive acaricide‑based tick control, culling or supervised imidocarb treatment of 160+ infected horses, and extensive tracing and testing of horses sold from the premises, with no further ranch‑linked tick-borne transmission detected after completion of the control program.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term movement of chronically infected horses between an EP‑endemic sister ranch in Brazil and the south‑Texas ranch, combined with suitable tick habitat and limited initial tick control, allowed establishment of local vector‑borne transmission in a region that previously had eliminated EP. Increased interstate and international trade in high‑value horses, and gaps in pre‑movement EP testing at the time, further contributed to the extensive spread among ranch horses. Internal mechanisms: Experimental work during this event showed that Amblyomma cajennense and Dermacentor variabilis were competent vectors for T. equi in this setting, broadening the recognized vector range (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation at the system level), but there is no clear evidence that the parasite itself evolved increased virulence or altered host range in this outbreak.
Review: retain – This record accurately captures the large 2009 south‑Texas ranch outbreak, including order‑of‑magnitude case numbers (≈292/360 horses on the index ranch, >400 infected overall), the key tick vectors (Amblyomma cajennense/A. mixtum and Dermacentor variabilis), and the linkage to a Brazilian sister ranch. Geographic fields (Northern America, United States, south Texas) and classification as a re-occurrence in a previously endemic subregion (not a new continental or subregional emergence) are appropriate. No substantive changes were required beyond minor wording harmonization, but a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether they prefer Texas ranch–associated infections detected off‑ranch be counted within this event or within the broader multi‑state episode below.

Countries: United States of America [2009] (multiple states; at least 16 states detecting infected horses)
Host: Horses, especially Quarter Horse racehorses involved in sanctioned and unsanctioned racing across multiple U.S. states
Event summary: From early 2009 through late 2010, expanded surveillance following the Florida and Texas equine piroplasmosis events identified hundreds of additional T. equi– and Babesia caballi–infected horses across at least 16 U.S. states, with about 540+ positives reported in federal risk assessments and committee reports. Many of these horses were apparently healthy Quarter Horse racehorses and other performance horses, and epidemiologic investigations linked a substantial proportion of the multi‑state cluster to unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing circuits, extensive interstate movement, and iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission via shared needles, illicit blood‑doping and contaminated multidose vials. The cluster led to new EP testing requirements at some racetracks, long‑term quarantine and supervised treatment programs for infected horses, and targeted outreach to racing sectors, after which the number of newly detected positives associated with these pathways declined markedly, although sporadic EP cases continue to be detected in the U.S.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑volume movement of racehorses between states and across the Mexican border, coupled with high‑risk husbandry practices (blood‑doping, reuse of needles and IV equipment, and possible informal blood transfusions) created multiple mechanical transmission routes that bypassed the need for tick vectors; prior to 2009, limited routine EP testing in racing sectors allowed accumulation and silent spread of carrier horses. Internal mechanisms: Genotyping studies suggest a limited number of T. equi introduction sources rather than widespread parasite diversification, and there is no evidence of increased intrinsic virulence; the primary mechanism is efficient human‑mediated blood‑borne spread in mobile, high‑density equine populations, representing a large-scale re-occurrence rather than evolutionary re-emergence.
Review: retain – This entry appropriately treats the 2009–2010 multi‑state U.S. detection of ≈500+ EP‑positive horses (largely linked to racing circuits and iatrogenic transmission) as a single, epidemiologically related re-occurrence episode, in line with USDA pathway assessments and subsequent reviews. The impact is large (hundreds of infected horses across ≥16 states) and clearly within the top tier of global T. equi emergence events, so it should be retained. No corrections were needed to geography or event‑type coding; a note of caution is that some horse counts in federal summaries may overlap with those from the Texas ranch outbreak, so final quantitative impact comparisons should recognise this potential double counting.

Countries: Ireland [2009] (County Meath – Thoroughbred racing stable near Dunshaughlin)
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses and a pony at a racing stable in County Meath, Ireland
Event summary: In June 2009 several Thoroughbred racehorses at a yard near Dunshaughlin, County Meath, developed fever, anemia and poor performance, and laboratory investigation confirmed equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, constituting the first officially reported EP outbreak in Ireland. Subsequent testing of 60 equids on the premises (59 racehorses and one pony) found 28 animals positive by serology and/or PCR, prompting quarantine of the yard, movement restrictions, and tracing of recent horse movements, although no competent EP vector ticks were identified and there was no evidence of wider geographic spread. After infected horses were managed under strict biosecurity and no additional foci were detected, Ireland continued to be regarded as EP‑free, and the event was closed as a limited import‑associated incursion highlighting the vulnerability of EP‑free regions to introduction via international horse movement and local iatrogenic spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of one or more T. equi–infected horses or contaminated blood products from endemic regions into a high‑density racing yard, along with close contact and potential reuse of needles or other equipment among valuable Thoroughbreds, likely enabled limited local mechanical transmission in a country with few or no established EP tick vectors. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication of a novel strain or altered parasite behaviour; the event is best interpreted as first detection and intra‑continental emergence of T. equi in Ireland driven by horse movements and management practices rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified Ireland 2009 as a first detection and intra-continental emergence event but substantially underestimated its scale (describing only three clinically ill horses). I updated the event summary and impact to reflect official reports indicating 28 of 60 horses on the premises tested positive, and clarified that competent vector ticks were not demonstrated and spread was likely mechanical and limited to the yard. I added a more detailed event report from The Horse and a peer‑reviewed retrospective analysis as key sources; because I changed numerical impact and interpretation of transmission mode, this row should be reviewed, but it clearly remains one of the most important recent European emergence events and should be retained.

Host: Horses of various breeds in the south‑west of the Netherlands, including two with autochthonous clinical Theileria equi infection and additional subclinical indigenous cases
Event summary: Between May and September 2010 a cross‑sectional survey of 300 randomly selected horses in the south‑west of the Netherlands, initiated after detection of an apparently indigenous Babesia caballi case, identified low‑level exposure to equine piroplasms and four horses considered truly indigenous infections, including two with clinical Theileria equi infection and two additional subclinical carriers. These affected horses had no history of travel outside the Netherlands and grazed in areas where the tick vector Dermacentor reticulatus had recently established, providing the first evidence of autochthonous T. equi transmission in a country previously regarded as non‑endemic. Follow‑up surveillance of horses and expanding D. reticulatus populations indicated that T. equi prevalence remained low and focal, and the Netherlands continues to be considered non‑endemic with only sporadic locally acquired cases associated with newly suitable tick habitats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: North‑westward expansion and establishment of Dermacentor reticulatus tick populations in the Netherlands from the mid‑2000s, likely driven by climate and land‑use changes, increased the ecological suitability for EP transmission, while the importation or movement of infected equids from endemic European regions seeded T. equi into these new vector‑supported environments. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for a novel T. equi strain in this event; emergence is best explained by geographic range expansion of competent tick vectors (geographic range expansion of the transmission system) combined with horse movements, enabling local autochthonous transmission in an area previously free of indigenous EP.

I changed the event year to 2010–2010 and updated the country field accordingly, and slightly rephrased the summary to match the Vet Parasitol paper (four truly indigenous cases, two clinical T. equi infections). Source URLs already pointed to the primary study and relevant European reviews and were therefore retained; because timing and impact details were adjusted, this event is flagged for review but clearly remains among the major European emergence events.

Countries: Austria [2020] (eastern Austria – Güssing/Burgenland farm with 18 resident horses)
Host: Domestic horses on a single farm in eastern Austria, including a pregnant Austrian Warmblood mare, her foal and multiple subclinical T. equi–infected pasturemates
Event summary: In 2020 a 23‑year‑old pregnant Austrian Warmblood mare from a pasture near Güssing in Burgenland, eastern Austria, was admitted with fever, anemia and icterus, and subsequent microscopy, PCR and sequencing confirmed Theileria equi infection despite the mare never having left Austria, constituting the first documented autochthonous equine piroplasmosis case in the country. Follow‑up investigations of the same farm over the next two years sampled 18 resident horses and local ticks, revealing that initially two horses showed clinical disease while 12 of the remaining 16 were subclinically infected, and by the second year a total of 16 of 18 horses had evidence of T. equi infection, with multiple questing ticks (Dermacentor reticulatus, Ixodes ricinus and Haemaphysalis concinna) also PCR‑positive for the same T. equi genotype E. Quarantine, tick control and management changes limited further clinical cases but the persistence of infected horses and infected ticks on the premises indicated establishment of a local transmission focus in Austria, raising concern that T. equi could become endemic in suitable parts of the country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of T. equi into an Austrian farm via movement of infected horses from neighbouring endemic regions (notably an imported Hungarian horse sharing pasture with the index mare) into an area where several tick species, including Dermacentor reticulatus, had recently expanded their range created conditions for local transmission; climate‑driven shifts and changes in land use likely facilitated this vector expansion. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing showed that all equine and tick isolates belonged to T. equi genotype E, with no evidence of a novel highly virulent lineage; the emergence reflects geographic and ecological expansion of the parasite–vector system into a previously non‑endemic country combined with the long carrier state in horses, rather than intrinsic changes in parasite virulence or host range.
Review: review – This significant recent emergence episode in Austria was absent from the original dataset but clearly belongs among the top T. equi events because it documents both the first autochthonous clinical case and a two‑year farm‑level study in which 16 of 18 horses and multiple tick species were infected in a previously non‑endemic country. I added a new event row starting in 2020 and extending through the two‑year follow-up (2020–2022), classified as first detection and intra-continental emergence in Western Europe, with drivers focused on importation of infected horses and northward expansion of Dermacentor and other ticks. Because this is a newly added and complex episode, it should be reviewed by a subject‑matter expert, but its inclusion materially improves coverage of recent European emergence linked to vector range expansion.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [source of infected cattle]; Comoros [2003] (Grande Comore)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus and Bos taurus crossbreds)
Event summary: In 2003, following importation of zebu cattle from Tanzania, East Coast fever caused by Theileria parva was introduced into Grande Comore in the Union of Comoros, an island previously free of the disease. The infection, carried by Rhipicephalus appendiculatus ticks on Muguga‑cocktail‑vaccinated cattle, spread rapidly during 2003–2004 and caused a severe epidemic that decimated the island’s cattle population, with participatory assessments later estimating livestock losses on the order of 10% or more. Subsequent control measures, including restrictions on cattle imports, intensified tick control and adaptation of husbandry practices, reduced incidence, but T. parva and its vector became established and the island remains at risk of recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of live cattle from Tanzania without adequate pre‑movement screening for T. parva or tick infestation; use of Muguga‑cocktail‑vaccinated animals that carried vaccine‑strain parasites into a naïve island cattle population; suitable island climate for establishment of Rhipicephalus appendiculatus and limited local veterinary capacity to recognise and contain a new tick‑borne disease. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of existing Muguga‑cocktail genotypes rather than a novel strain, but into an immunologically naïve host population and new ecosystem, leading to marked local geographic range expansion and high transmission intensity (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Enhanced Transmission via abundant vector–host contact).
Review: retain – Well‑documented, high‑impact introduction of East Coast fever to Grande Comore with major cattle losses; geography (Eastern Africa, Comoros) and classification as re-occurrence at subregion level (disease long‑present elsewhere in Eastern Africa) are consistent with the protocol. Tanzania is appropriately noted as the infection source rather than a new emergence location; no structural changes recommended.

Countries: Australia [2006] (initially coastal New South Wales; spread to Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event summary: From 2006 onward, cattle in coastal New South Wales, Australia, began experiencing outbreaks of severe haemolytic anaemia and mortality linked to virulent genotypes of Theileria orientalis, particularly Ikeda and Chitose, in herds previously considered affected only by benign T. orientalis. Over the subsequent decade, hundreds of clinical outbreaks of bovine anaemia associated with T. orientalis were reported along the eastern seaboard and into South Australia and Western Australia, with substantial production losses in both dairy and beef systems and widespread detection of pathogenic genotypes in cattle and Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks. Although the spatial spread of Ikeda into new areas largely stabilised after about 2015, clinical cases continued within the endemic zone through at least 2022, managed via improved diagnostics, tick‑control and herd management but with oriental theileriosis now recognised as a major endemic constraint.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expanded movement and trading of cattle within eastern and southern Australia, including movement of infected breeder stock between tick‑free and tick‑endemic areas; widespread presence of H. longicornis and other Haemaphysalis ticks in coastal and temperate regions; intensification of grazing systems and climatic conditions favourable to ticks. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and introduction of the virulent Ikeda genotype (often with co‑infection by Chitose and other types) into herds historically exposed only to benign T. orientalis strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), with higher parasitaemia and anaemia and apparent fitness advantages that facilitated rapid spread and establishment (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Major emergence of pathogenic T. orientalis Ikeda in Australia with hundreds of outbreaks and sustained impact; event period extended from 2006–2014 to 2006–2022 to reflect continued clinical activity. Inter-continental emergence was set to No because T. orientalis was already present in Oceania; under the project rules, genotype-level novelty is captured as re-emergence, not inter-continental emergence. Recommended to retain as one of the largest events, but classification and time window should be checked by a domain expert.

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event summary: In August 2012, index cases of severe anaemia and mortality due to Theileria orientalis Ikeda type were identified on dairy farms in Kamo (Northland) and Reporoa (Waikato) in New Zealand, where only benign T. orientalis types had previously been recognised. During 2012–2013 the epidemic of Theileria‑associated bovine anaemia (TABA) spread rapidly across the upper North Island, and by August 2014 at least 633 infected herds had been reported, with substantial economic losses from deaths, production drops and movement restrictions. After 2014, the disease was managed through enhanced surveillance (Ikeda declared a new‑to‑New‑Zealand organism in 2012), rollout of rapid qPCR diagnostics, tick‑control measures, movement management and farmer awareness, leading to a decline in new severe outbreaks even as Ikeda became established in cattle and Haemaphysalis longicornis populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of T. orientalis Ikeda into New Zealand, likely via imported cattle or biological material from endemic countries; established populations of H. longicornis ticks in North Island regions that enabled rapid local transmission; routine seasonal movements of pregnant and lactating cows between Northland, Waikato and other areas that disseminated infection; high within‑herd tick burdens on pasture in suitable climatic zones. Internal mechanisms: A virulent Ikeda genotype entering a cattle population previously infected mainly with benign Chitose and Buffeli types (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), capable of causing high parasitaemia and severe anaemia; efficient transmission by a competent vector already adapted to local environments (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), resulting in fast geographic spread within the country.
Review: review – Large, well-documented epidemic of T. orientalis Ikeda in New Zealand with >600 affected herds and major economic impact; clearly qualifies as a top emergence event. Reclassified as re-emergence (novel pathogenic genotype in a host system where T. orientalis was already present) rather than a mixed re-occurrence/re-emergence event, in line with the project rule that strain-level novelty should be captured as re-emergence, not intra/inter-continental emergence. Recommended to retain with this corrected classification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Viet Nam [2014] (aborted dairy heifers imported from Australia); China [2014] (Taiwan region, same imported cohort)
Host: Cattle (imported pregnant dairy heifers)
Event summary: In 2014, an outbreak of oriental theileriosis occurred in pregnant dairy heifers imported from Australia to Viet Nam, with abortions and clinical signs prompting investigation of both the affected heifers in Viet Nam and animals from the same shipment before export and after arrival in Taiwan. Multiplex tandem PCR on 112 cattle samples showed Theileria orientalis DNA in about 72% of animals, with very high prevalences and parasite loads in aborted heifers in Viet Nam and in cohorts shipped to Taiwan, and genotyping revealed Chitose and Ikeda types closely related to Australian outbreak strains. The episode, which linked severe disease in imported cattle in Asia to infection acquired in Australia, highlighted the risk of moving subclinically infected T. orientalis Ikeda/Chitose carriers through live‑cattle trade and led to calls for stricter pre‑export screening and biosecurity measures for oriental theileriosis.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance trade in pregnant dairy heifers from eastern Australia to Viet Nam and Taiwan without prior molecular screening for T. orientalis genotypes; transport stress and periparturient immunosuppression that likely precipitated clinical disease and abortion in infected heifers; presence or potential presence of competent Haemaphysalis vectors in destination countries. Internal mechanisms: High burdens of virulent Ikeda and Chitose genotypes in exported animals (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and long‑distance dissemination), which are strongly associated with clinical oriental theileriosis and abortion, demonstrating the capacity of these genotypes to cause transboundary disease even when infection is acquired pre‑export.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first reported outbreak of oriental theileriosis in imported cattle, with severe disease in heifers shipped from Australia to Viet Nam and high infection levels in animals sent to Taiwan. Classified as re-emergence (spread of pathogenic Ikeda/Chitose genotypes into additional production systems within Asia via trade) rather than inter-continental emergence, because T. orientalis was already established in both source and destination continents. Recommended to retain as a major transboundary emergence episode, but timing (2014) and country listing (Viet Nam plus Taiwan region under China) should be double-checked against full-text data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [Virginia 2017; additional affected eastern and mid-Atlantic states including West Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Maryland, New York, Kansas and others 2018-2025]
Host: Cattle (beef and dairy herds)
Event summary: In early autumn 2017, a beef herd in Albemarle County, Virginia, experienced unexplained anaemia and mortality that was traced to infection with the virulent Ikeda genotype of Theileria orientalis, marking the first recognition of this pathogenic genotype in North America, where only benign T. orientalis types had previously been reported. Over the following years, PCR‑based surveillance of cattle and ticks documented establishment and spread of T. orientalis Ikeda across Virginia and into multiple eastern and mid‑Atlantic states, with the parasite detected both in clinically affected herds and in invasive Asian longhorned ticks (Haemaphysalis longicornis), and bovine infectious anaemia due to Ikeda emerging as a significant concern for the U.S. cattle industry. By the mid‑2020s, Ikeda‑associated theileriosis had been reported in at least 16 U.S. states, and while control remains challenging due to the lack of approved chemotherapeutics and the expanding range of H. longicornis, awareness, laboratory diagnostics, extension guidance and research on vaccines and tick control have all increased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of T. orientalis Ikeda into the United States, probably via movement of infected cattle or biological material from endemic regions in Asia or Australasia; invasion and rapid spread of H. longicornis, first recognised in the U.S. in 2017 and now established in many eastern states; interstate movement and commingling of subclinical carrier cattle that facilitate parasite dissemination; historically limited surveillance for Theileria in North American cattle and ticks, which delayed recognition of the problem. Internal mechanisms: A virulent Ikeda genotype capable of causing marked anaemia, abortion and mortality in naive herds (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity) and well adapted for transmission by H. longicornis and possibly other ticks (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)), enabling rapid spread once introduced.
Review: review – Major emergence of T. orientalis Ikeda in North America with ongoing spread across many U.S. states; clearly among the most consequential recent events. Inter-continental emergence was set to No because non-pathogenic T. orientalis was already present in North America prior to 2017; this episode instead represents re-emergence driven by introduction of a virulent genotype. Event period extended to 2017–2025 to reflect documented continuing spread; recommended to retain with this corrected classification and time span.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [2020] (Hebei Province, Zhangjiakou, confined dairy cattle)
Host: Cattle (confined dairy herds)
Event summary: In June 2020, a confined dairy herd in Zhangjiakou, Hebei Province, China experienced an outbreak of piroplasmosis‑like illness with anaemia and deaths in adult cows, and laboratory investigation showed that two‑thirds of sampled animals were infected with Theileria orientalis. Molecular characterisation of the major piroplasm surface protein (MPSP) and 18S rRNA genes demonstrated the presence of both Chitose (type 1) and Ikeda (type 2) genotypes, and experimental infection indicated that Ikeda was the predominant and pathogenic type responsible for disease, representing one of the first clearly documented clinical outbreaks of Ikeda‑associated oriental theileriosis in Chinese dairy cattle. The episode raised awareness that pathogenic T. orientalis genotypes, previously regarded as mostly benign in China, can cause severe disease in intensive dairy systems and highlighted the need for improved surveillance, tick control and biosecurity in rapidly modernising herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and confinement of dairy production in Hebei with high animal densities and introduction of high‑producing but more susceptible cattle; exposure of naive or partially immune animals to infected ticks or iatrogenic transmission within the herd; limited prior recognition of T. orientalis Ikeda as a cause of serious disease in Chinese cattle, which may have delayed control responses. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and predominance of the virulent Ikeda genotype in an affected herd (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity), with high within‑herd infection prevalence and mortality in clinically affected animals, consistent with patterns seen in Australasia and New Zealand.
Review: review – Newly added event describing a high-mortality outbreak of T. orientalis Ikeda in confined dairy cattle in Hebei, China, which is among the clearest examples of clinical Ikeda emergence in Eastern Asia. Classified as re-emergence because T. orientalis (including Ikeda) had been detected previously in China, but this was one of the first large, well-characterised clinical outbreaks in intensive dairy cattle. Recommended to retain, with timing and herd-scale impact (number of deaths) to be confirmed from the full Chinese-language and supplementary materials.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; Ixodes persulcatus and Ixodes ricinus ticks; small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: Throughout the 1990s, the Russian Federation experienced the highest documented national burden of tick-borne encephalitis, with annual case numbers generally between 5,000 and 10,000 and peaks above 10,000 cases in the mid-1990s, driven largely by large foci in Western Siberia, the Urals and parts of the Far East. Incidence in some oblasts, such as Tomsk, Kemerovo, Novosibirsk and the Altai Republic, frequently exceeded 10–20 cases per 100,000 population and occasionally surpassed 70 per 100,000, far above the European average. After these mid-decade peaks, incidence remained elevated relative to the 1970s and 1980s, with substantial year-to-year variability linked to rodent and tick population dynamics and changing human outdoor activity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Socio-economic changes and reduced public health resources in the post-Soviet period, including declines in vaccination coverage, increased occupational and subsistence activities in forested areas, intensification of forestry and recreation in the taiga, and land-use and climatic shifts that favoured Ixodes persulcatus and rodent hosts, all contributed to greatly increased human exposure to infected ticks. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate the emergence of a single novel viral lineage as the main cause; instead, the episode reflects amplification and geographic spread of long-established Siberian and Far Eastern TBEV subtypes (geographic range expansion – inherent), with a high proportion of severe focal neurologic forms in Western Siberia.
Review: review - New high-impact event added for the very large national TBE burden in Russia during the 1990s (5,000–10,000 cases per year with peaks >10,000). Classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic subregion (Eastern Europe, including Western Siberia and the Far East by UNSD convention), driven primarily by socio-economic and ecological changes rather than a new strain. No events from Russia were present in the original dataset despite its global dominance in case numbers for this period, so this episode is likely among the top 10 most impactful and should be retained after expert verification.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (clinical TBE); Ixodes ricinus ticks; small mammals (rodent reservoirs)
Event summary: From 1993 onwards, the Baltic states and adjacent parts of northeastern Poland experienced a sudden and sustained surge in human tick-borne encephalitis incidence, with national case rates increasing several-fold compared with the 1980s. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania all saw sharp step-changes in 1992–1993, and in some counties incidence rose more than 10–30-fold, elevating the region to one of the highest-burden TBE areas in Europe. Elevated incidence persisted through the late 1990s, with marked spatial heterogeneity across counties, before stabilising at a high but fluctuating level under the influence of vaccination and public health measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post-socialist socio-economic transitions in the early 1990s (changes in agricultural practices, land abandonment, increased subsistence farming, reduced rodent and tick control), together with climate variability favouring tick survival and activity, are considered key to the abrupt increase in TBE incidence in the Baltics and neighbouring Poland. Internal mechanisms: No single novel viral strain was identified as causal; the episode is interpreted primarily as ecological and socio-economic amplification of established European-subtype TBEV transmission cycles.
Review: review - Retained as a major high-incidence episode for the Baltic states and northeastern Poland. Corrected the emergence-type classification by setting intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because the virus and human disease were already established in these subregions and the main signal was a sharp resurgence in incidence, not first spread into new subregions. Re-occurrence remains true, reflecting socio-economic and ecological drivers of resurgence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Czechia [1990]; Slovakia [1990]; Hungary [1990]; Slovenia [1990]; Croatia [1990]; Poland [1990]; Austria [1990]
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wild rodents
Event summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, many Central and Eastern European countries, especially Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia, parts of Poland and Hungary, and selected alpine and pre-alpine regions of Austria and Croatia, reported sustained increases in TBE incidence compared with the 1970s–1980s. In Czechia, national data showed a marked rise in annual TBE cases from the early 1990s through 2008, and similar trends were documented in neighbouring countries as established enzootic foci intensified and new local foci appeared. By the late 2000s, incidence had stabilised at a higher level with pronounced year-to-year variability driven by climate and host dynamics rather than a single outbreak wave.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warmer winters and earlier springs, changes in forest management and deer abundance, increased outdoor recreation and mushroom or berry picking, and reduced pesticide use collectively expanded suitable habitat and host availability for Ixodes ticks and increased human exposure. Internal mechanisms: No dominant novel genotype was linked to this regional trend; instead, the event reflects a broad geographic range expansion and intensification of existing European-subtype TBEV foci (geographic range expansion – inherent) under changing environmental and human-behavioural conditions.
Review: review - Event retained as a broad regional resurgence in Central and Eastern Europe. Cleaned the sub_regions field to use only UNSD categories (Eastern Europe; Southern Europe) instead of the previous free-text mixture, and set intra_continental_emergence from true to false because the countries involved were already within known endemic subregions; the main feature was a long-lasting increase in incidence (re-occurrence) and expansion of local foci rather than first entry into a new subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wild rodents
Event summary: In 1994, tick-borne encephalitis was identified for the first time in Italy in Belluno Province (Veneto), marking recognition of an autochthonous alpine focus at the southern edge of the known European range. Over the subsequent decade, additional human cases and TBEV-positive ticks were documented in other alpine and pre-alpine areas of northeastern Italy near the Slovenian border, with modest but persistent annual case numbers. These foci have remained active through the 2010s and early 2020s, with fluctuating incidence influenced by local vaccination uptake, tourism and environmental conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensified eco-tourism and outdoor recreation in forested alpine landscapes, land-use changes and favourable local climate created conditions for persistence of ixodid ticks and virus circulation at higher elevations and more southerly latitudes. Internal mechanisms: The circulating strains belong to the European TBEV subtype; available evidence suggests local establishment of this subtype in new mountainous habitats (geographic range expansion – inherent) rather than emergence of a distinct genotype.
Review: review - Retained as the first recognised autochthonous TBE focus in Italy and a key southward range extension. Restricted the countries field to Italy only and limited the sub_regions entry to Southern Europe, because Slovenia already had long-standing endemic foci and should not be treated as part of a first-detection event. The emergence-type classification (first_detection and intra_continental_emergence) is appropriate for Italy under the UNSD regional scheme.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wildlife reservoirs (rodents, deer)
Event summary: From 2001, when TBE became nationally notifiable in Germany, surveillance documented a rising trend in reported cases, particularly in Bavaria and Baden‑Württemberg, with smaller but increasing contributions from neighbouring federal states. Annual confirmed TBE cases in Germany generally increased over the 2000s and 2010s, peaking at around 584 cases in 2018, while some adjacent regions in Austria and Switzerland also experienced fluctuating but generally elevated incidence amid high vaccination coverage. After 2018, Germany continued to report several hundred cases annually, with year-to-year oscillations linked to environmental conditions and patterns of human outdoor exposure.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enhanced surveillance and mandatory notification increased detection, while mild winters, increased recreational use of forested and peri-urban landscapes, and high deer densities supported more abundant Ixodes tick populations and more frequent human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: This episode is best interpreted as re-occurrence and geographic spread of existing European-subtype TBEV foci at the western fringe of their distribution, driven by ecological and climatic factors rather than emergence of a clearly new strain.
Review: review - Event retained as a major long-term resurgence and westward spread of TBE within Germany. The countries field was narrowed to Germany only, because Austria and Switzerland had well-established endemic foci and long-standing vaccination programmes and were not experiencing a new emergence starting in 2001; they are mentioned only for contextual comparison. The re-occurrence classification remains appropriate; no intra- or inter-continental emergence flags are needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (food-borne and tick-bite associated TBE); small ruminants (goats, sheep, cows as virus source in milk); Ixodes ricinus ticks
Event summary: Between 2007 and 2016, Slovakia reported the highest documented occurrence of alimentary (food-borne) tick-borne encephalitis in Europe, with multiple outbreaks linked to consumption of unpasteurised goat, sheep or cow milk and cheese, including a large outbreak in eastern Slovakia in 2013 that affected dozens of people. Similar but generally smaller food-borne TBE outbreaks occurred in the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and other countries during this period, highlighting alimentary transmission as a clinically important complement to tick-bite exposure in endemic areas. Most outbreaks subsided rapidly once contaminated dairy products were withdrawn from sale and pasteurisation or boiling of milk was reinforced, although sporadic alimentary events have continued to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cultural practices involving consumption of raw milk and artisanal cheeses from small ruminants grazing in endemic forest-edge pastures created opportunities for alimentary TBEV transmission; limited awareness of this route and lack of systematic pasteurisation in some rural settings allowed multi-person outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: The events involved European-subtype TBEV strains capable of surviving and remaining infectious in milk and dairy products; the prominence of alimentary outbreaks represents functional re-emergence via a different transmission route (enhanced transmission through food) rather than a novel genotype, and in some foci may reflect high viral loads in livestock following intense tick exposure.
Review: review - Retained as a distinct re-emergence episode characterised by large alimentary outbreaks, with Slovakia as the main hotspot. Sub_regions was restricted to Eastern Europe because all listed countries fall in this UNSD subregion. The emergence classification was adjusted to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) to reflect the prominence of a re-emerging transmission route (food-borne infection) involving established European TBEV strains, rather than a generic resurgence driven mainly by external factors.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Norway (coastal Agder & Telemark, and western coast) [2015]; Denmark (Bornholm and new foci in Zealand and Jutland) [2018]; Sweden (western and higher-latitude expansion) [2010s]; Finland [2010s]
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wildlife reservoirs (rodents, deer)
Event summary: In the mid‑2010s, Nordic countries documented expansion of human TBE cases into new coastal and higher-latitude foci, including increasing incidence along the Norwegian and Swedish coasts and newly recognised foci in Denmark beyond the long-known endemic island of Bornholm, where autochthonous cases in 2018–2019 highlighted spread to mainland Zealand and Jutland. Case counts in Norway, Sweden and Finland rose over 2015–2019 compared with earlier years, although absolute numbers remained lower than in Baltic or Central European hotspots. These northern foci have persisted, with interannual variability linked to climate and small-mammal population cycles and ongoing gradual spread northwards along the Scandinavian coastline.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Warmer temperatures, longer vegetation seasons and milder winters at higher latitudes have improved overwinter survival and seasonal activity of Ixodes ticks; changes in deer and rodent populations and human outdoor behaviour (recreation, second homes, forestry work) have increased human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: Expansion represents geographic range expansion of existing European TBEV lineages into newly suitable northern habitats (geographic range expansion – inherent) rather than emergence of novel variants.
Review: review - Retained as a major intra-continental range expansion episode into new foci in the Nordic countries. Kept the focus on spread into new geographic areas (intra_continental_emergence = true) and set re_occurrence to false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence; the main signal is establishment of new northern and western foci rather than mere resurgence in long-recognised localities.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; roe deer (Capreolus capreolus as sentinel host)
Event summary: In 2015, TBEV was detected for the first time in the Netherlands in Ixodes ricinus ticks from Sallandse Heuvelrug National Park, and in 2016 the country reported its first two autochthonous human TBE cases, with a third case in 2017, confirming endemic transmission in at least two forested areas. Subsequent surveillance in roe deer, rodents and ticks identified several additional microfoci in the eastern and central Netherlands, with one to several human cases reported most years but overall incidence remaining low. The emergence of these foci marked a clear westward extension of clinically recognised TBE in Europe into a country that had previously considered all TBE cases to be imported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely contributors include movement and increasing densities of deer and small mammals, landscape connectivity of mixed forests and heathlands from central Europe into the eastern Netherlands, and favourable microclimatic conditions for ticks; improved clinical awareness and targeted testing also aided detection of the first human cases. Internal mechanisms: Viral sequencing indicates circulation of European-subtype strains closely related to those in neighbouring endemic countries, including a divergent Salland strain and viruses closely related to those later detected in the UK, consistent with geographic spread and local establishment (geographic range expansion – inherent) rather than a de novo variant.
Review: review - Retained as a key first-detection and intra-continental emergence event on the western fringe of the endemic area. Corrected the countries field to include only the Netherlands, because France has long-standing endemic foci and Belgium’s first confirmed autochthonous cases occurred later (2020). The emergence classification (first_detection and intra_continental_emergence) is now correctly tied to the Netherlands as a new endemic country.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Lithuania [2018]; Czechia [2018]; Germany [2018]; Sweden [2018]; Austria [2018]; Latvia [2018]; Slovakia [2018]; Slovenia [2018]; Poland [2018]; other EU/EEA countries [2018-2020]
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus ticks; wildlife reservoirs
Event summary: Between 2018 and 2020, EU/EEA countries experienced two of the highest regional TBE peaks on record. In 2018 they reported 3,212 cases (over 3,000 confirmed), with particularly high incidence in Lithuania, Czechia, Germany, Slovenia and Sweden, and Germany alone recording around 583 cases. After a moderate year in 2019, notification rates rose again in 2020 to 3,817 reported cases (3,734 confirmed), despite possible under-ascertainment during the COVID-19 pandemic. These peaks reflected synchronised amplification of TBEV activity across many established European foci rather than a single outbreak constrained to a few countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Favourable weather for ticks (warm, humid spring and summer), high rodent and deer densities, intensive human outdoor activity in forests and rural areas during climatically favourable seasons, and suboptimal vaccination coverage in several high-incidence countries (especially in the Baltics and parts of Central Europe) likely increased human exposure and disease burden. Internal mechanisms: The 2018 and 2020 peaks exemplify how climate variability and host–vector dynamics can trigger major regional re-occurrence within existing enzootic cycles without requiring the emergence of a fundamentally new viral variant.
Review: review - Retained as a major multi-country re-occurrence episode capturing record-high regional case totals. Updated the year field from a single year (2018) to 2018–2020 and clarified in the summary that both 2018 and 2020 represent EU/EEA-wide peaks, with 2019 as an intermediate year. Emergence classification remains re_occurrence only, as there is no evidence that these peaks reflected spread into new subregions or continents.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; deer (sentinel hosts)
Event summary: In 2018–2019, large-scale surveillance of wildlife and questing ticks in the United Kingdom first detected European-subtype TBEV in ticks from Thetford Forest and the Hampshire–Dorset border, and in July 2019 a probable locally acquired human TBE case was reported after a tick bite in southern England. Over the following years, further infected ticks were found in additional foci in England and Scotland, and by 2022–2023 the UK had confirmed its first PCR-positive domestically acquired human TBE cases, bringing the cumulative number of UK-acquired cases to a small handful. National risk assessments concluded that although overall risk remains low, TBEV is now established in limited foci in England and Scotland with potential for further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely northwestern expansion of infected ticks and wildlife hosts from endemic regions in continental Europe, facilitated by changes in deer and rodent movements, habitat connectivity and local climate, combined with targeted surveillance and testing that enabled recognition of previously unrecognised foci. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing demonstrates European-subtype TBEV closely related to strains from continental Europe, including those in the Netherlands, consistent with recent geographic range expansion rather than independent evolution; this represents intra-continental emergence into a new subregion (the UK) within an already affected continent.
Review: review - Retained as a first-detection and intra-continental emergence event for the United Kingdom. Countries and sub_regions were restricted to the UK/Northern Europe to avoid conflating this event with contemporaneous, but epidemiologically distinct, trends in Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, which are already covered in other events. The classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence is appropriate for the UK, where TBEV was not considered present before 2019.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus ticks; wild rodents
Event summary: Between 2019 and 2023, the Baltic countries reported 4,361 surveillance-confirmed TBE cases (Estonia 583, Latvia 1,055, Lithuania 2,723), corresponding to incidences of approximately 8.8, 11.2 and 19.4 per 100,000 person‑years, respectively, making them the highest-incidence TBE countries in Europe. Despite recommendations for universal vaccination of residents older than one year, more than 98% of TBE cases occurred in unvaccinated individuals, indicating persistent gaps in vaccine uptake. By 2023, incidence remained high but somewhat stabilised, with public health programmes emphasising vaccination, tick-bite prevention and enhanced awareness among populations and clinicians.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High environmental suitability for ticks and rodent reservoirs, extensive human use of forests and rural landscapes for work and recreation, and low to moderate vaccine coverage contributed to sustained high incidence; socio-economic patterns and health-seeking behaviour also influence under- and over-reporting. Internal mechanisms: The burden reflects endemic circulation of European TBEV strains rather than new variants; the re-occurrence at very high incidence in 2019–2023 underscores how incomplete vaccination and favourable ecologic conditions can maintain high disease impact in long-established foci.
Review: retain - Event appropriately captures the very high recent TBE incidence and vaccine-impact assessment in the Baltic states, based on detailed national surveillance and vaccine-effectiveness data. Classification as re_occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with a resurgence and persistence of disease in long-established endemic foci driven mainly by vaccination gaps and favourable ecology.

Host: Wild tilapine species (e.g. Sarotherodon galilaeus, Oreochromis aureus and other tilapia) in Lake Kinneret; farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), red tilapia and O. niloticus × O. aureus hybrids in ponds and cages
Event summary: From 2009, wild tilapia in Lake Kinneret (Sea of Galilee) and nearby Israeli farms began to suffer recurrent seasonal die‑offs, with high mortality in fry, juveniles and adults and prominent hepatic and neurological lesions not attributable to known agents. Between 2011 and 2013, Israeli researchers isolated a previously undescribed 10‑segment negative‑sense RNA virus from diseased fish, demonstrated its pathogenicity in experimental challenges and designated it Tilapia lake virus (TiLV). These outbreaks caused substantial production and catch losses in Israel and represent the first documented global emergence and virological characterization of TiLV in tilapia populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensification of Nile and hybrid tilapia culture in Israel, dense stocking in ponds and cages, seasonal warm water in Lake Kinneret and frequent movement of live fry and broodstock among farms favoured amplification and local spread of an initially unrecognized virus. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel orthomyxo‑like virus capable of systemic infection with high mortality in several tilapia species and hybrids, efficient horizontal transmission and environmental persistence, enabling establishment in both lake and farm systems (novel strain/genotype emergence plus enhanced transmission).
Review: review – Original row incorrectly combined Israel and Ecuador and treated them jointly as a first/global and inter‑continental emergence event. This revised event is restricted to Israel, with continent/sub-region corrected to Asia/Western Asia, countries limited to Israel [2009], and inter_continental_emergence set to No. First_global_emergence and first_detection remain Yes because this is the earliest documented TiLV detection in tilapia. Ecuador is now covered in a separate South American emergence event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) fingerlings and juveniles in intensive pond and tank systems
Event summary: Beginning in 2011, an intensively managed tilapia farm in Ecuador experienced recurrent outbreaks of a new liver disease in Nile tilapia fingerlings, later termed syncytial hepatitis of tilapia (SHT), with cumulative mortalities often exceeding 80–90%. Investigations through 2013 linked the lesions to a segmented negative‑sense RNA virus, and subsequent molecular work showed that the causative agent was TiLV and that the Ecuadorian strain shared about 97–99% nucleotide identity with Israeli isolates. These outbreaks were the first confirmed TiLV disease events in South America and demonstrated that the virus had already spread inter‑continentally from its original focus in Israel into a major Latin American tilapia‑producing country.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of industrial tilapia culture in Ecuador using a single farm-bred line, very high fry and fingerling stocking densities, and suboptimal water quality created strong amplification conditions once TiLV was introduced; movements of broodstock and seed within Ecuador and international trade in improved tilapia lines are the most plausible pathways for virus introduction from abroad. Internal mechanisms: a highly virulent TiLV lineage capable of causing SHT with very high mortality in young tilapia, genetically closely related to the Israeli strain, consistent with long‑distance spread of the same viral lineage rather than independent evolution, illustrating geographic range expansion driven by host and seed movement.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first major TiLV outbreak in South America (syncytial hepatitis of tilapia in Ecuador), which was previously only mentioned implicitly in the combined Israel–Ecuador row. Classified as an inter‑continental emergence (spread from Asia to South America), with years and impact based on SHT case and risk-factor studies; this clearly ranks among the top global TiLV emergence events and should be retained after expert checking of the exact start year (2011 vs. 2012).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in earthen ponds and cages in the Nile Delta and other major aquaculture areas
Event summary: From the early–mid 2010s, Egyptian tilapia producers reported a recurring "summer mortality" syndrome characterized by unexplained die‑offs of market‑size Nile tilapia during the warmest months, with little response to antibacterial treatments. An epidemiological study in 2015 found that about 37% of surveyed farms in major producing governorates were affected, with average mortality around 9% and an estimated production loss of roughly 98,000 tonnes of tilapia worth about US$100 million; subsequent virological work demonstrated the presence of TiLV in many affected farms and linked the virus to these events. Although control measures, awareness and diagnostics were gradually scaled up, TiLV became established in Egypt, representing the first confirmed incursion and large‑scale impact of the virus in Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Egypt’s dense network of tilapia ponds and cages in the Nile Delta, high dependence on tilapia for domestic fish supply, warm summer conditions and extensive internal movements of seed and food fish created ideal conditions for rapid establishment and spread once TiLV was introduced from overseas. Internal mechanisms: TiLV strains detected in Egypt belonged to the same general lineage as Israeli and Ecuadorian viruses and caused systemic disease with farm‑level mortalities typically in the 5–15% range but sometimes higher, illustrating geographic range expansion into Africa without evidence of major attenuation or host shift.
Review: retain – This event correctly captures the first major African TiLV outbreak associated with Egypt’s ‘summer mortality’ syndrome, including scale (≈37% of farms affected and losses around US$100 million) and its role as the inter‑continental emergence into Africa. Continent and sub‑region (Africa/Northern Africa) and classification (inter‑continental emergence only) are consistent with the definitions; no additional splitting or major corrections are needed.

Countries: Thailand [2015]; Indonesia [2016]; Malaysia [2016/2017]; Philippines [2017]; Taiwan Province of China [2017]
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia and red tilapia hybrids in cages, ponds and hatcheries; some affected broodstock and seed stocks
Event summary: In 2015–2016, tilapia farms in several provinces of Thailand experienced severe outbreaks with 80–90% cumulative mortality in juvenile and grow‑out fish, and laboratory investigations confirmed TiLV as the etiologic agent, marking its first recognized emergence in mainland South‑eastern Asia. Retrospective and prospective testing soon showed that genetically related TiLV strains were present in outbreaks and surveillance samples from other South‑east Asian countries, including Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, and in Chinese Taipei, often linked to substantial farm‑level losses and disruption of seed supply chains. As awareness grew, affected countries, FAO, NACA and WOAH issued alerts, and national services rolled out PCR‑based diagnostics, movement controls and improved farm‑level biosecurity; despite these measures, TiLV became established across much of the regional tilapia industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and high connectivity of tilapia farming in South‑eastern and parts of Eastern Asia; intense trade in live fry, fingerlings and broodstock among hatcheries and grow‑out farms; and initially limited awareness or diagnostic capacity enabled fast dissemination of TiLV once it entered the region. Internal mechanisms: TiLV displayed efficient horizontal transmission and high virulence in multiple Oreochromis species and hybrids across diverse production systems, supporting its classification as an intra‑continental emergence into new Asian sub‑regions driven by geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission rather than major viral attenuation or host change.
Review: review – Retained as a major intra‑continental emergence event into South‑eastern Asia, but sub_regions have been corrected to include both South‑eastern Asia and Eastern Asia because Chinese Taipei/Taiwan lies in Eastern Asia. Countries and approximate start years are consistent with outbreak and OIE notification reports, but the exact naming of "Taiwan Province of China" should be harmonised with the project’s Country sheet in a subsequent manual review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [2015]; Uganda [2016]; Kenya [2018]
Host: Farmed and wild Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in and around Lake Victoria (cages, ponds and open lake)
Event summary: From about 2015, producers around Lake Victoria began reporting unexplained mortalities in cage‑ and pond‑reared Nile tilapia, prompting regional investigations in the Tanzanian and Ugandan sectors of the lake. PCR‑based surveys of fish sampled from the Tanzanian part of Lake Victoria in 2015 and from the Ugandan part in 2016 confirmed TiLV infection in both farmed and wild tilapia, and phylogenetic analyses linked these East African viruses closely to strains from Israel and Thailand; later reviews report that the virus has spread throughout the lake ecosystem, including Kenyan waters. TiLV is now considered established in the Lake Victoria basin, and riparian states have launched surveillance plans, farmer training and biosecurity guidance, although eradication from this large, interconnected freshwater system is viewed as unrealistic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid growth of cage and pond aquaculture on Lake Victoria, transboundary hydrological connections, and frequent movement of live tilapia between hatcheries and farms around the lake created multiple opportunities for TiLV introduction (most likely from earlier African or Asian foci) and subsequent dissemination within the shared water body. Internal mechanisms: TiLV’s ability to infect both farmed and wild Nile tilapia and to persist in open freshwater systems underpins its geographic range expansion and environmental maintenance in Lake Victoria, with no clear evidence so far of major genetic adaptation specific to East African populations.
Review: review – Event retained as the key intra‑continental emergence of TiLV into Eastern Africa via Lake Victoria. Countries and years have been adjusted to reflect sample collection years reported for Tanzania (2015) and Uganda (2016); Kenya is kept in the country list with an estimated start year of 2018 based on later syntheses indicating spread throughout all riparian states, but there is less direct primary surveillance data than for Uganda and Tanzania. This row should be reviewed by regional experts to confirm whether Kenya should remain explicitly listed and whether the start year is appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia and red tilapia (Oreochromis spp.) in ponds and cages in Córdoba department
Event summary: In 2016, tilapia farms in Córdoba department, Colombia, experienced outbreaks with lethargy, skin lesions, abnormal swimming and substantial cumulative mortalities, raising suspicion of TiLV following earlier alerts about the virus in the region. A cross‑sectional investigation during 2016–2017 sampled seven farms and confirmed TiLV infection by nested RT‑PCR and sequencing in three of them, with farm‑level morbidity reported at 50–100% and mortality ranging from roughly 30% to 87% in affected ponds. This was the first official report of TiLV in Colombia and indicated that the virus, already present in Ecuador, had become established more widely in South American tilapia aquaculture.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive pond farming of Nile and red tilapia in Córdoba with high stocking densities, variable water quality and substantial movement of fingerlings between farms favoured amplification once TiLV was introduced; regional trade in tilapia seed or broodstock from other infected South American or Asian sources is the most likely introduction pathway. Internal mechanisms: Colombian TiLV segment 3 sequences showed around 97% nucleotide identity with the Israeli reference strain, consistent with introduction of an already well‑adapted lineage capable of causing severe disease and high mortality in local production systems without major additional viral evolution.
Review: review – New event added because TiLV emergence in Colombia involves multiple farms with very high mortalities and is widely cited as a major outbreak. Classified as re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region (the virus was already present in Ecuador), rather than intra‑continental emergence, in line with the project rule that spread to new countries within the same sub‑region should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. Recommended for retention, with a check that no larger South American events have been overlooked.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Peru [2017]; Peru – Piura, Lambayeque, San Martín (including Laguna Azul) [2018]
Host: Wild and farmed Nile tilapia and tilapia hybrids in rivers, reservoirs and aquaculture systems in northern coastal and Amazonian regions
Event summary: By late 2017, Peruvian authorities received reports of unusual mortalities in cultured and wild tilapia in northern and Amazonian regions, prompting emergency surveillance targeting TiLV. In early 2018, the national fisheries health authority (SANIPES) confirmed TiLV in farmed tilapia from multiple regions (including Piura and Lambayeque) and in wild tilapia from Laguna Azul in San Martín, and Peru filed an immediate notification to the WOAH; these findings followed earlier TiLV outbreaks in Ecuador and Colombia and signalled wider South American establishment of the virus. Peru responded with temporary restrictions on live tilapia movements, heightened monitoring and technical assistance to affected communities, which helped limit further spread but did not eliminate TiLV from wild or farmed stocks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: informal and formal movement of live tilapia for aquaculture and stocking of natural water bodies across South American countries, limited early diagnostic capacity and co‑farming with other species likely enabled TiLV introduction from existing foci in the region into new watersheds in Peru. Internal mechanisms: TiLV maintained high virulence in both farmed and wild tilapia in Peru, with some outbreaks approaching complete stock loss, illustrating persistent high pathogenicity and the virus’s capacity to persist in open freshwater environments without clear evidence of attenuation or major host shift.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region, but the Countries field has been corrected to include only Peru, with regional detail captured in brackets, and to remove the earlier speculative reference to "possibly Colombia and Ecuador with earlier farm outbreaks". Those earlier outbreaks are now represented explicitly in separate Ecuador and Colombia events. Coding as re_occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with TiLV already being present in the South America sub‑region via Ecuador and Colombia.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in ponds and cages; farmed Mozambique tilapia (O. mossambicus) and tilapia in polyculture; feral tilapia and hatchery broodstock in parts of India and Bangladesh
Event summary: Around 2016–2017, outbreaks with lethargy, skin erosions and very high cumulative mortality (>80%) in farmed Nile tilapia were reported from multiple locations in West Bengal and Kerala, India, and detailed investigations confirmed TiLV infection through PCR, sequencing, histopathology, cell culture and bioassays. Following regional alerts in 2017, Bangladesh implemented targeted surveillance of grow‑out farms and hatcheries in 2017 and 2019; TiLV was detected in the majority of farms experiencing unusual mortalities and in asymptomatic broodstock from six hatcheries, revealing widespread circulation across at least eight districts. Together these linked episodes marked the first recognized emergence and establishment of TiLV in Southern Asia, prompting national guidance on seed movement, farm biosecurity and continued surveillance, although the virus is now regarded as endemic in many affected areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid and sometimes poorly regulated expansion of tilapia aquaculture in South Asia, reliance on imported or locally multiplied improved tilapia strains (including GIFT), frequent movement of live seed, polyculture with carps, poor water quality and limited diagnostic capacity facilitated the introduction and silent spread of TiLV in India and Bangladesh. Internal mechanisms: South Asian TiLV isolates cluster genetically with Thai and Israeli lineages and retain high virulence in Nile and Mozambique tilapia, supporting a scenario of long‑distance introduction of existing virulent strains followed by efficient horizontal transmission, rather than evolution of a new attenuated or host‑shifted variant.
Review: review – New intra‑continental emergence event added for Southern Asia, aggregating strongly linked high‑mortality outbreaks in India with subsequent multi‑district detection in Bangladesh. This region was missing from the original set despite clear evidence of severe farm‑level impacts and wide TiLV circulation. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (first occurrence in the Southern Asia sub‑region), with years based on the first confirmed Indian outbreaks and Bangladesh surveillance; both countries and dates should be cross‑checked against any newer national reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in commercial pond and recirculating systems; some imported live tilapia stocks
Event summary: In 2017, TiLV was detected in Mexican tilapia aquaculture and formally reported to the World Organisation for Animal Health in 2018, indicating that the virus had reached Central America and was present in multiple production facilities across several states. In February 2019, a suspected TiLV outbreak in a U.S. tilapia facility led to the isolation and full-genome characterization of two TiLV isolates from moribund Nile tilapia, and phylogenetic analysis showed that these U.S. viruses clustered closely with Thai strains, consistent with introduction via international movements of live fish rather than from neighbouring farms. Following the Mexican and U.S. detections, authorities in both countries and industry groups increased surveillance, tightened health certification and import controls for live tilapia and emphasised farm-level biosecurity to prevent wider establishment and trade disruptions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in live tilapia broodstock and fingerlings, including imports from TiLV-endemic regions in Asia and possibly South America, facilitated transboundary and transoceanic introduction into Mexico and, separately, the United States; incomplete health screening of imported stocks and high farm connectivity amplified the risk. Internal mechanisms: TiLV maintained its pathogenic phenotype under North American farm conditions, and genome analyses showed close relatedness to Asian lineages, indicating recent introduction with limited divergence and demonstrating the virus’s capacity for inter‑continental spread without the need for major adaptive change.
Review: review – Original event correctly identified Mexico and the United States as a key emergence episode but misclassified the geography as solely "North America" and listed only the Northern America sub‑region. This revised row sets continents to South America and North America (reflecting Mexico’s placement in South America|Central America in the project’s Country sheet) and sub_regions to Central America and Northern America, and it clarifies that the principal classification is inter‑continental emergence due to first establishment in the Northern America continent. Start years for Mexico (2017) and the U.S. farm outbreak (2019) have been aligned with OIE notifications and the genomic characterization study; these details should be re‑checked against any additional national data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Southern sea otter (Enhydra lutris nereis)
Event summary: Between 1998 and 2001, investigators documented extensive Toxoplasma gondii infection and disease in southern sea otters along the California coast, revealing that a high proportion of live and dead otters were seropositive and that toxoplasmosis was a frequent cause of mortality. Over the subsequent few years, follow‑up work showed that a substantial fraction of the southern sea otter population had been exposed and that roughly one‑third of examined deaths involved toxoplasmosis as a primary or contributing cause, firmly establishing the parasite as a major impediment to sea otter recovery. This multi‑year coastal episode gradually abated locally as carcass numbers fluctuated, but chronic environmental contamination and continued exposure have kept toxoplasmosis an ongoing conservation concern for sea otters.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Land‑based pollution and coastal freshwater runoff carrying oocysts from domestic and feral cats into nearshore marine habitats were identified as key risk factors, with proximity to river outflows and anthropogenic development associated with higher infection risk in otters; shellfish such as mussels concentrate oocysts and act as exposure pathways. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced transmission, with a terrestrial felid parasite establishing a significant disease burden in marine mammal hosts; some isolates from sea otters showed distinct genotypes, but available evidence indicates that environmental loading and exposure, rather than a single hyper‑virulent strain, are the predominant mechanisms.
Review: Decision: review. Corrected the event start year from 1997 to 1998 and updated the country annotation to [California 1998] to match necropsy and stranding analyses that quantify T. gondii–associated mortality in southern sea otters from 1998–2004; classification as a re‑emergence episode (host expansion into a marine mammal with strong environmental drivers) and other fields remain appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Hawaiian monk seal (Neomonachus schauinslandi)
Event summary: From 2001 onward, protozoal infections, predominantly Toxoplasma gondii, were recognized as causes of fatal disseminated disease in endangered Hawaiian monk seals, with initial cases occurring in stranded adults and a captive animal. Over the period 2001–2015, at least eight confirmed and additional suspect monk seal deaths due to disseminated toxoplasmosis were documented around the main Hawaiian Islands, including the first confirmed case of vertical (congenital) transmission in this species. By the mid‑2010s and into the 2020s, toxoplasmosis had become one of the leading disease‑related causes of death in monk seals, prompting recognition of the parasite as a major barrier to the species’ recovery and leading to calls for feral and free‑roaming cat management in Hawaiʻi.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large populations of feral and free‑roaming domestic cats on the Hawaiian Islands shed oocysts that are transported via stormwater, streams and sewage into coastal habitats, where monk seals are exposed; ongoing urbanization and inadequate control of outdoor cats have sustained high environmental oocyst loading. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven primarily by host expansion and enhanced transmission into a naïve marine mammal population; available reports highlight severe disseminated disease rather than a clearly defined novel strain, although non‑archetypal genotypes circulating in Brazil and elsewhere suggest that genetically diverse strains can have high virulence in animals.
Review: Decision: retain. This row accurately summarizes the 2001–2015 series of Hawaiian monk seal mortalities attributable to disseminated toxoplasmosis, with correct geography (Northern America/United States), host, timeframe and classification as re‑emergence driven by expansion of T. gondii into an endangered pinniped population; primary NOAA case series support the numbers and interpretation, and no major omissions or misclassifications were identified.

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries), purebred Suffolk ewes
Event summary: During the 2005 lambing season, a flock of purebred Suffolk ewes on a Texas farm experienced a severe toxoplasmosis abortion storm in which only 14 healthy lambs were born while 38 abortuses, mummified and weak or stillborn lambs were delivered and at least 13 additional fetuses were presumed lost based on ultrasound examinations. Serologic testing showed that 35 of 37 ewes had antibodies to T. gondii, most with very high titers, and viable T. gondii (designated TgShUs55) with an atypical genotype highly virulent for mice was isolated from the brain and heart of an aborted lamb, confirming the parasite as the primary cause.
