In the following lambing seasons, the flock largely returned to normal productivity with only sporadic losses, consistent with development of protective immunity among previously affected ewes and absence of further large‑scale toxoplasmosis‑induced abortions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak likely resulted from heavy environmental contamination of feed or pasture with oocysts shed by local cats, combined with a group of susceptible pregnant ewes in mid‑ to late gestation, creating conditions for near‑synchronous exposure and fetal infection. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by an atypical, highly virulent T. gondii genotype (TgShUs55) that caused extensive abortion and neonatal mortality and by efficient vertical transmission from chronically infected ewes, illustrating the role of parasite genetic diversity and congenital infection in severe ovine toxoplasmosis.
Review: Decision: review. New row added for a previously omitted but widely cited 2005 abortion storm in a Suffolk sheep flock in Texas, where >50 pregnancies were lost and an atypical, mouse‑virulent genotype (TgShUs55) was isolated; this episode is likely among the most impactful modern livestock outbreaks of ovine toxoplasmosis and fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by a novel strain. Please verify numerical details and wording directly against Edwards & Dubey (2013) before finalizing.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event summary: In January–February 2010, a semi‑intensive Dorper–Santa Inês sheep flock of about 200 pregnant ewes in Serro, Minas Gerais State, Brazil, experienced an outbreak in which around 40 ewes aborted or delivered stillborn lambs. Necropsy and histopathology of an aborted fetus revealed characteristic necrotizing encephalitis with tissue cysts, and immunohistochemistry was strongly positive for T. gondii, while cultures and PCR for bacterial and other protozoal causes were negative, confirming toxoplasmosis as the main aetiology. Following diagnosis and implementation of improved management and biosecurity measures, the outbreak subsided and the owner reported no further major reproductive problems in the flock in the following year.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Semi‑intensive husbandry with ewes confined before lambing, presence of cats on the property, and likely contamination of feed or housing with sporulated oocysts created conditions for a point‑source exposure around mid‑gestation, a period when T. gondii infection is highly likely to cause abortion or stillbirth in sheep. Internal mechanisms: This was a re‑occurrence of endemic ovine toxoplasmosis in a previously affected subregion, characterized by efficient transplacental transmission and severe fetal disease in a flock that previously had few reproductive issues; no genotyping was reported, so there is no direct evidence for a novel strain beyond the typical pathogenic field variants known to circulate in Brazil.
Review: Decision: review. Reclassified the emergence type from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because the case report does not document a new genotype, host shift or other intrinsic change in T. gondii; the episode represents a sizeable but otherwise typical abortion outbreak in an already endemic subregion driven mainly by management and environmental factors. All geographical fields, host and impact description are consistent with the Brazilian report and have been retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic goats (Capra aegagrus hircus)
Event summary: Around 2011, a commercial goat herd in the Brazilian Midwest (State of Mato Grosso) experienced an outbreak of abortions, with seven fetuses submitted for necropsy to the Federal University of Mato Grosso veterinary pathology laboratory. Histopathology showed necrotizing encephalitis and mononuclear pneumonia in aborted fetuses, and nested PCR on fetal brains was positive for T. gondii while testing for Brucella abortus, Neospora caninum and bacteria was negative, indicating toxoplasmosis as the primary cause of the outbreak. After diagnosis, the outbreak was managed and no further large clusters of reproductive losses were reported on the farm in the following year, though the episode highlighted T. gondii as an under‑recognized cause of caprine abortion in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive environmental contamination with cat‑shed oocysts on a semi‑intensive goat farm, combined with climatic and management conditions conducive to oocyst survival (warm, humid environment, access of cats to feed and housing), likely led to synchronized exposure of pregnant does. Internal mechanisms: This event is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence of caprine toxoplasmosis in an already endemic area, driven by vertical transmission and severe fetal pathology rather than by a clearly documented new strain; nonetheless, very high serologic titers in aborting does and lesions typical of toxoplasmosis are consistent with infection by a virulent local field strain.
Review: Decision: review. Changed the emergence classification from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because the primary report describes a localized abortion outbreak in goats within an endemic region, with no evidence for a novel genotype, host expansion or other intrinsic change in T. gondii; geographic information and outbreak description remain accurate. The episode is retained as a substantial caprine abortion event but should not be interpreted as strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), growing–finishing pigs
Event summary: In 2020, a commercial finishing pig farm with about 1,500 pigs in the state of Santa Catarina, southern Brazil, experienced an outbreak of fatal systemic toxoplasmosis characterized by fever, anorexia, apathy and locomotor deficits, with a reported mortality of 3.8% in the growing–finishing herd. Necropsies of seven pigs revealed multifocal pale skeletal muscle lesions, lymphadenomegaly, hepatosplenomegaly and non‑collapsed lungs, and histology plus immunohistochemistry demonstrated widespread T. gondii tachyzoites and bradyzoites in multiple organs; multilocus PCR‑RFLP and microsatellite genotyping identified a non‑archetypal genotype #278, marking the first report of systemic toxoplasmosis in pigs with prominent muscle lesions. The outbreak was controlled through culling of affected animals and improvements in biosecurity, but it highlighted that clinically severe toxoplasmosis can re‑emerge in modern intensive swine systems and has implications for animal health and food safety.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Outdoor access of domestic and wild animals to pig‑sheds due to lack of perimeter fencing, combined with potential contamination of feed or water with cat‑shed oocysts, likely introduced T. gondii into the finishing herd; intensive housing with many pigs per shed facilitated exposure once contamination occurred. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by an atypical, non‑archetypal genotype (#278) capable of causing systemic, often fatal disease in pigs, a host where infection is usually subclinical; the unusual prominence of necrotizing myositis and muscular lesions suggests heightened tissue tropism and/or virulence compared with typical Type II strains more commonly described in pigs.
Review: Decision: review. Corrected the event year from 2022 to 2020 and updated the country annotation accordingly, based on the primary report which states that the farm contacted veterinarians after a sharp rise in mortality in February 2020; the original row appears to have conflated the publication year (2022) with the outbreak year. The classification as re‑emergence driven by an atypical genotype and the description of clinical impact and mechanisms are otherwise well supported and have been retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic goats (Capra aegagrus hircus)
Event summary: In the early 2020s, a small goat farm (10 does) in the State of Paraíba in Northeast Brazil experienced an abortion storm in which seven does aborted and another produced twins of which one was stillborn and the other weak and underdeveloped, resulting in an estimated 80–90% pregnancy loss attributed to toxoplasmosis. Serology showed very high IgG titers to T. gondii in all does, and ITS1 PCR followed by multilocus PCR‑RFLP genotyping of placental, colostrum and fetal tissues identified the atypical ToxoDB genotype #13 as the sole strain involved, confirming vertical transmission from dams to fetuses. After the outbreak, the herd was managed more carefully, but the event underscored that highly pathogenic non‑archetypal genotypes circulating in Northeast Brazil can cause devastating reproductive losses even in very small caprine herds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Semi‑intensive goat production without estrus synchronization, common in the Northeast of Brazil, together with inadequate facilities and likely access of cats to feed and housing, created conditions for widespread exposure to sporulated oocysts; limited routine diagnostic investigation in the region meant that similar outbreaks may go unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence, with the abortion storm linked to a highly virulent non‑archetypal genotype #13 that is common in local chickens and pigs and has shown high lethality in experimental infections in mice, indicating strong pathogenic potential in multiple hosts.
Review: Decision: retain. This row faithfully reflects the small‑herd abortion storm in Paraíba linked to atypical genotype #13 as described by Vilela et al. (2023/2024), including the scale of losses, host species and genotyping results. The exact calendar year of the on‑farm abortions is not specified in the source, so the event year is appropriately left approximate (~2021–2022) and flagged in the quality notes; classification as re‑emergence due to a highly pathogenic non‑archetypal genotype is appropriate.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), including neonatal and suckling piglets, lactating sows, and weaned growers on state and cooperative farms in Havana Province and other affected regions
Event summary: Beginning in February 2003, pig farms in Havana Province, Cuba, reported explosive outbreaks of gastroenteritis in sows and piglets, with very watery yellow diarrhea, vomiting and near 100% mortality in newborn litters, eventually affecting almost all recently farrowed sows and their litters on many farms. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf)) Laboratory investigation isolated coronavirus particles from diarrheic piglets, confirmed them as TGEV by electron microscopy, virus isolation, RT‑PCR and sequencing of the 5′ spike gene, and showed the Cuban strain to be closely related to a contemporary US TGEV isolate, indicating recent introduction of a typical enteric TGEV lineage. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf)) At the peak of the epidemic, at least 15 outbreaks in Havana Province alone involved about 23,201 sick pigs, 10,547 deaths and 5,256 culls, after which herd immunity and control measures allowed mortality to subside and TGEV to transition toward lower‑level endemic circulation with sporadic cases reported up to at least 2008. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): The epidemic is interpreted by Cuban investigators as a classic virgin‑soil introduction of TGEV into a previously unexposed national pig population, with no earlier clinical or serologic evidence of infection; likely drivers include introduction via contaminated pigs, semen or pork products from TGEV‑endemic countries, combined with relatively dense pig production around Havana and biosecurity gaps that permitted rapid farm‑to‑farm spread. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Partial S‑gene sequencing showed the Cuban strain grouped closely with a recent Midwestern US TGEV isolate, with only a few amino‑acid substitutions and no deletions characteristic of PRCV, supporting the interpretation that this was a typical, highly enteropathogenic TGEV genotype whose severe impact reflected the extreme susceptibility of an immunologically naïve host population rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent variant. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf))
Review: review – New event added. Strong evidence from Cuban case reports and molecular analyses shows a large virgin‑soil TGE epidemic beginning in 2003 with >23,000 cases and >10,000 deaths in Havana Province alone; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 TGEV events and represents an intra‑continental emergence into the previously TGE‑free Caribbean sub‑region of the South America continent grouping. Classification set to intra‑continental emergence, with first_global_emergence and first_detection kept false because TGEV was globally recognized in pigs since the 1940s.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), primarily 1–21‑day‑old suckling piglets and pregnant/lactating sows in intensive farrow‑to‑finish herds in Buenos Aires and Córdoba Provinces
Event summary: From 2010 onwards, three large farrow‑to‑finish pig herds in Argentina experienced sudden outbreaks of severe vomiting and watery diarrhea in 1–21‑day‑old piglets, accompanied by diarrhea, inappetence and agalactia in sows, leading to pre‑weaning mortality reportedly approaching 90–95% in affected litters and markedly elevated overall pre‑weaning losses during the main episode. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) In response to a 2014 national serologic survey that first detected TGEV antibodies in a small, clinically mild herd and triggered Argentina’s initial OIE notification, archived intestinal tissues from earlier high‑mortality neonatal diarrhea cases (2010–2015) were re‑examined and confirmed as TGEV by electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization while testing negative for PEDV and rotavirus A, demonstrating that clinically significant TGEV infection had been present in the national herd for several years before official recognition. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) The acute herd‑level outbreaks subsided over weeks to months as susceptible piglets died and herd immunity developed, and subsequent surveillance indicates that TGEV likely persists at low, under‑diagnosed prevalence in Argentine swine as part of a broader complex of enteric coronaviruses. ([repozytorium.piwet.pulawy.pl](https://repozytorium.piwet.pulawy.pl/bitstream/handle/123456789/724/s12917-024-04364-6.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=2))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): The Argentine episode appears to reflect introduction of TGEV into previously naïve or minimally exposed commercial herds, probably via movement of infected pigs, semen or contaminated transport and equipment from TGEV‑endemic regions, coupled with intensive, high‑density farrow‑to‑finish production and limited awareness and diagnostic capacity for swine coronaviruses in Argentina, which allowed several years of unrecognized circulation before formal notification. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and limited molecular data indicate a disease pattern consistent with classical enteric TGEV rather than a distinct new genotype, suggesting that the high impact arose from geographic range expansion of a typical, highly virulent TGEV strain into an immunologically naïve pig population, with severe disease concentrated in very young piglets lacking maternal antibodies. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763))
Review: review – Event retained but corrected. (1) Adjusted the event time span from 2011–2015 to 2010–2015 and the country tag from “Argentina [2011]” to “Argentina [2010]” to match the Argentine case‑series, which identified three TGEV‑confirmed outbreaks between 2010 and 2015. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) (2) Set the ‘first_detection’ flag to false because this category refers to the first detection of the pathogen in the host system globally; TGEV was first detected in pigs in the USA in 1946, so Argentine outbreaks represent national‑level and intra‑continental emergence within South America, not global first detection. ([anipedia.up.ac.za](https://anipedia.up.ac.za/publications/transmissible-gastroenteritis/1017.html?utm_source=openai)) (3) Slightly revised the event summary and mechanism to avoid over‑specific, weakly supported details (for example, specific mention of replacement gilt movements) while keeping the core interpretation that this was a major intra‑continental emergence into the South America sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), including sows and suckling and recently weaned piglets on small farrow‑to‑finish farms on Tahiti Island
Event summary: In August 2011, two commercial pig farms in Teva I Uta commune on Tahiti Island, French Polynesia, experienced explosive outbreaks of diarrhea and vomiting in sows and piglets, with reported mortality of 100% in non‑weaned piglets and about 50–76% in weaned piglets, resulting in 738 cases and 547 deaths among roughly 2,975 susceptible pigs across the two herds. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) Differential diagnosis and serology performed in France confirmed infection with transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV) using a differential TGEV/PRCV ELISA, and the territory submitted an immediate WOAH notification classifying the event as the first occurrence of TGE, indicating introduction into a previously TGE‑free island population in Oceania. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) The outbreaks burned out over time without vaccination, with mortality spontaneously ceasing after affected piglets died and biosecurity measures were reinforced, and no subsequent large‑scale TGE epidemics in French Polynesia have been widely reported. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): WOAH’s epidemiologic investigation noted no live‑pig imports in 2011 and identified swill feeding of untreated restaurant waste by an itinerant butcher as the most plausible source of TGEV introduction, implying long‑distance movement of virus in contaminated pork products to a naïve pig population; high pig density within affected farms and absence of prior immunity in French Polynesia then permitted rapid within‑herd transmission and extreme piglet mortality. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available information does not indicate unusual genetic changes in the virus; clinical pattern and severity are consistent with classical enteric TGEV infection in immunologically naïve herds, so this event is best interpreted as inter‑continental geographic range expansion of a typical TGEV strain into Oceania rather than emergence of a novel variant. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf))
Review: review – New event added. WOAH’s immediate notification for French Polynesia in 2011 documents two severe on‑farm TGE outbreaks and explicitly labels them as the first occurrence of this listed disease in the territory; given the absence of prior records of TGE in Oceania, this episode is appropriately classified here as an inter‑continental emergence of TGEV into Polynesia rather than as a re‑occurrence linked to earlier continental epidemics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses (Equus caballus) slaughtered for human consumption; domestic pigs and wild carnivores as background reservoirs
Event summary: Between 1990 and 1998, several very large trichinellosis outbreaks in Italy and France were traced to raw or undercooked horse meat, including a Barletta (Italy) epidemic with >500 human cases in 1990 and large multi-focal outbreaks in France and Italy in 1993 and 1998 linked to imported horses from Eastern Europe. These episodes confirmed that horses—previously considered an unusual host—could develop sufficient Trichinella muscle burdens to seed major food-borne epidemics despite relatively low infection prevalence. In response, the EU and importing countries introduced mandatory Trichinella testing and tighter traceability for horse carcasses, which sharply reduced horse-meat-associated trichinellosis by the early 2000s, although low-level infection and sporadic risk in horses persist.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing international trade in live horses and carcasses from Eastern Europe to France and Italy, combined with absence or inadequacy of Trichinella testing in horses and long-standing culinary traditions of eating raw or lightly cooked horse meat (e.g. steak tartare), created conditions for continent-scale food-borne outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of encapsulated Trichinella spp. (mainly T. spiralis) into horses used as a major food source; no new parasite species were involved, but recognition of horses as an efficient vehicle for human infection effectively expanded the realized host range in the domestic cycle.
Review: Decision: retain. New high-impact multi-country event added, because large horse-meat epidemics in Italy and France during 1990–1998 caused hundreds to >500 human cases and directly triggered EU-wide Trichinella controls on horses, clearly placing this episode among the most consequential modern emergence/re-emergence events for Trichinella spp. in food animals. Classified as re-occurrence (resurgence linked to horse-meat trade and food habits) and re-emergence (host expansion to horses as a major food animal), without intra- or inter-continental emergence, consistent with the genus being long established in Europe.

Countries: Argentina [multiple central and southern provinces including Buenos Aires, Córdoba, San Luis 1990-2005]
Host: Backyard and smallholder domestic pigs; occasionally wild boar and other suids (background)
Event summary: From 1990 through 2005, Argentina experienced repeated large trichinellosis outbreaks associated mainly with home-produced pork products from backyard pigs in several central and southern provinces, with some individual outbreaks involving hundreds of human cases. Over this 15-year period, >5,000 human cases were reported nationally, giving Argentina one of the highest incidences worldwide and reflecting intense circulation of Trichinella spiralis in poorly controlled domestic pig systems. Progressive strengthening of veterinary inspection, enforcement against feeding pigs raw offal, and public-health campaigns about the risks of raw sausages led to a gradual decline in incidence after the mid-2000s, although sporadic outbreaks continue to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional backyard pig rearing with home slaughter, feeding pigs uncooked food scraps and offal, lack of systematic meat inspection, and cultural preference for undercooked or raw pork sausages created ideal conditions for sustained Trichinella transmission in domestic pigs and frequent large human outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No new Trichinella species or genotypes were implicated; this event reflects amplification and persistence of established T. spiralis domestic cycles rather than biological innovation.
Review: Decision: retain. New event added to represent the very high cumulative burden of trichinellosis in Argentina (over 5,000 human cases between 1990 and 2005, largely from domestic pigs), which clearly ranks among the most impactful modern episodes for this genus. Classified as re-occurrence driven by husbandry and food-processing practices; no evidence for novel parasite biology.

Countries: Romania [1990-2011; Western and North-Eastern regions particularly affected]
Host: Backyard and farm pigs; wild boar (Sus scrofa); bears and other wildlife as sylvatic reservoirs
Event summary: Following the political and economic transition around 1989, Romania entered a prolonged period (approximately 1990–2011) of very high trichinellosis incidence, with tens of thousands of human cases nationally and thousands of infected pigs detected at slaughter, as Trichinella spiralis and T. britovi flourished in backyard pig and sylvatic cycles. Abattoir data from large western counties between 1998 and 2011 show infection in hundreds of thousands of slaughtered pigs and wild boar, with markedly higher prevalence in household pigs than in commercial farms, while epidemiological reviews estimate that Romania alone accounted for roughly half of all human trichinellosis cases reported in Europe during 1986–2007. Strengthened veterinary controls, EU-aligned meat inspection, restrictions on feeding pigs raw waste and carcasses, and public education gradually reduced incidence after the early 2000s, but Romania remains an important endemic focus with recurrent outbreaks linked to home-slaughtered pigs and game.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post-communist socio-economic upheaval, dismantling of large state farms, expansion of backyard pig keeping, breakdown or evasion of meat inspection, feeding pigs with uncooked slaughter waste, and culturally embedded traditions of home slaughter and communal consumption of raw or undercooked pork products (e.g. winter pig feasts) drove intense transmission. Internal mechanisms: No novel Trichinella species or resistance traits were implicated; the episode is best understood as a large-scale re-occurrence driven by external social and economic changes amplifying long-established T. spiralis and T. britovi cycles in domestic pigs and wildlife.
Review: Decision: retain. The original ChatGPT event (“1998–2011, Western and North-Eastern Romania”) has been broadened to 1990–2011 to align with WHO/EID and Romanian data showing that Romania experienced an exceptional, country-wide resurgence with ~28,500 human cases during 1986–2007, mainly in the 1990s. Classification as re-occurrence (external socio-economic drivers) without re-emergence (no clear parasite change) is retained. This long-running episode is clearly one of the most impactful modern Trichinella events and should remain in the top ten.

Host: Backyard domestic pigs (primary); dogs and other meat sources occasionally implicated but peripheral to the main domestic pig cycle
Event summary: In the early to mid-1990s, central Chinese provinces such as Henan experienced multiple community trichinellosis outbreaks caused by pork from Trichinella-infected backyard pigs, including a documented series of seven outbreaks around Zhengzhou between 1992 and 1996 with about 250 confirmed human cases and many more exposed. These events formed part of a wider national pattern: reviews of 1964–1999 data estimate hundreds of outbreaks and many thousands of human infections in China, with pork accounting for more than 95% of identified sources. Subsequent control programmes, including strengthened meat inspection, improved pig husbandry, and educational campaigns on cooking pork thoroughly, reduced incidence after 2000 but did not eliminate the risk, with further outbreaks recorded in Yunnan, Tibet, Hubei and other provinces.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High prevalence of Trichinella spiralis in backyard pigs, feeding of pigs with uncooked food wastes and carcasses, unregulated home slaughter without inspection, and traditional consumption of raw or undercooked pork dishes all contributed to frequent large outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel Trichinella species or genotypes; these outbreaks represent re-occurrence and amplification of endemic T. spiralis domestic cycles in central China.
Review: Decision: retain. New event added because central China’s pig-associated outbreaks in the 1990s, exemplified by the seven Henan outbreaks (≈250 cases) and embedded within >10,000 national cases over several decades, are among the largest documented Trichinella episodes outside Europe. Classified as re-occurrence in long-endemic domestic pig systems; no intra- or inter-continental emergence involved.

Host: Horses (Equus caballus); domestic pigs (background endemicity)
Event summary: In 1993, Trichinella infection was documented for the first time in horses slaughtered in Romania, against a backdrop of well-established Trichinella circulation in domestic pigs and humans. Although no linked human cases were identified from these specific horses, the finding showed that horses in Romania could enter the domestic cycle and potentially act as sources of large epidemics, as had occurred in Italy and France. The detection led Romanian and EU authorities to include horses in Trichinella surveillance and meat inspection schemes, alongside pigs and game.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The post-communist expansion of informal meat production and trade, including horse slaughter, in a context of high Trichinella prevalence in pigs and wildlife increased opportunities for spillover into horses. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of existing Trichinella lineages (mainly T. spiralis) into horses in the domestic cycle; no novel species were implicated, but the event underscored the capacity of horses to serve as food-borne sources of infection.
Review: Decision: review. The event description and classification as re-emergence (host expansion to horses) are broadly accurate and supported by Romanian reviews, but only a small number of horses were infected and no human cases were linked, so the direct impact is modest. Given numerous much larger outbreaks (Romania-wide pig epidemics, Chinese and Argentine pork outbreaks, major horse-meat epidemics, the 2003–2004 Izmir outbreak), this 1993 detection is unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful global emergence events; retain for now as a species–host milestone but consider excluding if the dataset is trimmed strictly to the top ten.
Review Comment: unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful global emergence events;

Host: Pork from illegally slaughtered domestic pigs and/or wild boar (Sus scrofa) used in raw meat dishes; wild boar as a likely reservoir
Event summary: Between December 2003 and January 2004, a very large trichinellosis outbreak with about 418 human cases occurred in the Izmir area of western Türkiye after consumption of raw or undercooked spiced meatballs made with pork from illegally slaughtered suids. Epidemiologic investigations pointed to meat from free-range pigs and/or wild boar that had bypassed official veterinary inspection, and Trichinella britovi was identified as the etiologic agent in humans and meat samples. This outbreak revealed substantial, previously under-recognized circulation of Trichinella in suid populations in western Türkiye and highlighted the risk posed by illicit pork and game meat in a predominantly Muslim country where pig meat is not widely consumed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Illegal slaughter and marketing of pigs or wild boar outside official abattoirs, preparation of traditional raw meat dishes (e.g. çiğ köfte–type products) with contaminated pork, and low awareness of trichinellosis risk in areas where pork consumption is culturally restricted allowed a single contaminated batch to infect several hundred people. Internal mechanisms: No new Trichinella species or host switch was involved; the event represents a large re-occurrence in a low-visibility suid reservoir revealed through a spectacular food-borne outbreak.
Review: Decision: retain. New high-impact event added: the 2003–2004 Izmir outbreak (≈418 human cases) is one of the largest modern trichinellosis epidemics outside Eastern Europe and clearly surpasses several previously listed low-impact detection events. Classified as re-occurrence driven by illicit pork/wild boar meat and raw-meat dishes; not an inter-continental or intra-continental emergence because Trichinella spp. were already endemic in the region.

Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [Gilan and other northern provinces mid-2000s]
Host: Wild boar (Sus scrofa); carnivores (e.g. golden jackal, fox) as background sylvatic reservoirs
Event summary: In the mid-2000s, larvae from a wild boar in Gilan Province in northern Iran were initially reported as Trichinella murrelli, apparently indicating the first occurrence of this North American species in Asia and in wild boar. However, subsequent molecular work demonstrated that this isolate had been misidentified and actually belonged to T. britovi, which, together with T. spiralis, had been circulating for decades in Iranian wildlife. Later surveys confirmed low-prevalence T. britovi infection in wild boar from several northern provinces, reinforcing the view that Iran harbours a long-standing sylvatic Trichinella focus with wild boar as a key bridge host for high-risk minority hunters and consumers.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing predator–prey and scavenging interactions among wild boar and carnivores in forested northern Iran maintain a sylvatic Trichinella cycle, while recreational and subsistence hunting by religious minorities provide an interface for spillover to humans; increased sampling and molecular diagnostics in the 2000s enabled species-level identification in wild boar. Internal mechanisms: Taxonomic clarification rather than true species introduction—reclassification of a supposed T. murrelli isolate as T. britovi; modest host expansion in that T. britovi was now confirmed in wild boar as well as carnivores, but with no evidence of major changes in parasite biology or regional distribution.
Review: Decision: review. The original event incorrectly treated this as a genuine inter-continental emergence of T. murrelli into Asia; the description and coding have been updated to reflect later evidence that the isolate was in fact T. britovi and that Trichinella spp. had long been present in Iranian wildlife. Inter-continental emergence has been set to No and the event is now coded as re-emergence (clarified species identity and host range). Because the impact is limited to low-prevalence wildlife infection with no major documented animal or human outbreaks, this event is unlikely to be among the top ten by impact and should be reconsidered for exclusion if space is constrained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic pigs; hunted wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event summary: Between 2006 and 2013, national surveillance in Spain documented Trichinella larvae in both domestic pigs and wild boar, primarily T. spiralis and T. britovi, with 384 infected pigs (0.0001%) and 1,399 infected wild boar (~0.2%), confirming ongoing domestic and especially sylvatic circulation. In 2014, Trichinella pseudospiralis was isolated from a wild boar hunted in Girona Province, Catalonia, marking the first detection of this non-encapsulated species in the Iberian Peninsula. This finding expanded the known European range of T. pseudospiralis and highlighted that areas previously regarded as low risk could harbour non-encapsulated Trichinella, detectable only through artificial digestion and molecular typing.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growth of wild boar populations, expansion of recreational hunting, and demand for free-range/organic pig production increased contact between domestic pigs, wild boar and wildlife carcasses, maintaining Trichinella transmission. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and/or first recognition of T. pseudospiralis in Iberian wild boar, representing re-emergence of the genus in the region via a new non-encapsulated species; detection depended on improved diagnostic and molecular tools rather than an obvious change in parasite biology.
Review: Decision: review. The original coding as intra-continental emergence has been corrected to re-emergence only, in line with project rules that new species or genotypes in regions where the genus is already endemic should not be labelled inter- or intra-continental emergence. The event is important for documenting the first Iberian detection of T. pseudospiralis and sustained Trichinella circulation in Spanish pigs and wild boar, but involves only a single known non-encapsulated-species isolate and no very large animal or human outbreaks; it may fall below the global top ten by impact and should be retained only if species-range expansions are prioritized alongside large epidemics.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [2013]; Italy, southern regions including Calabria/Basilicata/Apulia [2013-2016]
Host: Wild boar (Sus scrofa); occasionally free-range pigs
Event summary: From roughly 2013 to 2016, Italy recorded several trichinellosis outbreaks linked to wild boar hunted in regions previously classified as negligible risk for Trichinella, including a well-described outbreak in southern Italy in which consumption of undercooked wild boar sausages led to dozens of human cases caused by T. britovi. Retrospective analysis of Italian data from 1985–2016 indicates that most animal Trichinella detections (n≈354) involved wild boar, with occasional domestic pigs and other species, but these 2013–2016 outbreaks signalled a southward shift of enzootic foci into new hunting areas. Italian and EU reference laboratories subsequently emphasized systematic testing of wild boar carcasses from all regions and reinforced public advisories on thoroughly cooking game meat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and increased density of wild boar populations, spread of boar into new habitats, growth of recreational hunting, and inconsistent application of Trichinella testing to animals from putatively low-risk regions facilitated renewed human exposure. Internal mechanisms: No novel species or genotypes were identified; the outbreaks represent re-occurrence of T. britovi in wild boar at the periphery of its known range rather than parasite evolution, although the geographic shift broadened the realized endemic area within Italy.
Review: Decision: review. The original event has been reclassified as re-occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because the evidence points to geographic spread and increased detection of existing T. britovi foci in wild boar, without clear parasite change. These Italian wild-boar outbreaks are epidemiologically important for Europe but involve tens rather than hundreds of human cases and modest numbers of infected animals compared with the very large episodes in Romania, Argentina, China and Türkiye; they may or may not fit within a strict global top ten and are therefore flagged for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Backyard pigs used for traditional figatelli sausages; wild boar (background source in Corsica)
Event summary: In 2015, three human trichinellosis cases were reported in south-eastern France after consumption of raw figatelli sausages produced in Corsica from pork contaminated with Trichinella britovi, despite long-standing EU-mandated carcass testing. Investigations showed that pigs had been slaughtered illegally and the figatelli label carried insufficiently visible warnings that the product must be thoroughly cooked, allowing infected meat from backyard pigs or wild boar to enter artisanal processing chains. Following the outbreak, French authorities tightened labelling requirements for figatelli and reinforced veterinary controls and surveillance for Trichinella in Corsican outdoor pigs and wild boar.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cultural preference for eating raw or rare figatelli, gaps in labelling and enforcement of Trichinella testing in small-scale Corsican pig systems, illegal slaughter, and potential mixing of meat from free-range pigs and wild boar enabled the parasite to persist in localized production niches even as industrial pork was essentially Trichinella-free. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was identified; this episode represents a localized re-occurrence of T. britovi in Corsican backyard pig/wild-boar systems, with risk amplified by human behaviour and regulatory lapses rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Decision: review. The event description is supported by national French and ECDC sources, but the original classification has been adjusted to re-occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because no parasite change was documented; the outbreak was driven by illegal slaughter, inadequate labelling and traditional consumption of raw figatelli. With only three confirmed human cases and a very local animal reservoir, this event is more important as a regulatory case study than as a top-ten global impact episode and is therefore flagged for review when prioritising events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United States of America [1990] (California beef herds)
Host: Beef cattle (bulls and breeding cows) under natural service systems
Event summary: In 1990, a random survey of California cow–calf beef herds found that about 15.8% of herds had at least one bull infected with Tritrichomonas foetus, confirming substantial ongoing bovine trichomoniasis in western US beef operations and quantifying its prevalence at the herd level. The survey showed that infection was widespread yet clinically unapparent in bulls, with impacts expressed as reduced pregnancy rates and extended calving seasons in naturally serviced herds. These findings underpinned subsequent regulatory attention and testing requirements in several western states, although trichomoniasis has persisted as a chronic reproductive constraint in extensive beef systems relying on natural service.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive cow–calf operations depending on natural service, commingling of multiple herds on shared rangeland, and lack of routine trichomoniasis testing for breeding bulls allowed persistent transmission; low producer awareness meant infection was often only suspected after marked reproductive loss. Internal mechanisms: typical bovine T. foetus biology—lifelong asymptomatic colonisation of the preputial mucosa in older bulls and highly efficient venereal transmission—supports stable endemicity in herds using natural mating.
Review: Retain – Verified via state veterinary sources and reviews that a 1990 California survey found ~15.8% of beef herds with at least one infected bull and that T. foetus was long‑established in North America; geography, timing and classification as re‑occurrence (endemic disease documented with renewed attention) are appropriate, and sources are relevant to this event.([cdfa.ca.gov](https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/ahfss/Animal_Health/trich_Q_and_A.html?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Beef and mixed‑purpose cattle herds, breeding bulls and cows under natural service
Event summary: In 1992, pilot and cross‑sectional studies in the two main livestock‑rearing areas of northeastern Costa Rica used the InPouch TF system to detect Tritrichomonas foetus infection in bulls, finding farm‑level prevalences up to around 15–18% and bull‑level prevalences of about 4–7%, and demonstrating that bovine trichomoniasis was common in local cattle herds. The work identified risk factors such as Bos taurus breed and bull age over 4 years and linked infection to management practices based on untested natural‑service bulls, indicating potential for significant reproductive and economic losses in the national herd. Although no discrete epidemic wave was reported, these studies represented the first detailed, country‑level quantification of bovine trichomoniasis in Costa Rica and catalysed recognition of the disease as an important endemic reproductive problem in Central American beef systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: reliance on natural mating in many herds, limited veterinary reproductive monitoring, and movement or sharing of untested bulls between farms facilitated endemic circulation; low prior awareness and lack of systematic bull testing allowed infection to accumulate before detection. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for genotype change; disease patterns were consistent with canonical bovine T. foetus biology, with chronic asymptomatic carriage in bulls and transient but fertility‑reducing infection in cows leading to early embryonic loss and extended calving intervals.
Review: Review – The 1992 Costa Rica work clearly documents significant endemic infection and economic impact but global first emergence of T. foetus in cattle occurred decades earlier in Europe and other regions; the original classification as “first_detection = Yes” has therefore been changed to No, and no intra‑/inter‑continental emergence flag is applied because earlier circulation in the Americas is well documented though not previously quantified in Costa Rica, so this event is best treated as the first detailed national prevalence study rather than discovery of the parasite in the host system.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0167587792900136?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Beef cattle herds using natural service on rangeland, especially extensively managed herds with bulls on public allotments
Event summary: From 1997 through 2010, surveillance in Wyoming, USA, documented persistent Tritrichomonas foetus infection in breeding bulls, with individual‑bull prevalence peaking at 2.69% in 1999 and remaining around 0.6–1.5% in the early 2000s before declining under intensified control. In 2000 the state implemented a mandatory control programme (“Chapter 15” rules) requiring testing of bulls used on public grazing allotments or traded for breeding and culling of positive animals, gradually reducing prevalence to 0.21% by 2010 and eventually to zero recorded positive bulls by 2017–2019. This period represents a major endemic re‑occurrence and subsequent successful suppression of bovine trichomoniasis as a significant cause of reproductive loss in western US rangeland beef systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive range‑based cow–calf systems with multi‑herd commingling on public lands, frequent bull sharing or leasing, and initially minimal regulation created sustained opportunities for parasite transmission, while economic pressure to retain older bulls increased the reservoir of chronically infected animals. Strong regulatory measures—obligatory testing and culling of positive bulls, movement restrictions, and requirements for negative certification before sale or turnout—acted as powerful external drivers that reversed the trend. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype was implicated; persistence is explained by the long‑term carrier state of infected bulls and efficient venereal transmission in multi‑sire breeding groups, whereas the parasite’s limited environmental survival constrains indirect routes.
Review: Retain – Wyoming’s long time‑series (1997–2019) and state‑wide control programme are well documented and clearly high impact; the event correctly captures 1997–2010 as the main period of measurable prevalence and initial control, and classifying it as re‑occurrence (endemic disease under changing control pressure) is acceptable; no field edits were required beyond cross‑checking prevalence figures and regulatory details.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6954593/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Beef cattle (Asturiana de la Montaña and other beef breeds) kept under extensive, natural‑service systems
Event summary: Between roughly 2007 and 2015, bovine trichomoniasis re‑emerged as an important endemic reproductive disease in parts of Spain, particularly in extensively managed beef herds in northern and other beef‑producing regions. Surveys of Asturiana de la Montaña cattle reported very high Tritrichomonas foetus prevalence—about one‑third of tested bulls and around 40% of sampled herds infected—while retrospective national diagnostic data for 2011–2015 showed T. foetus in approximately 13% of bulls and 21% of herds tested, indicating substantial ongoing circulation in Spanish beef systems. These findings contrasted with the near‑eradication of trichomoniasis from most European dairy herds through artificial insemination and prompted recognition of the disease as endemic but geographically limited within Spain and a target for testing‑and‑culling control efforts in extensive beef production zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continued reliance on natural service in extensive beef systems, retention of older bulls for multiple breeding seasons, communal grazing and bull sharing among smallholders, and limited routine trichomoniasis testing or certification before breeding all favoured parasite persistence and spread; comparatively low adoption of artificial insemination in beef herds reduced the protective effect seen in dairy sectors. Internal mechanisms: available data show typical bovine T. foetus genotypes without evidence of increased virulence; the resurgence is best explained by management‑driven amplification of a historically present parasite, whose biology—lifelong asymptomatic carriage in bulls and fertility‑reducing, often subclinical infection in cows—supports ongoing endemicity where natural mating predominates.
Review: Retain – High bull‑ and herd‑level prevalences and associated control studies in Asturiana de la Montaña herds and wider Spanish beef regions are well supported by primary data; Spain had documented T. foetus infection before 2000, so this episode appropriately represents re‑occurrence in extensive beef systems rather than first emergence, and no corrections to geography, timing or event‑type classification were needed.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1090023311003741?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Spain [2012]; France [2012]; Portugal [2015]; Hungary [2012]; Poland [2012]; Italy [2013, 2015; infection limited to zones]
Host: Predominantly beef cattle herds using natural mating in affected EU Member States
Event summary: From 2012 to 2016, World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) notifications summarised by EFSA recorded bovine trichomoniasis in several EU Member States, with Spain reporting disease limited to one or more zones throughout the period, France reporting disease present nationally, and Portugal, Hungary, Poland and Italy reporting infection limited to zones in particular years. These notifications, together with earlier sporadic reports from Spain and other European countries, indicate that pockets of Tritrichomonas foetus infection persisted in beef‑cattle regions across Southern, Western and Eastern Europe at a time when most dairy herds were free of the parasite due to widespread artificial insemination. The episode represents re‑occurrence and formal recognition of geographically limited trichomoniasis foci across multiple European subregions, prompting its assessment under the EU Animal Health Law and highlighting trade‑related risks linked to movement of infected breeding cattle within the Union.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement and trade of live breeding cattle between Member States, combined with pockets of beef production that rely heavily on natural mating and retain older, potentially infected bulls, favoured the maintenance and dissemination of T. foetus within Europe; the absence of EU‑wide mandatory trichomoniasis testing for cattle movements meant infected bulls could be introduced into otherwise free herds. Internal mechanisms: available evidence points to typical bovine T. foetus genotypes rather than novel variants; parasite persistence was driven by its capacity for chronic colonisation of the bull preputial mucosa and efficient venereal transmission, with spatial spread shaped more by management and trade networks than by intrinsic changes in transmissibility or virulence.
Review: Review – EFSA’s assessment and earlier literature make clear that bovine trichomoniasis had been present in multiple European countries long before 2012 and was largely suppressed—but not eradicated—by artificial insemination, so WOAH notifications between 2012 and 2016 represent persistence and re‑occurrence of localized foci rather than first spread into new European subregions; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been changed from Yes to No, re_occurrence from No to Yes, the countries list has been restricted to Member States with documented bovine reports (removing the Netherlands, where recent monitoring describes T. foetus as not detected in cattle), and the host description was simplified to cattle to avoid conflation with wildlife or non‑bovine trichomonads.([efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2017.4992?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Breeding bulls in beef herds in Pernambuco State (north‑eastern Brazil)
Event summary: In 2016, a PCR‑based survey of breeding bulls in Pernambuco State in north‑eastern Brazil detected Tritrichomonas foetus in about 6–7% of bulls and found that roughly one‑fifth of sampled properties harboured at least one infected bull, confirming active bovine trichomoniasis foci in the region. Infection was detected only in bulls sampled on farms and not in slaughterhouse animals, underscoring breeding bulls as the principal reservoir and suggesting that infected males were maintained within breeding herds across multiple seasons. The study highlighted the potential for ongoing reproductive losses in regional cow–calf systems and recommended incorporating trichomoniasis diagnosis and removal of positive bulls into regional animal‑health programmes to limit further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: natural‑service breeding on numerous small and medium‑sized cow–calf operations, limited systematic screening of bulls before use, and animal movements between herds and local markets allowed T. foetus to persist and spread; low awareness of the disease and absence of targeted control measures in parts of north‑eastern Brazil contributed to its under‑recognition and continued impact. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype was implicated; disease dynamics reflected typical bovine trichomoniasis biology, with chronic infection in bulls and transient yet fertility‑reducing infection in cows, and the main determinants of herd‑level emergence were management practices and the age structure of breeding bulls rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – The Pernambuco study documents a clear, regionally important endemic focus with quantifiable bull‑ and herd‑level prevalence and appropriate emphasis on management‑related drivers; classification as re‑occurrence is justified given long‑standing reports of bovine trichomoniasis in Brazil, and geography, timing and sources are consistent with the primary article and regional reviews.([bjvm.org.br](https://bjvm.org.br/BJVM/article/view/56?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: South Africa [North West Province c. 2010s]; additional southern African countries with reported bovine T. foetus infection (e.g. Namibia, Botswana)
Host: Beef cattle herds and breeding bulls in southern African communal and commercial grazing systems
Event summary: During the 2010–2020 period, molecular surveys using real‑time PCR assays (e.g. VetMAX T. foetus tests) and culture‑based studies documented Tritrichomonas foetus infection in breeding bulls in the North West Province of South Africa and in other southern African cattle populations, revealing notable prevalence where testing was undertaken. In Namibia, multilocus genotyping of positive field isolates showed that cattle‑associated T. foetus formed a distinct genotype compared with strains characterised elsewhere, indicating regional diversification of the parasite even though disease presentation remained consistent with classical bovine trichomoniasis. Taken together, these studies show that bovine trichomoniasis remains an under‑diagnosed but significant cause of infertility and early embryonic loss in beef herds across parts of southern Africa, particularly in communal and extensive systems, and have prompted calls to integrate T. foetus surveillance and control into broader reproductive‑health programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive and communal grazing systems with multi‑herd mixing, reliance on natural service, limited routine reproductive health monitoring, and movement of untested bulls between herds and communal pastures favour chronic circulation; historically limited diagnostic capacity meant the disease was often overlooked until more sensitive PCR‑based assays became available. Internal mechanisms: while most southern African field isolates tested appear phenotypically typical for bovine T. foetus, multilocus sequencing has identified a distinct Namibian genotype among cattle isolates, indicating parasite diversification in the region; this genotype does not yet appear to confer clearly higher virulence, but its emergence, together with biological traits such as lifelong colonisation of the bovine preputial mucosa and efficient venereal transmission, underpins the classification of this episode as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence driven by genotype variation plus management conditions.
Review: Review – Southern African studies report appreciable T. foetus prevalence in cattle and, importantly, a genetically distinct Namibian cattle genotype; the original entry treated this solely as re‑occurrence and stated that no novel genotype was involved, which conflicts with the Parasitology paper documenting a new multilocus genotype from Namibia; the event has therefore been reclassified as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence (genotype‑driven), the mechanism_or_driver description updated to include genotype diversification, and the key Cambridge article added to the source list, while keeping the broad 2010–2020 timeframe and regional aggregation as an approximate summary of linked endemic foci.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/parasitology/article/novel-genotype-of-tritrichomonas-foetus-from-cattle-in-southern-africa/ED3D5DEEB0CF304734EC2BDB1972D13A?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United States of America [Florida beef herds, survey published 2004]
Host: Beef bulls and breeding cows in Florida cow–calf herds using natural service
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, a large statewide survey of beef bulls in Florida estimated that approximately 30% of sampled herds had at least one Tritrichomonas foetus–positive bull, with overall bull‑level prevalence near 6% and much higher herd‑level prevalence (about 54%) in very large herds of ≥500 cows; infection was more common in herds in southern Florida and in older bulls. Follow‑up analyses showed that T. foetus infection was associated with herd size, extensive management, and particular bull‑management practices, and that affected herds experienced reduced pregnancy percentages and altered calving patterns, confirming bovine trichomoniasis as a major endemic cause of reproductive loss in the southeastern US beef industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: widespread use of natural service in Florida cow–calf systems, large herd sizes with multi‑sire breeding groups, and importation or sharing of untested bulls increased opportunities for venereal transmission; limited routine screening before the survey allowed infection to remain largely undetected until reproductive performance declined. Internal mechanisms: no novel parasite strain was identified; the observed patterns are consistent with typical bovine T. foetus biology, in which older bulls become life‑long carriers and efficiently transmit the parasite to susceptible cows, which then suffer early embryonic loss and extended calving intervals.
Review: Review – This high‑impact Florida survey was missing from the original dataset despite documenting one of the highest well‑characterised herd‑level prevalences (~30% of herds, with >50% prevalence in very large herds) and substantial reproductive impact in a major US beef‑producing state; it has been added as a new event classified as re‑occurrence in an already endemic region, using the 2004 publication year as a proxy for the early‑2000s sampling period, with a recommendation that a human reviewer refine the exact sampling years if needed for finer temporal resolution.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0093691X0300236X?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United States of America [Texas statewide testing 2010]
Host: Beef bulls submitted for Tritrichomonas foetus testing from cow–calf herds across Texas
Event summary: In 2010, the Texas Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory system—which performs the vast majority of Tritrichomonas foetus testing in the state—analysed 31,202 bull samples for bovine trichomoniasis and found about 3.7% positive overall, with apparent prevalence peaking near 5.5% during the summer breeding season and a significant spatial cluster of infection identified in south‑eastern Texas. The large dataset confirmed that T. foetus infection was endemic across Texas beef herds and allowed mapping of high‑risk areas at county level, providing baseline information for monitoring the effectiveness of control efforts and underpinning later economic analyses of the benefits of reducing bovine trichomoniasis prevalence in the US beef industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive cow–calf operations using natural service, commingling of herds on shared rangeland, and variable uptake of trichomoniasis testing prior to breeding contributed to sustained circulation; the concentration of cases in certain south‑eastern counties suggests local husbandry and animal‑movement patterns further amplified risk. Internal mechanisms: infection patterns match canonical bovine T. foetus biology, with persistent infection in older bulls as the main reservoir; no novel genotype or altered virulence was reported, and the spatial clustering is best explained by contact networks rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review – A 2010 state‑wide Texas dataset with more than 31,000 bulls tested and clearly defined temporal and spatial patterns of infection represents one of the largest single‑year bovine trichomoniasis surveillance efforts globally and was absent from the original list; this event has been added and classified as re‑occurrence in an endemic region, with event timing, prevalence estimates and the presence of a south‑eastern spatial cluster taken directly from the PubMed abstract and subsequent modelling work, but a human reviewer may wish to refine county‑level detail if finer spatial granularity is required.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22192771/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Australia [northern beef regions; Queensland and Western Australia abattoir-sourced bulls]
Host: Beef bulls slaughtered from extensively managed northern Australian cow–calf herds
Event summary: An abattoir‑based survey of bulls from northern Australian beef herds, published in 2022, sampled 606 bulls from 134 properties in Queensland and Western Australia and detected Tritrichomonas foetus infection in 29 animals (4.8%) overall; after accounting for clustering at the property level the estimated apparent prevalence was about 1.9%, with several postcode regions in northern Australia showing apparent prevalences above 10%. Infection was concentrated in older bulls, with no positives detected in animals younger than roughly 30 months and an estimated prevalence of nearly 7% in the oldest age class, supporting the view that bovine trichomoniasis persists as an under‑diagnosed cause of reproductive loss in northern Australia’s extensive cow–calf systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of breeding bulls into extensive northern beef herds, long bull service lives with many older animals retained, reliance on natural service in remote regions, and limited routine diagnostic screening have allowed low‑to‑moderate prevalence T. foetus infection to persist largely unnoticed until systematic abattoir surveillance was undertaken. Internal mechanisms: infection patterns mirror classical bovine T. foetus biology, with infection essentially restricted to older bulls that act as life‑long carriers, and no novel genotype has been reported; the observed geographic clustering reflects management zones and property locations rather than any known intrinsic changes in the parasite.
Review: Review – This northern Australian abattoir survey is one of the few recent, large‑scale prevalence studies from Oceania and demonstrates non‑trivial T. foetus prevalence in older bulls and postcode‑level hotspots (>10% apparent prevalence) in key beef regions; it has been added and classified as re‑occurrence in a country with a long history of bovine trichomoniasis, with the 2022 publication year used as event year because the sampling period is not clearly visible from the accessible text, so a human reviewer may wish to adjust the exact sampling years if they are needed.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9305749/?utm_source=openai))
