Host: Pink pigeon (Nesoenas/Columba mayeri) – an endangered endemic columbid on Mauritius; other sympatric columbids (e.g. spotted dove, Madagascar turtle-dove) as reservoirs.
Event summary: By the early 1990s, trichomonosis caused by Trichomonas gallinae had become established in captive and wild pink pigeons on Mauritius, likely introduced earlier with non-native pigeons and doves, and was increasingly recognised as a major conservation threat to this critically endangered species. Between about 2002 and 2006, necropsy and epidemiological studies showed that trichomonad infections were a leading cause of post‑fledging mortality, with very high prevalence and frequent fatal ingluvitis in chicks, constraining population recovery despite intensive management interventions. Following these findings, conservation programs implemented improved surveillance, targeted treatment, and management of reservoir columbids, which reduced but did not eliminate trichomonosis as an ongoing constraint on pink pigeon recovery.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historic introduction and persistence of non-native pigeons/doves on Mauritius provided a chronic reservoir for T. gallinae; small, inbred pink pigeon populations with limited genetic diversity were highly susceptible; supplemental feeding, captive-breeding and release practices brought birds into close contact, enhancing transmission. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – parasite spilled over from introduced columbids into a naive endemic columbid; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – infection caused high nestling and juvenile mortality, with trichomonosis the dominant cause of death in some cohorts; Novel Strain/Genotype Presence – molecular work identified multiple lineages in Mauritian columbids, with some associated with severe disease, indicating circulation of particularly pathogenic variants.
Review: Decision: Retain. This is a well-documented, high‑impact conservation event for an endangered endemic columbid on Mauritius, supported by primary studies showing very high T. gallinae prevalence and substantial chick mortality in 2002–2006.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17699078/?utm_source=openai)) The 1992 start year reflects early recognition of trichomonosis in the population and is somewhat approximate but still within the correct decade of establishment; main impact years (2002–2006) are captured in the summary. Emergence type as re-emergence (long‑present parasite spilling over into a new, highly vulnerable host within the same subregion) is appropriate, with no evidence to justify first/global or intra-/inter‑continental emergence labels.

Host: House finch (Carpodacus/Haemorhous mexicanus), Northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos), corvids (e.g. scrub jay Aphelocoma californica, American crow Corvus brachyrhynchos, Common raven Corvus corax) and other passerines; parasite maintained in local pigeons and doves.
Event summary: From the early 2000s through about 2010, trichomonosis began to be recognised as a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in free-ranging passerines in western North America, particularly house finches and various corvids in California, overturning the prior belief that serious T. gallinae disease in the region was largely confined to columbids and raptors. Case series and prevalence studies in northern California documented frequent association of T. gallinae with severe upper alimentary tract lesions and very high case fatality in house finches, along with infections in corvids and mockingbirds. Following this recognition, T. gallinae became established in the literature and surveillance systems as an important cause of sporadic but sometimes locally severe mortality events in North American passerine communities, even though population-level declines have been less dramatic than in European finches.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urbanisation and widespread backyard bird feeding created dense aggregations of house finches and other passerines at feeders and water sources, facilitating oral–oral transmission; close proximity of wild birds to domestic and feral pigeons enabled repeated spillover events. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – T. gallinae, historically considered a parasite of columbids and raptors, caused clinically significant disease in multiple passerine taxa; Novel Strain/Genotype Presence – molecular work showed that parasites from house finches and corvids belonged to particular lineages within the T. gallinae complex (e.g. strain g7), suggesting adaptation to passerine hosts; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – severe ingluvitis and high case fatality in affected house finches and corvids indicate that some lineages are highly pathogenic in these new hosts.
Review: Decision: Review. This represents a genuine emergence of T. gallinae as a clinically important pathogen of wild passerines in western North America, supported by detailed pathological and prevalence studies in California.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19278788/)) However, the original start date (~1997) appears to have been influenced by confusion with mycoplasmal conjunctivitis in house finches; the revised 2000–2010 window is a more realistic approximation for the period over which trichomonosis was first recognised and characterised in these hosts, but the exact first‑case year remains uncertain and should be refined if local surveillance records are available. The event has been restricted to the United States, with Canadian Maritime finch emergence now treated as a separate event, and the Canadian CVJ article has been moved to that new row’s sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2005]; Ireland [2007]
Host: Primarily European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and Eurasian chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs); other garden passerines occasionally affected; reservoir in local columbids (e.g. feral pigeons, doves).
Event summary: In spring–summer 2005, a novel, highly pathogenic lineage of Trichomonas gallinae was first recognised causing trichomonosis in British finches, with carcasses of greenfinches and chaffinches submitted from gardens across England and Wales. In 2006–2007, reports of sick and dead finches at feeding stations surged and post-mortems showed trichomonosis as the dominant cause of infectious mortality, leading to an estimated loss of about 1.5 million breeding greenfinches and marked declines in chaffinch survival across Great Britain and later in Ireland. Through the late 2000s the epidemic became endemic with recurring seasonal outbreaks but somewhat lower incident numbers, and greenfinch populations partially stabilised at a much reduced level.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density aggregation at garden feeding stations promoted oral–oral transmission via contaminated food and water; widespread supplementary feeding and cool, moist conditions at feeders favoured parasite survival; lack of prior exposure in finches left them immunologically naive. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular typing identified a single clonal “finch epidemic strain” of T. gallinae distinct from most columbid strains; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – this strain showed efficient transmission in passerines via shared food and water sources; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – infection caused severe necrotic ingluvitis and rapid mortality, producing strong population-level impacts; Host Expansion (Spillover) – pathogen spilled over from columbids into finch species where it had not previously caused recognised epidemics.
Review: Decision: Retain. This is correctly captured as a major re-emergence event driven by a clonal finch epidemic strain causing unprecedented population declines of greenfinches and chaffinches in the British Isles.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0012215&utm_source=openai)) The 2005–2010 window appropriately covers the initial emergence and the years of peak epidemic impact; Ireland’s first major mortality in 2007 is consistent with surveillance data. Emergence type is correctly set to re-emergence only (not intra-/inter-continental), since T. gallinae was long endemic in European columbids before jumping into passerines.

Host: Purple finch (Haemorhous purpureus), American goldfinch (Spinus tristis), and occasionally other finches (e.g. pine siskin), with T. gallinae also present in sympatric rock pigeons (Columba livia).
Event summary: Beginning in 2007, widespread mortalities of purple finches and American goldfinches were reported at garden feeders in the Canadian Maritime provinces, and necropsies identified trichomonosis due to Trichomonas gallinae as the primary cause of death. Over the period 2007–2011, at least 18 sites across the region experienced trichomonosis-related mortality events in passerines, and molecular work showed that many isolates belonged to the same finch epidemic strain (subtype A1) responsible for the British greenfinch declines, alongside additional local strains. After initial emergence, trichomonosis became an established, recurrent cause of mortality in Maritime finch populations, raising concerns about long-term welfare and potential population impacts despite more limited documented declines than in Britain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-density congregation of finches at backyard feeders and birdbaths facilitated oral transmission via contaminated seed and water; cool, moist late-summer and autumn conditions favoured parasite survival; proximity to urban pigeons provided a reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – T. gallinae, historically associated with columbids, caused severe disease and death in wild finches; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular characterisation revealed presence of the European finch epidemic strain A1 in Maritime finches and rock pigeons, along with additional genotypes, indicating introduction and local diversification; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – a high proportion of dead finches at feeders showed severe upper alimentary tract lesions consistent with rapidly fatal trichomonosis.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). The original LLM output merged Canadian Maritime finch emergence with the western U.S. passerine episode, but available data show that Maritime outbreaks from 2007 onward constitute a distinct, well-documented emergence with repeated multi-site mortality events and clear molecular evidence of the European finch epidemic strain A1.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2839828/?utm_source=openai)) Separating this into its own row avoids over-aggregation of epidemiologically unlinked episodes and aligns better with the project rule that linked episodes should be merged only when occurring in the same outbreak area or clearly connected neighbouring countries.

Host: European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and Eurasian chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs), with spillover to other local finches; likely maintained in sympatric columbids.
Event summary: Around 2008, finch trichomonosis emerged in southern Fennoscandia, with marked mortality and subsequent declines in European greenfinch and to a lesser extent chaffinch populations, following its initial establishment in Britain. From 2008 to roughly 2011, surveillance and molecular studies documented rapid spread of the same finch epidemic strain across Finland, Sweden and Norway, and by 2009 disease and excess finch mortality were reported at feeders in Denmark, accompanied by strong reductions in breeding and wintering greenfinch numbers in affected regions. After the initial wave, finch trichomonosis became established but less explosively epidemic, contributing to long-term depressed finch populations in Northern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal migration of chaffinches and other finches between Britain and Fennoscandia transported infected birds and seeded new foci; shared high-density feeding at winter gardens and feeders in Northern Europe promoted local amplification. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – molecular analyses showed Fennoscandian finches carried an identical ITS/SSU rRNA finch epidemic strain to that in Britain, implying a single successful lineage with high transmissibility; Host Expansion (Spillover) – maintenance in migrating finches allowed colonisation of previously less-exposed Northern European passerine communities; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – traits of the epidemic strain facilitated persistence and spread into cooler northern climates when suitable host densities were present.
Review: Decision: Review. This event correctly represents the major extension of the finch epidemic strain into Fennoscandia and associated greenfinch declines.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21935745/?utm_source=openai)) However, two corrections were necessary: (i) Norway’s first confirmed finch trichomonosis cases occurred in 2008, not 2009, so the country year has been updated; and (ii) the intra_continental_emergence flag has been set to false, because T. gallinae was already endemic in Northern European columbids and this episode reflects re-emergence via host expansion and spread of a particular clonal lineage, not first presence of the parasite in a new subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild columbids: European turtle dove (Streptopelia turtur), stock dove (Columba oenas), wood pigeon (Columba palumbus), collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), with pathogenic lineages capable of causing mortality and spillover to raptors and finches.
Event summary: In the early 2010s, systematic molecular surveys across western and southern Europe revealed very high prevalence of Trichomonas gallinae in wild columbids, including turtle doves and stock doves, in Germany, Spain, Italy and Malta, with many birds infected by pathogenic lineages previously associated with mortality in columbids, raptors and finches. During this period, concern grew that trichomonosis was contributing to declines in already vulnerable species such as the European turtle dove, particularly along key migration flyways linking breeding grounds in western and central Europe with staging areas in the Mediterranean and winter quarters in Africa. Following these findings, trichomonosis was increasingly integrated into conservation assessments and management planning for European columbids, although infection remained widespread and endemic across much of the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Agricultural intensification and landscape change reduced food resources and potentially weakened columbid populations; high congregation at watering and feeding sites on migration flyways and in agricultural landscapes facilitated transmission; long-distance migration linked breeding and wintering areas, allowing continental‑scale dissemination; supplementary feeding of gamebirds and doves in some areas further increased contact rates. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – multiple genetic lineages were identified, including pathogenic “lineage A/B” (genotype B) shared with UK columbids and finches; Host Expansion (Spillover) – circulation of pathogenic lineages in columbids increased the risk of spillover into raptors and passerines; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – dominance of widely distributed pathogenic lineages indicates successful adaptation for broad geographic spread and use of multiple columbid hosts.
Review: Decision: Review. This row is best interpreted as a re-emergence/re-recognition of widespread, often pathogenic T. gallinae lineages in European columbids, with potential additive impacts on already declining turtle dove populations, rather than as an intra-continental emergence event; the intra_continental_emergence flag has therefore been set to false.([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1132905621/34)) The 2010–2015 window and listed countries reflect the timing and geography of key molecular surveys rather than discrete outbreak years, and should be regarded as approximate; nevertheless the event is retained because of its significance for conservation planning and the demonstration that highly pathogenic genotypes (including the finch epidemic-linked lineage) are widespread along major flyways.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeon (Patagioenas fasciata monilis); with secondary spillover documented in predators such as spotted owls during mortality events.
Event summary: In winter 2014–2015, Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeons in California experienced the most widespread and longest-duration avian trichomonosis epidemic ever recorded for this species, with mortality events (≥5 birds) reported from 25 counties and total deaths estimated to exceed 18,000 birds. The outbreak began in November 2014, coinciding with severe multi-year drought and unusually warm conditions that concentrated pigeons at a limited number of water sources, and continued through June 2015, with heavy adult mortality documented in both wintering and breeding areas. This epidemic followed earlier but smaller trichomonosis outbreaks in band-tailed pigeons and, together with hunting mortality, has been implicated as a major factor constraining recovery of an already declining upland game bird population.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptional drought and elevated winter and spring temperatures in California reduced surface water availability and concentrated band-tailed pigeons at remaining water sources, greatly increasing contact rates and environmental contamination; high acorn production in preceding years influenced winter aggregation patterns; continued legal harvest added to disease-related mortality in a declining population. Internal mechanisms: Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – T. gallinae subtype A2 was the predominant parasite and, together with the newly described species Trichomonas stableri, produced severe necrotic upper digestive tract lesions and high case fatality; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – trichomonosis epidemics occurred across much of the Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeon range in California; Dual-pathogen Dynamics – co-circulation of T. gallinae and T. stableri complicated the aetiology but both are highly pathogenic trichomonads contributing to the same disease syndrome.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). Large-scale, drought-associated trichomonosis epidemics in Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeons are among the highest-mortality T. gallinae events documented since 1990, with the 2014–2015 epidemic alone estimated to have killed over 18,000 birds across 25 counties and clearly linked to population-level impacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6068076/?utm_source=openai)) This event was missing from the original LLM output and is added here as a major re-occurrence (not first emergence) in a region where T. gallinae epizootics have recurred for decades; classification as re_occurrence rather than re_emergence is appropriate because the primary drivers are environmental aggregation and drought rather than documented appearance of a new T. gallinae genotype within this host system.

Host: European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and European goldfinch (Carduelis carduelis) in wintering flocks; likely spillover from or co-circulation with infected columbids.
Event summary: In winter 2016–2017, a major outbreak of finch trichomonosis was documented in European greenfinches and goldfinches wintering in the Boulonnais region of northern France, with large numbers of sick and dead birds observed at feeding sites and in nearby habitats. Necropsy and molecular analyses confirmed T. gallinae infection consistent with the finch epidemic lineage, and concurrent mortality in Brittany and other areas indicated that the epidemic extended across a broad area of western France. The outbreak subsided after winter, but highlighted that the finch epidemic strain had spread from earlier foci in the British Isles and Fennoscandia into western continental Europe, potentially contributing to local declines of affected finch populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Winter feeding stations in northern France concentrated mixed-species finch flocks, enabling efficient oral transmission; climatic conditions and high winter bird densities favoured sustained local circulation; long-distance migrants likely introduced the strain from previously affected regions. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – the same highly transmissible finch epidemic lineage appears to have driven mortality in continental finches; Host Expansion (Spillover) – notable involvement of European goldfinch, broadening the susceptible passerine host range; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the epidemic lineage continued its spread into new western European wintering areas.
Review: Decision: Review. The French 2016–2017 outbreak is a genuine high-impact episode with substantial winter mortality in greenfinches and goldfinches and clear molecular confirmation of the finch epidemic lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452646/?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as both intra‑continental emergence and re-emergence is inconsistent with project rules, because T. gallinae was long established in western European columbids and this episode reflects spread of a known lineage and host expansion within an already affected continent; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to false, with re-emergence retained as the primary event type.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/Bos indicus); wildlife (especially African buffalo and other game) as important reservoir hosts, though the documented production impact was on cattle mortality.
Event summary: In 1990 a severe outbreak of African animal trypanosomosis (nagana) occurred in the tsetse‑infested areas of north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal, South Africa, where tsetse and AAT had long been present but livestock case numbers had been relatively low in preceding years. During a major drought, high tsetse densities and limited grazing drove cattle into heavily infested thickets, leading to an explosive epidemic in which about 10,000 cattle died and over 100,000 were treated with trypanocides under an emergency control programme. Integrated measures based on mass chemotherapy and intensive dipping with pyrethroid insecticides reduced tsetse challenge and infection prevalence over subsequent years, although low‑level endemicity and periodic local flare‑ups have persisted in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Severe drought and land‑use changes in north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal in the late 1980s forced communal and commercial cattle herds into dense thicket habitats with high densities of Glossina austeni and G. brevipalpis, while gaps or changes in vector control allowed tsetse populations to rebound and contact rates with cattle to increase. Internal mechanisms: Parasitological and molecular surveys indicate that infections in cattle in this focus are dominated by T. congolense, with T. brucei not consistently detected and no specific novel genotypes reported; the outbreak is therefore best interpreted as a classic re‑occurrence of endemic AAT driven by ecological and control‑system changes rather than by documented evolutionary change in the parasites.
Review: review – retain; major AAT outbreak with ~10,000 cattle deaths and >100,000 treatments in north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal is well documented and clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes. Narrative was adjusted to emphasise that cattle infections in this focus are dominated by T. congolense (T. brucei is not consistently detected), treating the event as part of the multi‑species AAT complex under this EPP rather than implying strong T. brucei involvement. Classification as re‑occurrence and the geographic coding (Southern Africa, South Africa) are consistent with project definitions and should be kept, but the updated wording and cross‑species framing merit human review.

Countries: Brazil [1995] (Pantanal wetlands—Poconé, Paiaguás, Nabileque subregions); Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [1996-1997] (lowland departments of Santa Cruz and Beni, including wetland provinces such as Velasco, Ñuflo de Chávez, Guarayos, Chiquitos and Beni).
Host: Beef and dairy cattle (Bos taurus and Bos indicus crossbred herds); additional mortality recorded in wild marsh deer (Blastocerus dichotomus), but quantified impact is for cattle.
Event summary: From 1995 to the late 1990s, large outbreaks of bovine trypanosomosis caused by Trypanosoma vivax swept through the Brazilian Pantanal wetlands and adjoining Bolivian lowlands. The first recognised cases occurred in 1995 in cattle near Poconé in the northern Pantanal, where herds showed fever, anemia, abortions, severe weight loss and deaths, and parasitological surveys confirmed high T. vivax prevalence. In 1996–1997 the disease spread widely through wetland provinces of Santa Cruz and Beni in Bolivia, with contemporaneous reports attributing up to 150,000 cattle deaths—around 5% of Beni’s 5‑million‑head herd—and marked production losses across affected ranches, prompting emergency treatment campaigns and economic analyses that estimated the total cost of the 1995 outbreak complex at roughly 4% of affected brood‑cow value (around US$160 million). Following intensive chemotherapeutic control and adjustments to grazing and trade practices, overt mortality declined and T. vivax became established as an endemic constraint in the Pantanal–Beni cattle systems rather than a short‑lived epizootic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and long‑distance movement of infected cattle from northern Brazil, where T. vivax was already present, into the previously unaffected Pantanal, together with extensive droving of large herds along wetland trails and the very high abundance of biting tabanid flies during the rainy season, created ideal conditions for rapid mechanical transmission between herds across the Brazil–Bolivia border. Naïve cattle populations with no prior immunity, sparse veterinary infrastructure in remote ranching areas, and delayed recognition of trypanosomosis as the cause of disease all amplified the scale and impact of these outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not pinpoint a novel parasite genotype; instead, the episode reflects the expansion and amplification of an established T. vivax lineage into new wetland ecosystems via mechanical transmission, so it is best classified as a very large re‑occurrence/recrudescence of AAT within the South America sub‑region rather than as first detection or an inter‑/intra‑continental emergence event.
Review: review – new event added. The 1995–1997 Trypanosoma vivax epizootic in the Brazilian Pantanal and Bolivian lowlands caused very large cattle losses (local reports of ~150,000 deaths in Beni and an estimated economic impact of ~US$160 million) and is widely cited as a major AAT event, clearly qualifying for inclusion among the top post‑1990 emergence episodes. Classified as a re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region because T. vivax had been present elsewhere on the continent for decades and there is no strong evidence of a novel strain; mechanical transmission and cattle movements are the dominant drivers. Event should be retained but cross‑checked against any separate EPP entry that may exist for T. vivax to avoid double counting.

Host: Cattle (village and transhumant herds)
Event summary: Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, village cattle in Kénédougou Province, south‑western Burkina Faso, experienced persistent, high burdens of African animal trypanosomosis despite intensive chemoprophylaxis and treatment campaigns, indicating a major episode of control failure. Field studies using parasitological, mouse‑based and PCR methods in multiple villages showed widespread infections with T. congolense and T. vivax, with T. brucei‑group trypanosomes also detected, and many cattle relapsed after treatment with isometamidium chloride or diminazene aceturate, demonstrating multi‑drug resistance. Over this period, cattle condition and productivity deteriorated and routine chemotherapy became increasingly ineffective, and the episode ended only when resistance was recognised and control strategies (including drug‑use policies and vector control) were revised, although resistant strains remained entrenched in the area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy reliance on chemotherapy in the Kénédougou cattle corridor, with frequent, sometimes farmer‑administered dosing and limited veterinary oversight, created strong selection pressure for drug‑resistant trypanosomes; continued high tsetse challenge and movement of cattle between villages maintained intense transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multiple studies using the standard mouse test and PCR confirmed the emergence and spread of trypanocidal‑drug‑resistant trypanosome populations (primarily T. congolense, with T. vivax and some T. brucei‑group parasites) resistant to both isometamidium and diminazene, a clear example of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than environmental change alone.
Review: retain – Kénédougou is one of the best‑documented foci of multi‑drug‑resistant AAT, with field and laboratory evidence of widespread resistance to both isometamidium and diminazene and clear production impacts across many villages. Geographic coding (Western Africa, Burkina Faso) and classification as re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance align with the project’s definitions. No structural changes were needed beyond adding the core field‑study PubMed citation; event should be kept as one of the key post‑1990 AAT emergence episodes.

Countries: Uganda [2000] (central and south‑eastern cattle corridor; districts including Kaberamaido, Soroti and neighbouring areas)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus‑dominant mixed herds) and other livestock (goats, sheep) in the cattle corridor
Event summary: During the early 2000s, Uganda’s central and south‑eastern cattle corridor experienced a marked increase in African animal trypanosomosis, with districts such as Kaberamaido declaring emergency situations: surveys found around 9–10% of screened cattle infected in some subcounties, and many animals showed severe clinical disease. National assessments around this time estimated that approximately 100,000 cattle were dying annually from nagana in the wider cattle corridor, coinciding with overlapping epidemics of human T. brucei rhodesiense sleeping sickness in the same region. In response, Uganda and partners mobilized substantial funding (about US$9.8 million from the African Development Bank in 2008) and implemented intensified tsetse control, livestock treatment and community‑based surveillance, which gradually reduced mortality and prevalence, though nagana remained a chronic constraint on livestock production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased cattle movements along the cattle corridor, restocking initiatives into endemic sleeping‑sickness areas, high densities of tsetse flies in riverine and bush habitats, and under‑resourced veterinary and vector‑control services all contributed to the resurgence of AAT. The overlap of zoonotic T. b. rhodesiense foci in livestock and humans further complicated control and likely increased awareness and reporting. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence that novel animal‑infective T. brucei strains or other genetic shifts were responsible for this resurgence; instead, the episode reflects re‑occurrence driven mainly by ecological and socio‑economic factors (livestock movement, weak control systems) and possible but poorly quantified drug resistance.
Review: retain – this row captures the widely recognised early‑2000s resurgence of nagana (and overlapping rhodesiense sleeping sickness) along Uganda’s cattle corridor, with credible though approximate estimates of ~100,000 cattle deaths per year and major external funding for control. Time bounds (2000–2005) are necessarily approximate but broadly consistent with reported emergencies in Kaberamaido and the subsequent AfDB‑funded control project. Classification as re‑occurrence (rather than emergence or re‑emergence) appropriately reflects the dominant role of livestock movement and control‑system weaknesses rather than confirmed parasite change; no corrections were required.

Countries: Ethiopia [2001] (western Ethiopia—Ghibe Valley, Metekel, Upper Didessa, FITCA project areas)
Host: Cattle (smallholder and project herds in tsetse‑infested zones)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, several western Ethiopian tsetse‑infested zones (including the Ghibe Valley, Metekel and Upper Didessa) recorded persistently high prevalence of bovine trypanosomosis despite long‑standing control efforts, marking a significant resurgence of nagana. Field trials and follow‑up studies in cattle under natural challenge showed frequent relapse infections with T. congolense and, to a lesser extent, T. brucei‑group parasites after treatment with isometamidium and diminazene, and earlier work in Ghibe had already demonstrated triple resistance to diminazene, isometamidium and homidium. Meta‑analyses of Ethiopian data report prevalences exceeding 10% in some late 1990s–early 2000s studies in these areas. Continued poor treatment responses and sustained transmission signalled a shift from manageable endemicity to a difficult‑to‑control, high‑impact situation, which gradually improved only as vector control and drug‑use policies were adjusted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of cattle production into high‑challenge tsetse habitats, limited availability of alternative control methods, heavy reliance on a small set of trypanocides obtained from both formal and informal markets, and often suboptimal dosing practices fostered conditions for drug resistance and persistent transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multiple studies from the FITCA project and related research documented reduced efficacy and laboratory‑confirmed resistance of circulating trypanosome populations (especially T. congolense) to isometamidium and diminazene; together with earlier evidence of triple‑drug‑resistant T. congolense in Ghibe, this constitutes a clear re‑emergence event characterised by antimicrobial resistance and increased persistence of infections rather than simple ecological re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – this row consolidates well‑documented evidence of multi‑drug‑resistant AAT in western Ethiopia (Ghibe, Metekel, Upper Didessa) in the late 1990s–early 2000s. The geographic coding (Eastern Africa, Ethiopia) and classification as re‑emergence driven by confirmed resistance to isometamidium and diminazene are consistent with the event definition. Although burden estimates are indirect (prevalence data and reports of repeated relapse), this focus is widely cited as a major AAT problem area and plausibly belongs among the top post‑1990 events; no changes to coding were necessary.

Countries: Sudan [2010] (Blue Nile State, Kurmuk District; cattle infected after grazing in neighbouring Ethiopian tsetse‑infested areas)
Host: Cattle (Kenana and Fulani breeds)
Event summary: In June 2010 an acute outbreak of bovine trypanosomiasis occurred in Kurmuk District of Blue Nile State, south‑eastern Sudan, involving indigenous Kenana and Fulani cattle that had crossed the border to graze in Ethiopia’s tsetse‑infested belt and then returned to Sudan. The outbreak was characterized by high morbidity and mixed infections with up to four Trypanosoma species (including T. vivax, T. congolense, T. brucei‑group parasites and T. simiae) in affected cattle, leading to substantial production losses and prompting urgent veterinary investigation and laboratory confirmation. Control efforts focusing on treatment of infected herds, improved management of cross‑border grazing and targeted vector control gradually reduced case numbers, and the outbreak subsided as cattle movements and grazing patterns were modified and trypanocidal treatments were applied more systematically.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal transboundary movement of cattle from relatively lower‑risk Sudanese areas into high‑challenge Ethiopian tsetse belts exposed naïve or partially protected animals to intense infection pressure, and returning animals carried parasites back into Blue Nile State; limited veterinary infrastructure and surveillance capacity in this remote border area delayed recognition and response. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was attributed to the introduction of different parasite variants via cross‑border movement, but no specific novel genotype or resistance mechanism was conclusively identified, so this event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by livestock movements and high tsetse challenge rather than by documented genetic change in the trypanosomes.
Review: review – retain but with corrected geography. The 2010 Kurmuk outbreak is clearly centred in Blue Nile State, Sudan, with Ethiopian tsetse belts acting as an exposure source during seasonal grazing; accordingly, the event is now coded to Northern Africa/Sudan only, with Ethiopia mentioned in the narrative rather than as a second affected country/sub‑region. Classification as re‑occurrence (acute outbreak in a known tsetse‑trypanosomosis setting) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence remains consistent with the definitions. Human review is recommended to confirm that limiting the formal country list to Sudan matches how other cross‑border episodes are treated in the wider dataset.

Countries: Uganda [2010] (Karamoja region; Moroto, Kotido, Nakapiripirit and neighbouring districts)
Host: Cattle and donkeys (primary documented hosts), with probable involvement of goats and sheep in pastoral systems
Event summary: From around 2010 onwards, the semi‑arid Karamoja region in north‑eastern Uganda, historically underserved and long considered peripheral in AAT control planning, experienced growing burdens of African animal trypanosomosis that significantly constrained pastoral livelihoods. Detailed surveys documented appreciable prevalence of trypanosome infections in cattle and donkeys and widespread reports from pastoral households of substantial cattle losses, poor traction, low milk yields and herd depletion, leading national authorities to list AAT among the top livestock health constraints in Karamoja. By the mid‑2010s the Ugandan government launched an emergency cattle treatment and tsetse control project in Karamoja, after which prevalence declined in targeted areas but the region remained classified as a priority focus for AAT control rather than a low‑risk zone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and concentration of cattle herds around limited water sources, vegetation changes, chronic insecurity and remoteness that limited access to veterinary services, and under‑investment in tsetse control likely increased local Glossina abundance and contact rates, while increasing connectivity with higher‑risk neighbouring areas may have introduced more infected animals. Internal mechanisms: Available reports emphasise environmental, management and service‑delivery drivers rather than specific novel strains or resistance; thus the episode is interpreted primarily as a re‑occurrence and intensification of AAT within an under‑served part of the Eastern Africa sub‑region rather than as an intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence driven by parasite change, although unquantified drug resistance may contribute to persistence.
Review: review – retain but reclassified. Under the project’s rules, intra‑continental emergence refers to first spread into a new UNSD sub‑region; Karamoja lies within the already endemic Eastern Africa sub‑region (Uganda), and published work describes a neglected, high‑burden focus rather than first appearance on a new continent or in a new sub‑region. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to “no” and re_occurrence to “yes”. This still recognises Karamoja as a major 2010s AAT constraint but frames it as a resurgence in an under‑served area rather than a distinct continental emergence; human review is advised to confirm that this interpretation is applied consistently across the dataset.

Host: Horses (primary clinical cases), with donkeys and mules considered resistant carriers in rural equid populations
Event summary: From around 2000, routine dourine surveillance and clinical reporting in South Africa began documenting renewed widespread infection in equids, reversing earlier expectations that the disease was disappearing from the country. Between 2000 and 2010, national records compiled for the OIE NTTAT network indicate roughly 900 confirmed dourine cases—over 700 in the Eastern Cape alone—with further confirmed complement‑fixation–positive cases recorded in multiple provinces. Over the subsequent years to about 2015, at least 100 additional seropositive horses were detected country‑wide, after which annual case numbers declined but sporadic positives continued to occur under ongoing targeted surveillance, so dourine remains an endemic controlled disease rather than eradicated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of natural breeding in rural and communal horse populations, movement of breeding stallions between provinces, and limited resources for systematic pre‑breeding testing and culling allowed long‑established dourine foci to persist; socio‑economic constraints and the value of horses for transport and livelihood made aggressive stamping‑out difficult outside high‑value studs; surveillance intensity varied over time, contributing to apparent temporal fluctuations in case counts. Internal mechanisms: Available data and the long‑standing presence of the Onderstepoort (OVI) T. equiperdum strain suggest no clearly documented emergence of a novel, more virulent or drug‑resistant lineage during this period; the episode is best interpreted as large‑scale re‑occurrence of endemic dourine driven by management and control factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New event added to capture a major, well‑documented re‑occurrence of dourine in South Africa, where national reports and NTTAT/WOAH summaries describe approximately 900 confirmed cases from 2000–2010 and about 100 additional cases to 2015, with cases in most provinces. Classified as re‑occurrence in Southern Africa because dourine has been present in this subregion for more than a century and no clear evidence of a novel strain or resistance pattern was found. Time bounds and national case totals should be re‑checked against full WOAH WAHIS series if finer temporal resolution is needed, but the event clearly belongs among the most impactful modern dourine emergence episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Horses (primary clinical cases), with donkeys and mules examined for carrier and clinical states
Event summary: From August 2005 to January 2007, a cross‑sectional field study in the Arsi‑Bale highlands of Ethiopia systematically documented dourine as a major, ongoing health problem of local horses, with disease widely recognized by owners and seasonal peaks during the breeding season. Serological screening of 646 horses showed high seroprevalence (about 19–28% depending on the test used), and characteristic genital and neurologic signs were commonly observed, while donkeys and mules were also examined to identify clinical and carrier infections. The episode reflects intense endemic transmission and substantial productivity and welfare losses in a long‑affected area, with dourine persisting beyond the study period under similar management and limited control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional breeding systems relying on uncontrolled natural mating, communal use of stallions, and absence of systematic pre‑breeding dourine testing maintained a high force of venereal infection; inadequate access to veterinary services and lack of an eradication or movement‑control programme allowed infection to persist at high prevalence; seasonal breeding (June–September) concentrated transmission and clinical case recognition in specific months. Internal mechanisms: No new strain, host expansion or drug resistance was demonstrated; the event is best interpreted as a high‑burden re‑occurrence of long‑established dourine in Ethiopian highland horses rather than an evolutionary shift in T. equiperdum.
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2005–2007 Arsi‑Bale highlands survey by Hagos et al. and is appropriately classified as re‑occurrence within Eastern Africa, since dourine has been endemic in Ethiopian equids for decades. Country, sub‑region and time span (August 2005–January 2007) are correctly represented, and the selected article is an appropriate primary source; no corrections recommended.

Host: Horses (breeding stallions and mares on affected studs)
Event summary: In May 2011 dourine reappeared in Italy when a Friesian stallion in Sicily tested complement‑fixation–positive during routine stud examinations, leading to the investigation of a clinically affected mare and confirmation of dourine by serology, clinical signs and histopathology. Subsequent tracing and nationwide surveillance from June to December 2011 uncovered several outbreaks in southern Italy and other regions, ultimately identifying around 20 positive horses and demonstrating re‑establishment of infection in a country that had been officially free since the late 1990s. Through 2012, Italian authorities implemented strict movement controls, targeted surveillance and stamping‑out of infected animals; by around 2012 the outbreak was considered resolved and Italy worked toward re‑establishing recognised dourine‑free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of infection via an imported or previously infected breeding horse, combined with gaps in pre‑import or pre‑breeding dourine testing, allowed the parasite to enter an officially free equine population; intensive natural mating networks among breeding horses facilitated onward sexual transmission before detection, while initial diagnostic limitations delayed confirmation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterisation of the Italian outbreak strain indicates a T. equiperdum lineage closely related to other Trypanozoon parasites but does not clearly support increased virulence or drug resistance; the episode is best explained by reintroduction of an established parasite into a susceptible horse population rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Event retained but the time span has been corrected from 2011–2013 to 2011–2012 to better match OIE immediate notifications and EU reference‑laboratory presentations describing a 2011/2012 dourine outbreak in Italy. Classification as re‑occurrence in Southern Europe (infection reappearing in a country previously officially free of dourine) remains appropriate, and no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags are warranted because dourine has long been present in Europe. Source list was slightly strengthened by adding the clinical re‑emergence paper while retaining the original outbreak‑diagnosis and case‑report articles.

Host: Horses (nationwide horse populations, with first confirmed dourine case in a stallion)
Event summary: Within a SATREPS‑supported programme running in the mid‑2010s, Mongolia intensified investigation of non‑tsetse‑transmitted horse trypanosomoses, and in 2014 a stallion with genital swelling and neurologic signs was definitively diagnosed with dourine, yielding the first directly confirmed Trypanosoma equiperdum isolate in the country (strain IVM‑t1). Building on this, a nationwide serological survey collected more than 3,600 horse sera across all provinces and found an overall 4–5% seroprevalence for non‑tsetse‑transmitted trypanosomes (surra and dourine combined), with higher prevalence in several central provinces, showing that these infections constitute a widespread endemic problem. By about 2018, Mongolia had mapped the broad distribution of non‑tsetse equine trypanosomosis and confirmed local dourine transmission, but ongoing surveillance was recommended as the disease could not be eliminated and clinical cases continued to appear sporadically.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large free‑ranging horse populations managed under extensive pastoral systems, combined with near‑universal use of natural mating, create favourable conditions for venereal transmission of dourine; historically limited access to specific diagnostics meant dourine likely circulated undetected until targeted projects introduced molecular and serological testing; the strong cultural and economic importance of horses complicates culling‑based eradication. Internal mechanisms: The IVM‑t1 strain shows typical T. equiperdum features, including defective maxicircle kinetoplast DNA, but no clear evidence has been published of novel virulence, expanded host range or drug resistance; the emergence signal largely reflects first confirmed detection and mapping of an existing infection rather than recent evolutionary change.
Review: review – Event retained but the emergence‑type classification has been corrected by setting intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because dourine had already been officially reported in China and other parts of Asia within the same UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Asia), so the first confirmed Mongolian case does not represent spread to a new sub‑region. The first_detection flag is kept to indicate the first confirmed T. equiperdum infection in Mongolian horses, and the summary has been aligned more explicitly with 2014 as the year of the IVM‑t1 case. Countries, continent and sub‑region are correct, and the cited articles and WOAH/NTTAT abstracts are appropriate primary sources for this episode.

Host: Horses (working/ranch horses; outbreak on a large beef-cattle ranch)
Event summary: In 1994–1995, surra due to Trypanosoma evansi caused a severe outbreak among ranch horses in the Pantanal Mato-Grossense wetlands of Brazil, with one herd losing 48 of 95 horses (51% mortality) and at least one neighboring ranch reporting similarly catastrophic losses. Epidemiological and serological investigations showed that T. evansi had been (re)introduced into the southern Pantanal in the early 1990s after an apparent absence from local horse populations, and that infection was now maintained by a multi-host system involving horses, dogs and wild reservoirs such as coatis and capybaras under very high tabanid-fly challenge. Over subsequent years, recurrent surra outbreaks and endemic transmission in the Pantanal became recognized as a major constraint on equine health and on cattle ranching operations that depend on horse traction, with modeling studies later estimating thousands of horse deaths and multi-million dollar annual losses if the disease is left uncontrolled.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal flooding in the Pantanal concentrates domestic livestock and wildlife on small areas of dry land during the wet season, greatly increasing contact rates and exposure to biting flies; intensive cattle marketing with long-distance, on-foot movements of large cattle lots and their working horses promotes spread of infected animals between ranches; limited access to timely diagnosis and effective trypanocides, combined with the high working and cultural value of horses, amplifies the perceived impact when outbreaks occur. Internal mechanisms: Isolates from Pantanal outbreaks show typical Trypanosoma evansi morphology and isoenzyme patterns without evidence of a novel strain; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-introduction and amplification of an existing South American lineage (re-occurrence) driven by ecological conditions, husbandry practices and vector abundance rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review – Newly added event. Strongly supported by Silva et al. (1995) and subsequent FAO/EMBRAPA work showing >50% horse mortality in an affected herd and recurrent outbreaks causing several hundred equine deaths annually, plus modeled annual losses of ~US$2.4 million in the Pantanal horse population.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8644453/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence within the South America subregion (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because T. evansi was already long-established elsewhere in South America.

Countries: Spain [1997] (Canary Islands – especially Gran Canaria, later other islands)
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event summary: In 1997–1998, Trypanosoma evansi was detected for the first time in Spain and in Europe when a dromedary camel imported from Mauritania to Gran Canaria showed chronic surra and parasitaemia; subsequent surveys during 1997–1999 found seroprevalence around 6–9% in camels across multiple Canary Islands, confirming local establishment rather than a single imported case. Follow-up control programmes with treatment of parasitologically and/or serologically positive camels reduced prevalence but did not completely clear infection, leaving a persistent focus on two Gran Canaria farms. Over the following decade the Canary Islands remained the only endemic European focus, with sporadic clinical cases but ongoing surveillance due to the risk of onward spread via camel movements.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected camels from enzootic North African countries (e.g. Mauritania, Morocco) into the Canary Islands with inadequate pre-import trypanosomosis testing; high densities of mechanical vectors (Stomoxys calcitrans and possibly tabanids) in camel farms favoured local transmission; limited awareness of surra risk and historical EU trade rules that did not list T. evansi infection in camels allowed entry and establishment. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a distinct genotype relative to North African strains; emergence here is best explained by geographic range expansion via livestock movement, ecological suitability for mechanical vectors and high local camel density, rather than parasite change.
Review: Review – Keep as major event (first established T. evansi focus in Europe), but event types have been corrected. Set first_detection='No' because global first detection in animals occurred in India in the 1880s, and retained inter_continental_emergence='Yes' to reflect the first occurrence with local transmission in the European continent. Sub-region (Southern Europe) and country coding (Spain [1997], Canary Islands) are consistent with the UNSD scheme, and sources now emphasise primary Canary Islands seroprevalence and control studies.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11018734/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Thailand [2000] (Khon Kaen Province, equine breeding farm)
Host: Horses; mules
Event summary: During June–July 2000, a severe surra outbreak occurred on an equine breeding farm in Khon Kaen Province in north‑east Thailand, where Trypanosoma evansi was confirmed parasitologically in surviving animals. About 40% (19/47) of horses and 10% (1/10) of mules were suspected to have died from surra, and 42% of pregnant mares aborted or produced stillborn foals. Remaining horses and mules were treated with diminazene aceturate and followed for several weeks with parasitological tests, haematocrit and serology, which documented clearance of detectable parasitaemia after treatment but also highlighted drug toxicity and the scale of production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The outbreak occurred on a farm in an area where surra is endemic in cattle and buffaloes, and is consistent with spillover and amplification when large numbers of equids are kept together under high biting-fly pressure; shared grazing and watering with other livestock, plus seasonal abundance of tabanid and stable flies, likely promoted intense mechanical transmission. External drivers include limited availability of trypanocides (diminazene as the only registered product at that time) and potential underestimation of equine surra risk in local health planning. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence and intensification of an existing endemic parasite in the South‑eastern Asia subregion, rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Review – Newly added as a high-impact re-occurrence event. The Khon Kaen breeding-farm outbreak caused ~40% mortality in horses and very high abortion/stillbirth rates in mares, and is widely cited as a key example of severe equine surra in South‑east Asia.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401702003047?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic South‑eastern Asia subregion, not as intra-/inter‑continental emergence.

Countries: Philippines [2002] (southern Philippines, multiple villages in Mindanao/Agusan del Sur)
Host: Water buffalo (carabao); cattle (minor); other village livestock
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2006, cross-sectional surveys in 71 villages in southern Philippines identified a substantial burden of Trypanosoma evansi infection in 1,732 water buffaloes, with seroprevalence reaching 13–100% in high‑risk areas and strong associations with poor reproductive performance and mortality. The work revealed that surra had been causing major but under-recognized production losses in buffalo-dependent smallholder systems in Mindanao. Subsequent modeling showed that a typical village herd under moderate to severe surra could lose the equivalent of tens to hundreds of thousands of US dollars annually through mortality, reduced calving and the need to import replacement animals, prompting the disease’s recognition as the country’s second most important livestock disease and informing national control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Traditional free-grazing and communal watering of buffaloes and cattle in lowland agro-ecosystems, high densities of biting flies during the wet season, and socio-economic constraints limiting access to veterinary services and trypanocides all favoured persistent transmission and recurrent outbreaks; long-distance movements of animals for draught and breeding likely helped maintain high-force-of-infection foci. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was highlighted; the episode represents re-occurrence and intensification of long-established surra in the South‑eastern Asia subregion due to management and environmental drivers, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – This event is well supported by large cross-sectional datasets and economic modeling showing very high seroprevalence and major impacts on buffalo population dynamics and village economies in Mindanao.([researchportal.murdoch.edu.au](https://researchportal.murdoch.edu.au/esplorows/assetMapper?instCode=61MUN_INST&path=https%3A%2F%2Fresearchrepository.murdoch.edu.au%2F3407&utm_source=openai)) Classification as a major re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) in South‑eastern Asia is appropriate and has been left unchanged.

Countries: Israel [2006] (southern Dead Sea area, desert farm)
Host: Dromedary camels; horses; donkeys
Event summary: In September 2006, the first clinical cases of surra in Israel were diagnosed on a secluded desert farm in the southern Dead Sea area when a chronically wasted camel and, two months later, a mare showed high trypanosome parasitaemia and neurological signs, with fatal outcomes despite treatment. Over the next two years, a longitudinal study of the farm documented Trypanosoma evansi infection in 8 of 10 camels, 3 of 7 horses and 6 of 13 donkeys, with several animals acting as asymptomatic carriers detected by PCR and reverse dot-blot assays. The outbreak, recognized as the first reported T. evansi outbreak in domestic animals in Israel, led to intensive monitoring, treatment with melarsenoxide cysteamine and heightened awareness of surra risk in the Middle East.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The affected farm kept mixed equid and camel herds in an arid area where T. evansi is known from neighboring countries (e.g. Jordan); introduction of infected animals or contact with infected camels from the wider region combined with local mechanical vectors (tabanid flies) likely initiated the outbreak, which then persisted because of carrier animals and limited prior experience with surra diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite genotype was implicated; the episode is best interpreted as a notable re-occurrence of T. evansi within the Western Asia subregion, manifesting as the first recognized multi-species farm outbreak in Israel rather than a genuine inter-continental or subregional emergence.
Review: Review – Newly added event. The Israeli Dead Sea farm outbreak is well documented as the first recognized multi-species T. evansi outbreak in domestic animals in Israel, with high infection prevalence in camels, horses and donkeys.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20926194/?utm_source=openai)) It is coded as re-occurrence within Western Asia because T. evansi had already been reported in neighbouring Middle Eastern countries, so this is not an intra-/inter-continental emergence.
