Host: Dromedary camels; co-located sheep (ovine exposure, limited infection)
Event summary: In July 2006, five camels were imported from the endemic Canary Islands to a mixed camel–sheep farm in Aveyron, southern France; by October one imported camel died with trypanosomes observed in blood smears, marking the first outbreak of Trypanosoma evansi in metropolitan France. Further testing revealed infection in five camels (both imported and locally born) and serological evidence of exposure in some neighboring sheep, indicating local mechanical transmission rather than mere importation. Infected camels were treated with melarsomine, and follow-up parasitological and serological monitoring over subsequent months showed clearance of detectable infection and no spread beyond the index farm.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Legal importation of camels from an endemic region (Canary Islands) into continental Europe without mandatory surra screening; abundant tabanid horseflies and stable flies (Stomoxys calcitrans) on the farm during summer facilitated mechanical transmission between camels and possibly sheep; lack of recognition of T. evansi as an EU trade-relevant pathogen at the time delayed specific preventive surveillance. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was implicated; outbreak dynamics primarily reflect introduction of heavily infected camels from a nearby endemic focus (Canary Islands) and efficient vector-mediated spread in a naïve host population, i.e. geographic range expansion within Europe rather than parasite change.
Review: Review – Recommended to retain as a key intra-continental emergence event (first autochthonous outbreak in Western Europe), but the emergence coding has been clarified: first_detection is now 'No' (global first detection occurred in the 19th century) while intra_continental_emergence remains 'Yes' for spread from the Southern European Canary Islands focus into Western Europe with local transmission. A duplicate ELISA follow-up article URL was removed, and an EFSA/WOAH risk assessment retained as a regional context source.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18540034/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Spain [2008] (mainland – Alicante Province, mixed camel–horse farm)
Host: Dromedary camels; horses
Event summary: In 2008, an outbreak of surra was detected in a mixed camel and horse farm in Alicante Province on mainland Spain about six months after importation of a dromedary from the Canary Islands, which presented weight loss, weakness and anaemia with confirmed Trypanosoma evansi infection. Screening of the herd identified 18 infected animals (16 camels and 2 horses) by serology, with parasitaemia confirmed in most infected camels, demonstrating substantial in situ transmission in a previously unaffected area of mainland Europe. Infected animals were isolated and treated, and follow-up showed interruption of transmission and apparent eradication of the outbreak from the farm and surrounding area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of an infected dromedary from the endemic Canary Islands to mainland Spain without prior surra testing; presence of competent mechanical vectors and mixed-species (camel–equine) management provided opportunities for cross-species transmission; under-appreciation of surra risk in EU trade policy delayed inclusion of T. evansi in relevant health certificates, enabling repeated introductions from the Canaries into mainland Europe. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for genotype change; emergence in mainland Spain is best interpreted as geographic spread and re-occurrence within the existing Southern Europe subregion, amplified by management conditions and vector abundance.
Review: Review – Recommended to retain as one of the principal European emergence events, but reclassified from intra-continental emergence to re-occurrence because the outbreak occurred within the same UN subregion (Southern Europe) and country (Spain) as the pre-existing Canary Islands focus; according to the project rules, spread to a new area or province within the same subregion should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. first_detection has been set to 'No' for the same reason as other post-1990 events.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001706X16301413?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Spain [2014] (Gran Canaria, Canary Islands – two camel farms)
Host: Dromedary camels
Event summary: Nearly two decades after Trypanosoma evansi became established in Canary Islands camels, a new localized outbreak was detected starting in 2014 on two epidemiologically linked farms in Gran Canaria with increased seroprevalence and clinical surra cases. Card agglutination testing and PCR confirmed infection in multiple camels, suggesting persistence and resurgence of a residual focus rather than a fresh introduction. A structured surveillance and control programme, including movement controls, establishment of a lazaret for PCR-positive camels and repeated testing of the archipelago’s camel census from 2017 onward, was implemented, and by 2019 no PCR-positive animals were detected and only a few seropositive but clinically normal camels remained, indicating substantial control of the outbreak though formal eradication has yet to be declared.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Incomplete elimination of T. evansi from some herds after earlier control campaigns, continued local presence of mechanical vectors (Stomoxys calcitrans) and animal movements between linked farms allowed a residual focus to recrudesce; absence of systematic, island-wide surveillance prior to 2014 delayed recognition of rising infection levels. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or host jump reported; this episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by gaps in control and surveillance within an endemic island system rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – This event appropriately captures a documented resurgence of T. evansi in Gran Canaria in 2014–2015 and its subsequent control under an official surveillance programme; coding as re-occurrence (with all emergence flags 'No') is consistent with the guidance, and no structural corrections were required.([accedacris.ulpgc.es](https://accedacris.ulpgc.es/bitstream/10553/124121/1/1-s2.0-S0001706X23001778-main.pdf))

Host: Goats (Capra hircus)
Event summary: Around 2015–2016, molecular surveys in Cebu Province reported the first PCR-confirmed detection and identification of Trypanosoma evansi in goats in the Philippines, in a setting where surra had long been recognized in buffaloes and other livestock. Among 251 goats sampled on four farms, 33.9% tested positive for T. evansi by ITS1-PCR, showing that small ruminants were participating substantially in local transmission cycles rather than acting as rare incidental hosts. The findings raised awareness that goats could serve as additional reservoirs or clinical hosts in Philippine surra foci and led to recommendations that they be included in surveillance and control programmes in mixed-species smallholder systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed-species smallholder farming systems in Cebu, where goats, cattle and buffaloes share grazing and watering points under substantial biting-fly pressure, likely facilitated spillover from traditional large-host reservoirs into goats; absence of routine diagnostics in goats previously meant infections went undetected. Internal mechanisms: This event reflects host expansion in a known endemic subregion; while no new genotype was specifically implicated, the detection demonstrates parasite adaptability to goats and has been classified as re-emergence because of expansion of the recognized host range within the same subregion, rather than as a simple re-occurrence or first detection.
Review: Review – Recommended to retain as an important host-range expansion event but reclassified to avoid over-use of the 'first_detection' label. first_detection is now 'No' at the global host-system level, and the event is coded solely as re-emergence, consistent with guidance that new host use (host expansion) within an endemic subregion should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-occurrence.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405939020300654?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apis cerana; Apis mellifera
Event summary: During the 1990s, a second Nosema species parasitizing the Eastern honey bee Apis cerana was morphologically and molecularly characterized in China and named Nosema ceranae, confirming a long‑overlooked microsporidian distinct from Nosema apis.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0932473996800599?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent work showed that by the late 1990s to early 2000s N. ceranae was already infecting Apis mellifera in Eastern Asia, with PCR and sequencing from Taiwan and mainland China demonstrating that many nosemosis cases previously attributed to N. apis were in fact due to N. ceranae.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2007/01/m6062.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By around 2004, the parasite had been clearly recognized as a distinct pathogen of A. mellifera in the region, marking a confirmed host expansion from A. cerana to A. mellifera and setting the stage for its subsequent global spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and regional movement of managed honey bee colonies in Eastern Asia; close proximity of Apis cerana and Apis mellifera in shared landscapes and mixed‑species apiaries; limited biosecurity around bee movements and queen trade. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from Apis cerana to Apis mellifera; enhanced transmission traits facilitating efficient infection and persistence in the new host; inherent capacity for geographic range expansion once established in globally traded A. mellifera stocks.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the description of Nosema (Vairimorpha) ceranae from Apis cerana and its early host expansion into Apis mellifera in Eastern Asia; geography and timing are broadly consistent with Fries et al. 1996 and Huang et al. 2007. I added primary taxonomic and host‑switch references (Fries 1996; Huang et al. 2007) to replace some generic web summaries, but did not alter the core classification (treated here as first detection of the N. ceranae subtype plus re‑emergence of nosemosis in a new host).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0932473996800599?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apis mellifera
Event summary: From 1999 onwards, Spanish laboratories began receiving increasing numbers of diseased Apis mellifera samples with nosemosis, and retrospective molecular diagnostics later showed that most infections, even in archived samples from 1999–2002, were due to Nosema ceranae rather than Nosema apis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai)) Between about 2000 and 2005, N. ceranae prevalence rose sharply in Spain and neighboring European countries such as France, Switzerland and Germany, coinciding with widespread reports of colony depopulation, poor productivity and increased winter mortality.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai)) By 2004–2005, N. ceranae had become the predominant Nosema species in many affected European apiaries, and severe colony losses in Spain and parts of Western Europe effectively marked the recognized emergence of N. ceranae‑driven nosemosis on the European continent.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large‑scale movement and trade of queens and colonies within Europe; intensification of beekeeping; climatic conditions in Mediterranean and temperate Europe that favored long transmission seasons; interactions with other stressors such as Varroa destructor, viruses and nutritional stress. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and successful colonization of A. mellifera; enhanced transmission compared with N. apis (reduced seasonality, ability to maintain high infection levels year‑round); increased virulence/pathogenicity manifested as rapid depopulation and colony weakening; geographic range expansion from an Asian origin into Europe.
Review: retain – This event captures the well‑documented emergence of N. ceranae‑associated nosemosis in Spain and adjacent Western/Southern European countries around 1999–2005, with correct continent/sub‑region coding and appropriate classification as an inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence of nosemosis due to a new parasite species. The timing and impact align with longitudinal Spanish data and early European surveys, so no structural changes were made.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Apis mellifera
Event summary: In the mid‑2000s, Nosema ceranae was first molecularly confirmed in Nosema‑positive Apis mellifera worker samples from eastern Canada and the central United States, demonstrating that the parasite had recently colonized temperate Northern American honey bee populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17897670/?utm_source=openai)) During 2006–2010, additional surveys across many U.S. states revealed high prevalence of N. ceranae, often coinciding with reports of unexplained colony depopulation and heavy winter losses during the period when colony collapse disorder (CCD) was first recognized.([ars.usda.gov](https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=248454&utm_source=openai)) By about 2010, N. ceranae had become the predominant Nosema species in much of the USA and Canada, with most Nosema‑positive samples containing N. ceranae alone and only a small minority harboring N. apis or mixed infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation and interstate movement of colonies and package bees within North America; extensive migratory pollination services that facilitate pathogen spread among regions; co‑stressors including Varroa mites, viral infections, pesticides and nutritional stress that may amplify disease impact. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and global spread of N. ceranae into Northern American A. mellifera populations; enhanced transmission and persistence leading to high within‑colony prevalence; possible increased virulence contributing to rapid adult mortality and colony depopulation; partial ecological replacement of N. apis by N. ceranae.
Review: review – Mexico was removed from this event because the project’s Country sheet assigns Mexico to the Central America sub‑region under the South America continent; this North American event now covers only the USA and Canada and its start year has been adjusted to 2006 to match the first molecular detections there. The summary was rewritten to focus on U.S. and Canadian data, and a Mexico‑specific source was moved to the South/Central America event below. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Northern America with concurrent re‑emergence of nosemosis is still appropriate.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17897670/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Brazil [1979]; Mexico [1995]; Argentina [2005]; Uruguay [2005]; Chile [2005]; Colombia [2007]; Ecuador [2010]
Host: Apis mellifera (Africanized and European lineages)
Event summary: Retrospective molecular studies of archived Africanized Apis mellifera drones from southern Brazil revealed that Nosema ceranae had been present there since at least 1979, decades before its formal description, indicating an undetected long‑term presence in South America.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201113001286?utm_source=openai)) Later work on historical Africanized bee samples in Mexico showed that N. ceranae had parasitized A. mellifera in Central America since at least 1995, while from the mid‑2000s onward surveys in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador documented widespread N. ceranae infections in managed honey bee colonies, often co‑occurring with or supplanting N. apis.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3896/IBRA.1.50.2.09?utm_source=openai)) By about 2015, N. ceranae was recognized as a common and sometimes dominant Nosema pathogen across much of South and Central America, with high infection prevalence but variable association with overt colony losses depending on local climate, bee lineage and co‑stressors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive movements and admixture of Africanized and European A. mellifera stocks in South and Central America; limited veterinary oversight of bee movements; warm climates that favor year‑round brooding and pathogen transmission; co‑exposure to pesticides, deforestation and habitat changes that can stress colonies. Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing host adaptation of N. ceranae to Africanized A. mellifera, followed by wider geographic expansion and recognition; enhanced transmission and chronic infection dynamics enabling decades of largely silent spread; re‑emergence of nosemosis as N. ceranae reached higher prevalence and interacted with additional stressors, sometimes displacing N. apis as the main Nosema species.
Review: review – This event was expanded to cover both South America and Central America (Mexico), reflecting the project’s geography where Central America is a South America sub‑region, and the event period was updated to 1979–2015 to capture retrospective detections in Brazil (1979 samples) and Mexico (1995 samples) while still emphasizing the main emergence wave after 2000. The countries list now includes Mexico [1995], and the re_occurrence flag was set to false to avoid prohibited co‑occurrence with inter‑continental emergence; re_emergence remains true because a new Nosema species altered disease dynamics in regions previously dominated by N. apis. Sources were updated to include both the Brazilian retrospective study and later Mexican work showing long‑term presence of N. ceranae in Africanized bees.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201113001286?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apis mellifera
Event summary: By the mid‑2000s, Nosema ceranae was detected in Apis mellifera colonies in New Zealand as part of a global survey, indicating that the parasite had reached Oceania and become established in local honey bee populations.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai)) Within a few years, N. ceranae was also confirmed in Australian honey bee colonies, with molecular studies documenting its presence alongside N. apis and other pathogens across multiple states.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201112000560?utm_source=openai)) Through the late 2000s and early 2010s, N. ceranae became widespread in major beekeeping regions in Australia and New Zealand, although the severity of clinical disease and association with overt colony losses varied with climate, bee stocks and co‑infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of queens and bee packages from Europe and the Americas into Australia and New Zealand; regional movements of managed colonies for pollination and honey flows; warm temperate climates that can support nearly continuous brooding and pathogen replication. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental geographic range expansion into Oceania; efficient oral–fecal transmission via shared food, comb and water sources; potential increased virulence compared with N. apis under some environmental conditions; ongoing displacement of N. apis as the dominant Nosema species in parts of the region.
Review: retain – Evidence from global surveys and regional studies supports first establishment of N. ceranae in New Zealand and then Australia in the mid‑2000s, with correct assignment to Oceania (Australia and New Zealand) and appropriate classification as inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence. No geography or type‑coding changes were required; only top‑level references were checked against primary literature.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Germany [2000]; Denmark [2005]; Poland [2005]; Czechia [2005]; Hungary [2005]; Romania [2005]
Host: Apis mellifera
Event summary: Following its initial emergence in Southern and Western Europe, Nosema ceranae continued to spread across Northern and Eastern European honey bee populations from the early 2000s onward, with longitudinal surveillance in northeast Germany documenting a continuous increase in N. ceranae prevalence over more than a decade without complete replacement of N. apis.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2010/03/m09154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) During this period, N. ceranae infections became common in countries such as Germany, Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Hungary and Romania, often in the context of multifactorial colony losses where Nosema was one of several stressors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7302437/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, N. ceranae was established across most European subregions, fundamentally altering the epidemiology of nosemosis in A. mellifera by reducing seasonality and promoting more chronic, year‑round infection patterns.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing intra‑European trade and movement of queens, nucleus colonies and production colonies; exposure to pesticides, habitat changes and variable nutrition that may have increased bees’ susceptibility; interactions with Varroa mites and viral infections. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion within Europe from initial foci in the southwest into cooler temperate climates; enhanced transmission and persistence facilitating establishment in Northern and Eastern Europe; re‑emergence in previously affected subregions driven by a novel Nosema species with distinct epidemiology; partial but not universal displacement of N. apis, altering the temporal pattern and impact of nosemosis.
Review: review – Germany is classified as Western Europe in the project’s Country sheet, yet this event also includes Denmark (Northern Europe) and several Eastern European countries; I therefore added Western Europe to the sub_regions field so that all listed countries are represented by their correct UNSD sub‑regions. The event otherwise appropriately captures intra‑continental spread and re‑emergence of N. ceranae within Europe, supported by long‑term German surveillance and broader European distribution data.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2010/03/m09154.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apis mellifera (indigenous and imported lineages)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, surveys of indigenous honey bees in Saudi Arabia using microscopy and PCR detected both Nosema apis and Nosema ceranae, with N. ceranae reported for the first time in the country and mapped across multiple regions.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.00270-07?utm_source=openai)) Around the same time, Iranian investigators reported the first molecular detection of N. ceranae in Apis mellifera colonies in Iran, adding to evidence that the parasite had spread into Western and Southern Asia and the broader Middle East.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22347302/?utm_source=openai)) Over the following years, N. ceranae became recognized as a widespread component of the pathogen complex affecting honey bees in this region, though its specific contribution to colony losses has varied among studies and often interacts with other stressors.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional movements and importation of queens and colonies between Western/Southern Asian countries and from Europe/Asia; arid and semi‑arid climates that can stress colonies and modulate disease expression; co‑occurrence of other pathogens and pesticide exposures. Internal mechanisms: Intra‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae from Eastern and Central Asia into Western and Southern Asia; establishment in locally adapted A. mellifera populations; host expansion and possible strain diversification suited to hot, dry conditions; re‑emergence of nosemosis in areas where only N. apis had previously been known.
Review: review – Iran is assigned to Southern Asia in the project’s geographic scheme, whereas Saudi Arabia lies in Western Asia; the sub_regions field was therefore expanded to "Western Asia; Southern Asia" so that both countries are correctly represented. The event’s interpretation as intra‑continental spread and re‑emergence of nosemosis driven by N. ceranae in the Middle East/West Asia remains valid and is supported by first‑detection papers from Saudi Arabia and Iran and regional reviews.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22347302/?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apis mellifera intermissa; Apis mellifera adansonii
Event summary: Around the late 2000s, Nosema ceranae was first reported infecting African honey bee subspecies when molecular and microscopic surveys detected the parasite in Apis mellifera intermissa colonies in Algeria, providing the earliest confirmed record of N. ceranae in North Africa.([sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.14103?utm_source=openai)) Shortly thereafter, a PCR‑based study in Benin showed that only N. ceranae (and not N. apis) was present in sampled Apis mellifera adansonii colonies, revealing the parasite’s arrival in West Africa and documenting its prevalence in local apiaries.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254861124_Determinants_et_contraintes_de_la_production_du_miel_dans_le_Nord-Ouest_du_Benin_Cas_des_communes_de_Natitingou_et_de_Tanguieta?utm_source=openai)) Over 2009–2012, these findings, together with continent‑wide disease inventories, established that N. ceranae had recently invaded African A. mellifera lineages, although infection remained patchy and was not yet clearly linked to large‑scale colony collapses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected colonies, queens and beekeeping equipment from Europe and other regions into North and West Africa; increasing long‑distance trade and translocation of colonies; environmental changes and agricultural intensification that may stress local honey bee populations and facilitate novel pathogen establishment. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae into African A. mellifera subspecies (A. m. intermissa and A. m. adansonii); host adaptation to African lineages; re‑emergence of nosemosis in regions previously affected mainly by N. apis, now involving a second Nosema species with different chronicity and seasonality.
Review: review – A new event was added to represent the first confirmed presence of N. ceranae in African honey bees, based on reports from Algeria (A. m. intermissa) and Benin (A. m. adansonii) around 2009–2011 and syntheses showing that, at the time, these were the only well‑documented African records. This event is coded as an inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Africa with re‑emergence of nosemosis due to a new parasite species. The precise start year and country‑specific dates may be refined as additional historical data are uncovered, but the inclusion of an African first‑detection event is necessary to capture a major geographic expansion of this EPP.([sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.14103?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Apis mellifera
Event summary: After Nosema ceranae had already been reported from African honey bee subspecies in North and West Africa, a focused molecular survey of 69 colonies on two of the Comoros Islands in the South‑West Indian Ocean confirmed that N. ceranae was also established in Eastern Africa.([thehive.icipe.org](https://thehive.icipe.org/all-prp/1478/?utm_source=openai)) The 2023 study found high infection prevalence and spore loads in Apis mellifera colonies on Grande Comore and lower but still substantial prevalence on Mohéli, demonstrating successful colonization of these oceanic islands despite their relative isolation. Over subsequent monitoring, N. ceranae came to be regarded as an important component of the pathogen complex on the Comoros, and together with data from neighboring islands it suggested that N. ceranae‑associated nosemosis is now widespread in the South‑West Indian Ocean region, even though clear links to large‑scale colony losses remain limited.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movements of honey bee colonies, queens and equipment among South‑West Indian Ocean islands and between these islands and continental Africa; traditional, low‑biosecurity beekeeping and honey hunting in Comoros; environmental stressors such as drought and fluctuating forage availability that may influence disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Intra‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae within Africa from earlier foci (e.g. North/West Africa and other SWIO islands) into the Comoros Archipelago; successful establishment in locally adapted A. mellifera lineages; re‑emergence of nosemosis in a region where Nosema infections were poorly characterized previously, now involving a parasite that tends to cause chronic rather than highly seasonal disease.
Review: review – The original Africa event treated the Comoros Islands as the first inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Africa, but more recent syntheses and primary studies show that the parasite was reported earlier in Algeria and Benin. I reinterpreted the Comoros record as an intra‑continental emergence within Eastern Africa/SW Indian Ocean, set the event year and country‑specific year to 2023 to match the published molecular survey, and re‑coded the type fields accordingly (first_detection and inter_continental_emergence set to false; intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence set to true). I also added the recent population‑genetic study of V. ceranae in the SW Indian Ocean as a supporting source.([thehive.icipe.org](https://thehive.icipe.org/all-prp/1478/?utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event summary: From late 2011, large commercial pig farms in northern China that had long used Bartha‑K61 gE‑deleted vaccines began reporting severe pseudorabies outbreaks with high piglet mortality, abortions and respiratory disease despite high vaccination coverage, indicating the emergence of more virulent PRV variants. During 2012 these outbreaks spread rapidly across major swine‑producing provinces in northern and eastern China, and by 2013–2014 highly pathogenic variant strains such as HeN1, TJ and ZJ01 were causing substantial losses in southern China as well, with illness in large numbers of pigs and frequent vaccine failures documented in outbreak investigations. Between roughly 2014 and 2017, molecular surveillance showed these variant genotype II strains becoming dominant across much of the country, prompting development and rollout of updated gE‑deleted vaccines based on variant strains and intensified control programs, which reduced but did not eliminate circulation of variant PRV in Chinese herds. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/1/13-0531_article))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of high‑density, industrial pig production in China, frequent live‑pig movements among provinces, and long‑term, near‑universal use of Bartha‑K61‑based vaccines created strong selection pressure and many opportunities for evolution and spread of fitter field strains. Biosecurity gaps, especially in breeding and nursery units, facilitated farm‑to‑farm transmission once variants appeared. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular analyses showed that post‑2011 isolates formed a distinct "variant" clade within genotype II, with characteristic insertions and amino‑acid substitutions in several glycoproteins (notably gC, gD and gE) compared with earlier Chinese and Western strains; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – experimental infections demonstrated higher mortality and more severe respiratory and neurologic disease, including in older pigs, than classic strains; Enhanced Transmission/Immune Escape – variant strains infected pigs previously vaccinated with Bartha‑K61 and induced strong gE antibody responses, indicating partial vaccine escape; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – within China, variants spread from initial foci in northern and eastern provinces to most major swine regions, but remained within an already endemic continental range. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386699/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. This is clearly one of the largest post‑1990 emergence events for PRV and should be retained, with classification as re‑emergence in an already endemic Asian sub‑region rather than as inter‑continental spread. PRV was long established in Chinese pigs, and outbreak investigations from 2011–2013 demonstrate that a more virulent, partially vaccine‑escape genotype II variant clade drove unprecedented epidemic activity across many provinces. The 2011–2017 time span reasonably captures the emergence, explosive spread and early control period, even though lower‑level variant circulation persists beyond 2017. The geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China) and host (domestic pigs) are correct. Mechanism/driver text has been edited to remove an incorrect reference to African swine fever–related restocking, which occurred after 2018 and did not drive the initial variant epizootic, and to emphasize molecular evidence for gC/gD/gE changes and vaccine escape documented in primary outbreak reports. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/1/13-0531_article))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Farmed mink (Neovison vison)
Event summary: In 2014, a large commercial mink farm in Shandong Province, eastern China, experienced a sudden outbreak of acute respiratory and neurologic disease in which roughly 3,500 of about 4,000 mink (≈87%) died within one week; PRV was isolated from affected animals, and follow‑up PCR testing showed additional PRV‑positive mink on other farms in the province. Around the same time, a separate severe outbreak occurred in farmed mink in Liaoning Province in northeastern China, where animals fed raw pig offal developed diarrhea, neurologic signs and 80–90% mortality, causing major economic losses in the local fur industry. Genetic and phylogenetic analyses indicated that mink isolates clustered closely with contemporary Chinese "variant" PRV strains circulating in pigs and associated with vaccine failure, consistent with spillover from infected swine herds into mink populations via contaminated pig by‑products. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very high densities of farmed mink in Shandong and Liaoning, routine use of uncooked pig offal and other abattoir by‑products in mink feed, and concurrent circulation of highly pathogenic PRV variants in regional pig herds created repeated opportunities for transmission of virus‑contaminated tissues to a highly susceptible carnivore host. Weak separation between pig abattoirs and fur‑animal operations and lack of heat‑treatment of feed were key proximal risk factors. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – mink isolates belonged to the same variant genotype II lineage that had recently emerged in Chinese pigs and that showed reduced neutralization by antibodies elicited by Bartha‑K61‑based vaccines; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – outbreaks in mink were characterized by per‑acute clinical signs and very high case fatality in clinically affected animals; Host Expansion (Spillover) – these events represent efficient spillover and adaptation of swine‑origin PRV variants to farmed mink, with PCR surveys indicating that infection was widely distributed in regional mink populations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. A 2014 outbreak on a Shandong mink farm killed roughly 3,500 of 4,028 animals (≈87% mortality) in a single week, and a contemporaneous Liaoning outbreak in pig‑offal‑fed mink had 80–90% mortality, both caused by genotype II "variant" PRV closely related to vaccine‑resistant swine strains. These episodes produced major, well‑documented losses in China’s fur industry and clearly rank among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for this virus, yet they were missing from the original dataset. They have therefore been added as a single linked episode in Eastern Asia, classified as re‑emergence with host expansion (spillover from pigs to mink) in an already endemic country, not as inter‑continental emergence. Geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China) and year (2014) follow the primary outbreak descriptions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Humans (occupationally exposed farm workers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers)
Event summary: In 2017, clinicians in China reported a first molecularly confirmed human ocular infection with pseudorabies virus in a swine‑exposed worker who developed febrile illness followed by severe bilateral endophthalmitis; sequencing showed the viral strain to be closely related to emergent highly pathogenic PRV variants circulating in pigs. Over the following years, additional patients with acute encephalitis and/or retinal necrosis were identified in several Chinese hospitals, and a multicenter cohort study of 472 encephalitis patients from 2016–2018 detected PRV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid of six individuals with rapidly progressive panencephalitis, most of whom had occupational contact with pigs or pork. By around 2022, case reports and systematic reviews had compiled more than a dozen well‑documented, often severe or fatal human neuro‑ophthalmic infections linked to PRV exposure in China, coinciding temporally and geographically with the spread of variant genotype II strains in the country’s pig population and raising concern about an expanded zoonotic host range. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/6/pdfs/17-1612.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑intensity swine production in China with persistent circulation of variant PRV strains, close and sometimes unprotected contact between pigs and farm workers, veterinarians, butchers, and slaughterhouse staff, and limited initial awareness of PRV as a potential human pathogen created repeated opportunities for zoonotic exposure. Wider use of metagenomic next‑generation sequencing for unexplained encephalitis increased the likelihood that PRV infections would be detected rather than remaining idiopathic. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – accumulating human case reports, almost all with direct or indirect exposure to pigs or raw pork products in China and with viral sequences clustering within the post‑2011 variant genotype II lineage, suggest that these strains have a greater capacity to infect humans than earlier PRV variants; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – human infections typically manifested as rapidly progressive encephalitis and/or bilateral retinal necrosis with high morbidity and frequent long‑term neurologic or visual sequelae; Novel Strain/Genotype – at least one human PRV isolate (hSD‑1/2019) has been recovered and shown experimentally to be closely related to contemporary Chinese variant strains and highly pathogenic in pigs; Enhanced Transmission – no sustained human‑to‑human transmission has been documented, with infections still appearing to be limited to direct zoonotic exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7897889/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. Severe PRV encephalitis and neuro‑ophthalmic disease in humans have been increasingly reported in China since around 2017, with case series and systematic reviews documenting more than a dozen well‑characterized patients and a recent Journal of Virology review summarizing 34 suspected human infections since 2011, all linked to swine exposure and variant genotype II strains. These events are important for this EPP and should be retained, but the original coding of both "first detection" and "re‑emergence" was inconsistent with the project rules. Because this row belongs to an animal‑host entry (pigs as the primary host system) and human infections represent host expansion of a long‑established pathogen rather than first appearance of the virus in the livestock host system, first_detection has been set to "No" and the event is treated purely as re‑emergence with host expansion in an already endemic Eastern Asia sub‑region. Geography, time span (2017–2022 as the initial period of recognized cases), and host description remain appropriate and are supported by the cited medical literature. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/6/pdfs/17-1612.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Domestic pigs (small commercial herd in Iowa; non-commercial outdoor herd in Texas)
Event summary: On 30 April 2026, routine surveillance testing run by USDA’s National Veterinary Services Laboratories detected antibodies to pseudorabies virus in a small commercial swine facility in Iowa; traceback showed that five boars had recently been sourced from an outdoor herd in Texas where additional pigs also tested positive, representing the first reappearance of pseudorabies in U.S. commercial swine since national eradication was declared in 2004. In response, APHIS and state animal‑health authorities in Iowa and Texas imposed quarantines on the affected premises, established nested two‑ and five‑mile surveillance zones, depopulated and properly disposed of all pigs in the Iowa index herd and the Texas source herd, and implemented extensive epidemiologic tracing and testing of linked herds while trading partners introduced temporary restrictions on some live‑pig and genetics exports. By mid‑June 2026, all swine premises in the two‑mile zone had completed required follow‑up testing with no further detections, movement restrictions were lifted, the affected site had been cleaned, disinfected and fallowed, and a final report was submitted to the World Organisation for Animal Health confirming that the United States had again achieved freedom from pseudorabies in commercial swine, limiting long‑term impacts largely to the directly affected herds and short‑term trade disruptions. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/agency-announcements/usda-confirms-pseudorabies-swine-herds-iowa-texas?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued endemic circulation of PRV in U.S. feral swine and in outdoor or low‑biosecurity production systems created a reservoir from which infection could be introduced into otherwise PRV‑free commercial herds. Movement of infected or latently infected boars from a non‑commercial outdoor herd in Texas into the Iowa facility, combined with imperfect source‑herd biosecurity and limitations of pre‑movement testing, appears to have enabled this rare breach of eradication. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – available reports describe the detection as reintroduction of PRV rather than emergence of a genetically distinct variant; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – not relevant; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – clinical signs and outcomes were consistent with typical pseudorabies in domestic pigs, without evidence of unusual severity; Enhanced Transmission – standard direct contact transmission between pigs is presumed; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – this episode represents a re‑occurrence of PRV in a historically affected country and region rather than expansion into a new geographic area. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113510000891?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: retain. The April–June 2026 detection of PRV in a small commercial herd in Iowa with a direct link to an outdoor herd in Texas, followed by rapid depopulation, zoning and surveillance and formal restoration of U.S. PRV‑free commercial status, is well documented by USDA APHIS and state sources and clearly represents a significant re‑occurrence in a previously disease‑free commercial system. Coding this event as re_occurrence (Yes) and re_emergence (No) in North America is appropriate: PRV has a long history in U.S. domestic pigs and remains widespread in feral swine, and there is no evidence that the Iowa/Texas detections involved a novel strain, new host, or spread to a new continent or sub‑region. The geographic fields (North America; Northern America; United States of America [2026]) match the country and sub‑region lists, and although only two linked herds were directly affected, the event had notable trade and regulatory consequences that make it one of the more impactful recent episodes for this virus. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/agency-announcements/usda-confirms-pseudorabies-swine-herds-iowa-texas?utm_source=openai))

Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans
Event summary: In late 1992, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) of epidemic subtype IC re‑emerged in western Venezuela, with initial equine and human cases reported in Trujillo State and neighboring Andean valleys, followed by a larger wave of disease in 1993 that also affected Zulia State. Equids developed severe neurologic signs and high mortality, and human cases of febrile and encephalitic illness were reported, but transmission remained geographically confined to western Venezuela rather than spreading continent‑wide. Emergency equine vaccination campaigns and vector‑control activities, together with the end of the rainy season, reduced mosquito densities and susceptible horse numbers, and epizootic activity waned by early 1994.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Nearly two decades without major epizootics allowed substantial cohorts of unvaccinated horses to accumulate in areas where enzootic subtype ID VEEV circulated in rodent–mosquito cycles; favorable rainfall and humidity in 1992–1993 increased vector abundance in lowland forests and agricultural valleys, promoting amplification and spillover into equines and humans. Internal mechanisms: Comparative genetic studies show that the 1992–1993 subtype IC epidemic strains arose from closely related enzootic subtype ID viruses in western Venezuela, acquiring mutations associated with increased equine virulence and viremia, which enabled horses to serve as efficient amplification hosts and drove this episode of viral re‑emergence.
Review: retain – 1992–1993 western Venezuela subtype IC epizootic is well documented as a re‑emergence of equine‑virulent virus derived from enzootic subtype ID, confined to Venezuelan states such as Trujillo and Zulia; geography, timing and classification as re‑emergence rather than intra-/inter‑continental emergence are appropriate and supported by molecular and epidemiologic studies.

Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (sporadic)
Event summary: In 1993, an outbreak of Venezuelan equine encephalitis in coastal areas of Chiapas State, southern Mexico, produced neurologic disease and high mortality in horses and some human febrile illnesses, representing the first confirmed equine epizootic caused by subtype IE viruses in the region. Virus isolates from sick equines and mosquitoes showed that previously enzootic IE lineages had acquired equine virulence, permitting efficient amplification in horse–mosquito transmission cycles and spread among multiple lowland foci. Targeted equine vaccination and vector‑control measures, combined with depletion of susceptible horses and seasonal declines in mosquito abundance, brought the epizootic under control within that summer.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense mosquito populations in lowland tropical habitats, growth of equine populations with minimal prior exposure or vaccination, and close contact between horses and long‑standing enzootic VEEV foci on the Pacific coastal plain allowed spillover and amplification. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic and experimental infection studies demonstrate that the 1993 outbreak strains belonged to a subtype IE lineage closely related to enzootic progenitors but bearing mutations that conferred equine virulence and higher viremia, enabling horses to serve as effective amplification hosts; this represents re‑emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence rather than simple recurrence of earlier IAB/IC epidemic viruses.
Review: retain – 1993 Chiapas epizootic is correctly placed in South America | Central America (Mexico), accurately described as the first confirmed equine epizootic due to subtype IE with documented genetic adaptation for equine virulence, and appropriately classified as re‑emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence, because VEEV was already established in the Central American sub‑region.

Host: Humans; equines (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event summary: Beginning in April 1995 in Falcón State, an epizootic of Venezuelan equine encephalitis caused by subtype IC virus swept east and west through much of northern Venezuela in largely unvaccinated equine populations, producing extensive equine deaths and tens of thousands of human febrile and neurologic illnesses. By mid‑1995 the epidemic crossed the border into La Guajira Department of northern Colombia, where household surveys and clinical surveillance estimated roughly 75,000–100,000 human infections, including several thousand neurologic cases and hundreds of deaths, alongside substantial equine mortality and major socio‑economic disruption. Large‑scale emergency equine vaccination with live‑attenuated TC‑83 and inactivated vaccines, movement restrictions, vector‑control efforts and seasonal reductions in mosquito densities curtailed transmission, and the epidemic subsided by late 1995 with only residual activity into early 1996.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: After about 20 years without major epizootics, large cohorts of unvaccinated horses accumulated across northern Venezuela and adjacent Colombia; unusually heavy rains and humid conditions in 1995 increased mosquito vector densities, and movement of viremic equids and humans along trade and travel routes facilitated spread into La Guajira. Weaknesses in routine equine vaccination and vector control allowed rapid amplification once epizootic virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and phenotypic analyses indicate that the 1995 epidemic virus belonged to an epizootic IC lineage closely related to enzootic ID strains from the region and to viruses from the 1992–1993 Venezuelan outbreak, with mutations associated with high equine viremia and efficient mosquito transmission; this supports classification as viral re‑emergence of an equine‑virulent lineage rather than simple recurrence of long‑silent epizootic strains.
Review: retain – 1995 Venezuela–Colombia epidemic is a key high‑impact event with scale and geography consistent with primary sources (≈75,000–100,000 human cases and extensive equine mortality in northern Venezuela and La Guajira, Colombia); classification as re‑emergence of subtype IC virus in a previously affected sub‑region is appropriate and no geographic or type‑coding corrections are needed.

Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (sporadic, mild febrile illness)
Event summary: In June–July 1996, Venezuelan equine encephalitis recurred in southern Mexico when an outbreak due to subtype IE virus affected horses in several localities in Oaxaca State, with 32 equine cases and 12 deaths among roughly 2,500 animals under observation and virus isolated from clinically affected horses. This epizootic represented geographic spread and renewed activity of the equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage that had caused the 1993 Chiapas outbreak, raising concern that equine disease could become established more widely along the Pacific coast. Rapid implementation of equine vaccination, movement controls and vector control in affected communities contained the outbreak within weeks and prevented extensive human encephalitis or further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistence of the equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage in southern Mexico following the 1993 Chiapas epizootic, incomplete vaccination coverage among horses, favorable ecological conditions with abundant mosquitoes in lowland tropical and subtropical habitats, and local movement of equids allowed introduction and amplification in Oaxacan foci. Internal mechanisms: Genetic comparisons show that 1996 outbreak strains fall within the same equine‑virulent IE lineage identified in 1993, with no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype; the 1996 event is therefore best interpreted as re‑occurrence of a previously emergent equine‑adapted lineage driven primarily by ecological and husbandry factors rather than a fresh episode of viral re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event (1996 Oaxaca outbreak) is correctly located and quantified, but the emergence type has been adjusted from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because genetic and epidemiologic data indicate continued circulation of the same equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage responsible for the 1993 epizootic, with no new distinct strain arising in 1996; classification change and revised mechanism text should be checked and accepted or reverted by a domain expert.

Host: Equines; possibly humans (limited clinical recognition)
Event summary: Around the end of 1999 and early 2000, small focal outbreaks of Venezuelan equine encephalitis occurred in western Venezuela (Carabobo and Barinas States) in areas previously affected by the 1995 epidemic, with nine foci reporting equine neurologic disease and approximately 35 equine deaths consistent with VEE. Virus isolation and serologic testing confirmed circulation of subtype IC VEEV in these post‑epizootic foci, but the outbreaks remained localized and did not expand into a wider regional epizootic or cause large documented clusters of human neurologic disease. Continued vaccination of horses in high‑risk areas, quarantine of affected premises and natural seasonal declines in mosquito vectors led to rapid reduction of detectable IC transmission and a return to low‑level activity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Post‑epizootic ecological conditions in western Venezuela, including residual populations of competent mosquito vectors, intermittent accumulation of susceptible young horses where vaccination coverage was incomplete, and climatic variability at the end of the rainy season, favored localized recurrence of VEE. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate that viruses from these outbreaks were subtype IC strains closely related to the 1995 epidemic virus, with no major adaptive changes; this pattern is consistent with post‑epizootic persistence or reintroduction of the existing IC lineage, so the 2000 outbreaks are best categorized as re‑occurrence driven by environmental and host‑population factors rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: retain – 2000 focal outbreaks in Carabobo and Barinas are documented in post‑epizootic surveillance with ≈35 equine deaths, clearly representing localized recurrence of the 1995 subtype IC lineage within the same Venezuelan sub‑region; classification as re‑occurrence and restriction of geography to Venezuela are appropriate, and impact is sufficient to count among the larger post‑1990 VEEV animal events.

Host: Equines; possibly humans (sporadic or subclinical infection)
Event summary: In late September 2003, two small ranch‑level outbreaks of equine encephalitis were detected in the municipality of Arismendi, Barinas State, western Venezuela, with 5 equine deaths among 24 susceptible animals and serologic evidence of infection with both Eastern and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses in surviving horses. These events occurred in a region previously affected by the 1995 VEE epidemic and by the 2000 post‑epizootic outbreaks, and virologic and serologic investigations confirmed low‑level VEEV activity but did not show widespread equine disease or a marked increase in human cases. Rapid implementation of movement restrictions, equine vaccination on nearby farms and vector control, together with the small scale of the foci, limited the episode to a short‑lived, highly focal recurrence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Localized lapses in vaccination in small equine herds, combined with favorable local environmental conditions for mosquito breeding along riverine habitats in Barinas State, promoted short‑term transmission of VEEV (and co‑circulating EEEV) in a limited area. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence and serologic data indicate that viruses involved were closely related to the subtype IC lineage responsible for the 1995 epidemic and the 2000 focal outbreaks, with no evidence of a distinct new epidemic genotype; the episode therefore represents re‑occurrence of existing lineages under suitable ecological conditions rather than a major new emergent strain.
Review: review – The 2003 Barinas outbreaks are real but involved only two ranches and five equine deaths with mixed VEEV/EEEV serologic findings; they are correctly located and categorized as re‑occurrence, but their very small size means they may fall below the intended threshold of the ten most impactful post‑1990 events and could be considered for exclusion in the final curated list.

Host: Equines; humans (sero‑evidence and sporadic febrile illness); rodents and mosquitoes in enzootic cycles
Event summary: From 2003 to about 2010, surveillance in the Gulf Coast region of Mexico documented ongoing Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus activity in coastal lowland states such as Veracruz, Tabasco and Tamaulipas, with sporadic equine infections, human seroconversions and frequent virus isolations from mosquitoes, sentinel hamsters and other vertebrates indicating endemic‑enzootic circulation of subtype IE VEEV. Transmission fluctuated seasonally and geographically but repeatedly recurred in similar wetland and floodplain habitats, occasionally infecting horses and people but without the large equine epizootics seen on the Pacific coast in the 1990s. Continued vaccination of horses in high‑risk areas, vector surveillance and targeted public‑health monitoring limited the scale of outbreaks, and by about 2010 documented VEEV activity in these Gulf‑Coast sites had declined to low or serologically inferred levels, although enzootic circulation almost certainly persists.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent enzootic VEEV cycles in rodent–mosquito systems in tropical wetlands and coastal plains of the Gulf Coast region, expansion of equine and bovine populations into floodplain pastures, incomplete routine vaccination, and environmental conditions such as heavy rains and river flooding that boosted mosquito densities all sustained recurrent low‑level transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses of isolates collected during 2003–2010 show continued circulation of subtype IE lineages closely related to earlier Mexican strains, with no evidence that a new more virulent epizootic subtype had emerged; equids generally developed low or undetectable viremias, suggesting they were not the primary amplification hosts in this region. Consequently, the 2003–2010 Gulf‑Coast Mexico activity is best classified as re‑occurrence of established enzootic lineages with intermittent spillover to equines and humans, rather than a distinct episode of viral re‑emergence or inter‑continental spread.
Review: review – Event correctly summarizes long‑term subtype IE activity along Mexico’s Gulf Coast, but continent and sub‑region have been restricted to South America | Central America (Mexico) and the country list simplified to a single Mexico [2003] entry, because documented transmission during 2003–2010 occurred only in Mexican states and northward spread into the United States remained hypothetical; these geographic corrections should be confirmed and accepted.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; rodents (sylvatic reservoirs); mosquitoes (Culex (Melanoconion) spp.)
Event summary: In the first half of 2006, clinic‑based febrile surveillance in Iquitos, an Amazonian city in northeastern Peru, detected a marked increase in Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus infections, with 63 laboratory‑confirmed human cases representing approximately a five‑fold rise over baseline incidence from 2000–2004. Cases occurred across multiple urban and peri‑urban neighborhoods, many distant from forested areas, indicating that sylvatic subtype ID VEEV was being transmitted in or very near the city rather than only in rural forest habitats as previously recognized. After intensified vector surveillance and public‑health messaging and as mosquito densities and transmission declined later in the year, case numbers returned toward endemic levels, although enzootic VEEV circulation in the surrounding Amazon Basin persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and housing into forest margins around Iquitos, high rainfall and flooding that increased breeding sites for Culex (Melanoconion) mosquitoes, and increased human use of peri‑urban forested areas created more frequent contact between people and enzootic VEEV transmission sites, leading to an urban‑proximal outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed that viruses from the 2006 outbreak belonged to the Panama/Peru subtype ID genotype already circulating in the region, with no clear evidence of a newly evolved epidemic subtype; the episode therefore represents re‑occurrence of an enzootic lineage in a new ecological context (urban and peri‑urban exposure) rather than emergence of a novel equine‑virulent strain.
Review: retain – 2006 Iquitos outbreak, with 63 laboratory‑confirmed human VEEV infections and evidence of urban/peri‑urban transmission of subtype ID, was previously omitted yet clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 VEEV episodes in terms of human case numbers; it is correctly coded as a South America | South America (Peru) re‑occurrence of an enzootic lineage rather than a first detection or epizootic equine event.

Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (suspected sporadic cases)
Event summary: Between 2009 and 2013, Colombian veterinary surveillance recorded renewed Venezuelan equine encephalitis activity in multiple lowland departments, with 49 laboratory‑confirmed equine cases reported from 13 departments and additional serologically exposed animals, most frequently in Córdoba, Magdalena and Valle del Cauca. These cases occurred against a background of endemic arboviral transmission and extensive equine movements, but represented a clear resurgence of clinically apparent VEE in equids after several years without major reported animal disease or human outbreaks. Outbreak foci were managed through local quarantine, intensified vaccination campaigns in risk areas and vector‑control measures, and although sporadic cases continued, no large human VEE epidemic comparable to 1995 was reported during this period.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased movement and trade of horses, including informal or poorly controlled transport between departments and across borders, created opportunities for spread of VEEV into new herds; suboptimal vaccination coverage, large susceptible equine populations in tropical lowland areas below ~1,200 m elevation, and climatic conditions favorable for mosquito vectors (rainy seasons and flooding) promoted amplification and spillover. Internal mechanisms: Available information from Colombian reports and regional phylogenetic work suggests involvement of established epizootic/enzootic subtype I lineages rather than a novel variant, with no evidence that a new equine‑virulent strain emerged during 2009–2013; this multi‑year episode is therefore best categorized as re‑occurrence of VEEV in previously affected Colombian sub‑regions.
Review: retain – 2009–2013 Colombian equine VEEV activity, with 49 laboratory‑confirmed equine cases across 13 departments and clear evidence of renewed clinical disease in horses, was missing from the original dataset yet is a substantial multi‑year re‑occurrence within South America | South America; coding as a Colombian re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence is appropriate and brings the event list closer to capturing the ten most impactful post‑1990 episodes.

Host: Horses, cattle, one llama (epizootic in mixed livestock herds, primarily equids, with cattle affected on many premises)
Event summary: Beginning in April 1995, vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) spilled over from endemic foci in northern Mexico into horses and cattle in the southwestern United States, initiating an epizootic that spread along river valleys in New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Arizona and adjacent areas over the 1995 season. Subsequent years saw additional activity, including Indiana serotype outbreaks in 1997–1998, with repeated introductions and overwintering leading to recurrent disease in western US states and substantial numbers of quarantined operations. The multi‑year cycle waned as cooler weather reduced vector activity and movement controls, surveillance and biosecurity measures were implemented, ending this epizootic lineage in the late 1990s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: seasonal abundance of hematophagous insect vectors (black flies, sand flies, biting midges) along riparian corridors; livestock movements and grazing patterns that brought horses and cattle into high‑vector river valleys; warm climatic conditions favoring vector survival; and management practices concentrating susceptible animals at shared water sources. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a distinct VSNJV lineage from endemic Mexico, followed by emergence of an Indiana serotype lineage later in the cycle, representing viral genetic diversification and range expansion within Northern America; efficient vector‑borne transmission in equids and cattle facilitated rapid local spread and supported limited overwintering between years.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected continent/sub-region/country fields so this row now represents the well-documented 1995–1998 western US epizootic, with Mexico treated as the endemic viral source rather than a separate outbreak country; this aligns with UN subregion coding and the event description, which focuses on disease impact in US livestock. Classification as re-emergence driven by distinct New Jersey and Indiana lineages introduced from endemic areas is supported by phylogenetic work, but a specialist may wish to consider whether the 1997–1998 Indiana-serotype outbreaks should be summarized more explicitly or split into their own event if finer resolution is needed.

Host: Horses and cattle (majority of clinical premises equine, with substantial bovine involvement; some other domestic species incidentally affected)
Event summary: In 2004, a large vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) epizootic emerged in horses and cattle in New Mexico, Texas and Colorado, following circulation in endemic northern Mexican regions, and by late 2004 about 294 premises in 43 US counties were affected. Continued overwintering and expansion produced an even larger 2005 wave, with hundreds of affected premises across nine US states and linked activity in northern Mexico, and limited residual activity persisting into 2006 in Wyoming and nearby areas. The epizootic ended after colder weather reduced vector populations and authorities implemented depopulation of high‑risk pastures, strict movement controls and heightened surveillance, with subsequent years showing no comparable multi‑year activity until the next major cycle.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated viral introductions from endemic Mexican foci into the US border region; high densities of horses and cattle along rivers and irrigated pastures; warm, wet conditions favoring black flies and biting midges; and interstate movement of equids for competition and ranching that disseminated infection between states. Internal mechanisms: molecular epidemiology shows that 2004–2006 outbreaks were driven by a specific VSNJV lineage closely related to strains circulating in Mexico, with evidence for viral persistence (overwintering) between 2004 and 2005 and for continued evolution as the virus spread; viral traits supporting persistence in local reservoirs and efficient vector-borne transmission underpinned re-emergence across multiple seasons.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected Mexico’s country-specific start year from 2003 to 2004 so that country timing now falls within the stated 2004–2006 epizootic window and reflects sequencing evidence that Mexican and US isolates from this period form a common outbreak lineage. Classification as a re-emergent, cross-border multi-year episode with extensive US impact is well supported by APHIS reports and molecular epidemiology, and this event clearly belongs among the major VSV emergence episodes since 1990.

Host: Horses, cattle (with sporadic involvement of other domestic ruminants)
Event summary: Around 2009, vesicular stomatitis reappeared in the southwestern United States in horses and cattle, following several quiet years after the 2004–2006 cycle, with outbreaks linked to virus lineages maintained in endemic Mexican regions. Transmission persisted into 2010 with a moderate number of affected premises across familiar high‑risk states such as New Mexico, Texas and Colorado, prompting quarantine and movement restrictions but not reaching the scale of the 2004–2006 or later 2014–2016 and 2019–2020 epizootics. Cooler seasonal conditions, vector decline and standard control measures (movement controls, enhanced surveillance, and precautionary biosecurity at livestock operations) allowed the outbreak to fade by late 2010.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: cyclical build‑up of competent insect vectors in the southwestern US; introduction of virus from endemic Mexican foci via animal movements or vector dispersal; and climatic conditions permitting localized transmission but with more limited geographic spread than in earlier epizootics. Internal mechanisms: available genetic data indicate that virus involved was closely related to existing VSNJV lineages without evidence for major antigenic or host-range shifts; therefore the episode is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven by external ecological and movement factors rather than a novel re-emergent strain.
Review: Decision: review. Updated geography to treat this as a US-only re-occurrence (Northern America/Northern America; United States [2009]) and removed the earlier Mexico [2008] tag, which actually refers to a Mexican endemic isolate later linked to the 2012–2015 lineage rather than to a documented 2009 cross-border outbreak. Added the APHIS 2009 cumulative report as a more directly relevant source, but because this episode involved relatively few premises compared with large US and Ecuadorian outbreaks, it may fall below the top-10 impact threshold and should be reconsidered at prioritization stage.
