Host: Horses and cattle (index premises in equids with cattle exposure)
Event summary: In 2012, a vesicular stomatitis outbreak was detected in the southwestern United States, with vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) identified on equine premises in New Mexico and a small number of additional livestock herds investigated in the region. Epidemiologic and phylogenetic analysis showed that the 2012 virus was most closely related to a lineage previously detected in Veracruz, Mexico in 2000, indicating a relatively recent introduction from endemic Mexican reservoirs rather than persistence of the 2004–2006 outbreak viruses. Following targeted quarantines, movement restrictions and biosecurity measures, the outbreak was contained to a limited number of premises and ended with the seasonal decline in vectors and strict surveillance to exclude foot‑and‑mouth disease and other vesicular infections.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of VSNJV from endemic Mexican regions into US border states via movement of infected animals or insect vectors; heightened summer vector activity around irrigated pastures and riparian areas; and high livestock densities in affected counties. Internal mechanisms: genetic analysis demonstrated a distinct viral genotype, different from the 2004–2006 lineage yet related to Mexican 2000 isolates, indicating re-emergence through a new viral introduction and phylogeographically distinct lineage rather than simple reactivation of earlier US outbreak strains.
Review: Decision: review. Restricted geography to the United States only (Northern America/Northern America; United States [2012]) and removed Mexico as an outbreak country because the 2012 episode was confined to New Mexico and neighboring US areas, with Mexican 2000 isolates serving only as ancestral references. The event is correctly classified as re-emergence due to a distinct VSNJV genotype, but given its small scale relative to major US cycles and the large 2018 Ecuador outbreak, its inclusion among the top 10 highest-impact events warrants re-evaluation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses and cattle (mixed‑species outbreaks on farms in northeastern Brazil)
Event summary: Between June and August 2013, vesicular stomatitis outbreaks occurred on multiple farms in Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte states in northeastern Brazil, affecting horses and cattle with vesicular lesions clinically indistinguishable from foot‑and‑mouth disease. Diagnostic workup confirmed vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus subtype 3 (VSIV‑3, Alagoas virus) as the cause, and molecular analyses indicated that the viruses formed a distinct clade relative to historical VSIV‑3 strains, representing renewed viral activity of this subtype in the region after a long quiet period. Control efforts focused on quarantine, clinical management and movement restrictions, and the wave of outbreaks subsided by late 2013 as vector populations declined and affected premises recovered.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: endemic circulation of vesicular stomatitis viruses in parts of Brazil, with climatic and ecological conditions in northeastern states favoring vector populations; close contact among horses and cattle on mixed farms; and limited prior exposure or vaccination against VSIV‑3 in equids and cattle. Internal mechanisms: re-emergence of the Alagoas VSIV‑3 subtype as a distinct lineage, with molecular data showing a separate clade associated with the 2013 outbreaks; vector-borne transmission by local insects (likely biting flies and midges) facilitated rapid spread between animals on affected properties.
Review: Decision: retain. Removed a secondary summary link (madbarn.com) in favor of the primary JVDI article and a Brazilian sero-epidemiologic study, which together provide stronger peer-reviewed evidence for the scale and genetic distinctness of the 2013 VSIV-3 Alagoas outbreaks. This event represents the documented re-emergence of an important Indiana subtype in Brazil after decades of sparse detection and is a key South American counterpart to the major US cycles.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses, cattle, and other equids (mules, donkeys) on hundreds of premises
Event summary: In late 2013 and early 2014, vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) was detected in northern Mexican states such as Sonora and Chihuahua, and in May 2014 index cases were confirmed in horses in Texas, with rapid spread to New Mexico, Colorado and Nebraska. Over 2014–2015 this lineage expanded widely, ultimately affecting more than a thousand quarantined premises across eight US states and causing one of the largest recorded VS outbreaks in recent decades, before tapering off with only sporadic detections through the final release of quarantines in early 2016. The episode concluded after aggressive quarantine and movement controls, heightened awareness among veterinarians and producers, and seasonal decline of insect vectors reduced new infections and allowed all affected premises in Mexico and the United States to be cleared.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high densities of horses and cattle in affected western and central US states; intense summer vector activity along rivers and irrigated cropland; livestock and equine movement (shows, sales, interstate grazing) that disseminated infection; and cross-border connectivity with endemic VSNJV circulation in northern Mexico. Internal mechanisms: phylogeographic and modeling studies show that a single VSNJV lineage overwintered between 2014 and 2015, with viral evolution occurring in unsampled hosts and vectors as it expanded into new states; this capacity for multi-season persistence and northward range expansion underpins classification as a major re-emergent multi‑year epizootic.
Review: Decision: retain. Adjusted event years to 2013–2016 and kept Mexico [2013] plus United States [2014] to reflect phylogenetic and surveillance evidence that the 2014–2015 US outbreak was preceded by VSNJV detections in northern Mexico and concluded with final US quarantines in early 2016. Also corrected the continent label from “North America” to “Northern America” for consistency with the Country reference sheet; this multi-year, cross-border VSNJV lineage is clearly one of the highest-impact emergence events in the period.

Host: Cattle, horses and one mule (mixed herds on several farms in Maranhão state)
Event summary: In 2016, vesicular stomatitis outbreaks were reported on multiple cattle farms in Maranhão state in northeastern Brazil, where cattle, horses and a mule showed vesicular lesions, prompting investigation for foot‑and‑mouth disease. Laboratory testing confirmed infection with Alagoas vesiculovirus (VSAV, a VSIV subtype) closely related to, but genetically distinct from, viruses identified in the 2013 Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte outbreaks, indicating ongoing viral evolution and spread within northeastern Brazil. After implementation of on‑farm quarantines, movement restrictions and supportive care, clinical cases declined and the outbreak series ended as environmental conditions became less favorable for vector transmission.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: endemic VS circulation in northeastern Brazil; large cattle herds co‑grazed with equids; and environmental conditions (warm, humid climate with abundant insect vectors) that supported recurrent VSAV transmission. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show that the 2016 VSAV strains in Maranhão formed a clade related to, but distinct from, the 2013 viruses, providing evidence of re-emergence via an evolving lineage; vector adaptation to local conditions and persistence in regional reservoirs likely facilitated multi‑year activity.
Review: Decision: review. This row accurately describes the genetically distinct VSAV lineage causing the 2016 Maranhão outbreaks and is well supported by molecular and clinical data, but the number of affected farms was modest compared with the 2018 Ecuador and major US cycles. Retain for now as a key example of South American re-emergence of the Alagoas subtype, but its priority relative to other medium-sized events should be reassessed if a strict cap of 10 highest-impact episodes is enforced.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cattle primarily, with some equids implicated in endemic transmission foci
Event summary: In 2018, Colombia’s veterinary authority (ICA) reported a marked increase in notifications of vesicular stomatitis (estomatitis vesicular) in cattle herds, with numerous foci concentrated in departments such as Santander, Norte de Santander, Cesar and Antioquia where the disease is endemic. This resurgence led to intensified vaccination recommendations and reinforced surveillance, as VS cases complicate differential diagnosis with foot‑and‑mouth disease in a country striving to maintain FMD‑free status with vaccination. The elevated incidence declined after targeted vaccination campaigns, improved reporting and seasonal changes reduced vector populations, although VS remains a common vesicular disease in Colombian cattle and occasional equids.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: endemic VSV circulation in Colombia combined with favorable climatic conditions for vectors in 2018; high cattle density with frequent animal movements between farms and grazing areas; and gaps in vaccination coverage contributing to a larger‑than‑usual outbreak year. Internal mechanisms: reports emphasize established VSIV/VSNJV circulation without clear evidence of a novel strain or major host shift; thus the 2018 surge is categorized as a re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental conditions, herd immunity gaps and control program performance rather than viral genetic innovation.
Review: Decision: review. The Colombian surge in 2018 is well documented by ICA as an unusually high notification year in endemic departments, justifying classification as a re-occurrence in South America. However, the number of affected herds and geographic impact are smaller than for Ecuador’s 2018 multi-hundred-outbreak epizootic, so this row should be revisited when ranking events by continental and global impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds across coastal, Andean and Amazonian regions; other domestic species were not reported clinically affected)
Event summary: In 2018, Ecuador experienced a very large vesicular stomatitis epizootic, with approximately 399 registered bovine outbreaks reported across most provinces over a short period, especially between September and November. Molecular analysis of vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) and Indiana virus (VSIV) isolates showed that 2018 strains formed closely related clades distinct from, yet descended from, variants associated with a smaller 2004 Amazonian outbreak, indicating renewed epizootic activity arising from enzootic circulation. As climatic conditions shifted, vector pressure decreased and control measures such as movement restrictions and on-farm biosecurity were implemented, outbreak notifications declined and the widespread national wave subsided.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: favorable climatic conditions and abundant insect vectors in the Amazon, coastal lowlands and Andean highlands; high cattle densities and frequent movements of animals to auctions and between farms, particularly in coastal and highland regions; and long-term endemic circulation of VSV in Ecuador that provided viral reservoirs for rapid spread when environmental conditions were suitable. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses demonstrate that 2018 VSNJV and VSIV strains clustered in South American clades with two main Ecuadorian subclades (Amazonian and Andean/coastal), with close ancestry to 2004 Ecuadorian and Colombian variants, supporting classification as a major re-emergent epizootic driven by evolution and amplification of existing regional lineages rather than introduction of an entirely novel serotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Newly added row for the 2018 Ecuador outbreak, which involved about 399 recorded bovine outbreaks and nationwide spread over multiple ecological regions, clearly placing it among the most impactful VSV events in South America since 1990. Classified as re-emergence based on molecular evidence linking 2018 strains to earlier 2004 Ecuadorian and Colombian variants, with strong external drivers (vectors, climate, cattle trade) documented in primary sources; this event should be considered a core component of any top-10 VSV emergence list.

Host: Horses and cattle (index and majority of premises equine, with many mixed equine–bovine herds; some small ruminants and camelids affected)
Event summary: A large vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus (VSIV) outbreak began in June 2019 in the southwestern United States, with the first confirmed index premises in horses in Texas and New Mexico and rapid spread to Colorado and Wyoming, then further expansion to Oklahoma, Nebraska, Utah and Kansas over the season. By the end of 2019, approximately 1,144 VSV‑affected premises were identified in 111 counties across eight US states, representing the largest recorded VSIV incursion in recent decades and affecting primarily horses but also many cattle herds. The 2019 wave ended with the onset of winter and aggressive control measures, but evidence of overwintering and continued circulation in vectors and livestock set the stage for a follow‑on outbreak in 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: incursion of VSIV from endemic areas into US border states; extensive vector habitat along rivers and irrigated lands in affected states; dense populations of horses and cattle on pasture during peak vector season; and livestock movements for shows, sales and grazing that carried virus between regions. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses of VSIV from the 2019 outbreak revealed low genetic diversity consistent with a single incursion followed by rapid expansion, and later work showed that the same lineage successfully overwintered, with 2020 sequences nested within 2019 viruses, demonstrating re-emergence through persistence and adaptation to the North American ecological context.
Review: Decision: retain. Updated geography to treat this as a United States–only event (Northern America/Northern America; United States [2019]), removing Mexico [2018] because Mexican strains are implicated as ancestral sources but official data show no comparably large Mexican outbreak in 2018–2019. With 1,144 affected premises across eight states, this VSIV incursion is one of the largest VSV outbreaks in at least 40 years and clearly merits inclusion as a major re-emergent episode.

Host: Horses and cattle (numerous mixed‑species premises; some small ruminants)
Event summary: Following the large 2019 incursion, vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus re-emerged in 2020 across parts of the central United States, with virus overwintering and causing new infections in horses and cattle from spring through late summer. The 2020 episode affected about 326 premises in 70 counties, with notable eastward spread into Kansas and Missouri for the first time in several decades, alongside continued cases in previously affected western states. Vector control, on‑farm biosecurity, quarantines and movement restrictions, combined with the seasonal decline in biting flies and midges, eventually curtailed transmission and the outbreak ended by late 2020, although the event highlighted the potential for VSIV to expand into new areas of the US livestock belt under favorable conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: overwintering of the 2019 VSIV lineage in the US, likely in local reservoirs or insect vectors; favorable climatic conditions in 2020 that supported high vector densities in both traditional western foci and more easterly states; and livestock movements that facilitated establishment of infection in Kansas and Missouri. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic and genomic analyses show 2020 viruses forming a monophyletic subset of 2019 sequences, consistent with re-emergence via persistence of the same lineage; viral traits supporting survival across seasons and efficient transmission by local insect vectors underpinned geographic range expansion into new parts of Northern America.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected the countries list to "United States of America [2020]" and removed Mexico [2019] as well as state names (Kansas, Missouri) that had been incorrectly formatted as countries, while keeping the description of eastward spread within the US. This row appropriately captures the expansion year of the 2019 VSIV lineage, which overwintered and re-emerged to affect hundreds of premises and new US regions, and together with the 2019 incursion forms one of the most consequential modern VSV epizootic cycles.

Host: Horses predominantly, with some cattle and a few non-domestic species (e.g. rhinoceros) affected on mixed or zoological premises
Event summary: In May 2023, vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) was confirmed on an equine premises in San Diego County, California, marking the first VS outbreak in that state since the early 1980s, and cases soon appeared in additional California counties as well as isolated premises in Nevada and Texas. Between May 2023 and January 2024, about 319 VSV‑affected premises were identified across 19 California counties plus one county in Nevada and two in Texas, with most clinical disease reported in horses but some cattle and zoo animals also affected, prompting extensive quarantines and movement restrictions. As vector activity diminished over winter and control measures (vector management, movement controls, heightened surveillance) took effect, new case reports ceased and the 2023–2024 outbreak was declared resolved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely incursion of VSNJV from endemic areas via infected insect vectors into southern California, followed by local amplification under favorable climatic conditions that supported high densities of biting midges and black flies; high concentrations of horses at equine facilities and events in affected regions; and limited prior exposure to VSV in California, which had not seen an outbreak for decades. Internal mechanisms: virologic investigations during the outbreak detected VSNJV RNA in multiple vector species (including Culicoides midges and black flies) and indicated a relatively homogeneous viral lineage consistent with a single recent introduction that expanded within the western US; the ability of this lineage to exploit new ecological niches in California underlies its classification as a significant re-emergent epizootic in Northern America.
Review: Decision: retain. Newly added row summarizing the 2023–2024 US VSNJV outbreak, which involved roughly 319 affected premises across California, Nevada and Texas and represented the first vesicular stomatitis activity in California since the early 1980s. The event is treated as a US-only re-emergence with strong evidence for vector-borne introduction and spread, and its scale and geographic novelty justify inclusion among the highest-impact modern VSV emergence episodes.

Host: Humans (primary reported), with local Culex pipiens mosquitoes, urban birds and likely incidental equines contributing to transmission cycles
Event summary: In summer–autumn 1996, West Nile virus re‑emerged in Romania, causing a large outbreak of neuroinvasive disease centred on Bucharest and the southern Danube plain after decades with little recognized activity in Eastern Europe. Intense transmission in urban Culex mosquitoes feeding on birds and humans led to several hundred confirmed neuroinvasive cases and multiple deaths before incidence declined with the end of the mosquito season. The outbreak subsided as temperatures fell and vector populations dropped, but it signalled renewed epidemic potential of WNV in Eastern Europe and prompted establishment of sustained human, mosquito and bird surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban expansion with abundant breeding sites for Culex pipiens, warm summer conditions and limited prior surveillance or awareness facilitated intense local amplification in Bucharest and surrounding areas. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not support emergence of a novel lineage here; amplification of existing lineage 1 strains in dense urban bird–mosquito cycles produced a pronounced re‑occurrence of severe human disease in a previously affected subregion.
Review: review – Retain this event as one of the major modern WNV outbreaks; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) are consistent with historical evidence. Updated source URLs to rely on WHO Disease Outbreak News and primary outbreak investigations (Tsai et al., Lancet; Savage et al., EID) instead of general Wikipedia pages; no other fields changed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Domestic geese and other birds, wild migratory birds, humans; likely local horses as incidental hosts
Event summary: From 1997 onward, a more virulent strain of West Nile virus emerged in Israel, first recognized through unexpected mass mortality and neurologic disease in domestic geese and other birds in an area where WNV had previously been regarded as largely non‑pathogenic for birds. Over the 1998–2000 transmission seasons, this lineage caused repeated bird die‑offs and a large human outbreak in 2000, with several hundred confirmed cases and dozens of deaths, indicating intense local bird–mosquito amplification and spillover to humans and other mammals. Activity decreased after targeted vector control and seasonal cooling reduced mosquito abundance, but the episode demonstrated that newly introduced or evolved WNV variants could markedly increase pathogenicity in avian and mammalian hosts in an already endemic region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of farmed geese and wild birds along major Afro–Eurasian flyways, irrigated agriculture and peri‑urban water bodies in Israel enhanced opportunities for virus amplification and contact between birds, mosquitoes and humans. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and establishment of a more virulent lineage 1 strain closely related to the NY99 genotype, capable of causing severe disease and high mortality in birds and humans; this represents re‑emergence driven by increased virulence/pathogenicity of the virus in a region where WNV was already endemic.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the major 1997–2000 Israeli bird and human outbreak driven by a more virulent lineage 1 strain, but intra_continental_emergence was set incorrectly. WNV had long been endemic in Western Asia, so this episode is best classified as re-emergence without intra-continental emergence; intra_continental_emergence has been set to false and re_emergence retained as true. Countries have been restricted to Israel [1997–2000], as clear evidence for major contemporaneous outbreaks in Cyprus or the State of Palestine during this specific episode is lacking in reviewed sources. Source URLs were updated to outbreak-specific EID and PubMed articles.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Northern America; Caribbean; Central America; South America
Countries: United States of America [1999]; Canada [2001]; Mexico [2002]; Cayman Islands [2001]; Jamaica [2001]; Puerto Rico [2002]; Belize [2003]; Guatemala [2003]; Honduras [2003]; El Salvador [2003]; Nicaragua [2003]; Costa Rica [2003]; Panama [2004]; Colombia [2004]
Host: Wild birds (especially corvids and other passerines), zoo and captive birds, horses, humans, domestic dogs and cats, other incidental mammals
Event summary: In 1999, West Nile virus was detected for the first time in the Western Hemisphere during an outbreak of encephalitis and extensive bird deaths in New York City, marking the introduction of the virus into North America. Over the next several years, the introduced lineage 1 strain spread rapidly via migratory birds and competent Culex vectors across the continental United States, into Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean and parts of Central and northern South America, leading to massive mortality in wild birds and more than 27,000 documented equine infections alongside tens of thousands of human cases. By around 2004 the virus had become established across much of the Americas, with incidence declining from early epidemic peaks but with continued endemic seasonal transmission in birds, horses and humans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable translocation of an infected bird or mosquito via air or ship travel to New York, followed by rapid spread along bird migratory routes and through abundant urban and rural Culex breeding sites in temperate and subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a lineage 1 NY99 genotype highly adapted to naïve North American bird species and local Culex mosquitoes, enabling efficient bird–mosquito–bird transmission and rapid geographic range expansion; subsequent minor genetic changes (e.g. WN02 genotype) improved local adaptation but did not constitute a new lineage for emergence-type classification.
Review: review – Retain as a key event describing the introduction and hemispheric spread of WNV in the Americas; geography, timing and hosts are appropriate, and inter_continental_emergence remains correctly set to true. However, first_detection has been set from true to false because WNV was detected in animals and humans decades earlier in Africa and Europe; this episode represents first detection in the Americas, not in the host system globally. Source URLs already include detailed primary and review articles and were not otherwise modified.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild birds (especially raptors), horses, humans
Event summary: In 2004, a West Nile virus lineage 2 strain previously thought to be restricted to sub‑Saharan Africa was first detected in a northern goshawk in Hungary, signalling introduction of this lineage into Central Europe. Between 2008 and the following transmission seasons, the lineage 2 strain spread across Hungary and into eastern Austria and neighbouring countries, causing outbreaks in birds of prey, horses and humans and establishing a new enzootic focus distinct from earlier European lineage 1 circulation. Transmission intensity later stabilised as surveillance and vector control improved and the virus became endemic in local bird and mosquito populations, but this episode marked a major genetic and ecological shift in European WNV.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movements of migratory birds along Central European flyways likely carried lineage 2 from Africa or elsewhere in Eurasia into Hungary, while warm summers and wetland habitats supported Culex mosquito proliferation and overwintering. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of a novel lineage 2 genotype in Europe, representing re‑emergence of WNV in affected subregions through a genetically distinct, efficiently transmitting strain rather than simple resurgence of historical lineage 1 viruses.
Review: review – Retain this as a major re-emergence event driven by introduction of lineage 2 into Central Europe. WNV was already present in Eastern and Western Europe before 2004, so intra_continental_emergence has been set to false; re_emergence remains true to reflect the appearance and spread of a genetically distinct lineage. Added the central EID article on lineage 1 and 2 strains in Central Europe; other details (countries, timing, hosts) are consistent with reviewed literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Horses, livestock (cattle, small ruminants), wildlife (e.g. wild ungulates), humans (sporadic)
Event summary: Between 2008 and 2015, intensified surveillance in South Africa revealed a substantial burden of West Nile virus lineage 2 infection among horses with neurologic disease, with about 7% of over 1,000 sampled horses testing positive and roughly one‑third of infections proving fatal. Concurrent infections were also documented in livestock and wildlife, showing that WNV was causing more recognised clinical disease in multiple animal species than previously appreciated in this endemic region. Case numbers fluctuated seasonally and by year and were influenced by rainfall and horse population dynamics, but WNV has remained an important cause of equine encephalitis in southern Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental conditions favouring Culex vectors (wet summers, irrigation, water storage), expansion and concentration of horse populations, and improved veterinary diagnostic capacity together led to increased detection of WNV disease in equids and other animals. Internal mechanisms: Predominant circulation of lineage 2 strains with clear neurotropic potential in horses and evidence of pathogenic strains, representing re‑emergence through enhanced recognition and possibly local adaptation of lineage 2 viruses rather than appearance of a completely new lineage.
Review: retain – This episode is well documented as a substantial burden of lineage 2-associated neurologic disease in horses and other animals in South Africa and fits the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogenic lineage 2 strains and improved detection. Geography, hosts, timing and event-type coding are appropriate, and existing sources (EID surveillance report plus general WNV overview) are adequate for this dataset; no structural changes were made.

Host: Humans, horses, domestic birds and wild birds, mosquitoes (Culex pipiens)
Event summary: In summer 2010, Greece experienced its first major epidemic of West Nile disease when a lineage 2 strain, closely related to the Central European lineage 2 cluster, was detected in Culex mosquitoes and caused a large human outbreak centred in Central Macedonia. During this season, more than 250 human cases (with a high proportion neuroinvasive) and multiple equine cases were reported, alongside infection in local bird populations, marking a dramatic emergence of WNV disease in Greece despite prior serologic evidence of circulation. Transmission decreased after the mosquito season ended and was somewhat lower, but recurrent, in subsequent years, indicating establishment of an endemic focus seeded by this 2010 lineage 2 introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Wetland and rice‑growing landscapes around Central Macedonia supportive of large Culex pipiens populations, combined with hot summers and positioning on major migratory bird routes, created favourable conditions for amplification of the introduced lineage 2 virus. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and local expansion of the Nea Santa–Greece–2010 lineage 2 strain, which showed efficient transmission in local mosquitoes and birds and caused severe neuroinvasive disease in humans and horses, consistent with re‑emergence via a new genetic lineage in a previously less‑affected subregion.
Review: review – This event is correctly treated as a major Greek epidemic associated with introduction of a lineage 2 strain, but it does not constitute intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion because WNV was already established in Southern Europe (e.g. France, Italy). Intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to false, while re_emergence remains true to reflect emergence of a new lineage causing severe disease. Existing sources (Greek outbreak description, lineage 2 characterisation, and regional epidemiologic overviews) are appropriate and were retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Italy [2010]; Serbia [2012]; Romania [2010]; Russian Federation [2010]; Hungary [2010]; Austria [2010]; Croatia [2012]; Bulgaria [2012]
Host: Humans, horses, wild birds and sentinel poultry
Event summary: Following the 2004–2008 introduction of lineage 2 into Central Europe and the 2010 epidemic in Greece, West Nile virus activity expanded between 2010 and 2013 across Southern and Eastern Europe, including Italy, the Balkans, Romania, parts of European Russia and Austria, with multiple human and equine outbreaks. During these years, both lineage 1 and lineage 2 strains circulated, causing clusters of neuroinvasive disease in humans and horses and repeated detection in birds and sentinel poultry in new regions within affected countries. While annual case numbers varied with climate and vector abundance, by 2013 WNV had become entrenched along much of the Danube and Po river basins and Mediterranean coastal lowlands, and subsequent control efforts focused on targeted vector management and equine vaccination in high‑risk areas rather than eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive wetland and riverine habitats, irrigation agriculture and warming summers facilitated Culex breeding and viral overwintering, while bird migration enabled stepwise spread between river basins and coastal zones in Southern, Eastern and parts of Western Europe. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation and geographic expansion of both lineage 1 and lineage 2 viruses, with lineage 2 in particular showing strong adaptation to local ecosystems, representing re‑emergence driven by established but spreading strains rather than a completely novel lineage during this period.
Review: review – This multi-country 2010–2013 European episode is appropriately treated as a linked re-emergence period dominated by expansion of established lineage 1 and 2 strains, but two corrections were needed. First, WNV was already present in both Eastern and Southern Europe before 2010, so intra_continental_emergence has been set to false and the event kept as re_emergence. Second, Western Europe has been added to the sub_regions field to reflect inclusion of Austria, which is classified as Western Europe in the UNSD scheme. Countries and years remain consistent with regional outbreak summaries, and existing regional reviews were retained as sources.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Horses, humans, wild birds
Event summary: In 2010, West Nile virus caused the first recognised large outbreak of clinical disease in the Iberian Peninsula, with numerous equine cases and a small number of human neuroinvasive infections in Andalusia in southern Spain and confirmed human and equine cases in southern Portugal. The virus, which had been silently circulating in birds and occasionally humans in Iberia for years, established conspicuous local transmission cycles in wetlands and agricultural areas of the Guadalquivir and Tagus river basins, resulting in high attack rates in affected horse herds. Transmission declined after the mosquito season ended, but WNV has since recurred intermittently in Iberia, indicating that the 2010 episode marked the onset of more obvious endemic circulation with recurrent equine and occasional human disease.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Location of southern Spain and Portugal along major Afro‑Eurasian bird flyways, extensive wetland and rice‑growing areas, and warm summers allowed WNV, already present in local bird populations, to amplify in Culex mosquito populations and spill over to horses and humans. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and intensification of existing lineage 1 viruses into new foci within Southern Europe; there is no strong evidence of a novel genotype in 2010, so the key mechanism is re‑emergence of established strains into susceptible equine and human populations.
Review: review – The 2010 Iberian outbreak is rightly included as an important emergence of overt WNV disease in Spain and Portugal, but it was misclassified. WNV had been detected serologically in birds and humans in Spain and Portugal and a Spanish human neuroinvasive case was reported in 2004, so this episode is not first detection in the host system or a new UNSD subregion. First_detection and intra_continental_emergence have been set to false, and the event is recoded as re_emergence reflecting the first sizeable clinical outbreaks in Iberian horses and humans. Event summary has been slightly clarified and EID and regional papers on Spain and Portugal have been added to the source list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans, horses, wild birds
Event summary: In 2012, more than a decade after West Nile virus became established in North America, the United States experienced one of its largest resurgence years, with 5,674 reported human cases and 286 deaths, accompanied by increased detection of equine and avian infections in many states and parts of Canada. The resurgence was especially intense in the central United States, including Texas, where a severe regional outbreak resulted in over 1,800 human cases and more than 100 equine cases, driven by hot, dry conditions and altered water management that favoured Culex mosquitoes and amplified bird–mosquito transmission cycles. Case numbers fell again in subsequent years as weather patterns shifted and public health and veterinary responses intensified, but the 2012 season underscored the potential for major re‑occurrence of WNV disease even after long periods of endemicity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually warm temperatures and drought conditions in parts of the central United States, changes in water storage and irrigation, urban heat-island effects and possible lapses in vector control and personal protection promoted high Culex mosquito densities and contact with birds and humans. Internal mechanisms: The resurgence was largely driven by endemic North American lineage 1 strains already adapted to local ecosystems rather than by a novel genotype, so it represents re‑occurrence triggered mainly by climatic and ecological drivers rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – This row correctly captures the 2012 North American resurgence as a large re-occurrence year driven by climatic and ecological factors, with no clear evidence for an emergent viral genotype; event-type coding (re_occurrence only) is therefore appropriate. To strengthen documentation, CDC surveillance summaries and the EID paper on the Texas 2012 outbreak have been added to the source URLs alongside the existing overview sources. No changes were made to geography, timeframe or host description.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Italy [2018]; Greece [2018]; Serbia [2018]; Romania [2018]; Hungary [2018]; Bulgaria [2018]; Croatia [2018]; France [2018]; Austria [2018]; Slovenia [2018]; Germany [2018]; Spain [2018]; Portugal [2018]; Czechia [2018]
Host: Humans, horses (equids), wild and captive birds, mosquitoes (mainly Culex pipiens complex)
Event summary: In 2018, Europe experienced its largest recorded West Nile virus season, with an unusually early start to transmission and a marked increase in both human and equine cases compared with previous years across Southern, Eastern and parts of Western Europe. More than 1,500–2,000 autochthonous human infections and over 180 deaths were reported in EU and neighbouring countries, alongside approximately 285 notified outbreaks among equids in Italy, Hungary, Greece, Romania, France, Austria, Germany, Spain, Slovenia, Portugal and others, and widespread detections in wild and captive birds. Transmission gradually declined with the end of the mosquito season, but the 2018 episode highlighted the capacity of established WNV lineages in Europe to generate very large epidemics and epizootics when climatic and ecological conditions are highly favourable.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Exceptionally warm spring and summer temperatures, early onset of the mosquito season, episodes of drought followed by rainfall and extensive irrigated agriculture created optimal conditions for proliferation of Culex vectors and high contact rates with susceptible birds, horses and humans across much of southern and central Europe. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was driven primarily by already established lineage 2 (and to a lesser extent lineage 1) WNV strains rather than by emergence of a fundamentally new genetic variant, so it is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence within previously affected European subregions facilitated by environmental drivers and entrenched enzootic cycles.
Review: review – New event added to capture the record 2018 European transmission season, which was missing from the original dataset despite being one of the largest global WNV episodes in terms of human cases, deaths and equine outbreaks. Classified as re-occurrence because it involved dramatic amplification of established European lineages in previously affected Southern, Eastern and Western European subregions, driven largely by exceptional climatic and environmental conditions rather than emergence of a new lineage; all other emergence-type flags are set to false. Country and subregion lists reflect ECDC/EFSA data on heavily affected states, and sources draw on ECDC human and equine reports and recent European WNV overviews.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: China [1991-1992]; China, Taiwan Special Administrative Region [1991-1992]
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (Fenneropenaeus chinensis, Penaeus japonicus, Penaeus monodon and related cultured species)
Event summary: Origin: Around 1991–1992, intensive marine shrimp farms in coastal Fujian Province (China) and in Taiwan experienced sudden, pond-wide mortalities in penaeid shrimp, with histopathology and electron microscopy revealing a previously unrecognized large bacilliform DNA virus later named white spot syndrome virus (WSSV). Development: The outbreaks rapidly caused catastrophic losses in Chinese white shrimp and other cultured penaeids, with many ponds suffering 80–100% mortality within days, leading to collapse of major segments of the Chinese shrimp industry and the first detailed descriptions of white spot disease. End: By the mid‑1990s, WSSV was widely recognized as endemic in Chinese and Taiwanese shrimp aquaculture, and production partially recovered only after shifts in species, stocking practices and the adoption of improved biosecurity and diagnostics rather than true elimination of the virus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very intensive pond culture with high stocking densities, deteriorating water quality, and rapid expansion of shrimp farming created ideal conditions for amplification of a newly introduced virus; extensive movement and trading of live post-larvae and broodstock between hatcheries and farms facilitated farm-to-farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a highly virulent nimavirus capable of infecting multiple penaeid species; enhanced transmission via high viral shedding in water and cannibalism among shrimp; inherent capacity of the virus to persist in multiple crustacean hosts enabling establishment once introduced.
Review: Decision: Retain. This row correctly captures the earliest well-documented WSD outbreaks in Fujian (China) and Taiwan in 1992, with some reviews describing the onset as between 1991–1992. Country and subregion coding are consistent with the UNSD list, and classification as first global emergence (without a separate 'first detection' flag) matches the fact that WSSV appears to be a genuinely new pathogen in shrimp rather than a long-undetected agent.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Countries: Japan [1993]; Republic of Korea [1993-1994]; Thailand [1994]; India [1994-1995]; Malaysia [1994-1995]; Indonesia [1996]; Viet Nam [1997]; Philippines [1997]
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (mainly Penaeus monodon, P. japonicus, Fenneropenaeus indicus and related species)
Event summary: Origin: Following the initial emergence in China and Taiwan, WSSV spread in 1993 into shrimp farms in Japan and the Republic of Korea and, over the next few years, into Thailand, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Viet Nam and the Philippines, primarily via movement of infected broodstock and post-larvae across East and South-East Asian shrimp-producing regions. Development: Between about 1993 and 1997, these countries experienced repeated, often nationwide waves of white spot disease with acute pond mortalities of 80–100%, causing collapse or severe contraction of intensive shrimp industries in several nations and reshaping regional aquaculture practices. End: By the late 1990s, WSSV was entrenched across most Asian shrimp-farming zones, and although large epidemics continued, producers adapted through changes in stocking density, species choice (e.g. increasing use of Litopenaeus vannamei), and implementation of basic biosecurity and diagnostic screening, converting WSSV from an epizootic to an endemic constraint.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp aquaculture; extensive transboundary movement of live shrimp broodstock and post-larvae with limited or no pathogen screening; poor farm-level biosecurity and water exchange practices that allowed virus to spread via canal and coastal waters. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and broad host range of WSSV enabling infection of multiple penaeid species and other crustaceans; efficient waterborne and oral transmission (via cannibalism of moribund shrimp) leading to explosive within-pond epidemics; likely selection of genotypes well adapted to intensive Asian pond conditions.
Review: Decision: Retain. The timing, geography and qualitative impact of the 1993–1997 Asian pandemic are consistent with major reviews: WSSV moved rapidly from China/Taiwan into Japan, Korea, Thailand, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Viet Nam and the Philippines and caused industry-crashing losses. Continent and subregion labels are correct, and classification as intra‑continental emergence (spread to new Asian subregions) is appropriate. Note that other affected countries (e.g. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Cambodia) are not listed but this does not change the ranking of this episode among the largest global events.

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (primarily Litopenaeus vannamei and related species in Texas) and imported frozen commodity shrimp
Event summary: Origin: In 1995, WSSV was first detected in the Western Hemisphere when shrimp with gross signs of white spot disease were identified in U.S. retail outlets and an outbreak subsequently occurred on a shrimp farm in Texas, marking establishment with local transmission in North American aquaculture rather than isolated imported cases. Development: The Texas outbreaks and detection of WSSV in imported shrimp products prompted rapid changes in broodstock sourcing (shift to specific-pathogen-free lines), tighter controls on live animal imports, and heightened laboratory surveillance for WSSV in U.S. shrimp farms and processing facilities. End: Through these biosecurity responses, WSSV did not become continuously epidemic in U.S. shrimp farming, and subsequent North American production relied heavily on SPF stocks and improved management, although the virus remained a constant biosecurity threat through imported commodities and wild crustaceans.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in frozen and possibly live shrimp from WSSV-endemic Asian countries to North America, combined with initial gaps in screening and controls for exotic crustacean viruses; high-density pond culture in affected farms that allowed local amplification once the virus entered. Internal mechanisms: Broad environmental stability of WSSV virions in chilled or frozen product; efficient oral transmission when infected shrimp or processing wastes were used as feed or discarded into coastal environments.
Review: Decision: Retain. Multiple primary and review sources agree that WSSV was first diagnosed in the Americas in late 1995 on a Texas shrimp farm, with supporting evidence from imported commodity shrimp. Coding this as an inter‑continental emergence into North America (with in situ farm transmission) is therefore appropriate, and the country/subregion information is correct. No structural corrections were required.

Countries: Panama [1999]; Ecuador [1999]; Honduras [1999-2000]; Guatemala [1999-2000]; Nicaragua [1999-2000]; El Salvador [1999-2000]; Mexico [1999-2000]; Peru [1999-2000]; Colombia [1999-2000]
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (mainly Litopenaeus vannamei and P. stylirostris)
Event summary: Origin: In January 1999, WSSV was first detected causing white spot disease in farmed shrimp in Nicaragua, Honduras and Guatemala; within months it was found in farms in Panama and spread into major shrimp-farming areas of Ecuador, where by April 1999 it triggered an explosive epidemic. Development: Between 1999 and 2001 the virus disseminated rapidly throughout Central and South American shrimp industries (including the other listed countries), causing acute pond die-offs and, for example, an estimated 42% loss of production capacity in Ecuador alone (about 63,000 tonnes and US$280 million in the first year) and massive job losses regionally. End: By the early 2000s, WSSV had become endemic in much of Latin American shrimp aquaculture; Brazil and Venezuela initially remained exceptional by imposing strict bans on live crustacean imports, while affected countries rebuilt production via improved management, domesticated SPF stocks, and selective breeding for disease tolerance rather than eradication of the virus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High-volume transboundary movement of live broodstock and post-larvae of L. vannamei and P. stylirostris from multiple Latin American sources with limited health certification; rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp farms in estuarine systems; weak early-warning and contingency planning for exotic viral diseases. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent WSSV genotypes capable of causing nearly 100% mortality within 3–10 days post-onset; efficient transmission via water and carcasses that allowed entire farm clusters and coastal embayments to be infected during a single production cycle.
Review: Decision: Retain. This episode is widely recognized as one of the largest and most economically devastating WSSV pandemics, affecting most shrimp-farming countries in Central and South America from 1999 onward. The list of countries and timing (1999–2001) matches FAO and review sources; coding as an inter‑continental emergence into the South America continent (as defined in the project’s country list, including Central America) is appropriate. No changes to geography or classification were needed.

Host: Farmed Indian white shrimp (Fenneropenaeus indicus) and other penaeids in semi‑intensive coastal ponds
Event summary: Origin: Around 2001–2002, white spot disease was first confirmed in shrimp farms in Khuzestan Province (Abadan area) in southwestern Iran, representing the first documented WSSV outbreaks in the Middle East region. Development: The 2002 epidemic caused near‑total crop losses (approaching 100% mortality) in affected farms and led to a drastic reduction—by roughly two‑thirds—in Iranian shrimp production and exports, with PCR and histopathology confirming WSSV as the etiologic agent. End: Iranian authorities responded with emergency measures including harvest bans, movement controls, and later adoption of improved biosecurity and seed screening, which reduced but did not eliminate WSSV risk; white spot disease has since remained an ongoing constraint on shrimp farming in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation or regional transfer of infected broodstock or post-larvae from WSSV-endemic Asian sources; rapid expansion of semi‑intensive shrimp farming in coastal lagoons without robust health surveillance or quarantine; environmental stressors such as fluctuating salinity and temperature that increased disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a virulent WSSV genotype into a naïve shrimp population; high within-farm transmission via water and handling, facilitating near-total pond losses once infection was established.
Review: Decision: Review. The event description and impact are well supported, but the subregion has been corrected from 'Western Asia' to 'Southern Asia' to match the UNSD classification that places Iran in Southern Asia. The episode remains coded as an intra‑continental emergence within Asia (first documented WSSV outbreaks in the Middle East region), with other fields unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in coastal pond farms in southern (Santa Catarina/Laguna region) and later other Brazilian states
Event summary: Origin: After remaining free of WSSV during the 1999–2001 Latin American pandemic, Brazil experienced its first confirmed outbreaks in 2005, when farms in Santa Catarina (Laguna region) and subsequently other areas reported acute mortalities of L. vannamei and official notifications to the OIE confirmed WSSV. Development: The incursion led to the near collapse of the shrimp industry in southern Brazil, with production in the affected region reportedly falling from more than 4,000 tonnes in 2004 to well under 500 tonnes by 2006, and follow‑up studies detected WSSV in wild penaeid shrimp and other decapods in nearby estuaries, indicating establishment in local ecosystems. End: Brazil gradually rebuilt shrimp production by emphasizing health-screened or resistant stocks, strict biosecurity and surveillance, but WSSV remained enzootic in some areas and a continuing threat in combination with other viral pathogens such as infectious myonecrosis virus (IMNV).
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of WSSV into a previously WSSV‑free national industry, most likely via infected live shrimp or broodstock and/or contaminated products from other Latin American or Asian sources; high stocking densities and limited initial pathogen screening; co-circulation of IMNV that further stressed stocks and may have exacerbated losses. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and environmental stability of WSSV allowed rapid pond‑to‑pond spread through effluents and carcasses, while establishment in local wild shrimp populations created a persistent reservoir for reinfection of farms.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). Multiple Brazilian case studies and global reviews highlight the 2005 WSSV incursion as causing the collapse of the shrimp farming industry in southern Brazil and as the first confirmed WSSV outbreaks in the country after earlier success in keeping WSSV out. This episode involves very large regional production losses and represents a key step in the spread and establishment of WSSV in the Americas, so it merits inclusion among the top ten global events. It is correctly coded as a re‑occurrence within an already affected South American subregion rather than as a separate inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence.

Host: Farmed Indian white prawn (Fenneropenaeus indicus) and other penaeid shrimp in Egyptian coastal aquaculture
Event summary: Origin: In 2009, the Indian white prawn (Fenneropenaeus indicus) was introduced into Egypt as an alternative culture species, and soon after farmers in deltaic and lagoonal systems began experiencing large-scale mass mortalities; clinical signs, histopathology and PCR detection confirmed white spot disease caused by WSSV, representing the earliest well-documented WSSV outbreaks in Africa. Development: Over the following years (to at least the mid‑2010s), repeated WSSV outbreaks led to chronic production losses in Egyptian shrimp farms, indicating that the virus had become endemic and was recurring seasonally or under stress conditions; genomic characterization of local isolates showed they were closely related to Indian Ocean/Red Sea lineages. End: Although improved diagnostics, management practices and biosecurity were gradually introduced, WSSV remained an important constraint on Egyptian shrimp aquaculture, and Egypt became an established focus of African WSSV infection with potential for onward spread along the Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of WSSV through regional trade in live shrimp or broodstock and waterborne spread from the wider Indian Ocean/Red Sea system; expansion of shrimp farming in deltaic and lagoonal environments with limited initial health management; environmental stressors (temperature and salinity fluctuations, eutrophication) contributing to disease expression and recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of WSSV lineages in a naïve African subregion (Northern Africa), with persistent environmental and wild crustacean reservoirs enabling continued reinfection of farmed shrimp once the virus gained entry.
Review: Decision: Review. Based on the genome-announcement paper and associated Egyptian studies, WSD caused by WSSV has produced major losses in Egyptian shrimp farming since 2009, with strong clinical, histological and PCR evidence and a sequenced local WSSV genome. This makes Egypt 2009 the earliest clearly documented WSSV occurrence in Africa, so the event is now coded as an inter‑continental emergence (Africa as a new continent for WSSV in shrimp). The previous classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence has been removed because there is no evidence for major viral change driving the outbreaks, and Northern Africa is treated as the initial African subregion affected.

Host: Farmed whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and other penaeids in Red Sea coastal farms
Event summary: Origin: After WSSV was introduced to the Middle East, intensive shrimp farms along the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia began experiencing recurring white spot disease outbreaks, with major episodes reported during the winters of 2010–2011, 2011–2012 and 2013–2014. Development: These wintertime epizootics caused high mortalities and substantial production losses, threatening the viability of the national shrimp sector and prompting implementation of farm‑level and national biosecurity programmes focusing on water treatment, stock movement control and improved diagnostics. End: By the mid‑2010s, Saudi farms had reduced outbreak frequency through better biosecurity and management, but WSSV remained present in the region and continued to pose a seasonal re‑occurrence risk linked to cooler water conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Seasonal drops in water temperature during winter that increased host susceptibility and favored WSSV replication; high-density coastal pond systems with shared water sources; initial gaps in on-farm biosecurity and regional coordination of disease control. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of established WSSV lineages in a previously affected subregion, with outbreaks likely driven by virus persistence in wild crustacean reservoirs and pond sediments combined with high virulence and efficient waterborne transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. The timing and impact of repeated winter WSD outbreaks in Saudi Arabia are consistent with national and FAO/WOAH documentation, but there is no evidence that these episodes involved a novel WSSV strain or new host range. They are better interpreted as re‑occurring epidemics of established WSSV lineages in Western Asia triggered by seasonal and management factors. Accordingly, the event is reclassified with 're_occurrence' = Yes and 're_emergence' = No; other fields are retained.

Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (primarily Penaeus monodon and Fenneropenaeus indicus) in semi‑intensive coastal ponds
Event summary: Origin: In late August 2011, the first officially reported African outbreak of white spot disease occurred at a large shrimp farm near Quelimane in Zambezia Province, Mozambique, followed in May 2012 by a confirmed WSSV outbreak in a semi‑intensive shrimp farm in southwestern Madagascar along the Mozambique Channel. Development: These linked outbreaks caused heavy mortalities and severe economic losses, described as nearly crippling the regional shrimp industry, and triggered emergency responses including movement bans, culling of stock, and rapid establishment of surveillance and coastal barrier measures against further spread. End: Despite control efforts, subsequent studies demonstrated WSSV’s continued presence in farms and wild crustaceans in the Mozambique Channel, indicating that the virus had become established in the region’s coastal ecosystems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of WSSV into previously WSSV‑free Eastern African coastal systems, most likely via infected live shrimp or contaminated products from the Indian Ocean/Red Sea region; absence of prior surveillance and contingency plans; concentration of shrimp farms along the Mozambique Channel with shared hydrodynamics that facilitated rapid regional dissemination. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and environmental stability of WSSV, enabling efficient spread through farm effluents and wild crustacean populations; likely common origin of circulating genotypes in Mozambique, Madagascar and parts of the Middle East, as suggested by genotyping work.
Review: Decision: Review. WOAH and subsequent virological studies confirm major WSD outbreaks in Mozambique (2011) and Madagascar (2012) with heavy economic losses and establishment of WSSV in the Mozambique Channel. However, given strong evidence that Egypt had already experienced large WSD outbreaks since 2009, this episode is no longer treated as the first African occurrence. It is reclassified as an intra‑continental emergence into a new African subregion (Eastern Africa), with 'inter_continental_emergence' set to No, and the duplicated 'Eastern Africa; Eastern Africa' subregion entry has been simplified to a single 'Eastern Africa'.

Host: Farmed black tiger prawns (Penaeus monodon), farmed and wild penaeid prawns, and wild crabs in eastern Australia
Event summary: Origin: In November 2016, WSSV was first detected in Australia when black tiger prawns on a farm drawing water from the Logan River in southeast Queensland showed clinical signs of white spot disease, with laboratory confirmation on 1 December 2016 and rapid spread to six neighbouring farms and adjacent waterways. Development: The 2016–17 outbreak led to an estimated A$43 million loss in farm production, emergency destruction of stock, and a national suspension of uncooked prawn imports; despite intensive eradication efforts, WSSV was later found in wild prawns and crabs in Moreton Bay and, in 2022–2023, in biosecure farms and ponds in northern New South Wales, with genomic analyses indicating at least two distinct incursions. End: By 2023, authorities acknowledged that WSSV is likely to remain established in parts of eastern Australia’s wild crustacean populations, and management has shifted from attempted eradication toward long‑term containment, surveillance and strengthening of on‑farm biosecurity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of WSSV via imported uncooked prawns used as bait or food, combined with inadequate import risk controls prior to 2016; high recreational fishing activity and movement of potentially contaminated bait along the Logan River; tidal and estuarine hydrodynamics that facilitated spread from affected farms into wild crustacean populations. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of WSSV in naïve wild prawn and crab communities providing a persistent reservoir; high virulence and rapid transmission in intensive pond systems that amplified the virus during the initial incursion; at least two distinct viral lineages introduced into Australia, suggesting repeated long-distance introductions of WSSV genotypes already circulating elsewhere.
Review: Decision: Retain. The description is consistent with Australian government and independent reviews: WSSV was first detected in farmed prawns on the Logan River in late 2016, caused large production and response costs, and later established in wild crustaceans with further incursions into farms in New South Wales. Coding as an inter‑continental emergence into Oceania is appropriate, and continent/subregion and country assignments are correct. Aggregating the 2016–17 and 2022–23 incursions into a single 'emergence and establishment' episode is reasonable for a top‑level dataset, though users interested in finer temporal resolution could split them into separate events.

Host: Humans; sylvatic cycle involving non-human primates and Haemagogus spp. mosquitoes, with risk of spillover into Aedes aegypti–infested towns
Event summary: In 1995, a large jungle yellow fever epidemic emerged in the western Andean region of Peru after non-immune agricultural workers were recruited into newly expanded coffee-growing zones where virus was enzootically maintained. The epidemic spread through several highland departments, producing roughly 400–500 human cases and a very high case fatality ratio (around one-third of patients), and is described as the largest recorded jungle yellow fever outbreak in the Americas in recent decades. Intensive emergency vaccination campaigns targeting at‑risk Andean communities, coupled with vector control and the end of the rainy season, brought human transmission under control by late 1995, though the event highlighted the risk of urbanization in nearby Aedes aegypti–infested cities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of coffee cultivation into forested Andean foothills, recruitment of non‑immune workers from other regions, poor baseline vaccination coverage, and high vector densities in forest–edge and peridomestic environments created intense human exposure to sylvatic transmission foci. Internal mechanisms: Available phylogenetic work indicates circulation of established South American yellow fever virus lineages; the unusually large scale is best explained by ecological and social drivers rather than documented viral adaptation, so this is classified as re-occurrence with geographic range expansion rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – Added new event for the 1995 western Andean Peru epidemic, which produced ~440–500 cases with high fatality and is described by WHO/PAHO as the largest jungle yellow fever outbreak in the Americas during 1985–2012; this clearly qualifies among the ten most impactful post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence (no evidence of novel strain), with South America/South America subregion and Peru [1995] consistent with the UN country list.

Host: Humans; predominantly urban Aedes aegypti transmission with possible peri‑urban sylvatic links
Event summary: From March to late 2001, an outbreak of yellow fever occurred in Côte d’Ivoire, centred on the densely populated city of Abidjan, with about 128 suspected cases, 20 laboratory-confirmed cases and 14 deaths reported. Concern about explosive spread in this urban centre, considered the first urban yellow fever epidemic in Africa in roughly a decade, led to an urgent international appeal and rapid scale‑up of response activities. A 12‑day mass vaccination campaign that immunized approximately 2.6 million Abidjan residents, together with vector control and surveillance reinforcement, halted further urban transmission and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Low baseline yellow fever vaccination coverage in Abidjan, dense urban Aedes aegypti populations, high human mobility, and delays in recognizing early cases created conditions for an urban outbreak despite long-standing regional endemicity. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel viral lineage or increased virulence; the event reflects re-occurrence of yellow fever in an urban setting driven by immunity gaps and vector ecology rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – Added because WHO and PAHO describe the 2001 Abidjan outbreak as the first urban yellow fever epidemic in Africa in 10 years, triggering vaccination of >2.6 million people; despite modest case counts, its urban setting and massive response make it a high-impact event meriting inclusion among the major post‑1990 outbreaks. Sub-region corrected to Western Africa and country name aligned with the provided UN list.

Host: Humans; likely involvement of sylvatic cycle with non-human primates and Aedes spp. mosquitoes
Event summary: In early 2003, an outbreak of unexplained haemorrhagic fever was reported from the Imatong Mountains of southern Sudan (then part of Sudan), and field investigation confirmed yellow fever virus as the cause. The outbreak occurred in remote, conflict-affected districts with difficult access, and around 178 suspected cases and 27 deaths were documented, with the true burden likely higher because of surveillance gaps. Transmission declined after targeted outbreak response measures, including case management, vector control, and deployment of emergency vaccination in the affected localities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Population displacement and insecurity in southern Sudan, poor access to health services, low vaccination coverage, and favourable ecological conditions for Aedes vectors in forested highland areas enabled the reappearance of yellow fever. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses classified the viruses within an East African genotype that had circulated previously; no evidence of a novel strain or resistance was reported, so the outbreak is best viewed as a re-occurrence exploiting immunity and surveillance gaps.
Review: review – Retain as a well-documented Sudan outbreak with ~178 suspected cases and 27 deaths, but it is smaller than the subsequent 2005 South Kordofan and 2012 Darfur epidemics; if a strict ‘top 10’ is enforced, experts may ultimately drop this in favour of those larger Sudanese events. Sub-region has been corrected from “Eastern Africa” to “Northern Africa” to match the supplied UN classification for Sudan, and an additional peer‑reviewed source was added.

Host: Humans; primarily sylvatic/intermediate cycle in rural and nomadic populations with Aedes spp. mosquitoes
Event summary: Between September and December 2005, a large yellow fever epidemic occurred in South Kordofan State, Sudan, with over 600 suspected cases and around 180 deaths reported from multiple rural localities. The outbreak affected both settled communities and nomadic groups, in an area with limited health infrastructure and very low baseline vaccination coverage, and laboratory investigations also identified concurrent chikungunya virus circulation. A major emergency vaccination campaign supported by national authorities, WHO and partners, together with improved surveillance and the natural decline in vector densities, brought the outbreak under control by early 2006.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High densities of competent vectors in rural and forest-edge environments, extensive movements of largely unvaccinated nomadic populations, weak surveillance and delayed laboratory confirmation, and limited access to clinical care created conditions for wide spread in South Kordofan. Internal mechanisms: Available reports describe circulation of endemic East African yellow fever virus genotypes rather than a new variant; the epidemic is best explained by re-occurrence driven by ecological and social factors, not documented viral change.
Review: retain – Added because Sudan’s 2005 South Kordofan epidemic (≈615 suspected cases and 183 deaths) is highlighted by WHO and EMRO as one of the largest yellow fever outbreaks in the Eastern Mediterranean Region in recent decades and clearly belongs among the top global post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa (Sudan), with no evidence for viral re-emergence in the sense of intrinsic pathogen change.

Countries: Brazil [2008-2009]; Paraguay [2008] (urban and peri-urban focus); Argentina [2008-2009] (sylvatic focus); Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2008]
Host: Humans and non-human primates; Haemagogus/Sabethes forest mosquitoes; risk of urban Aedes aegypti involvement in fringe areas
Event summary: Around 2007–2009, yellow fever virus activity surged in several South American countries, with intense sylvatic transmission in parts of Brazil and Bolivia and smaller human outbreaks in Paraguay and northeastern Argentina, accompanied by widespread non-human primate die‑offs. Human cases occurred both in rural forested zones and, in Paraguay, in and around the metropolitan area of Asunción, raising concerns about urban yellow fever re‑establishment for the first time in decades. Coordinated emergency vaccination campaigns, enhanced surveillance of human and primate cases and focused vector control in high‑risk municipalities curtailed transmission and prevented sustained urban cycles.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deforestation, agricultural expansion and human encroachment into forest habitats increased contact with infected sylvatic mosquitoes and primates; movement of unvaccinated people between forested areas and towns infested with Aedes aegypti created opportunities for peri‑urban and limited urban transmission, particularly in Paraguay. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate circulation of established South American genotypes; the episode is best characterised as re-occurrence with geographic range fluctuations of existing lineages rather than emergence of a distinct new strain.
Review: review – Kept as a multi-country South American episode because Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina experienced increased human cases and extensive epizootics; however, case numbers (on the order of hundreds regionally) are smaller than in the 1995 Peru epidemic, Brazil 2016–2018, Angola/DRC 2015–2016 or Sudan 2012. Event type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence (no evidence for intrinsic viral change), and the country name has been standardised to “Bolivia (Plurinational State of)” to match the provided list.

Host: Humans; intermediate and sylvatic cycles with Aedes spp. mosquitoes and non-human primates
Event summary: From September 2012 to early 2013, a major yellow fever outbreak unfolded across all five Darfur states in western Sudan, initially detected as clusters of haemorrhagic fever with high mortality. By January 2013, health authorities and WHO reported around 847 suspected cases and 171 deaths, making it the largest documented yellow fever outbreak in Africa in more than 20 years at that time and leading to spillover cases into neighbouring Chad. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign covering millions of people, combined with intensified surveillance and vector control, progressively reduced transmission and the outbreak was eventually declared over.

Internal mechanisms: Epidemiologic and laboratory investigations indicate circulation of endemic African yellow fever virus lineages; the scale of the epidemic is attributed to social and environmental factors rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent or transmissible strain.

Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa (Sudan), with no evidence for pathogen-level re-emergence.
