Countries: Angola [2015-2016]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2016]; Kenya (imported) [2016]; China (imported) [2016]; Morocco (imported) [2016]
Host: Humans; predominantly urban Aedes aegypti cycle with contribution from sylvatic reservoirs
Event summary: In December 2015, yellow fever cases were detected in Luanda, Angola, heralding the country’s largest outbreak in 30 years and the biggest African epidemic since at least the early 1990s, which spread to many Angolan provinces and into urban areas of neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo. By late 2016, more than 7,000 suspected cases, 962 confirmed cases and almost 400 deaths had been reported across Angola and DRC, and viraemic travellers exported cases to Kenya, China, Morocco and other countries without seeding sustained local transmission. Massive emergency vaccination campaigns using standard and fractional dosing, combined with intensified vector control and global coordination under the newly launched Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy, eventually interrupted transmission and ended the epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid unplanned urbanization in Luanda and Kinshasa with high densities of Aedes aegypti, low vaccination coverage in many districts, intense intra‑African and international travel of unvaccinated workers, and limited global vaccine stockpiles all contributed to explosive spread and exportation. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked outbreak viruses to lineages previously circulating in Angola, indicating resurgence of existing strains; enhanced transmission resulted from dense human–vector contact and human mobility rather than documented increases in virulence or vaccine escape.
Review: retain – Confirmed as one of the largest and most disruptive modern yellow fever epidemics (≈7,334 suspected cases, 962 confirmed, ~393 deaths), depleting the global vaccine stockpile and directly triggering the EYE strategy; it clearly belongs in the top 10. Sub-regions have been narrowed to Middle Africa, reflecting that sustained transmission occurred in Angola and DRC, while Kenya, China and Morocco are correctly kept in the country list as imported cases without reclassifying the event as inter-continental emergence.

Host: Humans and non-human primates; sylvatic cycle with Haemagogus/Sabethes mosquitoes, with substantial spillover risk to urban Aedes aegypti
Event summary: From late 2016, Brazil experienced a massive sylvatic yellow fever epidemic starting in Minas Gerais and spreading through São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo, Bahia and other states, causing 778 confirmed human cases and 262 deaths in 2016–2017 and 1,376 confirmed cases and 483 deaths in 2017–2018, along with extensive die‑offs of non-human primates. The virus advanced southward and eastward into the Atlantic Forest and coastal belt, reaching areas close to major urban centres that had been considered risk‑free for decades, and numerous unvaccinated international and regional travellers (including from Argentina, Chile and Europe) acquired infection while visiting affected Brazilian states. Large‑scale emergency and preventive vaccination campaigns, adoption of a single‑dose policy and, in some areas, use of fractional doses, together with strengthened epizootic surveillance and vector control, eventually reduced transmission, and seasonal case numbers declined after 2018, though low‑level activity has recurred.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Encroachment into forested areas, ecological conditions favouring sylvatic vectors, low or uneven vaccination coverage in newly affected coastal and southeastern regions, and national and international travel of unvaccinated people into forested recreational and occupational settings all contributed to the magnitude and geographic expansion of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic work indicates that a yellow fever virus lineage from the Amazon region was introduced into southeastern Brazil and spread efficiently through multiple neotropical monkey species but does not demonstrate novel virulence or vaccine escape, so the event is best characterised as a large re-occurrence with major geographic range expansion rather than re-emergence driven by intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – Confirmed by WHO, PAHO, ECDC and CDC as the largest yellow fever epidemic in Brazil for many decades (over 2,100 confirmed human cases and hundreds of deaths) with major geographic expansion toward the Atlantic coast; this clearly fits among the top 10 global events. Event types have been adjusted so that only re-occurrence is marked (no strong evidence for intrinsic viral re-emergence), and the country list has been restricted to Brazil, with infections in travellers from Argentina, Chile and elsewhere treated as travel-related exposures rather than separate transmission foci.

Host: Humans; sylvatic and peri-urban cycles with Aedes spp. mosquitoes and non-human primates
Event summary: Beginning in September 2017, Nigeria detected confirmed yellow fever cases in Kwara State after many years without large reported outbreaks, signalling a resurgence that over 2017–2019 expanded to dozens of states with thousands of suspected cases and multiple confirmed clusters. Despite phased preventive and reactive vaccination campaigns under the EYE strategy, new foci continued to appear in 2019–2020, including high-fatality clusters in Delta and Enugu states and additional confirmed cases across several other states. Progressive scale-up of mass vaccination to tens of millions of people, together with strengthened surveillance and case management, has reduced incidence but transmission remains a recurrent threat in under‑immunized areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historically low yellow fever vaccination coverage, rapid population growth and urbanization, widespread Aedes infestation, health-system constraints and concurrent outbreaks of other diseases (e.g. Lassa fever, cholera, later COVID‑19) created conditions for sustained multi‑year resurgence. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not suggest emergence of a distinct, more virulent or transmissible lineage; the pattern is best interpreted as re-occurrence driven by immunity gaps, demographic change and vector ecology, with enhanced transmission through high human–vector contact and mobility rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – Nigeria’s 2017–2020 resurgence involved widespread, multi-year transmission with thousands of suspected cases across many states and very large vaccination operations, and is consistently cited in burden and EYE‑strategy evaluations as a major modern outbreak; it should remain in the top‑10 set. No changes to geography or event-type classification were needed beyond clarifying that this is re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence.

Host: Humans; non-human primates and mosquitoes in sylvatic and peri-sylvatic cycles
Event summary: Following the 2013 episode, Ethiopia experienced renewed yellow fever activity with an outbreak in August 2018 in Wolayita Zone (SNNPR) that caused 35 reported cases, and a larger outbreak in 2020 in Enor-Ener Woreda, Gurage Zone, with around 85 suspected cases and four deaths. These events occurred in districts identified as high‑risk in sub‑national risk assessments, reflecting expanding zones of sylvatic transmission and very low population immunity in parts of SNNPR and adjacent Oromia. Reactive vaccination campaigns in 2018 and 2020, embedded within Ethiopia’s engagement in the EYE strategy and combined with strengthened surveillance and risk mapping, halted active transmission in the newly affected areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and agriculture into ecologically suitable zones for yellow fever transmission, very low routine vaccination coverage before EYE implementation, and incomplete preventive mass vaccination in high‑risk districts facilitated spread into previously unaffected woredas. Internal mechanisms: Available data point to geographic range expansion and spatial clustering of existing viral lineages within an endemic country, without evidence of a distinct new genotype or resistance phenotype; therefore this is best described as re-occurrence rather than pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review: review – Retained as a combined 2018 and 2020 Ethiopia episode because together they represent a notable expansion of yellow fever risk zones within an endemic country and prompted substantial vaccination activities, but total case numbers remain modest relative to Sudan 2005/2012, Angola 2015–2016, Brazil 2016–2018 and Nigeria 2017–2020. Event-type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since available evidence points to spatial spread of existing lineages rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Sheep (Ovis aries) transported from Inner Mongolia to Hunan Province
Event summary: Origin: In 1994, an acute outbreak of yersiniosis occurred among a consignment of sheep transported from Inner Mongolia to Hunan Province in southern China, shortly after arrival at their destination. Development: Approximately 41% of the transported animals became clinically ill with acute systemic disease, and necropsy of affected sheep revealed multifocal lesions in skin, intestine, liver and lungs from which Yersinia enterocolitica biotype 3, a strain apparently distinct from previously reported ovine isolates in Europe and Oceania, was repeatedly cultured. End: The outbreak was limited to this transported group and resolved after the acute episode; the publication reports no further spread but emphasizes that the infection source remained undetermined and highlighted this event as a severe, unusual manifestation of ovine yersiniosis in China.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7953581/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Long-distance transport of sheep from Inner Mongolia to Hunan, associated crowding and stress, and movement into a different climatic region likely predisposed the flock to infection and severe clinical disease, although the original environmental or feed source of Y. enterocolitica was not identified. Internal mechanisms: All isolates from affected animals were identified as Y. enterocolitica biotype 3 and were described as apparently different from previously characterized ovine and caprine isolates in other countries, consistent with emergence of a distinct biotype with enhanced virulence for sheep in this setting.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7953581/))
Review: review – New high-impact ovine outbreak (China, 1994) added because it shows very high morbidity and mortality in sheep and involves a distinct biotype 3 strain; classified as re-emergence (strain/biotype change in a previously infected host system and subregion rather than first global emergence), with country and sub-region set according to the UNSD list and time span restricted to 1990+ as per protocol.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Domestic South American camelids (alpacas, Vicugna pacos) in a commercial breeding herd
Event summary: Origin: In autumn 2016, a commercial alpaca herd in Saskatchewan, Canada, experienced an abrupt onset of enterocolitis and sudden deaths among adults and crias, with an overall herd mortality of about 18.6%, prompting veterinary investigation. Development: Necropsy and laboratory testing of affected animals demonstrated Yersinia enterocolitica in multiple tissues and feces, and additional clinically affected alpacas were confirmed positive, establishing a herd-level outbreak of yersiniosis in a camelid species where only sporadic single-animal cases had previously been described in North America. End: Targeted antimicrobial treatment (oxytetracycline), supportive care, and farm biosecurity improvements were followed by cessation of new clinical cases, negative follow-up fecal cultures, and resolution of the outbreak, which was later reported as the first documented herd outbreak of yersiniosis in camelids in North America.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6625175/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Investigators noted multiple potential stressors and management-related risk factors, including overcrowding, suboptimal nutrition, and an abrupt drop in ambient temperature preceding the first deaths, which likely compromised immunity and facilitated expression of clinical yersiniosis in a naive alpaca herd. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was confirmed as Y. enterocolitica but no novel biotype, resistance profile or clear intrinsic virulence change was reported; disease expression is therefore best explained by exposure of a susceptible, previously unexposed camelid population to an endemic pathogen under stressful environmental and husbandry conditions, rather than by documented genetic innovation of the bacterium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6625175/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is real and clearly among the most impactful animal yersiniosis outbreaks post‑1990, but the original classification as re-emergence is adjusted to re-occurrence because no novel biotype, host jump at species level, or other pathogen-level change was demonstrated; year field has been normalised to the yyyy-yyyy format and the countries field simplified to 'Canada [2016]' to match the event-sheet specification, and source URLs were pruned to retain the primary case report and one independent summary.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Goats (Capra hircus) in a mixed-age meat goat herd (North West New South Wales)
Event summary: Origin: Between December 2020 and February 2021, a mixed-age herd of approximately 260 goats in the Gunnedah district of North West New South Wales, Australia, developed unexplained ill thrift, rapid weight loss, submandibular and facial oedema, diarrhoea and deaths after owners initially attributed the problem to internal parasites. Development: Fourteen goats were affected and eight died over several weeks; necropsy of a severely affected doe showed ulcerative enterocolitis and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, and culture of ileal contents yielded a profuse growth of Yersinia enterocolitica, while parasitism, coccidiosis, Johne’s disease and enterotoxaemia were excluded. End: Following institution of nutritional supplementation (grain and lucerne hay) and treatment of clinically ill animals with oxytetracycline, clinical signs abated, submandibular oedema resolved and no further deaths occurred, leading investigators to classify this episode as a yersiniosis outbreak likely facilitated by concurrent summer rainfall, temperature fluctuations and unusually high rodent numbers on the farm.([dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0005/1321862/Animal-Health-Surveillance-Issue-2021-1.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): The outbreak coincided with significant summer rainfall followed by a drop in ambient temperature and an exceptional local mouse plague, with rodents recognized as potential Yersinia carriers, as well as possible contribution from preceding parasite burdens and nutritional stress, all of which could have predisposed goats to infection. Internal mechanisms: The report did not identify a novel biotype or resistance phenotype; the episode is interpreted as re-occurrence of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in a susceptible goat herd under environmentally and nutritionally stressful conditions rather than emergence of a new strain.([dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0005/1321862/Animal-Health-Surveillance-Issue-2021-1.pdf))
Review: review – Newly added event capturing a well-documented outbreak of Y. enterocolitica yersiniosis in a 260-head goat herd in New South Wales with 14 clinical cases and 8 deaths; classified as re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion (Oceania) driven by environmental and management stressors, with continent, sub-region, and country fields aligned to the UNSD-based Country sheet and the event year spanning 2020–2021 to reflect the documented December–February timeline.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Viet Nam [1990]; Viet Nam [1992]; Viet Nam [1993]; Myanmar [1992]
Host: Humans; commensal and wild rodents in rural highland foci; fleas (primarily Xenopsylla spp.) as vectors.
Event summary: From 1990 onward, long‑standing plague foci in rural upland areas of Viet Nam and Myanmar experienced a marked resurgence, with Viet Nam reporting around 405 cases in 1990 and Myanmar rapidly escalating to 528 cases and 3 deaths in 1992 after years of lower activity. By 1992–1993, Viet Nam alone recorded approximately 437–481 human cases annually and Myanmar reported hundreds more, with clustered bubonic and some pneumonic cases across multiple villages in Magway, Sagaing and Mekong/central highland regions before intensified control was implemented. Strengthened surveillance, rapid antibiotic treatment, rodent and flea control, and socio‑economic change gradually reduced case numbers through the mid‑1990s, and by the early 2000s human plague in much of South‑eastern Asia had declined to sporadic or no reported cases although natural rodent foci persisted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Protracted conflict and population displacement, expansion of agriculture into upland forest habitats, poor housing and food storage favouring rodent infestation, and limited diagnostic and surveillance capacity in remote districts allowed long‑established Y. pestis foci in Myanmar and Viet Nam to generate large human outbreaks in the early 1990s. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate amplification of pre‑existing enzootic foci rather than emergence of novel genotypes; the key internal processes were efficient flea‑mediated transmission and high rodent densities in traditional rural production systems, rather than host expansion or major virulence change.
Review: review: New event added to capture the large early‑1990s resurgence of plague in South‑eastern Asia (Myanmar and Viet Nam), which reached several hundred cases per year and is clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes globally. Classified as re‑occurrence (not re‑emergence) because the disease was long‑established in these countries and no strong evidence of novel genotypes or host range shifts was found; no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is recorded since transmission remained within known endemic subregions. Countries and years are limited to those with the highest recorded national case counts (Viet Nam 1990, 1992, 1993; Myanmar 1992); this aggregation across two neighbouring countries is based on temporal overlap and similar ecological context rather than proof of a single epidemiologically linked multi‑country chain, so a specialist should confirm whether to keep them as one regional event or split by country.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1991]; United Republic of Tanzania [1994]; United Republic of Tanzania [1995]; United Republic of Tanzania [1996]; United Republic of Tanzania [1997]
Host: Humans; small mammals (especially Mastomys spp. and Rattus rattus) in the Western Usambara (Lushoto) and other foci; fleas (Xenopsylla spp. and others).
Event summary: In north‑eastern Tanzania, particularly the Western Usambara Mountains (Lushoto District), human plague re‑intensified from 1990 onward after earlier control successes, with 364 cases reported in 1990 and a major national peak of about 1,293 cases and 60 deaths in 1991. Through the mid‑1990s, annual epidemics continued in high‑altitude villages, with further large waves in 1994–1997 (approximately 444, 831, 947 and 504 cases respectively), affecting dozens of communities and generating thousands of cases over the decade despite repeated control efforts. Expanded surveillance, community education, rodent and flea control, and better access to antibiotics gradually reduced case numbers and case‑fatality rates after the late 1990s, though the Lushoto focus has remained a persistent natural plague hotspot with recurrent seasonal outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Settlement and cultivation of steep highland slopes, traditional grain storage inside houses, poor housing construction with earth floors, and sleeping on the floor promoted close contact between humans, rodents and fleas in Western Usambara villages; recurrent seasons of favourable temperature and humidity for flea survival, combined with limited access to timely care, allowed explosive plague waves. Internal mechanisms: Studies from Lushoto indicate that persistent transmission in local rodent‑flea systems, rather than introduction of new strains, underlies the repeated outbreaks; enhanced transmission within these established enzootic foci explains the large multi‑year epidemics rather than major genetic change in Y. pestis.
Review: review: New event added because repeated large epidemics in the Western Usambara (Lushoto) focus and other Tanzanian districts in the 1990s (notably ~1,293 cases in 1991 and hundreds of cases per year in 1994–1997) clearly place Tanzania among the most affected countries globally in this period. Classified as re‑occurrence within an established Eastern African focus; there is no evidence for first detection, or for intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or strain‑level re‑emergence. Years and case magnitudes are taken primarily from WHO compilations and Tanzanian retrospective analyses; this multi‑year aggregation is justified by the continuous, closely linked epidemic behaviour in the same focus, but experts may wish to split individual peak years into separate rows if more temporal resolution is desired.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; commensal and wild rodents (sylvatic reservoirs); fleas (vectors).
Event summary: In 1991 Namibia experienced a major bubonic plague epidemic in the north, notably in Ohangwena and neighbouring districts, with around 1,092 suspected human cases and 45 deaths following smaller outbreaks in 1989–1990. The outbreak spread across multiple rural communities as rodent die‑offs and high flea burdens around homes and grain stores facilitated rodent‑to‑human transmission until a national plague control programme with improved case detection, antibiotic treatment, and rodent and flea control was implemented. Over the following two to three years, reported human cases and deaths declined steeply and transmission was brought under control in the main epidemic focus, although natural Y. pestis foci persisted in local rodent populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High rodent densities around granaries and within poorly constructed houses, inadequate sanitation, cross‑border population movements, and limited prior surveillance in rural northern districts allowed rapid amplification of plague and delayed detection of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for a novel Y. pestis strain; the epidemic reflects intense amplification and geographic spread of existing plague foci in local rodent reservoirs, with enhanced flea‑mediated transmission under favourable environmental and socio‑economic conditions.
Review: retain: Event is real, well documented and one of the largest single‑year national plague epidemics since 1990 (about 1,092 cases and 45 deaths), clearly within the global top‑10 by impact. Sub‑region (Southern Africa), country assignment and classification as re‑occurrence in an existing focus are all consistent with WHO data and the Namibia control programme evaluation; no structural changes were made to this row.

Host: Humans; commensal rats and domestic guinea pigs (reservoir/bridge hosts); fleas.
Event summary: After decades with little reported activity, bubonic plague re‑emerged in northern Peru in 1992, with about 120 human cases in rural districts, and then expanded dramatically in 1993 when roughly 611 cases and 31 deaths were notified across 122 localities in Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad. Transmission continued in 1994 with an additional ~420 cases and 19 deaths, affecting both coastal and Andean communities where rodents and guinea pigs were kept inside homes and rat die‑offs preceded human illness. Intensified surveillance, insecticide campaigns, rodent control, improved clinical management, and long‑term control programmes in these departments led to a marked decline in annual case numbers after the mid‑1990s, although low‑level transmission and sporadic outbreaks have persisted in traditional plague foci.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rural poverty, crowding, storage of grain and other foodstuffs inside dwellings, and the widespread practice of rearing and slaughtering guinea pigs and other small mammals indoors created ideal conditions for rodent and flea proliferation and human exposure; lapses in sustained vector‑control and environmental management after earlier eradication efforts allowed the pathogen to re‑establish in domestic settings. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates reactivation of long‑standing natural plague foci in Andean and coastal Peru, with no clear signal of novel genotypes or host shifts; the resurgence is best explained by intensified transmission in pre‑existing rodent–flea cycles rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review: New event added because the early‑1990s Peruvian outbreaks (120 cases in 1992; ~611 in 1993; ~420 in 1994) represent the principal modern re‑emergence of plague in South America and clearly rank among the highest‑impact post‑1990 episodes by case and death counts. Classified as re‑occurrence in an established South American plague focus; there is no evidence of first detection, inter‑continental spread, or strain‑level re‑emergence. The time window and affected departments follow WHO/PAHO summaries; more detailed national data could be used in a future iteration to distinguish separate sub‑epidemics within this 1992–1994 episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans; commensal rats (Rattus spp.) as primary reservoirs; fleas (Xenopsylla spp.) as vectors.
Event summary: In late August 1994 India reported outbreaks of bubonic and pneumonic plague in several states after roughly 30 years without confirmed human cases, with WHO compiling about 876 cases and 54 deaths nationwide and other reports noting 693 serologically positive suspected cases and 56 deaths. The epidemic began in Beed district (Maharashtra) with bubonic disease and then spread to urban centres such as Surat (Gujarat), where overcrowding, poor sanitation, rat infestations and panic‑driven mass migration complicated control efforts and raised intense international concern about possible global spread. Rapid institution of antibiotic treatment, vector control, travel advisories, and strengthened surveillance halted transmission by mid‑October 1994; subsequent molecular work showed that the outbreak strains represented a distinct ribotype (designated S) of Y. pestis, underlining the episode as a modern urban re‑emergence of plague in India.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Deteriorating urban infrastructure, accumulation of garbage, proliferation of commensal rats in slums and unplanned housing, and severe crowding all facilitated rodent–flea–human transmission; mass movement of people out of affected cities in response to rumours and fear further disrupted control efforts and contributed to the economic and social impact. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing demonstrated that Y. pestis isolates from the 1994 outbreak belonged to a new ribotype (S), distinct from the historic Indian ribotype B, and that the same lineage was present in local rodents, fleas and patients, indicating clonal expansion of a distinct strain; this supports classification as re‑emergence driven in part by strain‑level genetic change, rather than a simple resurgence of an unchanged endemic lineage.
Review: review: Event is real and widely recognised as a major modern plague re‑emergence, with case and death estimates matching WHO and CDC summaries; it clearly belongs in the global top‑10 by impact because of both its size and its international public‑health consequences. The classification has been adjusted so that the event is coded as re‑emergence (true) but not re‑occurrence, in line with the instruction that categories are generally mutually exclusive and with evidence that the outbreak involved a distinct ribotype (S) of Y. pestis; external social and environmental drivers are still described in the mechanism field rather than encoded via a separate “re‑occurrence” flag. Source URLs have been expanded to include primary molecular and epidemiologic investigations of the 1994 Indian strains; a domain expert should review this balance between strain‑level novelty and long‑standing enzootic presence in India but the event’s inclusion is strongly supported.

Host: Humans; endemic rodent reservoirs (e.g. Rattus rattus and Malagasy rodents); fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis and others).
Event summary: From the mid‑1990s Madagascar experienced a dramatic resurgence of plague, with annual suspected case counts rising to about 1,147 in 1995, 1,629 in 1996 and peaking at roughly 2,863 cases and 176 deaths in 1997, mainly in the central highlands. These multi‑year epidemics manifested as recurrent seasonal waves of mainly bubonic plague in rural highland districts, occasionally extending towards larger towns, and were preceded by rodent die‑offs and high flea indices around houses and grain stores. With support from the Institut Pasteur de Madagascar and international partners, surveillance and laboratory confirmation improved, antibiotic treatment and community education were scaled up, and vector and reservoir control campaigns were re‑established, stabilising incidence by the early 2000s though Madagascar has continued to report hundreds of cases annually.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Socio‑economic decline, reduced investment in plague surveillance and vector control, encroachment of agriculture and housing into rodent habitats, and climatic conditions favouring flea survival collectively enabled explosive spread from long‑standing enzootic foci into human populations in the highlands. Internal mechanisms: Available genotyping suggests that these epidemics largely involved existing Y. pestis lineages circulating in Madagascar; the main internal process was enhanced transmission efficiency and geographic expansion of established rodent–flea cycles rather than emergence of novel strains or host shifts.
Review: retain: This multi‑year episode represents the single largest concentration of human plague globally in the 1990s, with annual case counts in Madagascar far exceeding those of other countries; it is unquestionably within the top‑10 events by impact. The event is correctly coded as re‑occurrence in an endemic focus rather than first detection or re‑emergence, and the time span and sub‑region (Eastern Africa) align with WHO and Institut Pasteur de Madagascar analyses. No structural changes were made beyond confirming figures against WHO compilations.

Host: Humans; peridomestic and wild rodents; fleas.
Event summary: During the 1996–1997 transmission season, the southern African plague belt experienced a pronounced regional upsurge, including a large bubonic outbreak in Namwala District, Southern Province, Zambia, where roughly 267 human cases and 26 deaths occurred between December 1996 and February 1997, and major epidemics in neighbouring Malawi and Mozambique. Malawi reported an outbreak totalling about 582 cases and 11 deaths in 1997 across Nsanje, Chikwawa and Ntchisi districts, while Mozambique notified approximately 825 cases and 18 deaths the same year, with most cases clustered in Mutarara and other districts after years of lower activity. These concurrent epidemics in adjacent countries prompted WHO‑supported responses with intensified case‑finding, antibiotic treatment, rodent and flea control, and community risk communication, after which reported case numbers declined markedly in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High rodent densities associated with seasonal agricultural production, poor rodent‑proofing of grain stores and dwellings, and favourable climate for flea survival drove epizootics in the border regions of Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique, while limited access to health care and weak early surveillance allowed human outbreaks to grow large before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Investigations in Namwala and affected districts documented infection in multiple rodent and flea species but did not identify major new genotypes; the events are best interpreted as amplification and geographic spread of long‑standing plague foci under conducive environmental and socio‑economic conditions rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review: This row has been revised to (i) restrict the sub‑region to Eastern Africa, consistent with the UNSD classification of Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia; (ii) extend the event year to 1996–1997 to cover the Zambian Namwala outbreak that began in December 1996; and (iii) add Malawi, which experienced 582 cases and 11 deaths in 1997 and forms part of the same regional upsurge in the southern African plague belt. The event is still coded as re‑occurrence rather than intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re‑emergence because all three countries had prior plague foci and there is no evidence of a novel lineage; however, grouping three national epidemics into a single regional episode is an analytical choice based on temporal and geographic contiguity rather than documented cross‑border transmission chains, and should be reviewed by a regional specialist.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans; rodents (reservoirs); fleas (vectors).
Event summary: In 2001 Zambia reported another major plague outbreak, this time centred on Eastern Province, with WHO global summaries indicating about 850 human cases but only three deaths, reflecting improved case management compared with earlier epidemics. The event followed reports of rodent die‑offs and a rapid rise in suspected bubonic cases in Nyanje area, Petauke District, before plague was recognised and response teams were mobilised, initially documenting several hundred suspected cases and a handful of deaths in early situation reports. As laboratory confirmation capacity, antibiotic treatment, and targeted indoor residual spraying and environmental management were scaled up across affected communities, transmission declined and reported cases from this area fell to zero in subsequent years, although plague has since reappeared sporadically elsewhere in Eastern Province.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Environmental conditions and agricultural practices that promoted rodent population surges around households and fields, combined with poor housing, limited rodent‑proof storage, and weak early surveillance in remote rural communities, allowed extensive epizootics and delayed recognition of human cases; once identified, improved clinical and vector‑control responses helped to keep mortality unusually low for a large African outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points to renewed amplification of existing plague foci rather than a distinct genotype or new host range; efficient flea‑mediated transmission in known rodent reservoirs, rather than pathogen evolution, underpinned the large but low‑fatality outbreak.
Review: review: Event is real and of major scale (~850 cases) and therefore belongs among the largest post‑1990 outbreaks, but the original version relied mainly on an early WHO Disease Outbreak News report (436 suspected cases and 11 deaths) without explicitly linking to the later WER global summary that revised the total to 850 cases and 3 deaths. The classification as re‑occurrence in Eastern Africa remains appropriate, and no intra‑/inter‑continental spread or strain‑level re‑emergence is supported by current evidence. Source URLs now include the WER article “Human plague in 2000 and 2001” alongside the outbreak notices and Zambian field investigations; figures in the summary text have been clarified to reflect this synthesis.

Host: Humans; wild rodents and other small mammals; fleas.
Event summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has long been one of the world’s main plague foci, and in 2003 reported a particularly high burden with about 1,092 human cases and 68 deaths, mainly from rural highland zones of Ituri and adjacent areas in the northeast. This peak capped more than a decade of sustained transmission with recurrent outbreaks in conflict‑affected, impoverished communities where rodent control and access to health care were extremely limited. Intensified international support, targeted surveillance in natural foci, and expanded access to antibiotics and vector control gradually reduced—but did not eliminate—plague incidence in subsequent years, and DRC remained one of the leading contributors to global plague case counts through at least 2014.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged armed conflict, population displacement into rodent‑rich environments, food insecurity, poor housing, and severely weakened health services combined to increase human exposure to sylvatic rodent reservoirs and to delay recognition and treatment of plague cases; isolation of highland communities further hampered control. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate long‑established plague foci in north‑eastern DRC with sustained rodent–flea transmission rather than recently introduced or genetically novel strains; high transmission intensity and human vulnerability within these endemic systems explain the large multi‑year burden.
Review: retain: This row correctly captures one of the single largest country‑year plague burdens in the modern era (2003 DRC) and stands in for a broader high‑incidence period in north‑eastern DRC from the late 1990s through the early 2010s; it is clearly within the global top‑10 by impact. The sub‑region (Middle Africa), event type (re‑occurrence in a long‑known focus), and lack of intra‑/inter‑continental emergence are consistent with WHO and recent ecological analyses; no structural corrections to the row were required, though an additional reference on 2004–2014 DRC plague ecology has been added at the top‑level source list.

Host: Humans; rodents (reservoirs); fleas (vectors).
Event summary: Beginning in August 2017 Madagascar experienced an unprecedented nationwide plague epidemic, with WHO and partners reporting roughly 2,119–2,417 suspected, probable and confirmed cases and 171–209 deaths by late November, about two‑thirds of which were pneumonic and many arising in urban centres including Antananarivo and Toamasina. The outbreak appears to have started from bubonic cases in the central highlands but rapidly evolved into urban pneumonic transmission with widespread person‑to‑person spread, extensive contact tracing, and international concern, and lower‑level transmission continued into early 2018 before returning to the country’s usual seasonal pattern of mainly rural bubonic plague. A massive national and international response—encompassing prophylactic antibiotics for thousands of contacts, infection‑prevention‑and‑control measures in health facilities, enhanced laboratory support, aggressive vector and reservoir control and sustained risk communication—ultimately interrupted urban pneumonic chains and curtailed the epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Endemic plague foci in Madagascar’s central highlands, seasonal increases in rodent and flea populations, heavy human mobility between rural highland communities and major coastal and capital cities, overcrowded urban housing, and weak infection‑prevention‑and‑control in health facilities collectively enabled rapid seeding and amplification of urban pneumonic transmission. Internal mechanisms: No entirely new genotype was demonstrated, but the outbreak highlighted how existing Y. pestis lineages can cause large‑scale human‑to‑human transmission when social and infrastructural conditions allow, effectively expanding the pathogen’s realized geographic and contact range without fundamental evolutionary change.
Review: retain: The 2017–2018 Madagascar epidemic is the largest urban pneumonic plague outbreak recorded in recent decades and is unquestionably among the most consequential post‑1990 emergence events globally by both case count and international concern. Its classification as re‑occurrence in an endemic focus (rather than re‑emergence or inter‑continental spread) is consistent with WHO and ECDC assessments, given the lack of evidence for a novel strain or sustained transmission outside Madagascar. No structural corrections to this row were needed beyond confirming case and death ranges against multiple situation reports.

Host: Farmed cervids (red deer, chital deer, elk, fallow deer and red deer–elk hybrids)
Event summary: From January 1990 to December 1993, multiple outbreaks of acute diarrhea, sudden death, and wasting occurred in farmed deer herds on at least eight farms in Ontario, Canada, predominantly affecting recently weaned 4–6‑month‑old calves in autumn. Veterinary diagnostic laboratories confirmed Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (mainly serotype III) as the primary pathogen in 25 necropsied deer from several cervid species, with severe enteritis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, and high on‑farm mortality often following cold, wet snaps after milder weather. After recognition of yersiniosis as an emerging health problem in the expanding farmed cervid industry and implementation of management changes (stress reduction around weaning, improved nutrition, and prompt antimicrobial therapy), affected herds recovered and subsequent control programs focused on husbandry and vaccination.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063879500700112))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of a new farmed deer industry in Ontario with increasing herd size; management‑related stressors including recent weaning, high stocking density, transport, and adverse autumn weather (sudden cold snaps, often with rain) repeatedly precipitated disease; likely environmental build‑up and recirculation of Y. pseudotuberculosis on affected farms over several seasons. Internal mechanisms: All characterized isolates in this series were Y. pseudotuberculosis serotype III, a lineage already associated with enteric disease in ungulates; there is no evidence for a novel genotype, and the pattern is most consistent with stress‑triggered expression of disease from an established environmental and host reservoir rather than de novo evolution.
Review: review – Event is real and well documented in farmed cervids in Ontario, but the original classification as a first_detection event was incorrect because Y. pseudotuberculosis had been reported in deer and other livestock in North America and elsewhere before 1990 (e.g., fallow deer in Michigan, farmed deer in Australia and New Zealand).([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063879500700112)) The emergence type has been changed to re_occurrence (stress‑ and weather‑driven resurgence in a previously affected subregion), and the Countries field has been simplified to a single entry (Canada [1990]) consistent with the event‑year convention. Duplicate URLs in the source list were removed. Recommend expert review but retain this as a major multi‑farm cervid outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Captive ruminants in a wildlife park (multiple ungulate species)
Event summary: In 1992, a wildlife park served by the Oklahoma Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory in the United States experienced an epizootic of acute, often fatal disease in several captive ruminants, which prompted necropsy and laboratory investigation. Microbiologic culture and histopathology confirmed Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection in the affected ruminants, and an epornitic of Y. pseudotuberculosis infection was identified in the vicinity during the same period, indicating wider circulation of the pathogen in the local environment. The report emphasized the zoonotic risk to people in contact with infected animals and recommended strict hygiene precautions; the episode is presented as a discrete outbreak limited to that period.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1644638/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species captive ruminant collections at a wildlife park with shared feed and water sources and likely exposure to fecal contamination from wild rodents and birds would have facilitated fecal–oral transmission; the concurrent epornitic in the surrounding area suggests environmental contamination or a common‑source exposure outside the enclosures. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or host jump was described; the episode is consistent with stress‑precipitated yersiniosis caused by established pathogenic Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages in susceptible captive ruminants rather than de novo evolution, and is therefore interpreted here as a major re‑occurring outbreak in a previously affected host group.
Review: review – New event added to capture the widely cited 1992 epizootic of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis in captive ruminants in a wildlife park, which likely represents one of the more impactful post‑1990 outbreaks in ungulates. Location has been coded as United States of America based on the Oklahoma Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory affiliation in the original report; the exact state and species composition are not specified in the abstract and should be verified from the full article. Emergence type is coded as re_occurrence (no evidence of a new strain or continent/subregion jump). Recommend expert review and retention as a major ruminant outbreak if full‑text details confirm this interpretation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) in a closed zoo colony
Event summary: In June and July 2003, a closed colony of approximately 115 Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) at the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, experienced an outbreak of yersiniosis in which seven bats died over a six‑week period. Post‑mortem examination and bacteriology showed that about 70% of the colony had mesenteric lymphadenopathy, hepatic abscessation, and/or splenomegaly consistent with Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection, and culture confirmed Y. pseudotuberculosis in many clinically affected and subclinically infected bats. Following recognition of the extent of infection, the colony was depopulated and the outbreak was highlighted as an important example of Y. pseudotuberculosis epizootics in captive bats and the need for rigorous hygiene, pest control, and surveillance because of the organism’s zoonotic potential.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19368235/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density housing and long‑term confinement in an indoor bat colony, with chronic accumulation of fecal contamination and probable exposure to rodent or insect vectors, created conditions favorable for amplification and rapid within‑colony spread of Y. pseudotuberculosis; concomitant stressors in the captive environment (social hierarchy, handling, diet or microclimate) may have further reduced resistance. Internal mechanisms: Although no entirely novel genotype was reported, the outbreak strain produced widespread systemic disease with high lesion prevalence in a bat species not traditionally regarded as a primary host, illustrating the capacity of established Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages to exploit new ecological niches in stressed captive wildlife rather than representing a de novo evolutionary event.
Review: review – New event representing the well‑documented 2003 Yersinia pseudotuberculosis outbreak in a closed colony of Egyptian fruit bats at the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York. Year, magnitude (7 deaths over 6 weeks in a colony of ~115 bats), and lesion patterns are taken from Childs‑Sanford et al. (2009) and related summaries.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19368235/)) Classified as a high‑impact re_occurrence event in a captive wildlife host; recommend retention, with a human reviewer confirming species numbers and any additional management details from the full article.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Mixed zoo mammals and primates: addax (Addax nasomaculatus), agouti (Dasyprocta spp.), giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), Arabian oryx (Oryx leucoryx), marmosets (Callithrix spp.), macaques (Macaca spp.)
Event summary: Between February and April 2012, the National Zoo at the Ramat Gan Safari in central Israel experienced a multi‑species outbreak of acute enteric and systemic disease that caused the deaths of 15 animals including addax, Arabian oryx, agouti, a giant anteater, and several New World and Old World primates. Necropsy and laboratory investigations consistently isolated Yersinia pseudotuberculosis biovar 1, serotype O:1b, from intestines, mesenteric lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and other organs, with severe fibrino‑hemorrhagic enterocolitis and necrotizing lymphadenitis, and no other primary pathogen identified. Following diagnosis, the zoo implemented biosecurity measures and supportive treatment; the outbreak was temporally associated with an unusually cold, wet winter, and no further yersiniosis cases were reported from the facility in subsequent years.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394106985_Outbreak_of_Yersinia_Pseudotuberculosis_in_a_Zoo_in_Israel))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Multi‑species husbandry in an open safari‑style ruminant yard with shared or adjacent enclosures created opportunities for fecal contamination of soil, feed, and water; the winter of 2012 in Israel was particularly cold and rainy, conditions known to favor Y. pseudotuberculosis persistence and trigger stress‑associated outbreaks. A nearby dump site attracting migratory birds was suggested as a possible source of introduction, and cross‑contamination from ruminant carcasses stored in a shared refrigerator likely spread infection to carnivores and primates.([ijvm.org.il](https://www.ijvm.org.il/sites/default/files/blum_sept_2023_internet.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain belonged to pathogenic biovar 1, serotype O:1b, and carried virulence genes inv and yadA, but did not represent a newly described genotype; disease reflects amplification of an existing zoonotic lineage in a stressed, susceptible zoo population rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: review – Event is strongly supported by Blum et al. (2023), which documents a 2012 multi‑species outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis at the Ramat Gan Safari.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394106985_Outbreak_of_Yersinia_Pseudotuberculosis_in_a_Zoo_in_Israel)) Emergence type as re_occurrence in Western Asia is appropriate, as Y. pseudotuberculosis had previously been reported from Israeli cattle and primates; there is no evidence that this was a first_detection or continent‑level emergence. The Review field now notes the unusually cold, wet winter and likely role of carcass handling and a nearby dump as drivers, and adds the official journal PDF URL alongside the ResearchGate copy. Recommend retention with minor human verification of the country/subregion coding and species list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Eurasian collared doves (Streptopelia decaocto) in a private aviary
Event summary: In February 2015, a private aviary in California, United States, experienced sudden, high mortality in a small flock of adult Eurasian collared doves, with four of nine birds dying over a short period. Two carcasses submitted to the California Animal Health and Food Safety (CAHFS) Laboratory showed numerous pale yellow foci in liver and spleen, and histology confirmed acute, fatal septicemia with multifocal necrotizing hepatitis and splenitis caused by Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, which was isolated from multiple organs. After diagnosis, the outbreak was managed at the aviary level through removal of dead birds and husbandry changes, and no broader spread beyond this small collection was reported in the case series.([meridian.allenpress.com](https://meridian.allenpress.com/avian-diseases/article/60/1/82/209905/Yersinia-pseudotuberculosis-in-Eurasian-Collared))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑density captive housing of doves with shared food and water sources, potential contamination of feed or water by feces from reservoir species (wild birds or rodents), and possible recent introduction of an infected bird into a naïve flock likely contributed to rapid within‑aviary transmission. Internal mechanisms: The cases illustrate the ability of established Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages to cause acute septicemia and high mortality in naïve columbids; there is no evidence for a novel genotype or host species jump, so the episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurring outbreak from environmental or reservoir sources in a susceptible host group.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the 2015 private aviary outbreak in Eurasian collared doves in California described by Stoute et al. (2016), including flock size, mortality (4/9), pathology consistent with acute septicemia, and interpretation as a localized outbreak without wider spread.([meridian.allenpress.com](https://meridian.allenpress.com/avian-diseases/article/60/1/82/209905/Yersinia-pseudotuberculosis-in-Eurasian-Collared)) Emergence type as re_occurrence (not first_detection or inter‑continental) is appropriate because avian yersiniosis due to Y. pseudotuberculosis had been reported globally for decades. No corrections beyond minor wording have been made, and the event appears to be a valid, if relatively small, outbreak within the top‑10 set.

Host: Captive rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) in a breeding or research colony
Event summary: In 2016, a captive colony of 18 rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) in China experienced an outbreak of systemic disease in which six animals died, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis serotype O:1a was identified as the causative agent. Standard bacteriologic, molecular, and serotyping methods confirmed the infection, and experimental infection of mice demonstrated the high pathogenicity of the outbreak strain, which carried multiple virulence genes and antimicrobial resistance determinants. This episode was notable as the first report of serotype O:1a infection in non‑human primates, and the authors concluded that this lineage represents a pathogen of concern for primate conservation and colony health.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Close confinement of rhesus monkeys in a captive breeding or research facility with shared housing, feed, and water likely facilitated rapid transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced, and stress associated with captivity, social hierarchy, and experimental or husbandry procedures may have predisposed some animals to severe disease. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain belonged to serotype O:1a, which had not previously been reported from non‑human primates, and demonstrated high virulence and antimicrobial resistance in experimental models, fulfilling the criteria for re_emergence driven by a new strain with altered pathogenic potential in an existing host system.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/))
Review: review – New event added to represent the EcoHealth‑reported 2016 outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis serotype O:1a in captive rhesus monkeys in China, with 6 deaths among 18 animals and experimental confirmation of high virulence.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/)) This is the first description of serotype O:1a in non‑human primates and therefore coded as re_emergence (novel strain in an existing host group) rather than simple re_occurrence. Country and subregion coding (China, Eastern Asia) are straightforward, but facility type (breeding vs research colony) is left generic because the abstract does not specify details; recommend human review of the full text to refine the host/facility description if needed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Capybaras (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) kept in captivity at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center
Event summary: In January 2020, the capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) group at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center in southern Spain experienced an outbreak of acute mortality in which five of seven animals (71% morbidity, 100% case fatality among affected) died within three days. Necropsy and histopathology revealed multifocal fibrinopurulent bronchopneumonia and generalized vascular lesions, and cultures from lung and other organs yielded Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, which was confirmed by PCR and MALDI‑TOF; two remaining adult males were treated prophylactically with marbofloxacin and survived. The authors described this as the first fatal outbreak of Y. pseudotuberculosis infection in zoo animals in Spain and stressed the potential implications for animal health, conservation of susceptible species, and public health.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Group housing of capybaras in an outdoor zoo enclosure with shared feed and water sources likely allowed fecal–oral transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced, and environmental or climatic conditions in winter may have favored bacterial persistence and stress‑associated susceptibility. Potential sources include contamination of water or feed by wild rodents or birds, although the exact source was not identified. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak demonstrates high susceptibility of capybaras to systemic Y. pseudotuberculosis infection, with rapid progression and high fatality, and represents the first reported fatal Y. pseudotuberculosis outbreak in this host species and in Spanish zoo animals; this is therefore coded as re_emergence driven by host expansion to a new, highly susceptible rodent species in a captive conservation setting.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686))
Review: review – New event added for the 2020 outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis in captive capybaras at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center in Spain, with 5 of 7 animals dying and confirmation by culture and molecular methods.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686)) This is explicitly described as the first fatal Y. pseudotuberculosis outbreak in zoo animals in Spain and the first in capybaras, justifying classification as re_emergence via host expansion rather than simple re_occurrence. Continent, subregion, and country coding (Europe, Southern Europe, Spain) follow the UNSD scheme. Recommend human review to confirm that this event is among the top‑impact zoo outbreaks selected for the top‑10 list, but available data strongly support retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Captive adult African lions (Panthera leo) in a zoological park in central North Carolina
Event summary: A zoological park in central North Carolina, United States, reported a cluster of systemic Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infections in adult African lions in which two 17‑year‑old male siblings and one 14‑year‑old female developed lethargy, anorexia, ataxia, and respiratory signs over several days; two of the three lions died despite treatment and were submitted for necropsy. Gross and histologic examination revealed multifocal necrosuppurative lesions in liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and mesenteric lymph nodes with abundant intralesional gram‑negative coccobacilli, and bacterial culture from liver, spleen, and lung yielded heavy growth of Y. pseudotuberculosis; in one lion the bacteria showed aberrant filamentous morphology, likely related to prior beta‑lactam antibiotic exposure. This was reported as the first description of disseminated Y. pseudotuberculosis infection in adult African lions, and an epidemiologic investigation into rodent, diet, and environmental sources did not identify a clear point source, although the outbreak was limited to this small group.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10406387211072822))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Semi–free‑range exhibit design with potential exposure of lions to wild rodents and birds, environmental contamination of soil and water, and feeding practices (including carcass feeding) likely provided multiple opportunities for oral exposure; advanced age and possible chronic health conditions in the affected lions may have increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: Histology and culture findings are consistent with disseminated infection by a typical pathogenic Y. pseudotuberculosis lineage; although unusual filamentous bacterial morphology was observed in one lion, this was plausibly attributed to prior cefovecin treatment rather than a fundamentally new genotype. The event is therefore interpreted as a notable but localized re_occurrence of yersiniosis in felids rather than re_emergence driven by a new strain or host jump.
Review: review – Event accurately reflects the African lion outbreak described by Womble et al. (2022), but the original dataset misclassified it as re_emergence; given the lack of evidence for a novel strain or host species jump (adult lions are the same species as previously affected cubs and other felids), the emergence type has been changed to re_occurrence.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10406387211072822)) The event year in the original work likely precedes the 2022 publication date, but the precise outbreak year is not given in the accessible text; the Countries field now notes that 2022 is the report year and that the event probably occurred in ~2020–2021, and this approximation should be checked against the full article and any associated epidemiologic study. Recommend expert review for timing but retain this as a major felid outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Captive parrots and passerine birds (e.g., eastern rosella Platycercus eximius, red‑rumped parrot Psephotus haematonotus) and other zoo birds in German collections
Event summary: Around 2023, German zoos including the Zoological‑Botanical Garden Wilhelma in Stuttgart documented sudden deaths of psittacine birds such as an eastern rosella and a red‑rumped parrot, which died within a few days of onset with minimal premonitory signs. Post‑mortem examinations revealed granulomatous or necrotizing hepatitis, pneumonia, and enteritis, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis was isolated from liver and other organs, fitting a pattern of high‑mortality avian yersiniosis previously reported in these collections; additional cases in other species were identified in retrospective and prospective surveillance between 2011 and 2024. The episode led to targeted fecal screening and environmental sampling in affected zoos, and during a one‑year monitoring period after the index cases, no further positive environmental samples were detected, indicating successful containment of that particular episode despite sporadic cases continuing over longer time scales.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11946000/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Outdoor mixed‑species aviary and zoo bird housing in temperate Central Europe exposes captive birds to wild birds and rodents that act as reservoirs, with seasonal factors (late autumn and winter) enhancing environmental survival of Y. pseudotuberculosis and physiological stress in birds; high stocking density and shared food and water sources facilitate fecal–oral transmission once introduced. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved established pathogenic Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages capable of causing septicemia in psittacines and other birds; no novel serotype or genotype was highlighted, so the episode most likely represents re_occurrence of a known zoo‑associated pathogen within susceptible aviary populations.
Review: retain – Event is consistent with the multi‑year dataset on Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infections in German zoo animals compiled by Hertwig et al., including sudden deaths in psittacine birds at Wilhelma and other facilities around 2023 and subsequent negative environmental surveillance.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11946000/)) Emergence type as re_occurrence (no new continent, subregion, or host species) appears appropriate, and continent/subregion/country coding matches the UNSD classification. No substantive corrections were required beyond aligning wording with the published study; retaining this event as one of the major recent avian outbreaks is justified.

Host: Zoo aviary birds in central California: hooded pitta (Pitta sordida), beautiful fruit dove (Ptilinopus pulchellus), golden‑crested myna (Ampeliceps coronatus)
Event summary: During winter and early spring 2025, a mixed‑species indoor aviary at a zoo in central California recorded the deaths of three exotic birds—a hooded pitta, a beautiful fruit dove, and a golden‑crested myna—over roughly three months, two of which showed only brief signs of respiratory distress, fluffed feathers, and lethargy before death. Necropsy and histopathology revealed necrotizing heterophilic and histiocytic hepatitis, splenitis, pneumonia, nephritis, myocarditis, and enteritis, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis was consistently isolated and identified as the primary pathogen, whereas other organisms such as Streptococcus gallolyticus were considered opportunistic. Following confirmation, the zoo instituted an 11‑month quarantine of the aviary (20 March 2025 to 20 February 2026) and conducted an extensive field investigation of potential environmental sources; no new cases of yersiniosis were detected for over a year after the outbreak ended, and the episode was considered contained.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13096001/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Enclosed mixed‑species aviary with shared food and water sources and likely exposure to reservoir hosts such as wild birds and rodents created ideal conditions for fecal–oral transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced; seasonal conditions during the cold, wet season may have favored bacterial persistence. A hooded pitta was suspected as a potential carrier bird based on epidemiologic investigation, and stress from captivity and interspecific interactions may have increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: A virulent Y. pseudotuberculosis lineage capable of causing systemic septicemia in multiple avian species was involved, but no novel genotype was reported; the outbreak demonstrates efficient spread and high pathogenicity of known Y. pseudotuberculosis strains in naïve zoo birds and is therefore classified as re_occurrence.
Review: retain – Event closely follows Resendiz‑Pozos et al. (2025), including the affected species, pathologic findings, outbreak timing, 11‑month quarantine period, and interpretation of the hooded pitta as a likely carrier.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13096001/)) Classification as a localized re_occurrence event in North America is appropriate; there is no evidence for a new strain or new continent/subregion, and the event clearly has substantial management impact for the zoo. No corrections beyond aligning URLs to the primary sources were needed, and the event should be retained as one of the major recent avian outbreaks.

EPP common name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Countries: United States of America (Maryland [1984 – first atrazine‑resistant biotype], Wisconsin [1990], Minnesota [1991], Michigan [2004])
Host: Mainly corn (maize) and soybean in the US Corn Belt, with resistant populations reported from maize and mixed row‑crop systems in affected states.
Event summary: In the mid‑1980s, a velvetleaf biotype in Maryland maize fields was found to survive normal atrazine treatments because it could rapidly detoxify the herbicide via enhanced glutathione S‑transferase activity; this represented one of the earliest documented cases of metabolism‑based triazine resistance in a broadleaf weed. During the 1990s and early 2000s, additional atrazine‑resistant velvetleaf populations were confirmed in Wisconsin (1990), Minnesota (1991) and Michigan (2004), indicating that resistance had either evolved repeatedly under strong selection or spread among fields across parts of the US Corn Belt. These resistant biotypes caused localized control failures in maize and soybean, forcing growers to change herbicide programmes and integrate alternative modes of action and cultural controls, and, because the resistant biotypes showed little or no fitness penalty, resistance is expected to persist in affected seedbanks even where atrazine use declines.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very intensive use of atrazine and related photosystem‑II–inhibiting herbicides in North American maize and soybean production created strong selection pressure on velvetleaf populations that were already widespread and economically damaging, with annual US yield losses and control costs for velvetleaf alone estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars by the 1980s. Internal mechanisms: Evolution of herbicide resistance via enhanced metabolic detoxification of atrazine (notably increased glutathione S‑transferase activity) and associated mechanisms, without a clear fitness cost, led to the emergence and spread of resistant biotypes in multiple US states; this is a clear example of re‑emergence driven by pesticide resistance rather than by a new introduction or host jump.
Review: Review – Added as a previously omitted but well‑documented major re‑emergence event for this species, based on the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database and primary studies documenting atrazine‑resistant velvetleaf biotypes in Maryland (1984) and additional US states from 1990–2004. Classified as re‑emergence (pesticide resistance) rather than first detection or intra‑continental emergence, since the species was already widespread in North American crops. Impact is substantial in terms of control failures, management cost and contribution to long‑term seedbanks, but the exact spatial extent and yield loss remain only partially quantified; inclusion and event years should be reviewed by a weed‑science specialist when harmonising event rankings across species.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Host: Primarily spring‑sown arable crops in lowland agricultural areas, especially sugar beet, maize, sunflower, soybean, potatoes, oil‑pumpkin and various vegetables.
Event summary: From 1991 onwards, distribution data from Austria, Czechia and Slovakia show that velvetleaf, formerly restricted mainly to scattered ruderal sites and occasional fields, began to spread rapidly across Central Europe’s lowland agricultural regions. During the 2000s, records revealed a marked increase in infestations within crop fields, with about 78% of all field records collected after 2000 and dense populations becoming frequent in sugar beet, maize, sunflower, soybean and vegetable rotations as agricultural area at risk expanded from roughly 27,000 ha in 1990–1999 to nearly 188,000 ha in 2000–2013. By 2013, velvetleaf was recognised as an invasive alien crop weed in these countries, prompting EPPO and national authorities to highlight its continued spread and to recommend measures to prevent further expansion into uninfested fields.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance human‑mediated dispersal from earlier invasion centres via contaminated grain, oilseeds, catch crops, supplementary animal feed, organic fertilisers and seed lots, together with seed transport on tillage and harvest machinery, facilitated the transition from scattered ruderal occurrences to widespread field infestations. Changes in cropping systems, especially the large area of spring‑sown row crops (sugar beet, maize, sunflower, soybean) and high soil disturbance and nutrient levels in modern intensive agriculture, further favoured its establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity (thousands of seeds per plant), very long‑lived seed banks, rapid early growth and strong competitive ability for light enabled inherent geographic range expansion from ruderal habitats into agricultural fields; there is no evidence that a novel genotype or herbicide‑resistant strain specifically drove this Central European expansion, so it is best considered a re‑occurrence driven by external drivers rather than genetic change.
Review: Retain – This event closely matches EPPO Reporting Service article 2018/044 and Follak et al. (2014), including the 1991–2013 time window, the focus on Austria, Czechia and Slovakia, and the quantified post‑2000 increase in field records and agricultural area at risk. Countries and sub‑regions (Austria in Western Europe; Czechia and Slovakia in Eastern Europe) are correctly assigned, and classification as re‑occurrence (expansion and intensification within previously affected sub‑regions without evidence of a new genotype) is appropriate. No corrections to geography, timing or emergence‑type coding are required; event should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 emergence episodes for this species.

EPP common name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Countries: New Zealand (Auckland and Waikato regions; >60 infested properties traced by 2014)
Host: Maize and maize silage on dairy and arable farms in Auckland and Waikato, with secondary spread into pastures where contaminated maize silage was fed out.
Event summary: Around 2011, a serious velvetleaf infestation was recognised on a Waikato farm where the weed was severely depressing maize yields, and subsequent tracing revealed that it had been present in the region for some time but misidentified or overlooked. Over the following years, investigations by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Waikato Regional Council and the Foundation for Arable Research (FAR) linked the incursion to movements of contaminated maize or maize silage and identified more than 60 infested properties across North and South Auckland and Waikato, leading to its declaration as an Unwanted Organism in 2012 and inclusion in regional pest management plans by 2014. This maize‑associated incursion was managed under an eradication/containment framework with strict farm hygiene and surveillance, substantially reducing known foci by the mid‑2010s, but it established the species as a regulated, high‑priority cropping weed in New Zealand before the later, larger fodder‑beet incursion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and local spread were driven by contaminated maize grain or maize silage and the movement of harvesting and feeding equipment between dairy and arable properties, allowing seed to be carried from infested maize fields into silage stacks and nearby pastures. Internal mechanisms: No evidence suggests a novel genotype or herbicide‑resistant strain; instead, the same traits that make velvetleaf a major weed elsewhere—vigorous seedling growth, rapid height gain, strong competitive ability in tall summer crops and long‑lived seed banks—enabled establishment once it was accidentally introduced into Waikato maize systems. This episode is therefore classified as a re‑occurrence within New Zealand’s North Island rather than as first detection or re‑emergence due to genetic change.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the earlier, maize‑associated New Zealand incursion that predates the national fodder‑beet outbreak but is clearly highlighted in FAR and regional council documentation as a separate, regionally important episode (first Waikato detection in 2011, Unwanted Organism status by 2012, >60 infested properties in Auckland/Waikato). Classified as re‑occurrence within the same continental and sub‑regional context, as velvetleaf had been present in New Zealand since the 1940s, and no novel resistance or host jump is involved. Event years (2011–2015) mark the period before the large fodder‑beet seed incursion becomes dominant; precise end‑date and impact magnitude should be checked against MPI surveillance reports during dataset harmonisation.
