EPP common name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Countries: New Zealand (national outbreak linked to contaminated fodder beet seed; properties affected across at least 11 regions, with more than 1,200 South Island properties traced to contaminated seed lines)
Host: Fodder beet and other forage crops (with additional occurrences in maize and in pastures where contaminated fodder beet or maize silage was fed), mainly within intensively managed livestock feed systems on arable and dairy farms.
Event summary: In the 2015/16 season, a major biosecurity incursion of velvetleaf was detected in fodder beet crops in the South Island of New Zealand, when plants were found in numerous paddocks sown with pelleted fodder beet seed imported from Europe that was later confirmed to be contaminated with velvetleaf seed. Over the next several years, national tracing and surveillance revealed that hundreds of properties—ultimately more than 1,200 South Island properties and additional farms in the North Island—had sown affected fodder beet seed lines, leading to detections of velvetleaf in fodder beet paddocks and adjacent areas in at least 11 regions and triggering intensive on‑farm management plans, import bans on specific seed lines, and strengthened border controls for coated seed. By the early 2020s, regional councils and MPI had concluded that complete eradication of all seedbank foci was unlikely; velvetleaf remained regulated as an Unwanted Organism managed under long‑term national and regional programmes aimed at containment and impact reduction in forage systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The primary driver was the accidental introduction of large quantities of velvetleaf seed as a contaminant in several pelleted fodder beet seed lines imported from Europe (notably from Italy and France) in 2014/15, which were then widely planted across New Zealand; movement of fodder beet and maize silage, livestock and agricultural machinery further spread seed within and between farms. Policy and management responses included emergency import bans on contaminated lines, tighter testing and certification requirements for imported fodder beet seed, national surveillance campaigns, and regionally coordinated containment and farm biosecurity plans. Internal mechanisms: Velvetleaf’s prolific seed production (estimates up to ~15,000–17,000 seeds per plant), very persistent soil seedbanks and competitive performance in high‑input fodder beet and maize crops underpinned its capacity to establish from relatively small seed contaminant loads; however, the episode is not associated with a novel strain or documented herbicide resistance, so it is best classified as a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven by external introduction pathways.
Review: Retain – This event accurately summarises the large fodder‑beet–associated incursion documented by MPI, regional councils and FAR, including its origin in contaminated pelleted fodder beet seed imported from Europe in 2014/15, subsequent detection from 2015/16 onwards across at least 11 regions, and national management response with more than 1,200 South Island properties linked to contaminated seed lines by the mid‑2020s. Countries and sub‑region coding (New Zealand within Australia and New Zealand, Oceania) are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate given earlier New Zealand presence. Description of scale and management has been cross‑checked against multiple official and industry sources; no changes to geography or event type were required, though wording could be further refined if more precise hectare or yield‑loss estimates become available.

EPP common name: hispid starbur, hispid starburr, bristly starbur
Host: Primarily associated with imported soybean and other grain commodities in port areas (Antwerpen and Gent), with plants establishing on unloading quays, near grain mills, grain dumps and other highly disturbed ruderal sites.
Event summary: Between 1997 and 2005, Acanthospermum hispidum was repeatedly recorded for the first time in Belgium as an alien “grain adventive” emerging from imported soybean and other cereals in the major ports of Antwerpen and Gent. The weed established small, transient populations on unloading quays, grain dumps and other disturbed port substrates, but remained rare and reluctant to flower in the Belgian climate. By the mid‑2000s most occurrences were ephemeral and confined to port infrastructure, with no evidence that the species had become widely naturalized in surrounding agricultural land, though continued trade meant that new introductions remained possible.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in contaminated grain (especially soybean) was the primary driver, with seeds arriving as contaminants in bulk commodities unloaded at the ports of Antwerpen and Gent; highly disturbed, open ruderal habitats on quays and grain dumps facilitated germination and short‑term establishment. Internal mechanisms: High propagule production (thousands of seeds per plant) and burr morphology enabling adhesion to materials and machinery aided local persistence in port environments, while broad ecological tolerance as a ruderal annual facilitated establishment in disturbed sites, although limited cold tolerance and daylength constraints likely restricted sustained reproduction in Western Europe.
Review: Review – Event retained as representing the first well-documented occurrence of A. hispidum in Europe as a grain-adventive weed in Belgian ports. Emergence-type coding has been corrected: ‘first_detection’ is set to No because global discovery predates this event by more than a century, ‘intra_continental_emergence’ is set to No, and ‘inter_continental_emergence’ is set to Yes to reflect first establishment on a new continent. Years, sub-region and country (Belgium [1997]) are consistent with the Belgian alien-flora account, and sources are appropriate (alienplantsbelgium for the event itself, POWO for corroborating distribution). Recommended for expert review mainly to confirm that no earlier pre‑1990 European records warrant redefining the timing of Europe’s inter-continental emergence.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: hispid starbur, hispid starburr, bristly starbur
Host: Invasive weed in multiple crops (e.g. rainfed annual crops, pastures), wastelands, roadsides and forest margins; reported from many Indian states including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Maharashtra, Telangana and others, often as a dominant invasive herb in disturbed terrestrial and swampland habitats.
Event summary: By around 2000, Acanthospermum hispidum—introduced to India earlier in the 20th century—had begun to expand markedly, being recorded in multiple states as an invasive alien herb in croplands, pastures and wastelands across the plains and up to at least 1500 m in the hills of Uttarakhand. During the 2000s and 2010s, a succession of regional floristic and invasive‑species surveys documented the weed as widely distributed and sometimes gregarious, especially in disturbed terrestrial and swampland habitats and along roads and forest edges, indicating a substantial increase in both range and local abundance. By about 2020 the species was consistently listed in national and regional compilations of India’s invasive alien flora, suggesting that it had become a common and persistent agricultural and ecological weed throughout much of Southern Asia’s lowland India, with no clear evidence that the expansion had yet stabilized.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion is strongly associated with intensification and expansion of annual cropping, overgrazed pastures, road building and other land‑use changes that create open disturbed ground; long‑distance dispersal is facilitated by movement of contaminated fodder, grain and soil, as well as vehicles and livestock. Internal mechanisms: The species is an aggressive colonizer of open sites, producing abundant, long‑lived burr‑type seeds that adhere to animals and materials, and it tolerates a wide range of tropical and subtropical climates from lowlands to mid‑elevations; these traits underlie its inherent capacity for geographic range expansion without evidence of a distinct new genotype or strain in India.
Review: Retain – Event appropriately captures one of the largest post-1990 emergence episodes for this species: the widespread expansion and recognition of A. hispidum as an invasive alien weed across India. Timing (c. 2000–2020), geography (Southern Asia, India) and emergence classification (re-occurrence driven by land-use change and disturbance, without evidence for a novel strain or host jump) align with multiple floristic and invasive-plant surveys. No corrections to years, countries, or emergence-type coding were required; host description and impact narrative are consistent with the cited Indian sources. This row should be retained as a major emergence event, with only routine checking needed if new quantitative impact data become available.

EPP common name: hispid starbur, hispid starburr, bristly starbur
Host: Agricultural crops (notably peanuts and other broadacre crops such as cotton, maize, sorghum, sugarcane and tobacco), as well as pastures and disturbed sites (creek flats, roadsides, waste places), with particular attention to infestations associated with imported peanut straw in Victoria.
Event summary: Before 2005, Acanthospermum hispidum was already established as a significant agricultural weed in parts of northern and eastern Australia (e.g. Queensland), where it infested cotton, peanut and other summer crops and pastures. In 2005 the species was detected for the first time in Victoria at Maffra in Gippsland, where it had spread from a batch of peanut straw imported from Queensland, raising concern about a southward range expansion into new cropping areas and prompting detailed impact and risk assessments for the state. Following detection, local control measures and awareness campaigns were implemented, and while climatic modelling suggests that much of Victoria is suitable for infestation, subsequent records indicate that the weed remained localized but continues to pose an ongoing risk of further spread wherever contaminated fodder or grain is moved.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The key driver for the Victorian emergence was intra‑national trade in contaminated agricultural products, specifically peanut straw transported from infested fields in Queensland; additional drivers include broadacre cropping systems, movement of contaminated fodder and seed, and disturbance of creek flats, roadsides and waste places that provide suitable establishment sites. Internal mechanisms: The weed’s high seed output, long seed longevity, rapid growth to reproductive maturity (within about two months) and burr morphology that enables adherence to livestock, wool and machinery enhance its invasive potential; its ability to significantly reduce crop yields (e.g. >20% peanut yield loss in Florida) and to contaminate wool and fodder further reinforces selection for persistence in agricultural landscapes and underpins its geographic range expansion within Australia.
Review: Review – Event retained as a well-documented range-expansion episode within Oceania, describing the first Victorian record in 2005 and associated concern over southward spread into new cropping areas. Emergence-type coding has been adjusted: ‘intra_continental_emergence’ is set to No because both the source (Queensland) and recipient (Victoria) lie within the same UN sub-region (Australia and New Zealand), and ‘re_occurrence’ is set to Yes to reflect renewed spread and local establishment within an already invaded sub-region driven by movement of contaminated fodder, without evidence of genetic change (hence ‘re_emergence’ remains No). Years, country annotation, host description and pathways are consistent with VicFlora and the Victorian Resources Online assessment. Recommended for expert review only to confirm that no earlier Victorian records exist and that this episode is among the most impactful recent emergence events for the species in Oceania.

Host: Rangeland and pasture vegetation (native perennial grasses and forbs), alfalfa and other perennial forage crops, and weedy vegetation in irrigated cropland of the western United States
Event summary: Around 1990, Russian knapweed infestations that had been present for decades in western U.S. rangelands began to expand rapidly, forming dense, nearly monospecific stands across large areas of semi‑arid grazing land and irrigated fields. By the late 1990s the species was estimated to infest roughly 557,000 ha in the western United States and was spreading at up to 14% per year in some regions, reaching about 1.2 million acres across 17 western states by 2000. As weed management programs, biological control initiatives and improved grazing and revegetation practices were implemented in the early 2000s, local populations were suppressed in some areas but the species remained a dominant, entrenched invader over much of its expanded range.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term overgrazing and soil disturbance in semi‑arid rangelands, expansion of irrigated agriculture and disturbed field margins, and widespread movement of contaminated hay, forage seed and soil facilitated rapid local and regional spread. Internal mechanisms: An extensive creeping rhizome system enabling vegetative spread, relatively low but sufficient seed production, and strong allelopathic effects that suppress neighboring plant germination and growth allowed Russian knapweed to displace native and desirable forage species and maintain dominance once established.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures a major 1990–2000 re‑occurrence episode in long‑invaded western U.S. rangelands, with acreage and spread rates supported by extension and research estimates.([extension.unr.edu](https://extension.unr.edu/publication.aspx?PubID=4109&utm_source=openai)) Geography, host system and emergence‑type coding (re‑occurrence only) are consistent with the definitions and the species’ much earlier arrival. I recommend keeping this row but noting that it forms part of a longer North American re‑occurrence episode that overlaps with Event 2; the two could be merged in a future revision to avoid double‑counting one broad invasion episode.

Host: Perennial forage crops and rangelands (alfalfa, hayfields, pastures) and disturbed rights‑of‑way in western and central United States and southern/central Canada
Event summary: During the 1990s, Russian knapweed expanded eastward and northward from core western U.S. populations into additional Great Plains and interior states and continued to increase in density where it was already present, while also spreading within Canadian prairie provinces and British Columbia. By the 2000s it was formally listed as a noxious weed in numerous U.S. states and Canadian provinces, with national and provincial agencies recognizing it as a serious invasive threat to forage production and ecosystem health. Through the late 2000s and around 2010, coordinated noxious‑weed, biocontrol and integrated weed management programs helped slow further spread in some jurisdictions, but the species remained widely established across Northern America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued movement of contaminated seed and hay between regions, road and rail corridors, and disturbance from cultivation and infrastructure development facilitated colonization of new areas within Northern America; formal policy recognition as a noxious weed generally followed after the biological invasion had already expanded. Internal mechanisms: Clonal expansion via rhizomes and long‑lived root systems, combined with allelopathy and strong competitive ability under semi‑arid conditions, enabled persistence and densification of stands once introduced into new landscapes.
Review: review – The episode of broader North American spread and policy recognition is real and important, and the emergence‑type coding as re‑occurrence (not intra‑ or inter‑continental) is appropriate because this is further spread within the already invaded Northern America sub‑region. However, Canada’s per‑country date was incorrect: Russian knapweed was introduced to Canada in the early 1900s, not the mid‑1990s.([inspection.canada.ca](https://inspection.canada.ca/en/plant-health/seeds/seed-testing-and-grading/seeds-identification/rhaponticum-repens?utm_source=openai)) I have changed the Countries field from “Canada [1995]” to “Canada [1990]” to indicate that this re‑occurrence episode is considered to begin (approximately) at the start of the 1990s rather than representing first arrival. This event overlaps strongly with Event 1 in both time and space; I therefore recommend retaining it but marking it for possible future merging with Event 1 into a single North American re‑occurrence episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Semi‑arid and arid rangelands, irrigated pastures, horticultural fields and roadsides in Argentina, affecting forage species and occasionally horses grazing heavily infested areas
Event summary: Russian knapweed was introduced into Argentina around 1920–1930 with contaminated alfalfa seed and by the 1980s already infested roughly 2,000 ha in the Valle Inferior del Río Negro irrigation scheme, with surveys showing more than half of irrigated farms reporting the weed. From the 1990s onward, the species spread from these irrigated foci into surrounding semi‑arid and arid rangelands and along roadsides in several provinces, forming dense patches that reduced forage production and occasionally caused neurotoxic “chewing disease” in horses grazing heavily infested sites. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, national reviews and invasion‑risk assessments listed Rhaponticum/Acroptilon repens among the most important invasive plants of Argentina’s rangelands, prompting monitoring and management programs but without achieving broad‑scale containment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and degradation of rangelands, intensification of irrigated horticulture, road construction and vehicle‑mediated dispersal, and movement of contaminated hay and livestock between ranches facilitated spread of Russian knapweed from initial irrigated foci across Argentine drylands. Internal mechanisms: Very deep root systems and pronounced allelopathic effects help the species dominate in water‑limited environments, while tolerance of semi‑arid climates and the ability to regenerate from rhizome fragments allow it to persist under grazing and partial control efforts.
Review: review – This event represents one of the major global impacts of Russian knapweed and should be retained, but several details required correction. Historical work from the Valle Inferior del Río Negro shows introduction in about 1920–1930, substantial spread by the 1960s and around 2,000 ha affected by the mid‑1980s, so the weed was not merely “localized” by the mid‑1990s.([repositoriodigital.uns.edu.ar](https://repositoriodigital.uns.edu.ar/bitstream/123456789/4564/1/Gajardo%20Acroptilon%20repens.pdf)) I have adjusted the Event Year to 1990–2015 and the country‑specific date to “Argentina [1990]” to align the episode with the start of the analysis window while acknowledging earlier invasion history, and rewritten the summary to reflect pre‑1990 expansion and the post‑1990 spread into wider rangelands documented in national reviews and risk‑assessment studies.([ri.conicet.gov.ar](https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/handle/11336/12543?utm_source=openai)) Emergence type as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental, not first detection) remains appropriate.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cereal crops (especially wheat and other winter cereals), vineyards, horticultural crops, irrigation channels and drains, and pastures in southern and eastern Australia
Event summary: By about 1990 Russian knapweed (creeping knapweed) was already present in parts of south‑eastern Australia but began to increase and spread within irrigated cropping regions and pastures, particularly in New South Wales and Victoria, where it invaded cereals, vineyards and horticultural crops. During the 1990s and 2000s it was detected and declared in additional Australian states, including South Australia, Western Australia and Queensland, and was recognized nationally as a serious invasive weed capable of reducing cereal yields by up to 80% and tainting flour and grain. Into the 2010s and up to 2020, strict biosecurity regulations, statewide eradication or containment programs, and farmer awareness campaigns have limited new incursions and aim to eradicate or contain remaining infestations, though scattered populations persist.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Irrigation development and intensive cereal and horticultural production created disturbed, moist environments favorable for establishment; spread was promoted by movement of contaminated seed and hay, water‑borne dispersal in irrigation channels, and machinery and soil transfer between farms and regions. Internal mechanisms: Strong allelopathic effects on neighboring plants, a robust rhizomatous root system, and tolerance of both semi‑arid and irrigated conditions facilitated aggressive local spread and allowed Russian knapweed to build dense stands that severely suppressed crop and pasture yields and posed toxicity risks to horses.
Review: review – The Australian episode is real and highly impactful, with national and state sources documenting widespread establishment in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia, recognition as a serious agricultural weed, and potential wheat yield losses of up to ~80%.([weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weed/CreepingKnapweed?utm_source=openai)) However, the original Countries field incorrectly treated Australian states (New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland) as if they were separate countries, which violates the coding rules that restrict this field to UN‑recognized countries. I have corrected the Countries field to “Australia [1990]” and left the description of state‑level spread in the narrative summary instead. Because the species arrived in Australia well before 1990, this is appropriately coded as a re‑occurrence episode (not first detection, not inter‑continental emergence).([pir.sa.gov.au](https://www.pir.sa.gov.au/aghistory/natural_resources/weeds_pests_disease_management/overview_period_histories/science_to_the_rescue_19211970?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Roadsides, abandoned fields and disturbed sites in the Iberian Peninsula (Spain), with potential to invade nearby pasture and rangeland habitats
Event summary: In 2011 botanists formally reported Russian knapweed for the first time from the Iberian Peninsula, documenting small populations in abandoned fields near Vilablareix (Girona, Catalonia) and in the Vinalopó valley (Alicante, Valencia), and re‑identifying a misassigned herbarium specimen collected in 1959. Over the subsequent few years the species was recorded at a handful of additional disturbed sites, prompting publication of a detailed floristic note describing Rhaponticum repens as a new alien plant for the Peninsula and highlighting its invasive behaviour in other continents. By the early 2010s the species remained very localized but under surveillance, and early detection allowed regional authorities and botanists to promote monitoring and control to reduce the risk of it becoming a major invader in Southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction likely occurred via contaminated seed lots or transported soil associated with international trade or transport corridors, with establishment favored by disturbed roadside and ruderal habitats in Mediterranean climates; the event represents spread into a new European sub‑region where the species is alien, rather than a change in the plant’s biology. Internal mechanisms: As elsewhere, rhizomatous growth, long‑lived root systems and allelopathic suppression of neighboring plants provide the capacity for local spread and competitive dominance, although at the time of first confirmed records in Iberia populations were still relatively small and localized.
Review: review – The Iberian event is valid as the first confirmed records of Russian knapweed in the Iberian Peninsula, and it is reasonable to include it among the top events as a key intra‑continental emergence into a new European sub‑region, even though impacts were still small. The original timing (2005–2010; Spain [2005]) was only inferred and not directly supported; the primary paper reporting this alien species for the Peninsula was published in 2011, while also noting a misidentified specimen from 1959.([collectaneabotanica.revistas.csic.es](https://collectaneabotanica.revistas.csic.es/index.php/collectaneabotanica/article/view/185?utm_source=openai)) I have therefore set the Event Year to “2011” and the country‑specific date to “Spain [2011]”. The earlier classification of this event as “first_detection” was inappropriate because the species has been known in the plant host system for centuries in its native Eurasian range; this flag has been set to false, while “intra_continental_emergence” remains true to reflect spread within Europe from native Eastern Europe into alien range in Southern Europe. I also replaced the ResearchGate link with the original Collectanea Botanica article URL as the primary source for this event.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) in irrigated rotations; associated weeds in neighbouring fields (Gooding County, Idaho)
Event summary: A triazine‑resistant Powell amaranth population was discovered in 1989 in a southern Idaho potato field treated with metribuzin, after growers noted repeated survival of pigweeds following standard programmes. Surveys showed the resistant biotype to be confined to the south‑eastern corner of Gooding County, where dense stands interfered with potato and neighbouring crops through the early 1990s. Subsequent physiological and molecular work, reported in 1992, confirmed high‑level resistance to several PSII‑inhibiting herbicides via a psbA Ser264→Gly mutation, forcing local shifts away from triazines and illustrating the risk of wider spread of this biotype.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance: a Ser264→Gly substitution in the chloroplast psbA gene confers high‑level resistance to PSII‑inhibiting triazines (for example metribuzin, atrazine) by reducing herbicide binding to the D1 protein. Drivers – decades of intensive triazine use in irrigated potato and associated crops, low diversity of herbicide modes of action and relatively limited crop rotation favoured selection and persistence of the resistant biotype in Gooding County.
Review: Retain – Event is well supported by Eberlein et al. 1992 and describes a clearly documented, localized triazine‑resistant Powell amaranth population in Gooding County, Idaho; year 1992 reflects the first peer‑reviewed report within the ≥1990 window while the 1989 discovery date is correctly given in the narrative, and classification as re‑emergence (herbicide‑resistant biotype in an already colonised subregion) with North America/Northern America/United States coding is consistent with the definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Host: Soybean (Glycine max) and other row crops in Ohio
Event summary: By the mid‑1990s, soybean growers in Ohio reported Powell amaranth surviving recommended rates of ALS‑inhibiting herbicides such as imazaquin, prompting greenhouse comparisons with known susceptible biotypes. In 1996, the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database records an ALS‑resistant Powell amaranth biotype in Ohio soybean, one of the first documented ALS‑resistant pigweed populations in the eastern Corn Belt. The resistant population reduced the effectiveness of widely used ALS herbicides, requiring growers to substitute or mix alternative modes of action and adopt more integrated weed‑management approaches.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via altered acetolactate synthase (ALS) target site, conferring resistance to imazaquin and likely cross‑resistance to other ALS‑inhibiting herbicides. Drivers – extensive reliance on ALS inhibitors in soybean and corn, often in reduced‑tillage systems with limited diversification of herbicide programmes, created strong selection pressure favouring ALS‑resistant Powell amaranth biotypes in Ohio.
Review: Review – Event (ALS‑inhibitor‑resistant Powell amaranth in Ohio soybean first confirmed in 1996) matches the dedicated case record in the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database and is appropriately classified as re‑emergence; I have replaced the generic secondary PDF citation with the specific case URL for better traceability, and recommend a light human check of the narrative wording against regional extension summaries, but no structural changes to timing or geography.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Host: Field corn (Zea mays), soybean (Glycine max) and wheat (Triticum aestivum) in Perth County and broader Ontario row‑crop systems
Event summary: In the late 1990s, Ontario corn–soybean–wheat growers observed poor control of Powell amaranth despite atrazine and ALS‑inhibiting herbicides such as imazethapyr and thifensulfuron‑methyl. By 1998, the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database reported ALS‑resistant and multiple‑resistant Powell amaranth populations in Ontario, and subsequent research from Perth County documented a biotype with extremely high resistance to both atrazine and imazethapyr. Through the early 2000s this multiple‑resistant biotype spread in local row‑crop systems, forcing major changes in herbicide programmes and illustrating the management challenges posed by dual target‑site resistance.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanisms – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with combined target‑site mutations in psbA (Ser264→Gly) and ALS (Ser652→Thr) conferring high‑level resistance to triazines and imidazolinones. Drivers – long‑term heavy use of triazine herbicides in Ontario corn, followed by intensive ALS‑inhibitor use in diversified corn–soybean–wheat rotations, selected first single‑site and then multiple‑resistant Powell amaranth populations, which were further favoured by reduced tillage and high weed seedbanks.
Review: Retain – Multiple resistance to imazethapyr and atrazine in Powell amaranth in Perth County, Ontario is well documented by the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database and Diebold et al. 2003; dates (first records in 1998 and characterisation through 2003), crops, herbicides and dual target‑site mutations are correctly represented, and classification as re‑emergence of a novel multiple‑resistant biotype within a pre‑existing weed species is appropriate.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Host: Carrots (Daucus carota) in muck soils near Keswick, Ontario; other vegetables
Event summary: In 1999, a dense Powell amaranth population surviving linuron and other PSII herbicides was identified in a muck‑soil carrot field near Keswick, Ontario after repeated control failures. Greenhouse and biochemical studies showed resistance to linuron and cross‑resistance to several triazines, later linked to a psbA Val219→Ile mutation. Over the following years, this resistant Powell amaranth became a serious weed in muck‑soil carrot and vegetable systems, increasing weed‑control costs and restricting effective herbicide options for growers in the affected area.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance to substituted urea (linuron) and PSII‑inhibiting triazines, associated with a Val219→Ile substitution in the D1 protein of PSII and possibly additional detoxification processes. Drivers – intensive and repeated use of linuron and Group 5 PSII herbicides in high‑value carrot production on muck soils, limited non‑chemical options and large local seedbanks provided strong selection pressure for the resistant Powell amaranth biotype.
Review: Retain – The Keswick, Ontario linuron‑ and triazine‑resistant Powell amaranth population in muck‑soil carrots, discovered in 1999 and characterised in subsequent thesis and journal work, is accurately located and timed, the mechanism (psbA Val219→Ile‑mediated PSII resistance with cross‑resistance to triazines) is correctly described, and treating this as a re‑emergence event (new resistant biotype of an existing weed) without intra/inter‑continental tags matches the project definitions.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Countries: United States of America [1992], United States of America – Michigan [2001]
Host: Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) and nursery crops in Michigan; mint and other perennial crops in Washington State
Event summary: Following earlier PSII‑resistant Powell amaranth populations in the Pacific Northwest, a biotype resistant to atrazine and diuron was reported in asparagus and nursery systems in Michigan by 2001, while Washington mint production had documented terbacil‑resistant Powell amaranth since the early 1990s. Surveys and later field work showed that PSII‑inhibitor‑resistant Powell amaranth became established in perennial crops and nurseries where tillage options were limited, and by the 2000s resistant biotypes were widespread enough in parts of the Columbia Basin and Michigan specialty crops to necessitate significant adjustments in herbicide programmes and integrated weed management.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance to multiple PSII inhibitors (for example terbacil, atrazine, diuron) via psbA mutations such as Ser264→Gly and associated cross‑resistance across Group 5 herbicides. Drivers – long‑term reliance on PSII‑inhibiting herbicides in perennial specialty crops (mint, asparagus, nursery stock) with few alternative modes of action and limited tillage or crop rotation, creating ideal conditions for selection and persistence of resistant Powell amaranth populations in the north‑western and Great Lakes regions of the United States.
Review: Retain – Linked PSII‑inhibitor‑resistant Powell amaranth populations in Washington mint (first recorded 1992) and Michigan asparagus/nursery crops (first recorded 2001) are supported by weedscience entries and Spring et al. 2016; the event is correctly treated as re‑emergence of resistant biotypes within an already established weed in Northern America, and the broad 2001–2010 window reasonably represents the main period when these cases became agronomically significant.

EPP common name: Powell's pigweed; Powell's amaranth; green amaranth
Host: Dry beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) and wheat (Triticum aestivum) in Manitoba
Event summary: In 2008, an ALS‑inhibitor‑resistant Powell amaranth population was confirmed in Manitoba, where plants in bean and wheat fields survived sulfonylurea herbicides such as thifensulfuron‑methyl and tribenuron‑methyl. Over subsequent seasons this biotype interfered with weed control in pulse–cereal rotations, causing localised yield loss and prompting growers to adjust herbicide programmes and diversify modes of action. The case marked the first documented ALS‑resistant Powell amaranth population in western Canada, raising concerns about further spread across the Prairies.
Mechanism or driver: Internal mechanism – Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via ALS target‑site mutation(s) conferring resistance to sulfonylurea herbicides (ALS inhibitors). Drivers – intensive and repeated ALS‑inhibitor use in bean–wheat and other Prairie rotations, limited herbicide diversity and large soil seedbanks promoted selection and establishment of the resistant Powell amaranth biotype in Manitoba.

As farmers shifted from transplanted to direct‑seeded rice and other upland cropping systems, Amaranthus spinosus became one of the most troublesome broadleaf weeds, with dense stands competing strongly with young rice plants and requiring greater weed control inputs. Internal mechanisms: Inherent traits of A. spinosus—high fecundity, wide germination temperature range, tolerance of salinity and water stress, and ability to emerge from shallow soil layers—enhanced its competitive ability in direct‑seeded rice and allowed rapid population build‑up under new management regimes rather than through a novel genotype.
Review: retain: Event correctly captures a major post‑1990 re‑occurrence episode in which A. spinosus became one of the most troublesome weeds of direct‑seeded and upland rice across South and South‑eastern Asia. Classification as re‑occurrence (no first/global or first‑detection role, and not a new sub‑region or continent) is consistent with the definitions, because the species was already widespread in these regions before 1990 and its increased impact is driven by shifts from transplanted to direct‑seeded systems and greater herbicide dependence. Countries and sub‑regions are appropriate at this coarse scale, though individual start years are approximate. Geography (USA – Mississippi, Northern America) and timing (grower observations in 2011, confirmation and characterization by 2013) are consistent with Nandula et al. 2014, later work on ALS resistance, and the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database. A. spinosus was already present elsewhere in the Northern Africa subregion (e.g. Egypt and Sudan, where it is treated as an introduced/naturalized species) prior to 2012, so the Tunisian record represents spread to a new country within an already invaded subregion, not introduction into a new subregion or continent. Review: review: As with Tunisia, this event was originally labeled as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence, but Amaranthus spinosus was already established in the Northern Africa subregion (e.g. Egypt, and since 2012–2016 Tunisia) before its first national record in Morocco. Under the given definitions, spread to a new country within the same sub‑region should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence. I therefore set first_detection to false and intra_continental_emergence to false, and marked re_occurrence as true to indicate further spread and increased incidence within a previously affected subregion driven by human‑mediated dispersal and disturbed habitats. Continent, sub‑region, country and year (Morocco, Northern Africa, 2021) match the EPPO 2023/100 report and underlying Flora Mediterranea paper; the event is retained but flagged for review because it is a national first record rather than a sub‑regional first emergence, and current agronomic impacts remain mostly prospective.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Countries: Hungary [1990]; Croatia [1990]; Serbia [1990]; Romania [1990]; Bulgaria [1990]; Ukraine [1990]; Russian Federation (southern European part) [1990]; Republic of Moldova [1995]; Bosnia and Herzegovina [1995]
Host: Primarily annual arable and forage crops (sunflower, maize, soybean, cereals) and fallow land/road verges in agricultural landscapes
Event summary: From around 1990, common ragweed populations already present in parts of the Pannonian Basin and south‑east Europe expanded explosively, colonizing large areas of arable land and disturbed habitats in Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, southern Russia and Ukraine and causing severe yield losses and allergenic pollen exposure. This expansion continued through the 1990s and 2000s, with ragweed becoming one of the most abundant weeds in many fields and along transport corridors, leading to some of the highest airborne ragweed pollen concentrations recorded in Europe and large increases in hay fever and asthma. By about 2010, the invasion front had reached cooler northern limits in Eastern Europe and the Black Sea region, with further spread slowing as populations approached climatic limits, prompting wide‑scale monitoring and control programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: profound socio‑economic and land‑use changes following political transitions in Eastern Europe in the late 1980s–1990s (farm restructuring, field abandonment, reduced weed control), expansion of road and rail networks and increased movement of contaminated grain and birdseed, and lack of effective regulation of seed impurities all facilitated rapid spread and build‑up of dense populations. Internal mechanisms: strong ruderal life‑history traits (high seed production and long‑lived seed bank), plus inherent tolerance to a wide range of soils and disturbance regimes, promoted dominance; no specific new strain is implicated, so this is classified as re‑occurrence driven mainly by external factors rather than documented genetic change.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the major 1990–2010 invasion episode in the Pannonian Basin and neighbouring Black Sea regions, which multiple studies identify as Europe’s main ragweed hotspot with extremely high pollen loads and widespread crop impacts; the spatial focus (Eastern and Southern Europe) and classification as re-occurrence driven predominantly by land-use and socio-economic change, rather than first occurrence or documented strain change, are appropriate and supported by EFSA, EPPO and regional invasion histories.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Arable crops (maize, sunflower, soybean), forage crops and urban/rural wasteland in the Rhône valley, Po Valley and adjacent regions
Event summary: In France and northern Italy, where common ragweed had been present since the 19th–20th centuries, the weed underwent a marked range and abundance increase from the early 1990s, especially in the Rhône valley and Po Valley where dense monocultures developed in fields and along infrastructure. Through the 1990s and 2000s this led to substantial yield losses in spring‑sown crops and a sharp rise in allergic rhinitis and asthma cases, with France later estimating hundreds of thousands of affected residents and tens of millions of euros in annual health‑related costs. By around 2015, intensive control, awareness campaigns and in parts of Italy the accidental establishment of the specialist beetle Ophraella communa began to locally reduce ragweed biomass and pollen loads, stabilizing or slightly decreasing impacts in some hotspots though the weed remains widespread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increased movement of contaminated crop and birdseed, expansion of transport networks, agricultural set‑aside and reduced tillage favoured ragweed establishment, while urban sprawl and disturbed riparian corridors provided additional habitat; climate warming may have lengthened the pollen season. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability and prolific seed production allowed rapid build‑up in crops; however, no specific novel strain has been identified, and the surge is best explained by land‑use and management changes (re‑occurrence). Biological control by Ophraella communa in northern Italy reduced pollen production locally but did not drive the initial emergence.
Review: retain – This event appropriately represents the well-documented 1990s–2010s surge of ragweed in the Rhône and Po valleys and adjacent regions, with very large health and agricultural impacts and detailed national cost estimates; treating it as a re-occurrence episode in long-invaded Western/Southern Europe (rather than new intra-/inter-continental emergence) is consistent with EFSA, ANSES and Italian invasion reconstructions, and listed countries match the main Western European hotspots.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Weed of annual crops (maize, soybean, peanut), orchards, plantations and disturbed non-crop habitats (roadsides, riverbanks) across northern and eastern China
Event summary: Common ragweed, first recorded in China in 1935 near Hangzhou, remained relatively localized until the late 20th century, when populations began to expand rapidly in northern and eastern provinces after about 1990. During the 1990s and 2000s the species spread along transport corridors and agricultural frontiers, so that by around 2010–2020 it was recorded as naturalized in more than 20 provinces spanning northern, central, eastern and parts of southern China, with dense infestations in some croplands and river basins. Recent analyses show continuing spread and niche filling in cooler northern provinces and along the southern periphery of its stable range, accompanied by increasing concern for both crop losses and pollen allergies and prompting local management and biological control studies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid economic development in China with major increases in road and rail networks, long‑distance movement of contaminated grain and forage seed, large‑scale land‑use change and disturbance, and climate warming that created more suitable thermal regimes all facilitated the spread from initial bridgehead regions. Internal mechanisms: reciprocal transplant and common‑garden studies indicate rapid evolution of invasive traits (e.g. higher growth and reproductive allocation in Chinese populations compared with native US populations) and regional adaptation to local climates, consistent with novel trait evolution and inherent geographic range expansion; together these justify classification as both intra‑continental emergence into new Chinese subregions and re‑emergence linked to genetic and phenotypic shifts.
Review: retain – The chronology (localized presence after first record in 1935 followed by rapid post-1990 expansion into >20 provinces) and mechanisms (trade- and infrastructure-driven spread plus well-documented rapid evolution of invasive traits and climatic adaptation) are consistent with EPPO distribution data and recent Chinese ecological/genomic studies; classifying this as both intra-continental emergence and re-emergence is therefore appropriate.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Countries: Türkiye [1998]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [1995]; India [2000]; Pakistan [2000]
Host: Weed of summer crops (maize, sunflower, soybean and other field crops), orchards and disturbed sites in lowland to submontane zones
Event summary: From the early 1990s, common ragweed, already present in parts of East Asia, was increasingly recorded spreading into additional regions of western and southern Asia, including Türkiye (with first confirmed records from 1998 and rapid spread in the Black Sea and Marmara regions) and later into parts of Iran, northern India and Pakistan where it colonized disturbed croplands and roadsides. Through the 1990s and 2000s, populations in these regions increased in abundance and extent, with the species becoming a problematic weed in some local farming systems and a source of seasonal pollinosis near urban centres, although impacts currently remain more localized than in central Europe or northern China. By about 2015, ragweed was recognized as part of the naturalized alien flora in several West and South Asian countries, with ongoing local spread and concern over future climatic suitability and potential for further invasion into higher elevations and new cropping systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing regional trade and transport, including movement of contaminated agricultural seed, grain and livestock feed from already invaded European and East Asian regions, and road construction that created disturbed habitat corridors, facilitated stepwise colonization of western and southern Asia. Internal mechanisms: pre‑adapted invasive traits (high fecundity, persistent seed bank) and broad climatic tolerance allowed establishment across a wide precipitation and temperature gradient; while some local adaptation is likely, there is currently limited direct evidence for region‑specific novel genotypes, so this episode is best treated primarily as intra‑continental emergence into previously uncolonized Asian subregions rather than as a documented re‑emergence driven by genetic change.
Review: review – Two corrections were made: (1) the start year for Türkiye was adjusted from 1990 to 1998, consistent with published invasion histories that identify 1998 as the first documented national record followed by rapid spread in the Black Sea/Marmara regions; (2) the event type was changed from intra-continental emergence + re-emergence to intra-continental emergence only, because current literature provides limited direct evidence of region-specific genetic or phenotypic innovation in West/South Asian populations beyond general pre-adaptation. Country years for Iran, India and Pakistan remain approximate (reflecting first substantial reports rather than earliest casual occurrences) and should be checked against national floras and weed surveys.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Weed of irrigated crops, orchards and disturbed urban/agricultural habitats in lowland Mediterranean-climate zones of North Africa
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, common ragweed, already naturalized elsewhere in Africa, was documented as part of the non‑native flora in Egypt and recorded as casual or locally established in Algeria and Morocco, indicating the presence of self‑sustaining foci in Mediterranean North Africa. Over the 2000s and 2010s the species persisted and likely expanded locally in irrigated and disturbed habitats, and by the late 2010s it was recorded for the first time from the wild flora of Tunisia, confirming its spread along the southern Mediterranean coast and the presence of multiple naturalized foci in the northern African subregion. By 2022, international alerts recognized common ragweed as part of the non‑native flora of Tunisia and broader North Africa, prompting concern about its future spread into additional agroecosystems and the potential emergence of new allergy hotspots on the African continent.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated seed, ornamental plantings and other trade pathways from Europe and Asia, combined with irrigated agriculture and disturbed roadside and urban habitats in Mediterranean North Africa, facilitated establishment; limited awareness and management allowed persistence and gradual spread. Internal mechanisms: there is currently no clear evidence of distinct African genetic lineages or novel adaptive traits; the invasion appears to be driven mainly by propagule pressure and suitable climate rather than demonstrated evolutionary change, so this episode is treated as an intra‑continental emergence within Africa rather than a first inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – This event was originally misclassified as an inter-continental emergence for Africa and described as marking the first establishment of ragweed on the continent; herbarium and floristic data show A. artemisiifolia has been naturalized in South Africa since at least 1896, and also listed as naturalized in Southern Africa and Egypt, so the North African episode represents spread into a new African subregion (Northern Africa) rather than first arrival on the continent. The event type has therefore been corrected to intra-continental emergence and the summary rewritten to remove the claim of first African establishment; the countries and timing (Egypt and neighbouring states with a later confirmed record in Tunisia in 2018) remain broadly consistent with EPPO and regional botanical sources but should be fine-tuned if more precise first-record dates become available.

EPP common name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Ruderal and agricultural weed of pastures, arable land, roadsides and urban wasteland, with pollen acting as a major aeroallergen for human populations in affected cities
Event summary: Although common ragweed has been present and naturalized in South Africa since at least the late 19th century, it was not previously regarded as a major aeroallergen until Ambrosia pollen was first consistently detected by the South African Pollen Network from 2019 onwards at several monitoring sites. During 2019–2024, aerobiological and eDNA metabarcoding studies demonstrated recurring Ambrosia pollen seasons in cities such as Durban, Potchefstroom, Pretoria, Johannesburg and Kimberley, and documented baseline sensitization to Ambrosia allergens in South African patients, highlighting ragweed as an emerging contributor to late‑summer respiratory allergy. By 2024, ragweed pollen was recognised as a growing aeroallergen of concern in South Africa, prompting calls for its inclusion in diagnostic testing panels and for improved management of established ragweed populations in urban and agricultural landscapes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing but previously overlooked naturalized populations of Ambrosia spp. in South Africa, combined with urban expansion, roadside disturbance and possibly favourable recent rainfall and temperature regimes, have increased the likelihood that ragweed reaches reproductive maturity and produces significant pollen near population centres; the establishment of a national pollen monitoring network since 2019 has also greatly improved detection and awareness of Ambrosia pollen. Internal mechanisms: no specific new African genotype has yet been identified; this episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a previously colonized subregion where external environmental change and improved monitoring have revealed a substantial aeroallergen burden rather than as a genetically driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – This new row has been added to capture the recent 2019–2024 recognition of common ragweed as a significant aeroallergen in South Africa, based on national pollen monitoring and sensitization data; it is classified as a re-occurrence in a subregion where the plant has been naturalized since the 19th century. The temporal bounds (2019–2024) are tied to the start of systematic pollen monitoring rather than to first botanical records, and some uncertainty remains about the exact onset and magnitude of health impacts, so the event should be retained but reviewed by a regional expert to refine dates and quantify burden.

EPP common name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Field crops (e.g. cotton, watermelon), orchards (avocado, date), degraded pastures, roadside and riparian vegetation
Event summary: Around 1990, Ambrosia confertiflora was first recorded in Israel near Zichron Yaakov and is reported as having been introduced to Palestine in the same period, most likely via contaminated seed mixtures for poultry and aquaculture imported from the southern USA and Mexico. From an initial focus near Shechem (Nablus) in the northern West Bank, the species spread rapidly along Nahal Shechem and downstream to the Alexander River, invading cultivated areas, riverbanks and nature reserves such as Wadi Qana. By about 2000 it had formed dense stands across parts of Samaria and the coastal plain, displacing native vegetation, invading agricultural land and establishing itself as a serious invasive weed in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction as a contaminant in imported seed mixes for poultry or aquaculture from the United States into the Nablus/Shechem area, followed by downstream dispersal along streams (Nahal Shechem, Alexander River) and facilitated by road construction, soil movement and intensive agriculture in the coastal plain and Jordan Valley. Additional spread was promoted by the absence of early coordinated control and by frequent disturbance along rivers, roads and in orchards and field crops. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity with production of numerous barbed achenes, efficient hydrochory (seed transport in rivers and wadis), vegetative spread from perennial rootstocks, and tolerance of a wide range of semi‑arid to mesic conditions, giving strong competitive ability in disturbed habitats and inherent capacity for geographic range expansion once introduced.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first well‑documented inter‑continental emergence of Ambrosia confertiflora into Asia (Israel and the State of Palestine), with large ecological and agricultural impacts. Corrected misclassification of the “first_detection” flag (now false, since global first detection predates 1990 in its native range) and standardized the country list to match the UN/Excel country list, setting both Israel and State of Palestine to [1990] based on national reports that date introduction into Palestine to 1990. Added Palestinian national‑report sources for introduction year and flagged the event for expert review mainly regarding the exact start year of widespread field detection in the West Bank, but recommend retaining the event and its classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode.

EPP common name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Riverside and wadi vegetation, degraded pastures, orchards (avocado, citrus, date), summer field crops (cotton, watermelon), urban and peri‑urban wasteland
Event summary: From the late 1990s into the 2000s, Ambrosia confertiflora underwent a massive expansion on both sides of the Green Line, especially along the Alexander River, Wadi Tirza and through Samaria into the northern Jordan Valley, where dense monospecific stands developed. During the 2000s and early 2010s the species spread further west into the Hefer Valley and the coastal plain and eastwards along wadis, invading orchards, pastures, summer field crops and protected areas while becoming one of the most harmful invasive plants documented in Israel and the occupied West Bank. By around 2017, infestations extended to additional regions including parts of Lower Galilee and the Negev, prompting coordinated national management plans and surveillance, although persistent populations remained entrenched along rivers, roadsides and agricultural landscapes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ongoing downstream transport of achenes in rivers and irrigation canals, movement of contaminated soil and machinery, expansion of irrigated agriculture and orchards, and lack of early coordinated management allowed rapid build‑up of seed banks and spread along linear corridors. Road and infrastructure development, together with repeated soil disturbance in orchards and row crops, further facilitated establishment and local dominance. Internal mechanisms: very high seed production with durable seed banks, vigorous clonal growth from perennial rootstocks, and ecological plasticity across semi‑arid to mesic habitats, leading to a dramatic increase in abundance and extent without evidence for a novel genotype; resurgence is therefore attributed mainly to external drivers (re‑occurrence) rather than evolutionary change in the weed.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major re‑occurrence episode representing the rapid expansion and intensification of the invasion in Israel and the State of Palestine from about 2000 to 2017, with extensive ecological and agricultural impacts and national‑level management responses. No change was made to the emergence‑type classification (re_occurrence = true, others = false), which is appropriate because the species was already present in Western Asia and no new genotype or host shift has been documented; this is a resurgence within the same sub‑region driven by external factors. The country string was standardized by replacing the vague “[2000s]” with “[2000]” for the State of Palestine to match the requested format; this year should be interpreted as the approximate onset of the large‑scale expansion phase rather than first introduction. Because the split between the 1990‑2000 and 2000‑2017 episodes is somewhat arbitrary along a continuum of spread, this event is flagged for expert review of the temporal boundaries, but it should be retained as one of the largest documented emergence episodes for this species.

EPP common name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Ruderal and disturbed vegetation along roadsides, agricultural field edges and other open disturbed habitats
Event summary: In 2023, Ambrosia confertiflora was documented for the first time as a naturalized alien in central Tunisia, marking the first well‑established Ambrosia species reported for the African vascular flora and the first known establishment of this species on the African continent. The plant was found forming small but established populations in several localities in central Tunisia, mainly in ruderal, disturbed habitats along roadsides and edges of cultivated fields, indicating local spread after an initially unnoticed introduction. At the time of reporting, populations remained geographically limited, but the authors highlighted a substantial risk of further expansion into disturbed and agricultural areas in North Africa if not managed early.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely accidental introduction via contaminated seed, fodder or grain trade from regions where Ambrosia confertiflora is established (e.g. the Americas or Western Asia), followed by establishment in road verges, waste places and agricultural margins that provide open, disturbed niches. Road construction, vehicle traffic and movement of soil along transportation corridors probably facilitated local dispersal of the burrs. Internal mechanisms: the same traits that promote invasiveness elsewhere—high reproductive output, buoyant and spiny achenes suited to animal and vehicle dispersal, vegetative regeneration from rootstocks, and tolerance of Mediterranean semi‑arid climates—underpin its initial geographic range expansion into North Africa; there is no specific evidence yet for novel genotypes, resistance or host shifts in Tunisian populations.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first confirmed inter‑continental emergence of Ambrosia confertiflora into Africa, documented by floristic work in central Tunisia and recognized as the first well‑established Ambrosia in the African vascular flora. Corrected misclassification of the “first_detection” flag (now false because global first detection of the species predates 1990 in its native range) so that the event is characterized solely as an inter‑continental emergence. The year 2023 is used as the detection/publication year; earlier unnoticed presence cannot be excluded but is not documented. Given that current populations are still geographically limited and impacts are mostly potential at this stage, the event is flagged for expert review in future updates (e.g. to adjust the date range or add further African countries if the species spreads), but it should be retained due to its high significance as the first continental establishment.

EPP common name: woollyleaf bur ragweed (woollyleaf bursage, bur ragweed, lagoonweed, woollyleaf franseria, woollyleaf povertyweed)
Host: Field crops (wheat and dry beans), vineyards (grapes), peach and loquat orchards, and adjacent disturbed grassland/roadside vegetation near Shfeya Junction in northern Israel.
Event summary: Ambrosia grayi, a perennial ragweed native to northern Mexico and the south‑central Great Plains of the USA, was first formally documented in Israel in June 2017, when a dense, spreading infestation was identified in vineyards, a peach orchard and adjacent cereal fields near the Shfeya agricultural school between Zikhron Ya’akov and Pardes Hanna. Over 2017–2024 the population persisted and expanded vegetatively within these cultivated fields, forming thousands of interconnected shoots over roughly 0.5–4 ha, prompting its categorization as an alien, quarantine weed and inclusion on the EPPO Alert List because of its potential to invade further agricultural land and contribute allergenic ragweed pollen. Intensive eradication efforts by Israel’s Plant Protection and Inspection Services and local land managers, including repeated herbicide treatments and delimiting a quarantine zone, have substantially reduced the infested area but have not yet achieved complete eradication by 2025, so the episode remains an ongoing, closely monitored inter‑continental introduction confined to a single focus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction into Israel was almost certainly unintentional, most likely via contaminated grain, animal feed, soil or machinery associated with agricultural trade, paralleling documented pathways for other alien Ambrosia species in the region. The infestation established in intensively managed agricultural landscapes (vineyards, orchards and arable fields) with repeated soil disturbance and irrigation, conditions that favor rhizomatous weeds and facilitate local spread along field margins, irrigation ditches and machinery tracks. Internal mechanisms: A. grayi reproduces vigorously via deep, long‑lived rhizomes capable of resprouting after drought and control measures, and can emerge across a broad range of temperatures (around 20/30 °C night/day) and soil moisture conditions, while producing a limited number of viable seeds that may aid occasional dispersal. This combination of clonal growth, stress tolerance and absence of specialized natural enemies in Israel underpins its ability to form dense colonies from a single introduction focus, although the small current range and aggressive eradication have so far constrained further expansion.
Review: retain – New inter‑continental emergence event added for introduction and establishment of Ambrosia grayi in Israel starting with formal detection in 2017. Supported by EPPO distribution and alert‑list records, Israeli botanical accounts (including the 2017 Kalanit article), and peer‑reviewed studies on distribution, allergenicity and weed biology; geographic fields (Asia, Western Asia, Israel) and event type (inter‑continental emergence only) are consistent with project definitions, and no evidence suggests additional multi‑country episodes that would warrant splitting this into multiple rows.

EPP common name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [≈1991, first identified near Anzali in Gilan Province; later spread along the Caspian coastal plain to Rezvanshahr, Talesh, Astara and other lowland sites]
Host: Invasive perennial weed of canals, wetland margins, roadsides, field margins and disturbed agricultural land in the humid Caspian lowlands of northern Iran
Event summary: Around the early 1990s Ambrosia psilostachya was first noted and later taxonomically confirmed from the Anzali area of Gilan Province on the Caspian coastal plain, representing the first well‑documented establishment of the species in the Southern Asia subregion. Subsequent surveys through the 1990s and 2000s showed rapid spread along canals, roadsides and wetland margins in Gilan and neighbouring provinces, with dense clonal stands forming in lowland agricultural landscapes. By the 2010s the species was regarded as an emerging invasive and quarantine weed in Iran, with management efforts focusing on mechanical removal and herbicide treatment of infested canals and fields but no realistic prospect of eradication in already colonized areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduced via contaminated crop seed, fodder or machinery associated with international trade, and then dispersed regionally along irrigation canals, road networks and other disturbed corridors in the humid Caspian lowlands. Expansion has been favoured by intensive irrigated agriculture, wetland drainage and continuous disturbance of field margins and canal banks. Internal mechanisms: Perennial rhizomatous growth, prolific clonal spread and abundant wind‑dispersed pollen and seeds promote local dominance and geographic range expansion without evidence for a distinct novel strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Cross‑checked with Tokasi et al. (2024, MDPI Plants) and earlier reports that cite an initial identification near Anzali in 1991 and confirm establishment and spread along the Caspian coastal plain through the 1990s–2010s.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/14/17/2611?utm_source=openai)) Asia already had A. psilostachya (e.g. Japan) before 1990, so classifying this as intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian subregion (Southern Asia) rather than inter‑continental emergence or first detection is appropriate. EPP common name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: Morocco [1994, first record near Settat; subsequent scattered records in northern and western Morocco]

Event summary: In 1994 Ambrosia psilostachya was documented for the first time in Morocco near Settat, adding a new country‑level occurrence within the already invaded Northern Africa subregion where the species had been naturalized in Algeria since at least 1918. Floristic work and later syntheses confirm its persistence in disturbed and ruderal habitats, with additional scattered sites reported in subsequent decades but no evidence of continent‑scale explosive spread. By the 2000s it was recognised as one of several alien ragweed species contributing to local allergenic pollen and ruderal weed floras in Morocco, although its documented impacts remain more localized than those of common ragweed (A. artemisiifolia).
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Secondary introduction within North Africa, probably via regional trade, contaminated crop material or movement of soil and road‑building materials, followed by spread along roadsides and other disturbed habitats. Internal mechanisms: Perennial rhizomes and seed production allow small founder populations to persist and expand locally once introduced, but available data suggest relatively limited regional spread compared with major invasion foci elsewhere.
Review: Decision: review. Floristic and aeroallergen syntheses confirm that A. psilostachya was first recorded in Morocco in 1994 near Settat and that it remains present mainly as localized populations in disturbed habitats.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394998562_Contribution_a_la_connaissance_de_la_flore_du_Maroc_notamment_de_plantes_exogenes_naturalisees?utm_source=openai)) However, Northern Africa already harboured established populations in Algeria from 1918, so the Moroccan record does not represent intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, nor a clear subregional resurgence. The previous coding of re_occurrence=Yes has therefore been corrected to re_occurrence=No to match the project definitions (spread into a new country within an already affected subregion). Given the apparently modest spatial extent and impact relative to major invasions in Italy, France, Iran and India, this event is flagged for expert review as a potentially lower‑priority, country‑level record that may fall below the top ten global emergence events for this species.

Internal mechanisms: Perennial life history with rhizomatous spread and wind‑dispersed pollen and seeds supports persistence of local foci once introduced, but available evidence points to a geographically limited naturalization rather than broad regional invasion.
Review: Decision: review (likely exclude). Tseng & Peng (2004) and subsequent Taiwanese databases clearly document a newly naturalized A. psilostachya population in Kaohsiung in 2000–2001, but show only a single small focus with no evidence of large‑scale spread or major impacts.([for.nchu.edu.tw](https://for.nchu.edu.tw/en/uploads/file/thesis/3eea2741-5e0b-44e3-bebb-f48042f27f4e.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Asia already harboured A. psilostachya (e.g. Japan, and later Iran) before 2000, so this Taiwanese record is not a global first detection and does not qualify as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. EPP common name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: Italy [pre‑1900 introductions to botanical gardens; major post‑1990 expansion along Tyrrhenian and Adriatic coasts and river corridors]
Host: Invasive weed of coastal dunes, sandy riverbeds, ruderal habitats and some agricultural margins in Italy
Event summary: Although Ambrosia psilostachya was first introduced to Italy in the 19th century (e.g. 1840s in a botanical garden) and recorded in the wild on the Tyrrhenian coast by the early 20th century, its most substantial expansion occurred from the late 20th century onward. Internal mechanisms: Strong clonal growth via rhizomes, tolerance of poor, dry and disturbed soils, high fecundity and efficient wind pollination enable rapid build‑up of dense stands once established, driving geographic range expansion and local dominance without evidence for a distinct new strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Recent reconstruction of the Italian invasion history shows that, after early introductions, A. psilostachya underwent major expansion from the 1990s onwards, now forming extensive populations along rivers and coastal dunes in Italy and representing one of the main non‑native strongholds of this species in Europe.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/11263504.2025.2485990?utm_source=openai)) Treating this as a re‑occurrence event (resurgence and spread within a subregion where the species has been present for more than a century) is consistent with the project’s definitions. No corrections to geography or event type were needed; this event clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for A. psilostachya.

EPP common name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: France [post‑2000 expansion from long‑established foci in Bouches‑du‑Rhône, Camargue and Hérault to additional Mediterranean and extra‑Mediterranean regions]
Host: Invasive weed of Mediterranean sandy grasslands and dunes, pastures, vineyards on sandy soils, and various ruderal habitats in France
Event summary: Ambrosia psilostachya was introduced to France at the end of the 19th century, with early records in Bouches‑du‑Rhône and subsequent spread to Camargue and Hérault during the first half of the 20th century. After a long lag phase, monitoring by French botanical conservatories and national databases revealed a marked increase in observations after about 2000, both in the core Camargue area (where it now forms dense stands in sandy grasslands and abandoned vineyards) and in other regions such as the Paris Basin, southern Saône‑et‑Loire, Alpes‑de‑Haute‑Provence, Var and Vaucluse. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional expansion in France appears linked to land‑use changes (abandonment of vineyards and pastures, urbanisation and infrastructure development), increased disturbance of sandy grasslands and road verges, and movement of contaminated soil or machinery between agricultural and construction sites; climate warming may also support persistence in more northerly regions. Internal mechanisms: A clonal rhizomatous growth form and tolerance of dry, sandy, nutrient‑poor substrates enable the formation of dense colonies that can dominate early‑successional and semi‑natural grasslands, promoting geographic range expansion within Western Europe without evidence for a distinct novel biotype.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). Multiple French sources document A. psilostachya as an emerging invasive species with a clear increase in the number and extent of populations since the 2000s, particularly in Camargue and other Mediterranean and western regions.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/283319666_Ecology_and_impact_of_an_emerging_invasive_species_in_France_western_ragweed_Ambrosia_psilostachya_DC?utm_source=openai)) This episode represents one of the main non‑native invasion foci globally and is therefore appropriately included among the largest emergence events. France lies in the UNSD Western Europe subregion, so coding continent=sub_regions as Europe/Western Europe and classifying the episode as re_occurrence (renewed expansion within a long‑invaded subregion) is consistent with the project rules.

Event summary: During the 1990s–2000s an unfamiliar ragweed was observed invading fields and common lands in Turuvekere taluk of Tumkur District, Karnataka, and was subsequently identified as Ambrosia psilostachya, representing its first confirmed occurrence in India. By the early 2010s surveys showed that western ragweed had colonized around 10 villages and invaded roughly 400 acres of cropland, horticultural and plantation fields and social forestry areas, forming dense stands that displaced grasses and increased management costs. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduced with contaminated imported seed, planting material or fodder, then spread within Tumkur District via local movement of soil, machinery, fodder and along road verges under semi‑arid conditions and grazing pressure. External drivers include agricultural intensification, land‑use change and insufficient early detection capacity. Internal mechanisms: The species’ perennial rootstock and extensive rhizomatous system, combined with tolerance of semi‑arid, sandy soils and the ability to regenerate after cutting or grazing, underpin rapid build‑up of dense stands and make control difficult, leading to regional range expansion within Southern Asia once established.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). Indian sources describe A. psilostachya as a new record for the country, restricted mainly to Tumkur District, but already invading about 400 acres of cropland, pastures and plantations and designated a quarantine weed, with dedicated delimiting surveys and eradication efforts undertaken.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122535/records/65de98846eef00c2cea09c3f)) This outbreak is clearly among the most impactful recent emergence events for the species in Asia and globally. Since Southern Asia already contained A. psilostachya in Iran by the early 1990s, the Indian outbreak is best coded as re_occurrence (a major increase in incidence within a previously affected subregion) rather than as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence or global first detection.

Host: Non‑crop ruderal vegetation and disturbed Mediterranean shrublands (roadsides, railways, waste ground) with occasional occurrence along agricultural field margins.

By the late 2010s, A. tenuifolia was still confined to a few coastal localities but was recognized in floristic surveys and allergenicity studies as a naturalized perennial ragweed of limited distribution in Israel.
