Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion facilitated by a perennial rhizomatous growth form, clonal spread via creeping roots, and tolerance of open, dry, disturbed Mediterranean habitats; local dispersal by seed and rhizome fragments allows maintenance of small but persistent colonies even though the species remains less invasive than other Ambrosia taxa in Israel.
Review: retain – Verified that A. tenuifolia was first recorded as an adventive plant in Israel in 1991 and that no earlier Asian records are known, so classification as a first detection for Western Asia and an inter‑continental emergence event is appropriate. Geographic fields (Asia / Western Asia / Israel) align with the UNSD scheme and sources consistently describe the taxon as a rare, localized perennial weed confined to a few coastal localities; no corrections to timing, geography or event type are required, and the cited floristic and allergenicity studies are relevant and sufficient for this event.

EPP common name: slimleaf bur ragweed, slimleaf burr ragweed, field ragweed
Countries: South Africa [≤2005 established alien; 2005–2015 continued persistence and local spread in Eastern Cape]
Host: Ruderal and semi‑natural vegetation (roadsides, disturbed grasslands) and agricultural field margins in Eastern Cape; potential weed of pastures and orchards, and a source of allergenic airborne pollen as part of the regional Ambrosia complex affecting humans.
Event summary: Ambrosia tenuifolia was introduced to South Africa well before 1990 and is documented as a non‑indigenous Asteraceae with naturalized populations, especially in the Eastern Cape Province. Through roughly 2005–2015, herbarium and checklist data confirm the continued presence and modest local spread of A. tenuifolia along roadsides, in disturbed grasslands and at field margins in Eastern Cape, consolidating its status as a localized alien ragweed alongside A. artemisiifolia and A. psilostachya. This long‑standing but patchy naturalization provided background inoculum for ragweed pollen in the region; from 2019 onwards, national aerobiological monitoring highlighted Ambrosia pollen as an emerging aeroallergen in several South African cities, although pollen loads are dominated by other Ambrosia species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Initial long‑distance introduction via contaminated seed or grain and subsequent regional spread along road and rail networks, together with ongoing disturbance of roadsides, overgrazed grasslands and urban fringes that maintain open ground suitable for colonization; climate warming may also favour persistence of subtropical ragweed species. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by clonal growth from rhizomes and a pioneer life‑history strategy (rapid colonization of bare soil, tolerance of drought and poor, sandy substrates) that allows survival and gradual spread in Eastern Cape landscapes, even though the species remains less abundant than other Ambrosia taxa.
Review: review – The presence of A. tenuifolia in South Africa (particularly Eastern Cape) is well supported by SANBI records and recent aerobiological work, but the specific 2005–2015 time span and its classification as a distinct “re‑occurrence” episode are weakly justified. Available sources indicate a long‑standing, localized naturalization rather than a clearly documented post‑1990 resurgence driven by external factors, and Ambrosia pollen impacts in South Africa appear to be dominated by other ragweed species. The re_occurrence flag has therefore been set to ‘false’, and this event is retained only provisionally as a description of ongoing establishment; it should be re‑evaluated to determine whether it truly ranks among the top 10 impact events for A. tenuifolia or whether South African impacts are better treated at the genus level.

EPP common name: slimleaf bur ragweed, slimleaf burr ragweed, field ragweed
Countries: Romania [1991–2020 (confirmed at C. A. Rosetti, Danube Delta; earlier reports from nearby villages are now treated as uncertain or refer to the same population)]
Host: Ruderal sandy sites, roadsides, disturbed grassland and an abandoned garden in the village of C. A. Rosetti (Danube Delta); potential invader of adjacent agricultural fields and pasture margins.
Event summary: In 1991, perennial ragweed plants collected from sandy roadsides and ruderal sites at C. A. Rosetti in the Danube Delta were deposited in the Bucharest agronomy herbarium and interpreted as Ambrosia psilostachya, masking the presence of A. tenuifolia in Romania for nearly three decades. Detailed taxonomic revision of these vouchers in 2019 and new field collections from the same locality in 2020 demonstrated that the perennial ragweed in the Danube Delta is in fact A. tenuifolia, revealing a naturalized population occupying about 100 m² with hundreds of shoots and scattered individuals in adjacent grassland and a derelict garden. Publication of this clarification in 2021 and an EPPO Reporting Service note in 2022 led to formal recognition of A. tenuifolia in Romania and identified the C. A. Rosetti population as a new Eastern European bridgehead for this species, with potential for further spread along sandy roadsides and into nearby agricultural and semi‑natural habitats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via contaminated seed or transport along the Danube corridor and regional road network from other invaded parts of Europe, coupled with disturbance of sandy soils, infrastructure development and land‑use change in the Danube Delta. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and strong clonal capacity (rhizomatous roots and root‑sprouting) that allow persistence and slow local expansion in warm, sandy, periodically flooded sites; the event primarily reflects taxonomic clarification and recognition of an already established population rather than evolution of a novel genotype or change in virulence, so it is best interpreted as a first detection and intra‑continental emergence into the Eastern Europe subregion rather than a re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Corrected the event year from “2010–2021” to “1991–2021” to reflect the earliest verified herbarium collection in 1991 and subsequent taxonomic revision and field surveys up to 2020–2021, and simplified the country field to emphasize the single confirmed locality at C. A. Rosetti while noting that other published localities are uncertain. With these adjustments, the event accurately represents the first confirmed detection of A. tenuifolia in Eastern Europe and its status as a localized but naturalized population in Romania, and classification as both a first_detection and an intra‑continental emergence (new sub‑region within Europe) is consistent with the definitions and with EPPO and primary taxonomic sources.

EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed

Event summary: From the early 1990s, giant ragweed rapidly increased in abundance across the US Corn Belt and parts of Canada as a major early‑emerging weed in conservation‑tillage and herbicide‑based soybean and maize systems. Through the 1990s and 2000s, regional surveys consistently ranked it among the most troublesome broadleaf weeds, with dense stands reducing soybean yields by 50% or more in heavily infested fields and threatening no‑till adoption. By around 2010, giant ragweed was widely established as a chronic management problem in many North American row‑crop regions, with persistent seedbanks and extended emergence periods sustaining infestations even where herbicide programs were intensified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of conservation tillage and no‑till systems, heavy reliance on a narrow set of post‑emergence herbicides, simplification of crop rotations (soybean–maize), and increased nutrient inputs created open, resource‑rich niches that favored large, early‑emerging annuals like giant ragweed. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity, long seedbank persistence, early season emergence and rapid growth giving strong competitive ability, and phenotypic plasticity in emergence timing and plant architecture allowed the species to capitalize on agronomic changes and dominate crop canopies.
Review: review – Retain as a major re‑occurrence event in the native North American range: timing, geographic scope and yield impacts are well supported by long‑term cropping‑system and survey studies. EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed

Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy, repeated use of ALS‑inhibiting herbicides (Group 2) in simplified soybean–maize rotations created strong selection pressure, while reduced tillage allowed survival and seed production of partially controlled plants. Internal mechanisms: evolution of ALS target‑site mutations and/or enhanced metabolism conferring high‑level resistance to multiple ALS‑inhibiting chemistries; resistant biotypes retained strong competitive ability and produced abundant seed, enabling them to dominate treated fields and increase in regional frequency.
Review: review – Retain as one of the largest internal re‑emergence events (evolution of ALS‑inhibitor resistance in the US Corn Belt). Start year adjusted to 1995–1996 (first field control failures) with 1998 as the year of formal confirmation, so the event window is now 1995‑2005. Countries field was simplified to “United States of America”, with state‑level details kept in the narrative. A peer‑reviewed conference paper on ALS resistance was added as a primary source, reducing reliance on a corporate news release and Wikipedia.([download.clib.psu.ac.th](https://download.clib.psu.ac.th/datawebclib/e_resource/e_database/agronomy/2002/Browse/pdf/A09-voglewede143234-Oral.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Host: Primarily glyphosate‑tolerant soybean and maize; also cotton; adjacent non‑crop habitats provide seed sources
Event summary: In 2004, glyphosate‑resistant giant ragweed was first confirmed in an Ohio soybean field, marking the earliest documented case of resistance to the dominant non‑selective herbicide used in glyphosate‑resistant cropping systems. Over the subsequent decade, additional resistant populations were confirmed across the eastern and central US soybean belt and parts of the Mid‑South, with growers reporting severe control failures, dense in‑crop stands and significant soybean and maize yield losses. By the mid‑2010s, glyphosate‑resistant giant ragweed was present in at least 10–11 US states, forcing widespread adoption of more complex herbicide programs and integrated tactics to keep infestations at manageable levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Massive expansion of glyphosate‑resistant crops from the late 1990s onward and repeated, often exclusive, use of glyphosate for in‑crop and fallow weed control created intense selection pressure; reduced tillage and limited crop‑rotation diversity further favored survival and spread of partially controlled plants. Internal mechanisms: evolution of glyphosate resistance, including non‑target‑site mechanisms (altered translocation, rapid necrosis response) and, in some populations, target‑site EPSPS mutations, conferred survival at field rates and enabled resistant biotypes to proliferate regionally.
Review: review – Retain: glyphosate‑resistant giant ragweed first confirmed in Ohio in 2004 and its spread across multiple US states in the 2000s–2010s clearly constitute a high‑impact re‑emergence event. Key documentation from the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database and US/Canadian research papers already present were kept as primary sources.([weedscience.org](https://www.weedscience.org/Pages/Case.aspx?ResistID=5278&utm_source=openai))

Event summary: In 2008, Canada confirmed its first glyphosate‑resistant giant ragweed populations in southwestern Ontario soybean fields after repeated control failures and follow‑up greenhouse tests. Over the early 2010s, surveys showed resistant biotypes to be more widespread in southern Ontario, with dense patches causing heavy yield losses where glyphosate remained the primary control tactic. By the mid‑2010s, management recommendations in affected regions had shifted toward diversified herbicide mixtures, pre‑emergence residuals and cultural measures to contain the spread and impact of resistant populations, and giant ragweed was recognised as Canada’s first glyphosate‑resistant weed.

Internal mechanisms: glyphosate resistance in giant ragweed populations, likely involving non‑target‑site mechanisms (reduced translocation, rapid necrosis) and possibly EPSPS target‑site changes, provided survival at field rates; the species’ early emergence and strong competitiveness then translated resistance into large yield and management impacts in affected fields.

EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Host: Maize, soybean and other summer crops in Northeast China; riverbanks, floodplains and disturbed urban/rural land; also an important source of allergenic pollen for humans
Event summary: Although introduced to China earlier in the 20th century (first records from Liaoning in the 1930s), giant ragweed underwent a marked expansion from the mid‑1990s onward in Northeast China, where it colonized riparian corridors and then invaded maize and soybean fields at high densities. During the 2000s and early 2010s, its range and local abundance increased across multiple provinces, with field observations and modelling studies documenting strong yield reductions in affected crops and significant suppression of native vegetation. By around 2015, giant ragweed had become one of the region’s most problematic invasive weeds, recognized both for its agricultural impacts and for heavy pollen production contributing to seasonal allergies in nearby urban areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased disturbance along rivers and transport corridors, expansion and intensification of summer crop production in Northeast China, and movement of contaminated grain and machinery facilitated spread; limited early detection and targeted control allowed populations to build large seedbanks. Internal mechanisms: high phenotypic plasticity, strong competitive ability under high nutrient and light conditions, and efficient dispersal along riparian and transport networks supported rapid geographic range expansion and high field densities, even without documented novel resistant biotypes during this period.
Review: review – Retain as a high‑impact invasion episode in Northeast China. Re‑typed from intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence to re‑occurrence only, because A. trifida has been present in China since at least the 1930s and the episode describes expansion and intensification within the same UN sub‑region (Eastern Asia), driven primarily by land‑use change and disturbance rather than a new genotype. EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Host: Roadsides, riverbanks and abandoned land; invasion into arable land including maize and soybean fields; major source of allergenic airborne pollen affecting human health
Event summary: In Japan, where giant ragweed was first recorded in 1952 at port locations, the species expanded markedly from about 2000 onward and is now widespread across much of the country, leading to its inclusion among Japan’s worst invasive alien species. During the 2000s and 2010s, dense stands developed along rivers, transport corridors and in some crop fields, locally reducing yields and displacing native flora while producing large quantities of allergenic pollen. Similar post‑2000 expansions and increasing allergenic and agronomic concern have been documented in the Republic of Korea. By around 2020, giant ragweed was widely recognized in these East Asian countries as both an agricultural and public‑health concern, and management guidelines emphasized early detection and coordinated mechanical and chemical control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of transport, trade and infrastructure development, coupled with frequent disturbance along rivers, roads and railways, created corridors for spread from initial introduction sites; incomplete control in urban and peri‑urban areas allowed large seed sources near cropland and residential zones. Internal mechanisms: high reproductive output, effective dispersal along waterways and disturbed linear habitats, and strong competitiveness in nutrient‑rich, open sites enabled long‑distance range expansion; high pollen production and allergenic potency amplified the perceived impact of invasion and spurred management responses.
Review: review – Retain as a major East Asian invasion event affecting both agriculture and public health. Re‑classified as re‑occurrence (no intra‑continental emergence), since A. trifida has been present in Japan since 1952 and the episode describes post‑2000 spread and impact within the same UN sub‑region (Eastern Asia). EPP common name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Host: Temperate grasslands of the Yili Valley (Xinjiang, China) and adjacent disturbed land; encroachment near cropland and settlements
Event summary: Beginning around 2013, giant ragweed invaded the hilly grasslands of the Yili Valley in Xinjiang, northwestern China, where it established dense stands on lower slopes and valley bottoms. Within roughly five years the weed formed single‑dominant communities in moist microsites, strongly suppressing native herbaceous species and reducing grassland productivity. By the mid‑2020s, field and experimental studies had documented that soil moisture strongly mediates the success of this invasion, and local managers regarded A. trifida as a serious emerging threat to temperate steppe ecosystems as well as nearby agricultural land in the Yili region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High soil moisture in low‑lying slope positions, local disturbance, and proximity to roads and settlements created favorable microsites in Yili grasslands; existing regional propagule pressure from invaded cropland and riparian zones allowed colonization of these new habitats. Internal mechanisms: strong growth response and competitive advantage under moist conditions, high fecundity and efficient seed dispersal along hydrological and anthropogenic pathways facilitated rapid dominance of invaded grassland patches once initial establishment occurred.
Review: review – Added new event to capture the well‑documented large‑scale invasion of Yili Valley grasslands (Xinjiang, China) since about 2013. This is one of the most impactful recent range expansions of A. trifida, with dense stands displacing native herbs and sharply reducing grassland productivity. It is classified as re‑occurrence because the species was already long established in China and this episode represents expansion into new habitats within the same country/sub‑region, driven mainly by environmental factors (especially soil moisture) and disturbance rather than a novel biotype.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40136506/?utm_source=openai))

Countries: Russian Federation [1990s–2000s expansion]; Ukraine [2000s]; Romania [2000s]; Hungary [2000s]; Serbia [2000s]; Croatia [2000s]; Italy [2000s]; France [2000s–2010s]; Montenegro [2024]
Host: Primarily riverbanks and floodplains, roadsides and disturbed land, with localized invasion of maize and sunflower fields; major producer of allergenic pollen affecting nearby human populations
Event summary: After scattered earlier records in the 19th and 20th centuries, giant ragweed expanded conspicuously in Central and Eastern Europe from about 2000 onward, with particularly rapid spread documented in parts of European Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Hungary and the western Balkans along major river systems and transport corridors. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability in fertile, disturbed soils, prolific seed production, and potential for long‑distance dispersal along rivers and human transport routes supported range expansion; European field studies suggest shifts in morpho‑functional traits that may enhance invasiveness in some invaded sites, supporting classification as re‑emergence in addition to intra‑continental spread.

The event has been re‑typed to intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence (with re‑occurrence set to No) to reflect spread into new European sub‑regions (Southern and Western Europe) alongside evidence of trait shifts in invaded populations, while respecting the rule that re‑occurrence should not co‑occur with intra‑continental emergence. Event summary: From about 2018, Wisconsin growers and researchers reported giant ragweed populations surviving labeled post‑emergence applications of PPO‑inhibiting herbicides such as fomesafen in soybean, despite existing resistance to ALS inhibitors and frequently to glyphosate. Subsequent greenhouse dose–response studies and field trials confirmed high‑level resistance to PPO inhibitors in several accessions and, in some cases, multiple resistance to ALS inhibitors and glyphosate as well. In response, Florida’s Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, together with USDA, expanded area‑wide management: large‑scale sterile insect technique (SIT) field trials were integrated with trapping, bait‑spray programmes, removal of preferred non‑commercial hosts around groves, and the creation and certification of Caribbean Fruit Fly Protocol "fly‑free" zones enabling export of grapefruit, oranges and other citrus to markets such as California, Texas, Japan and Korea. By around 1996, SIT evaluations and protocol‑driven management had reduced A. suspensa densities in designated citrus production zones to below detection thresholds for export certification, so that while the pest remained widely established in Florida, key protocol groves operated under lower, trade‑compatible population levels and reliance shifted toward monitoring, cultural control and post‑harvest treatments rather than emergency suppression.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The main external drivers were regulatory and market‑based rather than purely biological: the banning of ethylene dibromide as a fumigant, increasing domestic and international phytosanitary restrictions on fruit from caribfly‑infested areas, and the growth and geographic expansion of Florida’s citrus and specialty‑fruit industries made A. suspensa a major barrier to trade. Subtropical climatic conditions and a dense mosaic of commercial plantings and backyard host trees in central and south Florida allowed year‑round reproduction, maintaining high reinfestation pressure on export groves even where direct yield losses in citrus were often limited. California’s climate in parts of Los Angeles County, together with the abundance of backyard fruit trees and ornamental hosts in dense urban and suburban neighborhoods, provides permissive conditions for short‑term establishment following introduction. High levels of national and international travel and trade, especially through hubs such as the Los Angeles area, increase propagule pressure. Countries: United States of America (Pacific Northwest hazelnut industry – southwest Washington as the initial focus before 1990, with major spread through Oregon’s Willamette Valley from 1990 onward)

Event summary: In the decades leading up to 1990, Anisogramma anomala, endemic in eastern North America, was moved on infected nursery stock and scion wood into southwest Washington, where it became established on European hazelnut orchards and went largely unrecognized for several years. From roughly 1990 through about 2010, the disease front advanced at an estimated 2 km per year into Oregon’s Willamette Valley, the center of U.S. hazelnut production, resulting in a major regional epidemic that infected many orchards and forced extensive removal of highly susceptible cultivars such as ‘Barcelona’ and ‘Ennis’. By around 2010, widespread adoption of resistant cultivars, better sanitation and pruning practices, and targeted fungicide programs had greatly reduced new infections and allowed the regional industry to recover, even though the pathogen remains established in the landscape. ([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PHYTO.2001.91.12.1214?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The epidemic was driven primarily by long‑distance movement of infected but often asymptomatic Corylus planting stock from the eastern USA into the Pacific Northwest during the 1950s–1970s, followed by local nursery and ornamental plant movements that disseminated the pathogen within Washington and Oregon. The rapid expansion of large, genetically uniform orchards of very susceptible European hazelnut cultivars in a mild, wet climate created dense host populations where rain‑ and wind‑dispersed ascospores could sustain repeated infection cycles. Limited early awareness of the disease, its long latent period, and initially inadequate pruning and fungicide regimes allowed inoculum to build up to very high levels before effective management strategies were deployed. Internal mechanisms: Population studies indicate that the Pacific Northwest epidemic reflects introduction and expansion of a founder population from eastern North America, but there is no clear evidence for recent evolutionary change in virulence or host range; the event is therefore best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence in an already affected subregion, driven by human‑mediated spread and orchard design rather than by documented pathogen innovation. ([bpp.oregonstate.edu](https://bpp.oregonstate.edu/efb/location/maps-efb-epidemic?utm_source=openai))

Literature from APS journals, OSU epidemic maps and extension bulletins confirms timing, geography, spread (~2 km/year), and major production losses in Oregon and adjacent Washington. I have reclassified the event type from re_emergence=Yes to re_occurrence=Yes (with re_emergence=No) because the outbreak reflects human‑mediated introduction and expansion of an existing pathogen into a new intensive production zone within the same UNSD subregion, without clear evidence of recent pathogen evolution in host range or virulence; this aligns better with the project’s definitions of re‑occurrence vs. re‑emergence. In response, provincial authorities and growers implemented stricter movement controls, promoted aggressive removal of infected trees, and began an extensive replanting program with resistant cultivars and improved management practices, allowing slow recovery of production while the pathogen remains endemic in the region. Once introduced, the concentration of hazelnut orchards in the moist, cool lower Fraser Valley, combined with frequent spring rainfall events that favour ascospore release and infection, enabled rapid establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiological evidence indicates that British Columbia’s epidemic derives from the Pacific Northwest introduction rather than from a novel local lineage; no new virulence traits have been documented. Event summary: By the early 2000s, eastern filbert blight was causing severe disease in new commercial hazelnut plantings in southern Ontario, with some early orchards experiencing rapid decline and high tree mortality within just a few years of establishment. Over the 2000s and 2010s, as hazelnut acreage expanded in response to domestic processing demand and interest from Ferrero and other buyers, surveys and extension reports documented EFB in essentially all commercial orchards by 2018, with variable but often substantial disease incidence and repeated losses of susceptible cultivars. In the late 2010s, industry and research programs accelerated efforts to deploy resistant and tolerant germplasm, diversify cultivar choice, and refine fungicide and pruning strategies tailored to Ontario conditions, gradually shifting EFB from an almost prohibitive constraint on industry development to a chronic but more manageable production risk. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Ontario’s emergence event reflects expansion of commercial hazelnut acreage into environments where A. anomala was already present on native Corylus species, combined with widespread planting of susceptible European cultivars and selections originally bred under different pathogen populations. Market incentives created by Ferrero’s Brantford plant and rising hazelnut prices encouraged rapid orchard establishment from the mid‑2000s onward, often outpacing local experience with EFB management. Humid spring weather and frequent wetting periods favoured infection cycles, while the long latent period and initially limited adoption of pruning and fungicide programs allowed inoculum to accumulate in young blocks. Internal mechanisms: Available risk assessments and survey data suggest that Ontario harbours diverse, long‑established A. anomala populations distinct from those in the Pacific Northwest, and that some cultivars carrying resistance derived from western breeding programs show partial susceptibility under Ontario conditions. However, there is no clear evidence that these strains represent a newly evolved, more virulent form emerging during the 2000–2018 period; rather, the event is a re‑occurrence of a historically recognized constraint on hazelnut production, driven primarily by renewed planting of susceptible hosts into an endemic pathogen landscape and by mismatches between host resistance genes and existing local pathogen diversity. Review: review – Retain this event as a major emergence episode describing how EFB has constrained and reshaped the development of a commercial hazelnut industry in Ontario. OMAFRA’s Guide to Hazelnut Production and the 2018 survey summary confirm that EFB had been present at low levels for more than 15 years and was detected in all commercial orchards surveyed by 2018, while grower case studies (e.g. early Courtland plantings with massive losses around 2000–2003) illustrate severe impacts on initial orchards and highlight its role as the key disease limiting commercialization. I have reclassified the event type from re_emergence=Yes to re_occurrence=Yes (re_emergence=No) because the resurgence is best explained by expansion of C. avellana plantings into areas with long‑standing endemic pathogen populations and by cultivar choices, not by documented recent evolutionary change in A. anomala. EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) across the U.S. cotton belt, especially Texas High Plains and California’s San Joaquin Valley
Event summary: Beginning with major outbreaks in West Texas in 1991 and followed by severe mid‑season infestations in California’s San Joaquin Valley in 1994–1995, Aphis gossypii escalated from a sporadic pest to a key annual pest of U.S. cotton. During 1991–1997, mid‑season aphid populations frequently reached damaging levels over large acreages, with the 1995 San Joaquin Valley outbreak alone causing an estimated 5–6% lint yield loss and widespread sticky‑cotton problems that triggered multiple insecticide applications and emergency management discussions. By the late 1990s, improved understanding of aphid ecology, greater use of selective insecticides, conservation of natural enemies and better integration of aphid thresholds into IPM programs reduced the frequency of extreme outbreaks, although A. gossypii has remained a major management concern in parts of the U.S. cotton belt.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of broad‑spectrum pyrethroids and other insecticides against lepidopteran and lygus pests disrupted natural enemies, while adoption of plant growth regulators and higher nitrogen fertilization created lush, favorable host plants; hot, dry summers in key regions further favored aphid population growth and honeydew accumulation. Internal mechanisms: Field studies from this period documented substantial resistance of A. gossypii to several organophosphates and pyrethroids in parts of the U.S., contributing to control failures and justifying classification as a resistance‑linked re‑emergence of a previously minor pest.
Review: review – new event capturing the early‑ to mid‑1990s transformation of A. gossypii from a sporadic to key pest in the U.S. cotton belt, especially the 1991 Texas and 1995 San Joaquin Valley outbreaks; classification as re‑emergence (insecticide resistance plus agronomic changes) and the 1991–1997 window are well supported by extension and conference reports, but a curator should confirm the precise years and magnitude of yield losses using U.S. cotton loss survey data.

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in central Pakistan (Multan region)
Event summary: Between 1997 and 2000, bioassay monitoring of Aphis gossypii populations collected from cotton fields around Multan in central Pakistan revealed extremely high resistance ratios to seven pyrethroid insecticides compared with a susceptible laboratory strain. These findings indicated that field populations had evolved strong multi‑pyrethroid resistance, consistent with field reports of poor aphid control despite repeated sprays and prompting recommendations to modify insecticide programs and introduce alternative chemistries. Subsequent studies on Pakistani cotton aphid populations confirmed complex cross‑resistance patterns across organophosphate and carbamate insecticides as well, shaping regional insecticide resistance management strategies even though precise yield losses attributable to this resistance episode were not always quantified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroids in Pakistani cotton, often in mixtures and without sufficient rotation among modes of action, created strong selection pressure on A. gossypii populations; large contiguous cotton areas and limited non‑chemical control options further favored spread of resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Laboratory studies documented very high resistance ratios to multiple pyrethroids and changes in detoxification enzyme activity consistent with metabolic resistance and potentially altered target sites, making this a clear example of resistance‑driven re‑emergence of a long‑established pest.
Review: retain – Pakistan cotton aphid pyrethroid resistance between 1997 and 2000 is well documented by quantitative bioassays and clearly represents a major resistance‑driven re‑emergence event; geography (Southern Asia, Pakistan) and classification as re‑emergence are appropriate, though regional yield impacts are inferred rather than always reported explicitly.

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum), predominantly Bt cotton but also non‑Bt cotton in northern and central China
Event summary: Around 1999, shortly after rapid adoption of Bt cotton in the Yellow River and Yangtze River cotton regions of China, Aphis gossypii and other sucking pests resurged as secondary pests in fields where broad‑spectrum insecticide sprays targeting bollworm had been reduced. Over roughly 1999–2004, county‑ and household‑level surveys and economic analyses documented increasing aphid and other secondary pest problems across multiple northern provinces, leading to renewed insecticide use and concerns that these outbreaks eroded some of the anticipated economic and environmental benefits of Bt cotton. By the mid‑2000s, adjustments in integrated pest management, including more selective sprays, conservation of natural enemies and revised planting patterns, moderated aphid pressure, although A. gossypii has remained an important recurrent pest in Chinese cotton systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread adoption of Bt cotton reduced the need for frequent broad‑spectrum insecticide sprays that had previously suppressed a complex of secondary pests; in this new environment, combined with favorable weather and abundant host plants in surrounding landscapes, A. gossypii populations were able to increase to damaging levels. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel aphid biotype was implicated in this resurgence; available data are consistent with a re‑occurrence driven primarily by external agronomic and ecological change rather than by clear genetic change in the aphid.
Review: retain – this Bt‑cotton secondary‑pest resurgence in northern/central China (1999–2004) is well supported by economic and ecological studies and is among the most impactful modern A. gossypii outbreaks; classification as re‑occurrence (external agronomic driver) and geography (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) match UNSD regions and the event definition.

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) and, in some regions, nearby cucurbits and vegetables exposed to similar insecticide regimes in northern and eastern China
Event summary: From the late 1990s into the early 2000s, field monitoring in Shandong and other key cotton‑producing provinces of China documented rapid increases in resistance of Aphis gossypii to several major insecticide groups, including pyrethroids (e.g. fenvalerate), organophosphates (e.g. omethoate, carbosulfan) and later neonicotinoids (imidacloprid, acetamiprid). Comparative bioassays using samples collected in 1985, 1999 and 2004 showed resistance ratios climbing to very high levels in multiple cotton regions, and subsequent work revealed widespread and heterogeneous imidacloprid resistance across China, contributing to control failures on cotton and some cucurbit crops and raising concern about the sustainability of conventional chemical control programs. In the following decade, resistance‑management recommendations and rotation with alternative modes of action were promoted, but high and spatially variable resistance to several insecticide classes has persisted in many Chinese A. gossypii populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term, intensive use of organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids and later neonicotinoids on cotton and surrounding vegetable crops, often with limited rotation among chemistries, imposed strong selection for resistance. Internal mechanisms: Field and laboratory studies documented high resistance ratios to multiple insecticide classes and identified both enhanced detoxification (e.g. elevated esterases and P450s) and target‑site modifications (including nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and acetylcholinesterase changes), fitting the definition of a re‑emergence event driven by evolved insecticide resistance.
Review: review – end year adjusted from 2007 to 2004 so that the event aligns with years when very high resistance levels were directly measured (1985 vs 1999 and 2004) in Chinese cotton fields; classification as resistance‑driven re‑emergence is sound, but a curator may wish to consider whether post‑2004 resistance dynamics should be summarized as a separate, later episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in irrigated cotton systems of eastern Australia, mainly New South Wales and Queensland
Event summary: In the mid‑2000s, Australian cotton fields began to show declining control of Aphis gossypii with neonicotinoid seed treatments and foliar sprays that had previously been highly effective. By about 2010–2011, detailed bioassays confirmed strong resistance to imidacloprid and other neonicotinoids in cotton aphid populations from several cotton valleys, marking the first well‑documented neonicotinoid‑resistant A. gossypii populations on the continent and causing serious management difficulties in some seasons. From 2011–2012 onwards, industry‑wide resistance‑management programs, including rotation away from neonicotinoids, more selective aphicides and strengthened IPM guidelines, were implemented to slow further resistance increase and to recover acceptable control levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy reliance on neonicotinoid seed treatments and foliar sprays in Australian cotton, together with the aphid’s rapid parthenogenetic reproduction and multiple generations per season, created intense selection pressure; regional agronomic practices limited opportunities for susceptible immigration. Internal mechanisms: Bioassays and molecular work showed high levels of resistance to thiamethoxam and other neonicotinoids, likely mediated by overexpression of detoxification enzymes and changes in nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits, with cross‑resistance complicating management and necessitating formal resistance‑management strategies.
Review: retain – the Australian neonicotinoid resistance episode is well described and clearly among the most important resistance‑driven A. gossypii events globally; dates and geography are appropriate, though the precise onset (mid‑2000s) could be fine‑tuned by a curator using local monitoring records.

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cucurbit crops (melon, watermelon, zucchini, squash and pumpkin) in open‑field and greenhouse systems in southeastern and eastern Spain
Event summary: Cucurbit aphid‑borne yellows virus (CABYV) was first detected in 2004 in open‑field melon and zucchini crops in the Murcia region of Spain, where surveys already found high incidence of yellowing disease and Aphis gossypii as the dominant colonizing aphid. From 2004 through at least 2022, long‑term monitoring in major cucurbit‑growing areas (Murcia, Castilla‑La Mancha and Alicante) showed CABYV becoming the most prevalent virus in melon, squash, zucchini and watermelon, with incidences often exceeding 50–80% in symptomatic samples and frequent mixed infections with watermelon mosaic virus and other aphid‑borne viruses, leading to substantial yield and quality losses. By the early 2020s, CABYV remained widespread and difficult to control, and management focused on resistant or tolerant cultivars, cultural practices and vector management, but A. gossypii continued to drive recurrent, high‑impact virus–aphid outbreaks in Spanish cucurbit systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of cucurbit production in Mediterranean Spain, presence of multiple susceptible cucurbit hosts and weed reservoirs, and climatic conditions favorable to melon aphid population build‑up created conditions in which CABYV could become endemic; limitations of chemical vector control and increased organic production further complicated management. Internal mechanisms: No new aphid biotype has been implicated; the main biological factor is the inherent efficiency of A. gossypii (and to a lesser extent Myzus persicae) as a persistent vector of CABYV and other cucurbit viruses, so this episode is best described as a re‑occurrence of impact in a long‑established aphid–crop system rather than a genetically novel strain in the aphid.
Review: review – start year changed from 2011 to 2004 to reflect first detection and already high CABYV incidence in Murcia, and the event is now treated as a long linked episode of CABYV‑driven losses in Spanish cucurbits; classification as re‑occurrence (no new A. gossypii genotype) and geography (Southern Europe, Spain) are appropriate, but a curator may wish to refine quantitative estimates of yield loss.

EPP common name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in the southeastern U.S. cotton belt (e.g. Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Louisiana and neighbouring states)
Event summary: In 2017, cotton fields in coastal Alabama showing stunting, leaf rolling and blue‑green discoloration consistent with cotton blue disease were found to be infected with cotton leafroll dwarf virus (CLRDV), with abundant populations of Aphis gossypii present, marking the first confirmed CLRDV outbreak in U.S. cotton. Over the 2017–2019 seasons, CLRDV was detected across much of the southeastern and south‑central U.S. cotton belt, and in Alabama alone disease incidence of 3–30% in affected fields was estimated to have caused yield losses of about 560 kg/ha over roughly a quarter of the state’s cotton area in 2018, while surveys showed near‑100% infection in some sentinel plots even where symptoms were mild. By 2020, CLRDV had been confirmed in cotton in numerous states from Texas to Virginia, and although many U.S. cultivars proved tolerant and average regional yields remained acceptable, CLRDV and its efficient vector A. gossypii became a persistent concern, with management focusing on avoidance of highly susceptible varieties and improved understanding of vector ecology rather than on intensive aphid spraying, which has limited effect on this persistently transmitted virus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and rapid spread of CLRDV into an aphid‑rich, high‑value cotton production landscape created a new disease problem in a system where viral diseases of cotton had previously been negligible; widespread planting of cultivars of variable susceptibility and the presence of alternative host plants and aphid reservoirs favored virus establishment. Internal mechanisms: Aphis gossypii itself did not show evidence of new biotypes in this episode; instead, its existing capacity as the primary CLRDV vector in cotton, combined with persistent transmission biology, underpins the event, so it is best classified as a re‑occurrence of aphid impact mediated by a new virus rather than a re‑emergence caused by changes in the aphid.
Review: review – added to capture the major emergence of CLRDV in the U.S. cotton belt, where A. gossypii is the primary vector; geography (North America, Northern America, United States) and classification as a re‑occurrence (new virus in an established vector–host system) are appropriate, but exact yield loss estimates and the list of affected states should be rechecked against updated surveillance data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in rainfed grain production systems
Event summary: From the early 1990s through the mid‑2000s, ascochyta blight (black spot) dominated by Didymella pinodes became one of the most important constraints on field pea in southern and western Australia, with the pathogen present across virtually all pea-growing areas and causing frequent epidemics in seasons with cool, wet conditions. Meta‑analysis and field studies reported yield losses commonly around 10–25%, occasionally reaching 30–75% in severely affected crops, with national losses estimated at roughly AUD $20–25 million per year; these pressures led to development of tools such as the Blackspot Manager forecasting system, changes in rotations and sowing dates, and increased fungicide use, yet the disease has remained a major limitation on pea expansion.([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/8634086/ascochyta-blight-of-field-pea--pisum-sativum-?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of pea area into lower-rainfall and continuous-cropping zones; short or pea-on-pea rotations; retention of infected stubble that produces airborne ascospores; and seasons with prolonged cool, moist weather during early growth all favored intense epidemics and high carry‑over inoculum. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s hemibiotrophic lifestyle, prolific production of ascospores and pycnidiospores on residue and foliage, seedborne transmission, and the widespread use of cultivars lacking strong quantitative resistance underpinned a geographic and epidemic expansion of an already-adapted pathogen, without clear evidence of a single novel strain driving the outbreaks.
Review: Decision: review – This Australian episode clearly represents a high‑impact, multi‑year resurgence of D. pinodes in major pea areas and should remain among the top global events, but the original classification overstated internal evolutionary change. Re-emergence has been set from Yes to No because the literature attributes losses mainly to agronomic drivers (cropping intensity, rotation, environment, susceptible cultivars) and the polycyclic biology of an already established pathogen, without evidence for a distinct new strain or resistance-breaking genotype as the primary driver. All other geographic fields and sources are appropriate for this event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in Prairie grain systems
Event summary: Over the 1990s and 2000s, Didymella pinodes became the most common and economically important member of the ascochyta blight complex on field pea across the Canadian Prairies, where pea acreage expanded from under 0.1 million ha in the 1970s to around 1–1.5 million ha. Surveys and yield‑loss studies showed chronic mycosphaerella blight with average yield losses near 10% and reported losses up to 30–80% in heavily infected crops or trials under cool, wet conditions, making ascochyta/Mycosphaerella blight the primary foliar disease of pea in western Canada and a major constraint on both yield and seed quality.([collectionscanada.gc.ca](https://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/s4/f2/dsk2/ftp03/MQ37569.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of pea acreage in short rotations on the Prairies; use of cultivars bred mainly for resistance to Ascochyta pisi rather than D. pinodes; frequent cool, moist weather from late vegetative stages through pod fill; and widespread retention of infested residue and use of seed with low levels of ascochyta infection created persistent high inoculum pressure and favored severe epidemics. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes’ superior competitive fitness within the ascochyta complex, ability to survive for years in seed and residue, and efficient splash‑ and wind‑dispersed sporulation allowed it to dominate disease complexes and drive recurrent yield loss, but available evidence points to gradual selection within a long‑present population rather than emergence of a single novel genotype.
Review: Decision: review – This event represents a major, well‑documented regional re‑occurrence of severe D. pinodes–driven mycosphaerella blight in a very large production area and should remain in the high‑impact set. However, re_emergence has been corrected from Yes to No, as available Canadian work attributes the increasing dominance of D. pinodes primarily to cropping patterns, seedborne inoculum and environmental conditions rather than to a clearly defined new strain or resistance-breaking pathotype. The country, subregion and continent fields are consistent with the Canadian Prairies focus, and event-specific sources were replaced with Canada-focused extension and research documents that better quantify local impact.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in temperate Atlantic and northern French production regions
Event summary: From roughly 1990 through the mid‑2000s, Mycosphaerella blight caused by Didymella pinodes was consistently identified as the most destructive foliar disease of pea in France, particularly in Atlantic and northern production areas with cool, wet springs. Field trials and modeling studies indicated that in about seven years out of ten, Mycosphaerella blight reduced yields by around 20% on average, with documented loss ranges up to 30–70% under highly conducive conditions, prompting widespread preventive fungicide programs and intensive research on disease–yield relationships and resistance but without eliminating the pathogen as a chronic constraint on pea.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229642943_A_simple_model_of_pea_Pisum_sativum_growth_affected_by_Mycosphaerella_pinodes?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large and relatively intensive pea acreage in short rotations with cereals, frequent conservation of infected pea debris, and humid temperate weather during stem elongation and flowering provided repeated opportunities for early infection and rapid canopy blighting; economic incentives favored systematic fungicide programs rather than major shifts away from pea. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes’ ability to infect all aerial organs, produce abundant ascospores on senescent tissue, and cause substantial seed infection, combined with limited durable host resistance, maintained high pathogen pressure but there is no strong evidence that a discrete new genotype drove these French epidemics; this episode is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence in an established pathosystem.
Review: Decision: review – This new event has been added because French pea production is repeatedly cited as one of the systems most severely affected by D. pinodes, with long‑term average yield reductions of about 20% and higher losses in bad years, clearly placing it among the top global impact episodes. It is classified as a re-occurrence (chronic, climate‑ and management‑driven disease) with no evidence of a novel strain; geographic fields (Europe | Western Europe; France) match UNSD conventions. Sources focus on French yield‑loss quantification and population studies; this event should be retained after expert review of the chosen time window.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in highland rainfed smallholder systems
Event summary: Between the early 1990s and mid‑2010s, ascochyta blight of field pea, with Mycosphaerella/Didymella pinodes as the dominant pathogen, was repeatedly reported as one of the most widespread and destructive diseases of pea in the Ethiopian highlands, including Arsi, Bale and southern highland zones. Regional surveys and experiments indicate typical yield losses of 25–70%, with near‑total crop failure in susceptible landraces under persistently wet high‑altitude conditions, and more recent trials have shown grain yield more than doubling under intensive fungicide protection compared with unsprayed controls, underscoring the disease’s major impact on food security and income.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/350755059_Grain_Yield_and_Yield_Components_of_Field_Pea_Pisum_sativum_L_As_Influenced_by_Ascochyta_Blight_Mycosphaerella_pinodes_Disease_in_the_Highlands_of_Bale_Oromia?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and continued importance of field pea as a staple legume in highland Ethiopia; reliance on susceptible local landraces or only moderately resistant varieties; dense stands planted in cool, humid environments with long leaf‑wetness periods; and widespread use of farm‑saved seed carrying ascochyta infection all contributed to intense, recurrent epidemics. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes is considered the main pathogen within the Ethiopian ascochyta complex and shows strong aggressiveness on pea, but available studies emphasize high inoculum pressure and environment rather than distinct new genotypes; the episode is therefore best categorized as severe re‑occurrence rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Decision: review – This new African highlands event has been added because Ethiopian sources consistently rank D. pinodes–driven ascochyta blight as the most severe foliar disease of field pea, with large, quantified yield losses and widespread geographic extent, making it clearly among the most impactful modern episodes for this pathogen. It is classified as a re-occurrence (longstanding pathogen with repeated severe epidemics), with continent/subregion/country fields aligned to UNSD (Africa | Eastern Africa; Ethiopia). Given the societal importance of pea in Ethiopia, this event should be retained after further expert validation of severity estimates and time bounds.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in humid eastern Chinese production (e.g. Zhejiang Province)
Event summary: From the early 2000s through at least the mid‑2010s, repeated ascochyta blight epidemics affected field pea in humid eastern Chinese regions such as Zhejiang Province, where surveys of diseased crops at multiple locations recovered only Ascochyta/Didymella pinodes from 65 isolates, confirming it as the predominant causal agent. Chinese and global syntheses estimate typical yield losses of around 10–30% from ascochyta blight in China under conducive conditions, with greater reductions in susceptible cultivars, leading to recommendations for fungicide sprays and screening for improved resistance to manage this chronic, climate‑driven disease pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27148177/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of pea cultivation in warm, humid monsoon climates with frequent rainfall during vegetative growth and flowering; dense canopies; and use of susceptible local varieties or breeding lines created environments highly favorable to D. pinodes infection and spread. Internal mechanisms: The surveys and pathogenicity tests demonstrate that D. pinodes is well adapted to these environments and dominant within the ascochyta complex, but they do not implicate a discrete novel genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a significant regional re‑occurrence in an already globally distributed pathogen.
Review: Decision: review – This new event has been added to capture high, recurrent ascochyta blight pressure in humid eastern Chinese pea regions where surveys showed D. pinodes as the sole or dominant pathogen and reviews report substantial typical yield losses. It is classified as re-occurrence rather than emergence, because pea ascochyta blight and D. pinodes were known in China earlier, and no distinct new pathotype is described. Geography (Asia | Eastern Asia; China) follows UNSD; time bounds are approximate and should be validated against more detailed national data before final retention.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) and other solanaceous crops (e.g. tomato, pepper) in northern Mexico and the south‑western/central United States
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, a new potato disorder later termed zebra chip was first observed in commercial fields near Saltillo, Mexico, and by around 2000 similar symptoms appeared in potato fields in south Texas, USA. Over roughly 2000–2006 the disease intensified and became economically important, causing serious yield and quality losses in Texas and then in additional south‑western and central U.S. potato‑growing areas while remaining closely associated with high populations of the native potato/tomato psyllid. By the mid‑2000s, zebra chip and its B. cockerelli vector were recognized as a major production problem across much of northern Mexico and the western/central United States, prompting substantial research investment and major changes in insecticide use and crop management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic expansion of irrigated potato production in warm regions of northern Mexico and the southern United States, availability of year‑round solanaceous hosts, and movement of infested planting material and equipment facilitated high psyllid densities and rapid spread of the new disorder. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), a previously undescribed phloem‑limited bacterium vectored by B. cockerelli, converted a long‑known foliar pest into the driver of a severe tuber disease, representing a re‑emergence of the psyllid’s impact through a novel pathogen association and increased virulence/pathogenicity in potato relative to historical psyllid yellows.
Review: retain (minor correction). Event represents the primary modern emergence of zebra chip associated with B. cockerelli and CLso in Mexico and the southern/central USA, clearly one of the globally most impactful episodes (large yield and quality losses, tens of millions of dollars in damages). The event year has been slightly extended from 1994–2005 to 1994–2006 to reflect documentation that severe economic impacts in Texas continued through 2005–2006. Countries, continents and sub-regions correctly reflect Mexico (South America | Central America) and the United States (North America | Northern America). Classification as re-emergence (new pathogen association greatly increasing impact of a long-established pest) without first-detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate. Sources (Crosslin et al. 2010 Plant Health Progress; Nebraska Extension EC1905; reviews of zebra chip disease and B. cockerelli) are relevant and sufficient for this major event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Greenhouse and field tomato, capsicum, potato, tamarillo and other solanaceous crops
Event summary: In the summer of 2005–2006, Bactericera cockerelli invaded New Zealand, with the first authenticated detections made in May–June 2006 in glasshouses and nearby outdoor crops around Auckland. Over the next three years the psyllid spread rapidly by natural dispersal and human-assisted movement of infested nursery plants, becoming established across much of the North Island and the northern South Island and infesting greenhouse and field solanaceous crops. By 2009 the species was widespread and regarded as a serious invasive pest, leading authorities to abandon eradication and focus on long‑term management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade and the movement of infested plant material or contaminated packaging most likely introduced the psyllid from the Americas into New Zealand; once introduced, a suitable temperate climate, extensive greenhouse production and widespread solanaceous hosts facilitated establishment and rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: No major intrinsic biological change relative to American populations has been documented; this event primarily reflects geographic range expansion into a previously pest‑free continent, enabled by the existing association between B. cockerelli and CLso and the psyllid’s strong dispersal capacity.
Review: retain (minor clean‑up). Event correctly captures the first establishment of B. cockerelli in New Zealand as an inter-continental emergence into Oceania, which has had major economic consequences. Sub-region and country fields match the UNSD scheme (Oceania | Australia and New Zealand; New Zealand [2006]). The main edit is removal of a duplicated NZPPS article in the source list; remaining sources (Teulon et al. on incursion and dispersal, EPPO distribution record, and New Zealand pest-management papers) provide strong documentation of timing, spread and impact.

Host: Potato (field crops), tamarillo, greenhouse tomato and capsicum
Event summary: From 2008, soon after establishment of B. cockerelli, New Zealand growers and diagnosticians reported severe foliar symptoms and internal tuber discoloration in potatoes and other solanaceous crops resembling zebra chip. During 2008–2010, Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum was detected in symptomatic potatoes, tamarillo and other hosts, confirming a new plant disease complex tightly associated with the invasive psyllid. By the early 2010s, zebra chip and related disorders transmitted by B. cockerelli were causing major yield and quality losses in potatoes and tamarillo, triggering substantial industry investment in research, surveillance and integrated management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid nationwide spread and high densities of the recently introduced psyllid in both greenhouse and field production systems, coupled with susceptible cultivars and initially limited awareness and control experience, allowed CLso to disseminate widely before effective management practices were in place. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of CLso haplotypes in New Zealand via B. cockerelli constituted a novel strain/genotype emergence event for the region; the combination of an efficient vector and a new phloem‑limited bacterium resulted in increased virulence/pathogenicity compared with prior psyllid feeding damage alone, and created a high-impact vector–pathogen complex in key solanaceous crops.
Review: retain. This event correctly distinguishes the emergence of CLso and zebra chip disease in New Zealand (a re-emergence of B. cockerelli’s impact via a new pathogen association) from the earlier vector incursion. Oceania and sub-region coding are correct, and classification as re-emergence without intra-/inter-continental emergence matches the definitions. Sources (JIPM biology/management paper, Plant Health Progress review, EPPO distribution, national factsheets) are appropriate and specific to this disease phase.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) and other solanaceous crops
Event summary: From about 2009, large zebra chip outbreaks associated with dense populations of Bactericera cockerelli were documented in commercial potato fields in Honduras and subsequently in neighboring Central American countries, building on earlier reports from Mexico and Guatemala. Over the early 2010s, the psyllid–CLso complex spread and became established across key highland potato‑growing areas of Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and El Salvador, causing severe foliar symptoms, yield reductions and tuber quality defects at times affecting most plants in infested fields. By the mid‑2010s, zebra chip associated with B. cockerelli and CLso was considered widespread and economically important in multiple Central American countries, raising regional concern for the sustainability of potato and other solanaceous crop production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional trade and movement of seed potatoes and other planting material, limited vector control capacity, and continuous or overlapping potato cropping systems facilitated dissemination of the psyllid and CLso within the Central American highlands; suitable cool highland climates supported high vector and pathogen pressure. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks reflect the spread of existing CLso haplotypes A and B within established B. cockerelli populations rather than the emergence of new genotypes; the main mechanism is high inoculum pressure and efficient transmission by the psyllid, leading to a pronounced resurgence of disease severity in areas where psyllids had historically been present but zebra chip had not previously caused such large, multi-country epidemics.
Review: retain with corrections – review. This event appropriately captures a major regional resurgence of zebra chip in Central America but required several adjustments. (i) Country start years have been refined to better match available evidence: Honduras [2009] (severe outbreaks documented by 2009), Guatemala [2009] (disease known earlier but large regional epidemics evident by late 2000s), Nicaragua [2011] and El Salvador [2012] (following EPPO reporting of first CLso/B. cockerelli findings). (ii) Under the UNSD-based scheme, these countries all lie in the South America | Central America sub-region, so no intra-continental emergence flag is used, consistent with guidance not to treat spread to additional countries within the same sub-region as intra-continental emergence. (iii) The event is re-classified as re-occurrence only (re-emergence set to false): the available literature indicates regional spread of existing CLso haplotypes A/B and increased disease incidence driven mainly by external drivers (trade, cropping systems), without clear evidence for new genotypes or other intrinsic changes in B. cockerelli in this period. I extended the end year from 2013 to 2015 to include the Boynton Beach captures documented by FDACS, and clarified that the first inter-continental emergence into North America occurred earlier in California (1986), so this Florida sequence should not be coded as inter-continental emergence. Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Imported fruit and backyard or ornamental host trees (guava, citrus, stone fruits and other tropical/subtropical hosts) in urban and suburban areas
Event summary: Following the first Western Hemisphere record of Bactrocera correcta in Garden Grove, Orange County, California, in August 1986, the species was repeatedly detected in California from the early 1990s through 2012, mainly in the greater Los Angeles–Orange County region and other urban fruit-growing areas. Surveillance records compiled by state and federal agencies show numerous detections of individual flies and small clusters over this period, each prompting delimitation trapping, regulatory quarantines and localized eradication operations. Despite frequent incursions, intensified trapping, male-annihilation treatments and host-fruit removal meant that each detected infestation was declared eradicated, and B. correcta is still considered absent from California, though it remains a key target of the state’s invasive fruit fly detection network.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large volumes of air travel and trade between California and tropical fruit-producing regions in Asia, including both legal and smuggled shipments of fresh fruit, create repeated opportunities for introduction; widespread backyard plantings of guava and other host trees in urban and suburban landscapes provide resources where introduced flies can survive long enough to be trapped. Strong regulatory frameworks and public concern in California lead to rapid, resource-intensive responses each time a fly is detected. Internal mechanisms: No evidence indicates new strains or altered virulence; the incursions are driven by repeated introduction pressure acting on a polyphagous, high-fecundity species whose biology supports transient establishment but which has so far been eradicated whenever detected.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The California sequence is clearly one of the most important emergence-related episodes for this species because of the number of detections and the scale of eradication programmes. However, the previous classification treated it as an inter-continental emergence, whereas the true first inter-continental event for North America occurred with the initial 1986 detection in Orange County, which lies outside the 1990+ event window. I therefore classify the 1990–2012 sequence as re-occurrence only (inter_continental_emergence set to 'false') and retain the 1990 start as marking the beginning of a long period of recurrent detections. The summary is supported by the EENY/IN357 fact sheet, the APHIS host-plant PRA and analyses of tropical fruit fly incursions in California, but experts may wish to confirm whether later California detections (if any after 2012) should extend the end date.

Countries: United States of America – California (San Jose, Santa Clara County) [2025]
Host: Urban and suburban backyard and ornamental fruit trees (e.g. guava and other host fruits) in residential areas of San Jose
Event summary: Between 21 and 22 July 2025, three guava fruit flies were trapped in residential areas of San Jose, Santa Clara County, California, confirming a new breeding incursion of Bactrocera correcta into the San Francisco Bay Area. On this basis, the California Department of Food and Agriculture issued a Proclamation of Emergency Program, delimiting a roughly nine-square-mile treatment zone around the detection sites and initiating intensive male-annihilation treatments, with the option of foliar bait sprays and host-fruit removal where evidence of breeding populations occurred. The emergency programme was authorised through 17 May 2026 (three projected life cycles) to achieve eradication, and by mid-2026 CDFA’s guava fruit fly regulatory page listed no active quarantine boundaries, consistent with successful elimination of this incursion.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The San Jose infestation was almost certainly introduced via infested fruit carried in passenger baggage or informal trade from endemic regions of Asia, facilitated by the Bay Area’s dense international travel connections; the presence of numerous host trees in residential yards provided suitable habitat for a transient breeding population. Internal mechanisms: As in earlier California and Florida incursions, there is no evidence of a novel strain or enhanced virulence, and the event is best interpreted as a human-mediated geographic range expansion of a highly polyphagous fruit fly into a climatically suitable but non-native region, followed by eradication rather than establishment.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event is retained as a distinct high-impact re-occurrence episode because CDFA and Santa Clara County documents confirm a localized breeding infestation in San Jose and a substantial, multi-year emergency eradication programme. I corrected the timing and classification: official findings show that detections occurred between July 21–22, 2025, not in 2024, and that the emergency programme was planned through May 17, 2026; I therefore changed the event years to 2025–2026 and the country entry to 'United States of America – California (San Jose, Santa Clara County) [2025]'. I also re-set inter_continental_emergence to 'false' and re_occurrence to 'true' only, because North America’s inter-continental emergence occurred earlier in California (1986), and the 2025 San Jose infestation is another re-introduction into an already previously invaded continent. These corrections are based on the 2025 CDFA emergency proclamation and the County of Santa Clara information page and should be checked by an expert before finalisation.

Countries: Australia – incursions detected in Kununurra, Western Australia [1997–2001], outside the normal eastern coastal range

Event summary: In 1997, cucumber fruit fly was detected for the first time in Western Australia at Kununurra in the tropical Ord River irrigation area, representing an incursion beyond its usual eastern Australian coastal range. Over the period 1997–2001, occasional adult specimens continued to be found in Kununurra north of 29°S, prompting intensified surveillance and quarantine measures aimed at preventing establishment and southward spread. Subsequent distribution reviews concluded that the species had not established persistent populations in Western Australia and that detections south of 29°S should be treated as transient incursions, with Victoria and South Australia remaining free of the pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Anthropogenic movement of infested cucurbit produce or planting material within Australia, combined with expanding irrigated cucurbit production and favourable tropical climate in the Ord River region, likely introduced Z. cucumis into northern Western Australia and allowed short‑term population build‑up. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) at the warm tropical edge of its environmental niche within the Australia and New Zealand subregion, although the species did not achieve long‑term establishment beyond its historical eastern range.
Review: retain – The Western Australia (Kununurra) incursion between 1997 and 2001 is well supported by Dominiak & Worsley’s distribution review, the EPPO Reporting Service 2018/177 note, and the WA invertebrate incursions list. The event years, geography (Oceania / Australia and New Zealand subregion / Australia), and interpretation as a limited re‑occurrence within an already affected UNSD subregion (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) are consistent with project definitions. I have refined the event’s source_urls to cite the specific Dominiak & Worsley Part 1 paper and the WA incursions table instead of the generic ScienceDirect “Cucumis” topic page; no other field changes are recommended.

Countries: Australia [2025]; New Zealand (importing country affected via trade suspension; no evidence of establishment) [2025]
Host: Exported cucurbit crops including cucumber (Cucumis sativus), pumpkins and squash (Cucurbita spp.), zucchini, rockmelon and honeydew melon (Cucumis melo), and watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) produced in Z. cucumis–endemic areas of Australia
Event summary: In 2025, live larvae of cucumber fruit fly were detected in cucurbit consignments exported from Australia to New Zealand under the Winter Window pathway, revealing a failure in existing pre‑export mitigation measures for this endemic pest. Following notification by New Zealand’s Ministry for Primary Industries on 20 August 2025, Australia’s Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry issued Industry Advice Notice 2025‑46 and announced the immediate suspension of the Winter Window export pathway for cucurbits, temporarily halting trade of multiple cucurbit commodities to New Zealand while measures were reviewed. The incident was managed through investigation of pathway failures, updates to import and export requirements and corrective actions in Australian production and packing systems, with the pathway later reinstated once confidence in risk management was restored.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High volumes of cucurbit exports from Z. cucumis–endemic production regions in Australia to New Zealand under the seasonal Winter Window protocol, combined with limitations in field and postharvest risk‑mitigation measures, allowed infested fruit to pass through the system and be detected at destination, triggering suspension of the pathway and short‑term market access losses. Internal mechanisms: No reports indicate any novel genotype, resistance or host expansion; the event reflects operational and systems failures in managing an endemic pest, rather than biological change in the fly.
Review: review – The 2025 detection of live Z. cucumis larvae in Australian cucurbit consignments to New Zealand and the resulting suspension of the Winter Window pathway are clearly documented by DAFF Industry Advice Notice 2025‑46 and corroborated by Micor’s cucumber export page (which records the suspension and its lifting). Year, continent, UNSD subregion and the inclusion of both Australia and New Zealand in the countries field (with New Zealand only as the importing country imposing restrictions, and no evidence of establishment) are correct. I revised the mechanism_or_driver text to remove unsupported speculation about warmer winters and to focus on the documented trade pathway and systems factors, and I replaced general distribution papers in source_urls with the two regulatory documents that directly describe this event. Classification as a re‑occurrence (trade pathway failure for an endemic pest within the same UNSD subregion, with no inter‑continental emergence) is reasonable but somewhat interpretative, so I recommend that the event type be checked by the project team.
