Surveys using cuelure traps and fruit sampling during the early 2000s showed that the species became established and locally abundant on cucurbits and some other hosts throughout these new areas. By around 2006, Z. cucurbitae was widespread and regarded as a major cucurbit pest across much of Western and parts of Central and North‑eastern Africa, with ongoing management challenges but no clear continent‑wide eradication or containment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing regional trade and movement of infested cucurbit fruit and vegetables, weak quarantine at land borders, and expansion of irrigated vegetable production facilitated the rapid spread from long‑infested eastern Africa and Indian Ocean islands into West, Middle and North‑eastern Africa. Internal mechanisms: the species’ broad host range, high reproductive rate, and strong dispersal capacity underpinned its capacity for geographic range expansion within Africa (geographic range expansion – inherent).

Corrected sub_regions to include Northern Africa because Sudan is classified there in the UN/Excel scheme, and standardised the country list to use the official country names from the “Country” sheet (e.g. Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo). Classification as intra‑continental emergence (spread from previously infested Eastern Africa into new African sub‑regions) is appropriate and should be kept.

Host: Cucurbit crops and associated wild cucurbits
Event summary: During 2009–2013, first voucher‑confirmed records of melon fly were obtained from additional East African countries, notably Uganda, Burundi, Ethiopia, Malawi and Mozambique, extending its known range beyond earlier coastal East African foci in Tanzania and Kenya. Initial detections relied on trapping and larval rearing from infested cucurbits, which quickly showed that the species was established in smallholder and peri‑urban vegetable systems. By the mid‑2010s, melon fly was recognized as an invasive cucurbit pest across most of eastern Africa, with continued low‑ to moderate‑level populations in some new areas but a clear risk of severe yield loss if populations increased.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: spread was likely facilitated by cross‑border trade and informal movement of infested fruits, coupled with increasing cucurbit cultivation in East Africa and limited coordinated surveillance until the 2010s. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity, polyphagy on multiple cucurbit and some non‑cucurbit hosts, and thermal tolerance allowed establishment across a wide range of agroecological zones within Eastern Africa (geographic range expansion – inherent).
Review: Review – Keep this episode but reclassified it from “intra_continental_emergence” to “re_occurrence” and restricted sub_regions to Eastern Africa. Under the project’s definitions, intra‑continental emergence is reserved for spread into new UN sub‑regions; melon fly was already established in the Eastern Africa sub‑region (Tanzania, Kenya) since the 1930s, so the 2009–2013 expansion into additional Eastern African countries represents a major increase in incidence and range within an already affected sub‑region. Years and country first records match De Meyer et al. 2015. Classification as a re‑occurrence driven by external factors (trade, cropping expansion) is therefore more consistent with the scheme and should be reviewed and confirmed.

Countries: Benin [2004]; Burkina Faso [2000]; Cameroon [2002]; Côte d’Ivoire [1999]; Guinea [2000]; Mali [2000]; Niger [2004]; Senegal [2003]
Host: Field‑grown cucurbits (melon, cucumber, pumpkin, squash) in smallholder and peri‑urban systems
Event summary: Following initial detections in West and Central Africa around 1999–2004, melon fly populations built up substantially in the 2000s in irrigated vegetable zones of countries such as Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, Niger and Senegal. Field surveys and fruit sampling during this decade showed high infestation rates in cucurbit fields, with melon fly becoming one of the dominant cucurbit‑infesting tephritids in several regions. By the end of the 2000s, recurrent heavy infestation episodes and associated yield losses had turned the species into a key constraint on cucurbit production in many West African production basins, with farmers resorting to frequent insecticide applications and other ad hoc control measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of irrigated dry‑season vegetable production, monocropping of cucurbits near towns, and limited access to integrated pest management options created conditions for recurrent outbreaks; informal regional trade in fruits likely redistributed populations among countries. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability relative to native Dacus species on cultivated cucurbits and broad host use contributed to its dominance and repeated high‑density outbreaks (enhanced transmission/establishment; geographic range expansion – inherent).
Review: Retain – This row captures the shift from initial introduction (late 1990s) to recurrent, high‑impact infestations in key West and Central African cucurbit production basins during the 2000s. Countries, timing and impact are consistent with Vayssières et al. 2007 and subsequent work. Classification as re_occurrence (dramatic increase in incidence within already invaded West/Middle African sub‑regions) is appropriate. There is some temporal and geographic overlap with the 1999–2006 invasion row, but the focus here on outbreak intensity and yield loss justifies keeping it as a separate high‑impact episode; this should simply be noted when using the dataset to avoid double‑counting impacts.

Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [pre‑2010, high impact documented 2010s]; Kenya [pre‑2010, high impact documented 2010s]; Mozambique [2013; monitoring 2021-2023]
Host: Cucurbit crops (cucumber, zucchini, pumpkin, watermelon) and some other vegetables and fruits
Event summary: In the 2010s and early 2020s, studies from Tanzania, Kenya and Mozambique documented melon fly as the dominant cucurbit‑infesting fruit fly in many production areas, with high infestation levels and substantial yield losses. Surveys in eastern Tanzania found Z. cucurbitae infesting a wide range of cultivated cucurbits at higher rates than native Dacus species, while monitoring in Mozambique between 2021 and 2023 demonstrated widespread presence of the fly in multiple provinces. These findings indicated a sustained period of high pressure from melon fly on cucurbit production in Eastern Africa, with no large‑scale decline in populations despite increased monitoring and control efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ongoing expansion and intensification of cucurbit vegetable production, climatic conditions favorable to continuous generations, and limited adoption of area‑wide integrated pest management contributed to recurrent high infestation. Internal mechanisms: broad host range including wild and cultivated cucurbits, plus high fecundity and survival under local climatic regimes, promoted persistent high‑density populations (geographic range expansion – inherent; enhanced transmission).
Review: Review – This row is useful to characterise a prolonged period (2010s–early 2020s) of high melon‑fly pressure and economic impact in Eastern Africa, especially Tanzania and Kenya, with Mozambique representing the newer part of the range. Sub_regions have been corrected to Eastern Africa only, because all listed countries fall in that UN sub‑region in the project’s country sheet (Mozambique is not in “Southern Africa” under that scheme). Classification as re_occurrence (sustained or increased incidence in a previously known sub‑region) remains appropriate. Note that Mozambique’s 2021–2023 monitoring is also captured in a more focused Mozambique‑only row; analysts should avoid double‑counting if aggregating impacts.

Countries: United States of America – Hawaii [long-established; resistance characterized 2010s; field collections 2017]
Host: Cucurbit crops (watermelon, honeydew melon, cucumber, zucchini) and papaya under insecticide-based management
Event summary: In the 2010s, melon fly populations in Hawaii developed significant resistance to the spinosad‑based bait formulation GF‑120, which had been widely used for area‑wide suppression of tephritid fruit flies. Field populations collected from multiple farms on Oahu, Maui and Hawaii Island in 2017 displayed reduced susceptibility to spinosad in laboratory bioassays compared with historical baselines, indicating that resistant populations had evolved under prolonged selection pressure. This resistance undermined the effectiveness of a key management tool, leading to concerns about renewed damage in cucurbit and papaya crops and motivating research into resistance mechanisms and alternative control tactics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive and prolonged application of the GF‑120 spinosad bait in commercial cucurbit and papaya systems exerted strong selection pressure on local melon fly populations. Internal mechanisms: evolution of spinosad resistance in field populations (antimicrobial/pesticide resistance) and associated changes in detoxification pathways or target site sensitivity constitute a clear case of re‑emergence via reduced control efficacy.
Review: Review – This is a major re‑emergence event driven by evolved spinosad resistance in Hawaii, with good experimental support and clear management implications; it should be retained. Sub_regions has been standardised to the UN/Excel sub‑region name “Northern America”, with Hawaii specified in the countries field. Classification as re_emergence (biological change reducing control efficacy) is correct and consistent with the project’s definitions. Recommend retaining with these geographic clarifications.

Countries: Mozambique [2013 first detection; 2021-2023 documented multi-province spread]
Host: Field‑grown cucurbit crops (cucumber, zucchini, pumpkin and related cucurbits)
Event summary: After the first confirmed record of melon fly in Mozambique in 2013, a coordinated monitoring program from May 2021 to May 2023 surveyed cucurbit production areas in several northern and central provinces and found the species established with low to moderate populations across multiple regions. The surveys, motivated by the goal of establishing fruit production areas free of or with low prevalence of fruit flies, revealed that Z. cucurbitae was now widespread enough to pose a serious threat to cucurbit production, given published estimates of potential yield losses of 53–100% under heavy attack. By 2023, the pest was recognized as an emerging constraint on cucurbit production and a risk to trade, prompting recommendations for strengthened surveillance, movement controls on cucurbits and implementation of integrated pest management, though large‑scale population reductions had yet to be demonstrated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of cucurbit cultivation in northern and central Mozambique and inter‑provincial movement of infested cucurbit fruits likely facilitated spread from initial northern foci; the lack of prior systematic monitoring delayed recognition of its broader distribution. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity, multiple generations per year and the ability to achieve very high infestation levels in cucurbit hosts under suitable conditions explain the substantial yield loss potential observed elsewhere and anticipated in Mozambique (geographic range expansion – inherent; enhanced transmission).
Review: Review – Retain this as a clearly documented re‑occurrence/reinforcement of melon fly populations in Mozambique following the 2013 first record, with strong evidence of geographic expansion and emerging production risk between 2021 and 2023. Sub_regions has been corrected to Eastern Africa only, as Mozambique belongs to that UN sub‑region in the project country list. Classification as re_occurrence (increasing incidence in a previously known sub‑region driven by external factors) is consistent with the definitions. There is partial overlap with the broader Eastern Africa high‑pressure row (2010–2023); users should treat this as a more detailed, Mozambique‑specific sub‑episode within that wider pattern.

The fly rapidly spread across Tahiti and other French Polynesian islands, becoming the most damaging fruit fly species and triggering large‑scale biological control interventions with parasitoids such as Fopius arisanus. Within a few years the species spread through East, Central and West Africa, reaching at least 11 countries by 2005 and ultimately most mango‑producing regions of sub‑Saharan Africa, where it became the dominant fruit fly on mango, seriously damaging fruit production and disrupting export markets. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across much of sub‑Saharan Africa, with ongoing management relying on lure‑and‑kill, protein baiting and biological control, but with persistent high impacts on smallholder and commercial orchards.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance dispersal via trade and informal movement of infested mango and other host fruits within and between African countries; rapid expansion of mango cultivation and marketing; weak cross‑border phytosanitary controls; favorable tropical and subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, strong attraction to methyl eugenol facilitating mate finding, broad host range, and competitive superiority over native tephritids (e.g. Ceratitis cosyra), enabling displacement of resident species and geographical range expansion across multiple African sub‑regions.

Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion capacity and strong colonization ability of oceanic islands; competitive displacement of other tephritid species on key hosts (e.g. B. dorsalis out‑competing B. zonata and Ceratitis spp. in Mauritius), indicating increased ecological dominance; possible adaptive differentiation that facilitates survival in varied island microclimates.

Countries: China [1990–2010: rapid inland and northward expansion from long‑infested coastal areas in Guangdong and Hainan to Guangxi, Yunnan and central provinces such as Jiangxi, Hubei and the Chongqing region, with establishment north of the Yangtze River by the 2000s]
Host: Multiple fruit crops and wild hosts; major crops include citrus (mandarin, orange), mango, loquat, guava and other fleshy fruits
Event summary: From roughly 1990 to 2010 Bactrocera dorsalis expanded rapidly from long‑established coastal populations in South China (notably Guangdong and Hainan) into inland and more northerly parts of mainland China, including Guangxi, Yunnan and central provinces such as Jiangxi, Hubei and the Chongqing area. Genetic and historical trapping data indicate that coastal South China populations facing the South China Sea served as the main source, with strong gene flow and high propagule pressure driving stepwise colonization of previously uninfested inland fruit‑growing regions. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of commercial citrus, mango and other orchard crops in subtropical China, the development of dense road and market networks, and large internal trade in fresh fruit created abundant pathways for movement of infested fruit from coastal source areas to inland markets and orchards; mild winters and gradual climate warming increased suitability of central provinces. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, polyphagy, good flight capacity and strong gene flow among Chinese populations underpinned successful demographic and geographic expansion, with evidence of recent population growth and colonization of cooler inland environments consistent with inherent geographic range expansion rather than a single bottlenecked introduction.
Review: retain (modified): Corrected sub_regions to Eastern Asia only (previous reference to South‑eastern Asia was not supported by the China‑focused event), regularized the event year to 1990–2010 based on genetic and distribution data, and reclassified the event as re‑emergence within a previously affected UNSD subregion rather than intra‑continental emergence. Existing sources are appropriate and have been retained; event is clearly among the major post‑1990 range expansions and should be kept but flagged for expert review of the chosen 1990 start year.

Countries: Nauru [1992–1999: invasion and successful eradication]; Palau [1996]; French Polynesia [1996: first detected on Tahiti, then spread to Moorea and other Society Islands and later the Marquesas]
Host: Wide range of cultivated and wild fruit hosts; major damage reported in guava, mango, Polynesian chestnut and other tree fruits on affected islands
Event summary: Beginning in the early 1990s Bactrocera dorsalis invaded multiple Pacific islands where it had previously been absent. Around 1992 the fly was recorded in Nauru, where it became a serious pest before being eradicated by a coordinated male‑annihilation and bait‑spray campaign completed by the late 1990s. In July 1996 B. dorsalis was discovered on Tahiti in French Polynesia and rapidly spread to Moorea and other Society Islands, and in the same period it was first reported from Palau; on several islands it quickly displaced or added to existing polyphagous fruit flies and caused heavy damage to guava, mango and other fruit crops. Eradication was achieved in some locations (e.g. Nauru), whereas in French Polynesia the pest became established and long‑term classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus was implemented to reduce but not eliminate B. dorsalis populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing shipping and air traffic, and informal movement of fresh fruit between Asian source regions and remote Pacific islands, provided repeated opportunities for the introduction of infested fruit; once established, continuous fruiting of multiple hosts and limited quarantine capacity on small islands favoured spread within and between islands. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate, extreme polyphagy and strong attraction of males to methyl eugenol lures facilitated both invasion and detection, while the ability to coexist and eventually dominate over resident polyphagous fruit flies made B. dorsalis an especially disruptive invader in Pacific island fruit fly communities.
Review: retain (newly added): This high‑impact, multi‑island invasion (Nauru, Palau, French Polynesia) was previously omitted despite clear evidence of severe fruit damage, major management interventions and classical biological control programmes. It constitutes the first confirmed establishment of B. dorsalis in Oceania (UNSD Micronesia and Polynesia) after 1990 and clearly belongs among the top global emergence events; dedicated row added with continent/sub‑region coding aligned to UNSD and supported by primary Pacific fruit fly literature.

Countries: Australia [1993: papaya fruit fly (B. papayae, now B. dorsalis s.l.) trapped on Boigu, Dauan, Saibai and Darnley Islands in Torres Strait; 1995: detected on additional Torres Strait islands and near Cairns in mainland Queensland; 1999: official declaration of eradication from mainland Australia and Torres Strait]
Host: Papaya, mango, other tropical and subtropical fruits and some vegetables in northern Australia, threatening major horticultural industries and export markets
Event summary: In 1993 surveillance traps on several Torres Strait islands between Papua New Guinea and Australia detected the exotic papaya fruit fly, Bactrocera papayae, which is now regarded as conspecific with B. dorsalis and represented the first serious incursion of this species complex into the Australia and New Zealand subregion of Oceania. Despite rapid deployment of control measures, the fly reappeared on additional Torres Strait islands in 1995 and in October 1995 was found near Cairns in mainland Queensland, putting Australia’s papaya, mango and other fruit industries at high risk and prompting substantial domestic and export restrictions. A large, coordinated eradication programme combining male‑annihilation, protein‑bait spraying, host fruit destruction and intensive trapping eliminated the pest from the mainland and Torres Strait by 1999, but only after several years of costly emergency action and with ongoing surveillance to prevent reinvasion from nearby infested regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The incursion likely originated from recently infested areas of Papua New Guinea and Irian Jaya, with short‑distance natural dispersal across the Torres Strait and/or human‑mediated movement of infested fruit; high host availability and favourable tropical climate in northern Queensland allowed rapid build‑up once the fly reached the mainland. Internal mechanisms: As a member of the B. dorsalis complex, B. papayae exhibits high fecundity, broad host range and strong attraction to methyl eugenol, which together confer high invasion potential; however, absence of long‑term establishment in Australia reflects the intensity and effectiveness of eradication measures rather than any intrinsic biological limitation.
Review: retain (newly added): The papaya fruit fly/B. dorsalis incursion and eradication in northern Australia involved a large geographic area, major emergency control expenditure and significant trade implications, and is widely cited as a landmark invasive‑species management campaign. It clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for B. dorsalis sensu lato and was missing from the original dataset; added here as an intra‑continental emergence within Oceania (new UNSD subregion Australia and New Zealand).

Countries: Mauritius [1996–1999: first African record of B. dorsalis near Camp Carol close to the international airport, followed by rapid spread within the island and successful eradication after a nationwide control campaign]
Host: Mango, lychee, guava and other cultivated and wild fruits in Mauritius’ humid lowland and mid‑altitude production zones
Event summary: In June 1996 Bactrocera dorsalis was detected for the first time in Mauritius near Camp Carol, close to the main international airport, representing the earliest confirmed occurrence of this species in Africa. Within a short period the fly was found infesting mango, lychee and other fruits in several parts of the island, raising the risk of severe yield losses and export restrictions and prompting the launch of a nationwide male‑annihilation and bait‑spray programme. By 1999 B. dorsalis was no longer detected and the pest was officially declared eradicated, but this incursion highlighted the high vulnerability of African horticulture to oriental fruit fly invasions and foreshadowed later, more extensive colonization of mainland Africa and neighbouring islands.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The initial introduction likely occurred via imported infested fruit or luggage arriving by air, as suggested by first detection near the airport, with abundant hosts and suitable tropical climate on Mauritius enabling rapid establishment. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal ability typical of B. dorsalis facilitated quick spread within the island; however, intensive, well‑resourced area‑wide control (male‑annihilation, bait sprays, sanitation) was sufficient to overcome these biological advantages and achieve eradication.
Review: retain (newly added): The 1996–1999 Mauritius outbreak was the first confirmed African occurrence of B. dorsalis and required a nationwide eradication programme; it is explicitly highlighted in the invasion‑history literature for the Indian Ocean and Africa and should be treated as the inter‑continental emergence event for the African continent. This critical event was missing from the original dataset and has now been added with UNSD‑consistent coding and primary sources.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Western Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Kenya [2003]; Tanzania [2003–2004]; Uganda [2004]; Sudan [2004]; Benin [2004–2005]; Togo [2004–2005]; Senegal [2004]; Nigeria [2005]; Ghana [2005]; Côte d’Ivoire [mid‑2000s]; Cameroon [mid‑2000s]; Burkina Faso; Mali; Niger; Angola; Democratic Republic of the Congo; Congo; Equatorial Guinea; Guinea; Sierra Leone; Comoros [2005]; Mayotte [2007]; Madagascar [2010]; Mauritius [re‑detections 2013 and 2015 with eventual establishment]; South Africa and other Southern African countries [late 2000s–early 2010s]; plus numerous additional sub‑Saharan African countries where the species is now established
Host: Primarily mango and other tropical fruits (mango, citrus, guava, papaya) in smallholder and commercial orchards, but also a wide range of cultivated and wild fruit hosts across African agroecosystems
Event summary: In 2003 routine field surveys on the Kenyan coast detected an unknown Bactrocera of Asian origin that was later described as Bactrocera invadens and is now synonymized with B. dorsalis, marking the first major establishment of this species complex on the African mainland following the earlier but eradicated Mauritius incursion. Within just a few years the fly spread rapidly through East Africa and into West, Central and eventually Southern Africa as well as archipelagos such as the Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and, after earlier eradication, back into Mauritius, being recorded from more than 30–40 African countries by the early 2010s. Across much of sub‑Saharan Africa B. dorsalis quickly became the dominant fruit fly of mango and many other hosts, causing substantial yield and quality losses, market rejections and new phytosanitary barriers, so that by around 2015 it was widely regarded as a permanent, high‑impact pest and management focus shifted from eradication to long‑term integrated control and quarantine.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transcontinental introduction from Asia, likely via infested fruit from the Indian subcontinent, initiated the Kenyan coastal outbreak, and subsequent rapid spread across Africa was facilitated by extensive regional trade in fresh fruit, weak internal quarantine, year‑round availability of highly suitable hosts (mango, guava, citrus, papaya) and broadly suitable tropical to subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: The invading populations shared typical B. dorsalis traits of very high fecundity, strong flight and polyphagy; genetic studies show limited differentiation and signatures of recent demographic expansion, indicating one or few founding events followed by rapid range expansion and high gene flow across Africa. Compared with pre‑invasion fruit fly complexes dominated by Ceratitis spp., the arrival of this invasive B. dorsalis lineage represented a major re‑emergence of fruit fly damage driven by biological invasion and, after the earlier Mauritius episode, constitutes a continent‑wide intra‑continental emergence into new African subregions.
Review: retain (modified): This event is correctly among the largest global emergence events for B. dorsalis, but the original entry mis‑classified it as the inter‑continental emergence and understated the prior African incursion in Mauritius. The event has been reclassified as a major intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence within Africa following the earlier 1996–1999 Mauritius episode, sub_regions have been simplified to the four relevant UNSD African subregions, and countries have been expanded and annotated with example first‑record years using EPPO and regional syntheses. The narrative has been updated to acknowledge the Mauritius precedent and the role of both mainland and island invasions; sources remain appropriate and highly relevant. Flag for review to confirm the chosen 2003–2015 temporal window and country list capture the most impactful phase.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [2018–2020: Campania Region – initial detections around Palma Campania and Nocera Inferiore, with delimitation surveys and low‑level incursions detected through 2019–2020]
Host: Mixed fruit orchards in Campania, especially citrus and other tree fruits; adults and larvae intercepted in association with various fleshy fruits during surveys
Event summary: In 2018 pheromone traps and fruit inspections in mixed‑fruit orchards in the Campania Region of southern Italy captured adults and larvae belonging to the Bactrocera dorsalis species complex, providing the first confirmed field record of this high‑risk fruit fly in Europe and in the European Union. Following the initial detections near Palma Campania and Nocera Inferiore, national and regional plant protection services implemented delimitation surveys, intensified trapping and fruit inspections, and emergency phytosanitary measures including movement restrictions on host fruits and eradication treatments. Over 2019–2020 surveillance data indicated that the incursions remained localized and at low density, and regulatory reports framed the situation as a transient introduction rather than clear long‑term establishment, but the event is still treated as the first inter‑continental emergence of B. dorsalis into Europe with ongoing monitoring to prevent wider spread in Mediterranean fruit‑growing areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction into Campania was most likely via imported infested fruit from regions where B. dorsalis is established (Asia or Africa), facilitated by high volumes of international trade and passenger traffic into southern Italy, with the warm Mediterranean climate providing partially suitable conditions for establishment. Strong phytosanitary surveillance, particularly methyl‑eugenol‑baited trapping in high‑risk orchards and inspections of commercial fruit, enabled early detection and rapid response. Internal mechanisms: The species’ strong attraction to methyl eugenol and high dispersal ability underpin its invasion risk, but there is no evidence of local evolutionary change in the Italian populations; containment to date appears to reflect rapid regulatory and control action rather than intrinsic biological limits.
Review: retain (modified): The Italian incursion is appropriately included as the first confirmed field record in Europe and thus an inter‑continental emergence event, but the original row incorrectly flagged it as “first detection” in the host system globally. That flag has been removed (first detection is historical and occurred in Asia), and the text has been slightly adjusted to emphasize its status as an incursion with limited, possibly transient establishment. Sub‑regional and country coding remain correct; sources (Nugnes et al., ZooKeys records and EPPO reports) are relevant and sufficient.

Countries: China (Chongqing; Guangxi; Guizhou; Hubei; Hunan; Jiangxi; Shaanxi; Sichuan; Yunnan)
Host: Citrus spp., especially sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), mandarin (C. reticulata), pummelo (C. maxima), sour orange (C. aurantium), lemon (C. limon), hill lemon and related commercial citrus rootstocks and cultivars.
Event summary: From the early 1990s onward, Bactrocera minax caused recurrent, often severe damage across major citrus‑growing areas of south‑central and southwestern China, particularly in provinces along the Yangtze River basin such as Sichuan, Chongqing, Hubei, Hunan, Guizhou, Yunnan, Guangxi, Jiangxi and Shaanxi, with local reports of high infestation rates and major fruit losses. During this period, expanding citrus plantings in suitable mid‑elevation, subtropical environments and limited early adoption of integrated pest management allowed large and persistent populations to build up, prompting intensive research and the development of area‑wide control strategies. By the mid‑2010s, coordinated monitoring, baiting, orchard sanitation and other IPM measures in several provinces were reported to suppress B. minax infestations in treated orchards and substantially reduce insecticide use, although severe outbreaks have continued to occur in some areas into the 2020s and the pest remains a key quarantine concern with a large estimated suitable habitat (≈1.36 million km², about 14% of China’s land area).
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of citrus production in suitable mid‑elevation belts of the Yangtze basin; climate variability and generally warming conditions that favor survival and phenology of this univoltine, diapausing fly; fragmented smallholder orchards with poor sanitation and limited early adoption of coordinated management; domestic movement of infested fruit and nursery stock that facilitated spread among provinces. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent), reflecting exploitation of a broad range of subtropical–temperate citrus environments within China by a stenophagous citrus pest; no clear evidence in this period for distinct novel genotypes or strong insecticide resistance driving outbreaks, so changes are interpreted mainly as ecological range and population expansion rather than classic genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review. This row correctly represents the long period of high, recurrent damage caused by B. minax across the main citrus‑growing provinces of southern China and is clearly one of the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for this species. The time span has been extended from 1990–2015 to 1990–2025 to reflect evidence that severe infestations and detailed ecological studies continue into the early 2020s; the emergence type is kept as re‑occurrence within Eastern Asia because the pest was well established in this sub‑region before 1990 and there is no strong evidence of a distinct new strain or host shift. Sources are appropriate for documenting Chinese distribution, impacts and management; EPPO and other reviews are also consulted at profile level rather than duplicated here.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Bhutan; India – Sikkim; India – West Bengal
Host: Mandarin orange (Citrus reticulata) and other local mandarin landraces; sweet orange (C. sinensis) and other citrus where present.
Event summary: In the early 2000s, Bactrocera minax was documented as one of the most serious insect pests of citrus in Bhutan and nearby parts of northeastern India, with field studies in western Bhutan reporting that infestations could cause more than 50% fruit drop in mandarin orchards and national reports citing losses up to about 70% in some locations. Through the 2000s and 2010s, the fly became widely recognized across Bhutan and in Sikkim and West Bengal (India) as a key constraint on mandarin production, with heavy late‑season fruit drop and high larval infestation rates prompting development of phenology studies and basic IPM packages (trapping, baiting and sanitation). From the mid‑2010s into the early 2020s, governments and growers in Bhutan and Sikkim have implemented more structured monitoring and community‑based area‑wide control programs, which have reduced—but not eliminated—the severity of losses; recurrent outbreaks and severe fruit drop are still reported, and the fly remains a major constraint and quarantine concern for regional trade in fresh citrus.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: movement of infested citrus fruit and planting material from China into adjacent Himalayan regions; expansion of mandarin cultivation on mid‑hill slopes with limited pest management and poor orchard sanitation; smallholder production systems with minimal pesticide inputs and abundant unmanaged citrus trees acting as reservoirs; rugged terrain that complicates coordinated control. Internal mechanisms: primarily Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as the fly colonized climatically suitable mid‑elevation citrus zones in the eastern Himalayas; no strong evidence from this period of novel strains, host shifts beyond citrus, or resistance evolution driving outbreaks, so the event is treated as a major ecological and demographic re‑occurrence within an already affected sub‑region rather than a genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review. This event appropriately aggregates the Bhutan–northeastern India (Sikkim, West Bengal) outbreak complex into a single, linked episode characterized by very high mandarin fruit losses and long‑term economic impact. The time span has been extended from 2000–2015 to 2000–2025 to reflect that Chinese citrus fly remains the most serious citrus pest in Bhutan and a major problem in Sikkim and Darjeeling into the 2020s. In line with the project rules, spread within Southern Asia from earlier foci in the same UNSD sub‑region is not classified as intra‑continental emergence; the episode is therefore retained as a re‑occurrence event driven mainly by external agronomic and management factors. The cited sources (Dorji et al. 2006, Bhutan national surveys, and recent Sikkim AWCP work) are relevant and sufficient, so only the time span and narrative emphasis have been adjusted.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Primarily sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) and hill lemon, with damage also recorded in mandarin and other cultivated citrus.
Event summary: Although suspicious citrus fruit fly damage had been observed in eastern Nepal since at least the 1980s, Bactrocera minax was formally confirmed from collected adults in 2007, when specimens from Dhankuta and other mid‑hill districts were re‑identified as Chinese citrus fly rather than B. dorsalis. From about 2010 onward, and particularly since 2014, the species spread and increased rapidly in key citrus‑producing districts such as Sindhuli, Syangja, Gulmi, Lamjung and others, with reports of very high infestation levels and, in some orchards, near‑total pre‑harvest fruit drop that seriously threatened farmers’ incomes and citrus export agreements with China. In response to these escalating outbreaks, area‑wide control programs combining trapping, protein baiting and orchard sanitation were implemented in affected districts from the mid‑2010s onward, achieving substantial reductions in fruit loss in pilot areas but requiring sustained community coordination, and monitoring into the early 2020s still shows B. minax as one of the most destructive pests of Nepal’s citrus industry.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: misidentification of the pest as B. dorsalis until 2007 delayed species‑specific surveillance and management, allowing populations to build unnoticed; rapid expansion and commercialization of citrus (especially sweet orange and hill lemon) in Nepal’s mid‑hills, including export‑oriented production from districts such as Sindhuli and Syangja; poor orchard sanitation and limited access to effective control tools in smallholder systems; likely introduction and secondary spread via infested fruit and planting stock moving from Bhutan and northeastern India along trade and road networks. Internal mechanisms: chiefly Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as a pre‑adapted citrus specialist colonized climatically suitable mid‑hill environments; available literature does not yet demonstrate distinct novel genotypes, resistance or virulence shifts specific to Nepal, so this episode is classified as a major re‑occurrence driven mainly by external agronomic and trade factors rather than a clear genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review. This row correctly captures the first confirmed detection of B. minax in Nepal in 2007, the rapid subsequent spread into many mid‑hill citrus districts and the very high pre‑harvest fruit losses that followed. The time span has been extended from 2007–2020 to 2007–2025 to reflect continuing spread and area‑wide control initiatives documented into the early 2020s. Consistent with the project’s definitions, this episode is kept as a re‑occurrence event within Southern Asia: the sub‑region was already affected (India and Bhutan) before 1990, and spread to an additional country within the same UNSD sub‑region is not coded as intra‑continental emergence. The existing sources (national horticulture reports, research articles on AWCP and distribution) are relevant and retained; only the temporal bounds and wording of the summary have been updated.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Mango, guava, lychee and other fleshy fruits and vegetables in backyard trees and orchards in southern Mauritius
Event summary: On 5 June 1996, a single female oriental fruit fly was trapped near Camp Carol close to Mauritius’ international airport, and subsequent intensive trapping quickly revealed a localized but serious infestation in the south of the island, marking the first confirmed establishment of Bactrocera dorsalis in Africa.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Over 1996–1999, authorities implemented an island‑scale eradication campaign based on male annihilation and protein‑bait sprays, containing the population to roughly 150 km² and progressively driving trap catches to zero.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) After more than two consecutive years without detections, Mauritius declared B. dorsalis eradicated in mid‑1999 and EPPO recorded the African introduction as successfully eliminated, although the episode highlighted the continent’s vulnerability to this species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction was most likely via infested fruit or other plant material carried by air travellers or cargo from South or South‑East Asia into Mauritius, with detection aided by an existing area‑wide fruit fly monitoring network.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: High reproductive potential and broad host range allowed rapid build‑up after arrival, but the population remained geographically limited, enabling eradication using attractant‑based male annihilation and bait sprays before long‑distance secondary spread occurred.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). This event was missing in the original file but is clearly one of the most important post‑1990 emergence events for B. dorsalis: it represents the first documented establishment of the species in Africa (Mauritius), followed by a textbook area‑wide eradication, and is widely cited in EPPO and Mauritian sources.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classified as inter‑continental emergence (Asia→Africa) with first_detection and first_global_emergence set to No to respect the global‑scale definitions; sub‑region and country entries follow the UNSD list (Eastern Africa; Mauritius only). Flagged for awareness but not for further technical review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Kenya [2003]; United Republic of Tanzania [2003]; Uganda [2004]; Sudan [2004]; Benin [2004]; Cameroon [2004]; Senegal [2004]; Togo [2004]; Ghana [2005]; Nigeria [2005]; Angola; Burkina Faso; Chad; Congo; Côte d’Ivoire; Equatorial Guinea; Gambia; Guinea; Guinea-Bissau; Liberia; Mali; Mauritania; Niger; Sierra Leone; Mozambique [2007]; South Africa [2010]; other invaded sub-Saharan mainland countries
Host: Mango, guava, citrus, cashew and numerous other cultivated and wild hosts in smallholder orchards and commercial fruit production across sub‑Saharan Africa
Event summary: In 2003 a previously unknown Bactrocera fruit fly of Asian origin was detected in coastal Kenya and soon described as Bactrocera invadens, later synonymized with B. dorsalis; within a few years it became abundant in mango and citrus areas of Kenya and neighbouring countries.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-1417?utm_source=openai)) Between about 2003 and 2010 the species spread rapidly from East Africa across West, Central and parts of Southern Africa, with confirmed records from more than 20–30 mainland countries and documented mango yield losses exceeding 50–70% in some areas, prompting its listing as a major quarantine pest.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22251685/?utm_source=openai)) By the end of this episode B. dorsalis had become widely established across a contiguous area of over 8 million km², displacing several native Ceratitis species and forcing a shift from emergency measures to long‑term integrated pest management and export‑oriented quarantine systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth in intra‑African trade of fresh fruit, informal cross‑border movement of mangoes and other hosts, weak early‑warning systems and highly suitable tropical to subtropical climates across sub‑Saharan Africa favoured long‑distance jump dispersal and establishment.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22251685/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The invading populations (initially described as B. invadens) combined high fecundity, extreme polyphagy and strong attraction to methyl eugenol with the ability to exploit diverse climatic zones, supporting both geographic range expansion (to new African sub‑regions) and competitive displacement of native fruit fly species—hence classification here as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence (new invasive genotype) within Africa.
Review: Decision: review. Event is correctly included as one of the largest global emergence episodes (continent‑wide African invasion with major crop losses and many countries affected). However, several corrections were made: (i) added Southern Africa to the sub_regions and explicitly acknowledged spread into Mozambique (first trapped 2007) and South Africa (first detected 2010);([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-840?utm_source=openai)) (ii) clarified that this is not the first inter‑continental introduction into Africa, which occurred earlier in Mauritius (1996–1999), so inter_continental_emergence was changed from Yes to No; (iii) re‑classified the event as intra‑continental emergence (spread into new African sub‑regions) and re‑emergence (new invasive genotype within a continent where B. dorsalis had already appeared), and set first_detection to No to reserve that category for the global host‑system level. Country list remains illustrative rather than exhaustive but now better reflects the documented mainland range; further expert review could refine the exact end year and country‑specific first‑detection dates.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: French Polynesia [1996] (initially Tahiti and nearby Society Islands; later Austral and Marquesas archipelagos)
Host: Mango, guava, carambola and many other tropical fruits in smallholder and backyard plantings across French Polynesia
Event summary: In July 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first detected on Tahiti in French Polynesia, adding a fourth highly damaging invasive Bactrocera species to an already pest‑rich fruit fly fauna.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) Over the following decade it spread from the Society Islands to other archipelagos (including the Australs and, later, the Marquesas), rapidly becoming the dominant fruit fly and causing heavy infestations of mango, guava and other fruits.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) From 2002 onward, large‑scale classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus and other measures substantially suppressed B. dorsalis populations and reduced damage, though the species remains established and under ongoing management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensifying air and sea links and movement of infested fruit between Pacific islands, probably from Hawaii, introduced B. dorsalis into Tahiti and then facilitated its spread to other archipelagos; limited pre‑existing surveillance in remote islands delayed detection beyond Tahiti.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate, strong flight capacity and broad host range allowed B. dorsalis to rapidly dominate island fruit fly communities where other polyphagous species were already present, leading to ecological displacement and severe farmer losses until successful parasitoid‑based biological control was deployed.
Review: Decision: retain. The French Polynesia invasion is well‑documented, clearly post‑1990, and among the more consequential island invasions (large geographic spread within the territory and major changes in fruit fly communities). Classification as intra‑continental emergence (Oceania already had B. dorsalis in Micronesia and Hawaii before 1996) with other emergence‑type flags set to No is appropriate. Minor edits were made to the countries field to align with the UNSD country list (using French Polynesia as the country and archipelagos as sub‑national detail) and to clarify the invasion timeline; sources remain appropriate and no major additional events in Polynesia warrant a separate row.

Countries: Comoros [2005]; Mayotte [2007]; Madagascar [2010]; Mauritius [2013, 2015 reintroductions]; Réunion [2017]
Host: Mango, guava, citrus and other cultivated and backyard fruits on the western Indian Ocean islands of Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar, Mauritius and La Réunion
Event summary: After its establishment on mainland East Africa, B. dorsalis spread eastwards across the western Indian Ocean, being detected in Grande Comore in 2005, in Mayotte in 2007 and in Madagascar in 2010, where it rapidly joined existing polyphagous fruit flies as a key pest of mango and other fruits.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-2514?utm_source=openai)) Mauritius, where B. dorsalis had been eradicated in 1999, experienced new incursions detected in 2013 and again in 2015; the third invasion was not eliminated and the species is now considered present and widespread on the island.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9850006/?utm_source=openai)) In 2017 the fly was finally detected and quickly became widespread in La Réunion, completing a decade‑long island‑hopping invasion sequence that greatly increased fruit fly pressure on high‑value mango and other horticultural crops across the South‑West Indian Ocean.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUDO/distribution/RE?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Movement of infested fruit and plant material between East African coastal areas and island ports, regional passenger traffic, and trade between Indian Ocean islands and Asia created multiple introduction pathways, while favourable tropical climates and year‑round host availability fostered establishment on each new island.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9850006/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Independent introduction lineages from both mainland Africa and Asia, combined with high dispersal capability and strong competitive ability, enabled B. dorsalis to colonize island agroecosystems already occupied by other tephritids, increasing overall fruit fly damage; this justifies classification as re‑emergence (new invasive lineages in an already affected African sub‑region) and re‑occurrence for Mauritius (post‑eradication return).
Review: Decision: review. The Indian Ocean island invasion is rightly treated as a major multi‑country episode, but the original row required several corrections: (i) Seychelles was removed from the country list because B. dorsalis remains absent there apart from occasional interceptions at ports of entry;([www-pub.iaea.org](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Newsletters/ipc-96.pdf?utm_source=openai)) (ii) explicit first‑detection years for Comoros, Mayotte and Madagascar were added based on EPPO reporting;([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-2514?utm_source=openai)) (iii) Mauritius is now described as having reintroductions in 2013 and 2015 following its earlier eradication (now captured in a separate event), rather than as a simple post‑Kenya spread;([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9850006/?utm_source=openai)) and (iv) emergence‑type flags were set to re_occurrence and re_emergence (for new invasion lineages within an already affected African sub‑region) while intra‑ and inter‑continental emergence were set to No. Because invasion pathways and genetic structure are still being actively studied, an expert should review this consolidated island episode and decide whether to further split or refine it.

Countries: United States of America [2015] (Florida, Miami-Dade County – Redland agricultural area)
Host: Avocado, citrus, guava, mango, papaya, tropical vegetables and other hosts in the Redland production area and surrounding residential plantings
Event summary: In late August 2015, oriental fruit fly adults were detected in traps in the Redland agricultural area of Miami‑Dade County, triggering declaration of a major OFF outbreak and the establishment of a federal quarantine of about 98.6 square miles.([content.govdelivery.com](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDAAPHIS/bulletins/127b5f3?utm_source=openai)) By November 10, 2015, 157 adult flies and one larval infestation site had been confirmed, leading to intensive eradication measures including male annihilation, protein‑bait sprays, host removal and movement controls that significantly disrupted harvest and marketing of tropical fruits; affected producers later received more than US$1.6 million in compensation.([blogs.ifas.ufl.edu](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/miamidadeco/2015/09/29/oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-expanded-in-miami-dade-as-092815/?utm_source=openai)) After three fly‑free life cycles, APHIS and Florida authorities declared eradication and removed the quarantine on 13 February 2016, ending this re‑occurrence episode in a state that has seen multiple past OFF incursions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: One or more introductions of infested fruit or plant material from regions where B. dorsalis is established (Asia, Pacific or Africa), coupled with a highly suitable subtropical climate and dense plantings of preferred hosts in Miami‑Dade, enabled temporary establishment and rapid population increase.([ask.ifas.ufl.edu](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN240?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The fly’s inherent traits—high fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal—allowed it to quickly reach outbreak densities once introduced, necessitating an intensive, area‑wide eradication response using attractant‑based trapping, sterile male releases and chemical and cultural control.
Review: Decision: retain. This Florida outbreak is one of the most impactful recent B. dorsalis incursions in North America, with a large quarantine area and documented economic compensation, and it fits the definition of a re‑occurrence (previous OFF incursions in Florida, no evidence of novel strain or host jump). Minor numerical details in the original summary (fly counts and quarantine size) were tightened using APHIS and NAPPO reports,([content.govdelivery.com](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDAAPHIS/bulletins/127b5f3?utm_source=openai)) but the overall structure and emergence classification (re_occurrence = Yes; others No) are sound. No issues with country or sub‑region coding were found.

Host: Mixed fruit orchards (citrus, persimmon, stone fruits, grape) in Campania (Italy) and potential hosts near wholesale markets and airports in Austria and France where adults were trapped
Event summary: Between 2012 and 2018, nine adult Bactrocera dorsalis sensu lato were captured in methyl‑eugenol traps at several sites around Vienna, Austria, and identified as interceptions with no evidence of establishment.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-6656?utm_source=openai)) In 2018, a dedicated survey in mixed fruit orchards in Campania (Southern Italy) captured seven male B. dorsalis in methyl‑eugenol traps at Nocera Inferiore and Palma Campania, representing the first confirmed field detections of this species in European orchards and prompting emergency phytosanitary measures and delimiting zones.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6316371/?utm_source=openai)) From 2019 onwards, France reported sporadic male captures near the Rungis wholesale market, Orly airport and in a citrus orchard in Var, leading to increased surveillance and local regulatory actions; to date all findings are considered transient incursions linked to imported fruit, with no confirmed long‑term establishment anywhere in Europe.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUDO/distribution/FR?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Growing imports of tropical and subtropical fruits from Africa and Asia, passenger‑borne movement of infested fruit, and concentration of trade through major hubs (Rungis, airports, wholesale markets) have repeatedly introduced B. dorsalis into Europe, where Mediterranean and some temperate microclimates are potentially suitable for establishment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12470648/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ capacity to survive in a range of subtropical climates and its strong male response to methyl eugenol underpin both its invasion risk and the feasibility of early detection at very low densities; however, current evidence suggests repeated short‑lived incursions rather than sustained in situ transmission, so no emergence‑type category is ticked for this episode.
Review: Decision: review. The European detections are important as first records on this continent, but they mostly consist of isolated trap captures near trade hubs and one small cluster of males in Italian orchards, with no confirmed established populations. In line with the project’s exclusion of imported cases without in situ transmission from inter‑continental emergence, inter_continental_emergence was changed from Yes to No, and the event is now treated as a high‑priority detection/incursion episode without any emergence‑type flag set.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUDO/distribution/FR?utm_source=openai)) The year range was also adjusted to 2012‑2022 to encompass the Austrian interceptions and later French captures, and the countries list was limited to Austria, Italy and France where well‑documented official reports exist. Because the borderline between transient incursions and genuine establishment remains under close scrutiny, this row should be revisited as more surveillance data accumulate.

Countries: United States of America [2023] (California: Redlands area of San Bernardino and Riverside Counties; concurrent OFF quarantines in parts of Sacramento, Contra Costa and Santa Clara Counties)
Host: Citrus, avocado, grapes, stone fruits, figs, peppers, tomatoes and other fruit and vegetable hosts in commercial orchards and backyard trees within quarantined urban and peri‑urban areas of California
Event summary: In 2023, California detected unusually large numbers of oriental fruit flies, with a particularly severe outbreak centred on Redlands in San Bernardino and Riverside Counties where an OFF quarantine established on 27 September 2023 was repeatedly expanded to cover about 553 square miles and roughly 6,500 acres of commercial production.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/program-update/aphis-expands-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-san-bernardino-riverside-counties?utm_source=openai)) At the same time, additional OFF quarantines were declared in portions of Sacramento, Contra Costa and Santa Clara Counties, leading state authorities to describe the situation as the largest fruit fly infestation in California’s history and prompting substantial federal emergency funding.([universityofcalifornia.edu](https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/one-worlds-worst-pests-attacks-california?utm_source=openai)) Through 2024, APHIS and CDFA implemented intensive trapping, male‑annihilation, bait sprays and public outreach; by mid‑2024 the Sacramento and Santa Clara quarantines had been lifted following eradication, while work continued in remaining regulated areas as part of an expanded, statewide exotic fruit fly response.([wga.com](https://www.wga.com/news/cdfa-lifts-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-in-sacramento-county/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A combination of increased volumes of imported and passenger‑carried fresh produce, frequent movement of home‑grown fruit within California, and warm conditions conducive to overwintering contributed to multiple introductions and unusually sustained OFF populations in 2023–2024.([ask.ifas.ufl.edu](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN240?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ high fecundity, multivoltine life cycle and ability to exploit a wide host range in suburban and commercial plantings allowed rapid population build‑up once introduced, so that several separate but temporally overlapping outbreaks required large, coordinated state‑ and federal‑level eradication campaigns; these characteristics underpin classification as a major re‑occurrence rather than a new intra‑continental emergence.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). This large, multi‑county California outbreak was absent from the original dataset but clearly meets the criteria for a top‑impact emergence event: extensive quarantined area (hundreds of square miles), multiple commercial cropping systems affected, and substantial emergency funding and regulatory impact.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/program-update/aphis-expands-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-san-bernardino-riverside-counties?utm_source=openai)) It is coded as a re‑occurrence because California has experienced repeated OFF incursions since the 1960s, with no evidence that the 2023–2024 episode involved a fundamentally new strain or host jump. The countries, sub‑region and dates were cross‑checked against APHIS and CDFA reports; future expert review may wish to decide whether to split Redlands and the northern California quarantines into separate rows, but they are treated here as a single temporally linked episode for parsimony.

Countries: China (multiple provinces; progressive northward and inland expansion from long-established southern/coastal origin)
Host: Multiple cultivated and wild fruit and vegetable hosts (e.g. citrus, mango, guava, peach, other temperate and subtropical fruits)
Event summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, Bactrocera dorsalis expanded its range from long-established foci in southern China and adjacent South-East Asia northwards and inland across mainland China, invading new temperate and subtropical fruit‑growing regions. Genetic and distribution studies indicate stepwise spread and rapid population growth along major river valleys and transport corridors, leading to heavy infestations in central and eastern provinces where the fly had been absent or rare. By around 2010, the pest had become one of the most serious fruit flies in much of mainland China, with recurrent local outbreaks and evidence of overwintering in some central regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of fruit and vegetable production, increased domestic trade and transport of infested fruit within China, and regional warming trends improving climatic suitability in more northern and inland areas. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) supported by high dispersal ability, broad host range and high fecundity; evidence from population genetics and overwintering suggests some local adaptation to cooler climates at the expansion front rather than a single new genotype. (Supported by inland-expansion studies and global-distribution syntheses.)
Review: review – Retain this event as a major re‑emergence episode in Eastern Asia (large northward/inland expansion within China). Corrected the event type: set intra_continental_emergence to No because the spread occurs within a single UN sub‑region (Eastern Asia) and within one country, and kept re_emergence as Yes to reflect climatic and ecological drivers of resurgence. Subregion and country assignment match EPPO distribution and Zeng et al. 2019; timing and storyline are consistent with range-expansion studies, but exact onset and northern limits should be checked against the primary Chinese surveillance datasets.

Countries: Australia – Queensland (Torres Strait Islands [1993]; Cairns and wider wet tropics quarantine area [1995-1999])
Host: Papaya/papaw, mango, citrus, coffee berries, guava, tomato and many other tropical and subtropical fruits (≥35 host species recorded during surveys)
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, Bactrocera dorsalis (then known as papaya fruit fly B. papayae, now a synonym) moved from Papua New Guinea into Australia’s Torres Strait Islands and in October 1995 was detected infesting papaya near Cairns, marking the first major incursion of Oriental fruit fly into mainland Australia. The outbreak rapidly spread across a quarantine area of approximately 78,000 km² in north Queensland, where the fly bred in at least 35 fruit and vegetable species and threatened key tropical fruit industries. A national eradication campaign based on male annihilation, protein bait spraying and strict quarantine was implemented from late 1995 and, after four years of intensive operations, the pest was declared eradicated from mainland Australia in 1999, at a program cost of roughly AU$34 million and an estimated total industry impact of around AU$100 million.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: high propagule pressure from neighbouring infested regions (Papua New Guinea and Torres Strait), movement of infested fruit and limited early surveillance at the time, combined with favourable wet-tropics climate and dense plantings of susceptible hosts around Cairns. Internal mechanisms: broad host range, high reproductive rate and capacity to exploit both rainforest and cultivated habitats facilitated rapid build‑up from small founding populations; however, no specific resistance or novel strain was implicated, and the population was successfully eradicated using area‑wide male annihilation and bait control once detected. (Supported by Queensland government summaries and detailed analyses of the papaya fruit fly eradication campaign.)
Review: review – New event added to capture the major papaya fruit fly/Oriental fruit fly incursion in north Queensland, which was one of the largest OFF eradication campaigns globally in both area and cost. Classified as intra-continental emergence because it represents the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis sensu lato in the UN sub-region ‘Australia and New Zealand’ within Oceania, after earlier establishment in other Pacific sub-regions. Years, geography and impact metrics are well supported by Queensland government sources and eradication-campaign reports, but precise timing of initial island detections and full host lists could be further cross-checked against NAQS and QDPI technical reports.

Countries: French Polynesia [1996 (Tahiti); late 1990s–2000s spread to Moorea, Raiatea, Tahaa, Huahine and other Society, Marquesas and Austral Islands]
Host: Mango, guava, citrus, papaya and many other cultivated and wild fruits in orchards and backyard gardens
Event summary: In July 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was detected for the first time on Tahiti in French Polynesia, where it rapidly became the most damaging fruit fly species, displacing existing tephritids in many hosts. Over the following decade, the species spread from Tahiti to neighbouring Society Islands and then to other archipelagos within French Polynesia, including parts of the Marquesas and Austral Islands, causing heavy infestations in mango, guava, citrus and other fruits and triggering large-scale control efforts. An initial attempt at eradication on Tahiti and Moorea in 1997 was not fully successful, but subsequent area‑wide suppression and classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus reduced B. dorsalis populations and fruit damage, even though the pest remains established across much of the territory.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental introduction via infested fruit from other infested Pacific or Asian regions, followed by intense movement of fresh produce among islands and highly suitable tropical climates with extensive mixed-fruit plantings. Internal mechanisms: strong dispersal capacity, extreme polyphagy and competitive dominance over resident fruit fly species allowed B. dorsalis to become the primary frugivorous pest wherever it established; effective adaptation to local host plants and subsequent augmentation by parasitoid releases shaped long-term population dynamics rather than obvious emergence of novel genotypes. (Based on Pacific fruit-fly management syntheses and EPPO distribution data for French Polynesia.)
Review: review – New major event added for the invasion and spread of B. dorsalis in French Polynesia beginning in 1996, which is widely recognised as a devastating Pacific outbreak and a key source for regional biological-control case studies. Classified as intra-continental emergence because it represents first establishment in the Polynesia sub-region, after earlier presence in Micronesian islands. Timing and archipelago sequence are based on South Pacific Commission reports, EPPO distribution data and Pacific area-wide management literature and should be checked against primary island-level pest reports for finer dating.

Countries: Mauritius [1996 (first incursion, eradicated 1999); 2013 (second incursion, eradicated); 2015 onward (third incursion, establishment island-wide)]; Comoros [2005]; Mayotte [2007]; Madagascar [2010]; Réunion [2017]
Host: Diverse cultivated and wild fruits (including mango, citrus, guava and other tropical fruit crops)
Event summary: In 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first recorded on Mauritius, an Indian Ocean island off the African coast, where an intensive area-wide campaign combining bait sprays and male annihilation led to official declaration of eradication in 1999. From 2005 onwards, the species invaded the Comoros and then spread stepwise to Mayotte in 2007 and Madagascar by 2010, where it became the dominant fruit fly in many mango-growing areas, while Mauritius experienced at least two further incursions in 2013 and 2015, the latter leading to widespread establishment, and Réunion recorded its first invasion around 2017. Together these invasions produced a pattern of repeated long-distance introductions from Asia and from the African mainland, island hopping, occasional successful eradications and eventual establishment on most major south-west Indian Ocean islands, with substantial chronic fruit losses and increased insecticide use.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: human‑mediated movement of infested fruit between Asia, East Africa and the south-west Indian Ocean islands, dense tourism and trade links (air and sea traffic), and highly suitable tropical climates with abundant host fruit. Internal mechanisms: introduction of invasive genotypes capable of founding new island populations from few individuals, leading to strong founder effects and genetic bottlenecks, followed by rapid demographic expansion; genomic work supports two distinct invasion pathways (a western route via East Africa into Comoros–Mayotte–Madagascar and an eastern route directly from Asia into Mauritius and Réunion). Repeated eradications and reintroductions on Mauritius illustrate both the species’ high colonisation ability and the possibility of local elimination under intensive area‑wide management. (Supported by Deschepper et al. 2023 and EPPO/NPPO reports for Mauritius and other islands.)
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified to better match the definitions: treated as inter-continental emergence because the 1996 Mauritius incursion is the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis on the African continent, and re_emergence is kept to reflect repeated reintroductions and distinct invasion pathways; intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence flags were removed to maintain the mostly mutually exclusive structure of event types. The sub-region label was standardised to the UNSD term ‘Eastern Africa’. Country sequence and eradication/reintroduction history are consistent with EPPO reports and Deschepper et al. (2023), but finer dating for Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and the status of Réunion after 2017 should be double-checked against national reports.

Countries: United States of America – Florida (Tampa [1999], other central Florida localities [1999–2014], Miami-Dade County – Palmetto Bay/Redland/Miami [2015–2016])
Host: Urban and backyard fruit trees and vegetable crops (e.g. citrus, tropical fruits) in affected neighbourhoods and nearby smallholder plantings
Event summary: Beginning in 1999, Florida recorded repeated detections of Bactrocera dorsalis in urban and suburban areas, usually as single or few flies in traps around Tampa, Orlando and other central Florida locations, each triggering delimitation surveys and local treatments. In 2015, a much larger outbreak occurred in southern Miami‑Dade County, where 140 adult flies, 18 mated females and 8 larvae were detected in the Redland agricultural area and nearby suburbs, indicating an actively breeding population that prompted a major eradication program costing several million US dollars. By 2016–2018, eradication efforts had succeeded in removing the outbreak and the pest is still officially considered absent from mainland Florida, but sporadic new detections continue to occur and require rapid response to protect the state’s fruit industries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated introductions via infested fruit carried in passenger baggage or commercial shipments from infested regions (Asia, Hawaii, Africa); year‑round availability of suitable hosts in subtropical south Florida; and high human population density and travel volumes that increase introduction pressure. Internal mechanisms: high dispersal and reproductive capacity allow small founder populations to reach detectable levels quickly, as illustrated by the 2015 Redland focus, but there is no evidence of resistance or unusually adapted genotypes; outbreaks have remained transient because of aggressive trap-based detection, insecticide baiting and other eradication measures rather than intrinsic limitations of the pest. (Based primarily on Florida and federal regulatory reports and the American Entomologist review of Bactrocera spp. detections in Florida.)
Review: review – Event retained as a major high-cost re-occurrence episode in Northern America but reclassified: inter_continental_emergence was set to No because B. dorsalis has been present in the USA (Hawaii) since the 1940s and was first detected in Florida in 1964; the 1999–2018 detections represent repeated incursions and a significant 2015–2016 outbreak in a previously known sub-region. Re_occurrence remains Yes to reflect repeated reappearance driven by introduction pressure rather than evolutionary change. Timeline, trap counts and cost estimates are consistent with the American Entomologist review and Florida regulatory documents, but detailed cost figures and the formal end-date of eradication should be checked against primary FDACS/USDA reports.

Countries: United States of America – California (multiple counties including San Diego, Los Angeles – Pasadena/San Marino [2010], San Joaquin County [2010s], and other coastal and valley urban/agricultural areas)
Host: Wide range of fruits and vegetables in urban, peri‑urban and commercial orchards (e.g. peaches, plums, cherries, citrus, tomatoes, avocados)
Event summary: Since earlier introductions in the late 20th century, California has continued to experience repeated incursions of Bactrocera dorsalis, with a series of major detections and eradication projects from about 2000 onwards, particularly in southern California and the Central Valley. In 2010, for example, interior quarantine and eradication areas were established around Pasadena and San Marino in Los Angeles County and in parts of San Joaquin County after multiple flies were trapped, indicating localized breeding populations and prompting intensive bait spraying and quarantine restrictions. Through the 2000s and 2010s, California repeatedly implemented area‑wide male annihilation, bait treatments and quarantines whenever flies were detected; by around 2020 the pest remained officially non‑established on the mainland but continued to trigger costly emergency responses and ongoing debate about whether detections represent repeated introductions or low-level cryptic establishment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: continuous introduction pressure via infested fruit imported or carried from Hawaii, Asia and other infested regions; large urban populations with backyard fruit trees that provide cryptic host reservoirs; and high-value commercial fruit industries that make even small incursions economically consequential. Internal mechanisms: strong dispersal and reproductive capacity allow transient breeding populations to arise from small introductions, but intensive integrated eradication campaigns (attract‑and‑kill, sterile insect technique in some areas, strict quarantines) have so far prevented recognised long-term establishment; no clear evidence yet of genetic adaptation to California’s control tactics. (Supported by CDFA pest profiles and quarantine archives, as well as recent syntheses of B. dorsalis invasion history.)
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified as a re-occurrence episode rather than inter-continental emergence. B. dorsalis was first detected in California in 1960 and has shown a pattern of recurrent detections over many decades; the 2000–2020 window summarises a cluster of linked incursions and eradication programs in a region where the species is already known as a recurring invader. Re_occurrence is kept as Yes to reflect repeated reappearance under high propagule pressure, while inter_continental_emergence was set to No to avoid misclassifying these incursions as first arrival on a new continent. The counties and example years are supported by the CDFA interior-quarantine archive and recent invasion-history reviews, but the exact list of major outbreaks and their start/end dates should be cross-checked against CDFA regulatory notices for completeness.
