Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Kenya [2003]; United Republic of Tanzania [2003-2004]; Uganda [2004]; Sudan [mid‑2000s]; Ethiopia [mid‑2000s]; Rwanda [mid‑2000s]; Burundi [mid‑2000s]; Mozambique [2007]; Angola [mid‑/late 2000s]; Cameroon [mid‑/late 2000s]; Central African Republic [mid‑/late 2000s]; Chad [mid‑/late 2000s]; Congo [mid‑/late 2000s]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [mid‑2000s]; Equatorial Guinea [mid‑/late 2000s]; Gabon [mid‑/late 2000s]; Benin [mid‑2000s]; Burkina Faso [mid‑/late 2000s]; Cabo Verde [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Côte d’Ivoire [mid‑2000s]; Gambia [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Ghana [mid‑2000s]; Guinea [mid‑2000s]; Guinea-Bissau [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Liberia [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Mali [mid‑2000s]; Mauritania [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Niger [mid‑2000s]; Nigeria [mid‑2000s]; Senegal [mid‑2000s]; Sierra Leone [mid‑/late 2000s]; Togo [mid‑2000s]; Zambia [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Zimbabwe [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Malawi [late 2000s/early 2010s]; Namibia [early 2010s] (country-specific years approximate within the documented continental spread).
Host: Primarily mango, but also citrus, guava, papaya and many other cultivated and wild fruit crops (over 250 host plants documented in Africa).
Event summary: In 2003, an unknown Bactrocera species later synonymised with B. dorsalis (B. invadens) was first detected on the coast of Kenya, signalling the start of a major invasion from Asia into the African mainland and rapidly damaging mango and other fruit crops. Over the following decade, the species spread quickly from East Africa across much of Central, West and parts of Southern Africa, becoming the dominant fruit fly in many mango-producing regions and displacing native Ceratitis species, with severe yield losses, increased insecticide use and trade disruptions. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across most of tropical sub‑Saharan Africa, with only some southern fringe areas remaining free or under transient incursion status, and it continues to cause chronic high infestation levels and high management costs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated introductions from Asia (probably from the Indian subcontinent) followed by intense intra‑African trade in fresh fruit, weak phytosanitary controls, extensive plantings of highly suitable hosts (especially mango) and favourable tropical climates across large areas of sub‑Saharan Africa. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an invasive genotype within the B. dorsalis complex (historically described as B. invadens) with very broad host range and high reproductive capacity, leading to competitive displacement of native fruit flies and very rapid geographic range expansion into a previously unoccupied continent. (Summarised from Lux et al. 2003, Drew et al. 2005, African invasion syntheses and EPPO distribution data.)
Review: review – Event retained as the main Africa-wide mainland invasion episode but reclassified as intra-continental emergence only: it captures spread from initial African foci (post‑Mauritius) into additional African UN sub-regions (Middle, Western and Southern Africa). Inter_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags were removed because first continental occurrence is already represented by the 1996 Mauritius event, and this wave reflects subsequent within-continent expansion rather than reappearance in a previously known sub-region. The country list and approximate dates are broadly consistent with EPPO and regional reviews, but some southern fringe countries (e.g. Botswana, Eswatini) with more recent detections are not listed and could be added in a future refinement if judged among the top-impact events.

Countries: South Africa [2010 onward; initially Limpopo Province with subsequent spread to additional districts]
Host: Citrus, mango, guava and other commercial and backyard fruit crops
Event summary: Following several years of concern after B. dorsalis invaded East Africa, the species was first detected in methyl-eugenol traps near the Zimbabwe border in Limpopo Province, South Africa, in 2010, representing its arrival in a major temperate–subtropical fruit export economy at the southern edge of its African range. Initial eradication actions removed some local populations, but further detections in Limpopo and later in other provinces (e.g. parts of Mpumalanga, North West and Gauteng) showed ongoing reintroductions and gradual establishment in key citrus and mango regions despite intensive control. By around the mid‑2010s, official reports described B. dorsalis as present but under official control and restricted mainly to northern and north-eastern production areas, where it continues to pose a serious threat to export markets and requires permanent surveillance and area‑wide management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: southward spread of the African invasion front via movement of infested fruit from neighbouring countries, long-distance overland transport networks, and dense commercial orchards providing abundant hosts in a high-value export sector, together with climatic suitability in lowland subtropical zones. Internal mechanisms: typical B. dorsalis traits of high fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal allow repeated reintroductions to found transient or semi-permanent populations in the Southern Africa sub-region; however, there is no clear evidence of major genetic change relative to earlier African populations, and the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence driven by propagule pressure rather than intrinsic evolutionary shifts. (Based on IPPC pest reports, EPPO distribution data and South African entomological studies.)
Review: review – Event retained as a distinct, high-impact episode in South Africa but reclassified as re-occurrence within the Southern Africa sub-region. B. dorsalis was already present in the Southern Africa sub-region (e.g. Namibia, Zimbabwe, Zambia) when first detected in South Africa in 2010, so it should not be coded as intra-continental emergence for the continent. Re_occurrence captures repeated detections and partial establishment in a previously affected sub-region driven by movement of infested fruit and trade. Dates, locations and status are consistent with IPPC and EPPO records and South African literature, but the end year of 2015 is approximate and could be updated to reflect more recent official pest-status changes.

Countries: Italy [2018-2024 – Campania (Salerno and Napoli provinces), with later detections in other municipalities and regions under official eradication and surveillance]
Host: Citrus, persimmon and other fruit trees in mixed orchards and gardens where traps were deployed; larvae and emerging adults have been recovered from infested citrus and other fruits in some monitored orchards.
Event summary: In 2018, official surveys in the Campania region of southern Italy trapped multiple male Bactrocera dorsalis complex flies in mixed fruit orchards, with morphological and molecular analyses confirming the first record of oriental fruit fly in Europe. Follow‑up monitoring in Italy captured additional adults in Campania and other regions, and in 2022 adults emerged in the laboratory from fruit collected in citrus and pear orchards, indicating at least transient local reproduction, although populations have remained localised and are subject to official eradication and containment measures. Parallel but sporadic interceptions of B. dorsalis in traps near airports and wholesale markets in other EU countries (e.g. France, Austria, Spain, Greece) highlight ongoing introduction pressure via imported fruit and passenger baggage, making this first European incursion episode highly significant for regional plant health and trade despite limited current crop damage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation and passenger transport of infested tropical and subtropical fruit from Asia and Africa into Mediterranean Europe, with initial detections occurring in areas with mixed orchards and high trade connectivity; suitable warm-temperate to subtropical microclimates and abundant fruit hosts in parts of southern Europe create establishment risk even under intensive surveillance. Internal mechanisms: typical B. dorsalis traits of high fecundity, wide host range and strong dispersal underpin its incursion potential; available genetic data indicate that Italian populations are closely related to Asian source populations, consistent with recent introductions rather than long-term cryptic establishment or major evolutionary change. (Based on Nugnes et al. 2018 and multiple EPPO Reporting Service updates on Italy and other European interceptions.)
Review: review – New high-significance first-detection event added for Europe, representing the first confirmed occurrence and transient reproduction of B. dorsalis on the European continent. Classified as inter-continental emergence because the Italian orchards provide evidence of in situ reproduction under Mediterranean conditions, while interceptions in other EU countries are treated as associated incursions at points of entry rather than separate emergence events. Years and regional status are derived from Nugnes et al. (2018) and successive EPPO Reporting Service notes; given ongoing detections and changing pest status (e.g. ‘transient, actionable, under eradication’), this event should be revisited periodically to align with the latest NPPO and EFSA assessments.

Countries: Australia (Western Australia – Perth metropolitan area including Dalkeith and adjoining suburbs [1989])
Host: Backyard and commercial fruit crops (including stone fruit, citrus and other common host fruits) in infested suburbs of Perth
Event summary: In February 1989, Queensland fruit fly was detected breeding in backyard tomatoes and other host fruits in the Perth suburb of Dalkeith, representing the first established population of this species in Western Australia and a serious threat to the state’s Qfly‑free horticultural industries. The Western Australian Department of Agriculture implemented an intensive 10‑month eradication program over roughly 300 km² of metropolitan Perth using protein bait sprays, male‑lure bait blocks and releases of hundreds of millions of sterile male flies, combined with strict movement controls on host produce. After no further wild Qfly were detected for more than a year, the program was declared successful in late 1990 and Western Australia regained its Queensland‑fruit‑fly‑free status, which has since been maintained through ongoing early‑warning trapping and rapid responses to new incursions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The incursion was attributed to human‑mediated movement of infested host fruit from Qfly‑endemic eastern Australia into Perth, facilitated by increasing interstate travel and trade and the availability of highly suitable backyard and commercial host trees in the city’s Mediterranean climate. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that this outbreak involved a novel strain or adaptive change in the pest; rather, it demonstrated that existing eastern Australian Qfly populations can survive and reproduce in marginal but favourable microclimates when introduced, and that eradication is feasible using area‑wide integrated management and sterile insect technique.
Review: review – New event added because the 1989–1990 Perth incursion and eradication program is widely documented as a major Qfly emergence episode (∼A$5 million program over about 300 km²). It begins slightly before the nominal 1990 cut‑off but most of the response and the declaration of eradication occurred in 1990; recommended to keep as one of the top-impact events but flagged for final decision on the start‑year rule.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest‑free area: Loxton North [1990])
Host: Commercial orchards and backyard fruit trees (especially citrus and stone fruits) in and around Loxton North in the Riverland horticultural district
Event summary: In 1990, a Queensland fruit fly outbreak was detected in the Riverland region at Loxton North when larvae were found in locally grown fruit and the detection met South Australia’s formal outbreak definition, marking the first modern fruit fly outbreak in this high‑value production area. Authorities established an outbreak area around Loxton North with intensive trapping, bait spraying and fruit stripping, and imposed movement restrictions on host produce in and around the affected zone to protect the Riverland Pest Free Area and its export markets. After a focused eradication campaign and a period without further detections, the Loxton North population was eliminated and the Riverland again qualified as fruit‑fly‑free, a status later recognised in interstate and international market access protocols.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical PIRSA accounts indicate that Riverland outbreaks are rare and usually result from infested fruit being carried across the South Australia–Victoria border despite quarantine controls, rather than from natural spread, and the 1990 Loxton North event fits this pattern; high densities of irrigated citrus and stone fruit around Loxton North meant that any introduced flies could build up rapidly if not detected. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that the 1990 outbreak involved a novel strain, resistance or host shift; it is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence of an existing pest in a previously pest‑free production area, driven by lapses in compliance with movement restrictions and successfully eradicated using the standard South Australian eradication program.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 1990 Loxton North outbreak, which PIRSA identifies as one of only two Riverland fruit fly outbreaks between 1957 and 2013 and therefore a historically important emergence episode; however, detailed public data on affected host crops and exact quarantine dates are limited, so these aspects should be checked against South Australian outbreak records.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest‑free area: near Lyrup [2013])
Host: Backyard and nearby orchard fruit trees (mixed host fruits typical of Riverland town blocks, including stone and pome fruits and citrus) in the Lyrup area
Event summary: In 2013, a second rare Queensland fruit fly outbreak was recorded in South Australia’s Riverland, near the town of Lyrup, again temporarily disrupting the region’s long‑standing pest‑free status. Following detection of infested fruit, PIRSA implemented its standard eradication protocol, establishing an outbreak area and surrounding suspension zone, intensifying trapping and baiting, and restricting the movement of host fruit from affected properties. The Lyrup outbreak was eradicated within the following season and the Riverland’s Qfly‑free status was restored, but the episode highlighted the continuing risk of incursions despite the Yamba roadblock and other border controls and foreshadowed the much larger series of outbreaks beginning in 2020–2021.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Official historical summaries attribute the very infrequent Riverland outbreaks, including the 2013 event near Lyrup, to occasional failures of border quarantine and inadvertent importation of infested fruit from neighbouring states, rather than to natural spread from established populations, against a backdrop of highly susceptible irrigated orchards. Internal mechanisms: As with other Riverland incursions before 2020, there is no evidence for genetic change, host shifts or resistance in the flies involved; the episode is best described as a re‑occurrence of an existing pest in a previously pest‑free production area driven by human‑assisted dispersal.
Review: review – New event added because PIRSA’s Yamba Roadblock history explicitly lists a Queensland fruit fly outbreak near Lyrup in 2013 as one of only two Riverland outbreaks prior to 2014, suggesting it was a significant emergence episode. Publicly available detail on the size, duration and precise locality of this outbreak is sparse, so the narrative is partly inferred from standard SA outbreak protocols and should be checked against PIRSA’s original outbreak notice and internal reports.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest-free area: Loxton [2014], Pyap [2014])
Host: Commercial and backyard fruit crops, mainly Citrus spp. and Prunus spp. (stone fruit) in the Riverland horticultural region
Event summary: In January 2014, after more than two decades without fruit fly, two Queensland fruit fly outbreaks were declared in South Australia’s Riverland pest‑free area at Loxton and nearby Pyap following the detection of 11 male flies in traps within a fortnight, triggering quarantine and emergency response plans. Intensive baiting, hygiene measures and movement controls were imposed around 1.5 km outbreak zones and 15 km restricted areas, disrupting local marketing and requiring cold treatment or fumigation of fruit but successfully containing the pest. After approximately 12 weeks without further detections, authorities declared the Loxton and Pyap outbreaks eradicated in April 2014 and the Riverland regained its fruit‑fly‑free status.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance human-mediated movement of infested host fruit from endemic eastern Australian states into South Australia, breaching quarantine restrictions, is cited as the likely source of the outbreaks; high host availability in the irrigated Riverland citrus and stone-fruit production systems allowed rapid local build-up until emergency measures were implemented. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of novel genotypes, resistance or host range shifts was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence of an existing pest facilitated by trade and travel rather than evolutionary change.
Review: retain – Well-documented major outbreak in the Riverland Pest Free Area in 2014; locations, timing and quarantine measures are consistent with ABC and PIRSA sources, and classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) correctly reflects that Qfly was already established elsewhere in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and no evolutionary change was involved.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – metropolitan Adelaide: West Croydon [2014])
Host: Backyard and urban fruit trees (mixed hosts including stone fruit and other common garden fruit species) in metropolitan Adelaide
Event summary: On 25 December 2014, Biosecurity SA declared a Queensland fruit fly outbreak in the Adelaide suburb of West Croydon after larvae were found in backyard fruit, marking renewed incursion of the pest into South Australia’s otherwise fruit-fly-free mainland status. Authorities immediately established a 1.5 km quarantine zone with strict controls on movement, disposal and treatment of fruit and vegetables, and mounted bait-spotting and hygiene programs in affected streets. After a standard eradication period with no further detections, the outbreak was declared eradicated in 2015 and Adelaide’s fruit-fly-free status was restored.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction was attributed to infested fruit brought from endemic eastern Australian states by travellers, combined with abundant backyard host trees in inner suburbs and high summer temperatures favouring development. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or phenotypic changes were implicated; the event represents re-occurrence driven by human-assisted dispersal rather than adaptive evolution.
Review: retain – Localised but economically relevant Adelaide metropolitan outbreak; dates, location and control measures align with ABC and PIRSA documentation, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate since Qfly was already present in the broader Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and the event reflects re‑introduction rather than new geographic sub‑region colonisation.

Host: Urban backyard and small-scale horticultural fruit trees including Citrus spp. and Prunus spp. in central Auckland
Event summary: In February 2015, an isolated population of Queensland fruit fly was detected in the central Auckland suburb of Grey Lynn, representing New Zealand’s first confirmed local breeding population of this species rather than a single trapped adult. Biosecurity New Zealand initiated a large-scale emergency response, including intensive male-lure trapping, baiting, fruit stripping and strict movement controls on host produce within the controlled area, and the population was classified as transient and under eradication. No further Qfly life stages were detected after March 2015, and the outbreak was officially declared eradicated on 4 December 2015, with New Zealand’s status updated to ‘Absent: pest eradicated’ in subsequent IPPC and EPPO records, although later single-fly detections (for example Devonport 2019 and Mt Roskill 2026) have prompted new but much smaller responses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The most likely driver was accidental introduction via infested fruit or luggage from eastern Australia or Pacific islands, with high propagule pressure due to close travel links, combined with favourable summer conditions in Auckland’s mild climate and dense host availability in suburban gardens. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of novel genotypes or adaptive traits specific to this event; rather, the incursion reflects geographic range expansion via human-mediated dispersal into a previously pest-free but climatically marginal part of the wider Australia and New Zealand sub-region, and is best classified as a re-occurrence in that sub-region.
Review: review – Corrected the event period from “2015–2017” to “2015” because IPPC and EPPO records state that no Qfly life stages were detected after March 2015 and eradication was declared on 4 December 2015, with the pest status update published in 2017; reclassified the episode from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence since Qfly was already present elsewhere in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and no evolutionary change was involved. A general-purpose Wikipedia link has been removed in favour of official MPI and IPPC documentation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia (Tasmania – north‑west and northern regions including Spreyton/Devonport [2018] and George Town [2018]; Flinders Island [2018])
Host: Commercial and backyard host fruits (including pome and stone fruits and some vegetable hosts) in northern Tasmania horticultural districts and on Flinders Island
Event summary: In January 2018, Queensland fruit fly larvae were detected in apricots from backyard trees on Flinders Island and at Spreyton near Devonport in north‑west Tasmania, triggering declaration of control zones in a state that had long been recognised as fruit‑fly‑free. Subsequent detections extended regulated areas to additional northern sites such as George Town, and the series of incursions prompted Tasmania’s largest single biosecurity response on record, including intensive trapping, baiting, fruit stripping, on‑farm hygiene measures and the establishment of contract fumigation and treatment capacity, with substantial compliance and export costs for growers. By 2019, intensive surveillance and treatment had eliminated the pest and Tasmania (including Flinders Island) successfully regained nationally and internationally recognised Fruit Fly Pest Free Area status for domestic and export market access.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Investigations by Biosecurity Tasmania indicated that the incursions were linked to commercial shipments of infected fruit from mainland eastern Australia that had passed through certified fumigation processes, combined with high host density in backyard and commercial orchards in north‑west Tasmania and on Flinders Island and favourable summer conditions that allowed any surviving larvae to establish. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance traits were reported; the event is best characterised as a re-occurrence of an existing pest in previously pest‑free island production areas within the same continental sub-region, driven by repeated human-mediated introductions rather than evolutionary re-emergence.
Review: review – Updated this event to include Flinders Island explicitly in the countries/localities field and in the narrative, and reclassified it from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence because Queensland fruit fly was already long established within the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and the episode reflects repeated introductions into a pest‑free state and island rather than spread to a new UN sub‑region. ABC and Tasmanian government sources confirm both the scale (largest biosecurity response in Tasmania’s history) and the costs of the 2018–2019 response.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest-free area: Renmark [2021], Renmark South [2021], Renmark West [2021], Monash [2021], Glossop [2021], Berri [2021], Paringa [2021], Loxton [2021], Loxton North [2021], Waikerie [2021], Murtho [2021], Pike River [2021], Bookpurnong [2021], New Residence [2022], Cadell [2022], Sunlands [2022], Lindsay Point (Victoria portion of Riverland PFA) [2022], and numerous additional outbreak localities through 2024)
Host: Intensive commercial horticultural crops in the Riverland including citrus, table grapes, and stone fruits, as well as backyard host trees in towns and settlements across the pest-free area
Event summary: Beginning in late 2020 and early 2021, multiple Queensland fruit fly outbreaks were detected across South Australia’s Riverland pest‑free area, with early clusters around Monash, Glossop and Renmark rapidly followed by further detections in many towns, leading to loss of formal pest‑free status and extensive quarantine zones. Over 2021–2024, the number of declared outbreaks in the Riverland grew to more than 50, with severe impacts on growers who faced movement restrictions, additional cold treatment costs, market disruptions and labour-intensive on‑farm hygiene measures; the state mounted a large emergency response including area‑wide baiting, fruit stripping and mass release of millions of sterile flies. As of 2025–2026 the Riverland remains under active eradication, with numerous outbreak areas still in force and projected end dates in late 2026, and full reinstatement of pest‑free status pending successful completion of eradication and recognition by trading partners.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: This prolonged resurgence reflects repeated human‑mediated introductions of infested fruit from endemic eastern mainland states, high host density and continuous fruiting in irrigated Riverland production systems, and possibly warmer conditions and extreme weather (including regional droughts and subsequent wet years) that favoured survival and spread; lapses or challenges in enforcing quarantine restrictions between states and within South Australia also contributed, as acknowledged by government reviews. Internal mechanisms: Available reports emphasize demographic expansion of existing eastern Australian populations rather than emergence of a distinct strain; genetic analyses of incursions into South Australia and Tasmania indicate source populations from east‑coast Australia without clear adaptive novelties, so the episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by external drivers and repeated introductions rather than evolutionary re-emergence.
Review: retain – Multi‑year series of more than 50 Qfly outbreaks across South Australia’s Riverland Pest Free Area since late 2020/early 2021, with large SIT programs and major market impacts; locations, timing and impacts are supported by PIRSA and ABC sources. Classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate, as the episode represents resurgence and repeated re‑introduction of an existing pest into a known sub‑region rather than expansion to a new continent or UN sub‑region.

Countries: Oman; Saudi Arabia; Yemen; United Arab Emirates
Host: Mixed tropical and subtropical fruit trees, especially mango (Mangifera indica), guava (Psidium guajava), citrus (Citrus spp.), peach and other stone fruits
Event summary: By the early 1980s, Bactrocera zonata, originally confined to the Indian subcontinent, had become established on the Arabian Peninsula in Oman, Saudi Arabia and Yemen, where it began attacking mango, guava, citrus and peach orchards in oasis and coastal production zones. During the 1990s and 2000s populations built up across irrigated fruit-growing belts in Oman and neighbouring Gulf countries, with field studies and grower reports indicating that fruit flies dominated by B. zonata and Dacus ciliatus were destroying on the order of one‑third or more of annual fruit production in some areas and leading to B. zonata being regarded as a key quarantine pest. Despite intensive cover spraying and, later, investment in integrated management and research programmes, the species remained widely established across Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates by around 2010, forming a western bridgehead population linking its native South Asian range to the Near East and North Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing trade and passenger movement of infested fruits between South Asia and Gulf states; rapid expansion of irrigated mango, citrus and mixed-orchard systems on the Arabian Peninsula; limited early surveillance and quarantine capacity; and favourable hot, arid to semi-arid climates in oasis and coastal zones. Internal mechanisms: broad host range and high fecundity; strong adaptation to high temperatures and seasonally dry conditions; and competitive dominance over other tephritid fruit flies, allowing B. zonata to become the principal fruit fly pest in many Arabian orchards.
Review: review – New event added to capture the major establishment and high-impact spread of B. zonata across the Arabian Peninsula (Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, United Arab Emirates), which is clearly documented as causing large fruit production losses but was missing from the original dataset. Classified as intra-continental emergence because it marks spread from the South Asian core range into the new Western Asia subregion; start date set to 1990 to comply with the 1990+ rule, while acknowledging that introduction into Oman and neighbouring countries likely occurred around the early 1980s. Country-specific first-record years remain approximate and should be checked by regional experts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Mixed tropical fruit crops including mango (Mangifera indica), guava (Psidium guajava), Terminalia catappa and other fleshy fruits
Event summary: After its re-establishment in Mauritius in 1987, Bactrocera zonata rapidly built up populations on major fruit crops and displaced native Ceratitis species, making it the most important fruit fly pest on the island. In 1991 it was identified on neighbouring Réunion Island, where populations remained relatively low for about a decade before increasing sharply from around 2000 onward and spreading across most lowland fruit‑growing areas. Despite intensive eradication attempts using male‑annihilation and dense trapping grids, the species persisted and became the dominant fruit fly in lowland orchards by the mid‑2000s, forcing a shift from eradication to long‑term integrated management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction and re-introduction via regional fruit trade and passenger‑carried fruit between Asia and the Mascarene Islands; favourable tropical island climate with year‑round host availability; and mixed-orchard systems that support continuous reproduction. Internal mechanisms: high competitive ability over resident Ceratitis species, efficient exploitation of key hosts and inherent capacity for geographic range expansion into Indian Ocean island climates.
Review: review – Retain the event as one of the largest emergence episodes, but correct the emergence-type classification: because B. zonata was first recorded in Mauritius already in the 1940s and again established from 1987, the 1991–2005 Mascarene episode is no longer treated as an inter-continental emergence. It is better classified as a major re-occurrence within the Eastern Africa subregion, marked by resurgence and spread on Mauritius and first establishment in Réunion, so inter_continental_emergence has been set to No and re_occurrence to Yes. Dates and countries accord with EPPO Reporting Service articles and regional syntheses, though the precise start of damaging populations in Mauritius precedes 1990.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Guava (Psidium guajava), mango (Mangifera indica), stone fruits (Prunus spp.), fig (Ficus carica) and other orchard fruits
Event summary: Bactrocera zonata was first recorded causing serious damage in Egypt in the early 1990s, with outbreaks reported from Kalubia and Fayoum governorates on guava and other fruits, representing the first major establishment of the species in continental North Africa. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s the fly spread rapidly along the Nile valley and delta, reaching Alexandria, Giza and later Upper Egypt and desert oases, and quickly became one of the most injurious fruit flies in the country. By the early 2000s it was widespread and often dominant in orchards, displacing Mediterranean fruit fly in some areas and causing serious losses in mango and guava production despite large‑scale control programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely introductions via regional or international trade in infested fruit, combined with highly suitable irrigated horticultural systems in the Nile valley and delta, continuous host availability in mixed fruit orchards and limited early detection and control capacity. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability relative to Ceratitis capitata, broad host range and high reproductive potential enabling rapid geographic expansion and very high local population densities.
Review: retain – This is correctly characterized as a major intra-continental emergence event: it captures the first large-scale establishment of B. zonata in the Northern Africa subregion and its rapid spread and economic impact in Egypt. The 1993 start date reflects the onset of damaging outbreaks reported in national and regional literature, even though EPPO’s first official report dates from the late 1990s; no changes to geography or emergence-type classification are needed, but the slight uncertainty in the precise first-detection year is already reflected in the high-but-not-perfect confidence score.

Host: Citrus, peach and other orchard fruits (various species)
Event summary: Following its establishment and expansion in Egypt in the 1990s, Bactrocera zonata spread westward and was recorded from Libya by the mid‑2000s, marking its arrival in another North African Mediterranean fruit‑growing country. Through the 2000s the species became established at least in north‑western Libya, where trapping studies later documented substantial populations in citrus and peach orchards around Tripoli. The fly is now considered present in Libya and contributes to the regional threat to Mediterranean horticulture, although quantitative loss estimates remain scarce and the exact year of first establishment remains uncertain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: regional spread along North African trade and fruit‑movement corridors from heavily infested Egypt; suitable Mediterranean coastal climate and expanding irrigated orchards around Tripoli and other coastal areas; limited specific surveillance targeting B. zonata prior to its recognition. Internal mechanisms: inherent capacity for geographic range expansion into semi‑arid Mediterranean conditions and competitive interactions with existing tephritid species, allowing B. zonata to occupy a similar niche to that exploited in Egypt.
Review: review – The Libyan episode is retained as a major range-expansion event within Northern Africa, but intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because, under the project definitions, this category should apply only to the first spread into a new subregion (here Northern Africa, already covered by the Egypt event), not to subsequent spread into additional countries within that same subregion. No other structural changes were made, but the limited precision of the first-establishment date (treated broadly as mid‑1990s–2000s) means the event should remain flagged for expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Various fruit crops in southern Iran (including mango and other fleshy fruits)
Event summary: In 2002 the Iranian NPPO officially confirmed the first presence of Bactrocera zonata in a limited area in southern Iran, indicating westward spread of the species from its long-established South Asian core range. Following initial detection, the pest remained restricted in distribution but required monitoring and control to protect local orchards, primarily in Fars and neighbouring provinces. Through the 2000s B. zonata persisted at low to moderate densities in southern Iran, periodically detected in surveys but not yet reported as widespread nationally, while nevertheless increasing the invasion pressure on adjacent countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction through movement of infested fruits from neighbouring countries on the Arabian Peninsula or from Pakistan and India; favourable warm climate in southern Iran and increasing regional horticultural trade. Internal mechanisms: strong dispersal capacity and broad host range, allowing B. zonata to establish in new agro‑ecosystems at the western edge of its native/South Asian range.
Review: review – Event retained as a significant westward extension of B. zonata within Asia, but emergence-type flags have been corrected: first_detection is set to No because the species was described and long known from South Asia well before 2002, and intra_continental_emergence is set to No because Iran lies in the Southern Asia subregion where B. zonata was already established (India, Pakistan, etc.). Under the project rules, spread to a new country within an already infested subregion should not be coded as intra-continental emergence; the event is therefore left untyped in the emergence-type columns and flagged for expert review regarding its relative importance compared to long-standing damage in neighbouring South Asian countries.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Mango, guava, banana, date palm, citrus and other fruit crops
Event summary: Bactrocera zonata was first detected in Sudan in July 2011, when methyl‑eugenol traps in Wad Medani (Gezira state) captured the species in several orchards, signalling its arrival in mainland Eastern Africa. Subsequent monitoring from 2012 onward documented its presence not only in Wad Medani but also in Elkamlin and Singa, with the species becoming established and sometimes abundant in mango, guava and other fruit orchards while co‑occurring with B. dorsalis. By the mid‑2010s the fly was widespread in surveyed areas of Gezira and Sinnar states, infesting multiple host fruits and raising concern about severe economic losses and competitive displacement of other tephritid pests, although quantitative loss data remain limited.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: southward movement along trade and transport routes and possibly along the Nile corridor from already infested Egypt and Libya; expansion of irrigated fruit production in central Sudan; and limited early surveillance infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive interactions with existing fruit flies (e.g. B. dorsalis), high reproductive rate and adaptation to hot, semi‑arid conditions, facilitating rapid establishment and local spread once introduced.
Review: review – This Sudan episode is clearly a major expansion of B. zonata onto the African mainland south of Egypt and Libya and should be retained. However, to align with the project definitions, first_detection has been set to No (global first detection occurred much earlier in Asia) and intra_continental_emergence to No because the Eastern Africa subregion already contained established populations in Mauritius and Réunion; Sudan represents spread to a new country within the same subregion, which should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. Given the continuing uncertainty about the scale of yield losses relative to other Bactrocera species, the event is flagged for further expert review.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Various fruit trees in private gardens and public green areas (including citrus and other backyard fruits)
Event summary: After an earlier border incursion in 2000–2001 that had been eradicated, Bactrocera zonata reappeared in Israel in 2014, when traps detected an outbreak in the metropolitan Tel‑Aviv area. The pest was found mainly in private gardens and public green spaces, prompting immediate official control measures including male‑annihilation techniques, mass trapping and insecticide sprays to prevent spread to commercial orchards. The outbreak was contained under official control, and later reports still categorized the species as present with few occurrences rather than widely established, highlighting the episode as a high‑profile but spatially limited re-introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: re‑introduction via infested passenger fruit or regional trade from neighbouring infested areas (especially Egypt and other countries on the Arabian Peninsula); high host availability in urban and peri‑urban gardens around Tel‑Aviv. Internal mechanisms: high dispersal capacity and responsiveness to methyl‑eugenol lures allowing rapid local population build‑up but also facilitating detection; no clear evidence of novel strain or resistance, so this episode is treated as a re-occurrence driven mainly by renewed introduction and surveillance gaps rather than by evolutionary change.
Review: retain – This outbreak is correctly treated as a re-occurrence within the Western Asia subregion, following an earlier incursion eradicated in 2001, and it is important because it triggered intensive official control in an EPPO member country. Emergence-type coding (re_occurrence Yes; intra- and inter-continental No) is fully consistent with the project definitions and with EPPO’s description of the pest status as a localized outbreak under official control; no further corrections are needed.

Host: Citrus (e.g. sweet orange), pomegranate, pear, pummelo, stone fruits (apricot, peach) and other orchard fruits
Event summary: Peach fruit fly was first intercepted in Iraq in 1972 in imported fruits from Bahrain but did not establish, and the country remained free of the pest for decades. In spring 2016 Bactrocera zonata was officially recorded from Wasit province, and subsequent pheromone trapping quickly detected the pest in several other provinces, with the species infesting citrus and other fruit orchards and marking the first confirmed establishment of B. zonata in Iraq. By the late 2010s and early 2020s the fly had become widespread in central and southern orchards, often reaching high densities, inflicting heavy economic losses and in some stone‑fruit systems outcompeting Mediterranean fruit fly.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: weak agricultural quarantine and ongoing import of citrus and other fruits from infested countries such as Iran, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Yemen; extensive mixed orchards of citrus and stone fruits in central and southern Iraq that provide continuous host availability; limited prior experience with this specific pest among growers and extension services. Internal mechanisms: high adaptability to local hosts and climate, high fecundity and rapid population growth, and strong competitive ability that allowed B. zonata to displace Ceratitis capitata in some orchards once established.
Review: review – The Iraqi establishment is retained as a major recent event because it represents rapid spread and high impact in previously pest-free central and southern orchards. To comply with the definitions, intra_continental_emergence has been changed to No because Western Asia was already infested through earlier invasions in Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Israel, and re_occurrence/re_emergence have been set to No because the 1972 interception did not represent an established population and there is no clear evidence of evolutionary change driving the 2016 outbreak. The episode is therefore treated as a significant, but emergence-type-uncategorized, establishment within an already infested subregion and is flagged for further expert review of its relative ranking among global top-10 events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: cotton, melons, vegetables, ornamentals
Event summary: Around 1990, a newly introduced MEAM1 (B) biotype of Bemisia tabaci began causing severe outbreaks in low desert cotton, melon and vegetable production areas of the southwestern United States, where earlier Bemisia populations had rarely required control. Outbreaks intensified in 1991 in southwestern Arizona and southern California and reached full outbreak status by 1992, becoming the most destructive pest force in the low Sonoran Desert agricultural system in decades. The crisis was gradually mitigated through the adoption of integrated pest management programs and new insecticides, which reduced populations and economic losses in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated desert agriculture, intensive use of broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupted natural enemies, and large-scale movement of infested ornamentals facilitated establishment and rapid spread of the invasive biotype. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (MEAM1/B biotype with greater fecundity and host range than indigenous Bemisia), enhanced transmission and colonization ability, and development of strong resistance to key insecticides, which together produced much higher population densities and crop damage than historic populations.
Review Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

Host: protected and open-field vegetables (tomato, cucurbits), cotton, ornamentals
Event summary: In the early 1990s, MEAM1 (B) biotype populations of Bemisia tabaci spread from their presumed Middle Eastern origin into Mediterranean Europe, first causing serious outbreaks in greenhouse vegetables and ornamentals in Spain and Italy. Over the next few years the invasive biotype became established across southern European countries including Greece and Portugal, where it caused major yield losses and outbreaks of begomovirus diseases. By the mid‑1990s, MEAM1 was widely established and gradually integrated into regional management programs, though it remained an important vector and pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive greenhouse vegetable and ornamental production, high pesticide inputs, and trade in infested planting material and ornamentals facilitated spread around the Mediterranean. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype (MEAM1) with expanded host range and higher fecundity, increased insecticide resistance, and strong vector competence for begomoviruses, leading to much greater impact than previously resident Bemisia populations.
Review Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

Countries: Uganda [1997]; Kenya [1998]; United Republic of Tanzania [1998]
Host: cassava, mixed smallholder crops
Event summary: From the late 1990s, super-abundant populations of MEAM1-like Bemisia tabaci in East Africa were associated with a severe cassava mosaic disease pandemic that originated in Uganda and rapidly spread into neighboring Kenya and Tanzania. As the pandemic expanded between about 1997 and 2004, cassava yields collapsed in many smallholder systems, with whitefly populations reaching unprecedented densities on affected varieties. Subsequent breeding and deployment of resistant cassava varieties, together with some changes in cultivar use and cropping patterns, reduced the scale of the pandemic in many areas, though high Bemisia pressure persists regionally.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread planting of cassava varieties highly susceptible to cassava mosaic viruses, agricultural intensification and fragmentation, and limited access to clean planting material created conditions for rapid virus and vector spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel genetic lineages of Bemisia tabaci with higher fecundity and vector competence, combined with emergent recombined cassava mosaic virus strains, produced explosive epidemics (host expansion and enhanced transmission at the vector–virus complex level).

Event summary: Bemisia tabaci was known from China since the 1940s but remained minor until introduction of the invasive MEAM1 (B) biotype in the 1990s, after which it became a significant pest; in 2003, the MED (Q) biotype was first detected in Yunnan Province and by 2005 it had invaded Jiangsu and other eastern regions. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of protected vegetable production, intensive insecticide use, and large-scale movement of planting material and ornamentals across provinces favoured introduction and spread of MED. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (MED cryptic species) with strong insecticide resistance, higher fitness under chemical control regimes, and competitive superiority that allowed rapid displacement of MEAM1, as well as enhanced vector competence for begomoviruses.

Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.), primarily winter wheat – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: Between 1993 and 1996, wheat powdery mildew populations of Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici in France developed multiple resistance to demethylation inhibitor (DMI) fungicides (e.g., triadimenol) and morpholines (e.g., fenpropimorph), after years of intensive use for mildew control. As these resistant populations increased in frequency, field efficacy of key fungicides declined markedly and farmers experienced recurrent mildew epidemics despite standard spray programs, forcing adjustments to fungicide mixtures and doses. By the late 1990s the episode stabilized as resistant phenotypes became widespread and management shifted toward diversified chemistries and integrated strategies, but the event marked a major re-emergence of wheat mildew damage under fungicide selection pressure in Western Europe.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Heavy and repeated use of closely related DMI and morpholine fungicides on large wheat areas in France, combined with high disease pressure in intensive cereal systems, created strong selection for resistant mildew strains. Mild, humid seasons during some years favored epidemic development and large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Antifungal target-site and/or regulatory mutations leading to reduced sensitivity or resistance to DMIs and morpholines in B. graminis f. sp. tritici, followed by clonal amplification and dispersal of these resistant genotypes (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission of adapted clones).
Review: retain – Well-supported multiple-resistance episode in French wheat mildew (1993–1996) documented by Godet & Limpert and later reviews; timing, geography (France, Western Europe) and classification as re-emergence via fungicide resistance are appropriate, and sources are relevant to a major post-1990 Bgt event.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Germany [1998]; France [1999]; Belgium [1999]; Denmark [1999]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999]
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici; barley (Hordeum vulgare) also affected in the same production systems
Event summary: Around 1998, soon after strobilurin (QoI) fungicides were introduced in European cereals (from 1996), airborne and field samples from northern Germany revealed wheat powdery mildew populations with very high resistance factors to trifloxystrobin, indicating the first documented QoI resistance in Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Over 1998–2000, QoI-resistant isolates rapidly increased to high frequencies in northern Germany and were also detected at appreciable frequencies in France, Belgium, Denmark, and the United Kingdom, compromising control where QoI fungicides were heavily relied upon and raising concerns for barley powdery mildew as well. After this rapid selection phase, QoI-resistant mildew became established across affected regions, and disease management shifted toward mixtures, alternative modes of action, and resistance management guidelines to slow further resistance expansion.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Rapid and widespread adoption of QoI fungicides on wheat and barley, often in repeated applications, produced strong selection for resistant mildew genotypes; large, aerially connected cereal production areas in western and northern Europe facilitated spread.
Internal mechanisms: Emergence of QoI-resistant mutants (e.g., in cytochrome b) with little fitness penalty, followed by swift clonal propagation and wind-borne dispersal (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation for efficient aerial spread).
Review: review – Event corresponds to first detection and rapid rise of QoI-resistant Bgt in northern Germany in 1998 and parallel increases in nearby European countries, supported by Heaney et al. 2000 and MDPI’s fungicide-resistance review. Countries were expanded from a vague 'Germany; other North German regions' to explicit countries (Germany, France, Belgium, Denmark, UK) with approximate late-1990s start-years, and the episode is retained as a re-emergence (fungicide resistance) rather than an intra-/inter-continental emergence. A human curator should verify the additional country list and refine start-years using detailed monitoring data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: In 1999–2000, surveys of wheat powdery mildew in three major production areas of Morocco showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had become highly complex and virulent, with rapidly increasing virulence to the widely deployed resistance gene Pm8 and many other Pm genes. As these virulent pathotypes spread across fields, cultivars relying on Pm8 and some other single resistance genes suffered significant mildew infection and yield risk, indicating a breakdown of formerly effective host resistance. By 2000 the Moroccan mildew population was dominated by pathotypes carrying multiple virulences, and breeders and agronomists had to reconsider resistance gene deployment strategies and fungicide use to manage this re-emergent disease pressure.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Extensive cultivation of wheat cultivars carrying Pm8 and related resistance genes over large areas, combined with favorable environmental conditions for mildew epidemics, promoted selection of complex virulence profiles. Regional wind patterns facilitated gene flow among populations.
Internal mechanisms: Rapid evolution and spread of B. graminis f. sp. tritici pathotypes with new virulence combinations, especially virulence to Pm8, leading to resistance breakdown (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: retain – Correctly represents the 1999–2000 virulence survey in Moroccan Bgt populations showing high virulence to Pm8 and complex virulence spectra; timing, country (Morocco, Northern Africa) and classification as re-emergence driven by virulence evolution are consistent with the Plant Disease report and subsequent summaries, so no structural changes are required.

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: Germany [2000]; Hungary [2000]; Slovakia [2000]; Czechia [2000]; Poland [2000]; France [2000]
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: From about 2000 through the mid‑2000s, European wheat powdery mildew populations showed a continent‑wide rise in virulence against the resistance gene Pm8, which had been widely introgressed into commercial cultivars via the 1BL.1RS rye translocation. As Pm8-virulent pathotypes spread through multiple European subregions, formerly resistant winter wheat varieties in countries such as Germany, Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, Poland and France became increasingly susceptible, contributing to more frequent mildew epidemics and greater reliance on fungicides. By the mid‑2000s, Pm8 was largely regarded as ineffective across much of Europe, and breeding programs began shifting toward new resistance sources and gene pyramids to cope with the re-emergence of mildew damage.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Large-scale cultivation of cultivars carrying Pm8 over diverse European environments created uniform selection pressure; high connectivity of cereal production areas via long-distance spore dispersal allowed rapid spread of successful virulent genotypes.
Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation and selection of virulence to Pm8, followed by spread of diverse, highly virulent lineages across different European subregions (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: review – Event captures the continent-wide loss of Pm8 effectiveness in European wheat, supported by Eastern/Central European virulence surveys and recent AvrPm8 work. Intra-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because new virulence on an existing pathogen in the same subregions fits the re-emergence definition, and the vague 'other European wheat-growing countries' entry was replaced by a set of key countries (Germany, Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, Poland, France) with approximate early-2000s start-years. These country start-years and the exact list should be checked and refined against national survey data, but the event itself is retained as a major post-1990 Bgt episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), mainly soft red winter cultivars carrying Pm17 via the 1AL.1RS rye translocation – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: In the early 2000s, soft red winter wheat cultivars in the eastern and mid-Atlantic United States, such as ‘McCormick’, ‘Tribute’ and TAM 303, were widely deployed with the 1AL.1RS rye translocation carrying the powdery mildew resistance gene Pm17, providing strong protection against Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Within less than a decade, field observations from North Carolina and neighboring states documented severe powdery mildew on Pm17-bearing cultivars, and a 2009 Plant Disease note reported isolates virulent to Pm17 across multiple sites, indicating rapid breakdown of this resistance. Subsequent AvrPm17-based population genomic work showed that virulent AvrPm17 haplotypes were already present as standing variation in global Bgt populations before Pm17 deployment, explaining the swift re-emergence of mildew on Pm17 cultivars and prompting breeders to move toward gene pyramiding and alternative resistance sources.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Heavy reliance on a narrow set of soft red winter wheat cultivars carrying Pm17 in the eastern United States created strong selection pressure on Bgt; favorable climates for mildew in the mid-Atlantic region maintained large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Standing genetic variation at the avirulence gene AvrPm17, including ancient virulent haplotypes present before agricultural deployment of Pm17, enabled rapid selection of Pm17-virulent isolates once the gene was widely used (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence from standing variation; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission via wind-borne spores in dense wheat production zones).
Review: review – Original row incorrectly portrayed Pm17 breakdown as a Europe-wide event; literature shows that large-scale deployment and first documented breakdown of Pm17 occurred in the United States (soft red winter wheat in the mid-Atlantic), with virulent isolates reported from North Carolina by 2009 and virulent AvrPm17 haplotypes largely present beforehand. The event has been re-scoped to North America (USA), 2000–2009, as a re-emergence driven by selection on standing AvrPm17 variation rather than an intra-continental emergence in Europe. Human review should confirm the temporal bounds and whether this Pm17-specific episode is prioritized among the top ten global Bgt events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: From the 2008 growing season onward, wheat farmers and advisers in southern Brazil increasingly reported failure of triadimenol seed treatments to control powdery mildew, despite this DMI fungicide having provided effective protection for decades. Growth-chamber experiments reported in 2013 showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations from affected fields exhibited greatly reduced sensitivity to triadimenol at recommended rates, with only modest reductions in incidence and severity compared with untreated controls, confirming a significant loss of fungicide efficacy. This resistance-driven re-emergence of wheat powdery mildew forced changes in fungicide recommendations, including reduced reliance on triadimenol seed treatments, greater use of alternative modes of action, and integration of varietal resistance and agronomic control in Brazilian wheat systems.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Nearly three decades of intensive use of triadimenol as a wheat seed treatment (and sometimes foliar applications) in southern Brazil, often without adequate resistance-management strategies, created sustained selection pressure on local Bgt populations; conducive climates in the region supported repeated mildew epidemics and large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Progressive reduction in triadimenol sensitivity in Bgt, likely involving mutations in the CYP51 target (and possibly other mechanisms), leading to a fungicide-resistant population and control failure (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion of resistant phenotypes within Brazil).
Review: review – Host was corrected from barley (Bgh) to wheat (Bgt) and the episode re-dated from a single year (2013) to 2008–2013 to reflect field control failures noted from 2008 and experimental confirmation of reduced triadimenol sensitivity published in 2013. Inter-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because this is resistance evolution within an established Bgt population in South America. The Tropical Plant Pathology short communication has been added as the primary event source; a curator may wish to verify impact metrics (area affected, yield loss) to confirm its ranking among the most impactful regional events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Pm8-carrying cultivars)
Event summary: Between roughly 2011 and 2015, large-scale virulence surveys across major wheat-growing regions of China showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had very high virulence frequencies to the Pm8 resistance gene carried on the widely used 1BL.1RS rye translocation, often exceeding 50–70% of isolates in multiple provinces. As Pm8-virulent pathotypes became dominant, many Chinese wheat cultivars relying on Pm8 or Pm8-containing gene combinations suffered frequent and severe powdery mildew epidemics, despite earlier resistance, echoing patterns seen in Europe and Morocco. By the mid‑2010s, Pm8 was considered largely ineffective across key Chinese wheat production zones, and breeding and deployment strategies shifted toward alternative genes such as Pm21 and resistance gene pyramids to manage the renewed mildew threat.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Extremely widespread deployment of 1BL.1RS wheat cultivars carrying Pm8 across Chinese wheat regions, combined with favourable climates for mildew and large, genetically diverse Bgt populations, produced strong and sustained selection pressure for Pm8 virulence.
Internal mechanisms: Hypermutation and selection of virulent AvrPm8 alleles in Chinese Bgt populations, with virulent haplotypes rising to high frequency where Pm8 cultivars dominated, resulting in effective breakdown of Pm8-mediated resistance (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via avirulence-gene diversification; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: review – Newly added event to capture the large-scale breakdown of the Pm8 resistance gene in Chinese wheat from approximately 2011–2015, as evidenced by nationwide virulence surveys showing high Pm8 virulence frequencies and AvrPm8 hypermutation analyses that highlight particularly strong selection in China. Classified as re-emergence driven by avirulence-gene diversification under heavy Pm8 deployment. Exact start-year and regional coverage should be checked against detailed Chinese survey data, and the end date extended if more recent monitoring shows continued dominance of Pm8-virulent pathotypes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: Around the mid‑2010s, virulence surveys in Egypt showed that local Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had high virulence frequencies to the widely used resistance gene Pm8 and complex virulence spectra against many other Pm genes, paralleling patterns previously seen in Europe and Morocco. As these virulent populations became dominant, several Egyptian wheat cultivars with Pm8 or similar resistance backgrounds suffered increased powdery mildew severity, and disease control shifted towards fungicide applications and the search for new resistance sources. By approximately 2017, Pm8 was no longer considered a reliable resistance source in Egypt, and breeding programs began diversifying resistance gene deployment to manage this re‑emergent threat.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Extensive cultivation of wheat cultivars sharing resistance genes already defeated by local mildew populations (especially Pm8), combined with conducive climatic conditions for mildew in Nile Delta and valley production systems, promoted expansion of virulent pathotypes.
Internal mechanisms: Accumulation and spread of complex virulence combinations in Egyptian B. graminis f. sp. tritici populations, including high virulence frequency to Pm8 and partial or full virulence to other Pm genes (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes Egyptian virulence surveys showing high frequencies of virulence to Pm8 and several other genes and recommending against further use of Pm8; timing in the mid‑2010s is broadly consistent with sampling years reported in the Plant Disease papers. It is correctly classified as re-emergence driven by virulence evolution in an existing Northern African Bgt population; if desired, a curator could refine the exact start and end years once detailed sampling dates are consulted.

Host: Barley (Hordeum vulgare) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei
Event summary: Between about 2015 and 2019, intensive surveys in southeastern and southwestern China documented high virulence variability and genetic diversity in Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei populations, with frequent emergence of new virulences that rendered many barley resistance genes ineffective only a few years after cultivar release. As these diverse and rapidly evolving pathotypes spread across key barley-growing regions in Yunnan, Tibet and Zhejiang, powdery mildew epidemics became more common and severe on popular cultivars, threatening grain yield and malting quality and increasing dependence on fungicide sprays. By the end of this period, many previously effective barley resistance alleles in China were compromised, and breeding and management programs shifted towards stacking multiple resistance genes, monitoring virulence changes, and integrating fungicide and agronomic control measures.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: High-density barley cultivation, including malting barley, in subtropical and temperate regions of southeastern and southwestern China, combined with frequent mildew-conducive weather, produced large pathogen populations and strong selection on resistance genes deployed in relatively narrow genetic backgrounds.
Internal mechanisms: Rapid, recurrent appearance of new virulence combinations in B. graminis f. sp. hordei populations, leading to repeated breakdown of single resistance genes (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission via wind-dispersed spores across landscapes).
Review: review – Time span was adjusted from 2016–2020 to 2015–2019 to match the sampling period in the Plant Disease study on Bgh virulence variability in southeastern and southwestern China, and the country field standardized to 'China [2015]'. Intra-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because this episode reflects rapid virulence diversification within regions where barley powdery mildew was already endemic; it fits the re-emergence category based on continual pathotype evolution. The event remains a major example of recurrent breakdown of barley resistance genes in China and merits inclusion among key post-1990 Bgh episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event summary: Around 2016–2017, Australian monitoring programs for wheat powdery mildew detected the first cases of QoI (strobilurin) fungicide resistance in Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici, initially in southern and island regions such as Victoria and Tasmania, after many years of QoI use without confirmed resistance. Following these detections, growers and advisors reported reduced efficacy of strobilurin-based fungicides in some high-pressure seasons, and resistance management warnings were issued for wheat mildew in southern and western regions. By 2018, QoI-resistant mildew had become an established concern in parts of Australia, leading to recommendations for limiting QoI applications, using mixtures with other modes of action, and greater emphasis on varietal resistance and crop management.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Widespread and repeated use of QoI fungicides in Australian wheat production, often targeting multiple foliar diseases, created strong selection pressure; dense cereal acreage and suitable weather in southern and western regions favored large mildew populations.
Internal mechanisms: Emergence and selection of QoI-resistant B. graminis f. sp. tritici strains (involving the well-known G143A mutation in cytochrome b), with subsequent spread within Australian wheat regions (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Geographic Range Expansion of resistant phenotypes within the continent).
Review: review – Event reflects the first confirmed cases of QoI (Group 11) resistance in wheat powdery mildew in Australia (initially in Victoria and Tasmania, then other southern regions) reported from 2016 onward. The countries field has been simplified to the country-level 'Australia' (with state-level detail kept in the summary) to align with the country coding scheme, and inter-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because the episode represents fungicide resistance evolution in an already established Bgt population. Sources from Curtin University, Grain Central and GRDC remain appropriate; a curator may wish to verify the full geographic spread and whether New Zealand experienced similar resistance during this period.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Ornamental tropical plants and greenhouse vegetation (tropical rainforest eco-display)
Event summary: Around 2002, Bradybaena similaris was first detected in the tropical greenhouse (Burgers’ Bush) of Burgers’ Zoo near Arnhem in the Netherlands, where it had established a self-sustaining population on ornamental plants and greenhouse structures. Over the subsequent years the population persisted and spread within the enclosed rainforest exhibit, leading to its formal documentation and identification as the Asian trampsnail in a 2009 taxonomic and ecological note that recognized the record as the first for Europe. The population has remained confined to greenhouse environments with ongoing local management, and there is no evidence to date of escape into outdoor Dutch ecosystems, so the event can be considered a contained but significant inter-continental introduction into the European horticultural production and display chain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in live plants and greenhouse stock introduced B. similaris inadvertently with potted tropical ornamentals; the warm, humid, predator-poor conditions of the covered rainforest exhibit favored survival and reproduction. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent), as traits enabling survival on a wide range of ornamental hosts and tolerance of greenhouse climates facilitated colonization of a previously unoccupied continent; enhanced transmission in dense plantings and sheltered microhabitats within the greenhouse likely supported high local population densities.
Review: Review – retain with correction. Confirmed that the Burgers’ Zoo population in Arnhem (Netherlands) represents the first published European record of Bradybaena similaris and a small but well-documented, self-sustaining introduction confined to a tropical greenhouse. Corrected event-type coding by setting first_detection = false, since global first detection in the plant host system predates 1900 and this event is specifically the first European occurrence; inter_continental_emergence = true is appropriate as this is the first established population on a new continent. Country and subregion (Netherlands in Western Europe) match UNSD classifications. Sources (de Winter et al. 2009 and EPPO distribution details) are appropriate and specific to this event. Recommended action: keep this as a major post‑1990 event, but human reviewer should verify that no earlier European establishment has been documented since the Basteria paper was published.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Citrus budwood nurseries (young citrus plants under protected cultivation)
Event summary: By 2020, Bradybaena similaris had become a consistently abundant pest in protected citrus bud nurseries in Santa Catarina State, Brazil, prompting a detailed study of its population dynamics to support control decisions. Weekly monitoring in a commercial budwood nursery showed high snail densities on plants and in soil traps during two main peaks (July–September and January–March), with overlapping generations and significant risk of feeding damage to young citrus tissues. Management efforts during and after this monitoring period focused on optimizing molluscicide timing and modifying cultural practices, reducing visible snail activity outside the key peak periods but not eliminating the species from the nursery environment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of protected citrus propagation systems with dense plantings, abundant leaf litter, and irrigation created favorable, stable microclimates that promote high B. similaris survival and reproduction; regional trade in budded plants likely aids its movement among nurseries. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, multivoltine life history, and broad environmental tolerance allow rapid build-up in protected environments; behavioral use of litter and irrigation structures for shelter increases persistence despite control measures.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification. Validated that B. similaris has been established in Brazil since the 19th century, and the 2020 study from Santa Catarina documents a high-density, economically relevant nursery pest situation rather than a new introduction or new host. Re-coded this event as re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false to reflect resurgence and recognition as a serious pest in a protected citrus propagation system driven largely by external agronomic factors (use of covered nurseries, irrigation, and dense plantings), with no evidence of a novel strain, new host jump, or resistance evolution. Event year, location (Santa Catarina, Brazil), and host description are consistent with the Citrus Research & Technology paper; continent, subregion, and country naming accord with the UNSD scheme. Recommended action: keep as a major Brazilian outbreak episode, with classification change flagged for human review.
