Countries: Brazil (southern states – including Rio Grande do Sul, Paraná, Santa Catarina) [2010s]
Host: Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) and other fruit and vegetable crops, including vines, citrus, banana, coffee, and leafy vegetables
Event summary: During the 2010s, Bradybaena similaris was increasingly reported as a damaging pest in commercial strawberry fields and other horticultural crops in southern Brazil, culminating in studies published around 2019 that identified it among the principal terrestrial gastropods attacking strawberries and a wide range of other crops. Field surveys in Rio Grande do Sul and neighboring states documented heavy nocturnal feeding on strawberry fruits and foliage, as well as on vines, citrus, banana, coffee, and leafy vegetables, with growers reporting economic losses and contamination of harvested produce. Subsequent adoption of targeted molluscicide use, improved field sanitation, and modifications to irrigation and mulch practices helped moderate the most severe outbreaks, although the snail remains entrenched as a key gastropod pest in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of fruit and vegetable production with drip irrigation, plastic mulches, and abundant ground cover created moist refuges ideal for snail survival; regional transport of planting material and produce likely redistributed B. similaris among farms. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive capacity and broad host range increased its ability to exploit diverse crops, contributing to pronounced resurgence as an economically important pest in southern Brazilian horticulture.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification and minor wording clarification. Confirmed from the Ciência Rural paper and regional pest information that B. similaris has long been present in Brazil but emerged during the 2010s as a prominent pest of strawberries and other horticultural crops in southern states, with clear evidence of crop damage and grower concern. Updated event-type coding to re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false, because the outbreak reflects resurgence and spread within an already infested country/subregion driven by production intensification and favorable microhabitats, not a new host jump (strawberry was already known as a host) or documented evolutionary change. Adjusted the countries string slightly to make clear that multiple southern Brazilian states are involved while still treating Brazil as the country unit. Recommended action: keep as one of the main South American agricultural impact events, but human reviewer should confirm that it is not better merged with the citrus-nursery episode into a single, broader southern-Brazil horticultural outbreak period.

Countries: Argentina (Misiones) [2010s]; Argentina (Entre Ríos – southernmost South American record) [2019]
Host: Peridomestic vegetation, gardens, and agricultural plantations (including various crops in northeastern and east-central Argentina)
Event summary: Although Bradybaena similaris had a historical record from Misiones Province in the mid-20th century, a 2019 BioInvasions Records study documented nine new localities in Misiones and the first confirmed record in Entre Ríos Province, representing the southernmost occurrence of the species in South America. Surveys in urban and rural sites, including residential gardens, waterfalls, and agricultural plantations, showed that the snail was now widespread and established in northeastern Argentina and extending into temperate east-central areas, lengthening its latitudinal range by about one degree and appearing in places where it had previously gone undetected or misidentified. Following these findings, Argentine malacologists and plant protection services highlighted the need for monitoring its further spread and assessing risks both to agriculture and as a potential intermediate host of parasitic nematodes, while no specific nationwide crop-focused control program had yet been triggered.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regional movement of ornamental plants, nursery stock, and agricultural commodities among South American countries (notably from Brazil and Uruguay) likely transported B. similaris into and within Argentina; land-use change and expansion of irrigated agriculture and disturbed peridomestic habitats in northeastern and east-central provinces may have facilitated establishment. Internal mechanisms: Broad environmental tolerance and high colonization ability allow the species to persist in both subtropical Misiones and cooler temperate Entre Ríos, supporting continued geographic range expansion within Argentina.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification and clarification of historical context. The BioInvasions Records article confirms that B. similaris had an earlier record in Misiones (1956) and that the 2019 work adds numerous new localities plus a new southernmost record in Entre Ríos, implying both filling of distribution gaps and a modest latitudinal range extension. Because Argentina (and the broader South American subregion) were already known to harbor the species, this episode represents renewed spread and increased detection within a previously affected subregion, not a first introduction or documented genetic/phenotypic shift. Consequently, re-coded as re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false. Country, provinces, and timing (2010s, with a focal 2019 publication year) are consistent with the primary source. Recommended action: keep as a major South American range-expansion/resurgence event affecting peridomestic and agricultural habitats, noting for human reviewers that quantified crop loss data are still limited but the combination of agricultural risk and role as a parasite host justifies inclusion among top events.

Host: Vegetation along irrigation canals and adjacent cultivated fields (mixed crops)
Event summary: In 2019, Bradybaena similaris was recorded for the first time in Bangladesh when populations were discovered along an irrigation canal next to cultivated fields in Kayangghat in the country’s east, a finding later detailed in a 2020 BioInvasions Records paper. The snails were found in moist, disturbed vegetation bordering agricultural land, indicating that the species had already established locally by the time of detection and likely arrived through regional trade or transport from neighboring countries such as India, where it was already present. After publication, the EPPO Global Database listed the species as present in Bangladesh with no further details, and while large agricultural outbreaks have not yet been reported, authorities and researchers have recommended vigilance because the species is a known cosmopolitan pest of fruits, vegetables, and ornamentals and may expand into irrigated cropping systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of goods, vehicles, and plant material from neighboring India and other South Asian trade partners likely introduced B. similaris to eastern Bangladesh; the presence of irrigated agriculture and permanent canal systems created humid microhabitats favorable for its establishment. Internal mechanisms: High dispersal potential via egg-laying on soil and plant debris and the ability to exploit disturbed, human-dominated habitats contribute to spread and establishment within Southern Asia, but there is no evidence of a novel strain or host shift in this event.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification. EPPO distribution details and the BioInvasions Records article confirm that 2019 was the first confirmed national record of B. similaris in Bangladesh, within a Southern Asian subregion where the species was already known (e.g., India, Nepal). Accordingly, this is not a global first detection and not a new subregional or continental emergence, but rather spread into a new country within a previously affected subregion. Re-coded as re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false to reflect resurgence/expansion driven by trade and habitat conditions, without evidence of evolutionary change. Event year, locality (Kayangghat, east Bangladesh), and host context (canal-side vegetation adjacent to fields) align with the published record. Recommended action: keep as a key post‑2000 range-expansion event in Southern Asia, while noting that current agricultural impacts are more potential than realized and should be monitored.

Host: Lactuca sativa (cultivated lettuce)
Event summary: In June 1994, typical downy mildew symptoms were first observed on lettuce in commercial production areas of Natal (now KwaZulu‑Natal), South Africa, with angular chlorotic lesions and abundant white sporulation on leaf undersides. Surveys across ten lettuce‑growing sites documented an average of about 50% infection and severe leaf necrosis, and the pathogen was isolated and confirmed microscopically and via pathogenicity tests as Bremia lactucae. The outbreak highlighted downy mildew as a new constraint on lettuce production in this Southern African subregion and led to implementation of fungicide programs and monitoring to limit subsequent epidemics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and intensification of lettuce cultivation in Natal created new habitat for B. lactucae; suitable cool, moist winter conditions favored epidemic development. The 'first_detection' flag was set from Yes to No, as B. lactucae had been recognized on lettuce for decades and was already present elsewhere in Africa, whereas this episode fits the definition of intra‑continental emergence (first report in the Southern Africa sub‑region). Geography, host and mechanism now align well with the source, but the impact ranking as a top‑10 event should be confirmed by regional experts.

Host: Lactuca sativa (cultivated lettuce)
Event summary: From 2003 onward, severe downy mildew outbreaks began to affect lettuce production in São Paulo state, Brazil, with increasing difficulty in disease control and major yield and quality losses in intensively managed areas. Race‑typing of Brazilian B. lactucae populations between 2003 and 2011 using the sextet code system identified a succession of local races (SPBl:01 through SPBl:06 and later types), several of which emerged after 2006 and were associated with repeated resistance breakdown and severe epidemics in commercial cultivars. Continued monitoring through 2010–2011 confirmed that these novel races had become established in São Paulo’s lettuce districts, prompting recommendations for new resistant varieties, diversified Dm‑gene deployment and improved fungicide strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid intensification of lettuce production in São Paulo, year‑round cropping and dense plantings increased inoculum pressure; reliance on a narrow set of resistance genes and fungicides favored selection of new virulent types. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – multiple new races (SPBl series) with distinct virulence profiles; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – successive races overcame Dm‑mediated resistance in widely grown cultivars; possible Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance due to repeated fungicide use.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event captures a prolonged and well‑documented period in which multiple local races (SPBl:01–06 and later) emerged and spread in São Paulo, causing serious control failures and prompting large breeding and management responses; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for B. lactucae in South America. The timing, host, mechanisms and geographic focus agree with Brazilian monitoring studies; no structural changes are proposed, but future work could refine the end‑year if more recent São Paulo race data are incorporated.

Host: Lactuca sativa (primarily coastal and desert lettuce production in California and Arizona)
Event summary: Between 2015 and 2017, IBEB‑US monitoring in western US lettuce fields identified a group of Bremia lactucae isolates with a new virulence pattern that overcame several resistance genes used in commercial cultivars. Because this pattern was repeatedly recovered from different locations and seasons and persisted in the pathogen population, the consortium denominated it as race Bl:9US in 2018, extending the US race set beyond Bl:8US. Bl:9US contributed to renewed downy mildew problems in parts of coastal California and the desert production regions until cultivars with effective resistance and adjusted fungicide and hygiene programmes were adopted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive, year‑round lettuce production in the Salinas, coastal and desert valleys of California and Arizona, with high inoculum pressure and heavy use of race‑specific resistance and fungicides, favored selection of novel virulence types. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:9US represents a distinct virulence type stable over multiple years and locations; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – ability to infect cultivars carrying resistance to earlier US races (Bl:5–8US); Enhanced Transmission – persistence across major western‑US lettuce districts.

This new row was added to represent the emergence of race Bl:9US in the western United States, as described by the IBEB‑US press release and extension notes, which report repeated detections of the same virulence pattern in 2015–2017 followed by denomination in 2018. Because public sources provide limited quantitative yield‑loss estimates, the 2015–2018 window and qualitative impact assessment should be checked with regional specialists, but Bl:9US clearly marks an important race shift for US lettuce production. Countries: France [2016]; Germany [2016]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2016]; Belgium [2016]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2016]; Denmark [2016]; Norway [2016]; Sweden [2016]
Host: Lactuca sativa (open‑field and protected lettuce)
Event summary: In 2016, lettuce producers across north‑western Europe experienced unusually frequent and severe downy mildew outbreaks, including on cultivars carrying the then‑recommended set of Bremia resistances, and numerous isolates were collected for analysis. The International Bremia Evaluation Board Europe (IBEB‑EU) determined that one virulence profile was widely distributed across France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Scandinavia and Belgium, and in 2017 officially designated this new race as Bl:33EU. By late 2017 Bl:33EU was recognized as the most widespread race in Europe, and its establishment led to revisions of resistance descriptions and a push for new cultivars effective against Bl:33EU as well as strengthened chemical and hygiene measures to manage the elevated disease risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive European trade in lettuce seed and seedlings, dense year‑round production, and conducive cool, humid weather allowed rapid spread of a single successful race across multiple countries. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:33EU combined a virulence spectrum able to overcome many deployed Dm genes; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – its performance and spread across many production areas indicate superior fitness relative to many localized races it replaced.
Review: Decision: Retain. The description of Bl:33EU as a widely distributed race first evaluated from 2016 isolates and denominated in 2017, with confirmed presence in France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, Scandinavia and Belgium, is consistent with IBEB‑EU communications. Treating this as a re‑emergence event (new, more virulent race of an existing pathogen) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is appropriate, and the country and sub‑region assignments follow the press release wording; no structural changes are required.

Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – races Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU exhibited virulence patterns distinct from Bl:33EU and prior races; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – Bl:35EU, in particular, was described as a more aggressive variant of Bl:33EU able to break additional resistance sources; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – rapid colonization of many European subregions within a few seasons.

This row appropriately aggregates the emergence of Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU, which IBEB‑EU denominated in April 2018 on the basis of 2016–2017 surveys, and the listed countries match the union of territories reported for these races (Bl:34EU widely spread across western, southern and northern Europe; Bl:35EU mainly France plus parts of the Netherlands, UK and Germany). Because the 'countries' field does not distinguish which race occurs where and the bracket years [2016] are approximate for both, the event should be retained but marked for review if a future version separates Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU into more race‑specific, country‑level records.

Event summary: From 2016 onwards, IBEB‑EU monitoring began to detect a Bremia lactucae virulence pattern that was present across many European lettuce production areas and that overcame resistance effective against the then‑dominant race Bl:34EU. By 2017–2018 this virulence pattern represented roughly 16% of the isolates surveyed in 2017–2018 and had been found in multiple centres of lettuce production, including France, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Austria, Switzerland and Scandinavian countries. A formal evaluation launched in late 2018 led IBEB‑EU in April 2019 to denominate the representative isolate DE1620 as the new race Bl:36EU, prompting further adjustments of resistance claims and integrated control strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive, year‑round lettuce production across western and northern Europe, widespread deployment of similar combinations of resistance genes and fungicide programmes, and extensive trade in seed and young plants created strong selection for more virulent Bremia genotypes and facilitated their movement among regions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:36EU is described as a more virulent variant of Bl:34EU, able to break at least one additional resistance source; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – the race’s rapid rise to around 16% of surveyed isolates and broad geographic spread indicate a substantial fitness advantage under contemporary European production conditions.
Review: Decision: Review. This new row was added for race Bl:36EU, which IBEB‑EU denominated in 2019 after finding the underlying virulence pattern in about 16% of 2017–2018 isolates and documenting its spread across multiple European lettuce regions. Event years (2016–2019) and bracket years [2016] reflect that the race was first spotted in 2016–2017 but formally named in 2019; these approximations and the exact country set should be validated against national race‑monitoring datasets. Classified as re‑emergence because it represents a new, more virulent race of an already established pathogen, not spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region.

Host: Lactuca sativa (field lettuce, particularly in Mediterranean regions)
Event summary: From the late 2010s, French and Mediterranean lettuce producers reported recurring downy mildew problems in cultivars with up‑to‑date resistance, and IBEB‑EU surveillance identified a distinct virulence profile that had been present for several years in France and was increasingly found in Spain, Portugal and Italy. On 1 June 2021 IBEB‑EU formally denominated this profile as the new race Bl:37EU, with the type isolate FR19064 representative of a widely distributed, highly virulent population in these southern European countries. After its official recognition, Bl:37EU became a key target for breeders and resistance screening, and guidance to growers stressed the need to combine cultivars resistant to Bl:37EU with strict hygiene and fungicide programs to mitigate frequent outbreaks in Mediterranean lettuce production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of lettuce production in Mediterranean winter areas with conditions highly favorable to downy mildew and heavy reliance on genetic resistance led to strong selection for virulent pathotypes; regional trade in plant material facilitated spread among France, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:37EU represented a new virulence profile not covered by existing differential sets; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – its broad distribution and impact in resistant cultivars suggest enhanced ability to overcome multiple resistance factors; Enhanced Transmission – genetic traits enabling persistence and spread under Mediterranean conditions.
Review: Decision: Review. The event has been updated to reflect IBEB‑EU’s denomination of Bl:37EU on 1 June 2021, with an event window of 2018–2021 chosen to capture the period during which this virulence pattern was present and epidemiologically important in France, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Country bracket years were adjusted from [2016] to [2018], which better matches the 'several years' of prior occurrence mentioned in IBEB‑EU communications. Classification as re‑emergence only (new virulence profile in an existing European population) remains appropriate, but the start year and precise national spread should be validated against detailed monitoring data.

Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe
Countries: Spain [2021]; Italy [2021]; France [2021]; Portugal [2021]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2021]; Germany [2021]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2021]; Denmark [2021]; Sweden [2021]; Norway [2021]; Austria [2021]; Switzerland [2021]
Host: Lactuca sativa (diverse lettuce market types across Europe)
Event summary: By the early 2020s, continuing surveillance by IBEB‑EU documented further shifts in European B. lactucae populations, with many local outbreaks and increasing reports of disease in cultivars carrying resistance to earlier races, particularly in both southern and northern lettuce‑growing regions. In 2023, after evaluating isolates collected in 2021–2022, IBEB‑EU officially identified and named three additional races, Bl:38EU, Bl:39EU and Bl:40EU, noting that Bl:38EU occurred more frequently in southern Europe, Bl:39EU in northern Europe, and Bl:40EU across the whole continent. These newly recognized races contributed to renewed downy mildew pressure in affected areas until breeders confirmed that many newer varieties with broad resistance (e.g. Bl:29‑40EU notation) remained effective, and growers adjusted cultivar choice and integrated control measures accordingly.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: ongoing continent‑wide lettuce production with strong dependence on single‑race resistance and fungicides, plus favorable cool and humid periods, maintained high selection pressure for new virulence combinations; pan‑European movement of seedlings and seed disseminated successful races between regions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – three distinct races (Bl:38EU, 39EU, 40EU) with differing regional prevalence; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – Bl:40EU in particular established across Europe; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – ability of some new races to infect cultivars resistant to the previously dominant race set (Bl:16‑37EU).

The summary has been clarified to state that IBEB‑EU denominated Bl:38EU, Bl:39EU and Bl:40EU in 2023 on the basis of isolates collected in 2021–2022, consistent with the official press release. The country list and sub‑regions represent a reasonable union of areas where the three races are reported to be most frequent (Bl:38EU in southern, Bl:39EU in northern, Bl:40EU across Europe), but the bracket years [2021] are approximations rather than documented first‑detection years for each country. The event should be retained as a major recent re‑emergence episode, but national timing and impact could be refined in future updates.

Event summary: From 2022 onward, IBEB‑EU surveys began to detect a new Bremia lactucae virulence pattern in a growing share of European lettuce isolates, reaching about 3% of isolates in 2023 and 10% in early 2024. After a formal evaluation process, on 1 July 2024 IBEB‑EU denominated the French isolate REQ2301723 as the type isolate of race Bl:41EU, reporting repeated findings of this race in France, Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. Bl:41EU breaks several widely used resistance genes, including R53, R55 and R56, and rapidly became a major focus for breeders and advisors as a new threat to both open‑field and protected lettuce across western and northern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: highly intensive lettuce production across western and northern Europe, reliance on similar combinations of resistance genes and fungicide programs, and extensive intra‑European trade in seed and young plants created conditions for rapid spread and selection of a new, broadly adapted virulence type. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:41EU represents a distinct virulence profile, different from races Bl:38–40EU and able to overcome multiple contemporary resistance factors; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – its rapid rise in frequency and repeated detection across several countries indicate strong fitness under current European production and climate conditions.
Review: Decision: Review. This new event records the emergence of race Bl:41EU as described in the 2024 IBEB‑EU press release, which reports first occurrence of the underlying virulence pattern in 2022, increasing frequencies in 2023–early 2024 and official denomination on 1 July 2024, with confirmed presence in France, Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and the UK. The 2022–2024 window and bracket years [2022] are approximations aimed at capturing the period when Bl:41EU became epidemiologically important; as additional surveillance data become available, national start years and impact assessments should be refined. Classification as re‑emergence only is appropriate.

Host: Lactuca sativa (western-US head, romaine and baby leaf lettuce)
Event summary: From about 2022, IBEB‑US began to recover Bremia lactucae isolates with the IBEB‑D sextet code 45‑7‑2 from multiple western US lettuce districts, including locations in California and Arizona. Because isolates with this virulence profile were collected repeatedly over three years across several production areas, the representative isolate VP‑302 from San Benito County, California, was denominated on 1 July 2025 as the type isolate of the new race Bl:10US. Bl:10US was reported to overcome several commonly used resistance genes, including Dm25, Dm38 and Dm56, and was associated with renewed downy mildew pressure in some western‑US plantings until breeders and growers adjusted resistance packages and management practices.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large‑scale, continuous lettuce production in California and Arizona using similar resistance backgrounds and intensive fungicide use has created strong selection pressure for new virulent Bremia races; regional movement of transplants and seed links different production valleys and facilitates spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:10US shows a distinct and stable virulence profile not represented by races Bl:5–9US; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – its documented ability to defeat multiple major resistance genes; Enhanced Transmission – repeated recovery across multiple western‑US locations over several years indicates competitive fitness within the local pathogen population.
Review: Decision: Review. This newly added row summarizes the emergence of race Bl:10US in the western United States, based on the 2025 IBEB‑US press release and supporting industry communication detailing repeated detections across California and Arizona over three years and the race’s ability to overcome key resistance genes such as Dm25, Dm38 and Dm56. Because Bl:10US has only recently been denominated, its full agronomic impact is still developing; the 2022–2025 window should therefore be treated as provisional and revisited as more field data become available. Host: Cultivated Japanese plum (Prunus salicina), apricot (P. armeniaca), peach (P. persica) and nearby wild Prunus spp. (P. spinosa, P. cerasifera) in north‑eastern Italy (Friuli‑Venezia Giulia and adjacent areas).
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, severe decline of Japanese plum and other stone‑fruit trees in north‑eastern Italy led to intensive studies that demonstrated Cacopsylla pruni to be the highly efficient vector of ESFY phytoplasma, with both nymphs and adults transmitting the pathogen to very susceptible Japanese plum cultivars. In affected orchards, infection levels in some Japanese plum blocks reached 50–70% of trees, with high mortality and removal of heavily affected plantings, revealing ESFY as a major constraint on stone‑fruit cultivation in the region. Recognition of C. pruni’s vector role and the scale of losses triggered changes in Italian diagnostics, certification schemes and recommendations on managing both infected planting material and psyllid populations in and around orchards.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of plum and apricot production with highly susceptible Japanese plum cultivars, use and movement of infected nursery material, and the presence of unmanaged wild Prunus stands adjacent to orchards created landscapes with extremely high inoculum and vector pressure. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – studies in north‑east Italy showed that overwintered C. pruni adults acquire and retain ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’ through winter and transmit it very efficiently to susceptible Prunus hosts in spring, so once local vector populations and wild reservoirs were established, ESFY spread rapidly and repeatedly within orchards.
Review: review – Retain this as a key ESFY/C. pruni epidemic in Friuli‑Venezia Giulia and neighbouring areas. Reclassified the event type from re_emergence to re_occurrence (no clear evidence that recent genetic change in C. pruni, rather than external drivers and long‑standing vector competence, explains the outbreak) and set re_occurrence to true. Updated the source_urls to emphasise the original Italian transmission work and Mediterranean ESFY overview (EPPO Reporting Service 1999; Carraro & Osler 2003; Marcone 2010) instead of a more generic mix of references.

Host: Apricot (Prunus armeniaca) in experimental and commercial orchards in Languedoc‑Roussillon, with nearby wild Prunus domestica, P. cerasifera and P. spinosa acting as reservoirs.
Event summary: From 1994 to 2000, a major ESFY epidemic in apricot orchards in Languedoc‑Roussillon (southern France) prompted detailed epidemiological studies combining large‑scale insect trapping and molecular diagnostics. These studies identified Cacopsylla pruni as the main vector of ESFY in the region and linked its early‑spring flights from infected wild Prunus stands into orchards with primary infections in apricot seedling blocks. Although annual spread in monitored experimental orchards was modest, cumulative infection over several years led to significant tree loss and demonstrated that without early removal of infected trees and better management of nearby wild Prunus and psyllid populations, ESFY could progressively compromise regional apricot production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High density of susceptible apricot plantings, close juxtaposition of orchards and wild Prunus stands harbouring both C. pruni and ESFY phytoplasma, and initial lack of awareness of the vector’s overwintering and spring migration behaviour allowed sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – overwintered C. pruni adults moving from conifers back onto Prunus in early spring were shown to be important carriers of ESFY, with their migration phenology closely matching the window of host susceptibility and making them particularly effective vectors under southern French conditions.
Review: review – Event accurately reflects the Languedoc‑Roussillon epidemic and the French work that first quantified C. pruni’s role as ESFY vector. Adjusted the event classification from re_emergence to re_occurrence to match the definitions (vector and pathogen were already established in Southern Europe; the outbreak was driven by high local infection pressure rather than a new strain or host shift). Retained the Plant Pathology 2001 article as the main source and kept the period, geography and host description unchanged.

Host: Apricot orchards (Prunus armeniaca) in the Wachau valley and adjacent regions, plus nearby wild Prunus spinosa and P. domestica.
Event summary: In the early 2000s, ESFY became a major concern in apricot‑growing areas of the Wachau valley and surroundings in Austria, leading to detailed multi‑year epidemiological studies. Field work tracked Cacopsylla pruni population dynamics on apricot, blackthorn and plum using beating trays and sticky traps, revealing sustained vector presence and seasonal movement between wild and cultivated Prunus. These findings helped explain observed ESFY spread within orchards and underpinned Austrian guidelines recommending monitoring of C. pruni flights and management of nearby wild Prunus to limit future outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High‑value apricot production in river valleys bordered by unmanaged wild Prunus hedges, fragmented land ownership that complicated coordinated vegetation management, and pre‑existing ESFY foci in neighbouring countries created persistent regional infection pressure. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – continuous detection of C. pruni on both wild and cultivated hosts in the Wachau area and its proven vector status indicate that its life cycle and host preferences intrinsically support repeated reinfection of orchards once ESFY is present in the landscape.
Review: review – The Wachau valley episode is a genuine high‑impact ESFY focus in Austria and an important part of the cross‑border Central European epidemic. Event timing, geography and hosts are consistent with Austrian sources, but the emergence type has been simplified from mixed re_occurrence/re_emergence to re_occurrence only, reflecting that changes in management context and infection pressure, rather than documented biological change in C. pruni, drove the outbreak. Source_urls were adjusted to emphasise the BOKU thesis and regional distribution review as primary documentation.

Host: Plum, peach, apricot, nectarine and cherry orchards, and wild Prunus spp., in major stone‑fruit regions of Aragón, Catalonia, Extremadura and Valencia.
Event summary: In 2005–2006, Spain carried out intensive surveys in several stone‑fruit regions where ESFY‑like symptoms had become frequent, using yellow sticky traps and PCR diagnostics on both trees and psyllids. The surveys revealed substantial Cacopsylla pruni populations in Extremadura (Vegas Altas) and Catalonia (Baix Llobregat), with lower but detectable populations in Aragón and Valencia, and showed that a notable proportion of trapped adults carried ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’. Follow‑up work during the late 2000s and early 2010s demonstrated that ESFY and C. pruni were widespread in major Spanish stone‑fruit areas, particularly in Japanese plum orchards, and led to the integration of vector monitoring and wild Prunus management into national phytosanitary programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive plum and peach production in irrigated lowlands, widespread planting of susceptible Japanese plum cultivars, and abundant wild Prunus near orchards facilitated establishment and spread of the ESFY–C. pruni pathosystem in Spain. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – Spanish studies showed that local C. pruni populations acquire and transmit ESFY phytoplasma efficiently, and that their spring migratory flights from wild hosts into orchards coincide with key periods of host susceptibility, allowing rapid accumulation of infected trees once the pathogen is present in a production area.
Review: review – The Spanish episode is appropriately captured as an intensive survey and epidemic phase in multiple regions with high disease and vector incidence. Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting intra_continental_emergence to false (Spain lies in the same UNSD subregion, Southern Europe, as earlier ESFY foci in France and Italy, so this is not a new subregion) and by treating the event as a re_occurrence driven by spread into new production zones within an already affected subregion. Source_urls now clearly link to the original survey and nationwide epidemiological study, which better support the narrative.

Host: Stone‑fruit orchards (apricot, peach, plum) across Germany, together with widespread wild blackthorn (Prunus spinosa) stands.
Event summary: Between 2013 and 2017, Germany conducted a nationwide monitoring programme for ESFY and Cacopsylla pruni, sampling wild Prunus spinosa and orchards at dozens of sites. C. pruni was found on all surveyed P. spinosa stands and ESFY phytoplasma was detected in multiple regions at variable incidence, indicating that both vector and pathogen were widely established rather than confined to a few south‑western hotspots. The results shifted management emphasis from localised outbreaks to ongoing national surveillance and highlighted the role of blackthorn hedges as a continuous inoculum and vector corridor across the German landscape.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive networks of blackthorn hedgerows and mixed orchard–hedgerow landscapes allowed C. pruni and ESFY to persist and move over long distances, while increased diagnostic capacity and targeted surveys revealed the true breadth of the problem. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – high infection rates of C. pruni on wild P. spinosa, and its proven ability to transmit ESFY to orchards, underpin a system in which even moderate levels of infection in wild hosts can sustain recurrent spillover into commercial stone‑fruit blocks country‑wide.
Review: review – Retain this event as representing the transition from regional to nationwide recognition of ESFY and C. pruni in Germany. To follow the definitions more strictly, re_emergence has been set to false and the episode is classified as a re_occurrence in a country where both vector and pathogen were already established, with the main change being increased spatial extent and documented infection pressure. Existing sources (national monitoring study, earlier German work and the 2021 occurrence data paper) remain appropriate for this event.

Host: Apricot orchards and associated wild Prunus spp. (especially P. spinosa and feral P. cerasifera) in several Hungarian counties including Pest, Somogy, Vas and Veszprém.
Event summary: From the early 2010s, Hungarian surveys increasingly reported Cacopsylla pruni in western and central apricot‑growing areas where ESFY symptoms and tree decline were common. Field trapping and molecular testing confirmed the presence of C. pruni in orchards and surrounding hedgerows, and showed that a proportion of adults carried ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’, with about 30% of randomly sampled apricot trees infected and most symptomatic trees dying within a year. These findings demonstrated that ESFY, vectored by C. pruni, had become a major limiting factor for apricot production in the surveyed sites and led to formal inclusion of the vector and disease in Hungarian stone‑fruit health programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of apricot production in suitable Hungarian microclimates, combined with mixed orchard–hedgerow landscapes rich in wild Prunus and historical presence of ESFY, created favourable conditions for the build‑up of infection and vector populations. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – Hungarian studies confirmed that local C. pruni (biotype B) populations regularly colonise apricot orchards and can harbour and transmit ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’, so once infection is present, the vector’s life cycle supports recurrent and often lethal ESFY outbreaks in susceptible cultivars.
Review: review – The Hungarian event is supported by recent quantitative work showing high infection rates and severe apricot losses, and should be retained as one of the major ESFY/C. pruni episodes in Eastern Europe. However, EPPO and earlier literature indicate that ESFY and C. pruni have been present in Hungary since at least the 1990s, so this episode is more accurately coded as a re_occurrence in an already affected subregion rather than an intra‑continental emergence or re_emergence; the corresponding flags were adjusted accordingly. Sources were kept but their roles clarified, with the 2023 Agronomy paper and the Austria–Hungary epidemiological study providing the main evidence on impact and spatial extent.

Host: Mother‑plant orchard of apricot (Prunus armeniaca), Japanese plum (P. salicina), European plum (P. domestica), peach and nectarine (P. persica) in the Primorska region, plus surrounding wild Prunus spp.
Event summary: Between 2004 and 2006, a mother‑plant orchard established in 2001 with virus‑free material in the Primorska region of Slovenia experienced a severe ESFY outbreak. Molecular surveys showed that 70% of sampled apricot trees and all sampled Japanese plum trees were infected with ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’, while about half of sampled European plums and a smaller proportion of peaches and nectarines were also infected, often without clear symptoms; sudden wilting and dieback affected more than half of the apricot trees, which were subsequently removed. Cacopsylla pruni adults trapped near the orchard all tested positive for ESFY phytoplasma, indicating very high local infection pressure and revealing that the surrounding wild Prunus and vector populations posed a serious threat to the production of healthy planting material.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Establishment of a multi‑species mother‑plant orchard in a landscape with abundant wild Prunus and established ESFY, combined with use of material tested for viruses but not necessarily for phytoplasmas, allowed rapid build‑up of infection once the pathogen and vector were present. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – local C. pruni populations reached high densities on wild and cultivated Prunus and showed 100% infection in tested samples, so their seasonal movement between wild reservoirs and mother plants created an intense and self‑sustaining ESFY focus that was difficult to control by tree removal alone.
Review: review – Added this Slovenian mother‑plant‑orchard outbreak because the extremely high ESFY incidence in apricot and Japanese plum, the documented infection of C. pruni and the need to remove large parts of the orchard make it one of the most consequential ESFY/C. pruni events in Central–Southern Europe. Classified it as a re_occurrence in a region where both vector and pathogen were already present, driven by high infection pressure in a critical planting‑material source rather than by a new introduction or vector lineage. Sources were chosen to reflect the primary case study and broader distribution context, and this new row should be reviewed to confirm that the timing and host details match national surveillance data.

Host: Apricot (Prunus armeniaca), plum (P. domestica and P. salicina), peach (P. persica), almond (P. dulcis) and wild Prunus spp. in Mediterranean and Marmara provinces (notably Mersin, Adana, Bursa, Yalova and nearby areas).
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s, severe decline and dieback of apricot and plum trees were reported from several Turkish stone‑fruit regions, with symptoms of ESFY and large yield reductions. Surveys between 2004 and 2007 confirmed ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’ in symptomatic apricot, plum and almond trees in germplasm collections and commercial orchards, and pomological studies documented yield losses of up to 77% in infected apricot trees. Subsequent vector surveys in 2010–2011 found Cacopsylla pruni populations carrying ESFY phytoplasma in key fruit‑growing provinces such as Mersin, Adana, Bursa and Yalova, indicating that the full ESFY–C. pruni pathosystem had become established in important Turkish stone‑fruit areas at the eastern edge of the Mediterranean basin.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of early‑season apricot production in the Mediterranean coastal zone using susceptible local and imported cultivars, movement of infected propagation material, and the presence of wild Prunus and conifer overwintering sites near orchards favoured the introduction and local amplification of ESFY. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – Turkish C. pruni populations reached high densities on wild and cultivated Prunus and showed relatively high infection rates (around 23% of remigrant adults in some sites), supporting efficient transmission from wild reservoirs into orchards and allowing fast build‑up of disease once ESFY was introduced.
Review: review – Added this Turkish episode because combined plant and vector surveys document severe ESFY‑associated decline with large yield losses and confirm establishment of C. pruni as an infected vector in several major stone‑fruit regions, making it one of the most impactful non‑EU events. Treated it as a re_occurrence in Western Asia rather than an inter‑continental emergence, as C. pruni is native to the Western Palaearctic and had been recorded from Türkiye before 1990; the novelty lies in the intensity of ESFY outbreaks in commercial orchards. Sources focus on the original Turkish plant‑ and vector‑level studies plus the CAPS datasheet for distribution context; the row should be reviewed to refine the start/end years if more precise national data are available.

Host: Apricot orchards in the canton of Valais and other affected Swiss stone‑fruit plantings, together with surrounding wild Prunus spinosa and P. cerasifera hedges.
Event summary: During the 2010s, ESFY became an increasingly serious constraint on apricot production in the Swiss canton of Valais, where warm, dry valley floors support intensive stone‑fruit cultivation bordered by wild Prunus hedges. Field studies on the distribution and infection rates of Cacopsylla pruni in Switzerland showed that the psyllid is widespread on wild P. spinosa and P. cerasifera and that a significant proportion of adults carry ‘Ca. Phytoplasma prunorum’. By 2025, a federal study reported that about 75% of Valais apricot orchards were affected by ESFY, underscoring a prolonged, high‑impact re‑occurrence sustained by resident vector populations and wild reservoirs despite phytosanitary efforts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Concentration of susceptible apricot cultivars in valley orchards, proximity to unmanaged wild Prunus hedges acting as long‑term reservoirs, and a warming climate that favours vector survival and activity combined to create very high infection pressure in Valais. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation – C. pruni populations in Switzerland exhibit typical host‑alternating behaviour with high natural infection rates on wild hosts, allowing repeated reinfection of orchards from hedgerows even where symptomatic trees are removed, which makes long‑term management difficult without landscape‑scale interventions.
Review: review – Added this event to capture the very high and well‑documented ESFY incidence in Swiss Valais (around 75% of apricot orchards affected) and the associated role of C. pruni in Switzerland. Classified it as a prolonged re_occurrence in an already affected subregion, as both vector and pathogen had been present earlier but the combination of susceptible cultivars and wild Prunus hedges led to a sustained high‑pressure situation. Sources include the Agroscope 2025 summary, a Swiss vector‑epidemiology study and the CAPS datasheet; timing (2010–2025) is approximate and should be refined if national datasets specify a clearer onset period.

Host: Pyrus communis (commercial European pear cultivars in intensive orchards, especially in northern Italy’s pear districts)
Event summary: From the early 1990s through at least the mid‑2010s, Cacopsylla pyri remained the most economically important pest of pear in Italy’s main production regions, particularly in high-density orchards in Emilia‑Romagna and other northern districts, where repeated heavy infestations caused honeydew, sooty mould and fruit downgrading. Long-term reliance on organophosphate and pyrethroid insecticides contributed to resistance problems documented in European C. pyri populations, and after the banning of amitraz around 2005 Italian growers increasingly depended on abamectin, spirotetramat and other selective products alongside intensified monitoring and cultural measures. By the 2010s, integrated pest management strategies based on selective insecticides, conservation of natural enemies and host-plant resistance breeding reduced but did not eliminate pest pressure, and C. pyri continued to be the key pest and a major vector of pear decline phytoplasma in Italian pear orchards.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensification of pear production in northern Italy (large monoculture orchards, highly susceptible cultivars) and many years of frequent broad-spectrum insecticide applications created favourable conditions for C. pyri outbreaks and strong selection pressure on pest populations; regulatory withdrawal of older active ingredients (e.g. amitraz) further narrowed chemical options. Internal mechanisms: resistance to several organophosphate insecticides and pyrethroids has been demonstrated in European C. pyri, and Italian monitoring showed variation in susceptibility to abamectin and other compounds, consistent with ongoing selection for enhanced detoxification; the pest’s multivoltine life cycle, high fecundity and overwintering adults supported rapid responses to these pressures, making this a classic re‑emergence episode driven by evolved resistance and production intensification rather than by new geographic spread.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected the 'countries' field to 'Italy [1990]' so that the bracketed year represents the approximate start of the re‑emergence episode in this country, consistent with the event-year range. The event summary and mechanism text were revised to match the literature more closely by emphasising strong resistance to organophosphates and pyrethroids and monitored variation (rather than confirmed high-level resistance) in abamectin susceptibility, and by framing this as a resistance-driven re‑emergence in long-infested Italian pear regions rather than as any form of geographic emergence.

Host: Pyrus communis (commercial pear orchards, especially in Provence–Alpes–Côte d’Azur and other intensive pear regions)
Event summary: From about 1990 through 2000, pear psylla populations in the main French pear-growing areas, particularly around Avignon in southeastern France, developed very high levels of resistance to key organophosphate insecticides such as azinphosmethyl and phosmet and reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids and amitraz, leading to repeated control failures and heavy larval infestations with honeydew and sooty mould. Detailed bioassays in the mid‑1990s documented resistance ratios of roughly 25–180-fold for several organophosphates and lower but significant resistance to pyrethroids and amitraz, prompting renewed efforts to redesign control programmes and to screen for psylla-resistant pear germplasm. By the early 2000s, greater use of mineral oils, more selective insecticides and integrated pest management helped to partially restore control, but C. pyri remained a major pest and resistant genotypes persisted in French pear orchards.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: decades of intensive pear production in France with repeated applications of organophosphate and pyrethroid insecticides, withdrawal of some older pesticide classes and high cosmetic standards for fruit created very strong selection pressure and high carrying capacity for C. pyri. Internal mechanisms: French laboratory and field studies demonstrated high resistance ratios to azinphosmethyl and other organophosphates, cross-resistance to phosmet and monocrotophos, and reduced sensitivity to pyrethroids and amitraz, associated with altered acetylcholinesterase and enhanced detoxifying enzymes (esterases and mixed-function oxidases); these evolved changes are characteristic of re‑emergence driven by insecticide resistance rather than any new geographic intrusion.
Review: Decision: retain. Added this event to capture the well-documented 1990s insecticide-resistance crisis in French C. pyri populations around Avignon and other pear regions, which produced very high organophosphate resistance ratios and widespread control failures and is therefore among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for this pest. Classified as re‑emergence (internal change: evolution of resistance); no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. The time window 1990–2000 is an approximation covering the decade in which resistance was first quantified and widely recognised; more precise dating would require integrating detailed French resistance-monitoring datasets.

Host: Pyrus communis in commercial pear orchards
Event summary: Between roughly 1990 and 2005, Cacopsylla pyri resurged as a major limiting factor in Bulgarian pear production, with growers reporting marked increases in pest abundance and damage compared with the previous two decades. Intensive spraying with non‑selective insecticides led to widespread resistance or reduced efficacy of organophosphates, pyrethroids and amitraz and to disruption of natural enemy complexes, allowing severe recurrent infestations characterised by heavy honeydew, sooty mould and yield downgrading. After amitraz was banned around 2005, abamectin became the primary control option and provided improved but still incomplete suppression, prompting recommendations for more selective insecticides and stronger emphasis on biological control and integrated pest management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long-term frequent application of broad-spectrum insecticides in Bulgarian pear orchards increased carrying capacity for C. pyri by removing natural enemies and imposed strong selection pressure for resistance; structural factors (small orchards with limited adoption of integrated pest management) further constrained the feasibility of resistance-management strategies. Internal mechanisms: European and Bulgarian reports indicate cross-resistance in C. pyri to multiple organophosphates, pyrethroids and amitraz, together with high fecundity and many generations per year, which facilitated rapid increase and spread of resistant genotypes; these internal changes underpin the observed re‑emergence in impact without representing new geographic occurrence.
Review: Decision: retain. Updated the 'countries' field from a narrative phrase to 'Bulgaria [1990]' so that the bracketed value gives the approximate start of the resurgence episode in this country, consistent with the 1990–2005 event window. The summary and mechanism remain appropriate, reflecting Bulgarian and regional evidence of increased C. pyri damage and broad-spectrum insecticide resistance; classification as re‑emergence (driven by evolved resistance and natural-enemy disruption) is consistent with the event-type definitions and no intra- or inter-continental emergence is implied.

Host: Pyrus communis (commercial pear orchards in the Ebro Valley and southeastern Spain)
Event summary: From roughly 2000 to the mid‑2010s, Cacopsylla pyri intensified as the key pest of pear orchards in Spain, particularly in the Ebro Valley (Lleida area) and in southeastern regions such as Murcia, where it caused repeated severe honeydew deposition, sooty mould, fruit russeting and downgrading. Growers relied heavily on insecticide control, yet field monitoring and bioassays revealed reduced susceptibility or resistance to pyrethroids such as cypermethrin and lower efficacy of amitraz and abamectin in some orchards, leading to control difficulties and concern about resistance evolution; at the same time, the pest was implicated in the epidemiology of pear decline and peach yellow leaf roll associated with 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pyri'. Over time, research on natural enemies, alternative chemistries and integrated pest management helped to stabilise pest pressure in some orchards, but C. pyri remained the principal pear pest in major Spanish pear-growing regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion and intensification of commercial pear orchards in northeast and southeast Spain, combined with long-term heavy use of a limited set of insecticides, created strong selection pressure on C. pyri and disrupted natural enemy complexes; regulatory restrictions on certain older active ingredients further constrained rotation options. Internal mechanisms: toxicity bioassays and biochemical studies on field populations from the Ebro Valley documented elevated esterase, glutathione S-transferase and cytochrome P450 reductase activities and higher LC50 values to cypermethrin, consistent with emerging metabolic resistance; these changes underpin the re‑emergence of the pest as a difficult-to-control problem rather than any new geographic incursion.
Review: Decision: retain. This event was added because multiple studies from Lleida and southeastern Spain show that C. pyri is the principal pear pest in major Spanish production areas, with documented control difficulties and evidence of reduced susceptibility or resistance to pyrethroids and other insecticides, making it one of the more impactful post‑1990 emergence/re‑emergence episodes for the species. It is appropriately classified as re‑emergence driven by evolving metabolic resistance and management changes, without any intra- or inter-continental emergence component. The 2000–2015 time window is approximate and reflects the period during which Spanish sources repeatedly report control problems and resistance concerns; more precise dating would require a consolidated review of Spanish monitoring data.

Host: Pyrus communis in intensive pear orchards
Event summary: Between 2003 and 2006, monitoring in commercial pear orchards in the Czech Republic showed that Cacopsylla pyri was the main insect pest in intensive pear plantings and that some local populations displayed reduced sensitivity or resistance to commonly used insecticides. High initial infestation levels and immigration from untreated or differently managed plots contributed to control failures in certain orchards, prompting the evaluation and subsequent registration of insect growth regulators such as teflubenzuron (Nomolt 15 SC) and diflubenzuron (Dimilin 48 SC) and other selective products for C. pyri management. With adoption of these newer products and more structured resistance-management strategies, pest populations in trial orchards could generally be controlled without measurable yield loss, although the underlying resistance issues persisted and required continued surveillance.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive pear cultivation in selected Czech regions and repeated use of the same insecticide modes of action (organophosphates, pyrethroids and other broad-spectrum products) generated strong selection pressure on C. pyri and disrupted natural enemy communities; spatial heterogeneity in management (nearby untreated or differently treated orchards) facilitated reinfestation. Internal mechanisms: field experience and bioassays indicated the emergence and spread of C. pyri populations with reduced susceptibility or resistance to older insecticides, consistent with patterns seen elsewhere in Europe, and the pest’s multivoltine life cycle and ability to disperse between orchards amplified and spread these resistant genotypes, making this a re‑emergence in impact rather than a new geographic occurrence.
Review: Decision: retain. This event reflects a documented early‑2000s episode in Czech intensive pear orchards where C. pyri became the main insect pest and resistance or reduced sensitivity to older insecticides prompted registration of new insect growth regulators and changes in management, which is consistent with the definition of a resistance-driven re‑emergence. The geographic (Czechia in Eastern Europe) and temporal (2003–2006) assignments match the cited trials, and no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved, so only minor consistency checks were needed and no structural changes were made to this row.

EPP common name: field sandbur, coast sandspur, sandbur, southern sandbur, spiny burrgrass
Countries: China [2008] (Inner Mongolia – Tongliao and Chifeng in Horqin Sandy Land; neighboring parts of Liaoning and Jilin provinces)
Host: Natural and semi-natural sandy grasslands and pastures of the Horqin Sandy Land and surrounding rangelands; field margins, roadsides and disturbed sandy sites; dryland crops such as maize, sorghum, soybean and other field crops in infested zones; indirect impacts on grazing livestock via reduced forage quality and injurious burrs.
Event summary: Cenchrus spinifex (少花蒺藜草, treated historically as C. pauciflorus/C. incertus) was first recorded in Horqin district of northern China in 1983 and was recognized as a harmful weed in Liaoning by the mid‑1990s, but from 2008 onward systematic surveys in Tongliao and adjacent parts of Inner Mongolia documented a rapid increase in its abundance and area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10618509/?utm_source=openai)) Between 2008 and 2017 fixed monitoring plots showed steadily rising cover and seed bank densities, and by 2016 the Tongliao region accounted for nearly 80% of the national area infested, with large monodominant stands in Horqin sandy grassland and extensive occurrence along roadsides, crop fields and village margins.([journal30.magtechjournal.com](https://journal30.magtechjournal.com/bfnyxb/CN/10.3969/j.issn.2096-1197.2018.05.17)) Provincial early‑warning and control programs (manual removal, herbicides and monitoring) were launched in Liaoning and Inner Mongolia, but the species remained widely established by the late 2010s and continues to spread within northeastern China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The invasion in Horqin and surrounding areas has been promoted by extensive overgrazing, cultivation and other land‑use changes that leave large areas of bare, sandy soil, together with road construction and transport of soil, fodder and contaminated seed that facilitate long‑distance dispersal of burrs.([cjae.net](https://www.cjae.net/CN/10.13287/j.1001-9332.201705.040)) Semi‑arid temperate monsoon climate with variable rainfall favors opportunistic establishment in degraded grasslands. Internal mechanisms: C. spinifex produces large numbers of barbed burrs, forms a persistent soil seed bank with heteromorphic seeds differing in dormancy and germination, tolerates drought and low fertility, and strongly alters soil nitrogen pools and microbial communities in invaded sandy grasslands, enabling formation of pure stands and competitive exclusion of native forage species.([cjae.net](https://www.cjae.net/CN/10.13287/j.1001-9332.201705.040))
Review: review – Retain this as a major post‑1990 event capturing the rapid expansion and dominance of C. spinifex in Horqin and northeastern China, but reclassify it from inter‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence because the species was first found in Horqin in 1983 and documented as harmful in Liaoning by 1995 (pre‑1990 for first emergence on the continent).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10618509/?utm_source=openai)) Geography (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) and host description are appropriate, and sources are relevant Chinese scientific and government reports; dates remain approximate and should be checked against additional Chinese floristic records.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: field sandbur, coast sandspur, sandbur, southern sandbur, spiny burrgrass
Countries: Spain [1990] (Mediterranean and Atlantic coastal dunes, especially north‑eastern Spain and Cádiz province); Italy [1990] (Adriatic and Tyrrhenian coastal dunes); France [1990] (south‑western Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts, including Corsica); Switzerland [2015] (Monthey, industrial wetland near wastewater treatment plant); Croatia [2024] (Adriatic coast and ruderal sandy habitats)
Host: Coastal sandy beaches and dune systems (upper beach, shifting and fixed dunes); ruderal sandy strips along roads and military installations near the coast; occasional occurrence inland on sandy or gravelly ruderal sites; impacts mainly on native dune vegetation, recreation and animal/human welfare (injurious burrs) rather than on intensive crops.
Event summary: By the 1970s Cenchrus spinifex was already naturalized and locally invasive on sandy beaches along parts of the Spanish Mediterranean coast, and had spread widely on Italian coastal dunes in the post‑war tourism boom, becoming one of the most damaging invasive dune species there.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340080705_New_records_of_interesting_xenophytes_in_the_Iberian_Peninsula_Nuevas_citas_de_xenofitos_interesantes_en_la_Peninsula_Iberica)) From 1990 onwards, the species continued to expand and form dense infestations on Mediterranean and Atlantic beaches in Spain and Italy and was later confirmed for France (including Corsica), where it behaves as a noxious weed of coastal dunes.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235631409_A_taxonomic_revision_of_non-native_Cenchrus_sstr_Paniceae_Poaceae_in_the_Mediterraneanarea)) During the 2000s–2010s new naturalized populations were documented in additional Spanish provinces (e.g. Cádiz) and in Switzerland (Monthey) and by 2012 C. spinifex was placed on the EPPO list/Observation List of invasive alien plants; in 2024 it was reported for the first time from Croatia’s Adriatic coast, indicating ongoing spread into the north‑eastern Mediterranean.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340080705_New_records_of_interesting_xenophytes_in_the_Iberian_Peninsula_Nuevas_citas_de_xenofitos_interesantes_en_la_Peninsula_Iberica))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The European invasion has been facilitated by intense coastal tourism and infrastructure development after World War II, which created extensive disturbed sandy habitats on beaches and dunes; movement of sand and soil for beach nourishment and construction; and long‑distance dispersal of burrs on clothing, footwear, pets, livestock and vehicles, including via military bases and ports.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340080705_New_records_of_interesting_xenophytes_in_the_Iberian_Peninsula_Nuevas_citas_de_xenofitos_interesantes_en_la_Peninsula_Iberica)) Internal mechanisms: C. spinifex is highly adapted to open sandy substrates, producing many spiny burrs that adhere to animals and people (epizoochory) and forming persistent seed banks, allowing rapid colonization of drift lines and dunes. Its tolerance of drought and salt spray and ability to form dense mats enable it to out‑compete native dune vegetation, leading to altered dune plant communities and reduced recreational value of beaches.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235631409_A_taxonomic_revision_of_non-native_Cenchrus_sstr_Paniceae_Poaceae_in_the_Mediterraneanarea))
Review: review – New event added to capture a major, continuing post‑1990 invasion of coastal dunes and sandy habitats in southern and western Europe. Evidence from floristic surveys shows C. spinifex has been locally invasive on Spanish and Italian beaches since at least the 1970s and is now widely naturalized and considered a noxious/invasive dune weed, with ongoing spread documented by new national records (e.g. Switzerland 2015, Croatia 2024) and EPPO listing.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340080705_New_records_of_interesting_xenophytes_in_the_Iberian_Peninsula_Nuevas_citas_de_xenofitos_interesantes_en_la_Peninsula_Iberica)) Classified as re‑occurrence (not first detection) because introduction to Europe predates 1990; approximate start year (1990) and country‑specific years should be checked against additional national floras and herbarium records.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: field sandbur, coast sandspur, sandbur, southern sandbur, spiny burrgrass
Countries: Australia [1990] (inland southern and central Queensland, much of New South Wales, ACT, northern Victoria); Australia [2000] (southern South Australia and coastal south‑western Western Australia where it became more widely recognized and regulated)
Host: Pastures and rangelands on light, sandy soils in eastern and inland Australia; irrigated and dryland crops including vegetables, vines, citrus and hay; livestock (sheep, cattle) indirectly affected by burr injuries and fleece/hide contamination; recreational and urban green spaces, roadsides and disturbed sandy sites.
Event summary: Cenchrus spinifex was already naturalized and recognized as a problematic burrgrass in parts of eastern Australia by the 1970s–1980s, but during the 1990s and 2000s it spread and increased in abundance across inland southern and central Queensland, much of New South Wales and the ACT, and into northern Victoria, forming dense infestations in pastures, roadsides and disturbed sandy country.([keyserver.lucidcentral.org](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cenchrus_spinifex.htm)) Over the 2000s–2010s it became widely known under names such as spiny burrgrass or innocent weed and was listed as a declared weed or priority environmental weed in South Australia and other jurisdictions, prompting targeted control programs, inclusion on noxious/invasive plant lists and the development of integrated management guidelines.([pir.sa.gov.au](https://pir.sa.gov.au/biosecurity/weeds/declared-weeds/innocent_weed?utm_source=openai)) Despite herbicide use, competitive pastures and hygiene measures, the species remains widespread across much of eastern and southern Australia and continues to cause economic losses through livestock injuries, contamination of wool and hay, and control costs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of contaminated hay, grain, livestock and soil, together with burrs hitch‑hiking on wool, vehicle tyres and machinery, has dispersed C. spinifex from initial foci to much of eastern and southern Australia. Agricultural intensification, cereal stubble retention and irrigation created open, low‑competition niches in pastures and cropping systems, while disturbance along roads, stock routes and waterways facilitated establishment.([weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weed/SpinyBurrgrassSpinifex)) Internal mechanisms: The species produces large numbers of barbed burrs that adhere readily to animals and equipment, has a flexible life history (annual or short‑lived perennial depending on climate), and competes well on sandy, low‑fertility soils. These traits, combined with a persistent seed bank, support recurrent dominance in disturbed pastures and croplands, but there is no clear evidence to date of herbicide‑resistant biotypes driving this resurgence.([weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weed/SpinyBurrgrassSpinifex))
Review: retain – This captures a major, long‑running post‑1990 episode in which C. spinifex became widespread and formally regulated as a declared/noxious weed across eastern and southern Australia, with substantial impacts on pastures, crops and livestock.([keyserver.lucidcentral.org](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cenchrus_spinifex.htm)) Continent, subregion and country assignments are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate given pre‑1990 establishment and lack of documented resistant strains; dates and within‑country staging (1990 vs 2000) are approximate but acceptable, and could be refined with state floras if higher temporal precision is needed.

EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: Portugal [<1900; widespread by late 20th c.]; Spain [1990s–2010s]; France – Mediterranean coasts [19th–20th c.]; Italy (including Sardinia) [pre‑1980s; naturalized and locally invasive by 2000s]; Greece [1990s–2000s]; Croatia [1990s–2000s]; Slovenia [1990s–2000s]; Montenegro [2000s]; Bosnia and Herzegovina [2010s–2020s]; Cyprus [2011]
Host: Ruderal and arable-land vegetation associated with multiple crops (roadside and railway margins, fallow fields, gardens, orchards and urban greenspaces)
Event summary: After its 19th‑century introduction to Mediterranean France, Italy and Portugal, Euphorbia prostrata progressively spread around the northern Mediterranean and, from about 1990 onwards, showed marked expansion across Southern Europe. During the 1990s–2000s it colonized transport corridors and urban disturbed sites in Spain, Italy (including Sardinia), Greece and the former Yugoslav countries, becoming a frequent component of pavements, roadsides and railway margins and locally invasive in parts of Italy. By the 2010s it was documented from additional Mediterranean islands and coastal regions, including Bosnia and Herzegovina and Cyprus, and is now widely naturalised in lowland Mediterranean Southern Europe, although impacts are mostly limited to local dominance in disturbed patches rather than major agricultural losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of road and railway networks, increased trade and tourism in the Mediterranean, and urbanization facilitated repeated seed introduction and secondary dispersal along disturbed corridors and port cities. Frequent soil disturbance in verges, fallows, construction sites and urban greenspaces created open niches favorable for establishment of this small annual spurge. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) via traits typical of ruderal weeds (prostrate habit, rapid growth, high seed production, tolerance of trampling and drought) combined with enhanced human‑mediated dispersal of seeds in contaminated soil, gravel, horticultural material and vehicle movement.
Review: Review – Retain this as the main Southern European/Mediterranean episode but reclassify it as a re-occurrence rather than intra-continental emergence or re-emergence. The expansion after 1990 reflects increased abundance and spread within an already affected Southern European sub-region, driven by transport and urban disturbance, with no evidence of novel strains. Sub_regions were updated to 'Southern Europe; Western Europe' so that inclusion of France is consistent with the UNSD scheme, and Cyprus (first record 2011) was added to the country list; sources remain appropriate to document this regional spread.
