EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: Israel [introduced by 1948; invasive and very common in pavements, irrigated gardens and urban habitats by 1990s–2010s]; State of Palestine [20th century; naturalized in similar habitats by 2000s]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [2006 – first published national record, followed by scattered occurrences]
Host: Ruderal and irrigated ornamental vegetation in pavements, drip‑irrigated gardens, orchards, field margins and urban wasteland in Mediterranean and semi‑arid climates
Event summary: Euphorbia prostrata was first recorded as an American alien in the flora of Israel around 1948 and for several decades remained one of several low-growing spurges in disturbed sites. From the 1980s–1990s onward, the rapid expansion of drip‑irrigated gardening, ornamental planting and pavement networks across Israel and the Palestinian territories allowed the species to proliferate, and by the 1990s–2010s it was described as invasive throughout Israel and noted as the commonest spurge in sidewalk cracks. In 2006 it was reported as a noteworthy new record for the flora of Iran, and subsequent floristic and herbarium data confirm establishment at scattered sites in Western Asia, indicating a regional resurgence driven by human‑created habitats rather than change in the plant itself.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction and repeated spread with horticultural stock, soil and construction activities, together with the widespread adoption of drip irrigation and expansion of paved urban areas, created persistently moist, disturbed microsites in an otherwise seasonally dry region. Road construction and traffic further facilitated seed movement along urban and agricultural corridors. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by typical ruderal traits (small prostrate habit, high seed production, tolerance of compaction and drought); there is no evidence for novel genotypes or resistance, so resurgence in Western Asia is best attributed to external drivers rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Review – Newly added event to capture the clearly documented post‑1990 invasion and resurgence of E. prostrata in Western Asia, centred on Israel (where it is recorded as invasive throughout the country) and its first national record in Iran in 2006. Classified as re-occurrence in an already invaded Western Asian sub-region rather than intra-continental or inter-continental emergence, because presence in Israel predates 1990 and there is no indication of major genetic change. Countries and dates are based on Israeli adventive-plant lists, Danin’s account of American spurges entering with drip irrigation, and the Rostaniha note for Iran; further regional checking is advised.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: Bulgaria [first collected 1963; naturalisation documented 2009–2013]; Hungary [2011]; Czechia [2013]; Romania [<2012]; Serbia [2012]; Ukraine – Crimea [2010s]; Republic of Moldova [c. 2014–2019]
Host: Ruderal vegetation and arable-land weeds in urban parks, railway stations, river valleys, road verges and agricultural margins
Event summary: Between about 2009 and 2013, Euphorbia prostrata was documented as a previously overlooked but now spreading alien in Bulgaria, where herbarium and field surveys showed it to be naturalised across multiple floristic regions from the Black Sea coast to interior river valleys and mountains. In 2011 a population of roughly 100 plants was discovered in a city park in Szeged, marking the first confirmed record for Hungary and the wider Carpathian Basin and indicating ongoing northward expansion into temperate Europe. By the mid‑2010s to around 2020, additional first regional or national records were reported from the Czech Republic, Crimea and Moldova, confirming continued spread along railways, roads and urban habitats in Eastern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased traffic along trans-European road and rail corridors, intensification of trade and movement of soil and construction materials, and urban redevelopment created continuous networks of disturbed habitats favouring colonization. Climate warming likely improved overwintering and seed set in more continental and northern parts of Europe, reducing climatic constraints on establishment. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion enabled by ruderal life-history traits and tolerance of dry, compacted substrates, together with enhanced transmission via inadvertent seed transport on vehicles, railway ballast and contaminated soil around construction and industrial sites.
Review: Review – Retain this as the key intra-continental emergence episode into Eastern Europe, where the species appears in a new UNSD sub-region. I corrected the sub_regions field to 'Eastern Europe' only (the previous inclusion of Northern and Southern Europe did not match the listed countries) and removed the unjustified re_emergence flag; `intra_continental_emergence` remains Yes. The cited Bulgarian, Carpathian Basin, Czech and Crimean sources are appropriate for documenting this eastward and northward spread.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: Kazakhstan [2012 – Almaty Region]; Uzbekistan [2018–2019]; Russian Federation – Tomsk Region and other localities [2018–2021]
Host: Weed of anthropogenic habitats: wastelands, lawns, parks, gardens, fields, fallow lands, sidewalks, roadsides, railway embankments and river banks
Event summary: Around 2012 Euphorbia prostrata was first recorded from the Almaty Region of Kazakhstan, marking its documented arrival in Central Asia and showing that this American species had reached a previously uncolonised Asian sub-region. By 2018–2019 it was found as a weed in anthropogenic habitats in Uzbekistan and by 2018–2021 it was newly recorded in several localities in the Russian Federation, mostly along railway rights-of-way and urban disturbed sites. These findings together document a coordinated eastward and northward expansion across Central Asia and into continental parts of Russia, where the species is currently assessed as an alien of minor impact but clearly increasing its range.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of transport infrastructure, urbanization and trade across Central Asia and the Russian Federation has increased movement of contaminated soil, road materials and plant propagules, facilitating long-distance dispersal of ruderal aliens. Irrigation schemes, parks and gardens provide persistently disturbed, watered microsites in otherwise harsh continental climates. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion through pre-adaptation to hot, dry, nutrient-poor and compacted substrates typical of anthropogenic sites, with enhanced transmission via persistent seed banks and accidental transport with gravel and railway ballast enabling stepwise spread along transport corridors.
Review: Review – Retain this episode as an intra-continental emergence, because it documents the first confirmed records in the Central Asia sub-region (Kazakhstan and later Uzbekistan) and new records in Russia, within continents where the species was already established elsewhere. I simplified sub_regions to 'Central Asia; Eastern Europe' (dropping the non-standard 'Eastern Europe – Russia') and removed re_emergence, which is not supported by evidence of strain change. The Botanica Pacifica paper plus POWO provide adequate support for timing and geography.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Sub-regions: South-eastern Asia; Micronesia; Melanesia; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: Indonesia – Java, Madura, Philippines, Sulawesi, Lesser Sunda Islands, Moluccas, New Guinea [widespread by late 20th century and 2000s]; Papua New Guinea [mid‑20th century–2000s]; United States Minor Outlying Islands – Wake Atoll [first recorded 1960s; present on Peale Islet by 1994; confirmed as alien-invasive in 2019 surveys]; United States Minor Outlying Islands – Midway Atoll [recorded since at least the mid‑20th century; persistent 1990s–2010s]; Australia – Western Australia and other states [naturalised by late 20th century and present in multiple regions by the 2010s]
Host: Weed of disturbed ground in tropical agroecosystems and settlements, including fields, plantations, home gardens, roadsides, airfields and coastal installations
Event summary: By the late 20th century Euphorbia prostrata had become widely established as an alien weed in parts of tropical South‑East Asia and the Indo‑Pacific, including Java, the Philippines, Sulawesi, the Lesser Sunda Islands, the Moluccas and New Guinea, where it is recognised in invasive‑plant guides as a naturalised or invasive alien. On remote Pacific atolls such as Wake and Midway, the species was first recorded in botanical surveys during the mid‑20th century and by the 1990s–2010s it persisted as an alien‑invasive herb in disturbed sites such as airfields and coastal infrastructure. By the 2010s it was documented as an alien in Western Australia and remained common across multiple Indonesian islands and Pacific atolls, forming low mats that can dominate small disturbed patches but generally causing only minor ecological impacts beyond displacement of native ruderal species.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Military and civil aviation, shipping and coastal construction on islands have repeatedly imported soil and plant material contaminated with E. prostrata seed; continued human disturbance of airstrips, roads and settlements maintains open, compacted substrates ideal for establishment. Expansion of irrigated agriculture, plantations and peri‑urban gardens in Indonesia and neighbouring regions has multiplied suitable habitats. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by high seed production, rapid life cycle and tolerance of drought and saline spray; enhanced transmission via persistent seeds that are easily moved in construction materials, potted plants and on equipment, enabling colonisation of remote oceanic islands and scattered tropical settlements.
Review: Review – Retain this Indo‑Pacific episode but interpret it as a re-occurrence rather than intra-continental emergence, because most of the listed South‑East Asian and Pacific sub-regions were colonised before 1990 and the period 1990–2019 mainly reflects persistence and further local spread in disturbed sites. I therefore set `re_occurrence` to Yes and `intra_continental_emergence` to No, while leaving other fields and the source set (Indonesian invasive-plant guide, Pacific atoll surveys and Western Australian herbarium data) unchanged.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: South Africa [records from at least the late 19th century; widespread naturalised weed by late 20th century]; Zimbabwe [first recorded 1931; invasive and widely collected through the 20th century and into the 2010s]
Host: Ruderal weeds in urban areas, roadsides, agricultural margins and disturbed grasslands in warm, subtropical parts of Southern and south‑eastern Africa
Event summary: By the late 20th century Euphorbia prostrata had become naturalised in parts of Southern and south‑eastern Africa, with South African floristic treatments and herbarium data listing it as a non‑indigenous, naturalised species and regional data for Zimbabwe identifying it as an invasive alien weed. Through the 1990s–2010s it spread mainly in urban and peri‑urban disturbed habitats, where repeated soil disturbance and traffic allow it to form dense ground‑hugging mats in pavements, lawns and field edges. By around 2020 it was well established as a minor naturalised alien across warm lowland regions of South Africa and Zimbabwe, though it generally remained a low‑impact component of ruderal floras rather than a major agricultural pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urbanization, road expansion and increased vehicle traffic in Southern Africa have created extensive disturbed, compacted habitats and facilitated local seed dispersal along transport corridors. Movement of ornamental and horticultural plants, and associated potting media or contaminated soil, likely introduced the species initially and continues to redistribute it regionally. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion driven by broad ecological tolerance to heat and drought and a prostrate growth form that allows it to exploit small cracks and bare patches in pavements and heavily trampled sites; enhanced transmission via numerous small seeds that can adhere to soil on footwear, vehicles and machinery.
Review: Review – Retain this African episode but treat it as a re-occurrence of an already long-established alien rather than a new intra-continental emergence. Herbarium and floristic data show E. prostrata present in South Africa and Zimbabwe since the early–mid 20th century, with many later collections but no evidence of strain change. I changed sub_regions to 'Southern Africa; Eastern Africa' to match the Country sheet (Zimbabwe falls under Eastern Africa), set `re_occurrence` to Yes and `intra_continental_emergence` to No, and replaced the generic Wikipedia source with SANBI and Zimbabwe herbarium-based references that better document distribution and status.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Casual weed of grain import facilities, disused railway yards and later of nursery container plants (ornamental trees such as olives and palms) in port and industrial areas
Event summary: In 1992 Euphorbia serpens (as Chamaesyce serpens) was recorded for the first time in Belgium as a grain alien at the Versele‑Laga fodder mill in the inland port of Roeselare, followed in 1994 by a sizeable population along a railway siding in the Gent harbour canal zone, indicating repeated introduction with imported grain and some local establishment.([alienplantsbelgium.myspecies.info](https://alienplantsbelgium.myspecies.info/sites/alienplantsbelgium.be/files/dum53-54p35.pdf)) Later observations around Belgian nurseries showed E. serpens persisting as a low‑frequency weed in containers of Mediterranean ornamentals, but it has remained rare and largely confined to highly disturbed industrial habitats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in grain and oilseeds for cattle feed, and later trade in container‑grown Mediterranean ornamentals, introduced seeds repeatedly into Belgian ports and feed mills; open ballast, sandy spoil, and railway verges provided disturbed microsites for establishment.([alienplantsbelgium.myspecies.info](https://alienplantsbelgium.myspecies.info/sites/alienplantsbelgium.be/files/dum53-54p35.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: a mat‑forming, rooting‑at‑nodes growth habit and prolific seed production allow E. serpens to persist in ruderal microhabitats once introduced, but there is no evidence for new genotypes, resistance or major ecological shifts in Western Europe during this episode.
Review: review – Factual details and sources for the first Belgian records are sound, but I reset 're_occurrence' from true to false because these are first national records within an already occupied subregion (Western Europe) and do not represent a regional resurgence as defined in the protocol. All other emergence‑type flags remain false because this is neither a first/global detection nor spread into a new UNSD subregion; it is a minor but well‑documented adventive event that can be retained for historical context if space permits.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Asia
Countries: Switzerland [2004]; Greece (including Crete) [2007]; Turkey [2007]; Cyprus [2010]; Italy [2010, 2015]; Hungary [2013]; Bulgaria [2016]; Romania [2018]
Host: Weed of flower beds, pavements, cemeteries, irrigated gardens, roadsides and other urban/peri‑urban ruderal sites; locally in crop fields and plastic‑tunnel horticulture
Event summary: From the early 2000s onward, floristic surveys documented Euphorbia serpens spreading south‑ and east‑ward from its earlier Western and Central European range into new parts of Europe and adjacent Western Asia. First national records were published for Switzerland (2004), Greece and Crete (2007), Turkey (2007), Cyprus (2010), Italy (2010, with additional regional records by 2015), Hungary (2013), Bulgaria (2016) and Romania (2018), typically as a weed of flower beds, pavements, container plantings and other warm, disturbed urban habitats.([plant-journal.uaic.ro](https://www.plant-journal.uaic.ro/docs/2018/12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s authors concluded that E. serpens subsp. serpens was in an active phase of expansion of its secondary (alien) range across south‑eastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, though still mainly confined to ruderal and horticultural settings.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing trade in ornamental plants and potting substrates, movement of contaminated soil and construction materials, and road/rail traffic across the Mediterranean basin and Balkans supplied propagules to new cities and river valleys; many records are explicitly linked to imported container plants and recently built urban green spaces.([plant-journal.uaic.ro](https://www.plant-journal.uaic.ro/docs/2018/12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Warming climates in parts of Europe may also favor this C4 annual. Internal mechanisms: rapid germination, multiple generations per season, prostrate mat‑forming growth, and tolerance of trampling and heat allow E. serpens to exploit irrigated, nutrient‑rich ruderal sites and expand geographically wherever propagules arrive.
Review: review – Retain as a major multi‑country intra‑continental emergence episode. I corrected the 'sub_regions' field to use only UNSD categories (Western Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, Western Asia) and removed the informal 'South‑eastern Europe' label, but left the classification as 'intra_continental_emergence = true' since the event clearly represents spread into new European and West‑Asian subregions. Evidence and years follow Sîrbu & Şușnia (2018) and the EPPO reporting note.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia – Queensland [<2012]; Australia – New South Wales [<2012]; Australia – South Australia [2019, 2022-2023]
Host: Weed of coastal scrub, river floodplains, tracks, restoration sites and other disturbed ground; occasionally in agricultural fields and pasture margins
Event summary: By the early 2010s Euphorbia serpens was recognized in the Australian taxonomic literature as a naturalized weed in scattered localities in Queensland, western New South Wales and South Australia.([plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au](https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?lvl=sp&name=Euphorbia~serpens&page=nswfl&utm_source=openai)) Through the late 2010s and early 2020s, herbarium records and regional surveillance reports from South Australia documented the species more frequently in coastal reserves and along the River Murray floodplains, where it formed low mats in disturbed sites following floods and restoration works.([data.environment.sa.gov.au](https://data.environment.sa.gov.au/Content/Publications/Weeds%20Report%202022-23.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Recent regional weed assessments list matted sandmat as a low‑threat but established ruderal weed across several coastal management cells, indicating a shift from sporadic occurrences to a consistent, if still localized, component of disturbed vegetation in parts of southern Australia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Historical introduction via contaminated seed, fodder or soil associated with agriculture and horticulture, followed by ongoing disturbance in coastal reserves, floodplains and urban restoration sites, has promoted local spread and repeated re‑establishment after flooding and management activities.([plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au](https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?lvl=sp&name=Euphorbia~serpens&page=nswfl&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: a creeping, mat‑forming habit, rooting at nodes, a rapid life cycle and C4 photosynthesis enable quick colonization of bare, sun‑exposed soil under hot, dry Australian conditions, favoring re‑occurrence in disturbed habitats without evidence for novel genotypes or herbicide resistance.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures a documented increase in frequency and recognition of E. serpens as a naturalised weed in eastern and southern Australia, especially South Australia, based on NSW Flora Online and State Herbarium surveillance reports. I did not alter the emergence‑type coding ('re_occurrence = true') but note that earliest Australian records probably pre‑date 2010; this row should be interpreted as a resurgence and spread within an already colonised subregion rather than the first arrival in Australia.

Countries: China [1991 – first published records from Shanghai and Jiangsu; later widespread along roadsides and coastal sands in eastern mainland China and in Taiwan, where by the 2000s it was deliberately planted as orchard ground cover in pomelo and other citrus orchards in Tainan and nearby districts]
Host: Weed of sandy roadsides and coastal habitats in eastern China; deliberately managed ground‑cover and self‑sown weed in citrus and other orchards, melon fields and lowland farmland in the Taiwan region
Event summary: Around 1991 Euphorbia serpens was reported for the first time from China, as a weed of open ground in Shanghai and Jiangsu Province, marking its arrival in the Eastern Asia subregion after earlier introductions elsewhere in Asia.([rheedea.in](https://rheedea.in/storages/submission/file/1297225154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent floristic treatments and national databases describe the species as an American alien that has recently naturalized in western Taiwan and in lowland eastern China, where it occupies sandy roadside and coastal habitats.([tai2.ntu.edu.tw](https://tai2.ntu.edu.tw/species/415%20008%2009%200?utm_source=openai)) From the 2000s, Taiwanese agronomic extension materials promoted “匍根大戟” (E. serpens) as a low‑growing, easily managed ground‑cover in citrus and other orchards, especially in Tainan’s Madou district, and documented its rapid spread to near‑complete soil cover in some groves.([kmweb.moa.gov.tw](https://kmweb.moa.gov.tw/subject/subject.php?id=6274))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance introduction via contaminated seed, planting material and soil associated with trade, followed by regional promotion of grass‑covered orchards and reduced herbicide use in Taiwan, created strong propagule pressure and favorable management conditions for E. serpens in Eastern Asia.([rheedea.in](https://rheedea.in/storages/submission/file/1297225154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the species’ ability to root at stem nodes, its extremely low stature, rapid clonal and seed reproduction, and tolerance of trampling, drought and heat make it well suited both as a spontaneous weed in sandy coastal and roadside habitats and as a deliberately managed ground‑cover under tree crops, enabling substantial geographic and ecological range expansion without evidence of novel genotypes.
Review: review – New event added. It synthesizes the first published records of E. serpens in mainland China (Shanghai and Jiangsu in 1991) with evidence that the species has recently naturalized in Taiwan and is now widely used as a deliberate ground‑cover in citrus orchards. I classify it as 'intra_continental_emergence = true' because it represents spread of an already Asian alien into the Eastern Asia subregion and into new agro‑ecosystems. Exact arrival dates in Taiwan precede 1990 but the main agronomic adoption clearly intensified after 2000; users may wish to refine the start/end years based on additional regional data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Pakistan – Sindh Province, Khairpur District (cotton‑growing talukas including Kingri, Gambat, Khairpur, Sobhodero, Kotdiji, Thari Mirwah, Faiz Ganj, Nara) [1990s–2007]
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) fields and irrigation margins in semi‑arid irrigated agriculture
Event summary: Weed surveys in cotton fields of Khairpur District, Sindh, carried out in the 1990s and early 2000s, revealed Euphorbia serpens as one of the six most frequent and dense weeds, with an average frequency of about 67% and high plant densities across multiple talukas.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf)) The species, together with Trianthema portulacastrum, Dactyloctenium aegyptium and Brachiaria eruciformis, was identified as a dominant and "devastating" weed complex in cotton, indicating a substantial increase in abundance and competitive importance in this irrigated cropping system relative to earlier floristic accounts.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of irrigated cotton in Sindh, combined with inadequate or ineffective weed‑management practices and repeated tillage, created open, nutrient‑rich microsites that favored fast‑growing annual broadleaf weeds such as E. serpens; irrigated, hot conditions allowed multiple weed flushes within a season.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: small, numerous seeds, rapid germination, prostrate growth and the ability to root at nodes enable E. serpens to form dense mats between crop rows, intercepting resources and hindering mechanical weeding, thereby promoting re‑occurrence and increased dominance in cotton fields without documented evolution of herbicide resistance.
Review: review – New event added to represent the emergence of E. serpens as a high‑frequency, high‑density weed in cotton in Khairpur District, Sindh. The Pakistan Journal of Botany survey shows that by the mid‑2000s it ranked among the most assertive weeds across eight talukas, implying substantial agronomic impact. Because the species was already present in Southern Asia, I coded this as 're_occurrence = true' (resurgence of a previously known weed under changing agronomic conditions) rather than intra‑continental emergence. Earlier Pakistani records likely pre‑date the survey, so the 1990–2007 window should be interpreted as the period of documented dominance rather than first arrival.

Host: Weed of gardens and cultivated ground in urban environments (Baghdad city, including university gardens and adjacent fields)
Event summary: During field surveys in 2021–2022, Euphorbia serpens was observed for the first time in Iraq at multiple garden and field sites around the University of Baghdad (Al‑Jadriyah campus), where it formed local population patches; the species had not previously been mentioned in Iraqi floras.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366067711_New_record_for_Iraqi_Flora_from_the_Family_Euphorbiaceae_the_species_Euphorbia_serpens_Kunth_in_Iraq)) Herbarium specimens were deposited in the University of Baghdad herbarium (BUH 50470–50471), and the species was formally reported as a new record for the Iraqi flora in 2022, by which time it already occurred in several urban sites in Baghdad.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely accidental introduction through contaminated horticultural material (ornamental plants, potting soil or seed) into urban gardens and institutional plantings, combined with irrigation and soil disturbance that favor warm‑season ruderal weeds.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366067711_New_record_for_Iraqi_Flora_from_the_Family_Euphorbiaceae_the_species_Euphorbia_serpens_Kunth_in_Iraq)) Internal mechanisms: the plant’s ability to root at stem nodes, produce numerous seeds over a long flowering period (late April to early September) and tolerate trampling and heat supports rapid establishment and local spread once introduced, representing geographic range infill within Western Asia rather than expansion into a new continent or subregion.
Review: review – Evidence clearly supports this as the first national record for Iraq, but according to the project definitions 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' should not be used for each new country when the species is already established elsewhere in the same subregion (here, Western Asia: e.g. Iran, Gulf States, Palestine). I therefore set 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' to false and left all emergence‑type flags off; the event is best treated as a nationally important range infill rather than a continental‑scale emergence.

Countries: United States of America – Hawaiʻi (Kauaʻi [1984, 1988], Maui [2001], Oʻahu [2022–2023]); United States Minor Outlying Islands – Midway Atoll (Kuaihelani) [2015], Kure Atoll (Mokupāpapa) [1979; re‑determined 2025]
Host: Weed of coastal parks, beach dunes, urban roadsides and disturbed coastal military, research and conservation installations across the Hawaiian archipelago
Event summary: Herbarium records show Euphorbia serpens established on Kauaʻi by the mid‑1980s and later on Maui (2001), where it occupied sandy coastal vegetation and roadside habitats.([plantsofhawaii.org](https://plantsofhawaii.org/detail/%7B63F9BD2E-B082-4A2F-999C-F2182F6F17C4%7D?utm_source=openai)) In the early 2020s, new collections and a synthesis based on curated iNaturalist records documented scattered but established populations on Oʻahu (e.g. Oneula Beach Park and urban parks such as Ala Wai Community Park), indicating recent spread to the main population centre of Hawaiʻi.([plantsofhawaii.org](https://plantsofhawaii.org/detail/%7B63F9BD2E-B082-4A2F-999C-F2182F6F17C4%7D?utm_source=openai)) Botanical surveys on Midway Atoll (Kuaihelani) in the 2010s reported E. serpens as a naturalized component of the weedy flora, and a 2025 Hawaii Biological Survey paper clarified that earlier collections from Kure Atoll in 1979 and 1993 previously attributed to other Euphorbia species actually represented E. serpens, formalizing Kure as a new island record.([starrenvironmental.com](https://www.starrenvironmental.com/publications/2015-botanical_survey_of_midway_atoll-starr.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Together, these data indicate progressive colonization and recognition of E. serpens across both the main Hawaiian Islands and the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands over four decades.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance dispersal via contaminated soil, equipment and plant material transported among islands for military, research and conservation activities, coupled with disturbance in coastal parks, airfields and installations, created frequent colonization opportunities in the Hawaiian archipelago.([plantsofhawaii.org](https://plantsofhawaii.org/detail/%7B63F9BD2E-B082-4A2F-999C-F2182F6F17C4%7D?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: a hardy prostrate habit, rooting at nodes, high seed output and tolerance of salt spray, heat and trampling enabled the species to survive in harsh coastal environments and to re‑occur on multiple islands and atolls as a persistent ruderal rather than as a single large outbreak.
Review: review – I substantially revised this event. The original row misinterpreted the 2025 Bishop Museum note as a new record for Midway Atoll, whereas it actually documents a new island record and re‑determination for Kure Atoll, with Kure collections dating back to 1979 and 1993. I also (i) expanded the temporal window to reflect earlier herbarium records on Kauaʻi and Maui, (ii) clarified that Oʻahu records date from 2022–2023, and (iii) corrected the continent/sub‑region coding to match the Country sheet, treating Hawaiʻi as part of 'Northern America – United States of America' and Midway/Kure as 'Oceania – United States Minor Outlying Islands (Micronesia)'. The emergence‑type classification as 're_occurrence = true' is retained because these island records represent spread within an already colonised archipelago, not inter‑continental emergence.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa; conventional irrigated rice systems in multiple provinces)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, populations of Chilo suppressalis in China rebounded after a period of lower pest pressure and, by 1993, densities had increased markedly in major rice-growing regions, culminating in widespread outbreaks around 1996. The resurgence developed across large areas of the Yangtze River rice belt and other provinces, where both C. suppressalis and the yellow rice borer Scirpophaga incertulas caused heavy stem-borer damage, prompting renewed insecticide use and major yield-loss assessments. As management practices and planting structures were adjusted and new control tactics were introduced, these outbreak levels eventually declined in some areas, although the pest remained a key constraint on Chinese rice production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of hybrid rice, changes in planting dates and crop structure, and heavy reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides are cited as major factors behind the marked population increases and renewed outbreaks in Chinese rice fields in the early–mid 1990s. Internal mechanisms: No clear novel strain was implicated; the event is best characterized as a resurgence of established populations responding to agronomic and landscape changes rather than inherent biological innovation.
Review: Decision: retain. This row correctly captures the mid‑1990s resurgence of C. suppressalis in Chinese rice, as documented by Sheng et al. (2003) and later reviews, including timing (densities rising by 1993, major outbreaks and sustained high damage by 1996), geography (China/Eastern Asia), host (rice), and classification as a re-occurrence driven by agronomic change rather than by new genotypes. No structural corrections were required; minor narrative refinements could be made later but are not essential.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa), especially high-yielding hybrid and “super rice” cultivars, with occasional use of maize, wheat and sugarcane as secondary or overwintering hosts in the landscape matrix
Event summary: From the early 2000s through at least the mid‑2010s, Chilo suppressalis caused sustained, large-scale damage in Chinese hybrid and super-rice systems, representing one of the most impactful long-lasting emergence episodes for this pest. The event developed as super rice and intensified double-cropping systems expanded across the Yangtze basin and other regions, with national statistics indicating that C. suppressalis and allied borers damaged more than 14 million hectares of rice fields annually in China during much of this period, often requiring intensive insecticide use and additional IPM interventions. Expanded adoption of improved cultivation techniques, pheromone-based control and integrated management gradually reduced outbreak severity in some areas, though the pest remained entrenched and continues to pose a major production risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of high-yielding hybrid and super-rice cultivars, changes in planting density and sowing dates, longer growing seasons and stubble management practices created more favorable habitats and overwintering refuges; irrigation-based intensification and climate suitability maintained high population carrying capacity. Internal mechanisms: C. suppressalis biology (diapause capability, stem-boring habit, tolerance of wide temperature ranges) inherently supports persistence and geographic spread, but this episode is primarily driven by external agronomic drivers rather than documented new genotypes; it is therefore best categorized as a large-scale re-occurrence of an established pest.
Review: Decision: review. I corrected the geographic coding so that this event now refers only to Eastern Asia/China, and simplified the countries field from the vague “China [2000], multiple other Asian rice-growing countries” to “China [2000]”. The supporting literature (e.g., Sheng et al. 2003; Qu et al. 2011; recent resistance-monitoring syntheses) quantifies long-term damage and management responses specifically for China; similar chronic pressure elsewhere in Asia is real but less clearly documented as a distinct, linked 2000–2015 episode. Classification as a large-scale re-occurrence of an established pest remains appropriate, and the event is clearly among the top global episodes by area affected, but the revised row should be checked by a regional rice entomologist for temporal bounds and whether additional countries merit inclusion as a linked multi-country episode.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in intensively treated paddy systems
Event summary: Beginning around 2002, systematic resistance monitoring in eastern China showed that populations of Chilo suppressalis in key rice areas such as Lianyungang (Jiangsu) and Ruian (Zhejiang) were evolving resistance to multiple conventional insecticides. Over the subsequent decade, resistance ratios to several active ingredients (including organophosphates, carbamates, nereistoxin analogues and fiproles) increased significantly, reducing field efficacy and prompting changes in control recommendations and rotation strategies. By about 2011, monitoring data documented established, multi-insecticide-resistant field populations in several provinces, and management programs increasingly emphasized resistance management, IPM and alternative tools rather than sole reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of the same insecticide classes in high-value rice regions, often on successive generations within the same season, created strong selection pressure; dense planting and high pest pressure further favored survival of resistant individuals. Internal mechanisms: Evolution and spread of metabolic and target-site resistance to multiple insecticide modes of action in field populations of C. suppressalis, documented through bioassays and resistance monitoring, constitutes a clear re-emergence of the pest via pesticide-resistance mechanisms rather than geographic invasion.
Review: Decision: review. The conceptualization of this event as a resistance-driven re-emergence of C. suppressalis in Chinese rice from 2002–2011 is well supported by long-term bioassay data (e.g., He et al. 2013 and related Chinese monitoring studies), and the emergence types (re-emergence=yes; re-occurrence=no) are correctly used. I simplified the countries field to “China [2002]” (localities such as Lianyungang and Ruian are more appropriate in the narrative) and replaced a diamide-focused review with more directly relevant multi-insecticide resistance sources. The time window and list of chemistries under selection should be rechecked by a resistance specialist, but the event is clearly among the globally important episodes given the breadth of compounds affected and the large rice area involved.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in areas treated with diamide insecticides (chlorantraniliprole, flubendiamide and related compounds)
Event summary: Around 2013, shortly after diamide insecticides had been widely adopted to control rice stem borers, resistance to chlorantraniliprole and related compounds was first detected in field populations of Chilo suppressalis in Hubei Province, China. Over the next several years, reports of reduced field efficacy and elevated resistance ratios emerged from other eastern and central Chinese provinces including Hunan, Zhejiang, Shandong and Jiangxi, indicating rapid spread or independent evolution of diamide resistance in multiple C. suppressalis populations. By approximately 2016, resistance levels in some populations (e.g., in Jiangxi) had increased markedly, and although control failure was not yet universal, the episode forced adjustments to treatment thresholds, rotation schemes and integration with nonchemical measures to sustain effective management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread, intensive use of diamide insecticides in Chinese rice production beginning in the late 2000s created strong selection for resistant phenotypes; high pest pressure and frequent applications magnified selection intensity. Internal mechanisms: Genetic changes in C. suppressalis conferring reduced susceptibility to diamides, including target-site ryanodine receptor mutations (e.g., G4910/4946E) and metabolic mechanisms documented in multiple field populations, represent a classic pesticide-resistance-driven re-emergence, with evidence of moderate but persistent resistance across several provinces over multiple years.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly describes the first documented field resistance of C. suppressalis to diamide insecticides in China (initially in Hubei, then in other eastern/central provinces) and appropriately codes it as a re-emergence driven by pesticide resistance. I simplified the countries field to “China [2013]” and replaced a generic methods page with more specific monitoring and mechanism studies (e.g., Yao et al. 2017; Yao et al. 2016). The 2013–2016 window captures the initial emergence and rapid escalation of resistance; however, resistance has persisted and evolved further beyond 2016, so experts may wish to extend the end year or treat later intensification as a follow-on episode.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in irrigated rice systems, along with wild and cultivated grasses in nearby wetlands and canals
Event summary: During the late 20th and early 21st centuries, Chilo suppressalis expanded its range into the south of European Russia, where it had previously been absent, invading rice-growing and wetland areas along the lower Volga and Caspian regions. The invasion developed through gradual spread from existing foci in the Volga region and Transcaucasus, facilitated by irrigated rice cultivation, canal networks and suitable wetland habitats, and was documented by lepidopteran surveys that began recording C. suppressalis in south European Russia and adjacent regions. As populations became established, the species was added to regional faunal lists, and rice pest risk assessments started to consider it a potential or emerging threat in these newly colonized temperate areas, although large documented yield-loss outbreaks remained relatively localized.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated rice cultivation, canal networks and wetland habitats in the lower Volga and Caspian regions, together with increasing movement of plant material and climatic suitability, facilitated northward and westward spread from its historical Asian range and from earlier European foci in Spain and France. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype has been reported for the Russian invasion; the event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion supported by the species’ inherent tolerance of cooler climates and diapause capacity, allowing establishment in temperate Eastern Europe.
Review: Decision: review. I corrected the geographic metadata so that the continent is now “Europe,” the sub-region is “Eastern Europe,” and the countries field is simplified to “Russian Federation [approx. 1990s–2000s]”, removing non-standard text about Transcaucasus/Volga regions from the country field. On the basis of historical introductions into Spain and France well before 1990, this Russian episode is best interpreted as intra-continental emergence into a new European sub-region rather than inter-continental emergence. The underlying invasion is real but dates and exact rice-production impacts remain approximate, so the row should be rechecked against Russian faunal catalogues and any national pest reports.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and associated wetland grasses in European rice-growing landscapes
Event summary: In 2010, Chilo suppressalis was first reliably recorded from two localities in the Great Hungarian Plain, representing a new addition to the central/eastern European lepidopteran fauna and indicating spread within Europe from earlier foci in France and Spain. A few years later, in 2014, the species was documented from Nazaré on the Atlantic coast of Portugal, adding Portugal to the list of European countries where this rice borer is established or considered invasive. Following these detections, national and regional entomological and plant-health reports began treating C. suppressalis as an emerging invasive rice pest in the newly colonized areas, with monitoring and risk assessment emphasizing the potential for further spread into other suitable European rice-growing regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued expansion of C. suppressalis within Europe is associated with irrigated rice and wetland habitats in southern and eastern Europe, facilitated by irrigation networks, warm summers and movement of infested plant material or larvae in rice straw; climate-change-related warming may also improve overwintering success at higher latitudes. Internal mechanisms: The species’ diapause and cold-hardiness traits and its ability to exploit flooded rice and reed habitats support geographic range expansion, but there is no clear evidence of new genotypes specific to these invasions; this episode is therefore coded as intra-continental geographic expansion rather than a re-emergence based on biological change.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly captures post‑2000 spread of C. suppressalis into new European countries (Hungary and Portugal) and appropriately codes this as intra-continental emergence. I standardized the countries field to “Hungary [2010]; Portugal [2014]” and pruned the source list to emphasize primary faunistic records (microlepidoptera.hu for Hungary; SHILAP and distribution syntheses for Portugal and broader Europe) plus the CAPS datasheet, removing Wikipedia-based sources which are less authoritative. The biological and management implications (invasive status, potential spread into other rice areas) are broadly correct, but national plant-health records could be consulted to refine impact magnitude and confirm whether earlier, overlooked records exist.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in the irrigated paddies of the Ebro delta (Catalonia), with larvae also present in nearby wetland grasses
Event summary: From roughly 1990 through the end of the decade, Chilo suppressalis remained the principal insect pest of rice in Spain’s Ebro delta, causing recurrent local outbreaks that prompted intensive insecticide use and stimulated the development of new control strategies. Drawing on detailed studies of the pest’s larval development and phenology in the delta, regional plant-protection services and collaborators tested and refined mass trapping with synthetic sex pheromones throughout the 1990s, culminating in large-scale deployment. By about 2000, control of C. suppressalis in the Ebro delta relied predominantly on pheromone-based mass trapping, which substantially reduced the number of insecticide applications and overall control costs while maintaining acceptable levels of crop protection, effectively marking the end of this high-pressure resurgence phase.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Ebro delta comprises a large, continuous area of irrigated rice with favorable flooding regimes and abundant stubble, which historically supported high C. suppressalis populations; reliance on insecticides and lack of rotation further favored recurrent outbreaks. Regional investment in monitoring and in pheromone-based mass trapping was driven by the need to manage these chronic high populations more sustainably. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that novel strains or resistance traits unique to the Ebro delta were responsible for the resurgence; the episode is best viewed as a re-occurrence of an established European population under conducive agronomic and landscape conditions, followed by successful suppression via behaviorally based control.
Review: Decision: review (new event added). This row has been added to capture a major 1990s re-occurrence episode in the Spanish Ebro delta, where C. suppressalis was the dominant rice pest and where large-scale pheromone-based mass trapping was developed and adopted around 2000. The timing (1990s development work, mass trapping as the main control from 2000 onward), geography (Spain/Southern Europe, specifically the Ebro delta) and classification as a re-occurrence of an already established European population are consistent with Spanish plant-protection bulletins and extension reports. Precise start and end years are approximate, and quantitative information on hectares affected and yield loss is limited in the accessible literature, so this event should be reviewed by regional experts, but its inclusion is justified as one of the largest post‑1990 European emergence episodes for this pest.

Host: Apples (Malus domestica) and pears (Pyrus communis) in commercial orchards
Event summary: From about 1993, populations of Choristoneura rosaceana in southern Ontario apple and pear orchards began showing frequent control failures with standard organophosphate programs, prompting targeted resistance surveys. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s, laboratory and field assays demonstrated widespread organophosphate resistance and cross‑resistance to other insecticides across multiple Ontario production areas, and growers reported persistent leafroller damage despite repeated sprays. By the end of the decade, management programs were being redesigned around resistance‑management principles, alternative chemistries, and integrated pest management to restore control and reduce selection pressure on resistant populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term intensive use of organophosphate insecticides in apple and pear orchards, limited rotation of modes of action, and reliance on calendar sprays created strong selection pressure for resistant C. rosaceana populations; high host availability in large contiguous orchard landscapes facilitated persistence of resistant genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – biochemical and physiological mechanisms of resistance to organophosphorus insecticides were documented in field populations from southern Ontario, with associated cross‑resistance to some other products; increased virulence is not implicated, but resistance increased effective pest pressure by undermining previously effective control programs.
Review: Retain: Well documented, large-scale resistance-driven re-emergence affecting major southern Ontario apple and pear regions in the 1990s; geography, timing, host range, and classification as re-emergence (via insecticide resistance) are appropriate. No corrections required, but timing remains approximate to the main survey years.

Countries: Canada [early 1990s] (British Columbia – Okanagan, Similkameen and Creston Valleys)
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) and pears (Pyrus communis) in commercial orchards
Event summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, implementation of an area-wide sterile insect release programme for codling moth in southern British Columbia reduced the need for broad-spectrum summer sprays that had previously suppressed leafroller complexes in apple and pear orchards. As codling moth sprays were cut back, obliquebanded and threelined leafroller populations resurged in the Okanagan, Similkameen and Creston Valleys, causing noticeable increases in bud, leaf and fruit damage and economic concern among growers. By the late 1990s, provincial specialists and researchers had developed and promoted a dedicated integrated pest management programme based on Bacillus thuringiensis, insect growth regulators such as tebufenozide, and pheromone-based monitoring to bring leafroller damage back to acceptable levels under the new reduced-spray regime.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major changes in pest management, particularly the introduction of the codling moth sterile insect release program in the early 1990s and corresponding reductions in organophosphate cover sprays, removed incidental suppression of leafrollers and allowed C. rosaceana populations to resurge; large contiguous tree-fruit plantings in the southern interior provided abundant hosts. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic changes (e.g. new resistant strains) were implicated; the episode is best characterized as a management-driven re-occurrence rather than resistance-driven re-emergence.
Review: Review: Added new re-occurrence event for the 1990s resurgence of obliquebanded leafroller in British Columbia apple and pear orchards, linked to reduced broad-spectrum insecticide use after the codling moth sterile insect release program and subsequent adoption of a dedicated IPM programme. This episode affected major production valleys and is supported by provincial reports and research on leafroller populations; however, the start and end years are approximate and should be checked by a subject-matter expert.

Countries: United States of America [2000] (Washington – Columbia Basin, Wenatchee Valley, Yakima and Snake River areas; Oregon [early 2000s] – Milton-Freewater apple region)
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards
Event summary: In the early 2000s, Washington State and adjacent Oregon apple orchards experienced persistent oblique banded leafroller infestations despite standard insecticide programs, raising concern about emerging resistance. Field collections from numerous orchards across central Washington and nearby Oregon revealed markedly reduced susceptibility to several commonly used insecticides and documented resistance and cross‑resistance patterns across the region, confirming that resistant populations had spread in key production zones. By around 2006, regional management recommendations shifted toward rotation of chemistries, incorporation of mating disruption, and broader IPM tactics to mitigate resistance and restore acceptable control levels.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Decades of intensive, often prophylactic insecticide use against multiple apple pests, combined with large, high‑value orchards that favored repeated sprays, created strong regional selection for resistant C. rosaceana; coordinated area‑wide resistance management was initially limited, allowing resistant populations to persist and spread locally. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – documented resistance and cross‑resistance in obliquebanded leafroller populations to organophosphates and other insecticides in Washington apples; although transmission biology was unchanged, resistant populations had higher survival under spray regimes, effectively increasing pest pressure and damage potential.
Review: Retain: Supported by detailed resistance studies and regional extension reports showing widespread control failures and cross-resistance in Washington and adjacent Oregon orchards in the early 2000s. Geography, timing and classification as re-emergence driven by insecticide resistance are appropriate; no corrections made, but exact end year (2006) remains an informed approximation based on study and recommendation timelines.

Continent: South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)
Host: Wild and cultivated rosaceous and broadleaf hosts (including wild apples and ornamental/broadleaf trees)
Event summary: Around 2004, a comprehensive survey of Lepidoptera on the Baja California peninsula documented Choristoneura rosaceana in northern Mexico, representing the first confirmed records of the species in the country and extending its known range southward from the USA. During this period the moth was detected on native and cultivated hosts in lowland habitats, indicating that viable populations were established beyond the previously recognized US–Canada range. The species has since been considered part of the native North American fauna extending into northern Mexico, with phytosanitary concern focused on preventing further movement into new continents or regions via plants for planting.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely gradual natural range extension and/or previously undocumented occurrence associated with continuous temperate habitats from the south-western United States into northern Mexico; increased entomological sampling intensity and taxonomic work in Baja California enabled detection. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ broad host range and adaptability to diverse temperate and semi‑arid habitats facilitate persistence in northern Mexico; no specific genetic novelty is documented, but inherent ecological flexibility supports southward range continuity.
Review: Review: This event correctly captures the first confirmed records of C. rosaceana in Mexico (Baja California) and the associated southward range extension from the USA, and it is reasonable to treat it as an inter-continental emergence under the project’s scheme because it represents establishment in the 'South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)' region. However, first_detection has been set to No, since global first detection in the plant host system occurred much earlier in Canada/USA; the original classification conflated first records for Mexico with global first detection. The country description was also refined to refer specifically to the Baja California peninsula. Recommended for expert review to confirm that, despite limited quantified damage data, this range-extension event merits inclusion among the main post-1990 emergence events for this species.

Continent: South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards
Event summary: In 2011, Choristoneura rosaceana was reported for the first time as a pest of apples in the Ejido Vista Hermosa near Ciudad Cuauhtémoc, Chihuahua, marking its emergence as a new economic pest in northern Mexico’s highland apple belt. Surveys in infested orchards found larvae feeding in rolled leaves and on fruit clusters, with visible damage to developing apples, indicating that the moth had successfully colonized commercial apple production and could reach damaging densities under local conditions. Subsequent recommendations emphasized monitoring and adoption of management tactics based on experience from US and Canadian orchards to prevent the pest from becoming a chronic, high‑impact problem in Mexican apple regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive apple production in northern Mexico, movement of infested planting material or host plants from already infested North American regions, and relatively limited prior monitoring for this specific tortricid likely facilitated unnoticed establishment in Chihuahua orchards. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – although the moth already attacked apples elsewhere in North America, this event represents its establishment as an apple pest in a new production region; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – natural or human‑assisted spread from existing populations in northern Mexico or the south-western USA into the Chihuahua highlands contributed to this emergence.
Review: Retain: Accurately reflects the first report of C. rosaceana damaging apples in the Ciudad Cuauhtémoc region of Chihuahua and its emergence as a new economic pest in Mexico’s main apple-growing state. Classification as re-emergence (host expansion and range consolidation within an already infested subregion) is consistent with prior records from northern Mexico; geographic and temporal details match the primary source, so no corrections are proposed.

Host: Soybean (Glycine max), cotton (Gossypium hirsutum and other cultivated cottons)
Event summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, soybean looper populations in the southern United States surged in importance as a defoliating pest in soybean–cotton production systems, coinciding with intensive pyrethroid use. Field populations developed high levels of resistance to pyrethroid and other insecticide groups, leading to recurring late‑season outbreaks and control failures across the southern soybean belt. Management stabilized only after shifts in insecticide programs and integrated pest management tactics reduced reliance on single chemistries and incorporated additional control measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroid and other broad‑spectrum insecticides in soybean–cotton rotations, large contiguous areas of susceptible crops, and favorable warm, humid conditions that supported multiple generations per year. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (evolution of high resistance to pyrethroids and other chemistries), with resistance maintaining large populations despite control pressure; this indirectly increased effective reproductive rate but there is no clear evidence of increased virulence per se.
Review: Review – Event correctly represents major pyrethroid‑resistance‑driven outbreaks of soybean looper in the southern United States; re_occurrence has been set to No and re_emergence kept as Yes so that emergence types remain mutually exclusive while emphasizing that the key internal change was insecticide resistance in an already established pest. The 1990–1995 window is broadly consistent with reports of high pyrethroid resistance from the late 1980s into the early 1990s but could be fine‑tuned by a US cotton–soybean resistance historian. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267218002_Pyrethroid_Resistance_Levels_in_%27vo_Generations_of_Soybean_Looper_Lepidoptera_Noctuidae_on_Soybean_in_Mississippi_J?utm_source=openai))

Host: Soybean (Glycine max) (primary), with spillover to cotton and other broadleaf crops in some areas
Event summary: During the early 2000s, especially from the 2002–2003 soybean seasons onward, Chrysodeixis includens shifted from a historically secondary role to an emerging key pest of soybean across most major producing regions of Brazil. As soybean expanded rapidly into the Cerrado and other new frontiers and cropping systems intensified (no‑till and double‑cropping), repeated severe defoliation episodes were reported and control became increasingly reliant on foliar insecticides. By the late 2000s the species was widely recognized as a principal defoliator causing economically significant yield losses in Brazilian soybean, with its growing importance in neighboring Southern Cone countries setting the stage for later region‑wide outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of soybean into new frontiers (e.g. Brazilian Cerrado) with large, continuous monocultures; adoption of no‑till and double‑cropping systems increasing green cover and host availability year‑round; suppression of natural enemies and shifts in the pest complex associated with fungicide use and landscape simplification; climate variability (including El Niño–linked rainy seasons) favoring multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within South America associated with adaptation to extensive soybean landscapes and strong migratory ability, but without clear evidence of a discrete new biotype driving the initial outbreaks.
Review: Review – Event retained but refocused on Brazil, with the start year changed from 2000 to 2002 and the country list narrowed to Brazil [2002] because multi‑source evidence indicates that widespread outbreaks transforming soybean looper from a secondary to a key soybean pest began in the 2002/03 seasons in Brazil, whereas comparable dominance in Argentina and Paraguay arose later and is captured in a separate Southern Cone event. Emergence type has been simplified to re_occurrence (re_emergence set to No) since the main drivers appear to be cropping‑system and landscape changes plus climatic suitability rather than a clearly delimited new strain. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0085562615001089?utm_source=openai))

Host: Soybean (Glycine max)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s through approximately 2021, Chrysodeixis includens increased from a member of the noctuid defoliator complex to a consistently important and in some years predominant defoliating pest of soybean in northern and central Argentina and adjacent Paraguay. Field surveys, life‑table studies and biological work from Tucumán and other provinces documented high densities of soybean looper alongside, and later often exceeding, Rachiplusia nu and Anticarsia gemmatalis, raising concern about yield losses and the need for adapted economic thresholds. Over the 2010s and early 2020s, deployment of Bt soybean, refined sampling and insecticide use, and conservation of natural enemies helped limit but not eliminate recurrent outbreaks, and the species remains a key target in regional IPM programs.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large soybean area and intensified production systems in Argentina and Paraguay; similar landscape simplification and nearly season‑long host availability as observed in Brazil; regional climatic suitability supporting multiple generations; widespread use of foliar insecticides shaping the lepidopteran complex. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of high, damaging population densities across more of the Southern Cone soybean belt and high dispersal/migration maintaining genetic connectivity; possible buildup of insecticide tolerance, although for this episode the dominant signal is pest‑complex shift rather than a single resistance mutation.
Review: Review – Event kept as the main episode describing the rise of soybean looper to major soybean‑defoliator status in Argentina (and, more approximately, Paraguay), but the period has been extended back to 2005 to reflect studies from the 2005/06 season onward that already identify C. includens as one of the principal noctuid pests in Tucumán and other northern provinces. Emergence type has been adjusted to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because the resurgence is best explained by intensification of soybean production, complex shifts within the lepidopteran defoliator guild and management changes, while discrete new resistance mechanisms are treated in other events. The start year for Paraguay remains approximate (marked with “~2010”) and should be checked against national monitoring data. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41126143_Lepidopteros_noctuidos_plagas_en_el_cultivo_de_soja_en_Tucuman_Argentina?utm_source=openai))

Host: Soybean (Glycine max)
Event summary: Between roughly 2011 and 2016, large‑scale surveys across more than 35 million hectares of soybean in Brazil documented Chrysodeixis includens as the predominant lepidopteran pest in non‑Bt (glyphosate‑tolerant) soybean fields in virtually all major producing regions. These years were characterized by frequent and sometimes overlapping generations of soybean looper, high defoliation pressure and heavy dependence on foliar insecticide applications to prevent yield losses. The situation began to ease only with broader adoption of Bt soybean expressing Cry1Ac and better integration of IPM, which reduced defoliator pressure and insecticide use in some regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large and expanding soybean area under non‑Bt cultivars, especially before and during early adoption of Bt soybean; landscape simplification around soy and favorable climatic conditions in Central–West and other regions leading to long favorable seasons; intense reliance on foliar insecticides for defoliator control. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced dispersal and recolonization capacity allowing C. includens to dominate regional soybean pest communities; possible fine‑scale variation in insecticide susceptibility, although high‑level field resistance to Cry1Ac was not yet detected in this period.
Review: Review – Event retained as a distinct phase describing the 2011–2016 period when C. includens dominated non‑Bt soybean in Brazil and Cry1Ac soybean was widely evaluated; emergence type has been simplified to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because the main signal is a management‑ and landscape‑driven upsurge in an already widespread pest, while specific resistance evolution is handled in a separate insecticide‑resistance event. The cited large‑scale Cry1Ac and Bt/ conventional field surveys appropriately support the timing and scale. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4450/16/4/365?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Soybean (Glycine max), cotton (Gossypium spp.)
Event summary: From approximately 2013 onward, Brazilian populations of Chrysodeixis includens began to show clear, field‑evolved resistance to several chitin synthesis inhibitor (benzoylphenylurea) insecticides and variable susceptibility to other active ingredients used against soybean defoliators. As these chemistries lost efficacy in several regions, pest managers reported reduced control and higher survivorship of late‑instar larvae, forcing changes in spray programs and raising concern about resistance management in soybean and cotton. Over the latter 2010s, resistance monitoring and rotation strategies were introduced and, together with Bt crop deployment, helped limit but not eliminate resistance‑driven risk from this pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term, intensive use of benzoylphenylurea insect growth regulators and other insecticides in soybean and cotton landscapes, often with limited rotation of modes of action; high pest pressure and frequent applications in large contiguous production areas. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (field‑evolved resistance to chitin synthesis inhibitors such as teflubenzuron, novaluron and lufenuron, and documented variation in susceptibility to multiple insecticides); survival of resistant individuals enabling their disproportionate contribution to regional migratory populations.
Review: Retain – Event appropriately captures field‑evolved resistance of Brazilian soybean looper populations to benzoylphenylurea chitin‑synthesis‑inhibitor insecticides during the mid‑2010s, with classification as re_emergence (due to evolution of pesticide resistance) and other emergence types set to No in line with the scheme. Chemosphere and related resistance‑monitoring studies provide direct evidence of resistance levels, cross‑resistance patterns and approximate timing, and no higher‑impact insecticide‑resistance episode for this species in Brazil was identified that would supersede this one. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261219425000286?utm_source=openai))

Host: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), soybean (Glycine max), common bean and other legumes (Phaseolus spp.), eggplant (Solanum melongena), sunflower (Helianthus annuus)
Event summary: In Puerto Rico, Chrysodeixis includens has long been a severe pest of tomatoes, soybean and other broadleaf crops, with reports of up to 90% tomato fruit damage and complete defoliation in heavily infested fields. From around 2014, growers and resistance‑monitoring programs began reporting field failures and very high resistance ratios to key insecticides, particularly the diamide chlorantraniliprole, in soybean looper populations from Puerto Rican vegetable and seed‑production systems. By the late 2010s and early 2020s, bioassays and molecular work on the ryanodine receptor confirmed moderate to high diamide resistance, prompting recommendations for strict resistance‑management strategies and raising concern about potential spread of resistant migrants to the continental United States.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive, repeated use of diamide insecticides (e.g. chlorantraniliprole, flubendiamide) and other chemistries in year‑round vegetable and seed‑production systems in Puerto Rico; warm climate permitting multiple generations per year and continuous host availability; limited refuges from insecticide exposure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (field‑evolved resistance to diamides and other insecticide classes, including evidence of moderate chlorantraniliprole resistance and associated ryanodine‑receptor changes, as well as likely metabolic resistance); survival and buildup of resistant genotypes in an already severe pest, with potential for long‑distance migration to other parts of the Americas.
Review: Review – New event added to represent the emergence of moderate to high resistance of Puerto Rican soybean looper populations to diamide insecticides during roughly 2014–2023 in a context where C. includens was already a long‑established, very damaging pest of tomato, soybean and other crops. Classified as re_emergence because the defining feature is evolution of insecticide resistance, not spread to a new region; the 2014 start date reflects IRAC and monitoring reports of field failures, while upper bounds are based on recent RyR‑focused molecular studies and bioassays. Given that Puerto Rico’s cropped area is smaller than that of Brazil or the US mid‑south but resistance there has clear regional implications via migration, human experts should confirm whether this episode should remain among the top ten emergence events for this species. ([cotton.org](https://www.cotton.org/beltwide/proceedings/2005-2022/data/conferences/2022/paper/21635.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America (California: Davis and surrounding areas in the northern Central Valley)
Host: Chinese hackberry (Celtis sinensis) and other ornamental/amenity trees; citrus present in the broader region but this study focused on hackberry infestations.
Event summary: Following a severe population decline of citricola scale in northern California attributed to very cold winter conditions in 1990–1991, populations on Chinese hackberry trees in Davis, California began to recover starting in 1991. Between 1991 and 1994, a field study documented steadily increasing densities of female scales and crawlers on untreated hackberry trees each year, indicating a strong resurgence of this introduced subtropical species in urban landscapes. By 1994, high densities were again causing heavy honeydew and sooty mold accumulation, prompting evaluation of control options such as horticultural oil sprays and systemic insecticide trunk implants.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A period of unusually cold winter temperatures in 1990–1991 in northern California likely caused high mortality and a temporary crash in citricola scale populations, followed by milder winters that facilitated rapid resurgence. Urban plantings of Chinese hackberry provided abundant suitable host foliage and relatively low natural enemy pressure compared with better‑managed orchards. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance mechanism was reported for this event; the resurgence appears driven mainly by climatic recovery and host availability rather than documented genetic change.
Review: Retain – Event correctly describes the 1991–1994 post‑freeze resurgence of C. pseudomagnoliarum on Chinese hackberry in Davis, California, with geography and timing consistent with Dreistadt (1996). Classification as re-occurrence (resurgence in a long‑established subregion driven by climatic variation and urban host plantings, without documented genetic change) matches the study and soft-scale reviews. Impact is moderate and largely ornamental/urban rather than agricultural, so this event may be borderline for inclusion if a strict 'top 10 by economic impact' filter is later applied, but it is currently retained as one of the few well-documented post‑1990 resurgence episodes.
