Countries: United States of America (California: San Joaquin Valley citrus belt, including Fresno, Tulare, Kern and adjacent counties)
Host: Commercial citrus, especially sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) and other Citrus spp. in San Joaquin Valley orchards.
Event summary: From the early 2000s onward, citricola scale re‑emerged as a key soft scale pest in the San Joaquin Valley citrus industry after decades in which broad‑spectrum organophosphate and carbamate insecticides had suppressed its populations. As citrus growers increasingly adopted biologically based integrated pest management for California red scale, relying on selective pesticides and releases of the parasitoid Aphytis melinus, citricola scale populations built up on citrus foliage and twigs, causing substantial honeydew production, sooty mold growth, reduced tree vigor, and downgraded or culled fruit. By the 2010s–2020s, extension reports and field experiments documented that citricola scale was a serious and sometimes resistant pest in the San Joaquin Valley, with about 40% of sampled populations showing resistance to organophosphate insecticides and requiring alternative chemistries and refined IPM strategies to keep damage below economic thresholds.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: A major driver was the shift in citrus pest management in California towards selective insecticides and conservation/augmentation of parasitoids for California red scale, which reduced incidental suppression of citricola scale by broad‑spectrum insecticides. Expansion of high‑value citrus acreage in the San Joaquin Valley and the high economic value of cosmetically clean fruit increased the perceived impact of citricola scale honeydew and sooty mold. Internal mechanisms: Documented resistance to organophosphate insecticides in approximately 40% of citricola scale populations in the San Joaquin Valley indicates an adaptive re‑emergence mechanism based on pesticide resistance; there is likely cross‑resistance to carbamates, necessitating a shift to other active ingredients and timings of sprays that minimize disruption of natural enemies.
Review: Retain – Event appropriately captures the re‑emergence of citricola scale as a key pest of commercial citrus in California’s San Joaquin Valley from the late 1990s–2000s onwards. Classification as re-emergence (linked to pesticide resistance and management shifts) without intra-/inter-continental elements is consistent with UC IPM guidelines, classical biocontrol syntheses, and field efficacy studies documenting organophosphate resistance and sustained economic impacts. Dates are approximate but match the period when SJV citricola scale is consistently described as an 'emerging key pest' requiring specific control measures.

Countries: Cyprus [2005] (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus citrus-growing areas)
Host: Citrus spp. (commercial citrus orchards and associated host plants in Northern Cyprus).
Event summary: Between 2005 and 2007, a survey of scale insects in cultivated and non‑cultivated areas of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus recorded Coccus pseudomagnoliarum for the first time as part of the island’s Coccoidea fauna. During the survey, citricola scale was found on citrus and other host plants, and its presence was significant enough that the authors listed it among new country records and noted post‑harvest increases in populations alongside other soft scales. By the end of the survey period, citricola scale had become established in Northern Cyprus citrus ecosystems, although it was not yet highlighted as the dominant citrus pest due to the presence of other major scale species and their natural enemies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely drivers include regional trade and movement of infested citrus nursery stock or plant material between Türkiye and Northern Cyprus, which share close economic and logistical links in the eastern Mediterranean. Climatic suitability of coastal Northern Cyprus for subtropical soft scales and increasing intensity of citrus cultivation provided favorable conditions for establishment following introduction. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or resistance mechanism was described for the Northern Cyprus populations; the event is best interpreted as geographic spread and re-occurrence of an already widespread Mediterranean/West Asian pest in a new territory within the same subregion.
Review: Review – Event is a valid new-country record for C. pseudomagnoliarum in Northern Cyprus based on 2005–2007 surveys, but the emergence type has been corrected. Because the species had been established in the Western Asia subregion (e.g. Türkiye, Israel) for decades, this occurrence represents spread within an already affected subregion rather than a host-system-level first detection. 'first_detection' has therefore been set to false and 're_occurrence' set to true. Geographic assignment (Asia | Western Asia; country = Cyprus with specification of Northern Cyprus citrus areas) and timing (2005–2007 survey window) are retained. Impact appears limited (low densities, not a dominant citrus pest), so this event may be deprioritized if later evidence identifies additional, more damaging post‑1990 events.

Countries: Spain [2006] (Comunidad Valenciana: interior citrus-growing districts around Serra and other inland Valencia province orchards)
Host: Citrus spp. (mainly sweet orange and other commercial citrus varieties in interior Valencia citrus orchards).
Event summary: In 2006, the regional citrus phytosanitary surveillance program of the Comunidad Valenciana (Spain) detected Coccus pseudomagnoliarum for the first time in a citrus plot near Serra (Valencia), an area where this soft scale had not previously been recorded. Follow-up surveys during 2006–2008 showed that citricola scale was already widely distributed in many interior citrus-growing districts of Valencia province, although typically at moderate densities that rarely reached severe pest status. The species was therefore recognized as a 'new pest' in Valencian citrus, prompting detailed studies of its parasitoid complex and management, and its presence has since been incorporated into Mediterranean citrus IPM programs even though it remains generally less damaging than other key citrus pests in Spain.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction is most plausibly linked to movement of infested citrus plant material or propagative stock within the Mediterranean citrus trade, from regions such as Italy, Greece or California where the pest was already established, into the interior citrus districts of Valencia. The large area under citrus, relatively warm inland climate, and reduced use of broad-spectrum insecticides under Spanish citrus IPM programs created conditions that allowed citricola scale to establish and spread undetected for several years before formal detection. Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been presented for novel strains, resistance traits, or host shifts specific to Spanish populations; the event is best interpreted as geographic spread and re-occurrence within the already affected Southern Europe subregion.
Review: Retain – New event added to capture the introduction and spread of C. pseudomagnoliarum in the Valencian citrus industry, first detected in 2006 by the regional citrus surveillance program and subsequently found widely distributed in interior Valencia orchards. Classified as re-occurrence because the species had long been established in the Southern Europe subregion (Italy, Greece, Turkey), so this is spread to a new country within an existing subregion rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence or a global first detection. Sources consistently describe substantial concern, extensive monitoring and biological-control work but generally low–moderate infestation levels; given the importance of Valencia as a major citrus-producing area, this is considered one of the key post‑1990 emergence events.

Countries: Tunisia [2008] (Cap Bon citrus region and later other northern citrus-growing areas including Nabeul, Béja, Jendouba and Zaghouan districts)
Host: Citrus spp. (oranges, mandarins, lemons and other commercial citrus in Cap Bon and north-eastern Tunisian orchards).
Event summary: During surveys of citrus orchards in the Cap Bon region of Tunisia reported in 2008, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum was recorded for the first time as part of the Tunisian Coccoidea fauna, representing a new country record and, based on available literature, the first confirmed occurrence of this species in Africa. Subsequent faunistic work and national-scale surveys up to about 2011 documented citricola scale on citrus in additional northern Tunisian citrus regions, typically at low densities and in association with other scale insects such as Aonidiella aurantii and Saissetia oleae. Although citricola scale has not yet been identified as a major cause of yield loss in Tunisia, its establishment signifies an expansion of the pest’s range into North African citrus ecosystems, where it now forms part of a diverse alien scale insect complex.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The most likely pathway is trade and movement of infested citrus plant material (nursery stock, budwood or ornamental hosts) from Mediterranean countries where C. pseudomagnoliarum was already present (e.g. Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey) into Tunisian citrus regions. Climatic similarity between Cap Bon and other Mediterranean citrus zones, combined with high citrus planting density and historical under-appreciation of soft scale diversity, facilitated establishment and spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of novel strains, host shifts or resistance traits associated specifically with Tunisian populations; the event is best interpreted as inter-continental emergence due to geographic range expansion into Africa without documented intrinsic changes in the pest.
Review: Retain – New event added and classified as an inter-continental emergence, representing the first confirmed establishment of C. pseudomagnoliarum in Africa (Tunisia). Jendoubi et al. (2008) and later surveys document the species as a new record in Cap Bon citrus orchards and subsequently in other northern regions, with faunistic overviews confirming its inclusion among Tunisian citrus scale insects. Although current impact appears modest (low relative abundance and no major yield losses reported), the crossing into a new continent and a significant citrus-producing country warrants treating this as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events.

Countries: Syrian Arab Republic [2010] (Lattakia Governorate: Al-Ramma, Ein Al-Arus, Hmaimim, Albassa and nearby untreated citrus orchards)
Host: Citrus spp. in untreated citrus orchards of Lattakia Governorate.
Event summary: Around 2010, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum was reported as 'recently found' in Syria and recognized as a potential insect pest of citrus, with surveys in 2010–2011 documenting its presence on citrus trees in several districts of Lattakia Governorate. In untreated orchards, citricola scale caused economic damage primarily through heavy honeydew excretion and subsequent development of black sooty mold on leaves and fruit, reducing photosynthesis and marketability. During this period, researchers also characterized a diverse complex of parasitoids and predators associated with the scale, reflecting growing concern about its status in Syrian citrus production and the need for integrated management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction into Syrian citrus is most plausibly linked to regional movement of infested citrus planting material or fruit from neighboring Eastern Mediterranean countries (e.g. Türkiye, Lebanon) where C. pseudomagnoliarum was already present, coupled with favorable coastal climate and limited prior exposure of local natural enemy complexes to this specific pest. Economic and logistical constraints on pesticide use in some orchards may also have facilitated local population build-up. Internal mechanisms: Published studies emphasize phenology and natural enemies rather than intrinsic changes in the pest; there is no current evidence that Syrian populations possess unique resistance traits or host shifts, so the event is interpreted as re-occurrence and spread within the existing Western Asia subregion.
Review: Retain – New event added to describe the recent establishment and local build‑up of C. pseudomagnoliarum on citrus in Lattakia, Syria (2010–2011), which surveys characterize as a recently found pest causing economic damage via honeydew and sooty mold. Because the species had long been present in other Western Asia citrus regions (e.g. Türkiye, Israel), this is classified as re-occurrence (spread and resurgence within the same subregion) rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence or a global first detection. The event has moderate economic significance and substantial biological-control interest, justifying its inclusion among the limited number of post‑1990 emergence events for this pest.

Host: Soybean (Glycine max), maize/corn (Zea mays), cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) and other row crops in glyphosate-resistant (Roundup Ready) production systems, especially in no-till or reduced-tillage fields of the Midwest, Midsouth and Southeast
Event summary: After the introduction and rapid adoption of glyphosate-resistant (Roundup Ready) soybean in 1996 and subsequent glyphosate-based corn and cotton systems, Asiatic dayflower populations that had previously occurred at low densities in fields across parts of the US Midwest, Midsouth and Southeast began to increase and were first reported as troublesome weeds in no-till corn and soybean in the early 2000s. Through the 2000s, university weed science and extension reports from Iowa, Missouri and several other states documented Asiatic dayflower as a persistent broadleaf weed in glyphosate-resistant crops, characterized by extended emergence, survival of labeled glyphosate applications, and inclusion in regional lists of the most troublesome or hard-to-control soybean weeds. By the early–mid 2010s this weed shift had stabilized into a chronic management challenge in affected regions, with growers relying on diversified pre- and post-emergence herbicide programs and cultural practices to limit its impact on row-crop yields.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Rapid and widespread adoption of glyphosate-resistant soybean, corn and cotton from 1996 onward led to heavy reliance on glyphosate as the primary or sole post-emergence herbicide, reduced use of alternative herbicide modes of action, and increased use of no-till or reduced tillage. These management shifts created strong selection for weed species that are naturally tolerant of glyphosate and well adapted to minimally tilled, moist row-crop fields, allowing Asiatic dayflower to escape control and increase in density. Internal mechanisms: Commelina communis exhibits natural (inherent) tolerance to field rates of glyphosate, with partial survival at labeled doses and extended emergence that allows seedlings to escape the application window; there is no clear evidence of newly evolved glyphosate-resistant biotypes, and the event is best interpreted as a weed community shift driven by management rather than the appearance of a novel resistant strain. Life-history traits such as high seed production, prolonged emergence, and ability to root at stem nodes facilitate local population build-up and spread within affected production systems.
Review: review – Event is retained as a major emergence episode but reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence because current evidence indicates that C. communis in US glyphosate-resistant cropping systems is primarily exploiting pre-existing natural tolerance rather than a newly evolved herbicide-resistant biotype. Updated the mechanism_or_driver text to emphasize weed community shifts driven by glyphosate-dominated management and reduced tillage, and clarified that no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. Time span 1996–2015 is kept as an approximate period covering the main phase of weed shift and documentation, but the persistence of the problem beyond 2015 means dates should be treated as indicative and could be refined in a future pass.

Host: Soybean (Glycine max) and maize/corn (Zea mays) in rainfed and irrigated summer cropping systems of northeastern China (especially Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning provinces)
Event summary: From around the early 2000s, Asiatic dayflower populations in the major soybean- and corn-growing areas of northeastern China increased rapidly and became one of the three most troublesome weeds in soybean fields in this region, with dense infestations causing significant reductions in yield and quality. Surveys and genetic studies in Heilongjiang and neighboring provinces documented C. communis as the worst or dominant summer broadleaf weed in many fields, with long emergence periods, high seed production and poor control by the limited set of selective broadleaf herbicides available. By the late 2010s and early 2020s, prolonged and intensive use of atrazine and related herbicides had selected for C. communis populations with confirmed resistance to atrazine, and the species is now described as the dominant broadleaf weed in corn and soybean fields across northeastern China, with resistant biotypes and expanding distribution making management increasingly difficult through at least the mid‑2020s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Expansion and intensification of corn–soybean rotations in northeastern China, combined with widespread adoption of simplified herbicide programs and limited availability of effective selective broadleaf herbicides, created strong selection pressure favoring C. communis. Changes in farming systems (larger fields, reduced tillage and heavy reliance on a small number of herbicide modes of action, especially triazines) and climate conditions suitable for prolonged summer emergence further promoted its dominance. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field and laboratory studies from northeastern China have demonstrated C. communis populations with resistance to atrazine, associated with psbA gene over-expression, enhanced detoxification and high antioxidant enzyme activity; this resistance allows survival and reproduction under herbicide regimes that previously suppressed the species. Geographic and numerical expansion within its native range is facilitated by traits such as extended emergence, prolific seed production and rapid vegetative growth that allow C. communis to outcompete crops under current management, turning a previously less significant native weed into a dominant, high-impact pest in regional corn and soybean production.
Review: review – New event added to capture the major emergence of Commelina communis as a dominant and, in part, atrazine-resistant weed in corn and soybean systems of northeastern China. Classified as re_emergence because the high impact is closely linked to herbicide-resistant and highly adapted field populations within a region where the species was already present, rather than to spread into new continents or subregions. Time span 2000–2025 is an approximate linked episode covering its recognition as a worst or most troublesome weed in Heilongjiang province, subsequent dominance across northeastern China, and documented evolution of atrazine-resistant biotypes; exact onset and end years could be refined with more detailed Chinese-language agronomic data in a future revision.

Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event summary: In 1992, chestnut blight caused by Cryphonectria parasitica was detected for the first time in Germany on sweet chestnut in south‑western localities of Baden‑Württemberg, extending the pathogen’s range from already affected Italian, French and Swiss chestnut regions into central Europe. Subsequent monitoring through the 1990s and 2000s showed a limited number of scattered foci but confirmed in situ establishment of the pathogen in German chestnut stands. Disease has persisted at low to moderate levels in these areas, prompting continued surveillance and quarantine measures but without the landscape‑scale forest losses observed earlier in southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of infected nursery stock and other planting material within Europe, facilitated by regional trade in chestnut trees and insufficient early detection at import. Internal mechanisms: efficient local spread via rain‑dispersed conidia and airborne ascospores, and demonstrated adaptation of European C. parasitica populations to Castanea sativa, allowing successful colonization of more northerly German chestnut stands.
Review: review – Retain as a major post‑1990 event but reclassify as re_occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence, because Western Europe (France, Switzerland, etc.) was already affected before 1990; updated source list to use Germany‑specific first‑report and review articles instead of less relevant UK/Swiss references.

Countries: Iran (Islamic Republic of) [Gilan Province, 2001–2005 surveys; first published 2006]
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event summary: Between 2001 and 2005, severe dieback, cankers and mortality were observed on sweet chestnut trees in major chestnut‑growing forests of Gilan Province in northern Iran, and laboratory work repeatedly isolated Cryphonectria parasitica as the dominant pathogen from affected tissues. In 2006 this was formally reported as the first occurrence of chestnut blight in Iran, representing a major eastward extension of the disease into the easternmost native range of European chestnut within an Asian region where the pathogen had been known previously from India. Since then, chestnut blight has remained established in northern Iran, with damaging cankers and dieback in many stands, although the full spatial extent and long‑term impact on regional chestnut resources continue to be assessed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infected chestnut planting material or untreated wood from already infected regions in the Caucasus or Europe; humid montane climate and dense stands of susceptible C. sativa in Gilan facilitated establishment and local spread. Internal mechanisms: high pathogenicity of introduced C. parasitica strains on C. sativa, abundant production of asexual and sexual spores enabling rapid spread, and an apparent scarcity of hypovirulent (CHV1‑infected) strains, limiting natural attenuation of disease compared with some European regions.
Review: review – Event retained but event year adjusted to 2001–2005 to match survey data, and reclassified from intra‑continental emergence to re_occurrence because C. parasitica was already present in Southern Asia (India) by the early 1990s; country annotation and sources updated to rely on EPPO and primary Iranian field‑survey papers.

Countries: Azerbaijan [Great Caucasus chestnut forests; first symptoms 2003–2004, first official report 2008]
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event summary: Around 2003–2004, unusual cankers, dieback and mortality were first noted on sweet chestnut in the Great Caucasus region of Azerbaijan, and subsequent sampling confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica as the causal agent of chestnut blight. In 2008, a detailed plant pathology report formally documented C. parasitica on chestnut in Azerbaijan as a first country record, and by the late 2000s and early 2010s surveys showed the disease to be widespread and causing severe damage in most native chestnut forest districts. Through the 2010s and into the 2020s, chestnut blight has continued to drive high mortality and genetic erosion of local C. sativa populations and to impose significant socio‑economic impacts on chestnut‑dependent rural communities, while biological control with hypovirulent strains remains under evaluation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transboundary spread along the Caucasus, likely from neighbouring Georgia and/or Türkiye via movement of infected wood, bark or nursery stock, together with dense, genetically diverse native chestnut stands that provided abundant susceptible hosts; limited early surveillance and phytosanitary capacity in forest areas delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: aggressive C. parasitica genotypes introduced into a center of diversity for C. sativa, strong local spread via conidia and ascospores, and a historically low prevalence of hypovirus (CHV1), although CHV1‑infected strains and their potential for biocontrol are now being characterized.
Review: review – Retain as a high‑impact outbreak at the eastern edge of the European chestnut range but treat it as re_occurrence, not intra‑continental emergence, because Western Asia (notably Türkiye and Georgia) had long‑established chestnut blight; event types were corrected while existing first‑report and follow‑up sources remain appropriate.

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland – England (Warwickshire [2011], East Sussex [2011–2012])
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event summary: At the end of 2011, inspections of a five‑year‑old sweet chestnut nut‑production plantation near Leamington Spa (Warwickshire) revealed numerous trees with cankers and dieback, and laboratory testing confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica, marking the first detection of chestnut blight in the United Kingdom and in the Northern Europe subregion. Shortly afterwards, a second outbreak was found on a smaller plantation in East Sussex supplied from the same continental nursery source, and intensive surveys in 2011–2012 identified additional infected young chestnut trees linked to this planting material, although infections remained confined to recently planted stock. All known infected trees at these early sites were felled, uprooted and burnt, surrounding areas were surveyed within 3‑km radii, and strict movement controls for chestnut plants were implemented, leading to an apparent short‑term eradication of these initial outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction via international trade in infected nursery stock from mainland Europe, with several English sites traced back to a single French nursery; planting of many susceptible young chestnut saplings for nut production created concentrated host resources in previously disease‑free areas. Internal mechanisms: aggressive European C. parasitica strains capable of rapid canker formation and dieback on C. sativa, but the early foci were limited in extent and amenable to eradication because the pathogen had not yet established widely in surrounding woodland or older trees.
Review: review – Retain as the first established occurrence of chestnut blight in Northern Europe, i.e. a valid intra‑continental emergence event; restricted the list of affected counties in the “countries” field to Warwickshire and East Sussex to match EPPO first‑report information and avoid including later detections that belong to the 2016–2020 re‑occurrence episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland – England (Devon [2016], Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Cornwall, Derbyshire, Devon, Dorset, London, West Sussex [2017–2020]); Crown Dependencies: Jersey [2017–2019], Guernsey [2018–2020]
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut); Cryphonectria parasitica also detected on abandoned galls of Dryocosmus kuriphilus (Asian chestnut gall wasp)
Event summary: After the initial plantation outbreaks were thought to be eradicated, Cryphonectria parasitica was detected again in December 2016 on four mature sweet chestnut trees in woodland in Devon, representing the first confirmed establishment of chestnut blight in the wider environment in Great Britain. National surveys from 2017 to 2020 subsequently revealed multiple additional foci on sweet chestnut trees across several English counties and on the Channel Islands of Jersey and Guernsey, with genetic analyses revealing multiple introductions and a diversity of vegetative compatibility groups. By 2020, chestnut blight was officially regarded as present with restricted distribution in the UK, with limited but persistent disease at scattered woodland and landscape sites, and management shifted from pure eradication toward long‑term containment and evaluation of hypovirus‑based biocontrol.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued introductions of infected planting stock or wood products from continental Europe over at least two decades, coupled with increased planting of sweet chestnut for forestry and nut production; detection of the pathogen in abandoned galls of the invasive Asian chestnut gall wasp (Dryocosmus kuriphilus) suggests that this insect may provide a substrate or incidental vectoring mechanism for local pathogen survival and dispersal. Internal mechanisms: capacity of C. parasitica to establish on older woodland trees and persist in bark tissues and associated gall material; presence of multiple vegetative compatibility groups complicates classical hypovirus biocontrol, although Cryphonectria hypovirus 1 (CHV1) has been detected at some UK sites and is being evaluated to reduce canker severity and spread.
Review: review – Retain as a distinct re_occurrence episode in which chestnut blight became established in the wider environment of England and the Channel Islands after earlier eradication attempts; event‑type flags (re_occurrence only) are consistent with EPPO/EFSA descriptions, and the source list was cleaned to remove an unrelated EPPO article and duplicate links while keeping key UK distribution and research references.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Australia – Victoria (Ovens Valley, north‑east Victoria [2010 initial outbreak and follow‑up detections to 2020])
Host: Castanea spp. (commercial sweet chestnut orchards, primarily Castanea sativa and hybrids; occasional reports on Quercus spp. in the affected region)
Event summary: In September 2010, chestnut blight was detected for the first time in commercial chestnut orchards in the Ovens Valley of north‑east Victoria, Australia, where laboratory tests confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica on trees across at least six properties, marking the first established field outbreak of the disease in Australia and on the Oceania continent. An intensive eradication programme followed between 2010 and the late 2010s, during which more than 740,000 trees were inspected and over 5,000 diseased or at‑risk chestnut trees were removed under quarantine to protect an industry of roughly 350 growers concentrated in this region. Despite the initial campaign, low‑level infections persisted and additional foci were found in 2017–2019, and in 2019 the National Management Group concluded that eradication was no longer feasible, triggering a Transition to Management phase (2019–2020) and the current status of chestnut blight as an established but locally confined pathogen in Victoria.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected chestnut planting material or scion wood from overseas (likely Europe or Asia) into Australian nurseries in the early 2000s, including an earlier interception in post‑entry quarantine in Victoria in 2001, followed by escape into commercial orchards in the Ovens Valley; dense plantings of susceptible cultivars in a cool, humid montane climate facilitated establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: high aggressiveness of introduced C. parasitica lineages on Castanea spp., the ability of the fungus to remain latent in bark tissues for prolonged periods and sporulate profusely on cankers, and an apparent absence of established hypovirulent CHV1 strains in Australia, all of which undermined eradication despite rigorous sanitation and tree removal.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first established field outbreak of chestnut blight in Oceania and its decade‑long management; classified as an inter‑continental emergence into Australia based on official Agriculture Victoria and IPPC reports, and recommended for expert review of quantitative impact metrics (e.g. industry losses) as more data become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Algeria – Tizi Ouzou (Akfadou mountains, parc châtaigneraie [2023])
Host: Castanea sativa (sweet chestnut)
Event summary: In July 2023, mortality of sweet chestnut trees was reported in the parc châtaigneraie in the Akfadou mountain range of Tizi Ouzou, Algeria, where affected trees showed crown dieback with persistent withered leaves, trunk and branch cracks and cankers with orange pycnidial stromata and mycelial fans under the bark; morphological and DNA sequence analyses of EF‑1α and β‑tubulin genes confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica as the causal agent. Pathogenicity tests on detached chestnut twigs reproduced canker development and yielded the same fungus, and forestry archives indicated that the infected groves had originally been established with planting material from the Cévennes region of France, pointing to introduction via infected stock. This outbreak constitutes the first report of chestnut blight in Algeria and only the second documented African country record after Tunisia, representing a re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of the disease within the Northern Africa subregion and prompting calls for broader surveys and strengthened phytosanitary measures.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected chestnut planting material from France to establish groves in Tizi Ouzou, combined with suitable cool, humid montane conditions and a lack of prior targeted surveillance for C. parasitica in Algerian chestnut stands. Internal mechanisms: high virulence of the introduced C. parasitica lineage on C. sativa and efficient production of asexual spores on trunk cankers, enabling local spread within the small chestnut park and posing a risk of further dissemination to other plantings in North Africa.
Review: review – Newly added event reflecting the first confirmed occurrence of C. parasitica in Algeria (and second known African country record); classified as re_occurrence within Northern Africa because Tunisia was already affected, and summarised primarily from the 2025 Plant Disease note and EPPO distribution update; recommended for follow‑up once national survey data on spread and impact become available.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato); Capsicum annuum (pepper); Cucumis melo and other cucurbits
Event summary: From the late 1980s into the early 1990s, vegetable production in parts of Spain, Italy and France experienced severe epidemics of systemic tomato necrosis caused by cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) strains carrying necrogenic satellite RNAs, with the most intense phase around 1990–1992. In eastern Spain and southern Italy in particular, CMV–satRNA complexes caused systemic death of tomato plants and necrotic fruit, with reports that roughly 80% of tomato plants were lost over about 70% of the growing area and some fields suffered complete crop failure, and associated damage was also reported in pepper and cucurbit crops. The epidemic declined after growers and researchers deployed a mix of control measures, including withdrawal of the most susceptible cultivars, the use of attenuating satellite RNAs and other cross‑protection strategies, improved aphid management and sanitation, and by the mid‑1990s the incidence of necrogenic satRNAs in CMV populations in Spain had fallen sharply.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive open‑field and protected vegetable production along the Mediterranean coast, high densities of aphid vectors, and the presence of numerous CMV‑susceptible weed and crop hosts created strong inoculum pressure and facilitated rapid CMV spread; limited availability of CMV‑resistant tomato cultivars and dense plantings exacerbated the impact. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity were central, as specific necrogenic satellite RNAs (e.g. D‑satRNA and related CARNA‑5 variants) associated with existing CMV strains converted otherwise moderate infections into lethal systemic necrosis and fruit necrosis, effectively transforming CMV into a far more destructive pathosystem in tomato; the CMV–satRNA complexes also maintained effective transmission by aphids, so there was no trade‑off between virulence and spread.
Review: review – Added to capture the large CMV–necrogenic satellite RNA epidemics in tomato (and associated damage in peppers and cucurbits) in eastern Spain and parts of Italy and France, which caused reported losses of ~80% of tomato plants over much of the growing area and total crop failure in some fields. The event window is set to 1990–1992 to reflect the peak of these epidemics while respecting the 1990+ cut-off, even though the outbreak began in the late 1980s, and the country list is restricted to those with published evidence of necrogenic CMV–satRNA epidemics. Classified as re-emergence because CMV was already endemic in Southern Europe and the key novelty was the emergence and spread of highly virulent necrogenic satellite RNAs associated with existing CMV strains. Human review is recommended to confirm that the temporal bounds and country coverage match the intended episode granularity.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)
Event summary: In the 1980s and early 1990s cucumber mosaic virus was a major constraint on field tomato production in parts of China, and field trials summarised around 1990–1991 reported that CMV infection could reduce total tomato yield by roughly 25–50%. In heavily affected areas, abundant aphid vectors, mixed vegetable cropping with many CMV reservoir hosts and the absence of resistant tomato cultivars led to widespread infection and substantial reductions in marketable fruit quality and quantity. Subsequent adoption of integrated management, including deployment of attenuated CMV strains and satellite RNAs for cross‑protection in some regions, together with vector control and cultural practices, reduced the frequency and severity of such large CMV epidemics in Chinese tomato production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High aphid pressure, dense and mixed plantings of CMV‑susceptible vegetables and weeds, and the lack of effective CMV‑resistant tomato cultivars created conditions for rapid CMV spread and high disease incidence in Chinese tomato fields. Internal mechanisms: Available syntheses do not identify a single new genotype as responsible; rather, existing CMV populations (sometimes supporting satellite RNAs) reached very high prevalence under favourable ecological conditions, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re-occurrence of established CMV complexes in tomato rather than a distinct re-emergence driven by novel strains.
Review: review – New event added to represent CMV epidemics in Chinese tomato production where multiple syntheses report yield losses of roughly 25–50% of total yield attributable to CMV infection in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The 1990–1991 window is an operational approximation that captures the end of the eight‑year period of field trials reported by Tien and co‑workers while keeping within the 1990+ constraint; precise province‑level coverage and starting year could not be resolved from secondary sources. Classified as re-occurrence because CMV was already endemic in China and the published analyses attribute the impact mainly to high inoculum pressure and vector activity rather than clearly defined newly emerged CMV genotypes. A human curator should verify whether this Chinese episode should be retained among the top‑impact CMV events or further subdivided regionally.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Cucumis melo (melon); Capsicum annuum (pepper)
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, CMV was one of the predominant viruses infecting field‑grown melon and pepper in Spain, with large surveys of the main melon‑growing regions in 1995–1996 showing CMV (alongside WMV‑2) as the most frequently detected virus in symptomatic plants. Experimental infections in central Spain demonstrated that early CMV infection before flowering could reduce melon yield by about 50% overall and by roughly 60% compared with healthy controls, and severe CMV epidemics in some pepper plantings were reported to cause yield losses approaching 80% in bad years. After these outbreaks, integrated management strategies—combining control of aphid vectors, barrier crops and physical protection, removal of infected plants and weeds, and in some cases the use of mild strains or satellite RNAs for cross‑protection—helped to reduce CMV incidence and mitigate the most extreme yield losses, although the virus has remained a recurrent problem in Mediterranean cucurbit and pepper systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive greenhouse and open‑field horticulture along the Spanish Mediterranean arc, high early‑season aphid densities, mixed cropping of solanaceous and cucurbit hosts near perennial weed reservoirs, and the lack of widely adopted CMV‑resistant cultivars combined to favour rapid CMV spread; early infection before flowering was especially damaging in melon. Internal mechanisms: The epidemics reflected high prevalence of existing CMV populations (often in mixed infections with other cucurbit viruses and sometimes associated with satellite RNAs) rather than a single clearly documented novel strain, so they are best classified as severe re-occurrence events in an already CMV‑endemic region rather than as re-emergence driven by strain innovation.
Review: review – Added to represent the mid‑1990s CMV epidemics in Spanish melon and pepper, which are documented by surveys and field experiments showing CMV as one of the most prevalent viruses in melon fields and yield reductions of up to ~60% in melon and ~80% in pepper under early, severe infection. The 1995–1997 window aligns with the main melon surveys (1995–1996) and the 1997 impact study; pepper losses from this period are captured via later syntheses that cite Avilla et al. and Luis‑Arteaga et al. Classified as re-occurrence because CMV was already widespread in Southern Europe and there is no strong evidence that a single new CMV genotype was the primary driver; instead the impact reflects high inoculum pressure, vector abundance and mixed infections. Human review is advised to decide whether to keep this as a single multi‑crop event or split into separate melon and pepper entries if finer granularity is desired.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Capsicum annuum (hot and sweet peppers)
Event summary: In Korean pepper production, CMV pathotypes P0 and P1 had been endemic and highly damaging since the 1980s and 1990s, but their impact was reduced by widespread deployment of pepper cultivars carrying resistance effective against these pathotypes. From the early 2010s, and particularly after 2013, new CMV variants such as strain GTN and several related isolates were recovered from commercial pepper fields where they caused severe disease on cultivars previously resistant to P1, marking a resistance‑breaking re-emergence associated with renewed heavy losses in pepper production. Following these outbreaks, breeding efforts shifted toward broader‑spectrum resistance loci (e.g. cmr2) capable of controlling the new variants, and integrated aphid and crop management practices were emphasised to reduce CMV pressure in Korean pepper fields.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large areas of pepper grown as monocultures of CMV‑resistant cultivars imposed strong selection pressure on viral populations, while intensive production, overlapping cropping cycles and abundant aphid vectors promoted rapid spread once resistance‑breaking variants arose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity were demonstrated, as resistance‑breaking variants such as CMV‑GTN carry nonsynonymous mutations in RNA1 encoding the 1a protein that allow infection of P1‑resistant cultivars, while maintaining high fitness in the field; these changes reflect adaptation to the host resistance background rather than geographic spread and underlie classification of this episode as a re-emergence event.
Review: review – Event retained as a key CMV re-emergence episode in pepper but the time window has been corrected from 2010–2013 to 2013–2016 to align with the documented isolation of the resistance‑breaking strain CMV‑GTN from pepper in 2013 and the collection of additional resistance‑breaking isolates from P1‑resistant cultivars in 2016, rather than implying emergence already by 2010. The geographic assignment (Eastern Asia, Republic of Korea) and classification as re-emergence driven by resistance‑breaking viral evolution in an already affected subregion remain appropriate. A human curator may wish to refine the end year further if more detailed epidemiological information on the dominance period of these variants becomes available, but the current adjustments improve consistency with the primary literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)
Event summary: During a survey in January 2006 near Salem in Tamil Nadu, South India, tomato fields showing severe mosaic, leaf puckering and stunting were found to have more than 70% of plants symptomatic, and laboratory testing identified the causal agent as cucumber mosaic virus subgroup II. This was the first report of subgroup II CMV infecting tomato in India, where previous tomato infections had been associated predominantly with subgroup I strains, and it demonstrated that subgroup II variants had established in open‑field tomato with conspicuous disease and yield reduction. The discovery prompted recommendations for improved seed and seedling health management, stronger aphid control and attention to CMV subgroup structure when breeding and screening for resistance in Indian tomato and other solanaceous crops.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of tomato cultivation in southern India, often with limited vector control and proximity to other CMV hosts, facilitated introduction and establishment of subgroup II CMV in tomato fields. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence at the country/host level is central, as this outbreak represents the first documented occurrence of CMV subgroup II infecting tomato in India, indicating either recent introduction of subgroup II strains or successful host shift of existing subgroup II variants; this change in subgroup composition constitutes a re-emergence of CMV disease in a known host and subregion driven by viral diversification with potential implications for symptom severity and resistance specificity.
Review: review – Retained as an important re-emergence event representing the first report of CMV subgroup II infecting tomato in India, with field incidence greater than 70% in surveyed sites. The event’s source URL has been corrected to the Plant Disease note by Sudhakar et al. (2006, PD‑90‑1457B), which directly documents this outbreak; the previously cited CSIRO Plant Disease Notes PDF (DN08013) actually describes CMV subgroup IB on periwinkle and only references the tomato report secondarily. Geographic assignment (Southern Asia, India) and classification as re-emergence driven by a shift in CMV subgroup composition in tomato are appropriate, although quantitative yield‑loss estimates remain limited and could be refined if more data emerge.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Capsicum annuum (pepper); Solanum lycopersicum (tomato); Citrullus lanatus (watermelon)
Event summary: In the mid‑ to late 2010s, surveys of vegetable fields at multiple locations in Nigeria found cucumber mosaic virus infecting pepper, tomato and watermelon with typical mosaic, leaf deformation and stunting symptoms that farmers associated with yield reductions in smallholder and commercial systems. Molecular analyses of isolates from these outbreaks showed that Nigerian CMV populations belonged to subgroup IB but were unusually diverse and included at least one recombinant RNA1 segment, indicating ongoing in situ evolution of CMV in Nigerian agroecosystems. As awareness of this diversity increased, recommendations emphasised integrated management—removal of infected plants and weed reservoirs, seed health measures and aphid control—to limit further spread of divergent and recombinant CMV strains in West African vegetable value chains.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of vegetable production, frequent movement of infected planting material, high densities of alternative weed hosts and abundant aphid vectors in tropical agroecosystems favoured repeated CMV infection, mixed infections and long‑term virus persistence in Nigeria. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via recombination and accumulation of genetic diversity within subgroup IB was documented, with one Nigerian isolate identified as a putative recombinant and population‑genetic analyses indicating high diversity and predominance of purifying selection; these processes underlie CMV re-emergence in the same subregion with altered strain composition and potentially modified host‑range and pathogenicity profiles.
Review: review – Kept as a re-emergence event highlighting the discovery of genetically diverse subgroup IB CMV populations and a putative recombinant isolate infecting pepper, tomato and watermelon in Nigeria, representing the first detailed molecular description of such populations from West Africa. However, the underlying study is primarily a genetic survey of 106 samples collected from 16 locations, and while symptomatic plants and potential yield impacts are described qualitatively, quantitative estimates of national‑scale production losses are lacking, so its rank among the very largest CMV emergence events is somewhat uncertain. The event years (2015–2019) and Nigeria [2015] start year are approximate, reflecting the likely sampling period and prior Nigerian CMV reports rather than explicit dates in the paper. Human review is advised to confirm whether this episode should be retained among the top‑impact events or reframed as a key evolutionary/virological milestone for CMV in West Africa.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Capsicum annuum (commercial pepper cultivars carrying cmr1 resistance)
Event summary: In 2019–2020, growers in Antalya province, Türkiye, reported alarming CMV‑like symptoms on commercial pepper cultivars that carried the cmr1 allele conferring resistance to CMV pathotype P0, indicating breakdown of previously effective resistance. Field and greenhouse inoculation tests followed by complete genome sequencing confirmed that these plants were infected by a resistance‑breaking CMV‑P1 strain (rbCMV) capable of overcoming cmr1, and all tested resistant cultivars became systemically infected under experimental conditions. After this finding, local recommendations stressed the urgent need to deploy new resistance sources effective against CMV‑P1, alongside improved aphid management and sanitation, to restore control of CMV in Turkish pepper production.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive cultivation of cmr1‑based resistant pepper varieties in Antalya created strong, long‑term selection favouring CMV variants able to evade this single dominant resistance gene, while high aphid populations and intensive protected and open‑field pepper production enabled rapid spread once resistance‑breaking strains arose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity are clearly involved, as sequence comparisons showed SNP patterns characteristic of CMV‑P1 resistance‑breaking strains and all cmr1 cultivars tested developed systemic infection; this is a straightforward re-emergence event in which viral evolution overcame a major resistance gene rather than a geographic range expansion.
Review: retain – This event accurately describes the first report of CMV‑P1 resistance‑breaking strains infecting cmr1‑based resistant pepper cultivars in Antalya, Türkiye, during 2019–2020, as documented by Fidan et al. (2023). The geographic assignment (Western Asia, Türkiye), host specification (cmr1‑carrying Capsicum annuum cultivars) and classification as re-emergence driven by resistance‑breaking evolution in an already CMV‑endemic region are appropriate, and the Journal of Phytopathology article cited provides a suitable primary source. No changes to timing, geographic scope or emergence‑type classification are recommended, and this row can be retained as one of the major recent CMV resistance‑breaking episodes in pepper.

Host: A wide range of crops (e.g. potato, eggplant and other vegetables), pasture plants, fruit‑garden species and native flora in disturbed habitats
Event summary: Cuscuta campestris was first recorded in Japan in the 1970s at Fuchu, Tokyo, but by the 1990s–2000s the national invasive species database reported it from almost the entire country, parasitizing crops, ornamentals and native plants. During this period, the species transitioned from a localized alien to a widespread agricultural and environmental weed, prompting its inclusion in Japanese alien species reference works and attention under invasive species regulations. The expansion stabilised as a naturalised but problematic weed across much of lowland Japan, with management focused on on‑farm hygiene and local removal rather than eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Repeated accidental introductions in contaminated imported crop and afforestation seeds, combined with extensive agriculture and horticulture and a lack of early detection and rapid response, allowed C. campestris to spread from initial sites near Tokyo to much of Japan. Internal mechanisms: Highly persistent seed capable of surviving for many years in soil and the ability to parasitize many common crop and weed hosts facilitated its transition from localized introduction to widespread re‑occurrence and entrenched naturalization.
Review: retain – Evidence from the NIES invasive species database confirms first Japanese records of C. campestris in the 1970s at Fuchu (Tokyo) and near‑countrywide distribution by the 1990s–2000s; treating 1990–2010 as a re‑occurrence/intensification episode within Eastern Asia rather than first detection or (intra-/inter-)continental emergence is consistent with the definitions.

Countries: India [1990s; severe, widespread infestations documented in 2000s–2020s]
Host: Rainfed and irrigated pulses (lentil, chickpea, greengram, blackgram), oilseeds (niger/Guizotia abyssinica, linseed), chillies and other vegetables, and forage legumes (lucerne, Egyptian clover)
Event summary: From at least the 1990s, field dodder became one of the most serious parasitic weeds in pulses, oilseeds and fodder crops in parts of India, with weed‑science reports noting its spread across several central and eastern states. By the 2000s, experiments and reviews documented widespread infestations in crops such as lentil, chickpea, niger and linseed, with yield losses in heavily infested fields frequently estimated in the tens of percent and, for some hosts, up to around 80% in research trials. Through the 2010s–2020s, C. campestris has remained a chronic constraint on production in affected regions, with management relying on clean seed, crop rotation, tolerant varieties and pre‑emergence herbicides rather than any prospect of eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of pulse and oilseed cultivation under rainfed and irrigated systems, widespread use of farm‑saved and locally traded seed contaminated with dodder seed, and movement of infested hay and machinery facilitated the build‑up and regional spread of C. campestris. Internal mechanisms: Very small, hard seeds that survive for years in soil, plus an exceptionally broad host range on annual crops and weeds, underpin persistent re‑occurrence without clear evidence of novel biotypes or resistance evolution in this period.
Review: review – Newly added high‑impact event. Indian weed‑science reviews and field experiments document C. campestris as a major parasitic weed of pulses, oilseeds (especially niger and linseed), chillies and forage legumes across multiple states, with very large yield losses in susceptible crops after 1990; event years and subnational spread are approximated and should be refined against national floras and survey data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Australia [widely naturalised and impacting crops and pastures by 1990s; intensive management ongoing 1990s–2020s]
Host: Lucerne (alfalfa) seed and hay crops, other pasture legumes and fodder species, vegetables and horticultural crops, and broadleaf weeds and native plants along rivers, wetlands and pastures
Event summary: Although dodder was first reported damaging lucerne crops in south‑eastern Australia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, golden dodder (C. campestris) became much more widespread and problematic from the 1980s onwards, particularly in irrigated lucerne, pastures and some horticultural crops in New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and parts of Western Australia. Through the 1990s–2010s, state weed profiles and impact assessments described it as the weediest dodder species in Australia, causing substantial yield losses, seed‑lot contamination and quarantine of infested paddocks, and also threatening native vegetation along rivers and in inland wetlands. By the 2010s–2020s, golden dodder was regulated as a declared or noxious plant in several states, with dedicated biosecurity codes of practice, DNA tests for seed‑lot contamination and ongoing regional eradication or progressive‑containment programmes in key lucerne‑seed and irrigated districts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance spread has been driven mainly by contaminated lucerne and pasture seed, movement of infested fodder and machinery, and riverine dispersal along the Murray and other waterways; intensification of irrigated lucerne and pasture systems increased the area of suitable habitat, while strict export‑seed standards have made detection and reporting more systematic. Internal mechanisms: Extremely high seed production, long‑lived seed banks (often persisting for decades), and efficient parasitism of lucerne and other broadleaf hosts allow local populations to rebound after control efforts, supporting persistent re‑occurrence rather than discrete, self‑limiting outbreaks.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the long‑recognised but post‑1980s intensifying impact of golden dodder in Australian lucerne, pastures and some horticultural crops. National and state weed profiles and industry documents show that by the 1990s–2010s C. campestris was widespread in eastern and south‑eastern Australia, causing serious yield loss, seed‑lot rejections and environmental impacts; the 1990–2025 window therefore reasonably represents a prolonged re‑occurrence/intensification episode, though finer temporal resolution could be added from regional datasets.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Oilseed crops (especially noug/Guizotia abyssinica), lentil (Lens culinaris), linseed (Linum usitatissimum), various vegetables and coffee
Event summary: From the early 1990s, Ethiopian weed scientists began reporting Cuscuta campestris as a serious parasitic weed in noug and other oilseed and pulse crops, with national conferences in 1993 documenting its distribution and importance. Over subsequent decades the species spread within major noug‑ and lentil‑growing areas, with farmer surveys indicating typical lentil yield losses of about 14–29% in heavily infested fields and widespread damage also in noug and linseed. By the 2010s–2020s, C. campestris was regarded as one of the most important parasitic weeds in Ethiopia, entrenched across multiple crops and regions despite ongoing research and field trials on cultural and mechanical control methods.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of noug and lentil cultivation, movement of contaminated seed lots (particularly noug seed), dispersal by floodwaters (e.g. Awash River) and farm machinery, and limited access to clean seed systems facilitated rapid local spread and reinfestation. Internal mechanisms: Very high seed production and a long‑lived seed bank, combined with its broad host range on many dicot crops and weeds, underpin persistent re‑occurrence without requiring documented genetic change.
Review: retain – Ethiopian sources consistently describe C. campestris as one of the key parasitic weeds of noug, lentil and linseed with substantial yield losses and progressive spread since at least the early 1990s; classifying this as a long‑running re‑occurrence/intensification episode in Eastern Africa driven by contaminated seed and cropping changes, without clear evidence of novel strains or resistance, is in line with the emergence‑type definitions.

Countries: Kenya [~2000], United Republic of Tanzania [~2000], Uganda [~2005]
Host: Diverse native shrubs and trees, pasture and grassland species, crops including legumes and other dicots, and invasive weeds
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, field dodder was reported as invasive in parts of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, with CABI and regional factsheets describing it as a serious holoparasitic weed in Eastern Africa. Over the next two decades, ecological and phylogeographic studies documented Cuscuta campestris among the Cuscuta species rapidly spreading in Kenyan and neighbouring ecosystems, parasitizing crops, native plants and other invasive weeds and threatening biodiversity and agricultural production. By the late 2010s, regional reviews highlighted dodders as an emergent threat to Eastern African farmlands and natural vegetation, prompting calls for improved surveillance, taxonomy and integrated management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Land‑use change, habitat disturbance, intensification of agriculture, and increased movement of contaminated crop and pasture seed across Eastern Africa facilitated wider establishment; lack of awareness and limited control options allowed infestations to build up in both cropland and natural habitats. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range, rapid vegetative spread along host canopies, and prolific, persistent seed production promote geographic range expansion and make local eradication extremely difficult, but no specific novel strain or resistance evolution has yet been documented in this region.
Review: review – CABI/EAfrinet and regional ecological work confirm that C. campestris is invasive in parts of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda and poses a growing threat to farmlands and native vegetation, but specific first‑detection years by country are poorly documented; the 2000–2020 window and approximate country start dates are therefore provisional and should be cross‑checked against national floras, herbarium records and additional agronomic literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Forage and pasture legumes (e.g. Medicago, Trifolium) and associated weeds on arable and pasture land
Event summary: A floristic survey on Limnos (NE Aegean, Greece) around the late 2000s reported Cuscuta campestris as a new alien invasive taxon for the island, among species affecting the local agricultural economy. Subsequent EPPO reporting in 2012 treated C. campestris as invasive in parts of Greece, consistent with establishment and spread from initial foci on Limnos and other sites into forage crops and disturbed land. The outbreak on Limnos has persisted as an agricultural weed problem, contributing to the broader recognition of C. campestris as an invasive alien plant within Southern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction to Limnos likely occurred via contaminated forage or pasture seed, with local agricultural disturbance and movement of machinery assisting spread along field margins and pastures. Internal mechanisms: Pre‑adaptation to Mediterranean climates and efficient parasitism of common pasture legumes enabled rapid establishment once introduced; however, there is no evidence that this population represents a genetically distinct or more virulent strain relative to other European populations.
Review: review – Retain the Limnos island outbreak as a meaningful European agricultural event, supported by floristic records and EPPO listing C. campestris as invasive in Greece, but correct the emergence‑type coding: because the species was already present elsewhere in Southern Europe before 2008, spread to Limnos represents re‑occurrence within the same UNSD sub‑region rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to “No” and re_occurrence to “Yes”.

Host: Vegetable crops including potato and other market‑garden species, together with numerous wild dicot hosts in field margins, forest edges and along streams
Event summary: In 2010, Cuscuta campestris was observed for the first time in north‑west Tunisia (Mogods region), adding a new non‑chlorophyllous holoparasite to the country’s flora and to the North African weed flora. By the mid‑2010s, the species was recognised as an invasive alien with the potential to severely damage cultivated crops in affected areas and to spread further within Northern Africa if not contained.

Internal mechanisms: The same traits seen elsewhere—holoparasitic growth on many hosts, dense mats that smother vegetation and a persistent seed bank—allow rapid build‑up once established, so that even relatively small initial incursions can quickly become agronomically significant.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first confirmed records of C. campestris in Tunisia in 2010 and subsequent severe infestations of vegetable and potato fields and nearby wild vegetation by 2013, as documented by El Mokni et al. Countries: New Zealand [1941 naturalised; targeted wetland outbreaks recognised 2010s–2020s]

Review: retain – DOC, the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network and the Official Pest Register agree that C. campestris has been naturalised since the 1940s but only recognised as a high‑risk environmental and pasture weed in restricted Waikato wetlands from the 2010s onwards, with Unwanted Organism status granted in 2022; treating 2010–2025 as a re‑occurrence/intensification episode within the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region is therefore appropriate.

Countries: Chile [late 1990s, Aysén Region – Chile Chico area]; Argentina [pre‑existing populations in Neuquén and Río Negro as likely sources]

Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – existing life-history traits and tolerance of cooler temperate conditions allowed codling moth to colonize these more southern, ocean-influenced climates when fruit hosts became available; no special new genetic strain is indicated beyond normal dispersal.

This represents a major southward range expansion within an already affected UNSD subregion (South America), so the correct event type is re-occurrence driven by geographic range expansion and human movement of infested material, not intra-continental emergence (which is reserved for the first entry into a new UNSD subregion). Countries: United States of America [1991]; Canada [early 1990s, British Columbia]
Host: Apple and pear orchards in western United States (Washington, Oregon, California, Utah) and adjacent Canadian pome-fruit regions (British Columbia)
Event summary: In the early 1990s, monitoring in apple and pear orchards in western U.S. states showed that codling moth populations had evolved substantial resistance to the organophosphate insecticide azinphos-methyl after decades of intensive use, causing control failures and high fruit damage. Through the 1990s, resistance levels in some Washington and Utah orchards were strongly associated with prior insecticide selection pressure, and cross-resistance to several other insecticide classes was observed, leading to widespread concern and economic losses. By the late 1990s, this crisis drove large-scale adoption of pheromone-based mating disruption and integrated pest management programs across Washington, Oregon, California and neighboring British Columbia, which gradually reduced reliance on high-rate organophosphate sprays and restored better control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged, intensive use of organophosphate insecticides (especially azinphos-methyl) and other broad-spectrum chemistries in western North American orchards, combined with relatively limited early resistance-management practices, created strong selection pressure; tightening regulatory scrutiny of organophosphates also constrained options. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – codling moth populations evolved resistance to azinphos-methyl with documented resistance ratios in multiple orchards, and cross-resistance to carbamates, chlorinated hydrocarbons and pyrethroids; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – not relevant; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – not primary here; this event reflects mainly resistance evolution and consequent resurgence in damage.
Review: review – Field surveys in Washington and Utah during 1991–1992 documented significant azinphos-methyl resistance in many codling moth populations, and subsequent work linked this to long-term organophosphate use and helped trigger large-scale adoption of mating disruption and IPM in western North America. The event description, geography (USA plus adjacent British Columbia) and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in a long-infested region) are appropriate. A key peer‑reviewed source (Knight et al. 1994, J Econ Entomol, doi:10.1093/jee/87.2.285) has been added to strengthen the evidence base; otherwise no structural corrections are needed and the event should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 episodes.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jee/article-pdf/87/2/285/19237572/jee87-0285.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Countries: China [initial focus in Xinjiang; rapid spread during the 1990s–2010s to >131 counties in at least seven northwestern and north-central apple‑growing provinces]
Host: Commercial apple and pear orchards in northwestern and north-central China, initially concentrated in Xinjiang and later expanding into additional apple-producing provinces.
Event summary: Codling moth was first detected in Xinjiang, China in the 1950s, but for several decades it remained largely confined to that region. Beginning in the 1990s, expansion of commercial apple orchards and improved transportation allowed the pest to spread rapidly eastward across northwestern China; by the 2010s it had been reported in over 131 counties in seven provinces and was causing 20–30% damage in some pome‑fruit orchards. As populations established in these new apple‑growing regions, growers adopted intensive chemical and CpGV-based control, and Chinese researchers initiated detailed invasion‑risk mapping and resistance‑surveillance studies to anticipate further spread into other major apple-producing zones.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28973489/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale expansion and intensification of apple production in northwestern and north-central China, along with construction of modern road and rail networks that increased movement of infested fruit and packing materials, facilitated long-distance jumps from Xinjiang into new provinces. Climate-suitability analyses indicate that many of these regions offer favourable thermal and moisture regimes once the pest is introduced, and quarantine and sanitation measures were initially limited. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ high dispersal capacity, facultative diapause and tolerance of continental climates enabled successful colonisation of new Chinese production areas; emerging reductions in susceptibility to some organophosphates and carbamates have been reported but, so far, at modest levels compared with long‑standing resistance foci elsewhere.
Review: retain – This new event fills a critical omission: post‑1990 invasion and spread of codling moth across northwestern China, now a major apple-producing region. Multiple studies document that the pest, originally confined to Xinjiang, has since the 1990s spread to at least seven provinces and more than 100 counties, with substantial yield losses, and that Chinese programmes now monitor its distribution and insecticide susceptibility. The episode clearly ranks among the most impactful recent emergence events for codling moth and is correctly coded as re-occurrence (range expansion within an already affected UNSD subregion, driven mainly by external factors such as orchard expansion and transport).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28973489/?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern America; South America
Countries: Germany; France; Switzerland; Italy; Austria; Netherlands (Kingdom of the); Czechia; United States of America; Canada; Chile; Argentina
Host: Commercial apple, pear and walnut orchards worldwide, with codling moth targeted by chemical insecticides and CpGV biopesticides.
Event summary: From about 2000 through 2020, codling moth populations in major pome‑ and walnut‑producing regions of Europe, North America and South America progressively accumulated resistance to a broad suite of control agents, including organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids, neonicotinoids, insect growth regulators, diamides, spinosyns, avermectins, juvenile hormone mimics and CpGVs, leading to recurrent outbreaks and control failures in some intensive production areas. As resistance monitoring expanded, numerous cases of multi-class resistance and CpGV resistance were documented in European, North American and South American orchards, often after years of reliance on a narrow set of chemistries or biocontrol products. Over this period, regional and international management strategies shifted toward more diversified mode-of-action rotations, mating disruption, improved monitoring, and use of multiple CpGV genotypes, stabilizing codling moth control in many regions but leaving some high-pressure areas with chronic resistance challenges.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of pome-fruit and walnut production, long-term reliance on relatively few insecticide classes and single CpGV isolates, economic and regulatory pressures that concentrated use on particular chemistries, and expansion of organic production with heavy CpGV dependence all created strong and widespread selection pressure; climate warming in some regions may also have allowed more generations per season, amplifying selection. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – diverse resistance mechanisms across codling moth populations worldwide, including enhanced detoxification, target-site mutations, and multiple independent CpGV resistance types (I–III); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – repeated evolution of resistant genotypes in different regions and hosts; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – more relevant to the CpGV viruses, which were selected for higher virulence against resistant hosts; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – secondary but present as codling moth continued to colonize new orchards and marginal climate niches, often facilitated by human movement of infested fruit and plant material.
Review: review – This row intentionally aggregates a long, multi-country episode of escalating multi-class insecticide and CpGV resistance across Europe, North America and South America, which is well documented in global reviews and regional studies and clearly represents one of the highest-impact codling moth emergence patterns since 2000. The classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence of an established pest) is appropriate. However, the countries listed are not exhaustive, and resistance has also been reported from additional regions (e.g. parts of Asia and Oceania); for now the row is retained as a high-level summary for major Western Hemisphere and European production areas, but a human reviewer may wish either to split it into more regional episodes or expand the country list if finer resolution is required.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048357521001565?utm_source=openai))
