Host: Organic and integrated apple orchards (and other pome fruits) heavily reliant on CpGV-based biopesticides in southwest Germany and southeast France.
Event summary: Around 2003, an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany reported serious codling moth damage despite repeated applications of commercial Cydia pomonella granulovirus (CpGV) formulations based on the Mexican isolate CpGV‑M, and similar failures were soon observed in France. Laboratory bioassays on larvae collected in 2003–2005 confirmed an at least 1000‑ to >60,000‑fold reduction in susceptibility to CpGV‑M compared with susceptible strains, marking the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus product. Over 2003–2006, resistant field populations were reared and characterized (e.g. CpR/CpRR1 in Germany and RGV in France), and genetic studies showed that this "type I" resistance was dominant and largely linked to the Z sex chromosome, explaining its rapid rise and severe control failures in affected organic orchards.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Nearly two decades of intensive CpGV‑M use in European organic and low‑input orchards, often as the cornerstone control tactic, created strong selection pressure; high codling moth pressure in some orchards and limited rotation with alternative effective modes of action compounded this pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of high-level resistance to CpGV‑M, with 1,000–100,000‑fold resistance factors; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – not applicable to the pest, though resistance forced selection and deployment of more virulent CpGV genotypes; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – emergence of resistant codling moth genotypes carrying a Z‑linked, dominantly inherited resistance trait (type I CpGV resistance) that sharply reduced mortality from CpGV‑M.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus (CpGV-M), originating in an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany around 2003 and shortly thereafter in France, with extremely high resistance ratios and clear evidence of dominant, Z-linked inheritance. The geographic scope, timing and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in previously well-controlled orchards) are well supported by primary literature and need no correction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630735/?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America [early 2000s, Michigan]; (similar resistance issues also reported earlier and contemporaneously in western U.S. orchards)
Host: Apple orchards in Michigan (and other U.S. pome-fruit regions), where codling moth was controlled with a range of insecticides with different modes of action.
Event summary: In the early 2000s, codling moth populations from Michigan apple orchards were tested and found to exhibit significant resistance to multiple commonly used insecticides, including organophosphates (azinphos-methyl and phosmet), pyrethroids (lambda-cyhalothrin) and certain insect growth regulators and oxadiazines, while showing little or no resistance to some newer chemistries. These findings followed decades of heavy insecticide reliance and mounting regulatory pressure on older organophosphates, and some orchards experienced reduced control and increased codling moth injury. Over the subsequent years, these resistance data prompted adjustments in spray programs, greater emphasis on rotation among modes of action, and gradual integration of non-chemical tactics to restore codling moth management efficacy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term, repeated use of organophosphates and other broad-spectrum insecticides in Midwestern apple orchards, limited rotation among active ingredient classes, and regulatory constraints on key insecticides all intensified selection pressure; economic incentives for cosmetically perfect fruit encouraged frequent treatments. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – laboratory bioassays demonstrated 2‑ to 16‑fold resistance factors to several compounds (organophosphates, pyrethroids, and insect growth regulators) in some Michigan codling moth populations; no clear evidence of major fitness costs, supporting persistence; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – selection of resistant genotypes within local codling moth populations with modified target sites and/or elevated detoxification metabolism.
Review: retain – The Michigan event is well grounded in a detailed resistance study showing broad-spectrum resistance (up to 16‑fold) to multiple insecticide classes and associated field performance issues, and it illustrates an important North American focus of multi-class resistance outside the Pacific Northwest. The geographic scope, timing (early 2000s) and classification as re-emergence are appropriate, and the cited Pest Management Science paper plus the global resistance review provide strong support; no structural changes were necessary.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18383486/?utm_source=openai))

Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Germany [mid‑2000s]; France [mid‑2000s]; Switzerland [mid‑2000s]; Italy [mid‑late 2000s]; Austria [mid‑late 2000s]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [late 2000s]; Czechia [late 2000s–early 2010s]
Host: Primarily organic and some integrated apple orchards (plus other pome fruits) across multiple European apple‑growing regions relying heavily on CpGV.
Event summary: Following the first confirmed CpGV resistance in Germany and France in 2003–2005, similar codling moth populations with drastically reduced susceptibility to CpGV‑M were detected from the mid‑2000s onward in numerous orchards across Western and Central Europe. By the early 2010s, resistance had been documented in at least 38–40 apple plantations in Germany, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria, the Netherlands and Czechia, with some populations 1,000–100,000 times less susceptible to CpGV‑M than typical susceptible larvae and causing severe fruit damage in organic orchards. During roughly 2004–2015, resistance monitoring programs and virulence management strategies were developed, and new CpGV isolates and mixtures with different genome backgrounds (e.g. I12, NPP‑R1, CpGV‑R5 and others) were identified and registered to overcome resistance, allowing damage in many resistant orchards to be brought back under economic control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued, widespread reliance on CpGV‑M‑based products as the primary control in organic pome‑fruit systems, often with limited rotation between CpGV genotypes; regional coordination gaps that allowed resistant populations to spread between orchards; increasing market demand for organic fruit, expanding CpGV use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – spread and diversification of CpGV‑resistant codling moth populations, with type I resistance common and later additional resistance profiles; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – not central here, but resistance allowed higher survival through virus-sprayed canopies, effectively enhancing pest population persistence; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – selection of multiple resistant codling moth lineages across Europe, as well as selection and deployment of new CpGV genotypes (genome groups B–G) that partially or fully overcame the resistance.
Review: review – This row summarizes the broader European spread of CpGV-M resistance beyond the original German and French orchards, which is well supported by surveys documenting roughly 38–40 resistant plantations across at least seven countries by the early 2010s. The event is appropriately classified as re-emergence and linked to intensive CpGV-M use. The start year has been adjusted to 2004 (2004–2015) to align better with the timing of confirmed resistant populations across multiple countries, and the country-specific timing has been slightly generalized ("mid‑2000s" etc.) to avoid implying more precise onset years than the monitoring data support. An additional Europe-wide survey reference has been added for distribution details; a human reviewer may further refine the within-country start years if needed.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122439/records/64747290bf943c8c79829564?utm_source=openai))

Countries: Germany [North Rhine‑Westphalia, population NRW‑WE, first detected mid‑2010s]
Host: Apple orchards in western Germany (North Rhine‑Westphalia) where CpGV products had been used intensively for codling moth control.
Event summary: After the spread of type I CpGV resistance in Europe, a codling moth population from an apple orchard in North Rhine‑Westphalia, Germany (designated NRW‑WE), was identified around the early–mid 2010s that displayed a qualitatively different resistance pattern: larvae were highly resistant not only to CpGV‑M (genome group A) but also to multiple other CpGV genome groups (C–E), with no clear Z‑linked inheritance. Through 2010–2017, laboratory selection and crossing experiments defined this as "type II" CpGV resistance, characterized by strong cross‑resistance across CpGV genotypes and a more complex, likely autosomal mode of inheritance. This new resistance type posed a major challenge to resistance management because some of the previously resistance‑breaking CpGV isolates were no longer fully effective.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged and repeated application of CpGV products, including resistance‑breaking isolates, in some German orchards with sustained codling moth pressure; limited refuges of susceptible moths; possible regional movement of already partially resistant populations. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – emergence of a novel "type II" CpGV resistance in codling moth, conferring broad cross‑resistance to multiple CpGV genome groups beyond CpGV‑M; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – evolution of genetically distinct resistant codling moth lineages (e.g. NRW‑WE, and derived CpR5M and CpR5S strains) with non‑Z‑linked, probably autosomal dominant resistance mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – resistance allowed larvae to survive in virus‑treated orchards, effectively enhancing population persistence and spread under CpGV selection.
Review: retain – The description of type II CpGV resistance in the NRW‑WE population in western Germany matches the primary literature on this resistance form, including its broad cross‑resistance to multiple CpGV genome groups and autosomal inheritance. The event is correctly localized (North Rhine‑Westphalia) and classified as re-emergence driven by a new resistance mechanism in a long-infested region, with no intra- or inter-continental spread claimed. No corrections beyond minor wording (capitalisation of North Rhine‑Westphalia) were needed.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203626/?utm_source=openai))

Countries: Germany [northeastern Germany, population SA‑GO, first detected mid‑2010s]
Host: Apple orchards in northeastern Germany (SA‑GO population) relying on CpGV products for codling moth control.
Event summary: In the 2010s, another German codling moth field population from northeastern Germany (termed SA‑GO) was found to have yet another distinct pattern of CpGV resistance, with differential responses to CpGV isolates from several genome groups and a complex inheritance involving both autosomal and Z‑linked components. Laboratory studies showed that this "type III" resistance differed from previously described type I and type II resistance in its genetic control and spectrum of cross‑resistance, complicating the choice of effective CpGV genotypes for control. Over several years, this population served as a model to understand multi‑locus virus resistance in codling moth and to refine virulence‑management strategies in affected orchards, while additional CpGV mixtures were developed to maintain control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued intensive CpGV use in some orchards despite existing resistance issues, leading to further selection; local management practices that may have favored successive selection for more complex resistance patterns; limited influx of fully susceptible moths. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – emergence of "type III" CpGV resistance in SA‑GO codling moth population, combining resistance to CpGV isolates from genome types A and E and other groups; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – evolution of a distinct resistance genotype with mixed Z‑linked and autosomal inheritance and broad cross‑resistance; this represents further adaptive diversification of codling moth under prolonged baculovirus selection; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – not central, as this is primarily a resistance‑driven resurgence.
Review: retain – The SA‑GO population event accurately captures the discovery and characterization of type III CpGV resistance in northeastern Germany, including its mixed autosomal and sex-linked inheritance and complex cross-resistance profile. The geographic attribution (Germany only) and classification as re-emergence driven by a novel resistance genotype are appropriate, and the cited Journal of Virology articles provide strong support; no corrections were required.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5561285/?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America [Washington State, WA3 population from organic apple orchards – CpGV resistance confirmed in bioassays published 2022]
Host: Organic apple orchards in Washington State, USA, where codling moth had been controlled for many years using CpGV-M–based products (primarily Cyd‑X).
Event summary: During the 2010s, some organic apple orchards in Washington State experienced increasing codling moth damage despite regular applications of CpGV-M–based products such as Cyd‑X. To investigate possible resistance, five codling moth colonies (WA1–WA5) collected from these orchards were screened at a discriminating concentration of CpGV-M; colony WA3 showed markedly reduced susceptibility, with survivors able to reproduce. Subsequent tests demonstrated that WA3 was resistant not only to CpGV‑M but also to all commercial CpGV products then registered in the USA, making it the first confirmed case of CpGV resistance in North America and prompting evaluation of new CpGV isolates that remained effective against this population.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35735870/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Many Washington organic orchards had relied for years on a single CpGV-M formulation as a primary codling moth control tactic, with limited rotation among CpGV isolates or non-viral modes of action, under high codling moth pressure and with few alternative tools compatible with organic certification. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of a codling moth population (WA3) with substantially reduced mortality at discriminating CpGV-M doses and cross-resistance to multiple CpGV products; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – selection of resistant genotypes in Washington that likely share some features with previously described European CpGV resistance types, although the detailed genetic basis is still under investigation.
Review: retain – This new row captures a major omitted event: the first documented CpGV resistance case in the USA (WA3 population from Washington State), confirmed by discriminating-dose bioassays and published in 2022. The episode is clearly important for global CpGV use because it shows that resistance is not restricted to European codling moth populations. The geography, host system and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in a long-infested region) are appropriate; the start year is approximate, reflecting a build-up of unexplained control failures during the 2010s culminating in the 2022 publication, and could be refined if more precise field-detection dates become available.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35735870/?utm_source=openai))

EPP common name: chufa flatsedge, chufa, yellow nutgrass, yellow nutsedge
Host: Arable crops (especially maize, potatoes, vegetables, forage and roughage crops) on sandy and irrigated soils in the Netherlands and Flanders (Belgium)
Event summary: In 1975, yellow nutsedge was first recorded as an alien plant in the Netherlands, probably introduced with imported gladiolus corms from North America, and by the early 1980s it had begun to spread explosively in maize fields on light, sandy soils in the eastern and southern parts of the country; similar introductions with contaminated planting material led to the first record in Flanders (Belgium) around 1985. Through the 1980s–2000s, repeated planting of gladiolus and other root and tuber crops on new land, together with movement of contaminated soil and farm machinery, allowed Cyperus esculentus to colonize an increasing share of arable land in both the Netherlands and northern Belgium, and by the 2010s at least tens of thousands of hectares (roughly 5–15% of Flemish cropland) were infested, prompting its designation as a quarantine or noxious weed with mandatory reporting and strict restrictions on cropping infested parcels. By the early–mid 2020s, yellow nutsedge remained entrenched across much of Flanders and parts of the Netherlands despite intensive mechanical and chemical control, leading to long-term government- and university-led integrated management projects aimed at reducing tuber banks and preventing further spread rather than achieving full eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental introduction via contaminated gladiolus planting material imported from North America; annual movement of gladiolus and other bulb crops to new fields, which redistributed tubers across the landscape; intensive maize, potato, vegetable and forage production on sandy soils with frequent cultivation and soil movement; dispersal of tubers and infested soil on machinery, harvesters and processing residues; and later policy changes that replaced quarantine reporting with compulsory control and cross-compliance obligations (including bans on root, tuber and bulb crops on infested parcels), reflecting the scale of agronomic impact. Internal mechanisms: very high vegetative reproduction via rhizomes and durable stem tubers (up to hundreds–thousands of tubers per plant), long tuber survival in soil, tolerance of the cool temperate climate of northwestern Europe, and the ability to persist and reproduce under repeated tillage and partial herbicide control, all of which favor rapid patch expansion and make eradication from infested fields extremely difficult once established.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to represent the major intra-continental emergence and subsequent large-scale invasion of Cyperus esculentus in the Western Europe sub-region (Netherlands and Belgium/Flanders). Multiple floristic and extension sources document first alien records in the Netherlands in 1975 with rapid spread in maize fields by the early 1980s, followed by introduction into Flanders around 1985 and current estimates of at least 15,000–25,000+ ha of infested cropland plus legal bans on root, tuber and bulb crops on contaminated fields and mandatory control measures. This episode clearly ranks among the most impactful modern emergence events for this species in terms of area affected, production risk and regulatory response. It is coded as intra-continental emergence (first establishment in UN Western Europe as a weed) rather than re-emergence, because there is no evidence that a novel resistant or otherwise distinct biotype is driving this invasion. A human reviewer should confirm the precise start/end years used, the choice to treat the Netherlands and Belgium as a single linked episode, and whether other Central European hotspots (e.g. parts of Germany or Austria) should be rolled into this row or described separately.

EPP common name: chufa flatsedge, chufa, yellow nutgrass, yellow nutsedge
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and soybean (Glycine max) in rice–soybean production systems in Arkansas
Event summary: In the early 2010s, rice growers in eastern Arkansas began reporting yellow nutsedge plants surviving field-rate applications of the ALS-inhibiting herbicide halosulfuron in rice–soybean rotations, with widespread control failures first noted in 2012 and raising suspicion of a resistant biotype. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long-term, intensive use of ALS-inhibiting herbicides in Arkansas rice and soybean systems with limited diversification of herbicide modes of action; widespread adoption of ALS-based programs in imidazolinone-resistant rice; continuous or frequent rice–soybean rotations providing repeated selection pressure on nutsedge populations; and management practices that allowed surviving plants to set tubers and replenish the propagule bank. Internal mechanisms: a target-site mutation in the ALS enzyme (Trp574-Leu) conferring very high resistance and cross-resistance to multiple ALS-inhibitor families, combined with clonal tuber-based reproduction that stabilizes and spreads the resistant genotype once selected, and reduced translocation and efficacy of glyphosate on the resistant biotype, further complicating chemical control.

The event year is updated to 2012–2025 and the country label to "United States of America – Arkansas [2012–2025]" to align with reports of halosulfuron failures in 2012 and the herbicide-resistance database listing 2013 as the first year of confirmed resistance, with persistence thereafter. The emergence type remains re_emergence, reflecting evolution of an ALS target-site mutation and cross-resistance within an already long-established weed species. Key primary sources on first confirmation and mechanism (Pest Management Science 2014 article and USDA-ARS summary) have been added alongside existing Weed Science papers and the herbicide-resistance database entry, which are more appropriate than relying only on later glyphosate-efficacy studies. EPP common name: chufa flatsedge, chufa, yellow nutgrass, yellow nutsedge

Event summary: Between roughly 2015 and 2018, a peanut grower in Webster County, Georgia, repeatedly used the ALS-inhibiting herbicide imazapic in the same field for four consecutive peanut seasons and eventually reported a sharp decline in yellow nutsedge control, suggesting evolution of resistance. Mechanism or driver: Drivers: atypical continuous peanut monoculture over four consecutive seasons in Webster County, Georgia, with repeated use of imazapic as the primary postemergence nutsedge control; limited rotation of herbicide sites of action across the broader production system; and persistent, high yellow nutsedge pressure that ensured survival and reproduction of partially controlled plants. Internal mechanisms: evolution of an Ala-205-Val mutation in the ALS gene that confers resistance to imazapic, along with phenotypic traits of resistant biotypes such as somewhat delayed emergence that can reduce exposure to standard application timing; clonal propagation via tubers that quickly fixes and amplifies the resistant genotype within infested fields once selected.

Event is retained as the first documented ALS-inhibitor-resistant yellow nutsedge biotype in peanuts but its temporal bounds, sources and emergence-type interpretation have been tightened. The year range is broadened to 2015–2024 and the country label to "United States of America – Georgia (Webster County) [2015–2024]" to cover the four consecutive peanut seasons with intensive imazapic use that preceded detection in 2019 and the subsequent research period, while still anchored by 2019 as the first confirmed resistance year in the international resistance database. The event remains classified as re_emergence because it involves a new ALS target-site mutation (Ala-205-Val) and altered herbicide response in an already established weed species. The generic weedscience species page has been replaced with the specific Georgia resistance case entry, and Arkansas-specific Weed Science papers have been removed from this event’s sources to avoid conflating distinct biotypes. Host: Gleditsia triacanthos (honeylocust) in urban plantings and nurseries
Event summary: Around 1992, characteristic pod galls of Dasineura gleditchiae were first observed on honeylocust street trees near Budapest, indicating introduction of the North American midge into Hungary. Event summary: In 1997, Diaphorina citri was detected for the first time in southeastern Iran near the Pakistan border, in association with trees later confirmed to be infected with huanglongbing (HLB), marking the onset of a serious citrus disease complex in the country. Event summary: In June 1998, Diaphorina citri was detected for the first time in the United States on orange jasmine hedges and dooryard citrus in Palm Beach County, Florida, establishing the pest on a new continent and raising concern about future citrus greening. By the mid‑2010s, D. citri and HLB were entrenched throughout Florida, forcing a long‑term shift toward intensive vector control, tree removal, and replanting strategies with major economic losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction likely via human‑mediated movement of infested ornamental Murraya plants, followed by rapid regional spread aided by dense commercial citrus plantings, mild subtropical climate, and long periods of leaf flushing; industry structure and initial regulatory delays allowed the pest to build large populations before greening was detected. Internal mechanisms: Highly efficient acquisition and transmission of Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus by D. citri, high fecundity and multiple overlapping generations, and adaptation to Florida’s climate led to enhanced transmission and severe re‑emergence of the HLB pathosystem on a new continent.

Host: Citrus spp. (especially lime and sweet orange) in commercial and backyard plantings

The event evolved into a persistent regional problem as coordinated control programs attempted to limit further disease spread and maintain citrus production in the face of dual vector‑borne disease pressures.

Internal mechanisms: Efficient vectoring of CLas in an environment where susceptible citrus and other phloem‑limited pathogens (e.g., witches’ broom) were present, along with the insect’s capacity to exploit irrigated oases and orchards in otherwise harsh climates, contributed to significant re‑emergence of citrus disease problems in western Asia.

Host: Direct-seeded upland and rainfed rice (Oryza sativa) and rainfed maize (Zea mays) in smallholder fields
Event summary: From the 1990s onward, the expansion of direct-seeded upland rice and intensified rainfed maize production in parts of north-east and eastern India and neighbouring Nepal was accompanied by shifts in weed communities, with Digitaria setigera reported among the dominant grassy weeds in rainfed maize in Odisha and in upland direct-seeded rice in Nagaland during 2009–2010. Weed surveys and management trials in dry/direct-seeded rice in South Asia through the 2000s and 2010s repeatedly listed D. setigera as a frequent late-emerging grass weed that contributed to yield losses where weed control was inadequate. By the late 2010s, integrated weed-management recommendations for these systems (sowing method, stale seedbeds and selective herbicides) explicitly targeted D. setigera together with other competitive grasses, but the species remained a recurrent component of cereal weed floras in parts of Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread adoption of dry/direct seeding in rice and expansion of rainfed maize, driven by labour shortages, water constraints and mechanisation, created aerobic, highly disturbed seedbeds that favour colonising grass weeds; limited or poorly timed weed control further allowed Digitaria setigera to increase in abundance. Internal mechanisms: No specific new biotypes or resistance traits have been reported for D. setigera in these systems; its emergence reflects inherent colonising traits of a native annual grass—high seed production, tolerance of intermittent drought and repeated disturbance, and persistence in the soil seed bank—leading to re-occurrence and increased weed importance in long-cultivated cereal landscapes rather than true geographic or host-range expansion.
Review: Added new high-impact event. Multiple weed-survey and management studies from the 1990s–2010s (e.g. Rout & Satapathy 1996 for maize in Odisha; Kikon & Gohain 2017 for upland direct-seeded rice in Nagaland; Agronomy Journal of Nepal 2021; Paiman et al. 2020) consistently identify D. setigera as one of the dominant grassy weeds in direct-seeded rice and rainfed maize in parts of Southern Asia, affecting staple crops over large areas. Because the species is native/long established in this region and no novel genotypes or resistance have been documented, the event is correctly coded as re-occurrence only (no intra- or inter-continental emergence, no first detection). This pan-regional cereal-weed resurgence was missing from the original file but is likely among the most impactful post-1990 emergence episodes for D. setigera and should be retained.

Countries: United States of America [Hawaiʻi indigenous/long established; mainland southeastern USA (Florida and nearby states) naturalized by the 1990s–2000s]
Host: Weed in disturbed sites, pastures, roadsides, lawns and natural areas (including subtropical mainland southeastern USA and protected areas such as Everglades National Park and coastal conservation lands)
Event summary: Before 1990, Digitaria setigera was already indigenous or long established on the Hawaiian Islands, where it occurs in lowland mesic forests, pastures and roadsides across most main islands. Over roughly the 1990–2015 period, the species came to be documented as a naturalized grass in the southeastern mainland United States, especially in South Florida (Miami-Dade County, Everglades National Park, coastal beaches and Keys), where it occupies disturbed uplands, roadsides and some natural areas. By the mid-2010s D. setigera was listed in invasive/naturalized plant databases and Floras for Florida, but it remained a relatively localized component of the regional crabgrass flora compared to more aggressive congeners such as D. sanguinalis and D. ciliaris.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased trade and movement of contaminated soil, turf, nursery stock and seed, along with expanding networks of roads, urban landscapes and managed pastures in subtropical Florida, facilitated dispersal of D. setigera from its earlier stronghold in Hawaiʻi and the wider American tropics into mainland southeastern USA; coastal and urban disturbance created suitable niches in conservation areas and along beaches. Internal mechanisms: Generalist colonising traits typical of crabgrasses—annual or short-lived perennial habit, prolific seed production, tolerance of mowing and trampling, and ability to exploit bare, nutrient-enriched soils—underpin this re-occurrence and spread within the Northern America sub-region; there is no evidence of new genotypes or herbicide resistance driving the expansion.
Review: Retain but change emergence-type coding. Floristic databases (GRIN-Global, IRC South Florida, Invasive Plant Atlas, EDDMapS) show D. setigera long established and indigenous/naturalized in Hawaiʻi and later naturalized at scattered sites in South Florida and adjacent southeastern states. Under the project’s geography, these all lie in the same sub-region (Northern America), so expansion from Hawaiian populations to mainland Florida is best treated as a re-occurrence/increase within an already occupied sub-region rather than intra-continental or inter-continental emergence. Accordingly, 'intra_continental_emergence' is set to "false" and 're_occurrence' to "true"; 'first_detection' remains "false" because the species was described globally in 1817. The time window 1990–2015 is kept as an approximate period during which mainland naturalization became documented, but actual first arrival likely predates 1990 and this uncertainty is noted by keeping confidence at 0.5.

Countries: Australia [Northern Territory and some offshore territories native or long established; Queensland naturalized and increasingly recorded from the mid-20th century onward]
Host: Weed in tropical and subtropical pastures, open woodlands, roadsides, disturbed coastal habitats and occasionally around croplands in northern Australia and offshore Australian territories
Event summary: By the late 20th century Digitaria setigera was recognised in Australian floras as widespread in tropical northern Australia and several offshore territories, native or long established in the Northern Territory and islands such as Christmas and Cocos (Keeling), but treated as a naturalised weed in parts of Queensland. Through the 1990–2025 period, additional collections and state censuses confirmed its presence in Queensland (especially between Townsville and Cairns and in the Cape York region) and recorded both the species and D. setigera var. setigera as introduced land plants, indicating persistent populations in pastures, roadside verges and disturbed woodlands that occasionally encroach on croplands. Despite this broad distribution and its inclusion among widespread tropical grass weeds, D. setigera has not been singled out as a major cause of crop yield loss relative to more aggressive Australian pasture and crop weeds, and its impact is mainly through cumulative competition and ground cover in grazing systems and disturbed lands.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive grazing systems, land clearing, burning and road construction in northern Australia have created abundant disturbed habitat and dispersal corridors, while the movement of livestock, hay, machinery and soil between properties and via coastal shipping promotes regional spread of D. setigera seeds. Internal mechanisms: The species shows the life-history traits typical of problem Digitaria weeds—prolific seed set, tolerance of grazing and mowing, and ability to establish on bare or lightly vegetated soils—which support repeated re-occurrence and local increases in abundance within already occupied sub-regions; there is no evidence that novel genotypes, increased virulence or herbicide resistance are currently driving its spread.
Review: Retain with clarification and keep coded as re-occurrence. Flora of Australia, AusGrass2, Queensland herbarium data and regional fact sheets agree that D. setigera is native or long established in the Northern Territory and some offshore islands and has been present, but often overlooked, in Queensland since at least the mid-20th century, where it is now treated as a widespread but generally minor weed of pastures and disturbed woodlands. Because the species was already present in this sub-region well before 1990, the 1990–2025 window reflects continued documentation and local increases in abundance rather than a new introduction; there is no evidence for spread into a new continent or sub-region or for genetic change, so only 're_occurrence' is set to "true". The summary text has been lightly edited to emphasise long pre-1990 presence and the moderate, mainly pastoral impact, and this row is flagged for review if future work identifies more clearly quantifiable yield-loss episodes elsewhere that would displace it from a top-10 list for this species.

Countries: Ecuador [Galápagos, Isabela Island – Puerto Villamil, early 2000s]
Host: Ruderal vegetation and associated ornamental, horticultural and urban plantings in and around Puerto Villamil (Isabela Island, Galápagos), with potential to spread to nearby agricultural plots and natural vegetation
Event summary: Around the early 2000s, an inventory of introduced plants in Puerto Villamil on Isabela Island, Galápagos, recorded Digitaria setigera as a casual, sexually reproducing alien grass in disturbed urban sites, with herbarium collections from the town area in 2003. The species persisted in human-modified habitats around Puerto Villamil and was flagged by Galápagos biosecurity programmes as a potential source of propagules to nearby agricultural lands and the surrounding national park. Management attention focused on early detection and control of incipient populations to prevent further spread from this urban introduction focus into more pristine island habitats, and D. setigera has so far remained a localized but monitored component of the introduced flora.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance human-mediated dispersal of seeds via shipping, cargo, soil, ornamental plant material and visitors into the rapidly growing tourist town of Puerto Villamil, combined with extensive disturbance and nutrient enrichment along roadsides, gardens and waste ground, created suitable microsites for establishment. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype has been reported; emergence reflects the species’ general traits as a small-seeded, fast-growing annual grass adapted to disturbed tropical sites, now expressing as intra-continental spread from earlier American mainland and Caribbean populations to the oceanic Galápagos archipelago.
Review: Retain but re-code emergence type. Floristic syntheses (e.g. Vega et al. 2018, Biota Colombiana, POWO) show that D. setigera is already naturalized across much of the American tropics, including the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America and numerous South American countries (Colombia, Guyana, Surinam, French Guiana, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia), well before the Galápagos record. This means the Puerto Villamil occurrence is not the first presence of the species on the South American continent and should not be coded as 'inter_continental_emergence' or 'first_detection'. Instead, it represents spread into a new island area within an already colonised continent, so 'intra_continental_emergence' is set to "true" and 'first_detection' to "false". The underlying sources (PLOS One inventory plus distribution syntheses) are appropriate; the event is retained because new establishment on a highly sensitive oceanic archipelago has substantial conservation significance even if current abundance is low.

Countries: Austria [Upper Austria, St. Peter am Hart, first voucher 2010]
Host: Alien grass in arable land (notably maize fields) and disturbed ruderal habitats in the Eastern Alps (Upper Austria)
Event summary: In 2010, Digitaria setigera was first recorded from St. Peter am Hart in Upper Austria, with subsequent confirmation in an overview of alien grasses in the Eastern Alps that treated it as an annual neophyte, ephemeral and not yet invasive. During the early 2010s, records remained confined to a small area in Upper Austria, where the species appeared sporadically in maize fields and ruderal sites but often failed to persist without continued disturbance. By the mid-2010s, D. setigera was still assessed in European floristic treatments as a recently introduced neophyte of East African and southern Asian origin with very limited distribution in the Eastern Alps and no evidence yet of significant invasiveness.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction via contaminated grain or crop seed, fodder, or agricultural machinery associated with intensive maize-growing and transport corridors in the Eastern Alps, together with warming climates that allow survival of thermophilic grasses in lowland Austria. Internal mechanisms: No specific new genotype has been reported; the event represents the first confirmed establishment of this tropical Asian species on the European continent, enabled by its general life-history traits (annual habit, prolific seeding, tolerance of disturbance) rather than by demonstrable evolutionary change.
Review: Retain as the first European event but correct geography and coding. The Austrian neophyte catalogue and Neilreichia review document D. setigera from St. Peter am Hart (Upper Austria) in 2010, with status described as an annual, ephemeral neophyte and no earlier European field populations confirmed; no robust evidence could be found for naturalized occurrences in Italy during the same period. Accordingly, the countries field has been restricted to Austria [2010] and the sub_regions field to Western Europe, and Southern Europe/Italy has been removed. Because global description of the species dates to 1817, 'first_detection' should be "false", while this episode still represents the first established population on the European continent, so 'inter_continental_emergence' remains "true" and 'intra_continental_emergence' stays "false". Event years have been shifted to start at 2010 to match the earliest voucher citation, and the row is flagged for review in case additional pre‑2010 European records are uncovered.

Countries: Fiji [Western Viti Levu, Nadroga/Navosa and Ba provinces, 2023]
Host: Weed in vegetable crops, particularly eggplant fields, and surrounding disturbed ground in lowland agricultural areas
Event summary: In 2023, a weed survey of eggplant agroecosystems in the Fijian provinces of Nadroga/Navosa and Ba recorded Digitaria setigera among 40 weed species present in and around fields, with the grass forming a low-abundance component of the Poaceae-dominated weed flora. Across 24 farm surveys, D. setigera was present but contributed less than 1% of total weed flora by relative abundance, co-occurring with more dominant grasses such as Cynodon dactylon, Echinochloa colona and Eleusine indica and with several problem sedges and broad-leaved weeds. The study highlighted the need for integrated weed management but did not identify D. setigera as a primary target species, and there is currently no evidence of rapid spread or major yield losses in Fijian vegetable systems attributable specifically to this grass.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of smallholder vegetable production for export, repeated soil disturbance, limited crop rotation and imperfect weed control in western Viti Levu provide niches for opportunistic grass weeds, while local movement of contaminated seed, soil and farm machinery facilitates spread among fields. Internal mechanisms: As an indigenous or long-established grass in much of the tropical Pacific, D. setigera’s presence in these eggplant systems is best interpreted as a re-occurrence and modest increase in prominence within already occupied island landscapes, driven by its generalist traits (rapid growth, prolific seeding, tolerance of tropical conditions and repeated disturbance) rather than any documented herbicide resistance or other evolutionary change.
Review: Retain but flag as a low-impact re-occurrence. POWO and Pacific floras treat D. setigera as indigenous or long established in the tropical Pacific, including Fiji, so this 2023 record in eggplant fields reflects local re-occurrence/increased visibility in cropped land rather than a new continental or sub-regional incursion. The Deesh et al. (2024) survey shows D. setigera accounting for only about 0.7% of the recorded weed flora, far less than several other grasses and sedges, which suggests limited current agronomic impact. Given the small number of well-documented post‑1990 events for this species, this Fijian episode can be kept for completeness, but it should be considered a candidate for exclusion if future work identifies additional, more impactful emergence events (e.g. in major cereal systems or large-scale American invasions).

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: Russian wheat aphid, first recorded in Ethiopia in the 1970s, caused some of its most severe documented outbreaks in the early 1990s in the highland barley and wheat belts. During these seasons, small‑plot and field studies reported barley yield losses commonly exceeding 40% and in some cases over 70%, and wheat losses approaching or exceeding 80% in badly infested fields, making RWA the dominant insect constraint on highland barley and wheat production. Through the mid‑1990s, wider use of systemic insecticides, identification and deployment of more tolerant barley lines, and adjustments in sowing dates and crop management reduced the frequency of catastrophic losses, although the aphid remained entrenched and continues to flare up under favorable cool, dry conditions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of rainfed wheat and barley in high‑altitude zones, frequent drought‑stressed seasons that favored aphid survival and limited plant compensation, and poor initial access to resistant cultivars or affordable insecticides allowed large RWA populations to build up in the early 1990s. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, parthenogenetic reproduction and good adaptation to Ethiopian highland barley landraces underpinned explosive population growth, but no distinct new virulent biotype was reported from Ethiopia at that time, so this episode is treated as a severe re‑occurrence driven primarily by external agronomic and climatic factors.
Review: retain – Event reflects one of the globally most severe RWA outbreaks, with well‑documented barley and wheat yield losses in Ethiopia’s highlands in the early 1990s. Classification as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate because RWA had been established in Eastern Africa since the 1970s and the episode represents a dramatic resurgence in an already affected sub‑region without evidence for a new biotype. Sources were checked and supplemented to include peer‑reviewed Ethiopian yield‑loss studies.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: Introduced into the United States in 1986, Russian wheat aphid spread rapidly through the western Great Plains and by the 1991–1992 seasons caused its most damaging outbreak phase, infesting millions of acres of winter wheat and barley across 17 western states. Economic assessments for 1987–1993 attribute several hundred million to nearly US$900 million in direct and indirect losses to RWA in the western USA, with 1991–1992 among the peak years for infested acreage and yield loss. In the mid‑1990s, a combination of intensive insecticide use, biological control introductions and especially the deployment of resistant cultivars carrying gene Dn4 reduced average losses and shifted the pest from crisis level to a manageable but still important constraint.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large contiguous areas of susceptible dryland winter wheat and barley, favorable cool and dry conditions in several early 1990s seasons, and the initial lack of resistant cultivars or effective natural enemies allowed extremely high aphid densities and widespread crop losses during 1991–1992. Internal mechanisms: The invasive North American RWA population showed high reproductive rates and good cold tolerance but was not yet differentiated into multiple virulent biotypes; this episode is therefore interpreted as a major re‑occurrence (dramatic increase in incidence and impact) in a previously invaded sub‑region rather than as re‑emergence driven by new strain evolution.
Review: retain (newly added) – This event was missing from the original list but is clearly among the top global post‑1990 emergence episodes for RWA, with very large infested areas and economic losses in the western United States during 1991–1992. Classified as re‑occurrence because it represents the peak of a multi‑year invasion in a sub‑region where the species was already established and there is no evidence that a novel biotype was responsible.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare), oats (Avena sativa), rye (Secale cereale)
Event summary: Following its first South American record in Chile in 1987–1988, Russian wheat aphid was detected in Argentina in 1991 at Malargüe, Mendoza, and soon after in wheat fields in Buenos Aires province, marking its spread into one of the continent’s major wheat belts. Through the mid‑1990s the pest became established across key cereal‑growing regions such as Bahía Blanca, with high local aphid densities, characteristic foliar streaking and rolling, and documented economic importance for bread wheat and malting barley production. By the late 1990s, RWA was widely distributed in Argentina’s wheat region, and management had shifted from detection and containment to ongoing integrated control based on monitoring, selective insecticides and the gradual development of resistant or tolerant cereal germplasm.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated movement of infested plant material and wind‑borne spread from Chile into neighboring Argentine cereal areas, combined with extensive areas of susceptible wheat and barley in dry, sunny climates, facilitated rapid establishment and regional spread. Internal mechanisms: The invasive South American populations possessed the species’ inherent capacity for parthenogenetic reproduction, high intrinsic growth rates and adaptation to dryland cereals; early Argentine work did not document distinct virulence biotypes, so this episode is interpreted primarily as a major geographic range expansion within an already invaded continental sub‑region.
Review: review – Retain as a major South American emergence event, since RWA became an economically important pest in Argentina’s main wheat region from 1991 onward. Corrected misclassification by setting intra‑continental emergence to No, because RWA was already present in the same UNSD sub‑region (“South America”) via Chile prior to 1990; spread into Argentina represents country‑level expansion within an existing sub‑region rather than first occurrence in a new sub‑region. Countries field was simplified to the country‑level with provinces described in the summary, and a key Argentine field study (SciELO article from Bahía Blanca) was added as a more directly relevant source.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: After its initial emergence as a major pest in South African wheat in 1978, Russian wheat aphid remained entrenched, and by 1993 the country experienced one of its largest recorded outbreak seasons in the summer‑rainfall dryland wheat and barley areas. National estimates indicate that in 1993 large areas of dryland wheat suffered substantial yield reductions and that cumulative direct losses from the late 1980s through 1993 were on the order of tens of millions of South African rand. Intensified chemical control, gradual adoption of RWA‑resistant wheat cultivars and improved agronomic practices helped to bring infestations back to more manageable levels in subsequent seasons, though the pest continued to be a key constraint in susceptible cultivars.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive planting of susceptible wheat cultivars, favorable cool and dry conditions for aphid population build‑up, and limited early‑season control allowed very high aphid densities during the 1993 season, translating into large national yield and monetary losses. Internal mechanisms: No distinct new biotype was associated with this particular year; the outbreak reflects the invasive South African population’s ability to reach economic thresholds rapidly under conducive environmental conditions, so it is classified as a severe re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Event corresponds to a well‑documented peak outbreak year in South Africa with large national yield and economic losses. Classification as re‑occurrence (no new biotype, dramatic resurgence in an already affected sub‑region driven by weather and cropping patterns) is consistent with definitions. No structural corrections were needed beyond clarifying the nature of the losses in the summary.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: Following earlier establishment of Russian wheat aphid in parts of Eastern and South‑Eastern Europe (including Hungary and FYR Macedonia by 1989 and Serbia by 1990), the pest was first detected in the Czech Republic around 1996 as part of its broader expansion through the Carpathian Basin. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, RWA became a regular component of the cereal aphid complex in south‑eastern Moravia and other lowland wheat and barley areas, sometimes reaching locally damaging densities and prompting concern about its potential to cause significant yield losses. By about 2002, surveys documented its presence at multiple sites in the Czech part of the Carpathian Basin, but overall pest status remained moderate relative to the severe impacts seen in South Africa and North America, and management relied mainly on general cereal aphid monitoring and broad‑spectrum control measures where needed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Gradual natural spread along river corridors and plains of the Carpathian Basin, assisted by wind‑borne dispersal and regional movements of infested cereals, allowed RWA to colonize Czech cereal fields after establishing in neighboring Hungary and Slovakia. Internal mechanisms: The populations involved do not appear to represent a distinct new strain; establishment reflects the species’ inherent capacity for colonization and overwintering in temperate cereal regions, representing continued geographic range expansion within Europe rather than a strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – The original event correctly identified RWA’s spread into Czech cereal areas as part of its Carpathian Basin expansion but mis‑dated the first record (set to 1993) and classified it as intra‑continental emergence. The year has been adjusted to 1996 with the episode extended to 2002 to reflect primary distribution data, and intra‑continental emergence is now set to No because RWA was already present in the same UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Europe) in Hungary and other countries before 1990. A dedicated Carpathian Basin distribution paper was added as a key source. Event is retained but flagged for review because its overall impact appears moderate compared with African and American outbreaks and could be replaced if stronger evidence emerges for more impactful post‑1990 events elsewhere (e.g. Iran or Kenya).

Countries: United States of America – Colorado [2003], Kansas and other Great Plains states [mid‑2000s]
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: In 2003, a new Russian wheat aphid biotype, designated RWA2, was detected in southeastern Colorado and neighboring Great Plains wheat areas and was distinguished by its ability to damage cultivars carrying the resistance gene Dn4 that had previously provided effective control. Over the mid‑2000s this virulent biotype spread across major winter wheat regions in Colorado, Kansas, Texas and other western and central Great Plains states, causing renewed economic losses despite the prior success of Dn4‑based resistant varieties. By around 2010, RWA2 and additional virulent biotypes had largely displaced the original RWA biotype in many areas, and breeding programs and integrated pest‑management strategies were re‑oriented to deploy new resistance sources (e.g. Dn7) and adjust chemical and agronomic tactics.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy reliance on Dn4‑based resistant cultivars over large acreages created strong selection pressure favoring genotypes able to overcome this resistance, while extensive volunteer cereals and winter wheat acreage provided continuous host availability and corridors for spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the virulent RWA2 biotype and related Dn4‑virulent forms represents Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence, as shown by differential damage on Dn4 and Dny host lines and molecular work demonstrating altered gene expression in virulent aphids; this episode is therefore classified as re‑emergence driven by genetic adaptation to resistant hosts rather than as geographic emergence.
Review: review – Event clearly represents a major re‑emergence episode in North America associated with the evolution and spread of Dn4‑virulent biotype RWA2 and related genotypes and should be retained. The original classification incorrectly marked this episode as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence; intra‑continental emergence has been set to No because RWA was already widespread across the Northern America sub‑region and the key novelty lies in virulence evolution rather than spread to a new UNSD sub‑region. Sources were cross‑checked and a Colorado technical bulletin documenting the 2003 discovery and 2004–2008 spread of RWA2 has been emphasized.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s, South African researchers documented the appearance of new Russian wheat aphid biotypes able to damage cultivars previously considered resistant, beginning with RWASA2 in 2005 and followed by RWASA3 (2009) and RWASA4 (2011). These biotypes progressively overcame combinations of Dn1, Dn2, Dn3, Dn4 and other resistance genes deployed in commercial wheat, and during seasons such as 2005–2006 growers reported severe damage and significant localized yield losses even in fields planted to resistant cultivars. In response, wheat breeding programs intensified efforts to pyramid multiple resistance genes and to identify new sources of resistance, while integrated pest management recommendations were updated; although some control was regained, the durability and cost of resistance‑based management were substantially affected.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term, large‑scale planting of cultivars with similar RWA resistance backgrounds, combined with continued high pest pressure in South Africa’s summer‑rainfall wheat areas, imposed strong selection for resistance‑breaking aphid genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Successive Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence events (RWASA2–RWASA4) with increased virulence to multiple Dn genes underpin this re‑emergence, with South African populations showing biotypic and genetic differentiation relative to earlier invasive populations; this episode thus represents re‑emergence due to genetic adaptation to resistant hosts rather than simple resurgence of existing biotypes.
Review: review – Retain as a major re‑emergence episode in South Africa linked to successive resistance‑breaking biotypes, but extend the event period from 2005–2010 to 2005–2011 to encompass the first reports of RWASA4. Classification as re‑emergence is appropriate and was left unchanged; other emergence‑type flags remain No because the episode does not involve spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region. A South African extension article specifying years of detection for RWASA1–RWASA4 has been incorporated as a more precise source.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Australia – South Australia [2016], Victoria [2016], New South Wales [2016-2017], Tasmania [2017], Western Australia [2017-2020]
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare), other small grains and grass hosts
Event summary: In May 2016, Russian wheat aphid was first detected in wheat near Tarlee in South Australia, representing its first confirmed occurrence in Australia and the wider Oceania region. Within months, intensive surveillance found infestations across much of South Australia’s cereal belt and into Victoria and southern New South Wales, with subsequent detections in Tasmania in early 2017 and Western Australia by 2017–2018, raising major concern for wheat and barley industries, including organic growers with limited chemical options. By about 2020, RWA was established across large parts of southern Australia’s grain‑growing regions, and authorities shifted from emergency response to long‑term integrated pest management based on surveillance, action thresholds, conservation of natural enemies and selective insecticide or seed‑treatment use where warranted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: One or more accidental introductions via infested plant material, fodder or stowaway aphids from already infested continents, followed by wind‑borne dispersal across large, contiguous cereal landscapes in southern Australia and favorable temperate climates, enabled rapid establishment and spread; organic and low‑input systems were particularly vulnerable due to limited control options. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) to a previously uninvaded continent, supported by the aphid’s parthenogenetic reproduction, ability to exploit multiple cereal and grass hosts and capacity for long‑distance wind dispersal; no distinct Australian‑specific biotype has been emphasized, so this is treated as an inter‑continental emergence rather than a strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the first incursion and rapid establishment of RWA in Australia and should be retained as the sole inter‑continental emergence episode for this pest after 1990. The original classification set both first_detection and inter‑continental emergence to Yes; first_detection has been reset to No to align with the definition that this flag refers to the first detection of the EPP in the host system globally, which for RWA predates 1990, while inter‑continental emergence remains Yes to reflect first establishment in Oceania with in situ spread. Wikipedia was removed from the event‑level sources and replaced or supplemented with official Australian government and industry resources that more directly document detection dates and spread.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event summary: Around 2018, a highly virulent South African Russian wheat aphid biotype, later designated RWASA5, was first detected on multiple wheat fields in the Free State province and shown to overcome all known resistance genes present in commercial cultivars. By the early 2020s, RWASA5 had spread within major wheat‑growing areas of South Africa, and extension bulletins highlighted the absence of effective resistant cultivars, the potential for substantial yield losses in both wheat and barley, and concern about possible spread into neighboring Southern African countries. Management responses have focused on intensified monitoring for RWASA5, accelerated breeding to identify new resistance sources effective against this biotype, and integrated chemical and agronomic strategies to limit damage while longer‑term genetic solutions are developed.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued large‑scale planting of cultivars carrying a limited set of resistance genes and the presence of multiple earlier South African biotypes provided strong selection pressure for an even more virulent biotype, while regional trade in seed and grain and movement of infested plant material increase the risk of further spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity are central, as RWASA5 can damage plants carrying resistance genes that were effective against RWASA1–RWASA4, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by further biotypic evolution within South African RWA populations.
Review: review – Event is retained as a major recent re‑emergence episode because RWASA5 poses a serious threat to South African wheat and barley production. The start year has been corrected from 2015 to 2018 to align with reports of the first field detections and early distribution surveys, and the countries field has been restricted to South Africa, as neighboring states are currently described mainly as at risk rather than confirmed RWASA5 foci in available sources. Classification as re‑emergence remains appropriate, driven by a newly recognized, highly virulent biotype; new South African research articles and extension pieces documenting RWASA5 were added to strengthen sourcing.
