EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [1990] (Arkansas rice-growing regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded rice production systems
Event summary: In 1990, propanil-resistant barnyardgrass (Echinochloa crus-galli) was first documented in Arkansas rice fields, following decades of intensive propanil use as the primary post-emergence grass herbicide, and resistant populations spread rapidly within major rice counties over the early 1990s, causing severe control failures and yield losses; the event stabilized only after growers began diversifying herbicide programs and integrating additional pre-emergence products and cultural tactics.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Heavy, recurrent use of propanil in monoculture rice with limited herbicide rotation; expansion of high-input flooded rice acreage; limited non-chemical weed management.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of propanil-resistant E. crus-galli biotypes under strong selection pressure; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – not vector-based, but agronomic practices (continuous rice, flooding) favored rapid population build-up and seedbank enrichment of resistant plants.
Review: retain - This row correctly describes the first confirmation and rapid spread of propanil-resistant barnyardgrass in Arkansas rice, a globally important emergence event. I left the temporal and geographic framing unchanged but replaced the generic Wikipedia source with primary literature documenting 1990 confirmation and statewide spread (Carey et al. 1995; subsequent mechanism work). Classification as re-emergence only (no intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because the species was already long established in North America.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [1998] (quinclorac-resistant barnyardgrass first confirmed in Louisiana; multiple resistance to propanil and quinclorac confirmed in Arkansas [1999] with spread to additional southern rice-producing states by the early 2000s)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and semi-flooded systems
Event summary: In 1998 quinclorac-resistant E. crus-galli was documented in Louisiana rice fields, and by 1999 Arkansas confirmed barnyardgrass biotypes with resistance to both propanil and quinclorac, marking the first major multiple-herbicide-resistant grass problem in U.S. rice; resistant populations spread across additional rice-growing states by the early 2000s, undermining the two main post-emergence herbicides and forcing costly, complex control programs; the episode has persisted with chronic management difficulties, though diversified herbicide mixtures and rotation have partially contained further spread.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Sequential and frequent use of propanil and quinclorac in the same rice fields; limited crop rotation; economic pressure to rely on chemical control.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – independent evolution and subsequent spread of quinclorac resistance, followed by multiple resistance to both propanil and quinclorac in some biotypes; Enhanced Transmission – prolific seed production and dispersal via machinery and irrigation water facilitated rapid regional spread of resistant populations.
Review: review - Retain as a major event, but I broadened the time window to 1998–2003 to cover confirmation and early spread of quinclorac and multiple resistance, and simplified the country field to avoid unsupported state-level dating for Texas and Missouri. Louisiana 1998 quinclorac resistance and Arkansas 1999 propanil+quinclorac multiple resistance are well documented by weedscience.org and Weed Technology articles. The original use of the intra-continental emergence flag was incorrect for a resistance trait and has been set to re-emergence only, in line with the definitions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Italy [2000] (Po Valley rice-growing regions, especially Lombardy and Piedmont)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and water‑seeded rice systems
Event summary: From about 2000 onwards, northern Italian rice growers in the Po Valley began reporting barnyardgrass escapes after treatments with propanil and newer ALS‑inhibiting herbicides, and surveys over the 2000s confirmed multiple E. crus-galli populations with high resistance to azimsulfuron, imazamox, penoxsulam and other ALS inhibitors, with several populations also showing cross‑resistance to the ACCase inhibitor profoxydim; by roughly 2011, ALS and ALS+ACCase multiple-resistant barnyardgrass had become widespread in Italian rice fields, seriously reducing the effectiveness of the main post‑emergence herbicides and prompting recommendations for integrated weed management and rotation of herbicide modes of action.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Long‑term reliance on a narrow suite of ALS‑ and ACCase‑inhibiting herbicides in intensive rice monoculture in the Po Valley; limited crop rotation and non‑chemical weed control.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – target‑site ALS mutations (e.g. Trp574Leu and other substitutions) and, in some populations, ACCase target‑site changes conferring high‑level cross‑resistance to multiple ALS chemistries and low‑ to moderate‑level resistance to profoxydim; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant genotypes becoming dominant within Italian rice agroecosystems and replacing susceptible barnyardgrass populations.
Review: retain - New row added: multi‑herbicide‑resistant barnyardgrass in Italian rice (ALS and ACCase resistance) is clearly one of the globally important emergence episodes, with numerous resistant populations across the main Po Valley rice area and documented cross‑ and multiple resistance patterns. Dates and modes of action are aligned with the Italian cases in the International Herbicide-Resistant Weed Database and detailed ALS/ACCase target‑site studies; the event is classified purely as re‑emergence (evolution of resistant biotypes) rather than spatial emergence of the species.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [2000] (especially Arkansas rice region, with spread to neighboring rice-producing states)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and furrow-irrigated systems
Event summary: From the early 2000s through the 2020s, Arkansas and neighboring U.S. rice states experienced a sustained escalation of herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass problems, with populations evolving resistance to ALS inhibitors, ACCase inhibitors, propanil, quinclorac, clomazone and newer auxin herbicides, leading to complex multi-resistant biotypes that became the most troublesome weed in Arkansas rice and significantly increased weed management costs; surveys in the 2010s and early 2020s documented widespread producer concern, higher herbicide inputs and greater reliance on integrated management, while new herbicides such as tetflupyrolimet were explicitly developed and tested to help manage these resistant populations.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Long-term reliance on a narrow set of herbicide modes of action in rice; development of furrow‑irrigated and high-yield rice systems favoring barnyardgrass; limited adoption initially of non-chemical weed control; economic pressure to maintain high yields.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – sequential evolution and stacking of resistance to multiple herbicide classes (ALS, ACCase, synthetic auxins, propanil, others) in E. crus-galli; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity (operational) – resistant biotypes able to survive most standard programs and cause higher competitive yield loss; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – spread of multi-resistant genotypes across much of the Arkansas rice area and into neighboring states.
Review: review - This event is retained as a major, long‑running episode describing the accumulation of multiple resistance mechanisms in U.S. rice barnyardgrass. I corrected the emergence-type flags by removing intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence so that the event is classified solely as re‑emergence (sequential evolution of new resistance traits in an already widespread weed), consistent with the definitions. The time window and narrative match survey and research data on multi-resistant barnyardgrass in Arkansas rice.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: China: Hunan [2002], additional rice provinces in southern China [2000s]
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and double-cropping systems
Event summary: In 2002, quinclorac-resistant E. crus-galli was first confirmed in Hunan Province rice fields in south-central China, soon followed by additional resistant populations in other provinces after years of intensive quinclorac use for barnyardgrass control, leading by the late 2000s to widespread field control failures and serious rice yield losses in parts of southern China; resistance was partly mitigated when growers began rotating modes of action and adjusting water management, but resistant biotypes remain entrenched in many paddies.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Long-term, heavy reliance on quinclorac as the principal post-emergence herbicide against E. crus-galli; intensification of rice production with double-cropping and reduced labor for manual weeding.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of high-level quinclorac resistance (up to >100× recommended dose in some biotypes) with physiological changes in response and detoxification; Enhanced Transmission – barnyardgrass seed movement via flooded water, machinery, and contaminated seed facilitated rapid spread among adjacent paddies.
Review: review - Retain as one of the largest global emergence events: quinclorac-resistant barnyardgrass in Chinese rice is pervasive and well documented, with first confirmation in Hunan around 2002 and subsequent spread. I removed the intra-continental emergence flag so that the event is treated as re-emergence (a new resistant biotype of an existing weed) rather than geographic emergence of the species within Asia, in line with the project’s rules.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Brazil [2003] (especially Rio Grande do Sul and other southern rice regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa), mainly direct-seeded irrigated rice with Clearfield (imidazolinone-tolerant) cultivars
Event summary: During the 2000s, the rapid adoption of imidazolinone-tolerant (Clearfield-type) rice in southern Brazil led to intensive use of imidazolinone herbicides and selection of E. crus-galli populations with resistance to imidazolinones and often quinclorac, with surveys by 2009–2012 estimating that a very high proportion of barnyardgrass accessions in some rice areas carried imidazolinone resistance and caused major yield and quality losses; by the early 2010s this resistance had spread across much of the southern rice belt, and integrated programs combining clomazone and alternative post-emergence herbicides plus crop rotation were promoted to curb further expansion.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Large-scale deployment of imidazolinone-resistant rice technology; repeated, often exclusive use of imidazolinone herbicides in direct-seeded rice; economic incentives for simplified chemical-based weed management.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – ALS target-site mutations and non–target-site enhanced metabolism conferring resistance to imidazolinones and in some populations to quinclorac; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant genotypes became dominant within rice agroecosystems throughout southern Brazil, replacing susceptible barnyardgrass populations.
Review: retain - This Clearfield-based Brazilian episode is a high-impact, multi‑resistance event in a million‑hectare rice region and should clearly remain among the top 10. I only standardised the emergence classification to re‑emergence (evolution of imidazolinone and quinclorac resistance) and tightened the country/year wording to reflect introduction of Clearfield rice in 2003 and high resistance frequencies by 2009–2012, as reported in Brazilian surveys.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Republic of Korea [2008] (direct-seeded rice areas in Taean, Gimje and other mid-west regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in direct-seeded and puddled rice systems
Event summary: Around 2008, South Korean rice farmers began to experience frequent failures of ALS- and ACCase-inhibiting herbicides on barnyardgrass, and resistance surveys conducted in 2012 across 155 E. crus-galli var. crus-galli accessions from Taean, Gimje and other mid-west rice areas showed that 42 accessions were resistant to at least one ALS or ACCase inhibitor and 10 accessions carried multiple resistance to both modes of action; these multi-resistant populations, recorded in the International Herbicide-Resistant Weed Database as the first multiple-resistant barnyardgrass in Korea, rapidly reduced the efficacy of the dominant post-emergence herbicides and forced adoption of more complex mixtures, rotation of modes of action and integrated management in Korean rice systems.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Long-term, repeated use of ALS- and ACCase-inhibiting herbicides in direct-seeded rice with limited rotation of chemistries; high selection pressure from simplified weed-control programs.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – cross- and multiple resistance to several sulfonylurea and imidazolinone ALS inhibitors and to ACCase inhibitors such as cyhalofop-butyl, fenoxaprop-ethyl and metamifop, associated with target-site changes and likely enhanced metabolism; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant biotypes detected across multiple key rice districts in mid-western Korea.
Review: retain - New row added: multiple resistance to ALS and ACCase herbicides in South Korean barnyardgrass is a major, well-documented episode (42 of 155 accessions resistant and 10 showing multiple resistance in nationwide surveys) and is clearly among the top global emergence events for this weed. The event is classified as re‑emergence of resistant biotypes; continent and subregion fields follow UN definitions (Asia/Eastern Asia).

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in paddy rice systems
Event summary: Around the early 2010s, barnyardgrass biotypes collected from Lu-jiang County in Anhui Province and other rice areas in central–southern China were confirmed resistant to multiple herbicides including quinclorac and ALS inhibitors such as penoxsulam and bispyribac, indicating a shift from single- to multiple-resistance within key rice production zones; these multi-resistant populations spread locally and became a major constraint on herbicide-based weed control, prompting increased research into resistance mechanisms and greater emphasis on diversified chemical programs and cultural tactics.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Continued use of a narrow set of post-emergence herbicides (quinclorac, penoxsulam, bispyribac) in intensive rice systems; limited crop diversification and manual weeding due to labor shortages.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – stacked resistance to quinclorac and several ALS-inhibiting herbicides associated with both target-site ALS mutations and elevated detoxification; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – multiple-resistant biotypes spreading across multiple central and southern Chinese rice provinces.
Review: retain - This event captures the first well-characterised Chinese multi-resistant barnyardgrass biotypes (quinclorac + ALS inhibitors) in central–southern rice regions and should be retained as part of the top 10. I only adjusted classification to remove intra-continental emergence so that the event is labelled purely as re‑emergence of new resistant biotypes, which matches the project rules that new strains/biotypes are not coded as geographic emergence.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Uruguay [2013] (major irrigated rice regions in eastern and northern Uruguay)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in direct dry-seeded rice systems
Event summary: From about 2013 onward, Uruguayan rice growers began to experience recurrent barnyardgrass control failures, and more than 40 E. crus-galli biotypes collected between roughly 2013 and 2015 from rice regions across the country were later shown to include numerous populations resistant to quinclorac, imazapyr + imazapic, penoxsulam and, in some cases, propanil; the 2019 national report confirmed herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass for the first time in Uruguay and highlighted that quinclorac-resistant biotypes were widespread across rice areas, reducing herbicide options and prompting calls to redesign production systems around more diverse cultural and chemical weed management.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Long-standing reliance on a small set of herbicides (especially quinclorac and imidazolinone mixtures) for barnyardgrass control in direct dry-seeded rice; limited adoption of non-chemical weed control at landscape scale; regional spread risk from neighboring resistance hotspots in South America.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of barnyardgrass biotypes with resistance to quinclorac, imazapyr + imazapic, penoxsulam and sometimes propanil, with several biotypes showing multiple resistance; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment and early spread of resistant E. crus-galli biotypes throughout Uruguay’s rice agroecosystems.
Review: retain - Uruguay’s first confirmation of herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass involved multiple modes of action and biotypes distributed across essentially all national rice regions, threatening a major export crop. I corrected the event start year to 2013 (in line with weedscience.org entries for quinclorac and imazapic/imazapyr resistance) and reclassified it as re‑emergence (new resistant biotypes of a long-established weed) rather than first detection or intra-continental emergence. Given the national scale and multiple resistance, I recommend retaining this as one of the top 10 events.

EPP common name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in southern Chinese rice fields (post-emergence herbicide–intensive systems)
Event summary: A large survey of 58 E. crus-galli populations collected in 2021 from rice fields in Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan Provinces revealed widespread resistance to key post-emergence herbicides including ALS inhibitors (bispyribac-sodium, penoxsulam), ACCase inhibitors (cyhalofop-butyl, metamifop) and synthetic auxins (quinclorac, florpyrauxifen-benzyl), with many populations resistant to two or three modes of action, indicating a recent, severe escalation of multiple resistance in southern China; resistant populations have continued to challenge rice production through the mid‑2020s, while research has identified target-site mutations and upregulated detoxification genes underpinning the resistance and informing new management recommendations.
Mechanism or driver:
Drivers: Continued intensive use of a limited suite of post-emergence herbicides in high-yield southern Chinese rice systems; climatic suitability for multiple rice crops per year; limited alternative weed management strategies.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – high frequency of multiple resistance to ALS, ACCase, and auxin herbicides linked to ALS (e.g., Trp574Leu, Pro197His) and ACCase (Asp2078Glu) target-site mutations and strong upregulation of detoxification genes (P450s, GSTs, UGTs); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – multiple-resistant populations spreading throughout the surveyed provinces and posing risk to broader South China rice areas.
Review: retain - This recent South China episode documents extremely high frequencies of multiple resistance (ALS, ACCase and auxin herbicides) across 58 surveyed populations in Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan, with clear evidence of stacked target-site and metabolic mechanisms. I removed the intra-continental and re‑occurrence flags so that the event is treated as re‑emergence of highly multi‑resistant biotypes in an area where the weed is long established. Given the breadth of resistance and the importance of these rice regions, this event should be retained as one of the top 10.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Vegetables, fruit orchards (including citrus and other tree fruits), oil palm plantations, other plantation and field crops
Event summary: In 1990, Malaysian vegetable systems reported Eleusine indica biotypes resistant to the ACCase-inhibiting herbicides fluazifop and propaquizafop and to the PSI inhibitor paraquat, marking the start of a herbicide‑resistance problem in this weed in the country. Over the 1990s, resistant goosegrass spread across vegetable and plantation systems, and in 1997 a Teluk Intan fruit orchard reported severe control failure of glyphosate, with field and follow‑up trials confirming an 8–12‑fold glyphosate‑resistant biotype – the first such case globally in this species. Through the 2000s–2020s, repeated herbicide selection across oil palm, orchards and other crops led to multiple resistance to ACCase inhibitors, glyphosate, glufosinate, PS II inhibitors and oxidative phosphorylation uncouplers, making E. indica one of Malaysia’s most complex herbicide‑resistant weeds and a persistent management challenge.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive year‑round vegetable and plantation production with heavy reliance on a small set of post‑emergence herbicides (paraquat, fluazifop, glyphosate and others); limited rotation of modes of action; labour constraints favouring chemical over manual control; expansion of perennial crops (e.g. oil palm, fruit trees) where goosegrass thrives in inter‑rows. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via multiple target‑site mutations in ACCase (e.g. Trp‑2027‑Cys and other substitutions) and EPSPS (e.g. Pro106 substitutions and, in some populations, double EPSPS mutations), EPSPS overexpression and amplification, and non‑target‑site mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through prolific seed production and seed dispersal in plantation landscapes; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Malaysian agro‑ecosystems as resistant biotypes colonized diverse crops and plantation environments.
Review: Decision: retain – Key Malaysian herbicide-resistance milestones (ACCase and paraquat resistance in vegetables around 1990; first glyphosate-resistant biotype from a Teluk Intan orchard in 1997; subsequent evolution of multiple resistance including EPSPS double mutations) are supported by FAO, weedscience.org and mechanistic studies. No changes were made to geography, years or event typing; classification as re-emergence (novel resistant biotypes of an established weed) is appropriate and the event clearly ranks among the largest global Eleusine indica emergence episodes.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Coffee plantations (central coffee zone), rice, herbicide-resistant maize and cotton rotations
Event summary: In 2006, studies in Colombia’s central coffee zone documented Eleusine indica populations with reduced susceptibility to glyphosate in coffee plantations, signaling the emergence of resistance in a key perennial crop system. During the late 2000s–2010s, goosegrass control problems spread into rice and rotations with herbicide‑resistant maize and cotton, where glyphosate and paraquat were used intensively before and after crop establishment. By around 2016–2021, detailed dose–response and physiological studies confirmed high‑level resistance to both glyphosate and paraquat in goosegrass from central Colombia, with resistance factors up to about 10 for glyphosate and 7 for paraquat, making this the first confirmed multiple resistance (EPSPS + PSI) case for E. indica in the country and a serious threat to rice and HR‑crop productivity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive use of glyphosate in coffee, HR maize and HR cotton systems and paraquat for burndown in rice rotations; limited diversification of weed control tactics; increased technification and large‑scale monocropping of rice and HR crops. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence involving EPSPS target‑site mutations and/or overexpression, together with mechanisms conferring paraquat resistance (reduced uptake/translocation and altered oxidative stress responses), leading to multiple resistance to EPSPS and PSI inhibitors; Enhanced Transmission via prolific seed production and spread along mechanized production corridors.
Review: Decision: retain – Weedscience.org and Cenicafé reports confirm glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in Colombian coffee from 2006 and later glyphosate+paraquat multiple resistance in maize/rice systems, matching the stated timing, crops and mechanisms. The event is correctly framed as a national, multi‑crop re-emergence driven by resistance evolution rather than geographic spread; no structural corrections were needed.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Soybean, maize (corn), cotton and other grain/row crops
Event summary: From the mid‑2000s, Eleusine indica populations began to increase sharply in Brazilian soybean, maize and cotton fields under glyphosate‑based conservation tillage, initially as a troublesome but controllable grass weed. Over the 2010s, repeated glyphosate use in glyphosate‑resistant crop systems and heavy reliance on ACCase herbicides selected glyphosate‑ and ACCase‑resistant goosegrass across major producing regions, with resistant populations documented and spreading in South, Southeast and Central‑West Brazil. By the early–mid 2020s, reviews identified goosegrass as Brazil’s most troublesome weed in grain systems, infesting over 60% of grain‑producing areas and capable of reducing yields by more than 50% if uncontrolled, with multiple resistance to glyphosate and ACCase inhibitors now common.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Massive expansion of glyphosate‑resistant soybean, maize and cotton; widespread adoption of no‑till systems with glyphosate‑dominated weed control; limited rotation of herbicide modes of action; high cropping intensity and reduced tillage favouring E. indica establishment; economic incentives for low‑labour chemical control. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via EPSPS target‑site mutations, EPSPS gene amplification/overexpression, and ACCase target‑site mutations; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as highly adapted resistant biotypes expanded from local foci to dominate grain production landscapes.
Review: Decision: retain – Recent Brazilian syntheses document Eleusine indica infesting more than 60% of national grain area with potential yield losses >50% and multiple resistance to glyphosate and ACCase inhibitors, supporting this as one of the largest global emergence events. The timing (mid‑2000s onset with strong escalation through the 2010s–2020s), geography (Brazil, South America) and classification as re-emergence via resistance evolution are appropriate; no corrections were required.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: United States of America [2010 – Mississippi, cotton]; United States of America [2011 – Tennessee, soybean]; United States of America [2015 – southeastern turf and golf courses]
Host: Cotton and other glyphosate-resistant row crops; some turfgrass systems
Event summary: Around 2010, glyphosate‑resistant Eleusine indica was first confirmed in Mississippi cotton fields in the United States, following years of intensive in‑crop glyphosate use in glyphosate‑resistant cotton and soybean systems. Over the first half of the 2010s, additional glyphosate‑resistant goosegrass populations were detected in other southeastern states, including Tennessee soybean fields, alongside previously established dinitroaniline‑resistant biotypes in cotton and goosegrass resistance to various herbicides in turfgrass. By 2015–2016, work on a Tennessee goosegrass population showed that a Pro106Ser mutation in EPSPS alone could confer glyphosate resistance, illustrating a clear genetic mechanism and highlighting goosegrass as an emerging, multi‑herbicide‑resistant weed threat in US row crops and turf.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term reliance on glyphosate in glyphosate‑resistant cotton, soybean and maize with minimal diversification of weed control; historical dependence on dinitroaniline pre‑emergence herbicides in cotton; high selection pressure in warm‑season turfgrass under frequent herbicide applications. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via EPSPS Pro106Ser and other mutations, plus earlier dinitroaniline resistance arising from altered microtubule targets; Enhanced Transmission through seed movement with farm machinery and in turf sod; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as resistant biotypes adapted to both agricultural fields and managed turf environments.
Review: Decision: retain – USDA‑ARS and weedscience.org confirm first US glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in Mississippi cotton in 2010, followed by Tennessee cases with an EPSPS Pro106Ser mutation and numerous earlier dinitroaniline‑resistant populations in cotton and turf. Geography, timing and framing as a re-emergence via resistance evolution (not an inter‑continental spread event) are accurate; only minor clarifications to the country field (making Tennessee and turf systems explicit) were made for clarity.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: China [~2010 – orchards and tea]; China [2020 – direct-seeded rice]; China [2018-2024 – sugarcane and citrus in Guangxi]
Host: Orchards (citrus and fruit trees), tea plantations, direct-seeded rice, sugarcane
Event summary: From the early 2010s, Eleusine indica became a dominant weed in Chinese orchards and tea plantations, where heavy glyphosate use led to the evolution of glyphosate‑resistant populations with EPSPS overexpression and Pro106 mutations. Around 2020, a goosegrass population from direct‑seeded rice in Jiangsu was confirmed to have multiple resistance to cyhalofop‑butyl (ACCase inhibitor) and glyphosate, coinciding with a shift toward direct‑seeding practices and increased grass‑weed pressure. By the early 2020s, multiple‑herbicide‑resistant goosegrass populations were also reported in sugarcane and citrus in Guangxi Province, including combined resistance to glyphosate, paraquat and PS II inhibitors, causing serious control failures in perennial crop systems and threatening rice and sugarcane yields.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Transition to direct‑seeded rice and reduced tillage, favouring grass‑weed proliferation; intensive glyphosate, ACCase inhibitor and glufosinate/PS II herbicide use in orchards, tea and sugarcane; climatic suitability for C4 grasses in southern China; limited integration of non‑chemical weed management. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via ACCase target‑site mutations (e.g. Asp‑2078‑Gly) conferring cyhalofop resistance, EPSPS overexpression and point mutations for glyphosate resistance, and EPSPS amplification plus non‑target‑site mechanisms underpinning multiple resistance to glyphosate, paraquat and PS II herbicides; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Multiple Resistance (stacked resistance to several modes of action); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as resistant biotypes spread within southern Chinese agro‑ecosystems.
Review: Decision: retain – Chinese studies document glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in orchards/tea, multiple resistance to cyhalofop-butyl+glyphosate in direct‑seeded rice (Jiangsu) and complex multi‑resistance in sugarcane and citrus in Guangxi, matching the crops, geography and mechanisms described. The event is correctly treated as a re-emergence via new resistant biotypes in an already widespread weed; no changes to event type or core structure were needed.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: Indonesia [2012 – oil palm nurseries and plantations]; Indonesia [2019 – North Sumatra plantations]; Indonesia [2020-2023 – Lampung, Riau, West Kalimantan, Java, Bangka Belitung, South Sulawesi, North Sumatra (maize)]
Host: Oil palm plantations and nurseries; maize (corn) fields
Event summary: By the early 2010s, Indonesian oil palm nurseries and plantations were reporting Eleusine indica becoming dominant after repeated herbicide use, with early work noting poor control by glyphosate and the need for alternative graminicides. In 2012–2019, glyphosate‑ and paraquat‑resistant goosegrass was confirmed in North Sumatra oil palm, and subsequent studies showed additional resistance to ammonium glufosinate and widespread multiple‑resistant populations in Riau and West Kalimantan. By 2023–2025, greenhouse screening of maize‑field populations across six major maize‑producing provinces found widespread atrazine resistance and emerging mesotrione resistance in goosegrass, indicating multiple resistance across PS II and HPPD inhibitors on top of previously documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance and raising concerns for both oil palm and maize productivity.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Monoculture oil palm with frequent non‑rotated use of glyphosate, paraquat and glufosinate in plantation inter‑rows; intensification of maize production with heavy reliance on atrazine–mesotrione mixtures; lack of crop and herbicide rotation; limited awareness of resistance principles among smallholders. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance indices up to ~4–6, confirmed glufosinate resistance in some biotypes, and greenhouse evidence of PS II (atrazine) and HPPD (mesotrione) resistance; involvement of both target‑site and metabolic (non‑target‑site) mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission through extensive seed production and local movement on contaminated machinery within plantation and maize landscapes.
Review: Decision: retain – Indonesian oil palm and maize studies consistently report glyphosate-, paraquat- and glufosinate-resistant goosegrass in North Sumatra, Riau and West Kalimantan and more recent atrazine/mesotrione resistance in maize across multiple provinces, justifying a single linked national event. The timing, geography and classification as re-emergence due to multiple herbicide resistance are appropriate; minor clarifications were added to the country field to make the provincial spread explicit but no re-typing was needed.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Sub-regions: Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Countries: Ethiopia [1990]; Kenya [1990]; Uganda [1990]; United Republic of Tanzania [1990]; Malawi [1990]; Zambia [1990]; Zimbabwe [1990]; Nigeria [1990]
Host: Finger millet (Eleusine coracana) and other smallholder cereal systems, plus associated crops
Event summary: Since at least the 1990s, Eleusine indica has been recognized as a severe weed competitor of finger millet and other small cereals across East, Southern and parts of West Africa, where it shares ancestry and ecological niches with the crop species Eleusine coracana. As smallholder cereal production intensified with limited access to selective herbicides, goosegrass spread in fields and along paths and fallows, increasingly competing for water and nutrients in drought‑prone environments. By the 2000s–2020s, agronomy manuals and extension materials for finger‑millet management in Eastern, Southern and West Africa (e.g. Northern Plateau State in Nigeria) routinely highlighted Indian goosegrass and related wild Eleusine as key yield‑limiting weeds requiring proactive cultural and manual control, reflecting a sustained re‑occurrence and intensification of its impact rather than a new geographic invasion or herbicide‑resistant biotype.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of finger‑millet and other cereal cultivation under low external input conditions; frequent drought and high temperatures favouring C4 grasses like E. indica; limited availability and affordability of selective herbicides, leading to primarily manual control and allowing chronic low‑level infestations to increase; soil disturbance and grazing patterns that create open niches for annual grasses. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) and Enhanced Transmission through prolific seed production and efficient colonization of disturbed, droughty soils; no specific herbicide‑resistance mechanism has been documented as a major driver in these regions, so the event is characterized as Re‑occurrence driven by external agronomic and climatic factors rather than Re‑emergence via genetic change.
Review: Decision: review – The characterization of Eleusine indica as a chronic, severe weed of finger millet and small cereals in East and Southern Africa is supported by PROTA/PROSEA and finger-millet weed-management reviews, and Nigerian data indicate major goosegrass infestation in Northern Plateau State, justifying inclusion of Western Africa and Nigeria. However, the start year (1990) and multi‑country coverage are approximate rather than based on specific dated outbreaks, and impacts are inferred rather than quantified; I therefore expanded the sub_regions and countries to include West Africa/Nigeria and replaced Wikipedia citations with more specialised agronomy sources, but recommend expert review of the temporal window and country list.

EPP common name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: Mexico [2016 – Veracruz and Puebla citrus region]
Host: Persian lime and orange citrus groves
Event summary: Between roughly 2010 and 2016, intensive glyphosate use (3–4 applications per year for 15+ years) in Persian lime and orange groves in the Gulf of Mexico citrus region selected Eleusine indica populations with reduced glyphosate susceptibility, culminating in the first confirmed glyphosate‑resistant goosegrass in Mexico around 2016. Detailed physiological and molecular work on biotypes from Persian lime and orange groves in Martínez de la Torre, Veracruz, showed that resistant populations combined an EPSPS Pro106Ser mutation with EPSPS overexpression and reduced glyphosate translocation, giving resistance indices up to ~16 compared with susceptible biotypes. Subsequent management and economic analyses in nearby Persian lime groves documented that glyphosate‑resistant weeds (including goosegrass) substantially increased herbicide costs and forced growers to adopt alternative programmes based on glufosinate and residual herbicides, making this one of the most impactful Eleusine indica resistance episodes in Latin American perennial crops.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term near-exclusive use of glyphosate in Persian lime and orange groves in Veracruz and Puebla (4–6 applications per year at 720–1080 g ae ha−1) with little rotation of modes of action; economic incentives favouring cheap glyphosate over more expensive residual or diversified programmes; high perennial-crop value and year‑round groundcover producing continuous weed selection. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via an EPSPS Pro106Ser target‑site mutation plus EPSPS overexpression and non‑target‑site reduced translocation, conferring moderate‑to‑high glyphosate resistance in multiple goosegrass biotypes; Enhanced Transmission through seed dispersal within citrus orchards and along farm tracks.
Review: Decision: review – This new event was added because glyphosate-resistant Eleusine indica in Mexican citrus groves (Veracruz/Puebla) is well documented mechanistically (EPSPS Pro106Ser + overexpression and reduced translocation) and economically (resistant weeds significantly increase weed-control costs), and likely ranks among the top global Eleusine indica emergence episodes in perennial crops. I set the event window to 2016–2020 (first confirmed resistance around 2016, with management trials in 2014–2015 and ongoing impacts) and classified it as re-emergence driven by resistance evolution; subject-matter experts should confirm whether this timeframe and impact ranking are appropriate and whether to further refine the end year based on newer monitoring data.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Urban lawns, road verges and other disturbed ruderal sites in the Lyon agglomeration, with limited potential spillover into nearby gardens and field margins
Event summary: In 1995, Eleusine tristachya was first noticed in the Lyon agglomeration of eastern France on a roadside embankment at Chaponost and at a few additional disturbed urban sites, extending its known French range from earlier records confined to the south‑west Atlantic coast.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) Subsequent botanical surveys through the late 1990s and early 2000s recorded a small but increasing number of local populations around Lyon, indicating successful establishment in urban ruderal habitats while remaining much less expansive than the congener E. indica.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) By the mid‑2000s the species was regarded as locally naturalised in parts of Lyon but still rare in France overall, with spread largely limited to dry, disturbed sites along roads and in built‑up areas.([biblio.cbnpmp.fr](https://biblio.cbnpmp.fr/doc_num.php?explnum_id=7985))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion along transport corridors and in urban disturbed habitats in southern and eastern France, facilitated by vehicle traffic, movements of soil and construction materials, and warm, dry microclimates along roads and railways that mimic the species’ subtropical native conditions.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or physiological novelty has been reported for French populations; floristic treatments regard them as similar to South American material, so this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of pre‑existing genotypes rather than evolution of new biotypes.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2))
Review: Review – Reclassified this episode as a re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence. Eleusine tristachya was already recorded in south‑west France well before 1995, so the Lyon discovery represents a local resurgence within the same UNSD sub‑region (Western Europe), not colonisation of a new European sub‑region.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) The event is retained as one of the few well‑documented post‑1990 expansions in Europe, but its impact is modest (small ruderal populations with little documented crop damage), so it may be dropped if a stricter top‑10‑by‑impact filter is later applied.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Field margins, waste ground and cropped fields in Kanagawa Prefecture receiving cattle‑manure amendments (including vegetable and arable land adjacent to cattle feedlots)
Event summary: In 1998, Eleusine tristachya was collected for the first time in Japan in Kanagawa Prefecture, growing along fields fertilised with cattle manure near a feedlot, and Koba & Matsumoto (2003) described it as a newly naturalised alien grass.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) Subsequent observations at and near the original sites showed that populations persisted and set seed over multiple years, indicating successful establishment in disturbed agricultural margins and waste ground. Japanese naturalised‑plant lists compiled in the 2000s then treated E. tristachya as a casual to naturalised exotic with a restricted distribution, completing an inter‑continental colonisation from South America to eastern Asia while the species remained a minor weed.([rib.okayama-u.ac.jp](https://www.rib.okayama-u.ac.jp/wild/kika_table.htm))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction as a contaminant of cattle feed or forage imported from regions where Eleusine tristachya is common, with subsequent spread via manure application to fields; establishment was facilitated by disturbed, well‑drained soils in peri‑urban agriculture and transport of contaminated soil or machinery.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No herbicide resistance, host shift or other specific evolutionary changes have been documented in Japanese populations; establishment appears driven primarily by propagule pressure and environmental suitability rather than novel biotypes.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2))
Review: Retain – Evidence from Koba & Matsumoto (2003) clearly documents Eleusine tristachya as newly naturalised in Japan from collections in 1998 near manure‑amended fields, with no prior Japanese records.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) At the time of that work the species was known to be naturalised in North America and Africa but not in Asia, and later databases list only Japan and the Caucasus as Asian regions of naturalisation.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2)) Given the lack of older, well‑dated Caucasus records, classifying this as an inter‑continental emergence into Asia is reasonable, though future herbarium studies could refine which Asian region holds the true earliest record.

Host: Perennial tree and vine crops (especially almond, walnut and prune orchards) and adjacent non‑crop ground in California’s Central Valley and other warm regions of the western United States
Event summary: Although threespike goosegrass has been present in California since at least 1967,([wcngg.com](https://wcngg.com/2019/09/01/threespike-goosegrass-presents-orchard-challenges/)) it was only from the late 2000s and early 2010s that growers and weed scientists began reporting it as a serious problem in tree‑nut orchards of the Central Valley. Extension blogs and trade articles from the 2010s describe rapidly expanding, dense patches in almond, walnut and prune orchards, where the low, tufted growth interferes with irrigation and mechanical nut harvest and proves difficult to control with standard glyphosate‑based programmes.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Herbicide trials conducted between 2016 and 2019 at multiple orchard sites confirmed the species’ poor response to glyphosate alone and evaluated alternative pre‑emergence and post‑emergence herbicide combinations, leading to updated management recommendations and underscoring a sustained resurgence of Eleusine tristachya as a key orchard weed through at least 2023.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/675acd4e0ce2cede71d18f38))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of California tree‑nut acreage and a shift toward glyphosate‑based, reduced‑tillage orchard‑floor management created wide strips of disturbed, irrigated ground in which tufted, warm‑season grasses such as threespike goosegrass can thrive; repeated glyphosate use, limited mechanical disturbance and traffic along tree rows facilitated the build‑up and spread of dense clumps.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Internal mechanisms: Greenhouse dose–response work and field trials show that established E. tristachya plants survive very high glyphosate rates and often resume growth, indicating strong innate or slowly selected tolerance, but there is still no published molecular evidence for specific target‑site or metabolic resistance mutations in this species; the episode is therefore best interpreted as a re‑occurrence driven by management practices and physiological tolerance rather than a clearly defined new resistant biotype.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses))
Review: Review – Updated the event period from 2010–2020 to 2010–2023 to reflect the continued importance of threespike goosegrass in California nut orchards and recently published herbicide‑trial data.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/675acd4e0ce2cede71d18f38)) Reinterpreted the episode as a management‑driven resurgence within an area where the species has been present since at least 1967, keeping the classification as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence, because field and greenhouse studies show strong tolerance and poor control with glyphosate but do not yet document a specific resistance mutation.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Source URLs were adjusted to emphasise orchard‑specific extension and peer‑reviewed literature (UCANR blog, West Coast Nut article, HortTechnology trials, Calflora distribution) and to drop a mechanistic paper on glyphosate resistance in Eleusine indica that did not provide primary data on E. tristachya.

Host: Citrus spp. (especially satsuma mandarin and other susceptible cultivars in northern Uruguay)
Event summary: From the mid-1990s, as Uruguay expanded export-oriented satsuma mandarin and other citrus production in its northern regions, citrus scab caused by Elsinoë fawcettii became a major constraint, with field trials reporting that up to 98% of fruit in untreated plots had to be rejected for the fresh market due to severe scab lesions. Intensive reliance on benzimidazole fungicides for scab control selected for resistant E. fawcettii strains, and by the late 1990s benzimidazole-tolerant populations were documented in northern Uruguay, causing frequent spray failures and serious quality losses. By around 2000, adoption of alternative fungicides and improved management reduced disease incidence in treated blocks to below about 1–8%, stabilising export quality but at the cost of more complex and expensive spray programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of export-oriented citrus production in northern Uruguay in the 1990s increased the area planted to susceptible satsuma mandarins and other cultivars, while humid conditions and dense canopies in commercial orchards favoured severe scab epidemics; heavy, repeated use of benzimidazole fungicides created strong selection pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antifungal resistance (emergence of benzimidazole-tolerant E. fawcettii strains documented by Bernal 2000 and cited in EFSA and EPPO assessments); associated shifts in pathogen population structure under fungicide selection pressure.
Review: Decision: Review (new high-impact event added). Rationale: EFSA pest categorisation and the EPPO datasheet report that in Uruguay, up to 98% of fruit in untreated plots had to be rejected because of citrus scab and that benzimidazole-tolerant strains of E. fawcettii were detected in the northern citrus area in the late 1990s, with Bernal (2000) providing primary evidence of resistance and fungicide trials. This clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for this pathogen. The event is classified as re‑emergence because the pathogen was already present in Uruguay before 1990 and the key novelty is the evolution of fungicide-resistant strains and associated epidemic severity. The 1995–2000 period is inferred from the JICA citrus protection project window and the timing of Bernal’s 2000 report and should be checked against the original proceedings paper for more precise start and end years.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Citrus spp. (mainly lemons and other susceptible citrus in commercial orchards)
Event summary: In October 1999, citrus orchards in New Zealand were found to harbour Elsinoë fawcettii populations resistant to the systemic benzimidazole fungicide benomyl, confirming active citrus scab in the country and reduced efficacy of a key control product. Over the following seasons around 2000–2001, surveys and research showed benomyl‑resistant strains becoming prevalent in affected orchards, complicating management of scab on lemons and other susceptible citrus. Growers responded by shifting to alternative fungicides and integrated control strategies, stabilising disease losses but with higher management costs and the need for resistance‑management programmes.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive use of benzimidazole fungicides in New Zealand citrus orchards selected for resistant E. fawcettii populations; humid coastal climates favoured repeated infection cycles. Internal mechanisms: Antifungal resistance (development of benomyl-resistant strains); possible associated shifts in pathogen population structure under fungicide selection pressure.
Review: Decision: Retain. Evidence from the EPPO Reporting Service 2002/107 and the EPPO Global Database confirms that benomyl resistance in Elsinoë fawcettii was first observed in New Zealand citrus orchards in October 1999 and that this followed earlier establishment of the pathogen in the country. The event is correctly classified as re‑emergence because it reflects the evolution of fungicide resistance (an internal change in the pathogen) in an already affected subregion, not a new geographic occurrence. Geographic fields (continent: Oceania; sub-region: Australia and New Zealand; country: New Zealand) are consistent with UNSD groupings, and the selected sources are appropriate and specific to this resistance episode.

Countries: China [2010s, major citrus-growing provinces including Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan, Zhejiang]
Host: Multiple Citrus spp. (including satsuma mandarin, pomelo, lemons, tangelos and other commercial citrus cultivars)
Event summary: In the early 2010s, Chinese researchers collected Elsinoë fawcettii isolates from major citrus‑growing regions across China to investigate serious scab problems on a range of citrus cultivars. By 2014, pathogenicity and molecular analyses revealed at least 11 distinct pathotypes in China, including a newly described SM pathotype and additional host‑specialised variants affecting key commercial citrus types. Recognition of these diverse and sometimes newly defined pathotypes highlighted that citrus scab had diversified and adapted to different citrus hosts in China, prompting renewed efforts to tailor cultivar choice and fungicide programmes to local pathotype structure and helping stabilise disease impacts where those measures were adopted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large-scale, diverse citrus production across humid regions of China provided multiple host niches and continuous inoculum; climate conditions (warm, wet) favoured repeated infection cycles and selection for locally adapted strains. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (identification of at least one new pathotype – SM – and additional host-specialised pathotypes of E. fawcettii); host expansion and increased host specificity across different citrus cultivars; underlying genetic diversification documented by ITS and ISSR markers.
Review: Decision: Retain. Hou et al. (2014) and Hyun et al. (2009) document substantial pathotype and genetic diversity of E. fawcettii in China and worldwide, including the description of new pathotypes (such as SM) and evidence of host-specialised variants, which fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by internal evolutionary change rather than simple geographic spread. The geographic assignment (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) accords with UNSD classifications, and the sources used (primary Chinese pathotype study, global pathotype study, and supporting molecular/physiological work) are appropriate for this event. No corrections to event type or geography are required, but specific years of isolate collection (early 2010s) are inferred from the paper and thus the 2014 end date should be treated as approximate.

Countries: Georgia [2015, western Black Sea citrus belt]
Host: Citrus spp. (mandarin, lemon, orange, grapefruit in western Georgia)
Event summary: Between 2015 and 2017, systematic surveys in western Georgia documented citrus scab caused by Elsinoë fawcettii in nearly all surveyed orchards and citrus species, revealing widespread disease across the country’s humid Black Sea citrus belt. As the surveys progressed, high incidence and severity were reported across multiple municipalities, indicating that scab had become a major problem in this previously under‑documented citrus area of the EPPO region. Subsequent management actions focused on fungicide use, sanitation and regulatory attention helped to limit further spread beyond western Georgia, but citrus scab remains established there.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Favourable humid subtropical climate in western Georgia, expansion and intensification of citrus cultivation, and historically limited targeted control likely facilitated the build-up and high incidence of citrus scab; improved survey intensity in 2015–2017 also revealed the true extent of disease. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance mechanism was reported for Georgia; the event reflects increased incidence and documentation of existing E. fawcettii populations rather than demonstrated genetic change.
Review: Decision: Review (retain provisionally). EPPO distribution data indicate that E. fawcettii has been present in Georgia since at least the 1980s (CABI Disease Map 125, 1986), with the 2015–2017 surveys showing that the pathogen is now widespread and causing high incidence across western Georgia. On that basis, the episode is best interpreted as a resurgence or increased recognition of disease in an already infested subregion rather than a first detection or new continental spread, so classification as re‑occurrence (with other emergence types set to “No”) is reasonable. However, published sources provide limited quantitative information on temporal trends in incidence prior to 2015, so the extent to which this represents a true resurgence versus improved survey coverage should be confirmed by expert review; no changes were made to the original event coding, but the event is flagged for further scrutiny.

Countries: Portugal (Azores Islands) [2021, São Miguel; 2023–2025, additional islands under eradication]
Host: Citrus deliciosa, Citrus limon, Citrus reticulata and other citrus in small orchards on São Miguel and other affected Azorean islands
Event summary: In July 2021, an official survey on São Miguel Island in the Azores (Portugal) detected citrus plants showing typical scab lesions, and laboratory analyses confirmed Elsinoë fawcettii as the causal agent—representing the first confirmed occurrence of this pathogen in Portugal and in European Union territory. Subsequent delimiting surveys and EPPO reports documented additional outbreaks on São Miguel, and later on Faial and Santa Maria islands, but not yet in mainland Portugal, leading national authorities and the EU to treat the incursion as a quarantine emergency under eradication. Ongoing eradication efforts, movement restrictions on citrus plants, and regulatory surveillance from 2021 through at least 2025 aim to prevent establishment and further spread within the Azores and to avert introduction into mainland Mediterranean citrus‑growing regions.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infected planting material or nursery stock into the Azores, combined with humid island conditions and sprinkler irrigation that favour scab development; increased phytosanitary surveillance under EU citrus health regulations enabled its detection. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance mechanism has yet been specifically reported in this incursion; its significance lies in geographic range expansion of an already cosmopolitan pathogen into a previously unaffected continent (Europe) and regulatory region (EU/EPPO).
Review: Decision: Review (classification corrected). EPPO distribution records and EFSA’s earlier pest categorisation indicate that E. fawcettii was long present in other continents but absent from the EU/European continent until its first detection in the Azores in 2021, and EPPO Reporting Service 2022/021 explicitly labels this as the first report for Portugal and the EPPO region’s second confirmed country after Georgia. Accordingly, the event is correctly an inter‑continental emergence into Europe, not a global first detection. The original row incorrectly set the 'first_detection' flag to 'Yes'; this has been changed to 'No' because first detection in the citrus host system occurred decades earlier in the Americas, whereas this episode represents first detection only in a new continent. Geographic fields (Europe, Southern Europe, Portugal – Azores) and the time span 2021–2025, reflecting initial detection and subsequent outbreaks under eradication, are supported by New Disease Reports and EPPO/NPPO updates and have been retained.

Countries: New Zealand (notably Central Otago and Nelson apple districts)
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event summary: From 1991 a national shift from conventional apple production relying on broad-spectrum insecticides to integrated and organic fruit production systems in New Zealand allowed woolly apple aphid populations to rebound in some regions, after decades of suppression by organophosphates. During the mid‑1990s, orchards in Nelson and in Central Otago (Clyde Research Centre) experienced marked surges of WAA during the transition phase, with infestation levels high enough to require specific aphicide interventions and detailed research on biological control. By about 1998–2000, colonization by the parasitoid Aphelinus mali and predator communities stabilized and suppressed WAA to acceptable levels in integrated and biological production blocks, effectively ending the outbreak phase though the pest remained present at low densities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Major production‑system change from conventional programs dominated by broad-spectrum organophosphates to integrated and organic systems emphasizing selective insecticides, which removed chronic chemical suppression of WAA and initially left a gap before natural enemies fully re‑established. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – no specific new biotype documented, but WAA’s ability to exploit unsprayed canopies and rootstocks facilitated rapid population build‑up once chemical pressure was relaxed; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – not at continental scale, but local expansion within and between orchards during the transition.
Review: retain – Well supported by New Zealand monitoring and integrated fruit production literature documenting a WAA resurgence in Clyde and Nelson orchards during the 1990s as broad-spectrum insecticides were removed. Continent, sub-region and country fields are correct, and classification as re-occurrence (management-driven resurgence in an already infested sub-region) matches the definitions. No changes were made.

Countries: United States of America (especially Washington and other Pacific Northwest apple regions)
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event summary: In the early 2000s, apple pest management programs in the U.S. Pacific Northwest reduced or phased out many delayed‑dormant and summer organophosphate sprays, which had previously kept woolly apple aphid largely incidental. Following this change, extension surveys and grower reports documented a noticeable rise in both incidence and severity of WAA infestations on trees and roots, making it again a key concern in Washington and neighboring states. Over the subsequent decade, growers adapted by altering insecticide choices, encouraging biological control, and refining monitoring; these measures moderated but did not eliminate recurring WAA problems, and the pest remains a chronic management issue in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Regulatory and market-driven reduction of broad-spectrum organophosphates, adoption of selective insecticides and mating‑disruption programs for other pests, and potential negative impacts of some new chemistries on parasitoids and predators of WAA. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – WAA’s waxy covering and protected root habitats reduced susceptibility to many newer chemistries, enabling resurgence once organophosphate pressure was removed; no specific resistance mutation is documented but functional tolerance to commonly used selective products is implied by management failures.
Review: retain – Supported by WSU extension and other North American sources showing that woolly apple aphid increased in incidence and severity in the Pacific Northwest after organophosphate use declined in the early 2000s. Geography (North America – Northern America, USA) and coding as a re-occurrence driven by management changes are appropriate. No field values were changed.

Countries: South Africa (Western Cape and other commercial apple regions)
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event summary: By the mid‑2000s, woolly apple aphid had become one of the key insect pests affecting export‑oriented apple orchards in South Africa’s Western Cape and newer production areas, after earlier historical outbreaks linked to breakdown of rootstock resistance. During this period, monitoring studies and industry reports highlighted WAA as a continuing cause of tree decline, fruit contamination and export rejections, with subterranean populations particularly problematic. In response, South African researchers and growers expanded monitoring programs and trialed new management tactics, including optimized use of parasitoids, cultural practices, and experimental biological controls (entomopathogenic nematodes and fungi), which helped reduce but did not completely remove WAA as a constraint on apple production and market access.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and expansion of South African apple production for export, which increased the economic visibility of WAA damage and phytosanitary risk; orchard floor and soil management practices influencing subterranean colonies; historical reliance on rootstock resistance that had been eroded earlier by resistance-breaking WAA biotypes. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – earlier emergence (documented by the 1960s) of WAA biotypes able to overcome M.793 and MM.109 rootstock resistance in Elgin created a genetically adapted pest complex persisting into the 2005–2015 period; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – continued spread and persistence of root and canopy colonies within orchards; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – difficulty of controlling subterranean colonies and their role as reservoirs sustaining arboreal infestations.
Review: retain – South African literature and industry reports consistently describe woolly apple aphid as a major pest of export apples in the Western Cape, with persistent problems from subterranean colonies and past breakdown of rootstock resistance. The 2005–2015 window reasonably captures the modern export-focused period when WAA remained highly impactful, even though serious issues began earlier. Geography and classification as a management-driven re-occurrence in an already infested sub-region are acceptable; no field edits were made, but users should note that this row summarises a long-standing problem rather than a sharply delimited outbreak.

Countries: Argentina (main documented context; pest present more broadly in South American pome‑fruit regions)
Host: Malus domestica, Pyrus communis, Cydonia oblonga (apple, pear, quince)
Event summary: Throughout the 2010s, Argentine phytosanitary and extension documents continued to describe woolly apple aphid as a widespread and economically relevant pest in pome‑fruit orchards, particularly on susceptible rootstocks and in intensive production systems. National pest profiles and technical manuals report damage to shoots, roots and fruit, including galling, premature defoliation and sooty mould in heavily infested orchards, indicating that high population levels can cause serious tree decline and quality losses. These sources recommend regular monitoring, resistant rootstocks and integrated chemical and biological control, but do not indicate eradication, so WAA remains a chronic management concern in parts of Argentina and neighbouring South American production areas.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of commercial pome‑fruit production areas in Argentina; climatic and management conditions favoring survival of both root and canopy colonies; possible disruption of natural enemies by insecticide programs targeting other pests. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – the species’ ability to form dense, wax-protected colonies on multiple plant organs and to overwinter on roots sustains high orchard-level populations once established; no specific resistance or new genotype was documented in the 2010s in Argentina.
Review: review – Retained as a candidate high-impact event representing the long-standing importance of woolly apple aphid in Argentinian pome-fruit orchards, supported by SINAVIMO and INTA documents. However, available sources describe WAA as a chronic, economically relevant pest rather than documenting a discrete 2010–2020 resurgence clearly linked to external drivers. Accordingly, the re_occurrence flag has been changed from true to false, and the event_summary wording has been softened to avoid overstating evidence for national high-impact “episodes.” Further expert review is recommended to confirm whether this chronic pressure should be represented as one of the top emergence events and whether the 2010–2020 window is the most appropriate.

Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event summary: In 2019, a targeted survey of apple orchards at Fushoushan farm in central Taiwan detected woolly apple aphid for the first time in the country, representing a new incursion into Taiwanese pome‑fruit production. The survey examined 12,082 apple trees between June 24 and July 5, 2019, finding 2,531 trees colonized by WAA, an orchard-level infestation rate of about 21%, with colonies showing an aggregated spatial pattern concentrated in higher‑elevation blocks. Following this discovery, researchers modelled the potential suitable distribution of the pest across Taiwan’s highland apple areas and recommended urgent control measures at Fushoushan plus intensified surveillance in nearby mountain farming zones to prevent further spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infested plant material or nursery stock into Taiwan’s high-elevation apple orchards, combined with climatic suitability of cool mountainous areas; the pest was treated as a quarantine organism due to its absence from Taiwan prior to this detection. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – intrinsic capacity of WAA to colonize new apple-growing regions with climates similar to existing infested areas; no evidence yet for novel strain, host expansion beyond apple, or changed virulence, so emergence is best interpreted as range expansion rather than genetic innovation.
Review: retain – The 2019 Fushoushan farm survey is clearly documented as the first record of woolly apple aphid in Taiwan, with quantified infestation (about 21% of 12,082 trees) and spatial analyses. Continent and sub-region (Asia – Eastern Asia) and the use of “Taiwan [2019]” as the country are geographically correct. Because WAA was already established elsewhere in Eastern Asia (e.g. China, Japan), the event is rightly not coded as first/global emergence, first detection (global) or intra-/inter-continental emergence. No field values were changed.

Countries: Belgium [2010] (Sint-Truiden region, representing Western European apple-growing areas with similar resurgence)
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event summary: From roughly 2000 onwards, regulatory withdrawal and restricted use of broad-spectrum insecticides in European apple orchards, coupled with increased reliance on selective crop protection products and biological control, allowed woolly apple aphid populations to rebound in many Western European production regions. In Belgium’s Sint-Truiden apple belt, a decade of detailed field monitoring from 2010–2020 documented recurrent high WAA pressure on trees and roots, prompting development of a knowledge-based decision support system to time interventions while conserving the parasitoid Aphelinus mali. Similar experiences reported from other Western European apple-growing areas led to renewed focus on WAA monitoring, trunk-targeted spray technologies and organic-compatible tactics, indicating a sustained resurgence phase rather than isolated minor outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: European policy-driven withdrawal and restriction of organophosphate and other broad-spectrum insecticides, adoption of integrated and organic production schemes, and milder winters that improve overwinter survival of WAA colonies; orchard intensification in key apple belts such as Sint-Truiden. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) at orchard scale – dense wax-protected aerial colonies and hidden root colonies make WAA less susceptible to newer chemistries and allow rapid recolonization once broad-spectrum suppression is removed; no clearly documented novel biotype has been linked specifically to this Western European resurgence.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well-documented resurgence of woolly apple aphid as one of the most serious apple pests in Western Europe following withdrawal and restriction of broad-spectrum insecticides, with intensive monitoring in Belgian orchards during 2010–2020. Classified as re-occurrence in a previously infested sub-region because the increase is driven by changes in pesticide policy, production systems and climate, not by a clearly identified new WAA strain. Time window (2010–2020), continent/sub-region (Europe – Western Europe) and the use of Belgium as the focal country are well supported but should be checked by experts for potential refinement of the country list and exact outbreak period.

Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), mainly intensively managed winter wheat
Event summary: From the late 1970s through the 1980s, wheat powdery mildew in China expanded from a largely local problem in the Yangtze River basin to a much wider distribution as wheat production intensified and semi-dwarf, high-yielding cultivars replaced traditional landraces. In 1990 and 1991, favourable weather, high planting densities, heavy nitrogen use and expanded irrigated area triggered a nationwide crisis in which powdery mildew epidemics affected wheat in roughly two dozen provinces, with tens of millions of hectares exposed and several million tonnes of grain lost each year. Following emergency fungicide use, adjustments in agronomic practices and greater attention to resistance breeding, national epidemic intensity declined somewhat after the early 1990s, although powdery mildew has remained one of the most important foliar diseases of Chinese wheat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification of wheat production in China, including increased plant population densities, higher nitrogen fertilizer inputs, expansion of irrigated area in northern regions and widespread adoption of high-yielding, semi-dwarf cultivars, created dense, humid canopies highly favourable for powdery mildew epidemics; conducive weather in 1990–1991 allowed the pathogen to spread across most wheat-growing provinces. Internal mechanisms: No single new strain is highlighted; the event is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven mainly by cropping-system and climatic factors acting on existing B. graminis f. sp. tritici populations, although local adaptation of mildew populations to modern cultivars likely contributed.
Review: review – New event added. Large-scale wheat powdery mildew epidemics in China in 1990–1991, affecting about two dozen provinces and many millions of hectares with multi-million-tonne yield losses, clearly qualify among the most impactful modern events for B. graminis. Classified as re-occurrence (disease resurgence in an already affected region driven mainly by intensification and weather) rather than first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence. Geography (Asia/Eastern Asia, China) and timing (1990–1991) are based on national surveys and review articles; specific provincial breakdowns are not listed and could be refined by a human reviewer.
