Countries: Germany [1998]; France [2003]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Denmark; Netherlands (Kingdom of the); Belgium
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) and barley (Hordeum vulgare) in intensive cereal production systems
Event summary: In the mid- to late 1990s, new single-site fungicides such as strobilurin (QoI) compounds and quinoxyfen were introduced widely for control of wheat and barley powdery mildew in north-western Europe, where B. graminis was already endemic on cereals. Within a few years of large-scale use, high-level QoI resistance in wheat powdery mildew was first detected in airborne samples from northern Germany in 1998, and by the early 2000s reduced sensitivity or resistance to both QoIs and quinoxyfen was reported from Germany, France and other nearby countries, leading to field control failures and the need to change spray programmes. By the mid-2000s, fungicide-resistant mildew populations were established across much of Northern and Western Europe, and powdery mildew re-emerged as a costly disease despite intensive chemical control, prompting the development of specific resistance-management guidelines for cereals.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very large and intensive cereal production systems in Northern and Western Europe, combined with heavy reliance on single-site fungicides (especially QoI strobilurins introduced from 1996 onward and quinoxyfen introduced in 1997), created strong selection pressure for resistance in B. graminis populations on wheat and barley; frequent applications over large areas amplified this effect. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/pesticide resistance – wheat and barley powdery mildew populations evolved target-site and related mutations (for example in cytochrome b for QoIs and in other targets for quinoxyfen and sterol biosynthesis inhibitors) that conferred reduced sensitivity or practical resistance to multiple fungicide classes, allowing the pathogen to cause damaging disease despite previously effective products and fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by internal pathogen change.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re-emergence episode, but details adjusted. Event years narrowed to 1998–2005 to match the period from first detection of high-level QoI resistance in wheat powdery mildew in northern Germany (1998) through widespread reports of QoI and quinoxyfen resistance and associated control problems across North-West Europe. Country list now highlights Germany [1998] and France [2003] where specific resistance detections are documented, while retaining other affected countries (UK, Denmark, Netherlands, Belgium). Classification as re-emergence (pesticide resistance) with intra- and inter-continental emergence marked ‘no’ is consistent with B. graminis being long-established on cereals in these regions. Human reviewer should confirm whether the end year should be 2005 or extended, given that multiresistance has continued to diversify after this period.

Host: Triticale (×Triticosecale) – hybrid cereal of wheat and rye
Event summary: In the early 2000s, breeders and pathologists in France and Germany began to report unusual powdery mildew infestations on triticale, a cereal hybrid that had previously been regarded as largely free of this disease, with first official trial infections documented around 2001 and subsequent observations in Belgium and Poland. As triticale acreage in Europe nearly doubled after 2000, mildew epidemics became increasingly frequent and severe, with reports from Central Europe of yield losses approaching one quarter of the crop in susceptible varieties and a first major national epidemic in Switzerland in 2005, leading to routine fungicide treatments and a shift in breeding priorities toward mildew resistance. By the mid-2000s, powdery mildew was widely recognised as a significant and economically important disease of triticale across Western and parts of Eastern Europe, marking the establishment of a new host–pathogen combination within the B. graminis complex.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of triticale cultivation in Europe from the late 1990s onward created large, contiguous areas of a relatively new cereal host that shared landscapes with wheat and rye, exposing it to high levels of B. graminis inoculum and favouring selection for triticale-adapted mildew. Limited initial genetic diversity for mildew resistance in commercial triticale cultivars further facilitated epidemics. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and novel strain/genotype emergence – molecular and population-genetic analyses indicate that the mildew infecting triticale represents a newly emerged lineage, B. graminis f. sp. triticale, formed by hybridisation and introgression between wheat and rye powdery mildew lineages and/or recent host-range expansion from B. graminis f. sp. tritici, resulting in a pathogen population able to infect triticale efficiently and in some cases also wheat, consistent with re-emergence driven by internal evolutionary change.
Review: review – Event retained but substantially revised. The original LLM row correctly identified host-range expansion to triticale as a key emergence phenomenon but limited it to France and used a broad 2000–2010 window; here the event years are narrowed to 2001–2005 to match documented first detections in French and German official trials, early reports from Belgium and Poland, and the first major Swiss epidemic in 2005. Geographic scope is expanded to Western and Eastern Europe with explicit country annotations where first observations or epidemics are reported. The mechanism description is updated to reflect current evidence that triticale mildew represents a recently emerged hybrid/host-expanded lineage within B. graminis. Classification as re-emergence (internal evolutionary change and host expansion) with intra-/inter-continental emergence marked ‘no’ is appropriate because B. graminis was already endemic on cereals in these European regions before triticale was widely grown. Human reviewer should check the exact first-report years per country and whether additional affected countries (e.g. Switzerland’s neighbours) warrant inclusion.

Countries: Argentina [1983 detection in Azul district; widespread in central Buenos Aires Province by the 1990s and now present in additional provinces such as Córdoba and San Luis]
Host: Soybean (Glycine max), sunflower (Helianthus annuus), maize (Zea mays), wheat and other cereals
Event summary: From the early 1980s, toothed spurge populations (now recognised as Euphorbia davidii) appeared in isolated soybean fields in the Azul district, central Buenos Aires Province, and by the early–mid 1990s the weed had spread across roughly 80–85% of the district’s cropland, becoming abundant in soybean, sunflower, maize and short‑cycle wheat. Through the 1990s and 2000s, demographic studies documented rapidly increasing field densities (often 20–200 plants m−2 and up to 300–900 plants m−2) and strong competitive effects, with about 30% soybean yield loss (≈700 kg ha−1) at 100 plants m−2 and significant reductions in pods per plant and other yield components. Into the 2010s and early 2020s, large and persistent soil seed banks (>20 000 seeds m−2) and variable sensitivity to glyphosate have made the species a chronic and difficult‑to‑control weed in conservation‑tillage soybean systems, prompting development of population‑dynamics models to support integrated management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of soybean and other summer crops in central Argentina; adoption of no‑till and reduced tillage systems that favour annual broadleaf weeds with persistent seed banks; and heavy reliance on glyphosate in transgenic soybean, which selected for populations tolerant to typical label rates. Movement of contaminated grain, seed and machinery within the Pampas facilitated spread between districts. Internal mechanisms: very large, long‑lived soil seed bank and strong seed dormancy; high fecundity; and high competitive ability at relatively low densities leading to major yield losses. Populations show variable sensitivity to glyphosate, suggesting early evolution of reduced herbicide susceptibility, although fully confirmed resistance biotypes have not yet been documented.
Review: Review – Retain this as the primary high‑impact event for Argentina but reclassify it as re‑occurrence (resurgence of an already introduced alien in the South America sub‑region driven mainly by changes in cropping systems and herbicide regimes) rather than re‑emergence, because there is no clear evidence that a novel biotype or strain triggered the outbreak. The event period is extended from 1990–2015 to 1990–2024 to reflect continuing high densities and yield losses documented into the 2010s–2020s; countries, hosts and sources remain appropriate and the event is clearly among the top global emergence episodes for this species.

Countries: Russian Federation [1961–1968 initial invasive focus in North Ossetia and near Pyatigorsk], Ukraine [1989 first record at Odessa port; 1990s spread along railways and later into sunflower fields], Republic of Moldova [1970s railways and arable land]
Host: Railway‑side ruderal vegetation; sunflower and other arable crops (onion, cereals, row crops, vineyards)
Event summary: Euphorbia davidii, first recorded (as E. dentata) as an invasive weed in the North Caucasus (European Russia) in the 1960s, expanded markedly from the mid‑1990s as contaminated grain cargo introduced it to major Ukrainian railway hubs and industrial sites, from which it spread along tracks and into nearby fields. During the late 1990s and 2000s, numerous new populations were reported along railways and in crop fields across Ukraine, additional regions of European Russia and neighbouring Moldova, with densities exceeding 30 plants m−2 in some abandoned Brassica and sunflower fields. Although detailed yield data are scarce, field observations indicate noticeable competition in sunflower and cereals and increasing concern about its further spread into additional arable land within Eastern Europe.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: large volumes of imported grain and oilseeds contaminated with E. davidii seed entering Black Sea ports and inland terminals, onward movement along dense railway networks, and extensive disturbance in industrial zones and along tracks that provided abundant open habitat; in some areas, reduced tillage and fallowing of fields facilitated establishment from roadside sources. Internal mechanisms: strong adaptation to disturbed, drought‑prone and nutrient‑rich soils and close association with transport corridors (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) with effective long‑distance transport as seed contaminants); a persistent soil seed bank supports local re‑occurrence once populations are established.
Review: Review – Retain this regional re‑occurrence event but update the country annotations to reflect current evidence: earliest European records are from North Ossetia and Pyatigorsk in the 1960s, Moldova in the 1970s and Ukraine from 1989 (Odessa port), with major spread along railways and into fields occurring in the 1990s–2000s. Classification as re‑occurrence (expansion within the already affected Eastern Europe sub‑region) remains appropriate, and the sources used (EPPO datasheet and Barina et al. 2013) are relevant, but the revised years and wording should be checked and aligned with any future updates to Ukrainian and Russian floristic syntheses.

Countries: France [1997], Belgium [1986 casual port and rail‑yard records], Netherlands [1964 casual roadside and car‑park records, later re‑identified as E. davidii], Switzerland [2011 industrial zone, Bussigny‑près‑Lausanne]
Host: Maize, soybean, vineyards and other summer crops; railway ballast and verges; riverbanks and ruderal habitats
Event summary: From 1997 onwards, E. davidii was repeatedly recorded in southern and later central France, initially in a vineyard near Nîmes and subsequently along railways, roadsides, riverbanks and in summer crops such as maize and soybean, with some maize fields hosting thousands of individuals. At the same time, port‑ and rail‑associated populations were documented in Belgium and the Netherlands, and an industrial infestation was found in Switzerland in 2011, all linked to grain and oilseed handling and transport corridors. By the 2010s–2020s, the species had become an established though still patchy agricultural invader in parts of France and a recurrent transient or localized weed around transport hubs in neighbouring Western European countries, prompting EPPO to assess its potential economic impact if it spread further into arable zones.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated introduction as a seed contaminant of imported soybean and maize grain into major Western European ports, subsequent redistribution along national and trans‑European railway networks, and the presence of disturbed, sparsely vegetated ballast, field margins and riverbanks that favour establishment; in cropping systems, maize and soybean rotations with reduced tillage have allowed build‑up of populations at field edges that can move into crops. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity and persistent seed bank enabling rapid population growth once established, phenological fit to late‑summer cropping systems, and strong competitive ability evidenced by very high plant densities in maize fields (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) and effective unintentional seed movement with bulk grain).
Review: Review – Retain this Western Europe event but restrict the sources to those that directly document French and neighbouring records (EPPO datasheet, the Girod & Fried conference abstract on France, and Barina et al. 2013) and remove URLs specific to Hungary and Spanish flora updates, which are not directly relevant to this episode. Classification as re‑occurrence within the already affected Western Europe sub‑region is appropriate, because casual records in the Netherlands and Belgium pre‑date the large French outbreak.

Host: Soybean and other summer crops (Italy); railway‑side ruderal vegetation and surrounding arable land (Romania, Bulgaria)
Event summary: In 1996, E. davidii was reported from northern Italy and soon after began to colonize railway verges and, later, soybean fields, where densities of 50–300 plants m−2 indicated strong competition with the crop. Around 1997 the species appeared along railway lines in eastern Romania (e.g. Iași, Buzău, Tecuci, Movileni), and by 2009 it had also been recorded in Bulgaria, mainly associated with rail infrastructure but with incursions into adjacent fields. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, these Southern and Eastern European populations persisted and slowly expanded along rail corridors and into nearby crops, raising concerns that this intra‑continental spread into new parts of the Mediterranean and Black Sea agricultural zones could precede broader establishment in regional cropping systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: contamination of imported grain and oilseeds entering ports on the Adriatic and Black Seas, followed by secondary dispersal via rail transport through Italy, Romania and Bulgaria; frequent disturbance and herbicide‑treated strips along railway ballast provided ideal establishment sites connected to surrounding arable land. Internal mechanisms: adaptation to warm, summer‑rainfall Mediterranean and sub‑continental climates and to coarse, well‑drained substrates, plus a large and dormant seed bank that allows populations to persist even when above‑ground plants are intermittently controlled (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Review – Retain this linked Italy–Romania–Bulgaria episode as the main intra‑continental emergence into Southern Europe, but correct the sub‑region field to include both Southern Europe (Italy) and Eastern Europe (Romania, Bulgaria) in line with the UN/UNSD regional classification. EPPO and Barina et al. (2013) support the timing and pathways. Classification as intra‑continental emergence is appropriate because this episode includes the first confirmed establishment of E. davidii in the Southern Europe sub‑region (Italy); spread into additional Eastern European countries within the same sub‑region is treated as part of the same linked episode rather than re‑occurrence in a separate row.

Host: Maize and sunflower (primary), other arable crops
Event summary: In 2007, dense populations of E. davidii were first recorded in arable fields in the Vojvodina region of northern Serbia, between the villages of Aleksa Šantić, Pačir and Đurđin, marking the species’ emergence within the southern Pannonian cropping region. Over the following six years the weed spread and formed increasingly dense patches in maize and sunflower fields, with infested areas expanding from about 3 ha to 7 ha in the monitored blocks and observational reports of sunflower crops suffering reduced plant and head size and up to 300 ha being taken out of sunflower production in favour of less valuable crops. By around 2014, despite trials with various herbicide treatments (notably high‑rate glyphosate) the species was recognised as a significant invasive agricultural weed in Serbia, with ongoing monitoring and management experiments recommended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated grain or seed (likely from other infested European areas) combined with intensive maize and sunflower cultivation in Vojvodina and limited crop rotation options that allowed rapid build‑up in specific fields; mechanical operations and local seed movement facilitated spread between neighbouring farms. Internal mechanisms: high seed production and a persistent seed bank that make eradication difficult once established, and strong competitive ability in row crops leading to economically significant yield impacts (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Review – Retain this event as a major high‑impact outbreak in Serbia but change the event type from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence. The Southern Europe sub‑region was already invaded by E. davidii through its earlier establishment in northern Italy; Serbian crop‑field infestations therefore represent a resurgence and spread within an already affected sub‑region, not the first intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region. The magnitude of impact (sunflower taken out of production on hundreds of hectares) justifies keeping this as a separate key event.

Countries: Hungary [2011, with farmer reports of presence since 2008]
Host: Maize
Event summary: In late August 2011, E. davidii was detected for the first time in Hungary in a maize field at Igar (Fejér County), where it had initially been misidentified as E. dentata before taxonomic revision. During the subsequent seasons, surveys and weed‑vegetation studies recorded the species at additional maize and sunflower sites, with ground cover in some maize fields ranging from 0.1% to 30%, indicating substantial local infestations within the national cropping mosaic. By the mid‑2010s, Hungary regarded E. davidii as a newly established but spatially limited agricultural weed requiring monitoring and preventive measures to limit further spread from the initial outbreak area.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction as a contaminant of maize seed or grain, as suggested by the Hungarian plant protection authorities, coupled with intensive maize production and climatic conditions suitable for late‑summer annual broadleaf weeds; absence of early detection allowed the first population to flower and set seed before control was implemented. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity and efficient seed dispersal within fields via tillage and harvest operations, and a life cycle synchronized with maize phenology, supporting re‑occurrence within the same Eastern Europe sub‑region rather than a single transient incursion (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Retain – This event accurately captures the first documented establishment and subsequent spread of E. davidii in Hungarian maize fields within the already invaded Eastern Europe sub‑region. Classification as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with earlier records from European Russia and Ukraine, and the sources (EPPO Reporting Service, Hungarian weed‑science article and EPPO datasheet) are appropriate. No structural changes are required beyond noting that farmers reported the weed from about 2008.

Countries: Australia [problematic weed of summer crops and fallows in northern New South Wales by 1995–1996; additional records in New South Wales and Queensland thereafter; new naturalised record confirmed for South Australia and the Northern and Yorke region in 2020–2021]
Host: Weed of cultivation and arable fields (especially grain sorghum and other summer crops, fallows and field margins); also roadsides and disturbed sites
Event summary: By the mid‑1990s, E. davidii had been recognised as a troublesome annual weed of fallows and summer crops in northern New South Wales, with herbicide evaluation trials in 1995–1996 showing poor control by several commonly used products and highlighting its tolerance to some knock‑down herbicides. During the 2000s it became more widely recognised as an introduced weed of cultivation in eastern Australia, particularly in grain‑growing regions, and herbarium and flora accounts documented its presence in New South Wales and Queensland. In 2020–2021, the State Herbarium of South Australia reported E. davidii as a new naturalised record for South Australia and the Northern and Yorke Landscape region, confirming its spread into additional Australian cropping landscapes; by the early 2020s, the species was considered a localised but potentially expanding agricultural weed across several Australian states.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental introduction as a contaminant of imported grain or seed from the Americas, followed by spread within Australia through movement of contaminated harvest machinery, soil and local seed, together with widespread cultivation of summer crops and fallows in suitable climates. Internal mechanisms: ecological plasticity allowing survival as a weed of cultivation across different Australian climatic zones and soil types; high seed output and persistent seed banks that support establishment from low propagule numbers; and partial tolerance to several herbicides, requiring targeted control strategies.
Review: Review – Retain this as the key inter‑continental emergence event for Oceania but broaden the event period to 1995–2021 to capture the documented herbicide‑trial evidence of serious infestations in northern New South Wales in 1995–1996 as well as the later recognition of the species as naturalised in South Australia. The added Australian Weeds Conference paper provides direct agronomic and herbicide‑response data for the mid‑1990s outbreak; PlantNET, Lucid and the SA Weeds Report support its current distribution. Classification as inter‑continental emergence remains appropriate because this describes establishment of E. davidii in a new continent.

Countries: Uzbekistan [first confirmed naturalised and invasive populations in the Fergana Valley and other regions documented by 2024]
Host: Ruderal and rocky habitats (roadsides, riverbanks, rocky slopes and disturbed ground); locally present near or in agricultural land and considered a potential weed of sunflower, cereals and other row crops based on earlier records in the wider region
Event summary: In the early 2020s, E. davidii was recorded for the first time in Uzbekistan, with field and herbarium studies documenting naturalised populations in the Fergana Valley and other parts of the country and leading to its recognition as a new invasive species for the flora of Central Asia. These records prompted inclusion of Uzbekistan in the EPPO distribution for E. davidii and confirmation of the species as a naturalised alien in national floristic projects. Although most documented stands so far are in ruderal and rocky habitats such as roadsides, river valleys and rocky slopes, earlier agronomic literature from the former Soviet Union indicates that the same taxon (then treated as E. dentata) can behave as a weed of sunflower, onions, cereals and row crops in neighbouring regions, raising concern that the newly established Central Asian populations could invade nearby agricultural land.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction most likely as a contaminant of grain or seed moved along Eurasian trade routes (including imports from already infested parts of the EPPO region), combined with increasing disturbance along roads, railways and irrigation infrastructure in Central Asia. Internal mechanisms: broad climatic tolerance and the ability to establish on dry, rocky and ruderal substrates; high seed production and a persistent seed bank that favour local spread once established; and proven weediness in similar continental climates elsewhere, suggesting strong inherent potential for geographic range expansion.
Review: Review – Add this new event as the first confirmed inter‑continental emergence of Euphorbia davidii into Asia (Central Asia), based on recent floristic work in Uzbekistan and EPPO’s distribution update listing the species as present and invasive there. At present the species is mainly documented in ruderal and rocky habitats, and direct quantitative evidence of crop yield loss is lacking, but the combination of invasive behaviour, naturalisation across multiple localities and prior evidence of the taxon as a weed of sunflower and cereals in the wider region justifies including this as one of the major global emergence events. Further monitoring should clarify the extent of agricultural impact.

Host: Arid and semi-arid rangelands, roadsides and disturbed fields on sandy or stony soils in southern Tunisia; weed in pastures and agricultural fringes.
Event summary: During the 1990s, Euphorbia glyptosperma was reported in floristic treatments of the arid and Saharan zones of Tunisia as a naturalized weed in disturbed rangelands and field margins, representing the first documented establishment of this North American species in Africa. By the end of the decade it was considered a regular component of some sandy and stony habitats in southern Tunisia, though still localized and largely associated with anthropogenic disturbance. Subsequent decades saw the species persist regionally without clear evidence yet of continent-wide expansion, but it provided the bridgehead for later spread elsewhere in North Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely accidental introduction with contaminated seed lots or grain and other traded plant material into arid agricultural and pastoral systems of southern Tunisia, combined with land-use change, overgrazing and soil disturbance that created open, sandy or stony microsites for colonization. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – a small, fast-growing annual producing many seeds and tolerating drought and nutrient-poor, disturbed substrates, facilitating establishment in North African desert and steppe environments without evidence for novel strains, herbicide resistance or host shifts.
Review: review – New event added to represent the likely first inter-continental emergence of E. glyptosperma in Africa, based on the Libyan paper’s citation of Chaieb & Boukhris (1998) and its statement that the species has been naturalized in Tunisia since the 1990s. The exact first-detection year and detailed habitat information in Tunisia are inferred rather than directly checked in the original flora, and the decade-long date range (1990–1999) is approximate; a regional botanist should verify the Tunisian record, timing and whether this event merits inclusion among the top-impact events.

Host: Ruderal and arable-land vegetation including disturbed field margins, railway verges, urban wasteland and riverine alluvial sands in Eastern Europe.
Event summary: From 1997 onwards, Euphorbia glyptosperma was recorded for the first time in Eastern Europe when naturalized populations were collected in multiple regions of south-eastern European Russia (Volgograd, Saratov, Astrakhan, Kalmykia, Dagestan and neighbouring areas), mainly along railways, roadsides and disturbed steppe margins. In 2005 the species was discovered in Romania along a railway near Ciurea (Iași County), and by 2009–2011 it had spread to additional Romanian sites around Galați and onto alluvial sands along the lower Siret River, while a small population was photographed in 2011 in northern Crimea, confirming its presence in Ukraine. By roughly 2017, floristic syntheses treated E. glyptosperma as a naturalized alien across parts of Eastern Europe, though still largely confined to disturbed and riverine sandy habitats.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance human-mediated dispersal with contaminated cereal or other seed lots and via transport infrastructure (railways, ports and major roads) appears to be the primary pathway into south-eastern European Russia, Romania and Crimea, with secondary spread along river corridors such as the lower Siret. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ annual life cycle, high seed production, tolerance of drought and nutrient-poor, disturbed substrates, and ability to exploit man-made habitats (ballast, levees, urban ruderal sites) facilitate its colonization of new areas within Europe; there is no clear evidence for novel genotypes or herbicide resistance specific to Eastern European populations.
Review: review – Event retained but corrected: (i) start year adjusted from 2005 to 1997 to reflect earlier collections in south-eastern European Russia; (ii) the Russian Federation entry now explicitly notes collections from 1997–2006; and (iii) the event summary was updated to integrate Russian, Romanian and Crimean records into a single Eastern Europe intra-continental emergence episode. Classification as intra-continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Europe) remains appropriate, but an expert should confirm whether additional Eastern European countries beyond Russia, Romania and Crimea/Ukraine need to be incorporated or split into separate episodes.

Countries: Peru (Arequipa region, Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve) [2010]
Host: High Andean puna grasslands, shrublands, roadsides and disturbed patches within and around the Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve in southern Peru; weed in natural and semi-natural pastures and open ground.
Event summary: By around 2010, floristic inventories of the Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve in Arequipa, southern Peru, documented Euphorbia glyptosperma as part of the vascular flora, noting it as a widely distributed species in South America and present in high Andean vegetation associated with Polylepis woodlands and puna grasslands. These records indicate that the species had successfully established self-sustaining populations in the central Andes, representing a major inter-continental range extension from its native North American range. Subsequent surveys suggest that E. glyptosperma persists in disturbed high-Andean habitats of southern Peru, though its broader South American distribution and agricultural impact remain poorly quantified.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction with contaminated seed, grain or fodder and movement along road networks serving Andean pastoral systems, together with grazing pressure and land-use change that create open microsites in puna grasslands and shrublands. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – tolerance of high-elevation cold, drought and disturbance and a weedy annual life history allow E. glyptosperma to colonize Andean rangelands once propagules arrive; there is no clear evidence yet for evolved changes in virulence, herbicide resistance or host range in South American populations.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first well-documented inter-continental emergence of E. glyptosperma in South America (Peru), based on floristic syntheses for the Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve and global distribution overviews. The event year is set to 2010 to reflect the date of the main published flora, but introduction may predate this; quantitative impact data are minimal and much of South America is unsampled. A regional botanist should verify the earliest Peruvian records, clarify whether the species is truly alien rather than overlooked native, and decide if this event ranks among the top-impact emergence episodes for the species.

Host: Ruderal weed in disturbed sites, roadsides and agricultural surroundings on sandy soils in the Sabha and Ariggiba regions of south-western Libya.
Event summary: Between 2023 and 2024, Euphorbia glyptosperma was collected from multiple localities in the Sabha and Ariggiba regions of south-western Libya, where it formed naturalized populations in disturbed sandy habitats, roadsides and fields. These finds represent the first confirmed records of the species for Libya but follow earlier reports that it had already become a naturalized weed in neighbouring Tunisia since the 1990s, indicating expansion within the Northern Africa subregion rather than a continent-wide first arrival. By the time of publication, Libyan populations were mapped and discussed as a potentially expanding alien weed, though their distribution was still limited to a cluster of sites in the south-west and no large-scale agricultural impacts had yet been documented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Probable accidental introduction into Libya via contaminated seed or grain shipments, or other traded plant materials moving within the Mediterranean basin and between North African countries, assisted by road transport networks radiating from Sabha and Ariggiba and by local agricultural disturbance creating bare, sandy ground. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ prostrate, seed-prolific growth form and tolerance of hot, arid, sandy soils allow it to establish in semi-arid Libyan environments once introduced; there is currently no evidence for novel genotypes, herbicide resistance or host-range shifts relative to other extra-limital populations.
Review: review – Original event retained but reinterpreted: evidence from the Libyan paper indicates that E. glyptosperma had already been naturalized in Tunisia since the 1990s, so the Libyan records represent re-occurrence within the Northern Africa subregion rather than an inter-continental emergence for Africa. Accordingly, the emergence-type flags were changed from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence, and the summary now frames Libya as the first national record within a region where the species was already established. A regional expert should confirm the Tunisian status, check for any other earlier African records, and validate whether this Libyan expansion should be kept as one of the major emergence events.

Internal mechanisms: characteristic invasive‑weed traits such as prolific seed production, explosive dehiscence and tolerance of disturbed, semi‑arid Mediterranean conditions enable naturalization in Northern Africa without evidence of new genetic change.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401132662_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_Euphorbiaceae_-A_new_distributional_record_for_the_flora_of_Libya))

EPP common name: milk purslane, prostrate spurge, spotted spurge, spotted sandmat

EPP common name: milk purslane, prostrate spurge, spotted spurge, spotted sandmat

Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, rapid life cycle, tolerance of trampling and heat‑exposed substrates such as pavement joints, and a creeping mat‑forming habit favour establishment and local dominance in heavily disturbed urban sites, supporting re‑occurrence at much higher densities; however, current evidence links expansion to these pre‑existing traits rather than to a newly evolved strain or host shift.

EPP common name: milk purslane, prostrate spurge, spotted spurge, spotted sandmat

Internal mechanisms: The same pre‑adapted traits seen elsewhere—low, mat‑forming growth, rapid seed production, and tolerance of drought and trampling—allow the species to exploit open patches in heavily managed urban landscapes and along infrastructure, driving re‑occurrence and progressive naturalisation across multiple Western European countries without evidence for a discrete new genetic lineage.

EPP common name: milk purslane, prostrate spurge, spotted spurge, spotted sandmat
Host: Warm‑season turfgrass systems, particularly seashore paspalum and other managed turf on golf courses and sports fields in the south‑eastern United States
Event summary: In a seashore paspalum turf field in Georgia, USA, long‑term exclusive use of the ALS‑inhibiting herbicide metsulfuron for broadleaf weed control led by about 2010 to noticeable control failures against dense populations of Euphorbia maculata. Subsequent greenhouse and molecular studies published in 2016 confirmed an acetolactate synthase (ALS)–resistant spotted spurge biotype requiring more than ninety‑fold higher metsulfuron rates for comparable injury relative to susceptible plants and carrying a Trp574Leu target‑site mutation that confers resistance to ALS inhibitors; the biotype also showed cross‑resistance to another ALS inhibitor, trifloxysulfuron. This finding represents the first documented case of herbicide‑resistant spotted spurge, and more broadly the first confirmed herbicide‑resistant broadleaf weed species in turfgrass systems in the United States, with important implications for future control costs and strategies wherever similar selection pressures occur.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Prolonged, repeated application of the same ALS‑inhibiting herbicide (metsulfuron) for more than two decades in warm‑season turfgrass created intense selection pressure favouring rare resistant individuals within dense spotted spurge populations. Internal mechanisms: A point mutation in the ALS gene (Trp574Leu) in the resistant biotype confers high‑level target‑site resistance to metsulfuron and related ALS‑inhibiting herbicides, representing a clear re‑emergence mechanism via pesticide resistance; continued seed production and potential pollen‑mediated gene flow raise concern about spread of this resistance trait to other populations and sites.
Review: Review: This new event is added because the confirmation of an ALS‑herbicide‑resistant Euphorbia maculata biotype in Georgia turfgrass represents a qualitatively different and globally significant emergence mechanism (pesticide resistance) within the species’ native North American range; it is classified as re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial/pesticide resistance, with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence component. The 2010–2016 time span brackets the first documented field control failures and subsequent publication of the resistance study, but users should confirm whether resistance has since spread to other states or hosts and consider whether additional rows are needed if distinct resistant populations are documented elsewhere.

EPP common name: eyebane, upright spotted spurge, nodding spurge
Sub-regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: Austria [~1990]; Hungary [~1990]; Switzerland [~1990]; Bulgaria [~1990]; Italy [~1990]; Romania [~1990]; France [~1990]; Portugal [~1990]; Spain [~1990]
Host: Arable land margins, railways and roadsides, urban wasteland, gardens and other ruderal habitats adjacent to a variety of crops and orchards
Event summary: Building on 19th–20th century introductions into Mediterranean Europe, Euphorbia nutans was widely reported between about 1990 and 2010 from railways, arable field margins and urban ruderal sites in Western, Southern and parts of Eastern Europe, including Austria, Switzerland, Hungary, Bulgaria, Italy, Romania, France, Portugal and Spain. During this period, national floras and invasive‑species syntheses increasingly treated it as a naturalized neophyte and an alien weed of orchards and other crops, though usually localized along disturbed corridors rather than dominating crop fields. By around 2010 the species was established across much of warm‑temperate Europe as a scattered but persistent ruderal and minor agricultural weed, with further expansion continuing into the 2010s.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑distance trade, rail and road traffic, and urbanization created abundant disturbed habitats and transport corridors that facilitated secondary spread of E. nutans across Europe; Mediterranean‑climate regions and irrigated ruderal sites provided suitable microhabitats. External drivers (transport, disturbance, climate) rather than changes in the plant itself underpin this renewed spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) via traits typical of Chamaesyce‑type Euphorbia (small annuals with high seed production, rapid life cycle and tolerance of trampling and disturbance), and enhanced dispersal along linear habitats such as railways.
Review: retain (with corrections): Supported by GRIN/POWO distribution data and recent European floristic work showing long‑term but still expanding naturalization across Mediterranean and Central Europe, and by an EPPO weed survey listing E. nutans as an alien troublesome weed in European orchards. Reclassified the event from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the expansion reflects external drivers (rail transport, disturbed habitats) acting on an existing alien lineage rather than documented genetic change. Kept the 1990–2010 window and country list as approximate, but note that many introductions pre‑date 1990 and that exact starting years by country would need refinement from national floras and herbarium data.

EPP common name: eyebane, upright spotted spurge, nodding spurge
Countries: Australia [naturalized in New South Wales pre‑1990; scattered records increasing by 1990–2010]; New Zealand [naturalized by 1883; additional localities recorded post‑1990]

During this period, regional checklists and databases documented its occurrence at multiple localities in northern New Zealand and in Australian towns, often in gardens, pavements and other urban or peri‑urban disturbed sites. Review: retain: Event appropriately characterizes continued ruderal and garden‑weed occurrence in Australia and New Zealand after 1990, drawing on New Zealand floras and global distribution databases. Event type as re_occurrence (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate, given that introductions to both countries pre‑date 1990 and there is no evidence for trait change. EPP common name: eyebane, upright spotted spurge, nodding spurge

Event summary: Within its native range in the United States, Euphorbia nutans has long been part of the flora, but from about 2000 to 2020 it became increasingly recognized in extension literature and weed manuals as a nuisance weed in nurseries, container crops, lawns, pastures and certain agricultural settings. Publications from states such as Arkansas and Tennessee, together with nursery weed‑management guides, highlighted nodding spurge as a common broadleaf weed of disturbed, irrigated substrates, sometimes appearing abundantly in pastures, hayfields and nursery beds. Despite its nuisance status, infestations were typically managed with standard broadleaf herbicides and cultural practices, so by 2020 the species was regarded as a persistent but manageable weed rather than a driver of large‑scale production losses.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensification and expansion of container‑based nursery production, irrigation, and long‑distance movement of potting media and nursery stock provided ideal conditions and dispersal pathways for this small annual broadleaf weed; reduced tillage and conservation pasture management may have favoured its persistence in some systems. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence of herbicide resistance; instead, basic life‑history traits (fast growth, prolific seeding, tolerance of repeated disturbance and a broad habitat range from lawns to catfish ponds) underpin its success as a nursery and turf weed within its native range.
Review: retain: Event is well supported by multiple North American sources (Arkansas weed manual, nursery‑weed control guides, state extension bulletins and herbarium records) that document E. nutans as a frequent weed in container nurseries, pastures and disturbed agricultural habitats during the 2000s–2010s. Event type as re_occurrence is appropriate because the species is native and long present; the episode reflects increased prominence as a weed under changing production systems rather than range or trait novelty. Minor textual nuances (e.g. attribution of some nursery‑weed comments to E. humistrata rather than E. nutans) have limited impact on the overall characterization but could be refined in a future edit.

EPP common name: eyebane, upright spotted spurge, nodding spurge

Internal mechanisms: No novel traits were identified; the event reflects geographic range expansion (inherent) of an existing alien lineage into new but ecologically similar railway‑corridor habitats within the already affected Eastern Europe subregion.

Adjusted the event type by removing re_emergence (no documented change in the organism) and retaining re_occurrence to represent spread within the existing Eastern Europe subregion driven by external dispersal. Internal mechanisms: Standard ruderal traits (annual life cycle, high seed production, tolerance of mowing and trampling) facilitated establishment in lawns and orchards, but there is no evidence of novel genotypes or increased aggressiveness compared with populations elsewhere.

EPP common name: eyebane, upright spotted spurge, nodding spurge
Host: Weed in farmlands (including olive groves and other crops) and disturbed sites in several agricultural regions of Morocco
Event summary: During field surveys in 2023 and 2024, Euphorbia nutans was recorded for the first time in Morocco as a naturalized weed in farmlands across several agricultural regions, including sites under olive trees and near seaports. Review: retain (new event): Added as a major recent emergence episode in Northern Africa, based on Tanji & Khamar’s study and the corresponding EPPO reporting note that identify E. nutans as a new naturalized weed for Morocco with multiple farmland occurrences. Internal mechanisms: As elsewhere, E. serpens' annual life cycle, prolific seed set, tolerance of heat and drought, rooting at stem nodes and C4 photosynthesis support rapid colonization of disturbed, well‑drained soils, enabling geographic range expansion within Western Asia; there is no evidence of novel strain emergence or herbicide resistance specifically associated with the Iraqi populations.
Review: review – Retain as the first documented national record for Iraq, but correct and flag for review. Updated the event year to '2021-2022' to match the primary paper, which reports collections during two growing seasons 2021–2022 with publication in 2022, rather than the broader and partly speculative '2020-2022' span. Adjusted the habitat/host description to reflect that records come from university fields and gardens in Baghdad rather than generalized 'agricultural surroundings'. Set 'first_detection' and 're_occurrence' to false, since this is neither the first detection in the plant host system globally nor a resurgence in a previously known Iraqi subregion. Pruned event-level sources to the dedicated Iraqi floristic paper plus EPPO for general context, removing a second article that focuses on Euphorbia maculata rather than E. serpens.

Host: Casual weed in ornamental planters, pavement and sidewalk cracks, and an abandoned citrus grove in urban and peri‑urban sites around Reggio Calabria (Southern Italy), associated with mixed ruderal and ornamental vegetation rather than specific crops.

Urbanization, road and pavement construction, and abandonment of small orchards and citrus groves create disturbed, open habitats in which the species can establish. Internal mechanisms: The plant’s mat-forming habit, C4 photosynthesis, tolerance of periodically dry, nutrient‑poor substrates, and high seed production promote persistence in cracks, planters and ruderal sites, supporting local range expansion in disturbed Mediterranean environments, but there is no current evidence of increased invasiveness, new genotypes or resistance traits in the Calabrian populations compared with previously established European populations.

The original entry incorrectly dated the Calabrian record to '2015–2021' and implied long-standing presence along riverbanks and agricultural margins; these have been corrected to a first record in 2022 confined to planters, sidewalk and pavement cracks, and an abandoned citrus grove in Reggio Calabria, as reported in Musarella et al. ("New Alien Plant Taxa for Italy and Europe: An Update"). Emergence-type flags have been set to false for all categories because this event does not represent first detection in the plant host system, nor a new continent or subregion, nor a documented resurgence. Host: Field and greenhouse vegetables (tomato, pepper, lettuce), strawberries and numerous ornamentals where damage was dominated by Tomato spotted wilt virus epidemics driven by F. occidentalis
Event summary: After first becoming established in Dutch glasshouses in 1983, western flower thrips spread southwards through the late 1980s into Mediterranean horticultural zones of Spain, France, Italy, Portugal and Greece, where Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) rapidly re‑emerged as the most serious disease of many vegetables and ornamentals. During the early–mid 1990s, explosive F. occidentalis populations along the Mediterranean coast drove large TSWV epidemics in tomato, pepper, lettuce and ornamentals, causing severe yield and quality losses and disrupting existing IPM programmes. By the late 1990s, F. occidentalis‑associated TSWV outbreaks were entrenched across much of Southern Europe, forcing widespread adoption of resistant cultivars, intensive vector control and new integrated management strategies.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FRANOC/distribution/NL))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive greenhouse and open‑field horticulture along the Mediterranean coast; high volumes of intra‑European trade in ornamentals and vegetable seedlings; climatic suitability for outdoor overwintering in southern Europe; and high local inoculum of TSWV and other tospoviruses in crops and weeds. Internal mechanisms: a highly efficient vector relationship between F. occidentalis and TSWV; introduction of insecticide‑resistant invasive thrips lineages from North America; and emergence of TSWV strains able to overcome host resistance genes, together producing a re‑emergent, continent‑scale epidemic complex.([resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1461-9563.2003.00192.x))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (i) Added France and Greece, and clarified approximate first‑record years for each Mediterranean country based on regional TSWV and F. occidentalis literature, to better reflect the scale of the 1990s epidemic. (ii) Reclassified the event as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence: spread from the original outbreak focus in the Netherlands into the new Southern Europe subregion represents intra‑continental emergence for F. occidentalis, while the dramatic resurgence of TSWV mediated by the new vector is correctly captured as re‑emergence. Rationale: This episode is one of the globally most impactful events due to very large areas affected and documented yield losses, so it should be retained but flagged for expert review of country list and timing.

Countries: Netherlands [1983], Denmark [1985], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1986], Germany [late 1980s], Belgium [late 1980s], Sweden [early 1990s], Norway [early 1990s]
Host: Greenhouse ornamentals (especially chrysanthemum, rose, gerbera, carnation, pelargonium) and vegetables (cucumber, tomato, pepper, lettuce) in temperate glasshouse systems
Event summary: From the early 1980s through the early 1990s, western flower thrips invaded commercial glasshouses across the Netherlands and neighbouring Western and Northern European countries, rapidly becoming the dominant thrips pest on ornamentals and vegetable crops. By the early 1990s, infestations in Dutch, Danish, British and German glasshouses were causing up to 20% yield loss in crops such as cucumber and severely disrupting established biological control programmes, as heavy insecticide use against F. occidentalis undermined parasitoids and predatory mites. This invasion episode marked the transformation of F. occidentalis into a major glasshouse pest across much of temperate Europe and set the stage for the continent‑wide TSWV epidemics of the 1990s.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FRANOC/distribution/NL))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive, year‑round glasshouse production of ornamentals and vegetables in the Netherlands and neighbouring countries; large‑scale movement of infested planting stock and cuttings among European greenhouses; and climatic buffering by glasshouses that allowed the invasive thrips to thrive in regions with otherwise unsuitable winters. Internal mechanisms: selection and global dissemination of highly insecticide‑resistant F. occidentalis strains from North American glasshouses; polyphagy and high fecundity enabling rapid buildup on many crops; and efficient transmission of TSWV and INSV, which greatly magnified the economic impact of even moderate thrips densities.([resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1461-9563.2003.00192.x))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. New event added to capture a major, previously omitted emergence episode: the early‑1990s transformation of F. occidentalis into a dominant glasshouse pest across Western and Northern Europe, which severely disrupted IPM and preceded the better‑documented Mediterranean epidemics. Classified as re‑emergence (introduction and spread of an insecticide‑resistant invasive strain causing dramatic increases in incidence and control failures in a subregion where TSWV and other viruses were already present). Country list and approximate timing should be checked by a regional expert.

Countries: Kenya [1989], Uganda [1990s], United Republic of Tanzania [1990s]
Host: French beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) grown for export, plus other vegetables (tomato, onion) and ornamentals in highland greenhouse and field systems
Event summary: Western flower thrips was first detected in Kenya around 1989 on export French beans and soon became established throughout the main highland production zones, where it quickly emerged as the most destructive thrips pest on French beans and other vegetables. During the 1990s and 2000s, F. occidentalis spread within the Eastern Africa subregion into Uganda and Tanzania and became a key pest and quarantine concern on French beans, tomatoes and other vegetables, with growers often applying 12–15 insecticide sprays per season and yet still suffering 20–80% yield and quality losses. By about 2010 the species was widely entrenched across Eastern Africa’s major vegetable belts, its impact amplified by tospovirus transmission and burgeoning insecticide resistance, and it is now a primary driver for development of thrips IPM and post‑harvest disinfestation systems in the region.([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/research-for-development-outputs/genetic-structure-and-diversity-of-western-flower-thrips-frankliniella-occidentalis-in-a-french-bean-agroecosystem-of-kenya))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of export‑oriented French bean and other high‑value vegetable production under favourable highland climates; intensive use of greenhouses and continuous cropping, providing year‑round habitat; heavy reliance on broad‑spectrum insecticides leading to strong selection pressure; and regional trade in seed, pods and ornamental cuttings facilitating spread among farms and countries. Internal mechanisms: high reproductive rate, short generation time and polyphagy on many crop and weed hosts; development of resistance to commonly used insecticides in East African populations; and high efficiency as a vector of TSWV and related tospoviruses, which can cause up to 80% yield loss in tomato and other crops in the region.([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/research-for-development-outputs/genetic-structure-and-diversity-of-western-flower-thrips-frankliniella-occidentalis-in-a-french-bean-agroecosystem-of-kenya))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Overall event retained as a major emergence episode for Eastern Africa, with timeline (Kenya first detected ~1989) and regional spread confirmed. Main change: event sources updated to rely more heavily on peer‑reviewed and institutional reports documenting first detection, genetic structure, dispersal, yield loss and spray intensity; less relevant or inaccessible sources were replaced. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (new African subregion) plus re‑emergence (introduction of an invasive, insecticide‑resistant strain leading to dramatic increases in incidence) appears appropriate but should be double‑checked by regional experts, particularly for the approximate first‑record years in Uganda and Tanzania.

Host: Horticultural and ornamental crops including tomato, pepper, potato, lettuce, onion, groundnut, grapes, stone fruits and cut flowers in open field and protected cultivation
Event summary: Western flower thrips was first reported in South America from Peru in the late 1970s, but its regional impact surged in the 1990s as the invasive greenhouse strain established and spread through Brazil, Chile, Argentina and neighbouring countries. By the mid‑ to late 1990s it had become a serious pest of fruit, vegetable and ornamental crops in central Chile and multiple regions of Brazil, where F. occidentalis joined or displaced native thrips as a principal vector of TSWV and other tospoviruses. Through the 1990s and 2000s, devastating tospovirus epidemics in tomato, pepper and other crops were reported in Argentina and Brazil, with local yield losses sometimes reaching 80%, and F. occidentalis is now recognised across much of South America as a key invasive thrips driving virus disease complexes in intensive horticulture.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/320938986_First_Record_of_Frankliniella_occidentalis_in_Greece))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of intensive vegetable and fruit production for domestic and export markets; large‑scale movement of ornamentals and propagative material within and into South America; and favourable climates in many Andean and subtropical regions. Internal mechanisms: introduction of invasive, insecticide‑resistant F. occidentalis lineages; highly efficient transmission of TSWV, Groundnut ringspot virus and Tomato chlorotic spot virus in tomato, pepper and other crops; and polyphagy that allows the pest to persist on weeds and alternative hosts between crop cycles, maintaining high virus inoculum pressure.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FRANOC/distribution/CL))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. New event added to fill a major omission: the 1990s–2000s spread and establishment of F. occidentalis as a key pest and virus vector in South American horticulture. Classified as re‑emergence at continental scale because earlier presence (e.g. Peru in the late 1970s) was followed by a dramatic increase in incidence and impact associated with invasive insecticide‑resistant lineages and large tospovirus epidemics. Approximate country years and host list should be checked by South American specialists, and it may be useful to refine which tospoviruses are dominant in each subregion.

Host: Mixed ornamentals and cut flowers (glasshouse and nursery crops), vegetables and seed crops (e.g. lettuce, pepper, tomato) and later field crops affected via Tomato spotted wilt virus
Event summary: In May 1993, western flower thrips was first detected on ornamentals near Perth in Western Australia, marking its introduction into the Australian portion of the Australia–New Zealand subregion. During the mid‑ to late 1990s the pest spread to other Australian states and became established in greenhouse ornamentals and vegetables and in some outdoor horticultural crops. Its arrival coincided with, and contributed to, severe TSWV outbreaks in vegetables and ornamentals in eastern and south‑eastern Australia, where it displaced or supplemented native thrips as a vector and necessitated major changes in virus and thrips management.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FRANOC/reporting))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: imports of infested cut flowers and ornamental plant material, particularly into Western Australia; protected cropping systems that provided suitable year‑round habitat; and increasing areas of intensive horticulture in coastal and irrigated regions. Internal mechanisms: invasion by insecticide‑resistant greenhouse lineages of F. occidentalis; high fecundity and polyphagy facilitating rapid establishment on many hosts; and its superior efficiency as a vector of TSWV relative to native thrips, which led to large disease outbreaks in susceptible crops.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/1744-7917.12721))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Kept as a major emergence event for Australia but with corrected classification: inter‑continental emergence is set to “No”, because Frankliniella occidentalis (or a closely related taxon) was already present in New Zealand by the 1980s, so the Australian incursion represents spread within the Australia–New Zealand subregion rather than the first occurrence in Oceania. The event is instead treated as re‑emergence of an invasive, insecticide‑resistant strain in a subregion where related lineages were already present. Host range and linkage to TSWV epidemics are supported but could be further refined by an Australian specialist.

Countries: Canada [1995], United States of America [pre‑1990, widespread greenhouse populations]
Host: Greenhouse ornamentals and vegetables (e.g. chrysanthemum, poinsettia, cucumber, pepper) in commercial glasshouses, particularly in Ontario and neighbouring regions
Event summary: By the mid‑1990s western flower thrips was well established in greenhouses across the United States and Canada, but in 1995 severe resistance to organophosphates, carbamates and pyrethroids was documented in multiple greenhouse populations in the Niagara region of Ontario, with clear control failures. Over the following years, similar multi‑class resistance problems were reported in additional North American greenhouses, leading to persistent, damaging thrips populations and increased virus transmission despite intensive spraying. These resistance outbreaks forced a shift towards resistance‑management strategies and greater reliance on biological control agents in North American protected horticulture.([hero.epa.gov](https://hero.epa.gov/reference/5203879/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: very frequent, often weekly applications of broad‑spectrum insecticides in greenhouse ornamentals and vegetables; continuous year‑round production in enclosed glasshouses, which allowed strong selection for resistance; and movement of infested plant material among commercial facilities. Internal mechanisms: rapid evolution of resistance to multiple insecticide classes, mediated by enhanced detoxification enzymes and modified target sites; high reproductive rate and haplodiploid genetics that facilitated the spread and fixation of resistance alleles; and behaviour (cryptic feeding in flowers and crevices) that further reduced exposure to contact insecticides.([hero.epa.gov](https://hero.epa.gov/reference/5203879/))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event retained as a major re‑emergence episode characterised by multi‑insecticide resistance in North American greenhouse populations. Minor textual clarification of the country field (explicitly dating Canadian resistance to 1995 and acknowledging earlier widespread establishment in the USA) has been added. Classification as re‑emergence only (no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) remains appropriate, as the species was already long‑established in the subregion and this episode is driven by internal evolutionary change (resistance).

Host: Ornamental and cut‑flower crops (Alstroemeria, Gypsophila and other ornamentals in nurseries and botanical gardens)
Event summary: In 1996 surveys of nurseries and botanical gardens in Sri Lanka detected western flower thrips on Alstroemeria and Gypsophila, representing the first report of the species in the country and, as far as current evidence indicates, the first occurrence in the Southern Asia subregion. Over the late 1990s it became established in multiple ornamental and cut‑flower nurseries, reflecting local spread in protected cultivation, and raised concerns about possible future spillover into vegetable and other horticultural crops in Sri Lanka and neighbouring countries.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3692))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: importation of infested ornamental planting material and cut flowers from regions where F. occidentalis was already invasive; concentration of susceptible hosts in protected nurseries and botanical gardens; and initially limited awareness and surveillance for exotic thrips. Internal mechanisms: high reproductive rate on ornamental hosts; polyphagy enabling persistence on diverse nursery plants; and efficient short‑distance dispersal within and between greenhouses.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3692))
Review: Decision: RETAIN. This event corresponds well to the documented first report of F. occidentalis in Sri Lanka and likely the first incursion into the Southern Asia subregion. Classification as first detection and intra‑continental emergence (new Asian subregion, given earlier records in Western and Eastern Asia) is appropriate, and no clear higher‑impact event in Southern Asia before India’s incursion has been identified. No changes other than clearer wording in the summary; still, a regional expert may wish to confirm that no earlier reliable records exist elsewhere in Southern Asia.

Host: Greenhouse and open‑field vegetables (pepper, cucumber, tomato, lettuce, corn, tobacco), ornamentals and other horticultural crops
Event summary: Western flower thrips was first intercepted in 2000 on flowers at an international floriculture exhibition in Kunming, Yunnan Province, and a self‑sustaining population was first reported in 2003 on protected crops near Beijing. Between 2003 and about 2010, the pest expanded rapidly from initial foci in Yunnan and Beijing to numerous provinces across China in both greenhouse and open‑field vegetable and ornamental systems, causing increasingly severe damage and virus transmission. By 2015, F. occidentalis was widespread across much of China, with repeated outbreaks on vegetables, ornamentals and tobacco and significant economic losses reported.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10231115/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: international trade in cut flowers and ornamental plants introducing the pest via Kunming; explosive growth of protected vegetable and flower cultivation across China; human‑mediated movement of infested planting material between provinces; and broad climatic suitability across many regions for establishment. Internal mechanisms: multiple introductions and bridgehead effects producing genetically structured invasive populations; high fecundity and polyphagy; geographic range expansion facilitated by adaptation to diverse climates; development of insecticide resistance in some Chinese populations; and efficient transmission of TSWV and other tospoviruses, amplifying yield impacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10231115/))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event kept as one of the largest and best‑documented emergence episodes. Corrections: (i) intra‑continental emergence set to “No” because F. occidentalis was already present in the Eastern Asia subregion (e.g. Japan from 1990 and Republic of Korea from 1994) before its establishment in China, so spread into China represents expansion to an additional country within the same subregion rather than a new subregion. (ii) re‑emergence set to “No” because this is the first establishment of the species in China, not a resurgence in an area where it was previously established. The event is now classified purely as country‑level first detection, with regional spread described narratively.

Countries: Spain [late 1990s], (primarily Almería and Murcia greenhouse complexes)
Host: Greenhouse vegetables (especially pepper and tomato), ornamentals and some fruit crops in intensive Mediterranean greenhouse complexes
Event summary: From about 2000 through the late 2000s, western flower thrips populations in intensive greenhouse production areas of south‑eastern Spain (notably Almería and Murcia) developed high levels of resistance to multiple insecticides, including methiocarb, formetanate, acrinathrin and later spinosad. During this decade, growers reported severe control failures and increasingly frequent thrips and TSWV outbreaks despite intensive spray programmes, making F. occidentalis one of the most difficult greenhouse pests to manage. By around 2010, resistance‑driven resurgences of western flower thrips had become a major constraint on greenhouse vegetable and ornamental production in Southern Europe, prompting the adoption of resistance‑management strategies and biological control.([nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ps.1620))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extremely intensive insecticide use in Mediterranean greenhouses, with up to 19 sprays per crop cycle and limited rotation of modes of action; continuous, overlapping crops providing year‑round habitat; and high density of connected greenhouse enterprises facilitating movement of resistant populations. Internal mechanisms: rapid evolution of high‑level resistance to acrinathrin, methiocarb, formetanate and later spinosad in Spanish F. occidentalis populations; metabolic resistance involving elevated esterase and P450 activity and target‑site modifications; and maintenance of resistance alleles under continual chemical selection, leading to re‑emergence and persistence of damaging thrips populations despite control efforts.([nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ps.1620))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event retained as a major resistance‑driven re‑emergence episode but country scope narrowed explicitly to Spain, where robust data exist on high resistance levels and control failures; evidence for similarly severe resistance in other Southern European countries is weaker. Classification as re‑emergence only remains appropriate, as the species and tospoviruses were already established and the resurgence is driven by internal resistance mechanisms. A regional expert may consider whether Italy, Portugal or Greece experienced comparable resistance problems that merit inclusion in this or a separate event.

Countries: India [2014–2015 (first confirmed records), later detections in the Nilgiris and other localities]
Host: Tomato (initial detection near Bengaluru, Karnataka) and occasional records on other crops and ornamental hosts, with potential to utilise a wide range of vegetables, field crops and ornamentals
Event summary: In 2014–2015, western flower thrips was formally reported for the first time from India on tomato near Bengaluru, Karnataka, based on morphologically and molecularly confirmed specimens, although earlier reports are considered doubtful. Subsequent surveys initially struggled to relocate the species around Bengaluru, suggesting a transient or localised population, but by 2016 a breeding population including males was confirmed on Erythrina in the Nilgiris, indicating establishment at least in parts of southern India. By around 2020, F. occidentalis was recognised by Indian researchers and NPPOs as a high‑risk invasive thrips with the potential to spread widely across India’s large horticultural and field‑crop systems and to vector multiple tospoviruses, prompting development of surveillance and management recommendations even though documented large‑scale outbreaks remain limited so far.([databases.nbair.res.in](https://databases.nbair.res.in/insectpests/Frankliniella-occidentalis.php))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: increasing imports and domestic movement of ornamental and vegetable planting material, including cut flowers and nursery stock; rapid expansion of polyhouse and net‑house cultivation that favours invasive thrips; and limited initial diagnostic capacity to distinguish F. occidentalis from morphologically similar native thrips. Internal mechanisms: invasion by genetically distinct F. occidentalis lineages documented by barcoding; strong polyphagy enabling use of many Indian crop and non‑crop hosts; and a high potential to vector TSWV and other tospoviruses, raising concern that small current foci could seed much larger future epidemics.([databases.nbair.res.in](https://databases.nbair.res.in/insectpests/Frankliniella-occidentalis.php))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event retained as a country‑level first‑detection episode of high strategic importance, but the strength of evidence for widespread establishment and major economic impact by 2020 is weaker than for other events. Corrections: intra‑continental emergence set to “No” because F. occidentalis was already present in the Southern Asia subregion (Sri Lanka from 1996 and Iran from 2004). The summary now more explicitly reflects the current uncertainty around distribution and impact, so this row should be re‑evaluated as more post‑2020 data on establishment and damage in India become available.

Countries: South Africa [1990 Western Cape; rapid spread during the early 1990s to all major stone‑fruit regions]
Host: Peach and other stone fruits (Prunus persica and other Prunus spp.), and to a lesser extent pome fruits such as apple (Malus domestica), pear (Pyrus communis) and quince (Cydonia oblonga) in commercial orchards
Event summary: Around 1990, Grapholita molesta was formally recorded for the first time in South Africa in Western Cape peach orchards, following an accidental introduction probably in the late 1980s on infested budwood. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) The pest population rapidly built up in peach and other stone‑fruit plantings, with up to six generations per year and reported losses of up to about 60% of fruit in badly affected orchards, prompting intensive insecticide programmes and later mating‑disruption trials. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) Through the 1990s the moth became established across all major stone‑fruit‑growing districts of South Africa, after which it was managed as a key quarantine and production pest but remained widespread in commercial orchards. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/aesa/article/101/1/197/8488))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction via illegal or inadequately controlled movement of infested peach budwood and possibly fresh fruit into Western Cape production areas; expansion and intensification of commercial Prunus orchards providing abundant hosts; initially limited surveillance and awareness delaying detection until populations were well established. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) enabling survival and reproduction in Mediterranean‑type climates of Southern Africa, combined with multivoltinism and good local dispersal that allowed rapid build‑up once introduced.
Review: review – Retain as a major post‑1990 emergence event, but the original classification has been corrected: Africa already harboured G. molesta in North Africa and on islands before 1990, so the South African episode is an intra‑continental emergence (new sub‑region within Africa), not an inter‑continental one, and it is not a global first detection. Year, country and impact description were cross‑checked against Afromoths, EPPO Reporting Service articles and the CABI compendium, and event‑specific South African sources were added to the URL list; these adjustments should be checked by a regional specialist.

Countries: New Zealand [first detected 1976 Auckland; severe damage and intensive control in North Island stone‑fruit districts, especially Hawke’s Bay, during the 1980s–1990s]
Host: Commercial summerfruit (peaches, nectarines, apricots and plums; Prunus spp.) and, to a lesser extent, apples in North Island orchards
Event summary: After its initial discovery in Auckland in 1976, Grapholita molesta spread through North Island stone‑fruit areas and by the 1980s–1990s caused severe damage episodes, with reports of up to 100% infestation in unsprayed peach crops in parts of Hawke’s Bay. ([nzpps.org](https://nzpps.org/_journal/index.php/pnzppc/article/download/11643/11493/13120)) Through the 1990s, overlapping generations attacked both shoots and fruit, leading to frequent downgrading or rejection of fruit for processing and driving intensified spray programmes and evaluation of mating‑disruption thresholds in affected orchards. ([nzpps.org](https://nzpps.org/_journal/index.php/pnzppc/article/download/11643/11493/13120)) By the late 1990s and early 2000s, integrated pest management using targeted insecticides and pheromone‑based monitoring reduced, but did not eliminate, the pest, which remained a chronic production problem in the main North Island summerfruit districts. ([nzpps.org](https://nzpps.org/_journal/index.php/pnzppc/article/download/11643/11493/13120))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High host density in intensive summerfruit plantings; historic spray programmes aimed primarily at leafrollers (e.g. Epiphyas postvittana) that sometimes left windows of inadequate control for G. molesta; economic pressures encouraging reductions in broad‑spectrum organophosphate use under Integrated Fruit Production schemes, which initially allowed resurgence of oriental fruit moth in some orchards. Review: review – Event retained as a major linked outbreak episode representing re‑occurrence of a previously introduced pest in New Zealand orchards, but the year field has been standardised from the informal '1990s (linked outbreaks)' to the required '1990‑1999' format while keeping the original temporal interpretation. Emergence type coding (re‑occurrence only) is consistent with a resurgence driven by external management changes rather than a new continent or sub‑region invasion, and sources (NZ Plant Protection and CABI) appropriately document impact and management.
