Countries: Lithuania [1992–1994 records from Klaipėda, Utena, Vilnius and Panevėžys districts; later eradicated]
Host: Primarily peach and other Prunus spp. and apple (Malus domestica) where cultivated or present in gardens; detections were mainly via pheromone trapping rather than large commercial infestations
Event summary: In the early 1990s, Grapholita molesta was detected for the first time in Lithuania, marking its appearance in the Baltic part of Northern Europe beyond the species’ typical climatic range, with registrations in several districts between 1992 and 1994. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=55f34380020309efc6dcd31d6a0d7806d1f31145&repid=rep1&type=pdf)) Males were captured intermittently in pheromone traps in gardens and small orchards, indicating low‑level presence but not yet widespread establishment, and no major commercial crop losses were reported. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=55f34380020309efc6dcd31d6a0d7806d1f31145&repid=rep1&type=pdf)) Subsequent surveys in the mid‑1990s failed to detect the pest and EPPO now lists Lithuania as 'absent, pest eradicated', suggesting that this was a transient incursion rather than a lasting colonisation. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/LASPMO/distribution/LT))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Trade‑mediated introduction of infested fruit into a region outside the natural climatic range of the species; occasional mild years that may have allowed survival of small founder populations; limited local peach cultivation constraining establishment. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=55f34380020309efc6dcd31d6a0d7806d1f31145&repid=rep1&type=pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) at the cooler margin of suitability, reflecting the species’ ability to exploit scattered host trees and complete at least part of its life cycle under marginal climatic conditions, though in this case establishment was apparently not sustained.
Review: review – Event retained as a documented but low‑impact introduction at the northern climatic margin of the species, and correctly treated as an intra‑continental emergence because Northern Europe had previously been free of G. molesta. However, the 'first_detection' flag has been set to false, since first detection refers to the global host system, not to detections in individual countries, and additional detail on transient status (eradicated) has been added using EPPO data; given its very limited impact, this event could be considered for exclusion if a fuller global ranking showed more than ten larger post‑1990 episodes.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: India [2010–2012 Jammu & Kashmir – Anantnag, Ganderbal, Kupwara, Kargil and Leh districts]
Host: Apple and other pome and stone‑fruit trees (Malus domestica, Pyrus communis, Prunus spp.) and associated rosaceous vegetation in temperate orchards and surrounding habitats in the western Himalaya (Jammu & Kashmir).
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2012, surveys of tortricid moths in several districts of Jammu & Kashmir (Anantnag, Ganderbal, Kupwara, Kargil and Leh) recovered Grapholita molesta, which the authors reported as new to India. ([entomoljournal.com](https://www.entomoljournal.com/archives/?ArticleId=2126&issue=4&vol=5&year=2017)) Adults were collected in orchards and surrounding vegetation in the western Himalaya, indicating that the species had become established locally in a major apple‑ and stone‑fruit‑growing region rather than being only an isolated interception. ([entomoljournal.com](https://www.entomoljournal.com/archives/?ArticleId=2126&issue=4&vol=5&year=2017)) Subsequent catalogues and databases list G. molesta as an introduced fruit‑tree pest present with restricted distribution in Jammu & Kashmir, and the species is regulated as a quarantine pest for fruit imports into India. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340173790_Catalogue_of_Tortricidae_Latreille_1802_Lepidoptera_Tortricoidea_of_India))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via trade in infested fruit or planting material from already infested regions of Eurasia, combined with expansion of temperate apple and stone‑fruit cultivation in the western Himalaya and improved interest in monitoring tortricid pests. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) and ecological plasticity enabling establishment in high‑altitude Himalayan orchards; multivoltinism and broad host range in Rosaceae that favour persistence once small founder populations are present.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first confirmed national record of G. molesta in India, an important fruit‑producing country. Because the pest was already present elsewhere in the Southern Asia sub‑region (e.g. Iran), this spread into Jammu & Kashmir is coded as re‑occurrence within a previously affected sub‑region rather than intra‑continental emergence; all other emergence‑type flags remain 'no'. The year range, country and sub‑region assignments are based on the 2010–2012 Jammu & Kashmir surveys and subsequent catalogues and EPPO distribution data, but earlier undetected presence in the wider region cannot be ruled out, so this event should be reviewed by regional experts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Russian Federation [2010 Krasnoyarsk kray and Republic of Khakassia, southern Siberia]
Host: Apples, pears and stone‑fruit trees (Prunus spp., Malus domestica, Pyrus communis) in private and institutional orchards, as well as larvae in imported fruit at wholesale markets
Event summary: Between 2010 and 2012, pheromone‑trap monitoring in southern Siberia (Krasnoyarsk kray and Khakassia) detected Grapholita molesta for the first time in this cold continental region, with males captured both at fruit markets and in orchards and larvae found in fruits. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Trap catches and larval findings showed that at least part of the population was completing its life cycle locally, indicating northward expansion beyond the pest’s historical climatic range within the Eastern Europe (Russia) subregion. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Following these detections, quarantine phytosanitary zones were established and ongoing monitoring and regulatory measures were implemented to contain further spread and protect developing fruit industries in these Siberian areas. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased inflow of infested fruit into Siberian cities and markets from southern regions where G. molesta is common; gradual climate warming leading to milder winters and longer growing seasons, relaxing thermal limits on survival and development north of earlier range margins. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) via the species’ capacity to survive at lower winter temperatures than previously recorded; enhanced transmission due to multiple generations in favourable microclimates within river valleys and orchards, allowing establishment from relatively few introductions; practical host expansion from peach‑dominated systems to mixed orchards of apples, plums and cherries under Siberian conditions.
Review: review – Event retained as a key example of re‑emergence at the cold climatic margin of the species’ range, but the emergence‑type coding has been adjusted so that only 're_emergence' is marked 'yes'; 're_occurrence' has been set to 'no' to respect the intended mutual exclusivity of categories (apart from re‑emergence co‑occurring with inter‑/intra‑continental emergence, which does not apply here). Continent and sub‑region coding (Europe/Eastern Europe, including the whole Russian Federation) were checked against the project’s geographical scheme, and the description now explicitly notes that this represents a northward extension within an already affected sub‑region.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Belgium [2021 confirmed male from Genk, Limburg, in a garden‑centre area]
Host: Larvae are expected to use cultivated stone‑fruit trees (Prunus spp.) and possibly pome fruits in gardens and small orchards, inferred from the species’ biology elsewhere; no major damage in Belgian commercial orchards has yet been documented.
Event summary: Although Grapholita molesta had previously been intercepted in Belgium on imported fruit, its occurrence in the wild fauna remained unconfirmed until a male was reliably identified from a garden‑centre context in Genk (Limburg) in 2021, based on genitalia examination. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363186555_Interessante_waarnemingen_van_Lepidoptera_in_Belgie_in_2021)) This record led to inclusion of the species in Belgian Lepidoptera catalogues as an exotic with a very limited distribution, indicating that the moth can at least survive locally in Western European climates where it had long been considered absent or extremely rare. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/318221368_Crop_Protection_Compendium_Oriental_Fruit_Moth_Grapholita_molesta_Busck_CABI_Compendium)) Since 2021, only sporadic records have been reported and no major damage outbreaks in Belgian commercial orchards have been documented, so the episode currently represents a marginal range extension rather than a major agricultural emergence. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363186555_Interessante_waarnemingen_van_Lepidoptera_in_Belgie_in_2021))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Horticultural trade in infested fruits and ornamental or fruit‑tree planting material from regions in southern or central Europe where G. molesta is well established; availability of suitable host trees in gardens and small orchards that can act as stepping stones for establishment. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) to cooler, more maritime climates and the moth’s ability to maintain small, low‑density populations on scattered hosts, increasing the chance that repeated introductions eventually give rise to detectable local populations.
Review: review – Event retained as the first confirmed record of G. molesta in Belgium but downgraded in emergence‑type coding: Western Europe already had long‑established populations in neighbouring countries, so this should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence, and 'first_detection' is inappropriate because global first detection occurred much earlier; all emergence‑type flags are therefore set to 'no'. The sources from the Belgian Lepidoptera project and Phegea article adequately document the 2021 record; Wikipedia is kept only as a supplementary overview. Given the very limited impact so far, this event is flagged for possible exclusion if future work needs to focus strictly on the most consequential post‑1990 events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum), grain legumes, cereals, oilseeds, tomatoes and other summer crops
Event summary: In 1990–1991, cotton and other summer crops in eastern Australia suffered severe damage from Helicoverpa armigera as long‑standing resistance to pyrethroids, organophosphates and carbamates culminated in widespread field control failures, with combined management costs and yield losses from H. armigera and H. punctigera estimated at about A$150 million. Over the early 1990s, extremely high spray frequencies and escalating resistance in H. armigera maintained outbreaks and economic losses, prompting the development and implementation of a national insecticide resistance management strategy that restricted pyrethroid use and promoted rotations and non‑chemical measures. These measures, together with subsequent adoption of Bt cotton, progressively reduced outbreak severity and stabilized bollworm pressure, though high resistance levels persisted and continue to require tight resistance management and integrated pest control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: highly intensive irrigated cotton and summer‑crop production with heavy reliance on a narrow set of broad‑spectrum insecticides, plus favorable warm conditions allowing multiple H. armigera generations per season. Internal mechanisms: evolution and spread of multiple resistance mechanisms in H. armigera populations to pyrethroids and other insecticides, including a chimeric cytochrome P450 (CYP337B3) and other metabolic and target‑site changes, which increased survival under chemical control and led to a re‑emergent, high‑impact pest situation in an already infested region.
Review: review – Retain as a major event. Adjusted event years from 1990–1993 to 1990–1991 to match published estimates that place the largest Australian bollworm losses (~A$150 million) in the 1990–1991 seasons and emphasize this period as the peak of the resistance crisis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3458352/?utm_source=openai)) Reclassified the event from both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence to re‑emergence only, because the defining feature is the evolution of insecticide resistance (internal change in the pest) rather than purely external drivers. Geographic fields, hosts and sources are appropriate and consistent with Australian cotton pest‑management literature; recommended for human QC but to be kept in the top‑impact list.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cotton (Gossypium spp.), pigeonpea and chickpea (Cajanus cajan, Cicer arietinum), other pulses and field crops
Event summary: During the 1990s, Indian cotton and pulse crops experienced severe and recurrent Helicoverpa armigera infestations, with pod and boll damage often exceeding 40–60% in unprotected fields and large yield losses reported across major cotton belts. From the early to late 1990s, resistance monitoring revealed very high and geographically widespread resistance in H. armigera to synthetic pyrethroids and significant resistance to organophosphates and carbamates, coinciding with extremely frequent insecticide sprays and frequent control failures; total damage costs in cotton alone were estimated at roughly US$500 million in the 1997–1998 season.([oar.icrisat.org](https://oar.icrisat.org/5239/?utm_source=openai)) By the end of the decade, this resistance‑driven crisis led to national insecticide resistance management programs and helped motivate the later rapid adoption of Bt cotton to suppress H. armigera populations.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: expansion of irrigated cotton and pulse cultivation, high baseline bollworm pressure, and intensive, often poorly regulated use of multiple insecticide classes (including frequent tank mixes and off‑label doses), which increased selection pressure and disrupted natural enemies. Internal mechanisms: rapid evolution of multi‑class insecticide resistance in H. armigera, including enhanced detoxifying enzyme systems (esterases, P450s) and other physiological adaptations documented across many Indian cotton‑growing districts, resulting in a dramatic re‑emergence of this long‑present pest at much higher damage levels.
Review: review – Retain as a major event. This row correctly captures the large 1990s resistance crisis in India, including severe yield losses and prominent documentation of multi‑class insecticide resistance in H. armigera.([oar.icrisat.org](https://oar.icrisat.org/5239/?utm_source=openai)) Re‑typed the event as re‑emergence only (not re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence) because the key driver is genetic resistance evolution in the pest within an already infested subregion. Time span 1990–1999 is coarse but reflects the decade‑long crisis described in resistance and IRM literature; exact peak years (particularly 1997–1998) are noted in the summary. Geographic fields and sources are appropriate; recommend human QC but keep as one of the top global events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Cotton, maize, soybean, peanut and other smallholder field crops
Event summary: In the early 1990s, northern China experienced exceptional Helicoverpa armigera population explosions, with particularly severe first and second generation outbreaks in Hebei Province in 1992 that infested nearly 800,000 ha of cotton and about 600,000 ha of wheat, with larval densities locally reaching nearly 200 larvae/m².([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4546?utm_source=openai)) These outbreaks, linked to favorable weather, abundant host crops and escalating insecticide resistance, persisted through the mid‑1990s and caused major yield losses, making cotton bollworm the principal constraint on cotton production. In response, the Chinese government launched a major Bt‑cotton development program in 1992 and commercial Bt cotton planting began in 1997, after which H. armigera pressure and related yield losses in cotton and associated crops declined sharply.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive monoculture of cotton, wheat and other hosts in northern China, with heavy reliance on chemical insecticides and favorable climatic conditions in 1991–1992 that enhanced overwinter survival and early season population build‑up. Internal mechanisms: significant pre‑existing and further evolving resistance in H. armigera populations to widely used insecticides, combined with high dispersal capacity and fecundity, which produced a dramatic re‑emergence of bollworm outbreaks in a long‑infested subregion and set the stage for Bt‑cotton adoption.
Review: review – Retain as a major event. Verified against EPPO and Chinese cotton‑pest reviews that 1992–1993 in Hebei and surrounding provinces represented unprecedented bollworm outbreaks associated with insecticide resistance and favorable climate, and that these crises directly motivated the national Bt‑cotton program.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4546?utm_source=openai)) Re‑typed the event as re‑emergence only, removing re‑occurrence, because internal resistance evolution and consequent surge in pest densities are central. Time window 1992–1995 reasonably brackets the main outbreak years described in the literature.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Cotton (Gossypium spp.), with spillover to other field crops in affected regions
Event summary: In 1994, cotton‑growing areas of Pakistan experienced a major Helicoverpa armigera outbreak, during which growers responded with very frequent applications of pyrethroids and other insecticides; resistance monitoring showed that moderate resistance levels present in 1991–1993 escalated to very high levels from 1994 onwards.([cotton.org](https://www.cotton.org/beltwide/proceedings/1998/abstracts/483.cfm?utm_source=openai)) Over the 1994–1997 seasons, H. armigera remained one of the most destructive pests of Pakistani cotton, with widespread control failures and substantial yield losses reported across several cotton‑producing regions. This re‑emergent, resistance‑driven bollworm problem led to calls for more coordinated resistance‑management strategies and more diversified control tactics in Pakistan’s cotton sector.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: intensive cotton cultivation under hot, favorable conditions for multiple H. armigera generations, coupled with heavy and often repeated use of a limited set of insecticide modes of action, especially synthetic pyrethroids and endosulfan, in response to rising pest pressure. Internal mechanisms: rapid increase in resistance levels in H. armigera populations to cypermethrin, endosulfan and several organophosphates, as documented by discriminating‑dose bioassays across Pakistan, which transformed a long‑present pest into a re‑emergent, high‑impact threat over several seasons.
Review: review – Added as a new event. Pakistan’s mid‑1990s cotton bollworm outbreak and associated jump to very high resistance levels (following the 1994 outbreak) are clearly documented and are comparable in scale and importance to the Indian and Chinese resistance crises, making this one of the top global emergence episodes for H. armigera.([cotton.org](https://www.cotton.org/beltwide/proceedings/1998/abstracts/483.cfm?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑emergence because the pest was already established in Southern Asia and the key driver was internal evolution of multi‑class insecticide resistance. Some quantitative impact details (exact yield‑loss estimates by year) remain uncertain in the accessible literature, so this row is flagged for expert review before finalization.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Bt cotton (Cry1Ac‑expressing cultivars)
Event summary: By about 2010, after more than a decade of widespread Bt cotton cultivation in northern China, resistance monitoring detected reduced susceptibility of Helicoverpa armigera populations to Cry1Ac and provided evidence of field‑evolved resistance in at least one area (Qiuxian, Hebei).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19764057/?utm_source=openai)) Over the next few seasons, these resistant populations contributed to localized increases in boll damage and higher larval survival on Bt cotton in some counties, though large‑scale crop failure was avoided through continued refuge cropping and integrated pest management. Continued resistance monitoring, adjustments to refuge strategies and diversification of control tactics have since limited the spread and impact of high‑level Cry1Ac resistance, but this episode marked a clear evolutionary shift and ongoing re‑emergence risk in Bt‑based cotton systems.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extremely high adoption rates of single‑toxin Cry1Ac Bt cotton across northern China with relatively limited and spatially patchy structured refuges, imposing strong and prolonged selection pressure on H. armigera. Internal mechanisms: genetic changes conferring resistance to Cry1Ac (including increased frequency of resistance alleles and altered midgut receptor interactions), documented as field‑evolved resistance in at least one region, representing a re‑emergence of the pest in Bt‑cotton systems despite previous successful suppression.
Review: retain – Keep as a major event. Evidence from resistance‑monitoring and early‑warning studies in northern China clearly documents field‑evolved Cry1Ac resistance in H. armigera by around 2010, with localized agronomic impacts and substantial implications for long‑term Bt‑cotton sustainability.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19764057/?utm_source=openai)) The existing classification as re‑emergence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental components) is appropriate, and the geographic and temporal framing is consistent with the underlying literature. No structural corrections were needed; only flagged for continued monitoring as resistance frequencies evolve.

Countries: Brazil [2013], Paraguay [2013], Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2013], Argentina [2013], Uruguay [2013]
Host: Soybean, cotton, maize, tomato, beans and other row crops
Event summary: In the 2011/2012 and especially the 2012/2013 cropping seasons, Brazilian growers in the Cerrado and Northeast reported unprecedented damage to soybean, cotton and other crops by heliothine larvae, and in early 2013 diagnostic work confirmed the first official molecular records of Helicoverpa armigera in Brazil, marking its invasion of the New World.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0080134&utm_source=openai)) Over 2013–2014, the pest rapidly spread through Brazilian production regions and into neighboring Paraguay, Bolivia, Argentina and Uruguay, with light‑trap monitoring and field surveys documenting very high moth densities and serious yield losses, sometimes approaching one‑third or more in badly affected soybean and cotton fields, along with frequent control failures and sharply increased insecticide use. Emergency regulatory approvals for additional insecticides and biocontrol agents, together with intensified monitoring and the progressive integration of H. armigera into regional IPM and resistance management programs, helped reduce outbreak intensity in subsequent seasons, although the species is now established as a permanent major pest across large parts of South America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: introduction of an Old World H. armigera lineage into a landscape with extensive year‑round host availability (large, nearly continuous plantings of soybean, maize, cotton and horticultural crops), suitable tropical and subtropical climates, and existing insecticide‑based management frameworks geared to other Helicoverpa species; high volumes of trade in agricultural commodities and propagative material likely facilitated multiple incursion pathways. Internal mechanisms: invading populations carried high genetic diversity and pre‑existing broad insecticide and Bt‑toxin resistance alleles, as well as high dispersal ability and polyphagy, enabling rapid population build‑up, host exploitation and continent‑scale range expansion throughout South American cropping belts.
Review: review – Retain as the primary inter‑continental emergence event. Confirmed that H. armigera was first officially reported from Brazil in 2013 and quickly detected in Paraguay, Argentina, Bolivia and Uruguay, with very high moth densities and substantial yield losses documented during the 2012/2013 and 2013/2014 seasons.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pat/a/NhNkn3X9Xb3hGxdXZnSTsBP/?utm_source=openai)) Adjusted Uruguay’s bracketed start year from 2014 to 2013 to reflect evidence that captures and confirmations in soybean occurred from the 2013/2014 season onward.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/305721658_Primer_registro_de_ocurrencia_de_Helicoverpa_armigera_Hubner_1808_Lepidoptera_Noctuidae_en_soja_en_Uruguay?utm_source=openai)) Re‑set re_emergence to false, as this is the first establishment in the South American continent rather than a reappearance in a previously infested subregion, and retained only inter‑continental emergence to align with the definitions. This row already includes the main regional outbreak impacts and should remain the core representation of the South American incursion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Continent: South America; South America; Northern America
Countries: Brazil [2013], Caribbean (e.g. Puerto Rico [2014]), United States of America – Florida detections [2015]
Host: Maize, cotton and other field crops in the Caribbean and nearby U.S. territories/states
Event summary: Within about a year of its confirmation in Brazil, Helicoverpa armigera was detected in the Caribbean, with the first U.S. detection recorded when a single male was trapped in San Germán, Puerto Rico in September 2014 and molecularly confirmed shortly thereafter, marking the species’ establishment in at least part of the Caribbean basin.([pestalerts.org](https://www.pestalerts.org/nappo/es/official-pest-reports/617/)) In 2015, a single male was caught in a pheromone trap in Bradenton, Florida, representing the first detection of H. armigera in the continental USA, but with no evidence of establishment despite continued surveys.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4924)) Subsequent trap‑based studies from 2018–2021 documented a consistent presence of H. armigera within mixed Helicoverpa populations in high‑input field crops in southern Puerto Rico, confirming establishment there and underscoring the risk of further spread into the wider Caribbean and North American mainland.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6635935/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑distance dispersal from heavily infested South American regions via natural flight and human‑mediated movement on agricultural commodities, combined with suitable subtropical climate and large areas of maize and other host crops in Puerto Rico and parts of the Caribbean that can support establishment. Internal mechanisms: high migratory capacity, broad host range and pre‑existing resistance traits that favor survival in maize and cotton agroecosystems, enabling establishment in Puerto Rico and posing an ongoing invasion risk to the continental United States, even though only isolated detections (without establishment) have so far been recorded in Florida.
Review: review – Retain as a key event, but with clarified timing and classification. Adjusted the event years to 2014–2016 so that the start aligns with the first molecularly confirmed detection and establishment evidence from Puerto Rico in September 2014;([pestalerts.org](https://www.pestalerts.org/nappo/es/official-pest-reports/617/)) Florida detections in 2015 remain included but explicitly described as isolated trap captures without establishment. Following the definitions, removed the inter‑continental emergence flag: establishment is documented only in Puerto Rico, which falls in the Caribbean subregion of the South America continent in the provided country scheme, while Florida records represent interceptions without in situ spread and thus do not qualify as inter‑continental emergence. Intra‑continental emergence is retained to reflect spread from the South American subregion into the Caribbean subregion. This episode is important for its implications for North American risk rather than for very large realized yield losses, and is therefore flagged for expert review but recommended for inclusion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, noctuelle de la tomate, "ver de lépi du maïs"
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in the Estill–Ulmer–Cameron–Holly Hill cotton belt of South Carolina; damage documented primarily in cotton, with probable spillover to local maize and other hosts.
Event summary: In 1996, cotton fields near Estill, South Carolina experienced severe control failures of Helicoverpa zea, with heavy boll damage despite pyrethroid insecticide treatments. Laboratory bioassays on larvae and adults collected from these fields confirmed strong resistance to several pyrethroids, and by 1997 resistant moths were detected at additional South Carolina locations, indicating local spread of resistant populations. Changes in insecticide programmes and the subsequent adoption of Bt cotton reduced the frequency of catastrophic control failures, but pyrethroid‑resistant H. zea persisted as an important management problem in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroid insecticides in cotton in the southeastern United States created strong selection pressure, while large contiguous cotton acreage and favourable climate supported high population densities and rapid selection. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of resistance to multiple pyrethroid active ingredients (e.g. cyhalothrin, cypermethrin, permethrin), with resistance to cyhalothrin expressed as an incompletely dominant trait; inherent high dispersal capacity and multiple generations per year facilitated spread of resistant alleles within the cotton belt.
Review: review – Major pyrethroid resistance outbreak in cotton in South Carolina, USA (1996–1998) is well documented and represents a high‑impact re‑emergence event driven by evolution of multi‑pyrethroid resistance. Type‑of‑emergence classification has been corrected to treat this as re‑emergence only (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), because the resurgence is clearly linked to genetic changes in the pest rather than purely external factors. Geographic fields (North America / Northern America / United States of America) conform to the UNSD scheme and match the locations reported in Brown et al. (1998) and subsequent resistance monitoring. Sources are appropriate and specific to this episode; row should be retained with this corrected classification.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261219498000386?utm_source=openai))
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, noctuelle de la tomate, "ver de lépi du maïs"
Host: Bt cotton producing Cry1Ac (single‑toxin Bollgard) and, later, two‑toxin cotton (Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab or Cry1Ac + Cry1F) targeting heliothine pests, with H. zea as a primary pest in the southeastern and mid‑south cotton belt.
Event summary: After the commercialization of Bt cotton (Cry1Ac) in 1996, H. zea populations in the southeastern and mid‑south United States were exposed across millions of hectares with only moderate toxin dose and limited non‑Bt refuge. Around 2002–2004, resistance monitoring began to detect decreased susceptibility to Cry1Ac and later cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab in several cotton‑belt states, and by the late 2000s some fields experienced unexpected boll damage on Bt cotton and required supplemental insecticide sprays. With broader deployment of pyramided two‑toxin cultivars and adjustments in scouting and spray thresholds, regional crop failure was avoided, but Cry1Ac/Cry2Ab resistance alleles became established in H. zea populations and laid the groundwork for more widespread Cry1/Cry2 resistance problems in the following decade.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive, long‑term planting of single‑toxin Cry1Ac Bt cotton, followed by rapid adoption of two‑toxin Bt cotton, in the southeastern and mid‑south United States; overlapping exposure to related Cry1 toxins in Bt maize; declining availability and/or use of structured non‑Bt refuges; and favourable climate allowing multiple H. zea generations per year. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field‑evolved resistance to Cry1Ac and partial cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab, documented by increased survival at diagnostic toxin concentrations and elevated resistance ratios in bioassays; inherent high mobility and multivoltinism of H. zea facilitated spread of resistant genotypes within the existing North American range.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re‑emergence episode capturing the first broadly documented field‑evolved resistance of H. zea to Cry1Ac (and associated cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab) in U.S. Bt cotton. EPP common name: bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, noctuelle de la tomate, "ver de lépi du maïs"
Host: Pyramided Bt cotton (dual‑gene and triple‑gene varieties such as Cry1Ac + Cry1F, Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab, and Cry1Ac + Cry1F + Vip3A) and Bt corn (including events expressing Cry1Ab, Cry1Fa, Cry1A.105, Cry2Ab2 and Vip3Aa) grown across major cotton and maize production areas of the southeastern and south‑central United States.
Event summary: From about 2016 onward, large‑scale monitoring across the southeastern United States documented that many Helicoverpa zea populations had developed widespread practical resistance to Cry1 and Cry2 proteins in both Bt cotton and Bt corn, with frequent unexpected boll and ear damage despite use of pyramided traits. By 2020–2021, field trials and resistance monitoring indicated that triple‑gene cotton including Vip3Aa still provided effective control, but resistance allele frequencies to Cry1 and especially Cry2 were high and early warning signs for Vip3Aa resistance were emerging, prompting recommendations to adjust deployment strategies and resistance‑management plans to preserve Vip3A efficacy.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued intensive cultivation of Bt corn and cotton over large contiguous areas of the southern United States; widespread planting of pyramided Cry1/Cry2 traits with relatively few non‑Bt host refuges; and cropping patterns that maintain high densities of H. zea across seasons. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – widespread practical resistance to Cry1Ac, Cry1Ab, Cry1A.105, Cry1Fa and Cry2Ab2 documented through diet and plant bioassays, with high resistance ratios and high frequencies of resistance alleles; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – genomic and phenotypic evidence of resistant genotypes associated with Cry1Ac/Cry2Ab resistance; inherent life‑history traits (high mobility, polyphagy and multiple generations per year) allowed resistant genotypes to persist and spread within the existing North American range, while susceptibility to Vip3Aa was still generally high but threatened by detectable resistance alleles in some Texas and southeastern populations.
Review: review – This row summarises the broad, multi‑state phase (approximately 2016–2021) in which practical resistance of H. zea to Cry1 and Cry2 proteins in Bt cotton and Bt corn became widespread across the southeastern and south‑central United States, as documented by multi‑state bioassays, field injury data and increased use of foliar insecticides. Type‑of‑emergence coding has been corrected so that the episode is classified solely as re‑emergence (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), reflecting that the resurgence is driven primarily by resistance evolution rather than external factors alone. Sources (regional resistance surveys, Vip3Aa resistance‑allele studies and USDA ARS field efficacy work) are appropriate and up‑to‑date for this episode, but the row is flagged for expert review as new data on Vip3Aa field performance and resistance may justify further subdivision or extension of the event period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10058025/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Coffea arabica in mostly older shade and sun coffee plantations at mid-elevations
Event summary: Between 2002 and 2003, El Salvador experienced a nationally significant coffee leaf rust epidemic as Hemileia vastatrix caused unusually heavy defoliation in many aging, rust-susceptible Coffea arabica plantations at low and mid elevations, against a backdrop of record-low international coffee prices and structural overproduction that had already weakened farm finances. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) As fungicide use, fertilization and renovation were cut back, rust incidence and severity rose sharply and contributed to marked drops in national coffee output and export revenue compared with the 1990s, prompting concern over the long‑term viability of the sector and early policy discussions on renovation and diversification. ([ipsnews.net](https://www.ipsnews.net/2002/07/coffee-central-america-el-salvador-bears-brunt-of-severe-crisis/?utm_source=openai)) In subsequent years, production partially stabilized at a lower level, but many highly affected farms were not fully rehabilitated, and this episode highlighted vulnerabilities in El Salvador’s coffee sector that later exacerbated the impacts of the 2012–2013 regional Big Rust epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): The epidemic coincided with a period of global coffee overproduction and historically low prices around 2000, which sharply reduced profitability and led many Salvadoran growers to delay pruning and renovation, reduce fertilizer inputs, and apply fewer or no fungicide sprays, leaving dense, old stands of rust-susceptible arabica varieties with high inoculum levels. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Favourable weather for rust infection—frequent rains and prolonged leaf wetness at key times in the 2002–2003 seasons—further accelerated epidemic development. Internal mechanisms: Available accounts attribute the outbreak mainly to management and climatic factors rather than the emergence of a clearly novel hyper‑virulent race; the episode is therefore interpreted here as a re‑occurrence of established rust populations under conditions of economic stress and conducive climate, not a re‑emergence driven by pathogen genetic change.
Review: Decision: review. This new row has been added to represent the 2002–2003 El Salvador coffee leaf rust epidemic, which multiple regional syntheses identify as one of the few clearly documented severe national CLR outbreaks in Mesoamerica prior to the 2008–2013 Big Rust wave and link to the early‑2000s coffee price collapse and under‑investment in crop management. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Classification as a re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) reflects the absence of evidence for a single novel virulent rust race driving the event. Because quantitative loss estimates vary and the relative contribution of rust versus market forces is still debated, this row should be retained but reviewed by a coffee‑rust specialist to confirm that it meets the project’s impact threshold for inclusion among the largest post‑1990 emergence events.

Countries: Colombia [2008]; Costa Rica [2012]; Guatemala [2012]; Honduras [2012]; El Salvador [2012]; Nicaragua [2012]; Panama [2012]; Mexico (southern coffee areas, e.g. Chiapas, Oaxaca, Veracruz) [2012]; Jamaica [2012]; Dominican Republic [2012]; Peru [2013]; Ecuador [2013]
Host: Coffea arabica (primarily); some Coffea canephora in mixed systems
Event summary: From 2008, Colombia began experiencing unusually severe coffee leaf rust epidemics that caused an average 31% drop in national coffee production between 2008 and 2011 compared with 2007, as rust spread widely in susceptible arabica plantings under unusually wet and cool conditions and high input costs limited effective control. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) In 2012–2013, the epidemic extended and intensified across Central America, southern Mexico and several Caribbean countries (notably Jamaica and the Dominican Republic), where regional coffee output fell by roughly 16–20% relative to pre‑epidemic harvests, many smallholder farms reported 30–50% yield losses, and severe outbreaks were also reported in Peru and Ecuador by 2013, prompting phytosanitary emergencies and large‑scale renovation programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8271816/?utm_source=openai)) From about 2014–2015 onward, national and regional control efforts, farm‑level renovation and pruning, and some recovery in prices gradually reduced epidemic intensity and allowed production to partially rebound, although the pathogen remained endemic and rust continued to cause chronic losses in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Multiple analyses attribute the 2008–2013 'Big Rust' wave to a conjunction of prolonged periods of unusually high rainfall and reduced diurnal temperature range in parts of the Andes and Mesoamerica that favoured rust infection and survival; sustained low or volatile coffee prices and/or rising input costs that reduced profitability and led farmers to cut back on fertilization, fungicides and renovation; aging, densely planted, rust‑susceptible arabica stands, including high‑altitude farms where rust had previously been minor; and weakened public extension and research systems that limited early warning and coordinated response. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The epidemic largely reflected massive build‑up and spread of existing rust populations in susceptible varieties; while very large pathogen populations and widespread planting of cultivars carrying single major resistance genes (e.g. Catimor derivatives and Lempira) were associated with increased genetic diversity and breakdown of resistance in some countries, subsequent race analyses have not identified a single novel hyper‑virulent lineage uniquely responsible for the crisis, so the event is best classified as a dramatic re‑occurrence driven primarily by external socio‑economic and climatic factors.
Review: Decision: review. This event is correctly retained as a single linked, multi-country 'Big Rust' episode spanning Colombia (from 2008) and, from 2012–2013, most of Central America, southern Mexico, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, Peru and Ecuador, in line with regional syntheses that describe a continuous wave of high-intensity epidemics rather than isolated outbreaks. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) I have (i) adjusted the event year from 2008–2014 to 2008–2013 to match the period in which the main epidemic peaks are consistently reported, while recognising that severe losses in parts of Peru and Ecuador continued into 2014–2015; and (ii) refined the country list to name Jamaica explicitly and to avoid an unsourced catch‑all reference to 'other Caribbean producers (e.g. Haiti)', for which comparable epidemic‑scale documentation could not be found. ([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/members/community/newsroom/releases/Pages/BigRusts_PhytoReview.aspx?utm_source=openai)) Classification as a re-occurrence (with intra- and inter-continental emergence marked 'No') remains appropriate, because the fungus was already long established in the affected subregions and current evidence points to climatic and management drivers plus incremental race diversification rather than a single new hyper‑virulent strain. Given the complexity of this regional crisis, the revised year range and country list should be reviewed by a coffee‑rust expert before final adoption.

Countries: United States of America – Hawaii: Maui [2020]; Hawai‘i Island [2020]; O‘ahu [2021]; Lana‘i [2021]; Kaua‘i [2021]; Moloka‘i [2021]
Host: Coffea arabica (commercial and backyard coffee in Hawaii)
Event summary: In October 2020, coffee growers and extension agents in Maui and on Hawai‘i Island observed characteristic yellow-orange leaf lesions that were confirmed by state and federal laboratories as coffee leaf rust, marking the first known establishment of Hemileia vastatrix in Hawaii and the first in situ spread of the pathogen in the Northern America continent as defined in this project. ([hdoa.hawaii.gov](https://hdoa.hawaii.gov/blog/main/nr20-17-clrconfirmedonhawaiiisland/?utm_source=openai)) Over late 2020 and early 2021, the disease rapidly spread within infected islands and was subsequently detected on O‘ahu and Lana‘i, and by mid‑2021 confirmations on Kaua‘i and Moloka‘i meant that all major Hawaiian coffee‑growing islands were affected, threatening a coffee industry valued at tens of millions of dollars annually and increasing production costs through new fungicide and sanitation requirements. ([dab.hawaii.gov](https://dab.hawaii.gov/blog/main/nr21-17clrkauaimolokai/?utm_source=openai)) From 2020 onward, Hawaii implemented strict quarantines on movement of coffee plant material, multi‑agency surveillance, and promotion of fungicide programs and resistant varieties, which have slowed but not eradicated the disease; coffee production continues under ongoing rust management with substantially higher disease risk.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers (external): Genetic analyses and atmospheric modelling indicate that long-distance dispersal of urediniospores from Latin American rust populations—likely via wind currents and/or contaminated plant material or clothing of travellers—introduced Hemileia vastatrix into Hawaii, which had previously been free of CLR despite being a long‑standing coffee‑growing region. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2309-608X/8/2/189?utm_source=openai)) Climatic suitability of many Hawaiian coffee zones (warm temperatures, frequent dew or rainfall and cloud cover) facilitated establishment and rapid local spread once the pathogen arrived, while initial absence of regulatory measures specific to rust in a previously rust‑free region may have delayed early detection. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing shows that Hawaiian rust populations are closely related to Latin American genotypes and do not represent a novel race with unique virulence; the key internal factor is the pathogen’s inherent capacity for prolific spore production and long-distance aerial dispersal colonizing a naïve host population, rather than the evolution of a new high‑virulence strain. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2309-608X/8/2/189?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Multiple official and peer‑reviewed sources confirm that coffee leaf rust was first detected on Maui in October 2020 and in the Kona coffee district of Hawai‘i Island in November 2020, and that by mid‑2021 it had been found on O‘ahu, Lana‘i, Kaua‘i and Moloka‘i, establishing the pathogen across all major Hawaiian coffee-growing islands. ([dab.hawaii.gov](https://dab.hawaii.gov/blog/main/nr21-17clrkauaimolokai/?utm_source=openai)) Prior to this incursion, Hawaii was one of the last significant coffee regions globally without CLR, so this episode represents the first established occurrence of Hemileia vastatrix in the Northern America continent (in the project’s regional scheme) with clear in situ transmission, justifying its classification as an inter-continental emergence event. Later reports of CLR on small numbers of ornamental coffee plants in continental Florida are not treated as a separate emergence event because coffee is not commercially grown there and current evidence indicates very limited, non‑epidemic impact. ([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-09-23-1869-PDN?utm_source=openai))

Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event summary: During the 1991/1992 soybean season, soybean cyst nematode (SCN) was first detected in Brazil in commercial fields in the Cerrado, including areas near Nova Ponte (Minas Gerais), Chapadão do Céu (Goiás), Campo Verde (Mato Grosso) and Chapadão do Sul (Mato Grosso do Sul), after growers reported patches of stunted, yellow soybeans. Surveys through the mid‑1990s revealed additional infested fields across central Cerrado states and later into southern production areas such as Paraná, São Paulo and Rio Grande do Sul, indicating that SCN was already widely established and spreading under intensive soybean monoculture. By the late 1990s the nematode was recognized as a major constraint on Brazilian soybean production, affecting millions of hectares and prompting national recommendations for crop rotation, resistant cultivars and strict hygiene, although eradication proved impossible and SCN remains entrenched with highly variable field‑level densities.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of soybean monoculture into the Brazilian Cerrado, widespread use of continuous soybean or short rotations, and frequent movement of contaminated soil on machinery, trucks and seed lots allowed SCN to invade and spread among newly opened production frontiers. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity and multiple generations per season, combined with long‑term survival of eggs within durable cysts and efficient root invasion, enabled rapid population build‑up and persistence once fields were infested, facilitating geographic range expansion within the South America subregion.
Review: Review: Retain as a major South American emergence event. Adjusted event year from 1991–1992 to 1991–1997 to reflect multi‑year spread documented by Embrapa surveys and the 1993 Plant Disease report; kept the event classified as re_occurrence (South America’s first SCN record was Colombia 1983, so Brazil is not a continental or subregional first). Continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and the mechanism description appropriately emphasizes Cerrado soybean expansion and soil movement. Sources were focused on Embrapa Ageitec, early Brazilian survey publications and EPPO distribution data; no further structural changes recommended, but timing and impact estimates could be refined with additional Brazilian loss data.

Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event summary: From about 1996 onwards, soybean cyst nematode re‑emerged as the most damaging pathogen of soybean across the United States and Ontario, Canada, with national disease‑loss surveys consistently ranking SCN above all other soybean diseases. Analyses of loss data for 1996–2016 estimated cumulative yield losses approaching US$32 billion in the United States alone—more than US$1.5 billion annually—driven in part by SCN populations able to reproduce on widely used PI 88788‑based resistant cultivars and by expanded soybean acreage. By the late 2010s SCN was endemic across most of the U.S. soybean belt and a large share of Canadian soybean land, and management shifted toward more diverse resistance sources, nematode‑protectant seed treatments and intensive outreach, although substantial, often “hidden” yield losses continue each year.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of soybean cultivation in the U.S. and Canada, frequent soybean‑after‑soybean rotations, and heavy reliance on a narrow set of resistance sources increased selection pressure and allowed SCN populations to build to damaging densities. Internal mechanisms: Evolution and spread of virulence phenotypes capable of reproducing on PI 88788 and related resistance genes, combined with long‑term cyst survival and efficient belowground transmission, produced a large‑scale re‑emergence in terms of economic impact despite the nematode’s long‑standing presence in North America.
Review: Review: Retain as a key global re‑emergence episode with the largest documented economic losses. Corrected type classification by setting re_occurrence=No and re_emergence=Yes, reflecting that heightened impact was driven largely by virulence evolution and intensification rather than a simple resurgence. Simplified the countries field to “United States of America [1996]; Canada [1996]” to match event‑sheet formatting, while the 1996–2016 window remains aligned with published loss estimates. Sources (Tylka & Marett distribution/loss analysis, University of Minnesota Extension, CFIA risk documents and EPPO) appropriately support the magnitude and extent of this episode, though Canadian‑specific loss figures could be added in a later refinement.

Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event summary: During the 1997/1998 season, soybean cyst nematode was detected for the first time in Argentina in the core soybean‑growing region (“región núcleo sojera”) of Córdoba and Santa Fe, where patches of stunted, chlorotic soybeans prompted nematological analyses confirming Heterodera glycines. Internal mechanisms: The nematode’s high reproductive potential, capacity for several generations per season, long‑term egg survival in cysts and ability to exploit susceptible local cultivars allowed small initial foci to expand into a widely distributed, economically important pest within little more than a decade.

The 1997–2008 time window follows Argentine extension literature that dates first detection to the 1997/1998 campaign and notes that SCN emerged over the subsequent decade as a key soybean pathogen. Event summary: In summer 2000, soybean cyst nematode was detected for the first time in Europe when three commercial soybean fields near Pavia in Lombardia, northern Italy, with long‑standing yellow‑dwarf symptoms were found to harbour dense, reproducing populations of Heterodera glycines. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive capacity, survival of eggs in resilient cysts and the ability to complete multiple generations per year in temperate climates facilitated establishment and persistence in a new continent, representing geographic range expansion from Asia and the Americas into Europe.

Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event summary: Although soybean cyst nematode had long been known from temperate northeastern and northern China, in 2008 it was detected for the first time on soybean in Zhejiang province in subtropical eastern China, marking a southward extension beyond its traditional cool‑climate range.
