Host: Vegetable crops (beans, tomato, eggplant, potato, melon, celery, carrot) and ornamentals (gerbera, chrysanthemum and others) in protected and open-field production
Event summary: In 1990, Liriomyza trifolii was first recorded in Japan at Hamamatsu in Shizuoka Prefecture and rapidly spread nationwide, reaching almost all prefectures except a few northern ones by around 2000. Surveys and control trials from the early 1990s documented very high populations on greenhouse and field vegetables and on ornamentals such as gerbera and chrysanthemum, with marked insecticide resistance and serious crop damage. Over the following decade the species became a widespread invasive pest integrated into Japanese IPM and quarantine regulations, with parasitoid-based biological control and careful insecticide choice used to reduce its impact.([nies.go.jp](https://www.nies.go.jp/biodiversity/invasive/DB/detail/60040e.html))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction with infested ornamental and vegetable seedlings (especially gerbera and chrysanthemum) and expansion of intensive protected-cultivation systems provided continual host availability; frequent insecticide applications disrupted natural enemies and favoured resistant L. trifolii. Internal mechanisms: Strong insecticide resistance documented from 1990 onward, together with high reproductive rate and broad host range, allowed rapid build‑up and spread and justify classifying this as a re‑emergence event at the regional scale.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjaez1957/36/3/36_3_183/_article/-char/ja))
Review: retain – Added as a new high‑impact event capturing the 1990–2000 nationwide invasion of Japan, supported by the NIES invasive species database, EPPO reporting, and Japanese studies documenting insecticide-resistant outbreaks; coded as re‑emergence (resistant invasive lineage) rather than intra‑continental emergence or first detection, in line with the global-scale definitions.

Countries: Philippines [Luzon – major onion-growing areas of Central Luzon (e.g. Nueva Ecija) 1990s–2004]
Host: Bulb onion (Allium cepa) grown after rice in Central Luzon, with L. trifolii also affecting other vegetable crops locally
Event summary: Although Liriomyza trifolii was already present in Luzon by the mid‑1980s, from the early 1990s through the early 2000s it expanded and became the dominant leafminer in onion-growing areas of Central Luzon, particularly Nueva Ecija. Field studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s describe very high larval densities, extensive mining damage, and heavy reliance on insecticides, with reports that L. trifolii caused havoc in the onion industry during this period. By the mid‑2000s, the pest was established as a key component of the onion pest complex, with ongoing management based on chemical control, parasitoids and cultural practices rather than eradication.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/LIRITR/distribution/PH))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of dry‑season onion cultivation after irrigated rice in Central Luzon, coupled with intensive insecticide use and movement of planting material and produce, created favourable conditions for L. trifolii population build‑up and persistence. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity and polyphagy enabled rapid exploitation of onion and other hosts; some tolerance to commonly used insecticides was suggested by poor control in frequently sprayed fields, but available sources emphasise external drivers more than documented novel genotypes, so the event is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.([ukdr.uplb.edu.ph](https://www.ukdr.uplb.edu.ph/journal-articles/5748/))
Review: retain – New event added to represent the well‑documented 1990s–early 2000s onion outbreaks in the Philippines, which caused large production losses and intensive insecticide use; classified as re‑occurrence in an already infested subregion (South‑eastern Asia) driven mainly by cropping systems and chemical control practices.

Host: Open-field vegetable crops including beans, tomato, pepper, melon, cucumber, pumpkin, lettuce, cabbage and onion
Event summary: In 1991, Liriomyza trifolii was reported for the first time from Tonga, adding Polynesian vegetable systems to a Pacific distribution that already included Guam and other Micronesian islands. The fly quickly reached damaging levels on a wide range of vegetables, with serpentine leaf mines reducing photosynthetic area and marketability and prompting concern among growers. The pest subsequently became established as part of the endemic leafminer complex in Tonga, managed mainly with insecticides and limited cultural measures rather than eradicated.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-5390))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing inter-island trade in fresh vegetables and planting material from previously infested Pacific islands, combined with growth of intensive smallholder vegetable production, facilitated the jump from Micronesia to Polynesia. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range and good adaptation to tropical climates supported successful establishment in Tonga; no specific evidence of novel resistance or strains has been reported for this event.
Review: retain – Event is well supported by EPPO Reporting Service 1991/14 as the first confirmed record in Tonga and effectively marks intra‑continental emergence into the Polynesia subregion; no major corrections were needed beyond re‑checking the subregion and impact description.

Countries: India [Andhra Pradesh 1993; spread documented by 1996–2004 to Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Haryana, New Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Kerala]
Host: Castor bean and other field and vegetable crops (various legumes and vegetables in affected states)
Event summary: From 1993 onwards, Liriomyza trifolii was first recorded in Andhra Pradesh on castor bean and then rapidly detected in multiple Indian states including Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, with later reports from Gujarat, Haryana, New Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and finally Kerala by 2004. Field observations indicated that the species became widespread in castor-growing areas and other horticultural crops, contributing to substantial leaf mining damage and prompting local research on management and natural enemies. By the mid‑2000s, L. trifolii was established across much of India’s main horticultural belt as a regular pest, with management relying on insecticides and emerging IPM recommendations rather than attempts at eradication.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/LIRITR/distribution/IN))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of castor and vegetable production in semi‑arid and irrigated systems, together with internal trade in seedlings and produce from already infested regions, facilitated progressive spread across India. Internal mechanisms: The fly’s polyphagy and ability to exploit varied climates in Southern Asia underpinned its geographic range expansion, but available evidence does not clearly point to novel genotypes or resistance specific to India, so this is treated as intra‑continental emergence into a new UN subregion (Southern Asia) rather than as re‑emergence.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/LIRITR/distribution/IN))
Review: review – Original row incorrectly treated Kerala 2003 as the first detection in India; this has been replaced by a linked episode 1993–2004 that reflects EPPO distribution data showing earlier records from Andhra Pradesh and many other states, and “first_detection” has been set to No while “intra_continental_emergence” is retained to reflect first establishment in the Southern Asia subregion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Faba bean (Vicia faba) in irrigated field systems (New Halfa scheme)
Event summary: In the mid‑1990s, field studies on sowing dates of faba bean in the New Halfa irrigation scheme in Sudan documented heavy infestations by Liriomyza trifolii, representing the first detailed record of this pest from the country. By that time, L. trifolii was already widespread in other parts of Africa, but its recognition as a serious faba bean pest in Sudan raised concern about potential yield losses and appropriate planting strategies. Subsequent work treated the leafminer as an established component of the pest complex in irrigated legume systems in Sudan rather than an eradication target.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3890))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated faba bean and movement of infested seed or plant material from other African countries where L. trifolii was already present likely introduced the pest into the New Halfa scheme. Internal mechanisms: Generalist feeding on legumes and tolerance of semi‑arid irrigated environments underpinned establishment; no specific resistant strain or novel genotype has been implicated in this local emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the UN subregion from “Eastern Africa” to “Northern Africa” in line with the country list, and removed both “first_detection” and “intra_continental_emergence” flags because L. trifolii was already present in multiple African subregions including North Africa (e.g. Tunisia 1992) before this record; event is now treated as a country‑level emergence with moderate impact whose ranking among the top 10 African events should be reassessed.

Host: Various vegetable crops and ornamentals (e.g. tomato and other greenhouse and field vegetables; ornamental plants)
Event summary: Between July 1995 and September 1996, a national survey of agromyzid leafminers in Jordan identified Liriomyza trifolii, together with L. huidobrensis and L. sativae, for the first time in the country on vegetables, ornamentals and weeds. The species was found at multiple locations, showing that it had already become established and was contributing to leafminer damage in commercial fields and greenhouses. Since then, L. trifolii has remained present in Jordan as part of the regional leafminer complex managed within broader IPM and quarantine frameworks, without any attempt at eradication.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-2274))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of infested seedlings, cuttings and vegetables from neighbouring Mediterranean and Near Eastern countries where L. trifolii was already present, along with intensification of irrigated and protected vegetable production, favoured establishment in Jordan. Internal mechanisms: Polyphagy and adaptation to warm, semi‑arid climates facilitated establishment, but there is no clear evidence of a novel strain or major resistance change specific to this episode.
Review: review – Maintained the event as Jordan’s first country record but removed the “first_detection” and “intra_continental_emergence” flags because L. trifolii was already present in the same UN subregion (Western Asia) in Israel and Lebanon before 1990; this is now treated as a within‑subregion spread event of moderate, regionally focused impact.

Countries: Federated States of Micronesia [Yap and Pohnpei 1996–1997]
Host: Beans and other vegetable crops in field and garden production
Event summary: Surveys carried out in the mid‑1990s in the Federated States of Micronesia recorded Liriomyza trifolii on beans in Yap and Pohnpei, with growers reporting economic losses from leafmining damage. By the time these findings were summarized in a 1998 EPPO report, the species appeared established in parts of Micronesia following earlier presence on nearby islands such as Guam. The fly has since remained part of the local vegetable pest complex, with control based largely on insecticides and limited biological control, rather than being eradicated.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3592))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Short-distance spread within the Pacific through inter‑island trade in vegetables and planting material, and natural dispersal among closely spaced islands, allowed L. trifolii to move from earlier Pacific foci into Yap and Pohnpei. Internal mechanisms: Existing adaptation to humid tropical climates and broad host range supported establishment; there is no indication of a distinct invasive genotype, so no re‑emergence classification is applied.
Review: review – Adjusted the event year from 1998 (year of the EPPO report) to 1996–1997 to better reflect the timing of the field surveys, and removed the “re_occurrence” flag because this is better interpreted as first country records within an already infested Micronesian subregion rather than a resurgence in a previously affected area.

Countries: Argentina [≤2002]; Chile (Juan Fernández Islands) [≤2002]; Mexico [≤2002]; Saint Martin [≤2002]; Virgin Islands (unspecified) [≤2002]
Host: Multiple vegetable and ornamental crops, including beans and other horticultural hosts in open-field and protected cultivation
Event summary: A neotropical Agromyzidae survey published in 2002 reported Liriomyza trifolii for the first time from Argentina, the Juan Fernández Islands of Chile, Mexico, Saint Martin and the Virgin Islands, extending its known range within Central and South America and the Caribbean beyond earlier records from countries such as Colombia, Peru and several Caribbean islands. These new records indicated that L. trifolii had recently expanded southward and into additional islands, establishing on vegetables and ornamentals and adding to existing leafminer complexes that already caused concern for quarantine and yield losses. Following this expansion, the fly has remained part of the pest fauna across much of the Neotropics, routinely managed with insecticides and some biological control rather than targeted for eradication.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-2289))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of infested chrysanthemum cuttings and vegetable seedlings through regional and international trade, together with growth of protected and intensive horticulture in the Neotropics, facilitated spread into additional American countries and islands. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate, polyphagy and ability to exploit greenhouse and warm open‑field environments underpinned successful establishment, but there is no clear evidence that a novel genotype triggered these expansions, so the event is classified as re‑occurrence (further spread within already infested subregions) rather than intra‑continental emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12241706/))
Review: review – Reinterpreted this EPPO 2002 report as a re‑occurrence/expansion within already infested Neotropical subregions rather than as “first_detection” or “intra_continental_emergence,” because L. trifolii was already present in South America, Central America and the Caribbean before these new country records; country list and impact narrative were retained but the emergence-type flags were corrected.

Countries: China [Guangdong 2005; Hainan 2006; Jiangsu and a growing number of southern and eastern provinces by 2008 and into the 2010s]
Host: Wide range of vegetable crops (beans, tomato, pepper, cucumber and others), ornamentals, and other horticultural hosts in open fields and greenhouses
Event summary: Liriomyza trifolii was first recorded in mainland China in 2005 in Guangdong Province and was detected soon after in Hainan and additional provinces such as Jiangsu, with rapid spread across much of southern and eastern China over the subsequent decade. As it expanded, L. trifolii invaded intensive vegetable and ornamental systems already colonized by other invasive leafminers, and under heavy insecticide use it began to displace L. sativae as the dominant species in some regions, causing severe damage and prompting extensive research on its ecology and management. Through the 2010s the species remained a widespread invasive pest in China, with ongoing efforts to develop IPM strategies based on resistance management, competitive interactions and biological control.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048357522000219))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Very intensive vegetable and ornamental production in subtropical and warm‑temperate China with frequent insecticide applications created strong selection pressure and reduced effectiveness of natural enemies, while large domestic and international trade in seedlings and fresh produce facilitated repeated introductions and secondary spread. Internal mechanisms: Documented insecticide resistance and enhanced competitive ability relative to L. sativae, together with thermal adaptation and broad host range, allowed L. trifolii to expand its range and dominate leafminer communities in parts of China, justifying its classification as a re‑emergence event in an already infested continental region.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048357522000219))
Review: review – Retained the Chinese invasion as a major event but removed the “first_detection” and “intra_continental_emergence” flags because L. trifolii was already present in the Eastern Asia subregion (e.g. Taiwan 1988, Japan 1990) before 2005; the event is now coded solely as re‑emergence, reflecting the role of insecticide-resistant invasive populations and species displacement.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Countries: Australia [Kununurra, Western Australia; Torres Strait and Northern Peninsula Area, Queensland; Greater Darwin region, Northern Territory]
Host: A wide range of vegetable, pulse and ornamental crops (e.g. celery, beans, brassicas, cucurbits, tomatoes, ornamentals) in northern Australian production and backyard systems
Event summary: In 2021, Liriomyza trifolii was detected for the first time on the Australian mainland, with separate finds near Kununurra in northern Western Australia and in the Torres Strait and Northern Peninsula Area of Queensland, followed shortly by detections in the Greater Darwin region of the Northern Territory. These incursions marked the establishment of the American serpentine leafminer in northern Australia after years of being considered an exotic threat, triggering national biosecurity responses including containment zones, surveillance and communication campaigns to growers. As of the mid‑2020s the pest remains established in parts of northern Australia, with ongoing efforts focused on limiting spread into major southern vegetable and nursery production regions and integrating it into preparedness and IPM programmes alongside other invasive Liriomyza species.([ippc.int](https://www.ippc.int/es/countries/australia/pestreports/2021/07/liriomyza-trifolii-american-serpentine-leafminer-in-queensland-and-western-australia/))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International and regional movement of plant material and produce through northern Australian entry points (Torres Strait, northern ports and air routes), coupled with suitable tropical to subtropical climates and continuous host availability, enabled introduction and establishment; prior preparedness projects had highlighted this invasion pathway. Internal mechanisms: Invasive populations share traits seen elsewhere, such as broad host range and partial resistance to commonly used insecticides, but because this is the first establishment in the Australia and New Zealand subregion rather than a resurgence in a previously infested area, the event is coded as intra‑continental emergence (new UN subregion in Oceania) without an additional re‑emergence label.([dpird.wa.gov.au](https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/pests-weeds-and-diseases/animal-pests-diseases/pest-insects/american-serpentine-leafminer/))
Review: review – Retained as a major event but corrected the year field to “2021-ongoing” and removed the “first_detection” and “re_emergence” flags, leaving only “intra_continental_emergence” to reflect first establishment in the Australia and New Zealand subregion of Oceania; reasoning is based on NPPO pest reports and Australian government factsheets documenting ongoing, regionally restricted establishment.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: China [1988] (first detected in Tanghai County, Hebei; by 2003 present in at least 11 provinces and the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and wild Poaceae/Cyperaceae in and around irrigated rice fields
Event summary: After first detection of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus in Tanghai County, Hebei Province, China in 1988, parthenogenetic populations rapidly established in irrigated rice on the northeast coast. Through the 1990s and early 2000s the weevil expanded southwards and inland along irrigation networks and rice belts so that by late 2003 it infested more than 400,000 ha of rice across 11 provinces plus the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin, with local yield losses of 10–80% in severely affected paddies. By the early 2000s the invasion front had approached climatic limits in northern and western China, and national surveillance, quarantine and integrated chemical and agronomic control programmes were intensified to manage this now widely established invasive pest.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of infested rice seedlings, straw and other plant material; dense irrigated rice monocultures interconnected by canals and rivers; expansion of high-yielding rice production into suitable temperate areas; and incomplete quarantine enforcement facilitated spread from the initial coastal focus. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (invasive parthenogenetic California-derived lineage distinct from native bisexual U.S. populations), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (strong flight and effective use of irrigation infrastructure for dispersal), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent physiological tolerance allowing colonization of cooler, more northerly rice-growing zones within Eastern Asia).
Review: review – Retain this as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events because it represents the large invasive outbreak in mainland China, but corrected the emergence‑type classification: intra_continental_emergence is set to No (the spread occurred within the already infested Eastern Asia subregion, not into a new UN subregion) and re_emergence is kept as Yes to reflect a dramatic increase in incidence in an already affected subregion driven by the parthenogenetic invasive lineage. The description of invaded area and impact was aligned with Chen et al. 2005 and EPPO RS 2006/062 (≈11 provinces plus Beijing and Tianjin by 2003); a human review is recommended to confirm the choice of re_emergence (rather than re_occurrence) at subregional scale.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: Italy [2004] (initial foci in Lombardia, then spread across Piemonte; later new foci in Emilia-Romagna and Veneto)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and associated wild grasses and sedges (Poaceae, Cyperaceae) in and around paddy fields
Event summary: In 2004, parthenogenetic females of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were first detected in rice-growing areas of western Lombardia (Abbiategrasso and Vigevano) in Northern Italy, constituting the first record for both Italy and Europe. Over the following decade the pest invaded the entire rice-growing area of Piemonte and Lombardia and, by 2013–2014, new foci were discovered near Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna and near Verona in Veneto, several hundred kilometres from the original outbreak. By 2014 the weevil was firmly established across Northern Italy’s main rice belt, though reported economic losses remained generally localized and modest due to intensive monitoring and chemical and agronomic management.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely transcontinental introduction via infested plant material or straw, probably from North America or already invaded parts of Asia, with the first established Italian foci occurring close to major trade and air-transport hubs in the Milan area; subsequent spread facilitated by the fragmented but extensive network of rice paddies and waterways, and by movement of rice straw, machinery and soil between farms. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence at continental scale (establishment of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage in Europe), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (adult dispersal by flight and use of semi-aquatic habitats), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent traits enabling survival and reproduction in temperate European rice agroecosystems).
Review: review – This event correctly represents the first introduction and spread of L. oryzophilus in Europe, but the emergence‑type flags have been adjusted: first_detection is set to No because the first description of the species as a rice pest dates to the 1880s in the United States, and re_emergence is set to No because this is a true first establishment event for Europe. Inter_continental_emergence remains Yes to capture the first occurrence on a new continent. EPPO RS 2005/005, RS 2015/073 and Lupi et al. 2015 support the timing, regional spread and generally modest economic impact; the row should be retained with these corrected classifications.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Countries: France [2014] (initial finds in two rice plots in eastern France, later confirmed in Bouches-du-Rhône/Camargue and other Camargue rice areas)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in Camargue and other French rice-growing areas; associated wild grasses and sedges (Poaceae, Cyperaceae) in irrigation and field margins
Event summary: In 2014, Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus was first notified from France when adults were detected in two rice plots in the eastern part of the country and soon after confirmed in the main Mediterranean rice area of Camargue (Bouches-du-Rhône), indicating a secondary introduction from already infested regions. Over the next several seasons the weevil spread through many Camargue paddies and additional rice parcels, with French monitoring reports noting an increasing number of infested fields and concern about potential yield losses where control was not applied. By 2021, the NPPO of France considered the species present and widespread in national rice-growing areas, and management relied on targeted insecticide treatments, agronomic measures and continued surveillance to protect previously pest-free zones and track economic impact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Secondary introduction from other invaded European regions (particularly Italy and possibly Spain) via movement of infested rice plants or straw, shared harvesting machinery, and regional trade in rice seed and by-products; the dense, irrigated rice landscape of the Camargue provides highly suitable habitat and hydrological connectivity that facilitates local spread. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage already present in other parts of Europe, with Geographic Range Expansion (inherent cold and heat tolerance) enabling colonization of Mediterranean Western Europe; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via strong adult dispersal and exploitation of irrigation canals and adjacent wild hosts.
Review: review – This row has been added to capture a major emergence event that was previously omitted: first detection in France in 2014 followed by spread leading to a current official status of “present, widespread” in national rice-growing areas. It is classified as intra_continental_emergence (first establishment in the Western Europe subregion of an invasive lineage already present in Southern Europe). The timing and distribution are supported by the EU 2014 harmful organisms report, EPPO distribution details for France and Ferrand (2017); the event should be treated as one of the top global emergence events for this pest, but the narrative and time window (2014–2021) should be checked and refined by a domain expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: Greece [2016] (Central Macedonia, Axios river delta near Thessaloniki)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in deltaic paddy fields, with likely use of associated wild grasses and sedges as ancillary hosts
Event summary: In July–August 2016, during mosquito surveillance in rice fields in the Axios river delta of Central Macedonia, Greece, adult Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were collected and identified morphologically and by COI DNA barcoding, marking the first record of the species in Greece and the Balkans. This finding showed that the European invasion, previously centred in Italy, had expanded eastwards within Southern Europe into a new rice-producing country, although at that time no severe economic damage had yet been documented in Greek paddies. Following confirmation, Greek authorities and researchers initiated further surveys around the Axios delta to delimit the infestation, investigate likely introduction routes and assess potential agronomic impacts.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Secondary spread within Europe, most likely via trade and movement of contaminated plant material, rice straw or machinery from already infested areas (e.g. Italy), combined with the availability of large areas of flooded rice and interconnected water networks in the Axios delta that favour establishment and local dispersal. Internal mechanisms: Continued exploitation of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage without evidence of new genotypes, Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (effective dispersal in irrigated Mediterranean deltas), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) as the species occupies additional parts of the Southern Europe rice belt.
Review: review – This event remains important as it documents expansion of the European invasion into the Balkans, but its categorization and sources have been updated. Intra_continental_emergence is set to No because the spread is to a new country within the already affected Southern Europe subregion rather than to a new UN subregion, and re_occurrence is set to Yes to reflect renewed occurrence and increased regional incidence within an already infested subregion driven mainly by trade and irrigation networks rather than further genetic change. The source list has been focused on EPPO RS 2017/162 and Giantsis et al. 2017, removing a largely irrelevant U.S. agronomic study; human review is advised to confirm the choice of re_occurrence and the spatial scale at which it is applied.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in Ebro Delta paddies; detection also via DNA metabarcoding of insectivorous bat (Pipistrellus pygmaeus) faeces
Event summary: In August 2018, adults of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were collected from rice crops at several localities in the Ebro Delta in Catalonia, Spain, and later confirmed taxonomically, representing the first record of the species in the Iberian Peninsula. In 2019, DNA metabarcoding of faeces from Pipistrellus pygmaeus bat roosts in the same delta area again detected rice water weevil DNA, corroborating its establishment in the landscape. By the early 2020s the pest was known from major European rice-producing countries including Italy, France, Greece and Spain, although in Spain economic damage was still considered limited and mostly confined to parts of the Ebro Delta where chemical and agronomic controls are implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Secondary spread of the established European invasive population, probably via movement of infested plant material, machinery or straw from other invaded countries, interacting with intense rice monoculture and extensive wetlands in the Ebro Delta that favour establishment and local dispersal; use of insectivorous bats as “natural samplers” enabled early detection. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage, Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (successful colonization of irrigated Mediterranean delta systems), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) into Iberian rice-growing zones.
Review: review – This event is retained as a key marker of spread to the Iberian Peninsula, but its emergence‑type classification and sources have been corrected. Intra_continental_emergence is set to No (spread occurred within the already infested Southern Europe subregion), while re_occurrence is set to Yes to indicate renewed occurrence and increased incidence in that subregion driven by secondary dispersal of the invasive lineage. An incorrect EPPO link that pointed to the Greek first‑report article has been removed, leaving EPPO RS 2021/152 and Montauban et al. 2021 as the primary sources; a human check is recommended to confirm that the 2018–2019 window and impact description match national monitoring data.

Countries: Grenada [1994]; Trinidad and Tobago [1995]; Saint Kitts and Nevis [1996]; Saint Martin/Sint Maarten and other Netherlands Antilles islands including Curaçao and Sint Eustatius [1996-1997]; British Virgin Islands [1997]; United States Virgin Islands [1997]; Saint Vincent and the Grenadines [1997]; Puerto Rico (including Vieques and Culebra) [1997-1998]; other Eastern Caribbean islands (e.g. Anguilla, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Montserrat, Barbados, Bahamas) [1996-2000]; Guyana [1997]; French Guiana [1997]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [1999]; Belize [1999]; Mexico (Caribbean and Gulf coastal states) [1999]; other Central American states (e.g. Costa Rica, Nicaragua) [late 1990s].
Host: Wide range of ornamentals and crops (especially Hibiscus spp. and other Malvaceae, plus major crops including citrus, cocoa, cotton and soursop)
Event summary: Starting with its detection in Grenada in 1994, hibiscus mealybug caused severe damage to ornamentals, fruit trees and field crops and then spread rapidly north and south through the Lesser Antilles, reaching many eastern Caribbean islands, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and jumping to Belize, Mexico and northern South America (Guyana, French Guiana, Venezuela) by the late 1990s. Regional trade in infested planting material and favourable tropical climates allowed the pest to become widely established across the Caribbean Basin, with estimated losses of many millions of US dollars in Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago before large-scale classical biological control campaigns using parasitoids such as Anagyrus kamali and Gyranusoidea indica brought populations under better control.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4434?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid long‑distance movement of infested nursery stock and planting material among Caribbean islands and onto adjacent mainland territories; inadequate early quarantine for mealybugs; dense plantings of highly susceptible ornamentals in tourist areas and diversified smallholder systems with many alternative hosts, combined with favourable warm, humid climates. Internal mechanisms: Extreme polyphagy and high reproductive potential; inherent capacity for geographic range expansion in tropical climates; efficient local dispersal of crawlers by wind, animals and on contaminated plant material, allowing rapid build‑up and spread in newly invaded territories.
Review: review – This is a real, high‑impact emergence episode (first large-scale invasion of the Caribbean/Central American–northern South American region) and should be retained. Start year adjusted from 1993 to 1994 to match EPPO and FAO reports that first confirmed the pest in Grenada in November 1994, and country list expanded/clarified (including Mexico [1999]) based on EPPO distribution summaries and regional biological‑control reports. The classification as an inter‑continental emergence (first occurrence in the South America continent, which here includes Central America and the Caribbean) remains appropriate. Key supporting sources include EPPO RS 1995/235 and 1996/207, FAO Special Alert 263, the EPPO datasheet, and Caribbean biological‑control case studies.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4434?utm_source=openai))

Countries: United States of America – California (Imperial and neighbouring counties) [1999]; United States of America – Florida (Broward and Miami‑Dade counties) [2002]; United States of America – Texas, Louisiana, Georgia and other south‑eastern states with limited foci [early 2000s].
Host: Primarily ornamentals (Hibiscus spp. and other woody ornamentals), with additional infestations on various fruit trees and landscape plants in residential, nursery and urban plantings
Event summary: After the pink hibiscus mealybug had already become established in Hawaii in the 1980s, it was detected on the continental United States in California and northern Baja California in 1999 and then in Florida in 2002, where it caused localized but intense damage to ornamentals in nurseries and residential landscapes. Over the early 2000s the pest was found in additional Gulf and south‑eastern U.S. states, prompting eradication attempts, regulatory actions and large‑scale classical biological control releases that largely prevented the species from becoming a widespread, persistent outbreak pest across U.S. agriculture despite very high estimated potential economic impacts.([invasivespeciesinfo.gov](https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/terrestrial/invertebrates/pink-hibiscus-mealybug?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International and regional trade in infested nursery stock and ornamentals from Caribbean and other infested areas into U.S. coastal states; widespread use of highly susceptible ornamentals in urban landscapes; suitable subtropical climates in southern California, Florida and the Gulf Coast. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, short generation time and ability to exploit many ornamental and fruit hosts; capacity for geographic range expansion into warm temperate zones; initial lack of effective native natural enemies prior to deliberate introduction of parasitoids such as Anagyrus kamali and Gyranusoidea indica and predators such as Cryptolaemus montrouzieri.
Review: review – Event is real and among the most important emergence episodes because it marks the establishment and subsequent containment of M. hirsutus on the continental United States. However, it was misclassified as an inter‑continental emergence in the original file: North America was already colonised in 1983–1984 via Hawaii, so spread to California and Florida in 1999–2002 represents a major re‑occurrence within an already infested continent rather than the first continental record.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6359081/?utm_source=openai)) Sub‑regions have been restricted to Northern America and Mexico/Central American countries were removed from this row to avoid mixing two continents and double‑counting spread already covered under the Caribbean–Central America episode. Recommended action: retain as a major event but keep flagged for expert review of the exact list of affected U.S. states and the end date of the episode.

Countries: Brazil – Roraima [2010]; Brazil – Espírito Santo [2012]; additional Brazilian states in northern, north‑eastern, central‑western and southern regions (e.g. Pará, Maranhão, Bahia, Pernambuco, Mato Grosso, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina) [2012-2014].
Host: Fruit crops (e.g. soursop, citrus, carambola, grapevine and other fruit trees), ornamentals (especially Hibiscus) and various spontaneous hosts in and around orchards, vineyards and urban plantings
Event summary: In 2010, hibiscus mealybug was recorded for the first time in Brazil in the northern state of Roraima on hibiscus and several other hosts, representing a southward extension from previously infested parts of northern South America. Over the following few years the pest spread rapidly within Brazil, being found by 2012 in Espírito Santo in the south‑east and subsequently in multiple northern, north‑eastern, central‑western and southern states, where it attacked a broad range of fruit and ornamental hosts and triggered concern about impacts on crops such as cocoa and grapevine. By about 2014, the species was established in at least 11 Brazilian states, and research and extension focused on documenting its host range, natural enemies and suitable integrated management options.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/BR_rr?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Internal Brazilian movement of infested planting material (especially ornamentals and fruit trees) from the initial focus in Roraima; expansion of perennial crop and ornamental plantings across climatic zones favourable for mealybug development; limited early awareness and surveillance, which allowed populations to build up before detection in new regions. Internal mechanisms: Strong capacity for geographic range expansion across tropical and subtropical climates; polyphagy on numerous cultivated and wild hosts; effective local dispersal via crawlers and human‑assisted movement on nursery stock, enabling rapid colonisation of distant production regions once introduced.
Review: review – This is a genuine, high‑impact expansion episode in Brazil and should be retained, but several corrections were necessary. Evidence from EPPO RS 2013/009 and Brazilian studies shows that the first record in Brazil was in Roraima in 2010, not São Paulo, and that subsequent spread involved many states including Espírito Santo and several in the north‑east, central‑west and south.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/BR_rr?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence has been changed to re‑occurrence, because South America (including the ‘South America’ UN sub‑region) was already infested (e.g. Guyana, French Guiana, Venezuela, Suriname) before 2010; Brazil represents further spread within an already affected sub‑region, driven by trade and internal plant movement rather than a first occurrence on a new continent or sub‑region. Recommended action: retain but have a regional expert review the precise list of Brazilian states and the chosen end year for the episode.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Ornamental and landscape plants (notably Hibiscus rosa‑sinensis and other ornamental shrubs) and, to a lesser extent, fruit crops such as grapevine and guava in urban and peri‑urban settings
Event summary: Surveys in 2010 revealed that hibiscus mealybug was present throughout Cyprus, mainly on ornamental hibiscus in private gardens and garden centres but also occasionally on grapevine and guava, representing a major new outbreak focus in the eastern Mediterranean part of the pest’s native/long‑established Asian range. The finding, formally reported in 2011, triggered official control and intensive surveillance, as the pest became widely established in urban and tourist areas and raised concern about potential spread to mainland Mediterranean agriculture and the wider EPPO region. During the first half of the 2010s, management in Cyprus focused on containment, monitoring and promotion of biological control to limit damage in city parks, gardens and nearby crops.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-185?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction with infested ornamental plants imported from already infested parts of the Middle East or wider Asian range; high densities of susceptible ornamentals in coastal resort and urban landscapes; Mediterranean climates with mild winters and warm summers that favour survival and reproduction. Internal mechanisms: Continued geographic range expansion at the fringes of a long‑established range; broad host spectrum allowing establishment on common ornamental and fruit species even at low initial densities; initially limited presence of specialised natural enemies at the point of introduction, increasing the likelihood of establishment and rapid population growth.
Review: review – This event corresponds to the well‑documented discovery and rapid spread of M. hirsutus on Cyprus and is important because it marks establishment in the eastern Mediterranean and within the EPPO region, but the original row had major geographical and classification errors. Cyprus is classified as Asia/Western Asia in the provided country list, not Europe/Southern Europe, so continent and sub‑region have been corrected accordingly.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/CY?utm_source=openai)) Because the pest was already widespread in Asia (including several other Western Asian countries) long before 2010, this outbreak is better described as a re‑occurrence (regional resurgence on a new island within an already infested sub‑region) rather than an inter‑continental emergence, so the inter‑continental flag has been set to false and re‑occurrence to true. The event has also been re‑dated to 2010–2015 to reflect the first-record year documented by the Cyprus NPPO and EPPO RS 2011/069. Recommended action: retain as a major episode but keep flagged for expert review, especially regarding whether later detections in Greece and Türkiye should be treated as an extension of this same Mediterranean episode or as separate minor events.

Countries: Mexico – Tabasco State (cacao) [2014-2016]; additional Mexican cacao- or shade‑tree‑growing states in the Gulf and south‑eastern region [mid‑2010s].
Host: Cacao (Theobroma cacao) as a newly emphasized, economically important host, alongside other perennial crops and associated shade or border plants
Event summary: After hibiscus mealybug had been present in Mexico on ornamentals and other hosts since the late 1990s, severe infestations were reported in cacao plantations in Tabasco in the mid‑2010s, where the pest damaged shoots, leaves and pods and caused noticeable yield loss and dieback. The mealybug exploited both cacao and associated shade or border plants, and its emergence as a key pest in cacao systems prompted detailed studies of damage symptoms, host associations and local natural enemies. By the late 2010s, management recommendations specific to cacao (monitoring, cultural measures and compatible biological and chemical controls) were being developed, illustrating the pest’s capacity to re‑emerge as a serious problem on new, high‑value perennial crop hosts within an already infested region.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281034453_Biological_Control_of_Pink_Hibiscus_Mealybug_Project_Manual?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of cacao cultivation in warm, humid lowland regions with diverse shade trees and border vegetation that serve as alternative hosts; movement of infested planting material and pruned branches between farms; limited initial monitoring of mealybugs in cacao systems, allowing populations to build before being recognized as a major problem. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and re‑emergence on a major new economic host (cacao) within an already infested landscape; high adaptability and polyphagy of M. hirsutus, enabling successful exploitation of cacao tissues and associated shade plants; potential development of locally adapted populations or shifts in natural enemy complexes that increased its prominence in cacao relative to earlier ornamental‑focused infestations.
Review: review – This cacao‑focused episode is real and well documented for Tabasco, Mexico, and illustrates a clear host‑range driven re‑emergence of M. hirsutus within an already infested country, so it is appropriate to keep it as one of the major events. The main correction needed was geographic: Mexico belongs to the Central America sub‑region within the South America continent group in the project’s country list, so the sub‑regions field has been restricted to Central America rather than “Central America; South America.”([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/media/data/reporting/rs-2011-04-en.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑emergence (rather than a new inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with the fact that the pest had been present in Mexico on other hosts since 1999 and that the novelty here lies in its rise to prominence on cacao. Recommended action: retain but keep flagged for review to confirm the relative importance of this host‑shift episode compared with other possible crop‑specific re‑emergence events (e.g. on grapes or mulberry in Asia).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) in university glasshouse trials
Event summary: In 2003, larvae of Manduca sexta were discovered causing defoliation on tomato trial plants in two glasshouses at Humboldt University in Berlin, Germany, representing an accidental introduction of this American solanaceous pest into Europe. The infestation was traced to adults that most likely escaped from a nearby research rearing facility where M. sexta was maintained, and their progeny developed on tomato plants under protected cultivation before being detected. All larvae were removed and the crop was chemically treated; follow-up inspections found no additional specimens, and German authorities and EPPO subsequently classified the incursion as eradicated and the species as absent from Germany and the wider EPPO region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Human-mediated escape of adult Manduca sexta from a nearby laboratory/rearing facility into adjacent tomato glasshouses, combined with the presence of suitable host plants and favorable protected-climate conditions that allowed temporary local reproduction. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains, resistance, or host shifts in this episode; the event reflects a short-lived anthropogenic geographic range jump into a new continent rather than evolutionary change in the pest.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures the only well-documented inter-continental incursion of Manduca sexta: a 2003 tomato glasshouse outbreak in Berlin, Germany, with larvae feeding on tomatoes, eradication by removal and chemical treatment, and subsequent official status as “absent, single occurrence, eradicated.” Continent (Europe), subregion (Western Europe), and country (Germany [2003]) are consistent with the UNSD scheme and EPPO reporting. Classification as inter-continental emergence is appropriate because there was local reproduction and feeding on host plants in a new continent, not merely detection of imported material with no in situ development. No evidence was found for other larger emergence events (e.g. establishment in Europe, Africa, or Asia) between 1990 and 2025, and the cited EPPO reporting article plus the German and English Julius Kühn-Institut express PRAs are the most relevant primary sources for this event, so the event is retained without modification.

Host: Apple trees (Malus domestica) – trunk and branch cankers (perennial canker) and associated bull’s‑eye rot of fruit in Washington State orchards
Event summary: Around 1990–1995, perennial canker and associated bull’s‑eye rot caused by Neofabraea perennans were documented as serious problems in apple orchards in eastern Washington State, USA, with trunk and limb cankers plus latent fruit infections leading to substantial tree decline and postharvest losses. Studies conducted in 1987–1990 showed abundant conidial production on cankers during cool, wet periods and highlighted high infection risk around winter pruning, consistent with the heavy disease pressure seen in the early 1990s. Improved pruning sanitation, removal of cankered wood, and adjustments to irrigation and fungicide programs subsequently reduced inoculum levels and limited further spread within affected orchards.([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/backissues/Documents/1992Articles/PlantDisease76n11_1109.pdf))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Shift to high‑density plantings on dwarf rootstocks, use of overhead irrigation, and longer cold‑storage periods favored canker development and latent fruit infections; limited awareness of Neofabraea canker epidemiology delayed effective management. Internal mechanisms: No clear novel genotype was described; impact appears mainly linked to enhanced transmission and perennation via abundant sporulation on cankers and infected fruit, increasing inoculum pressure in intensively managed orchards.
Review: retain – Evidence from Grove (1992) shows that perennial canker and bull’s‑eye rot caused by N. perennans were chronic and economically important in eastern Washington through 1987–1990, with severe bull’s‑eye rot outbreaks in the mid‑1980s; treating the early 1990s as a major re‑occurrence episode in the same subregion is consistent with the dataset scope. Geography and event‑type coding (re‑occurrence only) match the definitions, and the sources used are appropriate.([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/backissues/Documents/1992Articles/PlantDisease76n11_1109.pdf))

Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards and long‑term storage in southern Brazil (Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul)
Event summary: In the 1995–1996 seasons, bull’s‑eye rot was first reported in commercial apple orchards in southern Brazil and the causal agent was identified as Neofabraea perennans, leading to serious postharvest losses on ‘Fuji’ and other cultivars during long‑term cold storage and marking the first establishment of this pathogen on apples in South America. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s the disease became widespread in the main production areas of Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, with lesions appearing after several months in storage and causing high cull rates in export lots. Later taxonomic studies showed that many Brazilian bull’s‑eye rot epidemics were actually caused by newly described Neofabraea species (N. brasiliensis and N. actinidiae), but historical reports and extension bulletins confirm that N. perennans was present and initially regarded as the main etiological agent in this period.([educapes.capes.gov.br](https://educapes.capes.gov.br/handle/capes/901976?mode=full))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive apple production and long‑term controlled‑atmosphere storage in southern Brazil, combined with movement of nursery stock and fruit from temperate production regions, facilitated introduction and establishment of Neofabraea spp. Internal mechanisms: Initial outbreaks were driven by latent infection biology and efficient survival on pruning wounds and fruit rather than documented novel genotypes; later work showed diversification into regionally adapted species (N. brasiliensis, N. actinidiae), indicating ongoing evolutionary adaptation of the Neofabraea complex to Brazilian environments.
Review: review – Retain the event but with corrected timing: Brazilian sources consistently state that bull’s‑eye rot on apples was first observed and attributed to N. perennans in the 1995–1996 seasons, so the event year has been updated from 1996–2002 to 1995–2002 and the country tag to “Brazil [1995]”.([educapes.capes.gov.br](https://educapes.capes.gov.br/handle/capes/901976?mode=full)) Classification as an inter‑continental emergence (first establishment of N. perennans on apples in South America with substantial storage losses) is appropriate. However, later work shows that other Neofabraea spp. now dominate Brazilian bull’s‑eye rot, so the share of impact attributable specifically to N. perennans is uncertain and should be reviewed by subject‑matter experts.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Pear (Pyrus communis, mainly ‘Packham’s Triumph’) and other pome fruit in Western Cape orchards and storage
Event summary: From around 2012 to 2015, bull’s‑eye rot (lenticel decay) began to be recognised as a postharvest problem on ‘Packham’s Triumph’ and other pears in the Western Cape of South Africa. A dedicated MSc study and industry surveys detected Neofabraea alba as the main causal agent on apples but also recorded conidia of Neofabraea perennans and N. kienholzii on pear and apple fruit, and identified N. perennans on Packham’s Triumph pears, representing the first reports of this species on pome fruit in South Africa and, by extension, in Africa. Although N. perennans was not the dominant species in the complex, the finding triggered further surveys and incorporation of Neofabraea lenticel decay into postharvest risk assessments and control programmes for export pears.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/fr/records/6a32c781c5555e957fa7d328))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of Neofabraea spp. (including N. perennans) with infected nursery stock or fruit into Western Cape orchards, combined with cool, wet winters and increasing use of long‑term cold storage for export pears, favoured expression of latent infections. Internal mechanisms: This episode mainly reflects geographic range expansion of existing lineages into a new continent rather than documented novel genotypes; the strong capacity of Neofabraea spp. for latent lenticel infection and survival during storage underpins their impact.
Review: review – Retain as the first confirmed record of N. perennans on pome fruit in Africa, but correct the timing and event‑type coding. Published MSc work and industry reports indicate that N. perennans and N. kienholzii were first detected on pears and apples in the Western Cape around 2012–2013, not as early as 2008, so the event window has been updated to 2012–2015 and the country tag to “South Africa [2012]”.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/fr/records/6a32c781c5555e957fa7d328)) Re‑emergence has been set to No because this is a first detection on the continent rather than a resurgence driven by genetic change; inter‑continental emergence remains Yes. The summary and sources have been revised to clarify that N. alba is the predominant species and N. perennans occurs at low frequency, so the quantitative impact attributable to N. perennans should be further assessed.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards and cold storage in Poland
Event summary: From around 2010 to 2015, bull’s‑eye rot caused increasing postharvest losses in stored apples in Poland, and a survey of fruit from major production regions identified three Neofabraea species—N. alba, N. perennans and N. kienholzii—with N. alba dominant and N. perennans present in a minority of samples. The disease manifested after long‑term cold storage, when apparently healthy fruit at harvest developed characteristic sunken, brown, bull’s‑eye lesions, leading to substantial culling of susceptible cultivars. The work confirmed that Neofabraea spp., including N. perennans which had already been reported in Poland in the 1960s, are important components of the postharvest rot complex, and it supported the adoption of molecular diagnostics, revised fungicide programmes and improved orchard sanitation and storage practices to limit future outbreaks.([bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12449))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased use of long‑term controlled‑atmosphere storage, widespread planting of susceptible cultivars and changes in permitted postharvest fungicides likely favoured Neofabraea spp. over other storage pathogens. Internal mechanisms: The Polish study did not demonstrate specific novel genotypes or resistance traits in N. perennans; the pattern is more consistent with re‑occurrence driven by management and storage conditions than with documented re‑emergence due to evolutionary change.
Review: review – Keep the event but re‑interpret its type. Molecular work from Poland shows that N. perennans was already reported there in the 1960s and that N. alba is the dominant species in recent outbreaks, with N. perennans recovered from only about 5% of symptomatic apples.([bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12449)) Accordingly, the event has been recoded from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence (no evidence of new N. perennans genotypes) in a previously affected subregion. Because the quantitative contribution of N. perennans to losses is modest relative to N. alba, the importance of this event for this specific EPP should be reviewed before final inclusion among the top global events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Apple trees and fruit (Malus domestica) – cankers and bull’s‑eye rot in the U.S. Pacific Northwest
Event summary: Between about 2012 and 2018, growers in the U.S. Pacific Northwest reported renewed problems with perennial canker of apple trees and bull’s‑eye rot of stored fruit, and field studies showed Neofabraea perennans and N. kienholzii to be the main species associated with cankers and fruit decay. Experiments in commercial orchards during 2012–2014 quantified infection timing and showed that fruit infections initiated near harvest could lead to substantial losses after several months in cold storage, while complementary work on twig inoculations clarified when cankers develop most readily. These findings, together with fungicide‑efficacy trials, underpinned adjustments in pruning timing, wound protection, and integrated pre‑ and postharvest fungicide programmes that allowed the industry to reduce disease severity to more manageable levels.([rex.libraries.wsu.edu](https://rex.libraries.wsu.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Timing-of-Perennial-Canker-Development-in/99900547488001842))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Aging high‑density orchards with accumulated inoculum in cankers, restrictions or shifts in available fungicides, and continued reliance on long storage periods increased the relative importance of Neofabraea perennans and related species. Internal mechanisms: The renewed impact reflects efficient latent infection and sporulation under cool, wet conditions; available data do not yet demonstrate stable fungicide resistance or distinct new genotypes of N. perennans, so this episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven mainly by management and climatic factors.
Review: review – Retain as a major recent episode but adjust the event type. Plant Disease articles on infection timing, canker development and fungicide efficacy document a pronounced resurgence of N. perennans‑associated cankers and bull’s‑eye rot in Pacific Northwest apples from 2012 onward, with substantial research and management responses.([rex.libraries.wsu.edu](https://rex.libraries.wsu.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Timing-of-Perennial-Canker-Development-in/99900547488001842)) However, they do not present clear evidence of novel N. perennans genotypes or stable fungicide resistance, so re‑emergence has been set to No and the event is classified as a re‑occurrence driven largely by orchard structure, fungicide programmes and storage practices.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica; e.g. ‘Fuji’, ‘Granny Smith’, ‘Cripps Pink’) in Chilean export orchards and cold storage
Event summary: In 2017–2018, apple lots from Chile stored for export began to show typical bull’s‑eye rot symptoms, and isolation plus multilocus sequencing confirmed Neofabraea perennans as the causal agent, leading to a 2020 disease note reporting the first occurrence of this species causing bull’s‑eye rot of apple in Chile. The disease became evident after extended cold storage, with slightly sunken, circular brown lesions developing on fruit from some orchards and raising concern about postharvest quality for distant markets. Following confirmation of N. perennans, Chilean producers and advisors strengthened orchard sanitation, adjusted fungicide applications around infection periods and implemented stricter storage and fruit‑selection practices to limit spread and economic impact, while continuing to manage N. alba, the previously recognised bull’s‑eye rot pathogen in the country.([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-12-19-2561-PDN))
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased volume of long‑stored export apples from cool, wet production zones in Chile, combined with regional and international movement of planting material and fruit, likely facilitated introduction and establishment of N. perennans. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s inherent ability for latent infection and survival during long cold storage underpins its success; there is no direct evidence of a novel Chile‑specific genotype, but its appearance in a previously N. perennans‑free South American country suggests geographic range expansion of existing lineages adapted to intensive storage systems.
Review: review – Retain as a well‑documented national emergence but correct the event‑type coding and sources. A 2020 Plant Disease note demonstrates that N. perennans was newly detected causing bull’s‑eye rot of apple in Chile in 2017–2018; earlier Chilean work had only found N. alba as the bull’s‑eye rot pathogen.([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-12-19-2561-PDN)) Because N. perennans was already present in Brazil, this Chilean outbreak does not represent inter‑continental emergence, and there is no evidence for genetic change in the pathogen, so re‑emergence has been set to No and all emergence‑type flags are left as No. The Brazilian thesis has been removed from the event‑level sources and replaced with the earlier Chilean characterization paper as more relevant context for the local species shift.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban/amenity plantings, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
Event summary: In 1999, Obolodiplosis robiniae was reported from Victoria on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, marking its spread within North America from its native eastern U.S. range to western Canada. The midge established on ornamental and planted black locust trees in urban areas, where conspicuous marginal leaf-roll galls were observed. The event represented westward geographic expansion within the continent rather than a new host association, and the pest has since persisted locally without evidence of continent-wide outbreaks comparable to those later seen in Eurasia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of infested nursery stock or ornamental black locust saplings across North America, combined with widespread planting of Robinia pseudoacacia in western Canadian cities, likely enabled colonization of Vancouver Island. Internal mechanisms: The species’ multivoltine life cycle and high fecundity, together with the high suitability of black locust foliage, supported establishment but no specific novel strain or resistance trait was reported in this event.
Review: Decision: retain. The 1999 detection on Victoria, Vancouver Island, is documented in European invasion syntheses and Csóka (2006) as an early extra-native-range record within North America, and there is no evidence of earlier western Canadian establishment. Classification as a minor within-continent range expansion (no intra- or inter-continental emergence flag under the UNSD subregion scheme) is appropriate, and although impact was limited compared with later Eurasian and New Zealand invasions, this stepping-stone event is retained because the total number of major episodes for this species is below ten.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban trees, shelterbelts and plantations; occasionally ornamental Robinia spp.
Event summary: Around 2002, Obolodiplosis robiniae was first detected in eastern Asia, with sudden appearance of characteristic leaf-margin galls on black locust in Japan and the Republic of Korea, representing the first established populations of the species outside North America. By 2004 the gall midge was recorded in China (Qinhuangdao City, Hebei Province) and then rapidly spread across multiple provinces, infesting roadside trees and plantations. The event marked a major inter-continental invasion from North America into Asia and set the stage for further expansion and local outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: International trade in live plants and nursery stock of Robinia pseudoacacia, including asymptomatic material carrying eggs or early-instar larvae in young leaflets, is considered the primary pathway for trans-Pacific introduction and rapid regional spread; extensive planting of black locust in East Asia (for shelterbelts, afforestation, and ornamentals) provided abundant habitat. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate and multiple generations per growing season, together with good dispersal ability of adults, promoted rapid population build-up; genetic studies indicate substantial genetic variation in Chinese populations consistent with multiple introductions and/or large founding populations, facilitating successful colonization and spread.
Review: Decision: review. This event correctly captures the first established populations outside North America in East Asia (Japan and Republic of Korea in 2002; China in 2004) and is appropriately classified as an inter-continental emergence into Asia. Country dates and interpretation are supported by Kodoi et al. 2003 for Japan and Korea and by Yang et al. 2006 and subsequent genetic work for China. The source list has been refined to emphasize primary East Asian references rather than a European-focused review; otherwise no changes to timing, geography or event-type flags are required.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Sub-regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: Italy [2003]; Czechia [2004]; Slovenia [2004]; Croatia [2006]; Germany [2006]; Hungary [2006]; Slovakia [2006]; Ukraine [2006]; Luxembourg [2006]; Netherlands (Kingdom of the) [2007]; Switzerland [2007]; Austria [2007]; France [2007]; Poland [2007]; Serbia [2007]; Romania [2007]; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2007]; Sweden [2008]; Denmark [2009]; Spain [2010]; Russian Federation [≤2010]; Albania [≤2010]; North Macedonia [≤2010]
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban landscapes, roadsides, shelterbelts and plantations; ornamental Robinia cultivars in parks and gardens
Event summary: In July 2003 Obolodiplosis robiniae was first reported in Europe from Paese near Padua in northeastern Italy, where heavy galling of black locust foliage was observed, and by 2004–2006 it had spread into Central and Eastern Europe, including Czechia, Slovenia, Hungary, Slovakia, Croatia, Germany and Ukraine. Between 2006 and 2010 the gall midge rapidly colonized much of Western and Northern Europe, with first records from countries such as the Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria, France, Poland, Serbia, Romania, the United Kingdom, Luxembourg, Sweden, Denmark, Spain and additional Balkan and Russian localities, often causing conspicuous defoliation of amenity and roadside black locust. Although densities later declined in some regions due to parasitoid build-up, the species has remained widely established across Europe and now occupies most areas where black locust is planted.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The primary driver was continent-wide movement of infested nursery and landscaping stock of Robinia pseudoacacia, combined with the widespread use of this invasive tree in forestry, erosion control and ornamental plantings across Europe; human-assisted jump dispersal was followed by natural spread along road networks and river corridors. Internal mechanisms: The midge’s host specialization on an already widely invasive tree, its multivoltine life cycle and ability to exploit young foliage, and the initial absence or low abundance of specialized natural enemies in Europe allowed rapid population growth and dispersal; later, introduction and spread of the parasitoid Platygaster robiniae contributed to natural regulation but did not prevent continent-wide establishment.
Review: Decision: review. This row appropriately represents the inter-continental emergence of O. robiniae into Europe and its rapid spread across Southern, Central, Eastern, Western and Northern Europe, in line with Duso & Skuhravá 2003, Skuhravá et al. 2007, EPPO RS 2008/202 and later syntheses. The countries list has been updated to include Hungary [2006] and Romania [2007], which are explicitly reported as early, often heavily infested areas, and reordered slightly while retaining approximate entries (≤2010) for Albania, North Macedonia and the Russian Federation where only regional summaries are available. Event-type flags remain correct (inter-continental emergence only) and the episode is clearly among the largest global emergence events for this species.
