EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia in urban plantings and street trees in southwestern France and Belgium
Event summary: After initial detection in Belgium and then France in the mid‑2000s, Obolodiplosis robiniae populations built up dramatically in 2007 in parts of southwestern France, especially Dordogne and Gironde, where black locust trees experienced heavy galling and premature leaf drop. During the 2007 growing season, high densities of galls were reported in streetside and ornamental plantings, drawing attention from plant protection services and leading to targeted monitoring. By 2008, however, field surveys recorded a sharp decline in visible damage in the same areas due to high parasitism by the introduced parasitoid Platygaster robiniae, and the outbreak subsided to lower, more stable levels of infestation.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Dense planting of susceptible black locust in urban and peri‑urban landscapes, combined with the recent arrival of the gall midge and initially low levels of natural enemies, allowed rapid population growth in southwestern France; mild climatic conditions further supported multiple generations per season. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported, but enemy release followed by subsequent build-up of the specialist parasitoid Platygaster robiniae created a boom‑and‑bust dynamic, with the initial outbreak representing a re‑occurrence driven largely by ecological imbalance (low parasitism) rather than genetic change in the pest.
Review: Decision: review. The 2007–2008 outbreak and subsequent collapse of O. robiniae populations in southwestern France (Dordogne, Gironde) and previously infested Belgium is well documented by EPPO RS 2008/202 and associated national reports, and its classification as a re-occurrence (not a new inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because populations were already established in Europe. Country timing has been corrected so France is now listed as [2007–2008] instead of [2005–2007], aligning with EPPO’s account of first French records in 2007 and high damage followed by parasitoid-driven decline in 2008, while Belgium remains [2005–2007] to reflect earlier detection with confirmation and peak damage by 2007.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Countries: China [2004] (initially Hebei Province, later many northern and eastern provinces)
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia plantations, shelterbelts and urban trees in northern and eastern China
Event summary: In 2004 Obolodiplosis robiniae was first recorded in China from Qinhuangdao City in Hebei Province, and in subsequent years it spread rapidly across northern and eastern Chinese regions where black locust is widely planted. During the late 2000s and early 2010s, high infestation levels were documented in shelterbelts, plantations and urban trees, with multiple generations per season causing repeated galling and, in heavy outbreaks, partial defoliation and growth reduction. As the midge became established throughout much of the Chinese range of black locust, it transitioned from an emerging invader to a chronic foliar pest whose impact varied among regions and years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: The Chinese outbreak was facilitated by extensive, often monocultural plantings of Robinia pseudoacacia for afforestation, sand stabilization and urban greening, which created continuous host corridors; long-distance movement of infested plants and nursery stock between provinces further accelerated spread. Internal mechanisms: Population genetic analyses indicate relatively high genetic diversity in Chinese O. robiniae populations, consistent with multiple introductions and/or large founding populations, which may have enhanced adaptive potential and colonization success; life‑history traits such as multivoltinism and efficient exploitation of young leaves supported repeated, high‑density infestations once the species was established.
Review: Decision: retain. This event accurately summarizes the first discovery of O. robiniae in China in 2004 (Qinhuangdao, Hebei) and the subsequent decade of rapid spread and frequent heavy infestations across northern and eastern China, as described by Yang et al. 2006 and Du et al. 2020, and appropriately treats it as a major re-occurrence episode within Eastern Asia following the earlier 2002 East Asian introduction. No corrections to geography, timing or emergence-type flags are required.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Countries: New Zealand [2009] (Auckland, then Bay of Plenty, Hawke’s Bay, Northland, Taupo, Waikato, Wairarapa, Wellington, Canterbury and other regions)
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia in parks, shelterbelts and amenity plantings across New Zealand
Event summary: In early 2009 the New Zealand biosecurity surveillance system detected Obolodiplosis robiniae for the first time, with samples from black locust trees collected at high‑risk sites and confirmed as the North American gall midge, representing its arrival in Australasia. Over the following decade the species spread widely through much of New Zealand, with distribution records from Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Hawke’s Bay, Northland, Taupo, Waikato, Wairarapa, Wellington, Canterbury and other regions, where repeated galling of Robinia foliage was observed. By the early 2020s the pest was considered established nationwide, causing recurring cosmetic damage and some defoliation on black locust, though impacts on native flora were judged low and management focused mainly on monitoring rather than eradication.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction was most likely via infested ornamental or forestry plant material of Robinia pseudoacacia imported from regions where O. robiniae was already established (Asia or Europe), with subsequent within‑country spread along human transport corridors and through local planting and movement of black locust. Internal mechanisms: The midge’s strict association with Robinia pseudoacacia, combined with its ability to complete several generations per year under New Zealand conditions, promoted establishment; later reports of heavy parasitism by a previously unrecognized parasitoid wasp suggest that natural enemy recruitment may begin to moderate populations, although this did not influence the initial establishment phase.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2009 detection and subsequent spread of O. robiniae across New Zealand are well supported by national surveillance reports (Biosecurity 92, Forest Health News 195; MPI Surveillance 48(3) 2021) and comparative invasion analyses, and correctly represent the first established populations in Oceania. Classification as an inter-continental emergence into a new continent, with modest but persistent impacts on ornamental black locust, is appropriate and no corrections are needed.

EPP common name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban parks, roadside plantings and shelterbelts in the southern Caucasus and northeastern Türkiye
Event summary: In 2013 the black locust gall midge was first recorded in the Caucasus region of Western Asia, with galls detected on Robinia pseudoacacia in Georgia, followed later in the decade by records from Armenia (initially in plantations near Dilijan and then in parks in Yerevan) and, in 2019, from north‑eastern Türkiye near the Georgian border. During the 2010s and early 2020s the species spread locally along urban plantings, shelterbelts and roadsides in these countries, forming characteristic leaflet-margin roll galls and occasionally causing noticeable foliar damage on ornamental and amenity black locust trees. This episode represents an intra‑continental range expansion of an already widespread Eurasian invader into a new UNSD sub‑region (Western Asia), rather than a new inter‑continental introduction.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Likely short- to medium-range human-assisted transport of infested Robinia pseudoacacia planting stock and vehicles along Black Sea and Transcaucasian transport corridors from already infested areas in southern Russia and eastern Europe, combined with widespread planting of R. pseudoacacia as an ornamental and shelter tree in Georgia, Armenia and northeastern Türkiye. Internal mechanisms: The same life-history traits that facilitated earlier invasions—multivoltinism, strong association with black locust and high dispersal capacity of adults—supported colonization of fragmented urban and roadside host patches; current evidence does not indicate distinct Western Asian strains or major changes in virulence relative to other Eurasian populations.
Review: Decision: review. This new row has been added to capture the documented post‑2013 expansion of O. robiniae into Western Asia, with first records from Georgia (2013), subsequent findings in Armenia (Dilijan plantations and Yerevan parks) and a 2019 detection in northeastern Türkiye, as reported by EPPO, Mirumyan & Skuhravá (2022) and Sinchuk & Sinchuk (2025). It is appropriately classified as an intra-continental emergence within Asia into a new UNSD subregion, following earlier establishment in Eastern Asia, but onset years for Armenia are approximate (≤2021) and should be rechecked against future national updates.

Host: Black gram (Vigna mungo) grown as a rabi crop in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India
Event summary: During the 2018–2019 rabi season in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India, field trials and observations reported exceptionally high infestation of black gram by the stem fly Ophiomyia phaseoli, with average plant infestation exceeding 40% in the latest sowing dates and plot-level incidence reaching up to 100% in some observation periods. This episode led the authors to describe O. phaseoli as having attained major pest status on black gram in this region for the first time, with severe tunnelling and basal stem damage in young plants threatening yields across an important production area. Subsequent pest and breeding reviews on black gram have cited stem fly (O. phaseoli) as a recently emerging or resurging internal feeder in Andhra Pradesh, although detailed multi-year regional impact data beyond the 2018–2019 season are still limited.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increased cultivation of black gram as a rabi crop in rice fallows in southern Andhra Pradesh, together with periods of high maximum temperatures (around 36–38 °C) and declining relative humidity during late February–March, created highly favourable conditions for rapid build-up and survival of Ophiomyia phaseoli populations. Additional contributing factors likely include limited adoption of targeted stem-fly management, cropping calendars that expose seedlings during peak favourable weather, and possibly changes in insecticide use patterns that did not effectively target stem fly. Internal mechanisms: no evidence has been presented for novel strains, pesticide resistance or host shifts in this episode; the event is therefore interpreted as a climate- and management-driven resurgence of an existing pest within a previously affected subregion rather than a re-emergence driven by evolutionary change in the fly.
Review: retain – This new row has been added to capture the 2018–2019 episode in which Ophiomyia phaseoli reached major pest status on black gram in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India. It is classified as a re-occurrence event (re_occurrence = true; re_emergence = false) within Southern Asia because O. phaseoli has long been present on black gram and other pulses in South Asia, and the episode represents a documented surge in pest importance in a major production zone, driven by weather and management conditions rather than first establishment in the subregion or demonstrable genetic change. The event fits the project’s emphasis on high-impact post‑1990 emergence episodes (very high local infestation levels in a large cropping area and subsequent recognition as an “emerging pest” in the regional literature), although the exact spatial extent and aggregate yield loss remain to be quantified. Recommended decision: retain as one of the principal post‑2005 emergence events for O. phaseoli, with a note that future updates should revisit its ranking if more quantitative impact data become available.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Maize (Zea mays) and other summer row crops in temperate arable systems
Event summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, fall panicum began to appear as a new and increasingly troublesome weed in maize fields of north‑west Germany, having previously occurred in Western Europe mainly as an occasional grain alien and ruderal plant. During the 1990s–early 2000s it spread and naturalised as a regular agricultural weed in Flanders (Belgium), especially on sandy soils between Brugge and Gent and in parts of Antwerpen and Limburg, where it became frequent in maize fields and disturbed arable land. By the mid‑2000s the species was considered a well‑established but locally concentrated C4 grass weed in Western European maize‑growing regions, managed but not eradicated by herbicide programmes and tillage.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive maize cultivation, grain imports through major ports, reduced tillage and other conservation‑tillage practices created open, moist, disturbed habitats favourable to C4 annual grasses; herbicide regimes that selectively suppressed broadleaved weeds also indirectly favoured grass weeds. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype was documented; the episode is best interpreted as geographic range and habitat expansion within Western Europe driven by the species’ inherent colonising ability, rather than clear‑cut herbicide resistance evolution.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly captures the shift from casual grain alien to established maize-field weed in north‑west Germany and Flanders and fits the definition of a re‑occurrence within an already invaded sub‑region. Continent, sub‑region and countries match the UNSD scheme, and classification as re_occurrence (without intra/inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate. The only change made was to remove a Canadian weed inventory from the event-level source list because it is not specific to this Western European episode; the remaining European floristic sources adequately support timing and status, but the 1990 start year and omission of nearby Western European countries (e.g. the Netherlands) should be checked by a human reviewer.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Weed in disturbed sites, moist road verges, waste ground and arable field margins
Event summary: Around 2001, fall panicum was first discovered in Slovenia near Lendava, close to the Hungarian border, representing spread from previously invaded Central European countries where it was already established. In 2003, systematic flora mapping in Hungary recorded the species for the first time as a new element of the Hungarian adventive flora, with populations in western, southern and northern parts of the country on disturbed, periodically wet soils. Over the next few years the grass persisted at multiple scattered Hungarian localities, remaining locally common in disturbed habitats but still in an early invasive phase.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Stepwise spread from established populations in Austria, Croatia and other Central European countries along river valleys, transport corridors and disturbed land; likely introduction via contaminated grain, birdseed mixtures, and vehicle or rail traffic. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) from Western/Southern Europe into Eastern Europe and the Pannonian Basin, facilitated by the species’ annual life cycle, prolific seed production and tolerance of moist, disturbed soils; no specific novel strain or resistance mechanism was reported.
Review: Decision: retain. Independent floristic sources confirm first national records near Lendava (Slovenia, 2001) and multiple Hungarian localities from 2003 onward, and these countries fall in different UNSD sub‑regions (Southern vs Eastern Europe); therefore classification as an intra‑continental emergence into a new European sub‑region is appropriate. No changes were required to continent, sub‑regions, timing or emergence‑type flags, and the event plausibly represents one of the largest post‑1990 spread episodes for this species in Europe.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Arable fields (summer annual crops), disturbed grasslands and transport‑corridor vegetation
Event summary: After its initial discovery in 2003, fall panicum continued to spread within Hungary, with new localities documented in the North Hungarian Mountains and other regions by the early 2010s as it colonised disturbed sites and arable land. Through the 2010s numerous additional records led Hungarian botanists to recognise the species as an invasive alien grass with a rapidly expanding distribution and increasing importance in summer annual crops and secondary habitats. By around 2020 the weed was considered established and spreading in multiple Hungarian regions, prompting updated assessments of its invasion status and recommendations for monitoring and control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Continued disturbance along roadsides, railways and field margins, intensive summer‑annual crop production, and propagule influx via regional grain and birdseed trade favoured the persistence and spread of existing populations; climate warming may also enhance the performance of C4 annual grasses in Central Europe. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of novel biotypes or herbicide resistance has been reported; the expansion is mainly due to demographic increase and geographic range expansion of already‑introduced genotypes within the same sub‑region.
Review: Decision: review. The event appropriately treats the 2010s as a re‑occurrence within Eastern Europe, reflecting rapid demographic expansion in Hungary rather than spread to a new sub‑region or evolution of resistance, so the emergence‑type flags are consistent with definitions. I added a more specific Hungarian distribution paper (Apró közlemények) to complement the generic Kitaibelia search URL, but the start year (2010) and the extent to which fall panicum is truly among the most impactful summer‑annual weeds in Hungarian agriculture should be checked by a regional expert.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Flooded and non‑flooded rice (Oryza sativa) and associated irrigated arable systems
Event summary: Although fall panicum had been known as a maize and ruderal weed in Italy and France since the mid‑20th century, it became increasingly prominent as a rice‑field weed in northern Italy and neighbouring Southern European rice regions from the mid‑1990s onward, coinciding with broader changes in rice agronomy. Through the 2000s and 2010s, weed surveys and management reviews list P. dichotomiflorum among the important grass weeds in flooded and dry‑seeded rice, particularly where herbicide programmes shifted and direct‑seeding practices expanded. By around 2020 the species was considered a recurrent, sometimes problematic component of the rice weed flora in parts of Italy (and locally France and Spain), requiring integrated management within evolving herbicide and water‑management strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Changes in European rice cultivation, including increased use of direct seeding, alterations in flooding regimes, and herbicide programmes that reduced broadleaf weeds and favoured grass species, created niches for fall panicum in paddy systems; movement of contaminated rice seed and machinery between fields and countries further facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: The event largely reflects ecological and agronomic shifts enabling an already‑present alien grass to colonise rice systems; specific herbicide‑resistant biotypes of P. dichotomiflorum have not been clearly documented in these regions, so this is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by external management changes and the species’ inherent tolerance of wet, disturbed conditions rather than a confirmed case of resistance evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Multiple independent rice‑weed management reviews and conference proceedings corroborate that P. dichotomiflorum has become a recurrent component of weed floras in Italian and, to a lesser extent, French and Spanish rice systems since the mid‑1990s, driven by shifts to direct seeding and changing herbicide regimes. The event is correctly treated as a re‑occurrence (no new continent or sub‑region, and no clearly documented resistance evolution) and appears to represent one of the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for this species in Southern European agriculture, although precise start and end years remain approximate.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Rice-based cropping systems (paddy and dry-direct-seeded rice), ditches and ridges around fields, and other irrigated summer crops
Event summary: By the 1990s, fall panicum—introduced earlier from North America—was present as a scattered naturalised grass in parts of eastern China and Japan, especially along ditches, bunds and disturbed moist ground near rice fields. As rice production in eastern China and parts of Japan shifted toward mechanised direct seeding, reduced tillage and intensive fertilisation from the late 1990s through the 2010s, the species increasingly colonised paddy margins, ditches and dry-seeded rice fields, and Chinese surveys began listing it among common alien agricultural weeds that are difficult to control chemically because they are grasses like rice. By around 2020 it was widely recognised in eastern China and some Japanese rice-growing regions as an established invasive grass in rice-based systems, usually as part of mixed grass-weed complexes, and recommendations for integrated management and monitoring were issued even though it rarely dominated fields alone.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of rice-based cropping in eastern China and Japan, increased use of dry-direct seeding, and infrastructure such as irrigation channels and bunds created extensive disturbed, seasonally wet microsites ideal for fall panicum; long-distance transport of contaminated grain and birdseed further contributed propagules. Internal mechanisms: Available literature treats the species as a typical invasive C4 annual grass with high fecundity and broad ecological tolerance; no specific herbicide-resistant biotypes or novel genotypes have been clearly documented in East Asia during this period, so the episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence driven by external agronomic change and inherent colonising ability rather than by detectable evolutionary change.
Review: Decision: review. This new event has been added because recent Chinese and Japanese literature consistently identify P. dichotomiflorum as a naturalised invasive or common alien agricultural weed in rice-based systems, implying substantial area and management impact, and thus it likely belongs among the species’ top post‑1990 emergence episodes. However, the timing of initial introduction to East Asia predates 1990 and exact years when it became agronomically important are poorly constrained; the 1995–2020 window, country list and interpretation as a re‑occurrence (rather than inter‑continental emergence) should be checked and refined by regional specialists.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Maize (field and silage corn) and other summer row crops in irrigated and rainfed systems
Event summary: In 1981, Spanish weed scientists documented a fall panicum population in maize fields that was resistant to the photosystem II inhibitor atrazine, representing one of the earliest confirmed herbicide-resistant weed cases in the Iberian Peninsula and Europe; these resistant biotypes persisted in parts of north‑eastern Spain into the 1990s and 2000s under continued triazine use. Through the 2000s–2010s, intensive maize production with repeated use of atrazine and later ALS-inhibiting herbicides such as nicosulfuron maintained selection pressure on fall panicum, and the species remained a recurrent C4 grass weed in some Spanish corn-growing regions. In 2022, new maize fields in Catalonia and Aragón were reported with poor control by nicosulfuron and subsequent studies confirmed enhanced-metabolism-based resistance to ALS inhibitors, signalling a further re‑emergence of fall panicum as a multiple-herbicide-resistant weed and prompting calls for diversified weed management strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term monoculture or short rotations with maize, heavy reliance on triazine herbicides (e.g. atrazine) followed by widespread adoption of ALS-inhibiting herbicides (notably nicosulfuron) created intense and sustained selection pressure on fall panicum populations in parts of Spain; conservation tillage and limited mechanical weeding further reduced non-chemical control options. Internal mechanisms: First, atrazine-resistant biotypes evolved via enhanced metabolic detoxification mechanisms, and later maize populations with resistance to ALS inhibitors (nicosulfuron) were documented, with evidence for enhanced metabolism and, in other regions, target-site mutations; together these constitute clear cases of pesticide resistance evolution that fit the definition of re‑emergence driven by internal change in the weed rather than by external drivers alone.
Review: Decision: review. This new event is added because atrazine-resistant and, more recently, ALS-resistant fall panicum in Spanish maize represent well‑documented, high‑impact resistance cases, including the first herbicide‑resistant fall panicum reported globally and one of the earliest herbicide-resistance cases in the Iberian Peninsula. The episode is correctly coded as a re‑emergence (internal evolutionary change via herbicide resistance) within an already invaded Southern European sub‑region, but the chosen 1990–2025 time window (using 1981 only in the narrative), the geographic focus within Spain, and the balance between atrazine and ALS resistance should be reviewed by a herbicide-resistance specialist to confirm that this is indeed among the ten most impactful emergence episodes for the species.

EPP common name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata) and other maize production systems in the U.S. Midwest
Event summary: In 2019, a sweet-corn grower in Wisconsin (USA) reported fall panicum escapes following applications of the ALS-inhibiting herbicide nicosulfuron, prompting collection of seed from surviving plants and formal resistance testing. Greenhouse and molecular studies published in 2022 demonstrated high-level resistance to nicosulfuron (with plants surviving multiple times the labelled rate) and identified an Asp‑376‑Glu substitution in one copy of the ALS gene, confirming the first documented case of herbicide resistance in fall panicum in the United States. Although currently known from a limited number of Midwestern sweet-corn fields, this resistant biotype has re‑emerged as a management concern in systems previously relying on nicosulfuron, and extension bulletins now recommend alternative herbicide programmes and integrated management to prevent wider spread.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Heavy and repeated reliance on nicosulfuron as the main post‑emergence grass herbicide in sweet-corn production, combined with limited non-ALS herbicide options and reduced tillage, created strong selection pressure on fall panicum populations in affected fields. Internal mechanisms: Target-site resistance evolved via an ALS gene mutation (Asp‑376‑Glu) in at least one gene copy, conferring high-level resistance to nicosulfuron; this clear evolutionary change in the weed’s herbicide sensitivity constitutes a classic re‑emergence event driven by internal mechanisms and requiring substantial adaptation of management practices.
Review: Decision: review. This newly added event is strongly supported by peer‑reviewed experimental work and extension reports confirming ALS target‑site resistance in a Wisconsin fall panicum population, and it is notable as the first herbicide‑resistant fall panicum case reported in the United States. It is appropriately classified as a re‑emergence (internal evolutionary change) within the native North American range, but the temporal bounds (2019–2022), the restriction to U.S. Midwest sweet-corn systems, and the judgement that this episode is among the globally most impactful events for this species should be validated against any future data on the geographic spread and agronomic significance of this resistant biotype.

Host: Humans (rural and forest-fringe populations, including migrant workers in Amazonian departments)
Event summary: In 1995, Peru experienced a major resurgence of jungle yellow fever, with outbreaks reported from at least seven Amazonian and Andean-foothill departments and on the order of 470–500 reported human cases and an estimated case-fatality of around 40%. The epidemic was concentrated among unvaccinated agricultural workers, loggers and other migrants entering forested areas, and it strained regional health services as cases were referred to departmental hospitals from remote zones. National authorities, PAHO and partners responded with intensified surveillance, health education and targeted vaccination in affected departments, and incidence declined after 1995, although Peru has continued to report smaller numbers of sylvatic yellow fever cases in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid colonization of Amazonian forests and foothills (road building, logging, agriculture, hydrocarbon exploration) brought large numbers of non-immune workers into enzootic yellow fever foci with abundant Haemagogus/Sabethes vectors and non-human primate reservoirs; routine vaccination coverage in these populations was very low. Internal mechanisms: Available virological work indicates circulation of South American genotype II viruses endemic to Peru rather than a fundamentally novel strain; the outbreak mainly reflects intense amplification of existing enzootic virus in newly exposed human populations (re-occurrence) rather than true re-emergence driven by viral evolution.
Review: Review: Newly added event. This 1995 jungle yellow fever epidemic in Peru, with roughly 470–500 reported cases and high case fatality across at least seven departments, is widely cited as one of the largest yellow fever outbreaks in the Americas since the 1950s and clearly belongs among the top post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence in the South America subregion because the virus and transmission cycle were long established there and no strong evidence points to a distinct new genotype or host shift driving the epidemic. Case counts vary somewhat across sources; values in the summary are given as rounded ranges and should be checked against national surveillance or PAHO country profiles before finalization.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (rural populations in Mamou, Labé, Kankan and surrounding areas)
Event summary: In September 2000, a large yellow fever epidemic erupted in Guinea, affecting mainly inland prefectures such as Mamou, Labé and Kankan and causing hundreds of suspected cases in rural communities. Between early September 2000 and early January 2001, authorities reported around 688 suspected cases and 225 deaths, and Médecins Sans Frontières and partners launched mass vaccination despite a global vaccine shortage. Transmission declined after emergency vaccination campaigns and vector control, and the epidemic was brought under control by early 2001, though Guinea remained recognized as an at‑risk country for future outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High proportions of unvaccinated populations due to gaps in routine immunization, ecological suitability for sylvatic transmission, and limited vaccine stocks that delayed mass campaigns; population movements and seasonal climatic conditions likely enhanced vector abundance. Internal mechanisms: Evidence suggests continued circulation of endemic West African YFV lineages rather than a distinct novel genotype; the main mechanism was resurgence of transmission in an under-immunized population, not major viral evolution.
Review: Retain: This was a large, high-fatality epidemic (≈688 suspected cases, 225 deaths) in a West African country with documented historical transmission. Classification as re-occurrence in Western Africa is appropriate; no evidence supports intra- or inter-continental emergence or a novel viral genotype. Source set (Lancet letter, MSF operational reports) is appropriate and focused on this event.

Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban residents of Abidjan and other affected areas)
Event summary: From March to December 2001, Côte d’Ivoire experienced a major yellow fever outbreak that began in the western town of Duékoué and progressed eastwards to Abidjan, ultimately causing about 280 reported cases (32 laboratory-confirmed) and six deaths across 11 of 62 health districts, with many cases in large urban centers including Abidjan. The epidemic spread along transport corridors into densely populated neighborhoods with heavy Aedes aegypti infestation, raising concern about explosive urban transmission and prompting international alarm. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign that immunized more than 3.7 million people in Abidjan and other affected districts, combined with vector control and strengthened surveillance, curtailed urban transmission and the outbreak was declared over by late 2001.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: High population density in Abidjan, abundant urban Aedes aegypti breeding sites, and immunity gaps due to limited prior vaccination in affected districts, combined with introduction of virus from sylvatic or rural foci into an urban setting with intense human–mosquito contact. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate circulation of known West African YFV lineages rather than a novel genotype; the key internal factor was efficient urban transmission by Aedes aegypti in a largely susceptible urban population rather than genetic change.
Review: Review: Event is correctly identified as an important urban yellow fever epidemic in Western Africa, but the original summary understated case numbers and deaths. Updated the event_summary to reflect published estimates (~280 reported cases, 32 confirmed, 6 deaths, 3.7 million people vaccinated) and to clarify that spread began in Duékoué and moved east to Abidjan. Classification as re-occurrence in a historically endemic West African subregion is appropriate; no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. Sources are now clearly anchored in Med Trop and WHO documentation.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (rural populations and displaced persons in what is now South Sudan, especially Eastern Equatoria and surrounding areas)
Event summary: In 2003, a large yellow fever outbreak was detected in the Imatong Mountains and surrounding areas of what was then southern Sudan (now South Sudan’s Eastern Equatoria), representing the first major confirmed yellow fever epidemic in East Africa since the 1960s despite earlier serologic evidence of virus circulation. The outbreak progressed in rural and semi-rural communities with numerous suspected and laboratory-confirmed cases and substantial mortality before it was fully recognized. Following case confirmation, national authorities, WHO and partners undertook reactive vaccination and strengthened surveillance, and transmission waned as the dry season progressed and control measures took effect.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-term low-level sylvatic circulation in East Africa combined with humanitarian crisis conditions, displacement and limited health services in conflict-affected southern Sudan, which allowed extensive human–vector contact and delayed detection. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate involvement of known East African YFV lineages without compelling evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype; the event mainly reflects ecological spillover and expansion into susceptible human populations within an already affected subregion (re-occurrence), not appearance in a new UNSD subregion.
Review: Review: Geographic coding has been aligned with the Country sheet by listing the country as South Sudan [2003] (the outbreak area corresponds to territory that is now South Sudan), while keeping the subregion as Eastern Africa. Previously labelled as intra-continental emergence; this is incorrect because yellow fever had already been documented in the Eastern Africa subregion (e.g. earlier Sudan and Ethiopia epidemics). Re-classified intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No and re_occurrence from No to Yes. Sources (EID article and related CDC report) appropriately describe both the size and East African context of this outbreak.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban residents, particularly around Asunción)
Event summary: In early 2008, Paraguay reported its first yellow fever cases since the 1970s, with confirmed and suspected cases initially identified in rural San Pedro Department and then in urban and peri-urban areas around Asunción, including several fatalities. Although the number of confirmed human cases remained relatively small (on the order of two dozen), the detection of probable urban transmission near the capital in a largely unvaccinated population triggered major regional concern and an urgent appeal for vaccine supplies. Intensive mass vaccination campaigns, supported by PAHO/WHO and neighboring countries and reaching more than a million people, along with vector control, halted transmission within months and no large subsequent outbreaks have been reported in Paraguay since.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of sylvatic YFV or infected vectors into an urbanized, highly susceptible population with minimal routine vaccination, coupled with abundant Aedes aegypti breeding sites in and around Asunción; delays and uncertainty in early recognition contributed to heightened risk. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects resurgence of long-established South American YFV rather than a new strain; no clear evidence indicates that viral genetic changes drove increased virulence or transmissibility in Paraguay. The global impact derived largely from the potential for urban spread and the stress on vaccine stockpiles, rather than absolute case counts.
Review: Retain: Although numerically smaller than some African epidemics, this episode was the first recognized urban yellow fever outbreak in the Americas in decades and led to emergency vaccination of over a million people and serious concern about potential international spread. Classification as re-occurrence in the South America subregion is appropriate. Source set (PAHO/WHO, PHAC, PLoS NTD analysis) adequately documents both the modest case count and the large-scale response.

Host: Humans (rural populations in northern Uganda districts)
Event summary: Between October 2010 and January 2011, northern Uganda experienced a sizeable yellow fever outbreak with 181 suspected cases and 45 deaths, characterized by fever and hemorrhagic signs and notable case-fatality. The epidemic evolved across multiple districts among rural populations engaged in farming and forest or swamp-related activities, reflecting intense exposure to sylvatic vectors and primate reservoirs. Following confirmation, Uganda and partners launched reactive vaccination campaigns, strengthened surveillance, and implemented vector control, and the outbreak subsided by early 2011, though Uganda has since remained a high-risk country with additional outbreaks in 2016, 2019 and 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large pockets of unvaccinated adults and children in high-risk ecological zones, occupational exposure in forest and swamp farming areas with non-human primates present, and limited routine vaccination before the outbreak; seasonal rainfall patterns likely favored vector proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic data suggest typical East African YFV strains closely related to earlier regional viruses; the main mechanism was resurgence of endemic virus in susceptible human populations (re-occurrence) rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Retain: This was the largest documented yellow fever outbreak in Uganda and an important example of East African resurgence within an already affected subregion. Classification as re-occurrence in Eastern Africa is appropriate, and the case and death counts have been aligned with the primary investigation (181 suspected cases, 45 deaths). Sources (IJID article and WHO DON) are appropriate.

Host: Humans (rural communities, displaced populations and traditional miners across the Darfur states)
Event summary: From September 2012 to early 2013, a massive yellow fever outbreak struck Sudan’s Darfur region, with approximately 847–849 suspected cases and 171 deaths reported across all five Darfur states, making it the largest yellow fever epidemic in Africa in at least two decades. The outbreak began in remote mining and rural areas of Central Darfur and spread to dozens of localities, including camps for internally displaced persons, before being recognized and laboratory-confirmed. A large emergency vaccination campaign, coordinated by Sudan’s Federal Ministry of Health, WHO and partners and ultimately targeting several million people, along with intensified surveillance and vector control, progressively reduced transmission, and no new cases were reported after early 2013.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Protracted conflict and population displacement in Darfur created crowded, poorly serviced settlements with limited access to routine vaccination, while traditional gold mining and other outdoor occupations brought non-immune adults into high-contact environments with Aedes vectors; delays in recognition and limited early laboratory capacity allowed the outbreak to grow before control measures were deployed. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work links the outbreak virus to contemporary East African YFV lineages (including links to Uganda 2010) rather than a novel genotype; the epidemic is best characterized as a major re-occurrence of yellow fever in Sudan driven by ecological and programmatic factors, not by fundamental viral change.
Review: Review: Newly added event. The 2012–2013 Darfur epidemic, with ≈847–849 suspected cases and 171 deaths across all Darfur states, is widely recognized as the largest African yellow fever outbreak in at least 20 years and clearly merits inclusion among the top post‑1990 events. Coded under Sudan in the Northern Africa subregion, consistent with the Country sheet. Classified as re-occurrence because Sudan had experienced earlier yellow fever outbreaks and available phylogenetic data indicate reintroduction/expansion of existing East African lineages rather than a new genotype or continental spread. Case numbers and timeline are well supported by WHO, NEJM and national/IFRC reports but should be cross-checked with final national surveillance data for exact totals.

Countries: Angola [2015]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2016]
Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban populations in Luanda and other Angolan provinces; urban and peri-urban populations in Kinshasa and surrounding provinces of DRC)
Event summary: In December 2015, an urban yellow fever outbreak began in Viana municipality of Luanda, Angola, and over 2016 spread to all provinces, causing more than 4,000 suspected cases and over 100 deaths, largely in unvaccinated urban populations. The virus was exported to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where autochthonous urban transmission occurred in Kinshasa and border provinces during 2016, and infected travelers carried the Angolan strain to several non-endemic countries, including China, although no sustained transmission was documented outside Africa. A massive emergency vaccination campaign—using dose-fractionation to stretch limited global supplies—combined with vector control and intensified surveillance ultimately interrupted urban transmission in Angola and DRC by late 2016, with mop-up activities continuing into 2017.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Large, densely populated urban centers with low yellow fever vaccination coverage and extensive Aedes aegypti infestation; high population mobility between rural and urban areas and across borders; global vaccine stockpile limitations that necessitated fractional dosing; concurrent global attention to Zika diverting some resources and focus. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed the outbreak strain was closely related to viruses from a 1971 Angolan outbreak, indicating reactivation and spread of existing Central African lineages rather than emergence of a novel genotype, though efficient urban amplification via Aedes aegypti represented a critical internal transmission mechanism. Imported cases to Asia and elsewhere remained part of this linked outbreak and did not generate independent inter-continental emergence events because no local onward transmission occurred.
Review: Review: Subregion coding has been corrected to Middle Africa only; there was no confirmed autochthonous transmission in West African countries during this episode, and Angola plus DRC are both classified as Middle Africa in the Country sheet. The event was previously labelled as intra-continental emergence, but yellow fever had long been endemic in Middle Africa, so this is better classified as a major re-occurrence in an already affected subregion, driven by low urban vaccination coverage and vector ecology. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence was changed from Yes to No while retaining re_occurrence = Yes. Source list has been refocused on WHO, ECDC and peer-reviewed outbreak analyses; the Wikipedia synthesis is no longer needed as a primary reference for this row.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (mainly rural and peri-urban residents in Southeast and South regions) and non-human primates (multiple Neotropical monkey species)
Event summary: From late 2016 through 2019, Brazil experienced the largest sylvatic yellow fever epidemic in roughly 70 years, beginning in the Midwest/North regions and rapidly spreading into previously low-risk Southeast states (Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo) and later parts of the South, causing more than 2,000 confirmed human cases and hundreds of deaths, as well as extensive epizootics in howler and other monkeys. The epidemic developed as virus lineages moved along forest corridors into densely populated regions with substantial immunity gaps among adults and intense epizootics in non-human primates, with multiple clusters of infections in forest-fringe communities and travelers and numerous exported cases to neighboring countries and Europe. Large-scale emergency vaccination campaigns, expansion of routine immunization to new regions, and improved surveillance progressively reduced cases, and human transmission declined markedly after 2018–2019, though YFV persists enzootically in Brazil.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and agriculture into Atlantic Forest and Cerrado biomes; high densities of susceptible non-human primates and Haemagogus/Sabethes mosquito vectors in forested areas; large unvaccinated adult populations in Southeast and South Brazil due to prior classification of these areas as low-risk; domestic and international travel that exported cases. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses identified a distinct lineage (BR-YFV_2016/18) with an inferred most recent common ancestor around 2015, representing geographic expansion of existing Amazonian lineages; while definitive increases in virulence have not been proven, the successful invasion of previously low-risk ecological zones and intense epizootics support classification as re-emergence driven in part by viral lineage dynamics (“geographic range expansion (inherent)”) rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Review: The event remains one of the most impactful post-1990 yellow fever epidemics, with >2,000 confirmed human cases and very large epizootics and geographic spread into densely populated Southeast and South Brazil. However, labelling it as intra-continental emergence is not consistent with the UNSD subregion definition, because transmission remained within the long-affected South America subregion. Intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to No, while re_emergence remains Yes to reflect the emergence and spread of a distinct viral lineage into new ecological zones within Brazil. Source set is appropriate (Viruses, PLoS NTDs, Scientific Reports, WHO DON).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (rural and peri-urban populations across multiple Nigerian states)
Event summary: In 2017, Nigeria confirmed its first yellow fever cases in over two decades, starting with an outbreak in Ifelodun LGA, Kwara State, and then reporting widespread suspected and confirmed cases across many states through 2018–2019. The outbreak developed into a nationwide resurgence, with thousands of suspected cases reported and multiple confirmed clusters, particularly during late 2018, highlighting large immunity gaps despite prior vaccination campaigns. Multi-phase reactive and preventive mass vaccination campaigns, coordinated by Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control, WHO, and partners under the EYE strategy, along with enhanced surveillance and risk communication, progressively reduced transmission, though sporadic outbreaks and clusters have continued in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Declining or incomplete yellow fever vaccination coverage in many Nigerian states, rapid urbanization with Aedes aegypti proliferation, and limitations in surveillance and laboratory capacity that delayed early confirmation and response; population mobility across states facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Available analyses attribute the resurgence to existing West African YFV lineages in under-immunized populations rather than emergence of a new resistant or more virulent strain; the event is best characterized as re-occurrence driven by external factors such as immunity gaps and health system constraints.
Review: Retain: This multi-year resurgence involved large numbers of suspected cases across many Nigerian states and is clearly among the most consequential recent yellow fever events in West Africa. Classification as re-occurrence in Western Africa is appropriate; historical data show extensive prior transmission in Nigeria, and there is no indication of a fundamentally new viral genotype. Sources (IJID article, BMC Infectious Diseases review, Africa Check/WHO data) are appropriate for magnitude and drivers.

Countries: Guinea [2020]; Senegal [2020]; Nigeria [2020]; Ghana [2021]; Cameroon [2021]; Chad [2021]; Central African Republic [2021]; Côte d’Ivoire [2021]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2021]; Niger [2021]; Republic of the Congo [2021]; Gabon [2020]
Host: Humans (populations in multiple high-risk districts across West and Central/Middle Africa)
Event summary: From late 2020 through 2021, multiple yellow fever outbreaks were detected across West and Middle Africa, beginning with confirmed clusters in Guinea and Senegal despite prior nationwide preventive mass vaccination campaigns, and followed by outbreaks and confirmed cases in Nigeria, Togo and Gabon and then at least nine countries in 2021, including Cameroon, Chad, Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Niger, Nigeria and Republic of the Congo. These episodes represented a region-wide resurgence in areas with known historical transmission but, in some instances, recent vaccination efforts, with cases occurring in hard-to-reach districts with weak surveillance and substantial population movement, raising concerns about undetected spread to neighboring countries. Intensified implementation of the Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy—through reactive vaccination, catch-up campaigns, risk communication, and surveillance strengthening—gradually contained distinct outbreaks, though yellow fever remains a serious ongoing threat in the region.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Persistent immunity gaps even after mass vaccination (e.g. missed populations, nomadic groups), health system weaknesses in conflict-affected or remote areas, population displacement and cross-border movements, and environmental conditions conducive to Aedes spp. vectors; COVID-19 disruptions likely affected routine immunization and surveillance, compounding risk. Internal mechanisms: The pattern indicates resurgence of endemic regional YFV lineages across multiple countries rather than emergence of a single new strain; no clear evidence suggests major changes in virulence or transmissibility, so the main mechanism is re-occurrence driven by external programmatic and ecological factors.
Review: Review: This row appropriately treats the 2020–2021 multi-country upsurge in West and Middle Africa as a linked regional resurgence. Subregion coding has been corrected to “Western Africa; Middle Africa” to match the listed countries; references to a generic “Central Africa” and “Eastern Africa” in the sub_regions field were inconsistent with the Country sheet and have been removed. Because all affected countries lie within historically endemic subregions and there is no evidence of new continental spread or a unique genotype, intra_continental_emergence has been changed from Yes to No while retaining re_occurrence = Yes. Country list now matches the main WHO West & Central Africa summary, with explicit start years for each country; smaller East African outbreaks in 2020 (e.g. Ethiopia, Uganda, South Sudan) remain outside this particular multi-country West/Middle Africa episode.

Host: Primarily sheep, goats, cattle and camels; occasional human myiasis cases
Event summary: In 1988–1989, New World screwworm was introduced into north‑western Libya, probably via infested livestock imported from South America, and by 1990 an explosive outbreak was affecting an estimated 25,000–40,000 km² of coastal livestock‑producing areas with thousands of myiasis cases. Intensive surveillance, movement control, insecticide treatment and mass release of sterile flies were scaled up through 1990–1991, sharply reducing new animal cases and preventing spread into neighboring North African countries. By April–June 1991 the last cases were detected and more than 600 million sterile flies had been released, and eradication was declared later in 1991 with no further transmission detected in Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: accidental introduction of infested animals through international livestock trade, limited early awareness of the parasite in North Africa, and high densities of susceptible small ruminants in coastal farming systems facilitated rapid establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: strong inherent dispersal ability and reproductive rate of C. hominivorax supported geographic range expansion into a previously non‑endemic continent, but there is no evidence that novel strains, resistance or increased virulence played a role in this event.
Review: Retain – This row correctly represents the only documented establishment of Cochliomyia hominivorax outside the Americas and its first inter‑continental emergence into Africa. Country (Libya), sub‑region (Northern Africa), and continent (Africa) are correctly assigned, and the 1990–1991 window captures the peak control and eradication phase while the narrative appropriately notes the 1988–1989 introduction. Event type as inter‑continental emergence (without re‑occurrence/re‑emergence) is consistent with definitions, and the cited FAO/IAEA and peer‑reviewed sources are appropriate; no field changes required.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Primarily cattle, but also small ruminants, horses and dogs
Event summary: In July 1998, following decades of endemic New World screwworm myiasis and mounting economic losses, Jamaica launched a national eradication programme with FAO/IAEA and USDA support, targeting an island-wide population that caused year‑round infestations in cattle, goats, pigs, horses and dogs. From November 1998 to October 2004, surveillance recorded on the order of hundreds of animal screwworm cases per month, prompting progressive intensification of control, including weekly releases of about 16 million sterile flies from August 1999, farmer outreach and improved wound management. Despite logistical challenges and slower-than-expected progress, these area‑wide measures substantially reduced infestation pressure and transformed the problem from an acute burden into a managed endemic threat, laying the groundwork for longer‑term suppression and protection of screwworm‑free areas in the wider Caribbean.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: long‑standing endemicity of C. hominivorax in Jamaica, high densities of susceptible livestock, inadequate wound management and limited early access to SIT created persistently high screwworm burdens and significant economic losses, motivating an intensive eradication campaign. Internal mechanisms: no evidence indicates a novel strain, resistance or increased virulence; this episode reflects severe re‑occurrence of typical screwworm populations until area‑wide integrated pest management and sterile‑fly releases began to reverse the trend.
Review: Review – This event represents a major, well‑documented re‑occurrence in an already endemic Caribbean territory and merits inclusion among the top episodes. However, the original row mis‑stated timing and case numbers. The event year has been corrected to 1998–2004 to match the national eradication programme (start of government programme in July 1998, sterile fly releases from 1999, and surveillance data reported through October 2004), and the summary has been revised to rely on Jamaica‑specific surveillance and economic impact rather than misattributing regional case totals from other countries. Classification as re‑occurrence (without intra/inter‑continental emergence) remains appropriate because the parasite was long established in Jamaica and no novel strain was involved. Sources (FAO/IAEA monograph, IAEA/Jamaica documents and subsequent analyses) remain suitable, but this corrected row should be checked by a human reviewer before finalization.

Host: Wild Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium), domestic dogs, cats, pigs and at least one raccoon; sporadic livestock risk around affected areas
Event summary: In mid‑2016, wildlife biologists in the Florida Keys began observing severe, maggot‑filled wounds and deaths in endangered Key deer, and laboratory analysis in September–October 2016 confirmed New World screwworm—marking the first autochthonous U.S. detection in more than three decades after national eradication. The infestation spread across several Lower Keys islands through late 2016, killing over a hundred Key deer and infesting a small number of pets and other mammals, while USDA and Florida authorities responded with quarantine measures, mandatory inspections of animals leaving the Keys, insecticide treatments, and aerial release of tens of millions of sterile flies. Intensive control through early 2017 eliminated local transmission, and by March 2017 the Florida Keys outbreak was declared eradicated, with continued surveillance to ensure no persistence or spread onto the mainland.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: most evidence points to accidental introduction of infested animals or flies from endemic regions in the Caribbean or Latin America into the Florida Keys, combined with a dense, naïve Key deer population and favorable warm, humid conditions. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses suggest the outbreak derived from a single source population but did not demonstrate a novel strain, so the event is best characterized as re‑occurrence fueled by normal reproductive and dispersal traits of C. hominivorax rather than by newly evolved virulence or resistance.
Review: Retain – The Florida Keys 2016–2017 outbreak is accurately captured as a high‑impact re‑occurrence in a previously endemic subregion (southern U.S.) with substantial ecological consequences for Key deer. Continent and sub‑region labels (North America / Northern America) and country (United States of America) align with the country list, and no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flag is warranted because the species had historically been established in this subregion. The host list, timeline and control description match USDA/APHIS, state reports and genetic studies; the source set favours primary and official documents, so no URL changes are needed.

Countries: Panama [2023], Costa Rica [2023], Nicaragua [2024], Honduras [2024], El Salvador [2024], Guatemala [2024], Belize [2024], Mexico [2024]
Host: Cattle, other livestock (sheep, goats, pigs, horses), companion animals and wildlife; numerous human myiasis cases in several countries
Event summary: After more than two decades of containment of New World screwworm south of the Darién biological barrier, Panama experienced a sharp rise in cases in 2023—from a baseline of a few dozen detections annually to many thousands of animal infestations—and declared a nationwide animal health emergency as the parasite spread beyond the traditional buffer zone. During late 2023 and through 2024, the infestation moved north through Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, Belize and into multiple Mexican states, generating tens of thousands of animal cases and hundreds to thousands of documented human myiasis cases, while straining sterile fly production capacity and prompting trade restrictions on livestock. By 2025, Central American and Mexican authorities, in collaboration with FAO, COPEG, WOAH, PAHO and USDA, had intensified SIT releases, surveillance and cross‑border coordination, but transmission remained active across much of the region with substantial economic losses and ongoing risk of further spread northward.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: failure of the long‑standing sterile‑fly barrier in Darién due to a combination of factors—including funding and capacity constraints, aging infrastructure, and high livestock movement across porous borders—allowed screwworm populations from endemic South America to re‑establish in Panama, then spread rapidly through Central America and Mexico; climate conditions favourable to year‑round fly reproduction and limited awareness in previously screwworm‑free communities further promoted expansion. Internal mechanisms: available genomic and epidemiological studies point to re‑invasion by existing South American C. hominivorax lineages rather than emergence of a novel strain with new traits, so the event is best characterized as a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven primarily by external control and surveillance failures and by the species’ inherent dispersal and reproductive capacity.
Review: Review – This row correctly captures the very large, ongoing re‑occurrence of New World screwworm in Central America and Mexico following breach of the Darién barrier, and it is clearly among the most impactful modern events for this species. However, several technical corrections were required: (1) continent/sub‑region fields have been simplified to the single values “South America” and “Central America” instead of duplicated entries; (2) country‑specific start years have been updated to reflect national first‑detection reports (Panama and Costa Rica in 2023; Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, Belize and Mexico in 2024); and (3) the event type has been re‑classified from “re‑occurrence + intra‑continental emergence” to “re‑occurrence only”, because all affected Central American countries and Mexico were historically endemic and the episode represents re‑invasion of previously infested subregions rather than first presence in a new sub‑region. The source list already includes key FAO, COPEG, CDC, CRS and USDA/APHIS documents that best describe this outbreak; no URL additions are essential, but this corrected classification and timing should be reviewed by a human expert.

Sub-regions: Africa: Northern Africa, Eastern Africa, Western Africa; Asia: Western Asia, Southern Asia
Countries: Eritrea [1992]; Sudan [1992]; Saudi Arabia [1992]; Yemen [1992]; Mauritania [1993]; Ethiopia [1993]; India [1993]; Pakistan [1993]
Host: Rainfed and irrigated cereal and pulse crops (e.g. sorghum, millet, wheat) and rangeland vegetation in coastal Red Sea zones and Sahelian interior
Event summary: From late 1992, desert locust populations along the Red Sea coasts of Eritrea, Sudan, Saudi Arabia and Yemen became gregarious following above‑average rains and formed swarms that initiated a regional upsurge. Over 1993–1994, successive generations spread west into Sahelian West Africa (e.g. Mauritania) and east across the Arabian Peninsula into India and Pakistan, causing significant damage to crops and pasture across multiple African and Asian countries before extensive control operations and deteriorating breeding conditions reduced populations. By mid‑1994, the upsurge had collapsed as dry conditions returned in key breeding areas and intensive ground and aerial control campaigns suppressed remaining swarms.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Unusually heavy and sustained rainfall along the Red Sea coastal plains and adjacent deserts in 1992 created persistent green vegetation, allowing multiple overlapping breeding cycles and gregarization; limited early warning capacity and delayed large‑scale control enabled populations to expand and spread across the Sahel and into Southwest and South Asia. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of host shift, novel genotype, or resistance—expansion was driven by favorable moisture and vegetation enabling normal migratory and reproductive behavior over a wide area (geographic range expansion mediated by climate rather than inherent trait change).
Review: review – Event correctly represents the major 1992–1994 upsurge and its classification as re-occurrence only is appropriate. Sub-regions were updated to include Northern Africa (Sudan and Egypt belong to this UN sub-region) and to make explicit coverage of Eastern and Western Africa and Western/Southern Asia. The duplicate, non-standard entry “Sudan (inland Sahel zones) [1993]” was removed so that each country appears once with a single start year. Additional affected countries (e.g. Algeria, Chad, Djibouti, Egypt, Gambia, Morocco, Oman, Senegal, Somalia, Western Sahara) documented in FAO/Showler syntheses are not individually listed here; if full exhaustiveness is required, this row should be further expanded using FAO Desert Locust Bulletins.

Sub-regions: Africa: Western Africa, Northern Africa; Asia: Western Asia
Host: Rainfed crops (cereals, pulses) and rangeland vegetation in coastal and interior desert agro‑pastoral systems
Event summary: Beginning around 1996, new desert locust upsurge foci developed in Mauritania and Yemen, linked to favourable rainfall in traditional recession breeding areas and a cyclone-induced wet period on the southern Arabian Peninsula. During 1997–1998, these populations expanded and produced swarms that affected agricultural and pastoral areas in Saudi Arabia and Sudan, prompting renewed international concern and the establishment of strengthened preventive control programmes in the Central Region. As seasonal rains diminished and preventive strategies improved, the upsurge was progressively brought under control and had largely subsided by 1998.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Episodes of above‑average rainfall in the Central Region (Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal areas) and parts of West Africa created green vegetation, while institutional weaknesses and limited resources delayed rapid intervention, allowing another upsurge to develop; political and security constraints in parts of the region further hampered control. Internal mechanisms: no documented change in strain, virulence, host range, or pesticide susceptibility compared to previous plagues; dynamics are consistent with typical desert locust responses to transient wet conditions and vegetation growth in core recession zones.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the cyclone-triggered 1996–1998 upsurge and its treatment as a re-occurrence is consistent with current evidence. Sub-regions were corrected to “Africa: Western Africa, Northern Africa; Asia: Western Asia” because Sudan is categorized as Northern Africa in the country sheet and no Eastern African countries are explicitly listed in this row. The country list is deliberately limited to the main foci highlighted in FAO EMPRES reporting (Mauritania, Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Sudan); East African countries (e.g. Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Egypt) did experience infestations and control operations during the late stages of this upsurge but are not enumerated here to avoid over-complicating this row. Sub-regions: Africa: Western Africa, Northern Africa, Middle Africa, Eastern Africa; Asia: Western Asia; Europe: Southern Europe
Countries: Mauritania [2003]; Mali [2003]; Niger [2003]; Senegal [2003]; Cabo Verde [2003]; Burkina Faso [2003]; Chad [2003]; Morocco [2003]; Algeria [2003]; Libya [2004]; Tunisia [2004]; Nigeria [2004]; Guinea [2004]; Guinea-Bissau [2004]; Gambia [2004]; Egypt [2004]; Sudan [2004]; Ethiopia [2004]; Spain [2004]; Portugal [2004]; Greece [2004]; Israel [2004]; Jordan [2004]; Lebanon [2004]; Saudi Arabia [2004]; Syrian Arab Republic [2004]
Host: Rainfed and irrigated cereals (millet, sorghum, wheat), pulses, horticultural crops and rangeland/forest vegetation across Sahelian, Maghreb, Red Sea and Mediterranean agro‑ecosystems
Event summary: From late 2003, unusually heavy summer rains in the western Sahel allowed desert locust populations in Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Senegal and neighbouring countries to build up rapidly and gregarize, initiating the largest upsurge in West and North Africa since the late 1980s. Through 2004, swarms multiplied and spread across most of Western Africa and into Northern and Middle Africa, causing extensive crop and pasture losses, and then moved north and east into the Maghreb, the Canary Islands and parts of Southern Europe (Spain, Portugal, Greece) as well as Western Asia (including Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and Syria). Massive international control operations and the onset of drier conditions by 2005 reduced locust densities, and the plague gradually collapsed, although lingering impacts on food security persisted in vulnerable Sahelian countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Above‑normal rainfall and resulting persistent green vegetation in the Sahel in 2003 triggered rapid population growth, while delays in early intervention due to limited resources and institutional weaknesses allowed the situation to escalate into a full plague; high poverty and dependence on rainfed agriculture in the Sahel and Maghreb greatly amplified the food security impact. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel genotypes or resistance driving the upsurge—the scale reflected favourable climatic conditions and the species’ inherent capacity for long‑distance migration; however, high mobility and reproductive potential allowed rapid geographic range expansion across West/North Africa, parts of Southern Europe and the Near East once control lagged behind population growth.
Review: review – This row correctly captures the magnitude and geography of the 2003–2005 plague and its classification as a large re-occurrence event spanning Africa, Western Asia and Southern Europe. Country names were aligned with the project’s country list: “Cape Verde” was changed to “Cabo Verde”, and the subnational label “Canary Islands – Spain [2004]” was replaced with the sovereign country “Spain [2004]”. Portugal [2004] was added because multiple technical sources document swarms reaching southern Portugal during this plague. The sub-regions already matched the included countries and did not require modification. An EPPO report summarizing the outbreak (including total treated area) was added to the source list to complement Wikipedia with more technical documentation. Per-country start years (especially for some Sahelian and Mediterranean states) remain approximate and could be fine-tuned using FAO Desert Locust Bulletins if higher temporal precision is required.

Sub-regions: Africa: Eastern Africa; Asia: Western Asia, Southern Asia
Countries: Yemen [2019]; Saudi Arabia [2019]; Oman [2019]; Iran (Islamic Republic of) [2019]; Pakistan [2019]; India [2019]; Ethiopia [2019]; Somalia [2019]; Kenya [2019]; Eritrea [2019]; Djibouti [2019]; Sudan [2019]; South Sudan [2020]; Uganda [2020]; United Republic of Tanzania [2020]; Nepal [2020]; Kuwait [2020]
Host: Rainfed and irrigated cereals and pulses, horticultural crops and rangeland vegetation in the Horn of Africa, Arabian Peninsula and Southwest/South Asian dryland farming systems
Event summary: Following tropical cyclones Mekunu and Luban in 2018, exceptionally heavy rainfall created large areas of green vegetation in the Empty Quarter of the Arabian Peninsula, enabling desert locust populations in Saudi Arabia, Oman and Yemen to breed unchecked and form large swarms that by early 2019 began spreading. Throughout 2019–2020, swarms invaded Southwest Asia (Iran, Pakistan, India, later Nepal and Kuwait) and crossed the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden into the Horn of Africa, where Ethiopia, Somalia and Kenya experienced their worst locust infestations in decades, soon followed by Eritrea, Djibouti, Sudan, South Sudan, Uganda and Tanzania, severely threatening regional food security. Intensified ground and aerial control operations coordinated by FAO, combined with changing weather patterns and the eventual drying of key breeding areas, progressively reduced locust populations so that by late 2021 the upsurge was largely brought under control, although localized infestations persisted in parts of Yemen and the Horn of Africa.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Sequential intense tropical cyclones in 2018 (Mekunu and Luban) over the Arabian Peninsula produced widespread and prolonged flooding in normally hyper‑arid areas, creating ideal breeding conditions; limited surveillance and access in conflict‑affected Yemen and remote desert areas allowed multiple undetected generations, while climate variability (including unusually wet conditions in East Africa) and high regional vulnerability (conflict, poverty, COVID‑19 disruptions) amplified agricultural and food security impacts. Internal mechanisms: the upsurge was driven by climatic anomalies and the species’ intrinsic migratory and reproductive behavior rather than documented genetic change or resistance; nonetheless, the event illustrates how climate‑driven habitat suitability shifts can expand the effective range and frequency of large‑scale outbreaks of an already established pest.
Review: review – The 2019–2021 upsurge is correctly identified as one of the most impactful desert locust events in recent history and is properly classified as a large re-occurrence driven by climatic anomalies, conflict and surveillance/control gaps rather than by genetic change. The country list was retained but the country-specific start years were normalized so that square brackets indicate the first year of clear involvement within this upsurge: “Yemen [2018/2019]” was replaced with “Yemen [2019]” (2018 cyclone-driven breeding is treated as a precursor rather than the onset of the upsurge), and “Kuwait [2019/2020]” was replaced with “Kuwait [2020]”, reflecting available evidence that swarms reached Kuwait during the main expansion phase. No additional countries were added, although FAO sources indicate that some Gulf and Near Eastern states (e.g. United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan) experienced localized swarms; these are considered minor in terms of crop impact relative to the listed core countries. If a fully exhaustive country list is desired, further extraction from FAO Locust Hub/Bulletins is recommended.
