Countries: Puerto Rico [2006–2008]; United States of America (Florida, North Carolina) [2012–2013]; Brazil [2013]
Host: Maize (Bt and non-Bt), primarily Zea mays
Event summary: Around 2006, unexpectedly severe damage by fall armyworm was observed in Cry1F Bt maize in Puerto Rico, marking the first documented case of field-evolved resistance of S. frugiperda to a Bt maize event and leading to withdrawal of TC1507 maize there. During the early 2010s, subsequent monitoring and bioassays documented high levels of Cry1F resistance in fall armyworm populations in mainland USA (Florida, North Carolina) and in Brazil, with larvae surviving on Bt maize plants in the field. This resistance has persisted in Puerto Rico despite removal of Cry1F maize and contributed to reduced efficacy of single-toxin Bt hybrids across parts of the Americas, driving shifts to pyramided Bt traits and integrated resistance-management strategies.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extensive and continuous planting of single-toxin Cry1F Bt maize hybrids (TC1507 and related events) in warm tropical and subtropical production systems with high fall armyworm pressure; inadequate refuge compliance in some areas; year-round cultivation enabling multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field-evolved resistance to the Cry1F Bt toxin (and cross-resistance to some other Cry1 toxins) mainly via changes in midgut receptors such as ABCC2 and reduced Cry1F binding, increasing larval survival and damage on Bt maize.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with modifications). Changes made: (1) Updated Event Year from "2006" to "2006-2013" so the row clearly covers the linked Cry1F resistance episode in Puerto Rico, southeastern USA and Brazil, consistent with reports of initial field-evolved resistance in Puerto Rico from 2006 onward and subsequent confirmations in Florida/North Carolina and Brazil around 2012–2013.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22537834/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Corrected continent and sub-region fields to follow the UNSD scheme: Puerto Rico is placed under South America | Caribbean, the United States under Northern America | Northern America, and Brazil under South America | South America. (3) Refined country-year annotations to Puerto Rico [2006–2008], USA [2012–2013], and Brazil [2013], which better matches the timing of documented resistance detections. Event-type classification as re-emergence (due to evolution of Bt resistance in an already established pest within its native continental range) and not as intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and has been retained. Rationale: This is clearly one of the most impactful post-1990 events for FAW because it marks the first field-evolved resistance to a Bt maize event globally and triggered major changes in resistance management; it should be kept as a major re-emergence episode but flagged for the minor structural corrections above.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Sao Tome and Principe [2016]; Nigeria [2016]; Benin [2016]; Togo [2016]; Ghana [2016–2017]; Zambia [2016–2017]; Democratic Republic of the Congo [2016–2017]; Burundi [2017]; Kenya [2017]; United Republic of Tanzania [2017]; South Africa [2017–2018]; Malawi [2017–2018]; Uganda [2017–2018]; Rwanda [2017–2018]; Ethiopia [2017–2018] (plus spread to most other sub-Saharan African countries by 2018)
Host: Primarily maize (Zea mays), but also sorghum, millet and other cereals and some vegetable crops
Event summary: In early 2016, fall armyworm was detected for the first time outside its native Americas on São Tomé and Príncipe and nearly simultaneously in maize fields in southwestern Nigeria, Benin and Togo, where severe outbreaks on maize were initially misattributed to indigenous Spodoptera species and then confirmed as S. frugiperda by morphological and molecular diagnosis. Over 2016–2018 the pest spread rapidly across Western and Middle Africa into Eastern and Southern Africa, becoming established in most sub-Saharan countries and causing extensive damage to smallholder maize and other staple crops. By 2018, fall armyworm infestations and associated yield losses had stabilized at high levels across much of the region, prompting FAO and partners to launch the Global Action for Fall Armyworm Control and national IPM programs to reduce its impact.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Accidental introduction of S. frugiperda from the Americas to West Africa, likely via trade or transport of infested plant material or contaminated cargo; favorable tropical and subtropical climates with year-round host availability (maize and other cereals); widespread monoculture maize, limited early detection capacity, and constrained access to effective, safe control tools in many smallholder systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – strong flight capacity (on the order of tens of kilometres per night) and broad host range facilitated rapid colonization across diverse African agro-ecological zones; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – adaptation of invasive populations to local climatic regimes and cropping calendars, enabling continuous breeding and spread across Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with corrected event-type classification). Changes made: (1) Adjusted emergence-type flags so that this episode is coded solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Africa outside the native Americas), with first_detection and intra_continental_emergence set to "false". This follows the rule that event types should generally be mutually exclusive, and that spread within Africa to additional sub-regions (Western, Middle, Eastern, Southern Africa) is considered part of the same inter-continental invasion episode rather than separate intra-continental events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5082806/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Confirmed that the listed countries and years (Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Sao Tome and Principe in 2016; Zambia, DRC and others in 2016–2017; East and Southern African countries mainly in 2017–2018) are consistent with EPPO, IPPC and FAO reporting, though additional African countries experienced outbreaks in the same period. (3) Continent and sub-region fields already matched the UNSD classification and were left unchanged. Rationale: This is unequivocally one of the largest FAW emergence events globally in terms of area affected, yield loss and number of countries, and should definitely be retained; the corrections concern only the technical coding of the emergence type.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia
Countries: Yemen [2018]; India [2018]; Sri Lanka [2018]; Bangladesh [2018]; Myanmar [2018]; Thailand [2018]; China (Yunnan) [2019]; China (multiple maize-producing provinces) [2019–2020]; Viet Nam [2019]; Lao People's Democratic Republic [2019]; Cambodia [2019]; Indonesia [2019]; Philippines [2019]; Nepal [2019]; Pakistan [2019–2020]; Japan [2019–2020]; Timor-Leste [2019]; Brunei Darussalam [2019–2020]; Malaysia [2019]; Republic of Korea [2019]
Host: Primarily maize; also sorghum, rice, sugarcane and some vegetable and forage crops
Event summary: In mid-2018, fall armyworm was first reported from Yemen and soon after from maize fields in southern India (Karnataka), marking the pest’s arrival in Asia following its invasion of Africa and the Near East. Over late 2018 and 2019, it spread rapidly across Southern Asia and South-eastern Asia, with confirmed detections and damaging outbreaks in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and neighboring countries, and by early 2019 it was detected in China’s Yunnan Province before spreading into many maize-producing provinces and other East Asian territories. By 2020–2021, fall armyworm had become established throughout much of Asia, including countries such as Viet Nam, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Japan and the Republic of Korea, causing significant damage to maize, sorghum and other crops and triggering regional action plans, national emergency responses and FAO-coordinated training and monitoring under the Global Action for Fall Armyworm Control.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long-distance migration of moths from already infested regions (likely via the Arabian Peninsula and/or eastern Africa into the Indian subcontinent), aided by monsoon wind systems; intense regional and cross-border trade in plant products; continuous availability of host crops in tropical and subtropical agro-ecosystems; limited initial awareness and preparedness among farmers and extension systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – high dispersal ability, broad thermal tolerance and polyphagy allowed colonization across diverse Asian climates and cropping systems; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – rapid build-up of populations in multi-cropping systems, with some evidence of adaptation to local cropping calendars and possibly differing host-use patterns between the so-called ‘rice’ and ‘corn’ strains.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with geography and type corrections). Changes made: (1) Corrected the continent field to "Asia" only and removed the reference to "Africa (Near East/North-east Africa)"; under the UNSD scheme, Yemen is classified in Asia | Western Asia, so this episode is purely Asian in the continent column, even though it is epidemiologically linked to the African invasion.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-6437?utm_source=openai)) (2) Replaced the informal "Asia (Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia); Africa (Eastern Africa – Yemen often grouped with Western Asia/Near East in FAO reporting)" wording with a standardized sub-region list: "Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia". (3) Updated the country list to explicitly include Malaysia [2019] and the Republic of Korea [2019], which are highlighted by FAO’s FAW map and EPPO/Scientific Reports as part of the early invasion front in East and South-east Asia, and removed any implication that Yemen belongs to Africa.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fall-armyworm/monitoring-tools/faw-map/en/?utm_source=openai)) (4) Adjusted emergence-type flags so this event is classified solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Asia), with first_detection and intra_continental_emergence set to "false" to respect the rule that event types are generally mutually exclusive. Rationale: This Asia-wide invasion, which rapidly involved more than a dozen countries and large maize areas, clearly ranks among the most impactful FAW emergence events and should be retained. Wikipedia is used only as a secondary, cross-checked source; primary dating and country information rely on FAO, EPPO and USDA GAIN reports.
