Countries: Australia [2020]; Papua New Guinea [2020]; Solomon Islands [2021]; New Zealand [2022]
Host: Maize, sorghum and other cereals; some vegetable and forage crops
Event summary: In late January 2020, fall armyworm was detected for the first time in Oceania on the Torres Strait islands of Saibai and Erub (Australia), with subsequent confirmations on mainland Queensland and then other northern states, marking its arrival in the region. During 2020 the pest was also reported in Papua New Guinea and by 2021 it had been detected on Melanesian islands such as the Solomon Islands, establishing a continuous presence across much of the tropical Asia–Pacific corridor. Between 2020 and 2022, fall armyworm spread through key maize- and sorghum-growing regions of northern and eastern Australia and, via wind-assisted migration, reached New Zealand where initial eradication efforts gave way to long-term management once the pest proved widespread, leading to emergency regulatory responses and rapid deployment of biological and chemical control options across affected countries.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Natural migration of moths from already infested parts of Southeast Asia via prevailing winds and island stepping-stones into northern Australia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and later New Zealand; high connectivity through regional trade and movement of plant materials; favorable tropical and temperate climates and extensive maize and sorghum production in northern Australia and parts of Oceania. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the invasive populations’ broad climatic tolerance enabled establishment in new subtropical and temperate environments in Oceania; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – rapid build-up in local maize and sorghum systems led to persistent populations requiring new biological control and biopesticide approaches (e.g. nucleopolyhedrovirus-based products and parasitoid wasps) for sustainable management.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with geography, country list and type corrections). Changes made: (1) Standardized the sub_regions field to the UNSD names "Australia and New Zealand; Melanesia" instead of the mixed "Oceania (Australia and New Zealand; Melanesia)" labelling. (2) Removed Timor-Leste from the country list because it is classified under Asia | South-eastern Asia and its first detection is more appropriately captured within the Asian invasion event; its inclusion under Oceania conflicted with the Country sheet.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fall-armyworm/monitoring-tools/faw-map/en/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Added Solomon Islands [2021] and New Zealand [2022] as key Oceania detections, supported by EPPO and MPI/EPPO reports documenting first records in these countries.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/LAPHFR/reporting?utm_source=openai)) (4) Adjusted emergence-type flags so the event is coded solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Oceania), setting first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to "false" in line with the general rule that event types are mutually exclusive. (5) Added the New Zealand MPI page on fall armyworm as a more specific source for the 2022 New Zealand detection and subsequent shift from eradication to long-term management, while retaining IPPC and EPPO pest reports for Australia and Papua New Guinea. Rationale: Taken together, the invasion of Australia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and New Zealand constitutes the major Oceania-wide emergence episode for FAW and should be retained as one of the top global emergence events.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (general population)
Event summary: In early 2007, clinicians on the Yap Islands in the Federated States of Micronesia noted an outbreak of rash, conjunctivitis and arthralgia initially suspected to be dengue, but laboratory testing identified Zika virus as the cause, marking the first recognized large outbreak of Zika fever and the first documented transmission outside Africa and Asia. The outbreak spread widely in the small island population, with 49 confirmed and 59 probable cases and serologic evidence that roughly three-quarters of residents were infected. Transmission declined over subsequent months as the susceptible population was exhausted and vector control and community protection measures were implemented, with no further large outbreaks reported there afterward.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of Zika virus via travel from endemic regions in Asia into an immunologically naïve island population with abundant Aedes mosquitoes and limited prior arboviral immunity; small, highly connected communities that facilitated rapid person–mosquito–person transmission. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transmission in dense Aedes populations and a high proportion of asymptomatic infections facilitating silent spread; geographic range expansion inherent to the virus as it moved from Asia to Micronesia, representing an inter-continental jump.
Review: retain – Event is real, correctly dated and clearly among the major emergence episodes (first large outbreak and first spread outside Africa/Asia). Country name was standardized to match the Country sheet (“Micronesia (Federated States of)”), but classification as an inter-continental emergence remains appropriate and no substantive issues were identified.

Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women and fetuses/newborns possibly affected)
Event summary: In 2007, during a large outbreak of febrile illness in Libreville and northern Gabon initially attributed mainly to chikungunya and dengue, virologic investigations detected Zika virus in Aedes albopictus mosquito pools and retrospectively in human samples, revealing substantial but previously unrecognized Zika circulation as part of the mixed arboviral epidemic. Subsequent analyses suggested that many thousands of people may have been infected with Zika virus alongside chikungunya and dengue, and later work raised the possibility of an associated rise in microcephaly and other adverse pregnancy outcomes during that period. As the rainy season ended and vector densities fell, reported febrile cases diminished and the outbreak subsided within several months, but the true burden and congenital impact of the Zika component likely remained underestimated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Recent invasion and rapid spread of Aedes albopictus in urban Gabon, high vector densities during the rainy season, co-circulation of chikungunya and dengue viruses that complicated diagnosis, and limited arboviral surveillance capacity leading to under-recognition of Zika infections. Internal mechanisms: Apparent adaptation of Zika virus to Aedes albopictus as an efficient urban vector, enabling large-scale transmission in a previously low-recognition setting and representing a notable re-emergence of Zika in Central Africa.
Review: review – This major Central African outbreak, with strong entomological and retrospective evidence for extensive Zika transmission and probable microcephaly impact in Gabon in 2007, was missing and has been added as a re-emergence event in Middle Africa. Classification as re-emergence (rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence) reflects long-standing Zika presence in Africa but a dramatic resurgence linked to a new predominant vector (Aedes albopictus); wording and scale should be checked against any additional outbreak reconstructions.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Countries: French Polynesia [2013]; New Caledonia [2014]; Cook Islands [2014]; Chile [2014]
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; Guillain–Barré syndrome patients)
Event summary: Beginning in October 2013, French Polynesia experienced a large Zika virus outbreak across its archipelagos, with over 8,000 suspected cases and an estimated attack rate near 10% of the population, representing the largest Zika outbreak to that date and the first where neurological complications such as Guillain–Barré syndrome were clearly recognized. In 2014, travel from French Polynesia seeded outbreaks in other Pacific islands including New Caledonia and the Cook Islands and led to introduction of Zika virus to Easter Island, part of Chile, marking the first documented autochthonous transmission in South America. By 2015, the Pacific outbreaks waned as herd immunity accumulated and control efforts intensified, but the virus had established a foothold in the Pacific that likely facilitated subsequent spread to mainland South America.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Increasing air and maritime travel among Pacific islands (tourism and cultural links) that moved infected persons from French Polynesia to other islands; high densities of competent Aedes vectors in tropical island settings; limited prior population immunity across the Pacific; constrained vector-control capacity in small island health systems. Internal mechanisms: Efficient vector-borne transmission by Zika’s Asian lineage; recognition for the first time of a strong association with Guillain–Barré syndrome and later congenital malformations, reflecting either intrinsic neurotropism of the circulating strain or improved ascertainment of severe outcomes; geographic range expansion from Polynesia to Melanesia and into South American territory (Chile, via Easter Island).
Review: review – Event correctly captures the large French Polynesia–centred Pacific outbreak and the first documented autochthonous transmission in South America (Easter Island/Chile). The previous classification set both intra- and inter-continental emergence to “Yes”, which is inconsistent with the rule that only re-emergence can co-occur; it has been corrected to inter-continental emergence only, and the Chile entry in the country list has been standardized (Chile [2014] with Easter Island detail moved to the narrative).
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub-regions: South America; Central America; Caribbean; Northern America
Countries: Brazil [2015]; Colombia [2015]; Suriname [2015]; El Salvador [2015]; Guatemala [2015]; Honduras [2015]; Mexico [2015]; Panama [2015]; Paraguay [2015]; Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) [2015]; Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2015]; Ecuador [2015]; French Guiana [2015]; Guyana [2015]; Peru [2015]; Argentina [2016]; Uruguay [2016]; Belize [2016]; Costa Rica [2016]; Nicaragua [2016]; Puerto Rico [2015]; United States Virgin Islands [2015]; Martinique [2015]; Guadeloupe [2015]; Saint Martin (French Part) [2015]; Saint Barthélemy [2015]; Curaçao [2015]; Aruba [2015]; Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba [2015]; Dominican Republic [2015]; Haiti [2015]; Jamaica [2015]; Barbados [2015]; Grenada [2015]; Saint Lucia [2015]; Saint Vincent and the Grenadines [2015]; Trinidad and Tobago [2015]; Turks and Caicos Islands [2016]; Antigua and Barbuda [2016]; Anguilla [2016]; Cuba [2016–2017]; United States of America [2016]
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns with congenital Zika syndrome; Guillain–Barré syndrome patients)
Event summary: In early 2015, Brazil confirmed autochthonous Zika virus transmission, likely introduced from the Pacific by travellers, and over the following months the virus spread explosively through Brazil with an estimated 1.5 million infections and an unprecedented surge in microcephaly and other congenital central nervous system malformations in infants. Between mid‑2015 and late 2016, Zika spread throughout South and Central America, the Caribbean and parts of Northern America, with PAHO/WHO documenting hundreds of thousands of reported autochthonous cases and 40+ countries and territories in the Region of the Americas affected, while locally acquired cases also occurred in Florida and Texas in the continental United States. By 2017, incidence declined sharply across the region as a result of accumulated population immunity, aggressive mosquito-control campaigns and public health warnings, and WHO declared the Public Health Emergency of International Concern over in late 2016, although sporadic transmission and congenital Zika syndrome cases continued to be reported.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of the Asian lineage of Zika virus into a highly urbanized region with widespread Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes; large-scale international travel and mass events that facilitated viral movement; dense urban populations with inadequate water, sanitation and housing that favoured vector breeding; limited prior Zika immunity in the Americas; and health-system constraints in vector control and prenatal screening. Internal mechanisms: Strong neurotropism and teratogenicity of the circulating Asian/American lineage leading to congenital Zika syndrome and microcephaly; possible increased transmissibility in urban Aedes populations; geographic range expansion across an entire new continent, including first documented autochthonous transmission in Northern America; enhanced recognition of sexual transmission as an additional, though minor, route of spread compared with vector-borne transmission.
Review: review – This event appropriately aggregates the large 2015–2017 epidemic across South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Northern America and correctly marks it as an inter-continental emergence because it includes the first autochthonous transmission in Northern America (continental United States). The continent label has been corrected from “South America; North America” to the defined “South America; Northern America”, and some country labels were standardized (e.g. Puerto Rico, United States of America), but the overall structure and impact description are sound and should be retained.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event summary: In October–November 2015, Cabo Verde reported its first epidemic of Zika virus infection, with rapid spread across the archipelago and over 7,500 suspected cases recorded in the 2015–2016 season. During the outbreak, at least 18 microcephaly cases and additional suspected congenital Zika syndrome outcomes were identified, representing the first large African outbreak associated with congenital malformations and molecularly linked to an imported Asian-lineage virus closely related to strains circulating in Brazil. Transmission subsided by mid‑2016 as the outbreak burned through the susceptible population and intensive vector-control activities, pregnancy surveillance and public health messaging were implemented.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of the Asian/American lineage of Zika virus from Brazil into Cabo Verde via air travel; presence of abundant Aedes mosquitoes and suitable climate in a largely Zika-naïve island population; limitations in sustained vector control and water/sanitation infrastructure; increased movement between Brazil and Lusophone West Africa. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a novel strain/genotype (Asian lineage) into the region with demonstrated teratogenic potential; geographic range expansion within Africa beyond historical African-lineage foci; high susceptibility of the local population allowing a large outbreak and clear detection of congenital Zika syndrome.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the size and significance of the Cabo Verde outbreak (first large African epidemic with clearly documented congenital Zika syndrome caused by the Asian lineage). Geographic coding (Western Africa, Cabo Verde) and classification as a re-emergence driven by introduction of a new lineage and new clinical phenotype are appropriate; no major corrections needed.

Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event summary: In 2016, Zika virus infection was confirmed in a resident of Angola and in a traveller returning from Angola to Europe, signalling previously unrecognized transmission of the Asian lineage of the virus in the country. Subsequent investigations and genomic analyses indicated that Zika was likely introduced from Brazil sometime between mid‑2015 and mid‑2016, and by 2017 Angola reported clusters of microcephaly in newborns consistent with congenital Zika syndrome. By late 2017, available data suggested that the outbreak had diminished, likely due to a combination of immunity build-up and vector control, though surveillance gaps meant the full size and duration of the epidemic were probably underestimated.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Travel links and migration between Brazil and Angola, including historical Lusophone connections, allowing trans-Atlantic introduction of the Asian lineage; high Aedes mosquito densities in urban Angolan settings with limited vector-control infrastructure; under-resourced surveillance that delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the Asian/American lineage into this subregion (replacing silent circulation of African lineages) with strong teratogenic potential; geographic range expansion within Africa; possible silent circulation before overt recognition via congenital cases, reflecting a high proportion of asymptomatic adult infections.
Review: retain – Event appropriately summarizes the Angola emergence of the Asian lineage with associated congenital Zika syndrome and treats it as a re-emergence in a continent where Zika was already endemic. Geographic assignment to Middle Africa and Angola is consistent with the Country sheet, and no clear misclassification or non-major status issues were found.

Host: Humans (general population, including migrant workers and residents in urban clusters)
Event summary: In 2016, after detecting an imported Zika case and genetically characterizing the virus, Singapore reported its first locally acquired Zika infections, with rapid emergence of large urban clusters in residential and industrial areas such as Aljunied Crescent and Sims Drive. Hundreds of autochthonous cases were identified over the following months despite intensive vector-control efforts, representing one of the most substantial documented Zika outbreaks in South‑eastern Asia’s urban settings, though no associated microcephaly or Guillain–Barré syndrome clusters were confirmed. By late 2016, case numbers had declined substantially as vector-control campaigns, heightened community awareness and seasonal changes reduced transmission, and no similar-scale outbreaks have been reported in Singapore since.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of Zika virus into a densely populated, highly urbanized city-state with widespread Aedes aegypti despite long-standing dengue control; intense human mobility within and between residential and workplace areas facilitating mosquito-mediated spread; challenges in fully suppressing vector breeding in construction sites and older housing estates. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transmission by Asian-lineage Zika viruses already adapted to urban Aedes aegypti; high asymptomatic fraction that allowed cryptic spread before outbreak recognition, though severe congenital outcomes were not documented in this event.
Review: retain – Event is well-supported and clearly one of the larger and better-characterized urban Zika outbreaks in South‑eastern Asia, with correct geographic coding (Asia, South-eastern Asia, Singapore) and classification as a re-occurrence in a region with long-standing Zika circulation but renewed, intensified transmission in 2016.

Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event summary: From early 2016, Thailand expanded nationwide Zika surveillance and rapidly confirmed locally acquired infections in multiple provinces, revealing that Zika had been silently circulating and was now causing noticeable outbreaks. Over 2016–2017, national data documented more than a thousand laboratory-confirmed infections distributed across at least 16 provinces, along with a small number of pregnancies and congenital anomalies temporally associated with maternal Zika infection. By 2018, reported case numbers had fallen as awareness, targeted vector control and routine surveillance improved, and Zika was recognized as an endemic but generally low-incidence arboviral infection in Thailand rather than a one-off explosive epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Longstanding presence of competent Aedes mosquitoes in Thailand, high background dengue transmission, favourable tropical climate, dense human populations and increased clinical and laboratory surveillance that improved detection of Zika from 2016 onward. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of Asian-lineage Zika virus without clear evidence of major new genetic changes, consistent with a re-occurrence driven primarily by environmental and surveillance factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – This substantial 2016–2017 outbreak in Thailand, with over a thousand confirmed infections and documented pregnancy exposures, was missing and has been added as a re-occurrence event in South‑eastern Asia. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or re-emergence) reflects evidence of earlier Zika circulation in Thailand and the absence of a clearly novel viral lineage; the summary and scale should be cross-checked against national surveillance reports for final inclusion.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women)
Event summary: After three autochthonous Zika cases were identified in Gujarat and one in Tamil Nadu during 2016–2017, India detected a much larger outbreak beginning in September 2018 in Jaipur, Rajasthan, followed by confirmed local transmission in parts of Madhya Pradesh. By late 2018, national and WHO reports documented at least 159 confirmed cases in Rajasthan and over 120 in Madhya Pradesh, including many pregnant women, prompting extensive vector control, household screening and intensified surveillance. These outbreaks were contained over several months without documented clusters of microcephaly or Guillain–Barré syndrome, but subsequent years saw additional, smaller Zika clusters in other Indian states, indicating ongoing low-level circulation in Southern Asia.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Widespread presence of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus in Indian urban and peri-urban settings, high human population density, climatic conditions suitable for arbovirus transmission, and increased clinical and laboratory surveillance following the Americas epidemic that enabled recognition of the 2018 outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of South-East Asian lineage Zika virus without clear evidence of novel genotype or major virulence change, suggesting that these events represent a re-occurrence of an established regional pathogen in a large, previously under-recognized national setting.
Review: review – India’s 2018 outbreaks in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh represent the country’s first large, well-documented Zika epidemics (hundreds of confirmed cases) and clearly belong among the major global emergence events. This row has been added as a re-occurrence in Southern Asia, given longstanding regional Zika evidence; country and year coding follow the Country sheet conventions and states are described in the narrative rather than in the country field.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

Host: Humans (general population in affected neighbourhood)
Event summary: In the summer of 2019, health authorities in the Var department in southern France detected a cluster of three Zika virus infections in residents with no travel history, indicating local mosquito-borne transmission in a neighbourhood of Hyères. Epidemiologic investigations and viral genetic analyses pointed to introduction of an Asian-lineage virus, probably from a traveller returning from a Zika-affected area in South-East Asia, and confirmed this as the first recognized local vector-borne Zika transmission in Europe. Intensive vector control around the cases and the onset of cooler weather were followed by no additional autochthonous cases, and the event remained a short-lived, geographically limited emergence.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Presence and seasonal abundance of Aedes albopictus in southern France, international travel from Zika-affected regions, and conducive summer climatic conditions that allowed a brief transmission chain in a small urban area. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of Asian-lineage Zika virus capable of being transmitted by European Aedes albopictus; no evidence of large-scale adaptation, but demonstration that local vectors can support short chains of transmission under favourable conditions, marking an inter-continental emergence into Europe.
Review: review – This small but epidemiologically important cluster in southern France constitutes the first documented local mosquito-borne Zika transmission in Europe and thus an inter-continental emergence event despite the very low case count. The row has been added with Europe/Western Europe/France coding and inter-continental emergence marked as “Yes”; outbreak size and timing are consistent with WHO and ECDC reports but should be rechecked when integrating with other European arbovirus emergence records.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Humans (community members, health-care workers)
Event summary: In early 1995, Ebola virus disease re-emerged in Kikwit and surrounding areas of Bandundu Region (now Kwilu), Democratic Republic of the Congo, when clusters of severe febrile haemorrhagic illness were first recognized among patients and hospital staff. The outbreak expanded rapidly through nosocomial transmission and close-contact care and funerary practices, resulting in roughly 315 cases and a case fatality ratio around 80%, with substantial infection of health-care workers. Intensive international response with isolation wards, barrier nursing, community education, and safe burials brought transmission under control, and the epidemic was declared over by mid-1995.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: extensive nosocomial transmission in a regional referral hospital with inadequate infection prevention and control; reuse of needles and syringes; close patient contact during caregiving and funerals; delayed recognition of viral haemorrhagic fever; limited laboratory and surveillance capacity. Internal mechanisms: no strong evidence for major phenotypic change relative to earlier Zaire ebolavirus strains; the event is best characterized as a large re-occurrence driven by health-system vulnerabilities and infection-control failures rather than viral evolution.
Review: Status: retained. Major Central African outbreak (~315 cases, high CFR) in a country and sub-region where Orthoebolavirus zairense was already established; classification as a re-occurrence without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence is appropriate and consistent with outbreak reconstructions.

Host: Humans (villagers handling infected wildlife, family caregivers, and health-care workers including a repatriated physician and a nurse in South Africa)
Event summary: In early 1996, an Ebola virus disease outbreak due to Orthoebolavirus zairense occurred in the village of Mayibout II in northeastern Gabon after villagers butchered and consumed a chimpanzee found dead in the forest, leading to dozens of cases and deaths and further spread through close household contact and funerals. Later in 1996, a second outbreak arose around Booué in central Gabon, again linked to contact with infected great apes and subsequent community and limited health-care transmission; together, the two Gabon outbreaks caused roughly 90–100 human cases with a high case fatality ratio. A physician infected in Gabon was evacuated to Johannesburg, South Africa, where nosocomial transmission to a nurse resulted in the first recognized human Ebola virus disease cases due to this species in Southern Africa, after which intensive infection control measures prevented wider spread and the episode ended.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: repeated zoonotic spillover associated with hunting, butchering, and consumption of infected chimpanzees and other wildlife; reliance on bushmeat in remote forest communities; limited awareness of Ebola and weak infection prevention and control in rural health facilities; international transfer of an infected clinician for specialized care enabling a nosocomial transmission event in South Africa. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses show closely related Zaire ebolavirus lineages across the Gabon outbreaks, compatible with multiple introductions from an enzootic reservoir rather than a fundamentally novel strain; the key emergence feature is geographic range expansion within Africa to a new UNSD sub-region (Southern Africa) via a secondary nosocomial cluster.
Review: Status: added. Captures the two substantial 1996 Gabon outbreaks (Mayibout II and Booué) plus the linked nosocomial transmission cluster in South Africa, which together form a major episode with cross-subregional spread; classified primarily as intra-continental emergence because it includes the first documented human cases due to Orthoebolavirus zairense in Southern Africa, while earlier 1994 Gabon activity is left out to keep within the top ~10 events.

Host: Humans exposed to infected wildlife (hunters, carcass handlers) and their community contacts
Event summary: From late 2001, Ebola virus disease outbreaks due to Zaire ebolavirus began along the forested border of northeastern Gabon and northwestern Republic of the Congo, with initial cases linked to handling carcasses of great apes and duikers found dead in the forest. Over several linked waves through 2002–2003, at least five clustered outbreaks occurred across villages in both countries, totaling roughly 300 cases and more than 250 deaths, with transmission sustained by close caregiving and funerary contact. Coordinated surveillance, quarantine, safe-burial measures, and reduction in hunting and carcass handling in affected zones eventually interrupted human-to-human spread and ended the episode by late 2003.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: recurrent zoonotic spillover associated with hunting and butchering of Ebola-infected ape and duiker carcasses; high wildlife mortality preceding human outbreaks; subsistence hunting and bushmeat trade; remote forest locations with delayed recognition and limited access to care and infection control. Internal mechanisms: outbreaks were caused by Zaire ebolavirus lineages within the known Central African diversity, with no clear evidence that genetic changes alone increased virulence; the episode is best viewed as a large geographic re-occurrence along the existing Middle African forest belt.
Review: Status: retained. Treating the closely spaced 2001–2003 Gabon/Republic of the Congo outbreaks as a single linked multi-year episode is consistent with project rules and literature; classification as re-occurrence in Middle Africa (rather than intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because all activity remained within an already affected UNSD sub-region and host system.

Host: Humans in rural communities of Kasai Occidental (including persons exposed to bats and caregivers)
Event summary: In mid-2007, Ebola virus disease reappeared in the Luebo and Mweka health zones of Kasai Occidental Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, when clusters of severe febrile illness and deaths were reported and confirmed as Zaire ebolavirus. The outbreak produced roughly 260–270 cases and around 185–190 deaths, with epidemiologic investigations linking early cases to exposure to bats and local hunting activities, followed by community and household transmission. Strengthened surveillance, isolation wards supported by international partners, community education, and safer burial practices progressively reduced transmission, and the outbreak was declared over in late 2007, with a small genetically related flare in 2008.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: likely spillover from fruit bats acting as reservoir hosts, with primary human cases in rural areas; traditional hunting and butchering practices; delayed recognition of Ebola among other causes of febrile illness; limited initial infection prevention and control in peripheral facilities. Internal mechanisms: molecular analyses indicated divergent Zaire ebolavirus strains compared with earlier DRC outbreaks, consistent with independent zoonotic spillover from bat reservoirs, but disease severity was similar to prior events; the episode is best classified as ecological re-occurrence in an already affected country and sub-region.
Review: Status: retained. This outbreak (plus the small 2008 flare) is one of the larger Central African Zaire ebolavirus episodes and is appropriately treated as a re-occurrence within Middle Africa with independent spillover from bats; no additional emergence category flags are warranted.

Sub-regions: Western Africa; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern America
Countries: Guinea [2013], Liberia [2014], Sierra Leone [2014], Nigeria [2014], Senegal [2014], Mali [2014], Spain [2014], United States of America [2014], United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2014], Italy [2015]
Host: Humans (rural villagers, urban residents, health-care workers, funeral participants, and international travelers/contacts)
Event summary: In December 2013, a zoonotic spillover of Zaire ebolavirus in southeastern Guinea (village of Méliandou, Guéckédou Prefecture) initiated a chain of human infections that went unrecognized for months, allowing Ebola virus disease to establish sustained transmission in Guinea and spread into neighboring Liberia and Sierra Leone by early to mid-2014—marking the first known emergence of Ebola virus disease caused by this species in West Africa. Through 2014–2015, intense community and nosocomial transmission in densely populated urban centers and across borders led to more than 28,600 suspected, probable, and confirmed cases and about 11,300 deaths across West Africa, with additional limited chains of transmission in Nigeria, Mali, Senegal, Spain, and the United States and imported cases detected in the United Kingdom and Italy. Massive international response efforts, including improved surveillance and isolation, community engagement, safe burials, border screening, and deployment of experimental vaccines and therapeutics, progressively reduced incidence, and WHO declared all known chains of transmission in West Africa stopped by mid-2016.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: initial spillover likely from a bat reservoir into a child in a forest-edge village; months of delayed detection and misattribution of early cases; high population mobility and porous borders in the Mano River region; fragile health systems with very limited infection prevention and control; rapid urbanization of affected capitals; traditional caregiving and funeral practices involving intense body contact; and community mistrust and resistance that slowed control measures. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses showed a Makona variant of Zaire ebolavirus that evolved during extensive human-to-human transmission, but without clear evidence of a single mutation dramatically increasing virulence; the unprecedented scale and geographic reach were primarily driven by social, demographic, and health-system factors. This episode is therefore classified as both intra-continental emergence (first sustained presence in Western Africa) and inter-continental emergence (first in situ transmission in Europe and North America) rather than as re-emergence.
Review: Status: retained with corrected classification. Re-emergence is set to false because this was the first recognized incursion of Orthoebolavirus zairense into the Western Africa sub-region and first sustained in situ transmission in Europe and North America, not a resurgence in a previously affected sub-region; dual intra- and inter-continental emergence flags are kept to reflect this multi-continent episode, but this use of multiple categories should be reviewed if strict mutual exclusivity of emergence types is enforced.
Review Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans in rural communities of Equateur Province (Boende and surrounding health zones)
Event summary: In mid-2014, shortly after the West Africa epidemic began, a separate Ebola virus disease outbreak due to Zaire ebolavirus occurred in Boende Health Zone, Equateur Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with an index case thought to be linked to handling or consumption of infected bushmeat. The outbreak caused about 66 cases and 49 deaths, largely confined to rural villages and associated health facilities, with transmission driven by caregiving and traditional funeral practices but limited geographic spread compared to West Africa. Aggressive case finding, isolation, safe burials, and international support brought the outbreak under control, and WHO declared it over in November 2014.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: independent zoonotic spillover likely from infected wildlife (e.g. bats or bushmeat) in a forested area; limited surveillance capacity and delayed recognition in remote Equateur Province; traditional burial practices and household caregiving facilitating early spread. Internal mechanisms: viral sequencing confirmed that the outbreak was due to Zaire ebolavirus but genetically distinct from the concurrent West Africa Makona lineage, representing a local re-occurrence from an endemic reservoir rather than spread from West Africa or emergence of a markedly more virulent strain.
Review: Status: retained. This moderate-sized outbreak in Equateur Province is epidemiologically distinct from the West Africa epidemic and represents a further re-occurrence within Middle Africa; classification as re-occurrence only (no intra-/inter-continental emergence, no clear viral change) is appropriate.

Host: Humans in Bikoro, Iboko and Wangata health zones (rural communities, urban residents in Mbandaka, and health-care workers)
Event summary: In May 2018, the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared its ninth Ebola virus disease outbreak after clusters of suspected viral haemorrhagic fever and deaths were reported from Ikoko-Impenge in Bikoro Health Zone, Equateur Province, and laboratory testing confirmed infection with Zaire ebolavirus. Cases subsequently appeared in the rural Iboko Health Zone and in the Wangata Health Zone of Mbandaka, a large river port city on the Congo River, raising concern about wider spread along major transport routes, but rapid deployment of treatment units, contact tracing, and ring vaccination helped limit transmission. The outbreak totaled 54 cases and 33 deaths and was declared over on 24 July 2018.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: zoonotic spillover in a remote forested area followed by person-to-person spread facilitated by limited local health infrastructure, movement along river and road networks, and traditional caregiving and burial practices; concern over spread from rural areas into the urban hub of Mbandaka. Internal mechanisms: genetic and epidemiologic data are consistent with a new local introduction of Zaire ebolavirus from an animal reservoir into a province with a history of Ebola outbreaks, without evidence that viral evolution substantially changed virulence or transmissibility; this episode is therefore categorized as a re-occurrence in Middle Africa.
Review: Status: added. The 2018 Equateur Province outbreak (54 cases, 33 deaths) is one of the larger Zaire ebolavirus events and the first documented incursion into a sizable urban center (Mbandaka) in western DRC; it was missing from the original dataset and is appropriately classified as a re-occurrence in Middle Africa.

Host: Humans in conflict-affected communities in North Kivu, Ituri and South Kivu Provinces, including health-care workers
Event summary: In August 2018, Ebola virus disease due to Zaire ebolavirus was detected in North Kivu Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, only days after a smaller Equateur outbreak elsewhere in the country ended, marking DRC’s tenth recorded Ebola outbreak and its first large epidemic in the densely populated, conflict-affected eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri (later also South Kivu). The epidemic spread across health zones in these provinces and ultimately caused around 3,470 cases and 2,280 deaths, with persistent transmission fueled by insecurity, attacks on health facilities, community mistrust, and frequent population movement; a small number of cases were detected in neighboring Uganda as cross-border importations without sustained local transmission. Deployment of a ring-vaccination strategy with rVSV-ZEBOV-GP, novel therapeutics in Ebola treatment units, and gradual improvements in community engagement and security eventually reduced case incidence, and WHO declared the outbreak over on 25 June 2020.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: complex humanitarian emergency in eastern DRC with ongoing armed conflict, population displacement, and attacks on health workers and treatment centers; weak and fragmented health infrastructure; high mobility across porous borders; burial and caregiving practices involving close contact; initial mistrust of response teams. Internal mechanisms: outbreak caused by Zaire ebolavirus, with genomic data consistent with a single spillover event followed by human-to-human transmission and ongoing within-epidemic evolution; despite viral diversification, social and security conditions, rather than a qualitatively more transmissible strain, explain the scale of the epidemic. Because cases detected in Uganda were importations with no sustained chains of transmission, the episode is classified as a large re-occurrence in Middle Africa rather than as intra-continental emergence into Eastern Africa.
Review: Status: retained with modification. Uganda has been removed from the country and sub-region fields and the intra-continental emergence flag is set to false because the few cases detected in Uganda during this period were cross-border importations without sustained in situ transmission; the episode is best characterized as a very large re-occurrence in a previously affected country and sub-region driven by conflict and health-system weaknesses.

Host: Humans in multiple health zones of Equateur Province
Event summary: On 1 June 2020, authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared the country’s eleventh Ebola virus disease outbreak after new Zaire ebolavirus infections were confirmed in Equateur Province, several years after the 2014 and 2018 outbreaks in the same general region had ended. Over the following months, the outbreak spread across multiple, often remote, health zones around the Congo River, resulting in about 130 confirmed and probable cases and more than 50 deaths, with challenges posed by difficult geography, lake and river transport, and the concurrent COVID-19 pandemic. Intensified surveillance, vaccination of contacts and frontline workers, improved case management, and logistics support eventually stopped transmission, and the outbreak was declared over in November 2020 after two full incubation periods without new cases.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: fresh zoonotic spillover or reactivation from a cryptic animal or human reservoir in a region with prior Ebola outbreaks; remoteness of many affected villages and dependence on river transport; weak routine health surveillance and competing health emergencies, including COVID-19, straining response capacity. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses indicate that the 2020 Equateur outbreak virus formed a distinct lineage of Zaire ebolavirus compared with both the 2018–2020 Kivu epidemic and earlier Equateur outbreaks, suggesting a new spillover and/or emergence from a persistent focus; this supports classification as both a re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region and a form of re-emergence driven by a distinct lineage rather than continuation of earlier chains of transmission.
Review: Status: retained. Evidence that the 2020 Equateur outbreak represented a genetically distinct Zaire ebolavirus lineage arising after earlier local outbreaks justifies labeling it as both re-occurrence and re-emergence within Middle Africa; magnitude (~130 cases) and mechanistic interest warrant its inclusion among major events.

Host: Humans in N’Zérékoré Region (Gouécké sub-prefecture and surrounding areas), including family members, funeral attendees, and health-care workers
Event summary: On 14 February 2021, the Ministry of Health of Guinea announced a new outbreak of Ebola virus disease in Gouécké, N’Zérékoré Region, after a cluster of deaths linked to a funeral was investigated and tested positive for Zaire ebolavirus. The outbreak, occurring in the same general area that seeded the 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic, resulted in 23 reported cases and 12 deaths and was contained through rapid case finding, isolation, contact tracing, and ring vaccination of contacts and health-care workers. Genetic analyses showed that viruses from this outbreak clustered within the earlier Makona diversity with far fewer mutations than expected for a fresh zoonotic spillover, strongly suggesting reactivation from a long-term persistent infection in a survivor rather than a new animal-to-human transmission; WHO declared the outbreak over on 19 June 2021.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: a likely relapse or delayed sexual transmission from an Ebola survivor infected during the 2013–2016 epidemic, with amplification at a funeral and in close household and health-care contacts; regional health systems strengthened since 2016 enabled much faster detection and response than in the earlier epidemic. Internal mechanisms: re-emergence from persistent human infection with Zaire ebolavirus Makona variant after more than five years, with limited additional genetic change compared with 2013–2016 viruses; this provides strong evidence for long-term viral persistence as an internal mechanism of re-emergence in a previously affected Western Africa sub-region rather than a new spillover or purely externally driven resurgence.
Review: Status: added. Although relatively small (23 cases), this outbreak is highly significant as a clear example of re-emergence driven by long-term persistence of Orthoebolavirus zairense in a human survivor in a previously affected Western Africa sub-region; accordingly it is classified as re-emergence only, without intra- or inter-continental emergence flags.

Host: Humans (local residents and travelers infected by local Aedes albopictus)
Event summary: In summer 2010, autochthonous dengue cases without travel history were detected in southern France and on the Pelješac peninsula in Croatia, demonstrating local transmission by Aedes albopictus after virus importation by viremic travelers. National and EU authorities intensified surveillance, case finding and vector control around the affected communities, and transmission ceased with the end of the mosquito season without progressing into a large epidemic.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Expansion and high densities of Aedes albopictus in southern Europe; increased travel from dengue‑endemic regions introducing viremic individuals; suitable summer temperatures enabling short-term transmission cycles; limited population immunity. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel viral traits; the event mainly reflects re‑occurrence of dengue transmission in Europe after many decades of silence, driven by geographic range expansion of the vector and human movement rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: Retained but reclassified: inter_continental_emergence has been set to false and re_occurrence to true. Historical records document large dengue epidemics in Europe (e.g. Greece 1927–1928) long before 2010, so Europe is not a new continent for dengue, and these clusters represent re‑appearance after a long silent period rather than inter‑continental emergence. The event remains important as the first confirmed autochthonous transmission in continental Europe in the modern era, though case numbers are small relative to major tropical epidemics; if a hard cap of 10 events is enforced, this would be somewhat borderline but still defensible for inclusion as a key temperate‑zone signal.

Host: Humans (local residents and visitors to Madeira Island)
Event summary: In October 2012, Portugal reported the first autochthonous dengue cases on Madeira Island, marking the first sustained dengue epidemic in Europe since the 1920s, with over 1,000 confirmed and more than 2,000 probable infections and numerous cases exported to mainland Europe. The outbreak was caused by DENV‑1 closely related to strains circulating in Venezuela and Brazil, likely introduced by travelers into a naive population with abundant Aedes aegypti. Intensive vector control, seasonal decline in mosquito populations, and public health measures led authorities to declare the outbreak over in early 2013.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of DENV‑1 via infected travelers from South America; dense local Aedes aegypti populations; favorable climate and urban conditions; immunologically naive human population; high tourist traffic facilitating both importation and exportation. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by an established competent vector; virus belonged to known DENV‑1 lineages without evidence of dramatically increased virulence; this represents re‑occurrence of dengue epidemic activity in Europe after a long hiatus.
Review: Retained and reclassified: inter_continental_emergence is set to false and re_occurrence to true. Madeira 2012 is well documented as the first large dengue epidemic in Europe since the inter‑war period, with >2,000 local cases, but dengue transmission had already occurred historically on the continent (including the major Greece epidemic in 1927–1928). It therefore represents a major regional re‑occurrence in a previously dengue‑silent setting rather than a first occurrence on a new continent.

Countries: United States of America (Florida – Key West/Monroe County) [2009]
Host: Humans (residents and visitors in Key West, Florida)
Event summary: In mid‑2009, dengue virus type 1 was identified in a visitor and subsequently in residents of Key West, Florida, and serosurveys showed 3–5% of Old Town residents had recent infection, confirming local transmission after decades without endemic dengue in the continental United States. Additional locally acquired cases occurred in Key West and other Florida counties in 2010–2011, with DENV‑1 detected in local Aedes aegypti populations and a distinct Key West viral sub‑lineage related to Central American strains. Aggressive vector control, public awareness campaigns, and seasonal decline in mosquito abundance curtailed transmission and prevented long‑term establishment.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Travel‑related introduction from the Caribbean/Central America, abundant Aedes aegypti in subtropical South Florida, high human–mosquito contact, and limited population immunity after a long dengue‑free period; urban environments with water‑holding containers supported breeding. Internal mechanisms: Local diversification of a DENV‑1 lineage (Key West sub‑lineage), but no clear evidence of increased virulence; the episode is best viewed as re‑occurrence of dengue transmission in a historically affected region rather than a novel inter‑continental emergence.
Review: Retained but corrected: inter_continental_emergence has been reset to false and re_occurrence kept as true. Dengue has a long history in the Americas, and autochthonous transmission in the United States occurred earlier in the 20th century and again in Texas and Hawaii before 2009, so Key West does not represent first occurrence on a new continent. It is, however, an important re‑establishment of local transmission in the continental USA after several dengue‑free decades, and is appropriate to retain as a major re‑occurrence.

Host: Humans (primarily urban residents in Lahore and Punjab Province)
Event summary: In 2011, Pakistan experienced its largest recorded dengue outbreak, centered in Lahore in Punjab Province, with approximately 22,000 reported cases and more than 300 deaths, far exceeding prior years’ activity. Co‑circulation of multiple serotypes (notably DENV‑2 and DENV‑3), intense urban crowding, inadequate vector control, and monsoon‑related breeding sites fueled rapid expansion of cases within Lahore and neighboring districts. Emergency vector control campaigns, clinical management improvements, and the end of the monsoon season gradually reduced transmission, though dengue has remained endemic with recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization and high population density, inadequate water and waste management enabling Aedes breeding, heavy monsoon rains, and limited sustained vector control; delayed recognition and health‑system overload contributed to high case fatality. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies show circulation of DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype related to strains already present in Pakistan, without strong evidence of a fundamentally novel viral lineage; increased severity largely reflects hyperendemic circulation and secondary infections rather than a new strain, so the event is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic setting.
Review: Retained but reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence only. Phylogenetic work on the 2011 Lahore epidemic indicates that the outbreak strains belonged to locally evolved DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype rather than a clearly new, more virulent variant, and key drivers were external (urban crowding, monsoon rains, limited control). This fits the definition of re‑occurrence (resurgence due to external factors) better than re‑emergence (which requires clear changes in the pathogen such as a new strain, host jump or resistance).

Host: Humans (local residents and domestic travelers, mainly exposed in urban parks)
Event summary: In August 2014, Japan reported its first autochthonous dengue case since 1945 in a patient infected in Tokyo’s Yoyogi Park, and by late October a total of about 160 locally acquired cases with no overseas travel history were confirmed around several Tokyo parks. Molecular analysis showed DENV‑1 closely related among cases, indicating a single introduction likely from an imported case and subsequent propagation by local Aedes albopictus populations in popular urban recreational areas. Closure and insecticide treatment of affected parks, public advisories, and the onset of cooler weather ended local transmission by late 2014, and dengue has not become endemic in Japan.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Importation of DENV‑1 by an infected traveler, dense Aedes albopictus populations in urban green spaces, high human visitation to parks, and summer temperatures permitting efficient transmission in a largely non‑immune population. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of markedly novel viral traits; the outbreak mainly illustrates how a single introduction can trigger transient re‑occurrence where competent vectors and favorable climate coexist.
Review: Retained without changes in emergence typing. Japan had sizeable dengue outbreaks in the 1940s, so the 2014 Yoyogi Park cluster is correctly captured as re_occurrence driven by travel‑related introduction, established Aedes albopictus and favorable summer conditions, with no clear viral innovation. It is a relatively small outbreak in absolute numbers but is an important indicator of dengue’s capacity to re‑appear in temperate East Asia.

Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban populations across multiple Indian states)
Event summary: In 2015, India experienced one of its worst dengue years in decades, with national surveillance indicating that reported dengue cases roughly doubled compared with 2014, exceeding about 80,000–100,000 suspected or confirmed cases and causing substantial mortality, particularly in Delhi and other large cities. Hyperendemic circulation of multiple serotypes, rapid unplanned urbanization, and water storage practices facilitated high Aedes aegypti densities and explosive transmission across many states. Intensified vector control campaigns, public education, and improved clinical management reduced case fatality and led to the typical seasonal decline in transmission toward the end of the year, though dengue has remained hyperendemic with recurrent large outbreaks.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Urban crowding, poor water and waste infrastructure, favorable monsoon seasons, and limited sustained vector control; large susceptible cohorts accumulated between epidemic waves; health‑system strain may have delayed effective responses in some areas. Internal mechanisms: Hyperendemic co‑circulation of multiple DENV serotypes raises risk of severe disease through secondary infection; however, no single novel genotype has been clearly implicated, so the event is best viewed as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic setting.
Review: Retained as a re_occurrence event. India has had dengue transmission for many decades, and 2015 is well documented as a year when nationally reported case counts roughly doubled relative to 2014, with major urban outbreaks. No strong evidence for viral novelty has been presented, so re_emergence is not appropriate. From a global top‑10 perspective this event is somewhat less exceptional than Sri Lanka 2017 or the 2019 and 2024 Americas epidemics, but it remains one of the largest recorded Indian dengue seasons and is reasonable to keep.

Countries: Brazil [2019]; Mexico [2019]; Honduras [2019]; Nicaragua [2019]; Colombia [2019]; multiple other countries across the Region of the Americas [2019]
Host: Humans (across tropical and subtropical urban areas in the Americas)
Event summary: In 2019, the Region of the Americas recorded its largest dengue epidemic on record to that date, with PAHO reporting more than 3 million cases and over 1,500 deaths, heavily affecting Brazil, Central America, Mexico, and several Caribbean nations. Following a relatively quiet 2017–2018, large susceptible populations, favorable climatic conditions, and persistent Aedes aegypti infestations allowed all four serotypes to circulate and drove explosive transmission across multiple countries. Intensive regional and national responses—including emergency vector control, risk communication, and strengthened clinical management—helped keep the overall case‑fatality rate below 1%, but transmission remained high into early 2020 before declining and later resurging in subsequent years.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Cyclical build‑up of susceptible populations, El Niño–linked and other climatic anomalies increasing mosquito breeding and survival, rapid urbanization with inadequate water and waste services, and high human mobility across borders; constrained vector‑control capacity limited sustained impact. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of all four DENV serotypes and shifting serotype dominance likely increased the probability of severe disease in previously exposed individuals, but no single novel strain has been clearly singled out; the event primarily represents a large-scale regional re‑occurrence.
Review: Retained without changes in emergence typing. This is clearly a major re_occurrence in a long‑endemic region, with >3 million cases and >1,500 deaths in the Americas and co‑circulation of all four serotypes. It remains an important benchmark event despite being surpassed in overall global burden by 2024.

Host: Humans (children and adults nationwide, with high incidence in several regions)
Event summary: In 2019, the Philippines experienced a massive dengue epidemic, with over 146,000 cases and more than 600 deaths reported by late July, prompting the Department of Health to declare first a National Dengue Alert and then a National Dengue Epidemic in August. Cases surged across multiple regions, driven by intense Aedes aegypti infestation, favorable weather, waning population immunity, and health‑system challenges following controversy surrounding a prior dengue vaccination program. Expanded community clean‑up campaigns, enhanced surveillance, and strengthened clinical management reduced mortality and, together with seasonal changes, led to declining case numbers later in the year.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions conducive to mosquito proliferation, high household water storage and waste, rapid urbanization, and reduced trust in some public‑health interventions; large susceptible cohorts after previous inter‑epidemic periods. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of multiple serotypes typical for hyperendemic settings; no clearly novel strain was identified as the main driver, so this represents a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic country.
Review: Retained as a major re_occurrence: national authorities declared a dengue epidemic in 2019 after an unusually large surge in cases and deaths, and the event is well documented. No evidence supports first/global emergence, inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence, or pathogen‑level changes, so the current categorization is appropriate. If the dengue dataset ultimately has to be reduced to 10 events, this could be weighed against other very large Asian epidemics (e.g. Sri Lanka 2017, Bangladesh 2019) for prioritization.

Host: Humans (especially residents of Dhaka and other major cities)
Event summary: Beginning in April 2019, Bangladesh experienced its largest dengue outbreak on record, with national data indicating over 100,000 confirmed cases and dozens of deaths by the end of the year, more than doubling prior peaks since dengue was first recognized in the country in 2000. The epidemic was initially concentrated in Dhaka, one of the world’s most densely populated megacities, before spreading to all 64 districts as population movements during religious holidays redistributed infected individuals and vectors. Emergency vector control, risk communication, and improved hospital triage and management helped reduce the case‑fatality rate, and case numbers declined with the end of the monsoon season though dengue has since remained a recurrent national threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Extreme population density and informal housing in Dhaka, inadequate water and waste infrastructure generating abundant Aedes breeding sites, heavy monsoon rains, and inter‑district human movement during holidays; limitations in sustained vector control and urban planning. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several DENV serotypes and potential shifts in serotype predominance contributed to severe disease risk, but no specific new genotype is clearly established as causal; the event is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence in an increasingly endemic setting.
Review: Retained as a major re_occurrence event. The 2019 Bangladesh epidemic is well documented as the largest since dengue was first recognized nationally in 2000, with >100,000 cases and nationwide spread. Available data implicate external drivers (urban crowding, monsoon rains, health‑system capacity) and shifting serotype predominance, but do not demonstrate a fundamentally novel viral strain, so re_emergence is not indicated.

Countries: Brazil [2024]; Argentina [2024]; Mexico [2024]; Colombia [2024]; Paraguay [2024]; Peru [2024]; Guatemala [2024]; Honduras [2024]; multiple other Latin American and Caribbean states [2024]
Host: Humans (populations across tropical and subtropical urban areas in the Region of the Americas)
Event summary: In 2024, dengue transmission reached unprecedented levels globally, with WHO receiving reports of about 14.4 million cases and 11,201 deaths across all six regions; more than 90% of these cases occurred in the Region of the Americas, where Brazil alone reported over 10 million cases and more than 6,000 deaths, and other Latin American countries such as Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, Paraguay, Peru, Guatemala and Honduras also experienced very large epidemics. These surges followed earlier peaks in 2019 and 2023 and were driven by favorable climatic conditions, rapid urbanization, widespread Aedes aegypti infestations and high mobility of people and virus lineages. Intensive international and national responses—including emergency vector control, updated clinical guidance, and deployment or pilot use of dengue vaccines in some countries—aimed to reduce severe disease and deaths, but the 2024 Americas outbreak nonetheless marked the highest regional and global dengue burden ever recorded.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Long‑term global and regional trends including urbanization, climate change increasing geographic and seasonal suitability for Aedes mosquitoes, resumption and intensification of international and regional travel after COVID‑19, persistent deficiencies in water and waste infrastructure, and limited scalable vector‑control tools; demographic growth has expanded populations at risk. Internal mechanisms: Hyperendemic circulation of all four DENV serotypes with shifting regional dominance and extensive serotype mixing increases the likelihood of severe outcomes among previously exposed individuals, but no single novel genotype explains the 2024 surge; the event reflects very large‑scale re‑occurrence and continued geographic expansion within a long‑affected region.
Review: Retained and scope clarified. The original entry treated this as a single "Global" event, which conflicts with the requirement not to merge events across continents; here the focus is explicitly on the Region of the Americas, which accounted for >90% of the ~14.4 million global cases and over 10 million cases in Brazil alone in 2024. The episode is correctly classified as re_occurrence, with no evidence of a new continent, new host system or clearly novel viral lineage. Separate 2024 events could be added for Asia and Africa if finer spatial detail is required.

Host: Humans (residents of multiple islands including Santiago, Maio, Fogo and Brava)
Event summary: From late September 2009, Cabo Verde reported its first known dengue epidemic, with thousands of suspected cases across the southern islands of Santiago, Maio, Fogo and Brava; by November, national and partner reports indicated more than 13,000–20,000 suspected infections and several deaths, making it at the time the largest recorded dengue outbreak in Africa. The epidemic, caused by DENV‑3 likely introduced from the Americas, spread rapidly through densely populated urban neighborhoods with abundant Aedes aegypti breeding sites and a largely dengue‑naive human population. Intensive emergency vector control, community clean‑up campaigns, clinical support and seasonal declines in mosquito density reduced transmission, and incidence fell sharply in early 2010, although Cabo Verde and the wider West African region have continued to report dengue activity thereafter.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Introduction of DENV‑3 via infected travelers (probably from Latin America), high densities of Aedes aegypti in urban areas, water storage and waste management practices favoring breeding, and a largely immunologically naive population in Cabo Verde; limited prior experience with dengue diagnosis and control delayed early recognition. Internal mechanisms: Virus belonged to known DENV‑3 lineages without evidence of unique resistance or virulence traits; the outbreak represents a dramatic re‑occurrence of dengue in the West African subregion, where dengue had been documented in countries such as Nigeria and Senegal decades earlier, rather than first emergence on the continent.
Review: Newly added and should be retained. WHO and MSF describe the 2009–2010 Cabo Verde epidemic as the country’s first dengue outbreak and, at the time, the largest recorded dengue epidemic in Africa, with >13,000–20,000 suspected cases. Because dengue virus had already been isolated from humans in West African countries such as Nigeria and Senegal in the 1960s–1970s, this is best classified as a major re_occurrence in a previously affected subregion, not as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence.

Host: Humans (urban residents of Guangzhou and surrounding districts)
Event summary: In 2014, Guangzhou in Guangdong Province experienced the largest recorded dengue outbreak in mainland China, with around 37,000–38,000 laboratory‑confirmed indigenous cases and several deaths, accounting for the great majority of dengue cases in China that year. After an imported index case in June, transmission expanded explosively during the hot, humid summer and early autumn, driven by very high densities of Aedes albopictus, high human–mosquito contact in crowded urban neighborhoods and widespread unprotected water containers. Intensive emergency vector control, community mobilization and the onset of cooler weather in late autumn curtailed transmission, but Guangzhou has remained the primary epicenter for recurrent dengue activity in China.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization, high population density, favorable climatic conditions for Aedes albopictus, abundant artificial containers and limited early vector control, together with repeated viral importations from dengue‑endemic areas in Southeast Asia. Internal mechanisms: Molecular investigations indicated circulation of DENV‑1 and DENV‑2 lineages closely related to strains from Southeast Asia, without evidence of a uniquely new genotype; the event therefore represents an extreme re_occurrence in a region where dengue had been present since the 1970s, not a new continental or subcontinental emergence.
Review: Newly added and appropriate to retain as a major event. Multiple epidemiological analyses describe the 2014 Guangzhou outbreak as the largest dengue epidemic ever recorded in mainland China, with >37,000 indigenous cases and strong concentration of national burden in one metropolitan area. Dengue was already recognized in southern China, so classification as re_occurrence (without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with the framework.

Host: Humans (nationwide, with highest incidence in Colombo and the Western Province)
Event summary: In 2017, Sri Lanka experienced its largest dengue epidemic since national notification began, reporting about 186,000 suspected cases and more than 400 dengue‑related deaths nationwide, with a marked concentration in the densely populated Western Province around Colombo. Following heavy rains and flooding that created extensive Aedes breeding sites, a shift from predominant DENV‑1 to a cosmopolitan DENV‑2 genotype associated with more severe disease coincided with explosive spread among older school‑age children and young adults and substantial strain on hospital capacity. Large‑scale vector control campaigns, triage and clinical management improvements, and the end of the southwest monsoon season led to a gradual decline in cases later in 2017, but dengue has remained a major recurrent public‑health threat.
Mechanism or driver: Drivers: Intense monsoon rains and flooding, high urban population density (especially in Colombo), suboptimal solid‑waste and water management, and limited sustained vector‑control capacity created ideal conditions for Aedes proliferation; health‑system crowding and delayed care seeking increased severity and mortality. Internal mechanisms: Virological investigations show a replacement of DENV‑1 by a cosmopolitan DENV‑2 genotype temporally associated with increased incidence and more severe disease, consistent with re_emergence driven by serotype/genotype change superimposed on an already endemic setting; this justifies coding both re_occurrence and re_emergence, as allowed by the framework.
Review: Newly added and strongly recommended for inclusion. WHO and peer‑reviewed analyses concur that 2017 was Sri Lanka’s largest dengue epidemic on record, with ~186,000 suspected cases and >400 deaths, and that a shift to DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype was temporally associated with the unprecedented severity. This fits both re_occurrence (major resurgence in a known endemic subregion) and re_emergence (pathogen‑level change in circulating serotype/genotype), which are allowed to co‑occur under the project’s rules.
